## Series Title Page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who Flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III;**

A chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, diligently corrected by comparison both with one another and with several manuscript codices; continually elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume or each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; enlarged by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any one of the Fathers has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers, and in what places in their works, have commented on each individual scriptural text.

The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, and the low price; above all, this collection, unified, systematic, and chronological, brings together for the first time in our library six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, gathered from works concerned with every age, place, language, and form.

**First Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of complete series in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# The Complete Works of Manlius Severinus Boethius

Most useful not only to students of the liberal disciplines but also to students of the higher faculties—indeed, indispensable for understanding Aristotle at his principal points—now printed for the first time with appropriate care, with the assistance of various editions. Of these, one, namely the books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, was printed with the greatest accuracy for the use of the Dauphin; another, superior in extent to all others and occupying the foremost place, is designated by the celebrated name of Glareanus, who restored arithmetic and music to their former brilliance, having enriched them with demonstrations and figures; the third, consisting of the theological treatises, recognizes the highly learned Vallin as its editor; finally, the fourth, which presents several previously unpublished monuments, is owed to the most illustrious Cardinal Mai.

# Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius’s Dialogues on Porphyry, Translated by Victorinus

## First Dialogue

[Col. 0009A] During the winter season we had withdrawn to the mountains of Aurelia. There, when the harsher south wind had driven away the night’s peaceful rest and disturbed our sleep, I decided to review those works which learned men had published, as it were, to sharpen the eyes of the understanding—eyes greatly darkened by obscurity—through certain introductory commentaries.

Fabius began the matter. Seeing me reclining on my couch and reflecting and meditating on these same subjects, he urged me to give him some instruction concerning them, as I had often promised. The opportunity was agreeable, since at that time both the greetings of friends and household affairs had ceased.

I therefore asked him about what subjects he wished me to unravel and explain. Then Fabius said:

“Since time is available for study [Col. 0009B], and this leisure may be converted into an honorable occupation, I ask you to explain to me what Victorinus, the orator who was almost the most learned man of his age, is said to have translated from Porphyry under the title *Isagoge*, that is, *Introduction to Aristotle’s Categories*. First, however, instruct me in certain teaching practices by which expositors and even commentators proceed, so that they may accustom the minds of their pupils to a certain teachability.”

Then I said:

“In every exposition teachers invariably set out six things in advance. First, they explain what the purpose of the work in question is—the point which among them is called *skopos*, ‘aim.’ Second, they explain its usefulness, which the Greeks call *chrēsimon*, ‘useful application.’ Third, they explain its order, which the Greeks call *taxis*, ‘arrangement.’ [Col. 0009C] Fourth, whether it is the genuine and proper work of the author to whom it is attributed, which is usually rendered by *gnēsion*, ‘genuine.’ Fifth, what the title of the work is, which the Greeks call *epigraphē*, ‘inscription.’ Because some people interpreted the purpose of each book improperly, uncertainty about the work’s title also arose among those less knowledgeable. Sixth, they state to what branch of philosophy the purpose of the book is directed, expressed in Greek as *eis poion meros philosophias anagetai*, ‘to what part of philosophy does it belong?’ All these matters, therefore, ought to be investigated and explained in every philosophical book.”

Then Fabius asked what the purpose of the *Introduction* was.

I replied:

[Col. 0009D] “Aristotle, who became the bridge to the *Introduction*, cannot be understood in any other way than by preparing for understanding the very matters about which he is going to dispute. Porphyry observed that in all things there were certain primary natures, from which everything else flowed as from some fountain; that these primary things both possessed subsistence and were called by the name ‘genus.’ [Col. 0010A] But a genus could never exist unless certain other things were subordinated to it, and those subordinated things were called ‘species.’ Moreover, a genus could never be the genus of only one species, but of several. Yet several species could not be multiple unless some distinction separated them. For if they were in no respect unlike one another, they would appear to be one species rather than several. That division and unlikeness among species are called by the name ‘difference.’

“Everything that differs in some respect must, moreover, be distinguished by certain individual and solitary natures. Let this suffice for the present.

“Porphyry therefore observed that all the dissimilarity of all things was divided between two principles of things, substance and accident, so that neither accident could exist without substance nor substance without accident. [Col. 0010B] An accident cannot exist without some foundation in substance; substance itself, however, cannot in any way be seen apart from an accident superimposed upon it. For example, color, which is an accident, exists in a body, which is substance. Conversely, when you see a body—that is, a substance—you perceive it as marked by an accident, namely by some color. Thus it follows that substance does not exist apart from accident, nor is accident separated from substance. Wherever substance has existed, accident immediately follows.

“Porphyry therefore considered that genera, species, properties, and differences were involved in these two things—accident and substance—and that these themselves function as genera for the subjects and underlying species which are marked by differences and properties. He decided to treat principally of genus, species, difference, and property. [Col. 0010C] Since this treatment will be useful in definitions, as we shall teach later, and since it is clear that anyone who places an accident in a general definition does not define correctly—a matter which will be treated in its proper place—he decided to give a preliminary account of accidents.

“Our most prudent teacher thus instructs us: we can receive complete knowledge in definitions only when what is useful has been stated and what is not useful has been excluded. The purpose of this work, therefore, is to treat of genus, species, differences, properties, and accidents.”

Then Fabius said:

“You have explained the purpose. Now explain the usefulness.”

“The usefulness and benefit of this work,” I replied, “are varied and manifold. First, [Col. 0010D] it is exceedingly useful for Aristotle’s *Categories*. We shall say what its usefulness there is when we discuss the title of that book. As for the other matters in which it is useful, I shall touch upon them briefly after making a division of philosophy itself.

“First, we must consider what philosophy itself is. Philosophy is love, pursuit, and, in a certain sense, friendship with wisdom. By wisdom I do not mean that which is concerned with certain arts and with some craftsman’s knowledge and expertise, but that wisdom which needs nothing, which is a living mind and the primal reason of things alone.

[Col. 0011A] “Here the love of wisdom is the illumination of an intelligent mind by that pure wisdom, and, in a certain way, its withdrawal and summons back to wisdom itself. Thus the pursuit of wisdom may equally be understood as the pursuit of divinity and friendship with that pure mind.

“This wisdom confers upon the entire race of souls the merit of its divinity and restores them to the proper power and purity of their nature. From this arise the truth of speculation and thought, and the holy and pure chastity of actions. This matter becomes a division and partition within philosophy itself.

“Philosophy is a genus, and it has two species: one called *theōrētikē* [Col. 0011B], the other *praktikē*—that is, speculative and active. There will be as many species of speculative philosophy as there are things in which a just consideration through speculation is found. And as many as are the varieties of actions, so many are the species and varieties of virtues.

“Thus the speculative or contemplative part, *theōrētikē*, has a threefold division, and this part of philosophy is divided into three species. One part concerns *intellectibles*, another *intelligibles*, and another natural things.

“Then Fabius interrupted me, astonished at what this new expression might be, since I had called one part of the speculative discipline ‘intellectible.’

“‘Understand,’ I said, ‘that I have never found the word used in Latin; I coined it myself by composing the term. An intellectible is that which, being one and the same in itself and always subsisting [Col. 0011C] in its own divinity, is grasped not by any of the senses but solely by mind and understanding. This belongs to the contemplation of God and to the consideration of the soul’s incorporeality, and is pursued through the investigation of true philosophy. The Greeks call this part *theologia*, theology.

“The second part is the intelligible. By thought and understanding it receives the first, the intellectible, and comprehends those things which are the causes of all celestial works belonging to the supreme divinity, together with whatever beneath the lunar sphere is capable of existing in a more blessed mind and purer substance.

“Finally, it concerns the condition and state of human souls. All these, although previously they had been intellectible substances together with those higher realities, degenerated through contact with bodies from intellectibles into intelligibles. Thus they are not so much understood as themselves understanding [Col. 0011D]; and they are more blessed in the purity of their understanding whenever they apply themselves to intellectibles.

“The third species of the speculative discipline concerns bodies and the science and knowledge of them: it is physiology, which explains the natures and properties of bodies. The second, the substance of intelligibles, is placed in the middle, because it possesses both the animation and, in a certain manner, the vivification of bodies, as well as the consideration and knowledge of intellectibles, as has been said.

“The active philosophy, which we have shown above to be called practical, also has a threefold division. The first is concerned with the care of the self, raising, adorning, and increasing the self through all the virtues, admitting nothing unwillingly of which it would not rejoice, and doing nothing of which it would have to repent.

[Col. 0012A] “The second undertakes the care of the commonwealth and ministers to the welfare of all through the resourcefulness of its prudence, the balance of justice, the steadfastness of courage, and the endurance of temperance.

“The third distributes and orders the duties of the household through a moderate arrangement. There are also further subdivisions of these, but for the present we should refrain from pursuing them.

“In order that these matters may be known and the foregoing understood, the discipline which the Greeks call *logikē*, and which we may call rational, yields a most necessary and abundant fruit. Through the correct rational method of speech it determines what is true and what is appropriate, without being led astray by any deviation or bypath of error.

[Col. 0012B] “Some have judged this discipline to be a part of philosophy; others have judged it not to be a part, but an instrument and, in a certain sense, a piece of equipment. The reason that led each group to this judgment will have to be recalled in another work.

“This discussion of genus, species, difference, property, and accident prepares for us, as it were, a road in every branch of philosophical knowledge. For when we are taught what a genus is and what a species is, we understand that philosophy is a genus, while its species are undoubtedly the speculative and the active, *theōrētikē* and *praktikē*. By the same reasoning we can consider whether logic is a species.

“Knowledge of difference is useful to us for recognizing the differences among the species of philosophy themselves. Knowledge of property is useful for understanding what appears to belong by its solitary nature and to be innate in the substance of each species of philosophy. [Col. 0012C] Knowledge of accident is useful because through it we can discern what is primary in things and what belongs to them secondarily and contingently.

“Thus the knowledge of these five things, by a branching and many-forked force, pours itself into all the parts of philosophy.

“It is no less useful in grammar, when we call speech a genus and measure the eight parts of speech through species, differences, and properties. Knowledge of this matter is also exceedingly friendly and closely connected with rhetoric. For in this way we can divide rhetoric into three kinds of cases and dissect them according to their underlying constitutions.

“There is also great, useful, and abundant knowledge of definitions, which belong to logic. Unless you treat definitions through genera, species, differences, and properties, no end can ever be imposed upon definitions.

[Col. 0012D] “For if you define something, you must first state what genus it belongs to; genus and species are completed in this way. Whenever you state the genus of some thing, you make that to which you apply the genus its species. For example, if you define what a human being is, you say that a human being is an animal. Since you have applied ‘animal’ to ‘human being,’ you have declared animal to be the genus and human being to be the species. But merely indicating the genus in a definition is not sufficient. If you say only that a human being is an animal, would you by that definition have depicted a human being rather than an ox, an ass, or a horse?

“Differences must therefore also be added, by which the thing being defined is separated from other species. Thus you say that a human being is a rational animal. [Col. 0013A] Since several species are frequently found under the same difference—for example, God and human being are both under ‘rational’—the use of property is extremely valuable, so that you may state what the species being defined alone retains as its own and proper characteristic.

“The definition of a human being therefore takes this form: ‘A human being is an animal’—animal being the genus; ‘human being’ the species; ‘rational’ the difference; and ‘capable of laughter’ the property. Accidents, however, have no use in definitions.

“Knowledge of these five things is therefore useful in definitions, so that you may neither omit what is useful nor add what contributes nothing.

“It is equally useful in division, since without knowledge of these matters no thing can be correctly distributed or divided. What proper distribution of genera or species could there be by division if we were not guided by knowledge of the things themselves that are being divided?

[Col. 0013B] “The truth of demonstrations is also principally established through these matters: through what you divide, you either demonstrate the thing being divided or something else. Marcus Tullius, in the first book of the *Rhetoricians*, since he properly and orderly arranged the division of kinds of cases, set out the proof of this matter through species and genera. He says that the same things may be placed above some things and below others, but cannot be both subordinated and superordinated to the same things.

“These are roughly the points about usefulness which we have thought should be stated for the present.”

Then Fabius said:

“I am greatly surprised that, when I was only beginning, you have presented to me matters so subtle and so thoroughly worked out. But please tell me: what was the entire purpose of this?”

I replied:

[Col. 0013C] “I shall tell you. The mind of the listener must be accustomed and imbued with a moderate degree of subtlety, so that, once it has first exercised itself here in the gymnasium of understanding and has, as it were, wrestled beforehand, it may complete what follows without any labor. But you may now state what remains.”

Fabius said:

“If I remember correctly, I think that the order remains.”

“Indeed,” I said, “this order is closely connected with the title. If you know one, you will know both.

“The order is this: all those who, after Porphyry, entered the study of logic began with this little book, because it was the first to advance to the point of extreme simplicity and thinness, preparing the path along which those who proceed farther must travel.

[Col. 0013D] “Aristotle, wishing to hand down to posterity the order and knowledge of dialectical and demonstrative discipline, saw that the power of demonstration and dialectic was contained in a single order of syllogism. He therefore wrote the *First Analytics*, which the Greeks call *Analytika*, ‘Analytica,’ and which ought to be read before anyone approaches anything in the art of dialectic or demonstration.

“In the *First Analytics* he treats above all of the order, combination, and figures of syllogisms. Since the syllogism is the genus of demonstrative and dialectical syllogism, he practiced dialectic in his *Topics* and arranged demonstration in the *Second Analytics*. The discipline which he had first assembled there for displaying syllogisms is also read earlier in one’s studies.

“Thus the *First Analytics* is taken up before the *Second Analytics*, which concerns demonstrative syllogism, and before the *Topics*, which concerns dialectical syllogism. Aristotle therefore drew together dialectical and demonstrative science and united them in his discussion of the analysis of syllogisms.

[Col. 0014A] “But since a syllogism must consist of propositions, he also indicated the book entitled *On Interpretation*, that is, *On Propositions*. All propositions, however, are composed of significant expressions. Therefore the book which he wrote on the ten categories—called by the Greeks *katēgoriai*, ‘categories’—concerns the first names of things and their significations.

“Aristotle saw that there was an infinite mixture and diversity among all things and words. To discover their order, he collected everything that could belong either to things or to expressions under ten primary expressions signifying the primary genera of things. But enough of Aristotle.

[Col. 0014B] “Porphyry, however, considered that if the categories were genera of things, and if the diversity of things and expressions were marked by species, differences, and properties, he also saw that accidents had great force within the categories. For Aristotle first divides all things into two parts, accident and substance, and he disperses accident among nine members. He says that a thing is either substance, whatever that thing may be, or, if it is an accident, it is either quality, quantity, relation, place, time, position, possession, action, or passion.

“Porphyry therefore gives us a preliminary preparation for the truest knowledge of these matters through this treatment of genera, species, differences, properties, and accidents.

[Col. 0014C] “Thus, just as syllogistic matters are read before demonstrative and dialectical matters; before syllogistic matters the first labor lies in propositions; before propositions, a little work is required in the categories; and before the categories there is much labor in the *Isagoge*, which treats of genera, species, differences, properties, and accidents—so the order requires that a brief preliminary account of these very matters be given.

“Rightly, therefore, this book of Porphyry appears to readers as a kind of thread, the first taster of their studies and, in a certain sense, their initiator. If what has been said is sufficient for this matter, we have also completed our discussion of the title. For by what other name could this book more suitably be called than ‘Introduction’? It is an entrance into Aristotle’s categories and admits those who approach them as through a kind of door.”

Then Fabius said:

“Please continue, and determine whether this work is genuinely and properly his.”

[Col. 0014D] “This is beyond doubt,” I replied, “for this style agrees with all Porphyry’s books. It is Porphyry’s practice, in matters of the greatest obscurity, to place in advance certain introductory explanations and preliminary tastings, as he did in another book on categorical syllogisms and likewise in many other matters which are weighty and distinguished in philosophy. Among earlier authorities this too is beyond doubt, and it is ignorance not to believe them.”

Then Fabius said:

“It remains for you to explain to what part of philosophy it is directed.”

I replied:

“I shall tell you. Since categories are fitted to propositions, syllogisms are composed from propositions, and demonstrative or dialectical syllogisms belong to the discipline of the logical art, it is also evident that the categories, which concern propositions and syllogisms, are connected with logical science. Therefore the introduction to the categories is also appropriately assigned to logical science.

“Since I have explained the matters that must be stated beforehand, let us now examine the structure and order of the text itself.”

Then Fabius said:

[Col. 0015A] “Before the explanation of the meaning proceeds, I wish to know why, although he could have said, ‘Since it is necessary,’ he said, in an inverted order, ‘When it is necessary.’”

I replied:

“Because there is no accident that does not rest upon the foundation of substance. Whatever provides firmness to anything superimposed must necessarily have existed before that thing itself. Just as no building can ever exist unless foundations are laid first, so no accidents can ever be superimposed unless the foundations of substance exist first.

“Something must first exist in order to take on the form of a quality, for ‘necessary’ is a quality. He therefore did not irrationally put ‘to be’ first and ‘necessary’ afterward; that is, after substance he applied the name of quality.”

Then Fabius said:

“You have explained this most subtly and clearly. But now let us examine the order and text of the work itself.”

[Col. 0015B]

# Text of the Work

Since it is necessary for Menantius, whether for the categories of Aristotle or for the discipline of definition, to know what genus is, what species is, what difference is, what property is, and what accident is—and, in general, for matters belonging to division or to proof, whose usefulness and knowledge are of great importance—I shall try to explain these matters briefly to you.

Although among the ancients these kinds of questions were proposed in lofty and magnificent terms, I shall explain them in simple language, with a certain conjectural consideration of the matters, and in another manner, on a moderate level.

Then I said: “We have indeed stated a few things above, but I do not think it unreasonable either to add something to them or to recall the same points again. The whole meaning is this: In writing to Menantius about the usefulness of the book, he gives a brief preliminary indication, so that the listener’s mind may arrive at the apprehension of these matters more diligently and in a more highly trained condition.

“He says that it is useful for Aristotle’s Categories because, when Aristotle divided the whole variety of significant expressions according to the different totality of things, and separated and distributed all things into substance and accident, he divided accident into nine parts, as I demonstrated above, and called these the most general genera—that is, γενικώτατα [most general]—because no other genera can be found above them.

“Therefore, if there are genera, they cannot exist without species. If species are subordinate to them, they will not be without differences. And if they retain differences, they will require properties. The categories of accident, moreover, are nine. Thus it was not unreasonable that an introduction to the Categories should be composed from this point, so that it might treat genera, species, differences, and properties, which appear to be inseparably embedded in the Categories themselves.

“Furthermore, Aristotle’s subtlety, before proceeding to the order of the categories, treated of equivocal and univocal terms. He defines equivocal terms as follows: ‘Equivocal are those things whose name alone is common, while the account of substance corresponding to the name is different’; that is, things which share only a name but differ in substance. Univocal terms, on the other hand, are those which are contained under the same name and under the same substance.

“Thus every genus can be predicated univocally of the species placed beneath it. Moreover, whatever is predicated univocally of any things has in those things one and the same definition, and genus and species are convertible. Animal and human being, for example, are univocal. ‘Animal’ is said by the name ‘animal,’ and the name ‘animal’ also applies to a human being, so that a human being is called an animal. The definition of animal is ‘an animate, sensible substance.’ If you apply this definition to a human being, you do nothing absurd: a human being can indeed be an animate, sensible substance. Yet animal is the genus, and human being the species. Genus and species, therefore, are predicated univocally.

“But things that are equivocal differ in their definitions; and where the definitions differ, the substance also differs. Where the substance differs, the genera are wholly different as well. It is therefore clear that, among equivocal things, neither genus nor species can properly be applied. For if someone calls a marble human figure and a living human being by the name ‘human being,’ he has given the same name to two substances, although their difference and definition are unlike. A human being and a statue do not have one genus: a statue is inanimate, whereas a human being is animate. It is therefore clear that whatever is predicated equivocally is never contained under the same genera.

“Unless one has first acquired knowledge and understanding of genera, species, properties, and differences, one can never discern this force of equivocity. Aristotle likewise states what first and second substances are. He says that first substances are individual and singular bodies, such as Cicero, Plato, or Socrates. He calls species second substances, such as human being, and also the genera in which those species are contained, such as animal. None of this can be understood unless knowledge of genus and species has first been supplied.

“Aristotle also says that one substance is not separated from another by any difference insofar as it is substance. He likewise seeks the properties of substance, so that, as though substance were marked by some impressed sign, we may more easily recognize and explain what substance is. He did the same with accidents. He collected the properties of quantity, quality, and relation, and the same concern and diligence are conspicuous throughout Aristotle’s work.

“Do you see how the force of these five things is interwoven with the Categories and inseparably bound up with the powers of the categories? Porphyry therefore did not falsely promise us that knowledge of these five things would be useful for the Categories.

“We said above that the discipline of definition cannot be treated apart from genera, species, differences, and properties. But since there are certain genera which cannot have a genus—substance, for example, and the other things Aristotle established in the Categories—someone might say that these matters are of no use for understanding them, since a definition cannot be derived from a genus where no genus can be found, and if a thing has no genus, it is not a species.

“Once this has been granted, genera and species would be of no use in defining the most general genera. This is an utterly ridiculous and absurd proposition. For apart from knowledge of genera and species, how could anyone know those most general genera, when, if this knowledge of genera and species alone were lost, nothing at all about genera and species would be known?

“In those things above which no other genus can be found, no definition’s boundary can ever be applied; in their definition, genera and species will fall away, and only their differences and properties will shape the limit of the definition. Once you have separated what you are defining from all other things by means of the differences attached to it, and have shown its form and shape by marking it with its properties, do not labor to seek a genus which you cannot find. Species and genera are not required in those cases where, because the things themselves are most general genera, no genus can be found.

“Yet in those things which do have a genus, if the definition is not derived from the genus, the conclusion of the definition is defective. It is beyond doubt that accident contributes nothing to definitions. Definition seeks to delineate substance, whereas accident does not identify substance. Accident, therefore, contributes nothing to definition.

“Knowledge of genus and species is consequently necessary, so that, if what one intends to define is not a most general genus, one may derive the definition from its genus. If it is a most general genus, one should not labor to seek a genus which cannot be found. It is equally defective either to seek genera in the most general genera or to fail to derive a definition from the genus in subordinate genera.

“Differences and properties, whether the genera are more general or subordinate, retain the greatest usefulness. And since certain points concerning definition have been stated, let us also gather a few observations about these matters themselves, more rationally and subtly.

“Let the genus be animal, the species human being, the difference rational or mortal, and the property capable of laughter. Let us omit accident, since it is inconvenient for definitions.

“Whoever defines a species separates it from other genera by means of the genus. Thus, if someone asks, ‘What is a human being?’ and the answer is ‘An animal,’ the speaker has separated the human being from all genera that are not animals. If someone states a difference and applies it to the species, he separates things under the same genera by means of differences.

“For when you say that a human being is a rational animal, although an ox and a horse are also species of animal, the addition of ‘rational’ separates and distinguishes the species human being from the other species under the same genus. When you supply properties, you separate things under the same differences.

“For when you say ‘neighing’ or ‘capable of laughter,’ the former is proper to a horse, the latter to a human being. Although a horse is under the same difference as an ox and a dog—all are irrational—the addition of ‘neighing’ divides the horse from the other species under the same difference.

“Human being and God are under the same difference, namely rational, since both are rational; nevertheless, human being and God are separated by the added difference mortal. But they are distinguished more naturally and substantially by the property ‘capable of laughter,’ which only a human being possesses. This can be understood more clearly in other things in which no species is separated by such a difference. For since irrational things—horse, ox, and dog—are under the same difference, there is no other substantial difference that separates them.

“There may be accidental differences that separate them, such as differences of form; but the property ‘neighing,’ added to horse, separates the horse from the other species under the same difference by the distinction of its property.

“We must therefore repeat from the beginning: genera separate things in definitions from other genera; differences separate species themselves that are placed under the same genera; properties separate species that are subordinate to the same differences.

“But since the matter of definition has been treated fully, let us address the force and subtlety of proof and division.

“Every division is twofold: either one separates an entire body into different parts, or one distributes genera through species. If, then, someone less skilled in these five things wishes to divide things, there is no doubt that through ignorance he will often dissolve them from species into genera. This is the most disgraceful error, and it happened to Hermagoras in the first discussion of his Rhetoric. He fell into such clouds of error that he placed two genera under a part of a coordinate genus.

“If he had recognized the force and truth of division, and had acquired the discipline of genera, species, properties, and differences, he would never have been so vigorously censured by Marcus Tullius for the error of such a foolish division.

“In proofs, however, the fruitfulness of this work is so great that no proof of anything whatever can ever arise apart from these matters. For what could you properly demonstrate if, because you do not know its differences, you cannot know what the thing itself is? What could you properly expound if, because you do not know its genus, you are ignorant of the source from which the thing itself derives? Or what could you demonstrate rationally in proofs if, because you do not know its species, you cannot recognize what the very thing is about which you wish to prove something?

“What if you omit properties? You will never be able to enclose any thing within the boundary of its proper proof. But if you do not perceive the force and nature of accidents, when treating the substance of anything you will mingle the empty name of accident equally in definitions and proofs.

“Once these matters are known, therefore, division and definition will remain complete and stable; when they are unknown, proof will be weak, unstable, and mutilated.

“Porphyry—not Victorinus—therefore promises to explain these matters briefly and moderately. He would not be serving as an introduction if, from the beginning, he established for us all the matters for which this clear introduction prepares us. The highly learned restraint of his discussion thus preserves the proper mode of an introduction, tempering by some light of his teaching the path of those entering into the deepest darkness of things.

“He says that matters had been discussed by the ancients in profound and magnificent inquiry, whereas he himself has now arranged them sparingly and briefly. What, however, was discussed about these matters by the ancient interpreters of philosophy, he merely touches upon and passes over.

“Then Fabius said: ‘What is that?’

“And I replied: ‘This: he says that he will entirely pass over the genera and species themselves—whether they truly subsist, or are held only in understanding and thought; whether they are corporeal or incorporeal; and whether they are separate or joined to sensible things themselves. Since this would be a profound discussion, he promised to remain silent about it. Let us, however, with the reins of moderation applied, touch upon each matter to a moderate extent.’

“Of the questions, then, which he promises to pass over and omit, the first is whether genera and species themselves are real, or are merely imagined as bare and empty things in acts of understanding. The question is of the following kind:

“Since the human mind is manifold, through the quality of the senses it understands things subject to the senses; and, having formed from these a conception through a certain act of contemplation, it prepares a path for itself toward understanding incorporeal things. Thus, when I see individual human beings, I recognize that I have seen them, and profess that I understand them because they are human beings.”

“From this understanding, therefore, as though strengthened by knowledge of sensible things, the mind raises itself to a higher act of understanding and contemplation. It then conjectures the species human being itself, which is placed under animal and contains individual human beings, and understands that incorporeal thing whose bodily particulars it had previously apprehended while sensing and understanding individual human beings.

“For it is impossible to call that specific human being which constrains all of us within the scope of its name corporeal, since we have conceived it solely through mind and understanding. Thus the mind, relying upon the beginnings of things, is elevated to a higher and incorporeal understanding.

“From this it follows that the mind is not only an artificer in understanding incorporeal things through sensible things, but also in fabricating and even falsifying things for itself. For from the form of a horse and a human being, understanding itself constructed for itself the false species of centaurs.

“These acts of mental contemplation, which proceed from the perception of things to understanding, and are either understood or at least imagined, the Greeks call Φαντασίαι [phantasiai]; we may call them ‘images’ or ‘appearances.’

“Thus they now ask about genera, species, and the other things: whether these are truly subsistent and are understood as possessing, in a certain manner, essence and stability, so that we understand the species human being as truly and completely derived from individual bodies; or whether they are fabricated by a certain imagination of the mind, as in that verse of Horace:

> If a painter wished to join a horse’s neck  
> to a human head—

“something which neither exists nor could exist, but is fabricated solely by a false act of mental contemplation.

“This is a very acute and subtle inquiry, and one that will be exceedingly useful for the matter at hand. For we must know whether these things truly exist; there could be no discussion or contemplation of them if they did not exist.

“But if you weigh the truth and integrity of things, there is no doubt that they are real. For since all real things cannot exist without these five things, you cannot doubt that these five things themselves are truly understood. They are interwoven and, in a certain manner, joined and compacted within all things.

“Why would Aristotle discuss the first ten expressions signifying genera of things? Why would he collect their differences and properties, and principally discuss accidents, unless he had seen these matters embedded in things and, in a certain manner, united with them?

“If this is so, there is no doubt that they are real and are held by a determinate act of mental contemplation. This is also confirmed by Porphyry’s own agreement. For, as though it had already been established and known that they truly subsist in this way, he does not hesitate to introduce another question when he says: ‘Whether these things are corporeal or incorporeal.’

“That question would be exceedingly trivial and absurd—whether they were corporeal—unless it had first been established that they existed.”

“This inquiry too, which is by no means useless, is resolved as follows. No one doubts that they are incorporeal; although they are grasped by no senses, what they are becomes clear through the mind’s contemplation.

“For it is primary in the nature of incorporeals that an incorporeal thing can in a certain manner be the source of a corporeal thing.” But corporeal things cannot be prior to incorporeals. Since substance is a genus, while corporeal and incorporeal are species of substance, this matter shows that corporeal is not a genus: incorporeal is subordinate to substance, that is, to the genus. If corporeal were a genus, an incorporeal species would never be placed beneath it.

“Observe most attentively what you have never before observed.”

“The genus itself has species; species, however, are separated by differences and shaped by properties. Certain species are found which, under the division of a genus, possess contrary functions: under animal, rational and irrational are contraries; under rational, mortal and immortal are also contraries.

“If animal, in a solitary act of understanding, were neither rational nor irrational, where would these differences in the species have arisen, since they had not previously existed in the genus? But if the genus—that is, animal—contains both things within itself, so that it is both rational and irrational, two contraries would occur in one and the same thing, which is impossible.

“I shall therefore touch briefly upon the question and say that the genus is not both things—that is, rational or irrational, or whatever else species divide among themselves by contrariety. Rather, by its own force and power, the genus contains these things, while it itself is none of them. The nature of genus will become clearer in this way: it is neither incorporeal nor corporeal in itself, yet it can produce either from itself, as will become more evident in the second book.

“Species, however, is sometimes corporeal and sometimes incorporeal. If you place human being under substance, you have posited a corporeal species; if you place God under it, you have posited an incorporeal species.

“The same applies to differences. If they divide corporeal or incorporeal species, they will sometimes be incorporeal and sometimes corporeal. Thus, if you oppose four-footed to two-footed, the difference is corporeal; but if you oppose rational to irrational, the difference is incorporeal. Properties are likewise treated in the same way.

“If a property corresponds to a species, then, if the species is incorporeal, the property will be incorporeal; if the species is corporeal, the property will be claimed as corporeal.

“Accident is treated in the same way. For if it happens to incorporeal things to be incorporeal, it is clear that, in the mind, knowledge is an accident and is evidently incorporeal. But whatever accidents belong to corporeal things are clearly corporeal, as when someone says that I have curly hair as an accident.

“Thus genus in itself is neither of the two, but it can produce both kinds from itself. Species, differences, properties, and accidents, once they have been received into contrary species, will accordingly be called either corporeal or incorporeal.

“There are, however, some to whom this very matter may appear complete and who define these things as incorporeal alone. They say that genus is not considered insofar as it exists by its own nature, but insofar as it is a genus.

“Thus, if substance is a genus, it is not considered insofar as it is substance, but insofar as it has species beneath it. Likewise, if species is corporeal and incorporeal, they are not considered insofar as one is called God or human being, but insofar as they are under a genus.

“Differences too are not considered insofar as something is two-footed or four-footed, but insofar as it is a difference. For four-footedness is not itself a difference unless there is something two-footed from which it differs. Thus it is not four-footed or two-footed that is being considered, but that which lies between two-footed and four-footed, namely difference.

“The same applies to property. Whatever belongs properly to something is considered as a property insofar as it belongs solely to the species of which it is said to be the property. ‘Capable of laughter’ is not a property of human being insofar as it is laughter, but insofar as only a human being can laugh. It is indisputably clear that these matters are incorporeal.

“Accidents, in turn, are of the same kind as the things to which they belong, as was said above. But those who hold this view seem to prove it by Porphyry’s own statement, who, as though it had already been established that these things are incorporeal, says: ‘And whether they are separate or joined to sensible things.’

“If these things had ever been corporeal, it would be absurd to ask whether corporeal things were separated from or joined to sensible things, since sensible things themselves are corporeal.

“The question is of the following kind: some incorporeal things do not admit bodies at all, such as animal or God; some cannot exist without bodies, such as the first incorporeality after boundaries; and some exist in bodies but can also exist apart from bodies, such as the soul.

“The question is therefore to which kind of incorporeality these five things belong: whether to those which are entirely separated from body, or to those which cannot be separated from bodies, or to those which are sometimes joined and sometimes separated.

“It appears that they can both be separated and joined. For when corporeal things are divided through genera into species, and their properties and differences are named, these things are plainly sensible—that is, corporeal. But when a discussion is held about incorporeal things, and those things are divided by means of the very entities that lack body, they are operating around corporeal things.

“If this is so, there is no doubt that these five things belong to the same genus, one which can both exist apart from bodies and endure conjunction with bodies. Yet they do so in such a way that, if they are joined to bodies, they are inseparable from bodies.

“If they are joined to incorporeals, however, they are never separated from incorporeals, and they contain both powers within themselves. For if they are joined to corporeals, they are of the same kind as that first incorporeality after boundaries, which never departs from body; but if they are joined to incorporeals, they are of the same kind as the mind, which is never joined to body.

“Porphyry therefore promised to remain silent about these matters and to treat them briefly and moderately, adopting a different consideration or conjecture concerning things. This is equivalent to saying:

“‘Since these matters are relevant to the Categories, to definitions, to divisions, and to proofs, I undertake to discuss them for that reason. I shall discuss them only to the extent that they contribute to the matters just mentioned, not to the extent that anything whatever might be treated concerning these genera, species, and the other matters themselves.’

“For those matters, as he himself says, require a more serious treatment. He confessed that he follows the teaching received from the Peripatetics—that is, from the Aristotelians. The Stoics, who also wished to treat these matters, are not wholly accepted by Porphyry; for that reason he says that he takes the method of discussion from the Peripatetics.

“Then Fabius questioned me as follows: ‘What was it that you said earlier, when you were treating incorporeals—that there are certain incorporealities which always subsist around body, such as the first incorporealities after boundaries? What incorporeality is this, or what boundaries do you mean? I do not understand.’

“And I replied: ‘The discussion is lengthy, and will contribute nothing to the matter we are now investigating. But I shall say briefly that by “boundaries” I meant the extremities of the figures dealt with in geometry. As for the incorporeality which exists around boundaries, if you take up the first book composed by the most learned man Macrobius Theodosius, the book he wrote On the Dream of Scipio, you will learn about it more fully and abundantly. But let us now proceed to what follows.’

“Then Fabius said, ‘As you wish,’ and at the same time began as follows.

## On Genus

‘For neither genus nor species appears to be named simply, that is, in only one way. “Genus” is said to be a collection of certain things related to one another and in some manner related to something else; hence the genus of the Dardanids is spoken of.

“Again, genus is said to be the beginning of any generation, either from the begetter or from the place in which someone was born.’

‘The rest,’ he said, ‘is generally clear.’

“Then I said: ‘If you first examine the force of equivocation, you will carefully recognize the division of genus. It is agreed that the name “genus” is applied equivocally to the things subordinate to it.

“‘Equivocal’ are things which are one in name but are widely different in their account of substance and distinct in definition. For example, let someone call this statue a Venus. Venus herself and the statue of Venus therefore agree in one designation, since the name Venus belongs to both. But if someone defines what each is, he will establish one account and definition for the true Venus, and another for the stone.

“If we observe that things called by one word but constituted by different definitions are equivocal, the participation in genus established by Porphyry will, as I think, become clear once it has been examined. For everything that is led from genus into species is univocal, not equivocal.

“Univocal is what can be called by the same name and constituted by the same definition. Thus animal is the genus and human being the species, but the same human being is also an animal. Genus and species—that is, animal and human being—can therefore be called by the one name animal, so that both are called animals; nor do their definitions differ.

“For if you give the definition of animal and say that an animal is an animate, sensible substance, it will not be absurd to apply this definition to a human being and say that a human being is an animate and sensible substance, just like an animal. But this has been stated above.

“If, then, univocal things are constituted by one name and the same definition, while equivocal things share one name but are not contained under one definition of substance, whatever is univocal—as animal, the genus, is univocal with respect to its species—involves genera and species. Whatever is equivocal, such as ‘ram,’ which is equivocal because it signifies several things, does not involve participation in genus and species. Such participation is not present in things that are classified as species and genera.

“For what knowledge of genus and species could there be in things whose definition and complete account of substance are divided apart?

“Porphyry therefore divides the name ‘genus’ into three forms, but as equivocal forms, not as univocal ones: that is, these forms are contained under one name, genus, but differ because their own properties are distinct. In this way he divides it into three parts.

“First, he says, ‘genus’ is called the collection of many people among themselves who derive the name of their genus from some one person—for example, Romans derive their genus from Romulus and are said to be of the same genus.

“Second, he says that ‘genus’ is the beginning of any generation, either from the begetter or from the place in which someone was born. Thus we say that Aeneas is descended from Anchises and is Trojan by race.

“Third, genus is that under which a species is subordinate.

“Victorinus, however, reduces the two higher genera to one. He declares that both the agreement of a multitude with one another through the same designation of genus, and the line of descent from a genus and the place in which someone was born, belong to one word and designation, genus.

“He himself adds something that can apply only to the Latin language. He says that genus is used in a second way, as in ‘an honorable kind of case.’ The Greeks do not consider these kinds of cases to be genera in the art of rhetoric, but call them σχήματα [schemata], that is, figures. They recognize only the principal genera: demonstrative, deliberative, and judicial. They themselves call these εἴδη [eidē], that is, species of rhetoric; but we call them genera of cases.

“The third genus is the one Porphyry sets forth: that under which species distributed by differences are subordinate.

“Since, however, Victorinus is about to treat the third genus, let us accept his fault—or, if that is what it turns out to be, his correction—with fairness and goodwill. Let us now return to the earlier meaning of genus in Victorinus and undertake to unravel and explain it as he expresses it.

“‘Genus,’ he says, ‘is said to be a collection of certain things related to one another and in some manner to something else.’

“Here he has indicated both things: the kinship of a multitude among itself and the tracing of a line. For when he says that genus is a collection of certain things related to one another in some manner—that is, joined to one another by some kinship—he indicates kinship. And when he adds ‘and to something else,’ he signifies the line of genus. Individual members touch that line and join themselves to one another by their connection with one origin of generation; many, joined and related through the same line, constitute the genus.

“The order is therefore as follows: ‘Genus is said to be a collection of certain things related to one another in some manner and to something else,’ that is, related to the line of someone through the genus. Thus he indicates kinship through ‘collection,’ and designates the tracing and line of genus through the relation in some manner to something else.

“What follows expresses this more plainly and clearly, when he says: ‘Again, genus is said to be the beginning of any generation, either from the begetter or from the place in which someone was born.’

“He explains more fully what he had gathered above in a compressed and elaborate brevity. He says that genus is again said either from generation—that is, from the one by whom someone was begotten—or from the place in which someone was born.

“If the particle ‘again’ is connected with the words ‘or from the place in which someone was born,’ the meaning does not waver, and the order is: ‘Genus is said to be the beginning of any birth, either from the begetter or, again, from the place in which someone was born.’

“Or the explanation will certainly be simpler if we take the earlier meaning of genus—that is, the collection of certain things related in some manner to something else—as referring solely to the kinship of a multitude, while assigning the tracing of a line and birth from a place to the lower meaning. Even so, one meaning of genus signifies, in a certain manner, both the kinship of a multitude, the line from a begetter, and birth from a place.

“All these matters concern the designation of anyone’s origin. It is therefore not unreasonable that everything belonging to the generative origin of anyone should be contained under one meaning of genus.

“Strictly speaking, however, and according to the simplest explanation, Victorinus established four meanings of genus, adding one to Porphyry’s three: the honorable genus of a case. The four meanings of genus are therefore: the kinship of a multitude, the tracing of a line, the genus of a case, and the genus of species.

“The second division of genus in Victorinus follows: genus as the kind of case which the Greeks, as has been said, call not genera but σχήματα [figures].

“The mode of the third meaning of genus is that genus is said to be that to which a species is subordinate—that is, the genus from which species derive. He says that this has perhaps been arranged in accordance with the likeness and equality of the higher meanings.

“For genus is the beginning of its species, just as Romulus is the beginning of those who are related and joined to him as Romans. Likewise, the name Romulus contains all Romans, just as species are contained under the name of a genus.

“For just as the descendants of Dardanus receive within themselves the earlier name Dardani, derived from Dardanus, so animal, when it has, for example, human being and horse as species, does not refuse to contain both horse and human being within the name animal, so that they themselves are called animals.

“Species are therefore contained under genera in the same way as related people are contained under the person from whom they happened to derive that relationship. For genus is both the beginning of its species and a collection containing many species within itself.

“Again, the first name of kinship and of generation itself is a beginning; and under that one name alone, the diversity of human names and genera is gathered through participation in the name and genus. This is what he says in the following words:

“‘In another way, genus is said to be that to which species are subordinate, perhaps named according to the likeness of the higher meanings. For genus is a certain beginning of those things that are beneath it, and it appears to contain the multitude of all things beneath it.’

“The word ‘appears’ has been added with great caution. If all these things were in no way different, there would be one meaning of genus, both the meaning that is distributed into species and the meaning that is divided among kinships.

“But there is such a difference between these genera: the genera of those species which themselves have other species beneath them are genera equally with respect to species of equal rank.

“Human being and horse, which are beneath animal, cannot be said to be earlier one than the other with respect to time and the beginning of birth. For if one thing were earlier and another later, and someone wished to place them under the name of one genus, he could not do so. Genus is genus equally for its species.

“And if genus is genus equally for its species, the species themselves are considered equal to one another in time and origin.

“But this is not so with genera that produce kinships. Whoever Capis’s father was—the Capis who founded Capua—if he fathered only one son, Capis, and from that one son the kinship and union of the Capuans proceeded, this differs from a genus to which species are subordinate. A genus can never be the genus of one species alone, but only of several.

“Yet the genus that is the beginning of kinships can gather and assemble a kinship from one son alone; a genus understood through species cannot do this unless several species are subordinate to it.

“It is therefore clear that the genus which gathers kinship differs from the genus from which species are divided.

“It can also differ in this respect: a genus—that is, the beginning of kinship—can have beneath it two persons born from it at unequal times, one of later origin and the other older. This is not true of genera and species. For, as was said above, species cannot properly be placed under a genus unless they are equal by nature, not merely by convention.

“Once these matters have been explained, the following comes next.

“Since genus has now been mentioned so many times, the discussion among philosophers concerns its final meaning. They explain it by defining it as follows:

> Genus is that which is predicated, in answer to the question ‘what is it?’, of several things differing in species.

He says “so many times” because he wishes to demonstrate this for the third time; and this has been admitted for the sake of a clear progression in the work. Since *genus* is a name applied to many things, its [Col. 0025D] first meaning had to be stated in full, so that, after the other meanings had been rejected, the one about which the discussion was to proceed might be selected.

When he says “in this way, since *genus* is mentioned so many times,” that is, for the third time, among philosophers—on whose account he is about to treat the final meaning of *genus* that he mentioned—the discussion and examination turns upon that genus which has species beneath it. As for the higher meanings of *genus*, namely kinship and the place in which someone was born, these belong to historians or poets; the second genus belongs to rhetoricians; the third to philosophers.

There is also an order in these discussions. Whenever matters arise that can be called by many names, and it is necessary to discuss and explain them under one of those names, everything is first arranged [Col. 0026A] in order, so that what is selected may be distinguished from what is rejected. But those things that are to be rejected and cast aside are mentioned first. What is taken up for discussion and treatment is named afterward. Thus here the later meaning of *genus* has been placed last: he has undertaken to discuss it, but first to define it, circumscribe it by a certain boundary, and make it clear. For unless a thing has first been established as what it is, its treatment will be regarded as empty speculation.

He therefore defines *genus* as follows:

> Genus is that which is predicated of several things differing in species, in answer to the question “what is it?”—

as, for example, *animal*. The definition is of this kind: all things that differ have some difference between them by which they appear to be distinct and different. Moreover, if something is a genus and species are placed beneath it, [Col. 0026B] two or more species must necessarily be posited under the genus, since there cannot be a genus of only one species.

But if there are several species, they must necessarily be divided by some difference; otherwise they could not be several. For if they differed in nothing, they would not be several species, and the name of genus would disappear. It is therefore clear that those species are placed under a genus which, distributed by differences, are constituted as several in number through divisions corresponding to those differences.

Accordingly, since it was stated above that in every definition the beginning of the definition must be drawn from the genus, if you wish to define any species, you will necessarily name its genus first, and will first apply the name of the genus to the species that you are defining. You say primarily that this species is what that genus is—the genus under which the species you are defining [Col. 0026C] has been placed. Afterwards, by differences and properties, you exclude it from the others by a certain delimitation of the definition.

For if you say that *animal* is *man*, *animal* is the genus and *man* the species. Thus you have predicated the name *animal*, that is, the genus, of *man*, that is, of the species, when you have said that man is an animal. But if you could apply the name of a genus to a single species in a definition, you would predicate the name of the genus of it. Yet there is nothing to prevent species from being species of their genera in an unequal manner; indeed, it is always necessary that whatever things are genera should be predicated of the species subject to them, whether in definitions or in any other questions.

But since a genus is predicated of species, we must recognize how it is predicated. For if you ask, “What is man?” and someone answers “Animal,” [Col. 0026D] he appears to have answered correctly and completely—and indeed he has. When you asked what man is, he answered “animal”; that is, the genus is predicated of the species in answer to the question “what is the species?” You asked what the species was, and he applied to the species about which you had asked the name *animal*, that is, the genus.

A full and proper definition of *genus* has therefore been given: genus is that which is named of several things differing in species, in answer to the question “what is it?”, as *animal*. For *animal* is named in answer to the question “what is it?” with respect to man, horse, ox, raven, serpent, and many other things that differ by differences and species.

But whether he said that genus is that which is predicated of several species differing by differences, in answer to the question [Col. 0027A] “what is it?”, or that genus is that which is predicated of several differences differing in species, in answer to the question “what is it?”, makes no difference. For whether the differences differ in species or the species differ by differences, the meaning is the same.

Whether, for example, rational and irrational, which are differences, distinguish man and horse in species, or whether the species man and horse are divided and distinguished by the differences rational and irrational, makes no difference. Thus the division of genus has been made full and complete.

Definitions, however, are made in two ways. One kind of definition is the definition that, as has been said, is drawn from a genus. But there are certain highest genera which cannot have another genus above them, such as the ten categories established by Aristotle. The definition of these things—[Col. 0027B] whose genus cannot be found, since they themselves are genera of everything that belongs to them—we shall provide.

What the Greeks call *ὑπογραφοὶ λόγοι* (“descriptive accounts”), the Latins may call *subscriptive accounts*. Subscriptive accounts are demonstrations and, in a certain way, indications of the property of that thing which, although it is itself the most general genus and no genus of it can be found, must nevertheless be defined.

Aristotle, wishing to define substance, the most general genus, and being unable to find any genus of it, says that it is a subject—a certain property, demonstration, and descriptive account of the thing itself. For substance is subject to everything. An accident, which he divides into nine parts, cannot exist apart from substance. Therefore, whatever things [Col. 0027C] must be defined, if they do not have a genus, must be given a certain descriptive and demonstrative account of them.

Thus, since he now thought that *genus* itself had to be defined, he did not draw the definition from a genus, but supplied a certain demonstration and property of genus. I mean that Porphyry has given this definition—and in a certain sense a description and demonstration—for subordinate genera as well as for those that are highest.

For if a genus has another genus, and that genus in turn has another, and another after that, the account proceeds to infinity unless there is some genus above which no genus exists. But if there is such a genus, this definition must necessarily fit it clearly and orderly as well.

I do not mean genus in the sense that *animal* is a genus of *animal*, nor [Col. 0027D] that *man*, which is a species, is a species of *man*, or *horse* of *horse*. I mean that by which animal itself is a genus of man and horse. For animal, taken by itself, is the genus of nothing; nor is man, taken by itself, a species of anything; nor is horse, taken by itself, a species of anything. They are genera and species only in relation to participation in something else.

Since horse and man are under animal, animal is not a genus with respect to itself, but with respect to horse and man. Likewise, the things called species—man and horse—are not species with respect to horse and man, but species with respect to animal.

I therefore say that genus and species do not mean the substances themselves in which genus and species are found, but the very participation or relation of higher things to lower, and of lower things to higher. This participation, [Col. 0028A] is one and the same in higher genera, higher species, subordinate genera, and subordinate species. Since no genus of this participation could be found, the definition of genus that has been given was not drawn from a genus; rather, a subscriptive, demonstrative, and, in a certain way, designative account of genus was supplied.

Then Fabius said:

> Subtle indeed, by Hercules, and something we have scarcely ever heard before. But please continue. For now the stars themselves are, in a manner of speaking, vying with one another, and night is being overcome by daylight.

Then I said:

> What follows is the first and brief division of all things.

For he says:

> Of the things that are spoken of, some are spoken of with reference to one thing, as are all individuals, such as Socrates, this person, and that person. Others are spoken of with reference to a plurality, such as genera, species, [Col. 0028B] differences, properties, and accidents. For these are not commonly names belonging to one individual. There is a genus, such as animal; a species, such as man; a difference, such as rational; a property, such as capable of laughter; an accident, such as white or sitting. Genus differs, then, from those things that are spoken of with reference to unity, because genus is predicated of several things.

This is a brief and distinct division, as was said above. For every thing is either the name of one thing or of several things. This is what he means when he says: “Of the things that are spoken of, some are spoken of with reference to unity, as are all individuals.”

What this means must be explained briefly. Every genus has species beneath it; species are separated by differences and explained by properties. Accidents occur secondarily in species, but primarily in individuals that are under [Col. 0028C] species. What this means will be stated later.

Genera, then, are spoken both of species, of the differences that distribute those species, of the properties that constitute the species, and of those accidents which, although they primarily belong to individuals, are said to be present in species. Let us demonstrate this by examples.

Let *animal* be the genus, *man* the species, *rational* the difference, *capable of laughter* the property, and *standing* or *walking*, or something measured in the body, such as being three feet tall, the accident.

Animal, which is a genus, is predicated of the species, that is, of man. For you say that man is an animal. Moreover, you also predicate the genus of the difference of the species. For you say that rational is an animal.

Nothing prevents the genus from being predicated in the same way of the property. For if you ask, “What is capable of laughter?” it is not [Col. 0028D] absurd to name animal.

Accidents, however, are primarily in individuals in this way, and secondarily in species. If someone says that particular men, for example Cicero, are sitting or standing, or whatever else he pleases, the same must also be true of the species man. For if Cicero is sitting, man too is sitting; if Cicero is walking, man too is walking. Therefore, if any accidents arise in individuals and, having been carried over, reside in species, genus can also be named of those accidents. For if someone asks, “What is walking?” the proper answer is “animal.” Nothing can walk except an animal.

Individuals are beneath species, such as Cicero and Virgil under man; and the genus of the species can be predicated [Col. 0029A] of those individuals. For if you ask, “What is Cicero?” you may properly answer “animal.”

Thus genus is named with respect to species, differences, accidents, properties, and individuals. Species, however, is no longer predicated of genus or of differences, but only of properties and of the individuals subject to it: of individuals because it is above them, and of properties because it is equal to them.

Let us see what this means. All genera surpass and exceed their species. We say that genera exceed species in that genera possess a greater power than species. Man, which is a species, is only man. Animal, which is a genus, is not only man, but also horse, ox, or anything else placed under animal. Thus the greater force of the genus is rightly predicated of the lesser species subject to it. [Col. 0029B]

There are also things that are equal to one another, such as properties and species. Man is a species; capable of laughter is a property. Whatever is capable of laughter is therefore man, and whatever is man is capable of laughter. Thus neither the power of capable-of-laughter surpasses that of man, nor that of man surpasses that of capable-of-laughter; they are equal and can be predicated of one another. Thus, if you ask, “What is man?” the answer is “capable of laughter”; and if you ask, “What is capable of laughter?” the answer is “man.”

Accordingly, whatever things are superior are predicated of those that are inferior; and whatever things are equal are mutually predicated of one another. But those things that are inferior and lesser cannot be predicated of superior and more comprehensive things, such as genera and species. For you will never correctly predicate a species of a genus.

Thus species is predicated of property as something equal. But since, under species, [Col. 0029C] individuals are found one by one, and since we call “individuals” those things that cannot be divided into any species or into any further parts—such as Cato, Plato, Cicero, and every individual human being—we do not divide these into parts, whereas we divide animal into species, namely man and horse, and man itself, the special species encompassing particular men, into Cato, Plato, Virgil, and all the separate human beings distributed beneath it. An individual man, that is, Cicero, cannot be distributed into any others.

For this reason he was called *ἄτομον*, that is, “indivisible” or “individual.”

Species, then, which is predicated equally of properties, is predicated of individuals as something superior [Col. 0029D] to them, since the species man is greater than any particular individual. Cicero is only Cicero, whereas man is not only Cicero. And if species is predicated of individuals, it is also predicated of the accidents of individuals.

Thus species is not predicated of the genus above it, nor of the difference, because difference—as we shall now demonstrate—is above species. But it is predicated of the property, to which it is equal, and of the individual, which it surpasses.

Difference, however, is predicated both of species and of properties, accidents, and individuals. For rational, which is a difference, is predicated of man, which is a species. Rational, which is a difference, is also predicated of capable-of-laughter, that is, of the property. For something is said to be capable of laughter because it is rational.

If man is rational and man is capable of laughter, [Col. 0030A] it is clear that what is capable of laughter can also be called rational. And if difference is predicated of species, while species is predicated of individuals, difference must also be predicated of individuals. For you say, “What sort of person is Cicero?”—“Rational.”

If difference is predicated of individuals, while accidents belong to individuals, differences must also be predicated of accidents. Property, however, since it is always the property of one species, is predicated of only that one species to which it belongs. Capable-of-laughter, which is a property, is predicated only of the species man.

If it is predicated of the species man, and species is predicated of individuals, there is no doubt that property is also predicated of individuals. For if man is an animal capable of laughter, Cicero and Virgil are also correctly called [Col. 0030B] animals capable of laughter.

If property is correctly predicated of individuals, it is also correctly predicated of the accidents that belong to those individuals. Accidents themselves, moreover, are predicated both of species and of all the other things, and especially of individuals.

We say “a white horse” and “a white man”; again, “a black horse” and “a black Ethiopian.” If this is so, we also say “a black animal.” We say “a rational black thing” and “an irrational black thing,” since horse and Ethiopian man may be black. We also say “a black thing capable of laughter” when some human being is black. And we say “a black individual” when some particular man is identified as being from Ethiopia.

Since this is so, it is clear that genus is predicated of several things, namely species, differences, accidents, properties, and individuals. [Col. 0030C] Likewise, difference is predicated of several things, namely species, properties, accidents, and individuals; property is predicated of several things, namely species, individuals, and accidents; species is predicated of several things, namely individuals and accidents; and accident is predicated both of genus and species, property, difference, and individuals.

If this is so, it is clear that these five things are predicated of several things. But an individual, since it has nothing beneath it, is predicated with reference to a certain singularity and unity. Cicero is one person, and the name applies to one person.

Thus individuals, which are spoken of with reference to unity, are subject to all the superior things. Genus, species, and difference are predicated of properties or accidents, although they may also be predicated of one another; but they are predicated equally of individuals, as was demonstrated above.

Individuals [Col. 0030D], however, since they have nothing beneath them into which they can be divided and distributed, are predicated of nothing other than themselves, which are single and one.

This is what he means when he says:

> Of the things that are spoken of, some are spoken of with reference to unity, as are all individuals, such as Socrates, this person, and that person. Others are spoken of with reference to a plurality, such as genera, species, differences, properties, and accidents. For these are not commonly names belonging to one individual.

It is as though he said: “These are commonly predicated of several things, not of one thing, as individuals are.”

He then supplies an example of what genera, species, differences, properties, and accidents are, saying:

> There is a genus, such as animal; a species, such as man—

the species man, which we previously placed under animal along with the other [Col. 0031A] animate beings;

> a difference, such as rational—

by which the species man is distinguished from irrational animal;

> a property, such as capable of laughter—
