which no other animal, rational or irrational, possesses. For no animal laughs except man alone. Therefore, although some of the heavenly powers are rational animals, capable of laughter is not their property, since they do not laugh. Correctly, then, capable of laughter is predicated as the property of man alone;

> an accident, such as white, black, and sitting—

since these are not part of the substance of human beings, they are rightly called accidents.

For if what we call an accident belonged to the substance of any species, then, when the accident was removed, the substance of the species to which it belonged would also perish. Since rationality belongs to the substance of man, if rationality were removed, [Col. 0031B] the substance of man would necessarily perish, because it occurs within the substance and nature of the species itself.

But if white or black, or any other accidents, are removed, the species itself in which they occurred remains. For not every man is white, nor is every man black; and if one or the other is absent, the species of the person in question does not perish. Therefore these are rightly called accidents, as though they were not innate in the substance but came from outside.

Now, since he has shown what genus is and has distinguished and distributed those things that are spoken of with reference to unity from those that are predicated of several things, he explains the differences of genus itself—both from those things spoken of with reference to unity and from those that belong to plurality, namely difference, species, property, and accident.

He says that genus differs from those things that are [Col. 0031C] predicated only of individuals, that is, from those that are spoken of with reference to unity, because genus is predicated of several things, whereas individuals are predicated of single things.

But since this difference between genus and individuals was shared by differences, species, properties, and accidents, he divides and separates genus from those other differences themselves. He demonstrates this as follows:

> Genus differs from those things that are spoken of with reference to unity because genus is predicated of several things.

Genus therefore differs from the remaining things. First it differs from species, because species, although predicated of several things, is not predicated of things differing in species but of things differing in number.

First, then, he demonstrates the difference between genus and species, a difference that proceeds from genus. Although difference is above species, it is not placed above a subordinate species but [Col. 0031D] above the most specific species.

For although the difference rational is placed above man, which is the most specific species, that difference itself is nevertheless a species of the genus under which the most specific species is placed. For beneath animal, rational is placed before man.

Thus, although both genus and species are predicated of several things, genus is predicated of several species in answer to the question “what is it?”, whereas species is no longer predicated of several species but of several individuals.

There are, as was said, certain most general genera above which no other genus can be found. There are also species beneath which no other species can be found. That species is called complete which is never [Col. 0032A] a genus, that is, beneath which there are no species. For if there were species beneath it, it too could be a genus.

A species that is truly a species, then, has no other species beneath it, as man does. Since man is a species, the individual men beneath him are not called his species but individuals.

For if man were the genus of individual men, and if a genus, as has been said, were predicated of several things differing in species in answer to the question “what is it?”, then, if the species man were predicated as a genus of individual men, individual men would differ from one another in species.

But individual men do not differ in species. Whatever does not differ in species, if something is predicated of it, is not predicated as a genus of species. Thus man is not predicated of individual men as a genus of several things [Col. 0032B] differing in species, but of several things differing in number. For individual men differ from one another only in number, not in species.

Therefore, since genus is predicated of its subjects in such a way as to be predicated of several things differing in species, whereas species is predicated of its subjects in such a way as to be predicated of several things differing in number, genus and species agree in that both are predicated of several things and both answer the question “what is it?”

For if you ask, “What is man?” the answer is “animal,” that is, the genus. And if you ask, “What is Cicero?” the answer is “man,” that is, the species.

They differ, however, in this: although both are predicated of several things and both answer the question “what is it?”, genus is predicated of things differing in species, whereas species is predicated of things differing only in number. Porphyry [Col. 0032C] demonstrates this as follows:

> From the remaining things that are predicated of several things, genus differs first from species. For although species is predicated of several things, it is not predicated of things differing in species but in number. For man, although it is a species, is predicated of Socrates, Plato, and Cicero, who differ not in species but in number. Animal, however, which is a genus, is predicated both of ox and of horse, which differ from one another in species, not merely in number.

This is equivalent to saying that genus has one additional difference from species. For genus and species agree in that both are predicated in answer to the question “what is it?”, as was said. Genus and species likewise agree in that both are predicated of several things. They also agree in that both are predicated of things [Col. 0032D] differing in number.

For individual men are divided from one another in number just as much as man is divided from horse, ox, deer, or any other animate beings. Genus differs from species, however, because genus is predicated of several things differing in species, whereas species does not have this feature.

I think it makes no difference whether we say that one thing is predicated *to* another or that one thing is predicated *of* another. The understanding is the same in either case. If animal is predicated of man, then animal is likewise predicated of man. For when you have asked, “What is man?” you answer, in response to the question concerning man, that man is an animal.

But now we must consider what follows. What, then, comes next?

[Col. 0033A]

> Genus differs from property because property is called the property of each species to which it belongs, and also of the things beneath that species, namely individuals. For capable of laughter belongs only to man and, of course, to individual human beings. Genus, however, is always applied not to one species but to several things differing in species.

He appears here to be saying that every property, if it belongs to one species, is then truly a property. For if it does not belong to one species but to two or more, it is not a property of two or more things but will be common in the account of substance.

It is therefore clear that a property adheres individually to the one species of which it is the property. Since the species man alone laughs, capable of laughter is properly and individually applied to man. A property is therefore always applied to one species. [Col. 0033B]

Property differs from genus in this respect: genus is always named of several species, whereas property is named of only one species, the species of which it is the property. If you say “capable of laughter,” it is applied to only one species, man.

Genus agrees with property in that both are named of several things. Genus is named of several species, and it is also named of the individuals beneath species. If man and horse are animals, then Cicero too will be an animal, and every individual horse will likewise be called an animal.

Property is similarly predicated of several things. It is predicated of each species and of the individuals beneath the species. If man is capable of laughter, Cicero and Virgil are also capable of laughter, and all those who are named individually are called capable of laughter.

Genus and property [Col. 0033C] also agree in that both are predicated in answer to the question “what is it?” Genus is predicated of species in answer to that question. If you ask, “What is man?” you answer “animal.” Property too is predicated in answer to the question “what is it?” If you ask, “What is man?” you may properly predicate capable of laughter.

They also agree in that genus and property are predicated of several things differing in number. Individual animals—man, horse, raven, and the rest—differ from one another in number in the same way as individual men do.

Property differs from genus, however, because genus is predicated of several species, whereas property is named of only one species, the species of which it is the property.

But the difference between genus and property is not the same as the difference between species and genus. Species is not predicated of any species at all, whereas property, although not predicated of several species, is always applied [Col. 0033D] to the one species of which it is the property.

After this he discusses the difference between genus and difference and accident, saying:

> Genus differs from difference and from accidents because, although these too are predicated of several things differing in species—namely differences and accidents that occur commonly—they are not named in answer to the question “what is it?” when we respond to those who ask; rather, they show what sort of thing it is.

He reserved difference and accident for later because he intended to state one difference and distinction common to them both. Difference and accident each demonstrate the quality of a species: difference demonstrates its substantial quality, while accident demonstrates an accidental quality, not a substantial one. [Col. 0034A]

Since genus is above species and species is subject to genus, genus shows what the species is, and species shows what the individual is. Species, however, can be separated only by differences. They are distinguished and distributed by substantial qualities, that is, by qualities that declare their substances.

Since animal is a genus and man and horse are species, the separation by difference shows what sort each species is: we say that the species man is rational and the species horse irrational.

If someone asks, “What is man?” the answer is “animal.” But if someone asks, “What sort of thing is man?” the answer is “rational.” Thus difference is always named not in answer to the question “what is it?” but in answer to the question “what sort of thing is it?”

There is no doubt that the same is true of accident, since quality itself [Col. 0034B] is included among the parts of accident. In the Categories, quality is named among the other nine parts of accident. If someone asks what sort of species a raven is, the immediate answer is “black.”

Genera therefore agree with differences and accidents in that they are predicated of several species. Just as genus has several species beneath it, so does difference. We call both God and man rational. Accident too is predicated of several species. We call man, horse, raven, ebony, and many other species black.

Genus and difference also agree in that difference, like genus, is equally predicated of individuals. If Cicero is an animal, which is genus, then Cicero is also rational, which is difference.

They also agree in that they are predicated of things differing in number [Col. 0034C], as was demonstrated above with respect to the others.

They differ, however, because, as was said, genus is named in answer to the question “what is it?”, whereas difference and accident are predicated in answer to the question “what sort of thing is it?”

If you ask, “What is man?” you name the genus and say that man is an animal. But if you ask what sort of thing he is with respect to difference, I answer “rational”; or, with respect to accident, “black” or “white,” or whatever quality belongs to the person about whom the question is asked.

Having distributed these matters, he begins again from the beginning to state the distinctions themselves, saying:

> Hence genus, by being predicated of several things, differs from those that are predicated of individuals, that is, from individuals. By being predicated of things differing in species, it differs from species and properties. By being named in answer to the question “what is it?”, it is distinguished from differences and commonly occurring [Col. 0034D] accidents, since these two declare what sort of thing it is.

He says that genus differs from individuals because genus is predicated of several things, as was stated. He gathers together and reduces to one the differences between property and species.

Since species is predicated of several things that differ not in species but in number, whereas property is predicated of only one species and of the individuals beneath that species, species and property nevertheless have an equal difference from genus: neither is predicated of several things differing in species.

For species cannot predicate anything of species at all; nor can property, since property is predicated not of several species but only of the one species whose property it is. If this is so, [Col. 0035A] species and properties are separated from genus by one difference.

Accident and difference are likewise separated from genus by one and the same difference: genus is named in answer to the question “what is it?”, whereas difference and accident are named in answer to the question “what sort of thing is it?”

Porphyry collects these differences for constructing the account of genus as sparingly as possible, intending to prove the same differences later in many ways. For the present, insofar as is sufficient, he says that he has established an adequate account of genus, saying:

> If this is so, the definition of genus has been made neither too short nor too long.

He says that he has given a perfect and complete definition of genus, since the definition has been made neither greater nor smaller, but has been composed equally and proportionately with genus. This must be demonstrated as follows.

We know that certain things which are predicated of other things exceed the things of which they are predicated, as genera and species do. For animal, which is a genus, exceeds man, which is a species, in that the name of the genus can also be applied to a horse, an ox, and other things. Therefore, if someone gives a definition to any thing that exceeds it, and makes the definition greater than the thing being defined, the definition will not be complete or proper, since, if the definition is greater, it embraces not only the thing it defines but also whatever other things the scope of that definition will encompass.

Thus the definition of the greater predicables will itself be greater, while the definition of the lesser will also be lesser. Accordingly, animal, which is greater, is defined as follows: “Animal is an animate, sentient substance.” But man, which is lesser than animal, is defined as follows: “Man is a rational, mortal animal, capable of laughter and learning.” Since animal is greater than man, the definition of animal will also be greater than the definition of man. For “animate, sentient substance” says more than “rational, mortal [animal].” Animate, sentient substance, like animal itself, includes not only man but also horse, ox, and other species of this kind.

If, therefore, someone applies the greater definition, that of animal, to man, defining man as follows—“Man is an animate, sentient substance”—the definition is not complete, since a horse and an ox can also be animate and sentient substances, although they are not species of man. If, on the other hand, someone applies the lesser definition to the greater thing, he makes the account deficient and, in a certain sense, truncated. For if someone wishing to define animal says, “Animal is a rational thing, capable of laughter and learning,” the definition will not be complete, since there are animals that can evade and escape the scope of this definition. An ox is an animal, yet it is neither rational nor capable of laughter.

Only those things, therefore, should be regarded as well defined that are constituted by equal definitions. We can discover when a definition is equal in the following way. Among all predicables, whenever a greater predicable is predicated of some lesser one, the relation cannot be reversed so that the lesser is predicated of the greater. For greater things are always predicated of lesser things, and lesser things never of greater things.

For example, if someone says that man is an animal, he cannot reverse the statement and say that animal is man. In relation to its genus, man is nothing other than animal; but, in relation to its species, animal can also be something other than man. Equal predicables, however, are always mutually convertible. Since “capable of laughter” belongs only to man, “capable of laughter” can be predicated of man, and man can also be predicated of “capable of laughter.” For whatever is man is capable of laughter, and whatever is capable of laughter is man.

Therefore, whatever definitions can be converted are true and equal; whatever cannot be converted is either greater or lesser and cannot be equal. If you say that man is an animate and sentient substance, the statement is true. But if you reverse it and say that an animate and sentient substance is man, you will not have spoken entirely truly. For something can be animate and sentient without being man.

Likewise, if you say that a rational, mortal thing, capable of laughter and learning, is an animal, you will have spoken truly. But if you reverse the statement and say that an animal is a rational, mortal thing, capable of laughter and learning, you will not have spoken entirely truly. For something can be an animal without being rational or capable of laughter.

Therefore, whenever the definition is greater than the thing defined, if the thing defined is mentioned first and the greater definition is then attached to it, the definition may be true. If you first say that the lesser thing is man and then attach the greater definition to it—“Man is,” followed by “an animate, sentient substance”—the result is true. Man necessarily is an animate, sentient substance.

If, however, you first state the definition and then introduce the thing defined, the statement cannot be wholly true. For if you first say “an animate, sentient substance” and then introduce the lesser thing by saying “is man,” so that the result is “An animate, sentient substance is man,” this is not wholly true. Something can be an animate and sentient substance without being man.

But if the definition is lesser than the thing defined, then, when the definition is stated first, the resulting statement is true; when it is stated afterward, it is false. If you state the lesser definition—“a rational, mortal thing, capable of laughter and learning”—and then add “is an animal,” the statement is true: “A rational, mortal thing, capable of laughter and learning, is an animal.” For every thing that is rational and mortal, and capable of laughter and learning, is necessarily an animal.

If, however, you reverse the order and first state the greater thing and then attach the lesser definition, the statement cannot be wholly true. If you say first “Animal is” and then add “a rational, mortal thing, capable of laughter and learning,” the statement is not wholly true. For something can be an animal without being rational or mortal.

Thus, if the definition is greater than the thing defined, then, when the thing is stated first and the definition follows, the statement is true; but if the definition is stated first and the thing follows, it is false. With lesser definitions and greater things, the reverse is the case. If the definition is stated first and the thing follows, the statement is true; but if the thing is stated first and the definition follows, it cannot be wholly true.

With equal definitions, however, conversion is equally possible. Since the definition “rational, mortal animal” belongs only to man, it is an equal definition of man, because it can be applied to nothing else. Thus, if you first state the thing defined and then add the definition, the result is true: “Man is a rational, mortal animal, capable of laughter and learning.” If you reverse the order and first state the definition and then the thing—“Whatever is a rational, mortal animal, capable of laughter and learning, is man”—this too is true.

Thus, for definitions to be true, nothing greater or lesser should be fitted to them; definitions must be arranged equally and appropriately. Porphyry, therefore, not being unaware of this, says that he has made the definition of genus neither greater nor lesser.

And Fabius said: “It remains to discuss species.”

“Tell me,” I said, “what follows?”

And Fabius said: “This, I think, is the order.”

## On Species

“Species” too is spoken of in many ways. The form of each individual human being is called species. Again, the beauty of the face is called species, which is why we call especially beautiful people *speciosi*, “handsome” or “beautiful.” Species is also that which is placed under a genus: thus we call man a species of animal, since animal itself is a genus; and white a species of color.

Then I said: “I take the name ‘species’ to be equivocal in the same way as ‘genus,’ since he indicates that it too is called by many names.”

“For,” he said, “species is also called the shape of a body, and perhaps many other things besides.”

Since no treatment was being given of these meanings, they were rightly omitted. Yet Victorinus seems to have erred here. Since the species and the face of any human being are the same thing, he presented the beauty of the face as though it were another meaning of species—as though the beauty of the face were not just as much the whole species. For if someone is beautiful in his entire body, he is beautiful also in his face.

Leaving these matters aside, let us turn to that species which is placed under a genus and constitutes a genus. For, as has been said, substances themselves are not classified by the name of species or genus unless they have been arranged in relation and comparison with one another. The fact that man is an animal does not make animal his genus merely because he is an animal; rather, animal is his genus because it contains under itself the species of man, horse, and the other animals. For this reason he says: “Thus we call man a species of animal, although animal itself is a genus.” Man would not be called a species unless the designation “animal” were predicated of him as a superior term.

But to show that genera and species do not occur only among substances, but are also connected among the designations of all the categories, he did not give an example only from substance; he also gave one from the remaining category of accidents. For when he says, “and white a species of color,” he places it in the division of quality among the accidents.

Since there is a certain connection, comparison, and relation between them, genera and species cannot exist apart from their mutual relation. Nothing can be concluded in their definitions unless they are named in relation to one another. If the substance of the genus is placed above the species, and the substance of the species is placed beneath the genus, and predication is completed in relation to them, there is no doubt that, when it is necessary to define genus, we must rightly predicate species, and that, when it is necessary to define species, we must rightly predicate genus.

This distinction was therefore also preserved in the definition of genus, when the definition of genus was given. For it was said that something is a genus when it is predicated of distinct species. Now, however, we must say that species is what is placed under a genus.

Its definition can be given in several ways. It can again be said that species is that of which genus is predicated in respect of what it is. Both statements signify that species is placed beneath genus. The first definition makes this explicit. The second is not of the same form, since lesser things are always placed beneath greater things. Genus is predicated of something in respect of what it is; and it is beyond doubt that genus is the greater term. If this is so, there can be no obscurity or error in saying that species, which is lesser, is placed beneath its greater genus.

Thus the meaning of the second definition differs in no way from that of the first. Species would not be placed beneath genus unless genus were predicated of species in respect of what it is.

The third definition of species, however, has been gathered in a complete account and demonstrates the force and nature of species itself. For it says that species is what is predicated in respect of what it is of several things differing in number. This definition ought also to have been made perfectly clear from the preceding account of genus.

But I shall explain it only as far as corrected brevity permits. First, a few things must be said about genera and species themselves.

Since there are certain genera that have species and can themselves be species of other genera, there is no doubt that they function in a twofold relation of comparison: in relation to some things they are called species, and in relation to others genera. But if we examine the matter along a single thread and order, and, whenever a genus of some thing has been found, seek another genus of that genus, and then another and another, the inquiry will again become inexplicable and endless if there is nothing at which intellect and reason can come to rest.

Since, however, there are many foundations of knowledge that cannot be brought to an end by the mind if it proceeds indefinitely, we must necessarily say that, in ascending, we can reach something above which, although it is itself a genus of other things, we cannot find another genus. This is called the first genus, the greater genus, or the most general genus.

If, in the case of genus, our ascent comes to a halt at some point, there is likewise no doubt that, in descending, we again come to a kind of limit at a fixed endpoint among species. When we have descended through species and reached that species which has no species beneath it, we call it the last species, the greater species, or the most specific species.

But if a species contained several things differing in species, it would rightly be called not a species but a genus. Since, however, it contains things not differing in species, it must contain pluralities that are similar to one another. If it contains a plurality, and what contains is always greater than what is contained, species will be predicated of that plurality.

Species, then, will be predicated of several things differing in number, in respect of what they are. When species is predicated of lower things, it indicates a higher species and substance. For when we ask, “What is Cicero?” the answer immediately given is “A man.”

Since, therefore, species has been defined in three ways, the first two definitions belong not only to species but also to subordinate species. For there is a species that is itself also a genus. Let the most general genus be substance; beneath it, body; beneath body, animate body; beneath animate body, animal; beneath animal, man; and beneath man, individuals. We shall examine this division more fully later; for now, this much is sufficient.

Substance, then, is the greater genus, and man the greater species, so that substance can never be a species, nor man a genus. Animate body or animal, however, is called a species in relation to what is above it and a genus in relation to what is below it.

If someone wishes to express animate body, animal, or man and says, “Species is what is placed beneath a genus and of which genus is predicated in respect of what it is,” this definition includes both the greater species—that is, man—and subordinate species, such as animate body or animal. Animate body, animal, and man are all placed beneath a genus, and “what it is” is predicated of all of them, as has been said.

If, however, someone wishes to indicate by a definition that species which is truly species—the most specific species, which is only a species and never a genus—he will define it as follows: “Species is what is predicated in respect of what it is of several things differing in number.”

This definition will never apply to subordinate species. For subordinate species can also be taken as genera if they are predicated of things beneath them. If they can be taken as genera, then, when taken as genera, they will be predicated not only of several things differing in number but also of things differing in species, since they are genera.

But this does not occur in the greater species: it is never predicated of things differing in species. Therefore this later definition belongs solely to the greater species, and it excludes and rejects the other subordinate species. Porphyry demonstrates this as follows:

> This will become clearer from what we are saying if expressed in this way: In all the categories there are certain greater genera and greater species, and there are other intermediate terms. The greater genera are those above which no other genus can be found. The greater species are those beneath which no species is found. The intervals between them contain both genera and species, each being compared with what is above and below it, so that it is called a genus in relation to one and a species in relation to the other.

“There are,” he says, “certain things whose genera cannot be found, and these are rightly called greater genera, since nothing greater than them can be found. For if these are genera—and a genus is greater than everything placed beneath it—then, if they have no genus, nothing greater than them can be found. Since nothing greater than them can be found, they are rightly called greater genera.

“There are also certain other things that are called greater species, beneath which no other species is placed. For that species appears greater, more complete, and truly a species which is never a genus than one which can at some time be a genus. If the truer species is the one that is only a species and never a genus, it is rightly called the greater species.

“Thus the interval between the greater species and the greater genus is filled by subordinate genera and subordinate species. We call all those things subordinate which, in relation to what is above them, are taken as species, and, in relation to what is below them, as genera. This is because, if you arrange all things in relation to what is below them, they are genera; if in relation to what is above them, they are species; and if you relate them both to what is above and to what is below, they are found to be both genera and species.

“For this reason they are called subordinate genera and species: arranged in a kind of sequence and order toward what is below, they are recognized as genera, and toward what is above, as species.”

Yet they can be genera and species in such a way that what is a genus is not again placed beneath itself as a species. For if, as was shown earlier, a genus is greater than its species, there is no doubt that a greater thing cannot be placed beneath a lesser. Therefore he says that they are called a genus in relation to one thing and a species in relation to another, since it would in no way be appropriate for the same thing to be both genus and species in the same relation.

He gives an example of this so that what he says may be more readily understood. He makes the following division.

He places substance as the greater genus. Beneath substance are body and incorporeal substance. Beneath body are animate body and inanimate body. Beneath animate body are sentient animal and insentient animal, such as oysters or shellfish, sea urchins, trees, and other things of this kind, which possess the soul of life but not the capacity of sensation. Beneath animal are rational animal and irrational animal. Beneath rational animal are mortal and immortal. Beneath mortal is man. Beneath man are individual human beings—that is, individual bodies, namely Cicero and Virgil, and those who have already been divided into separate individuals.

Substance, therefore, which comes first, is taken as the greater genus. It is solely a genus and not also a species, because no higher genus is ever found above it. Man, on the other hand, is solely a species, since it contains no other species beneath it. Individual human beings differ not in species, as has been said, but in number.

Body, which we previously placed beneath the genus substance, is taken as a species in relation to substance and as a genus in relation to animate body. Animate body is a species in relation to body and a genus in relation to animal. Animal appears as a species in relation to animate body and a genus in relation to rational animal. Rational animal is a genus in relation to mortal and a species in relation to animal. Mortal is a genus in relation to man and a species in relation to rational animal. Man, however, being above individuals, has nothing of the nature of genus; it is called solely a species.

If it is desired to transfer and apply this division to other things, the following principle must be observed: whatever has no genus that can be found above it should be called the greater genus; and whatever has no species beneath it—that is, whatever is placed above individuals—should be called the greater species.

For if something is a genus, it must be placed above things differing in species. But the greater species cannot be placed above things differing in species; otherwise it could never properly be called a species.

Therefore, just as the genus that is superior and has no genus above it is called the greater genus, so the species that has no species beneath it but only individuals is rightly called the greater species.

The things placed in the middle, however, do not have the same relation. Since they can be species, they are not greater genera; and since they can be genera, they are never predicated as greater species. In relation to the things above them they are species; in relation to the things beneath them they are placed in the position of genus.

Since all things have two possible forms—either genera are placed above them or species are placed beneath them—the two extremes, namely the most general genus and the most specific species, contain only one relation each. The former is only a genus and never appears as a species; the latter is only a species and is never called a genus.

The subordinate terms, however, which occupy the middle, have both forms—that is, both relations. As has been indicated repeatedly, they possess both, in a certain way, the parentage of genus and the derivation of species.

Nor should it perhaps disturb us that the most specific species has something beneath it. Man, although it is the greater species, has individual human beings beneath it. Although it is above individuals, it never changes the form of its specificity. Since it has beneath it individuals that it contains, and since those individuals belong to one species and do not differ from one another by any property of substance, it is called the species of the individuals it contains. Thus man is called a species of animal because it is contained under animal, and it is the species of individual human beings because it contains those who will never differ from one another in species.

The definition, therefore, of the greater genera and greater species is as follows:

A greater genus is said to be that which is always a genus and never a species, and above which there is no genus. Again, a greater species is that which is always a species and never a genus, which is never divided into species, and which is predicated in respect of what it is of several things differing in number.

The other terms, as has often been said, can be both genera and species, depending on whether they are compared with what is above or what is below.

This point must be considered with the greatest care. Among different nations, in a lineage where some kinship is traced through blood, the peoples of different relationships can be led back to a single head of the lineage. Since the Romans are descended from Romulus, Romulus from Mars, and Mars from Jupiter, the lineage of the Romans can be traced back to Jupiter.

Likewise, since the Athenians are descended from Minerva, and Minerva from Jupiter, the lineage of the Athenians can be traced back to the same Jupiter as its origin. Similarly, since the Persians are descended from the Sun, and the Sun from Jupiter, the Persians too can be led back to the same Jupiter as their proper origin.

Thus very different peoples can be raised to a single kinship. The same does not occur with species and genera. Different genera can never be brought together beneath one genus.

Aristotle established ten categories of the first genera, which, like a kind of fountain, poured forth upon all the lower things a certain origin and lineage. Since these genera are the most general, and no higher genus can be found above them, they cannot be reduced to one genus.

If the ten first genera cannot be reduced to one genus, neither can the things beneath those genera—namely, their species and subordinate genera—ever be brought under one genus. For if their first genera cannot be led back to one superior genus, there is no doubt that the things beneath them will not permit themselves to be controlled and contained by one genus.

If substance, quality, quantity, and the other categories cannot be placed beneath some other common genus, since they themselves are the greater genera, neither can anything that belongs to substance—that is, anything beneath the same genus, such as animal or man—or anything belonging to quality or quantity be brought under some common genus.

A genus can never be found that, by a solitary and proper act of understanding, could contain these ten genera within itself as species.

Someone might object: “If all these ten genera truly subsist, can they not in some way be called substances or beings?” For this expression is a grammatical inflection from *esse*, “to be,” and has been formed through an abuse of the participle because of the narrowness and compression of the Latin language.

These things, then, can be called beings, as has been said. And *ens* itself—that is, “being”—may perhaps appear to be their genus, but falsely. For all things that are named equivocally with respect to one another never share the containment of one and the same genus. Since their substances differ, there is no doubt that the definition of the genus itself will also differ.

When these things are called beings, they are predicated not univocally but equivocally. Substance is a being, and quality is likewise a being. If someone were to give the account and definition of substance and of quality, the same account could not apply to both. It is therefore clear that substance and quality are predicated equivocally, not univocally.

But if they are predicated equivocally, they cannot be placed at the source of one and the same genus. There is therefore no single genus among genera and species that can control and contain within itself diverse genera of things.

Then Fabius said: “You have treated all these matters abundantly, and they have been rehearsed frequently throughout this discussion. But proceed to what follows.”

“I shall,” I said. “For I think the following comes next.”

Aristotle therefore established ten genera in the Categories, which are the greater genera. The things that are the greater species, however, are always very numerous, though not infinite in number. The individuals beneath the greater species, on the other hand, are always infinite.

He means that there are far more species than genera. For a genus has very many species beneath it. Since the ten genera are the first genera of all things, the most specific species are not merely ten but more than ten, though they are not infinite.

The individuals beneath the greater species, however, are infinite, and their entirety can never be grasped by any knowledge. For what is infinite cannot be enclosed within any limit of knowledge.

Therefore, every division and every science of ours should descend from the greater genera through the subordinate genera down to the greater species. By remaining there, we can receive and retain a complete knowledge of what is above. But if someone wishes to comprehend individuals through knowledge and learning, he labors in vain.

We are therefore instructed to proceed from the greater genera through the intermediate divisions down to the greater species, so that, by dividing the subordinate genera with specific differences, we descend from the greater genera to the greater species.

Specific differences are those that disclose any given species. They disclose species in the following way. If someone begins with substance, places body beneath substance, animate body beneath body, animal beneath animate body, rational animal beneath animal, and mortal beneath rational animal, and places all these species of substance together with their differences, the species of man will be formed.

For animate body is a difference from inanimate body. Animal, in turn, is a difference from insentient things; rational is a difference from irrational; and mortal is a difference from immortal things. When all these are joined together, they disclose one species, namely man.

When you say “animate body,” “rational animal,” and “mortal”—differences that have been placed beneath one another in subordinate order—you have demonstrated man.

There are also other differences of the following kind, as when one says “an animal capable of rhetoric,” since only man can be an orator. But this is not a specific difference, nor does it complete the substance and nature of man; it merely indicates a particular art and branch of knowledge.

The differences and species that are useful in divisions are therefore those from which the thing called the greater species is formed. This is called a specific difference because it can produce the greater species.

Once the descent has reached the greater species, the individuals beneath the greater species must be left aside, and no knowledge of them should be sought. For they are not only infinite, but whatever they contain within themselves also becomes infinite.

Rhetoric, for example, is a species. But when it is distributed among individual human beings, it becomes divided among individuals and thereby becomes both particular and infinite. For if all the rhetors who exist or have existed were counted, there would never be an end to this enumeration, especially since individual human beings could continue to become rhetors throughout infinitely extended future time.

Then Fabius said: “So this was what he meant when he said:

> Moreover, when either arts or disciplines have begun to exist as individuals in separate human beings, they cannot at all acquire or possess an account by which they may be comprehended.”

And I: “This,” I said, “is what happens when arts or disciplines, which were previously gathered together as one within their species, come to individuals—that is, when they are dispersed through individual human beings into an infinite and innumerable multitude. [Col. 0045A] This occurs because the same principle is at work which Porphyry himself did not fail to state. For a genus, although one, is productive of many species. Many species are found under one genus because the species separate and disperse among many things the genus from which they flow. The genus, however, gathers together many things, just as it is itself divided again by many species.

“For human being, crow, and horse, which are species, are equally animals insofar as they fall under ‘animal.’ The name ‘animal’ thus contains all its species within itself. And if the name ‘animal’ applies to human being, crow, and horse, there is no doubt that the genus which contains these things under itself is divided and multiplied by the species into which it is separated. The genus therefore gathers species [Col. 0045B] into itself, while the species by their own nature disperse the genus itself.

“The genus is therefore collective of its species and, in a certain way, unifying. The species, divided from the genus, are in a certain way multiplicative. Accordingly, whoever ascends to the higher genera gathers and unifies the whole multitude of species through the genera. But when one descends from the higher genera to the lower species, every unity of the superior genera is separated into species with many branches and divisions.

“What he means by ‘the multitude must be grasped’ is equivalent to saying, ‘the multitude must be made’: for when you divide a genus into species, you take those species to be many, although you yourself have made them so. The species likewise do not differ from this unifying and, in a certain way, collecting function of the genus. For they too bring the infinity of individuals back to one [Col. 0045C] form.

“The species of individual human beings, which is ‘human being,’ is collective in this way. For all individual human beings, in relation to the species ‘human being,’ are one human being—that is, the first species which contains and constrains us. Yet the species itself is divided and split among us many. Everything that is singular and individual divides that from which it arises. Everything that is not singular and individual, but can be divided, does not by itself divide what is beneath it more than it gathers it.

“Once these matters have been clarified, it is evident both that a genus is a genus of many species and that a species constrains many individuals beneath it. For if things that are lower disperse, divide, and scatter into a multitude, there is no doubt that superior things are always fewer than inferior ones.

“The categories, however, which are predicated one of another or related to one another, are arranged as follows. Every thing will be either greater, lesser, or equal to another. Everything that is greater can be predicated of what is lesser. Thus, since ‘animal’ is greater than ‘human being,’ ‘animal’ can be predicated of ‘human being’; but what is lesser is not predicated of what is greater.

“Since animal includes both human being and horse, if you wish to predicate ‘animal’ of ‘human being,’ this predication is valid only to the extent that animal includes human being as one of its parts. Now reverse the statement and say that ‘animal is that which is human being.’ Animal is human being only to the extent that it is the part of animal which contains the species ‘human being.’ In those other parts of animal which contain something other than the species ‘human being,’ the designation ‘human being’ does not apply. For if you say ‘animal—that is, what is human being,’ the part in which animal is horse will not be human being; therefore the terms are not universally convertible.

“For if you say, ‘Every human being is an animal,’ that is true. If you say, ‘Every animal is a human being,’ that is false.

“If greater things are predicated of lesser things because every greater thing contains the lesser within itself, while lesser things are not predicated of greater things because greater things exceed and, in a certain way, surpass the definition of the lesser, there is no doubt that things which are equal can be converted with one another.

“Things are equal when they are neither lesser nor greater; that is, when, if they are applied to any species, they belong to the whole of that species and to no other. Every human being is risible, and no other species can properly be called risible. Therefore, because these terms are equal, they are convertible. You may say: ‘What is a human being?’ ‘A risible being.’ ‘What is a risible being?’ ‘A human being.’ Likewise: ‘What is a neighing being?’ ‘A horse.’ ‘What is a horse?’ ‘A neighing being.’

“If greater things are always predicated of lesser things, the superior things must be genera, and all subordinate things must be lesser. And if all subordinate things are lesser, then, when someone descends through subdivision to the ultimate species, whatever genus is predicated of things immediately adjacent to it will also be predicated of subordinate things.

“Substance has, toward what lies below it, a genus immediately subordinate to it, namely body; while its species in relation to itself is body. Substance is therefore predicated of body. For if someone asks, ‘What is body?’ the answer is ‘substance.’ Beneath body is animate body, and beneath animate body is animal.

“Since substance is predicated of body because it is superior to body, substance must also be superior to everything to which body is superior. If body is predicated of animate body and of animal, substance will likewise be predicated of animate body and of animal. Thus whatever is superior is predicated not only of things immediately beneath it but also of things much farther below.

“For if superior things are greater than the species immediately adjacent to them, they will be much greater than those things of which those adjacent species are themselves greater. Therefore, wherever a species is predicated, the genus of that species will also be predicated. If one species is greater than something, the genus of that species will be much greater than the thing of which the species is greater. It will therefore be predicated of it in the same way in which the species was previously predicated.

“And if this is so, there is no doubt that the genus of that genus, which could be predicated of the thing of which the species was predicated, can also be predicated of that of which both the species and the genus of the species were predicated. If someone says that Cicero is a human being, and animal is the genus of human being, it is not absurd to predicate animal of Cicero. Since substance is the genus of animal itself, it is likewise not improper to predicate substance of Cicero. For superior things are predicated of inferior things; and if inferior things have still other things beneath them, the first genus will also apply to those lower things, and may properly be predicated of them.

“Thus a species is predicated of an individual as a more special term; the highest genus is predicated of all subordinate things and of the most special species. For substance is predicated equally of body, animate body, sensible body, rational animal, mortal being, and human being. The highest genus is also predicated of their individuals, as has been said: Cicero, for example, may be called a substance.

“A species, however, is predicated of nothing except individuals, as stated above; and individuals themselves are predicated of nothing except themselves, that is, of their own individual instances. The nature of individuals is that the properties belonging to individuals remain in those individual beings alone and are transferred to no others; therefore they are predicated of no others.

“Whatever property Cicero may possess will never belong to Cato, Brutus, or Catullus. But the properties of human being—namely rational, mortal, and risible—can belong to many and to all individuals. Every human being, considered individually, is rational, mortal, sensible, and risible. Therefore those things whose properties can belong to others can be predicated of others.

“But things whose property does not belong to others, except to themselves individually, cannot be predicated individually of anything other than themselves.

“We must therefore repeat that every individual is contained by a species, while the species itself is constrained by a genus. The highest genus is, as it were, the single whole body of all things, and is never a part. An individual, however, is always a part and never a whole.

“A species is rightly called both a part and a whole: it is a part in relation to the genus and a whole in relation to individuals. For it divides the genus, as has been said, and gathers individuals.

“Yet a species is a part of something else—namely, of a genus—but it is not the whole of a part; it is the whole of parts. For the genus is one, while the species of one thing—that is, the species of one genus—are many, and each species is a part.

“And since individuals are many and infinite under one species, which gathers those individuals, that species is not the whole of one thing—that is, it is not the whole of a part—but the whole of many things, that is, of parts. For there are many individual parts beneath it, and their whole is called the species, namely ‘human being.’

“But enough has been said about genus and species. And since they are calling us to the morning greetings, let us transfer what remains to the coming watches of the night.”

## SECOND DIALOGUE

[Col. 0047]

## ON DIFFERENCE

[Col. 0047B]

“Many grave and splendid things have been granted to us by nature our mother, as well as to the other living creatures. She has cultivated us as a kind of benevolent artisan of humanity, first granting us minds and reason for reckoning and reflection, and afterward, once reason had been discovered, conferring speech upon us. It is as though she had wished and commanded us to differ from beasts not through the senses of the body but through the divinity of the mind.

“When the mind has joined itself to itself and has not departed from the vitality of its own nature, then, just as it is of an eternal kind, so it also makes its fame among posterity and its life of glory equal to the most infinite stretches of time. But if the mind allows itself to become subject to the body through depraved desires and permits itself to be ruined and corrupted, it follows the nature of the body. For nothing of its vitality remains after the body when all its labor and study have been expended upon bodily things and upon the body.

“Therefore we must take care to make ourselves better and more diligent—not in that respect in which we can differ in nothing from cattle, but in that by which, through the likeness of heavenly virtues, we may deserve the glory of eternity through distinguished deeds and words.

“But enough of this for another time; now I shall return to my subject.

“When the customary night’s study and wakefulness had come around again, Fabius—captivated, I believe, by the subtlety of the previous discussion, or by that eagerness and desire for learning and hearing which he possessed—rose more attentively than ever and came to me. After we had exchanged greetings, he asked me to continue the work I had promised.

“‘I shall do so willingly,’ I said, ‘since there is nothing in life that I would rather do, and since your eagerness increases this pleasure for me, which is exceedingly gratifying. Since yesterday’s discussion explained species, I have decided that the beginning of the next exposition should be taken from the following discussion of difference.’

“Then Fabius said: ‘You explained genera and species very fully during last night’s watches. But, as I hear, the treatment of differences is subtler and more refined.’

“‘Not without reason,’ I replied, ‘for differences, understood in various ways, will also possess various powers. At one time they will be genera, at another species, and at another differences; but this will be demonstrated later. For now, the text is as follows, as I believe:

> Every difference is spoken of both commonly, properly, and most properly.

“He also indicates that difference is called by many names. He says that difference occurs in these three ways: when differences are common, proper, or most proper.

“Common differences are those by which we differ either from everyone else or from ourselves. Sitting, walking, and standing are differences. If you walk while I sit, we differ in the very posture and activity of walking. Likewise, if I am sitting now but later walk, I will differ from myself by a common difference.

“Proper differences are those which depict the form of each individual through some natural property—for example, if someone has gray eyes or curly hair. Such features are proper to each individual human being, with which that person is born.

“Most proper differences are those which remain in the substance itself and alter the whole species through their description and difference, as rationality or mortality is a difference of human being.

“The common and proper differences make individuals within the same species differ from one another: the former through common differences, the latter through proper differences. Most proper differences, however, alter the whole nature and substance of any species and separate and distinguish it from other species.

“Since common and proper differences do not alter the species but merely make its form and condition differ in a certain way, they are said to make something ‘altered’—that is, not to make it wholly other, not to transform it completely, but in a certain way to produce difference and distance. Therefore they are not called ‘making another,’ that is, transforming, but rather ‘making something altered,’ that is, not making it wholly other.

“The third kind, namely the most proper difference, makes something other because it is substantial and inserted into the nature of the species itself. For although human being and horse had one substance insofar as they were animals, the arrival of rationality completely separated the species and made it fundamentally other.

“Thus common and proper differences are called ‘making something altered,’ whereas most proper differences are called ‘making something other.’

“It is therefore established that some differences make something other, while others make something altered. Those which make something other are substantial; they change the whole nature and species and are called specific differences. For they can constitute any species, separate it from all others, and compose its form and nature.

“If you posit ‘mortal’ and ‘rational’ as differences and add them to animal, there is no doubt that, when you produce the species ‘human being,’ they perfect that species. They are therefore called specific because they change the nature and constitute the substance of whatever species is concerned.

“The other differences produce nothing except something altered, since one thing differs from another either through some property of form or through some condition or disposition relating to action.

“Only that most proper difference which we call specific can properly be used in the division of a genus. The others contribute nothing to substance but serve only to mark, in a certain way, difference and distance within a similarity of the same kind. You can find nothing in them except alteration, since they do not constitute species but distinguish species already constituted and completed through their own properties.

“He then says:

> Returning now to what was said above, we must state that some differences are separable and others inseparable.

“This introduces another division. Earlier he separated difference into three parts, and afterward gathered those three into only two classes, saying that some make something other and others make something altered. Now a third division is again made of those original three. He says that some are separable and others inseparable.

“Just as in the earlier division two kinds—common and proper—made something altered, while the single most proper kind remained as the one that made something other, so now also in the division into separable and inseparable: only the common difference is separable; the other two are inseparable. Blindness of the eyes, blond hair, and bodily height are proper differences; rationality and mortality are most proper differences. These can never be separated from the species ‘human being.’

“Sitting and running, which are common differences, are separated from individuals and then added again.

“Among inseparable differences, some arise in themselves and others accidentally. Those which arise in themselves flow from most proper differences; those which arise accidentally are poured forth from proper differences alone. An inseparable accident is whatever befalls each species through an inseparable proper difference.

“Although proper and most proper differences are inseparable, they never change the superior form and nature. The most proper always produces something other; the proper always produces only something altered.

“Moreover, inseparable proper differences may belong to someone to a greater or lesser degree. Inseparable most proper differences neither increase through an accumulation of intensity nor diminish through reduction. One person may be born taller, another darker, another with thinner hair, and another with fairer hair; these are inseparable proper differences.

“But the most proper difference—namely rationality—admits neither more nor less. All human beings, insofar as they are human beings, are equally rational and mortal. For if a genus could be more or less a genus, differences too could increase through intensity or decrease through diminution. But animal is not more a genus for human being than for horse, nor more for horse than for other creatures; it is equally the genus of all its subjects.

“Thus the differences of species, which we call specific differences, do not admit more or less. For if the definition of human being is ‘rational, mortal animal,’ and this is likewise the definition of each individual human being, there is no doubt that the definition always applies equally to every individual human being and fits none more or less than another.

“And if this is so, the parts of the whole definition, which are the differences, will likewise be such that they apply to no one more or less, but always equally and appropriately. The parts of this definition are ‘rational’ and ‘mortal.’ Rational and mortal, therefore, which are most proper differences, do not admit more or less.

“From this division of separable and inseparable differences, then, we consider differences in three ways. They are either separable or inseparable; and inseparable differences are either in themselves or accidental.

“Those which arise in themselves are of two kinds: some divide the genus, while others shape and constitute the species. The former matter has already been discussed. We must now discuss those which divide the genus and constitute the species.

“Whenever a genus is divided into species, if those species are subdivided again and one descends from the higher genera through subordinate genera to the highest species, there will be a twofold and double division. For if you consider contrary differences, the division is one of genera; if you consider subordinate genera, it is the constitution of species.

“If we divide genus—that is, substance—as it was already divided in the discussion of species, then substance will be the highest term, followed by animate and inanimate body; beneath animate body, sensible and insensible; beneath sensible body, that is, animal, rational and irrational; beneath rational, mortal and immortal.

“These differences are species if they are considered in opposition to one another in the division, and they divide the genus in this way. Since we placed animate body and inanimate body beneath substance, if you consider animate body in opposition to inanimate body, you have divided substance.

“But if you consider subordinate genera within these differences, you will constitute a species. If you look at animate body and sensible body, which is beneath it, you have considered animal. Likewise, if you take rational difference in opposition to irrational difference, you have divided the genus common to both, namely animal.

“If, however, you take rational difference and mortal difference in the same sequence, you have unquestionably indicated the species ‘human being.’ Thus, when taken in one way, these differences become divisions of the genus—that is, differences dividing genera. When taken in another way, they become constitutive of species, that is, differences which disclose and constitute species.

[Col. 0051B]

> If you consider contrary differences, you will divide the genus; but if you consider subordinate differences, you will constitute the species.

“The power of differences, both separable and inseparable, retains the other three things—genus, species, and accident—in such a way that, when their comparison is altered, these same things are themselves also altered.

“If you consider the differences rational and mortal in opposition to irrational and immortal, they are differences dividing a genus. But if you compare those same differences, rational and mortal, with what is superior, they will be species of the animal which contains them.

“If you consider rational and mortal in relation to their subject, human being, you will contemplate genera and constitutive differences of it.

“But from those other inseparable differences, namely the proper ones, arise the differences of inseparable accidents. Blindness of the eyes, curvature of the nose, and other such features are inseparable accidents. The same applies to separable accidents, that is, common differences. Staying awake, sleeping, running, and sitting are separable accidents.

“He says:

> Thus substance has been composed above all things, and its divisible differences are animate and inanimate.

“Here he displays contrary differences in species. When he says:

> This difference, animate and sensible, joined to substance will complete animal,

“he displays constitutive differences of species. Thus, being understood in various ways, differences have acquired various powers and forms.

“Both divisible and constitutive differences are called specific, and in divisions of genera and in definitions they alone are useful. The other inseparable differences that arise accidentally are useless, and still more useless are those formed by separable difference and distinction.

“Those who have treated the division of differences declare that specific differences are such as those by which species possess something in excess of their genus. This must be explained briefly.

“There is a controversy over whether the genus contains within itself the differences of its species or not. For example, animal contains beneath itself the species rational and irrational, namely human being and, for example, horse. The question is whether animal possesses both rationality and irrationality—that is, the differences of human being and horse by which the species placed beneath animal differ from one another.

“If animal, which is the genus, is neither rational nor irrational, then the species placed beneath it will not possess these differences. For if the genus does not possess these differences, from where will the species obtain the differences by which they differ from one another?

“But if someone says that these differences are present in the genus—for species would not have differences unless the genus had them first—this entails an even greater difficulty. Since the species placed under a genus are equal, and human being and horse are equally placed under the genus animal, neither human being precedes horse nor horse human being; both are equally called species of animal.

“Therefore, if rational and irrational are equally under the same genus, they will also exist at the same time. And if they exist at the same time and the genus possesses these differences—so that the genus by its own nature, namely animal, is rational and irrational—there is no doubt that the same thing would substantially retain two contraries at one time. This cannot happen.

“What, then, are we to say? We must say that the genus does not possess these differences in actuality—the term the Greeks call ἐνέργεια, ‘actuality.’ Yet it is not devoid of them in potentiality, since it gives rise to these very differences in its species.

“The distinction between actuality and potentiality must be explained more precisely. The difference between actuality and potentiality is like the difference between a laughing human being and one who can laugh but is not laughing. The former performs the act itself; the latter merely has the power and does not perform it.

“The same applies to animal. Human being is rational in actuality. Human being is always rational and nothing else; horse is always irrational, and its irrationality exists in actuality. But animal itself does not perform rationality or irrationality, nor are these differences present in it in actuality; they are present in it in potentiality. For animal can produce from itself both rational and irrational species.

“Since species contain differences in actuality, while the genus contains them in potentiality, species are rightly said to possess differences in excess of their genus. What the genus can do—that is, produce differences—the species not only can do but actually do. For the differences are placed and formed within the species themselves.

“There is another definition of difference, which says that difference is what is predicated of many species in respect of what kind of thing they are.

“Difference can be predicated of many things. ‘Rational,’ for example, is predicated of human being: human being is rational. It is also predicated of God: God is called rational, but not in respect of what God is, rather in respect of what kind of thing God is.

“For if someone asks what kind of human being he is, the immediate answer is ‘rational.’ If you ask what kind of being God is, you may likewise say, without absurdity, ‘rational.’

“In the same way irrationality is predicated of horse, ox, fish, and bird. If you ask what kind all these are, they are called irrational.

“This, then, is a good and correct definition: difference is that which is predicated of many things differing in species in respect of what kind of thing they are. The same account applies to mortal and to the other differences.

“What follows is a very difficult passage, made obscure more by Victorinus the translator than by Porphyry, who proposed it. He says that every corporeal thing consists of matter and form.

“If you speak of a statue, for example, the statue consists of bronze and the shape which its maker imposed upon it. Bronze is the matter from which it is made; the shape—that is, the form—is what gives form to the bronze. If you form a human being from bronze and the shape of a human being, the shape will be the form of the human being, while the bronze will be its matter.

“The same applies to genus. The genus is taken in the manner of matter, while the difference is taken in the manner of form. For just as every thing consists of matter and form, so every species consists of genus and difference.

“Genus is to human being as bronze is to a statue. Difference is to human being as the shape from which the bronze has been fashioned is to the statue. Just as from some shape fashioned out of bronze comes the species of whatever statue it may be, so, when difference—that is, rationality—comes to genus, namely animal, the species ‘human being’ is formed.

“These things are therefore proportional to one another.

“Proportion is the comparison of one thing with another related thing in a similar relation. If, for example, you compare two with four, the proportion is double. If you compare twenty with forty, the proportion is likewise double. Four is therefore to two in the same proportion as forty is to twenty, since both are a double comparison of numbers.

“Thus the proportion—that is, the comparison—between matter and form is the same as the proportion between genus and difference; and these four things are proportional to one another. For just as the species of any formation is formed from matter and shape, so the species of any animate or inanimate thing is formed from genus and differences. Victorinus seems to have understood this less adequately.

“For what Porphyry called ἀνάλογον—that is, ‘proportional’—he understood as though it were ἄλογον, meaning ‘irrational.’ Therefore, in the passage where the text reads:

> For all things consist of form and matter, and form itself is irrational,

“the word ‘irrational’ must be removed.

“Likewise, a little farther below, where it reads:

> Every genus is similar to matter and consists irrationally,

“the word ‘irrational’ must be removed and ‘proportionally’ inserted, so that the passage reads: ‘and it consists proportionally.’

“For the proportion of shape to matter in producing the form of any corporeal thing is the same as the proportion of difference to genus in producing the species of any animate or inanimate thing.

“Another definition follows, of this kind:

> They say that difference is what can separate whatever falls under the same genus.

“And they are right. Since human being and horse fall under the same genus, because both are animals, when rational or irrational comes in, it divides and distinguishes horse and human being, which are under the same genus.

“Those differences, then, are able to separate things that fall under the same genus.

“There is another definition:

> Differences are that by which each thing differs from another.

“Human being and horse differ through the differences rational and irrational, although they are one in relation to their genus. This is what he says:

> Difference is that by which individuals differ, because the genus exists in itself, and those things which are rational—that is, we—and those things which are irrational.

“Human being, horse, and bird are all one genus, namely animal. Animal is the genus of all these.

“But if, in the passage where it says ‘because the genus exists in itself,’ you alter the wording and make it read ‘those which are animals in themselves,’ the meaning will be clearer. Here ‘genus’ has been improperly used in place of ‘animal,’ and the order would be:

> Difference is that by which individuals differ, namely those things which are animals in themselves, and those which are rational are animals—that is, we—and those which are irrational are animals.

“If the passage were read in this way, there would be no error at all. As it stands, the word ‘genus’ must be understood as being used in place of ‘animal.’

“Likewise, gods and human beings are both rational, yet they differ and are distinguished by the addition of mortality.

“Thus difference is that by which individuals differ. But this must not be understood without qualification. Only those differences should be considered of this kind which contribute to substance and to what a thing is, and which can be parts of the substance of a species.

“If horse and human being, whose genus is one—animal—differ from one another through the qualities rational and irrational, nevertheless rationality and irrationality are present in the substance of the species themselves in the following way. Horse cannot exist without irrationality, nor human being without rationality.

“Therefore these differences contribute to the being of the species to which they belong, and they are parts of its substance. Since human being consists of these differences—namely rational and mortal—the sole presence of rational or mortal is a part of the substance of human being. For if both together make one human being, there is no doubt that each of them must be considered a part contributing to the production of the substance of human being.

“Therefore any differences which do not contribute to being and are not parts of the substance of a species cannot be called specific differences, even if only one species possesses them.

“If human being sails, for example, he may be called a ‘sailing animal.’ But sailing does not enter into the substance of human being. Human being does not subsist because he sails, even though no other animal may possess this ability—that is, even though no other animal may be able to sail.

“The same applies to being a rhetorician or grammarian. We do not regard as specific those differences which do not contribute to being but merely indicate some art or knowledge, even if a particular species of animal alone possesses one of them.

“Therefore, whenever we state the definition that difference is that by which individuals differ, we must understand it to signify the difference which contributes to being and which is a part of the substance of some species. Those which do not contribute to being, although they belong to particular individuals, must not be included among this kind of differences.

“But since we have discussed difference, let us explain the property.”

Then Fabius said: “As I understand it, that follows.”

## ON PROPERTY

“Property is spoken of in four ways. It is called property when it belongs to one species, even if it does not belong to all its members.”

And I said: “Then properties are divided in four ways. For there is a property that happens to belong to one species, even if not to all its members, such as being a rhetorician, geometer, or grammarian. All these belong only to one species, namely the human species, [Col. 0055A] though not to everyone. For not all human beings are grammarians, rhetoricians, or geometers. Therefore this is called a property because it belongs to one species, even if not to all its members.

“There is also another property that belongs to all members, though not to that species alone. Being two-footed belongs to every human being. For every human being is two-footed; but being two-footed does not belong only to the human species, since it also belongs to birds.

“And there is a third property, which belongs to all members, to that species alone, and at some particular time—for example, growing pubic hair at puberty and becoming gray in old age. For this happens to all human beings, and to no other species except the human species, and at a particular time: a definite period has been established for adolescents to reach puberty and for the elderly to become gray-haired. For no one reaches puberty at the age of six or seven, or becomes gray at twenty, unless something new should happen [Col. 0055B] to him.

“The fourth property is that which belongs to one species, to all the individuals under that species, and at all times. For being capable of laughter belongs only to one species, namely the human species, and to all the individuals under that species, and at all times. For there has never been a time when any human being was unable to laugh. But by ‘capable of laughter’ I mean by potentiality, not by actuality. For even if a human being does not laugh, nevertheless, because he can laugh, he is called capable of laughter.

“These are complete and true properties: those that belong to one species, to all its members, and at all times. For these can be converted with their species.
