If you ask, ‘What is a human being?’ you may answer, ‘A being capable of laughter.’ If you ask what a being capable of laughter is, you will predicate ‘human being.’ But the other properties—being two-footed or being a grammarian—are indeed properties, but they cannot be converted. For a grammarian is always a human being, but a human being is not always a grammarian. Conversely, a human being is always two-footed, but not every two-footed creature is a human being.

“Being capable of neighing is similarly more properly a property of the horse. For this property can likewise be converted with its species. If you ask what a horse is, you will answer, ‘A being capable of neighing.’ If you ask what a being capable of neighing is, ‘Horse’ will be predicated.

“But since we have spoken of properties, let the following discussion concern accidents.”

Then Fabius said: “Porphyry defines an accident as follows.”

## ON THE ACCIDENT

“An accident is that which can be added or removed without the destruction of that in which it exists.”

This seems to mean that an accident is something without which the thing to which it belongs can nevertheless exist. For example, if someone’s face should happen to become red through some chance occurrence, when the redness departs the face remains unharmed, just as it was not harmed when the redness appeared.

An accident is therefore divided into separable and inseparable. A separable accident is, for example, sitting or walking. An inseparable accident is, for example, when one says “a black crow” or “a white swan”; these accidents cannot be separated.

A question nevertheless arises: whether the preceding definition is true and includes the name of every accident. Since there are, as he himself says, certain inseparable accidents, this definition seems unable to apply to them. For if they cannot be separated, the definition that says “an accident is that which can be added or removed without the destruction of that in which it exists” is not true of them. Since they are inseparable, they cannot be removed.

But this very difficult question is resolved as follows: this definition of accidents is given in terms of potentiality, not actuality, and of conception, not reality. It is not because an Ethiopian or a crow actually loses its color, but because, in our conception, it can exist without that color. For it is true that black color never leaves an Ethiopian or a crow. But if someone conceives that the Ethiopian or crow could lose this color, then only the color of the feathers would change in the crow, and the bird would be white in color while retaining the species and form of a crow, if one conceives this possibility. In the case of a human being—that is, an Ethiopian—once the black color had been lost, his species would be white, just as that of other human beings. Thus this is not called an accident because it actually occurs, but because, if it could occur, the substance receiving this accident would not perish. [Col. 0056B]

He demonstrates this in the following way:

“An understanding may also be supplied of a white crow and of an Ethiopian, so that the crow, having lost its color, remains in the nature of its proper substance, destined to lose its color without the destruction of that in which the color existed.”

For nothing relevant to the species prevents an Ethiopian or a crow from remaining in the nature of its proper substance after losing its color.

There is another definition, which is as follows:

“An accident is that which can belong or not belong to something.”

For whatever does not become part of a substance, we call an accident—that is, something not implanted in the substance but coming from outside. Things that can either belong or not belong are therefore called accidents, because they are not included in the account of the substance. If they were included in the account of the substance, they could never fail to exist; and if they did not exist, they could never come to exist. For since, for example, rationality belongs to the substance of a human being, a human being can never become irrational, because irrationality is not in the substance of a human being.

From this comes another definition:

“An accident is that which is neither a genus, nor a species, nor a difference, nor a property.”

Since genus, species, difference, and property belong to substance and display the substance of whatever thing is in question, whatever is none of these is rightly predicated as an accident.

Having thus completed and clarified the subjects he proposed—that is, genus, species, properties, differences, and accidents—he now proceeds to those features that are common to all of them and to the ways in which they differ.

## ON WHAT IS COMMON TO GENUS, DIFFERENCE, SPECIES, PROPERTY, AND ACCIDENT

First he explains what they have in common with one another, and afterward the features belonging to each individually. He says that what they all have in common is that they are predicated of several things.

A genus is predicated of species and individuals; in the same way, a difference is predicated of species and individuals. A property is also predicated of a species and of individuals. A species, however, is predicated only of individuals.

For genus—for example, animal—is predicated of horses, human beings, oxen, and dogs, that is, of species. [Col. 0057A] It is also predicated of the individuals contained under those species. For just as the species dog, horse, and human being are animals, so each individual horse or human being is predicated as an animal.

Differences are predicated of species and individuals in the following way. Human being and horse are species. But “rational” is predicated as a difference of the species human being, and in the same way of Cicero. Since an individual falls under the species human being, Cicero himself is also called rational.

A property is predicated of a species when one says that the species human being is capable of laughter; and when one says that Cicero is capable of laughter, since Cicero is an individual, it is shown that a property is predicated of individuals.

A species is predicated only of its own individuals. For one asks, “What is Cicero?” and the answer is “A human being.” [Col. 0057B]

An accident is predicated of individuals and afterward of species. If someone says, “A human being is sitting”—which is a separable accident—then whoever sees a particular human being, that is, an individual, sitting, also predicates the same of the species, saying, “Cicero is sitting.” Cicero, however, is a human being; therefore, a human being is sitting.

In the same way, an inseparable accident is predicated of species and individuals.

Having completed the discussion of what all these have in common, he first explains the common features and differences of genus and difference.

## ON WHAT IS COMMON TO GENUS AND DIFFERENCE

First he says that genus and difference have in common that species are contained under both. The genus animal contains the species human being and horse. Moreover, rational, which is a difference, contains both human beings and gods. Irrational, which is a difference, contains horses, oxen, and birds.

But genus contains in such a way that it always contains more species than a difference does. For genus also contains the differences themselves. Genus—that is, animal—contains both the species under rational and those under irrational: it contains the species under rational and also those under irrational. But the difference rational does not contain irrational; it contains only human beings and gods. Genus therefore contains more than difference.

There is another common feature. If something is predicated of a genus in such a way that it is its genus, and is also predicated of the species under the genus of which it is predicated, then that thing is called a genus; and it is likewise predicated of the individuals under those species.

Animal is the genus of human being, and “animal” is predicated of animal as a genus of substance. For substance is the genus of animal. Thus the substance that is predicated as the genus of human being—that is, animal—is also predicated of human being itself: human being is called a substance. This genus of the genus is also predicated of individuals that are under the species. For Cicero, who is an individual under the species human being, is called a substance. [Col. 0057D]

The same applies to difference. If one difference is predicated of another difference so that it is understood as a difference, it will be predicated of the species under the difference of which it is predicated, and of the individuals under that species.

“Using reason” is predicated of the difference rational as a related difference. But rational is predicated of human being; therefore “using reason” will also be predicated of human being. “Using reason” is likewise predicated of Cicero, who is an individual under that species—namely, the species of which the difference rational is predicated, and of which the related difference “using reason” is predicated.

Thus genus and difference have this in common: things predicated of a genus as its genus are also predicated of the species under that genus and of their individuals; and things predicated of a difference as a difference are also predicated of the species under that difference and of their individuals.

There is another common feature: just as, when a genus is destroyed, its species are destroyed, so, when a difference is destroyed, the species under that difference are destroyed. If animal should perish, human being and horse would immediately perish. But if the difference rational should perish, gods and human beings would perish, and nothing capable of using reason would remain.

## ON THE PROPERTIES OF GENUS AND DIFFERENCE

After demonstrating their common features, he indicates their properties and differences. He says that the first difference is that by which genus differs not only from differences but also from species, properties, and accidents.

For genus is predicated of many more things than are difference, species, accident, or property. Genus—animal—is predicated of quadrupeds, bipeds, reptiles, that is, snakes, and swimming creatures, that is, fish. But quadruped, which differs from biped, is predicated only of those that have four feet, such as a horse or ox. It cannot be predicated of the other things—bipeds, reptiles, or swimming creatures—of which the genus is equally predicated.

Genus is also predicated of more things than species. Although human being is a species and is predicated only of individuals, human being is not predicated equally of a horse, ox, or dog. Animal, however, which is a genus, is predicated of many species—human being, horse, dog, and ox—and of all the individuals under them.

Genus exceeds property in the extent of its predication. Property always belongs to one species and is predicated of the individuals under that species. Genus, however, is predicated of many species and properties and of the individuals under them.

Genus is predicated of far more things than accidents. Although white may perhaps be an inseparable accident of one swan, animal is predicated not only of the swan but also of all animals, both white and non-white. An accident, however, is predicated only of those in which it is contained inseparably or separably. It is primarily predicated of individuals. It is therefore clear that genus is predicated of many more things than accidents are, since accidents are primarily predicated of individuals, whereas genera are predicated of individuals, species, and differences.

But now let us understand those differences by which genus is divided, not those by which species are formed.

The point is this: we have said that there are two forms of differences, some divisive and others constitutive. We called constitutive those which, placed under the same line and descending through subordinate genera, form and perfect a particular species, such as rational or mortal, which constitute the species human being. We called the others divisive: they divide a genus but do not form a species, such as rational and irrational, mortal and immortal.

The present discussion concerns those differences that divide a genus, not those that constitute a species. Those that divide a genus are treated among the proper class of differences; those that constitute a species are treated within the substance of species and genera.

Rational is the genus of mortal; mortal is the genus of human being; and these constitute the species. But rational and irrational are not species, nor are they genera. Mortal and immortal are likewise neither genera nor species. Therefore, since these retain the proper force of differences and cannot be genera or species of one another, let us now take up those differences in which, with respect to genus and species, there is no commonality.

There is also a difference between genus and difference. Genus is prior to its proper differences. If you remove the genus, you remove all the differences at once. If you remove animal, rational and irrational do not remain. But if you remove rational, animal remains.

Even if both differences are destroyed—rational and irrational—something can nevertheless be conceived as a living, sentient substance, namely animal. Thus, when genus is removed, it takes all the differences with it. When the differences are removed, they do not destroy genus with them, [Col. 0059C] because genus remains in conception: animal can be conceived apart from the differences, by grasping only its definition in the mind and saying that it is a living, sentient substance.

Things that are such that, when they themselves are destroyed, they destroy other things, but are not themselves destroyed when the others are destroyed, are prior to those things that can destroy them.

There is also another difference: genus is always predicated in answer to “What is it?”, as has been said, whereas difference is predicated in answer to “What sort of thing is it?” But this has been repeated frequently and should therefore be omitted here.

There is another difference: one genus is always assigned to every species. Human being has only one genus, being called animal; but several differences can be assigned to one species. Human being is rational, which is a difference, and mortal, which is likewise a difference, and sentient; by all these it differs from other things. For by being sentient it differs from non-sentient things, by being rational from irrational things, and by being mortal from immortal things.

There is also the difference mentioned above. Genus relates to species as matter, whereas difference relates to it as form. Just as a form, entering bronze as matter, produces a statue, so a difference entering animal—that is, genus—such as rational or irrational, produces the species human being or beast.

These, then, are the common features and properties of genus and difference that he has discussed. There may perhaps be others, but for the sake of brevity they must be passed over and omitted.

[Col. 0060A]

## ON WHAT IS COMMON TO GENUS AND SPECIES

Now the common features and properties of genus and species are discussed. He says that genus and species have in common being predicated of several things, as has been stated. Genus is predicated both of several species and of their individuals. Similarly, species is predicated of the many individuals under it.

Here, too, those species are meant that are species in the fuller sense. If subordinate species are meant, they will appear to be genera no less than species. For subordinate species are also genera, and it would be absurd and inappropriate to discuss here the common features and differences of genera among themselves. Let us therefore take only those species that are called species in the fuller sense.

There is another common feature: just as genus is prior to species, so species are prior to individuals. If you remove genus, you remove species. If you remove species, genera do not perish. But if you remove species, individuals die; if individuals perish, species remain.

There is another common feature between them: just as genus declares what the whole is, so does species. Whatever is rational or irrational is declared by genus to be an animal. For whatever is rational or irrational is said to be an animal; thus the whole is declared by genus as to what it is.

But what the whole diversity of human beings—that is, of individuals—is, is declared by species alone, when “human being” is said. For a Scythian, an Indian, and every individual thing whatsoever are all included under the single name human being, that is, the species.

## ON THE PROPERTIES OF GENUS AND SPECIES

Having explained the common features of genus and species, he proceeds to their properties and differences, saying:

“Genus and species differ in that genera contain species, whereas genera are never contained by their proper species.”

As has been said, in this discussion subordinate species must be disregarded and species in the fuller sense must be considered. Genus contains many species, one of all of them, and the whole in relation to all and each individually. If this is so, and genus is greater than each of its species and is therefore said to contain them, there is no doubt that the genera which contain species cannot themselves be contained by those species.

Moreover, all genera lie prior. [Col. 0060D] This seems to mean that all genera are prior to the species contained under them. Just as prime matter is prior to the thing that, entering matter, establishes and shapes its form, so genus is prior to the species that a difference, entering it, forms and constitutes. Unless difference enters genera, species will never be constituted. Therefore genera lie prior—that is, they preside over—and are older than their species.

Consequently, if genera are destroyed, species will also perish. If you remove animal, you remove human being and beast. But if species are destroyed, genus will not immediately perish. If human being perishes, animal is not thereby destroyed, for another species will remain of which animal, that is, genus, may be predicated.

Thus genera are prior to their species. Moreover, all genera are predicated univocally of species, whereas species are never predicated of genera.

This, I believe, was already said in yesterday’s nocturnal study. Genera are always predicated univocally of species. Human being is both human being and animal. Animal, however, is the genus of human being, and animal is predicated of human being. Since animal is predicated and human being is said to be an animal, animal and human being are called by the same name, animal. The same definition will also apply to both. For animal is a living, sentient substance, and it is not absurd to say this of a human being. If a human being himself is called an animal, it is not absurd to say of a human being that he is a living, sentient substance.

Genus, therefore, is predicated univocally of its species, because the same name and the same definition apply. But species are not only not predicated univocally of their genera; they are not predicated of them at all. For no lesser thing can be predicated of a greater. Since species are lesser than their genera, they can be called of their genera neither univocally nor in any other way.

“Moreover, all genera exceed in the complex of the species placed under them, while species exceed their genera in their proper differences.”

What he says amounts to this: everything that is a genus contains several species under it; everything that is a species and has several things beneath it has differences. Genus—animal—exceeds and surpasses the species human being in this respect: human being is only human being, whereas animal is not only human being but also ox, bird, and other things of this sort.

Species, however, exceed their genera because they possess in actuality the differences that their genera do not possess. As was said above, genera contain in potentiality the differences possessed by the species placed under them, but not in actuality. Therefore the species human being, or another species such as horse, exceeds its genus animal in this respect: animal in itself is neither rational nor irrational, whereas human being is rational and horse lacks reason.

It is also said that a species can never become a genus in the fuller sense, and a genus can never become a species in the fuller sense. This shows that the discussion concerns not subordinate species but the more specific and most specific species.

What does he mean? Things that are genera in the fuller sense can never become species in the fuller sense; nor can species in the fuller sense at any time become genera in the fuller sense. A species is never a genus. Whatever is a species will not be a genus, and whatever is a genus will not be a species. It is therefore clear that these discussions concern species alone, not subordinate species. For subordinate species can also be genera, whereas species in the fuller sense—as he says—can never be genera.

After discussing the common features and differences of genera and species, he proceeds to genera and properties.

## ON WHAT IS COMMON TO GENUS AND PROPERTY

The common feature of genus and property is that they adhere to and embrace species.

He says that genus and property resemble one another in this respect: every genus never departs from its species. The same applies to properties. If you say “human being,” you immediately name animal along with human being, since animal is the genus of human being, that is, of the species.

But even if you say “human being,” you immediately name its property along with the human being, for every human being is capable of laughter. Thus genus and property are always inserted into and, in a manner of speaking, glued to their species.

Similarly, genus is predicated of species, and property is predicated of those that participate in it. He says that all species are equally subordinated to the same genus, and that genus is named in relation to them, just as properties are predicated of those capable of participating in them.

Genus is equally said of human being, horse, ox, and the other animals, just as being capable of laughter—the property—is said of Hortensius, Cicero, and each of the individuals contained under the same species, namely the species of which the property “capable of laughter” can be predicated.

They also have in common that they are predicated univocally. Just as genus is predicated univocally of its species, as has been said, so property is predicated univocally of the species of which it is the property. Whoever is a human being is also capable of laughter.

If someone says that a human being is a rational and mortal animal, and says that a being capable of laughter is a rational and mortal animal, he will not be wrong. Thus genus is predicated univocally of its species, and properties are predicated univocally of the species whose properties they are.

## ON THE PROPERTIES OF GENUS AND PROPERTY

The two differ in that genus is prior, while property is posterior. If genus is prior to species, whereas property adheres to only one species and is equal to it, there is no doubt that genus, which is greater than species, is also greater than the property of the species.

For in order that there be a being capable of laughter, animal comes first. Before any species can be formed, there must first be a genus into which properties and differences may enter, as has been emphasized frequently.

Moreover, genus is predicated of several species. Genus—animal—is predicated of many, whereas property—being capable of laughter—is predicated only of the species human being. Hence properties can always be predicated convertibly of their species, but species can never be predicated of genus.

For not everything that is an animal is a human being, nor is everything that is an animal capable of laughter. What is called an animal may be a horse and capable of neighing. But everything that is a human being is capable of laughter, and everything that is capable of laughter is a human being. Properties and species can therefore convert with one another and be predicated reciprocally.

Furthermore, whatever is the property of a species belongs to all members of that species and to that species alone. Being capable of laughter belongs to all human beings and occurs only in the human species.

Animal, however, which is a genus, even if it belongs to one species, does not belong to that species alone. Animal belongs to every human being, but not only to human beings, because it also belongs to beasts and other animals.

Here one must understand those properties that are properties in the fuller sense—that is, those properly called complete properties, which belong to one species and to all its members.

Genus and property therefore differ in this respect as well: properties belong to one species and to all the individuals in that species; genera belong to all the individuals in the same species and under the same genus, but not to one species alone, since a genus is always predicated of several species.

Hence, when a property is removed, genus is not removed; but when genera are removed, properties are also removed. If you remove the property “capable of laughter,” being capable of neighing and being capable of swimming remain. But if you remove genus, you remove the species as well. If you remove species, the properties belonging to the species perish along with them.

Thus, when genera are removed, properties are removed; but when properties are removed, genera are not removed at the same time.

## ON WHAT IS COMMON TO GENUS AND ACCIDENT

Having completed the discussion of the differences between genera and properties, he turns to the common features and properties of genera and accidents. He attributes one common feature to them: that they are predicated of several things.

Just as genus is predicated of several species, so a separable or inseparable accident is predicated of several species. Black is predicated of a crow and an Ethiopian; moving is predicated of a horse and a human being—the former being an inseparable accident, the latter a separable one.

Because genus and accident are farther removed from one another, he mentioned only this one common feature and set aside the investigation of any others that might perhaps exist.

## WHAT THE DIFFERENCE IS BETWEEN GENUS AND ACCIDENT

Genus differs from accident in that genus is prior to species, whereas accidents are posterior to species.

It was demonstrated above that genera are always above species, lie prior to them, and are greater than them. Animal is prior to human being; therefore, when animal is destroyed, species are also destroyed, whereas destroyed species do not destroy genera.

An accident, however, must necessarily exist after the species themselves. Something must first exist to which it can happen. No accident can exist apart from that to which it happens. Therefore something to which the accident happens must exist before the accident itself. Every accident must consequently be found after species, and still more after individuals, to which it can primarily happen.

It should also be added that those participating in a genus participate equally, just as every genus is equally the genus of its species, as has often been said, and all species participate equally in their genus. Horse and human being are equally animals; neither horse is more animal than human being, nor human being more than horse.

Accidents, however, are not participated in equally. Since moving is a separable accident, some species that participate in the same accident may move more slowly or more quickly than others. The same applies to an inseparable accident. One person may have darker eyes, while another, though his eyes are also dark, may have them almost purple. Accident therefore admits of increase and decrease. What is called white may be called whiter or less white, and the same applies to other things of this kind.

Thus the two differ in this respect: things that participate in a genus participate in it equally, whereas things that participate in an accident perhaps do not participate equally.

It should also be added that genera are prior not only to individuals but also to species, whereas accidents are posterior not only to species but also to individuals. Accidents happen primarily to individuals, as has been said.

There is also the difference already mentioned: genus is predicated in answer to “What is it?”, while accident is predicated in answer to “What sort of thing is it?” or “What is its condition?” If one asks what Socrates is, the answer is “A human being” or “An animal.” If one asks what sort of person he is, the answer may be “Bald” or “Flat-nosed,” which are inseparable accidents. If one asks what his condition is, the answer may be “He is lying down,” “He is sitting,” or whatever else he happens to be doing.

Since the substance of genus has now been distinguished from species, difference, property, and accident, he proceeds to what follows.

There are twenty differences. For since there are five things, and each of them differs from the other four and likewise has four differences, five times four produces twenty differences. Genus differs from species, property, difference, and accident: this makes four differences. Species differs from genus, property, difference, and accident: these are another four, which together with the first make eight. Difference differs from species, property, genus, and accident: another four are added, making twelve. Property differs from genus, species, difference, and accident: four more are added to the twelve, making sixteen. If the differences of accident from the remaining four are also included, four more are added to the sixteen, completing all twenty differences.

These are twenty in such a way that, for a sufficient account of the doctrine, only ten differences are counted. Genus was said to differ from difference, species, property, and accident: these were four differences.

If we say that difference differs from species, property, and accident, it is superfluous to mention difference from genus as a difference, since it was already mentioned when we discussed the differences of genus from difference. For, in my view, difference differs from genus in the same ways that genus differed from difference. Therefore the difference by which difference is distinct from genus must be left aside, since it was already stated above when the distinction between genus and difference was given.

There remain three differences by which difference itself differs from species, property, and accident. Since the superior genus had four differences from the others, and difference now has three distinctions from the others, these make seven distinctions.

Species was already said to differ from genus when we discussed the way genus differs from species. What difference differs from species was demonstrated when we said how difference is distinguished from species. There therefore remain two differences of species—namely, its differences from property and accident—which, added to the preceding seven, make nine differences.

There remains one difference between property and accident to be stated. How property differs from genus was stated when we discussed how genus differs from property. How it differs from species was stated earlier when we enumerated how species differs from property. How it differs from difference was also stated when difference was separated from property.

But now let us see how difference is distinguished from species, property, and accident.

## ON WHAT IS COMMON TO DIFFERENCE AND SPECIES

Difference and species have in common that a species admits the individuals under it equally, and individuals participate equally in the species itself. All human beings are equally human beings and participate equally in humanity.

The same applies to difference. All human beings are equally rational, and all who participate in rationality, which is the difference, participate in it equally.

There is another common feature: just as a species never abandons those whose species it is and over whom it stands, so difference never abandons those whom it causes to differ from others.

When Socrates is under the species human being, the species human being never abandons him. Socrates is always a human being. Similarly, when Socrates is rational, the difference rational never abandons him. Socrates is always a rational animal.

## ON THE PROPERTIES OF DIFFERENCE AND SPECIES
Species and difference, however, differ from one another in that difference is always predicated in answer to the question “what sort of thing is it?” Thus, when asked what sort of animal Socrates is, the answer is “rational”; species, by contrast, is predicated in answer to the question “what is it?” Thus, when asked what Socrates is, the answer is “a human being.” For the quality of human beings is rationality—but not simply any quality. The quality that is taken as a difference is the one that, entering into a genus, constitutes a species; having arisen from a substantial quality, it has become a substantial and specific difference. This, then, is called a difference of such a kind, and it is predicated of the human being in answer to the question “what sort of thing is it?” [Col. 0065D] The same is true of the differences among other things.

For a difference is often found in several species. The difference “quadruped,” for example, belongs to the species of ox, horse, and dog; and the difference “rational” belongs to human beings and angels. A species, on the other hand, presides over no things other than the individuals placed under it. For nothing else is a human being except an individual, such as Socrates, Plato, or Cicero. Hence it follows that, if the difference is removed, the species too is removed. For if you remove “rational,” you remove “human being.” But if you remove the species, the difference remains. For if you remove “human being,” the difference “rational” as applied to an angel remains.

There is also this difference: a difference can be joined to another difference, so that from them some [Col. 0066A] species may be formed. Thus the differences “rational” and “mortal,” joined together, produce the species of a single human being. But species joined to species never constitute a species from themselves. For if you join “human being” to “ox,” no species is formed from them. Someone might perhaps say: “From the union of donkey and horse a mule is born.” But this is not so. For what is born from the union of individuals is itself an individual. If, however, you join the species “donkey” and “horse” themselves in the abstract, no species is ever constituted from them. For the fact that individuals can mingle does not therefore mean that the species of those individuals pass into one another’s substance. It is consequently clear that joined species cannot compose one species, whereas joined differences are constitutive [Col. 0066B] of one species.

These matters having been completed, let us turn to what difference and property have in common.

## THE COMMON FEATURES OF DIFFERENCE AND PROPERTY

Difference and property have in common that those things which possess a difference, and from which that difference is participated, participate in it equally. For when the difference “rational” is present in human beings, and all human beings participate in the rational difference, there can be no doubt that all human beings are equally rational and participate equally in rationality.

The property “capable of laughter,” on the other hand, belongs equally to all human beings: all human beings are equally capable of laughter. They also have this in common: just as something is called “capable of laughter” in potential even if it is not laughing, [Col. 0066C] so too someone is called “two-footed” in potential even if one of his feet is lacking. For what is said is not what actually is, but what can be. Because a person can laugh, he is called “capable of laughter”; because he can have two feet, he is called “two-footed.” Therefore property and difference never depart from those in which they have taken their place. A human being is always capable of laughter, even if he is not laughing; always two-footed, even if one foot is lacking. For in these differences and properties, as has been said, what can be in potential is considered, not what actually is.

## THEIR DISTINCTIVE FEATURES

They differ from one another in that difference is predicated of several species, whereas property is predicated of one. The difference “mortal,” for example, is predicated of [Col. 0066D] human beings, oxen, horses, and other living creatures; and “rational” is predicated both of God and of human beings. But “capable of laughter” is predicated only of the single species, human being.

Hence it follows that every difference, since it contains several species, is greater than the species under it; and therefore it can itself be predicated of species. But a species cannot be predicated of the difference itself. For the predication cannot be reversed. Since “human being” is said to be rational, it cannot conversely be said that “rational” is that which is human being. For what is rational may also be not a human being but a god.

Property, however, since it is always fitted equally to one species, is converted with that species in equal order and designation. For it is said: “What is a human being?” “A being capable of laughter.” “What is a being capable of laughter?” “A human being.”

Having treated these matters, [Col. 0067A] the discussion passed to difference and accident.

## THE COMMON FEATURES OF DIFFERENCE AND ACCIDENT

Difference and accident have in common that they are predicated of several things. Difference is predicated of both human being and God, since both are rational; and accident is predicated of both human being and horse, as when a human being is black because he is an Ethiopian, and a horse is black.

They also have this in common: an inseparable accident, whatever species it belongs to, is present inseparably in all members of that species, just as a difference is. Thus the inseparable accident “black” belongs inseparably to a raven and to all ravens. The same is true of difference. Since it happens to a human being to be two-footed, being two-footed is always present in all human beings.

## THEIR DISTINCTIVE FEATURES

[Col. 0067B] They differ from one another in that every difference contains species, whereas it is not itself contained by species. If a difference has several species beneath it, as has been said, it will be greater than the species placed beneath it. If it is greater, no species can contain it. For what is greater can never be contained by what is lesser. Thus “rational” contains human being and God; but “human being” does not contain “rational.”

Accidents, however, sometimes contain and sometimes are contained. They contain because one accident often has two species beneath it: “black,” for example, contains Ethiopian and raven. They are contained because one substance often has two, three, or any number of accidents. If someone is gray-eyed, [Col. 0067C] curly-haired, white, or tall, one individual in whom all these accidents occur embraces and contains them all. Therefore the species that contains that individual—which has received several accidents in itself—is comprehensive of those accidents.

Furthermore, difference is never increased or diminished.

What he means is this: the rationality present in each species is neither more nor less. No human being is, in respect of substance, more rational or less rational than another human being. But accident is both increased and diminished. One person is called taller, another faster, another more curly-haired; and there is no doubt that all these are accidents.

Moreover, contrary differences are always unmixed.

[Col. 0067D] By “unmixed,” he means unmixable—things that cannot be mixed. For the rational cannot be mixed with the irrational, nor can they agree in one species. Contrary accidents, however, can plainly coexist in one species. Black and white can coexist not only in one species but even in one individual. For someone may be white-skinned while nevertheless having black hair.

Thus it has been stated how species differs from genus and from difference, when we discussed the distinction between genus and species and between difference and species.

## THE COMMON FEATURES OF SPECIES AND PROPERTY

Now we shall discuss what remains concerning the common features of species and property. [Col. 0068A] They have one feature in common: they are mutually predicated of one another. Since they are equal to one another, the species “human being” belongs to no property other than “capable of laughter,” and “capable of laughter” belongs to no other species than human being. Hence it is said: “What is a human being?” “A being capable of laughter.” “What is a being capable of laughter?” “A human being.”

They also have this in common: every property is predicated equally of the things placed beneath it. All human beings, for example, are equally capable of laughter; and species too is predicated equally of the things placed beneath it. For all individual human beings are equally called human beings by one and the same name.

## THEIR DISTINCTIVE FEATURES

They differ in that a species can also be the genus of another species, whereas a property cannot. Here, however, we must understand the species that is subordinate, not the species [Col. 0068B] that is most properly a species and can never be a genus. We must therefore understand only the subordinate species, which can also be a genus. For “mortal,” while it is a species of the genus “rational,” is the genus of human being. “Capable of laughter,” however, can never be predicated of any other species, nor can it be the property of anything else, as it is the property of human being. For those things are always properties, as has been said, which are invariably fitted to one species alone and to no other.

Next, species comes first, and property follows. What he means is this: for any species to have a property, it must first exist and be constituted. A human being must exist before he can be capable of laughter; it is not necessary for “capable of laughter” to exist first in order for there to be a human being. Since a property is called a property, it does not stand on its own unless it belongs to some species. Therefore that of which it is the property must exist before the property itself.

Moreover, species is always understood in actuality [Col. 0068C] in whatever subject it belongs to. Species is always actual, not merely potential. A human being is genuinely, actually, and in operation a human being; he can never be a non-human being. But “capable of laughter,” which is a property, is predicated only potentially, even if it is not actual. Anyone may not laugh; nevertheless, because he can laugh, he is called capable of laughter. Species and property therefore differ in this respect: species is always actual and operative, whereas property is sometimes only potential.

Further, things whose definitions differ are necessarily themselves different. Every definition defines a substance. Therefore, if things have the same substance, they are indicated by the same definition. If things are given the same definition, they are predicated as the same substance. But if things differ in definition, they also differ in substance. Things that differ in substance are entirely different from one another.

[Col. 0068D] Since, then, the definitions of property and species differ, species itself and property also differ from one another. The definition of species is: to be under a genus and to be predicated, in answer to the question “what is it?”, of several things differing in number. The definition of property, however, is: to belong to one species alone and to be predicated of all the individuals under that species. Since their definitions differ, species itself consequently differs from property.

## THE COMMON FEATURES OF SPECIES AND ACCIDENT

After this he transferred the discussion to the common features of species and accident, [Col. 0069A] and says that they have few features in common apart from the single fact that both are predicated of several things. For they appear to differ greatly in their own substance and in their capacity to undergo or produce what happens to something: the thing to which an accident belongs and the thing that is the accident. The thing to which the accident belongs is, as it were, a foundation for the accident. But that which is the accident cannot exist in its own substance apart from the thing to which it belongs.

## THEIR DISTINCTIVE FEATURES

Their distinctive features are as follows: species is predicated in answer to the question “what is it?”, whereas accident is predicated in answer to the questions “what sort of thing is it?” and “in what condition is it?”

If someone asks what Socrates is, the answer is “a human being.” If someone asks what sort of person he is, he is called bald or snub-nosed. If someone asks in what condition he is, he is called seated or lying down.

They also differ in this respect: each substance has one species. [Col. 0069B] The substance of a human being has only one species, that of human being. Likewise, the substance of a horse has only one species, that of horse. But one substance often contains several accidents. In the same horse, for example, one part may often be black and another white. It may also possess tallness, height, an aquiline head, and other features of this kind.

The same substance possesses not only inseparable accidents but also separable ones. Someone may perhaps be swift, physically strong, an archer, and so forth.

It should also be added that species are known beforehand—that is, they are understood beforehand; [Col. 0069C] in other words, they are known to exist before accidents are. A thing in which an accident occurs must exist before the accident that occurs in it. Since species is the subject of the accident, the place in which the accident occurs, species is therefore understood to exist before the accident.

Accidents arise afterward—that is, they come from outside and are extraneous to any substance, even when they are inseparable.

This too is a point of separation between them: all things that participate in a species participate in it equally. Socrates, Cicero, and Plato are equally human beings. But those that participate in an accident do not participate in it equally, even when the accident is inseparable. Although being black is an inseparable accident of Ethiopians, one of them may be blacker than another, and they do not all participate equally in that blackness.

## THE COMMON FEATURES OF PROPERTY AND ACCIDENT

It remains, then, to discuss the common features of property and accident. [Col. 0069D] What property differs from species, genus, and difference has already been shown above.

Property and inseparable accident have in common that the things which participate in them, and in which they are considered, never exist without them. A human being does not lose the capacity for laughter, nor does an Ethiopian or a raven lose blackness. Therefore those things that participate in properties and accidents cannot exist without these—namely, properties and accidents. Otherwise this common feature might appear to conflict with the preceding definition of accident.

[Col. 0070A] For accident was defined as that which can be added or removed without the destruction of the thing in which it is. Now it may seem that these things cannot exist without their accidents, whereas earlier it was said that an accident could be removed without the destruction of the thing in which it is. But this is meant not to say that, if an inseparable accident is removed, the thing to which it belongs perishes; rather, since it cannot be separated, that thing cannot exist without it.

Inseparable accident and property also have another feature in common: just as a property belongs to every member of the species to which it belongs and always belongs to it—that is, every human being is always capable of laughter—so too every inseparable accident is an inseparable accident of every member of its species and always is so. Every raven, for example, is black, and every raven is always black.

Their only common feature with separable accidents is that, just as property is predicated [Col. 0070B] of many individuals, so accident too can be predicated of many individuals. Many people run, and many also walk; these are separable accidents, just as many can be capable of laughter.

## THEIR DISTINCTIVE FEATURES

They differ in that property always belongs to one species, whereas accident belongs to several. Accident occurs in several species, both animate and inanimate: ebony is black, a raven is black, and an Ethiopian human being is black. But “capable of laughter” belongs to nothing except human being.

Property is therefore predicated conversely, because it contains one species and is equal to that species alone. [Col. 0070C] Accident, however, cannot be predicated conversely, because it has several species beneath it. One cannot say that whatever is black is ebony, merely because one says that whatever is ebony is black. Something can be black without being ebony.

Furthermore, every property is given equally to the things placed beneath it, and is participated in equally by them. Socrates, Cicero, and Vergil equally participate in the capacity for laughter and are equally capable of laughter. But accident is not always an accident in an equal degree. One person may be taller, another faster. The former is a separable accident, the latter an inseparable one.

There may perhaps appear to be other properties and common features belonging to them. But for now, insofar as is sufficient for an introduction, let these matters suffice.

Now, Fabius, everything relevant to an introduction to Porphyry has been treated for you more fully and abundantly. [Col. 0070D] Later, if you should ever need me—especially for your studies, which have never lacked honor—I shall gladly and willingly comply, as your encourager, with these same pursuits.

Fabius then said: “You promise me these things with a father’s affection. But I shall never withdraw from these studies, especially with you as my teacher, from whom, if life permits, I shall perhaps acquire the whole discipline of Aristotle’s logic.”

“And I shall do so,” I replied, “with the greatest pleasure. But since, as Petronius says, the morning sun has already smiled upon the rooftops, let us rise; and whatever remains can be treated later with more careful consideration.”

[Col. 0071]

## COMMENTARIES OF ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS ON PORPHYRY, TRANSLATED BY HIMSELF (C)

## BOOK ONE
[Col. 0071A] The second labor of the exposition undertaken—the labor that will set forth the sequence of our translation—now demands our attention. In this matter I fear that I may have incurred the fault of an overly faithful translator, since I have rendered the text word for word, matching and comparing one expression with another. The reason for this undertaking is that in writings where knowledge of things is sought, it is not the charm of polished expression but incorruptible truth that must be conveyed. Accordingly, I shall seem to have accomplished much if, in books of philosophy composed in Latin, nothing more is missed from the Greek writings by reason of the sincerity of a wholly faithful translation.

And since philosophy has been established as the highest good for human minds, so that reason may proceed by a kind of thread along its path, we must begin with the faculties of the soul itself. Three powers of the soul altogether are detected in the cultivation of living bodies. One of these supplies bodily life, so that the body may grow by being born and endure by being nourished. Another provides the faculty of sensation and judgment. The third is supported by the power of mind and reason.

The task of the first of these is to attend to the creation, nourishment, and sustenance of bodies, but it provides no judgment either of reason or of sensation. This is the power of herbs and trees and of whatever is held fast to the earth by its roots. The second is composite and joined together: taking the first power for itself and establishing it as a part of itself, it receives varied and manifold judgments concerning whatever it is capable of apprehending. For every animal that possesses sensation is likewise born, nourished, and sustained.

The senses, however, are diverse and extend to the number five. Thus whatever is merely nourished but does not also sense possesses only this much; whereas whatever can sense is also shown to have the first power of the soul—namely, that of being born and nourished—subject to it.

[Col. 0071B] Those in whom sensation is present do not merely apprehend the forms of things by which they are struck when the sensible body is present; even when it is absent and the sensible objects have been removed, they retain images of forms previously apprehended through sensation and construct memory, preserving each image for a shorter or longer time according to the capacity of the animal. But they receive these imaginings as confused and indistinct, so that they cannot produce anything from their combination and composition. For this reason they can indeed remember, though not all things equally; but once forgetfulness has intervened, they cannot gather up and recall their memories. They have no knowledge of the future.

The third power of the soul, which draws along with it the preceding powers of nourishment and sensation and uses them as servants, as it were, and as obedient instruments, is wholly established in reason. It is engaged either in the firmest contemplation of present things, or in understanding absent things, or in investigating things unknown. This power alone is available to the human race. It not only receives the images of the senses in a complete and orderly form, but also, through the full activity of understanding, unfolds and confirms what imagination has suggested.

Thus, as has been said, for this divine nature, the things it grasps through the senses are not sufficient for knowledge; it can also give names both to insensible things conceived through imagination and to absent things, and it discloses through the imposition of words what it has grasped by the reasoning of the intellect. It is also proper to this nature that, by means of what is known to it, it should investigate what is unknown, and desire to recognize not only whether each thing exists, but also what it is, what sort of thing it is, and why it is.

The nature of human beings alone, as has been said, has received this threefold power of the soul. The power of this soul is not without the movements of understanding, since in these four functions it exercises the force proper to reason. For it either investigates whether something exists, or, once it has established that it exists, asks what it is. If it also possesses through reason knowledge of both matters, it investigates what sort of thing each is and examines in it the remaining features of its accidents. Once these have been understood, it asks why the thing is so, and likewise investigates this by reason.

[Col. 0071C] Since, then, the activity of the human mind consists in being always engaged either in apprehending present things, in understanding absent things, or in investigating and discovering things unknown, there are two matters on which the power of the reasoning soul expends all its effort. One is to know the natures of things by a sure method of inquiry; the other is to arrive first at knowledge of what moral seriousness will subsequently put into practice. In investigating these matters, there must necessarily be many things that lead the inquiring mind far from the straight path, as happened in many cases to Epicurus, who supposes that the world is composed of atoms and measures the good by bodily pleasure.

It is clear that this happened to him and to others for the following reason: through inexperience in disputation, whatever they had grasped by reasoning they supposed also to occur in the things themselves. This, however, is a great error. Things do not behave in reasoning as they do in numbers. In numbers, whatever results on the fingers of someone counting correctly must without doubt also occur in the things themselves: if the calculation happens to yield one hundred, there must also be one hundred things subject to that number. But this does not hold equally in disputation. Whatever the flow of speech may discover is not thereby fixed in nature as well.

It was therefore necessary that those should be deceived who, having cast aside the science of disputation, investigated the nature of things. For unless one has first arrived at knowledge of which reasoning follows the true path of disputation and which follows a merely plausible one, and unless one has recognized what can be trusted and what is suspect, the incorruptible truth of things cannot be discovered through reasoning.

[Col. 0072A] Since the ancients, often led astray by many errors, gathered false and mutually contradictory conclusions in disputation, and since it seemed impossible that, when contrary conclusions had been drawn concerning the same matter, both should be true—namely, the conclusions reached by reasoning that disagreed with itself—while it was uncertain which reasoning ought to be believed, it seemed appropriate first to consider the true and complete nature of disputation itself. Once this had been understood, it would then also be possible to determine whether what had been discovered through disputation had been grasped as true.

From this, then, arose the expertise of the logical discipline, which prepares methods of disputation, the reasonings themselves, and means of distinguishing them, so that it may be possible to recognize which reasoning is sometimes false and sometimes true, which is always false, and which is never false.

Its power, moreover, is judged to be twofold: one part lies in discovery, the other in judgment. Marcus Tullius also clearly expressed this in the book entitled *Topica*, saying:

> Since every careful method of discussion has two parts, one of discovering and the other of judging, Aristotle, as I indeed believe, was the foremost master of both. The Stoics, however, worked diligently on one of them: for they carefully pursued the method of judging, the science they call dialectic; but the art of discovering, which is called topical and which was more useful for practical purposes and certainly prior in the order of nature, they left entirely aside.

[Col. 0072B] But since there is the greatest usefulness in both, and since, if we have leisure, we intend to pursue both, we shall begin with the one that is prior.

Since, then, the fruit of this inquiry is so great, the whole attention of the mind must be devoted to this exceptionally skillful discipline, so that, once our first steps have been firmly grounded in the truth of disputation, we may easily arrive at a certain grasp of things themselves.

And since we have already explained the origin of the logical discipline, it seems to remain for us to add whether it is altogether a part of philosophy or, as some maintain, an equipment and instrument by which philosophy discovers knowledge and the nature of things.

On this question I observe the following opposing views. Those who think that logic is a part of philosophy employ arguments of roughly this kind. They say that philosophy unquestionably has parts, the speculative and the active. The question concerns this third, rational part—that is, logic—whether it should be counted among them; but there can likewise be no doubt that it is a part of philosophy.

For just as the investigation of natural matters and of the other subjects placed under the speculative part belongs to philosophy alone, and just as philosophy alone examines moral matters and the other subjects that fall under the active part, so too it deals with this part—that is, with the matters subject to logic—and philosophy alone judges them.

[Col. 0072C] If, then, the speculative and active parts are parts of philosophy because philosophy alone treats of them, for the same reason logic will be a part of philosophy, since this subject of disputation is subject to philosophy alone.

They argue as follows: Since philosophy is concerned with these three matters, and since the subjects of active and speculative inquiry distinguish them—the former seeking the natures of things, the latter seeking morals—it is beyond doubt that the logical discipline is distinguished from the natural and moral disciplines by the special character of its subject. For the subject of logic is propositions, syllogisms, and other matters of this kind; neither the speculative part, which considers not speech but things, nor the active part, which attends to morals, can equally provide this subject.

If, then, philosophy consists of these three parts—speculative, active, and rational—which are separated from one another by their own distinct and threefold ends, and if the speculative and active disciplines appear to be parts of philosophy, there is no doubt that the rational discipline must likewise be shown to be a part of philosophy.

Those, however, who regard logic not as a part but as an instrument of philosophy bring forward arguments of roughly the following kind. They say that the end of logic is not like the end of the speculative and active parts. Each of those two parts aims at its own proper conclusion: the speculative part perfects knowledge of things, while the active part perfects morals and institutions, and neither is directed toward the other. The end of logic, however, cannot be complete in itself but is in some way joined and bound to the other two parts.

For what is there in the logical discipline that ought to be desired for its own sake, except that this accomplishment of the art was devised for the investigation of things? To know how an argument reaches its conclusion, or which argument is true and which plausible, aims specifically either at directing this science of reasoning toward knowledge of things or toward discovering those things which, when brought into the practice of human life, produce happiness.

[Col. 0072D] Therefore, since the speculative and active disciplines have their own definite ends, whereas the end of logic is directed toward the other two parts, it is clear that logic is not a part of philosophy but rather its instrument.

There are, however, further arguments that may be made on either side; it is sufficient for us briefly to have noted what has been said.

We distinguish this dispute in the following way. Nothing, we say, prevents the same logic from serving at once in the capacity of a part and in the function of an instrument. Since it retains an end of its own, and since that end is considered by philosophy alone, it must be regarded as a part of philosophy. But since the end of logic—which philosophy alone contemplates—offers its service to the other parts of philosophy, we do not deny that it is an instrument of philosophy.

The end of logic, however, is the discovery and judgment of arguments. It will not seem surprising that the same part should also be established as a kind of instrument if we turn our attention to the parts of the body. Through them something is done so that we may use them as instruments, as it were, and yet within the whole body they nevertheless occupy the place of parts.

The hands, for example, seem to have the specific function of handling, the eyes of seeing, and the other parts of the body their own particular functions. Yet, when referred to the utility of the whole body, they are found to be certain instruments of the body, and no one would deny that they are also parts.

[Col. 0073A] Likewise, the logical discipline is a certain part of philosophy, since philosophy alone is its teacher. It is also an instrument, since through it philosophy investigates the truth that has been sought.

But since, so far as concise brevity has allowed me, I have explained the origin of logic and what logic itself is, we must now say a few things about the book that we have undertaken to expound at present.

For in its title Porphyry announces that he is writing an introduction to Aristotle’s *Categories*. I shall briefly explain what this introduction is worth and what preparation it provides for the reader’s mind.

Aristotle composed the book entitled *On the Ten Categories* with the intention of comprehending the infinite diversities of things—which could not fall under knowledge—within a small number of genera. Thus what could not, because of its incomprehensible multitude, be brought under disciplined knowledge would, through the small number of genera, as has been said, become accessible to the mind and subject to knowledge.

Aristotle therefore considered that there are ten genera of all things: one substance and nine accidents, namely quality, quantity, relation, where, when, position, having, doing, and being acted upon. Since these are the highest genera, above which no other genus can be placed, the whole multitude of things must be found through the species of these ten genera.

These genera are distributed according to all their differences from one another. They appear to have nothing in common except their name, since all are predicated as beings: substance is, quality is, quantity is, and so forth with all the rest. The verb “is” is predicated of all in common, but they do not possess one common substance or nature; they have only the name in common. Thus the ten genera discovered by Aristotle are distributed according to all their differences from one another.

[Col. 0073B] But things that are separated by certain differences must have something proper to themselves by which each is claimed for a distinct and solitary form. What is proper, however, is not the same as an accident. Accidents can come and go, whereas properties are so inherent that those whose properties they are cannot exist without them.

Since this is so, and since Aristotle discovered the ten genera of things—things that the mind can grasp by understanding or that a disputant can express in speech (for whatever we grasp intellectually we make known to another through speech)—it came about that, for understanding these ten categories, a treatment of five of these matters became necessary: namely, genus, species, difference, property, and accident.

Genus is necessary because one must first learn what genus is in order to recognize that those ten things which Aristotle placed before all others are genera. Knowledge of species is likewise extremely important, so that it may be recognized which species belongs to each genus.

For if we do not know what species is, nothing prevents us from being thrown into confusion by error. It can happen that, through ignorance of species, we often place a species of quantity under relation, or assign the species of any one of the first genera to some other genus, and thus produce a confused and indistinguishable mixture of things. To prevent this, the nature of species must first be known.

[Col. 0073C] Knowledge of the nature of species is useful not only so that we do not exchange among themselves the species of the primary genera, but also so that, within any given genus, we may know how to select the proximate species appropriate to each genus—for example, so that we do not immediately say that animal is a species of substance rather than body, or that human being is a species of body rather than animated body.

The knowledge of differences, however, occupies the most important place in these matters. How do we know that quality differs from substance, or that the other genera differ from one another, unless we know their differences? And how can we distinguish their differences if we do not know what difference itself is?

Ignorance of difference introduces this error into our thinking, but it also removes all judgment concerning species. For differences give form to all species. If difference is unknown, species must likewise be unknown. How, then, could we recognize any difference if we were entirely ignorant of what this name signifies?

The usefulness of property is also so great that Aristotle himself investigated the properties of the individual categories. Who could have detected what their properties are before learning what property itself is? This knowledge of property is useful not only for those properties expressed by individual names, such as “capable of laughter” as a property of a human being, but also for those employed in place of definitions.

For all properties enclose the subject matter within a certain limit of description. I shall also mention this more suitably in its proper place.

Who could doubt how much the knowledge of accident contributes, when one sees that nine of the ten categories possess the nature of accidents? How shall we regard them as accidents if we are wholly ignorant of what accident is? This is particularly so because neither the knowledge of differences nor that of property can be understood unless we firmly grasp the nature of accident.

[Col. 0073D] For through ignorance it may happen that an accident is substituted for a difference or a property. That this is faulty is also demonstrated by definitions: although definitions themselves consist of differences and the definitions of each thing are made proper to it, they nevertheless appear not to admit an accident.

When, therefore, Aristotle had gathered together the ten genera of things, containing beneath them species differing in number, and when these species would never be diverse unless they were separated by differences; when he had resolved all things into substance and accident, and accident into the other categories; and when he had pursued the properties of certain categories—he taught about these categories themselves, but passed over as though in a brief note what genus was, what species was, what difference was, what that accident was about which we must now speak, and what property was.

[Col. 0074A] Therefore, so that those approaching Aristotle’s categories would not be ignorant of what each of the matters mentioned above signified, Porphyry wrote this book concerning knowledge of these five things. Once it had been examined, and once it had been considered what each of the things he had set forth above designated, the understanding would more easily learn the matters that Aristotle placed before it.

This, then, is the intention of the book that Porphyry, as has been said, indicated in the very inscription of its title that he had written as an introduction to the categories.

Yet although the intention of this book is directed toward this one end, its usefulness is not simple but manifold, extending into matters of the greatest importance. Porphyry himself mentions this at the beginning of the book, saying:

> Since it is necessary, Chrysaorius, both for understanding Aristotle’s doctrine of the categories and for assigning definitions, and generally for all matters involved in division and demonstration, to know what genus, what difference, what species, what property, and what accident are, I shall attempt, by giving you a concise account of these matters, useful for the study of them, to approach briefly, as though by way of an introduction, what the ancients have said. I shall refrain from the more advanced questions, while offering a moderate treatment of the simpler ones.

The usefulness of this book is spread in four directions. For it is of great benefit to readers both for the subject toward which its purpose is directed and for other matters which, although outside its purpose, nevertheless provide readers with no less benefit. Through this little work there is an easy understanding of the Categories, a complete presentation of definitions, a correct examination of divisions, and a most reliable establishment of demonstrations. The more difficult and demanding these matters are, the more perceptive and diligent a reader’s mind they require.

It must be said, however, that the same thing occurs in all books. For first, if their purpose is recognized, one can assess how much benefit may arise from it; and although many other things of this kind follow a book, as usually happens, [Col. 0077C] nevertheless it appears to have most immediately that usefulness to which its purpose is directed, as the book itself, which we have taken up, explains. Since its purpose is to provide an easy understanding of the Categories, there is no doubt that this is its principal usefulness, although definition, division, and demonstration are no less its companions.

Some principles of these matters are suggested to us here. The sense is as follows: “Since,” he says, “knowledge of genus, species, difference, property, and accident is useful for Aristotle’s Categories and his doctrine, and also for the presentation of definitions, for division, and for demonstration, because knowledge of these matters is useful and exceedingly fruitful, I shall attempt, by giving a concise account, briefly [Col. 0077D] to explain what the ancients discussed at length and in detail.” For the work would not be concise unless it compressed the whole undertaking through brevity. And since he was writing an introduction, he says that he will willingly avoid deeper questions, while treating the simpler ones with moderate conjecture—that is, he will address the obscurity of simpler questions by applying to them a certain reasoned process of conjecture.

The whole meaning of this kind of preface is such as to flatter the beginner’s mind both with its abundant usefulness and with its accessibility. But it must be explained what further meaning is concealed by the depth of the words.

In Latin speech, as in Greek ἀναγκαῖον, *necessarium* has several meanings. Marcus Tullius, with a different meaning, says that someone is “necessary” to him and to us. We likewise say that something is necessary when, for example, we say that it is necessary for us to go down to the forum; in that expression a certain usefulness is signified. There is also another meaning, as when we say that it is necessary for the sun to move—that is, that it must move. The first meaning may be set aside, for it is entirely unrelated to the *necessarium* that Porphyry uses here.

The other two meanings seem to contend with one another for the meaning appropriate to this passage, in which Porphyry says: “Since it is necessary, Chrysaorius.” For, as has been said, *necessarium* signifies both usefulness and necessity. Both meanings seem to fit this passage. For it is supremely useful to discuss the matters mentioned above concerning genus, species, and the others; and there is also the greatest necessity, because unless these matters have first been understood, the things for which they serve as preparation—the Categories—cannot be known. For the Categories cannot be learned apart from knowledge of genus and species. Nor does definition leave out genus and difference; and how useful this treatment is in the other matters will become apparent when division and demonstration are discussed.

But although it will be necessary for these five matters, which are to be discussed here, to come to knowledge before the things for which they serve as preparation, Porphyry did not use the word here in the sense in which he wished it to signify necessity, but rather usefulness. The very structure and connection of the discourse make this perfectly clear. No one uses reason in such a way as to say that a necessity is referred to something else. Necessity exists in itself, whereas usefulness is always referred to that for which something is useful, [Col. 0078C] as is the case here.

For he says: “Since it is necessary, Chrysaorius, both for the doctrine of the Categories that is found in Aristotle …” If, then, we understand *necessarium* here as “useful,” and translate the word accordingly by saying, “Since it is useful, Chrysaorius, both for Aristotle’s doctrine of the Categories to know what genus is, and so forth,” the order of the words accords with correct understanding. But if it is changed to mean “necessary,” so that we say, “Since it is necessary, Chrysaorius, both for Aristotle’s doctrine of the Categories to know what genus is, and so forth,” the order of the words does not accord with correct understanding.

Therefore we need not linger over this matter any longer. Although there is indeed the greatest necessity, in the absence of knowledge of these matters, of being unable to reach the things toward which this treatise is directed, the word *necessarium* is not used here with reference to necessity, but rather to usefulness.

Now, although the matter has already been mentioned above, let us briefly discuss how knowledge of genus, species, difference, property, and accident is useful for the Categories.

Aristotle established in the Categories ten genera of things, which would be predicated of all other things. Thus, whatever could come under signification, if it retained a complete signification, would be subordinated to one of the genera of which Aristotle treats in the book entitled *On the Ten Categories*. To refer something to another as to a genus is like subordinating a species to a genus. But this cannot in any way be done apart from knowledge of species; nor can we recognize what species themselves are, or to which genus they more properly belong, unless their differences are known. If the nature of differences is unknown, it will altogether be unknown which differences belong to each species.

Accordingly, it must be understood that if Aristotle treats of genera in the Categories, and the nature of genera must be known, knowledge of species accompanies that knowledge. But once this is known, what difference is cannot remain unknown—although in the same book there are many matters concerning which no understanding at all becomes available unless the reader brings the greatest expertise in genus, species, and difference. Thus Aristotle himself says: “Of different genera, and of genera not subordinated to one another, the species and differences are different in themselves.” This is impossible to understand if these matters are unknown.

Aristotle also investigates the property of each Category with the greatest care. Thus, after much discussion, he says that the property of substance is that it is capable of receiving contraries while remaining numerically one; that the property of quantity is that only in it is something called equal or unequal; and that the property of quality is that by it we propose one thing as like or unlike another. He proceeds in the same way with the others, explaining what the property of a contrary is, what belongs to opposition according to relation, what belongs to privation and possession, and what belongs to affirmation and negation. He treats these matters as though the nature of property were already known to those who are expert in them.
