If someone does not know this nature, he undertakes in vain the discussions concerning these matters.

It is already clear that accident occupies the greatest place among the Categories, since by its own name it encompasses nine Categories. From this it is evident how great the usefulness of this book is for the Categories.

What he says about the easy recognition of its usefulness for the presentation of definitions can be understood if the division of the account of substance is first established. The account of substance is presented in one way in description and in another way in definition. The account found in description gathers together a certain property of the thing whose substantial account it reveals; it not only shapes what it displays through a property, but itself also becomes a property, which necessarily enters into definition as well.

For if someone wished to give an account of quantity, he could say: “Quantity is that according to which something is called equal or unequal.” Just as he has placed the property of quantity in the account of quantity, and the whole account itself is proper to quantity, so description both gathers a property and itself becomes proper.

Definition, however, does not itself gather a property, but it too becomes proper. For one who displays substance joins genus to differences, reducing what is common in itself and shared by many to unity, and makes it equal to the one species that he defines.

Thus knowledge of property is useful for description, since only a property is gathered in description, and the description itself becomes proper, just as definition does as well. For definition, however, genus is placed first, followed by the species to which that genus is applied, and then the differences by whose conjunction with the genus the species is defined.

But if these matters seem to someone more compressed than the method of exposition requires, he should know that we have reserved this exposition for our own judgment, as was said in the first edition, so that the first edition might suffice for a simple understanding of this book, while this later edition is intended for deeper investigation by those whose knowledge has already been nearly confirmed and who no longer stumble over individual terms.

This book is also so useful for making divisions that, without knowledge of the matters discussed in its course, partition would occur by chance rather than by reason. This will become clear if we divide division itself—that is, if we divide the word *division* according to the things it signifies.

There is a division of a genus into species, as when we say: “Of colors, one is white, another black, and another intermediate.” Again, there is division whenever a word signifying several things is explained and the number of things signified by that word is displayed. Thus someone may say: “The word ‘dog’ signifies several things: this barking quadruped, a heavenly constellation, and a sea creature,” all of which are separated from one another by definition.

Division is also said to occur whenever a whole is separated into its proper parts, as when we say: “A house consists in one respect of foundations, in another of walls, and in another of a roof.” This threefold division is called partition according to itself.

There is another division, called division according to accident. This too occurs in three ways: either when we divide an accident among its subjects, as when I say, “Some goods are in the soul, others in the body, and others external”; or when we distinguish a subject by its accidents, as in: “Some bodies are white, others black, and others of an intermediate color”; or when we separate an accident into accidents, as when we say: “Some fluid things are white, others black, and others of an intermediate color.” Again, some white things are hard, others fluid, and some soft.

Since every division is therefore made either according to itself or accidentally, and each partition is threefold, and since in the threefold division according to itself one form of division is the separation of a genus into species, this cannot in any way be done apart from knowledge of genus, nor apart from knowledge of the differences that must be taken in the division of species.

It is therefore clear how useful this book is for this division, since at its very beginning it treats genus, species, and differences.

The second division, which is according to the significations of a word, is likewise not unrelated to the usefulness of this book. We can recognize in only one way whether a word whose division we are seeking to make appears to be equivocal or a genus: namely, if the things it signifies are defined. If the things that fall under a common signification are enclosed within one definition, they must be species, and the common term is their genus. But if the things designated by the proposed word cannot be included in one definition, no one doubts that the word is equivocal and not common to the things of which it is predicated as a genus, since the things it signifies under its common name cannot be comprehended in one definition.

If, therefore, it is clear from definition what a genus is and what an equivocal word is, and if definition proceeds through genera and differences, can anyone doubt that the authority of this book has great force in this form of division as well?

How, then, is that division according to itself which divides a whole into parts distinguished, and how will it not rather be thought to be a division of genus into species, unless genus, species, and their differences have previously been treated by some method of instruction? For why should someone not say that the foundations, walls, and roof are species of a house rather than its parts?

But once it is recognized that the name of a genus can wholly apply to each species, whereas the name of a whole cannot apply to each of its parts, it will become clear that one division is the division of genus into species and another the division of a whole into parts. That the name of a genus applies to each species is shown by the fact that both a human being and a horse are individually called animals. But neither a roof, nor walls, nor foundations is ordinarily called a house individually. Only when the parts have been joined together do they properly receive the name of the whole.

As for the division that occurs according to accident, no one is unaware that, when the accident and the force of genus and differences are unknown, it may easily happen that an accident is divided among subjects as though it were a genus among species; and finally ignorance will most shamefully confuse the whole order of partition.

Now that we have shown how this book is useful for division, let us speak about demonstration, so that the person who has labored with the most vigilant intelligence and most skillful effort in so great a discipline may not become entangled in matters arduous and difficult.

Demonstration—that is, the certain gathering of reasons for some matter under investigation—is formed from things naturally known beforehand, from appropriate premises, from first principles, from causes, from necessary propositions, and from things inhering in themselves.

Genera are naturally prior to species, and species naturally prior to properties. For species flow from genera. Likewise, it is clear that species are naturally prior to the individuals subordinated to them. Whatever is prior is also naturally foreknown and better known than what follows.

Something is called first and known in two ways: according to us and according to nature. For us, those things are more known which are closer to us, such as individuals, then species, and finally genera. But according to nature, in the opposite way, those things are more known which are least close to us. Therefore, the farther genera extend from us, the clearer and more naturally known they will be.

Substantial differences are those which we recognize as inhering in themselves in the things demonstrated. Knowledge of genera and differences must come first, so that in each discipline it may be understood what principles are appropriate to the thing being demonstrated.

No one who understands that a species cannot exist without genus and difference doubts that these very things—genera and differences—are necessary. Genera and differences are causes of species. For species exist because their genera and differences exist; when placed in demonstrative syllogisms, these are causes not only of the thing demonstrated but also of the conclusion, as the *Posterior Analytics* will explain more fully.

Since it is therefore highly useful both to circumscribe anything through definition, to resolve it through division, and to establish it through demonstrations, and since these activities can neither be understood nor practiced apart from knowledge of the matters discussed in this book, who could ever doubt that this book is the greatest aid to the whole of logic? Apart from it, the other matters that possess great force within logic provide no access to instruction.

But Porphyry remembers that he is writing an introduction and that he must not go beyond the form appropriate to instruction. For he says that he will refrain from deeper questions and touch upon simpler ones with moderate conjecture. He sets out the deeper questions that he promises to defer as follows:

> Next, concerning genera and species, whether they subsist or are posited only in bare acts of understanding; whether they are corporeal subsistents or incorporeal; and whether they are separated from sensibles or exist in sensibles—I shall refuse to speak about these matters. For such an undertaking is exceedingly profound and requires a more extensive investigation.

“I pass over the deeper questions,” he says, “lest, by thrusting them prematurely upon the reader’s mind, I disturb the beginnings and first principles of this work.” But lest he thereby seem altogether negligent, so that the reader might think that nothing beyond what he himself had stated was concealed, he added the very matter whose treatment he promised to defer. In this way he would not leave the reader in complete obscurity by refusing to discuss these matters at all, while one strengthened by knowledge might recognize what could rightly be investigated.

The questions he promises to leave unspoken are highly useful and secret; learned men have attempted them, but they have not been resolved by many. The first is of this kind:

Everything that the mind understands it either conceives as something established in the nature of things and describes to itself through reason, or it depicts as something nonexistent through empty imagination. Therefore the question arises concerning the understanding of genus and the others of this kind: do we understand species and genera in such a way that they are things which exist and from which we derive a true understanding, or are we deceiving ourselves when we form things that do not exist through a vain imagination?

If it is established that they exist and we say that understanding is conceived from things that exist, then another, greater, and more difficult question produces doubt: the very nature of genus is exceedingly difficult to distinguish and understand. For since everything that exists must be either corporeal or incorporeal, genus and species must belong to one of these. What, then, will that which is called genus be? Is it corporeal or incorporeal? For its nature cannot be carefully considered unless it is recognized in which of these it should be placed.

But even when this question has been resolved, every ambiguity is not removed. For if genus and species are said to be incorporeal, something remains that besets and holds the understanding and demands to be released: do they subsist around bodies themselves, or do they also appear to be incorporeal subsistents existing beyond bodies?

There are two forms of incorporeal things. Some can exist beyond bodies and, separated from bodies, persist in their own incorporeal being, such as God, mind, and soul. Others, although incorporeal, cannot exist beyond bodies, such as line, surface, number, and individual qualities. Although we declare these to be incorporeal, because they are not extended through three dimensions, nevertheless they are in bodies in such a way that they cannot be torn away or separated from them; or, if separated from bodies, they cannot persist in any way.

Although these questions are difficult to resolve while Porphyry himself refuses them for the moment, I shall nevertheless undertake them in such a way that I neither leave the reader’s mind anxious nor spend my own time and effort on matters beyond the scope of the task undertaken. First I shall propose a few points amid the ambiguity of the question; afterward I shall attempt to untie and explain the same knot of doubt.

Genera and species either exist and subsist, or they are formed in the understanding and by thought alone. But genera and species cannot be things that exist. This is understood from the following considerations.

Whatever is common to several things at one time cannot be one thing in itself. What is common belongs to many, especially when one and the same thing is wholly present in many at one time. For however many species there are, there is one genus in all of them—not because the individual species take some parts from it as though they were portions, but because each has the whole genus at the same time. Thus the whole genus, being present at the same time in several species, each taken singly, cannot be one thing. For it cannot happen that, when the whole is present as one in many at the same time, it is numerically one in itself.

If this is so, genus cannot be one thing, and consequently it will not exist at all. For everything that exists exists because it is one; the same must be said of species.

But if genus and species do exist while being many rather than numerically one, genus will not be the ultimate genus. It will have another genus placed above it, whose single name will encompass that multiplicity. Just as several animals, although they possess some similarity, are nevertheless not the same and therefore lead us to seek their genus, so too, since the genus that is in many things is multiple and therefore possesses a similarity to itself that is a genus but is not one because it is in many, another genus of that genus must be sought. Once it has been found, by the same reasoning stated above a third genus will again be sought. Thus the reasoning must proceed to infinity, since no limit of the discipline will appear.

But if there is one genus numerically, it cannot be common to many. For if one thing is common, it is common either in parts, in which case it is no longer wholly common, since its parts properly belong to individuals; or it passes at different times into the uses of those who possess it, so that it is common, as with a well or a spring, or a jointly owned slave or horse; or it becomes common to all at one time, but not in such a way as to constitute and form the substance of those to whom it is common, as with a theater or some spectacle that is common to all the spectators.

Genus cannot be common to species in any of these ways. It must be common in such a way that it is wholly present in each, at one time, and capable of constituting and forming the substance of those to whom it is common.

Therefore, if genus is neither one, because it is common, nor multiple, because another genus must be sought for that multiplicity as well, it will appear that genus does not exist at all. The same must be understood of the other things.

But if genera, species, and the rest are grasped only by acts of understanding, then every act of understanding either arises from an underlying thing in accordance with the way the thing is, or, if it does not accord with the way the thing is, it is false. An act of understanding that is grasped from no underlying thing cannot be formed from nothing.

If the understanding of genus, species, and the others arises from an underlying thing in such a way that it accords with the way the thing itself is, then they are not posited merely in understanding but also subsist in the truth of things. Again, then, one must inquire what their nature is—the question investigated above.

But if the understanding of genus and the others is indeed derived from an underlying thing, yet not in accordance with the way the thing subject to understanding is, then the understanding must be false. For an understanding that arises from a thing but does not accord with the way the thing is is false: it understands the thing otherwise than it is.

If, then, genus and species neither exist nor have a true understanding when they are understood, there is no doubt that all concern with discussing these five proposed matters must be abandoned, since the inquiry would concern neither a thing that exists nor something from which anything true could be understood or stated.

This, for the present, is the question concerning the matters proposed. With Alexander’s agreement, we shall resolve it by the following reasoning.

We do not say that every act of understanding which arises from an underlying thing but does not accord with the way the underlying thing itself is must appear false and empty. False opinion, rather than understanding, occurs only in things formed through combination.

If someone combines and joins in understanding things that nature does not permit to be joined, no one is unaware that the result is false—for example, if someone joins a horse and a human being in imagination and forms a centaur.

But if this occurs through division and abstraction, the matter is not in fact as the understanding represents it; nevertheless, that act of understanding is not false. For there are many things that have their own being in other things and cannot be completely separated from them, or, if separated, cannot subsist in any way.

To make this clear through a familiar example: a line is something in a body, and what it is belongs to the body; it retains its being through the body. This is shown as follows: if it is separated from the body, it does not subsist. For who has ever apprehended through any sense a line separated from a body?

But when the mind receives from the senses confused and mingled things together with bodies, it distinguishes them through its own power and thought. The senses deliver all incorporeal things of this kind, which have their being in bodies, to us together with the bodies themselves. The mind, however, which has the power both to join what is separate and to dissolve what is joined, distinguishes what the senses deliver as confused and conjoined with bodies, so that it contemplates and sees it as an incorporeal nature in itself and without the bodies in which it is embodied.

The properties of incorporeal things mingled with bodies are different, even when they are separated from the body.

Genera, species, and the others are therefore found either in corporeal things or in things that are corporeal. If the mind finds them in incorporeal things, it immediately possesses an incorporeal understanding of genus. But if it observes the genera and species of corporeal things, it removes from bodies, as it is accustomed to do, the nature of incorporeal things and contemplates it alone and pure, as it is in itself.

Thus, when the mind receives these things mingled with bodies, it divides and contemplates the incorporeal elements.

Let no one, therefore, say that we think of a false line because we grasp it in the mind as though it existed beyond bodies, although it cannot exist beyond bodies. Not every act of understanding that is grasped from underlying things otherwise than those things themselves are should be considered false. Rather, as was said above, the act of understanding is false when it does this through composition—for example, when someone joins a human being and a horse and thinks that a centaur exists.

But when someone does this through divisions, abstractions, and assumptions drawn from the things in which such elements exist, the result is not only not false; it is the only act of understanding capable of discovering what is true in the property of a thing.

Such things, then, exist in corporeal and sensible things. They are understood apart from sensibles so that their nature and property may be perceived.

Accordingly, when genera and species are conceived, their similarity is gathered from the individual things in which they exist: from individual human beings, dissimilar from one another, the similarity of humanity is gathered. When that similarity is conceived by the mind and truthfully perceived, it becomes a species. Again, when the similarity of diverse species is considered—a similarity that cannot exist except in the species themselves or in their individuals—it produces a genus.

Thus these things exist in individuals, but they are conceived as universals. A species should be regarded as nothing other than a thought gathered from the substantial similarity of a number of dissimilar individuals; a genus is a thought gathered from the similarity of species.

When this similarity exists in individuals, it becomes sensible; when it exists in universals, it becomes intelligible. In the same way, when it is sensible, it remains in individuals; when it is understood, it becomes universal.

Genera and species therefore subsist around sensibles, but they are understood apart from bodies. For it is not impossible for two things to be different in reason while existing in the same subject, as with a curved and a concave line. Although these things are defined by different definitions and have different acts of understanding, they are nevertheless always found in the same subject: the same line is both concave and curved.

The same applies to genera and species—that is, to individuality and universality. They have one subject, but a thing is universal in one way when it is conceived and singular in another way when it is sensed in the things in which it has its being.

With these matters settled, the whole question, as I think, has been resolved. Genera and species themselves subsist in one way but are understood in another. They are incorporeal, but, joined to sensible things, they subsist in sensibles. They are understood apart from bodies, as though subsisting by themselves and not having their being in other things.

Plato, however, thinks that genera, species, and the rest are not only understood as universals but also exist and subsist apart from bodies. Aristotle, on the other hand, thinks that they are understood as incorporeal and universal but subsist in sensibles. I have not thought it appropriate to judge between these opinions, for that belongs to a deeper philosophy. We have pursued Aristotle’s position more diligently, not because we especially approve it, but because this book was written for the Categories, of which Aristotle is the author.

Now I shall attempt to show you how the ancients, and especially the Peripatetics, treated these matters and the questions proposed in a plausible manner.

Having passed over the questions that he declares to be deeper, Porphyry desires a moderate treatment appropriate to an introductory work. But lest the omission of these questions itself be considered a fault, he first stated how he intended to treat the proposed matters and on whose authority he would rely as he undertook the work.

By promising to treat the matter moderately, with the difficulty of obscurity removed, he invites the reader’s mind to rest content and remain silent concerning what he is about to depict. He confirms what he is going to say by the authority of the Peripatetics. Thus he says that he will discuss “these matters”—that is, genera and species, concerning which he had raised the preceding questions—and “the proposed matters,” that is, differences, properties, and accidents, in a plausible manner.

By “plausibly” he means “with verisimilitude,” which the Greeks call λογικῶς or ἐνδόξως. We often find λογικῶς used by Aristotle to mean “with verisimilitude” and “plausibly,” and likewise in Boethius and Alexander. Porphyry himself also frequently uses this word with this meaning. In our translation, however, we omitted the expression that he calls λογικώτερον, which we might have rendered “more reasonably.”

The other meaning seemed far better and more accurate: that he promised to speak plausibly, that is, in a way not contrary to the opinion of beginners and readers, which is proper to an introduction. Since the secret of higher doctrine is repugnant to the minds of unlearned people, an introduction must be such that it does not go beyond the opinion of those who are entering upon the subject.

Therefore, as it seems to us, we have translated it better as “plausibly” than as “reasonably.” He says that the ancients discussed these same matters, but that he is following above all the treatment which the Peripatetics, under Aristotle’s leadership, left behind, so that the whole discussion may be suited to the Categories.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0085]

[Col. 0085D] At the beginning of expositions it is customary to ask why each thing is placed before the others in the order of arrangement. Thus, in the present case, one may ask why he placed genus before species, difference, property, and accident, since he treats it first.

We shall answer that this appears to have been done rightly. Everything universal encloses the other things within itself, but is not itself enclosed by them. It is therefore of greater importance and belongs to a more fundamental nature, since it restrains the others in such a way that, by the magnitude of its own nature, it cannot be contained by them.

Genus therefore contains within itself species, their differences and properties, and also accidents. Thus it was right to begin with genus, which restrains and contains the others by the magnitude of its nature.

Moreover, those things should always be considered prior which, if removed, cause the others to perish; the others are posterior, because when they are posited, the things that complete the substance of the rest follow. This is the case with genus and the others.

For if animal, which is the genus of human being, is removed, neither human being, which is the species, nor rational, which is the difference, nor risible, which is the property, nor grammatical, which is the accident, will remain. When the genus is destroyed, everything is destroyed.

But if you establish that something is a human being, or grammatical, or rational, or risible, it must also be an animal. For if it is a human being, it is an animal; if it is rational, risible, or grammatical, it does not depart from the substance of animal.

When genus is removed, therefore, the others are destroyed; when the others are posited, genus follows. Genus is therefore prior by nature, and the others posterior.

Genus was rightly placed first in the discussion. But since the word “genus” signifies many things, this is what he says:

## ON GENUS

> It appears that neither “genus” nor “species” is said in a simple manner.

Wherever an expression is not simple, its signification is multiple. He first distinguishes and separates the significations of this name, so that he may place before our eyes the signification of genus that he is going to discuss.

But since neither genus, species, difference, property, nor accident is simple in signification, why did he say only of these two—genus and species—that they are not said simply, when property, difference, and accident are themselves multiple in signification?

The answer is that, while avoiding length, he named only species, and did so lest genus alone be thought to have a multiple signification.

He enumerates the first signification of genus as follows:

> For “genus” is also called a collection of things related in some way to one thing and to one another, according to which signification the genus of the Romans is spoken of from its relation to one person. I mean Romulus and the multitude who are related to one another in some way by the kinship that comes from him, this being called a genus in distinction from other genera.

One meaning of “genus,” he says, is that which applies to a multitude and derives its beginning from some single individual, to which that multitude is so joined that its members are united both to that individual and to one another through the principle of that same individual. Thus, when “the genus of the Romans” is spoken of, the multitude of Romans, deriving its name from one Romulus, is joined both to Romulus himself and to one another, as it were by a certain inheritance of name. For the very association that descended from Romulus binds and gathers all Romans together among themselves under one name of genus.

[Cols. 0088A–C] It appears, however, that he has divided this meaning of genus into two parts when he introduced a connective conjunction, saying: “Genus is said to be a collection of things related in some way to one thing and to one another,” as though both that genus were said to be related in some way to one thing, and this genus again were said to consist of things joined to one another under the meaning of a single genus. But this is not so at all. For the same association propagated from some single individual both refers the whole multitude to that individual who is the founder of the genus and connects and contains the multitude among itself under one name of genus.

Therefore, one should not think that he made a division, but that he disclosed everything that had to be understood in this meaning of genus. The order of the words is to be understood as a hyperbaton: “Genus is said to be both a collection of things related in some way to one individual, and a collection of things related in some way to one another”; the repetition of “collection” is understood. There is also a zeugma, whose meaning he illustrated with an example: “According to this meaning, the genus of the Romans is spoken of, from the relation to one individual.” I mean, from the relation of Romulus and of the multitude that again has among itself, in some way, the kinship that derives from him—Romulus—called a genus by distinction from other genera, namely from other multitudes. For this multitude, having in some way a kinship both to one individual and to one another, was called a genus, so that it might be distinguished from others: the genus of the Romans was separated from the genus of the Athenians and from the rest.

Thus the complete order of the words is: “Genus is said to be both a collection of things related in some way to one individual, and a collection of things related in some way to one another; according to this meaning, the genus of the Romans is spoken of, from the relation to one individual. I mean, from the relation of Romulus and of the multitude—called by distinction from other genera—namely, of human beings who have among themselves in some way the kinship that derives from him, that is, from Romulus.” So much for this matter. Now we must speak of the second meaning of genus.

[Cols. 0088D–0089D] Genus is also spoken of in another way: that which is the principle of each person’s generation, either from the one who begot him or from the place in which he was begotten. Thus we say that Orestes derives his genus from Tantalus, and Hyllus from Hercules. Again, we say that Pindar was Theban by genus, but Plato Athenian; for a fatherland is the principle of each person’s generation, just as a father is. This appears to be the most straightforward meaning of genus. For those are called Romans who descend from the stock of Romulus; and Cecropidae are those who descend from the stock of Cecrops, together with their nearest kin.

There are altogether four principles that primarily produce each thing. One is the cause called productive, such as a father is of a son; another is material, such as the stones are of a house; the third is form, such as rationality is of a human being; the fourth is that for the sake of which something is done, such as victory is the purpose of a battle. There are also two principles of each thing that are said to be such by accident, namely place and time. Since everything that comes into being also exists in a place and at a time, whatever is born or made in a place or at a time is said to have that place or that time accidentally as its principle.

Of all these, in this second meaning of genus he takes two that appeared suitable to the meaning of genus, one from each group. From the causes that are primary he takes the productive cause; from those that are accidental he takes place. For he says: “Genus is spoken of both from the one by whom someone was begotten”—which is the productive cause among the primary causes—“and from the place in which someone was produced,” which is the accidental cause of a principle.

Accordingly, this second meaning contains two things: the one from whom someone was produced, and the place in which someone was born, as the examples also demonstrate. We say that Orestes derives his genus from Tantalus. For Tantalus begot Pelops, Pelops begot Atreus, Atreus begot Agamemnon, and Agamemnon begot Orestes. Thus this genus is spoken of from procreation.

But we say that Pindar was Theban because he was born at Thebes and thereby received such a name of genus. Yet since the one from whom each person is begotten differs from the place in which he is born, the meanings of genus that derive from the begetter and from the place appear to be different, although, in enumerating the second part, he made them one.

But lest the meaning of genus appear to be twofold, he joined them by analogy, saying: “For a fatherland is the principle of each person’s generation, just as a father is.” Yet since in meanings it often happens that something appears to be close to the thing signified, and since he added two meanings of genus—namely, that of multitude and that of the begetter—he judges and distinguishes to which the name “genus” more appropriately belongs, saying that this is the most straightforward meaning of genus: that which is derived from the begetter. For those are most properly Cecropidae who descend from Cecrops, and those are Romans who descend from Romulus.

But if this is so, the meanings of genus again appear to be confused. If those who derive their origin from Romulus are most properly Romans, and this is the meaning that derives from the begetter, where is the other meaning that he also enumerated first, namely, a collection of a multitude related in some way both to one individual and to one another?

For those who look more carefully, there are very many differences. It is one thing to derive a genus from some first begetter; it is another thing for many people to constitute one genus. The former can occur through a direct line of blood and need not spread into a multitude, as when a family descends through only sons. To this the second meaning of genus is suited, the meaning derived from the begetter; the first meaning, however, exists only in a multitude.

There is also this difference: the first meaning does not seek the first principle of procreation but, as he himself says, is satisfied that the multitude be related in some way to that from which the principle of such a genus is taken. The second meaning, however, derives its force solely from the begetter.

Likewise, within that first meaning of multitude, the particularity of the second meaning is contained. Thus, within the genus of the Romans there is the genus of the Scipios, since the Scipios are Romans by nature. For, being joined both to Romulus and to the other Romans according to their relation to Romulus, they are Romans. They are called Scipios, however, according to the second meaning of genus, because Scipio was the beginning of their family and bloodline.

[Cols. 0090A–C] First, then, genus was called the principle of each person’s generation; afterward it was also called the multitude of those who derive from one principle, such as Romulus. By dividing and distinguishing that multitude from others, we said that the whole collection was the genus of the Romans.

The meaning is easy and straightforward, provided that one ambiguity is resolved. For earlier he referred the meaning of multitude to the name “genus,” and afterward to the beginning of procreation. Now, however, he appears to call the meaning that he had previously counted first—the meaning of procreation—the earlier one, and the later meaning—the meaning of multitude—the later one. This may seem contrary if one considers the order of the discussion arranged above.

But here he is not speaking about himself; he is speaking about the customary usage of human language. In that usage, he says, the meaning of genus was originally the one derived from the begetter; with the passage of time, however, through linguistic usage, the name “genus” was transferred also to a multitude related in some way to some individual.

He said this because above he had stated: “For this appears to be the most straightforward meaning.” Thus, from this meaning—which he called the most straightforward, namely, the second—there seemed also to have been derived the name now applied to the multitude. For originally among human beings “genus” meant what someone derived from a begetter; afterward, through linguistic usage, a multitude related in some way to someone also came to be called a genus, for the sake of distinction among peoples, so that there might be differentiation of name and association among them.

Having completed these matters, he comes to the third genus, which is treated by philosophers and is of great use for the dialectical discipline. For history and poetry deal more with the beginnings of these genera. The third genus, however, is considered among philosophers, and he speaks of it in this way:

> Genus is also spoken of in another way: that under which species are placed, perhaps named by analogy with the foregoing. For such a genus is a certain principle of the species that fall under it, and it appears also to contain the whole multitude of the species that are beneath it.

[Cols. 0090D–0091A] Above he proposed two meanings of genus; now he attempts to show a third. He thinks that this one was named by analogy with the preceding meanings.

The two meanings stated above are these. In the one, the name “genus” contained a multitude joined to it by a certain antiquity of origin; in the other, genus was derived from each begetter, who is the principle of those who are begotten.

Since, then, two meanings of genus had previously been proposed, he now adds a third, the one spoken of among philosophers: that under which species are placed. It is believed to have been called genus for this reason, according to a probable interpretation, because it has some likeness to the preceding meanings. For just as the genus that is predicated of a multitude encloses a multitude under a single name, so genus also restrains and contains many species. Again, just as the genus spoken of according to procreation is a certain principle of those begotten from it, so genus is established as the principle of its species.

Therefore, since it resembles both of the others, it is plausible that it borrowed the name “genus” in this meaning also from the preceding meanings.

Since, then, genus is spoken of in three ways, the discussion among philosophers concerns the third. They also assigned it by describing it, saying that genus is what is predicated of several things differing in species in answer to the question “what is it?”, such as animal.

[Cols. 0091B–0092B] The philosophers rightly take the third genus for discussion, for this alone reveals substance. The others show either from what something exists or how it is divided from other human beings into one kind of form, as it were, of a people.

For the genus that contains a multitude does not reveal the substance of the multitude that it contains; it merely gathers the people under one name, so that they may be separated from a people of another genus. Likewise, what is called genus according to procreation does not reveal the substance of the thing produced, but only that it was the beginning of its procreation.

The genus under which species are placed, however, informs the substance of the species by way of difference. And since among philosophers the greatest question is what each thing is—for we seem to know each thing only when we recognize what it is—he rejects the others and discusses the genus that is chiefly treated among philosophers, which he also assigned by the description appended below.

He carefully says “describing,” not “defining.” For a definition is made from a genus, whereas genus cannot have another genus. This is more obscure than can be made clear at the first approach. It can happen that a thing which is a genus for one thing is placed under another genus; but when it is placed under that genus, it is not placed there as a genus but as a species.

Thus it cannot be placed under anything insofar as it is a genus; when it is placed under something, it becomes a species. Since this is so, it is shown that genus itself, insofar as it is genus, cannot have a genus.

If he had wished to encompass genus by a definition, he could not have done so in any way. Genus would have no other genus that could be placed above it. Therefore he says that a description, not a definition, has been made.

A description, as was said in the preceding book, is a kind of representation of a thing from its properties, a depiction, as it were, in certain colors. When several features come together in such a way that all of them taken together are equal to the thing to which they are applied, unless this collection is made from a genus or from differences, it is called a description.

The description of genus is therefore this: “Genus is what is predicated of several things differing in species in answer to the question ‘what is it?’”

Three things are required in genus: that it be predicated of several things; that it be predicated of things differing in species; and that it be predicated in answer to the question “what is it?” Since he himself discusses this matter more fully later, let us indicate briefly its meaning by an example.

Let animal be given to us as the form of a genus. It is undoubtedly predicated of certain things, namely, of human beings, horses, oxen, and the rest; but these are several things. Animal, therefore, is predicated of several things.

Human being, horse, and ox are such that they differ from one another, and not by some moderate difference but by the whole species, that is, by the whole form of their substance, of which animal is predicated. For human being, horse, and ox are called animals. Animal, therefore, is predicated of several things differing in species.

But in what way does this predication occur? For animal is not immediately given as the answer to everything one may ask. If one asks how large a human being is, animal is not, I think, the answer; that question belongs to quantity, not to substance.

Likewise, if one asks what sort of thing a human being is, the answer animal does not fit this question either. In every other question as well, one will find the answer animal inappropriate and useless, except for the question that asks what something is.

When we ask what a human being is, what a horse is, and what an ox is, the answer will be “animal.” Thus the name animal is predicated, in answer to the question “what is it?”, of human being, horse, ox, and the rest. Hence animal is predicated of several things differing in species in answer to the question “what is it?”

And since this is the definition of genus, animal must be the genus of human being, horse, and ox.

[Cols. 0092C–0094D] Every genus, however, is understood in one way in itself and in the thing, and in another way with reference to the predication of something else. Its own property constitutes it as what it is. Relation to something else makes it a genus.

Thus, if you ask about the substance of animal itself, I will say that it is an animated and sentient substance. This definition displays the thing in itself as it is, without reference to anything else. But when we say that animal is a genus, we are not, I think, then speaking of the thing itself under this name, but of the account according to which animal can be referred in predication to the other things subject to it.

Accordingly, the character and form of genus consists in its ability to be related by predication to those things which, although several and different in species, are predicated of them only with respect to their substance. He added the explanation of this definition by examples, saying:

> Of things that are predicated, some are predicated of one thing alone, such as individuals—for example, Socrates, and “this” and “this particular thing”; others are predicated of several things, as genera, species, differences, properties, and accidents in general, but not properly of any one thing. Genus is, for example, animal; species, human being; difference, rational; property, capable of laughter; accident, white, black, sitting.

Porphyry makes a division of all things that are predicated in any way. Therefore, in order to distinguish and separate the predication of genus from all the others, he proceeds in this way.

“Of all things that are predicated,” he says, “some are predicated of singularity, others of plurality.” By predication of singularity he means anything that has some one subject of which it can be said: things whose subjects are individual, such as Socrates and Plato; this white thing present in this snow; or this bench on which we are now sitting.

He does not mean every bench—for that is universal—but this bench now placed beneath us. Nor does he mean the white thing that is in snow—for white and snow are universals—but this white thing that is now seen to exist in this snow. For this cannot be predicated of every other white thing that is in this snow, since it has been brought down to singularity and constrained into an individual form through participation in an individual.

Others are predicated of several things, such as genera, species, differences, properties, and accidents in general, but not properly of any one thing.

Genera are predicated of their several species; species are predicated of their several individuals. Human being, for example, which is a species of animal, has beneath it several human beings of whom it can be predicated.

Likewise, horse, which is subordinate to animal as a species, has many individual horses of whom it is predicated.

A difference can also be predicated of several species, such as rational of human beings, of God, and of the heavenly bodies, which, as Plato holds, are animated and endowed with reason.

A property, although predicated of one species, is nevertheless said of many individuals placed under that species. Thus capable of laughter is predicated of Plato, Socrates, and the other individuals subordinate to human being.

An accident is also said of many things. White and black, for example, can be predicated of very many things separated from one another both in genus and in species. Sitting too is predicated of many things: a human being sits, an ape sits, and birds also sit, although their species are widely different.

But since an accident can be an accident in general or properly an accident of some individual, he qualified his statement by saying “accidents in general, but not properly of any one thing.” For those accidents that occur properly to an individual become individual and are capable of being predicated of one thing alone. Those understood in general, however, can be said of several things.

Thus, as was said of snow, the white thing in this snow placed before us is not an accident in general but an accident proper to this snow, which is presented to the eyes and made available for examination. In the same way, from something that could be predicated in general—for white can be said of many things, such as a white human being, a white horse, and white snow—it comes about that this white thing can be predicated of one snow alone, through whose participation it too has become singular.

In general, if we consider all genera, species, differences, properties, and accidents in themselves, insofar as they are genera, species, differences, properties, and accidents, it is clear that they are predicated of several things. But if we consider them in the things in which they exist, measuring them according to the form and substance of their subjects, it turns out that they appear to be brought from plurality of predication to singularity.

Animal, which is a genus, is predicated of several things. But when we consider this animal in Socrates, it is brought from plurality of predication to singularity. For Socrates is an animal, and the animal itself becomes individual because Socrates is individual and singular.

Likewise, human being is predicated of several human beings; but if we consider the humanity that exists in the individual Socrates, it becomes individual, because Socrates himself is individual and singular.

A difference such as rational can be said of several things, but in Socrates it is individual. Capable of laughter, when predicated of several human beings, becomes unique in each one. Likewise, an accident in general, such as white, although it can be said of several things, is individual when observed in each singular body.

A more convenient division could have been made in this way:

Of things that are spoken of, some are predicated with reference to singularity, others with reference to plurality. Of things predicated of several, some are predicated according to substance, others according to accident. Of things predicated according to substance, some are said in answer to “what is it?”, others in answer to “what sort of thing is it?” Genus and species are predicated in answer to “what is it?”, while difference is predicated in answer to “what sort of thing is it?”

Again, of things predicated in answer to “what is it?”, some are predicated of several species, others of no species. Genera are predicated of several species; species are predicated of none.

Of things predicated according to accident, some are predicated of several things, such as accidents, while others are predicated of one thing alone, such as properties.

Another division could also be made as follows:

Of things that are predicated, some are predicated of individuals, others of several things. Of those predicated of several, some are predicated in answer to “what is it?”, others in answer to “what sort of thing is it?”

Of those predicated in answer to “what is it?”, some are said of species that differ from one another, such as genera, and others are not, such as species.

Of those predicated in answer to “what sort of thing is it?” of several things, some are predicated of things differing in species, such as differences and accidents in general; others are predicated of one species alone, such as properties.

Of those predicated in answer to “what sort of thing is it?” of several things differing in species, some are predicated in substance, such as differences; others are predicated of things that occur in common, such as accidents.

From this division the definitions of these five things can be collected in the following way:

> Genus is what is predicated of several things differing in species in answer to “what is it?”
>
> Species is what is predicated in answer to “what is it?” of several things that do not differ in species.
>
> Difference is what is predicated of several things differing in species in answer to “what sort of thing is it?” and in substance.
>
> Property is what is predicated of one species alone in answer to “what sort of thing is it?”, but not in substance.
>
> Accident is what is predicated of several things differing in species in answer to “what sort of thing is it?”, but not in substance.

We have made these divisions in order to separate all these things from one another. Porphyry, however, had another purpose. He was not now hastening to distinguish everything from everything else, but only to separate the others from the form and property of genus.

For this reason he divided all things that are predicated either into those predicated of individuals or into those predicated of several things. Those predicated of several things he said were either genera, species, or the rest; and, adding examples of these as well, he continues:

> Genera therefore differ from those things that are predicated of one thing alone, because they are said of several things. They differ again from those that are predicated of several things: from species, because although species are predicated of several things, they are not predicated of things differing in species but in number. For human being, although it is a species, is predicated of Socrates and Plato, who differ from one another not in species but in number. Animal, however, although it is a genus, is predicated of human being, horse, and ox, which differ from one another in species, not merely in number.

[Cols. 0095A–B] Genus also differs from property because a property is predicated of one species alone, of which it is the property, and of the individuals under that species. Thus capable of laughter is predicated only of human being and of particular human beings.

Genus differs from difference and from accidents in general because, although differences and accidents in general are predicated of several things differing in species, they are not predicated in answer to “what is it?” but rather in answer to “what sort of thing is it?” or “how is it disposed?”

When asked what the thing is of which these are predicated, we shall answer with the genus, but we shall not answer with differences or with accidents in general. For these are not predicated of the subject in answer to “what is it?” but rather in answer to “what sort of thing is it?”

When asked what sort of thing a human being is, we say rational; when asked what sort of thing a raven is, we say black. Rational is a difference, while black is an accident. When we are asked what a human being is, we answer animal; animal is the genus of human being.

Now he attempts to separate genus from all the other things that are predicated in any way, as follows.

Since genus is predicated of several things, it immediately differs from those that are predicated of one thing alone and that have some one individual and singular subject. But this difference of genus from those predicated of one thing alone is common to it with the others—namely, species, difference, property, and accident—since they too are predicated of several things.

[Cols. 0095C–0096C] He therefore gathers the individual differences of these from genus, so that the nature of genus alone may be brought before the mind’s view. He says: “Genus differs from those that are predicated of several things: first from species, because although species are predicated of several things, they are not predicated of things differing in species but in number.”

A species cannot have several species beneath it; otherwise it would be called a genus, not a species. For if genus is what is predicated of several things differing in species in answer to “what is it?”, and species is predicated of several things in answer to “what is it?”, then, if the additional condition that it be predicated of things differing in species is added, the form of species passes over into genus.

This can rightly be understood by an example. Human being, although it is a species, is predicated of Socrates, Plato, and the rest, which are not separated from one another in species, as human being is separated from horse or ox, but in number.

There is, however, some difficulty about what it means to differ in number. Something appears to differ in number whenever one number differs from another, as one herd of cattle, perhaps containing thirty cattle, differs in number from another herd containing one hundred cattle. For they do not differ insofar as they are a herd, nor insofar as they are cattle; they differ only in number, since one group has more and the other fewer.

How, then, do Socrates and Plato differ not in species but in number, when Socrates is one and Plato is one, and one unit does not differ in number from another unit?

What has been said about things differing in number must be understood in this way: they differ in counting, that is, they are different while they are being counted. When we say “This is Plato” and “This is Socrates,” we have made two units; and when, touching with a finger, we say “This is one” of Socrates, and again of Plato “This is one,” the same unit has not been counted in Socrates as in Plato.

Otherwise it could happen that, when Socrates was touched a second time, Plato would also be indicated; but this does not happen. Unless you touch Socrates either mentally or with your finger, and likewise touch Plato, you do not make two things while counting them.

Therefore things that differ in number are distinct in counting. Since species is predicated of things differing in number, but not of things differing in species, while genus is predicated of several things differing in species—such as ox, horse, and the others that differ from one another in species, not merely in number—this is the additional feature that genus possesses over species.

If we give the complete definition of genus, we shall state it in this way: genus is what is predicated of several things differing in species, not merely in number, in answer to “what is it?” Species, however, is what is predicated only of several things differing in number in answer to “what is it?”

[Cols. 0096D–0097B] Genus differs from property because a property is predicated of one species alone, of which it is the property, and of the individuals under that species. A property can always belong to one species and never leave it or pass to another; for this reason it is called a property.

Thus capable of laughter belongs to human being. It is predicated both of the species of which it is the property and of the individuals under that species: capable of laughter is said of human being, of Socrates, of Plato, and of the others contained under the name human being.

Genus, however, is not predicated of one species alone, as has been said, but of several. Genus therefore differs from property in that it is predicated of several species, whereas property is named of one species alone, of which it is predicated, and of the individuals under it.

The difference between genus and difference and accident is concluded by one separation. For these are not predicated in answer to “what is it?” and by this very fact they are separated from genus. In other respects they are close to genus, since they are predicated of several things and of things differing in species, but not in answer to “what is it?”

If someone asks what sort of thing a human being is, the answer is rational, which is a difference. If someone asks what sort of thing a raven is, the answer is black, which is an accident. But if someone asks what a human being is, the answer is animal, which is a genus.

When we say that he said “not predicated in answer to ‘what is it?’ but rather in answer to ‘what sort of thing is it?’,” this statement encounters a difficulty of the following kind.

Aristotle thinks that differences ought to be predicated in substance. But what is predicated in substance shows what the thing of which it is predicated is, not what sort of thing it is, but what it is. Hence difference does not appear to be predicated in answer to “what sort of thing is it?”, but rather in answer to “what is it?”

The matter is resolved in this way: difference ordinarily reveals substance in such a way as to determine a quality concerning the substance, that is, to express a substantial quality. What has been said therefore amounts to this: “It does indeed appear to signify substance and to be predicated in answer to ‘what is it?’; but the more accurate account is that, although it reveals substance, it is nevertheless predicated in answer to ‘what sort of thing is it?’”

[Cols. 0097C–0098B] Thus genus, by being predicated of several things, is divided from those that are said of one thing alone, such as individuals. By being predicated of things differing in species, it is separated from those that are predicated like species or like properties. By being predicated in answer to “what is it?”, it is divided from differences and accidents in general, which are not individually predicated in answer to “what is it?” but in answer to “what sort of thing is it?” or “how is it disposed?”

We have said that these three features give form to this third meaning of genus: being predicated of several things, of things differing in species, and in answer to “what is it?” Each of these parts distributes and separates genus from the other things that are predicated in any manner. Summarizing them briefly, he says:

The fact that it is predicated of several things divides genus from those that are predicated of one individual alone.

“Individual” is used in several ways. An individual is what cannot be divided at all, such as a unit or a mind. An individual is also what cannot be divided because of its solidity, such as a diamond. An individual is also that whose predication does not apply to other similar things, such as Socrates. For although the other human beings are similar to him, the property and predication of Socrates do not apply to the others.

Therefore genus differs from those that are predicated of one thing alone in that it is predicated of several things.

Four things therefore remain: species, property, difference, and accident. Let us gather the differences of these from genus.

Genus is separated from those that are predicated like species or like properties by the difference according to which genus is said to be predicated of things differing in species. For species is not predicated of any other species at all, while property is predicated of one species alone; consequently neither is predicated of things differing in species.

Again, genus differs from difference and accident because it is predicated in answer to “what is it?”, while those are called by way of “what sort of thing is it?”, as was said.

Accordingly, genus differs from those predicated of one thing in the quantity of predication, since it is predicated of several. It differs from species and property in the nature of the subjects, since genus is said of things differing in species, whereas species and property are not. Genus is likewise divided from difference and accident in the quality of predication. For there is a certain quality of predication: either being predicated in answer to “what is it?” or being predicated in answer to “what sort of thing is it?”

The description of genus, therefore, contains neither anything superfluous nor anything lacking.

Every description or definition must be equal to the thing defined. For if the definition is not equal to the thing defined, then, if it is greater, it will also contain something else, and it will not necessarily always display the substance of the thing defined; if it is less, it does not attain a complete definition of the substance. For everything that is greater is predicated of what is less, as “animal” is predicated of “human being”; but what is less is not predicated of what is greater. No one can truly say, “Every animal is a human being.” Therefore, if the predication is to be convertible, it must be equal.

This can occur if it contains neither anything superfluous nor anything deficient, as in the very description of genus. For it was said that genus is what is predicated of several things differing in species in answer to the question “what is it?” This description can be converted with genus: if we say that whatever is predicated of several things differing in species in answer to the question “what is it?” is a genus, the converse is possible. Thus, as he says, the description of genus contains neither more nor less.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0097]

[Col. 0097D] The preceding discussion of genus may perhaps seem to have exhausted the entire treatment of species as well. For since genus is predicated in relation to something—that is, in relation to species—the nature of genus cannot be known if one does not know what species is. But since their consideration and distinction are different according to their own natures, although they are intermingled in combination, he proceeds to divide everything just as he set it out individually in the preface. Accordingly, after discussing genus, he first treats species, about which a question may indeed be raised.

If the reason for placing genus before all the others was that, by the magnitude of its nature, it contained the rest, it would not have been proper to place species before difference in the order of treatment, since difference contains species—especially since differences themselves give form to species. What gives form is prior to that which is perfected by its formation. Species, therefore, is posterior to difference, and the treatment of difference ought consequently to have come first. This would also agree with the preface, in which he established the order suggested by the natural order, saying that it is useful to know what genus is and what difference is.

This question must be answered because everything that is predicated in relation to something else always derives its substance from opposites. Thus there can be no father unless there is a son, nor a son unless there is a father preceding him; the name of one depends upon the other. The same can be seen in genus and species. A species is not a species except in relation to a genus, and again a genus cannot be a genus unless it is referred to a species. Nor should genus and species be thought to be certain substances or absolute things, as was also said above. Rather, whatever exists as a property of nature becomes genus or species when it is referred either to what is below or to what is above.

Since, therefore, the relation of these things mutually establishes them, their treatment has rightly been made continuous. Beginning with species, he says as follows:

## ON SPECIES

“Species” is used, first, of the form of each individual, as in the statement: “First, the species is worthy of rule.” But “species” is also used of what falls under an assigned genus, in which sense we ordinarily say that human being is a species of animal, since animal is a genus; white is a species of color; and triangle is a species of figure.

Just as above he distinguished the equivocal meanings of genus, so he does the same here with species, saying that the meaning of species is not simple. He gives two meanings, although it is clear that there are more; he passed over them so as not to confuse the reader’s mind with excessive length.

He says, first, that the figure of each individual is called its species, a figure produced by the combination of accidents. The wording “of each individual” is very carefully chosen, for this species is spoken of according to accident: it is the form belonging to each individual. It does not arise from some substantial form but from accidents.

There is another species of substantial form, called humanity. This is not something placed beneath animal, as though it were a subject, but is as it were the quality itself that displays the substance. It is different both from the form accidentally inhering in each body and from that which derives genus into its parts.

There are, finally, several things which, although identical, are understood as related in different ways to one thing and another. Consider humanity itself. If you regard it in itself, it is a species that determines a substantial quality. If you place it beneath animal in thought, it brings about animal’s participation in itself, is separated from the other animals, and becomes a species of the genus.

But if you consider the property of each individual—that is, the manly appearance, the firm gait, and the other features by which individuals are shaped and, in a certain way, depicted—this is the species of accident according to which we say that a particular person is suited to rule because of the outstanding dignity of his form.

To this he adds another meaning of species: namely, the species that we place beneath a genus. We, however, propose that species has three meanings: first, a substantial quality; second, the particular form proper to each individual; third, the species of which he is now speaking, which is placed beneath a genus.

We should believe that he omitted the meaning we have added because of its obscurity—since it would require a deeper and more learned understanding—and silently passed over it while presenting the others. He adds the following examples of this species: human being as a species of animal, white as a species of color, and triangle as a species of figure. For all these are called species of things that are genera: animal of human being, color of white, and figure of triangle.

When assigning the genus, we also recalled species, saying that genus is what is predicated of several things differing in species in answer to the question “what is it?” And we say that species is what is placed beneath an assigned genus.

[Col. 0100B] Earlier, when he assigned the description of genus, he introduced the name of species into the definition of genus, saying that genus is what is predicated of several things differing in species in answer to the question “what is it?” Thus he defined genus through the name of species. Now, when he attempts to define species, he uses the designation of genus, saying that species is what is placed beneath a genus. A question may rightly be raised against this statement.

Every definition ought to clarify the thing it encloses and make it clearer than it was when indicated by its name. A definition must therefore be formed from things that are better known than the thing defined. When he described or defined genus through the name of species, he used the word “species” as though it were better known than “genus,” and thus described genus through what was better known.

But now, when he wishes to include species within the term of a definition, he uses the name of genus and reverses the relation of the concepts. Thus, in the description of genus the term “species” is supposed to be better known, while in the description of species the term “genus” is supposed to be better known. This is impossible. If the term “genus” is better known than “species,” he ought not to have used the name of species in the definition of genus. But if the name “species” is more easily understood than “genus,” the name of genus ought not to have been added to the definition of species.

He answers this question by saying:

“We must understand that, since genus is the genus of something and species is the species of something, it is therefore necessary to use both of them in the accounts of each.”

Everything that is predicated in relation to something else derives its substance from that of which it is predicated. If, therefore, the definition of each substance must display its property, then in things that are mutually related a description is rightly formed from one another.

Since genus is the genus of species, it derives both its substance and the term “genus” from species; therefore the name of species had to be invoked in the definition of genus. Since species derives what it is from genus, the name of genus could not be omitted from the description of species.

But since the qualities of species are diverse—for some species can also be genera, while others remain only species and do not pass into the nature of genus—he gives a multiple definition of species, saying:

“They therefore assign species in this way also: Species is what is placed beneath an assigned genus and of which the genus is predicated in answer to the question ‘what is it?’ Further, species may also be assigned in this way: species is what is predicated of several things differing in number in answer to the question ‘what is it?’ But this latter assignment belongs to the most specific species, which is species alone and not also a genus; the other definitions may also belong to species that are not most specific.”

He forms species through three definitions. Two of these apply to every species and, by their conclusion, determine all things that are called species in any way. The third does not apply in this manner.

There are two forms of species. One species can at some time also be the genus of another; the other is only a species and does not pass into the form of genus. The first two definitions—the one stating that species is what is placed beneath a genus, and the one stating that species is that of which genus is predicated in answer to the question “what is it?”—apply to every species.

These definitions show only that species is placed beneath genus. The definition that says species is what is placed beneath genus signifies the force of species in its relation to genus. The definition that says species is that of which genus is predicated in answer to the question “what is it?” again signifies the form that species retains from the predication of genus.

To be placed beneath genus and to have genus predicated of it are the same thing, just as to be subordinated to genus and to have genus placed above it are the same thing. If all species are placed beneath genus, it is clear that every species is included within this scope of description.

But the third definition speaks only of that species which is never a genus and remains species alone. This species is not predicated of things differing in species. For if genus has more than species in that it is predicated of things differing in species, then a species which is predicated of subjects but not of things differing in species will be a species of a superior genus but will not be the genus of its subjects.

Therefore, the predication that species has in relation to its subjects, if it is such that it is not predicated of things differing in species, distinguishes it from those species that can be genera and shows that it is species alone, without possessing the predication of genus.

The third description of species, which is called more properly species and most specific species, is therefore defined as follows: species is what is predicated of several things differing in number in answer to the question “what is it?”—for example, human being. Human being is predicated of Cicero, Demosthenes, and the others who, as was said, differ from one another not in species but in number.

Of the three definitions, two encompass both most specific and non-most-specific species; the third encompasses only the final species. To make this clearer, he begins somewhat further back and illustrates the matter with appropriate examples:

“But what is being said will become clear in the following way. In each category there are certain most general things and, again, other most specific things; between the most general and the most specific there are others which are called both genera and species, though in relation to different things.

The most general is that above which there is no other genus supervening. The most specific is that after which there is no other lower species. Between the most general and the most specific there are other things which are both genera and species, taken in relation to different things.

Let this be clear in the category called substance. Substance itself is a genus; beneath it is body; beneath body is animate body; beneath animate body is animal; beneath animal is rational animal; beneath rational animal is human being; and beneath human being are Socrates, Plato, and the particular human beings.

Of these, substance is the most general and genus alone; human being is the most specific and species alone; body is a species of substance but a genus of animate body; animate body is a species of body but a genus of animal.

Again, animal is a species of animate body but a genus of rational animal; rational animal is a species of animal but a genus of human being; human being is a species of rational animal but is not also the genus of particular human beings—it is species alone.

Everything that comes immediately before individuals and is predicated of them will be species alone and not also genus.”

We stated earlier that Aristotle arranged ten categories. He called them categories because they are predicated of all the other things. Whatever is predicated of something else, if the predication cannot be converted, is greater than the thing of which it is predicated.

Thus these categories were shown to be the greatest of all things, since they are predicated of all things. Within each of these categories there are certain most general genera and a long series of species, descending from the greatest to the least.

Those things which are predicated of the others as genera, but are not subordinated to any others as species, are called most general genera, because no other genus is placed above them.

The lowest things, which are predicated of no species, are called most specific species, because they receive the complete name of each thing and are constituted in the pure and unmixed property of the thing under investigation.

But since species has the name “species” from the fact that it is subordinated to a genus, it will be a simple species if it is subordinated to genus in such a way that it is not placed above any other species as a genus.

For a species that is subordinated to one genus in such a way that it is placed above another is not a simple species; it contains a certain admixture of genus. But the species that is subordinated to genus in such a way that it is not placed above any other species is species alone and simple species. It is therefore both most properly a species and called most specific.

Between genera that are most general and species that are most specific there are certain intermediate things which, in relation to those above them, are species, and in relation to those below them, genera. These are called subordinate genera because they are genera in such a way that one is placed beneath another.

What is genus alone is therefore called the most general genus. Those things which are genera in such a way that they can be species, or species in such a way that they can sometimes be genera, are called subordinate genera or species. What is species in such a way that it cannot be the genus of another is called the most specific species.

Having understood these matters, let us take an example from one category, so that from it we may recognize what occurs in the other categories and in the other genera and species, following the same thread and order.

Substance, then, is the most general genus, for it is predicated of all the others. Its first two species are corporeal and incorporeal, since what is corporeal is called substance, and what is incorporeal is likewise predicated as substance.
