Beneath corporeal substance is placed animate and inanimate body. Beneath animate body is placed animal. For if you add “sensible” to animate body, you produce animal. The remaining part—that is, the species—contains inanimate body and sensible body.

Beneath animal are rational and irrational. Beneath rational are God and human being. For if you place mortal beneath rational, you constitute human being; if immortal, God.

By “God” I mean corporeal God, for the ancients called this world God and honored it with the name Jupiter. They also called God the sun and the other heavenly bodies, which both Plato and a very large chorus of learned men believed to be animate.

Beneath human being are individual and singular human beings, such as Plato, Cato, and Cicero. Their number does not admit an infinite plurality. The following description places an example of this matter before the eyes.

[Col. 0103C]

[Col. 0103D] The description given above shows the order of predication from the most general down to individuals. In it substance is called the most general genus because it is placed above everything and is itself placed beneath nothing. It is called genus alone for the same reason.

Human being is species alone because Plato, Cato, and Cicero, above whom it is placed, do not differ from one another in species but only in number.

Corporeal, which is placed second after substance, is shown to be both a species and a genus: it is a species of substance and a genus of animate body. Animate, in turn, is a genus of animal and a species of corporeal. Animate, together with its proper difference, which is sensible, is therefore rightly called the genus of animal.

Animal is the genus of rational, and rational is the genus of mortal. Since rational and mortal are nothing other than human being, rational is a species of animal and a genus of human being.

Human being itself is not, as was said, the genus of Cato, Plato, and Cicero, but species alone. Nor is human being a species only of the difference rational; it is also called the species of Cato, Plato, and the others, though for a different reason.

Rational is a species because rational is divided into mortal and immortal, and human being is mortal. The same human being is a species of Plato and the others because, in the form of all of them, human being is the substantial and ultimate likeness.

There is also a rule common to all: those species are most specific which are placed above individuals alone, such as human being, horse, and raven—not bird, since there are many species of birds. Only those are called species whose subjects are so similar to one another that they cannot have a substantial difference.

Throughout this entire arrangement, the prior genera are joined with the inferior things to produce the subsequent species. Thus, for body to be substance, it is joined with corporeality, and corporeal substance is body.

Likewise, for it to be animate, corporeal substance is joined with animation, and it is animate corporeal substance—that is, substance having a soul. For it to be sensible, the same three superior elements are joined to it.

What is sensible is therefore nothing other than corporeal, animate substance retaining sensation; the whole of this is animal.

All the superior elements, joined to rational, produce rational animal. Finally, all the superior elements terminate in human being: that is, substance with rational and mortal added. Human being is corporeal, animate, sensible, rational, and mortal substance.

We give the definition of human being by saying “mortal rational animal,” including in animal substance, corporeal, animate, and sensible. In the remaining species and genera, genera are divided or species described in this same manner.

Just as substance, because it is supreme and has nothing above it, is the most general genus, so human being, because it is a species after which there is no other species and no other thing that can be divided into species, but only individuals—for Socrates, Plato, and this white thing are individuals—is species alone and the final species, or, as was said, the most specific species.

Those that are in the middle are species of the things above them and genera of the things that follow them. Therefore they have two relations: one toward what is above, according to which they are called species of those things, and one toward what follows, according to which they are called genera of those things.

The extremes, however, have one relation. The most general genus has a relation to what follows, since it is the supreme genus of all; but it has no relation to what is above, since it is supreme, the first principle, and, as we said, has no other genus supervening above it.

The most specific species likewise has one relation: that toward what is above, of which it is a species. It does not have a different relation toward what follows, but the same one, since it is also called the species of individuals.

Species is called the species of individuals as something containing them; it is called the species of superior things as something contained by them.

The name of genus is also shown by analogy with species. Just as genus is called the most general genus because it has no genus above it, as substance does, so species is called the most specific species because it has no species beneath it but only individuals, as human being does.

For species’ having nothing beneath it means that it stands above things which cannot be divided into unlike things, as genera are divided, or into like things, as species are divided.

Those things established between the most general genera and the most specific species are called both species and genera. They are subordinated to some things, while other things are subjected to them; and they can be divided either into unlike things or into like things.

Since there are two relations, as it were two opposed comparisons, which occur throughout all genera and species—one looking toward what is above, as in the case of species subordinated to their genera, and the other looking toward what is below, as in the case of genera placed above their own species—the most general genera retain only one relation, namely the one embracing what is below. They do not have the relation directed toward what is placed above, since the most general genus is subordinated to nothing.

Similarly, the most specific species possesses one relation, by which it is compared only with genera. It does not have the relation directed toward what is below, since it is placed above no species.

The subordinate genera, however, employ both relations. They possess the relation directed toward what is above, because subordinate genera have a genus placed above them, and they possess the relation by which they are predicated of what is below, because subordinate genera have species subordinated to them.

Thus corporeal retains in relation to substance the relation by which it can be placed beneath a genus, and in relation to animate the relation by which it can be predicated of a species.

Although the most specific species are themselves placed above individuals, they do not have the relation of something placed above them. This is because the things subordinated to the final species are such that, insofar as they are one substance, they do not have a substantial difference but only an accidental one.

Consequently, they appear to differ at least in number. They may therefore almost be said both to stand above several species and, in a certain way, to be placed above nothing at all.

For since species displays substance, and the substance of all the individuals placed beneath the species is one, it is in a certain way placed above none if one considers substance. But if one considers the accidents, there come to be several things of which species is predicated—not through a diversity of substance but through a multitude of accidents.

Thus genus always has several species beneath it, since it is predicated of things differing in species, and difference belongs only to plurality. Species, however, can sometimes stand above one individual.

For if, as is reported, there is only one phoenix, the species “phoenix” is predicated of only one individual. The species “sun” is likewise understood to have only one subject. Accordingly, species does not in itself necessarily contain a multitude. Even if there is only one individual, the concept of species does not perish, since it stands above certain parts that are, as it were, its similars.

For if you divide a little bronze rod, insofar as it is called bronze, both the parts and the whole are understood to be the same.

It was therefore said that species, although placed above individuals, possesses only one relation—namely, the one by which it is species. When species is subordinated to what is above, it is called species and is the species of superior things as something subjected to them; it is the species of inferior things because their substance is displayed by it.

Species is not the species of individuals in the same way that genus is the genus of species. Genus is part of substance, as animal is part of the substance of human being. The remaining parts—rational and mortal—are added to animal in order to define the substance of human being.

But human being is the whole substance of Socrates and Cicero. No substantial difference is added to human being to make Socrates or Cicero, as rational and mortal are added to animal so that human being may be enclosed in a complete definition.

Therefore the most specific species is species alone, and it possesses only this relation: toward what is above, because it is contained by those things; toward what is below, because it forms and contains their substance.

They therefore define the most general genus in this way: although it is a genus, it is not a species; and there is no other genus supervening above it.

They define the most specific species as that which, although it is a species, is not a genus; and which, although it is a species, can no longer be divided into species. It is also defined as that which is predicated of several things differing in number in answer to the question “what is it?”

Those things in the middle between the extremes are called subordinate genera and species. Each of them can be species and genus, taken in relation to different things.

Those that rise above the most specific species up to the most general are alternately called genera and species: Agamemnon, Atrides, Pelopides, Tantalides, and finally Jupiter. In families, they are generally traced back to one principle—for example, to Jupiter.

After showing the nature of genera and species and their difference, he recalls their order of definition and description. First, he introduces the definition of the most general genus, saying that the most general genus is that which, although it is itself a genus, has no genus placed above it—that is, it is not a species—and above which there will be no other genus supervening.

For if it had another genus supervening above it, it would by no means be called the most general genus.

The most specific species is described in this way: although it is a species, it is not a genus. This is stated by opposition, since opposites are sometimes described from opposites. For “being placed above” is opposed to “being placed beneath”: genus is placed above, while species is placed beneath.

If the first genus is such because it is placed above in such a way that it is not subordinated, then the final species is such because it is subordinated in such a way that it cannot be placed above anything else. The definition of opposites has therefore rightly been made from opposites.

There is another description of species: although it is a species, it is never divided into species—that is, it cannot be a genus. For if every genus is the genus of species, whatever is not divided into species cannot be a genus.

There is yet another definition: it is predicated of several things differing in number in answer to the question “what is it?” This definition was often demonstrated above.

We must now attend to the point mentioned somewhat earlier: one individual can be the subject of a species. Thus the unique individual phoenix is the subject of the species phoenix; this luminous body is the subject of the species sun; and the species of the world or the moon is placed above its single individual.

If this is so—if species is predicated of any one individual, as of the phoenix—how is it appropriate to say that species is predicated of several things differing in number? For some things, such as phoenix, sun, and moon, are not predicated of things differing in number.

The explanation is the one of which we gave a brief account above; although somewhat intricate, it will most suitably resolve the difficulty.

Everything beneath the most specific species—whether it is infinite, constituted in a finite number, or reduced to singularity—remains a species so long as some individual exists. A species is not destroyed by the diminution of its individuals if even one remains, because, as was said, even if there are several individuals, they do not have substantial differences.

This cannot properly be said of genus, which stands above things separated from one another by substantial difference. Genus stands above species formed by different differences.

If one of them perishes and the species is reduced to unity, the account of genus can no longer be the account of genus, since genus is predicated of things differing in species. The same is not true of species. For even if the nature of all the individuals has been destroyed and the predication of the species placed beneath them has been reduced to the singularity of one individual, it is still species and remains so.

Those things which perish and are lacking are of the same kind as that which remains and lies beneath them.

The statement that species is predicated of several things differing in number can rightly be excused in two ways. First, because there are far more species predicated of numerous individuals than there are species to which only one individual appears to be subordinated.

Second, because many things are spoken of according to possibility, even when they are not always so in actuality. Thus a human being is called capable of laughter even if he is not actually laughing, because he can laugh.

In the same way, species is predicated of things differing in number. The species phoenix would be predicated of several phoenixes if there were more than there are now, when it is reported that there is one. Similarly, the species sun is now spoken of this one sun that we know; but if several suns are imagined and conceived in the mind, the name “sun” would nevertheless be predicated of several individual suns no less than it is now predicated of this one.

Thus species is said to be predicated of several things differing in number, although there are some species that are named of individual subjects one by one.

Those called subordinate genera can be defined in this way: a subordinate genus is one that can be genus and species in the manner found in families, which both beget and are begotten. The example given below also shows this: Agamemnon, Atrides, Pelopides, Tantalides, and finally Jupiter.

For Atreus, the son of Pelops, is, as it were, a species of Pelops and a genus of Agamemnon. Similarly, Agamemnon is related to the Pelopides and the Tantalides; Pelops is related to Tantalus, and Tantalus to Jupiter, as species; while Tantalus is related to Pelops and Pelops to Atreus, as though they were genera. Jupiter is, as it were, the most general genus of these.

But in families they are generally traced back to one principle, for example to Jupiter.

But this is not how matters stand among genera and species. For being is not the one common genus of all things, nor are all things of the same genus under one highest genus, as Aristotle says. Rather, as was said in the Categories, let the ten primary genera be posited as ten primary principles. And if someone calls all things beings, he will, he says, name them equivocally, not univocally. For if being were one common genus of all things, all beings would be called beings univocally; but since there are ten primary genera, “being” is common only in name, not also in the account corresponding to the name “being.”

Since, when speaking of subordinate genera, he had set forth the example of a certain family extending from Agamemnon to Jupiter, whom he placed last out of reverence for the deity, he now explains this more fully. For, according to the ancient theologians, Jupiter is referred back to Saturn, Saturn to Heaven, and Heaven in turn is traced back to the most ancient Ophion, whose beginning is none. Therefore, lest what is found in families be thought to exist also in things, so that all things might be referred back to one originating principle of their [Col. 0108D] name, he determines that this cannot occur in genera and species. For just as every family may have one principle, so there cannot be one principle of all things.

There were some who held that all existing things have one genus, called “being” (*ens*), derived from what we say, “is.” For all things are, and “to be” is predicated of everything. Thus there is substance, there is quality, there is quantity, and the remaining categories are likewise said to be; nor would anything be treated concerning them unless it were established that these things, which are called the categories, exist. Since this was so, they posited being as the ultimate genus of all things, since it was predicated of everything. Inflecting the participle from what we say, “is,” they called it in Greek ὄν (*on*), and in Latin *ens*, “being.”

[Col. 0109A]

But Aristotle, that wisest investigator of principles, rejects this opinion. He does not think that all things can be reduced to one first principle, but holds that there are ten genera in reality. Since these differ from one another, they are not brought back to any common principle. He establishes these ten genera as substance, quantity, quality, relation, where, when, position, having, doing, and being acted upon—whatever in fact was at issue, since “being” was predicated of all of them. For all the things mentioned above are said to be genera. He therefore examined and rejected the argument, saying that not every common name also forms a common substance, and that one must not infer that something is a common genus merely because a common name is predicated of several things.

[Col. 0109B]

Those to whom the definition of the common name applies will rightly be judged species of that common name, and the common term will be predicated of them univocally. But where it does not apply, the term is merely common in sound, and there is no common substance.

This is made clearer by examples as follows. We predicate “animal” as the genus of human being and horse. Let us therefore give the definition of animal: “an animate, sensible substance.” If we refer this to a human being, it will be “an animate, sensible substance,” and the definition is not marred by any falsity. Again, if we refer it to a horse, it will be “an animate, sensible substance”; that too is true. This definition therefore applies both to animal, which is common to human being and horse, and to horse and human being, which are posited as species of animal. Hence human being and horse, both being animals, are predicated univocally.

[Col. 0109C]

But if someone were to call a painted human being and a real human being by the common name “animal,” let him define animal, if he wishes, as “an animate, sensible substance.” This definition applies to the human being who is alive, but not at all to the painted one, since the latter is not an animate substance. Therefore the definition of the common name—that is, of animal—cannot apply to the living and painted human beings alike. “Animal” is not a common genus, but it is called a common term because the name *animal* signifies several things in the living and painted human being, not as a genus but as a term with several significations. A term with several significations is called equivocal, just as the term that signifies a genus is called univocal.

[Col. 0109D]

Accordingly, although what is called “being” is predicated of all the categories, since no definition of it can be found that can be applied to all the categories, it is not predicated of them univocally—that is, as a genus—but equivocally, as a term with several significations.

This reasoning also proves that what we call being cannot be the genus of the categories. For one thing cannot have two genera unless one is subordinate to the other, as animal and animate are genera of human being, with animal subordinated to animate as though it were a species. But if two things are so equal to one another that neither is ever subordinated to the other, neither can be the genus of the same species.

[Col. 0110A]

Being and one, therefore, are subordinate to neither other. For we cannot say that being is the genus of one, nor that one is the genus of being. For what we call being is one, and what we call one is being; but genus and species are by no means mutually convertible. If, therefore, being is predicated of all the categories, one is also predicated of them. Substance is one, quality is one, quantity is one, and so on. If, because being is predicated of all these, it is the genus of all, then one too, because it is predicated of all, will be the genus of all. But one and being, as has been demonstrated, are not subordinate one to the other. There would therefore be two equal genera of each of the categories, which cannot happen.

[Col. 0110B]

Since this is so, Porphyry determined the matter by saying that, in reality, things cannot all be reduced to one principle in the way that everything in a family is reduced to one principle. Nor can there be one common genus of all things, as Aristotle holds. Rather, he says, the first ten genera are set above them, as was stated in the *Categories*, like ten first principles. No further account is presently sought; accepting Aristotle’s authority, we believe that these ten genera are subordinate to no other genus. If someone calls them “beings,” he will name them equivocally, not univocally. For no single definition according to their common name can be applied to all of them, and this prevents anything from being predicated of them univocally. If it were predicated univocally, the common name predicated of all would be their genus. But if it were a genus, the definition of the genus would apply to the species. Since this does not happen, what we call being is common to them as a term by the signification of its word, not by reason of a common substance.

[Col. 0110C]

There are therefore ten most general genera. The most specific species, however, are finite in number, though not infinite. The individuals that come after the most specific species are infinite. Therefore Plato ordered that, when descending from the most general genera to the most specific species, one should stop. He advised descending through the intermediates by dividing with specific differences, but leaving the infinite aside, since no science of them can be formed.

Since knowing the nature of species belongs to the division of the genus, and since knowledge cannot be infinite—for no intellect encompasses the infinite—he therefore pursues with the greatest propriety the number of genera, species, and individuals. He says that the number of the highest genera is known, since Aristotle discovered ten categories, which are to be placed before all things as their genera.

[Col. 0110D]

Species, however, are much more numerous than genera. For although there are ten highest genera of things, and although many species rather than one are subordinated to each genus, the nearest species are themselves subordinate genera under the highest genera until they descend to the ultimate species. Thus, plainly, many species must be distributed under each genus. The most specific species are much more numerous than the subordinate genera, since one descends to them through the multitude of subordinate genera, and they are much more numerous than those genera. This is especially evident because they are lower, and subordinate genera are always divided into a greater number of subjects.

[Col. 0111A]

It is clear that the species of the ten genera are much more numerous than those of any one genus. Nevertheless, although they are more numerous, they are contained within a determinate number. Anyone who examines the matter carefully and follows the species of all the genera can readily recognize that number. The individuals under each species, however, are infinite, either because they are so numerous and situated in such diverse places that they cannot be gathered and comprehended in one account by knowledge or number, or because, existing within generation and corruption, they at one moment begin to be and at another cease to be.

For this reason the highest genera, the subordinate genera, and the species—especially the most specific species—are called such: because they are finite in number, knowledge can enclose them within a limit. Individuals, however, cannot be so enclosed in any way. Therefore Plato ordered that division should proceed more from genera than from species, even from the most specific species. Through those things that are finite in number he ordered one to descend by dividing; but when one arrived at individuals, he advised stopping, lest one gather together what nature does not permit to be gathered, namely, the infinite. In this way he approves the division of genera into species, so that the division terminates in specific differences.

[Col. 0111B]

We shall discuss specific differences more fully under the heading where difference is treated. Here it is enough to say that they are the differences by which species are formed, as the rational and mortal differences form the human being. Thus, when we divide animal into rational and irrational, and separate mortal from immortal, and likewise divide the other genera by differences of this kind, these differences form the species subordinated to them. Plato held that division should continue until one reached the most specific species, and should then stop rather than pursue the infinite, since there could never be either knowledge or enumeration of individuals.

[Col. 0111C]

When, therefore, we descend to the most specific species, we must proceed by division through multiplicity. When, however, we ascend to the most general genera, we must gather multiplicity into one. For a species is the collection of many into one nature, and a genus even more so. Particulars and singulars, by contrast, always divide into multiplicity what is one. Through participation in a species, many human beings are one human being; but in particulars and singulars, one common thing becomes many. For what is singular is always divisive, whereas what is common is collective and unifying.

To divide is to dissolve into multiplicity what had previously been one. Every division, moreover, meditates upon composition and conjunction in the opposite direction. What, while being one, is divided by separation is composed again by uniting its several parts. Thus, as was said above, a species gathers together the likeness of individuals. But likeness is nothing other than a certain unity of quality. It is therefore clear that a species gathers together the substantial likeness of individuals.

[Col. 0111D]

Genera, in turn, draw together the substantial likeness of species and reduce them to themselves. Again, differences distribute the unity of the genus into species, while accidents divide the unity of the species among singular and individual persons. Since this is so, whenever one descends from genus to species by division, one must always produce multiplicity. But when one ascends from species to genera by composition, one must gather and unite within species the several qualities of likeness that had been diverse in the species’ differences.

[Col. 0112A]

The same point can also be considered as follows. Just as the infinite individuals gather into one substantial likeness, so individuals distribute their proper species infinitely. All individuals are therefore disaggregating and divisive. Species and genera, however, are collective: species are collective and unifying with respect to individuals. Genera are collective with respect to species. To put it this way, the genus distributes species, and species are led from individuals into multiplicity; but the genus gathers many species together. The species, in turn, brings a singular and particular multiplicity to the unity of singularity. Thus genus is more unifying than species.

[Col. 0112B]

For species gathers only individuals, whereas genus gathers both species and the individual, singular persons belonging to those species. He uses an appropriate example when he says: through participation in the species—that is, in human being—Cato, Plato, Cicero, and the many other human beings are one: that is, the thousands of human beings, insofar as they are human beings, are one human being. Yet there is one human being who is a species; when he is considered in relation to the multitude of human beings subordinated to him, they become many. Thus many human beings are one in the specific human being, and the specific human being is one in many individuals. The specific is therefore one in an infinite plurality. Accordingly, what is singular is divisive, while what is common, since it is one of many, as genus and species are, is collective and unifying.

Having assigned what genus and species are—genus being one, while species are many—for the division of a genus is always into several species—he now says that genus is always predicated of species, and that all higher things are predicated of lower things, but species is predicated neither of its nearest genus nor of higher things; for it is not convertible with them.

[Col. 0112C]

Either equals must be predicated of equals, as “neighing” of horse, or greater things of lesser things, as animal of human being. Lesser things, however, are not predicated of greater things. For one does not say that animal is human being, as one says that human being is animal. Whatever things a species is predicated of, the genus of that species is necessarily also predicated of them, as is the genus of the genus, all the way up to the most general genus.

If it is true to say “Socrates is a human being,” and “a human being is an animal,” and “an animal is a substance,” then it is true to say that Socrates is an animal and a substance. Whenever higher things are predicated of lower things, therefore, species is predicated of an individual, while genus is predicated both of species and of individuals. The most general genus is predicated of genus, of genera if there are several intermediate and subordinate ones, of species, and of individuals.

[Col. 0112D]

The most general genus is said of all genera, species, and individuals subordinated to it. A genus that precedes the most specific species is said of all the most specific species and of individuals. Species alone is said of all individuals. An individual, however, is predicated of one particular thing only. Thus “Socrates,” “this white thing,” and “this man coming, the son of Sophroniscus,” if Socrates is his only son, are called individuals.

[Col. 0113A]

He briefly recalls everything said above in the following manner. When, he says, we have assigned what genus and species are, and have also comprehended them in their definitions, and have taught that genus is always divided into a great many species, we add this: all higher things are predicated of lower things, but lower things are by no means predicated of higher things. He then properly treats the points useful for understanding the mode of predication.

He shows that one genus is always divided into many species once the definition of genus has been assigned. For he defined genus as that which is predicated of several things differing in species, in answer to the question “what is it?” But there are no several things differing in species except several species. The genus is divided among those things of which it is predicated. It has therefore been shown from the assignment of the definition that one genus always has several species.

[Col. 0113B]

Since this is so, genus is predicated of species, species of individuals, and all higher things of lower things, but lower things in no way of higher things. I shall explain briefly why this happens. We have said that higher things are substantial genera. Whatever are genera are more extensive than each individual species. For a genus would not be divided into many species unless it were greater than each species.

Since this is so, the name of the genus applies to the whole species. The magnitude of the genus is not merely equal to that of the species; it also exceeds the species itself. Therefore every human being is an animal, because both human being and the other animals are contained within the term “animal.” But no one would say that every animal is a human being. The name “human being” does not extend to the whole of animal, because, being the lesser term, it cannot in any way equal the scope of the genus.

[Col. 0113C]

Thus the greater are predicated of the lesser, but the lesser are not convertible so as to be predicated of the greater. If, however, there are things that are equal, they must be mutually convertible according to the equality of their nature, as “neighing” and “horse.” For they are so equal to one another that there is no horse unless it is neighing, nor can one say what a neighing thing is unless it is a horse. Thus every neighing thing is a horse, and every horse is a neighing thing.

Since this is so, higher things are predicated not only of their nearest lower things but also of the lower things of the lower things. For if it is admitted that higher things are predicated of lower things, then the lower things of lower things are even lower in relation to the higher things. Thus substance is predicated of animal, which is lower; but human being is lower than animal, and therefore substance is also predicated of human being. Again, Socrates is lower than human being, and therefore substance is predicated of Socrates.

[Col. 0113D]

Species, then, are predicated of individuals; genera are predicated both of species and of individuals, but this cannot be converted. For neither are individuals predicated of species or genera, nor are species predicated of genera. Thus the most general genus can be predicated of all subordinate genera, species, and individuals beneath it, but nothing is predicated of the most general genus itself.

[Col. 0114A]

The ultimate genus is that which is placed immediately before the most specific species, without an intermediate term. It can be said only of the most specific species and of their individuals. Species, as has been said, are predicated of individuals, while individuals are predicated of singular things.

Thus Socrates and Plato are individuals. Those things are especially individuals that fall under pointing out and indication by the finger, such as “this bench” and “this man coming.” Also individual are things marked out by some distinctive accident. If someone wishes to point out Socrates without saying “Socrates,” lest another who happens to bear that name be indicated, he may say “the son of Sophroniscus,” if Sophroniscus had only one son.

Individuals can be indicated most readily either by being shown to the senses themselves—by the eyes, the finger, or touch—even without a spoken name; or by some proper name, if only one person has acquired that name; or by their parents, if they are the parents’ only child; or by any other accident through which their singularity is demonstrated. For accidents stand in relation to one subject alone, and their predication or designation does not pass to another, as the predication of genus passes to species and that of species to individuals.

[Col. 0114B]

Individuals are called such because each of them consists of properties, the collection of which will never be found identically in anything else. The properties of Socrates will never be identical in any other particular individual. The properties of human being, however—I mean of the common human being—will be identical in many, indeed more properly in all particular human beings, insofar as they are human beings.

Since above he called something an individual, he now attempts to explain the reason for this name. For only those things that are common to several are divided; each of these is divided within the things of which it is common and whose nature and likeness it contains. But those things in which the common nature is divided participate in that common nature, and the property of the common thing belongs to those among whom it is common.

[Col. 0114C]

The property of individuals, however, is common to no one. The properties of Socrates—for example, if he was bald, snub-nosed, had a prominent belly, and other bodily features, or particular habits of character, or a distinctive voice—did not belong to anyone else. These properties, which had come to him from accidents and had joined together to form his appearance and figure, belonged to no other person. What belongs to no other person cannot be a property common to anyone. And what has no property common to anyone has nothing that participates in its property.

But what is such that no one participates in its property cannot be divided among things that do not participate in it. Therefore those things whose properties do not belong to another are rightly called individuals. The property of human being, however—that is, of the species—belongs to Socrates, Plato, and the others, whereas the properties arising from accidents that belong to them do not belong in any way to another singular individual.

[Col. 0114D]

An individual is therefore contained under a species, and a species under a genus. Genus is wholly a whole, individual wholly a part, while species is both whole and part—but part of one thing and whole not of another thing, but in relation to other things. For a whole exists in its parts.

[Col. 0115A]

Enough has been said concerning genus and species: what the most general genus is, what the most specific species is, which things are genera and species, which are individuals, and in how many ways genus and species are spoken of.

He now briefly reviews everything he has dealt with above at greater length, saying that an individual is contained by a species, while species themselves are contained by a genus. He gives the reason for this by saying that every genus is a whole, whereas an individual is a part.

[Col. 0115B]

For genus, insofar as it is a whole, contains the whole, and it can also be a species. A whole is not a species insofar as it is a genus, but insofar as it is something subordinated to a genus. Genus, therefore, insofar as it is genus, is a whole in relation to species, since it always contains them. An individual, however, is always a part, for it never encloses anything through its own property.

Species is both a part and a whole: a part of the genus, but a whole in relation to individuals. When it is a part, it is referred to singularity; when it is a whole, to plurality. Since one genus is placed above several species, each species is a part of the genus—that is, of the one genus. Since a species is placed above several individuals, it is not a whole of one individual but of many.

[Col. 0116A]

For this reason it is called a whole: because it contains and confines many things. For something may be a part even if it is the part of one thing; but for something to be a whole, one thing cannot be the whole of one thing. Thus species is a part of one thing, namely the genus, but a whole in relation to others, namely the individuals.

Concerning genus and species, therefore, it has been said what the most general genus is—namely, that to which no other genus is superordinate—and what the most specific species is—namely, that beneath which no species is subordinated. It has also been said which things are both genera and species: the subordinate genera, to which something is superordinate and something subordinate; which things are individuals: namely, those whose properties cannot belong to another; and in how many ways genus and species are spoken of.

[Col. 0116B]

Genus consists either in multitude, or in procreation, or in participation in substance. Species, however, consists in form or in subordination to a genus, as has been sufficiently explained. Having completed these matters, I shall bring the book to an end, reserving the fourth section for the treatment of difference.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0115]

[Col. 0115B]

In discussing difference, the question that arose concerning the order of placement in the treatment of genus and species need not arise in the same way. There we recalled asking why genus was placed before everything else, so that it should come first for discussion, and why species was introduced after genus. Here, however, it is superfluous to say why difference was taken up after species, since the question has already been asked why it was not placed before species. If it seemed strange that species had been placed before difference in the order of discussion because difference is more comprehensive and more extensive than species, why should anyone wonder if the same difference is placed before property and accident? For property is always of one species, as will be shown later; accident displays a certain external nature and is not predicated in substance at all; whereas difference contains both, and is predicated of several species and in substance. But enough of this: let us now return to Porphyry’s own words.

# ON DIFFERENCE

[Col. 0115D]

Difference is spoken of commonly, properly, and most properly. In the common sense, one thing is said to differ from another because it differs by some otherness in whatever way, whether from itself or from another. Socrates differs from Plato by some otherness; he also differs from himself as a boy when he has now become a man, and from himself when acting when he is at rest. He is always regarded as differing in some mode of being disposed by such othernesses.

In the proper sense, one thing is said to differ from another when it differs from another by an inseparable accident. An inseparable accident is, for example, curvature of the nose, grey-blue eyes, and a scar when it has hardened over a wound. In the most proper sense, one thing is said to differ from another when it differs by a specific difference, as a human being differs from a horse by the specific difference of rationality.

[Col. 0116B]

We have said that one thing differs from another in three ways: by genus, species, or number. In all these cases one thing differs from another either by certain substantial differences or by accident. Things differing by genus or species are separated by certain substantial differences, because genera and species are formed by certain substantial differences.

For when a human being differs from a tree by genus, the quality of being animate and sentient makes the difference. For, when sentience is added to animation, it makes an animal; when it is removed from animation, it makes what is inanimate and insentient—namely shrubs. Thus human being and tree differ by genus, for both cannot be placed under the genus animal. They differ generically by the difference of sentience, which forms the genus of only one of the two things proposed, namely of the human being, as has been said.

[Col. 0116C]

Those that differ by species plainly also differ by substantial differences, as human being and horse differ by the substantial differences of rationality and irrationality. But things that are individuals and differ only in number differ solely by accidents, which are either separable or inseparable.

Separable accidents include moving and sleeping: one differs from another because the one is overcome by sleep while the other is awake. They also differ by inseparable accidents, because one is taller in stature and the other is not.

[Col. 0116D]

Since this is so, Porphyry gathers these varieties of differences into a threefold number and gives them the names that he will use later, saying: every difference is called either common, proper, or most proper. He takes common difference to be that which indicates any accident and consists in a certain otherness: for example, if Plato differs from Socrates because the former sits and the latter walks, or because the former is old while the latter is young. A person can certainly differ even from himself, if he now does something whereas earlier he rested, or if he has now become an adolescent whereas he formerly lived in tender infancy.

[Col. 0117A]

These are called common differences because they can be no one’s proper differences and indicate separable accidents alone. For standing and sitting, doing something and not doing it, belong to many—indeed to all—and plainly are separable accidents. Things differing in these respects are said to differ by common differences.

Moreover, being a child, an adolescent, or an old man are likewise truly separable accidents. For by the necessity of nature itself we advance from childhood to adolescence, thence to old age, and finally from this to extreme old age. Perhaps there may be doubt whether each person’s bodily appearance can in any way be separated. But appearance too is separable, for no one’s appearance remains enduring and stable.

[Col. 0117B]

Thus a father returning from abroad cannot recognize the boy whom he left at home if he sees him again as an adolescent: the appearance that had been there before is always changed, and the very otherness by which we differ from another is always different. It is established, then, that this common difference applies especially to separable accidents; proper difference signifies inseparable accidents.

Such cases are these: if someone is born with grey-blue eyes or a curved nose. So long as the nose and eyes remain, the one will always be grey-eyed and the other always curved-nosed; and this is by nature. Other things, however, happen to bodies by accident: for example, if a wound is covered over by a scar, and this has hardened, it makes a proper difference. For one person differs from another because this one has a scar and that one does not.

[Col. 0117C]

Finally, among all these separable and inseparable accidents, some are natural and others external. Natural ones include childhood, youth, and the whole formation of the body. Grey-blue eyes and curvature of the nose are likewise natural. The preceding examples are of separable accident by nature, while the latter are of inseparable accident.

Walking or running, on the other hand, come externally: these are brought about not by nature but by will alone. Nature has given only the power, not the act. These are examples of externally arising separable accident. An example of externally arising inseparable accident is a scar that has hardened over a wound.

The differences called most proper are those which form not an accident but substance, such as the rationality of a human being. For a human being differs from the rest because he is rational or mortal.

[Col. 0117D]

These, then, are most proper differences, because they display the substance of each thing. If the former are called common because they are separable and belong to all, and the others proper because they cannot be separated even though they are among accidents, those are rightly called most proper which not only cannot be separated from their subject but also perfect the species and substance of their subjects themselves.

From these three varieties of difference—common, proper, and most proper—arise distinctions by genus, species, or number. Distinctions by number arise from common and proper differences; distinctions by genus and species arise from most proper differences.

[Col. 0118A]

Every difference universally, when it comes to a thing, makes it altered; but common and proper difference make it altered, whereas most proper difference makes it another thing. For among differences, some make a thing altered and others make it another thing. Those that make it another thing are called specific; those that make it altered are simply called differences. For the difference rational, when added to animal, makes it another thing and makes the species of animal. But the difference of moving makes it altered from what is at rest. Therefore the former makes another thing, the latter merely an altered thing.

Every difference makes one thing distant from another. But that which makes an altered thing is either common, comprehensive, or belongs to some proper or most proper mode of difference; hence whatever is diverse from another for any reason is called altered. But if this diversity is accompanied by being diverse through some specific difference, it is called not merely altered but also another thing. Alteration, then, is comprehensive, while being another thing is contained within the scope of alteration. Thus everything that is another thing is altered, but not everything altered can be called another thing.

[Col. 0118B]

Accordingly, if diversity has arisen through certain accidents, the thing has indeed become altered. For diversity considered in any manner or through any differences makes alteration intelligible. But a thing does not become another thing unless one is separated from another by a substantial difference.

Thus common and proper differences, because they are differences of accidents, as has been said, produce only an altered thing, not another thing. Most proper differences, however, because they belong to substance and are predicated in the form of the subject, produce not only what is altered—which is common to substantial and accidental difference—but also another thing. This belongs only to the difference that contains the substance and form of the subject.

[Col. 0118C]

These differences that make another thing are called specific because they make a species; once they have formed it by substantial differences, they make it so diverse from others that it is not merely another but is predicated as wholly another thing. The division, therefore, is as follows: among differences, some make an altered thing, others another thing. Those that make an altered thing are called differences simply and without qualification; those that make another thing are called specific differences.

[Col. 0118D]

To make clearer what an altered thing is and what another thing is, they are defined by the following account or explained by an example. Another thing is what differs in the whole account of its species, as a horse differs from a human being, because the difference rational, when added to animal, makes a human being and establishes him as another thing than a horse.

Again, if one human being sits and another stands, one human being is not thereby made diverse from another as a human being; rather, alteration alone separates them, making the one who stands altered from the one who sits. Likewise, if one has black eyes and the other grey-blue eyes, nothing has changed so far as the form of humanity is concerned; according to such differences, therefore, alteration alone exists.

[Col. 0119A]

But if a horse lies down while a human being walks, horse is another thing than human being and is altered: altered in two ways, but another thing only once. It is altered because it is wholly diverse in species and is another thing; for, as has been said, everything that is another thing is also altered. It is also altered because it differs by accidents, because the one lies down and the other walks. But it is another thing only once, because it is separated by the differences rational and irrational, which are specific and are called substantial. An altered thing, then, is what is diverse from something else in any respect.

Accordingly, divisions into genera and species are made according to differences that produce something other, and definitions are assigned from the genus together with differences of this kind. According to those differences that produce only alteration, however, there are merely alterations and changes in the condition of something.

Since at the beginning of this work he stated that knowledge of the differences of genus and species, of the proprium and of the accident, was useful for division and definition, he now, having divided differences themselves, separates and distinguishes which differences are suited to divisions and definitions and which are not. Since, then, the division of a genus into species must be made so that those species differ from one another in every respect of substance, he does not approve the adoption for division of differences that signify either separable or inseparable accidents, nor of differences that produce only alteration and cannot constitute and form anything else. For differences that produce alteration are useless for division. Common and proper differences must therefore be excluded from the division of the genus, and only the more proper differences must be adopted. For these produce something other, as the division of a genus appears to require. The same more proper differences would also be highly useful for definition. Common and proper differences are excluded as useless: since common and proper differences carry an accident of a different genus, they conform nothing with respect to substance, whereas every definition attempts to display substance. Specific differences, however, are those which, as stated above, form a species and complete its substance; these are the more proper differences. They are therefore adopted both in the division of a genus and in the definition of species. In the present context they are divisive and are suited to the partition of the genus. Thus, since as divisive differences they constitute something other than what previously existed, in the definition of substance they produce the formation of the species. Since they are more proper and produce something other, and are specific because they produce something other, they are suited to divisions; but because they form the species, they are suited to definitions. Common and proper differences, since they produce not something other but only alteration, and do not display substance at all, are equally excluded from division and definition.

Beginning again from what was said above, it must be stated that some differences are separable and others inseparable. To be in motion and at rest, to be healthy and ill, and whatever is closely related to these, are separable. But to be hooked-nosed or snub-nosed, rational or irrational, are inseparable. Among inseparable differences, some are so in themselves and others accidentally. For rationality belongs to a human being in itself, as do mortality and the capacity to receive learning. But being hooked-nosed or snub-nosed belongs accidentally and not in itself.

Above, he divided differences in a threefold division, saying that they were either common, proper, or more proper. Then, in another division, he cut the same differences into two parts, saying that some produce something other and others alteration. Now he makes a third division of them, saying that some are separable. It is possible for numerous divisions to be made of one thing that has many differences, as is clear from the very nature of differences. For if every division is distributed through differences, then things with many differences must also have many divisions. Thus an animal may be divided as follows: of animals, some are rational and others irrational. Again, some are mortal and others immortal. Again, some have feet and others do not. Again, some feed on plants, others on flesh, and others on seeds. It should therefore be no surprise that a multiple division of difference has been made. First, when he cut the members into three classes, he named them common, proper, and more proper. The second division included common and proper differences under the name of what produces alteration, while it placed the more proper differences under what produces something other. The third division, in which he says that some differences are separable and others inseparable, joins one class to the separable differences that produce alteration, while it encloses the remaining classes under the term “inseparable difference.” For one class among those producing alteration—that is, the proper difference—and the remaining class, which was shown to produce something other—that is, the more proper difference—are said to be inseparable differences. Their subdivision is as follows: of inseparable differences, some are in themselves and others accidentally; those in themselves are the more proper differences, while those according to accident are the proper differences.

Something is said to belong in itself when it forms the substance of something. For if any species is what it is because it is constituted by a substantial difference, that difference belongs to its subject in itself, and not accidentally or through some other intermediary—just as blackness adheres to a person’s face through the heat of the sun. Rather, by its own presence it forms the species that it preserves, as rationality forms a human being. This sort of difference belongs to a human being in itself: a human being is a human being because rationality is present; if it departed, the species “human being” would no longer remain. No one is unaware that these substantial differences are inseparable. They cannot be separated from the subject unless the subject’s nature has been destroyed. Those inseparable differences that belong according to accident are the ones called proper, such as being hooked-nosed or snub-nosed. They are called accidental because they accrue externally to an already constituted species and contribute nothing to the substance of the subject.

Those differences, then, that belong in themselves are understood in the account of substance and produce something other. Those that belong according to accident are understood neither in the account of substance nor as producing something other, but only as producing alteration. Further, those that belong in themselves do not admit of more and less, whereas those that belong accidentally, although inseparable, admit of increase and decrease. For neither is a genus predicated in degrees of greater and less of that of which it is the genus, nor are the differences of the genus according to which it is divided. They are what complete the account of each thing; but each thing’s being is one and the same, admitting neither increase nor decrease. Yet being hooked-nosed or snub-nosed, or being colored in some particular way, can be intensified or diminished.

Having properly divided the differences, Porphyry shows the distance between them and repeats one distinction that he made above. After saying that there were three kinds of differences—common, proper, and more proper—he said that proper differences, like common differences, produce alteration but not something other, reserving the latter exclusively for more proper differences. Now he repeats the same point, saying that the inseparable differences that display substance—that is, those belonging in themselves to the subjects, forming and completing them—produce something other. But those that are proper, that is, inseparable differences according to accident, belong neither to substance nor produce something other, but only, as stated above, produce alteration.

There is another difference between those differences that belong according to substance and those that belong accidentally: those that display substance cannot be intensified or diminished, whereas those that belong accidentally increase by intensification and decrease by remission. This is proved as follows. Each thing’s own being cannot increase or decrease. A human being cannot have more or less of his humanity today or at any other time. He cannot be more or less a human being than himself, nor can one human being be more a human being than another human being or than an animal. Both are equally called animals and equally called human beings. If, then, each thing’s own being can be enlarged neither by increase nor reduced by diminution—and this can easily be shown from the fact that genera and species are not varied by intensification or remission—it is beyond doubt that differences which form the substance of each species likewise admit neither the losses of remission nor the increments of intensification.

Thus substantial differences admit neither intensification nor remission, for this reason: each thing’s being is one and the same and does not admit increase or decrease. Let this serve as an example. A genus cannot be said to be more or less a genus for anything, since it is imposed equally upon everything as a genus. Differences also, because they divide the genus and form the species, complete the essence of the species and therefore admit neither intensification nor remission. Inseparable differences according to accident, however, such as being snub-nosed, hooked-nosed, or colored in some way, admit both intensification and remission. One person may be somewhat blacker, another more snub-nosed, and another less hooked-nosed. But the fact that not all human beings are equally rational and mortal does not appear to be admitted by the nature either of species or of differences.

Since, then, three kinds of difference are considered—some separable and others inseparable—and among the inseparable some belong in themselves and others accidentally—and again, among the differences that belong in themselves, some are those according to which we divide genera into species, while others are those according to which the things divided are specified—consider, for example, that all the differences of this kind of animal are animate and sensible, rational and irrational, mortal and immortal. The difference “animate and sensible” is constitutive of the substance of animal, for animal is an animate, sensible substance. The differences “mortal and immortal,” and likewise “rational and irrational,” are divisive differences of animal, since by them we divide genera into species.

A complete and ultimate division of differences is now made, as follows: some differences are separable and others inseparable; among the inseparable, some are accidental and others substantial; among the substantial, some are divisive of the genus and others constitutive of species.

When he says, “Since three kinds of differences are considered,” he is referring to the fact that in the first division of differences he said that some were common, some proper, and some more proper. He then showed that these three kinds of difference were partly separable and partly inseparable: common differences were separable, while proper and more proper differences were inseparable. He divided inseparable differences by saying that some were considered according to accident and others according to substance, and that those considered according to accident were the ones called proper, while the more proper were considered according to substance. He then subdivides those that belong according to substance, saying that some divide the genus and others form the species.

For easy understanding of this point, let the arrangement of species and genera from the third book be transcribed: first, substance; under substance, corporeal and incorporeal; under corporeal, animate and inanimate; under animate, sensible and insensible; under these, animal; under animal, rational and irrational; under rational, mortal and immortal; and under mortal, the species human being, which thereafter is placed above individuals alone.

In this division, all these are called specific differences, for they are differences of genera and species. They are divisive differences of genera but constitutive differences of species. This is proved as follows. Substance is divided by the differences corporeal and incorporeal; corporeal is divided by animate and inanimate; animate is divided by sensible and insensible. Thus substantial differences divide genera, and are called divisive differences of genera.

But if these same differences, descending from the genus and dividing the genus, are collected and joined into a unity in which they can be combined, species are formed. Since animal is a species of substance—for everything superior is predicated of what is inferior, and whatever is inferior will also be a species of what is superior—the differences animate and sensible, when referred to genera, are divisive; when referred to the species, they become constitutive of animal and form and establish its substance, shaping its definition, so that animal is an animate, sensible substance.

Substance, then, is the genus; animate and sensible are its divisive differences and the constitutive differences of animal. Likewise, animal is divided by rationality and irrationality, and by mortality and immortality. But rationality and mortality, which had been divisive of animal, when joined together become constitutive of a human being; they complete his species and form and complete the whole account of his definition. If irrationality is joined with mortality, a horse or any other animal that does not use reason results. Rationality joined with immortality forms the substance of God.

Thus the same differences, when referred to genera, become divisive of genera; when considered in relation to lower species, they form the species and, through a suitable combination, constitute their substance. It has been asked how these differences could be called constitutive of species when the difference irrational and the difference immortal appear to produce no species. We answer first that Aristotle’s view is that the heavenly bodies are not animate. What is not animate cannot be an animal; what is not an animal cannot be rational. Rather, he maintains that these bodies, because of the simplicity and perpetuity of their motion, are eternal. There is therefore something composed of these two differences, namely irrational and immortal.

If, however, Plato’s view is to be accepted instead, and the heavenly bodies are to be believed animate, then no subject can belong to these differences. For whatever is irrational is subject to corruption and generation and therefore cannot be immortal. Nevertheless, since these differences belong to the number of substantial differences, if they could somehow be joined, they too could produce their nature and species. To understand what power they have to produce substance and form a species, let us look to proper and common differences. Even when these are joined, they constitute neither species nor substance in any way. If someone speaks while walking—these being two common differences—or if he is tall and white, is his substance for that reason constituted by them? Certainly not. Why? Because they are not of the same genus as those things that can constitute and conform a substance.

Thus these differences—irrational and immortal—even if they cannot have some substance as their subject, could nevertheless produce a substance if they could in any way be joined and combined. Moreover, irrational joined with mortal produces the substance of an irrational animal. Therefore irrational is a constitutive difference. Likewise, immortal joined with rational produces God. Therefore immortal is a difference that forms a species. If these differences cannot be joined to one another, that does not remove the capacity that belongs to their nature.

These differences that are divisive of genera become complete and constitutive of species. Animal is divided by the differences rational and irrational, and again by the differences mortal and immortal. But rational and mortal are constitutive differences of a human being; rational and immortal are constitutive of God; irrational and mortal are constitutive of irrational animals. Likewise, the highest substance, although it is divided by the differences animate and inanimate, and sensible and insensible, when animate and sensible are gathered together with substance, they complete animal; animate and insensible complete a plant.

He shows that differences have a twofold use: one by which genera are divided, and another by which species are formed. Differences do not merely partition genera; while dividing genera, they also produce the species into which the genera are led. Thus those that divide genera become constitutive of species. His own example is this: the differences of animal are divisive—rational and irrational, mortal and immortal—for by these the predication of animal is divided. Everything that is an animal is either rational or irrational, either mortal or immortal. But these differences, which divide the genus animal, constitute the substance and form of the species.

Since a human being is an animal, he is produced through the differences rational and mortal, which had previously divided animal. Since a horse is an animal, it is constituted through the differences irrational and mortal, which had previously divided animal. God, however, since he is an animal—if we are speaking of the sun—is produced through the differences rational and immortal, which the division just mentioned showed to divide the genus.

Here, as we have said, God must be understood as corporeal, like the sun, heaven, and other things of this kind. Plato confirms that these are animate and rational, and antiquity, in its veneration, accepts them under the name “gods.” The differences are also shown to derive from the first genus, that is, substance. Since its divisive differences are animate and inanimate, and sensible and insensible, the differences sensible and animate, when joined together, produce animate, sensible substance, which is animal. It was therefore rightly said that the differences that are divisive of genera are also constitutive of species.

Since, then, the same differences, taken in one way, become constitutive and, in another way, divisive, they are all called specific. They are especially needed for divisions of genera and definitions of species—not, however, the inseparable differences according to accident, and still less the separable differences.

[Col. 0124D] No one is unaware that all differences proceeding from a genus divide the very genus from which they proceed. But when those that divide the genus are applied to subsequent species, they form their substances and complete them. Thus the differences that are constitutive of species are the same as those that are divisive of genera, although they are considered in different ways. When referred to the genus, they are found to be divisive of the genus because they are viewed in an opposed division. But when joined together they can produce something, they are constitutive of species.

Since this is so, the differences that divide the genus are rightly called divisive; those that constitute a species are called specific. But the differences that constitute a species are those that divide the genus. Therefore the same differences that are constitutive of species are called specific. Hence those that are divisive of genera and those that are constitutive of species are rightly called specific.

It is therefore clear that these must be employed in the division of a genus and in the definition of species. Since they are divisive, the genus must be divided through them; since they are constitutive, species must be defined through them, for the things by which each thing is constituted are also the things by which it is defined. A species is constituted by the divisive differences of the genus, which are specific. Rightly, then, these alone, both in the division of genera and in the definition of species, are placed among the specific differences.

This, then, is the account of specific differences. But from those that contain either separable or inseparable accidents nothing can be assumed for the division of genera or the definition of species. The reason is that divisive differences divide the substance of the genus, and constitutive differences constitute the substance of the species. Inseparable accidents, however, form the substance of no species; consequently, separable accidents are even less suited to the division of genera or the definition of species. They are altogether unlike substantial differences.

Inseparable accidents perhaps have this in common with specific differences—that is, with substantial differences: they likewise do not leave their subject, just as specific differences do not. Separable accidents do not even possess this characteristic. They can be separated not only by possibility and by the reasoning of the mind, but also in actuality and through the presence of action; they are altogether changed by variations in coming and departing.

[Col. 0125C] In defining them, they also say: “Difference is that by which a species exceeds its genus.” A human being has more than an animal in being rational and mortal. Animal itself is none of these things. For from where would species obtain their differences? Nor does the genus possess all opposites, for then it would have opposites simultaneously. Rather, as they prove, it possesses all the differences beneath it potentially, but actually none. Thus neither does anything arise from things that are not, nor will opposites be simultaneously in the same thing.

He concludes the definition of specific differences by saying that substantial differences are defined by some people through a description of this kind. A specific difference is that by which a species exceeds its genus. The genus is animal, the species human being. A human being therefore contains within himself the differences that constitute him—rational and mortal. Every species retains within itself the differences constitutive of its form and cannot exist apart from them, since it is perfected by their combination.

If, then, animal alone is the genus, while a human being is a mortal rational animal, a human being has more than an animal in possessing rationality and mortality. Is that by which the species exceeds the genus, and by which it has more than the genus, therefore the specific difference?

But a question appears to arise against this definition, deriving its starting point from two propositions known in themselves. One is that two contraries cannot be in the same thing; the other is that nothing comes from nothing. Contraries cannot endure one another in such a way that they are simultaneously in the same thing, and nothing can come into being from nothing. Everything that comes into being has something from which it can be produced and formed.

These propositions generate the following question. It has been said that a difference is what a species has more than its genus. What, then? Must we say that the genus does not have the differences that the species has? And from where would the species obtain differences that the genus does not have? Unless there is something from which they come, differences cannot enter into the species. If the genus does not have these differences but the species does, the differences appear to have entered the species from nothing, and something to have been made from nothing—something that the proposition stated above declares impossible.

But if the genus contains all the differences, and differences are divided into contraries, it will follow that animal, which is the genus, possesses rationality and irrationality, mortality and immortality simultaneously. Thus two pairs of contraries would be in the same thing, which cannot happen. Nor is it customary for one part of a body to be white and another black in this way within a genus. For the genus, considered in itself, has no parts except insofar as it is referred to species. Whatever it has, therefore, it will retain not in parts but in the whole extent of itself.

It is nevertheless not doubtful that the genus has contrarieties in its parts: animal has rationality in a human being, but its contrary in an ox. But now we are not asking about species, for it is established that this is what has been said. We are asking whether the genus itself, considered in itself, can have and contain within the scope of its substance the differences that species possess.

We resolve this question as follows. Anything that is can not-be, but in another way can be and in another way not-be. Socrates, for example, when he is standing, sits potentially but does not sit actually. When he is standing, it is clear that he is not performing the action of sitting but rather the immobility of standing. Yet when he is standing, he does sit—not because he is already sitting, but because he can sit. Thus actually he does not sit, but potentially he does sit.

An egg is likewise an animal and is not an animal. It is not an animal actually, for it is still an egg and has not yet advanced into the living development of an animal; but it is an animal potentially, because it can become an animal once it has received the form and species of life.

Thus the genus has these differences and does not have them: it does not have them actually, but it has them potentially. If animal is considered in itself, it does not have the differences. If it is reduced to species, it can have them, but distributively, so that nothing contrary can occur within it as a whole in relation to its species separately.

Accordingly, if the genus itself is considered in itself, it is without differences. But if it is referred to species through the distribution of species, it will retain contraries as though in its parts. Thus the differences that the genus retains potentially have not come from nothing, nor are both contraries in the same thing, since the thing called “genus” does not actually have contrary differences in itself.

The impossibility asserted by the proposition that contraries cannot be in the same thing consists in this: contraries cannot be in the same thing actually. But there is nothing to prevent two contraries from being in the same thing potentially and not actually. What we called contraries Porphyry now calls opposites. For “opposite” is the genus of “contrary”; all contraries, when considered in themselves, are opposites.

They also define it in this way: “Difference is that which is predicated of several things differing in species with respect to what sort of thing it is.” Rational and mortal, when predicated of a human being with respect to what sort of thing a human being is, are said with respect to quality, not with respect to what the thing is. If we ask what a human being is, the appropriate answer is “animal.” If we ask what sort of thing he is, we will appropriately assign “rational and mortal.”

There are three questions to which genus, species, difference, proprium, and accident are answers: what is it, what sort of thing is it, and how is it situated?
