If someone asks what Socrates is, it is appropriate to answer through genus and species, either “animal” or “human being.” If someone asks how Socrates is situated, the proper answer is an accident—for example, that he is sitting or reading, and so forth. But if someone asks what sort of person Socrates is, the answer will be a difference, proprium, or accident: for example, rational, capable of laughter, or bald.

In the case of the proprium, the following observation must be made: something can be called a proprium when it is predicated of one species. An accident, however, is something that designates a quality not signifying substance. A difference is something that displays substance. When someone asks what sort of thing each thing is, if we wish to give a quality of substance, we predicate a difference. This difference is never predicated of only one species, as mortal or rational, but of several.

That which is predicated of several species differing from one another, in answer to the question “what sort of thing is the thing in question?”, is a difference. Hence he gave the following definition: “Difference is that which is predicated of several things differing in species with respect to what sort of thing each is.” Explaining the cause and rationale of this definition, he says:

For things composed of matter and form, or constituted in likeness and proportion to matter and form, are as follows. A statue consists, with respect to matter, of bronze, and with respect to form, of shape. Likewise, both the universal and the particular human being consist proportionally, with respect to matter, of the genus and, with respect to form, of the difference. The whole of this—animal, rational, mortal—is a human being, just as the statue is a statue.

He said above that differences were predicated with respect to the quality of a species. Now he explains the reasons why a difference is the quality of a species. All things, he says, either consist of matter and form or acquire substance in likeness and proportion to matter and form. Everything corporeal subsists from matter and form. Unless there is a bodily subject to receive form, nothing at all can exist. If there had been no stones of such size, there would have been no walls or buildings; if there had been no wood, not even a table, which is made from the matter of wood, could exist.

When matter has been supplied and lies ready, and form comes upon it, the particular corporeal thing is produced, subsisting from matter and form. A statue of Achilles, for example, is completed from the matter of bronze and the form of Achilles himself.

It is clear that corporeal things subsist from matter and form. Incorporeal things, however, have, in likeness to matter and form, earlier and more ancient natures superimposed upon one another. Differences coming upon these produce something that, in the same way as a body, appears to consist as if from matter and shape. Thus, when differences are added to a genus, a species is produced.

As in the statue of Achilles bronze is the matter, while the form is the quality and particular shape of Achilles, from which the statue of Achilles is produced and apprehended by the senses, so in the species human being, its matter is the genus animal, and the quality rational, coming upon it, produces rational animal—that is, the species. The genus is therefore a kind of matter for the species, while the difference is, as it were, the form of its quality.

What bronze is in the statue, the genus is in the species. What the shaping figure is in the statue, the difference is in the species. What the statue itself is in the statue—namely, what is formed from bronze and figure—the species itself is in the species, since it is composed from genus and difference. If, then, the genus is a kind of matter for the species, while the difference is its form, and every form is a quality, every difference is rightly called a quality. Since this is so, it is rightly given in answer to those who ask what sort of thing something is.

They also describe differences as follows: “Difference is that which is naturally suited to divide things belonging under the same genus.” Rational and irrational divide human being and horse, which belong under the same genus, animal.

[Col. 0128C] Since this definition is customary and already plainly displayed, he has nevertheless clarified it further by the light of an example. All differences are called differences because they cause species included within one genus to differ from one another. Human being and horse, for example, differ through their proper differences. For just as a human being is an animal, so also is a horse; therefore they do not differ at all with respect to genus. Those that do not differ in any way with respect to genus are distributed through differences.

When rationality is added to the human being and irrationality to the horse, the horse and the human being, which had belonged under the same genus, are distributed and made distinct by the addition of differences.

They also assign the definition in this way: “Difference is that by which individual things differ from one another.” Human being and horse do not differ according to genus. We and irrational animals are animals; but the addition of rationality separates us from them. We and the gods are likewise rational; but the addition of mortality separates us from them.

Some people explain what they intend through a defective and unsound account in defining it. They say that difference is that by which each thing is distinct from another. In this definition it makes no difference whether they say this or conclude as follows: “Difference is that which is difference itself.” For they have used the term “difference” in the definition of the same difference, saying, “Difference is that by which individual things differ from one another.”

If difference is still unknown unless it is clarified by a definition, how can we recognize what it means to differ? The person who has used the term “difference” in the definition of difference itself has contributed nothing further to our knowledge.

Moreover, this definition is common and vague. It does not include substantial differences alone but any accidental differences as well: “Difference is that by which individual things differ from one another.” Things that are the same in genus differ through their differences. Thus, although human being and horse are the same in the genus animal, since both are animals, they differ through the difference rational. Although gods and human beings are placed under rationality, they differ through mortality.

Rationality, then, is the difference of a human being from a horse, and mortality is the difference of a human being from a god. In this way substantial differences are collected. But if Socrates is sitting while Plato is walking, sitting and walking will be differences, although not substantial ones. This definition seems to include these as well when it says, “Difference is that by which individual things differ from one another.” For in what way could Socrates differ from Plato except through accidents?

That too would be a difference according to the preceding definition. Those who saw that the definition had a vague and common conclusion criticized it and appended a more precise formulation.

On examining the matter more closely, however, they say that not every dividing feature that separates things belonging to the same genus is a difference, but only one that contributes to being, that is, one which is a part of it and of the being of the thing. For something naturally suited to sailing will not be the difference of human beings, even if it is a property of human beings. For we say that some animals are naturally suited to sailing, others not, thereby dividing human beings from the rest; but being suited to sailing will not complete the substance, nor will it be a part of it, but only a certain aptitude. Therefore, because it is not a difference of the kind that are called specific differences, specific differences will be those that make one species different from another and that are taken into the account of what the being of a thing is. Enough, then, has been said about differences.

[Col. 0129C]

The sense of this passage is as follows. Since above he said that some had defined difference as that by which individual things differ from one another, he says that others, examining the nature of difference more carefully, did not think that the definition proposed above was correct. For not everything that causes things placed under the same genus to differ can be called a difference of the kind now under discussion, that is, a specific difference.

There are many features that divide species placed under one genus while nevertheless doing nothing to constitute their substance. They do not seem to be specific differences except those that contribute to what it is to be—that is, those that are included as parts in the definitions of something. Such is the case with “rational” in the definition of human being. It constitutes the substance of a human being, contributes to the being of a human being, and is part of its definition. Therefore, unless it contributes to what it is to be and is a part of the being of the thing, it cannot in any way be called a specific difference.

What, then, is the being of a thing? Nothing other than its definition. For when someone asks of any thing, “What is it?”, anyone who wishes to show what its being is gives its definition. Therefore, if something is part of a definition, it will be a part of that which indicates what the being of each thing is. A definition is what displays and expresses what each thing is; and it is shown that the being of each thing is established through the assignment of its definition.

Those differences, however, that do not contribute to substance but introduce some external accident are not called specific differences, even though they make species placed under the same genus differ. Thus, if someone were to say that the difference between a human being and a horse is being suited to sailing, since a human being is suited to sailing whereas a horse is not, then, although horse and human being belong to the same genus, animal, the added difference “being suited to sailing” would distinguish the horse from the human being. But being suited to sailing is not of such a kind as to constitute the substance of a human being, as rationality does, which is a substantial quality. It merely displays, in a certain way, an aptitude and an opportunity for doing or not doing something; for this reason it is not called a specific difference.

It follows that not every difference that distributes species placed under the same genus can be specific, but only one that contributes to the substance of the species and is taken as part of its definition. He therefore concludes that specific differences are those that make species differ from one another through substantial distinctions. For if the being of each thing is whatever is substantial in it, then whatever differences are substantially diverse make the species in which they occur different and distinct in their entire substance; and these differences are taken as parts of definitions. For if a definition displays substance, and substantial differences produce species, substantial differences are parts of definitions.

[Col. 0129D]

## On Property

Property is divided into four kinds. First, that which occurs in one species alone, even if it does not occur in every member of that species, is a property—for example, being a physician or a geometer in a human being. Second, that which occurs in every member of a species, even if it is not exclusive to that species, as being two-footed in a human being. Third, that which occurs in every member of one species alone, but only at some time, as becoming gray-haired in old age in a human being. Fourth, that which occurs in every member of one species alone and always, as being capable of laughter in a human being. For even if a person does not always laugh, he is nevertheless called capable of laughter—not because he always laughs, but because he is naturally suited to laugh at all times. This is always natural to him, just as neighing is natural to a horse.

These are properly called properties because they are convertible: everything that is a horse is capable of neighing, and everything capable of neighing is a horse.

[Col. 0130A]

It was said above that all properties derive from the class of accidents. For whatever is predicated of something either informs its substance or inheres in it according to accident. Nothing, however, displays the substance of any thing except genus, species, and difference: genus and difference display the substance of a species, while species displays the substance of individuals. Whatever therefore remains is placed among accidents.

But since accidents themselves have some difference among them, some are called properties and others, by the earlier and more ancient name, accidents. We shall speak of accidents a little later. For now, concerning properties, which are divided into four kinds—not as though one property-genus could be divided and cut into four species, but the statement “they divide” must be understood as though he were saying “they name,” that is, “they call property fourfold”—he enumerates the meanings of this fourfold designation, in order to show what is a suitable and appropriate naming of property.

He therefore says that the first property is an accident that belongs to one species in such a way that it is in no way coextensive with that species, but falls short of it and remains below it, as being a physician is said to be a property of a human being because it cannot belong to any other animal. One should not ask whether this can be predicated of every human being, but only whether being a physician can be said of anything other than a human being. This meaning of property is called “belonging to one alone,” even if it does not belong to every member. For it belongs only to the species, even if not to every member of it: being a physician belongs only to human beings, but it is not present as a learned accomplishment in all human beings.

A second property is defined in the opposite way: it belongs to every member, although not exclusively to that species. It is of such a kind that it embraces the whole species and extends beyond it. Since there is nothing among the members of the species that does not use this property, we say that it belongs to every member. Since it extends to other species as well, we say that it does not belong to that species alone. Such is being two-footed in a human being. Being two-footed is a property of a human being: every human being is two-footed, although human beings are not the only two-footed creatures, since birds are also two-footed.

The two meanings of property mentioned above therefore each lack something. The first lacks universality, the second exclusivity. If we join them, we obtain “belonging to every member and to that species alone.” But we have removed something regarding time. If “sometimes” is added, this becomes the third designation of property: belonging to every member and to that species alone, but only sometimes. Such is becoming gray-haired in old age or reaching puberty in youth. Every human being reaches puberty in youth and becomes gray-haired in old age, and only human beings do so. Reaching puberty belongs to human beings alone, but only sometimes; for it does not occur at every time, but only in youth.

This determination of property is complete insofar as it belongs to every member and to that species alone, but it loses something when we add “sometimes.” If we remove that qualification, we obtain the complete and simple meaning of property: a property is that which belongs to every member, to that species alone, and always; for example, being capable of laughter in a human being and being capable of neighing in a horse. Every human being, and only a human being, is capable of laughter, and is so always; similarly, every horse, and only a horse, is capable of neighing.

[Col. 0131A]

Nor should the fact that a human being does not always laugh disturb us. For what is a property of a human being is not laughing but being capable of laughter; this exists not in actuality but in capacity. Therefore, even if a person does not laugh, because he nevertheless can laugh, being capable of laughter is said to belong always to every human being and to human beings alone, and is appropriately called a property. For if it is separated from the species in actuality, it is in no way separated from it in capacity.

He has therefore stated four meanings of property. The first occurs when an accident belongs to the subject species in such a way that it belongs only to that species, even if not to every member—for example, medical expertise in a human being. The second occurs when it does not belong only to that species, but is always joined to every member of it—for example, being two-footed in a human being. The third occurs when it belongs to every member and to that species alone, but only sometimes—for example, reaching puberty in youth in a human being. The fourth occurs when it belongs to every member, to that species alone, and always—for example, being capable of laughter.

For this reason the other kinds cannot be converted. What belongs only to a species but not to every member is not coextensive with it. The species can be predicated of the property, but the property cannot be predicated of the species. Someone who is a physician can be called a human being, but a human being cannot thereby be called a physician.

Again, what is a property of something in such a way that it belongs to every member but not to that species alone can itself be predicated of the species, but the species cannot be predicated of it. “Two-footed” can be predicated of “human being,” but “human being” cannot in any way be predicated of “two-footed.”

Again, what belongs to every member and to that species alone, but only sometimes, cannot be reciprocated, because it lacks something by reason of time and does not belong simply. We can say, “Everyone who reaches puberty is a human being,” but we do not say, “Everyone who is a human being reaches puberty,” since someone may never reach youth and therefore may not reach puberty. The property of human beings is not simply reaching puberty, unless perhaps reaching puberty is not a property of human beings at all, but only reaching puberty in youth. Even when someone has not yet reached youth, or has already passed beyond it, this property is said to belong to him—not in the form in which it can occur when he is outside youth, but in the form in which it occurs when he is in youth. Therefore, what does not extend through every period of time, even if it belongs to every member of a species, but is restricted to some particular time, is not called a complete and absolute property.

The fourth kind is that which belongs in such a way that it embraces the species alone, belongs to every member, and is free from temporal limitation. Such is being capable of laughter, which differs greatly from the preceding kind, since whatever is capable of laughter can always laugh. Again, whoever can reach puberty in youth does not possess this capacity always in youth, since youth itself is not permanent. This fourth meaning of property, which no temporal definition restricts, is complete; for this reason it is also convertible, and property and species are predicated reciprocally of one another. Every human being is capable of laughter, and everything capable of laughter is a human being.

[Col. 0131B]

## On Accident

An accident is that which is present and absent without the corruption of the subject. It is divided into two kinds: separable and inseparable. Sleeping is a separable accident; being black belongs inseparably to a raven and to an Ethiopian. Yet one can conceive both a white raven and an Ethiopian shining with whiteness, without corruption of the subject.

It is also defined in this way: an accident is that which can belong or not belong to the same thing, and which is neither genus, species, difference, nor property, but always subsists in a subject.

Now that everything proposed has been determined—namely genus, species, difference, property, and accident—it remains to say what they have in common and what is proper to each.

[Col. 0132C]

As was said above, everything predicated of something is predicated either substantially or accidentally. Since things predicated substantially contain the substance and definition of that of which they are predicated, and since they are prior to and greater than what is produced from substantial predicates, it follows that when things said substantially perish, those whose nature and substance they formed must perish at the same time.

Since this is so, things said accidentally, because they do not inform the substance, can be present and absent without corruption of the subject. For only those things can corrupt the subject when they are absent that constitute and conform what is substantial. Things that do not constitute substance, such as accidents, neither inform nor corrupt the substance when they are present or absent.

An accident, then, is that which is present and absent without corruption of the subject. It is divided into two parts: one accident is separable, another inseparable. A separable accident is sleeping or sitting. An inseparable accident is the black color of an Ethiopian or a raven.

Here a difficulty arises. It has been defined as follows: an accident is that which is present and absent without corruption of the subject. Yet the same accident is sometimes called inseparable. If it is inseparable, it cannot be absent. It was therefore pointless to state that an accident is something that can be present and absent, since there are some accidents that cannot be separated from their subjects.

But things that cannot be separated in actuality can often be separated in the mind and in thought. If qualities separated from their subjects by the mind’s reasoning do not destroy them but remain and endure in their own substance, they are understood to be accidents.

Let us therefore suppose that the black color cannot be removed from an Ethiopian. If we separate it mentally and in thought, the Ethiopian will be white. Does the species therefore perish? Certainly not. Likewise, if we separate the black color from a raven in imagination, the bird nevertheless remains, and the species has not perished.

[Col. 0132D]

Therefore, when it is said that something is present and absent, this must be understood not in reality but in the mind. Otherwise, we would often separate substantial attributes that cannot be separated at all in reality by the mind and in thought. For example, if we remove rationality from a human being—a quality that we cannot separate from him in actuality—but separate it through the imagination of the mind, the species of human being immediately perishes. This does not happen with accidents. When an accident is removed in thought, the species remains.

There is also another definition of accident, framed through the exclusion of all the others: an accident is that which is neither genus, species, difference, nor property. This definition is extremely vague and very general. For genus too could be defined as that which is neither species, difference, property, nor accident; and species, difference, and property could be defined in the same way.

But when many things can be defined by the same likeness of definition, the description is not limiting or enclosed. It is especially far from the completeness of a definition when it displays the form of one thing through the negation of other things.

With all this completed—that is, genus, species, difference, property, and accident—and with their boundaries described as far as the brevity of an introductory treatment required, he proceeds to examine them collectively. He will show what differences these five things, discussed above, have among themselves and what they have in common, with moderate analysis, so that it may become clear not only what each of them is, but also how they are related to one another.

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0133]

[Col. 0133C]

Having completed individually everything he proposed and having briefly brought each matter, insofar as its consideration permitted, to the limits of knowledge, he now treats not the nature of the individual items—genus, difference, species, property, or accident—but their relation to one another.

Since he is collecting the common features and differences of things, he does not consider those things in themselves, but according to how they are related to other things. This takes place in two ways: by similarity, when he examines their common features, and by dissimilarity, when he examines their differences. Since this is so, we too, following the philosopher’s steps as we have done up to now for the sake of clearer understanding, shall begin with the common features belonging to genus, species, difference, property, and accident.

[Col. 0133D]

All five share the fact that they are predicated of many things. Genus is predicated of all the species under it and of individuals; difference is predicated similarly. Species, however, is predicated of the individuals under it. Property is predicated both of the species of which it is the property and of the individuals under that species. Accident is predicated both of species and of individuals.

Thus “animal” is predicated both of horses and of oxen, which are species, and of this horse and this ox, which are individuals. “Irrational” is predicated of horses and oxen, and likewise of their individual members. “Human being,” moreover, is predicated of individual human beings. “Capable of laughter” is predicated both of human being and of individual human beings. Finally, “black” is predicated of a raven and of ebony, and of their individual instances; this is an inseparable accident. Similarly, “to move” is predicated of human being and horse, and of their individual instances; this is a separable accident. It is predicated primarily of individuals, but secondarily also of the things that contain the individuals.

Before discussing the relation of each item to each of the others, he first considers the relation that all of them appear to have to one another. This is one common feature that includes all five proposed things through the plurality of their predication: all are predicated of many things.

In this respect, therefore, they all share something. Genus is predicated of many things, and so are species, difference, property, and accident. Accordingly, they have one common and undivided feature: being predicated of many things.

Porphyry indicates how this predication of many things occurs in each case and shows of how many things each of the proposed items is predicated. He says that genus is predicated of many things, that is, of species and of the individuals of species. Thus “animal” is predicated of human being and horse, and of the individuals that fall under them.

Genus is also predicated of the differences of species, and rightly so. Since species are informed by differences, and since genus is predicated of species, it follows that it is also predicated of those things that constitute the substance and form of species. Thus genus is also predicated of differences, and not of one difference only but of several. For what is rational is said to be an animal, and what is irrational is likewise said to be an animal.

[Col. 0134C]

Genus is therefore predicated of species and differences, and of the individuals under them. Differences, in turn, are predicated of many species and of their individuals. Thus “irrational” is predicated of horse and ox, which are several species, and in the same way it is said of the individuals under them. For whatever is predicated of a universal is also predicated of an individual.

If a difference is predicated of species, it will also be predicated of the subjects belonging to the same species.

Species, however, is predicated only of its own individuals. For it cannot happen that what is the lowest species, and what is truly and most properly called a species, is further divided into other species. If this is so, only individuals remain below the species. Species is therefore rightly predicated only of its own individuals, as “human being” is predicated of Socrates, Plato, Cicero, and the others.

Property likewise is predicated of the species of which it is the property. Otherwise it would not be the property of anything. For whatever is said of something alone, and of every member of it, and always, is shown to be its property. Since this is so, property is predicated of the species, as “capable of laughter” is predicated of “human being,” for every human being is capable of laughter.

It is also predicated of the individuals of the species of which it is predicated. Socrates, Plato, and Cicero are capable of laughter.

Accident, on the other hand, is predicated both of several species and of individuals of different species. A raven and an Ethiopian are said to be black, and this Ethiopian and this raven, which are individuals, are likewise said to be black. They are called black according to the quality of blackness; this is an inseparable accident.

Separable accidents inhere in even more individuals, as “to move” in human beings and oxen; both move. Again, the individuals under human being and ox are often said to move.

It must be observed, on Porphyry’s authority, that accidental predicates are said primarily of the individuals in which they are present. Secondarily, they are referred to the universals of the individuals; thus the predication of lower things is transferred to higher things. Since blackness is said to be present in individual ravens, it is also said to be present in the species raven. Since this quality of accidental blackness affects all the individual members, we also predicate the same blackness of the species, saying that the species raven is black.

[Col. 0135A]

In all this it may seem surprising that he did not say that genus is predicated of property, nor that species is predicated of property, nor that difference is predicated of property, but only that genus is predicated of species and differences; difference of species and individuals; species of individuals; property of species and individuals; and accident of species and individuals.

For it can happen that things with a more extensive predication are predicated of all the lesser things, and that things equal to one another are convertible. Hence genus is predicated of differences, species, properties, and accidents. Thus, when we say, “What is rational is an animal,” genus is predicated of difference; when we say, “What is a human being is an animal,” genus is predicated of species; when we say, “What is capable of laughter is an animal,” genus is predicated of property; and when we point to a raven or an Ethiopian and say, “What is black is an animal,” genus is predicated of accident.

Again, when we say, “What is a human being is rational,” difference is predicated of species. When we say, “What is capable of laughter is rational,” difference is predicated of property. When we say, “What is black is rational,” pointing to an Ethiopian, difference is predicated of accident.

Likewise, when we say, “What is capable of laughter is a human being,” species is predicated of property. When we say, “What is black is a human being,” pointing to an Ethiopian, species is predicated of accident.

In the same way, when we say, in pointing to an Ethiopian, “What is black is also capable of laughter,” property is predicated of accident. Conversely, accident can be predicated of the other four as a whole, since it is predicated primarily of the individual things and is thereby also predicated of the higher terms. Since Socrates is an animal, he is rational, capable of laughter, and a human being. Since baldness, which is an accident, is present in Socrates, the same accident is predicated of animal, rational, capable of laughter, and human being. Thus accident is predicated of the other four.

This is a deeper question, and there is not enough time to resolve it. For now, let the understanding of beginners attend only to this: some predicates are made in the direct order, while others are made in an oblique order. “A human being is moved” is direct, whereas “what is moved is a human being” presents the proposition in reversed expression. Porphyry therefore took the proper proposition throughout. If anyone considers the force of predication and resolution by comparing the individual predications, he will find that Porphyry counted those expressions that are in the proper order, while setting aside those whose predication is in reversed order.

[Col. 0135B]

It is common to genus and difference that they contain species. Difference also contains species, although not as many as genus does. For although “rational” does not contain irrational things as “animal” does, it nevertheless contains human being and god, which are species.

Whatever is predicated of genus as genus is also predicated of the species under it. Likewise, whatever is predicated of difference as difference is also predicated of the species that arise from it.

Since genus is animal, not only are substance, animate, and sensible predicated of it, but all these are also predicated of every species under animal, down to individuals. Since the difference is rational, “to use reason” is predicated of it as a difference. It is not only predicated of what is rational, but also of the species under rational.

It is also common to genus and difference that, when genus or difference is removed, the things under them are removed at the same time. Just as, if animal does not exist, neither horse nor human being exists, so, if rational does not exist, there will be no animal that uses reason.

[Col. 0135C]

After the common feature that appeared to belong to all of them, he seeks the similarities and differences of each item in relation to the others. Since genus and difference have the more universal predication among the five proposed things—genus containing both species and differences, while differences contain species and are in no way contained by them—he first collects the similarities of genus and differences.

He first sets out the following similarity. He says that genus and difference have in common that they enclose species. For just as genus has species under it, so does difference, although not as many as genus has.

Since genus also encloses difference, and does not confine and retain only one difference under itself, it must have more species under it than any one of the differences it contains. Thus “animal” is predicated of rational and irrational. If this is so, it will also be predicated of the species placed under rational and of those placed under irrational.

There is therefore something common to animal and rational—that is, to genus and difference: just as genus is predicated of god and human being, so rational, which is a difference, is predicated of god and human being.

But this predication does not extend as widely as that of animal, that is, of genus. Animal is predicated not only of god and human being, but also of horse and ox, which rational does not reach.

Whenever we include god under animal, we do so according to the opinion of those who affirm that the sun, the stars, and the entire world are animate; they also called these things “gods,” as has often been said.

A second common feature of genus and difference is that whatever is predicated of genus as genus is also predicated of the species under it, and whatever is predicated of difference as difference is likewise predicated of the species under that difference.

The meaning may be explained as follows. There are several things predicated of genera as genera. For example, animate and substance are said of animal, and are said of it as genera. These are therefore predicated of the things under animal, again as genera. For both animate and substance are genera of human being, just as they were previously genera of animal.

Likewise, among differences there are certain differences that are predicated of differences themselves. Two differences are said of rational. For what is rational either uses reason or possesses reason. To use reason is one thing, and to possess reason another, just as to possess sensation is one thing and to use sensation another.

A sleeping person possesses sensation but does not use it. In the same way, a sleeping person possesses reason but does not use it. Therefore “to use reason” is a difference of rationality, while human being is placed under rationality. “To use reason” is therefore predicated of human being as a difference. For a human being differs from the other animals because he uses reason.

[Col. 0135D]

It has therefore been demonstrated that just as what is predicated of genus is said of the things subject to the genus, so what is predicated of difference is said of the things subject to their differences.

A third common feature is that just as, when genera are removed, species perish, so, when differences are destroyed, the species of which those differences are predicated perish. It is common to universals that when they perish in substance, their subjects perish as well.

The first common feature demonstrated that genera are predicated of species, as are differences. Because of this similarity, if genera are removed, species perish. In the same way, the species under differences must perish if their universal differences are destroyed.

An example is the following. If animal is removed, human being and horse are removed, since they are species placed under animal. If rational is removed, human being and god are removed, since they are placed under the difference rational.

So much for the common features. He now considers the dissimilarity between genus and difference.

[Col. 0136A]

It is proper to genus that it is predicated of more things than difference, species, property, and accident. Animal is predicated of human being, horse, bird, and serpent. “Four-footed,” however, is predicated only of things having four feet; human being is predicated only of individual human beings; and “capable of neighing” only of horse and of the individuals belonging to it. Accident likewise is predicated of fewer things than genus.

One must understand here the differences by which genus is divided, not those that complete the substance of genus.

Moreover, genus contains difference potentially. For of animal, one part is rational and another irrational. Differences, however, do not contain genera.

Furthermore, genera are prior to the differences placed under them, and for this reason they remove those differences together with themselves, but are not removed by them at the same time. When animal is removed, rational and irrational are removed; but differences do not remove genus. Even if all the differences perish, the substance “animate, sensible” can still be conceived, and this is animal.

Moreover, genus is predicated in answer to “What is it?”, while difference is predicated in answer to “What sort of thing is it?”, as was said.

Moreover, there is one genus for each species—for example, animal is the genus of human being—but there are several differences, such as rational, mortal, and receptive of intellect and learning, by which human being differs from other things.

Moreover, genus is analogous to matter, while difference is analogous to form. Since there are also other common and proper features of genus and difference, let this suffice for now.

The definition of what a property is has been given with an appropriate and complete term. But, by an abuse of language, those attributes are also called the properties of anything whatsoever which, in each thing, contain a distinction from others, although those very attributes are common with others. [Col. 0138D] Strictly speaking, what is proper to a human being is that which is present in every human being, only in human beings, and always, such as the capacity for laughter. By an improperly extended expression, however, rationality is also called a property of the human being—not a property in itself, since the nature of human rationality is common to human beings and the gods—but rationality is called proper to human beings in order to distinguish them from cattle, which are not rational. The reason is that whatever someone possesses as his own is called his property; therefore, whatever distinguishes someone from another may, without absurdity, be called his property.

But when he now says that it is proper to a genus to be predicated of more things than the other four, this is a property of the genus of the same kind as what is ordinarily called a property in itself: namely, that it is present always, only, and in every instance of the genus. For it belongs only to the genus that it is predicated more broadly and abundantly than difference, species, property, and accident. [Col. 0139A]

But this may be said of those differences, properties, and accidents which fall under some genus: of differences, that is, which divide any given genus; of species, which are formed by the difference dividing the genus; of the property belonging to the species under that genus which is divided by the differences; and of accidents which adhere to the individuals belonging to that species encompassed by the designated genus.

Examples make this clearer. Let the genus be *animal*; let *quadruped* and *biped* be the differences contained under animal; let *human being* and *horse* be the species established under the same genus; let *capable of laughter* and *capable of neighing* be the properties of those species; and let *swift* and *warlike* be the accidents which occur in the individuals contained under the species human being and horse. [Col. 0139B]

Animal, therefore, which is a genus, is predicated of quadruped and biped, which are differences. But quadruped is not predicated of biped; it is said only of those animals which have four feet. The genus, therefore, is predicated more broadly than the difference.

Again, human being is predicated of Plato, Socrates, and others; but animal is predicated not only of human individuals, but also of the individuals of other irrational kinds. The genus, therefore, is predicated more broadly than the species.

Again, since the property of a horse is its capacity for neighing, and since a genus is predicated more broadly than a species, the predication of the genus also exceeds the predication of its property.

An accident too, although it may be present in more things, is often found more narrowly restricted than a genus: for example, *warlike* is properly said only of a human being, and swiftness is found in only a few animals. Thus the genus is predicated more broadly than the difference, the species, the property, and the accident. [Col. 0139C]

This, then, is one property of the genus by which the genus is separated and distinguished from all the others.

“But,” he says, “one must now understand those differences by which the genus is divided, not those by which the genus is formed.” For the latter, by which the genus is formed, are undoubtedly predicated more broadly than the genus itself. Thus *animate* and *corporeal* extend beyond *animal*, although they are differences of animal—not divisive differences, but rather constitutive ones. For everything superior is predicated of what is inferior. Whatever is predicated of inferior things, however, and cannot be converted with them, is predicated more broadly than those inferior things.

After this he shows another property of the genus by which it is separated from the differences placed under the same genus. [Col. 0139D] Every genus contains its differences potentially, whereas a difference cannot contain a genus. Animal potentially contains the rational and the irrational; rationality or irrationality, however, cannot contain animal.

He says that animal contains its differences potentially because, as was stated above, the genus has all its differences beneath it potentially, but not actually. From this another property arises. When the genus is removed, the difference perishes: when animal is removed, rationality, which is a difference, is destroyed. But if rationality is removed, irrational animal remains.

Someone might object: What if I remove both differences at once—will the genus be able to remain? [Col. 0140A] We say that it can. For each thing derives its substance not from the things of which it is predicated, but from the things by which it is constituted. Thus the genus can remain when its divisive differences have been removed, provided that those differences remain which constitute the form and substance of the genus itself.

Since animal is constituted by the differences *animate* and *sensible*, if these remain and are joined together, animal cannot perish, even if those things of which animal is predicated—namely, rational and irrational—perish. For each thing, as has been said, derives the character of its substance from that by which it is constituted, not from that of which it is predicated.

Moreover, although the genus contains both differences potentially, it does not, in itself, place or enclose either of them within itself actually. If, then, it does not contain them actually but only potentially, it can also be separated from them actually. For the very fact that it contains them potentially meant that it did not contain them actually. Since the genus does not actually contain every difference, it is also actually separated from those differences. [Col. 0140B]

Again, there is another property of the genus, recognized from the character of its predication. Every genus is appropriately given as the answer to the question “What is each thing?” Thus animal is predicated of human being in the category of what it is. A difference, however, is not so predicated, but in the category of what sort of thing it is; for every difference consists in quality.

But this property is of the kind we mentioned above—not a property in itself, but one stated in relation to a certain difference. Otherwise it is common to the genus and the species that they are predicated in answer to the question “What is it?” But because the genus differs from the difference in this respect—because the difference is predicated in the category of what sort of thing something is, whereas the genus is predicated in the category of what it is—it is called a property of the genus, not in itself, but in comparison with the difference. [Col. 0140C]

The same principle must be observed in all the remaining cases. Whatever is called a property of the genus in such a way that it is common to nothing else, but is possessed by this genus alone and always, is called a property in itself. Whatever is common with something else is called a property not in itself, but in relation to the difference of the other thing.

There is another separation between genus and difference: a single genus is always present in a species, namely its proximate genus. There may be several superior genera, as in the case of human being, whose genera are animal and substance; but the proximate genus of human being is animal alone. Several differences, however, can belong to one species, such as rational and mortal to human being. [Col. 0140D]

Thus a definition is formed from one genus but several differences, as in the definition of human being: animal, rational, and mortal.

There is another distinction: the genus occupies, as it were, the place of a subject, while the difference occupies the place of form. The genus is a kind of matter which receives a shape; the difference is the form which, supervening upon the species, completes its substance and account.

For this reason he separated the difference from the genus by several distinctions, because this difference contains a certain great likeness to the genus: it is universal, and, apart from the genus, is the greatest among the other things. But although many other common features and many properties of the genus and the difference can be found, “let these suffice for now,” he says. [Col. 0141A] For it is enough, for distinguishing them, to select whatever differences are appropriate, even if not everything that can be said is collected.

Genus and species have in common, as has been said, that they are predicated of several things. Let species be taken as species alone, and not as genus, if the same thing is both species and genus. They also have this in common: that they are prior to the things of which they are predicated, and that each is in a certain way the whole of what it contains.

He enumerates three common features of genus and species. The first is that both are predicated of several things: the genus is predicated of species, as has been said, while the species is predicated of individuals. But now he is speaking of a species which is species only, such as human being—that is, one which is not also a genus, but is a lowest species. [Col. 0141B]

If we posit a species which can also be a genus, and say that it has in common with genus that it is predicated of several things, it makes no difference whether we say that the genus itself has this in common with itself, namely, being predicated of several things. For such a species is not only a species but also a genus.

It is also common to them that both are prior to the things of which they are predicated. Everything predicated of several things, if it is stated in the proper order, as was said above, is prior to the things of which it is predicated.

They have this further feature in common: genus and species are each the whole of the things which they contain and encompass within their own scope. For the genus is the whole of all its species, and the species is the whole of all its individuals. Genus and species alike unite many things; and whatever unites many things, bringing them back to the form of unity, is rightly called their whole. [Col. 0141C]

They differ in that the genus contains species, whereas the species is contained and does not contain genera. For the genus is predicated of more things than the species.

Moreover, genera must lie prior to species and, when formed by specific differences, complete them. Hence genera are naturally prior, and when they are removed they remove the species with them, although they are not themselves removed by the species. For if a species exists, its genus exists; but if a genus exists, a species will not necessarily exist.

Genera are predicated univocally of species, but species are not predicated of genera.

Moreover, genera exceed the species beneath them by containing them, whereas species exceed genera by their proper differences. Further, a species will never become the most general, nor will a genus ever become the most specific. [Col. 0141D]

Having completed the discussion of what genus and species have in common, he now treats their distinction. He says that genus differs from species because the genus contains species, as animal contains human being, whereas species does not contain genera; human being is not predicated of animal.

Thus the species is contained by genera but never contains genera. For whatever is predicated more broadly contains that which is predicated more narrowly. Since the genus is predicated more broadly than the species, it is necessary that the species be contained by the genus, while the genus is in no way included within the scope of the species’ predication.

The reason is that the genus, by always receiving a difference, makes a species. That is, a genus, whose predication is broadest, is narrowed and contracted by differences into a species. For a difference joined to a genus altogether produces a species and contracts it from universality and the broadest predication into the narrow limit of a species. [Col. 0142A]

Animal, whose predication is in itself widely and extensively distributed, contracts and narrows into the single species human being when it receives the differences rational and mortal. Thus the species is always smaller than the genus and is therefore contained by it, but does not contain it. When the genus is removed, the species is removed: if the whole is taken away, the part will not remain. If the species is removed, however, the genus remains. Thus, when animal is removed, human being is also destroyed; if human being is removed, animal remains.

This is also why the genus is predicated univocally of the species: the species receives the definition and name of the genus, but not conversely, since the species does not appear to be received by the genus. Inferior things receive the substance of superior things. [Col. 0142B]

If you define animal and say that it is an animate, sensible substance, or if you predicate animal of human being, you will have spoken truly. If you also predicate the definition of animal of human being and say that human being is an animate, sensible substance, there will be nothing false in the proposition. But if you give the account of human being as animal, rational, mortal, these features do not apply to animal; for what is animal cannot be called rational and mortal animal.

Thus, just as the species receives the name of the genus, so it also receives its definition. And just as the genus does not receive the name of the species, so it is not shown by the definition of the species. Whatever has both a name and a definition predicated of something is predicated univocally of it. Since both the name and the definition of the genus are predicated of the species, the genus is said univocally of the species. [Col. 0142C]

Since neither the name nor the definition of the species is predicated of the genus, the univocal predication is not convertible.

Genera differ from species in another way: genera surpass their species by containing other species, while species surpass genera by the multitude of their differences. Animal, which is a genus, surpasses human being, which is a species, because it contains not only human being but also ox, horse, and other species which it includes within the range of its predication.

A species such as human being surpasses its genus, animal, by the multitude of its differences. For the genus does not actually possess rational or mortal differences; genus retains no differences actually, whereas species have those differences attached and implanted in their substance. Human being is rational and mortal, but genus is not. Animal is neither mortal in itself nor rational. [Col. 0142D]

If, then, the genus contains more than one species, while species are formed by many differences, the genus surpasses the species by containing species, whereas the species surpasses the genus by the multitude of differences.

There is also this difference: since the genus is first of all things, it can never descend so far as to become the last; and since the species is below everything, it can never rise so high as to become the highest of all. Therefore a species will never become the most general, nor a genus the most specific. [Col. 0143A]

Among the differences that have been stated, some distinguish genus from species specifically and in conjunction with it; others distinguish not only genus from species but also genus from the remaining things. For if we seek to recognize the proper rule of distinction, we must consider not only the differences that have been mentioned, but also those concerning the other items.

Genus and property have in common that they follow the species. If something is human being, it is animal; and if something is human being, it is capable of laughter.

They also have in common that the genus is predicated equally of its species, and the property of the individuals that participate in it. Human being and ox are equally animals, and Cicero and Cato are capable of laughter. [Col. 0143B]

Finally, they have in common that they are predicated univocally: the genus of its proper species, and the property of those things of which it is the property.

For the time being he says that genus and property have three common features. The first is that they follow the species in the same way as the property. Once a species has been posited, we must understand both the genus and the property, for neither leaves its own species: if something is human being, it is animal; if something is human being, it is capable of laughter. Thus, just as the genus does not depart from the species, so the property does not depart from the species of which it is the property.

They also have in common that participation in the genus is equal, just as participation in the property is equal. Every genus is participated in equally by its species, while a property adheres equally to all individuals.

It is clear that the property is equal to the genus in respect of participation. [Col. 0143C] Human being is not more animal than horse or ox; insofar as they are animals, they equally derive the name animal—that is, the name of the genus. Cato and Cicero are equally capable of laughter, even if they do not laugh equally. For they can be called capable of laughter insofar as they are suited to laughing, not because they always laugh.

Thus the things belonging under a genus receive the genus equally, just as the things belonging under a property receive the property equally.

The third common feature is that, just as the genus is predicated univocally of its proper species, so the property is said univocally of its species.

Since the genus contains the substance of the species, not only its name but also its definition is predicated of the species. But because the property does not leave the species, is always equal to it, does not extend to another species, and does not fall short of it, it also gives its definition to the species. [Col. 0143D]

Since a name belongs to only one species and is equal to it, there can be no doubt that its definition also applies to that species. Thus, just as the genus is predicated univocally of species, so the property is predicated univocally of its species.

They differ, however, because the genus is prior and the property posterior. Animal must exist first, and afterward be divided by differences and properties.

Moreover, the genus is predicated of several species of which it is the genus, whereas the property is predicated of only one species of which it is the property.

Further, the property is predicated convertibly of that of which it is the property, whereas the genus is predicated convertibly of nothing. For if something is animal, it is not necessarily human being, nor, if something is animal, is it necessarily capable of laughter. But if something is capable of laughter, it is human being, and conversely. [Col. 0144A]

Moreover, the property is present in every instance of the species to which it belongs, only in that species, and always. The genus is present in every species of which it is the genus and always, but not only in that species.

Further, when properties are removed, they do not at the same time remove the genera; but when genera are removed, they remove the species whose properties they are. Therefore, when the things of which they are the properties are removed, the properties themselves are removed at the same time.

Again, he takes a property which is called a property in relation to something else. He says that it is a property of the genus to be prior to properties.

The genus must be prior, since it is placed beneath the differences like matter; when the differences arrive, it becomes a species, together with which the properties arise. If the genus is prior to the differences, and the differences are prior to the species, while properties are coequal with species, there is no doubt that properties are posterior to genera. [Col. 0144B]

Accordingly, it was said to be a property of the genus that it is prior to properties. This is common to the genus and the difference. For the differences which form the species are considered prior to the properties. Indeed, they are prior to the species themselves, which they determine by their proper nature.

But, as was said, this property must be understood in relation to the distinction of property, not as the property in itself established above.

Again, genus differs from property because the genus is predicated of several species, whereas the property is not. For there is no genus unless it produces several species from itself, and there is no property if it can be common to any other species.

Thus the genus has several species beneath it, as animal has human being and horse; but the property has only one, as the capacity for laughter has human being. From this difference another property arises: the genus is predicated of species, but is itself not placed beneath anything in predication; property and species, however, exchange places in convertible predication. [Col. 0144C]

Predication proceeds either from greater things to lesser things, or from equal things to equal things. The genus, therefore, which is greater, is predicated of all its species; but species, being lesser, are not predicated of genera. Thus animal is said of human being, but human being is in no way predicated of animal.

The property, however, since it is equal to the species, is predicated and placed before it equally. Thus capable of laughter is said of human being: every human being is capable of laughter, and the converse also holds: everything capable of laughter is human being.

Property also differs from genus in that property is present in one species, in every instance of it, and always; genus retains two of these features but differs in one. It is present in its species always and in all of them, but not only in them. [Col. 0144D]

For this was proper to properties alone: to contain only one species; whereas it belongs to genera to contain several. Properties, therefore, each possess one species, while genera do not possess only one. The property is thus present in one species alone, always, and in every instance; the genus is present in every instance and always, but not only in that species.

Thus the capacity for laughter belongs only to human being, whereas animal belongs to human being but not only to human being; for it is also present in all the things we call irrational.

Moreover, if we remove the genus, the species are destroyed. If animal does not exist, human being will not exist. If we remove the species, however, the genus is not destroyed: if human being does not exist, animal will not perish. [Col. 0145A]

Species and properties, however, since they are equal, destroy one another reciprocally. If the capacity for laughter does not exist, human being will not exist; if human being does not exist, the capacity for laughter will not remain. Thus genera destroy the species placed beneath them but are not mutually destroyed by those species; species and properties, on the other hand, destroy and are destroyed by one another.

Genus and accident have in common that they are predicated of several things, as was said, whether the accident is separable or inseparable. For *to be moved* is predicated of several things, and *black* is predicated of crows, Ethiopians, and certain inanimate things.

Nothing among the other categories is so far removed from the nature of genus as accident. [Col. 0145B] The genus displays the substance of whatever it is the genus of, whereas accident is far removed from substance and comes from outside. Accident therefore has no more evident feature in common with genus than being predicated of several things.

The genus is predicated of several species; accident, however, is predicated not only of several species but also of animate and inanimate genera. Thus *black* is said of a rational human being, an irrational crow, and inanimate ebony. *White* is said of a swan and marble; *to be moved* is said of a human being, a horse, stars, and things that are agitated. These are examples of separable accidents.

Genus differs from accident because the genus is prior to species, whereas accidents are posterior to species. Even if an inseparable accident is taken, that which the accident affects is nevertheless prior by nature to the accident. [Col. 0145C]

Things that participate in a genus participate in it equally, whereas things that participate in accidents do not participate equally. For participation in accidents admits of increase and diminution, whereas participation in genera does not.

Accidents principally inhere in individuals; genera and species, however, are naturally prior to individual substances.

Genera are predicated of the things beneath them in the category of what they are; accidents are predicated in the category of what sort of thing each is or how each is disposed. If asked what sort of person an Ethiopian is, you answer, “Black”; and if asked how Socrates is disposed, you answer, “He is sitting” or “He is walking.”

He first proposes this distinction between genus and accident: the genus is prior to species, since it occupies the place of matter and, when formed by differences, produces species; accident, however, is found to be posterior to species. [Col. 0145D]

That which something happens to must exist first, and the accident itself must supervene afterward. For if there is no subject to receive it, the accident cannot exist. Since the genus is subject to species, species cannot exist unless the genus is posited beneath them like matter. Accidents, however, cannot exist unless species are posited beneath them. It is therefore clear that the genus is prior to species, whereas accidents are posterior to species.

Again, there is another difference: the genus can receive neither increase nor diminution. Consequently, those that participate in a genus receive its name and definition equally. All human beings are equally animals, and horses likewise; and when human being, horse, and the other animals are compared with one another, they are predicated equally as animals. [Col. 0146A]

Participation in an accident, however, is capable of increase and diminution. You will find someone walking a little longer and someone somewhat blacker; and if you consider Ethiopians themselves, you will find that not all are covered with black color to the same degree.

There is another difference: every accident principally subsists in individuals, whereas genera are prior to species and individuals. Unless individual crows were affected by blackness, the species crow could in no way be called black. Thus accidents appear to be posterior to individuals.

For if that which something happens to is prior to the thing that happens to it, there is no doubt that individuals are prior and accidents posterior. Genera and species, however, are considered above individuals, because they are predicated of all of them and constitute their substance by their proper predication. [Col. 0146B]

It may be said that genera and species too are found to be posterior to individuals. Unless individual human beings and individual horses exist, the species human being and horse cannot exist; and unless the individual species exist, their genus animal cannot exist.

But we must remember that it was said above that the genus does not derive its substance from the things of which it is predicated, but rather from that by which its substance and form are completed—namely, its constitutive differences.

Thus, if the genus is not destroyed when its divisive differences are removed, but remains in those differences which are constitutive of it and complete its form and definition, and if the divisive differences of the genus are prior to its species—for they form and constitute the species—it is not doubtful that the genus can remain in its own substance even when the species perish. The same must likewise be said of species: their substance remains. [Col. 0146C]

Species are formed by superior differences, not by posterior individuals. Since this is so, species also subsist before individuals. Accidents, however, cannot exist unless there are things which they affect, and they affect nothing prior to individuals. For individuals, subject to generation and corruption, are continually changed by various accidents.

He also counts the distinction mentioned above: since the genus signifies a thing and is predicated of substance, it is stated in answer to the question “What is it?” Accident, however, is stated in answer to the question “What sort of thing is it?” or “How is the thing disposed?”

If you ask about a quality, an accident will be given as the answer: “What sort of thing is a crow?” “Black.” If you ask how it is disposed, another accident is given: “It is sitting,” “it is flying,” or “it is croaking.” [Col. 0146D]

Since accident is divided into the nine categories—quality, quantity, relation, place, position, possession, time, action, and passion—all the remaining categories are included in the question “How is it disposed?” Quality, however, is usually given in response to an inquiry about quality. If we are asked what sort of thing an Ethiopian is, we answer with an accident, namely, “black.” If we ask how Socrates is disposed, we say either that he is sitting, walking, or in some other of the accidental states mentioned above.

It has been said how genus differs from the other four. [Col. 0147A] It also happens that each of the other things differs from the remaining four. Since there are five things, and each differs from the other four, one might think that four times five gives twenty differences among them all. But the matter is not arranged in that way. Rather, when the later items are enumerated, the second is surpassed by one difference because that difference has already been counted; the third by two, the fourth by three, and the fifth by four. Thus all the differences amount to ten: four, three, two, and one.

It has been stated how genus differs from difference, species, property, and accident. There are therefore four differences of genus.

How difference differs from genus was stated when the way in which genus differs from difference was explained. It remains to say how difference differs from species, property, and accident; thus there are three. [Col. 0147B]

How species differs from difference was stated when the way in which difference differs from species was explained. How species differs from genus was stated when the way in which genus differs from species was explained. It remains, therefore, to say how species differs from property and accident; these are two differences.

It remains to say how property differs from accident. For how property differs from genus, species, and difference was already stated in the differences of those things from property.

Thus, taking four differences of genus in relation to the others, three of difference, two of species, and one of property in relation to accident, there are ten differences in all. Of these, the four belonging to genus in relation to the remaining items have been demonstrated above. [Col. 0148A]

Since he intends to set forth in the same way the differences and common features of genus in relation to difference, species, proprium, and accident, and likewise those of the others, he first states how many all the differences can be that arise when the things set out above are compared and combined with one another. There are twenty. For since there are five things, and each of these things differs from the other four, five times four differences are produced, as is shown by the example of the letters placed beside one another.

Let there be five things, as it were five letters, *a, b, c, d,* and *e*. Let *a* differ from the other four, namely *b, c, d,* and *e*: there will be four differences. Again, let *b* differ from the other four, namely *a, c, d,* and *e*: there will again be four, [Col. 0148B] which, joined to the preceding ones, make eight. Then *c*, the third, differs from the remaining four, namely *a, b, d,* and *e*. These four differences, added to the preceding eight, produce twelve. Fourth, if *d* is compared with the other four, it likewise differs from those same four, namely *a, b, c,* and *e*. Thus four more will be produced, which, added to the preceding twelve, make sixteen. If finally *e* differs from the other four, namely *a, b, c,* and *d*, four further differences will be produced; combined with the earlier ones, they complete twenty. Let the arrangement therefore be as follows.

[Col. 0147] [Col. 0147C]

This being so, the same consideration will also be applied to genera, species, and the other categories. There will therefore be four differences by which genus is separated from difference, species, proprium, and accident. Again, there will be four by which difference is distinct from genus, species, proprium, and accident. Again, four of species in relation to genus, difference, proprium, and accident. Also four of proprium in relation to genus, difference, species, and accident. Moreover, four of accident in relation to genus, difference, species, and proprium. Taken together, these explain all twenty differences.

But this will be so if the nature of number and the alternation of comparison are taken into account. For if the attentive reader looks to the actual natures of the differences, he will find the same differences counted repeatedly. For by the same respect in which genus differs from difference, [Col. 0147D] difference is distant from genus; and by the same respect in which difference is distant from species, species is separated from difference; and the same applies in the other cases. Thus, in the arrangement of the differences that I set out above, I have counted the same ones several times.

But if we remove the similarities among the differences, there will be ten differences in all, which, for the purposes of the present discussion, must be taken as distinct and dissimilar. Let genus differ from difference, species, proprium, and accident: these are four differences, as we have already said. Let us likewise take difference: it will first be distant from genus, and then [Col. 0148C] from species, proprium, and accident. But how it differs from genus has already been explained, when we said how genus differs from difference. Once this comparison has therefore been removed, since it has already been mentioned, three discrepancies remain, by which difference is separated from species, proprium, and accident. Joined to the preceding four, these produce seven differences.

Next, if species is taken, it will have four differences according to numerical distinction, when it is compared with genus, difference, proprium, and accident. But the first two comparisons have already been stated. For how species differs from genus was stated when we were explaining how genus differs from species; and how species is distant from difference was mentioned when we were giving the differences of difference in relation to species. [Col. 0148D] Once these have been removed, two complete and untouched discrepancies remain: those of species in relation to proprium and accident. Joined to the seven, these make nine differences.

If proprium is considered numerically, it will have four differences—when compared with genus, difference, species, and accident—but three of these have already been stated above. For how proprium differs from genus was explained when we showed how genus differs from proprium. Again, how proprium differs from difference was demonstrated in gathering the distance between difference and proprium. [Col. 0149A] And how proprium differs from species was explained when we were saying how species is distant from proprium. One difference therefore remains: that of proprium in relation to accident. Joined to those already given, it completes ten differences.

Accident could indeed have four differences in relation to the others, unless all of them had already been shown to have been used up. For how genus, difference, species, and proprium differ from accident has been demonstrated above; and there are no more differences of accident in relation to the others than of the others in relation to accident. Thus, since the number of things is five, if the first is taken, there are four differences; if the second, three, and the differences of the second thing in relation to the others are exceeded by only one difference of the first in relation to the others. For when the first has had [Col. 0149B] four, the second retains three; if the third is taken, it will have two differences, which are exceeded by two of the first four differences; if the fourth is taken, it will have one difference, which is exceeded by three of the first four differences; and the fifth, since it will have no new difference at all, is exceeded by all four of the first differences. In this numerical progression, therefore, the count extends to ten: four, three, two, one—so that genus has four, difference three, species two, proprium one, and accident none.

The first comparisons of genus contain four new differences. The second comparisons, those of difference, contain three new differences: one was counted above, and it is exceeded by only one of the first four new differences. [Col. 0149C] The third comparison, that of species, has only two new differences, since we recognize that two were counted above; it is exceeded by only two of the first four new differences. Proprium retains only one new difference, since three were counted above, and it is exceeded by three of the first new differences. The comparisons of the fifth, accident, retain no new difference, and therefore it is exceeded by all four of the first differences of genus.

In this way, then, the twenty differences, according to number, are contracted into ten according to dissimilarity. Yet, so that we may also recognize these differences according to dissimilarity not only in the number five but in every other number, the following rule may be given, which will discover the complete dissimilarity of differences [Col. 0149D] in any plurality of things.

From the number of proposed things subtract one, and multiply what remains after the subtraction by the whole numerical sum. Half of the result of the multiplication will equal the plurality contained by the differences of the proposed things. Let there be four things, *a, b, c,* and *d*. I subtract one from these, leaving three. I multiply these by the whole number, four: the result is twelve. If I take half of this, there will be six. Thus there will be six differences when four things are compared with one another: *a* retains three differences in relation to *b, c,* and *d*; again, *b* has two in relation to *c* and *d*; and *c* has one in relation to *d*. Joined together, these complete the number six. [Col. 0150A] For the present, it is enough simply to have given this rule, without proof. In the exposition of the Categories, the reason why this is so will also be explained.
