The common feature of difference and species is that they are participated in equally: for particular human beings participate equally in man, and equally in the difference “rational.” It is also common to them that they are always present in the things that participate in them. Socrates is always rational, and is always a human being.

It has often been said that the things which constitute substance are neither contracted by diminution nor increased by intensification: for what each thing is is one and the same. If difference displays the substance of species, and species that of individuals, both are equally separated from intensification [Col. 0150B] and diminution, and consequently they are participated in equally. For all individuals are mortal and rational in the same way as human beings. If being a human being is the same as being rational, and all human beings are equally human beings, they must necessarily be equally rational.

Difference also has another feature in common with species: just as species do, differences do not abandon the things that participate in them. Socrates is always rational. For Socrates, who participates in rationality, is always a human being, because he participates in humanity. Therefore, just as differences do not abandon the things that participate in them, so species are always attached to the things that participate in them.

The proprium of difference is to be predicated in answer to “what sort of thing is it?”; the proprium of species is to be predicated in answer to “what is it?” [Col. 0150C] For even if “human being” is taken as a quality, it will not be a quality simply, but according to the fact that differentiating features, arriving in addition to the genus, constituted it.

Furthermore, difference is often considered in several species, as “quadruped” is found in several animals differing in species; species, however, is found only in the individuals that fall under one species. Furthermore, difference is prior to the species beneath it: if “rational” is removed, “human being” is destroyed; but if “human being” is destroyed, “rational” is not removed, since God remains. Furthermore, difference can be combined with another difference: “rational” and “mortal” are combined in the substance of human being. Species, however, cannot be combined with species so as to generate another species. A particular mare is mixed with a particular ass for the generation of a mule, but a mare simply, that is, universally, joined to an ass [Col. 0150D] would never produce a mule.

[Col. 0150D]

Having explained the common features of difference and species insofar as their instruction required, he now gathers their dissimilarities, saying: Species differ in that they are predicated in answer to “what is it?”, whereas difference is predicated in answer to “what sort of thing is it?”

A question could arise concerning this difference. If humanity itself, which is a species, is a certain quality, why is species said to be predicated in answer to “what is it?”, when it appears to be a certain quality because of a particular property of its nature? We answer that difference alone is a quality, whereas humanity is not merely a quality but is completed by quality. Difference, arriving upon [Col. 0151A] a genus, makes a species. Thus the genus is formed by a certain quality of difference so that it may proceed into a species. The species itself is indeed qualified according to its difference, which is a pure and simple quality, by which the species is completed and conformed; but the species is not itself a pure and simple quality. Rather, it is a substance produced from qualities. Therefore, difference, which is purely and simply a quality, is rightly answered in terms of “what sort of thing is it?”; species, however, in terms of “what is it?”, even though species itself is also a certain quality—not a simple quality, but one informed by other qualities.

There is again another difference: difference contains several species beneath it, whereas species presides only over individuals. Rationality includes both human being and God; “quadruped” includes horse, ox, dog, [Col. 0151B] and the rest; human being, however, includes only individuals. The same reasoning applies to the other species.

For this reason the definitions also followed: difference was called that which is predicated of several things differing in species in answer to “what sort of thing is it?”; species, that which is predicated of several things differing in number in answer to “what is it?” Differences are therefore of a higher nature than species, since they contain species. If someone removes a difference, he also removes the species: if someone removes rationality, he destroys both human being and God. If someone removes human being, however, rationality remains established in the other species. Difference therefore differs from species in that one difference can contain several species, whereas species cannot do so in any way.

There is another difference: one species is composed from several [Col. 0151C] differences, whereas no species-substance is joined together from several species. Human being is produced from the combination of “mortal” and “rational”; but no species is ever formed from the combination of species.

If someone objects that a horse mixed with an ass produces a mule, he would not be speaking correctly. Individuals joined to individuals may perhaps produce other individuals; but horse simply, that is, universally, and ass universally, can neither be mixed nor produce anything if they are combined in thought. It is therefore clear that many differences can converge upon the substance of one species, whereas species can in no way converge upon the nature of another species.

Difference and proprium have in common [Col. 0151D] that they are participated in equally by the things that participate in them: rational things are equally rational, and things capable of laughter (*risibilia*) are equally capable of laughter. It is also common to both that they are present always and in all cases. For even if the biped is maimed, what it is naturally fitted to be is still predicated of it; and “capable of laughter” is likewise always predicated of what is naturally fitted to have it—not in the sense that it is always laughing.

He now continues, in connected discourse, with the common features of difference and proprium. He says that it is common to proprium and difference that they are participated in equally: all human beings are equally rational and equally capable of laughter. The former is so because it displays substance; the latter because it is equal to its proper species and does not abandon the species subject to it.

He adds another feature common to them: difference is always equally present in its subjects, [Col. 0152A] like proprium. Human beings are always rational, just as they are always capable of laughter. But an objection could be raised: a human being is not always biped, although “biped” is a difference, if he is maimed by the loss of one foot. We resolve the question in the following way. Propria and differences are said always to be present in their subjects not because they are always actually possessed, but because they can always be possessed naturally. If someone is maimed in the foot, this does not affect the nature, just as the proprium is not removed merely because a human being does not laugh. These are said to be always present not because they are actually present, but because they can be present by nature. We say that “always” here means by nature, not in actuality.

For it can never happen, through the property of nature itself, that a human being is not always biped, even if it can happen that he is maimed in [Col. 0152B] one foot or both, or even born with a defective foot. In such cases, it is not the species and substance that are diminished, but the individual who is born.

The proprium of difference is that difference is often predicated of several species, as “rational” is predicated of human being and God; proprium, however, is predicated of only one species, whose proprium it is. Furthermore, difference follows those of which it is the difference, but the implication is not reciprocal. Propria, however, are predicated reciprocally of the things whose propria they are, because they are convertible.

Difference differs from proprium because difference encloses several species and is predicated of all of them; proprium is joined to and equal to one species alone. “Rational” is predicated of human being and God; “quadruped” of horse and the other quadrupeds. “Capable of laughter,” [Col. 0152C] however, contains only one species, namely human being. Thus difference always follows species, whereas species does not follow difference.

Species and proprium, however, accompany one another in reciprocal predication. Something is said to follow when, after one thing has first been named, the other is subsequently correctly named. Thus, if I say, “Every human being is rational,” I have placed human being first and the difference second; difference therefore follows species. But if I reverse the terms and say, “Every rational thing is a human being,” the proposition is not true. Species therefore does not in any way accompany difference. Proprium and species, however, follow one another reciprocally because they can be converted: “Every human being is capable of laughter,” and “Everything capable of laughter is a human being.”

Difference and accident have in common [Col. 0152D] that they are predicated of several things. It is also common to difference and inseparable accidents that they are always and in all cases present in their subjects: “biped” is always present in all crows, and “black” likewise.

He proposes two common features of difference and accident. One is common to difference and both inseparable and separable accidents; the other separates separable accident from them. Only inseparable accident is included in the second common feature.

It is common to difference and all accidents that they are predicated of several things. For separable and inseparable accidents alike are predicated, like difference, of several species and individuals. Thus “biped” is predicated of crow and swan, and of the individuals that fall under crow and swan. [Col. 0153A] Likewise “white” and “black,” which are inseparable accidents, are predicated of the same crow and swan. We say “walk,” “stand,” “sleep,” and “wake” of the same things; these are separable accidents.

The other common feature seems to include only those accidents that are inseparable. For just as difference always clings to the species subject to it, so inseparable accidents also never appear to abandon their subject. As “biped,” which is a difference, never abandons the species of crows, so neither does “black,” which is an inseparable accident. Difference does not abandon its subject because it completes and perfects its substance; an accident of this kind is inseparable because it cannot be separated. It could not be an inseparable accident if it ever abandoned its subject.

[Col. 0153B]

They differ in that difference contains and is not contained. Rationality contains human being and God. Accidents, however, in a certain way contain, because they are present in several things, and in a certain way are contained, because subjects are not receptive of one accident only but of many. Difference is not subject to intensification or diminution, whereas accidents admit of more and less.

Furthermore, contrary differences cannot be mixed, whereas contrary accidents can be mixed. Such, then, are the common features and properties of difference and the other categories. How species differs from genus and difference has been stated when we were explaining how genus and difference differ from the others. It remains to say how species differs from proprium and accident.

[Col. 0153C]

After giving the common features of difference and accident, he now discusses their differences and first proposes the following: Every difference, he says, contains a species. Rationality contains human being, because rationality is predicated of more things than the species “human being.” For it extends beyond the substance of human being and reaches as far as God.

Accidents, however, sometimes contain and sometimes are contained. They contain because any one accident is accustomed to be present in several species: “white,” for example, in swan and stone; “black” in crow, Ethiopian, and ebony. They are contained because several accidents occur in one species, so that the species appears to contain several accidents. When it happens to an Ethiopian to be black, it also happens to him to be flat-nosed and curly-haired. Since all these are accidents [Col. 0153D] of the Ethiopian, the species “human being” appears to include within itself several accidents.

An objection could be made: differences too are contained in one way and contain in another, since rationality contains human being—being predicated of more things than human being—but is also contained by human being, because human being contains not only this difference but also “mortal.”

We answer as follows: whatever is predicated substantially of several things cannot be contained by the things of which it is predicated. Consequently, difference is not contained by species, even if several differences inform the species. Accidents, however, are contained because accidents constitute the substance of a species in no act of predication. [Col. 0154A] In fact, accidents are not properly called universals when they are predicated of several species, whereas differences are especially and properly called universals.

Whatever things are universals of other things must necessarily also contain the substance of those things of which they are universals. Consequently, because differences display substance, they lack intensification and diminution: each substance is neither capable of contraction nor of relaxation. Accidents, however, since they make no claim to constitute substance, increase through intensification and decrease through diminution.

There is also this difference between them: contrary differences cannot be combined so as to produce something from them, whereas contrary accidents can be combined, and some intermediate can arise from either contrary. Nothing can be combined into one thing from rational and irrational; [Col. 0154B] from white and black, however, when combined, an intermediate color is produced.

Having explained the distances of difference from the other categories, it remains to speak of species. We previously gathered its differences in relation to genus when we discussed the differences of genus in relation to species; and we also stated the distances of species from difference when we displayed the dissimilarities of difference in relation to species. It remains, therefore, to join species to proprium and accident by their common features, and then to separate them by their differences.

The common feature of species and proprium is that they are mutually predicated: if something is a human being, it is capable of laughter; and if it is capable of laughter, it is a human being. “Capable of laughter” is to be understood according to what is naturally fitted to laugh, as has often already been said. It is also common to them that they are participated in equally: species are equally present in the things that participate in them, and propria equally in the things [Col. 0154C] whose propria they are.

[Col. 0154C]

He says that proprium and species have in common reciprocal predication of one another. For just as species is predicated of proprium, so proprium is predicated of species: as human being is capable of laughter, so what is capable of laughter is a human being. He recalls that this has already been stated, and adds the reason for their common feature: namely, that species are participated in equally by individuals, just as the propria are equally present in the things whose propria they are.

This reason does not appear to be suited to the conversion of predication, but rather to another similarity: just as species are equally participated in by individuals, so too are propria. Socrates and Plato are equally human beings, just as they are equally capable of laughter. We should therefore perhaps take the added statement as introducing another common feature: [Col. 0154D] “species are equally present in the things that participate in them, and propria in the things whose propria they are.”

Or should it rather be understood in this way, as though he were saying: Species and propria are equal? Since species are the species of the things that participate in species themselves, and propria are the propria of the things that participate in propria, species and proprium are equally present in both sets of things—that is, species do not exceed the things that participate in species, nor do propria exceed the things that participate in propria. And since these are the propria of species, it is necessary that species and proprium be equal and mutually predicated.

Species differs from proprium because species can also be the genus of other things, whereas it is impossible for proprium to be the genus of other species. Species also subsists before proprium, whereas proprium comes to be later in the species: human being must exist first for “capable of laughter” to exist.

Furthermore, species is always actually present in its subject, whereas proprium is sometimes present in actuality but always in potentiality. Socrates is always actually a human being, but he is not always actually laughing, although he is by nature always capable of laughter.

Furthermore, things whose definitions differ also differ themselves. The definition of species is to be under a genus and to be predicated of several things differing in number in answer to “what is it?”, along with other features of this kind. The definition of proprium is to be present in one species, in all instances of it, and always.

[Col. 0155A]

He says that the first difference between proprium and species is that species can sometimes be transferred into other species, that is, can be a genus. Thus animal, although it is a species [Col. 0155B] of animate being, can be the genus of human being. But he is not now speaking of those species that are most specific; and he appears to fall into the following confusion: although he had proposed to speak of the species that are ultimate, he now discusses those that are subordinate and often occupy the position of genus.

Propria, however, can in no way be genera, because they are equal to the most specific species. Since they cannot be genera, neither can the propria that are equal to them be genera.

Again, species always subsists before proprium. Unless there is a human being, “capable of laughter” cannot exist. Although the two are simultaneous, the conception of the substance precedes the account of the proprium. For every proprium is placed in the genus of accident. It differs from accident in that it contains the force [Col. 0155C] of proper predication around one single species only; accident, when it contains, can be extended to many species.

Since substances are prior to accidents, and species is a substance while proprium is an accident, there is no doubt that species is prior and proprium posterior.

Species are also distinguished from proprium by the nature of actuality and potentiality. Species is always actually present in individuals; propria, however, are not always present in actuality, but always in potentiality. Socrates and Plato are actually human beings, but they do not always actually laugh. They are called capable of laughter because, even if they are not laughing, they can nevertheless laugh.

Thus species is always present in its subjects by nature, just as proprium is; but species is always present in actuality, whereas proprium is not always present in actuality, as has been said.

Again, since definition displays substance, and things whose [Col. 0155D] definitions are different must have different substances, the definitions of species and proprium are different; therefore their substances are different. The definition of species is to be under a genus and to be predicated of several things differing in number in answer to “what is it?” This has frequently been explained above, and there is no need to repeat it here. Proprium is defined as that which is present in one species, in all instances of it, and always. Since the definitions differ, species and proprium plainly differ according to the boundaries of their natures.

The common feature of species and accident is that both are predicated of several things. Their other common features, however, are rare, because accident and that which suffers the accident are very far apart.

[Col. 0156A]

He says that the common similarity of species and accident is that both are predicated of several things. He says that their other common features are rare because that which happens as an accident and that to which it happens are widely different. The thing that suffers the accident is the subject and underlying bearer; the thing that occurs as an accident is superimposed and belongs to an arriving nature. Likewise, what is placed beneath is a substance, whereas what is predicated as an accident comes from outside.

All these considerations produce a great difference between the subject and the accident. Nevertheless, other common features of species and inseparable accident can also be found, such as always being present in subjects. Human being is equally always present in individual human beings, and inseparable accidents are present in individual things. [Col. 0156B] It is also common that, just as species is predicated equally of the individuals it contains, accidents are predicated of several individuals. “Human being” is predicated of Socrates and Plato; “black” and “white” are predicated of the several crows and swans in which they occur.

The distinctive features of the two are as follows: species is predicated of the things whose species it is in answer to “what is it?”; accident is predicated in answer to “what sort of thing is it?” or “how is it disposed?”

Furthermore, each substance participates in one species but in several accidents, both separable and inseparable. Species can also be understood before accidents, even if the accidents are inseparable. The subject must exist first for something to happen to it. Accidents belong to a later genus and to an adventitious nature.

Participation in species is equal; [Col. 0156C] participation in accident, even if the accident is inseparable, is not equal. One Ethiopian will have a more or less intense color than another Ethiopian with respect to blackness.

It remains to speak of proprium and accident. How proprium differs from species, difference, and genus has already been stated.

What he now promises to explain concerning the proprium of species and accident must be understood as the proprium mentioned above, spoken of in comparison with differing things. Species is predicated in answer to “what is it?”, whereas accident [Col. 0156D] is predicated in answer to “what sort of thing is it?” By this difference species is distinguished not only from accidents but also from differences and propria; and not only species, but genus as well.

Moreover, the fact that species is predicated in answer to “what is it?”, while accident is predicated in answer to “how is it disposed?”, is also common to species and genus. Genus too is distinguished from accident by predication in answer to “what is it?” and “how is it disposed?”

Likewise, each substance appears to contain one species. Thus Socrates is contained by the one species human being, and consequently only the species human being is immediately related to Socrates. Again, an individual horse has the one species horse immediately above it, and the same applies to the other cases. One species therefore presides over each substance, whereas more than one accident is joined to each substance. Several accidents always come upon each substance: Socrates is bald, flat-nosed, gray-eyed, and has a protruding belly. The same can be said [Col. 0157A] of the number of accidents in other substances.

Next, species are always understood before accidents. Unless there is a human being to whom an accident occurs, there can be no such accident; and unless there is some substance to which an accident can be joined, it will not be an accident. Every substance is contained by its proper species. Species is therefore rightly understood first, and accidents later, since, as he says, they belong to a later genus and to an adventitious nature.

Things that do not inform substance are rightly called adventitious in nature and later in genus. They are present in substances that have already been informed by differences.

Again, since species displays substance, and substance, as has been said, is without intensification and diminution, participation in species does not admit intensification or diminution. Accident, however, even if it is inseparable, can vary through increase and decrease of intensification [Col. 0157B] and diminution, as with the inseparable accident that belongs to Ethiopians, blackness. In some it can be present so as to approach dark brown; in others, so as to be exceedingly black.

It remains now to pursue the common features and differences of proprium and accident. How proprium differs from genus, species, and difference was demonstrated above, when we showed how genus, species, and difference differ from proprium. What remains is to consider the commonality and difference that join proprium to accidents or separate it from them.

The common feature of proprium and inseparable accident is that the things in which they are considered never exist apart from them. For just as human being does not subsist apart from “capable of laughter,” so an Ethiopian does not subsist apart from blackness. And just as proprium is present always and in all instances, so too is inseparable accident.

[Col. 0157C]

Since proprium is always present in species and never abandons them in any way, and since inseparable accident cannot be separated from its subject, this appears to be common to them: the things in which they are present cannot exist apart from their propria and inseparable accidents.

He compares inseparable accidents with proprium because, as was said concerning species, similarities between species and accident are exceedingly rare; consequently, common features between proprium and accident are even more difficult to find. Accident is customarily divided into contraries: inseparable accident and separable accident. Things that are divided into contraries under a genus participate in nothing other than the predication of that genus. [Col. 0157D]

If proprium is a certain inseparable accident, it differs greatly from separable accident; for that reason, he does not seek any similarities between proprium and separable accident. But since proprium itself differs from inseparable accidents according to certain fixed principles, common features and differences between them can also be found.

One of these is the one explained above; the second is that, just as proprium is always present in every instance of its species, so too is inseparable accident. Just as “capable of laughter” is present in every human being and always, so blackness is present in every crow and always attached to it.

[Col. 0158A]

They differ in that proprium is present in one species alone, as “capable of laughter” is present in human being; inseparable accident, such as blackness, is present not only in an Ethiopian but also in a crow, in coal, in ebony, and in certain other things.

Furthermore, proprium is reciprocally predicated of the thing whose proprium it is; inseparable accident is not reciprocally predicated. Participation in propria is equal, whereas in accidents one thing participates more and another less.

There are also other common features and properties of the matters discussed, but these are sufficient both for distinguishing them and for presenting their common features.

The first difference between a proprium and an accident is that a proprium is always predicated of one species alone, whereas an accident is not; its predication extends to many substances and species of different kinds. For example, “risible” is predicated of nothing other than a human being. But “black,” which is an inseparable accident in certain cases, belongs both to a crow and to an Ethiopian, which differ in species, and to a crow and ebony, which differ not merely in species but also in genus. Hence, in the case of propria, conversion is maintained equally, but in the case of accidents it is not.

For since propria have their being in individual things and comprise all their proper species, they are predicated in convertible order. For whatever is risible is human, and whatever is human is risible. Black, however, does not behave in this way: it can be predicated of those things in which it is present, but those things cannot be converted and referred back so as to be predicated of black. For “black” is predicated of coal, ebony, a human being, and a crow, but these are not predicated of black. Things that contain many items can be predicated of the things they contain; but things contained cannot in any way be predicated of the things containing them.

Again, a proprium is participated in equally, whereas an accident varies through degrees of diminution and intensification. Every human being is equally risible, but an Ethiopian is not equally black: as has been said, one is found to be somewhat less black, another exceedingly black.

Enough has now been said about the differences between a proprium and an accident. It remained to explain the common features and properties of an accident in relation to the other things; but these have already been enumerated when we set out the similarities and differences of genus, difference, proprium, and accident. Perhaps a mind instructed and sharpened by these matters will discover, besides those we have now mentioned, other common features and differences among the five things set out above. But for distinguishing them and comparing their similarities, what has been said is generally sufficient.

Since we are also reaching the harbor of the work we promised, and since we have disclosed the entire sequence of this book—first translated into Latin prose by the rhetorician Victorinus and afterward rendered by us in a twofold exposition—we here set a conclusion to this lengthy work, which contains a discussion of the five things and serves the Categories.

[Col. 0159]

# ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS, FOUR BOOKS ON ARISTOTLE’S CATEGORIES. (C)

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0159A]

Having completed the matters arranged for the Categories of Aristotle according to Porphyry’s instruction, I have also written these commentaries on the Categories, following a continuous exposition in a moderate style. I have not mixed into it any treatment of more advanced questions, but, observing a due measure in making things clear, I have wished neither to burden the reader with brevity nor to confuse him through excessive length.

Accordingly, the intention of this work should first be briefly disclosed. It is as follows. With things already existing before us and remaining principally established in their own natural constitution, the human race alone arose with the ability to impose names upon things. Thus it came about that the human mind, proceeding through everything individually, attached particular words to particular things. For example, it called one body “human being,” another “stone,” another “wood,” and another “color.” Again, whoever had begotten another from himself it named by the word “father.” It also defined a measure of magnitude by means of a proper form of name, saying that something was two feet long or three feet long, and so on in the same way with other things.

When all the names had been arranged, the mind returned to the properties and forms of the words themselves. It called that form of word which can be inflected through cases a noun; that which can be distributed through tenses, a verb. The first imposition of names, therefore, was that by which something subject either to the understanding or to the senses was designated. The second consideration was concerned with observing the individual properties and forms of the names, so that the primary name might be the very word for the thing—for example, when any particular thing is called “human being.”

When that very word, namely “human being,” is called a noun, this does not refer to the signification of the noun itself, but to its form, because it can be inflected through cases. Thus the first imposition of the noun was made according to the signification of the word, whereas the second was made according to its form. The first imposition was that names should be imposed upon things; the second, that the names themselves should be designated by other names.

For since “human being” is the word for the substance that is subject, what is called “human being” is the noun of “human being,” that is, the designation of the noun itself. We ask, “What sort of word is ‘human being’?” and the proper answer is, “A noun.”

The intention of this work, then, is to discuss the first names of things and the words signifying things—not insofar as they are formed according to some property or form, but insofar as they are signifying. For whatever is said of a substance, whether as doing or undergoing something, is not treated as though one of these could be inflected through cases and the other varied through tenses, but as though it signified either a human being, a horse, some individual thing, or a species or genus.

The intention of this work, therefore, is to treat words signifying things insofar as they are signifying. This is a position suitable to the time and purpose of an introductory and straightforward exposition. Following Porphyry, we have now arranged it in the form that seemed easier and clearer.

There is, however, a plan to discuss the intention, usefulness, and order of the work in three questions, in another commentary that I have proposed to compose on these same Categories for more learned readers. One of those questions is what the intention of the Categories means. There, after setting out the opinions of different writers, we shall teach which view our own judgment also follows. Let no one be surprised that our present position does not agree with that one, when he sees how much more advanced the other is, and that minds not greatly initiated could scarcely have been capable of it. We have written this work to provide moderate instruction for them.

Those whom we are preparing to admit to this science must therefore be affected and, so to speak, disposed by a moderate exposition at the very doors of this discipline. Let the reader recognize that this is the reason why the position of the two works has been changed: the former is adapted to perfect Pythagorean science and doctrine, while this one is adapted to the explanatory instruction of beginners.

But let us now return to our subject. For the present, let the intention of the Categories be the one stated above: to discuss the first words signifying the first genera of things, insofar as they are signifying. Since things are infinite, it is necessary that there also be infinitely many words signifying them; but there can be no knowledge of the infinite, for the infinite cannot be comprehended by the mind. What cannot be encompassed by reason cannot be enclosed within the limits of any science. Therefore there is no science of the infinite.

Aristotle, however, does not here deal with the infinite significations of things. Rather, by establishing ten Categories, he determined the classes to which the infinite multitude of signifying words should be referred. For example, when I say “human being,” “wood,” “stone,” “horse,” “animal,” “lead,” “tin,” “silver,” “gold,” and other things of this kind—which are unquestionably infinite—all these are reduced to one word, “substance.” This one name of substance includes these and any other words of the same kind, however infinite their number may be.

Again, when I say “two-footed,” “three-footed,” “six,” “four,” “ten,” “line,” “surface,” “solidity,” and whatever other things of the same kind are infinite, they are all contained under one name, “quantity,” so that all these are placed under quantity.

Again, when I say “white,” “knowledge,” “good,” “bad,” and other things of this kind, which are also infinite within their genus, there is nevertheless one name, “quality,” which includes them all. The same applies to the other Categories.

Thus Aristotle enclosed the indeterminate and infinite multitude of diverse things within the very small number of the ten Categories, so that things which could not fall within knowledge because they were infinite might be confined within the comprehension of science by being defined according to ten proper genera.

The ten Categories, then, are genera of the significations of infinite numbers of words. Since every signification of words concerns things, however, and since the things signified by words are signified insofar as the words are signifying, they necessarily signify genera of things.

To sum up the intention: this book contains a treatment of the first words signifying the first genera of things, insofar as those words are signifying.

[Col. 0161B]

Since the intention has been explained, the usefulness of the work must now be stated briefly. Although infinite things were signified by infinitely many words and, as has been said, could not enter into knowledge, through the definition by which the division of the ten Categories was made we acquire a science of all things and of the signifying words.

This is why, for those moving toward logic, this book is the first to be read. Since all logic is constituted by the reasoning of syllogisms, syllogisms are joined together from propositions, and propositions consist of speech, the first usefulness of this book is to recognize, through the definition of its proper science, what each expression signifies.

This examination of the ten Categories is also extremely useful to us in Aristotle’s physical doctrine and in the knowledge of moral philosophy, as will become clearer to those who proceed through each subject individually.

For the same reason, the order of the book is also appropriate. Since simple things are prior by nature to composite things—for composite things are composed from simple ones—and since this work discusses simple words signifying things, this first book of Aristotle is learned by beginners according to the primary nature of simplicity itself.

Nor is there much doubt about what part of philosophy the intention of this book concerns. Since the person who treats signifying words will also treat things to some extent, and since things and the signification of things are joined together, the more important discussion will be the one concerning expressions; second will be the discussion formed from the reasoning of things.

Since every logical art concerns discourse, and since this work principally treats words, its principal reference is to logic, although it is also related to the other parts of philosophy. I have principally discussed here what are in a certain way its simple elements, namely expressions.

This is Aristotle’s book, and not the book of any other author, because throughout philosophy he himself agrees with the discussion of this work. Its brevity and subtlety also do not differ from Aristotle. Otherwise, a person writing about syllogisms would appear to have produced an interrupted and incomplete work if he had either omitted propositions or passed over the treatment of the first words in which the propositions themselves are contained.

Although there is another book of Aristotle that discusses the same matters and contains almost the same material in different wording, this book has the stronger claim to authenticity.

Archytas also composed two books entitled *Universal Accounts* (*Καθόλους Λόγους*), in the first of which he arranged these ten Categories. For this reason, certain later writers suspected that Aristotle was not the inventor of this division, since a Pythagorean had written the same things. The philosopher Iamblichus is not insignificant among those who hold this view.

Themistius does not agree with him, however. Nor does he concede that this was Archytas the Pythagorean of Tarentum, who had lived for some time with Plato. Rather, he supposes that it was some Peripatetic Archytas, who gave authority to a new work by the antiquity of the name. But more about this elsewhere.

There remains the title, which was various. Some entitled it “On Things,” others “On the Genera of Things”; the same and similar error confused them all. For, as we have shown, this work does not treat the genera of things or things themselves, but expressions signifying the genera of things.

Aristotle himself makes this clear when he says: “Of things said without any combination, each signifies either substance or quantity.” If he were making a division of things, he would not have said “signifies”; for a thing is signified, it does not itself signify.

This too is a very strong argument that Aristotle is examining not things but expressions signifying things: he says, “Each of the things said is itself not said in any affirmation by itself, but from their combination with one another an affirmation comes about.” Things, if they are joined together, do not in any way produce an affirmation, for affirmation exists in discourse.

Therefore, if the Categories joined together make an affirmation—and affirmation exists only in discourse—then the things joined together to produce an affirmation are words signifying things. The treatment of the Categories, accordingly, concerns not things but words. Those who entitled the work “On Things” or “On the Genera of Things” were therefore mistaken.

Some add that this book should be read before the *Topics*, which is extremely absurd. Why not rather before the *Physics*? As though this book were less useful in physics, when the *Prior Analytics* are read before the *Topics*, and the book *On Interpretation* is read before the *Prior Analytics* as an introduction to knowledge.

Why, then, did they not more appropriately entitle this book as preceding either *On Interpretation* or the *Prior Analytics*? The position implied by this title must therefore also be rejected, and we must say that, since there are ten primary genera of things, there necessarily had to be ten simple words said of the things subject to them. For everything that signifies is said of the thing that it signifies. The book must therefore be entitled *On the Ten Categories*.

But perhaps someone may ask: If the discussion itself concerns words signifying things, why does Aristotle discuss things themselves? The answer is that things are always joined with their proper signification, and whatever occurs in things is also found in the words for things. Therefore, in discussing words, he rightly took the properties of signifying expressions from those things that were signified, that is, from things themselves.

There may perhaps be another question: Why, when Aristotle divided discourse into ten Categories here, did he divide it into only two parts in the book *On Interpretation*, namely verb and noun?

The difference is that there he divides the forms of words, whereas here he treats significations. Thus he is not contradicting himself. In *On Interpretation* he considers noun and verb according to a certain form of the word: one can be inflected through cases, the other varied through tenses. Here, however, the discussion is not according to these forms, but insofar as the words are signifying expressions.

Accordingly, by making different divisions in different matters and treatments, he will not be marked by any contradiction. Nor does he now divide discourse itself; rather, he distributes words among the multitude of genera. Since there are ten genera of things, he divides words into ten Categories—not according to discourse, but according to the signification of things—and treats them accordingly.

For this reason it was in a certain way necessary to mix a discussion of things into the treatment, so that, as has been said, the properties of expressions might appear in no other way than through things. Thus he begins the sequence of his discussion not properly with things, but with the Categories, that is, with the very words signifying things, insofar as they are signifying.

But if he is discussing the Categories, why does his first treatment concern equivocal, univocal, and denominative expressions? Obviously, certain matters are always set out in advance by those who discuss a subject, so that, once they have been established, instruction in what follows may be easier. In geometry, for example, terms are first presented, and afterward the sequence of the theorems is worked through.

So here too he explained whatever could be useful for the discussion of the Categories before proceeding to the Categories themselves. Since I have now explained what needed to be said beforehand, let us come to the sequence and text of the discussion itself. What usefulness equivocal, univocal, and denominative expressions possess will be treated according to the definitions and accounts of each individually.

## ON EQUIVOCAL EXPRESSIONS

Equivocal expressions are those whose name alone is common, whereas the account of substance corresponding to the name is different—for example, “animal,” “human being,” and what is painted. Their name alone is common, whereas the account of substance corresponding to the name is different. For if someone assigns an account of what each of them is, namely what makes each of them an animal, he will assign a proper account to each.

[Col. 0163D]

Every thing is indicated either by a name or by a definition. For we either call the thing subject by its proper name, or show what it is through a definition.

For example, we call a certain substance by the name “human being,” and we give its definition by saying that a human being is a rational, mortal animal. Since every thing is disclosed either by a definition or by a name, four differences arise from these two, namely name and definition.

For all things are joined either by the same name and the same definition, as “human being” and “animal”; both can be called animals, and both are joined by one definition. An animal is an animate, sensible substance, and a human being likewise is an animate, sensible substance. These are called univocal.

Other things are joined neither by names nor by definitions, such as fire, stone, and color, which differ by the nature of their proper substances. These are called diversivocal.

Others are called by different names but are subject to one definition and designation, such as “sword” and “blade.” These have many names, but what they signify is disclosed by one definition; this is called multivocal.

Others agree in name but differ in definition, as a living human being and a painted human being. Both may be called animals or human beings. But if someone wishes to define a painting and a human being, he will apply different definitions to each. These are called equivocal.

Since it has been explained what equivocal expressions are, let us follow each clause of Aristotle’s definition.

[Col. 0164B]

“Equivocal,” he says, means things which are not equivocal in themselves unless they are predicated under one name. Since they derive their being equivocal from a common word, he rightly says, “They are called equivocal.” For they are not equivocal in themselves, but are called equivocal.

Equivocation occurs not only in nouns but also in verbs. For example, when I say *complector te* (“I embrace you”) and *complector a te* (“I am embraced by you”), although the one word is *complector*, the manner of doing is one thing and the manner of undergoing is another. Thus there is equivocation here as well: the one word *complector* is defined by different accounts of doing and undergoing.

Equivocation is also frequently found in prepositions and conjunctions. Therefore, when Aristotle says, “whose name alone is common,” “name” must be understood as every signification of things through a word. It means every expression, not merely a proper or appellative noun—something belonging only to the kind of word that can be inflected through cases—but every signification of things by which we predicate words imposed upon things.

“Alone” is used in two ways. It is used once when we say that something is one, as when we say, “The world is alone,” meaning that it is one. It is used in another way when we indicate division from something else, as when someone says, “I have only a tunic,” meaning that I do not also have a cloak, with reference, that is, to the division between tunic and cloak.

Here, then, Aristotle says, “The name alone is common,” as though he meant that the definition also is not common: equivocal things are joined by name but disagree in definition.

“Common” is likewise used in many ways. Something is called common when it is divided into parts; then the whole is no longer common, but its parts become the property of individuals, as with a house.

Something is called common when it is not divided into parts but passes in turn into the use of those who possess it, as a common slave or horse.

Something is also called common when, through use, it becomes the property of each person, but after use is returned to common ownership, as with a theater. While I am using it, it is mine; when I leave, I return it to common use.

Something is also called common when, although not divided into parts, it comes as a whole at one time to each of several people. A voice or a speech, for example, reaches the ears of many people whole and undivided at one and the same time.

According to this last meaning of “common,” Aristotle thinks that the word is common to equivocal things.

[Col. 0165A]

For in a painted human being and a living human being, the whole word “animal” is said of both. He introduces the expression “whereas the account of substance corresponding to the name is different” in order to make clear that if the definitions are given in any other way than according to the name, the whole definition immediately slips and becomes unstable.

First, then, something must be said about the property of definition. Those are certain definitions which are convertible. If you ask, “What is a human being?” and answer, “A rational, mortal animal,” the answer is true. If you ask, “What is a rational, mortal animal?” and answer, “A human being,” this too is true.

But if someone says, “What is a human being?” and answers, “An animate, sensible substance,” the answer is true. If he then asks, “What is an animate, sensible substance?” and answers, “A human being,” this is not true in every case, because a horse too is an animate, sensible substance, but is not a human being.

It is therefore established that those definitions are complete which can be converted.

This occurs in the case of things that are not common but belong to one thing alone, as when a definition is given for the name “human being.” “Animal” is a common name. If someone says, “A human being is an animate, sensible substance,” the statement is acceptable, even if it is not convertible, because the definition has been given under a common name.

But if the definition is given for one name alone, then the definition must be made according to that name. It must be correctly given in such a way that the definition of a human being is “a rational, mortal animal,” not “an animate, sensible substance.” The former is given according to the name “human being,” the latter according to the name “animal.”

The same can also occur with names that are predicated commonly of two things. If the account of substance is not given according to the name, univocal things can sometimes become equivocal and equivocal things univocal.

For example, human being and horse are univocal under the name “animal,” but they can become equivocal if they are not defined according to that name. Human being and horse are called animals by a common name. If, then, someone gives the definition of a human being as “a rational, mortal animal,” and that of a horse as “an irrational, neighing animal,” he has given different definitions, and univocal things will have been changed into equivocal ones.

This happens because the definitions were not given according to “animal,” which is their common name, but according to “human being” and “horse.” If the definition had been given according to the common name “animal,” it would have been as follows: a human being is an animate, sensible substance, according to the name “animal”; and likewise a horse is an animate, sensible substance, again according to the name “animal.” According to the same word “animal,” horse and human being are predicated univocally.

Again, equivocal things become univocal in the following way. Suppose someone says that Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles, and Pyrrhus of Epirus are univocal, because both are called by one name, Pyrrhus, and both are rational, mortal animals. Here, a definition given according to the name “human being” has made equivocal things univocal.

But if the account of the definition were joined to the name “Pyrrhus,” whether through their parents or through their homeland, they would have to be defined by different definitions.

The phrase “according to the name” has therefore rightly been added, because if the definition is made in another way, it cannot remain stable and frequently leads to various errors along with it.

“Account” is likewise used in many ways. There is the account of the soul; there is the account of calculation; there is the account of nature, namely the very likeness of things being born; and there is the account given in definitions or descriptions.

Since the most general genera have no genus above them, while individuals do not differ through any substantial difference, and since a definition is drawn from genus and difference, no definition can be found either for the most general genera or for individuals.

Definitions can, however, exist for subordinate genera, since they have both differences and genera. But those whose definitions cannot be given are delimited only by descriptions.

A description is something that designates any given thing by a certain property of its own. Whether, therefore, it is a definition or a description, each indicates the account of the substance. Thus, when Aristotle said “the account of substance,” he included both the name of definition and that of description.

Some equivocal expressions are so by chance, others by deliberate arrangement. By chance, for example, Alexander the son of Priam and Alexander the Great: chance brought it about that the same name was given to both.

By deliberate arrangement are all those names imposed by human choice. Some of these are based on likeness, such as a painted human being and a real human being, the example Aristotle now uses.

Others are based on proportion, such as “principle”: in numbers, the principle is the unit; in lines, it is the point. This is called equivocation according to proportion.

Others descend from one source, such as a medical instrument and a medicinal drug; this equivocation descends from one medicine.

Others are referred to one thing, as when someone says, “The journey is healthful” and “Food is healthful” (*salutaris esca est*). These are equivocal because they are referred to the one word “health.”

Why does Aristotle treat equivocal expressions before univocal ones? Because the ten Categories, although different in their definitions, are called by one common name of predication. We call them all Categories. Since the Categories themselves are genera of things, however, they are predicated univocally of the things subject to them.

Every genus is predicated univocally of its proper species. It was therefore more appropriate to discuss first the common name of all the Categories, as though Aristotle would afterward explain how each individual Category is predicated of its proper species.

But if, as has been said, the intention of this book concerns not things but names, why does it treat equivocal things rather than equivocation? Equivocal are the things; equivocation is a word.

The reason is that the name itself contains no equivocation unless there are different things of which the word is predicated. Thus equivocation derives its substance from the things themselves, and the discussion was more appropriately begun with them.

There appears, however, to be another kind of equivocation which Aristotle entirely rejects. Just as we speak of a human being’s foot, so we also speak of the foot of a ship and the foot of a mountain. All such expressions are used by transference.

Transference, however, does not belong to any proper property. Therefore, things are never equivocal through transference unless the things subject to them are called by proper and immutable names.

Their general consideration is as follows. Not every transference is separated from equivocation, but only that in which, for the sake of ornament, a name is transferred from one thing already named to another thing that has its own name.

For example, since a certain person is already called a “charioteer,” someone may also call him a “pilot.” If, for the sake of ornament, he calls the person who is a pilot a “charioteer,” “charioteer” will not be an equivocal name, although it signifies different things, namely the driver of a chariot and the helmsman of a ship.

But whenever one thing requires a name while another thing already bears the name from which the name is transferred, then the transference retains the character of equivocation. Thus the name “human being” has been transferred from a living human being to a painting.

This is enough about equivocal expressions. Let us now discuss univocal expressions.

## ON UNIVOCAL EXPRESSIONS

Univocal expressions are those whose name is common and whose account of substance corresponding to the name is the same—for example, “animal,” “human being,” and “ox.” Both are called animals by a common name, and the account of substance is the same. For if someone assigns the account of what each of them is, namely what makes each of them an animal, he will assign the same account.

After defining equivocal expressions, Aristotle turned to the definition of univocal expressions. In them, the only difference is that equivocal things are separated by their definitions, while univocal things are joined by the same definition as well. Everything else that was said in the definition of equivocal expressions also applies to the designation of univocal expressions.

For just as the definition of equivocal things was made according to the name of the equivocal things, so in the case of univocal things the account of substance will be assigned according to the name.

Univocal things are either genera in relation to species or species in relation to species. Genera are univocal with respect to species, as “animal” and “human being.” Since animal is the genus of human being, a human being is called an animal; therefore both animal and human being are called animals.

If you define both according to the common name, you say that an animal is an animate, sensible substance. If you likewise say of a human being, insofar as he is an animal, that he is an animate, sensible substance, you will find nothing false in the statement.

Species are univocal with respect to species when they are contained under one and the same genus, as human being, horse, and ox. Their common genus is animal, and they are named animals by the common name.

According to the one name common to them, “animal,” one and the same definition will be assigned to all of them: all are animate, sensible substances.

Aristotle therefore took his example according to the latter designation of univocation, in which species are univocal with respect to species, as human being and ox, which fall under the same genus.

## ON DENOMINATIVE EXPRESSIONS

Denominative expressions are those which, differing from something else only in case, have their appellation according to the name—for example, “grammatical” from “grammar,” and “brave” from “bravery.”

This definition also contains nothing obscure. The ancients called certain transformations of names “cases,” such as “just” from “justice,” “brave” from “bravery,” and so forth. This transformation of a name was therefore called a case by the ancients.

Accordingly, whenever one thing participates in another, through that participation it acquires both the thing and its name. For example, a certain human being, because he participates in justice, derives from it both the thing and the name: he is called “just.”

Denominative expressions, therefore, are those which differ from a principal name only in case, that is, only in transformation. Since “justice” is the principal name, the transformed name “just” is produced from it.

Denominative expressions are therefore those which, differing from a principal name only in case—that is, only in the alteration of the name—have their appellation according to the principal name.

Three things are necessary for denominative words to be constituted. First, one must participate in the thing; next, in the name; finally, there must be some transformation of the name.

When someone is called “brave” from “bravery,” there is a certain bravery in which that brave person participates. He also participates in the name, for he is called “brave.” There is finally a transformation, since “brave” and “bravery” do not end in the same syllables.

If something does not participate in the thing, it cannot participate in the name either. Therefore whatever does not participate in the thing cannot be denominative.

Again, things which participate in the thing but not in the name are also distinct from the nature of denominatives. For example, suppose that someone participates in virtue itself, while we call him by no other name than “wise.” “Virtue” and “wisdom” are separated by their names. Here, then, he participates in the thing but not in the name.

Therefore “wise” is not said to be denominated from virtue, but from wisdom, in which he participates, with which he is joined by name, and from which he differs through transformation.

Again, suppose there is no transformation, as when a certain woman is “musical.” She participates in the discipline of music and is called musical. This appellation, however, is not denominative but equivocal, since by one name both the discipline and the woman are called musical.

Since the endings of the syllables are similar, the name is similar, and there is no transformation, such expressions cannot be denominative. Whatever is called denominative, therefore, will participate both in the thing and in the name, and will differ through some transformation of the word.

These matters, which he judged necessary for the Categories, he set out beforehand. He rejected multivocal and diversivocal expressions because he did not consider them useful for the present discussion.

Nevertheless, both must be defined briefly. Multivocal expressions are those for which there are several names but one definition, as “shield” and “buckler.” These have several names but one definition. The same applies to “Marcus Porcius Cato,” for one thing is subject to all these names.

Diversivocal expressions are those whose name is neither the same nor whose definition is the same, such as “human being” and “color,” and anything altogether distinct from another both in its name and in the account of its definition.

Some of the things said are spoken according to combination, while others are spoken without combination. Those spoken according to combination include “the human being runs” and “the human being wins.” Those spoken without combination include “human being,” “ox,” “runs,” and “wins.”

After he had sufficiently explained, insofar as the present work required, the conjunction of definitions and names—since a division must be made of the primary names signifying the primary genera of things, which differ not in name but in genus—he now shows what an utterance made without the combination of any term is. For those things are said to be without combination which are uttered according to the simple sound of a name, such as “man” and “horse”; for nothing additional is joined to them. Those things are said according to combination which are linked by some conjunction, such as “either Socrates or Plato,” or which are joined according to some accident. For when, for example, walking has come upon Socrates, we say, “Socrates walks”; and this utterance is according to combination, because when I say “Socrates walks,” I have joined Socrates with walking. By the phrase “of the things that are said,” however, he wishes to demonstrate nothing other than that he has arranged a discussion of the primary names of things in this little book. For what are said are the names of things; it is these that we properly name.

[Col. 0169A]

Of things that are, some are said of a certain subject but are not in a subject; for example, “man” is said of a certain man as its subject, but is not in any subject. Others are in a subject but are not said of any subject. By “being in a subject” I mean that which, although it is in something, is not in it as a part, and cannot exist without that in which it is. For example, a certain grammatical knowledge is in a subject, namely, in the soul, but is not said of any subject; and a certain white thing is in a subject, namely, in a body—for every color is in a body—but is not said of any subject. Others are both said of a subject and are in a subject; for example, knowledge is in a subject, namely, in the soul, and is said of a subject, as of this particular grammatical knowledge. Others are neither in a subject nor said of a subject, such as some particular man or some particular horse; for none of these is either in a subject or said of a subject. In general, individual things that are singular in number are said of no subject; but nothing prevents some of them from being in a subject, for a certain grammatical knowledge is in a subject but is said of no subject.

Here Aristotle gathers the entire multitude of expressions into the smallest possible division. For when he distributes the names of things among ten categories, no division greater than this can be found; nothing can exist to which an eleventh category could be added. Every thing is either substance, quantity, quality, relation, action, passion, time, place, possession, or position. Accordingly, there will also be as many expressions signifying these things; and this is the greatest division, to which nothing further can be added. The smallest division, on the other hand, is the division into four: substance and accident, universal and particular. For every thing is either substance, accident, universal, or particular. Just as nothing could be added to the ten higher categories, so nothing can be taken away from these four. No smaller division than these four can be made, nor any greater division than one in which the categories are enclosed within the limit of ten.

I shall explain briefly why the division was made into these four. The first division of all things is into substance and accident. But since substance cannot be uttered unless it is understood either universally or particularly—for when I say “man,” I have stated a universal thing, because this name is predicated of many individuals, whereas when I say “Socrates” or “Plato,” I have stated a particular thing, since “Socrates” is said of no subject—accident too is divided in the same way. For when I say “knowledge,” I have uttered a universal thing, because knowledge is predicated both of grammar and of rhetoric and of all the other things subordinate to it. But if I say “Plato’s knowledge,” since every accident that comes to an individual becomes individual, I call it particular knowledge; for Plato’s knowledge, like Plato himself, is particular.

Therefore, since neither substance nor accident can in any way be uttered unless, in its name, it assumes either the force of universality or that of particularity, the division into four was rightly made: every thing is either substance or accident, and each of these is either universal or particular.

[Col. 0170B]

From these four, combinations arise. When universality comes together with substance, universal substance results, such as “man” or “animal.” A universal is that which is capable of being predicated of many. A particular, however, is that which is predicated of no subject. Thus there is one combination of universality and substance, so that the result is universal substance. If particularity is joined to substance, particular substance results, such as “Socrates” or “Plato,” and anything individual found in substance.

When universality is mixed with accident, universal accident results, such as knowledge. Although knowledge is an accident and cannot exist apart from the soul in which it occurs, it is nevertheless universal, because it can be predicated of grammar or of other species subject to it. When particularity is joined to accident, particular accident results, such as Plato’s or Aristotle’s knowledge.

Thus four combinations arise: universal substance, particular substance, universal accident, and particular accident.

It is in no way possible for an accident to pass into the nature of substance, or substance into that of accident. An accident does indeed come to substance, but not so that it becomes substance. For although color, which is an accident, comes to substance, color is not thereby already substance. Nor, because substance receives color, does color thereby become substance. Therefore substance does not pass into the nature of accident, nor accident into the nature of substance.

Nor do particularity and universality pass into one another. Universality can indeed be predicated of particularity, as “animal” is predicated of Socrates or Plato, and particularity can receive the predication of universality; but this does not mean that universality is particularity, nor again that what is particular becomes universal.

Therefore, wishing to arrange the four combinations—universal substance, universal accident, particular substance, and particular accident—Aristotle supplied not their names but their descriptions. And since he could not find definitions of the most general genera, he used descriptions, saying that substance is what is not in a subject, while accident is what is in a subject. Every accident is in a subject, as color is in a body and knowledge in a soul, and every accident has a substance as its subject. For if someone removes the substance, the accident will not exist. Thus substance is a kind of place in which the nature of accident can subsist.

Substance itself subsists through itself and is therefore called substance. It does not depend upon any other subject; rather, it is the subject of all things. Otherwise, if substance could be in some subject, it would be an accident. For every accident is in a subject, and whatever is in a subject is an accident. If substance were in some subject, it would immediately become an accident; but substance cannot be an accident, as we have shown above. Therefore, since accident is in a subject, while substance is not an accident, substance is not in a subject.

The description of universality is: to be predicated of a subject. For every universal is predicated of particular subjects. Since “animal” or “man” is universal, it is predicated of Socrates and Plato. We say that Socrates is an animal and a man. Since knowledge is a universal accident, it is said of grammatical knowledge as its subject; for grammar is knowledge.

Particularity, however, since it is the ultimate of things and has nothing subject to it, is predicated of no subject. Since universality is predicated of a subject, while particularity is not universality, particularity will not be predicated of a subject.

Where things differ, their definitions also differ. So it is in these cases: since substance and accident differ, their definitions also differ. Since accident is in a subject, substance will not be in a subject. Since universality is predicated of a subject, while particularity differs from universality, particularity is not predicated of a subject.

Aristotle accordingly intermingled these descriptions as follows: “Of things that are, some are said of a certain subject but are in no subject,” intending, of course, to demonstrate universal substance. What he said—“are said of a subject”—indicates the universal; what he added—“are in no subject”—indicates substance. Thus, by saying that certain things are said of a subject but are in no subject, he attempts to demonstrate universal substance. For, as has often been stated, what is said of a subject is universal, and what is in no subject is substance. These taken together—being said of a subject and being in no subject—demonstrate universal substance.

[Col. 0171D]

After universal substance he placed particular accident, saying: “Others, however, are in a subject but are said of no subject.” What he said—“are in a subject”—indicates accident; what he added—“are said of no subject”—indicates particularity. For accident is in a subject, while particularity is predicated of no subject.

Therefore, whatever thing itself is in a subject but is predicated of no subject is a particular accident, such as a certain grammatical knowledge—that is, the grammatical knowledge of Aristarchus or of some individual person. Since it belongs to an individual person, it too has become individual and particular. Thus, since a certain grammatical knowledge is in the soul, it is an accident; and since it is predicated of no subject, it is particular.

For just as Aristarchus himself is said of no subject, so also his grammatical knowledge is predicated of no subject. He does not say that grammar itself is particular, but that a certain grammatical knowledge is particular—that is, the grammar of some individual person, which the particular person retains as his own possession of knowledge.

And since he introduced an incorporeal accident that occurs in the soul, namely grammar, which is in the soul, he also gives another example that is corporeal. He says: “A certain white thing is in a subject, namely, a body, for every color is in a body.” Here too he does not say that every white thing is particular, but that the white thing that has come to belong to an individual body is particular.

The particular white thing is also shown to be in a subject in the following way. Color, which is the genus of white or of some particular white thing, is in a body and is in a subject. Therefore, whatever has its genus in a subject is itself also in a subject. For all species and individuals are contained within their proper genus and possess its nature.

Since, however, “being in something” is said in many ways, I shall briefly explain what Aristotle intends by “being in a subject.” Something is said to be in something in nine ways. We say that something is in a place, as in the marketplace or in the theater. We also say that something is in something as in a vessel, as grain is in a bushel-measure. Something is also said to be in something as a part in a whole, as a hand is in a body. It is said to be in something as a whole in its parts, as a body is in all its parts. Again, it is said to be in something as a species in a genus, as man is in animal, or as a genus is in its species. We also say that something is in something as being at an end: since happiness is the end of a good life, if someone is happy, he is at the end of a good life. We also say that something is in something as in one who has power, as the administration of the state is in the emperor. We also speak of a form in matter, as the likeness of Achilles is in bronze or marble.

Thus something is said to be in something in nine ways: in a place, in a vessel, as a part in a whole, as a whole in its parts, as a species in a genus, as a genus in its species, at an end, in one who has power, and as a form in matter.

Of these, Aristotle mentions only three, though he joins two together and separates the other. He says: “By being in a subject I mean that which, being in something, is not there as a part, and cannot exist without that in which it is.”

The meaning is as follows: “I call that an accident which is in a subject—that is, which is in another thing in such a way that it is not a part of it and cannot exist without some subject”; for example, when color is in a body, it is not a part of the body, and if color is separated from the body, it exists nowhere. Every color is in a body alone.

An accident, therefore, is that which is always in another subject in such a way that it is not a part of it; when it is separated from that in which it is, it is reduced to nothing and cannot exist by itself without another subject.

By saying “not as a part,” he wished to exclude the meaning of being in something according to which we say that parts are in a whole. For a subject is not such that its accident is a part of it. By saying “it is impossible for it to exist without that in which it is,” he excluded the meaning according to which something is said to be in a vessel or in a place. For what is in a vessel or in a place can be separated from the vessel or place: grain that is in a bushel-measure can be removed from the measure, and a person can depart from the theater. An accident, however, cannot be separated from that in which it is.

Thus he posited only three meanings: the one according to which something is said to be in a vessel, the one according to which it is said to be in a place, and the one according to which a part is in a whole. But he distributed “in a vessel” and “in a place” under one statement when he said, “It is impossible for it to exist without that in which it is.”

Perhaps someone might say that the definition is not true: namely, that things are in a subject when they are in another thing not as parts and cannot exist without that in which they are. Socrates, or any man, although he is not an accident, is nevertheless always in a place and cannot exist without a place.

The answer is that Socrates can change places and exist apart from the place in which he was. Finally, if we understand the matter intellectually, substance subsists through itself, whereas accidents do not subsist through themselves.

But if someone should also object that accidents can change places—for if an apple is held in the hand, the hand is filled with the apple’s odor, and odor, which is an accident, can pass into another subject—the answer is that Aristotle does not say that an accident cannot change its place. Nor does he say that it is impossible for it to exist without that in which it was, but without that in which it is.
