This signifies that an accident can indeed change its place, but cannot subsist without some subject.

Therefore the definition of what is in a subject is correct and complete: it is in another thing not as a part, and it is impossible for it to exist without that in which it is. This was stated according to the meaning in which we say that a form is in matter. For if a form is in matter, it cannot in any way subsist through itself.

After showing what a particular accident is—namely, what is in a subject and is not predicated of a subject—and after giving the definition of a thing that exists in a subject, namely, that when it is in something it is not there as a part and cannot exist without that in which it is, he returns, in the continuing discussion, to universal accident, which he defines in the following way.

After defining the thing that is in a subject and after giving examples of particular accident, he proceeds to universal accident, saying that there are other things that are in a subject and are predicated of a subject. This signifies universal accident. Since it is said of a subject, it is universal; since it is in a subject, it is an accident. Thus being in a subject and being predicated of a subject demonstrate universal accident.

He also gives suitable examples of this combination. He says that knowledge is in a subject, namely, in the soul; for unless there were a soul in which it existed, there would be no knowledge, because knowledge is an activity of the soul. Inanimate things know nothing.

[Col. 0173D]

From this he proceeds to the presentation of particular substance, which he explains as that which is neither in a subject nor predicated of a subject. For what is not in a subject is substance, and what is not predicated of a subject is particularity. Therefore a thing’s being neither predicated of a subject nor in a subject makes it particular substance.

Thus he joined together four things with their proper combination, not according to their proper names but according to their proper principles and definitions. In place of universal substance he set that which is not in a subject and is predicated of a subject. For particular accident he said that which is in a subject and is not predicated of a subject. He designated universal accident by saying that which is both in a subject and said of a subject. In place of particular substance he inserted that which is neither in a subject nor predicated of a subject:

“Simply, however, individual things that are singular in number are said of no subject; but nothing prevents some of them from being in a subject, for a certain grammatical knowledge is in a subject.”

Every particular thing will be either substance or accident. When I say “Socrates,” I have signified an individual and particular substance. When I say “a certain grammatical knowledge,” I have stated an individual and particular accident.

[Col. 0174B]

Individuals are things that can be divided neither into other species nor into other individuals. Just as animal is divided into species, man and horse, and man into individual men—that is, Socrates, Plato, and the others—so Plato and Socrates are not divided into others.

The same must also be said of accidents. Just as knowledge is divided into species, grammar and rhetoric, and grammar itself into particular grammars, which particular people know, so a particular grammar itself is not divided into particular grammars.

Thus individuals are whatever things are singular in number and are not divided into any further multiplicity either according to species or according to individuals.

Every individual, since it is particular, is not predicated of a subject. But everything that is not predicated of a subject will be either substance, as Plato, or accident, as a certain grammatical knowledge.

Among these particulars—namely, substance and accident—which are not predicated of a subject, substance is not in a subject, whereas accident is in a subject. Thus those individuals that are substances cannot be in a subject, while other individuals that are spoken of according to the nature of accident may be in a subject without impediment.

This is what he says: “Simply, however, individual things that are singular in number are said of no subject; but nothing prevents some of them from being in a subject. For a certain grammatical knowledge is in a subject, but is said of no subject.”

[Col. 0174D]

This is what he preferred to demonstrate: that particular accidents and particular substances have in common that they are not predicated of a subject. For he said: “Simply, however, individual things that are singular in number are said of no subject.” We must understand this as meaning “whether they are substances or accidents,” but not that no individuals are in a subject. For individual accidents may be in a subject. A certain grammatical knowledge, although it is individual and is not predicated of a subject, is nevertheless in a subject, namely, in the soul.

To state the point collectively, the meaning is this: all individual things whatever are said of no subject, but not all are not in a subject. For although particular substance is not in a subject, as Plato, particular accident is in a subject, as a certain grammatical knowledge in the soul.

It should also be noted with great care what the order of the proposition is. There are four combinations made from four things, two of which differ in nature—substance and accident—and two in quantity—particularity and universality. Having joined and combined all four, he arranged them with their sides opposed.

He first posited universal substance, saying that it is not in a subject and is said of a subject. After this first position, which differs from the others in all respects, he placed beneath it a thing opposed to it, namely particular accident, which is in a subject and is not predicated of a subject. By saying “accident” he separated it from substance; by adding “particular” he separated it from universal.

Again, on another side of the division, he arranged universal accident, saying that it is in a subject and is predicated of a subject. Finally, he stated particular substance, contrary to the accident above it, as that which is neither in a subject nor predicated of a subject, opposing particularity of substance to the universality of accident.

To make our meaning clearer, we have appended a figure and description in which we have marked the upper side with substance and accident, and inscribed the remaining side with the title of particularity and universality, depicting Aristotle’s combination angularly and by its sides.

[Col. 0175C]

When one thing is predicated of another as of a subject, whatever things are said of what is predicated are all also said of the subject. For example, “man” is predicated of a certain man, while “animal” is predicated of man; therefore animal will also be predicated of a certain man. For a certain man is both man and animal.

[Col. 0175D]

When he was previously discussing things that are in a subject—that is, accidents—he established, in the course of the discussion, the definition of a thing constituted in a subject and unable to persist in any way apart from a subject. He said that it is something that is neither a part of anything nor able to persist in any way without a subject.

Having made clear what it is to be in a subject, he now explains what it is to be predicated of a subject. Predications occur in two ways: one according to accident, and the other of a subject. For “white” is predicated of man, since we say “a man is white”; and again “animal” is predicated of the same man, since we say “a man is an animal.”

The first predication, “A man is white,” is according to accident. For the accident “white” is predicated of the subject “man,” but not in respect of what the thing is. Since white is an accident and man a substance, an accident cannot be predicated of a substance in respect of what it is. Therefore this predication is called predication according to accident.

To predicate of a subject means to predicate one thing of another in its very substance, as animal is predicated of man. Since animal is both a substance and the genus of man, it is predicated of man in respect of what he is.

Therefore only those things are said to be predicated of a subject which are placed in the substance and definition of any thing. Whenever such a predication occurs—when one thing is predicated of another as of a subject, that is, is said of its substance, as animal is said of man—the following property must necessarily occur: if something is predicated of what is itself predicated, as of a subject—that is, in its substance—the same thing that is said of the predicate is necessarily said also of the subject of that predicate.

For example, man is predicated of Socrates in respect of what he is. When asked what Socrates is, we answer “a man.” But animal is said of man in respect of what he is; for animal is predicated in the substance of man. Thus animal is predicated of man, and man of Socrates, in respect of what they are, as of subjects.

Therefore, by this consequence, animal will also be predicated of Socrates in respect of what he is. When asked “What is Socrates?” one may answer “an animal.”

It is therefore evident that if one thing is predicated of another as of a subject—for example, man of Socrates—and, of the thing that is predicated, another higher thing is again predicated as of a subject—for example, animal of man—then this same thing must also be predicated of the subject of that of which it is itself said. Thus animal is predicated of Socrates, since Socrates is the subject of man, of whom animal is predicated.

The definition is therefore established that whenever one thing is predicated of another as of a subject, if something can be said of what is predicated in respect of what it is, that same thing can also be predicated of what was previously the subject.

Perhaps someone might say that what has been stated is not at all true. For when man is predicated of Socrates—Socrates is a man—and species is predicated of man—for man is a species—Socrates is not said to be a species. Again, when animal is predicated of man, and genus is predicated of animal—for animal is a genus—man does not possess the name “genus”; man is not said to be a genus, but only a species.

To this one must reply that they have paid insufficient attention. The definition concerns predication of a subject: that which is predicated in respect of what each thing is and in its substance. But species is not predicated of man in respect of what he is. For if someone gives the definition of man, he has not named species; “species” is merely a designating name, indicating whether the name “man” is predicated of several things differing in species or only of individuals.

Since man is predicated only of individuals, it is called a species; and since animal is said of things differing in species, we call animal a genus. In a certain sense, these are names of names.

Therefore neither genus is predicated of animal, nor species of man, in respect of what it is; they merely designate how man and animal are predicated of their proper subjects, as has been said.

It is therefore not surprising that the predication of the predicate which is not itself said of a subject cannot reach the subject of those things that are said of a subject.

[Col. 0177A]

Different genera that are not arranged subordinately have different specific differences, such as animal and knowledge. The differences of animal include walking, flying, having two feet, and living in water; none of these belongs to knowledge, for knowledge does not differ from knowledge by being two-footed.

With subordinate genera, however, there is nothing to prevent the differences from being the same. For higher genera are predicated of lower ones. Therefore whatever differences belong to the predicate will also be the same differences belonging to the subject.

[Col. 0177B]

Since “genus” is said in many ways, let us adopt only the sense that is relevant to the present discussion. A genus is said to be that which is predicated of several things differing in species, in answer to the question what a thing is: thus animal is predicated of a human being, a horse, a dog, an ox, and other things, all of which differ from one another in species. A species, on the other hand, is that which is predicated of several things differing numerically, in answer to the question what a thing is: thus human being is predicated of Cato, Socrates, Plato, Virgil, Cicero, and of individual human beings, who do not differ from one another in species but only differ numerically.

A difference is that which distinguishes species placed under the same genus by a property of their own. Thus, although horse and human being are one in respect of genus—for each is an animal—the difference “rational” and “irrational” [Col. 0177C] separates and distinguishes them. For by a certain quality, namely rationality and irrationality, each departs from the definition of its proper substance. Therefore a difference is that which is predicated of several things differing in species, in answer to the question what sort of thing it is. For this very difference, irrationality, is predicated of many things differing in species, such as a swan, a horse, and a fish. Although all these differ from one another in species, they are united by the quality of irrationality.

But a difference is not predicated of several things differing in species in every case. Some differences are predicated of only one species: for example, heaviness is properly said of earth alone, and lightness of fire alone. Nor is a species always predicated of several things differing numerically. The species “world” [Col. 0177D] is said of only one world, and the species “phoenix” of only one phoenix. Yet it has been defined in this way because a difference is more often predicated of several things differing in species than of one alone. In the same way, a species is more often found to be predicated of several things differing numerically than of one single and individual thing.

With these points established, there are certain genera called “most general,” above which no genus can be found; and there are species beneath which no other species can be found. Between these are others called “subaltern genera,” which are species of higher genera but genera of lower species. Thus substance is a genus, and is most general, since no genus can be found above it; human being is a species, since no species can be found beneath it. Animal, however, [Col. 0178A] is a species in relation to substance, but a genus in relation to human being.

The signification of the ten categories therefore demonstrates nothing other than the ten genera of things that we call most general. Consequently, whenever the most general genera differ, their species too will differ; and whenever species differ, since they are separated and formed by differences, the differences of the different species will also differ.

Animal and knowledge, for example, differ in every respect: animal is a substance, whereas knowledge belongs to the category “relative”; and since the genus of animal is substance, while the genus of knowledge is “relative,” they are wholly distinct from one another. The differences of knowledge and animal are likewise separated by every quality. The differences of animal include “two-footed” and “four-footed.” For one animal differs from another in that one is two-footed, such as a human being or a bird, another four-footed, [Col. 0178B] such as a horse or an ox, and another many-footed, such as an ant or a bee. Knowledge, however, has no differences of this kind, since knowledge does not differ from knowledge by being two-footed.

It is therefore evident that whenever genera are different, the differences of their species are also distinct. This is what he says: “The differences of genera that are different and not arranged subalternately are different according to species.” He confirmed this by adding an example, saying that the differences of animal and knowledge are different, since “two-footed” is a difference of animal but not of knowledge.

This has been said of different genera, that is, genera that are not subaltern. If the genera are subaltern, however, nothing prevents their differences from being sometimes the same and sometimes different. Thus bird is a species of animal and is also a genus of crow; bird is therefore a subaltern genus. The differences of animal are “rational” and “irrational,” [Col. 0178C] but rationality is not a difference of bird, since no bird differs from another bird by being rational. Therefore, in this case, the differences of the subaltern genera are not the same.

If, however, someone should identify as differences of the genus—namely, animal—the facts that some animals feed on grass, others on seeds, and others on flesh, these differences apply to the subaltern genus bird. Among birds there are some that eat seeds, some that eat grass, and some that eat flesh, such as the vulture and the kite. Therefore, among subaltern genera there is nothing to prevent the differences from being the same and again from differing.

This happens because what is said of the predicate [Col. 0178D] can also be predicated of the subject. Thus what is said of the genus can also be said of the species. This is what he means when he says: “With subaltern genera there is nothing to prevent the differences from being the same.” For higher genera are predicated of lower genera.

When he said that there is nothing to prevent the differences from being the same, he seems in a certain way to have intended to show that some differences can be the same while others can be different. Yet he appears to introduce the opposite point when he says: “Whatever the differences of the predicate may be, they will also be those of the subject.” For earlier he had said that there is nothing to prevent the differences of subaltern genera from being the same; here he declares that they are all the same. He says: “Whatever the differences of the predicate may be, they will also be those of the subject.” This passage has entangled many people in serious [Col. 0179A] errors, so that they have thought the text should be emended rather than understood as it stands.

They therefore propose to read it as follows: “Whatever the differences of the subject may be, they will also be those of the predicate.” But this must be rejected, since it is impossible for the predication of what is posterior to extend to the higher thing. When it is said, “Whatever the differences of the subject may be, they will also be those of the predicate,” this means that the predication of the subject returns to the predicate, which cannot happen.

It must instead be said that there are certain differences that complete the predicate and give form to its species; these are called, by a common name, “specific” differences. When I say “animate” and “sensible,” if these are joined to substance, they immediately produce the definition and species of [Col. 0179B] animal. For animal is an animate, sensible substance, and these differences are called specific and completing differences.

There are other differences that themselves complete nothing and produce no species, but merely divide a genus, such as “rational” and “irrational.” These divide the genus animal. For animal is divided by the rational and irrational difference.

Accordingly, those differences that divide a genus may sometimes be the same and sometimes not the same. Thus animal has the divisive difference “rational,” but bird, which is a subaltern genus, may not have it. Again, a subaltern genus may have the same divisive differences—for example, the very differences mentioned above. Since the differences by which animal is divided—those that feed on flesh, grass, and seeds—can be the same [Col. 0179C] in the subaltern genus bird, these divisive differences may also be different.

The differences that are completing and specific, however, cannot fail to be predicated of the subject. Since animal has differences that complete it and bring about its species—namely, “sensible” and “animate”—these differences cannot fail to be predicated of human being, which is the subject of animal. For all specific differences are predicated of the things whose species they complete. “Sensible” and “animate” are predicated of animal as of a subject; but animal is predicated of human being as of a subject. Therefore “animate” and “sensible” must also be predicated of human being as of a subject.

This is what he stated earlier when he said: [Col. 0179D] “Whenever one thing is predicated of another as of a subject, whatever is said of the thing that is predicated is also said of the subject.” This is rightly understood of all genera.

Thus divisive differences may sometimes be common to the subjects and sometimes different, whereas specific and completing differences cannot fail to be common to the subjects. When Aristotle says that “with subaltern genera there is nothing to prevent the differences from being the same,” this should be understood of divisive differences: there is nothing to prevent these from being the same, although they may also be different.

But when he says, “Whatever the differences of the predicate may be, they will also be those of the subject,” this should be understood of specific differences. Since these give form to the species of anything and are predicated of the thing they form as of a subject, they will be predicated of whatever is predicated as a subject of that thing which the differences themselves form; and they cannot fail to be predicated of it. [Col. 0180A] Therefore there is nothing in this theorem that ought in any way to be emended.

Of things said without any combination, each signifies either substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, possession, action, or being acted upon.

Substance, to give a figurative example, is “human being” or “horse.” Quantity is “two cubits” or “three cubits.” Quality is “white” or “grammatical.” Relation is “double,” “half,” “greater,” or “less.” Place is “in the Lyceum” or “in the marketplace.” Time is “yesterday” or “last year.” Position is “sitting” or “lying.” Possession is “shod” or “armed.” Action is “cutting” or “burning.” Being acted upon is “being cut” or “being [Col. 0180B] burned.”

Each of the things mentioned, taken by itself, is not expressed in an affirmation or negation; but affirmation or negation arises from their combination with one another. Every affirmation or negation appears to be either true or false. But among things said without any combination, each taken singly is neither true nor false—for example, “human being,” “white,” “runs,” or “wins.”

After the smallest division into four—namely, substance, accident, universality, and particularity—he is now about to deal with the greatest division, which is made into ten. No larger enumeration can be found, [Col. 0180C] since eleven categories cannot be found, nor can any genus beyond ten be rightly conceived. For this reason he makes an enumeration of this kind, but not a division.

A division is generally the division of a genus into species. But the categories cannot be a division, since they do not have one genus; they are rather an enumeration. Some people nevertheless contend that the enumeration has not been properly arranged. Some remove certain items as superfluous; others add items to what they regard as an incomplete work; still others alter the order. That they are not thinking correctly must be explained elsewhere.

He says: “Of things said without any combination.” So clearly is he about to discuss not things but words that he says “are said.” Things, properly speaking, are not said; words are. His addition that each signifies either substance or something else makes it evident [Col. 0180D] that he is discussing words. For things do not signify; they are signified.

Things are said without combination, as has been stated, whenever they are uttered with a single understanding and in a single expression. They are said with combination whenever they are joined together by some conjunction or by the coupling of an accident.

He himself shows what results from things said without combination when he says: “Each of the things mentioned, taken by itself, is not expressed in any affirmation; but affirmation arises from their combination with one another.” Every affirmation appears to be either false or true. But among things said without combination there is neither truth nor falsity, as in “human being,” “white,” “runs,” and “wins.”

Here, therefore, [Col. 0181A] he signifies that things said without any combination do not possess the force of an affirmation. If someone says “human being,” “white,” “ten,” or anything else in a simple manner, no truth or falsity will be found in it, whereas every affirmation is either true or false.

He therefore declares universally that the categories are entirely outside the scope of affirmation. But when these same items are joined together in some combination, they necessarily become propositions containing truth or falsity.

Not every combination, however, makes a proposition. If I say “Socrates in the marketplace,” that is not yet a proposition. But if someone says “Socrates walks in the marketplace,” then a proposition is formed, which is either an affirmation or a negation. Affirmations and negations appear to be either true or false; and therefore whatever is neither true nor false is not a proposition.

Thus truth and falsity are produced by a certain combination [Col. 0181B] from things said without combination. Aristotle has introduced affirmation alone here because every affirmation is prior: negation removes what affirmation first establishes. It is prior in signification, though not in genus; this will become clear elsewhere.

Aristotle shows most clearly that he intends to discuss not things but words when he says: “Affirmation arises from their combination with one another.” Affirmation or negation does not arise from the combination of things but from the combination of expressions. Truth and falsity do not reside in things, but in understandings and opinions, and subsequently in words and statements.

This is enough on that point. [Col. 0181C] Things said with combination are therefore those formed from complete expressions joined together, such as “Socrates walks.” Both “Socrates” and “walks” are complete expressions, and when joined they form an affirmation.

But if someone says “flame-bearing,” “many-sounding,” or “wave-wandering,” the utterance is not with combination, because it has not been formed from two complete expressions.

Definitions of these ten categories [Col. 0181D] cannot be found, because the things they signify are most general. Substance, quantity, and quality appear never to be subject to any genus. Since every definition is derived from a genus, a genus that is not subject to another genus is left outside definition.

For the moment he has supplied appropriate examples for all the categories; later he will discuss each one more extensively. Since no definition can be found for them, they are characterized by certain properties. Having now discussed them fully, let us proceed to the treatment of substance.

## On Substance

Substance, in the proper, primary, and fullest sense, is that which is neither predicated of a subject nor present in a subject—for example, some particular human being or some particular horse.

Secondary substances are called the species in which those things that are called substances in the primary sense are present. These include the species themselves and the genera of those species. Thus some particular human being is in the species human being, while animal is the genus of that species. Secondary substances, therefore, are such things as human being and animal.

The question arises why he began his treatment of the categories with [Col. 0182A] substances. Every thing is either in a subject or is not in a subject. Whatever is in a subject depends upon a subject, since it cannot subsist in its own proper nature. Since substance underlies all things, nothing that is in a subject can remain apart from substance.

That nature is prior without which other things cannot exist. Substance therefore appears to be prior by nature. It was not unreasonable, then, for him to take first in his discussion what is prior by nature. He could not provide a definition of substance, but after giving the preceding example he offers a kind of description by which we may recognize what substance is: namely, not being in a subject. Substance is not in a subject.

He divides substances in a certain way [Col. 0182B] when he says that some are primary and others secondary. By primary substances he means individuals; by secondary substances, the species and genera of individuals.

Since primary and secondary substances share the property of not being in a subject, the addition that primary substances are not predicated of subjects separates primary from secondary substances. An individual substance, insofar as it is a substance, is not in a subject; and insofar as it is individual, it is not predicated of a subject.

Primary substances are therefore those that are neither in a subject nor predicated of a subject, such as Socrates or Plato. Since they are substances, they are in no subject; and since they are particular and individual, they are predicated of no subject.

Secondary substances [Col. 0182C] share with primary substances the fact that they are not in a subject, but their distinctive feature is that they are predicated of a subject. Secondary substances are universal, such as human being and animal. Human being and animal are not in any subject, but they are predicated of some subject.

Primary substances are therefore particular, while secondary substances are universal.

He properly calls individuals substances because we collect the species “human being” and the genus “animal” only from knowledge of individuals. Since generality is understood from the perceptions of individual things, individuals and singular things are rightly called substances in the proper sense.

Individual substances are also said to be primary [Col. 0182D] because every accident first comes to be in an individual and only afterward in secondary substances. Since Aristarchus is grammatical, and Aristarchus is a human being, Aristarchus is a grammatical human being. Thus every accident first comes to an individual; only in the second place is that accident thought to come to the species and genera of substances.

It is therefore correct that what is first a subject should be called substance in the primary sense. Primary substance is said to be substance in the fullest sense because whatever is most subject to other things can most properly be called substance.

Primary substance is most subject to other things. [Col. 0183A] Everything is either predicated of primary substances or is present in them, including genera and species. Genera and species are predicated of their individual subjects: animal and human being are predicated of Socrates—that is, secondary substances are predicated of primary substances. If they are accidents, they are present primarily in primary substances.

Since accidents are primarily in primary substances, and secondary substances are predicated of primary substances, primary substances are subject to secondary substances and accidents. Since primary substances are most subject both to the subsistence of accidents and to the predication of secondary substances, they are called substances in the fullest sense.

He says that not every species and not every genus is a secondary substance, but only those that contain primary substances, such as human being and animal. Human being contains Socrates, that is, an individual substance. Animal contains both an individual and a species, namely human being and some particular human being.

He therefore considers those genera and species that are predicated of [Col. 0183B] primary substances to be secondary substances. He expresses this as follows: “Secondary substances are called those in which the species that are called substances in the primary sense are present.” He then gives examples of these species and of their genera, as if he were saying: “I do not mean all genera or all substances, but only those species in which individuals—that is, primary substances—are present, and the genera of those species, that is, of those species that contain primary substances.”

This seems to have been said so that no one would think that color, which is a genus, or white, which is a species, should be called a secondary substance. These do not contain primary substances beneath them.

Someone may ask how primary substances can be individuals, [Col. 0183C] since whatever is removed first removes what comes afterward, whereas when what comes later is removed, what comes earlier does not perish. If human being perishes, Socrates too will immediately perish; but if Socrates dies, human being does not immediately perish. If, therefore, the removal of genera and species destroys individuals, while the removal of individuals leaves genera and species, it would seem more appropriate to call species and genera primary substances.

But this is not the correct way to understand the nature of individuals. The whole substance of individuals is not contained in one Socrates or in any one human being, but in the several individual human beings. Genera and species are not understood from one individual alone; they are conceived by the reasoning of the mind from all individual things.

We also always think that things nearer to the senses [Col. 0183D] should be named by words that are correspondingly nearer to them. The first person who used the word “human being” did not conceive the universal formed from individual human beings; rather, he conceived in his mind some particular and individual being and imposed upon it the name “human being.”

Therefore, when individual human beings are removed, human being does not remain; and when individual animals are removed, animal perishes. Since this book deals with the signification of words, he rightly called those things primary substances to which words were first applied. Words were first imposed on things that could first fall under the senses. What is presented to the senses is first of all the individual, so he rightly placed individuals first in the division.

The same reasoning solves the question of why, although intelligible substances [Col. 0184A] such as God and the mind are naturally first, he did not call them primary substances. This work deals with names. Names were first applied to things that were principally subject to the senses; things belonging to intelligible incorporeality were considered later in the imposition of names. Since this work is principally concerned with names, and since the first words in the work dealing with words were said of individual substances that are first subject to the senses, individual and sensible substances were rightly established as primary substances.

Although there are three substances—matter, form, and the substance composed and compacted from both—here he has proposed neither form alone nor matter alone, but the two mixed and composed together. [Col. 0184B] The parts of substance are themselves simple and uncompounded; from them substance is constituted, namely form and matter. He later mentions these in passing when he says that the parts of substances are themselves substances.

This is enough on that point. Let us now turn the course of our exposition to what follows.

It is clear from what has been said that, of things predicated of a subject, both the name and the account must be predicated of the subject. Thus human being is predicated of some human subject; its name is also predicated, since one predicates “human being” of some human being. The account of human being too will be predicated of some human subject. For a particular human being is both a human being and an animal. Therefore both the name and the account are predicated of the subject.

Of things that are in a subject, however, in most cases [Col. 0184C] neither the name nor the account is predicated of the subject. In some cases the name may nevertheless be predicated of the subject, whereas it is impossible to predicate the account. For example, white is in a subject, namely a body, and is predicated of the subject, since one says “the body is white”; but the account of white is never predicated of the body.

All other things are either predicated of primary subjects, or are in those same subjects. This is evident from the examples that will be presented individually. Animal is predicated of human being, and therefore of some particular human being; for if it were predicated of none of the individual human beings, it would not be predicated of human being at all. Again, color is in a body, and therefore in some particular body; for if it were not in any individual body, it would not be in body at all.

Therefore all other things are either predicated of primary subjects [Col. 0184D] or are in those same subjects. If primary substances did not exist, it would be impossible for anything else to exist.

Everything that has been mentioned is either in a subject or predicated of a subject. But not everything that is in a subject is predicated of its proper subject. Whatever is in some subject is predicated of its proper subject: white, for example, is predicated of body, since one says “the body is white.”

Since secondary substances are either species or genera of primary substances—for the species of Socrates is human being, and animal is its genus—and since a genus is predicated univocally of the species and individuals subject to it, secondary substances are predicated univocally of their subject species.

The definition of primary and secondary substances [Col. 0185A] is the same when taken as one. Animal, human being, and Socrates are joined by one definition, since each is an animate, sensible substance. Secondary substances are therefore predicated of their proper subjects, namely primary substances, by a univocal predication.

Among things that are in a subject, sometimes the name itself [Col. 0185B] is not predicated of the subject. Virtue, for example, is in the soul, but virtue is not predicated of the soul. Sometimes the name is predicated denominatively: grammar is in a human being, and from grammar the denominative term “grammatical” is predicated.

Often the name itself is predicated of the subject. [Col. 0185C] Since white is in body, one says “the body is white.” Whether the name is not predicated, is predicated denominatively, or is predicated by its proper name, the definition of what is in the subject is never predicated of its proper subject.

Thus white is in the subject body, and the name “white” is predicated of body; but the definition of white is in no way predicated of body. “White” and “body” cannot be defined by one and the same account.

Furthermore, if every accident is in a subject, and substance is a subject, substance differs from accident. The definition of substance also differs from that of accident, since the definition of a subject cannot be the same as the definition of what is in the subject.

This is what he says: “Of things that are in a subject, in most cases neither the name nor the account is predicated of the subject,” as with virtue in the soul. He adds: “In some cases the name may nevertheless sometimes be predicated,” in some cases denominatively and in others by the direct name.

With respect to secondary substances, predication always reaches primary substances. If a particular human being is both human being and animal, and so forth, one definition of animal will suitably apply both to human being and to a particular human being.

He shows even more clearly that individual and particular substances are substances in the fullest sense. Since every thing is either substance or accident, and since some substances are primary and others secondary, there is a threefold division: every thing is either an accident, a secondary substance, or a primary substance.

To present this division in outline, [Col. 0185D] we may say as follows. Every thing is either in a subject or not in a subject. Among things that are in a subject, some are predicated of a subject and some are not. Among things that are not in a subject, some are predicated of no subject and others are predicated of a subject.

Thus every thing is either in a subject or not in a subject. It is either in a subject and predicated of a subject; or in a subject and predicated of no subject; or not in a subject and predicated of a subject; or not in a subject and predicated of no subject.

If, having established these distinctions, we separate primary substances, secondary substances and accidents remain. Secondary substances are those that are not in a subject and are predicated of a subject. Therefore they do not retain their existence except insofar as they are predicated of something.

Secondary substances are predicated of primary substances. Therefore their being [Col. 0186A] secondary substances depends upon their predication of primary substances. They would not be secondary substances unless they were predicated of primary substances.

Things that are in a subject, on the other hand, could not subsist at all unless they rested, as it were, upon primary substances as their foundation. Therefore everything that exists apart from primary substances will be either a secondary substance or an accident.

Secondary substances are predicated of primary substances; accidents are in primary substances. Hence everything is either predicated of primary substances, as secondary substances, or is in primary substances, as accidents.

Aristotle presents this as follows: [Col. 0186B] “All other things are either said of the principal subjects, or are in those same subjects.” Here too he gives entirely accurate examples. He says that if an accident were in no particular subject-body, it would not be in body at all. For if it were in none of the individuals, it would be said to be in nothing generally.

Similarly, unless animal were predicated of individual and particular human beings, it would not be predicated of human being at all. Therefore, since secondary substances are predicated because primary substances exist, and since accidents are something because primary substances are subject to them, if primary substances did not exist, neither would the things predicated of them remain, nor would the things present in those subjects remain.

Species is more of a substance than genus among secondary substances, [Col. 0186C] because it is closer to primary substance. If someone were to identify what a primary substance is, he would identify it more clearly and appropriately by presenting its species than by presenting its genus. In identifying some particular human being, for example, he will identify him more clearly by saying “human being” than by saying “animal.”

The former is more proper to that particular human being, whereas the latter is more common. If one presents a particular tree, one will identify it more clearly by saying “tree” than by saying “plant.”

It is established that individual substances are primary substances [Col. 0186D] in the fullest and proper sense. Secondary substances, namely genera and species, are not substances in an equal degree, just as they do not stand at an equal distance from primary substance. Since species is closer to primary substance than genus, species is more of a substance than its proper genus.

Human being is closer to Socrates than animal is, and therefore human being is more of a substance. Animal too is a substance, but it is less so than human being. This occurs because in every definition the species is more suitably predicated of the primary substance than the genus.

If someone wishes to show what a certain Socrates is, he will indicate the substance and property of Socrates more closely by saying that he is a human being than by saying that he is an animal. That Socrates is an animal he shares with other beings that are not human beings, namely with a horse and an ox. That he is a human being he shares with no others except those contained under the same species, human being.

Therefore the designation will be closer to the signification [Col. 0187A] when a species is given of an individual than when the name of the genus is predicated. Again, if someone wishes to designate some individual tree and says “tree,” he will indicate more closely what the thing is than if he names it “plant.” Plant is the genus of tree, for plant is predicated also of things that are not trees, such as stalks and lettuces.

It is therefore clear that species are more of a substance because they are closer to primary and most substantial things. A species assigned in answer to the question what a thing is gives a more appropriate and evident identification, whereas a genus is more distant and more common.

Furthermore, primary substances are called substances in the fullest sense because they are subject to everything else, while everything else is either predicated of them or is in them. Species stands to genus in the same way that primary substances stand to all other things. Species is subject to genus, for genera are predicated of species, whereas species are not reciprocally predicated of genera.

From this too it is evident that species is more of a substance than genus.

[Col. 0187B] He confirms again, by a stronger argument, that species are more substantially substances. For he demonstrates that this is so by means of a likeness. Since all substances are either primary or secondary, and since secondary substances are either genera or species, whatever among species and genera is found to be more like primary substances will rightly be thought more substantially a substance. Primary substances are called substances in the highest degree for this reason: everything else is so subject to them that other things are either in them as accidents or are predicated of them as secondary substances. Whatever, then, applies to primary substances also applies to species. Species are subject to all accidents, and genera are predicated of species, whereas species are not predicated of genera. Therefore [Col. 0187C] genera are not subject in the same way as species. Species are not predicated of genera. Thus, just as primary substances are subject to secondary substances and accidents, so species are subject both to accidents and to genera. Genera, although subject to accidents, are not themselves subject to species. Consequently, the likeness of species to primary substances is greater than that of genera. If the likeness of species to substances of the highest degree is greater, then species themselves will be more substantially substances.

But no one should suppose that we mean that things which are genera cannot be species; rather, they cannot be species insofar as they are genera. Insofar as something is a species, it is not predicated of higher things; but insofar as it is a genus, it will be predicated of that of which it is the genus. Consequently, genera themselves cannot be subject to the things of which they are genera, whereas species cannot be predicated of the things of which they are species.

Among the species themselves, none that is not a genus is more substantially a substance than another. For one cannot assign “man” more familiarly to any particular man than one can assign “horse” to any particular horse. Likewise, among primary substances, no one is more substantially a substance than another. For no particular man is more substantially a substance than a particular ox.

It was also stated, as Porphyry very clearly taught in his book on genera, species, differences, properties, and accidents, that some things are only genera, whose genus cannot be found, while others are only [Col. 0188A] species, which cannot be divided into other species. These are predicated of several things differing in number in answer to the question “what is it?” Thus “man” is said of individual men, and “horse” of individual horses, and “ox” of individual oxen. Those placed under their proper species do not differ from one another in the form of their proper nature. Species of this kind, such as man and horse, which preside only over individuals, cannot be genera and are therefore always equally substances. The name “horse” is assigned to any individual horse just as closely as the name “man” is assigned to any individual man. Accordingly, if these species, which are not genera, stand at an equal distance from primary substances, they will rightly be thought to be equally substances. This does not mean that all species are equally substances, but that those which are equally distant from primary substances are so.

For it may happen that, among the species of some higher genus, one species is compared with its proper species and appears to be a less substantial substance than that species. Suppose, for example, that someone says that bird is a species of animal, and likewise that man is a species of animal. Bird and man are not equally substances, because bird is higher than man. Man is not divided into other species, for it is more properly a species. Bird, however, can be divided into other species, such as hawk and vulture; although both are birds in species, they nevertheless differ from one another. Hawk and vulture are species in the proper sense, for they preside only over individuals. Therefore man and hawk are equally distant from primary substances and are equally substances. Man and bird, however, are not equally substances, since bird is higher than man; man is therefore more substantially a substance.

Thus, whatever species are equally distant from their individuals are equally substances. Since those species which are not genera are equally distant from primary substances, they are said to be equally substances. It is also clear, without requiring exposition, that primary substances themselves are equally substances. A particular man and a particular horse, since they are individuals, are primarily, properly, and supremely substances. Consequently, among substances of the highest degree, substance cannot be found either in greater or in lesser measure. Individuals, therefore, are equally substances.

It is therefore appropriate that, after primary substances, only the species and genera of other things are called secondary substances. [Col. 0188D] For among the things that are predicated, these alone indicate the primary substance. If someone assigns what a particular man is by assigning his species or genus, he will assign it more familiarly and make it clearer by saying “man” or “animal.” Whatever else anyone assigns, however, he will assign as something external—for example, “white,” “runs,” or anything of that kind. Thus these alone are rightly called the secondary substances of other things.

Aristotle shows, in due and appropriate order, that after primary substances—that is, individuals—genera and species have been established as secondary substances. This is a firm and straightforward proof. He says: “After the primary substances, genera and species have rightly been called secondary substances.” For in definitions, whenever the substance of anything is displayed, nothing other than genus and species reveals primary substances. If someone asks what Socrates is, he is called “man” or “animal”; and when asked what Socrates is in answer to the question “what is it?”, one rightly answers that he is man or animal. Therefore secondary substances show what primary substances are. If someone, apart from secondary substances, were to answer the question “what is the primary substance?” with something else, he would give a wholly inappropriate answer—for example, if, when asked what Socrates is, someone answered “white,” “he runs,” or something of that sort, which is not a secondary substance. Whoever says anything about a primary substance apart from secondary substances never gives an appropriate answer. Since none of the things that are not secondary substances declares what a primary substance is, and since secondary substances are genera and species, species and genera are rightly called secondary substances after primary substances.

Furthermore, primary substances are called substances properly because they are subject to everything else, while everything else is either predicated of them or is in them. Just as primary substances are related to everything else, so the genera and species of primary substances are related to all the remaining things. For everything else is predicated of them. You say that a particular man is grammatical; therefore you also say that man and animal are grammatical. The same applies in other cases.

There is also the following proof concerning the same matter, by which he confirms with the soundest reasoning that genera and species have rightly been placed after primary substances. Individuals are called primary substances for the reason that they are subject to everything else. Since they are placed beneath secondary substances for the purpose of predication, and secondary substances are predicated of them, and since they are placed beneath accidents so that accidents may exist, they are therefore primary substances.

Just as primary substances are subject to all accidents, so too are secondary substances. Since a particular man is subject to accidents, man and animal are also placed beneath an accident. Since a particular man is grammatical—that is, Aristarchus is a grammatical man—man is grammatical, and animal is grammatical as well. Consequently, primary substances are subject to accidents in the primary place, and secondary substances in the secondary place. Just as primary substances are subject both to accidents and to secondary substances, so secondary substances are subject to accidents. Secondary substances are species and genera. Aristotle therefore rightly proposed that, after primary substances, species and genera are secondary substances.

It is common to every substance not to be in a subject. For a primary substance is neither said of some subject nor is it in a subject. Secondary substances likewise exist in this respect, since none is in a subject. “Man,” for example, is said of some subject, namely an individual man, but it is not in a subject; for man is not in some man. Similarly, “animal” is said of some subject, namely a particular man, but animal is not in some man.

After enumerating substances and dividing them by proposing that some are primary and others secondary, [Col. 0190A] since no definition of substance had been given, Aristotle—because the most general genus is not contained by definitions—wishes to investigate a certain property, as though it were a sign by which we might recognize substance. First he proposes what can occur commonly in substances themselves; afterward he asks what is proper to them. He puts these matters first so that he may reach the true property without error and finally state what is truly proper to substances.

“Property” is signified in three ways. There is a property that belongs to every member of a species but not only to that species, such as being two-footed in the case of man. Every man is two-footed, but man alone is not, since birds too are two-footed. Or it belongs only to a species but not to every member of it, as being grammatical belongs to a certain man but not to every man; not every man is grammatical. The third meaning of property is what belongs to every member and only to that species, and always belongs to it, such as the capacity for laughter. Every man is capable of laughter, and man alone among animals laughs.

Of these, then, the first two mentioned above—where we said that certain properties belong either to every member but not only to the species, or only to the species but not to every member—appear to depart from the truth of properties. The third, which belongs to every member and only to the species, is truly a property. The former are called consequences, but are not truly properties; the last is truly a property.

Accordingly, whatever properties Aristotle finds that belong either only to some substances and not to all, or to all and not only to those substances, he rejects as not truly established in the nature of each thing. He posits instead the last kind, which can belong to every substance and only to substance. For those are properties that are convertible: if something is a man, it is capable of laughter; if something is capable of laughter, it is a man. Only those things can be converted which belong to every member and only to that member, since they will belong neither more to one thing nor less to another. Let us therefore proceed to the exposition and explanation of the passage itself.

What he says, then, is this: it is common to all substances that they are not in a subject. Primary substances, that is, individuals, are not in a subject. This is demonstrated with complete clarity by the following consideration. A particular substance can never be an accident of something. Secondary substances, however, possess a certain appearance of being in a subject. They seem to be in subjects—that is, in primary substances—but this is false. Secondary substances are merely predicated of primary substances; they are not in them.

“Animal,” for example, is said only of a certain man; it does not also subsist in some man as in a subject. The following consideration proves this. Whatever is in a subject has its individual instances also in a subject. Since color is in a body as subject, a particular color likewise rests upon a body as subject. But since primary substances, that is, individuals, are not in a subject, neither can their universals—that is, secondary substances, which are genera and species—rest upon some subject. Thus secondary substances have primary substances subject to them only for purposes of predication; they are not also accidents of primary substances.

There is also a very strong argument that secondary substances are not in a subject: everything that is in a subject can change, while the subject in which it is does not change. A color that is in a body can change while the same body remains, so that it becomes black from white. When primary substances remain, however, secondary substances do not change.

The proof that Aristotle himself gives to show that secondary substances are not in a subject is as follows. He had already taught that, in the case of certain things which are in a subject, their name can be predicated of the subjects, but never their definition. “White,” although it is in a body, is said of the body, and whiteness is predicated of the body; but the definition of whiteness is different from the definition of body. Secondary substances, however, are predicated of primary substances both in name and in definition. A particular man is an animal and a man; and a particular man is defined by the account of man and of animal.

To state the matter with the greatest exactness: everything that is in a subject is said equivocally of the subject. Secondary substances, however, are named of primary substances not equivocally but univocally, because, as has been said, they agree both in name and in definition. Therefore, just as primary substances are not in a subject, so secondary substances will lack a subject. It is common, then, to all substances, both secondary and primary, not to be in a subject; and whatever is a substance consequently exists in no subject.

But it may be asked whether this belongs only to substance or also to other things. If it belongs only to substance, then, since we have shown that it belongs to every substance that it is not in a subject, “not being in a subject” is called the true property of substance. For that was said to be most properly a property which belonged to all things and only to them. Aristotle confirms with the soundest proof that not being in a subject is not proper to substance, saying:

“Furthermore, among the things which are in a subject, nothing prevents their name from sometimes being predicated of the subject, but it is impossible for their definition to be so predicated. In the case of secondary substances, however, both their name and their definition will be predicated of the subjects; for you will predicate the definition of man and of animal of a particular man. Therefore substance will not be among the things which are in a subject. But this is not proper to substance, for difference too belongs among the things which are not in a subject. ‘Two-footed’ and ‘capable of walking’ are said of a subject, namely man, but are not in a subject; for two-footed is not in man, nor is capable of walking in man. The definition of the difference is also said of the thing of which the difference itself is predicated. Thus, if ‘capable of walking’ is said of man, the definition of ‘capable of walking’ will also be predicated of man, for man is capable of walking.”

He says that this is not proper to substance because the same condition is found in differences: no difference is in a subject. The following point is relevant. If a difference were in a subject, it would be predicated of the subject only in name and not also in definition. A difference, however, is predicated univocally of that of which it is said. If someone says that “capable of walking” is a difference of man, the definition of the difference will also appropriately apply to man. “Capable of walking” means “able to walk on the ground with the feet,” and man too is something that walks on the ground with the feet. Thus there can be one account both of the difference and of that of which the difference is predicated. That is, they can be joined both in the designation of the name and in the determination of the definition.

If the difference were in a subject, it would in no way be predicated univocally of that subject. Therefore not being in a subject is not proper to substance, since difference also possesses it. Difference is not substance. Otherwise, it would be proper to substance not to be in a subject. Difference, however, is not an accident, for then it would be in a subject.

Everything is either an accident or a substance—that is, it is either in a subject or not in a subject. Accidents are all those things which do not enter into the substance of their subject and which, when changed, do not destroy the nature of the substance. If, however, the destruction of something also destroys its subject, we do not properly call that thing an accident. A difference is predicated of several things differing in species in answer to the question “what sort of thing is it?”

Difference, however, is not substance. If it were substance, it would not be predicated of a subject in answer to the question “what sort of thing is it?” but in answer to the question “what is it?” Nor is it merely a quality, for then it would be an accident and would be in a subject.

Or is difference rather composed of substance and quality, so that the thing of which it is predicated is destroyed along with the destruction of the difference? Consider heat. When heat is in water, the water can remain in its substance after the heat has been removed; heat is in the water as its subject, and when it is removed the water does not perish. The same heat is also in fire, but when the heat is removed, the fire necessarily perishes. In fire, therefore, this quality of heat exists substantially and is a proper, that is, substantial, difference.

We must therefore conclude that difference is neither substance alone nor quality alone, but a substantial quality composed of both, which remains in the nature of its subject. Because it participates in substance, it is not an accident; because it is a quality, it is distinct from substance. It is thus a certain middle between substance and quality. Since it is not in a subject and is not substance, not being in a subject is not a property of substance.

After this he says that we must not be disturbed by the possibility that we might be forced to admit that parts of substances, which are in the whole as though in some subject, are not substances. Parts of substances are in a subject, but not as accidents. We see that certain parts of substances are in the whole as though they were in a subject: the head is in the whole body, and the hand is in the whole body. Form and matter, which are parts of a composite substance, are also in the composite substance itself. He therefore warns us lest we should at some point suspect that parts of substances are not substances but accidents merely because they are in a subject. He says:

“Let not the parts of substances disturb us, as though they were in the whole as in a subject, so that we might perhaps be forced to admit that they are not substances. For we did not say that things are in a subject in such a way that they are, as it were, parts in something.”

This gives the reason why no one should suspect that these things are accidents. Those things are defined as being in a subject which are in a subject without being a part of it; this was said above. “I call that being in a subject which, while it is in something, is not there as a certain part, and cannot exist separately from that in which it is.” Since, therefore, accidents are in a subject in such a way that they are not parts of the subject, while parts of substances are in the whole in such a way that they are not in a subject, no one can rightly suspect that parts of substances are parts of accidents.

Substances and differences also share the fact that everything predicated from them is predicated univocally. For everything so predicated is predicated either of individuals or of species. There is no predication from a primary substance, since it is not said of any subject. Among secondary substances, the species is predicated of an individual, while the genus is predicated both of a species and of an individual. Differences likewise are predicated of species and of individuals.

Primary substances also receive the account of species and genera, and species receive the account of their genus. Whatever is said of the predicate is also said of the subject. Similarly, species and individuals receive the account of differences. Things are univocal when they have both a common name and the same account. Thus everything derived from substances and differences is said univocally.

Having shown that not being in a subject is common to differences and substances, he proposes another common feature of substances and differences. Since some substances are primary and others secondary, and since primary substances are individuals, and individuals cannot have a subject, there is no predication from individuals. Secondary substances, however, are predicated of individuals—that is, of primary substances—and are said of them univocally. The name and the definition of secondary substances are predicated of individuals.

Of an individual, both species and genus are predicated. Thus of Plato—that is, of a particular man—both “man” and “animal” are said. A particular man is an animal, and the account of each is predicated of the individual. We say that a particular man is an animal, rational, mortal—the definition of the species, that is, of man. Again, we say that a particular man is an animate and sensible substance—the definition of the genus, that is, of animal.

A species also receives both the definition and the name of its genus. “Animal” is predicated of man, for man is said to be an animal, and this same man also receives the account of animal. We say that man is an animate and sensible substance.

It is therefore clear that genera and species are predicated univocally of individuals, and genera univocally of species. That is, in every predication of a secondary substance, it is said of its subjects by a univocal appellation. This is shared by difference. For a difference is also predicated univocally both of the species of which it is said and of the individual belonging to that species.

If “capable of walking” is a difference predicated of a particular man, a particular man is said to be capable of walking—for example, Plato and Cicero. Individuals of whom the difference is predicated also receive the definition of the difference. “Capable of walking” means “able to walk on the ground with the feet.” One could therefore define a particular man according to the name of the difference by saying that Plato is something able to walk on the ground with the feet.

The same occurs with the species of a particular man, that is, with man. Since man, the species itself, is capable of walking, it can be defined as follows: “Man is something able to walk on the ground with the feet.” Differences, therefore, are also said univocally of the things of which they are predicated.

Since secondary substances are said univocally of the things of which they are predicated, and differences in the same way, all predications made from substances or differences will also be predicated univocally of their subjects. The reason why secondary substances are predicated univocally of primary substances is the one Aristotle taught above when he reminded us that whatever is said of the predicate is also said of the subject.

All specific differences of a genus are predicated both of the species and of the individual. Since animal is constituted by the differences “animate” and “sensible,” these same differences will be predicated both of the species, that is, man, and of the individual, that is, a particular man. Since this has been stated above, it is sufficient to have said it here as briefly as the exposition requires.

Every substance also seems to signify a this-something; and in the case of primary substances it is indubitably and truly the case that they signify a this-something. What is signified is an individual and one in number. In the case of secondary substances, however, although the form of the name seems similarly to signify a this-something when someone says “man” or “animal,” this is not true. Rather, it signifies a certain sort of thing. For what is subject is not one in the way that a primary substance is; “man” and “animal” are said of many.

Nor does it signify merely a certain quality in the way that “white” does. “White” signifies nothing other than a quality, whereas genus and species determine a quality in the sphere of substance. For they signify a certain sort of substance; and the determination is greater in genus than in species, since “animal” encompasses more than “man.”

Since above he had stated two consequences of substance—namely, not being in a subject and having everything predicated of it univocally—and had separated them from what is most proper to substance because they also appeared to be common to differences, he adds another point which likewise makes this not proper to substance: it is not found in every substance.

Just as quantity signifies “how much” and quality signifies “what sort,” so substance also seems to signify a this-something. When I name Socrates, Plato, or some individual substance, I signify a this-something. But this does not belong to all substances. In the case of individuals, since they are particular and singular in number, it is true that substances signify a this-something.

The same is not true of secondary substances. Secondary substances are not single or numerically singular; species contain many individuals within themselves, and genera include many species within themselves. Therefore, when I say “man,” I do not signify a this-something. The name “man” is not singular, since it is predicated of many individuals; rather, it signifies a certain sort of thing. For when “man” is said, what sort of substance it is is shown.

This quality is determined around substance. Just as individuals possess species and genera of quality, and just as quantity encompasses individual quantities within species and genera, so the species and genera of individual substances are secondary substances.

When I say “man,” therefore, I signify a substance of such a kind as is predicated of several things differing in number in answer to the question “what is it?” Thus, when I have said “man,” I signify a certain sort of substance—one, namely, that is named of individuals. The same applies to genus. When I say “animal,” I signify a substance of such a kind as is said of several species.

There is therefore a quality, such as white, which is always in a substance, but not in such a way as to destroy the substance itself; for whiteness does not possess the property of substance. This quality which is predicated of substances determines a quality around substance and shows what sort of substance it is. If a man is rational, then the substance too will be rational; but “rational” is a quality.

Secondary substances therefore show what sort of substance something is. Consequently, it is not proper to substance to signify a this-something. Secondary substances show not a this-something but a certain sort of thing, as has been said; yet they show a certain sort of thing in such a way that they determine the quality itself around substances. For the quality of secondary substances is in individuals, since it is naturally predicated of them, and the individuals themselves are substances.

The quality of secondary substances is therefore terminated around individuals, that is, around those which are primary. Determination is greater whenever the boundary itself encompasses many things, and lesser whenever it encompasses fewer. Thus genus gathers together more things, while species gathers together fewer.

When I say “animal,” I include man, ox, and all other animals under this one name. When I say “man,” however, I include only individual men within the signification of the name. Determination is therefore greater through genus than through species, and the determination is a determination of quality around substance—either because substantial quality exists in genus and species, or because it is said according to a certain commonality of subjects.

Quality in itself, such as white, signifies neither the substance of anything nor any commonality, as genus displays the commonality of its species and species that of its individuals. Another property of substance must therefore be sought.

[Col. 0195D] Substance also has the property of having nothing contrary to it. What could be contrary to a primary substance, such as a particular man or a particular animal? Nothing is contrary to them. Nor is anything contrary to man or animal. But this is not proper to substance, since it also belongs to many other things, such as quantity. Nothing is contrary to a quantity of two cubits or three cubits; nor is anything contrary to ten or to any such quantity.

Unless perhaps someone says that many is contrary to few, or large to small; but no determinate quantity has any contrary.

He adds another property of substance, saying that nothing is contrary to substance. He confirms this by induction through individual cases. Man is not contrary to man, horse, or any other animal. If someone should perhaps say that, since fire and water are substances, fire is contrary to water, he would be mistaken. Fire is not contrary to water; rather, the qualities of fire are opposed to the qualities of water.

Heat and cold are contraries, as are moisture and dryness. Since these qualities are found in different ways in fire and in water, they appear to make the substances themselves contrary, but they do not. The point can be proved from all other substances as well, among which no one will be able to find anything contrary.

But this is not proper to substance alone, since determinate quantity too lacks contraries. Two is not contrary to three, nor two to four, nor anything of this sort. For if we say that three is contrary to two, why should we not also posit four or five as contrary to two? No reason can be offered why, if three is contrary to two, four or five should not be contrary to two. If this is so, then four, three, five, and every number that differs from two would become contrary to two; and one thing would have many contraries, which is impossible. Quantity therefore has no contrary.

If someone says that large is contrary to small, or many to few, even if he confirms that these are quantities, they are not determinate quantities. For the speaker does not define how large the large is or how small the small is; the same applies to many and few. If someone calls these quantities, he will admit that they are indeterminate and undefined.

Aristotle says that determinate quantity has nothing contrary to it, such as two or three, a line, or a surface. Even if some quantities have contraries and others do not, this does not affect the present point, since it is established that certain quantities do not have contraries. If this absence of a contrary also occurs in quantities, then it is not proper to substance.

If someone places large and small among quantities, the matter is clear—as Aristotle himself will later show—that these are not quantities but relatives: large is said in relation to small. When we come to those passages, we shall pursue the order of the subject more carefully. Now that it has been made clear both that nothing is contrary to substance and that this is not proper to substance, since the same is also found in quantities, let us turn to the path of exposition concerning the next property.

Substance appears not to admit of more and less. I do not mean by this that one substance is not more or less substantially a substance than another; this was stated because it is so. Rather, I mean that each substance, precisely insofar as it is what it is, is not said to be more or less. If this substance is man, it is not more or less man, either in relation to itself or in comparison with another. One man is not more a man than another, as one thing is whiter than another, or one thing better than another.

The same thing can also be said to be more or less in relation to itself. A body, when it is white, is said to be whiter now than before; and when it is hot, it is said to be hotter or less hot. Substance, however, is not said to be more or less substance. A man is not said to be more a man now than before, nor is anything else that is a substance. Substance therefore does not admit of more and less.

This property is not stated without qualification, but with a certain distinction. For he says that substance admits neither more nor less—not by saying that one substance is not more of a substance than another. For a certain man, since he is a substance, is more of a substance than “man,” that is, than the species; and man is more of a substance than animal, that is, than the genus. Therefore he is not saying that no substances are more substances than other substances; this has already been stated, since it is so—that is, since such cases are found.
