For above he said that primary substances, that is, individual substances, are substances in the fullest sense, while among secondary substances species are more substances than genera.

Therefore he is not saying that no substance is more of a substance than another substance, but that, in respect of what it is itself, no substance is said to be more or less a substance. Thus, if man is a substance, he is not saying that man is not more or less a substance: an individual man is more of a substance, while the species is less of one when referred to the primary, that is, individual, substance. Rather, he says that, in respect of what it is itself—that is, man—man will not be more or less man. Accordingly, he does not say that man is not more or less a substance, but that man, in respect of what he is himself, is not more or less man. For no man is more or less man; and the same point may be observed in comparison with himself.

For a man is not more man in relation to himself; nor, if he is compared with another, provided that they belong under the same conjunction or classification, will one individual man compared with another individual man be more or less man. Nor will the species itself be more or less man in relation to itself. This is clear in substances; in qualities, however, there can be more and less. White can become whiter than itself and admit more and less, so that it is whiter or less white. It can also be whiter than another white thing, as a lily is whiter than wool; and less white than another white thing, as wool is less white than a lily, and a swan less white than snow. The same is true of other qualities, such as the good and the hot.

For these can be altered by time and brought into a greater or lesser degree: something good can become better or worse, and something hot hotter or cooler. But a human being, who is a substance, will not now be more human than he was before, nor later be more or less human than he is now. Therefore, although substance does not admit more and less, this will nevertheless not be its property.

But why this is not its property Aristotle himself passed over in silence, as though it were known. We add, however, that not only do substances fail to admit more and less, but many other things do as well. One circle will not be more or less a circle than another, nor will a double be more or less double. For four is equally double in relation to two, and ten in relation to five. Therefore, since the same is true in other cases, this should not be regarded as a property of substance.

But all these features, whatever they are that are found in all substances, are nevertheless not properties of substance, since they are also found in other things. They are called consequences of substance. For all these things follow substances: wherever there is a substance, the features mentioned are found—namely, not being in a subject, having predicates predicated univocally from them, signifying a certain individual thing, having nothing contrary to them, and not admitting more and less.

Those features, however, that are not found in all substances are accidents of substances, and therefore are not properties. If they are not properties, they do not yet demonstrate what substance is like. Therefore, if we are to know the quality of substance properly, a property of the following kind must be sought for it: one that belongs both to substances alone and to all substances. This is the property that he himself proposed.

[Col. 0198B] The property that seems most especially to belong to substance is that, while remaining one and the same numerically, it is receptive of contraries. In the case of other things that are not substances, no one will be able to produce anything that, while remaining one and the same numerically, is receptive of contraries. For example, a color that is one and the same numerically will not be both white and black; nor will the same action, one numerically, be both vicious and virtuous.

The same applies to other things that are not substances. Substance, however, while remaining one and the same numerically, is capable of contraries. Thus a certain man, while remaining one and the same numerically, is at one time black and at another white; he is hot and cold, vicious and virtuous.

Nothing of this sort appears in any other thing—unless someone should perhaps object that statement and opinion are receptive of contraries. The same statement appears to be true and false: for example, if the statement “someone is sitting” is true, then when he rises, that same statement will be false. The same is true of opinion. If someone truly thinks that a person is sitting, when the person rises, he will falsely think the same thing, retaining the same opinion about the same subject.

But even if one grants this, there is nevertheless a difference. The things that are in substances become receptive of contraries by undergoing change. For what was hot and becomes cold has changed; it has been altered. What was white and becomes black, and what was virtuous and becomes vicious, have likewise changed. The same applies in other cases: each thing, by undergoing change, becomes receptive of contraries.

Statement and opinion, however, remain entirely unmoved in themselves. When the thing changes, a contrary condition comes about in relation to them. The statement “someone is sitting” remains the same, but when the thing has changed it becomes at one time true and at another false. The same applies to opinion. Therefore, even if one grants that statement and opinion are receptive of contraries, substance is at least receptive of contraries in a proper sense, because it is capable of them through its own change.

Aristotle says that it is especially the property of substance that the same thing, one numerically, is receptive of contraries, saying nothing contrary to what he said earlier. There he had said that substances are not contrary to substances; here he says that substances are not themselves contraries, but that things can receive contraries in themselves. Thus one and the same man is now healthy and at another time ill, while illness and health are contraries.

Therefore, since it has been established that substance can receive contraries, it must be demonstrated how this belongs to substances alone. For it is found in none of the other categories. In quality, one quality will not remain the same and one numerically while receiving contraries. The same thing, one numerically, will not be white and black: when it has been white and is later changed into black, the entire species of the quality has changed, and what is contrary is no longer one and the same numerically but something different.

Similarly, the same action, one numerically, will not be both good and bad; rather, one action will be good and another bad, so that they are different and not the same numerically. The same is found in the other categories.

Substance itself, however, since it is one and singular numerically, receives contraries. Thus the same one man, when he has been bright and white and is darkened by the sun, is changed from white into black and transformed into its contrary, receiving both contraries in himself. The preceding discussion sufficiently demonstrates that this belongs to none but substances.

If someone should object that statement and opinion, one and the same, are receptive of contraries, because when I say “Cicero is sitting,” or think that he is sitting, while he truly sits, both the statement and the opinion about him are true; but when he has risen, the same opinion or statement—“Cicero is sitting”—remains, although it is false, since he is not sitting. Thus opinion and statement seem to be the same and one numerically, now true and now false, and to receive contraries.

But this is false, because statement and opinion do not receive contraries. For even if one grants that statement and opinion are receptive of contraries, they are not so in the same way as substance. Substance, when receiving contraries, is itself changed: Cicero himself, receiving illness in himself, changes from healthy to ill, and, having changed, himself receives contraries.

Speech or opinion, however, remains itself unchanged; when the things about which it speaks or judges have changed, it is itself found to be false or true. Substance itself changes together with the contraries it receives; statement and opinion, because the things about which they are spoken or formed change, appear to be true or false.

When I say “Cicero is sitting,” if he has risen, the statement itself has undergone nothing; rather, the thing about which the statement was made has changed. The person who was sitting has risen, and for this reason the true statement has become false. Therefore substance itself, by receiving contraries, is changed, as has been said; but statement and opinion do not change. Instead, when the thing around which they are concerned changes, they become true or false.

Thus the property of substance will be understood to be receptive of contraries in such a way that, having itself changed, it receives contraries—not in such a way that, when the thing changes, it itself remains unchanged and immutable. This has been said only in case someone should think that statement and opinion are receptive of contraries; in fact, statement and opinion are not receptive of contraries. Aristotle himself adds again:

This is not true. Statement and opinion are not said to be receptive of contraries because they themselves receive anything contrary; rather, they are so called because some affection has occurred around something else. For according as the thing is or is not, the statement is said to be true or false—not because the statement itself is receptive of contraries. For statement and opinion are not moved by anything at all. Therefore they will not be receptive of contraries, since no affection of contraries has occurred in them. Substance, however, because it itself receives contraries, is said to be receptive of contraries. It receives illness and health, whiteness and blackness, and, by receiving each of these things itself, is said to be receptive of contraries. Therefore it will be the property of substance, while remaining the same and one numerically, to be receptive of contraries through its own change. And concerning substance, let this suffice.

He says that statement and opinion themselves are receptive of no contrary. For falsity and truth are not inherent in statement or opinion; they appear to be receptive of contraries because, as he himself says, they are concerned with some other affection—that is, with the fact that something is the object of an opinion or statement.

For the opinion or statement that someone is sitting or not sitting is concerned with sitting and not sitting, which are contraries. Thus, because they concern other things that are contrary to one another, when those things change, statement and opinion appear to become contrary—not because they themselves receive contraries, but because they concern contrary affections of things.

For neither statement nor opinion changes; only the things about which the statement and opinion are made change—namely, sitting and not sitting. Therefore, since statement and opinion themselves receive no affection and nothing contrary occurs in them, they do not appear to be receptive of contraries. Substance, however, because it itself receives a contrary, is said to be receptive of contraries.

Cicero, by receiving health, becomes healthy; by receiving illness, he becomes ill. But statement and opinion, as has been said, do not receive contraries. Therefore it will be the property of substance to be receptive of contraries.

But someone might perhaps ask why, although fire is hot, it never receives cold, and why, although water is moist, it never receives dryness. Since these are opposed, substance does not appear to be receptive of every contrary, and this property of substance would be weakened, since it is not found in all substances.

The answer must be that substances appear to receive those contraries that are not inherent in their nature. Otherwise, a thing does not receive whatever is present in it substantially. We say that something receives what comes from things external and is constituted outside its substance.

Since being hot is inherent in the substance of fire, fire does not receive heat. Therefore fire is receptive neither of heat nor of cold. It does not receive heat because heat adheres immutably to its nature and substance; it does not receive cold because the nature of heat belonging to fire spontaneously rejects its contrary.

Therefore, if there is something that fire receives—that is, something externally situated—it must also receive its contrary, while remaining itself one and singular. The same must be said of water. Just as fire does not receive heat, water does not receive moisture, for moisture is in a certain way naturally inherent in it.

For this reason the heat of fire and the moisture of water are said not only to be qualities but also substantial qualities of fire and water. Water, however, because it does not substantially possess either cold or heat in itself, is said to be receptive both of cold and of heat.

Therefore he is not speaking of contraries that are present substantially, but of those that each substance can receive—that is, of what can be applied to it externally. It is clear that this is found in all substances. For since Cicero is healthy and ill, man is healthy and ill; and if man is healthy and ill, animal is healthy and ill.

But animal and man are considered in two ways: first, as predicated of many; second, as substances. Insofar as they are predicated of many, they are not receptive of contraries. Thus animal, insofar as it is predicated of species, is neither wise nor foolish; and man, insofar as he is predicated of individuals, is neither healthy nor ill. But insofar as they are substances, and insofar as they stand above individual substances, they are receptive of contraries.

Therefore it will be the property of substance alone to be receptive of contraries. Let this suffice concerning substance. The sequence of the second book will begin with an exposition of quantity.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0201]

[Col. 0201B] Although the duties of the consulship prevent us from devoting all our leisure and complete attention to these studies, it nevertheless seems to belong to some form of public service to instruct our fellow citizens in a work produced by night-long labor. Nor shall I deserve ill of my fellow citizens if, after the ancient virtue of men has transferred to this one republic the affairs, domination, and empire of all other cities, I at least train the morals of our state in the arts of Greek wisdom, insofar as anything remains to be done.

Therefore even this does not fall outside the duty of the consul, since it has always been the Roman custom to honor more and more by imitation whatever was beautiful and praiseworthy anywhere among the nations. I shall therefore begin and weave together the argument and the order of the work I have undertaken.

## ON QUANTITY

[Col. 0201C] Of quantity, one kind is discrete, another continuous; and one kind consists of parts that have position in relation to one another, while another consists of parts that do not have position. Discrete quantity is, for example, number and speech. Continuous quantity is line, surface, and body. In addition to these there are also time and place.

The parts of number have no common boundary at which its portions are joined. Thus, if five is a portion of ten, the five and five are not joined at any common boundary; they are always discrete and separate. Likewise, three and seven are not joined at any common boundary. In number, one cannot find a common boundary of the parts; they are always discrete and separate.

Therefore number belongs to the discrete, and speech likewise belongs to the discrete. That speech is a quantity is clear, for it is measured by the short and long syllable. I mean speech produced by the voice, since its portions are not joined at any common boundary. There is no common boundary at which its syllables are joined; each syllable is divided and stands on its own.

After treating substance, the reason why he proposed to discuss quantity rather than quality is that everything that exists, as soon as it exists, falls under number. Every thing is either one or many; and the knowledge of quantity gathers together the one and the many.

But not every thing, as soon as it exists, immediately receives some quality. Matter itself falls under the principle of quantity, since it is one, but not under quality; for the matter itself is, for the time being, free from all qualities, while it is affected by the addition of a certain form and thereby receives quality. In itself it is numerically one but has no quality. Therefore, if every thing, as soon as it exists, falls under number, whereas not every thing immediately receives quality as soon as it exists, he rightly proposed quantity first.

There is also another reason why he treats the nature of quantity first. Every body, in order to be a body, consists of three dimensions: length, breadth, and height. In order for it to be a body with a quality, however, it must be white, black, or something else. Since being a body comes first and being a white body afterward, it will be prior for a body to consist of three dimensions than for it to be white.

But the three dimensions are quantities both numerically and through the continuity of space. Length, breadth, and height are counted among quantities, whereas white belongs to quality. Therefore, if consisting of three dimensions is prior to being white, quantity will be prior to quality. Accordingly, the discussion of quantity has rightly been proposed first.

There is yet another reason: quantity has more features resembling those of substance. Just as nothing is contrary to substance and substance does not admit more and less, so too with quantity. Nothing is contrary to quantity, nor does quantity admit more and less, as we shall show shortly. Quality, however, receives contraries, such as white and black, and more and less, such as whiter and blacker, whitest and blackest. For whatever can receive increase can also receive diminution.

Since quantity is more like substance, he rightly proposed to discuss quantity after substance.

He says that quantity has two differences. For one quantity is discrete and separated, while another is continuous. After this division he divides quantity again in another way. He says that one quantity consists of parts having position in relation to one another, while another consists of parts that do not have position.

That one thing can be divided in different ways is clear. Thus one may divide animal by saying: “Of animals, some are rational and others irrational.” Again one may divide the same thing in another way: “Of animals, some are walking and others not walking”; and again, among those animals, some feed on flesh, others on grass, and others on seeds.

Here one and the same thing has been divided according to a different order and method. Aristotle therefore divided the same name, quantity, in different ways: into what is discrete and what is continuous, and into what has position of its parts and what does not. The second division will be discussed later; for now, let the first be treated.

He states the first division as follows: “One quantity is continuous and another discrete.” Discrete is that whose parts are joined by no common boundary. Continuous is that whose parts have some common boundary at which they appear to be joined.

He gives number and speech as examples and species of discrete quantities. Speech is a discrete quantity, and number likewise; no one doubts that number is a quantity. It is discrete because, although the number ten consists of five and five, no connection can be found that joins one five to the other so as to make the whole ten into a single body.

If someone says that ten consists of three and seven, no common boundary can be found by which three and seven are joined so as to produce one complete whole of ten. This can be observed in every number. No number has parts such that some common boundary joins them; the parts themselves are always separate and discrete. Such a quantity is called discrete.

Number, therefore, is a discrete quantity. He says that speech is a quantity because every speech consists of a noun and a verb, and these consist of syllables. Every syllable is either long or short. But long and short are without doubt quantities. Who, then, would doubt that what consists of quantities is itself a quantity?

Speech itself, although it is a quantity, is also discrete. When I say “Cicero,” which is a part of speech, the parts of this name—*ci*, *ce*, and *ro*—are joined by no common boundary. We cannot find a common boundary by which the syllable *ci* is joined to *ce*, or *ce* to *ro*. Therefore speech also appears to be a discrete quantity.

But someone might perhaps say that the common boundary by which these syllables are joined, so that they signify something, is their signification itself. In the name “Cicero,” the common boundary of the syllables would be its signification. For if *ce*, which is in the middle, were placed first, *ro*, which is last, in the middle, and *ci*, which is first, last, the name that was previously “Cicero,” with its syllables transposed, would signify nothing.

The answer is that whatever is uttered in a certain speech, whether it signifies something or signifies nothing, has no common boundary among its syllables. For if someone says that, after the syllables have been rearranged, “Cicero” has become “ceroci” and has lost its signification, the syllables are nevertheless equally joined at no common boundary.

If someone should posit that this very expression signifies something—for example, that “Cicero signifies something”—then a signification has indeed been added, but no boundary has thereby been added to the syllables. Therefore, whether the name signifies something or nothing, its parts are discrete and separate and are joined by no common boundary.

Since in Greek *logos* (λόγος) also means a thought of the mind and reasoning within oneself, and since *logos* also means speech, I added this qualification so that no one, when Aristotle said that *logos*, that is, speech, is a discrete quantity, would think that he meant the *logos*, that is, the reasoning, which each person arranges in his own thought.

I mean speech produced by the voice. In Latin, the terms for speech and reasoning are distinct. In Greek, however, one word, *logos*, serves for both reasoning and speech. Therefore, so that the translation should not be blamed for being misleading, I added this qualification as well: “I mean speech produced by the voice.”

Among the Romans there is no other speech than speech produced by the voice, whereas among the Greeks there is another *logos*, which takes place in the thought of the mind. Therefore, so that nothing should be lacking, I translated even this qualification, although it is less applicable to Latin speech. I have explained in this exposition why I did so. Let this suffice concerning discrete quantity.

Continuous quantity is, as has been said, that whose parts have a common boundary. Examples are line, surface, and body, and in addition to these time and place. Aristotle himself indicates this in the following words:

“Line is continuous, for it is possible to take a common boundary at which its portions are joined—the point; and the common boundary of the surface is the line, for the portions of a plane are joined at a certain common boundary. Similarly, in the case of body you can take a common boundary, either a line or a surface, at which the portions of the body are joined.”

After explaining discrete quantity, he proceeds to the species of continuous quantity. Continuous quantities are, as has been said, those whose parts have some common boundary, as in the case of a line.

If someone divides a line, which is length without breadth, he makes two lines in the division, and each of the divided lines has a point at its extremity. For the boundaries of lines are points. Therefore, although the line had not previously been divided, the two points that appear after the division at the ends of the two lines are understood to have existed together before the division; in the division they become separate.

Thus the common boundary of the parts of a line is understood to be the point—that is, something so small that it cannot itself be divided or cut into parts.

A surface, which is breadth without height, likewise has a line as the common boundary of its parts; a solid body has a surface. For a surface that is divided produces two lines through its respective parts, just as a divided line produces two points at its opposite ends. When a solid body is divided, it produces two surfaces in the two parts of the division. When those surfaces were joined and undivided, the point was understood as the common boundary of the parts of the line; the line as the common boundary of the surface; and the surface as the common boundary of the solid body.

A sign of the continuity of a body is that if one part is moved, the entire body moves; and if the entire body moves, its neighboring parts will certainly move at the same time. Thus, if a small rod lies made of bronze, wood, or any other metal, and someone moves one of its ends or any part of it, the whole rod is immediately moved.

This happens because its parts are joined by a certain common boundary, and when one part is moved, that common boundary moves the other parts. The same is not true of discrete things. If there are ten, and I move one, the others do not move; the remaining nine stay still. If a bushel is full of grain, and I move one grain of wheat, all the grains will not immediately be moved, because the multitude is discrete and one grain does not appear to be connected with another by any common boundary.

But if one part of the grain itself is moved, the whole body of the grain must be moved.

This is not being said to claim that a line consists of points, or a surface of lines, or a solid body of surfaces. Rather, the point is the boundary of a line, the line the boundary of a surface, and the surface the boundary of a solid body; no thing consists of its boundaries.

Therefore the point of a line is not a part but the common boundary of its parts. The line of a surface, and the surface of a solid body, are not parts but common boundaries of their parts. It follows that line, surface, and the thickness of a solid body are continuous quantities. To these he adds further examples.

[Col. 0205B] Time and place are also of this kind. The present time joins the past and the future. Place likewise belongs to continuous things. The portions of a body occupy a certain place, and these portions are joined at a certain common boundary. Therefore the portions of place that contain the individual parts of a body are joined at the same boundary as the portions of the body. Place, therefore, is continuous, since its portions are joined at one common boundary.

He declares that time and place also belong to continuous quantity. That time is a quantity is shown by the fact that it is considered in extension, that is, in length and shortness. That it is continuous is shown by the fact that the parts of time have some common boundary and middle point at which their extremities are joined.

The parts of time are the past and the future; the present time is their common boundary. For the present is the end of the past and the beginning of the future.

Place likewise belongs to continuous things. By “place” we mean whatever holds the parts of a body, whether above, beside, or beneath it. If all the parts of a body occupy some place, and the place surrounding the body is spread through the whole extent and through the parts of the body, all the parts of the body will be occupied by parts of place.

If this is so, the common boundary that joined the parts of the body also joins those places that belong to the parts of the body. Place is therefore continuous in the same way as body. A common boundary is found in the parts of place just as in the parts of body, because the place of the body is spread throughout the whole body.

When he said, “Of this kind are also place and time,” he was speaking above about continuous quantities and added time and place to the continuous, saying, “Of this kind are also time and place,” that is, of continuous quantities. But after the division of continuous and discrete quantity, he begins another division again from the beginning.

[Col. 0206A] “Moreover, some quantities consist of parts that have position in relation to one another, while others consist of parts that do not have position. Thus the parts of a line have position in relation to one another. Each of them is situated somewhere, and one can take and designate where each is situated on a plane and to which of the other parts it is joined. Similarly, the parts of a plane have a certain position; for in the same way it can be shown where each lies and which parts are joined to one another. The same applies to solid body and place.”

[Col. 0206B] He again distinguishes the differences of quantity. Some quantities consist of parts that have position in relation to one another; others consist of parts that have no position.

Those parts are said to retain position whose nature has these three features: first, that the parts are somewhere; second, that they do not perish; and third, that the parts themselves join together and continue in their proper arrangement. A line is an example.

If a line is placed on a surface, you can recognize where its parts are: its beginning is on the right, its middle in the middle, and its extremity on the left. These are said to remain while the parts themselves remain. For the parts of the line do not perish but remain in the place where they are.

You can also show which part of the line is joined to which part—that is, to which part the beginning of one part and the end of another are connected. You can say, for example, “Here this part, the half, ends,” pointing out the place where it ends; and, again, “Here another part of the whole line begins.”

Thus, when a line is placed on any surface, its parts retain some place, the parts themselves do not perish, and anyone can recognize where the extremity of one part is joined and at what place the parts continue in relation to one another.

The same occurs in a surface. The parts of a surface are somewhere, they themselves do not perish, and it can be shown where one part is joined to another. Solid body has the same feature, and the parts of place are likewise continuous with those parts to which the parts of the body are themselves continuous, as was said above.

Therefore place will have the same nature as the whole of solid body. Place too belongs to the same kind of quantity as solid body: it consists of parts that have position in relation to one another. Place itself, therefore, consists of parts that have position in relation to one another.

Three things must therefore be considered, as was said above, if the parts are to appear to have position in relation to one another: the place in which the parts themselves are situated; the fact that those parts do not perish; and the fact that there is containment and continuity among the parts.

If someone should say that place lacks this feature because it is not itself in a place—for everything is in a place, but place itself cannot be in a place—the answer is that surface, solidity, and line are said to have position of their parts because they are in a place, their parts remain, and those parts are continuous.

Therefore place itself, all the more, is said to have position of its parts, since its parts neither perish nor cease to be joined together continuously and permanently.

Let this suffice concerning things that consist of parts having position in relation to one another. He now adds what concerns things that do not have position.

In number no one can show how its portions have any position in relation to one another, where they are situated, or which of its portions are connected with one another. The same is true of the parts of time. For the parts of time do not remain; and how could what does not remain have any position? Rather, you would say that time has a certain order of parts, so that one portion of time is earlier and another later.

The same applies to number: one is counted before two, and two before three. Thus numbers have a certain order, but one will not easily find position in them. Speech is similar. Its parts do not remain; something has been said and is no longer available to be taken up. Therefore its parts will not have position, since nothing remains.

Some things, then, consist of parts that have position in relation to one another, while others consist of parts that do not have position.

These, then, retain no position of their parts in relation to one another because it is clear that something is lacking in them from among the features mentioned above. [Col. 0207C] Number is itself discrete, and its parts are not joined to one another but are altogether separate. For this reason it does not belong among those things whose parts have some position in relation to one another. Nor could you show in what place any number lies. A thing is said to have position when—as has been stated—it is placed in some location, and when that position consists of parts that remain and are joined and connected to one another, so that it can be shown where each part lies and which part is connected to which. In number none of this is present. For it is not shown to be situated in any place, nor are its parts joined together. Thus, of the three features we have mentioned, number lacks two: position in a place and continuity of its parts. Time, although its parts are continuous, is nevertheless not said to have position of its parts because its parts do not remain but are always [Col. 0207D] moving and continually passing away. It is always being whirled along in swift motion and, like flowing water, never rests in any station. Since its parts do not remain, it is not said to consist of parts that possess position in relation to one another.

Yet although these things cannot have a position of their parts, they nevertheless possess a certain order, which they retain apart from the position of their parts. We say that two comes before three, and three before four; and the same order is plainly found in time: the future comes after the present, and the present after the past. Thus, even though these things do not have any position of their parts, they nevertheless retain an order.

[Col. 0208A] What he says—“but you will not, to any great extent, apprehend position”—amounts to saying that you will not apprehend it at all. “To any great extent” appears to have been added in place of “altogether,” as if he had said: “But you will not apprehend position at all.” The reason is that continuity itself gives some appearance that the thing might possess a position of its parts, but this is not actually so. For although quantities may be continuous, if they lack even one of the features mentioned above, they cannot possess a position of their parts.

The water discharged by a pipe retains its position while it is falling; but when the already-poured water mingles with the waves, it loses the position of its parts. A river likewise, when it flows into the sea, appears both to possess a position of its parts and to be continuous so long as the river’s surface has not yet mingled with the seawater. But when the outermost part of the river is touched by the sea’s influx, it plainly appears to lose its entire position. [Col. 0208B]

Speech is similarly constituted. It is not itself situated in any place, nor are its parts joined to one another in any way; rather, they are separate from one another. When its parts have been spoken, they do not remain. This is what he means when he says: “It has been spoken, and it cannot be taken up again any further.” For as soon as speech is uttered, it immediately passes away and cannot remain in any way. Consequently, as soon as something has been spoken, its parts cannot be displayed or grasped by demonstration.

Speech, therefore, also belongs among those things that do not have a position of their parts. Whether it has an order is doubtful. If a speech signifies something, as does *Cicero*, there is a certain order in it: the first syllable uttered is *ci*, the second *ce*, and the third *ro*; and [Col. 0208C] it derives its order rather from its signification. But if it signifies nothing, it is not said to have an order, as with *scindapsus*, which signifies nothing. Whether one places the second syllable first, the last syllable first, or mixes up the order and sequence of the syllables in any fashion, the result is the same. In significant words, an order is said to exist because, if that order is altered, the force of the signification is overturned. Here, however, where there is no signification, it makes no difference how the parts are arranged.

Thus speech has an order of its parts in some cases, but in others the order itself cannot be found. Or perhaps something that signifies nothing cannot be called speech, and there is no speech that lacks order.

According to the earlier division of quantity, in which it was said that some quantities are continuous and others discrete, there are five continuous quantities and two discrete ones. [Col. 0208D] The continuous are line, surface, solid body, place, and time. The discrete are number and speech. In the second division, however, in which he says that some quantities consist of parts having position in relation to one another, four retain position: line, surface, body, and place. Three do not have position: of these, two always retain an order, namely time and number. Speech has an order if it signifies something; if it signifies nothing, it is disordered—assuming that something signifying nothing can be called speech.

Having stated this, he concludes by saying: “Some things, then, consist of parts that have position in relation to one another, while others consist of parts that do not have position.” Having completed this division, he proceeds to the remaining matters, showing which things are properly called quantities and which are so called accidentally. [Col. 0209A]

The only things called proper quantities are those we have mentioned; everything else is called a quantity accidentally. For by looking to these things we call other things quantities as well: white is called “much” because its surface is extensive; an action is called “long” because its duration is great; and a motion is called “much” because it lasts a long time. None of these, taken individually, is called a quantity in itself. If someone is asked how long an action is, he defines it by time, assigning its measure in years or in some other way. If he assigns how extensive a white thing is, he defines it by its surface. Whatever the extent of the surface, he will say that the white thing is of that extent. Therefore only the things mentioned are called quantities properly and in themselves; nothing else is a quantity in itself, but only accidentally.

[Col. 0209B] Something is said to be such primarily when it is in itself what it is shown to be. It is such accidentally when it is not such in itself but is said to be such through something else. Thus color belongs to whiteness in itself: according to the nature of white, whiteness is said to be a color. But when a human being is called colored, this is not said of him in himself, because color is not present in a human being insofar as he is a human being; rather, because he possesses color, he is called colored.

Thus, just as white is in itself a color because color is a certain natural genus, while a human being is called colored because he possesses color, so white is called a color in itself and primarily, whereas a human being is called colored accidentally.

The same applies to quantities. All the things mentioned—line, surface, [Col. 0209C] body, number, speech, and time—are called quantities in themselves and according to their proper nature. If other things are called quantities according to some quantity, they are not named so in themselves but accidentally. Thus white is called “much,” not because whiteness is a quantity, but because the surface in which the white exists is extensive. If the space in which the white exists is extensive, the white will be extensive. Therefore white is not called “much” because whiteness itself possesses some quantity in itself, but because it is constituted in some quantity, namely a surface. According to the surface—which is a quantity and is extensive in itself—white is called “much.” It is not so called according to itself, and therefore white is called “much” neither in itself nor primarily, but accidentally.

[Col. 0209D] An action is likewise called long because it has been performed over a long period of time. We call an illness extensive when it lasts a long time, and a motion extensive because it has taken place over a long period, as when someone runs for a long time. But if someone were to call a run “extensive” because it was extremely swift, he would not be using language appropriately. Swiftness is not a quantity but rather a quality: according to it we are described as swift, that is, as belonging to a certain kind, not as having a certain quantity.

That something is called extensive according to quantity is shown by the very definition of the things. If someone wished to show what an extensive white thing is and to enclose it within the proper limit of a definition, he would have to say that white is extensive when it lies in an extensive surface; and that motion [Col. 0210A] and action are extensive when they are completed over a long period of time.

Thus, because we look to proper quantities and refer other things to them when we call them quantities—such as white to surface, which is a true quantity, and a run, or any motion or action, to time, which itself is truly a quantity—these things are not called quantities in themselves, but are named through those things that are properly called quantities. Since what is not so in itself is so accidentally, all things other than those previously enumerated among quantities are rightly said to be quantities accidentally and not in themselves. Therefore only those quantities that were listed above are properly and in themselves called quantities. The others are not quantities in themselves but, as he himself says, perhaps quantities accidentally.

After the division into continuous and discrete, into that which has a position of its parts and that which does not, and into quantities that are primarily and in themselves so and those that are quantities accidentally, he proceeds, as usual, to the properties by which quantities may be discovered.

Moreover, nothing is contrary to quantity. In the case of determinate quantities this is obvious: nothing is contrary to a two-cubit measure, a three-cubit measure, a surface, or anything of that kind. Nothing is contrary to them. Unless perhaps someone says that “much” is contrary to “few,” or “large” to “small”; but none of these is a quantity. They are rather relative terms. Nothing is called small or large in itself, but only in relation to something else. A mountain is called small, while millet is called large, because the former is smaller within its own kind and the latter larger within its own kind. Their relation, then, is to something else. For if large or small were said in itself, a mountain would never be called small and millet large.

Again, we say that there are more people in a village and fewer in a city, even though there are many more people in the city. Likewise, we say that there are many in a house but few in a theater, although there are more people in the theater. Further, a two-cubit or three-cubit measure, and each of the things of this kind, signifies quantity, whereas large or small does not signify quantity but rather relation, since “large” or “small” looks to something else. It is therefore clear that these are relative terms.

Moreover, whether one considers these to be quantities or not, nothing is contrary to them. For what cannot be grasped in itself but is referred solely to the relation of another—how could anything be contrary to it? [Col. 0210D]

Further, if large and small were contraries, it would follow that the same thing could receive contraries simultaneously and that these very things would be contrary to themselves. For the same thing can simultaneously be small and large: it is small in relation to one thing and that very same thing is large in relation to another. Thus it is possible for the same thing to be small and large at the same time, and so it would receive contraries simultaneously.

But nothing appears capable of receiving contraries simultaneously. Substance does appear to be receptive of contraries, but no one is simultaneously healthy and ill, or simultaneously white and black; nor is there anything else that receives contraries simultaneously. The same thing would also turn out to be contrary to itself. For if large were contrary to small, while the same thing were simultaneously small and large, it would be contrary to itself. But it is impossible for a thing to be contrary to itself. Therefore large is not contrary to small, nor much to few. Consequently, even if someone does not classify these as relatives but as quantities, they will still have nothing contrary to them.

A determinate quantity is one confined by some numerical limit, such as two or three, and things expressed in this way, as when one says two cubits, three cubits, and so forth. Things determined by some proper signification also belong here, such as surface and solidity. For what they are and what quantities they are is recognized; and because they are determinate, none of them has a contrary. A two-cubit measure is not contrary to a three-cubit measure, just as one number is not contrary to another. Nor is a surface contrary to solidity, nor anything of this kind to another.

[Col. 0211B] But since some indeterminate things display a certain appearance of quantity, such as large and small, which seem to be contraries, Aristotle opposes these to one another, saying that they are not quantities but rather relatives. We shall support this with his own arguments.

Yet it is not peculiar to quantity to lack contraries. Not every quantity is without contraries. As we proceed through each case, we must consider which species of quantity have no contraries and which do.

A line has no contrary, for one line is not contrary to another. If someone says that a straight line is contrary to a curved line, he is mistaken. A curved line is not contrary to a straight line insofar as both are lines, but insofar as one is curved. In such cases it is not lines that appear to be contrary, but straightness and curvature. [Col. 0211C] Therefore, insofar as it is a quantity, a curved line is not contrary to a straight line, but insofar as it has a certain quality. Since curvature and straightness are contraries, a line receives contrariety according to its being curved or straight, not according to its being a line. Thus a line, insofar as it is a line, lacks a contrary.

Nor is one surface contrary to another surface. Someone might perhaps say that a white surface is contrary to a black surface. The same answer must be given: they are not contrary insofar as they are surfaces, but insofar as whiteness and blackness are present in them—and who would doubt that these are contraries? In the same way, if someone calls a smooth and a rough surface contraries, he is refuted by the fact that the surfaces possess contrariety not according to their quantity but according to the quality of roughness and smoothness.

Nor is anything in any way contrary to body. If someone says that the incorporeal is contrary to body, he will be refuted because every contrariety is expressed by proper names, such as good and bad or white and black. Corporeal and incorporeal, however, are not expressed according to contrariety but according to privation and possession. The incorporeal is a privation of body.

Nor is anything contrary to time. If night seems to be opposed to day, it is not insofar as either is time, but insofar as day is bright air and night dark air. Air is neither time nor quantity; light and darkness are qualities, not quantities.

[Col. 0212A] Speech also, although it appears to have a contrary, does not possess a contrary opposition. True and false speech appear to be contraries, but “true” and “false” apply to speech according to its signification. When speech signifies what is, it is true; when it indicates what is not, it is false. Speech, however, is counted as a quantity not according to what it signifies but according to what is uttered. According to what is uttered, speech is composed of long and short syllables, which measure speech not according to what it signifies but according to its utterance.

It is also clear that number has no contraries. Two is not contrary to three, nor three to four, nor is any other number contrary to any other number.

Place, however, possesses a certain contrariety, for up and down are contraries. [Col. 0212B] Some nevertheless maintain that “up” and “down” do not belong to quantity but rather signify relations, which the Greeks call *scheseis* (σχέσεις). The part that is toward our head is called “up,” while the part beneath our feet is called “down.” Thus we predicate “up” and “down” with reference, in a certain way, to a relation to ourselves.

Herminius likewise says that “up” and “down” are not places but, in a certain way, a position of place. There are such things as “up” and “down,” but for something to be of a place is not the same as for it to be a place: the position of a place is a position in a place, but place itself is not position.

But if someone considers the entire form of the universe—how the circumference of the sphere encompasses the shape of all things, while the earth lies at the center—then, since in a sphere nothing is outermost except what occupies the boundary of its middle [reading uncertain], whatever is at the outermost curve of the heavens will be called “up,” while what is at the center will be called “down.” [Col. 0212C]

Thus “up” and “down” are contraries according to place: “up” in heaven and “down” on earth, because they are far removed from one another. Hence contraries are later defined in this way: contraries are whatever are farthest apart from one another. This definition was evidently drawn from the fact that heaven and earth are distant from one another and appeared to be at the greatest distance, the former being “up” and the latter “down.” Since “up” and “down” are called contraries for no other reason than that they are far separated from one another, they define a contrary as something that is maximally distant. Aristotle expresses this in the following way.

[Col. 0212D] Contrariety appears most clearly in quantity with respect to place. For they posit “up” as contrary to “down,” calling the place in the middle “down,” because the distance from the middle to the boundaries of the universe is great. They also appear to derive from these the definition of other contraries: whatever things are greatly distant from one another and belong to the same genus, they determine to be contraries.

[Col. 0213A] In every sphere the earth is at the center, as the ordered rotation of the stars itself demonstrates. He also added the reason why such places are called contraries: there is a great distance between the center and the boundaries of the universe. By the boundaries of the universe he means the outermost curve of the heavens.

From this contrariety of place he likewise demonstrates the definition of other contraries: things that are far apart from one another within the same genus are defined as contraries. But since the order of the discussion of quantity should not be disrupted by this matter of contrariety, and since we had said that nothing is contrary to the individual quantities in the cases discussed above, we have inserted this contrariety of place, leaving some matters in the middle aside. Let us now return to the earlier discussion so that the order of the exposition may continue coherently.

Earlier, when he proposed that nothing is contrary to quantity, he said that nothing could be contrary to a two-cubit measure, a three-cubit measure, a surface, or anything of that kind. Since these quantities are determinate, nothing appears to be contrary to them, whether two or three. But since some things are indeterminate and appear both to be quantities and to have contraries, he added the following:

[Col. 0213B] “Unless someone says that much is contrary to few, or large to small.” None of these, however, is a quantity, but rather a relative. Nothing is called large or small in itself, but is referred to something else. A mountain is called small, while millet is called large, because the former is smaller within its own genus and the latter larger within its own genus. Their relation, then, is to something else. For if small or large were said in itself, a mountain would never at some time be called small, nor millet at some time large.

Again, we say that there are more people in a village and fewer in a city, although there are many more people in the city. Likewise, we say that there are many in a house but few in a theater, although there are more people in the theater.

[Col. 0213C] Moreover, a two-cubit measure, a three-cubit measure, and everything of this kind signify quantity, whereas large and small do not signify quantity but rather relation, since large and small are considered in relation to something. It is therefore clear that these are relatives.

Just as he showed above that determinate quantities have no contraries, saying that nothing is contrary to a two-cubit measure or to a surface, so indeterminate things such as large and small, many and few, provide an appearance of contrariety. But the answer is that these are not quantities. For every quantity is said in itself. A two-cubit measure, a three-cubit measure, two, three, and a surface are referred to nothing else. Large and small, however, cannot be said without reference to something else. When you say “large,” you refer it to the comparison and proportion of something else. [Col. 0213D]

The Aristotelian example itself proves the same point. If large and small were said in themselves and not in relation to something else, we would never call a mountain small and millet large. If large and small were not said in relation to something else, a mountain would always be called large and millet always small. But when we compare a hill with the height of Mount Atlas, we call it a small mountain; and when we compare millet with other, smaller grains of millet, we call that millet large. In general, whatever is called large or small is named by reference to a species of the same genus: we compare mountain with mountain, millet with millet, and other things in the same way.

Much and few are said in the same manner. [Col. 0214A] If there are a hundred people in a village, we say that there are many people. But if there are a hundred in a city, we call them few, comparing them now with the smallness of villages and now with the size of cities. Again, if there are fifty people in a house, they are many; but in a theater they are few, because we call them few in the theater when we compare them with the number that ought to be present in a theater.

Moreover, since large and small always consist in being referred to something else, while we call individual quantities by their own names without comparing them to anything else—three, two, four, a line, and a surface—large and small, many and few are separated from the division of quantity. They are not quantities but rather relatives.

Further, whether someone considers them quantities or not, nothing will be contrary to them. [Col. 0214B] For what cannot be taken in itself but is referred solely to the relation of something else—how could anything be contrary to it?

This is also proved by the strongest argument: none of the quantities mentioned above has a contrary, with the possible exception of place. Even if someone places large and small, or many and few, among quantities, and this is conceded, they still are not subject to contraries because they are always referred to something else. Every contrary subsists in itself and is not expressed by comparison or relation to another. Good is not called the good of evil, nor evil the evil of good; each subsists in its own nature and expression. Whatever things are contraries are so in the same way. Since large and small do not subsist in themselves but are referred to the relation of something else, they cannot be contraries.

[Col. 0214C] Further, if large and small are contraries, it follows that the same thing receives contraries simultaneously and that these very things are contrary to themselves. For the same thing can simultaneously be small and large: it is small in relation to one thing and that very same thing is large in relation to another. Thus it is possible for the same thing to be small and large at the same time, and so it would receive contraries simultaneously.

But nothing appears capable of receiving contraries simultaneously. Substance appears to be receptive of contraries, but it does not receive them at the same time. No one is simultaneously healthy and ill, nor simultaneously white and black; nor does anything else simultaneously receive contraries.

The same thing would also turn out to be contrary to itself. For if large is contrary to small, while the same thing is simultaneously small and large, it would be contrary to itself. [Col. 0214D] But it is impossible for a thing to be contrary to itself. Therefore large is not contrary to small.

This is established and remains unalterable in its proper reasoning: one and the same thing cannot receive contraries at one and the same time. Substance, for example, is receptive of contraries. A human being, being a substance, receives illness and health, but not at the same time; he receives whiteness and blackness, but at different times. That one and the same thing should receive both contraries at one and the same time is impossible.

If, however, someone posits large and small as contraries, an impossibility follows: one and the same thing would receive both contrarieties at the same time, and these same things could be contrary to themselves. Let us posit that [Col. 0215A] large is contrary to small. One and the same thing can be large and small at the same time. A measure of ten feet, for example, is large when compared with a measure of two feet, but the same measure is small when compared with a measure of one hundred cubits. The same thing can therefore receive largeness and smallness at the same time. For one and the same thing, when compared with something larger and something smaller, is both large and small.

But if large is contrary to small, and the same thing receives both largeness and smallness at the same time, it follows that the same thing receives both contraries at the same time. This is impossible. [Col. 0215B] Since the same thing cannot receive contraries at the same time, but one and the same thing can receive both largeness and smallness, largeness and smallness are not contraries.

If someone nevertheless posits large and small as contraries, the same reasoning shows that one and the same thing is contrary to itself. For if small is contrary to large, while the same thing—as I have shown—can be both small and large when compared with different things, then the thing that is small and large could be contrary to itself. But this is impossible. Therefore small and large are not contraries.

After this reasoning and this very firm argument concerning contrariety, he discusses the contrariety of place, which we have already addressed above. It should therefore be passed over, lest a repetition of the exposition become tedious rather than instructive.

[Col. 0215C] Quantity does not appear to admit of more and less. A two-cubit measure is not more two-cubit than another two-cubit measure; nor is this so in number, as when three is compared with five. For three is not said to be more a number than five, nor [Col. 0215D] are three things more three than another three. Nor is one time called more or less time than another. In none of the things mentioned is “more” or “less” said at all. Therefore quantity does not admit of more and less.

He has once again added a property which, although it is not peculiar to quantity, he has left unexplained as to why it is not peculiar to it. We must demonstrate this ourselves. What he says is this: quantity does not admit of more and less. No number is more or less a number than another number. Three, when compared with five, is neither more nor less a number; and three things, compared with one another, are neither more nor less three. Time likewise does not admit of more and less. One time can be longer than another time, but it cannot be said to be more time or less time than another.

The same has also been shown in the case of substance. One human being is not more or less a human being than another. The same applies to quantity. Since this is also true of substance, it is not a property peculiar to quantity. Quantity has this feature as well, as he himself showed in the following order. Since he had already said this about substance and now proposes the same point concerning quantity, he neglected to mention that it is not peculiar to quantity. When discussing substance, he said that substances never admit of more and less; therefore, when he established the most distinctive properties in the customary manner, he returned to this point. [Col. 0216A]

The most distinctive property of quantity is that it is called equal and unequal. Each of the quantities mentioned is called equal and unequal. A body is called equal and unequal; time is called equal and unequal; number is called equal and unequal; and speech is called equal and unequal. The same applies to each of the other things mentioned: each is called both equal and unequal.

[Col. 0216B] In other things that are not quantities, however, “equal” and “unequal” do not appear to be used very often. An affection or disposition is not commonly called equal and unequal, but rather similar and dissimilar. White is not commonly called equal and unequal, but similar. Therefore it is a property belonging most distinctly to quantity to be called equal and unequal.

The property of quantity is most clearly indicated by the fact that equality and inequality are named according to quantity. Individual quantities are called equal and unequal: one line is equal to another line, and again unequal; one surface is called equal or unequal to another surface; and a body is called equal or unequal. Number, time, and place likewise are called equal and unequal.

In other things that are not quantities, however, it is not easy for equality or inequality to be named. Dispositions, therefore, which are called affections, are not called equal or unequal but rather similar and dissimilar. A disposition or affection is [Col. 0216C] an accommodation and application to some thing. If someone is reading grammar but has not yet fully learned it, he has a certain disposition toward it—that is, he is affected by it and possesses something accommodated and, as it were, akin to it.

Two people can be similarly disposed or affected, but they cannot in the strict sense be equally so. Two things may be similarly white, but not equally white. For if someone says of two similarly white things that they are equally white, he is not using the word correctly. Everything equal and unequal is constituted in measure and quantity.

Just as similar and dissimilar are not said of quantity, so equality and inequality are not properly named of any other thing except quantity. Therefore it is a property of quantity to be called equal and unequal.

Since the discussion of quantity is complete, let us proceed to the order of relatives. After the treatment of quantity, he enters upon the third category, that of relatives, and defines relatives in this way.

## On Relatives

Relatives are those things which are said to be what they are as belonging to other things, or which are otherwise related in some way to something else. For example, “larger” is said to be what it is as belonging to another: something is called larger than something else. “Double” is likewise said to be what it is as belonging to another, for something is called the double of something else. The same applies to all other things of this kind.

Why, then, he discusses things that are relative, while for the moment omitting the treatment of quality? The reason is that, once quantity has been posited, it is necessary that there be a greater and a lesser. Since the relative immediately follows quantity, therefore, the sequence of the relatives has rightly been arranged after quantity [Col. 0217A]. There is also this reason: earlier, when he was treating quantity, mention was made of relatives when the greater and the lesser were discussed. Therefore, so that the exposition might remain continuous and its division not be interrupted, he proposed to treat relation after completing the discussion of quantity.

When he says, “But things are called relative in this way,” he shows that, unlike quantity—which can be understood by itself and singly—and likewise unlike substance, quality, and each of the other categories, each of which, as is evident, can be understood by itself and singly, the relative cannot be grasped in thought by itself and singly, so that we could say that something exists as a relative in isolation. Whatever is recognized in the nature of relation must necessarily be considered together with something else. For when I say “master,” it is nothing by itself if “servant” is absent. Therefore [Col. 0217B], since the naming of one relative immediately draws another along with it, a relative cannot exist by itself. For this reason Aristotle did not say, “A relative is called such,” but, using the plural, said, “Relatives are called such,” thereby showing that the understanding of relatives consists not in singularity but in plurality.

Aristotle himself shows that there is no independent nature of relatives subsisting without some conjunction with another, when he says that those things are relative which are called what they are in relation to others. For he teaches that relatives are formed through some conjunction with another: they are called what they are in relation to others. That which is a master is called the master of another, namely, of a servant.

Whether we call them “relatives” or “things related to something,” it makes no difference. A thing is said to be related to something when, although it is nothing by itself, it is established in relation to another, as with “master.” If that to which it is said—namely, “servant”—is absent, the master does not exist; for “master” is said in relation to a servant. It is therefore clear that, if the servant is absent, the master cannot be called a master. Thus “master” is said relatively, that is, in relation to a servant. They are also called relatives because their naming is always referred to something else, as “master” is referred to “servant.” Hence it makes no difference how the expression is formulated.

This definition is thought to belong to Plato, and Aristotle corrects it somewhat later. Of relatives, some are referred to by the same cases, some by different cases, and some have no case at all. Aristotle indicates this when he adds, “or in some other way in relation to another.”

What this means is shown by almost the very wording of the text. When I say “master of a servant,” I have joined the nominative to the genitive; and if I reverse the relation in the same way, I say “servant of a master,” where again the nominative is referred to the genitive. The same is true of “father of a son” and “son of a father,” and of “teacher of a pupil” and “pupil of a teacher.” These things, then, are called what they are in relation to others in the same way, since “of others” is expressed by the genitive case.

Other relatives, however, do not preserve the same case in the corresponding expression. “Sense” is the sense of a perceptible thing. Whatever is perceptible can be sensed, and whatever can be sensed is perceptible. Here “sense” is fitted to the genitive expression “of a perceptible thing,” since it is said to be the sense of a perceptible thing. But if the relation is reversed [Col. 0218A], it becomes: “A perceptible thing is perceptible by sense.” In this relation the nominative is joined to the seventh case, that is, the ablative, in the expression “a perceptible thing is perceptible by sense”; it is not reversed according to the same case as in the earlier expression. For we say, “Sense is the sense of a perceptible thing,” where the nominative is again referred to the genitive. This relation does not allow itself to be fitted to the seventh case in the same way.

The same applies to knowledge. “Knowledge is the knowledge of a knowable thing,” since what is known is what can be known, and what can be known is knowable. Yet this relation is not reversed by the same method or into the same case. We say, “A knowable thing is knowable by knowledge.” The first relation is to the genitive, while the second reversal is to the seventh case.

Some relations are also reversed according to the same cases, as when we say, “The greater is greater than the lesser,” and “The lesser is less than the greater.” “Double” and “half” are also relatives, and they too are reversed by the same cases. For “double is the double of half,” while “half is half of double.”

There are also other relatives, which he himself added as follows:

> But these too are relative: state, disposition, knowledge, sense, and position. For all the things just mentioned are called what they are in relation to others, or in some other way in relation to another, and not in any other way. A state is called the state of something, learning the learning of something, and position the position of something. The same is true of the others.

Knowledge and sense have already been discussed above. Now we must discuss state, disposition, and position.

A disposition is a movable application to some thing [Col. 0218C]. Thus, if someone near a flame becomes warm, he is said to be disposed toward heat—that is, to possess some application and conjunction with heat. Affect is the same as disposition, so that no error may arise from the introduction of a new term. Since disposition is a certain conjunction with another thing, or an affect arising from another thing, it is easily movable; for it changes more quickly.

A state is a firm and not easily changeable acquisition of a disposition or affect. Thus, if someone walking in the sun becomes darker, he is said to be disposed toward blackness and affected by blackness. But if that blackness has more strongly and unchangeably infected the body, it is called a state. Hence a state is an affect grown old. Every state, therefore, is a disposition or affect, but not every [Col. 0218D] disposition or affect is a state.

To say no more, this too is evident concerning state and disposition: a state is an unchangeable affection, whereas a disposition is not similar, but is a certain affect and conjunction with something that can easily be changed.

Position is the placement of some thing, such as standing, sitting, leaning, reclining, and other things of this kind. For one who stands is said in a certain way to be positioned and placed; the same is true of one who sits or reclines, and anyone who is situated according to the other positions is said to be positioned. Therefore standing, sitting, and reclining will be positions.

But since we have explained what these are, let us now see whether they are relatives. That state is said relatively is proved by the same consideration that showed other things to be relatives, as happened with sense and knowledge. For it was said that sense is the sense of a perceptible thing because a perceptible thing is something that can be sensed. Thus a state is the state of something that can be possessed. A thing capable of being possessed is one that can be possessed; a state is the state of that thing which can be possessed. Therefore a state is the state of something capable of being possessed, while a thing capable of being possessed is capable of being possessed by a state, since through the state we possess those things that can be possessed.

The same applies to disposition. A disposition is the disposition of something disposed, and a disposed thing is disposed by disposition. The disposition of heat is the disposition of something warm—that is, of something disposed toward heat. In the same way, what is disposed toward heat is disposed by the disposition of heat. It is as though we said: every affect is the affect of something affected, and everything affected is affected by an affect. Heat becomes heat in something warm, and something warm becomes hot through heat.

Position too is relative. A position is the position of something positioned, and a positioned thing is positioned by a position. This should be understood according to the preceding account of state and disposition. The fact that the species of position are relative also proves that position is relative. Standing is the standing of something standing, and one who stands stands by standing. The same can be said of sitting and reclining.

Therefore state, disposition or affect, and position are relatives. All these are reversed either by corresponding or by different cases, though the cases are nevertheless suitable to the predication.

Among those relations that are reversed according to cases, some are predicated by the same word, while others are predicated by different words. When I say, “Like is like a like,” “Equal is equal to an equal,” and “Unlike is unlike an unlike,” the entire predication is made with the same words [Col. 0219C] and the same names. But when I say, “Double is double the half,” or “Greater is greater than the lesser,” the predication is made with different words.

Since he presented the definition of relatives by saying, “Relatives are called those things which are called what they are in relation to others, or in some other way in relation to another,” we have already explained what is meant by “called what they are in relation to others.” We must now investigate what is meant by “or in some other way in relation to another.”

Aristotle himself establishes this by suitable examples in the proper order. He says:

> Relatives, then, are whatever are called what they are in relation to others, or in some other way in relation to another. Thus a mountain is called great in relation to another. “Great” is said relatively; “like” is said like something; and all such things are likewise said relatively. Sitting, standing, and reclining are also certain positions; position is said relatively. To recline, stand, or sit, however, are not themselves positions, but are denominatively named from the positions just mentioned.

Since reclining, standing, and sitting are called positions, and since every position is relative, the matter has been sufficiently covered above. We must now explain what he means by “or in some other way in relation to another.”

In the relation by which we say “son of a father” and “father of a son,” no conjunction is mixed in, except that the force of the cases alone joins the members of the predication. But when I say “a great mountain,” referring it to another, smaller one, I propose it in this way: “the great mountain in relation to the small mountain,” and “the small mountain in relation to the great.” Here no force of cases is involved. Although an accusative may seem to be included, it does not carry the force of this relation; rather, it is the preposition that governs the accusative.

When I say “the great mountain toward the small mountain,” the preposition alone contains the force of the relation. If someone were to say “the great mountain the small mountain,” the expression would signify nothing definite. Therefore, although the accusative case occurs in the proposition, it does not here bear the force of a case; the preposition does.

This is what he means by “or in some other way in relation to another.” Since he had previously said that relations are formed according to cases, but some relations are held by no cases, he added “or in some other way in relation to another,” as if he were saying: every relation is either formed by cases—which he demonstrated by saying “whatever are called what they are in relation to others”—or it exists apart from cases, as the statement “or in some other way in relation to another” teaches. This completes the point.

But although position is relative, and its species are relative—sitting and standing are relative—“to sit” and “to stand” are not relations. “To stand” and “to sit” are denominatively derived from standing and sitting. Every denomination, however, is not the thing from which it is named. “Grammarian,” for example, is not the same thing as grammar, from which it is named.

Therefore, if “to sit” is denominatively derived from sitting, and “to stand” from standing, while sitting and standing are relatives, “to sit” and “to stand,” which are denominatively derived from relatives, are not included under the genus of relatives. In general, whatever is denominated from any positions can be referred not to relatives but to the predication called situs, or position.

There is also contrariety in relation. Virtue is contrary to vice, although both are relative, and knowledge is contrary to ignorance. Contrariety, however, is not found in all relatives. For nothing is contrary to double, nor to triple, nor to any of the like.

Just as in the case of substance and quantity he investigated whether it was proper to them to receive contraries, so now he considers in the case of relatives whether it is proper to relatives to be able to receive contraries. Since virtue and vice are both states—for virtue is an affection of the mind directed toward the good and difficult to change, while vice is an affection directed toward the bad, likewise difficult to change and enduring over time—then, since vice and virtue are states, and every state has been shown to be relative (for a state is the state of something capable of being possessed), virtue and vice will be relatives. But they are contraries. Therefore relatives do not refuse to receive contraries.

Someone might ask: why, then, does he shortly afterward count virtue, vice, and state itself among qualities? There is no difficulty in one thing being subsumed under different genera according to different significations.
