Socrates, insofar as he is Socrates, is a substance; insofar as he is a father or son, he is relative. Thus, when predication is directed toward one thing and then another, nothing prevents the same thing from being placed under different genera.

The same applies to state, virtue, and vice. State can be placed among qualities because people are called qualified by it: we say that some people possess a state of something. Virtue is also a quality because people are called good by it; according to that quality—namely, goodness—we call people qualified, that is, good. The same applies to vice.

A state itself, when referred to another predication, again becomes relative. For a state is the state of something capable of being possessed, and is therefore relative; and what is the virtue of something is virtue in relation to that thing; and what is the vice of something is likewise relative to it. Nothing, therefore, prevents the same things, when directed toward different objects, from being assigned to different predications.

We cannot understand the relative itself apart from some other category. We consider father and son according to substance [Col. 0221B], and master and servant likewise according to substance. For the one who is a master and the one who is a servant are substances. We consider double and triple according to quantity, since they consist in quantity. Knowledge and ignorance are considered according to quality, for according to these we are called qualified, namely, knowing and ignorant.

Therefore, since no one can understand relatives by themselves apart from another category, they are said to be capable of receiving contraries according to the categories in which the relation is understood. Socrates himself is a substance, but substance does not receive a contrary. Father and son, however, are predicated according to substance; for there is no father or son unless there is substance. Since, therefore, they are said according to substance, they lack contrariety.

Again, double and half are said according to quantity, and quantity has been shown not to have contraries. Therefore neither double nor half contends with contraries. Quality, however, receives contrariety: good and bad are opposed according to quality, and therefore good and bad are not free from contraries.

Thus, according to the categories under which relatives are predicated, if those categories receive contraries, relation also receives them. But if those categories previously reject contrariety, then the relative that is predicated according to them is never divided by contrariety. Therefore, receiving contraries is not proper to relation. It is not found in relation alone, since quality also has it, nor can it be considered in all relatives. In relatives that are predicated according to categories that do not receive contrariety—such as father and son according to substance, or double and half according to quantity—contraries are in no way found.

What belongs neither to one category alone nor to all is not proper to it. Therefore, it is not proper to relation to have contraries.

Relatives appear rather to receive greater and lesser. Like and unlike are said in degrees of greater and lesser, and equal and unequal are likewise said in degrees of greater and lesser, although both are relatives. For like is said like something, and unequal is said unequal to something. Not all relatives, however, receive greater and lesser. Double is not said to be more or less double, nor is anything of that kind.

We must now ask whether it is proper to relation to receive greater and lesser. Here the same reasoning applies as was given concerning contraries. Whatever is predicated according to categories that do not receive contraries themselves lacks contraries. In this case, however, equal and unequal are said according to quantity, yet they receive greater and lesser. For something is said to be more equal or less equal. Likewise, something is said to be more like or less like.

Someone might ask why, if equal and unequal are terms of quantity, and quantity does not receive greater and lesser, equal and unequal increase through intensification and diminish through remission. The answer is that, just as substance itself, insofar as it is substance, is not a property, while receiving contraries is a property of it, so too this is considered in quantity. What is proper is not the very thing of which it is the property, but some other quality or affection arising externally [Col. 0222B].

For it is an affection of quality, and equal and unequal may be called a certain quality. Since this property is not identical with the thing of which it is the property, to be called equal or unequal is not a property of quantity itself, but a certain quality and affection of quantity.

This, moreover, is said relatively, for it is called what it is in relation to another. We call equal what is equal to an equal, and similarly we call like what is like a like. Yet not all relatives receive greater and lesser. No one can say that something is more or less double. Whether ten is compared with five or four with two, each is equally double and each is equally half.

Quality also receives greater and lesser, for we say “whiter” and “less white.” Therefore, since the reception of greater and lesser belongs neither to every relation nor to relation alone, and since relation receives greater and lesser through quality, it is not proper to relation to receive greater and lesser.

All relatives are predicated in relation to correlatives: “servant of a master,” “master of a servant,” “double of half,” “half of double,” “greater than lesser,” “less than greater,” and similarly in other cases. Sometimes, however, they differ in case according to the wording, as “knowledge of a knowable thing” and “a knowable thing by knowledge,” or “sense of a perceptible thing” and “a perceptible thing by sense.”

The statement of the author is clear and not obscure. He says that all relatives are predicated in relation to correlatives, as he makes clear by his own examples. Every relative is predicated in relation to another in such a way that the thing to which it is predicated appears capable of being reversed in relation to it. This is what he means by saying: “All relatives are predicated in relation to correlatives.”

To reverse means that, if the first thing is said in relation to the second, the second is again said in relation to the first. Let the first be “father” and the second “son.” We say, “The father is the father of the son.” This can then be reversed by placing “son” first and making the predication, “The son is the son of the father.” Thus the father is said in relation to such a thing, namely, the son, which is itself reversible; and the son, which is said in relation to the father, is said in relation to such a thing as can itself be reversed when predicated of the son.

All relatives are of this kind. Every relative is predicated in relation to something that can itself be reversed in predication. Yet they are not all expressed through the same form of speech. Some are reversed by the same cases, as was said: “The father is the father of the son,” and “The son is the son of the father.” Others are not reversed by the same cases, as “Knowledge is the knowledge of a knowable thing.” Here the genitive is used. But “A knowable thing is knowable by knowledge” uses the seventh case in the predication.

Others are joined and reversed without any case at all, as “The great mountain is toward the small,” and “The small is toward the great.” Thus all relatives are predicated in relation to correlatives, although they are not reversed according to the same cases. Aristotle himself says this when he adds: “But sometimes they differ in case according to the expression.” What he added was made with great care.

Sometimes, however, a relation will not appear capable of being reversed unless the thing to which it is referred is assigned appropriately. If the one making the assignment errs, as when a wing is assigned to a bird, “bird of a wing” is not reversible. For “wing of a bird” was not assigned appropriately. A wing is not said to belong to something insofar as it is a bird, but insofar as it is winged. Many other things have wings that are not birds. Therefore, if the assignment is made appropriately, the relation is reversible: “A wing is the wing of something winged,” and “The winged thing is winged by a wing.”

Sometimes it may also be necessary to invent names if a name has not been established and the relation must be assigned appropriately. If an oar is assigned to a ship, the assignment will not be suitable. For an oar is not said to belong to something insofar as it is a ship, since there are ships without oars. Therefore it is not reversible: a ship is not said to be the ship of an oar.

Perhaps, however, the assignment will be more suitable if it is formulated in this way: “An oar is the oar of something oared,” or in some other way. The name has not been established, but the relation becomes reversible if it is assigned appropriately: “An oared thing is oared by an oar.” The same applies to other examples. A head is assigned more appropriately to something headed than to an animal, for an animal does not have a head insofar as it is an animal; there are many animals that do not have heads.

Above he proposed the reversal of relatives and said that whatever is relative is predicated, whether by the same or by different cases, in relation to correlatives. This occurs because every relative derives its being from the relation and comparison of another. If both things are opposed as relatives, they are called relatives and receive an equal force and naming.

If father and son are both relatives, and father is predicated in relation to son, then, since son is also relative, son too will be predicated in relation to something else. But son is the son of no one except a father. Thus these names take their beginning from one another’s naming. Therefore, things that mutually confer their substance are rightly predicated in relation to one another. This is understood in all relatives.

Such reversal, however, cannot take place in one way indiscriminately. Unless each thing is predicated appropriately in relation to that to which it is said, no such reversal occurs. If we say “the head of an animal,” we cannot say “the animal of a head.” Thus the expression, as given, cannot be reversed in any way.

This is what he means when he says that not all relatives appear capable of being reversed unless the thing to which they are said is assigned appropriately. If the person making the assignment errs and produces an unsuitable predication, the reversal does not proceed. The appropriate assignment by which relatives can always be reversed is as follows.

When I say “a wing is the wing of a bird,” it cannot be reversed into “a bird is the bird of a wing,” because the predication was not appropriately made. A bird does not have a wing insofar as it is a bird. Many things have wings without being called birds, such as bees and bats, and anything else of that kind. Therefore, the wing belongs to the bird not insofar as it is a bird, but insofar as it is winged. For it has a wing because it is winged, and whatever is winged will have wings.

Thus, when the predication is made in this way, it retains and preserves the reversal: “A wing is the wing of something winged,” and “A winged thing is winged by a wing.”

The same applies to the head. If someone says, “The head is the head of an animal,” he will not adapt the force of the predication appropriately. An animal does not have a head insofar as it is an animal; there are many animals without heads, such as oysters, shellfish, and other creatures of this kind. Therefore, one must say, “A head is the head of something headed,” and “A headed thing is headed by a head.” Do you see how a suitable predication has produced in itself the reciprocal conversion and reversion of the word?

The same must be considered in the other example proposed by Aristotle. If an oar is said to be the oar of a ship, it cannot in any way be reversed so that a ship is called the ship of an oar. There are ships that do not use oars at all, such as boats propelled only by a pole; therefore the relation is not reversible.

One must therefore say, “An oar is the oar of something oared,” and “An oared thing is oared by an oar.” It will also be necessary to invent a name if none has been established. Just as “son of a father” and “father of a son” are predicated through reciprocal conversion, and both names are in use, so, if a name is lacking, you must invent something yourself, as in “a wing is the wing of something winged.” “Winged” has been newly formed and was never used before.

Since we have established that it is necessary to invent names, we shall also explain, in the following order, the art of forming them. But this should be done only after I have cleared up a point raised by certain people who, out of a desire to criticize Aristotle, make the following objection.

They say that being predicated in relation to correlatives is not exclusive to relation. If someone says, “When the sun is above the earth, it is day,” and “When it is day, the sun is above the earth,” these statements too admit reversal, although they are admittedly excluded from the definition of relatives. Therefore, they say, this reversal does not apply only to relatives.

Iamblichus offered two solutions to this problem, one very weak and the other very strong. He says that nothing is inconsistent with Aristotle’s position if other things too are reversible. Aristotle did not say that this belonged only to relatives; he said that it belongs to all relatives. This cannot be denied in any way. Since Aristotle did not say that the property belonged only to relatives, the objection does not impede the judgment of this excellent philosopher.

But this is rather an appeal to an accidental circumstance than to nature, and a flight toward another refuge rather than the construction of a defense from the authority of Aristotle’s own words [Col. 0225A].

Iamblichus offered another, entirely weighty, reason. He says that it is proper to relatives to be reversed not according to their naming but according to some relation. When someone says, “When the sun is above the earth, it is day,” and “When it is day, the sun is above the earth,” he shows no relation, but only sequence. For the sun’s being above the earth follows when it is day, and when the sun runs its course above the earth, day follows.

But when someone says, “The son is the son of the father,” and “The father is the father of the son,” he declares a relation, comparison, and, in a certain way, the inclusion of both things. The same can be observed in every other relation. Since all relatives are said according to a certain relation and inclusion between one another, their reversal must also be made according to that inclusion and relation. In this matter we too readily yield to the authority of Iamblichus, who speaks with such force.

We must now explain the art of inventing names wherever they are lacking. Aristotle himself teaches it in these words:

> Thus, in cases where a name has been assigned, someone may perhaps easily obtain the appropriate term by giving to the things to which they are reversed names derived from those that are first, as in the examples just mentioned: from “wing,” “winged,” and from “oar,” “oared.” Therefore all things that are said relatively, if they are assigned appropriately, are said in relation to correlatives.

Since some things are said relatively in such a way that, unless they are fitted appropriately, there is no reversal, while in all relatives one must expect a reversal, Aristotle himself shows what this appropriateness is and how relations ought to be assigned.

If something is said relatively but cannot be reversed, a denomination formed from the thing that is said immediately restores the reversal. Thus “wing” is said of a bird, and this predication is correct in itself but unsuitable to the nature of relation. Since “bird” cannot be said of a wing in return, the usual reversal of relatives is restored if a denomination is formed from the original predication.

When we say “wing of a bird,” it is unsuitable to say “bird of a wing.” But if a denomination is formed from “wing,” so that we say “winged,” the reversal remains. We say, “A winged thing is winged by a wing,” just as we say, “A wing is the wing of something winged.”

The same occurs with an oar. Since an oar is said to belong to a ship, and “ship of an oar” cannot be produced by any reversal, if a denomination is formed from “oar,” reversal is immediately restored according to custom. We say, “An oar is the oar of something oared,” and this is reversible into its counterpart: “An oared thing is oared by an oar.”

Therefore the name must be invented from the thing stated first. Thus, from “wing,” since a wing is first said in relation to a bird, but a bird cannot be reversed in relation to a wing, a denomination is formed so that we say “winged.” This is what he means when he says that names should be given to the things to which they are reversed from those that are first.

The first predication is from “wing.” We say, “a wing of a bird,” and we seek to reverse this predication in relation to “wing.” Therefore, from the thing stated first, a name must be invented for the thing to which it is reversed. The name “winged” must be formed from “wing,” which is said first, and fitted appropriately to the thing to which the relation is reversed. The name “winged” itself is denominated from “wing.” The same may be understood in all other relatives.

For if relatives are assigned to anything else rather than to that to which they are properly said, they are not reversible. I mean that even among those things that are unquestionably called reversible, and for which names have been established, none is reversible if it is assigned to accidental features rather than to the things to which it is properly said.

Thus, if “servant” is assigned not to a master but to a human being, a biped, or something of that kind, it is not reversible. The assignment is not suitable.

He offered another argument showing that, if relations are not returned appropriately, they cannot be reversed. Someone might perhaps say that wing and head are not relatives. Even if this were conceded, no one could deny that servant or son is always predicated in relation to something else. Therefore, even in the case of things that are admittedly relatives, the proper reversal of relation disappears if the relation is not assigned appropriately and to the thing to which it is properly said.

Although “servant” is relative, unless it is returned in relation to a master—that is, to the thing to which it is appropriately said—there is no reversal. Let it be said that someone is the servant of a human being, or the servant of a biped. It cannot be reversed so that someone says “a biped is the biped of a servant” or “a human being is the human being of a servant.” The same applies to son.

Thus, if what is relative is predicated in relation to external features, there is no reversal. When he says “accidental,” he does not mean that human being is an accident, or that being a biped inheres accidentally as a difference of human being. Rather, it is sometimes part of Aristotle’s customary usage to say that things predicated secondarily and externally are predicated according to accident.

A servant is first related to a master, and only secondarily to a human being. For it is because the master is a human being that the servant is said to be the servant of a human being. And because the master is a biped, the servant is said to be the servant of a biped. Thus he says “according to accident” in the secondary sense, wishing to show that an extraneous and unsuitable predication is made if someone refers a servant to a human being or a biped rather than to a master.

It is therefore clear that this applies even to things that are admittedly relatives and for which names are established. The names “servant” and “master” are in use, unlike “oared” and “winged,” where no such names existed until Aristotle himself invented them. Since this is so, it is clear that, if such things are not fitted together appropriately, the predication will not preserve its reversal.

Furthermore, if the thing to which a relative is said is assigned appropriately, then, once all the other accidental features have been removed and only that thing to which it was assigned remains, it will always be said appropriately in relation to it.

Thus, if “servant” is said in relation to “master,” and all the other features that are accidental to the master are removed—such as being a biped, capable of knowledge, or a human being—while the master alone remains, “servant” will always be said in relation to that master. For “servant” is said to be the servant of a master.

But if the thing to which it is said is not returned appropriately, then, once all the others have been removed and only the thing to which it was returned remains, it will not be said in relation to that thing. Let “servant” be assigned to “human being,” and “wing” to “bird,” and let the fact that the human being is a master be removed. The servant will no longer be said in relation to the human being, since, if there is no master, there is no servant.

The same applies to the bird. Remove from it the fact that it is winged, and the wing will no longer be a relative, since, if there is no winged thing, the wing will not be the wing of anything. Therefore one must assign the thing to which the relative is appropriately said.

If a name has already been established, the assignment will be easy. But if there is no name, it may be necessary to invent one. If the relations are returned in this way, it is clear that all relatives will be predicated reciprocally.

Another powerful argument he adds, namely that in every relative predication only the appropriateness of the designation is to be sought. For that to which the predication of relatives remains when all other things perish, and with the perishing of which the predication “relative” does not remain while all other things endure, is that to which the relation of the name is appropriately referred. For one who is a master is also a human being, also bipedal, and also capable of receiving knowledge. Yet a slave will not be predicated in relation to any of these if he is not a master; but if he is a master, even if any one of these other attributes perishes, nothing prevents the predication. Let “slave” be predicated in relation to “master,” and let the rest be removed from him. Let what belongs to him as human, bipedal, and capable of receiving knowledge perish; when all these have perished, let “master” alone remain. Although the others have perished, “slave” is nevertheless still said in relation to “master,” but it is not said in relation to “human being.” For when the name “master” has perished, there is no predication of “slave” in relation to “human being.” If, however, “slave” is not referred to “master,” and the name “master” perishes while all the others remain, there will be no predication. For let “master” be removed while “human being,” “biped,” and “capable of receiving knowledge” remain: one cannot say “slave of a human being” or “slave of a biped.” When “master” does not remain, “slave” perishes. Therefore, while “master”—that to which “slave” is appropriately fitted—remains, the predication remains even though all the others perish; but when “master,” to which the appropriate predication belongs, is removed while all the others remain, there is no predication.

The same applies to a wing. Unless it is referred to something winged, the predication is not intact while all other things remain. Indeed, not only is there no conversion, but there will be no predication at all unless the relation is assigned to that to which the term is appropriately said to belong. This also provides a method and means of recognizing, when many things are present in a nature, the thing in relation to which the relation is chiefly predicated. For since a master is a human being, an animal, capable of receiving instruction, and bipedal, the following shows to which of these we may refer the name “master” or “slave.” The relation is most properly predicated of that which, while it remains and the others are removed, preserves the predication, and with whose removal, while the others remain, the predication is interrupted.

Having established these points, he concludes the force and meaning of the whole argument. He says that all things which are relatives are converted in equal predication; and this is of the following kind. Whatever things are equally predicated of one another, and are reversed when conversion is made, are founded upon an equal nature and measure, as are proper things and species. Relatives likewise must be equal if they are to be converted. For if one thing is greater and the other smaller, they do not admit conversion. In “a bird’s wing,” “bird” is narrower in extension than “wing”: many things have wings without being birds, and therefore conversion does not follow. In “a ship’s oar,” the ship is greater than the oar: there are many ships whose oars are absent, and therefore no conversion can exist in these cases. But if the terms are equal, as “son” and “father,” conversion does not fail. For there is never a son except of a father, and again there is never a father except of a son. Therefore whatever is predicated as relative must be equal.

If a name has been established for these things, one must use the established names. If no name has been established, one must invent a name from the terms present in the first predication, as was said above. If, then, everything relative is predicated appropriately of that to which it is said, the predication will be equal, and the reciprocal nature of conversion will immediately follow. It is therefore established that all relatives are spoken of in relation to correlatives. To this he adds another property.

## Relatives Are Seemingly Simultaneous by Nature

Relatives appear also to be simultaneous by nature, and in many cases this is true. In some cases, however, it is not true. For at the same time there are “double” and “half”; when something is half, it is double; when something is master, it is slave; and when something is slave, it is master. Other things of this kind are similar. These also remove one another simultaneously. For if there is no double, there is no half; and if there is no half, there is no double. The same applies to all other things of this kind.

Things are said to be simultaneous when, if either one is posited, the other necessarily follows, and when either one is removed, the other is in every way destroyed—for example, “father” and “son.” When there is a father, it is necessary that there also be a son; when there is a son, there is a father. Again, if the son perishes, it is clear that the father also perishes—not because the substance itself perishes, as Priam perishes when Hector perishes, but because the relation itself perishes. Therefore, since the name “son” perishes when the name “father” is removed, and the name “father” perishes when the name “son” is removed; and since, when “father” is posited and established in substance, the name “son” is also introduced, while when the name “son” is posited, that of “father” follows and is never separated from it, father and son are said to be simultaneous.

Things are therefore simultaneous when they either destroy one another or bring one another in; and he himself discusses these matters later. For the present, however, he has explained that this too belongs to relatives: that they are simultaneous. When there is a double, there is a half, and when there is a half, there is a double. The proof of this is that when the double is removed, the half perishes; and again, when the double is established, the half is established. Therefore, since double and half are relatives, and are simultaneous by nature—that is, in their very essence—it is clear that this also occurs in relatives, namely, that they appear to be simultaneous by nature.

The same applies to slave and master. Since, when either is removed, both perish, and when either is established, both subsist, it is clear that slave and master, being relatives, are simultaneous by nature. But they are simultaneous in such a way that this belongs to relatives, although it does not apply equally to all relatives. For there are some relatives of which one is prior by nature, as he again adds.

## The Knowable and Knowledge

It does not appear to be true of all relatives that they are simultaneous by nature. The knowable seems naturally prior to knowledge. For ordinarily we acquire knowledge after things have already subsisted. In few cases, or perhaps in none, will anyone find knowledge coming into being simultaneously with the knowable.

He has proposed that it is not true of all relatives that they appear to be simultaneous by nature. He proves this from the fact that, since knowledge is relative—for knowledge is said to be knowledge of a knowable thing—knowledge cannot exist unless there is some thing that can be known. This thing must be prior, as in the discipline of mathematics. We know that a triangle has its three interior angles equal to two right angles. Therefore what could be known must have existed first, and knowledge suited to that thing must have come afterward. This is what he means when he says: “For ordinarily we acquire knowledge after things have subsisted.” First things are constituted and, as it were, set before us; then the account of knowledge follows.

Therefore it is not true of all relatives that they are simultaneous by nature. Since knowledge and the knowable are relatives, the knowable is prior to knowledge. His qualification—that in few cases or perhaps in none will anyone perceive knowledge to have come into being simultaneously with the knowable—is to be understood as follows. The mind invents certain things for itself, such as a chimera, a centaur, and other things of this kind. These are known when the mind has conceived them. They begin to exist when they first occur in thought. They are therefore known when they have entered into thought, and these have being and being-known simultaneously. For since they arise in thought, they immediately begin to exist; but when they are present in reason, their knowledge is grasped. Thus, as soon as they exist, they are known, and their knowledge is joined to their essence.

Before the chimera was conceived, just as it had not existed in anyone’s thought, so there was no knowledge of it. After it had been constituted by the imagination of minds, knowledge of it followed together with that imagination. For this reason he says that it can be perceived in few cases that the knowable exists simultaneously with knowledge, as in the case of the chimera, which, being knowable, came into being together with knowledge of it.

But since nothing that does not persist in substance or stand in truth can be known—for knowledge is the apprehension of the truth of things—and since whatever the mind invents or discovers by imagination is not constituted in substance and truth, such things are not said to be knowable. Therefore there is no knowledge of things that subsist by imagination alone. For this reason he expressed his doubt by saying “in few cases or perhaps in none.” Anyone who examines these very few cases according to true reason and inquiry will judge that they are none. If someone were to say that there is some knowledge of the chimera, although there is not, then even if this false claim were granted, there would still be only a few cases in which knowledge and the knowable were simultaneous by nature. In the case of many things, knowledge arises only after they have been set before us and constituted.

Consequently, it is not true of all relatives that they are said to be simultaneous by nature. Just as it is false to say that this occurs in no relatives, so it is also false to say that it occurs in all relatives. He develops this discussion at greater length.

Moreover, when the knowable is removed, knowledge is removed simultaneously, but knowledge does not simultaneously remove the knowable. For if there is no knowable thing, there is no knowledge; but if there is no knowledge, nothing prevents there from being a knowable thing—for example, the quadrature of the circle, if indeed it is knowable. Knowledge of it does not yet exist, but the thing itself is knowable.

We have said that things are simultaneous whenever, when either is established or removed, both are established or removed together. For when it is established that there is a father, the son is also established, and the father simultaneously introduces the substance of the son. In the same way, the son simultaneously introduces the name of the father, for there is no son except of a father. Likewise, when one is removed, both must perish.

One thing, however, is said to be prior to another in several ways; but what we are now investigating is the following. Those things are said to be prior which, when they themselves are removed, remove other things, but when they are introduced and established do not simultaneously introduce those other things—for example, “one” and “two.” When one is removed, two also perishes. For how could there be a doubling of one in two if one perished? But when one is established and posited, two does not yet exist. The doubling of one has not yet taken place. Therefore those things are said to be prior which, when removed, destroy other things, but when introduced do not bring the others in simultaneously.

That the knowable and knowledge are not simultaneous is proved by the fact that, if someone removes a thing that is knowable, he will also remove knowledge. No knowledge can remain if the thing that can be known perishes. But if you establish that something is knowable, knowledge does not necessarily follow. The things that we now know existed for us when we were infants and remained in the substance of their own nature, but knowledge of them was not present in us. There are also many arts whose existence in accordance with their own nature we perceive, but whose neglect has removed knowledge of them. I myself greatly fear that this may be said most truly of all the liberal studies.

Therefore, if the removal of knowledge also destroys the knowable, while the introduction of the knowable neither brings nor establishes knowledge, then what can be known is prior to that which, as it were, comprehends and embraces it through knowledge.

He has supplied an especially obscure example for this matter. In geometry there is commonly a proposition of the following kind. We are instructed, given a four-sided area, to construct a triangle equal to it, and we do this as follows. Let the four-sided area be **AB**. We must construct a triangle equal to the area **AB**, and let the area **CDEF** be double the area **AB**. Draw the diagonal **CF**. I say that triangle **CDF** is equal to the area **AB**, because the area **CDEF** is double the area **AB**. Therefore **AB** is half of the area **CDEF**, for the diagonal **FC** divides the whole area **CDEF** into two equal parts. But things that are halves of the same whole are equal to one another. Therefore triangle **CDF**, and likewise triangle **CEF**, is equal to the area **AB**.

Given, then, the area **AB**, the equal triangle **CDF** has been constructed, as was required. In the same way, the problem is posed of making a square equal to a circle.

A square, then, is that which has equal sides and all four angles equal—that is, right angles. It seems not to have been discovered in the time of Aristotle. It was discovered later, but since its demonstration is lengthy, it must be passed over. This is what he means by “the quadrature of the circle.” Just as, while the square remains, a line drawn obliquely produces a triangular figure, so, without altering the circle, angles placed around it and directed equally toward the circle’s own sides give rise to the form of a square. We have depicted this by conjecture, as far as we could. For when a square equal to a given circle is constructed, the measure of that circle is reduced to the quadrature of the circle.

This, then, is what he says: “the quadrature of the circle”—that is, the construction of a square equal to the circle, if this can be done. If the thing is knowable, knowledge of it has not yet been discovered. In Aristotle’s time no one had yet constructed a square equal to a circle. If there is some knowledge of it that has not yet been found, then certainly the knowable is prior, and knowledge comes afterward. Although the quadrature of the circle could have been known while Aristotle was alive, no knowledge of it had yet been discovered. Therefore what could be known was prior to any knowledge of the thing itself.

Moreover, when the animal is removed, knowledge does not exist, whereas there may be very many knowable things.

He adds another, stronger argument that the knowable is prior to knowledge. It is evident that, if a discipline perishes through neglect, knowledge perishes, but the knowable remains. By “knowable” I mean what can be known. If no animal existed at all, there would be no one capable of knowing anything, and knowledge itself would perish completely. Nevertheless, nothing prevents those things from existing which, while an animal remains, the mind of an investigator could grasp through the process of knowledge.

## The Sensible and Sense

The same applies to what concerns sense. The sensible appears to be prior to sense. When the sensible is removed, sense is removed simultaneously; but sense does not simultaneously remove the sensible. For senses exist around and in a body, and when the sensible is destroyed, the body is also destroyed, since a body is sensible. When there is no body, sense too has been removed. Thus the sensible removes sense simultaneously, whereas sense does not remove the sensible. When the animal perishes, sense indeed perishes, but the sensible does not. Such things are sensible as a hot body, something sweet, something bitter, and all other things that are sensible.

He proposes that this be found in the case of the senses. He says that the sensible is prior to sense, establishing this as plausible by the common definition of prior things. For it was said that those things are prior which, when removed simultaneously, perish together, but which do not themselves perish simultaneously when other things are removed. Thus we say that the orb of the sun is prior to its own light: when the orb is removed, the light that comes from it will not remain at all; but when the sun’s light is removed, the orb remains.

So here too, in the case of sensibles and sense itself, he proposes that when what can be sensed is removed, sense is entirely removed. Sense cannot exist when it finds nothing that it can sense. But if sense altogether perishes, the sensible remains; and he confirms this with evident examples.

For since the things that exist are either incorporeal or, at any rate, corporeal, and whatever can be referred to bodily matter is subject to the variety of the senses, while whatever belongs to incorporeal things is grasped by the intellect through reason and contemplation, and since all sense is in a body, if the body perishes, sense is overturned altogether. There is no body at all, incorporeal things cannot be sensed, and the things that could be sensed have been destroyed.

But if sense is removed, sensibles remain. Since sense is an effect of animals, the destruction of the two is equal: whether you remove the animal, sense perishes, or whether the senses are destroyed, the animals too have been removed. Yet when animals, together with their proper senses, have been overthrown and destroyed, bodies that do not possess a soul remain. If, after animals have been removed and the senses destroyed, inanimate bodies subsist—and bodies are things that can be sensed—then, when animals capable of sensing have perished, sense has been overthrown while the sensible remains.

Therefore, just as the destruction of the sensible destroys sense, so the loss of sense is not accompanied by the extinction of sensibles. This too can be proved by the following argument. Before we actually sense something, there is no sense of it. Before we taste something sweet, the tasting of sweetness does not yet exist; but what can be tasted—that is, honey or anything else—exists according to the rationale of its own nature. Accordingly, Aristotle’s authority confirms that what can be sensed is prior, and sense comes afterward.

Moreover, sense comes into being simultaneously with the thing sensed, since the animal and sense come into being together. But the sensible exists before sense. Fire, water, and other things of this kind, from which the animal itself is constituted, exist before the animal exists at all, and therefore before sense. Hence the sensible appears to be prior to sense.

In composite things, and in things joined together from other things, those things which compose something are prior in substance to the thing they compose. Since the body of an animal is made from fire, air, water, and earth, these must be prior to the animal itself, which those elements combine. The same is clear in other cases. Since a book is made from verses, the nature of verses is prior to that of the book. And since a verse consists of words, names, and the other things that grammarians call the parts of speech, these from which the verse itself is constituted must be prior to the verse.

Therefore sense also supervenes upon animals once they have been composed. Since an animal consists of the four elements, and sense always accompanies the nature of animals, sense must come into being and arise together with the animals themselves. If sense arises together with animals—that is, with composite things—then, just as the things from which the animal is constituted are prior to the animal, so those things are prior to sense, which arises together with the animal and from which the animal’s nature is composed.

An animal is joined together and composed from the four elements. Therefore the four elements are prior to sense. But the four elements are bodies, and every body is sensible. The sensible, therefore, is prior to sense. Sense arises with the composite thing, whereas the things that compose it are both sensible and prior to the composite.

Universally, if two things exist simultaneously, and either one of them is prior to some other thing, then the other will also be prior to it. This applies to animal and sense: both exist and arise simultaneously. Since the four elements, which are sensible, are prior to the animal, they must also be prior to sense. Accordingly, he concludes by saying: “Therefore the sensible appears to be prior to sense.”

Some people, including Porphyry, maintain that it is true of all relatives that they are simultaneous by nature. They assert that the knowable and the sensible do not precede sense and knowledge, but exist simultaneously with them. Since Porphyry’s discussion is brief, I shall not hesitate to append it. He says:

“If there is no knowledge of anything, that thing, although it can subsist through itself, cannot be knowable. For example, if knowledge of Forms perishes, the Forms themselves may perhaps remain and continue in their prior nature, but they will not be knowable. For when there is no knowledge capable of comprehending them, the things themselves cannot be known. Every thing is known through knowledge; if knowledge does not exist, it cannot be known. Moreover, a thing that cannot be known is not knowable.

“The same applies to the sense of one who tastes. If the sense of taste perishes, honey may perhaps remain, but it will not be tasteable. Likewise, if sense altogether perishes, the things that could be sensed may exist, but they will not be sensibles once sense has perished.

“And perhaps knowledge and sense should not be considered according to those who know or sense, but according to the nature itself that can be grasped through sense. For whatever is sensible by nature must also have, in its own nature, the proper sense by which it can be sensed. And whatever can be known by nature could never be learned unless some knowledge of it were present in its nature.”

This is Porphyry’s position. But let us return to Aristotle’s order and text, for he added other questions as well.

## Whether Any Substance Is Relative

He raises the question whether no substance is said to be relative, as appears to be the case, if this is understood with respect to certain secondary substances. In the case of primary substances, it is true: neither whole primary substances nor their parts are said to be relatives. For an individual human being is not said to be someone’s individual human being, nor an individual ox someone’s individual ox.

The same applies to parts. A particular hand is not said to be someone’s particular hand, but someone’s hand; and a particular head is not said to be someone’s particular head, but someone’s head.

The same is true of secondary substances, and this is the case in most instances. A human being is not said to be someone’s human being, nor an ox someone’s ox, nor wood someone’s wood, but it is said to be someone’s possession. In such cases, then, it is clear that the thing is not relative. In some secondary substances, however, there is a certain difficulty: a head is said to be someone’s head, and a hand someone’s hand, and so with each of the things of this kind. Therefore these things appear perhaps to be relatives.

Against the arguments given above, he raises the following knot of a question. Since the first definition of relatives had been that those things are relatives which, in their very being, are said to belong to others, according to this definition certain substances may appear to be relatives. If this is so, substances pass over into the definition of accidents. For since relative things are accidents, if we grant that certain substances are relatives, we shall judge that they must be placed among accidents. But this is contradictory. A substance is not in a subject, whereas an accident is in a subject. How, then, could the same thing both be in a subject and not be in a subject?

Whether a certain substance can receive the account of an accident must be investigated as follows. Primary substances themselves are not said to be relatives, nor are the parts of primary substances, which we also count among primary substances. Socrates is not said to be someone’s individual Socrates; a human being is not said to be someone’s individual human being; an ox is not said to be someone’s individual ox. Nor are the parts of primary substances, which are themselves also primary substances, so called. A head is not said to be someone’s particular head, but simply someone’s head; and a hand is not said to be someone’s particular hand, but simply someone’s hand.

Therefore neither primary substances nor their parts can be said to be relatives. If we examine secondary substances as well, they too will not be said to be relatives. An animal is not said to be someone’s animal, nor a human being someone’s human being. If someone says that there can be someone’s animal—for example, my horse or anything else—it is not said to belong to someone insofar as it is an animal, but insofar as it is a possession. Thus it is not said to be someone’s animal, but an animal’s possession, someone’s possession.

Therefore neither primary substances, nor their parts, nor secondary substances are said to be relatives. But the parts of secondary substances are said to be relatives in respect of what they are. A head is said to be someone’s head, if we call the thing possessing a head “the headed one”; and a hand is said to be someone’s hand, if we wish to form a name from “hand” to which the hand can be referred, just as the head is referred to the headed one. The same applies to other things.

But if the parts of secondary substances are accidents, then the secondary substances themselves will also be accidents; or, if this is not acceptable, secondary substances will consist of accidental parts, which cannot happen. What, then, must be said? Either the definition of relatives must be rejected, or the difficulty must be resolved in another way.

Once the earlier definition has been posited and established—the definition that says that those things are relatives which are said to be what they are of others—the knot of this question cannot be resolved. Aristotle himself testifies to this by adding the following:

“If, then, the definition of things that are relatives has been adequately assigned, it is either extremely difficult or impossible to show that no substance is said to be relative. But if the definition has not been adequately assigned, and there are relatives for which their very being consists in having some relation to others, perhaps something will be said of these. The earlier definition follows all relatives, but it is not the case that their being relative consists in this, that they are said to be what they are of others.”

Once the earlier definition of relatives has been proposed and confirmed, it will be difficult—or perhaps impossible—to defend the claim that some substances are not relatives. For if those things are relatives which are said to be what they are of others, then what is a head is said to be a head of the headed one. Substance, therefore, which is a head, will have a relative relation; and thus it will be both a relative substance and an accident, which is impossible.

Since this difficulty follows from the arrangement once the earlier definition has been proposed and established, and since the account is therefore shown not to be a complete definition, the designation must be altered. He says that the definition given above is not complete, and that things are not relative merely because they are said to be what they are of others, but rather those things for which their very being consists in having some relation to others.

To readers who examine the passage carelessly and with little attention, however, it may appear that Aristotle has included in the definition the very thing that ought to have been defined, which is a serious fault. For if a definition is taken in order to designate the thing under inquiry, what definition could be clearer than one that uses the thing itself which it defines in the statement of the definition? A definition is given so that the thing whose being is in doubt may be made clear through its definition. But if it introduces into the definition the very thing that it defines, the definition is no clearer—just as if someone wishing to define “human being” were to say that being human is precisely being human.

In the same way, to those who do not consider the matter carefully, Aristotle will appear to have given the following definition of relatives: that things are relative for which their very being consists in having some relation to others—as though he were saying, “Those things are relative which somehow relate themselves to something.”

But to those who consider the matter more minutely and acutely, the force of the complete definition will readily and truly appear. We do not consider “relative” in the sense of merely being said to be relative, but in the sense of being relative in their very being. For those things are relatives which we consider in a certain comparison and relation. Consider the number four. It is said to be what it is—namely, four—and it is also called something else, namely, double, when it is compared with two.

But when we speak of the number four, “four” refers to the nature of the number four itself. “Double,” however, does not refer to the four as such, but to the two in relation to which the four is called double and in relation to which it is double by its proper relation. The number two is both two and half: it is two according to its own nature, but half according to its relation to four.

Accordingly, we consider relatives in a certain comparison and relation. Four, insofar as it is four, is not said to be relative; but insofar as it is double, it is relative to two, that is, when compared with two. Nor does two, insofar as it is two, refer to anything; but insofar as it is half, it is compared with four.

Therefore, for four to be double, it needs not two but half; and for two to be half, it needs not four but double. Do you see how, by a certain relation and comparison, things retain one character in their own nature while nevertheless being something else in relation to one another? They borrow this not from their own nature but from one another. For the number that is double derives from the half what it is as double, while the half derives from the double what it is as half.

This happens incidentally to things that are relative. Without anything itself undergoing change or alteration, things become relative. Nothing in the four having been changed, it is itself double if it is referred to two; and with nothing in the two having been changed, two is half if it is said in relation to four.

Therefore the being of relatives—that is, their nature and substance—is this: that what they are is referred to something else. They are not merely said to be referred to something else; they actually are so referred. This is what he means when he says that there are relatives for which their very being consists in having some relation to others—as though he were saying that their substance consists in being referred to another, and that they are such that what they are is referred to another and their being consists in being referred to another.

But not everything that is said in relation to another derives its being from another. The earlier definition is broader. It surpasses the definition of relatives, for it includes things that are not relatives. Just as when I say “human being,” it is necessary that the human being be mortal, but when I say “mortal,” it is not necessary that the thing be human, so too things that derive from another what they are, possess their being in relation to another, and refer their own being to the designation of another; but things that are merely said in relation to another do not necessarily have their own being referred to something else, so as to receive the later definition.

The point may be briefly stated as follows: whatever things satisfy the definition that their very being consists in having some relation to another also possess the definition according to which relatives are those things that are said to be what they are of others. But things that possess the latter definition do not necessarily possess the former. Thus things that are relatives are also said to be relative, but things said to be relative are not necessarily relatives.

If the later definition is accepted—the definition that those things are relative for which their very being consists in having some relation to another—the earlier difficulty can be resolved. We can then state what Aristotle pursued in the later discussion.

When he says, “The earlier definition follows all relatives, but their being does not consist in this, that they are said to be what they are of others,” the meaning is that something is not called relative merely because it is said to be what it is of another. Rather, a thing is properly included under the name “relative” whenever it is not only said in relation to something else, but its very being consists in having some relation to another.

He therefore added what properly follows from this definition.

## Knowledge of Relatives and Their Correlates

From these considerations it is clear that if someone knows definitely one of the things that are relatives, he will also know definitely that to which it is said to be relative. For if someone knows something that belongs among relatives—and the being of relatives consists in having some relation to another—he also knows that to which this thing is related.

He confirms as a property of relatives, according to the definition given above, that if someone knows definitely what a relative is, he will also know definitely the thing to which it can be referred. For relatives are things whose being consists in having some relation to another: thus, for four to be double, it derives this relation from two. If someone knows that the number four is double, he will necessarily also know that two is its half, since four is double in relation to two.

It is impossible that someone should know definitely that a thing is relative without also knowing definitely that to which the thing is said to be relative. One proof of this follows from the definition. Those things are defined as relatives whose substance consists in having some relation to another. If I know that the number four is double because it is joined in some relation to two, no one can know that four is double without knowing that two is half. The same should be considered in every case.

For if someone does not know to what one of the relatives is referred, he will also be ignorant whether it is related at all. Aristotle expresses this in the following words:

“For if he does not know at all that to which this has some relation, he will not know that it has some relation either. This is clear in individual cases. For example, if someone knows definitely what is double, he immediately knows definitely what it is double of. But if he knows no definite correlate, he does not know the double itself, nor whether it is double at all.

“The same applies to a particular thing. If someone knows definitely what is better and what it is better than, he must know the latter as well. But indefinitely he will not know that this thing is better than what is worse. That may be an opinion, but not knowledge. For he will not know precisely what is better than what is worse; if this were so, nothing would be worse than it.

“It is therefore clear that if someone knows definitely one of the relatives, he must also know definitely that to which it is said to be relative.”

He pursues examples of this matter as well, saying: If we know that the double is relative to something, we also know that of which it is the double; but if we do not know that of which it is the double—while the fact that something is the double of anything derives from its having a half—we cannot know whether the thing that is double is actually double. If, therefore, we know definitively that some thing is double, it is necessary that we also know definitively of what it is double. Thus, if someone knows definitively that Anchises is the father of Aeneas, he will also recognize that Aeneas is definitively the son; or, if he knows indefinitely that someone is a father, he will likewise know indefinitely that he is the father of a son. Again, if someone knows indefinitely that Aeneas is a son, he will also know indefinitely that he is the son of a father. It is therefore clear that, whenever things that are relative are known definitively to be relative to something, that to which they are referred must also be known definitively. With Aristotle as our authority, we prove that this is not the case in substances; he concludes the sequence of this question as follows:

> To know the head, and the hand, and each of these individually—which are substances—is to know definitively what they are. But it is not necessary to know to what they are said to belong. For it is not necessary to know definitively whose head or whose hand this is; therefore these will not be relatives. But if these are not relatives, it will be true to say that no substance is among the relatives.

In the case of the head, he says, and the hand, and other substances, it is not true that, if someone knows that one of these belongs to someone and is referred to something, he will consequently know definitively to whom it is referred. For if someone, with his head and all his limbs covered, were to extend a hand outside, it is clear that that hand is someone’s hand; but whose hand it is cannot be stated definitively. Similarly, if, with one’s eyes covered and one’s face veiled, one were to look at someone’s head, one would have no doubt that the head belongs to someone, but one could not definitively say whose it is. Therefore, since these things are such that, if someone knows definitively that they belong to someone, he cannot know definitively whose they are, substances are separated from the definition of relatives—a definition according to which, if any one relative thing is known definitively to be related to something, that thing to which it is referred is likewise known definitively.

Yet this further point must be added, which is altogether true: in definitions, the thing itself that is being defined ought not to be included. For many things are expressed and defined in one way, but understood in another. Thus, if someone says that white is a color contrary to black, this can also be understood of a body; for both the color is called white and the body that participates in white is called white. Therefore, lest anyone think that “white” has been defined as something referring to the participation of white and of a body, it should be stated in this way: “White is what, when it is present in something, is a color contrary to black.” Thus we take the thing itself into its definition. Aristotle, that is, placed among the probable arguments of the *Topics* the claim that the thing itself being defined ought not to be included in the definition. Now, after the discussion of relatives, the diligent teacher urges us to undertake a more extensive treatment of these matters, saying:

> Perhaps it is difficult to give a confident account of such matters unless they have often been examined; yet it will not be useless to have raised doubts about each of them.

He would never have said this unless he were calling us back to a more rigorous exercise of intelligence and investigation. Since this is his exhortation, we too shall not shrink from setting forth, in other matters, the doubts and solutions concerning these questions.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0239]

### [Col. 0239A]

The customary question at the beginning is why, after discussing the category of relation, he undertook the discussion of quality. This question is excessively inquisitive. It would indeed have been surprising if, after the order of quantity, he had not immediately begun with quality; but since he mixed a certain relation into quantity and continued the discussion of relation, it is not surprising that, once the digression on relation had been completed, he returned to the order of quality. Indeed, the sequence is also correct for this reason. For after great and small there immediately follows proportion and a certain comparison with something else, so that something is greater or lesser, equal or unequal; and these are relatives. After these, passions necessarily arise, which do not differ from the nature of quality: white, black, hot, cold, and whatever resembles these, all of which are included in the predication of quality.

The title of the present treatment is “Of the Quale and of Quality.” The question is why it was not sufficient for him to say either “Of the Quale” or “Of Quality.” This can be resolved as follows. We say that *quale* (“what kind of thing”) is used in more than one way, whereas *quality* is used simply. For we call both the quality itself and the thing that participates in that quality a *quale*: whiteness is a quality, while what participates in whiteness is called white. But we also commonly call whiteness itself a *quale*, that is, the quality properly speaking; and we call white a *quale*, namely that which participates in the quality previously described. Thus we commonly call both the quality itself and the thing that participates in the quality *qualia*, whereas *quality* is used simply. For only the thing itself that can be participated in is called a quality. The thing that participates is not included under the term “quality”: whiteness is a quality, but white is not a quality.

The terms *quale* and *quality* therefore differ in that the former is used in two ways, while the latter is used simply. Consequently, although some deny that this is Aristotle’s title and assert that it was marked by a later addition, we nevertheless say that he used both expressions in order to display a certain similarity of names, so that it might appear to make no difference whether the category appended is called “quale” or “quality”; for, as we have said, *quale* sometimes signifies the thing itself and sometimes quality.

Let the definition of quality, then, be taken from the things themselves. When I say “definition”—a term that we used above in the case of the other categories as well—no one should think that I intended to indicate a general definition. Rather, let the term “definition” be understood here as a description. In the case of the most general genera, one should not seek a definition, but rather a description of their nature. For no definition can be found of a thing that is itself a genus and has no genus above it. Accordingly, once these matters have been proposed and established, we must begin the discussion of quality.

## OF QUALITY

[Col. 0240A]

> I call quality that according to which certain things are said to be of a certain kind.

Here it is asked why the most learned of all disputants included quality within such a blameworthy definition. When we wish to know what quality is, he answers us in this way: “Quality is that according to which certain things are said to be of a certain kind.” For what he says—“according to which they are said to be of a certain kind”—is no less obscure and difficult to know than if he had spoken only of quality itself. For if those things are of a certain kind that possess quality, then, in order for them to be known as such, quality must first be known.

Moreover, it makes no difference whether he said that quality is that according to which certain things are said to be of a certain kind, or as if he had said that quality is that which is quality. For, wishing to define quality in this way, he says: “That according to which certain things are of a certain kind.” Again, if someone wished to define certain things as being of a certain kind, he could say in the same way that they are things that retain some quality in themselves. But if what quality is is shown through *quale*, and what *quale* is is shown through the quality previously mentioned, it would make no difference to say that quality is quality, or that quality is that which is quality, or that it is that according to which certain things are said to be of a certain kind.

But if an orderly general definition could have been placed in this most general genus, the determination would rightly seem blameworthy. As things stand, however, the objection is pressed in vain, since, as has often been said, he added this expression in place of a description rather than as a definition. Therefore, if it is merely a designation and, in a sense, a sketch of the thing being investigated, and not a definition, it is an absurd criticism to blame it—before considering the nature of description—for establishing less familiar things through more familiar ones.

Who could doubt that those who are of a certain kind are more familiar than the quality itself through which they are said to be of that kind, just as any white thing is more familiar than whiteness itself? For if whiteness is a quality, while white is denominated from whiteness, that is, from quality, then white will be called a *quale*, named from the quality whiteness. And if, as has been said, white is more familiar than whiteness, then the *quale* will be more familiar than quality, just as a grammarian is more familiar than grammar. A grammarian, too, is a *quale*, being so denominated from grammar, that is, from a quality.

Everything subject to the senses is more familiar to us than what is not grasped by the senses. Therefore, nothing prevents someone who is describing and, in a sense, designating the nature of the thing being investigated from establishing less familiar things through more familiar ones.

Quality is among the things spoken of in many ways, and one species of quality is called habit and disposition. Habit differs from disposition in being more permanent and longer lasting. Such are sciences and virtues. For science appears to belong to things that are permanent and very difficult to change, provided that one understands science in even a moderate sense—unless perhaps a major alteration has occurred through illness or something of that sort. Virtue is similar: justice, temperance, and each of the qualities of this kind do not seem capable of being easily removed or readily changed.

Affections, by contrast, are said to be things that are easily moved and quickly changed: heat and coldness, health and illness, and others of this kind. A person is affected in some way with respect to these, and is quickly changed, passing from hot to cold and from health into illness. The same applies in other cases, unless perhaps, through the passage of time, an affection also happens to pass into the nature of the thing, so that it becomes incurable or difficult to move—an affection that anyone would then call a habit.

He proposes that quality is spoken of in many ways. This has led some into error, so that they suspected Aristotle of believing that “quality” is an equivocal term. For if everything equivocal is spoken of in many ways, and according to Aristotle quality itself is also called in many ways, then, according to Aristotle, the name “quality” is equivocal.

We, however, maintain that “spoken of in many ways” means that a term is not named with only one signification. Something is said to be spoken of in many ways both when it is used equivocally and when it is predicated in different ways of its species. Such plurality of appellation is common even in names that are spoken of as genera of species, or as equivocal terms of their subjects. For “animal” too is spoken of in many ways. If there are many species subordinated to animal, then the term itself is also, in a certain way, named in many ways.

That Aristotle did not refer this plurality to equivocation, but rather proposed quality as a genus, is shown by his saying that one species of quality is called habit and affection. For when he says that habit and affection are species of quality, who could doubt that he regarded quality itself as having the force of a genus?

But why does he say that there is one species of quality when he has proposed two, namely habit and affection? The question arises. For if habit and affection are one and the same, the repeated proposal of the same thing is superfluous; but if they differ, we must investigate why they differ. That they do not differ in genus is established in advance by the fact that both are placed under quality. It remains, therefore, that they differ either in species or in number. But if they differed in species, Aristotle would not have placed them under one species. It follows, then, that they differ neither in genus nor in species, but in number.

Habit and disposition are the same in species, but differ in number and in a certain individual quality. I use “disposition” indistinguishably for what is also called affection. For just as Socrates does not differ from Plato according to the species of humanity itself, but they are separated only by the quality proper to their individual persons, so disposition and habit also differ—not, indeed, in precisely the same way. Rather, just as Socrates, while a child and later after reaching puberty, differed from himself, so too do habit and disposition. Habit is a firm disposition, while affection is an unstable habit.

Thus, just as one white color differs from another if one remains in a painting while the other immediately perishes, except that the one that is more permanent belongs to habit and the one that is easily destroyed belongs to affection, so there is no other difference between habit and disposition. Although habit is more permanent and disposition easily changeable, they differ only in the duration of their permanence. Hence habit and disposition do not differ in genus or species.

Accordingly, Aristotle rightly included under the designation of one species things that differed only in number, not in species. Their proper difference is that habits are dispositions that remain for a very long time, while disposition is a habit that is easily changed. Examples of these may be found as follows. Habits include arts, disciplines, and virtues. An art does not seem easily changeable and remains for a very long time. Indeed, the art itself takes care that it does not perish through use and practice. Who, possessing knowledge of grammar, has lost it without the intervention of some force or more powerful affection? It is reported that a certain outstanding orator, consumed by illness and fevers, lost all his literary learning, while remaining sound and self-possessed in other matters and vigorous in every respect.

Discipline too is difficult to change. Who, knowing that a triangle has three interior angles equal to two right angles, has lost this knowledge except through the force, as has been said, of some stronger affection? Virtues too must be placed in the same category. Virtue is not virtue unless it is difficult to change. For someone is not just merely because he has judged justly once, nor is someone an adulterer because he has committed adultery once; rather, this requires that the will and intention should have remained.

In his *Ethics*, Aristotle declares that virtues are not sciences, as Socrates thought, but habits. It is therefore established that habits are stably permanent and difficult to change, with only this qualification: they may be driven out and destroyed by some greater force bringing about a change.

Examples of affections are heating, cooling, illness, and health, since a person is in some way disposed and affected with respect to them, though he does not immutably possess the quality of heat or cold, nor perpetual health or perpetual illness. Moreover, if some conditions are hardened immutably in bodies through a long illness, so that they have in a certain way passed into the nature of the body, as when someone who has been struck develops an incurable scar, then for that person a habit has been formed out of disposition and affection. Hence it was rightly said that dispositions, when they grow old, become habits. For whenever a disposition becomes permanent and difficult to change, it must no longer be called a disposition or affection, but a habit.

It is clear that they wish those things to be called habits that are longer lasting and difficult to change. For in disciplines, those who do not retain much but are easily changed are not said to possess a habit, although they may be better or worse disposed toward the disciplines. Habit therefore differs from disposition in this: the latter is easily changed, while the former is longer lasting and difficult to change.

### [Col. 0243A]

That habits are qualities difficult to change and extremely long-lasting is confirmed by this argument: when some science is taught to people, if they do not learn it thoroughly, we do not say that they retain a habit of the subject they are learning. Someone learning letters who, before acquiring a fluent command of speech, reads in a somewhat halting and broken manner, syllable by syllable, through lack of skill, is said to be disposed and affected toward literacy; nevertheless, we do not yet say that he possesses the habit.

The same is therefore true in other matters. All those who are disposed toward some thing, and who are in some way affected with respect to it, but do not possess a lasting reception of it, we judge to be disposed toward that thing, but we do not say that they possess a habit. Aristotle therefore rightly proposes habit as longer lasting and more permanent, and disposition as easily changeable and not enduring.

### [Col. 0243B]

> Habits are also dispositions, but dispositions need not be habits; those who retain habits are in some way disposed through them, whereas those who are disposed do not necessarily retain a habit.

The meaning is that everyone who possesses a habit also possesses a disposition within that same habit. But if someone possesses a disposition, it is not necessary that he also retain a habit.

“Habit” derives its name from *having*, because it is possessed either immutably or with difficulty subject to change—for example, gray eyes, a hooked nose, or knowledge and learning in some art. Whoever possesses such things is also said to be disposed toward them. But if someone is disposed toward something, it is not necessary that he also possess a habit. Thus, if someone, being carelessly clothed, is shaken by the cold, he is then disposed toward cold, but he does not thereby retain a habit of it.

The genus seems to preserve the same analogy. A genus is predicated more broadly, and wherever a species is present, the name of the genus is immediately present as well. But wherever a genus is present, the name of the species does not necessarily follow. Thus, if someone is a human being, he must be an animal; but if someone is an animal, he is not immediately called a human being.

Therefore, since whatever is a habit is a disposition, while whatever is a disposition is not necessarily a habit, disposition appears to be a kind of genus of habit. But the more accurate account is that, wherever there is increase and decrease, the genus of increase cannot be decrease. For just as, in the case of white and whiter, white cannot be the genus of whiter—for white and whiter are the same, except that they differ only in degree, since whiter grows and extends through a certain increase and intensification—so habit and disposition, being the same, differ only in degree. Habit is, in a certain way, greater, more developed, more permanent, and firmer than disposition.

Therefore disposition is not the genus of habit, and, in the same way, habit is not a species of disposition. Yet some habits are such that they did not grow out of disposition, nor did they reach a complete state through some still-undurable quality. Such are the curvature of the nose or blindness of the eyes, if it has occurred suddenly. These began from the habit itself, without any preceding disposition; for perhaps no one was ever disposed toward them who did not already possess them.

Other habits arise through the increase and aging of a disposition, as in the case of activities belonging to arts and disciplines. At first a person is disposed toward them; later he acquires a habit. Other things reach the status of habit not through increase but through a certain alteration: milk, which is changed from a liquid and solidified into cheese; or wine, which, from being sweet and through its own power, is converted into a sour taste and flavor.
