For it is not more wine then than it was before, when it was sweet; rather, through a certain alteration it has passed into another quality and habit.

Enough, then, has been said about the first species of quality.

Another genus of quality is that according to which we call people boxers or runners, healthy or unhealthy, and, in general, everything that is spoken of according to natural capacity or incapacity. For things of this kind are not so called because they are disposed in some particular way, but because they possess a natural capacity or incapacity to do something easily or to suffer nothing easily. Thus people are called boxers or runners not because they are disposed in some particular way, but because they possess a natural capacity to do these things easily.

People are called healthy because they possess a natural capacity not to suffer easily from whatever external events may occur; they are called unhealthy because they possess a natural incapacity not to suffer easily. The same applies to soft and hard. Something is called hard because it has the capacity not to be easily cut, while something is called soft because it has the corresponding incapacity.

### [Col. 0244C]

He recalls that the second species of quality is that which proceeds from a certain natural capacity or incapacity. This is illustrated as follows. When we look at people with strong bodies who are not yet boxers and have not been trained in this art, we nevertheless call them boxers—not because they are already boxers, but because they could become so. And when we look at people with light bodies and small calves, we suppose that they are easily moved and swift in running, although they have not yet entered a running contest and are not runners; nevertheless, we may call them runners according to their capacity—not because they already run, but because they could run.

In the same way, we call people healthy or unhealthy when we judge them, on the basis of a strong or more fragile body, to be suited either to health or to illness. Hence we can call some sick people healthy and some healthy people unhealthy. They are not called healthy or unhealthy because they are already actually healthy or ill, but because they may remain healthy for a longer time or may become ill.

The question arises why, although the subject proposed is the species of quality, he spoke of a genus of quality and not of a species. For he says: “Another genus of quality is that according to which we call people boxers or runners, healthy and unhealthy.” But those who ask this appear to be unaware that only that is a genus which has no other genus above it, and only that is a species which contains no species beneath it. Things that lie between the most general genera and the most specific species can commonly be called both genera and species.

Accordingly, since Aristotle is discussing a species of quality that is not yet a most specific species but rather the first species of a genus, and a species of the sort that can also be a genus, there is nothing absurd in placing it both in the role of species and in that of genus.

But although certain qualities produce a denomination by which a thing is called what it is—for example, white from whiteness, luxurious from luxury, or anything of this kind—the situation is not the same in things that are spoken of according to natural capacity. The art of boxing itself is not proposed as the source from which we call people boxers. For people are not called boxers because they practice the use of the art of boxing, but because they are naturally disposed toward it according to their capacity. Consequently, those whom we call boxers are not named from boxing, nor can they be denominated from it; rather, boxers are named from the art of boxing.

A boxer is someone who uses the art of boxing, and the same can be seen in the other cases. In these matters, therefore, there is no definite quality from which the other things receive their names. Yet if some quality must be found and expressed, it is the one Aristotle himself indicates in this way: that which is according to the capacity to do something or the incapacity to suffer something.

We call people boxers and runners because they possess the capacity to do something—that is, to run and to be boxers. We call people healthy because they too possess, in a certain way, an incapacity to suffer something. For someone who suffers less from external events is secure in health, and one who is secure in health can truly be called healthy.

There is another quality that is spoken of according to an incapacity to suffer something: this applies to those whom we call unhealthy. They possess an incapacity not to suffer something, because they possess the capacity to suffer something quickly. If someone is one who easily suffers something from external events, he is capable of being very easily subject to illness; according to this capacity we call him unhealthy, even if he is healthy.

The same applies to hard and soft. Something hard has the capacity not to be cut quickly; for what is hard is divided with great difficulty by any cutting. Something soft has the incapacity to be cut with difficulty. Since what is soft is cut easily, we call it soft according to its incapacity to be cut with difficulty.

This, then, is the second species of quality. Let us now proceed to the third.

### [Col. 0245D]

The third species of quality consists of passive qualities and affections. Such are sweetness, bitterness, astringency, and everything related to these. Heat and cold, whiteness and blackness also belong here. That these are qualities is clear: whatever receives any of them is called such according to them. Thus honey, because it has received sweetness, is called sweet; and a body, because it has received whiteness, is called white. The same applies in the other cases.

He proposes a third genus of quality, which we convert into a part and species of quality: passive qualities and affections. These differ greatly from one another. Yet since both are qualities, he first teaches both together and afterward explains what their difference appears to be. He first presents examples of their similarity.

In teaching what passive qualities are, he says “sweetness or bitterness, heat and cold, blackness and whiteness, and things related to these.” He confirms that the things included above are qualities by the same reasoning through which, at the beginning of his discussion of quality, he had explained what quality itself is. For he had declared the definition of quality to be: “that according to which we are called such-and-such.” But if we are called such according to quality, and something is called bitter or sweet from bitterness or sweetness, and black or white from blackness or whiteness, who could doubt that these are qualities to which the definition of quality applies?

Whatever things fall within the boundaries of the same description are always believed to be of the same nature. Thus, if something receives the definition “a mortal rational animal,” it is clearly a human being. Therefore, if the things he called passive qualities or affections receive the definition of quality, because those who receive them are called such-and-such, it is established that these too are qualities.

Passive qualities are not called so because the things that receive them suffer something. Honey is not called sweet because it has suffered something, nor is anything else of this kind. Heat and cold are likewise called passive qualities, not because the things that receive them have suffered something, but because each of the things mentioned produces an affection according to the quality of the senses. They are therefore called passive qualities: sweetness produces a certain affection according to taste, heat according to touch, and the same is true of the others.

He had established sweetness, bitterness, cold, heat, whiteness, and blackness as examples of passive qualities. Although these are passive qualities, they are not called so in one and the same way; rather, the reasons why all these things are called passive qualities are very different.

Sweetness and bitterness, heat and cold, are first called passive qualities not because sweet things suffer something externally, nor because bitter things have acquired the harsh taste and bitterness of their flavor through some affection. Honey has not suffered something so that sweetness should be part of its nature, nor has wormwood been stained by any external affection with the horror of bitterness.

Therefore, such things and those resembling them are not called passive qualities because they themselves have suffered something, but because certain affections are produced in the senses by them. From honey, which is sweet, a certain sweetness is left in the sense of taste; heat and cold likewise produce a certain affection in the senses. We suffer sweetness when we taste something sweet, and we undergo in our senses an affection of the sort corresponding to the quality of heat and cold.

Accordingly, heat and cold, bitterness and sweetness, are called passive qualities because, according to the quality of the senses, they produce some affection in us—not because they themselves suffer something externally.

### [Col. 0247A]

Whiteness and blackness, and the other colors, are not called passive qualities in the same way as those just mentioned. They are called so because these qualities themselves arise from certain affections.

Since passive qualities are also said to include colors, namely whiteness and blackness, he now explains how they can be called passive qualities in a way different from bitterness and sweetness, heat and cold. Bitterness and sweetness were called passive qualities not because they themselves suffered something externally, but because they produced affections. Whiteness and blackness, by contrast, are called passive qualities not because they introduce affections into the senses, but because they arise from certain other affections.

Aristotle appears to have considered this in a certain way when he subsequently proposed the following:

> Since many changes of color occur through some affection, it is clear that this is so: someone becoming ashamed becomes red, someone afraid becomes pale, and the same applies to each of these cases.

This is transferred, with exceptionally acute reasoning, from affections of short duration to passive qualities that persist for a very long time. The probability of the argument proceeds as follows. The qualities of colors are shown to arise from affections: since shame is a certain affection, redness arises from it; and since fear is regarded as an affection, pallor fixes itself upon the face and features of the person who is afraid.

Therefore, since these colors appear to arise from a certain affection, it is plausible that the same process also occurred in natural coloration. When someone is ashamed, all the blood moves into the face and, as if it were about to reveal the offense, pours itself outward; so too redness arises from the movement of the blood and its being poured into the open surface. Accordingly, if this happens through an unnatural affection, the face is suffused with a natural redness.

Pallor occurs whenever the blood moves from the face into the inner regions around the heart. If this too is produced by a natural affection, it is plausible that the same coloration is generated and impressed upon the face. Therefore, whether pallor occurs through illness, which is not natural, or through some natural event involving an affection, and likewise in the other cases, such conditions are called passive qualities because they arise from certain affections. Aristotle himself confirms this in the following words:

> Therefore, if someone has naturally suffered something of this kind, he ought to have a similar color. For the affection that has now occurred in the body through shame, and the same affection according to a natural process, will produce the same result, so that the natural color will be similar.

For whether someone suffered something before birth that caused the blood to leave the face, or whether, in some other way, the blood moved from the infant’s face inward, the natural pallor stained the face. Whatever are now unnatural affections and dispositions—when these colors stain the face or the whole body—will, if they occur naturally, cause the face to be seen marked with similar colors.

At present, when heat on the surface of the face has cooked the blood lying there, the redness of the scorched blood produces the color of blackness. If the same thing occurred through some affection in the face of an unborn infant, it is plausible that the same affection would stain the body as it received that color. Therefore, the things found in colors are called passive qualities not because they themselves suffer something, but because they arise from certain affections in the body and face of anyone.

### [Col. 0247D]

> Whatever, then, takes its beginning from such events and from affections that are difficult to change and permanent are called passive qualities. Thus, whether pallor or blackness has arisen according to the natural substance, they are called qualities. For we are called such according to them; or, whether through a prolonged illness or through heat something of this kind has occurred—blackness or pallor—and does not easily pass away or remains throughout life, these too are called qualities. For we are likewise called such according to them.

He therefore states that whatever conditions of this sort originate from affections that are difficult to change and permanent are called passive qualities. Whether pallor or blackness has been produced in accordance with the natural substance, they are called qualities, since we are called such according to them. Likewise, if through a prolonged illness or through heat something of this sort occurs—blackness or pallor—and it does not easily pass away or remains throughout life, these too are called qualities, since we are similarly called such according to them.

It provides a certain indication by which, once it has been considered, we may recognize which of all those qualities mentioned above ought to be called qualities. For if these qualities have arisen either by chance or by nature in such a way that their departure is slow and their alteration difficult, they are called qualities. For if someone becomes pale either through illness or by nature, and the pallor remains in his body, then it is called a quality. This is found not only in bodily defects but also in affections of the mind. For if someone, either by nature [Col. 0248C] or later through some other circumstance, takes delight in continual feasting, and this delight somehow remains in the very dissolution of his mind and is difficult for him to relinquish, it has become a passible quality, because those in whom it arises are called qualified according to it. For someone in whom blackness remains is called black; someone for whom the pleasure of continual feasting is permanent is called a glutton. The sign, therefore, in passible qualities is that they are immovable and permanent. But concerning things of the kind that are very easily altered and exist only in a temporary state, Aristotle’s view appears to be as follows.

Whatever arises from things that are easily dissolved and quickly pass away is called a passion, and scarcely a quality at all [Col. 0248D]. For we are not called qualified according to such things. Someone who has become red through embarrassment is not called red, nor is someone who has become pale through fear called pale; rather, he is said to have undergone something. Therefore such things are called passions, but not qualities. Likewise, in the soul, passions and passible qualities are spoken of in the same way. Whatever comes into being immediately from passions that are difficult to remove is called a quality, such as madness, anger, and other things of this kind; for we are called qualified according to them—that is, angry and mad. Likewise, any other derangements that are not natural but have arisen from certain circumstances, if they are slow to pass away or altogether immovable, are also qualities of this kind, since we are called qualified according to them. But whatever arises from things that pass away easily [Col. 0249A] and quickly is called a passion. Thus, if someone becomes more irascible when distressed, he is not called irascible because he is more irascible in such a passion; rather, he is said to have undergone something. Therefore such things are called passions, but not qualities.

What judgment he would make concerning affections that adhere to minds or bodies only for the present time and for a moment, he himself stated in an unambiguous account. For after declaring that those things which arose from certain passions and nevertheless remained unalterably in their subjects were passible qualities, he now calls affections that exist in subjects in such a way as to pass away quickly not qualities but passions. If someone has been stained red through embarrassment, since that redness does not remain, he is not called red [Col. 0249B]. If he were called red, that redness itself would also be a passible quality, since it would remain for a very long time in the body that underlies it. But since someone who has become red through embarrassment is in no way called red, while qualities are those according to which we are called qualified, the redness of embarrassment is not a quality but a certain passion. For if it were a quality, those affected by that redness would be called red—that is, qualified—but this is not so. Affections of this kind, therefore, which do not last long, are not called qualities but rather passions. For someone who becomes red through embarrassment is said to have undergone something.

The same reasoning applies to passions of the soul. If someone is angry for a moment, no one would rightly call him irascible for that reason; but if such a defect has constantly remained in someone’s soul, then he may be so called [Col. 0249C]. For if someone has been harmed in body either by nature or through illness, so that he acquires perpetual madness or immovable irascibility, he is called either mad or irascible. And any derangements which, as he himself says, have remained either according to nature or through circumstance are counted among passible qualities, because we are called qualified according to them. But those which, as has been said, do not remain and instead pass away easily, we call not qualities but merely passions.

But since he enumerated three species of quality—one according to which habits and dispositions are spoken of; another according to which the natural power or incapacity of things subject to them is prepared for doing or undergoing something; and a third according to which passible qualities are spoken of—and divided this third species in a twofold manner, saying that some qualities are passible because they themselves produce certain passions, while others are passible because they arise from certain passions, one may ask how these passible qualities also differ from that first species of quality, which is established according to habit and disposition. For if someone has experienced heat and cold, he certainly possesses a passible quality, yet he is also situated in the disposition and affection belonging to that very thing. For he is disposed toward the same heat and cold that he has received and possesses. Aristotle himself, seeing this, counted heat and cold in both species: for he called heat and cold both a disposition and a passible [Col. 0249D] quality.

The solution to this question is as follows. Nothing prevents one and the same thing from being assigned to two genera or species on account of different causes. Thus Socrates is called “relative” insofar as he is a father, but he is a substance insofar as he is a human being. So, in the case of heat and cold, insofar as someone appears to be disposed according to them, they are counted under disposition; but insofar as they arise from certain passions, they are called passible qualities.

Passible qualities themselves differ from habit—that is, passible qualities differ from habits—in that, in most cases, habits are attained through arts and sciences, so that the habit itself is perfected by a certain order and progression. Passible qualities, however, are not attained in this way. Their difference from the second species, which is spoken of according to natural power or incapacity, is also asked about; and their difference is perfectly clear. For we say that something is spoken of according to the species of natural power not according to its present activity, but according to what it is capable of being. Cold and heat, however, and sweetness or bitterness, are considered not according to what they may become but according to what they already are. Thus this third species differs from the second in that the second is spoken of according to possibility, while the third is spoken of according to actuality.

As for what we earlier called indiscriminately by the name of passions and affections, there is also a short question concerning this. We shall find that a passion appears to differ from an affection. For if certain bodies have been heated in such a way that they are also able to emit some heat from themselves, they are called affected by heat [Col. 0250C]. But if they have merely received heat for a moment, we call these things passions and distinguish them from affections. Thus there is a continuous increase among passions, affections, and habits: when a passion has been enlarged, it passes into an affection; when an affection has been increased, it is transformed into a habit.

This is sufficient to have stated concerning the third species of quality. He now confirms the force and nature of the fourth species by a most truthful discussion, up to the point where the division of quality comes to rest. We too must moderate the length of our discussions. We must also see to it that sufficient brevity is applied to the order of the exposition, so that obscurity does not accompany brevity, nor does an insufficiently restrained discourse disfigure clarity through wearisome prolixity.

[Col. 0250D] The fourth genus of quality is figure and the form that remains constant around each thing. In addition to these there are straightness and curvature, and anything similar to them. For according to each of these, something is said to be qualified: a triangle or a quadrilateral is said to be something qualified, and likewise something straight or curved. And each thing is called qualified according to its form.

The fourth species of quality is that which is perceived according to each form and figure. A figure is something such as a triangle or a square; the form of that figure is a certain quality. Thus the figure is a triangle or a square, while the form of the triangle or square itself is a certain quality. Hence we also call human beings well-formed. For a figure that is either more beautiful, or ordinary, or constituted in some other way is called a quality and a form [Col. 0251A]. No one doubts that these are qualities. For from figure one is called “figured,” and from form “well-formed.” Moreover, a triangle is denominated from triangulation, and a square from squaring.

But if those things are qualities according to which something is called qualified, no one can doubt that form and figure are qualities, since everything that participates in them is called qualified from them. But since, among the species of continuous quantity, both the triangle and the surface have been enumerated, the surface itself is a quantity, while the composition of the surface is a quality. For a figure is, as geometers define it, something contained under one or more boundaries. Under one, as a circle; under more than one, as a triangle or square. Therefore the space itself enclosed by the lines mentioned above is called a surface, which is a quantity. For a surface, since it consists in a certain extension and space, is a quantity; but its composition is a quality. Since three lines, joined together by their appropriate endpoints, have enclosed one space contained by three angles formed by three lines, that very space which they enclose can be referred to quantity; but the fact that it is enclosed by three lines is a quality, for it is a triangular figure.

The same may also be said of a line. Since length without breadth is called a quantity, the fact that it is straight or curved is referred back to quality.

Rarified and dense, rough and smooth may indeed be thought to signify quality [Col. 0251C], but things of this kind are regarded as foreign to the disposition that belongs to quality. For each of the two seems rather to signify a certain position: something is dense because its parts are close to one another, and rarefied because they are separated from one another; something is smooth because its parts lie evenly in a straight line, and rough because one part projects while another is lower. Perhaps other modes of quality will also appear, but those most commonly mentioned are nearly all of them. The qualities, then, are the things stated above; the qualified are those which are denominatively called according to them, or in some other way from them.

Some things appear to be qualities because certain things are denominated from them—for example, “smooth” from smoothness, “rough” from roughness, and “dense” and “rare” from density and rarity [Col. 0251D]. These too therefore seem capable of being counted among qualities. But to those who consider the matter rationally, judging not merely by what is said to the ears but also by mind and intellect, it is clear that these should not be placed among qualities.

For what we call “rare” is a certain position of parts, not a quality. The parts are separated from one another in such a way that a foreign body can be admitted between them; for this reason a sponge and pumice stones are called rarefied, since a twig or something else can be inserted into their cavities, so that it lies among the gaps between the parts. This is why they are called rarefied. Dense, on the other hand, is so called because its parts are so near and tightly joined to one another [Col. 0252A] that no body can enter between them, as in iron or diamond. A certain position of parts, therefore, belongs to these things, not a quality.

Nor does what is called smooth differ in this respect. Its parts are positioned in such a way that neither projects above nor falls below the other, but they are joined with equal extremities. For this reason there is a certain smoothness, as when a hand drawn across it perceives the smoothness produced by parts joined in equality, as in silver. Roughness, on the other hand, is an unequal position of parts, with some projecting and others depressed, as in a file, whose parts are some raised and others lowered.

Thus, according to each particular position of the parts, rarity, density, roughness, or smoothness belongs to bodies. These things, therefore, are not spoken of according to quality but rather according to position. Position, however, has been named in the category of relation. These things are therefore not qualities but rather relatives.

Here Aristotle ends his enumeration of the species of quality. We must not, however, suppose that the only qualities are those he listed above. He himself testifies that there are also other qualities, which he has now neglected to enumerate all together. There are many reasons why he neglected them. The first is that this book occupies the place of an elementary introduction: it does not convey perfect knowledge but merely opens an approach and a kind of bridge toward entry into the higher parts of philosophy. Therefore, if this is so, he ought to say only as much as would suffice for beginners, lest their minds, not yet firmly established in knowledge, be confused by the subtlety of a manifold doctrine.

What is lacking here he supplied in the books entitled Μετὰ τὰ φυσικά (“After the Physics,” or “Metaphysics”) [Col. 0252C]. For that work is prepared for those who are complete, not for beginners. There is also another reason: he wished to encourage us to seek out other qualities, allowing us to discover something not only from our own teachers but also from ourselves.

Accordingly, he concludes that the things he listed above, which are most commonly spoken of, are qualities, while those things are called qualified which are spoken of according to the qualities mentioned above. But since he added “or in some other way from these,” the sequence of the exposition proceeds after first setting out Aristotle’s words.

“In most cases, and almost in all, they are denominated, as white from whiteness, grammatical from grammar, and just from justice; and likewise in other cases” [Col. 0252D].

In some cases, however, because names have not been assigned to the qualities, it is not possible for something to be denominated from them. Thus “runner” or “boxer,” when these terms are used according to natural aptitude, are not denominated from any quality. No names have been assigned to the aptitudes according to which these people are called qualified, as names have been assigned in the case of disciplines, according to which people are called boxers or athletes in accordance with an affection. Boxing and athletics are names of disciplines; those who are affected by them are denominatively called qualified from them.

Sometimes, even when a name has been assigned, the thing called qualified according to it is not denominated from that name. Thus someone is called “studious” from virtue. For he is called studious because he possesses virtue, but he is not denominatively called from virtue. This, however, is not the case in most instances [Col. 0253A]. Those things called qualified are either denominated from the qualities mentioned above or are called qualified in some other way from them.

There are, he says, many qualities which, once established and given their proper names, provide the basis for the denominative naming of other things. These are the examples he himself explained most clearly. Since whiteness is the name of a certain quality, “white” is said from it. In the same way, grammar is the name of a thing, and those qualified according to it are called “grammatical.” Grammarians, then, are named from grammar. This is the case in most instances: when a quality has a name, if something is called qualified according to that quality, its designation is derived from the quality itself.

There are other qualities which have no established name, although things are called qualified according to them. These things are called qualified because they participate in some other quality, but they are not called qualified according to the quality from which, if a name had been assigned to it, they could have been named [Col. 0253B]. This occurs in the quality spoken of according to natural power. For although those who are named according to that power are called qualified, they nevertheless, as has been said, are not called by any proper name.

Those called boxers are named from the art of boxing because they are in some way affected with respect to that same art of boxing. They are therefore predicated as boxers from the art of boxing. Those who are not yet boxers but can become so are called “boxers” not according to the art itself—that is, boxing—but according to the power of the art of boxing. No proper name, however, has been assigned to that power.

For just as runners are named from running, athletes from athletics, and boxers from boxing, by distinct terms belonging to the qualities, the same is not true of the natural power of each thing. Running—the natural power according to which we call people runners—and, likewise, the power of boxing or the power of practicing athletics, have no distinct names of their own.

Why is someone called a runner, if we are asked about someone who is not yet a runner? We answer: according to natural power. Why is someone called an athlete? In the same way, we reply that it is according to natural power. Therefore a boxer who is not yet a boxer is also named from that same natural power.

If this natural power had a proper name, it would be designated by distinct terms, just as happens with those qualities for which a proper name has been established, such as running, athletics, and the art of boxing. This is what he means when he says that, in some cases, because names have not been assigned to the qualities, it is impossible for anything to be denominatively named from them.

His purpose is to show that a runner who is already running is named from running, whereas a runner who is called a runner according to the power of running is not named from running but only from a power for which no proper name has been established. Therefore all things that are called qualified according to natural power are denominated from no quality, because the qualities from which they could be denominated lack proper names.

But things that are such that they are called qualified not according to power but according to affection are denominatively named from the qualities toward which they stand in some relation [Col. 0254A]. Aristotle expressed this in the following way: the case is not the same with natural power as it is with the disciplines according to which boxers and athletes are called qualified according to affection. Boxing and athletics are names of disciplines, and those who are involved with them are denominatively called qualified from them.

He therefore taught that everything which might appear to be named from certain qualities is not in fact predicated from qualities, as in the case of qualities that have no proper name. He also showed that this occurs in most cases, so that qualified things are denominatively named from the qualities proposed.

It remains for him to say that there are certain qualities for which a name has been established, yet those who participate in them are not denominatively named from them. Virtue is an example. For since virtue is a quality—it is a certain habit, and every habit is a quality—whoever participates in virtue is not denominatively named according to it.

In denominative naming, the name must always remain the same. But in someone who participates in virtue there is no denominative form derived from “virtue.” Someone who participates in goodness is called good; someone who participates in justice is called just; and so on. But someone who participates in virtue is called either upright or wise. Neither “upright” nor “wise,” however, is denominatively derived from “virtue,” since both names are very different from “virtue.” This is what he says: “Sometimes, even when a name has been established, the thing called qualified according to it is not denominatively named.”

He does not omit to give an example of this, although it cannot be found in many cases. There are few cases, as he himself says, in which, once the name of a quality has been established, those who participate in it are not called qualified according to that higher quality.

He assigns to these qualities a numerical plurality, from which the things that participate in them are called qualified. For, as he said above, “in most cases, and almost in all, they are denominated.” Therefore the definition is correct and has been set out in its proper order.

At the beginning, it was stated only that a quality is that according to which things are called qualified. But since there are certain qualities that lack proper names, while those who participate in them are called by their own terms, as in the case of natural power; and since, again, there are certain qualities that do have proper names, while no denominative designation from those proposed qualities is applied to things affected with respect to those qualities, he added that qualified things are called either denominatively from all qualities in which they participate or in some other way [Col. 0254D].

That is, either, when the quality has a name, they are not called according to that name, as in the case of virtue; or the quality itself has no assigned name, as in the case of natural power. Thus, in these two qualities—one in which, despite the existence of a name, the things that possess it are not called qualified according to that name, and the other in which no name has been assigned to the quality itself—neither predication is denominative.

To conclude the whole account of quality, he says that qualified things are named from qualities either denominatively or in some other way. Thus they are not denominatively named: sometimes they are called according to power, and sometimes according to the same quality of virtue—for virtue and wisdom are the same quality.

He therefore concludes that those things are called qualified which are denominatively named from these qualities or are called qualified in some other way from them.

After all the qualities have first been arranged in order and their conclusion established, each property is investigated in the customary sequence.

There is also contrariety according to quality. Justice is contrary to injustice, whiteness to blackness, and so forth. Likewise, things called qualified according to them are contrary, as just to unjust and white to black. But this is not the case in all instances: no contrariety exists between red or pale or other intermediate colors, although these are qualities.

[Col. 0255B] He says that some things in the category of quality are contraries, and he proves this by examples. Whiteness and blackness are contraries, as are all things that participate in whiteness and blackness. This is what he means by “and the qualified things that are called according to them.” For just as whiteness is contrary to blackness, so white is contrary to black.

But this is not a property of quality. Although red and pale are qualities, as are other colors of this kind, there is no contrariety among them. No one says that anything is contrary to red or to pale. Since white and black are certain extremes of colors and are very far apart, they are contraries; intermediate colors, however, have no contraries.

For if someone posits red as contrary to black, and contraries are very far apart, then blackness will be very far from redness; and whiteness, in turn, is very far from blackness. Therefore redness and whiteness would both be contrary to blackness, and two contraries would be found for one thing, which cannot happen. Redness, therefore, is not contrary to blackness. The same can be shown concerning the other intermediate colors: they have no contrary.

Accordingly, if these colors have no contrary, contrariety is not found in every quality. And if this is so, receiving contraries is not a property of quality.

Nor is contrariety found even among the figures that are manifestly qualities. A circle is not contrary to a square, nor a square to a triangle; indeed, no figure can be contrary to any figure. It is therefore clear that receiving a contrary is not a property [Col. 0255D] of quality.

But since certain things within quality appear to be contrary to one another, such as justice and injustice, a certain question commonly arises from this. Some say that injustice is not contrary to justice, because they think that what is called injustice is a privation of justice, not a contrariety. They say that contraries are named by their proper names, not by the privation of their contrary—for example, white is named in opposition to black—but that justice has some contrary whose proper name has not yet been discovered. This is entirely false.

Many dispositions are expressed by the vocabulary of privation, such as illiberality and imprudence. These would never be opposed to virtues, which are habits, unless they too were habits and remained immutably in the souls of those who possessed them [Col. 0256A].

Nor is it true that all privations are expressed by negation. Deafness, although it is a privation of hearing, is expressed without a negation; blindness is treated in the same way. No one says “non-hearing” or “non-seeing,” or anything of this kind; rather, deafness and blindness are simply named by their proper terms, although hearing and sight belong to habit, while deafness and blindness must be placed among privations. Justice, therefore, is contrary to injustice.

He accordingly gives a rule for the genus under which contraries are appropriately placed. Aristotle prescribes this rule in the following words:

“Furthermore, if one of two contraries is qualified, the other will also be qualified. This is clear if one sets out the other categories individually. For if justice is contrary to injustice, and justice is qualified, then injustice too is qualified. None of the other categories will fit injustice—not quantity, not relation, not place, nor anything else of this kind at all, but only quality. The same applies to other things that are contraries according to quality.”

If, he says, it is clear that one of two contraries is placed under quality, it will at the same time be clear that its contrary is also appropriately placed under quality. At the same time, he demonstrates that injustice is a quality. If justice is most plainly a quality, since it is neither relation, place, time, nor any other category and cannot be placed under any genus except quality, and if injustice is contrary to it, there is no doubt that injustice too must be attached to quality. Since he expressed this more clearly and made it evident through the light of his examples, we must move on to another matter.

Quality admits of more and less. One white thing is called whiter than another, and one just thing is called more just than another. Qualities themselves also admit of increase. For when something is white, it can become whiter, though this does not apply to all qualities but to many.

One may hesitate, however, to say that justice is more or less justice than another justice. The same question arises concerning other affections. Some doubt whether justice is said to be more or less justice than another justice, or health more or less health than another health. They do say that one person possesses less health than another, and that one person possesses less justice than another; and they speak similarly of grammar and other affections. Things called qualified according to these affections unquestionably admit of more and less [Col. 0256D]. One person is called more grammatical than another, more just, and healthier; and the same applies to other cases.

He also introduced another property, which, after examining the matter, he excluded from the complete property of quality. He says that qualities can be intensified or diminished. One thing, he says, can be called whiter than another, as snow is whiter than silver, and some marbles are whiter than others. We also say that one thing is more or less just than another. Something can become more just and even most just.

Wherever there are comparisons, it is clear that more and less are spoken of. In this way, whiteness itself, or another quality, grows through intensification and diminishes through relaxation, not only when compared with another quality of the same species but also when compared with itself. Silver, for example, is said to be whiter now than before, after it has been polished [Col. 0257A].

Yet although this is so, receiving more and less is not a property of quality. Quality alone does not receive more and less, for this intensification and relaxation are also found in relatives. We can say that one equal thing is more equal or less equal than another, and the same applies in other cases of this kind.

Nor do all qualities receive more and less, as he himself states: “But this is not the case in all instances, but in many.” For one may doubt whether justice is said to be more justice than another justice, and the same applies to other affections. Some doubt this, saying that justice is not called more or less justice than another justice, nor health more or less health than another health [Col. 0257B]. They do say that one person has less health than another, and that one person has less justice than another.

There have been three opinions on this matter. Some held that more and less can be found in all things according to their relation to matter. For they regarded it as proper to matter and bodies to grow through intensification and diminish through relaxation. This was the view of certain Platonists.

Another opinion held that more and less should not be spoken of according to the most certain and most genuine arts and virtues, but could be spoken of according to intermediate ones. Thus grammar and justice themselves are not called more grammar or more justice, but there are certain intermediate arts in which this can occur.

The third is the view Aristotle discusses. He thinks that habits themselves do not grow through intensification or diminish through relaxation, but that those who participate in them can be brought under the judgment of comparison, so that more and less may be said of them.

Health itself and justice itself are not one more or less than another. No one says that one health is more health than another health. We can say only that someone has more health—that is, that he is healthier, more healthy, or less healthy. We therefore say that qualities themselves do not receive more and less; but those who are called qualified according to them fall under comparison, as more just, healthier, and more grammatical.

Grammar itself—that is, literacy—does not receive more and less. No one says that one thing is more grammatical than another. Rather, we speak of the person who participates in grammar. We call him literate, deriving the term from literacy. “Literate,” however, receives more and less. Thus the grammarian Donatus, when he had reached a more advanced age, was more grammatical—that is, more literate—than when he had first come to studies of this kind.

Although these matters stand as described, we nevertheless find some qualities in which comparison cannot unquestionably be found, such as those he next sets out.

A triangle and a quadrilateral do not appear to admit of more and less, nor does any other figure.

These things, which have been discussed under the fourth species of quality, admit of more and less in no way. No one says that one circle is more a circle than another, or that one triangle is more a triangle than another. One may say that one is larger, but not that it is more a triangle [Col. 0258A].

The reason is as follows. The definition of a triangle is “a figure contained by three straight lines.” Whatever things receive this definition—whatever things are contained by three straight lines—are properly triangular in form. The same applies to the circle, which is defined as follows: “A circle is a plane figure contained by one line, to which all the lines drawn from one point within it are equal.” Again, the definition of a square is: “A square is contained by four equal lines and four right angles.”

Whatever things therefore receive the definition of a circle or of a square are equally circular or square in form; whatever do not receive it are not so at all. Whatever things receive the definition of any form are entirely identical with that form: what receives the definition of a circle is a circle; what receives the definition of a square is a square; what receives the definition of a triangle is a triangle; what receives the definition of an oblong, or figure longer in one direction than the other, is such an oblong; and the same applies in the other cases.

But if something does not receive the definition—for example, a triangle does not receive the definition of a circle—it is in no way a circle. Nor can one say that, between a square and a triangle, since neither receives the definition of a circle, the square is more a circle and the triangle less a circle. Both are entirely separate from the account of a circle. Aristotle treats this matter in the following words:

“Whatever things receive the definition of a triangle and of a circle are all similarly triangles or circles. But of those that do not receive the definition, no one is said to be more one than another. For a square is no more a circle than an oblong figure, since neither of them receives the account of a circle. In general, if neither receives the account proposed, one will not be said to be more than the other. Not all qualified things, therefore, receive more and less.”

None of the things mentioned above, therefore, is a property of quality [Col. 0258D].

For if this is what a definition does—demonstrate the account of each substance—then whatever things differ in definition will themselves also differ in the nature of substance. Correctly, therefore, if certain things do not receive the definition proposed for a given thing, whether triangle or square, they are separated from that thing’s nature. Accordingly, neither triangle, nor square, nor circle, nor anything of this kind admits of more and less. But although these are qualities, not all qualities admit of more and less equally. And if neither intensification nor diminution occurs in every quality, nor in quality alone—for you find the same thing in relation—then admitting more and less is not peculiar to quality. What, then, should be said to be peculiar to quality? He himself set this out most clearly below.

Similar and dissimilar are predicated according to qualities alone. For one thing is not similar to another according to anything other than that by which it is qualified. Therefore it will be peculiar to quality that things are called similar and dissimilar according to it.

“Only qualities,” he says, “retain similarity and dissimilarity.” For although similarity is relative to something, nevertheless we do not call something “similar” unless we call it so because of what quality it has. If the same quality exists in two things, the things in which it exists are similar; nor is there any other category according to which something could be called similar or dissimilar. As for all the other categories, it is clear that similarity is predicated of none of them. If someone should assert that similarity and dissimilarity can be predicated according to quantity, it has been shown that according to quantity what is predicated is not similar and dissimilar, but equal and unequal. Since, then, as we proceed through each case, this is found in all qualities and is manifestly found in no other category, he rightly established it as peculiar to quality.

But since, in treating of things related to something, he counted dispositions and habits among relatives, while now he has also assigned these same things to quality, he raised a question for himself: why, if he had previously subordinated them to the things related to something, he has now placed those very things under qualities. For earlier he showed that things differing from one another cannot have the same species, when he says: “Of different genera, and of genera not arranged subordinately, the species and differences are different.” Since, therefore, relation and quality are different genera, the same species ought not to be subordinated to both. This is what he says:

> But one ought not to be disturbed, lest someone say that, while making a statement about quality, we have inserted much concerning relatives. For we said that habits and dispositions belonged to things related to something; yet the genera in almost all qualities are said relatively, though none of the individual things themselves is so said. For since knowledge is a genus, it is itself said to belong to another, since one speaks of someone’s knowledge. But none of the individual things themselves is said to belong to another as what it is: grammar is not called someone’s grammar, nor music someone’s music, except perhaps according to the genus; and these are called relative in this way: grammar is called someone’s knowledge, not someone’s grammar, and music someone’s knowledge, not someone’s music. Therefore individual things are not related to something.

He resolves this question with a very strong argument, namely with these words: “For almost all the things included in these genera are said relatively. But none of the things taken individually—that is, the species—is of this kind.” This is the argument that the Greeks call *epicheirēma* (ἐπιχείρημα). In such affections and habits, which are among the genera, only those that are genera can be reduced to relatives; those that are species of those genera cannot be counted among relatives, but among qualities. Thus knowledge, being a habit, has other habits beneath it, grammar and geometry. Knowledge itself, therefore, insofar as it is a genus, is always related to something: we speak of someone’s knowledge. But no one says that grammar, which is its species, is someone’s grammar. Let grammar, if possible, be said to be Aristarchus’s grammar. But everything that is said relatively is convertible. Thus Aristarchus would also be called “grammar’s Aristarchus,” which cannot be done. Grammar, therefore, is not said to be Aristarchus’s in the manner of a relative.

There is also this argument: it is genera of this kind, not species, that are called relative. Although the species themselves are not called relative—for grammar is not called someone’s grammar—if a species is nevertheless sometimes related to something, it is not related according to itself but according to its genus. Thus, since grammar is a species of knowledge, and knowledge is relative, if someone attempts to relate grammar to something, he cannot predicate it as relative according to grammar itself, but according to knowledge, that is, according to its genus. For grammar is not called someone’s grammar, but perhaps someone’s knowledge. Grammar, therefore, is not said to be relative according to grammar, but according to knowledge.

This is what he means when he says that grammar and music are not called someone’s grammar or someone’s music, except perhaps according to their proper genus: grammar is called someone’s knowledge, not someone’s grammar. Thus nothing belonging to the individual species is predicated by way of a relation. The genera of these species, however, are relative, as I said shortly above. When he says, “For almost all genera among qualities are said relatively, though none of the individual things themselves is so said,” he wished to show that the genera themselves of habits and dispositions are relative, whereas the species of those genera, which he said are individual, are in no way predicated relatively. He called them “individual” for this reason: grammar is one thing, and music likewise one thing, whereas knowledge is not one thing. He therefore rightly called the species of knowledge individual.

It is consequently established that the genera of such habits are called relative, while the species are referred to nothing else by their proper predication. Since, then, he has shown that such species are not relative, he now confirms that they are qualities.

> We are also called qualified according to the individual things. For we possess these things. We are called knowledgeable because we possess particular kinds of knowledge. Therefore these individual things will also be qualities, according to which we are called qualified. These, however, do not belong to the things related to something.

It was confirmed above that those things are qualities according to which certain people are called qualified. We are called grammarians not because we possess universal knowledge, but because we possess grammar itself. And it is more accurate to say that we are called knowledgeable because we are grammarians than to say that we are called grammarians because we retain some knowledge. No one is called a grammarian or knowledgeable from general knowledge, but only from particular knowledge. Therefore, since we are called qualified from these species of habits, the species themselves must be counted among qualities.

But when someone participates in grammar, the genus is also predicated of him; and according to it he is connected not only with grammar but also with knowledge. He is called knowledgeable for this reason. Since, then, someone who possesses grammar is called both knowledgeable and a grammarian, no one can participate in any knowledge who does not possess particular kinds of knowledge. For someone who lacks all the species must also lack the genus itself. Since, therefore, we possess these species and are called qualified according to them, we are called knowledgeable and grammarians from grammar; and it has been shown that these species themselves are not related to something. Such habits, which are species within the other category, that of relatives, are therefore rightly counted among qualities.

If someone is still reluctant to accept this, he adds something else by which he will dissolve the entire knot of the question. He says:

> Furthermore, if the same thing happens to be both qualified and relative, there is nothing contradictory in counting it under both genera.

Although it is true that one and the same thing cannot be subordinated to two different genera in the same respect, nevertheless it is appropriate for one and the same species to be subordinated to two genera according to different respects. Thus, as was already said above, although Socrates is a substance and “father” is relative, and although substance differs from relation, there is nevertheless nothing contradictory in subordinating the same Socrates to substance insofar as he is a human being, and to relation insofar as he has a son.

Accordingly, if one and the same thing is subordinated to two entirely different genera according to different aspects, there is no contradiction. In the same way, habits are placed under relation insofar as they are habits of something, but are counted under quality insofar as certain people are called qualified according to them. Therefore there is nothing contradictory in counting one and the same thing under two genera, or, if the case requires it, under several, according to the different powers of its nature.

Since, then, the discussion of quality has been completed, let us also turn the course of our exposition toward the remaining categories.

## ON DOING AND BEING AFFECTED

Doing and being affected admit of contrariety and of more and less. Heating and cooling are contraries, as are being heated and being cooled, and being pleased and being saddened. Therefore doing and being affected admit of contrariety and of more and less: heating is said to occur more and less, as is being heated, and being saddened. Doing and being affected therefore admit of more and less. Let this suffice concerning them.

Having worked through the four categories that seemed to require some questioning and consideration, he touches upon the rest lightly and briefly. Concerning doing and being affected, nothing is discussed in this book except that they admit of contraries and of intensification and diminution according to Aristotle; in his other works, however, he treated these matters fully and completely. Thus he discussed doing and being affected in the books entitled *On Generation and Corruption* (Περὶ γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς). Nor was his discussion of the other categories less extensive in his other works: for example, he treated “where” and “when” in the *Physics*, and investigated all these matters more deeply and subtly in the books he called *Metaphysics* (Μετὰ τὰ φυσικά).

Regarding doing and being affected, he himself stated most clearly that they can admit contraries. We say that fire heats and cools, which plainly belongs to doing. We say that water is heated and cooled, which likewise belongs to the category of being affected. He demonstrates with the clearest examples that they also admit more and less. Thus one speaks of heating more and less, and of being heated more and less. So much for this matter, since he himself set it out with complete clarity.

The distinction between them is as follows: in doing, an act proceeding from one thing into another is considered with respect to the thing from which it proceeds; in being affected, that act is considered in the thing into which it proceeds. For in the *Physics* it has been shown that act and passion exist simultaneously. For the present, let this suffice concerning doing and being affected.

It was also said, among things related to something, that being situated is named denominatively from positions. Concerning the remaining categories—when, where, and having—nothing further is said because they are evident, except what was stated at the beginning: “having” signifies being shod or being armed; “where,” being in the Lyceum or in the marketplace; “when,” being yesterday. Other matters concerning these categories have also been stated. Let what has been said about the proposed genera suffice.

## ON SITUATION AND POSITION

[Col. 0262C]

Position was counted among things related to something because it is itself the position of something. But since everything that is denominated from another is different from that from which it is denominated—for example, the person who is a grammarian is different from grammar, although “grammarians” are denominated from grammar—so, although position is relative, whatever is said denominatively from positions does not belong to the genus of relatives.

Position itself is relative, but “positioned” is denominated from position. For a standing is a standing of something. But since “to stand” is denominated from “standing,” it is not placed in the genus in which standing was placed. Therefore this category is not found under relation. But since we cannot reduce or adapt this genus to anything else, we must say that it has its own genus. Thus “to recline” comes from “reclining,” “to stand” from “standing,” and so forth—matters that Aristotle declines to pursue because they are perfectly clear. He says:

> Concerning the remaining things—that is, when, where, and having—because they are evident, nothing further is said about them than what was stated at the beginning.

He then supplies the examples mentioned above.

## ON WHERE AND WHEN

We should speak briefly about the predication that is “where” and “when.” Just as something cannot be relative in itself unless it derives its nature from something else, so neither can “when” and “where” exist unless there is a place and a time. “Where” is accompanied by place, and “when” by time.

Time and “when” are not the same, nor are “where” and place. Rather, once a place has first been proposed, if some thing is situated in it, it is said to be “where.” Again, if a particular thing exists at a particular time, it is said to be “when.” Thus the Apollinarian Games, since they occur at a time, are said to be “when” when we say that they occur.

These categories also have their own differences. “Where” is sometimes spoken of indefinitely: we say that someone, such as Socrates, is somewhere. At other times it is spoken of definitely: for example, in the Lyceum or in the Academy. “Where” also has certain contraries according to the place itself in which something is: being above and being below are predicated as kinds of “where.”

It is likewise clear that there are variations of time in the category called “when.” Future, present, and past things fall under “when.” We say that Scipio was once a Roman consul; that now he is the ruler of the East, who is presently called Anastasius; and that someone will exist in the future—statements that are made according to the category of “when.”

## ON HAVING

Having is something that comes from outside, is not innate in the thing that possesses it, and consists in retaining within oneself something other than the possessor itself, as in being armed or being clothed. Having is to hold clothes and weapons, which were not born together with the possessor and are not joined to him by any common nature or property. But since Aristotle was silent about these matters, we too must now omit a longer treatment of them.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0263]

[Col. 0263B] Once all the categories had been completed, many people had previously asked why he had entered into this discussion of opposites, which seemed beyond the work’s intended subject. Andronicus, however, does not think that this is an addition by Aristotle; at the same time, he believes that Aristotle perhaps did not make this addition concerning opposites, things simultaneous, priority, motion, and equivocation because he wrote this little book before the *Topics*, and thought these matters unnecessary for that work. He did not fail to recognize, of course, that in the *Topics* there had been a sufficient treatment, insofar as arguments were concerned, both of all the matters added here and of the categories themselves. Yet the *Categories* are useful for understanding the *Topics*.

So much for Andronicus. Porphyry, however, does not think that this addition is empty or devoid of reason. He gives the following explanation. Just as many things that presented themselves to common conceptions of the mind were set out by Aristotle at the beginning of this book—for example, equivocal, univocal, and denominative terms, and all the matters stated up to the discussion of substance for the usefulness and understanding of the categories themselves—so there were also certain matters that were indeed present in common understanding but nevertheless required a more subtle method of division. These were carefully added so that their proper nature might be grasped, lest a mind led astray by false opinions should be deceived.

He says that this is also shown by the order of the titles, which is coherent and consistent with reason: the addition was highly useful and necessary. First he discussed opposites; afterward, things that are simultaneous; then things that are prior; afterward he discussed motion; and finally he brought the sequence of the book to an end with a discussion of the equivocation of “having.”

The reason is that in all the categories he had first asked whether they could have contraries. In the case of things related to something, he said that the great cannot be contrary to the small, but is opposed to it. He passed over what it means to say “opposed,” so as not to break the continuity of the order of discussion. Here, therefore, he properly teaches first what he had omitted there.

In the case of relatives he also touched briefly on things that arise prior by nature and things that arise simultaneously by nature; now he explains these matters carefully. The categories of doing and being affected are those in which a kind of motion and activity are considered. It was therefore necessary to speak of motion for anyone wishing to show the nature of doing and being affected. And who could doubt that demonstrating the equivocation of any term is highly useful? Since “having” is also a category, it was neither inappropriate nor superfluous to discuss the equivocation of “having.”

## ON OPPOSITES

We must discuss the several ways in which things are customarily opposed. One thing is said to be opposed to another in four ways: either as a relative, or as a contrary, or as habit and privation, or as affirmation and negation. Each of these is opposed in the following manner: to give an illustration, things are opposed as relatives, as double is opposed to half; as contraries, as good to bad; as habit and privation, as blindness to sight; and as affirmation and negation, as “he sits” to “he does not sit.”

It is also asked whether the term “opposition” is predicated equivocally. For we say that things are opposed in four ways: as contraries, as relatives, as habit and privation, or as affirmation and negation. The question, therefore, is whether there is some equivocation among these four differences, or whether the very thing we call “opposite” is predicated in the place of a genus, and is therefore univocal.

On this matter the Stoics and Peripatetics held different opinions, and the Peripatetics themselves followed different positions. Since the Stoics’ view would require a lengthy discussion, let it be passed over. Some Peripatetics think that the name “opposite” is predicated equivocally of its subjects. They make this claim because Aristotle said: “We must discuss the several ways in which opposites are opposed”—that is, the several ways in which the matter pertains to equivocation.

Those who judged more correctly, however, say that the name “opposition” ought to be predicated in the place of a genus. For although the name “opposition” is predicated of its subjects according to four oppositions, the definition also applies to them. Opposites are things that cannot exist simultaneously in the same thing, in the same respect, at the same time, and in relation to one and the same object. This is found in each of the individual opposites.

White and black, which are contraries, cannot exist simultaneously at the same time in one and the same body or part of a body. Nor can a slave and his master be the same slave and the same master at the same time. Nor can habit and privation exist together: who would say that sight and blindness can exist simultaneously in one and the same eye? And no one doubts how opposed affirmation and negation are, or that they cannot exist simultaneously in the same thing.

Therefore, if the things placed under opposition receive the name and definition of opposition, why should there be any doubt that “opposition” is not predicated equivocally? With these matters established, let us proceed to the distinctions and differences among them.

Things opposed as relatives are said to be what they are relative to their opposites, or otherwise related to them. For example, double, insofar as it is double, is said to be the double of another—namely, the double of something. Knowledge is also opposed to the knowable as a relative, and knowledge is said to be what it is of the knowable; the knowable is likewise said to be what it is in relation to its opposite, namely knowledge. We call something knowable in relation to something—in other words, in relation to knowledge.

Whatever things, therefore, are opposed as relatives are said to be what they are of other things, or are related in some other way to one another.

The matters that are spoken of as relative opposition are clear and familiar in themselves, and have already been understood from the preceding discussion of relation. Things are relative whenever they are said to be what they are of other things, or are related to them in some other way: a slave is the slave of a master, and a master is the master of a slave; the great is said in relation to the small, and the small in turn is related to the great.

If this is found in all relatives, there is no doubt that it can also be observed in those things that are opposed as relatives: they are said to be what they are of their opposites, or are related in some other way to their opposites. If a slave is opposed to a master, the master is called the slave’s master—that is, the master of his opposite. Again, if a master is opposed to a slave, the slave is called the master’s slave. The small is opposed to the great, and the great to the small—that is, to its opposite.

This must necessarily be found in all oppositions according to relation. Accordingly, let this be the property of things opposed as relatives: they are related to their opposites and are said to belong to their opposites.

Having established these points, he teaches the difference by which things said according to contrariety differ from and disagree with things said according to relation. He says:

> But things opposed as contraries are in no way said to be what they are of one another; rather, they are said to be contraries of one another. For the good is not called the good of the bad, but its contrary; nor is white called the white of black, but its contrary. Therefore these oppositions differ from one another.

[Col. 0266A] It was said of things opposed according to relation that they are said to be what they are in relation to what is opposed to them. Contraries, however, are themselves opposed to one another, but are not said to be what they are of their opposites; instead, they are called contraries.

The matter is as follows. We say that good is contrary to bad, and again that bad is contrary to good. We also think that black is contrary to white, and likewise white to black. Yet although we think this, we do not say that they are what they are of their opposites. If we said that good is what it is of its opposite, we would not say that good is contrary to bad, but that good is the good of bad. Nor would one predicate that black is contrary to white, but that black is the black of white.

For this would be to say what black is of its opposite: to say that black is the black of white. Since this is not said, things that are opposed to one another as contraries are not said to be what they are of their opposites. But since we say that good is contrary to bad, and black contrary to white, although they are not said to be what they are of their opposites, they are nevertheless named in relation to their opposites as contraries.

This is what he means when he says: “They are in no way said to be what they are of one another; rather, they are said to be contraries of one another.” For the good is not called the good of the bad; that would be to predicate it as what it is of its opposite. Instead, we say that good is contrary to bad.

Accordingly, things opposed according to relation differ from things opposed according to contrariety in this respect: things opposed according to relation are said to be what they are of their opposites, whereas things opposed as contraries are not predicated by the name of what they are of their opposites, but merely as contraries. Thus good is said to be the contrary of its opposite, bad. We say that good is contrary to bad, but we do not say that good is the good of bad.

Having shown the difference between opposition according to relation and contrariety, he now pursues the difference and distinction among contraries themselves.

> Whatever contraries are such that, in the things in which they naturally occur or of which they are predicated, it is necessary for one of them to be present, none of these has an intermediate. But where it is not necessary for one of them to be present, there is something intermediate. Thus illness and health naturally occur in the body of an animal, and it is necessary for one of them to be present in the animal’s body, either illness or health. Even and odd are predicated of number, and it is necessary for one of them to be present in a number, either odd or even. There is nothing intermediate between them—neither between illness and health nor between even and odd.

But where it is not necessary for one of them to be present, there is something intermediate. Black and white naturally occur in a body, but it is not necessary for one of them to be present in every body; for not every body is either white or black. “Bad” and “good” are predicated of a human being and of many other things, but it is not necessary for one of them to be present in everything of which they are predicated; for not everything is either bad or good.

There is something intermediate between them: between white and black, brown and pale, and all the other colors; between bad and good, whatever is neither bad nor good. In some cases names have been assigned to things that are intermediate, as between white and black, brown, pale, and the other colors. In other cases it is not easy to assign a name to the intermediate, but it is determined by negating both extremes, as “neither good nor bad,” or “neither just nor unjust.”

A brief division of contraries should be made in this way. Some contraries have an intermediate, others do not. Among those that have something intermediate, some have several intermediates, while others have only one. Some of these intermediates are called by their own names; in other cases the intermediates themselves lack proper names and are designated by negating the contraries.

Let us now return to the beginning and confirm what has been said with appropriate examples. Contraries that lack an intermediate are such that one of them must be present in their proper subject, as illness and health. Every body in which illness and health occur is either ill or healthy. Since illness and health lack an intermediate, one or the other must therefore be present in the subject in which both naturally occur and of which they are predicated.

For illness and health naturally occur in an animal’s body—that is, they customarily occur there—and every animal is naturally such that it can be either healthy or ill. Since either healthy or ill is predicated of an animal’s body, and since these contraries lack an intermediate, it is necessary that either illness or health exist in every animal body.

Accordingly, among things that lack an intermediate, one must necessarily be present in the subject; and whenever things are such that one of them must be present in the subject, there is no intermediate between them. Contraries that have an intermediate, however, are not such that one of them must be present in the subject.

In things lacking an intermediate, one of the contraries must be present in the subject because there is no intermediate capable of existing between them in the underlying substance. Thus, since evenness and oddness have nothing intermediate between them in number—for every number is either even or odd, and there is nothing else that could thereby exist in number—every number is either even or odd.

In things that include some intermediate between them, however, it is not necessary that one of the contraries always be present. An intermediate may exist, as in color. White and black differ as contraries, but they have an intermediate, red or pale. Therefore not every body is white or black, because an intermediate between white and black can sometimes be found in underlying bodies.

We see a red body, such as a rose, and many other flowers produced by the mildness of spring. It was therefore rightly said that, among things that have no intermediates, one of them is always present in the subjects; and that wherever one of them must be present, there cannot be any intermediate there.

In the same way, things that have intermediates do not necessarily have one of the contraries present in their subjects; and where neither contrary need necessarily be present in the subject, there can undoubtedly be some intermediate. In some cases there are several intermediates, in others only one.

Between white and black there are several intermediates: red, as has been said, and pale, and likewise blue, and many other colors of this kind. Between hot and cold there is only one intermediate, which is called warm.

Among things with one intermediate, some have a name assigned to that intermediate, while others do not.
