A name has been assigned to the intermediate between hot and cold, for we call it “warm.” Aristotle himself said that between the bad and the good there is something that is neither good nor bad. Since good and bad are contraries, but it is not necessary for everything capable of receiving good or bad to be either good or bad, he therefore said that good and bad, although contraries, have an intermediate whose name has not been established. Nevertheless, one will find it among the natures of these contraries.

Later writers said that between good and bad there are things called indifferent—such as things that lie between virtue and vice, which are themselves contraries: wealth and beauty, which, as the Stoics think, are neither bad nor good. For this reason they called them indifferent. But among earlier writers there was no term “indifferent”; it was invented by later writers.

Aristotle, who never used this term, says that good and bad have some intermediate, but that it is called by no name; instead, he defines it through the negation of both contraries. He says that the intermediate between good and bad is what is neither good nor bad, just as the intermediate between just and unjust is what is neither just nor unjust.

Lest it seem inappropriate to define something by negations, he himself says: “In some cases it is impossible to assign a name to the intermediate; instead, it is defined by the negation of both.” For where there is one intermediate, if both contraries are removed, only the intermediate will remain. Thus, since good and bad have one intermediate, once good and bad have been removed, only what is neither good nor bad remains.

The whole division should therefore be stated again briefly. Among contraries, those of which one must always be present in the things in which they naturally occur have no intermediate between them: health and illness in a body, evenness and oddness in number. But those contraries that, in the things in which they can exist, are not such that one of them must be present embrace some intermediate quality between them: whiteness and blackness have red between them; cold and heat have warmth.

Of these, some contain only one intermediate, while others contain many. Between white and black there are many: pale, blue, and others. Between hot and cold there is only one, warmth.

Among those that retain one intermediate, some have names assigned to them, as in the case of heat and cold: warmth is the intermediate between heat and cold. In some cases no name has been assigned, as in the case of good and bad, or just and unjust. In these cases the intermediate has no name, but is defined by negating both contraries. We say that the intermediate between good and bad is what is neither good nor bad, and that the intermediate between just and unjust is what remains when both contraries have been removed: what is neither just nor unjust.

Privation and habit are said to concern things that come to be around the same object, as sight and blindness around the eye. Speaking universally, both of these are said to concern whatever is naturally suited to receive the habit.

In the ordered sequence, he now treats the third species of the proposed opposition, namely that which is spoken of according to habit and privation. In it he establishes one similarity that it shares with contrariety. Just as contraries concern the same thing—for white is always in a body, and black likewise is always in a body; and since justice is always implanted in the soul, injustice is also a defect of the mind—so things spoken of according to privation and habit must always be found around the same thing.

Thus, since sight is a habit—we possess sight—and sight is in or around the eye, blindness, which is the privation of sight, does not exist apart from the eye. Hearing, too, is a habit, and since it is around the ears, its privation, which is called deafness, likewise does not depart from the ears. Whatever has a habit, therefore, is also the thing around which the privation of that habit is considered.

From this he gives a rule: universally, he says, privation occurs in whatever is naturally suited to receive the habit. He then adds, in continuous order, what it means to be deprived:

We say that each thing capable of possessing a state is deprived of that state when it does not possess, in any way, what it is naturally constituted to have, at the time when it is naturally constituted to have it.

Aristotle concluded what deprivation is by this definition. For not everything that lacks sight is called blind, nor is everything that does not perceive hearing deaf. No one would call a wall blind, or a stone deaf, or anything of that kind. [Col. 0269D] Rather, we say that only those things are deprived of a state which either possessed the state and lost it, or could possess it but do not. We do not call a wall blind because sight could not naturally arise in it. Nor would anyone, with sufficient propriety, pronounce very young puppies blind when they lack sight. At that age they cannot yet naturally possess sight. But if, after the days have passed during which their eyes can naturally open and receive the light, they do not possess sight, it is clear that they are blind. Oysters, likewise, are not called toothless, since by nature they do not have teeth; nor do we call infants toothless when they have not yet reached the age at which they can have teeth. [Col. 0270A] We use the term when either someone who previously had teeth has lost them, or when someone has no teeth at the age at which he ought naturally to possess them. Thus, if one of the children has produced no tooth at all by the seventh year, we rightly call them toothless. This is what he means when he says:

> We call something toothless not because it does not have teeth, nor blind because it does not have sight, but when that which ought to have them does not have them. For some things have neither teeth nor sight from birth, but they are not called toothless or blind.

That is, we do not call everything that does not see blind, nor everything that does not have teeth toothless. There are many things that either cannot naturally possess these faculties at all or cannot possess them at a particular time. Deprivation exists whenever the one who can naturally possess a state does not possess it, and [Col. 0270B] at the time when, by nature, it is already possible for him to have it; or when someone who possesses and retains a state loses it through some external accident. Thus, in the case of children who have already grown up, if they do not have teeth: since they are human beings, they can have them, and if they lose them after possessing them, they are called toothless. If, however, their teeth never grow at all, then, since it could naturally have happened that children of that age and adults possessed teeth, we call them toothless and deprived of the state of having teeth, because this condition has arisen through some accident or through the interference of illness.

“To be deprived” and “to possess a state” are not the same as the state and the deprivation. Sight is the state, and blindness is the deprivation. But possessing sight is not sight, nor is being blind blindness. Blindness is a kind of deprivation, whereas being blind is being deprived, not the deprivation itself.

[Col. 0270C] Here the matter is demonstrated with the greatest accuracy: whether the things that fall under deprivation and state are themselves deprivations and states, or not. Since sight is a state and blindness a deprivation, while possessing sight falls under the state and being blind under the deprivation, the discerning observer sees clearly that possessing what is possessed is something different from the thing possessed itself. For three things are present in that which has a state: the one who possesses it, the thing possessed, and the act of possessing. Thus there is the one who sees, sight itself, and that which arises from both—the one who sees and sight—which is seeing.

Seeing differs from the one who sees, and seeing also differs from sight. For what is produced is one thing, and the producer another. The one who sees performs the act of seeing; [Col. 0270D] therefore seeing is different from the one who sees. Seeing also differs from sight: what is produced is one thing, and that by which something is done another. Seeing is accomplished through sight. Seeing, therefore, differs from sight itself, which brings about seeing. Yet seeing is possessing sight, possessing sight is retaining a state, and sight is the state itself. State, therefore, is not the same as what falls under the state—that is, retaining any given state.

The same reasoning applies to deprivation. Here too there are three things: the one who is deprived, the act itself that takes place, namely being deprived, and that of which one is deprived, namely the deprivation itself. If the possessor differs from possessing the state, then the one who is deprived also differs from being deprived. And if possessing the state differs from the state itself that is possessed, [Col. 0271A] then necessarily being deprived differs from the deprivation itself by which someone is deprived. Therefore neither what falls under the state can be called the state, nor what falls under the deprivation the deprivation. It was rightly said, then, that possessing a state is not the state, and being deprived is not the deprivation. Aristotle adds a still stronger argument, which he expresses as follows:

> Further, if blindness and being blind were the same, both would be predicated of the same thing. But a human being is called blind, whereas blindness is in no way predicated of a human being.

“If,” he says, “blindness were the same as being blind, then whatever was said to be blind would also be called blindness. [Col. 0271B] But we say that a human being is blind, whereas no one calls the human being himself blindness. Since the predication is different in the two cases, and blindness is not predicated of the thing of which being blind is predicated, while the thing of which being blind is predicated cannot itself be called blindness, there is no doubt that being blind is different from blindness—that is, being a deprivation is different from being deprived.” Although they differ, however, they fulfill an equivalent role in opposition, as he himself says:

> These too appear to be opposites: being deprived and possessing a state, just as deprivation and state are opposites. The mode of opposition is the same; for just as blindness is opposed to sight, so being blind is opposed to possessing sight.

[Col. 0271C] Deprivation and state, then, are opposed to each other in equal proportion, as are the things contained under deprivation and state. For if deprivation and state—that is, blindness and sight—are opposed to each other, why should seeing and being blind not likewise be opposed to one another? Therefore, although these things differ, the mode of opposition in them is equal.

What lies under an affirmation and a negation is neither an affirmation nor a negation. An affirmation is an affirmative sentence, and a negation a negative sentence; but none of the things that fall under affirmation and negation is a sentence. They are the things themselves. These too, however, are said to be opposites of each other, like affirmation and negation, because their mode of opposition is the same. For just as the affirmation “she is sitting” is opposed to “she is not sitting,” so the things placed under the two are opposed: someone’s sitting and someone’s not sitting.

[Col. 0271D] He has now passed to the fourth kind of opposition, which is said to be according to affirmation and negation. An affirmation is that which joins one thing to another through a certain participation; a negation is that which separates one thing from another through a certain disjunction. Thus: “Every human being is an animal.” The sentence joins animal to human being, for the human being participates in his proper genus, namely animal. A negation is: “A human being is not a stone.” The person who negates separates the nature of stone from humanity. Much will be said about these matters in the book *On Interpretation*. A fuller discussion of them should therefore be deferred to another time.

Aristotle, however, marked out the definitions of affirmation and negation in the simplest and almost cursory manner, for the sake of those who are being instructed, saying that negation and affirmation are negative and affirmative sentences. If he had defined the matter more carefully and subtly, he would not have defined affirmation by means of an affirmative sentence. For if what an affirmation is remains in doubt, it is no clearer or more evident what an affirmative sentence is. Whoever does not know what an affirmation is will therefore certainly not know what an affirmative sentence is. He was more indulgent in defining it here because in the book *Περὶ ἑρμηνείας* (*On Interpretation*) he supplied the true and complete force of the definition of both.

[Col. 0272A] The same reasoning applies to the things that fall under affirmation and negation as applied to those that were placed under deprivation and state. Just as state and deprivation are not the same as possessing a state and being deprived, so being an affirmation or negation is not the same as what falls under affirmation and negation. [Col. 0272B] For example, the affirmation is: “Socrates is sitting”; the negation: “Socrates is not sitting.” What falls under the affirmation is Socrates’ sitting—that is, the doing of what the affirmation states. What falls under the negation is Socrates’ not sitting—that is, not doing what the negation removes.

This is proved by the fact that every affirmation and every negation is a sentence, as the definition and determination given above demonstrate. Sitting and not sitting—that is, doing and not doing—are not sentences. Since affirmation and negation are sentences, what lies under affirmation and negation is said to differ from the affirmation and negation themselves. Yet they preserve the same similarity in that the things spoken of according to affirmation and negation are themselves opposed to one another. Just as the affirmation “Socrates is sitting” and the negation “Socrates is not sitting” are opposed, so too Socrates’ sitting and not sitting are opposed according to a determinate kind of similarity.

[Col. 0272C] Since four kinds of opposition have now been stated, let us follow Aristotle’s lead and gather their differences. There are six in number. If there are four things and we wish to show that they differ from one another, we find only six differences. When we set the first apart from the second, third, and fourth, there are three differences. It is unnecessary to show separately that the second differs from the first. Once we have established the distance of the first from the second, we have shown how the second differs from the first.

[Col. 0272D] Leaving aside, then, the difference between the first and second things, we must show the differences between the second and third and between the second and fourth. These are two; joined to the preceding three, they make five. What remains is the distance between the third and fourth. The difference of the first from the second and third has already been shown, since we demonstrated that the first differs from the second and in the same way from the third.

The examples prove this. When we propose that the opposition according to relation differs from the oppositions according to contrariety, deprivation and state, and affirmation and negation, there are three differences. When the opposition according to deprivation and state is shown to differ from contraries and from affirmation and negation, there are two differences. Joined to the preceding three, these complete the five. We omitted the difference between state and deprivation and the opposition according to relation because we previously showed how relational opposition differs from state and deprivation. There is no doubt that the difference is equal in both cases, since each has been shown to differ from the other.

[Col. 0273A] One difference remains: that between contraries and affirmation and negation. We omitted the difference between contraries and relational opposition and the opposition according to state and deprivation, since we showed above how the latter differs from contrariety. Since, then, the number of their differences has been established, let us proceed to the order of the work that follows.

[Col. 0273B]

That deprivation and state are not opposed in the manner of relatives is clear. For the very thing that is an opposite is not said of the other: sight is not called the sight of blindness, nor is it said of blindness in any other way. Likewise, blindness is not said in relation to sight. Blindness is indeed called a deprivation of sight, but blindness is not called sight. Further, all relatives are predicated reciprocally. Therefore, if blindness belonged to the class of relatives, it would necessarily be converted toward that to which it was related. But it is not converted. Sight is not called the sight of blindness.

[Col. 0273C] The other differences, which were set out above in the discussion of the difference between contraries and relatives, are also clear. Aristotle said that there is one difference between contraries and relatives: contraries are not converted in the manner of relatives. No one says that malice is the malice of goodness, or that goodness is the goodness of malice, as one says that a son is the son of a father and again that a father is the father of a son.

[Col. 0273D] The same difference is found in the things expressed according to deprivation and state. Things opposed as relatives are referred back to one another, and all are predicated in relation to their opposites. But state and deprivation do not behave in the same way. No one says that sight belongs to blindness, nor again that blindness belongs to sight. Therefore, since relatives are predicated of their opposites and are spoken reciprocally—for since a father is opposed to a son, the father is called the father of the son, that is, in relation to his opposite, and conversely the son is called the son of the father—since this is not said of the things according to deprivation and state, for although sight is opposed to blindness, sight is not called the sight of blindness, according to the opposition of deprivation and state, it follows that nothing belonging to this opposition is predicated of its opposite, nor is it converted. Blindness is not called the blindness of sight. Deprivation and state have therefore rightly been counted not in the same species as relatives, but in another.

[Col. 0274A]

That the things said according to deprivation and state are not opposed in the manner of contraries is clear from the following. Where there is no intermediate between contraries, one of the contraries must necessarily be present in the things in which they naturally occur, or of which they are predicated. There was no intermediate between things of which one had to be present in the subject capable of receiving them, such as sickness and health, and odd and even.

[Col. 0274B] Where there is an intermediate, however, it is never necessary that one of the contraries be present in every subject capable of receiving them. It is not necessary that every subject capable of receiving them be white or black, or cold or hot, since there may be some intermediate between them. There was an intermediate between these contraries, and one of them did not necessarily have to be present in the subject—except in those things in which one is present by nature, as hot is present in fire and white in snow. In such cases it is determinately necessary that one be present, not either one indifferently. Fire cannot be cold, nor snow black. Thus it is not necessary that one of the two be present in every subject capable of receiving them; but in those things in which one is naturally present, it is determinately possible for one, and not the other, to be present.

[Col. 0274C] I have shortened the text because the matters being discussed have already been stated above, and because a longer exposition might produce some weariness, which we have avoided by dividing the text in this way. Aristotle first places before our eyes all the differences among contraries. I shall recall them as briefly as I can. He says that, among contraries without intermediates, one must always be present in the thing capable of receiving those contraries, as sickness and health are always found in an animal’s body, and neither has any intermediate opposed to its contrary. Every animal body is therefore always either sick or healthy, and one of health or sickness is always present in the thing that receives these contraries.

Among contraries that have some intermediate, however, it is not necessary that one always be present in the thing to which they occur. Thus white and black are both contraries, but since they have an intermediate, such as red, and since these qualities always occur in bodies, it is not necessary that every body be either white or black. It may happen that their intermediate occurs in a given body.

[Col. 0274D] This is the case with things that are not without an intermediate, which we call mediated contraries, except in those things in which one contrary is naturally inherent, such as white in snow and hot in fire. In such cases one contrary must always occur, not the other and not either indifferently, but one definitely. Fire does not become hot at one time, cold at another, and then lukewarm, which is intermediate between the two; rather, it is always kindled by its natural heat. Snow does not at one time become black, at another red, or change into any other colors; it is always white.

Since this is so, if the things opposed according to state and deprivation are shown to differ from contraries without intermediates, from those that include some intermediate quality, and also from those that, although mediated, belong definitely to some subject, then it has been completely demonstrated that the things according to state and deprivation differ from contraries. Let us therefore retain, on Aristotle’s authority, the manner in which they differ.

[Col. 0275A] In deprivation and state, neither of the alternatives just described is true. It is not always necessary that one of them be present in the subject capable of receiving them. What has not yet acquired the nature required for seeing is called neither blind nor possessed of sight. These are therefore not contraries of the sort that have no intermediate; nor are they contraries of the sort that have an intermediate, for one of these must be present in every subject capable of receiving them.

[Col. 0275B] When a thing has come to be naturally capable of possessing sight, it will then be called either blind or possessed of sight. But it is not determined that one rather than the other will be present; either may occur. It is not necessary that the thing be either blind or sighted, but only that whichever occurs may occur. In contraries with an intermediate, however, it was never necessary that one be present in every subject capable of receiving them, but only in some subjects, and in those subjects one definite contrary was present, not merely whichever happened to occur. It is therefore clear that the things opposed according to deprivation and state are not opposed as contraries in either manner.

He first gives the differences by which the things opposed according to state and deprivation differ from contraries without an intermediate. In contraries without an intermediate, one of the contraries must always be present in the subject underlying them. It is not so in state and deprivation. Not every thing always possesses either a state or a deprivation. There is a time when it possesses neither, as with puppies whose eyes have not yet opened naturally. We do not say that they possess the state, since they do not see, nor that they are deprived of sight, since, being still very young, they cannot yet naturally possess sight.

[Col. 0275C] Thus, among things opposed to each other according to deprivation and state, one of the two is not always present in the underlying subject. Among immediate contraries—that is, contraries without an intermediate—one of the two is always present in the subject capable of receiving them. The opposition according to state and deprivation therefore differs from the opposition according to contraries.

But there are also contraries that are naturally present in something, such as white in snow, hot in fire, and black in a raven. The opposition of deprivation and state differs from these as well. Things that are present by nature are determinate and do not change, as white is present in snow. Snow is not sometimes white and sometimes black; it is only white. A raven is not sometimes white and sometimes black; it is only black.

[Col. 0275D] In deprivation and state, however, one member cannot belong to a thing determinately in this way. Either deprivation or state may always occur. This is what he means when he says: “One is not determinate, but either this or that.” We should understand that it is not necessary that the thing be determinately either blind or possessed of sight. A puppy that does not yet see by nature will either acquire the state—that is, sight—or be deprived of it and become blind. But neither one is determined; either may occur indeterminately. This opposition therefore differs from contraries that occur immutably in certain things by nature.

[Col. 0276A] It remains to show that this opposition differs from mediated contraries. In those contraries, it is not always necessary that one of them be present in the subject, because their intermediates can occur in underlying substances. Thus a thing may be neither white nor black when these qualities do not belong to it by nature but only accidentally. Both may be absent from bodies because red or pale, which are their intermediates, may occur in them.

It is not so in deprivation and state. Once a thing can naturally possess the state, it cannot lack both alternatives. When a puppy has naturally become capable of seeing, it is said either to possess the state and to be sighted, or to possess the deprivation and to be blind. From the time when nature permits it to possess either one, it will always retain one of the two: either deprivation or state.

[Col. 0276B] Therefore, if in contraries that have an intermediate it is possible for neither contrary to be present in the subject, whereas in deprivation and state, from the time when the subject can naturally retain either, it is impossible for it not to possess one of them, these mediated contraries also differ from the things opposed according to deprivation and state. It was already shown that this opposition differs both from contraries that belong by nature and from those without an intermediate. It was therefore rightly stated that the opposition of deprivation and state differs from those things that are opposed as contraries.

[Col. 0276C] Further, when a subject capable of receiving contraries exists, it is possible for it to change into either one of them, unless one contrary belongs to it naturally, as hot belongs to fire. What is healthy can become sick, what is white can become black, what is diligent can become morally bad, and what is morally bad can become diligent. A morally bad person can be led toward better habits and instruction; if he makes even slight progress and becomes better, then, once he has taken even a small step forward, it is clear that he will either be completely transformed or will make very substantial progress. He will always become more readily disposed toward virtue, or toward whatever improvement he has begun to make. It is therefore likely that he will make further progress, and as this continues, he will be completely restored to the contrary state, unless the process is interrupted by time.

[Col. 0276D] In deprivation and state, however, it is impossible for the change to take place in both directions. Change occurs from state to deprivation, but from deprivation to state it is impossible. Someone who has become blind does not see again; someone who was bald does not again grow hair; and when someone has lost his teeth, the teeth do not grow back.

He again posits another difference between contraries and the opposition called that according to state and deprivation. Contraries can change into one another in alternating succession. What is hot can become cold, and what is cold can again be changed into the quality of heat. The only exceptions, as has been said, are those things in which one of the contraries is naturally inherent; only in such things can no reciprocal change occur.

[Col. 0277A] In things that occur in subjects accidentally and not by nature, however, there is always change into the contrary: a healthy animal body becomes sick, and a sick body again becomes healthy. It is also true that the path from good toward evil always seems easier, and that the change from moral excellence to wickedness is very easy, as is taught by the example from Terence: “From labor, an easy slope toward lust.” Although the passage from the shamefulness of vice to the virtues is difficult, Aristotle nevertheless confirms that it can occur.

For this philosopher holds that the virtues are not kinds of knowledge, as Socrates says, nor are they natural, as the Stoics say, but are teachable and implanted in human minds through a certain habituation in the good. Therefore, if someone is subject to any previous vices, and a better discourse receives him, so that he is adorned by the companionship and conversation of wise people, something will be corrected from the allurements of his former vices. He will cast some of them off and proceed somewhat more freely toward better things.

[Col. 0277B] Thus at first he is less bad, then not bad, and afterward gradually somewhat good. If this kind of improvement occurs very frequently, is not cut short by the brevity of time, and is not hindered by the limit imposed by death, there is no doubt that he may be transformed from the worst condition into a perfect state of virtue through good habits and conversation with the wise.

[Col. 0277C] There is therefore a change from good to evil and again from evil to good, and this occurs among contraries. It does not occur in state and deprivation. There is indeed a change, but only one, which cannot be reversed in any way. He says: “There is change from state to deprivation, but from deprivation to state it is impossible.” He demonstrates this most clearly through examples. Who has ever become sighted after being blind? Who has ever become covered with hair after being bald? Who, after losing his teeth, has had other teeth grow again? Therefore, if reciprocal change occurs among contraries but does not occur in deprivation and state, this opposition differs from the opposition according to contrary qualities.

[Col. 0277D] Whatever things are opposed as affirmation and negation are plainly opposed in none of the ways just mentioned. Only in these cases is it always necessary that one of the two be true and the other false. In contraries, it is not always necessary that one be true and the other false; nor is it so in relatives or in state and deprivation. Health and sickness, for example, are contraries, and neither is true or false. Double and half are opposed as relatives, and neither of them is true or false. The same applies to the things said according to deprivation and state, such as sight and blindness.

In general, none of the things expressed without any combination is either true or false; yet the things just mentioned are expressed without combination.

Having explained the differences by which relatives differ from contraries, deprivation and state from relatives, and deprivation and state from contraries, we must now consider how the things opposed according to affirmation and negation differ from all of these. Aristotle gives a distinctive sign of affirmation and negation, so that we may always recognize them and say that anything not possessing this sign differs from the opposition of affirmation and negation.

[Col. 0278A] In affirmation and negation, negation cannot fail to occur in this way: if the affirmation is true, the negation must immediately be false; and if the negation is true, the affirmation cannot escape the mark of falsehood. Thus, if someone says, “Socrates is walking,” and it is true that Socrates is walking, it is false that he is not walking. Conversely, if it is true that he is not walking, it is false that he is walking.

[Col. 0278B] No one can find this division between truth and falsehood in the other oppositions. In relatives, not only is it unnecessary for the opposition itself to divide between truth and falsehood, but no truth or falsehood at all is found in them. If someone says simply “father,” or again “son,” he asserts neither something true nor something false.

The same applies to contraries. Good is contrary to evil, but if someone names “good,” or simply pronounces “evil,” there is neither falsehood nor truth in the predication. The same is true of things according to state and deprivation. If someone names sight or blindness, neither is true or false.

This occurs because everything in which truth or falsehood is found is expressed with some combination. Things uttered simply lack the expression of truth and falsehood. Aristotle himself says this when, at the beginning, he enumerates all the categories: each of the things expressed in isolation is not stated in any affirmation, but truth and falsehood arise through a certain combination of these categories. Aristotle teaches that outside some combination it is impossible for truth or falsehood to be found in speech.

[Col. 0278C] The point is also clear from an example. If I say, “Socrates is a human being,” the statement is either true or false. But if I say only “Socrates,” or again only “human being,” there is neither truth nor falsehood in it. Since every affirmation is uttered with a combination, truth or falsehood can be found in it. Relatives, however, are spoken simply and without any combination. The same applies to contraries and to the things opposed according to state and deprivation, such as father and son, good and evil, sight and blindness. Since these are spoken without combination—and where there is no combination, there is neither falsehood nor truth, whereas truth or falsehood is found only in affirmations and negations expressed with combination—the opposition according to affirmation and negation differs from all the other kinds described above.

[Col. 0278D] This may seem especially to occur in contraries expressed with combination. “Socrates is healthy” is contrary to “Socrates is sick.” But even in these cases it is not necessary that one always be true and the other false. When Socrates exists, one is true and the other false; but when he does not exist, both are false, for when Socrates does not exist at all, neither “he is sick” nor “he is healthy” is true.

[Col. 0279A] In deprivation and state, when the subject does not exist, neither is true; but when it does exist, it is not always the case that one is true and the other false. Possessing sight is opposed to being blind, just as state is opposed to deprivation. When Socrates exists, it is not necessary that one of these be true and the other false. When he has not yet been naturally constituted to possess sight, both are false; and when Socrates does not exist at all, both are likewise false, both “he possesses sight” and “he is blind.”

[Col. 0279B] Since certain contraries appear to be expressed with combination, and since truth or falsehood is found in them even though they are neither affirmation nor negation, Aristotle also explains how they differ from the combinations expressed according to affirmation and negation. Just as sickness is contrary to health, so “Socrates is sick” is contrary to “Socrates is healthy.” The sentence “Socrates is healthy” is also contrary to the sentence “Socrates is sick.” Truth and falsehood are therefore found in these.

[Col. 0279C] They differ from the opposition according to the force of affirmation and negation in the following respect: when the thing of which both are predicated exists, one or the other is true, provided that the contraries being predicated have no intermediate. Since sickness and health are immediate contraries, if Socrates is alive and exists, and one person says, “Socrates is healthy,” while another says, “Socrates is sick,” one must be true and the other false. A living Socrates is either sick or healthy. If it is true that he is sick, it is false that he is healthy; and if it is false that he is sick, it is true that he is healthy.

But if Socrates does not exist or does not exist at all, both statements are false, namely that he is sick and that he is healthy. One who does not exist at all can be neither sick nor healthy. Thus, among contraries, when the thing of which they are predicated exists, one predication is always true and the other false—namely, among those contraries that are expressed with combination and have no intermediate. When the thing does not exist, both contraries are false.

[Col. 0279D] The things said according to deprivation and state, however, even when predicated with combination and when the subject exists, do not necessarily have one true and the other false; and when the subject does not exist at all, both are false. For Socrates, while still in his mother’s womb and not yet born into the light, does not appear in the world, but he exists and lives. At that time he is neither sighted nor blind. He is not sighted because he has not yet been born into the light, but he is not called blind because he was not yet able to see.

[Col. 0280A] Thus, when the thing of which state and deprivation are predicated exists and subsists, it can happen that both predicates are false of it. If the thing of which they are predicated does not exist, both must be entirely false. When Socrates does not exist at all, it is false to say either that he is sighted or that he is blind. The person who sees and is blind is one who lives and subsists; but when the subject of the statement does not exist at all, both predicates are falsely asserted of it.

The same applies to puppies. Once they have been born, they do indeed exist, but they are neither blind nor sighted, because they cannot yet naturally possess sight. If they do not exist at all, it is again false to predicate either of these of them. In affirmation and negation, however, the situation is not the same, as Aristotle himself states.

[Col. 0280B] In affirmation and negation, whether the subject exists or does not exist, one of the two will always be true and the other false. If Socrates exists, it is clear that one of “Socrates is sick” and “Socrates is not sick” is true and the other false. The same applies when he does not exist: “Socrates is sick” is false, whereas “Socrates is not sick” is true. Only in these cases, therefore, is it proper that one of the two always be true and the other false—namely, in whatever things are opposed as affirmation and negation.

In affirmation and negation, he says, whether the subject matter subsists or does not exist at all, one is always found to be true and the other false. For it is clearly shown that saying that someone is ill is not the same as saying that he is not healthy, nor is being blind the same as not seeing. For someone who is ill cannot be ill unless he subsists. But “not being healthy” is different: even if someone does not exist at all, this negation can be predicated of him. For what does not exist at all cannot be healthy; and what cannot be healthy is certainly not healthy. The same applies to blindness and sight. For saying that someone is blind is not the same as saying that he does not see: someone who is blind subsists and lives in order to be blind, whereas “not seeing” can also be said of something that does not subsist at all. For what does not subsist at all cannot see, and what cannot see does not see. Therefore, in affirmation and negation, whether the subject of the statement exists or does not exist, one is always true and the other false. For when Socrates exists and is alive, if it is true to say of him that he sees, it is false to say that he does not see; and if it is true to say of him that he is healthy, it is false to say of him that he is not healthy. If the negations are true, the affirmations are false. But if the subject matter does not subsist at all, the affirmation concerning it is false, while the negation is always true. In our own time, when Socrates does not exist and does not subsist, if one person says, “Socrates sees,” and another says, “Socrates does not see,” it is false to say of him that he sees, but true to say that he does not see. For what does not exist at all cannot see, and what cannot see does not see. Thus it remains firm and unalterable that in affirmations and negations one of the two is always constituted true and the other false in predication.

Consequently, since in contraries and in things belonging to possession and privation, when both are predicated with a complex statement of something that does not subsist, both predicates are false, whereas this is not so in affirmations and negations, all the other oppositions differ from affirmation and negation. Four oppositions and six differences have therefore been exhibited: first, that between contraries and relatives; second, that between contraries and things belonging to possession and privation; third, that between contraries and the opposition according to affirmation and negation; fourth, that between relatives and the opposition according to possession and privation; fifth, that between relatives and the opposition according to affirmation and negation; sixth, that between privation and possession, on the one hand, and negation and affirmation, on the other. After these distinctions among oppositions, Aristotle transmits certain discussions concerning contraries that are useful for many questions.

A contrary to the good is necessarily the bad; this is evident through induction from individual cases, such as illness to health, injustice to justice, and cowardice to courage, and likewise in other cases. But to the bad, sometimes the good is contrary and sometimes the bad. For to poverty, which is bad, abundance is contrary, although abundance itself is also bad. Likewise, moderation, since it is contrary to both extremes, is good. But one will find something of this kind in only a few cases; in most cases the good is always contrary to the bad.

Here it is shown that every good is always contrary to a bad, but not every bad always contrary to a good. For whatever is good has only the bad as its contrary; but to a bad thing, both a good and a bad thing can be contrary. To health, which is good, illness, which is bad, is contrary. Again, to happiness, which is good, unhappiness, which is also bad, is contrary. Yet one can find a bad thing that has two contraries, namely a good and another bad. Since contraries are those things that are farthest apart from one another, cowardice, being the worst disposition of the soul, has two contraries: rashness and courage. For the person who fears everything and is cowardly, and the person who fears absolutely nothing, in whom there is rashness, are far apart and differ from one another; consequently they are contraries, although both are bad. Again, since the good is contrary to the bad, and courage is good, cowardice will be bad, and cowardice will be opposed and contrary to courage. Thus two contraries are opposed to cowardice: rashness and courage. Rashness is contrary to it according to the greatest distance and degree of divergence between contrary dispositions. Cowardice, however, appears opposed to courage according to the quality of goodness and badness. It has therefore been sufficiently demonstrated that good things are always contrary to bad things, while bad things may also be contrary to bad things.

Induction is the collection of individual examples and the reduction of these, through knowledge and collection, to a universal conclusion. For example, if someone says that whoever knows music is a musician and is named from it, and that whoever knows medicine is a physician, and again whoever knows grammar is a grammarian, and from these individual cases gathers universally that whoever knows some art is designated by the name of that art—such as “grammarian” from grammar and “physician” from medicine—and so forth. Accordingly, Aristotle established what we said above concerning contraries by a very clear induction from examples. He also added that bad things can be contrary to bad things, though this is found in very few cases, whereas bad things are always contrary to good things. For even in those cases where bad things are contrary to bad things, they are nevertheless also contrary to good things: thus cowardice, because it is contrary to rashness, is at the same time contrary to courage. But it is not necessary that whatever bad thing is contrary to a good thing should immediately also be contrary to a bad thing. Illness, for example, is contrary to health, which is good, but it is not contrary to another bad thing. It was therefore rightly said that a bad thing is found to be contrary to a bad thing in fewer cases.

Furthermore, it is not necessary that if one contrary exists, the other must also exist. If everyone is healthy, health will exist, but illness will not. Likewise, if everyone is white, whiteness will exist, but blackness will not. Moreover, if being healthy is contrary to Socrates’ being ill, and it is impossible for both to belong to the same thing at the same time, it will not be possible that, when one contrary exists, the other should also exist. For when Socrates is healthy, he will not be ill.

It was said in the discussion of relatives that some relatives naturally exist simultaneously: when there is a son, there is a father, and when there is a father, he cannot exist without a son. Therefore father and son always exist simultaneously. This, however, is not the case with contraries. For he says that contraries do not necessarily always exist simultaneously. If no one is ill and everyone is healthy, health will exist but illness will not; while one contrary remains, the other may be entirely absent. Thus, if someone says the same thing about swans—since all swans are white—blackness will not exist among swans. The same point must also be referred to universals. For if all things that exist are white, blackness will not exist at all.

This seems to have been derived separately from particular cases. Two contraries cannot exist in the same thing at the same time: when Socrates is healthy, he is not ill; and while health remains, illness cannot exist. Nor is it necessary that, once one contrary has been posited, the other immediately follow. For if it were necessary that, once one contrary had been established, the other should immediately follow, the same Socrates could at one and the same time be both healthy and ill, which cannot happen. It is therefore not necessary that, when one contrary exists, another should immediately follow. Consequently, it can happen that, while one contrary exists, the other does not. This is also necessary in individual cases: in the case of Socrates’ being healthy, Socrates is not ill, and his being ill is contrary to Socrates’ health. For although Socrates is receptive of contraries, since he is a substance, he does not receive both contraries at one and the same time.

It is also clear that contraries naturally come to be concerning the same thing, either in species or in genus. Illness and health naturally occur in the body of an animal; whiteness and blackness occur simply in a body; and justice and injustice occur in the soul of a human being.

He teaches the things concerning which contraries can always exist. For he says that they occur concerning things that are either the same in genus or the same in species. Thus a body is one according to genus in the case of animals, since all animals have one genus, and illness or health is found concerning this body. Likewise, whiteness and blackness occur concerning every body without distinction, whether animal or inanimate, because every body itself is one according to genus; for their genus is substance. Justice and injustice are found in the soul. Every soul that receives justice and injustice is rational—that is, human. But all human beings are the same according to species; therefore all human souls are the same according to species, and justice and injustice are found concerning the same things according to species. Consequently, it has now been rightly concluded that all contraries are found concerning the same things either according to genus or according to species.

[Col. 0283B] It is necessary that all contraries either belong to the same genus, belong to contrary genera, or themselves be genera. White and black belong to the same genus, for color is their genus. Justice and injustice belong to contrary genera: the genus of the former is virtue, while that of the latter is vice. But good and bad do not belong to a genus; rather, they themselves are genera of certain things.

He shows the remaining point, namely where contraries can always be investigated. For all things that are contrary either belong under the same genus, belong under contrary genera, or themselves are genera. Contraries belong under the same genus, as white and black belong under one genus, namely color; for color is the genus of whiteness and blackness. These therefore belong under one genus. Other contraries are found under contrary genera, such as justice and injustice. The genus of justice is good, while that of injustice is bad; and bad is contrary to good. Justice and injustice therefore belong under contrary genera. Again, other things are themselves genera, such as good and bad. Both are genera of the good and bad things placed under them. This is not now said to mean that goodness and badness are subordinate to no other genus, for they are placed under quality. Rather, particular good and bad things have no other genera except good and bad in the general sense. Good and bad have therefore rightly been counted as the genera of other particular good and bad things. It was consequently stated most correctly that all contraries either belong under the same genus, as white and black belong under color; or under contrary genera, as justice and injustice belong under good and bad; or themselves are genera, as good and bad themselves are counted as the genera of justice and injustice.

## ON THE MODES OF “PRIOR”

One thing is called prior to another in four ways. First and most properly, according to time: one thing is called older and more ancient than another insofar as it has greater temporal duration and is earlier.

After explaining the discussion of opposites insofar as it concerned the present subject, he now discusses what can be called prior and posterior. He says that the first and proper sense, and the sense in which we ordinarily use “prior,” is when one thing precedes and surpasses another in time. When we speak properly according to temporal precedence, we call one thing more ancient and another older.

According to Porphyry, “more ancient” is used of inanimate things, whereas “older” is used of things that are not without life. Thus one might say that the war of the Thebans and Greeks was earlier than the destruction of Troy because it preceded it in time. For the sons of the leaders who perished in the Theban battle took part in the battles at Troy, such as Diomedes, son of Tydeus, and Sthenelus, son of Capaneus. This is so because even among inanimate things there is something called more ancient, as when we say that the rule of kings in the Roman state is more ancient than that of consuls and magistrates. Among living things, however, we use “older.” We say that Pythagoras is older than Socrates and Socrates older than Aristotle, because each precedes the other in time.

Thus one thing is properly called prior to another according to time. There were four differences of priority, as Aristotle himself says when he states: “One thing is called prior to another in four ways.” He briefly enumerates these individually, and added to them a fifth, which was unknown to the ancient philosophers. Since the first mode of priority has been discussed, let us speak of the second.

Second, one thing is prior when the consequence of its subsistence is not convertible, as one is prior to two. When two exist, it immediately follows that one exists; but when one exists, it does not necessarily follow that two exist. The consequence from one to the other therefore is not convertible: that from which the consequence of being is not convertible appears to be prior.

The second meaning of “prior,” he says, is understood not according to time but according to nature; and he says that it is that from which the consequence of subsistence is not convertible. For if two things are opposed in such a way that, if one exists, the other must exist, but if the other exists, the first need not exist, then that thing is prior which, once posited as existing, does not make it necessary that the other exist. This has been stated universally, but examples will make it clearer.

The number two and unity have this nature: if someone posits that two exists, he will also have shown that one exists, for one is included in two, and the number two cannot exist apart from two units. Consequently, if someone posits that the number two exists, it follows that one exists; thus, for two to exist, it needs unity. But if someone posits that unity exists, it is not yet necessary that two exist. The consequence of subsistence therefore is not convertible from unity. For when unity is posited, the quantity of the number two did not necessarily follow, because unity does not need two, whereas two needed unity. Unity is therefore prior to two.

If this is so, then whatever has the property that the consequence of subsistence is not convertible from it will be shown to be prior, on Aristotle’s authority, as in the case of human being and animal. When I say “human being,” I have immediately also said “animal”; but when I say “animal,” nothing has yet been said about human being. Every human being is an animal, but not every animal is a human being.

[Col. 0285A] Third, one thing is called prior according to a certain order, as in disciplines and in speeches. In demonstrative disciplines there is a prior and a posterior according to order: the elements in geometry are prior to the figures described from them, in their proper order. Principles are prior to theorems according to order, and in grammar the elements are prior to syllables; likewise in speeches the proem is prior to the narration according to order.

He gives a third meaning of “prior”: in geometry, he says, the elements are prior to the constructions. By “elements” he means what we call definitions, in which it is stated what a point is, what a line is, and what a figure is. Once these have been understood and firmly grasped by the mind, all the constructions of geometry are subsequently made; these are called problems and theorems. Since the elements are learned first and the transition to constructions occurs afterward, the elements are prior to the constructions according to order. For in order that a construction may be understood, the elements are taught first. In grammar too, the individual letters are taught before the syllables formed from them are joined together; consequently, in that same order, they are prior to syllables.

Orators, however, do not usually begin their cases with the narration, but with the exordium, because exordia are prior to narrations according to order. This, then, is the third mode of priority: that which is established according to the sequence of a certain order in any art.

Furthermore, apart from the senses already stated, what is better and more honorable appears naturally to be prior. People commonly call those whom they honor more highly and love more dearly “prior” in their own estimation. But this mode is almost entirely foreign to the ordinary meaning of priority. These, then, are approximately the modes of priority that have been mentioned.

He says that what is prior may appear to be something that is prior neither according to time, nor according to the consequence of subsistence, nor according to order, but simply because it is more valuable. Thus the sun appears prior to the moon, the soul to the body, and the intellect to the soul. He proves this by the fact that those who venerate certain persons and regard them as more honorable say that such persons are prior in their estimation; and those who have the greatest power in public affairs are called “prior” by those who venerate them most. But, as he himself says, this fourth mode just mentioned is the most foreign to the meaning of priority. It would be better to call such persons venerable and honorable; calling them “prior” is rather an abuse of language than a proper usage.

The fifth mode, which he himself added, is as follows.

It appears that, besides those already mentioned, there is another mode of priority. Among things whose consequence according to essence is convertible, that which is in any way the cause of the other is rightly called prior by nature. That there are things of this kind is clear. “Being a human being” is convertible, according to the consequence of essence, with a true statement about it. For if a human being exists, the statement “a human being exists” is true; and if the statement “a human being exists” is true, it follows that a human being exists. A true statement, however, is in no way the cause of the thing’s subsistence; nevertheless, the thing appears in some way to be the cause that the statement is true. For from the fact that the thing exists or does not exist, it is necessary that the statement be called true or false. Therefore, according to five modes, one thing is called prior to another.

We know that certain things can be converted in predication. If, among things that are convertible, one is the cause of the other and supplies, as it were, its natural subsistence, that thing is said to be naturally prior. He affirmed what he had proposed by a most suitable example. For if some thing exists, it is true to say of it that it exists. Again, if it is true to say of it that it exists, that very thing must exist—as, since a human being exists, it is true to say that a human being exists. And if it is true to say that a human being exists, there is no doubt that a human being exists.

Since these two are convertible with one another, let us now consider which of them is the cause of the other, so that the other may subsist and be able to exist. I see that the thing gives the true statement the beginning of its subsistence. Because a human being exists, it is true to say of him that he exists; but a human being does not exist because it can truly be said of him that he exists. The thing is the beginning of the statement insofar as truth is present, but a true statement does not make the thing subsist. Therefore it is prior that the human being exist, and posterior that something true be said of him.

Thus, although these things are convertible, one of them is nevertheless the cause of the other’s subsistence. For he says that, among things whose consequence according to essence is convertible, that is prior which is in any way the cause of the other. In this very statement concerning a human being, both are convertible, but the human being is the cause and beginning of the statement’s being true.

Aristotle puts it this way: “A true statement is in no way the cause of the thing’s subsistence. But the thing appears in some way to be the cause that the statement is true.” For the thing does not exist because the statement exists; rather, the statement is true because the thing itself subsists. Thus these are the five modes of priority. The first four mentioned above are: according to time; according to that from which the consequence of subsistence is not convertible; according to order; according to reverence; and according to conversion, when one thing is the cause of another’s subsistence. But since priority has now been discussed, he begins to speak of things that exist simultaneously.

## ON THE MODES OF “SIMULTANEOUS”

Things are called simultaneous simply and properly when their generation occurs at the same time; neither is prior or posterior to the other. They are therefore called simultaneous according to time.

When he was discussing prior things, he maintained that those are properly prior which are spoken of according to the force of temporal precedence. Therefore, when he discusses things that are simultaneous, he recalls the same point, and rightly so. For if time alone produces the greatest mode of priority, why should time not also produce a nature that is simultaneous? He therefore says that those things are called simultaneous both simply and properly which are brought forth in the origin of one and the same time. Just as those things are older and prior which are brought forth at an earlier time rather than at an equal time, those that do not precede one another in time are most correctly held to be simultaneous.

Things brought forth and produced at one time are called simultaneous according to time: that is, they have received their natural beginning and substance simultaneously. These, then, are called simultaneous according to time.

According to nature, however, things are said to be simultaneous whenever they are mutually convertible, with neither thing being the cause or principle of the other’s subsistence. Such are double and half: when something is double, it is half; and when it is half, it is double. Slave and master are likewise related, as are son and father. All such things, when one is posited, posit the other, and when one is removed, remove the other; they are always mutually convertible. For if I say “father,” it is necessary that “son” also be understood; if I say “son,” “father” immediately falls under consideration. If I remove one, I destroy both: if I remove son, there is no father; if I remove father, the son must also perish.

These are mutually convertible in such a way, nevertheless, that neither thing is in any way the cause of the other. For it is clear that father is convertible with son in predication, but the father is not the cause of the son’s existence, nor the son of the father’s. The point is as follows. If Aeneas had Ascanius as a son, we do not say that Aeneas was not the cause of Ascanius’ existence; rather, he was not the cause of his being a son. “Ascanius” denotes a particular substance; “son” cannot exist unless it is referred to something. When I name Aeneas, I have stated a substance; when I call him “father,” the expression has no meaning unless it is referred to a son. Thus Aeneas was the cause that Ascanius existed, but the father is not the cause that the son existed. For he becomes a father only when a son has come to be.

If these are not prior to one another in time, but the cause of anything is prior to that of which it is the cause, so that it may arise, there is no doubt that father and son—whose predications are equal in time—are mutually not causes, although the substances themselves are causes of their respective predications.

Nor should this be considered similar to what was said shortly before concerning a human being, namely that a true statement about him exists because he exists. There, when the thing existed, a true statement about it could then exist. It is prior that something exist, and afterward that something true be said about it. Here, however, it is not the case that one is first a father and afterward a son. As soon as there is a father, it is necessary that there be a son; as soon as there is a son, the predication “father” undoubtedly follows. Aristotle explains how this mode is simultaneous according to nature as follows:

Naturally simultaneous are those things whose consequence according to being is convertible, but neither is the cause of the other’s existence, as in the case of double and half. These are convertible: when something is double, it is half, and when something is half, it is double; but neither is the cause of the other’s existence.

Among those things that were said to be prior because they were convertible, although their consequence according to essence was convertible, one thing nevertheless appeared to be prior because one thing was the cause and principle of the other. This differs from things that are convertible and remove one another: since neither is the cause of the other, yet they are convertible, they are rightly said to be naturally simultaneous.

Things are also called naturally simultaneous when they are divided from one another in different directions out of the same genus. Those are divided in different directions which belong to the same division, such as walking, flying, and swimming. These are divided in different directions from the same genus according to one division: animal is divided into flying, walking, and swimming. None of these is prior or posterior to the others; rather, they appear to be simultaneous by nature.

He added this as a third mode of things that are simultaneous: those things are also simultaneous which are placed under a genus by an equal division. Thus, if someone posits animal as the genus of human being and horse, and divides human being and horse from the genus—that is, from animal—then human being and horse, because they belong under the same genus, are said to be simultaneous by nature.

The rule is appropriate in all genera. Whenever divisions of species are made, the species are naturally simultaneous; and if certain other things are placed under those species themselves, those things too are said to be naturally simultaneous with one another. Let animal, the genus, be divided into flying and walking; since these belong under the same genus, they are naturally simultaneous. If either of these is resolved into subordinate parts and species—for example, flying into birds that feed on seeds, those that feed on flesh, and those that feed on plants—these three species, which belong under flying, are again called naturally simultaneous. Aristotle puts it this way:

Each of these is again divided into species, such as walking animal, flying animal, and swimming animal. Those things, therefore, will also be naturally simultaneous that are from the same genus according to the same division. Genera, however, are always prior to species, for they are not convertible according to the consequence of being. When something is aquatic, it is an animal; but when something is an animal, it is not necessary that it be aquatic. Those things are therefore called naturally simultaneous which are convertible according to the consequence of being, but neither is the cause of the other’s existence; those which are divided from one another in different directions from the same genus; and, simply, those whose generation occurs at the same time.

For this reason it is impossible for a genus to have only one species. For if whatever belongs under a genus is simultaneous, and things cannot be simultaneous unless they are more than one, a genus cannot have one species under it. If there were only one, it could not be called simultaneous, since the point is that under the same genus certain things are ordinarily found that are naturally simultaneous. But this concerns species.

Genera, however, are always prior, for they are not convertible according to the consequence of subsistence. One mode of priority is that according to which those things are said to be prior whose subsistence is in no way convertible; this applies to genera as well. Genera are not convertible according to the consequence of subsistence in the following way. Let animal be a genus and human being a species. When I say that a human being exists, it follows that an animal exists. But if I say that an animal exists, the consequence of subsistence does not convert to human being. An animal can exist without being a human being. Therefore the consequence of subsistence is not convertible from animal to human being. Since, when human being is posited, animal is assured, but when animal is named, it is not necessary that human being exist, animal is prior to human being.

There is also this description of prior things: when removed, prior things remove other things with them, but when posited, they do not immediately posit them. When animal is removed, it also removes human being; but when animal is posited by saying that an animal exists, it does not immediately posit human being with it. Posterior things are the reverse. When posited, they immediately posit other things; when removed, they do not remove them. “Human being,” when stated, immediately brings animal with it, for every human being is an animal. But if human being is removed substantially, it is not necessary that animal also be removed, because the term “animal” can apply to several species. If this is so, animal will remain after human being has been removed.

He therefore concludes that there are three kinds of things that are simultaneous: those that are simultaneous according to time; those that are simultaneous according to nature, when both are convertible in such a way that neither is the cause of the other; and, third, those that belong to the same division under the same genus.

Since there was a certain motion involved in doing and undergoing, and he had added “doing” and “undergoing” to the categories, he now treats motions and declares that there are six in number.

## ON THE SPECIES OF MOTION

There are six species of motion: generation, destruction, increase, diminution, alteration, and change of place. It is clear that these motions are distinct from one another. Generation is not destruction, increase is not diminution, and change of place is not any of these. The same applies to the others.

In the *Physics*, Aristotle divided the species of motion in another way. He says that permutation is one thing and motion another, and that permutation has two species, generation and destruction. Motion, however, has three species: according to quantity, according to quality, and according to place.

Since this book was composed in a certain way as an introduction, he did not wish to make the account of division too subtle, lest he confuse the minds of beginners with a more refined division. He therefore divides motion in this way. One species of motion is according to substance, another according to quantity, another according to quality, and another according to place.

According to substance there are generation and destruction, for both occur in substance. Something is generated according to substance, and something is destroyed according to substance. According to quantity there are increase and diminution. For things are said to have increased when they have become greater in quantity, and to have diminished when something has been taken away from them. According to quality there is what is called alteration, namely alteration according to certain affections, which are clearly qualities. According to place there is movement in a straight line or a bending in a curve: movement in a straight line is, for example, from above downward, from the front backward, or from right to left. Conversely, if these directions are reversed and one proceeds straight ahead, the motions are the same.

It is also true that these are all the species of motion. They have nothing in common with one another except the name of their genus, since they are called motions. Generation is not the same as destruction: generation is an entrance into substance, while destruction is an exit from substance. Diminution is not the same as increase, nor is movement according to place similar to any of the preceding motions. Alteration, however, may perhaps raise a question, since it does not appear to differ from the preceding motions. He therefore proposes the question as follows.

In alteration there is a certain question: perhaps it is necessary that what is altered should be altered through one of the remaining motions. But this is not true. For it happens that something is altered according to almost all, or at least many, affections without any of the other motions participating. What is moved through an affection need not be increased, nor need it be diminished. The same applies to the others. Alteration will therefore be a motion distinct from those others. For if it were the same, what is altered would immediately have to increase or diminish, or undergo one of the other motions; but this is not necessary. Likewise, what increases, or moves through some other motion, would have to be altered.

In alteration there is another question: perhaps what is altered must be altered according to one of the remaining motions. For if everything that is altered is either generated, destroyed, diminished, increased, or necessarily moved according to place, there would be no doubt that the species called alteration differs in no respect from the preceding species. Aristotle rejects this by saying, “But this is not true.”

For what is altered is not necessarily generated or destroyed in every case. Someone who has stood in the sun for a long time, for example, becomes black from being white; he is said to have been altered according to color, but he has not been generated or destroyed. Nor has he undergone either increase or diminution, nor has he changed place. Someone can remain in one and the same place while being altered by affections coming from outside. Someone can also increase or decrease without undergoing alteration of quality. Aristotle expresses the point as follows:

But there are certain things that increase without being altered, such as a square: when a gnomon is placed around it, it increases, but nothing in it is altered. The same applies in other cases of this kind. Therefore the motions are distinct from one another.

What he says is this: “If,” he says, “a gnomon is added to a square, the square grows, but is not altered. Therefore, when the gnomon is removed, the square is diminished, but is not altered.”

Let the square be *a b c d*, and let its diagonal *b c* be drawn. Let its four sides—*a c, a b, b d, a c*—be divided into equal sections at the points *g, e, h, f*, and let the lines *g h* and *f e* be drawn. The square *a d* is thus divided into four squares, namely *e g, f g, e h,* and *h f*. When any three of these that lie around the same diagonal are removed, the resulting figure is called a gnomon. Thus, if one removes these three—*e g, g f,* and *f h*—the gnomon *m n* is found [Col. 0291A]; this gnomon *m n* is separated from the square *a b e h*. The whole square *a d* has indeed been diminished, having been made smaller from so large a size, but it has not altered the form of a tetragon. If, however, the tetragon *e h* alone is present and a gnomon, namely *m n*, is placed around it, the tetragon has grown and become larger, but has not been altered. For all tetragons are alike in their proper quality.

If alteration were a kind of motion not wholly distinct from the preceding kinds, there would be no doubt that whatever is altered would always have to be altered according to one of the modes of the earlier motions: it would either be generated, corrupted, diminished, increased, or undergo some change according to place. Since this is not the case, this kind of motion differs from all the preceding [Col. 0291B] kinds of motion. But it was shown above that the five preceding kinds of motion differ in every respect from substance itself. Consequently, these six kinds of motion likewise differ from one another and are distinct.

[Col. 0291C]

In general, rest is contrary to motion. In the individual cases, each motion has its own contrary: corruption is contrary to generation, diminution to increase; and, in the case of place, rest according to place is contrary to change according to place. More particularly, however, change into the contrary place seems to be opposite: for example, downward movement is opposite to upward movement, and upward movement to downward movement.

He now explains the contraries of motions. To the genus itself—that is, to motion—he says that rest is contrary, for motion has rest as its contrary. But the motions themselves are contrary to one another in the individual species of motion: corruption is contrary to generation, although both generation and corruption are motions; likewise, diminution is contrary to increase. Thus these species possess contrariety in a different way from that in which we previously showed that the genus possesses it. Motion itself has rest as its contrary. But among the motions of the species, not only rest but also other motions are contrary: corruption is contrary to generation, and diminution to increase. In the case of movement according to place, however, the contrariety is similar to that of the genus. For movement according to place likewise has rest according to place as its contrary: to move from place to place is contrary to not moving, and not moving according to place is rest, while moving according to place is transport or locomotion. More particularly, he says, movement into the contrary place is contrary to change according to place.

Suppose that something is above and remains there at rest, and afterward undergoes a motion by which it moves downward. Although rest is contrary to the earlier upward motion, a motion of this kind, which proceeds into the contrary place, is much more contrary to that upward motion. The same thing occurs in the other motions: if something is on the right and moves toward the left, its motion is said to have been made into the contrary place. The same may be observed in the other motions as well. But Aristotle doubts whether anything can be contrary to the remaining motion—that is, alteration—and he proposes the question as follows:

[Col. 0292B] “It is not easy to assign what is contrary to the remaining one of the motions listed. It seems, however, that nothing is contrary to it, unless someone also opposes rest according to quality in this case, or change into the contrary quality, just as, in the case of change according to place, rest according to place—or change into the contrary place—is opposed to it. For alteration is change according to quality.”

From the analogy of the motions we also infer their contraries. Since he found rest according to place to be contrary to motion according to place, and since every alteration that occurs according to some affection is an alteration according to quality, he posited rest according to quality as the contrary of this motion.
