Thus, if a stone is cold and remains so, that quality has remained and is at rest; but if it becomes warm, that quality has been altered, and the alteration itself is contrary, since a motion has occurred and a change according to quality has taken place in the stone’s warmth, whereas in its coldness there had been rest according to the same quality.

Consequently, although this motion may seem to have no contrary at all, just as it was said above that rest according to place is contrary to transport according to place, why should rest according to quality not also be said to be contrary to alteration according to quality? For the definition of alteration is transport according to quality: whenever the quality of anything is moved, a transport takes place—that is, according to quality.

If, however, transport according to place seems to have as its contrary not only rest according to place but also transport into the contrary place, then alteration according to quality will likewise have as its contrary not only rest according to quality but, above all, alteration into the contrary quality. Thus, if something is white and becomes red, the alteration itself, by which it changes from white into red, is contrary to the rest that could have continued in the white color. For if something changes from white into black, it undergoes the greatest alteration, and this is contrary to the preceding alteration, because it has been changed into the contrary quality. This is what he says:

[Col. 0293A] “Therefore, rest according to quality will be opposed to alteration according to quality, or alteration into the contrary quality will be opposed to alteration according to quality—for becoming white is opposed to becoming black, since it is altered when the change into the contrary quality takes place.”

This too is made clear by the most evident example. Since the matter of motions has now been explained, let us expound the equivocation of *having* that follows.

## On the Various Modes of Having

“Having” is said in many ways. It may mean a habit or disposition, or any other quality: we are said to have some learning or virtue. Or it may mean quantity, as in the case of someone who has magnitude; for one is said to have a magnitude of three cubits or four cubits. Or it may mean things situated around the body, such as a garment or tunic. Or it may mean something in a part, as a ring in the hand. Or it may mean a part itself, as a hand or foot. Or it may mean something in a vessel, as wheat in a bushel or wine in a jar; for a jar is said to have wine, and a bushel to have wheat. All these things, therefore, are said to be had as being in a vessel. Or it may mean possession: we are said to have a house or a field. A man is also said to have a wife, and a wife a husband.

But the mode just mentioned seems the most foreign to what is meant by “having.” For by “having a wife” we signify nothing other than that they live together. Perhaps, however, other modes of “having” will also appear. Nearly all the modes customarily mentioned have now been enumerated.

It is clear that the mode of having is equivocal. “Having” is said in so many ways that it is nevertheless predicated equivocally. We are said to have some quality, such as a habit or disposition. We are also said to have knowledge or virtue. We are said to have quantity, since we are said to be five or four feet in measure. Likewise, we are said to have something in the parts of the body, and to have the parts themselves: we are said to have fingers and rings on our fingers. We are also said to have something around the body, such as a tunic or any other garment.

Something is also said to be had in a vessel, such as wheat in a bushel or wine in a jar; these things are said to be had as being in a vessel. Someone is also said to have a wife. This signification, however, is common to none of those mentioned above, but—as Aristotle himself thinks—is altogether different from the category of having. For we do not properly “have” wives; rather, when someone is said to have a wife, this signifies that the wife dwells with him. We use “having” in the sense of dwelling, as in the expression “they have Socrates,” that is, “they dwell with Socrates and honor him.”

Aristotle therefore himself says that there may perhaps be some modes of having beyond those that are customarily stated, and he urges us to undertake a further inquiry, so that we too may ask by what other modes, besides those previously mentioned, “having” may be predicated. Enough, then, has been said about the equivocation of having.

Someone might perhaps wonder why, although he previously named “having” as a genus, he now presents it as equivocal. The question may be resolved as follows. It is not absurd for the same category to be predicated now univocally and now equivocally. It is predicated univocally above, when he proposed examples of the same species, such as being shod or being armed; for having is the genus of things of that sort. It is predicated equivocally in the modes that we have explained above.

If the predication of having also possesses certain proper species, while the very name itself is used in several ways, there is nevertheless nothing incongruous in counting it as a genus. For it is sufficient to demonstrate that the predication of having is a genus if it contains beneath itself certain divisions and species.

[Col. 0293]

# Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius: Two Books on Aristotle’s *On Interpretation* (C)

## First Edition, or Shorter Commentaries

## Book One

[Col. 0293D] This book is acknowledged to possess great authority among the Peripatetic school. In it Aristotle carefully examines the nature of simple propositions, but the difficult path of its exposition is obstructed and, compressed by lofty ideas, does not leave easy access to understanding. Therefore we have supplied an explanation of this book in two commentaries. To the extent that a brief and obscure discourse comprehends the meanings of the propositions for simple minds, we have expanded upon it in this treatment of the work. What requires a deeper acumen of reflection will be clarified in the sequence of the second edition.

For now, let the reader expect from me only that he may gradually and in detail, according to the order of the discourse and the text, understand what is hidden by the narrowness of brevity. First, however, we must briefly demonstrate the purpose of this work. This book is entitled in Greek *Περὶ ἑρμηνείας* (*Peri hermēneias*), which in Latin means *On Interpretation*. I shall explain briefly, therefore, what interpretation is.

Interpretation is a significant utterance signifying something by itself. Whether it is a noun that signifies by itself, as “human”; or a verb, as “I run”; or what grammarians call a participle; or a pronoun; or a sentence joined from these, as “A human runs”; or, in any other way, whether a noun, a verb, or a sentence joined from these signifies something by itself—it is called an interpretation.

Accordingly, although there are certain parts of a sentence that signify nothing by themselves but indicate something when joined to others, such as conjunctions and prepositions, we do not call these interpretations. For an interpretation, whether simple, like a noun or verb, or composite, like a sentence joined and connected from these, must either signify by itself if it is simple, or, if it is composite, must be joined from elements that signify by themselves. Interpretation, therefore, is an utterance signifying something by itself.

[Col. 0295B] Since nouns and verbs are interpretations, every sentence formed from predicative elements that signify by themselves is also called an interpretation. And since there are many interpretations, among which is also the sentence in which truth or falsity can be found—that is, the enunciative sentence, which is to be treated in this book—Aristotle gave the book its title from the common and comprehensive term.

For a noun and a verb are interpretations, and so too is a sentence of the following kind: “Every human is an animal.” But in this sentence the hearer understands truth or falsity. The sentence “Every human is an animal” is true or false. The command “Give me the book” is also an interpretation, but no one can find truth or falsity in it. For “Give me the book” can be neither true nor false.

Since, then, he is going to discuss only those sentences in which truth and falsity are found—sentences that we call enunciations or propositions and that are interpretations—and since he must speak about what nouns and verbs are and what force they retain in signification, he rightly entitled the book *On Interpretation*.

Nor should it disturb us that there are certain interpretations that he does not treat in this book. It is as if someone, while discussing the human being, had given his work the title *On the Animal*: although he would not be discussing every animal, he would nevertheless rightly give the book its name from “animal,” since he was going to discuss some animal. Likewise, although Aristotle does not treat every interpretation, he gives the book its title from the common and general term *On Interpretation*, since he must discuss one interpretation, namely the enunciation, as well as nouns and verbs, which are simple interpretations.

The purpose of this book is to discuss the simple enunciative sentence. A simple enunciative sentence is one in which there is truth or falsity, but in which the whole order of the sentence is proposed without a conjunction, as in: “A human exists,” “A human is an animal,” “A human runs,” “A frightened human runs.” These propositions are proposed without a conjunction, and they are called predicative sentences, since they contain a noun and a verb.

Sentences of the following kind, however—“If the sun is above the earth, it is day”—are called double, hypothetical, and also conditional sentences. They posit that if this is the case, that is the case: if the sun is above the earth, it is day. Such sentences are not simple, for “the sun exists” and “it is day” are two propositions, which the single conjunction “if” joins and combines. No treatment of these, therefore, will be given in this book.

Since he is going to treat simple enunciative sentences—that is, simple affirmation and simple negation—and since affirmations and negations are joined with verbs and nouns, as in the affirmation “A human runs,” where “human” is a noun and “runs” a verb, and again in “A human does not run,” where the negation is joined to the same noun and verb, he is rightly going to discuss first simple affirmation and simple negation, and in general the simple enunciation.

Since every simple enunciation is joined from verbs and nouns, he begins his discussion with nouns and verbs. Once these have first been brought to knowledge, the entire nature of the sentence is most easily revealed. He himself begins his treatment of what must be discussed throughout the book as follows.

## On Signs

“First it is necessary to establish what a noun is and what a verb is; afterward, what negation, affirmation, enunciation, and sentence are.”

He says that at the beginning of this discourse on enunciation it is necessary to establish—that is, define—what a noun is and what a verb is. For, as has been said, these are capable of forming every sentence. The sentence is the genus of other sentences.

There are five principal kinds of sentence. The first is the optative or prayerful sentence, as in: “Almighty Jupiter, if you are moved by any prayers.” The second is the imperative, as in: “Bring me the weapons.” The third is the interrogative, as in: “Where are your feet taking you, Moeris?” The fourth is the vocative, as in: “Come here, O Meliboeus!” The fifth is the enunciative sentence, in which truth or falsity is discerned.

The enunciative sentence has two species: affirmation and negation. Affirmation is, for example, “A human is an animal.” Negation is, “A human is not an animal.” Verbs and nouns, therefore, constitute a sentence. The sentence is the genus of enunciation, and enunciation is the genus of affirmation and negation.

Thus there are certain elements that join together to form a sentence, namely nouns and verbs; Aristotle first discusses these. Then he takes up the final two species of proposition and says that he will discuss affirmation and negation. After these he proposes their genus, enunciation. Finally he treats what is greatest among them, the sentence.

The order has, in a certain way, been reversed: proceeding from the species, he reaches their first genera. By beginning with affirmation and negation and rising to enunciation, which is their genus, he ascends. From enunciation he raises the subject of the work to the genus of enunciation, which is the sentence. Nevertheless, he discusses all these in a different order. First he explains the sentence, then enunciation, then affirmation, and finally the definition of negation—in other words, in reverse order. This will become clear later.

The fact that he proposed negation before affirmation makes no difference, since all the species are equally related to one another and are subordinated equally to one genus. Therefore, if affirmation and negation are species of enunciation, it is proper to propose either one first without distinction. How affirmation and negation are species of enunciation, and how enunciation is their genus, will be shown in the second edition.

There are, therefore, things in speech that are signs of affections in the soul, and things written that are signs of things in speech. And just as letters are not the same for everyone, neither are spoken expressions the same. But the affections of the soul, of which these spoken expressions are the first signs, are the same for everyone; and the things of which these affections are likenesses are likewise the same. These matters have been discussed in the works *On the Soul*. They belong to another inquiry.

Since he is shortly going to propose “significant” in the definitions of noun and verb, he first explains what it is that all significant things signify—that is, what the noun and verb themselves designate.

The whole meaning of the passage is as follows. There are three things from which every conversation and discussion is completed: things, thoughts, and utterances. Things are what we perceive through the reasoning of the mind and distinguish through understanding. Thoughts are what enable us to learn the things themselves. Utterances are what signify what we grasp in thought.

Besides these three there is something else that signifies utterances: letters. For the writing of letters is a signification of utterances. Since there are therefore four things—things, thoughts, utterance, and letter—the thought conceives the thing; utterances designate the thought; and letters signify the utterances themselves.

Thought is an affection of the soul. Unless someone undergoes in the reasoning of the soul a certain likeness of the thing he understands, there is no thought. When I see a circle or a square, I conceive its shape in my mind, and its likeness is formed for me in the reasoning of the soul. The soul undergoes the likeness of the understood thing; hence thought is both a likeness of the thing and an affection of the soul.

Of these four, two are natural and two are established by human convention. Utterances and letters are established by human convention; thoughts and things are natural. This is confirmed by the fact that different peoples use different utterances and letters, because they themselves composed the utterances they would use and the letters with which they would write.

No one established thoughts or things; they exist naturally. What is a horse among the Romans is not a deer among barbarians. Rather, among different peoples the nature of things is the same. Nor do barbarians think that what we understand to be a horse is a dog. The account of substances and thoughts is established identically among peoples who are otherwise most diverse.

Thus two of these four—utterances and letters—are established by human convention, and two—things and thoughts—according to nature.

What he now says is that utterances signify thoughts, while letters signify the utterances themselves. Thoughts are affections of the soul; utterances and letters are not natural. For just as the utterance is not the same among all peoples, neither is the letter. But you will find that thoughts and things are the same among all peoples, however diverse.

This is what he says:

[Col. 0298A] “There are, therefore, things in speech that are signs of affections in the soul.”

That is, he says, the utterances signify thoughts, which are affections of the soul, and they are their significations. The things in speech signify those affections and are their signs. For all understanding and every conception of the mind is signified through them.

When he adds, “and things written are signs of things in speech,” this has the same force as if he had said: “Written letters are signs of the spoken words and nouns.” He has therefore shown that utterances signify thoughts and letters signify utterances. He now discusses their nature, saying:

“Just as letters are not the same for everyone, neither are utterances the same.”

This serves to show that utterances and letters are established by convention, not by nature. For utterances and letters differ among different peoples; and just as the letters are not the same among all people, neither are the utterances. Therefore they are established by convention, a point he passed over as obvious. For what varies among individual peoples is manifestly established not by nature but by convention.

When he adds, “But the affections of the soul of which these are first signs are the same for everyone, and the things of which these are likenesses are likewise the same,” he intends to declare that things and thoughts are natural. For, as has been said, thoughts are affections of the soul and likenesses of things.

He is therefore saying this: The things of which these—that is, the utterances mentioned above—are signs are the same affections of the soul for everyone; and just as the letters are not the same, neither are the utterances. The affections of the soul signified by these utterances are the same for everyone; the utterances signify those affections, namely thoughts. Thought, therefore, is an affection of the soul and is not different among human beings. Thus the conception of the mind and the affection of the soul are natural among all human beings. The things that occur in utterances are their signs.

He also teaches that the things of which thoughts and affections of the soul are likenesses are established not by convention but by nature. For the things of which thoughts are likenesses—and thoughts are affections of the soul—are the same among everyone.

This is what he says:

“And the things of which these are likenesses,” namely, the affections of the soul, which are likenesses of things, “are likewise the same.”

It is as if he had said: The things of which thoughts are likenesses—the thoughts that are affections of the soul—are the same among everyone.

When he says, “of which these are first signs,” he means the following. He is speaking of utterances: the affections of the soul of which utterances are the first signs are the same among everyone. For an utterance signifies both the thought of a thing and the thing itself. When I say “stone,” I designate both the thought of stone and the stone itself, that is, the substance itself. But it signifies the thought first and the thing second.

Thus not everything that an utterance signifies is an affection of the soul, but only what it signifies first. The thought is signified first; the thing second. Thoughts are affections of the soul. Therefore, the affections of the soul of which utterances are first signs are the same among all human beings.

There is also another textual form that reads as follows: “Of which these are first signs, these are affections of the soul for everyone; and the things of which these are likenesses are likewise these things.” If the text is written in this way, it seems to say the following: He shows what the utterances are signs of, and what the affections of the soul in turn are signs of. It is as though he said: The things signified by utterances, of which they are signs, are affections of the soul; and, again, the things of which these affections of the soul are likenesses are things. It is as though he had said once more: The things of which the things present in thoughts and affections of the soul are likenesses are those things.

But he does not wish to prolong the discussion of these matters. For he says:

[Col. 0299B] “These matters have been discussed in the works *On the Soul*. They belong to another inquiry.”

For it is one matter to discuss the thoughts of the soul as the principal subject, and another to take up as much of the subject as may pertain to logical expertise. It therefore belongs to another inquiry to discuss the affections of the soul as the principal subject.

Just as in the soul sometimes there are thoughts without truth or falsity, while sometimes there is a thought in which one of these must necessarily be present, so it is also in speech. Falsity and truth concern combination and division.

Since he is going to speak about the enunciation in which truth and falsity are found, he rightly proposes first to show in what utterance one of these two—that is, either truth or falsity—can be found.

Every utterance signifies something perceived by the mind, and therefore whatever arises from the thoughts of the mind is indicated through utterances. He is therefore now saying this: There is a certain likeness between thoughts and utterances. Just as there are certain simple things that are conceived by the reasoning of the mind and established in the understanding, in which neither truth nor falsity is found, so it is also with utterances.

A simple thought, such as the thought of a human being or a horse, contains neither falsity nor truth. When I understand a human being and the substance itself simply, I retain nothing true or false in my thought. If I then perceive running through a thought of the mind, that thought too—because it retains the apprehension of a simple thing—is removed from truth and falsity.

But when I join a human being and running, and form something from them in my understanding, if I express it in speech it will be of this kind: “A human runs.” Then, from this combination and conjunction of substance and accident, a thought is formed in which there can be either falsity or truth.

Therefore, just as in thought there are sometimes simple things devoid of truth and falsity, and sometimes things in which truth or falsity must necessarily be present, so it is also in speech. If an utterance conveys a simple thought devoid of truth and falsity, the utterance itself is likewise left outside truth and falsity. But if it conveys a thought that contains truth or falsity in itself, it too retains the signification of truth or falsity.

By saying, “Falsity and truth concern combination and division,” he has taught in what utterance we can find enunciations. Whenever we join and combine a substance with an accident, or connect one thought with another so that a proposition can be formed in thought, the same thing takes place in speech.

Thus there is an affirmation, as in “A human runs.” For he has combined and joined “human” and “runs,” and from this an affirmation has arisen that contains truth or falsehood.

There is now a negation if I join the negative adverb “not” to this and divide and separate the substance from the accident, as in “A human does not run.” The word “not,” which is a negative adverb, has divided and separated the human from running, and from this a negation has again been formed, signifying truth or falsity.

It was therefore rightly said that affirmation consists in combination and negation in division, and that the nature of truth and falsity depends upon them [Col. 0300B].

Nouns and verbs themselves are like simple thoughts without combination or division, as “human” or “white,” when nothing is added; for they are neither true nor false.

He now continues, in a connected discussion, to explain what thought is without truth or falsity. Those things that are called simple, he says, are like simple thoughts, which are grasped by the pure apprehension of the soul without any combination or division.

“Human” and “white” are themselves simple and signify something, but they designate neither truth nor falsity. Every simple noun or verb is excluded from truth and falsity.

And therefore, since, as has been said, everything in speech signifies affections of the soul, simple utterances without combination or division are like those thoughts that simple understanding conceives without combination or division. In these and similar cases neither truth nor falsity is found.

Unless something is added—so that you either establish the thing you understand simply as existing in itself, or join something to it according to existence—there will be no truth or falsity. If I simply say “human,” and add nothing, such as the verb “is,” to form “A human is,” or something similar, such as “A human lives,” which has the same force as saying “A living human exists,” no truth or falsity can be understood.

For unless something of this kind is added, either establishing the thing understood as existing in itself—as when I say “A human is,” designating that a human exists in itself—or adding an accident that signifies the same thing as existence, as in “A human lives,” no truth or falsity can be understood. Life has been joined to the human, and “lives” signifies the same as “is living.”

He demonstrates this with a most suitable example.

A sign of this is the following: “Goat-stag” signifies something, but not yet something true or false, unless “is” or “is not” is added, either simply or with reference to time.

The subtlety of this example has great force. It is not only those nouns or verbs that are simple that are separated from falsity and falsehood; even those that are composite, if they are uttered simply, are separated from them.

“Goat-stag” (*hircocervus*) is a composite noun signifying goat and stag. But unless either “is” or “is not” is added, so that we say “A goat-stag is” or “A goat-stag is not,” no thought of truth or falsity can arise from it. Although it is composite, when uttered simply it is not yet related to truth or falsity. If someone says only “goat-stag,” he enunciates nothing. If he enunciates nothing beyond designating a composite noun, the hearer understands only that noun.

When he says “either simply or with reference to time,” he intends to prevent us from thinking that an enunciation is formed only when the present tense is added to the noun. When the present tense is added, as in “A goat-stag is” or “A goat-stag is not,” there is already truth or falsity in these expressions.

But a proposition makes an enunciation not only when it designates the present tense, but also when it designates the past, as in “A goat-stag was,” or the future, as in “A goat-stag will be.”

This, therefore, is what he means by “either simply or with reference to time.” An enunciation formed simply is formed with reference to the present. For what we call the present is not a time but the boundary between times. Time is either future or past.

Truth or falsity cannot therefore be found in the expression “goat-stag” unless “is” or “is not” is added: either the present, which is expressed simply, or a tense, which is past or future. If someone says “A goat-stag is,” he has spoken simply, that is, with reference to the present. But if someone says “A goat-stag will be” or “A goat-stag was,” he has spoken with reference to time, namely the future or the past.

Having prefaced these useful points, he now approaches, in the course of his discussion, the definition of the noun.

## On the Noun

A noun, therefore, is a significant utterance according to convention, without time, no part of which is significant when separated.

Every definition is completed by a genus and differentiating features. Accordingly, he took “voice” as the genus for the definition of the noun. The remaining features that he set out he added as differentiations. The exposition of this term is as follows: “A noun,” he says, “is a voice.” But some voices are significant, while others signify nothing. A noun signifies that of which it is the name. A noun, therefore, is a significant voice. Among significant voices, some are significant by nature and others not by nature. A voice is significant by nature when it naturally indicates such things as pain or joy. Voices that are not significant by nature [Col. 0301D] are those which we say exist by convention. Those exist by convention which human beings have established for themselves, as when someone says: “Let this substance be called gold, this stone, this water,” and similarly in other cases. Such voices, therefore, exist by convention—that is, according to the decision of the people by whom those names were formed. Voices of this kind, which exist by convention, exist according to the decision of those who established them.

But a noun does not signify by nature. For among different peoples the names are different. What is different among different peoples does not exist by nature, but according to the decision of those who established the names, and according to the convention of those who imposed them. Otherwise, if [Col. 0302A] names existed by nature, then just as things that are sweet among the Romans are not bitter or sour among the Scythians, but are sweet among them too and among all peoples in the same way, so all human beings would use the same names if names existed by nature. Since, therefore, names do not exist by nature and do not signify by nature, they exist according to convention—namely, according to the decision of those who established and originated them, and by whom the names themselves were impressed upon things. A noun, therefore, is a significant voice according to convention.

Among significant voices that exist according to convention, some bring time along with their signification, while others are predicated apart from time. Those that bring time along with them include *curro* (“I run”) and *lego* (“I read”), or *cucurri* (“I ran”) and *legi* (“I read”), and all such words are verbs. Every verb is accompanied by time. [Col. 0302B] Nouns, however, are without time. When I say “Socrates,” “Plato,” “whiteness,” or anything of this kind, they lack time. A noun, therefore, is a significant voice according to convention, without time.

Among significant voices that exist according to convention and without time, some have parts that signify something outside themselves, while others have parts that designate nothing outside themselves. The expression “Socrates with Plato and the other disciples,” which is an utterance, is significant and exists according to convention. Its parts, which are nouns, exist according to convention and without time. For there is not even an image of time in it; but it possesses the feature that its parts signify something outside themselves. The whole utterance is “Socrates with Plato and the other disciples”; but its part “Socrates,” if separated from the whole utterance, signifies something. [Col. 0302C] A part of a noun, however, signifies nothing outside itself. For in the noun “Socrates,” whose meaning remains when it is separated from the whole connection, the parts signify nothing outside themselves. Neither *So*, nor *cra*, nor *tes* designates anything outside the whole noun. Therefore the definition has been established with complete correctness: a noun is a voice that designates according to convention, without time, no part of which signifies anything separately. He teaches this through the examples he has proposed.

In the noun *equiferus* (“horse-wild” or “horse-like wild creature”), *ferus* (“wild”) signifies nothing by itself, as it does in the utterance *equus ferus* (“a wild horse”).

For if there is an utterance that says *equus ferus*, it signifies two things: a horse and something wild. One is a substance, the other a quality. But whoever says *equiferus* uses one noun, and there is one subject corresponding to what it signifies; [Col. 0302D] consequently, this combination signifies one thing as well. If the whole combination signifies one thing, then a part separated from it designates nothing outside it. In the whole noun *equiferus*, *ferus* does contribute to the signification, but by itself signifies nothing. If we were to suppose that *ferus*, the word “wild,” signified something by itself, it would no longer be a part of the noun, but would itself be a complete noun, and would have the parts *fe* and *rus*. Since nouns have one subject and the whole noun signifies one thing—whether it is ambiguous or not—for *canis* (“dog”) is ambiguous, yet as a whole it signifies first a barking animal, then a celestial body, and again a marine creature—since, therefore, every noun as a whole signifies one thing, its separated part, as though detached from the entire composition in which it contributed to the signification of one thing, signifies nothing outside itself. [Col. 0303A] He now gives the differences between simple and compound nouns.

But compound nouns do not behave in the same way as simple nouns. In simple nouns the part is in no way significant; in compound nouns, however, the part does wish to signify something, but when separated it signifies nothing—for example, in *equiferus*, *ferus*.

“Simple,” he says, “are those parts of a noun which do not consist of other parts; they reveal nothing, not even an imagined signification,” as in the noun *homo* (“human being”): neither *ho* nor *mo* signifies anything, nor are they thought to signify anything, precisely because the noun is simple. In compound nouns, however, since they are reduced from two significant elements into one signification, [Col. 0303B] the part does wish to signify something, but when separated it designates nothing. In *equiferus*, it does provide some impression of signification, and is thought to signify *ferus*. This is what he means when he says: “It does wish to signify something, but when separated it signifies nothing outside itself.” If *ferus* itself is called a part of the noun, it is called half of the noun *equiferus*; but half a noun designates nothing. Therefore *ferus*, when it contributes one signification together with the other part of the noun, namely *equi-*—that is, *equiferus*—designates nothing outside itself when separated. But if the word is once again placed externally, not as part of another noun, it signifies something by itself, like a noun. Thus the contribution of the parts is not the same in simple and compound nouns. The parts of simple nouns neither signify anything themselves [Col. 0303C] nor are thought to signify anything. The parts of compound nouns, however, do wish to signify something, give an impression of signification, and are thought to signify something, but retain no signification separately.

“According to convention.” For no noun exists by nature, but only when it becomes a sign.

A noun signifies according to convention when it becomes the sign of something—that is, when it signifies some thing, as with *scindapsus*. As long as nothing is assigned to this voice as its subject, *scindapsus* is not a noun. For it belongs to a noun to signify a subject, whereas *scindapsus* does not signify a subject. It is therefore not a noun. [Col. 0303D] Again, it belongs to the one who establishes a word to establish a subject, while it belongs to a noun to signify a subject. For nothing would be called a noun unless it derived this designation from the signification of a subject, especially since *nomen* (“noun,” “name”) is said to be so called as though from *notamen* (“mark” or “sign”). Thus, when *scindapsus* signifies a subject, it is a noun. It is therefore established that a noun exists according to convention, but only when it becomes a sign—that is, when it signifies some subject.

“For inarticulate sounds also designate something, such as the sounds of animals, none of which is a noun.”

Earlier, in the definition, he had said that a noun exists according to convention, not by nature. He now demonstrates this more carefully, saying that nothing is naturally a noun. For this reason it is not enough for the definition to say that it is a significant voice; it must also add that the significant voice exists according to convention. Otherwise [Col. 0304A] many inarticulate sounds signify something: a whistle, for example, sometimes signifies something. We also clearly observe that the voices of wild animals and dumb creatures are sometimes endowed with a certain signification. A particular sound of dogs signifies anger, and the neighing of horses often seeks out the company of another horse. But these sounds signify naturally, and therefore are not nouns. Whatever signifies naturally is not a noun.

This is enough on that point. Let us now see how the definition was constructed. When he said that a noun is a voice, he derived the genus of the definition. When he subsequently added that it is significant, he separated the noun from insignificant voices. By saying “according to convention,” he divided the nature of the noun from voices that signify naturally. By saying “without time,” he referred [Col. 0304B] to its difference from verbs. By saying that no part of it signifies anything separately, he intended to show that a noun differs from utterances. Up to this point, then, the entire definition of the noun has been discussed, and it has been made clear by which differences a noun can be distinguished from other voices. He now investigates more carefully whether those things that seem to fall under the definition of the noun are in fact nouns.

“‘Not-human,’ however, is not a noun. Nor has a name been established by which it ought to be called. For it is neither an utterance nor a negation; but let it be an indefinite noun, since it is alike in relation to whatever is and whatever is not.”

He now discusses what sort of things ought to be considered those which fall under the definition of the noun but nevertheless do not seem to be complete nouns. By carefully distinguishing these matters, [Col. 0304C] he brings the definition of the noun to complete precision.

There is uncertainty about what the expression “not-human” is. It is not an utterance. Every utterance is joined together from verbs and nouns. The expression “not-human” consists of two parts, but retains only one noun within itself and has no verb. The negative particle *non* (“not”) is neither a noun nor a verb. Nor is the expression a negation. For every negation signifies what is true or false. But “not-human” is neither true nor false. Unless, as he said above, something proximate to being is added to what is, no account of truth or falsity is completed in any combination of parts of an utterance.

Yet “not-human” is not a noun. Every noun [Col. 0304D] signifies one determinate thing, as when we say “human being”:” it signifies a substance, and not just any substance, but one that is rational and mortal. The same applies to the other nouns. Whoever says “not-human” removes the human being, but does not define what he wishes to indicate by that signification. For whatever is not human can be a horse, a dog, a stone, or anything else that is not human. Since the negative particle removes what can be signified determinately, but does not state determinately what is to be signified, each hearer understands many and indefinite things. “Let it be called,” he says, “an indefinite noun.” For “not-human” signifies as many things as there are things excluded from the definition of the human being.

Aristotle was the first to devise this term, [Col. 0305A] calling it an indefinite noun. Among earlier thinkers there was indeed this same uncertainty, but no term had been assigned to the distinction by which a determinate noun differs from a noun presented together with a negation. Aristotle himself attests to this when he says: “Nor has a name been established by which it ought to be called.” No one had established a term by which what we call “not-human” should be called; but Aristotle, with clear insight, judged that such a category should be called an indefinite noun.

“‘Of Cato’ or ‘to Cato,’ and all such forms, are not nouns, but cases of a noun.”

“Every case,” he says, “is a case of something else.” Thus every case appears to be an inflection of something else. Therefore what we call *hujus Catonis* (“of this Cato”), *huic Catoni* (“to this Cato”), and other forms of this kind are cases of nouns. Hence these are also called inflections; but every inflection is an inflection of something. What is inflected is prior to the result that is produced by the inflection. Since what we call *Cato* is a noun and is primary, it differs [Col. 0305B] from its inflections. The genitive and the other cases are inflections of the nominative. No one would correctly say that the nominative itself is a case. For if what we call *Cato* belonged to some case, it would be necessary to show which case it could be. But no case is predicated before what we call *Cato*. Since, therefore, *Cato* is the noun of no inflection, it is not a case at all.

The other cases, which are formed by inflecting the nominative, are *Catonis* (“of Cato”), *Catoni* (“to Cato”), and *Catonem* (“Cato” in the accusative). If [Col. 0305C] things produced by inflection differ from that which is inflected, then all these cases—*Catonis*, *Catoni*, and *Catonem*—differ from *Cato*, that is, from the primary noun. But *Cato* is a noun; therefore the cases are not nouns. For the case itself is one thing, and the thing of which it is the case is another.

Since all these forms are cases of a noun, they are not nouns. For this reason the ancients wisely called all the cases—genitive, dative, accusative, vocative, and ablative—by their own distinct names. The first they sometimes called the “straight” case, as though inflected from no other, and sometimes called it the nominative, using the name of the noun itself. Aristotle now pursues this point: the cases of nouns seem not to be nouns, but merely inflections of nouns, that is, cases.

[Col. 0305D] His reasoning is the same in other respects, but differs in this: when “is,” “was,” or “will be” is added, it is neither true nor false, whereas the noun always is so, as in “It is Cato’s” or “It is not Cato’s,” since it does not yet say anything true or false.

“The reasoning,” he says—that is, the definition of the noun and of the case of the noun—is the same. For just as a noun is a significant voice according to convention and without time, whose part signifies nothing separately, so also is a case. It is a voice and a designation according to convention, and its separated parts signify nothing outside themselves. Therefore the definition and account of the noun and of the case of the noun are the same.

But one difference is added between them: every noun, when joined with “is” or “is not,” makes either an affirmative or a negative utterance, as in “Socrates is” or “Socrates is not.” [Col. 0306A] Since truth or falsity arises here, it must be an utterance. In cases, however, even if one adds “is” or “is not,” no affirmation or negation results. For neither truth nor falsity applies to them. If someone says “It is of Socrates,” “It is not of Socrates,” “It is of Cato,” or “It is not of Cato,” without adding what is or is not the case, then by joining “is” or “is not” to a simple case he makes an incomplete utterance, detached from falsity and truth. Therefore it is not an utterance.

A noun consequently differs from a case in that a noun, when joined with “is” or “is not,” produces something true or false. A case neither says what is true nor lies. For without the addition of something else, it is truncated and incomplete. But why is this relevant? So that the definition of the noun might be completed in its entirety. The definition of the noun [Col. 0306B] now stands as follows:

> A noun is a significant voice, according to convention, without time, no part of which is significant separately, signifying something determinate, and, when joined with “is” or “is not,” making an utterance.

So much for the noun. He now determines the verb with the greatest care.

## On the Verb

“A verb is that which additionally signifies time, no part of which signifies anything separately, and which is always a sign of things predicated of something else.”

A verb differs from a noun only in this respect: a noun is without time, as has already been said, whereas a verb draws the force of time into its significations. The definition of the verb would indeed be complete if everything else that had been placed [Col. 0306C] in the definition of the noun were also included, with only this difference: that the verb additionally signifies time. The definition would then be: “A verb is a significant voice according to convention, no part of which signifies anything separately.” But since those features are common to nouns and verbs, while the distinctive property of the verb is that it additionally signifies time, he wished to define the verb by the property of the thing defined—namely, by that which separates the verb from the definition of the noun.

He carefully says “additionally signifies.” Nouns signify time, as “day” and “year,” for these are nouns of times. But a verb properly signifies time in addition to something else. Primarily it designates either an action or a passion, as when I say “I accuse” or “I am accused.” Along with the signification of the action or passion itself, it also brings with it the force of time, since that action or passion cannot be other than present, future, past, [Col. 0306D] or something between these.

“And it is always a sign of things predicated of something else.” The sense is this: every verb signifies some accident, and an accident is always predicated of something else. For if every verb designates either action or passion, and action and passion are counted among the accidents, every verb signifies the force of an accident. But an accident is always predicated of that which is its subject, as “white” is predicated of a body and “hard” of iron. Therefore all verbs designate things of this kind, which are always predicated of something else. This is what he means when he says that the verb is a sign—that is, a signification—of things predicated of something else. The same point could be expressed as follows: “A verb always signifies accidents, whose nature is always to be predicated of something else.” For whatever something is a sign of, that very thing which is the sign designates.

[Col. 0307A] “I say that it additionally signifies time: *cursus* (‘running’) is a noun, whereas *currit* (‘he runs’) is a verb, since it additionally signifies being-now.”

Above, in the definition of the noun, he stated that a noun is without time. He now demonstrates this by a careful example. The same category, when referred to a noun, is shown without the additional signification of time; but when referred to a verb, it appears with time. *Cursus*, simply stated as a noun and as the name of a thing, is without time. But when it is brought into an action, which always belongs to a verb, [Col. 0307B] it immediately takes on the property of a verb and the signification of time. *Currit* (“he runs”) is a verb: it signifies an action and, together with that action, indicates time, for it shows that the action is taking place now—that is, in the present time.

It is said to “additionally signify” for this reason: what we call *currit* signifies a certain action, but together with that action the present time is introduced into the signification itself. Hence he carefully says “additionally signifies.” This subtlety concerning verbs is remarkable in Aristotle.

“And it is always a sign of things said of something else, such as things that are predicated of a subject or are in a subject.”

“Always,” he says, “a verb signifies things that are predicated of something else.” Although his statement is very brief, he himself indicates what these things are. Aristotle’s practice is [Col. 0307C] to say that accidents are “in a subject.” He also says that these same accidents are predicated of a subject, because all things that are accidents are predicated of and are in a subject, whether denominatively or in some other way.

He now means, therefore, that the verb signifies something that is always an accident, and that this accident is either always in a subject or is predicated of a subject.

There is another exposition, as follows: a genus is always predicated of its species, which is said to be its subject. Among accidents, therefore, some are individual and others general. The individual accidents are merely in a subject, as any accident belonging to a particular body. Other accidents are general and are predicated of other accidents as of subjects, such as color, for color is predicated of whiteness, blackness, and the rest.

Thus he now says that every verb signifies something that is predicated of something else. This may be a particular accident that is merely in a subject, [Col. 0307D] as in *currit*. For *cursus* (“running”) is not predicated of any other subject; it is merely in a subject. Or the accident may be general and universal, so that it is predicated of another accident as of a subject, as when I say *movetur* (“it is moved”). What we call *movetur* is predicated of the subject *cursus*, for what runs is moved. A verb therefore signifies either a particular accident that is merely in a subject or a universal accident that is predicated of another accident as of a subject.

So far he has distributed the definition of the verb. He now separates from the account and property of the verb those things that might fall under the definition of a verb [Col. 0308A] but are not verbs, just as he did with the noun.

“‘He does not run’ and ‘he does not work’ are not verbs, I say. For they additionally signify time and are always predicated of something. No name has been assigned to this difference, but let it be an indefinite verb.”

Just as he did with the noun, so now with the verb he proceeds toward a complete definition of the verb and its property. He says that *non currit* (“he does not run”) is not a verb. The reason is that every verb designates something determinate. It will shortly be shown in what sense *non currit* is indefinite, and that it is not an utterance either.

In the expression *non currit*, there are neither two verbs, nor two nouns, nor a noun and a verb—the only combinations that can join to form an utterance. Nor is it a negation. For the whole expression is [Col. 0308B] an incomplete sentence. But, he says, the earlier thinkers did not assign a name to it either. The distinction represented by *non currit* and *non laborat* (“he does not work”), which differs from the pure and simple verb *currit* and *laborat*, had not been designated by any term among the earlier thinkers.

He called what is expressed by *non currit* and *non laborat* a “difference,” distinguishing it from *currit* and *laborat*. But since the ancients had assigned no name to it, Aristotle himself established one, saying: “Let it be an indefinite verb.”

Otherwise, the likeness of this category creates a serious difficulty. The category itself is a voice that designates according to convention, is predicated of something else, and additionally signifies time—precisely the same as the verb *currit*. It is seen to differ from it only in this respect: the latter is a definite verb, [Col. 0308C] while the former is indefinite. He now pursues continuously the reason why it is indefinite.

“Since it is alike in relation to whatever is and whatever is not.”

“An indefinite verb,” he says, “is so called because, although it is always predicated of something else” (*non currit* is predicated of something else), it can be predicated equally of an existing thing or of a nonexistent thing. Thus, in the statement “A human being does not run,” the human being is an existing, subsisting thing. What is expressed by *non currit* is therefore predicated of a human being, that is, of an existing thing.

Again, we say “A chimaera does not run.” But a chimaera does not exist and does not subsist [Col. 0308D] at all. Yet it can truly be said of it that it does not run at all. Thus *non currit* is said both of a thing that subsists and exists among realities and of a thing that neither exists nor can exist. For this reason it is called an indefinite verb.

There is another reason as well. When someone says *currit* (“he runs”), he definitively signifies the action that the person performs. But when he says *non currit* (“he does not run”), he seems to remove running, but does not disclose whether the person sits, lies down, walks, or does something else. Since both existing and nonexistent things are indefinite, and since the verb is predicated of all of them, and since what it removes is determinate while what it leaves open is indefinite, it is for this reason called an indefinite verb.

“Similarly, *curret* (‘he will run’) and *currebat* (‘he was running’) are not verbs, but cases of a verb. A verb additionally signifies present time, whereas those forms signify the times around the present.”

Just as he distinguished cases from nouns, he now separates cases of verbs from the account of verbs. [Col. 0309A] *Curret* (“he will run”), which signifies the future, *currebat* (“he was running”), which retains part of the past, and *cucurrit* (“he ran” or “has run”), which is a complete and perfect past, are not verbs but cases of verbs. The present either anticipates the future or leaves the past behind. For this reason the future time extends toward the present, while the past begins from the present. Thus the verb primarily contains what is present, and the complete verb is that which signifies the present.

Forms that signify something beyond the present are not verbs but cases of verbs. Here too, as in the case of nouns, he reveals the difference between verbs and cases. He says: “Every verb signifies present time. Cases of verbs [Col. 0309B] signify the time that is around the present and encompasses it.” The future and past times, which encompass the present and are around it, surround what is present. Whatever signifies either future or past time—times that encompass the present and are around it—is called not a verb but a case of a verb.

The complete definition of the verb is therefore as follows:

> A verb is a significant voice according to convention, with time, no part of which is significant separately, signifying something determinate and retaining the signification of the present.

That a part of a verb designates nothing outside itself is clear from the fact that not even a part of a noun signifies anything outside itself.

“Verbs uttered by themselves are therefore nouns, and signify something. For the person who says one establishes an understanding, and the person who hears it comes to rest.”

[Col. 0309C] He enters upon a very subtle point, but its meaning is as follows: every verb uttered by itself and without being joined to anything else possesses, in a certain way, the character of a noun and is truly a noun. When I say “A human being runs,” the word *currit* (“runs”) becomes a complete verb because I refer it to the human being; for it is unquestionably always predicated of something else. But if I say *currit* by itself, I in a certain way make *currit* its own thing, joining it to nothing else, and it becomes a noun for me.

The Greeks likewise sometimes add prefixed articles to verbs uttered by themselves, as in τὸ τρέχειν (*to trechein*, “running”) and τοῦ τρέχειν (*tou trechein*, “of running”). If someone says, “What is running is faster than what is walking,” in the first expression he has joined the nominative article, saying “what is running”; in the second [Col. 0309D] he calls the article ablative, saying “than what is walking.”

It is as though someone were to say, with nouns, “What is a bench is lighter than what is a door.” In the expression “what is a bench,” we have joined a prefixed article to *bench* itself, as though we were saying “this bench.” In what we again call “what is a door,” we use it as though we were saying “this door” in the relevant case.

So too, when we say “What is running is faster than what is walking,” we place “what is running” as though we were saying “this running,” and “than what is walking” as though we were saying, in a genitive form, “walking,” as if it had been transferred to a noun and expressed as “by this walking.” Verbs uttered by themselves are therefore nouns.

[Col. 0310A] Aristotle himself offers a proof of this. When we say a simple noun, the hearer’s understanding begins with our utterance, follows the speaker’s voice while we pronounce it, and comes to rest when the noun has been completed. When I say *Hippocentaurus* (“Hippocentaur”), the hearer’s understanding enters with the first syllable and does not come to rest until the end of the whole noun. When the hearer has heard the final syllable, he immediately understands what has been said and comes to rest in that understanding.

The same is true of the verb. When we say *currere* (“to run”), the hearer’s understanding proceeds through its syllables, *cur*, *re*, and again *re*. But when he hears the final syllable, immediately grasping the signification of the whole verb, his understanding comes to rest. A verb uttered by itself is therefore similar to a noun and is in a certain way a noun.

For just as in the case of a noun [Col. 0310B] the speaker establishes the hearer’s understanding with the utterance of the final syllable and the completion of the whole noun, and the hearer comes to rest without his understanding proceeding further, so a verb too, if uttered by itself, establishes the hearer’s understanding. If it is joined with something else, however, the hearer’s complete understanding has not yet been established. When I say “Socrates walks,” the complete sentence does not reside in *ambulat* (“walks”) alone, although it is a verb, but in the whole expression, “Socrates walks.”

Again, when I say “To walk is to move,” the sentence is not established in either of these verbs individually, but the hearer comes to rest in the whole utterance. Since, when one verb is predicated of another verb as its subject, [Col. 0310C] the hearer joins the signification of both verbs, he does not consider the verb that is uttered by itself, but refers it to the other: in “to walk is to move,” he refers walking to movement; in “Socrates walks,” he refers walking to Socrates.

A verb therefore becomes complete when it is referred to something else. But if it is predicated simply, the verb is a noun, because, just as a noun when uttered establishes the hearer’s understanding, so too does a verb.

[Col. 0310D] “But it does not yet signify being or not being; for being or not being is not a sign of a thing.”

Although a verb, he says, is a noun and signifies something determinate when uttered by itself, it nevertheless does not by itself make an utterance or establish anything true or false. This is what he means by saying: “But if you say ‘is’ or ‘is not,’ it does not yet signify.” He refers what he says—“if it is”—to affirmation, and “or if it is not” to negation. For none of these things is signified by the verb uttered as described above.

When I say *currit* (“he runs”), *currit* itself does signify something, but it does not yet signify that something is or is not. For “is” or “is not” is not a sign of the thing. This amounts to saying that the expression *currit* does not signify that running itself exists or does not exist. If it signified this, one would say *currere est* (“running is”) or *currere non est* (“running is not”). But *currit* does not designate that the thing itself exists or does not exist.

It is uttered alone and is a certain understanding, but it signifies neither affirmation nor negation, because it neither posits the thing as existing nor removes it. He shows this by saying: “For ‘is’ or ‘is not’ is not a sign of a thing.” That is, no verb is predicated in such a way that it is a sign of the thing of which it is predicated, insofar as that thing exists or does not exist.

“Nor, if you say ‘is’ itself by itself, does it signify anything, for it additionally signifies a certain combination, which cannot be understood without the things combined.”

[Col. 0311A] The verb *est* (“is”), when joined with another verb or noun, ordinarily makes a proposition, as in *homo est* (“a human being is”) or *currere est* (“to run is”). But if *est* itself is uttered alone, he says, it is neither true nor false, although almost all simple utterances are formed from it. Therefore, even if you say *est* itself by itself, it does not signify that something is or is not—that is, it neither affirms nor denies—because *est* uttered simply is nothing.

This does not mean [Col. 0311B] that it signifies absolutely nothing, but that it possesses neither truth nor falsity. It is not nothing with respect to signification, but with respect to the signification of truth and falsity, which is the matter now under discussion.

He shows why it indicates nothing true or false. The word *est* is used in two ways to designate truth or falsity. First, it may establish a single thing by its own combination, as when I say *homo est* (“a human being is”): *est*, joined and combined with *homo*, establishes that the human being exists, and an utterance results. Second, two things may be joined together through the combination and connection of the verb, as in *homo animal est* (“a human being is an animal”). The human being and the animal are joined and connected through the expression “a human being is an animal.”

Therefore, if every signification of truth and falsity in an utterance lies in the word *est* when it establishes something through its own combination or joins and combines two things, then its force, as displayed in utterances and propositions—in the designation of truth and falsity—[Col. 0311C] exists nowhere apart from the combinations in which it normally performs this function. This is what he means by saying: “It additionally signifies a certain combination, which cannot be understood without the things combined.”

[Col. 0311D] When I say *est* by itself, I have signified nothing concerning what is or is not. If I am to make an utterance, I must combine it with something, as in *homo est* (“a human being is”) or *homo animal est* (“a human being is an animal”). Since all its force in the expression of truth and falsity refers to combination, when it is said apart from combination, it does not designate outside the combination what it is able to designate within it. Once combined, however, it can display truth and falsity in an utterance.

No one can understand the function of *est* without the things combined with it. It was therefore correctly said to “additionally signify a certain combination,” one that could not be understood without the things combined.

## On the Utterance

“An utterance is a significant voice, some part of which is significant when separated, as a phrase, but not as an affirmation or negation.”

Everything composite takes on the nature of those things from which the whole body of the composite is constituted. Therefore, since an utterance consists of verbs and nouns, which are significant, an utterance too is rightly defined as significant. But an utterance differs from the things of which it is composed—that is, nouns and verbs—in this respect: their parts signify nothing outside themselves, whereas a part of an utterance signifies something when separated. For if a noun and a verb are parts of an utterance, and these signify by themselves, there is no doubt that, when separated, the parts of an utterance signify something. What they signify, however, he will show in the definition that follows.

Thus the parts of utterances signify as a diction, always; not always as an affirmation or a negation. Here he calls “diction” the simple naming of a verb or noun. For there are certain utterances whose parts signify as an affirmation, such as the utterance, “If it is day, it is light.” What we say, “it is light,” is a part of the whole utterance, and it signifies in such a way as to constitute a kind of affirmation. But not every utterance has an affirmation as a part. For this very utterance, “it is light,” contains as parts what we call “light” and, again, what we call “is”; yet neither of these is an affirmation, but only a simple diction. Every utterance, therefore, has a diction as a part, but not every utterance has an affirmation. It was therefore rightly said that the parts of an utterance signify as a diction, not as an affirmation. What a diction is, however, he himself will demonstrate more clearly shortly afterward.

I say, for example, “man”: it signifies something, but not that it is or is not; it will be an affirmation or a negation if something is added. But not one syllable of “man.”

What he had stated above, saying that the parts of an utterance signify as a diction, not as an affirmation, he demonstrated with a fitting example: “Man,” he says, “is a diction, and it is a part of an utterance if it is placed within a complete utterance, as in ‘man is an animal.’” Therefore, what we call “man” is a certain diction, but it is not an affirmation. Since this noun, that is, “man,” is a part of an utterance and is not an affirmation, he teaches that the statement is true that the parts of an utterance signify as a diction, not as an affirmation.

He also teaches that this noun is not an affirmation because truth or falsity is always found in an affirmation, whereas a noun stated simply is neither true nor false. Therefore, this noun, “man,” does not signify as an affirmation, but denotes something simple; thus it signifies something as a diction. If something is added to this diction, such as the verb “is,” or any other verb capable of producing an enunciation, it will be an affirmation. For if someone says, “Man is,” or “Man lives,” an affirmation is produced. This is what he says: “but it will be an affirmation or a negation if something is added.” For if something is added, or if what has been added is denied, in such a way that an enunciation can be constituted, an affirmation or a negation is produced. If someone says, “Man lives,” it is an affirmation; “Man does not live,” a negation.

He teaches that a diction is a sound signifying by convention in itself through what he says: “but not one syllable of ‘man.’” For one syllable of “man” is not a diction, because, when separated, it signifies nothing by itself, as “ho” and “mo,” and in the other cases, as we showed above. Every part of this kind that signifies nothing by itself is not a diction, but only denotes and co-signifies something placed within the whole noun, as he shows in the following example:

[Col. 0313A] For in “shrew-mouse” (“sorex”), “king” (“rex”) does not signify, but the sound is presently [only a sound]. In compound words, however, it does signify something, but not in itself, as has been said.

In the word “sorex,” he says, “rex” seems indeed to signify something; but since it co-signifies with the whole noun rather than denote anything by itself, as was already said above, it does not signify by itself. For he taught above that the parts of a noun, when separated, signify nothing at all. Therefore, when he says “but not in itself,” he means that in “sorex,” “rex” signifies nothing by itself, but merely co-signifies something which it denotes together with the entire composition of the noun, since both the syllable “so” and “rex,” joined into one, denote what “sorex” is through the whole conjunction of the syllables.

[Col. 0313B] Every utterance is significant, not as an instrument, but, as has been said, by convention.

Plato established that nouns are natural, and attempted to prove this from the fact that an utterance is a kind of equipment and, in a certain way, an instrument for expressing thoughts to one another. Natural equipment, however, is natural, just as the eyes are instruments for seeing, and seeing is a natural activity. Therefore the eyes too must be natural. Likewise, an utterance is the natural equipment and instrument of things—that is, of thoughts. Therefore the utterance itself is also natural.

Aristotle, however, says that an utterance is not according to nature but according to convention. Consequently, neither is an utterance natural equipment. When he says “not as an instrument,” he does not mean that thoughts are not conveyed through this instrument, but only that an utterance is a matter of convention, through which we display our own thoughts. For whatever has parts that are conventional is itself also conventional. But the parts of an utterance are the noun and the verb, and these are conventional, not natural. The utterance itself, therefore, is according to convention and imposition, but is not constituted naturally.

The complete definition of an utterance is therefore this: “An utterance is a significant sound according to convention, whose parts signify something outside themselves.”

Not every utterance is enunciative, but only that in which there is truth or falsity; these are not present in all utterances. A prayer, for example, is an utterance, but it is neither true nor false.

There are, as we have already said above, many kinds of utterance. The first kind is optative, as in: “Would that the immortal gods grant you this disposition!” The second is vocative, as in: “Hey, you!” The third is imperative, as in: “Take this; give it, Portion.” The fourth is deprecatory, as in: “Almighty Jupiter, if you can be moved by any prayers.” The fifth is enunciative, as in: “It is day”; “It is not day.”

Truth and falsity are present only in this last kind of utterance, and not at all in the others. Wishing to show that there are many utterances and that not every utterance is enunciative, Aristotle added: “A prayer is indeed an utterance, but neither true nor false.” For a prayer is counted among the kinds of utterance, but no nature of truth or falsity is discerned in it.

The others, then, may be left aside. Their consideration belongs more appropriately to rhetoric or poetry. The enunciative utterance, however, belongs to the present inquiry.

“Let us leave,” he says, “the deprecatory, optative, vocative, and imperative utterances to poets and orators.” For the other kinds of utterance are adopted by them either to arouse or to move the emotions. We philosophers, however, who are concerned with the distinction between truth and falsity, treat only that utterance in which either of these can be recognized. Since an enunciation contains either truth or falsity, let us too discuss enunciation.

There is one primary enunciative utterance, affirmation, and then negation; all the others are one by conjunction.

Some enunciative utterances are one in themselves, as “Man is an animal”; others are one through conjunction, as “If it is day, it is light.” “Man is” and “animal is” are two utterances, but when the conjunction “if” is added, they become one. Among those that are one in themselves, the first is affirmation and the second negation. For negation removes what affirmation previously established, and negation divides what affirmation joined together. Among enunciative utterances that are one in themselves, therefore, affirmation is first and negation follows. Others are not one in themselves, but although naturally multiple, become one through conjunction.

Every enunciative utterance must consist of a verb or of a case of a verb. For “the definition of man,” unless “is,” “will be,” “was,” or something of this kind is added, is not yet an enunciative utterance.

In Aristotle’s Greek text it does not stand as we placed it above, but rather in this form: “For ‘of man,’ if not ‘is,’ ‘will be,’ or ‘was,’ and so forth.” The philosopher leaves implicit what he was speaking about, namely, the definition, which the Greeks call λόγος (*logos*). But since he had been discussing an utterance above—also called λόγος (*logos*) by the Greeks—when he wished to speak of the “definition of man,” and since it signifies neither truth nor falsity unless “is,” “will be,” or “was” is added to it, he used the common term and referred it back to the λόγος (*logos*) of which he had been speaking earlier, so that we should understand not an utterance but rather a definition.

We now satisfy those who may perhaps criticize us as learned in Greek speech and ask why we added to our translation what was not present there. In serving the easier understanding of Latin speech, we added this because, when the discussion concerned an utterance, the sense could not be transferred to “definition” unless this was added.

The whole passage, however, has this meaning: if enunciative utterances are simple, verbs constitute them. An enunciation cannot be made from two nouns alone; it is made from a noun and a verb, as “Man lives.” It can also be made from verbs alone, as “To walk is to move.” It can also be made from a case of a verb, as “Socrates was” or “It will be day.” For “will be” and “was” are cases of the verb. Consequently, simple enunciative utterances are constituted chiefly by verbs alone.

He gives an example in which there are several nouns but which, without the addition of a verb, does not attain the proper form and signification of an enunciation, as in the definition of man. (For the definition of man is the definition of a species.) If “is,” “is not,” or something of this kind is added to it, it can become an enunciation. For if someone says, “Rational mortal animal,” no falsity or truth is yet understood in it. But if “is” is added, so that it becomes “Rational mortal animal is,” an enunciation is completed without any doubt. The verb alone, therefore, contains a simple enunciative utterance.

Why, then, is “two-footed walking animal” one thing and not many? For it will not be one merely because the words are spoken closely together. To deal with this is the subject of another inquiry.

While discussing simple and unified utterances, he inserted the definition of man, and now says this about it. The definition of man has indeed been inserted as though it were one utterance. But why it is one utterance, he says, we shall now omit discussing. For it must not be considered one merely because it is spoken continuously and with its parts close together: “two-footed walking animal.” It might seem that their continuity, spoken under one emission, makes a single enunciation; but Aristotle denies this. For an utterance is not one merely because it is spoken closely and continuously. Why it is one belongs to another inquiry, and he discusses it in the books entitled *Metaphysics*, a work belonging to first philosophy. We, however, must demonstrate this in the second edition.

An enunciative utterance is one either because it signifies one thing or because it is one by conjunction. Utterances are multiple when they signify many things and not one, or when they are unconjoined.

He declares that there are two ways in which utterances are one or many. An utterance is one either when it signifies one thing or when it is one through conjunction, as in “Rational mortal animal is man.” No one can divide the meaning of this utterance into many significations; it signifies one thing, and it is one apart from conjunction.

Another utterance is one through conjunction, as “If it is day, it is light.” An utterance is therefore one either because it signifies one thing or because it is joined by conjunction.

Utterances are multiple when they signify many things, as “The dog moves.” A hearer may understand this as referring to a barking dog, a sea-dog, or the Dog in the heavens. Since it signifies many things, it is not one utterance but several.

There are also utterances that are multiple both in themselves and in number and signification, and that are joined by no conjunction, as if someone says: “The sun exists; there will be peace; it is night; the heavens revolve.” Although these signify many things, they are joined by no conjunction, and therefore they are called multiple utterances.

In sum, among one utterances, some are one in signification and others one through conjunction. Among utterances that are not one, some are multiple in signification, while others are multiple because they are joined by no conjunction.

A noun and a verb, then, are diction alone, since it is not possible to say that one enunciates something by means of a sound signifying something—whether someone asks a question or not—but only when the speaker himself produces it.

Through this statement he explains what a simple diction is. He says that a verb and a noun appear to be dictions alone and not affirmations, and he adds the reason for this view. Verbs and nouns are dictions alone because, when they are spoken simply—whether by someone producing them, that is, saying them voluntarily, or by someone responding to another’s question—neither truth nor falsity can be understood from them.

If someone says by itself, “Socrates,” or again, by itself and simply, “walks,” it produces neither truth nor falsity. But if, when another asks, “Is Socrates walking?” someone replies, “He is walking,” and someone wishes to consider the verb “walks” by itself, there is no enunciation. It becomes an enunciation only when it is joined to the preceding question; then an enunciation arises from the conjunction of the question and the response.

No one can say that a mere noun or verb, whether spoken voluntarily by someone and not in response to another’s question, or spoken in answer to a question, constitutes an enunciation.

This is the sense of the passage. The order of the words, however, is as follows: “A noun and a verb are diction alone, since, when a sound signifying something is thus produced”—that is, when a noun or verb is simply uttered—“it is not possible to say that one enunciates.” For we cannot say that someone who has uttered a simple noun or a simple verb has enunciated something, whether another has asked a question or not, but only that the speaker himself has produced it voluntarily.

Of these, one enunciation is simple, such as something concerning something or something from something. Another is joined from these, like an utterance that is already composite.

He now explains what a simple and what a composite utterance is. A simple utterance consists of two terms. The terms are nouns and verbs, which we predicate in a simple proposition, as in “Socrates discusses.” “Socrates” and “discusses” are terms. The lesser term, which is put forward in the enunciation, such as “Socrates,” is called the subject and is placed first; the greater term, which is predicated, is placed afterward, such as “discusses.”

Whatever proposition is made from one subject and one predicate is called a simple enunciation.
