This is what he says: “Of these”—that is, of enunciative utterances—“one enunciation is simple, such as something concerning something”: one predicate, which is “something,” is predicated of one subject, which is “something.”

This pertains to affirmation: to predicate something of something. Negation, however, consists in separating one thing from another by predication, as in “Socrates does not discuss.” There I separated “to discuss,” one term, from “Socrates,” another term, by denying the predicate.

There are other enunciative utterances called composite, which are composed from simple utterances, as “If it is day, it is light.” “It is day” and “it is light” are two simple enunciative utterances, because each consists of two terms. The whole utterance, “If it is day, it is light,” is composed from these two simple utterances. This is what he says: “Another is joined from these,” that is, from simple enunciative utterances, “like an utterance that is already composite,” since its whole body is joined together from those utterances which I have already shown to be simple.

A simple enunciation is a significant sound concerning something that is or is not, according as the times have been divided.

[Col. 0317A] After discussing composite and simple utterances, he approaches the definition of enunciation through affirmation and negation. He says: “An enunciation is a sound signifying an affirmation or a negation, either in past time, present time, or future time.”

What he said, “concerning something that is,” he referred to affirmation; what he added, “or is not,” he referred to negation. What follows, “according as the times have been divided,” he referred to the nature of the individual times. Whether someone says, “Socrates lives,” “Socrates does not live,” “Socrates lived,” “Socrates did not live,” or “Socrates is going to live,” “Socrates is not going to live,” since each is an affirmation or a negation, and since each belongs to one of the times divided into future, present, and past, each retains the complete nature of a simple enunciation.

[Col. 0317B] An affirmation is an enunciation of something concerning something. A negation is an enunciation of something from something.

For the definition of affirmation and negation, he took the term “enunciation” as the genus. An affirmation occurs whenever we predicate something of something together with the verb “is,” as when we say, “Man is an animal”: we predicate “animal” of “man.” Whenever we separate something from something by predicating it negatively, there is a negation, as in “Man is not a stone”: we separate “stone” from “man.” Thus the definition of affirmation and negation has been correctly made.

## OF THE SUBJECTS AND PREDICATES OF ENUNCIATIONS

Since it is possible to enunciate both that what is is not, and that what is not is, and that what is is, and that what is not is not; and since, with respect to things outside the present time likewise, it is always possible to deny whatever one affirms and to affirm whatever one denies, it is clear that every affirmation has a negation opposed to it, and every negation an affirmation. Let this be contradiction: opposed affirmation and negation.

He now divides enunciations according to whether they can be made about things that are or about things that are not, whether in affirmation or in negation. For he says that it is possible to enunciate that what is is not, as when someone says, “No man is an animal.” Here he proposed that what is should not be. This is a false negation.

It is also possible to enunciate that what is not is, as when someone says, “Every stone is an animal.” He has established that what is not is; this is a false affirmation.

It is possible to enunciate that what is is, as when someone says, “Every man is an animal.” He confirms that what is is, and this is a true affirmation.

It is possible to enunciate that what is not is not, as when someone says, “No stone is an animal.” He proposes that what is not is not, and this is a true negation.

This applies not only to the present time but also to those times that lie outside the present. This is equivalent to saying that it is possible to enunciate in the present time in such a way that there is a true or false negation, and likewise a true or false affirmation; but it is also possible to do so in the past and future, which lie outside the present.

For likewise it is always possible to deny what is affirmed and again to affirm what is denied by another. If falsity is opposed to every truth, and truth likewise to every falsity; and if it is possible to utter falsehoods both in affirmation and in negation, it follows that an affirmation is opposed to every negation and a negation to every affirmation.

Here, then, he explains what is called contradiction. Contradiction is the opposition of an affirmation and a negation. When one person affirms what another denies, the conflict between the two propositions is called contradiction. This is what he says: “Let this be contradiction: opposed affirmation and negation.” When an affirmation is opposed to a negation, there is contradiction.

But which affirmation is opposed to which negation, and what kind of opposition these propositions have, he reveals in what follows. For not every negation is opposed to every affirmation, but only those that he himself defines below. Thus contradiction consists of opposed affirmation and negation; and which are opposed is set out in the following order of exposition.

I say that they are opposed when the same is predicated of the same, not equivocally; and whatever other qualifications of this kind we determined against sophistical difficulties.

He shows that opposition arises in affirmations and negations when the same subject and the same predicate occur in the negation as were proposed by someone in the affirmation. For if an affirmation is opposed to a negation, one must always be true and the other false. If both are false or both true, they are not opposed, since they do not destroy one another. But if one is false and the other true, the true one destroys the false one; and if one is true, the other immediately departs from truth.

If, however, either the subject or the predicate in an affirmation is equivocal, the propositions are not opposed. For if someone says, “Alexander carried off Helen,” and another denies this by saying, “Alexander did not carry off Helen,” since “Alexander” is an equivocal name, both may be true: the negation if the statement concerns Alexander the Great, and the affirmation if it concerns Alexander of Troy. Therefore these are not opposed.

He says that those propositions are opposed which have the opposition of the same predicate concerning the same subject, so that no equivocation causes diversity. This is what he means by: “I say that they are opposed when the same is predicated of the same, not equivocally.” The predicate opposed in the negation must be the same predicate that occurred in the affirmation, and the negation must concern the subject about which the affirmation was previously made.

He discusses this more carefully in the book he calls *On Sophistical Refutations* (*Περὶ σοφιστικῶν ἐλέγχων*). There he distinguishes the arguments of sophists—whom in Latin we may call deceptive reasoners—who construct fallacious syllogisms from propositions that do not divide truth from falsity. He identifies the arguments by which they customarily capture and entangle their respondent.

Therefore, he now says that those qualifications must also be observed which were determined against the troublesome character of arguments. What those qualifications are, let the text of the second edition await from me.

Since some things are universal and others singular, I call universal that which is naturally predicated of many; singular, that which is not, as “man” is universal, while “Plato” belongs among singular things.

[Col. 0319A] He shows how every proposition is formed. The nature of a proposition is completed according to the things that are signified. Some things are universal and others particular.

The universal is what is predicated of many, as “man” is said of many and is therefore universal. The singular is any individual thing whose predication does not extend to anything subordinate to it, such as Plato or Socrates.

He teaches their nature through examples, saying: “Man is universal, whereas Plato belongs among singular things.” For if that is universal which is predicated of many, “man” is universal, since it is said of many individuals. If, on the other hand, that is singular which is predicated of nothing else, Plato is singular. Individuals are predicated of no other things.

Since some things are universal and others singular, it is clear that every affirmation or negation is constituted through these.

It is necessary to enunciate that something inheres or does not inhere, sometimes in one of the things that are universal and sometimes in one of the things that are singular.

Every proposition has either a singular or a universal subject, whether it assents through affirmation or rejects through negation. If someone says, “Man is an animal,” or “Man is not an animal,” he proposes that a universal thing, namely man, either is or is not an animal. This is what he says: “It is necessary to enunciate that something inheres or does not inhere, sometimes in one of the things that are universal.”

Since “man” is universal, the affirmation proposes that “animal” inheres in it. This is what is said by “Man is an animal”; the negation, “Man is not an animal,” says that it does not inhere.

If someone says, “Socrates discusses,” or “Socrates does not discuss,” he joins or separates being and not-being from one of the singular things. This is what he means by: “sometimes in one of the things that are singular.” Since Socrates is something singular, discussion is joined to him by affirmation and separated from him by negation.

If, then, one enunciates universally concerning a universal that it is or is not, these will be contrary enunciations. By a universal enunciation concerning a universal I mean one such as “Every man is white” and “No man is white.” But when the enunciation is not universal concerning universals, the propositions are not contrary, although what is signified may at times be contrary.

[Col. 0319D] Every affirmation and every negation is either universal, particular, or indefinite.

An affirmation is universal when someone says, “Every man is an animal.” The subject “man” is universal, since it can be predicated of many; and the predicate has been made universal as well. We have said, “Every man is an animal.” We have not only posited “man,” which is universal, but also added “every,” a universal determination, to the universal subject, “man.” This is a universal affirmation.

If someone says, “No man is an animal,” he again adds to the universal thing “man” the universal determination expressed by “no.” Thus, whether in affirmation or negation, when someone utters them universally, he proposes a universal concerning a universal.

He does not propose a universal concerning a universal whenever he says, “Man is an animal” or “Man is not an animal.” Although “man” is a universal thing, no universal determination—“no” or “every”—has made the affirmation or negation universal.

Therefore it must be repeated: a universal affirmation is one in which a universal is predicated affirmatively and universally; a universal negation is one in which a universal is predicated negatively and universally. Propositions of this kind are contrary.

For it is impossible that wherever a universal affirmation is true, a universal negation should also be true, or conversely. Nevertheless, both may be found false, as in “Every man is just” and “No man is just.” Here both are false. But one may be true and the other false, as in “Every man is an animal” and “No man is an animal.” Here one is true and the other false.

It is impossible, however, for both to be true. Since both can be false, they are not contradictories but contraries. Why they are called contraries will have to be explained elsewhere.

Particular propositions are of this kind: “Some man is an animal”; “Some man is not an animal.” These are called subalterns. A particular affirmation is subaltern to a universal affirmation; likewise, a particular negation is subaltern to a universal negation.

Both particular propositions may be true, or one may be true and the other false; but both cannot be false. Thus, in “Some man is just” and “Some man is not just,” both are true. When we say, “Some man is an animal” and “Some man is not an animal,” one is true and the other false. Affirmation and negation of this kind are called particular subcontraries.

Therefore these too are not called opposed, because they may sometimes both be found true. Their diagram should be as follows:

[Col. 0320D] [Col. 0321A]

Neither the superior universals nor the inferior particulars, therefore, are opposed, because the inferior propositions may both be true, while the superior may both be false.

Contradictories are opposed, as he himself says, when one considers the diagonal propositions: when a universal affirmation is compared with a particular negation, as “Every man is just” and “Some man is not just.” These cannot both be true or both false; in every case one is true and the other false.

Likewise, when a universal negation is compared with a particular affirmation, they are found to be opposed, as “No man is just” and “Some man is just.” One is always true and the other false. If you examine this with any terms whatsoever, our account will not differ.

Let the fullest diagram be set out in this way.

[Col. 0321B]

[Col. 0321C] The determinations of universals are “every” and “no”; that of particulars is “some.” Propositions to which neither a universal nor a particular determination has been added are called indefinite, and they resemble particulars, as “Man is just” and “Man is not just.”

Both may be true, as in this very example. One may also be true and the other false, as in “Man is an animal” and “Man is not an animal.” They cannot both be false, however; and these, as was said, are called indefinite.

Apart from these, all propositions concerning singulars are such that contradiction can be found in them, as “Socrates is an animal” and “Socrates is not an animal”; “Socrates is just” and “Socrates is not just.”

If no equivocation of the predicate or subject, no difference of tense, or anything else that determines individual propositions interferes, one is always true and the other false.

Since, then, we have examined all these matters in common and expressed what each kind is as far as brevity allowed, let us now return to the text, since the time has come.

“If, then,” he says, “one enunciates universally concerning a universal that it is or is not, the enunciations will be contrary.” Someone enunciates universally concerning a universal whenever he makes either a universal affirmation or a universal negation.

When he says, “Every man is an animal,” he has enunciated universally concerning the universal “man” by the addition of “every.” If he again says, “No man is an animal,” he similarly enunciates universally concerning the universal “man” through what he says, “no”; and the propositions are contrary.

Which propositions he calls contrary he makes clear through the example that follows: “I call a universal enunciation concerning a universal one such as ‘Every man is white’ and ‘No man is white.’” One is a universal affirmation and the other a universal negation; above, in the diagram, we showed that these are contrary.

But when the enunciation concerning universals is not universal, the propositions are not contrary. Whenever propositions are indefinite and a universal is not proposed universally, they are not contrary. For the affirmation “Man is just” and the negation “Man is not just” are not contrary. Both may be true at the same time and in the same thing, namely man; in contraries this is impossible.

What he added—“although what is signified may at times be contrary”—has this meaning: the propositions themselves are not contrary, but what they signify may sometimes be contrary.

If someone says, “A man is white,” and another denies it by saying, “A man is not white,” the propositions themselves are not contrary. But “a man is not white” may signify something contrary. For “a man is not white” may signify that he is red, pale, brown, or black; black is contrary to white.

Therefore what is not white may be black. Thus, although the propositions themselves are not contrary, what is said may sometimes signify something contrary to the preceding affirmation. If “a man is not white” signifies that he is black, since what is black is not white, the propositions themselves are not contrary, because both may be true. But what is signified may sometimes be contrary. He demonstrated what kind of propositions these are by supplying examples.

I call it not enunciating universally concerning those things that are universal when one says, “The man is white” and “The man is not white.”

He demonstrated most clearly what it means for something universal to be predicated non-universally, saying:

Although “man” is universal, he does not use the enunciation universally. For “every” does not signify a universal thing, but that it is predicated universally.

The word “every” gathers together that to which it is predicated and brings it into one whole, as when one says, “Every man is just”: it excludes no man. Rather, it gathers together the whole of humanity, and a universal predication is made concerning the universal thing “man” when we say “every man.” Since “man” is universal, what is added—“every”—co-signifies universality with this universal, and the universal thing is predicated universally.

But where a universal is predicated, it is not true that it is predicated universally.

This sentence has instructed us where rightly to place the determination of universality. For it teaches that this universality, which we call the universal determination, must always be placed as a term with the subject, never with the predicate. For if someone says, “Every human being is an animal,” he has spoken correctly, placing “every” with the subject, that is, with “human being.” But if he says, “Every human being is every animal,” he has spoken falsely. Therefore he does not mean this when he says that a universal is predicated: for example, “animal” of “human being.” For “animal” is universal. Although it is predicated of every human being, it is not correct to predicate this very universal—namely, “animal”—universally, so as to say “Every animal is a human being.” Nor does he allow this to be correctly done merely in such cases; rather, he grants that it is correct in no affirmative proposition. For he says:

> No affirmation will be true in which a universal predicate is predicated universally, as in “Every human being is every animal.”

Why this occurs I shall explain briefly. The predicate is always either greater than, or equal to, the subject. It is greater, for example, when I say, “A human being is an animal”: “animal” is predicated, and “human being” is the subject. But “animal” is greater than “human being,” for it is predicated of more things than “human being” itself. Again, the predicate is equal when we say, “A human being is capable of laughter”: “human being” is the subject and “capable of laughter” the predicate. But “human being” and “capable of laughter” are equal, since being capable of laughter is proper to a human being. It is impossible, however, for the predicate to be found less than the subject. Therefore, if the predicate is greater, it is false to add a universal determination to the predicate, as in the example he himself gave, “Every human being is every animal.” If it is equal, the determination is superfluous, as if someone were to say, “Every human being is every being capable of laughter.” Thus one ought not to predicate a universal predicate universally.

I therefore say that an affirmation is opposed contradictorily to a negation when the affirmation signifies universally and the negation non-universally, as in:

- “Every human being is white.”
- “Not every human being is white.”
- “No human being is white.”
- “Some human being is white.”

He subsequently explains precisely what contradiction is. For he says that propositions are opposed contradictorily whenever a particular negation denies a universal affirmation, and whenever a particular affirmation destroys a universal negation. When it is said, “Every human being is white,” the negation that says, “Not every human being is white,” universally removes, with respect to the same subject, what the universal affirmation had established. The former posits that every human being is white. The latter says “not every,” as though it granted that someone is white but removed universality alone. This is what he means when he says that one proposition signifies universally, the other that the same thing is not signified universally. Just as the affirmation signifies universally by saying “human being,” so too the negation signifies a universal, since it too contains “human being.” But it teaches that this very universal does not hold universally—that is, that not everyone is white—whereas the affirmation had posited universally that every human being is white.

The same applies to the negations that we earlier set out in angular form and described as contradictories. Here he now calls these same propositions “contradictorily opposed.” The fact that he opposed to the universal affirmation “Every human being is white” the particular negation “Not every human being is white” amounts to the same thing as saying, “Some human being is not white.” For if not every human being is white, then some human being is not white.

Contraries, however, are a universal affirmation and a universal negation, as in:

- “Every human being is just.”
- “No human being is just.”

Accordingly, it is impossible for these to be true simultaneously. But the propositions opposed to them can sometimes be true of the same subject, as in:

- “Not every human being is white.”
- “Some human being is white.”

He fully works through all the propositions and says that the contraries are a universal affirmation and a universal negation. We too described these above. Here, however, he now demonstrates that these same propositions are opposed as contraries. He also adds that it is impossible for them ever to be known as simultaneously true of the same subject. For just as the nature of contraries cannot be found in the same subject—for nothing can be both black and white at one and the same time—so too it cannot happen that contraries are simultaneously true.

When he adds, “But the propositions opposed to these can sometimes be true of the same subject,” he indicates a particular affirmation and a particular negation. For a particular affirmation is opposed contradictorily to a universal negation, while a particular negation is opposed to a universal affirmation. The propositions opposed to contraries can therefore sometimes be found true of the same subject: that is, it can happen that both a particular affirmation and a particular negation are true, as in:

- “Some human being is white.”
- “Some human being is not white.”

Both are true.

## On the Rules of Opposed Propositions

Whatever contradictions are universal with respect to universals must have one member true and the other false.

And whatever propositions concern singulars, such as “Socrates is white” and “Socrates is not white,” likewise have one necessarily true and the other necessarily false.

He is speaking of contradictorily opposed propositions and of singular propositions, saying that one must always be found true and the other always false. For he means that, among the contradictions of things that are universal and universally predicated, one is always true and the other false. The contradictions of universals predicated universally are propositions in which universals are predicated particularly. For a universal affirmation or a universal negation is predicated universally; their contradictories are particular affirmations or particular negations, when compared angularly with them.

Among these contradictions, then—those of universals universally predicated—one is always true, while the other is always found false. The same holds for singulars. For, provided that no variation of equivocation interferes, and provided that the predicate is the same, the subject the same, the time one and the same, the respect one and the same, and the manner one and the same, one proposition is always true and the other false; they divide between themselves the nature of truth and falsehood.

But among propositions concerning universals that are not predicated universally, it is not always the case that one is true and the other false.

He says that propositions which are determinate neither by a universal nor by a particular determination do not always have one true and the other false; sometimes both are found true. In propositions concerning universals that are not predicated universally, the form is:

- “A human being is white.”
- “A human being is not white.”

In this case both can be true at one and the same time. For although “human being” is universal, the name is not predicated universally. Nor is it predicated particularly, since neither “some,” “no,” nor “every” has been added.

He teaches that propositions of this kind do not divide truth and falsehood between themselves, as follows:

> For it is simultaneously true to say that there is a white human being and that there is not a white human being; and that there is a beautiful human being and that there is not a beautiful human being. For if he is ugly, he is not beautiful; and if something is coming to be, it is not yet.

This statement demonstrates that an indefinite affirmation and an indefinite negation can both be found true. For it is true to say, “There is a white human being” and “There is not a white human being.” The proof is this: if it is true to say, at one and the same time, “There is a black human being” and “There is a white human being,” and if the one who is black is not white, it is true to say simultaneously that there is a white human being and that there is not a white human being.

Again, if it is true to say simultaneously that there is a beautiful human being and that there is an ugly human being, and if the ugly person is not beautiful, it is true to say at one and the same time that a human being is beautiful and that a human being is ugly. Achilles was beautiful, whereas the lame Thersites was ugly.

Again, if it is true to say that there is a white human being, and if at the same time a human being is coming to be white, no contradiction prevents there being a white human being and, again, a human being coming to be white. But the person who is becoming white is not yet white. It is therefore true to say that there is a white human being and that there is not a white human being.

This is what he means when he says, “and if something is coming to be, and is not.” For when it is coming to be, it is not yet; nevertheless, one can say that there is a white human being and that a human being is becoming white, so that both statements are true. Both can therefore truly be said:

- “There is a white human being.”
- “There is not a white human being.”

This may suddenly appear incongruous. The reason is that “There is not a white human being” appears to signify at the same time that no human being is white. But it signifies neither the same thing nor necessarily both at once.

He responds to an unspoken human doubt. When we say, “There is a white human being” and “There is not a white human being,” both appear to be true, yet sometimes this seems incongruous. For if it is true to say, “There is a white human being,” how can it be true to say, “There is not a white human being”?

This seems incongruous to some because “There is not a white human being” appears to signify as though we were saying, “No human being is white.” But that is not true. For “There is not a white human being” does not signify the same thing as “No human being is white.” Although, when we say “No human being is white,” we simultaneously signify that there is not a white human being, the two expressions do not necessarily signify the same thing.

When we say “A human being is not white,” it is not necessary to understand that we are also saying “No human being is white,” nor are the two always simultaneous. Sometimes they are simultaneous—namely, when the universal negation is stated first. But when the indefinite negation is stated first, the universal negation is not simultaneously joined to it.

For if I say, “No human being is white,” I have simultaneously said that a human being is not white. But if I say, “A human being is not white,” the universal negation “No human being is white” has not thereby also been stated, since there may be some non-white person of whom it is said, “A human being is not white,” without everyone being non-white. Thus “There is not a white human being” and “No human being is white” are not necessarily simultaneous.

It is clear, however, that there is one negation of one affirmation. For the negation must negate the same thing that the affirmation affirmed, and of the same subject—whether of one of the singulars or of one of the universals—either universally or non-universally.

This too is an argument that an indefinite negation and a universal negation do not signify the same thing and are distinct from one another. If there is one negation of one affirmation, then the affirmation opposed to “There is not a white human being” is “There is a white human being.” But the affirmation opposed to “No human being is white” is “Some human being is white.” These affirmations are different: “There is a white human being” and “Some human being is white.” Therefore the negations proportionally opposed to them are also different.

The negation “No human being is white” is therefore distinct from the negation “There is not a white human being.” He teaches that there is one negation of one affirmation and demonstrates this as follows: the negation must negate the predicate that the affirmation predicated; and, again, with respect to the same subject, the negation must remove the predicate that the affirmation previously joined to it. If this is done, there is no doubt that one negation belongs to one affirmation.

Whether this takes place with universals predicated universally, or indefinitely and non-universally, or with singulars, the nature of the propositions is one and the same: naturally, one affirmation has only one negation. He proves this by induction.

I mean, for example:

- “Socrates is white.”
- “Socrates is not white.”

In this proposition the subject is the same and the predicate is the same. In the midst of the examples he adds:

> But if the negation predicates something else of the same subject, or the same thing of another subject, it will not be opposed, but will be different from it.

The sense is this: if the negation predicates something other than what the affirmation predicated, or if it predicates of another subject the same thing that was predicated in the affirmation, the propositions are not opposed to one another but are merely different.

For if someone says, “Socrates is debating,” and another replies, “Socrates is not walking,” the predicate is different, and the propositions are different and not opposed. This is what he means by “something else,” for the negation has predicated something other than what the affirmation predicated.

But if someone says, “Socrates is debating,” and another replies, “Plato is not debating,” the same predicate has been predicated of another subject. The propositions are different from one another and not opposed. This is what is meant by “the same thing of another [subject].”

If both are different, the propositions are even more clearly different. Having established these points, he returns to the proposed examples and opposes one negative enunciation to one affirmation, comparing angular with angular, negative with affirmative, particular with universal, and indefinite with indefinite.

To the proposition “Every human being is white” he opposes “Not every human being is white.”

To “Some human being is white” he opposes “No human being is white.”

To “A human being is white” he opposes “A human being is not white.”

After this he concludes the discussion, saying:

> That one affirmation is opposed contradictorily to one negation, and which propositions these are, has been stated. That some are contrary, and which propositions these are, has also been stated; and that not every opposition is true or false, and why and when it is true or false, has likewise been stated.

He briefly reviews the fact that some propositions are contrary and others contradictory, and says that he demonstrated more carefully in the preceding discussion which these are. It is also clear that not every opposition of an affirmation and a negation—which he now commonly and improperly calls “contradiction”—is true or false. He recalls that he has explained when and why they are not true or false.

## On One Affirmation and One Negation

An affirmation and a negation are one when one thing is signified of one thing, whether a universal is predicated universally or not in the same way.

We have already explained above what one affirmation is, and it is no burden to teach the same thing again here. Aristotle has repeated the point: one affirmation is that which signifies one thing of one thing—that is, which has a predicate of this kind and a subject of this kind, so that each signifies a single thing.

For if the predicate signifies one thing, it is simple and one. If the subject likewise signifies one thing, and not several, it is again simple and one. Accordingly, if one predicate belongs to one subject, both signify single things and not several. Thus the signification of the proposition is simple, and a proposition that signifies one thing is one.

The same must also hold in universals predicated universally and in particulars, which must be opposed to universals. He supplies examples of these as well:

- “Every human being is white.”
- “Not every human being is white.”
- “There is a white human being.”
- “There is not a white human being.”
- “No human being is white.”
- “Some human being is white.”

For he says that “Every human being is white” is one proposition, and that its opposite, “Not every human being is white,” is likewise one.

> If “white” signifies one thing. But if one name has been assigned to two things from which no one thing results, there is neither one affirmation nor one negation.

“If ‘white,’” he says, “signifies one thing; but if it signifies several things, there is neither one affirmation nor one negation.” This must also be observed in the subject, namely, that the subject’s signification be simple.

He teaches that a proposition is not one if the predicate—or any other word in the proposition—signifies several things, as follows:

> But if one name has been assigned to two things from which no one thing results, there is neither one affirmation nor one negation.

There are certain things that signify several features, from all of which, when joined together, one thing can be formed. The name “human being” signifies animal, signifies mortal, and also designates rational; but these, when joined together, form one thing, namely, a rational mortal animal. All these together constitute one human being.

There are also other names that designate two or more things of this kind from which, when joined, no one thing can result. For example, “free.” Dionysius is called free, and a person is also called free in the sense of freeborn; but “Dionysius” and “freeborn,” when joined together, produce nothing.

Therefore, he says, if either the subject or the predicate is such that it signifies several things from which no one thing can result, the proposition is neither one affirmation nor one negation. He confirms this by means of a contrived example:

> Suppose that someone assigns the name “garment” to a human being and a horse, and says, “The garment is white.” This is neither one affirmation nor one negation. For it makes no difference from saying, “A human being and a horse are white.” But this makes no difference from saying, “A human being is white” and “A horse is white.”

Let us suppose, he says, that a horse and a human being are called “garment,” and that they have this name in common. If someone says, “The garment is white,” because “garment” designates both a horse and a human being, he appears to say that a horse and a human being are white. But this is equivalent to saying, “A horse is white” and “A human being is white.”

These are two propositions, not one. Therefore the proposition “A human being and a horse are white” is also double; consequently, the proposition “The garment is white” is double as well. For the double signification of the subject—namely, “garment”—has made the propositions double.

If someone says that “The garment is white” signifies one thing because it signifies “A human being and a horse are white,” that is impossible. For no one thing results from a human being and a horse such that the proposition could signify one thing. Therefore the proposition either signifies several things or, if it does not signify several things, signifies nothing at all. For there is no such thing as a “human-being-horse” that could be spoken of and understood as one thing. This is what he says:

> If, then, these signify several things and are several propositions, it is clear that the first proposition also signifies several things or signifies nothing, for there is no such thing as a human-being-horse.

If these propositions signify several things and are several propositions, it is clear that the first proposition—that is, “The garment is white”—signifies several things or nothing. It signifies nothing because, if a proposition has an equivocal term, and the things signified by the equivocal name are joined without coming together into one substance, such a conjunction—which connects things unrelated to one another—has no intelligible meaning.

Thus, in “The garment is white,” the proposition cannot be one if “garment” signifies a horse and a human being, unless the horse and the human being together produce one thing. But these terms are such that this proposition must either be multiple or signify nothing. For if “human being” and “horse” are joined, nothing results. There is no such thing as a human-being-horse. He demonstrates this by saying:

> For there is no such thing as a human-being-horse.

He explains with complete clarity why he has now introduced this point. When he was discussing propositions that divided truth and falsehood between themselves, he added that propositions with either an equivocal predicate or an equivocal subject do not divide truth and falsehood. Both may be true, as in the propositions:

- “He is a free human being,” if “free” is referred to freeborn status;
- “He is not a free human being,” if “free” is referred to Dionysius.

The statement is therefore correct:

> Hence, in these cases too, it is not necessary that one contradiction be true and the other false.

For when the proposition signifies several things, the multiple signification in the negation and affirmation does not destroy either one through the other. But if there is one affirmation and one negation, since both cannot be true of the same thing, one must always be true and the other false.

## On Future Contingents

In the case of things that are and things that have happened, an affirmation or a negation must be true or false. In the case of universals predicated universally, one must always be true and the other false, and the same applies to singular things, as has been said. But in the case of things said of universals non-universally, this is not necessary; this too has already been discussed.

He says that, in the case of present and past things, contradictory enunciations are determinate: one is always true, and the other is always definitively false. For example, suppose someone says:

> “All the Fabii who advanced to battle against the Veientes through a private conspiracy perished.”

If this is denied in the form:

> “Not all the Fabii who advanced to battle against the Veientes through a private conspiracy perished,”

one must indeed be true and the other false; but the affirmation is definitively true and the negation definitively false. For when what happened is said to have happened, the statement is definitively true; if it is denied to have happened, the denial is definitively false.

Thus, whether the contradiction is formed in universals predicated universally by means of particular opposition, or in singulars such as Socrates and other individuals, the same applies to past things. For example:

- “Socrates was killed by poison.”
- “Socrates was not killed by poison.”

The affirmation is definitively true, and the negation is definitively false.

The same must also hold for present things. If, while Socrates is debating, someone says, “Socrates is debating,” and another denies it, then, just as Socrates’s debating is determinate with respect to the present time, so the affirmation retains determinate truth and the negation determinate falsehood.

The same applies in the case of universal affirmations and negations in which a particular affirmation or a particular negation is opposed. This is what he means when he says, “In things that are and things that have happened”—that is, in present and past things—one is always definitively true and the other definitively false, whether one is universal and the other particular.

He demonstrates this by saying that, in the case of universals predicated universally, one is always true and the other false, or in the case of singular and individual predicates. This is what he indicates when he adds, “And in the case of singular things, one is true and the other false.” But after speaking of contradictories, he adds that, in the case of indefinite propositions, it is not necessary that one always be true and the other false.

He means that, in the case of things said of universals non-universally, it is not necessary to posit one as true and the other as false. For it can happen that both indefinite propositions are true.

In singular propositions, however, and in future propositions, the situation is not the same.

Some propositions signify merely that something inheres, as when, while Socrates was alive, someone said, “Socrates is bald,” and another denied it: “Socrates is not bald.” The first posited baldness as inhering in Socrates; the second separated baldness from Socrates.

Other propositions are necessary, as when someone says, “It is necessary for the sun to return to Aries every year.” For by predicating a necessary thing that occurs necessarily, he made the entire proposition necessary.

Other propositions are contingent. Although their actuality is not yet present, it is possible for them to occur in the future. For example:

- “Alexander will dine today.”
- “Alexander will not dine today.”

When these statements are made, dining does not yet inhere in Alexander, but it may come to inhere, and it may happen that he dines today. For that reason we call them contingent: it is possible for them to occur, since the event has not yet happened.

As has been said, such events do not yet inhere; they belong to the future. But what does not yet inhere, though it can come to inhere, is not necessary, because it retains the nature of being capable either of existing or of not existing. It may happen that Alexander dines today, and again it may happen that he does not dine today.

We call this possibility of occurring or not occurring “either-way possibility” (*utrumlibet*). In such matters either alternative is possible: either the affirmation or the negation. It is not necessary that either the affirmation or the negation occur. Since the affirmation is not necessary, the occurrence of the negation is not excluded. Conversely, since the negation is not necessary, it sometimes happens that the affirmation occurs. This capacity for occurring and not occurring is therefore called “either-way possibility,” because in such cases either the affirmation or the negation may occur.

Aristotle now tries to establish by a very powerful argument that, just as in past and present matters it is necessary not merely that one of an affirmation and a negation be true and the other false, but that one be definitively true and the other definitively false, so this is not the case with what are called contingent things.

It is necessary that either the affirmation or the negation be true, but it is not necessary that either one specifically be true and the other specifically false.

If we say, “Alexander is to be washed,” and someone else denies it, saying, “Alexander is not to be washed,” then the whole matter must necessarily turn out one way or the other: either he will be washed or he will not be washed. One must be true and the other false—the affirmation, if he is washed, or the negation, if he is not washed.

But it is not necessary that the affirmation specifically be true, because the negation may occur. Nor is it ever determined that the negation must be true and the affirmation false, because the negation may fail to occur.

Thus, throughout the contradiction, one must be true and the other false. But that one specifically be true and the other specifically false, as in past and present things, is in no way possible according to the nature of these matters.

Aristotle first proves this in propositions concerning singular predicates. He then teaches that the same principle must be understood in universals. This is why he says, “In singular propositions and in future propositions, the situation is not the same”—that is, in the singular propositions with which he first deals and in future propositions, meaning contingent propositions, the manner of true and false propositions is not the same as in past and present propositions.

In past and present matters, the entire body of the contradiction is divided between truth and falsehood, and one is definitively true, so that someone who knows the matter can say with certainty that the affirmation is true, or again that the negation is true. Even if no one says so, the nature of the past or present time has already made the matter determinate, and the event itself is certain.

But in matters that are contingent and future—that is, variable and unstable—the entire body of the contradiction is divided between truth and falsehood, but this truth and falsehood are indeterminate and changeable. No one can say that the affirmation is true, since it is not necessary that the affirmation be true: the negation may occur. Nor can one say that the negation is true, since it is not impossible for the affirmation to occur. Finally, since either alternative may occur, neither one can naturally be definitively and certainly true.

The arguments by which he develops this will become clear as follows:

> For if every affirmation or negation is true or false, and everything must either be or not be, then, if one person says that something will occur in the future and another denies this very same thing, it is clear that one of them must speak the truth, if every affirmation or negation is true or false. For both will not be true simultaneously in such cases.

If everything proposed in affirmations and negations is definitively true or false, it follows that what those affirmations and negations signify must either occur or not occur. This is what he means when he says, “For if every affirmation or negation is definitively true or false.” He adds “every” precisely because he is trying to prove that, in future or contingent matters, affirmations and negations are not definitively true or false.

If one person says that something will occur and another denies it, both cannot occur. For who would say that, when one person says “Socrates will dine” and another says “Socrates will not dine,” both are true of one and the same matter?

This cannot happen. Therefore one of them will speak truly and the other falsely. Suppose that one of them is definitively true or false. If every affirmation and negation is definitively true or false, and if both the person affirming and the person denying cannot both speak truly in contradictions, then one must speak the truth and the other falsehood—one definitively true and the other definitively false.

If this holds for all affirmations and negations, so that one is definitively false and the other definitively true, whatever the true proposition says will happen must happen, and whatever it says will not happen must not happen. This is what he means when he says, “It is clear that one of them must speak the truth.” For an affirmation and a negation cannot agree in such matters—that is, in contradictory propositions.

Whatever a definitively true affirmation states must happen, and whatever a definitively true negation states must not happen. He proves this as follows:

> For if it is true to say that something is white or is not white, it must be white or not white. And if it is white or not white, it is true to affirm or deny it; and if it is not, the speaker lies, and if he lies, it is not. Therefore either the affirmation or the negation must be true or false.

He draws an example from present things to show how a judgment concerning the future might arise. He says that the consequence among things is such that the truth of a proposition follows upon the subsisting thing, and that the being of the thing of which the proposition speaks accompanies the truth of the proposition.

If this stone, or anything else, is white, it is true to say of it that it is white; and the implication is reversible. For if it is true to say of it that it is white, it is without doubt white, and it must be white. Thus the thing follows the truth, and the truth follows the thing of which the proposition is made.

Again, if this stone is not white, it is true to say of it that it is not white; and if it is true to say of it that it is not white, it cannot be the case that it is white, since it is truly said not to be white.

The same applies to falsehoods. If something is not, and someone asserts that it is, he lies. And if someone lies about something, the thing about which the lie is made does not exist. Thus, if something is not white but someone falsely says that it is white, it necessarily follows that the thing about which he lied is not white.

Truth therefore is convertible with the thing that exists, and the existing thing with the truth; falsehood is convertible with the thing that does not exist, and the non-existing thing with falsehood. If this holds in all matters, whatever is said truly or falsely is convertible with the thing that exists or does not exist, whether the proposition is a negation or an affirmation. One must always be true and the other false.

But if one is definitively true, an impossible consequence follows from this position. For everything that is or comes to be will come to be necessarily; nothing will occur by chance, and nothing that is will be capable of being or not being. Nothing will remain within the governance of free choice; everything that occurs will be necessary.

For if it is definitively true to say of anything that it will be, that thing must certainly be going to be, and it cannot happen that it does not occur. It is true to say of it that it will be, and this could not truly be said unless it were necessary that it be. Therefore, if in every affirmation and negation either the affirmation or the negation concerning the future is definitively true or false, it is necessary that either what the definitively true affirmation says will occur, or what a false negation says will occur.

The same reasoning applies to falsehood. What will not be is falsely said to be going to be; and what is falsely said to be going to be will necessarily not be. Likewise, what will be is falsely said not to be; and what is falsely said not to be will necessarily be.

Just as a necessary event follows a true proposition, so that what it says comes to pass, so a necessary event follows a false proposition, so that what the false proposition says does not come to pass.

If, then, every affirmation or negation concerning the future always definitively divides truth and falsehood, there will be a necessary outcome for the things predicated, and everything will occur—or fail to occur—by necessity. Chance, possibility, and free will will all perish.

The syllogism is therefore as follows: if every affirmation is definitively true or false, and the negation is subject to the same rule, then everything will occur according to an unavoidable necessity. But if this is so, free will perishes. That is impossible. Therefore it is not true that every affirmation or negation is definitively true or definitively false.

The claim that everything occurs by necessity if those propositions are definitively true or false is demonstrated by the following syllogism:

Every definitive truth or falsehood concerning the future establishes by necessity the occurrence or non-occurrence of the thing, whether it will occur or will not occur.

But all future propositions are definitively true or false.

Therefore, in all things there will be a necessity of occurring or not occurring.

For this conclusion Aristotle introduced the statement that follows:

Nothing, therefore, either is or comes to be, neither by chance nor indifferently; nor will it be, nor will it not be; rather, everything occurs by necessity and not indifferently—for either the one who affirms is speaking truly, or the one who denies.

For chance, and that which is “indifferent,” are thereby abolished, and free will is also taken away if everything that will happen is destined to happen by necessity. He proves the preceding conclusion—that everything occurs by necessity—by saying, “For either the one who says it is true, or the one who denies it.” If, then, the truth of things is converted into necessity, either the one who denies is speaking truly, or the one who affirms; and it is necessary that everything happen by necessity. For if things will not happen by necessity, they will not be definitely true—something he adds immediately:

“Similarly, it would either happen or not happen; for that which is indifferent is no more disposed in one way than in the other, nor will it be.”

He explains the nature of the contingent by explaining what “indifferent” means. The indifferent is that whose outcome is undetermined—that is, what may equally be or not be. This is what he means by “it would similarly happen or not happen.” For it does not have one single direct and necessary course, either toward affirmation or toward negation; rather, it is no more disposed to be so than not to be so. The indifferent is that which retains an equal course both toward happening and toward not happening. For nothing is more disposed to be so than not to be so—that is, it is equally disposed toward being and non-being. Nothing is more disposed to happen than not to happen.

Moreover, if something is white now, it was true to say earlier that it would be white; consequently, it was always true to say of anything that has happened that it is or will be.

He sets against himself a powerful argument by which he might show that affirmations and negations are definitely true or false, and says that care must be taken lest one be forced to suppose that what has already happened could truly have been said, before it happened, to be going to happen. Thus, if Socrates dined last night, it was true to say yesterday morning that he was going to dine; consequently, it would also have been definitely true if this had been predicated of him. Everything that happens, therefore, could have been truly predicated as definite. This is what he means by saying, “If something is white now, it was true to say earlier that it would be white.” For if something is white now, it was true to say beforehand that it would be white; consequently, it was also definitely possible to predicate truly whatever has happened. The outcome of the thing itself confirms this.

He again meets this objection by the same reasoning. The person who says these things cannot escape the snare of the preceding argument; the same considerations once again surround him and press him with the same difficulties.

But if it was always true to say that something is or will be, it cannot fail to be or fail to be in the future. [Col. 0334C] Now what cannot fail to happen is impossible not to happen; and what is impossible not to happen must happen. Everything, therefore, that is going to happen must happen. Nothing, then, will be indifferent or occur by chance; for if it occurs by chance, it does not occur by necessity.

With remarkable skill he brings the preceding argument back to the same difficulty. He says: If it is true that everything that has happened could have been definitely and truly predicted as going to happen, then, since the necessity of the thing follows the truth of the proposition, what was truly and definitely predicated could not fail to occur. But if it could not fail to occur, it was impossible for it not to occur. And what is impossible not to happen must happen. Its outcome, therefore, follows by necessity. Nothing, then, will be indifferent or occur by chance. For if it can occur by chance, it is not destined to occur by necessity; but if it is not destined to occur by necessity, it is not impossible for it not to happen; and if it is not impossible for it not to happen, it can fail to happen; and if it can fail to happen, it cannot be definitely and truly predicted. For whatever is definitely and truly predicted is destined to occur by necessity, whereas what occurs by chance does not occur by necessity.

But it is not possible to say that neither alternative is true—that is, that it will neither be nor not be. For first, when the affirmation is false, the negation will not be true; and when the negation is false, it is possible for the affirmation not to be true.

The diversity of future contingents consists in four distinctions. Either both what is affirmed and what is denied concerning the future will be true, or both will be false; or one will be definitely true and the other definitely false; or one will be true and the other false indeterminately. He previously demonstrated that both the affirmation and the negation cannot be true in propositions concerning future contingent matters, by saying: “It is clear that it is necessary to say that one of them is true, if every affirmation is true or false.” For both will not be true simultaneously in such cases. It is impossible for anyone to find both propositions true in the opposition of contradictories.

Now he shows that it is not even possible for both to be false. He says: “But it is not even possible for us to say that neither is true”—that is, neither the affirmation nor the negation. Both would be false, namely the affirmation and the negation, if neither what the affirmation said would happen nor what the negation said would not happen were the case. It would then follow that neither what the affirmation predicated as being would be, nor what the negation asserted as not being would not be. If someone says this, he continues, the first absurdity and impossibility is that, in a contradictory proposition, when the affirmation is false, the negation is not true; and, conversely, when the negation is false, the affirmation is also false. This occurred only in contraries, not in contradictory opposition. In contradictory opposition one of the two must always be true and the other always false.

Further, if it is true to say that something is white and large, both must be the case. If it will be so tomorrow, it must be so tomorrow. But if it will neither be nor not be tomorrow, then it will not be indifferent, as in the case of a naval battle. For it would follow that the naval battle would neither occur nor fail to occur. These, then, are the absurd consequences, and others of the same kind, if, in every affirmation and negation—whether in propositions stated universally about universals or in propositions concerning singular things—it is necessary that one of the opposites be true and the other false. Nothing would be indifferent among things that happen; everything would be and come to be by necessity.

Consequently, there would be no need either to deliberate or to conduct business, as when we say, “If we do this, that will happen; but if we do not do this, that will not happen.” Nothing prevents one person from saying a thousand years in advance that something will happen and another from not saying so. Whatever one of them could then have truly said would therefore happen by necessity. Nor does it make any difference whether someone has stated the contradiction or not stated it. For it is clear that things stand thus even if one person has not affirmed and another has not denied. Things will be or will not be, not because of denial or affirmation, nor more after a thousand years than at any other time. Consequently, if things were always so ordered that one proposition could be truly stated, it was necessary that this should happen; and everything that happens was always so disposed as to happen by necessity. For whenever someone truly says that something will happen, it cannot fail to happen; and whatever has happened was always such that it was true to say that it would happen.

He adds another point to make the claim appear even more incongruous. Whatever is predicted concerning the future, if it is truly predicted, will happen. If someone says in the present that some animal is white or large-bodied, and says this truly, that animal must be white and large-bodied. Likewise, if someone truly says of the future that this animal will become white tomorrow and will be of larger build, then tomorrow both things must occur: it must become white and become larger-bodied.

But if something is falsely predicated, what is said must not be the case, if the proposition is an affirmation. Thus, if someone falsely affirms that a naval battle will occur, the event predicated by the false affirmation must not occur. If, however, the negation is false, what the false negation predicted would not happen must happen. But if both propositions are false, what is said will not necessarily occur, because the affirmation is definitely false; nor will what is said necessarily fail to occur, because the negation is definitely false.

Thus what is indifferent in reality is altogether abolished. For both alternatives are necessary and occur by necessity, and that necessity is impossible. If one person says that a naval battle will occur tomorrow and another denies it, saying that it will not occur, and both statements are false, then the naval battle must not occur tomorrow, because the affirmation that says it will occur is false. Yet, again, the naval battle must occur tomorrow, because the negation that says it will not occur is itself false. It will therefore be necessary both that the naval battle occur and that it not occur—which is impossible and contrary to the ordinary structure of thought.

It is not true, therefore, that both propositions together—that is, the affirmation and the negation—are false. These, he says, are the absurd consequences, and others of the same kind, if someone says that, whether concerning things that are universal and universally predicated or concerning things stated as singular in propositions, one of the propositions must definitely be true and the other definitely false. Such absurdities, he says, and others like them, will follow.

He is referring to the preceding arguments, in which he showed that everything occurs by necessity if someone says that one proposition is definitely true and the other definitely false. The other absurd and impossible consequences that accompany the assertion that one proposition is definitely true are these: if someone proposes that one is true and the other false, he removes—as was said above—the indifferent character of things and establishes that everything is or comes to be by necessity, with nothing occurring by chance and nothing arising from one’s own will. It follows that neither conducting business nor undertaking any action would be useful, although all such matters are handled by deliberation; deliberation itself would be superfluous, since everything that is going to happen must necessarily happen.

For what could anyone say? “If I do this, that will happen to me; but if I do that, this other thing will happen.” Nothing prevents one person from affirming that something ought to be done and another from denying it, since everything occurs under the force of necessity. For if someone had truly predicted beforehand everything that is happening now, who could doubt that the things that have happened occurred through the unalterable force of necessity? This is what he means by saying: “Therefore whatever it was true to say at that time will necessarily be the case.”

But lest it seem incongruous that we judge the outcome of things not from the nature of the things themselves but from the truth and falsity of propositions, he removes the difficulty himself by saying: “Nor does it make any difference if someone has stated the contradiction or not stated it.” To remove and abolish deliberation—to show that human beings ought not to deliberate at all—it is of little importance whether something is predicted beforehand. Whether something is said or not said, whatever can be truly predicted must occur even if it is not predicted. It is truly predicted because it can truly be predicted; and it can truly be predicted because it will occur immutably.

Thus it will happen if it is truly predicted—not merely if it is predicted, but even if it can be truly predicted. Whether it is predicted or not predicted, whatever can be truly predicted will happen by necessity. For, he says, it is clear that if things stand in this way, whether one person affirms and another denies, if the event is going to occur, the denial does not hinder it; and if it is not going to occur, the affirmation does not help it. It will or will not happen, not because of denial or affirmation, nor will time alter this force of nature.

Things believed to occur after a thousand years will occur in the same way as things destined by necessity to occur after any period of time. Hence, if at every time things are so ordered that one proposition can definitely be called true and the other definitely false, everything that has happened or will happen occurs according to the immutable order of things.

This is what he means by saying that each thing that occurs must occur—that is, if everything were so ordered as to happen by necessity. He confirms this with the preceding argument, saying: “Whenever someone truly says that it will happen, it cannot fail to happen.” The event follows necessity, necessity follows truth, and whatever has happened was always such that it was true to say that it would happen; for the truth of the proposition arises from the necessary outcomes of things.

But these consequences are not possible. For we see that there is a beginning of future events, arising from what we deliberate and do, and that among things which are not always actual it is altogether possible both to be and not to be—similarly, among things in which both alternatives are possible, to happen and not to happen.

Many such cases are evident to us. For example, it is possible for this garment to be cut up, but it may not be cut up; rather, it may wear out first. Similarly, it is possible for it not to be cut up. For it would not be possible for it to wear out first unless it were possible for it not to be cut up. The same applies to other things that come to be, whatever are said to be possible in this way.

It is therefore clear that not everything either is or comes to be by necessity. Some things are indifferent, and in their case the affirmation is no more true than the negation; other things occur more often in one way, and in most cases one alternative occurs, although the other can also occur, while the opposite occurs only rarely.

This is a long hyperbaton: we explain it first and connect it afterward. It is clear that we are the origin of some things, such as our actions. If someone does something by deliberation, he himself is the origin of whatever he accomplishes through deliberation. Whatever is brought about by the skill of deliberation begins with the deliberating person.

Some things are not actual but potential. This potentiality does not operate by necessity—that is, something may happen without its being necessary that it happen. Thus it is possible for this or any garment to be cut with iron, but it is not necessary that it be cut. Perhaps, through use, it will become worn and will be undone by daily friction. It can therefore be cut, but perhaps it will not be cut; rather, it will wear out before it can be cut.

Again, it may happen that it is not divided. For it would not be possible for it to wear out unless it were first possible for it not to be cut. Some things, therefore, can happen, but it may turn out that they do not happen. There are thus some possible things that are not necessary, and the same reasoning applies to other things that come to be.

For whatever comes about through someone’s deliberation has the deliberating person himself as its origin, not necessity; and whatever is possible will occur in a changeable manner. Things described according to some possibility do not occur according to necessity. It is therefore clear that not everything either is or comes to be by necessity, but that some things equally come to be or fail to come to be. This is what it means for something to occur indifferently.

Other things happen more often but fail to happen more rarely. It is equally possible, for example, that one meet a friend while leaving the house; such an event occurs and occurs equally. Other things happen more frequently than they fail to happen, as when a sixty-year-old turns gray. Yet it can happen in such a way that it is not impossible for it not to happen.

This is what he means: “Other things occur more often in one way and in most cases in the other,” as when, among sixty-year-olds, becoming gray occurs more often than not becoming gray. Nevertheless, the other alternative can occur—namely, that someone does not become gray—while the first alternative is not unavoidable—namely, that he does become gray.

The hyperbaton is arranged as follows: “But if we see that these things are impossible”—that is, that we ourselves are the origin of certain things, and that whatever is possible can happen and can fail to happen—“and if it is possible both for them to be and not to be, it is clear that not everything occurs by necessity. Some things occur equally often in either way; others occur in most cases but fail to occur in fewer cases, although it is not necessary that they fail to occur.”

Therefore, it is necessary that what is, be when it is, and that what is not, not be when it is not. But it is not necessary that everything which is be, nor that everything which is not fail to be. For it is not the same thing for everything that is to be necessarily when it is, and for it simply to be by necessity. The same applies to what is not.

The same reasoning applies to contradiction: everything must either be or not be, and it must either be going to be or not be going to be. Yet one must not say, by dividing the alternatives, that one of them is necessary. I mean that it is necessary either that there be a naval battle tomorrow or that there not be one tomorrow. But it is not necessary that there be a naval battle tomorrow, nor is it necessary that there not be one tomorrow. It is necessary only that it either be or not be.

He now describes what temporal necessity is. He says that whenever anything exists, it must undoubtedly exist. For it cannot be the case that, while it exists, it does not exist. Conversely, whatever does not exist must not exist when it does not exist; for it cannot be the case that, when it does not exist, it exists.

But if, when something exists, it must exist, this is not simple necessity—such as the necessity that the sun rise absolutely—but temporal necessity. Thus, when I am sitting, it is not for that reason necessary in itself and without reference to the present time that I sit. For while I am sitting, it cannot be the case that I am not sitting, and at that time I must be sitting; but sitting itself is not necessarily inherent in me, since I can stand.

Similarly, when I am not sitting, I must then not be sitting, but not sitting is not necessarily inherent in me, since I can sit. Therefore what exists is necessary when it exists, and what does not exist cannot, while it does not exist, come to exist. Yet not everything that exists or does not exist is necessarily so apart from reference to the present time; nor is everything necessarily absent when it is not, without any mention of the present time.

Consequently, he says, it is not the same to exist with temporal necessity—as I do when I am sitting—and to exist simply by necessity—as mortality belongs to a human being. Nor is it the same for something not to exist necessarily when it does not exist—as sitting is not present in me when I am not sitting—and for something simply not to belong to me by necessity, such as having three eyes or immortality. This is what he means by saying, “The same applies to what is not.”

The reason for this statement follows: “The same reasoning applies to contradiction: everything must either be or not be, and it must either be going to be or not be going to be.” The reasoning, he says, is similar in contingent contradictions and in things that are temporally necessary when they exist but are not simply necessary.

In future and contingent contradictions, the contradiction as a whole must have one true part and one false part. Thus, if someone affirms that there will be a naval battle tomorrow, that is not necessary. And if someone denies that it will not occur, then it is necessary that it either be or not be, but it is not necessary that it be, nor again is it necessary that it not be. It is necessary only that it either be or not be.

Therefore, the contradiction as a whole will have one true part and one false part, but one of them will not be definitely true and the other definitely false. In past events we speak as follows: “Romulus founded Rome”; “Romulus did not found Rome.” One is true and the other false, but in this case the affirmation is definitely true and the negation definitely false. Since what has happened cannot fail to have happened, a contradiction concerning the past is therefore definitely true or false.

In future propositions, however, the case is not the same—namely, in those that signify contingent matters. Thus, if I say, “Philoxenus is going to dine,” and “Philoxenus is not going to dine,” one proposition is true and the other false in the contradiction as a whole, but no one can divide them by saying that either the affirmation is established as definitely true or the negation is.

Before he dines, it is undetermined and variable whether he will dine. Once he has dined, the matter becomes determinate in the past. Therefore, in future contradictions it is necessary that something either be or not be. But it is not necessary that one thing happen and the other fail to happen.

Where, then, is the similarity between contingent contradiction and temporal, rather than simple, necessity? It lies in this: just as what exists must exist when it exists, although it is not simply necessary that it exist apart from the addition of the time, so in a contingent contradiction it is necessary that either the affirmation or the negation be true, but it is not necessary that either the affirmation be simply and definitely true or the negation. Either alternative may be established by the event as the one possessing determinate truth.

Since propositions are true in the same way as things are, it is clear that, whenever things are so constituted that either alternative may occur and their contraries are possible, the contradiction must likewise be constituted in the same way. This occurs in things that are not always and are not always not. In such cases one part of the contradiction must be true or false—not this particular one or that particular one, but either one; one may indeed be more likely to be true, but it is not yet definitely true or false.

It is therefore clear that it is not necessary for every pair of opposed affirmation and negation to have one true and the other false. Things do not stand in the same way in what is not yet actual but is nevertheless capable of being or not being, as they do in what already is; rather, they stand as has been said.

Things, he says, have a certain kinship with the expressions that designate them by their proper signification. Consequently, a statement that designates and signifies a thing will be constituted in the same way as the thing itself. Thus, if the thing does not exist, the statement is false; if the thing exists, the statement is true; and if the statement is true or false, what is said either will be or will not be, so that thing and statement correspond to one another.

Therefore, if a thing has not been established with determinate necessity, the statement that designates the thing itself is not definitely true. Accordingly, in matters where it is possible not only for something to be but also for it to fail to be, affirmation and negation stand indifferently; and just as it is possible for the thing itself both to be and not to be, so too it will contingently follow that the contradiction is indefinitely true and false.

He himself explains where this occurs. He says: “In things that are not always and are not always not,” for only such things can both be and not be—things that are not always and are not always not. If they always existed, their state could not change, and therefore they would exist by necessity; if they always did not exist, it would be necessary for them not to exist.

For just as the nature of things that come to be is variable, so one part of the contradiction has variable truth. It is always true or false, but neither one part is definitely so: it is not determined that this one is true or that one, but either may be. Just as the state of things itself is changeable, so too the truth or falsity of propositions is uncertain.

It may happen that, in some cases, one proposition is true more frequently, but it is not always true; and that another is true more rarely, but it is not necessary that it always be false. He demonstrated this by saying that one is “more likely to be true,” not that it is already always true or false.
