He concludes the entire question concerning propositions about future contingents and says: “It is clear that it is not necessary for all affirmations and negations to be definitely true.” The phrase “definitely” is lacking in the text and must therefore be understood. Among propositions that are contingent and future, one is never definitely true and the other definitely false.

For, he says, things do not stand in the same way in what is not yet actual but is capable of being or not being as they do in what is already actual, but rather as has been said. Things belonging to the present time are definite in their being, and so the truth and falsity of propositions concerning them are also definite.

Things that are not yet actual but nevertheless can be or not be are future in such a way that they do not arise by necessity. They can be one way, but they can also be the other way. In such matters contradiction will stand as has been said.

It has been said that everything must either be or not be, and that it must either be going to be or not be going to be. It is not, however, necessary by division and definiteness that one of these alternatives be the case.

There were four possibilities: that both propositions be true, which he removed by saying, “For both will not be true simultaneously in such cases”; that both be false, which he overturned by saying, “But it is not even possible to say that neither is true”; or that one be definitely true and the other definitely false, which he destroyed by the argument through which he showed that everything would happen by necessity if this were admitted.

Since those alternatives are not possible, it follows that one proposition is true and the other false in the contradiction; but just as the things themselves are future in a changeable and indeterminate manner, so the utterances too are expressed with variable, non-definite truth and falsity.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0341]

## ON INFINITE UTTERANCES

[Col. 0341B]

Since an affirmation is something signifying something about something, and this is either a name or an unnamed expression, while there must be one thing and the affirmation must be about one thing—and a name has already been discussed, as has the “unnamed” expression—“not-man” is not, strictly speaking, a name, but an infinite name. For an infinite name signifies something indefinite in a certain way, just as “does not run” is not a verb, but an infinite verb. Every affirmation and negation, therefore, will consist either of a name and a verb or of an infinite name and a verb.

Apart from a verb there is no affirmation or negation. Expressions such as “is,” “will be,” “was,” “may be,” and other verbs of this kind belong among the forms that have been established. For they co-signify time.

After discussing the truth and falsity of past, present, and future time, he now sets out the force of the simple predicative proposition. He says that a simple affirmation signifies one thing about one thing—that is, it predicates one thing of one subject. The subject is either a name or what the ancients called an “unnamed” expression, but Aristotle called an infinite name.

It was said earlier that “man” is a name, whereas “not-man” was called an unnamed expression by the ancients but is now called an infinite name. Since it is clear that a simple proposition predicates one thing of one thing, every simple proposition will consist either of a name and a verb or of an infinite name and a verb.

This is what he means by saying, “For ‘not-man’ I do not call a name, but an infinite name.” A name, he says, signifies everything definite. “Not-man,” although it can designate any one of the things that are not men, is indefinite and uncertain in what it designates. Since there are many things that are not men and it can signify any one of them, it is unknown what it signifies.

Just as “does not run” is not simply a verb but an infinite verb, so names accompanied by “not” are not names but infinite names. The subjects in propositions will therefore be either names or infinite names. Apart from the verb there is no affirmation or negation. He has thus made entirely clear which part of speech holds the leading position in a simple proposition.

For if a simple proposition cannot be formed without a verb, it is evident that the entire force of a simple proposition is contained in verbs. Every proposition will contain either “to be,” “to have been,” “to be going to be,” or something of this kind. For someone who says “he runs” says that he is running; someone who says “he ran” proposes that he was running; and someone who says “he will run” says that he will be running.

If, then, every proposition retains in its utterance either being, having been, being going to be, or something similar, it is clear that it cannot exist apart from a verb. For these expressions—“was,” “is,” and “will be”—are verbs, as can be recognized from the points established and acknowledged above, when we said that verbs are those expressions that co-signify time. “Is,” “was,” and the others carry with them a signification of time.

Therefore the first affirmation and negation will be:

“Man is”; “man is not.”

Next:

“Not-man is”; “not-man is not.”

Again:

“Every man is”; “not every man is.”

“Every not-man is”; “not every not-man is.”

The same reasoning applies in the other times.

He supplies examples of simple propositions. We said above that simple propositions are those joined from two terms. Since every definite expression precedes an infinite name, and “not-man” is not a name but an infinite name, whereas “man” is definite, he correctly placed first among his examples the propositions formed from the definite name. He says: “Therefore the first affirmation and negation are, ‘man is,’ ‘man is not.’”

Then he adds affirmations and negations involving the infinite name, saying: “‘Not-man is,’ ‘not-man is not.’” After this, joining universality to them, he repeats the same propositions. He first gives those formed from a definite name, and second those formed from an infinite name.

It is therefore necessary to understand that the quantities that determine universals and particulars do not belong among the terms. Since a proposition consisting only of two terms is simple, he counts among simple propositions the proposition that says, “Every man is,” even though it contains three parts of speech. Thus determiners are not counted among the terms.

In the same way, he says that, by the same reasoning, simple propositions are formed in the other times, such as:

“Man was”; “man was not.”

“Not-man was”; “not-man was not.”

The same method applies in the other tenses as well. By “other times” he means those apart from the present—that is, the past and the future. Here, however, he has spoken only of propositions that have one subject and one predicate. He will now discuss those that have one subject and two predicates. Whether these too are simple must be discussed in the exposition of the second edition. For the present, apart from demonstration, let us understand them to be simple.

But when a third expression is predicated as an adjacent term, the oppositions are then said in two ways. I mean such a case as “a just man is”: by the third term I mean the name or verb that is added in the affirmation. Therefore there will be four propositions, two of which will stand in a consequential relation to the affirmation and negation, like privations, while the other two will not.

I mean that “is” will be attached either to “just” or to “not just”; consequently, the negation will also be formed in the same way. There will therefore be four propositions. We understand what is being said from the examples written below:

“A just man is.”

Its negation: “A just man is not.”

“A not-just man is.”

Its negation: “A not-just man is not.”

In this passage, “is” and “is not” are attached both to “just” and to “not just.” These, therefore, are arranged as was said in the *Prior Analytics*. They stand in corresponding relations.

The same applies if the affirmation contains a universal name, as in:

“Every man is just.”

“Not every man is just.”

“Every man is not just.”

“Not every man is not just.”

But it is not similarly possible for the diagonal propositions to be true, although it is possible on occasion.

One subject and two predicates: he mentions how these can occur in a proposition. For if the expression is of this form—“a just man exists”—then “just” is the predicate, while “man” is the subject. We should not now consider what was said first and what later, but rather that being just is more universal than being a man: for something that is not a man can be just, such as God; and again, something can simply exist while not being a man. Therefore, although “exists” and “just” are first spoken in the expression “a just man exists,” since they are more universal, it is not “man” that is predicated of them, but they are predicated of “man,” and “man” is their subject. From these, therefore, he says that a twofold opposition and four propositions arise, adding below examples of them: “I mean that ‘exists’ will be attached either to ‘just’ or to ‘not just.’” For if someone produces two affirmations by saying, “A just man exists” and “A not-just man exists,” these, since they are two affirmations, will have two negations.

For if we have attached the verb “exists” to “just” in the proposition “A just man exists,” and in the proposition “A not-just man exists” have again joined the same verb to “not just,” then, since the negation “not,” joined to the verb “exists,” produces the opposition of negation, it is clear that the expression “does not exist” must again be joined both to “just” and to “not just,” so that the negations become: “A just man does not exist” and “A not-just man does not exist.”

He therefore correctly said: “If ‘exists’ is attached to ‘just’ and ‘not just,’ the negation too will be attached to ‘just’ and ‘not just.’” The four propositions he identifies are these:

- “A just man exists”: in this affirmation, we have joined the verb “exists” to “just.”
- Its negation: “A just man does not exist.”
- “A not-just man exists”: here “exists” is joined to “not just.”
- Its negation: “A not-just man does not exist”: here too, in the negation “does not exist,” the expression is attached to “not just.”

What he says—“I mean that, as in ‘a just man exists,’ a third [element], a noun or verb, is attached in the affirmation”—means the following. “Third,” he says, means that the verb “exists” is attached. “Man” and “just” are two elements to which the verb “exists” is added. He said “noun or verb” because earlier too he taught that verbs themselves are nouns, at the point where he says: “Verbs, when uttered by themselves, are nouns.”

What follows contains an extremely difficult meaning, which he has compressed in his customary brevity. In the middle of the entire argument he adds: “Therefore there will be four of these, of which two will stand in relation to affirmation and negation according to consequence, like privations, while the other two will not.” Alexander, Porphyry, Aspasius, and Herminus offer several interpretations of this statement. What Porphyry, the most distinguished of the commentators, said about it will be discussed elsewhere. Since Alexander’s simpler explanation seems preferable, we have inserted it here for the sake of brevity.

Privative propositions are those that predicate a privation. A privation is present, for example, when someone says “unjust,” since this deprives a man of justice. Thus the privative affirmation is: “A man is unjust.” The privative negation is: “A man is not unjust.”

Yet the former is not a complete affirmation in meaning—for it removes something—but a privative affirmation, since it retains the form of an affirmation while predicating a privation and removing something from that of which it joins the privation, as in the proposition “A man is unjust,” where it removes justice from man. Nor is the latter a pure negation. For by driving away the privation, as in “A man is not unjust,” it retains the state, that is, justice. But since the negation removes what the affirmation predicates, although such a negation has, as it were, the meaning of restoring the state, because it removes the privation it is called a privative negation.

This, then, is what he now says. Since there are four propositions, two formed from finite terms—“A just man exists” and “A just man does not exist”—and two from infinite terms—“A not-just man exists” and “A not-just man does not exist”—the two that have an infinite term, one being an affirmation, “A not-just man exists,” and the other a negation, “A not-just man does not exist,” stand in relation to affirmation and negation—that is, they retain the same form as affirmation and negation—and are similar, in affirming or denying something, to privative propositions.

For just as “A man is unjust” is not merely an affirmation but a privative affirmation, so “A not-just man exists” is not merely an affirmation, but an affirmation containing an infinite term and a certain privation. What is meant by “unjust” is equivalent in understanding to what would be meant by “not just.” Again, just as “A man is not unjust” is not merely a negation but a privative negation, since although it restores the state, it denies the privation, so “A not-just man does not exist” is not merely a negation, but a negation formed from an infinite term.

Because it denies an infinite term, and by denying the infinite term deprives the subject, it resembles a privative proposition. For if being unjust is equivalent to being not just, then not being unjust will be equivalent to not being not just.

Thus these two propositions that contain an infinite term are, with respect to the appearance and form of affirmation and negation, similar to privative affirmations and negations. The other two, which predicate a simple and definite term, are entirely removed from any similarity to privations. For “A just man exists” is not at all like “An unjust man exists,” although both are affirmations: the former is simple, the latter privative. Nor is “A just man does not exist” joined by any rational similarity to “An unjust man does not exist,” although both are negations: the former is simple, the latter privative.

Therefore the propositions formed with an infinite term stand in the same relation as privations. “A not-just man exists” is similar to “An unjust man exists”; and “A not-just man does not exist” is similar to “An unjust man does not exist.” Privations, however, are not joined to simple propositions, or to those formed from finite terms. No one would say that “A just man exists” is equivalent to “An unjust man exists,” nor that “A just man does not exist” can be compared with “An unjust man does not exist.”

It was therefore correctly said of these four propositions that two stand in relation to affirmation and negation as privations do, while the other two are simple and lack any similarity to privations. What he calls “according to consequence” should be understood as though he had said “according to similarity.” Things that are similar to one another do not, in a certain way, depart from one another and follow one another.

The two simple propositions are therefore set out first, followed by the two privative propositions, and finally those formed from infinite terms, so that affirmations are placed under affirmations and negations under negations.

**Affirmation:** A just man exists.  
A just man does not exist.  
**Negation.**

**Affirmation:** An unjust man exists.  
An unjust man does not exist.  
**Negation.**

**Affirmation:** A not-just man exists.  
A not-just man does not exist.  
**Negation.**

[Col. 0345B] But these, he says, are arranged in this way and bear the same relation of similarity to one another as was stated in the *Analytics*, that is, the treatises of resolution. He wrote two analytical books on syllogism. In the first of these he discussed the consequence between propositions formed from a finite term and an infinite term.

There is a similarity between the simple affirmative proposition formed from a finite term and the negative proposition containing an infinite term. The affirmation “A just man exists” is similar to the negation “A not-just man does not exist.” The simple negation formed from a finite term also corresponds to the affirmation formed from an infinite term. For “A just man does not exist” is similar to “A not-just man exists.”

We have postponed explaining how these are similar to one another and how they maintain their proper order in consequence. They may nevertheless be set out briefly, so that one of their properties may be displayed. Let there be an affirmation of a finite term, with beneath it the negation of an infinite term; and likewise a negation of a finite term, with beneath it the affirmation of an infinite term.

**Affirmation:** A just man exists.  
A just man does not exist.  
**Negation.**

**Angular propositions**

**Angular propositions**

**Negation:** A not-just man does not exist.  
A not-just man exists.  
**Affirmation.**

In this arrangement, then, the negation formed from an infinite term is placed beneath the affirmation formed from a finite term, and the affirmation formed from an infinite term is placed beneath the negation formed from a finite term. Since the angular propositions are indefinite, all of them can be true together, except in cases where the predicates either belong naturally to their subjects or cannot naturally belong to them.

For example, if someone says “A man is an animal,” the proposition “A man is a non-animal,” which is angular, can never be true together with it, because animal is naturally seen to inhere in the substance of man. Again, if someone says “A man is a stone” and “A man is not a stone,” these too cannot be true together, because it is naturally impossible for a stone to inhere in man.

But when the propositions concern things that do not inhere naturally, although they can inhere, as in the examples given above, the angular propositions are always true together. For both “A just man exists” and “A not-just man exists” can be true. Again, “A just man does not exist” can be true if it is said of Sulla, and “A not-just man does not exist” can be true if it is predicated of Cato.

Thus, in the case of indefinite propositions, if the things predicated do not inhere naturally but can inhere, the angular propositions can always be true together. But if we set out propositions with a determination of quantity, they must be stated as follows: “Every man is just”; its negation, “Not every man is just.” Again: “Every man is not just”; its negation, “Not every man is not just.” These should be arranged so that the negation is beneath the affirmation and the affirmation beneath the negation.

**Affirmation:** Every man is just.  
Not every man is just.  
**Negation.**

**Not true together**

**True together**

**Negation:** Not every man is not just.  
Every man is not just.  
**Affirmation.**

[Col. 0347A] Here, then, he displays a certain difference. In the case of indefinite propositions, if the predicates did not inhere naturally but could nevertheless inhere in the subjects, the angular propositions could unquestionably always be true together. Affirmations corresponded to affirmations, and negations to negations.

But in propositions stated with a determination of quantity the arrangement is not the same. The affirmations do not correspond to one another in any way. For if “Every man is just” is true, “Every man is not just,” which is angular, can never be true; and no example will be found in which this differs.

The particular negations, however, which are angular to one another, can sometimes be true together. For in cases where the predicates do not naturally belong to their subjects but can belong to them, a particular negation can correspond to its angular particular negation. Thus “Not every man is just” corresponds to the angular proposition “Not every man is not just,” though in a different way from the indefinite propositions.

In those propositions, “A just man exists” corresponded to the angular proposition “A not-just man exists.” Again, “A not-just man does not exist” corresponded to “A just man does not exist,” which was placed angularly.

But in these propositions—that is, those determined according to quantity—the two universal affirmations, “Every man is just” and “Every man is not just,” can never be true together. The angular negations, however, which are particular—“Not every man is just” and “Not every man is not just”—are true together when the predicates can both belong and fail to belong.

Thus the angular propositions do not correspond to one another in the same way in the propositions that are determinate as they do in those that are indefinite. This is what he demonstrates by saying: “But the angular propositions cannot similarly be true. Sometimes, however, they can.”

In the former case both angular propositions agree with one another; in the latter, the angular affirmative propositions can never be true together, while the other angular propositions, which are particular negations, can sometimes be true together. His own words make this clear: “But the angular propositions cannot similarly be true. Sometimes, however, they can.”

They cannot be true together in the same way because the universal affirmations whose angular propositions they are can never be true together, whereas this occurred in the indefinite propositions. He said “sometimes they can” when comparing the angular propositions that are particular negations, provided that the predicates are not natural to the subjects but can nevertheless inhere in them.

These two propositions, then, are opposed. There are others in which “non-man” is added as a kind of subject: “A non-man is just”; “A non-man is not just.” Also: “A non-man is not-just”; “A non-man is not not-just.” There are no further oppositions beyond these; taken by themselves, they stand outside the preceding ones, using “non-man” as a term.

He again shows that there are other propositions, in some of which the infinite term is not the predicate but the subject, while in others both terms are infinite. If someone says “A non-man is just,” since “non-man” is the subject and is an infinite term, this is called a proposition formed from an infinite subject. The same is true of the negation “A non-man is not just.”

There are other propositions that appear to be formed from both an infinite predicate and an infinite subject, such as “A non-man is not just” and “A non-man is not not-just.” In these, “not just” is the predicate and “non-man” the subject; both are infinite terms.

Thus, when the verb “exists” is the third predicate, no more propositions than those already mentioned can be found. Either both predicate and subject will be finite, as in “A man is just” and “A man is not just”; or only the predicate will be infinite, as in “A man is not just” and “A man is not not-just”; or the predicate will be finite and the subject infinite, as in “A non-man is just” and “A non-man is not just”; or both predicate and subject will be infinite, as in “A non-man is not just” and “A non-man is not not-just.” Beyond these, no further propositions in which the verb “exists” is the third predicate can be found.

But those that have an infinite subject, or both terms infinite, are additional to the preceding propositions, which either have an infinite predicate or have both terms finite. Therefore they are said to stand outside the former propositions, maintain no consequence with them, and are arranged as in the proposition “A non-man is just,” where the infinite term “non-man” is used as though a finite term had been placed.

This is what he means by “using ‘non-man’ as a term.” For the infinite term is placed as though it were a finite term, since it occupies the place of a term; although, even when so placed, it is still a term. An infinite term is not simply a term, but when joined to an infinite expression it is nevertheless a term.

In propositions where “exists” is not used, he does the same thing with “to run” or “to walk,” as though “exists” had been added. Thus: “Every man runs”; “It is not the case that every man runs.” “Every non-man runs”; “It is not the case that every non-man runs.”

One should not say “Not every man,” but rather add the negation “not” to “man.” For “every” does not signify the universal itself, but signifies that something is predicated universally. This is clear from “A man runs”; “A man does not run”; “A non-man runs”; “A non-man does not run.” These differ from the preceding propositions because they are not universal.

Therefore “every” or “no one” signifies nothing other than that an affirmation or negation is made universally of a term. The remaining cases must likewise be opposed in the same way.

There are, he says, certain propositions that are predicated with “exists.” Others cannot be predicated with the verb “exists,” as in “A man walks” and “A man runs.” But in these it makes no difference whether one says them in the ordinary form—“A man runs” and “A man walks”—or predicates them with the verb “exists.” For saying “A man runs” and “A man walks” is the same as saying “A running man exists” and “A walking man exists.”

Accordingly, in such propositions it makes no difference whether they are proposed with the verb “exists” or with the activity of the verb added without “exists.” The same applies to universal propositions. When we say “Every man runs,” “Every man does not run,” “Every non-man runs,” and “Every non-man does not run,” the meaning is the same as if we said “Every man is running,” “Every man is not running,” “Every non-man is running,” and “Every non-man is not running.”

He also teaches that it makes a great difference whether the negation is joined to the given term or to the determination. If it is joined to the subject-term, it produces an infinite term, as in “Every non-man runs.” If it is joined to the determination, it produces a negation, as in “Not every man runs.”

Thus, if the negation is placed not with the universal determination but with the thing and term, it produces an infinite term, as in “non-man.” But if the negation is placed not with the thing that is universal but with the universal determination, it is a negation. For when we say “not every,” “every” is not itself a universal, but signifies that the thing of which it is said is spoken of universally.

When we say “every man,” “man” is the universal itself, while “every” is not a universal but signifies that the universal thing, namely man, has been spoken of universally. Therefore whenever the negation is placed with the determination that indicates that some universal thing has been spoken of universally, it constitutes not an infinite term but a negation.

This is what he means when he says: “One should not say ‘not every man,’ but add the negation to ‘man,’ for ‘every’ does not signify the universal, but that something is said universally.” “Every” itself is not a universal term, nor is it a term at all; added to a universal predicate, it makes that predicate be enunciated universally.

He proves that these are not universal terms but merely determinations signifying universally in the following way. When we say “A man runs,” “A man does not run,” “A non-man runs,” and “A non-man does not run,” the subjects in these propositions are universal, but they are not predicated universally.

They differ from propositions in which we say “Every man runs” and “No man runs,” because the latter predicate a universal universally, whereas the former do not predicate a universal universally. It is therefore clear that “every” and “no one” are not universals, but make what is predicated as universal be enunciated universally.

Accordingly, the same arrangements must be made with “Every man runs.” If we wish to form an infinite term, we must not say “Not every man runs,” but rather add the negation “not” to the term while preserving everything else in the proposition. The same applies if we wish to form an affirmation from an infinite term.

But if we attach the negation to the universal determination of a universal thing, the result is not an affirmation of an infinite term but a negation of a proposition formed from a finite term.

Since the negation of “Every animal is just” is the proposition signifying “No animal is just,” it is clear that these will never be true together, nor in the same subject. Their opposites, however, can sometimes be true, namely “Not every animal is just” and “Some animal is just.”

Since these, he says, are contraries, they cannot be true together or in the same subject. They can indeed be true alternately and at different times, but not simultaneously. Thus, someone might say that in the Golden Age all men were just, while in the Iron Age no man is just. Both propositions can be true, but not at the same time.

This is what he means by “neither true together.” What follows—“nor in the same”—means, namely, in the same subject. Thus, if we refer “Every living thing is just” to the heavenly powers, it is true; but if we refer “No living thing is just” to horses, both are true, though not in the same subject. The former retains its truth with respect to divine beings, the latter with respect to horses.

But the propositions that are opposed to these—that is, the particular propositions—can be true together when the higher universal propositions are both false. He has shown which these are by the clearest example: “Not every animal is just,” which is a particular negation, and “Some animal is just,” which is a particular affirmation.

The following propositions correspond to them: “No man is just,” and “Every man is not just.” The proposition “Some man is just” is opposed to “Not every man is not just.” For it is necessary that someone exist.

He previously showed that a universal affirmation and a universal negation are contraries and cannot be true together. Now he shows that the universal negation with a finite term agrees with the universal affirmation containing an infinite term, and that the particular affirmation opposed to the universal negation with a finite term agrees with the proposition opposed to the universal affirmation containing an infinite predicate, namely the particular negation retaining an infinite predicate.

They may first be set out as follows:

**Negation — Corresponding — Affirmation**

No just man exists. — Every man is not just.

**Opposed — Opposed**

**Affirmation — Negation**

Some just man exists. — Not every man is not just.

**Corresponding**

The universal negation “No man is just” has as its opposite the contradictory particular affirmation “Some man is just.” Again, the universal affirmation containing an infinite predicate is “Every man is not just.” Its contradictory opposite is the particular negation containing an infinite predicate: “Not every man is not just.”

These propositions destroy one another. But the universal affirmation containing an infinite term—“Every man is not just”—follows from the negation “No man is just.” For if it is true that no man is just, it is true that every man is not just.

Their opposites likewise agree with one another. For if it is true to say that some man is just, it is true to say that not every man is not just. For if not every man is not just, it is necessary that someone be just.

It is clear that the same applies to singular propositions. If it is true to deny what is asked, then what is affirmed is also true. For example: “Do you think Socrates is wise?” “No.” Therefore: “Socrates is not wise.”

But in universal propositions the proposition stated in the same way is not true. The negation is true, as in: “Do you think every man is wise?” “No.” Therefore “Every man is not wise” is false. But “Not every man is wise” is true. The latter is opposed to the question; the former is contrary to it.

Whenever someone asks about singular things and the person questioned denies, the questioner correctly joins the negation to the singular term and forms an affirmation from an infinite term. Thus, if someone asks, “Do you think Socrates is wise?” and the other answers “No,” the correct conclusion is: “Therefore Socrates is not wise.”

From the respondent’s negation and the infinite term “not wise,” the affirmation “Socrates is not wise” is formed. This applies to singular propositions.

But if the same is done with universals predicated universally, a negation rather than an affirmation results. If someone asks, “Do you think every man is wise?” and the other answers “No,” it is not necessary to conclude, “Therefore every man is not wise.” This is false, nor does it follow necessarily from the respondent’s answer.

Rather, the conclusion should be: “Therefore not every man is wise.” For when someone asks, “Do you think every man is wise?” and the other denies it by saying “No,” you must conclude: “Therefore not every man is wise.”

This proposition is opposed to the question, that is, contradictory to it. You asked a universal affirmation: “Do you think every man is an animal?” He answered “No.” You will conclude the particular negation: “Not every man is an animal.” This divides the true from the false.

But if, in response to the question by which you asked for a universal affirmation, he denies it and you conclude the proposition “Therefore every man is not wise,” you will make the contrary proposition rather than the contradictory one. For “Every man is not wise” agrees with “No man is wise.”

Therefore it makes no difference whether someone gives this affirmation from an infinite term or gives, from a finite term, the universal negation that does not divide truth from falsity with the universal affirmation you asked about. Only those propositions should be concluded in which one is true and the other false.

Thus the conclusion in universal propositions should not be formed in this way: when a universal affirmation has been asked and someone responds with a negation, one should not conclude a universal affirmation formed from an infinite term. Rather, one should conclude a particular negation formed from a finite term.

Those propositions that are contradictory according to infinite terms or verbs—such as “non-man” or “not just”—may appear to be negations without a noun or verb, but they are not. Every negation must be either true or false.

Someone who says “non-man,” saying no more than “man” but rather less, is neither true nor false unless something is added.

[Col. 0352A] When he was discussing propositions formed from infinite terms, he took infinite terms alone and examined what they appear to be. Expressions, he says, that are opposed according to contradictory terms or verbs—such as “man” and “non-man,” “runs” and “does not run”—whenever a finite term is compared with an infinite one, appear to be something like negations.

But this is not so, since every negation is either true or false. Someone who says “does not run,” “does not work,” or “non-man” has stated neither something true nor something false, and has perhaps signified less of the true or false than someone who uses a finite term.

For someone who establishes a finite term has not yet enunciated anything true or false, but because he has posited something finite, such an utterance is closer to truth—by positing something finite—than an utterance that posits something infinite. Just as expressions that signify something are closer to producing an enunciation than those that signify nothing, so in the case of infinite terms less truth or falsity is apparent than in all expressions that are finite.

Still less does “non-man” or “does not run” designate anything true or false unless something is added that can produce an enunciation.

What he says—that these may appear to be “negations without a noun and verb”—is added because infinite nouns or verbs are neither simply nouns nor simply verbs, and “non-man” and “does not run” appear to be negations. If that were so, they would appear to be negations without a noun or verb.

He also adds that the person who says “non-man” is “not more” true or false than one who says “man,” but rather less. For the person who says “man” establishes a thing; the person who says “non-man” removes the thing itself but adds nothing. Consequently, the person who says something infinite of man enunciates considerably less than the person who uses a finite term.

It signifies, however, that “Every non-man is just” is identical with none of those propositions, nor is its opposite, “Not every non-man is just,” identical with any of them. But “Every non-just non-man exists” signifies the same as “No just non-man exists.”

The propositions in which infinite terms are subjects, he says, signify something quite different and are not identical with propositions stated according to either finite or infinite predicates. For “Every non-man is just” signifies nothing identical with “Every man is just,” “No man is just,” “Every man is not just,” or “No man is not just.” It resembles none of these.

Nor does its particular negation, “Not every non-man is just,” signify the same as any of the propositions described above, or as any of their opposites.

But the propositions formed from two infinite terms resemble universal negations having an infinite subject. Thus “Every non-man is not just” signifies the same as and agrees with “No non-man is just.” The former retains both terms as infinite; the latter has a finite predicate but an infinite subject. The former is an affirmation formed from two infinite terms, while the latter is a universal negation formed from a finite predicate and an infinite subject.

Transposed nouns and verbs signify the same thing, as in “A white man exists” and “A man white exists.” For if this were not so, there would be several negations of the same affirmation. But it has been shown that there is one negation of one affirmation.

The negation of “A white man exists” is “A white man does not exist.” But if “A man white exists” is not the same affirmation as “A white man exists,” its negation will be either “A non-man is not white” or “A man is not white.” The former is the negation of “A non-man is white,” while the latter is the negation of “A white man exists.” Therefore there would be two negations of one affirmation.

Since, therefore, the same affirmation and negation result when the noun and verb are transposed, this is clear.

Whenever, he says, nouns and verbs are rearranged, the meanings of the propositions remain the same. But whenever the negation is rearranged, they do not remain the same. If someone says “A non-man is white” and “A man is not white,” the meaning is not the same when the negation is moved and transposed.

But when one says “A white man exists” and again “A man white exists,” the transposed nouns and verbs signify the same thing, and the affirmations are identical. For if someone denies this, it follows that one affirmation has two negations. Yet it was shown above that this cannot happen, but that one affirmation always has one negation.

The negation of the affirmation “A white man exists” is “A white man does not exist.” But if the affirmation “A man white exists” is not identical with the affirmation “A white man exists,” its negation must also be different. It would be either “A non-man is not white” or “A man is not white.”

But “A non-man is not white” has its own affirmation, namely “A non-man is white.” And “A man is not white” is the negation of “A man white exists.”

If their affirmations are different, then their negations will also be different. Therefore, if someone says that the affirmation “A white man exists” differs from “A man white exists,” he must also concede that their negations differ. The negation of “A white man exists” is “A white man does not exist”; the negation of “A man white exists” is “A man white does not exist.” Thus these two negations—“A man white does not exist” and “A white man does not exist”—would differ from one another.

Again, when we say “A white man exists” and deny it by saying “A white man does not exist,” if both are said of the same man, one must be true and the other false. Thus, if “A white man exists” is said of Socrates, then “A white man does not exist” is its negation.

It was earlier posited that “A white man does not exist” is the negation of “A white man exists.” But now we show that “A man white does not exist” is also the negation of “A white man exists,” since both divide truth and falsity between them.

For it cannot happen that, when “A white man exists” and “A man white does not exist” are said of one and the same man, both are true. If they sometimes agree in truth in the form in which they are now stated, this happens because they are indefinite, not because they are formed by transposing nouns and verbs. Thus it would follow that one affirmation has two negations. What we have said will become clearer in the diagram below.

**Contradiction**

A white man exists. — A white man does not exist.

**Contradiction**

[Col. 0354B] **Contradiction**
## A human is white. A human is not white.

Contradiction.

## ON COMBINED AND DIVIDED STATEMENTS

But to affirm or deny one thing of several things, or several things of one thing, is not one affirmation or one negation unless one thing is formed from the several. By “one” I do not mean merely that one noun has been posited. For the things do not form one thing in this way: “A human is perhaps an animal, and biped, and gentle”; yet from these there is something that becomes one. But from “white,” “human,” and “walking” no one thing is formed. Therefore, even if someone affirms one thing of these, it will not be one affirmation, but one utterance containing several affirmations. Nor, if these things are predicated of one subject, will it be one affirmation; likewise, there will be several.

The Peripatetics devoted much consideration to distinguishing which propositions were one and which were many. Accordingly, he now says that if one thing is predicated of several things in affirmative or negative propositions, or if several things are again predicated of one thing, and even if one name has been assigned to those several things, or one thing is predicated of a single name signifying several things, then, unless one thing is formed from all of them, there is neither one affirmation nor one negation.

For if someone says, “A rational biped animal is a human,” he has placed one human under several predicates. Taken separately, these are several things; but together they shape a single substance. For when animal, rational, and biped are joined, one substance is formed: a rational biped animal, which is a human. Although these expressions, taken separately, are many—for if someone says “animal,” then again “rational,” and after an interval “biped,” each signifies something distinct—when joined together they make one nature. This is what he means by: “A human is perhaps an animal, and biped, and gentle; yet from these one thing is formed.” It is as though he said: “Human” signifies several things, but only if what is signified is stated separately. For it designates animal, biped, and gentle. We say that a human is an animal, biped, and gentle; but, joined together, these constitute one gentle biped animal, which is a human.

Therefore, although several predicates are asserted of one subject, since one thing is formed from all of them, there is consequently one affirmation and one negation. But if two things are subject to one predicate, and no single thing can be formed from them, there is neither one affirmation nor one negation. For if someone says, of a certain white human who is walking, “A white walking human exists,” white and walking do not come together into one nature, nor is one thing formed from both in such a way that these two joined predicates constitute the substance of anything. Therefore, whether they are affirmed or denied, whether they are subjects or predicates, there will be neither one affirmation nor one negation, although the utterance is one. There are as many affirmations and negations in it as there are terms from which no single thing is formed.

Whether one thing is predicated of several things or several things of one thing, the procedure is the same. Thus, if someone says, “A human is a rational biped animal,” since one thing is formed from these, it is one proposition. But if someone says, “A human is a white walker,” since no single thing is formed from these, it is not one proposition.

Furthermore, if one name has been assigned to several things from which no one nature results when they are joined, and some other thing is predicated of that single name, there is neither one affirmation nor one negation. “Marinus” and “this barking thing” are both called by the one word “dog.” If someone therefore says, “A dog is an animal,” since no one thing results from what “dog” signifies when its meanings are joined—for no single substance consists of a dog, a barking thing, and a sea-dog—that proposition is multiple, signifies many things, and is not one. He therefore teaches how one ought to answer questions of this sort, saying:

> If, then, a dialectical question is a request for an answer—either for a proposition or for one part of a contradiction—and a proposition is one part of a contradiction, there will not be one answer to these. For there is not one question, even if the proposition is true. This has been stated in the *Topics*. At the same time it is clear that even the question “What is this?” is not itself a dialectical question. The questioner must provide the respondent with a choice as to which part of the contradiction he wishes to state. The questioner must determine whether this is a human or is not this.

The sense is as follows. Whoever asks a question, if he does not depart from the art of dialectic, asks in order to receive an answer. The answer may be either the whole proposition or one part of the contradiction. If someone asks, “Is the soul immortal?” the respondent will answer either “It is” or “It is not.” This is one part of the whole contradiction. For the contradiction is: “The soul is immortal; the soul is not immortal.” Thus “is” and “is not” are its parts.

But if someone asks, “Is the soul immortal or not?” the respondent may answer, if he wishes to state the whole proposition: “It seems to me to be immortal,” or again, “It seems to me not to be immortal.” Thus whoever asks for an answer asks either for a proposition or for one part of a contradiction. A proposition is one part of a contradiction: that is, every affirmation has one negation, and in two propositions there is one contradiction. Therefore, whoever utters a proposition signifying several things does not make a proposition to which there is one negation. Consequently, a question that signifies several things should not receive one answer, even if it is true.

If someone asks whether a dog is a substance, although it is true to say “It is a substance,” since both the barking dog and the sea-dog are substances, one answer must not be given to the question as it stands. One must ask: “Which dog do you mean?” If he says that he means the sea-dog, or again the barking dog, then, once the question has been made into one proposition and given one determinate meaning through that specification and definition, one answer should be supplied.

He recalls that these matters have been discussed in the *Topics*. It is likewise clear that the question “What is this?” is not a dialectical question. He explains what the form of a dialectical question should be. He says: If someone asks, “What is an animal?” this is not a dialectical question. A dialectical question must give the respondent the choice of affirming or denying what is stated. Thus, if someone asks, “Is the good contrary to the bad?” the respondent is given the choice of affirming or denying. He may say either “It is” or “It is not.”

But someone who asks, “What is an animal?” leaves no room for either affirmation or negation. What could he say when asked, “What is an animal?” To answer “Is it not?” would be inappropriate. In the same way, if he says “It is an animal,” he has not answered the question. Only that question is dialectical in which the respondent is given the choice of selecting from the question whichever part of the contradiction he wishes and stating it, either affirmatively or negatively. The questioner must determine, for example, whether an animal is a human or is not, so that the respondent may choose whichever part of the contradiction he wishes from that question.

Since some predicates are compounded so that the whole of what is predicated separately becomes one predicate, while others are not, what is the difference? It is true to say of a human, separately, “animal” and “biped,” and to say these as one: “animal biped.” It is likewise true to say “human” and “white,” and these as one. But if someone is a cithara-player and good, it does not follow that he is a good cithara-player. If, because each is said separately, both were also said together, many absurdities would follow.

For it is true to say of a human both “human” and “white.” Therefore, the whole would also be true. Again, if “white” and “the whole” could be joined, a human would be “white white,” and this would proceed to infinity. Likewise, there would be “a musical white walking person,” with the same terms repeatedly entangled to infinity. Moreover, Socrates is Socrates, and he is a human; therefore, “Socrates Socrates human.” If he is human and biped, then “human human biped.” Since simply saying that all combinations are formed produces many absurdities, this is evident. We shall now explain how combinations should be formed.

After explaining the unity of a proposition and defining what a dialectical proposition is, he now turns to cases in which several things are often truly predicated separately of one subject, but, when predicated together, are sometimes true and sometimes false.

If someone says, “Marius is bad,” that may perhaps be true. Again: “Marius is a commander,” and this too is true. Yet the two, joined together, are not true in the sense expressed by “Marius is a bad commander,” for he is the best commander of all. Again, “A human is an animal” is true, and “A human is a biped” is true, and these are also true when joined. For if someone says, “A human is an animal biped,” that is true.

He therefore undertakes to give the rule governing such cases: when things separately predicated are true together, and when they are false. The sense is as follows, while the order of the discussion is this. Some things, he says, are truly predicated together of something in such a way that their predicate is one and their form agrees with what could truthfully have been predicated separately. Thus, in the expression “animal biped,” these predicates are spoken of a human in combination and composition, and in a certain way form one predication. Separately, “animal” and “biped” can both be predicated: we say, “A human is an animal,” and again, “A human is a biped.”

There are other combinations that do not work in this way. It is true to predicate their components separately, but false to predicate them together. The difference between these cases, and when one or the other occurs, must be explained; he teaches this by examples.

Of a human, he says, it is true to predicate separately “animal” and “biped,” and also to predicate them as one, by saying “animal biped.” Likewise, of any human—for example, Socrates—we can say, “That human is white,” and again, “That one is a human”; and, joining these as one, say, “That human is a white human.”

Sometimes, however, someone is a cithara-player and unskilled, while being a good human. If it is said of him that he is a cithara-player, this is true; and if it is said that he is good, this too is true. But it does not follow that, because he is both a cithara-player and good, he is therefore a good cithara-player. He may be extremely unskilled while nevertheless being a good human.

If, merely because each predicate is stated separately, both may also be stated together, many absurdities would follow. If someone claimed that everything truly said separately could also always be said truly together, many absurd and impossible consequences would result.

For of a human we can say that he is a human, and again that he is white; so we could also say together of him, “A human is a white human.” Again, of a white human we can say that he is a human and that he is white; therefore these too would be joined: “A human is a human white white.” For if it is true to say of a human that he is a human, and of a white person that he is white, and all this may be stated truly, then “a human is a human white white” would also be true.

And if it is again true to predicate “white” of this human white, and to predicate “white” of him, and once more to predicate “white” of the human, then there would be “a human white white white,” and this would proceed to infinity.

Similarly, if it is true to say of a human that he is musical, white, and walking, and these are again stated together, we would have “a human is a musical white walker.” Again, of one who is musical, white, and walking, we can say that he is white, walking, and musical. These would then be stated together again: “a human is white white, musical musical, walking walking.” Such continual combinations produce the same superfluous expression.

The same thing happens with individuals. If Socrates is Socrates and a human, there will be “Socrates Socrates human.” If Socrates is Socrates, a human, and a biped, there will be “Socrates Socrates human biped.” Again, if this same person is biped and human, there will be “Socrates Socrates human human biped biped.” No one fails to see how absurd all this is.

We must therefore not say that everything predicated separately can always be predicated together. He therefore explains which things can truly be said together and which cannot, among those that were first said separately and truly. Up to this point, he has demonstrated only that if someone says that combinations can be made simply and in every way, many absurdities must result. How combinations are actually formed must now be established and examined.

Of predicates and the things of which they are predicated, whatever is said accidentally, whether two predicates are predicated of the same subject or one of one another, will not form one thing. Thus: “A human is white and musical.” White and musical are not the same. Both are accidents of the same subject. Even if it is true to say “white musical,” “white musical” will not thereby be one thing. For “white musical” is said accidentally. Therefore, “white musical” will not be one thing. Consequently, neither is “good cithara-player” simply one thing, whereas “animal biped” is. The latter are not accidental.

Among predicates, he says, and the subjects of which they are predicated, there are two possibilities. Either two accidents are predicated of one subject—for example, “Marius is bad,” “Marius is a commander”—or one accident is predicated of a subject and another accident is predicated of that predicate, as when someone says, “Cicero is bald; the bald man is an orator.” Here “bald” is predicated of the subject Cicero, while “orator” is predicated of “bald.”

This is what he means by: “Whatever is said accidentally, whether of the same subject or one of another.” “Of the same” means that two accidents are predicated of one subject; “one of another” means that one accident is predicated of another accident, while the accident of which it is said is itself predicated of another subject.

When predication takes this form, the accidents cannot be joined and combined into one. If someone says, “A human is white; a human is musical,” these, joined together, do not form one thing, such as “musical white.” Or if “musical” is predicated of “white,” while “white” is predicated of “human,” and one says “that white musical thing,” “white musical” is still not one thing, nor do all the things that can truly be predicated separately come together into one substance.

They appear capable of being predicated of one another because they are predicated of the same subject, not because one thing is formed from them; both are accidents. Therefore, “white musical” will not be one thing. But since the human is both white and musical, because both occur accidentally in one subject, “white” is accidentally predicated of “musical.”

Nor, again, if someone is a cithara-player and good, can he therefore be called a good cithara-player. Good and cithara-player are not such that one thing can be formed from them. But because both occur in the same subject, they are accidentally predicated of one another.

It is perhaps better to say: “A human is an animal; a human is a biped,” and to join these in saying “animal biped.” In that case the predication is made according to substance, not accidentally.

Furthermore, neither are predicates that are contained in another to be combined. Therefore, neither “white” repeatedly, nor “human human animal” or “biped,” is correct, since biped and animal are contained in human.

He has shown that things predicated separately and accidentally cannot be predicated together. Now he also teaches that even things predicated substantially are not always to be predicated together. This rule applies both to accidents and to substantial things.

Whenever something is contained in a predicate, and we wish to predicate that contained item separately as well, then, if we again join the two predicates together, the result is incongruous predication. Sometimes this is apparent in the very utterance; sometimes it is found in the nature and content of the term.

Suppose someone is a white human, and it is said of him, for example, “Callias is a white human.” If one then wishes to add “white” again, the result is highly inappropriate: “Callias is a white human white.” This is because “white” was already contained in “white human,” which had previously been predicated of Callias. This is what he means by: “Therefore, neither white repeatedly.”

Other cases do not involve this in the utterance itself but in the nature of the thing. If someone says, “Socrates is Socrates,” and again, “Socrates is a human,” and joins these together by saying, “Socrates is Socrates human,” he has not made a correct predication. For “human” was already present in Socrates, and “human” has again been predicated of Socrates.

Thus, whoever wishes to predicate these joined terms—Socrates and human—of Socrates is doing nothing other than saying, “Socrates is a human human,” because the nature of human is present in Socrates.

Again, if someone wishes to predicate “human” and then “animal” of some human, saying “A human is a human and animal,” he makes an incongruous predication. For “a human is an animal”; hence combining the two is no different from saying “A human is an animal animal.”

Likewise, if someone predicates “human” and then “biped” of a human and wishes to state these together, he will make an improper predication. Whoever says “A human is a human biped” says nothing different from one who says “A human is a biped biped,” since a human is a biped.

Therefore, neither things that are contained in another in the utterance itself, when separately predicated, nor things that are not contained in the utterance but only in nature and substance, are correctly joined.

But if they are neither accidents nor one contained in the other, and they are predicated separately, then they are correctly predicated together. If someone says of a human that he is an animal, he has spoken truly; and if he says that he is a biped, this too is true. If he joins these, he produces the expression: “A human is an animal biped,” and this is correctly predicated. For neither are they accidents, nor is one contained in the other.

“Animal” is not taken in the definition of “biped,” and therefore animal is not substantially contained in biped. Only those things are substantially contained in something that are included in its definition. Thus, animal is included in the definition of human, and biped is likewise included in the definition of human; therefore biped is contained in human.

Consequently, only those things predicated separately are correctly predicated together that are neither accidents nor contained one in another, either in the utterance or in nature. This becomes clear if the definition of one of them is considered.

For example, if the question is whether “human” and “biped” can both be predicated together of a human, “human” must be defined. If “biped” appears in the definition of human, one must say that biped is contained in human, and that both cannot be predicated together of a human. For when one says “a human is a human biped,” this is equivalent to saying “a human is a biped biped,” which is incongruous.

It is true to say of something both with qualification and simply—for example, that a certain human is a human, or that a certain white human is a white human.

Earlier he asked whether everything that is truly predicated separately is also truly said when joined. Now he examines and considers whether everything that is truly said together is also truly predicated simply.

We say that Socrates is a certain human, and again we say simply that Socrates is a human. Likewise, we say, for example, that Callias is a white human, and we predicate “white” simply of him, saying, “Callias is white.”

He therefore asks whether this holds in every case: whether everything that it is true to predicate together is also true to state simply. But this does not occur in every case. For if a predicate has something opposed to the predication itself added to it, then that predication cannot be made simply.

Thus, if someone says of the already dead Socrates, “This body lying here is a dead human,” he speaks truly; but he cannot simply say, “This body lying here is a human.” This is because something opposed to human—namely, dead—has been added to the predicate “human.” For it has been said: “This body lying here is a dead human.” In a certain way, dead and human are opposites. If we consider their definitions, this can easily be seen. A human is animate, whereas the dead are without the soul. Since there is therefore a kind of opposition according to privation and possession between human and dead, both may be truly predicated together, but one of them—“human”—cannot be predicated simply and apart from “dead” of the corpse. This is what he means:

> Not always; but whenever, in the added expression, one of the opposites is present and a contradiction follows, the simple predication is not true but false—as when one calls a dead human a human. When the opposite is not present, it is true. Or rather, whenever it is present, it is always untrue; when it is absent, however, it is not always true. For example, “Homer is something,” such as a poet. Therefore, does he exist or not? For “being” is predicated accidentally of Homer because he is a poet, but it is not predicated of Homer in itself.

Both elements—the predicate and what is added to it—are accompanied by a contradiction arising from their opposition. Since human and dead are opposites, an opposition-based contradiction accompanies and follows them. We say: “Whoever is a human lives; whoever is dead does not live.” But “lives” and “does not live” constitute a contradiction. Therefore, in predications of this kind, it is not true to predicate one element simply.

When no such opposition is joined to the predicate, it may be truly predicated simply. But even this is not always the case. More accurately, one should say that whenever the opposition is present, it is never true to call simply one of the things that are truly predicated together. When the opposition is absent, it is not always true to predicate simply one of the things that are truly said together of something.

If someone says, “Homer is a poet,” he speaks truly. But if he says, “Homer exists simply, apart from being a poet,” this is false. Yet existence and poet are not opposites. Therefore, whenever there is no opposition among the predicates, it does not always follow that something is truly predicated simply.

When opposition is present, however, it is always false to state simply and apart from the other one of the predicates that are said together. When we say of Homer that he is something—that is, that Homer is a poet—that is true. But should we also say, in himself, that he exists? Or rather, is existence predicated of Homer not simply but accidentally?

It is not because he exists, but because he is a poet—and because being a poet happens to belong to him—that we predicate that Homer is something, namely a poet. Therefore, we do not predicate of Homer that he exists in himself; rather, we predicate that he is something, namely a poet. He concludes in this way:

> Therefore, wherever there is no contrariety among the predicates, if definitions are stated in place of the names, and the predicates are predicated in themselves rather than accidentally, it will also be true to speak simply. But of what does not exist, because it is an object of opinion, it is not true to say that it is something. Opinion concerns it not because it exists, but because it does not exist.

In some expressions, opposition is not apparent when the names are stated. But once they are defined, the opposition immediately becomes clear. Thus, “human” and “dead” are not themselves opposite names, but when defined they are found to be opposites.

In such oppositions, then—or whenever something is predicated not accidentally, as existence is predicated of Homer in relation to his being a poet, which is accidental to Homer, but in itself and according to the subject itself—it is clear that whatever can truly be said together can also be truly predicated simply.

Thus, if someone says of a certain human, “This human is white,” he may have spoken truly; and again, “This one is white.” This too is true. The reason is that he did not predicate white of him because he had first said that he was a human, as existence is predicated of Homer because he is said to be a poet. Rather, he predicates white of him in itself. The predication is not accidental but is made in itself.

Therefore, it was correctly said that when, in joined predications, there is neither a certain opposition nor an accidental predication, the same things can also be predicated simply.

But of what does not exist, because it is an object of opinion, it is not true to say that it is something. Opinion does not concern it because it exists, but because it does not exist.

Some people, wishing to show that what does not exist exists in some way, used the following syllogism: “What is, is an object of opinion.” They concluded: “Therefore, what is not exists,” teaching that things that exist are rather objects of knowledge, not of opinion, while what does not exist is subject only to opinion and is not encompassed by any knowledge.

Aristotle examines this as follows. He says that something is not an object of opinion because it exists; rather, it is an object of opinion because it does not exist. But what does not exist is indeed something, although it exists not in itself but as an object of opinion. Just as Homer is something—namely, a poet—although he does not exist in himself, so what does not exist is indeed something—namely, an object of opinion, or of ignorance, or of non-knowledge—but it is not something existing in itself in nature.

## ON STATEMENTS OF MODALITY: THE POSSIBLE, CONTINGENT, IMPOSSIBLE, AND NECESSARY

After these matters have been determined, we must examine how affirmations and negations stand in relation to one another—namely, those concerning being possible and not possible, being contingent and not contingent, being impossible and necessary. For these involve certain difficulties.

Some propositions are uttered simply; others have a certain mode mixed into the statement. If someone says, “Socrates is disputing,” he has made a simple proposition. But if someone says, “Socrates is disputing well,” he has added a mode to the proposition he was stating: by saying “well,” he has indicated how Socrates is disputing.

He now examines how the affirmations and negations of propositions uttered with some mode stand in relation to one another. Thus, if someone says, “It is possible for this to happen,” and again, “It is not possible for this to happen,” how does the nature of affirmation and negation operate in these cases? The same question applies to “being impossible,” “being necessary,” “being contingent,” and “not being contingent.” Which of these are affirmations, which are negations, and which affirmation is correctly opposed to which negation?

We must examine all these matters, he says, since what had to be said concerning joined and simple predications has been settled. There is much dispute concerning the oppositions among propositions uttered with a mode. He proceeds in continuous discussion to explain what the difficulties are and how oppositions are to be found in these cases.

For if the propositions that contain expressions are mutually opposed as contradictions, then all those arranged according to being and not being are opposed in this way. Thus, the negation of “to be a human” is “not to be a human,” not “to be a non-human.” Likewise, the negation of “to be a white human” is “not to be a white human,” not “to be a non-white human.”

For if every expression must be either an assertion or a negation, it would be true to say that wood is “a non-white human.” But if matters stand in this way, then in every case where “being” is not expressly added, the expression used in place of “being” will have the same function.

Thus, the negation of “a human walks” is not “a non-human walks,” but “a human does not walk.” For there is no difference between saying “a human walks” and “a human is walking.”

Therefore, if this is so in every case, the negation of “it is possible to be” is “it is possible not to be,” not “it is not possible to be.” Yet it appears that the same thing may be possible both to be and not to be. For everything that is possible can be divided or can walk, and it is possible for it not to be divided and not to walk.

Every proposition is formed by a combination of verbs and nouns; therefore, he says, among propositions that contain such a combination—and whose nature lies in combination—only these are contradictions. Propositions are opposed according to “being” and “not being” as follows. Of the affirmation “a man is,” the negation is not “a non-man is,” but rather “a man is not,” so that affirmation and negation are “a man is” and “a man is not.” The proposition that says “a non-man is” is not the negation of the one that states “a man is,” but is the affirmation of the negation “a non-man is not.”

Again, when we say “a white man is,” the negation of this affirmation is not the proposition that says “a non-white man is,” but rather the one that says “a white man is not.” This is proved as follows: in contradictions, one must always be true and the other always false. Therefore, if the negation of the affirmation “a white man is” were “a non-white man is,” it would follow that one was true and the other false. But if someone says of wood, “It is a white man,” he speaks falsely; and if someone denies of that same wood, saying, “It is a non-white man,” this too is false. For the proposition “a non-white man is” means that a man exists, but is not white—and it is false to predicate this of wood. Thus both “a white man is” and “a non-white man is” are sometimes false, as in the case of wood; therefore they are not opposed to each other.

[Col. 0363D] Consequently, neither is the proposition “a white non-man is” the negation of “a white man is.” The negation of the latter must therefore be the proposition “a white man is not.” In these propositions one is always true and the other always false.

If this is so, contradiction is constituted according to being and not being. For when I say “a man is,” the negation is formed according to the “is,” namely, “a man is not.” Again, when I say “a white man is,” the negation is likewise formed according to the “is,” namely, “a white man is not.”

The whole sense is of this kind. In the wording of the text, however, the expressions appear obscure because of their similarity. It will become clearer if they are pronounced and understood in the following way.

For if, among propositions that contain a combination—that is, propositions whose nature lies in combination—the contradictions are opposed to one another, then those are contradictions that are arranged according to being and not being, such as the propositions we have set out above and whose examples he himself gives. Thus, of the proposition “to be a man,” the negation is “not to be a man.” This is the negation of the affirmation according to being and not being. Here one must understand that it is not the negation by which he says “to be a non-man,” so that the sense is: of the affirmation “to be a man,” the negation is “not to be a man,” not the proposition that says “to be a non-man.”

This concerns simple propositions. Again, in propositions in which a third term is predicated, of the proposition “to be a white man,” one must not understand that the negation is the one that says “to be a non-white man.” Here too one must understand instead that it is the proposition that says “not to be a white man,” so that the sense is this: of the affirmation “to be a white man,” the negation is not the proposition that says “to be a non-white man,” but rather the one that proposes “not to be a white man.” He confirms this by an example.

For, he says, if of everything there is either an affirmation or a true negation, then, since it is false to say of wood that it is a white man, it ought to be true to say of it that it is a non-white man, if this were the negation of the preceding affirmation. But both propositions are false. Therefore, this is not the negation of that affirmation.

Thus contradictions are opposed to one another according to being and not being. And if this is so, then in every case where “being” is not added, the expression used in place of “being” will have the same force.

There are certain propositions in which “being” is not added, but what is enunciated in them has the same force as if “being” were present. In the proposition “a man walks,” for example, the expression “walks” has the same force as if one said “a walking man is.” Therefore, in propositions that do not contain the verb “is,” if I attach the negation to the verb that has been placed in its stead, the resulting negation is the same as it would be if the negation were attached to “being.” Thus, in “a man walks,” “walks” is used in place of “is.”

The negation of the affirmation “a man walks” is therefore not “a non-man walks,” but rather “a man does not walk.” In the latter, the negation is joined to “walks,” which stands in the place of “is” and is joined to “man.” For “a man walks” is equivalent to “a walking man is.”

Therefore, if the same principle applies everywhere, then of the proposition “it is possible to be,” the negation is “it is possible not to be,” but not “it is not possible to be.” If, he says, contradiction is always formed according to being and not being, then contradiction must likewise be formed according to being and not being in propositions concerning possibility. In “it is possible to be,” the negation will therefore be “it is possible not to be,” not “it is not possible to be.” For if “it is not possible to be” were opposed to “it is possible to be,” the opposition would not have been formed according to being and not being.

Since he has taught above that contradiction is formed according to being and not being, one should say that the opposition belonging to “it is possible to be” is “it is possible not to be.” But another consideration now arises that moves us away from this opinion.

In all cases, either the affirmation is true or the negation is true. But in these cases both are true. For whatever can be is also capable of not being: since a man can walk, a man can also not walk; and whatever can be seen can also not be seen. Likewise, whatever can be cut or divided can also remain uncut and undivided. Thus both propositions are true of the same thing: “it is possible to be” and “it is possible not to be.”

The proposition “it is possible not to be” is to be understood as though we said, “It is possible that there be no rain today,” while it is also possible that there be rain. Why this is so, he himself demonstrates, saying:

The reason is that everything that is possible in this way is not always actual. Therefore, its negation will also belong to it. What is capable of walking can therefore also not walk, and what is visible can also not be seen.

But it is impossible for opposite propositions about the same thing to be true. Therefore, “it is possible not to be” is not the negation of “it is possible to be.” Otherwise, either the same thing would be affirmed and denied simultaneously, or affirmations and negations would not be opposed according to being and not being. If the former is more impossible, the latter must be preferred.

The point is this: whatever is possible in such a way that it exists actually and in operation cannot in any way not be. The heavens, for example, always actually possess motion. They are always moving, and we say, “It is possible for the heavens to move,” because the motion of the heavens is actual—that is, it is continually being performed in them. They are always moving. With this sort of possibility, therefore, the proposition “It is possible for the heavens not to move” cannot apply, since this is impossible.

Thus, in everything that exists actually, the two propositions “it is possible to be” and “it is possible not to be” cannot in any way both apply. In things that are not always actual but are capable of being, however, both propositions can apply: “it is possible to be” and “it is possible not to be.” Rain is not always actual, but it is possible for it to occur at some time; therefore, it is possible for it at some time not to occur.

This, then, is why both propositions are found to be true: in possibilities that are not always actual, both being and not being can occur. Therefore, if the negation of “it is possible to be” is “it is possible not to be,” then affirmation and negation will simultaneously be true of the same thing. Whatever possesses the affirmation—so that it is possible to be—will also possess the negation, so that it is possible not to be. Thus what is capable of walking, that is, what can walk, can also not walk; and what is visible, that is, what can be seen, can also not be seen.

But it is impossible for opposed and contradictory propositions about the same thing to be true simultaneously. In all cases, either the affirmation is true or the negation is true.
