If, therefore, by forming negations according to being and not being in propositions expressed according to some mode, we make both the affirmation and negation true, which cannot happen, then it must rather be said that negations according to being and not being are not to be formed, but according to the mode. If it is more impossible for affirmation and negation to be true simultaneously, then it is preferable that contradiction not be formed according to being and not being, but rather according to the mode.

When he says, “If the former is more impossible, the latter must be preferred,” this does not mean that both alternatives are impossible—namely, that affirmation and negation should be true and that contradiction should not be formed according to being and not being. The former, that affirmation and contradiction should be true simultaneously, is impossible. But that affirmation should not be formed according to being and not being, and that negation should not be formed according to being and not being, is not impossible. He therefore uses “more impossible” as though he were saying “less possible.” It is less possible for opposed propositions about the same thing to be true than for negations not to be formed according to being and not being.

Accordingly, what is more possible must be chosen: negations should be formed according to the mode rather than according to being and not being. He explains this more clearly, saying:

The negation of “it is possible to be” is “it is not possible to be,” and not “it is possible not to be.” The same reasoning applies to “it is contingent to be,” for its negation is “it is not contingent to be.”

These two propositions cannot be found true simultaneously. For if something is possible to be, it cannot be impossible for that same thing to be. This should not be considered only in the case of possibilities; the same reasoning applies everywhere.

In the case of “it is contingent to be,” its negation is not the proposition “it is contingent not to be.” The latter agrees with “it is contingent to be,” whereas the negation is the proposition “it is not contingent to be.” These two cannot be found true simultaneously.

[Col. 0366C] The same applies in other cases, such as the necessary and the impossible. For, just as in those cases “being” and “not being” are added, while the underlying thing is sometimes white and sometimes a man, so it is here.

“And in the other cases,” he says, “the same procedure must be followed.” The negation must be joined to the mode: if the expression is “contingent,” it must be joined to contingent; if “possible,” to possible; if “impossible,” to impossible; and if “necessary,” to necessary.

For, he says, just as in propositions that are not expressed according to some mode, and that propose that something is, “being” and “not being” are additions—that is, predicates—while the underlying things are the subjects, as in “a man is” and “a man is not,” where “man” is the underlying thing and “is” and “is not” are additions and predicates; or as in “it is white” and “it is not white,” where “white” is the underlying thing and “is” and “is not” are added and predicated—so in propositions expressed according to some mode, “being” is likewise the subject, as though it were a certain thing, while the mode is predicated of it.

For when we say “it is possible for there to be rain today,” we make “being” the subject and predicate “possible.” Thus the whole force of the proposition lies in the predicate, both in simple propositions and in propositions outside the modes, whenever we predicate that something is. In “a man is,” for example, the verb “is” contains the whole force of the proposition. Likewise, in propositions expressed according to a mode, the mode contains the whole proposition, whether it is “possible,” “contingent,” “impossible,” or “necessary.” These are predicated, while other things are said to be subjects.

This is what he means when he says:

“Thus in this place ‘being’ and ‘not being’ become subjects, while ‘being possible’ and ‘being contingent’ are additions determining, just as ‘being’ and ‘not being’ determine truth and falsity in those cases, so here in ‘being possible’ and ‘being not possible.’”

For just as, in simple propositions, if negations are formed according to being and not being, one is always true and the other always false, so in propositions expressed according to a mode, if the negation is adapted to the mode itself—as to an addition or predicate—truth and falsity are divided and determined in the additions.

This is what he means when he says: “Likewise, these also, in the case of ‘being possible’ and ‘being not possible.’” For opposition formed according to possible and not possible determines truth and falsity in the same way as negation according to being and not being in simple propositions and in propositions expressed outside the modes.

He therefore sets out, in all propositions expressed according to a mode, the oppositions of the corresponding negations. He says:

Of “it is possible not to be,” the negation is not “it is not possible to be,” but “it is not possible not to be.” Of “it is possible to be,” the negation is not “it is possible not to be,” but “it is not possible to be.” Therefore, “it is possible to be” and “it is possible not to be” will seem to follow one another. The same thing is possible to be and not to be. “Possible to be” and “possible not to be” are not contradictions of one another. Rather, “it is possible to be” and “it is not possible to be” are never simultaneously true of the same thing, for they are opposed. Likewise, “it is possible not to be” and “it is not possible not to be” are never simultaneously true.

Similarly, of “it is necessary to be,” the negation is not “it is necessary not to be,” but “it is not necessary to be.” Of “it is necessary not to be,” the negation is “it is not necessary not to be.” Of “it is impossible to be,” the negation is not “it is impossible not to be,” but “it is not impossible to be.” Of “it is impossible not to be,” the negation is “it is not impossible not to be.”

To demonstrate that “it is possible not to be” is not merely not the negation of “it is possible to be,” but is not a negation at all, he finds another negation for it. For of “it is possible not to be,” which he has placed in the position of an affirmation, the negation is found to be “it is not possible not to be,” with the negation added to the mode. Hence, he says, it follows that “it is possible to be” and “it is possible not to be” follow one another; for the same thing is possible to be as is possible not to be.

The reason they can follow one another is that they are not opposed. If they were opposed, they would destroy one another rather than follow one another, and would disagree rather than agree, as happens with “it is possible to be” and “it is not possible to be.” These are so separated from one another that they cannot be true simultaneously.

This occurs because they are opposed. Therefore, whenever the complete nature of opposition is to be established, the negation must be placed according to the mode. He explains this very clearly by adapting negations to the individual modes of the propositions and thereby producing complete natural oppositions.

But, he says, “it is possible not to be” cannot be simultaneous with “it is not possible not to be.” For it is clear that they are opposed, since the negation has been placed according to the mode, which is “possible to be.”

In the case of “it is necessary to be,” one should not say that its negation is the proposition “it is necessary not to be.” For the latter has another negation, since it is itself an affirmation, and its negation is the proposition “it is not necessary not to be.” Rather, “it is not necessary to be” must be opposed to “it is necessary to be”; and, as has been said, “it is not necessary not to be” is opposed to “it is necessary not to be.”

Likewise, of “it is impossible to be,” one should not say that the negation is “it is impossible not to be,” but rather “it is not impossible to be.” For “it is impossible not to be” is an affirmation, and its negation is “it is not impossible not to be.”

Universally, then, as has been said, “being” and “not being” must be placed as subjects, while the affirmation and negation that form the proposition must be added to “being” and “not being.” These are to be regarded as opposed expressions:

- possible / not possible
- contingent / not contingent
- impossible / not impossible
- necessary / not necessary
- true / not true

He gives a universal rule, saying that the same procedure must be followed in all cases, as we have already stated: “being” and “not being” are to be placed as subjects, while the modes themselves are to be made the affirmation and negation.

This is what he means by “the negation and affirmation that form these.” The modes themselves—that is, “possible,” “contingent,” and the others—are arranged as affirmations, while the negative adverb is joined to them for the purpose of forming negations. These are then added to “is” and “is not.”

Thus, just as in relation to one thing—namely, “man”—the verb “is” is an affirmation and “is not” a negation, and is predicated in propositions that are outside the modes, as in “a man is,” so in propositions containing a mode we must place “is” and “is not” as subjects. The modes themselves are then predicated of the subject we have arranged according to being and not being, either affirmatively when they are stated simply or negatively when they are accompanied by negation.

We must therefore regard as opposed expressions and negations those formed according to the modes; all their negations and affirmations are to be arranged in opposition.

## Oppositions

[Col. 0367]

| Affirmation | Negation |
|---|---|
| It is possible to be | It is not possible to be |
| It is contingent to be | It is not contingent to be |
| It is impossible to be | It is not impossible to be |
| It is necessary to be | It is not necessary to be |

## Oppositions

[Col. 0369]

| Affirmation | Negation |
|---|---|
| It is possible not to be | It is not possible not to be |
| It is contingent not to be | It is not contingent not to be |
| It is impossible not to be | It is not impossible not to be |
| It is necessary not to be | It is not necessary not to be |

[Col. 0369A] What he added concerning “true” and “not true” applies to the demonstration of all the modes. If someone says “the true is,” its negation is not “the true is not” (*verum non est*), but rather “the not-true is” (*non verum est*). Otherwise, the negation of “the true is not” would be “the not-true is not” (*non verum non est*).

The consequences are formed as follows when the propositions are arranged in order. “It is possible to be” is followed by “It is contingent to be,” and this in turn is convertible with it, as are “it is not impossible to be” and “it is not necessary to be.”

“It is possible not to be” and “it is contingent not to be” are followed by “it is not necessary not to be” and “it is not impossible not to be.”

“It is not possible to be” and “it is not contingent to be” are followed by “it is necessary not to be” and “it is impossible to be.”

“It is not possible not to be” and “it is not contingent not to be” are followed by “it is necessary to be” and “it is impossible not to be.”

Having completed everything that was discussed concerning the oppositions of the modes, he turns to their consequences. For this is what he says: which propositions of the modes mentioned above are followed by which propositions, and with which do they agree? We have arranged these into four orders and set out the consequences of the propositions in a single sequence. These points should first be noted, so that the reader may more easily understand what Aristotle says.

The following should be considered from the accompanying table:

- It is possible to be.
- It is possible not to be.
- It is contingent to be.
- It is contingent not to be.
- It is not impossible to be.
- It is not impossible not to be.
- It is not necessary to be.
- It is not necessary not to be.
- It is not possible to be.
- It is not possible not to be.
- It is not contingent to be.
- It is not contingent not to be.
- It is necessary not to be.
- It is necessary to be.
- It is impossible to be.
- It is impossible not to be.

He himself sets out the consequences described above. We must briefly give the reason why these propositions follow one another.

“It is possible to be” means that it may at some time be; this is “it is contingent to be.” Whatever is contingent to be is not impossible to be. But whatever is not impossible to be is not thereby necessary to be. It is not impossible for there to be rain today, but it does not therefore follow that there must be rain today. Whatever is not impossible to be is therefore not necessary to be. This is the first order of consequence.

The second order has the following consequence: “It is possible not to be” means that it may happen not to be; therefore, it is contingent that it should at some time not be. Whatever is possible not to be is contingent not to be. Whatever is contingent not to be may happen not to be; but whatever may happen not to be is not impossible not to be. Therefore, whatever is contingent not to be is not impossible not to be. But whatever is not impossible not to be is not thereby necessary not to be. For it is not impossible that there be no rain today; rain may occur, but it does not therefore follow necessarily that it will not rain today. Thus whatever is not impossible not to be is not necessary not to be. This is the character of the second order.

Let us now proceed to the third. Whatever is not possible to be cannot happen; and whatever cannot happen to be at some time is not contingent to be. Therefore, whatever is not possible to be is likewise not contingent to be. But whatever is not contingent to be must not be; whatever is never contingent can never be; and whatever can never be must necessarily not be. Thus whatever is not contingent to be is necessarily not to be.

But whatever is necessarily not to be cannot happen; and whatever cannot happen is impossible to happen. Therefore, whatever is necessarily not to be is impossible to be.

The fourth order is as follows. Whatever is not possible not to be cannot happen not to be; and whatever cannot happen not to be is not contingent not to be. Since, for example, it is not possible for the motion of the heavens not to be, it is not contingent that the heavens should not move. Therefore, whatever is not possible not to be is likewise not contingent not to be.

But whatever is not contingent not to be must be, as in the case of the heavens. The heavens must move, since it is not contingent that they should not move. Whatever must be cannot happen not to be; therefore, whatever must be is impossible not to be.

This, then, is the ordered consequence of the propositions established by Aristotle, concerning which he will shortly argue at greater length.

Thus “impossible” and “not impossible” follow “contingent” and “possible,” and “not contingent” and “not possible,” in a contradictory but reciprocal order. For “it is possible to be” is followed by the negation of “impossible,” while the affirmation follows the negation. “It is not possible to be” is followed by “it is impossible to be.” For “impossible to be” is an affirmation, while “not impossible to be” is a negation.

He now examines some points concerning the preceding account of the consequences. In the preceding tables, the negation of “possible” was followed by the affirmation of “impossible.” Conversely, the affirmation of “possible” was followed by the negation of “impossible.”

The same applies to “contingent.” The affirmation of “impossible,” namely “it is impossible to be,” was followed by the negation of “possible,” namely “it is not possible to be.” Again, when “impossible” was negated by the expression “it is not impossible to be,” this was followed by the affirmation of “possible,” namely “it is possible to be.”

The same applies to “contingent.” The affirmation of “impossible,” namely “it is impossible to be,” was followed by the negation of “contingent,” namely “it is not contingent to be.” The negation of “impossible,” namely “it is not impossible to be,” was followed by the affirmation of “contingent,” namely “it is contingent to be.”

Thus these propositions follow one another, but reciprocally. The affirmation of “impossible” follows the negation of “contingent” and of “possible.” The negation of “impossible” follows the affirmation of “possible” and of “contingent,” as the following table shows.

[Col. 0371]

| Affirmation | Contradiction | Negation |
|---|---|---|
| It is impossible to be | It is not impossible to be | — |
| It is not possible to be | It is possible to be | — |
| It is not contingent to be | It is contingent to be | — |

[Col. 0371A] This is why he says that the contradictory propositions follow one another, but reciprocally: all the contradictions placed in opposition are contradictory. “It is impossible to be” and “it is not impossible to be,” “it is contingent to be” and “it is not contingent to be,” and “it is possible to be” and “it is not possible to be” are contradictions.

They follow one another reciprocally because affirmation does not follow affirmation, nor negation negation; rather, negations follow affirmations and affirmations follow negations. This becomes clearer when one returns to the preceding table.

The sense is therefore this: the order and sequence of the expressions is as follows. Aristotle says that the contradiction consisting of “impossible” and “not impossible” follows “contingent” and “possible,” which are two affirmations and follow one another, as do “not contingent” and “not possible,” which are two negations. They follow one another contradictorily, since the contradictions are drawn into opposition, but reciprocally, so that affirmation follows negation and negation follows affirmation.

The reason is as follows. “It is possible to be,” which is an affirmation, follows the negation of “impossible,” namely “it is not impossible to be.” Conversely, “it is not possible to be,” which is the negation of “possible,” follows the affirmation of “impossible,” namely “it is impossible to be.” For “it is impossible to be” is an affirmation, while “it is not impossible to be” is a negation.

The same applies to contingent propositions. This, then, has been said concerning the consequence of possible and impossible propositions. He now discusses the consequence of necessary and possible propositions.

The necessary must be considered as follows. It is clear that the consequences do not arise in the same way, but that contraries follow one another, while contradictions stand outside. For the negation of “it is necessary not to be” is not “it is not necessary to be.” Both may be true of the same thing: what is necessary not to be is not necessarily to be.

What he says means this: in the propositions “impossible” and “not impossible,” “not possible” agreed with “impossible,” while “possible” agreed with “not impossible.” Thus the contradiction of “impossible” was followed, in reciprocal order, by the contradiction of “not possible.”

In propositions that predicate “necessary,” whether affirmatively or negatively, when the proposition that agrees with “possible” is followed, the contradiction of the proposition predicating “necessary” does not follow the contradiction of “possible.” Rather, the contrary of the contradiction of the proposition predicating “necessary” agrees with the contradiction of “possible.”

By “necessary propositions” I now mean propositions that, although they do not signify necessity in reality, nevertheless predicate “necessary,” whether affirmatively or negatively. The sense is therefore this: if one of the propositions predicating “necessary” agrees with a possible proposition, the contradiction of the proposition predicating “necessary” does not follow the contradiction of the possible proposition. Rather, the contrary of the contradiction of the proposition predicating “necessary” agrees with the contradiction of the possible proposition.

First, however, let us set out which propositions are contradictory and which are contrary. Of “it is necessary to be,” the contradiction is “it is not necessary to be,” while the contrary is “it is necessary not to be.” Again, of “it is necessary not to be,” the contradiction is “it is not necessary not to be,” while the contrary is “it is necessary to be.” Let these therefore be set out around the same subject, with the contraries and contradictions arranged together, so that what we have to say may be clearer.

| Relation | Proposition |
|---|---|
| Affirmation | It is necessary to be |
| Contradiction | It is not necessary to be |
| Negation | — |
| Contrary | It is necessary not to be |
| Affirmation | — |
| Affirmation | It is necessary not to be |
| Contradiction | It is not necessary not to be |
| Negation | — |
| Contrary | It is necessary to be |
| Affirmation | — |

[Col. 0371C] Having set these out suitably and briefly, we must show what sort of consequence can occur between them and the possible propositions.

“It is possible to be” is followed by “it is not necessary to be.” For whatever is possible to be is not necessary to be; whatever is possible to be is also possible not to be; but whatever is possible not to be is not necessary to be.

Therefore, “it is possible to be” is correctly followed by “it is not necessary to be.” But the negation of “it is possible to be”—namely, “it is not possible to be”—is not followed by the affirmation of “it is not necessary to be,” namely “it is necessary to be.” For the latter is the contradiction of the necessary affirmation. Nor can the propositions “it is not possible to be” and “it is necessary to be” be said to agree. Rather, the contrary follows: “it is not possible to be” is followed by “it is necessary not to be.”

But “it is necessary not to be” is not the contradiction of “it is not necessary to be.” Both can be true simultaneously of the same thing. Since it is necessary that cold fire not exist, it is not necessary that cold fire exist.

Consequently, these are not contradictions. The contrary of “it is necessary to be” is “it is necessary not to be.” “It is necessary to be” is the contradiction of “it is not necessary to be.” Therefore, the contradiction of “it is possible to be,” namely “it is not possible to be,” is not followed by the contradiction of “it is not necessary to be,” namely “it is necessary to be,” but by “it is necessary not to be,” which is contrary to “it is necessary to be.” The latter is itself the contradiction of “it is not necessary to be.”

This will be clearer from the following table.

| Proposition | Relation | Proposition |
|---|---|---|
| It is possible to be | Contradiction | It is not possible to be |
| It is not necessary to be | Contradiction | It is necessary to be |
|  | Contrary | It is necessary not to be |

[Col. 0373A] Since “it is possible to be” and “it is not possible to be” are contradictions, and “it is possible to be” is followed by “it is not necessary to be,” the contradiction of “it is necessary to be” does not follow the contradiction of “it is possible to be.” Rather, the contrary of the contradiction of “it is not necessary to be” follows it.

For if “it is not necessary to be” is the contradiction of “it is necessary to be,” while its contrary is “it is necessary not to be,” then “it is necessary not to be” follows “it is not possible to be,” which is the contradiction of “it is possible to be,” and which is followed by “it is not necessary to be.”

It is therefore correctly said that contradictions stand outside, while contraries agree with contradictions. For “it is possible to be” and “it is not possible to be,” which are contradictions, are followed by “it is not necessary to be” and “it is necessary not to be,” which are not contradictions, since both can be found true simultaneously of the same thing.

But if contradiction followed contradiction, then, just as “it is not necessary to be” follows “it is possible to be,” so “it is necessary to be” would follow “it is not possible to be.” This is incongruous. Since it does not follow, its contrary follows. The contrary of “it is necessary to be” is the proposition “it is necessary not to be.”

The same applies to “it is possible not to be,” whose contradiction is “it is not possible not to be,” a point Aristotle left unmentioned. “It is possible not to be” is followed by “it is not necessary not to be.” But its contradiction, “it is not possible not to be,” is not followed by the affirmation that is the negation of “it is not necessary not to be,” namely “it is necessary not to be.” For the negation of “it is necessary not to be” is “it is not necessary not to be.” But the contrary of that affirmation, “it is necessary not to be,” namely “it is necessary to be,” follows the negation “it is not possible not to be.”

The corresponding table is therefore as follows:

| Proposition | Relation | Proposition |
|---|---|---|
| It is possible not to be | Contradiction | It is not possible not to be |
| It is not necessary not to be | Contradiction | It is necessary not to be |
|  | Contrary affirmation | It is necessary to be |
[Col. 0373] Thus it comes about in a manner unlike what previously occurred in the case of things possible and impossible. There, contradiction followed contradiction, but conversely: affirmation followed negation, and negation followed affirmation. Here the manner is not the same. For although the upper propositions are contradictory, and the lower negation follows the affirmation, the contradictory affirmation does not follow the negation; rather, the contrary of that affirmation follows it. If one reads attentively, one will recognize that this has been fully set out according to the argument; and he discloses why this happens.

The reason why it does not follow in the same way as the others is that the contrary of “impossible” is equivalent to “necessary.” For what is impossible to be must necessarily not be—not merely “not to be,” but rather “not to be.” What, however, is impossible not to be must necessarily be. Therefore, if those propositions follow “possible” and “not possible” in the same way, these follow conversely, since “necessary” and “impossible” do not signify the same thing, but—as has been said—conversely.

The reason why the consequence according to contradiction does not occur in the same way in these propositions as in those concerning what is impossible and not impossible is that everything necessary is impossible in the contrary manner. For what is impossible to be is necessary not to be; what is impossible to be is not necessary to be. No one would say, “It is necessary to be” of what is impossible to be. Therefore it is not necessary to be, but rather what is impossible to be is necessary not to be. Thus, by conversion, the impossible and the necessary have the same force. For what, when joined to “to be,” makes “impossible,” makes “necessary” when joined to “not to be.” Therefore what is impossible to be is necessary not to be.

Again, what is impossible not to be is necessary to be. For example, it is impossible for heat not to be present in fire; therefore heat must be present. Hence here too the same conversion applies: what “impossible” effects according to “not to be” has the same force as “necessary” when posited according to “to be.” Accordingly, “necessary” and “impossible” have the same force in contrary directions.

If, then, “impossible” and “necessary” have the same force in contrary directions, it is clear why the propositions “necessary,” “possible,” and “not possible” do not follow one another in the same way as the propositions “possible” and “not possible” were followed by “impossible” and “not impossible.” For “not impossible to be” follows “possible to be.” Again, “possible to be” is accompanied by “not necessary to be.” On the other hand, since “impossible to be” follows “not possible to be,” “necessary,” which has the same force as “impossible” in the converse order, follows it: what is impossible to be is necessary not to be. Consequently, “not possible to be” is also followed by “necessary not to be.”

Again, since “not impossible not to be” agrees with “possible not to be,” it is also compatible with “not necessary not to be.” Since what is said to be impossible not to be is associated with “not possible not to be,” and since “necessary,” when rendered in the converse manner, has the same force as “impossible not to be,” what is impossible not to be is followed by what we call “necessary to be.” This, in turn, is followed by what we propose as “not impossible not to be,” namely, “not necessary not to be.” The matter is shown by the following arrangement:

| Agreeing | Agreeing |
|---|---|
| Not impossible to be | Impossible to be |
| Possible to be | Not possible to be |
| Not necessary to be | Necessary not to be |
| Agreeing | Agreeing |
| Not impossible not to be | Impossible not to be |
| Possible not to be | Not possible not to be |
| Not necessary not to be | Necessary to be |

[Col. 0375B] The cause, then, of the different consequence is that the conversion of the propositions “impossible” and “necessary” has been made in contrary directions. But after considering these matters in this way, he in a sense reproaches himself and turns the discussion toward another property of the consequence.

Or is it perhaps impossible to posit the contradictions of “necessary” in this way? For what is necessary to be is possible to be; otherwise its negation would follow. For it is necessary either to affirm or to deny. Therefore, if it is not possible to be, it is impossible to be. Thus what is necessary to be would be impossible to be—which is plainly incongruous.

“Perhaps,” he says, “we went wrong in arranging the consequences in this way.” For at that point we arranged matters so that what is possible would follow what is not necessary, placing the negation of the necessary after the possible. Now, however, he says that this must be reversed: one must not begin with the possible and subordinate to it the negation of the necessary; rather, the necessary must be placed first and the possible second. For the proposition that contains “necessary” seems also to contain “possible,” since what is necessary is likewise possible.

What is necessary to be is possible to be. For if someone denies this and says that what is necessary does not entail possibility, the negation of possibility will accompany what is necessary. For if it is false to say “It is possible to be” of what is necessary to be, it will be true to say “It is not possible to be.” In every case there is either an affirmation or a negation: if one is true, the other is false; if one is not true, the other must immediately be true. But we have said that “not possible to be” follows “impossible to be.” Therefore what is called “necessary to be” would be “impossible to be.” This, however, is incongruous. Therefore it is not true that “not possible to be” agrees with “necessary to be.” Hence possibility follows what is necessary.

But “possible to be” is followed by “not impossible to be,” and this in turn by “not necessary to be.” Thus it follows that what is necessary to be is not necessary to be—which is plainly incongruous.

We say that “possible to be” agrees with “necessary to be.” But this again seems false when one considers and examines the matter, because “not impossible to be” also agrees with and is compatible with “possible to be.” Yet what is called “not impossible to be” is followed by “not necessary to be,” whereas we proposed that “possible to be” should agree with and follow “necessary to be.” Therefore “not necessary to be” would follow “necessary to be,” and “impossible” would agree with it.

What, then, are we to establish amid these difficulties? “Possible to be” cannot agree with “necessary to be.” Otherwise “necessary to be” would be followed by “impossible to be.” But if “possible to be” agrees with “necessary to be,” it again follows that what is necessary is not necessary. This, however, is false. The way in which the matter stands will be explained shortly. For the moment, reversing the earlier sequence, we say that “possible to be” cannot follow “necessary to be,” nor do these propositions agree with one another: “possible to be” and “necessary to be.” Aristotle puts the matter as follows:

“But neither does ‘necessary to be’ follow ‘possible to be,’ nor does ‘necessary not to be.’ For both are possible to the former, whereas if either of the latter is true, those former propositions will not yet be true, since it is possible both to be and not to be. But if it is necessary either to be or not to be, it will not be possible to do both. It remains, therefore, that ‘not necessary not to be’ follows ‘possible to be.’ For this is true even of ‘necessary to be,’ since it is the contradiction of what follows ‘not possible to be.’ For the latter is followed by ‘impossible to be’ and ‘necessary not to be,’ whose negation is ‘not necessary not to be.’ Thus these contradictions also follow according to the foregoing method, and nothing impossible results from their being so posited.”

He teaches that “possible” does not agree with “necessary to be,” nor again with “necessary not to be.” For what is necessary to be cannot not be, whereas what is necessary not to be cannot be. When we say “possible to be,” we mean it as though it were also possible not to be. Thus what we call “possible to be” has both aspects: it is possible to be and possible not to be. But what says “necessary to be” removes not-being, and what says “necessary not to be” removes being. Therefore, if these propositions are true—“necessary to be” and “necessary not to be”—both the propositions “it can be” and “it can not be” are false.

For the proposition “necessary to be” destroys “possible not to be,” while the proposition “necessary not to be” overturns “possible to be.” Therefore neither follows the proposition “possible to be”: neither the proposition that says “it is necessary to be” nor the one that says “it is necessary not to be.”

The sense is indeed this. The verbal formulation, however, is as follows: “Neither does ‘necessary to be’ follow the proposition ‘possible to be,’ nor does ‘necessary not to be.’” For both are possible to the latter—that is, both to be and not to be are possible. What can be can also not be. But if either of the following is true—“necessary to be” or “necessary not to be”—the propositions “possible to be” and “possible not to be” will not be true. For what is possible to be is also possible not to be.

If, then, neither “necessary to be” nor “necessary not to be” follows “possible to be,” it remains that “not necessary not to be” agrees with it. This follows “possible to be.” Whatever can be, need not not be. For example, since a human being can walk, it is not necessary that the human being not walk.

This is true, he says, also of “necessary not to be.” That is, the proposition “not necessary not to be” is true as a contradiction opposed to “necessary not to be,” which it contradicts. Hence the latter follows “not possible to be.” The following arrangement must therefore be made:

| Affirmation | Impossible to be | Contradiction | Not impossible to be |
|---|---|---|---|
| Negation | Not possible to be | Contradiction | Possible to be |
| Affirmation | Necessary not to be | Contradiction | Not necessary not to be |

[Col. 0377A] For “not necessary not to be” is the contradiction of “necessary not to be,” which follows and agrees with “not possible to be.” The latter agrees with “impossible to be,” which in turn follows the final proposition, “necessary not to be,” whose contradiction is “not necessary not to be.” For “necessary not to be” is the affirmation, and “not necessary not to be” is the negation.

Accordingly, this consequence too occurs according to contradiction. “Impossible to be” and “not impossible to be” are contradictory; but the negation “not possible to be” follows the affirmation “impossible to be.” The affirmation “possible to be” follows the negation “not impossible to be.” “Not possible to be” and “possible to be” are contradictory; but the affirmation “necessary not to be” follows the negation of the possible, namely “not possible to be,” while the negation “not necessary not to be” follows the affirmation of the possible, namely “possible to be.”

Thus, when the propositions are arranged in this way, nothing impossible occurs. Everything agrees and is compatible, and, according to the foregoing relation between the possible and the impossible, affirmations and negations follow one another contradictorily in converse order.

The overall sense is this. Since neither “necessary to be” nor “necessary not to be” agrees with “possible to be,” it remains that “not necessary not to be” follows “possible to be.” It is true to say “not necessary not to be” of “necessary not to be,” and we understand that it is its contradiction. “Not necessary not to be” is the contradiction of what follows the negation of the possible, namely “not possible to be.” This is “necessary not to be,” since “not possible to be” is followed both by “impossible to be” and by “necessary not to be.” The negation of the affirmation “necessary not to be” is “not necessary not to be.” But this follows both “not impossible to be” and “possible to be.” Therefore these contradictions follow one another according to the stated method, namely, contradictorily and in converse order; and, when they are posited and arranged in this way, nothing impossible results.

Someone might ask whether “possible to be” follows “necessary to be.” For if it does not follow, its contradiction—“not possible to be”—will follow. And if someone says that this is not the contradiction, he must say that “possible not to be” itself is the contradiction of “necessary to be.” But both are false of “necessary to be.” Yet again, “possible to be cut” seems to be the same as “possible not to be cut,” and “to be” the same as “not to be.” Thus what is necessary to be would be capable of not being, which is false.

He has returned to the earlier question concerning the consequence of the possible and the necessary. He says that it may be doubted whether “possible to be” agrees with the proposition “necessary to be.” For whether one says that it agrees or that it does not agree, something impossible and incongruous results in either case.

If someone says that “possible to be” does not agree with “necessary to be,” it will agree with the negation of possibility, namely “not possible to be.” But if this agrees with it, then “necessary to be” will be the same as “not possible to be.” If someone again denies this and says that “not possible to be” is not the negation of “possible to be,” but rather that the negation is “possible not to be”—although that is false—even so, the latter cannot agree with “necessary to be.” For “possible not to be” becomes the negation of “possible to be.” If the affirmation “possible to be” does not follow the affirmation “necessary to be,” the negation “possible not to be” follows it. But it is false to say that what is necessary to be is possible not to be. What is necessary to be cannot be said to be capable of not being; rather, it cannot fail to be.

If someone says again that “necessary to be” follows and agrees with “possible to be,” an incongruity will likewise be found. For what is possible to be is also possible not to be. Therefore what is necessary to be would be possible not to be, and what is necessary would be contingent. But what is possible and contingent can readily be turned in either direction, toward being or toward not-being. What is necessary to be, however, has its occurrence closed off from the contrary statement. If it is necessary to be, it cannot happen that it not be; and if it is necessary not to be, it is impossible that it be.

Therefore whoever says that “possible to be” agrees with “necessary to be,” on the ground that what is possible to be can also not be and is therefore contingent, says that what is necessary to be can not be and is contingent—which is incongruous.

Resolving this difficulty, he proceeds as follows:

“But it is clear that not everything possible, whether to be or to walk, has the capacity of its opposite. There are cases in which this is not true. First, among things whose powers are not according to reason: fire is capable of heating and possesses an irrational power. Powers according to reason are therefore powers of many contraries, whereas irrational powers are not all so; but, as has been said, it is not possible for fire to heat and not to heat, nor is this possible for anything else that always acts. Other things, however, even according to irrational powers, can receive opposites simultaneously. This has been said because not every power is a power of opposites, nor is this true of everything said according to the same species.”

“There are many things,” he says, “that can be only what they are and cannot also be something else that they are not. Many things do not change from what they are. Others, however, can change, as the heavens can do only one thing, namely, move; its opposite, not moving, is impossible for them.

“Therefore not everything that is possible either to be or to walk—that is, not everything of which some possibility is predicated—also has the capacity of opposites, so that it could both do what it does and do the opposite, namely, not do what it does. In some things powers are predicated in such a way that it is not true to say of them that they can also do the opposites. This is the case even with things that possess a power apart from reason, such as fire.

“For fire is hot apart from reason. There is no account to give of why fire is hot; it is hot by nature. Although it can be hot, it cannot have the opposite state, namely, it cannot fail to be hot. Hence the very same powers that are according to reason are powers of many contraries.

“Powers according to reason—that is, powers in which there is some rational account—are not powers of one possibility only, but of many and contrary possibilities. For example, the power of medicine is to heal. Since the physician heals according to reason, and the physician possesses a rational power of healing, he can not only heal but also not heal. He can do more than one thing, and the opposite of what he can do is also possible: the opposite of healing is not healing. These are called contraries, for affirmation and negation are distinguished by contrariety.

“Irrational powers, however, are not all like this. As has been said, it is not possible for fire both to heat and not to heat. Nor, he says, does every power according to reason also have the capacity of opposites. Among irrational powers, however, the situation is not uniform. For although the power of iron to become hot is irrational—for iron does not become hot through reason, since it has no reason—it can also fail to become hot. Fire, on the other hand, although its power to heat is irrational, cannot both heat and fail to heat.

“Therefore it was correctly said that irrational powers do not all lack contraries, but only some of them, such as fire, which, although capable of being heated, is not capable of not being heated. He shows which irrational powers have only one capacity and not the opposite by adding, ‘nor anything else that always acts.’ For fire cannot do the opposite, but not fire alone: everything that is always actual can do only one thing, not many or opposite things. Thus the sun is always actually luminous and therefore cannot fail to shine; snow is always actually cold and therefore can never be non-cold.

“Whatever always acts is always in actuality in respect of what it is. It is clear that, just as fire does not admit cold, so those things also cannot admit their opposites. Fire cannot do the opposite because it always has its proper power in actuality. It is always hot.

“Not all irrational powers, however, as has been said, have only one capacity and cannot do the opposite. There are some irrational powers that can do both, such as the power to cut skin or not to cut skin. Skin can be cut, but it can also not be cut; these are opposites. Therefore some opposites are possible even according to irrational powers.

“The earlier statements were made to show that fire and whatever is always actual cannot do opposites, and to teach that not every power is a power of opposites. Some powers are truly such that they are actual and can do only one thing, and therefore are distinct from the power of opposites. This is found not only in powers according to reason but also in the species called irrational. For among the things called irrational powers, some can do not only what they are able to do but also the opposite, whereas others can do only one thing. Skin can be cut and not cut, and therefore it has the power of opposites; fire, however, although hot, cannot be cold, and therefore it has no power of opposites.”

Some powers are equivocal. “Possible” is not said in one uniform sense. In one sense it is said because something is true in actuality: for example, “It is possible to walk,” because someone is walking; and, generally, “It is possible to be,” because something is already actual and is. In another sense it is said because something may perhaps occur: “It is possible to walk,” because someone may perhaps walk. This latter power belongs only to movable things; the former belongs also to immovable things.

In both cases it is true to say “It is not impossible to walk” or “It is not impossible to be,” both of what is already walking and acting and of what is capable of walking. Thus it is not simply true to predicate “possible” of what is necessary, although one of its senses is true. Therefore, since the particular follows the universal, what exists necessarily entails the possibility of being, but not in every sense.

A brief division of possibility must be made. “Possible” is said in two ways. One kind of possibility is that in which something, while not being, can come to be; for example, while a human being is sitting, he is not walking but can walk. Another kind is that in which something, while being, is capable of being; for example, since fire is hot, it can be hot, and since a human being is sitting, he can sit.

The latter possibility has two species. In one, something is actual but can nevertheless not be: if someone is sitting, he can sit in such a way that he can also not sit. In the other, something, while actual, cannot not be: fire is hot, but it cannot be non-hot.

This is what he means by saying that some powers are equivocal. “Possible” is not said simply. In one sense it is said because something is true in actuality—that is, because it is and comes to be in actuality. Thus it is possible to walk because someone is already walking, and everything that is in actuality is altogether possible to be.

In the other sense, something may perhaps occur: it is possible to walk because someone will walk, that is, because something is not presently so but can become so. “It is possible to walk” may mean not that someone is now walking, but that someone is going to walk. These are things said not according to actuality but according to mere capacity: they are not yet actual, but can become so.

This possibility belongs only to movable things, whereas the former belongs also to immovable things. By “movable” he means all natural things subject to generation and corruption. Whatever is generated can be corrupted, and such things are always in motion, since generation itself is a kind of motion, as is corruption. Therefore, in things that are generated and mortal, the possibility that is not spoken of according to actuality but according to what is not yet but can be is truly found.

Such a possibility never occurs except in things that come into being and undergo death. Immovable things—those fixed and established in their own nature so that they cannot change or move—namely divine things, possess only the possibility that is spoken of according to actuality. Thus the sun is immovable in substance, although movable in place. Since it is immovable in substance and does not change or move away from it, it possesses light in such a way that it cannot fail to possess it.

In both kinds of things, movable and immovable, it is true to say “It is not impossible to be.” What is not yet actual but can be—for example, when a human being is not walking but retains the capacity to walk—is not impossible to be. Nor is it impossible for the sun to have light, which it eternally possesses in actuality.

Thus, in both movable and immovable things, the statement “not impossible to be” is true. The same is truly said both of what is acting and of what can act: it is not impossible to be. What is walking is not impossible to walk, and what is capable of walking—namely, what can walk—is not impossible to walk.

But since we said that the possibility which is according to actuality has two species, one in which something is actual and can never not be—for example, fire is actually hot and cannot ever be non-hot—and another in which something is actual but can nevertheless not be—for example, someone who is sitting can sit but can also not sit—the possibility according to actuality of this latter kind is in no way predicated of what is necessary.

What is actual and necessary to be exists in such a way that it cannot not be. This is what he means by saying that it is not simply true to say “possible” of what is necessary, where “possible” means what is actual but can nevertheless not be. The other sense, however, is true: what is actual in such a way that it cannot not be, and is always actual, is rightly predicated of what is necessary. What is necessary to be exists, but cannot not be.

Since the particular follows the universal, what exists necessarily entails what is capable of being, but not universally. For, he says, just as the species always follows the genus and its part follows the universal, so, if a human being exists, an animal exists—that is, if there is a particular and a species, the universal and genus must also exist.

If this is so, the proposition “possible to be” follows and agrees with the proposition “necessary to be,” but not every meaning of “possible” follows what is necessary. Things that can be although they are not yet actual are in no way predicated of what is necessary. What is necessary not only must be but also is. This is what he means by “but not universally.” For the possibility that is predicated of what is necessary already exists; it cannot be the possibility of what is not yet but may come to be.

Perhaps “necessary” and “not necessary” are the principle of all propositions, whether of being or of not being; the other propositions must be considered as their consequences.

“This,” he says, “is perhaps the principle for discovering the consequences of these propositions. If one places ‘necessary’ and ‘not necessary’ first, and ‘possible to be’ and the rest second, this is natural. For what is necessary is prior. If what is necessary consists in what is always actual, and what is always actual is eternal, while eternal things are the principles of all things, then we shall rightly take the beginning of our investigation into the consequences of these propositions from the necessary things, and, on account of them, from the negations of the necessary, namely, from the not-necessary.

“It is therefore established that the principles for discovering the consequences of these propositions must be taken from ‘necessary’ and ‘not necessary.’ For the propositions ‘possible to be’ and ‘contingent to be,’ as well as ‘necessary’ and ‘not necessary,’ follow as though they were naturally prior. Hence he says: ‘And the others,’ that is, ‘possible to be’ and ‘contingent to be,’ must be considered as their consequences. They must be considered as though ‘necessary’ and ‘not necessary’ preceded, while ‘possible’ and ‘contingent’ and the rest followed.”

It is clear from what has been said that what exists necessarily is actual. Therefore, if eternal things are prior, things that are actual are prior to things that exist in capacity; and things that are without capacity are actual, such as the first substances. Other things are actual together with possibility; these are prior by nature but posterior in time. Others are never actual but exist only in capacity.

“It is evident,” he says, “that everything that exists necessarily always exists according to actuality. Since fire is necessarily hot, it is also always actually hot. Therefore, if eternal things are prior to all non-eternal things, then things that are always actual are also prior to things that exist in capacity.

“He divides all these things. Some exist apart from capacity, in actuality alone, as the sun is moved not according to a capacity but in actuality. It does not possess the capacity for motion that is not yet actual but could become actual; it possesses actuality alone and is excluded from the capacity that exists apart from actuality.

“The first substances are also actual but never potential. By ‘first substances’ he means the divine and eternal substances, not those that he showed in the Categories to be first substances, namely, individuals. There he was speaking of those that are first for us; now he is speaking of those that are first by nature, namely the divine and eternal things.

“Others,” he says, “are actual together with capacity,” that is, they possess actuality and at some time possessed a capacity. A house that has already been built was once capable of being built; it first possessed the capacity, according to time, and afterward actuality. By nature, however, actuality is prior to capacity. For art itself anticipates actuality in thought: it first designs and produces the form of the house in itself. Therefore actuality is prior to capacity by nature, while capacity is prior to actuality in time.

“Others,” he says, “are never actual but always exist in capacity.” For example, number is potentially infinite, since one can always increase it indefinitely, but it is not actually infinite. Whatever number one takes is actually finite; whatever number one names is necessarily encompassed by a finite quantity, whether ten or one hundred. It is infinite in capacity because one can make it increase without limit, but no number is actually infinite.”

## Which Enunciations Are More Properly Called Contraries

Whether the contrary is affirmation opposed to negation, or affirmation opposed to affirmation—for example, whether “Every human being is just” is contrary to “No human being is just,” or to “Every human being is unjust”; and, in the case of “Callias is just,” whether the contrary is “Callias is not just” or “Callias is unjust”—which of these is contrary?

For if what is expressed in speech follows what is in the soul, and if there the contrary opinion is contrary—for example, “Every human being is just” is contrary to “Every human being is unjust”—then the affirmations expressed in speech must likewise stand in the same relation.

But if there too the opinion of the contrary is not contrary, then affirmation will not be contrary to affirmation; rather, the negation that has been mentioned will be contrary. Therefore we must consider which false opinion is contrary to the true opinion: whether the opinion of the negation, or the opinion that something contrary is the case.

I mean it as follows. There is a true opinion concerning the good, namely, that it is good. There is another false opinion, namely, that it is not good; and another, that it is evil. Which of these is contrary to the true opinion? And if one is contrary, in what respect is it contrary?

The issue under discussion is as follows. He asks why the proposition “Every human being is just” appears to have as opposites both “No human being is just” and, again, “Every human being is unjust.” Which of these is more properly contrary to the superior affirmation “Every human being is just”: the proposition “Every human being is unjust,” or the universal negation “No human being is just”? Likewise, which is contrary to the proposition “Callias is just”: “Callias is unjust,” or “Callias is not just”?

He proceeds to discuss the matter in this way. If, he says, things expressed in speech serve those that exist in the soul and agree with them in signification, then whatever is found in the soul’s opinions must also appear in speech. If, in the realm of opinion, the opinion that every human being is just has as its opposite—and most especially as its contrary—the opinion that every human being is unjust, then in speech too the affirmation “Every human being is just” will be more contrary to the affirmation “Every human being is unjust.” But if, in the realm of opinion, the former is not more opposed to that opinion than is the opinion “No human being is just,” then in speech too the universal negation will appear to be contrary. Thus both the affirmation “Every human being is unjust” and the negation “No human being is just” will be contrary to “Every human being is just.”

When he says, “But if even there the opinion of the contrary is not contrary,” the point is this. To be just and to be unjust are contrary, although they belong to the categories of possession and privation. Yet the predication now under discussion—that is, being unjust—is taken as the contrary. Therefore, if in the realm of opinions the affirmation of the contrary, namely of the unjust, is not contrary, then in speech also the affirmation will not be contrary; rather, the negation “No human being is just” will be contrary.

“Therefore,” he says, “we must consider to which false opinion the true opinion is contrary.” If something is good, it is true to say of it that it is good. Against this proposition it is false to say that it is bad, and it is also false to say that it is not good. We must therefore determine which of these is more contrary to the true affirmation that what is good is good: the false opinion that what is good is bad, or the opinion that what is good is not good.

This is what he means when he says: “I mean it in this way: there is a certain true opinion concerning the good, namely, that it is good; another is false, namely, that it is not good; and another, that it is bad. Which of these, then, is contrary to the true opinion?” That is, we must inquire whether it is the opinion that denies what exists, or the opinion that posits what does not exist, and which of these appears more contrary to the opinion that affirms what is.

But what he adds—“and if there is one, according to which it is contrary”—means the following. Some contraries have an intermediate between them, while others do not. In the case of contraries that have an intermediate, if someone denies one contrary, it does not follow that the other contrary is thereby understood. Since there is something between white and black, if someone says, “It is not white,” he has not thereby shown that it is black; it may be red, or anything else located among such contraries.

But in the case of contraries that have no intermediate, it makes no difference whether one denies the proposed thing or affirms its contrary. There is no difference between saying “It is not day” and saying “It is night.” To be not-day is the same as to be night, since there is nothing between night and day.

Thus, in such cases, the affirmation of the contrary has the same force as the negation of the proposed thing. This is what he now says: even if in some cases such propositions are found that the negation of the proposed thing and the affirmation of its contrary have the same force and signify the same thing, we must still ask according to which enunciation the proposition is more contrary—whether according to the one that says “It is not day,” or according to the one that asserts “It is night.” We must therefore investigate which of these, although both signify one thing, is more contrary to the proposition that says “It is day.” This is what he means by “and if there is one according to which it is contrary”: even if at some point the negation of a thing and the affirmation of its contrary signify one and the same, we must determine according to which of them the proposition is more contrary to the prior enunciation.

[Col. 0384A]

To suppose that contrary opinions are defined by the fact that they concern contraries is false. The opinion that the good is good and the opinion that the bad is bad may perhaps be one and the same opinion, and it is true—whether there are several opinions or one. These objects are contraries, but the opinions are not contrary because they concern contraries; rather, they are contrary because they differ contrarily.

[Col. 0384B]

The person who treats contrary propositions first correctly determines the nature of contraries. Some have thought that opinions are contrary when they concern contrary things, but Aristotle rejects this. He says that the definition is false if it determines that opinions are contrary because they concern contrary things.

For since good is contrary to bad, we can have the opinion that the good is good, and this opinion is true. We can also judge that what is bad is bad, and this opinion too is true. The opinions that the good is good and that the bad is bad concern contrary things; nevertheless, both are true. But two opinions cannot be contrary while both are true. It was therefore incorrectly defined that opinions are contrary when they concern contrary things.

When he says, “For the opinion that the good is good and the opinion that the bad is bad may perhaps be one and the same opinion, and true,” either he refers “the same” to what follows—that true opinions, insofar as they are true, are the same—or he means that it may be one and the same opinion to judge that what is good is good and that what is bad is bad. Whether they are one opinion or several, they cannot be contrary, precisely because they are simultaneously true.

These opinions are contrary, but they are not contrary because they concern contraries; rather, they are contrary because they are contrary. He means that the opinions existing in the soul are contrary, not because they concern contrary things, but because they make contrary judgments about one and the same thing. Thus, if one person judges of the good that it is good, while another judges of that same good that it is bad, these opinions are contrary and cannot both be true at the same time.

They concern one and the same subject, namely the good, but judge of it now well, now badly—in other words, they make contrary judgments.

[Col. 0384C]

If, then, there is an opinion that the good is good, and another that it is not good, there is also another opinion that it is something else which it is not and cannot be. None of the other opinions should be posited as contrary—not those that judge what is not to be, nor those that judge what is to be not. For both classes are infinite: those that judge what is not to be, and those that judge what is to be not.

Rather, we must consider the opinions in which error occurs. These are the opinions from which generations arise, and generations arise from opposites. Therefore error also occurs among opposites.

[Col. 0384D]

The beginning of this argument is the proposition that he takes as admitted and demonstrated: that one thing cannot have several or infinitely many contraries. Therefore one thing will have one contrary.

There is, then, an opinion of the good that it is good, and this opinion is true. There is also an opinion of the good that it is not good, and this opinion is false. There may also be an opinion that judges what is good to be something which it is not—for example, if someone says of what is good that it is bad, or that it is a quantity, or that it is something else that it is not. But the things that can be said of the good while not being the good itself are infinite.

Again, we can judge that many things do not belong to the good although they do. We can say that the good, though honorable, is not honorable; though useful, is not useful; or though desirable, is not desirable, along with many other possibilities. Thus the things we can judge of the good—that it is something which the good itself is not—are infinite. The things which we judge not to belong to the good although they do are likewise infinite.

Therefore neither the opinions that judge the good to be what it is not nor those that judge the good not to be what it is should be posited as contrary to the opinion that the good is good. This is what he means when he says: “None of the others is to be posited”—neither those that judge the good to be what it is not, such as saying of the good that it is bad, useless, or shameful, nor those that judge the good not to be what it is, such as saying of that same good that it is not desirable or not honorable.

Both classes are infinite: those that judge the good to be what it is not, and those that judge the good not to be what it is. These must therefore be rejected and not taken as the contrary opinion, because they are infinite, whereas the opposition of contraries is always determinate.

He then goes on to say which opinions should be posited as contrary: “But those in which there is error; and these are among the things from which generations arise.” Thus, he says, the only opinion that should be posited as contrary to the opinion that the good is good is the one in which error is first found.

He shows where error is first found by saying that error is most readily found among the things from which generations arise. Generation always proceeds from opposites. Whenever something becomes white, it does not come to be from the sweet, the hard, or the liquid, but from the non-white. Whatever becomes sweet does not come to be from the hot, the cold, the black, or any other quality, but from its opposite, namely the non-sweet. The same applies in other cases.

Every generation therefore arises from what the thing previously was not: the sweet from the non-sweet, the white from the non-white, and the hot from the non-hot. If generations arise from opposites, and error occurs among the things from which generations arise, then the first error occurs among opposites.

The first error is to judge that something which is does not exist. The second is to judge that something which is not exists. Thus, in the case of what is good, the first error is to judge that it is not good; the second is to judge that what is good is bad.

[Col. 0385A]

Consequently, contrariety must be posited most especially where the first error occurs. The first error occurs among the things from which generations arise. By generations I mean the things that come to be from what they previously were not.

Generations arise from opposites; therefore the first error occurs among opposites. But where the first error occurs, the most truly contrary opinions must be posited. Opposites, then, are most truly contraries. “To be good” and “not to be good” are opposites. Therefore “not to be good” is contrary to “to be good,” not “to be bad.” He confirms this with a further argument.

[Col. 0385B]

If what is good is both good and not bad—good in itself, and not bad accidentally—then the opinion that is true in each case is more truly the opinion according to the thing itself. If it is true, then the opinion that what is good is not good is false in itself, whereas the opinion that it is bad is false accidentally. Therefore the opinion of negation is more false concerning the good than the opinion of the contrary.

The argument is formed with great subtlety. The good, he says, is both good and not bad. One of these predicates belongs to it in itself, immediately and naturally—namely, that it is good. The other belongs to it accidentally—namely, that it is not bad. For it happens to what is good that it is not bad. Therefore what is good possesses being good more naturally than being not bad. The former belongs to it in itself; the latter, as has been said, accidentally.

If this is so, the proposition that affirms what belongs to a thing in itself is truer than the proposition that affirms what belongs to it accidentally. It belongs to what is good in itself to be good; accidentally, it belongs to what is good not to be bad. It is therefore truer and more immediate to say of the good that it is good than to say of it that it is not bad.

If this is so, the opinion that is false in itself will properly appear more false than the opinion that is false accidentally. For if the proposition that belongs to the thing in itself is more truly true, then the proposition that is false in itself is more immediately false.

This is what he means when he says: “In each case, the proposition that is in itself is more true, and, if it is true, more false.” Just as the proposition that is in itself is more true, so the proposition that is false in itself is rightly said to be more false—that is, the proposition that denies what is true in itself.

Thus the proposition “What is good is not good” is false in itself.

[Col. 0385C]

He connects this with the preceding argument in continuous exposition. It was said above that the opinion which judges what is good to be good is an opinion in itself. Therefore the opinion that judges what is good not to be good is false, and it is false concerning what is true in itself.

The opinion that judges what is good to be good is true in itself; but the opinion that judges what is good not to be good destroys the truth of the opinion that is true in itself. Whoever judges that what is good is good has an opinion according to the nature of the good itself. For this reason opinions of this kind are called opinions “in themselves.”

The opinion that what is good is not good will therefore also be false in itself, since it appears to remove the proposition’s truth in itself. But the same good is not bad accidentally. It is true to say of the good that it is not bad, but this is true accidentally. It happens to the good not to be bad.

The opinion that judges what is good to be bad removes “not bad” from what is good and destroys what is true of it accidentally. For the opinion that what is good is not bad is true, though accidentally. Therefore the opinion that what is good is bad is false accidentally, since it removes a proposition that is true accidentally.

Since what belongs in itself is more immediate than what belongs accidentally, the falsity of the opinion that is false in itself will be more deceptive than the falsity of the opinion that is false accidentally.

The opinion that judges what is good not to be good destroys the truth that belongs to it in itself. The opinion that judges what is good to be bad destroys, with respect to the thing’s accidental character, the truth that it is not bad. Therefore the opinion that says what is good is not good is more false than the opinion that says what is good is bad.

[Col. 0385D]

The person who has the contrary opinion is most false concerning individual things. For contraries are those that differ most widely with respect to the same thing. If one of these is contrary, and contradiction is more contrary, it is clear that contradiction will be the contrary.

[Col. 0386A]

The question was whether the affirmation of the contrary or the negation of the proposed thing could be more contrary to the affirmation of that proposed thing. He now says that those things which are more false are more contrary. Contraries are whatever differ most widely with respect to the same thing, as white and black differ with respect to color.

Therefore the things that are most false and most true are farthest apart. The enunciation of what exists in itself is most true; the enunciation that destroys what is true in itself is most false.

One of the affirmation of the contrary and the negation of the proposed thing must necessarily be more contrary. The more false and more contrary opinion is the one that conceives a contradiction—for example, the opinion that what is good is not good—rather than the opinion that what is good is bad.

Since things expressed in speech follow opinions, the negation of “Every good thing is good”—namely, “No good thing is good”—is more contrary than “Every good thing is bad.” Accordingly, in other cases as well, such as “Every human being is just,” “No human being is just” is more contrary than “Every human being is unjust.”

[Col. 0386B]

The opinion that what is good is bad is implicit. For since it judges that what is good is not good, it must necessarily contain the same judgment.

He adds to the preceding demonstration an argument showing that the proposition which denies is more contrary than the proposition which affirms the contrary. The affirmation of the contrary, he says, is implicit. Whoever judges that what is good is bad cannot do so without also judging that it is not good.

The proposition “What is good is bad” is therefore in a certain way double, since it also contains the proposition “What is good is not good.” But “What is good is good” is a simple proposition, and a simple proposition can have as its more contrary counterpart only a simple proposition. The negation “What is good is not good” is simple. It is therefore more contrary.

[Col. 0386C]

Furthermore, if the same arrangement must hold in other cases as well, then what has been said here appears to be correct. Either contradiction is everywhere more contrary than the affirmation of the contrary, or it is nowhere more contrary.

In cases where there is no contrary, the false proposition is the one opposed to the true one by contradiction. For example, whoever judges that a human being is not a human being is false. Therefore, if these propositions are contrary, then other propositions that are contradictions will also be contrary.

[Col. 0386D]

Either, he says, it is universally true that contradiction is more contrary than the affirmation of the contrary, or it is true nowhere. Either the same result must occur in other cases too, or even here it is not true that the proposition formed by contradiction—that is, by negation—is more contrary than the affirmation of the contrary.

Let us examine this, he says, in things that have no contrary, such as “human being.” If someone judges that a human being is a human being, the judgment is true. If someone judges that a human being is not a human being, the judgment is false. But if someone judges that a human being is a horse, no one would say that the proposition judging a human being to be a horse is more contrary than the proposition judging a human being not to be a human being.

Therefore, if in things that have no contrary the proposition formed by contradiction is contrary, then in things that do have contraries the proposition of negation, not the affirmation of the contrary, is more contrary.

[Col. 0387A]

Furthermore, the opinions “the good is good” and “the non-good is not good” are similarly related. So too are “the good is not good” and “the non-good is good.” What, then, is contrary to the true opinion “the non-good is not good”? It is not the opinion that says “it is bad.” For these may sometimes be true simultaneously, and a true opinion is never contrary to another true opinion.

There is something that is non-good and is bad. Therefore they may be true at the same time. Nor is the contrary opinion “it is not bad,” since this too is true; these propositions may likewise be true together.

It remains, then, that the contrary of the opinion “the non-good is not good” is the opinion “the non-good is good.” This latter opinion is false. Therefore, corresponding to the opinion “the good is good,” the contrary is “the good is not good.”

[Col. 0387B]

He attempts to discover the force of propositions through similarity and proportion of contrariety. Let us first arrange these propositions, and afterward explain as briefly as possible the force of Aristotle’s argument.

True: the good is good.  
False: the good is not good.  
True: the non-good is not good.  
False: the non-good is good.

[Col. 0387C]

Of these four opinions, two are true and two are false. “The good is good” is true; “the good is not good” is false. Again, “the non-good is not good” is true; “the non-good is good” is false.

This is the similarity and proportion among the four propositions. The relation of the opinion “the good is good” to the opinion “the good is not good” is the same as the relation of the opinion “the non-good is not good” to the opinion “the non-good is good.” Just as in the first pair one is true and the other false, so in the second pair one is true and the other false.

He first takes his example from the opinion “the non-good is not good.” Since this opinion is true, what shall we posit as its contrary? Shall it be the opinion that says “it is bad”? But that is not contrary. The proposition “what is non-good is not good” and the proposition “what is non-good is bad” can both be true. There are some non-good things that are bad.

Therefore the propositions “what is not good is not good” and “what is not good is bad” are not contrary. Contrary propositions cannot both be true, and a true proposition is never contrary to another true proposition.

Nor can the contrary be the opinion that says “what is non-good is not bad.” For some things may not be good without being bad. To break a branch from a tree for no useful purpose, if the tree is not harmed, is neither bad nor good.

[Col. 0387D]

Thus the opinions that what is non-good is non-good and that what is non-good is not bad may both be true. These too are not contrary. It remains, then, that the contrary of the opinion “the non-good is not good” is the opinion “the non-good is good.”

If the similarity described above is preserved among these four propositions—if the relation of “the non-good is not good” to “the non-good is good” is the same as the relation of “the good is good” to “the good is not good”—then the opinion “the good is not good” will be contrary to the opinion “the good is good.” The opinion “the good is not good” is therefore contrary to the opinion “the good is good.”

[Col. 0388A]

It is clear that it makes no difference if we formulate the affirmation universally. The universal negation will then be contrary to it. Thus, to the opinion that every good thing is good, the contrary is the opinion that none of the things that are good is good.

The opinion “the good is good,” if it is affirmed universally, is equivalent to the opinion that whatever is good is good. This is no different from saying “Every good thing is good.”

The same applies to the non-good. Thus, if the matter is arranged in opinion in this way, the affirmations and negations existing in speech are signs of what exists in the soul.

[Col. 0388B]

It is clear that the contrary of an affirmation is a universal negation concerning the same subject.
