To “Every good thing is good,” or “Every human being is good,” the contrary is “No good thing is good,” or “No human being is good.” Contradictories, however, are “Not every good thing is good” and “Not every human being is good.”

He also rightly recalls that it makes no difference whether, in opinions that are not formulated universally, these are contrary, or whether the opinions oppose one another universally. The same relation holds in the opinion that judges every good thing to be good: its contrary is the opinion that judges no good thing to be good.

When we say that what is good is good, and this is affirmed universally in an opinion, we must understand it as saying that whatever is good is good. This is no different from saying “Every good thing is good.”

[Col. 0388C]

Since that opinion is true, the contrary opinion is the one that says that whatever is good is not good. This is no different from judging that no good thing is good.

The same applies to the non-good. If we say “Everything that is non-good is not good,” and again “Everything that is non-good is good,” these propositions stand in the same contrary relation: one is true and the other false.

This is found most especially in contraries. Thus the entire discussion and question are brought to the following conclusion. If the things existing in the soul are principles of the things signified in speech, and speech is a sign of the soul’s affections, then whatever occurs in the soul must necessarily return in the same way in speech.

[Col. 0388D]

If universal affirmation and universal negation are contrary in opinion, then they will likewise be contrary in speech. The contrary will not be the proposition that affirms the contrary, but the proposition that denies what was previously proposed through universal opposition.

Thus, to “Every good thing is good,” or “Every human being is good,” the contrary is “No good thing is good,” or “No human being is good.” This is what he means by “nullum” (“no [good thing]”) and “nullus” (“no human being”). “Nullum” refers to the proposition “Every good thing is good,” while “nullus” refers to “Every human being is good.” They are arranged as follows:

“Every good thing is good”; its contrary is “No good thing is good.”

“Every human being is good”; its contrary is “No human being is good.”

He calls the propositions set out above contradictories—the angular propositions discussed when he was speaking about universal and particular propositions. Universal affirmation is opposed by contradiction to particular negation, and particular affirmation to universal negation.

[Col. 0389A]

It is clear that a true proposition cannot be contrary to another true proposition, whether the propositions are opinions or contradictions. Contraries concern opposites, whereas it is possible for the same person to speak truth concerning the same things. But contraries cannot simultaneously inhere in the same thing.

[Col. 0389B]

From what has been said above he also concludes that contraries cannot both be true at the same time, nor can two true propositions be contrary to one another. This is not merely the case with opinions, such that one true opinion cannot be contrary to another true opinion; it is also the case with propositions. It is impossible for two contrary propositions to be simultaneously true.

He establishes this by a syllogism of the following form. All contraries are opposites. Opposites cannot simultaneously inhere in the same thing. Therefore nature does not permit contraries to exist in one and the same thing. If two true predicates can belong to the same thing, while two contraries cannot belong to the same thing, then things that are contrary cannot both be true.

This is what he means when he says: “Contraries concern opposites.” Every contrary is an opposite, and it is impossible for things that are contrary not to be included among opposites. As he taught in the Categories, opposition is a genus of contraries.

[Col. 0389C]

But it is possible for the same person to speak truly concerning the same things. That is, two true statements can simultaneously be true and can both be truly predicated of the same thing. Thus, when we say that something is not good and that it is bad, both statements may be true at once. Some things, though not good, are nevertheless bad; ugliness, for example, is not good but is bad.

It is therefore possible for things that are true to be simultaneously and truly predicated, and for them to exist simultaneously in the same thing. But contraries cannot simultaneously inhere in the same thing.

[Col. 0390A]

Consequently, if true predicates can belong to the same thing, while contraries cannot belong to the same thing, things that are contrary cannot be simultaneously true. The converse follows as well: things that are simultaneously true cannot be contrary.

It is therefore impossible, whether in opinions or in propositions, for anyone correctly to judge as contrary two things that are true. We have expressed as much as the brevity of the exposition permitted. What a more profound treatment of this book will teach will be explained in the sequence of the second edition.

ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS, SECOND EDITION OF HIS COMMENTARY ON ARISTOTLE’S *ON INTERPRETATION*, OR THE GREATER COMMENTARIES

[Col. 0393]

BOOK ONE
[Col. 0393A] Alexander declares in his commentaries that he was impelled by this reason to undertake the exceedingly long labor of exposition: he differed on many points from the opinions of earlier writers. For me, however, there is a greater reason for pursuing the work, since scarcely anyone has undertaken a continuous sequence either of translation or even of commentary—except that Vegetius Praetextatus rendered the Prior and Posterior Analytics into Latin, not by translating Aristotle, but by translating Themistius; anyone who has read both readily understands this. Albinus, too, is reported to have written on these same subjects. I know that his books on geometry have been published, but I have been unable to find his work on dialectic, though I searched for it long and diligently. Therefore, whether he remained entirely silent, we shall discuss what he omitted; or whether he wrote something, we too, following the zeal of that learned man, shall labor in the same field of praise.

Although many of Aristotle’s doctrines are concealed by the most subtle art of philosophy, this book above all is compressed both by the sharpness of its arguments and by the brevity of its words. Consequently, more effort will be spent here on exposition than in the ten Categories.

First, therefore, what a voice is must be defined. Once this has been made clear and evident, the purpose of the entire book will become apparent. A voice is a striking of the air by the tongue, produced by an animal through certain parts of the throat called the arteries. There are, however, other sounds produced by the same breath, which the tongue does not strike, such as a cough. A cough is produced by a certain breath issuing through the arteries, but it is formed without any impression of the tongue, and for that reason it is not subject to those elements: it cannot in any way be written down. Therefore this is not called a voice, but merely a sound.

A voice may also be defined as a sound accompanied by some conception of signifying. For when a voice is uttered, it is produced for the sake of some signification. A cough, although it is a sound, does not come forth for the sake of any signification, but rather arises of itself.

Since, then, our breath is such that, if it is struck and formed in such a way that the tongue strikes it, it is a voice—if the tongue strikes it so that a determinate and circumscribed sound emerges as a voice, it becomes speech, which in Greek is called *lexis* (λέξις). Speech is an articulated voice. We shall not call this expression—that is, *lexis*—a “diction,” because we translate *phasis* (φάσις) as “diction,” and *lexis* as “speech.”

The parts of this speech are letters. When they have been joined together, they produce one connected and composite voice, which is called speech. Whether a voice signifies something, as does the expression “human being”; or signifies absolutely nothing; or can signify something when assigned as a name to something, as does “blitiri”—for this voice, although it signifies nothing by itself, will signify when assigned as a name to something—or whether it signifies nothing by itself but indicates something when joined with others, as conjunctions do: all these are called speeches. Thus the proper form of speech is a composite voice that can be represented in letters.

For speech to exist, therefore, a voice is required—that is, the sound struck by the tongue—and for the voice itself to be determined by the tongue into a sound that can be inscribed in letters, that same sound struck by the tongue is likewise required. But for this speech to be significant, something further must be added: there must be some conception of signifying through which what exists in the voice or in the speech is expressed.

Or the matter may be stated as follows. If, in the breath that we emit through the arteries, there is merely a striking of the tongue, it is a voice. If the striking is such as to reduce the sound to letters, it is speech. If, in addition, a certain force of conception is supplied, the voice becomes significant.

When these three things come together—the striking of the tongue, the articulated sound of the voice, and some conception of utterance—interpretation is produced. For interpretation is an articulated voice signifying through itself.

Consequently, not every voice is an interpretation. There are voices of other animals that do not fall under the term “interpretation.” Nor is every speech an interpretation, because, as has been said, there are certain speeches that lack signification and, although they signify nothing by themselves, signify when joined with others, as conjunctions do.

Interpretation, however, remains only in voices that are both articulated and significant through themselves. Thus the converse follows: whatever is an interpretation signifies something, and whatever signifies something is called by the term “interpretation.”

Hence Aristotle himself, in the books he wrote on the *Art of Poetry*, also taught that the parts of speech are syllables and conjunctions. Syllables, insofar as they are syllables, signify absolutely nothing; conjunctions, however, can co-signify, but by themselves indicate nothing.

In this book, on the other hand, he establishes the parts of interpretation as the noun and the verb, which signify through themselves. It is equally clear that a sentence is an interpretation, since it too is a voice joined from significant parts and is not without signification.

Since, then, Aristotle treats in this book not only the sentence but also the noun and the verb, and not merely speech but significant speech, which is interpretation—and since the name “interpretation” is applied to verbs, nouns, and significant speeches—the book itself has been entitled *On Interpretation*, after the common name of the things treated in it. We have arranged its exposition in Latin, drawing especially on Porphyry, though also translating from other authorities. He seems to us to excel both in keenness of understanding and in the arrangement of his arguments.

The first two parts of interpretation, then, will be the noun and the verb. Through these, whatever exists in the mind’s acts of understanding is indicated; through them the whole order of speech is constituted. And insofar as the voice itself signifies an act of understanding, it is divided, as has been said, into these two parts, noun and verb.

But insofar as the voice, through the mediation of acts of understanding, demonstrates things subjected to understanding, Aristotle divided the number of significant voices into the ten Categories. Here lies the difference between the purpose of this book and that of the Categories, whose subject is collected into a tenfold plurality. In this book the question concerns the number of significant voices insofar as it pertains to the voices themselves—namely, by which significant voices the mind’s acts of understanding are indicated. These are simple nouns and verbs, and sentences composed from them.

The purpose of the Categories, however, is to treat significant expressions of things insofar as the intermediary act of understanding in the mind signifies them. For the noun and the verb are certain qualities of voice, and they signify those same ten Categories. The ten Categories are never uttered without some quality belonging either to a verb or to a noun.

The purpose of this book, therefore, will be to treat significant expressions of things insofar as they signify the mind’s conceptions and acts of understanding. The purpose of the book on the ten Categories was stated in its commentary: it concerns significant expressions of things, and the number of divisions into which their signification can be distributed, insofar as those expressions are able, through the mediation of the senses and of acts of understanding, to indicate things subjected to understanding.

In the work on the *Art of Poetry*, however, he divides speech differently. He includes all the parts of speech, affirming that its parts are elements, syllables, conjunctions, articles, nouns, cases, verbs, and sentences.

Speech does not consist solely in significant voices. It extends beyond the significations of voices and continues as far as articulated sounds. For every syllable, and every other voice that can be written in letters, is included under the name “speech,” which in Greek is called *lexis* (λέξις). Interpretation, however, is not constituted in the same way. For it is not enough that it be a voice of the kind that can be recorded in letters; it must also signify something.

The rationale of the Categories, on the other hand, is established in the fact that these two parts of interpretation indicate things subjected to acts of understanding. For since ten things altogether are found in all nature, there will likewise be ten acts of understanding. Since nouns and verbs signify these acts of understanding, there will altogether be ten Categories, designated by verbs and nouns. But there are two entities—namely, the noun and the verb—that signify the acts of understanding themselves.

The elements of interpretation, therefore, are verbs and nouns; strictly speaking, however, the parts of which interpretation itself consists are sentences.

Some sentences are complete, others incomplete. Complete sentences are those from which what is said can be fully understood; incomplete sentences are those in which the mind still expects to hear something more fully, as in “Socrates with Plato.” For without anything being added, the understanding of the sentence still hangs suspended and falters, and the listener expects to hear something further.

There are five kinds of complete sentence:

The supplicatory, for example:

> Almighty Jupiter, if you are moved by any prayers,  
> Then grant aid, father, and confirm these omens.

The imperative, for example:

> Go now, my son; call the west winds and glide upon your wings.

The interrogative, for example:

> Tell me, Damoetas, whose flock is it—is it Meliboeus’s?

The vocative, for example:

> O father, O eternal power of men and things.

The enunciative, in which truth or falsity is found, for example:

> In the beginning, the nature of trees for planting is varied.

The last of these has two divisions, for there is both a simple and a compound enunciative sentence. A simple sentence is, for example, “It is day; it is light.” A compound sentence is, for example, “If it is day, it is light.”

In this book, therefore, Aristotle discusses the simple enunciative sentence and its elements, namely the noun and the verb. Since these are significant, and since a significant voice is included under the name “interpretation,” he entitled the book *On Interpretation* after this common term, as has been said.

Theophrastus, in the book he composed on *Affirmation and Negation*, treated the enunciative sentence. The Stoics, too, in the books they call *On Axioms* (Περὶ ἀξιωμάτων), likewise discuss these matters. They, however, examine both simple and non-simple enunciative sentences; Aristotle, in this book, considers nothing except the simple enunciative sentence.

Aspasius and Alexander, as in the case of Aristotle’s other books, also published commentaries on this one. Both, however, assert that Aristotle treated the sentence. For if, as they themselves say, to utter something in a sentence is to interpret, then the book *On Interpretation* was evidently written as a book about the sentence—as though only the sentence, and not verbs and nouns as well, were included under the term “interpretation.”

For verbs and nouns, which are the elements of interpretation, are called by the name “interpretation” just as much as the sentence is. Alexander added that the title was defective, since it did not indicate what kind of sentence the book discussed. For there are many kinds of sentences, as has been said. He thinks that it should either have been added or understood that Aristotle was writing about a philosophical or dialectical sentence—that is, one by which truth and falsity can be brought to light.

But once he accepts that only the sentence is called by the name “interpretation,” he has also gone astray in understanding the title itself. For suppose someone considered the title defective because it did not add what kind of sentence was under discussion. If someone asked, “What is a human being?” and another answered, “An animal,” he might then blame the respondent for having spoken incompletely about what a human being is, on the ground that he had not pursued all the differences.

Yet if “animal” shares certain other common features with “human being,” nothing prevents the person who said “animal” from having perfectly demonstrated what a human being is. Whether someone adds the differences or not, it is necessary that a human being be an animal.

The same applies to the sentence. If someone grants, as a first premise, that interpretation means nothing other than a sentence, why should the person who entitled the book *On Interpretation* be blamed for not adding what kind of interpretation he meant? It is sufficient that he gave the title of the book from some encompassing commonality, as we have shown above: since nouns, verbs, and sentences are all included under the single name “interpretation,” he demonstrated that the book concerns all of them when he called it *On Interpretation*.

But when he added that the only interpretation is that in which truth and falsity can be found in a sentence—such as an enunciative sentence—he was, as Porphyry says, fabricating rather than teaching the signification of the name. In this respect he is wrong both about the purpose of the book and about its title; but he did not err in the same way concerning his judgment of the book itself.

Andronicus does not think that this book is Aristotle’s, a view that Alexander refuted vigorously and accurately. Since antiquity judged Andronicus to be an exact and careful judge and discoverer of Aristotle’s books, it is thoroughly worthy of great wonder that he should have been mistaken in judging this book.

He attempts to show that the work is not Aristotle’s on the ground that Aristotle treats at the beginning of this book the mind’s acts of understanding, which he called “affections of the soul,” and mentions that he discussed them more fully in his books *On the Soul*. Since he called them affections of the soul, Andronicus says that they must mean sadness, joy, desire, or other states of that kind. He claims that the book is proved not to be Aristotle’s because Aristotle had treated none of these affections in his books *On the Soul*. He failed to understand that, in this book, Aristotle used “affections of the soul” not for emotional states but for acts of understanding.

Alexander adds many other arguments for why this work appears to be especially Aristotle’s. The doctrines stated here agree with Aristotle’s views concerning the enunciative sentence. The style itself is also more compressed because of its brevity, and for that reason does not differ from Aristotle’s obscurity. Moreover, when Theophrastus, as he often does in other matters, treats subjects similar to those previously treated by Aristotle, he also uses in his book on affirmation and negation certain of the same words that Aristotle used in this book.

Theophrastus himself provides evidence that this is Aristotle’s book. In every subject he discusses after his teacher, he touches lightly on what he already knows Aristotle to have said, while treating more carefully matters that Aristotle did not discuss. He did the same here. The subjects Aristotle treated in this book concerning enunciation he passed over lightly; what his teacher had left unmentioned he added with more subtle consideration.

He also adds this reason: Aristotle, being determined to write about syllogisms, could never have done so properly unless he had first made certain observations concerning propositions. This too seems clear to me when carefully considered: the book was prepared for the Analytics. Just as Aristotle discusses the simple proposition here, so in the Analytics he considers only simple syllogisms. Thus the simplicity of the syllogisms and propositions themselves seems to belong to no other work than the larger Aristotelian composition.

Therefore Andronicus should not be heeded when, because of the term “affections,” he separates this book from Aristotle’s works. Aristotle called acts of understanding “affections of the soul” for this reason: the acts of understanding that we customarily express in speech and utter in sentences arise from some cause and utility.

There was, for example, a certain utility and cause by which scattered human beings were gathered together, became willing to submit to laws, and established cities. Consequently, whatever comes about from some utility must also come from an affection. For just as divine things exist without any affection, no external utility can be attached to them. Things that are subject to affection, however, always find some cause and utility by which they are sustained.

Therefore such acts of understanding as are to be expressed to another through speech, since they seem to have been gathered together from some cause and utility, were rightly called affections of the mind.

What has been said about the purpose of the book, its title, and the fact that this book should be regarded as especially Aristotle’s will suffice. Its usefulness, however, will not be unknown to anyone who understands in what kind of sentence truth and falsity consist. For they exist only in this enunciative sentence.

The careful student will be able to recognize in the work itself what things divide truth and falsity; what things distribute truth and falsity as defined, or as variable and changeable; what things can be said when joined together, although they can be predicated separately; what things are said separately when they are not predicated together; what negations are, together with the modes of propositions; what their consequences are; and many other matters besides. Anyone who applies his mind with care to an investigation of these questions will experience their great usefulness.

But now let us turn to Aristotle’s own words.

## On Signs

[Col. 0398D] First, it is necessary to establish what a noun is and what a verb is; afterward, what negation, affirmation, enunciation, and sentence are.

Beginning the book, he first set out what topics he would treat throughout its entire course. For he says that one must first define the things about which one is going to argue. Here “to establish” must be understood as “to define.” For it is necessary to determine what all these things are—that is, what a noun is, what a verb is, and the other items that we have said are the elements of interpretation. Affirmation and negation, however, belong within interpretation. Therefore it is clear that noun and verb are the elements of affirmation and negation. For affirmation and negation are joined together from these when they are combined.

Here a question arises: why does he promise to define only two, [Col. 0399A] noun and verb, when there appear to be more parts of speech? The answer must be that Aristotle defined in this book only as much as was sufficient for what he had undertaken to treat. For he treats simple declarative speech, which is of such a kind that it is composed only by joining verbs and nouns. If someone joins a noun and a verb, as in “Socrates walks,” he has made a simple declarative sentence. A declarative sentence is, as I mentioned above, one that contains an indication of truth or falsity. But in what we say, “Socrates walks,” it is necessary that either truth or falsity be contained: if it is said while Socrates is walking, it is true; if while he is not walking, it is false.

A simple declarative sentence is therefore completed from nouns and verbs alone. It is consequently pointless to ask why he did not also propose the other things that appear to be parts of speech, since he undertook to divide the elements not of speech in its entirety, but only of simple declaration—although these two should properly be called parts of speech, namely noun and verb, since each signifies independently. Conjunctions and prepositions, however, signify nothing at all unless joined with other words. Participles are related to the verb, either because they derive from the gerundive form or because they contain tense in their proper signification. Interjections, pronouns, and adverbs are to be placed in the category of nouns, because they signify something definite where there is no signification either of passion or of action. If some of these cannot be inflected through cases, that is no impediment. For there are certain nouns called *monoptota*—“single-case” nouns.

Even if someone thinks that these points are too remote and not immediately relevant, let him nevertheless concede what we have already said above: it is not fair to criticize someone who proposes to discuss not speech as a whole, but only simple declaration, for taking into his definition only as much as he judged sufficient for the work he had undertaken. Therefore it must be said that Aristotle does not wish in this work to define the parts of every kind of speech, but only those of simple declarative speech—namely, noun and verb.

The evidence for this is as follows. After proposing the words, “First one must establish what a noun is and what a verb is,” he does not immediately say what speech is, but adds next what negation is and what affirmation is, [Col. 0399D] then what declaration is, and finally what speech is. If he were speaking about speech in general, after noun and verb he would have spoken not about affirmation and negation, and after these about declaration, but immediately about speech. But since, after introducing noun and verb, he proposed affirmation, negation, declaration, and finally speech, we must acknowledge what we stated earlier: he wished to divide the parts not of universal speech, but of simple declarative speech, which is divided into affirmation and negation. Its parts are nouns and verbs.

These preserve a simple understanding in themselves and are called expressions (*dictiones*), though they are not the only things so called. Other expressions also exist, such as incomplete or complete sentences, of which I have already taught above that there are several parts. Among them, declaration is a species of complete sentence. This too is either simple or compound.

Among philosophers and commentators there is disagreement about the species of simple declaration. Some say that affirmation and negation ought to be subordinated to declaration as its species; Porphyry is among them. Others do not agree at all, but maintain that affirmation and negation are equivocal, and that both are called by the single term “declaration,” while declaration is predicated of both as an equivocal name, not as a univocal genus. Alexander is the chief of this group. It does not seem useless to set out their disagreements.

First, however, we must explain the ways in which Alexander thinks that affirmation and negation are not species of declaration. Afterwards I shall add how Porphyry dissolved these arguments.

Alexander says that affirmation and negation are not species of declaration because affirmation is prior. He attempts to show that affirmation is prior on the grounds that every negation removes and destroys an affirmation. If this is so, the affirmation that is overthrown is prior to the negation that overthrows it. But things in which there is something prior and something posterior cannot be placed under the same genus, as was said in the section of the *Categories* entitled “On Things Simultaneous.”

Furthermore, he says, every negation is division, while affirmation is composition and conjunction. When I say “Socrates lives,” I have joined life to Socrates. When I say “Socrates [Col. 0400C] does not live,” I have separated life from Socrates. Negation, then, is a kind of division, while affirmation is conjunction; but division belongs to what has been composed and joined. Conjunction, therefore, which is affirmation, is prior, while division, which is negation, is posterior.

He also added that every declaration made through affirmation is simpler than one made through negation. For if the negative particle is removed from a negation, affirmation alone remains. From “Socrates does not live,” if the particle “not,” which is attached to the verb, is removed, “Socrates lives” remains. Affirmation, therefore, is simpler than negation. But what is simpler must be prior.

The same holds in quantity: what is less in quantity is prior to what is greater in quantity. Every sentence has quantity; but when I say “Socrates [Col. 0400D] walks,” the sentence is shorter than when I say “Socrates does not walk.” Therefore, if affirmation is lesser according to quantity, it must also be prior.

He added that affirmation is a kind of possession, whereas negation is privation; but possession is prior to privation. Affirmation, therefore, is prior to negation. And, not to follow each point individually, since by these and other arguments he demonstrates that affirmation is prior to negation, he separates them from a common genus. For he thinks that no species can exist under the same genus if something prior or posterior is discerned among them.

But Porphyry says that he taught affirmation and negation to be species of declaration in the commentaries he published on Theophrastus. Here, however, he dissolves Alexander’s argument in the following way. He says that one must not think that whatever things are prior to others in any manner whatsoever cannot be placed under the same genus. Only those things that are prior or posterior according to their being and substance cannot be placed under the same genus.

And this is rightly said. For if whatever is prior in any respect cannot share a genus with what is posterior, substance could not be a common genus of primary and secondary substances. Anyone who says this departs from the right order of reasoning. But just as, although there are primary and secondary substances, both are equally not in a subject, and their being depends on their not being in a subject, they are placed under one genus, that of substance.

[Col. 0401B] Likewise, although affirmations are prior to negations in the utterance of speech, nevertheless in their being and proper nature they participate equally in declaration. Declaration is that in which truth and falsity can be found. In this respect affirmation and negation are equal. For affirmation and negation participate equally in truth and falsity. Therefore, since affirmation and negation derive equally from declaration what they are, they ought not to be divided from the common genus of declaration.

It seems to me as well that Porphyry’s position should be followed: affirmation and negation should be subordinated to declaration as their common genus. For Alexander’s long and manifold arguments are answered when Porphyry shows that things which are prior cannot be placed under a common genus only when they are prior with respect to their own being and substance.

Syrianus, whose surname is Philoxenus, asks here why Aristotle, proposing negation first and affirmation afterwards, says: “First one must establish what a noun is and what a verb is, then what negation and affirmation are.” At first, he says, Aristotle stated nothing distinctive, since in cases where both affirmation and negation can occur, negation may be prior and affirmation posterior. Thus, concerning Socrates, if he is healthy, an affirmation may be fitted to him, so that one says, “Socrates is healthy”; and a negation of this kind may also be fitted to him, so that one says, “Socrates is not healthy.”

Since, then, affirmation and negation can both occur concerning him, it follows that negation occurs before affirmation. For before he was born it could be said of him, “Socrates is not healthy”: since he had not been born, he could not be healthy.

He added that Aristotle preserves the converse distribution of the proposition and its exposition. Here, after noun and verb, Aristotle first proposed negation, then affirmation, then declaration, and finally speech. But after defining noun and verb, he first defined speech, then declaration, third affirmation, and finally negation, which he had placed first here after the introduction of verb and noun. Thus, in order to preserve the reversed sequence, he says that negation was proposed first; in this explanation [Col. 0402A] he does not depart from Alexander’s position either.

He also added, and not without usefulness, that declaration ought to be understood as the genus of affirmation and negation. Although, as has been said, affirmation is prior in utterance, Aristotle nevertheless established it as equal to negation under declaration itself—that is, under what is equally true or false. He says that Aristotle confirms this as well. Aristotle put negation first and affirmation second, and this arrangement has no defect if affirmation and negation are placed as equals under declaration itself; for things that are equal retain nothing contrary when they are considered without distinction.

The order, then, is this: first he proposed the element of speech as a whole, namely noun and verb; next, negation and affirmation, which are species of declaration; third, their genus, declaration; and fourth, speech, which is the genus of declaration. He promised to give the definitions of all these. For the moment, however, leaving and passing over those definitions and postponing them to a later treatment, he now adds what verbs and nouns are, or what they signify.

Therefore, before we come to Aristotle’s actual words, let us discuss briefly and generally nouns and verbs, and the things signified by verbs and nouns.

Whether it is an interrogation and response, a continuous sequence of some speech, and the hearing and understanding of another person, or whether one person teaches while another learns, the whole order of speaking is completed through three things: things, concepts, and utterances. A thing is conceived by the intellect. [Col. 0402C] An utterance signifies the conceptions and understandings of the mind; the understandings themselves both conceive the things placed before them and are signified by utterances.

Since, then, there are three things through which all speech and conversation are completed—namely, the things that are presented, the understandings that conceive those things and are in turn signified by utterances, and the utterances that designate the understandings—there is also a fourth thing by which the utterances themselves can be designated: these are letters. Written letters signify the utterances themselves.

Thus there are four things: letters signify utterances; utterances signify understandings; understandings conceive things; and these things have a certain sequence that is neither confused nor accidental, but rests upon an established order of their nature. Things always accompany the understanding conceived from them; the utterance follows the understanding; and letters are the elements of utterances. For understandings arise after things have first been presented and established in their own substance. There are always understandings of things; once these have been established, the signification of an utterance immediately arises. Apart from an understanding, an utterance signifies absolutely nothing.

But because there are utterances, letters—which we call elements—were discovered so that the quality of utterances might be designated. For the purposes of cognition, however, the relation is reversed. Wherever the same letters exist and people use the same elements, they must also use the same nouns and verbs—that is, the same utterances. Those who use the same utterances likewise have the same understandings active in the conception of the mind.

But wherever the understandings are the same, it is clear that the same things are presented to their understandings. Yet this does not work in reverse in every respect. For wherever the things are the same and the understandings are the same, it does not immediately follow that the utterances are the same, or that the letters are the same.

When a Roman, a Greek, and a barbarian all see a horse, they have the same understanding of it, namely, that it is a horse, and the same thing is presented to them; the same understanding is conceived from the thing itself. But the Greek calls the horse by one word, the Roman uses another utterance to signify the horse, and the barbarian differs from both in designating it. Consequently, they also write their respective utterances with different elements.

It was therefore rightly said that, wherever the things and understandings are the same, it does not immediately follow that the utterances or the elements are the same. A thing precedes an understanding, an understanding an utterance, and an utterance letters; but this cannot be reversed. For if there are letters, no signification of an utterance immediately arises from them. To people who do not know letters, no set of elements signifies any noun, precisely because they do not know them.

Nor, if there are utterances, is it immediately necessary that there be understandings. For one will find many utterances that signify absolutely nothing; nor is a thing always presented to the understanding. There are understandings without any thing presented to them, such as those of centaurs or chimaeras, which poets have invented. Their understandings exist, but no substance is presented to them.

But if someone returns to nature and considers it carefully, he will recognize that whenever a thing exists, its understanding also exists. If not among human beings, then certainly in God, who, through the divinity of his own substance and in the proper nature of the thing itself, is ignorant of nothing. And if there is an understanding, there is also an utterance; and if there is an utterance, there are also its letters. If the letters are unknown, this has no bearing on the nature of the utterance itself.

For an understanding is not, as it were, a cause of utterances, nor is an utterance a cause of letters, so that when the letters are the same among some people, the nouns must necessarily also be the same. Likewise, when the things or understandings are the same among some people, it does not immediately follow that the words used for the understandings or things themselves are the same. Although the thing and the understanding of a human being are the same, this substance is nevertheless called by different people in different ways and by different names.

Therefore, although the utterances are the same, the letters may be different. Thus the noun “man,” although it is one noun, can be written with different letters: it can be written in Latin letters, in Greek letters, or in other forms of characters newly invented.

Since, then, wherever the things are the same, the understandings must also be the same; wherever the understandings are the same, the utterances are not necessarily the same; and wherever the utterances are the same, the elements are not necessarily the same, we must say that things and understandings, since they are the same among everyone, are established by nature. Utterances, however, are not naturally established in relation to letters, since they are changed by the differing conventions of human beings; they are established by convention.

We must therefore conclude that wherever the elements are the same, the utterances are also the same; wherever the utterances are the same, the understandings are the same; and wherever the understandings are the same, the things presented to them are also the same. Conversely, wherever the things are the same, the understandings are also the same; wherever the understandings are the same, the utterances are not the same; and wherever the utterances are the same, the words themselves—whether verbs or nouns—are not always designated by the same letters.

In the statements above we used “element” and “letter” interchangeably. I shall now briefly explain the difference between them. A letter is the inscription and figure of the smallest part of articulated utterance, whereas an element is the sound of that inscription. Thus, when I write the letter *a*, the form itself that is written with ink or a stylus is called a letter; the sound by which we pronounce that letter aloud is called an element.

Once this is understood, we must say that the person who teaches, the person who speaks in continuous discourse, and the person who asks a question stand in an opposite relation to those who learn, hear, or respond in these three respects: utterance, understanding, and thing. Letters may be left aside because of those who are unfamiliar with them.

The teacher, the speaker, and the questioner proceed from things to understanding and exercise the force and function of their action through nouns and verbs. For, given the things before them, they derive understandings from them and utter them through nouns and verbs. The learner, the hearer, and even the respondent, however, proceed from nouns to understandings and reach the things themselves. Receiving the speech of the teacher, speaker, or questioner, the learner, hearer, or respondent understands what each of them says; by understanding it, he also acquires knowledge of the things and comes to rest in that knowledge.

It was therefore rightly said that those who teach, speak, and ask questions stand in an opposite relation, with respect to utterance, understanding, and thing, to those who learn, hear, and respond.

Since there are four things—letters, utterances, understandings, and things—letters, immediately and principally, signify verbs and nouns. These, in turn, primarily signify understandings, and secondarily also designate things. Understandings themselves signify nothing other than things.

But the earlier thinkers—Plato, Aristotle, Speusippus, and Xenocrates—place sensations between things and the significations of understandings. In sensible things they posit certain images, in which the origin of the understanding itself consists. What the Stoics say about this matter must be passed over for the present.

From all this, however, we need to recognize only the following: what exists in letters signifies the speech that consists in utterance; the speech that exists in utterance designates the speech of the mind and understanding, which is formed by silent thought; and this speech of the understanding primarily conceives and designates the things presented to it.

Of these four, Aristotle says that two are established by nature—things and the conceptions of the mind, that is, the speech formed in understandings—because they are the same among everyone, though subject to change. The other two, nouns and letters, are established not by nature but by convention. He does not say that they are fixed naturally because, as was demonstrated above, not everyone uses the same utterances or the same elements.

And this is what he says:

“Thus the things that exist in utterance are signs of the affections that exist in the soul, and the things that are written are signs of the things that exist in utterance. And just as letters are not the same for everyone, so neither are utterances the same. But the experiences of the soul, of which these are the primary signs, are the same for everyone, and the things of which these are likenesses are the same.

“These matters, then, have been discussed in what has been said concerning the soul, for that is a different subject.”

Since he had first set forth the noun and the verb, and had promised to define whatever followed afterward, he meanwhile passes these matters over and says a little about the affections of the soul and their signs, namely, the spoken sounds. But why he inserted this at this point, most commentators have neglected to explain. So far as I know, only three have offered an account of the reason for this insertion, and that of Herminus is far removed from the truth of the matter. He says that Aristotle inserted his discussion of the signs of the soul’s affections in order to impress upon the reader the usefulness of the work he had undertaken. Since he was going to discuss spoken sounds, which are signs of the soul’s affections, he rightly announced that he would say something about them. For since no one is ignorant of the affections of his own soul, it is highly useful also not to be ignorant of their signs together with the soul’s affections; for they cannot be known except through the spoken sounds that are their signs.

[Col. 0405B] Alexander, however, gives another reason for this insertion. “Nouns and verbs,” he says, “are contained in simple interpretation. But an utterance is formed from nouns and verbs joined together, and in it truth or falsity is already found. Whether, therefore, any expression is simple, or is already a joined and composite utterance, it derives its force from the things signified. For their order and connection exist first in those things; afterward they overflow into the spoken sounds. Therefore, since the force of signifiers arises from the things signified, Aristotle first proposes to teach us about what the spoken sounds themselves signify.”

But Herminus must be rejected at this point. He has explained nothing of the kind that pertains to the causes of the proposition under discussion. Alexander, passing briefly over the immediately relevant understanding, did touch upon the reason, but did not explain the principal basis of Aristotle’s statement. Porphyry, however, placed this very cause and origin of the discussion more fully before our eyes. He unfolded the whole dispute and controversy among the ancient philosophers concerning the force of signification.

He says that, in the opinions of the ancient philosophers, it remained uncertain what, properly speaking, was signified by spoken sounds. Some thought that things were designated by spoken sounds and supposed that the names of those things were whatever was uttered in speech. Others contemplated certain incorporeal natures whose significations were whatever was designated by spoken sounds. In a certain way they imitated Plato’s incorporeal Forms, when he says “the man itself” and “the horse itself”: they did not conceive the individual underlying substance of any person, but that particular man and that particular horse universally and incorporeally. Thus they posited certain incorporeal natures, which they thought came first in signification and could be joined in significations with other things, so that some assertion or utterance might be formed from them.

Others thought that senses were signified by spoken sounds; others, that images or representations were signified. Since this controversy existed among earlier thinkers and had continued down to Aristotle’s time, it was necessary that anyone who was going to define the noun and the verb as significant should first state what they designate.

Aristotle does not think that nouns and verbs signify the things that underlie them, nor, indeed, sensations or images. In his work On Justice he makes clear that sensations are not what significant nouns and verbs signify, saying:

> Φύσει γὰρ διηνέχθησαντάτε νοήματα καὶ τὰ αἰσθηματα

This may be rendered in English as follows: “For intellects and sensations are different by nature.” He therefore thinks that sensation and intellect differ in some respect. But when he says that the affections of the soul are signified by spoken sounds, he is not speaking of sensations. Sensations are affections of the body. If, therefore, he had said that affections of the body are signified by spoken sounds, we should rightly understand him to mean sensations. But since he proposed that nouns and verbs signify affections of the soul, we must understand him to mean not sensations but intellects.

Yet since imagination too is a matter of the soul, someone might wonder whether perhaps by “affections of the soul” he means images, which the Greeks call φαντασίαι. But in the books On the Soul he most accurately and carefully separated these, saying:

> Ἔστι δὲ φαντασία ἕτερον καταφάσεως καὶ ἀποφάσεως, συμπλοκὴ γὰρ νοημάτων ἐστὶ τὸ ἀληθὲς ἢ ψεῦδος, τὰ δὲ πρῶτα νοήματα τί διοίσει τοῦ μὴ αὐτὰ φαντάσματα εἶναι; Ἦ οὐδ` αὐτὰ φαντάσματα ἀλλ` οὐκ ἄνευ φαντασμάτων.

This he translates as follows:

> Imagination is different from affirmation and negation. For truth or falsity is a combination of intellects; but in what would the first intellects differ from not being images? Certainly they are not themselves images, but they do not exist without images.

This statement shows that images are one thing and intellects another; affirmations and negations arise from the combination of intellects. Hence he also wondered whether the first intellects might be certain images. By “first intellects” we mean those that conceive a simple thing—for example, if someone says merely “Socrates”—and one wonders whether such an intellect, which contains in itself neither truth nor falsity, is an intellect or an image of Socrates himself.

[Col. 0406D] But on this point too he seems to speak clearly. He says: “Certainly these are not images, but they do not exist without images.” For what this utterance signifies—whether “Socrates” or something else—is not itself a simple image but an intellect; and this intellect cannot arise apart from an image.

Sensation and imagination are, as it were, certain first outlines upon which understanding rests as upon a foundation. Just as painters customarily sketch a body in lines and lay beneath the body the surface on which they will render a face by means of colors, so sensation and imagination are naturally placed beneath the soul’s apprehension. When some object falls under the senses or under thought, it is first necessary that a certain image of it arise. [Col. 0407A] Afterward a fuller intellect comes upon it, unfolding all its parts, which had first been taken up confusedly by imagination.

Imagination is therefore something incomplete. Nouns and verbs, however, signify not something truncated but something complete. Aristotle’s opinion is consequently correct: whatever is contained in nouns and verbs signifies neither sensation nor imagination, but only the quality of intellects.

For this reason the Peripatetics, following Aristotle, very rightly maintained that there are three utterances: one that can be written in letters, another that can be produced by the voice, and a third that is joined together in thought. One is contained in intellects, another in the voice, and the third in letters.

Since Aristotle therefore thought that what is signified by spoken sounds is intellect, and since he was going to place nouns and verbs among the significant things in their definitions, he rightly stated what they signify. In this way he restrained the reader’s error, arising from the many disputes of the ancients, by making his own position clear. Thus nothing in his statement is superfluous, nor is anything detached from the continuity of the order.

Porphyry asks why Aristotle said, “There are, therefore, the things that are in the voice,” rather than “There are, therefore, spoken sounds”; and again why he said “the things that are written” rather than “letters.” He resolves this as follows.

It has been said that among the Peripatetics there are three utterances: one contained in letters, another produced in the voice, and a third joined together in the mind. If there are three utterances, there is no doubt that the parts of utterance are also threefold. Since the verb and the noun are principally parts of utterance, there will be some verbs and nouns that are written, others that are spoken, and others that are handled in silent thought.

Therefore, since Aristotle proposed to begin by saying, “First it is necessary to establish what a noun is and what a verb is,” and since the nature of nouns and verbs is threefold, he showed which of them he intended to discuss and define. Because he is speaking of nouns and verbs that are produced by the voice, he explains the same point more clearly by saying:

> Therefore, the things that are in the voice are signs of the affections that are in the soul, and the things that are written are signs of the things that are in the voice.

It is as though he had said: those verbs and nouns that are produced in vocal utterance announce the affections of the soul. But those verbs and nouns that are written signify the verbs and nouns that are produced by the voice. Just as the verbs and nouns of vocal utterance signify conceptions of the mind and intellect, so those verbs and nouns that lie only in the forms of letters are significant of the verbs and nouns that we speak—that is, that we utter through the voice.

When he says, “the things that are in the voice,” the nouns and verbs must be understood. Again, when he says, “the things that are written,” the same must once more be supplied, namely, verbs and nouns. And when he adds, “of the things that are in the voice,” we must add, “of those nouns and verbs that vocal utterance produces and expresses.”

If nothing at all were lacking, the full statement would be this:

> Therefore, those nouns and verbs that are in the voice are signs of the affections that are in the soul, and those verbs and nouns that are written are signs of the verbs and nouns that are in the voice.

The latter clause must be understood generally, although what we have supplied may appear to be absent. The statement is therefore not disconnected, but continuous with the first proposition.

When Aristotle decided to define what the verb and the noun are, and since the nature of the noun and the verb is multiple, he clearly distinguished which noun and verb he wished to discuss. Beginning, then, with those nouns and verbs that are in the voice, he discussed what they signify. He said that these designate the affections of the soul. He also added by what those nouns and verbs that are in the voice are themselves designated: namely, by those expressed through the forms of letters.

But since not every voice is significant, whereas verbs and nouns never lack signification; and since not every voice that signifies designates something by convention, but some signify naturally—for example, tears, groans, and grief, and certain voices of other animals also naturally reveal something, such as anger shown by the barking of dogs and affection displayed by another of their sounds—verbs and nouns signify by convention.

He therefore did not say simply, “They are voices that are signs of the affections that are in the soul,” since verbs and nouns are not merely voices, but significant voices; nor are they merely significant voices, but voices that designate something by convention and not by nature. If he had said this, it would have had no bearing on the distinctive nature of verbs and nouns.

For this reason he did not speak generally of voices, but said only “the things that are in the voice.” Voice is something universal, whereas nouns and verbs are parts; and every part is in a whole. Since verbs and nouns are therefore within voice, it was correctly said, “the things that are in the voice”—as though he had said: since they are contained within voice, they designate intellects.

But this is similar to saying: a voice having a certain determinate character signifies intellects. For, as has been said, a noun and a verb are not merely voices. A coin too is not merely stamped bronze with a certain shape, so as to be called a coin; it must also serve as the price of something else. In the same way, verbs and nouns are not merely voices, but are posited for the signification of certain intellects.

A voice that designates nothing, such as *gargulus*, may indeed be called a noun by grammarians who attend to its form as a voice. Philosophy, however, does not consider it a noun unless it has been posited to designate some conception of the soul and can in that way signify something belonging to things. For a noun must be the noun of something. If a voice designates nothing, it is the noun of nothing; and if it is the noun of nothing, it is not even said to be a noun.

For that reason such a voice—that is, a significant voice—is called not merely a voice but a verb or a noun, just as a coin is called not merely bronze but, by its proper name, a coin, by which it is distinguished from other bronze.

Therefore Aristotle’s statement, in which he says “the things that are in the voice,” designates nothing other than a voice that is not merely a voice, but which, while being a voice, possesses some specific property and, in a certain way, the impressed form of an instituted signification.

Of these—that is, of the verbs and nouns that are in the voice—the things that are written are in a certain way significant. Thus what he says, “the things that are written,” must be understood as referring to verbs and nouns that are in letters.

There may also be another reason why he said “the things that are written.” We call both letters and written forms, as well as the voices signified by those same forms, by the name “letters.” Thus the letter *a* and the sound itself both receive the name of the letter, as does the form inscribed upon wax that signifies the sound.

Therefore, wishing to indicate by what verbs and nouns the things in the voice become apparent, he did not say “letters,” since that could also refer to sounds belonging to letters, but said “the things that are written,” to show that he was speaking of letters established in writing—that is, letters whose form can be impressed upon wax with a stylus or upon parchment with a reed pen.

Otherwise, even the things that exist in sounds would be referred to the nouns that are in the voice, since nouns and verbs are joined to those sounds. But Porphyry, judging between the two interpretations, says:

> What he says, “and the things that are written,” should be referred not rather to letters, but to the verbs and nouns that are placed in the inscription of letters.

It remains, then, to add why Aristotle did not say: “Therefore, the things that are in the voice are signs of intellects.” Instead he said: “Therefore, the things that are in the voice are signs of the affections that are in the soul.”

Although the things that are in the voice signify things and intellects, they signify intellects principally, while they signify the things comprehended by the intellect only secondarily, through the mediation of intellects. But the intellects themselves do not exist without certain affections that arise in the soul from the underlying things.

For anyone who has undergone the impression of a thing’s property, having grasped it intellectually, strives to express and designate it. When someone understands some thing, he must first receive through imagination the form and property of the thing understood; and there arises either an affection or a certain apprehension of the intellect together with an affection. Once this has been established and placed in the seats of the mind, there arises the will to indicate the affection to another. The act of continuing the understanding immediately follows from the power of the innermost reason, and utterance explains and pours it forth, relying upon the affection first established in the mind—or, more truly, the utterance advances while signification advances along with it and keeps pace with the movements of the utterance that signifies.

This affection comes about as though it were the impression of some form, but in the manner customary to what takes place in the mind. For a proper form exists naturally in each thing in one way, while the form of that thing is transferred to the mind in another way. Letters, that is, the signs of spoken sounds, are not entrusted in the same manner to wax, marble, and sheets of writing. The Stoics speak of imagination as transferred from things into the soul, but they always add the qualification “in the manner customary to what takes place in the soul.”

Therefore, since every affection of the soul seems to be a certain property of a thing, and since significant voices rely principally upon the signification of intellects and thereafter upon the signification of the things from which those intellects arise, whatever is significant in spoken sounds designates the affections of the soul.

These affections of the mind, however, are produced from the likeness of things. When someone sees a sphere, a square, or any other figure, he grasps it in the understanding of his soul by a certain force and likeness. Whoever has seen a sphere considers and thinks about its likeness in his mind; and having undergone in his mind a kind of image of it, he recognizes that of which he bears the image.

Every image retains the likeness of the thing whose image it is. When the mind therefore understands, it grasps the likeness of things. Thus, when we observe two bodies, one larger and the other smaller, and afterward, with the bodies removed from our senses, think of those same bodies while memory preserves the matter, we know and recognize which body we saw as smaller and which as larger. This could not happen unless the mind retained the likenesses of things that it had once undergone.

Since the affections of the soul that are called intellects are therefore certain likenesses of things, Aristotle, when he shortly afterward spoke of the affections of the soul, passed in continuous order to likenesses, since it makes no difference whether he called them affections or likenesses. The same thing is an affection of the soul and a likeness of a thing.

Alexander also attempts to explain this passage:

> Therefore, the things that are in the voice are signs of the affections that are in the soul, and the things that are written are signs of the things that are in the voice; and just as letters are not the same for everyone, so neither are spoken sounds the same.

He explains it in this way. Aristotle proposed, he says, that the things in the voice designate the intellects of the mind, and he proves this by an example. For the things in the voice signify the affections of the soul in the same way as the things that are written designate spoken sounds. Thus we should understand “and the things that are written” as though he had said: “Just as the things that are written”—and Alexander says that the things that are written are signs of spoken sounds, that is, of nouns and verbs.

He showed this by adding: “And just as letters are not the same for everyone, so neither are spoken sounds the same.” For it is a sign that the signification of the spoken sounds themselves is contained in letters: where the letters are varied and the things written are not the same, the spoken sounds too must necessarily be varied. Thus far Alexander.

Porphyry, however, since he posited three utterances—one contained in letters, the second resounding in verbs and nouns, and the third unfolded by the intellect of the mind—says that Aristotle means this when he says:

> Therefore, the things that are in the voice are signs of the affections that are in the soul.

He says that Aristotle was showing this, as though he had said:

> Therefore, the things that are in the voice—the verbs and nouns—are signs of the affections of the soul.

And since Aristotle showed what the spoken sounds were significant of, Porphyry says that he also taught by what signs verbs and nouns were disclosed. For this reason he added:

> And the things that are written are signs of the things that are in the voice.

It is as though he had said:

> The written nouns and verbs are signs of the nouns and verbs that are in the voice.

The statement is therefore not disconnected. Nor, as Alexander thinks, should the words “and the things that are written” be understood as though Aristotle had said: “Just as the things that are written—that is, the letters—signify the things that are in the voice, so the things that are in the voice are signs of the affections of the soul.”

First, nothing should be added to the simple sense. Second, such a brief sequence, like a necessary form of utterance, should not be broken by inserting a division. Third, if the signification of letters and spoken sounds is similar to the signification of spoken sounds and the affections of the soul, then, just as spoken sounds are changed by different letters, so the affections of the soul ought also to be changed by different spoken sounds. But this does not happen, since the same intellect can be signified by different spoken sounds.

Alexander attempts to prove the position I have mentioned above—that he understood the passage in this way—by the following argument. He says that the signification of letters and spoken sounds is also similar in this respect: just as letters signify spoken sounds not naturally but by convention, so spoken sounds too designate the intellects of the mind not naturally but by some convention.

But anyone who first accepts that Aristotle’s words “and the things that are written” were said as though he had said, “Just as the things that are written,” must equally and without doubt be in error concerning whatever he adds to this interpretation.

Accordingly, in our judgment, those who wish to hold the more correct view will attach themselves to Porphyry’s opinion. Aspasius too strongly agrees with the second opinion of Alexander that we set out above; for this reason he will be criticized by us as having fallen into the same error as Alexander.

Aristotle thinks that these signs—letters, spoken sounds, and the affections of the soul—are established in two ways: one by convention, the other naturally. This is what he means when he says:

> And just as letters are not the same for everyone, so neither are spoken sounds the same.

For if letters signified spoken sounds, and spoken sounds in turn naturally designated the intellects of the mind, all human beings would use the same letters and the same spoken sounds. But since the letters are not the same among all peoples, nor the spoken sounds the same, it is clear that they are not natural.

There are, however, two possible readings of the following passage. Alexander thinks that it should be read in this way:

> But of those things of which these are first signs, the affections of the soul are the same for everyone; and of those things of which these are likenesses, the things themselves are also the same.

Aristotle, he says, wished to separate the things that signify by convention from those that designate something naturally. He therefore inserted the point that the things that signify by convention are varied, whereas those that signify naturally are the same among all.

Beginning with spoken sounds and proceeding to letters, Aristotle first demonstrates that they are not naturally significant by saying:

> And just as letters are not the same for everyone, so neither are spoken sounds the same.

For if letters are proved not to signify naturally because they differ among different peoples, it will likewise be plausible that spoken sounds do not signify naturally, since the various nations of human beings converse with one another using different spoken sounds.

But wishing to teach that the likeness between intellects and the things underlying them is naturally established, he says:

> But of those things of which these are first signs, the affections of the soul are the same for everyone.

That is, the spoken sounds that are different among different peoples retain a signification: they signify the affections of the soul, and those affections are the same among all. For it cannot happen that what is understood as “man” among the Romans should be understood as “stone” among the barbarians. The same applies to all other things.

The sense, then, is that what spoken sounds signify does not change among all nations of human beings. The spoken sounds themselves are different among many peoples, as Aristotle showed above when he said, “Just as letters are not the same for everyone, so neither are spoken sounds the same.” But what the spoken sounds themselves signify is the same among all human beings and cannot be altered in any way. These are the intellects of things, which, since they are natural, cannot be changed.

This is what he means by saying:

> Of those things of which these are first signs—that is, the spoken sounds—the affections of the soul are the same for everyone.

He thus shows that the spoken sounds are different, but that those things of which the spoken sounds are significant—namely, the affections of the soul—are the same among all and cannot be changed in any way, since they are naturally established.

Nor does Aristotle intend here to speak only of spoken sounds and intellects. By indicating that spoken sounds and letters are not naturally established, through the fact that they are not the same among everyone, he again shows that the intellects that he calls the affections of the soul are natural, because they are the same among everyone. From these—that is, from the intellects—he proceeds to things.

He says:

> Of those things of which these are likenesses, the things themselves are also the same.

He means that things too are naturally the same among everyone. Just as the affections of the soul, which are taken from things, are the same among all human beings, so the things themselves, whose likenesses are the affections of the soul, are also the same among everyone.

Things, therefore, are natural as well, just as the likenesses of things are natural, and these likenesses are the affections of the soul.

Herminus, however, is opposed to this interpretation. He says that it is not true that the intellects of all human beings are the same, intellects of which spoken sounds are significant. “What,” he asks, “will be said in the case of equivocation, where one and the same form of a spoken sound signifies several things?”

He instead considers the following reading more correct:

> Of those things of which these are first signs, these are the affections of the soul for everyone; and of those things of which these are likenesses, the things themselves are also the same.

On this reading, Aristotle seems to have shown of what the spoken sounds are significant, or of what things the affections of the soul are likenesses.

According to Herminus, this should be taken simply, so that we say:

> Those things of which spoken sounds are significant are the affections of the soul,

as though Aristotle had said: “The affections of the soul are what the spoken sounds signify.” And again:

> Those things of which the things contained in the intellects are likenesses are the things themselves,

as though he had said: “The things are what the intellects signify.”

Porphyry, however, judges between the two positions with insight and subtlety, and favors Alexander’s opinion more. He says that the multiple signification of equivocal expressions must not be concealed. The person who speaks applies his mind to one particular thing, which he declares by a spoken sound that he understands; and the person who hears expects one particular intellect.

If, however, while both understand different things from one name, the person who has uttered the equivocal name makes clearer what he intended that name to signify, the hearer immediately grasps it, and the two agree upon one intellect. Thus the intellect again becomes one among those same people among whom the affections of the soul had initially been different because of the equivocation of the name.

For it cannot be that one who distinguished spoken sounds that signify by convention from natural things by saying that the spoken sounds are not the same for everyone would fail to show that the things he proposed to be natural were natural for the same reason—namely, that they are the same among everyone.

Alexander is therefore to be approved, whether on the basis of his own opinion or on Porphyry’s authority.

Since Aristotle said, however:

> Of those things of which these are first signs, the affections of the soul are the same for everyone,

Alexander asks, if nouns are names of things, why Aristotle said that spoken sounds are first signs of intellects.

A name is imposed upon a thing. When we say “man,” we signify an intellect, but it is nevertheless the name of a thing—that is, of a rational, mortal animal. Why, then, are spoken sounds not rather first signs of the things for which they are imposed than signs of intellects?

“Perhaps,” he says, “this was stated because, although spoken sounds are names of things, we do not use spoken sounds in order to signify things, but in order to signify the affections of the soul that arise in us from things. Therefore, since spoken sounds themselves are uttered for the sake of signifying those affections, Aristotle rightly said that they are first their signs.”

Aspasius is very troublesome on this point. “How,” he asks, “can the affections of the soul be the same among all, when opinions concerning justice and goodness are so different?”

Aspasius thinks that by “affections of the soul” Aristotle meant not incorporeal things, but only those things that can be grasped by the senses. This is entirely false. A person who is mistaken cannot be said ever to have understood. Perhaps he may be said to have had an affection of the mind, whoever thinks that what is good is not as it is but otherwise; but he is not said to have understood it.

When Aristotle speaks of likeness, however, he speaks of intellect. For it cannot happen that someone who thinks that what is good is evil has conceived in his mind the likeness of the good. He has not understood the underlying thing.

But since all things that are just and good are referred either to convention or to nature, if Aristotle is speaking of justice and goodness in the sense of what is called civil justice or civil injustice, then the affections of the soul are rightly not the same, since civil justice and civil goodness exist by convention, not by nature.

Natural goodness and justice, however, are the same among all nations. The same applies to God. Although his worship is diverse, the intellect of him as a certain most eminent nature is nevertheless the same.

We must therefore return briefly to the beginning. Aristotle has proceeded through the parts up to utterance. When he first said that he was going to establish what the noun and the verb are, he was speaking of the least parts of utterance. But when he spoke of affirmation and negation, he was already speaking of an utterance composed of verbs and nouns; these in turn are parts of an assertion. After the proposition concerning assertion, he proposed to speak of utterance, of which assertion itself is also a part.

And since, as has been said, utterance is threefold—what exists in letters, what exists in the voice, and what exists in intellects—Aristotle, intending to define the verb and the noun and to establish them as significant, first says what the verbs and nouns themselves are significant of.

He begins with those nouns and verbs that are in the voice, saying:

> Therefore, the things that are in the voice—

and he shows what they are significant of by adding:

> —are signs of the affections that are in the soul.

Again, he declares that the verbs and nouns established in letters are significant of the nouns and verbs themselves that are in the voice, saying:

> And the things that are written are signs of the things that are in the voice.

Since these four things—letters, spoken sounds, intellects, and things—are in a certain respect distinct, and since letters and spoken sounds exist by convention, whereas things and intellects exist by nature, Aristotle showed that spoken sounds are not natural but conventional by saying that they are not the same among everyone, but varied:

> And just as letters are not the same for everyone, so neither are spoken sounds the same.

To show that intellects and things exist naturally, he said that the intellects are the same among all, of which the spoken sounds are significant, and again that the things are the same among all, of which the affections of the soul are likenesses:

> Of those things of which these are first signs—that is, of the things that are in the voice—the affections of the soul are the same for everyone; and of those things of which these are likenesses, the things themselves are also the same.

He called them “affections of the soul” because it had already been carefully shown elsewhere that every sound of an animal is produced either from an affection of the soul or on account of an affection of the soul. He called the likeness an affection of the soul because, according to Aristotle, understanding is nothing other than receiving into the soul’s consideration the property and image of any underlying thing. He recalls that he discussed these affections of the soul more carefully in the books On the Soul.

But since it has been shown how verbs, nouns, and utterance are principally significant of intellects, whatever signification exists in the voice comes from intellects. Therefore anyone who wished to discuss spoken sounds correctly first had to examine intellects briefly.

What he earlier called “affections of the soul” and “likenesses,” he now calls more openly “intellect,” saying:

> Just as in the soul there are sometimes intellects without truth or falsity, and sometimes those in which one of these must necessarily be present, so too in the voice. Truth and falsity concern composition and division. Nouns and verbs themselves, when no addition is made, are therefore similar to intellect without composition and division, as in “man” or “white.” For at this stage there is not yet truth or falsity. The sign of this is the following: “goat-stag” signifies something, but is not yet true or false unless “is” or “is not” is added, either absolutely or with reference to time.
