Since a noun, a verb, and every sentence are significant of the affections of the soul, there is no doubt that the specific character of their signification arises from the very things which they designate in those utterances. This, then, is the whole continuous sequence of Aristotle’s argument.

“Since,” he says, “the first things signified by utterances are those which occur in the mind and thought, and since among thoughts we consider some to be simple, without an assertion of truth or falsity”—as when the character of a human being is presented to us in silent imagination, for from this simplicity of understanding no recognition of truth or falsity arises—“while some thoughts are composite and conjoined, and in them there is already some apprehension of either truth or falsity,” as when something else is added to any simple mental perception that establishes it as being or not being something: for example, when being or not being, or being white or not being white, is joined to the thought of a human being. For then conceivable sentences arise that participate in truth or falsity, as follows: “A human being exists”; “A human being does not exist”; “A human being is white”; “A human being is not white.” Of these, “A human being exists” and “A human being is white” are called compositions: the former joins being to “human being,” and the latter joins “human being” to “white,” by a predicative combination of thoughts. But if I add something to the thought of a human being, so that the result is “A human being exists,” “A human being does not exist,” “A human being is white,” or something of that kind, then truth or falsity arises in the thought itself.

“Therefore,” he says, “just as there are at times certain simple thoughts that are without truth and falsity, while there are others in which one of these is found, so it is also with utterance. For those utterances that announce simple thoughts are themselves likewise separated from falsity and truth. But those that signify thoughts in which truth or falsity has already been established must themselves also contain one or the other. For if someone says only ‘human being,’ or ‘white,’ or even ‘goat-stag’ [hircocervus], although these expressions do signify something, nevertheless, since they signify simple thoughts, it is clear that they lack the whole character of truth or falsity.”

The entire argument, then, has this form. Yet we must attend more carefully to what he means by saying, “Truth and falsity are concerned with composition and division”; also to what is meant by the statement, “Nouns and verbs themselves are, in the same way as thoughts, without composition or division”; and likewise to why he uses a composite noun, or why he employs as an example something that does not subsist, when he says, “For ‘goat-stag’ signifies something.” Nor must we pass over what is meant by “either simply or according to time.”

First, then, we must discuss what he means by saying, “Truth and falsity are concerned with composition and division.” The question is whether every truth concerns composition and division, or whether some do and some do not. It must also be asked whether truth and falsity are established in every composition or division, or whether they are not present universally, but operate only in some part of composition or division.

In opinions there is truth whenever an imagination is derived from the subject matter, or whenever the intellect receives the imagination in accordance with the way the thing itself is. Falsity, on the other hand, occurs whenever an imagination is presented to the intellect either not from the subject matter or otherwise than the thing itself is. Yet even here, in truth and falsity, nothing else is found but a certain relation of opinion to the subject matter. For whatever the relation of the imagination to the subject matter is, and however the imagination corresponds to the thing, that alone is perceived in this truth or falsity. No one, however, would call such a relation “composition.” Nor can any mode of division, even fictitiously, be understood in this case.

It must also be considered whether there is some composition or division among these matters that are called true or false according to their own substance, as in “the true pleasure of living well” and “the false pleasure of waging war.” It must likewise be considered that, in the greatest God, whatever is understood is understood not accidentally but substantially; for we believe that the things which are good in him belong to him substantially, not accidentally. If, then, we believe God to be substantial, and no one would call God false, and nothing accidental can occur in him, God himself must be called truth. Where, then, is composition or division in things that are naturally simple and are joined by no comparison with any other thing?

Therefore not every truth, nor every falsity, is constituted around composition and division. Rather, this applies only to what arises through a plurality of thoughts and in the utterance of speech. For in the relation between imagination and the thing itself there is no composition; but composition occurs in the conjunction of thoughts. When I say, “Socrates walks,” the conception that he walks is itself not a composition. But when, through the progression of thought, I join walking to Socrates, a composition has now taken place. If I express this in speech, the same composition recurs, and the force of truth or falsity appears in relation to it.

Accordingly, truth and falsehood are found only in those compositions about which the present inquiry is concerned: namely, in the noun and the verb, in negation and affirmation, and in enunciation and sentence. These, receiving from thoughts the nature of truth and falsity, preserve it in the utterance of speech.

I shall explain more fully a little later the division that belongs to negation and the composition that belongs to affirmation. For now, we must consider whether truth or falsehood arises with every composition and every division. This is altogether false. Who, for example, would say that the conjunction “Socrates and Plato,” or, if these names are divided from one another, “neither Socrates nor Plato,” possesses any significance of truth or falsity? We must therefore admit that neither every division nor every composition—that is, the composition or division found in a sentence—contains falsehood or truth.

But the following is entirely true: every truth and falsity found in a sentence arises in composition and division, although not every composition or division of a sentence retains truth or falsity. Thus, if Aristotle had said, “Truth and falsity are concerned with every composition or division,” he would have spoken falsely. But since he said simply, “Truth and falsity are concerned with composition and division,” we must judge that he spoke most truly and subtly. For those nouns that are called simple in such a way that they can in some manner designate truth or falsity are of a kind that retain within themselves, and within their signification, a certain composition. Thus, if someone says, “I read,” this is equivalent to saying, “I am reading.” That is a composition.

Likewise, whenever one person asks a question and another responds with a single utterance, it appears that even then a simple expression produces truth or falsehood. This is completely false. The hearer’s response is joined to the entire structure of the preceding enunciation. If someone asks whether the world is an animal, and another answers, “It is,” this single particle appears to contain truth or falsehood; but that is false. It is not a single expression: for one who considers the force of the response, it is equivalent to saying, “The world is an animal.”

When he says that nouns and verbs themselves are, in the same way as thoughts, without composition or division, he indicates what he had already said above: that things expressed in speech are signs of the affections of the soul. If they are signs, then, just as letters bear in themselves a likeness of utterances, so utterances bear a likeness of thoughts.

Since we have explained why he spoke of the likeness of verbs and nouns to the affections of the soul, and why he proposed that falsity and truth are concerned with composition and division, we must now explain what composition or division itself is, in which truth or falsity is found. Since he is considering a simple enunciative sentence, as he himself later explains in the section on division, saying, “The first and primary enunciative sentence is affirmation, and then negation,” he now intends to designate the composition that either establishes the substance of something or joins something according to being.

When I say, “Socrates exists,” I apply being to Socrates himself and establish it as his substance. But if I say, “Socrates is a philosopher,” I have composed philosophy and Socrates according to being. Or if I say, “Socrates walks,” the expression is equivalent to saying, “Socrates is walking.”

Whenever, therefore, there is a composition of this kind—one that establishes a verb or substance according to being, or joins things together—it is called an affirmation, and the nature of truth and falsity is perceived in it. Since every negation is constituted in relation to a predication, the negation of the affirmation “Socrates exists” is not “Socrates is not,” but “Socrates does not exist.” The word “not” is added to the being that was predicated of Socrates, so that we say that the thing which was previously said to exist does not exist.

Accordingly, since the negation separates whatever was established or joined according to being in the affirmation, whether the establishment of the substance itself or the conjunction effected by saying that something exists, it is called a division. When I say, “Socrates does not exist,” I separate being from Socrates. When I say, “Socrates is not a philosopher,” I separate Socrates from being a philosopher. This separation, which belongs to negation, he called division.

It is therefore clear that if the thought in the affections of the soul is simple, and the thought itself does not yet retain any nature of truth or falsity, its expression is likewise separated from both. But when a composition according to being, or a division, has occurred in thoughts—the thoughts in which truth and falsity are principally generated—then, since utterances receive their signification from thoughts, they too must be true or false according to the quality of those thoughts.

The example possesses the greatest force because of its novelty and refined subtlety. To demonstrate that a single noun is neither true nor false, Aristotle chose a noun that is composite, although no substance corresponding to it can be found. If, then, a single noun could retain truth or falsity, he selected the noun “goat-stag.” Since there is no substance corresponding to it anywhere among existing things, it appears to designate something false; but it does not designate any falsity. Unless “goat-stag” is said either to exist or not to exist, although the thing itself does not exist, the word by itself contains nothing false or true that can be discerned in the utterance.

To demonstrate the force of a simple noun, therefore—its complete lack of truth and falsehood—he selected as an example a noun to which no thing is subject. If a single noun could signify something true or false, then a noun designating as existing a thing that does not exist would be altogether false. But it is not false. Therefore truth and falsity will never be found in a simple noun.

Nor was it a matter of little importance that he did not choose a noun signifying absolutely nothing, but one which, while signifying something, could nevertheless not be true or false. This was so that the cause of truth and falsity would not appear to be the fact that it signified nothing, but rather the fact that it was uttered simply.

At the same time, this example also establishes that not only simple nouns, lacking composition, but even composite nouns cannot signify truth or falsity unless they possess some composition according to being or non-being, as was said above. It is as though he were saying: not only does a simple noun, apart from any composition, signify nothing true or false, but composite nouns likewise lack both unless “to be” or “not to be” is added to them, either simply or according to time.

He added this because enunciations are made in some cases in such a way that what is said of a thing is proposed according to its substance, while in other cases the very being that is added signifies not substance but a certain presence.

When we say, “God exists,” we are not saying that he exists now, but simply that he exists in substance; the expression refers rather to the immutability of his substance than to any particular time. But if we say, “It is day,” this does not refer to the substance of the day, but only to the establishment of time. For what it signifies is equivalent to saying, “It is now.” Thus, when we add “exists” to designate substance, we add it simply; but when it is added to signify something present, it is added according to time.

This is one explanation of the passage.

Another explanation is as follows. “To be something” is said in two ways: either simply or according to time. To be simply means to be according to the present time, as when someone says, “A goat-stag exists.” But the present spoken of here is not a time in itself; it is the boundary between times, for it is the end of the past and the beginning of the future. Accordingly, whoever uses the expression “to exist” with reference to the present uses it simply. Whoever joins it either to the past or to the future does not use it simply, but brings it into the sphere of time. For, as has been said, two times are posited: the past and the future.

If, then, someone speaks of the present, he speaks simply; but if he speaks of either the past or the future, he uses the enunciation according to time.

There is also a third explanation of this kind: sometimes we use time in such a way that we speak indefinitely. Thus someone may say, “A goat-stag exists,” “A goat-stag existed,” or “A goat-stag will exist.” These expressions are indefinite and simply stated. But if someone adds “now it exists,” “yesterday it existed,” or “tomorrow it will exist,” he adds time to the being that is stated simply.

According to one of these three explanations, therefore, we must understand what he means by saying that “to be” or “not to be” is added either simply or according to time.

To what he had proposed earlier—namely, that at times there is in the soul a thought without truth or falsity—he subsequently supplied, as though by way of consequence, the statement that nouns and verbs themselves are like simple thoughts, as in “human being” or “white.” But to the statement that there are thoughts in which one of these alternatives must already be present, he offered no immediate counterpart. It may be thought that he supplied it by saying, “But it is not yet true or false unless ‘to be’ or ‘not to be’ is added.” For this is a certain composition of thoughts in which one of these alternatives must already be present, since in the sentence either “to be” or “not to be” is added.

Accordingly, since he had proposed to discuss the noun and the verb, and since he had shown, with the deepest reasoning, the consequences linking utterances, letters, thoughts, and things, he returns to the definition he had first promised when he said, “First we must establish what a noun is and what a verb is.” He now proceeds to define what he had promised to define.

## On the Noun

A noun is a significant utterance, established by convention, without time, none of whose parts, taken separately, is significant. In the noun “horse-wild” [equiferus], “wild” [ferus] signifies nothing by itself, unlike in the sentence “a wild horse.”

Every definition is formed by establishing a genus and completed by combining differences. For if we gather the differences belonging to the proposed genus and adapt them to the one species that we wish to define, until the collection applies to one species alone, nothing further is required for constructing the definition. Thus, if someone defines “human being” by reference to its genus, which is “animal,” it is necessary to add two differences, namely rational and mortal, and to construct the expression “rational mortal animal” [animal rationale mortale]. When this definition is referred to the human being, it is a complete description of its rational nature and substance.

Aristotle, therefore, wishing to define what a noun is, first took its genus, saying that a noun is an utterance. He did this in order to separate what we call a noun from other things that are not utterances but merely sounds.

Sound differs from voice. Sound is a perceptible striking of the air, whereas voice is breath issuing through certain parts of the throat called the windpipe, and formed by some movement of the tongue. Voice belongs only to living creatures, while sound is sometimes produced also by the collision of inanimate bodies.

Since, then, he showed that a noun is a voice, he separated and distinguished this part of speech from other things that are not voices but merely sounds, and took “voice” as the genus of the noun.

There is also something else that occupies the place of a species and differs from a noun, namely the verb. There are also certain utterances that signify nothing at all, such as articulated sounds whose signification cannot be discovered, for example “scindapsus.”

To this genus, therefore, he again adds other differences. Just as he separated the noun, as a voice, from other sounds, so these differences divide and distinguish the noun from the other species included under voice. In adding that a noun is a significant voice, he separated the noun from those voices that signify absolutely nothing, such as syllables. For although the whole noun is composed of syllables, the syllables themselves signify nothing at all.

There are also voices composed of letters and syllables that have no signification, such as “blitiri.” Since, therefore, there appeared to be certain voices lacking signification, the noun—which is a voice always uttered as the designation of something—could not be defined otherwise than by first separating it from non-significant voices. Hence he says that a noun is a significant voice, separating voice from other sounds, and, by adding signification, from things under voice that designate nothing.

But this does not yet complete the definition. A noun is not the only significant voice. There are certain voices that signify something but are not nouns, such as those uttered by us in various emotional states: when someone groans, or when, driven by pain, he emits a cry. The one is a sign of pain in the soul, the other of pain in the body. Although they are voices and signify some affection of either soul or body, no one would call a groan or a cry a noun.

There are also voices of mute animals that signify something. The barking of dogs signifies the dogs’ anger; another, gentler voice expresses a kind of affection or caress. A further difference was therefore needed to separate the noun from all things that are voices and signify something but are not included under the term “noun.” Accordingly, he added that a noun is a significant voice not simply, but according to convention.

What is “according to convention”? It is what is established according to the determination and decision of the one who assigns the name. No noun is established naturally, nor is a thing ever named by a word arising from nature in the same way that the thing itself is naturally constituted. Rather, the human race, which is distinguished by reason and speech, imposed names, joining them by whatever letters and syllables it pleased, and assigned them to the substances of individual things.

This is demonstrated by the fact that, if nouns were natural, the same nouns would exist among all peoples, just as the senses, since they are natural, are the same among all peoples. All peoples look with eyes alone, hear with ears, smell with nostrils, receive tastes with the mouth, and judge by touch what is hot or cold, smooth or rough. Such things are, as has been said, the same among all peoples. The objects perceived are likewise unchanged, since they are naturally constituted.

Sweetness and bitterness, white and black, and all the other things perceived by the five senses are the same for everyone. What is sweet to Italians in their perception does not appear bitter to Persians, nor does what appears white to our eyes appear black to Indians—unless, perhaps, some disorder of the senses causes a change; but that has nothing to do with nature.

Since these things are natural, therefore, they remain the same among all peoples. If nouns likewise appear to be natural, they would be the same among all peoples and would undergo no alteration.

But the same human being is called by one word among the Latins, another among the Greeks, and by different words among barbarian peoples. This disagreement in assigning names is a sign that names were composed not naturally but according to the decision and will of those who assigned them to things.

The same point is shown by the fact that the names of individual people are often changed. The man whom we now call Plato was formerly called Aristocles; and the man now called Theophrastus was called Tirtamus by his parents before Aristotle gave him the name Theophrastus. When, within the same language, several names are assigned to one thing, this also shows that the thing is named not by natural but by imposed names. For if things were called by natural names, we would designate one thing by one name alone.

What purpose would be served, if names were natural, by there being several names for one thing, all converging upon the designation and indication of a single object? We say “sword,” “blade,” and “cutting sword” [gladius, ensis, mucro], and these three expressions converge upon one underlying substance.

It has therefore been shown that nouns are established according to convention—that is, according to the convention of those who assign them. It is as though he were saying that a noun is indeed a voice and significant, but not naturally significant: it is significant according to the convention and will of the one who assigns it. In this way he distinguishes it from voices that designate naturally, such as those that we utter in emotional affections, or those that mute animals attempt to produce.

But the difference stated above still does not establish the complete form and definition of a noun. The noun shares with the verb the fact that it is a designative voice established by convention. The added difference “without time,” however, distinguishes the noun from the verb. No noun co-signifies time; it belongs to the verb, whenever an affection or an action is signified, to draw along with it some force of time by which the thing is expressed as acting or being acted upon.

When I say “Socrates,” the expression belongs to no time. When I say “I read,” “I read [in the past],” or “I shall read,” the expressions are not without time. By adding to the noun that it is without time, therefore, the noun is separated from the verb.

No one should suppose that we believe that no noun signifies time. There are nouns that indicate time by their signification, as when I say “today” or “tomorrow”; these are nouns of time. But we mean that time is not co-signified along with the noun itself. To signify time is one thing; to co-signify time is another.

The verb signifies time together with a certain mode proper to it, as when it indicates the mode of an agent or a patient. An affection or an action is not expressed without time. We therefore do not say that a noun does not signify time, but that the signification of time does not follow along with the signification of the noun.

One difference remains. If it is added to the preceding differences, it will form almost the complete definition of a noun. This is the difference by which the noun is separated from a sentence.

There are certainly some sentences that are voices, significant, established by convention, and without time, such as “Socrates and Plato.” For this expression, since it is joined together from nouns, is not itself a noun, although it is a significant voice established by convention and is without time. To separate the noun from an expression of this kind, therefore, he added the difference “none of whose parts, taken separately, is significant.”

Since a sentence is joined together from verbs and nouns, and since it is clear that verbs and nouns are significant, it is beyond doubt that the parts of a sentence also signify something.

But the part of a noun, since the noun is simple, signifies absolutely nothing. Yet since every sentence, noun, and verb derives its power of signifying from the thoughts underlying it, sometimes one noun signifies many thoughts. Thus there can also be a noun that is not simple, because it does not designate only one affection or thought of the soul.

When I say “suburban” [suburbanum], the term retains the imagination of “urban,” but when it is separated from the whole noun and referred to the noun itself, it signifies nothing. Likewise, in “horse-wild” [equiferus], “wild” [ferus] seems indeed to signify something, but if it is separated from the whole composition, it designates nothing at all within that noun—namely, the noun in which, joined to the element “horse,” it co-signifies “horse-wild.”

For the whole composition designates one thought. Thus in a sentence “wild” signifies something, for “a wild horse” retains two thoughts. But in a noun it signifies nothing, because “horse-wild” designates one thought.

Perhaps, however, “wild,” in the part with which it is joined, co-signifies something, while in separation it signifies nothing. This, then, is what he says:

“Yet the case is not the same in simple and composite nouns. In the former, a part is in no way significant. In the latter, it wishes to be significant, but when separated it signifies nothing, as in ‘horse-wild,’ where ‘wild’ is concerned.

“‘According to convention,’ because no noun is natural, but becomes a sign when it is established. For inarticulate sounds also designate something, such as the sounds of wild animals, none of which is a noun.”

A simple noun, then, has no signification of any parts. A composite noun, however, has parts of such a kind that they seem, as it were, to attempt to signify something, but co-signify rather than signify anything independently.

By adding to the noun that its parts signify nothing when separated, he separated the noun from the sentence.

After explaining the force in the definition of a noun of the addition “none of whose parts, taken separately, is significant”—namely, that it separates the noun from the sentence—he also discusses why the phrase “according to convention” was added.

Since no signification of nouns is natural, but every noun designates by imposition, he therefore said “according to convention.” Whatever pleased the person who first assigned names to things is designated by those words.

Let us ask, then, who could affirm that names are natural when there is such great diversity among all peoples? Nor is the claim that no voice naturally designates anything. Rather, the claim is that nouns signify not naturally but by imposition.

Otherwise, the sounds of wild and mute animals would possess this feature. Their voices signify something: the neighing of a horse indicates the horse’s customary search for another horse; the barking of barking dogs indicates anger; and there are other examples of this kind.

But although the voices of mute animals signify by their own nature, they are not written down by any formulas of letters. A noun, however, although it is subject to letters, signifies nothing by itself before it is assigned to signify some underlying thing. Thus, when we say “scindapsus” or “hereceddyn,” these expressions signify nothing by themselves. But if they are assigned to designate some underlying thing, as when one says “a scindapsus human being” or “a hereceddyn stone,” then these expressions, which previously signified nothing by themselves, designate something by imposition and according to a certain convention of the one who assigns them.

Therefore, when a noun is significant, as he himself says, it becomes a sign. It becomes a sign when, according to the convention of the one who assigns it, a word that naturally designated nothing is given to signify an underlying thing. This is what he means by “it becomes a sign.” For if nouns signified naturally, Aristotle would never say of them that they “become a sign”; in that case they would not become signs but would already be signs.

Since nouns, then, are significant according to convention, whereas the inarticulate sounds of wild animals signify according to nature, the latter’s voices are not called nouns.

In general, we say that of all voices, some can be inscribed in letters and some cannot. Again, among those that can be inscribed and those that cannot, some signify and others signify nothing. Moreover, among all voices, some designate according to convention and others naturally.

A noun, therefore, is established according to convention, for by imposition it has become a sign of an underlying thing. No noun signifies naturally. For the signification of a noun is formed not according to nature but according to convention.

The inarticulate sounds of animals also signify, such as the sounds of wild beasts. He called them sounds because certain mute animals have no voice at all but merely produce a kind of clashing noise. Some fish make sounds not with a voice but with their gills; and, as Porphyry maintains, the cicada produces sound through its breast. None of these sounds is a noun.

This is not said to mean that no noun exists for the sounds produced by animals, but that animals do not use those sounds as nouns. Although an inarticulate voice signifies naturally, as in the barking of dogs, it is nevertheless called “barking”; the sound of a lion is called “roaring,” and that of a bull “bellowing.” These are nouns for the voices produced by mute animals.

But we do not say that their sounds have no nouns at all. We say rather that none of these sounds is such as to be a noun—that is, such that wild animals, using them as nouns, might converse with one another according to them. They possess signification, but, as has been said, their signification is natural.

A noun, however, is established according to convention.

“Not-man” [non homo] is not a noun; yet no noun has been imposed by which it should be called. For it is neither a sentence nor a negation. But let it be called an indefinite noun, since it applies similarly to whatever is, and to whatever is not.

“Of Cato” [Catonis], “to Cato” [Catoni], and all expressions of this kind are not nouns but cases of a noun. Their account is otherwise the same, but differs in this: when “is,” “was,” or “will be” is added, they are neither true nor false. A noun, however, with such an addition, always says something true or false; but “of Cato is” or “of Cato is not” does not yet say anything true or false.

Earlier he separated from the name everything that lay outside it by the additions mentioned above. Now, since there are certain expressions that fall under the definition of a name but nevertheless appear to differ from a name, he discusses them, so that what a name is may be explained in full.

For what we say—“not-man” or “not-horse”—is certainly not a sentence. Every sentence consists either of nouns and verbs, or solely of two or more verbs, or solely of nouns. But in “not-man” there is only one name, namely *man*; while *not* is neither a noun nor a verb. Therefore it does not consist of two verbs, or of a verb and a noun. There is no verb in it, and so what we call “not-man” is not a sentence.

It is superfluous to demonstrate that it is not a verb, since verbs always contain tenses, whereas no tense at all can be found in this expression. Nor is it a negation. Every negation is a sentence; but since “not-man” is not a sentence, it cannot be a negation. Moreover, every negation is either true or false, whereas “not-man” is neither true nor false. Its sense is not complete; for this reason also it is not called a negation.

Who, then, would call it a name, when every name—whether proper or appellative—signifies definitely? When I say “Cicero,” I have named one person and one substance; and when I say “man,” which is an appellative name, I have signified a definite substance. When, however, I say “not-man,” I do signify something—namely, whatever is not a man—but this is indefinite. A dog may be signified, or a horse, or a stone, or anything whatsoever that is not a man; and the expression is said equally of what exists and of what does not exist.

If someone says of the nonexistent Sulla, “not-man,” he signifies something that does not remain in substance or in the nature of things. If, however, someone says “not-man” of a stone, a piece of wood, or other existing things, he nevertheless signifies something; and the signification of this sort of word always extends beyond the thing it names. For when man is removed, whatever is other than man is signified by “not-man.” This differs greatly from a name: every name, as has been said, signifies definitely what is named, and is not said equally of what exists and of what does not exist. But this sort of expression is both designative and conventional, without tense; and, as has been said, its parts signify nothing independently.

Consequently, among the ancients there was uncertainty whether they should deny that this was a name, or whether they should admit it under the definition of a name by adding some qualification. Those who separated it from the category of name enclosed the definition of a name in this way: a name is a designative expression, conventional, without tense, of circumscribed signification, whose parts signify nothing independently. Since “not-man” does not designate a circumscribed thing, they separated it from the name.

Others did not proceed in this way. They said that it was a name, but not without qualification. They thought that it could be placed under the category of name by means of a certain addition, as follows: just as a dead man is not simply called “man,” but “dead man,” so this expression, which signifies nothing definite, should not be called simply a name, but an “indefinite name.” Aristotle is the authority for this view, claiming that he himself had discovered the term for the thing.

He says: “But it is not yet a name that has been established, by which it ought to be called.” By this he means that antiquity did not know what term should be applied to what we call “not-man”; indeed, until Aristotle no one knew what the expression “not-man” was. Aristotle gave this expression a name, saying: “But let it be an indefinite name”—not simply a name, since it does not signify within any circumscription, but an indefinite name, since it signifies several things and signifies them indefinitely.

This situation, however, is not confined to such expressions, which cannot be placed simply under the category of name. There are also certain others that possess all the properties of a name and signify definitely, but nevertheless, because of another difference, cannot be called names without qualification. Such are the oblique cases, as when we say *Catonis* (“of Cato”), *Catoni* (“to Cato”), *Catonem* (“Cato” in the accusative), and the others.

Their difference from a name is this: a noun in the direct case, joined with *est* (“is”) or *non est* (“is not”), forms an assertion. If someone says, “Socrates is,” this is true or false. If it is said while Socrates is alive, it is true; if it is said after his death, it is false. Thus it is an affirmation. If someone says, “Socrates is not,” he again produces a negation, in which truth or falsity is likewise found.

Therefore every direct-case name, joined with *is* or *is not*, produces an assertion. These oblique cases, however, joined with *is* or *is not*, do not complete an assertion in any way. An assertion is a complete sense of a sentence, one to which truth or falsity applies. If someone says, “It is Cato’s,” the sense is not yet complete: what belongs to Cato is not stated. The same is true of “It is to Cato” or “It is Cato” in the accusative.

Since, then, when joined with *is* or *is not* they do not complete an assertion, they differ in some respect from a name, although in every respect they are joined to the definition of a name. The difference is considerable: a direct-case name, joined with *is*, makes a complete sentence, whereas an oblique case makes an incomplete one.

When it was said that oblique cases joined with the verb *is* do not make a complete sentence, this does not mean that oblique cases cannot be joined with any verb in such a way as to complete a sentence needing nothing further. For when I say “Socrates is troubled,” there is an assertion. But this does not happen with every verb: only when joined with *is* or *is not* do these cases fail in every way to constitute a complete sentence.

This is what he means when he says: “But *Catonis*, *Catoni*, and all such forms are not names, but cases of a name.” Hence they also appear to differ: these forms are not called names. Those forms are more properly called names that are placed first—that is, those that point to something. The genitive does not point to something, but to someone’s or something’s; the dative, to someone or something; and the other cases function similarly. The direct case, which is first, points to a thing, as when someone says “Socrates.” For this reason it is called the nominative: it alone, in a certain way, possesses the force of a name and is a name.

It is plausible that the person who first imposed names upon things spoke in this way: “Let this be called man,” and again, “Let this be called stone.” Later usage brought it about that the name originally imposed in the direct case was extended to the other cases.

There is an even more important point: every case is the case of some name. Therefore, unless there is a name whose case it is, it cannot properly be called a case of a name. Every case is an inflection. The genitive, dative, and other cases are inflections of the nominative; consequently, they will be cases of the nominative. But every case that is formed from a name is a case of a name. The name, therefore, is the nominative.

A case of something, however, is different from the thing itself whose case it is. A case of a name, therefore, is not a name.

When he adds, “Its account, however, is in other respects the same,” he means this: the account and definition of an oblique case and of a name are the same in all other respects. Both are expressions, both are significant, conventional, without tense, and designate within a circumscribed signification. But, as he himself says, they differ because, when joined with *is*, *was*, or *will be*, they are neither true nor false.

A direct-case name, by contrast, completes an assertion without any doubt when joined with *is*, *was*, or *will be*, producing something true or false. This is what he indicated when he said that a name, joined with *is*, *was*, or *will be*, always makes something true or false. He gives the examples: “It is Cato’s” and “It is not Cato’s.” In these, as he himself says, nothing true or false is yet stated.

The complete definition of a name is therefore as follows:

> A name is a designative expression, conventional, without tense, of circumscribed signification, whose parts signify nothing independently, and which, when joined with *is*, *will be*, or *was*, completes the sense of a sentence needing nothing further and constitutes an assertion.

Since the matter of the name has been settled, let us proceed to the definition of the verb.

## On the Verb

A verb is that which co-signifies tense, whose part signifies nothing independently, and which is always a sign of things predicated of something else. I say that it co-signifies tense as follows: *cursus* (“running”) is a noun, whereas *currit* (“he runs”) is a verb, for it co-signifies being present now. A verb is always a sign of things said of something else—that is, of things belonging to or existing in a subject.

The complete definition of a verb is therefore as follows:

> A verb is a significant expression, conventional, which co-signifies tense, and no part of which is designative independently.

But since being an expression, significant, and conventional is common to the verb and the name, he omitted these features and began with what is proper to the verb. The property by which the verb is separated from the definition of the name is that it co-signifies tense.

Every verb retains a co-signification of tense, not a signification of tense. A name signifies tense; but a verb, while primarily signifying actions and passions, also derives from those actions and passions the force of tense. Thus, when I say *lego* (“I read”), the verb primarily indicates a certain action. Yet together with that signification of action it also introduces the present tense. For this reason he does not say that a verb signifies tense, but that it co-signifies tense.

The verb does not primarily signify tense—for that belongs to the name—but, together with the things it primarily signifies, it introduces and incorporates the force of tense. Since both the name and the verb are significant and conventional expressions, the addition to the verb that it co-signifies tense separates it from the name. As has often been said, a name can signify tense, whereas a verb co-signifies it.

Just as, in the definition of the name, he added that its separated parts signify nothing at all apart from the whole composition, on account of sentences composed of names, such as “Plato” and “Socrates,” so in the case of the verb he added that no part of the verb signifies independently, on account of the sentences that verbs compose, such as “to walk” and “to run.” These expressions are composed of verbs, and the individual verbs signify both within the sentence and apart from it. In the verb itself, however, this is in no way the case. Just as a part of a name signifies nothing when separated from it, so a part of a verb signifies nothing when separated from it.

He says that a verb is always a sign of things predicated of something else. This amounts to saying that verbs signify nothing other than accidents. Every verb designates some accident. When I say *cursus* (“running”), the thing itself is indeed an accident, but it is not expressed in such a way that it is said to be in or not to be in something. If, however, I say *currit* (“he runs”), then, presenting the accident as the action of something, I signify that it is in something.

Since what we call *currit* cannot exist apart from some subject—for it cannot be said apart from the one who runs—it is therefore said that every verb is significant of things predicated of something else. The verb *currit* signifies something predicated of another, namely, of the one who runs.

Once these points have been established, he explains by examples what he meant by saying that a verb co-signifies tense. He says: “I say that it co-signifies tense: *cursus* is a noun, whereas *currit* is a verb, for it co-signifies being present now.”

He has shown most clearly how the verb differs from the name by placing the verb and the name side by side. Since *cursus* is an accident and has been named in such a way that it is a noun, it does not co-signify tense. But *currit*, that is, the accident expressed as a verb, designates the present tense. The verb appears to differ from the name in that the former co-signifies tense, whereas the latter is predicated without any co-signification of tense.

After demonstrating that the verb co-signifies tense, he now recalls what he had already said above—namely, that the verb is always predicated of something else—and explains how it is predicated. He says: “And it is always a sign of things said of something else, such as things belonging to a subject or existing in a subject.”

By this he means that a verb signifies something in such a way that what it signifies is predicated of something else, but as an accident. Every accident is both in a subject and predicated of the substance that is its subject. When I say *currit* (“he runs”), I predicate this of a man, if that happens to be the case—that is, I predicate it of the subject—and the running itself is in the man. Hence the verb *currit* is inflected.

Thus, when he says that a verb is always a sign of things predicated of something else, he shows that verbs always signify accidents. For he says that the things designated by the signification of verbs are either in a subject or predicated of a subject.

There is another possible interpretation, since he habitually uses the expression “predicated of a subject” indifferently, sometimes as though he meant “to be in a subject,” and often, when he says that something is predicated of a subject, he signifies that it is in a subject. Since he wished to show that the signification of accidents is contained in verbs, he said that verbs always designate things that are predicated of a subject. But because this seemed obscure, he clarified it by adding “or in a subject,” explaining by the latter phrase what he had earlier meant by “of a subject.”

It is as though he had said: “A verb is always a sign of things predicated of something else, that is, of a subject. But lest this seem obscure to anyone, I say that being predicated of a subject is the same as being in a subject.”

A better interpretation may be the following, if we take him to have spoken in a similar way, as though he had said: “Every verb signifies an accident, but in such a way that what it signifies is either particular or universal.” We may refer “of a subject” to universality and “in a subject” to particularity alone.

When I say *movetur* (“it is moved”), the expression is indeed a verb and an accident, but it is universal. Motion has several species, and running falls under motion. If motion is to be defined, therefore, we predicate motion of running. Motion is thus a genus of running, and for this reason motion is predicated of running as of a subject. Running itself, since it has no further species, exists only in a subject—that is, in the one who runs. Motion, although it too exists in a subject, is nevertheless predicated of a subject.

Therefore he says that a verb is a sign of things predicated of something else, and adds: “such as things predicated of a subject or existing in a subject.” He means that verbs signify the force of accidents, but of accidents that are either universal or particular. When I say *moveor* (“I am moved”), the expression is something universal and is predicated of a subject, such as running. When I say *curro* (“I run”), it is particular; since it is not predicated of a subject, it exists only in a subject.

“Not-running,” however, and “not-working”—I do not call these verbs, although they co-signify tense and are always of something. No name has been established for this difference, but it becomes an indefinite verb, since it is found equally in what exists and in what does not exist. Similarly, *curret* (“he will run”) and *currebat* (“he was running”) are not verbs but cases of the verb; they differ from the verb because the latter co-signifies the present tense, whereas those forms concern the surrounding tenses—

Just as he said in the case of the name that “not-man” is not a name because it applies to many other things that are not men, and because it removes from the predication what it says of man, leaving nothing definite in the same predication—for what is not a man may be a centaur, a horse, or other things that either exist or do not exist—and therefore it was called an indefinite name, so likewise in the case of the verb, “not-running” or “not-working” is itself indefinite. It may be predicated not only of what exists, but also of what does not exist.

I can say, “The man is not running,” and what I say—“is not running” or “is not working”—I predicate of an existing thing, namely, a man. I can again say, “Sulla is not running,” although Sulla does not exist. Therefore what I call “is not running” applies both to an existing thing and to something that is nothing.

Someone might perhaps argue that this too occurs among finite verbs. I can say, “The horse is running” and “The hippocentaur is running,” predicating it of something that exists and of something that does not.

As for the expression that embraces the future and the past, he said that the future lies before the present tense, whereas the past is left behind it, and he used a new and remarkable expression when he said “embraces.” After laboring long and hard to translate it as far as Latin allowed, we could achieve only this. In Greek, however, it is expressed more elegantly. The wording is:

> τὰ δὲ τῶν πέριξ

Anyone skilled in Greek recognizes how much better it sounds in the Greek expression.

Verbs uttered in themselves are therefore names, and they signify something. The speaker establishes a sense, and the hearer comes to rest. But they do not yet signify that a thing is or is not; for a verb is not a sign of a thing’s being or not being, not even if one utters *is* itself in isolation. The word *is* itself is nothing, but it co-signifies a certain composition, which cannot be understood without the things composed.

At this point Porphyry mixes together much material from Stoic dialectic and from other schools, and he does the same in other parts of this book, that is, in his explanations. Sometimes this should be disregarded by us, since excessive explanation often produces greater obscurity.

Aristotle’s meaning here is as follows. “Verbs,” he says, “when uttered in themselves, are names”—not in the sense in which every part of a sentence is commonly called a name, as when we speak of the names of things, but because every verb uttered by itself, without the addition of the thing of which it is predicated, is akin to a name.

For if I say, “Socrates walks,” the word *walks* belongs entirely to Socrates. It has no independent understanding of its own. But when I say simply “walks,” I have spoken as though the action were in someone, that is, as though someone were walking; nevertheless, the signification of the verb stands by itself and retains its own sense.

For this reason, among the Greeks, verbs are sometimes uttered alone with the prefixed articles, as in:

> τὸ περιπατεῖν — “walking”  
> τοῦ περιπατεῖν — “of walking”  
> τῷ περιπατεῖν — “to or for walking”

If verbs are joined with nouns in a Greek sentence, the prefixed articles cannot be added unless the verbs are uttered alone.

Since verbs signify a thing, and do so in such a way that, although they signify things that are in something, they are nevertheless spoken according to themselves and through their own essence, they are therefore names. When Aristotle says, “Verbs uttered in themselves are names,” his meaning is as though he had said: “Verbs uttered alone and not joined with others are names.”

He offers the following argument for this. “The speaker establishes a sense,” he says, “and the hearer comes to rest.” This means that every name, when heard, occupies a certain amount of time as it proceeds through its syllables. During the temporal progression in which the name is spoken, the mind of the hearer also advances. When I say *imperterritus* (“undaunted”), the name proceeds through the syllables *im*, *per*, *ter*, and the rest; correspondingly, the mind of the hearer advances through those same syllables.

But once the speaker has completed the name and said *imperterritus*, just as the name comes to rest when its progression through the syllables is complete, so the mind of the hearer also comes to rest. When the hearer has heard the whole name, he receives its whole signification. The hearer’s mind, which followed the speaker’s syllables in order to understand what was being said, comes to rest when it has grasped the signification. This is what he means by saying: “The speaker establishes a sense, and the hearer comes to rest.”

The speaker, after uttering the whole expression, establishes the hearer’s mind. There is no further direction in which the understanding can proceed. Once the name has been completed, the hearer’s mind, which had been advancing, is settled and comes to rest through the explanation provided by the name. It does not proceed any further toward understanding, since the name’s signification has been made complete.

This is common to the noun and the verb, but only when the verb is spoken alone. If it is joined with a noun, the hearer’s understanding is not yet settled, since there remains something toward which the mind of the hearer can advance. When I say, “Socrates walks,” *walks* is not understood by itself but is referred to Socrates; the understanding comes to rest in the complete sentence, not in the verb alone. But if it is uttered alone, its signification comes to rest in the same way as does that of a name.

It was therefore correctly said that verbs uttered in themselves are names, because the speaker establishes a sense and the hearer comes to rest.

Alternatively, the better explanation may be that verbs uttered in themselves are names because they possess the signification of some thing. For although a verb retains the signification of a thing that always exists either in something else or is predicated of something else, it does not follow that it signifies nothing at all. Nor, because it signifies something that cannot exist apart from a subject, does it therefore signify the subject itself.

When I say *sapit* (“he is wise” or “he has taste”), it does not follow that the word signifies nothing because *sapit* cannot exist without the one capable of being wise or of tasting. Nor, when I say *sapit*, does the word signify the one who is wise as existing in another. What I call *sapit* is the name of a certain thing that always exists in another and is predicated of another; consequently, it also has a sense.

Whoever hears *sapit*, although he does not hear a thing existing independently—for it always exists in another, and the thing in which it exists has not been stated—nevertheless understands something. He relies upon the signification of the verb itself, establishes his understanding in it, and comes to rest, without seeking anything further for the sake of understanding, just as happens with a name.

Just as a name is the proper signification of a thing existing independently, so a verb is the signification of a thing that does not exist independently, but rests upon another as its subject and, in a certain way, as its foundation.

There is a difficulty here, for what he says does not seem true: “The speaker establishes a sense, and the hearer comes to rest.” Neither does the speaker establish a sense, nor does the hearer come to rest; something is lacking from the expression or the name. If someone says “Socrates,” the mind of the hearer immediately asks: What about Socrates? Does he do something, or does he suffer something? The hearer’s understanding is not yet at rest while it asks for one of these possibilities. The same is true of a verb. When I say *legit* (“he reads”), the mind of the hearer asks who is reading. Therefore the speaker has not yet established a sense, nor has the hearer come to rest.

We should understand Aristotle to have been referring to the following. Whenever a hearer receives a significant expression in his mind, his understanding relies upon it. When someone hears “man,” he comprehends in his mind what the thing he has received is, and establishes in his mind that he has heard “a rational mortal animal.” If, however, someone receives an expression that signifies absolutely nothing, his mind, strengthened by no signification or understanding, wanders and turns about, and comes to rest within no boundaries of designation.

Aristotle’s view is therefore correct: verbs uttered in themselves are names, and the speaker establishes a sense while the hearer comes to rest. This difficulty was raised by Aspasius and resolved by him.

After Aristotle has established that verbs uttered in themselves are names, he says: “But they do not yet signify that a thing is or is not.” This means that verbs do signify something, like names, but no affirmation or negation is thereby completed. When I say *sapit* (“he is wise”), there is indeed a certain signification, but it does not demonstrate that anything is or is not. That is, it is neither affirmative nor negative.

For, as he has already taught above, affirmation and negation are found in compositions of thoughts. Neither nouns uttered alone nor verbs produce an affirmation or any negation. Aristotle has shown in several ways that truth and falsity are established not in things but in thoughts. If truth or falsity existed in things, one thing alone would either be an affirmation or the negation contrary to it. But since truth and falsity are established in joined thoughts, the sentence is also an interpreter of opinion, thought, and the affections of the soul.

Therefore, without a composition of thoughts, truth and falsity in words do not appear to exist; consequently, apart from some composition, there is no affirmation or negation. Verbs uttered in themselves do signify something and are names of a thing, but they do not yet signify in such a way as to establish that something is or is not—that is, they do not produce an affirmation or a negation.

Just as the parts of a name or of a verb signify nothing individually, while all of them together designate something, so likewise in affirmations and negations the parts signify individually, but when joined together they designate what is true or false. When I say, “Socrates is a philosopher” or “Socrates is not a philosopher,” the parts, placed separately, rely upon their own proper signification but signify nothing true or false. Joined together, however, as in “Socrates is a philosopher,” they produce truth, or, in the contrary expression, falsity.

Since verbs uttered in themselves are names and signify something, and since they are parts of a composition that can produce truth or falsity, they nevertheless do not, in their own proper signification, designate either existence—which belongs to affirmation—or nonexistence—which belongs to negation. Unless the verb is supplied with the person or thing in which it exists, no assertion is produced. When I say *sapit*, unless I add “the one who is wise,” it is not a proposition.

What he adds—“For it is not a sign of a thing’s being or not being”—means that the verb *is*, or the indefinite verb *is not*, does not itself indicate that a thing exists or does not exist; it signifies nothing independently. For *being* is not posited except in some composition.

Alternatively, every verb uttered by itself does signify something; but it does not thereby signify that something is or is not. For it does not follow that, once something has been uttered, it signifies that it is or is not. This is what he means when he says: “For it is not a sign of a thing’s being or not being.” The verb that is spoken does not signify that the thing of which it is said exists or does not exist.

It is as though he had said: “The verb that is spoken is not a sign that the thing of which it is said is or is not.” A better interpretation is that the verb is not a sign of the thing of which it is predicated existing or not existing—whether subsisting or not subsisting. The former belongs to affirmation, the latter to negation. The sense is therefore: “The verb that is spoken is not a sign that the thing is established or not established.”

He adds: “Nor if you utter this very word *is* alone,” or, as we may put it, “Nor if you utter this very word *being* alone.”

Alexander says that *is* or *being* is equivocal. All the categories, which are not subordinated to any common genus, are equivocal, and *being* is predicated of them all. Substance is, quality is, and so forth. Thus, Aristotle seems here to say that *being*, or *is*, from which *to be* is derived, signifies nothing by itself.

Every equivocal term, when placed by itself, signifies nothing. Unless it is adapted, according to the will of the speaker, to particular things, it is not designative of anything by itself, precisely because it signifies many things.

Porphyry, however, offers another explanation, as follows. The expression we call *is* does not by itself point to any substance, but always signifies some conjunction—either of existing things, if it is simply added, or of something else through participation.

When I say, “Socrates is,” what I say joins Socrates to the things that exist. If I say, “Socrates is a philosopher,” Socrates participates in philosophy. Here too I join Socrates and philosophy. Therefore the word *is* possesses the force of a certain conjunction, not of a thing.

If it announces some proposition or combination, then, when uttered alone, it signifies absolutely nothing. This is what he means by saying: “Nor if you utter this very word *is* alone.” That is, when spoken alone it designates not only neither truth nor falsity, but nothing at all.

What follows makes this clear: “It signifies a certain composition, which cannot be understood without the things composed.” For if *is* possesses the force and proper position of a certain composition and conjunction, then, uttered alone and without a conjunction, it signifies nothing. When it is joined to the things that are composed, it can signify the very composition that it marks; but without the things composed, it is impossible to understand what it signifies.

Alternatively, what he says—“it is nothing”—should be understood not in the sense that it signifies nothing, but in the sense that, if uttered alone, it demonstrates nothing true or false. When it is joined to something else, an assertion is produced. A verb uttered simply produces no signification of truth or falsity.

The entire meaning is therefore as follows: verbs uttered in themselves are names, for the speaker establishes a sense and the hearer comes to rest. Although verbs signify something, they do not yet signify an affirmation or a negation. Although they designate a thing, they do not yet signify that the thing exists; nor, if we say *is* or *being* itself, can anything true or false be discovered in it. Although it signifies something, it is not yet true or false. An assertion arises in a composition, and truth or falsity arises in it. It is impossible to understand that truth or falsity apart from the things that are composed and joined together.

Enough, then, has been said about the verb and the name. In the second book we must consider the sentence.

## Book Two

[Col. 0433]

[Col. 0433B] To the extent that human labor cultivates the human race and fills it with the most blessed fruits of intelligence, if people devoted themselves with equal zeal to the care and exercise of the mind, they would not make use of virtue so rarely. But when idleness lets the spirits sink, the fertile soil of the mind immediately bristles with savage growth. I would not grant that this happens through the knowledge of labor, but rather through ignorance; for who skilled in labor has ever withdrawn from labor?

Therefore the power of the mind must be directed toward its task, and it is true that the mind is lost if its effort is relaxed. For my part, if the more powerful favor of divinity grants its assent, I have firmly resolved that, although there have been distinguished intellects whose labor and study have contributed much concerning these matters that we too are now treating in the Latin language, they have nevertheless not set forth the stages of the disciplines by arranging them in a certain order and sequence.

I shall translate every work of Aristotle that comes into my hands into Roman style and set down in Latin all their commentaries, so that whatever Aristotle has written concerning the subtlety of logical art, the seriousness of moral expertise, and the acuity of natural truth, I may translate in an ordered manner and illuminate with a certain light of commentary. I shall also render all Plato’s dialogues into Latin, either by translating them or by commenting upon them.

When these tasks have been completed, I shall not disdain to bring the views of Aristotle and Plato into a kind of harmony, and to demonstrate that they do not, as most people think, disagree about everything, but agree about most of the matters that are of greatest importance in philosophy. If life and leisure remain for me, I shall strive to accomplish this with the great usefulness of this work, and also with renown. In this undertaking, those who are consumed by no envy ought to be favorable.

But now let us return to the matter proposed. Aristotle, beginning the book, first proposed that the name should be defined, then the verb, then negation, after negation affirmation, and finally assertion, with the sentence last of all. Now, however, although he has spoken about the name and the verb, he proceeds in the reverse order to what he proposed last. He now treats first of the sentence, which he placed last in the arrangement of the work. He says:

## On the Sentence

A sentence is a significant expression, some part of which is significant when taken separately, as an utterance, but not as an affirmation or negation.

I mean this: “man” signifies something, but not that it is or is not. It will become an affirmation or negation if something is added, but not by adding a single syllable of “man.” For in the expression *sorex* (“mouse”), the syllable *rex* does not signify anything; it is merely a sound uttered at this point in isolation.

In compound expressions, the parts do signify something, but not according to themselves, as has been said.

Aristotle seems also to regard as speeches those utterances which consist of nouns or verbs, not only those which convey a complete thought, [Col. 0434D] such as “Socrates and Plato” and “to walk and to speak.” For although these do not express a complete thought, they are nevertheless composed of verbs and nouns. For he says that a speech is a significant utterance whose parts signify something separately—“signify,” he says, not “co-signify,” as in the case of a noun and a verb.

This is also shown by the fact that, when discussing the noun, he says that in *equiferus* (“wild horse”) *ferus* (“wild”) signifies nothing, just as it does in the speech *equus ferus* (“wild horse”). For *equus ferus* is an utterance composed of nouns, but it does not possess a complete sense; and he says, “just as in the speech ‘*equus ferus*.’” For if, according to [Col. 0435A] Aristotle, *equus ferus* is a speech, why should not other expressions consisting of nouns and verbs also appear to be speeches, although their sense is incomplete—especially since Aristotle himself defines a speech as follows: “A speech is a significant utterance, some part of which signifies separately”?

In those utterances, therefore, which are composed of verbs and nouns, the parts signify externally and do not co-signify. For if a noun and a verb signify separately, and in those utterances composed of verbs and nouns the parts signify externally rather than co-signify, then incomplete utterances composed of nouns and verbs are also speeches. For if every noun and verb is significant, and these utterances—that is, speeches—are composed of nouns and verbs, there can be no doubt that, [Col. 0435B] in utterances joined together from nouns and verbs, the parts signify independently. If this is so, and an utterance whose part signifies separately is itself significant, then, even if its sense is incomplete, it is clearly a speech.

But Alexander thinks that Aristotle’s addition—“whose parts signify as a phrase, not as an affirmation or negation”—should be understood as follows. There are, he says, some simple speeches joined together solely from verbs and nouns, and others that are composite, whose parts, when joined into a single body, already constitute speeches. Simple speeches have as their parts the elements from which they are composed, namely verbs and nouns, as in “Socrates walks.” Composite speeches, however, consist sometimes only of speeches, and sometimes also of affirmations, as when I say, [Col. 0435C] “Socrates walks, and Plato speaks”: both are affirmations. Or when I say, “I affirm that you, descendant of Aeacus, can defeat the Romans,” such a speech is composed of speeches, not of affirmations. [The Latin *Aio te Aeacida Romanos vincere posse* permits either “I say that you, descendant of Aeacus, can defeat the Romans” or “I say that the Romans can defeat you, descendant of Aeacus”; both *te* and *Romanos* are accusatives in the infinitive construction.]

The former is simplicity, the latter composition. But where there is something prior or posterior, it must undoubtedly be defined first which is prior, since it also precedes by nature. Therefore, since the simple speech is prior and the composite posterior, Aristotle first establishes the definition of the simple speech, saying that its parts signify “as a phrase,” not “as an affirmation,” using “phrase” to designate a simple noun or verb. In simple speeches, the parts are of this kind. In composite speeches, however, they are sometimes speeches alone and sometimes affirmations, as we have shown above.

[Col. 0435D] He adds the following point as well. Every definition, he says, ought neither to be narrower than the species defined nor to exceed it. If Aristotle had framed the definition in such a way as to say that the parts of a speech signify as speeches, and not as phrases, he would have excluded simple speeches from the definition. For the parts of simple speeches signify not as speeches but as simple verbs and nouns.

For if every speech contained speeches as its parts, then those very parts, which are speeches, would in turn be joined to other speeches; and again, the parts of those parts—which would likewise be speeches—would contain still other speeches as their parts. If anyone adopts this view, the account proceeds to infinity, and there will be no first speech having simple [Col. 0436A] parts. For a speech cannot be called first if it has other speeches among its parts; its parts are prior to it in composition. But if the reasoning is extended to infinity, no first speech is found, and, if there is no first speech, neither is there a last one. Thus, when the first and last have both been eliminated, everything in between is eliminated as well, and there will be no speech at all.

Accordingly, the definition would not have been correct had Aristotle said: “A speech is a significant utterance whose parts signify externally, as speeches.” But Alexander replies that even if some speeches contain speeches as their parts, it does not therefore follow that the parts of those speeches must be affirmations. For example: “Cease to inflame both me and yourself with your complaints.” One part of this speech is “Cease to inflame both me with your”; [Col. 0436B] the other, “and yourself with complaints.” Neither of these is an affirmation, although it appears to be a speech.

The definition would therefore not have been correct even if it had said: “A speech is a significant utterance whose parts signify something externally, as an affirmation.” For although such speeches have parts joined together from speeches, the entire body of the speech is not thereby composed of affirmations.

Since every speech contains verbs and nouns, which are simple phrases, but not every speech has affirmations or speeches as its parts, Aristotle establishes in the definition what is common to all, as though he were saying: “A speech is a significant utterance according to convention, whose parts necessarily signify something externally as phrases, though not always as affirmations or speeches.” [Col. 0436C] For it is impossible to find a speech whose parts do not necessarily signify something externally as a noun or verb, although one may find a speech in which its parts signify externally without being either speeches or affirmations.

If Aristotle had said, “A speech is a significant utterance whose parts signify something externally, as an affirmation,” he would not have included in the definition those speeches whose parts are speeches but not affirmations, such as the verse I have already cited above. If, on the other hand, he had said, “A speech is a significant utterance whose parts signify externally as speeches,” he would have left out of the definition those speeches whose parts are simple, such as “Socrates walks.”

But by saying that the parts of a speech signify as phrases, and not altogether as affirmations, he includes both simple [Col. 0436D] and composite speeches. He includes simple speeches because every simple and smallest speech is joined from a noun and a verb, which are simple phrases. He includes composite speeches because, although they contain speeches as parts, those parts themselves contain simple phrases, which are also parts of the whole body. Thus, when I say, “If it is day, it is light,” “It is day” and “it is light” are parts of the whole speech. But the parts of these parts are again “day” and “is,” and likewise “light” and “is”; these too are parts of the whole speech by which I say, “If it is day, it is light.” Yet “day,” “is,” and again “light” and “is” are simple phrases.

Consequently, even the parts of composite speeches invariably signify as phrases, not as [Col. 0437A] affirmations or as certain speeches. Aristotle therefore correctly established this definition.

Alexander explains the passage according to this interpretation. He adds that Aristotle often calls affirmations “phrases,” because, wishing to distinguish the matter, when he says that the parts of a speech signify as a phrase, he adds “not as an affirmation,” lest anyone understand “phrase” in this context as an affirmation—as though he were saying: “A phrase is of two kinds: one simple, the other an affirmation. The parts of a speech signify something externally as the phrase that is simple, not as the phrase that is an affirmation.” In a certain sense, the whole of Alexander’s interpretation rests upon this understanding.

Porphyry also agrees with this interpretation, though he differs from it on one point. His explanation is as follows. A phrase, he says, [Col. 0437B] is a simple noun, a simple verb, or something composed of two elements, as when I say “Socrates,” or again “walks,” or “wild horse.”

The term “phrase” also extends to speeches joined from simple verbs and nouns. When I say “Socrates and Plato,” or when there is a compound noun, such as *equiferus*, and “man,” these utterances, although joined and incomplete, are nevertheless called by the name “phrase.” The term also extends to complete speeches, which will subsequently be called enunciations.

An enunciation is simple, as when someone says, “Socrates walks.” This is called an affirmation; its negation is “Socrates does not walk.” Simple enunciations are therefore affirmations or negations composed of individual [Col. 0437C] verbs and nouns. Thus, when I say, “If it is day, it is light,” the whole utterance is not called a phrase. For it is composite and joined together from the speeches “It is day” and “it is light.” These are affirmations and are called phrases.

The affirmations themselves, which are phrases, again contain other simple phrases, such as “day” and “is,” and likewise “light” and “is.” Therefore, when I say “Socrates walks,” this speech has phrases as its parts—namely, a noun and a verb—which are indeed phrases, but not affirmations.

If, however, I say, “Socrates debated in the Lyceum with Plato and the other students,” this part of the speech—“Socrates in the Lyceum”—is itself a phrase, but not a simple noun or verb. It is a phrase, but not an affirmation; [Col. 0437D] nor is it an affirmation, but only an incomplete speech composed nevertheless of verbs and nouns.

If I say, “If a man is, an animal is,” this speech again has phrases as its parts, but neither as simple phrases nor as incomplete speeches; rather, they are complete, simple affirmations. One is “an animal is,” the other “a man is.” The whole speech itself, however, is not a phrase.

Similarly, if I say, “If an animal does not exist, a man does not exist,” this speech again appears to be composed of two simple negative phrases, though the whole is nevertheless not a phrase.

Thus the term “phrase,” beginning with simple nouns and verbs, advances even to incomplete speeches; nor does it stop with these, [Col. 0438A] but proceeds further to simple affirmations and negations, and there reaches the limit of its progression.

Since, therefore, not every speech has affirmations and negations as its parts—these being the complete enunciations of simple phrases—and since not every speech has incomplete speeches as its parts, while every speech nevertheless retains simple phrases, because every speech is joined from verbs and nouns, Aristotle says that the parts of a speech always signify as phrases, though not always as affirmations.

Alexander agrees with this, as I have already explained above, so that the careful reader may properly discern their differences and recognize the points on which their understanding agrees.

At this point Aspasius introduces an irrelevant objection. He says that Aristotle did not intend to establish a definition for [Col. 0438B] all speeches, but only for simple ones, which consist of two elements, namely a verb and a noun. But he is entirely mistaken. For even if a simple speech consists of simple verbs and nouns, it does not follow that a composite speech does not likewise have verbs and nouns among its parts. If this feature is common to simple and composite speeches—that they have simple phrases among their parts, though not affirmations—and if speeches that contain affirmations also have simple phrases among their parts, why he directs this objection against Aristotle is difficult to understand.

Syrianus, who is called Philoxenus, does not think that those speeches whose sense is incomplete are speeches, and therefore he thinks that they do not have parts either. When he says, “Plato [Col. 0438C] debating in the Academy,” he argues that, since this is not complete, it has no parts, supposing that everything incomplete is contained by no parts. Accordingly, when Aristotle says, “A speech is a significant utterance whose parts signify something externally,” Syrianus thinks that he is establishing as a speech only one that retains a complete sense, whose parts are verbs and nouns.

But this is ridiculous. For nothing composite can come into being without its proper parts.
