If a thing is to be composed of ten parts, those parts must nevertheless be added one by one before we reach the tenth; yet the parts that we place individually upon one another in order to compose the total body remain parts, even if we have not yet reached the thing that is being composed.

Therefore, if, [Col. 0438D] before the tenth part is reached, the parts of the thing already produced and composed are parts, there is no reason why the parts of an incomplete thing cannot be called parts. For parts are not said to belong only to a complete compound, and not to an incomplete one. If a complete noun has four parts, namely syllables, as in *Mezentius*, and I remove one syllable and say *mezenti*, or if I again place one or two syllables, such as *me* and *zen*, each of these syllables is nevertheless a part. Although the composition itself is devoid of sense and incomplete, it is still contained by parts.

Syrianus, therefore, is not to be heeded. Porphyry is preferable, since he follows Aristotle’s thought and meaning in such a way that he neither causes the true definition to collapse nor makes it differ from the facts in other respects.

So much for [Col. 0439A] these matters.

Porphyry says the following:

“Aristotle, wishing to show that not every speech has either only simple parts or composite parts, takes his example from simple expressions, saying that the parts of a speech signify as a phrase and not as an affirmation. Thus, in the speech ‘Plato debates,’ the parts are phrases, but not affirmations.

“But if the speech were instead ‘If Plato debates, he speaks the truth,’ or ‘Plato debates and speaks the truth,’ the components would be phrases, not merely as simple expressions but also as affirmations. For a simple phrase is neither an affirmation nor a negation; it becomes one only when something is added that possesses the force of an affirmation or a negation. This is what Aristotle means when he says: ‘I mean, for example, that “man” signifies something, but not that he exists or does not exist; yet it will be an affirmation or a negation [Col. 0439B] if something is added.’

“This is as though he were saying: a simple noun does not produce an affirmation or a negation unless either the verb ‘is’ is added, in which case it is an affirmation, or ‘is not,’ in which case it is a negation.

“As for the addition, ‘but not one syllable of “man,” and in *sorex* “rex” does not signify, but is at present merely a sound,’ the explanation is twofold. [The examples concern parts of Latin words: *homo* means “man”; *sorex*, “shrew,” contains the syllable *rex*, which as a separate word means “king” but has no such independent meaning within *sorex*.]

“What Aristotle said earlier—‘but it will be an affirmation or a negation if something is added’—referred to the phrase that he had proposed as simple when discussing the significant part of a speech. He now completes and explains this point by saying that not just anything added to a simple phrase immediately makes an affirmation or a negation, or even a speech. For if something that is not [Col. 0439C] significant in itself is joined to a simple phrase, it does not therefore produce a speech, an affirmation, or a negation.

“Nor does the addition of a single syllable of ‘man,’ which is not independently significant, produce any speech. If it is not a speech, it is not an assertion either, since assertions are a certain kind of speech. Thus, if someone takes one syllable from the word ‘man,’ attaches it to the whole simple phrase, and says ‘man’—or cuts off a part in any other manner and adds it to the whole body of the phrase—he will not thereby produce a speech. If this is so, he will produce neither an affirmation nor a negation, though these are kinds of speeches.

“Accordingly, the passage should be understood as though Aristotle had said: ‘I mean, for example, that “man” signifies something, but not that he exists or does not exist; yet it will be an affirmation or a negation if something is added—but [Col. 0439D] not if one syllable of “man” is added, nor if something that does not signify independently is added to any other phrase. Thus, in *sorex*, *rex* does not signify, but is at present merely a sound.’

“Therefore, if someone were to take *rex* as though it were a part and attach it to *sorex*, saying *sorex rex*, so that *rex* were a part of *sorex*, no speech would result, and consequently neither an affirmation nor a negation. For these are composed of utterances significant in themselves. But *rex*, as a part of *sorex*, signifies nothing by itself.

“Alternatively, the interpretation will be better if we do not apply the words ‘but not one syllable of “man”’ to the completion of a speech, but rather to the signification of a phrase. For earlier Aristotle said that the parts of a speech signify [Col. 0440A] as a phrase and not as an affirmation; he now plainly shows what a phrase is.

“He establishes phrases as utterances significant in themselves. Therefore, when he says ‘but not one syllable of “man,”’ it is as though he were saying: ‘A part of a speech signifies as a phrase. But these phrases themselves, when complete, are nouns and verbs, not parts of nouns and verbs.’

“For example, in ‘The wild-horse creature runs,’ *equiferus* is a phrase belonging to the whole speech, for it signifies as a part of the speech; but *ferus* co-signifies as a part of the noun, and therefore *ferus* is not a phrase.

“Consequently, if any other syllables occur within a part of a speech—that is, within a noun or verb—and signify nothing independently, although they are parts of a noun, then, since the noun is a part of the speech, they themselves signify nothing in the whole speech and therefore will not be phrases.

[Col. 0440B] “We must therefore understand Aristotle as though he were saying: ‘A speech is a significant utterance, some part of which signifies separately as a phrase, not as an affirmation. I mean, for example, that “man” signifies something and is a certain simple phrase. It is not a speech, because it is simple; nor is it an affirmation or a negation, because it does not signify that something exists or does not exist. It will become an affirmation when something is added that constitutes an affirmation or a negation.

“‘What we call “man” is a phrase because it signifies independently. But a syllable of the noun “man” is not a phrase because it signifies nothing. This is what he means by “but not one syllable of ‘man.’” Even if a syllable appears to signify, if it is nevertheless a part of a noun and co-signifies within the noun, it signifies nothing in the whole speech. [Col. 0440C] Nor is it a part of the speech.’

“He makes this clear by saying that in *sorex*, *rex* does not signify, but is at present merely a sound signifying nothing. From this it is proved that such particles are not phrases. A sound by itself is not a phrase; only a sound that signifies independently is a phrase.

“‘If there are nouns,’ he says, ‘that are composed of other elements, such as *equiferus*, they do indeed suggest a certain appearance of signification, but they signify nothing independently; they co-signify. In simple nouns, however, there is no appearance of signification at all, as in *Cicero*: its parts are simple in sound and, in their meaning, lie wholly outside any resemblance to or representation of a signification.

“‘In compound nouns he intends the part to signify, but not to have any separate signification. It co-signifies only because the entire [Col. 0440D] body of the compound noun designates something; when separated, however, as has often been said, it signifies nothing externally.’”

Every speech, then, is significant, not as an instrument, but, as has been said, according to convention.

That speeches exist according to convention is confirmed by the fact that their parts are conventional—namely, the noun and the verb. If every compound derives its nature from the elements of which it is composed, then an utterance joined from conventionally established utterances is itself formed according to convention and position. It is therefore clear that a speech exists according to convention.

Plato, however, in the work entitled *Cratylus*, establishes the matter differently. He says that language is a kind of equipment [Col. 0441A] and instrument for signifying those things that are naturally conceived by the intellect, and for distinguishing their concepts by means of words. If every instrument of natural things exists according to nature, as the eye is the instrument of sight, he also thinks that nouns exist according to nature.

Aristotle denies this, and Alexander supports the denial with many arguments, showing that speech is not a natural instrument. Aristotle uses the words as follows: “Every speech is significant, but not as an instrument,” as though he were saying: “Every speech is indeed significant, but not naturally.” For the word “instrument” indicates this, as though he were saying “to signify naturally.”

Those who deny that speech is an instrument do not say that it signifies naturally, but according to convention. [Col. 0441B] For the instruments of natural things are themselves natural. Aristotle uses “instrument” in place of “nature” because, as has been said, Plato proposed that the instruments of all the arts exist according to the nature of those arts.

Alexander proceeds to prove that speech is not an instrument in the following way:

“All equipment belonging to natural activities is itself natural. For example, since sensation is given by nature, its equipment is also natural, such as the eye. Similarly, since hearing is natural, we recognize that the ears, which are instruments of hearing, have been given to us naturally.

“But since speech exists according to convention and not naturally—for it is clear that the parts of speech have been established according to convention, namely nouns and verbs, as is shown by the [Col. 0441C] diversity of words among all peoples—since, therefore, every speech is shown to exist according to convention through these elements, and what exists according to convention does not exist according to nature, speech is not equipment. For the means and power of signification are not natural. And if speech is not natural, it is not equipment.”

By these and similar arguments he shows that speech is not equipment.

We must therefore say that voices and the powers by which words are impressed upon things are natural, but that voices are not naturally significant; they are significant by convention. Just as we are naturally receptive to the individual arts but do not possess them naturally, acquiring them instead through instruction, so the voice itself is natural, but signification through the voice is not natural.

For a voice by itself is neither a noun [Col. 0441D] nor a verb; it is a voice to which signification has been added. Just as movement is natural, whereas dancing already belongs to a particular art and convention; and just as bronze exists naturally, whereas a statue exists by convention or art, so the very capacity for signification and the voice are natural, but signification through the voice belongs to convention, not to nature.

Thus far Aristotle has spoken about speech in general. He now proceeds to its species. For he says:

“Not every speech is enunciative, but only that in which there is truth or falsity. This is not present in all speeches; for a prayer is indeed a speech, but it is neither true nor false. The others may therefore be left aside, since consideration of them is more appropriate to rhetoric or poetry; the enunciative speech belongs to the present inquiry.”

There are many species of speech, and they divide them in various ways. [Col. 0442A] The Peripatetics, however, distribute all the species and parts of speech into five classes.

By “species of speech” we mean a complete speech, not an incomplete one. I call those speeches complete which fill out and express a thought. Let our division be as follows.

Let speech be the genus. One kind of speech is incomplete, because it does not express a complete thought, as if I say “Plato in the Lyceum.” Another kind is complete. Of complete speeches, one is optative, as “May Bacchus, giver of joy, be present”; another imperative, as “Receive and give your pledge”; another interrogative, as “Where are you going, Moeris? Is it where the road leads into the city?”; another vocative, as “O you who rule gods and men with everlasting commands”; and another enunciative, as “It is day,” “It is not day.”

Only in the enunciative speech is the nature of truth or falsity discerned. [Col. 0442B] In the others neither truth nor falsity is found. Some say that there are many more species of complete speech; others report innumerable distinctions among them. But this is irrelevant to us. All the species of speech are suited either to orators or to poets; only the enunciative speech belongs to philosophers.

This, then, is what Aristotle means: not every speech is enunciative. There are very many speeches that are not enunciative, such as those I listed above. The enunciative alone is one in which truth or falsity can be found.

Since it is the task of dialecticians and philosophers to investigate that speech in which truth or falsity is found, while the others are suited to orators and poets, Aristotle rightly treats only this one—that is, the enunciative speech.

Up to this point, therefore, he has spoken about the parts of interpretation and about speech in general. [Col. 0442C] He now narrows the method of discussion to a particular species and treats one species of speech, namely one kind of interpretation, the enunciative kind. Enunciation is a species of interpretation; negation and affirmation are species of enunciation. Let us therefore take our starting point for examining the enunciative speech from Aristotle himself.

There is one primary enunciative speech, the affirmation; next comes the negation; all the others are made one by conjunction. Every enunciative speech must consist of a verb or of a case of a verb. For “the account of man,” unless “is,” “was,” “will be,” or something of this kind is added, is not yet an enunciative speech.

Why, then, is “a two-footed walking animal” one thing and not many? It will not be one merely because the words are spoken close together. This matter belongs to another inquiry.

[Col. 0442D] A single sentence is treated in two ways: either when it is one in itself, or when it is joined by some conjunction. Or, more precisely, it should be said as follows: some sentences are one by nature, others by arrangement. Sentences that are one by nature are those that cannot be dissolved into other sentences, such as “the sun rises.” Those that are one by arrangement can be dissolved into other sentences, such as “if a man is, he is an animal”; for this is separable into other sentences. Just as wood or stone, each separately, subsists in its own nature and is one, while a ship or house made from them, though composed of several parts, is one by art, not by nature, so too in sentences we call simple sentences, and sentences naturally one in themselves, those joined only by a verb and a noun. We call composite those that are divided into other sentences, as has been said. For in such sentences a conjunction joins many sentences together. Thus, if I say, “Plato is and Socrates is,” the conjunction “and” joins the two, and therefore what was not naturally and intrinsically one appears one by arrangement.

Naturally, however, affirmation and negation are the two parts of one sentence. But since Aristotle did not put it in that way—rather, he said, “There is one first declarative sentence: affirmation; then negation”—the following question arises. Does the word “first” refer to affirmation, so that negation is subsequent? Or did they refer “first” to the simple sentence, so that the second is the sentence formed by joining sentences together? Aristotle himself resolves this ambiguity. For he says, “There is one first declarative sentence, affirmation,” and, to show which he would call second, adds, “then negation,” thereby placing affirmation first and negation second.

If he had said, “There is one first declarative sentence, affirmation or negation, and then one by conjunction,” it would have been necessary to understand him as saying that the first sentence is the simple one whose parts are affirmation and negation, while the second is the one made one by some conjunction when it is formed from sentences. But because he joined the word “first” to affirmation, saying, “There is one first declarative sentence, affirmation,” and then added “then” to negation, saying, “then negation,” it must be said that he considered affirmation the first sentence and negation the second, to which he immediately appended “then.”

But again we encounter Alexander’s question. He denies that affirmation and negation ought to be placed under one genus, namely declaration, on the ground that no common genus can be found among things that are prior or posterior. But this has already been said above: everything that is prior or posterior in any respect must be separated from a common genus. Otherwise first and second substances would not be placed under one genus, substance. Likewise, simple and composite sentences—of which simple propositions are first and composite ones later—would not be contained under one genus.

Yet only those things should be thought incapable of being placed under the same genus which we recognize as prior or posterior in relation to substance. Things that are equal in relation to their own being may both be placed under the same genus without impediment. Since, therefore, affirmation and negation have the same being insofar as truth and falsity are found in them, and since declaration is that in which the account of truth and falsity is constituted, neither affirmation is prior nor negation posterior with respect to their signifying what is true or false. No one doubts that, because affirmation and negation participate equally in this, they can be placed under the same genus.

Affirmation and negation participate equally in declaration: declaration makes use of the signification of truth and falsity, and affirmation and negation equally display truth and falsehood. Declaration, therefore, must be posited as the genus of affirmation and negation. What Aristotle says—“There is one first declarative sentence, affirmation, then negation; other sentences are one by conjunction”—must therefore be understood as placing affirmation first and negation second, with the word “then,” in the order of utterance. Affirmation is prior and negation posterior only in utterance, not in the designation of truth and falsity. Thus nothing prevents affirmation from being considered prior to negation while both are nevertheless constituted under one genus, namely declaration.

As for what follows—“Every declarative sentence must consist of a verb or a case of a verb”—Aristotle, wishing to distinguish the meanings of expression, affirmation, negation, declaration, and contradiction, has mingled them together through excessive brevity and entangled them in obscuring clouds. He ought first to have established what an expression is, then what affirmation and negation are, and afterward what declaration and contradiction are. For the moment, however, he passes this over and now teaches how a declaration is constituted, saying that every declaration consists of a verb, since a simple expression is either a noun or a verb.

Every simple declaration is of such a kind that it always retains either a verb or something else equivalent to a verb in the predicate—as though he had said that it retains a verb or a case of a verb in predication. The subject term, however, is not always formed from a noun, whereas the predicate is always formed from a verb. Let the proposition be “the sun rises.” In this proposition, “the sun” is the subject, while “rises” is the predicate. I call both of these expressions terms. Whatever is said first in a simple declaration is the subject, as “the sun” here; whatever is said later is the predicate, as “rises” in the same proposition.

Every declarative sentence, therefore, if it is simple, must retain a verb in the predicate. Thus, when I say “the sun rises,” “rises” is a verb, or something equivalent to one, as in “Socrates does not walk.” “Does not walk” is an infinite verb: it is not a verb in the strict sense, but it retains the same force as a verb.

A case of a verb is also often used, as in “Socrates was.” The subject term, however, does not always consist in a noun. It may contain an infinite noun, as when I say “not-man walks”; and it may even be a verb, as when I say “to walk is to be moved.” Thus, as I think, it has been fully shown that the subject is not always a noun, whereas the predicate always consists solely in a verb.

Approving, then, that verbs are always placed in predicates, Aristotle added this qualification: unless “is,” “was,” or something of this kind is added, or something equivalent is appended, no declaration is produced. When I say “man is,” I have posited a verb in the predicate. But if I say “man lives,” this has the same force as saying “man is living.” He therefore taught that affirmation or negation cannot be constituted without a verb by saying: “For the account of man, if ‘is,’ ‘will be,’ ‘was,’ or something of this kind is not added, is not yet a declarative sentence.”

His meaning seems to be this. The definition of man is, for example, “two-footed walking animal,” and this account is an account of human substance. Unless “is,” “will be,” “was,” or any verb whatever, as was said above, is added to it, it does not become a declaration, for it is neither true nor false. If I merely say “two-footed walking animal,” no truth or falsehood follows. But if I say “the two-footed walking animal is,” or “is not,” affirmation and negation are immediately formed. Who could doubt that these are declarations?

When Aristotle was speaking of simple declarations, he said that the account of man—that is, the definition—is not a declaration unless “is,” “will be,” or something of this kind is added to it. He was thereby affirming that the account of the human definition, “two-footed walking animal,” is one sentence rather than many, and that if “is,” “will be,” or “was” were added to it, it would become a simple declaration.

The reason why such an expression is one now requires investigation. For “two-footed walking animal” does not consist merely of two terms, and the things it names are several. Aristotle therefore paused and sought the reason for his own proposition, although he now postpones stating it. He says: “Why, then, is ‘two-footed walking animal’ one thing and not many? For it will not be one merely because the words are spoken close together. But this belongs to another investigation.”

He is asking this as though he were speaking in his own person: “I was speaking about simple declarations generally, and I proposed that they cannot exist without a verb. To prove this, I took the definition of man as an example, and I said that unless ‘is,’ ‘will be,’ or ‘was’ is added to it, no declaration is produced—as though ‘two-footed walking animal’ were one sentence rather than many, and as though it were possible to form a simple declaration from it. But why ‘two-footed walking animal’ should be one sentence belongs, he says, to another investigation.”

That investigation concerns things, not propositions. For “two-footed walking animal” is not one sentence merely because it is spoken continuously and with its words joined together. If that were sufficient, we could call the following sentence one, since it is uttered continuously, even though it signifies many things: “Socrates is a philosopher, snub-nosed, bald, old.” We shall discuss later how such a sentence is multiple rather than one. For now, let it be clear that the sentence “Socrates is a philosopher, snub-nosed, bald, old” is not one but multiple.

If proximity in utterance and continuity themselves made a sentence one, this too could be one sentence, although it will plainly be shown not to be one. Therefore “two-footed walking animal” is not one sentence merely because it is uttered continuously and closely. Aristotle postponed stating the reason why it is one, but he explained it in the books entitled *Metaphysics* (Μετὰ τὰ φυσικά, “After the Physics”).

Theophrastus, however, taught the following concerning affirmation and negation. A definition is always one sentence, and it ought to be uttered continuously. That sentence is said to be one which signifies one substance. A definition—for example, the definition of man, “two-footed walking animal”—is one sentence because it indicates one subject, namely man. If it is uttered continuously and not in separate parts, it is one sentence both because it is spoken continuously and because it indicates the substance of one thing.

But if someone divides it and, by interrupting the utterance, distributes a single sentence signifying one thing, it becomes a multiple sentence. Thus, if he says “animal, walking, two-footed,” the whole sentence indicates one thing and has been spoken continuously. But if he says “animal,” then again “walking,” and after an interruption repeats “two-footed,” the sentence becomes multiple because it has been distributed by interruptions.

A further objection arises. Who would not rightly criticize the claim that a sentence which is one can become multiple through interruption in utterance, when continuity of utterance would not make one a sentence that is multiple by nature? Just as, in things that are naturally multiple, continuity of utterance cannot make a single sentence, so a sentence that is naturally one ought not to become multiple merely because it is interrupted, since it concerns one subject.

The solution is as follows. When we say “animal,” then after an interruption “walking,” and in the same way again “two-footed,” we do not say these as though all were joined into one. For there is “animal,” then again “walking,” and again “two-footed”; since these are several things and are said plurally, that is, distributively, they do not appear capable of being predicated distributively of one subject.

This is unlike the case in which I say “Socrates, philosopher, snub-nosed, bald, old.” This is not a simple sentence, even if it is uttered continuously, because the items do not tend toward one substance. They are accidents and come from outside the substance.

It can also be shown that neither sentences spoken by division nor sentences that do not tend toward one substance are one, in the following way. If someone says “animal,” then again “walking,” and again “two-footed,” there is not one animal, nor one walking thing, nor one two-footed thing. But if I say “two-footed walking animal” continuously and closely, there is one thing signified by the conjunction of these three terms, namely man.

Let us now turn our attention to expressions that signify several things but are spoken continuously, as when I say “Socrates the philosopher, bald, old.” This seems almost to be a definition of Socrates: “philosopher, bald, old.” But if such an account belonged to Socrates, it would not necessarily follow that everyone who is a philosopher, old, and bald was also Socrates. In many cases, therefore, continuity is incidental. Consequently, the expression does not signify one thing, even though it is uttered continuously.

If, then, one thing is signified by all the terms and they are uttered continuously, the sentence is one, as when the parts placed in a definition are certain parts of the defined thing, rather than accidents. Continuous utterance does contribute something toward completing a single sentence, but it is not sufficient by itself unless each term belongs to one subject. Hence Aristotle said that “two-footed walking animal” is not one sentence merely because it is spoken closely. Proximity in utterance is not sufficient to constitute one sentence, for otherwise nothing would prevent things that were naturally multiple from appearing one when uttered continuously and closely. Aristotle postponed presenting the account of this matter.

The sense, therefore, is as follows: “Every declarative sentence,” he says, “must consist of a verb or a case of a verb. For the account of man, which is itself also a sentence, is not yet a declaration unless ‘is,’ ‘will be,’ ‘was,’ or something of this kind is added to it.” This occurs only in simple declarations. It is not universally the case in those that are made one by conjunction, as he already said.

When I say “there is day,” the entire force lies in the verb. But if I utter a conditional sentence, “If there is day, there is light,” the entire force lies in the conjunction. For the conjunction alone contains the account of the truth or falsity of this proposition: “If there is day, there is light.” If the former is the case, the latter follows. Thus the entire force of this kind of proposition lies in the conjunction, whereas every simple proposition has its entire force placed in the verb.

Just as in what are called hypothetical or conditional propositions conjunctions hold the force of the proposition, so in simple propositions predication holds that force. Hence such propositions are also called in Greek κατηγορικαί, that is, “predicative,” namely, simple propositions in which predication possesses the force of the whole proposition. Aristotle therefore says that a simple declaration is formed from a verb or a case of a verb. Apart from that which contains the whole predicative proposition—namely, apart from the predication—no declaration is formed.

It follows that negation too is always attached not to the subject but to the predicate. When I say “the sun rises,” its negation is not “not the sun rises,” but “the sun does not rise.” Hence negation placed with the subject does not make a contrary proposition, whereas when placed with the predicate it produces a contrary. Aristotle was therefore right to say nothing about the subject. The subject term does not sustain the predicative proposition; only the predicate does, and by its own force confirms the whole declaration.

There is one declarative sentence either because it signifies one thing or because it is one by conjunction; there are multiple sentences because they signify several things rather than one, or because they are unjoined. Let a noun and a verb, therefore, be expression alone, since one cannot say that a voice signifying something in this way declares anything, whether someone is asking a question or not, but only when the speaker himself utters it.

Here it is shown that when Aristotle said, “There is one first declarative sentence, affirmation, then negation,” we should not think that he was speaking first of a sentence that is one by nature, but of affirmation. Otherwise, repeating the point here, he would have said: “There is one first declarative sentence, which signifies one thing.” Since he did not say this, it is clear that when he previously said “first,” he was not referring to a sentence that is one apart from conjunction, but to affirmation, which is plainly prior to negation. But this has already been stated above.

I shall explain briefly what this enumeration means. Properly understood, this passage removes many confusions and many errors in discussions about sentences. This is an interpretation that none of the interpreters before Porphyry perceived. For it is not the same thing for a sentence to be one or multiple as for it to be simple or composite. One differs from simple, and multiple likewise differs from composite.

A sentence is one when it signifies one thing; it is multiple when it signifies not one thing but several. This occurs in sentences such as “Cato is a philosopher.” This sentence is not one, for it does not signify one thing. It may show that Cato of Utica is a philosopher, but it may also show that Cato the Censor, the orator, is a philosopher. In this respect the sentence is not one; therefore it is true of Cato of Utica but false of the orator. We call sentences of this kind multiple.

But if a sentence signifies one thing, as when we say “it is written on the paper,” we call it one. Whether a sentence is one or multiple is therefore understood from what it signifies: if it signifies one thing, it is one; if several things, it is multiple.

Simple and composite sentences, however, must be referred not to signification but to the terms themselves, that is, to the expressions used in propositions. A simple declarative sentence is one that consists of only two terms, as “man lives.” Whether “every” is added to the proposition, as “every man lives,” or “no one,” as “no stone lives,” or “someone,” as “some man lives” or “some man does not live,” since the terms themselves are two, the proposition is called simple.

A proposition is composite if it declares more than two terms, as “Plato the philosopher walks in the Lyceum.” Here there are four terms. The same is true if there are three, as in “Plato the philosopher walks.” These propositions are likewise composite if “every,” “no one,” or “someone” is added to them.

Thus whether a sentence is one or multiple is understood from whether it signifies one thing or many, and judgment is always made according to its proper signification. Whether it is simple or composite, however, is recognized not from its signification but from the plurality of its verbs and nouns. If the proposition has more than two terms, it is composite; if it has only two, it is simple.

If every simple sentence—that is, every sentence consisting of two terms—always retained one signification, it could be called both one and simple without distinction, since the same sentence would be both one and simple. But since not every simple sentence signifies one thing, not every simple sentence is one.

It can therefore happen that a proposition is simple with respect to the composition of its expressions but multiple with respect to the signification of its assertions. There will consequently be a twofold distinction here: one simple sentence may be called both simple and one, while another may be simple but multiple.

Again, if every composite sentence also signified several things, we would call it indiscriminately multiple and composite. But it can happen that a proposition consists at times of numerous terms, more than two, yet displays one meaning. Thus: “a rational, mortal animal, capable of mind and learning.” These are several terms, but one substance is subject to them, namely man. Consequently, the meaning too is one.

But if someone says, “Socrates both walks, speaks, and thinks,” the items are multiple. Walking is one thing, speaking another, and thinking another. Thus a sentence may sometimes be composite yet one.

Since a composite sentence may sometimes be uttered continuously without conjunction, and sometimes joined by a conjunction, four distinctions arise from this. There is a sentence composite from terms uttered continuously, without conjunction, and displaying one meaning, as “a rational, mortal animal, capable of mind and learning.” This sentence is composite from many terms, but it has no conjunction. For in the expression “capable of mind and learning,” the conjunction “and” has no force in the proposition as a whole. It does not join propositions; it adds the skill of which man is understood to be capable. One substance, namely man, is subject to the entire expression.

Another is a sentence composite from terms not joined by a conjunction, multiple, and not signifying one proposition, as “Plato, the Athenian philosopher, disputes.” Being Plato is one thing, being a philosopher another, being Athenian another, and disputing another. These terms joined together do not produce one thing as a substance. Hence the sentence is multiple, but it is clear that it is joined by no conjunction.

Another is a sentence composite from unjoined propositions and multiple, as “Jupiter Optimus Maximus is; Juno the queen is; Minerva is the goddess of wisdom.” If someone utters these continuously as one sequence, they are several propositions and a multiple sentence, but they lack a conjunction.

Another is a composite sentence, whether from terms or from propositions joined by a conjunction, which is multiple and signifies many things. It is composite from terms if someone says, “Jupiter and Apollo are gods.” It is joined from propositions and signifies many things if someone says, “Apollo is a prophet, and Jupiter thunders.”

Besides these there is another composite sentence, formed from propositions joined by a conjunction, which signifies one thing, as when I say, “If there is day, there is light.” The two propositions “there is day” and “there is light” are joined by the conjunction “if.” But this sentence does not signify many things. It does not assert both that there is day and that there is light; rather, it asserts that if there is day, there is light. It therefore signifies a certain consequence, not the existence of the propositions. It does not say that both propositions exist, but that if one exists, the other follows. In this way both belong to one understanding.

Porphyry presents this proposition externally because it seemed to signify several things: the plurality of the propositions itself imitates a plurality of significations. But, as has been said, it does not signify several things; it signifies one consequence.

There are therefore two kinds of composite propositions signifying one thing. A composite sentence may signify one thing through unjoined terms, as “a rational, mortal animal is,” or it may be composite from propositions joined by a conjunction, giving the appearance of signifying several things while signifying one, as “if there is day, there is light.”

Since this is the division of composite and simple sentences, sentences are one in two ways and multiple in two ways. Whether uncomposed or composite, a sentence is called one in one way when it is joined by a conjunction, and in another when it signifies one thing. A sentence is called multiple in one way when it is not joined by a conjunction, and in another when it signifies several things.

This is what Aristotle says: “There is one declarative sentence that signifies one thing or is one by conjunction. There are multiple sentences that signify several things rather than one, or are unjoined.” For, as has been said, a sentence is one in two ways: either when it is joined by a conjunction or when it signifies one thing. A sentence is multiple either when it signifies many things or when it is joined without a conjunction. He called those sentences multiple that either retain a plurality of signification or exist apart from conjunctions.

When he says “or unjoined,” he includes the whole range. A proposition is multiple whether it is simple, as “Cato is a philosopher”; or whether it is composite from terms without a conjunction, as “Plato the Athenian disputes in the Lyceum”; or whether it is composite from propositions without a conjunction, as “man is; animal is”; or whether it is composite from terms joined by a conjunction, as “Jupiter and Apollo are gods”; or whether it is composite from propositions joined by a conjunction, as “Apollo is a prophet, and Jupiter thunders.”

Why did he say “multiple sentences that signify several things rather than one”? There are certain expressions that signify several things in their words but display one thing in their entire composition, as “a rational, mortal animal.” These terms signify several things: animal is one thing, rational another, mortal another; but taken together they signify one thing, namely man.

When I say “Socrates the Athenian philosopher,” the individual terms are several and, taken together, they are still several. These are accidents, and they do not inform any substance. This is what he said concerning sentences that are one either by conjunction or by signification, and concerning multiple sentences that are multiple either because they lack conjunction or because their signification is multiple.

What he later says about simple and composite sentences will be explained when the exposition reaches that point. For now, let us return to the order of the argument.

Since he had said above that the simple proposition, which the Greeks call κατηγορική, and which we can translate as “predicative,” is always constituted by the predication of a verb, but not always by a noun as subject—for sometimes an infinite noun, a case of a noun, or a verb is subject—when he said that a simple sentence is constituted by simple expressions, and it was clear that affirmation and negation are sentences, he made it clear that affirmation and negation are constituted and formed by expressions. Affirmation and negation are completed always by the expression of a verb functioning as predicate, but not always by the expression of a noun functioning as subject.

Having proposed this, he now explains what an expression is—the expression that forms predicative, that is, simple, propositions—saying: “Let a noun and a verb be expression alone.” He says “expression alone” because there are certain expressions that are at the same time affirmations or incomplete sentences, as was said above.

He shows why a noun and a verb alone are expressions. “For,” he says, “one cannot say that a voice signifying something in this way declares anything, whether someone is asking a question or not, but only when the speaker himself utters it.”

The sense is this. A declarative proposition is formed principally in two ways: by its proper nature and substance, and by its use and treatment. Its nature is that truth or falsity is found in it. Its use occurs when something is proposed by way of a question and an answer is given, as in “Is the soul immortal?” Or it occurs when someone declares and utters something by his own judgment, as when someone says of his own accord, “The soul is immortal.” Hence a definition of declaration based on its nature and substance is given as follows: “A declaration is a sentence in which there is truth or falsity.”

With respect to its use and treatment, a declarative sentence is what we propose when asking questions in order to hear something true or false. With respect to our utterance, it is what we show to be true or false when we make a proposition.

Since every declarative sentence is either placed in a question or uttered spontaneously, and since the nature and substance of both kinds of declaration consists in this—that whether it is placed in a question joined with an answer, or uttered by itself, it contains truth or falsity—he says that expressions do not contain truth or falsity, whether someone else asks the question or anyone at all utters and speaks them spontaneously.

If one person asks, “Is Socrates disputing?” and another answers, “He is disputing,” the expression “he is disputing,” when joined with the whole question, can be understood as part of a sentence signifying something true or false. But if it is understood by itself, “he is disputing,” although it was given in response to another person’s question, is left without truth or falsity.

The same applies if someone says “Socrates” or “walks” without anyone asking a question, but simply uttering the expression himself. It signifies neither something true nor something false.

Verbs and nouns, therefore, are expressions alone because they are simple. There were certain other expressions in sentences, composed of nouns and verbs, but they were not yet complete assertions, since they signified neither truth nor falsity, whether another person asked the question or someone uttered them spontaneously.

There will also be certain other expressions that retain truth or falsity when another person asks the question or when someone utters them spontaneously—namely, expressions in which there are two affirmations or negations. Hence the sense is as follows. The order of the words is this: “Let a noun and a verb be expression alone, since we cannot say that someone who signifies something in this way by voice—that is, by a verb or noun—declares anything. We cannot say that whoever signifies something by a verb or noun declares, whether someone is asking a question or whether he himself spontaneously utters a simple expression.” To declare is to utter a sentence that designates truth or falsity.

[Col. 0452A] Of these, one is a simple declaration, such as “something of something” or “something from something.” The other is composed from these, like a sentence that is already composite.

Since above he spoke of single and multiple utterances, classifying as “single” one that was either one by conjunction in its expression or one in signification according to its proper nature, and as “multiple” those that either lacked conjunction or comprised many significations; and since one utterance was one thing, a simple utterance another, a compound utterance another, and multiple utterances yet another, he now returns to the simple and compound, saying that a simple utterance is an enunciative sentence contained within two terms, one of which is the subject and the other the predicate.

When he says, “Of these, this is a simple enunciation”—meaning, of course, of enunciative sentences—he explains what he means by saying that “this is a simple enunciation,” and he himself supplies the qualification: “something of something,” where “to predicate” is to be understood. The sense is therefore as follows: among enunciative sentences, an enunciation is simple if we predicate one thing of one thing, as when I say, “Plato discusses”: I have predicated something—namely, “discusses”—of a certain Plato. This is a simple enunciation because it is joined together from two terms or parts.

If, however, it has more terms, and its parts exceed the number of two terms, those sentences are called compound sentences. A compound enunciation is of this kind: “If it is day, it is light.” For “it is day” and “it is light” are two simple enunciations which, joined together, produce one compound enunciation. This is what he means when he says, “But this”—that is, another sentence—“joined from these,” namely, from simple enunciations, “is now a kind of compound sentence.” For this is not a simple sentence. A simple sentence has only two expressions among its parts, whereas a compound sentence has sentences as well, like the one I have just given.

The order here is therefore the following, although he himself has confused it. First he dealt with affirmation and negation, explaining which was prior and which posterior. Then he spoke of single and multiple utterances, and finally of simple and compound utterances. But since he mixed certain matters together in the middle, we have continued the direct sequence of the argument by distinguishing them somewhat and have cut short Aristotle’s lengthy hyperbaton by joining its parts. For what he says does not seem to be equivalent throughout:

> “The first single enunciative sentence is an affirmation, and then a negation; other sentences are single through conjunction,”

and again when he says:

> “There is one enunciative sentence that signifies one thing, or is one by a single conjunction. Multiple sentences signify several things rather than one, or are without conjunction.”

and when he adds:

> “Of these, this is a simple enunciation, such as something of something or something from something; but this other, joined from these, is now a kind of compound sentence.”

The first statement—“the first single enunciative sentence is an affirmation, and then a negation”—he referred to the priority of affirmation, showing that affirmation is prior and negation posterior. For he says, “then negation”; hence the word “first” must be applied to affirmation, while what follows shortly afterward must be understood in connection with negation.

The statement “There is one enunciative sentence that signifies one thing, or is one by a single conjunction; but multiple sentences signify several things rather than one, or are without conjunction” was intended to teach which sentences ought to be considered single: those that signify one thing or those that conjunction makes one; and which ought to be considered multiple: those that retain many things in their signification or whose structure is not composed by any conjunction.

Finally, when he added:

> “Of these, this is a simple enunciation, such as something of something or something from something; but this other, joined from these, is now a kind of compound sentence,”

he referred to simple and compound sentences. By “simple” he meant those joined from only two terms; by “compound,” those joined from simple enunciative sentences. The complete order is therefore as follows:

> “The first single enunciative sentence is an affirmation, and then a negation.”

Then, with the intervening material omitted, the following should be inserted:

> “There is one enunciative sentence that signifies one thing, either by conjunction as one; but multiple sentences signify several things rather than one, either without conjunction.”

After this, with the subsequent intervening material likewise omitted, the following should be read:

> “Of these, this is a simple enunciation, such as something of something or something from something; but this other, joined from these, is now a kind of compound sentence.”

It is as though he had said:

> “Among enunciations, the first sentence is affirmative and the second negative. Among affirmations and negations, a sentence is single if it signifies one thing or is made one by conjunction. It is multiple if either its parts are joined by conjunction and it signifies many things, or it is not joined by conjunction. Of these, a simple sentence consists of two terms, such as something of something or something from something; another is compound, being joined from simple affirmations.”

When he says “something of something or something from something,” his meaning is this. “Something of something” signifies an affirmation, as when I say, “Socrates discusses”: I have predicated something—namely, “discusses”—of a certain Socrates, and an affirmation results. If I say, “Socrates does not discuss,” I have separated discussion from Socrates and taken it away from him; this is a negation. Affirmation predicates one thing of another and joins it to that other thing. Negation, by predicating anything whatsoever of any thing, removes it from that thing. Thus, by “something of something” he signified a simple affirmation; by “something from something,” a simple negation.

A simple enunciation is a significant utterance concerning something’s being or not being, according as the times are divided. An affirmation is an enunciation of something concerning something; a negation is an enunciation of something from something.

After completing his treatment of multiple and single enunciations, and likewise of simple and compound enunciations, he now treats the simple enunciation and concludes it with a definition, saying that it is a significant utterance of something’s being or not being. When he says that it is an “utterance,” he refers to its genus; when he calls it “significant,” he gives the utterance its differentia. The phrase “concerning something that is or is not” refers again to the difference among the things signified. The utterance itself, by which it is spoken, has as its function the signification of something. What it signifies, or concerning what it maintains a designation, belongs to the distinction among significant utterances. Thus the statement is equivalent to saying that an enunciation does not signify everything, but signifies that something is or is not.

An enunciation is therefore a significant utterance concerning something’s being or not being—that is, every enunciation is either an affirmation or a negation. “Being” is posited by affirmation; “not being” by negation. But because certain people failed to see how concisely he compressed the definition, they were led into a foolish error concerning falsity. They argue that affirmation and negation are not species of enunciation.

“If this,” they say, “is the definition of enunciation, every definition of a genus can be applied to its proper species—for every genus is predicated univocally of its proper species. There is no doubt, then, that this definition of enunciation, if enunciation is a genus, must also apply to affirmation and negation, provided that these are its species. But who would ever say that the definition ‘a significant utterance concerning something’s being or not being’ applies to affirmation? Affirmation cannot be a significant utterance concerning being and not being, but only concerning being. Nor can negation be a significant utterance concerning being and not being, but only concerning not being and never concerning being. Negation always removes; affirmation joins and establishes. Therefore, if this definition of enunciation cannot be predicated of affirmation and negation, affirmation and negation are not species of enunciation.”

Those who argue thus seem to be greatly mistaken, as though anything prevented affirmation and negation alike from being included under one and the same definition. I can say that affirmation and negation are significant utterances concerning something’s being or not being, so that “significant utterance” is common to both; “concerning something’s being” belongs to affirmation alone, while “concerning something’s not being” belongs to negation alone.

Nothing shorter could have been done unless, within the same definition, he both established the nature of enunciation and effected its division. It is as if he had said:

> “An enunciation is a significant utterance in which truth and falsity are designated; one of its species is affirmative and the other negative.”

He says instead:

> “An enunciation is a significant utterance concerning something’s being or not being.”

For when he says “concerning something’s being or not being,” this is equivalent to saying “which demonstrates truth and falsity.” Everything that posits something as being—for example, “It is day”—or as not being—for example, “It is not day”—demonstrates either truth or falsity. If something is posited as being or not being, truth and falsity are found in it.

Thus in his statement that it is a significant utterance concerning something’s being or not being, the meaning is as though he had said:

> “An enunciation is a significant utterance signifying truth and falsity.”

For signification concerning something’s being or not being is a demonstration of truth and falsity. Yet in the same definition he divided the species with remarkable brevity. It is as though he had said:

> “A significant utterance is an enunciation in which truth and falsity are demonstrated. One part of it is affirmative and the other negative.”

He says instead, “concerning something’s being or not being.” Signification concerning something’s being is affirmation; concerning what is not, negation. Thus the statement that an enunciation is a significant utterance concerning something’s being or not being gathers both under one act of understanding. What he said signifies both the demonstration of truth and falsity and the division between affirmation and negation.

Alexander, however, does not abandon his own view and is held by the same error as the others. He says that here too it is apparent that enunciation is not the genus of affirmation and negation, because in the definition of enunciation Aristotle used affirmation and negation as its parts.

Everything composite, and everything equivocal, can be defined either through its parts or through its significations. Thus, if someone wishing to define the number three said, “The number three is what is composed from one and two”; or if someone wishing to define “human” said, “A human is either a rational mortal animal, or an image made from such colors or from metal”; in this way an equivocal name is displayed through those things signified by the equivocal name itself.

Alexander therefore argues in the same way:

> “Enunciation,” he says, “is a significant utterance concerning something’s being or not being,”

as though he had said:

> “Enunciation is an utterance that is either affirmative or negative.”

He thus falls into the same error, failing to see how Aristotle both made a division and displayed the nature of enunciation by means of one definition. So far as I know, neither Porphyry nor any other commentator has noticed this explanation.

Aspasius also agrees with Alexander. Alexander says that Aristotle defined enunciation here in the same way as elsewhere, namely in the *Prior Analytics*. There he concluded the definition of the proposition—which is an enunciation—in the following terms:

> “A proposition is an affirmative or negative sentence of something concerning something, or of something from something.”

Aspasius follows him in this.

Porphyry, however, says that the subtlety of the definition is admirable. Enunciation, he says, is defined according to the total force of affirmation and negation, while affirmation and negation themselves are defined through their terms. For affirmation, consisting of two terms, signifies that something inheres in something, but its entire force is to affirm something. Negation likewise signifies that something does not inhere in something, but its entire force is to deny and separate something. Again, affirmation designates that something inheres in something, but its entire force is to posit something. When it demonstrates that something inheres in something, it posits something. Negation, by contrast, declares that something does not inhere in something, but its entire force is to remove.

“Therefore,” Porphyry says, “Aristotle now defines enunciation according to the total force of affirmation and negation when he says, ‘An enunciation is a significant utterance concerning something’s being or not being.’ This pertains to the force of negation and affirmation, as though he had said: ‘An enunciation is a significant utterance that either posits or removes something’—acts that are properly the powers of affirmation and negation.

“For if he had said, ‘An enunciation is concerning something’s being in or not being in something,’ he would appear to have defined enunciation through the terms of affirmation and negation. But when he says ‘concerning something’s being or not being,’ he defines it according to the entire force of both. In the affirmation ‘It is day,’ he shows, according to the terms, that something is present to something—for he applies ‘is’ to ‘day’—but the entire force of such a proposition is to declare that something is. Again, when I say ‘It is not day,’ I pronounce that something is not in something, but the entire force of the statement is to say that it is not. It is therefore clear, according to Porphyry, that enunciation is described according to the entire force of affirmation and negation, while affirmation and negation themselves are described through their terms.”

Aristotle says:

> “An affirmation is an enunciation of something concerning something,”

taking “enunciation” as the genus in the definition of affirmation. For enunciation, as has been said, is the genus of affirmation and negation. Aristotle himself demonstrates this more clearly when he assigns the name “enunciation” to the definition of both:

> “An affirmation is an enunciation.”

He refers “enunciation” to the genus, while what he adds—“of something concerning something”—he refers to the terms. In a simple affirmation, something is predicated by being enunciated of something, as in “It is day,” where the being of day is predicated.

Negation is likewise defined:

> “A negation is an enunciation of something from something.”

Here again “enunciation” is referred to the genus, while “of something from something” is referred to the terms. In the negation “It is not day,” by enunciating we remove being from day.

But so that he would not appear to have defined enunciation only with reference to the present time, he added that the definition of enunciation is also understood of the other times. He says:

> “An enunciation is a significant utterance concerning something’s being or not being, according as the times are divided.”

Time is divided into three parts: every time is either future, present, or past—or is mixed from these. Enunciation is therefore a significant utterance signifying either that something is or that it is not.

But since this expression designates the present time, he says that we are not speaking only about the present, but also about those times into which time is divided, so that this being and not being may extend into the future and the past. Thus enunciation may signify being and not being in such a way that it either posits or removes the present, as in “Socrates is” and “Socrates is not”; the past, as in “Socrates was” and “Socrates was not”; and likewise the future, as in “Socrates will be” and “Socrates will not be.”

In all these times, therefore, the entire force of enunciation consists in being or not being something—that is, in positing and removing. This is what he means by “concerning something’s being or not being, according as the times are divided,” as though he had said:

> “An enunciative utterance signifies that something is or is not, whether in the present, the past, or the future, according as time itself is divided.”

I shall briefly explain why the definition has this order. First he discussed the noun, then the verb, then the sentence, again enunciation, then affirmation, and finally negation.

Everything composite is posterior to its parts, while every genus is prior to its parts. In composites, therefore, the parts are prior to the whole; in genera and species, the parts are posterior to the whole. Again, in composites the whole is posterior to its parts, whereas in species and genera the whole is prior to its parts.

Since nouns and verbs were neither species of affirmation, negation, enunciation, nor sentence, but certain parts of all these by which they are joined together; since the sentence is the genus of enunciation; since enunciation is the genus of affirmation and negation; and since affirmation is prior to negation according to expression, as Aristotle himself attested—therefore, because sentence, enunciation, affirmation, and negation are all joined from nouns and verbs, nouns and verbs are prior to them all.

A noun signifies either a thing subsisting in itself or something as though subsisting in itself; a verb signifies an accident, or, as has been made clear above, an accident belonging to another. What subsists in itself is prior. Therefore what a noun signifies is prior to what a verb signifies, and the noun is prior to the verb.

Since noun and verb are prior to sentence, enunciation, affirmation, and negation—for parts are prior to the things composed from them—they were rightly defined before all the rest. Since the noun is prior to the verb, the noun was defined first and the verb afterward.

But since every genus is prior to its species, after these—that is, after noun and verb—he described the sentence by a definition. The sentence is both the proximate genus of enunciation and the higher genus of affirmation and negation. After the sentence he defined enunciation, which, although it is a species of sentence, is nevertheless the genus of affirmation and negation. After enunciation he defined affirmation, which, although it is a species co-equal with negation according to its proper genus, namely enunciation, is prior in expression, as he had already taught above when he said:

> “The first single enunciative sentence is an affirmation, and then a negation.”

But since we said above that he intended to define five things—what an utterance is, what an enunciation is, what an affirmation is, what a negation is, and what a contradiction is—he showed what an utterance is through the statement:

> “Let noun and verb alone be a diction (*dictio*).”

He defined enunciation through the statement:

> “A simple enunciation is a significant utterance concerning something’s being or not being, according as the times are divided.”

He defined affirmation through the statement:

> “An affirmation is an enunciation of something concerning something.”

He likewise defined negation when he said:

> “A negation is an enunciation of something from something.”

It remains, therefore, to discuss contradiction. He proceeds to explain what contradiction is, saying:

> “Since it is possible to enunciate both that what is is not and that what is not is, both that what is is and that what is not is not; and in the case of things outside the present times, the same applies throughout: whatever someone affirms can be negated, and whatever someone negates can be affirmed. It is therefore clear that every affirmation has a negation opposed to it, and every negation an affirmation; and let this be contradiction: opposed affirmation and negation.”

Having completed everything he promised to explain, he now comes in due order to the remaining subject, namely contradiction. He finds it in affirmations and negations, saying that every affirmation can have its proper negation opposed to it, and every negation can likewise have its proper affirmation established against it.

This follows from our knowing that some things are and others are not, and that we ourselves can say and think both that some things are and that they are not. From these four enunciations arise two pairs of contradictions.

If someone says that what is is not—for example, while Socrates is alive, says “Socrates is not alive”—he negates what is, and the negation is false. If someone affirms that what is not is—for example, when Socrates is not alive, says “Socrates is alive”—the affirmation is likewise false. If someone establishes in an enunciation that what is is—for example, while Socrates is alive, says “Socrates is alive”—the affirmation is true. But if someone denies that what is not is, the negation is true—for example, when Socrates is not alive, says “Socrates is not alive.”

Thus there are four enunciations: a true affirmation and a false negation, and again a true negation and a false affirmation. But affirmation is contained in two of them and negation in two. There are two contradictions.

This is what he means when he says:

> “Since it is possible to enunciate both that what is is not…”

Here he presents the false enunciation of negation. When he adds “and that what is not is,” he presents the false affirmation in an enunciation. What he says next—“and that what is is”—designates the true enunciation, because what is is expressed through a true affirmation. Further, when he says “and that what is not is not,” he gives the form of a true negation.

Thus, if what is can truly be said to be, and what is can falsely be predicated as not being; and if what is not can truly be enunciated as not being, while it can falsely be affirmed to be, it is clear that every affirmation has some opposed negation and that every negation produces a contradiction through the opposition of an affirmation.

If everything someone affirms can be negated, and everything someone negates can be affirmed, who could doubt that no affirmation can be established without a negation contradicting it, and no negation without an affirmation that can be found against it? Every affirmation therefore has an opposed negation, and every negation an opposed affirmation. Contradiction is therefore opposed affirmation and negation.

What opposition is will be explained later, as will what contradiction is; I shall demonstrate it afterward with the greatest precision.

When he says “and in the case of things outside the present times,” the meaning is as though he had said: just as affirmation and negation can be made in the present time, so too they can be made in the past or future. For just as what is can be established as being, so what was can be proposed as having been, and what will be can be affirmed under the form of the future, as when we say “Socrates was” or “The sun will be in Cancer in summer.”

Affirmation and negation are therefore established concerning the future and the past in the same way as concerning the present. The future and the past are outside and beyond the present time: the one has not yet come, and the other has departed.

He was therefore right to say that such affirmations and negations can also occur concerning things outside the present times. For concerning the past and the future, which are outside the present time, the same applies throughout—as he himself says: whatever someone affirms can be negated, and whatever someone negates can be affirmed. Hence it follows that in every time it is established that a negation can be opposed to every affirmation, and an affirmation opposed to every negation.

He now shows what sort of opposition must be taken in affirmation and negation. This is what contradiction is: opposed affirmation and negation. If these, when opposed, constitute contradiction, he properly proceeds to explain what kind of opposition must be present in them in order to constitute contradiction.

> “I mean opposition of the same predicate concerning the same subject, and not equivocally; and whatever other qualifications of this kind we have determined against sophistical importunities.”

Since a simple proposition consists of two terms, one subject and the other predicate—and since the subject is what is stated first, while the predicate is what is stated afterward—he says that affirmation and negation constitute a complete contradiction only through an opposition in which they have the same subject and the same predicate, so that neither subject nor predicate signifies more than one thing. Otherwise there will be neither contradiction nor any opposition.

For example, when I say “Socrates is white” and someone else says “An Ethiopian is not white,” the affirmation and negation are not opposed, because the subject is different while the predicate is the same. In the affirmation the subject was Socrates; in the negation it was an Ethiopian.

Again, when I say “Socrates is white” and someone else says “Socrates is not a philosopher,” the negation does not preserve opposition against the affirmation, because the predicates proposed in the two are different. In the affirmation “white” is predicated of Socrates; in the negation “philosopher” is predicated.

If both terms are different, there is even less opposition, as when I say “Socrates is a philosopher” and someone responds “Plato is not a Roman.” Here neither the subject nor the predicate is the same. These propositions are more fully diverse and are not joined in opposition to one another. Therefore both may be true at once; sometimes both may be false, and it may also happen that one is true and the other false. Things that do not destroy one another can be found either both false, both true, or one true and the other false.

We therefore do not say that propositions are opposed when either their subject or their predicate is different. Hence even those propositions whose subjects or predicates signify many things cannot preserve a contradictory negation.

If someone makes an equivocal name the subject and predicates something of it, then establishes a negation against such an affirmation, he will not create opposition. For example, when I say “Cato killed himself at Utica,” the name “Cato” is equivocal. It can signify either the orator or the man who led an army into Africa.

If, then, someone says “Cato killed himself at Utica,” he might be understood to mean Cato of Marcia. If someone replies “Cato did not kill himself at Utica,” he might have established the negation concerning Cato the Censor. But since Cato the Censor is different from Cato of Marcia, and the name “Cato” signifies different things, the affirmation and negation are different from each other.

The negation does not wholly destroy what the affirmation establishes. The affirmation establishes that Cato of Marcia killed himself at Utica. The negation says that Cato—if that is what is intended, the orator—did not kill himself at Utica. Thus they do not establish truth and falsity between themselves, because they differ from each other. Both are true: Cato of Marcia killed himself at Utica, and Cato the orator did not kill himself at Utica. The equivocal subject therefore prevents the affirmation and negation from constituting opposition in any way.

If the predicate is equivocal, contradiction likewise does not arise. Someone may say “Cato is brave,” predicating bravery of mind; another may reply “Cato is not brave,” referring to weakness of body. The equivocation in “brave” creates an ambiguity that cannot establish opposition.

If both terms—the subject and the predicate—are equivocal, the propositions are even more divergent and not opposed. They do not divide truth and falsity between themselves; it may happen that both are true, and sometimes that both are false.

The subject must therefore be one and the predicate one, so that what the affirmation predicates and joins, the negation may divide and separate; and what the affirmation predicates of the subject, the negation may deny of the same subject. For if both terms are equivocal, or either one of them is, the negation may remove something different from what the affirmation posited. No opposition will therefore arise.

This is why it must not be done in that way. The affirmation must have the same subject and predicate as the negation, and the negation must have the same subject and predicate as the affirmation. This is what he means when he says:

> “I mean opposition of the same predicate concerning the same subject, and not equivocally.”

“Of the same” refers to the predicate; “concerning the same” refers to the subject. The meaning to be supplied is:

> “I mean opposition of the same predicate concerning the same subject, but not equivocally; neither the subject nor the predicate should be equivocal, and even more properly both should signify one thing.”

He indicates this through the phrase “not equivocally.” But the absence of equivocation alone is not sufficient to establish a firm opposition. He also determined many other matters in the *Sophistical Refutations* against those who try to overturn the path of true reasoning by fallacious arguments: how propositions should be constructed and how the fallacy of arguments should be discovered.

This is what he means by:

> “And whatever other qualifications of this kind we have determined against sophistical importunities,”

as though he had said:

> “I say that affirmation and negation are opposed when the same predicate is predicated of the same subject; and I include whatever other matters of this kind have been determined in the *Sophistical Refutations* against the importunities of arguments.”

Since his concern here was different, he touched on the matter most briefly and conveniently. We, however, shall not hesitate to add, insofar as brevity permits, what he determined in the *Sophistical Refutations* for establishing the contradictory opposition.

Contradiction does not arise merely when equivocation is introduced into propositions. It also fails to arise when a univocal term is used in the negation. An opposition has contradiction when, if the affirmation is true, the negation is false, and if the negation is true, the affirmation is false.

When terms are taken univocally, it can happen that both the affirmation and the negation are true at the same time. For example:

> “A human being walks; a human being does not walk.”

The affirmation is true of a certain human being, and the negation is true of man taken specifically. Yet specific man and particular man are univocal. Therefore, when univocal terms are taken in this way, contradiction does not arise.

Nor does contradiction arise if the affirmation and negation are made with reference to different aspects. For example:

> “The eye is white; the eye is not white.”

In one respect it is white, and in another it is not white. Thus both the affirmation and the negation are true.

Nor is contradiction produced when the statements refer to different things, as in:

> “Ten is double; ten is not double.”

If I refer “double” to five, the affirmation is true; if I refer it to six, the negation is true.

Nor does contradiction arise if a different time is taken in the affirmation and negation, as in:

> “Socrates is sitting; Socrates is not sitting.”

Taken at one time, “is sitting” makes the affirmation true; taken at another, “is not sitting” makes the negation true.

Further, if someone states in the negation what he proposed in the affirmation but in a different mode, the force of contradiction is interrupted. If someone takes the affirmation as referring to potentiality and the negation as referring to actuality, affirmation and negation can be established as true at the same time. For example:

> “The puppy sees; the puppy does not see.”

It sees potentially, but does not see actually.

If contradiction is to be made, therefore, the same predicate must be predicated of the same subject—as he himself says—not equivocally but univocally, with reference to the same aspect, the same thing, the same time, and in the same mode. He pursued all these matters most carefully in the *Sophistical Refutations*. Here he recalls only a few and postpones the complete discussion to those books.

An enunciation concerns something’s being or not being. An affirmation concerns being, as in “Plato is a philosopher”; a negation concerns not being, as in “Plato is not a philosopher.” These two enunciations—“Plato is a philosopher” and “Plato is not a philosopher”—destroy one another and, being placed in a kind of conflict, constitute a contradiction.

Contradiction is the opposition of affirmation and negation in which it cannot happen that both are false or both true, but one is always true and the other false. If there are cases in which affirmation and negation do not divide truth and falsity, then something different is present in them, and they are not completely opposed.

Porphyry says that an argument supporting the claim that affirmation must be opposed to negation in such a way that, when one is true, falsity immediately arises in the other is supplied by our ordinary conversational practice. For whenever someone says that something is and another denies the same thing, we suspect that one of them is speaking the truth and the other is lying.

Moreover, if something either is or is not, and nothing intermediate between being and not being can be found; and if affirmation posits that something is while negation removes the same thing; then affirmation and negation are opposed, and such opposition constitutes complete contradiction, in which affirmation and negation cannot both be true simultaneously.

The nature of affirmation and negation belongs to a certain quality. Affirmation and negation are qualities of propositions. In addition to this quality, however, there is also the quantity of propositions, which must be discussed a little later.

Aristotle, wishing to teach us what contradiction is, first showed where it exists. Contradiction must exist in opposition.
