Since contradiction is therefore in opposition, while the kind of opposition that produces contradiction is not yet known, the opposition may lie either in the quality of oppositions, or in their quantity, or in both.

The quality of propositions, which consists in affirmation and negation, has been discussed. We shall now speak of quantity, so that once this too is understood it may become clear whether contradiction in propositions lies in quality, in quantity, or in both.

## On the Subjects and Predicates of Enunciations
Since some things are universal, while others are singular, I say that a universal is what is naturally predicated of many, whereas a singular is what is not so predicated. “Human being,” for example, is universal, while Plato is one of the singular things. Now it is necessary to state that something inheres or does not inhere sometimes in one of the universal things, and sometimes in one of the singular things.

Every proposition receives the distinctive character of its signification [Col. 0462C] from the concepts underlying it. But since concepts must be likenesses of things, the force of propositions is extended through concepts to things also. Therefore, whenever we wish either to affirm or to deny something, this is related to the quality of the intellect and of the mind’s conception. For whatever we conceive through imagination and understanding, when we place it in an affirmation or denial, we affirm or deny it. Propositions derive their force and distinctive character primarily from understanding, but secondarily from the things out of which the concepts themselves must be constituted. Hence a proposition participates both in quantity and in quality: in quality, certainly, through the very utterance of affirmation and denial, which one emits and expresses from one’s own judgment; in quantity, through the underlying [Col. 0462D] things that the concepts apprehend.

For we see that some qualities in things are of such a kind that they cannot belong to anything except one particular and singular substance. There is one kind of quality that is singular, such as Plato’s or Socrates’; another is shared with many and presents itself wholly to each and to all, such as humanity itself. There is, then, a certain quality of this sort that is wholly in each individual and wholly in all of them. Whenever we contemplate something of this kind in the mind, the mind’s thought is not led by this name to any one person, but to all those who participate in the definition of humanity.

Thus one quality is common to all, whereas the former is indeed incommunicable [Col. 0463A] to everyone else but proper to one. If it were permissible to coin a name, I would call that singular quality, incommunicable to any other subsistence, by a fictitious name of my own, so that the form of the present argument might become clearer. Let that incommunicable property of Plato be called “Platonity.” In this way we may give this quality the fictitious name “Platonity,” just as we call the quality of human beings “humanity.” Platonity, then, belongs to one human being alone, and not to just anyone, but to Plato alone; whereas humanity belongs both to Plato and to all the others included under this term.

Consequently, since Platonity belongs to one Plato, the mind of the listener refers the word “Plato” to one person and one particular substance. But when the listener hears “human being,” the understanding also refers to the many whom it knows to be included under humanity. Therefore, since humanity is common to all human beings and is wholly in each human being, all human beings retain humanity equally, just as one human being does. For if this were not so, the specific definition of “human being” would never fit the substance of an individual human being.

Since this is so, “human being” is called something universal, whereas Platonity itself and Plato are particular. Once this has been established, since that universal quality can be predicated both of all and of individuals, when we say “human being” it is ambiguous and open to doubt whether the term has been used of the species or of some particular individual, because the word “human being” can be said both of all [Col. 0463C] and of each individual included under the species humanity.

Accordingly, it is indefinite whether what we have said, “human being,” has been said of all human beings or of each individual and particular substance of a human being. If, then, we try to separate this quality of humanity by removing the ambiguity of the understanding, it must be determined either by extending it to plurality or by gathering it into numerical unity. For when we say “human being,” it is indefinite whether we mean everyone or one person.

But if “every” is added, so that the predication is “every human being,” or if “a certain” is added, then the distribution and determination of universality take place. The name that is universal—that is, “human being”—is uttered universally when we say “every human being,” or particularly when we say “a certain human being.” For “every” signifies universality [Col. 0463D].

Therefore, if “every,” which signifies the universal, is joined to “human being,” which is itself also universal, the universal thing, namely human being, is predicated universally according to the determination of quantity added to it. But if “a certain human being” is said, then the universal, “human being,” is uttered particularly because particularity has been added to it by the term “a certain”; and the universal thing is said particularly.

Yet although “a certain human being” is a particular predication, and Plato is also a particular predication—for “a certain human being” is said of one person, and Plato is said of one person—the two are not particular in the same way. Plato indicates one definite substance and property, which cannot belong to another [Col. 0464A]. “A certain human being,” however, determines the universal name itself particularly; but if “a certain” were absent, what we call “human being” would be universal and would therefore remain ambiguous. “Plato,” on the other hand, can never be universal.

Even if this name “Plato” should sometimes be imposed on several people, the name will not thereby be universal. Humanity, gathered from the natures of individual human beings, is in a certain way reduced to one conception and nature. But the name “Plato” might perhaps be common to many in respect of the word; nevertheless, the property of Plato would belong to none of them—that property or nature of the Plato who was the student of Socrates—even if they were called by the same name.

This is because humanity is natural, whereas a proper name is established by convention. Nor is it being said here that the name “Plato” cannot be predicated of several people, but rather that Plato’s property cannot. That property is not naturally said of many, as humanity is; and therefore Platonity itself is an incommunicable quality, as was said, whereas the universal quality is communicable, existing both in many and in individuals.

Thus, when I say “every human being,” I direct the proposition toward number. But when I say “Socrates” or “Plato,” I do not direct it toward number; rather, I confine and predicate the quality and property of one person within his individual and singular substance.

The two particularities—“a certain human being” and “Plato”—therefore differ especially in this respect: when I say “Plato,” I have designated by a name the human being whom I have named, and I have indicated the property of each person whom I name. But when I say “a certain human being,” I have merely removed number and reduced the proposition to unity. The particularity “a certain” does not tell me whom I am speaking about. A certain human being may be Socrates, Plato, Cicero, or any one of the individuals whose properties differ from one another in respect of their singularity and nature.

For this reason Theophrastus most appropriately called propositions of this kind, such as “a certain just human being,” particular indefinites. For they take away a part from “human being,” which is universal, whether in word or in nature. Yet they do not determine or define what that part itself is or by what property it is described.

He therefore called universal what is naturally predicated of many, such as “human being” [Col. 0464D], not what is said of many by convention, as the name “Alexander” is said of the Trojan and of the Macedonian, the son of Philip. The latter is said of many by convention, the former by nature.

He states with great precision that a universal is what is naturally predicated of many. He called the property and nature of the name and thing that is particular singular by saying, “But Plato is one of the singular things.” Then he continued: “Now it is necessary to state that something inheres or does not inhere, sometimes in one of the universal things and sometimes in one of the singular things.” This is as if he were saying: Every affirmation and denial demonstrates that something inheres or does not inhere. Whatever is enunciated is proposed either concerning being, as in “Plato is a philosopher”—for this proposition establishes that philosophy inheres in Plato—or concerning what does not inhere, as in “Plato is not a philosopher,” for this separates philosophy from Plato and proposes that philosophy does not inhere in him.

Therefore, since it is necessary either to say that something inheres in something or that something does not inhere in something, it is also necessary to understand whether the thing in which we say that something inheres is universal, as when we say “the human being is white,” showing that whiteness inheres in a universal thing, namely, the human being; or whether it is particular and singular, as when someone says “Socrates is white,” signifying that whiteness inheres in Socrates, a singular substance and incommunicable property.

But in singular things, whether something is affirmed or denied, there is one mode of opposition that possesses the force of contradiction. Since a singular and individual is not divided by any division, the contradiction made concerning it will also be simple [Col. 0465B].

In propositions concerning universals, however, there is not one mode of contradiction. For when I say “Socrates is a human being” and “Socrates is not a human being,” this is the only kind of opposition capable of producing contradiction, provided that all the conditions previously stated against the importunity of arguments are present.

But if the subject is something universal, predicated of many—as he himself says—then the opposition is not a simple contradiction. There are three differences among propositions made concerning universal things. One encompasses all, as when I say “every human being is an animal.” Another gathers and confines the force of a proposition from an indefinite and innumerable multitude into one, as when someone says “a certain human being is an animal.” A third directs the proposition neither toward plurality nor toward particularity, as in what is proposed without any determination: “the human being is an animal,” “the human being is not an animal.” For we have added neither “a certain,” which expresses particularity, nor “every,” which expresses universality.

Thus singularity is predicated simply, whereas universality is sometimes predicated universally, as in “every human being is an animal,” where the universal thing “human being” is predicated universally. Since “human being” is universal, the word “every” added to it makes universality be expressed universally.

Again, universality may be predicated particularly, as when I say “a certain human being is an animal.” “A certain” determines the particular, but when joined to the universal substance “human being,” it makes that substance be predicated particularly.

There is also the predication of a universal non-universally, whenever the universal name is simply posited without the addition of a universal or particular determination, as in “the human being is an animal.”

Determinations are terms that either spread a universal thing over the whole, as “every” does, or contract it to a part, as “a certain” does. “Every” and “a certain” determine the quantity of a proposition, and this quantity, joined with the quality of propositions, varies in four ways.

The quality of propositions consists in affirmation and denial. A proposition may affirmatively predicate a universal thing universally, as “every human being is an animal”; affirmatively predicate a universal thing particularly, as “a certain human being is an animal”; negatively predicate a universal thing universally, as “no human being is a stone”; or negatively predicate a universal thing particularly, as “a certain human being is not a stone” [Col. 0466A].

In propositions put forward with a universal determination, the negation must occur in the determinations themselves. Since the determination is universal of a universal thing, when we say “every human being is just,” if we deny it universally, we say “no human being is just.” The word “no” removes the universality that belongs to “every,” not the universality that belongs to “human being.”

Again, if I wish to deny the proposition “every human being is just” particularly, I will say “not every human being is just,” destroying by particular negation the force of the universality.

With particulars, however, the arrangement is different. If I wish to deny the particular determination of a universal thing, as in “a certain human being is just,” I will deny it particularly by saying “a certain human being is not just.”

This occurs because, if negative particles are placed with the predicates rather than with the determinations in universal propositions, the result has a certain similarity and ambiguity as to whether the proposition has been stated universally or particularly. For if, in opposition to the affirmation “every human being is just,” I put the proposition “every human being is not just,” it will seem to signify two things: first, that no human being is just, since it proposes that every human being is not just; and second, that there are some human beings who are not just, since it denies that every human being is just.

This does not prevent one person from being unjust and another just. For if someone is just, that does not conflict with the proposition “every human being is just” being false; the proposition does not mean that every human being is just if some are just and others unjust.

Since the proposition has a double signification, the definition of universal negation, “no,” removes the determination of the universal affirmation, “every.” Therefore, in particular negations, the negation must be attached to the universality of the affirmation. Thus, for “every human being is just,” the opposed negation is “not every human being is just,” not “every human being is not just,” lest it remain ambiguous whether the negation is universal or particular [Col. 0466D]. For, as has been said, the negation “every human being is not just” can signify both an interpretation of universality and a particular proposition.

Whenever something particular is removed, however, the negative particle is attached not to the determination but to the predicate. Thus, for “a certain human being is just,” one does not say “not a certain human being is just,” but “a certain human being is not just.” The negation is not attached to the particular determination “a certain”; rather, we say “a certain human being is not just,” attaching it to the predicate “just.”

Likewise, with indefinite propositions—those without “every,” “no,” or any other determination—the negative particle is always attached to the predicate, as in “the human being is not just” [Col. 0467A]. No one says “not the human being is just,” but “the human being is not just.”

With singulars also, I do not say “not Socrates is just,” but “Socrates is not just.” Unless ambiguity sometimes intervened, the negation would always be placed with the predicate.

Everything placed in a determination is of such a kind that it either gathers the whole affirmatively, as “every” does; removes the whole negatively, as “no” does; gathers a part affirmatively, as “a certain” does; removes a part negatively, as “a certain … not” does; or removes the whole particularly in a negative way, as “not every” does.

“A certain … not” and “not every” are particular negations. For whether someone takes away a part from the whole, what remains is particular, since it has departed from the completeness of the whole; or whether someone denies the whole while leaving a part, what remains is again particular. When I say “a certain human being is not just,” I have removed a part. Again, when I say “not every human being is just,” by denying every human being, I have indicated that there is someone who is not just.

Thus “not every” and “a certain” are perfectly clear determinations and subject to ordinary understanding. These two receive particular negations: “a certain … not” denies the particular determination, while “not every” denies the universal determination. Yet both negations, as has been said, contract the proposition into particularity.

The term “no,” however, seems to be a word with a distinctive character. “Not every,” as it is said, removes “every” by means of the negative adverb “not.” Again, in “a certain … not,” the adverb “not,” added to “a certain,” separates the particular from the subject term.

But “no” does not show within its own word what it separates. It seems in a certain way to be negation rather than affirmation. Yet it is neither an adverb nor a conjunction, since adverbs and conjunctions lack declension. The word “no,” however, is subject to genders and is inflected through cases. What, then, is it? Will it be a noun? But no negation is shown to be a noun. What it is must therefore be sought through this inquiry.

The word “no” appears to be equivalent to saying “not one.” For when someone says “no human being is an animal,” this has the same force as “not even one human being is an animal.”

The word “any,” however, is a diminutive of “one.” For “any” is the diminution of “one,” as if I were to say “no one.” Whoever denies even the diminution denies more, as when someone says, “He not only does not have a gem, which is the greater thing, but not even a little gem, which is the lesser.”

Thus whoever wishes to deny even one denies more if he says that not even the diminutive of one exists. If someone wishes to say that there is not even one human being in the theater, he should say: “Not only is there not one human being there, but not even any.”

Accordingly, when we say “no,” we place it before the noun as though we were saying “not even any.” The determination “no,” therefore, contains within itself the function both of negation and of a noun: of negation in the element “not even,” and of a noun in the element “any,” which is a diminutive of “one.”

Thus the greatest negation is made of the smallest thing, namely one, when it also removes the diminutive of one, namely “any.” Therefore negation immediately removes both “every” and “a certain,” since it removes even the diminutive of one by its predication, as in “no human being is just.”

This has precisely the force of saying “not any human being is just,” which is equivalent to saying “not one human being is just.” Since these matters have now been sufficiently discussed, let us proceed in due order to Aristotle’s words.

“If, then, one enunciates universally of a universal that it is or is not, these enunciations will be contraries. By ‘universal enunciation of a universal’ I mean, for example, ‘every human being is white,’ ‘no human being is white.’”

[Col. 0468B]

He intends to demonstrate the opposition of contradiction. But since he has mingled the path and the order of discovery, we too shall first set out a few matters in an ordered exposition, so that the reader may not be troubled by the darkness and obscurity of confusion.

Among all simple propositions—which the Greeks call categorical and which we may call predicative—there are four kinds. There is either a universal affirmation and negation, as “every human being is just,” “no human being is just”; or a particular affirmation and negation, as “a certain human being is just,” “a certain human being is not just”; or an indefinite affirmation and negation, as “the human being is just,” “the human being is not just”; or an affirmation and negation concerning a singular subject, as “Cato is just,” “Cato is not just.”

The truth and falsity of these do not relate to one another in the same way but differently. First we must discuss the universals and particulars, that is, those that are determined; afterward the remaining kinds will be considered.

Let the universal affirmation “every human being is just” be set out, together with the universal negation opposed to it, “no human being is just.” Beneath these, under the universal affirmation, let there be the particular affirmation “a certain human being is just”; under the universal negation, the particular negation “a certain human being is not just.” The following diagram demonstrates this:

**Universal affirmation:** Every human being is just.

**Universal negation:** No human being is just.

[Col. 0468D]

**Particular affirmation:** A certain human being is just.

**Particular negation:** A certain human being is not just.

These two—the universal affirmation and the particular affirmation—are called subalterns. Likewise, the universal negation and the particular negation are called subalterns, because particularity is always included under universality.

It must be considered that wherever the universal affirmation is true, the particular affirmation is also true; and wherever the universal negation is true, the particular negation is also true. For if “every human being is an animal” is true, “a certain human being is an animal” is true. And if “no human being is a stone” is true, “a certain human being is not a stone” is true.

But if the particular affirmation is false, as “a certain human being is a stone,” the universal affirmation “every human being is a stone” is false. The same applies to negation. For if the particular negation is false, as “a certain human being is not an animal,” the universal “no human being is an animal” is false.

Thus, just as the universals precede in truth, so the particulars precede in falsity.

The universal affirmation and the universal negation are called contraries. This is because contraries are by nature farthest apart from one another. If they have some intermediate between them, it is not always the case that one of them inheres in the subject. We cannot say that every body is either white or black, for a body may be neither white nor black, and both propositions may be false, since there is an intermediate color.

If, however, they have no intermediate, one of them must inhere in the subject. Thus, when we say that every body is either at rest or in motion, there is no intermediate between these, and every body must either remain at rest or move.

Contraries cannot be in the same thing at the same time. For it is impossible for the same thing to be both white and black, as is apparent in universal affirmations and negations.

Universal negative and affirmative propositions are very far apart. One posits something for all, while the other removes it from all and denies it entirely. The proposition “every human being is just” posits justice in every human being; the proposition “no human being is just” concedes that nothing included within the definition of humanity is just.

They therefore differ from one another as far as possible. Yet if the things they signify have some intermediate between them, it is not necessary that one be true and the other false, as in “every human being is just” and “no human being is just.” There may be an intermediate condition: it may be neither the case that no human being is just, since some are just, nor that every human being is just, since some are not.

Both propositions may therefore be false. It is not true either that every human being is just or that no human being is just. Consequently, in cases where some intermediate exists, the universal affirmation and universal negation may fail to divide truth and falsity; both may be false, following the example of contraries that contain some intermediate between them. In such cases both contraries may fail to inhere in the subject, as we have shown above.

In cases without an intermediate, however, one must always be true and the other always false. The propositions “every human being is an animal” and “no human being is an animal” are of this kind, because between being an animal and not being an animal there is no intermediate, at least according to the likeness of contraries that lack an intermediate. In such cases one of the alternatives had to inhere in the subject.

Thus the universal affirmation and universal negation may both be false. They may also divide truth and falsity, so that one is true and the other false; but they cannot both be true, just as it is true that contraries cannot exist together.

Universal affirmation and universal negation are therefore correctly called contraries.

The particular affirmation “a certain human being is just” and the particular negation “a certain human being is not just” have properties contrary to those of the universal contraries. The universals could not both be true, whereas they could sometimes both be false. The particulars, however, can both be true, but they cannot both be false. Thus “a certain human being is just” may be true, and “a certain human being is not just” may also be true; they cannot both be found false. In this respect they differ from contraries.

They nevertheless seem similar to them because, just as contraries sometimes divide truth and falsity, so one particular may be true and the other false: “a certain human being is an animal,” “a certain human being is not an animal.”

They preserve a stable and unalterable order of both likeness and contrariety. Since contraries may both be false, wherever both contraries are found false, both subcontraries are true. But since both contraries cannot be found true, both subcontraries cannot be found false.

For example, if “every human being is just” and “no human being is just” are false, the propositions beneath them—“a certain human being is just” and “a certain human being is not just”—are true [Col. 0470C].

But if the universals divide truth and falsity, so that one is true and the other false, the particulars do the same. Thus, in “every human being is an animal” and “no human being is an animal,” the universal affirmation is true and the negation false. Likewise, in “a certain human being is an animal” and “a certain human being is not an animal,” the particular affirmation is true and the particular negation false.

These are called subcontraries either because they are placed beneath contraries or because they themselves have properties contrary to those of the superior propositions under which they stand, as has been said.

In this direct opposition of contraries and subcontraries, both falsity may occur in the superior propositions, but never both truth; in the inferior propositions, both truth may occur, but never both falsity.

If, however, one considers the diagonals and opposes the universal affirmation to the particular negation, and compares the universal negation with the particular affirmation, one will find that one is always true and the other false.

It can never happen that, when the universal affirmation is true, the particular negation is not false, nor that, when the latter is true, falsity does not immediately follow in the former. Again, if the universal negation is true, the particular affirmation is false; if the particular affirmation is true, the universal negation is false.

This can be measured in the diagram given above and also in any other terms that the mind of the person considering the matter may construct. The same result will be seen. In the case of “every human being is just,” since this is false, “a certain human being is not just” is true. Again, in the case of “no human being is just,” since the negation is false, the affirmation “a certain human being is just” is true.

The universal affirmation and particular negation, which are diagonal, and likewise the universal negation and particular affirmation, which are also diagonal, are called contradictories. This is the contradiction that he seeks, in which one is always true and the other always false.

We have added the complete model of the preceding diagram, so that what has been conceived in mind and thought may be set before the eyes and thus be more firmly fixed in memory [Col. 0471B].

Since matters stand thus, let us examine indefinite and singular propositions [Col. 0471C]. First we must discuss the indefinite propositions.

Indefinite propositions do not by themselves divide truth and falsity. For when I say “the human being is just,” “the human being is not just,” it may happen that both indefinite propositions are true. We therefore separate them from contradiction. Contradiction, as has often been said, is constituted by the fact that it can never be found that both propositions are true or both false; one is always capable of truth and the other of falsity.

Those propositions that express universality indefinitely, however, possess the force of defined particulars. For “the human being is just” is equivalent to “a certain human being is just”; and “the human being is not just” is equivalent to “a certain human being is not just.”

The matter proves this: just as defined particulars may be true in some cases and divide truth and falsity in others, but can never both be false, so in indefinites signifying a universal it can happen that both are true. Thus, in “the human being is just,” “the human being is not just,” both may be true; it is impossible for both to be false. But one true and the other false is easily found in these terms—namely, in those that naturally and necessarily inhere in their subjects, or in those that cannot inhere.

Since being an animal necessarily inheres in a human being, if someone says “the human being is an animal” and this is denied—“the human being is not an animal”—or if one says “the human being is a stone” and “the human being is not a stone,” one proposition is immediately found true and the other false [Col. 0472A].

Therefore these form a contradiction with universals predicated universally. If the indefinite proposition “the human being is not just” is set in opposition to “every human being is just,” one is always true and the other false. Likewise, if the indefinite proposition “the human being is just” is opposed to “no human being is just,” the propositions distribute truth and falsity between them, just as the defined propositions of universals, opposed according to particular and universal quantities, produce contradictory oppositions.

It is therefore established that those propositions that express a universal non-universally, being indefinite and expressing neither particularity nor universality, do not themselves always divide truth and falsity between them, but are similar to defined particulars.

Singular propositions, however, possess one mode of opposition between them. If you put them forward with the same subject, the same predicate, concerning the same part, at the same time, in the same relation, and in the same manner, they distribute truth and falsity between them, as in “Socrates is just,” “Socrates is not just.”

There are therefore two contradictions: one occurs in universals when diagonally opposed particulars are set against them; the other occurs in singulars when all the determinations that he set out in the sophistical refutations are opposed.

Since we have shown how propositions are related and how they produce contradictory oppositions, let us proceed to Aristotle’s own words. Through what has already been understood, they can now be grasped readily.

The foregoing diagram makes the point more fully. He says that when a universal thing is designated universally, and someone affirms it universally, if another denies the same thing universally, the propositions are related as contraries. He makes his meaning clearer by saying: “By ‘universal enunciation of a universal’ I mean, for example, ‘every human being is white.’”

Since “human being” is universal, the enunciation in which “every human being” is said is universal concerning a universal human being. The universal thing, namely human being, is therefore predicated universally and affirmatively by the determination “every.”

Negatively, it will be said universally in this way: “no human being is white.” For “no” is a universal term added to the universal “human being.” Thus, when affirming and denying a universal universally, the affirmation and negation are contraries, as Aristotle himself testifies and as we have explained in the preceding discussion [Col. 0472D].

But when one speaks of universals non-universally, these are not contraries, although what is signified may sometimes be contrary. By “speaking non-universally of universals” I mean, for example, “the human being is white,” “the human being is not white.” Since “human being” is universal, the enunciation does not use it universally. For “every” does not signify a universal thing, but signifies that the thing is used universally.

In wishing to show what an indefinite proposition was like, it was necessary not only to remove the universal determination from the universal term, but also the particular determination; and it was necessary to say it in this way: “When, however, with respect to universals, [Col. 0473A] a proposition is neither universal nor particular, the propositions are not contrary.” But since he did not add “nor particular,” he seems not to be speaking about indefinites, in which neither universality nor particularity is present, but only about particulars, from which he removed the universal alone and not the particular as well. Yet he himself made clear what he wished to demonstrate by suitable examples. For he did not give examples of a particular proposition, but of an indefinite one. He says: “I mean not to state universally in the case of things that are universal, as in ‘a man is white,’ ‘a man is not white.’” If he had wished to indicate a particular proposition, he would have said: “a certain man is white, a certain man is not white.” But since he showed by the example what he meant, we too should understand his earlier proposition, which reads: “[Col. 0473B] When, however, with respect to universals, a proposition is not universal,” as lacking “or particular,” so that it removes both particularity and universality from the whole expression, as the examples later show that he is speaking not of particulars but of indefinites.

Why, then, does he say this? So that, if the propositions are neither universal nor particular—which must be understood—those propositions are not contrary. For those propositions are contrary which posit a universal term universally. Indefinite propositions, however, do not have a universal determination applied to a universal term. He therefore separated universality alone from indefinites, and not particularity as well, because he was separating indefinite propositions from contraries alone, not also from particulars.

What I mean is this: if he had wished properly to indicate indefinite propositions, he would have said that indefinites are neither particulars nor universals. Those propositions which are put forward with respect to a universal neither universally nor particularly—that is, which are neither universal nor particular—are indefinite. For propositions which are neither universal nor particular are neither contrary nor subcontrary. They are not subcontrary because they do not have a particular determination added; and they are not contrary because they do not have a universal determination.

But since he wished only to show that they are not contrary, and for the present wished to omit the question of subcontraries, he called those propositions indefinite which do not have a universally determined universal. Thus we should understand that they are not contrary. He did not add that they lack particularity because he wished to separate indefinites from contraries alone, not also from subcontraries.

Therefore, if he had wished to separate indefinites from both contraries and subcontraries, he would have said: “When, however, with respect to universals, a proposition is neither universal nor particular, the propositions are neither contrary nor subcontrary.” But since he did not wish at this point to show that they are not subcontrary, but only that they are not contrary, he did not add “or particular” to the statement “when, however, with respect to universals, a proposition is not universal.” If he had added this, he would have turned to the subcontraries, about which nothing had been added. Hence his meaning is this: propositions which are indefinite are not contrary because they lack universality.

Although they are not in themselves contrary, they can nevertheless signify contraries. The meaning of this is explained in various ways by the commentators.

Herminus says that indefinites can sometimes signify contraries, although they themselves lack contrariety, since they concern universal things but do not have a universal determination added—provided that this occurs only in cases where what is affirmed or denied belongs naturally to the subject. Thus, when we say “man is rational” and “man is not rational,” rationality is of such a kind that it belongs to the nature of man. The affirmation and the negation divide truth and falsehood between them, and in a certain way contraries are designated by them.

But this has no bearing upon the signification of contraries in indefinite propositions. Particular propositions too, in such cases, divide truth and falsehood between them, as in “a certain man is rational” and “a certain man is not rational.” According to Herminus, then, we see that these propositions too can signify contraries. Why, therefore, did he say of these propositions also that, although they are not contrary, what they signify is contrary?

Alexander says this: since these propositions are indefinite, nothing prevents them from being reduced, just as to particulars, so also to universals, which appear to be contrary. Thus, in the propositions “man is an animal” and “man is not an animal,” since these propositions are indefinite, they can be taken as though they were contrary. For if we say “man is an animal,” it can be understood as though we were saying “every man is an animal”; and again, “man is not an animal” can be heard as though we were saying “no man is an animal.”

But when one says “man walks” and “man does not walk,” the mind of the hearer is led not to contraries but to subcontraries. Hence indefinites can sometimes signify contraries, because, precisely by being indefinite, nothing prevents them from being reduced to the signification of contraries and universals.

This view does have some rational basis, but it does not fully explain what Aristotle says; and Alexander voluntarily rejected the better interpretation, which Porphyry approved. For there are certain negations which retain within themselves the contrariety of the affirmation that they deny. Thus, in “he is healthy” and “he is not healthy,” the expression “he is not healthy” signifies “he is ill,” which is contrary to being healthy.

Again, when we say “a man is white,” if we deny this by the proposition “a man is not white,” it may signify that the man is black; for one who is black is not white, and being black and being white are contrary. Thus certain negations and affirmations signify contraries, but this is not always so. For in “man walks” and “man does not walk” there is no contrary contained. Nothing is contrary to walking. Hence he says that it is established that these two propositions are not contrary because, although they are universal in subject, they are not stated universally. They can, however, sometimes signify contraries when the negation includes within itself the contrary of the affirmation.

Aspasius and Alexander do not approve this latter interpretation. We, however, say that Alexander’s view is not without rational basis, but that Porphyry’s is the better. For when Aristotle says, “When, however, with respect to universals, a proposition is not universal, the propositions are not contrary, although what they signify is contrary,” Alexander does not explain when the things signified can be contrary; he merely says when the propositions themselves can be contrary. Porphyry, on the other hand, carefully explains when what is signified can be contrary.

This is what Aristotle’s text itself expresses, although Alexander too perceived the same interpretation that Porphyry expounded. Nevertheless, as has been said, he voluntarily rejected it and confirmed for himself the view that this interpretation was displeasing.

In my judgment, either both interpretations should be accepted, or the latter should be considered the better. Aristotle himself indicates this to some extent below when he says:

“For it is possible at the same time to say truly that there is a white man and that a man is not white, and that there is a good man and that a man is not good. For if he is wicked, he is not good; and if something is coming to be, it is not yet.”

When we come to that passage, we shall explain its interpretation.

It must be recognized and retained in memory that whenever universal propositions are predicated universally, if one is affirmative and the other negative, both are always contrary, unless ambiguity, tense, or any of the other factors mentioned above prevents the opposition from being one of contrariety.

Nevertheless, not all propositions that are contrary either state a universal universally or consist of one affirmative and the other negative. Thus, in “Socrates is healthy” and “Socrates is ill,” neither is a universal stated universally, nor is one an affirmation and the other a negation; yet the propositions are contrary. What they signify is contrary. Therefore it was most correctly said that any propositions which state a universal universally, provided that one is affirmative and the other negative, are immediately and naturally contrary.

But propositions that are contrary need not either state a universal universally or consist of one affirmation and the other negation. Sometimes propositions can be contrary even though they do not signify a universal universally, but only in cases where what is affirmed belongs naturally to the subject of which the affirmation is made, as in the case of “animal” and “man.” When we say “man is an animal” and “man is not an animal,” since animal belongs to the nature of man, the affirmative and negative propositions appear to be contrary, although neither a particular nor a universal determination is added.

In the case where a universal is predicated, however, the expression “to predicate universally” is not true. For no affirmation will be true in which the universal predicate is predicated universally, as in “every man is every animal.”

What he says is as follows. Every simple proposition consists of two terms. Determinations of universality or particularity are often added to these, but he explains to which part these determinations should be added. Aristotle seems to hold that a determination ought not to be joined to the predicate term.

In the proposition “man is an animal,” the question arises whether the subject should be stated with a determination, so that the proposition is “every man is an animal”; or whether the predicate should be so determined that the proposition is “man is every animal”; or whether both should be determined, so that it is “every man is every animal.”

Neither of the latter alternatives is appropriate. A determination is never joined to the predicate, but only to the subject. For it is not true to say “every animal is every man.” The reason is that every predicate is either greater than the subject or equal to it. In “every man is an animal,” animal is greater than man. Again, in “man is capable of laughter,” the predicate “capable of laughter” is equal to man. But a predicate cannot be smaller than, and more restricted than, the subject.

Therefore, in predicates which are greater than the subject, such as “animal,” the proposition is plainly false if the determination of universality is placed on the predicate term. For if we say “man is an animal,” animal, which is greater than man, is contracted by this determination all the way down to the subject man, although the name “animal” can be applied not only to man but also to other things.

The same happens in things that are equal. For if I say “every man is every risible being,” then, if I refer the first determination to humanity itself, it is superfluous to add the determination. But if I refer it to each individual human being, the proposition is false. For when I say “every man is every risible being,” I seem to signify that each individual man is every risible being, which is impossible.

The determination, therefore, must be placed not on the predicate but on the subject.

Aristotle’s words are understood in this way and lead to this interpretation: “In the case of predicates which are universal, to add something universal to them, so that the universal predicate is predicated universally, is not true.” This is what he means: “In the case where the predicate is universal”—that is, where the predicate is universal and is predicated—it is not true to predicate the universal predicate universally.

In a universal predicate—that is, something which is universal and is predicated—it is not true to predicate the predicate itself, which is universal, universally, that is, with a determination of universality added. For it cannot happen that any affirmation is true in which a universal determination is predicated of a predicate that is already universal.

He makes the point clear by giving the example: “every man is every animal.” We have already said how unacceptable this is.

## On the Rules of Oppositions

I therefore say that an affirmation is opposed contradictorily to a negation when the affirmation signifies universally and the negation does not signify universally, as in “every man is white” and “not every man is white”; and “no man is white” and “a certain man is white.”

The universal affirmation and the universal negation, however, are contrary, as in “every man is just” and “no man is just.” Consequently, it is impossible for these to be true together, whereas it is sometimes possible for the propositions opposed to them to be true together, as in “not every man is white” and “a certain man is white.”

He shows in these words what a complete contradiction is. He says that contradictory opposition is any opposition which says that a universal thing is not universally the case, in opposition to one which proposes the universal thing universally. This is what he means:

“I say that an affirmation is opposed contradictorily to a negation when the affirmation signifies universally and the negation signifies the same thing without being universal.”

Thus, “every man is just” is opposed to “a certain man is not just,” which signifies a universal—man—but not universally, just as “not every man is just” does. This is contradictory opposition: if there is a universal affirmation, there is a particular negation; if there is a universal negation, there is a particular affirmation.

As has been said, only the angular propositions produce contradiction. The words are therefore obscure, but the meaning is clear. He says that an affirmation is opposed contradictorily to a negation, or a negation to an affirmation, whenever the proposition which signifies what the other proposition signified universally signifies the same universal thing non-universally, as in the examples mentioned above.

“Every man is just” signifies a universal thing universally. “Not every man is just,” which is opposed to that affirmation, denies the same universal man non-universally, saying “not every man is just.”

Again, “no man is just” denies a universal thing universally by saying “no.” But “a certain man is just” affirms a universal thing particularly and not universally: it proposes that some man is just, but it does not state man universally.

He thus pursues all the properties of propositions. He says:

“The universal affirmation and the universal negation are contrary.”

Just as he said above that propositions which signify a universal universally, whether affirmatively or negatively, are contrary, so now he repeats the same thing, saying that the universal affirmation and the universal negation are contrary. He gives examples to show that both are universal: “every man is just” and “no man is just.”

He then sets out their property, saying that it is impossible for propositions of this kind both to agree with one another in truth. But it is possible for both propositions opposed to them to be true. The propositions opposed to them are both particular: a particular negation is opposed to a universal affirmation, and a particular affirmation is opposed to a universal negation.

Consequently, these two particular propositions—one a negation and the other an affirmation—which are angularly opposed to the universal affirmation and universal negation, can sometimes be true together and of the same subject, as in “a certain man is just” and “a certain man is not just.”

“A certain man is just” is opposed to “no man is just,” while “a certain man is not just” is opposed to “every man is just.” Yet the two propositions “a certain man is just” and “a certain man is not just” agree with each other in truth.

This, then, is what he says: “It is possible for those opposed to these to be true together,” and he indicates this by the examples “not every man is white” and “a certain man is white.”

Once the two propositions—the universal affirmation and the universal negation—have been set out, we must provide the method by which their opposites are found. By “opposite,” I mean contradictory, not contrary or anything else.

Let the affirmation be “every man is just,” and the negation “no man is just.” Against the affirmation “every man is just” there appear to be these negations: “no man is just,” “a certain man is not just,” “not every man is just,” and finally the indefinite proposition “man is not just.”

Which of these, then, is established in contradiction to “every man is just”? I call an opposition contradictory when the affirmation and negation are neither both true nor both false, but one is always true and the other false.

If “no man is just,” the universal negation, is opposed to “every man is just,” the opposition is not contradictory, since both propositions are false. If “man is not just,” the indefinite proposition, is posited, it too does not produce opposition. Since it is indefinite, it can sometimes be understood as a universal negation, depending on what the hearer expects.

Consequently, it too does not produce opposition. For if it is heard in this way, when it is understood as contrary, it can happen that both propositions are found to be false.

It remains, therefore, that the contradictory proposition is either “not every man is just” or “a certain man is not just.” But these agree with each other. The person who proposes “a certain man is not just” says the same thing as the person who says “not every man is just.” For if a certain man is not just, not every man is just; and if not every man is just, a certain man is not just.

Thus both particular negations are contradictorily opposed to the universal affirmation. In these cases, they are neither both true nor both false, but one is true and the other false.

Again, let the universal negation be “no man is just.” The affirmations opposed to it appear to be “every man is just,” “man is just,” and “a certain man is just.”

But if “every man is just” is opposed to “no man is just,” both propositions can be false; therefore they are not contradictorily opposed. The proposition “man is just,” because it is indefinite, can also sometimes be understood as though it said “every man is just.” If this is how it is understood, it can sometimes be false together with the negation “no man is just”; therefore it is not opposed to it.

It remains, then, that “a certain man is just” is contradictorily opposed to “no man is just.”

The propositions must therefore be sought angularly: against the universal affirmation the proposition under the universal negation must be opposed; and against the universal negation the proposition under the universal affirmation must be established contradictorily. Wishing to show this, Aristotle says:

“Whatever, then, are contradictions of universals universally, one of them must be true and the other false. But whatever are contradictions among singulars, as in ‘Socrates is white’ and ‘Socrates is not white’—”

In propositions that are contradictory to universals predicated universally, truth and falsehood are always divided. The contradictory propositions are the particular negation of the universal affirmation and the particular affirmation of the universal negation. In these cases, therefore, one is always true and the other always false.

This is what he means: “Whatever, then, are contradictions of universals universally.” The sentence must be divided so that it is understood in this way: “Whatever, then, are contradictions of universal propositions proposed universally, one must be true and the other false.”

Here truth and falsehood are first divided between propositions opposed both in quantity and in quality: in quality, because one is a negation and the other an affirmation; in quantity, because one is universal and the other particular.

In the second case, namely among singular propositions, truth and falsehood are divided provided that no cloud of arguments is present, as in “Socrates is white” and “Socrates is not white.” One is true and the other false, provided, as has been said, that no ambiguity of equivocation prevents this.

But in the case of universals stated non-universally, one is not always true and the other false.

“For it is possible at the same time to say truly that there is a white man and that a man is not white, and that there is a good man and that a man is not good. For if he is wicked, he is not good; and if something is coming to be, it is not yet.”

He attempts to show that propositions which are stated with respect to universals but not universally are not always true or always false. He demonstrates this by means of contraries.

The proposition “a man is white,” and its negation “a man is not white,” are shown in this way not always to divide truth and falsehood between them. For if it is true that the two affirmations “there is a white man” and “there is a black man” are both true at the same time, it is also true that an indefinite affirmation and an indefinite negation can sometimes both be found true.

If it is true that there is a white man, it is likewise true that there is a black man. For while a Gaul may be found white, an Ethiopian is found exceedingly black at the same time. It is therefore true to say that there is a white man and that there is a black man. But the man who is black is not white. Thus it is true at the same time to say that there is a white man and that a man is not white.

The same applies to “good” and “wicked.” If it is true to say that there is a good man—for example, if someone says this of a philosopher—and it is likewise true to say that there is a wicked man—for example, if someone says this of Sulla—both statements would be true: there is a good man and there is a wicked man. But one who is wicked is not good.

It is therefore simultaneously true to say that there is a good man and that a man is not good.

Nevertheless, it may appear that he has said something contradictory and that the demonstration advanced through such examples is difficult, since the examples seem to involve contraries. White and black, good and wicked, are contrary; and someone may perhaps doubt whether contraries can be found in some subjects at the same time.

But he added another example in which the terms are not contrary, although negation arises from it in the same way as in the case of contraries. Suppose someone says “there is a good man,” and another says “a man is becoming good,” if, whether instructed by another or correcting himself, someone advances through some discipline of reason.

There is nothing contrary, then, between being good and becoming good; nor is the relation contrary in the way that being a good man and being a wicked man are contrary. Since there is no contrary involved, there is no doubt that both can be true at the same time.

But what is coming to be is not yet present while it is coming to be; therefore the man who is becoming good is not yet good. It is nevertheless true to say, together with “there is a good man,” that “a man is becoming good”; but the man who is becoming good is not a good man.

It is therefore true to say at the same time that there is a good man and that a man is not good, even though valid examples involving contraries have been given. Nothing prevents contraries from belonging at one time to different subjects. Hence it is established that indefinite propositions, by what he set out in the examples above, can sometimes appear true together and do not always divide truth and falsehood between them.

When he says, “But it will suddenly appear strange, because ‘a man is not white’ seems also to signify ‘no man is white,’” his meaning is as follows.

He said that the affirmative proposition “there is a white man” can be true together with “a man is not white.” He now observes that it may sometimes appear strange and incongruous to say that “there is a white man” and “a man is not white” can both be true at the same time, because “a man is not white” seems to convey an impression that no man is white.

For a negation of this kind—“a man is not white”—seems also to signify that no man is white. If someone said “a man is not white,” it might be thought that he meant “no man is white.”

But this, he says—that is, “a man is not white,” and again “no man is white”—does not signify the same thing, nor are the two always true together.

One who says “no man is white,” by determining the negation universally, makes a statement about the whole universal class. But one who says “a man is not white” does not deny the whole universal class, but is satisfied merely to deny it with respect to some particular. “No man is white” is false if even one man is white. But “a man is not white” is true if even one man is not white. Therefore the propositions do not signify the same thing.

I mean, moreover, that whenever it is said “a man is not white,” it does not immediately signify “there is no white man.” For when I say “no man is white,” this signifies “a man is not white.” The universal proposition contains the indefinite within itself.

But when we say “a man is not white,” it does not altogether signify “no man is white,” since the indefinite does not contain the universal within itself. We have shown above that indefinites possess the force of particulars.

Thus, when there is a universal negation, there is also an indefinite negation; but when there is an indefinite negation, there is not necessarily a universal negation. The consequence therefore does not convert according to subsistence. Hence the propositions are not simultaneous. For things that do not convert are not simultaneous, as the book of the *Categories* taught us.

Thus the negations “a man is not white” and “no man is white” neither signify the same thing nor are simultaneous, since they do not convert according to the consequence of subsistence.

Syrianus, however, attempts to show that an indefinite negation has the force of a determinate negation, and tries to establish this by many arguments, although Aristotle strongly opposes him. He endeavors to prove not only by his own arguments but also by Platonic and Aristotelian reasoning that “man is not just” is of the same kind as “no man is just.”

But, adhering to Aristotelian authority, we approve what Aristotle states truthfully. As for Syrianus’ claim that an indefinite affirmation has the force of a particular, whereas an indefinite negation has the force of a universal—a claim that would be false, and that both should properly be proposed as particulars—we have shown this above and have expressed it carefully in the books we composed on categorical syllogisms, especially in the first book.

Now Aristotle himself is also our witness, and Syrianus is refuted by a very simple argument. In the *Analytics* too, Aristotle says that no syllogism can be inferred from two indefinites, whereas from a particular affirmative and a universal negative a particular negative conclusion can be drawn.

If an indefinite affirmation and an indefinite negation had the force of a universal negation and a particular affirmation, Aristotle would never have said that these propositions do not yield a syllogism. The truer view is that nothing can be inferred from two particulars in any combination of propositions. He therefore said that nothing can be inferred from these propositions because he judged indefinite propositions to have the force of particulars.

Syrianus’ arguments are thus broken in many ways. But let us now turn the course of our exposition to what follows.

It is clear that one negation belongs to one affirmation. For the negation must deny the same thing that the affirmation affirmed, and of the same subject—whether a singular or a universal—and either universally or non-universally.

I mean, for example, “Socrates is white” and “Socrates is not white.” But if one proposition predicates something else of the same subject, or the same thing of another subject, it will not be opposed to the first proposition but will be different from it.

“Every man is white” is contradicted by “not every man is white.” “A certain man is white” is contradicted by “no man is white.” And “a man is white” is contradicted by “a man is not white.”

Here too it becomes apparent that an indefinite affirmation and an indefinite negation do not always consist respectively in truth and falsehood. It is also shown from this that an indefinite negation cannot have the same force as a universal negation, and that one negation is universal while the other is indefinite.

For if one negation appears to be opposed to each affirmation, and if the affirmation “a man is white” differs from the affirmation “a certain man is white,” they will also have different expressions as their negations. The indefinite affirmation “a man is white” will have an indefinite negation, namely “a man is not white.” But the affirmation “a certain man is white” will have as its opposed negation “no man is white.”

Therefore, if a determinate particular affirmation and an indefinite affirmation differ from one another, it is true that their contradictory negations will also be dissimilar. “No man is just” is therefore different from “a man is not just.” Aristotle now pursues this point.

He says that one negation can always be established against one affirmation, and he attempts to explain why: every negation has the same terms in its statement as the affirmation, but differs in its manner of stating them. What the affirmation posits, the negation removes; and what the affirmation joins as predicate to subject, the negation divides and separates.

Therefore, if the negation contains the same subject and the same predicate that the affirmation had previously posited, there is no doubt that one negation belongs to one affirmation. For if there were two negations, either the subject would have to be changed or the predicate.

Propositions of this kind, however, are not opposed. This is what he says: “If something else is predicated, or the same thing of another subject, the proposition is not opposed but different.”

The meaning is as follows. If the negation denies something other than what was in the affirmation—for example, if the affirmation is “a man is white” and the negation says “a man is not just”—the negation has predicated something different from what was established in the affirmation.

Or, if it says the same predicate of a different subject from the one in the affirmation—for example, if the affirmation is “a man is just” and the negation answers “a lion is not just”—the predicate is the same, but the subjects are different.

If, therefore, a proposition either predicates something else in its statement or predicates of another subject the same thing that the affirmation had previously posited, the affirmation and negation will not be opposed but merely different from one another. For they do not cancel each other.

He added a demonstrative confirmation of this point, showing that there cannot be more than one negation for one affirmation, whether in singular propositions, as in his own example “Socrates is white,” “Socrates is not white,” or in universals predicated universally, when particulars are established in contradictory opposition to them.

Thus, against the universal affirmative “every man is white,” the universal stated particularly is predicated negatively: “not every man is white.” Against the particular affirmative concerning a universal, “a certain man is white,” there is opposed the universally stated negative proposition, “no man is white.”

Against the affirmative proposition stated with respect to a universal but not universally—“a man is white”—there is opposed the negative proposition likewise stated with respect to a universal but not universally—“a man is not white.”

The expression “whether of some singulars” refers to the examples “Socrates is white” and “Socrates is not white.” What follows, “or of some universals universally,” appears to refer to the examples “every man is white,” “not every man is white,” “a certain man is white,” and “no man is white.”

When he adds “or non-universally,” he refers, in the case of universals, to the examples “a man is white” and “a man is not white.”

That one affirmation is opposed contradictorily to one negation, and which propositions these are, has been stated; that there are also other propositions which are contrary has been stated; which these are has been stated; and it has been stated that not every contradiction is true or false, together with the reason why and the circumstances in which it is true or false.

Hence he briefly recapitulates everything once more, saying [Col. 0483B] that he has already stated that one affirmation is opposed to one negation, and not in just any manner, but contradictorily—namely, in such oppositions in which truth and falsity are divided. He also recalls having explained which propositions he called contradictory: the universal affirmative and the particular negative, and again the particular affirmative and the universal negative. “I also discussed,” he says, “that some are contraries and others contradictories,” for the contraries are not the same as the contradictories. The contraries are the universal affirmation and the universal negation. “I explained this also,” he says: “that not every contradiction is true or false.” Here, however, he has used “contradiction” not strictly, but generally of propositions that are opposed either in a contrary manner [Col. 0483C] or in a subcontrary manner. For these did not always divide truth and falsity between themselves, so that one would always be true and the other false: it could happen that the contraries were found false together, and the subcontraries true together. But concerning those that are properly contradictories, he proceeds and recalls that he has already explained why one is true and the other false, and when this is so. The universal affirmation is opposed in contradiction to the particular negation because they differ from one another in every respect, both in quality and in quantity. The one is an affirmation, the other a negation; the one is universal, the other particular. Therefore it is impossible for both to be false or both to be true. When this is the case, it is clear that one is true and the other false. This is what he means when he says that he has explained “why and when” they are true or [Col. 0483D] false—namely, recalling why an opposition, and when, has one proposition always true and the other false: this occurs when they are arranged diagonally, because the propositions differ from one another both in quantity and in quality.

We must now explain when, among contrary or subcontrary oppositions, both are simultaneously false, or both simultaneously true, or one is found false and the other true. Among contraries, if things that do not naturally belong to a subject are predicated, both propositions are false. For example, whiteness does not naturally belong to a human being; therefore both propositions that predicate whiteness are false: “Every human being is white” is false, and “No human being is white” is false. But when both of these are false, the subcontraries are true, as in: “Some human being is white” [Col. 0484A] and “Some human being is not white.” If, however, something natural is predicated among the contraries, the affirmation is true and the negation false. Since it is natural for a human being to be an animal, the proposition “Every human being is an animal” is true, while “No human being is an animal” is false. In the same way, among subcontraries the affirmation is true and the negation false. But if something impossible is predicated, the affirmation is false and the negation true. Since it is impossible for a human being to be a stone, if we say “Every human being is a stone,” this is false; “No human being is a stone” is true. The nature of the subcontrary retains the same force: this affirmation is false, and the negation true.

## ON ONE AFFIRMATION AND NEGATION

An affirmation and a negation are one when one thing is signified of one thing, whether the subject is universal taken universally or not [Col. 0484B] in the same way; for example: “Every human being is white,” “Not every human being is white,” “A human being is white,” “A human being is not white,” “No human being is white,” “Some human being is white”—provided that “white” signifies one thing.

What we carefully explained above, he now presents more clearly himself. We said that a proposition is one when it signifies any one thing and not many, so that it has neither an equivocal subject nor an equivocal predicate. A proposition is one in the following sense. He now says that there is one proposition when one thing is signified—that is, when it has neither an equivocal subject nor an equivocal predicate—whether it is a universal affirmation, a universal negation, a particular negation, a particular affirmation, or either of the indefinite propositions, and whether they are set diagonally against one another. [Col. 0484C] That proposition is one which signifies one thing in affirmation or negation.

Here, however, a question arises: how can a universal affirmation signify one thing, when universality itself is predicated not of one thing but of many? When I say “Every human being is white,” I signify individual human beings, who are many, and thus designate many things in the very predication of the affirmation. Consequently, no universal affirmation or negation could signify one thing, because the universal itself, as has been said, is predicated of many individuals.

To this we reply that when something universal is stated, the structure of the entire proposition is brought, in a certain manner, to one collection; and its unity is applied not to particularity but to universality, which is one quality. Thus, when we say “Every human being is just,” we do not then understand the individual human beings separately, but whatever is said concerning the human being is said with reference to one humanity [Col. 0484D]. Therefore, whether it is a universal affirmation or a universal negation, even when it concerns singular things, these propositions can be one if they are held with one signification.

This is what he means when he says that the propositions he set out above—“Every human being is white,” “Not every human being is white,” “A human being is white,” “A human being is not white,” “No human being is white,” and “Some human being is white”—are regarded as one if, he says, “white” signifies one thing. For if “white,” which is predicated, signifies many things, or if “human being,” which is the subject, does not signify one thing, there is neither one affirmation nor one negation. He makes this clearer in what follows, saying:

[Col. 0485A] “But if one name is assigned to two things from which one thing does not result, there is neither one affirmation nor one negation.”

The sense is as follows: if one name signifies several things from which one thing cannot be constituted, the affirmation in which that name is either predicated or made the subject signifies many things. For example, in the case of “human being,” when we say “human being,” it signifies animal, rational, and mortal. Yet from these things, which it signifies as many, one thing can be constituted: a mortal, rational animal. Therefore, although the name “human being” signifies several things, nevertheless, because they come together in a certain way into one body, and by being joined together produce one thing, whenever the statement is made as though one thing were formed from what the name signifies, [Col. 0485B] it is clear that the name signifies the one thing produced by that entire conjunction. This is what he means when he says: “But if one name is assigned to two things from which one thing does not result, there is neither one affirmation nor one negation.”

For if any expression signifies things of such a kind that no single body can be formed from them when they are joined together, and the things signified by that one name cannot come together into one species of substance, the affirmation is not one. He skillfully demonstrates what sort of name does not produce one affirmation because it signifies several things from which one cannot be made, saying:

“If someone assigns the name ‘garment’ to a human being and a horse, and says ‘The garment is white,’ this is neither one affirmation nor one negation. For it makes no difference from saying [Col. 0485C] ‘A human being and a horse are white.’ This, however, makes no difference from saying ‘A human being is white’ and ‘A horse is white.’”

“If someone assigns the name ‘garment’ to a human being and a horse,” he says, “and places this name in a proposition, that proposition is not one but multiple.” For if, for example, “garment” is said of both a human being and a horse, so that when someone says “garment” he designates either a human being or a horse, then if someone states in a proposition, “The garment is white,” this is not one affirmation. For what he says—“The garment is white”—is equivalent to saying “A human being and a horse are white,” since “garment” has signified both a human being and a horse.

But to say “A human being and a horse are white” is no different from saying “A horse is white” and “A human being is white.” These are two propositions, and they are not alike, since their subjects are different. [Col. 0485D] Therefore, if these are two affirmations, the affirmation that says “A human being and a horse are white” is also double. And if this in turn is double, because “garment” has been assigned to signify both a human being and a horse, then when we say “The garment is white,” it signifies not one thing but many. Consequently, if an affirmation that designates many things is not one, neither will this affirmation be one, since either its predicate or its subject is equivocal. This is what he means when he says:

“If, then, these signify many things and are plural, it is clear that the first proposition also signifies many things—or signifies nothing. For there is no human-being-horse; therefore, in these cases it is not necessary that one contradiction be true and the other false. In the case of things that are and things that have come to be, however, [Col. 0486A] an affirmation or a negation must be true or false. And among universals taken universally, one must always be true and the other false; and in the case of singular things, as has been said. But in the case of things said of universals without being taken universally, this is not necessary; this too has been stated concerning them.”

“If ‘A horse is white’ and ‘A human being is white’ signify many things,” he says, “then the first proposition also—‘The garment is white’—from which these have proceeded, signifies many things. Or if someone says that it does not signify many things, he plainly admits that absolutely nothing is indicated by the signification of the proposition itself.”

A single name signifying many things could then converge upon one signification whenever [Col. 0486B] one substance could be joined and constituted from the things signified, as in the example given above, where “human being” signifies an animal that is rational and mortal—things that can be joined together into one. But if “garment” signifies both a human being and a horse, it designates many things, and those things do not come together into one body. For it cannot happen that someone is both a human being and a horse. Therefore it either signifies many things—which is true—or, if someone insists that it does not signify many things but something joined from what it signifies, then, since nothing can be joined from a horse and a human being, it signifies absolutely nothing.

This is what he said: “For there is no human-being-horse.” This must be read under a single accent, not pronounced separately as “human being” and then “horse,” but as “human-being-horse,” so that from the conjunction of these terms it becomes clear that absolutely nothing can be constituted.

The following sentence shows why he said this. [Col. 0486C] If a proposition is to be constructed in such a way that a negation of this kind is opposed to the affirmation, an opposition in which truth and falsity are divided so that one is true and the other false, the affirmation and the negation must each be one. This occurs if neither the subject nor the predicate signifies many things. But if either designates several things and is equivocal, then in propositions of this kind one will not always be true and the other false.

Herminus, however, holds the following view. What Aristotle says—“But if one name is assigned to two things from which one does not result, there is neither one affirmation nor one negation”—he applies, for example, to “A human being is capable of walking,” because what we call “capable of walking” can designate a biped, a quadruped, or a many-footed animal. “From all these,” he says, “one thing is formed: something having feet. [Col. 0486D] Therefore,” he says, “this affirmation does not signify many things.”
