But Aristotle’s position does not follow at all. For one thing is not formed from all these; neither the quadruped, the biped, nor the many-footed animal makes “having feet.” Here we have a number of feet, not one constitution of feet. Therefore Herminus must be set aside.

Aspasius, Porphyry, and Alexander also agreed with the exposition I have given above in the commentaries they published on this book. But so that Aristotle’s example may not continue to burden us with obscure darkness, let us examine the matter in some familiar example and expression. When we say “Ajax kills himself,” the statement designates both Ajax, the son of Telamon, and Ajax, the son of Oileus; and from these two no single thing can be formed. For nothing at all is joined together from two individuals. [Col. 0487A] Therefore such a proposition signifies many things.

But enough of this. He now determines that what he previously said about propositions did not concern every tense, but only the past and present, and explains how propositions stand with respect to truth and falsity in those tenses. In future matters, however, the judgment concerning a proposition is not the same as it is concerning the present and the past. In the latter cases, truth and falsity are already determined, whether when the event has occurred or when it is presently the case.

Thus, when I say “Brutus first established the consulship under King Tarquinius,” and another says “Brutus did not first establish the consulship under King Tarquinius,” one proposition is true and the other false; the affirmation is definitely true and the negation definitely false.

Similarly, in the present, when we say “It is spring” and “It is not spring,” if this is said [Col. 0487B] during spring, the affirmation is true—and definitely true—and the negation is false—and definitely false. But if it is said in autumn, the affirmation is definitely false and the negation is definitely true. For whether in the present or in the past, the truth of an affirmation or negation has already occurred.

In the future, however, the matter is not the same. Thus, when we say “The Franks will defeat the Goths,” [Col. 0488A] and someone denies it by saying “The Franks will not defeat the Goths,” one proposition is true and the other false. But no one can know, before the outcome, which is true and which is false. This is what he means when he says: “In the case of things that are and things that have come to be, an affirmation or a negation must be true or false; among universals taken universally, one must always be true and the other false; and in the case of singular things, as has been said.”

Thus, not only must one proposition always be true and the other false throughout the contradiction, but in the case of any singular proposition a determinate truth or falsity must also be found. In this way truth and falsity are divided in propositions concerning singular things. Among universals, however, when particular propositions are opposed to them, as has been said, one must be true and the other false, [Col. 0488B] but without the truth or falsity of the propositions being determinate in the manner explained above. Therefore, some discussion of future matters must follow.

Since we shall see that this is a larger work than can be discussed briefly here, and since we have extended the course of the second volume at greater length, let us here bring this wearisome prolixity to an end.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0487]

[Col. 0487B] To expound what the course of this book will contain belongs to a treatment almost too elevated to be discussed within the logical discipline. But since, as has often been said, thoughts are expressed through sentences, and it is evident that the things underlying them exist, there is no doubt that what belongs to things is often transferred in the same form to words. Therefore I rightly decided to disclose Aristotle’s most subtle opinions in a commentary arranged in two orders. For the earlier edition prepares, for those entering upon these more elevated and subtler matters, a kind of easier path. The second edition, however, which labors to make subtle opinions clear, is offered to those advanced in study and learning, so that they may read and learn from it. Accordingly, a few preliminary remarks must first be made, so that what we shall discuss later may not seem unfamiliar to those reading this.

The Greeks call categorical propositions those that are uttered without any condition attached to the proposition, as in: “It is day,” “The sun exists,” “A human being exists,” “A just human being exists,” “The sun is hot,” and other such statements proposed without the knot or bond of any condition. Conditional propositions, on the other hand, are of this kind: “If it is day, there is light,” which the Greeks call hypothetical propositions. They are called conditional because a certain condition is proposed, so that one says: “If this is, that is.” Those propositions which the Greeks call *categorical* we may call *predicative* in Latin. For if κατηγορία (*katēgoria*) means “predication” or “predicate,” why should κατηγορικαί (*katēgorikai*) propositions not also be called predicative propositions?

Some of these propositions signify what is everlasting: just as the things they signify always exist and never depart from their proper nature, so too the propositions themselves possess immutable signification. Thus, if someone says, “God exists,” or “God is immortal,” [Col. 0488B] these propositions, just as they are spoken of immortal things, likewise possess an everlasting and necessary signification; and this is not perceived merely within the nature of one time, but within that of every time. For when we say, “God is immortal,” or “God was immortal,” or “God will be immortal,” there is no deviation from the necessity proper to the signification.

We call propositions necessary when what is said either must have been, must be, or must certainly come to pass; and those that signify everlasting things possess everlasting necessity. For even if the nature of their truth is not manifest in these cases, nothing prevents the constancy of necessity from being fixed in nature. Thus, if it is unknown to us whether the stars are even or odd in number, it nevertheless cannot happen that they appear to be neither even nor odd; without any doubt, they are either even or odd. Every multitude retains one of these two properties in its nature. Accordingly, if one person says, “The stars are even,” and another replies, “The stars are not even,” or if one says, “The stars are odd,” and another replies, “The stars are not odd,” one of them necessarily puts forward the truth. Although which of them has spoken the truth is unknown to us, what is said must nevertheless exist immutably; and these are immutable necessary propositions.

Others do not signify everlasting things, yet are themselves necessary so long as the subjects remain concerning which the proposition affirms or denies something. Thus, when I say, “A human being is mortal,” so long as a human being exists, it is necessary that the human being be mortal. If someone says, “Fire is hot,” then so long as fire exists, the proposition is necessarily true.

Others depart from the nature of necessity and signify only what is contingent. These either stand equally with respect to affirmation and negation, or incline more frequently toward one side. They stand equally when someone says, “I must bathe today,” and “I must not bathe today.” Neither the negation nor the affirmation is more necessary, for neither is necessary in the same way as the other. Those that incline more toward one side are of this kind: someone says, “A human being grows gray in old age,” and “A human being does not grow gray in old age.” It happens more frequently that he grows gray, yet it is not excluded that he may not grow gray.

The nature of predicative propositions is gathered from the truth and falsity of things. As things are, so will be the propositions that signify them. [Col. 0489B] For if things possess some necessity in themselves, the propositions too are necessary. If, however, they merely signify that something is present—for example, if someone says, “A human being is walking,” thereby showing that walking is present in a human being—then they are beyond necessity, signifying only presence and entirely empty of necessity. If things are impossible, the propositions that indicate those things are called impossible propositions. If things come and go contingently, the proposition that reveals them is called a contingent proposition.

Since some times are future, others present, and others past, the things subject to time likewise vary according to these differences of time. Some belong to the present, others to the future, and others to the past. In the same way, some propositions are governed by the signification of past time, as when I say, “The Greeks destroyed Troy”; others by the present, as when I say, “The battle of the Franks and Goths is being joined”; and others by the future, as in, “The Persians and Greeks will die in war.”

With respect to past and present things, propositions are as stable and definite as the things themselves. What has happened has not not-happened, and what has not happened has not yet happened. Therefore, concerning what has happened, it is definitely true to say that it happened, and false to say that it did not happen. Again, concerning what has not happened, it is true to say that it has not happened, and false to say that it happened. The present too, in what is taking place, has a definite nature; and propositions about it must likewise possess definite truth or falsity. For of what is happening it is definitely true to say that it is happening, and false to say that it is not happening. Of what is not happening it is true to say that it is not happening, and false to say that it is happening.

The definition of propositions concerning the past or present has therefore already been discussed above. Now the order of the discussion turns to the truth and falsity of those propositions that are spoken of the future and that are contingent. He customarily calls “future” those things that he likewise customarily calls contingent. According to Aristotle’s view, a contingent thing is whatever comes about by chance, or through anyone’s free choice and personal will, or through nature’s capacity to turn in either direction—so that it may occur or not occur.

Thus, past and present things have a definite and settled outcome. What has happened cannot not have happened, and what is now taking place cannot, while it is taking place, not be taking place. But among future things, which are contingent, something can happen and can fail to happen.

Since we have set out above three modes of contingency, which we have discussed more fully in the *Physics*, let us provide examples of each. If yesterday I left the house and found a friend whom I had intended to seek, it was nevertheless possible, before I found him, that I might not find the person whom I did find. Once I had found him, or after I had found him, it was no longer possible that I had not found him.

Again, if I freely set out for the countryside last night, before this occurred it was possible that I might not set out. After I had set out, or while I was setting out, it was no longer possible that what was taking place might not take place, or that what had happened might not have happened.

Further, it is possible for this tunic that I am wearing to be torn. If it was torn yesterday, while it was being torn or after it had been torn, it was no longer possible that it should not be torn or should not have been torn. Before it was torn, however, it was possible that it should not be torn.

It is therefore clear that, in present and past things that are contingent, the outcome of those same things is definite and settled. In future things, however, either of two alternatives can occur, while neither one is definite; rather, the matter inclines in both directions, and either this or that must occur. Yet it is impossible for either one of the alternatives to occur definitely, or for the other to be definitely impossible. For contingent things are contingent in both directions.

What I mean is this: as I leave the house today, it is necessary that I either find a friend or not find him. In every case there is either an affirmation or a negation. But it is not necessary that I definitely find him; or, if that does not happen, it is likewise not necessary that I definitely fail to find him, as it was yesterday, when I left the house and found my friend. Yesterday it was definite that it was not true that I had failed to find him.

The case is not the same with contingent and future things. There is merely either this or that, and this is necessary: that one or the other must occur. But that one particular thing, or one particular outcome, should be definite and virtually certain cannot be the case beforehand.

In this respect the propositions concerning contingents and futures differ from those concerning past and present things. They are alike in that each contains either an affirmation or a negation, just as do propositions concerning past or present things. They differ in that past and present things have a definite outcome, whereas future and contingent things have an indefinite and uncertain outcome.

Some present or past things may nevertheless appear uncertain and indefinite, but only because we are ignorant of them, not because nature is. Although we do not know whether the stars are even or odd in number, it is nevertheless evident that one of these alternatives definitely obtains in the nature of the stars. It is unknown to us, but perfectly known to nature.

The case is not the same with “I shall see my friend today” or “I shall not see my friend today.” What will happen is unknown to us, and it is not known to nature either, since it does not occur naturally but by chance. Therefore propositions of this kind are referred not merely to our knowledge, but also to the knowledge of nature itself, according to an uncertain outcome and an unstable truth or falsity.

Such is the nature of the contingent: it may stand equally in both directions, as in “I must bathe today” and “I must not bathe today,” or it may incline more toward one side and less toward the other, as in “A person grows gray as he grows old” and “A person does not grow gray as he grows old.” One occurs more often, the other less often. Yet nothing prevents what happens more rarely from happening nevertheless.

Aristotle’s subtle treatment will therefore begin with singular propositions and open a way toward universals. Contradictions arose in two ways: either in singular propositions, or in universals universally predicated and opposed to one another.

[Col. 0491B] He proceeds from the three kinds mentioned above—chance, free choice, and possibility—which he called by one name, “either-way” (*utrumlibet*). He coined this name to indicate that these things do not have one fixed and certain outcome, but either of two outcomes, and that they can occur or fail to occur. This indicates an unstable nature, inclining in both directions without resistance from anything.

One must not, however, suppose that everything unknown to us belongs to the nature of the “either-way” and of the contingent. For if it is unknown to us that envoys have been sent from the Persians to the Greeks, it does not follow that their having been sent is an uncertain event. Nor, if medicine detects a fatal sign on a sick person’s face, so that nothing else is possible except that he will die, does it follow that, because through ignorance of the art we do not know that the sick man will die, his death should be judged “either-way” and contingent.

Only those things should unquestionably be regarded as of this kind that are unknown to us because their outcome cannot be known from their own nature—because, through their own instability, they incline in both directions; that is, because through their own instability and inconstancy they change toward either the outcome of affirmation or that of negation.

Among philosophers there is a dispute concerning the causes of things that occur: whether everything happens by necessity or whether some things happen by chance. On this matter there is great disagreement among the Epicureans, Stoics, and our Peripatetics. Let us briefly explain their views.

The Peripatetics, whose leader is Aristotle, affirm with the greatest authority and clearest reasoning that chance, free judgment, and necessity all exist in things that are and in things that are done. They prove in the *Physics* that chance exists whenever something is undertaken and the result does not occur for the sake of which the action was begun. Whatever then occurs should be regarded as occurring by chance; and chance does not occur without some action.

Whenever something other than what was expected occurs through the action being carried out, Peripatetic authority proves that it occurred by chance. If someone, while digging the earth or sinking a pit for the cultivation of a field, finds a treasure, the treasure was found by chance, though not without some action: the earth was dug when the treasure was found. But it was not the agent’s intention that the treasure should be found. Thus, something different succeeded for the person acting, although he was acting for another purpose.

Whatever occurs through an action, yet does not occur on account of the thing for which the action was begun, is therefore said to occur by chance. This belongs to the very nature of things, not to the weakness of our knowledge, as though some things appeared to be chance occurrences merely because they were unknown to us. Rather, they are unknown to us because whatever happens by chance in nature possesses neither a constant necessity nor a pattern of providence.

The Stoics, since they think that everything occurs by necessity and according to providence, measure what happens by chance not according to the nature of chance itself but according to our ignorance. They believe that something happens by chance when, although it occurs necessarily, it is unknown to human beings.

There is almost the same dispute between them and us concerning free choice. We posit free choice when, with nothing external compelling us, we judge and deliberate about what should or should not be done, and then undertake and complete the action after first forming an intention. Thus what is done takes its beginning from us and from our judgment, with nothing external either violently compelling or forcibly preventing us.

The Stoics, however, attributing everything to necessity, attempt to preserve freedom of will by reversing the order. They say that the soul naturally possesses a certain will toward which its own nature impels it. Just as inanimate bodies that are naturally heavy are carried downward toward the earth, while light bodies move upward, and no one doubts that this occurs by nature, so too they think that human beings and the other animals all possess a natural will, and that whatever we do occurs according to the will that is natural to us.

They add, however, that we will what the necessity of that providence has commanded. Thus a will is naturally granted to us, and we do voluntarily what we do, since the will is in us; yet the necessity of that providence constrains the will itself. Everything therefore happens by necessity, because the natural will follows necessity; and what we do proceeds from us because the will itself is from us and accords with the nature of the animal.

We, however, do not call free choice of will simply whatever someone has wanted, but what each person has arrived at through judgment and examination. Otherwise many animals too would possess free choice of will. We see them voluntarily avoid some things and voluntarily pursue others. If wanting or not wanting something were rightly included under the term “free choice,” this would belong not only to human beings but also to the other animals, though who does not know that they lack this power of free choice?

Free choice is what the very words reveal: a free judgment concerning the will. Whenever certain images converge in the mind and provoke the will, reason weighs them and judges among them; and after weighing and examining what seems better to it, it acts. Therefore we reject certain things that display the appearance of pleasure, though they promise usefulness, and we strongly endure other things that are bitter, even against our will.

Free choice therefore consists not in the will itself but in the judgment of the will; it lies not in imagination but in the weighing of imagination itself. For this reason we ourselves are the origins of certain actions, not merely followers of them. This is what it means to use reason and to use judgment.

Existence is common to us with the other animals; we are distinguished from them by reason alone. If the difference between us and the other animals lies solely in judgment, why should we doubt that using reason is the same as using judgment? If someone removes judgment from things, he has removed human reason; and once human reason has been removed, humanity itself cannot remain.

Our Peripatetics therefore judged better: they allowed chance to exist as something fortuitous in things, outside any necessity, and they placed free choice neither in necessity nor in something that, though not necessary, is nevertheless not within us like chance, but in the choice of judgment and the examination of the will.

There is also a disagreement between the Peripatetics and the Stoics concerning what is said to be possible. We can settle it briefly in this way. The Stoics define as possible what can happen, and say that what is prevented from happening is not possible. They refer this to our ability, so that what we can do is called possible, while what is impossible for us they deny to be possible.

The Peripatetics, however, placed possibility not in us but in nature itself. Thus some things are possible to happen in such a way that they are also possible not to happen. For example, it is possible for this pen to be broken, and it is also possible for it not to be broken. They refer this not to our ability but to the nature of the thing itself.

Opposed to this view is the doctrine that everything happens by fate, whose proponents are the Stoics. For what happens by fate follows from its primary causes. But if this is so, what does not happen cannot be changed into happening.

We, however, say that some things are possible to happen in such a way that those same things are also possible not to happen. We measure this neither by necessity nor by our own possibility.

With these matters clarified, it is enough to add that, since Aristotle firmly retained this view in his doctrine, it was easy for him to explain the character of contingent propositions concerning the future: they stand equally with respect to affirmation and negation, and either alternative can occur. Therefore they do not possess a determinate constancy of outcome. If they did, everything would be believed to happen by necessity. This will become clearer when we reach Aristotle’s own words.

Aristotle did not inappropriately or incongruously transfer a discussion of matters more elevated—and perhaps not immediately belonging to the art of logic—into a logical treatment when he spoke of propositions. For it would not be possible to establish the firm correctness and signification of propositions unless he had shown that this derives from things. Predicative propositions, as has been said, rest not upon speech or upon the combination of predicates, but upon the signification of things.

Now that everything that had to be said in preparation has been set forth, let us proceed to disclose and unravel Aristotle’s own opinions.

[Col. 0494A] “Among things that are and things that have happened, an affirmation or negation must be true or false: among universals, one is always true and the other false; among singular things, as has been said, this is so; but in the case of things that are not stated universally as universals, it is not necessary.”

Categorical propositions, which may be called predicative in Latin, as we have already said above, are judged by the complete rule of reasoning from the things that the propositions themselves signify. Those that we call hypothetical or conditional propositions derive their proper force from the condition itself, not from the things they signify. For when I say, “If a human being exists, an animal exists,” and “If a stone exists, an animal does not exist,” one proposition is consequent and the other contradictory. Therefore the entire force of the propositions turns upon their consequence and contradiction. It follows that not their signification but the condition constitutes the force and nature proposed by hypothetical utterances.

Predicative propositions, as has been said, derive their substance principally from things. Therefore, since some things belong to the present and others to the past, and since the event of things in the present or past is certain, the truth and falsity of predicative propositions concerning the past and present are likewise certain.

The mode of contradiction was twofold. Either universals were opposed angularly to particulars, or a singular affirmative signification destroyed a singular negation by contradictory opposition. In such cases one was always found to be true and the other false.

In indefinite propositions, however, it was not necessary that one be true and the other false, except in those cases in which truth and falsity were divided. In these cases—not only is one always true and the other always false, as in past and present propositions, but one retains a certain and definite truth, while the other retains a certain and definite falsity.

With propositions concerning the future, if they are necessary propositions, although they are expressed in the future tense, it is nevertheless necessary not only that one be true and the other false, but also that one be definitely true and the other definitely false. If I say, “The sun will enter Aries in the spring of this year,” and someone else denies this, one proposition is not merely true and the other false; the affirmation is definitely true and the negation definitely false.

Aristotle, however, does not usually call necessary things “future,” but rather those that are contingent. Contingent things are, as we said above, whatever stand equally with respect to being and not-being. Just as they have an indefinite being and not-being, so too affirmations and negations concerning them have an indefinite truth or falsity. One is always true and the other always false, but in contingent matters it is not yet known which is true and which false.

For just as, among things that must exist, existence is definite, and among things that cannot exist, non-existence is definite, so among things that can exist and can not exist, neither existence nor non-existence is definite. Truth and falsity are taken from whether the thing exists or does not exist. If what is said exists, the statement is true; if what is said does not exist, it is false.

Thus, in contingent and future matters, just as the existence and non-existence of the thing itself are unstable, existence or non-existence is nevertheless necessary in the sense that one or the other must obtain. Likewise, in affirmations that reveal contingencies, truth and falsity remain uncertain. Which is true and which false is unknown according to the nature of the propositions themselves; nevertheless, one must be true and the other false.

Porphyry, however, mixes in certain elements of Stoic dialectic. Since these are unfamiliar to Latin ears, and the very issue under discussion is thereby not recognized, we shall deliberately pass over them.

## ON FUTURE CONTINGENTS

With singular and future propositions, however, the situation is not the same. For if every affirmation or negation is true or false, and everything must either exist or not exist, then if one person says that something will happen and another does not say that same thing, it is clear that one of them must speak the truth, if every affirmation or negation is true or false. For in such matters both cannot be true.

If it is true to say that something is white or is not white, it must be either white or not white. If it is white or not white, then affirmation or negation is true; and if it is not so, the speaker is lying. If he is lying, it is not so. Therefore either the affirmation or the negation must be true or false.

Consequently, nothing either is, comes to be, or occurs by chance or by the “either-way”; nor will anything be or fail to be. Everything occurs by necessity, and nothing is “either-way.” Either the person who affirms speaks the truth or the person who denies does; likewise, either the thing would come to be or it would not come to be.

It has already been said above that there are two kinds of contradiction in propositions, and Aristotle now recalls this: in both, one must be true and the other false. But what is said about future and contingent matters will be better understood if we speak of contingencies that arise in singular contradiction.

A universal angular contradiction among contingents is of this kind:

“Tomorrow all the Athenians will fight in a naval battle.”

“Tomorrow not all the Athenians will fight in a naval battle.”

In singular propositions it is of this kind:

“Tomorrow Socrates will fight in the wrestling school.”

“Tomorrow Socrates will not fight in the wrestling school.”

One must not fail to recognize that the propositions “Socrates will die” and “Socrates will not die” are not contingent in the same way as “Socrates will die tomorrow” and “Socrates will not die tomorrow.” The former are not contingent at all, but necessary. Socrates will necessarily die. The latter, which define a time, are not themselves included among contingents, because it is uncertain to us whether Socrates will die tomorrow. It is not uncertain to nature, however. Therefore it is not uncertain to God either, who knows nature itself perfectly.

The genuinely contingent propositions are those that belong neither to nature nor to necessity, but either to chance, free choice, or the possibility of nature. They belong to chance when, for example, I leave the house and see a friend, without leaving for that purpose. They belong to free choice when something can be willed or not willed, and before it occurs it is uncertain whether I shall will it. They belong to possibility when, since something can occur and can fail to occur, it is uncertain beforehand which of the two alternatives will be realized.

Thus, “Tomorrow Socrates will debate in the wrestling school” is contingent, because it proceeds from free choice.

If in such contingents one proposition is always true and the other always false, and one is definitely true while the other is definitely false, and things correspond to words, then everything must either exist or not exist. Whatever comes to be comes to be by necessity. Nothing is possible that could also possibly not exist; free choice will not exist, nor will there be any chance in things, since necessity rules over everything.

In these matters—that is, in singular contradictions—both parties cannot speak the truth. Contradictories were propositions that could not exist together; nor can both of them, namely negations and affirmations, be false in contradictory propositions. For those propositions were contradictory that could not be true together. Therefore one will speak the truth and the other falsehood.

If nothing unstable is granted in such matters—that is, among contingents—so that outcomes arise according to a sequence and the utterance of truth and falsity remains uncertain, then whatever is said definitely to be true in an affirmation must necessarily exist; and whatever is said falsely in a negation must necessarily not exist. Everything therefore will either exist by necessity or not exist by necessity. There is consequently no chance, free choice, or possibility in things, if necessity governs all.

Aristotle takes the hypothetical proposition, “If everything said of the future is definitely true or definitely false,” and shows through the consequent reasoning that everything happens by necessity and nothing by chance, judgment, or the corresponding possibility. Once this has been posited—that one proposition is true and the other definitely false—everything follows by necessity.

He demonstrates this from the agreement of propositions with things in the following way. He proposes the condition and confirms its truth from the necessity of the things themselves. The condition is this: if every affirmation or negation expressed concerning the future is definitely true or false, then everything that happens happens by necessity, and nothing occurs by chance, by one’s own free will and judgment, or through any possibility—things which he has called by the term “either-way.”

He states the condition as follows:

[Col. 0496D] “For if every affirmation or negation is true or false”—we must understand “definitely”—“everything must either exist or not exist. If one person says that something will happen, while another does not say this very same thing, it is clear that one of them must speak the truth, if every affirmation or negation is true or false; for both will not be true at the same time in such cases.”

The sense is therefore this: “If,” he says, “every affirmation or negation is definitely true or false, then everything must either exist or not exist, according to what the affirmation posits or the negation removes. For if one person says that something exists and another says that this same thing does not exist, one affirms and the other denies. But in affirmation and negation placed in contradiction, one is always true and the other false. They cannot both be true.”

The discussion is not now concerned with subcontraries or indefinites. For subcontraries—that is, a particular negation and a particular affirmation—and indefinite propositions could both be true of the same subject. Contradictories, however, could not; for it is impossible that propositions which either form singular contradictions or stand in angular opposition among universals should ever be true simultaneously.

This is what he means by “for both will not be true at the same time in such cases”: both utterances will not be true in contradictory utterances. Once this condition has been posited—if every affirmation is definitely true or false—everything follows by necessity.

He attempts to demonstrate this consequence and correspondence between things and propositions by saying:

“For if it is true to say that something is white or not white, it must be white or not white; and if it is white or not white, it is true to affirm or deny; and if it is not so, the speaker lies; and if he lies, it is not so. Therefore either the affirmation or the negation must be true or false.”

Every affirmation and every negation, he says, is either true or false in accordance with the things themselves. He takes his examples from present matters. For just as utterances are related by necessity in the present, so they are related in the future.

Let us therefore examine in the present what necessity belongs to things and propositions. If a proposition stated of anything is true, the thing that it asserts must exist in the manner stated. If someone says that snow is white, and this is true, the necessity of the thing follows from the truth of the proposition. Snow must be white if the proposition predicated of it is true.

If someone says that pitch is not white, and this is true, it is equally clear that the thing follows the truth of the proposition.

Moreover, propositions follow the necessities of things. If something exists, it is true to say of it that it exists; and if something does not exist, it is true to say of it that it does not exist. Thus, according to the truth of an affirmation or negation, the necessity of the thing follows its substance; and the necessity of things accompanies the necessity of propositions.

The same applies conversely to falsities. If an affirmation is false, the thing of which it speaks must not be as the affirmation states. Thus, if the affirmation “Pitch is white” is false, pitch must not be white. Again, if the negation “Snow is not white” is false, snow must be white.

Conversely, if the thing does not exist, the affirmation concerning it is necessarily false. If the thing again does not exist, whatever negation may be uttered of it is false without question, and the contrary must be the case. Thus, if one can make the false negation “Snow is not white,” what this false negation says—namely, that snow is not white—does not exist as a fact. Snow is not non-white.

The falsity of both forms therefore corresponds to the necessity of things. If something exists, it is truly said of it that it exists; and if it is truly said that the thing of which something is truly predicated exists, then it must exist. But if what is said does not exist, the utterance is false; and if utterances are false, the things must not exist.

If these matters stand so, and it has been posited that every affirmation and negation is definitely true or false, then the truth or falsity of propositions follows the necessity of things according to their existence or non-existence: existence according to truth, as has been said, and non-existence according to falsity.

There will therefore be nothing by chance, by free will, or through any possibility. For the things we call “either-way” are those which, although they have not yet happened, can happen and can fail to happen. Once they have happened, they could not fail to have happened. For example, I may read Virgil’s book today. Since I have not yet done so, it can fail to happen, but it can also happen; and if I do it, I was able not to do it.

Everything called “either-way” is of this kind. He now explains more clearly what “either-way” is, saying:

An either-way possibility, then, is no more so than not so, nor will it be.

For an either-way possibility is one that is equally disposed toward being or toward not being; that is, it is necessary neither that it be nor that it not be. Some, including the Stoics, however, thought that Aristotle was saying that future contingents are neither true nor false. Because he said that they have no greater inclination toward being than toward not being, they interpreted him as saying that it made no difference whether they were considered false or true; for they held that they were neither true nor false. But this is false. Aristotle does not say that both are neither true nor false; rather, he says that each of them is either true or false. Yet not in the determinate manner of past propositions, nor in the determinate manner of present propositions. The nature of enunciative expressions is, in a certain way, twofold: in some, not only are truth and falsity found, but one is determinately true and the other determinately false; in others, one is true and the other false, but indeterminately and variably—and this by their own nature, not because of our ignorance or knowledge.

Accordingly, it was rightly said that, if every affirmation or negation were determinately true, nothing would come to be or exist either by chance or through what is called an either-way possibility, and nothing would contingently be or not be; rather, everything would either be or not be determinately, and everything would occur by necessity. For this is what follows for anyone who says either that what is affirmed is true or that what is denied is true. If this were true, then, just as something would come to be together with truth, so it would fail to come to be together with falsity—and likewise with whatever was said truly or falsely by the enunciations. But if this is impossible, and there are some things that do not exist by necessity, and we see that some things happen by chance, some by will, and some through the proper possibility of nature, it is pointless to think that, in future enunciations just as in past ones, one is determinately true and the other determinately false. Accordingly, this was one part of his argument; then, as though opposing an objection to himself, he enters upon another question with a stronger treatment.

Furthermore, if something is white now, it was previously true to say that it would be white. Therefore, it was always true to say of anything that has happened that it is or will be. But if it was always true to say that it is or will be, it cannot fail to be or fail to be in the future. And what cannot fail to happen is impossible not to happen. What is impossible not to happen must happen. Therefore, everything that will happen must happen; so nothing will be an either-way possibility, nor will anything happen by chance—for if it happened by chance, it would not happen by necessity.

To establish that not all future enunciations are determinately true or false, he takes, with the same argumentative force and from the same possible outcome, a different route of argument. Earlier, from things that had not yet happened, he inferred that, if they were truly predicted to happen, there could be only necessity in things. Now, however, he takes his argument from things that have happened: if they had been truly predicted before they happened, then the events of all things would be held in the chain of necessity. Those who say that even propositions concerning contingents have a fixed enunciative status according to truth and falsehood think that everything that has happened could have been predicted, since it would happen. For it was already present in nature, but the event itself disclosed this to us. Therefore, if everything that has happened exists, and the things that exist could have been predicted to happen, everything that is said must be either determinately true or determinately false, since its event is determinate in relation to the present time. Thus, whenever something happens, it was true to say that it would happen, even if it had not yet happened. The event itself proves that it was then true to say this: what could have been predicted did happen. If it had been predicted, then the thing that was going to happen would have been predicted with determinate truth.

Aristotle takes this and leads it by an exceedingly powerful argument to the same impossibility, joining the nature of the present time with the enunciation of the future. For he says that it is similar to enunciate about present things according to the necessity of truth and to enunciate about future things. If it is true to say that something is, then it must be; and if it is true to say that something will be, then without doubt it must be in the future. Everything, therefore, is destined to happen by necessity. He draws the argument toward the same impossibility. He derives the order of this impossibility from propositions that are easier to understand, though they have the same force, as follows:

“If it is always true to say that something is or will be, then whatever it was true to predict at that time cannot fail to be or fail to be in the future. For just as what is truly said to be present cannot fail to be, and the proposition that said it was true, so too, in the future, the proposition that says something will be, if it is true, cannot be false of what it predicts as future. But if what is predicted by a true proposition cannot fail to happen, it is impossible for it not to happen. To say ‘it cannot fail to happen’ is the same as saying ‘it is impossible for it not to happen.’ What is impossible not to happen must happen. For ‘impossible’ is the contrary predicate corresponding to ‘necessary,’ as he later teaches. What is impossible to be must necessarily not be. What must be cannot possibly not be; for what cannot possibly be is necessarily not. If this is so, opposites will also stand in the same relation. What is impossible not to be must be. But it has been said that things truly predicted cannot possibly not be; this is therefore to be by necessity. Accordingly, the things that are predicted are necessarily going to happen.”

Thus nothing is an either-way possibility, neither by chance nor in any way according to free choice, since the meaning of “either-way” has enclosed all of these notions. For when he says “either-way,” he includes possibility, chance, and free choice in its meaning.

Therefore nothing happens by chance. If someone says that certain things happen by chance, he again removes necessity from those things; for what happens by chance does not happen by necessity. But nothing happens by chance, since everything comes about by necessity whenever a true enunciation has predicted it. This impossibility results from what was granted earlier: that everything that has happened could have been determinately and truly predicted. For if what happened comes about by necessity, it was true to say that it would happen. But if it does not come about by necessity, but contingently, then it was not more properly true to say that it would happen, but rather that it happens contingently; for whoever says “it will be” introduces a certain necessity into the prediction itself.

This is understood from the fact that, if someone truly says that what is predicted will happen, it becomes impossible for it not to happen. But this means that it happens by necessity. Therefore, whoever says that one of the things that happen contingently will happen may be lying in saying that the thing that happens contingently will be future. Or, even if the thing he predicts does happen, he is nevertheless lying—not because the event is false, but because the mode of prediction is false. He ought to have said: “Tomorrow a naval battle will happen contingently.” This means: “If it happens, it will happen in such a way that it could have failed to happen.” Whoever says this speaks truly, for he has predicted the event contingently.

But whoever says, “Tomorrow there will be a naval battle,” as though it were necessary, makes the prediction in such a way that, even if it happens, he has not thereby spoken truly simply because he predicted it. What was going to happen contingently, he predicted as necessarily future. The falsity, therefore, lies not in the event but in the mode of prediction.

Just as, if someone saw Socrates walking and said, “Socrates is walking necessarily,” he would be lying—not in saying that Socrates is walking, but in predicting that he is walking necessarily—so also here: whoever says that something will happen, even if it happens, is still false, not about what happened, but about its having happened in the manner in which he predicted it would happen. If his statement were determinately true, the event would have to occur by necessity. Therefore, whatever he pronounces will happen without qualification, he predicts as necessarily future. Falsity, then, is found not in the event of the thing but in the enunciative manner of the prediction.

For in the case of contingents, if the enunciation is to be true, one must predict something in such a way that one does indeed say it will happen, while still leaving open the possibility that it will not happen. This is the nature of the contingent: to predicate something contingently in the enunciation. But if someone simply predicts that something which may happen contingently will happen, he predicts that the contingent thing will happen necessarily. Therefore, even if what is said does happen, he is nevertheless lying: the thing happened contingently, whereas he had predicted that it would happen necessarily.

There are therefore four modes of truth and falsity in enunciations concerning things predicted in the future:

1. That what is said will happen and will not happen—that is, that both the affirmation and the negation are true;
2. That it will neither happen nor fail to happen—that is, that both the affirmation and the negation are false;
3. That it will happen or will not happen, with one determinately true and the other determinately false;
4. Or again, that it will happen or will not happen, with both indeterminate according to truth and falsity, each tending equally toward truth and falsehood.

He has already taught that it is impossible for both being and not being to occur, when he said: “For both will not occur together in such cases.” He has also taught, to some extent, that in contingent and future propositions it is impossible for either being or not being to be determinate. Now he adds that it is impossible to say that neither being nor not being is the case—that is, that it is impossible for both future propositions to be false.

If, then, both are not true, both are not false, and one is not determinately true while the other is determinately false, what remains is that one is true and the other false, but not determinately: they are either-way and unstable, so that one or the other must happen, while it is impossible for either one particular outcome or its opposite to occur as something necessary and determinate. He now begins to demonstrate that both cannot be false.

“But in truth it is not possible to say that neither is the case, as though one could say that neither will happen nor will fail to happen. For, first, if the affirmation is false, the negation will not be true; and if the negation is false, it is possible for the affirmation not to be true. Furthermore, if it is true to say that something is white and large, both must be the case. If it is true to say that there will be a naval battle tomorrow, then there must be a naval battle tomorrow. But if there will neither be nor fail to be a naval battle tomorrow, it will not be an either-way possibility, such as a naval battle; for there must neither be a naval battle nor fail to be one.”

The meaning of this argument is as follows: he says that it cannot be said that neither of the propositions concerning contingents is true in the future. But this is no different from saying that both are false, and this is impossible in contradictories. Both cannot be found false, for this is proper to contradictories: they avoid the property of contraries. Thus contradictory propositions, just as they avoid the property of subcontraries in that they cannot both be true at once, also avoid the property of contraries in that they are not found both false at once. They therefore have this proper nature: they are neither simultaneously false nor simultaneously true. Consequently, one of them is always true and the other always false.

It is therefore impossible that, when the negation is false, the affirmation should not be true; and again, when the affirmation is false, that the negation should not be true. Hence it is not possible to say that both are not true. He indicated this by saying: “But in truth it is not possible to say that neither is true”—that is, it is not possible for us to say, or it is impossible to say, that neither is true, namely, in the affirmations and negations proposed concerning contingents and future things.

Those who thought Aristotle held both future propositions to be false would never have fallen into such great errors if they had carefully read what he now says. For it is not the same to say “neither is true” as to say “neither is determinately true.” The statements “there will be a naval battle tomorrow” and “there will not be a naval battle tomorrow” are not said to be wholly false together, but rather neither is determinately true, nor is either one of them determinately false. One is true and the other false, but neither one is determinate; either may be so contingently.

He added something else, saying that, if the truth of propositions depends upon the substance of things, then whatever is true to say in propositions must necessarily be the case. If it is true to say that something will be white, the necessary occurrence of the thing follows upon the truth of the proposition. Thus, if someone says that a certain thing will be white tomorrow, and says this truly, it will necessarily be white tomorrow.

Therefore, if someone truly says that neither of the propositions uttered about the future is true, then what those propositions say and signify must neither be nor fail to be. For if both the affirmation and the negation are false, neither what the affirmation says can happen nor what the negation says; therefore, by necessity, neither occurs—neither what the affirmation says nor what the negation says.

Thus, if the affirmation says, “There will be a naval battle tomorrow,” and is false, there will not be a naval battle tomorrow. Again, if the negation denies this, saying, “There will not be a naval battle tomorrow,” and this too is false, there will be a naval battle tomorrow. Therefore there will neither be a naval battle, because the affirmation is false, nor fail to be a naval battle, because the negation is false.

But even one’s own mind cannot formulate such absurdity. For who has ever said that something necessarily neither is nor fails to be? This is what the person says who holds that both future propositions are false.

The absurd consequences are therefore these, together with others of the same kind: if, in every affirmation and negation—whether in propositions universally stated about universals or in propositions concerning singular things—it is necessary that of the opposing propositions one be true and the other false, then nothing among things that come to be will be an either-way possibility; everything will be and come to be by necessity.

Consequently, there will be no need either to deliberate or to undertake action, as in: “If we do this, that will happen; but if we do not do this, that will not happen.” For nothing prevents one person, a thousand years in advance, from saying that something will happen while another does not say so. Hence, whatever of these things it was then true to say will necessarily happen.

Those who think that all future propositions are determinately either true or false are led to this impossibility. Nothing can happen either through free choice of will, through some possibility, or by chance; everything is subject to necessity. Some have even not hesitated to say that everything exists by necessity, and have attempted by various arts to join what is in our power with the necessity of things.

Some of these are the Stoics. They say that everything that happens comes about by the necessity of fate, and that everything governed by the reasoning of fate undoubtedly occurs by necessity. But they say that only those things are in our power and arise from our will which are brought to completion and fulfillment through our will and through ourselves by the power of fate.

“For,” they say, “our will is not in our power. We will and refuse the same things, whatever the necessity of fate has commanded.” Thus our will too appears to depend upon fate. Since certain things happen through our will and therefore through us, and since the will itself is produced by the necessity of fate, the things that we do by our own will are done because necessity has commanded them; compelled by necessity, we do the things we do.

In this way, by altering the meaning of free choice, they attempt impossibly to join necessity with what is in our power. For what is in our power is free choice, free from every necessity, independent, and under its own authority. We are, in a certain way, masters of these things, whether to do them or not to do them. But if the necessity of our fate also commands our wills, then the will itself will not be in our power but in fate; nor will there be free choice, but rather servitude to necessity.

Hence those who bind all acts and events with necessity say that we do not even bend the knee unless fatal necessity has ordered it. Nor do we scratch our heads; hence neither do we wash or do anything else. To this I would add doing anything successfully or unsuccessfully, or undergoing anything. Thus they maintain that there is neither chance, nor free choice, nor any possibility in things. Yet, fearing to destroy free choice, they invent another meaning for it, through which human freedom is nonetheless overturned.

Aristotle’s authority, however, confirms that these things are established and present in reality in such a way that he does not now explain what chance is, what possibility is, or what is in our power; nor does he prove and demonstrate that these exist in reality. But it is so evident to him that these things exist in reality that he declares the opinion that all future enunciations are true to be impossible precisely because it overturns chance, possibility, and free choice.

He thinks these are so established in reality that no demonstration concerning them is needed. Any argument that attempts to overturn possibility, chance, or what is in our power is judged impossible. The truth has already shown how chance is destroyed by determinate truth in future propositions. Now he explains with the greatest force of argument how that same determinate truth of future and contingent propositions removes the capacity for free choice, saying that all such things would be impossible if someone imagined one part of an enunciation to be determinately true or false.

Following Porphyry, when we undertook the exposition of this discussion, we said that Aristotle had earlier spoken of singular and future propositions because the discussion would be easier to understand if these matters were first considered in singular propositions. After carefully prefacing his remarks about singular propositions, he now speaks about universals stated universally and about the contradictions that arise in them.

He says:

“If, in every affirmation and negation, whether in those universally stated about universals or in those concerning singular things, it is necessary that of the opposites one be true and the other false, and nothing among things that come to be be an either-way possibility, but everything be and come to be by necessity…”

Alexander thinks that Aristotle spoke about singular and future propositions as though he meant future things subject to generation and corruption. For there are some future things that are not subject to generation and corruption, such as what is predicated of the sun, the moon, and the other heavenly bodies. But among those things whose nature is to come into being and perish, it is not always necessary that one proposition be true and the other false.

I reject neither interpretation. Both are supported by very sound reasoning. The entire meaning, however, is this: Aristotle overturns the claim that necessity alone rules in things. Everything that exists by nature is not without purpose. Human beings naturally deliberate. But if necessity alone rules in things, deliberation is pointless. Yet deliberation is not pointless, and it exists by nature. Therefore, necessity cannot rule everything in things.

The order is as follows. “The inconvenient consequences,” he says, “are these and others of the same kind: first, chance as it exists in things is overturned; second, possibility and the will of free choice are lost.” He then follows by explaining how these consequences arise:

“If, in every affirmation and negation, whether in those universally stated about universals or in those concerning singular things, it is necessary that of the opposites one be true and the other false, and nothing among things that come to be be an either-way possibility, but everything be and come to be by necessity…”

Those inconveniences arise if every affirmation and negation is determinately true or false, whether in contradictions formed universally or in singular contradictions. For then nothing is an either-way possibility; everything occurs by necessity, because the event of things necessarily follows the truth and falsity of propositions.

Thus, as he himself says, there will be no need either to deliberate or to undertake action: “If we do this, that will happen; but if we do not do this, that will not happen.” Deliberation is overturned if it is pointless, and whoever posits only the necessity of fate in things says that deliberation is pointless. Why should anyone deliberate if nothing can be accomplished through what he deliberates, when necessity governs everything?

Therefore, there will be no need to deliberate; or, if someone deliberates, he ought not to undertake action. To undertake action means to do something actively and practically—not to make a profit, but to pursue some cause or activity. No one would accomplish anything through his action or deliberation unless the necessity of fate commanded it.

He explained what deliberation is through the words: “If we do this, that will happen; but if we do not do this, that will not happen.” For deliberation always proceeds in this way. Suppose Scipio is deliberating: “If I lead the army into Africa, I shall remove Hannibal’s devastation from Italy; but if I do not lead it, Italy will not be rescued.” This means: “If I do this”—that is, if I lead the army into Africa—“this will happen”—that is, Italy will be rescued; “but if I do not do this”—that is, if I remain here—“this will not happen”—that is, Italy will not be rescued. The same applies in all other matters.

At the same time, he showed that there is no necessity in deliberations. For he says: “If I do this, this will happen; and if I do not, this will not happen.” But if there were necessity in things, whether someone did this or did not do it, what had to happen would happen. Therefore, what occurs through deliberation does not occur through the violence of necessity.

He added to deliberation the word “undertake action,” and the order is as follows: “Therefore there will be no need either to deliberate—for if we do this, this will happen, but if we do not do this, this will not happen—nor to undertake action. Nothing prevents one person, a thousand years in advance, from saying that this will happen, while another does not say so. Therefore, whatever of these things it was then true to say will happen by necessity.”

Nor should one undertake action—that is, begin any activity or carry on any enterprise. Deliberation comes first and action afterward, but he placed action after deliberation and inserted after the discussion of action all the points that had to be added concerning the nature of deliberation.

The order is this: “If necessity governs everything, there is no need to deliberate, since if we do this, this will happen to us, but if we do not do this, it will not happen. For it is pointless for one person to say and another to deny: ‘If we do this, this will happen,’ or ‘this will not happen.’ Whatever is going to happen will happen, whether one person conjectures through deliberation that it can happen—even if he does something else—or another denies through deliberation that it can happen—even if he does what he said. For whatever either of them has said truly will happen by necessity.”

But if one ought not deliberate at all, neither ought one to undertake action—that is, begin any enterprise. Whether someone begins or does not begin, whatever is necessary will unquestionably happen. Therefore one person will differ in nothing from another. We judge people better because they are better in deliberation. But when deliberation is pointless because necessity does everything, human beings do not differ from one another either.

Deliberation itself makes no difference, whether it is good or bad, when the outcome rests upon the administration of fate’s necessity. Therefore, if people of good counsel deserve praise and people of bad counsel deserve blame, this can be just only if bad action and bad counsel, and conversely good action and good counsel, are in our power and not in fate. For when the outcome of a thing is not bound by necessity, then there is also free choice of will, so that it is not enslaved to fatal necessity.

Therefore we must accept neither those who have arranged the simple orders of things in this world by chance alone, nor those who, treating the structure of the world as unmixed, also assign unmixed causes to actions. For neither do those who say that everything happens by chance judge rightly, nor are those who imagine that everything occurs through the violence of necessity sound in their opinion. It is not evident that everything is by free choice either. Rather, the causes and outcomes of all these things are mixed.

Some things happen by chance; some by necessity; and we also see that certain things are governed by free judgment. The will of our actions is in our power. Our will is, in a certain way, mistress of our actions and of the ordering of our whole life. But the outcomes are not in our power in the same way.

For when we do something by free choice for one purpose, chance may intrude from the same causes. Thus, if someone digs a pit in order to plant a vine and finds a treasure, digging the pit arose from free choice, but finding the treasure was brought about by chance alone. Nevertheless, chance had as its cause the action produced by the will. For if he had not dug the pit, the treasure would not have been found.

Some outcomes, however, are available to our wills; others are obstructed by a kind of violent necessity. Eating lunch, reading, and other such activities arise from our will, and often their outcomes likewise depend upon our will. But if a Roman should now wish to rule the Persians, the choice of will is in his power, while a harsher necessity holds back this outcome and prevents it from being brought to completion.

Thus chance, will, and necessity govern all things. None of these should be posited as ruling everything; rather, their power is mixed. Hence the mind of those who do wrong is considered more than the outcome, and the mind is punished rather than the completion of the act, because the will is free in us, although at times the course toward completion is held back.

But if everything happened either by chance or by necessity, there would be neither fitting praise for those who act well, nor retribution for wrongdoers, nor any just laws that assigned rewards to the good or penalties to the bad.

I now come to the question that is raised in many ways: whether divination remains if not everything in reality occurs by necessity. What applies to true prediction also applies to knowledge. Just as, when someone predicts truly, what is truly predicted must be the case, so whatever someone knows will happen must happen.

But divination does not know all things in such a way as to pronounce that they will happen by necessity. For this reason it frequently predicts in the following manner, as can easily be recognized in the books of the ancients: “This will happen; but if this occurs, it will not happen”—as though it could be prevented and happen in another way. If this is so, it does not happen by necessity.

Let us ask the question this way: if God knows all future things, must everything happen by necessity? If someone says that God’s knowledge of future events follows the necessity of those events, then, if not everything occurs by necessity, he will be forced to conclude that God cannot know everything. For the necessity of events follows God’s knowledge; if there is no necessity of events, divine knowledge is destroyed. And who could be so tormented by an impious line of reasoning as to dare say this about God?

Perhaps someone will say that, since it is impossible for God not to know everything future, it follows that everything exists by necessity, because it is impious to remove from God his knowledge of future things. But whoever says this must consider that, while trying to make God know everything, he is asserting that God knows nothing.

If someone claims to know that the number two is odd, he does not know it; rather, he is ignorant. Likewise, it is not knowledge within one's power; rather, to think that one knows it is a sign of weakness. Whoever therefore says that God knows everything and that, for this reason, everything will happen by necessity, says that God believes by necessity that everything will happen, including things that do not happen by necessity.

For if God knows that everything will happen by necessity, he is mistaken in his knowledge; not everything happens by necessity, but some things happen contingently. Therefore, if he knows that things which will happen contingently will happen by necessity, he is mistaken in his own providence.

God knows future things not as events that will occur by necessity, but as events that will occur contingently; he does not fail to know that something else could happen, while nevertheless discerning what does happen from the reasoning of the human beings and actions involved.

Therefore, if someone says that everything happens by necessity, he must also deprive God of benevolence. For his goodness produces nothing if necessity governs everything, so that God’s own doing good would in a certain way be by necessity and not by his own will. But if some things happen by his will, so that he is not confined by any necessity, then not everything happens by necessity.

Who, then, would be so impiously wise as to bind God himself with necessity? If someone says that everything happens by necessity, this further impossibility will also follow. We must therefore posit that some things in reality can happen by chance, some are effected by will, and some are bound by necessity. An argument that overturns any of these must be judged impossible.

Aristotle therefore does not unfairly lead the argument to impossibility when he says that possibility, chance, and free choice perish if one proposition among all future enunciations is always determinately true and the other always determinately false. For necessity follows from their truth and falsity, and this removes chance and free choice from reality.

Thus he now repeats the same point, saying that it makes no difference whether someone said a thousand years earlier that something would happen or someone else denied it. Things do not come to be or fail to come to be because someone says or denies them. But if it is necessary that events follow the person who says or denies them, then the things affirmed or denied will follow even if those persons do not say what, once they had said it, had to happen. They must happen even without anyone saying it. He puts it this way:

“But in truth it makes no difference whether someone has uttered the contradiction or has not uttered it. For it is evident that things are disposed in this way even if one person has not affirmed while another has denied. It will not be or fail to be because of denying or affirming, nor more in a thousand years than at any other time. Therefore, if throughout all time things were so disposed that one statement was spoken truly, it was necessary for this to happen; and each of the things that happen was always so disposed that it would happen by necessity. For when someone truly says that something will happen, it cannot fail to happen; and of what has happened, it was always true to say that it would happen. But if these consequences are impossible, we see that there is a beginning of future things, and that from what we deliberate and do, something comes about.”

Aristotle considers the outcome of things as necessary not from the truth of those who make predictions, but from the nature of the things themselves. He says that, although it is necessary that, whenever someone has truly predicted something, the thing he previously announced should come to pass, nevertheless the necessity of things does not depend on the truth of the prediction; rather, the truth of divination is assessed from the necessity of the things. It is not necessary for something to exist because something true has been predicted; rather, because it was necessarily going to happen, something true could therefore be predicted about it. If this is so, the one who predicts that something will happen, or denies it, is not the cause of its happening or not happening. Things are not necessary because of an affirmation or denial; rather, those things that are going to happen are necessary because they possess a certain necessity in their own nature, and whoever encounters that necessity makes a true prediction.

[Col. 0508B] Therefore, whatever things have now happened, it would have been true to say of them that they would happen, whether he had said so or not. Whatever things have now happened were necessarily going to happen. Necessity in things does not arise because someone says or denies something; rather, truth or falsity is found in an utterance because of the necessity of things. Thus, if even those things that have now happened could truly have been predicted as going to happen, and if, once this had been posited, the thing necessarily had to occur whether he predicted it or not, then everything that happens must necessarily be going to happen, and nothing at all in things is contingent either way. For if prediction contributes nothing to the necessity of things, and if it makes no difference whether someone predicts that something will happen or denies it,

[Col. 0508C] or whether no one predicts anything at all, either affirmatively or negatively, it is clear that there is no difference concerning the matter itself. For whether someone truly predicted long beforehand that something would happen, or did so a few days, hours, or moments beforehand, makes no difference. Whether someone predicted a thousand years beforehand what was necessarily going to happen, or a year, a month, a day, an hour, or a moment beforehand, would not alter the necessity of the thing that was going to happen. What difference would it make whether it was predicted or not? None. Nor does it matter whether it is predicted near the event or farther away.

If these things are so, and everything that has happened necessarily had to have been going to happen, all free choice perishes, all chance is abolished, and every possibility in things is excluded by necessity.

[Col. 0508D] At the same time, Aristotle confirms the necessity of things from the truth of the proposition itself, joining together the prediction and the contingent outcome. He says: “If things were so disposed that, at every time, each thing that happened was such that it could truly be predicted, it would necessarily happen”—that is, what was truly predicted would necessarily occur. For everything that happens and is truly predicted is so disposed that it exists by necessity.

The reason for this is that whatever someone says truly must happen. That truth is generated from the necessity of things. If, then, what has happened had also been truthfully announced as going to happen, there could be no doubt that everything arises by necessity. But if this is impossible, he says,

[Col. 0509A] for we see that certain things descend from the principle of free choice and from the source of our actions, why do we hesitate to exclude the frivolous argument for the necessity of all things and not to abolish the choice inherent in human life through the intervention of necessity? For what distinction would remain among human beings if the judgment of free choice perished? Why, finally, were laws enacted? Why the statutes of the state? Why legal opinions? Why institutions? Why are public customs and private actions held within the provisions of rulers and the bonds of judgments, if it is certain that nothing is permitted to human purposes? All these things are pointless if free choice does not exist, for we know that laws and the rest were established to restrain human minds.

If minds do not govern themselves, and some force of necessity drives them,

[Col. 0509B] there is no doubt that these laws are empty, since they are proposed to people who do nothing voluntarily.

But Aristotle himself proves how impossible these consequences are. His sound judgment removes neither chance, nor necessity, nor possibility in either direction of nature, nor free choice. Rather, combining all these elements, he holds that the world is composed of many things and is not governed simply by chance, or by necessity, or by the judgment of free will.

“If these things are impossible—for we see that there is a principle of future events, and that something proceeds from what we deliberate and do—”

These claims, he says, are impossible: that everything should arise by necessity. We ourselves are also principles of certain things, and our mind, formed by reason, and our actions, directed by reason, possess the principle of certain things.

[Col. 0509C] This is what is meant by saying that what is within us is disposed in a certain way: when nothing outside us prevents or compels us, we spring toward what appears right to us according to the judgment of reason.

Not everything, therefore, should be taken away by necessity. For the whole class of animals, insofar as they are animals, is subject to various things: some to nature, some to the courses of the heavenly stars, and some also to the reason and thought of mind and spirit. Trees and certain irrational animals are subject only to nature. Brute animals, because they do not possess free choice, are also subject to the decrees of the heavenly bodies. Human beings, however, are subject to nature, to the stars, and to their own will.

Many things we do or suffer under the dominance of nature, such as death or some similar bodily condition. Many things are also drawn along by the necessity inherent in the things themselves, such as those things that, although we wish to do them, we are nevertheless unable to do.

[Col. 0509D] But free choice of the will grants us many things that happen when we wish them to happen and would not happen unless we wished them. Hence nature, which is the principle of motion, participates both in the power of free choice and in the reason of the mind.

The soul, however, as though bound to bodies over which nature rules, participates in that nature to which it is bound through images, desires, the heat of anger, and the other things that bodies bring with them. Yet all things are subject to divine providence, and from the will of the divine beings we too depend upon that providence. Thus this discussion neither completely overturns the necessity of the heavenly bodies, nor removes chance from things, nor fails to strengthen free choice. But these matters are greater than can suitably be treated at present.

[Col. 0510A] We, therefore, are also principles of things, and many things in the world depend upon our deliberations and actions.

If the considerations brought forward by this reasoning are clear, while the proposition that every affirmation and denial concerning the future is true is not equally clear, why do we hesitate to evade the deceptive path of argument and to hold to what is both true and evident, rejecting what is supported by no truth and does not clearly appear?

Since he had already asked above why there should be no deliberating or conducting business, he now gives the answer to the statement that there should be no deliberating, saying that we are a principle of future events.
