And to the statement that there should be no conducting of business, he gives as his answer what he added: “and that we do something.” Thus the discourse has been compressed with such brevity

[Col. 0510B] that the necessity of its reasoning and order is contained within it.

And since, in the case of things that are not always actual, it is altogether possible both to be and not to be in the same way—things in which both alternatives occur, being and not being—therefore it is possible both to happen and not to happen. Many things are evident to us as being so disposed. For example, it is possible for this garment to be cut and yet not be cut, but to wear out first; and likewise it is possible for it not to be cut. For it would not be possible for it to wear out first unless it were possible for it not to be cut.

The same applies to other things that come into being and are spoken of according to this kind of potentiality. It is therefore clear that not everything either is or comes to be by necessity. Some things are contingent in either direction, and affirmation is no more true than negation. Other things occur more often and in most cases in one way, yet it remains possible for the other way to occur, while the contrary outcome occurs hardly at all.

[Col. 0510C] The continuous sense, connected with what precedes, is as follows. Above he said that, if these things were impossible—that is, if necessity governed everything—we nevertheless see that there is some principle of future events in us and in our actions and deliberations. To this he adds that there are certain things that are possible to be when they are not, and possible not to be when they are. These things would all be removed at once if necessity ruled everything. The sense is therefore joined to what precedes in this way.

The whole meaning of the argument should be understood as follows. Something is called possible when, by reason of its own nature, it can readily turn in either direction: when it does not exist, it can exist, and when it exists, nothing prevents it from not existing. In this way, therefore, we distinguish what we call possible from what is necessary.

[Col. 0510D] For it is one thing to say that it is possible for me to walk while I am sitting, and another to say that it is possible for the sun now to be in Sagittarius and, after a few days, to pass into Aquarius. In the latter case, the possibility is such that the event must also occur. We ordinarily call something possible when, while it does not exist, it can exist, and when it does exist, it can again not exist. If, then, someone subjects everything to necessity, he destroys the nature of possibility.

There are therefore three doctrines concerning possibility. Philo says that something is possible when the nature of the proposition itself can receive truth—for example, when I say that I shall reread Theocritus’ *Bucolics* today. If nothing external prevents it, this can, so far as it depends on itself, be truthfully predicted.

In the same way, Philo defines the necessary as that which, when true, cannot, so far as it depends on itself,

[Col. 0511A] ever be capable of falsehood. He defines the non-necessary as that which, so far as it depends on itself, can receive falsity. The impossible, according to its own nature, can never receive truth.

Philo also affirms that the contingent and the possible are one and the same. Diodorus defines the possible as what either is or will be; the impossible as what, being false, will not become true; the necessary as what, being true, will not become false; and the non-necessary as what either already is or will be false.

The Stoics, however, defined as possible what is capable of receiving a true predication, provided that nothing prevents it externally, although things that occur together with it may also come about along with it. The impossible is what can never receive truth because other things external to its outcome prevent it.

[Col. 0511B] The necessary is what, once true, cannot by any means receive a false predication.

But if everything happens by necessity, one must without hesitation adopt Diodorus’ incorrect doctrine. He held that, if someone died at sea, it had been impossible for him to die on land, a position that neither Philo nor the Stoics maintain. Yet although they do not say this, if they measure one side of a contradiction by the outcome of necessity, they are forced to agree with Diodorus.

For if someone has died at sea, it was necessary for him to die at sea; it was impossible for him to suffer death on land. But this is utterly false. They are consequently forced to accept all these impossibilities. For whoever definitely maintains that one side of a future contradiction is true introduces necessity alone into things.

[Col. 0511C] If someone perished in a shipwreck at sea, it does not follow that, if he had never sailed, he would have remained immortal on land.

Rather, the contradictions in propositions must be judged not from the outcome of things but from the nature of the things that receive those outcomes. If everything is now available to me for going to Athens, it is clear that, even if I do not go, I am nevertheless able to go; and once I have gone, it was possible for me not to go. This too is beyond doubt among those who correctly judge outcomes according to the nature of things.

What is possible, therefore, is not the same as what is necessary. Although what is necessary is possible, there is nevertheless another nature of possibility, external to it, which is distinct both from the impossible and from the necessary.

[Col. 0511D] Aristotle, holding this view concerning things that must always be necessary, believes that they have no affinity with contraries. Snow, for example, because it is always cold, is never associated with heat. Fire likewise is never akin to cold, since it always exists in the opposition of cold—that is, in heat.

Everything that is necessary, therefore, has no affinity with the contrary quality that it itself possesses. If fire had any affinity with cold, that affinity would be pointless, since fire never changes into the quality of cold. Yet we know that nature does not ordinarily perfect anything that has been born with a proper nature pointlessly.

Those things, then, are necessary that have no affinity with contraries; those things that do have such an affinity are not necessary. But since things appear to be joined by a certain natural affinity to both sides of a contrariety,

[Col. 0512A] their outcomes are possible in both directions. This piece of wood, for example, can be cut, but it nevertheless has an affinity with the contrary possibility, for it can also not be cut.

Water can become hot, but nothing prevents it from also being associated with cold. In general, whatever is neither always nor always not, but is sometimes and is sometimes not, has, precisely because it is and is not, some affinity with contraries.

Such things lie between the impossible and the necessary. The impossible can never be; the necessary can never not be. Between them is the proper nature of certain things, which is intermediate between both: it can be and can not be.

This, then, is what he now says: “We see,” he says, “that among things that are not always actual there are some that are possible both to be and not to be.” Those things are not always actual that have an affinity with both contraries. Fire is always actually hot, whereas water is not always so.

Accordingly, we see that among things that are not always actual there are certain possibilities both to be and not to be—that is, possibilities both to exist and not to exist. This occurs in things in which both alternatives are possible: being and not being. Thus water can be hot and can not be hot; it can become hot and can not become hot.

Many things are also evident to us as being so disposed that their outcome can turn in either direction without any impediment from anything. For example, a garment can be cut, but it may happen that it is not divided by iron before old age wears it out. It can also happen that any garment wears away gradually through use rather than being cut by iron.

[Col. 0512C] Likewise, it is possible not only for it to be cut, but for it to wear out before being cut. For it would not be possible for it not to be cut unless it were previously possible for it to wear out. When it wears out, it is not cut.

He shows that this occurs universally among things that come into being. “It occurs,” he says, “in things that are to be made.” Things to be made are all those in which there is generation and corruption. Whether something is produced by nature or by art, he calls it a thing to be made because it proceeds from making.

Among such things, then, some exist in potentiality and others in actuality. Water, for example, is hot in potentiality: it can become hot, while it is cold in actuality. It is actually cold, and the fact that the same thing can be actual and potential comes from matter.

For since matter is receptive of contrariety, and contains within itself an affinity with both contraries, when considered in itself it possesses none of the things that it receives, and is itself nothing in actuality, though everything in potentiality.

When it receives contraries, although it possesses one contrariety, it also possesses the other at the same time, though not in actuality. This is the case with the same water: its matter is receptive both of heat and of cold. When it has received either of them—heat or cold—it is, if circumstances so require, hot, and at the same time cold, though not in the same way. For perhaps it is actually hot and potentially cold.

[Col. 0512D] What exists in potentiality in things, therefore, comes from matter. Otherwise, divine bodies would have nothing at all in potentiality, but everything would be in actuality. The sun, for example, never has light potentially, but actually; nor does it have any darkness potentially. Nor is there rest anywhere throughout the whole heaven.

Things are therefore so disposed through matter that, taken in themselves, they are all in potentiality and none in actuality. But the nature present in matter distributes individual motions according to their proper proportions and assigns the particular properties of qualities to the individual parts of matter.

Nature has arranged some qualities as necessary, so that, as long as a thing remains what it is, the property remains in it—for example, heat in fire. As long as fire exists, it must be hot.

To other things, however, nature has attached qualities of which they can be deprived. The necessary quality forms the substance of each thing, for that quality is naturally joined to its matter. The other qualities are external: they may be admitted or not admitted. From this arise generation and corruption.

[Col. 0513B] From nature and matter, therefore, comes the possibility present in things. Along with this possibility, chance sometimes enters. Chance is an undetermined cause that falls without any reason; it is not nature, for nature accomplishes nothing in vain.

Nor is chance the free choice that consists in judgment and reason. Chance is external: because of another event, it suddenly and unexpectedly arises from certain things that have happened.

From this possibility of either alternative also arises the rational basis of free choice. For if it were not possible for something to happen, but everything either existed by necessity or by necessity did not exist, free choice would not remain.

Aristotle therefore rightly did not propose that everything occurs by chance, as Epicurus held, nor that everything occurs by necessity, as the Stoic held, nor again that everything happens by free choice. Rather, combining everything, he proposed that in a mixed world there are also mixed causes of things: some things occur by necessity, others by chance, others by free choice, and still others by possibility.

All these have one common name: “either way,” whether in chance, in will, or in possibility. But he divides them into classes.

[Col. 0513C] Of things that are “either way,” some are equally disposed toward affirmation and denial. For example, I may read Virgil today, and I may not read him. In either way, both alternatives are possible. This is what he means by saying that affirmation is no more true than negation. I can equally read Virgil now and not read him.

Others are not equally disposed. Although one outcome occurs more frequently in a given matter, it is not thereby prevented from occurring in the other way. For example, a human being’s hair turns gray in old age. This happens in most cases, but the other outcome can occur as well—that is, a person may not turn gray. The remaining phrase, “alterum vero minime, id est ut canescat” (“the other, however, least of all—namely, that he turns gray”), is textually unclear.

Thus, by the strongest and most compelling argument, he establishes that, in the case of possibility, chance, and free choice, a contradiction concerning the future is not definitely true or false on one side.

To this he adds the following:

“Therefore it is necessary that what is, when it is, should be; and that what is not, when it is not, should not be. But not everything that is must necessarily be, nor must everything that is not necessarily not be.

[Col. 0514A] For it is not the same for everything that is to be necessarily what it is when it is, and for it simply to exist by necessity. The same applies to what is not.”

Two modes of necessity are indicated. One is proposed together with the necessity of some accident; the other is expressed by a simple predication.

For example, when we say, “It is necessary for the sun to move,” we do not mean that the sun must move because it is moving now; rather, necessity enters into the sun’s motion because it will never not move.

The other kind, which is stated conditionally, is expressed as follows: “Socrates must be sitting when he is sitting,” and “Socrates must not be sitting when he is not sitting.” Since the same person cannot simultaneously sit and not sit, whoever is sitting cannot not be sitting at the time when he is sitting. Therefore, at the time when someone is sitting, he must be sitting; for it is impossible that, while he is sitting, he should not be sitting.

Again, when someone is not sitting, then, while he is not sitting, he must not be sitting. The same person cannot sit and not sit. Thus this conditional necessity is possible: when someone is sitting, then, while he is sitting, he sits necessarily; and when he is not sitting, then, while he is not sitting, he necessarily does not sit.

[Col. 0514B] But this necessity, which is proposed conditionally, does not carry simple necessity along with it. It is not simply necessary for everyone who is sitting to sit; rather, it is necessary with the added qualification “when he is sitting.”

When we say that the sun must move, we do not add “when it is moving.” We simply say, “The sun must move,” and this simple necessity concerning the sun completes the truth of the statement.

But in the conditional statement, “Socrates must be sitting when he is sitting,” if we remove the temporal condition “when he is sitting” from the proposition, the truth of the whole proposition disappears.

We cannot say that Socrates sits by necessity. He may also not sit. Socrates has a certain capacity and affinity both for sitting and for not sitting.

[Col. 0514C] Therefore, when we say that Socrates sits necessarily when he is sitting, we propose this with reference to an accident. When sitting happens to Socrates, then, at the time when it happens, it cannot not have happened to him. Otherwise the same thing would happen and not happen to the same person at the same time, which is impossible.

Accordingly, by attending to the accident, we say, “Socrates must be sitting,” but not simply so; rather, we add “when he is sitting.”

Just as it is false to say simply that an Ethiopian is white, although it is true that he is white in some respect—for there is whiteness in his eyes and teeth—so it is also false to say simply that Socrates must be sitting. It is true, however, to assign this necessity to some particular respect and not to predicate it simply, by saying “when he is sitting.”

Just as we say of the sun that it must simply move, so, if we say simply that Socrates must sit, the statement is false. But if we say of a marble statue of Socrates that it must sit—if, perhaps, it was formed in a sitting posture—the statement is true, and necessity can be predicated simply of such a Socrates. But such necessity cannot be predicated simply of Socrates himself.

[Col. 0514D] For it cannot be the case that Socrates must sit by necessity—except perhaps when he is sitting. At that time, because he is sitting and cannot not be sitting, he sits necessarily. Otherwise he sits simply and not necessarily, but contingently, since he can stand up.

What exists simply by necessity cannot alter that necessity. Since it is simply necessary for the sun to move, the sun cannot in any way stand still.

This, then, is what Aristotle says: everything that is, when it is, and everything that is not, when it is not, exists or does not exist conditionally and necessarily; but it does not exist or not exist simply and without condition.

Such simple necessity belongs only to those things that have no power or affinity toward opposites—for example, the sun in relation to rest, or fire in relation to cold.

[Col. 0515A] Aristotle says that it is not the same for something to exist necessarily when it exists conditionally, or not to exist when it does not exist, as it is to say simply that everything exists or does not exist by necessity.

In the first case, the condition makes the statement true; in the second, the nature of simplicity produces the truth.

The same applies, he says, to what is not. Not everything that is not must necessarily not be; rather, when it is not, it must not be, and here too this is conditional, not simple.

Having thus demonstrated two kinds of necessity—one conditional and the other simple—he returns again to the contradiction concerning the contingent future.

“And the same account applies to contradiction. Everything must either be or not be, and must either be going to be or not be going to be. Yet one must not say, by dividing the alternatives, that one is necessary.

[Col. 0515B] I mean, for example, that it is necessary either that there will be a naval battle tomorrow or that there will not be one, but it is not necessary either that there will be a naval battle tomorrow or that there will not be one. It is necessary that it either will be or will not be.”

He explained very clearly what position should be held concerning contingent and future propositions. He said that, in these cases, the entire contradiction has one side or the other true and the other false, but not in such a way that someone can divide the alternatives and answer that one is necessarily true and the other necessarily false.

For example, in the statements “The sun will set today” and “The sun will not set today,” someone might easily divide the alternatives and say that it is necessarily true that the sun will set today and necessarily false that it will not set.

[Col. 0515C] The nature and condition of the divine bodies are such that they have no affinity with opposites. Therefore, either what they are is so by necessity, or what they are not is necessarily not so.

Things that are subject to generation and corruption, however, are not like this. Precisely because they are generated and corrupted, they have an affinity with opposites. Therefore, in their case one may not take one side of a contradiction and declare it necessary, while proposing that the other necessarily does not exist.

Although one side of the whole contradiction is true and the other false, it is not known or determined to us which is which. The nature of the things proposed is uncertain. Thus, in the proposition “Socrates will read today” and “Socrates will not read today,” one side of the entire contradiction is true and the other false,

[Col. 0516A] for he will either read or not read; and this is evident in a confused way from the whole statement. But no one can divide the alternatives and answer either that it is true that he will read or that it is true that he will not read.

This is not because we, as listeners, are ignorant of future events, but because the same thing can both be and not be. Otherwise, if this resulted from our knowledge rather than from the variable and undetermined outcome of the things themselves, the impossibility would arise again that necessity governs everything.

What is necessary will not happen because of our knowledge. Even if we do not know, the outcome of the thing will nevertheless be fixed, and it will necessarily and indubitably be going to happen.

Since this cannot be so, and since there are certain things that do not arise by necessity but contingently, in these cases, although truth or falsity is found in either side of the whole contradiction, it is not possible for someone to divide the alternatives and say that one is true and the other false.

[Col. 0516B] He demonstrated this with the following example: “It is necessary that a naval battle will take place tomorrow or will not take place, but it will not necessarily take place tomorrow, nor will it necessarily not take place tomorrow.”

It cannot be possible for someone to divide the alternatives and make a definite prediction, saying, “It will happen tomorrow,” in such a way that this is truly said and occurs as a determinate outcome; or again, “It will not happen tomorrow,” in such a way that this likewise comes to pass.

Rather, only indeterminately is one side of the contradiction true and the other false—whichever side will in fact occur. The outcomes themselves are undetermined, and either one or the other may happen.

This is because the outcome of things does not depend upon certain earlier causes, as though there were a kind of chain of necessity. Rather, such things depend upon our judgment and free will, and in them there is no necessity.

[Col. 0516C] “But if,” he says, “statements are true in the same way as things are,” he has taken this from Plato, who said that statements correspond to things and are in some way related to them in their signification. If things are unchangeable and remain stable according to reason, the statement about them would also be true and necessary. But if a thing, because of the variability of its nature, never remained constant, there would likewise be no fixed truth in statements, and no demonstration would arise through such statements.

Taking this as excellently expressed, Aristotle says:

“Therefore, since statements are true in the same way as things are, it is clear that, whatever things are so disposed that either alternative may occur and their contraries may come about, the contradiction concerning them must likewise be so disposed. This occurs in things that are not always and are not always not.”

[Col. 0516D] Since, he says, statements are disposed in the same way as things, it is clear that, whatever things are so constituted that either alternative may occur and their contraries may come about, the contradiction concerning them must also be so constituted. This applies to the unstable and undetermined things of that nature.

If things have uncertain and undetermined outcomes, the contradiction made concerning those things must likewise have a variable and undetermined outcome.

What things are of this kind, whose outcomes are variable and undetermined, he demonstrated very clearly by saying that this occurs in things that are not always and are not always not.

[Col. 0517A] These are the things in which either alternative may occur. They are not always, since they can be destroyed; nor are they always not, since they can be generated and come into being.

These things have an affinity with opposites, as the outcome itself demonstrates in the proper substance of the things. Being and not being are opposites. What was not, when it is generated and comes into being, arises from what was not. It therefore has an affinity with being and not being—that is, with opposites.

If the very thing that exists is destroyed, it will not exist from what previously existed. It will therefore again have an affinity with opposites.

Thus, just as the outcome of things subject to generation and corruption is undetermined, so also are the sides of the contradictions concerning them, although one side of the entire contradiction is true and the other false. Which of these is true and which false is undetermined and undiscriminated.

“For of these it is necessary that one side of the contradiction should be true or false. Yet not this particular side or that, but either alternative; one is more often true, but not already definitely true or false. Therefore it is clear that it is not necessary for every affirmation and denial among opposites that one should be true and the other false.”

[Col. 0517C] Above he taught that, in matters where either alternative is possible, one side of the contradiction is not definitely true and the other definitely false. Now he draws an argument from what happens more frequently and what happens more rarely.

For above he showed that there are certain things that occur more frequently, yet it is not ruled out that their opposites may sometimes occur. The opposites can occur, though more rarely and less frequently.

Therefore, if, among things that occur in most cases, it is not necessary that one side be true and the other false, then, when someone says that a human being’s hair turns gray in old age and asserts that this happens by necessity, he will be lying. For it is also possible not to turn gray.

[Col. 0517D] If, then, in cases where one outcome occurs more frequently and the other more rarely, one side is not definitely true and the other definitely false, much less is this so where the outcomes of the opposites are equal. It is true to say that one outcome occurs more frequently, but it is not true to say that, because it occurs in this way, the opposite does not occur at all, even if more rarely.

[Col. 0518A] If, then, even in matters predicated of what happens in most cases one side is not definitely true and the other false, and still less in matters whose outcomes occur with equal and undetermined frequency, it is clear that, in future and contingent propositions, one side is not true and the other false.

This is what he argued at the beginning, in order to demonstrate it by the strongest argument:

“For things are not disposed in the same way in the case of what is as they are in the case of what is not, although it is possible for it to be or not to be, but in the way that has been stated.”

It refers the whole question back to the division of times made at the beginning. For he says that those propositions which are formed are predicated either in the present, or in the future, or in the past; and that those which are spoken of the past or the present possess determinate truth or falsity, whether they are spoken of eternal and divine things or of things coming into being [Col. 0518B] and passing away, in which either outcome may occur, so that they have a relation to opposites. In the case of future things, however, if someone were speaking of divine and immutable matters, he would likewise determine one to be true and the other false. For natures of this kind have no relation to opposites. But in the case of things subject to generation and destruction, when future events are predicated either affirmatively or negatively, the mode of truth is not determinate in the same way: one part of the entire contradiction is true and the other false, but it is by no means possible to determine one definitely as true and the other definitely as false.

[Col. 0518C] Here, however, he did not posit both times—namely, the present and the past—but only the present. For he said: “Nor does it stand in the same way in the case of things that are,” that is, in the case of things that are present. When he says “in the case of things that are not, but are nevertheless capable of being,” he is speaking of future things, which, although they do not yet exist, can exist. For a proposition stated in the present does not stand in the same way as one stated in the future, namely, in the case of things in which either outcome is possible and which belong to generation and destruction. In the former—in the present and past—one is definitely true and the other false. In the latter—in the future and contingent—the truth and falsity of propositions are not confined by any determination. [Col. 0518D] But since we have explained Aristotle’s view of future propositions as carefully as our ability allowed, let us now bring the length of the volume to an end.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0517]

[Col. 0517D] The sequence of this book—which among the Latins is entitled *On Interpretation*, but among the Greeks Περὶ ἐρμηνείας (*On Interpretation*)—is obscure in its expression, and obscure judgments have been added to it. For that reason I would not have unfolded it in such large volumes, unless, yielding nothing to the labor involved, I had wished in a second commentary to complete as plainly as possible what I had omitted concerning its profundity and subtlety in the first edition. Yet indulgence must be granted to its length, and the size of the work must be weighed against the obscurity of the book. Even so, there are stages in our work that satisfy both the reader’s diligence [Col. 0518D] and the eagerness of one who wishes to learn great matters with the greatest ease. After these two commentaries we shall produce a kind of abridgment of this book, using Aristotle’s own words in some passages and almost everywhere, except that what he expressed obscurely through brevity we shall make into a smoother sequence by adding a few words. Thus, as though between the brevity of the text and the diffuseness of the commentary, a style midway between them will proceed: gathering together what has been stated diffusely and expanding what has been written with extreme compression. But that will come later.

[Col. 0519A] Now, since Aristotle has shown above that in future contingent propositions truth and falsity are not divided by any fixed or determinate rule, and since he has embraced whatever was included above in an extremely extensive discussion, his present purpose is to set forth the number of categorical propositions—namely, all those which are formed with a finite or an infinite name. For in the first book it was said that a name is, for example, “man,” while an infinite name is “not-man.” Predicative, or categorical, propositions are those which consist of only two simple terms. They may be formed with a finite name, as in “man walks,” or with an infinite name, as in “not-man walks.” He therefore endeavors to give the number of these categorical and simple propositions, namely, all those formed by the addition of an infinite name.

[Col. 0519B] Since all propositions differ either according to quality or according to quantity: according to quality, because one is affirmative and another negative; according to quantity, because one embraces more and another fewer. By this distinction the propositions “man walks” and “not-man walks” differ from one another either according to quantity or according to quality.

For when I say “man walks,” I designate a certain quality of substance—that is, I designate man as walking—and a determinate thing and substance which declares that one species is capable of walking. But when I say “not-man walks,” I remove man as a determinate thing and signify innumerable other things. [Col. 0519C] Thus the proposition “man walks” seems to differ according to quality, whereas “not-man walks” seems rather to differ according to quantity.

Or perhaps the following is more correct: “man walks” has the simple name “man,” which is close to an affirmation, whereas “not-man walks” has the infinite name “not-man,” which seems analogous to a negation. But affirmation and negation differ according to quality, and these are analogous to an affirmation and a negation. They therefore differ more according to quality than according to any quantity.

Or perhaps the following is more correct still: just as the proposition “Socrates walks” stands in relation to “some man walks,” so “man walks” stands in relation to “not-man walks.” For if several people are walking, “some man walks” must be true. But if several are walking, it does not follow that Socrates is walking. Several may be walking while Socrates is not.

[Col. 0519D] When several are walking, therefore, “some man walks” is true. This happens because in saying “some man walks” we join particularity to universality—that is, to “man.” If any of those included under the universal, that is, under “man,” are walking, the proposition “some man walks” must be true. But when it is said “Socrates walks,” since “Socrates” concerns the property of one particular individual, unless Socrates himself has walked, it is not true to say “Socrates walks,” even if all human beings are walking.

Thus, just as “some man walks” is definitely true if several people are walking, whereas “Socrates walks” is not true unless Socrates himself is walking, so too in the case of “man” and “not-man.” The person who says “man walks” says that a certain animal walks, and determines this by the name and quality, saying “man walks.” But the person who says “not-man walks” does not overthrow everything, but only man; he declares that the remaining animals are capable of walking. Therefore, whether it is a horse, an ox, or a lion that walks, “not-man walks” is true; but “man walks” is not true if man himself is not walking.

[Col. 0520A] Thus, just as “some man walks” stands in relation to “Socrates walks”—in the former case, if several men were walking, “some man walks” would be true, while “Socrates walks” would not be true unless Socrates himself were walking—so also the same may be said of “man walks” and “not-man walks.” [Col. 0520B] For if several non-men are walking, it is true to say “not-man walks,” but it is not true to say “man walks” unless man himself is walking.

[Col. 0520C] They therefore seem to differ more according to definition and property than according to any whole quantity, any part of a quantity, or, again, any quality. For, as will be demonstrated later, the proposition “not-man walks” is an affirmation rather than a negation. Let this much have been said for the present.

## ON INFINITE ENUNCIATIONS

Since an affirmation is a statement signifying something concerning something, and this something is either a name or an unnamed expression, there must be one thing, and the affirmation must be about one thing. A name and an unnamed expression were mentioned earlier. For “not-man” is not, strictly speaking, a name, but an infinite name. In a certain way an infinite name signifies one thing. Likewise, “does not run” is not, strictly speaking, a verb, but an infinite verb.

Every affirmation and negation will therefore be formed either from a name and a verb, or from an infinite name and a verb. Apart from a verb there is no affirmation or negation. For “is,” “will be,” “was,” “comes to be,” and all other verbs of this kind belong among those that have been posited; they co-signify time. Thus the first affirmation and negation will be:

- “Man is.”
- “Man is not.”
- “Not-man is.”
- “Not-man is not.”

Again:

- “Every man is.”
- “Every man is not.”
- “Every not-man is.”
- “Every not-man is not.”

The same arrangement applies in the other times as well.

[Col. 0520D] In the second book, as I think, we stated beforehand that every simple enunciation—that is, every predicative proposition—consists of a subject and a predicate. Of these, the predicate would always be either a verb or something that could perform the same function, as if a verbal expression were supplied. Thus, when we say “man walks,” a verb is present; but when we say “man rational,” the verb “is” is understood, so that the complete meaning is “man is rational.” It is therefore necessary that the predicate always be either a verb or something analogous to a verb and capable of functioning in enunciations.

The subject, on the other hand, would either be altogether a name or something serving in place of a name. Consequently, this must be especially gathered: in every categorical proposition the subject is a name, while the predicate is a verb.

[Col. 0521A] But when he was discussing the name, he introduced another sort of name—one that was not a name simply and in itself, but was called an infinite name, namely, that which is expressed with the negative particle. Every proposition consists of the subjection of a name. A categorical proposition is one that either predicates or denies something of something, and that of which it predicates is a name. Since an infinite name is also sometimes called a name, every categorical proposition must always have as its subject either a name or what is called an infinite name. An infinite name is what he now calls an unnamed expression.

Every predicative proposition is therefore divided into two species. Its subject is either an infinite name, as when I say “not-man walks,” or a simple and finite name, as in “man walks.” The proposition formed from a finite and simple name has two species: it either places a universal name as subject, as in “man walks,” or a singular name, as in “Socrates walks.”

[Col. 0521B] The division is therefore as follows. Of all simple enunciations consisting of two terms, some have an infinite name as subject, while others have a finite and simple name. Of those that have a simple subject, some have a simple universal as subject, while others have a singular. Above he taught what the differences are among propositions that place a simple name in the subject: some are universal, some particular, and some indefinite; and according to quantity they differ in this way. According to quality, however, some are affirmative and others negative.

[Col. 0521C] The same applies to propositions enunciated with an infinite name as subject. Some of these are indefinite and others definite. Among the definite, some are universal and others particular. Here too they differ according to quantity, and no less according to quality: the same differences apply to infinite names in propositions. For we say that some are affirmative and others negative. The description placed below shows which are the simple affirmatives and negatives, and which are the affirmatives and negatives formed with an infinite name. We have also included all of them under their proper classifications, and likewise included indefinite propositions in both species, while omitting those having a singular subject from the simple propositions.

[Col. 0521D] The indefinite simple propositions are:

- “Man walks.”
- “Man does not walk.”

Opposed to these, according to the infinite name, are:

- “Not-man walks.”
- “Not-man does not walk.”

The universal propositions with a simple subject are:

- “Every man walks.”
- “No man walks.”

Opposed to these, according to the infinite name, are the universals:

- “Every not-man walks.”
- “No not-man walks.”

Again, the particulars with a simple subject are:

- “Some man walks.”
- “Some man does not walk.”

Opposed to these, according to the infinite name, are:

- “Some not-man walks.”
- “Some not-man does not walk.”

This is made clear by the description placed below.

### Indefinite propositions with a simple name as subject

“Man walks.” — “Man does not walk.”

[Col. 0522A]

### Indefinite propositions with an infinite name as subject

“Not-man walks.” — “Not-man does not walk.”

### Universal propositions with a simple name as subject

“Every man walks.” — “No man walks.”

### Universal propositions with an infinite name as subject

“Every not-man walks.” — “No not-man walks.”

### Particular propositions with a simple name as subject

“Some man walks.” — “Some man does not walk.”

### Particular propositions with an infinite name as subject

“Some not-man walks.” — “Some not-man does not walk.”

[Col. 0522B] In making this division, and making this division concerning propositions constituted of two terms, he says that all propositions are formed from a name as subject, and he takes for division only those formed from an infinite name and a finite name. He makes the principal division as follows: “Of propositions, some are from a finite name and others from an infinite name.”

Someone wishing to divide everything according to the differences among propositions ought indeed to include not only infinite names but also infinite verbs. But he knew that an infinite name preserves the kind of proposition in which it occurs: if it is used in an affirmative proposition, it preserves an affirmative enunciation, as in “not-man walks.” If in a negative proposition, it preserves a negative enunciation; it is negative, as in “not-man walks.” He therefore passed over the matter of verbs, because infinite verbs joined in a proposition do not complete an affirmation but a negation. Infinite verbs belong more properly to one quality of proposition, namely, the negative. For a negation is always formed from an infinite verb.

[Col. 0522C] Gathering these points together, he says: “Since an affirmation is a statement signifying something concerning a subject,” that is, predicating something, “this is either a name or an unnamed expression.” In other words, every proposition consists of a subject and a predicate, and the subject is either a name or an unnamed expression. An unnamed expression is one that removes the name proposed, as in “not-man.” The name “man” differs from the privation of the name, “not-man”; for that reason he called the latter an unnamed expression.

To show what sort of proposition he is discussing, he says: “There must be one thing, and the affirmation must be about one thing.” That is, a proposition must consist of two terms. He also recalls that he had already explained what an unnamed expression is: Aristotle would not call what we say, “not-man,” a name; rather, what he would not call a name simply, he calls an infinite name by adding this qualification. He does so because it signifies one thing, but an infinite thing. For the expression that removes the very signification of what we call “man”—namely, “not-man”—is one thing and takes away one intrinsic signification.

[Col. 0522D] Many matters are left to the understanding of the attentive. He also recalls that above he called “does not run” an infinite verb, not simply a verb. Since an affirmation is something concerning something, and its subject must either be a name or an unnamed expression—that is, an infinite name—there are two species of proposition. Every affirmation is formed either from a finite name and a verb, or from an infinite name and a verb; and the same applies to negation. For no affirmation will ever be found whose negation cannot also be found.

[Col. 0523A] If there are two species of affirmations, then there are also two species of negations. He also recalls what he said above: although a predicative, that is, categorical, affirmation and negation is formed from a name and a verb, and likewise from what is not a name but an infinite name and a verb, it is impossible for any affirmation or negation to exist apart from a verb, or apart from something that signifies the same thing, whether understood or expressed in some other way.

He also gives the verbs that occur in nearly all propositions, either in themselves or in words equivalent to them. “Is,” he says, “or will be, or was,” and any others that co-signify time, are verbs, as we can learn from what was set out and conceded earlier, when the definition of verbs was given: verbs are expressions that co-signify time. [Col. 0523B] Therefore, if these expressions co-signify time, there is no doubt that they are verbs; and apart from these or expressions equivalent to them, there is no proposition. It was therefore correctly said that a predicative proposition cannot be constituted apart from verbs.

Someone might justly raise the question why he has now said that enunciations cannot be constituted apart from a verb, when he had already said the same thing earlier, as though he had said nothing about it before. But this should not seem superfluous. Since a finite name with a negative particle is an infinite name, someone might perhaps think that “not-man” is a negation. If this were a negation, then “man” would be an affirmation. To prevent anyone from falling into this error, he said—and appropriately repeated—that an enunciation cannot exist apart from a verb, as though he were saying: no one should suppose that an infinite name is a negation or that a name is an affirmation. For affirmation and negation can never be constituted in any way apart from a verb.

[Col. 0523C] Here he also noted that an infinite verb signifies both a negation and an infinite verb. For what we call “does not walk” is both an infinite verb and a negation. If it is said by itself, simply and without any other additions, it is an infinite verb. But if it is pronounced with a name or with an infinite name, it is no longer understood as an infinite verb but as a negation. Thus the negative particle “not,” joined to “walks,” forms the infinite verb “does not walk”; but in the proposition “man does not walk,” it designates that man does not walk. For that reason he says that subjects in propositions may be either names or infinite names, but predicates cannot be anything other than verbs.

[Col. 0523D] For whether one places it in affirmations or in negations, one has undoubtedly predicated a verb. In a negation, “is not” is not an infinite verb but simply a verb; the addition of the particle “not” changes the entire quality of the proposition from affirmative to negative. He therefore rightly made no distinction among propositions according to infinite verbs. Infinite verbs are infinite when they stand alone. But when they are joined to an infinite name or a finite name, they are no longer infinite verbs but finite verbs. Together with the negation, however, they are understood in the complete proposition.

[Col. 0524A] If, as the Stoics wish, negations were attached to names, so that “not-man walks” were a negation, then when we say “not-man” it could be ambiguous whether this were an infinite name or a finite name joined with a negation. But since Aristotle holds that negations must be joined to verbs, infinite verbs are more liable to ambiguity: they may appear to be infinite or finite when joined with a negation.

The distinction is therefore made in this way: when an infinite verb is taken together with a name, it becomes a negation and a negative proposition, as in “man does not walk.” When stated by itself, it is an infinite verb, as in “does not walk.” For that reason, in propositions he made a distinction only between names and infinite names, and not between infinite verbs, because he was speaking of joined expressions—namely, names or infinite names together with verbs. In this combination, what is called an infinite verb by itself is a negation.

[Col. 0524B] Nor is it necessary that just as every proposition consists either of a finite name or of an infinite name, so it should also consist either of a finite verb or of an infinite verb. There is no infinite verb in propositions. Whenever something of this kind is placed by itself, as has been said, it is indeed a finite verb, but the negation joined to it deprives and destroys the whole proposition; and when an infinite verb is joined to names, it must produce a negation, whereas an infinite name joined to a verb does not necessarily produce a negation.

[Col. 0524C] For what we say—“not-man walks”—is an affirmation, not a negation. Since an affirmation must signify something concerning something, and an infinite name is something, whenever we say “not-man walks,” we predicate walking—that is, something—of not-man, that is, of something. But if we say “does not walk,” we do not so much predicate something of something as take something away from something. For the person who says “man does not walk” takes walking away from man; he does not predicate it of man. It is therefore a negation rather than an affirmation.

If it were an affirmation—that is, if the verb were infinite—it would predicate something of something. But now it removes something from something. It is therefore not an infinite verb, but rather a negation whenever it is taken as part of the whole proposition.

[Col. 0524D] He then places below the number of propositions that we also described above: first the infinite propositions, and afterward those opposed to them. Anyone who returns to those passages, or directs his attention here, will recognize carefully where our arrangement or Aristotle’s differs. We presented both contraries and subcontraries, whereas Aristotle presented only propositions opposed to one another contradictorily. Aristotle, however, says that the same differences among propositions that he proposed exist not only in the present time but also in the other two times, which are external. By “external times” he means those other than the present—namely, the past and the future.

When a third element is predicated as something adjacent, oppositions are then spoken of in two ways. I mean, for example, “a just man is.” By “third,” I mean a name or a verb that is added in an affirmation. There will therefore be four propositions, two of which will stand in a relation of consequence to the affirmation and negation, like privations, while the other two will not. I mean that “is” will be added either to “just” or to “not-just.” [Col. 0525A] The same applies to the negation. There will therefore be four.

We understand what is being said from the propositions written below:

- “A just man is.”
- Its negation: “A just man is not.”
- “A not-just man is.”
- Its negation: “A not-just man is not.”

Here “is” and “is not” are added to “just” and “not-just.” These propositions are arranged in the way stated in the *Analytics*.

What is being said is extremely obscure and has been explained carelessly by many writers. I shall enumerate their views with appropriate judgment.

[Col. 0525B] After he had dealt with propositions that consisted of two terms and had a subject that was either a name or, as he himself says, an unnamed expression—that is, an infinite name—he now turns to those in which a third element is predicated as something adjacent: one subject with two predicates. Thus, in what we say, “man is just,” “man” is the subject, while both “just” and “is” are predicated. There are therefore two predicates here and one subject.

Someone might perhaps ask why he said, “When a third element is predicated as something adjacent.” For the third element is not predicated; the second is. There are two predicates and one subject. But this was not said as though “is” were the third element predicated in the proposition “man is just.” Rather, because the third element is adjacent and is predicated, what is called “third” refers to its being adjacent. For in the proposition “man is just,” “is” is adjacent as the third element, while the predicate is no longer third but second.

[Col. 0525C] Thus the third element, counted as third, is adjacent; the second, counted as second, is predicated. This is what he means when he says: “When a third element is predicated as something adjacent”—not that the third element is predicated, but that the third element, which is adjacent, is predicated, that is, in the third position.

He therefore now examines propositions in which “is” is the third adjacent element and the second predicate. Just as, in propositions in which only “is” is predicated, he examined the subject “man” and considered how many differences the subject produced in propositions—whether the subject was a name or an infinite name—so here he speaks of the predicate and treats the differences of predicates.

[Col. 0525D] In propositions in which a third element is predicated as adjacent, the predicate, when taken as a name or an infinite name, produces different kinds of propositions. By predicate I mean “just” in the proposition “man is just.” “Just” is predicated of man; “is” is not predicated independently. But the third element is predicated as adjacent—that is, in the second position—and adjacent to “just.” The third element is predicated in the proposition as a whole, not as though it were some part of the whole proposition, but rather as an indication of its quality.

[Col. 0526A] For what we say—“is”—does not constitute the entire proposition, but demonstrates what kind of proposition it is, namely, that it is affirmative. For that reason he did not merely say “the third is predicated,” but “the third adjacent is predicated.” The third element is not simply placed as something predicated; it is adjacent in the second position and, as has been said, is predicated accidentally.

Aristotle may also be understood to have said that “is” is predicated in these propositions as a third adjacent element because it can sometimes be predicated by itself. For example, someone might say, “Socrates is a philosopher,” intending the proposition to mean “Socrates, the philosopher, lives.” Here “is” is used in place of “lives.” If someone speaks in this way, two subjects are found. “Is” alone is predicated, not the adjacent element. [Col. 0526B] For when we say “Socrates philosopher,” both are subjects.

But if someone says, “Socrates is a philosopher,” not to signify that Socrates is a philosopher and lives, but to signify by the enunciation that Socrates practices philosophy and is a philosopher, then one subject and two predicates are found. “Socrates” is the subject, while “philosopher” and “is” are predicates. “Philosopher” is predicated principally; “is” is adjacent to the name “philosopher” and is itself predicated, but not simply—it is predicated as adjacent.

[Col. 0526C] There are also other propositions of this kind, such as “Socrates debates in the Lyceum.” These consist of three terms. For the present, however, he says nothing about the nature of such propositions; he deals only with those in which a third element is predicated as adjacent, as in “man is just.”

Of these, then, there are two oppositions. Accordingly, there are rightly two oppositions consisting of four propositions. The matter is as follows. When a third adjacent element is predicated, what is predicated principally will be either a name or an infinite name. These will in turn be predicated either affirmatively or negatively. Thus the affirmation of a simple name and the negation of a simple name constitute one opposition and two propositions.

[Col. 0526D] Here “finite” and “infinite” apply not to the subject but to the predicate. Thus, in “man is just,” “just” is predicated; and this will be either a name or an infinite name. From these arise two affirmations and two negations:

- “Man is just.”
- “Man is not-just.”
- “A not-just man is not.”
- “A just man is not.”

This applies to indefinite propositions. Later it will also be shown that the same applies to those having a determination of universality or particularity. For the present, however, the order set out below indicates their number and opposition.

[Col. 0525] Simple affirmation. Simple negation. A man is just. One opposition. A man is not just. Affirmation from an infinite term. Negation from an infinite term. A man is non-just. One opposition. A man is not non-just.

[Col. 0525D] In the description given above I called those propositions simple in which a noun is predicated, as in “a man is just” and “a man is not just.” I call those propositions “from infinite terms” in which an infinite noun is principally predicated, as in “a man is non-just” and “a man is not non-just.” Whether “is” is predicated first or afterward makes no difference. Nor should it trouble us that Aristotle placed “is” first, whereas we place it last; the meaning is the same. Thus there are two oppositions, but four propositions, and these four propositions have been reduced from the number six to a smaller number.

For if the propositions had been simple and consisted of two terms, they would have been as follows: “A man exists,” “A man does not exist,” “A just thing exists,” “A just thing does not exist,” “A non-just thing exists,” “A non-just thing does not exist”; and these would have been six propositions. It would also be possible to add propositions formed with an infinite noun as subject, such as “A non-man exists” and “A non-man does not exist.” But he will discuss these later.

For the present, those six simple propositions have been reduced to four, because simple things, when naturally joined together, return as fewer things. Conjunction itself reduces the number: if there are ten things and they are joined one to one so that pairs are formed, the number resulting from the conjunction is five. Thus, in this case, there had been six propositions, as I showed above, which could also have been stated simply; but they have been contracted, and their number has been reduced through conjunction.

For the four propositions proposed were: “A man exists,” “A man does not exist,” “A just thing exists,” “A just thing does not exist.” These conjunctions have been reduced to two, since “man” joined with “just” produced two propositions: “A man is just,” “A man is not just.” Again, when the infinite term is predicated of that same man, two further propositions reasonably arise from the infinite predicate: “A man is non-just,” “A man is not non-just.” Thus there are two oppositions and four propositions.

Accordingly, from the six propositions—“a man,” “not a man,” “a just thing,” “not a just thing,” “a non-just thing,” “not a non-just thing”—there are three oppositions. But when “man” and “non-just man” are made subjects, only four propositions and a double opposition result.

It is therefore clear that those who said that more propositions are formed from propositions in which “is” is predicated as an adjacent third element than from those consisting of two terms did not understand the nature of things. Nature operates in such a way that things formed from several simple elements always return as fewer and more compact conjunctions.

He therefore says that, in propositions in which “is” is predicated as an adjacent third element, the expression “third” should be referred not so much to predication as to order, as he himself distinguished it when he said: “I mean, for example, ‘a just man exists’: I say that ‘is’ is a third element adjacent to the noun or verb in the affirmation; I do not mean,” he says, “that the third element is predicated.” Rather, “third” refers to adjacency in the order, not to predication: it is adjacent as a third element, but it is predicated as an adjacent element, that is, it is not predicated simply. For it has not been delimited above as a term, so that “is” would be a term in the proposition.

[Col. 0527D] Therefore, if someone wishes to resolve propositions into their terms, he does not resolve them into “is,” but into “man” and “just”; and there will be two terms: “man” as subject and “just” as predicate. The fact that “is” is predicated as an adjacent element, and that “third” refers to adjacency, is understood not in terms of the propositions’ terms but rather in terms of their quality, as has been said.

He says “noun or verb” for this reason: by saying that “is” is adjacent as a third noun, he showed that there are two first elements, namely “man” and “just.” He says “noun or verb” because verbs too are nouns. He had already said this when he stated that verbs, considered in themselves, are nouns.

After he had explained what he intended to show by the expression “is is predicated as an adjacent third element,” and had clarified that this refers to order rather than predication, he went on to explain how many propositions would result, saying: “Therefore these four will result.” He mentioned in these four a common feature, which I shall explain carefully shortly.

The feature is this: although there are four propositions, two of them will stand in relation to affirmation and negation according to the same consequence as privative propositions, whereas the other two will not. I shall demonstrate this feature in these propositions shortly. For now, let us consider how he says that the four propositions themselves are formed.

He says: “I mean that ‘is’ will be adjacent either to ‘just’ or to ‘non-just.’ For a twofold proposition will result.” If “is” is adjacent either to “just” or to “non-just,” the propositions will be these: “A man is just,” [Col. 0528B] “A man is non-just.”

Thus, he says, if “is,” placed affirmatively, is joined now with “just” and now with “non-just,” it produces two affirmative propositions. The same thing happens when the negation “not” is joined with it: it also produces two negative propositions, namely “A man is not just” and “A man is not non-just.” This is what he means when he says: “I mean that ‘is’ will be adjacent either to ‘just’ or to ‘non-just.’” If it is adjacent to “just,” it produces the affirmation “A man is just”; if it is adjacent to “non-just,” it produces the affirmation “A man is non-just.”

The negation joined with “is” does the same thing. The negation “not,” joined with “just” and “non-just,” produces two negative propositions opposed to the propositions mentioned above. If it is added to “just,” it produces the negation [Col. 0528C] “A man is not just”; if to “non-just,” “A man is not non-just.”

Why does this happen? Because both “is” and “is not” are adjacent to “just” and “non-just.” “Is,” joined with “just” and “non-just,” produces two propositions; then the negation “is not,” joined with “just” and “non-just,” produces two further negative propositions. Of these four, two oppositions result, as he said above.

When “is” is predicated as an adjacent third element, oppositions are spoken of in two ways. The whole meaning is therefore as follows:

“But since there is also another description of the passage, which says: ‘I mean that “is” will be adjacent either to “man” or to “non-man,” and therefore the negation as well; thus there will be four propositions,’ we understand what has been said from the material written below.”

“A man is just”; its negation: “A man is not just.”

“A man is non-just”; its negation: “A man is not non-just.”

For in this passage “is” and “is not” are adjacent to “man” and “non-man.” This troubled the commentators, who wondered how it could be that, although he had said above, “I mean that ‘is’ will be adjacent either to ‘man’ or to ‘non-man,’” he did not add “is” to “man” or “non-man” in his example and arrangement, but instead spoke of “just” and “non-just.”

We understand what is meant from what is written below: “A man is just”; its negation: “A man is not just.” “A man is non-just”; its negation: “A man is not non-just.” Afterward he added “is” and “is not” to “just” and “non-just,” which he had not mentioned earlier, whereas he had proposed that they be adjacent to “man” and “non-man.” Then he adds: “In this passage ‘is’ is adjacent to ‘man,’ and ‘is not’ to ‘man’”—although he had placed “is” and “is not” as adjacent to “just” and “non-just.”

[Col. 0529A] Alexander therefore also says that the fault lies in the text, not in the philosopher, who spoke correctly, and that the text should be emended. Yet he should not have been embarrassed if, instead of “man” and “non-man,” the author introduced “just” and “non-just.” For these are examples rather than an essential requirement of the propositions. When he said that “is” is adjacent to “man” and “non-man,” he took the expression as though “man” were predicated, as in “Socrates is a man,” or again, “Socrates is not a man.”

Thus, wishing to take whatever predicate might be used—now simple, now infinite—he introduced “just” and “non-just” indifferently. It makes no difference whether “man” and “non-man” are predicated or “just” and “non-just”; the only difference is that in the predicate the noun is sometimes taken as finite and sometimes as infinite. Alexander therefore ought not to have been troubled.

Nor did Porphyry and Herminus find this text troubling, although the philosopher wished to exercise us through it. They say that the examples here are of a finite and an infinite predicate, and that the free choice of predicate should be accepted equally. Even if, after saying that “is” and “is not” are adjacent to “man” and “non-man,” he had later added “white” and “non-white,” that would have been sufficient.

For the predicate must equally be taken as finite in some cases and infinite in others, whatever nouns are used. When he says that “is” and “is not” are adjacent to “man” and “non-man,” and then introduces “just” and “non-just” and adds “man,” we should not suppose that he intended to speak first of subjects, namely “man” and “non-man,” and then by mistake introduced “just” and “non-just” as predicates. Rather, he took “man” and “non-man” as though they were predicated of something, [Col. 0529C] as in the examples already given: “Socrates is a man,” “Socrates is not a man.” In these, “man” and “non-man” are predicated.

Again, if someone says, “A man is just,” “A man is non-just,” the difference is none. In one proposition the predicate is taken simply, in the other infinitely. It is as if I were to say, “Snow is white,” “Snow is non-white”: the structure is the same. The text should therefore not be blamed because, having first proposed that “is” be adjacent to “man” and “non-man,” it then introduced “just” and “non-just.” It makes no difference whether “just” or “non-just” is predicated, or “man” or “non-man,” provided that the predication is taken in one case as infinite and in the other as finite, when “is” is predicated as an adjacent third element.

The philosopher, therefore, whose ingenuity extends to all things, wished to exercise our understanding and intellectual activity, not to confuse us with a corrupt text. When, collecting what he had said above, he adds, “For in this passage ‘is’ and ‘is not’ are adjacent to ‘man,’” he means the following.

In the proposition that says “A man is just,” which he had proposed above, “just” is predicated of “man.” Now “is” is adjacent to “just,” and it will consequently also be adjacent to “man.” In the proposition that says “A man is not just,” “just” is predicated of “man,” while “is not” is adjacent to it. Therefore “is not” will also be adjacent to “man.” This is what he means by saying, “For in this passage ‘is’ and ‘is not’ are adjacent to ‘man.’”

For if “just” is predicated of “man,” while “is” and “is not” are adjacent to “just,” they will also be adjacent to “man,” as has been said.

Alexander also thinks that this text should be emended, and that it should be made to read as follows, [Col. 0530A] as we explained earlier: “For in this passage ‘is’ and ‘is not’ are adjacent to ‘just’ and ‘non-just.’” But the order of the entire sentence has been carefully explained. Whether the one reading or the other is present, neither should be altered. One has more material for intellectual exercise, while the other offers greater ease; but both arrive at the same understanding.

It remains, then, to explain more carefully what he means when he says: “Therefore these four will result, of which two will stand in relation to the affirmation according to the same consequence as privations, while the other two will not.”

This passage is compressed with great brevity and is difficult because of its excessive subtlety and obscurity. In the first edition of this work we passed over it in our exposition and gave, as in other passages, only a very brief explanation. Now, however, we ourselves shall disclose, as far as our ability permits, what truth the meaning contains and what lies hidden beneath this brevity. Let the reader apply his mind as much as he can. If some things appear a little obscure to him, let him attribute that to the difficulty of the subject; if they appear clearer than he expected, he should credit his own acumen.

But before I explain this passage as far as possible, let us first consider Herminus’s opinion. Herminus says that propositions with an infinite noun can be expressed in three ways. They may have:

- an infinite subject, as in “A non-man is just”;
- an infinite predicate, as in “A man is non-just”;
- both an infinite subject and an infinite predicate, as in “A non-man is non-just.”

Of these, he says, any propositions whose predicate term is an infinite noun are similar to those that express some privation. The propositions that express privation are those that say, “A man is unjust,” “A man is not unjust.” Therefore, propositions of the following kind—“A man is unjust,” “A man is not just”—are of this sort.

The propositions that agree with these, he says, are those formed from an infinite predicate, such as “A man is non-just,” “A man is not non-just.” For, he says, being an unjust man is the same as being a non-just man.

But those propositions that have either an infinite subject, as in “A non-man is just,” or both terms infinite, as in “A non-man is non-just,” do not agree with the privative proposition “A man is unjust.” For there is no similarity between “A non-man is just” and “A man is unjust,” nor between “A non-man is non-just” and “A man is not unjust.”

For the propositions that have an infinite noun in the predicate agree with the privative propositions. But those propositions that have either an infinite subject or both terms infinite are altogether different from the privative propositions.

Here Herminus, departing far from the complete meaning and reasoning of the passage, inserted propositions formed either from two infinite terms or from an infinite subject. As for what he meant by “according to the same consequence,” or which two propositions stood in consequence like privations, while the other two did not, he explained nothing clearly. The meaning is no less obscure after Herminus’s explanation than it was before it.

Following Porphyry, therefore, and agreeing with that learned man, we say that there are four propositions, two formed from finite nouns and two from infinite predicate nouns.

The propositions formed from finite nouns are as follows: the affirmation, “A man is just”; the negation, “A man is not just.”

The propositions formed from infinite predicate nouns are these: the affirmation, “A man is non-just”; the negation, “A man is not non-just.”

In what follows we shall call these propositions formed from infinite predicate nouns “infinite propositions.” Thus, in this exposition, the infinite affirmation is the proposition that says, “A man is non-just,” and the infinite negation is the proposition that says, “A man is not non-just.” In order that the proposition formed from an infinite predicate noun may be given a name, we shall call it “infinite.” The other two, which contain no infinite noun, neither as subject nor as predicate, we shall call “simple.”

[Col. 0531B] The simple propositions are therefore these: “A man is just,” “A man is not just.”

I call “privative propositions” any propositions that contain a privation. Privative propositions are of the following kind: “A man is unjust,” for injustice deprives the subject of justice; and again, “A man is not unjust,” for injustice once more deprives the subject.

Thus, since there are two simple propositions, one affirmative and the other negative, and two further privative propositions, one affirmative and the other negative, and also two further infinite propositions, again one affirmative and the other negative, I say that just as the privative propositions—the affirmation and the negation—stand in relation to the simple affirmations and negations, so too the infinite propositions will stand in relation to those same simple propositions, that is, according to the same consequence.

What I mean is this. First let the two simple propositions be arranged: the affirmation, “A man is just,” and again the negation, “A man is not just.”

Under these let the privative propositions be arranged: under the simple affirmation, the privative negation; under the simple negation, the privative affirmation. Thus, under the proposition “A man is just,” let there be placed “A man is not unjust,” and under the proposition “A man is not just,” let there be placed “A man is unjust.”

Again, under the privative propositions let the infinite propositions be arranged: under the affirmation, the affirmation; under the negation, the negation. Under the privative affirmation, “A man is unjust,” let the infinite affirmation “A man is non-just” be arranged. Under the privative negation, “A man is not unjust,” let the infinite negation “A man is not non-just” be placed.

The following arrangement illustrates this:

[Col. 0531B]

**Affirmation:** A man is just.  
**Simple propositions.**  
**Negation:** A man is not just.

**Negation:** A man is not just.  
**Privative propositions.**  
**Affirmation:** A man is just.

**Negation:** A man is not non-just.  
**Infinite propositions.**  
**Affirmation:** A man is non-just.

Having arranged these matters in this way, I say that just as the privative propositions—that is, the affirmation and the negation which say “a man is unjust” and “a man is not unjust”—stand in consequence to the simple propositions which propose “a man is just” and “a man is not just,” so too the infinite propositions, affirmation and negation—namely, “a man is not just” and “a man is not not-just”—will stand in consequence to those same simple propositions, “a man is just” and “a man is not just.” [Col. 0531C]

Let us see what the consequence is between the simple and privative propositions, so that we may learn whether the infinite propositions stand in relation to the simple propositions as the privative propositions stand to those same simple propositions.

The simple propositions are therefore arranged in the first order: the simple affirmation, “A man is just,” and the simple negation, “A man is not just.” Beneath these—that is, beneath the simple affirmation—are placed two negations: one privative, “A man is not unjust,” and the other infinite, “A man is not not-just.” Beneath the simple negation, “A man is not just,” are placed two affirmations: one privative, “A man is unjust,” and the other infinite, “A man is not-just.” [Col. 0531D]

One must also observe in the diagram that the affirmations and negations confront one another angularly. For the simple affirmation, “A man is just,” stands angularly opposite both affirmations, the infinite and the privative, which are “A man is not-just” and “A man is unjust.” Likewise, the simple negation, “A man is not just,” stands angularly opposite the two negations, the infinite and the privative.

In truth, the privative negation follows the simple affirmation. For if it is true to say, “A man is just,” it is true to say, “A man is not unjust,” since whoever is just is not unjust. [Col. 0532B] The privative negation therefore follows the simple affirmation, so that if the simple affirmation is true, the privative negation is also true, and the truth of the privative negation follows from the truth of the simple affirmation. [Col. 0532C]

The converse, however, does not hold; the simple affirmation does not follow the privative negation. For if it is true to say, “A man is not unjust,” it is not altogether true to say, “A man is just.” One may truly say of a horse that the horse is not an unjust man, since it is not a man at all. Therefore it is not an unjust man; but one cannot say of a horse that the horse is a just man. Thus the truth of the simple affirmation does not follow the truth of the privative negation, and therefore no connected and conjunctive proposition can be formulated or uttered here. [Col. 0532D]

It is not a true proposition to say, “If he is not an unjust man, he is a just man.” For it is true of a horse, as has been said, that it is not an unjust man, but it is not true that the horse is a just man. Therefore the simple affirmation does not follow the privative negation.

It has thus been shown that the privative negation follows the simple affirmation, whereas the simple affirmation does not follow the privative negation.

Let us again examine the consequence on the opposite side. In the other relation, the simple negation follows the privative affirmation, whereas the privative affirmation does not follow the simple negation. For if it is true to say, “A man is unjust,” it is true to say, “A man is not just”: whoever is unjust is not just. The truth of the simple negation, “A man is not just,” therefore follows the truth of the privative affirmation, “A man is unjust.” [Col. 0533A] But this does not work in the reverse direction.

For the privative affirmation does not follow the simple negation. If it is true to say, “A man is not just,” it is not altogether true that he is an unjust man. It is true of a horse to say that the horse is not a just man, since what is not a man at all cannot be a just man. But one cannot truly say of that same horse that the horse is an unjust man, since what is not a man cannot be an unjust man. Therefore the truth of the privative affirmation does not follow the truth of the simple negation, whereas the truth of the simple negation necessarily follows the truth of the privative affirmation.

Accordingly, this has been shown in both cases: the privative negation follows the simple affirmation, but the simple affirmation does not follow the privative negation; the simple negation follows the privative affirmation, but the privative affirmation does not follow the simple negation. [Col. 0533B]

Having established these points, let us discuss the infinite and privative propositions.

The privative and infinite affirmations agree with affirmations, and the negations with negations, in the following way. The privative affirmation, “A man is unjust,” agrees with the infinite affirmation, “A man is not just.” Both the privative affirmation and the infinite affirmation signify the same thing. Although they differ in the way the expression is formulated, they do not differ in signification, except that what the former posits as unjust—that is, as deprived of justice—the latter posits as not just. [Col. 0533C]

Likewise, the privative negation, “A man is not unjust,” agrees and corresponds with the infinite negation, “A man is not not-just.” It is clear that these two negations agree with each other in their consequence.

The privative negation, “A man is not unjust,” follows the simple affirmation, “A man is just.” Therefore the infinite negation also follows that same simple affirmation, namely, the one which says, “A man is just,” while the infinite negation proposes, “A man is not not-just.” Since the privative negation and the infinite negation agree with one another, if the privative negation follows it, the infinite negation also follows it. But the privative negation, “A man is not unjust,” follows the simple affirmation, “A man is just.” Therefore the infinite negation, “A man is not not-just,” also follows that same simple affirmation, “A man is just.” [Col. 0533D]
