The same thing happens again on the other side. The simple negation, “A man is not just,” followed the privative affirmation, “A man is unjust.” The simple negation, “A man is not just,” therefore also follows the infinite affirmation, “A man is not-just.” For if the privative affirmation and the infinite affirmation agree, the proposition which follows the privative proposition follows the infinite proposition as well.

The privative affirmation, “A man is unjust,” is followed by the simple negation, “A man is not just.” But the privative affirmation and the infinite affirmation signify the same thing and agree with one another. Therefore the simple negation, “A man is not just,” follows the infinite affirmation, “A man is not-just.” [Col. 0534A]

The converse, however, does not hold. We have now shown that the infinite negation follows the simple affirmation and that the simple negation follows the truth of the infinite affirmation. But it does not follow conversely that the finite affirmation follows the infinite negation, nor does the infinite affirmation again follow the simple negation. [Col. 0534B]

For if the privative negation, “A man is not unjust,” and the infinite negation, “A man is not not-just,” signify the same thing, and if—as we showed above—the simple affirmation, “A man is just,” does not follow the privative negation, “A man is not unjust,” then that same simple affirmation, “A man is just,” does not follow the infinite negation, “A man is not not-just.”

Again, on the other side, the privative affirmation, “A man is unjust,” signifies the same thing as the infinite affirmation, “A man is not-just.” But the privative affirmation, “A man is unjust,” did not follow the simple negation, “A man is not just.” Nor, therefore, does the infinite affirmation, “A man is not-just,” follow that same simple negation, “A man is not just.”

Although the reasoning and necessity of consequence demonstrate this, let us also teach what we have demonstrated by reasoning through examples. [Col. 0534C]

I say that the infinite negation, “A man is not not-just,” follows the simple affirmation, “A man is just,” just as the privative negation, “A man is not unjust,” also followed that same simple affirmation. For if it is true to say that a man is just, it is also true of that same man to say that he is not not-just. Whoever is just is not not-just, just as it was true to say that the same person who is just is not unjust. Therefore the infinite negation follows the simple affirmation, just as the simple privative negation also followed it.

But the converse does not hold. It is not immediately true that whoever is not not-just is just. A horse is not not-just, since it is not a man at all. What is not a man at all cannot be a not-just man. Yet, although it is true to say of a horse that it is not not-just, it is not true to say of it that it is a just man. [Col. 0534D]

Likewise, it would be true to say of the same horse the privative negation, “A man is not unjust.” This could also be said of a horse, but it was not true that the simple affirmation, “A man is just,” followed this privative negation. Therefore the simple affirmation, “A man is just,” does not follow the infinite negation, “A man is not not-just,” just as it did not follow the privative negation corresponding to the infinite negation, namely, “A man is not unjust.” [Col. 0535A]

In conclusion, then, one must say that the infinite negation follows the simple affirmation, just as the privative negation followed it; but the simple affirmation does not follow the infinite negation, just as it did not follow the privative negation.

Again, on the other side, the converse occurs in the same way. The simple negation follows the infinite affirmation, just as the same simple negation followed the privative affirmation. For whoever is a not-just man is necessarily not just, just as whoever is an unjust man is necessarily not just.

But if it is true to say, “A man is not just,” it is not altogether necessary that he be a not-just man. A horse is not a just man, since what is not a man at all cannot be a just man; but no one can say of that same horse that it is a not-just man. What is not a man cannot be a not-just man. Likewise, when we said, “A man is not just,” the privative affirmation, “A man is unjust,” did not follow. A horse is not a just man, but no one says of that same horse that it is an unjust man. [Col. 0535B]

In conclusion once more, one must say that the simple negation follows the infinite affirmation, just as the privative affirmation was also followed by the simple negation; but the converse does not hold. The infinite affirmation does not follow the simple negation, just as the privative affirmation did not follow it.

Thus there are four propositions: two simple and two infinite. The two simple propositions are “A man is just” and “A man is not just”; the two infinite propositions are “A man is not-just” and “A man is not not-just.” [Col. 0535C]

Of these four, two—namely, the infinite negation and the simple negation—follow two others. The infinite negation follows the simple affirmation: “A man is not not-just” follows “A man is just.” The simple negation follows the infinite affirmation: the infinite affirmation, “A man is not-just,” is followed by the simple negative proposition, “A man is not just.”

The other two—namely, the simple affirmation and the infinite affirmation—do not follow the infinite negation and the simple negation. This also occurs with the privative propositions: the privative affirmation does not follow the simple negation, although the simple negation follows it; and, conversely, the privative negation follows the simple affirmation, although the simple affirmation does not follow the privative negation. [Col. 0535D]

It was therefore correctly said that, of these four propositions—two simple and two infinite—two are consequents of two and have a certain consequence in relation to the others. The infinite negation and the simple negation follow the simple and infinite affirmations, just as the privative propositions do: the privative negation followed the simple affirmation, and the simple negation followed the privative affirmation. [Col. 0536A]

Thus two have consequence—that is, the infinite negation and the simple negation have consequence in relation to the simple and infinite affirmations—just as the privative propositions do. For the privative propositions are similarly related, as I have often shown above. The other two have no consequence at all. The simple affirmation does not follow the infinite negation, nor does the infinite affirmation follow the simple negation, just as it was with the privative propositions. For among the privative propositions, neither did the simple affirmation follow the privative negation, nor did the privative affirmation follow the simple negation.

The meaning is therefore this. There are four propositions, from which he had said that a twofold opposition is formed. These four are two simple propositions—affirmative, “A man is just,” and negative, “A man is not just”—and two infinite propositions—affirmative, “A man is not-just,” and negative, “A man is not not-just.” [Col. 0536B]

Of these, he says, two—namely, the infinite and simple negations—stand in consequence to the affirmations, so that these two negations, the simple and the infinite, follow the other two affirmations, the simple and the infinite, just as the privative propositions followed them.

The other two, he says, do not do so at all. That is, the two affirmations—the simple and the infinite—do not stand in consequence to the two negations, the infinite and the simple, which they did not follow, just as the privative affirmations did not previously follow those negations.

When he says “in consequence to the affirmation and negation,” this must not be understood as though there were only one affirmation or one negation. Rather, in the four propositions, two are affirmations and two are negations. The affirmations are the simple, “A man is just,” and the infinite, “A man is not-just”; the negations are the simple, “A man is not just,” and the infinite, “A man is not not-just.” [Col. 0536C]

The two affirmations—the simple, “A man is just,” and the infinite, “A man is not-just”—were followed by two negations: the simple negation, “A man is not just,” follows the infinite affirmation, “A man is not-just,” and, again, the infinite negation follows the simple affirmation.

Since, therefore, as has been said, the two negations, simple and infinite, followed the two affirmations, simple and infinite, and since this was also the case with the privative propositions, he accordingly said that, in relation to the affirmation and negation, two of these four propositions stand in consequence just as the privative propositions do.

He said “in relation to the affirmation and negation” because two negations follow two affirmations, whereas the other two do not: the two affirmations do not follow the two negations. The simple affirmation did not follow the infinite negation, nor did the finite affirmation follow the simple negation, just as it was not so among the privative propositions, as has often been shown above. [Col. 0536D]

Let no one suppose that we are saying that, among propositions of the same kind, negations follow affirmations. For we are not saying that the simple negation follows the simple affirmation. That is impossible. The simple affirmation and the simple negation never agree with one another; nor do the infinite negation and the infinite affirmation.

It cannot happen either that the negation which says, “A man is not just,” agrees with the affirmation which proposes, “A man is just,” or that the affirmation which says, “A man is not-just,” agrees with the negation which says, “A man is not not-just.” [Col. 0537A]

The privative negation, “A man is not unjust,” follows the simple affirmation, “A man is just.” But, they say, the simple affirmation, “A man is just,” does not follow the infinite negation, “A man is not not-just.”

To this one must reply that they do not correctly understand this consequence, and that there is no discrepancy in this kind of consequence among these propositions. Why did they not notice that the finite affirmation, “A man is just,” does not follow the infinite negation, “A man is not not-just”? This ought not to seem surprising. [Col. 0537B]

The reason why the simple affirmation, “A man is just,” does not follow the infinite negation, “A man is not not-just,” is that it did not previously follow the privative negation either. For the same simple affirmation, “A man is just,” did not follow the privative negation, “A man is not unjust.” This is precisely why it does not follow the infinite negation either. For the infinite and privative propositions agree with one another, as has often already been said above.

There is therefore no discrepancy. If the simple affirmation followed the privative negation, it would likewise follow the infinite negation. But since the simple affirmation does not follow the privative negation, it does not follow the infinite negation either. [Col. 0537C]

Those who assumed that the privative negation followed the simple affirmation and then claimed that there was a discrepancy in the same consequence because the simple affirmation did not follow the infinite negation ought not to have understood the discrepancy in this way. Rather, there would be a discrepancy if, in the same way that the privative negation followed the simple affirmation, the infinite negation did not follow the simple affirmation. But since the simple affirmation does not follow the privative negation, there is no discrepancy whatsoever.

In this respect, therefore, they differ and disagree in no way at all. Let us now examine the other matter in which they claim that there is a discrepancy between the consequence of the infinite and privative propositions in relation to the simple propositions, so that we may see whether they truly differ in that respect. [Col. 0537D]

They say that the simple negation, “A man is not just,” agrees and corresponds with the privative affirmation, “A man is unjust.” And just as the privative negation follows the simple affirmation, they say that the infinite affirmation, “A man is not-just,” does not likewise follow the simple negation, “A man is not just.” For, they say, the former does not follow the latter.

To this one must again reply that the reason why the infinite affirmation, “A man is not-just,” does not follow the simple negation, “A man is not just,” is that the privative affirmation, “A man is unjust,” does not follow the simple negation, “A man is not just.” If the privative affirmation followed the simple negation, the infinite affirmation would unquestionably follow that same simple negation as well. But since the privative affirmation does not follow the simple negation, the infinite affirmation does not follow the simple negation either, for the privative and infinite affirmations agree with one another. [Col. 0538A]

Those who wished to demonstrate a discrepancy between the consequence of the infinite and privative propositions in relation to the simple propositions—because, although the simple negation followed the privative affirmation, the infinite affirmation did not similarly follow the simple negation—ought not to have inferred the discrepancy in this way. Rather, it would have been necessary to say that there was some difference in the consequence if, in the same way that the privative affirmation, “A man is unjust,” followed the simple negation, the infinite affirmation, “A man is not-just,” did not follow the simple negation, “A man is not just.” [Col. 0538B]

But since the privative affirmation does not follow the simple negation in the same way that the infinite affirmation does not follow that same simple negation, it is clear that there is no discrepancy between them. On the contrary, their consequence is entirely alike in every respect. Those who wish to introduce this argument are therefore not reasoning correctly; rather, they are entangling an obscure meaning in still greater obscurities.

The statement that “two of them will stand in consequence to the affirmation and negation, as the privative propositions do, while two will not” must instead be understood as though it had said the following: [Col. 0538C]

Of the four propositions—two simple and two infinite—two affirmations, namely the simple and the infinite, are followed by two negations, namely the simple and the infinite, just as the privative propositions are also followed. Among the privative propositions, the simple affirmation was followed by the privative negation, and the privative affirmation was followed by the simple negation. The other two—that is, the simple affirmation and the infinite affirmation—have no consequence in relation to the negations, the simple and the infinite, just as the privative propositions likewise have no such consequence. For the privative affirmation did not follow the simple negation, nor did the simple affirmation follow the privative negation. [Col. 0538D]

Thus, then, there are four propositions, two simple and two infinite. Of these four—that is, of the two simple and the two infinite—two, namely the simple and infinite negations, follow the two affirmations, the simple and the infinite.

This is what he means when he says that they stand in consequence “to the affirmation and negation”: the negations follow the affirmations, just as was also said of the privative propositions. The other two—that is, the simple and infinite affirmations—do not stand in consequence to the two negations, the simple and the infinite, just as the privative propositions likewise did not stand in consequence in that direction. For the privative negation was not followed by the simple affirmation, nor was the privative affirmation followed by the simple negation. [Col. 0539A]

There is also another, simpler explanation, which Alexander published after many other explanations that he had considered. It runs as follows:

“There are four propositions,” he says, “two of which are infinite and two simple. The two infinite propositions stand in equal relation, according to affirmation and negation, to the privative propositions; but the two simple propositions do not stand in the same relation to those privative propositions.

“For the infinite affirmation agrees with the privative affirmation. The infinite affirmation, ‘A man is not-just,’ agrees with the privative affirmation, ‘A man is unjust.’ The infinite negation, ‘A man is not not-just,’ agrees with the privative negation, ‘A man is not unjust.’ These two, then—that is, the infinite affirmation and the infinite negation—stand in relation to the affirmation and negation just as the privative propositions do: they affirm or negate the same things that the privative propositions affirm or negate.

“But the other two do not do so—that is, the two simple propositions do not stand in the same relation to the affirmation and negation as the privative propositions do. For it is altogether impossible for the simple affirmation to agree with the privative affirmation. The proposition which says, ‘A man is just,’ does not agree with the proposition which says, ‘A man is unjust.’ Nor does the simple negation agree with the privative negation. The proposition which says, ‘A man is not just’—the simple negation—differs greatly from the proposition which says, ‘A man is not unjust’—the privative negation.

“Thus, since there are four propositions—the simple affirmation, the simple negation, the infinite affirmation, and the infinite negation—two of them, namely the infinite affirmation and the infinite negation, affirm or negate in the same way as the privative propositions. This is what he means when he says that they stand in relation to the affirmation and negation as the privative propositions do; the other two do not do so.

“For the two simple propositions do not affirm and negate in the same way as the two privative propositions. The simple affirmation differs from the privative affirmation, and the simple negation likewise differs greatly from and disagrees with the privative negation.” [Col. 0539B]

This, as we have said, is Alexander’s simpler explanation after many others. It is not to be rejected, but the earlier explanation appears to be more correct, as Aristotle himself confirms. For shortly afterward he says: “These propositions, then, are arranged in the way stated in the *Prior Analytics*.”

The consequence between the privative and infinite propositions and the simple propositions which I mentioned above was arranged at the end of the first book of the *Prior Analytics*, which the Greeks call *Analytica* (ἀναλυτικά). Porphyry says that there were some men of his own time who attempted to explain this passage. When they found, in the separate explanations offered by Herminus, Aspasius, and Alexander, many contradictions and disagreements resulting from their poorly composed interpretations, they concluded that this book of Aristotle could not be explained at all in a manner worthy of it. Many men of that period consequently passed over the entire teaching of the book, considering its obscurity inexplicable. [Col. 0539C]

We, however, passed over this passage very briefly in our first edition. But what we there set down briefly, for the sake of ease of understanding, we have here arranged at length, setting out the entire force and extent of the meaning. Since, therefore, we have expressed the preceding passage adequately, as it seems to me, let us now examine the order and meaning of the following text. [Col. 0539D]

## [Col. 0540A]

“Likewise, they are related when the affirmation has a universal subject, as in ‘Every man is just.’ The negation is ‘Not every man is just’; ‘Every man is not-just’; ‘Not every man is not-just.’ But it is not possible for the angular propositions to be true in the same way, although it is possible for them to be true sometimes.”

Having first discussed certain propositions that are infinite, he now speaks of those which are determinate through the addition of universality and particularity. He says that these too stand in the same way as those which were uttered without any determination—namely, the simple and the infinite propositions. [Col. 0540B]

When he says, “Likewise, they are related when the affirmation has a universal subject,” some have understood “likewise” to refer to the number of propositions and oppositions. For just as, in the case of the infinite and indeterminate propositions, there are two oppositions—one between the simple affirmation and the simple negation, and the other between the infinite affirmation and the infinite negation—so too, as was already said above, there are four propositions and a twofold opposition in the propositions that have determination according to universality and particularity.

One opposition is between the universal simple affirmation and the particular simple negation:

- “Every man is just.”
- “Not every man is just.”

This is one opposition.

The other is between the universal infinite affirmation and the particular infinite negation:

- “Every man is not-just.”
- “Not every man is not-just.”

Thus here too, since there are two oppositions, there will unquestionably be four propositions, just as in the propositions discussed above, which lacked determination. [Col. 0540C]

Others, however, who have examined Aristotle’s intention more deeply, say that the determinate propositions are not related merely in respect of the number of propositions and oppositions, but also in respect of consequence. For the consequence of the negations to the affirmations in the simple and infinite propositions which are uttered without determination is reproduced in the propositions which are uttered with determination.

But because not all things are alike in every respect, he added the qualification, “But it is not possible for the angular propositions to be true in the same way, although it is possible for them to be true sometimes.” [Col. 0540D]

The meaning is this: these propositions which are called infinite in accordance with determination stand in the same relation to the simple propositions, and the simple propositions to the infinite, as those propositions which were called indeterminate because they were uttered without determination stood in relation to one another. But they have a certain dissimilarity: the angular propositions among those uttered with determination are not true in the same way as those uttered without determination, whether infinite or simple.

Let us therefore first examine whether the same consequence exists in the determinate propositions as in those uttered indefinitely. Then let us examine what the dissimilarity is in the angular propositions.

Let not only the simple and infinite propositions be arranged, but also the privative propositions. First let them be arranged as follows.

The simple affirmation and the simple negation are first. These are indefinite, that is, without the addition of universality or particularity. Beneath them—beneath the simple affirmation—let the privative negation be placed; beneath the simple negation, let the privative affirmation be placed.

These too are indefinite. Beneath the privative affirmation and the simple negation let the infinite affirmation be placed. Beneath the privative negation and the simple affirmation let the infinite negation be placed. These too are indefinite and indeterminate, without any particular or universal qualification. [Col. 0541A]

Beneath these let the propositions be arranged which we call determinate, either by the quantity of universality or by that of particularity. First, let the universal simple affirmation be placed, opposite it the particular simple negation.

Beneath the universal simple affirmation let the particular privative negation be placed; beneath the particular simple negation, let the universal privative affirmation be placed.

Again, beneath the particular privative negation and the universal simple affirmation let the particular infinite negation be placed. Beneath the universal privative affirmation and the particular simple negation let the universal infinite affirmation be placed. [Col. 0542A]

The arrangement will be as follows:

| Proposition | Form |
|---|---|
| Simple affirmation | A just man exists. |
| Privative negation | An unjust man does not exist. |
| Infinite negation | A not-just man does not exist. |
| **Indefinite propositions** |  |
| Simple negation | A just man does not exist. |
| Privative affirmation | An unjust man exists. |
| Infinite affirmation | A not-just man exists. |
| **Determinate propositions** |  |
| Universal simple affirmation | Every man is just. |
| Particular privative negation | Not every man is unjust. |
| Particular infinite negation | Not every man is not-just. |
| Particular simple negation | Not every man is just. |
| Universal privative affirmation | Every man is unjust. |
| Universal infinite affirmation | Every man is not-just. |
[Col. 0541B] In the order of propositions that we described above, it is clear which are diagonal. For affirmations are diagonal to affirmations, and negations to negations; and, among those that are indefinite, affirmations are likewise diagonal. The simple affirmation, “A just man exists,” is diagonal to the privative affirmation, “An unjust man exists,” and to the infinite affirmation, “A non-just man exists.” Likewise, the simple negation, “A just man does not exist,” is diagonal to the privative negation, “An unjust man does not exist,” and to the infinite negation, “A non-just man does not exist.”

If one also considers the definite propositions, one will find the same thing without any doubt. For the universal simple affirmation, “Every man is just,” is diagonal to the universal privative affirmation, “Every man is unjust,” and to the universal infinite affirmation, “Every man is non-just.” Likewise, the particular simple negation, “Not every man is just,” is diagonal to the particular privative negation, “Not every man is unjust,” and to the particular infinite negation, “Not every man is non-just.”

Thus affirmations are diagonal to affirmations, and negations to negations; they are diagonal both in the order of indefinite propositions and in the order of definite propositions. Consequently, we must examine their consequence. It was said earlier that the indefinite simple affirmation is followed by the privative and infinite negations, but that the simple affirmation does not follow them. Again, the simple negation follows the infinite and privative affirmations, but they do not follow the simple negation.

If one again considers the order of the definite propositions, one will find the same thing. For the universal simple affirmation is followed by the particular privative negation and the particular infinite negation. If the universal simple affirmation, “Every man is just,” is true, then the particular privative negation, “Not every man is unjust,” is also true. This occurs because the proposition “Not every man is unjust” can mean the same as the simple proposition and resembles the particular simple affirmation, “Some man is just.” For if not every man is unjust, then some man is just; and the particular simple affirmation follows the universal simple affirmation. Whenever the universal affirmation “Every man is just” is true, the particular affirmation “Some man is just” is also true. But the particular privative negation, “Not every man is unjust,” agrees with the proposition “Some man is just.” Therefore the particular privative negation also agrees with the universal simple affirmation.

The proposition “Every man is just,” namely the universal simple affirmation, is therefore followed by the proposition “Not every man is unjust,” the particular privative negation. This particular privative negation, “Not every man is unjust,” is accompanied by the particular infinite negation, “Not every man is non-just.” And if not every man is unjust, it is true that not every man is non-just, since “unjust” and “non-just” mean the same thing. But the particular privative negation follows the universal simple affirmation. Therefore the particular infinite negation follows the universal simple affirmation and agrees with it, provided that the universal affirmation is true.

Consequently, the universal simple affirmation “Every man is just” is undoubtedly followed by the particular privative negation “Not every man is unjust” and the particular infinite negation “Not every man is non-just.” Thus here too negations follow an affirmation, but this is not reversible. For, as has been said, the particular privative negation “Not every man is unjust” agrees with the particular simple affirmation “Some man is just.” But the universal affirmation does not follow this particular affirmation; for even if it is true that some man is just, it does not therefore follow that every man is just.

Thus the universal simple affirmation “Every man is just” does not follow the particular affirmation “Some man is just.” The former may be false while the latter—that is, the particular affirmation—is true. But the particular simple affirmation agrees with the particular privative negation. Therefore the universal simple affirmation does not follow the particular privative negation either.

The universal simple affirmation “Every man is just” does not follow the proposition “Not every man is unjust”; rather, the particular privative negation agrees with the particular infinite negation. Therefore the universal simple affirmation does not follow the particular infinite negation. The universal simple affirmation “Every man is just” does not follow the particular infinite negation “Not every man is non-just.”

Thus the two particular negations, the infinite and the privative, follow the universal simple affirmation, just as they did among the indefinite propositions. For the two indefinite negations, the infinite and the privative, followed the indefinite simple affirmation, but not conversely. The universal simple affirmation does not follow the particular infinite and privative negations, just as the indefinite simple affirmation did not follow the indefinite privative and infinite negations. In this one respect, therefore, the definite propositions are similar to the indefinite ones: true negations accompany true affirmations, but the truth of negations is not followed by the truth of affirmations, nor do they agree in that direction.

[Col. 0543C–0544C] Let us now examine the other side, namely, how the particular simple negation follows the universal privative and infinite affirmations. The universal privative affirmation “Every man is unjust” is followed by the particular simple negation “Not every man is just.” For the proposition “Every man is unjust” agrees with the universal simple negation “No man is just”; if every man is unjust, no man is just.

But the universal simple negation is followed by the particular simple negation. If it is true that no man is just, it is true that not every man is just. Thus the universal simple negation agrees with the universal privative affirmation. Therefore the particular simple negation “Not every man is just” follows the universal privative affirmation “Every man is unjust.”

The latter also agrees with the universal infinite affirmation, since “Every man is unjust” and “Every man is non-just” signify the same thing. Consequently, the particular simple negation “Not every man is just” also follows the universal infinite affirmation “Every man is non-just.”

Here too, then, the two universal affirmations, the privative and the infinite, are followed by the particular simple negation “Not every man is just,” but this is not reversible. For the universal negation “No man is just” does not follow the particular simple negation “Not every man is just.” If it is true that not every man is just, it does not follow that no man is just.

The universal simple negation agrees with and signifies the same as the universal privative affirmation. Therefore the universal affirmation “Every man is unjust” does not follow the particular simple negation “Not every man is just,” just as the universal negation did not follow that same particular negation. The universal privative affirmation agrees with the universal infinite affirmation. Therefore the universal infinite affirmation “Every man is non-just” does not follow the particular negation “Not every man is just.”

Thus here too the particular simple negation follows the two universal affirmations, the privative and the infinite, just as the indefinite negative followed the two indefinite affirmations, the privative and the infinite. But the two universal affirmations, the privative and the infinite, do not follow the particular simple negation, just as the two indefinite affirmations, the privative and the infinite, did not follow the simple negation. The definite propositions, then, are similar to the indefinite propositions with respect to consequence.

The diagonals, however, are not similarly related. Among the indefinite propositions, the diagonal propositions can happen to be true simultaneously. If it is true that “A just man exists,” which is the indefinite simple affirmation, there is nothing to prevent the proposition “An unjust man exists” from also being true, and likewise “A non-just man exists,” which are the indefinite privative and infinite affirmations.

Again, it can happen that diagonal negations are simultaneously true: if “A just man does not exist” is true, there is nothing to prevent “An unjust man does not exist” and “A non-just man does not exist” from also being true. It is therefore possible for the indefinite diagonals to agree with one another in truth, but only with respect to terms which, as we taught in the second book of this work, are neither naturally present in a subject nor impossible to be present.

If someone says, “A rational man exists,” its diagonals cannot be true—namely, “An irrational man exists” and “A non-rational man exists.” Rationality belongs to man by nature. The same must be said of impossibles: if the terms are such that they are neither impossible to be present nor naturally present, as in the proposition “A just man exists”—for justice need be neither natural nor impossible for man to possess—it is clear that the diagonals always agree with one another in truth. The same is correctly said of diagonal negatives.

With terms that are neither natural nor impossible, therefore, the diagonals can always be simultaneously true: negations with negations and affirmations with affirmations. This applies to the indefinite propositions. But the definite propositions, which participate in universality and particularity, are not related in the same way.

With any terms whatsoever—whether possible, natural, or impossible—diagonal affirmations cannot agree with one another in truth. Diagonal negations, however, can agree with one another in truth only with terms that are neither natural nor impossible.

First, it must be demonstrated that diagonal affirmations cannot agree with one another in truth, whatever the terms may be. The propositions “Every man is just” and “Every man is unjust,” the latter being its diagonal, cannot both be true. For “Every man is unjust” differs in no respect from “No man is just.” But “Every man is just” and “No man is just,” being contraries, cannot both be true.

The proposition “No man is just” agrees with and is equivalent to “Every man is unjust.” Therefore “Every man is just” and “Every man is unjust” cannot both be true. The latter, “Every man is unjust,” also agrees, as has often been said, with “Every man is non-just.” Therefore these propositions cannot agree in truth with “Every man is just.”

The universal simple affirmation “Every man is just” therefore cannot, in any way, agree in truth with the universal privative and infinite affirmations “Every man is unjust” and “Every man is non-just,” which are its diagonals. This differs from the indefinite propositions, among which affirmations could agree with affirmations and negations with negations in truth. Among the definite propositions, diagonal affirmations cannot be simultaneously true.

It was therefore rightly said that, in all other respects, the consequence of the definite and indefinite propositions is similar. Negations agree in truth with affirmations, but affirmations do not altogether agree with negations; this similarity of consequence exists in both kinds, namely, in the definite and in the indefinite propositions. The difference is that the diagonals cannot similarly be true: among the indefinite propositions, both diagonal affirmations and diagonal negations can be true; among the definite propositions, diagonal affirmations can in no way be true simultaneously.

This will become clear if one proposes examples involving natural and impossible terms, as well as examples involving possible terms that are neither natural nor impossible. In every case one will find that definite affirmations cannot be simultaneously true with their diagonal affirmations.

What he added—“But it can happen sometimes”—means the following. Although definite diagonal affirmations cannot be simultaneously true with any terms whatsoever, it can nevertheless happen that negations are found to be simultaneously true with their diagonal negations. Thus the similarity extends to the infinite diagonals. Just as, among the indefinite propositions, diagonal negations could be simultaneously true when the terms were neither natural nor impossible, so here too, in the order of definite propositions, definite negations can be simultaneously true with definite diagonal negations when the terms are neither impossible nor natural.

The particular simple negation “Not every man is just” can be true simultaneously with “Not every man is unjust.” For it can happen that some men are just and others are not. In that case both propositions are true. “Not every man is just” is true because there are some unjust men; and “Not every man is unjust” is true because there may be some just men.

The latter also agrees with the particular infinite negation “Not every man is non-just,” for “Not every man is unjust” means the same as “Not every man is non-just.” Therefore these propositions too, as diagonals, can be simultaneously true. If some men are just and some unjust, it is true to say “Not every man is just,” because there are some unjust men; and it is true to say “Not every man is non-just,” because there are some just men.

Definite diagonal negations, then, can be simultaneously true, and this is similar to the indefinite propositions, among which diagonal negations, just as diagonal affirmations, agree with one another in truth.

The complete sense is therefore as follows: “Similarly,” he says, “the consequence of the propositions is related”—that is, it will be similar to what it was among the indefinite propositions—even if the affirmation contains a universal term, that is, even if definite affirmations and negations are posited. He demonstrated this through the examples placed beneath: opposite the universal simple affirmation “Every man is just” he set “Not every man is just,” namely, the particular simple negation. Then, proposing the universal infinite affirmation “Every man is non-just,” he set against it the proposition “Not every man is non-just.”

“These,” he says, “are similarly related with respect to consequence,” as the indefinite propositions were. How the indefinite propositions were related with respect to consequence has been shown above. But, he says, their diagonals cannot similarly be true. Among the indefinite propositions, diagonal affirmations could be simultaneously true; among the definite propositions, they cannot be simultaneously true. It can happen, however, that definite diagonal negations are simultaneously true, just as in the indefinite propositions described above.

The meaning is therefore complete.

Herminus, however, explains the passage differently, as follows: “Similarly,” he says, “four propositions will form two oppositions if two are simple and two infinite, provided that a determination is added.” If he demonstrates this, he will first propose the universal simple affirmation “Every man is just.” Against this he will place the particular simple negation “Not every man is just.” Beneath the universal simple affirmation he will place the universal infinite affirmation “Every man is non-just.” Against this, beneath the particular simple negation, he will place the particular infinite negation “Not every man is non-just.”

[Col. 0547]  
- Every man is just.  
- Not every man is just.  
- Every man is non-just.  
- Not every man is non-just.

[Col. 0547A] With these propositions arranged in this way, he says, two oppositions arise. For opposite “Every man is just” stands “Not every man is just.” This is because the universal simple affirmation and the particular simple negation are contradictorily opposed to one another; this constitutes one opposition.

Again, opposite the same simple affirmation “Every man is just” stands the universal infinite affirmation “Every man is non-just,” and this in a contrary mode. For “Every man is non-just” signifies the same as and agrees with “No man is just.” But “No man is just” is opposed in a contrary mode to “Every man is just.” Therefore “Every man is non-just” is also opposed as a contrary to “Every man is just.” This is therefore a second opposition.

There are thus two oppositions, just as there were among the indefinite propositions. Although the propositions there were opposed in another way, there were nevertheless two oppositions. But, as he himself says, they cannot be simultaneously true along the diagonal.

For since those propositions were indefinite, even the propositions situated along the diagonal could be simultaneously true, and all could be true with all. Anyone who returns carefully to the descriptions of the indefinite propositions will recognize this. Here, he says—that is, among the definite propositions—the situation is not the same.

He demonstrates it as follows. The proposition “Every man is just” does not agree with its contradiction, “Not every man is just.” Likewise, “Every man is non-just” does not agree with “Not every man is non-just.” For the latter agreed with its contrary.

Therefore, when the universal simple affirmation “Every man is just” is true, the proposition “Every man is non-just” is undoubtedly false. But, since the latter is false, its contradiction, “Not every man is non-just,” will be true. Thus the two diagonal propositions “Every man is just” and “Not every man is non-just” are sometimes found to be true. They can therefore sometimes be true, but not universally.

For if one begins with the particular infinite negation “Not every man is non-just,” the result is not the same—that is, the same truth does not follow. This is demonstrated in the following way. If “Not every man is non-just” is true, “Every man is non-just” is false, since the latter is opposed to it as its contradictory. But if “Every man is non-just” is false, it does not follow that “Every man is just” must be true, because these two are opposed to one another as contraries. We have shown above that contrary propositions can both be false.

Therefore, if “Every man is non-just” is false, it does not follow that “Every man is just” is true. It may happen that both are false. Thus it can happen that, when “Not every man is non-just” is true, “Every man is just” is false. The propositions therefore do not similarly agree with one another in truth along the diagonal.

Herminus, by saying this without a correct interpretation, confuses the order. If someone carefully understands either what Herminus says or what we said above, he will recognize how great the difference between the interpretations is. If he judges the preceding interpretation the better one and trusts us, he will rightly agree with it.

The two propositions mentioned above are therefore opposites. There are others, however, in which “non-man” is added as a sort of subject, such as:

- A non-man is just.
- A non-man is not just.
- A non-man is non-just.
- A non-man is not non-just.

There are not, strictly speaking, more oppositions than these. Those additional propositions will stand outside the former ones, each according to itself, using the expression “non-man” as a name.

[Col. 0548C] He had already said above that every subject consists either of a simple and definite name or, again, of an infinite name. He showed that their oppositions were two in number, comprising four propositions: two having a simple subject-name and two having an infinite one. He then considered cases in which the third adjacent term, “is,” is predicated.

There too he said that oppositions arise in two ways, namely, when the predicate is a definite or an infinite name. He demonstrated the consequence that these have among themselves, namely, the consequence that the privative propositions have in relation to the corresponding simple propositions formed from a definite name.

Since all the variation among these propositions occurs when “is” is predicated as the third term, the subject and predicate may both be definite, or the subject may be definite and the predicate infinite, as he discussed above when demonstrating their consequence; or the subject may be infinite and the predicate definite; or both subject and predicate may be infinite.

The propositions in which both are definite are:

- A man is just.
- A man is not just.

Those with a definite subject and an infinite predicate are:

- A man is non-just.
- A man is not non-just.

Their consequence was demonstrated above.

There are others that have an infinite subject and that use an infinite expression as a name, such as:

- A non-man is just.
- A non-man is non-just.

These propositions use “non-man” as their subject, that is, as a name, and “just” as their predicate. This is what he means when he says: “Others concern ‘non-man’ as an added subject.”

If one posits “non-man” as the subject and predicates of it either a definite name, “just,” or an infinite one, “non-just,” one will again produce two oppositions in each case.

[Col. 0549A] The four propositions are therefore these:

- A non-man is just.
- A non-man is not just.
- A non-man is non-just.
- A non-man is not non-just.

In these four propositions there are two pairs of oppositions. “Non-man” is the subject in both; in the first opposition, the definite predicate “just” is predicated, while in the second the infinite predicate “non-just” is predicated.

But those propositions that have an infinite predicate and a definite subject, or those whose predicate and subject are both definite, have some consequence among themselves. Those that we mentioned afterward—that is, those that have an infinite subject with either a definite or an infinite predicate—have no consequence in relation to the propositions that are formed with either a definite predicate or an infinite predicate from a definite subject.

This is what he means when he says: “Those, outside the former, will exist by themselves.” That is, he says that those propositions which retain an infinite subject in the order of propositions have no consequence in relation to the preceding propositions, which are formed from a definite subject.

After enumerating the propositions formed from two definite terms, namely, a definite subject and predicate, and those formed from a definite subject and an infinite predicate, he added the propositions formed from an infinite subject and a definite predicate, as well as those that appear to consist of two infinite terms.

Having enumerated these, he says: “There will not, strictly speaking, be more oppositions than these.” For every opposition, as was said above, is either formed from two definite terms, as in “A man is just” and “A man is not just”; or from a definite subject and an infinite predicate, as in “A man is non-just” and “A man is not non-just”; or from an infinite subject and a definite predicate, as in “A non-man is just” and “A non-man is not just”; or from two infinite terms, as in “A non-man is non-just” and “A non-man is not non-just.” It is impossible, for any reason, to discover a fifth opposition.

This, then, has been said concerning propositions in which the third adjacent term, “is,” is predicated.

[Col. 0549D] In propositions in which “is” does not function in this way, as in “to run” or “to walk,” the same arrangement is made as if “is” were added. Thus:

- Every man runs.
- Not every man runs.
- Every non-man runs.
- Not every non-man runs.

One must not say “not every man”; rather, the negation “not” must be added to “man.” For “every” does not signify a universal thing, but signifies that something is said universally.

This is clear from the following:

- A man runs.
- A man does not run.
- A non-man runs.
- A non-man does not run.

These differ from the preceding propositions in that they are not universal. Therefore “every” or “no one” adds no signification of its own except that it makes an affirmation or negation concerning a name universal. The remaining cases must consequently be constructed in the same way.

Certain propositions are those in which “is” is predicated as a third element [Col. 0550A], and this is discerned by the very sound and utterance. Others are those in which a verb is predicated such that “is” is not predicated as a third element, yet the verb “is” is joined with and contained within it. If such a proposition is resolved into a participle and the verb “is,” then what was previously predicated by a single verb will be predicated in the second place, and “is” will be predicated in the third place; the proposition thus becomes similar to one that also had the verb “is” in its utterance.

For if someone says, “Every human being runs,” there is one subject and another predicate in this proposition: “human being” is the subject, while “runs” is the predicate. We cannot suppose that there are three terms in this proposition merely because “every” is present, for “every” is not a term but a determination of the subject-term. [Col. 0550B] It signifies that the thing is universal—that is, that “human being” is subjected universally to running—when one says, “Every human being runs”; for there is no exception among human beings when the determination is that every one runs.

Therefore, what we call “every” is not placed in the position of a term, but is rather a determination of the subject-term. Consequently, in the proposition “Every human being runs,” there are two terms: “human being” and “runs.” Thus, although the verb “is” is not predicated in this same proposition, it is nevertheless contained potentially in the signification of the verb “runs.” For if someone resolves the proposition “Every human being runs” into a participle and the verb “is,” he will produce: “Every human being is running”; and the participle joined with the verb signifies the same thing as the verb.

The two expressions encompass the same meaning. When I say, “Every human being runs,” I declare that the activity is present in every human being; and when I say again, “Every human being is running,” I assert that the same activity is present in human beings. Therefore, the verb “runs” signifies the same thing as “is running.” In the proposition “Every human being runs,” although “is” is not uttered, it is predicated potentially. This is recognized from the fact that the whole proposition can be resolved into a participle and a verb.

Accordingly, just as an affirmation is formed from an infinite subject-noun, an affirmation cannot be formed in the same way from an infinite verb; rather, the force of negation is immediately recognized in it. For when we make an affirmation by saying, “Every non-human being runs,” placing “non-human being” as the infinite subject, we cannot in the same way say that an affirmation is made when we propose, “Every human being does not run.” This is already a negation.

Therefore, wherever “does not run,” “does not labor,” “does not walk,” or “does not read” occurs, a negation is made: in every case in which an infinite verb is predicated.

Someone may wonder, however, whether, just as an affirmation cannot be formed from an infinite verb but negation always arises from this category, so also, if the same proposition is resolved into a participle and a verb, an affirmation might be formed from the infinite participle. For one will ask whether, just as in the proposition “Every human being runs,” someone who proposes “Every human being does not run” cannot make an affirmation but unquestionably makes a negation, the same will hold when it is resolved into a participle and a verb. Thus, if someone says, “Every human being is running” [Col. 0551A], and the infinite participle “not-running” is introduced so that one says, “Every human being is non-running,” is this an affirmation, or rather a negation equivalent to “Every human being is not running”?

There were people who inferred the answer from many other considerations, and especially from a certain syllogism of Plato, so that they might learn from the authority of the most learned men what should be determined in this matter. For a syllogism cannot be formed from two negative propositions. In a certain dialogue Plato asks a syllogism of the following kind:

“Sense-perception,” he says, “does not apprehend the account of substance; what does not apprehend the account of substance apprehends the notion of truth. Therefore sense-perception does not apprehend the notion of truth.”

He appears to have formed a syllogism entirely from negative propositions, which cannot be done. Hence, they say that the infinite verb “does not apprehend” was used in place of an infinite participle—that is, “is not apprehending.” For in many other instances as well, an infinite verb is frequently found used in place of an infinite noun. Therefore, some have said that a verb always makes a negation when the infinite form is added.

Participles and nouns, however, if they are infinite, can make an affirmation. For this reason, whenever great men place an infinite verb and two negations in a syllogism, it is defended on the ground that the infinite form has been used in place of a participle, and that the participle is predicated in the proposition in the place of a noun. Alexander of Aphrodisias and many others held this view.

They say that affirmations cannot be formed from an infinite verb because, just as the negative particle joined to the verb “is” immediately completes a whole negation, so verbs that are infinite, or that contain within themselves the verb “is,” will not make an infinite affirmation but rather a negation. If someone says, “A human being is not running,” no one would call this an affirmation. If someone says, “A human being does not run,” this proposition likewise is not an affirmation, because the verb “runs” contains the verb “is” within itself.

Just as the negative particle joined to the verb “is” does not make an affirmation but rather a negation, so too, when negation is joined to another verb that contains the verb “is” within itself, it completes a full negation.

Aristotle, however, does not appear to distinguish these cases, but seems to hold the same view whether the verb “is” is placed with a participle or whether the verb that encloses and contains “is” within itself is used without a participle. For he says [Col. 0551D] as follows:

“In those cases in which ‘is’ is not suitable, as in ‘to run’ or ‘to walk,’ the expressions, when so placed, do the same as if ‘is’ were added.”

He then gives the example “Every human being runs.” In the proposition “Every human being runs,” the verb “is” is not suitable for insertion. Likewise, if someone says, “Every human being walks,” the verb “is” is not suitable for insertion there either. Yet such expressions are as though “is” had been added. He teaches this by an example.

For just as “Every human being is running” is an affirmation showing the presence of running, so also “Every human being runs” is an affirmation, equivalent in force and signification. He then proceeds to enumerate these affirmations from simple subjects, in which “is” is not suitable to be predicated, saying: “Every human being runs,” placing the middle determination “every” between the predicate, which is “runs,” and the subject, which is “human being.”

Against this he sets the simple negation: “Every human being does not run.” Again, he makes an affirmation from an infinite noun: “Every non-human being runs.” To this he opposes the negation of the infinite subject-noun: “Every non-human being does not run.” He proposed these expressions in order to show that the same thing occurs in propositions in which “is” is not suitable to be predicated as in those in which “is” is predicated as a third element.

But because, in the negation of the infinite noun, he substituted “Every non-human being does not run,” he says: “For one must not say, ‘Not every human being,’ but the negation must be added to ‘human being.’”

Someone might have objected that he had not correctly formed the negation of the affirmation “Every non-human being runs,” namely, “Every non-human being does not run,” but that the opposition should rather have been constituted as follows:

“Every non-human being runs; not every human being does not run.”

He demonstrates from this that the negation must be made as he himself arranged it. For he says: “One must not say, ‘Not every human being,’ but the negation must be added to ‘human being.’” The sense is this:

“Whenever,” he says, “we make a negation against the affirmation ‘Every non-human being runs,’ the negative particle ‘not’ is not to be joined to ‘every,’ but rather to the subject, which is ‘human being.’ When we say ‘Every non-human being runs,’ the negation must be made ‘Every non-human being does not run.’ One must not say ‘Not every human being does not run’; that is, the negative particle is not to be added to ‘every,’ but rather to ‘human being.’”

The reason is that “every” is not reckoned among the number of terms but belongs rather to its own force, that is, to determination. For “every” itself does not signify something universal; rather, it signifies that what is universal—namely, “human being”—is predicated universally. “Every” is a determination, since it indicates that what is universal, namely “human being,” is predicated universally.

Therefore, the determination “every” does not signify something universal in its own right, but rather that a universal noun is predicated universally. Accordingly, whenever negation is made in these propositions, the negation must be drawn toward the subject-noun rather than toward the determination. And so that no one may doubt that oppositions must also be formed in this way in other cases, consider propositions with a finite subject.

When we say, “Every human being runs,” and a contradictory negation is placed against it, the negative particle must be attached to the determination, so that against “Every human being runs” we have “Not every human being runs.” [Col. 0552D]

In propositions formed from an infinite subject-noun, however, whether in an affirmation or in a negation, the negation must not be separated from the subject-noun.

This can be recognized by a very simple argument if the determinations are temporarily removed and the propositions formed from an infinite subject-noun are examined as indefinite propositions. Let the indefinite affirmation be “A non-human being runs.” Against this will stand the negation “A non-human being does not run.”

If these propositions are made with universal terms—for “human being” is a universal term—but without an added determination, since they are predicated universally, that is, “every,” then in both the affirmation and the negation the negative particle has remained attached to the subject. The noun was always infinite, even when something determining was added; the negation must not be added to the determination but rather to the subject-noun. When the subject has been infinite in the affirmation, care must be taken that this same infinity reappear in the negation.

For just as a finite and simple term must be preserved in both affirmation and negation in indefinite propositions, so that we say “A human being runs” and “A human being does not run,” so also the same must be preserved in the proposition formed from an infinite subject-noun: what is the subject in the affirmation must remain the same in the negation.

If this occurs in indefinite propositions, why should it not also be required in those that are definite? Definite propositions differ from indefinite ones only in this: whereas indefinite propositions predicate universals, determined and definite propositions predicate the same universal with the addition and signification that it is predicated universally.

“Every” or “no one,” therefore, signifies nothing other than that what is called universal is predicated universally. Consequently, everything that was placed in the affirmation and negation of indefinite propositions must also be preserved in the same determined propositions. For “every” and “no one” are not terms but determinations of a universal term.

Having discussed these matters from Aristotle, let us also transfer from Syrianus—whom we have already mentioned as having the surname Philoxenus—the number of all the propositions considered in this discussion of the book, since it is exceedingly relevant and useful. First, it must be examined how many indefinite propositions there are in categorical propositions. For as many as the indefinite propositions are, so many will there be of the universal propositions, so many of the particular propositions, and so many of the propositions concerning singulars and individuals.

Let us first examine the affirmations in the following manner. There are four modes of propositions: they are either indefinite, universal, particular, or concerned with singulars and individuals. If, then, we determine how many indefinite affirmations there are, and multiply these by four, the number of affirmations is obtained. If this number is doubled, the number of negations is also obtained, as follows.

“Is” is either predicated alone or, together with something else, as a third element. If it is predicated alone, it is predicated either of a simple and finite noun or of an infinite noun. From these there are two affirmations:

- “Is a human being.”
- “Is a non-human being.”

Whenever “is” is predicated as a third element, there will be four affirmations:

- when the subject alone is infinite: “A non-human being is just”;
- when the predicate alone is infinite: “A human being is not just”;
- when both are finite: “A just human being is”;
- when both are infinite: “A non-just non-human being is.”

There will not be more propositions than these, as he himself says.

Since there are therefore six affirmations—two in which “is” is predicated and four in which it is predicated as an adjunct—if these are multiplied by four, twenty-four result. If these are again multiplied by two, the total rises to forty-eight. Thus there will be forty-eight affirmations and negations, whether “is” or the adjunct is predicated.

Since there are three other qualities of propositions, which are necessary, contingent, and signifying actuality or existence, and since all these propositions are uttered according to those qualities, if we multiply these forty-eight propositions by three according to the qualities of propositions, the total number of all the predicative propositions treated in this book will be one hundred and forty-four.

But now, setting aside these three qualities, we have written below the forty-eight propositions together with their negations. When they are multiplied according to the qualities of the propositions—necessary, contingent, and signifying actuality—there will be one hundred and forty-four.

> A human being is.  
> A non-just non-human being is.

| [Col. 0553] | |
|---|---|
| Is not a human being. | |
| Is every human being. | Is not every human being. |
| Is some human being. | Is not some human being. |
| Is Socrates. | Is not Socrates. |
| Is a just non-human being. | Is not a just non-human being. |
| Is every just non-human being. | Is not every just non-human being. |
| Is some just non-human being. | Is not some just non-human being. |
| Is a just non-Socrates. | Is not a just non-Socrates. |
| Is a non-human being. | Is not a non-human being. |
| Is every non-human being. | Is not every non-human being. |
| Is some non-human being. | Is not some non-human being. |
| Is a non-Socrates. | Is not a non-Socrates. |
| Is a non-just human being. | Is not a non-just human being. |
| Is every non-just human being. | Is not every non-just human being. |
| Is some non-just human being. | Is not some non-just human being. |
| Is a non-just Socrates. | Is not a non-just Socrates. |
| Is a just human being. | Is not a just human being. |
| Is every just human being. | Is not every just human being. |
| Is some just human being. | Is not some just human being. |
| Is a just Socrates. | Is not a just Socrates. |

| [Col. 0555] | |
|---|---|
| Is not a non-just non-human being. | |
| Is every non-just non-human being. | Is not every non-just non-human being. |
| Is some non-just non-human being. | Is not some non-just non-human being. |
| Is a non-just non-Socrates. | Is not a non-just non-Socrates. |

[Col. 0555A] Since Syrianus had gathered these propositions by calculation, we too have set them out individually, because confidence in the number will be easier if it is presented through examples. At the same time, someone who was badly educated had argued most perversely about these propositions, placing affirmations in the place of negations and, through negations, confusing the entire order. Therefore, so that no one might be led by his speech away from the truth of correct reasoning, we have arranged this material as an aid to a more lasting memory.

Since the negation contrary to “Every animal is just” is the one signifying “No animal is just,” it is clear that these contrary propositions will never be true together or of the same thing. Their opposites, however, will at some time be true together, namely “Not every animal is just” and “Some animal is just.” [Col. 0555B]

It was also demonstrated above with the greatest care that contraries sometimes divide truth and falsity between themselves if they are proposed either of natural things or of impossible things; but sometimes they can both be found false if they predicate things that are neither natural nor impossible.

They were said to be contraries when someone makes a universal utterance, whether affirmative or negative. Therefore, what he says now is this: “Contraries,” he says, “cannot be true together.” He did not say this without a certain determination of things. For he says:

“Since the negation contrary to ‘Every animal is just’—that is, contrary to the affirmation—is the one signifying ‘No animal is just’—that is, the negation—these, since they are contraries, cannot be true together.”

It is clear, he says, that they will never be true together or of the same thing.

What he said, “not true together,” has the following meaning. Nothing prevents both the universal affirmation and the universal negation from being truly proposed at different times. Thus, if someone says, “Every human being is just,” this would be most truly proposed if it were said in the golden age. If someone again says, “No human being is just,” this would be a true proposition if it were uttered in the iron age.

Thus it can happen that the universal affirmation and the universal negation are both true, although they are plainly contraries—but not at the same time. The former would hold in the golden age, if circumstances were such; the latter in the iron age. These times are different and do not coincide.

Therefore he correctly added that they can never be true together. What he added, “or of the same thing,” serves as another determination concerning the same matter. For again, the universal affirmation and universal negation can be true at the same time and together if they are not predicated of the same thing.

Suppose someone says, “Every animal is rational,” and predicates this of human beings; the affirmation is true. If someone says, “No animal is rational,” and predicates this of horses, the universal negation will also be true at one and the same time in opposition to the universal affirmation, but not of the same thing. The affirmation was made of human beings, whereas the negation was made of horses.

Therefore it was said that contrary propositions can never be true together or of the same thing—that is, neither at one and the same time nor of one and the same subject.

But since the opposites of these propositions are a particular negation opposed to the universal affirmation and a particular affirmation opposed to the universal negation, and since we said that these are called subcontraries because they undergo, in a certain way, something different from contraries, it is clear that just as contrary propositions cannot be true together, although they sometimes divide truth and falsity between themselves, so subcontraries sometimes divide truth and falsity between themselves when the contraries also divide them.

They can, however, be found true together when the universals and contraries are not both true. That they should be false together is impossible by any account of things.

No one, therefore, will ever be able to find contrary propositions true together and of the same thing. But the subcontraries, which are opposed to the universal propositions and contraries, can be found true when compared with one another, as in the very example he proposed:

- “Not every animal is just” is true.
- “Some animal is just” is also true.

Therefore nothing prevents subcontraries from being found true together, although contrary propositions cannot be true together.

Next comes “No human being is just,” followed by “Every human being is not just.” The proposition “Some human being is just” is opposed to “Not every human being is not just,” for it is necessary that there be someone who is just. [Col. 0556C]

He has already discussed sufficiently above the consequence of simple and infinite propositions. But now his purpose is not to show which particular affirmation follows a universal affirmation or negation, as he demonstrated above. Rather, he proposes to show which universal negation follows a universal affirmation, and which particular negation agrees with a particular affirmation.

He presents these four propositions, saying that the simple universal negation and the infinite universal affirmation follow one another and agree with one another; likewise, their opposites—the simple particular affirmation and the infinite particular negation—follow one another in truth and falsity and do not differ from one another in any way.

Let these four propositions be arranged as follows. First is the infinite universal affirmation:

“Every human being is not just.”

Under it is the simple universal negation that agrees with it:

“No human being is just.”

On the other side, against the infinite affirmation, is the simple particular affirmation:

“Some human being is just.”

Under this is the infinite particular negation:

“Not every human being is not just.”

| Infinite universal affirmation | Simple universal negation |
|---|---|
| Every human being is not just. | No human being is just. |
| Simple particular affirmation | Infinite particular negation |
| Some human being is just. | Not every human being is not just. |

[Col. 0557A] With these propositions arranged in this way, if the infinite universal affirmation “Every human being is not just” is true, then the proposition “No human being is just,” which is the simple universal negation, is also true. This becomes clearer from the examples below.

Let us say, “Every human being is not a quadruped.” This is true. Again, “No human being is a quadruped” is also true. If one of these is false, the other will also be false. For if “Every human being is not just” is false—as it is indeed false—then the simple negation “No human being is just” also makes a most false assertion.

Therefore the infinite universal affirmation and the simple universal negation agree with one another: if one is true, the other must be true; and if one is false, the falsity of the other follows.

The same thing occurs on the other side. For if “Some human being is just” is true, then “Not every human being is not just” is also true, since there is someone who is just.

“Not every” has the same force as if someone said “Some is not,” as becomes clearer in another example. If someone says, “Not every human being is just,” this means “Some human being is not just.” Therefore “not every” signifies “some is not.”

If someone proposes, “Some human being is not not-just,” that is, someone whom he says is not non-just, he confirms to be just. For the person of whom it is said that he is not non-just will be just.

Thus the proposition “Not every human being is not just” agrees with “Some human being is just.” But it does not agree with “Some human being is not just.” Therefore it does not agree with the proposition “Not every human being is not just.” [Col. 0557C]

Because this may perhaps appear somewhat obscure, the consequences of the propositions should be taken in the following way.

Let us posit that the infinite universal affirmation and the simple universal negation agree with one another, so that the truth or falsity of one is followed by the truth or falsity of the other.

If the infinite universal affirmation “Every human being is not just” is false, its contradictory opposite, the infinite particular negation “Not every human being is not just,” will be true. But when the infinite universal affirmation is false, the simple universal negation “No human being is just” is also false. Since this is false, its contradictory opposite, the simple particular affirmation “Some human being is just,” must be true.

Therefore, when the infinite universal affirmation is false, the infinite particular negation is true; and when the simple universal negation is false, the simple particular affirmation is true. But the infinite universal affirmation and the simple universal negation are false together and agree with each other in falsity. Consequently, the simple particular affirmation and the infinite particular negation will be true together.

Again, if the infinite universal affirmation is true, the infinite particular negation will be false, since it is opposed to it as its contradictory. If the simple universal negation is also true, the simple particular affirmation will be false. But if the infinite universal affirmation and the simple universal negation are true together, then the simple particular affirmation and the infinite particular negation will be false together.

Therefore these two—the simple particular affirmation and the infinite particular negation—also agree with each other in truth and falsity, and their truth and falsity follow one another.

Thus the affirmation and negation, both universal—one simple, the other infinite—follow and agree with one another. The particulars opposed to the universals—the simple affirmative and the infinite negative—also agree with each other. The correct order is therefore that just as the simple universal negation agrees with the infinite universal affirmation, so the infinite particular negation agrees with the simple particular affirmation. [Col. 0558B]

It is also clear that the same applies to singulars. If it is true to deny what it is also true to affirm, then, for example:

“Do you think Socrates is wise?”

“No.”

“Therefore Socrates is not wise.”

In universal propositions, however, the proposition expressed in the same way is not true. The negation is true, as in:

“Do you think every human being is wise?”

“No.”

“Therefore every human being is not wise.”

This conclusion is false. Rather:

“Therefore not every human being is wise”

is true. The latter is the opposite, whereas the former is contrary.

While discussing the consequence of propositions and explaining how they agree with one another, he briefly departed from that discussion in order to teach what follows in responses concerning singular propositions when the negative particle is added to their predicate, and what follows in propositions concerning universals when the negative particle is added to the predicate. For utterances must not be formed in the same way, since what follows from the two kinds of predication is not alike.

This becomes clear as follows. If someone, questioned about a singular, gives a negative answer, the person who asked can form a conclusion from an infinite predicate-noun by joining to it the negation that the respondent previously gave; and he will predicate this truthfully.

In the case of universals, however, it will be apparent that the same truth cannot follow if an affirmation is composed in this way.

Suppose someone asks another:

“Do you think Socrates is wise?”

If he answers, “No,” the questioner correctly concludes:

“Therefore Socrates is not wise.”

Likewise, let this be made clear in another example. If we ask someone:

“Is Socrates Roman?”

and he answers, “No,” we can correctly conclude:

“Therefore Socrates is not Roman.”

We form an affirmation from the negation that he gave and from the noun predicated in the proposition, producing an affirmation from an infinite noun:

“Socrates is not wise,” or “Socrates is not Roman.”

It was shown above that these are affirmations formed from an infinite noun.

If, then, someone asks about universal subjects in the same way:

“Is every human being wise?”

we will of course answer:

“No.”

The questioner then concludes by the same reasoning:

“Therefore every human being is not wise.”

Consequently:

“No human being is wise,”

for “Every human being is not wise” was shown to agree with “No human being is wise.”

It will therefore appear that a false conclusion has somehow been inferred from a true answer. Our response is that we gave a negation, but not one in which the negation was to be joined to the predicate. Rather, it was to be joined to the determination.

For we did not intend to remove wisdom from every human being when, upon being asked whether every human being was wise, we answered negatively. Rather, we intended to withdraw it from “every,” that is, from the determination, signifying that wisdom belonged to some and did not belong to others. Thus what we said, “No,” had the same force as “Not every.” [Col. 0559B]

If that negation is joined to the noun—that is, to “wisdom”—the universal affirmation “Every human being is not wise” is formed, and this agrees with the finite universal negation “No human being is wise.” But the latter is contrary to the question. For the question was, “Is every human being wise?” This contains a universal affirmation, to which the universal negation is contrary; and the infinite universal affirmation again agrees with that negation.
