Consequently, the infinite universal affirmation “Every human being is not wise” is also contrary to the simple universal affirmation placed in the question, namely “Is every human being wise?”

If, however, one says, “Not every human being is wise,” this is true and is opposed to the question. For against the question “Is every human being wise?” when the answer is “No,” and the negation is joined to “every,” a particular negation is formed:

“Not every human being is wise.”

This is opposed to the universal affirmation in the question. This is what he says:

“This is opposite, whereas that is contrary.”

The sense of his words is as follows. It is clear, he says, that in singulars, such as Socrates and whatever is individual, if it is true to deny what one is asked—that is, if someone truly gives a negative answer when asked something—then the questioner can make an infinite affirmation from the negation and the predicate-noun.

The example is:

“Do you think Socrates is wise?”

Response: “No.”

Conclusion: “Therefore Socrates is not wise.”

But the matter does not proceed similarly in universals. This is shown by the statement:

“In universals, the proposition expressed in the same way is not true.”

That is, the infinite affirmation formed from the predicate-noun and the respondent’s negation is not true. Rather, the negation is true, not the affirmation.

The example is:

“Do you think every human being is wise?”

Response: “No.”

False conclusion:

“Therefore every human being is not wise.”

This is false and does not function like the proposition previously given concerning a singular subject. Rather, the true proposition is:

“Therefore not every human being is wise.”

Here the respondent’s negation is joined to “every,” and a particular negation is formed. This is true and is also the opposite proposition. For when the universal affirmation “Is every human being wise?” is asked, the negative particle produces in the conclusion:

“Not every human being is wise.”

These propositions are opposed. The former is a universal affirmation, the latter a particular negation; the former, however, is contrary to the universal negation.

If the negation is joined to the predicate, an infinite universal affirmation is formed, which agrees with the finite universal negation. But this is contrary to the finite universal affirmation placed in the question. Therefore the infinite universal affirmation is also contrary.

The reason must be sought why, in the case of singulars, either the affirmation from an infinite noun or the negation agrees with the finite proposition, whereas in universals the universal affirmation from an infinite noun does not agree with the finite particular negation.

If someone says, “Socrates is non-wise” and “Socrates is not wise,” the meaning is the same, and the two propositions agree with one another. But if someone says, “Every human being is not wise” and again, “Not every human being is wise,” the two propositions do not agree with one another.

The reason is that in propositions with singular subjects there are not two oppositions but only one, namely the opposition that makes a negation. In universals predicated universally, however, there are two oppositions: one contrary and one contradictory.

Suppose, then, that there is an affirmation:

“Socrates is wise.”

Against this there is one opposition:

“Socrates is not wise.”

If someone says, “Socrates is not wise,” this will have no other meaning than “Socrates is not wise,” since we said that there is only one opposition in singulars. Therefore, whatever other forms occur will converge upon the same signification.

In universals predicated universally, however, the situation is different. If there is the universal affirmation:

“Every human being is wise,”

then against it stand both:

“No human being is wise,”

and:

“Not every human being is wise.”

The former is contrary; the latter contradictory.

The simple opposition therefore cannot agree with the infinite affirmation. The one removes the whole universal by means of a universal negation; the other removes a determinate part by means of a particular negation.

But the universal negation agrees with the universal affirmation formed from an infinite noun. This, therefore, will also differ from the finite particular negation. Since there are two oppositions in universals but only one in singulars, it is correct that the same truth and falsity should not follow from the same form of predication.

Those that are opposed according to indefinite names or verbs, as in “not-human” or “not-just,” will seem to be negations without a noun or verb, but they are not. For a negation must always be either true or false. Whoever says “not-human,” however, says no more than one who says “human,” but rather less; without the addition of something else, it is neither true nor false.

We know that propositions can be formed from indefinite names. Aristotle therefore resolves this question by taking the expression of the indefinite name in itself and discussing whether, when it is set against a definite name, it appears to constitute some sort of enunciative opposition. If someone takes what is called “not-human” and sets it against what we call “human,” it may perhaps seem to produce opposition to some extent. For since every negative particle added to a verb that contains a proposition produces a negation—even if some mode of proposition is not predicated, as will be demonstrated later—so too, when a negative particle is added to a name, it seems to produce a kind of negation. Thus, if “not” is joined to “human,” it produces “not-human.” This is what he means:

Those opposed according to indefinite names or verbs, as in “not-human” or “not-just,” seem to be negations without a noun or verb. For if someone says “he does not run,” this is a negation without a noun; and if someone says “not-human,” this too is a negation without a verb. These expressions, formed according to an indefinite name or verb, are opposed to the definite name or verb “human” and “runs.” They will therefore seem to be negations according to the indefinite name or verb that is predicated, but they are not.

The strongest reason proving that these are not negations is that every negation is true or false. What we call “not-human” or “does not run,” however, although the simple and definite expressions “human” and “runs” themselves signify nothing true or false, nevertheless signify even less that is true or false. It is not that the simple expressions signify something true or false; for this reason we say that indefinite expressions display less truth or falsity than simple ones. Yet although a simple noun or verb signifies nothing true or false, it nevertheless presents something definite: in “human,” for example, there is something definite and a single species. But whoever says “not-human” removes the species currently under consideration and suggests an indeterminate number of other things, positing none of them. Accordingly, although definite verbs or names cannot in themselves be true or false unless they are joined with other expressions, indefinite names or verbs are even less capable of truth or falsity, since they do not even posit the thing they signify; they merely remove it and establish nothing else in its signification. Finally, definite expressions are more closely related to truth and falsity in their intelligible content. The expression of an indefinite name is therefore less true or false than that of some simple and definite term.

[Col. 0561D] “Every not-human is just” signifies the same as none of those, nor is its opposite “not every not-human is just.” But “every not-just is not-human” signifies the same as “no just is not-human.”

After he has discussed propositions having an indefinite predicate at sufficient length, shown their oppositions, and demonstrated their consequences—and after briefly noting in the middle of the discussion that indefinite names are not negations—he now returns to propositions that have an indefinite subject, with either a definite or an indefinite predicate. First he teaches whether these propositions are identical, signify the same thing, and stand in any order of consequence to one another: namely, those formed from an indefinite subject, compared with those formed from an indefinite predicate or with those formed from two definite terms.

He says that these two propositions, “Every not-human is just” and “Not every not-human is just,” signify the same as none of those propositions formed either from two definite terms or from an indefinite predicate. Let the propositions formed from two definite terms or from an indefinite predicate be arranged as follows: first, let the simple universal affirmation be placed above; beneath it, let the universal negation formed from an indefinite predicate be placed, agreeing with the simple affirmation above. Conversely, let the simple universal negation be placed above, and beneath it the universal affirmation formed from an indefinite predicate, which plainly agrees with the preceding universal affirmation formed from an indefinite predicate.

> **Every human is just** — **No human is just**
>
> Agreeing
>
> Contrary
>
> Contrary
>
> Agreeing
>
> **No human is not-just** — **Every human is not-just**

Since the affirmations and negations have thus been arranged—having a simple subject and either an indefinite or a simple predicate—Aristotle now says that the propositions having an indefinite subject signify the same as none of the preceding propositions. For “Every not-human is just” agrees neither with “Every human is just,” nor with “Every human is not-just,” nor with “No human is just” or “No human is not-just.” All of these have “human” as their subject, whereas the former has “not-human.” Therefore its negation—that is, the particular negation of the universal affirmation with an indefinite subject—cannot agree with any of those having a definite subject. “Not every not-human is just” agrees neither with “Every human is just,” nor with “Every human is not-just,” nor with “No human is just” or “No human is not-just.”

But he does not mean that propositions formed with an indefinite subject differ from those formed with either a definite or an indefinite predicate while retaining a definite subject. For predicates can indeed be different while sometimes signifying the same thing. Thus “Every human is unjust,” although different from “No human is just,” may nevertheless signify the same thing when a privative affirmation has preceded. For it has been said that negations would undoubtedly follow preceding affirmations.

He therefore does not mean that propositions formed with an indefinite subject differ from propositions formed with a definite subject and either a definite or an indefinite predicate merely because they are different propositions. Rather, he means that they do not agree with one another at all, or do not signify the same thing—in other words, that in the full force of the proposition they are wholly dissimilar.

He has thus spoken of propositions having a definite subject and either an indefinite or a definite predicate. He now turns to their consequences: propositions formed with an indefinite name as subject and propositions formed from two indefinite terms. Just as above he taught the consequence between propositions formed from two definite terms or from an indefinite predicate, so now conversely he shows what consequence exists among those formed from two indefinite names or from an indefinite name as subject. He says:

“Every not-just is not-human” signifies the same as “No just is not-human.”

He shows that these two propositions alone are in question: the universal affirmation formed from two indefinite terms, “Every not-just is not-human,” agrees with the universal negation formed from an indefinite subject alone, “No just is not-human.” In these propositions the verb “is” is understood, so that the complete propositions are “Every not-just is not-human” and “No just is not-human.” For just as, among propositions having a definite subject and either an indefinite or a definite predicate, the affirmation with a definite subject and indefinite predicate—“Every human is not-just”—was followed by the simple universal negation formed from two definite terms, “No human is just,” so here, with the subjects merely exchanged, the same relation appears.

There, the universal negation formed from two definite terms followed the affirmation formed from a definite subject and an indefinite predicate. Here, likewise, the universal affirmation formed from two indefinite terms is followed by the universal negation formed from an indefinite subject. Both propositions are universal, and he has written down these two alone, showing only their consequence. He omitted the others because he thought they were easy to understand. But so that nothing may seem to have been left out, we add them here. The consequence is as follows:

- Every not-human is not-just.
- Every not-human is just.
- No not-human is just.
- No not-human is not-just.
- Some not-human is just.
- Some not-human is not-just.
- Not every not-human is not-just.
- Not every not-human is just.

[Col. 0563] Whoever examines these carefully will see that the two comparisons display a consequence and agreement most fittingly corresponding to the two [preceding] comparisons.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0563]

[Col. 0563C] We shall now undertake, with greater boldness and confidence, the greater part of the work that remains, although it is obstructed by major difficulties. We must not become weary in the individual sections, since we have begun to disclose and clarify the doctrine of the whole of dialectic. Accordingly, we shall weave together a continuous and orderly exposition.

Transposed names and verbs signify the same thing, as in “a white human is” and “a human is white.” For if this were not so, there would be several negations of the same proposition. But it has been shown that one proposition has one negation. The negation of “a white human is” is “a white human is not.” But if “a human is white” is not identical with “a white human is,” its negation would be either “a not-human white is not” or “a human white is not.” Yet the former is the negation of “a not-human white is,” while the latter is the negation of “a white human is.” Thus there would be two negations of one proposition.

He now teaches that, when names and verbs are transposed, and one is predicated earlier and the other later, they unquestionably retain the same signification. Whether someone says “a human is white,” “a white human is,” “a white human is,” or “a human white is,” or rearranges the order of predication in any other way, the signification unquestionably remains the same.

This may not be perceived in the same way by orators and poets as by dialecticians. For so far as the composition of speech is concerned, it makes the greatest difference in what order the verbs and names of a predication are uttered. It matters greatly, for example, whether Cicero’s words are said as he wrote them:

> “Nature brought you forth for this madness, desire exercised you, fortune preserved you,”

or instead:

> “For this madness nature brought you forth, desire exercised you, fortune preserved you.”

In the latter arrangement the grandeur of the sentence is diminished, and what stands out when it is composed in the former way shines less brightly and is less clearly disclosed to the ears and minds of men, even against their will.

Again, when Virgil says:

> “Pacique imponere morem” (“and to impose a custom upon peace”),

he could have preserved the meter by saying:

> “moremque imponere paci” (“and to impose a custom upon peace”);

but the sound would have been weaker, and the verse would not have been composed with such a splendid rhythmic impact as it is now.

Thus the changed order of words and names does not have the same force for orators and poets. Those concerned with composition find much ornament in the arrangement of words. Dialecticians, however, who have no concern for the elegance of speech and investigate truth alone, consider it irrelevant in what order words and names are rearranged, provided that they retain the same force in signification as before.

Yet even among dialecticians the same force and signification are not always preserved when the order of an expression is rearranged in every possible way. The negative particle “not” is of great importance and produces great differences when added in different places.

If someone says, “A white human is not,” he produces an indefinite negation. If someone says, “A human not-white is,” he produces an indefinite affirmation with an indefinite predicate. If someone says, “A not-human white is,” he likewise establishes an indefinite affirmation with an indefinite subject.

Again, if someone predicates, “Every human is not-just,” this agrees with “No human is just.” But if the same “not” is not placed with the universal determination, so that one says “Not every human is just,” this is no longer a universal affirmation with an indefinite predicate agreeing with a simple universal negation; rather, it is a simple particular negation.

Do you see, then, how many differences the negative particle produces when joined to different predications of names? Nevertheless, the same particle can, when placed in different positions, preserve the same force and signification in another way. If the particle “not” is placed together with its universal determination, and that entire expression is repeatedly transposed, the signification unquestionably remains the same.

If someone says, “Not every human is white,” this is a simple particular negation. If someone instead says, “Human—not-every—white—is” (*homo non omnis albus est*), the signification is the same. Or if one says, “Human—white—not-every—is” (*homo albus non omnis est*), this too does not depart from the preceding signification. Likewise, if someone rearranges it still further and says, “Human—white—is—not-every” (*homo albus est non omnis*), there is no difference from the original signification. In whatever other way the expression is rearranged, provided that the proper determination of universality is itself rearranged along with it, the same signification must always be preserved.

Similarly, if the same particle “not,” joined to another name or verb, is repeatedly transposed—as when we say “A just human is not,” “A human is not just,” and “A human is not just” (*non est homo justus*)—the same signification is retained. Accordingly, if only the negative particle is transposed and is not always predicated in the same order, it will produce many differences among propositions. But if it is transposed together with another name, as has been said, the same signification will remain through all the transpositions.

With these matters arranged, we must examine Aristotle’s demonstration that transposed verbs and names always have the same force and signification. He says:

> “Transposed verbs and names signify the same thing, as in ‘a white human is’ and ‘a human is white.’”

For these names and verbs, although transposed, retain the same signification. In the first expression “white” comes first and “human” second; in the other, “human” comes first and “white” second. If this is false, and the two expressions are not the same but differ from each other, something impossible and absurd follows: there will be two negations of one affirmation. But it has been shown that one affirmation has one negation.

Let us now see how, if the affirmations “a white human is” and “a human is white” are not identical but different, there can be two negations of one affirmation. Let them first be arranged as follows:

> A white human is.  
> A human is white.

The negation of the proposition “A white human is” will be “A white human is not,” since no other reasonable possibility can be found. Let the affirmation and its proper negation be arranged again:

> A white human is.  
> A white human is not.  
> A human is white. [Col. 0566A]

Since the negation of “A white human is” is “A white human is not,” if “A human is white” differs from the proposition “A white human is,” it will have another negation. Let that negation therefore be either “A not-human white is not” or “A human white is not.” Let the two affirmations first be set down alternately, with the negation of the first placed opposite it; against the second, let both of the negations just mentioned be written:

> A white human is.  
> A white human is not.  
> A human is white.  
> A human white is not.  
> A not-human white is not.

Once these have been distinguished, “A not-human white is not” cannot be the negation of “A human is white.” It is the negation of the proposition having an indefinite subject, namely “A not-human white is.” Likewise, whatever other negation one might posit, another affirmation can unquestionably be found corresponding to it. It follows that the negation of “A human is white” must be “A human white is not.”

But “A human white is not” is also the negation of the affirmation “A white human is.” This is proved by the fact that the two divide truth and falsity between them: if it is true that a white human exists, it is false that a human white does not exist.

If this is found to be true in some cases, that is recognized according to the definition of the proposition, not according to the form of the negation. In that respect the propositions are opposed more according to quantity than according to quality. This is shown if someone says, “Every human is white,” and “Not every human is white” is placed against it. It is evident that these divide truth and falsity between them: one must be true and the other false.

Therefore, even if the determinations are removed, the same opposition returns, although the proposition becomes indefinite. Just as, in the case of “Every human is just” and “Not every human is just,” when “every” and “not every” are removed, “A human is just” and “A human is not just” are opposed, so here too, when “every” and “not every” are removed, “A white human is” is opposed to “A human white is not.”

When the determinations are added, one is always true and the other false. But we have said that the negation of the affirmation “A white human is” is “A white human is not.” Thus “A white human is not” and “A human white is not” are two negations of one affirmation, namely “A human is white.” This would follow if “A human white is not” and “A white human is not” were different from one another, which in turn follows from the prior assumption that “A white human is” differs from “A human is white.”

But it is impossible for one affirmation to have two negations. Since it is evident that both “A white human is not” and “A human white is not” are opposed to the affirmation “A human is white,” these two negations are not different from one another; they agree with one another and differ only in the transposition of the name. In every other respect they are identical. If the negations are identical, the affirmations too are identical. It was therefore rightly said that transposed names and verbs preserve the same force and signification.

The entire sense is accordingly as follows, while the order of the words is this:

> “Transposed names and verbs,” he says, “signify the same thing.” An example of this is “A human is white” and “A white human is.” In these expressions the names are transposed.

For if this were not so—that is, if transposed names and verbs did not signify the same thing—something impossible and absurd would follow. He says that there would be several negations of the same thing, that is, several negations of the same affirmation. But this is impossible, since it has been shown that one affirmation has one negation.

He demonstrates as follows that, if transposed verbs and names did not signify the same thing, two negations would be opposed to one affirmation. The negation of “A white human is,” namely “A white human is not,” is properly opposed to that affirmation. But if “A human is white,” that is, the other affirmation, is not identical with “A white human is”—if it differs from the first proposition and does not agree with it—it will have some negation, either “A white human is not” or some other expression. Any such proposal can be refuted by the same reasoning, which he also uses here.

He says:

> “One is the negation of ‘A not-human white is,’ while the other is the negation of ‘A white human is.’”

Of the two negations he has posited—“A not-human white is not” and “A human white is not”—the former is the negation of the affirmation having an indefinite subject, “A not-human white is.” The latter, namely “A human white is not,” is the negation of “A white human is,” since it divides truth and falsity with it. Thus there would be two negations of one affirmation, which is impossible.

Since, then, it is clear that when a name and a verb are transposed the affirmation and negation remain the same, the point is established.

He confirms the preceding argument with this conclusion of the proposition. He has constructed the syllogism in the second hypothetical mode, which he calls indemonstrable, as follows: If the first is, the second is; but the second is not; therefore the first is not. That is: if, when verbs and names are transposed, the propositions are not identical, there are two negations; but this is impossible. Therefore the propositions are not different when the verbs and names are transposed.

# CONJUNCT AND DIVIDED ENUNCIATIONS

To affirm or deny one thing of several things, or several things of one thing, does not constitute one affirmation or one negation if no one thing is formed from the several. By “one” I do not mean merely that one name has been posited while no one thing is formed from its several significations. “Human,” for example, may perhaps be animal, tame, and two-footed, and one thing is formed from these; but from “white,” “human,” and “to walk,” no one thing is formed.

Therefore, even if someone affirms one thing of these, there will not be one affirmation, but one utterance and many affirmations. Nor, if he affirms these of one thing, will there be one affirmation; there will likewise be several.

Many people are confused by the obscurity of this passage and cannot adequately explain or clarify what Aristotle says. We have already stated that it was a matter of great concern among the leaders of the Peripatetic school to determine which affirmation or negation was one and which was several. They are not recognized by the sound of the utterance or by the number of terms. For one thing may indeed be predicated of one thing without the enunciation being one. Conversely, several things may be predicated of one thing, or one thing of several, and yet one enunciation may be formed from all of them. They took great care over this point, so that whenever the relevant rule arose, it would not remain unnoticed.

If someone says, “A dog is an animal,” this is not one enunciation, because “dog” signifies many things. But if someone says, “A human is a rational, mortal animal,” or “A rational, mortal animal is a human,” each is one enunciation. The reason is that one thing can be formed from all the terms, since from “animal,” “rational,” and “mortal,” taken together, one human is constituted.

There are also cases in which several things are predicated, from which no one thing can be formed or constituted—neither when they are predicated of something else nor when something else is predicated of them. In such cases there is one affirmation or negation only in appearance; in reality as many affirmations must be said to exist as there are things predicated of one thing or of which one thing is predicated.

Thus, when we say, “Socrates, bald, a philosopher, walks,” nothing single is joined together from baldness, philosophy, and walking, such that these might form something like one species. Therefore, whether these are predicated of one thing or one thing is predicated of them, the enunciation cannot be one. The general sense of the entire proposition is therefore this.

Let us now turn to Aristotle’s own words. He says:

> “To affirm or deny one thing of several things, or several things of one thing, if no one thing is formed from the several, is not one affirmation or one negation.”

If, he says, you predicate several things of one thing—as when you say, “Socrates is a philosopher, snub-nosed, and bald”—or, conversely, predicate one thing of several—as when you say, “Socrates, snub-nosed, philosopher, bald, is”—if no single thing is formed from the several things that you predicate or subject, just as one thing can be formed from what we predicate, namely “animated, sensible substance,” which becomes “animal,” then there is neither one affirmation nor one negation.

For several things are either predicated or subjected, from the collection of which no single species arises. If someone predicates one thing of one thing whose single name signifies several things, from which no one thing is formed, then again there is neither one affirmation nor one negation.

If someone says, “A dog is an animal,” the name “dog” signifies a barking animal, a celestial body, and a marine creature; nothing single is formed from these when they are joined together. Since no one thing can be formed from these several meanings, the name “dog” does not yield one affirmation or one negation when it is predicated or subjected, since it signifies many things from which no one thing can be formed.

This is what he shows by saying:

> “By ‘one’ I do not mean that one name has been posited, while no one thing is formed from those things.”

For one name can be predicated of one thing. But if one name signifies several things, from which no one thing is formed, there is neither one negation nor one affirmation. For it is not the single utterance that completes the enunciation, but the simplicity of what is signified—or, if several things are collected into one, their capacity to produce something single.

He then added an example that has misled many, saying:

> “For example, ‘A human is perhaps an animal, two-footed, and tame.’ But from these one thing is formed; from white, human, and walking, no one thing is formed.”

Some have thought that he spoke in this way to show, by way of example, that he was offering something like a definition, lest anyone suppose that he had proposed as the true definition of a human the formula “a two-footed, tame animal.” For this reason, they say, he added “perhaps,” and said “animal, two-footed, and tame,” so that no one would think that Aristotle considered such a formula to be the definition of a human.

Others did not understand it in this way. Rather, they interpreted Aristotle’s wording as expressing the following sense: “A human is that which is animal, two-footed, and tame.” From this, they say, one should understand that “human” stands equally in relation to what is human and to what is an animal, two-footed, and tame.

Accordingly, if to say “human” is the same as to say “animal, two-footed, tame,” then whenever several things are predicated of one thing—that is, when animal, two-footed, and tame are predicated of human—because what is one is equal to “human,” one thing is being predicated, although three utterances seem to be predicated.

But all these interpreters understand nothing at all. There is a better exposition, which Porphyry gave. Aristotle, he says, wishing to demonstrate which affirmation was one and which was not one, first said that to predicate several things of one thing, or to subject several things to one thing, is not to make one enunciation unless one thing is formed from those several things.

Then, observing that affirmations could still be several even among predicates that, although several, could nevertheless form one thing from themselves, he added the example:

> “A human is perhaps an animal, two-footed, and tame.”

What I mean is this: it is clear that if several things are predicated of one thing, from which no one thing can be formed, or if several things are subjected to one thing, from which no one thing is formed, there is neither one affirmation nor one negation.

But let us now consider several things from which one thing can be formed. We shall find that even among these there can sometimes be several enunciations according to the manner of utterance, and not one, although one thing can be formed from the several terms.

If someone says, “A rational, mortal animal is a human,” joining “animal,” “rational,” and “mortal” together continuously, this is one affirmation, because one thing is formed from them. But if there is some interval, as when someone says, “A human animal,” then again “rational,” and after pausing for a while says “mortal is,” this is neither one affirmation nor one negation. The interruption produces several enunciations.

Again, if the terms are spoken with conjunctions—“A human is animal and rational and mortal”—there are likewise several propositions. It makes no difference whether someone says this by pausing or by inserting conjunctions, or says:

> “A human is an animal; a human is rational; a human is mortal.”

These are plainly several propositions.

Seeing this, Aristotle said:

> “A human is perhaps an animal, two-footed, and tame.”

By “perhaps,” he means something like this: it may be that, concerning a human, an animal, a two-footed thing, and a tame thing, one thing is formed; but sometimes several propositions arise when a certain conjunction separates and distinguishes the terms.

For “human and animal” may perhaps form one proposition, “two-footed” another, and “tame” another. But from all these together one thing is formed; when they are uttered continuously, because one thing is produced from them, the proposition is one. The same does not happen in every case. From “white,” “human,” and “walking,” no one thing is formed.

If someone says, “Socrates, a white human, walks,” this is not one affirmation, because no species at all is formed from human, whiteness, and walking.

The conclusion is therefore that, even if one thing is predicated of several things from which no one thing is formed—as when one thing is predicated of a terrestrial barking dog, a celestial dog, and a marine dog—because no single thing is formed from them, and even if one thing is predicated of these several things, as when we say “dog,” a name signifying several things from which no one thing is formed does not produce one affirmation or one negation when it is predicated of something or subjected to something else. There will indeed be one utterance, but several affirmations.

Whether one thing is predicated of several things from which no one thing is formed, or several such things are predicated of one thing; whether one thing is predicated of one thing whose predicate signifies several things from which no one thing is formed; or whether that predicate is subjected to something else—in every case there is neither one affirmation nor one negation.

The rule is this: an affirmation is one if either two terms signify single things, or if several things are predicated of one thing or subjected to one thing in such a way that one thing can be formed from them, or if one name, whether predicated or subjected, signifies several things capable of being gathered together so as to constitute in some way a single species.

If, then, a dialectical question is a request for an answer—whether for a proposition or for the other part of a contradiction—and a proposition is one part of a contradiction, there will not be one answer to these cases. For neither is the question one, even if it is true. These matters were discussed in the *Topics*.

At the same time, it is clear that even the question “What is this?” is not a dialectical question. It must be given in such a way that the person questioned may choose which part of the contradiction he wishes to enunciate. The questioner must determine whether this is a human or not this.

Whoever uses a dialectical question either asks a simple question and puts a single proposition into the question, so that there may be a single answer to it, or, by asking both alternatives, states two propositions to which no simple answer can be given, but to which one entire proposition must be answered. For if the questioner says, “Is Socrates an animal?” the answer to this is either “Yes” or “No.” But if someone asks in this way, “Is Socrates an animal, or is he not?” there is no single answer to this. For if one answers “Yes,” it is unknown to which of the two one has assented, the affirmation or the negation; and if one answers “No,” it is again unknown which one wishes to deny, the affirmation or the negation. Therefore, to questions of this kind an entire proposition must be answered—that is, one or the other part of the contradiction, either the whole affirmation or the whole negation—so that one says either, “Socrates is an animal,” or, if this does not seem right, answers, “Socrates is not an animal.”

In matters composed of many elements from which no single thing can be formed, if a single question is made, the question itself is defective, as is the single answer to it. For whoever asks several questions in one, from which a single proposition cannot be formed, makes many questions; and if one answers them simply, even if the answer itself is true, one is nevertheless rightly reproved. A manyfold question requires a manyfold answer. For if the questioner says, “Is Socrates a philosopher, and does he read and walk?” it may be that he is a philosopher and reads but does not walk, or walks but does not read; it may also be that he both reads and walks. To such a proposition, therefore, there will not be one answer. For whoever asks, “Is Socrates a philosopher, and does he read and walk?” has asked either ignorantly or deceptively. If it should happen that Socrates is a philosopher, reads, and walks, and he answers, “Yes,” this answer too is censured. For one answer ought not to be given to several questions, even if the single answer truly answers them—as in this case, if he is both a philosopher and reads and walks.

[Col. 0571C] Therefore, if a dialectical question is a request for an answer through which a proposition may be made—just as when someone asks, “Is it day?” and another answers, “No,” from this a negation is formed, “It is not day,” or certainly the other part of an opposition when the question is, “Is it day, or is it not day?” so that the appropriate answer is either “It is day” or “It is not day,” that is, an entire proposition—those questions which are formed from several elements, when no single proposition can be made from them, are not simple questions. Accordingly, neither is a simple answer to be given to them. He recalls that he has discussed these matters in the *Topics*.

Again, since a dialectical question is a request for an answer—as was said above—either for a proposition or for the other part of a contradiction, as will be shown shortly, those ask incompetently who say, “What is an animal?” or “What is a human being?” For the person who asks dialectically must give the respondent the choice, arising from the question, of selecting either the affirmation or the negation. But whoever asks in such a way as to demand that the respondent say what a thing is is not asking a dialectical question.

Some people, however, ask in the following way: “Do you think that the soul is fire?” When the respondent denies this, they add: “Do you not think that there is some intermediate body between fire and air, so that the soul is such a thing?” When the respondent denies this as well, they continue: “Or perhaps do you rather think that the soul is water or earth?” When the respondent has agreed that the soul is neither earth nor water, they then, wearied by their questions, ask: “What, then, is the soul?” But this [Col. 0572A] is not a dialectical question; it is rather the question of a student wishing to learn something from a teacher. For one who wishes to learn something asks someone capable of teaching what the thing about which he is uncertain is. A dialectician, however, as has been said, ought to ask in such a way that the respondent has the opportunity to choose whether he wishes to affirm or deny.

For one must understand that every question is a request for an answer. A dialectical question, however, is not a request for just any answer, but for one that has an opposition in both directions. Therefore, the question “What is it?” is not a dialectical question. One must ask in such a way that the respondent can choose one or the other part of the contradiction on the basis of the question. The questioner must determine and define whether the thing said is the case or is not the case: “Is a human being an animal, or is he not?” Thus the respondent may give either the affirmation [Col. 0572B] or the negation.

What he said, namely, that a dialectical question is a request for an answer, either for a proposition or for the other part of a contradiction, means the following. Whoever asks for an affirmation either seeks that same affirmation—that the hearer should answer him accordingly—or seeks its contradiction. Thus, if someone asks, “Is a human being an animal?” and the other assents, he has returned the proposition, namely the one proposed by the questioner. But if, when someone asks whether a human being is an animal, the respondent says, “He is not,” he will be seen to have answered with a contradiction. The one asked for the affirmation; the other answered with the negation, which is a contradiction.

Again, if one asks for a negation and the other answers with a negation, he has returned the same proposition that the questioner had previously proposed. But if, when someone asks for the negation, the other answers with the affirmation, a contradiction has been given in answer. This, then, is what he means when he says that a question is a request for an answer; and he adds: a request for what kind of answer? Either for a proposition, if the respondent gives the same answer as the questioner asks for, or for the other part of the contradiction, if, when the questioner asks for the affirmation, the respondent answers with the negation, or if, when the questioner puts the negation into his question, the respondent returns the affirmation in his answer.

According to the Peripatetics, a question has two species: either it is a dialectical question, or it is not dialectical. The non-dialectical question has two species. One occurs when, taking an accident as our starting point, we ask to what it belongs—for example, when we see Cicero’s house and ask who lives there—or when we take the subject itself, or the thing, as our starting point, but ask what accident belongs to it—for example, if someone sees Cicero himself and asks where he is staying. This is one species of the questions that we ask non-dialectically according to accident.

The other species occurs when, putting forward a name, we ask what it is, seeking its genus, difference, or definition—for example, if someone asks what an animal is. Or it occurs when we take a definition or one of the things just mentioned and ask whose definition it is—for example, if someone asks, “Of what is ‘rational, mortal animal’ the definition?”

Since some predicates are predicated in combination, so that the whole of the things predicated outside the subject constitutes one predicate, while others are not, what the difference is must be determined. For it is true to say of a human being both that he is an animal and that he is two-footed, and these form one thing. It is also true to say of him that he is human and white, and these too form one thing. But it is not the case that, if he is a cithara-player and good, he is thereby a good cithara-player.

For if, because each is said separately, both were also said together, many absurdities would result. It is true to say of a human being both “human” and “white,” and therefore also “the whole.” Again, if “white,” then also “the whole.” Therefore there will be “a white human being,” and this will continue infinitely. Again, there will be “a musical white walking human being,” and these same terms will repeatedly be combined without end. Further, if Socrates is Socrates, Socrates is also human, and therefore “Socrates Socrates human.” And if he is human and two-footed, then “human human two-footed.”

Many things, when truly predicated individually, retain a true predication when someone joins them together and predicates them. There are other things which, when predicated separately and disjoined, are true, but which, when said together, do not retain the truth of their predication. The difference between these must therefore be recognized.

For if someone says, “Socrates is an animal,” he has spoken truly. If someone again predicates of Socrates that he is two-footed, this too is true. If these are said together, as in “Socrates is an animal and two-footed,” the combined statement does not depart from its proper truth. These belong to genus and difference, which are substantial to Socrates.

But the same thing may also occur when an accident is predicated. For if someone says, “Socrates is a human being,” this is true; and again, “Socrates is bald,” this too is true. If he joins them and says, “Socrates is a bald human being,” he will again make a true predication from the conjunction. In these cases, things which were individually said truly are truly predicated when joined.

There are, however, other cases in which the predicates are individually true, but lose the character of truth when joined. Thus, if someone says, “Socrates is good,” this is true; and again, “Socrates is a cithara-player,” this too is true. It is not necessary, however, that their conjunction be true, namely, “Socrates is a good cithara-player.” For he may be a good human being and, although he is a cithara-player, not be good in that capacity; he may be good in one respect, and in another merely knowledgeable in that art, without being accomplished in the art itself.

This will become clearer from the following example. If someone says, “Tiberius Gracchus is bad,” this is true; and again, “Tiberius Gracchus is an orator,” this too is true. But if, joining them, he says, “Tiberius Gracchus is a bad orator,” he will have spoken falsely, for he was an excellent orator. But lest anyone think that, in saying this, we are unaware that the definition of an orator is “a good man skilled in speaking,” these statements have been made as an example rather than as historical truth.

These points were proposed by Aristotle, whose words in the text stand as follows:

“Since some things,” he says, “are predicated in combination, so that one predicate is formed from them, among those things that are truly predicated outside the subject, while other things, although they were truly predicated separately outside the subject, do not form a true predication when joined, their difference must be investigated. Examples of these are as follows.

“Among those things predicated truly outside the subject which do not lose the nature of truth even when joined, an example is this: it is true to say of a human being that he is both an animal and two-footed; and again, it is true to say of the same human being, for example of Socrates, that he is an animal and two-footed. It is likewise true, if the circumstances permit, to say of the same Socrates that he is human and white outside the combination; and to predicate of the same person ‘animal and two-footed’ does not depart from the truth. These, then, are things that are truly predicated separately outside the subject and are also true when joined.

“But if something is predicated of someone as ‘a cithara-player,’ and this is true, and again he is predicated as ‘good,’ and this is true, it is not necessary to say that he is ‘a good cithara-player.’ For he may be merely a cithara-player and a good human being.” Thus far he has arranged the matter.

But since some people seemed to suppose that everything which was truly predicated separately could also rightly be said in combination, he argues against them that many absurdities and many impossibilities would follow if one said that everything which is truly predicated separately is also truly predicated when joined.

For it is true to say of a human being that he is human; thus, of Socrates, who is a human being, it is truly said that he is human. Again, it can truly be said of the same person that he is white. Therefore, if these are joined and predicated as one, it is true to say of some human being that he is a white human being. But it is true to say of a human being who is white that he is white. Therefore, even if these are joined, the predication will be: “Socrates is a white white human being,” since it was true to say of Socrates that he is a white human being; but it is true to say of a white human being that he is white. These joined produce the statement, “Socrates is a white white human being.”

If, moreover, you wish to predicate “white” again of the same white human being, this is true. Consequently, if you join them, the predication will be: “The human being is a white white white human being.” And this continues infinitely.

Again, if someone says of some human being that he is a musical human being, and speaks truly, and adds that the same human being is walking, he speaks truly. If he joins these and says that the human being is a walking musical human being, he speaks truly. But if it is true to predicate of some human being that he is a walking musician, and it is true to say of a walking musician that he is a musician, then that human being will be “a walking musical musical human being.” And since it is true to say of the same person that he is walking, it will again be true to say of him that he is “a walking walking musical musical human being.”

Further, Socrates is Socrates, and again he is human; therefore, “Socrates Socrates human.” But he is also two-footed; therefore, “Socrates Socrates human two-footed.” It is true to say of Socrates that he is “Socrates human two-footed.” But when I said “human,” I had already said “two-footed,” since every human being is two-footed. Therefore it is true to say of him that he is two-footed; and it was true to say that “Socrates is Socrates human two-footed.” There will therefore be a true predication: “Socrates is Socrates two-footed two-footed human.”

But again I said “human,” and in it I named another “two-footed,” since every human being is two-footed. Socrates, therefore, is “a human two-footed two-footed two-footed” person. When this is extended infinitely, excessive and superfluous verbosity results. It is therefore not possible that, in every respect, whatever is said outside the combination should be truly predicated when joined.

[Col. 0575A] Since, then, if someone simply says that combinations can be made, it follows that many absurdities must be stated, this is clear. We shall now say how the matter must be understood.

Among things that are predicated, and among the things of which they are predicated, whatever is said according to accident—whether two accidents are predicated of the same thing, or one accident is predicated of another—does not form one thing. Thus, “a human being is white and musical,” but the musical and the white are not the same; both are accidents of the same subject. Even if it is true to say “white musician,” the white musician will not thereby be one thing, for “white musician” is said according to accident. Therefore “white musician” will not be one thing, and consequently neither will “good cithara-player” simply be one thing.

Further, neither do those things form one thing which are contained in something else. Therefore neither “white” repeatedly, nor “human human animal” [Col. 0575B] or “two-footed,” is to be formed; for animal and two-footed are contained in human.

What he summarized above he now determines with the clearest reasoning. He says that, among things predicated truly outside the subject, a single true predication cannot be formed by joining those which are either accidents of the same thing, or cases in which, when one accident belongs to another, a further accident is predicated of that accident.

For if someone says of Socrates that Socrates is a cithara-player, and again that Socrates is good, and predicates both truly, he has predicated two accidents of one subject, namely Socrates. Consequently, one predication cannot be formed from them by saying, “Socrates is a good cithara-player.”

Again, if “musical” is predicated of Socrates—let Socrates indeed be musical—and if “white” is predicated of the musical person, and this too is perhaps true, it is nevertheless not necessary that the musical person be white. For if Socrates is musical, and white is predicated of that same musical person, musical is predicated of Socrates as subject, while white is predicated of the musical person, which is an accident; again, it is another accident. Therefore a single true proposition cannot be formed here by saying, “Socrates is a white musician.” For the musical person cannot always be white, but accidents have the nature of coming and going.

Thus, if the skin of a musical white person standing in the sun should be darkened by the heat, he will no longer be white, although he remains musical. Consequently, neither at the time when it was truly predicated that “Socrates is a white musician” was this a true and correct predication, since an accident does not have a nature that remains so as to be predicated always truly.

The reasoning of the words is as follows. “Since, then,” he says, “if someone says that combinations can be made in absolutely any manner—that is, that whatever one has predicated separately may be proposed as a combined and connected statement—it follows that many absurdities must be stated. For many impossibilities arise together, as he himself showed above when he led them into excessive verbosity by repeatedly repeating the same names.

“Now we say how the matter must be understood,” that is, how things which are said truly when separate ought to be predicated when joined. “Everything,” he says, “which is predicated of something, and again everything of which other things are predicated, is of two kinds. Either they are accidents, or they are substantial. Some predications are therefore according to accident whenever either two accidents are predicated of a substance, or an accident of an accident belonging to some substance. Other predications are not according to accident, whenever something is said substantially of something else.

“Of all things, then, which are said according to accident, whether two accidents are predicated of the same thing, or one accident is said of another accident, no single predication can be made from them, nor will they be one thing when joined. Thus, a human being is white and musical; but ‘white musical,’ since they do not converge into one form, does not make one proposition. White and musical are not the same; both are accidents of the same thing, but they are not the same.

“Nor, if we predicate white of the musical person—that is, an accident of an accident—and this is true, is it nevertheless necessary that what is musical be white. For it is not one thing. What is musical is white accidentally: since the very thing to which musical belongs is white, musical is therefore called white. But musical and white are not the same.

“Consequently, the same reasoning applies, so that a cithara-player cannot be the same thing as a good person, nor do these, joined into one body, make one thing, although they are truly predicated separately.

“But if someone predicates something substantially, and says two things separately, they can be brought into one proposition, since things which are substantially and truly set apart from one another can be placed together. For since a human being is both an animal and two-footed, he is an animal two-footed, and one predication is formed from these. Neither animal nor two-footed belongs to a human being according to accident. He demonstrates this by saying, ‘but animal two-footed’; for they are not according to accident.

“He adds also that things are not rightly joined which are contained, either covertly or in their expression, in one of the terms placed in the proposition. For this reason, one ought not to predicate white of a white human being, so that the predication ‘a white white human being’ may result, since white is already contained in ‘white human being.’ Again, for this reason one ought not to predicate two-footed of a human being, since, although it has not been uttered, one who is human is two-footed.

“But if someone predicates two-footed of a human being, he predicates two-footed of a thing having two feet, not by the difference that is ‘two-footed.’ Consequently, there will again be ‘a two-footed two-footed human being,’ since ‘two-footed’ is contained in ‘human being,’ and whoever says ‘human being’ with its difference says this as well. If someone therefore predicates two-footed once more of a thing having two feet, he will have predicated two-footed. Thus there will be ‘a two-footed two-footed human being,’ but it ought not to be predicated in this way. Two-footed is contained in human being; if two-footed is predicated again, an extremely tiresome repetition results.

“This is what he means when he says: ‘Further, neither those things which are in another,’ that is, which are contained in it—either by expression, as in ‘white human being,’ in which white is contained because it has already been said by expression, or potentially and by force, as in ‘human being,’ in which two-footed is contained, although it has not been uttered at all.”

It is true to say simply of something, for example, that a certain human being is a human being, or that a certain white human being is a white human being. But this is not always so; rather, it is so when something belonging to the opposites is present in what has been added. [Col. 0577A] The contradictory consequence is not true but false—for example, to call a dead human being “a human being.” But when the relevant feature is not present, it is true.

This question is the opposite of the preceding one. There it was asked whether things predicated separately would always be truly said when joined and combined. Here, however, the order is reversed, and it asks whether things that are truly predicated in combination are also truly said separately.

After Socrates’ death, we can say of this corpse, “It is a dead human being,” and by joining “human” and “dead” make one true predication from them. But merely to call the corpse “a human being” is not true. Again, of the same living Socrates it is true to say that he is an animal and two-footed, and it is separately true to say that he is an animal.

Therefore the question is what difference exists in this kind of predication: when things are said together and truly predicated of their subjects, whether in some cases they can also be truly said separately and outside the combination, while in other cases, if they are said simply apart from that combination, they are false.

He stated this as if in doubt. It should therefore be read as though he were asking in this way: “Is it true to say of something, in a combined and connected form, that it is something—for example, to say of a human being that he is human, or of a white person that he is white—so that something among these may also be predicated simply outside the combination? Or is this not always so?”

He gives a rule by which we may recognize whether things said in combination can also be said separately, or not. Whenever the predicates are such that, together with the other predicate, they do not contain a contradiction within themselves, they can also be said truly when separated. [Col. 0577C] But if they contain some contradiction within themselves, the predicates which are said together cannot be truly predicated separately.

Thus, one who calls a corpse “a dead human being” speaks truly; but he cannot truly call it merely “a human being.” The reason is that he first predicated it in combination, saying “dead human being,” and “dead” is attached to the predicate “human.” For when “dead” is predicated together with “human,” it contains a contradiction against “human.” A human being is an animal, whereas the dead is not an animal; therefore “dead” and “human” have a certain contradiction between them. The one is an animal, the other is not an animal.

Consequently, since these have a certain contrariety between them, “human” is not said by itself of a dead human being. The same applies if someone says that the hand of a statue is marble: he speaks truly. But merely to call it a hand, as it belongs to a statue, is false. A hand has the power to give and receive, whereas that hand does not. Therefore there is a certain contradiction between a hand and a marble hand: the one can give and receive, the other cannot. These are opposed to one another in the manner of a contradiction.

Thus, whenever something of this kind is predicated—for example, “human” of a corpse—and something is joined and attached to it which produces a contradiction against the predicate, as “dead” is attached here to “human,” and is simultaneously predicated of the corpse so as to produce a contradiction against “human” itself, the predication cannot be separated and stated individually as a true predication.

[Col. 0578A] But if this contradiction is absent, it can be done. In “Socrates is an animal and two-footed,” animal and two-footed are not opposed by any contradiction. Consequently, “animal” and “two-footed” can be said of him individually and simply.

The sense is therefore of this kind. The order of the words, however, is as follows. He spoke in doubt: “Is it true to say something of something in a composite and connected way, and again simply—for example, to say of some human being ‘human,’ or of some white person ‘white’—or is this not always so, but only when something among the opposites is present in what has been added?”

That is, in the thing which is added when something is predicated with another, there is something of such opposites as are followed by contradiction—an opposition which is immediately followed by contradiction, as the opposition of human and dead is followed by the contradiction “animal and not animal.” If this is the case, then it is not true to predicate the term simply, but it is false. Thus, although one can truly say “dead human being” in combination, one cannot truly predicate “human” alone of the same person.

When this opposition is not present in the things predicated, it is true both to predicate what one had predicated in combination and to predicate it simply. The added element is that in which this kind of opposition sometimes occurs, as in “dead human being,” where “dead” is added to “human.” Otherwise, “human” cannot truly be predicated of a corpse.

Or again: when the opposition is present, it is never true; but when it is absent, it is not always true either. For example, “Homer is something, namely a poet”; therefore, “Homer is,” or is he not? “Being” is predicated of Homer according to accident, because he is a poet; but “being” is not predicated of Homer in itself, simply because he is.

[Col. 0578C] Since above he had said that, when there was a contradiction in what was added, it was not true to predicate simply what had been said in combination, whereas, when there was no contradiction, it was true to say simply what had been said in combination, he now corrects this because it appeared not to be true in certain cases.

He says that what was stated above is true: whenever there is some contradiction in what is added, it is not true to predicate simply what was said in combination. But when no contradiction is present, it is not always true to predicate simply what was truly said in combination; sometimes it is true and sometimes false.

An example is the following. When I say, “Homer is a poet,” I have truly predicated “is” and “poet” together of Homer. But if I say, “Homer is,” this is false, although there is no contradiction between “is” and “poet,” nor is there in what is added any such opposition as would entail a contradiction.

The reason is as follows. We predicate “poet” principally of Homer when we say, “Homer is a poet.” But the verb “is” is predicated principally of the poet, and only secondarily of Homer. We do not predicate being because Homer is, but because he is a poet. Therefore, when what is principally predicated—namely “poet”—is removed, although “is,” which is attached to “poet,” contains no contradiction against “poet,” the predication “Homer is” does not become true.

“Being” is predicated according to accident, not principally. When the principal predication is removed, what was predicated according to accident is immediately found to be false.

As for what he added:

“Therefore, in all predicates in which no contrariety is present, if definitions are stated in place of names, and the predicate is predicated in itself rather than according to accident, in these cases it will also be true to say something simply. But of what is not, because it is an object of opinion, it is not true to say that it is something; for it is an opinion of it—not that it is, but that it is not.”

He gathers together in one argument what he said above. Whatever is predicated in such a way that it contains no contrariety either in the names or in its proper definitions is also true when predicated outside the combination and simply.

Thus, in “dead” and “human,” the names themselves contain no contradiction or contrariety. But if definitions are taken in place of these names, the opposition immediately becomes apparent. For if someone gives the definition of a human being, he says that it is a rational animal. If he gives the definition of the dead, he says that it is a body deprived of life and inanimate. From this the whole force of the contradiction appears.

Consequently, if definitions are taken in place of names, and some contrariety is seen to be present in them, or if something is predicated according to accident—as with Homer, when “poet” is predicated principally—then whatever was predicated in combination will not also be truly predicated simply.

But if there is no contrariety, and the predicates are predicated in themselves rather than according to accident, whatever is said truly in combination is also said truly simply.

There were some people who said that what is not is, joining the entire syllogism through the following propositions: “What is not is an object of opinion; what is an object of opinion is; therefore what is not is.”

He therefore says: if it is true, he says, to predicate of what is not that it is an object of opinion, then the verb “is” is predicated of the object of opinion, but of what is not it is predicated according to accident. Since what is not is an object of opinion, for this reason the verb “is” is predicated secondarily of what is not. Therefore we cannot simply say that what is not is.

For it is an object of opinion precisely because it is not. If it existed in itself, it would be an object of knowledge, not of opinion, just as Homer is said to exist because he is a poet, not because he exists in himself. Or certainly Homer is said to be a poet because his poetry exists and endures, just as we often say that certain people live on in their children.

Consequently, what is not is said to be an object of opinion because there is an opinion of it. It is not said to be so because what is not can exist as something in itself.

Having briefly treated and arranged these matters in order, he now turns to the modes of propositions, a matter of the greatest usefulness in dialectic, and begins a discussion of propositions. It remains now to discuss the modes of propositions and their oppositions. Many have questioned whether the mode of propositions stated without a mode is the same as that of propositions which are determined by their own modes and qualifications. He begins his inquiry into these matters as follows.

[Col. 0580A] **On Enunciations of the Modes of the Possible, the Contingent, the Impossible, and the Necessary**

These matters having been determined, we must examine how affirmations and negations stand in relation to one another—namely, those concerning what can be and what cannot be, what is contingent and what is not contingent, what is impossible and what is necessary—for these raise certain difficulties.

Every proposition is either uttered simply, without any mode at all, as in “Socrates walks,” “It is day,” or whatever is predicated simply and without any qualification. Others are expressed together with their proper modes, as in “Socrates walks quickly.” For a mode has been added to Socrates’ walking when we say that he walks quickly; for “quickly” signifies how he walks, which we predicate of his walking. [Col. 0580B] Likewise, if someone says, “Socrates is well educated,” he shows how Socrates is educated: he has not said merely “educated,” but has also added the mode of Socrates’ education.

But since there are other modes by which we say that something can come to be, cannot come to be, must be, or happens contingently, the question arises how contradiction ought to be constituted in these cases as well. For in propositions that are predicated simply and without any mode, the place of contradiction is easily recognized. The negation of the affirmation “Socrates walks,” if it is placed with the verb, as in “Socrates does not walk,” most correctly effects opposition by separating walking from Socrates. Again, if in the proposition “Socrates is a philosopher” someone places the negation with the verb “is,” [Col. 0580C] he will make a complete negation by saying, “Socrates is not a philosopher.” For in simple affirmations negation cannot be placed anywhere other than with the verb that contains the force of the entire proposition.

If, in the proposition “A human being is white,” someone does not state the negation as “A human being is not white,” but instead says “A human being is non-white,” the proposed negation is shown to be false by means of a stone. Let the question be asked whether that stone is a white human being. If he denies this, and, in giving the negation of “A human being is white,” uses the form “A human being is non-white,” one may say to him: “If the affirmation ‘A human being is white’ is not true of this stone, then the negation of it—namely, ‘A human being is non-white’—will be true of it.” Yet this too is false. For the stone is not a human being at all, [Col. 0580D] and therefore “a non-white human being” cannot be predicated of it. But if neither the affirmation nor the negation is true of it—and it is impossible for both contradictory affirmations and negations predicated of the same thing to be false—it is clear that the negation of the affirmation “A human being is white” is not “A human being is non-white,” but rather the negation by which it is proposed that “A human being is not white.”

Therefore, in propositions that are stated simply and without any mode, negation must nowhere else be placed except with the verb that contains the whole proposition. We have already discussed these matters sufficiently above. In propositions to which some mode is added, however, there is doubt whether the negative particle should be placed with that mode, or whether it should retain its place with the verb, as it did in propositions that were simple and without any mode.

[Col. 0581A] For if the negative particle retains its place with the verb, the proper character of contradiction disappears, and it no longer divides truth from falsity. A mode is a certain way of doing something whenever we say that something is possible, necessary, or anything of that kind. Thus, if someone says that I can now walk, and, placing the negation with the verb “walk,” denies it by saying that I can not-walk, the affirmation and negation, being contradictory propositions spoken of the same thing, will be found to be true simultaneously. For it is evident that I can both walk and not walk.

But if the negative particle is not correctly joined to the verb in this mode of possibility, then even in those cases in which it makes no difference whether negation is placed with the mode or with the verb, an opposition appropriate to this kind of proposition—one uttered with a mode—must be preserved. [Col. 0581B] Thus, in the proposition “Socrates walks quickly,” whether someone negates it by saying “It is not the case that Socrates walks quickly” (*Socrates velociter non ambulat*), placing the negation with the verb, or says “Socrates walks, but not quickly” (*Socrates non velociter ambulat*), joining the negative particle to the mode, the result will appear nearly the same. In either form the negation, suitably constructed, divides truth from falsity together with the affirmation.

But since there are several modes in which, if the negative particle is joined to the verb, it is not the negation of the affirmation stated above, the following proportion must therefore be preserved in all propositions according to their modes: the oppositions of all propositions are to be said to be formed in one and the same manner. In simple propositions, negation should negate the thing itself; in those that contain a mode, it should negate the mode.

[Col. 0581C] Thus, in “Socrates walks,” it negates the thing itself—that is, “walks”—and the proposition removes it by saying, “Socrates does not walk.” In propositions that contain a mode, however, it should agree that the thing exists but negate the mode. Thus, in “Socrates walks quickly,” the negation should say, “Socrates walks, but not quickly,” so that whether he walks or does not walk makes no difference. The negation opposed to it removes the mode, namely, walking quickly.

This does not happen in certain cases, however. For simultaneously with the mode itself, the thing also has to be removed, as in “Socrates can walk” and “Socrates cannot walk.” Here the negative particle, joined to the mode itself, cuts off both the mode and the thing. [Col. 0581D] This generally occurs in cases in which something is said not to take place, and the mode of the act itself is not added; rather, what is added is the mode of doing it in the future. For example, someone may say that Socrates is able to walk, not meaning that he is already walking, but that he knows it is possible for him to walk. If negation is joined to the possible, it will also seem to have removed the very thing of which that possibility was predicated.

If, however, someone says, “Socrates walks quickly,” he says that Socrates is doing something and joins a mode to that act, so that anyone may recognize how he does what he is said to do. In such cases the thing remains, while the mode is overturned, as was said above.

[Col. 0582A] Or is it perhaps more correct to say that propositions of this kind always remove the mode but do not destroy the thing of which the mode is predicated? This applies both where the thing is posited—as in “Socrates walks quickly”—and where the act itself is predicated as present, because it is being performed and carried out. It is clear that in such cases the mode is overturned, while the thing said to occur remains, as when we say, “Socrates does not walk quickly.” His walking has not been removed; only this negation has separated quickness from his walking.

In propositions that posit the possibility of doing something in the future by means of a mode, no act at all is posited, but only the mode. When negation is joined to that mode, it removes the mode. But the thing of which the mode was predicated does not remain, because even when it was predicated with the mode, it was not proposed that anything was actually being done or occurring. Thus, if someone says that it is possible for Socrates to walk, a mode has indeed been posited, but the thing itself has not been established as actual. For it has not been said that he walks, but that it is possible for him to walk.

[Col. 0582B] Negation therefore removes this possibility in the proposition “It is not possible for Socrates to walk.” But in that proposition the thing of which the mode was spoken does not remain. This occurs because even in the affirmation the thing of which the mode was predicated was not posited. Therefore the thing has not been destroyed by the negation, since the negation found it already unposited; only the mode has been removed, and that mode had itself been established by the affirmation.

[Col. 0582C] There is a great difference between placing negation with the mode and placing it with the verb. If it is placed with the verb, the predicate is separated from the subject, as in “Socrates does not walk.” For “walks,” which is the predicate, has been divided from the subject, “Socrates.” But if negation is placed with the mode, the predicate is not divided from the subject. Rather, the mode is separated from the predication, as in “Socrates walks, but not quickly.” This proposition does not separate walking from Socrates, but quickness from walking—that is, the mode from the predicate. This appears more easily and clearly in all cases in which things are predicated in such a way that they are said both to be possible and not to be possible.

We must define what the possible is, what the necessary is, and what it means for something to be [in being], and must show their significations. This will help us with the subtlety of the present discussion, will make clearer all that was said above concerning the contingent, and will reveal to us in the clearest light the meaning of the *Analytics*. [Col. 0582D]

Aristotle arranges four modes in this book, *On Interpretation*. Something is either said to be, to be contingent, to be possible, or to be necessary. “To be contingent” and “to be possible” signify the same thing, and there is no difference between saying “It is possible that there will be circus games tomorrow” and “It is contingent that there will be circus games tomorrow,” except that possibility can be removed by privation, whereas contingency cannot.

For sometimes a negation of possibility is brought against what is said to be possible, as in “It is not possible for it to be,” and sometimes a privation, as in “It is impossible for it to be.” What we call impossible is a privation of possibility. In the case of the contingent, although it signifies the same thing, only negation is opposed to it; no privation is found. Thus, if we wish to remove what is contingent, we say “not contingent,” and this is a negation. No one, however, would call “incontingent” a privation.

Although therefore “to be contingent” and “to be possible” have the same signification, according to Porphyry there is much difference among these propositions: some signify what is necessary and merely present, while others signify what is contingent or possible.

[Col. 0583A] When something is said to be, this is judged according to the present time. If something now belongs to someone or something, it is predicated as being.
