But what belongs in such a way that it always exists and never changes is said to be necessary, such as the motion of the sun and the eclipses of the moon when the earth intervenes. What is said to be contingent or possible is considered neither according to the present nor according to any unchangeability of its outcome; we look only to the extent promised by the proposition of contingency.

[Col. 0583B] For what is said to be possible or contingent is not yet actual, but may be. Whether it occurs or does not occur, because it can occur, the proposition is called contingent and possible. Propositions are not judged by their outcome, but rather by their signification, as follows.

If someone says, “It is possible that there will be circus games tomorrow,” this is a possible and contingent affirmation. If there are circus games tomorrow, nothing in the proposition’s contingent or possible status has thereby changed, so that what it promised as possible would appear to have been necessary. And if there are no circus games tomorrow, again nothing has changed so that it would appear necessary that there not be circus games. [Col. 0583C]

For, as has been said, these propositions are not judged according to their outcome, but according to the promise of the proposition itself. Whoever says that there can be circus games tomorrow says this: whether they occur or do not occur, there is nevertheless no necessity preventing them from not occurring.

Thus two of the four modes are the same—namely, the contingent and the possible. These two differ from the other two, and the latter two also differ from one another. The possible and the contingent differ from the proposition that says that something is, for the former proposes an affirmation according to the possibility of future time, whereas the latter concerns a present act.

Both propositions—the one signifying that something is and the one signifying that it is possible or contingent—are distinguished from the necessary proposition. For necessity not only requires that something belong to a thing, but that it belong immutably, so that what is said to be can never be unable to be. [Col. 0583D]

[Col. 0583D] Hence the consequences of the order also become evident. What is necessary cannot be said to be without also being said to be, to be contingent, or to be possible. Whatever is necessary both is and can be; for if it could not be, it would not exist at all. And if it did not exist, it would not be called necessary. Therefore everything necessary is said to be and is possible, but not everything that is is necessary.

[Col. 0584A] For some things can be without it being necessary that they be, as with Socrates’ walking and other examples drawn from separable accidents. Nor, again, does what contingently is or is possible immediately have to be necessary. Therefore “to be necessary” is followed by “to be” and “to be possible,” but neither “to be” nor “to be possible” is followed by necessity.

Again, everything that is is followed by being possible; for what is can be. If it could not be, it plainly would not be. But being does not follow upon being possible. What is possible can also not be, as it is possible for me to go out now, but it is not necessary for me to do so. For I am not going out now. Thus the whole consequence proceeds by stages: the necessary is followed by being and by possibility; being is in turn followed by possibility; but possibility is followed neither by being nor by necessity.

[Col. 0584B] It is therefore clear that there are two kinds of possible things: one that already follows necessity, and another that does not itself follow necessity. When I say, “It is necessary that the sun now be moving,” this is also possible. When I say, “It is possible for me now to pick up a book,” it is not necessary.

Aristotle is therefore rightly about to ask whether that which conforms to necessity is possible. When we reach the relevant passages, we shall recognize what this similarity among possible things means and how they can be distinguished.

But since we have explained the consequences of affirmative propositions, let us now examine the consequences of negative propositions. Of the four propositions formed from “to be,” “to be necessary,” “to be possible,” and “to be contingent,” there are four negations: “not to be,” “not to be necessary,” “not to be possible,” and “not to be contingent.”

Just as the affirmations “to be contingent” and “to be possible” were the same according to the similarity of their significations, so their negations are also the same. There is no difference between saying “It is not possible” and saying “It is not contingent.” [Col. 0584C]

The consequences among the affirmations were arranged as follows: necessary propositions were followed by those signifying that something is and by possible propositions. Those saying that something is were likewise followed by possible propositions; but possible propositions were followed neither by those signifying that something is nor by necessary propositions.

With negatives, however, the situation is reversed. The negation of possibility is followed by the negation of the proposition signifying that something is and by the negation of necessity. But the negation of necessity is followed neither by the negation of being nor by the negation of possibility.

Let all of them be arranged in this order:

- To be possible.
- Not to be possible.
- To be contingent.
- Not to be contingent.
- To be.
- Not to be.
- To be necessary.
- Not to be necessary.

The consequences of the affirmations should therefore be briefly repeated, so that it may become clearer how they are reversed in the negatives.

Being is followed by possibility and contingency. But being is not followed by possibility and contingency. Rather, necessity is followed by being, possibility, and contingency; whereas possibility and contingency are followed neither by being nor by necessity.

With negations the contrary is the case. “Not to be” is followed by “not to be possible” and “not to be contingent”: whatever cannot be, is not. But “not to be possible” does not follow from “not to be,” for what is not does not thereby become wholly prevented from being possible.

At present I do not see Trajan’s Forum, but it is not necessary that I not see it; for I may approach more closely and see it. [Col. 0585A] Again, neither “not to be possible” nor “not to be contingent” follows from “not to be,” nor does “not to be necessary.” For what is not cannot truly be said to be unable to be; rather, it can be said that it can either not be or be—that is, that it is not necessary for it to be.

But what cannot not be cannot truly be said to be not necessary for it to be; rather, it must be said that it is necessary that it not be—that is, that it have no essence.

[Col. 0585B] The negation of necessity, namely “not to be necessary,” is followed neither by “not to be” nor by “not to be possible.” While I am walking, it is not necessary for me to walk; no one walks out of necessity. Yet what is not necessary is not thereby prevented from occurring. For whoever walks is not required to walk, but merely can walk. Therefore what is not necessary to be is not wholly prevented from being.

The same reasoning applies to the non-contingent. The reversal of the negative therefore proceeds in a different way from that of the affirmations. [Col. 0585C] There, being and possibility followed necessity; possibility followed being; but neither being nor necessity followed possibility, nor, again, did necessity follow being.

Here, however, “not to be” follows “not to be possible” and “not to be necessary.” But “not to be necessary” is followed neither by “not to be” nor by either negation of possibility, the one that proposes that something cannot be.

Or should we rather say that the relation in negations is the same as in affirmations, as Theophrastus perceived with great acuity? In affirmations the consequence was that necessity was followed both by being and by possibility, whereas possibility was followed neither by being nor by necessity.

The same thing will appear to those who examine the matter thoroughly in the case of negations. For when negation enters into the necessary and produces the negation “It is not necessary for it to be,” it weakens the force of necessity and brings the whole proposition down to possibility. What is not necessary to be, once the rigidity of necessity has been broken, is brought over to possibility. But possibility was followed neither by being nor by necessity.

Therefore, when the negation says “It is not necessary for it to be,” it is correctly followed neither by “not to be” nor by “not to be contingent”; for it has weakened necessity and brought the proposition over to possibility.

[Col. 0585D] Again, whoever says “It is possible for it to be,” if the negation is added to it, removes the possible and, by the negative form, brings the whole proposition back to the permanence of necessity. Thus, “It is not possible” means that what is possible is not yet actual when it is said to be possible, but belongs to the future. When its negation is converted into necessity, it cannot change what is the case: what cannot be cannot come to be, and what cannot come to be must not be.

Thus this proposition, in which we say that something cannot be, has a certain necessary force. Yet being and possibility followed necessity. “Not to be necessary,” on the other hand, looks toward possibility.

Therefore “not to be necessary,” which also belongs to possibility, correctly follows the proposition “not to be possible,” which belongs to necessity. The orders of the propositions are different, but their force is the same: everything follows necessity, whereas necessity does not follow possibility.

[Col. 0586A] Here a rather difficult question arises. If possibility follows necessity, and “not to be necessary” is closely related to possibility, why does “to be necessary” not follow what we call “not to be necessary”? For if possibility follows necessity, and “not to be necessary” follows possibility, then necessity ought to follow what we predicate as “not necessary.”

The question is resolved in this way. Although “not to be possible” has the force of necessity, it nevertheless differs from necessity because necessity has an affirmative form, whereas “not to be possible” has a negative form. In the same way, “to be possible” and “not to be necessary” differ only in this respect: the former is affirmative, while the latter is negative, although their signifying force is the same.

[Col. 0586B] The affirmation of possibility and contingency followed necessity. Although “not to be necessary” imitates and agrees with possibility, it is nevertheless a kind of negation. Therefore the affirmation “to be necessary” is not followed by the negation through which we propose that something is not necessary.

This, then, was the solution to the question discovered by Theophrastus, a man of great learning. With these matters determined, let us proceed to what follows.

[Col. 0586C] As Aristotle himself says, there are many difficulties in these matters. But let us first set out the fullest sense of the entire text. Although it is long, I shall not hesitate to include it, lest the meaning appear to have been interrupted.

For if the contradictory statements of the things that comprise them are opposed to one another, whatever is arranged according to being and not-being is opposed in this way: the negation of “a human being is” is “a human being is not,” not “a non-human being is.” And the negation of “a white human being is” is “a white human being is not,” not “a non-white human being is.”

For if every statement is either an affirmation or a negation, it will be true to say of a piece of wood that it is not a white human being. If this is so, then in every case in which “to be” is not added, the expression used in place of “to be” will produce the same result. Thus the negation of “a human being walks” is not “a non-human being walks,” but “a human being does not walk”; for it makes no difference whether one says “a human being walks” or “a walking human being exists.”

As Aristotle examines these matters with precision, one must acknowledge that it is very different to define the force and nature of possibility itself [Col. 0586D] from the standpoint of its proper science, and to determine what a possible enunciation ought to be. For through the cognition of possibility one perceives only whether what is said can come to be, with no external cause preventing it. Even if such an impediment should occur, nothing in the condition of the prior possibility is thereby altered. But the judgment of the possible enunciation itself is very different; this will soon become clear from the discussion of possible enunciations themselves.

For just as it is not the same thing to answer those asking for the definition of “human being” and to include that definition under another term of definition, so it is not the same thing to discuss a possible enunciation and to discuss what possibility itself is. Hence it comes about that, although the possible and the contingent are identical in meaning, they appear to be different in enunciations. For above we taught that possibility and contingency have the same meaning: whatever could contingently happen is likewise possible, and whatever is possible could likewise happen contingently. Yet a possible enunciation is not the same as a contingent one. For if someone puts forward a possible affirmation and opposes to it a contingent negation, he will not produce a correct contradiction. If someone says that something or other is possible, and another replies by denying that the thing is contingent, although, so far as meaning is concerned, he has removed the former possibility, this must nevertheless not be called a contradiction, since different terms have been enunciated in the negation and in the affirmation. A possible affirmation must have a negation concerning possibility [Col. 0587B], not concerning contingency. The same applies to contingent propositions. If someone says that something is contingent, one must not oppose to him a negation of possibility, even though the possible and the contingent are identical.

It is therefore clear that the method for judging a mode in itself is entirely different from that for judging an enunciation in which the mode is predicated together with a qualification. Hence, although possibility and contingency are identical in meaning, Aristotle presents them as if they were different in the order of the modes.

One must also not overlook the fact that, for the Stoics, possibility appears to be more universal than necessity. For they divide enunciations in this way: “Of enunciations, some are possible and some impossible. Of possible enunciations, some are necessary and some not necessary. Again, of those that are not necessary, some are possible.” They foolishly and carelessly make the same possible thing both the genus of what is not necessary and its species [Col. 0587C]. Aristotle, however, recognizes as possible whatever can be non-necessary.

For the possible is not spoken of in the same way when something passes at some time from falsehood into truth, or again from truth into falsehood. Thus, if someone says now, because it is day, “It is day,” he speaks truly; but if he says the same thing at night, it is false, and the truth of the proposition has been changed into falsehood. There are therefore certain possibilities such that it may happen for them either to be or not to be; but they are not spoken of in the same way as those whose nature is not changeable, namely, those which we have called necessary. Thus, if someone says that the sun moves, or that it is possible for the sun to move, these propositions will never change from truth into falsehood.

But for the present we must say nothing about the disagreement between Aristotle and the Stoics [Col. 0587D]. The one matter that must be investigated with particular care is where the negation is to be placed in propositions in which some mode is predicated—that is, in propositions called possible, contingent, or necessary, and in all propositions that contain a mode.

Such propositions will truly be said to be according to a mode, just as others are said to be according to being, when their meanings contain the quality of subsistence of the thing of which they are predicated. Thus, when I say, “Socrates speaks well,” “well” is a certain mode of Socrates’ speaking. Therefore, just as in propositions that affirm the subsistence of some thing the negation is placed with that subsistence—for example, when we say “Socrates is,” the negation is attached to “is” when we deny, “Socrates is not” [Col. 0588A]—so also, in propositions that express a mode of subsistence, the negation must be placed with that mode which appears to have been added to the subsistence.

When we say, “Socrates speaks well,” the mode of the thing itself is what we predicate, namely, “well.” The negation must therefore be placed with this mode and qualification.

We call many propositions contingent, or possible, in which the mode itself is displayed, rather than being spoken of as something concerning the mode; instead, the mode is predicated of what is. For when we say, “It is possible to be,” we say that something exists, and add how it is: namely, “possibly,” so that it is said to be neither necessarily nor in any other mode, but only according to potentiality. Thus “being” becomes the subject, while the predicate is a mode—contingent, possible, necessary, or any other mode [Col. 0588B]. These propositions are therefore called propositions according to a mode; in them there is no uncertainty about substance. The discussion concerns only the mode and the qualification.

But if the mode is made subject and “being” is predicated, then the question concerns the substance of the thing, not the mode. Thus, if someone says, “The possible is,” declaring that the possible itself exists among things, no mode has been added to this proposition. When we speak of “the possible,” we do not, taken by itself, mean that it has a mode; rather, we perceive the separated part of the proposition as though it were joined with the whole proposition. When we join it to its proper proposition, the mode in which it is predicated becomes apparent.

When we say, “It is possible,” the phrase “it is” is a part of the proposition that signifies a mode. If we attach it to its own body by forming some proposition, we recognize what that mode asserts. Let us take the expression “It is possible” and join it to other predicates, thereby forming one enunciation, and say, “It is possible for Socrates to walk.” Do you not see the mode in the proposition, “possible,” so that, whether Socrates walks or does not walk, anyone may nevertheless recognize from the mode of the proposition itself that he can walk?

Thus, by removing a part from the whole, we contemplate a possible enunciation as though it were a complete proposition. The same procedure is customary with expressions that determine quantity. When we are uncertain whether “none” or “not all” should be posited in opposition to “all,” we consider these expressions as though they were complete propositions, although it is clear that they are determinations of propositions.

To conclude, in propositions that predicate a mode, all the other things are subjects—“to be,” “to walk,” “to read,” “to speak,” or whatever else is said to occur with some mode. But where the mode itself is made subject and “being” is predicated, so that there is a complete proposition, the proposition is not concerned with the mode. There the substance of the mode alone is proposed. Thus, when someone says, “The possible is,” he says that something among things is possible; again, “The contingent is” says that something among things is contingent; and “The necessary is” says that something among things is necessary. Here the discussion concerns not the mode but being alone.

Therefore, whenever “being” is made subject and the mode is predicated, as when we say, “It is possible for Socrates to walk,” the negation must be joined to the mode [Col. 0589A]. But whenever the mode is made subject and being is predicated, the negation must be placed with being. When we say, “The possible is,” we speak as though we were saying, “Possibility is”; and when we say, “The contingent is,” we speak as though we were saying, “Contingency is.” The negation must therefore be placed with being, and we must say, “The possible is not,” which has the same force as saying, “Possibility is not.” The same applies to contingency.

Yet one must not always assume, without careful examination, that the subject is whatever is said to occur first. Whatever is predicated is always what is predicated second. In some cases this is obvious; in others we determine from the meaning of the propositions which term is subject and which is predicate.

When I say, “A human being is an animal,” I must first say “human being” and then predicate “animal”; therefore “human being” is called the subject, while “animal” is predicated. But in propositions in which a mode is added, as when we say, “Socrates speaks well,” the sense is equivalent to “Socrates is speaking well.” Here “well” has been said first, and afterward “speaking is,” and it appears that what is said first, “well,” is the subject, while what is said afterward, “speaking is,” is the predicate.

But this is false. It can very easily be shown to be false from the fact that no one who hears “Socrates is speaking well” is unaware that he is speaking, whereas the force of the whole proposition is contained in the mode. Attention must therefore be directed not to whether he speaks—for that is beyond doubt—but to the mode, to what is expressed by “well.” For when someone says that Socrates speaks well, it is not enough to say that he speaks; he must also say that he speaks well.

The mode therefore contains the whole proposition. Yet, again, predication contains the whole proposition, and so in these propositions the mode is rather what is predicated.

We must therefore conclude universally that every contradiction involving modes is not formed according to the verb “to be,” nor according to a verb that itself contains “to be,” but rather according to the mode. Verbs are said to contain within themselves the notion of “being” when, for example, we say “he speaks,” since this has the same force as “he is speaking.” Therefore, whenever propositions contain some mode within themselves [Col. 0589D], there is no doubt that the negation ought not rightly to be applied to what posits being, but rather to the mode according to which something is said to be or to occur.

For every affirmation with a mode is such that the hearer’s attention ought not to be directed to what is said to be, but rather to how it is said to be. When we say, “Socrates speaks well,” we must not investigate whether he speaks, but rather direct the mind to how he speaks. This appears to contain the whole proposition.

Therefore, the negation opposed to “It is possible to be” is not “It is possible not to be,” but “It is not possible to be.” Similarly, the negation opposed to “It is contingent to be” is not “It is contingent not to be,” but rather “It is not contingent to be” [Col. 0590A]. The same procedure appears to apply to the modes “necessary,” “impossible,” and the others that Aristotle has passed over here in his customary brevity.

But since the excellence of a commentary consists not only in expressing the force of the meaning universally, but also in connecting what was stated above in confusion with the words and order of the text itself, let us now divide the discussion according to the order of Aristotle’s own words.

These matters having been determined, we must examine how negations and affirmations are related to one another—namely, those concerning “possible to be” and “not possible to be,” “contingent to be” and “not contingent to be,” and those concerning the impossible and the necessary. For they contain certain difficulties.

“It must be examined,” he says, “in what manner affirmations and negations appear to be opposed.” This concerns propositions containing some mode: those that are possible, contingent, necessary, impossible, true, false, good, bad, or whatever is predicated with some qualification. “For they contain,” he says, “certain difficulties,” and he immediately sets out what these difficulties are.

“If, of the expressions that comprise them, those are contradictions which are opposed to one another that are arranged according to being and not-being …”

The complete sense is as follows. In all complexes of propositions, that opposition is valid which is formed according to being and not-being. Thus, when we say “A human being is,” its negation is “A human being is not,” not “A non-human being is.” Again, of the proposition “A white human being is,” the negation is “A white human being is not,” not “A non-white human being is.”

He demonstrates this in the following way. “For if of everything there is either an affirmation or a negation, it will be true to say of wood that it is a non-white human being.”

This is stated briefly, but it appears capable of the following explanation. Let wood be the subject of two enunciations. Let it be clear to us that, of every subject, if the affirmation is true, the contradictory negation is false, and if the negation is true, the affirmation is declared false.

With wood as the subject, then, the affirmation “Wood is a white human being” is false. If this affirmation is false, its negation ought to be true. If the negation of the affirmation “A white human being is” is “A non-white human being is,” then this negation would be truly predicated of wood: anyone could say that wood is a non-white human being. But this cannot be done. It is plainly false to say that wood is a non-white human being. Whatever is not a human being at all cannot be a non-white human being.

Both propositions are therefore false: the affirmation concerning wood, “Wood is a white human being,” and the negation concerning it, “Wood is a non-white human being.” If both are false, the latter negation is not the negation of the former affirmation.

Another must therefore be sought which divides truth and falsehood with it. No other proposition is found opposed to “A white human being is” except “A white human being is not.” If the negation of the affirmation “A white human being is” is the proposition “A non-white human being is,” then, since the affirmation concerning wood is false, the negation stated of it would be true; it would be true to say of wood that it is a non-white human being. But this is impossible.

It is therefore clear that the proposition “A non-white human being is” is not the negation of the affirmation “A white human being is.” Rather, “A white human being is not” is the negation of the same affirmation.

Do you see, then, how in nearly all cases affirmations and negations are formed according to being and not-being? One proposition says that something is white, while the other denies this by saying that it is not white. Again, one says that something is a human being, while the other denies this by saying that it is not a human being. The same applies in the other cases.

“And if this is so, and in all cases in which ‘being’ is not added, the same will be done by what is said in place of ‘being,’ so that of the proposition ‘A human being walks,’ the negation is not ‘A non-human being walks,’ but ‘A human being does not walk.’ For it makes no difference whether one says ‘A human being walks’ or ‘A human being is walking.’”

Nor, he says, can this occur only in propositions arranged according to being and not-being. It also occurs in all propositions containing verbs of such a kind that the verbs themselves include the force of being—for example, “A human being walks” contains “is” within itself. “Walks” has the same meaning as “is walking.”

The negation must therefore be fitted to these verbs that contain being. For if every contradiction is formed according to being and not-being, and these verbs contain being in their proper signification, and are positioned as though being itself had been posited, it is clear that the negation ought to be placed with the verbs containing being, in accordance with the similarity of those propositions which, as explained above, are opposed to one another according to being and not-being.

Having stated these points, he continues by explaining what difficulty may result from them.

“Therefore, if this is so in all cases, of the proposition ‘It is possible to be,’ the negation is ‘It is possible not to be,’ and not ‘It is not possible to be.’ Yet it appears that the same thing can be and not be. For everything that is capable of being divided is also capable of not being divided; and everything capable of walking is also capable of not walking.”

[Col. 0591D] It was demonstrated above how, in enunciations that comprise propositions, oppositions are formed rather according to being and not-being. Aristotle now says: If this procedure must be followed in all propositions, so that their contradictions are posited according to being and not-being, then in propositions that declare something to be possible, the negation must not be framed as “It is not possible to be.” Rather, it must be constituted according to not-being, so that “It is possible not to be” is declared to be the negation of “It is possible to be.”

But if we say this, he continues, the affirmation and the negation do not divide truth and falsehood contradictorily between themselves. For everything that can be also can not be. Whatever can be divided can also not be divided, and whatever can walk can also not walk [Col. 0592A].

He next explains what kind of possibility this is: the kind by which, when something is said to be capable of occurring, it is nevertheless left capable of not occurring.

“The reason,” he says, “is that everything which is possible in this way is not always in actuality. Therefore negation will also belong to it. Thus what is capable of walking can also not walk, and what is visible can also not be seen.”

“But it is impossible for opposite statements concerning the same thing to be true. Therefore, of the proposition ‘It is possible to be,’ the negation is not ‘It is possible not to be.’ For from these alternatives it follows either that one simultaneously affirms and denies the same thing of the same subject, or that affirmations and negations are not formed according to the opposed notions of being and not-being. If the former is impossible, the latter must be preferred. The negation of ‘It is possible to be’ is therefore ‘It is not possible to be,’ and not ‘It is possible not to be.’ The same reasoning applies to ‘It is contingent to be,’ whose negation is ‘It is not contingent to be.’ The same applies in the other cases, such as the necessary and the impossible.”

The reason, then, why what is said to be capable of being can also not be is that everything we call possible is declared to be so in a way that does not require it always to be actual—that is, in a way that does not make it necessary. For whatever is always actual is necessary, as the sun is always moving. Its motion therefore always occurs.

But if someone says that I can walk, this is because the motion of walking does not always occur in me; there is also in me, at times, not walking. Thus it is truly said of me that I can not walk, while it is also truly said that I can walk. Whatever is not always actual therefore admits both of being possible and of being possible not to be.

What is walkable—that is, what can walk—can therefore not walk; and what is visible can fail to be seen. Accordingly, he teaches that the negation of “It can be” is not “It can not be.” The reason is that both are true in the case of things that, as Aristotle says, are not always actual.

From these alternatives, one of two consequences follows: either the same thing is simultaneously affirmed and denied of the same subject, or affirmations and negations are not formed according to the opposed notions of being and not-being. In other words, either affirmation and negation agree with each other if every contradiction is formed according to being and not-being—as happens with “It is possible to be” and “It is possible not to be”—or else being and not-being, or the verbs containing being, do not constitute contradiction in all affirmations and negations.

For the two propositions are identical in content and agree with one another. If someone calls them a contradiction, he says that a contradiction agrees with itself, which is impossible [Col. 0592D]. Alternatively, it must be admitted that in all affirmations and negations the opposing propositions are not formed according to being and not-being—that is, that contradiction is not formed in every case according to being and not-being, or according to verbs that contain being.

“If the former,” he says, “is more impossible, the latter will be preferred.”

Above he had posited two consequences of the preceding arguments: either affirming and denying one and the same thing of one and the same subject simultaneously—that is, making affirmation and negation predicates of the same thing at the same time, in agreement with one another—or forming contradiction otherwise than according to being and not-being.

Both appear in some way to be unacceptable. The first is plainly impossible, since affirmation and negation would agree; the second is inconsistent with other propositions in which it is clear that contradiction is formed in this way.

He now says that, since both alternatives are unacceptable, one must be chosen—that is, the less impossible one. It is less impossible for oppositions not to be formed according to being and not-being. Nothing prevents that. But it is more impossible for affirmation and negation to agree with one another. The former alternative must therefore be preferred: propositions containing a mode do not have the oppositions formed according to being and not-being, but rather those formed with respect to the mode [Col. 0593B].

He does not say that one alternative is more impossible as though the other were impossible. Rather, he refers to the fact that both appear somehow unacceptable, although one of them is unquestionably impossible. From this he also establishes the order of propositions enunciated according to a certain mode. They do not form their negations according to being, for he says:

“The negation of ‘It is possible to be’ is ‘It is not possible to be,’” adding the negation not to the verb “to be,” but to the mode “possible.” He says that the same reasoning applies to contingent propositions: the negation of “It is contingent to be” is “It is not contingent to be.”

He also teaches that the same appears to apply to the necessary and the impossible. Although the nature of this opposition has been expressed only briefly, it has nevertheless been expressed with complete truth. We discussed it at greater length above; if anyone attends more perceptively to the interpretation of that passage, he may connect it with this exposition as it proceeds step by step.

“For, just as in those cases ‘being’ and ‘not-being’ are additions, while the subjects are one thing white and another thing human being, so in this passage ‘being’ and ‘not-being’ become subjects, while ‘contingent’ and ‘possible’ are additions, determining, as ‘being’ and ‘not-being’ do in those cases, truth and falsehood—here in ‘being possible’ and ‘being not possible.’”

The negation of “It is possible not to be” is not “It is not possible to be,” but “It is not possible not to be.” Likewise, the negation of “It is possible to be” is not “It is possible not to be,” but “It is not possible to be.”

Therefore these propositions will appear to follow one another: “It is possible to be” and “It is possible not to be.” For the same thing is possible both to be and not to be. Such propositions are not contradictions of one another: “It is possible to be” and “It is possible not to be.” Rather, the contradictions are “It is possible to be” and “It is not possible to be”; these are never simultaneously true of the same subject, since they are opposed.

Nor are “It is possible not to be” and “It is not possible not to be” ever simultaneously true. The same applies to “It is necessary to be”: its negation is not “It is necessary not to be,” but “It is not necessary to be.” The negation of “It is necessary not to be” is “It is not necessary not to be.” The negation of “It is impossible to be” is not “It is impossible not to be,” but “It is not impossible to be.” The negation of “It is impossible not to be” is “It is not impossible not to be” [Col. 0594A].

He calls predicates “additions.” He therefore says that in propositions expressed without any mode, “being” and “not-being,” or verbs containing being, are always predicated; the things of which they are predicated are made subjects. Thus “white” is the subject when we say “White is,” and “human being” is the subject when we say “A human being is.”

Because predication in these propositions contains the whole proposition, that predication determines truth and falsehood. Being, or something containing being, is predicated. Contradictions are therefore rightly formed according to being and not-being.

But in the other propositions—that is, those in which some mode is predicated—being, or a verb containing being, is the subject [Col. 0594B]. The mode alone is predicated, in a certain sense. For when being is expressed without any mode, the substance of the thing itself is declared, and the question is, in a certain way, whether it exists. Therefore, when the affirmation posits being, the negation says “not-being.”

In propositions containing a mode, however, something is not said simply to be, but to be with some qualification. Being itself is not in dispute either for the affirmation or for the negation; what is in dispute is the qualification, that is, how it is.

Therefore, when someone says, “Socrates speaks well,” the negation is not “Socrates does not speak well,” but “Socrates speaks not-well.” For, as has been said, the hearer’s attention is directed not to being, nor to verbs containing being and thereby constituting the whole proposition, but rather to the mode, when the affirmation declares that something is [Col. 0594C].

If, then, the force of the whole proposition is contained in this, and what contains the force of the proposition is predicated, and oppositions are always formed according to what is predicated, the force of negation is rightly applied only to the modes.

Having established these points reasonably, he again explains that not only are “it can be” and “it can not be” not contradictions, but propositions of this kind, although they are formed with a mode and have a negation joined to being, are not negations at all; they are affirmations. For other negations of them can be found.

He says: “The negation of ‘It is possible not to be’ is ‘It is not possible not to be.’” So far, he says, is “It is possible not to be” from being the negation of “It is possible to be” that the proposition which says “It is possible not to be” is shown to be not a negation but rather an affirmation. An affirmation is never opposed to another affirmation as a contradiction.

It is shown to be an affirmation because another negation of it is found, namely, “It is not possible not to be.” He adds at the same time:

“Since there are two propositions which appear to be negations of the proposition ‘Something is possible to be’—namely, ‘Something is possible not to be’ and ‘Something is not possible to be’—from this it is recognized which of them is contradictory to the affirmation ‘Something is possible to be.’ For whichever divides truth and falsehood with it can rather be its negation than the one that agrees with it.”

“It is possible not to be” agrees with “It is possible to be,” as I have already shown. But if “It is not possible to be” is false, “It is possible to be” is true; and if this is again false, “It is not possible to be” is true. These propositions therefore divide truth and falsehood, as can easily be found in individual examples.

Let someone say that I can walk: he will have spoken truly. If someone says that I cannot walk, he has lied. Again, if someone says that the sun can stand still, he is lying. But if someone says that the sun cannot stand still, no one doubts the truth of his statement.

These propositions, then—“It is possible to be” and “It is not possible to be”—divide truth and falsehood. Those propositions, however, which say “It is possible to be” and “It is possible not to be” follow one another.

Those that agree with one another are not contradictions; those that divide truth and falsehood should rather be regarded as contradictions. This is what he means when he says: “Therefore they will also appear to follow one another.”

He identifies the propositions that follow one another: “It is possible to be” and “It is possible not to be.” He shows why they follow one another by adding: “For they are not contradictions of one another.” If they were contradictions, they would never follow one another.

He then declares which propositions are contradictions: “But ‘It is possible to be’ and ‘It is not possible to be’ are never simultaneously true.” He does not leave unexplained why they are never simultaneously true, for he says: “For they are opposed.” They are therefore never simultaneously true because they divide truth and falsehood, being opposed to one another.

He also teaches that the negation of “It is possible not to be” is “It is not possible not to be,” and from the same force passes to this proposition. He says: “But ‘It is possible not to be’ and ‘It is not possible not to be’ are never simultaneously true.” By this he shows that the one is affirmative and the other negative.

For universally, whenever one proposition posits the same thing of the same subject and another removes it, if one is affirmative and the other negative, and no ambiguity or universal qualification intervenes, they are contradictory opposites.

The remaining points, he says, are already so clear in themselves that they require no lengthy exposition. Yet certain matters must be interwoven into their order, so that what is clear in itself may be shown more clearly.

He proceeds in the same way through the other modes, saying which propositions are not the negations of which affirmations and which are, and opposing other negations to those he declares to be affirmations, so as to demonstrate that they are affirmations.

“Similarly,” he says, “the negation of the proposition ‘It is necessary to be’ is not ‘It is necessary not to be.’” For this is an affirmation, as he immediately proves by opposing a negation to it. Rather, the negation of “It is necessary to be” is “It is not necessary to be.”

He proceeds in the same way throughout, saying that the negation of “It is necessary not to be”—which he earlier declared not to be opposed to “It is necessary to be”—is “It is not necessary not to be.” For all propositions that have a negative particle joined to being, if they also contain a mode, must be regarded as affirmations.

The negation of “It is impossible to be” is not “It is impossible not to be.” For the latter does not have a negative particle attached to the mode, but rather the negation is “It is not impossible to be.” These two divide truth and falsehood between them. The proposition that has the negative particle attached to being is clearly an affirmation—namely, “It is impossible not to be”—and its negation is “It is not impossible not to be” [Col. 0596A].

He concludes briefly what he demonstrated above, saying:

“Universally, then, as has been said, being and not-being ought to be posited as subjects, while the negation and affirmation that produce this opposition ought to be added to being and not-being. These ought to be regarded as opposed expressions: possible, not possible; contingent, not contingent; impossible, not impossible; necessary, not necessary; true, not true.”

[Col. 0596B] “Universally,” he says, “as was already stated above, in propositions that have modes added to them, ‘is’ and ‘is not’ should rather be made subjects, while the modes are predicated. Therefore, for each individual mode—that is, according to each single mode—an affirmation and a negation must always be formed, so that, just as the predicated mode contains the affirmation, so the negative particle joined to the mode may contain the negation in its entirety.

“He proposes as opposed expressions the following: possible, not possible; contingent, not contingent; impossible, not impossible; necessary, not necessary. His addition of ‘true, not true’ is intended to include all modes. For ‘truly’ is indeed a mode, as are ‘well,’ ‘quickly,’ ‘gladly,’ ‘heavily,’ and whatever other modes there are. In these cases contradiction must be formed in this way: ‘It is true,’ ‘it is not true’; ‘to walk quickly,’ ‘not to walk quickly’; but not ‘to walk not quickly.’ Thus the negation must always be joined to the mode in the conclusion. For, as was already said above, those expressions always oppose one another that have negative particles joined according to their predications. In these propositions the modes are predicated, as we have already demonstrated above. Therefore, when the negation is placed according to the modes, it produces the complete force of contradiction.

“Once the oppositions of the modes have been dealt with, there will follow a subtle and useful treatment of the consequence and agreement of propositions. If ‘possible to be’ were said simply, the agreement of the propositions would appear simple and easy, and it would seem impossible to go wrong in their consequence. But since it is said in two ways according to different modes, the consequences of the propositions are not the same.

“What I mean is this. The possible has two divisions. One is that which, although it is not, can be. The other is that which is possible because it already exists. The first division belongs to corruptible and changeable things: mortal Socrates could exist when he did not yet exist, just as mortals who now exist are what they previously were not. A human being can speak when he is not speaking, and can walk when he is not walking. This division is therefore spoken of in relation to something that does not yet exist but nevertheless can exist.

“The other division of the possible is spoken of in relation to something that already exists actually, not merely potentially. It applies to both kinds of nature, namely, to everlasting things and to mortal things. For what exists in everlasting things is possible to be. Again, what exists in mortal things does not depart from the possibility of existing; it differs only in this respect: what exists in eternal things is in no way changed and must always exist, whereas what is found in mortal things can also not exist, and its existence is not necessary.

“When I am writing, the power of writing is present in me. Consequently, writing is possible for me. But since I myself am mortal, this power of writing is not necessary, for I do not write by necessity. When, however, we say that motion is present in the heavens, there is no doubt that the heavens must move. Thus, in mortal things, when something exists and can exist, its existence is not necessary; but in everlasting things, what exists must exist, and because it exists, it is possible to exist.

“Since the possible therefore has, primarily, two divisions—one spoken of in relation to what, although it is not, can exist, and the other predicated in relation to something that already exists actually, not merely potentially—this latter kind of possible, which already exists actually, produces two species: one that, although it exists, is not necessary; and another that, although it exists, also possesses the property that it must exist.

“This subtlety was not discovered by Aristotle alone. Diodorus too defines the possible in this way, saying that it is what either is or is not. Aristotle therefore takes what Diodorus says, ‘is not,’ to be the possible that, although it is not, can nevertheless come to be. What Diodorus said ‘is,’ Aristotle interprets as the possible that is called possible because it already exists actually.

“We have taught that the modes of this kind of possibility have two divisions: one that we call necessary, and another that we call non-necessary. This non-necessary kind has two further divisions: one that proceeds from potentiality to actuality; the other that has always been actual, while at some time the thing receptive of that actuality existed.

“The thing that proceeds from potentiality to actuality is receptive of both parts of the contradiction. Thus, I am now writing: I have come from potentiality to actuality, and, while acting, I can write. Before I wrote, I had the potentiality for writing; but from the potentiality for writing I came to the actuality of writing. Hence both belong to me: writing and not writing. For I can both not write and write, and this is in a certain way a contradiction.

“Therefore, whatever proceeds from potentiality to actuality can both do and not do, both be and not be. Thus, someone who is speaking could speak before he spoke, because he had the power to speak; and now he can speak because he is speaking. He can therefore speak, and he can also not speak.

“The other kind was never previously potential but was always actual, although at some time the thing itself was what is said to possess something potentially. This kind is adapted to only one outcome. Fire was never previously potentially hot so that it might later be perceived as actually hot; nor was snow previously potentially cold and then afterward actually cold. Rather, fire was at some time actually hot, and snow was at some time actually cold. Consequently, these potentialities are not adapted to both alternatives. Fire cannot undergo coldness, nor can snow ever produce heat.

“Therefore, this division must be made from the beginning. One part of the possible is that which, although it is not, can nevertheless be. The other is that which exists actually and is therefore called possible. For if it could not exist, it would not exist at all. This latter possibility, which is spoken of according to the mode in which something is already actual, has two divisions: one according to what we say exists by necessity; the other according to what we judge, although it exists, not to exist by necessity.

“This non-necessary potentiality has two further divisions. One is that which, because it comes from potentiality to actuality, admits both being and not being. The other is that which, because it has never ceased to be actual, was at some time what is said to be possible for it to be. It is adapted and possible for only one alternative, namely, the one it has always exercised actually: heat for fire, cold for snow, hardness for a diamond, liquidity for water.

“But no one should suppose that what we call ‘never having been potential’ belongs to the species of necessary possibility. Certain actualities in certain things—for example, heat in fire—can cease. In things that are necessary, however, not only must the quality never depart from the underlying thing, as appears even in fire, whose quality of heat does not depart from it; the underlying substance itself must also appear to be immortal. This does not occur in fire.

“Peripatetic doctrine considers the sun and the other bodies of this kind that are above and heavenly to be immortal. Therefore, consistently with itself, it teaches that the sun necessarily moves: not only does that motion never depart from the sun, but the sun itself will never cease to exist.

“Having stated these matters, we must now pursue more carefully the subject for which they were prefaced, namely, the consequence of propositions.

“The consequences are arranged as follows. ‘Possible to be’ is followed by ‘contingent to be’; the latter converts with it, as do ‘not impossible to be’ and ‘not necessary to be.’ ‘Possible not to be’ and ‘contingent not to be’ are followed by ‘not necessary not to be’ and ‘not impossible not to be.’ ‘Not possible to be’ and ‘not contingent to be’ are followed by ‘necessary not to be’ and ‘impossible to be.’ ‘Not possible not to be’ and ‘not contingent not to be’ are followed by ‘necessary to be’ and ‘impossible not to be.’ Let what we mean be considered from the table below.”

[Col. 0598D] Aristotle added this concerning the consequence of propositions, consistently with what we prefaced above. Although these matters are clear to those who examine them sharply, nevertheless, lest we seem to have added nothing here either, we shall pass through them in a very brief exposition.

First, he wished to demonstrate that whatever is said of the possible can also be said, with complete truth, of the contingent. Therefore he says that “possible to be” is followed by “contingent to be.” And lest anything here appear inconsistent, he adds, “and this converts with it,” so that we may understand that what is possible can be contingent, and what is contingent can be possible. Thus, things that convert with one another are equal and identical.

Whatever, therefore, can be called impossible is predicated in the same way of the contingent. Accordingly, he said that “contingent” and “possible” follow the proposition that says “not impossible to be” and the proposition that denies necessity, namely, “not necessary to be.” For he says:

“‘Possible to be’ is followed by ‘contingent to be,’ and this converts with it, as do ‘not impossible to be’ and ‘not necessary to be’”—as though he were saying: “Contingent to be also follows possible to be. These two convert with each other, but they are followed by not impossible to be and not necessary to be.”

No one is unaware how correctly this is said. What is possible to be is contingent to be, so that it is not impossible to be. For if it were impossible, it would not be said to be able to be; the force of impossibility would prevent its being. Therefore, what can be is not impossible to be.

Similarly, what is said to be possible to be is not necessary to be. This occurs because what we predicate as possible is readily convertible in both directions: it can come to be and it can not come to be. Necessity and impossibility, however, are confined to one or the other alternative. What is impossible to be can never be; and what must be can never not be.

Therefore, what we deny to be impossible we make agree with possibility. And what we again deny to be necessary we join to the same nature of possibility, so that it may be said in this way—or, to speak more accurately: what is possible can both be and not be. Again, what is impossible to be cannot be, and what must be cannot not be.

If, then, by adding a negation we break the force of the impossible proposition and say “not impossible to be,” we join to it that part of possibility in which we say that something can be. But if we lessen the force of the necessary proposition by negation, saying “not necessary to be,” the result is that we apply the proposition to that part which lies within possibility, namely, that it may not be.

Thus “not impossible to be” follows possibility because what is possible can come to be. The proposition “not necessary to be” likewise follows possibility because what is possible can also not be.

Put differently: of what is possible it is not correct to say that it is impossible, because it can come to be. Nor is it correct to say that what is possible is necessary, because what is possible to be can also not be. Therefore, if impossibility and necessity cannot correctly be predicated of possibility, their negations agree with possibility: “not impossible to be” and “not necessary to be.”

We must remember that the same reasoning always applies to the contingent and the possible—namely, to the possible that, although it does not yet exist, can nevertheless be or not be.

He gives another consequence in this way:

“‘Possible not to be’ and ‘contingent not to be’ are followed by ‘not necessary not to be’ and ‘not impossible not to be.’”

He gives this consequence for the same reason. He says that “‘possible not to be’ and ‘contingent not to be’” agree with “‘not necessary not to be’ and ‘not impossible not to be.’” This is because what can not be can also be, and what is contingent not to be is also contingent to be.

But what must not be cannot be; and what is impossible not to be cannot not be. Therefore these differ from the possible in both respects. For the proposition that says that something must not be contradicts possibility, which promises that something can be. Again, because possibility contains the force by which what can be can also not be, it strongly disagrees with the proposition that says that it is impossible not to be.

If, then, the proposition that predicates that something must not be, and likewise the proposition that says that something is impossible not to be, disagree with possibility, their negations are rightly thought to agree with possibility.

By “possible propositions” I mean those that display some possibility either in affirmation or in negation, without excluding the other alternative. Thus, the proposition that says that something can be is not excluded by the proposition through which it can be said that something can not be. Likewise, if someone says that it is possible for something not to be, this does not exclude its being possible for it to be.

Therefore I call the affirmation “it is possible to be” a possible proposition, and likewise the proposition “it is possible not to be.” In the propositions Aristotle sets out, in which he says “possible not to be,” it should not appear that he is speaking as though he intended to say that something is impossible when he says “possible not to be.” He says this proposition not in order to remove that possibility, but to say that it is possible for something not to be.

The verb “to be” must be understood and supplied with the word “possible,” so that when he says “possible not to be,” we understand “possible to be not to be,” that is, “possible for something not to be.”

He establishes a third consequence, in which he says that “‘not possible to be’ and ‘not contingent to be’” agree with “‘necessary not to be’ and ‘impossible to be.’” This is so clear that it requires no exposition. What is not possible cannot come to be; what cannot come to be must not be; and what must not be is impossible.

It is therefore correctly said that the proposition “something cannot be” and the proposition “something is not contingent to be” are followed by those that affirm that something must not be and those that affirm its impossibility.

What he says is this: “Not necessary to be” is contingent to be. “Necessary not to be” is not contingent to be—that is, it is not contingent to be—and is necessary not to be.

He gives the remaining consequence by saying that the propositions “‘not possible not to be’ and ‘not contingent not to be’” agree with those that propose “‘necessary to be’ and ‘impossible not to be.’” This too contains no obscurity.

What is not possible not to be is impossible not to be. For what we call “impossible to be” has the same force as “not possible to be.” What negation does in the interpretation in which we say “not possible,” privation does in the interpretation in which we say “impossible.”

That which is impossible not to be is plainly necessary to be. Therefore, what is not possible not to be is likewise plainly necessary to be. The same must also be said concerning the contingent.

He sets these out in this way so that they may be grasped not only by the mind and by reasoning but also so that understanding may be made easier by placing them before the eyes. To make the explanation clearer, we arrange them in two orders. In the first we have placed those that precede; in the second, those that follow. Thus, even for those who do not understand the reasons for them independently, there is considerable assistance in looking at the diagram and recognizing which proposition follows which.

[Col. 0602A]

Possible to be.  
Not impossible to be.  
Contingent to be.  
Not necessary to be.  
Possible not to be.  
Not necessary not to be.  
Contingent not to be.  
Not possible not to be.  
Not possible to be.  
Necessary not to be.  
Not contingent to be.  
Impossible to be.  
Not possible not to be.  
Necessary to be.  
Not contingent not to be.  
Impossible not to be.

Once this table has been made, no one who examines it carefully can find it ambiguous what Aristotle has treated generally concerning propositions and universally concerning their consequences. Since we do not wish to weary our readers, however, the remaining matters that he discussed individually concerning their consequences will be dealt with in the sixth volume.

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 0601]

[Col. 0601B] This sixth book brings to an end a long commentary, established through great labor and the passage of time. For the opinions of many authors have been gathered into one work, and we have spent nearly two continuous years in the toil of commenting.

Nor do I suppose that those who interpret matters unfavorably will think it glorious that what could have been said briefly was extended by us through a display of learning—not toward the knowledge of readers, but toward their weariness through prolixity. I should like to reply to them that they would not feel this so falsely if they had read through the brevity of the earlier commentary. For the obscurity of the extremely compressed and difficult language could not have been explained more briefly, and they will recognize how much is lacking for a complete understanding of this book.

What benefit each of the two works offers to readers seems to me most easily judged from this: when someone first takes this second edition into his hands, he is overwhelmed by the extensive variety of the subjects themselves, so that anyone unable to apply his mind to the greater matters begins to miss the brevity and simplicity of the first edition.

But if a reader approaches the two books of the earlier edition, he may perhaps think that he has acquired some contribution to knowledge. When at last he comes to know this second edition, however, he recognizes how much he had not known in the first. Nor should the length of the work deter people from reading it, since it did not prevent us from writing it.

But lest even this preface seem to extend too far, let us return to the sequence of Aristotle and to the matters he carefully pursues concerning the consequence of propositions.

[Col. 0601D] He arranged in the preceding description of the propositions what was to be examined generally and universally concerning propositions and their mutual consequences. Now he pursues, with the most careful treatment, what happens individually to each of them. For he says as follows:

“Therefore, ‘impossible’ and ‘not impossible’ follow ‘contingent’ and ‘possible,’ and ‘not contingent’ and ‘not possible,’ as contradictories, but conversely. For ‘possible to be’ is followed by the negation of ‘impossible’; while the affirmation follows the negation. For ‘impossible to be’ follows ‘not possible to be.’ For ‘impossible to be’ is an affirmation, while ‘not impossible to be’ is a negation.”

The consequence of propositions, as the preceding table teaches, has been established according to the possible and the necessary. This also led him to speak of contingent and impossible propositions and their consequences. Since the contingent agrees directly with the possible, while the impossible is related conversely to the necessary, as we shall explain shortly, he examines the possible, contingent, and impossible, asking how they relate to one another and what consequences they possess. He establishes the matter in this way, saying:

“Impossible and not impossible follow possible and not possible as contradictories, but conversely.”

This means the following. We know that the privative affirmation is the one that says “impossible to be,” and its negation is “not impossible to be.” Again, the possible affirmation is the one that says “possible to be,” and its negation is “not possible to be.”

The negation of the impossible therefore follows the possible affirmation. For what is possible is also not impossible. Otherwise, if the proposition “not impossible to be” did not follow possibility, its affirmation—that is, “impossible to be”—would follow it. What is possible would then be impossible, although it can come to be.

If impossibility does not follow possibility, therefore, “not impossible to be” follows possibility. But the affirmation of impossibility follows the negation of possibility. For what is not possible is impossible. Negation in propositions has the same force as privation.

The same applies to the contingent. What is contingent to be is not impossible. For if contingent and possible follow one another, and possible agrees with not impossible, then contingent and not impossible also signify the same thing.

Again, someone examining the matter will be able to see that “not contingent” and “impossible” appear to be the same, because “not contingent” expresses the same meaning as “not possible,” while “not possible” agrees with “impossible.” Consequently, “not contingent” also declares that something is impossible to be.

Thus the affirmation of impossibility follows the contradiction of possibility. But it does not follow affirmation as affirmation, nor negation as negation, but conversely: affirmation follows negation, and negation follows affirmation.

For the affirmation “possible to be” is followed by the negation of impossibility, “not impossible to be”; while the negation of possibility, “not possible to be,” is followed by the affirmation of impossibility, “impossible to be.”

The same must be said of the contingent. The affirmation of the contingent is followed by the negation of impossibility, while the negation of the contingent is followed by the affirmation of impossibility. For whatever is proposed concerning possibility is judged in the same way concerning the contingent.

They should therefore be arranged in this way: first, the affirmation of impossibility, and opposite to it, the negation of impossibility. Under the affirmation of impossibility should be placed the contingent and possible propositions that are followed by impossibility; under the negation of impossibility, the possible and contingent propositions with which the negation of impossibility agrees, as follows:

Impossible to be.  
Not impossible to be.  
Not possible to be.  
Possible to be.  
Not contingent to be.  
Contingent to be.

It is therefore clear that contradictions agree with other contradictions. It is also clear in this matter that affirmations agree with negations, and negations with affirmations.

The complete sense is as follows. The reasoning of the expressions is this:

“Impossible and not impossible”—namely, the contradiction consisting of two contradictions—“follow, as contradictories, contingent and possible, and not contingent and not possible.” One contradiction, “impossible and not impossible,” follows two contradictions: “contingent and not contingent,” and “possible and not possible.”

Although one contradiction therefore follows another contradiction, they nevertheless agree with each other conversely. For “possible to be” is followed by the negation of impossibility, as the preceding table teaches. The negation of possible, however, is followed by the affirmation of impossibility, for “not possible” agrees with “impossible.” The affirmation of impossibility is the one that says “impossible to be.”

Although the reasoning of the expressions is involved, anyone who returns, according to the preceding explanation, from Aristotle’s own words to the earlier passages, and supplies from our exposition what is lacking in those words, will find that the fullest sense does not depart from reason.

[Col. 0603D] The manner in which the necessary operates must now be considered. It is clear that the consequences do not arise in the same way, but that contraries follow. Contradictories, however, are outside the consequence. For “necessary not to be” is not the negation of “necessary to be”; rather, “not necessary to be” is its negation. Both can be true in the same subject. For what is “necessary not to be” is not “necessary to be.”

We learned earlier, from the comparison of the possible and the impossible, that the possible affirmation is followed by the negation of the impossible, while the possible negation is followed by the affirmation of the impossible.

Now, seeking to determine how the consequences of possible and necessary propositions arise, he says that they do not occur in the same way as those that arose from the comparison of the possible and impossible propositions.

In the latter case, opposite contradictions followed opposite contradictions: affirmation was followed by negation, and negation by affirmation. In the case of the impossible and necessary, however, the arrangement is different. Contraries follow, but contradictories and opposites remain outside and do not follow.

First, let us set out which are contraries and which are contradictories. The contradictory of the proposition “necessary to be” is “not necessary to be.” The contrary is “necessary not to be.” Thus, if someone says, “The sun necessarily moves,” the contradictory opposed to it is “The sun does not necessarily move,” while the contrary is “The sun necessarily does not move.”

A possible proposition is therefore followed by the contradictory of the necessary. But the contradiction of the possible is not followed by necessity. That would occur if opposites followed one another in these propositions. Rather, it is followed by the contrary of necessity.

Let us examine what necessary propositions agree with the opposition that says “possible to be.” The proposition “necessary to be” cannot agree with it. What is possible to be can also not be, whereas what is necessary to be cannot not be.

Therefore, if necessity does not follow possibility, the contradiction of necessity follows it. The proposition “possible to be” is not followed by “necessary to be,” but by the contradiction of necessity, “not necessary to be.”

Necessity does not agree with the contradiction of possibility. For we cannot say that the proposition “not possible to be” is followed by “necessary to be.” Rather, it is followed by the contrary of the necessary, “necessary not to be.” For when something is not possible to be, it must not be.

Let these propositions that follow be set out, together with the necessary propositions and with an indication of which is the contradiction and which the contrary:

Possible to be.  
Not possible to be.

Not necessary to be.  
Necessary not to be.

Contradictories: Necessary to be.  
Contraries: Necessary not to be.

No one can therefore doubt that the affirmation of possibility is followed by the negation of necessity, while the negation of possibility is not followed by the necessary but rather by the contrary of the necessary.

When “possible to be” is followed by the contradiction of necessity, namely “not necessary to be,” the contradiction of possibility, “not possible to be,” is not followed by necessity itself, but rather by the contrary proposition, “necessary not to be.”

The sense is therefore this. The sequence of the words is as follows: “The necessary,” he says, “must be considered as to how it arises,” that is, what consequences it possesses.

First he defines the matter by saying: “It is clear that it does not occur in the same way.” Here we must understand: “as it occurs in propositions that are possible and impossible.” Rather, contraries follow, while contradictories remain outside and do not follow.

For the contradiction of the possible is followed not by the contradiction of the necessary but, as we have taught above, by its contrary. Possibility is followed by “not necessary,” while “not possible” is followed by the proposition “necessary not to be,” not by “not necessary to be.”

Again, “necessary not to be” and “not necessary to be” are not contradictories. “Not necessary to be” is the negation of the necessary, whereas “necessary not to be” is contrary to the necessary. They are not contradictories opposed to one another, for both can be found simultaneously in one and the same subject.

He indicates this by saying: “For both can happen to be true in the same thing.” For “necessary not to be” is not “necessary to be.” Since it is necessary for a human being not to be a quadruped, it is not necessary for a human being to be a quadruped. If the latter were true, it would be necessary for a human being to be a quadruped, although it is necessary that he not be one.

It is therefore clear that “not necessary to be” and “necessary not to be” can sometimes be found together. Although they are opposed, they are not contradictories.

He then gives the reason why, although consequence is established according to the comparison of the possible, the same arrangement could not occur in the necessary:

[Col. 0605B] “The reason why the consequences do not follow in the same way as in the other cases is that the impossible, expressed contrarily, is rendered equivalent to the necessary. For what is impossible to be is necessarily not to be—not ‘to be,’ but rather ‘not to be.’ What is impossible not to be is necessary to be.

“Therefore, if those propositions followed possible and not possible in the same way, these follow conversely, because necessary and impossible do not signify the same thing, but, as has been said, conversely.”

“The reason,” he says, “why the consequence is arranged in this way in the necessary is that the necessary always agrees with the impossible in a contrary manner. What is impossible to be is necessary not to be; and what is necessary to be is impossible not to be.

“Thus a kind of contrariety arises. When impossibility is predicated of being, necessity is predicated of not being; and when necessity is predicated of being, impossibility is predicated of not being. Therefore impossibility and necessity have the same force, but are expressed in different ways.

“If necessity is expressed according to being, impossibility is expressed according to not being; and if impossibility is expressed according to being, necessity is expressed according to not being. This is why the conversion occurs in the opposite manner. Where there is ‘impossible to be,’ there is ‘necessary not to be.’ But ‘impossible to be’ and ‘not possible to be’ agree. Therefore ‘not possible to be’ and ‘necessary not to be’ agree.

“No one can doubt, then, that ‘necessary not to be’ follows the negation of possibility, because the impossibility that follows the negation of possibility agrees with the proposition ‘necessary not to be.’ This occurs because impossibility and necessity have the same force, as I have said, when they are proposed as contraries.

“The matter is therefore expressed as follows: ‘The reason why the consequences do not follow in the same way as in the other cases’—that is, as in those formed according to the possible and impossible—is ‘that the contrary of the impossible is rendered equivalent to the necessary.’ That is, impossibility, expressed and stated in the contrary manner, has the same force as necessity.

“If it is impossible to be, it is necessary not to be. But if it is necessary not to be, it is not possible to be. Therefore no one should say, ‘It is necessary to be,’ but rather, ‘It is necessary not to be,’ as though he had said: If it is impossible to be, it is necessary not to be.

“We must not suppose that ‘impossible to be’ is the same as ‘necessary to be.’ If, conversely, it is impossible not to be, then it is necessary to be. Thus impossibility and necessity, when converted conversely and expressed in contrary form, have the same force.

“If impossibility yields consequence in relation to possibility through a similar contradiction and through the conversion of contradictions, and if impossibility and necessity have the same force when predicated as contraries, there can be no doubt that the consequence here has rightly been given as contrary rather than opposite.

“Or should the matter be explained in this way? In the consequence of ‘impossible’ and ‘not impossible’ to the propositions that propose ‘possible’ and ‘not possible,’ the proposition ‘not possible’ was followed by the proposition ‘impossible to be.’ It is clear that, conversely, ‘impossible’ has the same force as ‘necessary not to be.’ This follows the proposition that impossibility also followed.

“The proposition ‘necessary not to be’ is contrary but equivalent to impossibility, and impossibility follows the proposition ‘not possible to be.’ Therefore ‘necessary not to be’ follows ‘not possible to be.’ The sense is that ‘impossible’ can have the same force as ‘necessary,’ when expressed conversely.

“The same arrangement applies: it is in the same way as was said concerning the consequence of ‘impossible’ to the propositions called ‘possible’ and ‘not possible.’”

Is it perhaps impossible to set out the contradictories of the necessary in this way? For that which necessarily is, is possible to be. For if not, negation will follow. In every case, it is necessary either to affirm or to deny. Therefore, if it is not possible to be, it is impossible to be. Thus what necessarily is would be impossible to be, which is absurd. But from that which is possible to be, it follows that it is not impossible to be. This, however, is what it means that it is not necessary to be. Therefore it follows that what necessarily is is not necessary to be—which is plainly absurd. Yet neither does “necessary to be” follow from “possible to be,” nor does “necessary not to be.” For both belong to the possible, whereas, if either of these is true, the former will not yet be true. For it is possible simultaneously both to be and not to be. But if it is necessary either to be or not to be, it will not be possible to do both. It remains, therefore, that “not necessary not to be” follows from “possible to be.” For this is true also of “necessary to be”: that which is necessary to be is not necessary not to be. This is the contradictory of the proposition that follows from “not possible to be.” For “impossible to be” and “necessary not to be” follow from the latter. The contradictory of “necessary not to be” [Col. 0607A] is “not necessary not to be.” These contradictories, therefore, also follow according to the manner stated above. And nothing impossible results when they are so posited.

The conversion of the propositions made earlier was such that the possible proposition was followed by the negation of the necessary.
