With these propositions so arranged, however, it did not follow that a contradiction was followed by a contradiction, nor that the converse relation held—as it did in the case in which the consequence of the possible and the impossible was being considered—for the contradiction of the necessary, namely “not necessary to be,” followed the possible proposition. Necessity, however, did not follow the contradiction of the possible; rather, the contrary of necessity did. Wishing to alter this, Aristotle intends to arrange the consequences so that, in a similar manner, contradiction agrees with contradiction, but conversely. He arranges the matter in the following way.

He says: “Perhaps I was mistaken in beginning the consequence of the necessary and the possible from the possible, rather than from the necessary, so that its agreement with the latter might be concealed.” For he had posited “possible to be” as the antecedent, and “not necessary to be” as agreeing with it by way of consequent. That was the earlier arrangement. Now he reverses it and says: “Perhaps, through an error, we arranged these consequences in such a way that we first posited ‘possible to be’ and then joined to it, as its consequent, the negation of the necessary, which says ‘not necessary to be.’ Or rather, is the truth not that, when the necessary is posited first, possibility—which agrees with necessity—should follow? For it appears that every necessary proposition is followed by possibility. If anyone denies this, he must admit that the negation of the possible follows necessity. For in every case there is either affirmation or negation. Therefore, if the possible does not follow the necessary proposition, the negation of the possible follows it.” Thus one might say that the correct consequence is: “What is necessary to be is not possible to be.” But it was said earlier that the impossibility agrees with the proposition that asserts “not possible to be.” Yet “not possible to be” follows necessity, and therefore impossibility will also follow necessity. The correct consequence of the propositions will thus be: “If it is necessary to be, it is impossible to be.” But this cannot be.

If, therefore, impossibility does not follow necessity, while the proposition that declares something unable to be follows the impossible proposition, then the negation of possibility—namely “not possible to be”—does not agree with the necessary proposition. And if this does not agree with the necessary assertion, its affirmation will agree with it. Possibility, therefore, follows necessity. The correct consequence of the propositions will thus be: “If it is necessary to be, it is possible to be.”

But again another difficulty arises from this. For if someone says that the possible proposition agrees with necessity, then, since the proposition “not impossible to be” agrees with possibility, and again the proposition “not necessary to be” agrees with it—as the preceding order taught—it will follow that the proposition “not necessary to be” agrees with the necessary proposition. The correct consequence would therefore be: “If it is necessary to be, it is not necessary to be.” But this too is impossible. If that is so, something impossible must be rearranged among the consequences of the propositions, so that the reasoning may agree with itself. Either, then, the first statement was made incorrectly—namely, that the negation of the necessary follows the affirmation of the possible, so that “not necessary to be” follows “possible to be”—or else we have wrongly understood the possible proposition to agree with the necessary, which is utterly absurd. For no one would say that possibility is contrary to necessity. It follows, indeed, that what is necessary cannot fail to be, and the consequence is correct: “If it is necessary to be, it is possible to be,” just as the contradiction of the necessary proposition should not follow the possible proposition.

When these things are said, however, we should understand that possibility follows necessity, so that what is necessary is said to be possible. This is a point intended for those who examine the matter more deeply. For it is one thing to say that a thing must be, and another to say that it is possible. What is possible in itself does not become necessary in every respect. For if something is necessary, it cannot happen not to be. But what is possible can also not be; therefore what is possible will not be necessary.

I say, moreover, that neither does the proposition that is wholly contrary to necessity follow possibility. For the proposition contrary to the necessary is the one that says, “It is necessary not to be.” No one will compel this to agree with possibility. For what is necessary not to be cannot be. But what is possible can both be and not be. Therefore the necessity predicated according to being does not follow possibility, because possibility can also not be, whereas necessity according to being cannot not be. Again, necessity predicated according to not-being differs from possibility and does not follow it, because the necessity that is said according to not-being cannot be, whereas the possible can both be and not be.

Thus, so that neither the opposed negation of the necessary may follow possibility—the one that asserts “not necessary to be”—nor the affirmation of necessity itself, which says “necessary to be,” nor its contrary, which says “necessary not to be,” there appear to be four propositions:

> It is necessary to be.  
> It is not necessary to be.
>
> It is necessary not to be.  
> It is not necessary not to be.

If, therefore, neither the proposition that says “it is necessary to be,” nor its opposite, “it is not necessary to be,” nor the contrary of necessity, whose meaning is “it is necessary not to be,” agrees with possibility, then it remains that the fourth proposition agrees with it: “It is not necessary not to be.” This fourth proposition, in a certain way, also agrees with necessity, whereas necessity itself does not agree with possibility at all. For everything that is necessary to be is also possible to be, and it is not necessary that it not be.

The proposition “it is not necessary not to be” agrees with necessity for the following reason: the proposition “it is necessary not to be” is contrary to necessity, while its opposite is “it is not necessary not to be.” Therefore the proposition that is contradictory to the affirmation opposed to it will agree with it. Anyone who examines the matter more attentively and returns fully to what was written above will readily understand this.

If, then, as was said, “possible to be” is followed by the proposition “not necessary not to be,” its opposite, “necessary not to be,” will follow the negation of the possible. The consequence will therefore be:

> If it is possible to be, it is not necessary not to be.  
> If it is not possible to be, it is necessary not to be.

The consequence has therefore been reversed: contradiction follows contradiction, but conversely, as was said above concerning impossibles. Here the negation follows the affirmation of the possible—the negation that destroys the necessary, namely “not necessary not to be”—while the necessary affirmation according to not-being follows the negation of the possible. Here too, therefore, the same conversion occurs: contradiction follows contradiction, but conversely, so that affirmation agrees with negation and negation with affirmation. We believe this will become clearer if it is placed before the eyes; and therefore let the order of the arrangement below remind us most plainly of the argument:

> It is possible to be. It is not possible to be.
>
> It is not necessary not to be. It is necessary not to be.

The whole meaning is as follows. The order of the discourse is this: After Aristotle had discussed the consequence of the possible and the impossible, saying that contradictions agree with contradictions, but conversely—that affirmation agrees with negation, while negation agrees with affirmation—he says that we must now examine how the same consequence occurs in the case of the necessary.

Having examined the necessary as well, he did not find the same relation. For when he had said that the negation of the necessary agrees with possibility, the necessary affirmation did not agree with the negation of possibility. In giving the reasons for this, he criticized the proposition that had made impossibility equivalent to the contrary of necessity. Wishing to correct this, he said:

“Or perhaps,” he says, “it is impossible to set out the contradictions of the necessary in such a way that we say that the negation of the necessary agrees with possibility.”

He adds a certain difficulty, which runs as follows. “What is necessary to be,” he says, “is without doubt possible to be. For if it is not—if what is necessary is not possible—the negation of possibility follows. For in every matter it is necessary either to state, that is, to affirm, or to deny. In every matter, either the affirmation or the negation is true. Therefore, if it is not possible to be—that is, if this is ‘not possible to be,’ which is impossible—what is necessary to be will become impossible. The proposition ‘impossible to be’ follows the proposition ‘not possible to be’; thus something impossible will be asserted, namely that what is necessary to be is impossible to be. But this is absurd.” He therefore taught that possibility follows necessity.

Now he adds another point. Since he said above that the negation of the necessary affirmation agrees with the possible proposition, he now raises a difficulty about the same matter, saying:

“But from that which is possible to be, it follows that it is not impossible to be. For what is possible is not impossible. But what is not impossible to be is not necessary to be. Therefore, if ‘not impossible to be’ follows possibility, ‘not necessary to be’ also follows the possible proposition. There can be no doubt that, if possibility follows necessity, the negation of the necessary follows the necessary affirmation. Thus it follows that what is necessary to be is itself not necessary to be, which is absurd.”

It is therefore established that the opposite negation of the necessary affirmation does not follow the possible affirmation. For this reason, as we said above, that must be removed: the negation of the necessary must not follow the possible affirmation, so that possibility may follow necessity. Since this cannot happen in any way, the opposite must be removed: the negation opposed to necessity must not follow possibility.

Therefore “not necessary to be” does not follow possibility. And because he had left all these matters unspoken in the middle of his discussion, he added to what had been said above: “But neither does the necessary follow ‘possible to be.’” By this he included the point that necessity does not agree with possibility. Nor is this all; he also shows more clearly the meaning of “necessary not to be.” For “both,” he says, “can happen to the possible”—namely, both being and not-being. But if either of these—the necessary according to being or the necessary according to not-being—is true, those alternatives will not be true. He himself explains this by speaking of the possible in both ways: “For it is possible simultaneously both to be and not to be.” This, then, is what he means when he says, “Both can happen to it.”

“But if,” he says, “it is necessary to be or not to be”—that is, if it cannot not be, and if it cannot be—it will not be possible for both to hold. If it is necessary to be, it will not be able not to be; or if it is necessary not to be, it will not be able to be. Thus three propositions do not follow possibility: “not necessary to be,” “necessary to be,” and “necessary not to be.”

It remains, therefore, that the fourth proposition, which is opposed to the affirmation of the necessary according to not-being, follows possibility: namely, “not necessary not to be” follows “possible to be.” But because possibility agrees with the necessary, this proposition also agrees with the necessary. For this is what he said: “This is true also of necessary being.” For what is necessary to be is not necessary not to be. The proposition “not necessary not to be” is therefore the contradiction of the affirmation that follows the negation of possibility, namely “not possible to be.”

For when the affirmation “possible to be” is followed by the negation of the necessary according to not-being, “not necessary not to be,” this negation of the necessary according to not-being is the contradiction of what follows the negation of possibility. The latter—that is, the negation of possibility—is followed by the impossible. For the negation of possibility is the proposition “not possible to be,” and this is followed by “impossible to be,” to which “necessary not to be” agrees.

The negation of the possible proposition is therefore followed by “necessary not to be,” whose contradiction is “not necessary not to be.” Thus it too comes about that contradiction follows contradiction, but conversely. This is what he means when he says: “These contradictions also follow according to the manner stated above”—namely, so that affirmation follows negation and negation follows affirmation.

When the consequences are arranged in this way—so that the possible affirmation is followed by the negation of the necessary according to not-being, while the negation of the possible agrees with the necessary affirmation according to not-being—nothing either absurd or impossible results. Having explained these matters, Aristotle adds further difficulties.

Someone might raise the question whether “possible to be” follows “necessary to be.” For if it does not follow, contradiction will follow, namely “not possible to be.” And if someone says that this is not the contradiction, he must say that the contradiction is “possible not to be.” Yet both are false of what is necessary to be. But again it seems that the same thing is possible both to be cut and not to be cut, both to be and not to be. Therefore what is necessary to be will be contingent not to be; but this is false.

Above, Aristotle arranged the consequences so that possibility followed the preceding necessary proposition. Now he himself raises a difficulty about the same point. For whether he arranges possibility as agreeing with necessity or someone denies this, either alternative appears incongruous.

If someone denies that possibility agrees with necessity, he says that the negation of possibility will agree with the necessary proposition. For if someone refuses to allow the proposition “possible to be” to agree with the proposition “necessary to be,” he cannot deny that the negation of possibility agrees with necessity. There would then be a complete consequence: “If it is necessary to be, it is not possible to be,” since the consequence “If it is necessary to be, it is possible to be” is false.

But if it cannot happen that the negation of possibility agrees with the necessary affirmation, then it is true that the possible affirmation agrees with the necessary. Yet here too there will be a greater difficulty. For everything that is possible to be is also possible not to be. But if possibility follows necessity, what is necessary will be able both to be and not to be, according to the nature of possibility that agrees with necessity. This is impossible. Possibility therefore does not follow necessity.

If possibility does not follow necessity, however, its negation follows—namely “not possible to be.” The difficulties that arose earlier, when we treated this passage, will therefore recur. Someone might refuse to take the negation of possibility to be “not possible to be,” choosing instead “possible not to be.” Although he assigns the negation to the affirmation in an improper order—for it was said above that whenever propositions are expressed according to their modalities, the negation ought to be applied to the modalities rather than to the words—we must nevertheless concede this point. By refuting the false position of the argument even with this concession, which some may consider useful for its defense, we may establish the truth more firmly and deeply.

Let the negation of possibility, then, be what they themselves wish: “possible not to be.” But this too does not agree with necessity. For if someone says that “possible to be” does not follow “necessary to be,” the contradiction of the possible immediately follows necessity. If someone takes the contradiction of the possible to be “possible not to be” and thinks that this agrees with necessity, then, according to him, the correct consequence would be: “If it is necessary to be, it is possible not to be.” But this cannot happen. For what is necessary to be cannot not be.

If, therefore, possibility does not follow necessity, what is necessary will be contingent. For “possible” and “contingent” have the same meaning. The negations of possibility—whether “not possible to be” or “possible not to be”—will agree with necessity. But both alternatives are impossible. If these do not follow, their affirmation follows—that is, possibility. But this too cannot happen, as we have shown repeatedly above.

This question is resolved by Aristotle himself in the following order. Since the sense of the question stated above is such, let us examine the actual words and the order of the discourse. He says:

“Someone might raise the question whether ‘possible to be’ follows ‘necessary to be’”—that is, whether possibility agrees with necessity. “For if it does not follow”—that is, if someone denies that possibility follows necessity—the contradiction of possibility follows. For if possibility does not follow, its contradiction follows, namely “not possible to be.” He omitted what would follow from these premises, namely the impossible.

The point is this: if possibility does not follow necessity and the contradiction of possibility agrees with it, the correct consequence would be: “If it is necessary to be, it is not possible to be,” which is absurd. And if someone does not say that this is the contradiction—that is, if someone denies that the contradiction of possibility is “not possible to be”—he must certainly say that the contradiction of possibility is “possible not to be.” But both are false of what is necessary to be. For what is necessary cannot be not possible; and again, what is necessary cannot be possible not to be.

Again, it seems that the same thing is possible both to be cut and not to be cut. Possibility is common to affirmation and negation, for what is said to be possible to be can both be and not be. But this is false when predicated of the necessary. For if the necessary is, it cannot not be; and if it is not, it cannot happen in any way.

If someone says that possibility follows necessity, that same possibility also agrees with the contingent. Thus what is necessary to be will be contingent not to be—that is, what is predicated as necessary to be will be contingent. For if what is possible to be can not be, and what can not be is contingent not to be, then there can be no doubt that, if possibility follows necessity, contingency follows it as well.

We can speak of the contingent in the form of a negation, saying “it is contingent not to be.” Therefore what is necessary to be will be contingent not to be. But this is false.”

Such, then, is the order of the discourse. As in almost all the other passages, it is perplexed and tightly compressed: sometimes the similarity of the enunciations, sometimes what is omitted, makes the meaning implicit and obscure. If one connects Aristotle’s words with the sequence of our exposition, separates by our exposition what has been confused there because of the similarity, and supplies from here what is lacking in Aristotle’s wording, the reasoning of the whole will become clear.

Now, since he has proposed the question, he immediately pursues it in the following words:

> It is evident that not every possibility, whether of being or of walking, has the power of opposites. But there are cases in which this is not true. First, among things that can act without reason: fire is capable of heating and has an irrational power. Therefore rational powers are powers of many, even contrary, things. Irrational powers, however, are not all such; rather, as was said, it is not possible for fire both to heat and not to heat, nor for whatever else always acts. Other things, however, can, even through irrational powers, receive opposites simultaneously. But this has been said because not every power is a power of opposites, nor are all things that are spoken of according to the same species such powers.

Having raised the question concerning the consequence of the possible and the necessary—and since, if possibility agreed with necessity, an absurdity resulted, while if possibility in turn followed necessity, necessity itself, with which possibility agreed, would receive both being and not-being—he now resolves the incongruous ambiguity through a reasonable argument.

He says that Aristotle was not truly concerned that possibility, by following necessity, would break the nature and rigor of necessity itself, so that what was necessary would be changed into contingency. For not everything that is possible to be is also possible not to be. There are many things that contain only one power and are in no way suited to negation, as with the possibilities produced by irrational activity. Although it is possible for fire to heat, it is not possible for it not to heat. This power therefore cannot have opposites.

For if a power can have opposites, it can both be and not be, both do and not do. A power that cannot have opposites, however, can do only one thing: it gives affirmation alone and rejects negation. If someone posits that possibility agrees with necessity, this does not mean that necessity itself must thereby be changed into contingency, with which possibility agrees. For not everything possible can do both—that is, both be possible to be and be possible not to be.

Therefore not every possible agrees with the contingent. Aristotle teaches this in the following way: among things that can act without reason, the possibility that is called possibility does not have opposites. Thus “fire heats” is irrational. There is no reason why fire heats, for there is no reason underlying anything that occurs naturally. Therefore those things whose power is irrational cannot have opposites. Fire cannot both heat and not heat.

For if they could do both, they could do opposites. “To heat” and “not to heat” are opposites. Since irrational powers therefore do not have the capacity to perform opposites, those things that occur according to reason can retain the activity of opposites, so that whatever is conceived through will and reason is effective in both directions. For it is both possible and not possible for me to practice medicine; likewise, it is possible both to walk and not to walk. Whatever someone wills through the reasoning or desire of the soul is said to proceed from reason.

In all such cases there is a power that is effective in both directions—that is, in affirmation and negation—so that the thing may both be and not be. Among irrational things, although it may occur that the power called irrational cannot have opposites, nevertheless not every irrational power lacks opposites. Water, for example, is cold and moist. It can therefore readily become colder and become moist; but when changed into something hot, it may lose the power of becoming cold, while it cannot lose the power of moistening so long as it remains water.

Consequently, not every power is effective with respect to opposites. The power that is effective with respect to opposites is the one that operates through rational movements. The power that is not effective with respect to opposites is found only among irrational powers, though not among all of them. For there are irrational powers that can do both, as in the case mentioned concerning the coldness of water.

The entire force of the argument is therefore as follows. Let us now explain the order of the words.

“It is evident,” he says, “that not every possible thing—whether possible to be or possible to walk—has the power of opposites.” This is clearly not said so that we should suppose that everything which can walk, or everything which can be, cannot have opposites—that is, cannot not be. The text may appear to say this, but no one should understand it in that way. Rather, it should be understood as follows:

“It is evident that not every possible thing, as we commonly use the term when we say ‘it is possible to walk,’ has the power of opposites.” For not every power applies equally to affirmation and negation. Some powers can do only one thing, as we have already said.

This becomes clearer if we put it in the following form: “It is evident that not every possible thing also has the power of opposites,” since we frequently predicate “possible” both of being and of walking. Whoever considers the matter in this way will more easily recognize what the words of the text signify, provided that one approaches obscure meanings with patience and assent, attending primarily to the author’s meaning, even if the grammatical order of the words does not fully support it.

Once this has been established, it is evident that not all powers are effective with respect to opposites. There are some in which it is not true to say that they have the power of opposites. An example is given from things that can act irrationally—that is, not according to some reason—whose powers cannot be explained by reference to a reason, since this belongs to their nature. Thus, because fire is capable of heating, no rational account can be given of why it heats. This is naturally present in it. The power of fire therefore does not have opposites, even though it is irrational.

Powers that are rational, however, and operate according to rational power, are powers of many, even contrary, things. For whatever is governed by reason is naturally suited to both opposites. The same powers therefore belong to many things that are contrary. If it is possible for me to walk, since this occurs through reason and will, it is also possible for me not to walk. This is not the power of one thing only, but of many things, and of contrary things.

Although “to walk” and “not to walk” are in a certain sense affirmation and negation, Aristotle now arranges them in the place of contraries. In all rational powers, then, it is clear that they belong to many contraries and have the power of opposites.

Things that do not operate according to reason, however, although some of them have the power of opposites, do not all have it. Water has the power of cooling—which is irrational—and, again, another power of heating when it itself has been heated. But this is not found in all irrational powers. Fire, as was said, appears to have only the power of heating.

This is what he means when he says: “Irrational powers are not all such”—that is, not all have the power of opposites. “Rather, as was said, it is not possible for fire both to heat and not to heat.” The rule applies generally to things that cannot have contraries: those that always contain one thing in actuality. Fire is always hot; the sun is always in motion; and the same applies to other things of this kind. This is what he indicates when he says, “nor whatever else always acts.”

Other things, however, can have certain opposites, even through irrational powers, as was said of water. But he says that this was stated for the following reason: so that we may understand that nothing contrary results if someone says that possibility agrees with necessity. For since not every possibility has the power of contraries, the possibility that agrees with necessity is the one that does not have contraries but always performs one thing.

This is what he means when he says: “But this has been said because not every power is a power of opposites, nor are all things that are spoken of according to the same species such powers.”

The meaning is this: not only can not everything called possible be a power of contraries, but even among things belonging to the same species, some cannot have contraries, such as those belonging to irrational powers. Although all irrational powers belong to one species insofar as they are irrational, even among these it cannot be found that all have the same power of contraries, as is shown by the example of fire.

Although the power of fire is irrational, it is nevertheless not such as to be transferred to contraries. It was therefore correctly said that not all things belonging to the same species can be powers of contraries. Although the power of fire belongs, together with all other irrational powers, to the species “irrational power,” it nevertheless does not have the power of opposites.

We said earlier that this point could begin to resolve the entire question, though it did not yet dissolve it with complete force. But Aristotle added, in a continuous argument, what most directly guides and settles the difficulty:

> Some powers are equivocal. “Possible” is not said simply, but in one sense because the thing is true in actuality—for example, “it is possible to walk” because one is walking, and “it is possible to be” because what is called possible already exists in actuality. In another sense, it is said because the thing may perhaps act—for example, “it is possible to walk” because one may perhaps walk. The latter power belongs only to movable things; the former belongs also to immovable things. In both cases it is true to say that it is not impossible to walk or to be, and that what is walking both acts and is capable of walking. Thus “possible” is not simply true to say of the necessary, but the other sense is true. Therefore, since the particular follows the universal, what exists by necessity follows what is possible to be, but not universally.

What this passage contains, which Aristotle has now proposed, we carefully set out in the fifth book [Col. 0616C], and we shall now explain it briefly. We undertake this labor of exposition for the sake of explanation and instruction, not to increase tedious length by prolixity.

The entire meaning is therefore as follows. “Possible,” as we frequently use the term of things, is not said in a simple sense. And since “possible” is derived from “power,” “power” itself is likewise equivocal. This is evident from the fact that some possibilities are spoken of not because they are being actualized, but because nothing prevents their being actualized. Thus, if someone is sitting with respect to a healthy body, after all the other things that could impede walking have been removed, one may say that he is able to walk—not because he is walking, but because absolutely nothing prevents him from walking.

Other possibilities are spoken of in this way because they are already actual and being actualized. Thus, if someone says of a walking man that he is able to walk [Col. 0616D], that possibility which is not expressed according to some present actuality but according to what he could do is called a “possibility” because his power does not prevent him from doing it. But the possibility that is already acting and actual is called the actuality itself.

There are therefore two meanings of “possibility”: one designates a possibility that exists as a power but is not according to actuality; the other signifies a possibility that exists in actuality. This possibility that is already actual either passes from power into actuality, or has naturally always been actual. Thus, when a man is sitting and therefore is not walking, he is nevertheless able to walk, and so he passes from power into actuality. [Col. 0617A] The sun, however, when it moves, never passes from power into actuality, for it has never at any time failed to perform this movement. Nor has fire, insofar as it is now hot, at some time not been hot.

That possibility, then, which is spoken of according to some actuality, contains within itself two species. One designates an actuality of possibility that cannot fail to be; this is called “necessary,” since it never passes from power into actuality but has naturally remained actual. The other is one that may also fail to be—namely, one that has migrated from power into actuality. Although it is actual, this is not necessary.

This latter kind of possibility, which passes from power into actuality, exists only in movable things—that is, in things capable of being moved. These are corporeal things. We shall explain a little later by what arguments incorporeal things are shown not to be movable. [Col. 0617B] Those things that have remained always actual by the quality of their own nature are found both among movable things—for example, heat in fire, which is always actual and has never existed merely as a power—and among immovable things. These are incorporeal and divine things.

Therefore, possibility that has migrated from power into actuality belongs only to corruptible and corporeal things. Possibility that has always been actual is common to divine and corporeal things.

To touch briefly upon the whole argument, then, it should be stated as follows: possibility is equivocal and has many meanings. There is one possibility that, although it is not itself actual, can exist in actuality; and for this reason it is called a possibility. There is another that is already actual. This latter is not equivocal but a genus. For beneath it are species: one possibility that is actual but has migrated from power, and another that is actual but has not migrated from power. The one that has not migrated from power is called necessary, since it never leaves its subject. The one that passes from power into actuality is, without any doubt, called non-necessary, because it can at some time leave its subject.

Accordingly, of both of these—namely, possibilities spoken of either as powers or as actualities—a common predicate may be made if we say that both are “not impossible.” For it is true to say both of one who can walk although he is not walking and of one who is already walking that it is not impossible for them to do what they can do or are doing.

But since there are two meanings under the term “possibility”—one possibility that is not actual, and another that is actual—the possibility spoken of according to power cannot be applied to the necessary, nor can it ever agree with necessity. It remains, therefore, that necessity be placed under that plurality of possibilities which is actual. Yet this too has one species that passes from power into actuality, and this is non-necessary; hence necessity cannot be placed under that species either.

It remains, then, that since no one denies that what must be is possible, and since what is spoken of as existing in power also falls under the possible, necessity is not to be placed under that possibility which exists merely as a power. Nor is it to be placed under that actual possibility which can leave its subject. Rather, it must be placed under that actuality which cannot leave its subject. Thus necessity is a possibility that never leaves either actuality or its subject [Col. 0618A], because it did not come into actuality from power.

Necessity will therefore be a species of possibility, if it is placed where there is a possibility that is always actual. And if the genus follows the species, and wherever the species is found the genus cannot be absent, then the genus proper to its species—namely, possibility—follows its species, necessity, but not every possibility. That possibility which exists merely as a power, not also in actuality, does not follow necessity; nor does the possibility which, although actual, can leave its subject. Only that possibility follows necessity which, although actual, can never depart from its subject.

Possibility therefore follows necessity, and nothing impossible results—provided that the possibility in question is actual and never ceases by nature to exist in its subject.

The whole meaning is of this kind; the force of the words, however, is as follows. “Some powers,” he says, “are equivocal.” This is said because not every power is equivocal. There is a power that functions as a genus, namely the power predicated according to actuality.

He then explains how some powers are equivocal, saying: “The possible is not spoken of simply.” He divides it in this way: one possibility is so called because it is true in actuality—for example, “it is possible to walk,” because the person is already walking; and, universally, “it is possible to be,” because what is called possible already exists in actuality.

Nothing could demonstrate this more clearly than calling that possible which is already being done. If someone were to deny that it is possible to be, Aristotle says that such a person would be saying that what is impossible both comes to be and exists; but this exceeds every measure of rationality.

He gives the other part of the meaning of possibility as follows: “The other is what perhaps will act,” and he supplies this example: “It is possible to walk, because he will perhaps walk.” Thus the reference is not to what is already being done, but to what may perhaps be done—that is, to what nothing perhaps prevents from being done.

“And this,” he says, “is a power found only in movable things”: namely, the power spoken of according to power, not according to actuality. As has been said, by “movable things” he means bodies alone. The other kind—that which exists in actuality—is also found in immovable things. For this reason he added the words “and in immovable things,” so that we would not suppose that actuality as possibility exists only in divine things, but also in mortal and corporeal things.

In both cases it is true to say that it is not impossible to walk or to be: both what is already walking and acting, and what is capable of walking. “In both,” he says, means that one predicate can apply to both meanings. We can say that it is not impossible either for what is already walking to walk, or for what can walk but is not walking to walk. This is what he indicated by the term “walkable.” For “walkable” is that which is not actually walking but nevertheless can walk.

He adds: “Thus it is not true to say simply of the necessary that it is possible.” That is, possibility, insofar as it is predicated equivocally, cannot be predicated simply, universally, and altogether of the necessary. Not every possible therefore agrees with the necessary. But “the other”—namely, the possible in the other sense—is truly predicated of the necessary; that is, the possible spoken of according to actuality and immutability.

Therefore, since what exists by necessity follows its own part—that is, its species, or what is universal, namely, the genus—it follows that what can be is possible, but not every possibility. For the possibility predicated in actuality that can leave its subject does not follow necessity. Only that possibility follows necessity which, although actual, neither passes from power into actuality nor can leave its subject.

These, then, are Aristotle’s statements on the matter.

What we postponed, however, was the demonstration that immovable things are divine, and that only bodies are movable. It must now be shown briefly. It is clear that there are six species of motion, as Aristotle arranged them in the *Categories*, although he altered this account in the *Physics*. For the present, however, let us proceed as though there were altogether six.

If reason demonstrates that divine and incorporeal things are moved according to none of the species of motion, it follows by an ordered argument that divine things are not moved. Things that are neither generated nor corrupted, neither increased nor diminished, nor transferred from place to place—for they are wholly present everywhere through the fullness of their nature—cannot be understood as divine things; nor are they altered by any affections.

But if the nature of divine things is not changeable according to any of these motions, it is evident that they are altogether not movable, and that these six motions occur only in bodies. It is sufficient to have touched briefly upon the many reasons and arguments that can be given on this subject.

Now, since Aristotle has taught that not every possibility agrees with necessity and has identified the possibility that does agree with it [Col. 0619C], he again sets out from memory what follows from what, and what ought to be placed first and what afterward, saying:

> There is perhaps a principle of all things, whether of being or of not being, namely, what is necessary and what is not necessary. The other matters must be considered as consequences of these. It is clear from what has been said that what exists by necessity exists in actuality. Therefore, if the prior things are eternal, and what exists in actuality is prior to what exists in power, then those things that are without power exist in actuality, such as the primary substances. Other things exist in actuality together with possibility: in nature they are prior, but in time they are posterior. Other things are never actual but exist only in power.

After explaining what he thought about the consequence of the possible and the necessary, he adds this in a way that corrects the preceding order. Since above, beginning from the possible, he reduced all the other propositions to the possible and the contingent and to their agreement, he now reasonably changes this, so that one should begin not with possibility but with necessity.

For if someone considers the preceding arrangement more carefully, the possible and the contingent were placed first, and the meaning of all the others was related to them. This now seems to require alteration. He says that it may perhaps be more correct for the sequence of propositions to begin with necessary things.

The whole meaning is as follows. Since necessary things are eternal, and eternal things are the principles of all other things that are not eternal [Col. 0620A], what is necessary must appear to be prior to all the others. The sequence should therefore be arranged in the same way, so that necessity is proposed first, followed afterward by possibility and the rest. The sequence would be as follows:

> It is necessary to be. It is not necessary to be.
>
> It is not possible not to be. It is possible not to be.

Do you see, then, that first “it is necessary to be” and “it is not necessary to be” have been proposed? In the second place, the remaining propositions have been referred to the agreement and consequence of necessity.

This, then, is what he meant by saying that there is perhaps a principle of all things, whether of being or of not being: namely, what is necessary. The starting point for examining propositions should be taken from the necessary, and this should determine, by consequence and agreement, the being or not being of the other propositions.

Since “it is necessary to be” was placed first, the proposition “it is not possible not to be” agrees with it. The principle of the proposition “it is not possible not to be”—which announces that something cannot not be, for it removes the possibility that has not yet been actualized—is necessity, with which it agrees without any doubt.

Again, since “it is not necessary to be” agrees with “it is possible not to be,” the principle of the proposition that establishes something as possible is the proposition “it is not necessary to be.”

Therefore, whether necessity is proposed affirmatively or negatively, it appears to be a kind of principle of the rest, and the remaining propositions should be judged as agreeing with these—that is, with the necessary propositions. This is what he means by saying: “The other matters must be considered as consequences of these” [Col. 0620C].

He then shows why this occurs, saying that necessary things exist in actuality, as has often been demonstrated above. Necessary things are eternal, and eternal things are prior to those whose powers are not yet actual. It is therefore clear that things which are actual and do not come from power into actuality are prior.

We are speaking of an actuality that does not come from power into actuality, but has always remained actual through the constitution of its own nature. Thus fire is hot, the sun moves, and other things of this kind have never left actuality; actuality has never been absent from them, nor have they ever come to this actuality from power.

Since things of this kind have always existed, and whatever always exists is prior to all other things, they will also be prior in power according to their proper nature. But things that are prior are always eternal; and, again, these same things are necessary in actuality. It is therefore necessary that things actual be prior to things potential.

Aristotle next divides things in the following way:

Some things are always actual and have not come from power. These are things that have no powers, but are always actual. Other things have passed again from power into actuality. In these, substance and actuality are posterior to power in time but prior in nature.

For in all things what is actual is prior to and more noble than what is potential. What exists in power is still hastening toward actuality and is therefore an imperfection; it becomes perfected when it eventually reaches actuality. It is evident that what is perfect is nobler and prior to what is imperfect.

If things that came from power into their own actuality were first in power and afterward in actuality, then their actuality is posterior to their power if we consider time, but prior to that same power if we consider nature. This is what he means by saying that some things exist both in possibility and in actuality, but have their actuality posterior to their possibility in time and prior in nature.

There are also some things in which there is only power and never actuality, such as infinite number. Number can increase without limit. Whatever number is stated—one hundred, one thousand, ten thousand, or any other—must be finite. Therefore number is never actually infinite. Since it can grow without limit, we say that it is infinite only in power, not in actuality.

The same applies to time. However much time one names, it is finite; but because time can increase without limit, we say that time is infinite in power, not in actuality. Nothing can actually be infinite.

When we said above that things which are always actual are primary substances, this should not be understood in the way Aristotle speaks of primary substances in the *Categories*, where he calls individuals primary substances. Here he calls those things primary substances which are always actual, because, as has been said, things that are always actual are the principles of all other things. Consequently, they must be primary substances.

## Which Propositions Are More Properly Called Contrary

> Whether affirmation is contrary to negation, or affirmation to affirmation, and speech to speech—for example, whether “Every human being is just” is contrary to “No human being is just,” or whether “Every human being is just” is contrary to “Every human being is unjust”; and in the case of “Callias is just,” whether the contrary is “Callias is not just” or “Callias is unjust”—which of these is contrary?

After examining the consequences of propositions and arranging them through subtle inquiry, a question now arises that offers such great usefulness that its importance is apparent to readers at the very outset. It is evident that an opposed negation always attacks an affirmation, and especially that universal negation destroys universal affirmation. It is also not unknown that a privative affirmation—which affirms the contrary—likewise destroys the proposition of the contrary itself.

The question is which more thoroughly destroys and attacks an affirmation: whether the universal negation, or the affirmation of the contrary or privation.

Let the affirmation be established as follows: “Every human being is just.” Two propositions destroy it: the universal negation, which says “No human being is just,” and the affirmation that predicates the privation of justice, namely, “Every human being is unjust.”

The affirmation “Every human being is just” is therefore destroyed both by its proper universal negation, “No human being is just,” and by the privative affirmation, “Every human being is unjust.” Since it is destroyed by both, and since what destroys a thing appears to be contrary to what it destroys, while, as has been said, it is destroyed by two propositions, and two things cannot be contrary to one thing, it must be asked which of the two propositions mentioned above—universal negation or privative affirmation—is contrary to the universal affirmation stated earlier.

No one who considers the matter fails to see how useful this question is. Unless Aristotle had investigated and resolved it, there would be considerable doubt whether two things could be admitted as contrary to one thing, which plainly cannot occur. For when two things destroy one thing, who would doubt either that one thing is opposed to two, or that, when two things destroy one thing, it is necessary to ask which of them appears to be more contrary?

We call them contrary—not according to the mode Aristotle explained in the *Categories*, but merely insofar as one thing destroys another thing, or one proposition destroys another proposition. The question is therefore posed in roughly this form: according to which proposition is universal affirmation more thoroughly destroyed—according to universal negation, or according to a proposition that predicates privation or anything else that, through its opposition, displays the force of a contrary?

It should also not escape notice that there is an ambiguity between universal privative affirmation and universal negation as to which is opposed to the contrary. For it was already said above that universal negation is contrary to universal affirmation. Here, however, that is not what is being said; rather, the question concerns which more thoroughly destroys the thing. For what more thoroughly destroys it will appear to be more contrary.

For this reason Aristotle did not propose the question only with universal propositions. He also added particular propositions, lest anyone suppose that he was referring to the kind of contrariety he discussed either in the *Categories* or earlier when speaking of universal affirmation and negation, where affirmation and negation were not contrary in the case of particulars.

If we correctly remember what was established above, universal affirmation and universal negation were said to be contrary. But here he also establishes the question with respect to just and unjust, which is a matter of possession and privation rather than any genuine contrariety.

Therefore, as we have said, the present question must be understood as asking which proposition more immediately and effectively destroys and eliminates which other proposition. The method of investigating this will be as follows.

If what exists in speech follows what exists in the soul, and if there the opinion of a contrary is contrary—for example, “Every human being is just” and “Every human being is unjust”—then affirmations existing in speech must likewise be related in the same way. But if the opinion of a contrary is not contrary there, then affirmation will not be contrary to affirmation either; rather, the negation that has been mentioned will be contrary.

We must therefore consider which true opinion is contrary to a false opinion: the opinion corresponding to negation, or the opinion that takes contraries as its objects.

I put the matter this way: there is a true opinion of the good, namely, that the good is good. There is another, false opinion, that the good is not good. There is another that it is evil. Which of these, then, is contrary to the true opinion? And if there is one, according to which is it contrary?

This is the investigation: which is more contrary to universal affirmation, universal privative affirmation or universal negation? The basis of the inquiry is that nearly every property which must occur in spoken expressions derives from the opinions that the expressions signify.

What must therefore be investigated in expressions must first be discerned in opinions. For since the significations of expressions derive from the opinions signified by those expressions, it cannot be that the properties of expressions are not first found in opinions. We must therefore examine how these matters stand when placed in opinions, and whatever is discovered in them may reasonably be transferred to expressions.

The inquiry should first be conducted in opinions as follows. If the opinion corresponding to universal privative affirmation is more contrary to the opinion corresponding to simple universal affirmation than is the opinion corresponding to universal negation, then it is clear that universal privative affirmation more thoroughly destroys simple universal affirmation than universal negation does.

But if this greater contrariety is not found, and instead the opinion corresponding to universal negation more thoroughly destroys the opinion corresponding to universal affirmation than does the opinion corresponding to privative affirmation, then it is established that universal negation is more contrary to universal affirmation than privative affirmation is.

To discover this, the following procedure must be used. Let one opinion be true, and let two false opinions be set against it, one an affirmation of privation and the other a universal negation. Of the two false opinions, whichever reason finds to be more false, we shall say is more contrary to the true opinion.

Let there therefore be three opinions, one true and two false. Let the true opinion be this: that what is good is good. This is the opinion Aristotle calls the opinion of the good, because it is good. Let one false opinion be that what is good is not good; this is what Aristotle calls the false opinion of the good, because it is not good. Let the remaining opinion be that what is good is evil; this is the opinion Aristotle calls the opinion of the good, because it is evil.

Of these three opinions—one true and two false—it must be asked which is more contrary to the true opinion. But since it often happens that negation and privation signify the same thing, especially in contraries where there is no intermediate state, he adds: “And if there is one, according to which is it contrary?”

This means the following. In contraries where there is no intermediate state, negation has the same force as privation. In contraries where there is an intermediate state, privative affirmation and negation do not have the same signification.

Suppose, for example, that the contraries are immediate: “having been generated” and “not having been generated.” In immediate contraries, privative affirmation has the same force as negation. But it is not the same in things that have an intermediate state.

For it is not equivalent to say that someone is evil and to say that he is not good. When the good is denied, the mind of the hearer may suspect some intermediate condition. But when evil is posited, the whole suspicion of the hearer is directed toward the contrary. They therefore do not signify the same thing.

Nevertheless, because privation or contrariety often agrees with negation, whenever propositions are found in which privative affirmation differs in no way from negation, Aristotle thinks that it must be asked according to which utterance or opinion the proposition or opinion is contrary to the true affirmation or opinion.

Although they sometimes signify the same thing, we use these propositions in different ways. One who posits negation says that what is is not; one who posits privation says that what is not is. Since, therefore, the propositions have in a certain way a different starting point and a different intention, even when they have the same signification, it must be asked which of them is more contrary to the true proposition, and according to which movement of the mind the true proposition is more thoroughly destroyed.

This is what he means by saying: “And if there is one, according to which is it contrary?” He is not saying that negation and privation are altogether one and the same, but only that they are the same in cases where they are identical—namely, in immediate contraries.

Even when they signify the same thing, however, they do not express it according to one and the same movement of the mind. One person posits the contrary or privation, while another posits negation. The question is therefore according to which of these the proposition is more contrary: whether according to the proposition that posits privation, or according to the one that posits negation.

He next indicates what the nature of contrariety is.

For it is false to think that contrary opinions are defined by the fact that they concern contraries. The opinion that the good is good and the opinion that the evil is evil are perhaps the same opinion and true, whether they are multiple or one. These things are contrary, but the opinions are not contrary because they concern contraries; rather, they are contrary because they concern them contrarily.

The meaning has been briefly explained, but it has been constructed with the utmost logical precision. In discussing contraries, he first sets out how opinions can be contrary. Some people thought that opinions were contrary when they concerned contraries, but this is shown to be false.

For even if good and evil are contrary, it does not immediately follow that contrariety must arise in an opinion about good and evil. Suppose someone forms the opinion that the good is good, and again forms the opinion that the evil is evil. Although he has the same kind of opinion about good and evil—namely, that the one is good and the other evil—the opinions are not contrary.

For it is not contrary to think that what is good is good and that what is evil is evil; both opinions are true. The contrariety of opinions is recognized through truth and falsity.

Opinions can be contrary in this way: they proceed, as it were, from the same affection of the mind—that is, from opinions that recognize something as true. Therefore, if someone has an opinion concerning one of two contraries and forms some judgment about contraries, it does not immediately follow that contrariety occurs in the opinions.

Contrariety of opinions does not therefore consist in the fact that they concern contraries or are formed about contraries. Rather, contrariety arises in opinions whenever someone forms contrary opinions about one and the same thing.

Thus, let some proposed thing be good. If someone forms a contrary opinion about it—saying of the same thing that it is good and again that it is evil—the opinion that holds what is good to be good is true, while the opinion that holds what is good to be evil is false.

True and false are contrary. We therefore rightly call contrary those opinions that truth and falsity separate, even if they do not concern contraries but are expressed contrarily about one and the same thing.

It was therefore rightly said that contrary opinions should not be defined by the fact that they concern contraries, but rather by the fact that they form contrary judgments about the same thing.

The order of the words is as follows [Col. 0625B]: “To think,” he says, “that contrary opinions are defined by the fact that they concern contraries”—that is, by the fact that they form some opinion about contraries—is false.

He himself explains how it is false. The opinion that the good is good and the opinion that the evil is evil are perhaps the same—that is, they are not contrary opinions but are identical. He then adds the reason why they are the same: “and true.” They are the same because they are true.

Contrariety, as has been said, is situated in truth and falsity. Therefore, if the opinions agree in truth, they will appear to be the same in truth and falsity. Nor does their number interfere with this. Whether there are several opinions or one, insofar as they are true they are the same.

“These,” he says, “are contrary”—that is, the matters involved in the opinions—but contrary opinions are not found in the fact that the opinions concern contraries or form judgments about contraries. Rather, their contrariety arises from the fact that they form contrary opinions about one thing. This is what he means by “but rather because they are contrary.”

Here “contrary” is used adverbially, as if he had said: “They are more properly contrary because they form contrary opinions,” with the words “about one thing” understood. For if they do not form contrary opinions about one thing, but about several things, they may not be contrary. Anyone who carefully and prudently considers this will readily perceive it.

If, then, there is an opinion that the good is good, and another that it is not good, and yet another that it is something else which is not and cannot be, none of the other opinions should be posited—not any opinions that hold that what is not is, nor any that hold that what is is not. For both classes are infinite: those that suppose what is not to be, and those that suppose what is to be not.

Rather, the opinions to be considered are those in which there is falsehood. These are the opinions from which generations arise; and generations arise from opposites. Therefore falsehoods also arise from opposites.

He brought his valid conclusion to a close in the briefest possible words. Its force, stated concisely, is this. Whoever wished to know about the contrariety of propositions ought first to determine what sort of infinity there is among propositions and then to adapt the force of contrariety to it. For in every pair of contraries, one thing is contrary to one thing. But if there is some infinity among propositions, that entire infinity cannot be contrary to one proposition. This is the point at which the whole argument begins. [Col. 0626A]

In propositions, therefore, one must expect not merely that a false proposition is contrary to a true one, but that, among all false propositions, the one false proposition is contrary to the true proposition which is single and not infinite. Propositions can be infinite and false; there can also be one finite proposition which is likewise false and which must reasonably be regarded as contrary to the true proposition.

Thus, wishing to establish that negation is more contrary to affirmation than an affirmation which posits the contrary, he says this. There can, he says, be an opinion which supposes that what is the case with each thing is the case. There is also another opinion which judges that what is not the case is the case with that thing. There is another which thinks that the thing in question does not possess what it does possess. Again, there is another which judges that the thing itself is not what it is. [Col. 0626B]

To make this clear by an example, he takes the proposition concerning which someone might form an opinion: namely, “what is good.” If someone believes that this good thing is good, he will have a true opinion. But if someone judges that this good is what it is not, he will have a false opinion—for example, if someone judges that the good is harmful, useless, or unjust. Such a person will hold of the good opinions about things that are not the case, and this is false.

Again, whoever judges that what the good possesses it does not possess will hold opinions such as these: “the good is not useful,” “the good is not just,” “the good is not to be desired.” He too is mistaken. But if there is someone who judges that the very thing which is good is not good—not judging that what is not is bad, nor that what it possesses in itself is to be desired, but judging that the thing which is good, that is, goodness itself, is not good—then he will judge that the good is not good. [Col. 0626C]

All the other opinions, therefore, are infinite. For by many examples we can collect false propositions which, although they do not concern each thing itself, we nevertheless assert of it. Thus, concerning the good itself, I can say that it is bad, shameful, unjust, to be avoided, dangerous, and whatever else no one will find in the good. These are infinite.

Again, I can say that what the good possesses is not in the good—for example, “the good is not useful,” “the good is not to be desired,” “the good is not what increases.” These too are infinite. But when an opinion removes from a thing what that thing is, it can do so only once. For nothing further can be effected by the assertion that what is good is not good. Thus, all the other opinions, whether they judge that what is not the case is the case or that what the good possesses it does not possess, are false, but false infinitely. [Col. 0626D]

Here, however, he uses “good” as though he were saying “goodness.” If someone judges that goodness itself is not good, he is both false and false in a determinate way. But among false propositions which are determinate and numerically single, that one appears more and more immediately contrary to the truth, since one thing is always contrary to one thing.

Accordingly, this is rightly more contrary: the proposition which denies what the thing is, rather than the one which denies what it possesses or affirms that it possesses what it does not possess. But, in bringing this to a close, he did not use a straightforward formulation; instead, he diverted the argument toward something else, and this caused considerable confusion.

For after saying that we ought not to posit as more contrary to the true opinion those propositions which are infinite, he added the following: “but those in which there is error; and these arise from those from which generations also arise.” This closes the argument with the following meaning: opinions contrary to true opinions are to be opposed to them when the beginning of the error is present in them. Errors arise from the same things from which generations also arise; generations, however, arise from opposites. [Col. 0627A]

The point is this. Every generation arises from a change of what previously existed. For unless what previously existed has ceased to be, generation cannot occur. Everything that comes to be is transformed in some way into another form of substance. Thus, when what previously existed is no longer present, something comes to be, and it is something other than what it was. Likewise, whoever judges that what any given thing is, is not, is in error.

For whoever thinks that what is good is bad is mistaken; but it cannot become bad in any other way than by not being good. The same applies in the other cases. Error, therefore, and the beginning of error occur when someone judges that what a thing is, is not that thing. [Col. 0627B]

This error arises from the same things from which generations arise. For every generation, as he said, arises from deprivation: what becomes sweet does not arise from what is white, but from what is not sweet; and what becomes white does not arise from what is hard, but from what is not white. The other generations likewise proceed from their opposites, and this is the first error.

If, then, the first error occurs among the things from which generations arise—where falsity is most complete and closest to the true opinion—and if these are found only among opposites, that is, among affirmations and negations, there is no doubt that the opinion of negation is more contrary to the opinion which affirms something contrary. [Col. 0627C]

Such is the meaning. The wording, however, runs as follows:

“If, then, there is an opinion concerning the good that it is good”—an opinion which is true—“and there is also an opinion that it is not good”—which is false and determinate—“and there is another that it is something else, which is not and cannot be”—that is, an opinion which attributes to it what is not the case—“none of the others is to be posited,” neither the opinion that what is not the case is the case, that is, which thinks that the proposed thing is what it is not, nor the opinion that what is the case is not, that is, the opinion which denies in thought what the proposed thing possesses.

Why are these not to be regarded as contrary opinions? He explains: “For both are infinite”—both those which suppose that what is not the case is the case and those which suppose that what is the case is not. “But those are to be posited in which there is error,” that is, in which the beginning of error is present.

But from where is the beginning of error derived? It is derived from the things from which generations also arise. And from where do generations arise? From opposites. For every generation, as has been said, arises from the fact that what previously existed is no longer what it was, and this tends toward negation. Therefore error and the beginning of error are found among opposites, where generations also occur, and from these the error itself arises. [Col. 0627D]

If, then, what is good is both good and not bad—“good” in itself, and “not bad” accidentally—for it happens to be not bad—then in each thing that which is in itself is more true, and also more false, since it is more true. Therefore the opinion that what is good is not good is the false opinion concerning what is in itself. But the opinion that it is bad is the opinion concerning what is accidental. Accordingly, the false opinion concerning the good which is a negation will be more false than the one which is a contrary. [Col. 0628A]

Although we explained all this most carefully in the commentary on the first edition, lest the exposition of this book appear too abbreviated, we shall explain the same matters here as well, repeating them. The argument proceeds as follows:

“If, when a true proposition has been posited, there are several false propositions which destroy it, that one among them will be more contrary to the true proposition which is more false.”

We must therefore ask which, among several false propositions, is more false, so that it may appear more contrary to the true proposition. This must be determined by truth. For although something can be said truly and in itself, or accidentally, that nevertheless most fully possesses the nature of truth which is said according to the thing itself rather than what arises accidentally. [Col. 0628B]

Thus, if someone forms the opinion concerning the good that it is good, he has a true opinion according to the thing itself. But if someone judges that the good is useful, he will indeed have a true opinion, but this truth is accidental to the good. For it happens to the good to be useful as well.

Consequently, the opinion which judges that the good is good is true in itself, that is, true according to the thing itself. The opinion which judges that what is good is useful is true only accidentally of the good. Therefore the former, which judges that what is good is good, is closer to the nature of goodness than the latter, which judges that what is good is useful. If this is so, the former is truer, since it is true according to the thing itself, rather than the latter, which appears to be true accidentally. [Col. 0628C]

Once this has been established, the same must be said about falsity. For the false proposition which is contrary to that true proposition which is in itself [F: “which is true in itself”] is more false than the one which destroys the true proposition which is accidental. If the proposition which says something true about the very nature of the thing is truer, then the one which destroys the truer proposition will be more false. And if the latter, although true, is less so because it makes a statement about an accident of the thing, then the proposition which destroys the less true proposition will likewise be less false.

With these points established, let us now see how they apply to the opinions or propositions under discussion. [Col. 0628D] Let the example be the same as above: what is good is good and is not bad. The former is according to the thing itself; the latter is accidental to it. For what is good is good by nature, whereas that it is not bad belongs to it in a secondary and almost accidental way.

Therefore the opinion concerning the good that it is good is truer and closer to nature than the opinion concerning the good that it is not bad. If, then, the proposition which destroys the truer opinion is more false than the one which destroys a true opinion that is nevertheless less true, it is evident that negation is more false than the affirmation which posits the contrary.

For negation says that what is good is not good, whereas the contrary affirmation says that what is good is bad. The negation that what is good is not good destroys the opinion which is true in itself, namely, that the good is good. But the contrary affirmation that what is good is bad destroys the true opinion which is accidental, namely, that what is good is not bad. [Col. 0629A]

It is therefore established that the opinion which says that what is good is not good is more false than the one which thinks that what is good is bad. If what is more false is more contrary, then the opinion of negation is more contrary than the contrary affirmation.

Once the meaning has been clarified, the actual words must be demonstrated. “If, then,” he says, “what is good is good and is not bad”—the former in itself, that is, what is good is said to be good; the latter accidentally, that is, what is good is said not to be bad. For it happens to it not to be bad. But in each thing that which is in itself is more true. For what exists according to the nature of each thing is closer to the thing whose nature it is. [Col. 0629B]

Therefore truth according to the thing itself, because it is closest to the thing, is truer than truth according to an accident. This is what he says: “But in each thing that which is in itself is more true.” If this is so, then the falsehood which destroys the opinion or proposition that is true in itself is also more false, since what is true in itself is truer than what is true accidentally of the thing. This is what he means by “if it is true.”

He confirms the point with an example: “Therefore the opinion that what is good is not good is false of what is in itself.” That is, it is opposed to the opinion which was true in itself. This is what the words show when he says: “Therefore the opinion that what is good is not good is false of what is in itself”—it is the falsity opposed to the proposition which is true in itself, for falsity is opposed to truth.

“But the opinion that it is bad is false of what is accidental.” That is, the opinion which judges that what is good is bad is false, and it is suited to the proposition which is true accidentally, namely, the opinion that what is good is not bad.

“Therefore the opinion concerning the good which is negation will be more false than the one which is the contrary,” that is, negation is more contrary than the affirmation of the contrary. For although both are predicated of the good, negation is nevertheless found to be more false. [Col. 0629C]

When he said that it happens to the good not to be bad, this should not be understood in the way in which we usually say that something happens to a subject. For this cannot come to be. Here “happens” must be understood as meaning that it is said in a secondary place: primarily, what is good is said to be good; secondarily, it is said not to be bad. This is drawn from the analogy of substance and accident. Every substance is, primarily, a subject; secondarily, it is white, two-footed, accidental, or whatever else can happen to substances. [Col. 0629D]

The person who holds a contrary opinion is most false concerning each particular thing. For contraries are those things which differ most with respect to the same thing. If, then, one of these is contrary, but contradiction is more contrary, it is evident that contradiction will be the contrary. [Col. 0630A]

The force of the entire argument, stated as briefly as possible, is this. Everything true is either true in itself or true accidentally, and consequently everything false must likewise be either false in itself or false accidentally. It is established that what is true in itself is truer than what is true accidentally. Whoever holds about a thing an opinion contrary to what the thing itself is must be especially false.

For opinions are contrary whenever, concerning one and the same thing, they are furthest removed from one another. Therefore what is more false will also be contrary. For what is farther from the truth is more false. Among opinions which differ most from one another, those are contrary. The contrary opinion, therefore, is the one which is most false. [Col. 0630B]

As has been said, that is most false which is false in itself, that is, which destroys the proposition that is true in itself. This is negation. Negation, therefore, is contrary to affirmation rather than the affirmation which posits the contrary.

This meaning is contained in the following words: “But the person who has a contrary opinion is more false concerning each particular thing.” Anyone may be false even without holding a contrary opinion concerning the same thing, but the person who thinks something contrary is more mistaken.

He explains why this is so: “For contraries are those things which differ most with respect to the same thing.” This is why the most false opinions are opposed as contraries: contrariety is found only among things which differ most widely.

“If one of these is contrary”—that is, if one of these propositions, whether the one which is false in itself or the one which is false accidentally, must be contrary—“but contradiction is more contrary.” That is, negation is more false. By saying, “but this is more contrary,” he means: “but the contradiction is more false,” that is, “negation is more false.” If the matters are as stated above, he concludes, it is evident that this—the contradiction—will be contrary. [Col. 0630C]

But the proposition “that what is good is bad” is implicit. For whoever judges it bad must perhaps necessarily also hold the very opinion that it is not good. [Col. 0630D]

After showing that negation is more properly contrary because it is more false than the affirmation which asserts the contrary, and after explaining through the distinction of falsity that the contrary proposition or opinion is the one which denies the proposed thing, he now attempts to establish the same point from simple and implicit propositions and opinions.

He says that the affirmation which posits the contrary is implicit rather than simple. It is implicit because whoever judges that what is good is bad must immediately also judge that what is good is not good. For it cannot be bad in any other way than by not being good. [Col. 0631A]

Thus whoever judges that what is good is bad both judges that the good thing is bad and judges that it is not good. This opinion concerning the good is therefore not simple, since it contains within itself the opinion that it is not good.
