But whoever judges that what is good is not good is not thereby necessarily required to judge that it is bad. For something may be neither good nor bad. This is found particularly in things in which some intermediate state can be found; he added this point with great care.

Once these matters have been established, since the opinion of the contrary is not simple, whereas the negation is simple, it necessarily follows that the simple opinion appears more contrary to the simple opinion.

The simple opinion concerning the good—that it is good—is true. The simple opinion concerning the good—that it is not good—is false. The simple negation, therefore, is contrary to the simple opinion concerning the good that it is good: namely, the opinion concerning the good that it is not good. [Col. 0631B]

The entire force of this argument is drawn from the following consideration. Whenever one proposition is true and there are two propositions capable of destroying it, if one of them can destroy the true proposition without needing the other, whereas the other cannot destroy that same proposition without the first, then the one which is sufficient to itself and does not need the other in order to destroy the proposed proposition must be called more contrary.

The true proposition concerning the good—that it is good—can be destroyed by negation alone. The negation which says that it is not good is sufficient by itself for the destruction of that true proposition. But the opinion that it is bad is not sufficient by itself unless it is aided by the other proposition, namely, that what is good is not good. [Col. 0631C]

The contrary affirmation destroys the true proposition only because it brings negations with it. It is therefore clear that the proposition which is sufficient by itself for the destruction of the true proposition rightly appears more contrary than the one which is not sufficient by itself unless the force of a negative proposition is added to it.

Moreover, if the same arrangement must be found in other cases as well, the argument will appear sound here too. Either contradiction is contrary everywhere, or nowhere. In cases where there is no contrary, the false proposition opposed to the true one is nevertheless false: for example, whoever thinks that a human being is not a human being is false. If, then, these are contrary, the other propositions which are contradictions are contrary as well. [Col. 0631D]

What we say about these propositions, he says, ought to be firm if it is found in all cases. For it is not likely that negations should be contrary in some propositions, while affirmations which posit the contrary should be contrary in others. But if the same thing is found in all propositions and contradictions—namely, that contradiction, that is, negation, is more contrary than the proposition which contains the contrary—there is no doubt that this reasoning holds universally.

If, on the other hand, in other cases the proposition which posits the contrary is more contrary than negation, then it is equally evident that this is not so here. For wherever contrariety can be found, there is a question as to which is contrary: whether the proposition which affirms the contrary or the proposition which denies the proposed thing.

Therefore we must examine the matter in cases where there is no doubt how it is to be understood. There is no doubt in cases where contrariety is absent, as in substances. Here only negations are contrary. [Col. 0632A]

If, then, the opinion concerning a human being that he is a human being is opposed by the opinion concerning a human being that he is not a human being, it is evident that in other cases as well, where contrariety is found, negation should occupy the place of contrariety.

For if, in cases where contrariety exists—as in good and bad—it were evident that the proposition which denies the good is not more contrary to the opinion that what is good is good than the proposition which asserts the bad, then negation ought not to be contrary in cases where there is no contrariety. What purpose would it serve for negation to be contrary when we speak of a human being, who has no contrary, but not to be contrary when we speak of the good, which does have a contrary, with the proposition which posits the contrary taking its place instead?

Wherever negation is turned, it must preserve its force everywhere.

Thus, what Aristotle says amounts briefly to this: if negation is contrary in other cases, it is evidently contrary here too. But if it is not contrary in other cases, then it will not be contrary in the cases mentioned above either. Rather, in all the other cases where no contrariety is found, contradiction occupies the place of contrariety; therefore it will occupy the same place, and no other, in the cases where contrariety is present. [Col. 0632B]

He explains this in the following words: “Moreover, if the same arrangement must be found in other cases, the argument will appear sound here too.” For if the same arrangement is necessary in all other cases, it will also be found in the cases mentioned above, and what has been said will appear to have been said most appropriately.

“Either contradiction is contrary everywhere, or nowhere.” In some cases, therefore, one will find a contrary proposition, and in others not. But in cases where there is no contrary—for example, in substances, where there is no contrariety—there is nevertheless a false proposition opposed to the true one.

The Categories taught us this, if we remember correctly. In such cases there is indeed a false opinion opposed to the true opinion, but it is clear what sort of opinion it is. Where there is no contrariety, the contrariety of contradiction is evident: whoever thinks that a human being is not a human being is false. Here the only contrariety to the true proposition is contradiction. [Col. 0632C]

If, then, these are contrary, the other propositions which are contradictions are contrary as well. That is, if negations are contrary in cases which do not have contrariety—and some propositions must be contrary—then in all other cases also, including those in which some contrariety exists, as with the good and the bad, negation occupies the place of contrariety. [Col. 0632D]

Moreover, the propositions “concerning the good, that it is good” and “concerning what is not good, that it is not good” are similarly related; and to these correspond “concerning the good, that it is not good” and “concerning what is not good, that it is good.”

What, then, is contrary to the true opinion concerning what is not good, namely, that it is not good? It is not the opinion that it is bad, for sometimes both will be true. But a true opinion is never contrary to a true opinion. For something which is not good may be bad, and therefore both opinions can be true at the same time.

Nor is it the opinion that it is not bad, for this too is true; both opinions may likewise be true at the same time. It follows that the contrary of the opinion concerning what is not good, that it is not good, is the opinion concerning what is not good, that it is good. For this is false.

Accordingly, the opinion concerning the good, that it is not good, is contrary to the opinion concerning the good, that it is good. [Col. 0633A]

He confirms everything said above once more by a stronger argument based on proportion. Proportion is a similarity among things in relation to one another. If four things are posited, of which two are antecedent and the remaining two consequent, and if the first stands to the second as the third stands to the fourth, then the first must stand to the third as the second stands to the fourth.

We recognize this most easily and briefly through numbers. Let the first number be 2, the second 6, the third 4, and the fourth 12. Here the antecedent numbers are 2 and 4, and the consequent numbers are 6 and 12. As 2 is to 6, so 4 is to 12. For just as 2 is one-third of 6, so 4 is one-third of 12. [Col. 0633B]

Accordingly, as one antecedent stands to its consequent, so one antecedent will stand to the other consequent; and as one antecedent stands to the other antecedent, so one consequent stands to the other consequent. Two is half of the antecedent number 4, and 6 is half of 12. [Col. 0634A]

This is what is observed in every proportion: if, among four proposed things, the first stands to the second as the third stands to the fourth, then the first stands to the third as the second stands to the fourth.

Let this numerical proportion now be transferred to the force and nature of propositions. Let there be two first propositions, one antecedent and the other consequent, and again two others, one antecedent and the other likewise consequent, with a certain similarity between them.

If the first is “concerning the good, that it is good,” this is followed by “concerning the good, that it is not good.” Again, let the third antecedent be “concerning what is not good, that it is not good,” followed by the fourth, “concerning what is not good, that it is good.” [Col. 0634B]

**Antecedents — Consequents**

1. Concerning the good: that it is good. | 2. Concerning the good: that it is not good. |

3. Concerning what is not good: that it is not good. | 4. Concerning what is not good: that it is good. |

Let us therefore observe in these propositions what the similarity of the proportions is. As the first proposition, “concerning the good, that it is good,” stands to the second, “concerning the good, that it is not good,” so the third, “concerning what is not good, that it is not good,” stands to the fourth, “concerning what is not good, that it is good.”

For just as “concerning the good, that it is good” is a true proposition, while “concerning the good, that it is not good” is false, so likewise “concerning what is not good, that it is not good” is true, while “concerning what is not good, that it is good” is false.

If this is so, and the opinion concerning the good that it is good is related to the opinion concerning the good that it is not good in the same way as the opinion concerning what is not good that it is not good is related to the opinion concerning what is not good that it is good, then, as the first stands to the third, so the second will stand to the fourth. [Col. 0633C]

As the opinion concerning the good that it is good stands to the opinion concerning what is not good that it is not good—both being true—so the opinion concerning the good that it is not good stands to the opinion concerning what is not good that it is good—both being false. As the first stands to the third, so the second stands to the fourth. [Col. 0634B]

This proportion having been demonstrated, let the same propositions be arranged in a changed order. Let the first opinion be “concerning what is not good, that it is not good,” followed by “concerning the good, that it is good”; under these, let the third antecedent be “concerning what is not good, that it is good,” and the fourth consequent be “concerning the good, that it is not good.”

**True**

**Antecedents — Consequents**

1. Concerning what is not good: that it is not good. | 2. Concerning the good: that it is good. |

3. Concerning what is not good: that it is good. | 4. Concerning the good: that it is not good. |

**False** [Col. 0633]

As was demonstrated above, the opinion concerning what is not good that it is not good stands to the opinion concerning the good that it is good in the same way as the opinion concerning what is not good that it is good stands to the opinion concerning the good that it is not good. Just as the former pair is simultaneously true, so the latter pair is simultaneously false; the proportion is the same.

Accordingly, as the first proposition, concerning what is not good that it is not good, stands to the third, concerning what is not good that it is good, so the second proposition, concerning the good that it is good, stands to the fourth, concerning the good that it is not good. [Col. 0633C]

We must therefore ask how the first stands to the third, so that from this we may examine how the second stands to the fourth. I say that the opinion which judges that what is good is not good is contrary to the opinion which judges that what is not good is good.

Suppose, for the sake of argument, that it is rather contrary to the opinion which judges that what is not good is good that which judges that what is not good is bad. But this cannot be. Contrary opinions can never be true simultaneously, whereas these opinions can be true simultaneously. [Col. 0634C]

If someone thinks that parricide, which is not good, is not good, and also thinks that the same parricide, which by nature is not good, is bad, he holds both opinions truly. Therefore the opinion which judges that what is not good is not good is not contrary to the opinion which judges that what is not good is bad.

Again, let the opinion concerning what is not good that it is not good be opposed to the opinion which judges that what is not good is not bad. This too is not contrary. For it is possible that what is not good is also not bad. Not everything which is not good is immediately bad; some things may be not good and yet not bad.

If someone judges that a stone lying uselessly—which is not good in itself—is not good, he judges truly. If he also thinks that the same stone, which is not good in itself, is not bad, no falsity enters into his opinion. [Col. 0634D]

Therefore, since the opinion concerning what is not good that it is not good is sometimes found to be true together with the opinion concerning what is not good that it is bad, and sometimes together with the opinion concerning what is not good that it is not bad, it is contrary to neither.

It remains, then, that the contrary opinion is the opinion concerning what is not good that it is good. This opinion judges that what is not good is good. It is therefore the opinion concerning what is not good that it is good, since it judges that what is not good is good.

Thus the opinion concerning what is not good that it is not good is contrary to the opinion concerning what is not good that it is good. [Col. 0635A]

The opinion concerning what is not good that it is good stands to the opinion concerning what is not good that it is not good in the same way as the opinion concerning the good that it is good stands to the opinion concerning the good that it is not good. The first and the third are contrary. Therefore the second and the fourth, according to the similarity of the proportion, are without doubt contrary.

The point can also be understood more simply as follows. If the opinion concerning the good that it is good and the opinion concerning what is not good that it is not good are similar according to truth, while the opinion concerning the good that it is not good and the opinion concerning what is not good that it is good are likewise similar according to falsity, then, if one of the false opinions is found to be contrary to one of the true opinions, the other false opinion will be contrary to the other true opinion. Similarity alone produces this result. [Col. 0635B]

It has been shown that one false opinion is contrary to one true opinion in the following way: the opinion which says that what is not good is good is contrary to the opinion which judges that what is not good is not good.

It follows that the opinion which judges that what is good is not good is contrary to the opinion which judges that what is good is good. From this it follows that negation, rather than the affirmation which posits the contrary, is contrary to true affirmation.

The perplexing meaning has therefore been clarified in the ways we have described. The order of the words is as follows:

“Moreover,” he says, “the opinion concerning the good that it is good and the opinion concerning what is not good that it is not good are similarly related”—both being true—“and above these are the opinion concerning the good that it is not good and the opinion concerning what is not good that it is good”—both being false.

“To the true opinion concerning what is not good that it is not good, what is contrary?” This is expressed almost as a question. “It is not the opinion which says that it is bad, since both may sometimes be true.” This cannot occur among contraries, for a true opinion is never contrary to a true opinion.

How can both be true? Because something which is not good may be bad, and therefore both can be true simultaneously. Nor is the contrary the opinion that it is not bad, for these too may sometimes be true simultaneously, especially in things which lie between good and bad.

It follows that the contrary of the true opinion concerning what is not good that it is not good is the false opinion concerning what is not good that it is good; the two cannot be found true simultaneously.

He therefore returns to the proportion established above and says that the opinion concerning the good that it is not good is contrary to the opinion concerning the good that it is good. Whoever considers the foregoing more carefully will not be mistaken either about the meaning of the whole argument or about its order. [Col. 0635C]

It is evident, moreover, that it makes no difference even if we posit the affirmation universally. For the universal negation will be contrary to it, just as to the opinion which judges that everything which is good is good there is contrary the opinion that none of the things which are good is good. [Col. 0636A]

In the foregoing argument he explained everything concerning indefinite propositions. But since someone might perhaps suspect that the same account could not apply to propositions that are determinate, and that it might make some difference whether the same demonstration applied to determinate propositions, he adds this: it makes no difference whether someone applies to universal propositions—which are now unquestionably determinate—the same demonstration that he previously made concerning indefinite propositions. For if someone arranges determinate propositions according to the foregoing arrangement of indefinite propositions and examines them in accordance with the method stated above, he would find no other contrary to the opinion of universal affirmation than the opinion of universal negation. For there is no difference between indefinite and determinate propositions except that indefinite propositions are without a determination, whereas determinate propositions are accompanied by an indication of determination, either universality or particularity. This is what he means when he says that it makes no difference even if the affirmation is stated universally: for the universal negation will be contrary to the universal affirmation, as, for example, the opinion that “everything that is good is good” is a universal affirmation, while the contrary is the opinion that “none of the things that are good is good,” which is a universal negation.

For the proposition “the good is good,” if “good” is taken universally, [Col. 0636C] is identical with the opinion that whatever is good is good. This differs in no way from “everything that is good is good.” The same applies to what is not good.

He gradually brought the indefinite proposition into likeness with the universal proposition. He says that whatever the indefinite proposition may be, if whatever we customarily add in speech is added to it, it becomes universal. Thus the proposition in the affirmation that predicates “everything” of the subject is no different from the opinion or proposition “whatever is good is good,” if, so to speak, “whatever is good is good” is added to it; it differs in no way from the opinion “everything good is good.” Therefore the force of the foregoing demonstration is the same in indefinite propositions as in universal propositions, which differ slightly—not in the quality or force of the proposition, but in quantity. For universality is opposed to quantity. The meaning is indeed as follows; the words are these.

Above he had proposed that it makes no difference whether a proposition is indefinite or universal. He now explains why it makes no difference in this way. The proposition “the good is good”—that is, the indefinite affirmation—if “good” is taken universally, that is, if “good” is stated universally, is identical with the opinion “whatever is good is good.” In other words, it does not differ from the opinion that whatever is good is good; and this opinion differs in no way from the proposition plainly stated universally, namely, “everything that is good is good.” The same applies to what is not [Col. 0637A] good: that is, we say “not good” by the same reasoning. For the proposition or opinion that something is not good, if universality is added to it, differs in no way from the proposition plainly stated universally, namely, “everything that is not good is not good.”

Therefore, if the matter stands thus in the case of opinion—and the affirmations and negations that exist in speech are signs of what exists in the soul—it is clear that the contrary of an affirmation is a universal negation concerning the same subject. Thus the contrary of “everything good is good,” or “every human being is good,” is “nothing” or “no one.” The contradictory propositions are “not everything” or “not everyone.”

Above he brings all the arguments together for the good and reduces the whole force of the question to a conclusion. For he had previously stated that the contrarieties of negations and affirmations should be weighed in relation to opinions. Now, having discovered in the case of opinions that the contrary is the universal negation, he applies the same conclusion to propositions, which are plainly utterances signifying the affections of the soul. At the beginning of the book he taught that significant utterances truthfully indicate the affections of the soul. Now, as though he were proving that the contrary of a universal affirmation had been found among opinions to be the universal negation rather than an affirmation asserting the contrary of the universal affirmation, he likewise holds that the same applies to utterances: namely, that the contrary of a universal affirmation is not an affirmation positing a contrary object, but a universal negation; and that the contradictories are those in which, when there is a universal affirmation, there is found a particular negation. This has indeed been stated most fully, and there is no error in the words. But, leaving nothing ambiguous, as in the other matters, we shall also follow the sense and order of the words themselves.

For he says: “Therefore, if the matter stands thus in opinion”—that is, if the negation is found to be contrary to the opinion of affirmation rather than an affirmation positing a contrary—“and the affirmations and negations that exist in speech are signs of those that exist in the soul.” For just as there is an affirmation and negation in speech, so also there is one in opinion, whenever the soul in its thought affirms or denies something. We shall explain this more carefully elsewhere. Thus, since the affirmations and negations that exist in speech [Col. 0637D] are signs of the affirmations and negations that exist in the soul, “it is clear that the contrary of an affirmation is a universal negation concerning the same subject.” He added “concerning the same subject” so that we would not say that affirmations and negations are contrary when they concern different things. Rather, he says that the affirmation and negation concern one and the same thing, with one affirming it universally and the other denying it universally.

Examples are these: the contrary of “everything good is good,” or “every human being is good,” is “nothing”—that is, “no good thing is good”—or “no one”—that is, “no human being is good.” The contradictory is either “not everyone,” that is, “not every human being is good,” contrary to “every human being is good,” or “not everything,” that is, “not everything good is good,” contrary to “everything good is good.” It is therefore established that, among the propositions he set out above, the proposition “no just human being is just” is more contrary to the affirmation “every human being is just” than is “every human being is unjust.”

It is also clear that a true proposition cannot be contrary to a true proposition, nor can an opinion be contrary to an opinion, nor a contradiction to a contradiction. For contraries are concerned with opposites. But it is possible for someone to speak the truth about the same things. Contraries, however, cannot belong simultaneously to the same subject.

After this, the book brings its discussion to an end with an investigation and demonstration by which he attempts to show the following, although it is already clear and evident to everyone: two true propositions are not contrary. The beginning of this argument is as follows. Things that are contrary are opposites. Opposites cannot belong simultaneously to the same subject. Therefore contraries cannot belong simultaneously to the same subject. But things about which something can be said truly at the same time can belong simultaneously to the same subject. Things that cannot belong simultaneously to the same subject cannot be the subjects of simultaneously true propositions, whether affirmation or negation. But contraries cannot belong simultaneously to the same subject. Therefore propositions that state the truth simultaneously are not contrary.

For things about which an affirmation and a negation can both be true at the same time can belong simultaneously to the same subject. Consequently, propositions that are true at the same time are not contrary. This is the meaning; the words themselves are arranged as follows.

“It is also clear,” he says, “that a true proposition cannot be contrary to a true proposition”—that is, two true propositions cannot be contrary—“nor an opinion, nor a contradiction.” If one true opinion is not contrary to another true opinion, still less is a contradiction, which arises from opinions, contrary to one. Here he has used “contradiction” for “contrariety,” for contradiction itself was not under discussion. “Contraries are those that concern opposites”: that is, every contrary is an opposite. But it is possible for the same person to speak the truth concerning the same things, because only of such things can both negation and affirmation be true simultaneously, as they can belong simultaneously to the same subject. Contraries, however, cannot belong simultaneously to the same subject. The conclusion therefore follows that, of those things concerning which both affirmation and negation are true at the same time, both can belong simultaneously to the same subject, whereas contraries cannot belong simultaneously to the same subject. Therefore things that are true at the same time cannot be contrary.

Our labor, too, now rests in a tranquil harbor. For, as I think, nothing has been left undone that belonged to a complete understanding of this book. Therefore, if by diligence and devotion we have successfully completed the task undertaken, it will be very useful to those who desire to acquire knowledge of these matters. But if we have not achieved what we intended—namely, to unravel the most obscure doctrines of this book—our labor will at least harm no one, and, if it proves unnecessary, no one will object to it.

So that nothing further might be sought in these works of Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, we have added the books of Aristotle’s Prior Analytics and Posterior Analytics, rendered into Latin by this author, striving everywhere not to appear to have been deficient in our service.

[Col. 0639]

THE TWO BOOKS OF ARISTOTLE’S PRIOR ANALYTICS, WITH ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS AS INTERPRETER. (G,S)*

BOOK ONE

CHAPTER ONE. On the proposition, term, and syllogism.

[Col. 0639A]

[Col. 0639B] First, it must be stated what the subject and aim of the inquiry are: they concern demonstration and demonstrative knowledge. Next, it must be determined what a proposition is, what a term is, what a syllogism is, and what a perfect and an imperfect syllogism are. After that, we must determine what it means for one thing to belong wholly in another, or not to belong in another, and what we mean by “being predicated of everything” or “being predicated of nothing.”

A proposition, then, is an affirmative or negative statement of something concerning something. This is either universal, particular, or indefinite. I call it universal when something belongs to everything or to nothing; particular when something belongs to something, or does not belong to something, or does not belong to everything; and indefinite when it signifies that something belongs or does not belong, whether universally or particularly, as in “the knowledge of contraries is the same” or “pleasure is not good.”

A demonstrative proposition differs from a dialectical proposition because a demonstrative proposition is the assumption of one side of a contradiction. For the person demonstrating does not ask a question but makes an assumption. A dialectical proposition, however, is a question concerning a contradiction. It makes no difference if a syllogism is produced from either kind, since both the demonstrator and the questioner syllogize by assuming that something belongs or does not belong to something. Thus a syllogistic proposition will simply be an affirmation or negation of something concerning something, in the manner stated. A demonstrative proposition will be one that is true and is assumed through first principles. A dialectical proposition, for the person asking, is a question concerning a contradiction; for the person syllogizing, it is an assumption of what appears and is probable, as was stated in the Topics.

What a proposition is, and how a syllogistic proposition differs from a demonstrative and a dialectical proposition, will be explained more carefully below. For present purposes, let what has now been said suffice as our determination.

I call a term that into which a proposition is resolved, such as the predicate and that of which it is predicated, whether “to be” or “not to be” is added or separated. A syllogism is an utterance in which, certain things having been posited, something other than what has been posited follows necessarily because of those things. By “because of those things” I mean that the consequence arises on account of them. To arise on account of them means that no additional term from outside is needed for the necessity to follow.

I call a syllogism perfect when it needs nothing else besides what has been assumed in order for the necessity to be evident. An imperfect syllogism is one that needs one or more things which, although necessary through the terms contained in it, have not been assumed in the propositions. For one thing to belong wholly in another, and for one thing to be predicated of another in every instance, are the same. We say that one thing is predicated of everything when it is impossible to take anything belonging to the subject of which the other is not said; and similarly in the case of “of nothing.”

CHAPTER TWO. On the conversion of absolute propositions.

Since every proposition concerns either belonging, necessary belonging, or possible belonging, and since, under each of these descriptions, some propositions are affirmative and others negative, and since among both affirmatives and negatives some are universal, some particular, and some indefinite, a universal negative proposition concerning belonging must be converted universally. For example, if no pleasure is good, then no good is pleasure.

An affirmative proposition must indeed be converted, but not universally; it must be converted particularly. Thus, if every pleasure is good, then some good is pleasure. A particular affirmative must necessarily be converted particularly. For if some pleasure is good, then some good will be pleasure. A negative particular proposition, however, need not be converted. For if a human being does not belong to some animal, it does not follow that an animal does not belong to some human being.

Let the universal negative proposition a–b be taken first. If a belongs to no b, then b will belong to no a. For if it belongs to some—for example, c—the assertion that no b is a will not be true, since c is one of the things that are b. But if a belongs to every b, then b belongs to some a; for if it belonged to none, a would belong to no b, whereas it was posited that it belongs to every b.

The same applies if the proposition is particular. For if a belongs to some b, then b must belong to some of the things that are a; for if it belonged to none, a would belong to no b. But if a does not belong to some of the things that are b, it does not follow that b does not belong to some a. For example, let b be animal and a be human being: a human being does not belong to every animal, whereas an animal belongs to every human being.

CHAPTER THREE. On the conversion of modal propositions.

The same arrangement applies to necessary propositions. A universal negative is converted universally, while both affirmative forms are converted particularly. For if a necessarily belongs to no b, then b necessarily belongs to no a; for if it could belong to some, a too could belong to some b. But if a necessarily belongs to every or to some b, then b must necessarily belong to some a; for if it did not belong necessarily, a would not necessarily belong to some b.

A particular negative proposition is not converted, for the same reason that we stated above.

In the case of possible propositions, since “possible” is said in several ways—for we call both what is necessary, what is not necessary, and what is possible “possible”—the affirmative propositions will behave similarly in conversion in every case. For if a can belong to every or to some b, then b can belong to some a; for if it belonged to none, neither would a belong to any b, as was previously shown.

With negative propositions, however, the case is not the same. Those things are said to be possible either because they necessarily do not belong or because they do not belong necessarily; these behave similarly in conversion. For example, one might say that it is possible for a human being not to be a horse, or that white may belong to no garment. In the former case the non-belonging is necessary, whereas in the latter it is not necessary; and the proposition is converted in the same way. For if it is possible for no human being to be a horse, it is possible for no horse to be a human being. And if it is possible for white to belong to no garment, it is possible for a garment to belong to no white thing. For if it necessarily belonged to some, white would necessarily belong to some garment; this was previously demonstrated.

The same applies to the particular negative proposition.

But propositions in which “possible” is spoken of as occurring for the most part, or according to what things naturally tend to be, do not behave in the same way in negative conversions, depending on how we determine the possible. In these cases the universal negative proposition is not converted, while the particular negative proposition is converted. This will become clear when we discuss possibility.

For the present, let it be enough for us to make clear from what has been said that “may belong to none” or “may not belong to some” has the form of an affirmation, since “is possible” is arranged in the same way. Whatever is predicated as adjacent to “is” always produces an affirmation, for example “is not good,” “is not white,” or simply “is not this.” This too will be shown in what follows; the other cases will behave similarly in their conversions.

CHAPTER FOUR. On the syllogistic and non-syllogistic modes of the absolute propositions of the first figure.

Having established these matters, we shall now discuss through what means, when, and how every syllogism comes about; afterward we shall discuss demonstration. We must speak of the syllogism before demonstration because the syllogism is more universal: every demonstration is a kind of syllogism, but not every syllogism is a demonstration.

Whenever three terms are related to one another in such a way that the last is contained wholly in the middle, and the middle either is contained wholly in the first or is wholly excluded from it, there must be a perfect syllogism concerning the extremes.

I call the middle that which is itself in another and has another in itself; it is also middle in position. The extremes are that which is itself in another and that in which another is contained. For if a is predicated of every b, and b of every c, then a must be predicated of every c. What it means to predicate of everything was stated earlier.

Likewise, if a is predicated of no b, while b is predicated of every c, then a will belong to no c.

But if the first term follows every middle term while the middle belongs to no last term, there will be no syllogism concerning the extremes. For nothing necessary follows on account of these premises, since it is possible for the first term to belong both to every last term and to no last term. Consequently, neither a particular nor a universal conclusion is necessary. Where nothing necessary follows, there will be no syllogism through these premises.

The terms for “belonging to everything” are animal, human being, horse; for “belonging to nothing,” animal, human being, stone.

Again, when neither the first belongs to the middle nor the middle belongs to any last term, there will likewise be no syllogism. The terms for belonging are knowledge, line, medicine; for not belonging, knowledge, line, unit.

When the terms are universal, it is clear in this figure when there will and will not be a syllogism, and that whenever there is a syllogism, the terms must be related in the way we have described; and when they are so related, it is clear that there will be a syllogism.

But if one of the terms is universal in relation to another, while the other is particular, then, whenever the universal is placed with the major extreme, whether affirmatively or negatively, and the particular with the minor extreme affirmatively, a perfect syllogism must result. Whenever the terms are arranged with the minor extreme, or in any other way, it is impossible.

By the major extreme I mean the term in which the middle is contained; by the minor, the term that is contained under the middle.

Let a belong to every b, and b belong to some c. Then, if “to be predicated of everything” means what was stated at the beginning, a must belong to some c. And if a belongs to no b, while b belongs to some c, then a must not belong to some c. For what “of nothing” means has also been determined. Therefore there will be a perfect syllogism.

The same applies if the proposition b–c is indefinite, since the syllogism will be the same whether the indefinite or the particular is assumed.

But if a universal proposition is placed with the minor extreme, whether affirmative or negative, there will be no syllogism, whether the other proposition is affirmative, negative, indefinite, or particular. For example, if a belongs or does not belong to some b, while b belongs to every c.

The terms for belonging are good, disposition, prudence; for not belonging, good, disposition, ignorance.

Again, if b belongs to no c, while a belongs or does not belong to some b, or does not belong to every b, there will likewise be no syllogism.

The terms for universal belonging are white, horse, swan; for belonging to none, white, horse, raven.

The same applies if a–b is indefinite.

Nor, when a universal proposition, affirmative or negative, is placed with the major extreme and a particular negative proposition with the minor extreme, will there be a syllogism, whether the particular proposition is taken indefinitely or particularly. For if a belongs to every b, while b does not belong to some c, or does not belong to every c, then from the fact that the middle does not belong to some c it does not follow that the first belongs to all or to none of them.

Let the terms be animal, human being, white; and then let swan and snow be taken as things of which human being is not predicated. Animal is predicated universally of one of these, but of the other it is predicated of none; therefore there will be no syllogism.

Again, let a belong to no b, while b does not belong to some c. Let the terms be inanimate, human being, white; and then let swan and snow be taken as white things of which human being is not predicated. Inanimate is predicated universally of one of these, but of the other it is predicated of none.

Moreover, since the proposition “b does not belong to some of the things that are c” is indefinite, and it is also true that b belongs to none, and also that it does not belong to every one because it does not belong to some, if these terms are taken as belonging to none, it is clear from what was stated earlier that no syllogism results. Therefore it is clear that, when the terms are related in this way, there will be no syllogism, for there would also be no syllogism in these cases.

The same can be shown if the universal proposition is negative.

Nor, if both intervals are stated particularly and affirmatively or negatively, or if one is affirmative and the other negative, or if one is indefinite and the other determinate, or if both are indefinite, will there be a syllogism in any way.

The common terms for all these cases are animal, white, horse; and animal, white, stone.

It is clear from what has been said that, if there is a particular syllogism in this figure, the terms must be related in the way we have described. If they are otherwise related, no syllogism results.

It is also evident that all syllogisms in this figure are perfect, since they are all completed through what was assumed at the beginning; and that every problem is demonstrated through this figure, whether it concerns belonging to everything, belonging to nothing, belonging to something, or belonging to something not being the case.

I call this kind of figure the first.

CHAPTER FIVE. On absolute syllogisms in the second figure.

But whenever the same term belongs universally to one thing and to no other, or belongs universally to both or to neither, I call this kind of figure the second.

In this figure, I call the middle what is predicated of both; the extremes are the things of which it is predicated. The major extreme is the one placed nearer the middle, and the minor is the one farther from the middle. The middle is placed outside the extremes, while the first term is first in position.

A perfect syllogism, then, is in no way produced in this figure. A syllogism is nevertheless possible both when the terms are universal and when they are not universal.

When the terms are universal, a syllogism occurs whenever the middle belongs universally to one term and to no instance of the other, even if the negative proposition is assigned to either term; otherwise it occurs in no way.

Let m be predicated of n universally negatively and of x universally affirmatively. Since the negative proposition is convertible, n belongs to no m; but m was assumed to belong to every x. Therefore n belongs to no x, as was previously shown.

Again, if m belongs to every n, but to no x, then n will belong to no x. For if m belongs to no x, then x belongs to no m; but m belonged to every n, and therefore x belongs to no n. Again, since the negative proposition is convertible, n belongs to no x. The syllogism is therefore the same as before, and these cases can also be demonstrated by leading to the impossible.

It is therefore clear that a syllogism results when the terms are related in this way, but that it is not perfect. For the necessary conclusion is completed not only from what was assumed at the beginning, but also from other propositions.

But if m is predicated of every n and of every x, there will be no syllogism.

The terms for belonging are substance, animal, rational account; for not belonging, substance, animal, stone, with substance as the middle.

Nor is there a syllogism when m is predicated of neither n nor x.

The terms for belonging are line, animal, human being; for not belonging, line, animal, stone.

It is therefore clear that, if a syllogism is produced from universal terms, the terms must be related in the way stated at the beginning. If they are otherwise related, no necessary conclusion results.

But if the middle is universal in relation to one of the terms, then, whenever it is universal in relation to the major term, whether affirmatively or negatively, and particular in relation to the minor term, and opposite to the universal proposition—by “opposite” I mean that if the universal is negative, the particular is affirmative, or if the universal is affirmative, the particular is negative—a particular negative syllogism must result.

For if m belongs to no n, while it belongs to some x, then n must not belong to some x. Since the negative proposition is convertible, n belongs to no m; but m was assumed to belong to some x. Therefore n does not belong to some of the things that are x. The syllogism is produced through the first figure.

Again, if n belongs to every m, while x does not belong to some m, then n must not belong to some x. For if x belonged to every n, and m were predicated of every n, then m would necessarily belong to every x; but it was assumed not to belong to some.

And if m belongs to every n, while it does not belong to every x, there will be a syllogism, since n does not belong to every x. The demonstration is the same.

But if m is predicated universally of x and not universally of n, there will be no syllogism.

The terms for belonging are animal, substance, raven; for not belonging, animal, white, raven.

Nor is there a syllogism when m is predicated of no x and of some n.

The terms for belonging are animal, substance, stone; for not belonging, animal, substance, knowledge.

When the universal proposition is opposite to the particular, it has been stated when there will and will not be a syllogism.

But when the propositions belong to the same form—for example, when both are negative or both affirmative—there will be no syllogism in any way.

Let them first be negative, with the universal proposition assigned to the major extreme, so that m belongs to no n while it does not belong to some x. It is possible, then, for n to belong both to every x and to no x.

The terms for belonging to none are black, snow, animal. Terms for belonging to every one cannot be supplied if m belongs to some x but not to some other x. For if n belonged to every x, and m belonged to none, n would belong to no x that m belonged to; but it was posited that m belonged to some. Therefore terms cannot be taken in this way.

This must be shown from the indefinite case. Since it is true that m does not belong to some x, and if it belongs to none, while no syllogism results when it belongs to none, it is clear that no syllogism will result now either.

Again, if the propositions are affirmative and the universal is similarly assigned, so that m belongs to every n while it belongs to some x, then it is possible for n to belong both to every x and to no x.

The terms for belonging to none are white, swan, stone. Terms for belonging to every one cannot be supplied, for the same reason as before; this too must be shown from the indefinite case.

But if the universal proposition is assigned to the minor extreme, so that m belongs to no x while n does not belong to some m, then n may belong both to every x and to no x.

The terms for belonging are white, animal, raven; for not belonging, white, stone, raven.

The same applies if the propositions are affirmative.

The terms for not belonging are white, animal, snow; for belonging, white, animal, swan.

It is therefore clear that, if the propositions belong to the same form, and one is universal while the other is particular, no syllogism results in any way.

Nor does one result if the terms belong to both subjects, or do not belong to both, or belong to one but not the other, or belong to neither universally, or if the propositions are indefinite.

The common terms for all these cases are white, animal, human being; and white, animal, inanimate.

It is therefore clear from what has been said that, if the terms are related to one another in the manner stated, a syllogism necessarily results; and if a syllogism results, the terms must be related in this way.

It is also evident that all the syllogisms in this figure are imperfect, since they are all completed by assuming further propositions, which either necessarily belong to the terms or are posited as hypotheses, as when we demonstrate by the impossible.

It is also evident that no affirmative syllogism is produced through this figure, but that all are negative, both universal and particular.

CHAPTER SIX. On absolute syllogisms in the third figure.

[Cols. 0645C–0647A]

If one thing belongs to every instance of the same subject, while another belongs to none, or both belong to every instance, or both to none, I call this the third figure. By “middle” in this figure I mean that of which both are predicated; by “extremes,” those which are predicated; by “major extreme,” that which is farther from the middle; and by “minor,” that which is nearer. The middle is placed outside the extremes, while the last in position is the middle.

A perfect syllogism, then, is not produced in this figure. A syllogism is nevertheless possible, both universally and non-universally, when the terms are related to the middle. It is universal when both *p* and *r* belong to every *s*, since *p* must belong to some *r*. For, since an affirmative proposition converts, *s* will belong to some *r*. Therefore, since *p* belongs to every *s*, and *s* to some *r*, *p* must belong to some *r*. The syllogism is formed through the first figure.

It is also possible to make the demonstration by reductio ad impossibile and by exposition. For if both belong to every *s*, let one of the things that are *s* be taken—for example, *n*. Then both *p* and *r* will necessarily belong to it; therefore *p* will belong to some *r*. And if *r* belongs to every *s*, while *p* belongs to no *s*, there will be a syllogism, since *p* must not belong to some *r*. The mode of demonstration will be the same, by converting the proposition *r–s*. This can also be shown by reductio ad impossibile, as in the preceding cases.

But if *r* belongs to no *s*, while *p* belongs to every *s*, there will be no syllogism. The terms for belonging are: animal, horse, human; for not belonging: animal, inanimate, human. Nor is there a syllogism when both are predicated of no *s*. The terms for belonging are: animal, horse, inanimate; for not belonging: human, horse, inanimate; the middle is inanimate.

It is therefore clear, in this figure also, when and when not a syllogism arises from universal terms. When both terms are affirmative, there will be a syllogism, since one extreme belongs to some instance of the other. When both are negative, there will be no syllogism. When one is negative and the other affirmative, if the major is negative and the other affirmative, there will be a syllogism, since one extreme does not belong to some instance of the other. If the arrangement is reversed, there will be no syllogism.

If one proposition is universal with respect to the middle and the other particular, then, if both are affirmative, a syllogism must result; indeed, it does so if either of the terms is universal. For if *r* belongs to every *s*, while *p* belongs to some *s*, then *p* must belong to some *r*. Since an affirmative proposition converts, *s* will belong to some *p*. Therefore, since *r* belongs to every *s*, while *s* belongs to some *p*, *r* will belong to some *p*, and consequently *p* will belong to some *r*.

Again, if *r* belongs to some *s*, while *p* belongs to every *s*, *p* must belong to some *r*, for the demonstration is the same. It is also possible to demonstrate this by reductio ad impossibile and by exposition, as in the preceding cases.

But if one proposition is affirmative and the other negative, and the affirmative is universal, then, when the minor is affirmative, there will be a syllogism. For if *r* belongs to every *s*, while *p* does not belong to some *s*, then *p* must not belong to some *r*. For if *p* belonged to every *r*, and *r* to every *s*, *p* would belong to every *s*, whereas it did not. This is also shown without deduction, by taking one of the things that are *s* to which *p* does not belong.

When the major is affirmative, however, there will be no syllogism—for example, if *p* belongs to every *s*, while *r* does not belong to some *s*. The terms for belonging to every instance are: animate, human, animal. For belonging to none, it is impossible to supply terms if *r* belongs to some *s* but not to others. For if *p* belongs to every *s*, while *r* belongs to some *s*, then *p* will belong to some *r*, although it was posited that it belongs to no *r*.

But the point must be stated as in the preceding cases. When the proposition says indefinitely that something does not belong to some instance, and what belongs to none is truly said not to belong to some instance, no syllogism resulted when the proposition was that it belonged to none. It is therefore clear that there will be no syllogism.

If the negative term is universal, then, when the major is negative and the minor affirmative, there will be a syllogism. For if *p* belongs to none of the *s*, while *r* belongs to some *s*, *p* will not belong to some *r*. Here again the first figure results by converting the proposition *r–s*. When the minor is negative, however, there will be no syllogism.

The terms for belonging are: animal, human, wild creature; for not belonging: animal, knowledge, wild creature. The middle in both cases is wild creature.

Nor is there a syllogism when both propositions are negative, one being universal and the other particular. The terms when the minor is universal with respect to the middle are: for belonging, animal, human, wild creature; for not belonging, animal, knowledge, wild creature. When the major is universal, the terms for not belonging are: raven, snow, white. For belonging, it is impossible to supply terms if *r* belongs to some *s* but not to others. For if *p* belongs to every *r*, while *r* belongs to some *s*, *p* will belong to some *s*. But it was posited that it belongs to none; this is to be shown from the indefinite case.

Nor will there be a syllogism if both belong to some middle, or both do not belong, or one belongs and the other does not, or one belongs to some while the other does not belong to every instance, or the propositions are indefinite. The common terms for all these cases are: animal, human, white; animal, inanimate, white.

It is therefore clear, in this figure also, both when and when not a syllogism arises, and that when the terms are related as stated, a syllogism necessarily results, while if there is a syllogism, the terms must be so related. It is also clear that all the syllogisms in this figure are imperfect, since they are all completed by the addition of certain propositions.

It is also clear that it is impossible to syllogize universally through this figure, whether negatively or affirmatively.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Three Figures and the Indirect Syllogisms Related to One Another

[Cols. 0647B–0648A]

It is clear, moreover, that in all the figures a syllogism is sometimes not produced. When both terms are affirmative or both negative and are particular, nothing at all follows necessarily. But when one is affirmative and the other negative, and the negative is taken universally, a syllogism always results from the minor extreme to the major—for example, if *a* belongs to every *b* or to some *b*, while *b* belongs to no *c*. For, by converting the propositions, *c* must not belong to some *a*.

The same holds in the other figures, since a syllogism is always produced by conversion.

It is also clear that an indefinite proposition, when substituted for a particular affirmative, will produce the same syllogism in all the figures.

It is clear as well that all imperfect syllogisms are completed through the first figure. For all are completed either demonstratively or by reductio ad impossibile, and in both cases the first figure is involved. In demonstrative proofs, the perfect syllogisms are completed because they were closed by conversion, and conversion produces the first figure. In demonstrations by reductio ad impossibile, the proof is made through the first figure because, once the falsehood has been posited, a syllogism results through that figure.

For example, in the last figure, if *a* and *b* belong to every *c*, then *a* belongs to some *b*. For if it belonged to none, while *b* belonged to every *c*, *a* would belong to no *c*, although it belonged to every *c*. The same applies in the other cases.

It is also possible to reduce all syllogisms to universal syllogisms of the first figure. In the second figure, it is clear that they are completed through those syllogisms, though not all in the same way: the universal ones through the converted negative proposition, while both particular forms are reduced by reductio ad impossibile.

The particular syllogisms in the first figure are completed in themselves. Yet it is also possible to demonstrate them by the second figure through reductio ad impossibile. For example, if *a* belongs to every *b*, and *b* to some *c*, then *a* will belong to some *c*. For if it belonged to none, while *b* belonged to every *a*, *b* would belong to no *c*. This is known through the second figure.

The demonstration is similar in the negative case. If *a* belongs to no *b*, while *b* belongs to some *c*, *a* will not belong to some *c*. For if *a* belonged to every *c*, while *b* belonged to none of *a*, *b* would belong to no *c*. This was the middle figure.

Therefore, since the syllogisms in the middle figure are all reducible to universal syllogisms of the first figure, while the particular syllogisms of the first figure are reducible to those in the middle figure, it is clear that the particulars too will be reduced to the universal syllogisms of the first figure.

The syllogisms in the third figure, when the terms are universal, are immediately completed through those syllogisms. But when they are particular, they are established through the particular syllogisms of the first figure; and these have been reduced to the universal ones. Therefore the particular syllogisms of the third figure are also reduced to them.

It is consequently clear that all syllogisms are reducible to universal syllogisms of the first figure.

Thus it has been stated how the syllogisms that show that something belongs or does not belong are related both to those in the same figure, to one another, and to those in the other figures.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Syllogisms from Necessity in the Three Figures

[Cols. 0648B–0648C]

Since belonging, belonging necessarily, and possibly belonging are different—for many things belong without belonging necessarily, while others belong neither necessarily nor at all, though they may possibly belong—it is clear that the syllogism in each of these cases is also different. The terms are not related in the same way: one proposition concerns what is necessary, another what simply belongs, and another what is possible.

In necessary propositions, then, the arrangement is nearly the same as in propositions concerning simple belonging. When the terms are posited in the same way, both in propositions concerning simple belonging and in those concerning necessary belonging or non-belonging, a syllogism will or will not result in the same way. The difference lies in the fact that what is necessary to belong or not to belong is attached to the terms. For the negative proposition converts in the same way, and we shall likewise assign belonging to all and predication of every instance.

Accordingly, in the other cases it will be shown through conversion, in the same way, that the conclusion is necessary, just as in the case of simple belonging.

In the middle figure, however, when one proposition is a universal affirmative and the other a particular negative, and again in the third figure when one is a universal affirmative and the other a particular negative, the demonstration will not proceed in the same way. Instead, it is necessary to make an exposition of some object to which neither proposition belongs and to construct the syllogism about it. The conclusion will be necessary in that case. If the conclusion is necessary about the object exposed, it will also be necessary about that particular object, since the exposed object is itself one such object. Each syllogism is formed in its proper figure.

## CHAPTER IX. Mixed Syllogisms from One Necessary and One Absolute Proposition in the First Figure

[Cols. 0648D–0649A]

Sometimes, when only one proposition is necessary, the syllogism also becomes necessary, but not whichever proposition it may be: it is necessary when the proposition belonging to the major extreme is necessary.

For example, suppose *a* necessarily belongs, or necessarily does not belong, to *b*, while *b* simply belongs to *c*. With these propositions, *a* will necessarily belong, or not belong, to *c*. For since *a* necessarily belongs, or does not belong, to every *b*, and *c* is one of the things that are *b*, it is clear that *c* will necessarily have one of these relations to *a*.

But if *a–b* is not necessary while *b–c* is necessary, the conclusion will not be necessary. For if it were, it would follow that *a* necessarily belongs to some *b*, through the first and third figures. But this is false, since it is possible for *b* to be such that *a* belongs to none of it.

This is also clear from the terms. Let *a* be motion, *b* animal, and *c* human. Human necessarily belongs to animal, but animal does not move necessarily; therefore neither does human. The same demonstration applies if *a–b* is negative, since the proof is identical.

In particular syllogisms, if the universal proposition is necessary, the conclusion will also be necessary. If the particular proposition is necessary, the conclusion will not be necessary, whether the universal proposition is negative or affirmative.

First, let the universal proposition be necessary, and let *a* necessarily belong to every *b*, while *b* belongs only to some *c*. Then *a* must necessarily belong to some *c*, since *c* is subordinate to *b*, while *a* necessarily belonged to every *b*. The same applies if the syllogism is negative, since the demonstration is the same.

But if the particular proposition is necessary, the conclusion will not be necessary. Nothing impossible follows, just as in universal syllogisms, and the same holds in negative cases.

The terms are: motion, animal, white.

## CHAPTER X. Mixed Syllogisms from One Necessary and One Absolute Proposition in the Second Figure

[Cols. 0649B–0650A]

In the second figure, if the negative proposition is universal and necessary, the conclusion will be necessary. If the affirmative proposition is necessary, the conclusion will not be necessary.

First, let the negative proposition be necessary. Let *a* belong to no *b* necessarily, while *c* simply belongs to *a*. Since the negative proposition converts, *b* necessarily belongs to no *a*. But *a* belongs to every *c*; therefore *b* necessarily belongs to no *c*, since *c* is subordinate to *a*.

The same applies if the negative proposition is assigned to *c*. For if *a* necessarily belongs to no *c*, then *c* necessarily belongs to no *a*, while *a* belongs to every *b*. Therefore *c* necessarily belongs to none of the things that are *b*. The first figure results.

Again, the same holds if the proposition *b–c* is negative, since it converts in the same way.

But if the affirmative proposition is necessary, the conclusion will not be necessary. Let *a* necessarily belong to every *b*, while *c* simply belongs to none of *a*. By converting the negative proposition, the first figure results. It was shown in the first figure that, when the proposition concerning the major is not necessary and negative, the conclusion is not necessary; therefore in these cases also the conclusion will not be necessary.

Furthermore, if the conclusion were necessary, it would follow that *c* necessarily does not belong to some *a*. For if *b* necessarily belonged to no *c*, then *c* would necessarily belong to no *b*; but *b* must belong to some *a*, since *a* necessarily belonged to every *b*. Therefore *c* must necessarily not belong to some *a*. Yet nothing prevents taking an *a* of such a kind that every *c* may possibly belong to it.

It is also possible to show by assigning terms that the conclusion is not necessary without qualification. Let *a* be animal, *b* human, and *c* white, and let the propositions be taken in the same way. It is possible for animal to belong to no white thing; therefore human will also belong to no white thing, but not necessarily. For it is possible for a human being to become white, though not while animal belongs to no white thing. Thus, under these conditions, the conclusion is necessary, but it is not necessary without qualification.

The same holds in particular syllogisms. When the negative proposition is universal and necessary, the conclusion will also be necessary. But when the affirmative universal proposition is necessary and the negative proposition particular and not necessary, the conclusion will not be necessary.

First, let the negative proposition be universal and necessary. Let *a* necessarily belong to no *b*, while *c* belongs to some *a*. Since the negative proposition converts, *b* will necessarily belong to no *a*, while *a* belongs to some *c*. Therefore *b* will necessarily not belong to some of the things that are *c*.

Again, let the affirmative proposition be universal and necessary, and let it be assigned to *b*. If *a* necessarily belongs to every *b*, while *c* does not belong to some *a*, it is clear that *b* does not belong to some *c*, but not necessarily. The terms for the demonstration will be the same as in universal syllogisms.

Nor, if the negative proposition is particular and necessary, will the conclusion be necessary. The demonstration is made through the same terms.

## CHAPTER XI. Mixed Syllogisms from One Necessary and One Absolute Proposition in the Third Figure

[Cols. 0650B–0651C]

In the last figure, when both terms are universal with respect to the middle and both propositions are affirmative, if either proposition is necessary, the conclusion will also be necessary.

If one proposition is negative and the other affirmative, then, when the negative proposition is necessary, the conclusion will also be necessary; but when the affirmative proposition is necessary, the conclusion will not be necessary.

First, let both propositions be affirmative, and let *a* and *b* belong to every *c*. Let *a–c* be necessary. Since *b* belongs to every *c*, *c* will belong to some *b*, because a universal proposition converts particularly. Therefore, if *a* necessarily belongs to every *c*, and *c* belongs to some *b*, *a* must necessarily belong to some *b*, since *b* is subordinate to *c*. The first figure results.

The same will be shown if *b–c* is necessary, since *a–c* converts, so that *c* belongs to some *a*. Therefore, if *b* necessarily belongs to every *c*, *b* will necessarily belong to some *a*.

Again, let *a–c* be negative and *b–c* affirmative, with the negative proposition necessary. Since the affirmative proposition converts, *c* will belong to some *b*. But *a* necessarily belongs to no *c*; therefore *a* will necessarily belong to none of *b*, since *b* is subordinate to *c*.

If the affirmative proposition is necessary, however, the conclusion will not be necessary. Let *b–c* be affirmative and necessary, while *a–c* is negative and not necessary. Since the affirmative proposition converts, *c* will necessarily belong to some *b*. Therefore, if *a* belongs to none of the things that are *c*, while *c* belongs to some of the things that are *b*, *a* will not belong to some of the things that are *b*, but not necessarily. For it was shown in the first figure that, when the negative proposition is necessary, the conclusion is not thereby necessary.

This is also clear from the terms. Let *a* be good, *b* animal, and *c* horse. Good may belong to no horse, while animal necessarily belongs to every horse; but it is not necessary that some animal be not good, since it is possible for every animal to be good.

Or, if this is not possible, let the terms be “awake” and “asleep.” Every animal is capable of these states.

If, then, the terms are universal with respect to the middle, it has been stated when the conclusion will be necessary.

But if one term is universal and the other particular, and both propositions are affirmative, then, when the universal proposition is necessary, the conclusion will also be necessary. The demonstration is the same as before, since the particular affirmative proposition also converts.

If *b* necessarily belongs to every *c*, while *a* is subordinate to *c*, then *b* must necessarily belong to some *a*. If *b* belongs to some *a*, then *a* must necessarily belong to some *b*, since the proposition converts. The same applies if the universal proposition *a–c* is necessary, since *b* is subordinate to *c*.

But if the particular proposition is necessary, the conclusion will not be necessary. Let *b–c* be particular and necessary, while *a* belongs to every *c*, though not necessarily. By converting *b–c*, the first figure results, with the universal proposition not necessary and the particular proposition necessary. But when the propositions are so related, the conclusion was not necessary; therefore it will not be necessary in these cases either.

This is also clear from the terms. Let *a* be wakefulness, *b* biped, and *c* animal. It is necessary that *b* belong to some *c*, while *a* may belong to every *c*; but *a* does not necessarily belong to some *b*, since it is not necessary that any biped be asleep or awake. The same terms will show the point if *a–c* is particular and necessary.

If one term is affirmative and the other negative, and the necessary proposition is universal and negative, the conclusion will also be necessary. For if *a* necessarily belongs to no *c*, while *b* belongs to some *c*, *a* must necessarily not belong to some *b*.

But when the affirmative proposition is necessary—whether universal or particular—or when the particular negative proposition is necessary, the conclusion will not be necessary. The other cases will be stated in the same way as those already discussed.

The terms when the universal affirmative proposition is necessary are: wakefulness, animal, human; the middle is human. When the particular affirmative proposition is necessary, they are: wakefulness, animal, white. Animal necessarily belongs to some white thing, while wakefulness may belong to no white thing; but it is not necessary that wakefulness not belong to some animal. When the particular negative proposition is necessary, the terms are: biped, motion, animal; the middle is animal.

It is therefore clear that there is no syllogism concerning simple belonging unless both propositions concern simple belonging; but a necessary syllogism results even when only one proposition is necessary. In both affirmative and negative syllogisms, one proposition must resemble the conclusion. By “resemble” I mean that if the conclusion concerns simple belonging, the corresponding proposition concerns simple belonging; and if the conclusion is necessary, the corresponding proposition is necessary.

It is therefore also clear that there will be no conclusion that is either necessary or concerned with simple belonging unless a proposition signifying necessity or simple belonging has been assumed.

This is nearly sufficient as an account of how a syllogism concerning necessity is formed and how it differs from one concerning simple belonging.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Non-necessary Possible

[Cols. 0651D–0652D]

We shall now discuss the possible: when, how, and through which propositions a syllogism arises.

By “possible” and “possibility” I mean that which, although not necessary, becomes nothing impossible when it is posited as belonging. For “necessary” is also called “possible,” equivocally.

That this is the meaning of possibility is clear from the opposed affirmations and negations. “It is not contingent to be,” “it is not possible to be,” “it is impossible to be,” and “it is necessary not to be” are either the same or follow one another. Therefore their opposites—“it is possible to be,” “it is not impossible to be,” and “it is not necessary not to be”—will likewise be either the same or mutually consequential.

Of every subject, an affirmation or negation is true. Thus what is contingent will be necessary, and what is non-necessary will be contingent.

All propositions concerning possibility happen to convert into one another. I do not mean affirmative propositions into negative ones, but those that have an affirmative form according to opposition: “it is possible to be” converts with “it is possible not to be”; “it is possible to belong to every instance” with “it is possible to belong to none” or “not to every”; “it is possible to belong to some” with “it is possible not to belong to some”; and similarly in the other cases.

Since what is possible is not necessary, and what is not necessary may possibly not be, it is clear that if *a* may belong to *b*, it may also not belong to *b*. If it may belong to every instance, it may also not belong to every instance. The same demonstration applies to particular affirmations.

Such propositions are affirmative in form, for “to be possible” is posited in the same way as “to be,” as was previously stated.

Having established these points, we say again that “possible” is used in two ways. In one sense it means what usually happens but may fail to happen, while not being necessary—for example, a human being’s becoming gray, increasing, decreasing, or anything that is naturally the case. Such a thing does not possess necessity continuously, since a human being is not always present; yet whenever a human being exists, the event occurs either necessarily or for the most part.

In another sense, “possible” means what is indefinite, that which can occur either in one way or in the opposite way—for example, an animal’s walking, or an earthquake occurring while an animal is walking, or anything that happens by chance. Nothing is naturally disposed more toward one outcome than its opposite.

Therefore both kinds of possibility convert according to opposed propositions, though not in the same way. What is naturally disposed to occur converts with what occurs without necessity. In this way it is possible for a human being not to become gray. The indefinite possible converts with what is neither more naturally disposed to occur in one way nor in the other.

Scientific knowledge and demonstrative syllogism do not arise from the indefinite, since its middle term is unordered. Most discussions and inquiries concerning such possibilities concern things naturally disposed to occur. It is possible to construct a syllogism from the indefinite, but this is not ordinarily the object of inquiry.

These matters will be defined more fully later. For now, we shall say when, how, and what kind of syllogism arises from possible propositions.

Since “it is possible for this to belong to that” can be understood in two ways, it may mean either that the subject to which this belongs is such that it can belong, or that it is possible for the predicate itself to belong. Thus, when *a* is said to be possible for *b*, this may signify either the subject of which *b* is predicated or the subject of which it is possible to predicate *b*. In the case where *a* is possible for every *b*, there is no difference.

It is therefore clear that “*a* may belong to every *b*” is said in two ways.

We shall first discuss the case in which *b* is possible for *c*, and *a* is possible for *b*: what kind and what sort of syllogism results. In this case both propositions are taken according to possibility. But when *a* is possible for the subject of which *b* is predicated, one proposition concerns simple belonging and the other possibility. We must therefore begin with similar figures, as in the other cases.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Syllogisms from Two Possible Propositions in the First Figure

[Cols. 0653A–0654B]

When *a* is possible for every *b*, and *b* for every *c*, there will be a perfect syllogism, since *a* is possible for every *c*. This is clear from the definition, for we defined “possible for every instance to belong” in this way.

The same applies if *a* is possible for no *b*, while *b* is possible for every *c*: *a* is possible for no *c*. For if *a* is possible for none of the things to which *b* is possible, this means that no instance has been left among the things possible under *b*.

When *a* is possible for every *b*, while *b* is possible for no *c*, no syllogism results from the propositions as taken. But when the proposition *b–c* is converted according to possibility, the same syllogism results as before. For since *b* is possible for no *c*, it is also possible for every *c*, as was previously stated. Therefore, if *b* is possible for every *c*, while *a* is possible for every *b*, the same syllogism results.

The same applies when negation is added to both propositions together with possibility—for example, if *a* is possible for no *b*, and *b* for no *c*. From the propositions as taken, no syllogism results; but after they are converted, the same syllogism results as before.

It is therefore clear that when negation is added to the minor extreme, or to both propositions, either no syllogism results, or one results but is imperfect, since it necessarily arises through conversion.

If one proposition is universal and the other particular, then, when the universal proposition is assigned to the major extreme, the syllogism will be perfect. For if *a* is possible for every *b*, while *b* is possible for some *c*, *a* will be possible for some *c*. This is clear from the definition of possibility.

Again, if *a* is possible for no *b*, while *b* is possible for some *c*, *a* must be possible not to belong to some *c*. The demonstration is the same as in these cases.

But if the particular proposition is negative while the universal proposition is affirmative, and the propositions are similarly arranged—for example, if *a* is possible for every *b*, while *b* is possible not to belong to some *c*—no syllogism is evident from the propositions as taken. But after the particular proposition is converted, and *b* is posited as possible to belong to some *c*, the conclusion is the same as before, just as in the cases treated from the beginning.

If the proposition concerning the major extreme is particular and that concerning the minor universal, then, whether both are affirmative, both negative, of different forms, both indefinite, or both particular, there will in no way be a syllogism.
