For nothing prevents *b* from exceeding *a* and not being predicated of equal instances. Let *c* be taken among the things in which *b* exceeds *a*. For this *c*, it is possible for *a* to belong neither to every instance, nor to none, nor to some, nor not to some, since the propositions concerning possibility convert, and more things may possibly have *b* than *a*.

This is also clear from the terms. With the propositions related in this way, the first necessarily belongs to every instance of the last, while it is possible for it to belong to none. The common terms are: for necessary belonging, animal, white, human; for possible non-belonging, animal, white, garment.

It is therefore clear that, when the terms are related in this way, no syllogism results. Every syllogism concerns either simple belonging, necessary belonging, or possible belonging. But the conclusion here concerns neither simple nor necessary belonging. Therefore it must concern possible belonging; yet this is impossible. For it has been shown that, when the terms are so related, the first necessarily belongs to every instance of the last, while it is possible for it to belong to none. Thus the conclusion cannot concern possibility, since what was necessary has been shown to be possible.

It is also clear that, when the terms in possible propositions are universal, a syllogism is always formed in the first figure, whether the propositions are affirmative or negative. From affirmative propositions it is perfect; from negative propositions it is imperfect.

Possibility must be understood here not in the necessary sense, but according to the definition given; this distinction is sometimes overlooked.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Syllogisms from One Absolute and One Possible Proposition in the First Figure
If, however, one proposition is taken as inhering and the other as possible, whenever the proposition belonging to the major extreme signifies possibility, all the syllogisms will be perfect, and the conclusion will be possibility in the sense defined above; but whenever the proposition belonging to the minor extreme signifies possibility, all the syllogisms will be imperfect, as will the negative syllogisms—not possibility in the sense defined above, but necessary inherence in none, or not in all. For if we say that something is possibly in none, or not in all, necessarily, we mean that it is in none, or not in all. Let *A* possibly belong to every *B*, and let *B* inhere in every *C*. Since *C* is contained under *B*, while *A* possibly belongs to every *B*, it is clear that *A* possibly belongs to every *C* also; thus there is a perfect syllogism. Likewise, when the proposition *AB* is negative, while *BC* is affirmative, and the former is taken as possible and the latter as inhering, the syllogism will be perfect, since *A* possibly inheres in none of *C*. Thus it is clear that, when inherence is posited in relation to the minor extreme, perfect syllogisms result.

That syllogisms also result when the propositions are arranged contrariwise must be shown by reductio ad impossibile; at the same time it will become clear that they are imperfect, since the demonstration does not proceed from the propositions assumed. [Col. 0654D] First, it must be stated that if, whenever *A* exists, *B* must exist, then, whenever *A* can exist, *B* will necessarily be possible. Let things be arranged so that wherever *A* is possible, *B* is impossible. If, then, something else is possible, when it is possible it will come to be; but what is impossible, since it is impossible, will not come to be. At the same time, if *A* is possible and *B* impossible, it will be possible for something to come to be apart from *B*, and likewise to exist. For what comes to be, when it has come to be, exists.

Possibility and impossibility must be understood not only in coming-to-be, but also with respect to truth and existence in actuality, and in whatever other sense possibility is stated simply; for in all cases the relation will be similar. Furthermore, when *A* exists, *B* exists, not as though *B* would exist merely because some one thing, *A*, exists; for nothing follows necessarily from the existence of one thing alone, but from at least two, as when the propositions are arranged in the way stated according to a syllogism. For example, *A* is said of *D*, *D* of *E*, and *C* necessarily of *E*; and if both are possible, the conclusion will also be possible.

Therefore, just as if someone were to posit the propositions as *A* and the conclusion as *B*, it would follow not only that, if *A* exists necessarily, *B* exists simultaneously and necessarily, but also that if *A* is possible, *B* is possible. Once this has been shown, it is clear that if a false but non-impossible proposition is posited, what follows from the position will also be false but non-impossible. Thus, if *A* is false but not impossible, when *A* exists, *B* will also be false but not impossible. For it has been shown that when *A* exists, *B* exists, and that when *A* is possible, *B* is possible. But *A* was posited as possible, and therefore *B* will be possible; for if *B* were impossible, the same thing would simultaneously be possible and impossible.

With these points determined, let *A* inhere in every *B*, while *B* possibly inheres in every *C*. Therefore *A* must possibly inhere in every *C*. Suppose that it does not possibly do so, while *B* is posited as inhering in every *C*. This is false, but not impossible. If, then, *A* does not possibly inhere in every *C*, while *B* inheres in every *C*, *A* does not possibly belong to every *B*. For a syllogism arises through the third figure. But it was posited that *A* possibly inheres in every *C*. Therefore *A* must possibly inhere in every *C*. For when a false but non-impossible proposition is posited, what follows from it cannot be impossible.

It is also possible to make the first figure impossible by positing that *B* inheres in *C*. For if *B* inheres in every *C*, while *A* possibly inheres in every *B*, then *A* will possibly inhere in every *C*; but it had been posited that it is not possible for it to inhere in every case.

“Inheres in every” must not be determined according to a time, such as “now” or “at this time,” but simply—for it is by propositions of this kind that we construct these propositions and syllogisms. With a proposition taken as applying only now, there will be no syllogism. For perhaps nothing prevents “mover” from inhering at some time in every human being, if nothing else is moving, while “mover” possibly inheres in every horse, but “human being” possibly inheres in no horse.

Furthermore, let the first term be “animal,” the middle term “mover,” and the last term “human being.” The propositions will accordingly be arranged in the same way, but the conclusion will be necessary, not possible. For a human being is necessarily an animal. It is therefore clear that the universal must be taken simply, and not determined by time.

Again, let the universal proposition *AB* be negative, and let *A* inhere in no *B*, while *B* possibly inheres in every *C*. With these propositions posited, *A* must possibly inhere in no *C*. Suppose that it does not possibly do so, while *B* is posited as inhering in *C*, as before. Then *A* must inhere in some *B*, for a syllogism arises through the third figure. But this is impossible; therefore *A* possibly inheres in no *C*. For when a false but non-impossible proposition is posited, what follows from it is impossible.

This syllogism, then, is not about possibility according to the definition, but about necessary inherence in none. This is the contradiction of the hypothesis that was made. For it was posited that *A* necessarily inheres in some *C*, while the syllogism by impossibility establishes the contradictory proposition. [Col. 0656A]

Furthermore, it is clear from the terms that the conclusion will not be possible. Let *A* be “raven,” *B* “intelligent being,” and *C* “human being.” Thus *A* inheres in no *B*, since no intelligent being is a raven; *B* possibly inheres in every *C*, since intelligence belongs to every human being; but *A* necessarily inheres in no *C*. Therefore the conclusion is not possible.

Nor is it always necessary. Let *A* be “mover,” *B* “knowledge,” and *C* “human being.” Thus *A* inheres in no *B*, while *B* possibly inheres in every *C*; yet the conclusion will not be necessary, since it is not necessary that no human being move, but only that some human being move. It is therefore clear that the conclusion concerns necessary inherence in none. The terms should be chosen more suitably.

If a negative proposition belonging to the major extreme is posited as signifying possibility, there will be no syllogism from the propositions as assumed; but if the possible proposition is converted, there will be a syllogism, as in the preceding cases. Let *A* inhere in every *B*, while *B* possibly inheres in no *C*. With the terms arranged in this way, nothing necessary follows. But if *BC* is converted and *B* is taken as possibly inhering in every *C*, a syllogism will arise as before, since the terms are arranged in the same way by the position.

The same holds when both intervals are negative, if *AB* signifies non-inherence and *BC* signifies possible non-inherence. From the propositions as assumed, nothing necessary follows; but when the possible proposition is converted, there will be a syllogism. Let *A* inhere in no *B*, while *B* possibly inheres in no *C*. From these propositions nothing necessary follows. But if *B* is taken as possibly inhering in every *C*, which is true, while the proposition *AB* remains arranged in the same way, the same syllogism will again result.

If *B* is posited as not inhering in every *C*, and as not possibly failing to inhere, there will be no syllogism at all, whether the proposition *AB* is negative or affirmative. The common terms for necessary inherence are “white,” “animal,” “snow”; for impossibility of inherence, “white,” “animal,” “pitch.”

It is therefore clear that, when the terms are universal, and one proposition signifies inherence while the other is taken as possible, whenever the proposition belonging to the minor extreme is taken as possible, there is always a syllogism—sometimes from the propositions themselves, sometimes from the converted proposition, and sometimes in both ways; and the reason for this has been stated.

If one interval is taken as universal and the other particular, then, whenever the proposition belonging to the major extreme is universal and possible, whether negative or affirmative, while the particular proposition is affirmative and concerns inherence, there will be a perfect syllogism, just as when the terms are universal; the demonstration is the same as before.

But whenever the proposition belonging to the major extreme is universal, concerns inherence, and is not possible, while the other is particular and possible, whether both are posited affirmatively or negatively, or the one negatively and the other affirmatively, there will invariably be an imperfect syllogism. Some of these are demonstrated by impossibility, others by conversion of the possible proposition, as in the preceding cases.

A syllogism by conversion also arises when the universal proposition belonging to the major extreme signifies inherence or non-inherence, while the particular proposition is negative and is taken as possible. Thus, if *A* inheres or does not inhere in every *B*, while *B* possibly does not inhere in some *C*, then, by converting *BC* according to possibility, a syllogism results.

When the particular proposition is posited as non-inherence, there will be no syllogism. The terms for inherence are “white,” “animal,” “snow”; for non-inherence, “white,” “animal,” “pitch.” The demonstration must be understood as involving an indefinite proposition.

If the universal proposition is placed at the minor extreme, while the major proposition is particular—whether negative or affirmative, possible or concerning inherence—there will be no syllogism at all. Nor will there be one when particular or indefinite propositions are posited, whether they are taken as possible or as concerning inherence, or are interchanged. The demonstration is the same as before. The common terms for inherence are necessarily “animal,” “white,” “human being”; for impossibility of inherence, “animal,” “white,” “tunic.”

It is therefore clear that, when the proposition at the major extreme is universal, there will always be a syllogism, but never when it is at the minor extreme.

## CHAPTER XV. The Mixture of the Necessary and the Possible in the First Figure

When one of the propositions signifies necessary inherence or non-inherence, while the other signifies possibility, a syllogism will result when the terms are arranged as follows. It will be perfect when the necessary proposition is placed at the minor extreme.

If the propositions are affirmative, the conclusion will concern possibility, not inherence, whether they are universal or not universal. But if one proposition is affirmative and the other negative, then, when the affirmative proposition is necessary, the conclusion will concern possibility, but not necessary non-inherence. When the negative proposition is necessary, the conclusion will concern possibility and non-inherence, whether the terms are universal or not universal.

Possibility in the conclusion must be understood in the same way as in the preceding discussions. There will be no syllogism concerning necessary non-inherence, for “not necessarily inhering” is different from “necessarily not inhering.”

Since, when the terms are universal and affirmative, no necessary conclusion is produced, this is clear. Let *A* necessarily inhere in every *B*, while *B* possibly inheres in every *C*. There will therefore be an imperfect syllogism, since *A* possibly inheres in every *C*. That it is imperfect is evident from the demonstration; for it will be shown in the same way as in the preceding cases.

Again, let *A* possibly inhere in every *B*, while *B* necessarily inheres in every *C*. There will therefore be a syllogism, since *A* possibly inheres in every *C*, but not that it inheres. The syllogism is perfect, not imperfect, since it is completed immediately from the initial propositions.

If the propositions do not belong to the same figure, let the first be negative and necessary: let *A* necessarily inhere in no *B*, while *B* possibly inheres in every *C*. Therefore *A* necessarily inheres in no *C*. For suppose that *A* inheres in every or in some *C*. But *A* was posited as possibly inhering in no *B*. Since the negative proposition is convertible, *B* possibly inheres in no *A*. Yet *A* was posited as inhering in every or in some *C*. Therefore *B* will possibly inhere in no or not every *C*, whereas it had originally been assumed to inhere in every *C*.

It is also clear that there is a syllogism both concerning possible non-inherence and concerning non-inherence. Again, let the proposition be affirmative and necessary, while *A* possibly inheres in no *B*, and *B* necessarily inheres in every *C*. Thus there is a perfect syllogism, but not concerning non-inherence; it concerns possible non-inherence. For the proposition belonging to the major extreme has been taken in this way, and the argument does not lead to impossibility. If *A* is posited as inhering in some *C*, while *A* is posited as possibly inhering in no *B*, nothing impossible follows from these assumptions.

If the negative proposition is placed at the minor extreme and signifies possibility, there will be a syllogism by conversion, as in the preceding cases. When it signifies impossibility, there will not be a syllogism concerning necessity; nor will there be one when both propositions are negative and the proposition at the minor extreme is not possible.

The terms for inherence are “white,” “animal,” “snow”; for non-inherence, “white,” “animal,” “pitch.”

The same arrangement will hold in particular syllogisms. For when the negative proposition is necessary, the conclusion will concern non-inherence. Thus, if *A* necessarily inheres in no *B*, while *B* possibly inheres in some *C*, *A* must fail to inhere in some of the things that are *C*. For if *A* inheres in every *C*, it necessarily inheres in no *B*, and *B* necessarily inheres in no *A*. Therefore, if *A* inheres in every *C*, *B* possibly inheres in no *C*; but it had been posited that it possibly inheres in some.

When the particular affirmative proposition in a negative syllogism is necessary, as *BC* is, or when the universal affirmative proposition in an affirmative syllogism is necessary, as *AB* is, there will be no syllogism concerning inherence. The demonstration is the same as in the preceding cases.

If a universal proposition is placed at the minor extreme, whether affirmative or negative and possible, while the particular proposition is necessary, there will be no syllogism. The terms for necessary inherence are “animal,” “white,” “human being”; for impossibility of inherence, “animal,” “white,” “tunic.”

Likewise, when the universal proposition is necessary and the particular proposition possible, if the universal is negative, the terms for inherence are “animal,” “white,” “raven”; for non-inherence, “animal,” “white,” “pitch.” If the universal is affirmative, the terms for inherence are “animal,” “white,” “swan”; for impossibility of inherence, “animal,” “white,” “snow.”

Nor will there be a syllogism when the propositions are taken as indefinite, or when both are particular. The common terms are, for inherence, “animal,” “white,” “human being”; for non-inherence, “animal,” “white,” “inanimate.” For animal necessarily inheres in some white thing, and white necessarily inheres in some inanimate thing, and neither is possibly inhering in every case; the same holds with possibility. Thus these terms are useful for all the cases.

From what has been said it is clear that, with the terms similarly arranged, syllogisms both arise and fail to arise in the cases of inherence and of necessity. Yet when a negative proposition is posited in the case of inherence, the syllogism concerned possibility; when the negative proposition is necessary, it concerned both possibility and non-inherence.

It is also clear that all the imperfect syllogisms are perfected through the figures mentioned above, and how they are perfected.

## CHAPTER XVI. Syllogisms from Two Possible Propositions in the Second Figure

In the second figure, when both propositions are taken as possible, there will be no syllogism, whether they are affirmative or negative, universal or particular.

When one proposition signifies inherence and the other possibility, if the affirmative proposition signifies inherence, there will never be a syllogism; but if the negative proposition is universal, there will always be one.

The same holds when one proposition is taken as necessary and the other as possible. In these cases too, the possible element in the conclusions must be understood as in the preceding discussions.

First, it must be shown that in the case of possibility the negative proposition is not convertible. Thus, if *A* possibly inheres in no *B*, it does not follow that *B* possibly inheres in no *A*. Let this latter proposition also be posited, and let *B* possibly inhere in no *A*. Since, in the case of possibility, affirmations are convertible with negations, and contraries with their counterparts, it is clear that, if *B* possibly inheres in no *A*, *B* possibly inheres in every *A*. But this is false. For it does not follow that, if one thing possibly belongs to every member of another class, the latter necessarily possibly belongs to every member of the former. Therefore the negative proposition is not convertible.

Furthermore, nothing prevents *A* from possibly inhering in no *B*, while *B* necessarily fails to inhere in some *A*. Thus “white” possibly inheres in no human being, since it is also true to say that a human being is not white; but it is not true to say that a human being possibly inheres in no white thing, since many things necessarily fail to be white, and what is necessary was not possible.

Nor can the converse be shown by reductio ad impossibile. Suppose someone thinks that it is false that *B* possibly inheres in no *A*, and true that it does not possibly inhere in no *A*. For affirmation and negation are opposites. If this is true, *B* necessarily inheres in some *A*, and therefore *A* necessarily inheres in some *B*. But this is impossible. For it does not follow that, if *A* does not possibly inhere in no *B*, *A* necessarily inheres in some *B*.

“Does not possibly inhere in no one” is said in two ways: either because it necessarily inheres in some one, or because it necessarily fails to inhere in some one. For when something necessarily fails to inhere in some of the things that are *A*, it is not correct to say that it possibly fails to inhere in every one of them, just as when it necessarily inheres in some one, it is not correct to say that it possibly inheres in every one.

Suppose, then, that someone thinks that *C* possibly inheres in every *D*, but necessarily fails to inhere in some one. This is false, since, if it is possible, it inheres in every one. Rather, because it necessarily inheres in some, we say that it does not possibly inhere in every one.

Thus, opposed to the possibility of inhering in every case are both necessary inherence in some and necessary non-inherence in some; and likewise these are opposed to the possibility of inhering in none.

It is therefore clear that, for possibility and non-possibility understood in the sense defined at the beginning, one must include not only necessary inherence in some but also necessary non-inherence in some.

Once this is granted, nothing impossible follows, and therefore no syllogism results. It is clear from what has been said that the negative proposition is not convertible.

Once this has been shown, let *A* possibly inhere in no *B*, and in every *C*. By conversion, therefore, there will be no syllogism. For it has been stated that a proposition of this kind is not convertible.

Nor will there be one by impossibility. If *B* is posited as possibly inhering in every *C*, nothing false follows; for *A* will possibly inhere in both every and no *C*.

In general, if there is a syllogism, it is clear that the conclusion will be possible, since neither proposition has been taken as concerning inherence, whether affirmative or negative. But this is impossible in either way: if the conclusion is affirmative, it will be shown by the terms that inherence is not possible; if negative, that the conclusion is not possible but necessary.

Let *A* be “white,” *B* “human being,” and *C* “horse.” Thus white possibly inheres in every member of one class and in none of the other, but it is neither possible for *B* to inhere in *C* nor possible for it not to inhere. Since inherence is impossible, this is clear: no horse is a human being. But neither is possible non-inherence, since it is necessary that no horse be a human being, whereas what is necessary was not possible. Therefore there is no syllogism.

The same will be shown if the negative proposition is posited conversely, and likewise if both propositions are affirmative or both negative, for the demonstration will use the same terms.

The same holds when one proposition is universal and the other particular, when both are particular, when they are indefinite, or when the propositions are otherwise rearranged in any way; in every case the demonstration will use the same terms.

It is therefore clear that, when both propositions are posited according to possibility, no syllogism results.

## CHAPTER XVII. The Mixture of Inherence and Possibility in the Second Figure

If one proposition signifies inherence and the other possibility, then, when the affirmative proposition is taken as concerning inherence and the negative proposition as possible, there will never be a syllogism, whether the terms are taken universally or particularly. The demonstration is the same and uses the same terms.

But when the affirmative proposition is possible and the negative proposition concerns inherence, there will be a syllogism. Let *A* inhere in no *B*, while *C* possibly inheres in every *A*. By converting the negative proposition, *B* inheres in no *A*, while *A* possibly inheres in every *C*. Thus there is a syllogism that *B* possibly inheres in no *C*, through the first figure.

The same holds if the negative proposition is placed in relation to *C*.

If both propositions are negative, and one signifies non-inherence while the other signifies possible non-inherence, nothing necessary follows from the propositions as assumed; but when the possible proposition is converted, a syllogism results, namely that *B* possibly inheres in no *C*, as in the preceding cases. For the first figure is again produced.

If both propositions are affirmative, there will be no syllogism. The terms for inherence are “health,” “horse,” “human being.”

The same arrangement holds in particular syllogisms. When the affirmative proposition is about inherence, whether taken universally or particularly, there will be no syllogism; this is demonstrated in the same way and by the same terms as before.

When the proposition is negative, there will be a syllogism by conversion, as in the preceding cases.

Again, if both intervals are taken as negative, while the universal proposition signifies non-inherence, nothing necessary follows from the propositions themselves; but when the possible proposition is converted, there will be a syllogism.

If the proposition concerning inherence is negative and taken particularly, there will be no syllogism, whether the other proposition is affirmative or negative.

Nor will there be one when both propositions are indefinite, whether affirmative or negative, or when both are particular. The demonstration is the same and uses the same terms.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Mixture of the Necessary and the Possible in the Second Figure

If one proposition is necessary and the other signifies possibility, then, when the necessary proposition is negative, there will be a syllogism—not only that non-inherence is possible, but also that there is non-inherence; when it is affirmative, there will be no syllogism.

Let *A* necessarily inhere in no *B*, while *C* possibly inheres in every *A*. By converting the negative proposition, *B* inheres in no *A*, while *A* possibly inheres in every *C*. Thus, again, through the first figure, there is a syllogism that *B* possibly inheres in no *C*. At the same time it is clear that *B* does not inhere in any *C*. For suppose that it does inhere. If *A* possibly inheres in no *B*, while *B* inheres in some *C*, then *A* does not possibly inhere in some *C*, whereas it had been posited as possibly inhering in every *C*.

The same will be shown if the negative proposition is placed in relation to *C*.

Again, let one proposition be affirmative and necessary, and the other negative and possible. Let *A* possibly inhere in no *B*, while *C* necessarily inheres in every *A*. With the terms arranged in this way there is no syllogism, for it follows that *B* necessarily fails to inhere in *C*.

Let *A* be “white,” *B* “human being,” and *C* “swan.” Thus white necessarily inheres in every swan, while it possibly inheres in no human being; and a human being necessarily belongs to no swan. Since there is no syllogism concerning possibility, this is clear, for what was necessary was not possible.

Nor is there a syllogism concerning necessity, for a necessary conclusion follows either from two necessary propositions or from a necessary negative proposition.

Furthermore, with these assumptions it is possible for *B* to inhere in *C*. Nothing prevents *C* from being contained under *B*, while *A* possibly inheres in every *B* and necessarily inheres in *C*. Let *C* be “wakefulness,” *B* “animal,” and *A* “movement.” Movement necessarily belongs to what is awake, while it possibly belongs to no animal, and everything awake is an animal.

It is therefore clear that there is no syllogism concerning non-inherence, since, with the terms arranged in this way, inherence is necessary; nor is there one concerning the corresponding affirmative propositions. Therefore there will be no syllogism.

The same will be shown if the affirmative proposition is posited conversely.

If the propositions belong to the same figure and are negative, there is always a syllogism, by converting the possible proposition, as in the preceding cases. For if *A* necessarily fails to inhere in *B*, while *C* possibly fails to inhere in *A*, then, after the propositions have been converted, *B* necessarily inheres in no *A*, while *A* possibly inheres in every *C*. Thus the first figure results; and likewise if the negative proposition is placed in relation to *C*.

If the propositions are affirmative, there will be no syllogism. For there will be neither a syllogism concerning non-inherence nor one concerning necessary non-inherence, since no negative proposition has been taken, whether concerning inherence or necessary inherence. Nor will there be a syllogism concerning possible non-inherence, for, with the terms so arranged, it is necessary that *B* fail to inhere in *C*. Thus, let *A* be “white,” *B* “swan,” and *C* “human being.” Nor will there be a syllogism concerning the corresponding affirmative propositions, since it has been shown that *B* necessarily fails to inhere in *C*. Therefore there is no syllogism at all.

The same arrangement holds in particular syllogisms. When the negative proposition is universal and necessary, there will always be a syllogism, both concerning possible non-inherence and concerning non-inherence; the demonstration proceeds through conversion. When the proposition is affirmative, there will never be one. The same demonstration used for the universal cases, with the same terms, applies here.

Nor is there one when both propositions are affirmative, since the demonstration is the same as before.

When both propositions are negative, and the universal proposition is necessary and signifies non-inherence, nothing necessary follows from the propositions as assumed; but when the possible proposition is converted, there will be a syllogism, as in the preceding cases.

If both propositions are indefinite or particular, there will be no syllogism; the demonstration is the same and uses the same terms.

From what has been said it is clear that when a universal negative proposition is posited as necessary, there is always a syllogism—not only concerning possible non-inherence but also concerning non-inherence—whereas when the proposition is affirmative there is never one.

It is also clear that, with the terms similarly arranged, a syllogism both arises and fails to arise in the cases of necessity and of inherence. It is evident that all the syllogisms are imperfect, and that all are perfected through the figures already mentioned.

## CHAPTER XIX. Syllogisms from Two Possible Propositions in the Third Figure

In the last figure, when both propositions are possible, or when only one is possible, there will be a syllogism. When the propositions signify possibility, the conclusion will also be possible. When one signifies possibility and the other inherence, there will likewise be a syllogism.

When one proposition is necessary, however, if it is affirmative there will be no conclusion, neither necessary nor concerning inherence. If it is negative, there will be a syllogism concerning non-inherence, as in the preceding cases. Here too, the possible element in the conclusions must be understood in the same way.

Let the propositions first be possible, and let *A* and *B* possibly inhere in every *C*. Since the particular affirmative is convertible, and since *B* possibly inheres in every *C*, *C* possibly inheres in some *B*. Therefore, if *A* possibly inheres in every *C*, while *C* possibly inheres in some *B*, *A* possibly inheres in some *B*; for the first figure results.

If *A* possibly inheres in no *C*, while *B* possibly inheres in every *C*, then *A* must possibly fail to inhere in some member of the class *B*. Again, the first figure results through conversion.

If both propositions are negative, nothing necessary follows from the propositions as assumed; but when the propositions are converted, there will be a syllogism, as in the preceding cases. For if *A* and *B* possibly fail to inhere in *C*, then, when the possible non-inherence is transposed, the first figure again results by conversion.

If one of the terms is universal and the other particular, with the terms arranged as in the case of inherence, a syllogism will both arise and fail to arise.

Let *A* possibly inhere in every *C*, while *B* inheres in some *C*. Again, the first figure results through conversion of the particular proposition. For if *A* possibly inheres in every *C*, while *C* possibly inheres in some *B*, then *A* possibly inheres in some *B*.

The same holds if the proposition *BC* is made universal.

Likewise, if *AC* is negative and *BC* affirmative, one syllogism again results through conversion. But if both propositions are negative, one universal and the other particular, nothing necessary follows from the propositions as assumed; when the propositions are converted, however, there will be a syllogism, as in the preceding cases.

When both propositions are indefinite or particular, there will be no syllogism, for it is necessary that *A* inhere in every *B* and in no *B*.

The terms for inherence are “animal,” “human being,” “white”; for non-inherence, “horse,” “human being,” “the middle white.”

## CHAPTER XX. The Mixture of Possibility and Inherence in the Third Figure

If one proposition signifies inherence and the other possibility, the conclusion will state that something is possible, not that it inheres; and a syllogism will result when the terms are arranged as in the preceding cases.

Let the propositions first be affirmative, with *A* inhering in every *C* and *B* possibly inhering in every *C*. By converting *BC*, the first figure results, and the conclusion states that *A* possibly inheres in some *B*. For whenever one of the propositions in the first figure signifies possibility, the conclusion will also be possible.

The same holds if *BC* concerns inherence and *AC* possible inherence.

If *AC* is negative and *BC* affirmative, with either premise being one of inherence in either arrangement, the conclusion will be possible, for the first figure again results. It has been shown that, if one proposition in the first figure signifies possibility, the conclusion will also be possible.

If the possible proposition is negative and placed at the minor extreme, or if both propositions are negative, nothing follows from the propositions as posited; but when they are converted, a syllogism results, as in the preceding cases.

If one proposition is universal and the other particular, then, when both are affirmative, or when the universal is negative and the particular affirmative, the mode of the syllogisms will be the same. For all are completed through the first figure. It is therefore clear that the syllogism will concern possibility, not inherence.

If the universal proposition is affirmative and the particular negative, the demonstration proceeds by impossibility. Let *B* inhere in every *C*, while *A* possibly fails to inhere in some *C*. Therefore *A* must possibly fail to inhere in some *B*. For if *A* necessarily inheres in every *B*, while *B* has been posited as inhering in every *C*, then *A* will necessarily inhere in every *C*. This was shown earlier, but it had been posited that *A* possibly fails to inhere in some *C*.

When both propositions are indefinite or particular, there will be no syllogism; the demonstration is the same as in the universal cases and uses the same terms.

## CHAPTER XXI. The Mixture of the Necessary and the Possible in the Third Figure
If one of the propositions is necessary and the other contingent, then, if the terms are affirmative, there will always be a syllogism concerning contingency. When one term is affirmative and the other privative, if the necessary proposition is affirmative, the conclusion will concern contingent non-inherence; but if it is privative, the conclusion will concern both contingent non-inherence and non-inherence. There will not be a syllogism concerning necessary non-inherence, just as in the other figures.

Let the terms first be affirmative. Suppose that *a* necessarily inheres in every *c*, while *b* contingently inheres in every *c*. Since *a* necessarily inheres in every *c*, and *c* contingently belongs to some *b*, *a* will contingently inhere in, and fail to inhere in, some *b*; for this is the way it occurs in the first figure. The same will be shown if *b* is posited as necessary with respect to *c*, and *a* as contingent with respect to *c*.

Again, let one term be affirmative and the other privative, and let the affirmative term be necessary. Suppose that *a* contingently inheres in no *c*, while *b* necessarily inheres in every *c*. Here again the first figure results, and the conclusion is contingent non-inherence, since a privative proposition concerning contingency signifies non-inherence. It is therefore clear that the conclusion will be contingent; for when the propositions stood thus in the first figure, the conclusion was contingent.

But if the privative proposition is necessary, the conclusion will likewise concern both contingent non-inherence and non-inherence. Suppose that *a* necessarily does not inhere in *c*, while *b* contingently inheres in every *c*. On converting the affirmative proposition *b–c*, the first figure results, with a necessary privative proposition. When the propositions stood thus, it followed that *a* contingently does not inhere in some *c*, and also does not inhere in it; consequently, *a* must not inhere in some *b*.

When the privative proposition is placed with the minor extreme, if it is contingent, there will be a syllogism by converting the proposition, just as in the preceding cases. But if it is necessary, there will be none. For it is necessary that contingency should inhere both in every case and in no case.

Terms for inhering in every case: sleep, horse, sleeping man.  
Terms for inhering in no case: sleep, horse, wakeful man.

The same will hold if one of the terms is universal and the other particular with respect to the middle term. For if both are affirmative, the syllogism will concern contingency, not necessary inherence. When one proposition is privative and the other affirmative, if the affirmative proposition is necessary, the conclusion will concern contingency. But if the privative proposition is necessary, the conclusion will concern non-inherence, since the demonstration will proceed in the same way whether the terms are universal or not universal. The syllogisms must necessarily be completed through the first figure; consequently, what occurs in those cases must occur here as well.

When the privative proposition taken universally is placed with the minor extreme, if it is contingent, there will be a syllogism by conversion; but if it is necessary, there will be none. This will be shown in the same way and by the same terms as in the universal cases.

It is therefore clear in this figure also when and how there will be a syllogism, and when it will concern contingency and when it will concern inherence. It is also clear that all the syllogisms are imperfect and that they are completed through the first figure.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Demonstrative Syllogism

Since, then, the syllogisms belonging to these figures are completed through the universal syllogisms of the first figure and are reduced to them, this is clear from what has been said. That every syllogism without qualification is formed in this way will now become clear, once it has been shown that every syllogism that occurs is formed through one of these figures.

Every demonstration and every syllogism must therefore show either that something inheres or that it does not inhere. This may be shown universally or particularly, and either demonstratively or hypothetically. Of hypothetical argument, argument by impossibility is one part.

We shall first speak of demonstrative syllogisms. Once these have been shown, what concerns arguments by impossibility, and hypothetical arguments in general, will also be clear. If, then, it is necessary to syllogize that *a* inheres in or does not inhere in *b*, it is necessary to take something of something.

If *a* is predicated of *b*, the conclusion will have been assumed from the beginning. If *a* is predicated of *c*, while *c* is predicated of nothing else, nothing else is predicated of *c*, nothing other than *a* is predicated of *a*, and nothing else is predicated of *a*, there will be no syllogism. For when one thing is predicated of one thing, nothing follows necessarily. Hence another proposition must be assumed.

If *a* is predicated of something else, or something else of *a*, or something else of *c*, there is nothing to prevent there being a syllogism; but it will not be a syllogism concerning *b* from the propositions assumed. Nor, when *c* inheres in something else, and that in another, and this in something further, will there be a syllogism concerning *b* and *a* if the chain is not connected with *b*.

In general, we say that there can never be a syllogism concerning one thing and another unless some middle term is assumed that is related to both in some way through predication. A syllogism without qualification is formed from propositions; a syllogism concerning a particular subject is formed from propositions relating to that subject; and a syllogism concerning one subject in relation to another is formed from propositions relating those subjects. It is impossible to assume a proposition concerning *b* without either predicating or denying something of it, or, again, concerning *a* in relation to *b*, without assuming something common to both while predicating or denying something distinctive of each. Therefore something must be assumed that connects the predicates of both, if there is to be a syllogism concerning one subject in relation to another.

If something common to both must necessarily be assumed, this can happen in three ways: either *a* is predicated of *c* and of *b*; or *c* is predicated of both; or both are predicated of *c*. These are the three figures already described.

It is therefore clear that every syllogism must be formed through one of these figures. The same account applies even if the connection with *b* is made through several terms, for the figure remains the same in the case of several terms.

Since demonstrative syllogisms are concluded through the figures mentioned above, this is clear.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Hypothetical Syllogism

That the syllogisms leading to impossibility are also formed through these figures will be clear from the following. For all who conclude by impossibility syllogize something false. What was assumed from the beginning, however, they demonstrate hypothetically, when something impossible follows from positing the contradictory—for example, that the diagonal is incommensurable, because, on supposing it commensurable, odd numbers become equal to even numbers.

Thus they syllogize that odd numbers become equal to even numbers, but they demonstrate hypothetically that the diagonal is incommensurable, because a falsehood follows from the contradictory supposition. This is what it means to syllogize by impossibility: to show that something impossible follows because of the prior hypothesis.

Since, then, the demonstrative syllogism in arguments leading to impossibility is false, while what was assumed from the beginning is demonstrated hypothetically—and since we previously said that demonstrative syllogisms are concluded through these figures—it is clear that syllogisms by impossibility will also be formed through these figures.

The same applies to all other hypothetical syllogisms. In all of them a syllogism is formed concerning the substituted proposition, while what was assumed from the beginning is concluded either through an admission or through some other hypothesis.

If this is true, every demonstration and every syllogism must be formed through the three figures mentioned above. Once this has been shown, it is clear that every syllogism is completed through the first figure and reduced to its universal syllogisms.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Quality and Quantity of the Terms of a Syllogism

Further, in every syllogism at least one of the terms must be predicative and universal. Without a universal proposition there will be no syllogism, or it will not concern the proposed conclusion, but will beg what was assumed from the beginning.

Suppose, for example, that musical pleasure is choiceworthy. If one were to ask whether enjoyment is good without adding “every,” there would be no syllogism. If one were to ask whether some enjoyment is good, then, if it were a different enjoyment, the conclusion would not concern the proposed subject; but if it were the same, one would be assuming what was originally at issue.

This becomes even clearer in the figures. Suppose, for example, that the angles at the base of an isosceles triangle are equal. Let the lines *a–b* be drawn to the center. If one assumes that the angle *a–c* is equal to the angle *b–d*, without generally asking that the angles belonging to the semicircles be equal, and again that *c* is equal to *d*, without assuming the whole angle belonging to the segment, one will be begging the question.

Further, given that whole angles are equal, if equal angles are subtracted, the remaining angles—namely *e* and *f*—will be equal. But unless one assumes that from all equal angles, after equal angles have been subtracted, equal angles remain, one will again be begging the question.

It is therefore clear that every syllogism must contain a universal proposition. A universal proposition is shown through all the universal terms, while a particular proposition may be shown in this way or in another. Hence, if the conclusion is universal, the terms must also be universal; but if the terms are universal, the conclusion may nevertheless not be universal.

It is also clear that in every syllogism either both propositions or one of them must be similar to the conclusion. By “similar” I mean not merely that it is affirmative or negative, but also that it is necessary, inherential, or contingent. The other categories must also be considered.

It is clear in general when there will and will not be a syllogism, when it will be perfect, and that, if there is a syllogism, its terms must be arranged according to one of the modes described.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Number of Terms in a Syllogism

It is also clear that every demonstration will proceed through three terms, and not through more, unless the same conclusion is reached by different means—for example, *e* through *a* and *b*, and through *c* and *d*; or through *a* and *b*, and through *a* and *c*, and through *b* and *c*. There may be several middle terms for the same conclusion, but when this happens there are not one but several syllogisms.

Or again, both *a* and *b* may be established through syllogisms: *a* through *d* and *e*, and *b* through *f* and *g*; or one may be established by induction and the other by syllogism. If there are several syllogisms, there are also several conclusions, such as *a*, *b*, and *c*.

If, then, there are not several syllogisms but only one—and this cannot occur by means of several middle terms yielding the same conclusion, such as *e* through *a*, *b*, *c*, and *d*—the supposition is impossible.

Let *e* be the conclusion from *a*, *b*, *c*, and *d*. Then one of these terms must have been assumed in relation to another, one as a whole and the other as a part; for this was shown earlier, namely, that if there is a syllogism, some of the terms must stand in this relation.

Let *a* stand to *b* in this way. There will therefore be some conclusion from them: either *e*, or one of *c* and *d*, or something else besides these. If it is *e*, there will be a syllogism from *a* and *b* alone. Suppose that *c* and *d* are related in such a way that one is known and the other a part. There will then be some conclusion from them: either *e*, or one of *a* and *b*, or something else besides these.

If it is *e*, or one of *a* and *b*, there will be several syllogisms; alternatively, as sometimes happens, the same conclusion will have been reached through several terms. If the conclusion is something else besides these, there will be several syllogisms unconnected with one another.

But if *c* and *d* are not related in such a way as to produce a syllogism, they will have been assumed pointlessly, unless for the sake of induction, concealment, or some other purpose of that kind.

If the conclusion from *a* and *b* is not *e* but something else, and the conclusion from *c* and *d* is either one of these or something else besides them, there will be several syllogisms, and not a syllogism concerning the proposed conclusion. For the syllogism was supposed to concern *e*.

If no conclusion follows from *c* and *d*, their assumption will have been pointless, and there will not be a syllogism concerning what was assumed from the beginning.

It is therefore clear that every demonstration and every syllogism will proceed through three terms alone.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Number of Propositions and on Pros yllogisms

Once this has been made clear, it is evident that a syllogism proceeds from two propositions and not from more, for three terms yield two propositions—unless something is assumed, as was said earlier, for the completion of the syllogisms.

It is therefore clear that when, as in a syllogistic argument, the propositions through which the principal conclusion is reached are not equal in number—for some of the higher conclusions must themselves be propositions—the argument is either not syllogistic or has asked more questions than are necessary for the position.

When syllogisms are counted according to the principal propositions, every syllogism will consist of complete propositions but an excess of terms: there will be one more term than propositions, while the conclusions will be half as numerous as the propositions.

When the conclusion is reached through pros yllogisms, or through several non-contiguous middle terms—for example, *a–b* through *c–d*—the number of terms will likewise exceed the number of propositions by one. For either an external term is added, or an intervening middle term is placed between them. In either case, the intervals are one fewer than the terms, while the propositions equal the intervals.

The propositions, however, will not always be perfect while the terms are in excess; the reverse may also occur. When the propositions are perfect, the terms will be in excess; when the terms are perfect, the propositions will be in excess. For whenever a term is added, one proposition is added with it, no matter where the term is added.

Since, then, in one arrangement the propositions were perfect and the terms excessive, the same relation must be reversed when an addition is made.

The conclusions will not have the same numerical relation either to the terms or to the propositions. When one term is added, one conclusion is also added, and there will be one fewer conclusion than terms already present, since no conclusion is formed concerning the final term alone, but one is formed concerning every other term.

For example, if *d* is added to *a*, *b*, and *c*, two conclusions immediately arise, one concerning *a* and one concerning *b*. The same applies in other cases. If a term is inserted in the middle, the situation is the same: it will not produce a syllogism concerning one term alone. Consequently, there will be many more conclusions than terms or propositions.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Problems—That Is, on the Ease and Difficulty of Constructing and Refuting Propositions in Each Figure

Since we know from what syllogisms are formed, what each figure is like, and in how many ways each is demonstrated, it is clear to us which propositions are easy and which are difficult to establish. For a proposition that can be concluded in more figures and through more cases is easy; one that can be concluded in fewer figures and through fewer cases is more difficult to establish.

A universal affirmative is demonstrated only through the first figure, and through that figure only in one way. A privative proposition is demonstrated both through the first and through the middle figure: through the first simply, and through the middle in two ways.

A particular affirmative is demonstrated through the first and the last figure: simply through the first, and in three ways through the last. A particular privative is demonstrated in all the figures—once in the first, twice in the middle, and three times in the last.

It is therefore clear that a universal affirmative is the most difficult to construct but the easiest to refute. In general, universal propositions are easier to refute than particular ones. For if it is shown that something inheres in no case, or does not inhere in some case, the original universal affirmative has been refuted; of these, “does not inhere in some case” is not demonstrated in all the figures, while “inheres in no case” is demonstrated in two.

The same applies to privative propositions: if a proposition says that something inheres in every case, or that it inheres in some case, the original position has been refuted. This occurred in two figures.

With particular propositions, the situation is simpler: one demonstrates that something inheres either universally or nowhere.

For construction, however, particular propositions are easier, since they are demonstrated in more figures and through more modes. In general, it must not escape our notice that refutation works reciprocally: universals are refuted by particulars, and particulars by universals. But construction does not proceed from particulars to universals; rather, particulars are constructed from universals. For example, if something inheres in every case, it follows that it inheres in some case.

At the same time, it is clear that refutation is easier than construction. How every syllogism is formed, through how many terms and propositions, how these stand in relation to one another, which proposition is demonstrated in each figure and which in several figures or in fewer figures—all this is clear from what has been said.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Abundance of Propositions

How we shall always be able to syllogize concerning the proposed subject, and by what route we shall obtain the principles relevant to each matter, must now be discussed. It is perhaps not enough merely to consider the generation of syllogisms; one must also possess the ability to produce them.

Of all existing things, some are such that they are not truly predicated universally of anything else—for example, Cleon, Callias, and whatever is individual and perceptible. Other things are predicated of these; for both “man” and “animal” are predicated of them.

Other things are themselves predicated of other things, while nothing else is previously predicated of them; still others are predicated of other things and have other things predicated of them—for example, “man” is predicated of Callias, and “animal” of man.

Since some existing things cannot be said of anything else, this is clear. Nearly every perceptible thing is of this sort, so that it is predicated of nothing else, except accidentally. For sometimes we say that “white” belongs to Socrates, or that “this person” is Callias.

Since, however, in ascending we sometimes reach a stopping point, we shall discuss this again. For the present let this be assumed: it is not possible to demonstrate of such things except according to opinion. But these things are predicated of others, whereas singular things are not predicated of others; rather, other things are predicated of them.

It is clear that what lies between these extremes admits of both relations. Such things are predicated of others, and others are predicated of them; and almost all definitions and investigations are concerned chiefly with them.

With respect to each such thing, propositions should therefore be collected in the following way. First, collect the thing itself, its definitions, and whatever belongs properly to it; then collect whatever follows the thing. Again, collect what the thing follows, whatever cannot inhere in it, and the things in which it cannot inhere; but the last are not to be taken, since the privative proposition is convertible.

The consequences must also be divided: those predicated in the account of what the thing is, those predicated as proper attributes, and those predicated as accidents; and among the latter, those that hold according to opinion and those that hold according to truth.

The more numerous such propositions one possesses, the more quickly one will find a conclusion; the more truthful they are, the more one will demonstrate.

One must choose not merely what follows some individual, but what follows the whole thing—for example, not what follows some man, but what follows every man, since syllogism proceeds through universal propositions.

When the subject is indefinite, it is uncertain whether the proposition is universal; when it is definite, this is clear. The same method must be followed in selecting what follows the whole subject, for the reason given.

One must not take the consequence as following wholly in the converse sense. I mean that “every animal” does not follow “every man,” nor “every discipline” follow “music”; rather, one should take only the simple consequence, as we have indicated. The converse is both useless and impossible—for example, that every man is every animal, or that justice is every good. Rather, of that which has the consequence, it is said that the whole of the consequence is in it.

When the subject is contained under another subject, whose consequences we must collect, we should not select in the contained subject what follows, or does not follow, the universal. For these have already been taken in the higher subjects: what follows animal and man, and what does not inhere in animal, are treated similarly.

What is proper to each subject must be selected. For some properties belong to a species in addition to the genus; different species must necessarily have certain properties of their own.

Nor should one select as universal those consequences that follow the contained subject—for example, animal among the things that follow man. For if animal follows man, all these consequences must also follow; but such consequences are more suitable for selecting what belongs to man.

One must also select what usually follows the things that follow. For in problems, what usually occurs is relevant, and a syllogism proceeds from propositions that hold either usually, universally, or in some cases; the conclusion is similar to the principles of each thing.

Further, one should not select what follows everything. No syllogism will arise from such propositions, and the reason will become clear in what follows.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Rules for Finding the Middle Terms of Syllogisms

Those who wish to construct a proposition universally about one thing must examine, concerning the thing to be constructed, the subjects of which it is predicated; and, concerning the subject of which it must be predicated, whatever follows that subject.

If some one of these is identical with another, the one must inhere in the other. If the desired conclusion is not universal but particular, one must look for what follows both; for if some one of these is identical, it must inhere in some case.

When the conclusion must be that something inheres in no case, one must examine, concerning the subject in which it must not inhere, what follows that subject; and, concerning what must not inhere, what cannot inhere in it.

Alternatively, concerning what must not inhere, one may examine what cannot inhere in the same subject, and, concerning what does not inhere, what follows it. For if these are identical in both cases, it is impossible for one thing to inhere in the other in any case. Sometimes this produces a syllogism in the first figure, sometimes in the middle.

If the conclusion is that something does not inhere in some case, then, concerning what must not inhere, one must examine what follows it; and, concerning what does not inhere, what cannot possibly inhere in it. If some one of these is identical, it must not inhere in some case.

The matter will perhaps become clearer in the following form. Let *a* be the things that follow the subject, among which is *b*; let *c* be the things that follow the subject itself; let *d* be the things that cannot inhere in it. Again, let *e* be the subject itself; let *f* be the things that inhere in it; let *g* be the things that follow it; and let *h* be the things that cannot inhere in it.

If one of the things designated by *c* is identical with one of the things designated by *f*, then *a* must inhere in every *e*. For *f* inheres in every *e*, and *c* in every *a*; therefore *a* inheres in every *e*.

If *c* and *g* are identical, then *a* must inhere in some *e*. For the common term follows both *a* and *e*.

If *f* and *d* are identical, *a* will inhere in no *e* by a proper syllogism. Since the privative proposition is convertible, and *f* is identical with *d*, *a* inheres in no *f*; but *f* inheres in every *e*.

Again, if *b* and *h* are identical, *a* will inhere in no *e*. For *b* inheres in every *a*, but in the subject in which *e* occurs it inheres in no case. *b* was identical with *h*, and *h* inhered in no *e*.

If *g* and *d* are identical, *a* will not inhere in some *e*. For *a* does not inhere in what is *g*, since it does not inhere in *d*; and *g* is subordinate to *e*. Therefore *a* does not inhere in some *e*.

If *g* and *b* are identical, the syllogism will be converted. For *g* follows every *a*: *b* follows *a*, and *e* follows *b*, while *g* was identical with *b* and *a* follows *e*. It is not necessary that *a* inhere universally, but it must inhere in some case, because the universal affirmative is converted into a particular affirmative.

It is therefore clear that in every inquiry one must examine both sides in relation to the propositions mentioned, since all syllogisms arise through these.

One must also examine the things that follow and the things followed by each individual in relation to the primary and universal subjects. Thus *e* should be considered more in relation to *k–f* than to *f* alone, and *a* more in relation to *k–c* than to *c* alone. For if *a* inheres in *k–f*, and *e* inheres in *f*, then it also inheres in *e*. If *a* does not follow this, however, it is possible that *f* follows it.

The same must be considered among things that are identical. For if a consequence follows the primary subjects, it also follows the things subordinate to them; but if it does not follow the primary subjects, it may nevertheless follow the things subordinate to them.

It is clear that the inquiry proceeds through three terms and two propositions, and that all syllogisms are displayed through the figures mentioned. The conclusion that *a* inheres in every *e* is shown when something common to *c* and *f* is assumed; this is the middle term, while *a* and *e* are the extremes, and the result is the first figure.

The conclusion that *a* inheres in some *e* is shown when something common to *c* and *g* is assumed; this belongs to the last figure, with *g* as the middle term.

The conclusion that *a* inheres in no *e* is shown when *d* and *f* are identical. This may occur in the first or the middle figure: in the first, because *a* inheres in no *f*, given the convertibility of the privative proposition, while *f* inheres in every *e*; in the middle, because *a* inheres in no *d*, while *e* inheres in every *d*.

The conclusion that *a* does not inhere in some *e* is shown when *d* and *g* are identical. This belongs to the last figure, since *a* inheres in no *g*, while *e* inheres in every *g*.

It is therefore clear that all syllogisms are formed through the figures mentioned.

Nor should one select whatever follows everything, since no syllogism arises from such propositions. Construction does not proceed simply from consequences; and privation cannot be established through what follows everything. One thing must inhere in the one subject, and another must not inhere in the other.

It is also clear that other forms of inquiry based on selection are useless for producing a syllogism—for example, when the things that follow both subjects are identical, or when what follows *a* is identical with what cannot inhere in *e*, or when the things that cannot inhere in either subject are identical. No syllogism arises through these.

If the things that follow are identical—for example, *b* and *f*—the middle figure results, with both propositions affirmative. If what follows *a* is identical with what cannot inhere in *e*—for example, *c* and *h*—the first figure results, with a privative proposition attached to the minor extreme. If the things that cannot inhere in either subject are identical—for example, *d* and *h*—both propositions will be privative, either in the first figure or in the middle; in neither way will there be a syllogism.

It is also clear that one must select identical things according to the inquiry, not things that are different or contrary. First, the examination is undertaken for the sake of the middle term, and the middle term must be identical, not different. Second, when a syllogism happens to arise from contrary things, or from things that cannot inhere in the same subject, these cases are all reducible to the modes already stated.

For example, if *b* and *f* are contrary or cannot inhere in the same subject, a syllogism will result when they are assumed, namely, that *a* inheres in no *e*. But this does not arise from those terms themselves; it arises from the mode already described. For *b* inheres in every *a*, while *b* inheres in no *e*; therefore *b* must be identical with some one of the things designated by *h*.

Again, if *b* and *g* cannot belong to the same subject, it will follow that *a* does not inhere in some *e*. This is also a middle-figure case: *b* inheres in every *a*, while *g* inheres in no *b*. Therefore *g* must be identical with some one of the things designated by *d*. For the inability of *g* and *b* to inhere in the same subject makes no difference from the case in which *g* is identical with some *d*, since everything that cannot inhere in *a* has been included among the *d*.

It is therefore clear that no syllogism arises from these forms of inspection; and even if *b* and *f* are contrary, the syllogism is always produced by making *b* identical with some *h*. Thus those who investigate in this way are led to consider another necessary route, since the identity of *b* and *h* sometimes remains hidden.

## CHAPTER XXX. Assertoric Syllogisms Leading to Impossibility and Other Hypothetical Syllogisms

Syllogisms leading to impossibility stand in the same relation to demonstrative syllogisms. They too are formed through what follows and through what is followed by both subjects. The same inquiry applies in both cases: what is demonstrated demonstratively can also be syllogized by impossibility, and the same terms are used for both; likewise, what is demonstrated by impossibility can also be demonstrated directly.

For example, suppose that *a* inheres in no *e*. If one assumes that it inheres in some case, then, since *b* inheres in every *a* and *a* in some *e*, *b* will inhere in some *e*, although it inheres in no case.

Again, suppose that *a* inheres in some *e*. If *a* inheres in no *e*, while *e* inheres in every *g*, then *a* will inhere in no *g*, although it inheres in every case.

The same applies to the other propositions. In all cases, a demonstrative argument by impossibility will arise from what follows and from what is followed by both subjects.

For each proposition, the same inquiry is available both to one who wishes to syllogize demonstratively and to one who wishes to lead the argument to impossibility, since both demonstrations use the same terms. For example, if it has been demonstrated that *a* inheres in no *e*, and it happens that *b* inheres in some *e*, that is impossible. If *e* is assumed to inhere in no *b*, while *a* inheres in every *b*, it is clear that *a* inheres in no *e*.

Again, if it has been demonstrated directly that *a* inheres in no *e*, then, by assuming that it does inhere, one will demonstrate by impossibility that it inheres in no case. The same applies in the other cases.

In all arguments by impossibility, it is necessary to assume some common term other than the subjects, with respect to which the false syllogism will arise. When the proposition is converted, while the other remains similarly arranged, there will be a demonstrative syllogism using the same terms.

The demonstrative syllogism differs from the syllogism leading to impossibility in this respect: in the demonstrative syllogism both propositions are posited as true, whereas in the syllogism leading to impossibility one proposition is false. This will become clearer in what follows, when we discuss impossibility. For the present, it is enough that we understand that the same examination applies both to those who wish to syllogize demonstratively and to those who wish to lead the argument to impossibility.

In the other hypothetical syllogisms—those formed through substitution, or according to the quality of the subjects rather than according to the original subjects—the inquiry concerns the substituted subjects, not the original ones; but the method of inspection is the same. One must also consider and divide the various kinds of hypothetical syllogism. Each of the propositions mentioned is demonstrated in this way.

There is also another way of syllogizing some of these, namely, to establish universals hypothetically through particular inspection. If *c* and *g* are identical, and only *g* is assumed to inhere in *e*, then *a* will inhere in every *e*. Again, if *g* and *d* are identical, and *e* is predicated only of *g*, then *a* will inhere in no *e*. It is therefore clear that the inquiry must proceed in this way.

The same holds for necessary and contingent propositions. The inquiry is the same and proceeds through the same terms, and in the same order there will be a syllogism concerning contingency and inherence. In contingent cases one must also take what does not inhere but could inhere. For it has been shown that a syllogism concerning contingency is formed through these as well.

The same arrangement applies to the other forms of predication.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That the Syllogisms of All the Sciences Are Produced by the Preceding Rules

It is therefore clear from what has been said not only that all syllogisms can be formed by this method, but also that they cannot be formed by any other. Every syllogism has been shown to be formed through one of the figures mentioned; and these figures cannot be constituted in any other way than through what follows and what follows from each thing. The propositions and the assumption of the middle term arise from these. Hence it is impossible for a syllogism to be formed through anything else.

The method is therefore the same for everything, both in philosophy and in every particular discipline. One must collect, concerning each subject, what inheres and in what it inheres, and possess as many such propositions as possible. One must then examine the matter through three terms, refuting in one way and constructing in another.

For demonstrations according to truth, one must use what inheres according to the truths written about the subject; for dialectical syllogisms, one must use propositions that accord with opinion.

The principles of syllogisms have been stated universally, along with how they are arranged and how one must investigate them, so that we do not attend to everything that is said; so that we do not construct and refute the same propositions indiscriminately; and so that we do not construct universally or particularly, nor refute from all or from some, but attend to fewer and more determinate propositions.

In each individual case one must select what is relevant—for example, what concerns the good or a discipline. The proper propositions belonging to each subject are numerous. The principles concerning each subject therefore grow through experience. By this I mean, for example, that astronomical experience belongs to the astronomical discipline. Once the relevant appearances have been sufficiently collected, astronomical demonstrations were discovered in this way.

The same applies to every other art and discipline. Thus, if what inheres in each subject is collected, it will then be our task to set out the demonstrations readily. For if nothing is omitted from the historical record of what subtly and truly belongs to things, we shall be able to discover and demonstrate the relevant proposition concerning every subject for which demonstration is possible, and to make clear the case of what is not by nature demonstrable.

In general, then, we have almost stated how propositions should be selected. We have pursued the matter carefully in the work concerning dialectic.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Division and Its Syllogism
Because division by genera is a small part of the method just mentioned, it is easy to see that it is a kind of weak syllogism. For division asks for what must be demonstrated, but always syllogizes something superior.

At first this escaped all who used division. They tried to persuade themselves that it was possible to demonstrate substance and what a thing is. Hence they neither understood that those who divide were syllogizing, nor that they were syllogizing in the manner we have described.

[Col. 0674D] In demonstrations, whenever something must be syllogized, the middle term through which the syllogism is produced must always be less extensive, and not universal with respect to the first extreme. Division, however, aims at the contrary, since it takes a more universal middle term.

Let animal be that in which *a* is contained, mortal that in which *b* is contained, and immortal that in which *c* is contained; let human being be that whose term must be taken, namely *d*. The divider therefore takes every animal to be either mortal or immortal. But this means that everything is either *b* or *c*. Again, whoever divides always posits that human being is animal; thus, concerning *d*, he assumes that it is *a*. The syllogism therefore is that *d* as a whole will be either *b* or *c*. Hence one must take human being to be either mortal or immortal. For it is necessary that animal be either mortal or immortal; but that it is mortal is not necessary—it is merely assumed. Yet this was precisely what had to be syllogized.

[Col. 0675A] Again, whoever posits that *a* is mortal animal, *b* is footed, and *c* is footless, and human being is *d*, likewise takes *a* to be either *b* or *c*. For every mortal animal is either footed or footless. Concerning *d*, however, he assumes *a*, since he has taken human being to be mortal animal. Therefore it is necessary that human being be either footed or footless; but that it is footed is not necessary—it is merely assumed. Yet this, again, was what had to be demonstrated.

[Col. 0675B] In this manner, then, whenever they divide, they always take as middle a universal term concerning which the differences and the extremes are to be demonstrated. At the end, however, when they say that this is human being—or whatever it is that is being sought—they have demonstrated nothing. Thus the conclusion is necessary only because they have taken another route altogether: they do not establish the relevant possibilities, but assume them.

It is clear, moreover, that by this method one can neither refute anything nor syllogize anything accidental, proper, or generic, nor anything whose condition is uncertain in one way or another. Consider, for example, the question whether the diameter is commensurable or incommensurable. If one assumes that every length is either commensurable or incommensurable, and that the diameter is a length, it has been syllogized that the diameter is commensurable or incommensurable. But if incommensurability is assumed—the very thing that had to be syllogized—then there is no demonstration.

[Col. 0675C] The method is indeed this: let *a* be length, and let *b* be commensurable or incommensurable, while the diameter is *c*. But by this method one does not demonstrate that the diameter is commensurable or incommensurable.

It is therefore clear that this method of inquiry is not suitable for every investigation, and that even in the cases where it seems most appropriate it is not useful. From what has been said, it is clear both from what demonstrations are produced, how they are produced, and what must be examined in relation to each particular proposition.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Resolution of Syllogisms into Propositions

[Col. 0675D]

How we are to reduce syllogisms to the figures mentioned above must now be explained. This consideration remains, for if we examine both the generation of syllogisms and our ability to discover them, and in addition reduce completed syllogisms to the figures mentioned above, the purpose proposed at the beginning will be fulfilled. At the same time, what was stated earlier will be confirmed and made clearer, since matters stand as will be shown in what follows.

Everything that is true must, in every respect, be evident in itself.

[Col. 0676A] First, then, one should try to identify the two propositions of a syllogism, since it is easier to divide something greater into larger parts than into smaller ones; and larger parts are more composite than the things from which they are composed. Next, one should consider which proposition is universal and which particular. If both have not been taken, one should take the proposition that posits the other [the transmitted wording is elliptical]. For sometimes, in extending a universal proposition, people do not take the proposition contained in it, neither writing it down nor asking it. At other times they state the propositions through which the conclusion follows, but omit the propositions by which those propositions themselves are concluded, while asking some other question pointlessly.

One must therefore consider whether anything superfluous has been assumed or anything necessary omitted. The former must be removed and the latter supplied, until one arrives at two propositions; without two propositions it is impossible to reduce arguments in this way.

[Col. 0676B] In some cases it is easy to see what is missing, while in others it goes unnoticed. People seem to syllogize because something necessary follows from what has been posited.
