For example, suppose it is assumed that when substance has not been destroyed, substance is not destroyed, and that when the things from which substance is composed have been destroyed, what is composed of them is also destroyed. From these assumptions it is necessary that a part of substance be substance. Yet what has been assumed has not been syllogized; propositions are missing.

Again, if, when human being exists, it is necessary that animal exists, and when animal exists, substance exists, and when human being exists, substance exists necessarily, the conclusion has still not been syllogized. The propositions do not stand as we have said.

We are deceived in such cases because something necessary follows from the assumptions, and a syllogism is also necessary. But necessity extends further than syllogism: every syllogism is necessary, but not everything necessary is a syllogism. Therefore, if something follows necessarily from certain assumptions, one must not immediately try to reduce it. First one must identify the two propositions.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Resolution into Terms

[Col. 0676C]

Next one must divide the argument in this way into terms. The middle term must be established as the term spoken of in both propositions, for in every figure the middle term must occur in both.

If the middle term is both subject and predicate—or if it is predicated while something else is denied of it—the figure is the first. If it is both predicated and denied of something, the figure is the middle one. If other things are predicated of it, or if one thing is predicated of it while another is denied of it, the figure is the last. For this is how the middle term stood in the last figure. The same determination of the middle applies even when the propositions are not universal.

It is therefore clear that where the same term is not repeatedly stated in an argument, there is no syllogism, since the middle term has not been taken.

[Col. 0676D] Since we know what conclusions are contained in each figure, and in which figure the conclusion is universal or particular, it is clear that one must not examine every proposition in every figure, but must examine each proposition in its proper figure. Whatever conclusions are contained in several figures, we recognize the figure by the position of the middle term.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Necessity and the Position of Terms

[Col. 0677A]

It often happens, as was said earlier, that people are deceived about syllogisms because of necessity. Sometimes they are deceived because of the similarity in the arrangement of the terms, and this must not escape our notice.

For example, if *a* is predicated of *b*, and *b* of *c*, it will seem that, when the terms are arranged in this way, there is a syllogism. But there is neither anything necessary nor a syllogism.

Let *a* be “always to be,” *b* “intelligible Aristomenes,” and *c* Aristomenes. It is true that *a* is present in *b*, for intelligible Aristomenes always is; and *b* is predicated of *c*, for Aristomenes is intelligible Aristomenes. But *a* is not present in *c*, for Aristomenes is corruptible. Thus there was no syllogism with the terms arranged in this way. The proposition should instead have taken *a* universally of *b*. But the assumption that every intelligible Aristomenes always exists is false, since Aristomenes is corruptible.

Again, let *c* be Micalus, *b* be musical Micalus, and *a* be “will perish tomorrow.” It is true that *b* is predicated of *c*, for Micalus is musical Micalus. It is also true that *a* is predicated of *b*, for musical Micalus will perish tomorrow. But *a* is falsely predicated of *c*. This is the same as in the preceding case: it is not universally true that musical Micalus will perish tomorrow. Since this was not taken universally, there was no syllogism.

[Col. 0677B] This fallacy arises because we practically treat it as making no difference whether we say that this is present in that, or that this is present in everything of that kind.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Ecthesis of Terms

[Col. 0677C]

It often happens that an argument is false because the terms are not properly set out in accordance with the proposition.

Let *a* be health, *b* illness, and *c* human being. It is true to say that *a* can be present in no *b*, since health is present in no illness. Again, it is true to say that *b* is present in every *c*, since every human being is susceptible to illness. It will therefore seem to follow that health can be present in no human being.

The reason for this is that the terms have not been properly set out according to the expression. When the terms belonging to dispositions are substituted, there is no syllogism. Thus, if “healthy” is substituted for health and “ill” for illness, it is not true to say that being healthy can be present in someone who is ill. Since this has not been assumed, there is no syllogism—except a syllogism concerning what is possible. That, however, is not impossible, since health can be present in no human being.

The same falsehood will arise in the middle figure. Health can be present in no illness, but in every human being; hence it would seem to follow that illness is present in no human being.

[Col. 0677D] In the third figure, a falsehood arises concerning possibility. For health, illness, knowledge, ignorance, and, in general, contraries can all be present in one and the same thing, although it is impossible for them to be present in one another. This was acknowledged earlier. For when several things can be present in the same thing, they could also be present in one another.

It is therefore clear that in all these cases the fallacy arises from the setting out of the terms. Once the terms belonging to dispositions are substituted, nothing false follows. It is therefore evident that, in propositions of this kind, what belongs to a disposition must always be taken and posited as the disposition itself.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the Ecthesis of Composite and Oblique Terms in a Syllogism

[Col. 0678A]

One must not always seek terms that can be set out by a single name. Often there will be arguments in which no names are available for this purpose, and it will consequently be difficult to reduce such syllogisms. Sometimes, moreover, the attempt to find such terms will itself cause deception.

Suppose, for example, that *a* is “two right angles,” *b* is triangle, and *c* is isosceles. Then *a* belongs to *c* through *b*. But *a* does not belong to *b* through anything else, since a triangle possesses two right angles in itself. Thus *b* is not the middle term of *a* and *c*, although it is demonstrative.

It is clear, then, that the middle term must not always be taken as a single thing of this kind. Sometimes it must be taken as an expression, as also occurred in the example just given.

[Col. 0678B] When the first term is present in the middle, and the middle in the last, one must not assume that they are always predicated of one another in the same way—namely, the first of the middle and the middle of the last—and similarly with non-presence. Rather, whenever an expression means that something is the case and is truly said, one must take it as meaning that it is present.

For example, “the contraries have one science.” Let *a* be “there is one science,” and let *b* be contraries. Then *a* is present in *b*, not in the sense that the contraries have one science belonging to them as contraries, but because it is true to say of the contraries that there is one science of them.

Sometimes the first term is predicated of the middle, while the middle is not predicated of the third. For example, if wisdom is a science, and wisdom belongs to the good, the conclusion is that science belongs to the good. It is not that the good is a science, while wisdom is a science.

[Col. 0678C] Sometimes the middle is predicated of the third, while the first is not predicated of the middle. For example, if every science is a quality—or a contrary—and the good is both a contrary and a quality, the conclusion is that science belongs to the good. But the good is not a science, nor a quality, nor a contrary; rather, science belongs to all of them. The good is not a science, nor is the conclusion, in the direct sense, that it is a quality or contrary; rather, these belong to the good.

Sometimes neither the first is predicated of the middle nor the middle of the third, while the first is sometimes predicated of the third and sometimes not.

For example, if whatever has a science has a genus, and the good has a science, the conclusion is that the good has a genus. Yet no term is predicated of another. If whatever has a science has a genus, and the good has a science, the conclusion is that the good is a genus. Thus the first term is predicated of the extreme, but the terms are not predicated of one another.

[Col. 0678D] Non-presence must be taken in the same way. For “this is not present in that” does not always mean that this does not exist as that; sometimes it means that this is not that of which it is predicated, or that this is not present in that.

For example, there is no motion of a motion, nor generation of a generation; but there is [generation] of pleasure; therefore pleasure is not generation. Or again, laughter is a sign, but there is no sign of a sign; therefore there is no sign of laughter. The same applies in other cases where the intended conclusion is overturned because something is said in some way with reference to that genus.

Again, an opportunity is not an opportune time. Opportunity belongs to God, but an opportune time does not, since nothing contributes to God. The terms must therefore be taken as opportunity, opportune time, and God.

[Col. 0679A] The proposition must be taken according to the grammatical case of the name. In general, terms must always be established according to the declensions of names: “human being,” “good,” “contraries,” or “of a human being,” “of the good,” “of the contraries.”

Propositions, however, must be taken according to each case. One may say that something belongs to this, as equal; that it belongs to this, as double; that this is acting upon or seeing; that this is human being or animal; or that the name is inflected in any other way in accordance with the proposition.

The phrase “this belongs to that,” or “this is truly said of that,” must be taken as often as the predicates have been divided—whether in some particular way or simply, and whether the terms are simple or composite. The same applies to non-presence. These matters must be considered and determined in the best way.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Reduplication and Position of Syllogisms—that is, on Repetition and Position

[Col. 0679B]

A reduplicated expression in the propositions must be assigned to the first extreme, not to the middle. I mean, for example, that if the syllogism is “science belongs to justice because it is good,” the reduplication must be assigned to the first extreme.

Let *a* be “science because it is good,” let *b* be good, and let *c* be justice. It is true, then, that *a* is predicated of *b*, for science belongs to the good because it is good. It is also true that *b* is predicated of *c*, since justice is something good. Thus the resolution is achieved.

[Col. 0679C] If “because it is good” is assigned to *b*, however, the result will not follow. *a* will indeed be truly predicated of *b*, but *b* will not be truly predicated of *c*, since it is false and unintelligible to predicate “good because it is good” of justice.

The same applies if it is demonstrated that the healthy is teachable because it is good, or that the goat-stag is opinionable (*opinabilis*) because it exists, or that a human being is corruptible because it is perceptible. In every case the reduplication in the predicates must be assigned to the extreme.

The position of the terms is not the same when something is syllogized simply and when it is syllogized as something, in a certain respect, or in a certain manner. I mean, for example, the difference between demonstrating that the good is teachable and demonstrating that it is teachable insofar as it is good.

[Col. 0679D] When the teachable is demonstrated simply, the middle term must be “being”; but if it is demonstrated as teachable insofar as it is good, the middle term must be “a certain being.”

Let *a* be “science because it is a certain being,” *b* be “a certain being,” and *c* be good. It is true that *a* is predicated of *b*, for science is the science of some being, namely, of a certain being. It is also true that *b* is predicated of *c*, since *c* is a certain being. Therefore *a* is also predicated of *c*. Hence science belongs to the good because it is good. For “a certain being” is properly a mark of substance.

If, however, “being” is posited as the middle term, and “being” is stated simply of the extreme rather than “a certain being,” there will be no syllogism proving that science belongs to the good because it is good; it will prove only that science belongs to the good insofar as it is being. Let *a* be “science because it is being,” *b* be being, and *c* be good.

It is therefore clear that terms must be taken in this way in particular syllogisms.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Rules for Proper Resolution

[Col. 0680A]

One must take names that can substitute for names and expressions that can substitute for expressions. A name and an expression must each be taken in place of an expression whenever appropriate. This makes the setting out of the terms easier.

For example, it makes no difference whether one says that the *suspicabile* (“conjecturable”) is not a genus of the *opinabile* (“opinionable”), or that the *suspicabile* is not the same thing as the *opinabile*. For, if what is signified by the expression is the same, *suspicabile* and *opinabile* may be established as terms in place of the expression.

[Col. 0680B] But that pleasure is good is not the same as pleasure being what is good. The terms must therefore not be set out in the same way. If the syllogism is that pleasure is what is good, the term must be “what is good”; but if the syllogism is that pleasure is good, the term must be “good.” The same applies in other cases.

Nor is it the same to say, “to whatever *b* belongs, *a* also belongs universally,” and to say, “to whatever *b* belongs universally, *a* belongs universally.” For nothing prevents *b* from belonging to *c* without belonging to every instance of *c*.

Let *b* be something beautiful and *c* be white. If something beautiful belongs to some white thing, it is true to say that something beautiful belongs to the white; but it may not belong to every white thing.

Thus, if *a* belongs to *b* but not to everything of which *b* is predicated—whether *b* belongs to every *c* or only to some—then it is not necessary that *a* belong to *c*. This is not merely because it does not belong universally; it is not necessary that it belong to *c* at all.

[Col. 0680C] If *a* is truly predicated of everything of which *b* is predicated, then *a* will be predicated of everything of which *b* is predicated. But if *a* is predicated universally of everything of which *b* is predicated, nothing prevents *b* from belonging to *c* without *a* belonging universally to *c*, or without *a* belonging to *c* at all.

With three terms, then, it is clear that whatever *b* is predicated of universally, *a* is also predicated of universally. If *b* is predicated universally, so is *a*; but if *b* is not predicated universally, it is not necessary that *a* belong universally.

One must not suppose that any absurdity results from such an exposition. We are not concerned with whether something exists as an actual thing, but with the method by which we state the matter. A geometer, for example, speaks of a foot-long line and says that a line is straight and without breadth, although no such thing exists in this way. He does not use these assumptions as premises for syllogizing.

[Col. 0680D] In general, the demonstrator proves nothing from things that do not stand either as a whole to a part or as a part to a whole. We use exposition so that the learner may understand what is being said; we do not use it because demonstration would be impossible without such entities, in the way that a syllogism is impossible without its premises.

We must also not overlook the fact that, in the same syllogism, not all conclusions are established through one and the same figure. One conclusion may be established through one figure and another through another. It is therefore clear that resolutions must be carried out in the same way.

[Col. 0681A] Since not every proposition belongs to every figure, but propositions are arranged in each figure, it is clear that one must determine from the conclusion in which figure the proposition is to be sought.

In definitions of expressions, whenever an argument is directed toward one particular thing among those contained in a term, that thing toward which the argument is directed must be taken as the term, rather than the whole expression. This creates less confusion because of the length of the wording.

For example, if someone demonstrates that water is a moist drink, “drink” and “water” must be taken as the terms.

## CHAPTER XL. On the Resolution of Syllogisms to the Impossible and from Hypothesis

[Col. 0681A]

One must not try to reduce syllogisms from hypothesis, since they cannot be reduced from what has been posited. The assumptions have not been demonstrated syllogistically; they have all been granted by agreement.

Suppose someone posits that, if there is not one power of contraries, there is not one science of them either. He then argues that there is not one power of contraries, such as the power of making healthy and the power of making ill, since otherwise the same thing would simultaneously be healthy-making and illness-making.

[Col. 0681B] It has been demonstrated that there is not one power of all contraries; but it has not been demonstrated that there is not one science of them. Although this latter conclusion must be acknowledged, it is acknowledged not from a syllogism but from the hypothesis. This, then, is not a resolution of the conclusion that there is not one power, for that conclusion may have been syllogized, whereas the other was hypothetical.

The same applies to conclusions established through the impossible. This is not a resolution either. The reduction to the impossible is indeed established by a syllogism, but the other conclusion is not, since it follows from a hypothesis.

These differ from the preceding cases because in those one must first concede the hypothesis, if one is to grant the conclusion—for example, that if there is one power of contraries, there is also one science of them. In the present cases, however, people grant the conclusion without having first conceded it, because the falsehood is evident—for example, on positing the diameter as commensurable, since odd things are equal to even things [the transmitted wording is corrupt].

[Col. 0681C] Many and diverse terms are also determined from the condition, and these must be examined and properly noted. The differences among these cases, and the various ways in which they arise, will be discussed later. For the present, let it simply be clear to us that syllogisms of this kind cannot be reduced to the figures, and for what reason this is so.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the Reciprocal Reduction of Syllogisms from One Figure to Another

Whatever propositions are demonstrated in several figures can, if syllogized in one figure, have their syllogism reduced to another. Thus a negative syllogism in the first figure can be reduced to the second, and one in the middle figure to the first. Not all can be reduced, however, but only some; this will become clear in what follows.

If *a* belongs to no *b*, and *b* belongs to every *c*, then *a* belongs to no *c*. This is a syllogism in the first figure. If the negative proposition is converted, it becomes a syllogism in the middle figure, for *b* belongs to no *a*, while *c* belongs to every *a*.

The same applies when the syllogism is not universal but particular. If *a* belongs to no *b*, while *b* belongs to some *c*, then, by converting the negative proposition, the figure becomes the middle one.

Of the syllogisms in the second figure, universal syllogisms can be reduced to the first figure, but only one of the particular syllogisms can be so reduced.

[Col. 0681D] Let *a* belong to no *b*, and let *a* belong to every *c*. By converting the negative proposition, the result is the first figure: *b* belongs to no *a*, while *a* belongs to every *c*.

If the affirmative proposition is related to *b* and the negative proposition to *c*, *c* must be established as the first term. For *c* belongs to no *a*, while *a* belongs to every *b*. Therefore *c* belongs to no *b*, and hence *b* belongs to no *c*, since a negative proposition is convertible.

[Col. 0682A] If the syllogism is particular, then, when the negative proposition is related to the greater extreme, it can be reduced to the first figure. For example, if *a* belongs to no *b*, while *b* belongs to some *c*, then, by converting the negative proposition, the first figure results: *b* belongs to no *a*, while *a* belongs to some *c*.

When the affirmative proposition is particular, however, there is no reduction. If *a* belongs to every *b*, while *c* does not belong to every *b*, the proposition *a–b* does not admit the required conversion, and no syllogism results when it is converted.

Again, not all syllogisms in the third figure can be reduced to the first, whereas all those in the first can be reduced to the third.

Let *a* belong to every *b*, while *b* belongs to some *c*. Since the particular affirmative is convertible, *c* will belong to some *b*. Since *a* belonged to every *b*, a third-figure syllogism results.

[Col. 0682B] The same applies if the syllogism is negative. The particular affirmative is convertible, so if *a* belongs to no *b*, while *c* belongs to some *b*, the corresponding reduction follows.

Of the syllogisms in the last figure, only one is not reducible to the first: the case in which the negative proposition is not universal. All the others are reducible.

Let both *a* and *b* be predicated universally of *c*. Then *c* can be converted to each of them particularly. Thus *a* belongs to some *b*, and the first figure results: *a* belongs to every *c*, while *c* belongs to some *b*.

The same reasoning applies if *a* belongs to every *c* and *b* belongs to some *c*, since *c* is convertible with respect to *b*.

If *b* belongs to every *c*, while *a* belongs to some *c*, *b* must be established as the first term. For *b* belongs to every *c*, and *c* belongs to some *a*. Therefore *b* belongs to some *a*, and, since the particular affirmative is convertible, *a* will belong to some *b*.

[Col. 0682C] If the syllogism is negative with universal terms, the same procedure must be followed. Let *b* belong to every *c*, while *a* belongs to no *c*. Then *c* belongs to some *b*, while *a* belongs to no *c*; hence *c* is the middle term.

The same applies when the negative proposition is universal and the affirmative proposition particular: *a* belongs to no *c*, while *c* belongs to some *b*.

If the negative proposition is particular, there is no reduction. For example, if *b* belongs to every *c*, while *a* does not belong to some *c*, then, after converting *b–c*, both propositions become particular.

[Col. 0682D] It is clear that, in reducing figures to one another, the proposition related to the lesser extreme must be converted in both figures. Once it has been converted, the transition is made.

Of the syllogisms in the middle figure, one can be reduced to the third figure and one cannot. The one with a universal negative proposition can be reduced. If *a* belongs to no *b* but to some *c*, both propositions are converted with respect to *a*: *b* belongs to no *a*, while *c* belongs to some *a*. Thus *a* is the middle term.

When *a* belongs to every *b* but *c* does not belong to some *a*, there is no reduction, since neither proposition admits the required universal conversion.

Syllogisms in the third figure can be reduced to the middle when the negative proposition is universal. For example, if *a* belongs to no *c*, while *b* belongs to some or every *c*, then *c* belongs to no *a* and to some *b*.

If the negative proposition is particular, there is no reduction, since a particular negative proposition does not admit conversion.

[Col. 0683A] It is therefore clear that the same syllogisms cannot be reduced in these figures that could not be reduced to the first. It is also clear that, once syllogisms have been reduced to the first figure, these alone are closed by reduction to the impossible.

How syllogisms are to be reduced, and how the figures are reduced to one another, is clear from what has been said.

## CHAPTER XLII. On Infinite Syllogisms and the Rules of Consequence

In constructing or refuting an argument, it makes a difference whether one thinks that the expressions signify the same thing or different things: “not to be white” and “to be not-white,” for example. These do not signify the same thing. Nor is “to be not-white” the negation of “to be white”; the negation is “not to be white.”

[Col. 0683B] The reason is this. “It is possible to walk” stands to “it is possible not to walk” as “to be white” stands to “to be not-white,” and as “to know the good” stands to “to know not-good.” For “to know the good” does not differ from “to be knowing the good,” nor does “to be able to walk” differ from “to have the ability to walk.”

Consequently, their opposites—“not able to walk” and “able not to walk”—would likewise belong simultaneously to the same thing. For, if “not able to walk” signified the same as “able not to walk,” the same thing would at once be able both to walk and not to walk; likewise, the same thing would know both the good and the not-good. But affirmation and negation cannot belong simultaneously to the same thing.

[Col. 0683C] Thus “not to know the good” is not the same as “to know not-good,” nor is “to be not-good” the same as “not to be good.” In corresponding cases, if one is present, so is the other. Nor is “not to be equal” the same as “to be unequal.” The former has some underlying subject, namely the unequal; the latter has none, since not everything is equal or unequal, whereas everything is either equal or not equal.

Moreover, “there is a non-white piece of wood” and “there is no white piece of wood” do not hold simultaneously. If there is a non-white piece of wood, there is wood; but if there is no white piece of wood, it is not necessary that there be wood at all.

It is therefore clear that “to be not-good” is not the negation of “to be good.” If, of every one thing, either the affirmation or the negation is true, and the negation is not present, it is clear that the affirmation will be present in some way. Every affirmation has a negation, and in this case the negation is “it is not the case that there is not-good.”

[Col. 0683D] Let “to be good” be *a*, “not to be good” be *b*, “to be not-good” be *c* under *b*, and “not to be not-good” be *d* under *a*. Thus, of every thing, either *a* or *b* belongs to it, and not both to the same thing. Likewise, either *c* or *d* belongs to every thing, and not both to the same thing. Whatever *c* belongs to must necessarily have *b* belonging to it universally.

For if it is true to say that something is non-white, and true to say that it is not white, it is impossible for the same thing simultaneously to be white and non-white, or to be white wood and non-white wood. Therefore, if the affirmation is absent, the negation will be present.

But *c* does not always follow *b*. For what is not wood at all will be neither white wood nor non-white wood.

[Col. 0684A] Conversely, whatever *a* belongs to also has *d* belonging to it universally. For everything is either *c* or *d*. Since non-white and white cannot belong simultaneously to the same thing, *d* belongs to it: of what is white, it is true to say that it is not non-white.

But *a* does not belong universally to *d*. For of what is not wood at all it is not true to say that it is white wood. Thus *d* is true, while *a* is false, in the claim that it is white wood.

It is clear that *a* and *c* belong to no same thing, while *b* and *d* may belong to the same thing in some cases.

Privations stand to affirmations in the same way and according to the same arrangement. Let *a* be equal, *b* not equal, *c* unequal, and *d* not unequal.

[Col. 0684B] In the case of several things, some of which possess a certain attribute and others of which do not, the negation is likewise true. For example, “not all things are white,” “each thing is not white,” “each thing is non-white,” or “all things are non-white” are not equivalent; the latter claims are false.

Similarly, the negation of “every animal is white” is not “every animal is non-white,” for both are false. Rather, it is “not every animal is white.”

Since it is clear that “non-white” signifies something different from “not white,” the former being an affirmation and the latter a negation, it is clear that the method of demonstrating them is not the same.

[Col. 0684C] For example, the proposition that every animal is not white, or can fail to be white, is not demonstrated in the same way as the proposition that it is true to call it non-white; for this is to be non-white. But the propositions that it is true to call something white and that it is true to call it non-white are demonstrated in the same way: both are established affirmatively through the first figure.

The negation of “it is true to call it white” is not “it is true to call it non-white,” but “it is not true to call it white.”

If it is true to say that whatever is human is musical or non-musical, then whatever is animal must be taken to be musical or non-musical, and this has been demonstrated. But “whatever is human is not musical” is demonstrated destructively according to the three modes stated earlier.

[Col. 0684D] In general, this is the arrangement of *a* and *b*: they cannot both belong to the same thing, but one or the other must belong to everything. Likewise, the same applies to *c* and *d*. *c* follows *a*, but not conversely; *b* follows *d*, but not conversely; and *a* and *d* can belong to the same thing, whereas *b* and *c* cannot.

First, it is clear that *b* follows *d*. For one of *c* and *d* must necessarily belong universally to every thing. Whatever *b* cannot belong to, *c* cannot belong to either, since *c* entails *a*, while *a* and *b* cannot belong to the same thing. Therefore *d* follows *b*.

Again, since *c* does not follow *a* conversely, but everything is either *c* or *d*, *a* and *d* can belong to the same thing. *b* and *c* cannot belong to the same thing, since *c* follows *a*; otherwise something impossible would result.

It is therefore clear that *b* and *d* are not convertible with one another, since *a* and *d* can belong simultaneously to the same thing.

Sometimes people are deceived in arranging terms of this kind because they do not take the opposites correctly—namely, the pair in which one or the other must necessarily belong universally.

[Col. 0685A] Suppose *a* and *b* cannot belong simultaneously to the same thing, but one or the other must necessarily belong to everything; and suppose the same of *c* and *d*. If *c* follows *a* universally, it would follow that *b* necessarily belongs to everything that *d* belongs to. But this is false.

For if the negation of *a* and *b* is taken to be *f*, and the negation of *c* and *d* to be *g*, then either *a* or *f* must belong universally, since everything has either the affirmation or the negation. Likewise, everything must have either *c* or *g*. The affirmation and negation are such that whatever *c* belongs to universally has *a* underlying it; therefore whatever *f* belongs to universally has *g*.

Again, since one or the other of *f* and *b* belongs universally, and likewise one or the other of *g* and *d*, *g* follows *f*, and *d* follows *b*. This is what we know.

[Col. 0686A] But if *a* follows *c*, and *d* follows *b*, the result is false, since in such cases the consequence was the reverse.

For it is perhaps not necessary that either *a* or *f* belong universally, nor that either *f* or *b* belong universally. For *f* is not the negation of *a*: “not-good” is the negation of “good,” but “neither good nor not-good” is not the same as “not-good.” The same applies to *c* and *d*, since the negations that were taken are two.

# BOOK II

[Col. 0685]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0685A]

In how many figures, by what means, with how many propositions, at what time, and in what manner a syllogism is produced; furthermore, what one must observe when constructing and refuting arguments; how one ought to inquire into the proposed matter according to each art; and, in addition, by what route we shall take up the principles belonging to each case—we have now gone through these matters.

Since some syllogisms are universal and others particular, all universal syllogisms always establish more than one conclusion, whereas among particular syllogisms the affirmative ones establish more than one, but the negative ones establish only the conclusion. For some propositions are convertible, but a privative proposition is not convertible. The conclusion, however, is something predicated of something; hence some syllogisms establish more than one conclusion. For example, if it has been shown that *a* belongs to every or to some *b*, it is necessary that *b* belong to some *a*; and if *a* belongs to no *b*, then *b* belongs to no *a*. But this is different from the preceding case. If *a* does not belong to some *b*, it is not necessary that *b* fail to belong to some *a*; for *a* may belong to everything. This, then, is the common reason why universal and particular syllogisms establish more than one conclusion.

There is also another way of speaking about universal conclusions. Whatever terms occur either under the middle term or under the conclusion will all yield the same syllogism if the former are placed under the middle term and the latter under the conclusion. For example, if *a–b* is the conclusion through *c*, whatever terms fall under *b* or under *c* must all be said of *a*. For if *d* belongs to the whole of *b*, and *b* belongs to *a*, then *d* will also belong to *a*. Again, if *e* belongs to the whole of *c*, and *c* belongs to the whole of *a*, then *e* will belong to the whole of *a*. The same applies if the syllogism is negative.

In the second figure, however, only what falls under the conclusion will be established by syllogism. For example, if *a* belongs to no *b* and to every *c*, the conclusion is that *b* belongs to no *c*. If *d* falls under *c*, it is clear that *b* does not belong to it; but concerning what falls under *a*, it is not clear by syllogism that *b* does not belong to it. Nor, if *e* falls under *a*, is it clear by syllogism that *b* does not belong to *e*. Rather, the proposition that *b* belongs to no *c* has been demonstrated by syllogism, while the proposition that *a* is not *b* has been assumed without demonstration; consequently it does not follow by syllogism that *b* does not belong to *c*. [Col. 0685B]

In particular syllogisms, however, what falls under the conclusion will not necessarily be established. For no syllogism arises when the proposition taken is particular. What falls under the middle term, on the other hand, will all be established, though not by syllogism. For example, if *a* belongs to every *b*, and *b* belongs to some *c*, there will be no syllogism concerning what is placed under *c*, but there will be one concerning what is under *b*—though not on account of the syllogism previously produced. The same applies in the other figures as well. For what falls under the conclusion will not be established, whereas the other will be, but not by syllogism, since in universal cases what fell under the middle term was shown from an indemonstrated proposition. Therefore the same will not be the case here, nor will it be so in those cases. [Col. 0686A–B]

## Chapter II. That in the first figure a true conclusion may be drawn from false premises

The premises through which a syllogism is produced may therefore be true, or false, or one true and the other false; and the conclusion may necessarily be either true or false. From true premises, then, it is impossible to syllogize falsely; from false premises, however, it is possible to syllogize truly—not *because* of the explanation, but merely *that* the conclusion is so. A syllogism that proceeds *because of the explanation* cannot arise from false premises; the reason will be stated later.

First, that it is impossible to syllogize falsely from true premises is clear from the following. If, when *a* exists, *b* must exist, then, if *b* does not exist, *a* must not exist. If, therefore, *a* is true, *b* must also be true; otherwise the same thing would both exist and not exist at the same time, which is impossible.

But one must not understand this as though, because *a* is posited as a single term, something necessarily follows merely from the existence of some one thing; that is impossible. For what follows necessarily is the conclusion, and the terms through which it is produced are at least three, with two intervals and two premises.

If, then, it is true that *b* belongs to every *a*, and that *c* belongs to every *b*, then *a* must belong to every *c*, and this cannot be false; otherwise the same thing would both belong and fail to belong. Thus the one term *a* has been posited as yielding two premises. The same holds in negative propositions; it is impossible to demonstrate what is false from true premises. [Col. 0686C]

From false premises, however, it is possible to syllogize truly, both when both premises are false and when only one is false. But this does not happen in just any way; it occurs in the second figure if we take a whole proposition as false, whereas not every proposition can be taken as wholly false.

Let *a* belong to every *c*, but to no *b*, and let *b* also not belong to *c*. This is possible: no animal belongs to any stone, and no stone belongs to any human being. If, then, we take *a* to belong to every *b*, and *b* to belong to every *c*, *a* will belong to every *c*. Thus the conclusion is true from two wholly false premises: every human being is an animal.

The same is true in the negative case. Let *c* belong to no *a* and *b*, while *a* belongs to every *b*. For example, taking the same terms, neither animal nor human belongs to any stone, while every human being is an animal. If we take the term that belongs to everything as belonging to nothing, and the term that belongs to nothing as belonging to everything, the conclusion will be true from two false premises. The same will be shown if both propositions are false in some respect. [Col. 0686D]

If one premise is false, then, when the first is wholly false, the conclusion will not be true, though the second arrangement will yield a true conclusion.

By “wholly false” I mean false in the contrary of the truth: for example, if what belongs to no thing is taken as belonging to everything, or what belongs to everything is taken as belonging to nothing.

Let *a* belong to no *b*, and let *b* belong to every *c*. If, then, we take the proposition *b–c* as true, but take *a–b* as wholly false by taking *a* to belong to every *b*, it is impossible for the conclusion *a–c* to be true. For *a* belonged to no member of *c*, since *a* belonged to no *b*, while *b* belonged to every *c*.

Likewise, if *a* belongs to every *b*, and *b* belongs to every *c*, but the proposition *b–c* is taken as true and *a–b* as wholly false by taking *a* to belong to no *b*, the conclusion will be false. For *a* belongs to every *c*, since *b* belongs to every *c* and *a* to every *b*.

It is therefore clear that when the first premise, whether affirmative or negative, is taken as wholly false and the other as true, the conclusion is not true. [Col. 0687A]

But when it is not taken as wholly false, the conclusion may be true. For example, let *a* belong to every *c*, let *b* belong to some *a*, and let *b* belong to every *c*. Take animal, swan, and white: animal belongs to every swan, white belongs to some things, and white belongs to every swan. If we take *a* to belong to every *b*, and *b* to belong to every *c*, *a* will truly belong to every *c*, for every swan is an animal.

The same applies when the first proposition is negative. For it is possible that *a* belongs to some *b*, that *a* belongs to no *c*, and that *b* belongs to every *c*. For example, animal belongs to some white things, snow belongs to no thing, and white belongs to every snow. If, then, we take *a* to belong to no *b*, and *b* to belong to every *c*, *a* will belong to no *c*. [Col. 0687B]

If the proposition *a–b* is taken as wholly true while *b–c* is wholly false, the syllogism will nevertheless be true. Nothing prevents *a* from belonging to every *b* and to every *c*, while *b* belongs to no *c*, as with species of the same genus that are not subordinate to one another. Animal belongs to human being and horse, while horse belongs to no human being. If, then, *a* is taken to belong to every *b*, and *b* to belong to every *c*, the conclusion will be true although the proposition *b–c* is wholly false.

The same applies when the proposition *a–b* is universally negative. For it is possible that *a* belongs to neither *b* nor *c*, and that *b* belongs to no *c*, as with species from another genus: animal belongs neither to music nor to medicine, and music belongs to no medicine. If, then, *a* is taken to belong to no *b*, and *b* to belong to every *c*, the conclusion will be true.

Even if *b–c* is not wholly false but false in some respect, the conclusion will likewise be true. Nothing prevents *a*, *b*, and *c* from belonging to the whole of their subjects, while *b* belongs to some *c*. For example, animal belongs to every human being and to every biped, while human being belongs to some bipeds but not to every one. If, then, *a* is taken to belong to every *b*, and *b* to belong to every *c*, *a* will belong to every *c*, which was true. [Col. 0687C]

Similarly, when the proposition *a–b* is negative, it is possible that *a* belongs to no *b* and to no *c*, while *b* belongs to some *c*. Take a genus from another genus, together with its species and differentia: animal belongs to no wisdom and to no contemplation, while wisdom belongs to some contemplation. If *a* is taken to belong to no *b*, and *b* to belong to every *c*, *a* will belong to no *c*, which was true.

In particular syllogisms, too, it is possible for the conclusion to be true when the first proposition is wholly false and the second true; when *a–b* is false in some respect and *b–c* true; when *a–b* is true and the particular proposition false; and when both are false.

Nothing prevents *a* from belonging to no *b*, *c* from belonging to some *b*, and *b* from belonging to some *c*. For example, animal belongs to no snow, white belongs to some things, and snow belongs to some white things. If snow is taken as the middle term, animal as the first, and *a* as belonging to the whole of *b*, while *b* belongs to some *c*, the proposition *a–b* will be wholly false, *b–c* true, and the conclusion true. [Col. 0688A]

Likewise when the proposition *a–b* is negative, it is possible for *a* to belong to every *b*, for *a* not to belong to some *c*, and for *b* to belong to some *c*. For example, animal belongs to every human being, white does not belong to some things, and human being belongs to some white things. If human being is taken as the middle term, and we take *a* to belong to no *b* while *b* belongs to some *c*, the conclusion is true although the proposition *a–b* is wholly false.

If the proposition *a–b* is false in some respect while *b–c* is true, the conclusion will also be true. Nothing prevents *a*, *b*, and *c* from each belonging to some things, while *b* belongs to some *c*. For example, animal belongs to some beautiful things and to some large things, while beautiful belongs to some large things. If *a* is taken to belong to every *b*, and *b* to some *c*, then *a–b* will be false in some respect, *b–c* true, and the conclusion true.

The same applies when the proposition *a–b* is negative, since the same terms can be used and placed in the same way for the demonstration.

Again, if *a–b* is true and *b–c* false, the conclusion will be true. Nothing prevents *a* from belonging to every *b*, *c* from belonging to some things, and *b* from belonging to no *c*. For example, animal belongs to every swan, black belongs to some things, and swan belongs to no black thing. If *a* is taken to belong to every *b*, and *b* to belong to some *c*, the conclusion will be true although *b–c* is false. [Col. 0688B]

The same applies when the proposition *a–b* is negative. It is possible for *a* to belong to no *b*, for *a* not to belong to some *c*, and for *b* to belong to no *c*. For example, animal belongs to no number, white does not belong to some things, and number belongs to no white thing. If number is taken as the middle term, and *a* is taken to belong to no *b* while *b* belongs to some *c*, *a* will not belong to some *c*. This was true, although *a–b* was true and *b–c* false.

If *a–b* is false in some respect and *b–c* is also false, the conclusion will nevertheless be true. Nothing prevents *a* from belonging to some *b* and to some *c*, while *b* belongs to no *c*, as when *b* is contrary to *c* and both are attributes of the same genus. Animal belongs to some white things and to some black things, while white belongs to no black thing. If *a* is taken to belong to every *b*, and *b* to some *c*, the conclusion will be true. The same applies when the proposition *a–b* is negative; the same terms will be used and placed in the same way for the demonstration.

The conclusion will also be true from two wholly false premises. For it is possible for *a* to belong to no *b*, for *a* to belong to some *c*, and for *b* to belong to no *c*. For example, animal belongs to no number, animal belongs to some white things, and number belongs to no white thing. If *a* is taken to belong to every *b*, and *b* to belong to some *c*, the conclusion is true although both premises are false. [Col. 0688C]

The same applies when the proposition *a–b* is negative. Nothing prevents *a* from belonging to the whole of *b*, *a* from not belonging to some *c*, and *b* from belonging to no *c*. For example, animal belongs to every swan, animal does not belong to some black things, and swan belongs to no black thing. If *a* is taken to belong to no *b*, and *b* to some *c*, *a* will not belong to *c*. Thus the conclusion is true while both premises are false. [Col. 0688D]

## Chapter III. That in the second figure a true conclusion may be drawn from false premises

In the middle figure it is altogether possible to syllogize truly from false premises: when both premises are wholly false; when one is true and the other wholly false; when either one is false; when both are false in some respect; and when one is simply true while the other is false in some respect. This occurs in both universal and particular syllogisms.

If *a* belongs to no *b* and *c* belongs to every *a*, as animal belongs to no stone while it belongs to every human being, then, if the propositions are taken in their contraries—*a* belonging to every *b*, and *c* to no *a*—the conclusion will be true from two wholly false premises.

The same holds if *a* belongs to every *b* and to no *c*, for the syllogism will be the same.

Again, one premise may be wholly false and the other wholly true. Nothing prevents *a* from belonging to every *b* and to every *c*, while *b* belongs to no *c*, as with a genus and non-subordinate species. Animal belongs to every horse and every human being, while no human being is a horse. If, then, animal is taken to belong to the one universally and to the other not at all, one premise will be false and the other wholly true, while the conclusion will be true, whichever proposition is taken negatively. [Col. 0689A–B]

If one premise is false in some respect and the other wholly true, this too is possible. Let *a* belong to some *b*, *a* belong to every *c*, and *b* belong to no *c*. For example, animal belongs to some white things, to every crow, and white belongs to no crow. If *a* is taken to belong to no *b*, and to every *c*, the proposition *a–b* will be false in some respect, *a–c* wholly true, and the conclusion true. The same applies with the negative proposition transposed, since the demonstration uses the same terms. [Col. 0689C]

If the affirmative proposition is false in some respect while the negative one is wholly true, nothing prevents *a* from belonging to some *b*, from belonging to no *c*, and *b* from belonging to no *c*. For example, animal belongs to some white things, to no woodpecker, and white belongs to no woodpecker. If *a* is taken to belong to every *b*, and to no *c*, *a–b* is false in some respect, *a–c* wholly true, and the conclusion true.

If both propositions are false in some respect, the conclusion will be true. It is possible for *a*, *b*, and *c* each to belong to some things, while *b* belongs to no *c*. For example, animal belongs to some white things and to some black things, while white belongs to no black thing. If *a* is taken to belong to every *b* and to no *c*, both premises will be false in some respect, while the conclusion will be true. The same applies when the negative proposition is transposed, using the same terms. [Col. 0689D]

The same is clear in particular syllogisms. Nothing prevents *a* from belonging to every *b*, *a* from belonging to some *c*, and *b* from not belonging to some *c*. For example, animal belongs to every human being, white to some things, and human being does not belong to some white thing. If *a* is taken to belong to no *b*, and to some *c*, the universal premise is wholly false, the particular premise true, and the conclusion true.

The same applies when the affirmative proposition *a–b* is taken. It is possible for *a* to belong to no *b*, for *a* not to belong to some *c*, and for *b* not to belong to some *c*. For example, animal belongs to no inanimate thing, white belongs to some things, and inanimate does not belong to some white thing. If *a* is taken to belong to every *b*, and not to belong to some *c*, the universal proposition *a–b* is wholly false, *a–c* true, and the conclusion true.

If the universal proposition is true and the minor particular proposition false, nothing prevents *a* from belonging to neither *b* nor *c*, while *b* does not belong to some *c*. For example, animal belongs to no number and to no inanimate thing, while number does not belong to some inanimate thing. If *a* is taken to belong to no *b*, and to some *c*, the conclusion is true, the universal proposition true, and the particular proposition false. [Col. 0690A]

With a universal affirmative proposition placed in the same way, it is possible for *a*, *b*, and *c* all to belong to their subjects, while *b* does not belong to every *c*, as with genus, species, and differentia. Animal belongs to every human being and to every biped, while human being does not belong to every biped. If *a* is taken to belong to the whole of *b*, and not to belong to some *c*, the universal proposition is true, the particular proposition false, and the conclusion true.

It is clear that the conclusion will also be true when both premises are false, provided that *a* and *b* belong to one subject universally and to another not at all, while *b* does not belong to some *c*. If *a* is taken to belong to no *b*, and *c* to some *a*, both premises are false while the conclusion is true.

The same applies when the universal proposition is affirmative and the particular proposition negative. It is possible for *a* to belong to no *b*, for *a* to belong to every *c*, and for *b* not to belong to every *c*. For example, animal belongs to no discipline, to every human being, while discipline does not belong to every human being. If *a* is taken to belong to the whole of *b*, and not to belong to some *c*, both premises are false while the conclusion is true. [Col. 0690B]

## Chapter IV. That in the third figure, too, a true conclusion may repeatedly be drawn from false premises

In the last figure also, the conclusion may be true when both premises are wholly false; when both are false in some respect; when one is true and the other false; when one is false in some respect and the other wholly true; and conversely; and in all the other ways in which the premises can be arranged.

Nothing prevents neither *a* nor *b* from belonging to any *c*, while *a* belongs to some *b*. For example, neither human being nor biped belongs to any inanimate thing, while human being belongs to some bipeds. If *a* and *b* are taken to belong to every *c*, both premises will be wholly false, while the conclusion will be true.

The same applies when one proposition is negative and the other affirmative. It is possible for *b* to belong to no *c*, for *a* to belong to every *c*, and for *a* not to belong to every *b*. For example, black belongs to no swan, animal to every swan, and animal does not belong to every black thing. If *b* is taken to belong to every *c*, and *a* to no *c*, *a* will not belong to some *b*. The conclusion is true, while the premises are false. [Col. 0690C–D]

If both premises are false in some respect, the conclusion will be true. Nothing prevents both *a* and *b* from belonging to some *c*, and *a* from belonging to some *b*. For example, white and beautiful belong to some animal, and white belongs to some beautiful thing. If *a* and *b* are taken to belong to every *c*, the premises will be false in some respect, while the conclusion is true.

The same applies when the proposition *a–c* is negative. Nothing prevents *a* from not belonging to some *c*, *b* from belonging to some *c*, and *a* from not belonging to every *b*. For example, white does not belong to some animal, beautiful belongs to some animals, and white does not belong to every beautiful thing. If *a* is taken to belong to no *c*, and *b* to every *c*, both premises are false in some respect, while the conclusion is true. [Col. 0691A]

The same applies when one premise is taken as wholly false and the other as wholly true. It is possible for *a* and *b* to belong to every *c*, while *a* does not belong to some *b*. For example, animal and white belong to every swan, while animal does not belong to every white thing. With these terms, if *b* is taken to belong to the whole of *c*, and *a* to none of *c*, *b–c* will be wholly true, *a–c* wholly false, and the conclusion true.

The same applies if *b–c* is false and *a–c* true, using the terms black, inanimate, and swan.

If both premises are taken affirmatively, nothing prevents *b* from belonging to every *c*, *a* from belonging to no *c*, and *a* from belonging to some *b*. For example, animal belongs to every swan, black belongs to no swan, and black belongs to some animal. If *a* and *b* are taken to belong to every *c*, *b–c* will be wholly true, *a–c* wholly false, and the conclusion true. The same applies with *a–c* taken as true, since the same terms demonstrate the point. [Col. 0691B]

Again, when one premise is wholly true and the other false in some respect, it is possible for *b* to belong to every *c*, and for *a* to belong to some *c* and to some *b*. For example, biped belongs to every human being, beautiful does not belong to every human being, and beautiful belongs to some bipeds. If *a* and *b* are taken to belong to the whole of *c*, *b–c* will be wholly true, *a–c* false in some respect, and the conclusion true.

The same applies if *a–c* is true and *b–c* false in some respect, with the same terms transposed.

When one premise is negative and the other affirmative, it is possible for *b* to belong to the whole of *c*, for *a* to belong to some *c*, and, in such a situation, for *a* not to belong to every *b*. If *b* is taken to belong to the whole of *c*, and *a* to no *c*, the negative premise is false in some respect, the other wholly true, and the conclusion true. [Col. 0691C]

Again, since it has been shown that when *a* belongs to no *c* and *b* belongs to some *c*, it follows that *a* does not belong to some *b*, it is clear that when *a–c* is wholly true and *b–c* false in some respect, the conclusion may be true. If *a* is taken to belong to no *c*, and *b* to every *c*, *a–c* is wholly true, *b–c* false in some respect, and the conclusion is true.

It is also clear in particular syllogisms that the true conclusion may altogether arise from false premises. The same terms are to be taken; and when the premises are universal, in affirmative cases the affirmative form is to be used, and in negative cases the negative form. For it makes no difference, when one thing belongs to no other, to take it as belonging universally, nor, when it belongs to some thing, to take it universally for purposes of arranging the terms. The same applies to negative premises.

It is therefore clear that when the conclusion is false, the propositions from which the argument proceeds must be false, either all of them or some. When the conclusion is true, however, it is not necessary that any proposition, or all of them, be true.

Yet there are cases in which none of the things in the syllogisms is true, while the conclusion is likewise true, though not necessarily. The reason is that when two things are related in such a way that, if one exists, the other must exist, then, if the one does not exist, the other will not exist either; but when the one exists, the other need not exist. Moreover, if the same thing exists and does not exist, it is impossible that the other should exist necessarily.

For example, let it be necessary, when *a* is white, that *b* be large, and let it also be necessary, when *a* is not white, that *b* be large. When *a* is white, *b* must be large; and when *b* is large, *c* must not be white. Hence, if *a* is white, *c* must not be white.

When, among two existing things, the existence of one entails the necessary existence of the other, and when the first does not exist the other must not exist, then, if *b* is not large, *a* cannot be white. But if *a* is not white, *b* must be large. Thus, when *b* is not large, it follows necessarily that *b* is large—an impossibility. For if *b* is not large, *a* will necessarily not be white; and if, when *a* is not white, *b* is large, then, if *b* is not large, *b* will be large, as follows through three terms. [Col. 0692A]

## Chapter V. Circular demonstration in the first figure

To demonstrate circularly, and to demonstrate from one another, is to establish one proposition through the conclusion and, conversely, to take the other proposition as a premise and conclude the remaining proposition—the one that had been taken in the other syllogism.

For example, if one must show that *a* belongs to every *c*, and this is shown through *b*, then, if one again wishes to show that *a* belongs to *b*, one takes *a* as belonging to *c* and *c* as belonging to *b*, and *a* will belong to *b*. In the earlier syllogism, however, one had taken conversely that *b* belongs to *c*. Or, if one must show that *b* belongs to *c*, one takes *a* as predicated of *c*—which was the conclusion—and *b* as predicated of *a*, whereas earlier *a* had been taken conversely as predicated of *b*.

Otherwise it is not possible to demonstrate from one another. For if another middle term is taken, the demonstration is not circular, since none of the same propositions is being used. If one of these terms is taken, only one of the premises must be different; for if both were used, the conclusion would be the same, whereas it must be different. [Col. 0692B]

In cases involving nonconvertible propositions, a syllogism proceeds from the one indemonstrated proposition. For it is not possible through these terms to demonstrate that the middle belongs to the third term, or that the first belongs to the middle.

In cases involving convertible propositions, however, everything can be demonstrated through one another. Suppose *a*, *b*, and *c* are mutually convertible. Let *a–c* be shown through the middle term *b*. Then *a–b* may be shown through the conclusion and through the converse of the proposition *b–c*. Likewise *b–c* may be shown through the conclusion and through the converse of *a–b*. One must also demonstrate *c–b* and *b–a*, since only these propositions have been used in the demonstrations.

If, then, *b* is taken to belong to every *c*, and *c* to every *a*, there will be a syllogism concerning *b–a*. Again, if *c* is taken to belong to every *a*, and *a* to every *b*, it follows necessarily that *c* belongs to every *b*. In both syllogisms the proposition *c–a* has been taken as indemonstrated, since the other propositions had been proved. If we demonstrate this proposition, all the propositions will have been established through one another. If, then, *c* is taken to belong to every *b*, and *b* to every *a*, both premises are taken as demonstrated, and it necessarily follows that *c* belongs to *a*. [Col. 0692C–D]

It is therefore clear that demonstrations through one another and circularly are possible only in cases involving convertible propositions; in other cases they occur as stated earlier.

It also happens in these cases that the very thing being demonstrated is used in the demonstration. For *c–b* and *b–a* are demonstrated by taking *c–a* as the conclusion, while *c–a* is demonstrated through those propositions. Thus the conclusion is used as part of the demonstration. [Col. 0693A]

In negative syllogisms, demonstration from one another proceeds as follows. Let *b* belong to every *c*, let *a* belong to no *b*, and let the conclusion be that *a* belongs to no *c*. If one must again conclude that *a* belongs to no *b*—the proposition previously taken—one takes *a* as belonging to no *c* and *c* as belonging to every *b*, since this is the converse proposition.

If one must conclude that *b* belongs to *c*, one cannot convert *a–b* in the same way, since the propositions “*b* belongs to no *a*” and “*a* belongs to no *b*” are the same. Instead, one must take the proposition that to whatever *a* belongs to no thing, *b* belongs to everything. Let *a* belong to no *c*, which was the conclusion; and let *a* belong to no *b*. If *b* is taken as belonging to every such thing, then *b* must belong to every *c*. Thus, with three terms, each proposition has been made a conclusion, and circular demonstration is possible—that is, by taking the conclusion and, conversely, one proposition in order to syllogize the other. [Col. 0693B]

In particular syllogisms it is not possible to demonstrate the universal proposition through the others, but it is possible to demonstrate the particular proposition. That the universal cannot be demonstrated is clear: the universal is shown through universals, whereas the conclusion here is not universal. One must demonstrate it from the conclusion and the other proposition.

Furthermore, no syllogism results from a converted proposition, since both premises become particular. Let *a* belong to some *c* through *b*. If, then, *b* is taken to belong to every *a*, while the conclusion remains, *b* will belong to some *c*; this is a syllogism in the first figure, with *a* as the middle term.

If the syllogism is negative, the universal proposition cannot be demonstrated, for the reason already stated. The particular proposition cannot be demonstrated by simply converting *a–b*, as in universal cases; but it can be demonstrated by an additional assumption—for example, that to whatever *a* does not belong to some thing, *b* belongs to some thing. Otherwise, with the propositions arranged differently, no syllogism results, since the negative proposition is particular. [Col. 0693C]

## Chapter VI. The same circular demonstration in the second figure

In the second figure it is not possible to demonstrate the affirmative proposition in this way, but it is possible to demonstrate the negative proposition.

The affirmative proposition cannot be demonstrated because the two premises are not both affirmative. The conclusion is negative, whereas an affirmative conclusion was demonstrated from two affirmative premises.

The negative proposition is demonstrated as follows. Let *a* belong to every *b*, let *c* belong to no *a*, and let the conclusion be that *b* belongs to no *c*. If *b* is taken to belong to every *a*, and to no *c*, then *a* must belong to no *c*. This is a syllogism in the second figure, with *b* as the middle term.

If *a–b* is taken as negative and the other proposition as affirmative, the syllogism will be in the first figure. For *c* belongs to every *a*, and *b* belongs to no *c*; hence *b* belongs to no *a*, and therefore neither does *a* belong to *b*, with *c* as the middle term. Thus no syllogism results from the conclusion and one premise; but it does result when the other proposition is added. [Col. 0693D]

If the syllogism is not universal, the proposition that is universal cannot be demonstrated, for the same reason stated earlier. The particular proposition can be demonstrated when the universal premise is affirmative.

Let *a* belong to every *b*, let *c* not belong to every *a*, and let the conclusion be *b–c*. If *b* is taken to belong to every *a*, and *c* not to belong to every *a*, the conclusion follows that *a* does not belong to some *c*, with *b* as the middle term.

If the universal proposition is negative, the proposition *a–b* cannot be demonstrated after conversion. For then either both premises or one of them becomes negative, and there will be no syllogism. It will instead be demonstrated as in universal cases, if one takes the proposition that to whatever *b* does not belong to some thing, *a* belongs to some thing. [Col. 0694A]

## Chapter VII. Circular reasoning in the third figure

In the third figure, when both premises are taken universally, it is not possible to demonstrate one proposition through the other. For the universal is demonstrated through universals, but in this figure the conclusion is always particular. It is therefore clear that it is altogether impossible in this figure to demonstrate a universal proposition.

If one proposition is universal and the other particular, however, this will sometimes be possible and sometimes not. When both premises are affirmative and the universal premise concerns the minor extreme, it will be possible; when it concerns the other extreme, it will not.

Let *a* belong to every *c*, and *b* to some *c*, with the conclusion *a–b*. If the converse of the universal proposition is taken—that *c* belongs to every *a*—together with the conclusion, then it has been shown that *c* belongs to some *b*, but it has not been shown that *b* belongs to some *c*, although this is necessary if *c* belongs to some *b* and *b* to some *c*. But it is not the same for one thing to belong to some of another and for the other to belong to some of the first. One must instead assume that if this belongs to some of that, the other belongs to some of this; but once this is assumed, there is no longer a syllogism from the conclusion and the other proposition. [Col. 0694B–C]

If *b* belongs to every *c*, and *a* to some *c*, then *a–c* can be demonstrated when *c* is taken to belong to every *b* and *a* to some *b*. For if *c* belongs to every *b*, while *a* belongs to some *b*, it follows necessarily that *a* belongs to some *c*, with *b* as the middle term.

When one proposition is affirmative and the other negative, and the universal proposition is affirmative, the other can be demonstrated. Let *b* belong to every *c*, let *a* not belong to some *c*, and let the conclusion be that *a* does not belong to some *b*. If *c* is taken to belong to every *b*, while *a* already does not belong to every *b*, it follows necessarily that *a* does not belong to some *c*, with *b* as the middle term.

When the universal proposition is negative, the other cannot be demonstrated except as in the preceding cases. If *a* belongs to no *c*, and *b* belongs to some *c*, the conclusion is that *a* does not belong to some *b*. If one takes the proposition that to whatever *a* does not belong to some thing, *c* belongs to some thing, it follows necessarily that *c* belongs to some *b*. Otherwise the universal proposition cannot be converted so as to demonstrate the other, since in no way will there be a syllogism. [Col. 0694D]

It is therefore clear that in the first figure demonstration through one another is possible both through the first and through the third figure. When the conclusion is affirmative, it proceeds through the first figure; when negative, through the last figure, since one takes that to which the first belongs to no thing, while the other belongs to everything.

In the middle figure, when the syllogism is universal, demonstration is possible both through that figure itself, through the first figure, and through the last figure. When it is particular, it is possible through that figure itself and through the last figure.

In the third figure it is possible through that figure itself in all cases.

It is also clear that in the middle and third figures, syllogisms that are not produced through those figures themselves either do not conform to the circular demonstration described, or are imperfect. [Col. 0695A]

## Chapter VIII. Conversion of a syllogism

To convert a syllogism is to transpose the conclusion and produce a syllogism, so that either the extreme will not belong to the middle, or the latter to the former. For when the conclusion is converted and the other proposition remains, the remaining proposition must be destroyed; for if it follows, the conclusion will follow as well.

It makes a difference whether the conclusion is converted contradictorily or contrarily. The same syllogism does not result from either kind of conversion, as will become clear from what follows.

By “contradictory” I mean: “belongs to every” versus “does not belong to every,” and “belongs to some” versus “belongs to none.” By “contrary” I mean: “belongs to every” versus “belongs to none,” and “belongs to some” versus “does not belong to some.”

Let *a–c* have been demonstrated through the middle term *b*. If *a* is taken to belong to no *c*, and to every *b*, then *b* belongs to no *c*. If *a* belongs to no *c*, and *b* to every *c*, then *a* does not belong to every *b*, though it does not follow that it belongs to none; for a universal conclusion was not demonstrated through the third figure. [Col. 0695B]

In general, the proposition belonging to the major extreme cannot be destroyed universally by conversion; it is always destroyed through the third figure, since both propositions must be taken with respect to the minor extreme.

If the syllogism is negative, the same applies. Let *a* belong to no *c* through *b*. If *a* is taken to belong to every *c*, and *b* to no *a*, then *b* belongs to no *c*. If *a* and *b* belong to every *c*, then *a* belongs to some *b*, although it had belonged to none.

If the conclusion is converted contradictorily, the resulting syllogisms will likewise be contradictory and will not be universal, since one premise becomes particular and therefore the conclusion will be particular.

Suppose the syllogism is affirmative and is converted in this way. If *a* does not belong to every *c*, and *b* belongs to every *a*, then *b* does not belong to every *c*. If *a* does not belong to every *c*, and *b* belongs to every *a*, then *b* does not belong to every *c*. Likewise if the syllogism is negative: if *a* belongs to some *c*, and *b* belongs to no *a*, then *b* does not belong to some *c*, though not to none simply. If *a* belongs to some *c* and *b* to every *a*, then, as was taken at the beginning, *a* belongs to some *b*. [Col. 0695C]

In particular syllogisms, when the conclusion is converted contradictorily, both premises are destroyed; when it is converted contrarily, neither is destroyed. For it no longer happens, as in universal syllogisms, that the premise is destroyed through conversion when the conclusion fails, nor is either premise destroyed altogether.

Let *a* have been demonstrated as belonging to some *c* through *b*. If *a* is taken to belong to no *c*, and *b* to some *c*, then *a* does not belong to some *b*. If *a* belongs to no *c* and *b* to every *c*, then *b* belongs to no *c*. Thus both premises are destroyed.

If they are converted contrarily, neither is destroyed. For if *a* does not belong to some *c*, and *b* belongs to every *c*, then *b* does not belong to some *c*; but what was established at the beginning has not yet been destroyed, since it is possible for something to belong to some things and not to belong to others. Once the universal proposition *a–b* is removed, no syllogism at all results. For if *a* does not belong to some *c*, and *b* belongs to some *c*, neither premise is universal.

The same applies if the syllogism is negative. If *a* is taken to belong to every *c*, both premises are destroyed; if it is taken to belong to some, neither is destroyed. The demonstration is the same. [Col. 0695D]

## Chapter IX. Conversion of a syllogism in the second figure

[Col. 0696A]

In the second figure, the proposition belonging to the major extreme cannot be refuted contrariwise; however the conversion is made, and the conclusion will always be in the third figure. Since there was no universal syllogism in this figure, we shall refute the other proposition in it, likewise by conversion. By “likewise” I mean: if it is converted contrary to the original, then contrary; if oppositely, then oppositely.

Let \(a\) belong to every \(b\), while \(c\) belongs to none, and let the conclusion be that \(b\) belongs to \(c\). If, then, it is assumed that \(b\) belongs to every \(c\), while \(a\!-\!b\) remains as before, \(a\) will belong to every \(c\), for this produces the first figure.

[Col. 0696B]

But if \(b\) belongs to every \(c\), while \(a\) belongs to no \(c\), then \(a\) does not belong to every \(b\): this is the final figure. If \(b\!-\!c\) is converted oppositely, the same result will be shown for \(a\!-\!b\), while \(a\!-\!c\) will be converted oppositely.

[Col. 0696C]

For if \(b\) belongs to some \(c\), while \(a\) belongs to no \(c\), \(a\) will not belong to some \(b\); and again, if \(b\) belongs to some \(c\), while \(a\) belongs to every \(b\), \(a\) will belong to some \(c\). Thus the opposite syllogism is produced. The same will also be shown if the propositions stand conversely.

If the syllogism is particular, when the conclusion is converted contrary to the original, neither proposition is refuted, just as in the first figure; when it is converted oppositely, both are refuted. Let \(a\) belong to no \(b\), while \(c\) belongs to some \(b\), and let the conclusion be that \(b\) belongs to \(c\). If, then, it is posited that \(b\) belongs to some \(c\), while \(a\!-\!b\) remains as before, the conclusion will be that \(a\) does not belong to some \(c\); but the original proposition is not refuted, since it is possible for something to belong to some and not to belong to some.

Again, if \(b\) belongs to some \(c\), and \(a\) belongs to some \(c\), there will be no syllogism, since neither of the propositions assumed is universal; therefore \(a\!-\!b\) is not refuted. If, however, the propositions are converted oppositely, both are refuted—not if \(b\) belongs to every \(c\), while \(a\) belongs to no \(b\), for then \(a\) will belong to no \(c\), but to some \(c\). Again, if \(b\) belongs to every \(c\), while \(a\) belongs to some \(c\), \(a\) will belong to some \(b\).

[Note: [Col. 0696D] This passage is affected by some serious corruption.]

The same demonstration applies if the syllogism is universal and affirmative.

## CHAPTER X. On the converting syllogism in the third figure

In the third figure, when the conclusion is converted contrary to the original, neither proposition is refuted in any of the syllogisms; when it is converted oppositely, both are refuted in every case.

For suppose it has been shown that \(a\) belongs to some \(b\), and let \(c\) be taken as the middle term; let the propositions be universal. If, then, it is assumed that \(a\) does not belong to some \(b\), while \(b\) belongs to every \(c\), there is no syllogism concerning \(a\) and \(c\). Nor, if \(a\) does not belong to some \(b\), while \(c\) belongs to every \(b\), will there be a syllogism concerning \(b\) and \(c\).

[Col. 0696D]

The same will be shown if the propositions are not universal. For either both must become particular through conversion, or the proposition relating to the minor extreme becomes universal; but in this way there will be no syllogism, neither in the first figure nor in the middle figure.

If, however, the propositions are converted oppositely, both are refuted. For if \(a\) belongs to no \(b\), while \(b\) belongs to every \(c\), \(a\) belongs to no \(c\). Again, if \(a\) belongs to no \(b\), while \(c\) belongs to every \(b\), \(b\) belongs to no \(c\). The same applies if one proposition is not universal. For if \(a\) belongs to no \(b\), while \(b\) belongs to some \(c\), \(a\) will not belong to some \(c\). If \(a\) belongs to no \(b\), while \(c\) belongs to every \(b\), \(b\) will belong to no \(c\).

The same applies if the syllogism is negative. Let it be shown that \(a\) does not belong to some \(b\); let the proposition \(b\!-\!c\) be affirmative and the proposition \(a\!-\!c\) negative, for in this way the syllogism was produced.

[Col. 0697A]

When, therefore, the contrary of the conclusion is assumed, there will be no syllogism. For if \(a\) belongs to some \(b\), while \(b\) belongs to every \(c\), there is no syllogism concerning \(a\) and \(c\). Nor, if \(a\) belongs to some \(b\), while \(b\) belongs to no \(c\), was there a syllogism concerning \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\); therefore the propositions are not refuted.

When the opposite is assumed, however, both are refuted. For if \(a\) belongs to every \(b\), and \(b\) belongs to every \(c\), \(a\) belongs to every \(c\), although it was supposed to belong to none. Again, if \(a\) belongs to every \(b\), while \(a\) belongs to no \(c\), \(b\) belongs to no \(c\), although it belonged to every \(c\).

[Col. 0697B]

The same is shown if the propositions are not universal. Let \(a\!-\!c\) be universal and negative, and the other particular and affirmative. If, then, \(a\) belongs to every \(b\), while \(b\) belongs to some \(c\), it follows that \(a\) belongs to some \(c\), although it belonged to none. Again, if \(a\) belongs to every \(b\), while \(b\) belongs to no \(c\), then \(b\) belongs to no \(c\). But if \(a\) belongs to some \(b\), and \(b\) belongs to some \(c\), there is no syllogism.
