Nor is there one if \(a\) belongs to some \(b\), while \(b\) belongs to no \(c\). Therefore, in the former way the propositions are refuted, but in this way they are not.

[Col. 0697C]

It is clear from what has been said how, in each figure, a syllogism results when the conclusion is converted, and when it is converted contrary to a proposition, and when oppositely. It is also clear that in the first figure syllogisms are produced through the middle and final figures: the proposition relating to the minor extreme is always refuted through the middle figure, while that relating to the major extreme is refuted through the final figure; in the second figure, through the first and final figures, the proposition relating to the minor extreme always through the first figure, and that relating to the major extreme through the final figure; and in the third figure, through the first and middle figures, the proposition relating to the major extreme always through the first, and that relating to the minor extreme always through the middle.

What conversion is, therefore, how it occurs in each figure, and what syllogism results, is now clear.

## CHAPTER XI. On the syllogism through the impossible

A syllogism through the impossible is demonstrated when the contradiction of the conclusion is posited and the other proposition is assumed. It occurs in all the figures, since it is similar to conversion. Nevertheless, it differs in this respect: in conversion the syllogism is made after both propositions have been assumed, whereas a deduction to the impossible does not begin by conceding the opposite, but by what is manifestly true.

The terms stand similarly in both cases, and the same assumption is made in both. For example, if \(a\) belongs to every \(b\), and \(c\) is the middle term, then if it is supposed that \(a\) belongs either not to every \(b\) or to no \(b\), while \(c\) belongs to every \(b\), it is necessary that \(c\) belong either to no \(b\) or not to every \(b\). But this is impossible; therefore the supposition is false. The opposite is consequently true.

[Col. 0697D]

The same applies in the other figures, since whatever propositions admit conversion also admit a syllogism through the impossible.

Thus all other propositions can be shown through the impossible in all the figures; but the universal affirmative is shown in the middle and third figures, not in the first. For suppose that \(a\) does not belong to every \(b\), or belongs to no \(b\), and let the other proposition be assumed in either form—either \(a\) belongs to every \(c\), or \(b\) belongs to every \(d\), for in this way the first figure was produced. If, then, it is supposed that \(a\) does not belong to every \(b\), no syllogism will result, whichever proposition is assumed.

[Col. 0698A]

But if it is supposed that \(a\) belongs to no \(b\), and \(d\) is assumed, there will indeed be a syllogism concerning something false, but the proposition at issue will not be shown. For if \(a\) belongs to no \(b\), while \(b\) belongs to every \(d\), then \(a\) belongs to no \(d\); but although this is impossible, it follows only that the proposition “\(a\) belongs to no \(b\)” is false—not that “\(a\) belongs to every \(b\)” is true. If \(c\!-\!a\) is assumed, there is no syllogism, either when it is supposed that \(a\) does not belong to every \(b\); therefore it is clear that, in the first figure, “\(a\) belongs to every \(b\)” is not shown through the impossible.

The particular affirmative, the universal negative, and the particular negative are shown. For suppose that \(a\) belongs to no \(b\), while \(b\) is taken to belong to every or to some \(c\). It is then necessary that \(a\) belong to no \(c\) or not to every \(c\); but this is impossible. Let it be true and evident that \(a\) belongs to every \(c\). Therefore, if this is false, \(a\) must belong to some \(b\).

[Col. 0698B]

If the other proposition is taken with reference to \(a\), there will be no syllogism, nor when the subcontrary of the conclusion is supposed—that \(a\) does not belong to some \(b\). It is therefore clear that the opposite must be assumed.

Again, suppose that \(a\) belongs to some \(b\), and let \(c\) be taken to belong to every \(a\). It is then necessary that \(c\) belong to some \(b\); but let this be impossible. Therefore the supposition is false, and it is true that \(a\) belongs to no \(b\). The same applies if the proposition assumed is negative, \(c\!-\!a\). If the proposition is assumed with reference to \(b\), there will be no syllogism.

If the contrary is supposed, there will be a syllogism and an impossibility, but the proposition at issue will not be shown. For suppose that \(a\) belongs to every \(b\), and let \(c\) belong to every \(a\). It is then necessary that \(c\) belong to every \(b\); but this is impossible. Therefore it is false that \(a\) belongs to every \(b\), but it is not yet necessary that it belong to no \(b\).

[Col. 0698C]

The same applies if \(a\!-\!d\!-\!b\) is taken as the other proposition: there will be a syllogism and an impossibility, but the hypothesis is not refuted. Therefore the opposite must be supposed.

To show that \(a\) does not belong to every \(b\), one must suppose that it belongs to every \(b\). For if \(a\) belongs to every \(b\), and \(c\) belongs to every \(a\), then \(c\) belongs to every \(b\); if this is impossible, the supposition is false. The same applies if the other proposition is taken with reference to \(b\), and likewise if \(c\!-\!a\) is negative, for a syllogism is produced in this way. If the proposition assumed with reference to \(b\) is negative, nothing is shown.

If it is supposed not that \(a\) belongs to every \(b\), but that it belongs to some \(b\), it is not shown that it does not belong to every \(b\), but that it belongs to no \(b\). For if \(a\) belongs to some \(b\), while \(c\) belongs to every \(a\), \(c\) will belong to some \(b\); if this is impossible, it is false that \(a\) belongs to some \(b\), and therefore it is true that it belongs to no \(b\). But once this has been shown, what is true is refuted, since \(a\) did belong to some \(b\), though not to others.

[Col. 0698D]

Moreover, the impossibility does not arise because of the hypothesis, since the hypothesis will be false only if a false conclusion is syllogized from true premises—and that is not the case here, for \(a\) does belong to some \(b\). Therefore one must not suppose that it belongs to some \(b\), but that it belongs to every \(b\).

The same applies if we were to show that \(a\) does not belong to some \(b\). For if “not belonging to some” is the same as “not belonging to every,” the demonstration is the same in both cases.

It is therefore clear that in all syllogisms the contrary must not be supposed, but the opposite. In this way the result will be necessary and the principle will be plausible. For if, concerning everything, either the affirmative or the negative is true, once it has been shown that the negative is not true, the affirmative must be true. Again, if they do not posit the affirmative as true, it follows that the negative is true. But the contrary cannot in either way be made secure: it is not necessary that, if “belongs to no” is false, “belongs to every” should be true, nor is it plausible that, if one contrary is false, the other should therefore be true.

[Col. 0699A]

It is clear, then, that in the first figure all the other propositions are shown through the impossible, but the universal affirmative is not.

## CHAPTER XII. On the syllogism through the impossible in the second figure

In the middle and final figures the universal affirmative is also shown. Suppose that \(a\) does not belong to every \(b\), and let \(a\) be taken to belong to every \(c\). If, then, \(b\) belongs not to every \(a\), while \(c\) belongs to every \(a\), \(c\) does not belong to every \(b\); but this is impossible.

[Col. 0699B]

Let it be evident that \(c\) belongs to every \(b\). Therefore the supposition is false, and it is true that \(a\) belongs to every \(b\).

If the contrary is supposed, there will indeed be a syllogism leading to the impossible, but the proposition at issue will not be shown. For if \(a\) belongs to no \(b\), while it belongs to every \(c\), \(c\) belongs to no \(b\); but this is impossible. Therefore it is false that \(a\) belongs to no \(b\), but it does not follow that it belongs to every \(b\).

When \(a\) belongs to some \(b\), suppose that \(a\) belongs to no \(b\), while \(c\) belongs to every \(a\). It is then necessary that \(c\) belong to no \(b\); if this is impossible, it is necessary that \(a\) belong to some \(b\). If it is supposed not to belong to some \(b\), the result will be the same as in the first figure.

Again, suppose that \(a\) belongs to some \(b\), while \(c\) belongs to no \(a\). It is then necessary that \(c\) not belong to some \(b\), although it belonged to every \(b\). Therefore the supposition is false, and \(a\) belongs to no \(b\).

When \(a\) does not belong to every \(b\), suppose that it belongs to every \(b\), while \(c\) belongs to no \(a\). It is then necessary that \(c\) belong to no \(b\); but this is impossible. Therefore it is true that \(a\) does not belong to every \(b\).

[Col. 0699C]

It is clear, then, that all syllogisms are produced through the middle figure.

## CHAPTER XIII. On demonstration through the impossible in the third figure

The same applies in the final figure. Suppose that \(a\) does not belong to some \(b\), while \(c\) belongs to every \(b\); then \(a\) does not belong to some \(c\). If this is impossible, it is false that \(a\) does not belong to some \(b\), and therefore it is true that it belongs to every \(b\).

If it is supposed to belong to no \(b\), there will indeed be a syllogism and an impossibility, but the proposition at issue will not be shown. If the contrary is supposed, the result will be the same as in the preceding cases.

To show that \(a\) belongs to some \(b\), the same hypothesis must be assumed. For if \(a\) belongs to no \(b\), while \(c\) belongs to some \(b\), \(a\) does not belong to every \(c\); if this is false, it is true that \(a\) belongs to some \(b\).

[Col. 0699D]

When \(a\) belongs to no \(b\), suppose that it belongs to some \(b\), and also let \(c\) belong to every \(b\). It is then necessary that \(a\) belong to some \(c\), although it belonged to none. Therefore it is false that \(a\) belongs to some \(b\).

If it is supposed that \(a\) belongs to every \(b\), the proposition at issue is not shown. To show that it does not belong to every \(b\), the same hypothesis must be assumed. For if \(a\) belongs to every \(b\), while \(c\) belongs to some \(b\), \(a\) belongs to some \(c\); but this was not the case. Therefore it is false that \(a\) belongs to every \(b\), and consequently it is true that it does not belong to every \(b\).

If it is supposed to belong to some \(b\), the result will be the same as in the cases already discussed. It is therefore clear that in all syllogisms through the impossible the opposite must be supposed. It is also clear that in the middle figure the affirmative is shown in a certain way, and in the final figure the universal proposition.

## CHAPTER XIV. How the demonstrative proof differs from the proof leading to the impossible

[Col. 0700A]

The demonstration leading to the impossible differs from the ostensive demonstration in that it posits what it intends to refute and leads to an acknowledged falsehood, whereas the ostensive demonstration begins from acknowledged and true propositions.

Both therefore assume two acknowledged propositions; but the one takes both as premises from which a syllogism follows, while the other takes one of these and the contradiction of the conclusion as its premises. Hence in the former case it is not necessary that the conclusion already be known, or that one previously believe either that it is or that it is not; in the latter case it is necessary to know that it is not.

It makes no difference whether the conclusion is affirmative or negative, for the situation is the same in both cases.

[Col. 0700B]

Everything concluded ostensively can also be shown through the impossible, and everything shown through the impossible can be shown ostensively, using the same terms, though not in the same figures. When a syllogism through the impossible is produced in the first figure, what is true will be found in the middle or in the final figure: the negative conclusion in the middle figure, and the affirmative in the final figure. When the syllogism is produced in the middle figure, what is true will be found in the first figure in all the propositions. When the syllogism is produced in the final figure, what is true will be found in the first and middle figures: the affirmative in the first, and the negative in the middle.

Suppose, then, that it has been shown through the first figure that \(a\) belongs to no \(b\), or does not belong to every \(b\). The hypothesis was that \(a\) belongs to some \(b\); the other proposition assumed was that \(a\) belongs to every \(c\), while \(b\) belongs to no \(c\), for in this way the syllogism leading to the impossible was produced.

[Col. 0700C]

This is the middle figure if \(c\) belongs to every \(a\), while \(b\) belongs to no \(a\); and from these premises it is evident that \(b\) belongs to no \(a\). The same applies if it has been shown that \(a\) does not belong to every \(b\). The hypothesis is that \(a\) belongs to every \(b\); \(a\!-\!c\) is assumed universally, and \(b\!-\!c\) not universally. If the proposition assumed is negative, \(c\!-\!a\), the same result follows, for in this way also the middle figure is produced.

Again, suppose that it has been shown that \(a\) belongs to some \(b\). The hypothesis is that it belongs to no \(b\); \(b\) is assumed to belong to every \(c\), and \(a\) either to every or to some \(c\), for in this way the impossible will follow.

This is the final figure if \(a\) and \(b\) belong to every \(c\); and from these premises it is evident that \(a\) must belong to some \(b\). The same applies if \(b\) or \(a\) is taken to belong to some \(c\).

[Col. 0700D]

Again, suppose in the middle figure that it has been shown that \(a\) belongs to every \(b\). The hypothesis was that \(a\) does not belong to every \(b\); \(a\) is assumed to belong to every \(c\), and \(c\) to every \(b\), for in this way the impossible results.

This is the first figure, if \(a\) belongs to every \(c\), and \(c\) to every \(b\). The same applies if it has been shown that \(a\) belongs to some \(b\). The hypothesis was that \(a\) belongs to no \(b\); \(a\) is assumed to belong to every \(c\), and \(c\) to some \(b\).

[Col. 0701A]

If the syllogism is negative, the hypothesis is that \(a\) belongs to some \(b\); \(a\) is assumed to belong to no \(c\), and \(c\) to every \(b\), and thus the first figure results. The same applies if the syllogism is not universal but it has been shown that \(a\) does not belong to some \(b\). The hypothesis is that \(a\) belongs to every \(b\); \(a\) is assumed to belong to no \(c\), and \(c\) to some \(b\), and thus the first figure results.

Again, suppose in the third figure that it has been shown that \(a\) belongs to every \(b\). The hypothesis was that \(a\) does not belong to every \(b\); \(c\) is assumed to belong to every \(b\), and \(a\) to every \(c\), for in this way the impossible follows. This is the first figure.

The same applies if the demonstration concerns some particular case. The hypothesis is that \(a\) belongs to no \(b\); \(c\) is assumed to belong to some \(b\), and \(a\) to every \(c\).

If the syllogism is negative, the hypothesis is that \(a\) belongs to some \(b\); \(c\) is assumed to belong to no \(a\), and to every \(b\). This is the middle figure. The same applies if the demonstration is not universal, for the hypothesis is that \(a\) belongs to every \(b\); \(c\) is assumed to belong to no \(a\), and to some \(b\). This too is the middle figure.

It is therefore clear that, using the same terms, each proposition can be demonstrated both ostensively and through the impossible. Likewise, when the syllogisms are ostensive, it is possible to lead them to the impossible using the terms assumed, when the opposite proposition has been taken as the conclusion. For the same syllogisms result as those produced through conversion. Hence we immediately possess the figures through which each proposition will follow.

[Col. 0701B]

It is clear, then, that every proposition is shown in both ways, through the impossible and ostensively, and that one cannot be separated from the other.

## CHAPTER XV. On reasoning from opposite propositions

In which figure it is possible to syllogize from opposite propositions, and in which it is not, will become clear as follows.

By “opposite propositions” I mean, in linguistic form, four pairs: “belongs to every” and “belongs to none”; “belongs to every” and “does not belong to every”; “belongs to some” and “belongs to none”; and “belongs to some” and “does not belong to some.” In truth, however, there are three pairs, since “belongs to some” and “does not belong to some” are opposed only in expression.

[Col. 0701C]

Among these, the universal propositions “belongs to every” and “belongs to none” are contrary—for example, “all knowledge is commendable” and “no knowledge is commendable”; the others are contradictory opposites.

In the first figure, therefore, there is no syllogism from opposite propositions, either affirmative or negative. There is no affirmative syllogism because both propositions must be affirmative, whereas opposites consist of affirmation and negation. There is no negative syllogism because the opposites predicate and deny the same thing of the same subject, whereas in the first figure the middle term is not predicated of both: of one extreme something else is denied, while of the other the same thing is affirmed. These propositions, therefore, are not opposites.

## CHAPTER XVI. On reasoning from opposite propositions in the second figure

[Col. 0701D]

In the middle figure it is possible to produce a syllogism both from opposites and from contraries.

Let \(a\) be “good,” and let \(b\) and \(c\) be “knowledge.” If, then, one assumes both that all knowledge is commendable and that no knowledge is commendable, \(a\) belongs to every \(b\) and to no \(c\); therefore \(b\) belongs to no \(c\), and thus no knowledge is knowledge.

The same applies if, taking all commendable things as one term, one takes medicine as not commendable. For then \(a\) belongs to every \(b\), but to no \(c\), and therefore some knowledge will not be knowledge.

Again, if \(a\) belongs to every \(c\), but to no \(b\), let \(b\) be knowledge, \(c\) medicine, and \(a\) opinion. For by taking no knowledge to be opinion, one has taken some knowledge to be opinion.

[Col. 0702A]

This differs from the preceding case in that the affirmative proposition is converted with respect to the terms: previously it was related to \(b\), but now to \(c\). If one proposition is not universal, the same applies. The middle term is always that which is negatively predicated of one term and affirmatively predicated of the other.

Therefore it is possible to establish opposites, but not always or in every case. The terms falling under the middle must stand either as identical with one another or as whole to part. Otherwise it is impossible, for the propositions will in no way be either contrary or opposite.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the syllogism from opposite propositions in the third figure

In the third figure there will never be an affirmative syllogism from opposite propositions, for the reason stated in connection with the first figure.

There will, however, be a negative syllogism, both with universal and with non-universal terms. Let \(b\) and \(c\) be knowledge, and \(a\) medicine. If, then, one takes both that every medicine is knowledge and that no medicine is knowledge, \(b\) belongs to every \(a\), and \(c\) to no \(a\); therefore some knowledge will not be knowledge.

[Col. 0702B]

The same applies if the proposition \(a\!-\!b\) is not taken universally. For if some medicine is knowledge, and again no medicine is knowledge, it follows that some knowledge is not knowledge.

When the terms are taken universally, the propositions are contrary; when one is particular, they are opposites.

It must be understood that one can take opposites in the way described: “all knowledge is commendable,” and again “no knowledge,” or “some knowledge,” is commendable. This does not usually escape notice. One proposition can be syllogized through other questions, and assumed in the manner described in the *Topics*.

Since there are three oppositions among affirmations, opposites can be assumed in six ways: “every” and “none”; “every” and “not every”; or “some” and “none.” These can also be reversed with respect to the terms—for example, \(a\) belongs to every \(b\) and to no \(c\), or to every \(c\) and to no \(b\); or to the one universally and to the other not universally; and again with the terms reversed. The same applies in the third figure.

[Col. 0702C]

It is therefore clear both how many times and in which figures a syllogism from opposite propositions can be produced.

It is also clear that a true conclusion can be syllogized from false premises, as was said earlier. But this is not so from opposite propositions, for the syllogism is always contrary to the thing itself—for example, “good is not good,” or “animal is not animal”—because the syllogism proceeds from a contradiction, and the terms of the subject are either identical or one is the whole and the other a part.

It is also clear that in paralogisms nothing prevents a contradiction of the hypothesis from arising, as when one assumes that an odd number is not odd. For from opposite propositions a contrary syllogism will result; if one reasons in this way, the contradiction of the hypothesis follows.

[Col. 0702D]

One must consider that it is not possible in this way to conclude the contrary from a single syllogism—for example, that something good is not good, or some other such conclusion—unless a proposition of that kind is immediately assumed, such as that every animal is both white and not white, while man is an animal. Rather, one must either assume the contradiction, as that all knowledge is both opinion and not opinion, and then assume that medicine is knowledge but not opinion, as refutations are constructed; or proceed through two syllogisms.

Therefore, what has been assumed is contrary in truth only in the manner previously described.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On begging the question

To beg and accept the principle is, generally speaking, to assume in what is not a demonstration the proposition that is to be demonstrated. This occurs in several ways: when no syllogism is produced at all; when the demonstration proceeds through things less known or equally unknown; and when what is prior is demonstrated through what is posterior, since demonstration proceeds from prior and better-known things.

[Col. 0703A]

None of these, however, is strictly begging the principle. The reason is that some things are naturally known through themselves, while others are known through them: principles are known through themselves, whereas what falls under the principles is known through other things. Whenever someone attempts to demonstrate through itself something that is not known through itself, then the principle is begged.

This may be done by immediately demanding the proposition at issue. It may also be done by passing over the propositions that are naturally demonstrated through the relevant things and demonstrating them through what they themselves are naturally used to demonstrate. For example, if \(a\) is shown through \(b\), \(b\) through \(c\), and \(c\) is naturally shown through \(a\), those who syllogize in this way end up demonstrating \(a\) through itself. The same occurs with those who think they are constructing parallel lines: they fail to notice that they are assuming propositions that they cannot demonstrate, since the lines are not parallel.

[Col. 0703B]

Therefore those who syllogize in this way end up saying that each thing is what it is; and in this way everything would be known through itself, which is impossible.

Suppose, then, that someone is in doubt and assumes, as though certain, that \(a\) belongs to \(c\), and likewise that \(b\) belongs to \(c\), while demanding that \(i\) belong to \(b\). It is not yet clear that he has begged the principle; but it is clear that he has not demonstrated it, since the supposed principle of the demonstration is itself equally uncertain.

If \(b\) stands to \(c\) in such a way that they are identical, or that it is evident that they are convertible, or that one belongs to the other, then the principle is begged. For he will demonstrate that \(a\) belongs to \(b\) through those terms if they are convertible; but this is prohibited by the subject matter, not by the method.

[Col. 0703C]

If he proceeds in this way, he will do what has been described and will convert through three terms. The same applies if he assumes that \(b\) belongs to \(c\), when this too is equally uncertain. Thus, even if \(a\) belongs to \(c\), he has not yet begged the principle, but neither has he demonstrated it.

If \(a\) and \(b\) are identical, or if they are convertible, or if \(a\) follows \(b\), he begs the principle for the same reason. We previously established that what is not evident through itself will be shown through itself.

[Col. 0703D]

If begging the principle consists in showing through itself what is not evident through itself, this occurs when what is demonstrated and what demonstrates are equally doubtful—either because the same things are assumed to belong to the same things, or because the same thing is assumed to belong to the same things.

In the middle and third figures, begging the principle can occur alike in both propositions in affirmative syllogisms; in the third and first figures it can occur negatively when the same thing is denied of the same thing, though the two propositions are not alike. It likewise occurs in the middle figure, because the terms are not convertible in negative syllogisms.

Begging the principle occurs in demonstrations that proceed according to truth; in dialectical arguments, it occurs according to opinion.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the falsehood not arising because of this

The expression “the falsehood does not arise because of this,” which we often use in disputes, applies first to syllogisms leading to the impossible, when the proposition leading to the impossible contradicts what has been demonstrated. For one who does not contradict does not say “not because of this,” but rather that some earlier proposition is false. Nor does the expression apply to an ostensive argument, since such an argument does not posit the contradictory proposition.

[Col. 0704A]

Moreover, when something is refuted ostensively through \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\), one cannot say that the syllogism was produced “not because of” the proposition posited. We say that something occurs “not because of this” when, after that proposition has been refuted, the syllogism nevertheless remains complete. This does not happen in ostensive demonstrations: once a proposition has been refuted, the syllogism depending on it no longer exists.

It is therefore clear that the expression is used with arguments leading to the impossible, when the hypothesis bears such a relation to the impossible that, whether it is present or absent, the impossible nevertheless results.

[Col. 0704B]

The clearest case in which the falsehood does not arise because of the supposition is when the syllogism leading to the impossible is disconnected from the hypothesis by the intervening middle terms, as was said in the *Topics*. To posit as a cause what is not a cause is precisely this.

For example, if someone wishes to show that the diagonal is incommensurable, but attempts to establish by Zeno’s argument that motion does not exist and then derives an impossibility from this, the falsehood is in no way connected with the original proposition.

Another case occurs when the impossible is connected with the hypothesis, but does not arise because of it. This can happen both when one takes the connecting sequence below and when one takes it above. Suppose that \(a\) is posited as belonging to \(b\), \(b\) to \(c\), and \(c\) to \(d\), while it is false that \(b\) belongs to \(d\). If, after \(a\) is removed, \(b\) still belongs to \(c\), and \(c\) to \(d\), the falsehood will not arise because of the original hypothesis.

[Col. 0704C]

Again, someone may take the connecting sequence above: \(a\) belongs to \(b\), \(e\) to \(a\), and \(f\) to \(e\), while it is false that \(f\) belongs to \(a\). Here too the impossible remains after the original hypothesis has been refuted.

One must connect the impossible to the terms that derive from the original hypothesis; in this way it will arise because of the hypothesis. In the lower sequence, this means connecting it to the predicate term. For if it is impossible that \(a\) belong to \(d\), then after \(a\) is removed the falsehood no longer remains. In the upper sequence, it must be connected to the subject of predication. For if it is impossible that \(f\) belong to \(b\), then after \(b\) is removed the impossibility no longer remains. The same applies when the syllogisms are negative.

[Col. 0704D]

It is therefore clear that, when the impossible does not attach to the prior terms, the falsehood does not arise because of the original positing.

But is the falsehood then always caused by the hypothesis? Suppose that \(a\) is posited as belonging not to \(b\) but to \(k\), and \(k\) to \(c\), and \(c\) to \(d\); the impossible nevertheless remains. The same applies when the terms are taken in the upward sequence. Therefore, since the impossible results both when the hypothesis is present and when it is absent, the falsehood does not arise because of the positing.

One must not take the case in which an impossible results after some other proposition has been posited, but the case in which, after this proposition has been removed, the same impossibility is concluded through the remaining propositions. There is perhaps nothing strange in the same falsehood arising through several hypotheses—for example, that parallel lines meet, or that the inner angle is greater than the outer, or that a triangle has more than two right angles.

[Col. 0705A]

## CHAPTER XX. On false reasoning, counter-syllogism—that is, counter-reasoning—and refutation

A false argument arises because of the first falsehood. For every syllogism proceeds from either two propositions or more. If it proceeds from two, one or both of these must be false, since a false syllogism does not arise from true propositions. If it proceeds from more than two—for example, one part through \(a\) and \(b\), another through \(d\), \(f\), and \(g\)—some proposition among the higher ones will be false, and because of it the argument will be false. For \(a\) and \(b\) are concluded through those propositions; therefore the conclusion and its falsehood arise because of some one of them.

[Col. 0705B]

Those advancing the argument must try to conceal from respondents what we have instructed the latter to guard against. This will happen, first, if they do not syllogize the conclusions beforehand, but, after the necessary propositions have been assumed, the conclusions are not evident.

To avoid being counter-syllogized, one must be attentive when the argument is questioned without its conclusions being stated, so that the same proposition is not granted twice among the premises. We know that no syllogism is produced without a middle term, and the middle term is what is most often stated.

[Col. 0705C]

How one must attend to the middle term for each conclusion is clear from knowing what is demonstrated in each figure. This will not escape us, since we see how the argument is being supplied.

Further, the questions should not be asked in close succession, but as far apart as possible from the middle terms. For example, if one needs to conclude \(a\), \(d\), \(e\), and \(f\), with \(b\), \(e\), \(d\), and \(e\) as middle terms, one should inquire whether \(a\) belongs to \(b\), and then not whether \(b\) belongs to \(e\), but whether \(d\) belongs to \(e\), followed by whether \(b\) belongs to \(c\), and so on. If there is a syllogism through one middle term, one should begin with that middle term, for in this way the respondent will be most effectively kept unaware.

[Col. 0705D]

Since we know when and under what arrangement of terms a syllogism is produced, it is also clear when a refutation will and will not occur. With all affirmative answers, or with answers arranged alternately—one affirmative and the other negative—a refutation can result. For there will be a syllogism, and it will be produced when the terms stand in that arrangement. Therefore, if what has been posited is contrary to the conclusion, a refutation must result, since a refutation is a syllogism of contradiction.

[Col. 0706A]

But if nothing is affirmed, it is impossible for a refutation to result. There was no syllogism when all the terms were negative, and therefore there is no refutation. For if there is a refutation, there must be a syllogism; but when there is a syllogism, it does not necessarily follow that there is a refutation.

The same applies if nothing has been posited universally in accordance with the answers. For the definition of a syllogism and of a refutation will be the same.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the fallacy according to opinion
Sometimes, just as we were mistaken in the arrangement of the terms, a fallacy also arises according to opinion. This happens when the same thing belongs essentially to several subjects, while one person is unaware that it belongs to one of them and believes that it belongs to none, but knows that it belongs to another. For example, let *a* belong essentially to *b* and *c*, and let these likewise belong universally to every *d*. If, then, someone believes that *b* belongs to every *a*, and that this is true of *d*, but believes that *c* belongs to no *a*, and that this too is true of every *d*, he will possess knowledge and ignorance of the same thing in the same respect.

Again, one may be mistaken about things belonging to the same chain of predication. Suppose *a* belongs to *b*, *b* to *c*, and *c* to *d*, but someone believes that *a* belongs to every *b* and, again, to no *c*. He will simultaneously know and fail to believe that it belongs. Thus he thinks nothing other than what he knows, but does not believe it; for in some manner he knows that *a* belongs to *c* through *b*, as the particular is contained in the universal. Therefore, what he knows in some manner he altogether believes that he does not believe—which is impossible.

In the case mentioned earlier, if the middle term is not from the same chain of predication, it is impossible for him to believe both propositions on the basis of each of the two middle terms: for example, that *a* belongs universally to *b*, but to no *c*, while both of these belong universally to *d*. Yet it may happen that he takes the first proposition as contrary, either absolutely or in some respect. If he believes that *b* belongs to everything to which *a* belongs, and knows that *b* belongs to *d*, and also knows that *a* belongs to *d*, then, if he again believes that *c* belongs to nothing to which *a* belongs, he will not believe that *a* belongs to something to which *b* belongs. But what he believes universally of everything to which *b* belongs, he will once more fail to believe of some thing to which *b* belongs—or, absolutely, he will believe the contrary. Thus it is not possible for him to hold these opinions.

On the basis of both middle terms taken together, however, or of both propositions on the basis of one of them, nothing prevents him from believing that *a* belongs to every *b*, that *b* belongs to *d*, and again that *a* belongs to no *c*. A similar fallacy occurs in the case of particulars, just as we are mistaken about them. If *a* belongs to every *b*, and *b* to every *c*, then *a* will belong to every *c*. If, therefore, someone knows that *a* belongs to everything to which *b* belongs, he also knows that it belongs to what is *c*. Yet nothing prevents him from being ignorant that *c* exists. For example, let *a* be having two right angles, *b* be a triangle, and *c* be a perceptible triangle. Someone may believe that *c* does not exist while knowing that every triangle has two right angles. Thus he will simultaneously know and be ignorant of the same thing. For knowing that every triangle has two right angles is not simple: in one respect he has universal knowledge, but in the other he has knowledge of an individual.

Thus, universally, he knows that *c* has two right angles, but individually he does not know it; therefore he does not possess contrary beliefs. The same is true of the argument in the *Meno*, namely, that learning is recollection. We never happen to know an individual in advance; rather, by induction we acquire knowledge of particulars together, as though recognizing them. For some things, once we know them, we immediately know them—for example, that something has two right angles, if we know that it is a triangle—and the same applies in other cases.

Thus, we contemplate particulars universally, but do not know them in their own individuality. We may therefore be mistaken about them—not contrarily, but by possessing universal knowledge while being deceived about the particular. The same applies to the cases mentioned above. For the knowledge that proceeds through a middle term is not contrary to the knowledge that proceeds through a syllogism; nor is the opinion based on both middle terms contrary. Nothing prevents someone who knows both that *a* belongs to the whole of *b*, and that *b* belongs to the whole of *c*, from believing that *a* does not belong to *c*. For example, knowing that every mule is sterile and seeing this animal to be a mule, he may believe that this mule is pregnant. He does not know that this is *a* and that this is *c*, since he does not perceive the connection established through both middle terms.

It is therefore clear that even if someone knows one thing but does not know another, he will be deceived in the relation between universal and particular knowledge. We do not know any sensible object when it is outside perception; nor, even when we are perceiving it, do we know it except universally, and in the respect in which it possesses its proper knowledge—not in its actual realization. For “knowing” is said in three ways: universally, individually, or in actuality. Deception therefore also occurs in these three ways. Nothing prevents someone from both knowing and being deceived about the same thing, although not contrariwise.

The same occurs in someone who knows both propositions but has not previously worked through them. For someone who believes that a mule is pregnant does not possess knowledge in actuality, nor does he have, because of this opinion, a fallacy contrary to knowledge. The syllogism is contrary to the fallacy in the universal case.

But someone who believes that being good is being bad will believe the same thing to be both good and bad. Let being good be represented by *a*, being bad by *b*, and again being good by *c*. Since, then, he believes that the same thing is both *b* and *c*, he will believe that *c* is *b*, and similarly that *b* is *a*; consequently, he will also believe that *c* is *a*. Just as, if it were true of *c* that it is *b*, and of *b* that it is *a*, it would be true of *c* that it is *a*, so too in the case of opinion.

The same applies to being. Since *c* and *b* are the same, and again *b* and *a* are the same, *c* and *a* will be the same; and the same follows in opinion. This conclusion is necessary if someone grants the first premise. But perhaps it is false for someone to believe that being bad is being good except accidentally. For it is possible to hold this belief in several ways; this must be examined more carefully.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Conversion of Terms

When the extremes are converted, the middle term must also be converted with respect to both. For if *a* belongs to *c* through *b*, then, if the relation is converted and *a* belongs to everything to which it belongs, *c* and *b* are converted with respect to *a*; and *b* belongs to everything to which *a* belongs through the middle term *c*, while *c* is converted with *b* through *a*.

The same applies in the case of non-being. If *b* belongs to *c*, but *a* does not belong to *b*, then *a* will not belong to *c*. If, therefore, *b* is converted with respect to *a*, *c* will also be converted with respect to *a*. Let *b* belong to no *a*; then neither will *c*, since *b* belonged to every *c*. And if *b* is converted with respect to *c*, *a* will also be converted with respect to *c*. For whatever *b* belongs to, *c* also belongs to; and whatever *c* belongs to, *a* does not belong to. If *c* is converted with respect to *a*, then *b* will also be converted with respect to *a*. For whatever *b* belongs to, *c* also belongs; but wherever *c* belongs, *a* does not belong. Only this conversion begins from the conclusion; the others do not work in the same way, as in a predicative syllogism.

Again, if *a* and *b* are converted, and likewise *c* and *d*, while universally either *a* or *c* belongs, then *b* and *d* will also stand in such a relation that one belongs universally. For if *a* belongs to *b*, and *c* to *d*, and universally either *a* or *c* belongs, but not both simultaneously, it is clear that universally either *b* or *d* belongs, but not both. Thus, if what is ungenerated is incorruptible, and what is incorruptible is ungenerated, then what is generated must be corruptible, and what is corruptible generated. Two syllogisms have thereby been established.

Again, if universally either *a* or *b*, and either *c* or *d*, belong, but do not belong simultaneously, then, if *a* and *c* are converted, *b* and *d* will also be converted. For if *b* does not belong to something to which *d* belongs, it is clear that *a* belongs to it. But if *a* belongs, so does *c*, since they are converted; consequently *c* and *d* would belong simultaneously, which is impossible.

When *a* belongs to the whole of *b* and *c*, and is predicated of nothing else, while *b* belongs to every *c*, *a* and *b* must be converted. Since *a* is said of only *b* and *c*, while *b* is predicated both of itself and of *c*, it is clear that wherever *a* is said, *b* will also be said; and this will be true of every instance of *a*.

Again, when *a* and *b* belong to the whole of *c*, and *c* is converted with *b*, *a* must belong to every *b*. For *a* belongs to every *c*, and *c* belongs to *b* because they are converted; therefore *a* will belong to every *b*.

When two opposites are given—say, *a* is more choiceworthy than *b*, since they are opposites, and *d* is likewise more choiceworthy than *c*—if *a* and *c* are more choiceworthy than *b* and *d*, then *a* is more choiceworthy than *d*. For *a* is to be pursued and *b* avoided, since they are opposites; likewise *c* is opposed to *d*. If, then, *a* is to be chosen in preference to *d*, and *b* is to be avoided in preference to *c*, since each is to be avoided in the same way as the other is to be chosen, both *a* and *c* will be more choiceworthy than *b* and *d*. But they cannot be so in the same degree, since then *b* and *d* would also be equal.

If *d* is more choiceworthy than *a*, and *b* less avoidable than *c*, then what is less is opposed to what is less. But what is more choiceworthy is the greater good and the lesser evil, rather than the lesser good and the greater evil. Thus *b* and *d* as a whole would be more choiceworthy than *a* and *c*. But this is not the case. Therefore *a* is more choiceworthy than *d*, and *c* is less avoidable than *b*.

If every lover chooses, in accordance with love, that *a* should have such a relation as agreeing rather than not agreeing, represented by *c*, or agreeing rather than not being such as to agree, represented by *b*, it is clear that being such as *a* is more choiceworthy than agreeing. Therefore being loved is, in accordance with love, more choiceworthy than association; hence love is greater in friendship than association.

But if this is the supreme object, and this is the end, then agreement either does not exist at all or exists for the sake of being loved; for other desires and arts also arise in this way. How terms stand in conversions, and likewise in what is more to be avoided or more to be chosen, is therefore clear.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On *Epagōgē*, That Is, Induction

Since not only dialectical and demonstrative syllogisms are produced through the figures mentioned above, but also rhetorical syllogisms and, in general, every kind of persuasion, as well as the reasoning used in each art, this must now be discussed.

We believe everything either through a syllogism or through induction. If, then, there is induction, there is also an inductive syllogism: one syllogizes through one extreme by means of the other extreme. For example, if *b* is the middle term of the things represented by *a* and *c*, one proves through *c* that *a* belongs to *b*. This is how we conduct inductions.

Let *a* be long-lived, *b* be not having bile, and *c* consist of particular long-lived things, such as a human being, a horse, and a mule. Thus *a* belongs to the whole of *b*, for everything that does not have bile is long-lived; and not having bile belongs to every *c*. If, therefore, *c* is converted with *b*, and the middle term does not exceed the range of the particulars, *c* must belong to *b*.

It was previously shown that if two things belong to the same subject, and one of them is converted, the other will also belong when the predicate is converted. One must understand *c* as composed of all the particulars, for induction proceeds through all of them.

A syllogism of this kind belongs to a first and immediate proposition. Where there is a middle term, the syllogism proceeds through the middle; where there is none, it proceeds by induction. In a certain way induction is opposed to syllogism: the latter proves an extreme of a third term through the middle term, whereas the former proves an extreme of the middle term through a third term. By nature, therefore, the syllogism through the middle is prior and more knowable; but for us the syllogism through induction is clearer.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Paradigm, That Is, the Example

An example occurs when an extreme is shown to belong to the middle through something similar to a third term. The middle term must also be known to belong to the third term, and the first term to belong to the similar case.

Let *a* be bad, *b* be making war against neighboring peoples, *c* be the Athenians making war against the Thebans, and *d* be the Thebans making war against the Phocians. If, then, we wish to show that it is bad for the Thebans to make war, we must take as a premise that making war against neighboring peoples is bad. The credibility of this is derived from similar cases—for example, from the fact that it was bad for the Thebans to make war against the Phocians.

Since making war against neighboring peoples is bad, and making war against the Thebans is making war against neighboring peoples, it is clear that making war against the Thebans is bad. Since *b* belongs to both *c* and *d*, this is clear: both involve making war against neighboring peoples. It is also clear that *a* belongs to *d*, since it was not advantageous for the Thebans to make war against the Phocians.

That *a* belongs to *b* will be shown through *d*. The same applies if credibility is established through several similar cases, from the middle term to the extreme.

It is therefore clear that an example is neither a relation of whole to part nor of part to whole, but of part to part, when both fall under the same thing while one of them is known. It differs from induction because induction showed the extreme to belong to the middle from all the individual cases and did not connect the syllogism to the extreme, whereas the example both connects it and does not establish it from all the cases.

## CHAPTER XXV. On *Apagōgē*, or Deduction

Deduction occurs when it is clear that the first term belongs to the middle, but that the middle belongs to the last term is doubtful, although equally credible with, or more credible than, the conclusion.

It also occurs when there are fewer middle terms between the last term and the middle term, since in that case the relation happens to be closer to knowledge. Let *a* be teachable, *b* be learning, and *c* be justice. It is clear that learning is teachable; but whether justice is learning is doubtful. If, then, *b*–*c* is equally or more credible than *a*–*c*, this is deduction, since it is closer to knowledge through the assumption by which they took *a*–*c*, although they did not previously possess learning.

Again, deduction occurs if there are fewer middle terms between *b* and *c*, since this too is closer to knowledge. Let *d* be quadrangular, *e* rectilinear, and *f* a circle. If there is only one middle term between *e* and *f*, then proving through lunar figures that a circle is equal to a rectilinear figure will be closer to knowledge.

But when *b*–*c* is neither more credible than *a*–*c* nor accompanied by fewer middle terms, I do not call it deduction. Nor do I call it deduction when *b*–*c* is immediate, since what is immediate is knowledge.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Objection, Called *Enstasis*

An objection is a proposition contrary to another proposition. It differs from a proposition because an objection may be particular, whereas a proposition either cannot be particular at all or, in universal syllogisms, is not particular.

An objection is advanced in two ways and through two figures. It is advanced in two ways because every objection is either universal or particular; and through two figures because the propositions opposed to the original proposition are completed only in the first and third figures.

When someone demands that something belong universally, we object either that it belongs to nothing or that it does not belong to something. The first of these proceeds from the first figure, the second from the last figure.

Let *a* be one science, and *b* be contraries. Someone proposes, then, that there is one science of contraries. We object either that there is not one science of opposites at all; since contraries are opposites, this produces the first figure. Or we object that there is not one science of the known and the unknown; this produces the third figure. For according to the third figure it is true that the known and the unknown are contraries, but false that they have one science.

The same applies in a privative proposition. When someone demands that there not be one science of contraries, we object either that there is one science of all opposites, or that there is one science of some contraries, such as the healthy and the sick. The first objection proceeds from the first figure, the second from the third.

In general, in every universal objection, one must state the contradiction of the universal proposition—for example, if someone believes that there is not one science of all contraries, one must assert that there is one science of opposites. This must be in the first figure, since the middle term becomes universal in relation to what follows from the original premise.

But when the objection is universal only in relation to a particular case, it is called a proposition—for example, that the known and the unknown do not have the same science. Here the universal is contrariness in relation to those terms, and the third figure results, since the middle term is taken particularly, namely, the known and the unknown.

We attempt to state objections from the same terms from which we syllogize the contrary. Therefore we advance them only through these figures, since only in them are opposing syllogisms possible. In the middle figure it was not possible to affirm.

Moreover, even if such an objection were possible, it would require a very extensive argument, as in the middle figure. For example, if someone does not concede that *a* belongs to *b* because *c* does not follow from it, this would be made clear through other propositions. An objection should not require conversion to other propositions; it should immediately have the other proposition evident. For this reason there is no sign from this figure alone.

The other objections must also be examined: those arising from contraries, similarities, and opinion, and whether it is possible to take a particular objection from the first figure or a privative one from the middle figure.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Likely Sign, the Evidentiary Sign, and the Enthymeme

The likely sign and the evidentiary sign are not the same. The likely sign is a probable proposition. What people know to happen, not to happen, to exist, or not to exist in most cases is a likely sign—for example, that envious people hate, or that lovers cherish.

A sign, however, is intended to be a demonstrative proposition, whether necessary or probable. When one thing exists, another exists; or when one thing has occurred, another occurs earlier or later. Such a relation is a sign that the latter thing has occurred or exists.

An enthymeme, then, is an imperfect syllogism based on likely signs and evidentiary signs.

A sign is taken in three ways, according to the three figures: either in the first, the middle, or the third. For example, to show that a woman has given birth because she has milk proceeds through the first figure. The middle term is having milk: *a* is giving birth, *b* is having milk, and *c* is a woman.

To show that the wise are industrious because Pittacus is industrious proceeds through the last figure: *a* is industrious, *b* is wise, and *c* is Pittacus. It is true that *a* and *b* are predicated of *c*, but they do not state the first proposition because it is known; they assume the second.

To show that she has given birth because she is pale is intended to proceed through the middle figure. Since pallor accompanies women who have given birth, and this woman too has pallor, they believe that it has been shown that she has given birth. Let pallor be *a*, giving birth *b*, and a woman *c*.

If only one proposition is stated, there is merely a sign; if the other is also assumed, there is a syllogism. For example: Pittacus is generous, because ambitious people are generous and Pittacus is ambitious. Or again: the wise are good, and Pittacus is good and also wise. In this way syllogisms are formed.

The syllogism through the first figure is incontrovertible, if it is true, since it is universal. The one through the last figure is refutable: even if its conclusion is true, it is not universal, since it belongs to the third figure. Nor is it relevant as a syllogism, for if Pittacus is industrious, it does not follow that other people must therefore be wise.

The syllogism through the middle figure is always and altogether refutable, for no syllogism results when the terms stand in this relation. If what has given birth is pale, and this woman is pale, it does not follow that this woman has given birth.

The sign is therefore true in all the figures, but the differences just stated belong to them.

Should the sign, then, be divided in this way? Among these, the middle term should be taken as the proof, for a proof is said to be that which makes something known, and such is especially the middle term. Or should the inferences from the extremes be called signs, and that through the middle a proof? The most probable and most genuinely true sign is the one proceeding through the first figure.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Physiognomic Syllogism

It is possible to know natures if one grants that body and soul undergo change together in all the natural passions. Someone who learns music may perhaps change in some respect in soul, but this is not a passion among those naturally inherent in us; rather, it belongs to anger, desire, and natural movements.

If this too is granted, together with the principle that one sign belongs to one thing, and if we can identify the proper passion and sign of each genus, we shall be able to know natures.

For if a passion belongs specifically to an individual of some genus—for example, courage to lions—there must also be some sign, since things posited together are naturally associated. Let this sign be having large extremities, which also occurs in other genera, though not throughout them.

The sign is proper in this way because the passion is proper to the whole genus, not merely to one individual, as we ordinarily say. The same sign will therefore occur in another genus, and there will be a courageous human being and some other courageous animal. Each will therefore possess the sign, since there was one sign for one thing.

If these conditions hold, we shall be able to collect such signs among animals that possess only one distinctive passion; each passion has its sign, and since each thing must have one sign, we shall be able to know their natures.

But if an entire genus possesses two distinctive characteristics—for example, a lion is both courageous and sociable—how shall we know which of the signs belongs to which characteristic among the signs that properly follow? Perhaps we can determine this if both characteristics do not belong throughout another genus, and in those cases where they do not both belong throughout, one characteristic is present while the other is absent. For if something is courageous but not generous, and it possesses one of the two signs, it is clear that this sign is also, in the lion, the sign of courage.

Knowledge of natures occurs in the first figure because the middle term is converted with the first extreme, while the third term is exceeded and is not converted. Let courage be *a*, having large extremities *b*, and a lion *c*. Thus, whatever *c* belongs to, *b* belongs universally; and *b* also belongs to other things, while whatever *b* belongs to, *a* belongs universally, though not to many. If the relation is converted, there will be one sign for one thing; if it is not converted, there will not be one sign for one thing.

[Col. 0711]

# TWO BOOKS OF ARISTOTLE’S POSTERIOR ANALYTICS, TRANSLATED BY ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS (S)

## BOOK ONE

### CHAPTER I. On Things Previously Known

All teaching and all intellectual learning arise from pre-existing knowledge. This is clear to anyone who considers the matter in every field. Mathematical sciences arise in this way, and so does each of the other arts.

The same is true of arguments conducted by syllogism and by induction. Both produce teaching through what is previously known: the former taking its starting point from known things, the latter displaying the universal through what is evident in the particular.

Rhetorical persuasion proceeds similarly, either through examples, which is induction, or through enthymemes, which are syllogisms.

There are two ways in which prior knowledge is necessary. In some cases one must presuppose that the thing exists; in others one must understand what the term means; and in some cases both are necessary. For example, it is necessary to know that it is true to affirm or deny every proposition, and to know that a triangle signifies a certain thing. In the case of a unit, both are required: one must know what it signifies and that it exists. For these are not equally evident to us in every case.

Some things are known only by someone who already knows them; in other cases knowledge is acquired simultaneously. This occurs with whatever happens to fall under universals of which one already has knowledge. One may already know that every triangle has three angles equal to two right angles, but one learns simultaneously that the triangle inscribed in a semicircle is such a triangle.

For some things learning occurs in this way, and the final individual is not known through a middle term, as with whatever belongs to already existing individuals and not to some prior subject.

Before induction or the acquisition of a syllogism, one may perhaps be said to know something in one respect but not in another. Someone who did not know absolutely that the object before him had two right angles nevertheless knew in some way that a triangle has two right angles. It is clear that he knows it universally but does not know it absolutely.

Otherwise the ambiguity described in the *Meno* would arise: either one learns nothing, or one learns only what one already knows. It is not enough, as some attempt to resolve the problem, to ask: “Did you know of every pair that it is even, or did you not?” When the person answers yes, a particular pair is produced which he did not believe to exist, and consequently did not believe to be even.

They resolve the problem by saying that one does not know that every pair is even, but only that the thing one knows to be a pair is even. Yet one does know the object of which one possesses a true demonstration, and the object one has grasped. One has not grasped it as an individual of which one happens to know that it is a triangle or a number, but simply as every number and every triangle.

For one does not accept a proposition about “the number that you know” or “the rectilinear figure that you know,” but about every number and every rectilinear figure.

Nevertheless, nothing, in my view, prevents what someone learns from being both knowledge and ignorance in different respects. There is nothing strange in knowing in some way what one learns; what would be strange is knowing it in precisely the respect in which one is learning it.

### CHAPTER II. On the Ways of Knowing and on Demonstration

We believe that we know each thing simply—not in the sophistical sense, which is accidental—when we think that we know the cause because of which the thing is, that this cause is the cause of it, and that it cannot be otherwise.

It is therefore clear that knowing something of this sort is the relevant kind of knowledge. For those who do not know, as well as those who know, believe that things stand in this way; but those who know also possess knowledge. Therefore, whatever is known simply cannot be otherwise.

If there is another mode of knowing, we shall discuss it later. We say that to know is to understand through demonstration. By “demonstration” I mean an epistemic syllogism—that is, one that produces knowledge. I call it epistemic because, when we possess it, we know according to it.

If knowing is as we have defined it, demonstrative knowledge must arise from things that are true, primary, immediate, more knowable, prior, and causes of the conclusion. In this way the principles will be proper to what is demonstrated. There can be a syllogism without these conditions, but there will not be demonstration, since it will not produce knowledge.

The premises must be true, because what is not cannot be known—for example, that the diameter is commensurable. Demonstration proceeds from primary and indemonstrable premises, because someone who does not possess a demonstration of them cannot know them. To know things of which there is a demonstration, and to know them non-accidentally, is to possess their demonstration.

The premises must also be causes, more knowable, and prior. They must be causes because we know something when we know its cause; they must be prior because they are causes; and they must be more knowable not merely in the sense of understanding them in another way, but in the sense of knowing that they exist.

“Prior” and “more knowable” are used in two ways. What is prior by nature is not the same as what is prior for us, nor is what is more knowable by nature the same as what is more knowable for us.

By what is prior and more knowable for us I mean what is closer to perception. What is prior and more knowable simply is what is farther from perception. The most remote things are the most universal; the nearest are the individual things. These stand opposed to one another.

Demonstration proceeds from primary things, that is, from proper principles; for I identify the primary with the principle. The principle of demonstration is an immediate proposition. An immediate proposition is one for which there is no prior proposition.

A proposition is one part of an enunciation, affirming one thing of one thing. Dialectical reasoning accepts any proposition in this way; demonstrative reasoning determines one as true.

An enunciation is either part of a contradiction. A contradiction is an opposition that has no intermediate term in itself. The part of a contradiction that affirms something of something is an affirmation; the part that removes something from something is a negation.

Among syllogistic principles, I call a position one that cannot be demonstrated and that need not be possessed by someone who is to learn anything. A principle that anyone who is to learn must possess is called an axiom. There are principles of this kind, and this is the name we customarily give them above all.

Of positions, one that takes either part of an enunciation—for example, affirming or denying that something exists—is a supposition. A position without this is a definition, for a definition is itself a kind of position.

The mathematician posits that a unit is indivisible in quantity; this is not a supposition, since “what a unit is” and “that a unit is” are not the same.

Since one must believe and know the thing while possessing the syllogism that we call demonstration, and since demonstration consists of premises, it is necessary to know beforehand not only the primary premises—whether all of them or some—but especially those premises.

For whatever something exists because of, that cause is more important. For example, what we love for the sake of something else is more truly our friend. Therefore, if we know and believe because of the primary principles, we know and believe those principles more strongly, since the posterior conclusions are known and believed because of them.

One cannot believe more strongly what one knows than what one cannot know or be better disposed toward than if one knew it. This would happen unless someone previously knew the principles on account of which those who believe the demonstration believe it. For one must believe the principles—whether all or some—more strongly than the conclusion.

Someone who is to possess knowledge through demonstration must not only know and believe the principles more strongly than the demonstrated conclusion; nothing else must be more credible or more knowable to him than the principles opposed to those from which the syllogism of the contrary deception would arise. For someone who knows simply must be unchangeable.

### CHAPTER III. That Not Everything Is Demonstrative Knowledge

Some people, because they believe that the first principles must be known, think that knowledge does not exist. Others think that it exists but that there are demonstrations of everything. Neither view is true or necessary.

Those who altogether deny knowledge reduce the matter to infinity. They say that posterior things cannot be known through prior things unless there are first principles, and in this they are right: it is impossible to traverse an infinite series. If the series stops and these are principles, they will nevertheless be unknown, since there is no demonstration of them; yet they say that knowing consists only in demonstration.

If it is impossible to know the first principles, then neither can the things derived from them be known, either simply or properly, but only conditionally, provided that the principles exist.

Those who hold the second view agree that knowledge is knowledge only through demonstration, but claim that there is a demonstration of everything. Nothing, they say, prevents demonstration from proceeding in a circle, from things that stand in reciprocal relation to one another.

We, however, shall say that not all knowledge is demonstrative. Knowledge of immediate things is indemonstrable, and that this is necessary is clear. If it is necessary to know the prior things from which demonstration proceeds, and if these ultimately become immediate, then these immediate things must be indemonstrable.

We therefore say not only that there is scientific knowledge, but also that there is a certain principle of knowledge, through which we know the terms.

That circular demonstration is simply impossible is clear if demonstration must proceed from prior and more knowable things. The same things cannot simultaneously be prior and posterior to one another, except in different respects: one set may be prior for us, the other prior simply. In precisely this way induction makes something known.

If this is so, then “knowing simply” will not have been properly defined, but will have two meanings. Or does a different demonstration arise simply from what is more knowable to us?

Those who say that demonstration is circular incur not only the difficulty just stated but also the consequence that they say nothing other than: “If this is, then this is.” In this way everything is easily demonstrated.

It is clear that this occurs when three terms are posited. Whether one says that the circle is produced through many terms or through few makes no difference; through few means through two.

For when *a* is, *b* necessarily is; and when *b* is, *c* is. Therefore, when *a* is, *c* will be. But if, when *a* is, *b* necessarily is, and when *b* is, *a* is, this will be circular. Let *a* be that of which *c* is predicated: to say that, when *b* is, *a* is, is also to say that *c* is. But to say this is to say that, when *a* is, *c* is; and *c* is identical with *a*. Hence those who say that demonstration is circular say nothing other than: “When *a* is, *a* is.” In this way everything could easily be demonstrated.

Yet even this is possible only in things that follow one another reciprocally, as proper attributes do. From one premise alone it has been shown that nothing else follows necessarily. By “one” I mean not one term or one premise, since syllogizing is possible from two primary and minimal premises.

If *a* follows from *b*, and *c* follows from *a*, and these relations hold reciprocally, then if it is possible to demonstrate everything from reciprocal relations in the first figure, this has been shown in the discussions of syllogism.

It has also been shown that in the other figures either no syllogism is formed, or it does not concern the premises that have been accepted. Where the terms are not reciprocally predicated, circular demonstration is wholly impossible.

Since such cases are few in demonstrations, it is clear that it is both futile and impossible to claim that demonstration proceeds from reciprocal relations, and that this is why everything has a demonstration.

### CHAPTER IV. What “Of Every,” “In Itself,” and “Universal” Mean

[Col. 0716C]

Since it is impossible for that which is the object of knowledge simply to be otherwise, it will necessarily be knowable according to demonstrative knowledge. Demonstrative knowledge is the knowledge that we possess when we possess a demonstration; therefore demonstration is from necessary syllogisms. We must accordingly determine from what and of what sort demonstrations arise. First, let us define what we mean by “of every” [universal], “per se,” and “universal.”

By “of every” I mean that something is not true in one case but not in another, nor true at one time but not at another. Thus, if “animal” is predicated of every human being, then if it is true to say “human being,” it is also true to say “animal”; and if one is true now, the other is true now as well. [Col. 0716D] Likewise, if there is a point on every line. The indication of this is that we put forward counterexamples by asking whether the predicate is truly said of every case, or whether it fails in some case, or at some time.

Things are “per se” whenever they belong to a thing’s essence: for example, a line belongs to a triangle, and a point to a line. Their substance consists of these elements, and they are included in the account that states what the thing is. Those features which belong to the things themselves are also included in the account that states what they are: for example, straightness and circularity belong to a line; evenness and oddness, primeness and compositeness belong to number; “equilateral” (isopleurum) and “longer on one side” belong [to the triangle; the transmitted syntax is defective]. and whatever else belongs to these is included in the account stating what the thing is, on the one hand in the case of line, on the other in the case of number. I call each such feature “per se.” [Col. 0717A]

Features that belong to something in neither of these ways are accidental, such as musical or white in the case of an animal. Further, something is per se when it is not predicated of another subject, as “walking” or “white” is, since there is also some other thing that is walking or white. Substance, and whatever signifies a this-something, is not something other than what it is. Thus I call those things that are not predicated of another subject “per se,” and those that are predicated of a subject “accidental.”

In another sense, whatever belongs to each thing because of that thing itself is per se; whatever does not belong to it because of itself is accidental. For example, if a walking person flashed, the flashing would be accidental, since the person did not flash because he walked; this is what we call accidental. But if something that had been killed perished in consequence of being killed, then this would be per se, since it perished because it had been killed, although it is not accidental for what has been killed to perish. [Col. 0717B]

Thus the things that are called per se in objects of knowledge simply speaking are as follows: predicates either are present, or belong to their subjects because of those subjects themselves and necessarily. They cannot fail to be present, either simply or in one of two opposed ways—for example, straight or oblique in the case of a line, and even or odd in the case of number. For in the same genus there is either contrariety, or privation, or contradiction: for example, even and odd in the case of numbers, according to the relation in which one follows the other. Therefore, if it is necessary either to affirm or to deny, then it is also necessary that per se attributes belong to their subjects.

Let this, then, be our determination of “of every” and “per se.” By “universal” I mean that which is both of every subject, per se, and belongs to it insofar as it is itself. It is therefore clear that whatever is universal belongs necessarily to its subjects.

Something belongs per se and insofar as the thing itself is what it is—for example, a point and straightness belong per se to a line, since they belong to it insofar as it is a line; and two right angles belong to a triangle insofar as it is a triangle, since a triangle is per se equal to two right angles.

An attribute is universal when it is demonstrated to belong to every instance, and to the first instance. For example, having two right angles does not belong universally to every figure, although it can be demonstrated that a figure has two right angles; it cannot be demonstrated of every figure, nor does the demonstration use an arbitrary figure. A quadrilateral is indeed a figure, but it is not equal to two right angles; an isosceles figure does have two right angles, but it is not first—the triangle is prior. Whatever is first demonstrated to have two right angles, or anything else, has the universal attribute belonging to it in the primary sense, and the demonstration of this universal is per se. In the case of the other figures, it is universal in a certain respect but not per se. An isosceles figure is not universal in the strict sense, but only in a wider sense.

## CHAPTER V. How error can arise concerning the primary universal

We must not overlook the fact that it is often possible to err, so that what is demonstrated is not the primary universal, although it appears to be demonstrated as the primary universal. We fall into this error when either there is nothing else to take above the individual or individuals, or when such a higher item exists but is unnamed among things differing in species, or when what is demonstrated in part happens to be the whole. For things belonging to a part, the demonstration does indeed apply, and it will be “of every” case; nevertheless, it will not be a demonstration of the primary universal whose demonstration it appears to be.

Thus, if someone demonstrates that right angles do not intersect, the demonstration will appear to concern the primary universal because the attribute belongs to all right angles. But it is not such a demonstration unless it is made on the ground that they are equal in this particular way, but rather on the ground that they are equal in whatever way. If a triangle were nothing other than an isosceles triangle, the attribute would appear to belong to it insofar as it was isosceles.

Likewise, proportionality, insofar as it belongs to numbers, lines, solids, and periods of time, can be demonstrated separately in each case—as has sometimes been demonstrated. It is possible, however, for one demonstration to establish it of all these things, because there is no named item according to which numbers, lengths, periods of time, and solids are all one. Taken separately, they differ in species from one another. Yet the universal is now demonstrated. It did not belong to them insofar as they were lines or numbers, but insofar as they possessed that feature which is assumed to be universal.

For this reason, even if someone demonstrates, in one or more demonstrations, that every individual triangle has two right angles—equilateral, scalene, and isosceles separately—he has not yet come to know that the triangle has two right angles, except sophistically. Nor has he come to know this universally of the triangle, even if there is no triangle other than these. He has not come to know it insofar as it is a triangle, nor has he come to know every triangle; he has come to know it according to number, and not every case according to species, even if there is no case that he does not know.

When, then, does someone fail to know universally, and when does he know simply? It is clear that this is so if being a triangle is the same as being an equilateral triangle, or the same as being each individual kind, or the same as being all of them. But if being a triangle is not the same as being an equilateral triangle, but something different, and the attribute belongs to it insofar as it is a triangle, then he does not know it.
