Whether the attribute belongs insofar as something is a triangle or insofar as it is isosceles, and when the first universal exists concerning that thing of which the demonstration is made, is clear from the following. The first attribute remains when the isosceles and bronze are removed: two right angles belong to a bronze isosceles triangle, but when “bronze” and “isosceles” are removed, the attribute remains—not when the figure or the term is removed, but when the non-primary features are removed. To what primary subject, then, does it belong? If it belongs to the triangle, and belongs to it insofar as it is a triangle, then it also belongs to the other triangles, and the demonstration is of this universal.

## CHAPTER VI. That demonstration is from necessary premises and per se attributes

If demonstrative knowledge exists, and if it proceeds from necessary principles, then what is known cannot be otherwise. Things that are per se necessarily belong to their subjects, since they belong to them in the account of what they are. In some cases, these attributes belong to a thing’s essence when they are predicated of the thing, and one of two opposites must necessarily belong to it.

It is therefore clear that a demonstrative syllogism is formed from premises of this sort. Everything either belongs in this way or belongs accidentally; but accidents are not necessary. We must therefore speak in this way, or else establish as a principle that demonstration is necessary and that what is demonstrated cannot be otherwise. The syllogism, then, must be from necessary premises.

A syllogism may be from true premises without being demonstrative; but it is not from necessary premises unless it is demonstrative, since this is what belongs properly to demonstration. An indication that demonstration is from necessary premises is that we put forward counterexamples in this way when we seek to demonstrate to those who hold an opinion. If something is merely a matter of opinion, it is not necessary either that it be so altogether or that it be otherwise, except for the sake of argument.

This also makes clear that those are foolish who suppose that it is enough to grasp good principles if the proposition is plausible and true—for example, the sophists’ claim that to know is to possess knowledge. It is not the plausible or implausible that constitutes a principle, but the first item in the genus under investigation; nor is every truth a proper principle.

That the syllogism must be from necessary premises is clear from the following. If, when a demonstration exists, someone does not possess an account of the reason why, then he does not know. Suppose that \(A\) necessarily belongs to \(C\), while \(B\), the middle term through which it has been demonstrated, is not necessary. He does not know why \(A\) belongs to \(C\), since the reason why is supplied by the middle term, and the middle term may fail to belong, although the conclusion is necessary. [Col. 0719B]

Further, suppose that someone is ignorant now, although he possesses the account, and that the account and the thing itself remain preserved; he has neither forgotten nor previously known it, but the middle term will be destroyed unless it is necessary. He will therefore possess the account while the thing remains preserved, but he will not know; nor, consequently, did he know previously. If the middle term has not been destroyed, but it is possible for what is accidental to be destroyed, then it would be possible and contingent for the matter to stand in this way; but it is impossible for someone in such a condition to know.

Even if the conclusion is necessary, then, nothing prevents the middle term through which it was demonstrated from being non-necessary. It is possible to syllogize necessarily from non-necessary premises, and to derive a true conclusion from false premises. But when the middle term is necessary and the conclusion is necessary, the situation is analogous to the fact that what follows from true premises is always true.

Let \(A\) necessarily belong to \(B\), and let \(B\) necessarily belong to \(C\). Then \(A\) must necessarily belong to \(C\). But if the conclusion does not belong necessarily, it is not possible for the middle term to be necessary. Suppose that \(A\) belongs to \(C\) non-necessarily, while \(A\) belongs to \(B\), and \(B\) belongs to \(C\) necessarily. Then \(A\) will belong to \(C\) necessarily, contrary to the supposition.

Since demonstrative knowledge requires that the attribute belong necessarily, it is clear that the demonstration must also be possessed through a necessary middle term; otherwise there will be no knowledge, either of the reason why or of the fact. The necessary connection must therefore belong to the middle term. Otherwise the person will merely opine without knowing, if he opines that the non-necessary is necessary; or he will not opine in the same way, whether he claims to know through middle terms, through the reason why, or through immediate premises.

As for accidents that are not per se, according to the definition given, there is no demonstrative knowledge of them per se. It is not possible to demonstrate necessarily the conclusion concerning them, since the accident in question may fail to exist. I mean an accident of this sort.

Someone might nevertheless ask why these matters need to be examined, if the conclusion need not be necessary. For it makes no difference whether someone, when questioned about contingencies, subsequently states the conclusion. The question must not be put on the assumption that the conclusion is necessary because of the questions already asked, but rather because the respondent must say what follows from what has been stated, and must say it truly if the premises are true.

## CHAPTER VII. That demonstrations are from things that are per se and from eternal things

Since whatever is per se, and whatever belongs to each thing insofar as it is that thing, belongs necessarily to each genus, it is clear that scientific demonstrations concern things that are per se and proceed from such things. Accidents are not necessary. Therefore it is not necessary to know the reason why of a conclusion if the conclusion is an accident, even if the accident always exists. In the case of things that are not per se, such as syllogisms from signs, one will not know them per se, nor will one know the reason why.

To know the reason why is to know through the cause. For this very reason the middle term must belong to the third term, and the first term to the middle. It is therefore not possible to demonstrate by descending from another genus—for example, to give a geometrical demonstration in arithmetic.

There are three elements in demonstrations. First is the conclusion that is demonstrated, namely, what belongs per se to some genus. Second are the axioms, from which the demonstration proceeds. Third is the underlying genus, whose attributes and per se accidents the demonstration exhibits.

The premises from which a demonstration is formed may be the same. But when the genus is different—as in arithmetic and geometry—an arithmetical demonstration cannot properly concern accidents of magnitudes, unless magnitudes are numbers; how this is possible in some cases will be explained later. An arithmetical demonstration always has the genus concerning which the demonstration is made, and the same is true of the other sciences.

Therefore the genus must either be simply the same, or the same in some respect, if demonstration is to descend from one science to another. Otherwise it is impossible. For the ultimate and middle terms must necessarily belong to the same genus; if they did not belong per se, they would be accidental.

For this reason geometry cannot demonstrate that contraries are the object of one science; nor that two cubes constitute one cube; nor can one science demonstrate what belongs to another. It may demonstrate only what stands in relations such as one science’s being subordinate to another—for example, perspective to geometry, and harmonics to arithmetic.

Nor, if something belongs to lines but not insofar as they are lines and not from their proper principles, can it be demonstrated geometrically. For example, if the straight line is the most beautiful of lines, or if the circular line is the contrary in some respect, this does not belong to them insofar as they constitute their proper genus, but insofar as they share something common.

It is also clear that, if the propositions from which the syllogism is formed are universal, the conclusion of such a demonstration must be eternal, and, generally speaking, must belong to demonstration simply. There is therefore no demonstration, and no knowledge simply speaking, of perishable things. Such knowledge is only accidental and is not universal knowledge of the thing itself; it holds only at some time and in some way. In that case, one of the premises must be non-universal and perishable: perishable because the conclusion is perishable, and non-universal because one of the premises will hold while the other will not. Therefore the syllogism is not universal, but establishes only that the matter is so now.

The same applies to definition, since definition is either a principle of demonstration, a demonstration differing in position, or a certain conclusion of demonstration.

There are also demonstrations and knowledge of things that occur frequently, such as an eclipse of the moon. It is clear that, insofar as they are such things, they are always so; but insofar as they occur only in particular cases, they are not always so. The same is true of an eclipse and of other such things.

Since it is clear that one does not demonstrate each thing indiscriminately, but either demonstrates it from the principles proper to each thing, or demonstrates it insofar as it is that thing, one does not possess knowledge merely because it is demonstrated from true, indemonstrable, and immediate premises.

For it is possible to demonstrate in the manner of Bryson’s squaring of the circle. Such arguments demonstrate on the basis of something common, which also belongs to another subject; consequently, the same arguments may be applied to other, non-congeneric matters. One does not therefore know the thing according to what it is, but only accidentally, since the demonstration does not belong to the same genus.

We know each thing non-accidentally when we know it according to that in virtue of which it is derived from its own principles and insofar as it is that thing. For example, having two right angles belongs per se to the triangle, and is known from the principles proper to the triangle.

Therefore, if the attribute belongs per se to the subject, the middle term must necessarily be in the same immediate relation. If this is not so, but the relation is like that between harmonics and arithmetic, then such demonstrations are similar, but differ in kind. The fact belongs to one science, because the subject genus is different, whereas the reason why belongs to the superior science, whose per se attributes are under consideration.

It is clear from this that nothing can be demonstrated simply except from the proper principles of each thing, although the principles of these sciences may have something in common. If this is clear, it is also clear that the proper principles of each science cannot themselves be demonstrated. They would then be principles of all things, and the science possessing them would govern all sciences. For one who knows from higher causes knows more completely, since he knows from prior causes rather than from effects. If he knows more completely, and most completely, then that science will also be more complete and most complete.

But demonstration does not transfer to another genus except in cases such as those mentioned: geometry to mechanics or perspective, and arithmetic to harmonics.

It is difficult to know whether we possess knowledge from the principles proper to each thing, or not. We suppose that knowing consists in possessing a syllogism from true and primary premises, but this is not sufficient. The primary premises must also be congeneric with the subject.

## CHAPTER VIII. On principles, both variable and common, and proper and subordinate

By “principles in each genus” I mean those things whose existence cannot be demonstrated. We must determine what the first principles and the things derived from them signify. As for the principles themselves, the text is corrupt: “[F. quoad] … [an. quaedam?]”; it says that some must be assumed, while others must be demonstrated. For example, one must assume what unity is, what straightness is, and what a triangle is; one must also assume that unity and magnitude exist, but their other properties must be demonstrated.

The principles used in demonstrative sciences are of two kinds: some are proper to each science, while others are common. The common principles are common by analogy, because each is useful only to the extent that it applies to the genus falling under the science in question.

Proper principles include, for example, that a line is such-and-such, and what straightness is. Common principles include: “If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal.” Each of these is sufficient to the extent that it applies within its genus. The same principle may be used even if it is not taken universally—for example, in magnitudes alone, while the analogous principle in arithmetic applies to numbers.

Proper principles also include the things whose existence is assumed and around which the science conducts its investigation, namely, per se attributes. Arithmetic assumes units; geometry assumes points and lines. These sciences receive their existence and what it is to be for these things, while their per se attributes are investigated.

Each science assumes what its objects signify. Arithmetic, for example, assumes what even, odd, square, and cube signify; geometry assumes what irrationality, bending, and convergence signify. Their existence is demonstrated through common principles, and their properties are demonstrated from those principles. The same is true of astronomy.

Every demonstrative science concerns three things: first, the underlying genus, whose existence is assumed and whose per se attributes it investigates; second, the common axioms from which demonstrations proceed; and third, the attributes whose significance each science assumes. Some sciences may disregard certain of these. For example, they may not assume the existence of their genus if its existence is evident. It is not equally evident that number exists and that hot and cold exist. Nor need a science receive the meanings of attributes if these are evident, just as it need not receive the meaning of a common principle such as subtracting equals from equals, since that is already known.

Nevertheless, by nature these three things remain involved in every science: the subject concerning which it demonstrates, what it demonstrates, and the principles from which it demonstrates.

What must exist through itself, and whose existence is evidently necessary, is neither a supposition nor a petition. Demonstration is not addressed to external speech but to the reasoning in the soul, since a syllogism is not addressed merely to external speech either. One can always object to external speech, but not always to the internal reasoning.

Whatever a demonstrator accepts as demonstrable without demonstrating it—if he accepts something apparently true—constitutes a supposition for the learner, but not a supposition simply speaking; it is a supposition only for that learner. If he accepts something that no one believes, or something contrary to belief, then he begs the question.

Supposition and petition differ in this respect: petition is contrary to the learner’s opinion, or consists in accepting and using something demonstrable without demonstrating it.

Terms are not suppositions, since they do not say that something exists or does not exist; suppositions occur in propositions. One must merely understand the terms. This is not a supposition, unless someone should say that merely hearing a supposition makes it one. A conclusion follows from whatever things exist in the manner signified by those terms.

Nor does the geometer assume falsehoods, as some claim when they say that a geometer must not speak falsely, yet lies when he says that a line is one foot long although it is not, or that a line is straight although it is not straight. The geometer does not draw a conclusion about the particular line that he has posited, but about what is demonstrated through such a line.

Further, every petition and supposition is either wholly or partly such; terms are neither. It is not necessary, if demonstration is to exist, that species exist, or that there be one thing outside the many. It is necessary, however, that one thing be truly predicated of many. Otherwise there will be no universal. If there is no universal, there will be no middle term and therefore no demonstration. There must therefore be one and the same non-equivocal predicate of several things.

It is not possible for the same thing to be affirmed and denied at the same time; nor does a single demonstration assume this, except when it needs to demonstrate its conclusion in that way. Rather, it proceeds by taking the first term to be truly predicated of the middle and its negation not to be truly predicated. It makes no difference whether the middle term is assumed to exist or not; the same applies to the third term.

For if “human being” is assigned to something, it is true to say that it is an animal; and if “not human being” is assigned, the following words are textually uncertain. But if it is assumed only that every human being is an animal, and that no non-human is an animal, then it is true to say that Callias is an animal whether he is Callias or not, but not true to say that he is not an animal.

The reason is that the first term is not predicated only of the middle term but also of something else, because it is predicated of many. Therefore it makes no difference to the conclusion whether the middle term is both the same and not the same.

A common principle such as “to affirm or deny universally” is assumed in a demonstration by impossibility, but not always and universally; it is assumed only to the extent sufficient. What is sufficient is sufficient within the genus. By “within the genus” I mean the genus concerning which the demonstrations are made, as was previously stated.

All sciences share in the common principles. By “common” I mean the principles they use as though demonstrating from them, but not the principles from which they demonstrate their subject matter, nor the things they demonstrate.

Dialectic, by contrast, concerns all things, and if it attempts to demonstrate any common principle universally—such as what it is to affirm or deny everything, or to subtract equals from equals—it does so without being the science of any one defined subject or of any one genus. It does not ask questions in the way that one does when demonstrating, since one does not question someone who is demonstrating. The reason is that dialectic does not demonstrate that the same thing belongs to opposites. This has been shown in the discussion of syllogism.

## CHAPTER IX. The distinctiveness of each discipline, and the appropriateness of its questions

If a syllogistic question is the same as a contradictory proposition, and propositions differ according to each science, then there will necessarily be questions belonging to each science, from which the syllogism proper to each science is formed.

It is therefore clear that not every question will be geometrical, nor medical, nor similarly associated with the other sciences. A question is geometrical when something is demonstrated from geometrical principles, or when it concerns something that geometry demonstrates from those principles—for example, visible magnitudes. The same applies to the other sciences.

In such matters an account must be given from geometrical principles and conclusions. But the geometer, insofar as he is a geometer, need not give an account of the principles themselves. The same applies to the other sciences.

Nor should one question every person about everything, nor respond to every question about each thing; one should respond only to what has been determined according to the science in question.

If someone disputes with a geometer insofar as he is a geometer, it is clear that he disputes properly if he demonstrates something from geometrical principles, but not otherwise. It is also clear that he does not refute the geometer as geometer, but either accidentally or in some other respect. Therefore one should not dispute geometrically about non-geometrical matters, since the person arguing badly will escape notice. The same applies to the other sciences.

Since there are geometrical questions, are there also non-geometrical questions? There are questions belonging to each science, and questions arising from ignorance—for example, the sort of ignorance that is geometrical. Is a syllogism arising from ignorance, and from opposed premises, a syllogism or a paralogism?

A question arising from another art, such as music, is non-geometrical. A question about geometry—for example, the belief that parallel lines converge—is geometrical in one respect and non-geometrical in another. This is because there are two kinds of such error, just as there are two senses in which one may err about number: one is non-geometrical because one does not possess the relevant knowledge; the other is non-geometrical because one possesses it badly. Ignorance arising from the principles of the science is contrary to knowledge.

In instructional arguments the paralogism does not arise in the same way, because the middle term always occurs twice: one term is predicated of all of it, and it in turn of all another term, whereas the predicate itself is not said universally. These matters can be seen in thought, but they are concealed in speech. For example, whether every circle is a figure is unclear in speech; once it is written down, it is evident. Whether poems are circles is plainly false.

One must not bring a counterexample against a proposition if it is inductive. Just as a proposition that does not hold in most cases is not a proposition of the relevant kind, so it will not hold universally. From universal premises, however, it is clear that there is no counterexample, since propositions and counterexamples are the same: the case brought forward as a counterexample becomes a demonstrative or dialectical proposition.

It is also possible for some people to speak without syllogizing because they take consequences on both sides, as Caeneus does when he argues that fire occurs in a multiplied proportion. Fire, he says, is generated quickly, and this is the proportion. But this is not a syllogism. It would be one if the fastest proportion followed from a multiplied proportion, and if fire had the fastest proportion in change.

Sometimes, then, it is impossible to syllogize from the premises that have been accepted; sometimes it is possible, but does not appear so.

If it were impossible to demonstrate truth from falsehoods, resolution would be easy, since the terms would necessarily be convertible. Suppose that \(A\) exists, and that, because it exists, the things known to exist are \(B\). From these I shall demonstrate that the original thing exists. The terms that occur in mathematics are more readily convertible, since they contain no accident—as they differ in this respect from the matters discussed in dialectical arguments—but only definitions.

Demonstrations are increased not through middle terms but through the addition of premises. For example: \(A\) is predicated of \(B\), and \(B\) of \(C\); again, \(C\) of \(D\), and so on indefinitely. The extension may also proceed laterally: \(A\) is predicated of \(C\), and of \(E\), as in the case of number, whether determinate or infinite. Let \(A\) be an odd number of whatever magnitude, \(B\) an odd number, and \(C\) [a number]: \(A\) is thus predicated of \(C\). Let [\(A\)] be an even number of whatever magnitude, \(D\) [a number], and \(E\) an even number: \(A\) is therefore predicated of \(E\). [The variable assignments in the transmitted text are defective.]

## CHAPTER X. On demonstration of the reason why and of the fact

Since knowing the reason why differs from knowing the fact, the difference arises first within the same science, and in two ways.

First, a syllogism may not proceed through immediate premises. In that case the first cause is not taken, whereas knowledge of the reason why proceeds from the first cause.

Second, the syllogism may proceed through immediate premises, but not through the cause; rather, it proceeds through convertible terms and through what is better known. Nothing prevents one of two equally predicated terms from being better known without being the cause. In that case the demonstration will establish the fact through it.

For example, that the planets are near may be demonstrated through their not scintillating. Let \(C\) be planets, \(B\) not scintillating, and \(A\) being near. It is true to predicate \(B\) of \(C\), since planets do not scintillate; and it is true to predicate \(A\) of \(B\), since what does not scintillate is near. This is accepted either through induction or through perception. Therefore \(A\) belongs to \(C\), and it has been demonstrated that the planets are near.

This syllogism, however, is not a demonstration of the reason why, but of the fact. The planets are not near because they do not scintillate; rather, they do not scintillate because they are near.

It is possible to demonstrate the one through the other, and then the demonstration will be of the reason why. Let \(C\) be planets, \(B\) being near, and \(A\) not scintillating. Then \(B\) belongs to \(C\), since the planets are near, and \(A\) belongs to \(B\); hence \(A\) belongs to \(C\), and the syllogism will be of the reason why, since the first cause has been taken.

Again, the moon is demonstrated to be circular through its phases. If what increases in this way is circular, and the moon increases in this way, then it is clear that the moon is circular. This is a syllogism of the fact. If the middle term is reversed, however, the syllogism is of the reason why. The moon is not circular because it undergoes such phases; rather, because it is circular, it undergoes such phases.

Let \(C\) be the moon, \(B\) its increase, and \(A\) circularity.

When the middle terms are not convertible, and what is not the cause is better known than the cause, the demonstration establishes the fact but not the reason why. This is especially so when the middle term is placed outside the subject, since in such cases the demonstration is not of the reason why but only of the fact; the middle term is not stated as the cause.

For example, the reason why a wall does not breathe is that it is not an animal. If not breathing is caused by this, then being an animal must be the cause of breathing. If negation is the cause of not existing, affirmation is the cause of existing. Thus, if lacking measure is the cause of not being healed, measure will be the cause of being healed. Similarly, if affirmation is the cause of existing, negation is the cause of not existing.

But in demonstrations of this kind the foregoing condition does not hold, since not every animal breathes.

The syllogism establishing this cause is in the middle figure. Let \(A\) be animal, \(B\) breathing, and \(C\) wall. \(A\) belongs universally to \(B\), since everything that breathes is an animal; but \(B\) belongs to nothing that is \(C\). Therefore \(B\) belongs to no \(C\); the wall does not breathe.

Causes of this sort are compared according to superiority with the causes already mentioned. The greatest distance between the terms is taken as the middle term, as in Anacharsis’ saying that there are no flute players among the Scythians, since there are no vines.

Within the same science, and according to the position of the middle terms, these are the differences between the syllogism of the fact and the syllogism of the reason why.

The reason why also differs from the fact in another way: the two may be investigated by different sciences. This occurs whenever one science is subordinate to another—for example, perspective to geometry, mechanics to stereometry, harmonics to arithmetic, and the appearances of the heavens to astronomy.

Some of these sciences are nearly synonymous, such as mathematical astronomy and nautical astronomy, or mathematical harmonics and harmonics based on hearing. In these cases, knowledge of the fact belongs to the sensible or observational discipline, whereas knowledge of the reason why belongs to the mathematical discipline. The mathematical sciences possess demonstrations of causes, but often do not know the fact itself, just as those who consider universals often fail to know some particulars because they do not attend to them.

Such sciences concern things that are different in substance but use forms. Mathematical sciences concern forms, not a particular subject. If geometrical matters were concerned with some particular subject, they would not concern it insofar as they were geometrical.

Perspective stands to geometry in this way, and other sciences stand to it similarly. For example, in the case of the rainbow, knowing that it exists belongs to the physicist, whereas knowing why belongs to the perspectivist, either simply speaking or according to the discipline.

Many sciences that are not subordinate to one another stand in this relation, such as medicine to geometry. That circular wounds heal more slowly is for the physician to know as a fact; why they do so is for the geometer to know.

## CHAPTER XI. That the first figure is best suited to the highest degree of knowledge
Of the figures, the first is the one that most greatly produces knowledge. For the mathematical sciences derive their demonstrations through it—arithmetic, geometry, perspective, and, generally speaking, all those sciences that make the consideration of the “why” visible [Col. 0726D]. For either altogether, or most often and in the majority of cases, the syllogism through this figure—which is the figure of the “why”—is formed. Therefore it will also be the figure that most greatly produces knowledge, since to know the “why” visibly is the most proper kind of knowledge.

Further, through this figure alone it is possible to hunt after knowledge of the essence, the “what-it-is.” For in the middle figure no predicative syllogism is formed, whereas knowledge of the essence belongs to affirmation. In the last figure a syllogism is indeed formed, but not universally; and the “what-it-is” belongs to universals. For “man is a two-footed animal” is not, in a certain way, the essence. Moreover, the first figure requires nothing from the others, whereas the others are condensed and strengthened through it until they arrive at immediate propositions. It is therefore clear [Col. 0727A] that the first figure is most proper to scientific knowledge.

Just as it is possible for A to belong immediately to B, so too it is possible for A not to belong immediately to B. By “belonging immediately” I mean belonging, or not belonging, in such a way that there is no intermediate term; for otherwise the belonging would be through something else.

Whenever either A or B belongs universally to something, or both belong universally to something, it is not possible for A first not to belong to B. Let A belong universally to C. If B does not belong universally to C—for A may belong to some whole while B does not belong to that whole—there will be a syllogism establishing that A does not belong to B. For if C belongs to every A, while C belongs to no B, then A belongs to no B. Likewise, if B belongs to some whole—for example, to B itself—then, since D belongs to every B and to no A, A will belong to no B by syllogism. The same will be shown if both belong to some whole.

That B does not belong to the whole to which A belongs, or again that A does not belong to the whole to which B belongs, is clear from the arrangements of terms, whenever the arrangements are not mutually convertible. For if none of the things in the arrangement A, C, D is predicated of any of the things in the arrangement B, E, F, while A belongs universally to G, it is clear, given this arrangement, that B will not belong to G; otherwise the arrangements would be convertible. The same applies if B belongs universally to something.

But if neither belongs universally to anything, and A does not belong to B, then it is necessary that the non-belonging be immediate. For if there were an intermediate term, one of the two would necessarily belong universally to something. A syllogism would be possible either in the first figure or in the middle figure. If it were in the first figure, B would belong universally to something, since the proposition affirming this would be required. If it were in the middle figure [Col. 0727C], either possibility would arise: with a negative proposition posited for each, there would be a syllogism; but when both propositions were negative, there would not be one.

It is therefore clear that it is possible for one thing also not to belong to another immediately, both when this is possible and in the manner in which it is possible.

## CHAPTER XII. Ignorance and the syllogism of ignorance concerning what belongs or does not belong immediately

Ignorance, when spoken of not according to negation but according to a disposition, is deception produced through a syllogism. In the case of things that belong, or do not belong, immediately, this occurs in two ways. It occurs either when someone simply assumes that something is, or is not, the case, or when someone forms an opinion of it through a syllogism. Simple deception belongs to simple opinion, whereas the deception produced through a syllogism has several forms.

Let A belong to no B immediately. If, then, someone syllogistically concludes that A belongs to B by taking C as the middle term, he will be deceived through a syllogism. It is therefore possible for both propositions to be false, and it is possible for only one of them to be false. If A belongs to no C, and C belongs to no B, then, when both propositions are taken in the contrary form, both will be false.

C may stand in such a relation to A and B that C is neither subordinate to A nor universally contained in B. It is impossible for B to belong to anything universally, since it was first established that A does not belong to B itself; but A need not belong to everything that belongs universally to C. Thus both propositions are false.

It is possible, however, for one proposition to be taken as true, though not either one indifferently. The proposition A–C can be true, whereas the proposition C–B will always be false, because C belongs to no B. The proposition A–C may be true if A belongs immediately both to C and to B; for when the same thing is first predicated of several things, neither of them will belong to the other.

It makes no difference if the belonging is not immediate. Deception concerning belonging is produced in this way alone, since there was no syllogism concerning belonging in any other figure. A syllogism concerning non-belonging, however, occurs in both the first and the middle figures. Let us therefore first state in how many ways deception occurs in the first figure, and with what relations among the propositions.

It is possible for both propositions to be false—for example, if A belongs immediately both to B and to C. If A is taken as belonging to no C, while C is taken as belonging to every B, both propositions are false.

It is also possible for only one to be false. Under any such circumstances, the proposition A–C may be true while the proposition B–C is false. The proposition A–C may be true because A does not belong to everything, whereas the proposition C–B is false because C cannot belong to B, to which A belongs nowhere. Nor will the proposition A–C be true if it is taken in the other direction. If both propositions are true, the conclusion will also be true, as will the proposition C–B.

It is possible for one proposition to be true while the other is false. If B belongs both to C and to A, one of the two must be subordinate to the other. Thus, if A is taken as belonging to no C, the proposition will be false. It is therefore clear that whether one proposition is false or both are false, the syllogism will be false.

In the middle figure it is not possible for both propositions as a whole to be false. For when A belongs to every B, it will not be possible to find something that belongs universally to one term and to no member of the other. Yet this is how the propositions in the middle figure must be taken: one thing must belong to one term and not belong to the other, if there is to be a syllogism. If they are taken in this way as false, it is clear that the contrary propositions will stand in converse relation; but this is impossible.

There is nothing to prevent both propositions from being false in a particular respect. If C belongs to some A and to some B, then, if C is taken as belonging to every A and to no B, both propositions will be false—not as wholes, but in a particular respect. The same applies if the negative proposition is taken in the converse order.

It is possible for one proposition to be false, and either one may be false. Whatever belongs to every A also belongs to B. If C is taken as belonging to the whole of A but to no part of B, the proposition C–A will be true, whereas C–B will be false.

Again, whatever belongs to no B will not belong to every A. For if it belonged to A, it would belong both to A and to B, although it was assumed not to belong. If C is therefore taken as belonging to the whole of A and to no B, the proposition B–C is true, while the other is false.

The same result follows when the negative proposition is transposed. Whatever belongs to no A will not belong to no B. If C is taken as belonging to no part of A but as belonging to the whole of B, the proposition A–C will be true, while the other will be false.

Again, it is false to take something that belongs to every B as belonging to no A. For if it belongs to every B, it must belong to some A. If C is therefore taken as belonging to every B and to no A, the proposition C–B will be true, while A–C will be false.

It is therefore clear that, when things are immediate, a deceptive syllogism may arise both when both propositions are false and when only one is false.

## CHAPTER XIII. The syllogism of ignorance concerning what belongs mediately

In the case of things that belong, or do not belong, not immediately, when a syllogism of falsehood is produced through the proper middle term, it is not possible for both propositions to be false; only the proposition preceding the major extreme can be false.

By “proper middle” I mean the middle through which a syllogism of contradiction is produced. Let A belong to B through C. Since the proposition C–B must be affirmative if a syllogism is to be produced, it is clear that this proposition is always true, for it is not converted. The proposition A–C, however, is false, since, when this is converted, the contrary syllogism is produced.

The same applies if the middle term is taken from another arrangement—for example, D—if D belongs universally to A and is predicated universally of B. The proposition D–B must remain unchanged, while the other must be converted. Thus the former is always true, the latter always false; and this deception is generally the same as that produced through the proper middle.

If the syllogism is not produced through the proper middle, and the middle is subordinate to A but belongs to no B, both propositions must be false. They must be taken in the contrary form from the way in which the terms actually stand if there is to be a syllogism. When taken in this way, both become false. For example, if A belongs universally to D, while D belongs to no B, then, when the propositions are converted, a syllogism will result, and both propositions will be false.

When the middle term D is not subordinate to A, the proposition A–D will be true, while D–B will be false. A–D is true because D does not belong to A; D–B is false because, if it were true, the conclusion would also be true, whereas it was false.

When deception is produced through the middle figure, it is not possible for both propositions as wholes to be false. For when B is subordinate to A, nothing can belong universally to one term and to no member of the other, as was stated earlier. One proposition, however, may be false, and either one may be false.

If C belongs both to B and to A, and it is taken as belonging to A but not to B, the proposition A–C will be true, while the other will be false. Likewise, if C is taken as belonging to B but to no A, the proposition C–B will be true, while the other will be false.

If the syllogism of deception is negative, it has now been stated when and through which terms deception arises.

If it is affirmative, then, when it is produced through the proper middle, it is impossible for both propositions to be false. The proposition C–B must remain unchanged if there is to be a syllogism, as was stated earlier. Therefore C–A will always be false, since this is the proposition that is converted.

The same applies if the middle is taken from another arrangement, as was stated in the case of negative deception. The proposition D–B must remain, while A–D must be converted; and this deception is the same as the preceding one.

When the syllogism is not produced through the proper middle, if D is subordinate to A, the proposition A–D will be true and the other false. For A may belong to several things that are not subordinate to one another.

If D is not subordinate to A, it is clear that this proposition is always false, since it is taken affirmatively. The proposition D–B, however, may be either true or false. There is nothing to prevent A from belonging to no D while D belongs to every B—for example, animal belongs to science, and science belongs to music. Nor need it be the case that A belongs to no D, or that D belongs to no B.

It is therefore clear that, when the middle is not the proper middle, both propositions may be false together, and either one may be false.

The number of ways in which deceptive syllogisms can arise, and through which terms, both in cases that are without a middle and in cases that proceed through demonstration, is now clear.

## CHAPTER XIV. If a sense is deficient by nature, knowledge of its proper sensibles is also deficient

It is clear that if someone lacks one of the senses, some knowledge must also be lacking—knowledge that it is impossible for him to acquire, since we learn either through induction or through demonstration. Demonstration proceeds from universals, whereas induction proceeds from particulars [Col. 0730B].

It is impossible to contemplate universals except through induction. For even things spoken of by abstraction are made known through induction, when someone wishes to establish that there are certain things in each genus, even if they are not separable insofar as each is such a thing.

But it is impossible to induce without possessing sense-perception, since perception is of particulars. Therefore it is impossible to acquire knowledge of them: there is neither knowledge from universals without induction nor induction without sense-perception.

## CHAPTER XV. Of how many and what sort of terms a syllogism consists, and whether the regress upward or downward proceeds to infinity

Every syllogism is through three terms. It is possible to show that A belongs to C because it belongs to B, and B belongs to C. A negative syllogism has one proposition asserting that something belongs to something else, and the other asserting that it does not.

It is therefore clear that these are what are called principles and suppositions. Once they are taken in this way, it is necessary to show that A belongs to C through B; then again that A belongs to B through another middle, and that B belongs to C in the same way.

For those who syllogize according to opinion, and dialectically alone, it is clear that this is the only thing to be sought: that the syllogism be formed from premises that are as plausible as possible. Thus, even if there is in truth some middle term between A and B, but someone who syllogizes does not proceed through it, he still syllogizes dialectically.

For truth, however, one must seek what belongs to things themselves. The matter stands as follows. There is something that is predicated of another not accidentally. By “accidentally” I mean, for example, that we sometimes say that the white thing is a man, but do not similarly say that the man is white. For since there is not another thing that is white, but something white is a man, white is a man because being white happens to belong to man.

There are therefore certain things of this kind, namely, whatever are predicated according to themselves. If C is such a thing that it itself does not belong to another, but B belongs to it immediately and not through another middle, and again E belongs to D, and similarly D belongs to B, must this process come to a stop, or is it possible for it to proceed to infinity?

Again, if nothing is predicated essentially of A, but A belongs immediately to F, while the middle belongs to nothing prior, and F belongs to A, and this belongs to B, must this process also come to a stop, or is it possible here too to proceed to infinity?

The difference between this and the preceding case is that the former asks whether the process can begin from something that belongs to nothing else while something else belongs to it, and proceed upward to infinity; the latter begins from something that itself is predicated of another, while nothing is predicated of that other, and proceeds downward, if it is possible to proceed to infinity.

Further, is it possible for there to be infinitely many middle terms between determinate terms? For example, if A belongs to C and B is their middle, and between B and A there is another term, and between those another, can this continue to infinity, or is it impossible?

To inquire into this is the same as asking whether demonstrations proceed to infinity, and whether there is a demonstration of everything, or whether demonstrations conclude with one another.

The same question applies to negative syllogisms and propositions. Suppose, for example, that A belongs to no B immediately, or that there is some middle term to which A does not belong immediately—say, G, which belongs to every B—and again G does not belong to something prior, say H, which belongs to every B. In such cases either there are infinitely many terms to which the predicate does not belong in relation to prior terms, or the process comes to a stop.

With things that are not convertible, however, the matter does not stand in the same way. There is no equally predicable term of which one can say that it is predicated first or last, for all terms stand in the same relation to all others, whether infinitely many things are predicated of the term itself or both directions are infinitely indeterminate—unless conversion is possible in the same way. In one case the relation is accidental, in the other it is predicative.

## CHAPTER XVI. With the extremes determined, the highest and lowest, the middle terms are not infinite

Since it is not possible for the middle terms to be infinite when the predicates stand upward and downward, this is clear. By “upward” I mean toward what is more universal, and by “downward” toward what is more particular.

If A is predicated of C and there are infinitely many middle terms, among which B occurs, it is clear that the following will also occur: proceeding downward from A, one term will be predicated of another to infinity, since there are infinitely many middle terms before C is reached; and proceeding upward from C, there will likewise be infinitely many before A is reached.

If these consequences are impossible, it is impossible for there to be infinitely many middle terms between A and C. Nor does it make any difference if someone says that the terms A, B, and C are mutually contingent, so that they are not middle terms, while the others cannot be taken in this way. Whatever term among the B’s is taken, there will be infinitely many middle terms between A and it, or between it and C.

Does it make any difference whether the infinitely many terms begin immediately or not immediately? No, since the terms after these are infinite.

## CHAPTER XVII. The middle terms of a mediated negative proposition, by which it is reduced to an immediate proposition, are not infinite

It is clear also, in demonstrative reasoning, that the process comes to a stop, provided that it comes to a stop in both directions in predicative relations. Let it be assumed that it is not possible to proceed upward from the last term to infinity, nor from the first term to the last.

By the term “last” I mean that which itself belongs to nothing else, but to which something else belongs, as C. By “first” I mean that which itself is predicated of another, while nothing else is predicated of that other.

If these conditions hold, it is clear that the negative sequence too will come to a stop. This can be shown in three ways.

First, suppose that B belongs to every C, while A belongs to no B. The sequence concerning B and C must therefore proceed toward immediate propositions, since it is predicative. But the other sequence is also clear: if A does not belong to something prior, such as D, then A must belong to every B; and if A does not belong to something prior to D, that term must belong to every D. Thus, since the path downward comes to a stop, the path upward will also come to a stop, and there will be something to which A does not belong immediately.

Second, if B belongs to every A and to no C, then A belongs to no C. If this too requires demonstration, it is clear that it will be demonstrated either through the preceding method, through this one, or through the third.

The second method may be demonstrated as follows. Suppose that D belongs to every B but to no C. If something must belong to B, and this does not belong to C, while another thing belongs to D but does not belong to C, then, since belonging always comes to a stop at a higher term, non-belonging will also come to a stop.

The third method is this: if A belongs to every B, while C belongs to no B, then C does not belong to every thing to which A belongs. This too will be demonstrated through the preceding method or in a similar way.

The process therefore comes to a stop through these methods. If it proceeds in this way, B will again be taken as belonging to E, while C does not belong to every E, and the same procedure will continue. But since it was assumed that the downward sequence comes to a stop, it is clear that the sequence concerning what does not belong to C will also come to a stop.

It is also clear that even if the demonstration does not proceed along one path alone but along all of them—sometimes through the first figure, sometimes through the second, and sometimes through the third—the process will still come to a stop, since the paths are finite. A finite number taken finitely many times must itself be finite.

This establishes the point concerning non-belonging, provided that belonging too comes immediately to a stop.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The middle terms of a mediated affirmative proposition are not infinite

For those who investigate the matter logically, the point becomes clear in this way. In the case of predicates belonging to the essence, it is evident: if definition is possible, or if the essence is known, and it is impossible to traverse an infinite series, then the predicates belonging to the essence must be finite [Col. 0732D].

In general we speak as follows. It is truly possible to say that white walks, that the large thing is wood, that wood is large, and that a man walks. But saying it in one way differs from saying it in another. When I say that the white thing is wood, I mean that the thing to which being white happens to belong is wood; I do not mean that the subject indicated by the word “white” is wood. For neither the white thing, nor whatever is white, has become wood. Thus the statement is accidental.

When I say that wood is white, I do not mean that something else is white while wood happens to belong to it. For example, when I say that the musical thing is white, I mean that the man is white and that being musical happens to belong to him, whereas wood is the subject. The subject is what has become white, not something else besides what is wood or some wood.

If names must be assigned to these relations, let us call the first kind of statement predication, and the second either no predication at all or predication not simply but accidental predication. In the former case white is what is predicated, whereas wood is that of which it is predicated.

Let it therefore be assumed that the predicate is always predicated simply of that of which it is predicated, and not accidentally. Demonstrations proceed in this way. Thus, in respect of the essence, quality, quantity, relation, action, passion, place, or time, one thing will be predicated of one thing.

Moreover, terms signifying substance signify either a particular thing or some particular thing of that of which they are predicated. Those that do not signify substance but are said of some subject do not signify either what that subject is or that it is some such thing; they are accidents, as white is said of man. For man is neither white nor a white thing, but perhaps an animal; for man is an animal.

Whatever does not signify substance must be predicated of some subject, and “white” is not a “what,” since it is white only when some other thing is present as its subject. Species and genera are valid for this purpose, but monstrosities are not; and even if such things existed, they would contribute nothing to the argument, since demonstrations concern things of this kind.

Further, if this is not the quality of that, and that is not the quality of this, nor is one quality the quality of another, it is impossible for them to be predicated of one another in the same way. It may be true to say it in one way, but they cannot be predicated of one another with equal truth.

For will it be predicated as substance, or as genus, or as difference? It has been shown that such predicates will not be infinite, either upward or downward. Thus: man is two-footed; this is an animal; this is something else. Nor does animal proceed from man, while man proceeds from Callias, and then from something else, in respect of the essence. For it is possible to define every substance of this kind, and it is impossible to traverse an infinite series in thought. Therefore the predicates are not infinite either upward or downward; otherwise it would not be possible to define the thing of which infinitely many predicates were made.

Genera, then, are not predicated of one another equally. For what is itself some particular thing will not be predicated of a quality, or of anything else, except accidentally. All such predicates are accidents, and they are predicated of substances; but since they are not infinite upward, neither are the accidents infinite.

Each thing is predicated as signifying either some quantity, some quality, or something of this kind that belongs to substance. These categories are finite, and the genera of the categories are finite: either quality, quantity, relation, action, passion, place, or time.

It has been assumed that one thing is predicated of one thing. We do not say that things which are not relative are predicated of one another, since they are all accidents; some are accidents according to themselves, others according to the other mode.

We say that all these are predicated of some subject, but that an accident is not itself a subject. We do not posit any of these things as subjects—not that one thing is said to be another, but that one thing itself is predicated of others, and some things are predicated of other things. Nor, therefore, are the predicates infinite upward. There will be one thing predicated of one thing, and neither upward nor downward will the series be infinite, since the things of which accidents are predicated, whatever belongs to the substance of each thing, are not infinite. The upward series, therefore, and the accidents in both directions, are not infinite.

There must consequently be something of which one thing is first predicated, then another of this, and so on, until the process comes to a stop; and there must be something beyond which nothing further is predicated either of a prior term or of that term itself.

This is one mode of demonstration.

There is another. If the things of which certain prior terms are predicated are demonstrable, then the things that are demonstrated cannot stand in a better relation to them than knowing them; nor is it possible to know them without demonstration. If this is so, they are known through those prior terms. But we do not know these prior terms, nor do we stand in a better relation to them than knowing them, nor will we know them through these terms.

If, therefore, there is such a thing as knowledge through demonstration simply, and not from other premises or from a supposition, the predication of the middle terms must come to a stop. For if it does not, and one continually takes a higher term, everything will be demonstrable. But since it is impossible to traverse an infinite series, the things that are demonstrable will not be known through demonstration.

If, then, we do not stand in a better relation to them than knowing them, there will be no knowledge through demonstration simply, but only knowledge from a supposition.

Thus, from these considerations, someone may perhaps be persuaded logically of the point stated. Analytically, however, the matter is made clear more quickly through the following. In demonstrative sciences, predicates cannot be infinite either upward or downward, concerning the things with which the inquiry is concerned. For demonstration proceeds from things that belong to objects according to themselves.

“According to themselves” has two senses. It includes whatever belongs to things in respect of their essence, and whatever things themselves belong to in respect of their essence. For example, odd belongs to number, while number itself belongs to the account of odd; and again, multitude or divisibility belongs to the account of number.

Neither of these can be infinite, just as odd cannot be infinite in relation to number. For if another odd thing belonged to the thing to which this already belonged, and if number were first, it would belong to the things contained in it.

If things of this sort cannot be infinite in one thing, then they will not be infinite upward either. Yet everything must belong to the first term—for example, to number—and number must belong to those things. Thus they will be convertible, not exceeding one another.

Nor are those things infinite that belong to the essence; otherwise definition would be impossible. Therefore, if all predicates according to themselves are predicated in this way, and these are not infinite, the upward series will come to a stop, and consequently the downward series as well.

If this is so, it is already clear that demonstration does not merely require principles to exist and deny that everything is demonstrable, as some say in accordance with the principle. For if there are principles, not everything is demonstrable, and it is impossible to proceed to infinity. To be any one of these things is nothing other than for there to be no interval without a middle term, and for the term to be immediate; but all terms are divisible.

For by inserting a term within the interval, rather than taking the term as given, one demonstrates what is to be demonstrated. If this could proceed to infinity, there would be infinitely many intermediate terms within two terms. But this is impossible if predicates come to a stop upward and downward. That they do come to a stop has already been shown logically, and is now shown analytically.

## CHAPTER XIX. The elements of demonstrating mediated propositions are not infinite

Once these points have been demonstrated, it is clear that if the same thing belongs to two things—for example, A belongs both to C and to D—while neither is predicated of the other, either altogether or universally, it will not always belong according to something common.

For example, isosceles and scalene triangles have angles equal to two right angles according to something common, since they have this property insofar as they are figures, and not insofar as one is something other than the other. But this relation does not always hold.

Let B belong to C and D insofar as they are A. It will then be clear that B belongs to C and D according to some other common term, and that term according to another. Thus infinitely many terms between two terms would arise. But this is impossible. Therefore it is not necessary that the same thing always belong to several things according to something common, since otherwise there would be immediate intervals.

Nevertheless, the terms must belong to the same genus and arise from the same indivisible elements, if there is to be something common to what is demonstrated. For what is demonstrated cannot descend from one genus into another.

It is clear also that if A belongs to B, and there is some middle term, then it is possible to demonstrate that A belongs to B. The elements of this demonstration are these, and they are as numerous as the middle terms; for immediate propositions—either all of them or the universal propositions—are elements.

If there is no middle term, there will no longer be a demonstration; the path has reached the principles.

The same applies if A does not belong to B. If there is either a middle term or a prior term to which A does not belong, there will be a demonstration. If there is no middle term, there is no demonstration, but only principles. The elements are as numerous as the terms, since their propositions are the principles of demonstration.

Just as certain principles are indemonstrable—namely, that this is that, or that this belongs to that—so too are the propositions that this is not that, or that this does not belong to that, indemonstrable. Thus some principles affirm that something is, while others affirm that something is not.

Whenever it is necessary to demonstrate something, one must take what is first predicated of B. Let it be C; then likewise take A as predicated of C, and continue in this way without ever going outside the series. The proposition is not established by taking the being of A itself as what is to be demonstrated; rather, the middle term is continually condensed until the terms become immediate and one.

There is one term when the proposition becomes immediate, and one simple proposition is immediate, just as in other cases there is a simple principle. This immediate element is not the same everywhere: in heavy things it is the ounce, in melody the quarter-tone; in one field it is one thing, in another something else.

So in the syllogism the one is an immediate proposition; in demonstration and scientific knowledge, it is intellect.

In ostensive syllogisms concerning what is, nothing falls outside the sequence. In negative syllogisms, however, where the term that ought to belong does not fall outside the sequence, the process proceeds as follows. If A does not belong to B through C, and C belongs universally to B while A belongs to no C, then, if it is necessary to establish that A belongs to no C, a middle term between A and C must be taken, and the process continues in this way.

If it is necessary to demonstrate that D does not belong to E because C belongs universally to D but to no E, or not to every E, the sequence never goes beyond E, since E is the term to which the predicate ought not to belong.

In the third mode, the process goes beyond neither the term to which the predicate ought to belong nor the term that ought to be deprived of it.

## CHAPTER XX. That universal demonstration is superior to particular demonstration

Since every demonstration is either universal or particular, and the former is affirmative while the latter is negative, the question will arise as to which is superior. The same question applies to the demonstration that is said to demonstrate and to demonstration by reduction to the impossible.

Let us first investigate the universal and the particular. Having established this, we shall speak also of the demonstration that is said to demonstrate and of demonstration by reduction to the impossible.

It may perhaps seem to some who investigate the matter in this way that particular demonstration is superior. For if the demonstration through which we know more is the superior demonstration—and this is the excellence of demonstration—then we know each thing more when we know it according to itself than when we know it according to something else.

For example, we know the musical Coriscus more when we know that Coriscus is musical than when we know that a man is musical. The same applies in other cases.

Universal demonstration, however, demonstrates something else, not the thing itself. It demonstrates, for example, that an isosceles triangle has three angles equal to two right angles, not insofar as it is isosceles but insofar as it is a triangle. Particular demonstration, on the other hand, demonstrates the thing itself.

If, therefore, the demonstration according to the thing itself is superior, and particular demonstration is of this kind, then particular demonstration will be superior to universal demonstration, and demonstration according to the particular will be the better demonstration.

Furthermore, if the universal is not something apart from particulars, but demonstration produces the belief that the subject of its demonstration is something real and that this is a certain nature among existing things—for example, triangles apart from particular triangles, figures apart from particular figures, and numbers apart from particular numbers—and if a demonstration concerning being is superior to one concerning non-being, and one by which we shall not be mistaken is superior to one by which we shall be mistaken, then the universal has this character. For those proceeding by demonstration establish the universal as something existing proportionally: for example, that what is of such-and-such a kind will be proportional, although it is neither a line, nor a number, nor a solid, nor a plane, but something apart from these. If, then, the universal is more of this kind, and is less concerned with being than the particular, and if it produces a false belief, the universal will consequently be less worthy than the particular. In the first place, however, there is no more reason in the universal than in the particular for the following argument. [Col. 0736D] If what belongs to two right angles does not belong to the isosceles insofar as it is isosceles, but insofar as it is a triangle, then someone who knows that the isosceles has three angles equal to two right angles insofar as it is itself has less knowledge than someone who knows that it is a triangle. And, in general, if one does not know it insofar as it is a triangle, and then demonstrates it, there will not be a demonstration. But if one knows each thing insofar as it is what it is, one has greater knowledge. If, then, triangle extends over a wider range, the same argument applies; and if “triangle” is not equivocal, and if what has three angles equal to two right angles belongs to every triangle, then it is not the triangle insofar as it is isosceles that has this property, but the isosceles insofar as it is such a triangle has three angles. Therefore, universally, the person who knows knows more through what the thing is than the person who knows particularly. The universal is therefore superior to the particular.

Furthermore, if there is a single account and no equivocation, the universal will be no less particular in relation to certain things, but will be more so insofar as those things are more imperishable; whereas what is particular is more perishable. Moreover, there is no necessity for supposing that something exists apart from these particulars, since demonstrations establish one thing no more than another—namely, whatever does not signify a substance but either a quality, a relation, or an increase. If this is so, then demonstration is not the cause; rather, it is the hearer who supplies the supposition.

Furthermore, if demonstration is a demonstrative syllogism that proceeds from the cause and from the reason why, the universal is more of a cause. For whatever has something belonging to it in itself has that same thing as its cause; but the universal is first. The universal, therefore, is the cause, and consequently the demonstration of it is more worthy, since the universal is more a cause [Col. 0737C] and is more concerned with the reason why.

Moreover, we continue asking “why?” until we reach this point, since we then think that we know when there is no further explanation of why something either comes to be or exists. For the end and final limit is already of this kind: “For what purpose did he come?”—“To receive the money.” “For what purpose?”—“So that he might repay the person to whom he owed it.” “For what purpose?”—“So that he might not act unjustly.” Thus, proceeding until there is no further “why,” and nothing else for which it is a cause, we say that he came, existed, or came to be for this reason, as for an end; and then we know most fully why he came. If, then, the same holds in all causes and in all matters involving the reason why, and if we know those things most fully when they are causes in the same way as the purpose for which something is done is a cause, then in other cases also we know most fully when there is no further explanation that this is because of something else. Thus, when we know that the four exterior angles are equal because the figure is isosceles, we still lack the reason why it is isosceles: because it is a triangle; and why is it a triangle? Because it is a rectilinear figure. But if this no longer has a further reason why, then we know most fully. At that point the knowledge is universal. The universal, therefore, is superior.

Furthermore, whatever is more particular falls into the infinite, whereas the universal falls into the simple and the finite. Things insofar as they are infinite are not knowable, but insofar as they are finite they are knowable. Therefore things demonstrable universally are more knowable than things demonstrable particularly, and so they are more universal. Demonstration is more properly concerned with what is more demonstrable; for such things are simultaneously more closely related to one another. The universal is therefore more worthy, since it is more properly a demonstration. [Col. 0738A]

Furthermore, if the demonstration through which one knows both this and something else is more choiceworthy than the demonstration through which one knows this alone, then, possessing the universal, one knows the particular, whereas possessing the particular one does not know the universal. Thus the universal will also be more choiceworthy in this respect.

And again, universal knowledge is more knowledge through the middle term of a demonstration, since the middle term is nearer to the principle, and what is immediate is nearest of all; and the immediate is the principle. If, then, what proceeds from a principle is more certain than what does not proceed from a principle, and what proceeds more directly from the principle is more certain than what proceeds less directly, demonstration of this kind will be more universal and more worthy. For example, suppose that one must demonstrate that a belongs to d, and that b and c are middle terms, with b higher than c. If the demonstration proceeds through b, it is more universal. [Col. 0738B]

Some of the arguments just given are logical. The clearest indication that the universal is more fundamental is that, when we possess the universal proposition as prior, we in some way know the subsequent proposition as well, and possess it potentially. For if someone knows that every triangle has three angles equal to two right angles, then in a certain way he also knows potentially that the isosceles has angles equal to two right angles—even if he does not know that the isosceles is a triangle. But someone who possesses the latter proposition in no way knows the universal, either potentially or actually. The universal is grasped by thought, whereas the particular is completed through perception.

Let this suffice for what has been said concerning the superiority of the universal over the particular.

## CHAPTER XXI. That affirmative demonstration is superior to negative demonstration

[Col. 0738C]

That affirmative demonstration is superior to negative demonstration is clear from the following. Let the superior demonstration be the one that, with all other things equal, proceeds from fewer questions, suppositions, or propositions. For if these are known equally, knowledge will be acquired more quickly through them, and this is more desirable.

The reason why a demonstration from fewer propositions is better is universally as follows. If the middle terms are equally known, the earlier terms are better known. Suppose that, through the middle terms b, c, and d, one demonstrates that a belongs to e, while another demonstration establishes through b and c that a belongs to d. The propositions that a belongs to d and that a belongs to e are therefore similarly related; but that a belongs to d is prior to, and more knowable than, that a belongs to e, since the latter is demonstrated through the former. What is demonstrated through the prior is more credible. A demonstration through fewer terms is therefore superior, all other things being equal.

Both demonstrations use three terms and two propositions, but one assumes that something exists, whereas the other assumes both that something exists and that something does not exist. It consequently proceeds through more propositions and is therefore less worthy.

Furthermore, it has been shown that a syllogism cannot be formed from two negative propositions, but that one proposition must be of this kind and the other affirmative. In addition, one must make this further assumption: when an affirmative demonstration is extended, more propositions necessarily result, whereas in a negative syllogism it is impossible for more than one proposition in every syllogism to be negative. Let it be assumed that a belongs to nothing in which b belongs, while b belongs to every c. If it is necessary to extend both propositions again, a middle term must be inserted. Let d be the middle term between a and b, and e the middle term between b and c. It is clear that e is affirmative; d is affirmative with respect to b, but a is posited negatively with respect to d. For d belongs to every b, whereas a must belong to no d. Thus there is one negative proposition. The same method applies to the other syllogisms. The middle term of the affirmative terms is always affirmative in both propositions, whereas in the negative terms one proposition must be negative. Thus one proposition is of this kind, while the others are affirmative.

If that through which something is demonstrated is better known and more credible, and if a negative proposition is demonstrated through an affirmative proposition, but the latter is not demonstrated through the former, then the affirmative is prior, better known, and more credible. It will therefore be superior.

Furthermore, if the universal immediate proposition is the principle of a syllogism, in affirmative demonstration this principle is affirmative, whereas in negative demonstration it is a negative universal proposition. But the affirmative proposition is prior to and better known than the negative, since the negative is known through the affirmative, and affirmation is prior in the same way as being is prior to non-being. The principle of affirmative demonstration is therefore superior to that of negative demonstration, and what uses superior principles is itself superior.

It is also more fundamental, for without affirmative demonstration there is no negative demonstration. It is therefore clear that affirmative demonstration is superior to negative demonstration.

## CHAPTER XXII. That demonstrative proof is superior to proof by reduction to the impossible

[Col. 0739C]

The difference between direct demonstration and demonstration leading to the impossible must also be understood. If a belongs to no b, while b belongs to every c, then it necessarily follows that a belongs to no c. When these propositions are assumed, the direct negative demonstration shows that a does not belong to c.

A demonstration leading to the impossible proceeds as follows. If one must demonstrate that a does not belong to b, one assumes that a belongs to b and that b belongs to c; consequently, it follows that a belongs to c. But if it is known and granted that this is impossible, then a cannot belong to b. Thus, if it is granted that b belongs to c, it is impossible for a to belong to b. The terms are therefore arranged similarly.

The difference concerns which negative proposition is better known: whether it is better known that a does not belong to b or that a does not belong to c. When the conclusion—that the impossible does not hold—is better known, the demonstration is a demonstration through the impossible; when it is contained in a syllogism, it is demonstrative.

By nature, the proposition that a does not belong to b is prior to the proposition that a does not belong to c, since the premises from which the conclusion is derived are prior to the conclusion. The proposition that a does not belong to c is the conclusion, whereas the proposition that a does not belong to b is among those from which the conclusion is derived.

For if something can be removed, that does not make it the conclusion, while the propositions from which the conclusion is derived are something else. The proposition from which the syllogism proceeds stands in a relation either like that of a whole to a part or like that of a part to a whole. But the propositions “a does not belong to c” and “a does not belong to b” do not stand in such a relation to each other.

If, then, a demonstration from more worthy and more credible propositions is itself more worthy, and both demonstrations proceed from the non-being of something, but one proceeds from what is prior and the other from what is posterior, the demonstration by reduction to the impossible will simply be the superior negative demonstration. Consequently, affirmative demonstration is superior even to this. It is therefore clear that demonstration by reduction to the impossible is also superior to direct negative demonstration.
