## CHAPTER XXIII. Which knowledge is more certain, which is one, which is another, and how there can be several demonstrations of the same thing

Knowledge is more certain, and prior, when knowledge of the fact and of the reason why are the same, than when they are not the same, apart from knowledge of the reason why. Knowledge that is not subordinate is more certain than knowledge that is subordinate, as arithmetic is more certain than harmonics. Knowledge that proceeds from fewer assumptions is more certain than knowledge that proceeds by addition, as arithmetic is more certain than geometry. By “through addition” I mean, for example, that a unit is a substance without position, whereas a point is a substance with position; the latter is obtained through addition.

A science is one when it belongs to one genus and is composed of first principles, while its parts are either the attributes of that genus or the attributes belonging to it in itself. One science is different from another when their principles are neither derived from the same principles nor from the principles of another science. The sign of this is that, when the demonstrable objects are reached, they must belong to the same genus as the things demonstrated. Another sign is that the demonstrable objects are demonstrated by these principles within the same genus and are proximate to them.

There can be several demonstrations of the same thing, not only by taking a non-continuous middle term from the same order—for example, for things related as a to b, through c, d, and e—but also from a different order. Let a be “to undergo change,” d be “to move,” b be “to rejoice,” and e be “to rest.” It is true both that d is predicated of b and that a is predicated of d: for one who rejoices moves, and what moves undergoes change. Again, it is true that a is predicated of e and e of b: for everyone who rejoices rests, and what rests undergoes change. Thus there is a syllogism through different middle terms and not from the same order. Nevertheless, neither of the middle terms is predicated of the other. For the same e must belong to something in both demonstrations. The matter must be investigated through the different figures, in as many ways as it is possible for a syllogism concerning the same thing to be formed.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That there is no knowledge of things due to chance, nor through the operation of the senses

There is no demonstrative knowledge of what occurs by chance. What is due to chance is neither necessary nor frequent, but occurs outside these categories; demonstration, however, concerns one or the other of them. Every syllogism proceeds either through necessary propositions or through propositions that hold for the most part. If the propositions are necessary, the conclusion will also be necessary; if they hold for the most part, the conclusion will likewise hold for the most part. Therefore, if what occurs by chance is neither frequent nor necessary, there will be no demonstration of it.

Nor is knowledge acquired through perception. For perception is of such-and-such a thing, not of “this” in the universal sense; perceiving necessarily means perceiving something particular, and perceiving it here and now. But it is impossible to perceive the universal, which is present in all things. For it is neither this particular thing, nor now, nor here; otherwise it would not be universal. We call that which is always and everywhere universal. Since demonstrations are universal, while perception does not have this character, it is clear that knowledge cannot be acquired through perception.

It is also clear that if we perceived the triangle as having angles equal to two right angles, we would still seek a demonstration rather than, as some maintain, possess knowledge of it. Perception must be of particulars, whereas knowledge consists in knowing the universal.

Hence, even if we were above the moon and saw the earth obstructing the light, we would not thereby know the cause of the eclipse. We would perceive that it was being eclipsed, but not why; for perception is not of the universal. But by observing that this occurs repeatedly, and seeking the universal, we possess a demonstration. The universal becomes clear from several particulars. The universal is especially valuable because it reveals the cause. Knowledge of such a universal is therefore more valuable than perception and than knowledge of anything for which there is another cause.

The case of first principles is different. It is clear, then, that it is impossible to know any demonstrated object through perception, unless someone were to say that perception itself possesses knowledge through demonstration. There are, however, some matters that are reduced to a deficiency in perception among the propositions. If we could see certain things, we would not seek an explanation of them. But this would not be because we knew them simply by seeing; rather, from what we saw we would possess the universal. For example, if we saw a perforated glass and light passing through it, it would immediately be clear why it illuminates: because we would see separately in each case, while understanding simultaneously that the same holds in all cases. [Col. 0741C]

## CHAPTER XXV. That the principles of all syllogisms cannot be the same

It is impossible for the principles of all syllogisms to be the same, first when considered logically: some syllogisms are true, while others are false. Even if it is possible to syllogize truly from false premises, this occurs only once—for example, if a is truly predicated of c, while the middle term b is false. For neither does a belong to b nor b to c. If propositions are taken from these middle terms, they will be false, since every false conclusion follows from false premises, whereas a true conclusion follows from true premises; but the premises in question are partly true and partly false.

Moreover, false things do not arise from the same principles, since falsehoods can be mutually opposed, contrary, or impossible for them to exist together: for example, justice and injustice, fear and boldness, a human being and a horse or ox, or equal, greater, and lesser.

The same is true of opposites. The principles of all true things are not the same, since there are different principles for different genera. Nor do they coincide: units do not coincide with points, since units have no position, whereas points do.

The principles must either converge in the middle, or above, or below, or one set must lie inside the terms while another lies outside them. Nor can there be some common principles from which everything will be demonstrated. By “common” I mean principles such as “everything must either be affirmed or denied.” For the genera of existing things are different: some belong solely to quantities, others solely to qualities, and it is through the common principles that they are demonstrated. [Col. 0742A]

Furthermore, principles are not much fewer than conclusions. Principles are propositions, and propositions consist of terms that are assumed or inserted. Conclusions, however, are infinite, while terms are finite. Moreover, some principles are necessary, while other conclusions are contingent. Thus, from this point of view, it is impossible for the principles to be the same or finite, since the conclusions are infinite.

If someone says in another sense that some principles belong to geometry, others to numbers, and others to medicine, what else is he saying except that the principles of the sciences are different? It is ridiculous to say that they are the same, since the same things would have the same principles; everything would consequently become the same.

Nor does the demand that anything whatsoever be demonstrated from all principles amount to the claim that all principles are the same; that would be extremely foolish. This does not happen even in the evident sciences, nor is it possible in resolution. Immediate propositions are principles, and another conclusion is formed when an immediate proposition has been assumed.

If someone says that the first immediate propositions are the same principles, there is one such principle in each genus. But if it is neither possible to demonstrate anything whatsoever from all principles as required, nor, from another set of principles, to show that they belong to a single science, it remains that the principles of all things are proximate principles: some things proceed from one set, others from another. This too is clear, since it has been shown that the principles of things differing in genus are different.

Principles are of two kinds: those from which a demonstration proceeds, and those concerning which it proceeds. The former are common; the latter are proper—for example, number and magnitude. [Col. 0742C]

## CHAPTER XXVI. That knowledge and the knowable differ from opinion and the opinable

The knowable and knowledge differ from the opinable and opinion because knowledge is universal and necessary in the strictest sense, whereas what is necessary cannot be otherwise. There are some true things that can be otherwise. It is therefore clear that there is no knowledge concerning these things, since they could otherwise be different.

Nor is opinion intellect—for intellect is the principle of scientific knowledge—nor is it indemonstrable knowledge, which is the apprehension of an immediate proposition. Intellect, knowledge, and opinion, and what is said by means of them, are true. It follows that opinion concerns what is true or false and can be otherwise. It is the apprehension of an immediate, non-necessary proposition.

Opinion is uncertain in accordance with what appears in this way, and its nature is such. Moreover, no one thinks that he is merely opining when he believes that something cannot be otherwise; rather, he thinks that he knows it. But when he believes that something is so while recognizing that it could be otherwise, nothing prevents him from opining it. Thus opinion is concerned with what is contingent, while knowledge is concerned with what is necessary.

How, then, can opining and knowing not be the same? And why will opinion not be knowledge, if someone posits that everything one knows can also be opined? For the person who knows and the person who opines will proceed through the middle terms until they arrive at the immediate propositions. If the one knew, then the one who opined would also know, since opinion of the fact and opinion of the reason why would be involved, and the reason why is the middle term.

Or would someone who holds this view say that things cannot be otherwise in the way that the definitions through which demonstrations are made cannot be otherwise? In that case, he would not opine but know. But if he believes that the things are true without believing that these attributes belong to them according to their substance and species, then he will opine and will not truly know either the fact or the reason why. If he opines through immediate propositions, he will opine both the fact and the reason why; but if he does not proceed through immediate propositions, he will opine only the fact.

Opinion and knowledge do not wholly concern the same thing, but they concern the same thing in the way that truth and falsehood do in some sense. Thus knowledge and opinion can concern the same thing, and there can be both true and false opinion about it. As some say, however, if true and false opinion concern the same thing, absurd consequences follow: one would desire other things while not opining the things one falsely opines.

Since “the same” is said in many ways—sometimes as what can be otherwise, sometimes as what cannot be otherwise—it is absurd to opine that the diameter is commensurable. But the diameter, about which the opinions are held, is the same subject in both cases; what it is to be a diameter, however, is not the same according to the account.

The same applies to knowledge and opinion of the same thing. The former, for example, is that something is an animal, which cannot fail to be an animal; the latter is that it is a human being, which can fail to be a human being. The subject is the same—the human being—but it is not the same in the same respect.

From these considerations it is clear that it is impossible simultaneously to opine and to know the same thing in the same respect. One would then simultaneously hold the opinion that the thing could be otherwise and that it could not be otherwise. The same thing can be so in different respects, as has been said, but not in the same respect. Otherwise one would simultaneously possess contradictory opinions.

For example, one may hold that a human being is an animal insofar as he is an animal—for in that respect he cannot be a non-animal—but that he is a human being in another respect, in which this can be otherwise. The remaining question—how these matters should be distributed among intellect, knowledge, science, art, practical wisdom, and wisdom—belongs more properly to the study of nature in one respect and to ethical inquiry in another.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On acumen

Acumen is a certain capacity for recognizing the middle term instantly, without previous investigation. For example, someone sees that the moon always has its brightness directed toward the sun and immediately understands why this is so: because it is illuminated by the sun. Or, while arguing with a wealthy person, he recognizes that the person is borrowing money; or, because two people are friends, he recognizes that they are enemies of the same person. In every case, by seeing the middle causes, he recognizes the final causes.

Let “being bright toward the sun” be a, “being illuminated by the sun” b, and “the moon” c. Thus c—namely, the moon—has b, which is being illuminated by the sun; and b has a, which is being bright toward that from which it shines. Therefore c also has a through b.

# BOOK II

## CHAPTER I. The number of questions ordinarily asked in the sciences

The questions we ask are equal in number to the things that we truly know. There are four things we ask: the fact, the reason why, whether something exists, and what it is.

When we ask whether one thing belongs to another, or whether it belongs to it or not, we are asking the question of the fact. For example, when we ask whether the sun is eclipsed or not, we are asking whether the eclipse occurs. The sign of this is that, when we discover that it is eclipsed, we stop; and if we knew from the beginning that it was eclipsed, we would not ask whether it was.

When we know the fact itself, we ask the reason why: for example, knowing that the sun is eclipsed and that the earth moves, we ask why the sun is eclipsed and why the earth moves.

In other cases we ask whether something exists, such as whether a centaur or a god exists. Here I mean whether it exists simply, not whether it is white or not. When we know that it exists, we ask what it is—for example, what a god is or what a human being is.

These, then, are the things we ask, and these are the things we know when we discover them.

## CHAPTER II. That every question concerns the middle term

When we ask whether something exists or whether it exists simply, we are asking whether there is a middle term for it or not. When, having learned either that it exists, or whether it exists, whether particularly or simply, we ask again why it exists or what it is, we are then asking what the middle term is.

By “whether it exists” or “whether it is” I mean either particularly or simply. Particularly, for example, when we ask whether the moon is eclipsed or is increasing; for in such cases we ask whether something is or is not the case. Simply, when we ask whether the moon or night exists or does not exist.

Thus in every question we may ask either whether there is a middle term or what the middle term is. The middle term is the cause, and in every case this is what is sought. For example, when we ask whether the moon is eclipsed, we first ask whether there is some cause of the eclipse; once we know that there is one, we ask what it is.

The cause of the moon’s being eclipsed is not merely this or that particular attribute, but its substance simply, or not its substance simply but one of the things belonging to it in itself or accidentally. This is the middle term.

By “simply” I mean the subject—for example, the moon, the earth, the sun, or the triangle. By “what it is” I mean the eclipse, equality, or inequality, if the middle term is present or not.

In all these cases it is clear that what a thing is and why it is are the same. What is an eclipse? A deprivation of light from the moon through the interposition of the earth. Why is there an eclipse, or why is the moon eclipsed? Because the earth, being interposed, deprives it of light.

What is consonance? A numerical ratio between the high and the low note. Why is the high note consonant with the low? Because both the high and the low have a numerical ratio.

Is the high note consonant with the low? Is there a ratio between them in numbers? Having established that there is consonance, we ask what the ratio is.

That the question concerns the middle term is shown whenever the middle term is perceptible. For when we do not perceive it, we ask whether an eclipse exists or not. But if we were above the moon, we would not ask either whether an eclipse occurs or why it occurs; both would be immediately clear, since from perception we would also have acquired knowledge of the universal. Perception would tell us what is now obstructing the light and would make it clear that an eclipse is now occurring; from these observations the universal would be established.

As we have said, knowing what a thing is is the same as knowing why it is. This may concern something simply, not one of its attributes, or it may concern an attribute—for example, that two right angles are present, or that something is greater or lesser.

It is therefore clear that all the things we ask are questions concerning the middle term.

## CHAPTER III. The distinction between demonstration and definition: that they are not of the same thing

How the essence is demonstrated, what the method of introduction is, what definition is, and what things admit of definition, we shall explain by first setting out the difficulties concerning them. The starting point should be the matters that will be most appropriate to the arguments already given.

Someone may ask whether knowing by definition and knowing by demonstration are the same in respect of the same thing, or whether this is impossible. Definition appears to state the essence of a thing. But the essence is always universal and affirmative. Syllogisms, however, are sometimes negative and sometimes not universal. In the second figure all syllogisms are negative, whereas in the third figure they are not universal.

Moreover, not every affirmative syllogism in the first figure has a definition as its conclusion—for example, the proposition that every triangle has angles equal to two right angles. The reason is that to know something demonstrable is to possess a demonstration of it. If there is a demonstration in such cases, it is clear that there will not also be a definition of them. Someone may know it according to a definition without possessing a demonstration, since there is nothing to prevent the two from not being possessed simultaneously.

Induction is sufficient for conviction. If it were not, we would at some point know nothing by defining anything, neither things that belong to a subject in themselves nor things that belong to it accidentally.

Furthermore, if definition is a kind of knowledge of substance, it is clear that such things are not substances. It is therefore clear that there is not a definition of everything that has a demonstration.

But of what things is there a definition? Is every demonstration a definition, or not? The same argument applies here. There is one science of one thing insofar as it is one. If knowing what is demonstrable is possessing a demonstration, an impossibility follows: someone would know a thing through its definition without possessing a demonstration.

Furthermore, definitions are the principles of demonstrations, and it has already been shown that there are no demonstrations of these principles. Otherwise the principles would themselves be demonstrable, and there would be principles of principles, continuing to infinity; or the first definitions would be indemonstrable.

But perhaps the definition and the demonstration are not both of the same thing universally, but only of some things. This too seems impossible. The demonstration of a thing is not the same as its definition: definition states what the thing is and its substance, whereas demonstrations presuppose and assume what the essence is—for example, mathematical demonstrations assume what a unit is and what an odd number is, and so do the other sciences.

Moreover, every demonstration shows something of something, for example, that something is or is not. In a definition, however, nothing is predicated of something else: neither is “animal” predicated of “two-footed,” nor “two-footed” of “animal”; neither is “figure” predicated of “plane,” nor “plane” of “figure,” since a plane is not a figure, nor a figure a plane.

Moreover, demonstrating what a thing is differs from demonstrating that it is. Definition shows what a thing is, whereas demonstration shows that this belongs to that, or does not belong to it.

A different demonstration belongs to a different matter, unless one is a part of the whole. By this I mean the demonstration that an isosceles has angles equal to two right angles, if every demonstrated object is a triangle: the former is a part, the latter the whole. But “that it is” and “what it is” do not stand in this relation to each other; neither is a part of the other.

It is therefore clear that not every object of definition is the object of a demonstration, nor is every object of a demonstration the object of a definition. Thus, generally, nothing can possess both with respect to the same thing.

It is therefore clear that definition and demonstration are neither identical nor contained one within the other; for if they were, their subjects would stand in the same relation. These, then, are the difficulties up to this point.

## CHAPTER IV. That the essence of a thing is not demonstrated by a syllogism that assumes it twice

The question is whether the essence is a syllogism and a demonstration, as the preceding argument assumed.

A syllogism demonstrates something of something through a middle term. But the essence belongs properly to a thing, and in the account of what a thing is it is predicated of it; this must be convertible. For if a belongs properly to c, then it is also clear that it belongs properly to b, and that b belongs properly to c. Thus all the terms are convertible with one another.

Furthermore, if a belongs to every b in the account of what the thing is, and b is universally predicated of every c in the account of what the thing is, then a must be predicated of c in the account of what it is. But if someone does not make this assumption through a duplicating syllogism, it will not be necessary that a be predicated of c in the account of what it is.

Suppose, however, that a is predicated of b in the account of what it is, but b is not predicated of everything in the account of what it is. If both a and b possess the essence, then b will also be predicated of c in the account of what it is.

If, then, both terms possess the essence and what it is to be that thing, the essence will be prior in the middle term. In general, if one demonstrates what a human being is, let c be “human being,” a be the essence—whether “two-footed animal” or something else. If a is syllogistically predicated of c, a must be predicated of every b. There will therefore be another middle account for this, and that too will be what it is to be a human being. The argument consequently assumes what it ought to demonstrate, since b is already what it is to be a human being.

This must be considered in two propositions, and especially in the first and immediate propositions, since what is being said becomes most evident there. [Col. 0747A]

In demonstrations by conversion of what the soul is, or what a human being is, or anything else that exists, the argument begs the principle. For example, if someone thinks that the soul is the cause of life to itself, and that this is a number moving itself, he must assume that the soul is this very thing—that is, a number moving itself—in precisely the same sense.

For even if a follows b, and b follows c, it does not follow that c possesses a as its essence; it will only be true to say that c possesses a. Nor, if a is the essence and is predicated of every b, will it follow that a is the essence of c. For the essence of animal is predicated of the essence of human being, and it is true that the essence of animal is predicated of every essence of human being, just as animal is predicated of every human being; but it does not follow that they are one essence.

If, then, the terms are not assumed in this manner, it is not syllogistically established that a is the essence and substance of c. But if they are assumed in this manner, then what is being assumed is prior: namely, that b is the essence of c. Thus the conclusion has not been demonstrated, since what was present at the beginning has been assumed.

## CHAPTER V. That the essence cannot be established by division either
But neither is it possible to syllogize by division, as was stated in the discussion of resolution concerning the figures. For it is by no means necessary that the thing in question exist when these conditions are present, any more than induction demonstrates it. One must not ask for the conclusion, nor must it be among the propositions conceded; rather, it must necessarily follow when those propositions are present. If the respondent does not say whether “man is an animal” or “inanimate,” and the questioner then takes “animal,” he has not syllogized. Again, if he takes “every animal is either walking or aquatic,” and then takes “walking,” and that “man is wholly a walking animal,” the conclusion will not necessarily follow from what has been said; he has assumed this also. It makes no difference whether one says this in many steps or in few, for the procedure is the same.

The procedure is therefore not syllogistic when one proceeds in this way, and it is possible to syllogize about contingent matters as well. For what prevents all these predicates from being true of man, while nevertheless none of them states what he is, or demonstrates what his essence is? Further, what prevents one from adding something, removing something, or exceeding the substances? These matters may therefore be dismissed.

It is possible, however, to resolve the matter by taking all the elements in the essence and then making the division that was previously sought, leaving nothing out. This is necessary if everything falls under the division and nothing is left over, for the final species must be indivisible. Yet a syllogism is still not present. If the procedure makes us know the matter in some other way, that is not objectionable; for induction perhaps does not demonstrate either, but it nevertheless makes something evident. But one cannot call it a syllogism merely because, by selecting from the division, one arrives at a definition. For just as, in conclusions without middle terms, if someone says that when these things exist this other thing must exist, one may ask why it is so, so also one may ask in the case of divided terms: “What is man?” “A mortal animal, possessing feet, two-footed, without wings.” Why does he know each addition? He will give an account and exhibit it by division, on the supposition that every animal is either mortal or immortal, and so forth. But no such account is a definition. Thus he has made something evident through division, but the result is a definition, not a syllogism.

## CHAPTER VI  
### The definition cannot be demonstrated by taking the definition of definition, nor by the definition of the contrary

But is it possible to demonstrate what a thing is in substance by taking as a condition its essence, which is constituted by the things belonging properly to what the thing is? These are the only constituents of what the thing is, and everything proper to it is its being. Or has he again taken the essence, and taken it as belonging to this? In that case it must be demonstrated through a middle term.

Further, just as in a syllogism one does not take “what it is to syllogize” as a premise—for it is always the whole or part of a proposition, and a syllogism is composed of propositions—so neither should what a thing is be present in the syllogism; rather, it should be separate from the propositions laid down. If someone asks whether the matter has been syllogized or not, the answer is that this was the syllogism; and, in addition, that the essence has not been syllogized, since it was already assumed as the essence. Consequently, either a syllogism can exist without what the thing is, or it is possible to syllogize what the essence is.

And if one demonstrates it from a condition—for example, if divisibility belongs to evil, then indivisibility belongs to the contrary; whatever has a contrary has something contrary to it; good is contrary to evil, and indivisible is contrary to divisible; therefore indivisibility belongs to good—then, by assuming the essence, he demonstrates it. Yet what is taken for demonstrating the essence is something else.

For in demonstrations, one predicate belongs to another, but it is not the thing itself, nor is it something whose account is identical with it and convertible with it. The same difficulty arises both for those who demonstrate by division and for those who syllogize in this manner: why is man a walking, two-footed animal, but not simply an animal and a two-footed thing? From the premises taken, there is no necessity that the predicates form one thing; otherwise the same man would also be a musician and a grammarian.

## CHAPTER VII  
### He argues that what a thing is cannot be demonstrated

How, then, will the definer demonstrate substance, or what a thing is? For he cannot, as someone demonstrating from established premises, make it evident that some other thing must exist when those premises exist. That is demonstration. Nor can he do so as one who induces from particulars, when it is evident that the whole is so because it is not otherwise. For induction does not show what a thing is, but only that it is or is not.

What other method, then, remains? He cannot demonstrate it by sense-perception or by pointing. Further, how will he show what man is? For someone who knows what man is, or anything else, must also know that man exists. No one knows what a thing is when it does not exist; one knows only what the word signifies. Thus, when I say “goat-stag,” there is an account or name of what it signifies, but it is impossible to know what a goat-stag is.

But if he demonstrates both what it is and that it is, how will he demonstrate them by the same account? What a man is and the existence of a man are different things. Further, we say that everything except substance must be demonstrated as existing—whereas existence itself is not a substance, for it is not a genus. The demonstration will therefore show that the thing exists, as the sciences now do. The geometer, for example, assumes what “triangle” signifies and demonstrates that a triangle exists.

What, then, will the definer show concerning what a triangle is? Someone may know from the definition what it is, but if it exists he will not know; yet that is impossible. It is also clear from the present methods of defining terms that definers do not demonstrate that the thing exists. Even if there is a middle term from which something equal follows, one may still ask why the thing defined exists, and why a circle exists. One could even say that it is a bronze mountain; for definitions neither establish that the thing described can exist nor that it is the thing whose definition they claim to give. It is always possible to ask why.

If, then, the definer demonstrates either what the thing is or what the name signifies, but in no way demonstrates what the thing itself is, the definition will be an account of the name, signifying the same thing; but that is not adequate. First, there would then be definitions of non-substances and of things that do not exist, since even things that do not exist can be signified. Further, every account would be a definition, for one could assign a name to every account; then we would be disputing entirely by definitions, and the *Iliad* would be a definition.

Moreover, no science demonstrates that a name is the essence of the thing it signifies, and definitions therefore do not establish this either. From these considerations, definition does not appear to be the same as syllogism, nor does the syllogism and the definition belong to the same thing. Furthermore, definition neither demonstrates anything nor makes anything evident; neither what the thing is, nor through definition or demonstration can what the thing is be known.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### What it means for what a thing is to be demonstrated through something else

We must again examine which of the things said are correct and which are not, what definition is, and whether it is in some way a demonstration of what a thing is, or a definition, or neither.

As we said, to know what a thing is and to know the cause of its existence are the same, because there is some cause, and that cause is either the same as the thing or different from it. If it is different, it is either demonstrable or indemonstrable.

If it is different and can be demonstrated, there must be a middle term, and the demonstration must be in the first figure, for what is demonstrated is universal and affirmative. One way of demonstrating what a thing is through something else has now been investigated. In such cases, the essence must be a middle term, and the property must be the property of the property. Thus one account will demonstrate something, but the other will not demonstrate the essence of the same thing.

We have already said that this method is not a demonstration of what the thing is; it is a logical syllogism concerning what the thing is.

## CHAPTER IX  
### What a thing is and that it is

We shall explain how this can occur by beginning again from the start. Just as, when we ask why, we already possess the fact that something is, and sometimes the two become evident together, but it is impossible to know why before knowing that, so likewise it is impossible to know the essence without knowing that the thing exists. For it is impossible to know what a thing is while being ignorant whether it exists.

Sometimes we possess the fact accidentally, but at other times we possess the essence of the thing itself: for example, thunder is a certain sound in clouds; an eclipse is a certain privation of light; man is a certain animal; and the soul is something that moves itself.

Whenever we know only accidentally that such things exist, this has no relation to knowing what they are. For, since we do not know that they exist, it is impossible to ask what they are. If we do not possess the fact that a thing exists, asking what it is is to ask nothing. But when we possess what the thing is, the matter is easy. Thus, in the same way as we possess the fact that it exists, we also possess the answer to what it is.

Let us take an example among things whose essence we possess. Let an eclipse be A, the moon C, and the earth’s obstruction B. The question “Does the moon suffer eclipse or not?” is the question whether B exists. This is no different from asking whether the account of the eclipse exists, and whether, if this exists, we say that the other exists; or from asking which of the two contradictory accounts applies: whether the moon has two right angles, or does not have two right angles.

When we discover the fact and the reason together, we know the reason if it is obtained through a middle term; otherwise, we know the fact but not the reason. Let the moon be C, eclipse A, and the moon’s inability to cast a shadow when nothing lies between us and it B. If B—the inability to cast a shadow when nothing lies between us—is present in C, then A, eclipse, is present in C. It is evident that the moon is eclipsed, but not yet why. We know that there is an eclipse, but we do not know what it is.

When it is evident that A belongs to C, the question “Why does it exist?” is the question whether B is the earth’s obstruction, the moon’s turning, or the extinguishing of its light. This is the account of the other term, namely A itself; for an eclipse is the earth’s obstruction.

What is thunder? The extinguishing of fire in a cloud. Why does it thunder? Because fire is extinguished in a cloud. Let the cloud be C, thunder A, and the extinguishing of fire B. B is present in C, for fire is extinguished in the cloud; A belongs to B; and B is the account of A, the first term. If there is again another middle term for this, the account will be obtained through the remaining terms.

How what a thing is is taken and becomes known has therefore been explained. Consequently, there is no syllogism of what a thing is, nor a demonstration of it; yet it becomes evident through syllogism and demonstration. Thus it is not possible to know what a thing is without demonstration when it has another cause, but the demonstration is not a demonstration of the thing’s essence, as we also said in discussing the difficulties.

## CHAPTER X  
### The definition of what a thing is and the reason why

Some things have another cause, while others do not. It is therefore evident that among things whose essence is in question, some are without a middle term, such as principles. Their existence and what they are must be assumed, or otherwise made evident, as the arithmetician does. For he assumes what a unit is and that it exists.

But in the case of things that have a middle term, and whose substance and existence have some other cause, one must show through demonstration, as we said, though not demonstrate the essence itself.

Since definition is said to be an account of what a thing is, it is evident that one kind of definition will be an account of what the name signifies, while another will be an account that introduces names. For example, when we ask what “what a triangle is” signifies, we already possess the fact that it exists and ask why it exists.

It is difficult to grasp what we do not know to exist, for the reason given earlier: we know neither whether it exists nor whether it does not, except accidentally.

An account is “one” in two ways. In one way, it is one through conjunction, as the *Iliad* is one account. In another way, it exhibits one thing of one thing, not accidentally. The first kind is the definition of a term, as previously stated. The other is an account demonstrating why the thing exists. Thus the first signifies but does not demonstrate.

The second kind is evidently what the demonstration of the essence will be, differing from demonstration only in the arrangement of the terms. For it is different to say “Why does it thunder?” and “What is thunder?” The answer to the first is: “Because fire is extinguished in the clouds.” The answer to the second is: “A sound caused by the extinguishing of fire in a cloud.” Thus the same account is stated in one way and in another: in one form it is a continuous demonstration, in the other a definition.

Further, the definition of thunder is “sound in the clouds.” This is the account of its essence and is the conclusion of a demonstration. But the definition of immediate things is a positing of their essence and is indemonstrable.

There is therefore, first, a definition that is an indemonstrable account of what a thing is; second, a syllogism of what a thing is, differing from demonstration only in the arrangement of its terms; and third, the conclusion of a demonstration concerning what a thing is.

From what has been said, it is evident both how there is a demonstration of what a thing is and how there is not one, which things admit it and which do not. It is also evident in how many ways definition is spoken of, how it shows what a thing is and how it does not, which things admit definition and which do not, how definition is related to demonstration, when the two can belong to the same thing, and when they cannot.

## CHAPTER XI  
### Demonstration can proceed through any kind of cause

Since we believe that we know when we know the cause, and since there are four causes—one being what a thing was to be, another being that when this exists that must exist, another being what first set something in motion, and the fourth being that for the sake of which something is—we demonstrate all these through a middle term.

That when this exists that must exist is not established by one premise, but by at least two. This occurs when they have one middle term; once this middle term is taken, the conclusion must follow.

It is evident in this way why the angle in a semicircle is a right angle, or what must exist for it to be a right angle. Let the right angle be A, half of two right angles B, and the angle in a semicircle C. The cause of A—the right angle—in C—the angle in a semicircle—is B, for B is equal to A, and C is equal to B. Half of two right angles is a right angle; therefore, when half of two right angles exists, A is present in C. This was what it meant for the angle in a semicircle to be right. The same thing is also what the essence signifies in an account. Thus the cause of the essence itself has also been demonstrated through a middle term.

Why was the war against the Persians undertaken by the Athenians? What was the cause of the Athenians’ fighting? Because, together with the Eretrians, they had made an attack upon Sardis; this set the event in motion.

Let war be A, the prior engagement with the enemy B, and the Athenians C. B is present in C, for the Athenians were the first to engage; A is present in B, for they had first made war upon those who had acted unjustly. Thus A is present in B as the beginning of the war, and B is present in C, namely the Athenians, since they began first. Here the middle term is the first moving cause.

In cases where the cause is that for the sake of which something occurs, one asks, “Why does he walk?” “So that he may become healthy.” “Why is there a house?” “So that the vessels may be preserved.” The first is for the sake of becoming healthy, the second for the sake of preserving the vessels. There is no difference between asking why one ought to walk after dinner and asking for the sake of what one ought to do so.

Let walking after dinner be C, the food’s not rising toward the mouth of the stomach B, and becoming healthy A. In the fact that someone walks after dinner, there is the fact that the food does not rise toward the mouth of the stomach; and this is becoming healthy. B is therefore present in C, and A is present in B. The cause of A’s being present in C, as that for the sake of which it occurs, is B, the food’s not rising. This is like the account of the other term: “Why is B present in C?” “Because this is the condition of becoming healthy.”

The accounts must be exchanged in this way, and then the individual cases will become clearer. The generations in these cases are the reverse of the order in causes connected with motion. There, the middle term must come first; here, C itself is the extreme term, and what is for the sake of which something occurs comes last.

The same thing can also be both for the sake of which something occurs and necessary, as light passes through the hide of a lantern. It necessarily passes through, because what is contained in a small space is more finely divided and passes through larger pores, if indeed light comes through by passing out; and it does so for the sake of our not stumbling.

If something can exist, can it also come to be? For example, if thunder occurs because fire is extinguished, it is necessary that there be a hissing and a sound; and, as the Pythagoreans say, thunder occurs for the sake of threatening those in Tartarus, so that they may be afraid.

There are very many cases of this kind, especially among things that exist by nature and remain constant. Nature produces some for this purpose, while others occur by necessity. Necessity is of two kinds: one according to nature and aptitude, the other violent and contrary to aptitude. Thus a stone is carried upward and downward by necessity, but not by the same necessity.

Among things produced by intelligence, some do not arise from what is useless in itself—for example, a house or a statue—and are not produced by necessity, but for a purpose. Others arise by fortune, such as health and safety, especially in cases where things can occur either one way or another, while the generation itself is not due to fortune.

A good end therefore occurs for the sake of something either by nature or by art; nothing occurs by fortune for the sake of something.

The same cause belongs to things that are coming to be, to things that have come to be, and to things that will be, just as it truly belongs to things that exist: the middle term is the cause. Nevertheless, in existing things the cause is what exists; in things coming to be, what is coming to be; in things that have come to be, what has come to be; and in future things, what will be.

For example, why has an eclipse occurred? Because the earth has come to be in the middle. It occurs because the earth comes to be in the middle; it will occur because the earth will be in the middle; and it exists because the earth is in the middle.

What is crystal? Let it be taken as frozen water. Let water be C, frozen A, and the intermediate cause B, the complete absence of heat. B is therefore present in C, and in B is the fact of being frozen, which is A. Crystal comes to be when B comes to be; it has come to be when B has come to be; and it will be when B will be.

Thus the cause, and that for the sake of which something occurs, comes to be together with the thing when it comes to be, exists together with it when it exists, and is present in the thing that has come to be and in the future thing in the same way.

## CHAPTER XII  
### Coming to be and having come to be

In things that do not occur together, does the relation hold in continuous time? It appears that in such cases the causes are different: what has come to be is the cause of what has come to be later, what will be is the cause of what will be later, and what has already come to be is the cause of what comes to be afterward.

There is therefore a syllogism concerning A, which comes later than what has come to be. The beginning belongs to the things that have come to be, and similarly to things that are coming to be. But there is no syllogism from what is earlier to what is later—for example, it does not follow that, because this has come to be, that has come to be later. The same holds for the future.

For it will not be so over either an infinite or a finite time. Since it is true to say that this has come to be, it is true to say that this has come to be later. But it would be false to say that, in the interval, this has already come to be when the other has come to be; the same account applies to the future.

Nor does it follow that, because this has come to be, that will come to be. The middle term must have come to be at the same time: what has come to be with what has come to be, what is coming to be with what is coming to be, and what exists with what exists. But what will be and what exists cannot have come to be simultaneously.

Further, the time constituting the middle term cannot be either infinite or finite, for it would be false to say what occurs in the interval.

We must therefore examine what is continuous. Is the coming-to-be of things after what has come to be continuous? It is evident that what is coming to be is not continuous with what has come to be, nor what has come to be with what has come to be afterward. The terms are atomic. Just as points are not joined to one another, so neither are things that have come to be; both are indivisible.

Nor, for the same reason, is what is coming to be continuous with what has come to be. What is coming to be is divisible, whereas what has come to be is indivisible. As a line is related to a point, so what is coming to be is related to what has come to be; for there are infinitely many things that have come to be within what is coming to be. This is clearer in universal cases.

We must speak about these matters in connection with motion. So much has been established concerning how the middle cause is related to what comes to be next in generation: there must be a middle term, and the first terms must be immediate. Let A have come to be because C has come to be, with C having come to be later and A earlier.

The beginning is C, because it is nearest to the present, which is the beginning of time. But C has come to be if D has come to be. When D has come to be, A must also have come to be; the cause is C. For once D has come to be, C must have come to be, and once C has come to be, A must previously have existed.

If one takes some middle term, will it always fall outside because of infinity? What has come to be is not continuous with what has come to be, as has been said. Nevertheless, one must begin from a middle term and from the first present moment.

The same applies to what will be. If it is true to say that D will be, it is first necessary truly to say that A will be. The cause of this is C: if D will be, C will first be; and if C will be, A will first be.

The division in these cases is likewise infinite. What will be will not be continuous with what will be, and the beginning in these cases must also be taken without a middle term.

The same relation appears in works. If a house has been built, the stones must have been cut, and this has occurred because the foundation has been built, since if the house has been built, the foundation must have been built. If the foundation exists, the stones must previously have been cut. Again, if a house will be built, the walls will first be built; and this too is demonstrated through a middle term, since the foundation will be earlier.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### In things generated in a circle, demonstration is circular

We see that in things that come to be there is a certain circular generation, and this is possible when the middle term and the extremes follow one another. For in such cases they are convertible. It has already been shown above that conclusions are convertible; and this is what circularity is.

In practical cases the relation appears as follows: when the earth has been drenched, vapor must arise; when this has arisen, a cloud comes to be; when the cloud has come to be, water comes to be; and when water has come to be, the earth must have been drenched. This was the starting point. Thus the process has gone around in a circle: when any one of these exists, the other exists; when that other exists, the next exists; and when this exists, the first exists.

Some things come to be universally: they always and in every case either exist or come to be in this way. Others do not always do so, but are as they usually are. For example, not every male human being has a beard, but this is what usually occurs.

In such cases, then, the middle term must also hold usually. If A is universally predicated of B, and B universally of C, A must be predicated always and of every C. For this is what “universally,” “of every,” and “always” mean. But it was assumed that the matter holds usually. Therefore the middle term, which is present in B, must hold usually as well.

Thus the principles of things that usually occur will also be without middle terms, whenever things usually exist or come to be in this way.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### How the definition is to be investigated

We have already stated how what a thing is is to be assigned in terms, and how demonstration or definition belongs to it or does not. We shall now explain how one ought to seek the predicates belonging to what a thing is.

Among the things that always belong to each individual, some extend more widely, though not beyond the genus. By “extend more widely” I mean whatever belongs universally to each member of one class but also belongs to something else—for example, something that belongs to every triad but also to things that are not triads.

“Being” belongs to a triad, but also to number; “odd” belongs to every triad and extends more widely, since it also belongs to five, though not beyond the genus, for five is a number and nothing outside number is odd.

Such predicates must be taken until one has taken as many as are required, each of which extends more widely, but all of which together do not extend more widely. For this must be the substance of the thing.

“Number,” “odd,” and “prime in both senses”—both “not measured by a number” and “not composed of numbers”—belong to every triad. The triad, then, is a number that is odd and prime in both senses. Each of these predicates belongs to all odd numbers, whereas the last also belongs to two; but all of them together belong to nothing else.

Since we showed earlier that the predicates belonging to what a thing is are necessary, and that necessary predicates are universal, these predicates, when taken in this way as belonging to the triad and to anything else of the same kind, will constitute the necessary essence of the triad.

That this is substance is evident from the following. Unless this is the being of the triad, it must be some genus. Whether this genus has been named or not, it will extend more widely than the triad. Let it be granted that such a genus exists, belonging potentially to more things. If it belongs to nothing other than atomic triads, then it will be the being of the triad. Let this be assumed as the substance of each thing, namely the ultimate predicate in atomic things. The same argument applies to anything else; in the case of what has been demonstrated, this will be its being.

It is appropriate, when someone is investigating a whole subject, to divide the genus into the first atomic species—for example, number into triad and duality—and then to try to take their definitions, such as those of straight line, circle, and right angle.

After this, once one has taken the genus—whether it belongs among quantities or qualities—one should examine its proper attributes through the primary common features. For things composed of atoms, the features that agree will become evident from the definitions, because definition is the principle of everything: what is simple belongs intrinsically only to simple things, and belongs to other things through those simple constituents.

Divisions according to differences are useful for proceeding in this way, as was stated earlier. They are useful only for collecting what a thing is. They will appear to demonstrate nothing, but will immediately deceive us, as though one had assumed the answer from the beginning without division.

It makes a difference whether the first or a later predicate is predicated. For example, one may say “a tame, two-footed animal” or “a two-footed, tame animal.” If the whole consists of two elements, and “tame animal” is one thing, and from this together with the difference “man” or some other single thing is formed, the person making the division must assume what he is seeking.

Further, nothing should be left out of what a thing is. This is possible only in the following manner. Once the genus has first been taken, if one takes one of the divisions belonging to some lower class, everything will not fall under it. For example, not every animal is either wholly winged or divided according to wings; rather, every animal is winged or not winged. This is the difference of the animal. The first difference of animal is the one into which every animal falls.

The same applies to each of the other cases, including those outside the genera and those subordinate to them: for example, in the case of bird, every bird falls under it, and in the case of fish, every fish falls under it.

For someone proceeding in this way, it is easy to know that nothing has been left out. Otherwise, it is necessary to leave something out and not know it.

The definer who divides need not know everything that exists, although some say that it is impossible to know the differences belonging to each thing without knowing each thing, and that without knowing the differences it is impossible to know each thing. For what a thing does not differ from is the same as it; what it differs from is other than it.

The first claim is false. A thing is not other according to every difference. The same species contains many differences, but they do not concern substance or belong intrinsically.

Further, once the opposites and the difference have been taken, and everything falls under one side or the other, and the thing sought is taken as belonging to one of them and is known, it makes no difference whether one knows or does not know the other things of which the differences are predicated.

For it is evident that, if one proceeds in this way until reaching things in which there is no longer a difference, one will possess an account of the substance. And if everything falls into the division, there is no begging of the question, provided that the differences are opposites. For everything must be included under one or the other if this is their difference.

To establish a term through divisions, one must make three conjectures: first, that the predicates belonging to what a thing is are taken; second, that they are arranged in the proper order, with the first and the second identified; and third, that all of them really belong.

One of these concerns the first predicate and can be established in the manner in which we can syllogize an accidental predicate, namely by proving it through the genus.

The order will be correct if the first predicate is taken. This will be so if one takes what follows all the members of the genus, while not everything follows that predicate. There must be some predicate of this kind. Once it has been taken, the same method applies to the lower members. The first predicate among the remaining predicates will be the second, and the first of the succeeding series will be the third. When what is above has been removed, the first of the remaining continuous series will be taken. The same applies in the other cases.

That all the predicates belong is evident from the following procedure. First, according to the division, everything is either this or that; then this predicate is taken, together with the difference of the whole. At the extremes there is no longer a difference, or else the last difference does not differ in species from the whole.

It is evident that no further predicate is opposed to it. All the predicates belonging to what a thing is have been taken, and nothing is lacking; for there will be either a genus or a difference. The genus is the first predicate, and with the differences it has been taken completely. All the differences are present, since there is no further one. Otherwise there would be a difference in species; but the last predicate, as has been stated, does not differ in species.

One must investigate similarities and things without differences. First determine what all of them have in common; then examine other things that belong to the same genus as the first but differ from them in species. Once the same feature has been found in both groups, examine the features taken again to see whether they are the same, and continue until they converge into one account.

This will be the definition. If they do not converge into one account but into two or more, it is evident that what is predicated is not one thing but several.

For example, if we are asking what magnanimity is, we should examine certain magnanimous people whom we know and determine what one thing they all possess insofar as they are such. If Alcibiades, Achilles, and Ajax are magnanimous, what one thing do they all possess? They do not tolerate being wronged. One of them fought, another became enraged, and another killed himself.

The same inquiry must be made among others, such as Lysander and Socrates, assuming that they differ from the first group and include both fortunate and unfortunate people. Having taken these two groups, we should examine what they have in common: perhaps insensibility to fortune, or refusal to tolerate being wronged.

If there is no common feature, there will be two species of magnanimity. For every definition is always universal. A physician does not say that something is curable in one particular eye, but either states it universally or determines it by species.

## CHAPTER XV  
### Species are easier to define than genera

It is easier to define the particular than the universal; therefore one ought to ascend from particulars to universals. For equivocations are more concealed in universals than in things without differences.

Just as in demonstrations one must syllogize that a predicate belongs, so it is clear that the same holds in definitions. This will happen if, in each genus, one defines separately through the predicates said of each individual—for example, “similar” not in every case, but in colors and in shapes; and “sharp” in the case of a voice. In this way one may proceed toward the common, taking care that equivocation does not arise.

If one ought not to dispute by metaphors, it is evident that one ought not to define by metaphors either, nor to dispute concerning things said metaphorically; otherwise one would necessarily have to conduct the discussion through metaphors.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### Anatomy and analogy are important for determining problems
[Col. 0757D] To have our propositions before us, we must select decisions and divisions; in doing so, we must select according to the common subject-genus of all things. For example, if animals are under consideration, we should identify what belongs to every animal. Having accepted these, we should first determine what follows universally upon them—for example, if this is “bird,” what follows upon every bird—and so always proceed to what is nearest to it.

For it is clear that we shall then be able to state why the subsequent attributes belong to what falls under the common genus—for what reason, for example, they belong to a human being or a horse. Let animal be represented by *a*, and let *b* be an attribute that follows upon every animal; let *c*, *d*, and *e* be animals. It is therefore clear why *b* belongs to *d*: it belongs because of *a*. The same account applies in the other cases, and the same reasoning always holds elsewhere.

[Col. 0758A] Now we speak according to the common names that are assigned. But we must consider not only these things; if something else appears to be common, we must take it as such and then determine in what things it inheres and what follows upon it. For example, one should determine that animals with horns have several stomachs and do not have teeth in both jaws; likewise, one should determine what follows upon having horns. For it is clear why the attribute in question belongs to them: it inheres in them because they have horns.

Furthermore, there is another method: to select according to analogy. For to take one thing is not the same as what must be called by the same name—“self,” “spine,” and “bone”—although attributes follow upon these as upon things having one common nature of this sort.

[Col. 0758B] The propositions set forth are the same when they have the same middle term. For example, all the contrary states are one in genus, while some of them are the same in genus wherever they have differences by which they differ from other things or differ in another way: for example, why something resounds, why something appears, and why the rainbow exists. All these have one proposition in genus, since they are all reflections, but they differ in species.

Other propositions differ because their middle term is subordinate to another middle term. For example: why does the Nile flow more strongly at the end of the month? Because the closing month is more wintry. And why is the closing month more wintry? Because the moon is waning. These terms are related to one another in this way.

## CHAPTER XVII. On causes and effects, and whether one thing has several causes

Concerning a cause, and that of which it is the cause, someone may raise the question whether, when the effect exists, the cause also exists—for example, if [Col. 0758C] leaves fall or the moon is eclipsed, whether the cause of the eclipse or of the falling of leaves also exists: in the latter case, having broad leaves; in the former, the earth’s being in the middle. If not, there will be some other cause of these things.

But if the cause and the effect exist together—for example, if the earth is in the middle, the moon is eclipsed, or if a leaf is broad, leaves fall—then they will necessarily exist together and will be demonstrated through one another.

Let the falling of leaves be represented by *a*, a broad leaf by *b*, and a vine by *c*. If *a* belongs to *b*—for every broad-leaved plant sheds its leaves—and *b* belongs to *c*—for every vine has broad leaves—then *a* belongs to *c*, since every vine sheds its leaves. The middle term *b* is therefore the cause.

It can also be demonstrated that the vine has broad leaves because it sheds its leaves. Let *d* be “having broad leaves,” *e* be “shedding its leaves,” and *f* be “vine.” [Col. 0758D] *e* belongs to *f*, since every vine sheds its leaves; and *d* belongs to *e*, since everything that sheds its leaves has broad leaves. Therefore every vine has broad leaves, and the cause is the shedding of leaves.

If, however, the cases cannot occur together—for the cause is prior to that of which it is the cause—then the earth’s being in the middle is the cause of the moon’s eclipse, but the moon’s eclipse is not the cause of the earth’s being in the middle.

If demonstration proceeds through the cause, it establishes why something is so; if it does not proceed through the cause of the thing itself, it establishes only that it is so. Thus, one may know that the earth is in the middle, but not why this is so. That the moon’s eclipse is not the cause of the earth’s being in the middle, but that the latter is the cause of the former, is clear: for in the account of the moon’s eclipse there is the fact that the earth lies in the middle. Hence it is clear that the former will be known through the latter, but not the latter through the former.

[Col. 0759A] Can one thing have several causes? Indeed, if the same predicate is first predicated of several primary subjects, let *a* belong primarily to *b* and also to another primary subject *c*; let *b* belong to *d*, and *c* to *e*. Then *a* will belong both to *d* and to *e*. The cause of *a* belonging to *d* is *b*, while the cause of its belonging to *e* is *c*. Therefore, when the cause exists, the thing must exist; but when the thing exists, it is not necessary that every cause whatsoever exist. The cause must exist, but not every cause.

Or, if the proposition is always universal and the cause is something universal, is that of which it is the cause also universal? “Shedding leaves” is determined universally in some whole, and so also in the species belonging to it. It is therefore universal either in plants or in plants of a certain kind. The middle term must consequently be equal in extension to both the things in which it is the cause and the thing of which it is the cause, and the terms must be convertible.

[Col. 0759B] For example, why do trees shed their leaves? If it is because of the thickening of the moisture, then, if a tree sheds its leaves, thickening must be present; and if thickening is present not in every kind of thing but in a tree, then the tree sheds its leaves.

But is it possible that the same thing should not have the same cause in all cases, but one cause in one case and another in another? If the thing is demonstrated per se, and not according to a sign or an accidental feature, this is impossible. For the account of the extreme term is the middle term. If this is not the case, however, and the relation between the thing of which something is the cause and the thing to which it is a cause is considered accidentally, the propositions do not appear to be properly established.

If this is not so, the middle term will be similarly related. If the terms are equivocal, the middle term will be equivocal; but if they are related as members of one genus, the relation will be similar. Thus, in the question “why does something change?” the cause is analogous: it is one cause in numbers and another in lines, while it is the same cause insofar as they are lines, and another insofar as they possess a certain kind of increase. The same applies in all cases.

[Col. 0759C] The likeness of one color to another and of one figure to another may have one cause in one case and another in another, since “like” is equivocal in these cases. In figures, likeness perhaps consists in having corresponding sides and equal angles; in colors, it consists in their producing one sensation, or something else of this kind. Things that are the same according to analogy also have a middle term according to analogy.

The cause is related in this way both to one another and to that of which it is the cause, and to the thing for which it is a cause. Each is taken in relation to the thing of which it is the cause, but the thing of which it is the cause is more extensive. Thus, “four equal external angles” is more extensive than “triangle” or “quadrilateral”; but in all cases the relation is as it is in equal figures, since whatever has four equal external angles has the same middle term.

[Col. 0759D] The middle term is the account of the first extreme, and all sciences arise through definition. Thus, the shedding of leaves follows similarly upon the vine, the fig tree, and other plants, but not upon all things; rather, the cases are equal. If one takes the first middle term, the account of the shedding of leaves will be obtained. For in one case there is a first middle term, since all such things are of this kind; and subsequently there is another middle term, because the sap thickens, or for some other reason of this sort.

What, then, is the shedding of leaves? It is the thickening of the sap at the point of contact with the seed.

In figures, one should assign the sequence of the cause and that of which it is the cause in the following way. Let *a* belong to every *b*, and let *b* belong to each of the things represented by *d*, while *b* is more universal. Therefore *b* belongs universally to the things represented by *d*. By “universally” I mean that it is not convertible. The first universal is that which is not convertible with each individual thing, while all the things taken together are convertible with it and do not exceed it.

[Col. 0760A] Therefore, for the things represented by *d*, *b* is the cause of *a*. *A* must consequently extend to more things than *b*. If it does not, why should this rather be the cause of that?

If *a* belongs to all the things represented by *e*, those things will constitute some one whole distinct from *b*. For if they do not, how could one say that wherever *e* is, *a* is present universally, while wherever *a* is present, *e* is not universal? Why would there not be some cause by which *a* belongs to all the things represented by *d*?

But perhaps the things represented by *e* also constitute some one whole. This must be considered. Let them be represented by *e*. It is therefore possible for the same thing to have several causes, but not causes that are the same in species.

For long life in quadrupeds, the cause is the absence of bile; in flying animals, it is dryness, or some other cause. If one does not immediately arrive at an indivisible term, and there is not merely one middle term but several, then there are also several causes.

[Col. 0760B] Is the cause of the middle terms that which is related to the first universal, or that which is related to the individual terms? It is clear that the causes are those which are nearest to each thing of which they are causes. The first thing under the universal is the cause. Thus, if *a* belongs to *d*, *c* is the cause. For *a* belonging to *d*, *c* is the cause; and for *b* belonging to *c*, the same relation holds.

It is therefore clear what a syllogism and a demonstration are, what each of them is, and how each comes about; and at the same time the nature of demonstrative knowledge is clear, since it is the same thing.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How the principles are known, and what the state of the principles is

[Col. 0760C]

How the principles become known, and what the knowing state is, will become clear from what follows, once the initial difficulties have been raised.

It was stated earlier that it is impossible to know through demonstration unless one already knows the immediate first principles. Someone may nevertheless ask whether knowledge of immediate principles is the same as knowledge of other things, or different; whether there is scientific knowledge in both cases, or whether one is scientific knowledge while the other belongs to some other genus.

One may also ask whether these states come to be when they are not already present, or whether, when they are present, they remain concealed.

If we already possess them, it is strange that we should have cognitions more certain than demonstration and yet fail to recognize them. But if we do not possess them beforehand, how shall we come to know them and learn them from a condition in which no cognition previously exists? That is impossible, as we said in discussing demonstration.

It is therefore clear that it is impossible either to possess them—or to possess them while ignorant of them—or for them to come to be in those who do not possess the relevant state. It is necessary, then, to possess some capacity, though not one of the kind that is more honorable in respect of certainty.

This capacity appears to belong naturally to all animals. They possess an innate discriminative capacity, which is called sensation. When sensation is present, in some animals a perceptual retention remains, while in others it does not. In those in which it does not occur—either altogether or with respect to particular objects—there is no cognition beyond what they sense.

But in those that possess it, after they have sensed, one thing comes to be established in the soul. When many such instances have occurred, a difference of some kind arises: in some animals a certain account comes to be formed from such memories, while in others it does not.

[Col. 0761A] Memory, as we say, arises from sensation. From memory, when the same thing has often been remembered, comes experience. For the many memories, numerous in number, constitute a single experience. From experience—or from the whole universal that has come to rest in the soul, one apart from the many, when that one is the same in all cases—arise the principle of art and of knowledge. If it concerns coming-to-be, it is a principle of art; if it concerns what is, it is a principle of knowledge.

Thus, these determinate states are neither already present in us nor produced from other states that are more knowable; they arise from sensation. As in a battle, when a rout has occurred, one person makes a stand, then another stands beside him, and so on until the beginning is reached, so the soul is constituted in such a way as to be capable of undergoing this process.

[Col. 0761B] What was said earlier was stated before, but not clearly; let us say it again. When one of the undifferentiated particulars has come to a stand, the first universal is present in the soul. For although what is sensed is an individual, sensation is of the universal—for example, of a human being, not of Callias as such.

[Col. 0762A] Again, the process comes to a stand in these cases until indivisible and universal items have come to rest: for example, this kind of animal, and then animal, and similarly in each case.

It is therefore clear that we must come to know the first principles through induction. For sensation also produces the universal in this way.

Concerning the states by which we declare truth, some are always true, while others admit falsity, such as opinion and reasoning. Knowledge and intellect, however, are always true. There is no other genus of knowledge more certain than intellect. The principles of demonstrations are more knowable than demonstrations, while all knowledge is accompanied by reasoning; therefore there cannot be knowledge of the principles in the same sense.

Since nothing can be more true than knowledge except intellect, intellect must be the knowledge of the principles.

[Col. 0762B] These considerations also show that the principle of demonstration is not itself a demonstration, and therefore that there is no knowledge of knowledge. If, then, we possess no other true genus besides knowledge, intellect will be the principle of knowledge, and the principle of the principle. The same relation holds in every case with respect to the whole subject matter.

[Col. 0761]

## ON THE CATEGORICAL SYLLOGISM

ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS, INTRODUCTION TO CATEGORICAL SYLLOGISMS
[Col. 0761C] The ancient leaders of philosophy contributed much to the studies of those who came after them. Before reaching matters deeply shrouded in darkness, they first prepared the way by a kind of intellectual struggle: here, instruction is made easier by the brevity of a condensed summary; there, through what they call προλεγόμενα (“preliminaries”), a more accessible path is secured toward understanding. I have therefore resolved, as an imitator of this foresight, to open the entrances to obscure doctrines by the light of preliminary instruction, to devote the present work to syllogisms, in whose connections every reasoning is contained, and to preserve this manner of exposition: serving ease and understanding, we shall compress the ancients’ more expansive statements, present their propositions more briefly, and disclose what has been obscured by the unfamiliarity of improper language through the exactness of customary terminology.

But the reader who approaches this work should, we wish, first be asked not immediately to presume judgment upon matters he has never previously encountered, nor, if he has received something while still inexperienced and unsteady in the school of elementary disciplines, to think that he must embrace it and even venerate it. For some things are suited to tender ears that are still being instructed and formed, while others are reserved for minds made firm and stronger by learning. Therefore, if anything seems discrepant, let him not immediately object, but, having consulted reason, judge with a keener intelligence and subtler consideration what he himself thinks and what we are proposing.
