For the same thing will happen: what they learned at the very first entrance into their studies, once thoroughly examined and rather discovered, they will despise.

But if anyone now prefers to be a defender of his own knowledge—people whom the old and prolonged sluggishness of learning has seized have this fault also, that once they have grasped opinions they do not withdraw from them, lest, by learning in old age, they seem to have learned nothing at all up to old age—if, I say, they prefer to defend rather than alter what they have once absorbed through common studies, no one demands that they condemn what came before, but that they construct and join to it certain greater and higher things. For the method of different disciplines is not one and the same, since one and the same substance or material is treated by disciplines that are very different. A grammarian must discuss each part of speech in one way, a dialectician in another; nor do a mathematician and a physicist treat a line or a surface in the same manner. Hence one discipline does not obstruct another, but, joined through the consideration of many things, a true knowledge of nature is produced and explained from them all.

[Col. 0762C] But enough of this; let us now arrange our discussion of the matters proposed. Since this work concerns categorical syllogisms, and the structure of syllogisms is woven from propositions, while the parts of propositions are noun and verb, and a part is prior to that of which it is a part, let the first discussion be placed upon noun and verb, which are first; afterward we shall treat of the proposition and finally of the connection of syllogisms.

A noun is a significant utterance according to convention, without time, no part of which, when separated, is significant. This definition must be explained somewhat more clearly. We say that a noun is an utterance because utterance is the genus of nouns; and every genus is predicated of its species, while every definition is taken from a genus—for example, if you define a human being, you first say “animal,” which is its genus. Then you add the differences, which are “rational” and “mortal.” Thus, in the definition of noun, we too take “utterance” as the genus and attach the remaining features to utterance as differences, as when a noun is called a designative utterance.

For there are utterances that designate nothing, such as syllables; a noun, however, is a designative utterance, since a noun always designates that of which it is the name. “According to convention” is added because no noun signifies by nature, but according to the convention and will of the person who establishes and assigns it. For each thing is called by the name that pleased the person who first impressed a name upon it. There are, however, utterances that signify naturally, such as the barking of dogs: it signifies the dogs’ anger, while another of their sounds signifies caresses. Groans also designate pain, but they are not nouns, because they designate according to nature, not according to convention.

“Without time” distinguishes nouns from verbs, since verbs too are significant utterances according to convention, but differ from nouns because nouns are without time, whereas verbs are with time. “No part of which, when separated, is significant” separates nouns from discourse. For discourse too is a significant utterance according to convention and is sometimes without time, as in this verse:

> Nerine Galatea, sweeter to me than Hybla’s thyme.

But the parts of discourse, when separated from the whole discourse, designate; nothing outside the noun, however, designates. In those nouns that are simple forms, it is evident that no part signifies anything at all: in “Cicero,” for example, no separated part designates anything—not “ci,” nor “ce,” nor “ro.”

[Col. 0763C] But if a noun is compound, its separated parts seem to signify something. Yet, in the same noun, which is composed from both parts, the separated parts designate nothing. Thus, if I say “magister” (“teacher”), the parts of this noun are “magis” and “ter.” Taken externally and separated from the noun, they are not without significance, for each signifies quantity adverbially: “more” and “three times.” But since the compound noun “magister” signifies someone skilled and learned in some art, “magis” cannot designate either a part of the teacher or the teacher as a whole. In the same way, “ter” neither signifies the teacher as a whole nor the teacher in part—that is, it in no way designates the thing that is signified by the term “teacher.”

Thus the parts of compound nouns, when separated and dispersed, signify nothing of the thing they designated when joined into a single word; they may signify something else, but then they are not parts of the noun—they are nouns themselves. For what they signify when joined, they do not designate when divided and separated. Joined, “magis” and “ter” retained the meaning of “teacher”; when separated, therefore, they lose the whole meaning of “teacher.”

But lest anyone criticize the example given above and refuse to admit that “magister” is a compound noun, no one will deny that “vir fortis” (“brave man”) is a compound noun if it is pronounced with a single accent. Its parts, “vir” and “fortis,” which are said to signify within “vir fortis,” are not parts of a noun but nouns themselves. Nor will “vir fortis” be the name of one thing, but rather discourse, as is demonstrated by the combined signification of two nouns.

[Col. 0764A] But when “vir fortis,” pronounced with the force of a single accent, is not discourse but a noun, its parts cannot be nouns; and, since they are not nouns, they do not signify anything at all, neither natural affections nor actions, as verbs do. Therefore we must conclude that, whenever utterances retain their proper signification, they are not parts of nouns but nouns themselves; but whenever they have been joined into the form of a single noun, they are considered as its parts and lose the force of their proper signification. These matters have been sufficiently discussed in the commentary on Aristotle’s book Περὶ ἑρμηνείας (“On Interpretation”), and the treatment of the matter is too extensive to be fully unfolded now.

But since there are certain utterances that are designative, according to convention, and without time, whose parts signify nothing outside them, yet do not observe the properties and nature of a noun, they must first be distinguished and separated from the noun by adding differences, so that the force of the noun may clearly appear.

For a negation always added to a noun makes the utterance ambiguous: it can be attached neither to a verb nor to discourse, even when considered more closely, nor can it be attached to a noun. Thus, if someone says “non homo” (“not a human being”), it is a significant utterance. For it designates whatever is not a human being, according to convention. It has precisely those parts that it assumed for the signification either of the negation or of the word established by convention for a human being.

“Without time” separates the utterance “not a human being” from a verb, whose parts signify nothing outside it, so that it may not seem to be discourse. For “not a human being” is an utterance separated into the negative particle and “human being”; when separated within this expression, they signify nothing. “Not a human being” signifies either a horse, or a dog, or whatever—as has been said—is not a human being. But the negative particle signifies neither a human being, nor a horse, nor any substance. Likewise, “human being” cannot signify a dog or anything that is not a human being. Therefore, in the utterance “not a human being,” the separated parts signify nothing of the thing designated by the composition of the whole utterance.

[Col. 0764C] For this reason it cannot even be placed in discourse. If someone admits that the utterance “not a human being” is discourse, he will have to acknowledge that it is nothing other than a negation. Every negation, however, is either true or false. But someone who says “not a human being” announces neither truth nor falsehood.

Furthermore, if someone removes the negative adverb from any negation, an affirmation remains. But from the utterance “not a human being,” if one removes what is the negative adverb, “human being” remains—and this is not yet an affirmation. Therefore, if “not a human being” cannot be a negation, while it would appear to be nothing else if it were discourse, we must conclude that a negation joined to a noun cannot be discourse.

Every noun signifies something definite and determined, such as “human being,” “horse,” or “dog.” “Not a human being,” however, removes what the noun signifies but does not prescribe what it itself signifies. Therefore, since a negation joined to “human being” does signify something, but not something definite, let it be called an indefinite noun. A difference must therefore be added to the definition of noun, namely [Col. 0765A] that a noun is what, together with the other features already stated, has a definite signification.

Now, to those who do not look more deeply, the cases of nouns may also seem to be nouns. For who would think that such utterances as “of Cato,” “to Cato,” and the like, which are inflected from proper nouns, are not nouns? Yet these utterances differ from the noun by a certain difference. Every noun, when joined to a verb, produces and admits an enunciation with the nature of truth and falsehood, as in “Cato is” or “the day is.” But if a case is joined to “is,” there is neither an enunciation nor a complete sentence of discourse: “of Cato is” neither has a complete sense nor can indicate anything true or false. For this reason such forms are called not nouns but cases of nouns.

For when that from which something is inflected is first, while what arises from the inflection of the first is second, and the same thing cannot be both first and second, it is clear that the cases of nouns are not the same as nouns. Accordingly, grammarians call the others genitive, dative, accusative, and the other cases, while they call the first the nominative or “straight” case, because it has held the principal place in signification.

The full definition of noun must therefore be made complete and undiminished, as follows:

> A noun is a significant utterance according to convention, without time, no part of which, when separated, is significant; it designates something definite, and, when joined to a verb, produces an enunciation.

Thus “utterance” separates the noun from articulations and meaningless sounds; “designative” separates it from utterances that signify nothing; “according to convention” from utterances that signify something by nature; “without time” from the verb, which does not depart from the signification of time; “no part of which, when separated, is significant” separates it from discourse, whose parts signify outside it, as I shall explain shortly; “designating something definite” separates it from those utterances that join a noun with a negation and make indefinite nouns; and “when joined to a verb, producing an enunciation” separates it from cases, which, when joined to “is,” cannot complete and express a full sense.

Nearly all these features also apply to the verb, except that the verb is separated from the noun by its signification of time. For every verb designates an action or a passion, which cannot occur without an indication of time. The definition of verb is therefore this:

> A verb is a significant utterance according to convention, with time, no part of which, when separated, is significant,

as in “he runs” and “he conquers.”

But if negative adverbs are joined to verbs, they become indefinite verbs, just as we said that nouns become indefinite when negated. When “he runs” or “he conquers” designates something definite and determined, the addition of negation interrupts what is designated by the verb and does not determine what else it says happens. Moreover, negation may correctly be joined to a verb whether it is in what is or in what is not, as in “the human being does not run.”

The arguments that separated the indefinite noun from discourse or negation will also show that this is not discourse or a negative enunciation. But since we principally perceive present things, and it is clear that names were assigned by mortals to those things we conceive through present perception, it is correct to say that a verb always has the signification of present time, as in “he runs” or “he conquers.”

“He will run” or “he will conquer,” and “he will have run” or “he will have conquered,” are not verbs but cases of verbs, because they are inflected away from the signification of present time. The complete definition of verb is therefore as follows:

> A verb is a significant utterance according to convention, with the signification of time, no part of which, when separated, is significant; it designates something definite and present.

It remains for us to speak of discourse. But first it seems that we must show whether noun and verb alone are placed among the parts of discourse, or whether, as the grammarians wish, the remaining parts of speech should also be added to them.

For, considering the forms of utterances, grammarians enumerate eight parts of speech. Philosophers, however, whose entire treatment of noun and verb is established upon signification, have taught that there are only two parts of discourse: whatever possesses complete signification, if it signifies without time, they call a noun; if it signifies with time, they call a verb. Therefore they join adverbs and pronouns to nouns, since they signify something established and definite without time. Nor does it matter that they cannot be inflected through cases; it is not proper to nouns that they must be inflected through cases. For there are nouns that grammarians call indeclinable nouns (*monoptota*).

The participle, however, because it carries the signification of time, although it is expressed through cases, is rightly joined to the verb. Interjections, if they signify naturally, are to be joined neither to verb nor to noun. For the definitions of verb and noun do not allow them to be natural; they are established according to the convention of the person who assigns them. Therefore they will not be counted among the parts of discourse. For discourse signifies by convention; if discourse signified naturally, different peoples would not speak in different languages.

But if some interjections signify by convention, since they designate a definite affection without time, they are rightly counted among nouns. Those that themselves rest upon no proper signification but designate something when joined with others, such as conjunctions and prepositions, should not even be called parts of discourse. For discourse is joined from significant parts. Therefore noun and verb are rightly said to be the only parts of discourse.

Discourse is a significant utterance according to convention, whose parts signify something outside it as an expression, not as an affirmation. Discourse therefore has in common with both verb and noun that it is an utterance, that it is significant, and that it signifies according to convention. With the noun it shares, in some cases, the fact that it is without time, as in the Virgilian verse quoted above:

> Nerine Galatea, sweeter to me than Hybla’s thyme,

and the following:

> Whiter than swans, more beautiful than white ivy.

With the verb it shares the fact that it is sometimes expressed with the signification of time, as in:

> If you have any care for your Corydon, come.

But it differs from both in that the parts of discourse, when separated from the whole discourse, signify. The parts of discourse are noun and verb, which we showed to be significant when defining them. Therefore the parts of discourse signify as an expression, not as an affirmation—although sometimes they do signify as an affirmation, yet not always; they always signify as expressions.

An expression is a simple naming of a verb or noun. For when we say, “If it is day, there is light,” and wish to divide this whole discourse into parts, namely “it is day” and “there is light,” each part will signify as an affirmation. It is clear that “it is day” and “there is light” are affirmations. But if we dissect all the members of the whole discourse into smaller units, the final resolution will be into nouns and verbs. We shall say that the parts of the discourse set out above are “day,” “light,” and “is”; pronounced by themselves, these are not affirmations but merely expressions.

Since every discourse consists of verbs and nouns, it can be resolved into nouns and verbs. It is not possible, however, to turn every discourse into an affirmation. For example, if someone says “There is light,” its parts are “light” and “is”; no one is unaware that these are not affirmations but simple expressions. Since discourse cannot always be resolved into an affirmation, but can always be resolved into simple expressions, it was rightly said that the parts of discourse designate something outside it not as affirmations but rather as expressions.

The species of discourse, if we divide them very strictly, are five: interrogative, as:

> Where are you going on foot, Meris? Or by what road does the way lead into the city?

Imperative, as:

> Hand me the weapons.

Invocative, as:

> Gods of sea and land, and rulers of storms.

Deprecatory, as:

> Make the way easy, winds, and blow favorably.

Enunciative, as:

> I have a pipe joined from seven unequal reeds.

Of these, apart from the enunciation, none designates that something exists or does not exist. The others either ask, invoke, command, or pray. The enunciation alone always signifies that something exists or does not exist. Therefore truth or falsehood can be found only in the enunciation. Hence the definition of enunciation arises: an enunciation is that which announces what is true or false.

Cicero also calls this a *proloquium* (“proposition”), and it is partly simple and partly compound. A simple proposition proposes that something exists or does not exist, with the condition removed, as in “Plato is a philosopher.” A compound proposition consists of two simple propositions joined by a condition, as in “If Plato is learned, he is a philosopher.”

Among simple enunciations we find differences based either on quality or on quantity. Their difference in quality is that one is affirmative and another negative. An affirmative enunciation is one that signifies something of something, as in “Plato is a philosopher”: we predicate “philosopher” of Plato. A negative enunciation separates something from something by predication, as in “Plato is not a philosopher”: by this predication we have separated “philosopher” from Plato.

According to quantity, the differences among enunciations are that some are universal, some particular, some indefinite, and some singular. Universal enunciations are those which, whether they affirm or deny, nevertheless enunciate universally about a universal subject, as in:

> Every human being is wise.  
> No human being is wise.

“Human being” is something universal. For it constrains and contains many individuals under itself, and it is enunciated universally when “every” or “no” is added to it.

Particular enunciations are those which, whether affirming or denying, reduce the range of a universal subject to a part, as in:

> Some human being is wise.  
> Some human being is not wise.

Here the universality of “human being,” by the addition of a particular determination, has been diminished and reduced to a part.

Indefinite enunciations are those expressed without a determination of universality or particularity, as in:

> A human being is wise.  
> A human being is not wise.

Singular enunciations are those which, by affirmation or denial, propose something about a singular and individual, as in:

> Socrates is wise.  
> Socrates is not wise.

A particular proposition differs from a singular proposition in this respect: the particular posits some one individual but does not indicate who that individual is, as in “Some human being is wise”; the proposition does not declare which human being this is. A singular proposition, however, takes one individual and indicates who that individual is, as in “Socrates is wise”; it proposes that one individual—this Socrates—is wise.

Moreover, every particular proposition posits a universal term but removes its universality by adding particularity, as in “Some human being is wise.” “Human being” is a universal term, for it includes many things through its proper predication. But because “some” is said, “human being” is reduced to one individual; it would remain universal unless particularity had been added.

In singular propositions, however, an individual is always placed beneath the predicate term, as in “Socrates is wise.” Socrates is singular and individual. Therefore the particular proposition is one that removes a part from universality, while the singular proposition consists in the predication of a singular and individual.

The parts of simple enunciations are subject and predicate. The subject is that which receives the predication of the predicate, as in the proposition “Plato is a philosopher.” Plato is the subject, for “philosopher” is predicated of him, and in him it receives the predication of “philosopher.” The predicate is what is said of the subject. Thus, in the same proposition, “philosopher” is said of Plato, the subject.

The subject is always either less than or equal to the predicate. It is less, for example, in the proposition discussed shortly before: Plato cannot be equal to the name “philosopher,” nor is Plato alone a philosopher. The subject term is equal to the predicate if someone says “A human being is risible,” for the subject term “human being” is equal to the predicate “risible.”

Hence reciprocal predication can be produced: the subject and predicate can exchange places, so that what was previously the predicate becomes the subject, and what was previously the subject is predicated in reversed order. Thus one may say, “What is risible is a human being.” For all things that are equal are predicated of one another.

It is entirely impossible, however, for what is the subject to be greater than the predicate in any enunciation, since the nature of a predicate does not allow it to be smaller. Rather, what is equal or greater is always predicated of what is equal or smaller.

We call these parts of enunciations—namely, the predicate and the subject—terms. They are called terms because the final resolution is into them. Thus, in singular or indefinite propositions, we always find two terms and a verb that determines the quality of the proposition. In the proposition “Socrates is wise,” it is clear that “Socrates” and “wise” are terms. “Is” is not a term but an indication of quality; it signifies whether the proposition is negative or affirmative. Here the affirmation has been made by the verb “is” alone, fitted to the proposition. But if the negative adverb “not” were added, it would be said: “Socrates is not wise,” and in this way the quality would be changed from affirmation into negation.

Therefore “is” and “is not” are not terms but, as has been said, signify quality. The same applies in every respect to an indefinite proposition. If the expressions are “Socrates is” and “the day is,” “is” performs a double function: that of predicate, for it is predicated as a verb of Socrates and of the day; and that of a sign of quality, for, when placed alone, it produces an affirmation, while with the negative adverb it produces a negation.

But if the propositions contain differences of quantity, as universal and particular propositions do, the same force of the terms remains. “Every,” “no,” and “some” are not counted among the terms but signify the quality of the enunciations. Therefore what is subjected and what is predicated are rightly called terms, since the proposition is resolved only into them. The other elements added to simple enunciations either retain the quality of the propositions or signify quantity.

Some simple propositions have no terms in common, as “Plato is a philosopher” and “Virtue is good.” In each, something different is predicated of something different, and they have nothing in common in their manner of proposing. The first says that Plato is a philosopher; the second announces that virtue is good.

Others are joined through some participation in their terms. This can occur in two ways: either in the same order or through an alteration of order. In the same order it occurs in two ways: either by establishing simple terms in both propositions, or by making the participation of terms through opposition. This happens in three, and no more than three, ways, for negation is joined either to the predicate, or to the subject, or to both terms.

They also agree through an alteration of order in two ways: either through simple predication of the terms or through opposition of the same terms. This opposition of terms likewise admits three modes, when negation is joined either to the predicate, or to the subject, or to both.

Those propositions that share only one term also do so in three ways: either what is predicated in one proposition is the subject in the other; or the same thing is predicated in both; or the same thing is the subject in both.

Since we have made the most orderly division of all propositions that agree with one another, let us now discuss each separately. First we shall treat the agreement of propositions that share both terms but preserve the same order of participation. It is of this kind:

> Every human being is wise.  
> No human being is wise.

Both propositions make “human being” the subject and predicate wisdom; and although they agree in both terms, they are different because one is an affirmation and the other a negation.

Let this be said merely by way of example; the treatment of this kind of participation will be made fuller in the following manner. We have shown that the differences of all simple propositions are situated either in quality or in quantity. They are differences of quantity when propositions are expressed universally, particularly, indefinitely, or singularly [F. “are enunciated”]; they are differences of quality when some are affirmative and others negative.

If, therefore, we combine the two kinds of difference, eight mixed forms arise, which together contain quality and quantity. These are: universal affirmation, universal negation, particular affirmation, particular negation, indefinite affirmation, indefinite negation, singular affirmation, and singular negation.

Let us set aside the indefinite and singular forms and discuss the universal and particular forms. Let the universal affirmation first be set out:

> Every human being is just.

Its contrary is the universal negative proposition:

> No human being is just.

Under the universal affirmation let the particular affirmation be placed:

> Some human being is just.

Opposite this, let the particular negation be placed beneath the universal negation:

> Some human being is not just.

| Universal affirmation | Universal negation |
|---|---|
| Every human being is just. | No human being is just. |
| Some human being is just. | Some human being is not just. |
| Particular affirmation | Particular negation |
The universal affirmation and the universal negation of these propositions differ in quality but agree in quantity. For while the one is affirmative and the other negative, and therefore they differ in quality, both are universal and therefore agree in quantity. It is possible, then, for both of them to be false, or for one to be true and the other false; but they cannot both be true at the same time. For in the description just given, the affirmation “Every human being is just” and the negation “No human being is just,” although both are universal, are nevertheless neither of them true.

But if the affirmation is “Every human being is an animal,” and this is universally denied by saying “No human being is an animal,” or if the propositions are “Every human being is a stone” and “No human being is a stone,” one must be true and the other false. Accordingly, whenever predicates are asserted that can both belong to a subject and be separated from it, so that one proposition affirms them universally and the other denies them, both may be false; this is demonstrated by the examples given above. For justice can exist in human beings, but it is not so inseparably inherent in human beings that it cannot in any way be separated from them. Consequently, both “Every human being is just” and “Every human being is not just” may be false.

But if the predicate is such that it cannot be separated or abstracted from the subject, or such that it can never belong to the subject, and the universal affirmation is universally denied, one proposition will always be true and the other false. If the predicate cannot be separated from the subject, the affirmation will always be true and the negation false; but if the predicate is something that cannot belong to the subject, the affirmation will be false and the negation true. For since animal cannot be separated from human being, the proposition affirming that a human being is an animal is true, while the proposition denying it is false. Likewise, if something is predicated that cannot occur, and the affirmation “Every human being is a stone” is made while the opposed proposition denies this and grants that no human being is a stone, the negation is connected with truth, while the affirmation is joined to falsehood. No examples, however, can show a universal affirmation and a universal negation to be true simultaneously.

For this reason the universal affirmation and the universal negation are called contraries. Just as, among contraries that contain an intermediate, neither need be present in the subject—for example, a body may be neither black nor white, since there is something else it may be, such as red—while among contraries lacking an intermediate one of them must always be present in the subject, as every animal either sleeps or is awake, since there is no intermediate state between sleeping and being awake; so it is impossible for both contraries to be found simultaneously in the same thing.

The same applies to the universal affirmation and negation. They may both be false, as in the case of contraries that contain an intermediate; or one may be true and the other false, as is possible with contraries that lack an intermediate. But it is impossible for both propositions to agree in truth, just as no contraries can be present simultaneously. Therefore the universal affirmation and the universal negation are called contraries.

[Col. 0771C] These propositions do not always preserve such force through their opposition that they remain in perpetual and irreconcilable disagreement; nor do they always destroy one another. Although they differ in their assertions, they can agree in a common falsehood. If, therefore, one of them is removed, it does not necessarily follow that the other is true. For it may be that neither is true. Thus, if someone disproves the assertion that every just person is a human being, it does not follow that no human being is just.

The propositions placed beneath these—that is, the particular affirmation and the particular negation—are called subcontraries, because the particular shares a common subject with the universal. Since the universal propositions are understood to be contraries, the propositions placed beneath contrary universals must be subcontraries.

Their quantity is likewise the same, since both are particular; but their quality is different, since one is an affirmation and the other a negation. Although they appear to be subordinate to contraries, the particulars, in an inverse manner, agree with one another in truth rather than in falsehood. That one should be true and the other false, or that both should be true, is readily demonstrated by the examples already given; but they cannot both be false.

For if either proposition asserts something that cannot be separated from the subject or cannot belong to it, one proposition will be true and the other allied with falsehood. If what cannot be separated from the subject is predicated, only the affirmation possesses truth; but if what cannot belong to the subject is asserted, only the negation possesses truth. Thus, if one person says “Some human being is an animal” and another denies it by saying “Some human being is not an animal,” or if the propositions are “Some human being is a stone” and “Some human being is not a stone,” each pair of affirmation and negation divides truth from falsehood. In the former case the affirmation is true; in the latter, the negation is true.

But if something is asserted that can occur but can nevertheless at some time be separated from the subject, and both a particular affirmation and a particular negation are made, both must be true—for example, “Some human being is just” and “Some human being is not just.” They cannot both be false. Accordingly, even the propositions we call subcontraries do not always destroy one another, since at times they agree in truth.

If we seek propositions that disagree in every respect and mutually destroy one another, we must examine the angular propositions. These are the universal affirmation and the particular negation, or the universal negation and the particular affirmation. Their disagreement is so great that they never agree either in falsehood or in truth. Whenever the affirmation is true, the negation must be false; whenever the negation is true, the affirmation must possess falsehood.

Earlier we said that propositions have two kinds of difference, namely quality and quantity. These propositions differ in both respects. Since one is an affirmation and the other a negation, they differ in quality; and since one is universal and the other particular, they differ in quantity. Nor can they ever agree either in falsehood or in truth.

For if the propositions concern things that cannot be absent from the subject, one must always be true and the other false. If the predicate is such that it may either belong to the subject or not belong to it, the universals are always false and the particulars true. Thus, if one says “Every human being is just” and another denies it by saying “Some human being is not just,” the universal affirmation is false, while the particular negation is true. Similarly, if someone says “No human being is just,” the universal negation is false, while the particular affirmation is true. Thus, in cases where the predicate may either belong to the subject or be absent from it, the universals are associated with falsehood and the particulars possess truth.

But if the terms are such that they cannot be separated or divided from the subject, whether the proposition is universal or particular, truth will always remain with the affirmation and falsehood with the negation. Thus, if someone says universally that every human being is an animal, while another denies this particularly by saying that some human being is not an animal, the universal affirmation speaks truly and the particular negative proposition is false.

Likewise, if someone universally proposes the negation “No human being is an animal,” truth follows the particular affirmation, while the universal negation remains false. But if the predicates are such that they can never belong to the subject, whether they are asserted universally or particularly, truth adorns the negations and falsehood disfigures the affirmations. For if someone confirms that every human being is a stone, while another replies that some human being is not a stone, falsehood belongs to the universal affirmation and truth to the particular negation. If, however, someone universally denies this by saying “No human being is a stone,” and another affirms particularly that “Some human being is a stone,” truth belongs to the universal negation, while the particular affirmation is not free from falsehood.

Therefore, whatever alteration is made in the predicates or subjects, if one joins the universal affirmation with the particular negation, or the universal negation with the particular affirmation, while considering them individually, then, if one is false, the other will be true, and if one is true, the other must be found false. For this reason these propositions are called opposed and contradictory.

Thus far we have compared affirmations and negations whose intentions are turned in opposite directions, and have shown what disagreement and difference there is between them. We must now compare the universal affirmation with the particular affirmation, and the universal negation with the particular negation, with respect to their agreement in truth and falsehood. There is no disagreement between these propositions; consequently, the question appears to concern not their disagreement but rather their agreement.

First, therefore, the universal affirmation and the particular affirmation are called subalterns, because one lies beneath the other. That is, the particular affirmation is placed beneath and subordinate to the universal affirmation, like a part always lying within the extent of the whole. The same must be said of the universal and particular negations: they are called subalterns because the higher and broader universal negation encloses and contains within itself the particular negation.

These propositions agree in the following way. If the universals precede in truth, the particulars must also be true. Thus, if someone proposes universally, by affirmation, that every human being is an animal, and this is true, it brings with it the truth of its particular affirmation, namely “Some human being is an animal.” For if it is true that every human being is an animal, it is true that at least one is.

Likewise, if someone universally asserts that no human being is a stone and speaks truly, the particular negation subordinate to it preserves the same truth; nor does the person lie who says that some human being is not a stone. Thus, when the universal affirmation and negation speak truly, the particular affirmation and negation follow the universal propositions in truth.

But if the universals are false, it does not necessarily follow that the particulars must agree with the universals in falsehood. Consider the universal propositions “Every human being is just” and “No human being is just.” One is an affirmation and the other a negation, but both are false. The falsehood of the particulars does not necessarily follow from them. Someone may truly say that some human being is just, which is a particular affirmation; consequently, when the universals are false, it is not necessary that the particulars be true.

When the universal affirmation “Every human being is a stone” is called false, the particular affirmation “Some human being is a stone” is also false. But if the universal negation “No human being is an animal” is proposed falsely, the particular negation “Some human being is not an animal” is not thereby true.

Thus, when the universals remain true, the particulars must agree with the truth of the universals. But when falsehood adheres to the universals, the particulars may be either true or false: they are true if something is predicated that can belong to the subject and can be separated from it; both are false when the particular affirmation concerns something that cannot belong to the subject, or when the particular negation concerns something that cannot be separated from the subject. The examples given above make this clear.

But if particular propositions take precedence with respect to the consequence of truth and falsehood, the universal proposition corresponding to them agrees with them in the contrary manner. If the particulars are false, the universals must also be false. If, however, the particulars are true, the universals may be either true or false.

Thus, if the particular affirmation “Some human being is a stone” is false, the universal affirmation “Every human being is a stone” is also false. Likewise, if the particular negation “Some human being is not an animal” is false, the universal negation “No human being is an animal” is false.

But if the particular affirmation or negation is true, and the predicate is something that can be divided and separated from the subject, it is not in doubt that the universal affirmation and negation may be false. Since the particulars “Some human being is just” and “Some human being is not just” are true, it is clear that the universals subordinate to them are false, namely “Every human being is just” and “No human being is just.”

But if the particular affirmation asserts something that cannot be absent from the subject, the universal affirmation placed above it will be true. Thus, when someone says that some human being is an animal, the universal affirmation agrees with it in truth: “Every human being is an animal.”

If the particular negation proposes something that cannot belong to the subject, the truth of the universal negative necessarily follows the truth of the particular negation. Thus, when someone says that some human being is not a stone, the universal proposition “No human being is a stone” agrees with it in truth.

Consequently, when the universal propositions precede in truth, the particulars must be true; when the particulars precede in falsehood, the truth of the universals does not follow; when the universals remain false, the particulars need not speak falsely; and even when the particulars make true assertions, the universal propositions need not necessarily be true. The examples have taught us this. But so that the matter may become clear through a firm demonstration, let the following useful diagram be presented for making the relationships evident.

[Col. 0775A]

[Col. 0775B] From what has been said above it can be understood that contraries either divide truth and falsehood between them or can both be false, but cannot both be true; that subcontraries may both be true, or one true and the other false, but can never both utter a falsehood; and that angular propositions never agree either in truth or in falsehood, but one proposition is always true and the other always false.

We must now demonstrate that particulars cannot be false when the universals are true, whereas when the universals are false, the particulars may make statements that are not false.

I say, then, that if the universal affirmation is true, the particular affirmation will also be true. For if it were false, the universal negation opposed to the particular affirmation would be true; but the universal affirmation has been posited as true. In this way, therefore, both universals—the universal affirmation and the universal negation—would be true simultaneously. It has been shown that this cannot occur. It is therefore impossible, when the universal affirmation has been proposed as true, for the particular affirmation to be false.

Again, if the universal negation is true, I concede that the particular negation is also true. For if someone calls the particular negation false, he must necessarily admit that the universal affirmation opposed to it is true. But if the universal negation has been proposed as true, the universal negation and affirmation would therefore both be true at the same time. The examples given above have shown that this cannot happen.

But if the universal affirmation is false, the particular affirmation may state either falsehood or truth. Once this is granted, nothing impossible follows. For if the particular affirmation is false, the universal negation will be true; but if the particular affirmation is true, the universal negation will be false. Thus, when the universal affirmation is false, the universal negation may either agree with it in falsehood or disagree with it in truth. The preceding examples show that this is not impossible.

In the same way, if the universal negation is false, the particular negation may be either true or false, and nothing incongruous follows. If the particular negation is true, the universal affirmation will be false; if the particular negation is false, the universal affirmation will speak truly. Therefore, when the universal negation has been proposed as false, reason demonstrates that the universal affirmation may be either true or false, and this is not impossible.

Again, if the particulars are false, the falsehood of the universal also follows. For if the particular affirmation speaks falsely, the universal affirmation will likewise be false. If the universal affirmation were true, its opposed particular negation would be false; but we have established that the particular affirmation is false. Thus the particular affirmation and negation would both be false simultaneously, which the preceding discussion has shown to be impossible.

Likewise, if the particular negation is said to be false, the falsehood of the universal negation will agree with it. For if the universal negation were true, the proposition opposed to it—the particular affirmation—would be false. Thus both particulars, namely the affirmation and the negation, would be false at the same time, which, as we said, cannot occur.

But if the particular affirmation is true, the universal affirmation may be either false or true. If the particular affirmation is false, the negation must be true; if it is true, the particular negation will be false. Yet when the particular affirmation is true, it is not impossible for the particular negation to be either false or true.

Again, if the particular negation possesses truth, the universal negation may possess either truth or falsehood. If it is true, it is clear that the opposed particular affirmation is false; if it is false, the particular affirmation will preserve the truth. Thus, when the particular negation possesses truth, the particular affirmation may be either true or false, neither of which has been shown by the preceding discussion to be impossible. Let this suffice concerning the universals.

Let us now discuss indefinite and singular propositions. Indefinite propositions are those to which no indication of determination is added; they are uttered without the quantitative specification of universal or particular, as in “A human being is just” and “A human being is not just.” Although, as has been said, no indication of determination is added to them, they nevertheless possess the force of particular propositions.

For just as those propositions which we marked as subcontraries in the preceding diagram sometimes distribute truth and falsehood between one another and sometimes agree with one another in truth, yet never appear able simultaneously to speak falsely, so too with indefinite propositions. If the proposition expresses something that must always be present in the subject, the affirmation is true and the negation false, as in these propositions: “A human being is an animal”; “A human being is not an animal.”

But if an indefinite proposition expresses something that the nature of the subject does not admit, the negation is true and the affirmation is joined to falsehood, as in “A human being is a stone”; “A human being is not a stone.” Yet no case can be found in which both agree in uttering falsehood.

They nevertheless differ from universal affirmations and negations in this respect: however the subjects are altered, one will always be true and the other always full of falsehood.

An example of a predicate that always inheres in the subject is the following:

- Every human being is an animal.
- A human being is not an animal.
- No human being is an animal.
- A human being is an animal.

Here the indefinite propositions have the same force as the particulars.

An example of something that never inheres in the subject is:

- Every human being is a stone.
- A human being is not a stone.
- No human being is a stone.
- A human being is a stone.

Here too, in each opposition, the indefinite propositions opposed to the universals make one true and the other false.

Likewise, consider something that the nature of the subject can admit and that may nevertheless be absent from it:

- Every human being is just.
- A human being is not just.
- No human being is just.
- A human being is just.

Here too the indefinite propositions remain unchanged as particulars. When opposed to the universals through each pair of contrary propositions, they divide truth and falsehood between them, making one true and the other false.

Furthermore, whatever examples of terms are given, if we compare affirmations with affirmations and negations with negations, the truth of the indefinites follows from true universals. Thus, when the propositions “Every human being is an animal” and “No human being is a stone” are true, the indefinite propositions “A human being is an animal” and “A human being is not a stone” are also evidently true.

But if the falsehood of the universals precedes, the indefinite propositions may vary between truth and falsehood, as follows.

The universal proposition “Every human being is just” is false; but the proposition “A human being is just” contains truth in part of human nature. For if every human being does not possess justice, yet someone does possess it, one may truly say that a human being is just.

Likewise, when it is universally proposed that “No human being is just,” the proposition is false; but if the same is denied indefinitely, it does not differ from the truth. Since there is some human being who is not just, the person who says “A human being is not just” will not be lying.

Again, since the universal affirmation “Every human being is a stone” is false, the indefinite affirmation “A human being is a stone” is also false.

Similarly, since the negation “No human being is an animal” is false as a universal proposition, the indefinite negation “A human being is not an animal” is false as well.

Here too the resemblance to the particulars is preserved. In subaltern propositions, a true universality brought truth to particularity; but a false universality imposed on particulars neither the necessity of truth nor the necessity of falsehood. The same results arise from a comparison of universals and indefinites.

Again, if the indefinite propositions are first established as false, the universals must also be false. If it is false that a human being is just, it will be false that every human being is just, since the latter cannot be true if even one human being is not just.

Likewise, if the indefinite negation is false, the universal negation cannot be true. For example, if the proposition “A human being is not just” is false, justice cannot be universally denied of human beings if it is shown to be present in even one of them.

But if the indefinite propositions possess truth, the universals may be either true or false. Thus, when we say “A human being is just,” the proposition is true, for there is a human being who is not without justice. The universal negation will be false when someone says “No human being is just.”

But if something is affirmed indefinitely that cannot be separated or divided from the subject, the affirmative universal proposition “Every human being is an animal” will nevertheless be true.

If an indefinite negation proposes something that the nature of the subject does not admit—for example, if it says “A human being is not a stone”—its truth will not differ from that of the universal negative proposition “No human being is a stone.”

There is therefore no doubt that indefinites resemble particulars and possess the same force in signifying truth and falsehood. Enough has been said about them.

Let us now explain singular propositions, which are unlike the preceding ones in every respect. The preceding propositions established a universal subject of which they predicated a term; for this reason they also admitted differences of quantity. For whatever is universal can be uttered universally, particularly, or indefinitely.

But propositions that posit one thing, singularly and individually, cannot have differences of quantity. Consequently, only the difference of quality remains in them: one proposition is an affirmation and the other a negation.

A singular affirmation and a singular negation will therefore always distribute truth and falsehood between them, unless other circumstances interfere—circumstances that usually divert and distort the sense into different kinds of signification.

When the same predicate and the same subject occur in the affirmation and negation, are taken at the same time, uttered in the same manner, referred to the same thing, and proposed with respect to the same part, one of them must always be true and the other always false.

But if the terms are equivocal, or if they do not refer to the same time, or if a different manner is involved in the two propositions, or if they refer to different parts or to something else, both may be true.

Suppose, for example, that the affirmation uses an equivocal term and says, “Cato killed himself at Utica,” while the negation says, “Cato did not kill himself at Utica.” Both propositions are true, because “Cato” is equivocal. The praetorian Cato laid hands on himself at Utica, but the censorial Cato did not.

Likewise, let the affirmation be “It shines at night,” and let the negation answer, “It does not shine at night.” Here “to shine” is equivocal. Therefore nothing prevents both propositions from remaining true. The affirmation, when it says that it shines at night, refers to the light of the moon; the negation, when it denies this, refers to the light of the sun. Thus the equivocal predicate permits both propositions to remain true.

Again, if someone says of Socrates, “Socrates is sitting,” and another denies it by saying “Socrates is not sitting,” both may be true if they refer to different times. Socrates may be sitting now but not sitting at another time.

Again, if one person affirms that the color of the human eye is black while another maintains that it is not black, both may speak truly if the affirmation and negation refer to different parts of the eye. The part around the circumference, which surrounds the central pupil, is white; the circumference itself appears black.

Again, if Socrates is placed between two people and one says “Socrates is on the right,” while another replies “Socrates is not on the right,” truth may hold for both. Socrates is on the right of the person who stands at his left; but with respect to the person whose left side is joined to Socrates’ right side, Socrates is not on the right.

Likewise, if one person declares that an egg is an animal and another denies that an egg is an animal, both statements are compatible with truth. For an egg is potentially an animal but is not actually an animal.

Thus propositions concerning singular subjects distribute truth and falsehood between themselves—one must be true and the other false—provided that neither the subject nor the predicate is confused by equivocation; provided they refer to the same time, the same parts, the same manner, and the same thing to which the affirmation referred what is asserted in the negation.

For example:

- Socrates is bald.
- Socrates is not bald.

If the affirmation and negation are both proposed concerning the same Socrates; if the affirmation and negation use the same meaning of baldness; if both refer to the same part of the head; if both signify either actuality or potentiality; if no difference of time causes an error; and if the affirmation is not referred to one person while the negation is referred to another, then one proposition is always joined to truth and the other always retains falsehood.

Having explained the agreement of propositions that maintained both simple terms in the same order, we must now discuss the relation that preserves both terms and the same order, but in which negation is introduced. As has been said, this can occur in three ways: either only the predicate term, or only the subject term, or both terms are proposed with negation.

The resulting proposition consists either of an infinite subject, an infinite predicate, or two infinite terms. Whenever negation is added to a noun, the noun becomes infinite. For this reason the relation is said to be established through opposition. An infinite noun is always opposed to a simple noun: “human being,” “non-human being”; “animal,” “non-animal”; and so forth.

Since this is so, let the simple propositions be set out first, and from their nature let us derive the others. First, therefore, let the series of propositions be described—namely, the series joined by two finite terms—and from these simple propositions let the order of all the propositions joined with indefinite terms be arranged, so that affirmations are placed opposite affirmations and negations opposite negations.

| Every human being is rational. | Every non-human being is non-rational. |
|---|---|
| No human being is rational. | No non-human being is non-rational. |
| Some human being is rational. | Some non-human being is non-rational. |
| Some human being is not rational. | Some non-human being is not non-rational. |
| Every human being is grammatical. | Every non-human being is non-grammatical. |
| No human being is grammatical. | No non-human being is non-grammatical. |
| Some human being is grammatical. | Some non-human being is non-grammatical. |
| Some human being is not grammatical. | Some non-human being is not non-grammatical. |
| Every human being is a stone. | Every non-human being is a non-stone. |
| No human being is a stone. | No non-human being is a non-stone. |
| Some human being is a stone. | Some non-human being is a non-stone. |
| Some human being is not a stone. | Some non-human being is not a non-stone. |
| Every human being is just. | Every non-human being is non-just. |
| No human being is just. | No non-human being is non-just. |
| Some human being is just. | Some non-human being is non-just. |
| Some human being is not just. | Some non-human being is not non-just. |
| Every human being is capable of laughter. | Every non-human being is not capable of laughter. |
| No human being is capable of laughter. | No non-human being is not capable of laughter. |
| Some human being is capable of laughter. | Some non-human being is not capable of laughter. |
| Some human being is not capable of laughter. | Some non-human being is not not capable of laughter. |
[Col. 0779C] The property of the falsity or truth of these propositions must therefore be connected in such a way that universal affirmations and particular negations may either agree with one another in truth or falsehood, or divide truth and falsehood between them. For if something is predicated of a subject which either cannot be separated from the subject—for example, rationality from a human being—or can indeed depart from the subject but cannot equal the nature of the subject—for example, grammar from a human being—it follows that one is true and the other false.

For whoever says, “Every human being is rational,” speaks the truth; and whoever says, “Every non-human is non-rational,” will be lying. For divine substances possess reason, but they are not human beings. Likewise, if someone declares, “Every human being is grammatical,” he will have spoken falsely. But whoever proposes, “Every non-human is non-grammatical,” will have spoken truly. For whatever is not human cannot be grammatical.

But if something is predicated of a subject which either can never belong to the subject—for example, a stone to a human being—or, although belonging to it, can depart from it because it is greater than and more universal than the subject—for example, justice in relation to a human being—then falsity arises in both propositions. For if someone says, “Every human being is a stone,” he will have made a false proposition. In the same way, whoever says, “Every non-human is not a stone,” will also have spoken falsely, since flint is not human but is a stone.

Likewise, the proposition “Every human being is just” is false; from its falsity follows the falsity of “Every non-human is not just.” For justice is always present in divine substances, although humanity is not.

But if something is predicated of a subject which is always joined to it and nevertheless cannot exceed the subject—for example, risibility in relation to a human being—the judgment in both directions agrees in the truth of its signification. “Every human being is risible” is true, and “Every non-human is not risible” likewise retains its truth. For since risibility is proper to the human being, it is rightly said that whatever is not human is not risible.

All the same points are expressed in particular negation. For whether what is predicated of the subject is greater than the subject and cannot depart from it, as rationality is from a human being, or can depart from it but is greater than the subject, as grammar is from a human being, the propositions make one true and the other false.

Whoever says, “Some human being is not rational,” has proposed something false; but whoever responds, “Some non-human is not non-rational,” speaks truly. For the divine substance is not some human being, but it cannot lack the rationality of human nature.

Likewise, “Some human being is not grammatical” is true, but it is false if I say, “Some non-human is not non-grammatical.” The former is more correct, since whatever is not human cannot be grammatical.

But if what is predicated either can never truly be predicated of the subject, as a stone of a human being, or is indeed predicated and is greater than the subject but permits itself to depart and be separated from it, as justice from a human being, both propositions immediately retain their truth. For whoever says, “Some human being is not a stone,” will have spoken truly. If someone responds, “Some non-human is not non-stone,” he too will have spoken truly—provided that this is understood of flint and other such things which, although they are not human beings, are not non-stones.

Likewise, “Some human being is not just” retains its truth. Nor is the proposition false which proposes that some non-human is not not-just; for, as has been said, this is found in divine substances: they possess justice, although they are separated from the definition of humanity.

Again, if what cannot be absent and is equal to the subject is predicated of that subject—for example, risibility of a human being—falsehood affects both propositions. “Some human being is not risible” is false, and its falsity is matched by the proposition “Some non-human is not non-risible,” as though whatever is not human could be risible.

Thus, in universal affirmations and particular negations, truth and falsity are sometimes found together and sometimes divided between the two. Universal negations and particular affirmations, however, do not respond in the same way. Universal negations can say one thing truly and the other falsely, or both can be false. They can never both be true.

For if something which cannot belong to the subject is predicated of it, as a stone of a human being, one proposition is made true and the other false. Thus, “No human being is a stone” is true, whereas “No non-human is a non-stone” is false; for all animals other than human beings are non-stones in the same way as they are separated from human nature.

Whatever else is predicated of the subject cannot preserve truth in either proposition. If someone proposes, “No human being is rational,” he will have spoken falsely; and another who responds, “No non-human is non-rational,” is likewise convicted by reason of lying. A horse is a non-human, and no one would say that it participates in reason. No term, however, can demonstrate that both propositions are simultaneously true.

Particular affirmations, on the other hand, diverge in truth and falsity whenever something is said of the subject which can never belong to it, such as a stone. If someone declares, “Some human being is a stone,” the proposition is false; but if someone responds, “Some non-human is not a non-stone,” it retains the contrary truth, for a horse is a non-human and is not said to be a stone.

Whatever else is predicated of the subject causes the propositions to agree in the signification of truth. Thus, “Some human being is rational” is true, and “Some non-human is not non-rational” is likewise true; for a horse is a non-human and does not subsist by reason. No examples, however, will be found in which both are simultaneously false.

In this manner, then, the property of propositions must also be considered with respect to the other cases in which either the subject or the predicate is indefinite, in order to determine their agreement in truth and falsity. It is sufficient for us here to have briefly touched upon what occurs; we leave the examination of each case to the reader’s diligence, to be investigated through the appropriate terms.

Let the propositions consisting of two simple terms therefore be set out, and let those whose subject alone is negated face them on the opposite side.

### Simple propositions

Every human being is grammatical.

[Col. 0781] | [Col. 0783] |

### From finite subjects

Every human being is rational. | Every non-human is rational. |

No human being is rational. | No non-human is rational. |

Some human being is rational. | Some non-human is rational. |

Some human being is not rational. | Some non-human is not rational. |

Every human being is risible. | Every non-human is risible. |

No human being is risible. | No non-human is risible. |

Some human being is risible. | Some non-human is risible. |

Some human being is not risible. | Some non-human is not risible. |

Every human being is just. | Every non-human is just. |

No human being is just. | No non-human is just. |

Some human being is just. | Some non-human is just. |

Some human being is not just. | Some non-human is not just. |

[Col. 0783] |

Every non-human is grammatical. |

No human being is grammatical. | No non-human is grammatical. |

Some human being is grammatical. | Some non-human is grammatical. |

Some human being is not grammatical. | Some non-human is not grammatical. |

Every human being is a stone. | Every non-human is a stone. |

No human being is a stone. | No non-human is a stone. |

Some human being is a stone. | Some non-human is a stone. |

Some human being is not a stone. | Some non-human is not a stone. |

[Col. 0783A] In these universal affirmations, then, truth and falsity are distributed if something is predicated of the subject which cannot be absent from it, whether it is greater than the subject, as animal is greater than human being, or equal to it, as risible is equal to human being. In these cases one must be true and the other false. But whatever is predicated apart from these will not always result in one being true and the other false; nor can it be shown that both are simultaneously true.

In particular affirmations, if things are predicated which can pass beyond the subject, whether they cannot be separated from it, as animal from human being, or can be separated, as justice from human being, both propositions speak truly. Whatever is predicated apart from these is held by one proposition as true and by the other as false; but they cannot both be found false simultaneously.

Particular negations, however, if they predicate something which cannot depart from the subject, whether it is greater than the subject, as rational is greater than human being, or equal to it, as risible is equal to human being, will have one true and the other lying. But if anything apart from these is predicated, both are always shown to be true, so that common falsity can never fall upon them.

Let the propositions now be arranged in order: first, the simple propositions, and opposite to them those in which the predicate is negated with respect to the simple subject.

### Simple propositions

Every human being is a stone.

[Col. 0783] |

### From an indefinite predicate

[Col. 0783] |

Every human being is not a stone. |

No human being is a stone. | No human being is not a stone. |

Some human being is a stone. | Some human being is not a stone. |

Some human being is not a stone. | Some human being is not not a stone. |

Every human being is an animal. | Every human being is not an animal. |

No human being is an animal. | No human being is not an animal. |

Some human being is an animal. | Some human being is not an animal. |

Some human being is not an animal. | Some human being is not not an animal. |

Every human being is risible. | Every human being is not risible. |

No human being is risible. | No human being is not risible. |

Some human being is risible. | Some human being is not risible. |

Some human being is not risible. | Some human being is not not risible. |

Every human being is just. | Every human being is not just. |

No human being is just. | No human being is not just. |

Some human being is just. | Some human being is not just. |

Some human being is not just. | Some human being is not not just. |

Every human being is grammatical. | Every human being is not grammatical. |

No human being is grammatical. | No human being is not grammatical. |

Some human being is grammatical. | Some human being is not grammatical. |

Some human being is not grammatical. | Some human being is not not grammatical. |

[Col. 0783B] The universal affirmations in this group, then, if they predicate something which cannot belong to the subject, as a stone to a human being, or something which, although equal to or greater than the subject, cannot depart from it, as animal or risible from a human being, must always produce one truth and the other falsehood. Whatever else is predicated results in falsity for both, so that they cannot agree in truth.

Universal negations, if they predicate of the subject something which can both belong and not belong to it, and which exceeds it, as virtue exceeds human being, or something which can belong to it but cannot equal the subject, as grammatical exceeds human being, share in falsity. Whatever else is predicated results in one being true and the other false; but it cannot be shown that both are true.

Particular affirmations are simultaneously true if what is predicated can either belong or not belong to the subject, whether it is greater, as justice is greater than human being, or lesser, as grammatical is lesser than human being. If anything else is predicated, truth and falsity are distributed between them, so that they never jointly agree in falsity.

Particular negations likewise agree in truth with similar terms. For if something that can belong or not belong to the subject is predicated, whether it is greater, as just is greater than human being, or lesser, as grammatical is lesser than human being, both will retain truth. In all other predications one retains truth and the other falsity. Yet they will never both agree in expressing falsity.

Besides this agreement between propositions, those which pronounce the predicate with an added negation possess a feature peculiar to themselves, which cannot belong to the others. Universal affirmations agree with negations, and universal negations with affirmations; likewise particular affirmations with negations, and negations with affirmations, in such a way that they never disagree either in falsity or in truth.

We describe the order and sequence of these agreements. If one looks back at the propositions set out above, one will see that they are arranged in an angularly reversed manner.

[Col. 0785]

Every human being is rational. — They agree with — No human being is not rational.

Every human being is not rational. — They agree with — No human being is rational.

Some human being is non-rational. — They agree with — Some human being is not rational.

Some human being is rational. — They agree with — Some human being is not non-rational.

[Col. 0785A] This seems to occur in these cases alone because both orders of opposition are understood of the same subject. The proposition “Every human being is rational” predicates rationality of a human being; likewise, the proposition “Every human being is not rational” separates rationality from that same human being. Thus the simple affirmations rightly agree with the negation.

But in the other cases the subject is not understood to be the same. The proposition “Every non-human is rational” and the proposition “Every non-human is not risible” do not speak of a human being, but of whatever else is left outside the negation of “human being.” For that reason, as though they were foreign and unrelated to one another, they possess neither agreement in truth nor agreement in falsity.

I did not think that indefinite propositions should be added to those above, since we have shown that they resemble particulars. What occurs in indefinite propositions must be what commonly occurs in particulars.

Having dealt with propositions which share both terms and are set out in the same order, let us now discuss that agreement or participation of propositions which consists in agreement of both terms but in a change of order. The end of this discussion is to teach the conversion of propositions. For what else is it for propositions to agree with both terms after their order has been changed, except for propositions to be converted?

Propositions are said to be converted either with themselves or with others whenever, after the order of the terms has been changed—that is, when what was subject becomes predicate and what was formerly predicated becomes subject—they obtain truth or falsity together.

We have already said that there are four propositions distinguished by differences of quantity and sharing both terms without changing their order: universal affirmation, universal negation, particular affirmation, and particular negation.

Particular affirmation converts with itself in the primary way, and converts accidentally with universal affirmation. Universal negation likewise receives conversion with itself in the primary position and can be converted accidentally with particular negation. Universal affirmation cannot have a permanent conversion with itself, but can be converted accidentally with particular affirmation. Nor is the conversion of particular negation with itself stable and firm in the primary position; it converts secondarily and accidentally with universal negation.

All this is more easily explained by examples.

A particular affirmation, such as “Some human being is white,” easily converts with itself if we say, “Some white thing is a human being”; truth is preserved simultaneously in both. But if someone proposes, “Some human being is a stone,” and converts it by saying, “Some stone is a human being,” falsity remains in both. In this way particular affirmation receives conversion with itself.

Universal negation can likewise be converted. If someone states, “No human being is a stone,” and, with the terms converted, says, “No stone is a human being,” both retain truth. But if someone says, “No human being is an animal,” and proposes the same proposition with the terms converted, “No animal is a human being,” neither has lost its falsity. In this way universal negation also converts with itself.

Universal affirmation, however, does not preserve permanent conversion. Although universal affirmations can sometimes be converted when properties are predicated of species—for example, if someone says, “Every human being is risible,” he can change the order of the terms and say, “Everything risible is a human being”—this is not an equal and reliable conversion in every case. For when someone proposes, “Every human being is an animal,” can he truly convert it and declare that every animal is a human being? Since universal affirmation, when converted, sometimes fails to retain its proper truth, it is said not to be able to receive the nature of conversion.

Particular negation also sometimes appears capable of conversion. If someone declares, “Some human being is not a stone,” he will speak truly if he says, “Some stone is not a human being.” But this conversion is unstable and uncertain. For although some human being is not grammatical, it is false to say that some grammatical thing is not a human being. Thus this conversion immediately falls away from its own truth.

Of the four enunciations proposed above, therefore, two opposites—particular affirmation and universal negation—receive a firm and permanent conversion with themselves. The other two opposites—universal affirmation and particular negation—do not retain firm conversion. But because universal affirmation, which appears unstable in its conversion with itself, necessarily entails the truth of particular affirmation whenever it is true, if converted particular affirmation does not lose its proper truth, converted universal affirmation will likewise express the same truth as particular affirmation. This will be demonstrated by the following examples.

If someone proposes, “Every human being is an animal,” he will have spoken truly. Its subordinate particular affirmation, “Some human being is an animal,” is also true, because the truth of the universal affirmation preceded it. This particular affirmation can very truly be converted with itself: “Some animal is a human being.” Therefore the universal affirmation “Every human being is an animal” and the converted particular affirmation “Some animal is a human being” both retain the signification of truth.

Thus universal affirmation, which could not bear permanent conversion with itself, has been converted accidentally with particular affirmation. It is called accidental because particular affirmation converts with itself in the primary position, while universal affirmation, converted with particular affirmation, retains the same judgment in truth.

The same applies to universal negation. Since it can itself be converted in the primary position, the subordinate negation, when converted, reports the same judgment of truth.

Converted particular negation can agree in the signification of truth. If someone affirms, “No human being is a stone,” its conversion is, “No stone is a human being.” Since this precedes as true, it completes the truth of the subordinate particular negative, namely, “Some stone is not a human being.” Compared with the universal negation “No human being is a stone,” this particular negation, although differing in terms, is proposed with a similar truth.

Thus particular negation, which cannot convert with itself, can be converted accidentally with universal negation. This is accidental because universal negation can first convert with itself. Through its conversion with itself, it appears to obtain a judgment of truth similar to that of particular negation.

It must therefore be concluded that particular affirmation and universal negation preserve a firm and stable conversion with themselves. Universal affirmation and particular negation, however, cannot be firm in conversion; the former can be converted accidentally with particular affirmation, and the latter with universal negation.
