It remains to discuss the agreement or participation of propositions in which, after the order of both terms has been changed, a negative adverb is joined to one or both of them.

In these enunciations, the converted terms are said to be opposed, since each term, when prefixed by negation, appears opposed to the terms pronounced simply. This participation has three forms: negation may be joined only to the predicate, only to the subject, or negation may be attached to both terms.

First, examples should be set out; afterward, their agreement in truth and falsity will be discussed in the proper order. We shall begin with the case in which both subject and predicate are negated; next with the case in which only the subject is negated; and finally with the case in which the predicate is pronounced together with negation.

We shall construct their nature and order from the simple propositions. We have shown that there are four simple propositions established by differences of quantity.

Let the first be a universal affirmation proposing, “Every human being is an animal.” Opposite to it let there be a universal affirmation which is expressed not only with the terms converted but also with a negative adverb attached to each term, as follows: “Every non-animal is a non-human.”

Again, let the universal negation be proposed: “No human being is an animal.” Opposite to this let there be a universal negation with the terms converted together with negation: “No non-animal is a non-human.”

Likewise, let there be the simple particular affirmation, “Some human being is an animal.” Opposite to it let there be a particular affirmation which, with the terms changed in order, bears opposed negations on both: “Some non-animal is a non-human.”

Finally, let there be the simple particular negation proposing, “Some human being is not an animal.” Opposite to it let there be a particular negation which, with the terms changed in order, adds a negative adverb: “Some non-animal is not a non-human.”

### Simple propositions

[Col. 0787] |

### Converted, with both terms indefinite

Every human being is an animal. | Every non-animal is a non-human. |

No human being is an animal. | No non-animal is a non-human. |

Some human being is an animal. | Some non-animal is a non-human. |

Some human being is not an animal. | Some animal is not a non-human. |

[Col. 0787C] Although we know that there are several differences in this kind of participation, it is sufficient for the instruction of categorical syllogisms to have proposed only this much. Some of these propositions consist of simple names, while others consist of indefinite names.

The universal proposition “Every human being is an animal” consists of two finite names. It is evident that both “human being” and “animal” are finite names. The affirmation “Every non-animal is a non-human,” however, is joined through the placement of indefinite terms. We stated above, in the definition of the name, that “non-animal” and “non-human” are indefinite names; these stand in relation to the account of truth and falsity as follows: just as indefinite names, through the addition of negations, are opposed to simple names, so the conversion of propositions occurs in the opposite manner from what was found earlier in the simple propositions.

[Col. 0788C] In those propositions, universal affirmation and particular negation did not retain stable conversion. Particular affirmation and universal negation, when converted, most certainly preserved agreement either in truth or in falsity. Here everything is different.

Universal affirmation and particular negation convert with themselves through opposition; but the conversion of universal negation and particular affirmation is not reliable for agreement in truth or falsity.

Let us first treat universal affirmation. When it is true in simple terms, its conversion through opposition also preserves truth. Thus “Every human being is an animal” is true, and its conversion through opposition, namely “Every non-animal is a non-human,” must also be true. The sense of this proposition is that whatever is not an animal is not a human being, which no one doubts is true.

Likewise, if a universal affirmation constituted with simple terms is false, its conversion through opposition will also be shown to be false. For when we say, “Every stone is an animal,” it is false; and its conversion through opposition, “Every non-animal is a non-stone,” must also be false. The meaning of this enunciation is that whatever is not an animal is not a stone, which is plainly false, since a stone itself is not an animal.

If, then, universal affirmation agrees with its conversion through opposition in both truth and falsity, there is no doubt that simple universal affirmation is shown to have a stable conversion through opposition.

We shall say the same about simple particular negation. When it is false—for example, “Some human being is not an animal”—the proposition converted through opposition will likewise retain falsity: “Some non-animal is not a non-human.” For this enunciation gathers the meaning that something which is not an animal is a human being. Indeed, to be a human being is to be not a non-human.

But if the particular negation joined from simple terms is true, as in “Some stone is not an animal,” the converted proposition with opposition of the terms will also retain truth: “Some non-animal is not a non-stone.” The conversion signifies that some thing which is not an animal is a stone; for to be a stone is to be not a non-stone.

Since simple particular negation agrees with its proper conversion through opposition in the signification both of truth and of falsity, there is no doubt that simple particular negation can be converted through opposition of the terms in a certain and stable manner.

In universal negation, however, the conversion is neither permanent nor reliable. This may deceive someone who looks only to agreement in falsity. When the simple universal negation “No human being is an animal” is false, its conversion through opposition is also false: “No non-animal is a non-human.” For this proposition shows that whatever is not an animal is a human being; it signifies that whatever is not an animal is a human being, and proposes that there is no non-human which is not an animal.

But this agreement in falsity does not extend as far as truth. Suppose that the simple universal negation “No human being is a stone” is true. “No non-stone is a non-human” cannot be true. This conversion signifies that whatever is not a stone is a human being; for to be a human being is to be not a stone. It declares that there is no non-human which is not a stone, which is plainly false. For although I can mention many things which are not stones, they are nevertheless separated from human nature, such as a horse, a tree, and many others.

If, therefore, universal negation agrees with its proper conversion through opposition in falsity but does not agree in truth, it is rightly declared not to possess a permanent and uniform conversion.

The same reasoning applies to simple particular affirmation. Here too error is often detected when conversions of propositions are considered certain by looking not to agreement in falsity but only to agreement in truth.

When simple particular affirmation is true, as in “Some human being is an animal,” if its terms are converted with opposition and the proposition becomes “Some non-animal is a non-human,” it does not depart from truth. For what else does this enunciation signify than that there is something which, since it is not an animal, is not a human being either—for example, a stone, which lacks both the nature of animal and the nature of human being?

But this agreement in truth does not extend as far as falsity. What if simple particular affirmation is false, as in “Some human being is a stone”? Its conversion through opposition, “Some non-stone is a non-human,” will not therefore be false. Indeed, this stands firmly in truth, for the proposition makes it understood that there is something which, since it is not a stone, is not a human being either, such as a horse or a tree, which are enclosed by neither the definition of human being nor that of stone.

Since particular affirmation, when converted through opposition, agrees with itself in truth but disagrees with itself in falsity, it is correct to declare that terms joined with negation do not retain a firm and stable conversion.

Thus, in simple conversions apart from opposition, universal negation and particular affirmation are converted through a permanent and reliable exchange of terms, whereas universal affirmation and particular negation are not. When a simple proposition converts with itself through opposition of the terms, everything occurs in the contrary manner, as has been said.

Universal affirmation and particular negation retain a firm conversion of the negated parts. Universal negation converts with itself correctly in falsity, but disagrees with itself in truth. Particular affirmation agrees with itself in truth but disagrees in falsity.

A similar consideration applies to propositions in which, after the order of the terms has been converted, negation is joined only to the predicate or only to the subject. As we did above, we shall set out only the order of the propositions and briefly indicate what occurs, leaving the examination of each individual case to the reader’s diligence.

The simple propositions having been set out, let those which, after the order has been changed, pronounce the predicate with negation be compared with them on the opposite side.

### Simple propositions

Every human being is just.

[Col. 0789] |

### Converted from an indefinite predicate

Every human being is an animal. | Every animal is a non-human. |

No human being is an animal. | No animal is a non-human. |

Some human being is an animal. | Some animal is a non-human. |

Some human being is not an animal. | Some animal is not a non-human. |

[Col. 0791] |

Every just being is a non-human. |

No human being is just. | No just being is a non-human. |

Some human being is just. | Some just being is a non-human. |

Some human being is not just. | Some just being is not a non-human. |

Every human being is grammatical. | Every grammatical being is a non-human. |

No human being is grammatical. | No grammatical being is a non-human. |

Some human being is grammatical. | Some grammatical being is a non-human. |

Some human being is not grammatical. | Some grammatical being is not a non-human. |

Every human being is a stone. | Every stone is a non-human. |

No human being is a stone. | No stone is a non-human. |

Some human being is a stone. | Some stone is a non-human. |

Some human being is not a stone. | Some stone is not a non-human. |

Every human being is risible. | Everything risible is a non-human. |

No human being is risible. | Nothing risible is a non-human. |

Some human being is risible. | Something risible is a non-human. |

Some human being is not risible. | Something risible is not a non-human. |

[Col. 0791A] In these universal affirmations, then, if what is predicated of the subject can both belong and not belong to it, whether it is greater than the subject, as justice is greater than human being, or lesser, as grammatical is lesser than human being, or if what is predicated cannot belong at all, as a stone to a human being, both propositions must always be false. Whatever else is predicated results in one being true and the other false; but the two will never agree in truth.

In universal negations, if things are predicated of the subject which can be separated from it, whether they are greater, as justice is greater than human being, or lesser, as grammatical is lesser than the same human being, a false judgment will belong to both. Whatever else is predicated will make one true and the other false. But concordant truth is never found in these cases.

In particular affirmations, if things are predicated which can be separated and are either greater than the subject, as just is greater than human being, or lesser, as grammatical is lesser than human being, the affirmations will possess common truth. Any other predication will always make one true and the other false, but they will never both be false.

In particular negations the rule is that, whether what is predicated cannot belong to the subject, as a stone to a human being, or can be separated from it, while one is greater, as justice is greater than human being, and the other lesser, as grammatical is lesser than human being, both will retain truth. Whatever else is predicated will divide truth between one and falsity between the other; yet it will not happen that both are simultaneously false.

Let there also be set out a description in which the simple propositions are placed first and, facing them in opposition, those which, after the order has been changed, propose the subject together with negation.

### Simple propositions

[Col. 0791] |

### Converted from an indefinite subject

Every human being is an animal. | Every non-animal is a human being. |
No human is an animal. | No non-animal is a human.

Some human is an animal. | Some non-animal is a human.

Some human is not an animal. | Some non-animal is not a human.

Every human is capable of laughter. | Every non-laughable thing is a human.

No human is capable of laughter. | No non-laughable thing is a human.

Some human is capable of laughter. | Some non-laughable thing is a human.

Some human is not capable of laughter. | Some non-laughable thing is not a human.

Every human is a stone. | Every non-stone is a human.

No human is a stone. | No non-stone is a human.

Some human is a stone. | Some non-stone is a human.

Some human is not a stone. | Some non-stone is not a human.

Every human is just. | Every non-just thing is a human.

No human is just. | No non-just thing is a human.

Some human is just. | Some non-just thing is a human.

Some human is not just. | Some non-just thing is not a human.

Every human is a grammarian. | Every non-grammarian is a human.

No human is a grammarian. | No non-grammarian is a human.

Some human is a grammarian. | Some non-grammarian is a human.

Some human is not a grammarian. | Some non-grammarian is not a human.

[Col. 0793A] Of the propositions described above, then, the universal affirmatives, if predicates are asserted of the subject that can never be removed from it—whether the predicate is greater, as animal in relation to human, or equal, as capable of laughter in relation to human, or of such a kind that it cannot in any way belong to the subject, as stone in relation to human—will distribute truth to one and falsity to the other. But if anything other than these is predicated, falsity will attach to both, and there can be no place for a common truth of the propositions.

In the negatives, however, if universal and greater predicates are asserted—whether they are things that cannot leave the subject, as animal in relation to human, or things that can leave it, as justice in relation to human—falsity will adhere to both. Any other predicates make one true and the other false, so that both cannot share in the same truth. [Col. 0793B]

In the particular affirmatives, if greater predicates are asserted of the subject—whether they never cease to be joined to the subject, as animal in relation to human, or can nevertheless be separated from it, as justice from human—both will correspond to truth. Other predications, however, distribute truth or falsity to the propositions, with both sharing in falsity. [Col. 0794A]

Particular negatives, if they assert predicates that can be separated from the subject—whether the predicate is greater, as justice in relation to human, or lesser, as grammarian in relation to human—must necessarily both be true. But if anything else is predicated, one must be true and the other false, so that they cannot be found false simultaneously.

These points have been made concerning propositions that are uttered with a determiner. Indefinite propositions, since they correspond to the properties of particulars, will, when compared with universals, exhibit all the same features that the order of the particular propositions preserved in the preceding diagram.

There would remain propositions concerning singular subjects. Since discussing them would be lengthy, would contribute nothing to the purpose of the work, and since the reader will discover the same principles for himself by using as examples the propositions proposed above, they ought, it seems, to be passed over. [Col. 0794B]

AN. MANL. SEV. BOETHIUS, TWO BOOKS ON THE CATEGORICAL SYLLOGISM

[Col. 0793]

BOOK ONE

[Col. 0793C] The ancient Greeks left many works of great learning to their successors. In them, before coming to matters obscured by dense darkness, they make a kind of preliminary advance through a struggle of understanding. Thus, by way of introduction, learning becomes easier and more accessible; and through what they call προλεγόμενα (*prolegomena*), which we may call “preliminary statements” or “things to be stated beforehand,” a readier path is prepared toward understanding.

Therefore, not disapproving of this foresight, I too have decided to place, in a certain way, a bridge toward the most obscure matters, sampling each topic moderately. If something has been stated too briefly, I shall extend it for understanding by adding explanation. If Aristotle, in his customary manner, has confused something by altering nouns and verbs, I shall, in the service of understanding, restore it to familiar terminology. If, writing for the learned and touching only on the highest points by way of summary indication, he has merely pointed something out, I shall investigate it in the manner of an introduction by arranging some treatment of those matters.

But if anyone approaches this work for reading, let him be asked not to venture at once to judge matters he has never touched; and, if he has learned something in elementary disciplines, let him not regard it as inviolable, since a more rigorous treatment in philosophy often removes matters suited to tender ears. If something in this work does not seem right, let him not immediately object, but, having considered the reasoning, let him judge—with keener intelligence and more carefully worked-out reasoning—both what he himself thinks and what we propose. [Col. 0793D]

And let these matters stand thus. For, as I think, we have sufficiently [done] that they should taste the commentaries concerning which we have put these things forward, perhaps attracted by the pleasant flavor of subtlety; although they are unbridled and untamed creators, they will nevertheless submit to the impregnable authorities of ancient men. [Note: [Col. 0793] “Nos . . . acquiescent” (“we . . . they will submit”). The phrase appears confused, or perhaps defective.] But anyone who lacks Greek will labor over these passages, and over any similar passages elsewhere.

Thus this will be the law of this preface: no one should inspect our forum without understanding it and therefore finding fault with it. But, lest time be spent on prefaces that contribute nothing, we must begin, first removing the danger that anyone might accuse our discourse of barrenness. We are not pursuing ornate eloquence, but plainness; and if we achieve this, then, however inelegantly we speak, our purpose too will have been fulfilled. [Col. 0794C]

Since, however, the structure of syllogisms must be explained in this work, and a proposition precedes a syllogism, this little book will treat propositions. And since the parts of a proposition are a noun and a verb, while a part is prior to the thing of which it is a part, the first discussion must be placed first: a discussion of the noun and the verb.

A noun is a significant vocal expression established by convention, without time, no part of which is significant independently. “Vocal expression” is said because vocal expression is the genus of nouns. Every definition, however, is drawn from a genus: if you define a human being, you say “animal,” which is the genus, and afterward “rational,” which is the difference.

It is called “significant” because there are certain vocal expressions that signify nothing, such as syllables. A noun signifies that of which it is the noun. “Established by convention” means that no noun signifies anything by itself, but only according to the will of the person who establishes it. For each thing is called by the name chosen by the person who first imposed that name upon it.

There are vocal expressions that signify naturally, such as the barking of a dog, which signifies the dog’s anger, and another kind of vocal expression that signifies its affection. But these are not nouns, because they signify not by convention but by nature. “Without time” means that verbs too are significant vocal expressions established by convention, but differ in this: nouns are without time, whereas verbs are with time. [Col. 0795B]

“No part of which is significant independently” separates the noun from discourse. Discourse too is a vocal expression, significant, established by convention, and sometimes without time; but its parts signify, whereas the parts of nouns do not.

In the noun *Cicero*, no part independently signifies—not *ci*, nor *ce*, nor *ro*. Nor is the situation different when nouns are formed from two complete words. What signifies together in one word does not signify independently. In the noun *magister* (“teacher”), *magis* and *ter* signify together, since the word means “teacher.” But once *ter* and *magis* have been removed, neither will signify anything unless you choose to give that separate item the same name. For all nouns are established not naturally but conventionally.

This was discussed in the commentary on Aristotle’s book *Περὶ Ἑρμηνείας* (*On Interpretation*), and a fuller treatment of the matter is too extensive to be undertaken now. [Col. 0795C]

Let us therefore return to the noun. There are certain vocal expressions that are significant, established by convention, and without time, but whose nature is doubtful, such as *non homo*—properly, *non-homo* (“non-human”). For this signifies something and is established by convention, since it has been imposed as a term; but it is doubtful under what category it can be subsumed. It cannot be a noun, since every noun signifies something definite, whereas “non-human” removes whatever is definite. Nor can it be called discourse, since all discourse consists of nouns and verbs, while “non-human” consists neither of nouns nor of verbs. Much less can it be a verb, since every verb includes time, whereas “non-human” is without time.

What it is must therefore be considered. Since *non-homo* signifies something, but what it signifies is not contained in the word “human” itself—for a non-human may be a horse, a stone, a house, or anything that is not human, and since the things it can signify are infinite—it is called an “indefinite noun.” [Col. 0795D]

There are also certain vocal expressions that are significant, established by convention, definite, and whose parts signify nothing independently, such as the cases of nouns: *Ciceronis* (“of Cicero”), *Cicerone* (“by/with Cicero”), and so forth. These will not be nouns. For every noun joined to a verb indicates something true or false. If you say, “It is day,” this is either true or false. But if you join an oblique case, you produce neither truth nor falsity. If you say, “It is of the day,” you have indicated nothing that is or is not. Thus you will produce from this neither truth nor falsity. [Col. 0796A]

And the statement seems rightly made. For only that which the first namers of things, when imposing names on them, called a “noun” will properly be called a noun. The person who first imposed a name on the circus seems to have said: “Let this be called a circus.” And for that reason the first case is called the nominative, because it is the noun. They gave the remaining cases names other than “noun.”

The account must therefore be retraced from the beginning. “Vocal expression” was said because vocal expression is the genus of nouns; “significant,” because there are certain vocal expressions that signify nothing, so that the noun may be distinguished from them; “established by convention,” so that it may be separated from vocal expressions that signify naturally, such as the sounds of animals; “without time,” to distinguish it from the verb, which is with time; “no part of which signifies independently,” to distinguish it from discourse, whose parts are nouns and verbs and do signify; “definite,” to distinguish it from indefinite expressions; and “straight,” to distinguish it from the cases.

Nearly all the same features apply to the verb. A verb is a significant vocal expression established by convention, with time, no part of which is independently significant. [Col. 0796B] Since there is a significant vocal expression established by convention, with time, one part of which signifies nothing independently—such as *non albet* (“is not white”), for *albet* (“is white”), when joined with *non*, signifies together but does not signify independently—and since it indicates nothing definite—for what is not white may be red, black, pale, or anything that is not white—it is therefore called an “indefinite verb.”

*Faciebat* (“he was doing”) and *facturus* (“about to do”), as was said above concerning the noun, are not verbs but cases of verbs. The discussion of the verb must therefore be repeated from the beginning. It was said to be a vocal expression because vocal expression is its genus; significant, so that it may be distinguished from non-significant vocal expressions; established by convention, so that it may be separated from vocal expressions significant by nature; with time, so that it may be distinguished from the noun; signifying something present, so that it may be separated from the cases of the verb; and definite, so that it may be distinguished from indefinite expressions. [Col. 0796C]

It remains now to say what discourse is. It seems to be composed of a noun and a verb. But first let us consider whether the noun and the verb are the only parts of discourse, or whether there are also six others, as the grammarians believe, or whether some of these are to be converted into the functions of the verb and the noun. Unless this is first established, the whole account of propositions, and thereafter of syllogisms themselves, which are composed of propositions, will totter. For if the genus from which terms derive is unknown, everything will be unknown. [Col. 0796D]

The noun and the verb alone should be regarded as the two parts. The others are not parts but supplements of discourse. Just as the reins or straps of a chariot are not parts but, in a certain sense, fittings and, as has been said, supplements rather than parts, so conjunctions, prepositions, and other things of this kind are not parts of discourse but certain kinds of connective elements.

The so-called participle will be placed in the position of the verb, since it indicates time. The adverb, however, is a noun, for it has a definite signification without time; and the fact that it is not inflected through cases is no obstacle. Inflection through cases is not proper to every noun. There are some nouns that cannot be inflected and that grammarians call *monoptota* (“single-case forms”), but this belongs more to grammar than to the present inquiry.

Discourse is a significant vocal expression established by convention, whose parts signify something independently—not as an assertion. The fact that discourse is a vocal expression, significant, and established by convention is shared by the noun and the verb. For whatever has parts established by convention is itself established by convention. The parts of discourse are the noun and the verb. Since these are established by convention, discourse too is established by convention.

Dialecticians call nouns and verbs the terms of discourse. They are called “terms” because the analysis of the parts of discourse proceeds only as far as the verb and noun; no one should attempt to resolve discourse as far as the syllables of nouns or verbs, which are no longer significant. [Col. 0797A]

Discourse differs from a noun or verb in that its parts signify independently, whereas the parts of the verb and noun signify nothing independently.

A *dictio* (“expression”) is the naming of a single simple word, or a simple assertion. For this reason it was said that the parts of discourse signify as an expression—that is, as the naming of a simple word. In the discourse “Socrates walks,” each word signifies independently only as much as the naming of a simple word can signify.

How an expression does not signify as a simple assertion I have explained in the commentary on *Perihermenias* (*On Interpretation*). What an assertion and a negation are will be explained shortly.

There are five species of discourse in the narrowest division:

- interrogative, as “Do you think that the soul is immortal?”
- imperative, as “Take the book.”
- optative or supplicatory, as “May God bring it to pass.”
- vocative, as “Be present, O God.”
- enunciative, as “Socrates walks.”

In the first four there is neither truth nor falsity. Only the enunciative contains either truth or falsity. From it propositions arise.

An enunciation is divided into two parts: affirmation and negation. An affirmation is an enunciation of something concerning something. A negation is an enunciation of something away from something.

An affirmation is, for example, “Plato is a philosopher.” A negation is, “Plato is not a philosopher.” The affirmation asserts some philosophy of Plato—that is, it states that Plato is a philosopher. The negation, by enunciating some philosophy away from Plato, removes it; that is, it states that Plato is not a philosopher.

Of enunciative discourses, some are simple and others non-simple. Simple ones are, for example, “It is day” and “There is light.” Non-simple ones are, for example, “If it is day, there is light.” [Col. 0797D]

Simple affirmations and negations are some universal, some particular, and some indefinite. Universal propositions either affirm everything, as “Every human is an animal,” or deny everything, as “No human is an animal.” Particular propositions affirm or deny some individual, as “Some human is an animal” and “Some human is not an animal.” Indefinite propositions neither affirm nor deny universally or particularly, as “A human is an animal” and “A human is not an animal.”

A simple proposition is divided into two parts: subject and predicate. For example, in “A human is an animal,” “human” is the subject, while “animal” is predicated of the human. These parts are called terms. [Col. 0798A]

We define them as follows: terms are the parts of a simple proposition into which the proposition is divided primarily.

There is also a secondary division of a universal simple proposition. Thus, in the proposition “Every human is an animal,” “every human” is one term, and “is an animal” is the other. But this is a secondary division, whereas the other is primary. For the primary terms are the subject and the predicate.

“Is” and “is not” are no more terms than they are indicators of affirmation or negation; and “every,” “no,” and “some” are no more terms than they are indicators of whether something has been stated particularly or universally.

A proposition is therefore divided, as has been said, into that which is the subject and that which is predicated. By “subject” I mean “human” in the proposition “Every human is an animal”; by “that which is predicated” I mean “animal.” Whatever is predicated either exceeds and is more extensive than the subject, or is equal to it. A predicate is never found to be less extensive than its subject.

Let us demonstrate what we have said by different examples. The predicate exceeds the subject whenever some genus is predicated of something, as when one says, “Every human is an animal.” You cannot convert this and say, “Every animal is a human,” because animal is more extensive than human and exceeds it.

The predicate is equal to the subject whenever a property is predicated of something, as “Every human is capable of laughter.” You can convert this and say, “Everything capable of laughter is human.” But it cannot happen that what is predicated is less extensive.

The predicate is also said to precede, while the subject follows. For predication is better suited to constitute a proposition than is the subject. [Col. 0798C]

Some simple propositions have no term in common, such as “Every human is an animal” and “Virtue is good,” and propositions of this kind. Others do have terms in common. Of those that share terms, some share terms in both positions, while some share a term in only one position. Those that share one term do so in three ways; those that share both terms do so in two ways.

Let us therefore show by examples how propositions share one term in three ways. A term is common when it is the subject in one proposition and the predicate in another, as in “Every human is an animal” and “Every animal is animate.” In the first proposition animal is predicated of human; in the second, animal is the subject of “animate.” This is the first mode among those that share one term.

The second mode is when the common term is predicated in both propositions, as when someone says, “Every snow is white” and “Every pearl is white.” In both the first and the second proposition, “white” is predicated: in the first of snow, and in the second of pearl. This is the second mode among those sharing one term.

The third mode is whenever the common term is the subject in both propositions, as in “Virtue is good” and “Virtue is just.” In both propositions virtue is the subject, once in relation to “just” and once in relation to “good.” [Col. 0798D]

Thus propositions share one term in these three ways: either the common term is predicated in one and is the subject in the other; or it is predicated in both; or it is the subject in both.

Those that share both terms have two modes. Some preserve the same order, while others involve an exchange of order.

Those preserving the same order are propositions that assert or deny the same thing of the same thing, either universally or particularly. Universally: “Every pleasure is good,” and “No pleasure is good.” Again, particularly: “Some pleasure is good,” and “Some pleasure is not good.”

Those involving an exchange of order occur whenever the term that is subject in one proposition is predicate in the other, as in “Every good is just” and “Everything just is good.” In the first proposition good is the subject and just the predicate; in the second, just is the subject and good the predicate. [Col. 0799A]

Now, since some propositions preserve the same order and others exchange the order, we shall first speak of those that share both terms in the same order.

Since propositions are affirmative, negative, universal, particular, or indefinite, two of these differences concern quality and three concern quantity. Those differing in quality are affirmative and negative; those differing in quantity are universal, particular, and indefinite.

Affirmative and negative propositions show what a thing is or is not. Universal, particular, and indefinite propositions indicate the quantity of all, none, or some.

From these five differences—that is, universal, particular, indefinite, affirmative, and negative—six combinations arise, since each of the three differences belonging to quantity is joined to each of the two belonging to quality.

Thus there are:

- universal affirmative and universal negative: “Every human is just”; “No human is just”;
- particular affirmative and particular negative: “Some human is just”; “Some human is not just”;
- indefinite affirmative and indefinite negative: “A human is just”; “A human is not just.”

Thus six combinations arise from joining the two differences of quality to the three differences of quantity. Let us set aside the indefinite affirmatives and negatives and let the discussion concern only universals and particulars.

Let two universal propositions belonging to those propositions that share both terms in the same order be written below: one affirmative and the other negative. Let the universal affirmative be “Every human is just,” and let the universal negative opposing it be “No human is just.” [Col. 0799D]

Let a particular affirmation and a particular negation be placed beneath these, so that the particular affirmative is placed beneath the universal affirmative and the particular negative beneath the universal negative. Let the particular affirmative be “Some human is just,” and the particular negative opposing it be “Some human is not just.” The following diagram demonstrates this.

[Col. 0800A]

[Col. 0800B] In the foregoing diagram, therefore, the universal affirmative and the universal negative are contraries; the particular affirmative and the particular negative are subcontraries; and the universal affirmative and the particular affirmative, as well as the universal negative and the particular negative, are called subalterns. Diagonally opposed propositions are those at the angles, namely the universal affirmative and the particular negative, and likewise the universal negative and the particular affirmative: “Every human being is just,” “Some human being is not just”; “No human being is just,” “Some human being is just.” They may be defined in the following way.

Contraries are propositions in which one universally affirms of the same thing what the other denies. Subcontraries are propositions in which one particularly affirms of the same thing what the other denies. Subalterns are propositions in which both affirm or deny the same thing, one particularly and the other universally. Contradictories occur when one affirms of the same thing what the other denies, or one denies what the other affirms, the one generally and the other particularly. They are called contraries because what the universal affirmation posits, the universal negation removes. They are called subalterns because what the one posits universally, the other also posits particularly.

They are called subcontraries either because they are naturally placed beneath the contraries themselves, as the diagram shows, or because they differ from the contraries and are in a certain way contrary to them. For it is impossible for both contraries to be true at the same time, but it is possible for both to be wholly false; subcontraries possess the opposite force. For it is impossible for both subcontraries to be wholly false, whereas it is possible for both to be true at the same time, as will be explained more fully below.

They are called diagonally opposed because the universal affirmation or negation faces the particular affirmation or negation at an angle. Since each proposition has two differences, one according to quality and the other according to quantity—for example, a universal affirmative differs in quantity because it is universal, and in quality because it is affirmative—the other propositions likewise have two differences, one according to quality and the other according to quantity.

Subaltern propositions differ in only one respect, namely quantity: one is particular and the other universal. They retain no difference in quality, for both are affirmatives. The other propositions, namely contraries and subcontraries, differ in quality, because one is affirmative and the other negative; they do not differ in quantity, for both contraries are universals, and both subcontraries are particulars. Those called contradictories differ in both respects: one is a universal affirmation and the other a particular negation, while one is a universal negation and the other a particular affirmation.

Now that we have explained how they differ according to quality and quantity, let us explain their properties with respect to truth and falsity.

Of subaltern propositions, then, if the universal affirmative is true, the particular affirmative will also be true. For if “Every human being is just” is true, the proposition “Some human being is just” will also be true. For if every human being is just, then some are just as well.

The same applies to negative subalterns. If the universal negative is true, the particular negative will also be true. Thus, if “No human being is just” is true, “Some human being is not just” will also be true. For if no human being is just, then neither is some human being.

The converse, however, does not hold. If the particular is true, it does not necessarily follow that the universal is true. Thus, if “Some human being is just” is true, it does not necessarily follow that “Every human being is just” is true, since it is possible that not everyone is just. The same applies to the negative. If the particular negative “Some human being is not just” is true, it does not necessarily follow that the universal negative “No human being is just” is true, since it is possible that some are just.

Let us therefore state the rule concerning subaltern propositions: if the universals are true, the particulars must be true; but the converse does not hold. If the particulars are true, it does not necessarily follow that the universals are true.

Particulars, however, have the converse relation to universals with respect to falsity. As stated above, if the universals are true, the particulars are also true; and if the particulars are true, the universals are not necessarily true. But if the particulars are false, the universals will also be false. For if the particular “Some human being is just” is false, the universal “Every human being is just” will also be false. If “Some human being is just” is false, “No human being is just” is true; and if “No human being is just” is true, “Every human being is just” is false. Thus, when the particular is false, the universal is false.

Likewise, if the particular negative “Some human being is not just” is false, the universal negative “No human being is just” will also be false. For if it is false that some human being is not just, it is true that every human being is just; and if this is true, “No human being is just” is false. Therefore, when the particular is false, the universal is also false.

The converse does not hold: if the universals are false, the particulars do not necessarily have to be false. For if the universal “Every human being is just” is false, it does not necessarily follow that the particular “Some human being is just” is false. It may be that, although not every human being is just, some are just. Likewise, if the universal negative “No human being is just” is false, it does not necessarily follow that “Some human being is not just” is false. For if “No human being is just” is false, it is true that some are just; and it is also true that some are not just.

Returning, then, to the beginning, let us state what applies to subalterns: if the universals are true, the particulars are also true, but the converse does not hold. Likewise, if the particulars are false, the universals are also false, but the converse does not hold.

Contraries can never both be true. Sometimes, however, both may be false; at other times, one may be true and the other false. Both are false if someone says, “Every human being is a grammarian,” for this is false because not everyone is a grammarian, and “No human being is a grammarian,” which is false because not no one is a grammarian.

One is true and the other false if someone says, “Every human being is two-footed”: this affirmative is true, while “No human being is two-footed,” the negative, is false. Likewise, “Every human being is four-footed” is false, while “No human being is four-footed” is true.

Contraries, therefore, are sometimes both false and sometimes divide truth and falsity between them; but they can never both be true.

Subcontraries undergo the opposite condition. They can never be found both false, but sometimes both are true. Thus, “Some human being is a grammarian” is true, and “Some human being is not a grammarian” is also true, since one person may be a grammarian and another may not be.

At other times one is true and the other false. The affirmative “Some human being is two-footed” is true, while the negative “Some human being is not two-footed” is false. Likewise, the affirmative “Some human being is four-footed” is false, while the negative “Some human being is not four-footed” is true. It is never possible, however, for both to be false.

It remains for us to speak of diagonally opposed propositions. These can neither both be false at any time nor both be true; one is always true and the other false. This becomes clearer if one constructs whatever examples one wishes.

The subject also prompts us to consider certain indefinite propositions. Indefinite propositions have the same force as particular propositions. For it was said that if universal affirmatives or negatives are true in subaltern propositions, the particulars are also true. We now say that if universal propositions are true, the indefinites are also true.

If “Every human being is two-footed” is true, then “Some human being is two-footed” is true, and the indefinite proposition “A human being is two-footed” is also true. It was likewise said that if the particulars are false, the universals are also false. We must now add that if an indefinite proposition is false, the universal will also be false. If “A human being is four-footed” is false, then “Some human being is four-footed” and “Every human being is four-footed” will also be false. The same appears to apply to negatives.

It is therefore clear that all indefinites contain the same force as particular propositions.

It was also stated that subcontraries, which are particular affirmatives and negatives, can be true together; that they can divide truth and falsity between them; but that they cannot both be false. The same should be expected of indefinite propositions. They divide truth and falsity between them: if someone says, “A human being is two-footed,” this is true, while “A human being is not two-footed” is false. Likewise, “A human being is four-footed” is false, while “A human being is not four-footed” is true.

They can also both be true. If someone says, “A human being is a grammarian,” speaking of Donatus, this is true. Likewise, if someone says, “A human being is not a grammarian,” speaking of Cato, this is true. Thus we shall never find them both false. This too shows that indefinites are equal in power to particulars.

Furthermore, it was stated that diagonally opposed propositions—that is, the universal affirmative and the particular negative, and likewise the universal negative and the particular affirmative—cannot be true together or false together, but divide truth and falsity between them. The same applies to indefinites. The universal affirmative and the indefinite negative, or the universal negative and the indefinite affirmative, can neither be true together nor false together. They divide truth and falsity between them. If you say, “Every human being is two-footed,” this is true; if you say, “A human being is not two-footed,” this is false. Likewise, if you say, “A human being is four-footed,” this is false; if you say, “No human being is four-footed,” this is true. From this also it can be gathered that all indefinites are equal in power and force to particulars.

There are also certain propositions that themselves divide truth and falsity, such as “God thunders” and “God does not thunder.” But they divide truth and falsity between them only when the time, the subject, and the predicate are the same.

What I mean is this: if the subject is equivocal, they do not divide truth and falsity between them. If someone says, “Cato killed himself at Utica,” and it is answered, “Cato did not kill himself at Utica,” both may be true. For Cato the Younger killed himself, whereas Cato the Elder, the Censor, did not kill himself at Utica. This happens because the name “Cato” is used equivocally: it refers both to Cato the Elder, the Censor, and to Cato the Younger of Utica.

Likewise, if the predicate in a proposition is equivocal, the affirmation and negation do not divide truth and falsity between them. If someone says, “It shines at night,” and it is answered, “It does not shine at night,” both may be true. For a lamp can shine at night, whereas the sun cannot shine at night. This occurs because “to shine” is used equivocally of the light of a lamp and of the light of the sun.

Moreover, if the time expressed in the subject and predicate is different, the affirmation and negation do not divide truth and falsity between them. If someone says, “Socrates is walking,” and it is answered, “Socrates is not walking,” both may be true. For Socrates may walk at one time and not walk at another; he may instead be standing, sitting, or doing something else.

In propositions of this kind—“Socrates is walking,” “Socrates is not walking”—those propositions divide truth and falsity between them that are asserted of the same subject, with respect to the same predicate and the same time.

There are also propositions called contradictories. They are of the following kind: whenever a particular negation removes a universal affirmation: “Every human being is just,” “Not every human being is just”; and again, “No human being is just,” “Some human being is just.” In these, the universal determination is removed. But we shall discuss them elsewhere.

Since we have spoken of propositions that participate in the same order, let us now speak of those that participate through a change of order.

There are two modes among propositions that participate through a change of order. One is conversion by contraposition, as when one says, “Every human being is an animal; everything that is not an animal is not a human being.” The other is simple conversion, as when one says, “Every human being is capable of laughter,” and converts it to “Everything capable of laughter is a human being.”

In these cases, a conversion is produced merely by exchanging the terms when neither the predicate exceeds the subject nor the subject exceeds the predicate. In the proposition “Every human being is capable of laughter,” “human being” is the subject and “capable of laughter” the predicate; they have equal force. Therefore it can be converted so that “capable of laughter” is the subject and “human being” the predicate: “Everything capable of laughter is a human being.”

But where one term exceeds the other, the proposition cannot be converted. If one says, “Every human being is an animal,” this is true; nevertheless, when the terms are exchanged, the converted proposition cannot be true, for it is false to say, “Every animal is a human being.” This occurs because “animal” exceeds “human being.”

Conversion by contraposition is performed in the following way. Whenever the subject occurs in an affirmative proposition, it is changed and made the predicate of a negative proposition, while the predicate is made the subject. Thus, in “Every human being is an animal,” “human being” is the subject and “animal” is predicated of it. If someone converts it by contraposition, making “animal” the subject and “human being” the predicate, a negative particle is added to “human being,” producing: “Everything that is not an animal is not a human being.” The conversion is therefore:

“Every human being is an animal; everything that is not an animal is not a human being.”

But we shall discuss these matters later. For now, let us return to simple conversions.

Of the four propositions, two are universal—an affirmative and a negative—and two are particular—an affirmative and a negative. The particular affirmative and the universal negative convert into themselves when their terms are exchanged.

As stated, propositions convert when, after the terms have been exchanged, they are either both true or both false. If someone says, “Some human being is an animal,” this is true. Its conversion, “Some animal is a human being,” is also true. Likewise, “Some human being is a stone” is false, as is its conversion, “Some stone is a human being,” for this too is false.

The particular affirmative, therefore, converts into itself when the terms are exchanged.

The universal negative undergoes the same condition. If someone says, “No human being is a stone,” this is true, and it can be converted to “No stone is a human being,” which is also true. Likewise, “No human being is an orator” is false, and its conversion, “No orator is a human being,” is also false.

Of these four propositions, therefore, only the two diagonally opposed propositions convert into themselves: the particular affirmative and the universal negative. The other two do not convert into themselves. Neither the universal affirmative nor the particular negative converts into itself.

If someone says, “Every human being is an animal,” this is true. But if it is converted to “Every animal is a human being,” it is false. It cannot therefore convert into itself, since the converted proposition does not preserve the truth of the original.

Nor does the particular negative convert into itself. If someone says, “Some human being is not a grammarian,” this is true; but if it is converted to “Some grammarian is not a human being,” it is false, for every grammarian is a human being.

Let us repeat from the beginning: there are four propositions—the universal affirmation, the universal negation, the particular affirmation, and the particular negation. The particular affirmation and the universal negation, which are diagonally opposed, can convert into themselves. The universal affirmation and the particular negation, which are themselves diagonally opposed, can never convert into themselves.

Nor should it trouble us that certain universal affirmations and certain particular negations can be converted. One can say, “Every human being is capable of laughter,” and “Everything capable of laughter is a human being,” and both are true. Likewise, “Every human being is capable of neighing” is false, and “Everything capable of neighing is a human being” is also false.

Similarly, in the case of the particular negative, “Some human being is not a stone” is true, and “Some stone is not a human being” is also true. Again, “Some human being is not capable of laughter” is false; “Something capable of laughter is not a human being” is also false.

Universal affirmations and particular negations therefore appear capable of conversion, and they are converted—but not universally. By “universally,” I mean that propositions can be converted in every case.

These propositions can be converted in only two kinds of matter. If someone predicates the property of a species of the species to which it belongs, treating that species as the subject, conversion is possible. Since the capacity for laughter is a property of the human being, if one predicates “capable of laughter” and makes “human being” the subject, as in “Every human being is capable of laughter,” one can again make “capable of laughter” the subject and predicate “human being,” saying, “Everything capable of laughter is a human being.”

Universal affirmative conversions are simultaneously false in those cases where what is predicated cannot at any time truly be said of the subject. If someone says, “Every human being is a stone,” this is false. Again, “Every stone is a human being” is false, because at no time will “human being” truly be predicated of “stone,” nor “stone” of “human being.”

The opposite applies to particular negatives. They are false when they predicate a property, whether the property is made the subject or the predicate. If someone says, “Some human being is not capable of laughter,” this is false. Likewise, “Something capable of laughter is not a human being” is also false.

They are true when they predicate of the subject something that cannot at any time truly be affirmed of it. Thus, if one says, “Some human being is not a stone,” this is true. Again, “Some stone is not a human being” is true.

Universal affirmations, therefore, convert into themselves as true when they predicate a property; and they convert into themselves as false when they predicate something that can at no time be truly said of the subject. Particular negatives, likewise, are false when they predicate a property and true when they predicate something that can at no time be truly said of the subject.

Only in these cases can they be converted. In other cases they cannot be converted. Hence they do not convert universally. It remains, therefore, that in all other matters, as stated above, they do not convert.

It must also be understood that the particular affirmative, which converts into itself, can convert accidentally with the universal affirmative, which does not convert into itself. Likewise, the particular negative diagonally opposed to the universal affirmative, although it does not convert into itself, can convert accidentally with the universal negative, which does convert into itself.

We have shown how the particular affirmative and the universal negative convert into themselves. We must now demonstrate how the particular affirmative converts accidentally with the universal affirmative, and how the particular negative converts accidentally with the universal negative.

It was said above that if the universal affirmative is true, the particular affirmative is also true, and the particular follows from the universal. If “Every human being is an animal” is true, then “Some human being is an animal” is also true. For if every human being is an animal, then some human being is an animal.

But the particular affirmative converts into itself; therefore it also converts with the universal affirmative. If “Every human being is an animal,” then “Some human being is an animal.” The latter converts into itself in the following way: “Some human being is an animal”; therefore it may be converted to “Some animal is a human being.” Both propositions are true: “Every human being is an animal” and “Some animal is a human being.”

The particular affirmative is said to convert accidentally with the universal affirmative because it converts primarily with itself and only secondarily with the universal affirmative.

It remains to show how the particular negative, which does not convert into itself, converts accidentally with the universal negative, which does convert into itself. The reasoning is the same. Since, if the universal negative is true, the particular negative is also true, and since the universal negative converts into itself, the particular negative can convert with the converted universal negative.

Take the universal negative “No human being is capable of neighing” and convert it to “Nothing capable of neighing is a human being.” This proposition, the universal negative “No human being is capable of neighing,” entails the particular negative “Some human being is not capable of neighing.”

Now convert the universal “No human being is capable of neighing” to “Nothing capable of neighing is a human being.” Convert its particular negative, “Some human being is not capable of neighing,” to “Something capable of neighing is not a human being.” Both are true. “Nothing capable of neighing is a human being,” which is the converted universal negative, is true; and “Something capable of neighing is not a human being,” which is the conversion of the particular negative, is also true.

Why this is called accidental conversion was explained above.

The nature of accidental conversion is therefore clear. Whatever applies to the universal affirmative also applies to its diagonally opposed particular negative, for neither converts into itself. Whatever applies to the universal negative also applies to its diagonally opposed particular affirmative, for both can convert into themselves.

When propositions that can convert into themselves are joined to those that cannot, so that each proposition capable of self-conversion is joined to one incapable of it, and each incapable of self-conversion is joined to one capable of it, they produce the accidental conversions demonstrated above.

It remains to speak of conversions made by contraposition. First, their arrangement should be set out in the following diagram:

The contraposed conversion of the universal affirmative “Every human being is an animal” is “Everything that is not an animal is not a human being.”

The contraposed conversion of the universal negative “No human being is an animal” is “Nothing that is not an animal is not a human being.”

The contraposed conversion of the particular affirmative “Some human being is an animal” is “Something that is not an animal is not a human being.”

The contraposed conversion of the particular negative “Some human being is not an animal” is “Something that is not an animal is not not a human being.”

This is shown by the following diagram:

“Every human being is an animal” — “Everything that is not an animal is not a human being”

“No human being is an animal” — “Nothing that is not an animal is not a human being”

“Some human being is an animal” — “Something that is not an animal is not a human being”

“Some human being is not an animal” — “Something that is not an animal is not not a human being”

[Col. 0807B] With these propositions set out, the situation in contraposed conversions is the opposite of what was stated above concerning simple conversion of terms. In simple conversion, the particular affirmative and the universal negative convert into themselves, whereas the universal affirmative and the particular negative do not. In contraposed conversions, by contrast, the universal affirmative converts into itself by contraposition, and the particular negative also converts into itself. The universal negative and the particular affirmative do not convert into themselves by contraposition.

We shall prove this by examples. If the universal affirmative “Every human being is an animal” is true, its contraposed conversion “Everything that is not an animal is not a human being” will also be true. For whatever is not an animal is not a human being.

If the universal affirmative “Every animal is a human being” is false, its contraposed conversion “Everything that is not a human being is not an animal” will also be false. For it may be that something which is not a human being is nevertheless an animal. The latter proposition denies that anything which is not a human being is an animal.

Since, when the universal affirmative is true, its contraposed conversion is true, and when the universal affirmative is false, its contraposed conversion is false, there is no doubt that the universal affirmative can convert into itself.

We must now show how the particular negative converts into itself by contraposition. If the proposition “Some human being is not an animal” is false, its contraposed conversion “Something that is not an animal is not a human being” will also be false.

This proposition appears to say the same as: “There is something which is not an animal and is a human being.” For whoever says “not not a human being” signifies that what is not an animal is a human being. But this is plainly false, since every human being is an animal.

If the particular negative “Some animal is not a human being” is true, its contraposed conversion “Something that is not a human being is not an animal” will also be true. This is equivalent to saying: “A thing which is not a human being is not a non-animal, but is an animal.” Thus a horse and an ox are not human beings, yet they are not non-animals.

Therefore, if whenever the particular negative is false its contraposed conversion is also false, and whenever the particular negative is true its contraposed conversion is true, there is no doubt that the particular negative can convert into itself by contraposition. [Col. 0808B]

Now that we have shown that the universal affirmative and the particular negative can convert into themselves by contraposition, let us show that the universal negative and the particular affirmative cannot.

First, concerning the universal negative: if the universal negative is true, it does not necessarily follow that its contraposed conversion is true. But if it is false, its contraposed conversion must be false.

If “No human being is an animal” is false, its contraposed conversion “Nothing that is not an animal is not a human being” may perhaps be false. This is equivalent to saying: “There is nothing which is not an animal and is not a human being,” which amounts to saying that everything which does not possess animal life is a human being. This is plainly false.

Likewise, if the universal negative “No human being is a stone” is true, its contraposed conversion “Nothing that is not a stone is not a human being” will be false. This is equivalent to saying: “There is nothing which, although it is not a stone, is not a human being,” which amounts to saying that every thing whatsoever that is not a stone is a human being. This is false. For you will find innumerable things that are not stones and are not human beings.

Therefore, since if the universal negative is false its contraposed conversion is false, and if the same universal negative is true its contraposed conversion is also false, there is no doubt that the universal negative cannot convert into itself. What fails in one case cannot be established as a general rule.

It remains to show that the particular affirmative cannot convert into itself by contraposition. When the particular affirmative is true, its contraposed conversion will also be true. If “Some human being is an animal” is true, its contraposed conversion “Something that is not an animal is not a human being” is true. This is equivalent to saying: “There is something which does not possess animal life and is not a human being,” which is true. A stone does not possess animal life and nevertheless is not a human being.

Likewise, if the particular affirmative “Some stone is a human being” is false, its contraposed conversion “Something that is not a human being is not a stone” will be true. This is equivalent to saying: “There is something which, although it is not a human being, is not a stone,” which is true. A horse is not a human being and nevertheless is not a stone.

Therefore, since in some cases, when the particular affirmative is true, its contraposed conversion is true, and since in some cases, when the particular affirmative is false, its contraposed conversion is true, there is no doubt that particular affirmatives cannot convert into themselves by contraposition.

The universal negative and the particular affirmative, which are diagonally opposed, undergo opposite conditions in contraposed conversions. In the case of universal negatives, whether the universal negative is true or false, the contraposed conversions are always false. In the case of particular affirmatives, whether the particular affirmative is true or false, its contraposed conversion is true.

[Col. 0810A] We must therefore return to what was stated above and confirm it. In simple conversions of terms, the particular affirmative and the universal negative can convert into themselves. The universal affirmative and the particular negative cannot convert into themselves.

In conversions made by contraposition, the situation is the opposite. The universal affirmative and the particular negative can convert into themselves by contraposition; the universal negative and the particular affirmative cannot convert into themselves by contraposition. The universal negative and the particular affirmative, which are diagonally opposed with respect to the distinction of truth and falsity, undergo opposite conditions in relation to one another, as has been demonstrated.

Let this suffice concerning the categorical propositions of categorical syllogisms. If anything has been omitted here, it has been treated more carefully and precisely in the commentary on Aristotle’s *Perihermenias*.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0809]

The preceding series of the volume explained what pertains to the propositions of categorical syllogisms. Now, insofar as the measured scope of an introduction permits, we shall discuss the structure of categorical syllogisms themselves. Since the strength or weakness of every composite thing is found chiefly either in the elements of which it is composed or in the good or bad composition by which its praise or blame is determined—for if a house is built of strong or weak stones, it too is strong or weak; moreover, if its construction has received an even and skillful arrangement from the builder, the structure itself will rightly be a praiseworthy foundation of stability, whereas if its composition is less skillful, the entire structure, although arranged from good stones, will totter in its stability, unable to maintain itself—we too, following this same image, first explained the elements of which the syllogism itself consists, namely, propositions. Now, however, we shall discuss the connection and composition of syllogisms with one another.

You must remember that here I have undertaken to teach what is being introduced, not what has already been introduced. First I shall briefly show what it means for something to be “in every” thing or “not to be in every” thing. For if one thing is the genus of another, it will contain every species within itself [Col. 0809D], and the species is said to be in the whole of that genus. Let the genus be “animal” and the species “man.” Since man is less than animal, man is said to be in the whole of animal. For every man is an animal.

If someone therefore says that one thing is predicated of every other thing, the converse makes no difference. For just as man is in the whole of animal, so too animal is predicated of every man. To be “not in the whole,” however, occurs whenever one thing is entirely disjoined from another; for example, if you say, “Animal is in no stone,” since no animal is a stone; and if you say, “Animal is predicated of no stone,” since animal is said of no stone.

We therefore define “to be in the whole,” or “to be predicated of every,” as follows: something is said to be in the whole, or to be predicated of every, whenever nothing belonging to the subject can be found of which what is predicated cannot be said. For no man can be found of whom animal cannot be said. “Not to be in the whole,” or “to be predicated of none,” is said to occur whenever nothing belonging to the subject can be found of which what is predicated can be said. For nothing belonging to stone can be found of which animal can be predicated.

It should also be noted that “to be in the whole” is expressed conversely. For if something is predicated of every member of something, that of which it is predicated is said to be in the whole of what is predicated—for example, animal is said of every man. Man, however, is in the whole, that is, as a kind of part hidden within the whole animal. And if something is in every member of another thing, that thing of which it was said above to be in it is said to be in that whole; for example, the same animal, since it is in every man and is predicated of every one of them, has man in its whole: man is in the whole of animal.

With these points established, whenever we arrange letters in place of terms, we do so for the sake of brevity and concision: what we wish to demonstrate by means of the letters, we demonstrate universally. For perhaps, in some actual terms, it may be necessary to introduce something false. With letters, however, we never go astray, since we use them as though we were positing terms. In the letters themselves, unless the connection of the terms is sound and effective in itself, neither truth nor falsity will be found.

Whenever, therefore, we wish to show that one thing is predicated of every member of another, we set it out as follows. Let the first term be *a*, the second *b*, and let *a* be predicated of every *b*. Understand this as though we had taken *a* to mean “animal” and *b* to mean “man.” The same applies to negative propositions. For if we say, “*a* is predicated of no *b*,” this is equivalent to saying, “*a*, which is animal, is predicated of no stone,” where stone is *b*, and likewise with any similar cases.

Every simple syllogism is demonstrated and concluded through three terms. But first let us examine the figures of the syllogisms, and afterward discuss their modes and arrangements.

When three terms are so posited that they are near and connected with one another, there must be no more than three combinations, as follows. Let there be *a*, *b*, and *c*. Either *a* will be predicated of *b* and *b* of *c*; or *a* will be predicated both of *b* and of *c*; or these same terms *a* and *b* will be predicated of the term *c*.

Let *a* be “good,” *b* “just,” and *c* “virtue.” Either *a*, that is, good, will be in every *b*, that is, in every just thing, and it will be said, “Every just thing is good”; and likewise *b*, just, will be in every *c*, that is, in every virtue, and it will be said, “Every virtue is just.” The propositions will therefore be of this kind: “Every just thing is good,” and “Every virtue is just.”

Or *a*, that is, good, will be predicated of *b*, which is just, and of *c*, which is virtue, so that we have: “Every just thing is good,” and “Every virtue is good.”

Or else *a*, good, will underlie *b*, just, and *c*, virtue, so that we say: “Everything good is just,” and “Everything good is virtue” [Col. 0811B]. In this combination, *b* and *c* are predicated of the single term *a*.

Where *a* is predicated of every *b*, and *b* likewise of every *c*, I call this the first figure. It is defined as follows: the first figure is that in which the term that is subject is predicated of another. For *b*, which is subject to term *a*, is likewise predicated of term *c*.

The extremes of this figure I call the predicate and the subject, namely *a* and *c*. For *a* is predicated of term *b*, while term *c* is subject to term *b*. I call the middle that which is subject to one term and predicated of another, namely *b*. For term *b* is subject to term *a* and is predicated of term *c*.

The major extreme is that which is predicated first, namely *a*, since *a* is predicated of term *b*. The minor is that which is subject to the middle term, namely *c*, since term *c* is subject to the middle term *b*; for the middle term *b* is said of it. Term *a* is called the major term, that is, the term which is predicated, because every predicate is greater than that of which it is predicated.

In the conclusion, as in the first proposition, term *a* is always predicated. For *a*, good, is predicated of *b*, just, and we say, “Every just thing is good”; while the middle term *b* is predicated of *c*, and we say, “Every virtue is just.” From these the syllogism concludes: “Every virtue is good.” Thus *a*, good, is named of *c*, virtue, and for that reason we call *a* the major extreme.

We must also remember that things which are equal can be reversed and predicated of one another. Just as what is predicated is in the subject as a whole, so conversely what was subject will be in the former predicate as a whole. If *f* and *g* are two terms equal to one another, so that neither is greater than the other, then when you predicate *f* of every *g*, term *f* will be in every term *g*. But if you reverse them and predicate term *g* of term *f*, then again term *g* will be in every term *f*.

Let *f* be “capable of laughter” and *g* “man.” If, therefore, you predicate *f*, capable of laughter, and make *g*, man, the subject, *f* will be found in every *g*. For every man is capable of laughter. But if you predicate *g*, man, of *f*, capable of laughter, *g*, man, will be found in every *f*, capable of laughter. For everything capable of laughter is a man.

What terms are, and what predication or subjection is, was sufficiently explained in the preceding book on propositions. But lest we go wrong concerning what appears to be the converse of a universal affirmative—for this too was discussed above—we now wish only to show that only equal things in the whole are convertible. This is useful for the demonstration of syllogisms that proceeds in a circle, which we discussed in the *Analytics*.

This completes the first figure of categorical syllogisms.

The second figure occurs whenever term *a* is predicated of both terms *b* and *c*, as follows. If you say that *a*, good, is predicated of every *b*, just, so that the proposition is “Every just thing is good,” and then that *a*, good, is predicated of every *c*, virtue, so that you say, “Every virtue is good,” you have predicated only *a* of both terms *b* and *c*, and this will be the second figure.

The middle term in this figure is that which is predicated of both, namely *a*. The extremes are those which are subjects, namely *b* and *c*. The major extreme is that of which term *a* is first predicated, namely *b*, just; or, if it is first predicated of *c*, term *c* is found to be the major extreme. This is because the extreme of which the middle term is first predicated will itself be predicated in the conclusion, as will be demonstrated later. The minor extreme will be that to which the middle term is predicated later.

The third figure occurs whenever terms *a* and *b* are both predicated of one term *c*. If someone predicates *a*, that is, good, of *c*, that is, virtue, so that the proposition is “Every virtue is good,” and likewise predicates *b* of *c*, so that it is “Every virtue is just,” he produces the third figure.

In this figure the middle term is that which is subject to both, namely *c*. For terms *a* and *b* are predicated of term *c*. The major extreme is that which is predicated first, namely *a*; the minor is that which is predicated afterward, namely *b*. Or, if someone prefers to predicate *b* first and *a* afterward, the major or minor extreme will be determined according to the earlier or later predication. Here too, as in the other figures above, the major extreme is predicated of the minor in the conclusions.

Having explained the three figures of syllogisms, we must say that a perfect syllogism is one in which nothing is lacking for a complete and demonstrated conclusion from what has been taken and proposed above. A conclusion formed in the proper mode and order, lacking nothing, is completed through what it previously proposed.

An imperfect syllogism is one to which nothing is lacking for a complete conclusion, but in which, among the things taken in the propositions, something is missing by which it may be evident why the conclusion is so. These definitions, however, will all become clear later.

Now we must briefly explain how these figures arise. For from the same source from which they arise, they are again resolved. The second and third figures appear to arise and be generated from the first.

Let term *a* be in every term *b*, and let it be predicated of every such term; let term *b* likewise be predicated of every term *c*. This, as has been said, is the first figure of syllogisms.

If someone reverses the major extreme and proposition, making what was previously predicated into the subject, he will produce the second figure. For just as term *a* is predicated of term *b*, so *b* is predicated of *c*.
