If, therefore, it is reversed so that term *b* is predicated of term *a*, term *b*, which had previously been the middle term and subject to term *a*, is found to be predicated of term *c* and thus to be predicated of both terms.

Since *a*, good, was predicated of *b*, just, and *b*, just, was predicated of *c*, virtue, the propositions were: “Every just thing is good,” and “Every virtue is just.” If the first proposition, “Every just thing is good,” is reversed while “Every virtue is just” remains, it becomes “Everything good is just.” The propositions are therefore: “Everything good is just,” and “Every virtue is just”; and “just,” that is, *b*, is predicated of terms *a* and *c*. Thus, by reversing the major extreme of the first figure, the second figure of syllogisms is generated.

The third figure arises when the minor proposition is reversed. For if *a*, good, is predicated of *b*, just, so that we say, “Every just thing is good,” and *b*, just, is predicated of *c*, virtue, so that we say, “Every virtue is just,” then, if the first proposition remains unchanged and the second, “Every virtue is just,” is reversed to become “Every just thing is virtue,” all the propositions will be as follows: “Every just thing is good,” and “Every just thing is virtue.” Terms *a* and *c* are then predicated of *b*, just, and the connection of the third figure is produced.

Thus, by reversing the first and later extremes of the first figure, the third or second figure arises.

Each of these three figures, however, contains several modes of syllogisms, so that the modes stand under the figures as species stand under their genera. According to Aristotle, the first figure has four modes; Theophrastus and Eudemus add five further modes to these four, following Aristotle’s beginning in the second book of the *Prior Analytics*. This will be explained more fully later.

The second figure has four modes; the third, according to Aristotle, has six. Others add one more, as does Porphyry, following the authorities mentioned above.

Since, as was said in the preceding book, some propositions are affirmative and others negative, and among each of these some are universal and others particular, the propositions and conclusions of syllogisms are joined according to these distinctions.

The first mode of the first figure is formed from two universal affirmatives and yields a universal affirmative. If term *a* is in every term *b*, and term *b* is predicated of every term *c*, term *a* will be predicated of every term *c*. For if *a*, good, is predicated of every *b*, just, so that we have “Every just thing is good,” and *b*, just, is predicated of *c*, virtue, so that we have “Every virtue is just,” it necessarily follows that the extremes are predicated of one another, namely *a* and *c*, so that we have “Every virtue is good.”

The propositions and conclusion are therefore of this kind: if *a* is in every *b*, and *b* is in every *c*, term *a* will be predicated of every *c*. That is: “Every just thing is good”; “Every virtue is just”; and the conclusion: “Therefore every virtue is good.” This is the first mode of the first figure.

The second mode of the first figure occurs whenever a universal conclusion by negation is drawn from a first universal negative and a second universal affirmative. Let *a* be “evil,” *b* “good,” and *c* “just.” Term *a* is predicated of no term *b*: no good thing is evil. Term *b*, however, is predicated of every term *c*: every just thing is good. Therefore it follows that no just thing is evil, as in the following form: if term *a* is predicated of no term *b*, while term *b* is predicated of every *c*, term *a* will be predicated of no *c*. Thus: “No good thing is evil”; “Every just thing is good”; “Therefore no just thing is evil.”

The third mode of the first figure occurs whenever a particular affirmative is drawn from a universal affirmative and a particular affirmative. If *a*, virtue, is predicated of every *b*, that is, good, and *b*, good, is predicated particularly of some *c*, that is, just, then the conclusion will likewise be particular, so that *a*, virtue, is predicated particularly of some *c*, just.

If, therefore, term *a* is in every *b*, and term *b* is in some particular *c*, term *a* will be in some particular *c*, as follows:

> Every good thing is virtue.
>
> Some just thing is good.
>
> Therefore some just thing is virtue.

The fourth mode of the first figure is as follows: a particular negative is drawn from a universal negative and a particular affirmative. If term *a* is predicated of no term *b*, while term *b* is predicated of some term *c*, term *a* will not be predicated of some term *c*, as the following diagram shows. The propositions are:

> No good thing is evil.
>
> Some just thing is good.
>
> Therefore some just thing is not evil.

These are the four modes in the first figure that Aristotle set out in his *Analytics*. The remaining five modes were added by Theophrastus and Eudemus. Porphyry, a man apparently of the highest authority, seems to have agreed with them. They are as follows.

Since a particular affirmative converts with itself, whoever has shown in the conclusion that term *a* is predicated particularly of some term *c* has shown in that same conclusion that term *c* is again predicated particularly of some term *a*. For if the particular proposition in the conclusion converts with itself, then if term *a* is in some term *c*, term *c* will be predicated of some term *a*.

Likewise, whoever has proved a universal negative in the conclusion must also have proved its converse in that same conclusion. For a universal negative always converts with itself. If someone has proved that term *a* is predicated of no term *c*, there is no doubt that in this conclusion he has also proved that term *c* is predicated of no term *a*. For, as was said, a universal negative always converts with itself.

A universal affirmative is also contained in a twofold conclusion. Whoever shows that term *a* is predicated of every term *c* has also shown that term *c* is predicated particularly of some term *a*. For if someone proves that animal is predicated of every man, saying, “Every man is an animal,” he has necessarily also shown particularly that “Some animal is a man.”

Thus a universal negative and a universal affirmative, or a particular affirmative, are each concluded in two ways. Some propositions convert with themselves: the particular converts particularly, and the universal universally. Another proposition, although itself universal affirmative, converts with itself particularly. A particular negative, however, never converts with itself, and therefore retains a simple conclusion in itself.

What we have just said is shown by Aristotle in the second book of the *Prior Analytics*: Theophrastus and Eudemus, taking this as their starting point, turned their attention to adding other syllogisms to those of the first figure. These are called κατὰ ἀνάκλασιν, that is, “by a kind of refraction and conversion” of the proposition.

The fifth mode is formed from two universal affirmatives and yields a particular affirmative, as follows. If *a* is in every *b*, and *b* is in every *c*, one could indeed conclude that term *a* is in every term *c*. But since this universal proposition, as has been said, converts particularly, leaving aside the fact that term *a* is predicated of every term *c*, the conclusion is said to be that term *c* is predicated of some term *a*. This must be shown by an example.

If the propositions are: “Every just thing is good,” and “Every virtue is just,” one could indeed conclude that “Every virtue is good.” But since the proposition converts with itself in such a way that “Some good thing is virtue” is particular, a particular syllogism and conclusion are drawn from two universal affirmatives.

Its form is: term *a* is in every *b*, term *b* is in every *c*; therefore term *c* is in some *a*, as follows:

> Every just thing is good.
>
> Every virtue is just.
>
> Some good thing is just.

It is called “by conversion” or “by refraction” because what was concluded universally is converted and collected particularly.

The sixth mode of the first figure is formed from a universal negative and a universal affirmative, yielding a universal conclusion by conversion. If term *a* is in no *b*, while term *b* is in every *c*, one could indeed conclude that term *a* is in no *c*. But since the universal negative converts, we say that term *c* is in no *a*, as follows:

> No good thing is evil.
>
> Every just thing is good.

One could conclude:

> No just thing is evil;

but from these propositions, by conversion, we conclude:

> No evil thing is just.

The seventh mode of the first figure is formed from a universal affirmative and a particular affirmative, yielding a particular affirmative by conversion. If term *a* is in every *b*, and term *b* is predicated of some term *c*, term *a* can be predicated of some term *c*. But since the particular affirmative converts with itself, the conclusion is formed by conversion, and it is said that term *c* is predicated of some term *a*, as follows:

“Every good thing is virtue; some just thing is good.”

One could indeed conclude that “Some just thing is virtue,” but since the particular affirmative converts, we say that “Some virtue is just.”

The eighth mode of the first figure occurs whenever a particular conclusion is drawn from a universal affirmative and a universal negative. If term *a* has been predicated of every term *b*, while term *b* is predicated of no term *c*, it is not possible to conclude that term *a* is predicated of no term *c*. Why this is impossible was explained in the *Analytic* works.

But since the universal negative converts with itself, we can say and convert it so that term *c* is predicated of no term *b*, while term *b* is said to be predicated of some term *a*, since the universal affirmative converts particularly with itself. Therefore term *c* will not be predicated of some term *a*, as follows:

From “Every good thing is just” and “No evil thing is good,” one could not conclude that “No evil thing is just.” But it converts as follows:

> No good thing is evil.
>
> Some just thing is good.
>
> Therefore some just thing is not evil.

The ninth mode of the first figure is formed from a particular affirmative and a universal negative, yielding a particular negative by conversion. If term *a* is predicated of some term *b*, while term *b* is predicated of no term *c*, it cannot indeed be said that term *a* will not be predicated of some term *c*. Why this is impossible was also explained in the *Analytic* works.

But since the universal negative can be converted, it will be said that term *c* is predicated of no term *b*, while *b* is predicated of some term *a*. Therefore term *c* will not be predicated of some term *a*, as follows:

> Some good thing is just.
>
> No evil thing is good.
>
> Therefore some just thing is not evil.

Having completed the nine modes of the first figure, let us proceed to the four modes of the second figure. Let it simply be established that, just as in the first figure a universal affirmative, a universal negative, a particular affirmative, and a particular negative are all drawn as conclusions through the nine modes mentioned above, in the second figure neither a universal nor a particular affirmative can be concluded. Only negative conclusions can be drawn, whether particular or universal.

The first mode of the second figure occurs whenever a universal negative is drawn from a universal negative and a universal affirmative. If term *a* is predicated of no term *b* and of every term *c*, term *b* will be predicated of no term *c*. Let *a* be “good,” *b* “evil,” and *c* “just.” If someone says:

> No evil thing is good.
>
> Every just thing is good.

he concludes:

> No just thing is evil.

It is therefore clear that the major extreme is predicated of the minor in the conclusion.

Although all syllogisms of the second figure are true, the truth is not proved from themselves, but is completed through the modes of the first figure. For if term *a* is predicated of no term *b* and is in every term *c*, it has not yet been proved that term *b* is altogether predicated of no term *c*. But if someone turns this first mode of the second figure into the second mode of the first figure, the entire syllogism and its conclusion are proved by conversion.

For in the syllogism in which term *a* is in no *b* and the same term *a* is predicated of every *c*, if someone converts the proposition concerning *a* and *b* so that it becomes *b* and *a*—for every universal negative converts—then, if someone says that term *a* is predicated of no term *b*, term *b* will therefore be predicated of no term *a*. But term *a* is predicated of every term *c*. Thus the second mode of the first figure is produced: from a universal negative and a universal affirmative it draws a universal negative conclusion. The conclusion is therefore that *b* is predicated of no term *c*.

Through these conversions every syllogism and conclusion of the second and third figures is drawn and proved. Since they are not proved from themselves unless they are confirmed from what is prior, namely, the modes of the first figure, any syllogism found in the second or third figure is called an imperfect syllogism.

The second mode of the second figure occurs whenever, with the order of a universal affirmative and a universal negative reversed, a universal negative is again concluded. If term *a* is in every term *b* and is predicated of no term *c*, term *b* will be predicated of no term *c*. Let *a* be “good,” *b* “just,” and *c* “evil.” If someone says:

> Every just thing is good.
>
> No evil thing is good.

he concludes:

> Therefore no evil thing is just.

This combination and connection of propositions has a twofold conversion. It is shown from the second mode of the first figure as follows. If term *a* is in every term *b* and is predicated of no term *c*, the universal negative is converted. Thus term *c* will be predicated of no term *a*. If this is so, the syllogism will be of the following form: term *c* is predicated of no term *a*; term *a* is in every term *b*; therefore term *c* will be predicated of no term *b*. One conversion of the negative proposition has thus taken place.

But since we said that the conclusion is not that *c* is in no *b*, but that *b* is in no *c*, the universal negative conclusion is also converted here. Just as it was concluded that term *c* is predicated of no term *b*, so it is concluded that term *b* is predicated of no term *c*.

The third mode of the second figure occurs whenever a particular negative is drawn from a universal negative and a particular affirmative. If term *a* is predicated of no term *b* and is in some term *c*, term *b* will not be predicated of some term *c*. Let *a* be “good,” *b* “evil,” and *c* “just.” If someone says:

> No evil thing is good.
>
> Some just thing is good.

he must conclude:

> Some just thing is not evil.

This syllogism too is proved by conversion as follows. If term *a* is predicated of no term *b*, term *b* will be predicated of no term *a*. But term *a* is predicated of some term *c*. Thus the fourth mode of the first figure returns: it is formed from a universal negative and a particular affirmative and draws a particular negative. In this syllogism too it draws a particular negative, namely, that term *b* is not predicated of some term *c*.

The fourth mode of the second figure draws a particular negative from a universal affirmative and a particular negative. If term *a* is in every term *b* and is not predicated of some term *c*, term *b* will not be predicated of some term *c*. Let *a* be “good,” *b* “just,” and *c* “evil.” If someone says:

> Every just thing is good.
>
> Some evil thing is not good.

he concludes:

> Therefore some evil thing is not just.

This combination and arrangement of propositions cannot be proved by conversion. For a universal affirmative cannot convert with itself. This syllogism is therefore shown from the first figure not by conversion but by impossibility, since, if the particular negative conclusion is not drawn in this syllogism, something unreasonable and impossible follows.

This impossibility will be demonstrated through the first figure. I say that if term *a* is predicated of every term *b* and is not in some term *c*, the conclusion must be drawn that term *b* is not predicated of some term *c*. For if this is false, the proposition opposed to it will be true. Particular negatives have universal affirmatives as their opposites, as we taught in the preceding book.

If, therefore, the particular negative is not the conclusion here, the universal affirmative will be. Let the affirmation be universal, and let term *b* be predicated of every term *c*. But term *a* is predicated of every term *b*, and term *b* is said to be predicated of every term *c*. Therefore term *a* is predicated of every term *c*, which cannot happen. For we previously posited the proposition concerning *a* and *c* so as to say that term *a* is not predicated of some term *c*. This has therefore been demonstrated through the first mode of the first figure.

Thus every syllogism in the second figure is imperfect, and its proof is either reduced by conversion to the first figure or, from a hypothetical arrangement, demonstrated through impossibility, showing that it cannot be otherwise than through the first figure. The others too are proved by impossibility, as will be demonstrated shortly.

It remains to explain the modes and arrangements of the third figure. Before doing so, however, we must first observe that in the modes of the third figure a universal conclusion is never drawn. Whether the collections are negative or affirmative, they are always particular and never universal.

The first mode of the third figure is formed from two universal affirmatives and draws a particular affirmative. If terms *a* and *b* are predicated of every term *c*, term *a* will be predicated of some term *b* by conversion. For if term *b* is predicated of every term *c*, and the universal affirmative converts particularly with itself, term *c* is predicated of some term *b*. If this is so, the third mode of the first figure is produced: it is formed from a universal and a particular affirmative and concludes that term *a* is predicated of some term *b*.

Let *a* be “just,” *b* “virtue,” and *c* “good.” If someone says:

> Every good thing is just.
>
> Every good thing is virtue.

the conclusion is:

> Some virtue is just.

Others change the terms and wish to make this the second mode, so that *a* is virtue, *b* just, and *c* good, giving the following syllogism:

> Every good thing is virtue.
>
> Every good thing is just.
>
> Therefore some just thing is virtue.

Aristotle does not separate this from the preceding mode. He considers these two one mode. For that reason, we hesitated to say that there are seven modes of the third figure. Aristotle should rather be followed; therefore we shall say that there is another mode which can properly be regarded as the second.

The second mode of the third figure occurs whenever a particular negative is drawn from a universal negative and a universal affirmative. If term *a* is predicated of no term *c*, while term *b* is predicated of every term *c*, term *a* will not be predicated of some term *b*. For if term *a* is predicated of no term *c*, while *b* is predicated of every *c*, term *c* will be predicated of some term *b*. The universal affirmative converts particularly with itself. Thus, in the fourth mode of the first figure, it is concluded that term *a* is not predicated of some term *b*.

Let *a* be “evil,” *b* “just,” and *c* “good.” If someone says:

> No good thing is evil.
>
> Every good thing is just.

he must conclude:

> Therefore some just thing is not evil.

From this it must be observed that the major extreme is predicated in the conclusion.

The third mode of the third figure occurs whenever a particular affirmative is concluded from a particular and a universal affirmative. If term *a* is predicated of some term *c*, while term *b* is predicated of every term *c*, it is concluded by a twofold conversion that term *a* is predicated of some term *b*.

For since term *b* is predicated of every term *c*, while term *a* is predicated of some term *c*, and the particular affirmative always converts with itself, term *c* will be predicated of some term *a*. The propositions are therefore as follows: term *b* is predicated of every term *c*, while term *c* is predicated of some term *a*. If this is so, in the third mode of the first figure it is concluded that term *b* is predicated of some term *a*. Thus the particular affirmative is converted, and term *a* is predicated of some term *b*. There are therefore two conversions, one of the proposition and the other of the conclusion.

Let *a* be “just,” *b* “virtue,” and *c* “good.” If someone says:

> Some good thing is just.
>
> Every good thing is virtue.

he must conclude:

> Some virtue is just.

The fourth mode of the third figure occurs whenever a particular affirmative is drawn from a universal affirmative and a particular affirmative. If term *a* is predicated of every term *c*, while term *b* is in some term *c*, it is concluded by conversion that term *a* is predicated of some term *b*.

For if term *b* is predicated of some term *c*, term *c* is predicated of some term *b*, since the particular affirmative converts with itself. Thus the third mode of the first figure is produced: it is formed from a universal affirmative and a particular affirmative and draws a particular affirmative. The syllogism is therefore as follows: term *a* is in every term *c*, and term *c* is in some term *b*. Therefore term *b* is in some term *b*.

Let *a* be “virtue,” *b* “just,” and *c* “good.” If someone says:

> Every good thing is virtue.
>
> Some good thing is just,

he will conclude:

> Some just thing is virtue.

The fifth mode of the third figure occurs when a particular negative and a universal affirmative yield a particular negative conclusion. This mode, however, cannot be proved by conversion, but by impossibility, just as the fourth mode of the second figure was proved. For if term *a* is not predicated of some term *c*, while term *b* is predicated of every term *c*, term *a* will not be predicated of some term *b*. For if this were not so, it would be true that term *a* is predicated of every term *b*; but term *b* is predicated of every term *c*, and therefore term *a* would be predicated of every term *c*, which cannot happen. For term *a* was previously posited in such a way that it was not predicated of some term *c*. And if the universal affirmative is not in the conclusion—that is, if term *a* is predicated of every term *b*—there will be a particular negative contradictory to it, namely, that term *a* is not predicated of some term *b*. Let *a* be evil, *b* just, and *c* good. If someone therefore says:

> Some good is not evil.

> Every good is just,

he must conclude:

> Therefore, some just is not evil.

The sixth mode of the third figure occurs when a universal negative and a particular affirmative yield a particular negative by conversion. For if term *a* belongs to no term *c*, while term *b* is predicated of some term *c*, the conclusion follows that term *a* is not predicated of some term *b*. For if term *a* is predicated of no term *c*, while term *b* is predicated of some term *c*, then term *c* will be predicated of some term *b*, since a particular affirmative can be converted. Thus the syllogism is formed as follows: term *a* is predicated of no term *c*; term *c* is predicated of some term *b*; therefore term *a* is not predicated of some term *b*. Let *a* be evil, *b* just, and *c* good. If someone therefore says:

> No good is evil.

> Some good is just,

he concludes:

> Therefore, some just is not evil.

Having dealt with these matters, we must define what a syllogism itself is. It is defined as follows: a syllogism is an argument in which, when certain things have been posited and conceded, something other than those things that have been posited and conceded necessarily follows through the very things conceded.

We said that a syllogism is an argument because every definition is drawn from a general class, and the genus of a syllogism is an argument. What was said—“in which, when certain things have been posited and conceded”—should be understood as though it had said, “in accordance with which, when certain things have been posited and conceded.” For in order that a syllogism may be formed, something is first stated by the proposer, and the hearer concedes it. When he has conceded it, the proposer draws the conclusion and completes the syllogism. This is because doubtful matters are demonstrated through things conceded and proved; and true affirmation and true negation are conceded equally.

The remaining parts of the definition of a syllogism distinguish syllogisms that are not properly constructed from true syllogisms. For the phrase “in which, when certain things have been posited” indicates a plurality of assumptions—that is, of propositions. There are some who are thought to be syllogisms in which there is only one proposition and one conclusion. Such are the following: “You see; therefore you live”; “You are a human being; therefore you are an animal”; and others of this sort. The ancients did not admit these as syllogisms, for a syllogism is a collection of several things. But a collection can exist only of several things, and whoever posits one proposition does not collect. He therefore produces no syllogism. A syllogism must be established by two propositions, if it is to be as short as possible.

What was said—“something else necessarily follows than those things that have been conceded”—is because some people frequently construct syllogisms in which they conclude in the conclusion precisely what they had proposed, as in the following:

> If you are a human being, you are a human being;  
> but you are a human being;  
> therefore you are a human being.

For he concluded the same thing that he had proposed earlier. Therefore, to distinguish such cases, it was said that something else must follow than those things that have been conceded, as in all the preceding syllogisms that we set out among the modes and demonstrations of the three figures.

Syllogisms of the kind just mentioned are extremely absurd, because something that had previously been conceded as doubtful is collected in the conclusion. The phrase “necessarily follows” is relevant because there are often certain true propositions used for induction whose conclusion is in no way true. For example, someone might say:

> Whoever knows music is a musician,

and this is conceded; and:

> Whoever knows arithmetic is an arithmetician;  
> whoever knows medicine is a physician;  
> whoever knows the good is good.

When all these have been conceded, he might add:

> Whoever knows evil is evil.

This appears similar to the preceding statements, but is altogether false. For good people are not otherwise able to guard against evil unless they know evil. Therefore, because of conclusions drawn from propositions asserted by induction, it was added that conclusions in syllogisms occur necessarily—that is, follow by necessity.

There is also another explanation, but it has already been given in our *Analytica*.

The phrase “through the very things that have been posited” was said because of those who construct syllogisms in which either less, more, or something other than what ought to have been proposed is proposed. Syllogisms of this kind are formed as follows. If someone says:

> Socrates is a human being;  
> every human being is an animal;

and concludes:

> Therefore Socrates is animate,

he has proposed less than was required, since he did not say that every animal is animate. If he had proposed this, he would rightly have concluded that Socrates is animate, saying:

> Socrates is a human being;  
> every human being is an animal;  
> every animal is animate;  
> therefore Socrates is animate.

To propose more means that someone says:

> Every human being is an animal;  
> every animal is animate;  
> but the sun is in Aries;  
> therefore every human being is animate.

Here the insertion that the sun is in Aries is superfluous.

To propose something other than what is necessary occurs as follows:

> Every human being is an animal;  
> virtue is good;  
> therefore every human being is animate.

None of these propositions is relevant to what he wished to conclude.

The definition of a syllogism having been explained, let us proceed to the nature and resolution of the preceding modes, and first let them all be arranged in order.

## Modes of the first figure

### Eighth

| Mode | Propositions and conclusion |
|---|---|
| First | Every just thing is good. Every virtue is just. Therefore every virtue is good. |
| Second | No good thing is evil. Every just thing is good. Therefore no just thing is evil. |
| Third | Every good thing is a virtue. Some just thing is good. Therefore some just thing is a virtue. |
| Fourth | No good thing is evil. Some just thing is good. Therefore some just thing is not evil. |
| Fifth | Every just thing is good. Every virtue is just. Therefore some good thing is a virtue. |
| Sixth | No good thing is evil. Every just thing is good. Therefore no evil thing is just. |
| Seventh | Every good thing is a virtue. Some just thing is good. Therefore some virtue is just. |

> Every good thing is just. No evil thing is good. Therefore some just thing is not evil.

### Ninth

> Some good thing is just. No evil thing is good. Therefore some just thing is not evil.

## Modes of the second figure

| Mode | Propositions and conclusion |
|---|---|
| First | No evil thing is good. Every just thing is good. Therefore no just thing is evil. |
| Second | Every just thing is good. No evil thing is good. Therefore no evil thing is just. |
| Third | No evil thing is good. Some just thing is good. Therefore some just thing is not evil. |
| Fourth | Every just thing is good. Some evil thing is not good. Therefore some evil thing is not just. |

## Modes of the third figure

| Mode | Propositions and conclusion |
|---|---|
| First | Every good thing is just. Every good thing is a virtue. Therefore some virtue is just. |
| Second | Every good thing is a virtue. Every good thing is just. Therefore some just thing is a virtue. |
| Third | No good thing is evil. Every good thing is just. Therefore some just thing is not evil. |
| Fourth | Some good thing is just. Every good thing is a virtue. Therefore some virtue is just. |
| Fifth | Every good thing is a virtue. Some good thing is just. Therefore some just thing is a virtue. |
| Sixth | Some good thing is not evil. Every good thing is just. Therefore some just thing is not evil. |
| Seventh | No good thing is evil. Some good thing is just. Therefore some just thing is not evil. |

These, then, are all the modes of the three figures. The first four modes of the first figure are called indemonstrable and direct—that is, demonstrated without any conversion. They are called indemonstrable because they are not demonstrated through others, and perfect because they are established through themselves. They are called first because they are first in position and nature, and because all the others are resolved into them.

The remaining five modes of the first figure are imperfect and proceed by conversion. All the modes of the second and third figures are likewise imperfect, because they are demonstrated through the first four modes of the first figure; for they are resolved into those modes. Let us therefore consider their principles, since they are resolved into the very things from which they arise.

The fifth mode of the first figure is generated from the first mode of the first figure. With the first two propositions remaining unchanged, the conclusion of the first mode, converted particularly, produces the fifth syllogism, as the following arrangement makes clear:

| Original | Same |
|---|---|
| Every just thing is good. | Every just thing is good. |
| Every virtue is just. | Every virtue is just. |
| Every virtue is good. | Some good thing is a virtue. |

The sixth mode of the first figure takes its beginning from the second mode of the first figure. With the two preceding propositions of the second mode remaining unchanged, and the universal conclusion being universally converted, the sixth syllogism arises, as the following arrangement shows:

| Original | Same |
|---|---|
| No good thing is evil. | No good thing is evil. |
| Every just thing is good. | Every just thing is good. |
| No just thing is evil. | No evil thing is just. |

The seventh mode of the first figure arises from the third mode of the first figure. With the two preceding propositions remaining unchanged, and the particular affirmative in the conclusion being converted, the structure of the seventh mode is produced:

| Original | Converted |
|---|---|
| Every good thing is a virtue. | Every good thing is a virtue. |
| Some just thing is good. | Some just thing is good. |
| Some just thing is a virtue. | Some virtue is just. |

The eighth and ninth modes of the first figure are resolved into the fourth mode of the first figure; they do not take their beginning from it. The eighth is resolved into the fourth as follows. The first proposition of the fourth mode is universally converted into the second proposition of the eighth, and the first proposition of the eighth mode is converted particularly into the second proposition of the fourth mode; the same conclusion, namely, the particular negative, is then collected.

> No good thing is evil — universal negative.

> Some just thing is good — particular affirmative.

> Universally converted: Every good thing is just.

> Universally converted: No evil thing is good.

> Some just thing is not evil — the same conclusion.

> Some just thing is not evil.

The ninth mode is resolved into the fourth mode as follows. The first proposition of the fourth mode is universally converted into the second proposition of the ninth, and the second proposition of the fourth is converted particularly into the first proposition of the ninth; the same conclusion remains, namely, the particular negative.

> No good thing is evil — universal negative.

> Some just thing is good — particular affirmative.

> Particularly converted: Some good thing is just.

> Universally converted: No evil thing is good.

> Some just thing is not evil — the same conclusion.

> Some just thing is not evil.

Having resolved the five modes of the first figure into the four preceding ones, let us resolve the four modes of the second figure into the modes of the first figure. Three of these are proved by conversion, but the fourth by impossibility alone.

The first and second modes of the second figure are resolved into the second mode of the first figure. The first is resolved as follows. The first universal negative is universally converted, while the second universal affirmative remains unchanged; the same conclusion arises in both cases.

> **First mode of the second figure**

| Original | Converted or unchanged |
|---|---|
| No good thing is evil. | No evil thing is good. |
| Every just thing is good. | Every just thing is good. |
| No just thing is evil. | No just thing is evil. |

The second mode of the second figure is resolved into the second mode of the first figure as follows: the second proposition is converted, while the first remains; the conclusion is likewise universally converted.

> No good thing is evil — converted: No evil thing is good.

> Every just thing is good — remains: Every just thing is good.

> No just thing is evil — converted: No evil thing is just.

The third mode of the second figure is generated from the fourth mode of the first figure. When the universal negative is universally converted into the first proposition, while the second propositions remain unchanged, the same term and proposition of the syllogism are collected as follows:

> No good thing is evil — converted: No evil thing is good.

> Some just thing is good — likewise: Some just thing is good.

> Some just thing is not evil — the same: Some just thing is not evil.

The fourth mode of the second figure, since it could not be turned back into a mode of the preceding first figure by conversion when it was first established through conversion, was demonstrated by impossibility. It too is reduced to the preceding modes by impossibility. Since all the modes of the second figure are demonstrated by impossibility, we shall likewise resolve them all by impossibility, beginning with the fourth.

The fourth mode of the second figure is resolved into the first mode of the first figure by impossibility; the third into the second; the second into the third; and the first into the fourth. This will become clear in the following way.

If someone concedes these two propositions—namely, “Every good thing is a virtue” and “Some just thing is not a virtue”—he must also concede the conclusion, which is: “Therefore some just thing is not good.” For if this is false, its contradictory counterpart will be true, namely, “Every just thing is good.” But he conceded the first proposition of the fourth mode, namely, “Every good thing is a virtue.” From these he must conclude: “Therefore every just thing is a virtue.” But earlier he conceded the second proposition of the fourth mode, namely, “Some just thing is not a virtue.” Now, by conceding “Every just thing is a virtue,” he will conclude two contradictory counterparts simultaneously, which cannot happen.

This occurs because the conclusion of the fourth mode has been converted into the second proposition of the first mode. If the second proposition of the first mode is not collected in the conclusion of the fourth, the conclusion of the fourth—that is, the particular negative—will remain.

Let us not be disturbed by the fact that, in resolving the modes, we have used terms different from those used earlier in arranging them. For our concern now is not with the terms themselves, but with constructing and resolving the figures, modes, and combinations.

| Original | Resolution |
|---|---|
| Every good thing is a virtue. | Every good thing is a virtue. |
| Some just thing is not a virtue. | Every just thing is good. |
| Therefore some just thing is not good. | Therefore every just thing is a virtue. |

The third mode of the second figure is resolved into the second mode of the first figure as follows. If someone concedes the first two propositions of the third mode, he will also conclude the particular negative: “Therefore some just thing is not good.” For if this is false, its contradictory counterpart will be true, namely, “Every just thing is good.” But the other proposition has also been conceded, namely, “No good thing is evil.” From these he concludes: “Therefore no just thing is evil.” Yet he had previously conceded “Some just thing is evil.” Now he concedes “No just thing is evil,” thereby conceding two contradictory counterparts at the same time, which cannot happen. Once the universal conclusion—“Every just thing is good”—has been removed, the particular negative remains: “Some just thing is not good.”

| Original | Resolution |
|---|---|
| No good thing is evil — conceded. | No good thing is evil. |
| Some just thing is evil — contradictory counterpart. | Every just thing is good. |
| Therefore some just thing is not good — converted contradictory counterpart. | Therefore no just thing is evil. |

The second mode of the second figure is resolved into the third mode of the first figure as follows. If someone concedes the two propositions of the second figure, he also concedes the conclusion: “Therefore some just thing is good.” For if this is false, its contradictory counterpart, the particular affirmative “Some just thing is good,” will be true. But he also conceded the proposition “Every good thing is a virtue.” From this he must conclude “Some just thing is a virtue,” while he had already conceded the second proposition of the second mode, namely, “No just thing is a virtue.” Thus he concedes two contradictory counterparts at the same time, which cannot happen.

| Original | Resolution |
|---|---|
| Every good thing is a virtue — conceded. | Every good thing is a virtue. |
| No just thing is a virtue — contradictory counterpart. | Some just thing is a virtue. |
| No just thing is good — converted contradictory counterpart. | Some just thing is good. |

The first mode of the second figure is likewise resolved into the fourth mode of the first figure. Whoever concedes the two propositions of the first mode must also concede the conclusion. For if it is false, its contradictory counterpart will be true, namely, the particular affirmative “Some just thing is good.” But he also conceded “No good thing is evil”; from this he must conclude “Therefore some just thing is not evil,” while he had previously conceded “Every just thing is evil.” Thus he concedes two contradictory counterparts at the same time, which cannot happen. Once the particular affirmative “Some just thing is good” has been removed, “No just thing is good” remains.

| Original | Resolution |
|---|---|
| No good thing is evil — similar. | No good thing is evil. |
| Every just thing is evil — contrary. | Therefore some just thing is not evil. |
| No just thing is good — converted contradictory counterpart. | Some just thing is good. |

It remains for us to reduce the modes of the third figure to the first four. Five of them are resolved into the first four by conversion and impossibility; only the fifth is resolved into the preceding modes by impossibility alone.

The first mode of the third figure is resolved into the third mode of the first figure as follows. If the first proposition of the third mode of the first figure remains, and the second, particular proposition of the third mode of the first figure is universally converted, and becomes the second proposition of the first mode of the third figure, the same conclusion is collected, namely, the particular affirmative.

| Original | Resolution |
|---|---|
| Every good thing is just — remains. | Every good thing is just. |
| Some virtue is good — converted. | Every good thing is a virtue. |
| Some virtue is just — remains. | Some virtue is just. |

Or it may be done in this way, since earlier we described such a syllogism with the terms interchanged, and Aristotle does not regard it as different:

| Original | Resolution |
|---|---|
| Every good thing is a virtue — similar. | Every good thing is a virtue. |
| Some just thing is good — converted. | Every good thing is just. |
| Some just thing is a virtue — remains. | Some just thing is a virtue. |

The second mode of the third figure is resolved into the fourth mode of the first figure as follows. If the first propositions of the second mode of the third figure and of the fourth mode of the first figure remain, while the second proposition of the fourth mode of the first figure is universally converted and becomes the second proposition of the second mode of the third figure, the same conclusion is produced.

| Original | Resolution |
|---|---|
| No good thing is evil — remains. | No good thing is evil. |
| Some just thing is good — universally converted. | Every good thing is just. |
| Some just thing is not evil — remains. | Some just thing is not evil. |

The third mode of the third figure is resolved into the third mode of the first figure. If the first proposition of the third mode of the first figure and the second proposition of the third mode of the third figure remain, while the particular second proposition of the third mode of the first figure is particularly converted and becomes the first proposition of the third mode of the third figure, the conclusion arises by particular conversion.

| Original | Resolution |
|---|---|
| Every good thing is a virtue. | Every good thing is a virtue. |
| Some just thing is good. | Some good thing is just. |
| Some just thing is a virtue — particularly converted. | Some virtue is just. |

The fourth mode of the third figure is resolved into the third mode of the first figure. If the first propositions of both remain, and the particular second propositions are particularly converted, the same conclusions arise.

| Original | Resolution |
|---|---|
| Every good thing is a virtue — remains. | Every good thing is a virtue. |
| Some just thing is good — converted. | Some good thing is just. |
| Some just thing is a virtue — remains. | Some just thing is a virtue. |

The remaining sixth syllogism of the third figure is generated from the fourth mode of the first figure. With their first propositions remaining, and their second propositions altered only in their particular terms, the conclusion remains the same in both.

| Original | Altered |
|---|---|
| No good thing is evil — same. | No good thing is evil. |
| Some just thing is good — altered. | Some good thing is just. |
| Some just thing is not evil — remains. | Some just thing is not evil. |

The remaining fifth mode, just as it was previously proved by impossibility, is now also resolved by impossibility. In the same order in which one has been resolved, all the others must be resolved. The sixth mode of the third figure is resolved into the third mode of the first figure; the fifth mode of the third figure into the first mode of the first figure; the fourth mode of the third figure into the fourth mode of the first figure; the third mode of the third figure into the second mode of the first figure; the second mode of the third figure into the first mode of the first figure; and the first modes of the third figure into the second modes of the first figure.

The sixth mode of the third figure is resolved by impossibility into the third mode of the first figure as follows. If someone concedes the two propositions of the sixth mode of the third figure, he must also concede the conclusion: “Some just thing is not evil.” For if this is false, its contradictory counterpart will be true, namely, the first proposition of the third mode of the first figure: “Every just thing is evil.” But he also conceded the second proposition, “Some good thing is just.” From these he must conclude “Some good thing is evil,” since he had previously conceded the first proposition of the sixth mode of the third figure, “No good thing is evil.” Thus he concedes two contradictory counterparts at the same time, which cannot happen, as the following arrangement shows.

| Original | Contradictory counterpart |
|---|---|
| No good thing is evil — contradictory counterpart. | Some good thing is evil. |
| Some good thing is just — conceded. | Some good thing is just. |
| Some just thing is not evil — converted contradictory counterpart. | Every just thing is evil. |

In this way all the remaining modes of the third figure are referred to the first modes of the first figure, as the following arrangement shows. The fifth, which could not be resolved by conversion, has here been resolved by impossibility.

> Some good thing is not evil — contradictory counterpart: Every good thing is evil.

> Every good thing is just — conceded in both: Every good thing is just.

> Some just thing is not evil — converted contradictory counterpart: Every just thing is evil.

> Every good thing is a virtue — contradictory counterpart: No good thing is a virtue.

> Some good thing is just — conceded in both: Some good thing is just.

> Some just thing is a virtue — converted contradictory counterpart: No just thing is a virtue.

> Some good thing is just — contradictory counterpart: No good thing is just.

> Every good thing is a virtue — conceded in both: Every good thing is a virtue.

> Some virtue is just — converted contradictory counterpart: No virtue is just.

In the resolution of the second mode of the third figure into the first mode of the first figure, this impossibility occurs: he concedes two contraries at the same time, which cannot happen. For two contraries can never be found true simultaneously.

> No good thing is evil — contrary: No good thing is just.

> Every good thing is just — conceded in both: Every good thing is just.

> Some just thing is not evil — converted contradictory counterpart: Every just thing is evil.

In the following syllogism also, he concedes two things that are impossible:

> Every good thing is just — contrary: No good thing is just.

> Every good thing is a virtue — conceded in both: Every good thing is a virtue.

> Some virtue is just — converted contradictory counterpart: No virtue is just.

Nor should we be disturbed by the fact that in some cases the contrary proposition and conclusion are found, while in others the contradictory counterpart is found. For he is equally at fault whether he concedes both contraries or both contradictory counterparts. Just as contradictory counterparts can never be true at the same time, neither can contraries.

> Every good thing is a virtue — contrary: No good thing is a virtue.

> Every good thing is just — conceded in both: Every good thing is just.

> Some just thing is a virtue — converted contradictory counterpart: No just thing is a virtue.

## On the introduction to categorical syllogisms

I have set forth these matters concerning the introduction to categorical syllogisms, following Aristotle for the most part and borrowing some points from Theophrastus and Porphyry, insofar as the brevity permitted by an introduction allowed. If anything is missing, I shall express it more fully in my *Analytica*. For the present, insofar as the matter concerned only the form of categorical syllogisms, this work is complete and has been elaborated as a supplement to the introduction.

Nor should it disturb us if some propositions and conclusions presented here are false, since our subject has been not the truth of things but the connections, figures, and modes of syllogisms. Once these have been understood, if the subtlety of disputation draws anyone toward the thorough study of logic, let him first learn about ambiguous arguments; afterward, through these, he will examine truth and falsehood in matters themselves.

## AN. MANL. SEV. BOETHIUS, TWO BOOKS ON HYPOTHETICAL SYLLOGISM

### Book One
[Col. 0831B] Since I regard the greatest consolation of life as residing in learning and pursuing every branch of philosophy, I take up with greater pleasure—and, as it were, with some reward for my labor—the things that I compose to share with you. For although the contemplation of truth ought to be pursued for its own particular beauty, it nevertheless becomes more lovable when brought into common use. For there is no good that does not shine forth more beautifully when confirmed by the knowledge of many. What was previously suppressed by silence, and was already on the point of perishing in silence, now flourishes more broadly and is preserved from the destruction of oblivion through the participation of those who know; and a discipline likewise becomes more pleasurable when it commands one to be wise among those who share the same wisdom. If, moreover—as is now the case between you and me—things that are naturally pleasurable are brought into the fellowship of friendship, then the sweetness of study must necessarily be seasoned, as it were, with the most delightful flavor of affection.

For since friendship possesses this as its proper function: that it does not wish to have solitary thoughts, each person readily confides what he honorably thinks to no one more readily than to the one he loves. Thus it came about that, even if the immensity of the labor denied a path to the work I had begun, my spirit was nevertheless sufficient to accomplish what it had undertaken through contemplation of you. For what great thing would a love devoted to you accomplish if it remained within the limits of ease?

What, then, I found treated among Greek writers only by very few, and there only briefly and confusedly, but among Latin writers by none at all, my labor—though prolonged, yet effective in its undertaking—has cultivated and dedicated to your knowledge. For when you had acquired an ample understanding of categorical syllogisms, you often asked about hypothetical syllogisms, concerning which Aristotle wrote nothing. Theophrastus, however, a man capable of every branch of learning, merely sets out the main points of the subject. Eudemus proceeds along a broader path of instruction, but in such a way that he seems to have scattered certain seeds without producing any harvest of fruit.

Therefore, insofar as we have been able through our intellectual powers and our devotion to your friendship, we have undertaken diligently and carefully to elucidate and pursue with precision what those authors either stated briefly or omitted altogether. In this matter I count the reward of overcoming the difficulty as having been achieved if I seem to have fulfilled my obligation to your friendship, even if I do not seem to have satisfied the demands of learning.

Every syllogism [Col. 0832B] is contained in propositions that are definite and suitably arranged. Every proposition, however, is either categorical, which is called predicative, or hypothetical, which is called conditional. A predicative proposition is one in which something is predicated of something else, as in: “A human being is an animal.” Here “animal” is predicated of “human being.” A hypothetical proposition is one that, with a certain condition, declares that something exists if something else exists, as when we say: “If it is day, there is light.”

Hypothetical propositions are composed of categorical propositions, as will appear shortly. Hence a syllogism joined from categorical propositions is called categorical—that is, predicative—whereas one consisting of hypothetical propositions is called hypothetical—that is, conditional.

In order, therefore, that the difference between these syllogisms may be discerned, we must first examine their distinction in the nature of their propositions. For in some propositions a predicative proposition seems to differ from a conditional proposition in nothing except a certain manner of expression. Thus, if someone proposes “A human being is an animal,” and then states it again in this way: “If it is a human being, it is an animal,” the propositions differ to some extent in expression, but they do not seem to signify different things.

First, then, it must be said that a predicative proposition establishes its force not in a condition but in predication alone, whereas in a conditional proposition the basis of consequence is derived from the condition. Again, a predicative proposition is simple, whereas a conditional proposition cannot exist unless it is joined from predicative propositions. Thus, when we say “If it is day, there is light,” there are two predicative, that is, simple, propositions: “It is day” and “There is light.”

Furthermore, what most clearly reveals the property of each is this: a predicative proposition has one subject term and another predicate term. What is made subject in a predicative proposition seems to receive the name of what is predicated in that same proposition. Thus, when we say “A human being is an animal,” “human being” is the subject and “animal” the predicate; and “human being” receives the name “animal,” since the human being himself is proposed as being an animal.

But in the propositions called conditional, the mode of predication is not the same. For one thing is not altogether predicated of another; rather, it is merely said that one thing exists if another exists. Thus, when we say “If she has given birth, she has had intercourse with a man,” it is not being said that giving birth itself is the same thing as having intercourse with a man. It is merely proposed that birth could never have occurred unless intercourse with a man had occurred.

If, however, the property of one kind of proposition should occur within a single and identical proposition, the manner of understanding it will vary according to the form of the statement, as follows. When we say “A human being is an animal,” we make a predicative proposition; but if we propose it in this way—“If it is a human being, it is an animal”—the statement is turned into a conditional one.

In the predicative proposition, therefore, we shall attend to the fact that the human being himself is an animal, that is, that he takes upon himself the name “animal.” In the conditional proposition, by contrast, we understand that if there is some thing which is said to be a human being, there must be some thing which is called an animal.

Thus the predicative proposition declares that the thing it makes subject receives the name of the thing predicated. The meaning of a conditional proposition, however, is that something exists only if something else exists, even if neither receives the name of the other.

Accordingly, once propositions had been distinguished according to the character of their statements, syllogisms too acquired their names: some are called predicative, others conditional. For those whose propositions are predicative we call predicative syllogisms. But those in which the first proposition is hypothetical—for the assumption and the conclusion too may be predicative—are called hypothetical and conditional solely because of the nature of that one hypothetical proposition.

We have explained the simple, that is, predicative, syllogisms in two books, which we composed concerning their constitution. After the discussion of simple syllogisms, the order of treatment requires us to discuss non-simple syllogisms. The non-simple syllogisms are those called hypothetical, which in Latin we call conditional.

They are called non-simple because they are composed of simple propositions and are ultimately resolved into them. In particular, their first propositions derive the force of their own consequence from categorical, that is, simple, syllogisms. For if it is doubted whether the first proposition of a hypothetical syllogism is true, it can be demonstrated by a predicative conclusion.

The assumption in such syllogisms is seen to be predicative in many forms, and likewise the conclusion. Thus, when we say “If it is day, there is light; but it is day,” the assumption “It is day” is predicative. If it is questioned, it will be proved by a predicative syllogism: “There is light”; and so the conclusion again follows predicatively.

Moreover, every conditional proposition is joined from predicative propositions, as has been said. If, therefore, these propositions both receive their credibility from them and derive the order of their parts from them, categorical syllogisms must supply hypothetical syllogisms with the force of their conclusion.

But since we are speaking of hypothetical propositions, we must first explain what “hypothesis” signifies. Hypothesis, from which hypothetical syllogisms receive their name, is used in two senses, as Eudemus holds. For either something of such a kind is assumed through a condition agreed upon between the parties—something which cannot occur in any way—in order that the reasoning may be brought to its conclusion; [Col. 0834A] or, once a condition has been posited, a consequence is shown by the force of conjunction or disjunction.

An example of the former kind of proposition would be the following. Suppose we were demonstrating that all corporeal things subsist through the concurrence of matter and form. We then posit something that cannot occur according to the nature of things: we separate the whole nature of form from the underlying matter, if not in reality, at least in thought. Since nothing remains of corporeal things, we regard it as demonstrated and shown that the substance of corporeal things is constituted by the elements that agree with one another, and that when those elements are separated and withdrawn from one another, the substance perishes.

In this example, then, once the condition of agreement has been posited—so that for a little while we understand as occurring what cannot occur, namely, that form is separated from matter—we investigate what follows: namely, that bodies perish, in order to establish that they consist of those same elements from which they are constituted. Since the destruction of corporeal things follows, we rightly say that all corporeal things consist of form and matter.

But propositions of this kind, which arise from a condition of agreement, do not differ from those expounded in the treatises of the first book of the simple categorical system. Those that differ from simple propositions are propositions in which something is said to exist or not to exist if something has existed or not existed. These are always proposed with conjunctions, as when we say: “If it is a human being, it is an animal”; “If it is three, it is odd”; and other similar cases. For these are proposed in such a way that, if one thing exists, another follows.

Likewise, when we say “If it is a human being, it is not a horse,” the proposition is proposed in negation in the same way as the earlier one was proposed in affirmation. For here it is said: “If this exists, that does not exist”; and the other propositions are formed in the same manner.

Sometimes these may also be stated in this form: “When this exists, that exists,” as when we say “When it is a human being, it is an animal,” or “When it is a human being, it is not a horse.” This statement has the same force as the proposition proposed in the form: “If it is a human being, it is an animal”; “If it is a human being, it is not a horse.”

Hypothetical propositions are also formed through disjunction, as follows: “Either this is the case, or that is the case.” This proposition must not be considered identical with the one stated above in this form: “If this is the case, that is not the case.” The latter is not formed through disjunction, but through negation.

Every negation is indefinite, and for that reason it can occur both among contraries, among the intermediate states between contraries, and among disparate things. By “disparate” I mean things that differ from one another but do not conflict through contrariety, such as earth, clothing, fire, and the like. Thus: “If it is white, it is not black”; “If it is white, it is not red”; “If it is a discipline, it is not a human being.”

But in a proposition formed through disjunction, one of the alternatives must always be posited, as in: “Either it is day or it is night.” If we transfer to disjunction all the cases that properly belong to negation, the reasoning does not work. For what if someone says: “Either it is white or it is black”; “Either it is white or it is red”; “Either it is a discipline or it is a human being”? It may be that none of these is the case.

Since, therefore, a proposition through disjunction is posited only in definite cases in which one of the alternatives must occur, whereas separation through negation can be posited in all cases, including those in which the things do not mutually destroy one another’s nature, the distinction between them is clear.

Every hypothetical proposition, therefore, is formed either through connection—which includes, I declare, the mode formed through negation—or through disjunction. Both modes are composed from simple propositions.

Simple propositions are those which we called predicative in the first book of the introduction to the *Categories*. They are propositions in which something is predicated of something else, either affirmatively or negatively, as in: “It is day”; “There is light.”

If an intervening condition is added to these, the result is: “If it is day, there is light.” One hypothetical proposition is thereby joined from two categorical propositions.

Since every simple proposition is either affirmative or negative, hypothetical propositions can be formed through connection in four ways: either from two affirmatives, or from two negatives, or from an affirmative and a negative, or from a negative and an affirmative.

Examples of all these should be supplied, so that what we are saying may become clearer. From two affirmatives: “If it is day, there is light.” From two negatives: “If it is not an animal, it is not a human being.” From an affirmative and a negative: “If it is day, it is not night.” From a negative and an affirmative: “If it is not day, it is night.”

Since it has been said that the same thing is signified by the conjunction *si* (“if”) and by *cum* (“when”), when they are used in hypothetical propositions, conditionals can be formed in two ways: one accidentally, the other in such a way that they possess a natural consequence.

The accidental kind is formed as follows: “When fire is hot, the sky is round.” For the sky is not round because fire is hot. Rather, the proposition indicates that at the time when fire is hot, the sky is also round.

Other propositions possess a natural consequence. This too has two modes. In one, the consequence must follow, although that consequence does not arise through the positing of the terms; in the other, the consequence arises through the positing of the terms.

An example of the first mode is: “When it is a human being, it is an animal.” For this consequence is supported by unshakable truth. But a thing is not an animal because it is a human being; a genus is not a genus because it is a species. Rather, perhaps the beginning is derived from the genus, and the cause of essence can more properly be drawn from universals, so that it is a human being because it is an animal.

The genus is the cause of the species; nevertheless, the person who says “When it is a human being, it is an animal” establishes a correct and necessary consequence. Such a consequence does not proceed through the positing of the terms.

There are other hypothetical propositions in which a necessary consequence is also found, and in which the position of the terms itself supplies the cause of the consequence, as in: “If the earth is interposed, an eclipse of the moon follows.” This consequence is true, and an eclipse of the moon follows precisely because the earth has been interposed.

These, then, are definite propositions and useful for demonstration.

We divide hypothetical propositions into two simple propositions. The first, to which the conjunction is attached, we call the antecedent; the second, the consequent. Thus, in “If it is day, there is light,” we call the part that says “If it is day” the antecedent, and “There is light” the consequent.

In disjunctive propositions, however, the order of statement makes one part antecedent and the other consequent, as in: “Either it is day or it is night.” The part proposed first is called the antecedent, and the part proposed later the consequent.

This is sufficient concerning the parts of hypothetical propositions.

We must now explain something that is also stated by Aristotle: when the same thing exists or does not exist, it is not necessary that the same other thing exist. For example, if, when *a* exists, it is thereby necessary that *b* exist, then if the same *a* does not exist, it is not necessary that *b* exist merely because *a* does not exist.

For the demonstration of this matter, the definition of impossibility must first be given. It is as follows: that is impossible which, once posited, results in something false and impossible, precisely because the impossible proposition was initially posited.

Let it therefore be posited that, when *a* exists, *b* exists—that is, that there is such a consequence between *a* and *b* that, if the existence of *a* is granted, it is necessary to grant the existence of *b*. Let the proposition therefore be proposed: “If *a* exists, *b* exists.” I say that if *a* does not exist, it is not necessary that *b* exist.

First, then, let us consider what the consequence of the propositions is. If there is a conjunction of this kind—such that if *a* exists, *b* must also exist—then, if *b* does not exist, *a* too must not exist. This is known through the following demonstration.

If *a* exists, *b* must exist. I say that if *b* does not exist, *a* will not exist. For let it be posited that *b* does not exist, and, if possible, let *a* exist. But it has been said that if *a* exists, it must be granted that *b* exists.

Since, then, *b* does exist, *b* will not exist. For because we posit that *b* does not exist, *b* will not exist; but because we posit that *a* exists, *b* will exist. Therefore *b* will both exist and not exist, which cannot happen.

It is therefore impossible for *b* not to exist and *a* to exist. This is how we properly employ the firm demonstration.

The example will make it clearer. If there is a human being, there is an animal; if there is no animal, there is no human being. But it does not follow that if there is no human being, there is no animal, for there are many animals that are not human beings.

Thus, in the consequence of a connected proposition: if the first exists, the second must exist; if the second does not exist, the first will not exist. But if the first does not exist, it is not necessary that the second not exist, nor is it necessary that it exist. That is what we proposed to demonstrate earlier.

Let *a* exist, and let it be the case that whenever *a* exists, *b* must exist. I say that if *a* does not exist, it is not necessary that *b* exist. Nor do I mean that if *a* does not exist, it is necessary that *b* not exist; I mean only that it is not necessary that *b* exist.

For since it was demonstrated shortly before that if *b* does not exist, *a* necessarily does not exist, if it happens that the same term *b* does not exist, *a* will not exist. But if, when *a* does not exist, *b* must exist, then the same *b* will necessarily both exist and not exist. For because it happens that *b* does not exist, it will not exist; but because, if *a* does not exist, *b* must exist, that same term *b* will therefore both exist and not exist, which is impossible.

From these considerations, I believe it has been demonstrated that in the hypothetical consequence, if the first exists, it follows that the second exists; if the second does not exist, it follows that the first does not exist; but if the first does not exist, it does not follow that the second either exists or does not exist.

It is also evident that if the second exists, it does not follow that the first either exists or does not exist. Thus, in the proposition “If it is a human being, it is an animal,” if an animal exists, it does not follow that there is either a human being or no human being.

Likewise, if the first does not exist, it does not follow that the second necessarily either exists or does not exist. Thus, in the same proposition, if there is no human being, it is not necessary that there either be an animal or not be an animal.

Of all these, therefore, [the OCR reading *selae* is uncertain] only two consequences are stable and remain unalterably fixed: if the first exists, it follows that the second exists; and if the second does not exist, it necessarily follows that the first does not exist.

Having established these points, I shall add the following. Although every hypothetical proposition is not simple, but is joined from other propositions, there are nevertheless certain hypothetical propositions which, when compared with other conditionals, are considered simple.

Every conditional proposition is either connected or disjunctive. Since these are joined from predicative propositions, in connected propositions there must be four modes of this conjunction.

A hypothetical proposition is either joined from two simple propositions and is called a simple hypothetical proposition, as in “If *a* exists, *b* exists,” or, as we say, “If it is a human being, it is an animal.” For “It is a human being” and “It is an animal” are two simple propositions.

Or it is joined from two hypothetical propositions and is called composite, as when we say: “If, when *a* exists, *b* exists, and when *c* exists, *d* exists.” An example would be: “If, when it is a human being, it is an animal, and when it is a body, it is a substance.” “If, when it is a human being, it is an animal” is one hypothetical proposition; “When it is a body, it is a substance” is another. From these one proposition is joined, and it is called composite.

Or it is joined from one simple and one hypothetical proposition, as in: “If *a* exists, when *b* exists, *c* exists,” or, as we say: “If it is a human being, when it is an animal, it is a substance.” “It is a human being” is a simple proposition, while “When it is an animal, it is a substance” is shown to be hypothetical through the consequence expressed by the condition.

Or it is formed from a prior hypothetical proposition and a later simple proposition, as when we say: “If, when *a* exists, *b* exists, then *c* also exists.” For example: “If, when it is a human being, it is an animal, then it is also a body.” The proposition “If, when it is a human being, it is an animal” is hypothetical; the later simple proposition that follows this hypothetical proposition is “It is a body.” Since these too are not joined from simple propositions, they are called composite.

The propositions that consist of simple propositions and are called simple hypothetical propositions are constituted by two terms. By “terms” I now mean the parts of simple propositions that are joined together.

Composite hypothetical propositions that consist of two hypothetical propositions are joined by four terms. Those composed of a hypothetical and a simple proposition, or of a simple and a hypothetical proposition, are joined by three terms.

The differences and similarities of these simple and composite hypothetical propositions must therefore be discussed.

When propositions joined from simple propositions are compared with those joined from two hypothetical propositions, the consequence is the same and the proportion remains; only the terms are doubled. For the place occupied in hypothetical propositions composed of simple propositions by the simple propositions themselves is occupied in propositions composed of two hypothetical propositions by the conditions through which those propositions are said to be joined and connected.

In the proposition “If *a* exists, *b* exists,” and in the proposition “If, when *a* exists, *b* exists, and when *c* exists, *d* exists,” the part that is first in the proposition composed of two simple propositions—“If *a* exists”—occupies the same place in the proposition joined from two hypothetical propositions as the first part—“If, when *a* exists, *b* exists.”

For here the consequence has been established by the condition of conjunction between two propositions.

Likewise, the part that follows in the hypothetical proposition joined from both propositions—namely, “*b* exists”—has the same force in the proposition joined from hypothetical propositions as the part that follows there—namely, “When *c* exists, *d* exists.” The only difference is that, in the first proposition joined from simple propositions, one proposition follows another, whereas in the second proposition joined from hypothetical propositions, the condition of one consequence accompanies the consequence of another condition.

For to say “If *a* exists, *b* exists” means nothing other than that the proposition by which we say that *a* exists is accompanied by the proposition by which we predicate that *b* exists. But in the proposition introduced through hypotheticals, when we say “If, when *a* exists, *b* exists, and when *c* exists, *d* exists,” we mean that the consequence between *c* and *d* accompanies the consequence between *a* and *b*, so that, if the latter follows—once it has been posited that *a* exists and *b* exists—the former also undoubtedly follows, once it has been posited that *c* exists and *d* exists.

In propositions consisting of a simple and a hypothetical proposition, the relation is such that either a condition of consequence follows a proposition, or a proposition accompanies a condition of consequence.

When we say “If *a* exists, when *b* exists, *c* exists,” we wish it to be understood that the proposition by which we say “If *a* exists” is followed by the condition by which we say “When *b* exists, *c* exists”—that is, if *a* exists, it must be the case that term *b* is accompanied by term *c*.

But when we say “If, when *a* exists, *b* exists, *c* exists,” we mean nothing other than that the truth of one proposition follows from the consequence between two propositions: if *a* and *b* have a consequence between them, then it must be the case that the condition of the proposition by which we say that *c* exists follows truthfully—that is, if it is necessary, once *a* is posited, that *b* exist, it is also necessary that *c* exist.

The syllogisms of propositions joined from simple propositions and those of propositions joined from non-simple propositions will therefore be similar. Those joined from one simple and one hypothetical proposition will differ from the preceding ones, but will be similar to one another. It makes no difference to the modes of the syllogisms whether the first proposition is hypothetical and the second simple, or, conversely, the first simple and the second hypothetical, except perhaps with respect to the mere alteration of order.

Once the nature of the syllogisms consisting of propositions joined from simple propositions has been demonstrated, the nature of the syllogisms of propositions joined from hypothetical propositions also seems to have been demonstrated. And when the nature of the syllogisms consisting of a simple and a hypothetical proposition has been understood, the nature of the syllogisms produced by propositions in the reverse order is likewise shown.

There is also another species of propositions placed within a connection, which in a certain way occupies the middle position between propositions joined from simple and hypothetical propositions and those joined from two hypothetical propositions.

If one considers the number of terms, they seem to consist of three terms; if one directs one’s attention to the conditionals, they seem to be composed of two conditionals. This intermediate character arises because one of their terms is common to both conditionals.

These propositions are proposed according to the first, second, or third figure.

According to the first figure, they are formed as follows: “If *a* exists, *b* exists, and if *b* exists, *c* exists.” Here *b* is counted in both propositions. There are three terms: “*a* exists,” “*b* exists,” and “*c* exists”; but there are two conditionals: “If *a* exists, *b* exists,” and “If *b* exists, *c* exists,” since *b* is common to both. For this reason propositions of this kind occupy the middle position between propositions composed of three terms and those composed of four.

According to the second figure, the form is: “If *a* exists, *b* exists; if *a* does not exist, *c* exists.”

According to the third figure, it is: “If *b* exists, *a* exists; if *c* exists, *a* does not exist.”

This is sufficient concerning connected propositions.
