Disjunctive propositions always consist of contraries, as in: “Either *a* exists or *b* exists.” When one is posited, the other is removed; when one is removed, the other is posited. For if *a* exists, *b* does not exist; if *a* does not exist, *b* exists. Likewise, if *b* exists, *a* will not exist; if *b* does not exist, *a* will exist.

With these matters settled, let us return to connected propositions. In them either a proposition follows a proposition, a condition follows a condition, a proposition follows a condition, or a condition follows a proposition.

We must therefore explain which propositions seem to be consequents of which propositions; which differ from one another as greatly as possible in the manner of contrariety; and which disagree by contradictory opposition.

Among simple, that is, predicative, propositions, some are proposed without a mode and others with a mode. Those without a mode are any that signify simple existence, as in “It is day,” “Socrates is a philosopher,” and propositions stated in a similar manner.

Those with a mode are proposed as follows: “Socrates is truly a philosopher.” Here “truly” is the mode of the proposition.

But propositions stated with a mode involving necessity or possibility produce the greatest differences among syllogisms. A proposition involving necessity is stated thus: “It is necessary for fire to be hot.” One involving possibility is stated thus: “It is possible for the Trojans to be conquered by the Greeks.”

Hence every proposition either signifies that something inheres, signifies that something necessarily inheres, or, although something is not the case, declares that it can happen.

Of these, the proposition that signifies simple inherence is simple and cannot be reduced into other parts.

The proposition that signifies that something inheres necessarily is expressed in three ways. First, it may be similar to a proposition that signifies simple inherence, as when we say: “It is necessary for Socrates to sit while he is sitting.” For this has the same force as the statement “Socrates is sitting.”

A second meaning of necessity occurs when we propose: “It is necessary for a human being to have a heart while he exists and lives.” This expression seems to signify not that it is necessary for him to have it for as long as he has it, but that it is necessary for him to have it for as long as he is the one who possesses it.

A third meaning of necessity is universal and proper: it predicates necessity absolutely, as when we say “It is necessary for God to be immortal,” without any condition of determination being added.

“Possible” is likewise used in three ways. It may refer to what is possible to exist, as in “It is possible for Socrates to sit while he is sitting”; or to what can occur at every time while the thing remains to which the possibility of something occurring is attributed, as in “It is possible for Socrates to read,” for as long as Socrates exists, he can read; or to what can occur absolutely at every time, as in “It is possible for a bird to fly.”

It is therefore evident from these considerations that some propositions signify inherence, others necessity, and others contingency and possibility. Since necessity and contingency each have a threefold division, individual members of those divisions are related to propositions signifying inherence.

There remain, therefore, two necessary and two contingent propositions. Together with the proposition signifying inherence, these make five differences among propositions.

Of all these propositions, some are affirmative and others negative. An affirmative proposition signifying inherence is one that says “Socrates exists.” A negative one proposes “Socrates does not exist.”

Of necessary propositions, there appear to be two negations of affirmative propositions: one contrary and the other opposed. For of the proposition that says “It is necessary that *a* exist,” either the proposition that says “It is necessary that *a* not exist” or the proposition that says “It is not necessary that *a* exist” may be regarded as its negation.

The proposition “It is necessary that *a* not exist” is contrary to “It is necessary that *a* exist.” For both can be false, as when we say “It is necessary for Socrates to read” and “It is necessary for Socrates not to read.” Both statements are false. For when he reads, he does not read by necessity; and when he does not read, he is not compelled by any necessity to read. Both possibilities remain open.

But the proposition “It is not necessary that *a* exist” is opposed to “It is necessary that *a* exist.” One of these is always true, while the other is always false.

The same reasoning applies to contingent and possible propositions. To the proposition “It is possible that *a* exist,” there may be opposed the proposition “It is possible that *a* not exist,” or the proposition “It is not possible that *a* exist.”

The proposition “It is possible that *a* not exist” is called a contingent negation, and it can be true together with the affirmation “It is possible that *a* exist.” Thus we may say: “It is possible for Socrates to sit” and “It is possible for Socrates not to sit.” These are not called contraries, since they can be true simultaneously.

They are opposed, however, whenever possibility itself is negated, as when, against the proposition “It is possible that *a* exist,” the proposition “It is not possible that *a* exist” is set. This signifies that it cannot happen at all.

Since this is so, propositions signifying inherence, when stated without any mode, are negated fully by adding the negative adverb to “exists.” But when propositions stated with a mode are necessary, and negation is joined to “exist,” as in “It is necessary that *a* not exist,” the result is a necessary negation.

If, however, negation is placed before necessity itself, the negation of necessity is produced, strongly opposed to the affirmative proposition, as in “It is not necessary that *a* exist.”

Likewise, in contingent propositions, if negation is placed before “exist,” a contingent negation is formed, as in “It is possible that *a* not exist.” But if negation is joined to contingency itself, the negation of contingency is formed, strongly opposed to the contingent affirmation, as in “It is not possible that *a* exist.”

Since every proposition is proposed either universally, particularly, indefinitely, or singularly, a universal proposition is stated as “Every human being reads”; a particular proposition as “Some human being reads”; a singular proposition as “Socrates reads”; and an indefinite proposition as “A human being reads.”

It is therefore necessary, as was shown in the introduction to categorical syllogisms, that those propositions should seem most strongly opposed to one another which either affirm a universal while denying it particularly, or deny a universal while affirming it particularly; and, in the case of singular propositions, those which are placed respectively in affirmation and negation.

If the same reasoning is applied to contingent and necessary propositions, the same relation is found in necessary and contingent propositions. If someone says “It is necessary that every *a*-term exist,” and another denies this by saying “It is not necessary that every *a*-term exist,” he has made an opposed negation.

Likewise, if someone says “It is possible that every *a*-term exist,” and another denies it by saying “It is not possible that every *a*-term exist,” he has made an opposed negation. In both cases the negation removes the mode and extinguishes the signification of universality.

This must occur in simple and categorical propositions. We pursued their nature more carefully in the volumes that we entitled *On Interpretation* [Greek: *Περὶ ἑρμηνείας*] in the exposition of the second edition.

If someone therefore investigates the number of all conditional propositions, he will be able to discover it from the categorical propositions. First, it must be investigated in connected propositions composed of two simple propositions, as follows.

Since a simple hypothetical proposition is joined from two categorical propositions, one of them will signify either inherence, or simple contingent existence, or necessity in two ways. If these are affirmative, they will be proposed in an affirmative statement five times.

But since every affirmation has an opposed negation, a negative statement can likewise be pronounced five times. Thus, in the first proposition—which is one part of the hypothetical proposition—there will be ten modal propositions, consisting of affirmation and negation.

The second proposition, which is the other part of the hypothetical proposition, will likewise have the same number.
affirmations and negations; therefore its enunciations too will number ten. But since the first proposition is joined to the second by a certain consequence, so that they form one hypothetical proposition, all [Col. 0842A] ten affirmative and negative propositions will be applied to all ten affirmative and negative propositions. Thus, taken together, they produce one hundred propositions: those which are joined together from simple propositions.

By this method the number of propositions can also be found in propositions joined from a categorical and a hypothetical proposition, or formed from two conditionals. For propositions consisting of a conditional and a categorical proposition, or conversely of three categoricals joined together—if the combination of two predicative affirmations or negations signifies being, necessary being, or contingent being—produce five hundred combinations, since the third proposition will be affirmative or negative; and, if affirmative, it will signify in five ways: being present, or necessary presence in two ways, or contingent presence in two ways. It will likewise be negated in the same number of ways, so that altogether it will be stated ten times. Consequently, when the third proposition is joined to the two preceding propositions, combined and interconnected in one hundred ways, it produces one thousand combinations. For one hundred modes of the two propositions, combined with the ten modes of the third proposition, make one thousand. Ten times one hundred is one thousand.

Again, since a conditional proposition joined from two hypotheticals is connected with four categoricals, and the first two categoricals had been joined in one hundred combinations, it is necessary that the latter two also be connected in one hundred combinations. If, then, the modes of the one hundred superior categorical propositions are combined with the modes of the one hundred posterior categoricals, there will be ten thousand combinations. In propositions that vary in three figures, if the middle term is stated in the same way both in the first and in the second hypothetical, there will be one thousand combinations, corresponding to those formed from three categoricals. For in that case one and the same term will produce three, and no more than three, enunciations in both cases. It is stated in the same way in both, as follows: “If a is, b is; if b is, c is.” Here the term *b* is positioned both with respect to the term *a* and with respect to *c*, signifying presence. The same is to be understood of necessary and contingent propositions.

But if it is stated in this way: “If a is, b is, and if it is necessary that b be, c either is or is not,” the two conditional propositions become four predicative propositions. Consequently, according to the combinations formed from four predicatives, they make ten thousand combinations; and these numbers must be considered both in the first, second, and third figures.

We have indeed indicated how great the number of propositions could be, but the middle term is never enunciated in dissimilar ways. For, in order that a conclusion concerning the extremes may be formed, a middle term intervenes, and its common relation joins the extremes. If, however, the middle term is expressed in different ways in the two propositions, the extremes are not connected, and therefore no syllogism at all can be formed—especially since not even one proposition can properly be said to exist in which the middle term is enunciated dissimilarly.

The number of propositions would be far more numerous if we varied affirmative and negative propositions signifying presence, necessity, and contingency through universal and particular, or contradictory and subaltern, forms. But this is not appropriate, because the terms of conditional propositions are generally enunciated in an unlimited variety of ways. I therefore judged it superfluous to inquire into the multitude of propositions determined according to quantity, since conditionals are not usually stated in a determinate form. Hypothetical propositions, moreover, are for the most part expressed neither by necessity nor by contingency; rather, those are chiefly used in conversation which signify presence.

All of them, however—those which signify presence, those to which necessity is added, and those to which a predication of possibility is attached—intend to retain necessary consequence, for the term is applied accordingly. The necessity of a hypothetical proposition, and the rationale of the propositions from which its connections are joined, require consequence. Thus, when I say, “If Socrates is sitting and is alive,” it is not necessary either that he be sitting or that he be alive; but if he is sitting, it is necessary that he be alive.

Likewise, when we say, “The sun moves; necessarily it comes to setting,” this signifies the same as, “If the sun moves, it comes to setting.” For the necessity of a proposition consists in the unchangeability of its consequence. Again, when we say, “If it is possible for the book to be read, it is possible to reach the third verse” [the manuscript reading *termium* is evidently corrupt], the necessity of the consequence is again preserved. For if it is possible for the book to be read, it is necessary that it be possible to reach the third verse.

Only those propositions that destroy their substance are opposed to hypothetical propositions. The substance of hypothetical propositions consists in the continued validity of their consequence. If, then, someone properly opposes a conditional proposition, he will do so by destroying its consequence. For example, when we say, “If a is, b is,” he does not oppose it by showing either that a is not or that b is not; rather, after positing a, he shows that b does not immediately follow, but that a can be even if the term b is not present.

If the conditional proposition is negative, it is destroyed in the same way. Thus, when we say, “If a is, b is not,” one must not show either that a is not or that b is; rather, while a is, one must show that the term b can be present.

Hypothetical propositions are some affirmative and some negative. Here I am speaking of those which, being placed in a consequence, are said to exist in a connection. An affirmative proposition is, for example, “If a is, b is,” or “If a is not, b is not.” A negative proposition is, “If a is, b is not,” or “If a is not, b is not.” The consequent proposition must be considered in order to judge whether the proposition is affirmative or negative. The same will have to be understood of compound conditional propositions.

But concerning propositions placed in disjunction, I shall speak more suitably and fully when I have dealt with their syllogisms.

Some judge that hypothetical syllogisms, which we call conditional in Latin, consist of five parts, others of four, and others of three. I shall settle this controversy shortly, after first showing by what names the parts of such syllogisms are called. Since every syllogism is woven from propositions, the first is called either the proposition or the premise; the second is called the assumption; and what follows from these is called the conclusion.

For when we say, “If a human being is, an animal is; but a human being is; therefore an animal is,” the enunciation by which we say, “If a human being is, an animal is,” is called the proposition or premise; the one we add to it, “A human being is,” is called the assumption; and the third is called the conclusion, by which we show that whatever is a human being is an animal.

But since it often happens that the consequence expressed by the proposition is not credible, an approval or proof is often added to the proposition, by which what has been proposed is shown to be true. The assumption likewise often does not seem sufficient by itself to establish belief; support in the form of a proof is therefore added to it as well, so that it may appear true. Consequently, hypothetical syllogisms may sometimes have five parts, sometimes four, and sometimes three.

They will consist of five parts if both the proposition and the assumption require proofs. If either the proposition or the assumption requires proof, the syllogism is four-part. If neither requires approval, it remains three-part.

M. Tullius is also found to hold this view. For in the *Rhetorica* he affirms that some syllogisms are five-part and others four-part. Those who do not approve of extending the parts of such syllogisms beyond the number three do not consider the proofs of propositions and assumptions to be parts of the syllogism.

They do not consider there to be a proposition from which a syllogism can arise if the hearer does not assent to it. If the proof added to a doubtful proposition is itself doubtful, and by establishing credibility for the same proposition to which it is attached makes that proposition suitable for a syllogism, then the proposition begins to be a syllogism’s proposition only when, through the proof, it has been rendered such that something can be inferred from it. Something can be inferred from it only when, with the aid of the proof, it can be conceded by the hearer.

Therefore, the proof appears to be a certain limb, as it were a support, of a doubtful proposition or assumption, but not a part of the syllogism itself. Our view accordingly agrees more closely with those who declare that the syllogism consists of three parts. For any proof attached either to a proposition or to an assumption is called the proof of that proposition or assumption.

Since, then, it is referred not to the syllogism but to the proposition or assumption whose proof it is, it ought not properly to be regarded as a part of the syllogism. No one is unaware of the objection that the parts of parts are also said to be parts of the whole. But it makes a great difference whether those things are themselves primary parts of the whole, or whether they occupy the outermost position among secondary parts.

Furthermore, if a proposition is probable and evident by itself, the entire syllogism does not require proof. But if the proposition has no credibility by itself, it necessarily requires something like the testimony of a proof. The syllogism, therefore, does not require proof insofar as it is a syllogism; rather, the proposition requires it if it lacks credibility of its own. The same can also be said of the assumption.

It is therefore clear that the view asserting that the syllogism is joined from only three parts ought to be preferred. Moreover, if a proposition requires proof in order that belief in its truth may follow, it will be demonstrated by some syllogism. How, then, can a syllogism properly be called a part of a simple syllogism? For the proof of the proposition itself must either be a syllogism or arise from a syllogism.

These matters having been determined, we should now explain those syllogisms whose propositions, placed in a connection, consist of two terms. Their form is twofold. There are four formed through affirmation of the antecedent; these are the first and perfect hypotheticals. There are also four formed through negation of the consequent; since these require demonstration, they do not appear to be perfect. But from negation of the antecedent and affirmation of the consequent no syllogism at all is produced.

Let us first explain the number of all such propositions, so that recognition of the syllogisms formed from them may be easy. They are four:

“If a is, b is”;  
“If a is, b is not”;  
“If a is not, b is”;  
“If a is not, b is not.”

We must first discuss the prior and perfect syllogisms. Their first mode proceeds from the first proposition, as follows: “If a is, b is; but a is; therefore b is.” Since the first proposition merely states the condition that, if a is, the existence of the term b must follow, the assumption takes up and posits what precedes it and says, “But a is.” It follows, therefore, that b is, for this results from the consequence of the first proposition.

But if we posit what follows by taking it as the assumption, no syllogism is produced. Let the consequence be, “If a is, b is,” and let what follows be assumed in this way: “But b is.” It does not follow that a either is or is not.

This will become clearer from an example. Let the proposition be, “If a human being is, an animal is,” and let the existence of an animal—the consequent—be assumed. It will not be necessary that a human being either is or is not, since, although an animal exists, a human being may otherwise either be or not be.

The second mode is that in which the prior part of the proposition is repeated in the assumption. It proceeds from the second proposition set out above, as follows: “If a is, b is not; but a is; therefore b is not.” For this was what had been proposed: if a were, b would not be. Once the antecedent has been assumed, the conclusion concerning the consequent follows.

But if the consequent is assumed, no syllogism appears to result, because no necessity follows in this way: “If a is, b is not; but b is not; therefore a either is or is not.” It is not necessary that a either be or not be.

Let the proposition, for example, be, “If something is black, it is not white,” and let what follows be assumed: “But it is not white.” It will not be necessary that it be black or not black, because, although it is not white, it may be something intermediate.

The third mode is the mode of those syllogisms that proceeds from the third proposition, in which what precedes is posited in the assumption, as follows: “If a is not, b is; but a is not; therefore b is.” This conclusion again follows from the condition of the proposition, for what had been proposed was that, if a were not, b would be.

But if you reverse the relation and assume that b is—that is, what follows—it will not be necessary that what precedes either be or not be. An example of this cannot be found, because if it is proposed that, when a is not, b is, there appears to be no intermediate between a and b. In such cases, if one of the two is not present, the other must immediately be present; and if one is present, the other must immediately be absent.

Thus syllogisms seem in a certain way to arise from the consequent being posited in these cases. As far as the nature of the thing is concerned, this is so; but as far as the condition of the proposition itself is concerned, it does not follow at all. This is clear from what was said above. In both the preceding modes, when the consequent is posited, nothing is inferred with necessity. Here, however, in the third mode, insofar as the combination of propositions is concerned, when what followed is posited in the assumption, no syllogism is produced.

Insofar, however, as the nature of the things is concerned—things in which these propositions alone can be enunciated—the consequence appears necessary, as in: “If it is not day, it is night”; and from “If it is night,” it necessarily follows that it is not day. These syllogisms resemble those established in disjunction, which I shall mention shortly and to which I shall explain both their differences and their similarities.

The fourth mode proceeds from the fourth proposition, when it is stated thus: “If a is not, b is not; but a is not; therefore b is not.” Here too it is shown to follow from the proposition, which proposed that b would not be if the prior term a had not been present.

But if we assume what follows, no necessity appears possible. For example, if we say, “But b is not,” it will not be necessary that a either be or not be. Let the proposition be, “If an animal is not, a human being is not,” and let the assumption be, “But a human being is not.” It is not necessary that an animal either be or not be.

It has therefore been demonstrated that in syllogisms of this kind, if what precedes is assumed by being posited, the syllogisms are perfect, probable from the propositions themselves, and necessary. But if what follows is assumed by being posited, no necessity is produced, except in the third mode. Since that mode resembles syllogisms formed from enunciations stated disjunctively, it appears to preserve necessity in the things about which it can be proposed, although it does not preserve it in the combination of propositions. This is argued from the other three modes—first, second, and fourth—in which, when the consequent part of the proposition is assumed by being posited, nothing is accomplished with necessity.

We have sufficiently explained these syllogisms joined from two terms, in which the first part of the proposition is assumed by being posited, insofar as concerns the method of their construction. We must now discuss those in which the consequent of the proposition is taken in such a way that it is destroyed.

These too have four modes, since the prior part of the proposition cannot be destroyed in such a way that any necessity of syllogism follows. The first mode of these syllogisms proceeds from the first proposition, as follows: “If a is, b is; but b is not; therefore a is not.” Here the term b, which had been the consequent in the first proposition, has been destroyed in the assumption, so that the term a, which had been the first part of the proposition, may likewise be destroyed.

The necessity is proved in the following manner. What had been proposed was, “If a is, b is”; and the assumption has been made so that the consequent part of the proposition might be destroyed, namely, that b is not. I say that it follows that a is not. For if a can be present when b is not, the first proposition—which says, “If a is, b is”—will be pointless. Yet that proposition is valid: when a is, b is.

If, then, when b is not, a is—as the assumption proposes—the same b will both be and not be. It will not be, because the assumption proposes that b is not; but it will be, because if a is, b will be. This is impossible. Therefore, if b is not, a will not be.

This, then, is the first mode of those syllogisms formed by destroying the consequent part of the proposition. They are not perfect or self-evident, but require either the proof I mentioned above or some other proof in order to be shown true.

But if the first part of the proposition is destroyed, there will be no syllogism. Let us say, for example: “If a is, b is; but a is not.” It does not follow that b either is or is not, as is also demonstrated by an example. Let the proposition be, “If a human being is, an animal is”; but a human being is not. It will not be necessary that an animal either be or not be.

The second mode is based on contradiction in the assumption and proceeds from the second proposition. It is as follows: “If a is, b is not; but b is; therefore a is not.” Here again the second part of the proposition has been destroyed, for whereas the second part of the proposition said that b would not be, the assumption declares that b is.

Affirmation destroys the negation which follows from the assumption, so that a is not, as follows. Let the proposition be, “If a is, b is not,” and let b be present. I say that a will not be. For if a is, while b is, the same b will both be and not be. It will not be according to the first proposition, which says, “If a is, b is not”; but it will be according to the assumption, by which we say that b is.

But if the preceding part of the proposition is removed, no necessity will result. Let us say in such a proposition, “If a is, b is not”: “But a is not.” It does not follow that b either is or is not.

This is argued by the following example. Let us say, “If something is black, it is not white,” and let us assume that it is not black. It does not immediately follow that it is either white or not white, for there may be something intermediate.

The third mode is derived from the third proposition. It is stated as follows: “If a is not, b is; but b is not; therefore a is.” Here too the consequent part of the proposition has been assumed, and although it was affirmed in the proposition, it has been negated in the assumption; the consequence is valid and completes the syllogism in this way.

For if it is true that, when a is not, b is, I say that if b is not, a is. For if it were possible that, when b is not, a also not be, the first proposition would be pointless—the proposition that says, “When a is not, b is.” Then b would both be and not be: it would not be according to the assumption, which proposes that b is not; but it would be because, if the term a is denied, then, once the term b is posited as not being, b will be, since a is not. This is impossible.

Therefore it cannot happen that, when b is not, a is not. It follows, then, that when b is not, a is.

But if the prior part of the proposition, which is the antecedent, is removed, there is no syllogism. For when we say, “If a is not, b is,” and assume, “But a is,” nothing necessary follows—neither that b is nor that b is not—according to the nature of the combination itself.

Here too, as in the cases in which the second term was posited in the assumption, we must say that, according to the nature of the combination itself, no syllogism is produced; but according to the terms, in which alone such a proposition can be stated, it is necessary that, if a is, b is not. For this can truly be predicated only of contraries and of things that are immediate, that is, that have no intermediate. Thus, when we say, “If it is not day, it is night”: if it is not day, it will be night; if it is not night, it will be day; if it is day, it will not be night; and if it is night, it will not be day.

The fourth mode of these syllogisms descends from the fourth proposition. Its first proposition is: “If a is not, b is not; but b is; therefore a is.” Here too the second part of the proposition has been assumed, and since it had been posited with a negation, it has been destroyed by an affirmation; for affirmation destroys the force of negation.

Here too the necessity of the syllogism is contained in the same way. For if, after the proposition “When a is not, b is not” has been posited, b is assumed to be, I say that it follows also that a is. For if it is possible that, while b is, a is not, the first proposition is pointless—the proposition that declares that, when a is not, b is not. Thus once again the same b will both be and not be.

It will be b according to the assumption, for it says, “But b is.” But if, once this has been posited, a can be absent, b will again not be, because the first proposition says, “If a is not, b is not.” This is impossible.

But if the portion of the proposition that precedes is removed, nothing necessary follows. Let us say, for example: “If a is not, b is not”; and let us assume, “But a is.” It does not follow that b must necessarily either be or not be, as in this syllogism: “If an animal is not, a human being is not; but an animal is; therefore it is not necessary either that a human being be or that a human being not be.”

These four syllogisms are therefore called imperfect, because they do not possess in themselves an open and evident necessity of consequence; that necessity is supplied to them by proof.

To summarize briefly: in simple hypothetical syllogisms having propositions joined in a connection, however they are formed, if the first part of the proposition is assumed—if it is posited—four syllogisms will be self-evident and perfect. But if what follows is assumed, there is no necessity of syllogism, except in the third mode alone. That mode appears to retain the necessity of the conclusion not because of the nature of the combination, but because of the contrariety of the terms, in which alone such a proposition can be stated.

Thus, if something stated in the proposition is posited in the assumption, there must be four or five perfect syllogisms: four when the first part of the proposition is assumed by being posited, but five when the second part is assumed by being posited—if we attend not to the nature of the combination but to the terms.

But if something stated in the first proposition is removed in the assumption, and the consequent part of the proposition is removed, four imperfect syllogisms requiring proof will result. If, however, the prior part of the proposition is removed, there will be no necessity of syllogism, except in the third mode, in which the combination does not produce the necessity but the nature of the terms does.

Consequently, here too there are four or five syllogisms: four if the second part of the proposition has been destroyed, and a fifth if it is measured not by the nature of the combination but by the proper character of the terms.

Therefore, if the first proposition consists of two terms, there are eight or ten syllogisms, and no more.

Concerning these conditional syllogisms, whose propositions are connected and consist of two simple predicatives, enough has now been said. We must now discuss those syllogisms that are connected from a predicative and a hypothetical proposition, or from a hypothetical proposition and a predicative one.

The combinations of all these syllogisms will readily become clear if their number is first set out. The first are those which are connected from a predicative and a hypothetical proposition. They are as follows:

If a exists, and b exists, c exists. If a exists, and b exists, c does not exist. If a exists, and b does not exist, c exists. If a exists, and b does not exist, c does not exist. If a does not exist, and b exists, c exists. If a does not exist, and b exists, c does not exist. If a does not exist, and b does not exist, c exists. [Col. 0849C] If a does not exist, and b does not exist, c does not exist.

First, it seems that the nature of these propositions must be considered. For a conditional proposition is not produced by placing the condition in just any manner, but only when the consequent follows because of the condition that has been posited. For if someone says, “If a human being exists, then, since it is an animal, it is animate,” the appended condition does not seem to make the consequent necessary. For even if no human being exists, nevertheless, if something is an animal, it is animate. But if the proposition is framed as follows—“If it is a human being, then, since it is animate, it is an animal”—the basis of the consequent seems to reside in the condition. For it is not necessary that, since something is animate, it be an animal, unless it is a human being or something of that kind which is posited as animate. In that case, what is animate must be an animal: a human being, or any other such thing, is animate.

We must therefore proceed through the individual propositions and examine the nature of each of them in the following way. The first proposition, which says, “If a exists, and b exists, c exists,” must have this character: b must be able to exist even apart from a, although, if a exists, b cannot fail to exist. Again, the same term b must also be able to exist when c does not exist; nor must it be necessary, merely because b is posited, that c also exist. Rather, c must be necessary only when term b follows term a. Thus, let a be “human being,” b “animate,” and c “animal.” For “animate” can exist both apart from “human being” and apart from “animal.” But if something is a human being, it must be animate; and since animateness follows the essence of a human being, it follows that what is animate is an animal. [Col. 0850A]

Similarly, the second proposition, which says, “If a exists, and b exists, c does not exist,” must have this character: b must be able to exist apart from a, but, when a exists, b must necessarily exist as well. On the other hand, c must be such that it cannot exist together with a, although it can exist together with b, and can either exist or not exist with b. It must be unable to exist with b only when b follows a. Thus, let a be “human being,” b “animate,” and c “insensible.” For “animate” can exist apart from “human being”; but if something is a human being, it must be animate. “Insensible,” however, can either exist or not exist together with “animate.” Yet “insensible” and “animate” are incompatible when it is animate for the reason that it has been predicated to be a human being.

The third proposition must have as its term a something that can never exist together with term b. Term c, however, must be such that it can either exist or not exist when b does not exist; but c must be necessary only if b does not exist because term a has been predicated. Thus, let a be “human being,” b “inanimate,” and c “sensible.” For if something is a human being, it is not inanimate; but it can either be sensible or not sensible when it is not inanimate. There can indeed be things that are neither inanimate nor sensible, such as trees. Nevertheless, something must be sensible when it is not inanimate, if it is not inanimate for the reason that it has been predicated to be a human being.

Again, the fourth proposition must have this property: term b can in no way exist if a exists, whereas c can either exist or not exist if b does not exist. But c must be necessarily absent when b is absent, only if b is absent because term a was previously posited. Thus, let a be “human being,” b “inanimate,” and c “insensible.” For the inanimate will not exist if the thing is a human being; but the insensible can either exist or not exist if it is not inanimate. The insensible must be absent only when it is not inanimate, since it is not inanimate for the reason that it has been predicated to be a human being. [Col. 0850C]

The fifth proposition must likewise have terms of the following kind: if a does not exist, b must necessarily exist; if b exists, c can either exist or not exist. c must be necessary only when b exists, and b must exist because term a has been denied. Thus, let a be “animate,” b “insensible,” and c “nonliving.” If something is not animate, it immediately follows that it is insensible. “Nonliving,” however, can exist if it is insensible, as in the case of a stone; but something can also be insensible without being nonliving, as trees are. Yet, once “insensible” has been posited, it must necessarily be nonliving only when it is insensible for the reason that it is not animate. [Col. 0850D]

The sixth proposition requires terms of the following kind: b must necessarily exist if a does not exist; but, if b exists, term c can either exist or not exist. c must necessarily not exist when b exists, provided that b exists because term a has been posited as absent. Thus, let a be “animate,” b “insensible,” and c “living.” Something must be insensible if it is not animate; but, if it is insensible, it may fail to live, as a stone does, or it may live, as a tree does. Yet it must necessarily fail to live when it is insensible, if it is insensible because it has been posited as not animate. [Col. 0851A]

The seventh mode must be constructed with terms of the following kind: b cannot exist without a; but, if c does not exist, b can either exist or not exist. c must nevertheless necessarily exist if b does not exist, when b has been posited as absent because a has been denied. Let a be “animate,” b “sensible,” and c “nonliving.” Something cannot be sensible unless it is animate. Therefore, if it is not animate, it will not be sensible. But if it is not sensible, it may be nonliving, as stones are; it may also not be nonliving, as trees are. Yet, once “sensible” has been denied, it must necessarily be nonliving, if it is not sensible because it has been posited as not animate. [Col. 0851B]

The eighth proposition must be connected with terms of the following kind: term b cannot exist if a does not exist; but, when b does not exist, term c can either exist or not exist. c must nevertheless necessarily not exist when b does not exist, if b does not exist because term a was previously denied. Thus, let a be “animate,” b “sensible,” and c “living.” Something cannot be sensible unless it is animate. Yet, if it is not sensible, it can either be living or not living: not living, as stones are; living, as trees are. But it must necessarily not be living if it is not sensible, when it is not sensible because its being animate was previously denied.

It is therefore established from these propositions that term c, however b may be constituted, can be assumed either affirmatively or negatively in conditional propositions which, in the complete statement, are placed after predicative propositions. From these assumptions arise various combinations of syllogisms.

These matters having been clarified, something general should now be stated. Since there are eight propositions connected from a predicative and a hypothetical proposition—the propositions written above—four of them establish the consequence on the condition that term a exists, while four posit the condition so that term a does not exist. Syllogisms arise from them in the following way.

From the first proposition, “If a exists, and b exists, c exists”:

- “But a exists; therefore, since b exists, c exists.”
- Or: “But, since b exists, c does not exist; therefore a does not exist.”

That such an assumption is possible can be understood from the nature of the propositions described above.

From the second proposition, “If a exists, and b exists, c does not exist”:

- “But a exists; therefore, since b exists, c does not exist.”
- Or: “But, since b exists, c exists; therefore a does not exist.”

From the third, “If a exists, and b does not exist, c exists”:

- “But a exists; therefore, since b does not exist, c does not exist.”
- Or: “But, since b does not exist, c does not exist; therefore a does not exist.”

From the fourth, “If a exists, and b does not exist, c does not exist”:

- “But a exists; therefore, since b does not exist, c exists.”
- Or: “But, since b does not exist, c exists; therefore a does not exist.”

In these four propositions, in which term a is posited as existing, if the same term a is assumed, term c is shown either to exist or not to exist. The same applies if term c is assumed: if c is assumed not to exist when it exists, or to exist when it does not, term a will be shown not to exist.

From the fifth proposition, “If a does not exist, and b exists, c exists,” syllogisms arise as follows:

- “But a does not exist; therefore, since b exists, c exists.”
- “But a exists; therefore, since b exists, c does not exist.”
- “But, since b exists, c does not exist; therefore a exists.”
- “But, since b exists, c exists; therefore a does not exist.”

This proposition produces four syllogisms because, in these cases alone, when one thing does not exist, another can be posited as existing, where the contraries lack an intermediate. For in such cases, when one is removed, the other is posited, or, when one is posited, the other must be removed.

From the sixth, “If a does not exist, and b exists, c does not exist”:

- “But a does not exist; therefore, since b exists, c does not exist.”
- Or: “But, since b exists, c exists; therefore a exists.”

From the seventh, “If a does not exist, and b does not exist, c exists”:

- “But a does not exist; therefore, since b does not exist, c exists.”
- “But a exists; therefore, since b does not exist, c does not exist.”
- “But, since b does not exist, c does not exist; therefore a exists.”
- “But, since b does not exist, c exists; therefore a does not exist.”

Here too, for the same reason, four deductions are produced.

From the eighth, “If a does not exist, and b does not exist, c does not exist”:

- “But a does not exist; therefore, since b does not exist, c does not exist.”
- Or: “But, since b does not exist, c exists; therefore a exists.”

In these four propositions, if the nonexistence of a is assumed, the existence or nonexistence of c is concluded. But if c is assumed as not existing when it exists, or as existing when it does not, the existence of a is always concluded, except in the fifth and seventh modes, in which, when c is assumed to exist, a is shown not to exist.

The general rule for all of them, except the fifth and seventh modes, is that if term a is assumed in the manner in which it was posited in the first statement, the condition that follows is confirmed in the conclusion. But if the following condition is assumed in the opposite manner from that in which it was posited in the statement, the categorical proposition that comes first is destroyed. In the seventh and fifth modes, however, either term, assumed in either manner, produces a conclusion in both parts.

Thus there are sixteen, or rather twenty, syllogisms: eight when term a is assumed as it was posited, and eight when term c is assumed in the opposite manner from that in which it was placed in the proposition. Four more are added from the seventh and fifth modes, which produce conclusions in both directions. In the remaining combinations there is no necessary consequence.

To make the meaning clearer, I have written out the propositions with their terms, so that, according to the modes of assumption described above, the demonstration might proceed not by reasoning alone but also by example, making the instruction clearer to those who follow it.

If a is a human being, and b is animate, c is an animal.  
If a is a human being, and b is animate, c is not insensible.  
If a is a human being, and b is not animate, c is sensible.  
If a is a human being, and b is not animate, c is not insensible.  
If a is not animate, and b is insensible, c is nonliving.  
If a is not animate, and b is insensible, c is not living. [Col. 0853A]  
If a is not animate, and b is not sensible, c is nonliving.  
If a is not animate, and b is not sensible, c is not living.

The syllogisms produced from propositions of this kind—those in which the first is predicative and the second hypothetical—having now been dealt with, let us pass to those which are connected from a first conditional proposition and a second predicative proposition. Their total number must be set out, so that the reader may recognize what we are discussing.

If, when a exists, b exists, c exists.  
If, when a exists, b exists, c does not exist.  
If, when a exists, b does not exist, c exists.  
If, when a exists, b does not exist, c does not exist.  
If, when a does not exist, b exists, c exists.  
If, when a does not exist, b exists, c does not exist.  
If, when a does not exist, b does not exist, c exists.  
If, when a does not exist, b does not exist, c does not exist.

The first proposition must have terms of the following kind: a must be able to exist apart from b and c; but, if a exists, c must be necessary when b follows term a. Thus, let a be “animate,” b “human being,” and c “animal.” For “animate” can exist both apart from “human being” and apart from “animal.” But what is animate must be an animal when what is animate is a human being.

The second proposition must be constructed with terms such that a can exist apart from b and c, as well as together with them. Nevertheless, c must necessarily not exist when a exists, if b follows from the positing of a. Thus, let a be “animate,” b “human being,” and c “horse.” For something animate can be a human being or a horse. But what is animate must not be a horse if what is animate is a human being.

The third proposition is connected with terms such that a can either exist or not exist together with b and c; nevertheless, it must necessarily exist together with c if, when term a is posited, term b is denied. Thus, let a be “animate,” b “animal,” and c “insensible.” For what is animate can be an animal or not an animal, insensible or not insensible. But what is animate must be insensible if, when “animate” is posited, “animal” is denied.

The terms of the fourth proposition are such that a can either exist or not exist together with b and with c; but c must be separated from a in every way if, when a is posited, b is denied. Thus, let a be “animate,” b “animal,” and c “human being.” For what is animate can be either an animal or not an animal, and likewise can be either a human being or not a human being. Yet, when it is animate, it must not be a human being if, with “animate” posited, its being an animal is denied.

The fifth proposition is connected with terms such that, if a does not exist, b and c can either exist or not exist; but, when a does not exist, c must exist if, upon the denial of a, the existence of b follows. Thus, let a be “nonliving,” b “human being,” and c “animal.” For if it is not nonliving, human being and animal can either exist or not exist. But animal must be necessary when nonliving is denied, if the denial of nonliving is followed by the existence of a human being. [Col. 0854A]

The sixth proposition must be joined by members such that, if term a does not exist, b and c can either exist or not exist; but, when a is denied, c must necessarily not exist, when the affirmation of b accompanies the denial of a. Thus, let a be “nonliving,” b “human being,” and c “horse.” For what is not nonliving can either be a human being or a horse, or neither; but a horse must necessarily not exist when nonliving is denied, if the denial of nonliving is followed by the positing of a human being.

The seventh proposition must have terms such that, if a does not exist, b and c can both exist and not exist; but c must necessarily exist if the denial of a is followed by the denial of b. Thus, let a be “animal,” b “animate,” and c “nonliving.” If an animal does not exist, animate and nonliving can either exist or not exist. But, if an animal does not exist, nonliving must exist when the absence of an animal is followed by the absence of the animate.

The eighth proposition is one in which, when term a is denied, terms b and c can both exist and not exist. But c must necessarily not exist if term a is denied and the denial of term b follows. Thus, let a be “nonliving,” b “animal,” and c “human being.” If nonliving does not exist, animal and human being can either exist or not exist.

These matters having been clarified, the following general point must be made: the first four propositions establish the condition that a exists, whereas the later propositions establish it on the condition that a does not exist. From all of them syllogisms arise in the following manner.

From the first proposition, “If, when a exists, b exists, c exists”:

- “But, when a exists, b exists; therefore c exists.”
- Or: “But c does not exist; therefore, since a exists, b does not exist.”

That such conclusions are possible is recognized from the nature of the propositions described above, for term a could both exist and not exist together with b.

From the second, “If, when a exists, b exists, c does not exist”:

- “But, when a exists, b exists; therefore c does not exist.”
- Or: “But c exists; therefore, since a exists, b does not exist.”

From the third, “If, when a exists, b does not exist, c exists,” deductions arise in both directions:

- “But, when a exists, b does not exist; therefore c exists.”
- “But, when a exists, b exists; therefore c does not exist.”
- “But c does not exist; therefore, since a exists, b exists.”
- “But c exists; therefore, since a exists, b does not exist.”

This produces a deduction in both directions because these propositions could be placed among terms in which immediate contraries are found. In such cases, the positing of one removes the other, and the removal of one posits the other.

From the fourth, “If, when a exists, b does not exist, c does not exist”:

- “But, when a exists, b does not exist; therefore c does not exist.”
- Or: “But c exists; therefore, since a exists, b exists.”

From the fifth, “If, when a does not exist, b exists, c exists”:

- “But, when a does not exist, b exists; therefore c exists.”
- Or: “But c does not exist; therefore, since a does not exist, b does not exist.”

From the sixth, “If, when a does not exist, b exists, c does not exist”:

- “But, when a does not exist, b exists; therefore c does not exist.”
- Or: “But c exists; therefore, since a does not exist, b does not exist.”

From the seventh, “If, when a does not exist, b does not exist, c exists,” deductions arise in both directions:

- “But, when a does not exist, b does not exist; therefore c exists.”
- “But, when a does not exist, b exists; therefore c does not exist.”
- “But c does not exist; therefore, since a does not exist, b exists.”
- “But c exists; therefore, since a does not exist, b does not exist.”

Here too, for the same reason, a syllogism arises from either assumption. For it was said that one thing exists when another does not exist only in the case of immediate contraries.

From the eighth, “If, when a does not exist, b does not exist, c does not exist”:

- “But, when a does not exist, b does not exist; therefore c does not exist.”
- Or: “But c exists; therefore, since a does not exist, b exists.”

In all the syllogisms described above, the rule is this: if term b is assumed in the manner in which it was placed in the proposition, it concludes term c in the manner in which it was placed in that same proposition. But if term c is assumed in the opposite manner from that in which it was placed in the proposition, term b is shown in the conclusion in the opposite manner, except in the third and seventh modes. In those modes, even if term b is assumed in the opposite manner from that in which it was placed in the proposition, it concludes term c in the opposite manner from that in which it was placed; or, if term c is assumed in the manner in which it was placed in the proposition, it concludes term b in the same manner in which it had been placed in that proposition.

Consequently, there are sixteen, or twenty, syllogisms. When the first hypothetical propositions are assumed, there are eight; there are eight when the second, predicative propositions are assumed; and four are added from the third and seventh modes, which produce deductions in both directions. Thus, in these combinations of propositions also, there are altogether sixteen, or twenty, syllogisms. However you vary the assumptions in any other way, nothing necessary follows.

To make the entire account of the propositions and syllogisms clear, we have added examples, through which what was taught above may more readily become evident:

If, when a is animate, b is a human being, c is an animal.  
If, when a is animate, b is a human being, c is not a horse.  
If, when a is animate, b is not an animal, c is insensible.  
If, when a is animate, b is not an animal, c is a human being.  
If, when a is not nonliving, b is a human being, c is an animal.  
If, when a is not nonliving, b is a human being, c is not a horse.  
If, when a is not an animal, b is not animate, c is nonliving.  
If, when a is not nonliving, b is not an animal, c is a human being.

Enough has now been said about the syllogisms connected with propositions of this kind, which consist of a hypothetical and a predicative proposition.

Now we must discuss those syllogisms whose propositions contain three terms in such a way that they occupy an intermediate position between propositions constructed from a hypothetical and a predicative proposition, and those connected from two hypothetical propositions. We set them out here for this reason: like the preceding propositions, these too contain three terms, and the treatment will proceed more easily from similar cases to similar cases.

Their syllogisms are numerous, and none of them can be perfect, since they are not clear in themselves and require the assistance of a proof supplied from outside in order that they may be accepted as trustworthy. The proof of such syllogisms is itself a syllogism established in another order. As has been said, they are produced through the first, second, and third figures.

The propositions of the first figure are these:

If a exists, b exists, and if b exists, c exists.  
If a exists, b exists, and if b exists, c does not exist. [Col. 0856A]  
If a exists, b does not exist, and if b does not exist, c exists.  
If a exists, b does not exist, and if b does not exist, c does not exist.  
If a does not exist, b exists, and if b exists, c exists.  
If a does not exist, b exists, and if b exists, c does not exist.  
If a does not exist, b does not exist, and if b does not exist, c exists.  
If a does not exist, b does not exist, and if b does not exist, c does not exist.

If the method of deduction is such that the assumption establishes and confirms what the first statement declares, there must be sixteen combinations, of which only eight preserve the necessity of the consequence; the other eight seem to have nothing suitable for establishing belief. Again, if the assumption overturns what the first proposition establishes, there must likewise be sixteen combinations, of which eight are held by firm necessity, while the other eight are more often governed by unreliable variation. Syllogisms are produced in the first, second, and third figures.

We shall therefore explain all the modes of the three figures, beginning with the first, so that nothing is left unexamined.

The first mode of the first figure derives from the first proposition, when we state: “If a exists, b exists, and if b exists, c must necessarily exist.” If a exists, then c must also necessarily exist. The demonstration is as follows. If a exists, it follows that b exists; for the first proposition posits precisely that, if a exists, b exists. But if b exists, c exists; for this is what the second part of the proposition declares, namely, that if b exists, c necessarily follows. Once these points have been granted, it follows that, when a exists, c must also exist.

We call this syllogism imperfect because it required the testimony of a proof. The proof was a demonstration by means of a syllogism, by which we establish the necessity of such a consequence. For when the proposition was stated—“If a exists, b exists, and if b exists, c must exist”—and the assumption posited what the affirmation had established, namely a, and a conclusion following that assumption was said to be that c must necessarily exist, this would not be evident from the nature and property of the syllogism itself. A syllogistic proof was therefore added in the following way:

If a exists, b exists;  
but if b exists, c exists;  
therefore, if a exists, c must necessarily exist.

It is clear that the same procedure must be expected in the remaining cases.

This combination assumes and establishes what had first been posited in the proposition. But if someone assumes what followed by positing it, there is no necessary syllogism. Thus, we say: “If a exists, b exists, and if b exists, c must necessarily exist; but c exists.” It is not therefore necessary that b either exist or not exist. Since it is not necessary that b exist or not exist, it will not be necessary that a exist or not exist. The following example confirms this: “If it is a human being, it is an animal; and if it is an animal, it will be an animate body. But it is an animate body.” It will not therefore be necessary that it be an animal, and consequently not even that it be a human being.

The second mode of the first figure is as follows: “If a exists, b exists, and if b exists, c must necessarily not exist; but a exists. Therefore c does not exist.” Its demonstration is as follows. If a exists, b exists; this is shown by the first condition, namely, “If a exists, b exists.” But, since b exists, c must necessarily not exist. This was presented by the consequence in which it was declared that, if b existed, it would necessarily follow that c also did not exist. Therefore, if a exists, c will not exist.

But if the assumption posits what the proposition establishes last—namely, that c does not exist—there is no syllogism. For suppose the proposition is: “If it is a human being, it is an animal; and if it is an animal, it is not a stone. But it is not a stone.” It will not therefore be necessary either that it be or that it not be an animal. In the same way, neither will it be necessary that it be a human being. For if it is not a stone, it may be wood, or something else that is neither an animal nor included among human beings.

The third mode of the first figure arises when the assumption establishes what the first proposition posits. Its starting point is the third proposition, when we state: “If a exists, b does not exist, and if b does not exist, c must necessarily exist.” Here again, if term a is assumed in the manner in which it was placed in the first statement, we say: “But a exists; therefore c exists.” The proof is similar to those above: because a exists, b does not exist; because b does not exist, c exists; therefore, because a exists, c exists.

But if term c is assumed, nothing necessary follows. Thus, let the proposition be: “If it is a human being, it is not insensible; and if it is not insensible, it is an animal. But it is an animal.” It is not therefore necessary that it be a human being.

The fourth mode begins from the fourth proposition, which is formed from the following proposition: “If a exists, b does not exist, and if b does not exist, c also must necessarily not exist.” Here, if a exists, c must necessarily not exist. The demonstration is the same as in the preceding modes.

But if the nonexistence of c is assumed, there is no necessary combination. For suppose the proposition is: “If it is a human being, it is not irrational; and if it is not irrational, it is not inanimate. But it is not inanimate.” It is not therefore necessary that it be a human being.

The fifth mode descends from the fifth statement, whose first proposition is: “If a does not exist, b exists; and if b exists, c must also necessarily exist.” But a does not exist; therefore c must exist. Here too the previously stated condition produces a necessary consequence. But if c is assumed, no necessity follows. Let the proposition be: “If it is not irrational, it is rational; and if it is rational, it is an animal. But it is an animal.” It will not therefore be necessary either that it be or that it not be irrational.

The sixth mode is produced by the sixth proposition: “If a does not exist, b exists; and if b exists, c does not exist. But a does not exist; therefore c does not exist.” The demonstration is similar to those above. But if c is assumed, there is likewise no syllogism. For if the proposition is: “If it is not animate, it is inanimate; and if it is inanimate, it is not sensible,” and we assume: “But it is not sensible,” it will not therefore be necessary either that it be or that it not be animate.

The seventh mode derives from the seventh proposition: “If a does not exist, b does not exist; and if b does not exist, c must necessarily exist. But a does not exist; therefore c must necessarily exist.” But if c is assumed, nothing necessary follows. For if we state: “If it is not animate, it is not an animal; and if it is not an animal, it is insensible,” and assume: “But it is insensible,” it is not therefore necessary either that it be or that it not be animate.

The eighth mode is stated as follows: “If a does not exist, b does not exist; and if b does not exist, c must necessarily not exist. But a does not exist; therefore c does not exist.” But if c is assumed, there will be no necessity. For let us state: “If it is not animate, it is not an animal; and if it is not an animal, it must necessarily not be sensible. But it is not sensible.” It will not therefore be necessary that it not be animate—for example, trees, grasses, and whatever is nourished only by a living soul and not by a sensible soul.

In the first figure, then, there are sixteen combinations of hypothetical propositions from three terms, with what is posited in the proposition also posited in the assumption: eight when term a is posited in the assumption, and eight when term c is posited. If term a is assumed by being posited, there are eight necessary syllogisms; but if term c is assumed by being posited, no syllogism is produced.

The order of the syllogistic combinations will likewise be apparent if what had been posited in the proposition is removed in the assumption. There will be sixteen combinations: eight in which what follows is removed and which retain complete necessity, and eight in which what precedes is removed and which preserve necessity in the same manner.

Examples of all these must now be supplied.

The first mode is this: “If a exists, b exists, and if b exists, c must also necessarily exist. But c does not exist; therefore a does not exist.” But if we assume: “a does not exist,” nothing necessary follows. Let the proposition be: “If it is a human being, it is an animal; and if it is an animal, it must necessarily be animate. But it is not a human being.” It will not therefore be necessary that it either is or is not animate.

The second mode is: “If a exists, b exists, and if b exists, c must necessarily not exist. But c exists; therefore a does not exist.” But if we assume: “a does not exist,” it will not be necessary that c either exist or not exist. For let the proposition be: “If it is a human being, it is an animal; and if it is an animal, it is not a stone.” If we assume: “But it is not a human being,” it will not be necessary that it either be or not be a stone.

The third mode is: “If a exists, b does not exist, and if b does not exist, c must necessarily exist. But c does not exist; therefore a must necessarily not exist.” But if the assumption removes term a, nothing necessary follows. For let the proposition be: “If it is a human being, it is not inanimate; and if it is not inanimate, it must necessarily be animate. But it is not a human being.” It is not therefore necessary that it either be or not be animate.

The fourth mode is: “If a exists, b does not exist, and if b does not exist, c must necessarily not exist. But c exists; therefore a will not exist.” But if we assume that a does not exist, no necessity is found in the combination. For let the proposition be: “If it is a human being, it is not irrational; and if it is not irrational, it must necessarily not be inanimate. But it is not a human being.” It is not therefore necessary that it either be or not be inanimate.

The fifth is: “If a does not exist, b exists, and if b exists, c must also necessarily exist. But c does not exist; therefore a must necessarily exist.” But if term a is assumed, no syllogism will be produced. Let the proposition be: “If it is not irrational, it is rational; and if it is rational, it is an animal. But it is irrational.” It will not therefore be necessary that it either be or not be an animal.

The sixth is: “If a does not exist, b exists, and if b exists, c must necessarily not exist. But c exists; therefore a must exist.” But if term a is assumed, no necessity is found. Let the proposition be: “If it is not animate, it is inanimate; and if it is inanimate, it is not sensible. But it is animate.” It will not therefore be necessary that it either be or not be sensible.

The seventh is: “If a does not exist, b does not exist, and if b does not exist, c must necessarily exist. But c does not exist; therefore a must necessarily exist.” But if we assume term a, the combination produces no necessity. Let the proposition be: “If it is not an animal, it is not rational; and if it is not rational, it is irrational.” And let us assume: “But it is an animal.” It is not therefore necessary that it either be or not be irrational.

The eighth mode is formed by this proposition: “If a does not exist, b does not exist, and if b does not exist, c must necessarily not exist. But c exists; therefore a must exist.” But if term a is assumed, no necessity will follow. Let the proposition be: “If it is not an animal, it is not a human being; and if it is not a human being, it must necessarily not be capable of laughter. But it is an animal.” It will not therefore be necessary that it either be or not be capable of laughter.

Enough has now been said about the first figure. The second will be treated in the following volume.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0859]

[Col. 0859B] The second figure of conditional propositions consisting of three terms occurs whenever, from something being said either to be or not to be, it follows that two things are said either to be or not to be. Within the propositions themselves, and also within the conclusions, they vary in many ways according to the order of the assumption. To make this clearer, let all the propositions first be arranged in order. It must be stated in advance that propositions are sometimes set out in the same mode, and sometimes not. Of propositions in the same mode there is no syllogism. A proposition is in the same mode when we say: “If a is, b is, and if a is, c is not.” But if they are in different modes, they produce a syllogism.

[Col. 0859C] In the different-mode propositions of the second figure, such a proposition occurs in hypothetical syllogisms whose statements are composed of three terms, as when we propose: “If a is, b is; but if a is not, c is.” Let the following be understood as an example of this proposition: “If animal is, it is animate; if animal is not, it is insensible.” Here, therefore, the animal that is present is a; in both cases the same thing is proposed, but it is joined affirmatively to b and negatively to c. This is called predication in different modes. If, however, a were posited as being or not being in both cases, it would be called predication in the same mode.

Let all the propositions in different modes, then, be arranged as follows:

“If a is, b is; if a is not, c is.”

“If a is, b is; if a is not, c is not.”

“If a is, b is not; if a is not, c is.”

“If a is, b is not; if a is not, c is not.”

Here a has been posited as being with b, and as not being with c. [Col. 0859D] Let us again posit a as not being with b, and as being with c:

“If a is not, b is; if a is, c is.”

“If a is not, b is; if a is, c is not.”

“If a is not, b is not; if a is, c is.”

“If a is not, b is not; if a is, c is not.”

If, then, the proposition is in different modes, when b is assumed sixteen combinations result, of which only eight are syllogisms. Again, if c is assumed, sixteen combinations likewise result, but firm necessity is found in only eight syllogisms.

Let the first mode of the second figure, arising from the first proposition, be this: “If a is, b is; but if a is not, c is.” I say that, if b is not, c is. For since “if a is, b is,” according to the order of consequence it follows that, if b is not, a will not be. But if a were not, c would be. Therefore, if b is not, c will be. But if b is posited as being, nothing necessary follows. For suppose that b is: it is not necessary that a either be or not be. Nothing necessary, therefore, follows as to whether c is or is not—for example, let a be animal, b animate, and c insensible. If animal is, it is animate; but if animal is not, it is insensible. Yet if something is animate, it is not necessary that it either be or not be animal. Therefore it is not necessary that it either be or not be insensible.

If the c-term is assumed, however, then, if it is posited as not being, b will necessarily be; but if it is posited as being, there is no syllogism. For if c is not, a is; and if a is, b is. Therefore, if c is not, b is. But if c is, it is not necessary that a be—or perhaps it is necessary that a not be. For this proposition, “If a is not, c is,” applies only in cases in which one of the two must be. If c is, a will not be; but if a is not, nothing follows regarding b. For example, if something is insensible, it will not be animal; but if it is not animal, nothing requires that it either be or not be animate.

From the second proposition a syllogism results as follows: “If a is, b is; if a is not, c is not.” I say that, if b is not, c is not. The proposition is “If a is, b is”; the order of consequence is “If b is not, a is not.” But if a is not, c is not. Therefore, if b is not, c is not.

If b is posited as being, however, it is not necessary that c be. Let a be animal, b animate, and c rational, and let the proposition be: “If animal is, it is animate; if animal is not, it is not rational.” Yet if something is animate, it is not necessary that it be animal, and consequently it is not necessary that it be rational.

If the c-term is assumed, then, if c is affirmed, b will be; but if c is denied, there is no syllogism. For since, if a is, b will be, and if a is not, c will be, if c is, a will be. But when a is, b is; therefore, if c is, b will be. If c is not, however, nothing is necessary. For in the proposition “If animal is, it is animate; if animal is not, it is not rational,” let us assume that rational is not. It will not be necessary that animal either be or not be; consequently, neither will it be necessary that animate be or not be.

From the third proposition the syllogism is as follows: “If a is, b is not; and if a is not, c is.” I say that, if b is, c is. For since the proposition is “If a is, b is not,” it necessarily follows that, if b is, a is not. But if a is not, c will be. Therefore, if b is, c will be.

If b is not, however, nothing is necessary. Let a be animal, b inanimate, and c insensible. In the proposition “If animal is, it is not inanimate; if animal is not, it is insensible,” let us assume that inanimate is not. It will not be necessary that animal either be or not be; consequently, neither will it be necessary that insensible be or not be.

If the c-term is assumed, then, if c is not, b will not be; but if c is, there will be no necessity for the conclusion. For since the proposition is “If a is, b is not; but if a is not, c is,” the consequence is such that, if c is not, a is. For these terms are only spoken of when they are deprived of an intermediary. But if a is, b is not. Therefore, if c is not, b will not be. If c is, however, there is no syllogism. For in the proposition “If animal is, it is not inanimate; but if animal is not, it is insensible,” let someone assume that insensible is. It follows indeed that animal is not, but it does not follow that animate either is or is not.

From the fourth proposition there is a syllogism as follows: “If a is, b is not; if a is not, c is not.” I say that, if b is, c is not. For since the proposition is “If a is, b is not,” the consequence is that, if b is, a is not; and when a is not, c had been posited as not being. Therefore, if b is, c is not.

If b is assumed as not being, however, there will be no syllogism. Let a be animal, b inanimate, and c rational, and let the proposition be: “If animal is, it is not inanimate; if animal is not, it is not rational.” Let us assume that inanimate is not. It will not be necessary that animal be; consequently, neither will it be necessary that rational be.

Again, if the c-term is assumed, then, if c is posited as being, it will necessarily follow that b is not. But if c is not, there is no syllogism. For since the proposition is “If a is, b is not; if a is not, c is not,” it is necessary that, when c is, a also is; but if a is, b is not. Therefore, if c is, b will not be. If c is posited as not being, however, there is no syllogism—for example, in the proposition “If animal is, it is not inanimate; if animal is not, it is not rational.” If someone assumes that rational is not, it will not be necessary that animal either be or not be; consequently, neither will it be necessary that inanimate either be or not be.

In these four propositions, then, the a-term was posited as being with respect to b, but as not being with respect to c. If the order is changed, there will again be four other syllogisms. If the b-term is assumed, there will be four others, and likewise if c is assumed. On either side there will also be four combinations that produce no syllogisms.

Let the fifth proposition be: “If a is not, b is; if a is, c is.” I say that, if b is not, c will be. For let the assumption be made: “But b is not”; therefore a will be, since this was established as the order of consequence. But when a is, c is. Therefore, if b is not, c will be.

If b is posited as being, however, nothing necessary follows. For if b is, a will not be; but if a is not, nothing follows regarding c, and consequently there is no syllogism.

That a is not when b is is demonstrated by the proposition in which we say, “If a is not, b is.” This occurs only in immediate contraries. Let a be animal, b insensible, and c animate, and let the proposition be: “If animal is not, it is insensible; if animal is, it is animate.” If insensible is posited, it is necessary that animal not be. But it is not necessary that animate either be or not be.

If the c-term is assumed, then, if it is assumed negatively, it will produce a syllogism; if affirmatively, in no way. For if c is not, a is not. But if a is not, b is. Therefore, if c is not, b is. If c is, however, it is not necessary that a either be or not be. Consequently, neither is it necessary that b either be or not be. For if something is animate, it is not necessary that it either be or not be animal; and when animal is not, it is not necessary that insensible either be or not be. The proposition itself is the same as in the preceding cases.

Again, from the sixth proposition a syllogism is formed as follows: “If a is not, b is; and if a is, c is not.” I say that, if b is not, c will not be. For if b is not, a is; and if a is, c is not. Therefore, if b is not, c will not be.

If the b-term is assumed, however, the conclusion has no necessity. For if b is, a is not; this is clear from what was said above. But if a is not, nothing follows regarding c, since c was not present if a were. An example is: let a be animal, b insensible, and c inanimate. Let the proposition be: “If animal is not, it is insensible; if animal is, it is not inanimate.” Yet if something is insensible, it is not therefore animal; nor does it follow that it either is or is not inanimate.

If the c-term is assumed, then, if it is affirmed, a syllogism results. For if c is, a will not be; but if a is not, b will be. Therefore, if c is, b will be. If c is denied, however, nothing is necessary. For if c is not, it will not be necessary that a either be or not be; consequently, neither will it be necessary that b be or not be. For if inanimate is denied, it is not necessary that animal either be or not be, and consequently neither is it necessary that insensible either be or not be.

From the seventh proposition the conclusion is formed as follows: “If a is not, b is not; if a is, c is.” I say that, if b is, c will be. For since it was proposed that, if a were not, b would not be, a will be if b is. But if a is, c will be. Therefore, if b is, c will be.

If the b-term is denied in the assumption, however, there will be no necessity in the conclusion.
