For if b is not, nothing will necessarily follow as to whether a is or is not, and consequently neither as to whether c is or is not. For example, let a be animate, b animal, and c living, and let us state: “If animate is not, animal is not; if animate is, it lives.” If we assume that animal is not, it is not necessary that animate either be or not be, and consequently neither is it necessary that living be or not be.

If the c-term is assumed, then, if it is denied, the syllogism will have complete necessity; if it is affirmed, there is no conclusion. For if c is not, a will be; and if a is not, b will not be. Therefore, if c is not, b will not be. If c is affirmed, however, nothing is necessary. For whether it is necessary that a be or not be, nothing follows regarding b, as can be shown in the preceding terms. For if something lives, and if it is necessary that it be animate, it is nevertheless not necessary that it either be or not be animal. If it is not necessary that it be animate, it is not necessary that it either be or not be animal. But that it be necessary that it not be animate is impossible.

From the eighth proposition the conclusion is as follows: “If a is not, b is not; and if a is, c is not.” I say that, if b is, c is not. For if b is, a is; and if a is, c is not. Therefore, if b is, c will not be.

If the b-term is denied in the assumption, nothing is necessary. For if b is not, it will not be necessary that a either be or not be, and consequently neither will it be necessary that c be or not be. Let a be animate, b animal, and c inanimate. Let us propose: “If animate is not, animal is not; if animate is, it is not inanimate.” If we assume that animal is not, it will not be necessary that animate either be or not be; consequently, neither will it be necessary that inanimate be or not be.

If the c-term is assumed, then, if it is posited affirmatively, the syllogism will have necessity. For if c is, a is not; and if a is not, b is not. Therefore, if c is, b is not. If the c-term is denied in the assumption, however, nothing is necessary. For if c is not, it will not be necessary that a either be or not be. Consequently, neither will it be necessary that b be or not be. For if inanimate is not, perhaps it is necessary that animate be, but it is not necessary that animal be.

Terms can also be found in which it is not necessary that a be, as when we posit c as black and a as white: from “black is not” it does not follow that “white is.”

We have thus, I believe, explained all the same-mode combinations of the second figure. If the propositions are in the same mode, no syllogism at all results. They are in the same mode whenever the a-term is posited as being or not being simultaneously with respect to b and c, however b and c may vary.

Of the combinations called same-mode, none can be comprehended as producing a syllogism. These are all the same-mode combinations:

“If a is, b is; if a is, c is.”

“If a is, b is; if a is, c is not.”

“If a is, b is not; if a is, c is.”

“If a is, b is not; if a is, c is not.”

“If a is not, b is; if a is not, c is.”

“If a is not, b is; if a is not, c is not.”

“If a is not, b is not; if a is not, c is.”

“If a is not, b is not; if a is not, c is not.”

From assumptions made in any manner we can find their weak conclusion, entirely lacking necessity; and, following the modes described above, we can very easily discover terms by which it may be demonstrated that no stability whatsoever can be found in such combinations.

We have carefully shown how many syllogisms there are in the second figure and in how many ways they are formed. If the combinations are in different modes, eight syllogisms are formed when the b-term is assumed, and as many when the c-term is assumed. Thus there are sixteen syllogisms of the second figure. An equal number of combinations are formed when the b- and c-terms are assumed in ways that do not produce what they should, and from them nothing at all is inferred.

We must now speak of the third figure. In it there are just as many combinations and just as many syllogisms, but the propositions are set out in different modes. If they are in the same mode, no syllogism at all is formed, as was said concerning the second figure.

[Col. 0864A] Let us set out all the different-mode propositions of the third figure:

“If b is, a is; if c is, a is not.”

“If b is, a is; if c is not, a is not.”

“If b is not, a is; if c is, a is not.”

“If b is not, a is; if c is not, a is not.”

Here a has been proposed as being with b, but as not being with c. Again, let a be proposed as not being with b, but as being with c:

“If b is, a is not; if c is, a is.”

“If b is, a is not; if c is not, a is.”

“If b is not, a is not; if c is, a is.”

“If b is not, a is not; if c is not, a is not.”

The first mode of the third figure is therefore this: “If b is, a is; if c is, a is not.” This differs from the first mode of the second figure. There, if a was or was not, b and c were said to be. Here, however, if b or c is, a is proposed either to be or not to be.

The propositions are in different modes when in one part a is established as being and in the other as not being, as in the proposition just set out: “If b is, a is; if c is, a is not.” With these propositions posited, I say that, if b is, it is necessary that c not be. For if b is, a is; but if a is, c is not. Therefore, if b is, c is not.

If the b-term is denied, however, there is no syllogism. For if b is not, it will not be necessary that a either be or not be. Therefore, neither will it be necessary that c either be or not be. For example, let b be animal, a animate, and c dead, and let the proposition be: “If animal is, it is animate; if dead is, it is not animate.” Yet if animal is not, it is not necessary that animate either be or not be. For things that are not animals can be animate, such as trees; and they can be inanimate, such as stones. Consequently, if animal is not, it is not necessary that dead either be or not be. Many things are not animals and are not dead, such as stones; for things are called dead that once lived.

An affirmative assumption of the c-term, however, produces a syllogism. For if c is, b will not be. For if c is, a is not; but if a is not, b will not be. Therefore, if c is, b will not be.

A negative assumption of c establishes no necessity. For if c is not, it is not necessary that a either be or not be. Consequently, neither will it be necessary that b be or not be. For if dead is not, it is not necessary that animate either be or not be. Some things that are not dead are animate, such as trees; others, although not dead, are not animate, such as stones. Consequently, if dead is removed, it is not necessary that animal either be or not be.

From the second proposition the mode of drawing the conclusion is this: “If b is, a is; if c is not, a is not.” I say that, if b is, c will be. For if b is, a is; but if a is, c is. The proposition “If c is not, a is not” is converted in this way. Therefore, if b is, c is.

If the b-term is denied, no necessity for the syllogism results. For if b is not, it is not necessary that a either be or not be. Consequently, no necessity reaches c either, as is clear in these terms. Let b be animal, a animate, and c corporeal, and let the proposition be: “If animal is, it is animate; if corporeal is not, it is not animate.” If we assume that animal is not, it is not necessary that corporeal either be or not be.

But if the c-term is denied, there will be necessity for the syllogism. For if c is not, a is not; and if a is not, b is not. This is how the proposition can be converted. Therefore, if c is not, b will not be.

If c is affirmed, there is no necessity. For if something is corporeal, it is not necessary that it either be or not be animate. Consequently, neither is it necessary that it either be or not be animal.

The third proposition receives the following conclusion: “If b is not, a is; if c is, a is not.” I say that, if b is not, c will not be. For if b is not, a is; but if a is, c will not be. This is how the part of the proposition that said, “If c is, a is not,” could be converted. Therefore, if b is not, c is not.

If the b-term is affirmed, however, there is no necessity in the conclusion. For if b is, it is indeed necessary that a not be, but it is not necessary that c be. Let b be animate, a inanimate, and c animal. If someone proposes, “If animate is not, it is inanimate; if animal is, it is not inanimate,” and we posit that animate is, it follows that inanimate is not, but it is not necessary that animal be.

If the c-term is affirmed, a necessary conclusion results as follows. For if c is, a is not; and if a is not, b is. This followed from the proposition that said, “If b is not, a is.” Therefore, if c is, b is.

If the same c-term is denied, there is no syllogism. For if c is not, it is not necessary that a either be or not be. Consequently, neither is it necessary that b be or not be. For if animal is not, it is not necessary that inanimate either be or not be; consequently, neither is it necessary that animate either be or not be.

From the fourth proposition there is a syllogism as follows: “If b is not, a is; if c is not, a is not.” I say that, if b is not, c is. For if b is not, a is; but if a is, c necessarily is. This follows from the part of the proposition that says, “If c is not, a is not.” Therefore, if b is not, c is.

If the b-term is affirmed, however, there is no syllogism. It follows that a is not, but it does not follow that c either is or is not. For example, let b be insensible, a animal, and c animate, and let the propositions be: “If insensible is not, animal is; if animate is not, animal is not.” If insensible is, animal is not, but it is not necessary that animate either be or not be.

If the c-term is denied, a syllogism immediately results. For if c is not, a is not; and if a is not, b will be. This follows from the part of the proposition that says, “If b is not, a is.” Therefore, if c is not, b will be.

If c is, however, it is not necessary that a either be or not be. Consequently, neither is it necessary that b either be or not be. For if animate is, it is not necessary that animal either be or not be. Consequently, neither is it necessary that insensible either be or not be.

Up to this point we have arranged four modes in such a way that, however the b-term is constituted, the a-term is posited as being, while with respect to c it is posited as not being. Let us now establish the arrangement in which the a-term is said not to be with respect to b, but to be with respect to c, with the order accordingly changed.

That these propositions are all in different modes is shown by the fact that a is proposed affirmatively with respect to b and negatively with respect to c; or, if it is proposed negatively with respect to b, it retains an affirmative enunciation with respect to c.

The fifth proposition therefore produces a syllogism as follows. Let the proposition be: “If b is, a is not; if c is, a is.” I say that, if b is, c is not. For if b is, a is not; but if a is not, c is not. This followed from the proposition that said that, if c were, a also would be. Therefore, if b is, c is not.

If b is denied, however, there is no syllogism. For if b is not, it is not necessary that a be. Consequently, no necessity reaches c either. The same is clear in the terms. Let b be dead, a animate, and c animal, and let the proposition be: “If dead is, it is not animate; if animal is, it is animate.” If we assume that dead is not, it is not necessary that animate either be or not be. For things that are still animate, as well as things that never were animate, are not dead. Consequently, it does not follow that animal either is or is not. For what is not dead can be an animal, such as a living dog, and can also not be an animal, such as a stone.

If the c-term is affirmed, however, there will be a complete conclusion that b is not. For if c is, a is; and if a is, b will not be. This follows from the mode of the proposition set out above. Therefore, if c is, b will not be.

If c is denied, no necessity leads either to a or to b. For if animal is not, it is not necessary that either animate or dead be or not be.

The conclusion of the sixth proposition is this: “If b is, a is not; if c is not, a is.” I say that, if b is, c will be. For if b is, a is not; and if a is not, c will be. Such is the consequence in this part of the proposition. Therefore, if b is, c will be.

If the b-term is denied, nothing necessary follows. For if b is not, it does not follow with necessity that either a or c is present or absent. This is clear in the terms. Let b be dead, a animate, and c inanimate, and let the proposition be: “If dead is, it is not animate; if inanimate is not, it is animate.” If dead is not, it is not necessary that animate either be or not be. Consequently, neither is it necessary that inanimate either be or not be.

If the c-term is assumed, then, if it is placed in the negative, the conclusion that b is not will be established. For since c is not, a is; but if a is, b is not. Therefore, if c is not, b will not be.

If c is affirmed, nothing is necessary. For even if it is necessary that a not be, no necessity reaches the b-term. This is also clear in the terms: if something is inanimate, it is necessary that it not be animate, but it is not necessary that it be dead.

The syllogism of the seventh proposition is as follows. Let it be enunciated: “If b is not, a is not; if c is, a is.” I say that, if b is not, c is not. For if b is not, a will not be; but if a is not, c will not be. The same followed from the proposition that said that, if c were, a also would be. Therefore, if b is not, c will not be.

If b is affirmed, however, nothing is necessary. For if b is, it is not necessary that either a or c either be or not be. This is clear in the terms. Let b be animate, a animal, and c sensible, and let the proposition be: “If animate is not, animal is not; if sensible is, animal is.” If animate is assumed as being, it is not necessary that animal either be or not be, nor that sensible either be or not be.

If the c-term is used for the assumption, then, if it is affirmed, the conclusion will be firm; if it is denied, there is no syllogism. For if c is, a is; and if a is, b will be. This followed from the proposition that says, “If b is not, a is not.” Therefore, if c is, b will be.

If the same c-term is denied, nothing is necessary. For if c is not, no necessity compels either a or b to be or not be. For example, if sensible is not, perhaps animal is not, but it is not necessary that animate be.

There will also be terms in which it is not even necessary that a not be.

The eighth mode is that in which the proposition is set out as follows: “If b is not, a is not; and if c is not, a is.” I say that, if b is not, c is. For if b is not, a will not be; but if a is not, c will be. This followed from the part of the proposition that said, “If c is not, a is.” Therefore, if b is not, c will be.

If the b-term is affirmed, however, nothing is necessary. For if b is, it is not necessary that the a-term either be or not be; consequently, neither will it be necessary that c be or not be. Let b be animate, a animal, and c insensible, and let the proposition be: “If animate is not, animal is not; if insensible is not, animal is.” If we affirm the b-term in the assumption and say, “But animate is,” it is not necessary that animal or insensible either be or not be. Consequently, there is no syllogism.

If the c-term is denied, however, a syllogism immediately results. For if c is not, a is; but if a is, b will be. Therefore, if c is not, b will be.

If the c-term is affirmed, nothing is necessary. For even if it is necessary that the a-term not be, no necessity reaches the b-term. This is demonstrated by the following example: if something is insensible, it is not animal; but if it is not animal, it is not necessary that it either be or not be animate.

In propositions in different modes, then, whether the b-term or the c-term is assumed, eight syllogisms necessarily arise from each side. The remaining eight combinations on each side are deprived of necessity. But if the propositions are in the same mode, no syllogism at all exists.

They are called same-mode whenever the a-term is proposed as being or not being with respect to both terms. All the same-mode propositions are of this kind:

“If b is, a is; if c is, a is.”

“If b is, a is; if c is not, a is.”

“If b is not, a is; if c is, a is.”

“If b is not, a is; if c is not, a is.”

“If b is, a is not; if c is, a is not.”

“If b is, a is not; if c is not, a is not.”

“If b is not, a is not; if c is, a is not.”

“If b is not, a is not; if c is not, a is not.”

In these, by both the order of consequence in the propositions designated above and the examples, we can clearly and consistently recognize that no necessity at all is produced in the syllogisms.

Consequently, when a proposition is woven from three terms, sixteen syllogisms are formed from the first figure, sixteen syllogisms from the second, and just as many are gathered from the third. Thus there are forty-eight syllogisms from three terms in all.

It remains now to speak of those syllogisms that are connected by two hypothetical propositions. Their mode of consequence is similar to that found in propositions made from two categorical and simple propositions. For in all cases, if we wish to establish something, we assume the first part of the whole proposition; but if something is to be destroyed in the conclusion, the second part is denied.

Whether the first part is denied or the latter part affirmed, no necessity at all results, except in the fifth, seventh, thirteenth, and fifteenth propositions. In these cases it is not the nature of the combination but the property of the terms that produces the consequence, just as we have shown to occur in those syllogisms that consist of propositions containing two simple propositions.

I have set out all the propositions of these syllogisms that consist of two hypothetical propositions. When the reader has recognized their differences, it will be necessary to return to their examples, which are joined from simple and categorical propositions.

The differences among all propositions joined from two hypothetical propositions are as follows:

If, when a is, b is; and when c is, d is. If, when a is, b is; and when c is, d is not. If, when a is, b is; and when c is not, d is. If, when a is, b is; and when c is not, d is not. If, when a is, b is not; and when c is, d is. If, when a is, b is not; and when c is, d is not. If, when a is, b is not; and when c is not, d is. If, when a is, b is not; and when c is not, d is not. If, when a is not, b is; and when c is, d is. If, when a is not, b is; and when c is, d is not. If, when a is not, b is; and when c is not, d is.

[Col. 0868C] If, when a is not, b is; and when c is not, d is not. If, when a is not, b is not; and when c is, d is. If, when a is not, b is not; and when c is, d is not. If, when a is not, b is not; and when c is not, d is. If, when a is not, b is not; and when c is not, d is not.

In these propositions too, one must observe that, although there are sixteen, eight vary in such a way that in all of them the term a is posited as being, while the other eight vary in such a way that the same term a is said not to be. But they will not, in whatever way they are arranged, have the force of conditional propositions consisting of two hypotheticals. For if someone says, “If, when a human being is, it is an animal, and when it is animate, it is a body,” he has not made a proposition consisting of two conditionals. For it is not because it is animate that it is an animal, on the ground that whatever is a human being is an animal; nor does one condition follow from the other. But if you separate them and pronounce each independently, each has necessity in the consequence of its terms. For both “whatever is a human being is an animal” and “whatever is animate is a body” are true in themselves, and they are not joined by a condition.

Thus, in order that the nature of the individual propositions may become clear, each must be discussed. The first proposition, then, must be such that, if a is posited, the term b does not immediately follow; likewise, if c is posited, it need not be the case that the term d follows. But, when the term a is posited, the term c must be the case; and, when b is posited, the term d must be the case. Then it will happen that, if b follows upon the positing of a, d must follow upon the positing of c. Let the terms be a, “human being”; b, “doctor”; c, “animate”; d, “craftsman.” For, when a human being is posited, it need not be the case that he is a doctor; and, when something is animate, it need not be a craftsman. But if something is a human being, it must be animate; and if something is a doctor, it must be a craftsman. Once this is established, it follows that, if, when a human being is, he is a doctor, then, when something is animate, it is a craftsman.

The second proposition must be such that a and b can each exist apart from one another, and likewise c and d, but a cannot exist apart from c, while b and d cannot exist together. Then it follows that, if b follows upon the positing of a, d must not be the case when c is posited. Let a be “human being,” b “black,” c “animate,” and d “white.” A human being can exist either with or without blackness, and something animate can exist either with or without whiteness; but a human being cannot exist apart from being animate, nor can black exist together with white. Hence, if, when something is a human being, it is black, then, when it is animate, it is not white.

The terms of the third proposition must likewise be such that a can exist apart from b, but c can exist neither with a nor with d. Consequently, if b follows upon the positing of a, d must be the case when c is denied. Let a be “animate,” b “doctor,” c “inanimate,” and d “craftsman.” Something animate can exist apart from being a doctor, whereas the inanimate can be joined neither with the animate nor with the craftsman. Thus, if, when something is animate, it is a doctor, then, when it is not inanimate, it is a craftsman.

The fourth proposition must be constructed with terms such that a can exist either with or without b, and c likewise either with or without d. But a cannot in any way exist with c, nor b with d. Then it follows that, if b follows upon the positing of a, d is also denied when c is denied. Let a be “human being,” b “black,” c “inanimate,” and d “white.” A human being can exist either with or without blackness, and the inanimate can exist either with or without whiteness; nevertheless, a human being cannot exist with the inanimate, nor black with white. Therefore, if, when something is a human being, it is black, then, when it is not inanimate, it is not white.

The constituents of the fifth proposition are such that a can exist either with or without b, and c either with or without d; but a cannot exist apart from c, and b and d can never exist together, so that, if one is not the case, the other must be the case. Then it follows that, if b is denied when a is posited, d follows when c is posited. Let a be “human being,” b “sick,” c “animate,” and d “healthy.” A human being can exist either with or without sickness, and the animate either with or without health; but if something is a human being, it must be animate, and if it is not sick, it must be healthy. Thus, if, when something is a human being, it is not sick, then, when it is animate, it is healthy.

The sixth proposition requires terms such that a can exist apart from b, and c apart from d, either with or without being the case. But a cannot exist apart from c, nor d apart from b. Then it follows that, if b is not the case when a is posited, d is not the case when c is posited. Let a be “human being,” b “craftsman,” c “animate,” and d “doctor.” A human being can exist either with or without being a craftsman, and the animate either with or without being a doctor; but a human being cannot exist apart from being animate, nor a doctor apart from being a craftsman. Hence, if, when something is a human being, it is not a craftsman, then, when it is animate, it is not a doctor.

The terms of the seventh proposition are such that a can exist apart from b, but c can exist neither with d nor with a; b likewise cannot exist together with c. Thus it follows that, if b is denied when a is posited, d follows when the term c is denied. Let a be “animate,” b “healthy,” c “inanimate,” and d “sick.” The animate can exist either with or without health. But the inanimate can agree neither with the animate nor with the sick. Hence, if, when something is animate, it is not healthy, then, when it is not inanimate, it is sick.

The eighth proposition must likewise be joined with terms such that a can exist either with or without the term b, while c can exist neither with a nor with d, and d cannot exist apart from b. In this way it follows that, if b is denied when a is posited, d is not the case when c is denied. Let a be “animate,” b “craftsman,” c “inanimate,” and d “doctor.” The animate can exist either with or without being a craftsman. But the inanimate agrees neither with the animate nor with the doctor. A doctor, however, cannot exist apart from being a craftsman. Hence, if, when something is animate, it is not a craftsman, then, when it is not inanimate, it is not a doctor.

The ninth proposition arises if a and b cannot exist together, while c can exist apart from d but cannot exist with a. Then it follows that, if b follows when a is denied, d follows when c is posited. Let a be “inanimate,” b “doctor,” c “animate,” and d “craftsman.” For the inanimate cannot be a doctor, while the animate can exist without being a craftsman; and the inanimate and the animate cannot exist together. Hence, if, when something is not inanimate, it is a doctor, then, when it is animate, it is a craftsman.

The tenth proposition is joined by terms such that a can exist apart from b, and c apart from d, but a cannot exist with c, nor b with d. Thus it follows that, if b follows when a is denied, d must not be the case when c is posited. Let a be “inanimate,” b “black,” c “animate,” and d “white.” The inanimate can exist either with or without blackness, and the animate either with or without whiteness. But the inanimate and the animate cannot exist together, nor black with white. If, therefore, the inanimate is denied and black follows, then, when the animate is posited, white will be denied.

The eleventh proposition is such that neither a and b nor c and d can exist together, while a cannot exist without c, nor b without d. Thus, if b follows when a is denied, d must be the case when a is denied. Let a be “inanimate,” b “doctor,” c *invitale* (“nonliving”), and d “craftsman.” The inanimate cannot be a doctor; consequently, neither can *invitale* be a craftsman. But what is inanimate cannot fail to be *invitale*, and whoever is a doctor cannot fail to be a craftsman. Therefore, if the inanimate is denied and being a doctor follows, then, when being *invitale* is denied, being a craftsman follows.

The twelfth proposition must consist of terms such that a can exist apart from b, while c can exist either with or without d; but a cannot exist without c, nor b with d. Thus, if b follows when a is denied, d is also denied when c is denied. Let a be “inanimate,” b “white,” c *invitale* (“nonliving”), and d “black.” The inanimate can exist either with or without whiteness, and *invitale* either with or without blackness. But if the inanimate is human and is white, then, when it is not *invitale*, it will not be black.

The thirteenth proposition must be connected with terms such that a can exist apart from b, and c apart from d, while a and c, and likewise b and d, cannot exist together, so that, if one of each pair is not the case, the other must be the case. Thus it follows that, if b is denied when a is denied, d is affirmed when c is affirmed. Let a be “irrational,” b “sick,” c “rational,” and d “healthy.” The irrational can exist apart from sickness, and the rational apart from health; but the irrational and the rational cannot exist together, nor the sick and the healthy. If, however, when one of them is not the case, the other must be the case, then, if sickness is denied when the irrational is denied, health is posited when the rational is posited.

The fourteenth proposition must be constructed from constituents such that a can exist apart from b, and c apart from d, but a and c cannot exist together, so that, when one is not the case, the other must be the case; and d cannot exist apart from b. It follows that, if b is denied when a is denied, d is not the case when c is the case. Let a be “inanimate,” b “craftsman,” c “animate,” and d “doctor.” The inanimate can exist apart from the craftsman, and the animate apart from the doctor; but the inanimate does not agree with the animate, and the doctor is in no way separated from the craftsman. Hence, if, when something is not inanimate, it is not a craftsman, then, when it is animate, it is not a doctor.

The fifteenth proposition must have terms such that, if a is not the case, c must not be the case; while b and d are such that, when one of them is denied, the other must be the case. Thus it follows that, if b is denied when a is denied, d is affirmed when c is denied. Let a be “irrational,” b “healthy,” c “inanimate,” and d “sick.” If the irrational is not the case, the inanimate is not the case; moreover, the healthy and the sick cannot exist together, and whoever denies the healthy must necessarily affirm the sick, and conversely. Thus, if the healthy is denied when the irrational is denied, then, when the inanimate is denied, the sick is posited.

The sixteenth proposition consists of terms such that a cannot exist apart from c, while d cannot exist apart from b; and a and b, and likewise c and d, cannot exist together. It follows that, if b is denied when a is denied, d is denied when c is denied. Let a be “inanimate,” b “craftsman,” c *invitale* (“nonliving”), and d “doctor.” The inanimate cannot exist apart from *invitale*, nor the doctor apart from the craftsman; and the inanimate cannot exist with the craftsman, nor *invitale* with the doctor. Therefore, if the craftsman is denied when the inanimate is denied, then, when *invitale* is denied, the doctor is denied.

This account of the propositions whose examples we have set out above has been introduced so that their nature might become clear, not because the terms cannot exist in any other way. For, as was said above, it is not enough to join terms in just any manner for them to become hypothetical propositions conjoined from two conditionals. If someone says, “If, when a human being is, it is an animal, and when it is day, it is light,” he has not thereby made a proposition consisting of two conditionals, because the first condition is not the cause of the second condition. The account given above of the propositions demonstrates how it comes about that one condition follows another.

Since this is so, we must now speak of their syllogisms. From the first proposition a syllogism is formed as follows:

“If, when a is, b is, and when c is, d is. But when a is, b is; therefore, when c is, d will be.”

Or as follows:

“But when c is, d is not; therefore, when a is, b is not.”

That this can be the assumption is demonstrated by the nature of the propositions described above.

Likewise, from the second proposition:

“If, when a is, b is, and when c is, d is not. But when a is, b is; therefore, when c is, d is not.”

Or:

“But when c is, d is; therefore, when a is, b is not.”

From the third:

“If, when a is, b is, and when c is not, d is. But when a is, b is; therefore, when c is not, d is.”

Or:

“But when c is not, d is not; therefore, when a is, b is not.”

Likewise, from the fourth:

“If, when a is, b is, and when c is not, d is not. But when a is, b is; therefore, when c is not, d is not.”

Or:

“But when c is not, d is; therefore, when a is, b is not.”

From the fifth proposition four deductions are made. The terms are proposed in such a way that a valid conclusion is reached in both directions:

“If, when a is, b is not, and when c is, d is. But when a is, b is not; therefore, when c is, d is.”

Or:

“But when a is, b is; therefore, when c is, d is not.”

Or:

“But when c is, d is not; therefore, when a is, b is.”

Or:

“But when c is, d is; therefore, when a is, b is not.”

From the sixth:

“If, when a is, b is not, and when c is, d is not. But when a is, b is not; therefore, when c is, d is not.”

Or:

“But when c is, d is not; therefore, when a is, b is.”

From the seventh, likewise, four syllogisms are made:

“If, when a is, b is not, and when c is not, d is. But when a is, b is not; therefore, when c is not, d is.”

Or:

“But when a is, b is; therefore, when c is not, d is not.”

Or:

“But when c is not, d is not; therefore, when a is, b is.”

Or:

“But when c is not, d is; therefore, when a is, b is not.”

From the eighth proposition:

“If, when a is, b is not, and when c is not, d is not. But when a is, b is not; therefore, when c is not, d is.”

Or:

“But when c is not, d is; therefore, when a is, b is.”

Thus far we have shown how syllogisms are formed from propositions that proposed a to be the case and varied the remaining terms by affirming and denying them. Now we must say what syllogisms are formed from propositions that vary the remaining terms in such a way that they propose a not to be the case.

From the ninth proposition a syllogism is formed as follows:

“If, when a is not, b is, and when c is, d is. But when a is not, b is; therefore, when c is, d is.”

Or:

“But when c is, d is not; therefore, when a is not, b is not.”

Likewise, from the tenth:

“If, when a is not, b is, and when c is, d is not. But when a is not, b is; therefore, when c is, d is not.”

Or:

“But when c is, d is; therefore, when a is not, b is not.”

From the eleventh:

“If, when a is not, b is, and when c is not, d is. But when a is not, b is; therefore, when c is not, d is.”

Or:

“But when c is not, d is not; therefore, when a is not, b is not.”

From the twelfth:

“If, when a is not, b is, and when c is not, d is not. But when a is not, b is; therefore, when c is not, d is not.”

Or:

“But when c is not, d is; therefore, when a is not, b is not.”

From the thirteenth, which yields four syllogisms, as follows:

“If, when a is not, b is not, and when c is, d is. But when a is not, b is not; therefore, when c is, d is.”

Or:

“But when a is not, b is; therefore, when c is, d is not.”

Or:

“But when c is, d is; therefore, when a is not, b is not.”

Or:

“But when c is, d is not; therefore, when a is not, b is.”

Likewise, from the fourteenth:

“If, when a is not, b is not, and when c is, d is not. But when a is not, b is not; therefore, when c is, d is not.”

Or:

“But when c is, d is; therefore, when a is not, b is.”

The fifteenth again yields four deductions:

“If, when a is not, b is not, and when c is not, d is. But when a is not, b is not; therefore, when c is not, d is.”

Or:

“But when a is not, b is; therefore, when c is not, d is.”

Or:

“But when c is not, d is not; therefore, when a is not, b is.”

Or:

“But when c is not, d is; therefore, when a is not, b is not.”

From the sixteenth proposition:

“If, when a is not, b is not, and when c is not, d is not. But when a is not, b is not; therefore, when c is not, d is not.”

Or:

“But when c is not, d is; therefore, when a is not, b is.”

From all these, forty conclusions arise. Sixteen are obtained by assuming the first condition in the same manner in which it is posited in the proposition. Sixteen are obtained by assuming the second condition in the opposite manner from that in which it is placed in the proposition. Eight arise from the fifth, seventh, thirteenth, and fifteenth propositions by assuming the first conditions in the opposite manner from that in which they were expressed in the proposition, while the second conditions are assumed in the same manner in which they had been placed in the proposition. Therefore, so that the account of all the propositions and conclusions might become clear, we have set out all such enunciations together with their proper examples.

[Col. 0873] If, when a is a human being, b is a doctor; and when c is animate, d is a craftsman. If, when a is a human being, b is black; and when c is animate, d is not white. If, when a is animate, b is a doctor; and when c is not inanimate, d is a craftsman. If, when a is a human being, b is black; and when c is not inanimate, d is not white. If, when a is a human being, b is not sick; and when c is animate, d is healthy. If, when a is a human being, b is not a craftsman; and when c is animate, d is not a doctor. If, when a is an animal, b is not healthy; and when c is not inanimate, d is sick. If, when a is animate, b is not a craftsman; and when c is not inanimate, d is not a doctor. If, when a is not inanimate, b is a doctor; and when c is animate, d is a craftsman. If, when a is not inanimate, b is black; and when c is inanimate, d is not white. If, when a is not inanimate, b is a doctor; and when c is not *invitale*, d is a craftsman. If, when a is not inanimate, b is white; and when c is not *invitale*, d is not black. If, when a is not irrational, b is not sick; and when c is rational, d is healthy. If, when a is not inanimate, b is not a craftsman; and when c is animate, d is not a doctor. If, when a is not irrational, b is not healthy; and when c is not inanimate, d is sick. If, when a is not inanimate, b is not a craftsman; and when c is not *invitale*, d is not a doctor.

[Col. 0873B] Let these, then, be the formulations devised concerning those that are produced through connection.

[Col. 0873C] Those that are placed in disjunction appear to be attached to these and to assume the modes and forms that we said above were produced in connection from propositions joined out of two simple propositions. If, therefore, in the case of propositions set out in disjunction, I demonstrate, by analogy with their causes, the propositions that were placed in connection and joined from simple propositions, then as many modes and whatever kinds of conclusions there are in each of those propositions formed by connection must also be present in those which are pronounced by disjunction and shown to have the same force of connection.

We said above that there are four differences of propositions enunciated through connection, when they are joined from simple propositions, as follows:

“If a is, b is”;  
“If a is not, b is not”;  
“If a is, b is not”;  
“If a is not, b is.”

Through disjunction too, propositions have four differences, as follows:

“Either a is, or b is”;  
“Either a is not, or b is not”;  
“Either a is, or b is not”;  
“Either a is not, or b is.”

The first of these, which proposes “Either a is, or b is,” can be stated only in cases where one of the two must be the case, as with contraries that lack an intermediate. It is similar to the proposition that says, “If a is not, b is.” For the proposition that proposes “Either a is, or b is” understands that both cannot be the case together, and that, if one is not the case, the other follows as being the case. Thus, if a is not, b will be the case. But this is one of the propositions that above we counted among those formed through connection.

Therefore, whatever syllogisms are formed in the proposition “If a is not, b is,” must also be formed in the proposition that is proposed through disjunction, “Either a is, or b is.” In the former proposition they are formed in four ways. For whichever part of the proposition you assume—whether the antecedent or the consequent, whether in negative or affirmative form—it will produce a syllogism.

For if the proposition is “If a is not, b is,” then:

- if a is not, b will be the case;
- if a is, b will not be the case;
- if b is not, a will be the case;
- if b is the case, a will not be.

The same holds in the disjunctive proposition. For when it is said, “Either a is, or b is,” if a is the case, b will not be; if a is not the case, b will be; if b is not, a will be; and if b is the case, a will not be.

This is also made clear by the following example. If the proposition is “Either he is sick or he is healthy,” whichever of these is taken as the assumption, or denied, the other part will either be affirmed or denied in the following manner:

If he is healthy, he is not sick;  
if he is not healthy, he is sick;  
if he is sick, he is not healthy;  
if he is not sick, he is healthy.

Likewise, the disjunctive proposition that proposes “Either a is not, or b is not” is stated of things that cannot exist together in any way, even if it is not necessary that one of them be the case. It is similar to the connected proposition that proposes, “If a is, b is not.” For the proposition “Either a is not, or b is not” plainly means that, if a is, b cannot be. This may be demonstrated as follows. When it is proposed in this form, “Either a is not, or b is not,” if a is assumed to be the case, b will not be. Consequently, it is similar to the connected proposition that enunciates, “If a is, b is not.”

In this proposition, however, only two combinations generated syllogisms: if a were the case, b was not; and if b were the case, a was not. If a were not the case, it was not necessary that b either be or not be; and if b were not the case, it was not necessary that a either be or not be. Consequently, the disjunctive proposition must likewise have the same number of syllogisms and the same number of combinations that yield no conclusion by necessity. For when it is proposed, “Either a is not, or b is not,” it says: if a is, b will not; and if b is, a will not. But if a is not, it will not be necessary that b either be or not be; and if b is not, it will not be necessary that a either be or not be. This is evident in the following examples.

If someone says, “Either it is not white, or it is not black,” and assumes, “But it is white,” then it will not be black; or again, “But it is black,” then it will not be white. If he assumes that it is not white, it will not be necessary that it either be or not be black; and if he assumes that it is not black, no necessity will result as to whether it is or is not white.

Likewise, the proposition that proposes “Either a is, or b is not” is spoken of things that adhere to one another, and is proposed in propositions that proceed from the greater to the lesser. It is similar to the connected proposition that says, “If a is not, b is not.” For if someone says, “Either a is, or b is not,” and assumes, “But a is not,” then b will in every way not be. Thus, if a is not, b will not be. This is what the disjunction presupposed. In the connected proposition, if a were denied, or b affirmed, some syllogism resulted. But if a were affirmed or b denied, there was no necessity in the conclusion; the same occurs in the disjunctive proposition.

For when it is proposed, “Either a is, or b is not,” if a is not, b will not be. But if b is, a will be; whereas if a is, or if b is not, nothing is necessary.

This may be confirmed by the following terms. Suppose someone proposes, “Either it is an animal, or it is not a human being.” If it is not an animal, it will not be a human being; if it is a human being, it is an animal. But if it is an animal, it need not be a human being; and if it is not a human being, it need not follow that the animal perishes.

The proposition that says, “Either a is not, or b is,” can be proposed of things that adhere to one another, and can proceed from the lesser to the greater. It is similar to the connected proposition that says, “If a is, b is.” For when someone enunciates it in this way, if a is assumed to be the case, b immediately follows as being the case. In this proposition, if a were affirmed, it followed that b was the case; and if b were denied, it followed that a was not the case. But if a were denied or b affirmed, nothing necessary appeared to occur.

The same is true in the disjunctive proposition that says, “Either a is not, or b is.” If a is the case, b will be; if b is not the case, a will not be. But whether a is not or b is, no necessary syllogism follows, as is shown by this example: “Either it is not a human being, or it is an animal.” If we assume, “But it is a human being,” it will be an animal. If we deny that it is an animal, it will not be a human being. But if we deny that it is a human being or affirm that it is an animal, nothing necessary follows.

Consequently, from what has been said above it is clear how many syllogisms belong to disjunctive propositions, and by what differences they are distinguished from connected propositions. Connected propositions display a certain consequence in being or not being; those proposed through disjunction, however, are such that the alternatives cannot be true together.

One also finds connected propositions that mean that the terms cannot be separated from one another, as when we propose, “If a is, b is.” This proposition plainly means that, if a can be the case, b immediately follows as being the case. None of the propositions in disjunction, however, is proposed in such a way that the alternatives appear to exist together. For when we say, “Either a is, or b is,” or vary the same propositions in any other way, the conjunction used disjunctively means that they cannot be the case together.

Since the difference between them is extensive, we have added only a brief discussion of them here, because we said that as many syllogisms arise in propositions formed through disjunction as there were in the connected propositions. And since enough has been said about all hypothetical syllogisms that can be formed in any way, let us here bring the work to an end.

[Col. 0875]

ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS, BOOK ON DIVISION. (C)

[Col. 0875D] How great a benefit the science of division brings to students, and how highly this knowledge has always been esteemed in the Peripatetic discipline, is shown by the published book *On Division* by Andronicus, that most diligent old man; by the fact that the same work was approved by Plotinus, a philosopher of the highest authority [Col. 0876D]; and by its being taken up again by Porphyry in his commentaries on Plato’s book entitled *Sophist*, as well as by the usefulness of this introduction to the *Categories*, which Porphyry himself praised.

For he says that knowledge of genus, species, difference, property, and accident is necessary—not only for many other reasons, but also for the very great usefulness involved in division. Therefore, since its usefulness is so great and its doctrine so easy, I too, as with nearly everything else, have written it out for Roman ears in the manner of an introduction, treating the subject with appropriate precision and restrained brevity. My purpose is that neither the anxiety produced in readers’ minds by a discourse cut short and by an incomplete exposition, nor the suspicion that an inexperienced, untrained, and unaccustomed person might form—that the verbosity of these matters is superfluous—should arise; and that no malicious envy should obscure by oblique attacks what is naturally difficult and unknown to our people, but what has been organized by us with great labor and for the benefit of readers. Rather, let them open a path for scholarship, now by forgiving, now even by approving, instead of tightening the reins on the liberal arts by rejecting with shameless obstinacy whatever is new [Col. 0877B]. For who does not see how greatly the decline of the liberal arts is encouraged if, in the minds of human beings, there is never any despair of displeasing?

But enough of this. We must now divide the term “division” itself, and explain, according to each word, the properties and parts of each proposed kind. “Division” is said in many ways. There is division of a genus into species. Again, there is division when a whole is divided into its proper parts. There is another kind when a word having many meanings is divided into its proper significations. Besides these three, there is another division said to be made according to accident. This has three forms: one, when we separate a subject into its accidents; another, when we divide an accident into its subjects [Col. 0877C]; and a third, when we cut an accident into accidents—provided that both are seen to belong to the same subject.

Examples of all these must be supplied, so that the rationale of this entire division may become clear. We divide a genus into species when we say: of animals, some are rational and others irrational; of rational beings, some are mortal and others immortal. Or when we say: of colors, some are white, some black, and some intermediate.

Every division of a genus into species must be made either into two parts or into more. Yet a genus can have neither infinitely many species nor fewer than two. Why this is so will be demonstrated later.

A whole is divided into parts whenever we resolve it into the things of which each whole is composed—for example, when I say that a house is one thing insofar as it is roof, another insofar as it is wall, and another insofar as it is foundation; or that a human being is composed of soul and body. And when we say that the parts of a human being are Cato, Virgil, Cicero, and each of the individual human beings, although they are particulars, they nevertheless join together and constitute the force of the whole human being. For a human being is neither a genus, nor are individual human beings its species; rather, they are the parts by which the whole human being is constituted.

Division of a word into its proper significations occurs whenever one word having many meanings is explained and its plurality of meanings is displayed. Thus, when I say *canis*, which is a noun, it designates both a barking four-footed animal and the celestial body that shines near Orion’s foot as a baleful star. There is also another *canis*, a marine creature which, growing to an immense size of body, is called “blue.”

[Col. 0878A] There are two forms of this division. Either one noun signifies many things, or a sentence already composed of nouns and verbs does so. A noun signifies many things, as in the example just given. A sentence, too, designates many things, as in: “I say that you, descendant of Aeacus, are able to conquer the Romans.”

The division of a noun into its proper significations is called the division of equivocation; the distribution of a sentence into its proper significations is the distinction of ambiguity, which the Greeks call ἀμφιβολία (*amphibolia*). Thus a noun that signifies many things is called equivocal, whereas a sentence that designates many things is called amphibolous or ambiguous.

Among divisions made according to accident, the division of a subject into accidents is exemplified when we say: of all human beings, some are black, some white, and some of an intermediate color. These are accidents of human beings [Col. 0878B], not species of human beings; and the human being is their subject, not their genus.

The division of an accident into subjects occurs, for example, when we say: of all things that are desired, some are situated in the soul and others in bodies. For what is desirable is an accident of soul and body, not their genus; and the good situated in soul and body does not have these as species, but as subjects.

The division of an accident into accidents occurs when we say: of all white things, some are hard, such as pearls, and others liquid, such as milk. For liquidity, whiteness, and hardness are accidents here. White is divided into hard and liquid things.

When we speak in this way, we divide an accident into other accidents; but this kind of division can always be reversed from one side to the other. For we can say: of hard things, some are black and some white; and again, of liquid things, some are white and some black. We can then reverse the division once more: of black things, some are liquid and some hard; and of white things, some are liquid and others hard.

This division differs from all those mentioned above. We cannot divide a signification into words, since it is the word that is distinguished into its proper significations. Nor are parts divided into a whole, although a whole is separated into parts; nor are species divided into genera, although a genus is divided into species.

The statement made earlier—that this division takes place when both accidents happen to belong to the same subject—becomes clear upon closer inspection. When we say that among hard things some are white and some black, as with stone and ebony, it is evident that both hardness and blackness belong to ebony. A careful reader will discover the same point in the remaining cases.

Those who seek the highest operation of truth must first understand what property all these forms of division possess together, and by what individual differences they are separated from one another. Every division of a word, a genus, and a whole is called division according to itself. The remaining three are included under the distribution of accident.

The difference of division according to itself is as follows. The division of a genus differs from the division of a word because a word is separated into its proper significations, whereas a genus is divided not into significations but, in a certain way, into things generated from it. A genus is always the whole of its proper species, as the more universal is a whole in nature.

Equivocation, however, is called “more universal” with respect to the things signified; it is a whole in the word, but not a whole in nature. Division according to itself also differs from the distribution of a word in that the things falling under the same word have nothing in common except the name itself. Those placed under a genus receive both the name of the genus and its definition.

Moreover, the distribution of a word is not the same among all peoples. What is called *canis* among us, although it has many meanings in the Roman language, may perhaps be predicated simply in a foreign language; and what among us is designated by one name may perhaps be signified among them by several names. The division and distribution of a genus, however, remains the same among all. Hence the division of a word belongs to convention and usage, whereas that of a genus belongs to nature. What is the same among everyone belongs to nature; what varies among some belongs to convention. These, then, are the differences between genus, distribution, and word.

The division of a genus is also distinguished from the distribution of a whole because division of a whole is made according to quantity. Its parts, which together constitute the whole substance, are separated either in actuality or by the mind’s reasoning and thought. The distribution of a genus, however, is accomplished according to quality. When I place a human being under animal, the division is made according to quality. For the question is: what kind of animal is a human being? Since a human being is formed by a quality, the answer will be either “rational” or, in another respect, “mortal.”

Furthermore, every genus is naturally prior to its proper species, whereas a whole is posterior to its proper parts. The parts that join together to make a whole sometimes precede the perfection of their composite by nature alone, and sometimes also in temporal sequence. Hence we dissolve a genus into what is posterior, but a whole into what is prior.

This is also the reason for the true statement that, if a genus is destroyed, its species immediately perish; but if a species is destroyed, the genus is not thereby destroyed and continues to exist in nature. The reverse occurs in the case of a whole. If one part of a whole perishes, the whole no longer exists as the whole whose one part has been destroyed. But if the whole perishes, its parts remain distributed. Thus, if someone removes the roof from an intact house, he disrupts the whole that previously existed; but once the roof has been destroyed, the walls and foundation remain.

Moreover, the genus is matter for its species. Just as bronze, upon receiving a form, becomes a statue, so a genus, upon receiving a difference, becomes a species. The multiplicity of a whole’s parts is its matter, whereas their composition is its form. For just as a species consists of genus and difference, so a whole consists of parts. Hence a whole differs from each of its parts by the composition of the parts themselves, while a species differs from its genus by the conjunction of its difference.

Furthermore, a species is always the same as its genus in the relevant respect: a human being is the same as an animal, and virtue is the same as a state. A part, however, is not always the same as the whole. A hand is not the same as a human being, nor a wall the same as a house. This is clear in things whose parts are dissimilar.

The same does not seem equally clear in things whose parts are similar, as in a little rod of bronze. Its parts are continuous and are made of the same bronze, and therefore they appear to be the same as the whole. But this is false: perhaps such parts are the same in substance, but not in quantity.

It remains to give the differences between the distribution of a word and that of a whole. They differ in that a whole consists of parts, whereas a word does not consist of the things it signifies. A whole is divided into parts; a word is not divided into parts, but into the things that the word itself signifies. Hence, if one part is removed, the whole perishes; but if one of the things signified by a word with many meanings is removed, the word itself remains.

Now that the differences of division according to itself have been stated, let the distribution of genus be examined.

First, genus must be defined. A genus is that which is predicated of several things differing in species, in answer to the question “what is it?” A species is what we place under a genus. A difference is so called because we propose that one thing differs from another.

A genus is what is appropriately given in answer when someone asks what a thing is; a difference is what most correctly answers the question “what kind is it?” When someone asks, “What is a human being?” the correct answer is “animal.” When he asks, “What kind of thing is a human being?” the appropriate answer is “rational.”

A genus is divided sometimes into species and sometimes into differences, when the species into which the genus ought to be divided lack names. Thus we say: of animals, some are rational and others irrational. “Rational” and “irrational” are differences. But because there is no single name for the species “rational animal,” we put the difference in place of the species and join it to the higher genus. For every difference, when added to its proper genus, produces a species. Hence matter in one respect is genus, while form is difference.

When species are called by their proper names, the correct division of a genus is made not into differences but into species. This is why a definition is assembled from several terms.

If all species were called by their own names, every definition would be made from only two terms. For example, when I ask, “What is a human being?” why would I need to say “a mortal rational animal,” if “rational animal” were designated by a proper name, since, when joined with the remaining difference, namely “mortal,” it would complete the definition of a human being with perfectly sound reasoning and complete expression?

As things stand, however, the division of species is necessary for complete definitions; and perhaps the method of division and definition is the same. For one definition is composed by joining divisions together.

But since some things are equivocal and others univocal, and since we receive univocal things into divisions of genera, whereas in the case of equivocal things there is only a division of signification, we must first examine what is equivocal and what is univocal. Otherwise, if these matters deceive us, we may resolve an equivocal name into significative units as though they were species. Thus, once again, a definition is necessary for division. We determine by definition what is equivocal and what is univocal.

Some differences are per se, while others are accidental. Of these, some are immediately relinquishing, while others are immediately accompanying. Examples of relinquishing differences are sleeping, sitting, standing, and being awake. Examples of accompanying differences are having curly hair, provided it has not been artificially curled with a curling iron, and having gray eyes, provided they have not been disturbed by some external injury [Col. 0881A].

These differences must not be employed in the division of a genus. Nor are they suitable for definitions, since whatever is suitable for the division of a genus we most properly gather together for definitions as well. Only differences that belong per se are suitable for the division of a genus. For these inform and complete the substance of each thing, as rationality and mortality do in the case of a human being.

How, then, can we determine whether these differences belong to the class of immediately relinquishing, immediately accompanying, or permanently substantial differences? This must now be considered. It is not enough to know which differences we should employ in division; we must also know how to recognize correctly the differences that should be employed and those that should be rejected.

We must therefore first see whether the proposed difference can belong to every subject, and always belong to it. If it can be separated from the subject either in actuality or in thought, it must be excluded from the division of the genus.

If it is frequently separated both in actuality and in thought, it belongs to the class of differences that immediately relinquish, such as sitting, which is more frequently separated and is divided from its subject in actuality itself. Those that are separated from the subject only in thought belong to the accompanying differences. Thus we separate having gray eyes from the subject only in thought when we say, “There is an animal with gray eyes,” as in the case of any human being. Even if that human being did not possess such eyes, nothing would prevent him from being a human being.

There is another difference that cannot be separated in thought, and if it were separated, the species would be destroyed. Thus we say that it belongs to a human being that he alone can count or learn geometry; if this capacity is separated from a human being, the human being himself does not remain.

Yet these are not immediately among the differences that belong to substance. A human being is not human because he can perform these activities, but because he is rational and mortal. Those differences through which a species exists are therefore placed both in the definition of the species—for example, the definition of a human being—and in the division of its genus, which contains the species, namely the human being himself.

In general, we must say that whatever differences are such that the species cannot exist apart from them, but exists through them alone, must be taken either in the division of the genus or in the definition of the species.

Some things that differ must not be placed over against one another in divisions. Thus, in the case of animal, no one says that some animals are rational and others have two feet. Although rational and two-footed differ, they are not separated from one another by any opposition.

It is established that only those differences that differ from one another by some opposition can divide the genus when placed beneath it. There are four kinds of opposition: as contraries, for example good and bad; as possession and privation, for example sight and blindness.

There are also certain things in which it is difficult to determine whether they should be placed among contraries or among privation and possession: motion and rest, health and illness, wakefulness and sleep, light and darkness. But these matters may be treated elsewhere. For now, the remaining oppositions must be discussed.

The third opposition is according to affirmation and negation, as in “Socrates is alive” and “Socrates is not alive.” The fourth is according to relation, as in father and son, master and slave, double and half, the sensible and sense.

It must therefore be shown, with the greatest correctness, according to which of these four oppositions the division of a genus is made.

It is clear that there are four oppositions and that genera and species are separated by opposites. We must now say according to which of these four oppositions, and in what manner, species ought to be separated from a genus.

Let the opposition of contradiction come first. I call the opposition of contradiction that which is expressed by affirmation and negation.

In this opposition, negation by itself produces no species. When I say “human being,” “horse,” or something of this kind, these are species. Whatever someone puts forward by negation, however, does not declare a species. “Not being a human being” is not a species, since every species establishes being. Negation, on the other hand, separates whatever it proposes from being. When I say “human being,” I seem to have spoken of something that exists; but when I say “not human being,” I destroy the substance of a human being by negation.

Thus, in itself, negation has no place in the division of a genus into species. Nevertheless, it is often necessary to form a species by negation when the species that we wish to designate by a simple name has no name. Thus we say: of odd numbers, some are prime, such as three, five, and seven, and others are not prime, such as nine. Again: of figures, some are perfectly straight; and of colors, some are white, some black, and some neither white nor black.

Therefore, when no single name has been assigned to species, it is necessary to express them by negation. This is imposed by necessity, not by nature.

Accordingly, whenever we make a division by negation, an affirmation or a simple name should be stated first: “Of numbers, some are prime and others are not prime.” If the negation is stated first, understanding of the thing proposed becomes slower. When you first say that there are certain prime numbers, and then explain by an example or definition what kind they are, the hearer immediately understands what kind are not prime. If you proceed in the opposite order, either neither will be understood immediately, or both will be understood only later.

A division, however, which was devised because of the evident nature of a genus ought rather to lead to what is easier to understand.

Moreover, affirmation is prior and negation posterior. What is first ought also to be placed first in a division. It is also necessary that finite things always be prior to infinite things: the equal to the unequal, virtue to vices, the certain to the uncertain, and the stable and fixed to the unstable and changeable.

Everything expressed either by a determinate part of speech or by an affirmation is more finite than a noun joined with a negative particle or than a complete negation. Therefore division should be made according to the finite rather than the infinite.

If this causes anyone anxiety, or if these matters seem perhaps more obscure than he desires, that has nothing to do with me, since I make no promise to render knowledge easy. I do not present these matters for the untrained, but for those already instructed and who have advanced almost to a further stage of the entire discipline. What the order of this work—that is, of dialectic—is, I explained carefully when it was necessary for me to discuss the order of the Peripatetic discipline.

These, then, are the points stated concerning the opposition constituted by affirmation and negation.

The opposition according to possession and privation also appears similar to the one just discussed. Privation in a certain way negates possession, but they differ in that negation can always exist, whereas privation cannot always exist, but only when it is possible to possess the relevant possession. The *Categories* have already taught us this.

Thus privation is understood to be a certain form. It does not merely deprive, but also disposes the deprived subject itself in accordance with its own character. Blindness does not merely deprive the eye of light; it also disposes the eye itself, according to its own nature, as deprived of light. A blind person is said to be disposed and affected, in a certain way, toward privation. Aristotle also attests to this in the *Physics*.

Hence we frequently employ the difference of privation in the division of a genus. Here too, however, we must proceed in the same way as in contradiction. The possession, which is analogous to affirmation, must be placed first; then privation, which is analogous to negation.

Sometimes certain privations are expressed by the name of a possession, as in “bereft,” “blind,” and “widowed.” Sometimes they are expressed with a privative particle, as when we say “finite, infinite,” or “equal, unequal.” In such cases, “equal” and “finite” must be placed first in the division, while the privations come second.

Let these remarks suffice concerning the opposition of privation and possession.

With respect to the opposition of contraries, it may perhaps be questioned whether it should be understood as an opposition according to privation and possession—for example, whether white and black are such that white is the privation of black and black the privation of white. But this may be considered elsewhere. For now, it must be treated as though it were another kind of opposition, just as Aristotle himself arranged it in the *Categories*.

There are many divisions of genera according to contraries. For we generally reduce nearly all differences to contraries. But since some contraries lack an intermediate and others have one, division must be made accordingly. Thus, among colors, some are black, some white, and some neither.

Every definition and every division would be made with two terms if the lack of names, which often occurs, did not prevent it, as stated above. How both could always be made with two terms will become clear in the following way.

When we say that of animals some are rational and others irrational, “rational animal” tends toward the definition of a human being. But because “rational animal” has no single name, let us assign it the name “letter A.” Again, among things designated by the letter A—that is, rational animals—some are mortal and others immortal.

Therefore, if we wish to give the definition of a human being, we shall say: “A human being is mortal A.” For if the definition of a human being is “rational, mortal animal,” and “rational animal” is signified by the letter A, then “mortal A” has the same meaning as “rational, mortal animal,” since A signifies rational animal, as stated.

Thus the definition of a human being is made with two terms, the letter A and “mortal.” If names were found for everything, every definition would always be complete in two terms.

Division too, when names are available, is always divided into two terms. This becomes clear if someone supplies a name when a genus or difference lacks one. Thus we say: of figures, some are three-sided, some equilateral, some have two equal sides, and some are entirely unequal.

If this triple division were expressed with names, it would become a double division: among three-sided figures, some are equal and some unequal; among unequal figures, some have only two equal sides and others have three unequal sides—that is, all unequal sides.

Likewise, when we say that among all things some are good, some bad, and some indifferent—that is, neither good nor bad—the division would become twofold if it were expressed in this way: among all things, some are different and some indifferent; among different things, some are good and some bad.

Thus every division would be divided into two if names were not lacking for species and differences.

We said that the fourth opposition is according to relation, as in father and son, master and slave, double and half, the sensible and sense.

These have no substantial difference by which they are distinguished from one another. Rather, they possess a kinship by which they are related to one another and cannot exist without one another. Therefore a genus must not be divided into relative parts; this entire kind of division must be separated from genus.

For slave and master are not species of human being, nor are half and double species of number.

Since there are four kinds of opposition—affirmation and negation, possession and privation, contraries, and relation—the division according to relation must always be rejected, though not always by necessity; division according to privation and possession and according to contraries must be employed.

Contrariety, especially, must be placed among differences, but so too must privation, because something appears to be opposed contrary to possession—for example, finite and infinite. Although infinite is a privation, it is nevertheless formed through the conception of a contrary. For, as has been said, it is a certain form.

It is worth investigating whether genera are correctly divided into species or into differences. The definition of division is the distribution of a genus into its nearest species. Therefore, according to the nature and definition of division, a genus ought always to be separated into its proper species.

Sometimes this cannot be done, however, for the reason given above: many species lack names. Moreover, since some genera are first, some last, and some intermediate, the first is substance, the last animal, and the intermediate body. For body is the genus of animal, while substance is the genus of body.

Just as nothing can be found above substance that could be placed in the position of a genus, so nothing can be found below animal. A human being is a species, not a genus.

Therefore division into species will seem preferable, provided there is no lack of names. But if we do not possess names for all these things, it is appropriate to separate the first genera down to the last into differences.

This must be done in the following manner: divide the first genus into its own differences, not into those of a later genus; and again divide the later genus into its own differences, not into those of a still later genus. For the differences of body are not the same as those of animal.

If someone says, “Of substances, some are corporeal and others incorporeal,” he will have made a correct division, since these are proper differences of substance. If, however, he says, “Of substances, some are animate and others inanimate,” he has not correctly separated the differences of substance. These are differences of body, not of substance—that is, of the second genus, not of the first.

It is therefore clear that the division of prior genera must be made according to their proper differences, not according to those of a later genus.

Whenever a genus is resolved either into differences or into species, definitions or examples must immediately be supplied after the division has been made. If someone does not have an abundance of definitions, it is sufficient to add examples. Thus, when we say that of bodies some are animate, we may add “such as human beings or animals”; and that others are inanimate, “such as stones.”

A division, like a definition, must neither be deficient nor excessive. More species than fall under the genus must not be added, nor fewer, so that the division may be convertible with itself, as a definition is.

A definition is convertible in this way: “Virtue is the best disposition of the mind”; and again, “The best disposition of the mind is virtue.”

So too with division: every genus will be one of the things that exist, and a species will be the proper genus of something; again, any species will be the proper genus of something.

The same genus can be divided in many ways, as in the case of all bodies and of all things possessing some magnitude. Just as we can divide a circle into semicircles and into what the Greeks call τομεῖς (*tomeis*), which we call “sections,” and just as we can divide a square in one way by drawing a diagonal through its angle into triangles, in another way into parallelograms, and in another into squares [Col. 0885C], so too a genus may be divided in several ways.

For example, we say that of numbers some are even and others odd, and again that some are prime and others not prime. Of triangles, some are equilateral, some have only two equal sides, and some have all their sides unequal; and again, of triangles, some are right-angled, some have three acute angles, and some have one obtuse angle.

Thus one and the same genus can have multiple divisions.

It is very useful to know that a genus is, in a certain way, a single likeness of many species, displaying the substantial agreement among them. For this reason a genus is a collective unity of many species.

The species of one genus are disjunctive because they are formed by differences, as has been said. Therefore, under one genus there cannot be fewer than two species, since every difference consists in a plurality of things that differ [Col. 0885D].

Much has now been said about the division of genus and species. By following this path, an easier ability to proceed from the division of genus to the definition of species is opened up.

It is necessary not only to learn which differences we should employ for a definition, but also to master the art of definition through the most careful study. I shall omit the question whether any definition can be demonstrated, how it can be discovered through demonstration, and whatever Aristotle treated more subtly concerning it in the *Posterior Analytics*. I shall explain only the rule for defining.

Some things are higher, some lower, and some intermediate. No definition encompasses the higher things, because their superior genera cannot be found. The lower things, such as individuals, also lack specific differences. Consequently, they too are excluded from definition.

Intermediate things, however, which have genera and are predicated of other things—whether genera, species, or individuals—can fall under definition.

Given such a species, one that has a genus and is predicated of things below it, I first take its genus, divide the differences of that genus, and add a difference to the genus. I then consider whether that difference, joined with the genus, can be equal to the species that I have undertaken to circumscribe by a definition.

If it is less than the species, I take the difference that I had just placed with the genus as though it were a genus and divide it into its further differences. I then join these two differences to the higher genus. If this equals the species, it will be called the definition of the species. If it is still less, I divide the second difference again into others.
