I join all of them to the genus and again observe whether all the differences together with the genus are equal to the species being defined. Finally, I distribute the differences into further differences as many times as necessary, until, joined with the genus, they describe the species by an equal definition.

Examples will make this clearer.

If we are proposing to define the noun, the word “noun” is predicated of several nouns and, in a certain way, contains individuals beneath itself. I therefore define “noun” as follows.

I take its genus, which is “word,” and divide it: of words, some are significative and others are not. A non-significative word has nothing to do with a noun, since a noun signifies.

I therefore take the difference “significative” and join it to the genus, that is, to “word,” and say: “significative word.” I then consider whether this genus and difference are equal to “noun.”

But they are not yet equal. A word can be significative without being a noun. Some words designate pain, while others naturally signify affections of the soul; these are not nouns, as with interjections.

I therefore divide significative word into further differences: of significative words, some are according to human convention and others are natural. A word that signifies naturally has nothing to do with a noun, whereas a word that signifies according to human convention agrees with a noun.

Accordingly, I join these two differences—“significative” and “according to convention”—to “word,” that is, to the genus, and say: “A noun is a significative word according to convention.”

But again this does not equal “noun.” Verbs too are significative words according to convention. Therefore this is not the definition of a noun alone.

I divide the difference “according to convention” again and say: among significative words according to convention, some are with time and others without time. The difference “with time” is not joined to a noun, because it belongs to the signification of time by verbs, whereas nouns do not signify time.

It remains, then, that the difference “without time” agrees with a noun. I therefore join these three differences to the genus and say: “A noun is a significative word according to convention, without time.”

But again a complete definition does not result. A word can be significative, according to convention, and without time, and yet not be one noun but a combination of nouns—a sentence such as “Socrates with Plato and the students.” Although this sentence is incomplete, it is nevertheless a sentence.

Therefore the final difference, “without time,” must itself be divided by further differences. We shall say: among significative words according to convention and without time, some are such that a part of them signifies something independently; this belongs to a sentence. Others are such that a part of them signifies nothing independently; this belongs to a noun. For no part of a noun designates anything independently.

The definition is therefore formed as follows:

[Col. 0887B] A noun is a significative word according to convention, without time, no part of which, when separated, signifies anything independently.

Do you see, then, how correctly the definition has been constituted? For when I said “word,” I separated the noun from the other sounds; when I added “significative,” I separated the noun from non-…

I separated [it] from significant sounds; by [saying] “according to convention” and “without time,” I separated the property of a noun from naturally significant sounds and from verbs; and by proposing that its parts signify nothing outside it, I distinguished it from a sentence, whose parts signify something independently when separated. Hence every noun is enclosed by that definition, and wherever this definition is appropriately applied, you should have no doubt that the thing in question is a noun.

[Col. 0887C]

It must also be said that the genus in a division is wholly present, whereas in a definition it is a part. Thus a definition is as though its parts join together to form a certain whole, while a division is as though a whole were dissolved into parts. The division of a genus is therefore analogous to the division of a whole, and a definition to the composition of a whole. In a division of the genus, for example, “animal” is the whole of “human being,” since it contains the human being within itself. In a definition, however, it is a part: for the genus, joined with the other differences, composes the species. Thus, when I say that among animals some are rational and others irrational, and again that among rational beings some are mortal and others immortal, “animal,” “rational,” and “mortal” make up a whole; these three are constituents of the human being. But if in a definition I say, “A human being is a mortal rational animal,” these three unite to form one human being. Therefore both genus and difference are found to be parts of the human being.

[Col. 0887D]

Thus in a division the genus is the whole, and the species a part. In the same way, the differences are wholes, while the species into which they are divided are parts. In a definition, however, both the genus and the differences are parts, while the defined species is the whole. But enough of this for now.

Let us now discuss that division which is the division of a whole into parts. This was the second division after the division of a genus. For by “whole” we signify several things. A whole is, first, something continuous, such as a body or a line, or anything of this kind. We also call something a whole that is not continuous, such as a whole flock, a whole people, or a whole army. We likewise call that a whole which is universal, such as a human being or a horse. For these are wholes of their parts—that is, of human beings or horses—and therefore we also call each individual human being a particular.

[Col. 0888A]

That too is called a whole which consists of certain powers, as in the soul: one power is the power of knowing, another of perceiving, another of nourishing. These are parts, but not species.

Since, then, “whole” is said in so many ways, the division of a whole must be made—first, if it is continuous—into those parts from which the whole is evidently constituted. Otherwise there is no division. Thus you divide the body of a human being into its parts: the head, hands, chest, and feet; and in whatever other manner a correct division is made according to its proper parts.

But where composition is manifold, division too is manifold. Thus an animal may be divided into parts that have parts similar to themselves, such as flesh and bones, and again into parts that do not have parts similar to themselves, such as hands and feet. The same applies to a ship and a house.

[Col. 0888B]

We also dissolve a book into verses, verses into sentences, sentences into syllables, and syllables into letters. Thus syllables, letters, words, and verses appear to be certain parts of the whole book; yet, considered in another way, they are not parts of the whole but parts of parts.

One must not, however, examine everything as though the divisions were made in actuality, but rather as though they were made in thought and by reason. Thus we divide wine mixed with water into wines mixed with water—this is an actual division. We also divide it into wine and water, from which the mixture is composed—this is a division by reason, since the components can no longer be separated from one another in actuality.

A whole may also be divided into matter and form. For a statue is constituted in one way from its parts and in another way from matter and form—that is, from bronze and shape. In the same way, those wholes that are not continuous must also be divided; and likewise universals.

[Col. 0888C]

Thus, among human beings, some are in Europe, some in Africa, and some in Asia. The division of that whole which consists of powers must be made in the following way. One part of the soul is found in shrubs, another in animals; and again, of the part that is in animals, one is rational and another sensitive. These parts are in turn dispersed through further subdivisions. Yet the soul is not their genus but their whole: these are parts of the soul, not as parts of quantity, but as parts of some power or capacity.

[Col. 0888D]

For the substance of the soul is joined together from these powers. Hence this kind of division has something in common both with the division of a genus and with the division of a whole. The fact that the predication of any part follows the soul to which it belongs pertains to the division of a genus—for wherever a species is found, its genus immediately follows. But the fact that not every soul is joined with all the parts, but one with one set and another with another, must necessarily be referred to the nature of a whole.

It remains, then, to discuss the division of a sound into its significations. A sound is divided in three ways. It is divided into several significations, as in equivocal or ambiguous expressions. One name signifies several things, as in “dog.” Again, one sentence signifies several things, as when I say, “The Greeks defeated the Trojans.”

In another way, it is divided according to manner. For in this case the expression does not signify several things, but signifies one thing in several ways. Thus, when we say “infinite,” it signifies one thing, whose limit cannot be found. But we say this either with respect to measure, multitude, or species.

[Col. 0889A]

With respect to measure, as when we say that the world is infinite, since we mean infinite in magnitude; with respect to multitude, as when we say that the division of bodies is infinite, since we signify an infinite multitude of divisions; and with respect to species, as when we speak of infinite figures, since the species of figures are infinite. We also call something infinite with respect to time, as when we call the world infinite because its limit cannot be found in time. In the same way we call God infinite, since the limit of his higher life cannot be found with respect to time.

Thus this expression does not in itself signify several things, but is predicated in several ways of individual things, while nevertheless signifying one thing. A further mode of division is according to determination. Whenever any expression is uttered without determination, it produces uncertainty in the understanding. Thus “human being” is an expression that signifies many things. Since it is not enclosed within any definition, the listener’s understanding is carried among many waves and led astray by errors.

[Col. 0889B]

For what can any listener understand when the speaker does not enclose what he says within any determination? Unless someone defines it by saying, “Every human being walks,” or at least, “A certain human being walks,” and uses the name in accordance with that designation, the listener has no rational understanding of what is meant.

There are also other determinations. If someone says, “Give it to me,” no one understands what is to be given unless the understanding and a definite account of the determination are added. Or if someone says, “Come to me,” it is not known where or when the person is to come without a determination.

[Col. 0889C]

Everything ambiguous is indeed doubtful, but not everything doubtful is ambiguous. The examples just given are doubtful, but not ambiguous. In ambiguous expressions, each of two interpretations seems rationally to the listener to be what he has understood. Thus, when someone says, “I hear that the Greeks defeated the Trojans,” one person thinks that the Greeks defeated the Trojans, while another thinks that the Trojans defeated the Greeks; and each understands this rationally from the speaker’s own words.

But when I say, “Give me what you ought to give,” no listener rationally understands anything from the words themselves. He will conjecture what I did not say rather than clearly perceive, by some reasoning, what was not previously expressed.

[Col. 0889D]

Since, then, a sound is divided in so many ways—either according to significations, according to the mode of signification, or according to determinations—in those things divided according to signification, it is necessary to demonstrate by definition not only the significations but also the different things that are signified.

Aristotle carefully taught this in the *Topics*: among things called good, some are good, such as those that retain the quality of goodness, while others are not themselves called good by reason of any quality, but are called good because they make a thing good. One must practice this art especially, as Aristotle himself says, in opposition to sophistical harassment.

For if there is no underlying thing signified by a sound, it is not called designative. If, however, there is one thing signified by the sound, it is called simple; but if there are several, it is called multiple—that is, signifying many things. These distinctions must therefore be made correctly, lest we be trapped in some syllogism.

[Col. 0890A]

But if a sentence is amphibolous—that is, ambiguous—it may happen that what it signifies is possible in both ways, as in the example given above. For it could happen that the Greeks defeated the Trojans and that the Trojans overcame the Greeks. There are, however, other cases in which one interpretation is impossible, as when I say, “A human being eats bread.” This signifies that a human being eats bread and, again, that bread eats a human being; but the latter is impossible.

Therefore, whenever the matter concerns contention, both the possible and the impossible interpretations must be divided. Whenever it concerns truth, only the possible interpretation should be stated, and the impossible one left aside.

Since there are several kinds of expressions that signify several things, it must be said that some have their multiplicity of signification in a part of the expression, while others have it in the whole sentence. In the former case, the word or phrase itself is called equivocal. The whole sentence, however, is multiple by reason of equivocation. That which retains its multiplicity of signification in the whole sentence—as was said above—is called ambiguous.

[Col. 0890B]

The significations of equivocal expressions may be divided either by equivocation in sentences or by definition. Thus, when I say, “A human being lives,” the reference may be understood to be both a real human being and a painted one. The division may be made in this way: “A mortal rational animal lives”—which is true; “A representation of a rational mortal animal lives”—which is false.

The division may also be made by any addition that determines the genus, case, or some article. Thus, when I say, “Canna has been stained with the blood of the Romans,” the word indicates both a reed and a river. We divide it in this way by an article, saying, “This Canna has been stained with the blood of the Romans”; by gender, saying, “Canna was full of Roman blood”; or by case or number. In one instance it is singular only, in another plural; and the same applies to the other cases.

[Col. 0890C]

Some expressions are ambiguous according to accent, others according to spelling. According to accent, for example, *pone, pone*; according to spelling, *queror* and *quaeror*, one from inquiry and the other from lamentation. These are again divided according to spelling itself, or according to active and passive usage: *quaeror*, from inquiry, is passive, whereas *queror*, from lamentation, is active.

Ambiguous sentences must be divided either by addition, as in “I hear that the Trojans are being defeated, the Greeks having won”; by subtraction, as in “I hear that the Greeks have won”; by division, as in “The Greeks won; the Trojans were defeated”; or by some transposition. Thus, instead of saying, “I hear that the Trojans defeated the Greeks,” we may say, “I hear that the Greeks defeated the Trojans.” This ambiguity is resolved by any of these methods.

[Col. 0890D]

The signification of expressions must not, however, always be divided in the manner of a genus. In a genus all the species are enumerated. In ambiguity, by contrast, as many interpretations suffice as can be useful for the sentence that the ambiguous expression connects in either direction.

Enough, then, has been said about the division of a sound. The division of a genus and of a whole was also proposed and completed. Thus all the divisions considered in themselves have been treated with the greatest care, insofar as the brevity appropriate to an introduction allowed.

[Col. 0891A]

Now we shall discuss those divisions that arise accidentally. Their general rule is that whatever is divided must be separated into opposites. Thus, when we divide a subject according to its accidents, we do not say, “Some bodies are white and others sweet,” since these are not opposites, but rather, “Some bodies are white, others black, and others neither.”

The same method must be followed in the other accidental divisions, and one must pay particular attention not to say either too much or too little, as happens in the division of a genus. One must not leave out any accident belonging to the same opposition that is present in the subject and should be stated in the division; nor should one add anything that cannot be present in the subject.

[Col. 0892A]

The later Peripatetic school examined the distinctions among divisions with the greatest care, separating and distributing division in itself from division according to accident, and also distinguishing these divisions from one another. The ancients, however, used accident indiscriminately in place of a genus, and accidents in place of species or differences. Therefore it seemed to us very useful both to set forth what these divisions have in common and to separate them according to their proper differences. We have carefully presented the entire subject of division, insofar as the brevity of an introduction permitted.

# Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, *Book on Definition* (C, G, S)*
[Col. 0891B] The first discourse in speaking and disputing is always that which is called definition, as the dialectical authorities and M. Tullius himself repeatedly admonish us. For nothing can ever be brought into contest and controversy—provided that it belongs to discourse—unless the matter over which the future conflict will take place has first been fixed by a definition, so that it may be clear between the two who are about to undertake the lawsuit what it is about which the future question will deal. Hence the excellence of defining must be discerned not only as a matter of usefulness, because through this discourse the matter is always unfolded and because it is the discourse that explains what the thing under inquiry is, but also because, whenever it is applied as the principal element, it produces the greatest and clearest illumination of the matter whose question has been brought into opposition.

Indeed, if words [Col. 0891C] were either familiar to everyone, or always retained one and the same signification, and if they did not deceive hearers by ambiguous or obscure speech and mislead speakers through differing interpretations, definition would certainly not be thought necessary at all. But since names imposed upon things and individual words have been established according to the judgment of the person who decided that things should be called in this way, and since they have been so skillfully composed that they lead hearers by a certain indication toward the meaning of things rather than by an open declaration, I consider it extremely necessary to know what definition is and of what kinds and parts it consists, so that it may both most easily point out the thing it declares and, once the recognized methods of speaking have been learned, remove the weariness produced by its variety.

And first, so that we may seem to preserve order through instruction, a definition of definition itself must be supplied. [Col. 0891D] Definition is, as M. Tullius says in the *Topics*, “a discourse that explains what the thing being defined is.” This is so evident, and must be understood in such a way, that it seems necessary to declare both what genus definition belongs to, what it encompasses, and in what manner the same definition has been perfectly defined.

Names or words sometimes signify things, sometimes actions, sometimes individual statements, sometimes discourses; and although the genus of all these actions, statements, and discourses seems to be what we call discourse, nevertheless a thing, in its proper name and fixed signification, seems to be different from an action, different from a statement, and an individual and unique thing different from a discourse. [Col. 0892B] Therefore definition is not the word of an action, nor of any bodily or incorporeal thing, but is a discourse. For such an utterance as expresses what the thing under inquiry is is unquestionably called a discourse, just as an exordium, a narration, and the other things that we call parts of discourse are discourses. Thus definition too is a discourse.

But since this is a general name which, as we have said, also applies to exposition, narration, invocation, prayer, and all the other individual forms that are called discourses, a species has been added so that what has been set down generally may be brought to the particular matter under inquiry. For we were asking what definition is; and, to make this clear, M. Tullius added: “a discourse that explains what the thing being defined is.” Such a discourse is definition and nothing else. For [Col. 0892C] narration is indeed a discourse, but it does not explain what it defines; it explains what has happened. Likewise, the other individual discourses, established in their own functions and activities, are something different from this discourse, which explains what the thing being defined is. Thus the species has been added: the genus above is discourse, while the species is that discourse which explains what is being defined.

Finally, something has been added to declare more certainly and more properly what has been said: “explains what it is.” For there are other discourses that explain rather what something is like or how great it is. But this discourse explains none of these things; it explains only what it is. The cognition involved in this division is different, since it is one thing to know what something is like and another to explain what it is. The latter is contained in apprehending the substance of a thing, the former [Col. 0892D] in knowing its quality. This, then, is Cicero’s definition.

Nevertheless, let us make clearer by our own explanation what definition is. Everything demonstrated by discourse is shown either to exist, or what it is, or what it is like. When discourse is applied to declaring whether some thing exists, it is not definition. Likewise, when discourse shows what something is like, it is not definition. But when it shows what something is—the middle position between whether it exists and what it is like—it is definition. It is the middle position in this sense: there is by then no doubt whether the thing exists, while what it is like is located in the knowledge not of the person asking but of the person defining. This middle kind of discourse, I say, which shows what the thing under inquiry is, is called definition.

Every definition has an uncertain matter as its subject. Every thing, if it is certain, does not need definition; if it is uncertain, it is not yet a thing for us, and it seeks to be shown by definition. For every thing, if it is already a thing, is certain, as we have said. Once it is certain and possesses its qualities, by which it is easily comprehended, what it is is also easily recognized. For what something is can never be understood unless what it is like has first been comprehended.

Every definition is adopted either for the purpose of proving a thing, or, if the matter is under inquiry, of strengthening it, or, if some thing is already known to an opponent or hearer, of confirming it. Nevertheless, definition is used so that the same known thing may be held certain and fixed.

Every definition is either rhetorical discourse or dialectical discourse. If it is rhetorical, originating in contention, it divides itself through the parts of the matter under inquiry, and does not remain wholly occupied with its own subject in treating a single matter, so that, when the complete, certain, and perfect nature of each thing is known, the statements of the disputants may distribute that same thing among all its parts.

We retain the violation of a tomb as a certain, complete, and perfect matter when the intention and the deed of the violator are also present in the tomb that has been dug up, since someone seems to have undertaken it with the purpose of digging up and profaning the dead. Therefore, as we have said, violation of a tomb consists both in intention and in deed, and the matter of the violated tomb is complete through these two elements: someone opened the tomb in order to carry away its ornaments.

The same person, accused of violating the tomb, is brought to trial. Without doubt, the case requires a defining discourse and contention explaining what violation of a tomb is. But orators use the individual parts of the whole and complete deed, so that one may assert that violation of a tomb consists in the tomb’s having been opened, while another may argue that it consists in the intention. Thus the treatment of the defining discourse arises: when everything recognized as belonging to the violation of a tomb has been distributed among its parts and the individual orators have taken hold of those parts, they seem to use definition in the manner of contention.

Yet it is not properly called such a definition, since it is not certain, complete, or integral unless the discourse, expressing everything that belongs to the matter under inquiry, has declared what it is. This, however, is a captious and false definition, [Col. 0893D] not a certain rhetorical definition.

There is another definition also known to be suited to orators, which is very far removed from the excellence of defining. Through comparison it does not show what something is; rather, it concludes by discourse that one thing is like another, although the things are different. Thus, when it is asked what it is to receive something in the proper sense—a true and certain matter—it is nothing other than to take something offered by someone with one’s own hand.

By comparison M. Tullius defines Verres as having received money, since his companions, allies, and attendants received money. “Those companions of yours,” he says, “were your hands.”

Likewise, when it is asked what an enemy is, we say that an enemy is someone who has contrived some evil; and Cicero, using comparison, says: “An enemy is one who acts against the interests, will, honor, and dignity of everyone.” From this we conclude that such definitions are especially suitable to the contentions of orators, but are far removed from the excellence of definition. These definitions, nevertheless, which are suited to orators and poets, contain a fixed order in their explanation within a discourse.

M. Tullius has established instructions concerning this matter in the *Rhetorics*, according to which every definition—that is, every discourse explaining what the matter under inquiry is—is held together by these members and parts. First, our discourse must briefly contain what the matter under inquiry is; this is called the definition. Next, approval of that definition must be placed after it, by which we show that what we briefly set down in the definition is in fact so, proving it by rational arguments. Third, we introduce the application of the same definition to the species concerning which the question and judgment have been established. Thus, after defining the matter generally, saying that the thing under inquiry is of this kind, and then establishing through approval that what we define is true, we show in the third place that this is what happened, or that this is the matter under inquiry. This part of the discourse is called the deduction of the genus to the species.

Fourth, in our discourse we place the destruction of the opposing party’s definition. That is, we set forth how the opponents have defined the very matter concerning which we established a definition above, and we demonstrate that their definition is defective. We shall explain later in what way it is defective, for it has its own certain and integral parts, which we shall omit discussing for the present.

M. Tullius gives a brief definition of hostility, set out as follows: “Do you think there are greater hostilities than opposing wills and dissimilar pursuits among human beings?” As we said, this is a rhetorical definition, a discourse briefly concluded to show what hostilities are.

After this definition, approval is supplied: “The person who regards faith and the most sacred religious duty as fundamental in life—can he fail to be an enemy to someone who has plundered all the shrines?” In the remaining words that follow, one may observe that approval of a definition and the deduction of a definition into a species can be joined. For here Marcus Tullius approves that hostilities consist in opposing pursuits and dissimilar wills in such a way that he includes in his words the very species under inquiry.

Approval could have been given in this form: that those are hostilities which contain opposing wills; and, in the arguments supplied afterward, a statement could have been composed such as this: while one person preserves faith, another is faithless. There is no doubt that persons disposed toward one another in this way are believed to be enemies. Likewise, an irreligious person is an enemy to a religious man.

If, therefore, statements concerning different pursuits and wills had been supplied separately, there would have been approval alone, not also a deduction of the genus into the species. But since the discourse is now linked in this way—“He who regards the most sacred faith in life, and thinks religious observance necessary, is unquestionably an enemy to the man who has plundered shrines, violated every temple, and polluted the sanctuaries”—the deed of Verres, which is under inquiry, is also contained and enclosed here in a specific form, so that it is held together simultaneously with the approval and the deduction of the genus into the species.

After this is added, as we said, the destruction of the opposing definition, but by concession—that is, through a similar case: “Suppose that someone had inflicted an injury against my interests; would I properly profess myself his enemy?”

Let us therefore propose the opposing party’s definition as follows: “Hostilities exist when someone has either done or said something injurious against my interests.” M. Tullius destroys this definition by conceding that what has been defined is indeed so, while nevertheless showing that hostilities also exist in another way, when someone acts against the interests, honor, and dignity of everyone.

Thus a discourse concerning rhetorical definition must always be marked by four members: definition, approval of the definition, deduction of the definition to the species, and finally destruction of the opposing party’s definition. This, however, seems suited to rhetorical speakers, but not to philosophers.

[Col. 0895B] The definition proper to philosophers, on the other hand, is also suitable to orators; the orator adds it to his own material and to the adornment of his particular style. For the orator correctly expresses everything in speech that belongs to philosophers. He also uses argument, which is proper to philosophers, and also a necessary argument. Conversely, in their own disputes philosophers condemn everything belonging to orators: they do not at any point add a sign, or what is called the probable, and they entirely exclude every merely persuasive argument from the excellence of their discourse.

We shall therefore explain the definition proper to philosophers: how, in expressing things, it explains what something is and what it is like, and how it ought to consist of its parts.

We have already said that definitions are the principles of disputation. M. Tullius proves this both in all his dialogues and also in the book entitled the *Topics*, where he teaches that the first place of arguments is definition—that is, definition belongs to the place called “from the whole.” A definition must necessarily be applied to that place, so that the argumentative place “from the whole” is definition.

Moreover, as we said above, definition is said to explain the argument that comes from the whole. Therefore, in accordance with the instructions of all dialecticians and philosophers, we must hold to this: there is no definition except one that declares and displays the substance of the thing we wish to define before we understand it to be that thing.

To make this clearer, we shall show that no definition is certain, complete, and worthy of approval except the one that philosophers call substantial, in Greek οὐσιώδης (*ousiōdēs*). [Col. 0895D] What is substantial, however, must be explained elsewhere.

For present knowledge, let it suffice to note that whenever it is asked what something is, a certain and substantial definition can exist whenever we set down the genus of the thing under inquiry, as we said, and then add the remaining elements in discourse through differences.

It does not seem inappropriate to offer an example and then pass to the remaining obscure matters. The question is: what is a human being? Its genus is certainly animal. When, therefore, in the definition that explains what a human being is, I say “animal” and then connect the remaining elements, the definition will be substantial. For I have declared the substance of the human being when I said “animal.”

Likewise, when I ask what white or black is, if I say “white is a color,” because color is the genus of the matter under inquiry, white or black, the definition will already be substantial, since it begins from the genus and connects the remaining elements. This definition will be called substantial, proper, and complete.

This definition was approved by the philosophers, so that a definition made in any other way is never said to be a definition. Nevertheless, some people often transfer this name also to other things that are defined in another way.

M. Tullius explains substantial definition as follows: after setting down the genus of the thing under inquiry, we ought to add the species, so that we may separate by distinct commonalities those things that may be close to it; and we should insert differences until, by marking its expression, we arrive at what is proper to the thing under inquiry.

He himself adds examples in the *Topics*. But so that the reader may not be confused by legal examples, let us propose this one: “A human being is a rational, mortal, terrestrial, two-footed animal, capable of laughter.”

When “animal” is said, the substance of the human being has been declared. For, as we said above, animal is the genus of human being, and every genus is a substantial declaration of its species. But here, because “animal” was too broad, the species “terrestrial” was added; what is either aerial or aquatic has now been excluded. “Two-footed” was added because of the other animals that rest upon many feet. “Rational” was added because of those that lack reason. “Mortal” was added because of God.

When all the animals that could have corresponded to the elements placed above in the discourse have been distinguished and excluded, what is proper has been added at the end: only the human being laughs. Thus the definition is perfect in every respect for declaring what a human being is, since, after the genus was set down and all things that could correspond to it were excluded through differences, the discourse arrived at what is proper to the thing under inquiry.

This, then, is the Tullian instruction: the person who defines ought to insert and add differences in discourse until the statement reaches what is proper and can no longer be common.

Aristotle, however, says that a perfect and complete definition consists of genus and differences. We too taught above that it consists of genus and differences, when the inserted species, with its own difference, separated other things that could be similar.

Some people, nevertheless, more cautiously and fully in their teaching, establish certain parts of definition itself and say that the perfect definition which I call substantial ought to consist of five parts: genus, species, difference, accident, and property. But accident has very little force in a definition, while property has very great force.

They recall these matters correctly and truly, and they must not be judged foreign either to Aristotle, the founder of these arts, or to M. Tullius, who transmitted instructions concerning them. For an integral definition consists of these five parts, as of its own members. Aristotle too, in the books that he called the *Topics*, taught what genus, species, difference, property, and accident are. Moreover, many philosophers have embraced these matters in their books and explained their force and capacity.

[Col. 0897A] Since we have already disputed at greatest length in one book about these five matters, so that the interposition of one matter within another may not produce obscurity, or so that we may not repeat what has been said, we wish the reader, if he needs it, to turn to the book already written. Let him now observe that what has been omitted here should not be an impediment to him. For, once all these matters have been learned, he will retain the point through the necessity of the instruction.

In this substantial discourse we must insert species and differences until, after everything that could be the same has been excluded, we arrive at the point where what is proper is held as certain.

M. Tullius wished to define civil law and, as was required, began from the genus. He said at the beginning: “Civil law is equity.” This is the genus of law. But since equity is sometimes established and sometimes natural, while civil law is equity established by human beings, he therefore added: “Civil law is established equity.” After setting down the genus, he added the species and separated another species, namely natural equity.

But since the law of nations is also established equity and yet is not civil law, he added what could separate the law of nations: “among those,” says M. Tullius, “who belong to the same state.” With this species inserted, he described civil law.

There is still another thing that can be common with the former, namely the whole matter mentioned above. For it also applies to the law of religions and of all sacred things. The law of religions is equity, established equity, and equity among all those who belong to the same state. Yet we do not call that law civil law; it belongs to the pontiffs. Therefore, so that he might exclude it and define civil law down to what is proper to it, he added: “for securing one’s own possessions.”

Let us give another example placed in speeches, so that the matter may be explained more easily and clearly. M. Tullius defines what glory is, as I think, in these words: “Glory,” he says, “is the illustrious and widely spread reputation of right actions and very great services performed either toward one’s fellow citizens, or toward the state, or toward the whole human race.”

Glory, then, has been substantially defined when it was called reputation. For reputation is the genus of glory. Since reputation may now concern bad things and now good things, it is a genus to which the species “illustrious” has been added; and this is praise. For reputation concerning good things is praise, and it is illustrious. By this addition, therefore, inferior reputation has been excluded.

And since this praising reputation may now correspond to merit and now exceed merit—for often an opinion about someone has spread otherwise than the deed was performed—he therefore says “the reputation of services.” For those are services which, when we perform them, make us worthy to receive glory.

Cicero, therefore, who wished at that time to grant glory to Caesar when Caesar had presided over the state, divided these deeds or services, set down generally, into species. He added “both toward his fellow citizens, and toward the state, and toward the whole human race.” These are evidently species of right actions, subordinate to the proper definition of glory.

For glory now possesses a certain and true property in its parts. Everything that we provide is either given as though it were owed or as though it were not owed. When we act rightly, if the acts are only those that are owed, the illustrious reputation of actions is spoken of. But when we do more than what is owed, through the goodwill of providing and the kindness of giving, these are called services.

He therefore concluded both kinds of giving when he said: “the illustrious and widely spread reputation of right actions and very great services, both toward the state and toward all citizens—the reputation of services.”

From all this, I think it is clear that the definition which ought to be substantial should be expressed in this way: after setting down the genus of the thing under inquiry, and adding species together with differences, we proceed to what is proper to it, with all commonality excluded.

And if we wish to follow the judgment of the true philosophers, on the authority of the philosophers, no other statement will be called a definition. For the remaining kinds give rather an understanding of the thing; they do not, through the discourse applied, declare with complete fullness what that thing is. Nevertheless, since by a transferred use of the name the other discourses too, retaining the same function through an imaginative form of expression, are called by the same name and are said to be definitions, I think that the remaining species should be set down, so that we may more easily know what others say and, once the multiple forms of definition have been understood, the truth of defining may be readily disclosed, as was said above.

M. Tullius, treating in the *Topics* of the first three argumentative places—“from the whole,” “from the parts,” and “from the mark”—says that when the argument is from the whole, definition must be applied. For there the genus is set down, so that what the thing under inquiry itself is may be explained.

But when the argument is from the parts, this too is called definition, although by a transferred use of the name. When all the parts have been counted, the whole is thereby recognized. In this respect there is almost no difference between knowing all the parts of the whole from a definition that is from the whole, and grasping what the whole is from the enumeration of its parts.

Cicero calls this kind of definition an enumeration of parts, but assigns it to definition because the enumeration of parts also shows what the thing under inquiry is. The same is done by the definition set down above: since a discourse that shows what something is is called definition, there is no doubt that this too is called definition.

M. Tullius therefore sets down, explaining what is free—or, conversely, what is not free: “Since freedom is granted by the census, by the rod of emancipation, and by testament, and these are the means by which freedom is granted, if someone is free neither by the census, nor by the rod, nor by testament, then he is not free.”

Once the parts by which a free person is made free have been set down, a denial of freedom follows if none of these parts preceded in the granting of freedom.

Nor should it trouble you that the definition establishes what is not free, rather than what is. The reasoning and force of defining are equal and the same both when it shows what something is not and when, by means of a definition, it strips away and reveals what something is.

Although M. Tullius says differently in the same book of the *Topics*, that there are two kinds of definition: first, when what exists is defined; second, when what does not possess substance is defined—that is, what does not exist—and he enclosed and restricted this kind of division in the matters mentioned above.

He wished, however, to distinguish things that exist from things that do not exist. He says that those things exist which have a body underlying them, as when we define what water or fire is. But he wished those things to be understood as not existing whose substance does not seem to be bodily, such as piety, virtue, and freedom.

We, however, judge that all these things—whether they exist with a body or are, as it were, in a body, if they are understood in it so as to seem to exist either by themselves or in something else—are to be counted under one genus. Thus all those things are understood to exist that can have their own substance, whether bodily substances or, as is most certain and as they can properly be called, qualities.

Yet definition is also used when something that does not exist is shown. For definition is necessary so that we may teach what something is not. Therefore, if by division and enumeration of parts we say what freedom is, by the same division we shall show what freedom is not.

Definition will consequently also be made from parts: if I say, “If it is neither male nor female, it is not a human being”; likewise, “If it is neither slave nor free, it is not a human being.”

Here I think it should be noted that the parts are often taken from the very whole under inquiry for the purpose of defining it, and often not from that whole itself but from what happens to it, so that an enumeration of accidents can define what the whole is. For when the whole under inquiry is the human being, slave and free are not its parts but its accidents. When these are enumerated, what a human being is is shown.

I also think this should be noted: when definition is made from parts, it may happen that sometimes the whole is gathered from all the parts, as we have shown above; at other times the parts are enumerated in the definition in such a way that the whole is present in each individual part. Such is the case in controversies: “To bring assistance is to decree, to set out by sending troops, to come even if one has not fought, and to frighten the enemy so that they do not fight.”

Thus M. Tullius, in many places, and in his speech for Cornelius himself, when the question is what it is to diminish majesty, treats the matter as follows: that someone brought forward a bad law; that, by reading the code, he removed the right of veto; that he caused sedition. In all these instances, injured majesty is defined. But the individual items are so constituted that injured majesty—the whole—can be shown in each one separately.

The same principle holds in the speech for M. Caelius, where, through an enumeration of the evils by which criminal deception is produced, the definition is formed in such a way that criminal deception can be recognized in each individual species.

When we understand this clearly, another point is also evident: a certain notion, not the fullest account of the thing, is contained in this definition. The definition we set down above is far superior, since, after the genus has been established, the discourse brought forward for the declaration of the thing being defined indicates its substance.

I think it should also be added that there is no necessity in this enumeration of parts—where there is, in a certain sense, a definition—to include every part if the parts are infinite or the species very numerous and an enumeration must be made by division. I do not think that, in such an enumeration, all the innumerable items must be concluded. It is enough to produce an enumeration of very many, since, where the parts are infinite, it is not a fault to omit something.

Cicero set this down in the *Topics*: we can define civil law by enumeration. Civil law consists in laws, custom, and equity, but the whole of the law has not been enumerated, since it is also found in senatorial decrees, plebiscites, edicts, and the commands of rulers, and perhaps still in other things. But once a notion of the law has been given by enumerating some parts from among the infinite, we shall judge what civil law is by similar examples.

Thus the definition of which we are speaking is produced by division or partition. Through this same definition and partition, by enumerating either all the species or parts, if they are few, or many, if they are infinite, we are led to knowledge and a notion of the thing under inquiry.

Let us understand that a definition is “from the genus” when species are enumerated, and “a partition” when parts are enumerated. Accordingly, let us define animal. Since its species are infinite in number—human being, ox, horse, lion, fish, and the rest—we can declare what animal is by enumerating a few species.

But if I touch upon those species which are rather differences, and which themselves can be three in number—moist, terrestrial, and celestial—the animal will have been defined by an enumeration of all these things.

You will preserve the same method in an enumeration of parts. If we say, “The world is sea, land, and sky,” the world’s nature is explained by an enumeration of parts, though not of all its parts.

And if we wish to define what the world is by an enumeration that employs other infinite parts, then, since, as M. Tullius says, an enumeration of parts is often more extensive, we have this instruction: we must not regard it as a fault in an enumeration that something has been omitted when the parts are infinite. Therefore we can say: “The world is the sun, the moon, the stars, the air, and all that is in it, that is, the earth and the rest.” Although we have not stated the parts by enumerating them individually, we have shown what the world is by comprehending all the parts through the likeness of those that were mentioned.

Definition, then, may also be treated through an enumeration of parts. It is rationally permissible to put parts in place of species, just as the whole may stand in place of the genus; yet the genus is never called the whole, nor are species called parts.

Every genus of anything is, as it were, the whole in relation to its species; hence we properly call the whole the genus. In the same way we shall call parts species. For if the name “whole” is properly joined to the genus, the same reasoning allows us to enumerate parts as species under the designation of the whole.

I wish, however, to issue this careful warning: since there are two kinds of things, bodily and incorporeal, in both cases genus and whole are understood, and in the same way parts and species are named, but with the proper division of reasoning kept separate.

When the genus of a quality has been named, we should understand the species placed beneath it. But when “whole” is understood—not in the sense that its quality, which is signified, is always noticed in the genus, but as a certain substantial body—the whole is understood as having been cut and distributed into its own parts, as though it had received the division of some quantity. Whether that body is bodily or, as we said, incorporeal, we must attend to the relationship of both kinds, which exists either in quality or in quantity.

If we wish to name a thing according to quality, let us call it a genus and understand species to be placed beneath it. If we comprehend some quantity in what is the whole, we properly and rightly say that parts exist in the division.

Once that usage has been admitted and accepted permissibly, so that we may call species by the name of parts and may use the genus itself—which we said belongs to quality—under the designation of the whole without fault, nevertheless we must never use what belongs to quality, where the whole is to be named, as the genus. Nor shall we ever call species parts under the whole; we shall always call them parts.

The third definition is called “from the mark,” when the force of a word or name, situated in its composition, designates its own thing by a certain separation.

“Faith,” says M. Tullius, “is the doing of what is said.” Here one may observe that a name seems to be simple, yet is fashioned and compounded, so that, although its composition resounds obscurely in relation to its own things, we recognize the compounded word by distinguishing it into nearly the same syllables that state the thing signified.

But often a simple and pure word, not joined by any composition, will be used in definition from the mark, where there is the force which the Greeks call ἐτυμολογία (*etymologia*), while Cicero calls it *veriloquium*, “true-speech.” Yet what cannot be shown through a separation where there is no composition can nevertheless be explained by means of a declaration and a kind of derivation of the name, as *bonus* (“good”) from *bonitas* (“goodness”), *malus* (“bad”) from *malitia* (“badness”), and *sapiens* (“wise”) from *sapientia* (“wisdom”).

For when the thing is known in another name, what is derived from it and, in a certain sense, named from it easily leads to knowledge and shows what it is. Thus Cicero says that *consul* is derived from *consulere* (“to deliberate,” “to care for”), especially, he says, because the force of the name itself prescribes care for the state. This too must be called a kind of definition.

Although M. Tullius in the *Topics* made an argumentative place which he called “conjugate,” and which is adjacent to the place “from the mark,” nevertheless we shall rightly call it definition—not differently or contrary to him, but in accordance with the same instruction. When, by dividing a compound name into the things that it expresses, we understand what it signifies, the definition is from the mark. But when we begin to inquire from what a simple word has been derived, we have received an argument from the conjugate, as M. Tullius set it down. Nevertheless, we shall call it definition because it shows what something is, which is proper to definition.

These are the three principal substantial definitions that I have now set down: the definition from the whole, the definition from the enumeration of parts, and the definition from the mark. The first of these alone is truly called definition; the other two, by the honor and dignity of the name, because they show what the thing under inquiry is, will be called definitions, though not truly so.

Now let us return to the definition that is from the whole, because it can receive many forms within itself. From among these we shall divide those that we have been able to gather—for there may perhaps be others—and then we shall give their explanations, differences, and examples.

The first is therefore the one that in Greek may be called οὐσιώδης (*ousiōdēs*), and in Latin *substantialis*, “substantial.” The second is ἐννοηματική (*ennoēmatikē*), which supplies only a notion. The third is ποιότης (*poiotēs*), “quality,” which takes its name from quality. The fourth is ὑπογραφική (*hypographikē*), which M. Tullius calls *descriptio*, “description.” The fifth is κατὰ ἀντίλεξιν (*kata antilexin*), which in Latin we may render word for word. The sixth is κατὰ διαφοράν (*kata diaphoran*), “according to difference.” 

[Col. 0902A] Latin writers call this “of the same and of the other,” which may be called a difference.

The seventh is *κατὰ μεταφοράν*, that is, by transference. The eighth is *κατὰ ἀφαίρεσιν τοῦ ἐναντίου*, that is, by removing its contrary. The ninth is *κατὰ ὑποτύπωσιν*, that is, by a kind of representation. The tenth is *ὡς τύπος*, in Latin, “as an example” or “as it were.” The eleventh is *κατὰ ἔνδειαν πλήρους ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ γένους*, that is, by the deficiency of a complete thing from the same genus. The twelfth is *κατὰ ἔπαινον*, that is, by praise. The thirteenth is *κατὰ ἀναλογίαν*, that is, according to a ratio, which is called proportion. The fourteenth is *κατὰ τὸ πρός τι*, that is, by what is relative to something. The fifteenth is *αἰτιώδης*, attributing a cause.

We completed a full discussion of the first definition above, when we showed what a substantial definition is and of what parts it is composed. [Col. 0902B] The second is called *ἐννοηματική*, which we may call “notional,” though not by its proper name but by a common one. For in all the remaining definitions the notion of the thing is brought forward, while a substantial explanation is not given. This second kind, however, is always formed in the following way: when the thing to be defined has been proposed, without stating its genus, it explains what that thing is by words that lead the hearer toward the sense of the thing.

It is almost characteristic of this kind to define proposed things through superimposed names. Thus, if I say, “Man is that which presides over all animals by rational conception and exercise,” I have not actually said what man is; rather, by saying what he does, I have summoned him into recognition by a kind of sign. There are many other examples in M. Tullius’s *Rhetorics*, such as: “The honorable is a type of case toward which the hearer’s mind immediately inclines without our speech,” and likewise “the admirable,” from which the minds of those who are going to hear are alienated. He uses the remaining definitions in the second book when explaining the virtues.

[Col. 0902C] First, when he says what virtue itself is and gives its definition—“a disposition consonant with nature and reason”—he has supplied its genus by calling it a disposition; this is a substantial definition. But when he says, “Memory is that by which the mind recalls things that have been,” and likewise, “Intelligence is that by which it regards things that are,” and similarly, “Foresight is that by which something future is seen,” it is sufficiently clear that this is not a substantial definition but, as we said, the kind called in Greek *ἐννοηματική*. Here the notion of the thing is presented not by grasping its substance but by bringing forward the thing as known through its activity.

[Col. 0902D] The third species of definition is called *ποιότης*. By stating what sort of thing something is, it displays its quality. To put forward again the example used above, so that it may easily appear that several definitions can be made of one and the same thing: first we defined man substantially. Then, according to the mode of the second definition, we expressed his notion. Now, through the third definition, we shall explain what man is.

Man is the being in whom piety, justice, equity, and self-control are found, as well as wickedness, cunning, and the other vices; who is strong in intelligence, excels in the arts, and through knowledge of things either loves what he ought to do or, by discerning what is useless, despises, rejects, and casts it aside. Man is expressed through these qualities. For no other animal requires a life marked by these movements of the mind that designate quality, [Col. 0903A] but only this animal, man, is fulfilled by qualities placed and established in the mind, as though he were either a natural craftsman or a governor of life.

Some may think that this third kind and the second are common to one another. For often, in either of these, it is enough for the definition of the thing in question simply to name its distinctive property. Thus, if I say, “Man is that which laughs,” this is a property of man and of no other animal. Although all the other features by which man could be displayed are left unspoken, he is nevertheless declared solely through his own property.

[Col. 0903B] Cicero also said that this belongs to the genus of definition concerning property, which, as some think, can be applied to a notion. It can also be applied to this definition, which has received the name of quality. Hence some judge these two to be one and the same, without any fixed distinction between them, although it is sufficiently clear that the former can be completed by a notion without positing any qualities, as we explained above, whereas the latter can show what the thing is by positing qualities, even when its proper property is left unspoken.

We called the fourth definition *ὑπογραφική*, not assigning it a place as though it were a proper number, but joining the term to the account now presented in an established order, in order to make it easier to understand. For the fourth definition is not *ὑπογραφή*, which we have called “description,” and therefore should not be called fourth. Rather, because the order of the exposition required it, we have placed the numerical designation here.

The fourth definition, in Cicero’s treatment, is the definition “of the same and of another,” while he established the *ὑπογραφική* as fifth. But, leaving aside numerical order, we shall explain what *ὑπογραφική* is—what M. Tullius calls “description”—[Col. 0903C] by the reasoning already proposed and by an example. This is a form of speech that does not so much say what a thing is as explain by a circuitous presentation of words and deeds what each thing is.

This is called a descriptive definition, as when one asks what a miser, a cruel man, or a luxurious man is and describes the entire nature of the miser, the luxurious man, or the cruel man. This species of definition is called description in the manner of exhortation. For example: “A luxurious man is one who desires food not necessary but expensive and burdensome, who overflows with delicacies and is inclined toward lust.” These and other statements define the luxurious man, and they define him by description. This definition is always suitable for an orator. For praise of speech by circumlocution is assigned to it on account of its dignity, rather than the more concise and determinate speech that is, as it were, proper to the definition we earlier instructed should be substantial.

[Col. 0903D] For this reason, in many passages M. Tullius, when he says that something must be defined, does not prescribe that it be defined substantially, but rather that it be described. Thus he says: “When it is asked what a thief is and what a sacrilegious person is, it must be shown by their description.”

The fifth species of definition is the one we called *κατ’ ἀντίλεξιν*, which in Latin may be rendered “word for word.” This designates the thing whose nature is being asked about by another expression, in one single and particular term; it places what the thing is in one word and explains it by another word. Thus, “to be silent” is “to keep quiet”; likewise, “he drains the open side” means “he strikes”; likewise, when we call a limit an “end,” or interpret “ravaged” as “laid waste.” In general, whenever we explain the meaning of one word by another, clearer word, this is the fifth definition under discussion.

[Col. 0904A] M. Tullius used this in the *Topics* when, defining the locus of an argument, he said that it is a “seat.” Thus, by calling the thing whose name he sought by another designation, he showed by a word-for-word definition what a locus was: a seat. The Greeks call this *κατ’ ἀντίλεξιν*, as in: *ἀνὴρ ἐστὶν ὁ ἄνθρωπος*—“a man is a human being.”

The sixth species of definition is *κατὰ διαφοράν*, which we call “by difference.” Writers on the arts call it “of the same and of another.” Thus, when it is asked what distinguishes a king from a tyrant, and a difference is added, what each one is is defined.

[Col. 0904B] Indeed, every definition, as we taught above, comprehends what the thing in question is only when differences have been added and its proper feature has been grasped. Yet this does not seem to be the same method as the one now under discussion. For when a single difference has been placed between two things about which it is asked what they are, both are recognized. In the preceding cases, each thing is defined separately; here, two things that are almost known but confused through a certain community between them are separated by the added difference, through which what each is becomes known. Thus: “A king is modest and temperate, but a tyrant is cruel.”

This is the point of Terence’s statement: “I think it better to retain free men by modesty and generosity than by fear; this is the difference between a father and a master.” Likewise, M. Tullius, in his speech for Sextus Roscius, says: “There is no difference between this life refined by humanity and that savage life except right and force.”

[Col. 0904C] The seventh is *κατὰ μεταφοράν*, that is, by transference, as Cicero says in the *Topics*: “The shore is what the waves wash away.” Likewise: “Youth is the flower of life; old age is the setting of life.” This can be treated in various ways: sometimes so as to admonish, sometimes to designate, sometimes to censure, or to praise.

To admonish: “Nobility is the burden of one’s ancestors’ virtue upon posterity.”

To designate: “The head is the citadel of the body.”

To censure: “Riches are a long provision for a short life.”

To praise: “Youth is the flower of life.”

This definition can therefore be expressed in these and other ways. In this category, however, one must take care that the transference is neither far-fetched nor indecent.

A far-fetched transference is found in expressions such as “the crowd of the republic” or “the chaos of the laws,” which Tullius moderated in his speech for Sextus Roscius. He says: “As though it were an everlasting night.” Even here the definition may be understood as involving a comparison, receiving its moderation from the particle of likeness.

[Col. 0904D] An indecent transference occurs in two ways: when we define honorable things by shameful ones, or shameful things by honorable ones. Thus, if someone, defining consummation, were to call it “the tears of an exhausted Venus,” though he would better call it sweat. Or, conversely, if someone were to say, “Tears are the ejaculation of grief.” No moderation from the preceding qualification is granted to this fault. We must therefore avoid it with the greatest care.

The eighth species of definition is *κατ’ ἀφαίρεσιν τοῦ ἐναντίου*, that is, by removing the contrary of the thing being defined. Thus: “The good is that which is not evil.” We should use this kind of definition when the contrary is known. For when these two are understood in such a way that one cannot exist without the other, how can one be known unless both are comprehended?

[Col. 0905A] Therefore, when one of them is asked about—what it is—it cannot be comprehended by this definition if both are unknown, since they are naturally so bound together that the knowledge of one is connected with the necessary comprehension of the other. Such a definition is therefore in danger. We must know whether its contrary is familiar, so that, when the contrary has been removed, knowledge of the thing defined may be produced.

It is often better, therefore, when we are seeking to define something, to define its contrary; by removing that contrary, we shall clarify the thing in question. Thus, if “the good” is defined as “that which is beneficial with honor,” then what is not such a thing is evil.

[Col. 0905B] Cicero says in the *Rhetorics*: “Those things are necessarily demonstrated which can neither be done nor approved otherwise than they ought.” Let us posit the necessary and the unnecessary as contraries; understand that here we are positing as contraries all things by whose removal the thing in question is defined. Thus the unnecessary can be defined as that which can both be done and approved otherwise than it is said to be. When I remove this, I establish the definition of the necessary.

Such a definition can therefore properly be made, but in the manner I have explained. This is what M. Tullius prescribed in the *Partitiones*: that definition should often proceed from contraries.

Notions also fall under this definition when accidents are removed, as do all other things that are different. Likewise, when the contrary of an accident or of something consequent upon an accident is removed, as when someone says that substance is that which is neither quality nor quantity nor any of the remaining accidents; here things that are different are removed. The same applies if someone defining man removes all animals, either generally or specifically.

[Col. 0905C] God can be defined by this kind of definition. For since we cannot in any way know what God is, the removal of all existing things—which the Greeks call *ὄντα*—provides us with a knowledge of God by enclosing and removing the knowledge of known things. God is neither body, nor any element, nor soul, nor mind, nor sense, nor intellect, nor anything that can be grasped through these. When such things have been removed, what God is may be defined—especially if one adds that God is also that which cannot be defined.

A definition formed by removing the contrary of an accident or of something consequent upon it is of this kind: “To be awake is to use the senses; to sleep is not to use the senses.” Such definitions may naturally seem to agree with the definition we earlier called *ἐννοηματική*. [Col. 0905D] Yet the latter consists of the accidents or consequences of the thing we have defined; the former consists of contraries.

Thus the *ἐννοηματική* definition is formed from accidents, as M. Tullius teaches when he shows that Piso was not consul: “Did anyone, during the rest of that time, regard you as consul? Did anyone rise for you when you came into the Senate-house? Did anyone think that he ought to answer you when you were consulting him?”

The preceding and following speech in this passage rests upon this definition, by which he explains in various ways that Piso was not consul, teaching this also through what is contrary to the consul’s character in words, deeds, and thoughts. From consequences he defines a consul as follows: “He ought to possess a mind equipped with judgment, trustworthiness, dignity, vigilance, and care—in short, with the entire function of the consulship.” Thus far he proceeds from consequences. For all these are consequences of what I called “the function of the consulship,” and hence this is an *ἐννοηματική* definition.

[Col. 0906A] To make this clearer, I shall give another example. M. Tullius says in the same work: “What else is madness than not knowing men, not knowing the laws, not knowing the Senate or the state, and staining one’s own body with blood?” To collect consequent accidents is therefore the *ἐννοηματική* definition; but to remove the contrary of what one is defining is the definition we identified above as the eighth.

The ninth species of definition is *κατὰ ὑποτύπωσιν*, that is, by a certain representation. Thus: “Aeneas is the son of Venus and Anchises.” This kind always concerns individuals, which the Greeks call *ἄτομα*, “indivisible things.”

[Col. 0906B] This definition is required for names that are homonymous, but only for individuals, such as Ajax—Ajax son of Oileus and Ajax son of Telamon. It is also useful in a kind of speech in which shame or fear prevents one from naming someone.

“Those assassins,” says M. Tullius, “were describing me in this way,” in his speech *On His Own House*. In the speech for Fundanius he says: “Did you describe this very man, our necessary friend and competitor, whose zeal and favor have fortified this entire prosecution?” He was afraid to name him, and therefore he described him.

Likewise, in the speech for Cornelius: “These are matters of treason; read them as you were reading them, and from this you will understand that Cornelius is neither described nor indicated by the slightest suspicion.” This concerns proper names only. The other form is the preceding definition, which we called *ὑπογραφική*.

Thus, by genus, homeland, body, deeds, words, or circumstances, and by character, we designate by a mode of definition the one whom we do not wish to name.

[Col. 0906C] The tenth species is *ὡς τύπος*, which we rendered “as it were.” Thus, if it is asked what an animal is, one may answer: “For example, a human being.” Aristotle says in this way: *οὐσία ἐστιν ὡς ἄνθρωπος*—“substance is, for example, a human being.” For the example appended explains the thing being sought, and this is proper to a definition: to explain what the thing being sought is.

The eleventh species of definition is *κατ’ ἔνδειαν τοῦ πλήρους ἐξ αὐτοῦ γένους*, that is, by the deficiency of the complete thing from its own genus. Thus, if it is asked what a quadrans is, one may answer: “That from which a dodrans is lacking, so that it may be an as.”

[Col. 0906D] The twelfth species of definition is *κατ’ ἔπαινον*, that is, by praise. Thus M. Tullius says in his speech for Cluentius: “The law is the mind, spirit, judgment, and knowledge of the state.” We have indeed set out this example in order to show a definition. For M. Tullius, saying the same thing without using the form of a definition, simply arranged it as follows: “The mind, spirit, judgment, and knowledge of the state,” he says, “are placed in the laws.” As we taught above, he intended a definition to be nothing other than a form of speech.

M. Tullius therefore expressed the same matter in a different way, whereas we have transformed his speech into the form of a definition. This is very different from the method that proceeds by metaphor. For it is not a transference when the law is called the mind of the state; nor is it a genus, so that it could be regarded as substantial or *οὐσιώδης*. It is instead a consequence, and the same may be expressed by censure but without transference.

Thus the following may appear to be defined by Tullius: “Slavery is the worst of evils, to be repelled not only by war but even by death.” Although he began in this way—“Peace is tranquil liberty”—and there is a very great difference between peace and slavery, so that the definition may seem to be by difference, he did not briefly display the particular feature by which they differ. Rather, he defined each thing according to its own kind and showed by comparison how they differ; this was not a definition by difference.

[Col. 0907A] The earlier definition of peace will therefore be *ἐννοηματική*, proceeding from the consequences of the thing he was defining: “Peace is tranquil liberty.” The second is more a matter of censure. For it is neither a consequence of slavery nor any of the features we assigned to the *ἐννοηματική* definition; it is simply censure, declaring slavery to be the worst of all evils.

Nor is “evil” taken as a genus of slavery. For evil is a quality, while slavery is relative to something; since they are different things, evil cannot be the genus of slavery. The preceding definition of slavery is therefore rightly said to have been made by censure.

[Col. 0907B] The thirteenth species of definition is *κατὰ ἀναλογίαν*, that is, according to a ratio, which is called proportion. This occurs when something that may be discussed is said to be what another thing is, because of a similarity of relation. It happens when an inferior thing is defined by the name of a superior thing, and what is added explains what the inferior thing is.

The Greeks define it as follows: *Ἄνθρωπός ἐστι μικρόκοσμός τις*—“Man is a kind of lesser world.” Cicero used this method as follows: “Those who attach the greatest importance to an edict say that, apart from the edict, law is its soul.”

The fourteenth species of definition is *κατὰ πρός τι*, that is, “relative to something.” Thus: “A father is one who has a son.” Cicero says in the *Rhetorics*: “That is a genus which embraces several parts.” Likewise: “A part is that which lies under a genus.”

[Col. 0907C] The fifteenth species is *αἰτιώδης*. The Latins call it “according to the account of the thing.” Thus: “Day is the sun above the earth; night is the sun beneath the earth.” For the cause of its being day or night is the sun’s being above or beneath the earth.

There may perhaps be other species of definition. If anyone discovers one, let him add it to the number, provided that he carefully attend to this: perhaps what he has discovered can be assigned to one of these species. Nor should anyone again think that we have separated so many species without reason merely because some of them can coincide with one another. With a fuller and more careful consideration, he will see that they are all separated from one another by a great distinction.

Let him retain what I have often prescribed above: only that definition is properly so called which begins from a genus and descends to the proper feature of the thing being defined by separating through differences the features that could have been common.

[Col. 0907D] Let us now explain, as promised, the faults of definition.

The substantial definition, which we taught first and called the only true definition, admits two principal faults: either the defining statement embraces more than it should, or it declares less than the fullness of the thing requires. For a defining statement must be so composed in relation to the name whose thing it defines that it express an equivalent power of explanation to that name; and, conversely, the name and the definition, when compared with one another, must explain each other.

Thus, if one asks what man is, the correct answer is: “A terrestrial, rational, mortal, two-footed animal capable of laughter.” If this is reversed, “man” is the best equivalent. When one asks what a terrestrial, rational, mortal, two-footed animal capable of laughter is, the correct answer is: “Man.”

[Col. 0908A] But if one defines man as “an animate, sentient substance,” this does indeed explain man, since man is all these things; but if it is reversed, it will not hold. For an animate, sentient substance is not man alone. The definition therefore errs through excess, because it contains more than was sought.

In general, a definition is faulty if it posits a genus that extends beyond the thing itself; for, we say, the higher the genus, the more broadly it explains.

A definition also errs when it contains less than is necessary. Thus: “Desire is the longing to seek what belongs to another.” If this is similarly reversed, it does not remain valid, because the definition is less comprehensive than the thing named requires. Desire extends broadly; it is not merely avarice. The definition is therefore faulty because it is less comprehensive than the thing sought.

[Col. 0908B] It would be as though one said: “Desire is avarice.” If this were offered as an example and led the hearer to the whole of what desire is by a proposition of similarity, as in the case of avarice, it would be the species of definition we placed tenth, *ὡς τύπος*, “as an example.”

But here the example does not lead to the whole. It errs by passing over much while appearing to contain the whole, and therefore the name cannot be converted into the definition. If these two faults are avoided, the definition is complete—not only the substantial definition, but also the remaining species.

So much concerning the faults.
