[Col. 0908C] When Cicero taught in the *Rhetorics* that there are three faults, he said that a bad definition occurs when it describes common features, as in: “A seditious man is one who is a bad and useless citizen.” For this does not describe the force of a seditious man more than that of an ambitious man, a false accuser, or any wicked person. We said that this definition is faulty through excess.

He adds another fault, in which something false is asserted, as in: “Wisdom is the understanding required for seeking money.” Cicero added this fault to the two I mentioned.

He himself placed a third fault, which we have established as the second: a definition that does not contain anything substantial or significant. Thus: “Foolishness is an immeasurable desire for glory.” This is faulty because it comprehends less than it should, as M. Tullius expresses it. It is indeed a kind of foolishness, but it is defined only from one part, not from the whole genus.

Besides these, M. Tullius added two faults in the second book of the *Rhetorics*: a definition may be indecent or useless. This, as he himself says, is judged from the aspects of honor and usefulness.

We discussed the indecent definition above, when treating definition by metaphor; but there the fault lies in the word. It can also happen that an entire statement contains something dishonorable or comprehends something useless.

[Col. 0908D] In the first *Philippic*, M. Tullius taught that Antony was overturning Caesar’s acts, while Antony denied this. Each of them offered a definition to show what the act of one who, as a citizen wearing the toga, was active in the state with authority consisted in.

I taught above that there are four parts in establishing a definition: first, the definition itself; second, the approval of the definition; third, the application of the definition to a particular instance; fourth, the destruction of the opposing party’s definition.

Cicero defines the act of one who lives in public affairs with authority as laws; Antony defines it as written memoranda. Thus, in his speech, Cicero both defines, approves, applies the definition to a particular instance, and destroys the definition of the opposing party.

[Col. 0909A] Cicero’s definition is this: “And what could be so properly called the act of one who, as a citizen wearing the toga, has conducted affairs in the republic with power and authority, as a law?”

Then the approval of this definition follows in this way: “Ask for the acts of Gracchus: the Sempronian laws will be produced. Ask for Sulla’s acts, the Cornelian laws; ask what the third consulship of Gnaeus Pompey consists in: in what acts does it stand? Surely, in laws.” This is the approval.

Then the application of the definition to a particular instance is added: “If you ask Caesar himself what he had done in the City and in the toga, he answers that he had introduced many excellent laws.”

[Col. 0909B] The refutation of the opposing party’s definition follows. This is done in two ways. Either some one of all its faults is established in the refutation, or, once what the opponent says has been conceded, we approve by comparison that our position is more properly what the matter is.

M. Tullius does both here. He introduces the faults in order to show that the opposing definition is false, indecent, and useless. Then, conceding the opposing position, he confirms his own definition as superior.

Cicero proves the definition false by examining what follows from it. A definition is shown to be false if it does not possess its own proper feature, if it contains rather its contrary, if it does not retain its own consequence, or if it has been stated otherwise than according to common opinion.

[Col. 0909C] Here, then, since the question is what the act of a toga-wearing citizen conducting affairs in the state with authority is, and it has been said to be nothing other than laws, [Col. 0910A] we must observe what Antony had said—that it consisted of written memoranda. Cicero carefully considers the consequences and proves the definition false as follows:

“One who is in authority is in the state; when he has done something, he cannot alter the act. This belongs to a law: once it has been passed, it is never changed by the one who passed it. But written memoranda, because they are private acts, have the consequence that they may be altered and often may not be produced at all.”

Thus M. Tullius refutes the claim that written memoranda are acts, because they do not possess the consequences of acts. He says: “But he would either alter the written memoranda or not issue them; or, if he had issued them, he would not call these matters his acts. But, by concession [the transmitted reading is uncertain], I concede those very points and even wink at certain matters; [Col. 0910B] in the greatest matters, however—that is, in the laws—I do not think it tolerable that Caesar’s acts be undone.”

After this he adds a similar, twofold refutation: one from the faults, by which he calls the definition both indecent and useless; and then, by concession, he concludes from comparison that his own definition is superior.

He says that the opposing statement is indecent and useless: “Unless, perhaps, if he recorded something in a booklet as a reminder, that will be counted among the acts.” And although this is unjust and useless, it is defended in the following way: “Equity is a virtue; virtue itself is honorable; therefore inequity is indecent, because indecency is contrary to honor.” Thus, in the very words, he refutes the definition as indecent and useless.

Then he adds the final point by concession: “What he carried before the people in the centuriate assemblies will not be counted among Caesar’s acts.”

[Col. 0910C] I have thought that these matters are sufficiently established even for a discerning reader.

[Col. 0909]

# The Eight Books of Aristotle’s *Topics*, translated by Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius. (G,S)*

## Book One

### Chapter One. What Aristotle intends in the First Book of the *Topics*, and the kinds of reasoning

[Col. 0909D]

The purpose of this work is to discover a method by which we shall be able to reason syllogistically from probable premises about every proposed problem, and, while maintaining the discussion ourselves, say nothing contradictory.

First, therefore, we must state what a syllogism is and what its differences are, and how a dialectical syllogism is understood—for this is what the present undertaking seeks. A syllogism, then, is an argument in which, certain things having been posited, something other than what has been posited necessarily follows through what has been posited.

A demonstration is a syllogism when it proceeds from true and primary premises, or from premises that have received their status as principles of the relevant knowledge through certain primary and true propositions. [Col. 0910C] A dialectical syllogism, however, is one constructed from probable premises.

True and primary propositions are those that possess credibility not through other propositions but through themselves. For in the principles of the sciences one ought not to inquire into the reason why, but each principle itself must possess credibility in its own right.

Probable propositions are those that seem so to everyone, or to most people, or to the wise—and among the wise, either to all, to most, or especially to those who are most familiar with and approved in the matter.

A contentious syllogism is one drawn from things that appear probable but are not. The other is an apparent syllogism, proceeding either from probable premises or from premises that merely appear probable. For not everything that appears probable is also probable: nothing that is called probable has its entire appearance merely on the surface, as happens in the principles of contentious disputes; [Col. 0911A] for in such cases the nature of the falsehood is often immediately evident even to those who are capable of seeing only a little.

Therefore, let the first of the arguments just mentioned be called a syllogism, while the other may indeed be called a contentious syllogism, but not a syllogism, because it appears to reason but in fact does not reason at all.

Besides all the syllogisms mentioned above, there are also paralogisms peculiar to particular sciences, as occurs in geometry and its related disciplines. This method appears to differ from the syllogisms already mentioned: the pseudographer neither reasons from true and primary premises nor from probable ones, since he does not fall under that definition. He does not take premises that appear so to everyone, or to most people, or to the wise—either to all, to most, or to those most highly approved—but constructs a syllogism from propositions peculiar to the discipline that are not true. Thus, a pseudographer produces a paralogism by drawing semicircles improperly or by drawing certain lines in a way in which they ought not to be drawn.

Let these, then, be the kinds of syllogisms, stated in outline. In brief, concerning all that has been said above and what will be said afterward, let this much be established: since we do not choose to give an exact account of any of these matters, but wish to pass over them in a somewhat schematic fashion, we judge it entirely sufficient, in accordance with the proposed method, to be able in some way to recognize each of them.

### Chapter Two. To how many things dialectic and the discipline of disputation are useful

[Col. 0911C]

It follows from what has been said that we must state to how many things, and to which things, this undertaking is useful. It is useful for three things: exercises, conversations, and the disciplines belonging to philosophy.

That it is useful for exercises is clear from this: when we possess the method, we shall easily be able to argue about any proposed subject.

It is useful for conversations because, by taking account of the opinions of many people, we shall converse with them not from foreign doctrines but from their own doctrines, changing whatever they appear not to express well in their various formulations.

It is useful for the philosophical disciplines because, by being capable of doubting in both directions, we shall easily discern the true and the false in each matter, and in addition shall be able to approach the first principles of the disciplines. For it is impossible to say anything about the first principles of a given discipline from the principles proper to that discipline, since those principles are primary; but it is necessary to discuss them by means of probabilities drawn from what concerns the individual matters. [Col. 0911D]

This is proper, and especially distinctive, to dialectic, since, being investigative, it has a path to the principles of all methods.

We shall possess the method perfectly when we possess it in the same way as in rhetoric, medicine, and similar arts—that is, when from the things that occur we do what we choose. For neither will a rhetorician persuade in every manner, nor will a physician heal; but if he omits nothing among the things that can occur, we shall say that he possesses his discipline adequately.

### Chapter Three. From what, and from how many things, dialectical disputation consists

[Col. 0912A]

First, then, we must consider what the method consists of. If we determine how many and what sorts of arguments there are, what their subjects are, and how we may obtain an abundance of them, we shall have sufficiently accomplished our purpose.

The things from which arguments are constructed and the things about which syllogisms are constructed are equal in number and the same: arguments are constructed from propositions, while the subjects about which syllogisms are constructed are problems.

Every proposition and every problem indicates either a property, a genus, or an accident. For a difference, when it is general, must be ordered together with the genus.

Since a property in one case signifies what a thing is and in another case does not, let property be divided into the two parts just mentioned. Let that which signifies what a thing’s being is be called a definition; let the remainder, according to the common designation assigned to these matters, be called a property.

It is therefore clear from what has been said that, according to the present division, everything falls under one of four headings: property, definition, genus, or accident.

Let no one suppose that we mean that each of these, considered in itself, is a proposition or a problem, but rather that problems and propositions are constructed from them.

A problem and a proposition differ in their manner of expression. When one asks, “Do you think that ‘walking biped animal’ is the definition of man?” it is a proposition; and when one asks, “Is animal the genus of man?” it is likewise a proposition. But if the question is whether “biped animal capable of walking” is the definition of man or not, it becomes a problem. The same applies in other cases. Thus problems and propositions are rightly equal in number, since one can turn every proposition into a problem by changing its manner of expression.

### Chapter Four. Definition, property, genus, and accident

We must state what a definition, a property, a genus, and an accident are.

A definition is an expression signifying what a thing’s being is. It is given either as an expression in place of a name or as an expression in place of an expression; for some things signified by an account can also be defined.

Whenever someone gives a designation by a name in any manner, it is clear that he is not giving the definition of the thing, since every definition is a certain expression. Nevertheless, what is suited to a definition must be placed alongside it—for example, “what is honorable is decorous.”

Likewise, one may ask whether sensation and knowledge are the same or different; for much discussion arises concerning definitions as to whether things are the same or different. In short, everything contained under the same discipline as definitions may be said to be suited to a definition.

That everything just mentioned is of this kind is clear from the following. If we are capable of arguing that something is the same or different, we shall likewise easily be able to argue concerning definitions. For by showing that something is not the same, we shall refute the definition. The converse of what has just been said does not hold: showing that something is the same is not sufficient to establish a definition, but showing that it is not the same is sufficient to destroy one. [Col. 0913A]

A property is what does not signify what a thing’s being is, but belongs to that thing alone and is predicated convertibly of it—for example, “being capable of grammar” is a property of man. For if something is a man, it is capable of grammar; and if it is capable of grammar, it is a man.

No one calls something a property if it can belong to another thing, such as “sleeping” in the case of man—not even if, perhaps, it belongs exclusively to man for some period of time. If something of this kind is called a property, it will be called a property not absolutely but at some time or in relation to something. Thus, “being on the right” is at some time a property.

“Biped” is a property in relation to something—for example, of man in relation to horse and dog.

That none of the things that can belong to another is predicated convertibly is clear: it is not necessary that, if something is sleeping, it is a man. [Col. 0913B]

A genus is what is predicated of several things differing in species with respect to what a thing is.

Those things are said to be predicated with respect to what a thing is whenever the person questioned can answer what the proposed thing is. Thus, when asked what the proposed thing is in the case of man, it is appropriate to answer “animal.”

In the case of genus, it is appropriate to ask whether one thing belongs to the same genus as another or to a different genus. This too falls under the same method as genus. If we argue that animal is the genus of man, and likewise that good is a genus, we shall be arguing that these belong to the same genus; but if we show that one is a genus and the other is not, we shall be arguing that they do not belong to the same genus. [Col. 0913C]

An accident is what is none of these things—not a definition, a property, or a genus—but belongs to a thing; it is what may belong to, or fail to belong to, one and the same thing. Thus, sitting may belong to a certain individual and may fail to belong to that same individual.

The same is true of white: nothing prevents the same thing from being white at one time and not white at another.

A second definition of accident is better. When the first definition is given, one must already know what a definition, a genus, and a property are in order to understand it; the second is complete for knowing by itself what is being said.

Comparisons that in any manner are spoken of in relation to accidents should also be attached to accident—for example, whether what is honorable or what is advantageous is more choiceworthy, whether a life according to virtue or a life according to pleasure is more pleasant, and anything else expressed similarly. In all such cases, the question is which of two things the predicate belongs to more.

It is clear from these considerations that nothing prevents an accident from becoming a property at a particular time or in relation to something. Thus, although sitting is an accident, when someone sits alone it may at some time become a property; and when someone alone is sitting, it may be a property in relation to those who are not sitting. Therefore, nothing prevents an accident from becoming a property in relation to something or at some time, although it will not be a property absolutely.

### Chapter Five. That the other predicates contain something of what the definition contains

We must not overlook that whatever is said concerning property, genus, and accident can also be said concerning definitions.

For if we show that what is contained under the definition does not belong to that thing alone—as in the case of a property—or that what has been assigned in the definition is not a genus, or that one of the things stated in the definition does not belong to the thing—which may also be said in the case of an accident—we shall refute the definition.

Therefore, according to the account previously given, everything that has been enumerated will in some way be applicable to a definition.

But for this reason we should not seek one universal method for everything. It would not be easy to find such a method, and even if it were found, it would be altogether obscure and plainly disagreeable for the present undertaking.

If, however, a method is assigned for each of the determined genera, a passage through the proposed subject can easily be made from what is proper to each one. Therefore, in general outline, the division should be made as stated earlier, while the matters that are especially peculiar to each of the remaining categories should be attached to them. Let these be called matters applicable to definition and genus; nearly all the matters stated have already been attached to their individual subjects.

### Chapter Six. Sameness

First of all, we must determine how many senses “same” has. In outline, “same” appears to be divided in three ways: we ordinarily call things the same in number, in species, or in genus.

Things are the same in number when their names are multiple but the thing is one, such as “garment” and “clothing.” [Col. 0914C]

Things are the same in species when, although they are multiple, they do not differ according to species, such as man and man, horse and horse. For things of this kind are said to be the same in species whenever they belong to the same species.

Likewise, things are the same in genus whenever they belong to the same genus, such as horse and man.

Water from the same source, which is called “the same,” may appear to have some difference beyond the modes just mentioned. Not so: this too should be placed among things that are said in some manner to be of one species. For all such things appear cognate and related to one another. Every water is said to be the same in species as every other water because it possesses a certain similarity; water from the same source, which is called “the same,” differs in no other respect than that the similarity is stronger. Therefore, we do not separate “same” from things that are said in some manner to belong to one species. [Col. 0914D]

Most indisputably, however, “same” is said of what is one in number.

This too is usually explained in several ways, but most properly and primarily it applies when the same thing is designated by a name or definition, as “clothing” is designated by “garment,” and “biped animal capable of walking” by “man.”

Second, it applies when a thing is designated by a property, as man by “capable of knowledge,” and fire by “naturally borne upward.”

Third, it applies when a thing is designated by an accident, as Socrates by “sitting” or “musical”; for all these are intended to signify one thing in number.

That this is true can be learned especially from transferred designations. Often, when we command someone to call one of those sitting, we transfer the command when the person to whom we are giving it perhaps does not understand, taking the designation from the accident itself, which is more readily understood; we order him to call the person who is sitting or disputing to us. It is clear that we do this because we suppose that the same person is signified both according to the name and according to the accident.

Thus, “same,” as has been said, is divided in three ways.

### Chapter Seven. That every dialectical dispute concerns definition, property, genus, or accident, and where these are found

Since arguments are constructed from the matters previously stated, and through these matters and toward these matters there is, on the one hand, a certain confirmation by induction, anyone who considers each proposition and problem will see that it is constructed either from a definition, a property, a genus, or an accident.

There is also confirmation by syllogism. Everything predicated of something must either be predicated convertibly of the thing or not. If it is predicated convertibly, it will be a definition or a property. If it signifies what a thing’s being is, it is a definition; if it does not signify this, it is a property. For this was the property: that it is predicated convertibly without signifying what a thing’s being is.

If it is not predicated convertibly of the thing, it is either among the things stated in the definition of the subject or it is not. If it is among the things stated in the definition, it will be either a genus or a difference, since a definition consists of a genus and differences. If it is not among the things stated in the definition, it is clearly an accident, since an accident was said to be what is neither a definition, nor a genus, nor a property, but belongs to the thing.

After this, we must determine the genera of the categories in which the four differences mentioned are found. There are ten in number: substance, quantity, quality, relation, where, when, position, possession, action, and passion.

For definition, genus, property, and accident will always belong to one of these categories. All propositions signify either what a thing is, or what sort of thing it is, or how much it is, or some other category.

It is clear from the same considerations that a statement signifying what a thing is sometimes signifies substance, sometimes quality, and sometimes one of the other categories. For when, with man posited, someone says that what has been posited is man or animal, he states what it is and signifies substance. When, with white color posited, he says that what has been posited is white or color, he states what it is and signifies quality. [Col. 0915D]

Likewise, if, with a cubit of magnitude posited, he says that what has been posited is a cubit-long magnitude, he states what it is and signifies quantity. The same applies in the other cases.

Whenever any such thing is said of the same thing, or a genus is said of it, it signifies what the thing is; but when it is said of something else, it does not signify what it is, but how much, what sort, or one of the other categories.

Thus the subjects of disputes, and the things from which disputes arise, are these and so many. How we shall obtain them, and by what means we shall become well supplied with them, must be stated next.

### Chapter Eight. The dialectical proposition

First, then, let us determine what a dialectical proposition and what a dialectical problem are. Not every proposition and not every problem should be called dialectical.

No one will propose something that no one finds plausible, nor will anyone propose what is evident to everyone or to most people. The former has no plausibility, while the latter is not open to question.

A dialectical proposition is a plausible question, not unexpected either to everyone, to most people, or to the wise—and among the wise, either to all, to most, or especially to those who are most familiar with the matter.

Someone may propose what appears true to the wise, unless it contradicts the opinions of many.

Dialectical propositions also include things resembling probabilities, and things contrary to what appears probable when expressed by contradiction, as well as every opinion belonging to an established art.

If it is probable that the same discipline concerns contraries, it will also appear probable that the same sense concerns contraries. If there is one grammar, there will also be one flute-playing discipline; and if there are several grammars, there will also be several flute-playing disciplines, since these matters appear similar and related.

Likewise, things contrary to probabilities, when expressed by contradiction, appear probable. If it is probable that one ought to benefit one’s friends, it is also probable that one ought not to harm one’s friends. The contrary is that one ought to harm one’s friends; the contradictory is that one ought not to harm one’s friends.

Similarly, if one ought to benefit one’s friends, one ought not to benefit one’s enemies. This too is expressed by contradiction in relation to contraries, since the contrary is that one ought to benefit one’s enemies. The same applies in other cases.

A contrary to a contrary also appears probable by analogy. If one ought to benefit one’s friends and ought to harm one’s enemies, then the contrary will also appear to be that one ought to benefit one’s friends and ought to harm one’s enemies. Whether this is true or not will be shown in what will be said about contraries.

It is clear that all opinions belonging to established arts are also dialectical propositions. Someone will propose what appears true to those skilled in the relevant art—for example, what concerns geometry as a geometer and what concerns medicine as a physician.

### Chapter Nine. The dialectical problem and the dialectical position

[Col. 0916D]

A dialectical problem is an inquiry directed either toward choice and avoidance, or toward truth and knowledge, either in itself or as an aid to something else of this kind. It concerns something about which people either have no opinion in either direction, or about which most people hold an opinion contrary to that of the wise, or the wise contrary to that of most people, or about which the same people disagree with themselves.

Some problems are useful merely for knowing what should be chosen or avoided—for example, whether pleasure should be chosen or not.

Others are useful only for knowledge—for example, whether the world is eternal or not.

Others, in themselves, serve neither of these purposes but assist in matters of this kind. For most things we do not wish to know for their own sake, but for the sake of other things, so that through them we may know something else.

There are also problems about which contrary syllogisms exist. They contain a difficulty as to whether the matter is so or not, because there are persuasive arguments on both sides.

There are also problems about which we possess no argument, although they are important, since we judge it difficult to assign a reason for them—for example, whether the world is eternal or not. Someone may inquire into matters of this kind.

Let problems and propositions, then, be determined as has been stated.

A position is a remarkable opinion held by one of those familiar with philosophy—for example, that contradiction is impossible, as Antisthenes said; that everything is in motion, according to Heraclitus; or that being is one, as Melissus said. It would be foolish to concern oneself with every person who advances opinions contrary to common belief.

A position may also concern matters about which we possess an argument contrary to common opinions—for example, that not everything that exists is either generated or eternal, as the sophists say. For being musical or grammatical is neither generated nor eternal.

Even if this does not appear so to someone, it will nevertheless appear so because it has a persuasive argument.

A position, therefore, is a problem, but not every problem is a position, since some problems concern matters about which we hold no opinion in either direction.

That a position is also a problem is clear. It follows necessarily from what has been said that either most people will doubt the position in opposition to the wise, or both sides will disagree with themselves, since a position is a remarkable opinion.

Almost all dialectical problems are now called positions. It makes no difference how the matter is expressed; we did not divide them in this way because we wanted to fabricate names, but so that we would not overlook their differences when some of them differ from one another.

We should not consider every problem or every position, but only one that someone among those who require arguments would question, and not something requiring punishment or sense-perception.

Those who question whether the gods should be honored and parents loved require punishment; those who question whether snow is white require sense-perception.

Nor should we consider matters whose demonstration is close at hand, or matters whose demonstration is extremely remote. The former contain no difficulty, while the latter exceed what is appropriate for an exercise of intellectual ability.

### Chapter Ten. The kinds of reasoning and dialectical disputation

[Col. 0917D]

Having determined these matters, we must divide the kinds of dialectical disputation. One kind is induction, another is syllogism.

What a syllogism is has already been stated.

Induction is an advance from particulars to universals. For example, if an educated pilot is excellent, and an educated charioteer is excellent, then every person who is educated in a particular field is excellent.

Induction is more persuasive, clearer, more accessible to sense-perception, and common to more people; a syllogism, however, is stronger and more effective against those who contradict.

Let the kinds of the subjects of disputation, and the kinds of things from which disputations arise, then, be determined as stated earlier.

### Chapter Eleven. The instruments by which we obtain an abundance of syllogisms for disputation

[Col. 0918A]

The instruments by which we become well supplied with syllogisms are four.

The first is to obtain propositions.

The second is to distinguish in how many ways each thing is said.

The third is to discover differences.

The fourth is the consideration of similarity.

In a certain sense, three of these are also propositions. Each can be made into a proposition—for example, that what is choiceworthy is honorable, or pleasant, or useful; that sense differs from knowledge because someone who loses knowledge can acquire it again, whereas this is impossible in the case of sense; and that the healthy is related to health in the same way as the well-conditioned is related to good condition.

The first proposition is drawn from things said in multiple ways, the second from differences, and the third from similarities.

### Chapter Twelve. The obtaining of propositions

It has therefore been determined in how many ways propositions should be selected: one should put forward the opinions of everyone, or of most people, or of the wise—and among the wise, either of all, most, or those most highly regarded.

One should also put forward propositions contrary to what appears probable, as well as opinions belonging to an art. But contrary propositions should be advanced against apparent probabilities by way of contradiction, as was stated earlier.

It is also useful, in making selections, to choose not only probable propositions but also propositions resembling them—for example, that the same sense concerns contraries, since the knowledge of contraries is also the same.

Likewise, we see things by receiving something rather than by emitting it; the same applies to the other senses, since we also hear by receiving something rather than emitting it, and smell in the same way. The same applies to the other senses.

Furthermore, whatever appears so to everyone or to most people should be taken as a principle and an apparent position, since those who do not observe closely posit that something is not so in a particular case.

One must also select propositions from written disputations.

Descriptions should be made for each genus, setting them out separately—for example, descriptions of the good, of animal, and of the good as a whole—beginning with what each thing is.

The opinions of particular thinkers should also be recorded, such as that Empedocles said there are four elements of bodies. Someone will propose a statement because it was made by a person of recognized standing.

In outline, there are three parts of propositions and problems: some are ethical, some physical, and some logical.

Ethical propositions are of this kind: whether, if parents and laws disagree, one ought to obey parents rather than the laws.

Logical propositions are of this kind: whether the same discipline concerns contraries or not.

Physical propositions are of this kind: whether the world is eternal or not.

The same distinctions apply to problems.

It is not easy to assign by definition what each of the stated kinds is. Each must be learned by practice through induction, by considering them in accordance with the examples given above.

In philosophy one must investigate these matters according to truth; dialectically, however, one must proceed according to opinion.

One should select propositions that are as universal as possible, and make many into one—for example, that the same discipline concerns opposites, then that it concerns contraries, and then that it concerns relatives.

These propositions should themselves again be divided in the same way, as far as division can proceed—for example, into good and bad, white and black, cold and hot, and similarly in other cases.

Let what has been said about propositions suffice.

### Chapter Thirteen. Distinguishing things said in multiple ways
Itself, however, must be investigated in how many ways it is spoken, not only whatever things are said according to another mode, but also an attempt must be made to assign the accounts of them: for example, not only that “good” is said in one way of justice and courage, and in another way of what is useful and health-producing, but also that the former are so called because they themselves possess certain qualities, whereas the latter are so called because they produce something, and not because they possess some such qualities. The same applies in other cases. Whether something is spoken in many ways or in one way in species must be considered by these means.

First, one must examine the contrary, whether it is spoken in many ways, either in species or in name. For some things are immediately different even in their names: for example, the contrary of “sharp” in the case of the voice is “deep,” but in the case of magnitude it is “blunt.” It is therefore clear that “sharp” is spoken in many ways, since its contrary is so spoken. If this is so, “sharp” also is spoken in many ways. For there was a different contrary according to each of the two senses: the same “sharp” will not be contrary to “blunt” and to “deep”; yet “sharp” is contrary to both.

Again, the contrary of “deep” in the case of the voice is “sharp,” but in the case of magnitude it is “light”; therefore “deep” is spoken in many ways, since its contrary is so spoken. Likewise, “beautiful” is contrary in one case to what is ugly in an animal, and in another to what is harmful in a house; therefore “beautiful” is equivocal.

In some cases the names do not differ at all, but the difference in species is immediately evident, as with “clear” and “dark.” A voice is called clear and dark, and likewise a color. Thus their names differ in no way, but the difference in species is immediately evident; for a color is not called “clear” in the same way as a voice is called “clear.” This is also evident through perception: things that are the same in species are judged by the same sense, but what is clear in a voice and what is clear in a color are not judged by the same sense; the one is judged by sight, the other by hearing. Likewise, “sharp” and “blunt” are used of flavors and of magnitudes, but the one is apprehended by touch and the other by taste. These expressions differ neither in their names nor in themselves, nor do their contraries differ, for “blunt” is contrary to both.

Further, one should examine cases in which one thing has a contrary while the other has none at all. For example, the pleasure arising from drinking has as its contrary the distress arising from thirst, whereas the pleasure arising from contemplating that the diagonal is incommensurable with the side has no contrary. Therefore “pleasure” is spoken in many ways. Again, hatred is contrary to love as love is understood according to the mind, but love as understood according to bodily activity has no contrary. It is therefore clear that “love” is equivocal.

Further, one should examine the intermediate terms. If one thing has an intermediate while the other has none, or if both have intermediates but not the same ones, the terms are equivocal. For example, between clear and dark there is an intermediate in colors, namely dusky, but in the case of the voice there is none—or perhaps hoarse, as some say, claiming that a hoarse voice is intermediate. Therefore “clear” is equivocal, and similarly “dark.”

Moreover, if one of the two has several intermediates while the other has only one, as with clear and dark: colors have several intermediates, whereas the voice has one, namely hoarseness.

Again, one must examine the terms opposed according to contradiction, to see whether they are spoken in many ways. If one of them is so spoken, the term opposed to it will also be so spoken. For example, “not seeing” is spoken in many ways: in one sense, not possessing sight; in another, not exercising sight. If “not seeing” is spoken in many ways, “seeing” must also be spoken in many ways, since “seeing” is opposed in both cases to “not seeing”: possessing sight is opposed to not possessing sight, and exercising sight is opposed to not exercising sight.

Further, one must examine expressions spoken according to privation and possession. If one of the two is spoken in many ways, the other will be so spoken too. Thus, if “sensitive” is spoken in many ways—of the soul and of the body—then “insensitive” will likewise be spoken in many ways, of the soul and of the body. That these expressions are opposed according to privation and possession is clear from the fact that animals are naturally capable of possessing both kinds of sense, in soul and in body.

One must also examine the cases of the terms. If “justly” is spoken in many ways, “just” will also be spoken in many ways, since what is just corresponds to each of the senses in which “justly” is used. For example, if “justly” means both judging according to one’s own knowledge and judging as one ought, “just” will have the same multiplicity.

Likewise, if “health-producing” is spoken in many ways, “healthfully” will also be spoken in many ways. If “health-producing” means in one case what produces health, in another what preserves it, and in another what indicates it, then “healthfully” will be spoken either productively, preservatively, or indicatively. The same applies in other cases: whenever a term itself is spoken in many ways, its derivative forms will also be spoken in many ways; and if its derivative forms are so spoken, the term itself will be so spoken.

One must also examine the genera of the things predicated under the same name, to see whether they are the same in name. If they are not the same, it is clear that the term is equivocal. For example, “good” in food is productive of pleasure, in medicine productive of health, and in the soul a quality, such as being chaste, courageous, or just. The same applies to a human being. Sometimes “good” is also used of time—for one speaks of a “good time”—and most often of quantity, as when one speaks of a moderate quantity as good. Therefore “good” is equivocal.

Likewise, “white” means a color in the case of a body, but a well-sounding quality in the case of a voice.

Likewise, “sharp” is not said in the same way in all cases. A sharp voice is a swift voice, as those versed in harmonic numbers say; a sharp angle is one smaller than a right angle; and a sharp sword is one possessing a sharp angle.

One must also examine the genera of things that fall under the same name, to see whether they are different and not subordinate to one another, as with “horse”: a horse is both an animal and a vessel. The account corresponding to the name differs in these cases, for the former signifies an animal, while the latter signifies a vessel of a certain sort.

If the genera are subordinate to one another, however, their accounts need not be different. For example, “animal” and “bird” are genera of a crow. When we call something a crow and also call it an animal, we mean the same thing; therefore both genera are predicated of the same object. Likewise, when we call a crow a two-footed flying animal, we call it a bird as well; thus both genera and their accounts are predicated of the crow.

This does not occur with non-subordinate genera. When we call something a vessel, we do not call it an animal; nor, when we call it an animal, do we call it a vessel.

One must consider not only whether the genera in the subject are different and non-subordinate, but also whether this is so in the contrary. For if the contrary is spoken in many ways, it is clear that the subject term is also so spoken.

It is useful for examining definitions to consider a definition formed from a compound expression, such as “a white body” and “a white voice.” Once the specific element has been removed, the same account ought to remain. But this does not happen with equivocal terms, as in the cases just mentioned: one definition will be “a body possessing such a color,” while the other will be “a voice that sounds good.” Once “body” and “voice” have been removed, the same account does not remain in both cases; yet, if “white” were univocal, the same thing would have to be signified in both.

Often, moreover, an equivocal term is concealed even in the definitions themselves, and therefore it must be examined in the definition as well. For example, if someone says that “what is productive of health” or “what is indicative of health” is “what is moderately related to health,” this should not be rejected immediately. Rather, one must examine what he means by “moderately” in each case: whether in one case it means something such as producing health, and in the other something such as indicating what sort of condition the state is.

Again, one must examine terms that are not comparable according to “more” and “less,” or in a similar way, such as “a clear voice,” “a clear garment,” “a sharp flavor,” and “a sharp voice.” These are not called clear or sharp in the same way, nor is one of them called more clear or more sharp than another. Therefore “clear” and “sharp” are equivocal, since everything univocal is comparable: it is either said in the same way or one thing is said to be more so than another.

Since things belonging to different genera, and not arranged subordinately, have different species and differentia—as animal and knowledge have different differentiae—one must examine whether things under the same name but belonging to different and non-subordinate genera have different differentiae. For example, “sharp” as applied to a voice and to a magnitude: a voice differs from another voice by being sharp, and likewise a magnitude differs from another magnitude. Therefore “sharp” is equivocal, since different and non-subordinate genera have different differentiae.

Again, one must examine whether things that fall under the same name and belong to the same genus have different differentiae, as with color in bodies and in melodies. The color in bodies has as its differentiae the ability to gather together and to separate the visual field, whereas the color in melodies does not have the same differentiae. Therefore “color” is equivocal, since things belonging to the same genus ought to have the same differentiae.

Furthermore, since a species is not the differentia of anything, one must examine whether, among things that fall under the same name, one is a species while another is a differentia. For example, “clear” as applied to a body is a species of color, whereas as applied to a voice it is a differentia. A voice differs from another voice by being clear.

What is spoken in many ways must therefore be examined by these and similar methods.

CHAPTER XIV. On discovering differentiae, considering similarities, and the uses of the instruments.

One must examine differentiae within the same genera in relation to one another, for example, how justice differs from courage, and prudence from temperance. All these belong to the same genus, virtue. One must also examine one thing in relation to another when the things do not differ greatly, as in the question of how sense differs from knowledge; for where things differ greatly, their differences are altogether evident.

Similarity must be considered among things belonging to different genera: as one thing is related to another, so is another related to another. For example, as knowledge is related to the knowable, so sense is related to the sensible. Or, as one thing is present in another, so is another in another: sight is in the eye, mind in the soul, tranquility in the sea, and calm weather in the air; in both cases the common element is rest.

One should practice especially with things that are far apart, for it will then be easy to discern similarities in the remaining cases.

One must also consider things belonging to the same genus, to see whether some one thing is present in all of them. For example, if there is something identical in a human being, a horse, and a dog, then they are similar in that respect.

It is useful to have considered how many ways a term is spoken, especially for clarity. Once it has been made clear in how many ways a term is used, one will best know what is being posited.

It is also useful for constructing syllogisms about the thing itself rather than about the name. If it is unclear in how many ways a term is spoken, it may happen that the respondent and the questioner do not direct their understanding toward the same thing. Once the multiplicity has been made clear, however, the questioner will appear ridiculous if he does not direct the discussion toward the relevant sense of the term.

This is also useful for avoiding deception by false reasoning and for deceiving others instead. Those who know in how many ways a term is spoken will not be led astray, but will recognize when the questioner is not speaking about the same thing. They themselves can also deceive by an apparent argument, unless the respondent recognizes the multiplicity of the term.

This is not always possible, but only when, among the things spoken in many ways, some are true and others false.

Strictly speaking, however, this method is not appropriate to dialectic; therefore dialecticians should altogether avoid arguing about the name in this way, unless they cannot otherwise discuss the subject.

It is useful to discover differentiae both for syllogisms about sameness and difference and for knowing what each thing is. That differentiae are useful for syllogisms about sameness and difference is clear: once we have discovered any difference between the subjects, we shall show that they are not the same.

They are useful for knowing what each thing is because we customarily separate the proper account of each substance by attaching to it the differentiae that belong to it.

The consideration of similarity is useful for inductive arguments, for syllogisms from hypothesis, and for assigning definitions.

It is useful for inductive arguments because, by induction concerning individual cases among similar things, we believe that we bring in the universal. It is not easy to make an induction for those who do not recognize similarities.

It is useful for syllogisms from hypothesis because it is probable that, as one of a group of similar things is, so are the others. Thus, with respect to whatever subject we possess the ability to argue, we shall maintain that, as it is in these cases, so it is in the subject under discussion. By showing this, we shall also show the subject from hypothesis: by hypothesizing that as it is in these cases, so it is in the subject, we shall construct a demonstration.

Similarity is useful for assigning definitions because, when we can discern what is identical in each thing, we shall not hesitate to determine what genus should be placed in the definition of the subject. For the common element that is predicated in answer to “what is it?” will be its genus.

The consideration of similarity is likewise useful for defining things that are far apart: tranquility in the sea and calm weather in the air are the same in that both are rest; a point in a line and a unit in number are the same in that both are principles. Therefore, by assigning the common genus in all these cases, we shall believe that we are defining without irrelevance.

Those who give definitions almost always assign them in this way. They say that a unit is the principle of number and that a point is the principle of a line. It is therefore clear that they place the common genus of both under consideration.

These, then, are the instruments by which syllogisms are formed; the places to which the foregoing instruments are useful are the ones that must now be discussed.

BOOK TWO

[Col. 0923]

CHAPTER I. On universal problems and on the predicates for which “belongs” and “is” are convertible.

[Col. 0923B]

Some problems are universal and others particular. Universal problems are such as “every pleasure is good” and “no pleasure is good.” Particular problems are such as “some pleasure is good” and “some pleasure is not good.”

Both universal and particular problems have universal, constructive, and destructive forms in common. For by showing that something belongs to everything, we will also have shown that it belongs to something; likewise, if we show that something belongs to nothing, we will also have shown that it does not belong to everything.

First, then, one must discuss universal destructive problems, because such methods are common to universal and particular problems, and because positions concerning inherence are more often brought forward than positions concerning non-inherence, whereas those engaged in disputation refute them.

It is especially difficult to convert from an accidental predication to the proper naming of the thing. In a certain respect, and not universally, conversion occurs only in the case of accidents. For from a definition, a property, and a genus, conversion is necessary. For example, if “being a walking biped” belongs to some animal, then it will be true, on conversion, to say that that animal is a walking biped.

The same applies to the genus. If “animal” belongs to something, that thing is an animal.

The same applies to a property. If “being capable of receiving grammar” belongs to something, that thing will be capable of receiving grammar.

None of these belongs or fails to belong in a qualified way; rather, it belongs or fails to belong simply. With accidents, however, nothing prevents something from belonging in a qualified way, as with whiteness or justice. Therefore it is not sufficient to show that whiteness or justice belongs to something in order to show that it is white or just, since there remains the question in what respect it is white or just. Consequently, conversion is not necessary in the case of accidents.

One must also determine the errors that occur in problems. There are two kinds: either the speaker says what is false, or he transgresses the expression that was posited. Those who say what is false commit an error, as do those who say that what does not belong belongs to something. Those who call things by alien names—such as calling Plato “a human being”—transgress the naming that was posited.

CHAPTER II. Places for problems concerning whether something belongs or does not belong.

One place is to examine whether something belongs according to some other mode, although it has been assigned as an accident. The greatest error of this kind occurs concerning genera. For example, if someone says that being a color happens to white, being a color does not happen to white; rather, color is its genus.

It is also possible to determine the position by the naming used by the one who makes it, as when someone says that being a virtue happens to justice. Often, even when he does not explicitly determine it, it is clear that he has assigned a genus as an accident, as when someone says that whiteness is colored or that walking is moved.

No genus is predicated denominatively of a species; rather, genera are predicated univocally of their species, since species receive both the name and the account of their genera. Thus, someone who calls white “colored” has assigned neither a genus, since he has spoken denominatively, nor a property or definition, since a definition and a property belong to nothing else. Yet colored things include wood, stone, a human being, and a horse. It is therefore clear that he has assigned it as an accident.

Another place is to examine things that have been said to belong either to everything or to nothing, and to consider them according to species rather than in an unlimited way. Consideration is more effective by proceeding through a small number of cases, but one must begin with the primary divisions and then proceed successively to individuals.

For example, if someone says that opposites have one and the same science, one must examine whether the same science applies to things relative, to contraries, to things spoken according to privation and possession, and to things spoken according to contradiction. If it is not yet clear in these cases, one must divide them again down to individuals: for example, just and unjust, double and half, blindness and sight, being and not-being.

For if it is shown in any case that the science is not the same, we shall have refuted the problem. The same applies if it is shown that the supposed predicate belongs to nothing.

This place can be turned toward both construction and destruction. If, when we produce the divisions, the predicate appears in all cases and in no larger number of cases, we must demand that it be posited universally, or produce an exception showing that the matter is not so in some case. If the speaker does neither, he will appear absurd for refusing to posit it.

Another place is to formulate definitions of the accident and of the thing to which it belongs, or definitions of each in relation to the other, and then examine whether something false has been taken in the definitions as though it were true.

For example, suppose the question is whether God commits injustice. What is “to commit injustice”? If it means voluntarily harming someone, it is clear that God does not commit injustice, since God cannot harm.

Again, suppose that a good person is envious. What is an envious person, and what is envy? If envy is distress at the apparent prosperity of some good person, it is clear that a good person is not envious, for he would then be wicked.

Likewise, suppose that the resentful person is envious. What is each of the two? In this way it will become clear whether what has been said is true or false. If an envious person is one who is distressed at the prosperity of good people, while a resentful person is one who is distressed at the prosperity of bad people, it is clear that a resentful person will not be envious.

One must also take definitions of the terms occurring in the definitions themselves, and not stop until one reaches something known. For often, even when the whole definition has been given, what is being sought is not clear; but when a definition has been given for one of the terms occurring in the definition, it becomes clear.

Further, one should make the problem itself into a proposition and raise an objection to it. The objection will then be an argument against the position. This place is almost the same as the one that examines the things said to belong either to everything or to nothing, but it differs in manner.

Further, one must determine which expressions should be used in the sense accepted by the majority and which should not. This is useful both for construction and for destruction. For example, “health-producing” should be called what produces health, as most people say. But whether the subject under discussion is health-producing should no longer be determined according to common usage; it should be determined as a physician would determine it.

Further, if a term is spoken in many ways, while the position is that it belongs or does not belong, one must show one of the meanings of the term, if both do not apply. This should be used in cases where the ambiguity is concealed. If the multiplicity is not concealed, the opponent will object that what he himself was asking about has not been shown, but something else.

This place can be turned toward both construction and destruction. Those who wish to construct will show that one meaning belongs, if they cannot show that both do; those who wish to destroy will show that one meaning does not belong, if they cannot show that both do not.

For the destructive reasoner, however, nothing needs to be argued from a concession, whether the predicate was said to belong to everything or to nothing. If we show that whatever the thing may be does not belong, we shall have refuted its belonging to everything; likewise, if we show that it belongs, we shall have refuted its belonging to nothing.

For those constructing a position, however, it should first be conceded that whatever belongs to any one thing belongs to everything, if the assumption is plausible. It is not sufficient, in order to show that something belongs to everything, to argue from one case—for example, that because the human soul is immortal, every soul is immortal. One must first concede that if any soul is immortal, every soul is immortal.

This should not always be done, but only when it is difficult to state one common account applying to all cases, as the geometer does when he says that a triangle has three angles equal to two right angles.

If the term’s multiplicity has not remained concealed, then, both in destroying and in constructing, one must divide it according to the number of ways in which it is spoken.

For example, if someone says that something is useful or honorable, one must try either to construct or to refute both meanings with respect to the subject: that it is honorable and useful, or that it is neither honorable nor useful. If both cannot be established, one must show one of them, noting that one applies and the other does not. The same account applies if the term is divided into more than two meanings.

Again, there are terms that are spoken in many ways not because of equivocation, but in another manner. For example, one science may concern several things, either as an end or as things directed toward an end, as medicine concerns what produces health and what provides nourishment. Or the same science may concern both ends, as with contraries, since one end is no more an end than the other. Or it may concern what exists in itself and what exists accidentally.

For example, that a triangle has three angles equal to two right angles belongs to it in itself; that it is equilateral belongs to it accidentally, since it happens to the triangle to be equilateral. Through the latter fact we come to know that it has three angles equal to two right angles.

If, then, it is in no way possible for one science to belong to several things, it is clear that it is wholly impossible for it to do so; if it is possible in some way, it is clear that it is possible.

It is useful to divide a term according to all the ways in which it is spoken. If we wish to construct a position, we should posit whatever meanings apply, and divide only into those meanings that are useful for construction. If we wish to destroy it, we should posit whatever meanings do not apply and omit the rest.

This must be done when the number of meanings has remained concealed. One can then establish, from the same places, that a thing belongs to a given subject in one sense—either as an end, as something directed toward an end, or as something accidental—or that it does not belong in any of the stated senses.

The same applies to desire and to anything else said of several things. Desire is directed toward something either as an end, such as health; as something directed toward an end, such as the preparation of medicine; or as something accidental, such as a sweet thing in wine. It is not desired because it is wine, but because it is sweet: sweetness is desired in itself, while wine is desired accidentally. If the wine becomes bitter, it is no longer desired; therefore wine was desired accidentally.

This place is also useful in dealing with relatives, since things relative are almost always of this kind.

Further, one should transfer the discussion to a more evident name. Instead of “exact in opinion,” use “clear”; instead of “curiosity,” use “desire for superfluous things.” Once what has been said has been made more evident, the position will be easier to argue.

This place is common to both construction and destruction.

To show that contraries belong to the same thing, one must examine the genus. For example, if we wish to show that correctness and error belong to sense, then sensing is judging, and judging is either judging correctly or incorrectly; therefore correctness and error belong to sense.

Here the demonstration proceeds from genus to species, since judging is the genus of sensing: whoever senses judges in some way.

Again, one may proceed from species to genus. Whatever belongs to the species also belongs to the genus. For example, if knowledge is bad and good, then disposition also is bad and good, since disposition is the genus of knowledge.

The first place, however, is false for construction, while the second is true. It is not necessary that whatever belongs to the genus belong also to the species: an animal is flying and four-footed, but a human being is not. Whatever belongs to the species, however, necessarily belongs to the genus: if a human being is good, then an animal is good.

For destruction, the first place is true and the second false. Whatever does not belong to the genus does not belong to the species; but whatever does not belong to the species need not fail to belong to the genus.

Since it is necessary that, whenever a genus is predicated of something, one of its species also be predicated of it, and that whatever possesses a genus, or is denominatively named from a genus, must possess one of its species or be denominatively named from one of them, the following applies.

If knowledge is predicated of something, grammar, music, or some other science will also be predicated of it. If someone possesses knowledge, or is denominatively named from knowledge, he will possess grammar, music, or some other science, or will be denominatively named from one of them, as “grammatical” or “musical.”

If, therefore, something has been said to be moved according to its genus—for example, that the soul is moved—one must examine whether the soul can be moved according to some species of motion, such as increase, decrease, destruction, generation, or any other species of motion. If it is moved according to none of them, it is clear that it is not moved.

This place is common to both construction and destruction. If it is moved according to some species, it is clear that it is moved; if it is moved according to none of the species, it is clear that it is not moved.

When one lacks an argument for the position, one must proceed from definitions, whether definitions of the proposed thing or definitions that appear plausible; and if not from one definition, then from several. It is easy to argue from definitions, since argument from definitions is easy.

In the subject under discussion, one must consider what must be posited if a given thing exists, or what exists necessarily if the subject is given.

The person who wishes to construct must ask: if what exists is present, what subject will necessarily follow? For if that is shown to exist, the subject will also have been shown. The person who wishes to destroy must ask: if the subject is given, what follows? For if we show that what follows from the subject does not exist, we shall have refuted the subject.

Further, one must examine the matter with respect to time, to see whether there is any discrepancy. For example, if someone says that whatever is nourished necessarily grows: animals are always nourished, but they do not always grow.

Likewise, if someone says that knowing is remembering, the former concerns the present and the future, whereas the latter concerns the past. We are said to know present and future things—for example, that there will be an eclipse of the sun—but remembering cannot concern anything other than the past.

Further, there is a sophistical method of leading the discussion to the point at which one has the greatest capacity for argument. This point will sometimes be necessary, sometimes apparently necessary, and sometimes neither apparently nor actually necessary.

It is necessary when, after the respondent has denied something useful to the position, the argument is directed toward that matter. This can occur when the matter is one concerning which we have a plentiful supply of arguments.

The same applies when someone, having made an induction from the position, attempts to refute it. For once that has been refuted, the subject itself is also refuted.

It is apparently necessary when it seems useful and appropriate to the position but does not concern the point at issue in the disputation—whether the person conducting the dispute denies it, or whether, after making a probable induction from the position, he attempts to refute that very matter.

The remaining case is when it is neither necessary nor apparently necessary for the point at issue, and the respondent is refuted without reason.

One must avoid the last-mentioned method, for it plainly lies entirely outside and apart from dialectic. The respondent, too, ought not to take it badly, but should indicate, by positing what is not useful to the position, whatever does not seem to follow. He does posit it, however, since, when questioners have posited all such things, it commonly happens that they become more perplexed if they do not reach a conclusion.

Further, everyone who has said one thing has in a certain way said many things, because several things necessarily follow from each thing. For example, whoever has said “human being” has also said that it is an animal, living, two-footed, endowed with mind, and capable of receiving knowledge.

Therefore, when any one of the consequences is refuted, the original assertion is refuted as well. One must be careful, however, about making an assumption of this kind, since sometimes it is easy to refute the consequence, and sometimes the original position itself.

Whenever one of two alternatives must belong or fail to belong—for example, illness or health to a human being—if we can easily argue that one of them belongs or does not belong, we can also easily argue regarding the other.

This method can be turned in both directions. By showing that one belongs, we shall show that the other does not; and if we show that one does not belong, we shall show that the other does belong. It is therefore clear that this place is useful for both purposes.

Further, one should argue by transferring a name into a phrase when it seems much more appropriate to interpret it in that way than according to the established name. Thus, “magnanimous” should be taken not as “brave,” as it is ordinarily taken, but as “having a great soul,” in the same way as “confident” means “expecting good things.”

Likewise, “ingenious” should mean one whose genius is good. As Xenocrates says, an ingenious person is one who has received a good soul, since the soul itself is each person’s genius.

Since some things are necessary, others occur for the most part, and others may go either way, if what is necessary is posited as occurring for the most part, or what occurs for the most part is posited as necessary, either the thing itself or its contrary will always provide an opportunity for argument.

If what is necessary is posited as occurring for the most part, it is clear that the speaker is not saying that it belongs to everything, although it belongs to everything. Therefore he has made an error.

Likewise, if he says that what occurs for the most part is necessary, he says that it belongs to everything, although it does not belong to everything.

The same applies if he says that the contrary of what occurs for the most part is necessary. For the contrary of what occurs for the most part is always said to occur in fewer cases. If, for example, bad people occur for the most part, good people occur in fewer cases; therefore he has erred much more if he says that good people necessarily exist.

Likewise, if something that may go either way is said to be necessary, or to occur for the most part, the statement is false: what may go either way is neither necessary nor something that occurs for the most part.

It may also happen that someone makes the statement without determining whether he means “for the most part” or “necessarily.” If the matter occurs for the most part, one may argue as though he had said it was necessary.

For example, if someone says that wicked people ought to be disinherited without specifying the manner of necessity, one may argue as though he had asserted that this is necessary.

Further, someone may posit the same accident as two different things because the names are different. Thus Prodicus divided pleasures into joy, delight, and gladness, although all these are names for the same thing, namely pleasure. If, then, someone posits that rejoicing happens to gladness, he will be saying that the same thing happens to itself.

CHAPTER III. Other places for determining problems concerning the same things.

Since contraries are connected with one another in six ways, but produce contrariety when combined in four ways, one must take up the contraries in whatever manner will be useful both for refutation and for construction.

That they are combined in six ways is clear. For either each of the two contraries is connected with each of the other two contraries—and this occurs in two ways: for example, “to benefit friends and harm enemies,” or conversely, “to harm friends and benefit enemies”—or both are predicated of one subject, likewise in two ways: “to benefit friends and harm friends,” or “to benefit enemies and harm enemies”—or one is predicated of both, again in two ways: “to benefit both friends and enemies,” or “to harm both friends and enemies.”

The first two combinations mentioned do not produce contrariety. For “benefiting friends” is not contrary to “harming enemies,” since both are things to be chosen and belong to the same disposition; nor is “harming friends” contrary to “benefiting enemies,” since both are to be avoided and likewise belong to the same disposition. Yet what is to be avoided does not seem to be contrary to what is to be avoided unless the one is stated according to excess and the other according to deficiency. For an excess of things to be avoided appears to exist, and likewise a deficiency.

The remaining four combinations all produce contrariety. For “benefiting friends” is contrary to “harming friends,” since they belong to opposite dispositions: the former is to be chosen, the latter rejected. The same applies in the other cases. In each pairing, one is to be chosen and the other avoided: the former belongs to a good disposition, the latter to a bad one. It is therefore clear from what has been said that several contraries can come to belong to the same thing. Thus “benefiting enemies” and “harming friends” are contrary to “benefiting friends.”

Likewise, when one considers each of the others in the same way, two contraries will appear in each case. One should therefore take whichever of the contraries will be useful for the proposed position.

Further, if something has a contrary accident, one must consider whether that contrary belongs to the subject of which the accident has been stated. For if this contrary belongs to it, the other will not; it is impossible for contraries to belong simultaneously to the same thing.

Or consider a statement of the following kind: that, since something is present, its contraries must also be present—for example, if someone were to say that Forms are present in us. For then it would follow that the same Forms are both in motion and at rest, and also both perceptible and imperceptible. Those who posit Forms say that they are at rest, immobile, and intelligible. Yet if they are in us, it is impossible for them to be immobile. For when we are moved, everything that is in us must necessarily be moved at the same time. And it is clear that they would also be perceptible if they were in us, since through the sense concerned with sight we apprehend the form present in each thing.

Again, if an accident has been posited to which something is contrary, one must consider whether the subject that is receptive of the accident is also receptive of its contrary. The same thing is receptive of contraries. Thus, if someone were to say that hatred inheres in anger, hatred would be present in the form of rage, since anger is present there. One must therefore examine whether the contrary is also present in the form of rage, or rather in desire. For if it is not present in rage but in the desiring faculty, hatred does not inhere in anger.

The same applies if someone were to say that the desiring faculty is ignorant. For it would then also be receptive of knowledge, if it is receptive of ignorance. But this does not appear to be so: the desiring faculty does not appear to be receptive of knowledge.

Thus the refuter should use the place as has been stated. For one constructing an argument, the place that something actually has the accident is not useful, but the place that it may have it is useful. By showing that the subject is not receptive of the contrary, we shall show that the accident neither belongs to it nor may belong to it. But if we show that the contrary belongs to it, or that it is receptive of the contrary, we shall not yet have shown that the accident belongs to it; we shall have shown only that it may belong to it.

Since there are four kinds of opposition, one must consider, in contradictions, converse consequence, both for refutation and for construction. This may be grasped through induction. For example: if a human being is an animal, then “not-animal” is “not-human.” The same applies in other cases. Here there is converse consequence: “animal” follows from “human,” whereas “not-animal” does not follow from “not-human”; rather, conversely, “not-human” follows from “not-animal.”

In every case one should suppose the relation to be of this kind: if something is good, it is pleasant, and if it is not pleasant, it is not good; conversely, if it is not this, neither is it that. Likewise, if it is not pleasant, it is not good; and if it is good, it is pleasant. It is therefore clear that both implications are convertible: the consequence according to contradiction proceeds conversely.

With contraries one must consider whether the contrary follows from the contrary, whether they follow one another in opposition, or whether the consequence is converse, both for refutation and for construction. Such cases too may be grasped through induction, insofar as useful. Opposition is found, for example, in courage and cowardice. Virtue follows from courage, vice from cowardice; what is to be chosen follows from courage, and what is to be avoided from cowardice. Thus the consequences of these are opposed to one another: what is to be chosen is contrary to what is to be avoided. The same applies in other cases.

Converse consequence occurs, for example, when health follows from a good condition, whereas illness does not follow from a bad condition; rather, a bad condition follows from illness. It is therefore clear that in such cases the consequence is converse. Converse consequence rarely occurs among contraries; for the most part, they follow one another in opposition. If, then, neither does one contrary follow the other in opposition nor does the consequence proceed conversely, it is clear that neither of the things mentioned follows the other. But if this is so among contraries, then in the cases mentioned also one must follow the other.

The same examination must be made with contraries, privations, and dispositions. Yet in privations the consequence is not converse; rather, the consequence must always proceed in opposition. Thus sight follows from perception, while blindness follows from insensibility. Sense is opposed to insensibility as disposition to privation: one of these is a disposition, the other a privation.

Likewise, the same method should be used with a disposition and its privation, and with relatives. For here too the consequences proceed in opposition. If “triple” is “multiple,” then “subtriple” is “submultiple”; for “triple” is said relative to “subtriple,” and “multiple” relative to “submultiple.”

Again, if knowledge is opinion, then the knowable is opinable; and if sight is perception, then the visible is perceptible.
