An objection may be raised that in relatives consequence does not necessarily occur in the way stated. For the perceptible is knowable, whereas perception is not knowledge. This does not, however, appear to be a valid objection, since many deny that there is knowledge of perceptible things.

Moreover, what has been said is no less useful for establishing the contrary: if the perceptible is not knowable, neither is perception knowledge.

The same method applies to correlated terms and grammatical forms, both for refutation and for construction. Correlated terms are such as “just,” “a just person,” and “justice”; likewise “brave” and “bravery.” Also included are productive and preservative terms, correlated with that of which they are productive or preservative—for example, “health-producing” with “health,” and “disposition-producing” with “disposition.” The same applies in other cases. Such terms are ordinarily called correlated.

Forms of expression include “justly,” “bravely,” “health-producingly,” “disposition-producingly,” and whatever is expressed in the same manner. The expressions according to such forms also appear to be correlated—for example, “justly” with “justice,” and “bravely” with “bravery.”

Everything expressed according to the same correlation is called correlated: “justice,” “just,” “the just thing,” and “justly.” It is therefore clear that, once one of the terms expressed according to the same correlation has been shown—for example, “good” or “praiseworthy”—all the others have been shown as well. Thus, if justice belongs among praiseworthy things, then “justly,” “just,” and “the just thing” also belong among praiseworthy things.

“Justly” and “praiseworthily” are said to be in the same grammatical form, since “praiseworthily” derives from “praiseworthy,” just as “justly” derives from “justice.”

One must consider not only what has been stated but also the contrary of the contrary. For example, what is good is not necessarily pleasant; otherwise what is bad would be painful. Likewise, if justice is knowledge, injustice is ignorance; and if what is done justly is done knowingly and with experience, what is done unjustly is done ignorantly and with experience. If these implications do not hold, neither do the corresponding others. As in the point just mentioned, it will be more apparent that what is done unjustly is done with experience than without experience.

This place was discussed earlier under the consequences of contraries. For we are now proving nothing other than that the contrary follows from the contrary.

Further, the same applies to generations, corruptions, productive and destructive causes, for refutation and for construction. Whatever has good generations is itself good, and if it is itself good, its generations are good. If its generations are bad, it too is bad.

With corruptions the reverse holds: if the corruptions are good, the things themselves are bad; and if the corruptions are bad, the things themselves are good. The same reasoning applies to productive and destructive causes: whatever has good productive causes is itself good, whereas whatever has good destructive causes is itself bad.

### CHAPTER FOUR. Places from similarities, addition, more and less, the unqualified, and the qualified

[Col. 0932C]

Again, in similar things, consider whether they are alike. For example, if there is one science of many things, so too there is one opinion; and if having sight is seeing, having hearing is hearing. The same applies in other cases, both to things which are and to things which appear to be.

This place is useful for both purposes. For if this is so in one of similar things, it is so in the other similar things; but if it is not so in one, neither is it so in the other. One must also consider whether it is alike in one thing and in many. For sometimes it fails to accord: if knowing is thinking, then knowing many things would be thinking many things; but this is not true. For it is possible to know many things without thinking of them. But if this is not so, neither is the assertion that knowing is thinking.

[Col. 0932D]

Further, there are arguments from more and less. There are four places concerning “more.” One is this: if the greater follows from the greater, as, if pleasure is good, greater pleasure is greater good; and, if doing injustice is bad, doing greater injustice is greater bad. This place is useful for both purposes. For if, as stated, increase of the accident follows increase of the subject, it is clear that the accident belongs to it; but if it does not follow, it does not belong. This must be established by induction.

Another place is this: when one thing is predicated of two, if it does not belong to that to which it appears more to belong, neither does it belong to that to which it appears less to belong; and if it belongs to that to which it appears less to belong, it also belongs to that to which it appears more to belong.

Again, when two things are predicated of one, if that which appears more to belong to the other does not belong, neither does that which appears less to belong; or, if that which appears less to belong does belong, that which appears more to belong does also.

[Col. 0933A]

Further, when two things are predicated of two, if what appears more to belong to one does not belong, neither does the remaining predicate belong to the remaining subject; or if what appears less to belong to one does belong, the remaining predicate also belongs to the remaining subject.

Further, there are three arguments from what belongs, or appears to belong, alike, corresponding to the latter three places concerning “more.” For whether one thing belongs, or appears to belong, alike to two things: if it does not belong to one, neither does it belong to the other; but if it belongs to one, it belongs to the other. Or whether two things belong alike to one thing: if one does not belong, neither does the other; but if one belongs, so does the other. The same holds if two things belong alike to two things: if one does not belong to one, neither does the other belong to the other; but if one belongs to one, the other also belongs to the other.

[Col. 0933B]

Thus one may argue in so many ways from more and less and from what belongs alike. Further, there is argument from addition. If one thing, when added to another, makes it good or white, though it was not previously good or white, the thing added will be good or white, being of the sort that in fact makes the whole so.

Further, if something makes that to which it is added more such as it already was, it will itself be of that sort; and the same applies in other cases. This place is useful not in all cases, but in those in which increase of the very thing itself occurs. But it cannot be reversed for refutation. For if the added thing does not make the whole good, it is not yet clear that it itself is not good. For good added to bad does not necessarily make the whole good; nor does white added to black, or sweet added to bitter.

[Col. 0933C]

Again, if something is spoken of in terms of more and less, it also belongs without qualification. For what is not good or white is not called more or less good or white; evil is not called more or less good in any respect, but more or less evil. This place, however, cannot be reversed for refutation. For many things which are not spoken of in terms of more and less belong without qualification: a human being is not called more or less a human being, but is not therefore not a human being.

[Col. 0934A]

The same must be considered with respect to what is qualified, and to when and where. For if something is possible in a respect, it is possible without qualification; likewise with when and where. For what is impossible without qualification is possible neither in a respect, nor in a place, nor at a time.

An objection is that people are naturally earnest in a respect—for example, liberal or chaste—but are not naturally earnest without qualification; for no one is prudent by nature. Likewise, at a particular time it is possible for some corruptible thing not to perish, but it is not possible without qualification for it not to perish. Similarly, in a place it is expedient to use a certain regimen of life, as in unhealthy places, but it is not expedient without qualification. Further, in some place it is possible for only one thing to exist, but it is not possible without qualification for only one thing to exist.

[Col. 0934B]

Likewise, it is indeed good in a particular place to denounce one’s father, as among the Triballians, but it is not good without qualification. Or does this not signify “where,” but “for certain people”? For it makes no difference wherever they may be: it will be good for them everywhere among the Triballians.

Again, it is expedient to undergo medical treatment when one is ill, but not without qualification. Or does this not signify “when,” but being affected in a certain way? For it makes no difference at what time, provided that one is so affected.

What is said without qualification is what you call good, or its contrary, with no addition. Thus you do not say that sacrificing one’s father is good, but that it is good for certain people; therefore it is not good without qualification. But you call honouring the gods good without adding anything: it is good without qualification. Therefore whatever appears honourable, shameful, or anything of that kind with no addition will be said to be so without qualification.

## BOOK THREE

### CHAPTER ONE. Places concerning the better and the more choiceworthy

Whether one of two or more things is more choiceworthy or better must be discerned from the following considerations.

First, let it be determined that our inquiry is not concerned with things that are very far apart and greatly different from one another—for no one doubts whether happiness or wealth is more desirable—but with things that are close to one another and about which we are uncertain which should be preferred, since we see no superiority of one over the other.

It is therefore clear that in such cases, once one superiority, or several superiorities, have been demonstrated, the judgment will be established: the more choiceworthy is whichever of them is superior.

First, that which is more lasting or stable is more choiceworthy than that which is less so.

Also, that which a prudent person, a good person, a right law, or those selected as excellent in particular matters would choose, insofar as they are such; likewise that which experts in each field would choose; or that which the majority or everyone would choose—whether in medicine, building, or any other craft, where the majority or all physicians, builders, or practitioners choose it—or, generally, that which the majority, everyone, or everything chooses, as in the case of the good. For everything desires the good.

One must direct the argument toward whatever is useful for the point that is to be made. In general, that which is in accordance with the better discipline is better and more choiceworthy; for a particular person, however, that which is in accordance with that person’s own discipline may be so.

Next, that which is the same as what something is, rather than what it is not, within its genus is more choiceworthy—for example, justice is more choiceworthy than a just person. The former belongs to the genus “good,” whereas the latter does not; and the former is itself a good, whereas the latter is not. For nothing is called the same as its genus unless it belongs to that genus. Thus a white human being is not the same as color. The same applies in other cases.

That which is to be chosen for its own sake is more choiceworthy than that which is chosen for the sake of something else—for example, being healthy rather than exercising. The former is chosen for its own sake, the latter for the sake of something else.

That which is chosen in itself is more choiceworthy than that which is chosen incidentally—for example, that one’s friends should be just rather than that one’s enemies should be just. The former is chosen in itself, whereas we choose the latter incidentally, namely so that they may do us no harm.

This is the same as the preceding point, but differs in formulation. We choose that our friends should be just for their own sake, even if they owed us nothing and even if they were in India; but we choose that our enemies should be just for the sake of something else, namely so that they may do us no harm.

That which is the cause of good in itself is more choiceworthy than that which is its cause incidentally—for example, virtue rather than fortune. Virtue is the cause of good in itself, whereas fortune is its cause incidentally; and the same applies to anything else of this kind.

The contrary likewise holds. That which is the cause of evil in itself is more to be avoided than that which is its cause incidentally—for example, vice rather than fortune, since vice is evil in itself, whereas fortune is evil only incidentally.

That which is good without qualification is more choiceworthy than that which is good for someone in particular—for example, becoming healthy rather than undergoing surgery. The former is simply good, whereas the latter is good for someone who requires surgery.

That which is by nature is more choiceworthy than that which is not by nature—for example, justice rather than a just person. The former is natural, whereas the latter is acquired.

That which belongs to the better and more honorable is more choiceworthy—for example, what belongs to a god rather than what belongs to a human being, and what belongs to the soul rather than what belongs to the body.

What is proper to the better is better than what is proper to the worse—for example, what belongs to a god rather than what belongs to a human being. In what is common to both there is no difference between them; but in their proper differences one surpasses the other.

What exists in the better, earlier, or more honorable things is better—for example, health is better than strength and beauty. Health exists in the moist and dry elements—or, stated generally, in the things from which the animal is constituted earlier—whereas strength exists in sinews and bones, and beauty appears to be a certain proportionate arrangement of the limbs, which are later.

The end appears to be more choiceworthy than the things directed toward the end. Of two things, that which is nearer to the end is more choiceworthy. In general, what is directed toward the end of life is more desirable than what is directed toward some other end—for example, what aims at happiness rather than what aims at prudence. For what aims at happiness is more choiceworthy.

The possible is more choiceworthy than the impossible.

Further, when two things are productive of an end, the thing whose end is better is itself better. When there is a productive cause and an end, their superiority is proportionate when the end surpasses the other end by more than the one productive cause surpasses the other.

For example, happiness surpasses health by more than health surpasses what produces health. Therefore the productive cause of happiness is better than health. For by as much as happiness surpasses health, by that much the productive cause of happiness surpasses what produces health; but health surpasses what produces health by less. Hence the productive cause of happiness surpasses what produces health by more than health does. Therefore the productive cause of happiness is better than health.

It is clear, then, that the productive cause of happiness is more choiceworthy than health, since the same superiority is greater.

Further, that which is chosen for its own sake is better, more honorable, and more praiseworthy—for example, friendship rather than wealth, and justice rather than health and strength. The former are honorable for their own sake, whereas the latter are not chosen for their own sake but for the sake of something else. No one honors wealth for its own sake, but for the sake of something else; friendship, however, is honored for its own sake, even if nothing else were to be gained from it.

### CHAPTER TWO. Other places concerning the same problems

Further, when two things are very similar to one another and we cannot discern any superiority of one over the other, we must examine what follows from them.

When a greater good follows, that thing is more choiceworthy; but when bad consequences follow, that thing is more choiceworthy which has the less bad consequence. For although both things may be choiceworthy, there is nothing to prevent something troublesome from following one of them.

The consequences may be considered in two ways, since both what precedes and what follows may be consequences. Thus ignorance comes first for the learner, and knowledge later; in most cases, however, what comes later is better. One must therefore take whichever of the consequences is useful.

Further, more goods are more choiceworthy than fewer, either simply or when the one set includes the other—for example, many goods rather than a few.

An objection is that sometimes one of two things exists for the sake of the other; in that case the two are not more choiceworthy together than one alone. For example, becoming healthy and health are not more choiceworthy together than health alone, since we choose becoming healthy for the sake of health.

Things that are not goods may nevertheless be more choiceworthy than goods—for example, happiness and something else that is not a good, or justice and courage.

The same things are more choiceworthy with pleasure than without pleasure, and with freedom from pain than with distress.

Each thing is more choiceworthy at the time when it is more effective. Thus freedom from distress is more choiceworthy in old age than in youth, since it is more effective in old age.

Accordingly, prudence is also more choiceworthy in old age. No one chooses young men as leaders, because it is not established that they are prudent. Courage, however, is the reverse: action according to courage is more necessary in youth. The same applies to temperance, since young people are more troubled by desires than the old.

That which is useful at all times, or on more occasions, is more choiceworthy—for example, justice and temperance rather than courage, since the former are always useful, whereas courage is useful only sometimes.

That which, if everyone possessed it, would leave us in need of nothing else, is more choiceworthy than that which, if we possessed it, would still leave us in need of the other. This applies to justice and courage: if everyone were just, courage would be of no use; but if everyone were courageous, justice would be useful.

Further, the argument may proceed from corruptions and additions, generations and acquisitions, and contraries.

Whatever has bad corruptions is itself more choiceworthy; the same applies to removals and contraries. If the removal or contrary is more to be avoided, the thing itself is more choiceworthy. With generations and acquisitions the reverse holds: whatever has more choiceworthy acquisitions and generations is itself also more choiceworthy.

Another place is this: what is nearer to the good is better and more choiceworthy.

What is more similar to the good is more choiceworthy—for example, justice rather than a just person.

What is more similar to the better of two things is better. Thus some say that Ajax is better than Odysseus because he is more similar to Achilles.

The objection to this is that the claim is not true. For there is nothing to prevent Ajax from being more similar to Achilles in respect of something other than the respect in which Achilles is best, while one may be good and yet not similar in the same respect.

One must also consider whether the similarity holds in more ridiculous cases, such as a monkey being more similar to a human being than to a horse, even though the monkey is not better. For the monkey is not better than a horse, but it is more similar to a human being.

Again, with two things: if one is more similar to the better and the other to the worse, the one more similar to the better will be better.

This too admits of an objection. For there is nothing to prevent one thing from being only slightly similar to the better, while the other is very similar to the worse—for example, if Ajax is only slightly similar to Achilles, whereas Odysseus is very similar to Nestor.

The reverse is also possible: one thing may be more similar to the better in its worse aspects, and another more similar to the worse in its better aspects, as in the comparison of a horse with a donkey and a monkey with a human being.

That which is most distinguished is more choiceworthy than that which is less so.

What is more difficult is more choiceworthy, since we value more highly what we possess when it is not easy to obtain.

What is more proper to oneself is more choiceworthy than what is more common.

What is less encumbered is more choiceworthy, since that which is followed by no trouble is more choiceworthy than that which is followed by trouble.

Further, if one thing is better than another, then the best of the things belonging to the first is better than the best of the things belonging to the second. Thus, if a human being is better than a horse, the best human being is better than the best horse.

If the best of one class is better than the best of another, then the former class is simply better than the latter. Thus, if the best human being is better than the best horse, then a human being simply is better than a horse simply.

Further, those things which we wish our friends to share are more choiceworthy than those which we do not wish them to share.

Those actions which we prefer to perform toward a friend rather than toward just anyone are more choiceworthy—for example, acting justly and benefiting someone rather than merely appearing to do so. We wish more to benefit our friends than merely to appear to benefit them, whereas toward just anyone the reverse is true.

Things that are added to necessary things are better, and sometimes also more choiceworthy. For living well is better than merely living, and living well is something added to the necessary condition, whereas living itself is necessary.

Sometimes such things are better but not more choiceworthy. For what is better is not necessarily more choiceworthy. Philosophizing, for example, is better than making money, but it is not more choiceworthy for someone who lacks the necessities of life.

What is added to necessary things is present when, once the necessities have been secured, certain further goods are added. In general, what is necessary is perhaps more choiceworthy, while what is added to it is better.

That which need not be sought from another is more choiceworthy than that which must also be sought from another. This is the relation of justice to courage.

If one thing can be chosen without the other, whereas the other cannot be chosen without it, the former is more choiceworthy. Thus power without prudence is not choiceworthy, whereas prudence without power is choiceworthy.

Of two things, if we deny one in order to appear to possess the other, the one which we wish to appear to possess is more choiceworthy. Thus we deny that we love labor in order to appear talented.

Further, that for whose absence those who are distressed are less deserving of reproach is more choiceworthy.

And that for whose absence one should reproach someone more if that person is not distressed is more choiceworthy.

### CHAPTER THREE. Other places concerning the better and the more choiceworthy

Further, among things belonging to the same species, that which possesses its proper virtue is more choiceworthy than that which does not; and when both possess it, that which possesses more of it is more choiceworthy.

If one thing makes the thing to which it belongs good, whereas the other does not, the former is more choiceworthy. Thus what heats is hotter than what does not heat.

If both do so, that which does so more is more choiceworthy; or that which makes something good in a better and more primary way—for example, if one makes the soul good and the other the body.

Further, the argument may proceed from grammatical forms, uses, actions, and works, and from these back to one another. For they follow one another. If what is done justly is more choiceworthy than what is done bravely, then justice is more choiceworthy than courage; and if justice is more choiceworthy than courage, what is done justly is more choiceworthy than what is done bravely. The same applies in other cases.

Further, if, in relation to the same thing, one is a greater good and the other a lesser good, the greater is more choiceworthy; or if one thing is greater than another which is itself greater, it is more choiceworthy.

If two things are each more choiceworthy than one thing, that which is much more choiceworthy than the lesser of them is itself more choiceworthy.

That whose excess is more choiceworthy is itself more choiceworthy. Thus friendship is more choiceworthy than money, since an excess of friendship is more choiceworthy than an excess of money.

That for which one would rather be the cause oneself is more choiceworthy than that for which one would rather have another be the cause—for example, friends rather than money.

Further, from addition: if something added to the same thing makes the whole more choiceworthy, the thing added is more choiceworthy.

One must be careful not to extend this to cases in which one of the things added makes use of the other as a common instrument, or cooperates with it in some other way, while the remaining thing neither makes use of it nor cooperates with it. Thus a saw joined with the carpenter’s art is more choiceworthy, but a saw is not simply more choiceworthy.

Again, if something added to a lesser thing makes the whole greater, that which makes it greater is more choiceworthy.

The same applies to removal: if, when something is removed from the same thing, what remains becomes lesser, then that which has been removed is greater, since its removal makes what remains lesser.

If one thing is chosen for its own sake and the other for the sake of reputation, the former is more choiceworthy—for example, health rather than beauty. The limit of what is done for reputation is that one would not wish to possess it if no one knew of it.

If one thing is chosen both for its own sake and for the sake of reputation, while the other is chosen only for the latter, the former is more choiceworthy.

Whatever is more honored for its own sake is also better and more choiceworthy. That which is honorable in itself is evidently the thing which requires nothing else; we choose it more for its own sake.

Further, whenever something is said to be choiceworthy, it must be divided according to the reasons for which it is chosen—for example, whether it is useful, honorable, or pleasant. That which is useful for all or for more purposes is more choiceworthy than that which is not so useful.

If the same qualities belong to both, one must consider in which of them they belong more: whether the pleasant, the honorable, or the useful is present to the greater degree.

Again, that which is chosen for the sake of the better is more choiceworthy—for example, what is chosen for the sake of virtue rather than for the sake of pleasure.

The same applies to things to be avoided. That which more obstructs the virtues is more to be avoided—for example, illness rather than ugliness, since illness is a greater impediment both to pleasure and to being excellent.

Further, what has been proposed as to be chosen or avoided can be shown through similarity. The less choiceworthy is that which someone would equally choose and avoid, compared with what is to be chosen alone. Comparisons must therefore be made among the things themselves, as has been stated.

### CHAPTER FOUR. Rules concerning what is to be chosen and avoided: common places
The same topics are also useful for demonstrating anything whatsoever that ought to be chosen or avoided. For one must remove only the superiority that relates one thing to another: if what is more honorable is more choiceworthy, then what is honorable is choiceworthy; and if what is more useful is more choiceworthy, then what is useful is choiceworthy. The same applies to all other things that admit of such comparison.

In some cases, however, we immediately say, on the basis of the comparison with another thing, that both or one of them ought to be chosen. For example, when we say that one thing is good by nature and another is not good by nature: for it is clear that what is good by nature ought to be chosen. One should take as universal as possible the topics concerning “more” and “less,” since, when formulated in this way, they will be useful in more cases.

It is possible to make some of the topics already mentioned more universal by slightly altering their wording. For example: what is such by nature is more such than what is not such by nature. And if one thing does what possesses a given quality while another does not, then what sometimes does it is more such than what does not. If both do it, then what does it more is more such. Further, if, in relation to the same thing, one is more such and another less such. And if one is more such in relation to what is such, while another is such in relation to what is not such, it is clear that the former is more such.

Further, the same follows from addition: if something added to the same thing makes the whole more such, or if something added to what is less such makes the whole more such. The same applies to subtraction: when something has been removed, if what remains is less such, then the thing removed is more such. Things that are less mixed with their opposites are more such. Thus white is whiter insofar as it is less mixed with black.

Further, beyond the points mentioned earlier, that which more fully admits the proper account of the subject is more such. For example, if the account of white is “a color that separates sight,” then the account of whiter is “a color that separates sight more.”

If the problem is posed particularly rather than universally, all the topics that construct or destroy what has been stated universally are useful in the first instance. For by means of universal destructions or constructions we also demonstrate particulars: if something belongs to everything, it belongs to something; and if it belongs to nothing, it belongs to nothing in particular.

The most appropriate and common topics are those derived from opposites, correlatives, and inflected forms. For it is similarly plausible to suppose that, if every pleasure is a good and every pain an evil, then some pleasure is a good and some pain an evil. Likewise, if some perception is not a capacity, then some insensibility is not an incapacity; and if something opined is learned, then some opinion is learning. Again, if something among unjust things is good, then something among just things is evil; and if something among things unjustly regarded as evil is evil, then something among things unjustly regarded as good is good. If something pleasant ought to be avoided, then some pleasure ought to be avoided; and accordingly, if something pleasant is useful, then some pleasure is useful.

The same applies to things that destroy or generate. For if something destructive of pleasure or learning is good, there will be some pleasure or learning that is an evil. Likewise, if some destruction of learning is good, or some generation of evil is good, there will be some learning that is evil. For example, if forgetting the shameful things one has done is good, or remembering evil things is good, then knowing the shameful things one has done is evil. The same applies in other cases, since the same plausibility holds throughout.

Further, the same follows from “more” and “less,” and likewise from equality. For if something belonging to another genus is more such, while nothing belonging to that genus is such, then the thing under discussion will not be such either. For example, if some learning is more a good than pleasure, but no learning is a good, then pleasure will not be a good either.

The same applies in the case of equality, and in the same way it can both destroy and establish. From equality, both destruction and construction are possible; from less, only construction, not destruction. For example, if some capacity and learning are equally goods, and some capacity is a good, then some learning is a good. But if no capacity is a good, it does not follow that no learning is a good. Thus it is clear that from “less” one can establish only the conclusion.

Destruction can be derived not only from another genus but also from the same genus, when one takes what is most such. For example, if it has been proposed that some learning is a good, but it is shown that prudence is not a good, then no other learning will be a good either, since prudence appears most of all to be learning.

Further, this follows from a supposition when one asks, in the same way, whether something belongs or does not belong to one thing and to everything. For example: if the human soul is immortal, then other souls are immortal; but if this soul is not immortal, neither are the others. If it has been proposed that something belongs to one thing, one must show that it does not belong to one thing, since by the hypothesis it will follow that it belongs to nothing. If it has been proposed that it does not belong to one thing, one must show that it belongs to one thing, since in this way it will follow that it belongs to everything.

It is therefore clear that one who uses a hypothesis turns a problem posed particularly into one posed universally. For by inducing the person who admits it particularly to admit it universally, one asks him to concede that it belongs similarly to one thing and to everything.

When the proposition is indefinite, destruction is possible in one way. For example, if someone says that pleasure is a good, or that it is not a good, without determining anything further: if he says that some pleasure is a good, then, if the proposition is to be destroyed, one must show universally that no pleasure is a good. Likewise, if he says that some pleasure is not a good, one must show universally that every pleasure is a good. Otherwise destruction is impossible. For if we show that some pleasure is a good or is not a good, the proposition has not yet been destroyed.

It is therefore clear that destruction is spoken of in one way, whereas construction is spoken of in two ways. For if one shows universally that every pleasure is a good, or that some pleasure is a good, the proposition will have been established.

Likewise, if one must argue that some pleasure is not a good, then, by showing either that no pleasure is a good or that some pleasure is not a good, one will have demonstrated the conclusion in both ways, universally and particularly.

When the proposition has been determined, destruction is possible in two ways. For example, if it is proposed that a good belongs to one pleasure but does not belong to another: whether one shows that every pleasure is a good or that no pleasure is a good, the proposition will have been destroyed. But if someone proposes that only one pleasure is a good, destruction is possible in three ways: by showing that every pleasure is a good, that none is a good, or that more than one is a good.

In most cases where the proposition has been determined—for example, that prudence alone is the knowledge of the virtues—destruction is possible in four ways. For the proposition will be destroyed if one shows that every virtue is knowledge, that no virtue is knowledge, that some other virtue, such as justice, is also knowledge, or that prudence itself is not knowledge.

It is also useful to examine individual cases in which something has been said to belong or not to belong, just as in universal problems. Further, one must also examine genera, dividing them according to their species down to individuals, as was said earlier. For if it appears to belong to everything, or to belong to nothing after many examples have been presented, one should ask the other party either to concede the universal claim or to raise an objection in some case where it does not hold.

Further, in cases where an accident can be determined either by species or by number, one must examine whether it belongs to none of them. For example, if time is not moved and is not motion, one should enumerate the species of motion. For if none of them belongs to time, it is clear that time is not moved and is not motion. Likewise, that the soul is not a number can be shown by dividing number into its species, since every number is either odd or even. If the soul is neither odd nor even, it is clear that it is not a number. In this way, then, one must argue concerning an accident.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0941]

## CHAPTER ONE. What must be examined: ten topics concerning the genus of problems

[Col. 0941B]

After this, one must examine matters concerning genus and property. These are elements of the procedures relating to definitions, though disputants rarely investigate them in themselves.

If the genus of something that exists is proposed, one must first examine all things related to what has been stated, to see whether it is predicated of something else as well, as happens with an accident. For example, if “good” is proposed as the genus of pleasure, one must ask whether some pleasure is not good. For if this is evident, then “good” is not the genus of pleasure, since a genus is predicated of all the species that fall under it.

Next, one must examine whether it is predicated in the account of what the thing is, or merely as an accident. For example, white is predicated of snow, of the soul, and of what is moved by itself. Neither snow is, in its essence, white—for which reason white is not the genus of snow—nor is the soul, in its essence, moved, since motion happens to it, just as walking and being in the act of walking frequently happen to an animal.

Further, “being moved” appears to signify not what a thing is, but what it does or undergoes. The same applies to “white”: it does not indicate what snow is, but what sort of thing it is. Therefore neither is predicated in the account of what the thing is.

One must examine especially, in the definition of an accident, whether it fits the proposed genus, as in the examples just mentioned. For it is possible both to move oneself and not to move oneself, and likewise both to be white and not to be white. Therefore neither of these is a genus but an accident, since we call an accident that which can belong to something and also fail to belong to it.

Further, one must examine whether the genus and the species are not in the same division, but one is substance and the other a quality, or one a relative and the other a quality. For snow and swan are substances, whereas white is not a substance but a quality. Therefore white is not the genus of snow or of swan.

Again, learning is relative, whereas good and beautiful are qualities. Therefore beautiful or good is not the genus of learning, since the genera of relatives must themselves be relatives, as in the case of double: the genus of double is multiple, and multiple itself belongs among relatives.

To state the matter universally, the genus must be in the same division as the species. If the species is a substance, the genus must also be a substance; and if the species is a quality, the genus must also be a quality—for example, if white is a quality, then color is a quality. The same applies in other cases.

Again, one must examine whether the genus proposed must, or can, participate in the species placed under it. The definition of participating is receiving the account of that which is participated in. It is therefore clear that species participate in genera, but genera do not participate in species: the species receives the account of the genus, whereas the genus does not receive the account of the species.

One must therefore examine whether the proposed genus participates, or can participate, in the species—for example, if someone assigns something as a genus of being or unity. For the genus would then participate in the species, since being and unity are predicated of everything that is; therefore their accounts would also be predicated of everything.

Further, one must examine whether the species is truly predicated of something of which the proposed genus is not. For example, if being or knowable is proposed as the genus of the opinable, the opinable will be predicated of what is not, since many non-beings are opinable. But it is clear that being and knowable are not predicated of what is not. Therefore being and knowable are not the genus of the opinable, since the genus must be predicated of everything of which the species is predicated.

Again, one must examine whether none of the species can participate in what has been placed as the genus. For it is impossible to participate in a genus while participating in none of its species, unless one is a species in the first division of the species; for those species participate only in the genus.

Thus, if motion is proposed as the genus of pleasure, one must examine whether neither destruction nor alteration nor any of the other motions that are usually enumerated is pleasure. For it will be clear that none of the species participates in it. Therefore motion will not be the genus, since it is necessary that whatever participates in the genus should participate in one of its species.

Accordingly, pleasure will not be a species of motion, nor will it be one of the individuals or of anything that falls under the species motion. For individuals also participate in both species and genera, as a particular human participates in human and in animal.

Further, one must examine whether what has been placed under the genus is predicated of more things than the genus itself. For example, the opinable is predicated of more things than being, since both being and non-being are opinable. Therefore the opinable will not be a species of being, since a genus is always predicated of more things than its species.

Again, one must examine whether the genus and the species are predicated of equal numbers of things. For example, if, among things that all follow one another, one is proposed as the species and another as the genus, as being and unity, then, since everything that is is one, neither is the genus of the other, since they are predicated of equal things.

The same applies if “first” and “principle” are proposed as genera of one another. For a principle is first, and the first is a principle. Therefore either the two expressions signify the same thing, or neither is the genus of the other.

A general test in all such cases is that a genus and a difference are predicated of more things than the species, since the difference too is predicated of fewer things than the genus.

One must also see whether the proposed genus is absent from, or does not appear to be present in, one of the species that differ in species. For construction, the genus must belong to some species, since the same genus belongs to all species that differ in species. If it is shown to belong to one, it is clear that it belongs to all; and if it belongs to none, it is clear that it belongs to no species.

For example, if someone places lines that can be divided under the genus “indivisible,” then the proposed genus is not present in lines that have division, although all straight lines are alike in species.

## CHAPTER TWO. Other topics concerning genus

One must also consider whether there is some other genus of the species proposed that neither contains the proposed genus nor falls under it. For example, if someone proposes knowledge as the genus of justice, virtue is also a genus, and neither genus contains the other. Therefore knowledge would not be the genus of justice.

It appears that whenever one species falls under two genera, one of the genera is contained under the other. There is, however, a difficulty in certain cases of this kind. Prudence appears to some people to be both virtue and knowledge, although neither genus contains the other. Yet not everyone grants that prudence is knowledge.

If someone accepts that the preceding claim is true, it will nevertheless appear necessary that the two genera either be subordinate to one another or both fall under the same genus, as happens with virtue and knowledge. Both fall under the same genus, since each is a state and disposition.

One must therefore consider whether neither of the two genera is contained in the proposed genus. For if the genera are neither subordinate to one another nor both under the same genus, the proposed genus will not be the genus.

One must also consider the genus of the proposed genus, and so continually the higher genus, to see whether all such genera are predicated of the species and predicated in the account of what the thing is. Every higher genus must be predicated of the species in the account of what the thing is. If there is any discrepancy, it is clear that the proposed genus is not the genus.

Again, one must examine whether the genus participates in the species, either itself or through one of its higher genera. For none of the higher genera participates in what is lower. Thus, for destruction, one should proceed as has been said.

For construction, if the other party admits that the proposed genus belongs to the species but questions whether it belongs as a genus, it is sufficient to show that one of the higher genera is predicated of the species in the account of what the thing is. When one higher genus is predicated in the account of what the thing is, all its higher and lower genera, if they are predicated of the species, will also be predicated in that account. Therefore the proposed genus too will be predicated in the account of what the thing is.

That when one thing is predicated in the account of what the thing is, all the others also, if predicated, are predicated in that account, must be established by induction.

But if the mere belonging of the proposed genus is in question, it is not sufficient to show that one of the higher genera is predicated of the species in the account of what the thing is. For example, if someone proposes locomotion as the genus of walking, it is not sufficient to show that walking is motion in order to prove that locomotion is its genus, since other motions also belong to motion. One must show that walking participates in none of the things belonging to the same division except locomotion.

For it is necessary that what participates in a genus participate in one of its species according to the first division. If walking participates in neither increase nor decrease nor any other motion, it is clear that it participates in locomotion. Therefore locomotion will be the genus of walking.

Again, one must consider the things of which the proposed species is predicated as a genus, and whether the proposed genus is also predicated of those same things in the account of what they are. The same applies to all the things above the genus. If there is any discrepancy, it is clear that the proposed genus is not the genus.

For if it were the genus, both all the higher genera and the genus itself would be predicated in the account of what the things are, of those things of which the species is predicated in that account.

For destruction it is useful if the genus is not predicated in the account of what the thing is of the things of which the species is predicated in that account. For construction it is useful if it is so predicated. It will follow that the genus and species are predicated of the same things in the account of what they are, and therefore that the same species falls under two genera. The genera must therefore be subordinate.

If it is shown that the genus we wish to establish is not subordinate to the species, it is clear that the species will fall under that genus. Thus it will have been shown that this is the genus.

One must also examine the accounts of the genera, to see whether they fit the proposed species and the things that participate in the species. For the accounts of the genera must be predicated both of the species and of the things that participate in it. If there is any discrepancy, it is clear that the proposed genus is not the genus.

Again, one must examine whether a difference has been proposed as a genus. For example, if “immortal” is proposed as the genus of god: immortal is a difference of animal, since some animals are mortal and others immortal. It is therefore clear that the proposal is mistaken, since no difference is a genus.

That this is true is clear because no difference signifies what a thing is, but rather what sort of thing it is, as “capable of walking” and “two-footed.”

One must also examine whether a difference has been placed in the genus as a species. For example, odd has been placed under number, although odd is a difference of number and not a species. Nor does the difference appear to participate in the genus. For everything that participates in a genus is either a species or an individual. But a difference is neither an individual nor a species. It is therefore clear that a difference does not participate in a genus. Consequently odd will not be a species but a difference, since it does not participate in the genus.

Further, one must examine whether the genus has been placed in the species. For example, contiguity has been identified with continuity, mixture with tempering, or—as Plato defined it—locomotion with change of place.

For it is not necessary that contiguity be continuity; rather, the reverse is true: continuity is contiguity. Not everything contiguous is continuous, but whatever is continuous is contiguous.

The same applies in other cases. Not every mixture is a tempering, since a mixture of dry things is not a tempering. Nor is every change of place locomotion, since walking does not appear to be locomotion. “Locomotion” is used chiefly of things that change place involuntarily, as happens with inanimate things.

It is therefore clear that in the examples given the species is predicated of more things than the genus, whereas the opposite should be the case.

Again, one must examine whether a difference has been placed in the species. For example, immortal has been identified with god. It follows that it is predicated either of an equal number of things or of more things than the species. For a difference is always predicated either of an equal number of things or of more things than the species.

Further, one must examine whether the genus has been placed in the difference, as when color is identified with “that which brings together,” or number with odd. One must also examine whether a genus has been stated as a difference. For someone might make such a proposal, taking mixture as the difference of temperance, or change of place as the difference of locomotion.

All such cases must be examined by the same methods. A genus must be predicated of more things than a difference, and it must not participate in the difference. With the proposed identification, neither of these conditions can hold: the genus will be predicated of fewer things, and the genus will participate in the difference.

Again, if none of the differences of the genus is predicated of the proposed species, the genus itself will not be predicated of it. For example, neither odd nor even is predicated of the soul; therefore number is not predicated of the soul either.

Further, one must examine whether the species is prior by nature and destroys the genus simultaneously. This appears to be contrary to the nature of genus and species.

Further, if it is possible to leave behind what has been stated—such as the soul’s being moved, or an opinion’s being true or false—then neither of these will be the genus or the difference. For genus and difference appear to follow the species as long as the species exists.

## CHAPTER THREE. Other topics concerning genus

One must also examine whether what has been placed under the genus participates in something contrary to the genus, or whether it can participate in it. For the same thing will then participate simultaneously in contraries, since it never abandons the genus itself but also participates in what is contrary to it, or can participate in it.

Further, if the species shares something that is wholly impossible for the things under the genus, as when the soul shares life while no number can possibly live, then the soul will not be a species of number.

One must also consider whether the species is equivocal with the genus, using the points stated concerning equivocation. For genus and species are univocal.

Since one must examine all the species of every genus, one should see whether it is impossible for another species to belong to the genus stated. For if this is not possible, it is clear that what has been stated will not be a genus at all.

One must also consider whether something has been stated metaphorically and assigned as a genus. For example, if harmony is proposed as the genus of temperance. A genus is properly predicated of its species, whereas harmony is not properly predicated of temperance but metaphorically, since every harmony belongs to sounds.

Further, if there is something contrary to the species, it must be examined. The examination is conducted in several ways.

First, one must ask whether the contrary of the species is in the same genus, while there is no contrary to the genus. For contraries ought to be in the same genus if nothing is contrary to the genus.

When the genus has a contrary, one must examine whether the contrary of the genus is predicated of the contrary of the species. For this must be so if the genus has a contrary. Each of these points is made evident by induction.

Again, one must examine whether the contrary of the species is not in any genus at all, but the genus itself is contrary. For example, with good: neither good itself nor its contrary will be in a genus, but the genus itself will be contrary, as happens with good and evil. Neither is in a genus; rather, each is itself a genus.

Next, one must consider whether both the genus and the species have a contrary, and whether one pair has an intermediate while the other does not. For if the genera have an intermediate, the species will also have one; and if the species have one, the genera will also have one. This occurs with virtue and vice, and with justice and injustice, since both pairs have an intermediate.

An objection is supplied by health and illness: there is no intermediate between health and illness, whereas there is an intermediate between good and evil.

Further, one must examine whether there is an intermediate for both species and genera, but not in the same way—whether the intermediate for one pair is constituted by negation, while for the other it is a subject. It is plausible that the same should hold in both pairs, as with virtue and vice, and justice and injustice: in both cases the intermediate is constituted by negation.

Further, when there is no contrary to the genus, one must consider not only whether the contrary is in the same genus, but also whether there is an intermediate. For whatever contains the extremes also contains the intermediate, as color is the genus of white, black, and all the intermediate colors.

An objection is supplied by deficiency and excess: both belong to the same genus, namely evil, whereas the mean between them does not belong to evil but to good.

One must also consider whether the genus is contrary to something while the species is contrary to nothing. For if the genus is contrary to something, the species should also be contrary to something, as with virtue and vice, and justice and injustice. The same appears evident in other cases.

An objection is supplied by health and illness. Health as such is contrary to illness as such, whereas some particular illness, although a species of illness, is contrary to nothing—for example, fever and ophthalmia, and each of the other illnesses.

For destruction, then, one must examine the matter in all these ways. If the stated conditions are absent, it is clear that the proposed genus is not the genus.

For construction there are three methods. First, the contrary of the species should be in the proposed genus, while there is no contrary to the genus. For if the contrary is in this genus, it is clear that the proposed species is also in it.

Further, one should examine whether there is an intermediate in the proposed genus, since the genus that contains the intermediate also contains the extremes.

Again, if the genus has a contrary, one must examine whether the contrary of the genus is predicated of the contrary of the species. If it is, it is clear that the proposed species is in the proposed genus.

## CHAPTER FOUR. Other topics concerning genus

Again, in inflected forms and correlatives, one must examine whether they follow one another in the same way, both for destruction and for construction. For they belong or do not belong simultaneously to one thing and to all things. For example, if justice is a kind of knowledge, then acting justly is acting knowingly, and a just person is a knowing person. But if any one of these does not belong, neither does any of the others.

Again, one must examine things that stand in similar relations to one another—for example, whether pleasant relates to pleasure as useful relates to good. Both are productive of their respective correlatives.

If, therefore, pleasure is in some way a good, then something pleasant will be useful. For it will be productive of good, since pleasure is a good.

The same applies to generations and destructions. If building is working, then having built is having worked; and if learning is remembering, then having learned is having remembered; and if being dissolved is being destroyed, then having been dissolved is having been destroyed, and dissolution is a kind of destruction.

The same applies to things that generate and destroy, and likewise to capacities and their uses. In general, one must examine both for destruction and for construction according to every kind of similarity, as was said concerning generation and destruction.

For if what is destructive is dissolving, then being destroyed is being dissolved; and if what generates is productive, then being generated is being made, and generation is making. The same applies to capacities and uses generally: if a capacity is a disposition, then being capable is being disposed; and if the use of something is an activity, then using is acting, and having used is having acted.

If what is opposed to the species is a privation, destruction is possible in two ways.

First, one must ask whether its opposite is in the proposed genus. For a privation is either not in the same genus at all, or not in the final genus. For example, if sight is in the final genus of perception, blindness will not be a perception.

Second, if the privation is opposed both to the genus and to the species, but the opposite is not in the opposite, then the proposed species will not be in the proposed genus.

For destruction one should proceed as stated. For construction there is one method: if the opposite is in the opposite, then the proposed species will be in the proposed genus. For example, if blindness is a kind of insensibility, then sight is a kind of perception.

Again, in negations one must consider the converse, as was said in the case of accidents. For example, if the pleasant is what is good, then what is not good is not pleasant. If the relation does not hold in this way, the converse will follow: what is not good will be pleasant.

But this is impossible if good is the genus of pleasant, since something not good cannot be pleasant. For of things of which the genus is not predicated, none of the species is predicated either.

For construction, one must examine the matter in the same way. If what is not good is not pleasant, then what is pleasant is good; therefore good is the genus of pleasant.

If the species is relative, one must examine whether the genus is also relative. If the species is relative, so is the genus, as with double and multiple, since both are relatives.

But if the genus is relative, the species need not be relative. For learning is relative, but grammar is not.

And perhaps the earlier claim will not appear to be true either: virtue itself is good and virtue itself is honorable, and virtue is relative, whereas good and honorable are not relatives but qualities.

Again, one must examine whether the species is said relative to the same thing both in itself and through its genus. For example, if double is said to be double of a half, then multiple too must be said to be multiple of a half. If not, multiple will not be the genus of double.

Further, if the genus is not said relative to the same thing, neither is it said relative to the same thing in all its genera. For if double is multiple of a half, it will also be more than a half; and, in general, according to all the higher genera, it will be said relative to a half.

An objection is that it is not necessary for a thing to be said relative to the same thing in itself and in its genus. Knowledge is said to be knowledge of what can be known, whereas a state and disposition are not said to be of what can be known but of the soul.

Again, one must examine whether the genus and species are similarly said according to their inflections. For example, if both double and multiple are said to be of something, then the same applies to knowledge, since both knowledge and its genera—state and disposition—are of something.

An objection is that this is not always so. “Different” and “contrary” are said of something, whereas their genus, “diverse,” is not said of something but from something, since diverse means diverse from something.

Again, one must examine whether things said relatively according to their inflections are similarly convertible. For example, both double and multiple are of something, and their correlatives are also expressed by conversion: half and submultiple are likewise of something.

The same applies to knowledge and opinion. Both are of something, and the same is true of what is learned and what is opined. If in some case the conversion is not similar, it is clear that one is not the genus of the other.

Again, one must examine whether the species and genus are not said of equal things. They appear to be said similarly and equally, as in gift and giving. A gift is said to be of someone and to someone, and a giving is said to be of someone and to someone. Giving is the genus of gift, since a gift is an irrecompensable giving.

In some cases, however, the genus and species are not said of equal things. Double is double of something, whereas “exceeding” and “greater” are said both of something and in relation to something. For everything that exceeds or is greater than something exceeds or is greater in relation to something. Therefore these are not genera of double, since they are not said of equal things as the species.

Accordingly, the claim that species and genus are said of equal things is not universally true.

One must also examine whether the contrary of the proposed species has as its genus the contrary of the proposed genus. For example, if multiple is the genus of double, then submultiple ought to be the genus of half, since the genus of the opposite ought to be the opposite.

If, therefore, someone identifies knowledge with perception, then what can be known must be identified with what can be perceived. But this is not so, since not everything knowable is perceptible: some intelligible things are knowable. Therefore the perceptible is not the genus of the knowable; and if this is not the case, neither is perception the genus of knowledge.

Since, among things said relatively, some necessarily exist in or around the things to which they are related—for example, state, disposition, and commensurability, since none of these can exist in anything other than the things to which they are related—whereas others need not exist in the things to which they are related, although they can, as the knowable can exist in the soul, since nothing prevents the soul from possessing knowledge of itself, though this is not necessary, since the same knowable can exist in something else—and still others simply cannot exist in the things to which they are related, as a contrary cannot exist in its contrary, nor knowledge in what is knowable unless what is knowable is a soul or a human being—one must examine whether someone places in the genus something of the first kind in something that is not of that kind.

For example, if someone says that memory is a persistence of knowledge. For every persistence is in the mind and concerns it; therefore the persistence of knowledge is also in knowledge. Memory, then, would be in knowledge, since it is a persistence of knowledge. But this is impossible, since all memory is in the soul.

This topic is also common to accidents. For it makes no difference whether one says that the genus of memory is persistence or that persistence happens to it. If memory is in any way a persistence of knowledge, the same account will apply to it.

## CHAPTER FIVE. Other topics concerning the same matter
Again, if he has posited a state as an activity, or an activity as a state, what is so posited is not a genus. For example, if he says that perception is movement through the body: perception is a state, whereas movement is an activity. Likewise, if he calls memory a state retaining opinion, for no memory is a state, but rather an activity.

Those also go wrong who place a state among the accompanying powers, as with gentleness, self-control with respect to anger, courage, and justice, self-control with respect to fears and gains. [Col. 0949C] For a courageous person and a gentle person are said to be free from disturbance, whereas a self-controlled person is one who is disturbed but is not led by the disturbance. Perhaps, then, such a power follows upon both: if he is disturbed, he is not led by it. Yet “to exercise self-control” does not mean that one person is courageous and another gentle, but altogether that one is not disturbed by such things.

Sometimes they also posit as a genus what follows in some manner—for example, sadness as the genus of anger, and opinion as the genus of belief. Both of these do in some way follow the species assigned. Neither, however, is their genus. For whoever becomes angry becomes sad, sadness having first arisen in him; anger is not the cause of sadness, but sadness is the cause of anger. Therefore anger is not, simply speaking, sadness.

On the same grounds, belief is not opinion either. The same opinion can be held even by one who does not believe. [Col. 0949D] This would not be possible if belief were a species of opinion, since the same thing cannot continue to remain the same if it has been wholly changed from one species into another, just as the same animal cannot at one time be a human being and at another time not be one.

If someone were to say that necessarily whoever opines also has belief, then opinion and belief would be said equally of the same things; hence even so belief would not be a genus, since a genus must be predicated of more things.

One must also examine whether both have a natural capacity to occur in some one thing. For species and genus occur in the same thing—for example, white and color, grammar and knowledge. If, then, he has called shame fear, or anger sadness, species and genus do not occur in the same thing. Shame occurs in the rational part, fear in the spirited part, sadness in the appetitive part—for pleasure also occurs there [Col. 0950A]—whereas anger occurs in the spirited part. Therefore the things assigned are not genera, because they do not naturally occur in the same thing as their species.

The same applies if friendship is placed in the appetitive part: it will not be a kind of willing, since all willing occurs in the rational part.

This place is also useful with respect to an accident and the thing of which it is an accident, since an accident and that to which it belongs occur in the same thing. Therefore, unless they appear in the same thing, it is clear that the one is not an accident of the other.

Again, if a species is said to participate in a genus in some qualified respect, the genus does not appear to be participated in merely in some qualified respect. For a human being is not, in some qualified respect, an animal, nor is grammar, in some qualified respect, knowledge. The same applies in other cases.

One must therefore examine whether a genus is participated in only in some qualified respect—for example, if an animal is called perceptible or visible. [Col. 0950B] For an animal is perceptible or visible in some qualified respect: it is perceptible and visible with respect to the body, but not with respect to the soul. Therefore “visible body” and “perceptible body” will not be genera of animal.

Sometimes they also go unnoticed when they place the whole in a part, as with animal and animate body. For a part is in no way predicated of the whole. Therefore body will not be the genus of animal, since it is a part.

One must examine whether he has placed among powers or among things capable of acting something blameworthy or to be avoided—for example, a sophist, a slanderer, or a thief as someone capable of secretly taking what belongs to others. None of the persons mentioned is called such merely in virtue of being capable of this. [Col. 0950C] God and the virtuous person too can do what is wrong, but they are not thereby such persons; for all wrongdoers are called so with reference to their choice.

Moreover, all powers are powers of things that are choiceworthy. The powers of wrongdoers are choiceworthy, since we say that God and the virtuous person possess them. We call people capable of doing wrong “capable” in this respect. Therefore the genus of nothing blameworthy will be a power.

Otherwise it will follow that something blameworthy is choiceworthy, since there will be a blameworthy power.

The same applies if he has placed among powers, things capable of acting, or productive causes something that is honorable or choiceworthy for its own sake. For every power, and everything capable of acting or productive, is choiceworthy for the sake of something else.

The same applies if he has placed in one genus something that belongs to two or more genera. For some things cannot be placed in only one genus, such as a fraudulent person or a slanderer. The person who chooses but is incapable is neither; nor is the person who is capable but does not choose [Col. 0950D] a slanderer or fraudulent person. Rather, the person who has both characteristics is such. Therefore these things must not be placed in one genus, but in both of the genera mentioned.

Further, sometimes they assign the genus in the place of the difference, and the difference in the place of the genus—for example, astonishment as an excess of admiration, and belief as an intensity of opinion. For neither excess nor intensity appears to be a genus, but a difference. Astonishment appears to be excessive admiration, and belief intense opinion. Therefore admiration and opinion are the genera, whereas excess and intensity are differences.

Further, if someone assigns excess and intensity as genera, inanimate things will produce belief and astonishment. For the intensity and excess of anything belong to the thing of which they are the intensity and excess. If, then, astonishment is an excess of admiration, it will belong to admiration; [Col. 0951A] hence admiration will produce astonishment. Likewise, belief will belong to opinion if it is an intensity of opinion; hence opinion will produce belief.

Further, it will follow for anyone who assigns them in this way that he calls intensity intense and excess excessive. For there is an intense belief; if, then, belief is intensity, intensity will be intense. Likewise, astonishment is excessive; if astonishment is excess, excess will be excessive.

Neither of these, however, appears to be so—just as neither knowledge is knowledgeable nor movement moved.

Sometimes they also go wrong by placing an affection under the genus of that which is affected, as when they say [Col. 0951B] that immortality is everlasting life. Immortality appears to be an affection and an accident of life. That what is said is true will become clear if one admits that someone can become immortal from being mortal. No one says that he takes on another life; rather, some accident or affection comes to the same life. Therefore life is not the genus of immortality.

Again, if he says that the affection of something is its genus—for example, that spirit is moved air—spirit is rather the movement of air. For the same air remains both when it is moving and when it is at rest. Therefore air is not altogether spirit, since spirit exists even when the air is not moving, provided that the same air remains which previously was spirit. The same applies in other cases of this kind.

If, then, in this case too one must admit that moved air is spirit, [Col. 0951C] nevertheless the genus must not be assigned of all such things in which it is not verified, but only of those of which the genus assigned is truly predicated. For in some cases it does not appear to be verified, as with mud and snow. They say that snow is congealed water, and mud earth mixed with moisture; yet snow is not water, nor mud earth. Therefore neither of the genera assigned will be a genus. For a genus must always be verified of all its species.

Likewise, wine is not putrefied water—as Empedocles says, “In the wood the water rotted”—for it is not water in the simple sense.

## CHAPTER VI. Other Topics Concerning Genus

Further, if what has been assigned is not the genus of anything at all, [Col. 0951D] it is clear that it is not the genus of the thing in question either.

This should be considered from the fact that none of the things participating in the genus assigned differ in species—for example, white things do not differ in species from one another. But all species of a genus differ. Therefore white will be the genus of nothing.

Again, if he has called what follows everything a genus or a difference. For several things follow everything, such as being and unity; these belong among the things that follow everything. If, then, we assign being as a genus, it is clear that it will be the genus of everything, since it is predicated of everything. A genus is predicated of no more things than its species; [Col. 0952A] therefore unity too will be a species of being. It follows that of everything of which the genus is predicated, the species will also be predicated, since being and unity are predicated of everything without qualification. But a species must be predicated of fewer things.

If he has called what follows everything a difference, it is evident that the difference will be predicated of an equal number or a greater number of things than the genus. For if the genus too follows everything, the difference will be predicated of an equal number; but if the genus does not follow everything, the difference will be predicated of more things than the genus itself.

Further, if what is called the assigned genus is present in the subject species—for example, white in snow—it is clear that it will not be a genus, since a genus is predicated only of the subject species.

One must also consider whether the genus is not univocal with the species. For the genus is predicated univocally of all its species.

Further, when both the species and the genus have a contrary, if he places the better of the contraries in the worse genus [Col. 0952B], the remaining contrary will consequently be in the remaining genus, since contraries belong to contrary genera. Thus what is worse will be in the better genus, although the genus of the better appears itself to be better.

The same applies if, with the same relation holding equally to both, he places one in the worse genus and not in the better—for example, if he assigns to the soul what is itself agitation, or what is agitated. For the same thing appears equally to be at rest and in motion. Therefore, if rest is better, the thing ought to be placed in the genus of rest.

Further, from the more and the less.

For the person attempting to refute, if the genus admits of more and the species does not—neither the species itself nor what is predicated of it—then the assigned genus will not be a genus. For example, if virtue admits of degrees, but justice and the just person do not—yet one just person is said to be more just than another—then, if the assigned genus admits of more while neither the species [Col. 0952C] nor what is predicated of it does, the assigned genus will not be a genus.

Again, what appears to be more or equally so is not a genus; evidently, therefore, neither is what has been assigned a genus.

This place is especially useful in cases where several things appear to be predicated of a species in answer to “what is it?”, while it is not determined or readily apparent to us which of them is the genus—for example, in the case of anger, sadness, and the opinion that one is being slighted. For an angry person becomes sad and thinks that he is being slighted.

The same consideration applies when one species is compared with something else. For if what appears to be more or equally so is not in the assigned genus, it is clear that neither will the species assigned as a whole be in the genus. [Col. 0952D] This is how one must use the refutational procedure just described.

For the person attempting to establish the claim, however, this place is not useful if what has been assigned as genus, and the species, both admit of more. For nothing prevents two things that both admit of more from not being genus and species—for example, good and white both admit of more, but neither is the genus of the other.

Comparison of genera and species with one another is useful: for example, if this and that are equally genera; if one is a genus, then the other is too. The same applies if one is less and the other more—for example, if power is more the genus of self-control than virtue is, while virtue is also a genus and so is power.

The same may be said of species. If this and that are equally species of the subject, then if one is a species, the other is too; and if what appears less to be a species is one, then [Col. 0953A] what appears more to be one is also a species.

Further, for establishing the claim, one must examine whether the assigned genus is predicated in answer to “what is it?” of the things of which it is assigned as genus, when there is not one species assigned but several differing species. For it is evident that it will be a genus.

If it is present in the assigned species, one must also consider whether the genus is predicated in answer to “what is it?” of other species. For again the same thing will be predicated of several differing things.
