Since in some cases a difference too appears to be predicated of species in answer to “what is it?”, genus and difference must be separated by using the following criteria.

First, genus is predicated of more things than difference. Second, according to the account of what a thing is, it is more appropriate to state the genus than the difference. For someone who says that a human being is an animal [Col. 0953B] indicates what a human being is more fully than someone who says that he is capable of walking.

Further, the difference always signifies a quality of the genus, whereas the genus does not signify a quality of the difference. For someone who says “capable of walking” says that it is a certain kind of animal; but someone who says “animal” does not say that it is a certain kind of walking thing. Thus the difference must be separated from the genus in this way.

Since the musical person, insofar as he is musical, appears to be knowledgeable, and music is a kind of knowledge [Col. 0954A]; and since a person who is walking, insofar as he is walking, is moved, and walking is a kind of movement, one must consider in which genus he wishes to establish something according to the method stated. For example, if he says that knowledge itself is belief, because the knowledgeable person, insofar as he knows, believes, it is clear that knowledge will be a kind of belief. The same applies in other cases of this kind.

Further, since what follows something always does not convert with it, it is difficult to separate what is not a genus when one thing follows another universally, but the latter does not follow the former universally. For example, quiet follows rest, and divisibility follows number, but not conversely: not every divisible thing is a number, nor is every rest quiet.

One must use as a genus the thing that always follows, when the other does not convert with it; but when the other does not extend to all cases, one must comply with this difference.

[Col. 0954B] An objection to this is that non-being follows everything that comes to be—for what comes to be is not—but the converse does not hold, since not everything that is not comes to be. Nevertheless, non-being is not the genus of what comes to be, since non-being simply has no species. Such, then, are the considerations concerning genus.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0953]

## CHAPTER I. The Modes of the Proper Attribute

[Col. 0953B]

Whether what has been stated is a proper attribute or not must be considered by these means.

A proper attribute is assigned [Col. 0953C] either absolutely and always, or in relation to something else, or at some time.

An absolute proper attribute is, for example, the naturally gentle animal as a proper attribute of the human being.

A relational proper attribute is, for example, that of the soul in relation to the body: the soul is naturally suited to rule, whereas the body is naturally suited to obey.

An always-present proper attribute is, for example, the immortal animal as a proper attribute of God.

A temporal proper attribute is, for example, walking in the gymnasium as a proper attribute of some particular person at some particular time.

Of the proper attribute assigned in relation to something else, there are either two problems or four. If something is assigned of one thing and the same thing is denied of the other, only two problems arise, as when being two-footed is assigned as a proper attribute of a human being in relation to a horse. Someone can argue both that a human being is not two-footed and that a horse is two-footed; in either way the proper attribute is removed.

But if both are assigned to each of the two things, and both are denied of each [Col. 0953D], there will be four problems. For example, the proper attribute of a human being in relation to a horse is that the former is two-footed and the latter four-footed. One can argue that a human being is not two-footed and is naturally four-footed; and it is possible to argue that a horse is two-footed and is not four-footed. In whatever way the point is shown, the proposed proper attribute is refuted.

An absolute proper attribute is assigned to all things and separates the subject from everything else, as “an animal capable by nature of receiving instruction” does for a human being.

A relational proper attribute does not separate the subject from everything, but determines it from some specified thing—for example, virtue in relation to knowledge, since virtue comes to be in many things, whereas knowledge comes to be only in the rational part and in things possessing reason.

An always-present proper attribute is verified at every time and is never absent, as “composed of soul and body” is an attribute of an animal. [Col. 0954B]

A temporal proper attribute is verified at some time and does not necessarily follow always, [Col. 0954C] as walking in the marketplace is an attribute of some particular person at a particular time.

To assign a proper attribute in relation to something else is to state a difference, either one that holds in all cases and always, or one that holds for the most part and in the majority of cases.

An attribute that holds in all cases and always is, for example, the two-footedness of a human being in relation to a horse: every human being is always two-footed, whereas no horse is two-footed, ever.

An attribute that holds for the most part and in the majority of cases is, for example, the rational part’s ruling over the appetitive and spirited parts. The rational part rules, while the others obey. Yet the rational part does not always rule, since sometimes it is ruled; nor are the appetitive and spirited parts always ruled, since sometimes they rule, when the soul of a human being is depraved.

The most logical of proper attributes are [Col. 0954D] those that are absolute and always-present, and those that are relational. For a relational proper attribute gives rise to several problems, as we said earlier: necessarily there are either two or four problems.

More arguments arise concerning these. An absolute proper attribute requires arguments concerning many things and examination across many times. The absolute attribute requires arguments concerning many things, since it must be present in each of the things in which the proper attribute ought to inhere; therefore, if it does not separate the subject from everything, it has not been properly assigned.

The always-present attribute requires examination across many times. If it is not present, was not present, or will not be present, it is not a proper attribute.

In the case of a temporal attribute, we examine the particular time now under discussion. [Col. 0955A] There are therefore not many arguments concerning it.

A logical problem is one that gives rise to frequent and sound arguments.

A proper attribute stated in relation to something else must therefore be examined by means of the places concerning accidents: whether it belongs as an accident to this thing but not to that. Those that are always-present and absolute must be considered by the following methods.

## CHAPTER II. The Topics Concerning the Proper Attribute

First, one must consider whether the proper attribute has been assigned well or not. In the case of an assignment that is good or bad, there is one question: whether the proper attribute has been posited by means of things more known or less known.

For the person attempting to refute, it is defective if it has not been posited by means of things more known; for the person attempting to establish it, it is good if it has been posited by means of things more known.

An attribute has not been posited by means of things more known if the proper attribute assigned [Col. 0955B] is altogether less known than the thing of which it is said to be the proper attribute. It will not have been properly posited, since we assign a proper attribute for the sake of knowledge. We formulate both proper attributes and definitions for the sake of learning.

What is more known must therefore be used, since in this way knowledge will be more adequate. For example, someone who posits as the proper attribute of fire that it is most like the soul uses the soul, which is less known than fire. We know more clearly what fire is than what the soul is. Therefore “most like the soul” will not have been properly posited as the proper attribute of fire.

Another case occurs if it is not more known that this attribute belongs to this thing. For it must not merely be more known in itself; it must also be more known that it belongs to this thing. Someone who does not know that it belongs to this thing does not know it even if it belongs more clearly to that thing alone.

Whenever either of these conditions occurs, the proper attribute becomes obscure. For example, someone who posits as the proper attribute of fire that it is the thing in which the soul is naturally present first [Col. 0955C] uses something less known than fire, since it is less known whether the soul is in this thing and whether it is first in this thing. Therefore “the thing in which the soul is naturally present first” will not have been properly posited as the proper attribute of fire.

For the person attempting to establish the claim, if the proper attribute has been posited by means of things more known, and by means of things more known in both ways, it will have been properly posited in this respect. Some constructive topics concerning what is good show only that the assignment is good in this respect, while others show that it is good absolutely. For example, someone who says that perception is the proper attribute of an animal has assigned the attribute by means of things more known and more known in both ways. Therefore “to have perception” will, in this respect, have been properly assigned as the proper attribute of an animal.

Next, for the person attempting to refute, if one of the names [Col. 0955D] occurring in the proper attribute is used in several senses, or if the whole statement signifies several things, the proper attribute will not have been properly posited. For example, “to perceive” signifies several things: one thing is to have a sense, another is to use a sense. Therefore “being naturally capable of perceiving” will not have been properly posited as the proper attribute of an animal.

For this reason one must not use either a name used in several senses or a statement signifying several things, because equivocal language makes what has been said obscure. The person who must argue is left uncertain which of the several meanings is intended, although a proper attribute is assigned for the sake of learning.

Moreover, when someone assigns a proper attribute in this way, it is necessary to produce some refutation whenever someone [Col. 0956A] constructs a syllogism by using the equivocal expression against the opposing side.

For the person attempting to establish the claim, if neither any name nor the whole statement signifies several things, the proper attribute will, in this respect, have been properly posited. For example, neither “body” nor “most mobile toward the upper place,” nor the whole expression composed of these, signifies several things. Therefore “the most mobile body toward the upper place” will, in this respect, have been properly posited as the proper attribute of fire.

Next, for the person attempting to refute, if the thing of which the proper attribute is assigned is itself used in several senses, but it is not determined which of these is intended as the subject of the proper attribute, the proper attribute will not have been properly assigned. The reasons are not obscure from what was said earlier, since the same consequences must follow.

For example, “to know this” signifies several things: to have knowledge of this, to use [Col. 0956B] knowledge of this, to be the knowledge of this, and to use this knowledge. Therefore no proper attribute will have been properly assigned to “knowing this” if it is not determined which of these is intended as the proper attribute.

For the person attempting to establish the claim, if “this,” of which the proper attribute is being assigned, is not used in several senses but is one and simple, the proper attribute will in this respect have been properly posited. For example, since “human being” is said simply, “an animal gentle by nature” will, in this respect, have been properly posited as the proper attribute of a human being.

Next, for the person attempting to refute, if the same thing has been stated repeatedly in the proper attribute—for those who do this often fail to notice it in proper attributes, just as they do in definitions—the proper attribute will not have been properly posited. Repetition confuses the hearer; what is said necessarily becomes obscure, [Col. 0956C] and they appear to be merely repeating themselves.

The same thing is often stated in two ways. First, when someone names the same thing repeatedly—for example, if someone assigns as the proper attribute of fire “the most rarefied body among bodies.” Here “body” has been stated repeatedly.

Second, when someone uses statements in place of names—for example, if someone assigns as the proper attribute of earth “the substance that by nature among bodies is borne most toward the lower place,” and then uses “such substances” in place of “bodies.” For “body” and “such a substance” are one and the same. Thus “substance” has been stated repeatedly, and the proper attribute will not have been properly posited in either case.

For the person attempting to establish the claim, if he does not use the same name repeatedly, the proper attribute will in this respect have been properly assigned. For example, someone who says that the proper attribute of a human being is “an animal [Col. 0956D] capable of receiving instruction” has not repeatedly used the same name. Therefore, in this respect, the proper attribute of a human being will have been properly assigned.

Next, for the person attempting to refute, if he assigns as a proper attribute a name that belongs to everything, the assignment will be useless. For it separates nothing from anything, whereas what is stated in proper attributes ought to separate the subject. Just as in definitions, therefore, the proper attribute will not have been properly posited.

For example, someone who posits as the proper attribute of knowledge “an opinion that cannot be dissuaded by reason,” while using the term “one”—which belongs to everything—has used something of this kind as the proper attribute. Therefore the proper attribute of knowledge will not have been properly posited.

For the person attempting to establish the claim, if he uses nothing common but something that separates the subject from something else, [Col. 0957A] the proper attribute will in this respect have been properly posited. For example, someone who says that the proper attribute of an animal is “to have a soul” uses nothing common. Therefore “to have a soul” will, in this respect, have been properly posited as the proper attribute of an animal.

Next, for the person attempting to refute, if he assigns several proper attributes of the same thing without determining that he is assigning several, the proper attribute will not have been properly posited. For just as in definitions one must not add anything beyond the statement that indicates the substance, so in proper attributes nothing should be assigned in addition to the statement that makes the stated attribute proper.

Such an addition is useless. For example, someone who says that the proper attribute of fire is “the most rarefied and lightest” has assigned several proper attributes, since both are truly predicated of fire alone. Therefore “the most rarefied and lightest body” will not have been properly posited as the proper attribute of fire.

For the person attempting to establish the claim, if he assigns not several proper attributes of the same thing but one, [Col. 0957B] it will in this respect have been properly assigned. For example, someone who says that the proper attribute of the moist is “a body that can be drawn into every shape” assigns one proper attribute, not several. Therefore the proper attribute of the moist will, in this respect, have been properly posited.

Next, for the person attempting to refute, if he uses the thing of which he has assigned the proper attribute, or something belonging to it, the proper attribute will not have been properly posited. A proper attribute is assigned for the sake of learning; but the same thing is similarly unknown to itself, while something that belongs to it is posterior to it. Therefore it is not more known, and no one learns anything more through it.

For example, someone who says that the proper attribute of an animal is “the substance [Col. 0957C] of which a human being is a species” has used something belonging to the animal. Therefore the proper attribute will not have been properly posited.

For the person attempting to establish the claim, if he uses neither the thing itself nor anything belonging to it, the proper attribute will in this respect have been properly posited. For example, someone who posits as the proper attribute of an animal “to be composed of soul and body” has used nothing belonging to the animal. Therefore the proper attribute of an animal will, in this respect, have been properly assigned.

The same consideration must be applied in other cases: one must determine which things do or do not make the subject more known.

For the person attempting to refute, if he uses something opposite, or something naturally simultaneous, or something posterior, the proper attribute will not have been properly posited. An opposite does not make the subject more known; nor does something naturally simultaneous or something posterior.

For example, someone who says that the proper attribute of the good is “that which is most opposed to the bad” [Col. 0957D] has used the opposite of the good. Therefore the proper attribute of the good will certainly not have been properly assigned.

For the person attempting to establish the claim, if he uses neither an opposite, nor something naturally simultaneous in every respect, nor something posterior, the proper attribute will in this respect have been properly assigned. For example, someone who posits as the proper attribute of knowledge “an opinion that most produces belief” uses neither an opposite, nor something naturally simultaneous in every respect, nor something posterior. Therefore the proper attribute of knowledge will, in this respect, have been properly posited.

Next, for the person attempting to refute, if he assigns as a proper attribute not what always follows but what occurs only sometimes, the proper attribute will not have been correctly stated. For neither is the name necessarily verified of the thing in which we find the attribute present, nor is the name necessarily denied of the thing in which we find it absent. Therefore the proper attribute will not have been properly posited.

Moreover, when someone assigns a proper attribute of this kind, it will not be clear whether it is present, since the attribute itself [Col. 0958A] can be absent. Thus someone who posits as the proper attribute of an animal “sometimes to move and sometimes to remain at rest” has assigned a temporal rather than a proper attribute, and the proper attribute will in no way have been properly posited.

For the person attempting to establish the claim, if he assigns as a proper attribute what is necessarily always present, it will in this respect have been properly posited. For example, someone who posits as the proper attribute of virtue “that which makes its possessor virtuous” assigns what always follows. Therefore the proper attribute of virtue will, in this respect, have been properly assigned.

Next, for the person attempting to refute, if he assigns what is now a proper attribute [Col. 0958B] without determining that he is assigning a temporal proper attribute, the proper attribute will not have been properly posited.

First, everything that occurs contrary to custom requires an explicit determination, whereas it is customary for everyone, for the most part, to assign as a proper attribute what always follows.

Second, if he has not made the determination, it is unclear whether he wishes to posit what is now a proper attribute. Therefore no opportunity for reproach should be given.

For example, someone who posits as the proper attribute of a particular person “to sit with another particular person” has posited a present and temporal attribute. He will not have assigned the proper attribute well if he says this without specifying that it is only a present attribute.

For the person attempting to establish the claim, if he assigns a present proper attribute and explicitly determines that it is present, the proper attribute will in this respect have been properly posited. For example, someone who says that the proper attribute of a certain person is “to be walking somewhere now,” and makes the temporal qualification explicit, will have properly posited the proper attribute.

Next, for the person attempting to refute, if he assigns as a proper attribute [Col. 0958C] something whose presence cannot be known except by perception, the proper attribute will not have been properly posited. For everything perceptible, when it is outside perception, is obscure; it is hidden whether it is still present, since it is known only through perception.

This is true of things that do not necessarily follow always. For example, someone who posits as the proper attribute of the sun “the brightest heavenly body carried above the earth” uses as a proper attribute something known by perception—namely, “carried above the earth.” Therefore the proper attribute of the sun will not have been properly assigned. For when the sun has set, it will be obscure whether it is still being carried above the earth, since perception has then left us.

For the person attempting to establish the claim, if he assigns as a proper attribute something that is not evident through perception, or, if it is perceptible, something whose presence is necessarily evident, [Col. 0958D] the proper attribute will in this respect have been properly posited. For example, someone who posits as the proper attribute of a surface “that which is first colored” uses something perceptible—namely, being colored—but something whose presence is always evident. Therefore the proper attribute of a surface will in this respect have been properly assigned.

Next, for the person attempting to refute, if he assigns a definition as a proper attribute, the proper attribute will not have been properly posited. For a proper attribute must not indicate what a thing is.

For example, someone who says that the proper attribute of a human being is “a two-footed animal capable of walking” indicates what a human being is and has assigned a definition as the proper attribute. Therefore this will not have been properly assigned as the proper attribute of a human being.

For the person attempting to establish the claim, if he assigns as a proper attribute something that is predicated reciprocally but does not indicate what a thing is, [Col. 0959A] the proper attribute will in this respect have been properly assigned. For example, someone who posits as the proper attribute of a human being “an animal gentle by nature” assigns something predicated reciprocally, but not something that indicates what a thing is. Therefore the proper attribute of a human being will in this respect have been properly assigned.

Next, for the person attempting to refute, if he assigns a proper attribute without placing something in the answer to “what is it?”, the proper attribute will not have been properly assigned. For in proper attributes, as in definitions, one must first assign the genus and then add and separate the remaining elements.

Therefore a proper attribute not posited in this way will not have been properly assigned. For example, someone who says that the proper attribute of an animal is “to have a soul” [Col. 0959B] has not placed anything in which, or in answer to what, the animal is. Therefore the proper attribute of an animal will not have been properly posited.

For the person attempting to establish the claim, if he places something in the answer to “what is it?” concerning the thing whose proper attribute he is assigning and then adds the remaining elements, the proper attribute will in this respect have been properly assigned. For example, someone who posits as the proper attribute of a human being “an animal capable of receiving instruction” places something in the answer to “what is it?” and then assigns the proper attribute. Therefore the proper attribute of a human being will in this respect have been properly posited.

Whether a proper attribute has been assigned well or not well must therefore be examined by these means.

## CHAPTER III. Other Topics Concerning the Proper Attribute
Whether what has been stated is in every respect a property, or is not a property, must be considered from the following points. For those who construct an account of a property that has been correctly stated, the same topics will be used as for those who establish a property in every respect; they will be discussed in those places.

First, then, one examining a property destructively must consider each thing of which the property has been assigned: whether it belongs to none of them, whether it is not predicated of the thing in question, or whether it is not the property of each of them in accordance with that of which the property was assigned. For what has been posited as a property will not be a property—for example, since “not to be deceived by argument” is not predicated of the geometer (for a geometer is deceived when he constructs a false figure), “not to be deceived by argument” will not be the property of the scientist.

For one constructing the argument, if it is predicated of everything, and of that thing in respect of which it is predicated, it will be a property. For since “an animal capable of receiving instruction” is predicated of every human being, and of a human being as such, “an animal capable of receiving instruction” will be the property of a human being.

This is a topic for destructive examination if the expression is not predicated of everything of which the name and the account are predicated, or if the name is not predicated of everything of which the account is predicated. For the property will not be what has been posited as a property. Thus, since “an animal capable of receiving instruction” is predicated of God, whereas “human being” is not predicated of God, “an animal capable of receiving instruction” will not be the property of a human being.

For constructive examination, the point is whether the name and the account are predicated of the same things, and whether the account and the name are predicated of the same things. The destructive form is to ask whether the account and the name are not predicated of the same things, and whether the name and the account are not predicated of the same things. The constructive form is to ask whether the account and the name are predicated of the same things, and whether the name and the account are predicated of the same things. For what has been posited as a property will be a property: since “to have a soul” is predicated of an animal, and “animal” is predicated of whatever has a soul, “to have a soul” will be the property of an animal.

Next, for destructive examination, if he has assigned as the property of a subject what is said to belong to the subject. For what has been posited as a property will not be a property. Thus, since the person who assigned fire as the property of the most subtle body assigned as a property the subject of the predicate, fire will not be the property of the most subtle body. This is not a subject-property because the same property would then belong to several things different in species. For several things differing in species have certain attributes in common, and, if one assigns a property in this way, what is said of them all would be the property of the subject.

For constructive examination, if he has assigned as the property of the subject what belongs to the subject. What has been posited as not being a property will, in this way, be a property, provided that it is predicated of that subject alone, as was said. Thus, since the person who said that the property of earth is to be a body of the heaviest kind assigned as the property of the subject something that is said of earth alone, and it is predicated as a property, “to be a body of the heaviest kind” will correctly be posited as the property of earth.

Next, for destructive examination, if he has assigned as a property something that belongs by participation. For what belongs by participation contributes to the essence; and such a thing will be a certain differentia predicated of some species. Thus, since the person who said that the property of a human being is “to be a walking biped” assigned the property by participation, “to be a walking biped” will not be the property of a human being.

For constructive examination, if he has not assigned the property by participation, nor as indicating the essence, but has predicated it reciprocally of the thing. What has been posited as a property will be a property. Thus, since the person who posited as the property of an animal “what is naturally capable of perceiving” assigned neither a property by participation nor one indicating the essence, while predicating it reciprocally of the thing, “what is naturally capable of perceiving” will be the property of an animal.

Next, for destructive examination, if the property does not necessarily belong simultaneously with the name itself, but either later or earlier. For what has been posited as a property will not be a property—either never or not always. Since a person may happen to exist before or after walking in the marketplace, rather than at the same time as being a human being, “walking in the marketplace” will not be the property of a human being, either never or not always.

For constructive examination, if it necessarily and always belongs simultaneously, while being neither a definition nor a differentia. What has perhaps been posited as not being a property will be a property. Thus, since “an animal capable of receiving instruction” necessarily and always exists simultaneously with what it is to be a human being, while it is neither a differentia nor a definition, “an animal capable of receiving instruction” will be the property of a human being.

Next, for destructive examination, if the same property does not belong to things that are the same in the respect in which they are the same. For what has been posited as a property will not be a property. Thus, since “to appear good to some people” is not the property of what is to be pursued, neither will it be the property of what is to be chosen; for what is to be pursued and what is to be chosen are the same.

For constructive examination, if it is the property of the same thing in the respect in which it is the same. What has been posited as not being a property will be a property. Thus, since having a three-part soul is the property of a human being insofar as it is called a human being, it will also be the property of an earth-born being insofar as it is earth-born.

This topic is also useful in dealing with accidents, since the same attributes must belong, or not belong, to the same things in the respect in which they are the same.

Next, for destructive examination, if the same property in species does not always belong to things that are the same in species. For what has been stated will not be the property of what has been posited as its property. Thus, since a human being and a horse are the same in species, while “to stand by oneself” is not always the property of a horse, “to move by oneself” will not be the property of a human being. For “to move by oneself” and “to stand by oneself” are the same in species, insofar as each occurs to them as an animal.

For constructive examination, if the same property in species always belongs to things that are the same in species. What has been posited as not being a property will be a property. Thus, since it is the property of a human being to be a walking biped, it will be the property of a bird to be a flying biped. For both of these are the same insofar as the species of the former are under the same genus, being under animal, while the latter are related as the differentiae of the genus animal.

This topic is false when one of the things mentioned belongs to one species alone, whereas the other belongs to several species, as “to be a walking quadruped” does.

Since “same” and “different” are said in many ways, it is difficult for a sophist to assign a property to one thing and to one thing alone. For what belongs to something to which an accident belongs will also belong to the accident taken together with the thing to which it belongs. Thus, what belongs to a human being will also belong to a white human being, if the human being is white; and what belongs to a white human being will also belong to a human being.

Someone might, however, raise a captious objection concerning many properties, arguing that the subject is one thing when considered in itself and another when taken together with an accident. Thus, he might say that being a human being is one thing, and being a white human being another.

Further, he may make a distinction between a state and what is said according to the state. For what belongs to a state will also belong to what is said according to the state, and what belongs to what is said according to the state will also belong to the state. Thus, since “knower” is said of one affected according to knowledge, “not to be persuadable by argument” will not be the property of knowledge, for the knower too will be not persuadable by argument.

For constructive examination, it should be said that the thing to which an accident belongs and the accident taken together with that thing are not simply different, but are called different because their being is different. For being a human being is not the same as being a white human being.

Moreover, in speaking of grammatical cases, one should note that the knower is not *indissuasibile a ratione* but *indissuasibilis a ratione* (“not persuadable by argument”), and knowledge is not *indissuasibile* but *indissuasibilis a ratione*; for one who presses the point without qualification must be opposed without qualification. For anyone who presses the point without qualification must be opposed without qualification.

Next, for destructive examination, if, wishing to assign what belongs by nature, he states it in such a way that the expression signifies what always belongs. For what has been posited as a property will appear capable of being refuted. Thus, since the person who said that the property of a human being is “to be a biped” wishes to assign what belongs by nature, but by his wording signifies what always belongs, “to be a biped” will not be the property of a human being, since not every human being has two feet.

For constructive examination, if he wishes to assign a property that belongs by nature and signifies this by his wording in that way, the property will not be refuted on this account. Thus, since the person who assigned “an animal capable of receiving instruction” as the property of a human being both intends and signifies by his wording that it is a property belonging by nature, the property will not be refuted on the ground that “an animal capable of receiving instruction” is not the property of a human being.

Further, whenever things are said either as being according to some other primary thing or as being primary themselves, it is difficult to assign a property of such things. For if he assigns the property of what is according to something else, it will also be predicated of the primary thing; but if he assigns the property of the primary thing, it will also be predicated of what is according to something else. Thus, if someone assigns “to be colored” as the property of a surface, “to be colored” will also be predicated of a body; and if he assigns it as the property of a body, it will also be predicated of a surface. Hence the name and the account will not be predicated of the same things.

In many properties, some error commonly arises because the person assigning a property does not specify how, or of what kind of thing, he is assigning it. For everyone attempts to assign either what belongs by nature, as “to be a biped” in the case of a human being; or what belongs at present, as “to have four fingers” in the case of a particular human being; or what belongs in species, as “to be most subtle” in the case of fire; or what belongs simply, as “to live” in the case of an animal; or what belongs according to something else, as “to be prudent” in the case of a soul; or what belongs as primary, as “to be prudent” in the case of the rational faculty; or what belongs in that which possesses something, as “not to be persuadable by argument” in the case of a knower—for nothing else will be not persuadable by argument except by possessing something; or what belongs in that which is possessed, as “not to be persuadable by argument” in the case of knowledge; or what belongs in that which is participated in, as “to perceive” in the case of an animal—for something else, such as a human being, also perceives, but it perceives by participating in this; or what belongs in that which participates, as “to live” in the case of some animal.

Accordingly, whoever fails to add “by nature” commits an error, since what belongs by nature may fail to belong to the thing to which it belongs by nature, as “to have two feet” in the case of a human being. Whoever fails to specify that he is assigning what belongs at present assigns something that will not be of the kind that belongs at present, as “to have four fingers” in the case of a human being.

He must also indicate whether he is positing the property as primary or according to something else, since otherwise the name and the account will not be predicated of the same things—for example, whether he assigns “to be colored” as the property of a surface or of a body. He must also state whether he has assigned the property in what possesses something or in what is possessed.

Otherwise what has been assigned will not be a property. For if he assigns it in what is possessed, it will also belong to what possesses it; and if he assigns it in what possesses it, it will also belong to what is possessed. Thus, if “not to be persuadable by argument” is posited as the property of knowledge or of a knower, without also specifying whether it belongs in what possesses or in what is possessed, or in what participates or what is participated in, the property will also belong to certain other things.

For if he assigns it in what is participated in, it will belong to those that participate; but if he assigns it in what participates, it will belong to the things participated in. Thus, if he posits “to live” as the property of some animal, without also distinguishing in species that it belongs to only one of the things subordinate to the subject whose property he assigns, the property will not be properly assigned. For what belongs by way of superiority belongs to only one thing, as “to be lightest” belongs to fire.

Sometimes a person also errs by adding “in species.” For when he adds “in species,” the things mentioned ought to constitute one species; but this does not occur in certain cases, as with fire. For there is not one species of fire: coal, flame, and light differ in species, although each of them is fire.

For this reason, when “in species” is added, it is not necessary that what is stated belong to different species. It may belong more to some and less to others, as “to be most subtle” in the case of fire; for light is subtler than coal and flame.

This need not occur when the qualification is absent, and the name is more strongly predicated of what the account is more strongly verified of. If this is not so, there will not be a thing of which the account is more strongly verified, nor a thing of which the name is more strongly predicated.

Moreover, the same property belongs to what is simple and to what is maximal among things that are simple in this respect, as “to be most subtle” applies to fire. For it will be the same property of fire simply and of light, since light is the most subtle.

When, therefore, someone assigns a property in this way, one should argue against him; but this objection should not be conceded to him. Rather, as soon as he posits the property, it must be determined in what way he is positing it.

## CHAPTER IV. Another Topic Concerning Property

Next, for destructive examination, if he has posited the same thing as the property of the same thing. For the same thing indicates the essence of the same thing; and what indicates the essence is not a property but a definition. Thus, since the person who said that the property of what is honorable is “to be seemly” assigned the same property of the same thing—for the honorable and the seemly are the same—“to be seemly” will not be the property of what is honorable.

For constructive examination, if he has not assigned the same thing as the property, while predicating it reciprocally. What has been posited as not being a property will be a property. Thus, since the person who posited “an ensouled substance” as the property of an animal did not posit the same thing as the property of the same thing, and assigned it as a reciprocal predicate, “an ensouled substance” will be the property of an animal.

Next, one must also consider things composed of similar parts. For destructive examination, if what is the property of the whole is not predicated of the part, or what is the property of the part is not said of the whole. What has been posited as a property will not be a property. This happens in some cases.

Someone may assign a property among things composed of similar parts, sometimes considering the whole and sometimes understanding himself as speaking of what is said according to the part; but neither assignment will be correct. In relation to the whole, for example, since the person who said that “to be a great quantity of salt water” is the property of the sea assigned as the property of something composed of similar parts a feature that is not predicated of the part—for no part of the sea will be a great quantity of salt water—“to be a great quantity of salt water” will not be the property of the sea.

In relation to the part, for example, since the person who posited “to be breathable” as the property of air stated the property of something composed of similar parts, but assigned a feature that is true of some air and is not said of the whole—for not all air will be breathable—“to be breathable” will not be the property of air.

For constructive examination, if what is the property of each of the similar parts as a whole is predicated of each similar part. What has been posited as not being a property will be a property. Thus, since “to move downward by nature” is predicated of all earth, and is also the property of some earth taken as a whole, “to move downward by nature” will be the property of earth, in accordance with what it is to be earth.

Next, one must consider opposites, beginning with contraries. For destructive examination, if the contrary is not the contrary of the property. For the contrary will not be the property of the contrary. Thus, since injustice is contrary to justice, and what is worst is contrary to what is best, while what is best is not the property of justice, what is worst will not be the property of injustice.

For constructive examination, if the contrary of the contrary is a property, the contrary’s contrary will also be a property. Thus, since evil is contrary to good, and what is to be avoided is contrary to what is to be chosen, while what is to be chosen is the property of the good, what is to be avoided will be the property of the evil.

Second, among relatives, for destructive examination, if what is relative is not the property of what is relative. For what is relative will not be the property of what is relative. Thus, since “double” is said in relation to “half,” and “surpassing” in relation to “surpassed,” while “surpassing” is not the property of “double,” “surpassed” will not be the property of “half.”

For constructive examination, if what is relative is the property of what is relative, then the corresponding relative will be the property of the corresponding relative. Thus, since “double” is said in relation to “half” as two is to one, and “two to one” is the property of double, “one to two” will be the property of half.

Third, among states and privations, for destructive examination, if what is said according to a state is not the property of the state, then what is said according to the privation will not be the property of the privation either; and if what is said according to the privation is not the property of the privation, neither will what is said according to the state be the property of the state. Thus, since “to be insensible” is not said to be the property of deafness, neither will “to perceive” be the property of hearing.

For constructive examination, if what is said according to a state is the property of the state, then what is said according to the privation will be the property of the privation; and if what is said according to the privation is the property of the privation, then what is said according to the state will be the property of the state. Thus, since seeing is the property of sight, in accordance with the fact that we possess sight, not seeing will be the property of blindness, in accordance with the fact that we do not possess sight though we were born to possess it.

Next, among affirmations and negations, first, among the predicates themselves: this topic is useful only for destructive examination. If an affirmation, or what is said according to an affirmation, is the property of something, its negation, or what is said according to a negation, will certainly not be its property; and if a negation, or what is said according to a negation, is its property, the affirmation, or what is said according to an affirmation, will not be its property. Thus, since “to be animate” is the property of an animal, “not to be animate” will not be the property of an animal.

Second, among predicates and non-predicates, and among the things of which they are predicated or not predicated: for destructive examination, if the affirmation of an affirmation is not a property, neither will the negation of a negation be a property; and if the negation of a negation is not a property, neither will the affirmation of an affirmation be a property. Thus, since “animal” is not the property of a human being, “not-animal” will not be the property of a non-human being; and if “not-animal” does not appear to be the property of a non-human being, “animal” will not be the property of a human being.

For constructive examination, if the affirmation of an affirmation is a property, the negation of a negation will also be a property; and if the negation of a negation is a property, the affirmation of an affirmation will also be a property. Thus, since “not to live” is the property of a non-animal, “to live” will be the property of an animal; and if “to live” appears to be the property of an animal, “not to live” will also appear to be the property of a non-animal.

Third, among the subjects themselves: for destructive examination, if the property assigned is the property of an affirmation, it will not also be the property of a negation; and if the assigned property is the property of a negation, it will not be the property of an affirmation. Thus, since “to be animate” is the property of an animal, “to be animate” will not be the property of a non-animal.

For constructive examination, if the assigned property is not the property of an affirmation, it will be the property of a negation. But this topic fails, since the affirmation of a negation and the negation of an affirmation are not properties. For an affirmation does not belong to a negation at all, while a negation does belong to an affirmation, but does not belong to it as a property.

Next, among things divided into opposites: for destructive examination, if none of the things divided into opposites is the property of any of the remaining things divided into opposites, what has been posited will not be the property of the thing whose property it has been posited to be. Thus, since “sensible animal” is not the property of any of the other mortal animals, “intelligible animal” will not be the property of God.

For constructive examination, if any one of the remaining things divided into opposites is the property of any one of the things divided into opposites, the remaining one will be the property of the thing whose property was posited as not being a property. Thus, since it is the property of prudence to be naturally the virtue of the rational faculty in itself, and the same holds for each of the other virtues taken individually, it will be the property of temperance to be naturally the virtue of the appetitive faculty in itself.

Next, among grammatical cases, for destructive examination, if one case is not the property of another case, the corresponding case will not be the property of the corresponding case. Thus, since “well” is not the property of “justly,” “the good” will not be the property of the just person.

For constructive examination, if one case is the property of another case, the corresponding case will also be the property of the corresponding case. Thus, since “to be a walking biped” is the property of a human being, it will be the property of a human being to be called a walking biped.

The examination must not be restricted to the cases mentioned, but must also be applied to opposites, as was said in the preceding topics. For destructive examination, if the opposite case is not the property of the opposite case, the opposite case will not be the property of the opposite case. Thus, since “well” is not the property of “justly,” “badly” will not be the property of “unjustly.”

For constructive examination, if the opposite case is the property of the opposite case, the opposite case will also be the property of the opposite case. Thus, since “what is best” is the property of what is honorable, “what is worst” will be the property of what is dishonorable.

Next, among things that stand in a similar relation, for destructive examination, if what stands in a similar relation is not the property of what stands in a similar relation, neither will it be the property of the other thing that stands in a similar relation. Thus, since a builder stands in a similar relation to constructing a building as a physician does to producing health, while producing health is not the property of a physician, constructing a building will not be the property of a builder.

For constructive examination, if what stands in a similar relation is the property of what stands in a similar relation, it will also be the property of the other thing that stands in a similar relation. Thus, since a physician stands in a similar relation to being productive of health as a schoolteacher does to being productive of good condition, while being productive of good condition is the property of a schoolteacher, being productive of health will also be the property of a physician.

Next, among things related in this way, for destructive examination, if what is related in this way is not the property of what is related in this way, it will not be the property of the thing whose property it has been posited to be. Thus, since prudence stands in this relation to the honorable and the shameful, insofar as knowledge belongs to both of them, while “to be knowledge of the honorable” is not the property of prudence, “to be knowledge of the shameful” will not be the property of prudence. If “to be knowledge of the honorable” is the property of prudence, “to be knowledge of the shameful” will not be the property of the same thing, since it is impossible for one thing to have several properties.

For constructive examination, this topic is of no use, since what is related in this way is compared with several things.

Next, for destructive examination, if what is said according to being is not the property of what is said according to being, neither “to be corrupted” will be the property of what is said according to being corrupted, nor “to be generated” the property of what is said according to being generated. Thus, since it is the property of a human being to be an animal, “to be generated as an animal” will not be the property of “to become a human being,” nor will “to be corrupted as an animal” be the property of “to cease to be a human being.”

The same procedure must be applied from generation to being and corruption, and from corruption to being and generation, just as it has now been applied from being to generation and corruption.

For constructive examination, if what is ordered according to being is properly ordered, it will be a property. For what is said according to generation will also have as its property what is said according to generation, and what is said according to corruption will have as its property what is assigned according to corruption. Thus, since it is the property of a human being to be mortal, “to be generated as mortal” will be the property of “to become a human being,” and “to be corrupted as mortal” will be the property of “to cease to be a human being.”

The same procedure must be applied from generation and corruption to being, and to the processes arising from each of them, just as was said in the destructive form.

Next, one must consider the same subject. For destructive examination, if the property does not belong to the Form, or does not belong to it in the respect in which the property of the thing is assigned. For what has been posited as a property will not be a property. Thus, since rest does not belong to the man himself insofar as he is a human being, but belongs to him insofar as he is a Form, “to rest” will not be the property of a human being.

For constructive examination, if the property belongs to the Form, and belongs in that respect in which it is said of the very thing whose property was posited as not being a property. What has been posited as not belonging will be a property. Thus, since being composed of soul and body belongs to the animal itself, and belongs to it insofar as it is an animal, “to be composed of body and soul” will be the property of an animal.

## CHAPTER V. Another Topic Concerning Property

Next, among greater and lesser degrees: first, for destructive examination, if what is greater is not the property of what is greater. For what is lesser will not be the property of what is lesser, nor what is least of what is least, nor what is greatest of what is greatest, nor what is simply so of what is simply so. Thus, since “to be more colored” is not the property of a body that is more colored, neither will “to be less colored” be the property of a body that is less colored, nor will “to be colored” be the property of a body without qualification.

For constructive examination, if what is greater is the property of what is greater, what is lesser will be the property of what is lesser, what is least of what is least, what is greatest of what is greatest, and what is simply so of what is simply so. Thus, since “to perceive more” is the property of what lives more, “to perceive less” will be the property of what lives less; likewise, what belongs most to what is most, what belongs least to what is least, and what belongs simply to what is simply.

The same considerations apply from what is simple to the corresponding cases. For destructive examination, if what is simple is not a property, neither will what is greater be the property of what is greater, nor what is lesser of what is lesser, nor what is greatest of what is greatest, nor what is least of what is least. Thus, since being diligent is not the property of a human being, being more diligent will not be the property of a human being to a greater degree.

For constructive examination, if what is simple is the property of what is simple, then what is greater will be the property of what is greater, what is lesser of what is lesser, what is least of what is least, and what is greatest of what is greatest. Thus, since it is the property of fire to be carried upward by nature, it will be even more the property of more fiery fire to be carried upward by nature. The same considerations apply to the other cases of this kind.

Second, for destructive examination, if what is greater is not the property of what is greater, what is lesser will not be the property of what is lesser. Thus, since perceiving is more properly the property of an animal than knowing is the property of a human being, and perceiving is not the property of an animal, knowing will not be the property of a human being.

For constructive examination, if what is lesser is the property of what is lesser, what is greater will also be the property of what is greater. Thus, since being naturally gentle is less properly the property of a human being than living is the property of an animal, and being naturally gentle is the property of a human being, living will be the property of an animal.

Third, for destructive examination, if what is more properly the property of one thing is not its property, what is less properly its property will not be its property either. Conversely, if the former is its property, the latter will not be its property. Thus, since being colored is more properly the property of a surface than of a body, if it is not the property of a surface, it will not be the property of a body; and if it is the property of a surface, it will not be the property of a body.

This topic is of no use for constructive examination, since it is impossible for the same thing to be the property of several things.

Fourth, for destructive examination, if what is more properly the property of something is not its property, what is less properly its property will certainly not be its property either. Thus, since being a sensible animal is more properly the property of an animal than being divisible is, and being a sensible animal is not the property of an animal, being divisible will not be the property of an animal.

For constructive examination, if what is less properly the property of something is its property, what is more properly its property will also be its property. Thus, since perceiving is less properly the property of an animal than living is, and perceiving is the property of an animal, living will be the property of an animal.

Next, among things that belong in a similar way: first, for destructive examination, if what is similarly a property is not the property of that whose property it is similarly said to be, what is similarly a property will not be the property of that whose property it is similarly said to be. Thus, since desiring is similarly the property of the appetitive faculty as reasoning is the property of the rational faculty, and desiring is not the property of the appetitive faculty, reasoning will not be the property of the rational faculty.

For constructive examination, if what is similarly a property is the property of that whose property it is similarly said to be, what is similarly a property will be the property of that whose property it is similarly said to be. Thus, since “to be prudent” is similarly the primary property of the rational faculty, and “to be temperate” the primary property of the appetitive faculty, while “to be prudent” is the primary property of the rational faculty, “to be temperate” will be the primary property of the appetitive faculty.

Second, for destructive examination, if what is similarly a property is not the property of something, what is similarly a property will not be its property. Thus, since seeing and hearing are similarly properties of a human being, if seeing is not the property of a human being, hearing will not be the property of a human being.

For constructive examination, if what is similarly a property is its property, what is similarly a property will be its property. Thus, since it is similarly the property of the soul that one of its parts is primarily appetitive and that one of its parts is primarily rational, and since it is the property of the soul that one of its parts is primarily appetitive, it will also be the property of the soul that one of its parts is primarily rational.

Third, for destructive examination, if what is similarly the property of one thing is not its property, it will not be the property of the other thing either; and if it is the property of the former, it will not be the property of the latter. Thus, since burning is similarly the property of flame and coal, if burning is not the property of flame, it will not be the property of coal; and if it is the property of flame, it will not be the property of coal.

This topic is of no use for constructive examination. The topic drawn from things that stand in a similar relation differs from that drawn from things that belong similarly, because the former is taken according to proportion, not by comparing something that belongs to a thing, whereas the latter is drawn from something that belongs and is compared with another thing.

Next, for destructive examination, if, while assigning a property potentially, he does not assign it potentially in relation to what exists, although the potentiality cannot belong to it when the relevant thing does not exist. For what has been posited as a property will not be a property. Thus, since the person who said that “to be breathable” is the property of air assigned the property potentially—for something is breathable if it can be breathed—but assigned it also in relation to non-being, since when there is no animal that is naturally capable of breathing air, air may exist, although when there is no animal it is not possible to breathe, “to be breathable” will not be the property of air at that time. For there will be no animal of the kind capable of breathing; therefore “to be breathable” will not be the property of air.

For constructive examination, if, assigning a property in potentiality, he assigns it both to what exists and to what does not exist, although potentiality may belong to what does not exist. What has been posited as not being a property will be a property. Thus, since the person who assigned “to be capable of undergoing or producing something” as the property of what exists, assigning the property in potentiality, assigned it to what exists—for when it exists, it will be capable of undergoing or producing something—“to be capable of undergoing or producing something” will be the property of what exists.

Next, for destructive examination, if he has posited the property by way of superlative excess. For what has been posited as a property will not be a property. In such assignments the account and the name will not be verified of the same thing; for when the thing has been destroyed, the account will remain no less true, since the superlative attribute belongs to some existing thing. Thus, if someone assigns “the lightest body” as the property of fire, then, when fire has been destroyed, one of the bodies will still be the lightest. Therefore “the lightest body” will not be the property of fire.

For constructive examination, if he has not posited the property by way of superlative excess, it will, in this respect, have been correctly posited as a property. Thus, since the person who posited “an animal naturally gentle” as the property of a human being did not assign the property by way of superlative excess, it will, in this respect, have been correctly posited as a property.

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 0969]

## CHAPTER ONE. Topics Concerning Definition
The parts of the treatment concerning the terms of the argument are five. For either it is not at all true to say of the thing of which the name and account are predicated—for the definition of “human being” must be true of every human being—or, although it is a genus, it has not been placed in its genus, or has not been placed in the appropriate genus—for the person defining must add the differences after placing it in a genus, since the genus appears above all to signify the substance of the thing defined—or the definition is not proper—for a definition must be proper, as was said earlier—or, if the person who made the definition has done all the things mentioned, he has nevertheless not defined, nor stated what it is to be the thing defined. The remaining possibility is that, although he has defined it, he has not defined it well. [Col. 0969C]

If the name and account are not truly predicated of the thing, one must examine the matter by means of the places concerning accidents that have been stated. For there too the whole inquiry concerns whether something is true or not true: when we argue that an accident belongs to something, we state what is true; when we argue that it does not belong to it, we state what is not true. But if the account has not been placed in the appropriate genus, or if it has not been assigned as a proper account, one must investigate by means of the places stated concerning genus and what is proper. [Col. 0969D]

The remaining case—if the thing has not been defined, or has not been well defined—must be attacked in some way by argument. First, then, one must discover whether it has not been well defined. For it is easier to do anything at all than to do it well; clearly, therefore, the error is somewhat greater in this respect, since doing something well is more laborious. Hence the argument concerning this point is easier than the argument concerning the other.

There are two parts to what is not well done. One is the use of an obscure account. For the person defining must use, as far as possible, the clearest account, since a definition is assigned for the sake of knowledge. [Col. 0970B] The second is saying more in the definition than is appropriate, for everything added beyond what is necessary in a definition is superfluous. [Col. 0970C]

## CHAPTER II. Another place concerning definition

Again, each of the two matters just mentioned is divided into several parts. One place concerning obscurity is this: if what has been said is equivocal. For example, “generation is a leading into substance,” and “health is a commensuration of hot and cold.” “Leading” and “commensuration” are equivocal; it is therefore unclear which of the things signified by the terms used in several senses the speaker intends. [Col. 0970D]

Likewise, if the thing defined is itself said in several senses and the person dividing has not specified the sense, it is unclear to which of the definitions he has assigned the account. Consequently, it is possible to criticize the account as not applying appropriately to everything whose definition he has assigned. This is especially likely when the equivocation is concealed.

It is also possible to criticize the person defining whenever the expression assigned in the definition is used in several ways. For if it has not been stated sufficiently in any of the possible senses, it is clear that he has not defined it in that sense.

Another place is when the definition is stated metaphorically—for example, “knowledge is undivided,” “the earth is a nurse,” or “temperance is concord.” Everything obscure that is expressed metaphorically can be criticized as not being stated properly, since the definition will not fit what is said. Thus, in the case of temperance, every concord belongs to sounds. Moreover, if concord is the genus of temperance, the same thing will belong to two genera that do not contain one another; for neither concord contains virtue, nor virtue concord. [Col. 0971A]

Further, obscurity arises when unfamiliar names are used—for example, when Plato calls the eye “ciliumbre” [a corrupt or uncertain term], the spider “putrimordax” (“rotting-biter”), or the marrow “ossigenium” (“bone-born”). Everything unfamiliar is obscure.

Some expressions are stated neither by equivocation nor metaphor nor properly—for example, “law is the measure or image of things that are just by nature.” Such expressions are worse than metaphors. Metaphor makes what is signified in some way known through resemblance; everyone who uses a metaphor uses it on the basis of some resemblance. But an expression of this kind does not make the matter known, since there is neither a resemblance according to which law is a measure or image, nor is the expression ordinarily used in its proper sense. [Col. 0971B]

Therefore, if he says properly that law is a measure or image, he is speaking falsely. An image is something whose generation occurs through imitation, and this is not found in law. If he does not speak properly, it is clear that he has spoken obscurely, and more defectively than in any of the expressions stated metaphorically.

Further, one must consider whether the account of the contrary is not made clear by what has been said. For things that are properly assigned make their contraries clear as well.

Or, if the expression is stated in itself, one must consider whether it is unclear whose definition it is. This is like the expressions in ancient writings: unless someone had written a heading above them, it would not be known what each one referred to. If the definition is not clear, it must be examined by means of such considerations.

If he has said something superfluous in the definition, one must first consider whether he has used something that belongs to everything—either to all things without qualification or to all the things subordinate to the same genus as the things defined. For what is necessary must not be called superfluous. [Col. 0971C] The genus must separate the thing from other things, and the difference must separate it from some of the things within the same genus. But what belongs to everything without qualification separates nothing, while what belongs to everything within the same genus does not separate the thing from the others in that genus. Such an addition is therefore superfluous.

Or one must consider whether what has been added is indeed proper, but whether, once it is removed, the rest of the definition is still proper and signifies the substance. For example, in the account of “human being,” “capable of acquiring knowledge” is added superfluously; when it is removed, the remainder is still proper and signifies the substance. In general, anything is superfluous if, once it is removed, what remains makes the thing defined clear. [Col. 0971D]

The same applies to the definition of soul, if soul is defined as “a number moving itself.” For “that which moves itself” is soul, as Plato defined it. Is what is said proper, but, when “number” is removed, does it fail to signify the substance? Whichever way the matter stands, it is difficult to explain it fully.

In all such cases, therefore, one must use the argument according to what is useful. Consider the definition of phlegm: “the first undigested moisture from food.” There is only one first moisture, not several; therefore “undigested” is added superfluously, since, when it is removed, the remainder will be a proper definition. It is impossible for there to be another first moisture from food. [Col. 0972A]

But perhaps phlegm is not simply “the first moisture from food,” but “the first moisture from undigested food.” In that case “undigested” must be added, for if the definition were stated in the former way, it would not be true, since the first moisture is not necessarily the first moisture from all food.

Further, one must consider whether something stated in the account does not belong to all the things within the same species. Such a person has defined worse than one who uses something that belongs to everything. In the former case, if the remainder is a proper definition, the whole account will also be proper, since the addition of anything true to what is proper makes the whole account proper. But if one of the things stated in the account does not belong to all the things within the same species, it is impossible for the whole account to be proper. It will not be predicated reciprocally of the thing.

For example, “a walking, two-footed, four-cubit animal” is not predicated reciprocally of the thing, because “four-cubits-tall” does not belong to all the things within the same species. [Col. 0972B]

Again, one must consider whether the same thing has been stated repeatedly. For example, someone who defines desire as “an appetite for pleasure”: every desire is an appetite for pleasure, so “the appetite of desire” will also be “of pleasure.” The definition of desire thus becomes “an appetite for pleasure of pleasure.” For there is no difference between saying “desire” and “an appetite for pleasure”; hence both expressions will be “of pleasure.”

But perhaps this is not absurd. A human being is also two-footed; therefore “two-footed” will be identical with “human being.” Yet “human being” is “a walking, two-footed animal,” and so “a walking, two-footed animal” will be two-footed. Still, this does not make anything absurd. “Two-footed” is not predicated twice of the walking animal; it is predicated twice only if “a walking, two-footed animal” is said of a two-footed animal. Thus “two-footed” is predicated only once. [Col. 0972C]

The same applies to desire. “Being of pleasure” is not predicated of the appetite, but of the whole expression; hence here too the predication occurs only once.

It is not absurd to say the same name twice, but it is absurd to predicate the same thing repeatedly of something. Thus Xenocrates says that prudence is “definitive and contemplative of beings.” Since the definitive is a kind of contemplative, he says the same thing twice by adding “contemplative” again.

Likewise, those who say that refrigeration is “a privation of the heat that is according to nature” add “according to nature” superfluously, since every privation is a privation of what is according to nature. It is perhaps sufficient to say “a privation of heat,” since “privation” itself makes it clear that it is a privation of what is according to nature. [Col. 0972D]

Again, one must consider whether a particular has been added after a universal expression. For example, if clemency is defined as “a diminution of what is expedient and just,” since what is just is something expedient, it is included under what is expedient. “Just” is therefore superfluous: after stating the universal, he has added the particular.

Likewise, if medicine is defined as “the science of things productive of health in animals and human beings,” or law as “the image of things good and just by nature,” since what is just is something good, the same thing has again been stated repeatedly.

Whether a definition is well or badly made must therefore be examined by these and similar considerations.

## CHAPTER III. Another place concerning definition

Whether a person has defined and stated what it is to be the thing, or has not done so, must be examined by the following considerations. [Col. 0973A]

First, one must ask whether he has constructed the definition through things prior and better known. A definition is assigned for the sake of knowing what is said; but we do not know through just anything, but through what is prior and better known, as is the case in demonstrations—for all teaching and all learning proceed in this way. Clearly, then, whoever has not defined through such things has not defined.

If he had defined, there would be several definitions of the same thing. For it is clear that the person who defines through what is prior and better known has defined better; thus both would be definitions of the same thing. But this does not seem possible, since for each thing that exists there is one being, namely what it is to be that thing. If there were several definitions of the same thing, then the being of the thing would be the same as what is signified according to both definitions. But these are not the same, since the definitions are different. Clearly, therefore, whoever has not defined through what is prior and better known has not defined. [Col. 0973B]

To say that a definition is made through what is not better known can be understood in two ways. It may be made simply through what is less known, or through what is less known to us; either is possible.

What is prior is simply better known than what is posterior—for example, a point than a line, a line than a surface, and a surface than a solid; similarly, unity is prior to number, since it is the principle of every number, and an element is prior to a syllable.

For us, however, the contrary sometimes occurs. A solid is more perceptible to the senses than a surface, a surface more than a line, and a line more than a point. Hence the majority know such things more readily: the former can be grasped in any manner, whereas the latter must be comprehended by a more subtle and penetrating intellect. [Col. 0973C]

Simply speaking, therefore, it is better to try to know posterior things through prior things, since this is more scientific. But for those who are incapable of knowing through such means, it may perhaps be necessary to construct the account through things known to them. Such are the definitions of a point, a line, and a surface: all of them make the prior known through the posterior. A point is said to be the limit of a line, a line the limit of a surface, and a surface the limit of a solid.

It must not be overlooked, however, that those who define in this way cannot indicate what it is to be the thing defined unless what is better known to us also happens to be what is simply better known. For the person who defines well must define through genus and differences; and these are simply prior and better known than the species. The genus and the difference destroy the species, and thus are prior to it. [Col. 0973D]

They are also better known. Once the species is known, it is necessary to know the genus and its differences: whoever knows a human being also knows that it is a walking animal. But once the genus and difference are known, it is not necessary that the species be known. The species is therefore less known.

Further, if those who say that definitions are truly constructed from what is known to each person are correct, it follows that there will be several definitions of the same thing. What is better known to one person is not necessarily better known to another, and what is better known to one is not necessarily better known to everyone. Thus a definition would have to be assigned to each individual, if a definition must be made from what is better known to each person.

Moreover, for the same person, some things are at one time more known and at another time less known. At first, sensible things are more known; but after one has become more educated, the contrary is the case.
