Therefore, even for the same person, the same definition could not always be assigned if one admits that definitions are to be made through what is better known to each individual. [Col. 0974A]

Clearly, then, a definition must not be made through things of this kind, but through what is simply better known; only in this way will one and the same definition always be produced.

Perhaps what is simply known is not what is known by everyone, but what is known by those whose intellect is properly disposed—just as what is simply healthy is what is healthy for those whose bodies are in good condition. Each such matter must therefore be investigated carefully, while disputants should use the point according to what is useful.

It is especially possible to refute a definition decisively if it is possible to construct it neither from what is simply better known nor from what is better known to us. [Col. 0974B]

One place concerning what is not defined through better-known things is this: the definition indicates prior things through posterior ones, as we said earlier.

Another is this: if the account has been assigned to us by means of what is indefinite and in motion, although the thing defined is at rest and definite. What remains and what is definite are prior and better known than what is indefinite and in motion.

There are three places concerning the failure to define through prior things.

First, if one thing is defined through its contrary—for example, if good is defined through evil. Contraries are naturally known together, and some people even think that the same science concerns both. Hence one is not better known than the other.

It must not be overlooked that some things perhaps cannot be defined otherwise—for example, the double cannot be defined without the half, nor anything else that is essentially relative. In all such cases, being is identical with being related in a certain way. It is therefore impossible to know one without the other, since the other must necessarily be included in its account. [Col. 0974C]

All such things must therefore be understood, but they should be used in arguments according to what appears useful.

Another place is when the definition uses the thing defined itself. This can remain hidden when a different name from the name of the thing defined is used. For example, if the sun is defined as “a star appearing by day,” the person who uses “day” is using “sun,” since day is the sun’s passage above the earth.

To detect such cases, one should substitute an account for the name—for example, define day as “the sun’s passage above the earth.” It will then be clear that whoever says “the sun’s passage above the earth” has said “sun.” Thus anyone who uses “day” is using “sun.” [Col. 0974D]

Again, one thing may be defined by means of a thing divided from it in the same division. For example, “odd” is defined as “a number greater than an even number.” But odd and even are divided from the same genus, since both are differences of number.

Likewise, one must consider whether higher things have been defined through lower things. For example, an even number is defined as “a number divisible into two equal parts,” or a good disposition as “a virtue.” “Divisible into two equal parts” is derived from two things that are even, and virtue is a kind of good; hence these definitions use lower things.

The person who uses lower things must also use the things above them. Whoever uses virtue uses good, since virtue is a kind of good; similarly, whoever uses “divisible into two equal parts” uses “even,” since being divisible into two means being divisible into two equal parts. [Col. 0975A]

In general, then, one place is the failure to construct the account through prior and better-known things. Its parts are the considerations just stated.

A second place is this: the thing, though it exists, is not placed in a genus. This is an error in all cases in which what the thing is is not first stated in the account—for example, in the definition of body as “that which has three dimensions,” or in the definition of a human being as “that which knows how to count.” In neither case has it been said what it is to have three dimensions or what it is to know how to count.

The genus is intended to signify what the thing is, and it is placed first among the things stated in the definition.

Further, if the thing defined is said of several things, but the definition has not been assigned to all of them—for example, if grammar is defined as “the science of writing what is spoken.” It also requires the science of reading; the person who defines it as the science of writing assigns it no more to writing than to reading. [Col. 0975B]

Therefore, it is not another definition, but the person who includes both writing and reading, since there cannot be several definitions of the same thing. This is genuinely true in some cases, as has been said, but not in others—for example, wherever the thing is not essentially said of both.

Thus medicine is the science of producing health and disease. Health is predicated essentially of medicine, but disease only accidentally; producing disease is simply foreign to medicine. Therefore, the person who assigns the definition to both does not define it any more than the person who assigns it to one; indeed, he may define it worse, since anyone else could also produce disease.

Further, if, where the thing defined is related to several things, the definition has been assigned not to the better one but to the worse one. Every science and power appears to concern what is best.

Again, if what has been said has not been placed in its proper genus, the matter must be examined by the elements concerning genera, as was stated earlier.

Again, one must consider whether the definition leaps over genera. For example, someone defines justice as “a productive or distributive disposition of equality.” Whoever defines it in this way skips over virtue. By leaving out the genus of justice, he does not state what it is to be justice, since each thing’s substance is found in its genus.

This is the same as failing to place the thing in its proximate genus. Whoever places it in the proximate genus has stated all the higher genera, since all higher genera are predicated of lower things. Therefore, the thing must either be placed in its proximate genus, or all the differences by which the proximate genus is defined must be added to the higher genus. In this way nothing will be omitted, but the lower genus will be stated in the account in place of its name. [Col. 0975C]

The person who states only the higher genus does not state the lower genus: whoever says “plant” does not thereby say “tree.”

The same considerations apply to differences. One must ask whether the differences stated are differences of the genus. If the thing has not been defined through the specific differences of the thing, or if something has been stated that cannot be the difference of anything at all—such as “animal” or “substance”—it is clear that no definition has been given, since the things stated are the differences of nothing.

One must also see whether there is something divided from the stated difference in the same division. If there is not, it is clear that the stated difference will not be a difference of the genus, since every genus is divided by differences that are divided from one another in the same way—for example, animal is divided into walking, flying, aquatic, and two-footed. [Col. 0976A]

Or, if there is a difference divided from it in the same way, one must ask whether it is truly predicated of the genus. If it is not, it is clear that neither will be a difference of the genus, since all differences divided from one another in the same way are truly predicated of their proper genus.

Likewise, even if it is truly predicated of the genus, one must ask whether it makes the thing added to the genus a species. It is clear that the stated difference will not be a specific difference of the genus, since every specific difference together with the genus makes a species. If this is not a difference, neither will the other be one, since it is divided from this one in the same way.

Further, one must consider whether the genus has been divided by a negation—for example, when a line is defined as “a length without breadth.” “Without breadth” signifies nothing other than “which does not have breadth.” It will therefore follow that the genus participates in the species.

For every length either is without breadth or has breadth, since of everything either an affirmation or a negation is true. Thus the genus of line, since it is length, will either be without breadth or have breadth. But “length without breadth” is the account of one species, and likewise “length having breadth” is the account of another, since “without breadth” and “having breadth” are differences. The account of the species is composed of the difference and the genus; therefore the genus will receive the account of the species. [Col. 0976B]

The same applies to the differences, since one of the differences stated must necessarily be predicated of the genus.

This place is useful against those who posit that Forms exist. For if there is no Form of length itself, then in some way “having breadth” or “without breadth” will be predicated of the genus, since one or the other must be truly predicated of every length if it is to be predicated of the genus. But this does not happen: there are both lengths without breadth and lengths with breadth. Hence this place is useful only against those who say that the genus is numerically one—namely, those who posit Forms. They call length itself and animal itself genera.

Perhaps, however, in some cases the person defining must necessarily use a negation, as in privations. Thus the blind is “that which does not have sight, although it was naturally constituted to have it.”

There is no difference between dividing the genus by a negation and dividing it by an affirmation that necessarily has the negation as its contrary—for example, if length is defined as “having breadth.” “Having breadth” is divided from “not having breadth,” and nothing else; thus here too the genus is divided by a negation. [Col. 0976C]

Again, one must consider whether a species has been assigned as a difference. For example, someone defines abuse as “an insult accompanied by ridicule.” Ridicule is a kind of insult; hence ridicule is not a difference but a species.

Further, one must consider whether a genus has been stated as a difference—for example, when virtue is defined as “a good or excellent disposition.” “Good” is the genus of virtue.

Or is “good” not the genus but the difference? If it is true that the same thing cannot belong to two genera that do not contain one another—for neither does good contain disposition, nor disposition good, since not every disposition is good and not every good is a disposition—then they cannot both be genera. If disposition is the genus of virtue, it is clear that good is not the genus but rather the difference.

Moreover, “disposition” signifies what virtue is, whereas “good” does not signify what it is but what sort of thing it is. A difference appears to signify what sort of thing something is.

One must also consider whether the difference assigned signifies not what sort of thing the thing is but what it is itself. Every difference appears to signify what sort of thing something is.

Further, one must consider whether the difference belongs to the thing defined accidentally. No accidental attribute is a difference, just as none is a genus, since it is impossible for a difference to belong to something and not belong to it.

Further, if the difference, species, or some lower item is predicated of the genus, the person defining has not defined. None of the things stated can be predicated of the genus, since the genus is predicated of the greatest number of things. [Col. 0977A]

Again, one must consider whether the genus is predicated of the difference. The genus appears to be predicated not of the difference, but of the things that have the difference—for example, animal is predicated of human being, ox, and the other walking animals, but not of the difference that is predicated of the species.

For if animal were predicated of each difference, many animals would be predicated of the species, since differences are predicated of the species.

Further, all the differences would be either species or individuals, if they were animals, since every animal is either a species or an individual.

Similarly, one must examine whether a species, or some lower member of a species, is predicated of the difference. This is impossible, since the difference is predicated of more things than the species.

Further, it would follow that the difference is a species if one of the species were predicated of it. If human being is predicated of the difference, it is clear that the difference is human being. [Col. 0977B]

Again, one must consider whether the difference is not prior to the species. The difference must be posterior to the genus but prior to the species.

Further, one must consider whether the stated difference belongs to another genus, neither a genus contained by nor one containing the genus in question. The same difference does not appear to belong to two genera that do not contain one another.

If this is not so, it will also follow that the same species belongs to two genera that do not contain one another, since each difference entails its proper genus. For example, walking and two-footed entail animal. Therefore, if both genera are predicated of the thing of which the difference is predicated, it is clear that the species belonged to two genera that do not contain one another. [Col. 0977C]

Or is it impossible for the same difference to belong to two genera that do not contain one another, unless both are subordinate to the same higher genus? Walking animal and flying animal are genera that do not contain one another, and two-footed is a difference of both. Therefore one must add that neither is both subordinate to the same higher genus. In this case, both are subordinate to animal.

It is also clear that it is not necessary for every difference to entail its own genus. The same difference can belong to two genera that do not contain one another, but it is necessary for it to entail only one genus and all the higher genera—for example, two-footed entails animal, whether it is walking or flying.

One must also consider whether a place has been assigned as the difference of a substance. Substance appears to differ from substance by being somewhere; hence those who divide animal into walking and aquatic are criticized, as though “walking” and “aquatic” signified a place. [Col. 0977D]

But perhaps they are not rightly criticized in these cases. “Aquatic” and “terrestrial” do not signify being in something or being somewhere, but what sort of thing something is. If something is on dry land, it is still aquatic in the same way; likewise it is terrestrial. If it is in water, it is still terrestrial in the same way, although it will not be aquatic.

Nevertheless, whenever a difference signifies being in something, it is clear that the definition will be defective.

Again, one must consider whether an affection has been assigned as a difference. Every affection, when it becomes greater, detracts from the substance; but a difference is not of this kind. Rather, the difference appears to preserve more fully the thing of which it is a difference. It is simply impossible for each thing to exist without its proper difference: without walking, there will be no human being; and, to put it generally, whatever changes according to an affection does not have that affection as its difference. [Col. 0978A]

All such affections, when they increase, detract from substance. Therefore, if anyone assigns such a thing as a difference, he has erred. In general, things do not undergo alteration according to their differences.

One must also consider whether the difference assigned is the difference of something relative to something else, rather than of an absolute thing. Differences of relatives are themselves relative, as in the case of sciences: a science is called contemplative, practical, or productive, and each of these signifies a relation to something. It is contemplative of something, practical with respect to something, and productive of something.

One must also consider whether the person defining has assigned the relation to which each relative is naturally directed. In some cases, the only natural use of a relative is directed toward one thing and toward nothing else—for example, sight exists solely for seeing. In other cases, it is directed toward something else as well. Someone may use a jar for drawing water, for example; nevertheless, if someone defines a jar as “an instrument for drawing water,” he has erred, since this is not what it was naturally made for. [Col. 0978B]

A definition concerns what a thing is naturally made for—what a prudent person uses it for precisely as a prudent person, and what belongs to the proper science concerning each thing.

Further, one must consider whether the person defining has assigned the first relation when the thing is said in relation to several things. For example, prudence may be called the virtue of a human being or of the soul, but first it is the virtue of the rational part; in this respect both the soul and the human being are called prudent.

Further, if the subject is not receptive of the affection, disposition, or anything else of which it is said, the person defining has erred. Every disposition or affection naturally comes to be in the thing whose disposition or affection it is. Knowledge, for example, is in the soul, since it is a disposition of the soul. [Col. 0978C]

Sometimes people make mistakes in such cases—for example, those who say that sleep is “an incapacity of sense-perception,” doubt is “an equality of contrary reasonings,” and pain is “a separation of natural parts accompanied by violence.” Sleep is not in sense-perception, although it would have to be if it were an incapacity of sense-perception. Likewise, doubt is not in contrary reasonings, nor pain in natural parts, since inanimate things would suffer if pain were in them.

The definition of health is of the same kind, if health is “a commensuration of hot and cold.” For hot and cold must be healthy, since the commensuration of anything belongs to the things of which it is the commensuration. Health, therefore, would belong to hot and cold themselves. [Col. 0978D]

Again, those who define in this way may place what is produced in the producer, or conversely. Pain is not “a separation of natural parts,” but something productive of pain; nor is sleep “an incapacity of sense-perception,” but something productive of the other. Either we sleep because of incapacity, or we become incapable because of sleep.

Likewise, equality of contrary reasonings will appear to be productive of doubt. Whenever, in reasoning toward both alternatives, everything appears equally to occur according to either alternative, we will be in doubt about what to do.

Further, everything must be examined with respect to time wherever there is disagreement. For example, if the immortal is defined as “an animal that is now incorruptible,” then an animal that is now incorruptible will be immortal now. [Col. 0979A]

But perhaps this does not follow. “Now incorruptible” is ambiguous: it may mean that the thing is not being corrupted now, that it is not now capable of being corrupted, or that it is now of such a nature as never to be capable of corruption.

When we say that an animal is now incorruptible, we do not mean that the animal is now such, but that it is incapable of corruption at any time. This is identical with “immortal”; therefore it does not follow that it is now immortal in the sense of being immortal only now. [Col. 0979B]

Nevertheless, wherever it happens that what is assigned according to the definition belongs to the thing now or earlier, while what is signified according to the name does not belong to it, this place should be used in the manner stated.

One must also examine whether the thing defined is more commonly said according to some other account than according to the account assigned. For example, if justice is defined as “a power distributive of what is equal,” the just person is more properly one who chooses to distribute what is equal than one who merely has the power to do so. Justice therefore will not be a power distributive of what is equal, since the person who could distribute what is equal would then be most just.

Further, if the thing itself admits of degrees, whereas what is assigned according to the account does not, or conversely, what is assigned according to the account admits of degrees while the thing itself does not, the definition is defective. Both must either admit of degrees or neither, if what is assigned according to the account belongs to the thing. [Col. 0979C]

Further, if both admit of degrees but do not increase together, as when love is defined as “a desire for intercourse.” A person who loves more does not desire intercourse more. Thus the two do not increase together, although they would have to if they were the same.

Further, if, when two things are proposed, the thing itself is said more of one, but what is assigned according to the account is said less of that one. For example, if fire is “the most subtle body,” fire is more truly flame than light, whereas the most subtle body is less truly flame than light. Both would have to belong more to the same thing if they were identical. [Col. 0979D]

Again, one must consider whether one of the two things belongs equally to both proposed subjects, while the other does not belong equally to both but belongs more to one.

Further, one must consider whether the definition has been assigned to two things in accordance with each of them. For example, “good” is defined as “what is pleasant through sight or hearing,” and “being” as “what is capable of acting or being acted upon.”

Then the same thing will be both good and not good, and likewise both being and non-being. What is pleasant through hearing will be identical with good; therefore what is not pleasant through hearing will be identical with not good, since the same things will have the same opposites. The opposite of good is not good, while the opposite of what is pleasant through hearing is what is not pleasant through hearing. Clearly, therefore, what is not pleasant through hearing is identical with not good. [Col. 0980A]

If something is pleasant through sight but not pleasant through hearing, it will therefore be both good and not good. In the same way, we shall show that the same thing is both being and non-being.

Further, in the case of genera, differences, and all the other elements assigned in definitions, one must consider whether anything conflicts with those who substitute accounts for names.

## CHAPTER IV. Another place concerning definition
[Col. 0980B] But if what is being defined is a relative, either in itself or according to its genus, one must consider whether that to which it is related has not been stated in the definition, either in itself or according to its genus. For example, if knowledge has been defined as an unpersuadable opinion, or willing as desire without distress: for the substance of everything relative is related to something else, since for each of the relatives, being is in a certain way the same as being related to something. Knowledge, therefore, ought to have been called an opinion of the knowable, and willing a desire for the good. Likewise, if grammar has been defined as knowledge of letters, what it is related to ought to have been stated in the definition, either in itself or according to the genus to which it is related.

Or if, when something is said to be related to something, the end has not been stated [Col. 0980C]. The end in each case is what is best, or that for the sake of which other things exist. One must therefore state either the best or the ultimate end; thus desire is not desire of the pleasant, but of pleasure, for it is for the sake of pleasure that we choose what is pleasant.

One must also consider whether what has been stated as the object of the relation is a process of generation or an activity. Nothing of this sort is an end; rather, having acted and having generated are more truly ends than becoming and acting. Or is this not true in all cases of this kind? For almost everyone wishes rather to be enjoying pleasure than to have ceased enjoying it. Therefore one might more properly regard acting as an end than having acted.

Again, in some cases, if the definition has not determined how much, what sort, where, or according to the other relevant differences—for example, what kind and how much honor the ambitious person desires, since everyone desires honor—it is not sufficient to say that an ambitious person is one who desires honor [Col. 0980D]; the stated differences must also be added. Likewise, one must state how much money the miser desires, or what kinds of pleasures the intemperate person pursues. For someone who is mastered by just any pleasure is not called intemperate, but someone mastered by a particular kind.

Again, if someone has defined night as the shadow of the earth, an earthquake as a movement of the earth, a cloud as a density of air, or wind as a movement of air, how much, of what kind, where, and from what cause must also be added. The same applies in other cases of this kind. For by omitting any difference, one does not state what it is to be that thing; one must always argue from what the definition requires. Not every movement of the earth, nor every degree of shaking, will be an earthquake; likewise, not every kind or degree of movement of the air [Col. 0981A] will be wind.

Further, in the case of desires, one must add what appears to be the object, and the same applies in other cases. Thus willing is desire for an apparent good, and desire is desire for apparent pleasure. For those who desire are often unaware that what they desire is good or pleasant. Therefore it need not be good or pleasant, but only appear so; the definition ought accordingly to have been formulated in that way.

If someone has stated the definition in the manner just described, he must be led to the Forms by the person who maintains that Ideas exist. For there is no Idea of anything merely apparent; the Form itself, however, seems to be predicated of the Form itself—for example, desire itself of pleasure itself, and willing itself of the good itself. The will itself, therefore, will not be the will of an apparent good, nor desire itself the desire of an apparent pleasure. For it is absurd that the apparent good or pleasant thing itself should exist [Col. 0981B].

Further, if the definition is of a state, one must consider whether the definition applies to the possessor; and if it is of the possessor, whether it applies to the state. The same applies in other cases of this kind: if pleasure is defined as benefit, then the pleasant thing should be beneficial.

Speaking generally, in definitions of this kind the person defining in a certain way defines several things at once. For one who defines knowledge in a certain way thereby also defines ignorance; likewise the knowledgeable and the ignorant, knowing and being ignorant. Once the first has been made clear, the rest are in a certain way made clear as well. One must therefore examine all such cases to see whether anything is inconsistent, using the elements derived from contraries and correlatives.

Further, in the case of relatives, one must consider whether the genus to which one thing is related has been assigned, and whether the species has been assigned to the corresponding species. For example, if opinion is related to the object of opinion, and a particular opinion to a particular object of opinion; and if a multiple is related to a multiple, and a particular multiple to a particular submultiple. If it has not been assigned in this way, the error is evident.

One must also see whether the definition of the opposite has been stated as the opposite. For example, the definition of the half should be the opposite of that of the double. For if the double is what exceeds the half by an equal amount, the half is what is exceeded by the double by an equal amount.

The same applies to contraries. The account of a contrary will be the account of its contrary, according to a certain combination of contraries. For example, if what aids is productive of good, what harms is productive of evil—or productive of the destruction of good. One of these must necessarily be contrary to what was stated at the beginning. If neither contrary is contrary to the original definition [Col. 0981D], it is evident that neither of the accounts subsequently assigned will be the account of the contrary. Consequently, the definition assigned at the beginning was not correctly assigned.

Since some contraries are spoken of through the privation of the other—for example, inequality appears to be the privation of equality, since unequal things are called those that are not equal—it is clear that what is called contrary according to privation must be defined through the other term, whereas the other need not be defined through what is expressed according to privation. For neither is understood through the other.

One must therefore examine this error in the case of contraries—for example, if someone defines equality as the contrary of inequality. In this case he has defined it through what is expressed according to privation [Col. 0982A].

Further, the person defining in this way is compelled to use the thing defined. This becomes clear if the account is substituted for the name. Since it makes no difference to say “inequality” or “privation of equality,” equality will be the contrary of the privation of equality; thus the same term will have been used.

If neither of the contraries is expressed according to privation, but an account is assigned in the same way—for example, “good is contrary to evil”—it is evident that “evil is contrary to good” will also follow. For the account of contraries must be assigned in the same way. Thus again the definition will involve using the thing defined, since “good” occurs in the account of evil. Accordingly, since good is contrary to evil, and evil is nothing other than what is contrary to good, good will be contrary to the contrary of good. It is therefore clear that the same term has been used.

Further, if someone assigns what is expressed according to privation, but does not state of what it is the privation—whether of a state, a contrary, or anything else of which it is a privation—and if he does not add in what the privation naturally occurs, either without qualification or in what it first naturally occurs, he has erred. For example, if he calls ignorance a privation but does not say a privation of knowledge, or if he does not add in what it naturally occurs, or, having added this, does not state where it first naturally occurs—for example, not in the rational faculty but in a human being or in the soul—he has erred in omitting any of these points.

The same applies if someone does not say that blindness is a privation of sight in the eye. A proper definition must state what the thing is, of what it is a privation, and what it is that is deprived.

One must also see whether someone has defined something not expressed according to privation by means of a privation. A similar error appears in the case of ignorance among those who do not define ignorance according to negation. For someone who does not possess knowledge does not seem to be ignorant; rather, the ignorant person seems to be one who has been deceived. This is why we do not say that inanimate things or children are ignorant. Ignorance, therefore, is not defined as a privation of knowledge in this sense [Col. 0982C].

Further, if the grammatical cases of a name are similar, corresponding cases of the account should also be similar. Thus, if “what aids” is productive of health, “helpful” is productive of health, and “the helper” produces health.

One must also consider whether the stated definition can be applied to the Idea. In some cases it cannot. For example, Plato adds “mortal” in definitions of animals; but the Idea—for example, Man-itself—will not be mortal. Therefore the definition will not apply to the Idea.

In general, whenever “productive” or “passive” is added, the definition must fail to apply to the Idea. For those who maintain that Ideas exist consider the Ideas to be impassible and immovable. Against such people, therefore, arguments of this kind are useful.

## CHAPTER V. Other Topics concerning Definition

Further, if someone has assigned one definition common to all things spoken of equivocally, this must be examined. For things univocal are those for which there is one account corresponding to the name. Consequently, the definition assigned will not be the definition of any of the things included under the name, since it is applied equally to all the equivocal things.

Dionysius’ definition of life has suffered this defect, if life is “a movement belonging to the genus of things naturally serving nourishment.” For this is no more present in animals than in plants. Yet life does not seem to be spoken of according to one species: one kind is present in animals, another in plants [Col. 0983A].

It is therefore possible, by choice, to assign the definition in this way, as though the term were univocal and all life were spoken of according to one species. Nothing prevents someone who recognizes the equivocation and wishes to assign a definition from failing to notice the proper account and assigning instead an account common to both. But in either case he has committed an error.

When an equivocation has escaped notice, the questioner should treat the term as univocal. For the definition of one thing will not fit the other, and thus it will appear that the distinction need not be made, since the definition ought to fit every univocal instance. The respondent, however, must make the distinction.

Since some respondents call a univocal term equivocal when the assigned account does not fit everything, and call an equivocal term univocal even if the account fits both, one should in such cases secure a prior admission, or first establish whether the term is equivocal, univocal, or both. For people are more likely to concede something before they foresee what will follow.

If, without such a preliminary admission, someone says that a univocal term is equivocal because the assigned account does not fit this instance, one must consider whether the account fits the remaining instances. For if it does, the term will be univocal with respect to the others; but if it does not, there will be several definitions for the others. Two accounts corresponding to the name—the one assigned earlier and the one assigned later—will fit the same thing.

Again, if someone defines one of the things spoken of in several ways, while the account does not fit all the cases, and he refuses to admit that the term is equivocal, saying that the name itself does not fit all the cases because the account does not, one should reply that the customary name must be used, together with the name that follows it, and that such things must not be displaced, even though some of them should not be said to apply in the same way to the plurality of cases [Col. 0983C].

If a definition is assigned for something composite, one must consider, by removing the account of one of the components, whether the remainder applies to the other. For if it does not, it is evident that the account of the whole does not apply to the whole. For example, suppose someone defined a terminal straight line as “the boundary of a plane having boundaries, whose middle is added to the boundaries.” If the account of the terminal line is “the boundary of a plane having boundaries,” then the remainder, “whose middle is added to the boundaries,” ought to apply to the straight line. But the infinite has neither a middle nor boundaries, whereas it is straight; therefore the remainder is not the account of the remainder.

Further, if the thing defined is composite, but an equal-membered account is assigned as its definition, this must be examined. An account is called equal-membered when, however many components there are, there are the same number of names and verbs in the account. In such cases it is necessary to change either all or some of the names of the components, since no more names have now been stated than before. But the person defining ought to substitute an account for the names, preferably for all of them, or at least for most.

For in the case of simple things as well, someone who merely changes the name will not be defining—for example, substituting “garment” for “tunic.” It is an even greater error if he makes the substitution with less familiar names, as when he substitutes “earth-born shining one” for “white human being.” For he has not defined it, since the substituted expression is less clear [Col. 0984A].

One must also consider whether, by changing the names, he now signifies something different. For example, someone who calls contemplative knowledge “contemplative opinion.” Opinion is not the same as knowledge; but, if the definition is to be valid, the whole must also be the same. “Contemplative” is common to both accounts, but the remaining term differs.

Further, if, in changing one of the names, he has changed not the difference but the genus—for example, in the case just mentioned, since “contemplative” is less familiar than “knowledge.” “Knowledge” is a genus, whereas “contemplative” is a difference; the genus is more familiar to everyone because it is common. Therefore the substitution ought to have been made not in the genus but in the difference, since the latter is less familiar [Col. 0984B].

Or is this criticism absurd? Nothing prevents the difference from being expressed by the most familiar name and the genus by a less familiar one. Even so, given the circumstances, it is clear that the substitution of names should be made in the genus rather than in the difference. But if someone substitutes an account for a name rather than one name for another, it is evident that the definition of the difference should be assigned rather than that of the genus, since a definition is assigned for the sake of knowledge, and the difference is less known than the genus.

If a definition has been assigned for a difference, one must consider whether the same definition is common to something else. For example, if someone has called an odd number “a number having a middle,” it must be determined in what sense it has a middle. For “number” is common to both accounts, while the account of the odd has been added. But both a line and a body have a middle, although they are not odd; therefore this will not be the definition of oddness.

If “having a middle” is itself said in several ways, it must be determined in what sense it is having a middle. Otherwise there will be either a criticism or a syllogism showing that he has not defined the thing.

Again, if the thing whose account he has assigned is among existing things, while the thing falling under the account is not among existing things—for example, if someone defines white as “a color mixed with fire”—this is impossible, since an incorporeal thing cannot be mixed with a body. Therefore “color mixed with fire” does not exist, although white does.

Further, anyone who does not divide relatives according to what they are related to, but includes them under something more extensive, speaks falsely either in every case or in some cases. For example, if someone calls medicine “knowledge of being.” If medicine is the knowledge of none of the things that are, it is evident that the whole account is false; but if it is the knowledge of some of them and not of others, the account is false in some respect. For it must be knowledge of every being, if it is said to be knowledge of being in itself and not accidentally, as is the case with other relatives: every object of knowledge is referred to knowledge [Col. 0984D].

The same applies in other cases, since all relatives are convertible. Every object of knowledge, for example, is referred to knowledge.

On the other hand, if someone has correctly assigned an account not in itself but accidentally, he has assigned each relative not to one thing but to several. For nothing prevents the same thing from being being, white, and good. Thus, if he has assigned it to any of these, he has assigned it correctly, provided that he was assigning it according to an accidental relation.

Moreover, it is impossible for such an account to be the proper account of the thing assigned, since not only medicine but many other kinds of knowledge are related to being. Therefore each of them will be knowledge of being. It is consequently clear that such an account is the definition of no particular kind of knowledge, since a definition must be proper and not common.

Sometimes, however, people define not the thing itself but the thing in a good or perfected condition. Such would be the definition of a rhetorician and a thief, if a rhetorician is one who can discern what is plausible in each case and omit nothing, and a thief one who takes secretly. For it is clear that, when each is such, the one will be a good rhetorician and the other a good thief. For it is not simply the person who takes secretly who is a thief, but the person who wishes to take secretly [Col. 0985B].

Again, if something chosen for its own sake is defined as active or productive, or in any way as something chosen for the sake of another, this is an error. For example, if someone calls justice “preservative of laws,” or wisdom “productive of happiness.” Preserving and producing belong among the things chosen for the sake of something else.

Nothing, indeed, prevents something chosen for its own sake also from being chosen for the sake of another. Nevertheless, the person who defines what is chosen for its own sake in this way has still erred. For what is best for each thing, especially in its substance, is what is chosen for its own sake, and what is chosen for its own sake is better than what is chosen for the sake of another. Therefore the definition ought rather to signify that.

## CHAPTER VI. Other Topics concerning Definition

[Col. 0985C]

One must also consider whether the person who assigned a definition for something defined it as these things, as what results from these things, or as this together with that.

If he defined it as these things, it will follow that both and neither are present in the same subjects. For example, if he defined justice as temperance and courage: if there are two people, and each has one of the two qualities, both will be just, and neither will be just, since both have justice while neither has both qualities.

If what has been said does not yet seem entirely absurd, because the same thing can occur in other cases—nothing prevents both people from possessing one quality even though neither possesses both—nevertheless it will seem utterly absurd that contrary qualities should be present in the same thing [Col. 0985D]. This will happen if one person has temperance and cowardice, while the other has courage and prodigality; for both will possess justice and injustice. If justice is temperance and courage, injustice will be cowardice and prodigality. In general, all arguments that are suitable for showing that the parts are not the same as the whole are useful here. Yet the person who defines in this way appears to say that the parts are the same as the whole.

Such accounts are especially apt wherever the composition of the parts is evident, as in a house and similar things. For it is clear that, although the parts exist, nothing prevents the whole from not existing; therefore the parts are not the same as the whole.

If, however, he has not said “these things,” but “what results from these things” is what is defined, one must first consider whether it is natural for something single to come to be from the things stated. For some things are so related to one another that nothing single is formed from them, such as a line and a number.

Further, if the thing defined is naturally formed first in one particular thing, but the things from which he says it is formed are not first naturally formed in one thing, but each in the other, it is evident that it will not be formed from them. For wherever there are parts, the whole must also be present. Therefore the whole will not exist first in one thing, but in several [Col. 0986A].

If both the parts and the whole first exist in one thing, one must consider whether they do not exist in the same thing, but the whole in one and the parts in another. For wherever the whole is, the parts also seem to be.

Again, one must consider whether the parts are destroyed together with the whole. The converse must occur: when the parts are destroyed, the whole must be destroyed; but when the whole is destroyed, it is not necessary that the parts also be destroyed.

One must also consider whether the whole is good or bad while the parts are neither, or conversely whether the parts are good or bad while the whole is neither. For it is impossible either for something good or bad to be formed from things that are neither, or for something neither good nor bad to be formed from good or bad things.

Or consider whether one part is more good than another is bad, while what results from them is not more good than bad—for example, if imprudence results from courage and false opinion. Courage is more good than false opinion is bad. Therefore what results from them should follow what is stronger and be either simply good or more good than bad.

But is this not necessary unless both constituents are good or bad in themselves? For many productive things are not good in themselves, but when mixed with something become good, or conversely: both constituents may be good, while their mixture is bad or neither. This is especially clear in things that promote health and things that cause disease. Some medicines are such that each is good, but if both are administered in combination, the result is bad [Col. 0986C].

Again, if something is formed from a better and a worse thing, consider whether the whole is not better than the worse but worse than the better.

But is even this not necessary unless the things from which it is composed are good in themselves? For in the case of things that are not good in themselves, nothing prevents the whole from failing to be good, as in the examples just mentioned.

Further, consider whether the whole is of the same name as one of its constituents. It ought not to be, just as neither are syllables. None of the elements from which a syllable is composed has the same name as the syllable [Col. 0986D].

Further, consider whether the mode of composition has not been stated. It is not sufficient, for purposes of knowing what is being said, merely to state that it is formed from these things. For the substance of each composite is not merely what is formed from these things, but what is formed from them in this particular way, as in the case of a house. If these things are put together in just any way, the result is not a house.

If he has assigned it as this together with that, one must first state whether “this together with that” means this and that, or what results from them. For someone who says “honey with water” either says honey and water, or what results from honey and water. If he admits that this together with that is identical with any of the expressions just mentioned, the same considerations will apply as those stated earlier concerning both alternatives [Col. 0987A].

Further, when the phrase “one thing together with another” has been divided according to its several meanings, one must consider whether “this together with that” is true in no way. For the phrase may mean that one thing is with another in the same receptive subject, as justice and courage are in the soul; or in the same place; or at the same time. If what has been said is true in none of these ways, it is clear that the assigned definition will be the definition of nothing, since “this together with that” is true in no way.

If, after the several meanings of “one thing together with another” have been distinguished, it is true that both are present at the same time, one must consider whether it is possible for them not to be directed toward the same end. For example, if someone defined courage as boldness together with correct understanding, it is possible for someone to have boldness concerning plunder, but correct understanding concerning matters of health; yet a person who possesses these at the same time is not thereby courageous.

Further, if both are directed toward the same object—for example, medical matters—nothing prevents someone from having both a certain boldness and correct understanding concerning medical matters. Yet even so, the person who has these together is not courageous. Both must be directed neither merely toward one or the other of the two things, nor toward just any common object, but toward the end of courage—for example, the dangers of battle, or whatever is more properly its end [Col. 0987B].

Some definitions of this kind do not fall under the division just stated at all. For example, if anger is defined as distress together with an opinion of being slighted, the intention is to indicate that the distress arises because of such an opinion. But something’s arising because of this is not identical with its being this together with that according to any of the modes mentioned.

Again, if he has said that the whole is the composition of these things—for example, that an animal is the composition of soul and body—one must first consider whether he has stated what kind of composition it is. Thus, if he defines flesh or bone as a composition of fire, air, and earth, it is not sufficient merely to say “composition”; one must determine what the composition is and what kind it is. For flesh results from these things when they are composed in one way, and bone when they are composed in another [Col. 0987C].

Nor does either of the things mentioned seem to be altogether identical with composition. Every composition has dissolution as its contrary, whereas neither of the things mentioned has anything of this sort.

Further, if it is equally plausible either that every composite is a composition or that none is, then, since each animal is composite, it will not be a composition; nor, in fact, will any other composite be a composition.

Again, if contrary things are naturally present in the same subject in the same way, but someone defines the subject through only one of them, it is evident that he has not defined it. If this is not so, the same thing will have several definitions. For why is the person who defines it through one of them any more a definer than the person who defines it through the other, since both are naturally present in the same subject in the same way? Such is the definition of the soul, if the soul is “a substance capable of receiving knowledge,” since it is similarly capable of receiving ignorance [Col. 0988A].

If someone cannot argue against the whole definition because the whole is unknown, he must argue against some part, if that part is known and appears not to have been correctly assigned. For when a part is refuted, the whole definition is also refuted.

Whenever definitions are unclear to the person correcting them, and adapting them so as to make something clear and provide an argument, they must be examined in this way. For the respondent must either accept what has been assumed by the questioner, or himself make clear what has been arbitrarily asserted by the definition.

Further, just as in assemblies people introduce a law, and if the law introduced is better, they repeal the earlier one, so the same must be done with definitions, and another definition must be brought forward. For if the new definition appears better and makes the thing defined clearer, it is evident that the one previously posited has been overturned, since the same thing cannot have several definitions [Col. 0988C].

In relation to all definitions, an especially important element is to define the proposed object in relation to itself skillfully, or to adopt an appropriately stated definition. For one must examine it as though using a model, determining both what is lacking in the definition and what has been added superfluously, so that one may have a greater abundance of arguments.

So much, then, has been said concerning definitions.

# BOOK VII

[Col. 0987]

## CHAPTER I. Topics concerning Sameness and Difference

Whether one thing is the same as or different from another according to the most proper of the modes previously mentioned concerning sameness must now be discussed. The most proper sense of “the same” was said to be what is one in number. One must consider the matter through inflected forms, correlatives, and opposites.

For if justice is the same as courage, then the just person is the same as the courageous person, and acting justly the same as acting courageously; the same applies to opposites. If these are the same, then their opposites are also the same according to any of the stated kinds of opposition. For it makes no difference which of the two is taken as the opposite, since the result is the same.

Again, one must consider productive and destructive things, generations and destructions, and, generally, things that stand in similar relations to one another. Whatever things are simply the same have the same generations and destructions, and the same productive and destructive causes.

One must also consider which of two things is most emphatically said to be something, and whether the other is likewise most emphatically said to be that same thing. Thus Xenocrates identified the happy life with the excellent life because the excellent life is the most choiceworthy and happiest of all lives: what is most choiceworthy and greatest is one and the same in the highest degree [Col. 0988C].

In such cases, however, both things called greatest and most choiceworthy must be one in number. If they are not, it has not been shown that they are the same. For it does not follow, if the Peloponnesians and Lacedaemonians are the bravest of the Greeks, that the Peloponnesians are the same as the Lacedaemonians, since a Peloponnesian and a Lacedaemonian are not one in number. It is necessary, however, that one be included within the other—for example, that the Lacedaemonians be included among the Peloponnesians.

If this were not so, they would become better than one another, if neither were included in the other. For the Peloponnesians would have to be better than the Lacedaemonians, since they are better than all the others; and likewise the Lacedaemonians would have to be better than the Peloponnesians, since they too are better than all the others. Thus they would become better than one another [Col. 0989A].

It is therefore clear that what is called best and greatest must be one in number if it is to be shown that the things are the same. Accordingly, Xenocrates did not identify the two: the happy life and the excellent life are not one in number. It does not follow, therefore, that they are the same merely because both are most choiceworthy; one is subordinate to the other.

Again, consider whether one thing is the same as one thing, and another as another. For if both are not the same as the same thing, it is evident that they are not the same as each other.

Further, one must consider the attributes of these things and the subjects to which these attributes belong. Whatever belongs to one must belong to the other, and whatever has one of them as an attribute must have the other as an attribute. If anything is inconsistent, it is clear that the things are not the same.

One must also see whether both are not predicated in the same category, but one signifies a quality, while the other signifies a quantity or a relative. Again, whether their genera are not the same, but one is a good and the other an evil, or one a virtue and the other knowledge.

Or, if the genus is the same, whether the differences predicated of each are not the same, but one is said to be contemplative knowledge and the other practical knowledge; and similarly in other cases.

Further, one must consider degrees: whether one admits of “more” and the other does not, or whether both admit of “more” but not at the same time. For example, the person who loves more does not desire sexual intercourse more; therefore love and sexual desire are not the same [Col. 0989C].

Further, one must consider addition: if adding the same thing to both does not make the wholes the same, or if, when the same thing is removed from both, what remains is different. For example, if someone says that “double the half” and “multiple of the half” are the same, then, when the half is removed from both, the remainders ought to signify the same thing. But they do not, since “double” and “multiple” do not signify the same thing.

One must consider not only whether the positing of something already produces an impossibility, but also whether it is possible for the result to exist on the supposition. Thus those who say that the void and the air-filled are the same: if the air departs, the void will be no less a void—in fact, it will be more so—whereas what is filled with air will no longer be filled with air. Therefore, if, on the supposition of something—whether the supposition is true or false, for this makes no difference—one of the terms is destroyed while the other is not, they are certainly not the same [Col. 0989D].

Generally speaking, one must consider, from the things predicated of either term in any way and the things of which these predicates are said, whether there is any inconsistency. Whatever is predicated of one must be predicated of the other, and whatever has one of them predicated of it must have the other predicated of it.

Further, since “the same” is said in several ways, one must consider whether the things are the same in some other way. Things that are the same in species or genus need not be the same in number; one must therefore consider whether they are the same in this way or not.

Further, if one can exist without the other, they will not be the same, since one thing cannot be identical with another if it can exist without it.

These, then, are the Topics concerning sameness.

## CHAPTER II. Other Topics concerning Sameness in Definition
It is evident from what has been said that all the destructive lines of argument that apply to the same thing are also useful against a definition, as was said earlier. For if the name and the account do not indicate the same thing, it is clear that the account assigned will not be a definition. None of the constructive lines of argument, however, is useful for establishing a definition. For it is not sufficient, in order to construct a definition, to show that the thing signified by the account and the name is the same; the definition must also possess all the other features required of it. One must therefore always try to refute a definition in this way and by these means.

But if we wish to construct one [Col. 0990B], we must first know that few, or perhaps none, of those engaged in disputation establish a definition by syllogism; rather, everyone assumes as a starting point something of this kind, as do those working in geometry, arithmetic, and other disciplines of the same sort. Next, assigning what a definition is and how one ought to define belongs properly to another inquiry. For present purposes, however, it is enough to say only that it is possible for there to be a syllogism of a definition, and of the essence. For if a definition is an account indicating what it is for a thing to be, and if the elements included in a definition must be predicated of the thing alone in respect of what it is, while genera and differentiae are predicated of a thing alone in respect of what it is, it is clear that if someone takes those elements which alone ought to be predicated of the thing in respect of what it is, the account containing these elements will necessarily be a definition. For it is impossible for anything else to be a definition, since nothing else is predicated of the thing in respect of what it is. It is therefore clear that a syllogism can be constructed from a definition.

The means by which one ought to construct a definition have been treated more carefully elsewhere; for the present method, however, the same lines of argument are useful. One must examine contraries and other opposites, both whole accounts and their parts. For if opposites have opposite definitions, the definition stated for the proposed subject must necessarily be the one described.

Since contraries have several possible combinations, one must take from the contraries whichever definition most clearly appears to be contrary to the proposed definition. Thus one must examine whole definitions, as was said [Col. 0990D]. With respect to the parts, the procedure is as follows. First, one must consider whether the genus assigned has been assigned correctly. For if the contrary belongs to the contrary, while the proposed subject does not belong to the same genus, it is clear that it will belong to the contrary genus, since contraries must belong either to the same genus or to contrary genera.

We assume that contrary differentiae are predicated of contraries, as in the case of white and black: the former is divisive of sight, the latter congregative. Therefore, if contrary differentiae are predicated of the contrary, the differentiae assigned will be predicated of the proposed subject. Consequently, since both the genus and the differentiae have been assigned correctly, it is clear that the assigned definition will be a definition.

But is it not necessary for differentiae to be predicated of contraries only when the contraries belong to the same genus? When their genera are contrary, there is nothing to prevent the same differentia from being said of both, as in the case of justice and injustice: the former is a virtue, while the latter is a vice of the soul. Thus “of the soul” is said as a differentia of both, since there are both virtue and vice of the body as well. Still, it is true that contraries have either contrary differentiae or the same differentiae. Therefore, if contrary differentiae are predicated of the contrary, but not of this subject, it is clear that the differentia stated will be predicated of this subject.

In general, if a definition consists of a genus and differentiae, and the definition of the contrary is clear, the definition of the proposed subject will also be clear. For since the contrary belongs either to the same genus or to a contrary genus, and since the differentiae are likewise either contrary differentiae predicated of contraries or the same differentiae [Col. 0991B], it is evident that the proposed subject will have either the same genus as the contrary, and contrary differentiae—either all of them or some—or the remaining differentiae will be the same; or the differentiae will be the same while the genera are contrary; or both will be contrary, both genera and differentiae. Both cannot be the same; otherwise the definition of the contraries would be the same.

Another line of argument proceeds from inflected forms and cognates. Genera must correspond to genera and definitions to definitions. Thus, if forgetting is the loss of knowledge, then to forget will be to lose knowledge, and to have forgotten will be to have lost knowledge. Once any one of these has been admitted, the others must also be admitted.

The same applies if corruption is the dissolution of substance: to corrupt is to dissolve substance; “corruptively” corresponds to “dissolutively”; if that which corrupts is that which dissolves substance, then corruption is dissolution of substance. The same applies in other cases. Thus, once any one of these has been assumed, all the rest must also be conceded.

Another line of argument proceeds from things that stand in a similar relation to one another. If the healthy is productive of health, then the fit will be productive of good condition, and the helpful will be productive of good. For each of the things mentioned stands similarly in relation to its own end. Therefore, if the definition of one of them is “being productive of the end,” the definition of each of the others will be the same.

Another proceeds from what is more and from what is alike. The consideration based on likeness is useful whenever one can establish two things by comparing two with two. Thus, if this is more a definition of this than that is of that, and the latter is a definition in the lesser degree, the former too is a definition in the greater degree; and if this is a definition of this in the same way as that is of that, then, if one is a definition of one, the other is a definition of the other.

The consideration based on what is more is of no use at all when one definition is compared with two things, or two definitions with one thing. For it is impossible for one definition to belong to two things, or for two definitions to belong to the same thing.

The most useful lines of argument are those just mentioned, together with those from inflected forms and cognates. Accordingly, these must be especially retained and kept ready, since they are useful for the greatest number of cases. Of the other lines, the most useful are those that are most common. For example, one should examine particulars and consider species, asking whether the definition applies to them, since a species is univocal. This line of argument is useful against those who posit the existence of Forms, as was said earlier. Further, if someone has used a name metaphorically, or has predicated the same term of the same thing as though it were different, and likewise with any other common and effective line of argument, one should use it.

## CHAPTER III. The lines of argument for constructing and destroying predicates

That it is more difficult to construct than to destroy a definition is clear from what will be said later. For it is not easy to know for oneself, or to obtain from questioners, propositions of the following kind: that of the elements contained in the assigned account one is the genus, another the differentia; and that, in respect of what it is, genus and differentiae are predicated. Without these it is impossible to construct a syllogism of a definition. For if certain other things are also predicated of the subject in respect of what it is, it is uncertain whether the account in question or another is its definition, since a definition is an account indicating what a thing is.

This is also clear from the following considerations. It is easier to establish one conclusion than many, and, when destroying a definition, it is enough to argue against one point. Whatever that one point may be, by destroying it we shall destroy the definition. But in constructing a definition, it is necessary to establish everything that is contained in it.

Moreover, in constructing one must establish a universal syllogism. For the definition must be predicated of everything of which the name is predicated, and must also be convertible: everything of which the account and the name are predicated, if the definition assigned is to be proper. In destroying, however, it is not necessary to show this universally. It is enough to show that the account is not true of some one of the things falling under the name. Even when the universal must be destroyed, it is not necessary, in destroying, to establish the converse. For the person destroying the universal need only show that the account is not predicated of some thing of which the name is predicated; conversely, it is not necessary to show that of the things of which the account is not predicated, the name is likewise not predicated.

Further, if the account is present in everything included under the name but not in that alone, the definition has been destroyed. The same holds concerning what is proper and concerning the genus. In both cases, destruction is easier than construction.

This is clear in the case of what is proper from what has been said. For what is proper is usually assigned as a combination of several elements; hence, in destroying it, it is enough to destroy one element, whereas in constructing it one must collect all the elements by reasoning. Nearly everything else that can appropriately be said concerning a definition and what is proper follows the same pattern. For in constructing, one must show that the account is present in everything falling under the name, while in destroying it is enough to show that it is absent from one thing. If it is present in everything but not in that alone, the definition has likewise been destroyed, just as was said in the case of a definition.

In the case of the genus, construction has only one method: showing that the genus belongs to everything. Destruction, however, has two methods, since the original claim is destroyed if it is shown either that the genus belongs to no thing or that it does not belong to some one thing. Again, in construction it is not enough to show that it is present; one must also show that it is present as a genus. In destruction it is enough to show that it is absent from either some thing or from all things.

It appears that, as in other matters, destruction is easier than construction, so here too it is easier to destroy than to construct. In the case of an accidental predicate, a universal is easier to destroy than to construct. For in constructing, one must show that it belongs to everything; in destroying, it is enough to show that it does not belong to one thing.

With a particular claim the reverse is true, since construction is easier than destruction. In constructing, it is enough to show that it belongs to some thing; in destroying, one must show that it belongs to no thing.

It is clear why destroying a definition is easiest of all. The materials supplied by the many claims are numerous, and from many premises a syllogism is constructed more quickly; moreover, error is more likely in many cases than in few.

Further, in the case of a definition, one can argue by other means as well. For if the definition is not proper, or if the assigned term is not a genus, or if one of the elements contained in the definition does not belong, the definition has been destroyed. In the other cases, however, it is not possible to argue from terms or in all the other ways. Only arguments concerning the accident are common to all the predicates mentioned. Each of the elements described must be present; but if the genus is not present as what is proper, the genus has not yet been destroyed. Likewise, it is not necessary for what is proper to be present as a genus, nor for an accident to be present as a genus or as what is proper, but only that it be present. Thus it is not possible to argue from one of these predicates to another, except in the case of a definition.

It is therefore clear that destroying a definition is easiest of all, while constructing one is most difficult. For one must establish all the elements by reasoning: that the stated elements are present, that the assigned element is a genus, that the definition is proper, and, in addition to these, that the account indicates what it is for the thing to be. All of this must be done correctly.

What is proper is, among the other predicates, especially of this kind. Destruction is easier because it is usually constituted from several elements. Construction is most difficult because many things must be established, as well as that it belongs to the subject alone and is predicated convertibly of the subject.

Constructing an accident is easiest of all. For in the other cases one must show not only that the predicate is present but also the manner in which it is present; in the case of an accident, it is enough to show simply that it is present. Destroying an accident, however, is most difficult, because the claims supplied in its case are fewest: an accident does not signify how it is present.

Thus, in the other cases, destruction can be accomplished in two ways, either by showing that the predicate is absent or by showing that it is not present in the relevant manner. In the case of an accident, it can be destroyed only by showing that it is absent.

The lines of argument by which we shall have abundant means of arguing each of the various problems have now been enumerated almost sufficiently.

# BOOK VIII

[Col. 0993]

## CHAPTER I. Lines of argument for instructing the questioner

After this, we must discuss the order and the manner in which one ought to ask questions. First, the questioner must find the line of argument from which the argument is to proceed; second, he must question and arrange each point within his own mind; finally, as the third step, he must state the same things to the other person.

Finding the line of argument is a matter for the philosopher and the dialectician alike. Arranging it and questioning, however, belong specifically to the dialectician, since everything of this kind is directed toward another person.

For the philosopher investigating by himself, it is of no concern whether the respondent grants the premises through which the syllogism is formed, provided that they are true and known; for they are close to the principles, and he foresees what follows. Indeed, he may even proceed deliberately, since the axioms are especially well known and close at hand; scientific syllogisms are formed from them.

The lines from which one ought to take one’s premises have already been stated. We must now discuss order and questioning by distinguishing the propositions that are to be taken for the necessities of the argument. “Necessary” propositions are those through which the syllogism is formed. The propositions taken from these are of four kinds. They are introduced either for the sake of induction, as when a universal claim is to be made evident; or for enlarging the account; or for concealing the conclusion; or for making the account clearer. Apart from these, no proposition should be introduced. One must try to enlarge the argument and conduct the questioning by means of them.

Some propositions serve concealment for the sake of disputation. But since every undertaking of this kind is directed toward another person, they too must be used.

The necessary propositions through which the syllogism is formed should not be arranged at once; rather, one should go back to the highest principles. Thus, if one wishes to obtain the proposition that the same science concerns contraries, one should not ask for it immediately, but should first ask for the proposition concerning opposites. Once this has been assumed, the proposition that the same science concerns contraries can be established by syllogism, since contraries derive from opposites.

If the proposition concerning opposites is not established by induction, the person proposing it must take it in particular cases involving opposites. The necessary propositions must therefore be obtained either by syllogism or by induction—or some by induction and others by syllogism.

Those propositions that are especially evident should also be put forward first. For what will follow is always less evident in a digression and through induction. At the same time, one should put forward the necessary propositions themselves, and whoever cannot proceed in this way should be prepared to obtain them. The propositions taken for the sake of these are to be accepted for the sake of the necessary propositions.

Each proposition should be used in the following way: in induction, one proceeds from particulars to universals and from what is known to what is unknown. What is more readily known is what is known through perception, either simply, in a plurality of cases, or by the majority.

When concealing the argument, one should first collect the steps by which the syllogism of the original position is to be formed, and these should generally be numerous. This will happen if one syllogizes not only the necessary propositions but also some of those useful for establishing them.

Further, one should not state the conclusions, but later derive them by syllogism as though they were spontaneous. In this way one will depart as far as possible from the original position.

In general, the person who questions covertly should question in such a way that, when the whole argument has been questioned and the respondent states the conclusion, the reason for it is sought. This will happen especially by the method described above. For if only the final conclusion is stated, it is unclear how it came about, since the respondent has not foreseen from which premises it followed, because the earlier syllogisms were not divided into their parts.

A syllogism is least divided into its parts when its premises are not stated, but when the premises from which the syllogism is formed are themselves obtained.

It is also useful to take the premises from which the syllogisms are formed not consecutively, but alternately, moving from one conclusion to another. For when appropriate premises are placed next to one another, what follows from them becomes more evident.

When possible, one should also obtain a universal proposition through a definition, not in the terms themselves but in their cognates. For respondents deceive themselves through false reasoning when a definition is taken in a cognate form, if they do not concede the universal claim. For example, if one must obtain the proposition that someone who is angry desires punishment, one may take “anger” to be a desire for punishment arising from apparent contempt. Once this has been assumed, it is clear that the universal proposition previously chosen will be obtained.

But when the proposition is put directly in the terms themselves, the respondent often objects, since the matter admits of a more plausible counterexample—for example, that not everyone who is angry desires punishment, since we are angry with our parents but do not desire to punish them. Perhaps this is not a true counterexample, since for some people sufficient punishment consists merely in causing distress and making the offender regret his conduct; nevertheless, it has some plausibility, so that the respondent does not appear to reject the proposition irrationally. It is not equally easy to find a counterexample when the definition of anger is used [Col. 0995C].

Moreover, it is appropriate to put forward the proposition not for its own sake but for the sake of something else. For respondents avoid whatever is useful to the original position.

In general, one should make it as uncertain as possible whether one intends to assume the proposition put forward or its opposite. When it is uncertain which of the alternatives is useful to the original position, respondents are more likely to state what seems to them appropriate.
