One should also question by analogy. For this is both plausible and more effective at concealing the universal proposition. For example, just as knowledge and ignorance of contraries are the same, so too perception of contraries is the same; or conversely, once it has been established that perception of contraries is the same, one may establish the same of knowledge.

This resembles induction, but it is not the same. In induction, the universal is obtained from particulars; in cases of analogy, there is no universal under which all the similar things fall.

The questioner should sometimes also provide a counterexample against himself. Respondents are less suspicious of those who appear to argue fairly.

It is useful to state what is customary and what is commonly said. People are reluctant to disturb what is customary when they have no counterexample; and because they themselves use such expressions, they are cautious about challenging them.

Further, one should not proceed too assiduously, even when that would be entirely useful. For respondents resist those who proceed too assiduously.

It is also useful to present, by way of analogy, what is being proposed for the sake of something else, and not for its own sake. They are then more likely to accept it.

Further, one should not propose the proposition that must be obtained, but one whose consequence is what is required—that is, what follows necessarily. For they are more likely to concede it, since it is not equally evident from this proposition what will follow; and once this is granted, the other proposition is granted as well.

The proposition one most wants to obtain should be questioned last. For respondents are most resistant to the first questions, since most questioners begin with the points about which they are especially concerned.

With some respondents, however, it is useful to put forward the useful premises first. Insolent respondents most readily accept the first premises unless what will follow is entirely obvious; at the end they become insolent. The same is true of those who think themselves clever at answering. After accepting the first premises, they retract at the end, as though nothing had followed from what they had granted. They accept the first premises readily because they trust their own ability and think that they will suffer no harm.

It is also useful to prolong the argument and insert matters that have no bearing on it, as those who use a false proof do. When there are several premises, it is unclear where the falsehood lies; thus questioners sometimes conceal it by putting forward, in a hidden manner, premises that they would not have stated by themselves. One should therefore use the methods described for concealment.

## CHAPTER II. Other lines of argument for instructing the respondent

For ornament, one should use induction and the division of things that are related. What induction is has been made clear. Division is of the following kind: saying that one science is better than another either because it is more exact or because it concerns better objects; or saying that some sciences are theoretical, others practical, and still others productive. Each such device embellishes the account, but it is not necessary that it be stated for the conclusion.

For clarity, examples and analogies should be brought forward. The examples should be appropriate and drawn from things we know, such as examples from Homer rather than from Choerilus. In this way what is proposed will be clearer.

In discussion, syllogism should be used more with dialecticians than with the general public, whereas induction should be used more with the general public. These matters have been discussed both here and earlier.

In some cases, the person using induction can question universally; in others this is not easy, because no common name has been established for all the similar things. When a universal proposition must be obtained, people say that all such cases are alike.

It is extremely difficult to determine which things are of this kind and which are not. For this reason, disputants often disagree: some say that things are similar when they are not, while others doubt that things which are similar are similar.

Accordingly, in all such cases one should try to coin names oneself, so that the respondent cannot claim that the conclusion has not been stated in a similar manner, and the questioner cannot quibble by saying that things expressed alike have been expressed differently—for many things that are not expressed alike appear to be expressed alike.

When the person using induction has not been granted a universal proposition in several cases, it is fair to demand a counterexample. But when he himself has not stated that the cases are alike in some respects and unlike in others, it is not fair to demand one in certain cases but not in others. The person using induction must first demand a counterexample in this way.

A counterexample should not be brought against the proposition as stated unless there is only one case of the kind—for example, the duality of even numbers, where two is the only prime even number. The person presenting the counterexample must either produce one in another case or say that this case alone is of the relevant kind.

Against those who produce a counterexample to a universal proposition, but do so in a different sense—for example, to the claim that someone who has a color, foot, or hand that is not his own possesses such a thing, since a painter has a color that is not his own and a cook has a foot that is not his own—one must question by dividing the senses involved. For when the equivocation remains concealed, they may appear to raise a good objection against the proposition.

If the objection is not based on equivocation but genuinely obstructs the question by presenting a counterexample in the same sense, the person removing the objection must state the remainder after eliminating the point in which the counterexample lies, making the proposition universal until he obtains what is useful.

For example, in the case of forgetting and having forgotten, they do not concede that someone who has lost knowledge has forgotten, because while the knowledge has passed away he has lost it but has not forgotten it. The person removing the objection should state the remainder after eliminating the point in which the counterexample lies: “If he lost the knowledge while it remained available, then he has forgotten it.”

The same method applies against those who raise an objection to the claim that a greater good has a greater evil opposed to it. They say, for example, that health is a lesser good than good condition, but that the evil opposed to health is greater, since illness is a greater evil than bad condition.

Here too one must eliminate the point in which the counterexample lies. Once it has been removed, the respondent will be more likely to accept the claim: a greater good has a greater evil opposed to it, provided that one thing is compared with another in the same way that good condition is compared with health.

This should be done not only when the respondent raises an objection but also when he denies the proposition without producing one, because he anticipates something of this kind. Once the point in which the counterexample lies has been removed, he will be compelled to accept the proposition, since he will not anticipate that the remainder fails in some case. If he does not accept it, then, when challenged to produce a counterexample, he will have none to give.

There are propositions that are false in one respect but true in another. In these cases, it is fair to remove the false respect and leave the remainder true.

If the respondent does not produce a counterexample in several cases when a proposition is put forward, he should be asked to concede it. For a dialectical proposition is one for which, when it holds in most cases, there is no counterexample.

When it is possible to syllogize the same conclusion both without an impossibility and through an impossibility, this makes no difference to someone demonstrating rather than engaging in discussion. But a person engaged in disputation should not use a syllogism through impossibility. For if he reaches the conclusion without an impossibility, there is little chance that the respondents will object; but when he syllogizes through an impossibility, unless the falsehood is very obvious, they say that the proposition is not impossible, and thus the questioners fail to obtain what they want.

One should put forward propositions that hold in most cases. A counterexample either does not exist at all or is not apparent on the surface, since those who cannot see the cases in which the proposition does not hold accept it as true.

One should not turn the conclusion itself into a question. Otherwise, if the respondent refuses it, the syllogism will not appear to have been completed. Often, even when the questioner does not ask it as a question but draws it as a consequence, respondents deny it; and by doing so they do not appear to have been refuted before those who cannot see what follows from the premises that have been granted.

When the questioner does not state that the conclusion follows but asks for it, and the respondent denies it, it does not appear at all that a syllogism has been completed.

Nor is every universal question a dialectical proposition—for example, “What is a human being?” or “In how many ways is ‘good’ used?” A dialectical proposition is one to which it is possible to respond “yes” or “no.” The questions just mentioned do not admit such an answer. Therefore questions of this kind are not dialectical unless the questioner himself determines or divides the alternatives, as in: “Is ‘good’ used in this sense or not?”

Questions of this kind admit of an easy answer, either affirmative or negative. Therefore one must try to formulate such propositions in this way.

At the same time, it may perhaps be fair to ask the respondent, “In how many ways is ‘good’ used?” when, after the questioner has divided and proposed the alternatives, the respondent has conceded none of them.

Whoever questions one account for a long time is questioning badly. For if the respondent’s answer does answer the question, it is clear that the questioner is asking several questions, or repeatedly asking the same question. Thus he is either wasting time or has no syllogism, since every syllogism proceeds from a few premises.

If the respondent does not answer, why does the questioner not rebuke him or withdraw?

It is difficult to argue, but easy to maintain the suppositions themselves. Such suppositions include those that are naturally first and those that are naturally last. The first require a definition, while the last are established through many steps by anyone who wishes to take a continuous series from the first principles; otherwise the arguments appear sophistical. For it is impossible to demonstrate anything unless one begins from the proper principles and connects the argument through to the last conclusions.

Respondents attach no importance to defining, and even when the questioner defines a term, they pay no attention. Yet unless it is made clear what the proposed subject is, it is not easy to argue.

This happens especially with principles. Other things are demonstrated through them, but they cannot themselves be demonstrated through other things; each such principle must necessarily be known through a definition.

There are also positions that are difficult to argue because they are very close to a principle. It is impossible to find many arguments for them, since there are few intermediate steps between them and the principles through which what follows them must be demonstrated.

Among terms, those are most difficult to argue against that employ names whose meaning is initially unclear: whether they are used simply or in several senses, and further whether it is uncertain whether they are predicated of the defined subject literally or metaphorically.

Because they are obscure, no arguments are available; and because it is unknown whether the expression is being used without metaphor, there is nothing with which to reproach the respondent.

In general, whenever a problem is difficult to argue, one should suppose that it either requires a definition, belongs among things that have several senses, belongs among things said metaphorically of the defined subject, lies close to principles, or is difficult because it is not clear to us at the outset which of these ways accounts for the difficulty.

Once the source of the difficulty is clear, it is clear that one must either define, divide, or find intermediate propositions. For the final conclusions are demonstrated through these.

In many positions, when the definition has not been properly assigned, it is not easy to dispute or argue—for example, whether one thing has a contrary or several contraries. But once contraries have been defined in some manner, it is easy to show whether one thing can have several contraries or not. The same applies to other matters requiring definition.

Certain matters in the sciences also appear difficult to describe because of a deficiency in definition. For example, it is said that a line which cuts a plane *ad latus* (‘at the side’; technical sense uncertain) likewise divides both the line and the area. Once the definition has been stated, what is meant is immediately clear. For areas and lines undergo the same subtraction; and this is the definition of the statement in question.

In general, with the first elements, once definitions have been given—such as what a line is or what a circle is—it is easiest to demonstrate the relevant claims, although it is not possible to find many arguments for each of them, since there are few intermediate steps. If definitions of the principles are not given, however, the task is difficult, and perhaps altogether impossible.

The same applies to matters concerning accounts. One must therefore not fail to notice, when a position is difficult to argue, that it has been affected by one of the circumstances described above. When the matter concerns an axiom and a proposition, disputation is more laborious than when it concerns a position.

Someone might raise the question whether other assumptions should be added. If one does not add them, but demands that the dispute be conducted against them, one will impose a greater task than the original position required; but if one adds them, one will be reasoning from premises that are less credible.

If the problem is not to be made more difficult, they should therefore be added; but if the intention is to syllogize from more familiar premises, they should not be added. Or perhaps they should not be added for a learner unless they are better known, but should be added for someone already trained, if they appear to be true on their own.

It is therefore clear that one must not judge in the same way what ought to be assumed for a questioner and for a teacher.

This is almost sufficient concerning the manner in which one ought to question and arrange the argument.

## CHAPTER III. Lines of argument for the respondent.

Concerning the respondent, we must first determine what constitutes the proper task of a good respondent, just as we determined the task of a good questioner. The questioner’s task is to conduct the argument in such a way as to make the respondent say things more contrary to accepted opinion than those which necessarily follow from the position. The respondent’s task, however, is not to appear to suffer an impossibility or something contrary to accepted opinion on his own account, but on account of the position; for the other possibility is perhaps a fault: to assume at the outset what ought not to be assumed, and then in some way fail to preserve what has been assumed.

Since matters are indeterminate for those who conduct arguments for the sake of practice and experience—for the considerations are not the same for learners, teachers, and disputants, nor for those who practice with one another for the sake of examination—for a learner must always be granted what appears to be so, since no one attempts to teach what is false, whereas among disputants the questioner must altogether appear to be doing something, while the respondent must appear to be suffering nothing—and since, in dialectical encounters conducted not for the sake of contention but of experiment and examination, it has not yet been made clear how one ought to challenge the respondent, what one ought to grant, and what one ought not to grant, in order to preserve the position well or badly, let us ourselves attempt to say something, since, as I have said, nothing has been handed down by others.

The respondent must necessarily sustain the argument by assuming a position that is probable, improbable, or neither; and either simply probable, simply improbable, or indeterminate—probable or improbable for this person or for another. It makes no difference how the position is characterized, provided that it is probable or improbable; for the same method will apply to responding well, whether one grants or refuses what has been asked. For when the position is improbable, the conclusion must be probable; when the position is probable, the conclusion must be improbable. The questioner will always conclude the opposite of the position. If what has been assumed is neither probable nor improbable, the conclusion will likewise be of that kind.

Since a person who syllogizes well demonstrates what is proposed from things more probable and better known, it is clear that, when what is proposed is simply improbable, the respondent should grant neither what is not simply apparent, nor what is indeed apparent but appears less so than the conclusion. For when the position is improbable, the conclusion is probable. Therefore all the assumptions must be probable, and more probable than what is proposed, if what is less known is to be concluded through what is better known. Accordingly, if none of the questions has this character, the respondent should not assume it.

If the position is simply probable, it is clear that the conclusion is simply improbable. The respondent should therefore assume everything that appears to be so, and, among the things that do not appear to be so, whatever is less improbable than the conclusion. In this way the dispute will appear to have been conducted sufficiently well.

The same will hold if the position is neither improbable nor probable. In that case too, everything that appears to be so should be granted, and among what does not appear to be so, whatever is less improbable than the conclusion; for in this way the arguments will happen to become more probable.

If, then, what is assumed is simply probable or improbable, comparison must be made with what appears simply to be so. But if what is assumed is not simply probable or improbable, but probable or improbable for the respondent, he must judge by what appears and does not appear to himself whether it should be assumed.

If the respondent is defending another person’s opinion, it is clear that he must look to that person’s understanding when assuming or denying each point. Thus those who concern themselves with foreign opinions—for example, the claim that good and evil are the same, as Heraclitus says—do not grant that contraries cannot simultaneously be present in the same thing. This is not because such a claim appears true to them, but because, according to Heraclitus, that is what must be said. The same is done by those who take up one another’s positions: they challenge one another as though the person who assumed the position were making the claim. It is therefore clear what the respondent must conjecture, whether the position assumed is simply probable or probable for someone in particular.

Since everything asked must be either probable, improbable, or neither, and since what is asked may or may not pertain to the argument, the following rules apply. If what is asked appears to be so and does not pertain to the argument, it should be granted, with the statement that it appears so. For, once it has been assumed, the original position is not destroyed.

If it does not appear to be so and does not pertain to the argument, it should nevertheless be granted, while indicating that it does not appear to be so, in order to avoid absurdity.

If it pertains to the argument and appears to be so, one should say that it does appear so, but is very close to what was assumed at the outset, and that, once it is assumed, the proposed conclusion is destroyed.

If it pertains to the argument but is a highly probable assumption, one should say that this follows once it is assumed, but that what is proposed is highly absurd.

If it is neither probable nor improbable and does not pertain to the argument, it should be granted without any determination.

If it does pertain to the argument, one should indicate that, once it is assumed, the original position is destroyed. [Col. 1001B] In this way the respondent will not appear to suffer anything on that account, provided that he anticipates each point before assuming it; and the questioner will obtain a syllogism only after having assumed all the things more probable than the conclusion. Those who attempt to syllogize a conclusion from things that are not more probable plainly do not syllogize well. Therefore, when they ask questions in this way, the respondent should not grant them.

The same method must be used with things said obscurely or ambiguously. Since the respondent, rather than the learner, is permitted to say “I do not understand,” and since an ambiguous statement need not necessarily be affirmed or denied, it is clear that, whenever what is said is not plain, one should not hesitate to say “I do not understand.” Often something difficult arises because respondents grant propositions that questioners have not stated clearly.

If the statement is known but ambiguous, then, if what is said is wholly true or wholly false, it should simply be granted or denied. But if it is true in one respect and false in another, one must indicate that it is ambiguous, and say that this part is false while that part is true. For when the distinction is made only later, it remains unclear whether the ambiguity was also noticed at the beginning.

If the respondent did not foresee the ambiguity, but granted one interpretation while the questioner was directing the question toward another, he should say to the questioner who is leading toward the other interpretation: “I granted it with reference not to that interpretation, but to the other of the two.” Whenever several things fall under the same name or the same expression, ambiguity is easy.

If what is asked is clear and simple, the answer should be either “yes” or “no.”

Since every syllogistic proposition is either one of the propositions from which a syllogism is formed, or is taken because of one of them, it is clear that sometimes one proposition will be taken for the sake of another when several similar questions are asked. For universals are usually obtained either by induction or by analogy. All the particulars should therefore be granted, if they are true and probable; but one should attempt to produce a counterexample to the universal. For to block an argument without either a counterexample that exists or one that appears possible is merely contentiousness. If, then, a person who has no counterexample refuses to grant a universal that appears to hold in many cases, it is clear that he is being contentious.

Further, if he has no counterargument showing that the universal is not true, he will appear even more contentious, although this by itself is not sufficient. We have many arguments opposed to common opinions that are difficult to resolve, such as Zeno’s arguments that motion is impossible and that one cannot traverse the stadium. But this does not mean that propositions contrary to those arguments should not be granted. If, therefore, a person who has neither a counterargument nor a counterexample refuses to grant what is clear, he is plainly being contentious.

In disputes, a contentious response, apart from the methods already mentioned, consists in destroying the syllogism. One ought to sustain both the position and its definition, anticipating objections and arguing against them. For it is clear that one must oppose the points by which the questioners destroy what has been proposed.

One must be cautious about maintaining an improbable supposition. An improbable supposition may be so in several ways: it may entail absurd consequences, as when someone says that everything moves or that nothing moves; it may involve choosing a morally worse way of life; or it may be contrary to accepted counsels, such as the claim that pleasure is good or that it is better to commit injustice than to suffer it. People dislike someone who sustains such claims not as a matter of argument, but as though he genuinely held and asserted opinions of this kind.

Whenever an argument syllogizes something false, it must be resolved by destroying the point on account of which the falsity arises. For a person does not resolve an argument merely by destroying any proposition, not even if the proposition destroyed is false. An argument may contain several false propositions. For example, suppose someone assumes that a seated person is writing and that Socrates is seated; it follows from these assumptions that Socrates is writing. If, then, one destroys the proposition “Socrates is seated,” the argument is no more resolved than before, although the proposition destroyed is false; for the argument is not false on that account. If someone is seated but not writing, the same solution will no longer apply to such a case. Therefore it is not “Socrates is seated” that must be destroyed, but “a seated person is writing,” since not everyone who is seated writes.

A person resolves an argument completely when he destroys the proposition on account of which the falsity arises. A person knows the solution when he knows that the argument is false because of that proposition, as in cases where things are falsely described. It is not enough merely to produce a counterexample, even if the proposition destroyed is false; one must also identify the proposition on account of which the argument is false. In this way it will be clear whether the counterexample was made with foresight or not.

## CHAPTER IV. Common Topics for the Questioner and the Respondent

There are four ways of preventing a conclusion from being reached. One is by destroying the point on account of which the falsity arises. Another is by producing a counterexample against the questioner; for often this does not actually resolve the argument, but it prevents the questioner from carrying it further. The third is directed against the questions themselves. For it may happen that the desired conclusion does not follow from the questions as asked because they were badly formulated, but that it does follow once something is added.

If the questioner can no longer carry the argument further, the counterexample is directed against the questioner; if he can carry it further, it is directed against the questions.

The fourth and worst kind of counterexample is one directed against the time available. Some people produce counterexamples to matters that would require more time to discuss than is available for the present exercise. Thus, as was said earlier, counterexamples occur in four ways.

Strictly speaking, only the first of these is a resolution; the others are certain means of blocking and impeding conclusions.

The blame for an argument may concern the argument itself or the way in which the question is asked, and these are not the same. For most often an argument is not properly conducted because the respondent is responsible: he does not grant the propositions from which the argument should properly have been conducted in relation to the position. It is not the sole responsibility of either party to bring the common task to completion.

Accordingly, it is sometimes necessary to argue against the speaker rather than against the position, when the respondent observes propositions contrary to the questioner’s claims and thereby strengthens his own case. Those who behave contentiously and quarrelsomely thus make their exercises contentious rather than dialectical.

Moreover, since arguments of this sort are conducted for the sake of practice and experiment, not instruction, it is clear that one must syllogize not only the truth but also the falsehood, and not always through true premises but sometimes through false ones. For often, once a true proposition has been assumed, the disputant must destroy it. Therefore false propositions must sometimes be proposed; and when a false proposition has been assumed, it must sometimes be destroyed through false propositions. Nothing prevents someone from finding propositions that do not hold more convincing than true ones. Consequently, an argument constructed from what appears true to that person will persuade him more than it will assist him.

A person who carries an argument well must conduct it dialectically, not contentiously: he must deal with a geometer geometrically, whether the conclusion is false or true. What dialectical syllogisms are was stated earlier.

Since a bad participant is one who obstructs the common task, the same is plainly true of arguments. There is something proposed as a common task in these arguments also, except among disputants engaged in mere contention. In their case it is impossible for both parties to reach the same end, since several persons cannot defeat one person.

It makes no difference whether the fault occurs in responding or in questioning. The person who questions contentiously argues badly; and the person who, in responding, refuses to grant what appears to be so, or refuses to accept anything that the questioner wishes to ask, also argues badly.

It is therefore clear from what has been said that the blame assigned to the argument itself and the blame assigned to the questioner are not the same. Nothing prevents an argument from being bad in itself while the questioner, as far as possible, argues excellently against the respondent. For against contentious respondents it may perhaps not be possible immediately to take whatever propositions one wishes, but only such as can be made into syllogisms.

Since it is indeterminate when people take contrary propositions and when they take the propositions assumed at the outset—for people often state contradictory things on their own, and after initially denying something grant it later, because they commonly comply with the questioner both in contrary matters and in matters assumed at the beginning—disputes necessarily become bad. The cause is that the respondent grants some propositions of one kind and others of another kind. It is therefore clear that the questioners and the arguments should not be blamed in the same way.

There are five ways in which an argument may be blamed in itself.

First, when nothing is concluded from the questions—not what was proposed, nor anything at all—although the questions are false or improbable, and although all or most of the propositions on which the conclusion ought to rest are present, and although the conclusion does not follow whether certain propositions are removed, others added, or some removed and others added.

Second, when no syllogism is formed in relation to the position, from propositions of the sort and in the manner stated earlier.

Third, when a syllogism is formed only after certain propositions are added, and these are worse than the propositions asked, less probable than the conclusion, even if some propositions are removed. For sometimes people assume more than is necessary, and the syllogism does not arise merely because these propositions are present.

Further, an argument is defective if it concludes from things more improbable and less credible than the conclusion, or if it demonstrates from true propositions but through a greater amount of work than the problem itself requires. One should not suppose that syllogisms derived from all problems are equally probable and persuasive. Some of the questions are naturally easier, others more difficult. Therefore, if someone makes his challenge from propositions that are as probable as possible, insofar as this can be done, the argument has been properly conducted.

It is therefore clear that the blame assigned to an argument is not the same in relation to the problem and in itself. Nothing prevents an argument from being blameworthy in itself but praiseworthy in relation to the problem, or conversely, praiseworthy in itself but blameworthy in relation to the problem, when it is easy to conclude from several propositions that are both probable and true.

Sometimes an argument that reaches a conclusion will be worse than one that does not. The former may conclude from absurdities when the problem is not of that kind, whereas the latter may require propositions that are probable and true, and the argument may not yet have been formed from the assumptions.

Those who conclude something true through false propositions should not be blamed. A false conclusion must always be syllogized through false propositions, but it is sometimes possible to syllogize a true conclusion through false propositions, as was stated earlier. This is clear from the *Analytica*.

When an argument has been stated as a demonstration of something, if it contains anything else that has no relation at all to the conclusion, no syllogism will be formed from it. If it nevertheless appears to produce a conclusion, it will be a sophism, not a demonstration.

A *philosopheme* is a demonstrative syllogism; an *epichireme* is a dialectical syllogism; a sophism is a contentious syllogism; and an *aporeme* is a dialectical syllogism leading to contradiction.

If something is demonstrated from propositions that both appear to be so, but do not appear so equally, nothing prevents the demonstrated conclusion from appearing more convincing than one of the premises.

But if one proposition appears to be so and the other appears neither true nor false, or if one appears true and the other does not appear true, then, when they appear equally, the result will be equally so or not so; but when one appears more convincing, the conclusion will follow from the more convincing one.

There is also the same kind of fault in syllogisms when what can be shown through shorter means is demonstrated through longer ones, using elements that are extraneous to the argument. For example, suppose someone asks whether one opinion is more probable than another, and then asks whether each thing is most fully what it is, and whether what truly exists is what is capable of being opined. It would then follow that some things are more fully what they are. But is what is more probable also said to be more fully what it is, and is the opinion itself also true? Would this be more exact than is appropriate, as though one were demanding an excessive degree of precision?

The assumptions made were that the opinion itself is true and that each thing is most fully what it is, as though the opinion itself were more certain because it is true. But what greater fault is there than to make the cause of the argument escape notice in the very matter about which the argument is concerned?

An argument is manifest in one way, the most public and obvious, when it reaches a conclusion in such a way that nothing further needs to be asked. It is manifest in another way, and in the way most often mentioned, when the propositions have been assumed from which it is necessary that the conclusion follow—propositions which themselves have been established through conclusions—even if the highly probable proposition is omitted.

## CHAPTER V. Common Topics for the Opponent and the Respondent

A false argument is so called in four ways.

First, when it appears to reach a conclusion although it does not. This is called an apparent or contentious syllogism.

Second, when it does reach a conclusion, but not the conclusion proposed. This occurs especially in arguments that lead to an impossibility.

Third, when it reaches the proposed conclusion, but not according to the proper discipline. For example, something that is not medical may appear to be medically established; something that is not geometrical may appear to be geometrically established; or something that is not dialectical may appear to be dialectically established, whether the resulting conclusion is true or false.

Fourth, when it does not conclude through false propositions. In this case the conclusion may sometimes be false and sometimes true; for a false conclusion always requires false propositions, but a true conclusion may be reached without true propositions, as was stated earlier.

That an argument is false is rather the fault of the person who states it than of the argument itself. Yet this is not always the fault of the speaker, but only when the person who stated the false argument has concealed the fact from himself. For when we accept something additional from him together with several true propositions, and he destroys one of the truths that appear most firmly established—for such a set of truths constitutes a demonstration—then at least one of the propositions assumed must not be wholly true, and the result will be a demonstration of this fact.

If someone concludes something true through false and highly absurd propositions, his argument will be worse than one that syllogizes something false. The same will be true of an argument that concludes something false.

It is therefore clear that the first consideration regarding an argument in itself is whether it reaches a conclusion; the second is whether the conclusion is true or false; and the third concerns the kind of propositions from which it concludes. If it concludes from false but plausible propositions, it is reasonable. If it concludes from true but improbable propositions, it is defective. If the propositions are both false and highly improbable, it is plainly defective, either absolutely or in relation to the matter at hand.

How the questioner should ask for what was assumed at the beginning, and for its contrary, has been stated according to truth in the *Analytica*; it must now be stated according to common opinion.

People appear to beg the original assumption in five ways.

The clearest and first occurs when someone asks for the very thing that ought to be demonstrated. This may not easily remain concealed when the same words are used, but it is more likely to remain concealed in synonyms and wherever a name and its definition signify the same thing.

The second occurs when someone asks universally for what ought to be demonstrated particularly. For example, someone who argues that there is one discipline of contraries may assume that there is one discipline of all opposites. He appears to be asking, together with several other cases, for what he ought to have demonstrated in itself.

The third occurs when someone asks particularly for what he ought to demonstrate universally. For example, if the proposition concerns all contraries, he asks for it with respect to some of them. Here too he appears to be asking outside the proper demonstration for what ought to have been demonstrated together with several other cases.

Again, someone begs the question by dividing the problem. For example, if one must show that medicine concerns both the healthy and the sick, he separately assumes each of the two. Or someone may ask for one of two propositions that necessarily follow one another, as when, if it is necessary to show that the diameter is incommensurable with the side, he assumes that the side is incommensurable with the diameter.

Contraries are begged in the same way as the original assumption.

First, someone may ask for opposites according to affirmation and negation.

Second, he may ask for contraries according to opposition, such as asking whether good and evil are the same.

Third, someone may ask for a contradiction universally while presenting it particularly. For example, having assumed that there is one discipline of contraries, he asks whether the healthy and the sick have different disciplines; or, having asked this particular question, he attempts to take the opposition universally.

Again, someone may ask for the contrary of what necessarily follows from the propositions assumed. Or he may fail to assume the actual opposites and instead ask for two other propositions from which the contradictory opposition follows.

There is a slight difference between assuming contraries and begging the original assumption. The fault involved in begging the original assumption concerns the conclusion: by looking to the conclusion, we say that the original assumption has been begged. Contraries, however, are found in the propositions because the propositions themselves stand in some relation to one another.

For practice and training in arguments of this kind, one should first become accustomed to reversing arguments. In this way we shall acquire a greater supply of material for what is said and shall know several arguments from a few. To reverse an argument is to take its conclusion together with the remaining questions and destroy one of the propositions previously stated. For if there is no conclusion, one of the propositions must be destroyed, since, if all had been assumed, the conclusion necessarily would have followed.

For every position one should consider an argument both for and against it, and, once one has found such arguments, immediately seek their solutions. In this way one will simultaneously be trained both to question and to respond. Even if one has no one else available, one should gradually acquire within oneself the arguments relevant to the position. This provides a great abundance of material for compelling an opponent and considerable assistance in refutation, when one is ready to argue both for and against a position.

For this makes it possible to observe contraries, and to gain knowledge and philosophical expertise by seeing what follows from each supposition. The remaining task is to choose correctly between them. For this one must possess good judgment. In truth, good judgment consists in being able to choose the truth well and avoid the false. Those who are naturally well endowed can do this properly, since people readily discern what is presented as best when they love or hate it.

One must also know the arguments for the problems that arise most frequently, and especially for the first positions. Respondents often become weary in these matters.

Further, one must have a rich supply of definitions, and have reputable and primary premises ready to hand; for syllogisms are formed through these.

One should also attempt to retain the topics into which disputes most frequently fall. Just as in geometry one must first be trained in the elements, and in arithmetic one must have the basic numbers ready to hand—and it makes a great difference for this purpose to know another number multiplied by them—so too in arguments one must be ready with the principles and know the propositions by heart.

For just as, in the storehouse of memory, locations that have been arranged immediately make the things themselves come to mind, so these arrangements make one quicker at reasoning, because one looks to those fixed locations according to their number.

A common proposition should be stored in memory more readily than a position. To possess a moderate supply of principles and suppositions is difficult.

Moreover, one should become accustomed to making several arguments out of one, like those who conceal things with the greatest secrecy. This will occur if one departs as far as possible from the affinity of the matters under discussion. The most useful arguments will be those that are especially universal and capable of this treatment, such as the claim that there is not one discipline for several things. This applies equally to relatives, contraries, and cognates.

One should also remember to make arguments universal, even when one is disputing a particular case. In this way it will be possible to make several arguments out of one, just as rhetoricians do with enthymemes.

One should especially avoid bringing syllogisms against the same universal proposition.

One must always consider arguments when they are discussed through several common propositions. For all particulars are discussed within a universal, and the demonstration of what is universal is present in particulars, since nothing can be syllogized without a universal.

Practice should be conducted with inductive arguments for the inexperienced, and with syllogistic arguments for the experienced. One should attempt to obtain propositions from those practiced in syllogisms, and analogies from those practiced in induction, since each group is trained in its own kind.

In general, those who dispute for the sake of practice should attempt to produce either a syllogism about something, a proposition, a solution, or a counterexample—whether the speaker is right or wrong, whether it is oneself or someone else, and whether it is directed toward one matter or another. From these comes ability, and practice is undertaken for the sake of ability, especially with propositions and counterexamples.

For, to put it simply, the dialectician is skilled in proposing and producing counterexamples. To propose is to make one thing out of several. One must take one thing as the point to which the argument is directed. To produce a counterexample is to make several things out of one. For one either divides or destroys, granting one part and refusing another of the propositions proposed.

One should not dispute with everyone, nor practice against just anyone. With some people it is necessary for arguments to become defective, since one must avoid anyone who makes every attempt merely to appear victorious. It is entirely proper to attempt to conclude through a syllogism, but it is not honorable to stand ready to contend against just anyone.

For contentiousness necessarily arises from this. Those who are practiced in argument cannot refrain from disputing without quarrelling.

One should also have prepared arguments for problems of this kind, so that with the smallest supply of material one may possess arguments useful for the greatest number of cases. These are the most universal arguments, and those for which it is difficult to discover something readily at hand.

[Col. 1007]

# TWO BOOKS OF ARISTOTLE’S SOPHISTICAL REFUTATIONS, TRANSLATED BY ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS (S)*

## BOOK ONE

### CHAPTER I. What the Work Intends, and What a Sophistical Syllogism Is

[Col. 1007C]

[Col. 1007D] Concerning sophistical refutations and those that appear to be refutations—for they are deceptive arguments, but not refutations—we must speak, beginning naturally with the first principles.

That some arguments are syllogisms while others appear to be syllogisms although they are not is clear. For just as this occurs in other matters through a certain resemblance, so it occurs in arguments. Some things possess the proper form, while others only appear to possess it, swelling themselves up and composing their appearance out of what is borrowed. Some things are beautiful because of their beauty, while others merely appear beautiful because they have adorned themselves with cosmetics.

The same is true of inanimate objects. Some are genuinely silver, while others are genuinely gold; others are not silver or gold, but appear so to the senses, such as objects of litharge or of tin that appear silver, and objects dyed with bile that appear gold.

The same applies to a syllogism and a refutation. One is genuinely such, while the other is not but appears to be so because of inexperience. For inexperienced people, like those standing at a distance, look at things from afar.

A syllogism is an argument in which, once certain things have been assumed, something other than what has been assumed follows necessarily from those assumptions. A refutation is a syllogism together with the contradiction of the conclusion. The apparent refutations do not do this.

They appear to be refutations for many reasons, one of which is especially suitable and common: the use of names. Since it is impossible to bring the things themselves into a dispute, we use names in place of things as signs. We then suppose that what happens with names also happens with the things themselves, just as those who count with pebbles do.

But the resemblance is not exact. Names are limited in number, whereas the number of expressions is unlimited; things, however, are infinite in number. It is therefore necessary that several things be signified by one expression and one name.

Just as those who are not skilled at handling pebbles in calculation are deceived by those who are skilled, so in arguments those who are ignorant of the power of names are easily misled by deceptive arguments, both when they themselves argue and when they listen to others.

For this reason there is both an apparent syllogism and an apparent refutation, although neither truly exists.

### CHAPTER II. The Kinds of Disputations

Since some people consider it more worthwhile to appear wise than to be wise without appearing so—for sophistic wisdom is apparent wisdom that does not exist, and the sophist is a hunter of money through apparent but nonexistent wisdom—it is plainly necessary for such people to appear to perform the work of the wise more than to perform it without appearing to do so.

To state the matter in a general way, the work of the wise person in each field is not to lie about what he knows, but to be able to expose the person who lies. These are two distinct capacities: one consists in being able to give an argument, the other in being able to receive one.

Those who wish to act sophistically must therefore seek the kind of arguments just mentioned. Such a capacity is worthwhile to them, since it will make them appear wise, which is what they desire.

That this is the kind of argument they seek, and that they desire such a capacity, is clear in the case of those whom we call sophists. We must now discuss how many kinds of sophistical arguments there are, from what number of elements this capacity is constituted, how many parts the activity may have, and the other matters that contribute to this art.

There are four kinds of arguments used in disputation: demonstrative, dialectical, investigative, and contentious.

Demonstrative arguments are those that infer conclusions from the proper principles of each discipline, and not from what appears to be so to the respondent; for one must believe the person who makes the assertion.

Dialectical arguments are those that, from probable premises, establish contradictions.

Investigative arguments are those that infer conclusions from what appears to be so to the respondent, and from what someone who pretends to possess knowledge must necessarily know how to determine in other matters.

Contentious arguments are those that syllogize from what appears to be probable, but only apparently.

Demonstrative arguments were discussed in the *Analytica*; dialectical and investigative arguments were discussed elsewhere. We must now discuss quarrelsome and contentious arguments.

### CHAPTER III. The Aims of the Sophist, and Sophistical Topics in Expression
First, then, we must determine the things that those who contend and dispute in argument aim at. There are five in number: refutation, falsity, the paradoxical, solecism, and, fifth, making one’s opponent talk nonsense. This consists in repeatedly forcing him to say the same thing, or to say what is not the case but merely appears to be one of these things. For they chiefly wish to appear to refute; secondly, to demonstrate something false [Col. 1010A]; thirdly, to lead the opponent to what is paradoxical; fourthly, to make him commit a solecism—that is, to make him barbarize in his speech by the form of his expression. Finally, they aim to make him repeat the same thing again and again.

There are two modes of refutation: some arise from the expression, others independently of the expression. The devices that produce an appearance through the expression are six in number: equivocation, amphiboly, combination, division, accent, and the form of expression. The basis of this classification is that of induction, syllogism, and any other such method: the same names and the same expressions do not signify the same things in all their uses.

Arguments arising from equivocation are of the following kind: “Those who know learn.” For grammarians learn what has been handed down in writing [Col. 1010B]. “To learn” (*discere*) is equivocal: it may mean understanding for one who possesses a discipline, or acquiring a discipline.

Again: “Bad things are good,” since what is useful is good, while bad things are useful. For “useful” (*expediens*) is twofold: it may mean what is necessary, which commonly occurs in the case of bad things—for there is some bad thing that is necessary—or we may say that good things also are useful.

Further: “The same person is sitting and standing, sick and healthy.” For one who was rising is standing, and one who was recovering is healthy; yet he was rising while seated, and was recovering while sick. For “a sick person” or “a seated person” doing or undergoing anything whatsoever does not always signify the same thing: sometimes it means the person who is now sick or seated, and sometimes the one who was formerly sick or seated. Yet the person who was recovering was sick [Col. 1010C] while he was sick, whereas he is healthy not while he is sick, but after having been sick.

Arguments arising from amphiboly are of this kind: “I want to seize those who are fighting.” And: “Whatever someone knows, does he know that thing?” For it may be the person who knows, or the thing known, that is signified by the expression. Again: “Whatever someone sees, does he see that?” But he sees a column; therefore, the column sees.

Again: “Whatever you say exists, do you say that you exist?” You say that a stone exists; therefore, you are a stone.

And: “Can one say ‘silences’?” For “to say silences” has two meanings: it may refer to those who say that they are silent, or to the things that are said to be silences.

There are three modes of equivocation and amphiboly. The first occurs when a name or expression primarily signifies several things, as in “eagle” or “dog.” The second occurs when we are accustomed to speak in a certain way. The third occurs when a combined expression signifies several things, while, when separated, it signifies something simple; for example, “to know letters.” Perhaps each word separately signifies one thing—“to know” and “letters”—but together they signify several things: either to possess knowledge of the letters themselves, or to know something concerning letters.

Amphiboly and equivocation arise through these modes.

Arguments arising from combination are of the following kind: “It is possible for a seated person to walk,” and “for a non-writing person to write.” The meaning is not the same when one divides the expression and when one combines it: “It is possible for a seated person to walk,” and “for a non-writing person to write.” The same applies if one combines “a non-writing person writes.” It will then signify that one who is not writing has the power to write [Col. 1011A]; but if one does not combine the expression, it will mean that a person has the power to write whenever he is not writing.

Similarly: “He is now learning letters,” if he has learned the letters that he knows.

Further: “What can carry one thing can carry several things.”

Arguments arising from division include: “Five are two and three,” and “three are even and odd.” Also: “The greater is equal,” since the greater is equal to itself and is also still greater. The same expression, divided and combined, does not always appear to signify the same thing. For example: “I have set you down as a slave, being free.” And: “Achilles left fifty men, a hundred heroes.”

Arguments arising from accent are not easily constructed by dialecticians in speech without writing, but they are more readily found in written texts and poems. Thus some defend the poet against those who accuse him of speaking absurdly in the line:

> Nor will the turtledove cease to moan from the airy elm,

because he has used a penthemimeral caesura and the feminine form “turtledove.” They resolve the difficulty by accent, saying that “airy” (*aeria*) has a long final accent and should be referred not to “turtledove” but to “elm,” as an epithet ought to be.

The same applies to the passage concerning Nisus and Euryalus, when they understood that the Rutulians were buried in wine and sleep:

> The other animals throughout the lands were loosening their cares in sleep,  
> and their hearts, forgetful of toil.

Such, then, are the cases arising from accent.

Those arising from the form of expression occur when one thing is interpreted as though it were another—for example, a masculine term as feminine, or a feminine term as masculine; or when one of these is interpreted as the other; or when quality is interpreted as quantity, or quantity as quality; or an active term as passive, or a disposition as an action; and similarly in the other cases already mentioned under division.

There is something that is not among the things that can perform an action, although it can be signified by an expression as though it were such a thing. Thus “to be healthy” is said in the same form of expression as “to cut” or “to build,” although the former signifies a certain quality or condition, while the latter signify doing something. The same applies in the other cases.

Refutations arising from the expression therefore arise through these devices.

## CHAPTER IV. The Places of Sophistical Refutations Independent of Expression

There are seven kinds of captious arguments that arise independently of the expression. The first is through accident; the second through saying something simply, or not simply but in some respect, or somewhere, or at some time, or in relation to something; the third through ignorance of what refutation is; the fourth through the consequent; the fifth through assuming at the beginning what is at issue; [Col. 1011D] the sixth through taking what is not a cause as a cause; the seventh through making several questions into one.

Captions through accident occur whenever something is thought to belong in the same way to a thing and to its accident. For since many things belong accidentally to the same subject, it is not necessary that all the predicates belonging to the subject should also belong to every one of its accidents. Otherwise everything will be identical, as the sophists say. For example, if Coriscus is different from “man,” he is different from himself, since he is a man. Or, if he is different from Socrates, and Socrates is a man, they say that Coriscus has confessed that he is different from a man, because “man” happens to be that from which he said he was different.

The second kind arises when one thing is stated simply and another in some respect, but not absolutely. This occurs when what is said in part is taken as though it had been said absolutely. For example, “non-being is thinkable,” when what is thinkable is non-being. For “to be something” and “to be simply” are not the same.

Again: “What is not is,” if some one of the things that are is not—for example, if a man is not. For “not to be something” and “not to be simply” are not the same. The error appears because the expressions are very similar, and there is little difference between “to be something” and “to be,” or between “not to be something” and “not to be.”

Similarly, the error may arise from “in some respect” and “simply,” as when an Indian, although black all over, is white in his teeth; therefore, he is both white and not white.

Or, if both predicates are taken in some respect, contrary predicates may be thought to belong simultaneously. This is easy to observe in certain cases. For example, if one takes an Ethiopian to be black but says that he is white in his teeth, then, if he is white there, one may think that he is both black and not black and has completed a syllogistic argument [Col. 1012B].

In other cases the matter is frequently concealed, whenever something stated in some respect appears to follow simply, or whenever it is not easy to determine to which subject the predicate properly belongs. This occurs especially when opposites are distributed in the same way. For they appear either both or neither to be predicated simply. For example, if half of something is white and half black, is it white or black?

Arguments arising because the nature of a syllogism or a refutation has not been determined result from omitting part of the expression. A refutation is the contradiction of one and the same thing—not merely of a name, but of the thing; and not of a synonymous name, but of the same name; and it must follow necessarily from what has been granted, without including what was originally at issue; and it must concern the same respect, the same relation, the same manner, and the same time.

If something in this definition is omitted, someone may state what is false and nevertheless appear to refute another. Thus something may appear to be both double and not double: two is double one, but three is not double one.

Or the same thing may appear to be double and not double, but not in the same respect: it is double in length but not double in breadth.

Or it may be the same thing, in the same respect and in the same manner, but not at the same time; hence the refutation is only apparent.

Some transfer this kind of argument to those arising from the expression.

Arguments arising from assuming what was at issue in the beginning occur in as many ways as begging the question can occur. They appear to refute because one cannot easily observe that the same thing has been assumed as both identical and different.

Refutation through the consequent arises because people suppose that consequence is convertible. If one thing follows necessarily when another is present, they think that when the first is present the other must also be present. Hence errors also arise from opinions based on sense-perception. People have often supposed that honey is bile because yellow color follows honey. And because the earth becomes wet when it rains, they think that if the earth is wet, it must have rained; but this does not follow necessarily.

In rhetorical arguments, demonstrations based on signs arise from consequents. For example, those who wish to show that someone is an adulterer take what follows from adultery: that he is well-groomed, or that he is seen wandering about at night. Yet many people possess these characteristics, while the predicate in question does not belong to them.

The same occurs in argumentative reasoning, as in Melissus’ argument that the universe is infinite. He assumes that the universe is ungenerated—for nothing comes into being from nothing—and that whatever comes into being comes from a beginning. If, then, the universe did not come into being, it has no beginning; therefore, it is infinite. But this does not follow necessarily. For although everything that comes into being has a beginning, it does not follow that everything that has a beginning has come into being. Just as, although someone with a fever is hot, it does not follow that everything hot has a fever.

Arguments arising from taking what is not a cause as a cause occur when what is not the cause is assumed as though something happened because of it. This happens in arguments leading to the impossible, since in such arguments it is necessary to eliminate something among the propositions that have been posited.

If, among the necessary questions, one enumerates something that merely happens to lead to the impossible, the refutation will often appear to occur because of that proposition. For example: “Soul and life are not the same.” If generation is contrary to corruption, then some generation will be contrary to every corruption; death is a kind of corruption and contrary to life; therefore, life is generation and living is coming-to-be. But this is impossible; therefore, soul and life are not the same.

The conclusion has not actually been established. The impossible has followed accidentally, even though someone may not say that life and soul are identical. The only genuine premises are that life is contrary to death, since death is a corruption, and that generation is contrary to corruption.

Such arguments are therefore not simply inconclusive, but inconclusive with respect to the intended conclusion. The questioners themselves are often no less unaware that this is so.

Such, then, are the arguments arising from the consequent and from taking what is not a cause as a cause.

Arguments arising from making several questions into one occur when the plurality of questions is concealed and a single answer is assigned as though there were only one question.

In some cases it is easy to see that the questions are multiple and that one answer should not be given, as in: “Is the earth the sea or the sky?” In other cases it is less obvious, and since the question appears to be one, a person either agrees—because he cannot answer what has been asked—or appears to be refuted. For example: “Is this man and that man a man?” If someone strikes this man and that man, he will strike a man, not men.

Again, when some things are good and others not good: “Are all these things good or not good?” Whichever answer he gives, he will appear either to refute or to assert something false. For to say that something not good is good, or that something good is not good, is false [Col. 1013D].

Sometimes, however, when certain premises have been granted, the refutation will also be true. For example, if someone agrees that both one thing and several things may be called white, naked, and blind. If “blind” means what does not possess sight but is naturally fitted to possess it, then things that lack sight but are naturally fitted to have it will be blind. If, therefore, one thing has sight and another does not, both will be either seeing or blind—which is impossible.

## CHAPTER V. All Sophistical Refutations Are to Be Referred to Ignorance of Refutation

[Col. 1014A]

We must either distinguish apparent syllogisms and refutations in this way, or reduce them all to ignorance of refutation, by making this the starting point. For it is possible to resolve all the modes mentioned into the definition of refutation.

First, if the arguments are inconclusive, the conclusion must follow from the premises that have been posited, and must follow necessarily, so to speak, rather than merely appear to follow.

Next, the same applies according to the several parts of the definition. Among the arguments arising from the expression, some arise from doubleness, such as equivocation and amphiboly, and from similarity of form; for it is customary for all these to signify something else as well.

Combination, division, and accent arise because the expression or name is not the same, although it ought to be the same in the way that the thing itself is the same, if there is to be a refutation or a syllogism. For example, if it is syllogized that something is a tunic rather than a garment, but it is a tunic, that too may be true, but it has not been syllogistically established; a further question is still required concerning what signifies the same thing for the questioner.

The cases defined according to accident become clear from the definition of syllogism. The definition of syllogism and of refutation must be the same, with the addition of contradiction, since a refutation is a syllogism of contradiction. If, then, there is no syllogism concerning the accident, there is no refutation. For if, when these things are present, that thing necessarily is, it does not follow that “being white” has been established through a syllogism.

Similarly, if a triangle has three angles equal to two right angles, and it happens to possess a figure, or to be first, or to be a principle, the demonstration does not establish that it has a figure, or is first, or is a principle as such; it establishes this insofar as it is a triangle. The same applies in other cases.

Therefore, if a refutation is a kind of syllogism, there will be no refutation based on accident.

For this reason even experts and those who possess knowledge are refuted by the unlearned: the latter construct syllogisms based on accidents against the wise. Those who cannot divide the different senses either grant what they are asked or, when they do not grant it, think that they have granted it.

The cases arising from “in some respect” and “simply” occur because affirmation and negation do not concern the same thing: something may be white in some respect and not white in another respect, while “white simply” and “not white simply” constitute a negation. If, then, when someone grants that something is white in some respect, another takes this as a statement made simply, he has not produced a refutation; he merely appears to have done so because of ignorance of what a refutation is.

Most clearly of all, the cases mentioned earlier arise from the definition of refutation; this is why they have received those names. For an appearance is produced by omitting part of the expression. In all such cases, the common element must be the omission of part of the expression.

The cases arising from assuming what was at issue at the beginning, and from taking what is not a cause as a cause, are made clear by the definition. The conclusion must follow because these premises are present; this is absent in the case of what is not a cause. Likewise, what is assumed at the beginning is not included among the premises in arguments that beg the question.

The cases arising from the consequent are a subdivision of those arising from accident, since the consequent is accidental. It differs from accident in this respect: accident is assumed in relation to one thing alone—for example, that yellow, honey, white, and swan are the same—whereas the consequent always concerns several things. Things that are identical with one and the same thing are consequently required to be identical with one another; and this is why refutations through the consequent arise.

The assumption is not altogether true. For example, “white” belongs accidentally to snow and to a swan, but this does not make them identical. Again, in Melissus’ argument, he assumes that “having come into being” and “having a beginning” are the same, or that “becoming equal” and “having the same magnitude” are the same [Col. 1015B].

Because what has come into being has a beginning, and what has a beginning is assumed to have come into being, the two are treated as identical on the ground that both have a beginning, and therefore are finite.

Similarly, if things that become equal acquire the same magnitude, and things that acquire the same magnitude become equal, the consequent has been assumed. It is therefore clear that refutation through accident belongs to ignorance of refutation, and that refutation through the consequent belongs to the same class. This should also be examined more carefully in other cases.

The cases arising from making several questions into one consist in failing to articulate or divide the expression of the proposition. A proposition is one thing predicated of one thing. The same term may be applied to one thing alone and to a thing simply—for example, “man” and “one particular man.”

The same applies in other cases. If a proposition requires one thing to be predicated of one thing, then a question of this kind, stated simply, will also be a proposition. Since a syllogism consists of propositions, and a refutation is a syllogism, a refutation must also consist of propositions.

If, then, a proposition is one thing predicated of one thing, it is clear that these cases too belong to ignorance of refutation: an expression that is not a proposition appears to be a proposition. If the respondent gives an answer as to one question, there will be a refutation; if he does not give one, but appears to have done so, there will be an apparent refutation.

Thus all the places that have been mentioned fall under ignorance of refutation. Those arising from the expression do so because they produce an apparent contradiction, which is proper to refutation; the others do so because of the limits of the syllogism.

## CHAPTER VI. The Causes of Sophistical Deceptions and Captions

Deception occurs in cases involving equivocation and amphiboly because one cannot divide what is said in several senses. Some expressions are not easy to divide, such as “one,” “being,” and “the same.”

In cases involving combination and division, deception occurs because people think that a combined expression and a divided expression make no difference, as happens in many instances.

The same applies to cases involving accent. For an utterance pronounced with an acute accent and one pronounced with a grave accent do not appear to signify something different, whether in one instance or in many.

Cases involving the form of expression arise from the similarity of the wording. It is difficult to distinguish expressions that are alike from those that are different; for whoever can do this is nearly prepared to see the truth, and especially to understand what is being indicated.

We think that everything predicated of something is itself a thing, and we understand it as one thing. For “one” and substance seem most closely to follow what is a thing and what is being.

This place, therefore, must be assigned among those arising from the expression.

First, deception is more readily produced in those who examine a matter with others than in those who examine it by themselves. Examination with another proceeds through expressions, whereas examination by oneself proceeds no less through the thing itself.

Even by themselves, however, people may be deceived when they conduct their examination through an expression. Moreover, deception arises from similarity, and similarity arises from the expression.

In cases involving accident, deception occurs because one cannot distinguish what is the same from what is different, or one from many, nor determine which of the predicates belong to the subject and which to its accidents.

The same applies to cases involving the consequent, for the consequent is a part of accident.

Further, in many cases the consequent appears and is assumed in this way: if one thing is not separable from another, then the other is not separable from the first.

In cases involving omission of part of the expression, and in those involving “in some respect” and “simply,” deception arises because of a small difference. We concede universally as though nothing were signified by “what,” “in some respect,” “somewhere,” or “now.”

The same applies to cases that assume what was at issue at the beginning, to cases involving what is not a cause, and to all cases that make several questions into one. In all of them deception arises from a small difference, because we do not precisely distinguish the limits of the proposition or of the syllogism, for the reasons already stated.

## CHAPTER VII. The Places from Which False Captions Arise

Since we have identified the grounds on which apparent syllogisms arise, we also possess the grounds on which sophistical syllogisms and refutations arise.

By a sophistical refutation or syllogism I mean not merely an apparent syllogism or a refutation that does not exist, but also one that does exist while being apparently appropriate to the thing in question [Col. 1016D].

These are the arguments that do not refute according to the thing itself and that expose the ignorance of those who do not know; this was the distinctive feature of the tentative method. The tentative method is a part of dialectic; it can syllogize falsely because of the ignorance of the person who supplies the argument.

Sophistical refutations, even when they establish a contradiction, do not make the ignorance manifest. Indeed, they can impede even those who possess knowledge through such arguments.

That we possess arguments of this kind is clear in the following way. Whatever appears to the audience to have been syllogized in response to a question will also appear so to the respondent. Therefore, through these devices there will be false syllogisms, either in all cases or in some. For what an unexamined person thinks he has granted, a person being questioned will also place among the premises.

In certain cases, asking the question that is missing and producing an appearance of falsity occur together, as in cases involving the expression and solecism.

If syllogisms of contradiction arise from apparent refutation, it is clear that there will be as many false syllogisms as there are apparent refutations. For whenever any required condition is absent, there will be an apparent refutation: where the conclusion is not non-accidental; in cases arising from expression; in arguments leading to the impossible; in making two questions into one through the proposition; and in taking what is accidental in place of what belongs in itself, including its subdivision, the consequent.

Further, an apparent refutation arises when something occurs not in the thing but in the expression; when a universal contradiction is replaced by one concerning something particular; when the relation, respect, manner, or time is not the same; and when the argument fails in any one of these respects [Col. 1017B].

It also arises through failing to include what was assumed at the beginning, which produces the fallacy of begging the question.

We therefore possess as many categories as there are ways in which captious arguments arise. There are no further categories beyond these, while all cases fall under those that have been stated.

A sophistical refutation is not a refutation simply, but a refutation relative to a particular person; and the same applies to a syllogism.

If the argument does not assume that an equivocal term has one meaning, and if, in the case of similarity of expression, it does not assume merely the intended form, and likewise in the other cases, then there will be neither syllogisms nor refutations—not simply and not even relative to the person being questioned.

If the argument does make these assumptions, it will be a refutation relative to the person being questioned, but not a refutation simply. For it has not assumed one signification, but only an apparent one, and only in relation to that person.

## CHAPTER VIII. True and False Refutations

Those who use refutations must not attempt to grasp the grounds on which refutations occur without possessing knowledge of all the relevant things.

This knowledge does not belong to a single art, since the sciences are perhaps infinite. It is therefore clear that demonstrations too are refutations, and true ones. Whatever can be demonstrated can also refute someone who posits the contradictory of a truth.
