For example, if someone posits that the diagonal is commensurable, a demonstration will refute him by showing that it is incommensurable.

It will therefore be necessary to possess knowledge of all such matters. Some refutations follow from the principles and conclusions of geometry; others from those of medicine; others from those of the remaining disciplines.

False refutations will likewise be infinite. For there is a false syllogism corresponding to each art: a geometrical false syllogism in geometry, and a medical one in medicine. By “according to an art” I mean according to the principles of that art.

It is therefore clear that we must seek the places not of all refutations, but of those that belong to dialectic. These places are common to every art and every capacity. It belongs to the person who possesses knowledge of each particular discipline to examine the refutation appropriate to that discipline, whether it is genuinely a refutation or only appears to be one, and why it is so. But the refutation that proceeds from common principles and falls under no particular art belongs to dialecticians.

For if we possess the sources from which probable syllogisms can be constructed in any subject, we shall possess the sources from which refutations can be constructed. A refutation is a syllogism of contradiction; therefore, one or two syllogisms of contradiction constitute a refutation.

We thus possess the sources from which all such refutations arise. If we possess these, we also possess their solutions, since the objections to such arguments are their solutions.

We also possess the sources from which apparent refutations arise. But apparent refutations do not appear so to everyone, only to people of certain kinds. If one considers all the things that appear to anyone to be refutations, their number will be infinite.

It is therefore clear that it belongs to dialecticians to grasp the grounds on which, through common principles, there arises either a refutation or an apparent refutation, whether dialectical or apparently dialectical, or tentative.

## CHAPTER IX. Arguments Should Not Be Divided into Those Addressed to the Name and Those Addressed to the Meaning

[Col. 1018B]

There is no distinction between arguments of the kind that some people call “addressed to the name” and those “addressed to the meaning.” For it is absurd to suppose that some arguments are addressed to the name while others are different arguments addressed to the meaning, rather than the same arguments.

What does it mean for an argument not to be addressed to the meaning? It means that the person who thinks he is asking a question does not use the name with the meaning that the person questioned has given it. But this is precisely what it means to be addressed to the name.

An argument is addressed to the meaning when it proceeds according to the meaning that the respondent has given while understanding it.

If someone thinks that a name which signifies several things signifies only one, both the questioner and the respondent may proceed on that assumption. For example, “being” and “one” signify several things, but Zeno, both respondent and questioner taking “one” to signify one thing, asked the question found in the argument that all things are one [Col. 1018C]. Such an argument is directed to the name, or to the understanding of the questioner.

If someone thinks that the term has several meanings, it is clear that the argument is not directed to the meaning.

The first point concerning such arguments, then, is that they are directed to the name and to the meaning whenever the terms signify several things. The second point is that, in every case, being directed to the meaning does not lie in the expression itself, but in the way the respondent relates to what has been granted.

Third, it is possible for all such arguments to be directed to the name. For in this context “directed to the name” means “not directed to the respondent’s understanding.” If this were not true of all of them, there would be certain arguments directed neither to the name nor to the meaning, although those who make the distinction say that every argument is directed either to the name or to the meaning, and not that some are directed to neither.

Nevertheless, among syllogisms arising from the fact that a term has several meanings, some are directed to the name. It would be absurd to say that all arguments arising from the expression are directed to the name. There are certain captions that arise not because the respondent relates to them in a particular way, but because the argument itself contains a question with several meanings.

In general, it is absurd to discuss refutation without first discussing syllogism. For a refutation is a syllogism; therefore, syllogism must be discussed before false refutation, since such a refutation is an apparent syllogism of contradiction.

The cause of an apparent refutation will therefore lie either in the syllogism or in the contradiction, since the contradiction must be added. Sometimes it will lie in both [Col. 1019A].

In the case of “saying silences,” the cause lies in the contradiction, not in the syllogism. In the case of “what no one can give,” it lies in both. In the case of “the poem of Homer is a figure through a circle,” the cause lies in the syllogism. Whatever belongs to neither is a true syllogism.

Let us return to the point from which the discussion began. Are the arguments found in the sciences addressed to the meaning or not? If someone thinks that “triangle” has several meanings, and grants the proposition not with reference to the figure from which the conclusion that it has two right angles was drawn, was the argument directed to his meaning or not?

Again, if the name signifies several things but the respondent does not understand this and does not think that it does, how can the argument not be directed to his meaning? Or how should one question a person who does not make the division?

For example, suppose someone asks whether “to say silences” is possible or not—is it possible in one sense but not in another? If the respondent gives no answer at all, while the questioner continues the argument, is the argument not directed to his meaning, even though the expression appears to belong among those directed to the name?

There is therefore no special class of arguments directed to the meaning. Some arguments are directed to the name, but not all such arguments are refutations, nor even apparent refutations. There are apparent refutations that do not arise from the expression, such as those arising from accident and the remaining cases.

If someone demands that the respondent make the division—saying that by “saying silences” he means one thing, whereas the expression may also mean something else—that demand is itself absurd. For sometimes the question does not appear to have several meanings, and it is impossible for someone who does not recognize this to make the division.

Moreover, what else would such a demand be except an attempt to teach? It will clearly make the matter understood in a certain way to someone who neither considers nor knows nor supposes that the expression has another meaning. The same could be done even in cases where there is no ambiguity.

For example: “Are units equal to twos in fours?” The twos in question exist in the fours, but not in the same way as the other twos.

Again: “Is there one science of contraries or not?” Some contraries are known, while others are unknown.

Thus the person who makes this demand appears not to understand that teaching is different from disputing. The teacher should not ask questions but make the matter clear, whereas the disputant should ask questions.

## CHAPTER X. The Questioning Proper to the Tentative Method, and the Difference between the Contentious and the Sophistical
[Col. 1019D] Furthermore, to require someone to affirm or deny is not the act of one demonstrating, but of one conducting an examination. For dialectical examination is a kind of testing; therefore it investigates everything and examines not the person who knows, but the person who is ignorant and pretends to know.

Thus, whoever considers common matters according to their reality is a dialectician; whoever does so only apparently is a sophist. The contentious and sophistic syllogism is, in one sense, an apparent syllogism concerning the subjects on which dialectical examination is conducted, even though its conclusion is true. For it is deceptive with respect to the “because” (*propter quid*), and any deceptive arguments that are not actually demonstrations within the respective sciences appear to belong to those sciences.

For false geometrical constructions that are not contentious—since, insofar as they concern matters falling under a science, they are deceptive arguments—are not contentious merely because they are false; nor is a false construction concerning something true, such as Hippocrates’ quadrature by means of lunes. But when Bryson squared the circle, even if the circle could in fact be squared, his procedure was sophistic because it did not proceed according to the nature of the matter. Hence, when an apparent syllogism concerns these things, the argument is contentious: it is apparent according to the matter itself, and therefore deceptive and unjust.

For just as the injustice that occurs in a contest has a certain appearance and is a kind of unfair fighting, so in contradiction contentiousness is an unfair fight. In the former case, those who wish to win by any means try everything; so too do the contentious here. Those who behave in this way for the sake of victory itself appear to be contentious people and lovers of litigation; those who do so for the sake of the glory that belongs to wealth [Col. 1020B] are sophists. Sophistry is, as we said, a kind of money-making pursuit based on an apparent wisdom; for this reason they seek an apparent demonstration.

The lovers of litigation and the sophists may be found in the same arguments, but not for the same reasons. The same argument may be sophistic and contentious, but not for the same reason: insofar as it aims at apparent victory, it is contentious; insofar as it aims at wisdom, it is sophistic. For sophistry is a kind of apparent wisdom, not wisdom that actually exists.

Contentious argument is related to dialectic somewhat as false geometrical construction is related to geometry. From the same materials, by a deceptive mode of argument, contentious reasoning deceives in dialectic, just as false construction does in geometry. But a false construction is not contentious when it produces a false construction from principles and conclusions belonging to the science itself [Col. 1020C]. When it proceeds from matters belonging to dialectic, however, it is clearly contentious with respect to other matters. Thus the quadrature by means of lunes is not contentious, whereas Bryson’s is contentious.

The former cannot be transferred except to geometry, precisely because it is produced from geometry’s own principles. The latter can be transferred to many fields by anyone who does not know what is possible and what is impossible in each field. Thus it may be adapted to the procedure of Antiphon, or to the argument that it is better to walk after dinner—if someone does not say that this is better by means of Zeno’s argument—since that is not medicinal but common.

If, then, contentious argument is related to dialectic altogether as false construction is related to geometry, contentious argument will not necessarily proceed from principles belonging to any one determinate field.

## CHAPTER XI. That the arguments of dialecticians and those conducting examinations do not belong to a determinate genus

[Col. 1020D]

Dialectic does not concern any one determinate genus, nor is any demonstrative science universal. For not everything belongs to one genus; and even if everything did, it would not be possible for the things belonging to it to be governed by the same principles.

Therefore none of the sciences that demonstrate some determinate nature is interrogative, since it is not possible to offer either of two alternatives. A syllogism is not constructed from both alternatives, whereas dialectic is interrogative. If it demonstrated something, what would it demonstrate other than everything? Nevertheless, it does not interrogate its primary and proper principles [Col. 1021A]; for if these were not granted, it would no longer have anything from which to argue in response to an objection.

Examination has this character. It is not like geometry, but like what a person who does not know a subject would have. For it is possible for someone who does not know the subject to test another person who does not know it, provided that the tester offers premises not from what he knows, nor from the subject’s proper principles, but from consequences—things of such a kind that nothing prevents a knowledgeable person from being ignorant of them as a matter of technique, whereas the ignorant person must be ignorant of them.

It is therefore clear that examination is not the discipline of any determinate subject, because it concerns everything. All the sciences make use of certain common principles. Hence, in a certain way, all uneducated people use dialectic and examination. For everyone attempts, up to a point, to judge those who make assertions [Col. 1021B]; and the matters by which they judge are common. They themselves know no less about these matters, although those who speak may appear to be saying things far beyond them.

Everyone therefore conducts refutations, for without possessing a technical art they participate in what belongs technically to dialectic and to the art of syllogistic reasoning: they are examiners and dialecticians.

Since some things are many and concern everything, though they are not such as to constitute a nature or genus but rather negations, while other things are not of this kind but are proper to particular subjects, it is possible to conduct an examination from the former concerning everything. There is thus a certain art, though it is not like the demonstrative sciences.

Contentious argument is not altogether related to its subject as false construction is related to geometry. It is not deceptive by proceeding from the principles of some determinate genus; rather, the contentious person operates concerning every genus. These, then, are the places of sophistical refutations. It is not difficult to see that it belongs to the dialectician to consider them and to be able to produce them: the discipline concerned with propositions includes the whole of this inquiry. The apparent refutations have now been discussed.

## CHAPTER XII. The places used by sophistical questioners to lead to what is false or contrary to expectation

To demonstrate something false about a subject, and to lead the argument toward what is contrary to expectation, belong to the intended purpose of sophistic procedure.

The first means is to question in a certain manner; indeed, this occurs chiefly through questioning. To question without having a determinate objective is characteristic of those who hunt for such opportunities. For people who speak at random are more likely to make mistakes [Col. 1021D]; and they speak at random when they have no definite objective.

To ask about many things—even when the matter under discussion is determinate—and to claim that one is asking for whatever appears to be the case creates a certain capacity to lead the respondent toward what is unexpected or false. If the person questioned affirms or denies something that leads toward the points on which the questioner is prepared to argue, this may nevertheless cause less harm now than before, since the questioner returns to something connected with the original issue.

The device for arriving at something false or contrary to expectation is to refrain at once from asking a determinate question, but to say that one is asking because one wishes to learn. This enables the questioner to consider the place from which the argument may be drawn.

The proper sophistic device for demonstrating something false is to lead the argument toward propositions with which the questioner is abundantly supplied. To do this well or badly is as was explained earlier.

To lead someone toward what is contrary to expectation, one should consider what kind of person the opponent is and then ask about something that most people of that kind regard as unexpected. For each group has something of this sort. The means of obtaining such points is to take the positions held by each group as premises.

The appropriate solution in these cases is to show that the unexpected conclusion did not arise because of the argument. The contentious questioner always wants it to appear that it did.

One may also proceed from people’s desires and their evident opinions, since people do not desire and say the same things. They say the most respectable things, but desire what appears advantageous: for example, they say that one ought to prefer a good death to a life of pleasure, and to act justly rather than live wickedly in abundance; yet they desire the opposite.

Thus the person who argues from people’s desires should be led to their evident opinions, while the person who argues from those evident opinions should be led to their hidden desires. In either way it is necessary to make him say what is contrary to expectation, since the statements will contradict either evident or hidden opinions.

There is a very extensive means of making someone say what is contrary to expectation, as Callicles is represented as saying in the *Gorgias*:

“All the earlier thinkers, too, held that what occurs according to nature and what occurs according to law are opposed. For they say that nature and law are contrary, and that justice according to law is good, but according to nature is not good.”

The person who argues according to nature should therefore be confronted with what follows according to law [Col. 1022C], and the person who argues according to law should be led toward what follows according to nature. In either way it is possible to make him say what is contrary to expectation. What is according to nature is true to the speakers themselves, whereas what is according to law is what appears true to the majority.

It is therefore clear that those earlier thinkers, like those of the present day, attempted either to refute the respondent or to make him say what was contrary to expectation.

Some questions have a response that is contrary to expectation in either direction—for example, whether one ought to obey the wise or one’s father; whether one should do what is expedient or what is just; and whether it is preferable to suffer injustice rather than commit it.

One must lead the respondent toward what is contrary to the views of both the majority and the wise. If he speaks like those concerned with arguments, he should be led toward what is contrary to the majority; if he speaks like the majority, toward what is contrary to those concerned with argument. The former necessarily say that the just person is happy, whereas to the majority it is contrary to expectation that an unhappy person should be a king.

To lead someone toward such unexpected conclusions is the same as leading him toward the opposition between what is according to nature and what is according to law. Law is the opinion of the majority, whereas the wise speak according to nature and truth. What is contrary to expectation should therefore be sought from these places.

## CHAPTER XIII. The devices of verbal repetition and solecism

We have already shown what we mean by making someone repeat himself. All such arguments aim at producing this result if it makes no difference whether a noun or an expression is uttered.

“Double” and “double of a half” are the same. If, then, “double” is “double of a half,” it will be “double of half of a half.” Again, if “double of a half” is substituted for “double,” it will have been said three times: “double of half of half of a half.”

Consider also: “Is desire pleasure?” But desire is an appetite for pleasure. Therefore desire is an appetite for pleasure for pleasure.

All arguments of this kind concern relatives—things that are spoken of not merely as genera but as relatives in themselves, and are assigned to the same single relation: for example, the appetite of something, the desire of something, the double of something, and the double of a half. The same applies to things which, although they are not substances, belong altogether among the relatives of which they are habits, dispositions, or something of that kind.

In a statement predicated of such things, the relation is made explicit. For example: “An odd number is a number having a middle.” But it is a number; therefore a number is a number having a middle.

Again, if “snub” is a concavity of the nose, and the nose is snub, then the nose will be a nose that is a concavity of a nose.

Sometimes people appear to produce repetition when they do not, because they fail to ask whether “double,” when uttered by itself, signifies something or nothing; and, if it signifies something, whether it signifies the same thing or something different. Instead, they state the conclusion immediately, and because the word is the same, it appears that the thing and its signification are the same.

What sort of thing a solecism is has been stated earlier. Here, too, it is possible both to produce one without appearing to do so and to appear to produce one without actually doing so, as Levinus argued in the case of “Venus” being masculine. Someone who says *almam* commits a solecism according to Levinus, but does not appear to commit one to others; someone who says *almum* appears to commit one, but does not actually do so.

It is therefore clear that there is also an art capable of producing this effect, since many non-syllogistic arguments appear to produce solecisms, just as they appear to produce refutations.

Almost all apparent solecisms arise for this reason, especially when a grammatical case signifies neither masculine nor feminine but neuter. For *hic* signifies the masculine, *haec* the feminine, and *hoc* is intended to signify the neuter; yet the same form often signifies both masculine and feminine, as in “What is this? Calliope, wood, Coriscus.”

The masculine and feminine differ in all their cases, whereas the neuter forms differ in some cases but not in others. When the neuter form is given, they often draw a conclusion as though the masculine form had been stated. Similarly, they substitute one case for another.

The deceptive argument arises because the same form is common to several cases: at one time it signifies *hic*, at another *hunc*. The forms should instead signify their respective cases: when the meaning is *hic*, it should signify *hic*; when the meaning is *hunc*, it should signify *hunc*—for example, “Coriscus is” and “to be Coriscus” (*Coriscum*).

The same applies to feminine nouns. In every case, the forms of “is” and “to be” will likewise make the distinction.

In a certain way, the solecism in these matters resembles the refutations that arise because things are not similar or because they are expressed similarly in form. Just as there it arises in things, so here a solecism arises in names. For “human” and “white” are both a thing and a name.

It is therefore clear that one should attempt to construct a solecism from the cases that have been stated. These, then, are the species of contentious arguments, together with the parts of those species and the modes that have been described.

## CHAPTER XIV. Sophistic concealment and methods against troublesome respondents

[Col. 1024A]

It makes a considerable difference if the questions are arranged in a certain way so that the method remains hidden, as happens in dialectical arguments.

The following points should first be added to what has already been said. One means of producing a refutation is prolixity, since it is difficult to grasp many things at once. For the sake of prolixity, one should use the devices already introduced. One such device is haste, since slower respondents foresee less. Anger and contentiousness are useful as well, since disturbed people are less able to observe everything.

The elements that produce anger include making it evident that one wishes to act justly, while behaving shamelessly in every respect.

One should also alternate the questions, whether someone has several arguments directed toward the same point, or has one argument of one kind and another of the opposite kind. In this way the respondent is simultaneously compelled to attend either to several matters or to contrary matters.

In general, everything previously mentioned as useful for concealment is also useful in contentious arguments. Concealment is employed in order to remain hidden, and remaining hidden serves deception.

Against those who reject whatever they think is relevant to the argument, one should ask by means of a negation, as though one wished to assert the contrary, or should ask an equal alternative question. When what the questioner wishes to obtain is uncertain, they become less insolent.

When someone has granted particular cases to a person conducting an induction, the universal should often not be asked as a question; rather, one should use it as something already granted. They sometimes think that they themselves have granted it, and the audience also sees it as granted because of the preceding induction [Col. 1024C], as though the question had not been asked pointlessly.

Where the universal is not signified by a name, one should nevertheless use a similarity appropriate to the desired result, since the similarity generally goes unnoticed.

To obtain a premise, one should ask by comparison through the contrary. Thus, if one wishes to establish that one ought to obey one’s father in everything, one should ask: “Must one obey one’s parents in everything, or must one not obey them in everything?” One may also ask: “Should many things be conceded, or only a few?” For if it is necessary to concede something, many concessions will appear more likely.

When contraries are placed beside one another, smaller and larger things, and worse and better things, appear so to human beings.

A particularly effective and frequent way of making it appear that a refutation has been achieved is the sophistic slander of questioners. Although they have drawn no conclusion, they do not ask the final question; instead, they state it as though they had drawn a conclusion: “Therefore, this and this.”

It is also sophistic to introduce something contrary to expectation, which appears to require the respondent to answer, after having stated what seemed to follow from the beginning; then to ask: “Does this seem so to you?” For if the question is composed of the premises from which a syllogism proceeds, it must result either in a refutation or in something contrary to expectation. If the respondent grants the premise, there is a refutation; if he neither grants it nor appears willing to grant it, he admits what is contrary to expectation; and if he does not grant it but admits that it appears so, the result resembles a refutation.

Furthermore, as in rhetoric, one should similarly consider contraries in refutations: either those arising from the same speaker’s statements, or those arising from people whom he acknowledges to speak or act well. One should also consider those who appear to be of this kind, or similar people, or the majority, or everyone.

Just as respondents often make a double assertion when they are refuted, so, when a refutation is about to occur, one should sometimes use questions of the following kind against those who press the argument: “If this follows in one way, but not in another….” If the respondent grants the point, as Cleophon does in the *Mandrobulus*, one must also divide the remaining arguments away from the argument under discussion. If the respondent has anticipated the move, one should press him first and state the conclusion in advance.

Sometimes one should also argue toward something other than what has been stated, taking up that point if one cannot argue toward the proposed subject. This is what Lycophron did when the proposal was to praise the lyre by means of its art [Col. 1026A].

Against those who demand that one argue toward a particular point, one should do so after it appears necessary to assign the cause.

Among the points to be observed in general in refutations is that the respondent should state the contradiction—for example, deny what he affirmed or affirm what he denied—but not claim that the same discipline concerns contraries or that it does not concern them.

The conclusion should not be asked as though it were a premise. Some things should not be asked at all; rather, they should be used as already conceded.

The questions that should be asked, and how they should be asked, have been discussed in the exercises of disputation.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1025]

## CHAPTER I. The usefulness of knowing sophistic arguments and the preparation for resolving them

[Col. 1025B]

We must next discuss responding, how one ought to resolve such arguments, what should be resolved, and for what purpose arguments of this kind are useful.

They are useful for philosophy for three reasons. First, matters that arise chiefly from language make one better able to discern in how many ways each expression is used, and to distinguish what happens similarly and differently in things and in names.

Second, they are useful for investigations conducted by oneself. For a person who is easily deceived by another through a sophistical argument, without noticing it, is also very often deceived by himself in the same way.

Third, they are useful for reputation, since a person will appear to have been trained in every matter and inexperienced in none. If someone who participates in argument criticizes arguments without having any definite account of their defect, he gives the impression that he wishes to appear arrogant—not because that is true, but because of his lack of experience.

As for how respondents should resist such arguments, the answer is clear if we have correctly stated earlier the sources of deceptive reasoning and have sufficiently divided the fallacies that require investigation.

It is not the same thing to recognize an argument, to resolve its defect, and to be able to answer a questioner quickly. For what we know, when rearranged, we often fail to recognize.

Moreover, just as in other matters speed and slowness are produced chiefly by practice, so it is with arguments. Thus, even when a matter is clear to us, if we are not ready to respond immediately, we frequently lose the opportunity.

Sometimes what happens is like what occurs in the construction of geometrical diagrams. For there, too, we may sometimes be unable to reconstruct the correct figure even after resolving it. So it is with refutations: although we know why an argument occurs, we may nevertheless be unable to resolve the argument.

## CHAPTER II. The respondent’s apparent solution

First, just as we said that in constructing a syllogism one should sometimes choose what is more plausible rather than what is more true, so in resolving an argument one should sometimes prefer what is more plausible to what is true. Against contentious people one must resist altogether—not as against those who actually refute, but as against those who only appear to refute.

We do not say that they are constructing a syllogism; therefore, in order that they may not appear to do so, their argument must be corrected. If a refutation is a non-equivocal contradiction arising from certain premises, there is no need to distinguish amphiboly or equivocation—for these do not produce a syllogism—but one must distinguish them for no other reason than that the conclusion appears similar to a refutation.

The concern, then, is not to avoid being refuted, but to avoid appearing to be refuted. This is because the questioner uses amphibolous expressions, expressions that rely on equivocation, and other such devices that cast a true refutation into shadow and make it uncertain whether the questioner has refuted or not [Col. 1026C].

For, since at the end, once the argument has been completed, one may say that one is not denying the very same thing that one affirmed, but is denying it equivocally or amphibolously—even though the result may come as close as possible to the same thing—it becomes uncertain whether the respondent has been refuted. For it is uncertain whether he is now speaking truthfully.

If the questioner had distinguished the equivocal or amphibolous expression while asking the question, the refutation would not have been certain. Contentious people demand—now less than formerly—that the person questioned should, if possible, answer in this way, either “yes” or “no.”

But because questioners do not ask their questions properly, the person questioned must give some answer while correcting the defect in the question. Once the distinction has been made sufficiently, the respondent must say either “yes” or “no.”

If someone thinks that there is a refutation through equivocation, it will in a certain way be impossible for the respondent to escape being refuted. In things presented to the senses, it would be necessary to deny the name that he affirmed and affirm the name that he denied.

Indeed, the solution offered by some is of no use. They say that Coriscus is not musical and not non-musical, but that this Coriscus is musical and this Coriscus is not musical. The expression “Coriscus,” however, will have the same meaning as the expression “this Coriscus is musical” or “this Coriscus is not musical,” which they affirm and deny simultaneously.

Perhaps, however, they do not signify the same thing, since the name does not do so in the other case either; hence there is some difference. But if they assign “Coriscus” simply in one instance and add “some one” or “this” in the other, that is absurd. For one does not differ more than the other; whichever form is used, there is no difference.

The solution is therefore not to proceed in this way. Since it is uncertain whether someone who has not determined the ambiguity has been refuted, and since it is permitted to distinguish the ambiguity in arguments, it is clear that failing to determine the question and asking it simply is an error. Even if the respondent himself has not been refuted, the argument resembles a refutation.

People often become sluggish about distinguishing an amphiboly when they see one, because such cases are frequently proposed and they do not wish to appear troublesome on every occasion. Then, when they do not think that the argument has arisen for this reason, they often encounter something contrary to expectation. Since distinguishing the ambiguity is permitted, one should not hesitate to do so, as was stated earlier.

If someone makes two questions into one question, the deceptive inference will not arise through equivocation or amphiboly. The issue is whether this is a refutation or not.

For what difference is there between asking whether Callias and Themistocles are musical and asking whether two different people who had one name were musical? If the expression signifies more than one thing, more than one question has been asked.

If, then, it is not correct to regard a single answer as sufficient for two questions, it is clear that one should not answer simply in the case of equivocal expressions either—not even if the answer is true of all the things involved, as some think. For this is no different from asking: “Are Coriscus and Callias at home, or are they not at home?” Whether both are present or both absent, there are several propositions on either side.

The fact that it is true to say “yes” does not make the question one question. For it is possible to answer “yes” or “no” truthfully to ten thousand questions asked in this way; nevertheless, one should not give a single answer, since the argument would thereby be destroyed.

The same applies when the same name is imposed on different things. If one ought not to give one answer to two questions, it is clear that one should not say simply “yes” or “no” in the case of equivocal expressions either. For the person who says this gives an answer, although he has not really answered; in a certain way, he loses the point at issue in the argument because what has happened remains concealed.

As we said that some refutations appear to be refutations although they are not, so some solutions appear to be solutions although they are not. In contentious arguments, and in dealing with an equivocal expression, these apparent solutions may sometimes be more useful than true ones [Col. 1027D].

In matters that appear to be the case, the respondent should answer in accordance with the appearance. This will least make a refutation arise. If he is compelled to say something contrary to expectation, he should add that it merely appears to be so. In this way it will appear that neither a refutation nor something contrary to expectation has been produced.

Since it is clear how a question begs the original point, people think that, whenever the premises are closely related, one should refute them altogether and grant none of them, as though the original point were being begged.

When someone demands something that necessarily follows from the position but is false or contrary to expectation, the same response should be made. Things that follow necessarily appear to belong to the same position.

Moreover, when a universal is not taken by name but by similarity, one should say that it was not granted in that form and that the questioner has not taken it as he proposed. A refutation often arises for this reason.

When these points are prohibited, one must return to what has not been properly demonstrated and resist according to the determination already given.

In the case of names used in their proper sense, it is necessary to answer either simply or by making a distinction. But when we propose something by implication—when questions are not asked fully but in truncated form—a refutation arises for that reason. For example:

“Do you think that whatever belongs to the Athenians is the possession of the Athenians?”

“Yes.”

“Similarly, in other cases?”

“Certainly. A human being belongs among animals.”

“Therefore, a human being is the possession of animals.”

We say that a human being belongs among animals because he is an animal, and that Lysander belongs among the Lacedaemonians because he is a Lacedaemonian.

It is therefore clear that where what is proposed is ambiguous, one must not grant it simply.

When two things exist and, given one of them, the other appears necessarily to exist, whereas when the other exists the first does not follow necessarily, one should grant the lesser claim when asked about both. For it is more difficult to draw a conclusion from several things.

If the questioner argues that one thing has a contrary while another does not, then, provided that the argument is true, one should say that there is a contrary, but that the name of the other has not been supplied.

Some people say that, among the things stated, refusal to grant some propositions makes the respondent speak falsely, but refusal to grant others does not—for example, propositions that are ambiguous. For many people have not determined whether the soul of animals is corruptible or immortal.

When it is uncertain in which way what is proposed is ordinarily stated, the question concerns what are called opinions. These include both true beliefs and complete negations, as in “the diameter is incommensurable.”

Moreover, when someone transfers names in matters whose truth is in doubt, the deception will be especially concealed. Since it is uncertain how the truth stands, the speaker will not appear to be acting sophistically. Because the matter is doubtful, he will not appear to be speaking falsely; the metaphor will make the argument appear free from refutation.

Furthermore, whenever someone anticipates the questions that are about to be asked, one should press the point first and state the conclusion in advance. In this way one will most effectively prevent the questioner from proceeding.

## CHAPTER III. The proper solution: its places
Source/review notes: The source’s abbreviated half-verse/Iliad example has compressed or corrupt syntax; its printed Latin is preserved with a cautious approximate gloss.

Since a correct solution is the disclosure [Col. 1028D] of the false syllogism on account of whichever question the falsehood arises—“false syllogism” being used in two senses, either when the conclusion drawn is false or when, although there is no syllogism, one appears to exist—the solution just described will apply also to an apparent syllogism, through which a correction of the questions appears to arise. Thus it is possible to refute syllogistic arguments while solving the apparent syllogism by division.

Again, since some syllogistic arguments have a true conclusion and others a false one, those that are false in their conclusion can be solved in two ways: either by refuting one of the answers given to the questions, or by showing that the conclusion [Col. 1029A] does not hold in the proposed way. Those that are false in their premises can be solved only by refuting something, since their conclusion is true. Therefore, for anyone wishing to solve an argument, the first matter to examine is whether it actually forms a syllogism or not; next, whether its conclusion is true or false, so that we may solve it either by division or by refutation; and, in the case of refutation, again by one method or the other, as was previously explained.

There is a very great difference between solving an argument when one is being questioned and solving it when one is not being questioned. For it is difficult to foresee the issue, whereas when time is available it is easy to see it.

Of the refutations that arise through equivocation and amphiboly, some contain a question with several meanings, while others contain a conclusion expressed in several ways. Thus, in the argument “to speak silently,” [Col. 1029B] the conclusion has two meanings; in “not to know what one knows,” there is amphiboly in one of the questions. Sometimes a term is both double and not double, and sometimes it signifies two things—one thing being and another not being.

 In all cases where the ambiguity occurs at the end, unless the contradiction has first been secured, no refutation results, as in the case of “to see the blind”; for without contradiction there is no refutation. Where the ambiguity occurs in the questions, however, it is not necessary to deny in advance that the expression has two meanings, since the argument does not arise from that ambiguity itself but because of it.

At the beginning, therefore, one should answer an ambiguous term or expression in this way: “It is so in one respect, but not so in another.” Thus, concerning “to speak silently,” one should say that it is so in one respect and not so in another, and then proceed with [Col. 1029C] the relevant qualifications. Some things are advantageous in one respect and not in another, since “advantageous” is said in several ways.

 If the ambiguity escapes notice, it must be corrected at the end by adding to the question: “Is it ‘to speak silently,’ but not those who are silent?” The same applies in propositions that have several senses.

“Do you think that they know what they know?”—“Yes.”

“But not as knowing in that way; for ‘not to know’ is not the same as ‘not to be knowing in that way.’”

In general, one must resist the argument, even if the conclusion is drawn in a simple form. For the respondent has denied not the thing meant by the speaker but the name; consequently, this is not a refutation.

 It is also clear how arguments arising from combination and division are to be solved. If the expression signifies one thing when divided and another when combined, the contrary interpretation must be given. All [Col. 1029D] such arguments arise from combination and division.

“Do you think that the man whom you saw being struck was struck by the same person by whom this man was struck?” And: “By the person by whom he was struck, did you see him?”

This also has something of the character of an ambiguous question, although it arises from combination; for it is not ambiguous because of division, since the expression is not the same when divided and when combined.

 Thus *ora* and *hora*, when pronounced with different accents, signify different things, although in writing the same name is used, being written from the same letters and in the same way. In speech, however, the signs are no longer the same when pronounced. Hence the ambiguity does not arise from division.

It is clear that not all refutations arise from ambiguity, as some maintain. The respondent must therefore [Col. 1030A] divide the expression, for “to see with the eyes the man who was struck” is not the same as “to see with the eyes of the man who was struck.”

 The argument of Euthydemus is similar:

“Do you think that, although you are in Sicily, you have seen the ships now present in the Piraeus?”

Again:

“Do you think that a bad shoemaker can be good?” Let someone be good but a bad shoemaker; therefore he is a bad shoemaker.

“Do you think that disciplines (*disciplinae*) are good when their sciences or branches of knowledge (*scientiae*) are good? But a good discipline is ‘of evil’ (*mali*, genitive); therefore a good discipline is an evil (*malum*). Yet both the evil (*malum*) and the discipline are evil; therefore a bad discipline (*mala disciplina*) is an evil (*malum*).”

The printed wording deliberately shifts among *mali* (‘of evil’), *malum* (‘evil’), and *mala disciplina* (‘bad discipline’); those shifts create the apparent inference.

“Do you think that you are now telling the truth when you say that you have come into being?” Therefore you have come into being now.

Or does the divided expression signify something else? “To tell the truth now that you have come into being” does not mean “you have come into being now.”

 “Do you think that, in whatever way you are able to act, and with whatever things you are able to act, you will act in that way and with those things?” But although you are not playing the lyre, you have the power to play it; therefore, although you are not playing the lyre, you will play it.

[Col. 1030B] Or does he possess the power for this—to play the lyre while not playing it? Rather, he possesses it so that, whenever he does not play, he may play.

Some solve this argument in another way. If he has been given the power to do something, they say, it does not follow that the person who is not playing the lyre will play it. For it is not in every case the same thing to be able to do something and to do it in every way in which one is able.

But it is clear that this is not a good solution. For all arguments arising from the same source require the same solution, whereas the same solution cannot be adapted to every argument, nor even always to the question itself. It must be directed against the questioner, not against the argument.

 Arguments based on accent do not arise either in written expressions or in spoken ones, except in a few cases, such as this:

“Do you think that the house in which you live exists?”—[Col. 1030C] “Yes.”

“Do you mean ‘is there a house in which you live?’ Is *ne* the negation of ‘in which you live’?”—“Yes.”

“But you said, ‘There is no house in which you live.’ Therefore you deny that you live in a house.”

How this is to be solved is clear. The expression pronounced with the grave accent does not signify the same thing as when pronounced with the acute.

 It is also clear how one must resist arguments that arise because things that are not the same are treated as though they were expressed in the same way. We have the genera of the categories to guide us. In one case the respondent, when questioned, granted that something did not belong among the things signifying substance; in the other, the questioner showed that it belonged among relatives or quantities.

Some expressions appear to signify substance because of their wording, as in this argument:

“Do you think that it is possible for the same thing both to do and to undergo the same action at the same time?”—“No.”

“But it is possible for seeing and being seen to occur simultaneously and in the same respect.”

 Again:

[Col. 1030D] “Do you think that anything that undergoes an action can perform an action?”—“No.”

“Then ‘to be cut,’ ‘to be burned,’ and ‘to work’ are expressed in the same way, and all signify undergoing an action. Again, ‘to run’ and ‘to see’ are expressed in the same way with respect to one another. Yet seeing is doing something; therefore it is also undergoing something, and thus the same thing is both doing and undergoing.”

If someone, after granting that it is possible for the same thing both to do and to undergo the same action simultaneously, says that seeing and being seen can occur together, he has not yet been refuted unless he also says that seeing performs something and being seen undergoes something. That additional question is required. The listener, however, may suppose that it has already been granted, because “to cut” was granted to be doing something and “to be cut” to be undergoing something, along with whatever other expressions are similarly spoken.

 The listener himself supplies the remaining inference, as though the expressions had been used in the same way, although [Col. 1031A] they have not. The wording makes them appear similar.

The same thing occurs here as in equivocations. The person who is ignorant of the arguments thinks that the speaker has denied the thing, not merely the name, and therefore still requires the further question: if the respondent is considering only one of the meanings, is the term equivocal? Once this has been granted, there will be a refutation.

Arguments of this kind are also similar to those in which, if someone has something and later no longer has it, he is said to have lost it. For if he loses only one counter, he will no longer have ten counters.

 “Did he lose what he no longer has, although he had it before?” But a person need not lose as many things as he has.

The questioner therefore collects, from what he has, the number of things involved; for ten is among the things he has. If the question had been asked at the beginning in this form—“If someone does not have as many things as he previously had, has he lost that many?”—no one would have granted it, but would have answered “that many” or “some of them.”

[Col. 1031B] Moreover, someone may give what he does not have, since he does not possess only a single counter.

 “Did he not give what he did not have, but give it in the respect in which he did not have it?” For “only” signifies neither what, nor what kind, nor how much, but a relation to something—namely, “not together with another.”

The same applies if someone asks: “Do you think that someone can give what no one has?” If the respondent does not assent, the questioner may ask:

“If someone gives something quickly, can someone who does not possess ‘quickly’ give it?”

Having secured assent, he concludes that someone gives what he does not have. But it is clear that he has not formed a syllogism. For “quickly” is not what is given; rather, it is the manner in which it is given. Someone may give in a manner in which he does not possess it—for example, he may give pleasantly what he possesses, but give it painfully.

 Arguments of this kind are also the following:

“Do you think that someone can strike with his hand what he does not have?” Or: “Can he see with his eye what he does not have?” For he does not [Col. 1031C] possess only one eye.

Some solve these arguments by saying that the person may possess one eye alone, or may possess one thing and something else besides. Others say that he may possess what he has received in the relevant sense. For this person gave only one counter, and this person has, they say, only one counter from him; for he received it from him, and therefore this person has only one counter.

Others immediately refute the question by pointing out that it is possible to have what one did not receive—for example, someone may receive sweet wine and possess harsh wine if it has spoiled while being received.

 But all these solutions, as was said earlier, are directed not against the argument but against the person. If this were a genuine solution, it would be impossible to solve the corresponding contrary argument. The same applies in other cases: if “what is” is given as the solution, then “what is not” would also be a solution. If the expression is granted without qualification, [Col. 1031D] it yields a conclusion; if it does not yield one, the proposed answer is not a solution. In the preceding cases, however, even though all the premises were granted, we do not say that a syllogism has been formed.

Arguments of this kind also include the following:

 “Do you think that someone wrote what is written?” But what is written now is “You are sitting,” which is false. It was true when it was being written; therefore it was written as both false and true at the same time.

For “a false or true expression,” or “a false or true opinion,” signifies not the thing itself but a certain kind of thing. The same account applies to opinion.

Again:

“Do you think that what a learner learns is what he learns?” But someone learns something slowly or quickly. Therefore he did not say “what he learns” but “the manner in which he learns.”

Again:

“Do you think that what someone walks upon he tramples?” But he walks all day. Thus he did not say what he walks upon, but when [Col. 1032A] he walks.

 Similarly, when someone drinks a cup, he does not drink what he drinks, but that from which he drinks.

Again:

“Do you think that someone knows what he has discovered or learned?” Of these things, one he discovered and another he learned; yet neither of these is simply “both.”

Or is the expression “all” in one sense, while “not all” is meant in another?

Further, there is said to be a third man in addition to the man himself and to each individual man. For “man” and “the universal” signify not a this-something, but a certain quality, relation, manner, or something of that kind.

 The same applies here:

“Are Coriscus and musical Coriscus the same or different?” The one signifies a this-something, while the other signifies a certain quality; therefore it is not the same thing to define them.

Giving a definition does not introduce a third man; it merely grants what the thing itself is. For it will not be the case that what Callias is and what man is are both this-somethings.

[Col. 1032B] Nor does it matter if someone, having introduced the term, says that it signifies not a this-something but the same thing as a quality. For there will still be one thing common to many, such as man.

It is therefore clear that what is predicated universally of all things must not be granted to be a this-something, but must signify either a quantity, a quality, a relation, or something of that sort.

 In general, in arguments arising from wording, the solution must always be the opposite of the source of the argument. If the argument arises from combination, solve it by division; if from division, by combination. If it arises from the acute accent, the solution is the grave accent; if from the grave, the acute.

If the argument arises from equivocation, it must be solved by giving the contrary name. If someone has used “animate” and the conclusion is drawn by denying that it is not animate, it is clear that the solution is [Col. 1032C] “inanimate.” If “inanimate” was used and the conclusion drawn is that it is animate, one must say that it is inanimate.

The same applies to amphiboly.

If the argument arises from similarity of wording, the solution is the opposite expression:

 “Do you think that someone will give what he does not have?”—“Do you mean that he will give not what he does not have, but in the manner in which he does not have it—for example, only one counter?”

“Do you think that someone knows what he knows by learning or discovering?” Yet the question does not concern the things he knows.

And if the argument is that what someone walks upon he tramples, the answer is that the issue is not what he walks upon but when he walks.

The same applies in the other cases.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Solutions of the Arguments from Accident

 There is one solution common to all arguments arising from accident. Since it is indeterminate when one should say of a thing that what belongs to it accidentally [Col. 1032D] belongs to it in the same way—and since in some cases this appears to be so, while in others it is not said to be necessary—the answer should be framed uniformly for all cases: the accidental predicate does not necessarily belong to the thing in question. One must have a means of refuting the claim by stating what follows in the corresponding manner.

All the following arguments arise from accident:

“Do you know what I must ask you?”

“Come now, do you recognize the person who is coming, or the person who is covered?”

“Is the statue your work?”

“Is your dog the father?”

“Are few things few?”

 For it is clear in all these cases that what is said of the accident need not also be true of the thing itself. Only in things that are indistinguishable according to substance, and that are one and the same, do all predicates appear to belong in the same way.

[Col. 1033A] Being good is not the same as being about to be asked a question; nor are being someone who is coming, or someone who is covered, and being Coriscus the same.

Therefore, if I know Coriscus but do not know the person who is coming, it does not follow that I both know and do not know the same person. Nor, if this thing is mine and it is a work, does it follow that the work is mine; it may be my possession, my property, or something else.

The same applies in the other cases.

 Some solve these arguments by refuting the question. They say that it is possible to know and not know the same thing, but not in the same respect. Thus, although they do not know the person who is coming, they know Coriscus; they say that they know and do not know the same person, but not in the same respect.

Yet, as we have already said, arguments that arise from the same source ought to have the same solution. That will not be the case [Col. 1033B] if someone takes the relevant point to concern not “knowing” but “being” or “being in some relation,” which they themselves approve—for example, “If this is a father, it is your father.” For although this may be true in certain cases, and it may happen that the same person is both known and unknown, this has nothing in common with the argument just stated.

There is nothing to prevent the same argument from having several faults, but the disclosure of every fault is not a solution.

 It is possible to show that someone has formed a false syllogism without showing the reason why he has failed—for example, in Zeno’s argument that motion does not exist. Thus, if someone tries to draw a conclusion to an impossibility, he is at fault; and even if he forms a syllogism a thousand times, this is not the solution. For the solution was the disclosure of the syllogism through which the false conclusion arose.

[Col. 1033C] If he has not formed a syllogism, however, then whether he tries to draw a true or a false conclusion, the disclosure of that fact is the solution.

In some cases, perhaps, the same thing may both be known and not known; but this will not appear to be so in the present case. For one knows Coriscus as Coriscus and knows the person who is coming as the person who is coming. It is possible to know one thing and not know another—for example, to know what is white but not know what is musical. In this way the same person knows and does not know, but not in the same respect. In the present case, however, one knows both the person who is coming and Coriscus, both the person who is coming as coming and Coriscus as Coriscus.

 Those who solve the argument that every number is few make a similar mistake. They omit the fact that no conclusion has been formed and then claim that a true conclusion has been reached—for they say that everything is both many and few. They are mistaken.

[Col. 1033D] Some also solve the syllogisms by ambiguity, as in the argument that someone is your father, son, or slave. But it is clear that if a refutation appears to arise from a term used in several senses, the name or expression must properly have several meanings. No one properly says that this person is the son of that person if the latter is the son’s master; rather, the combination arises accidentally:

“Do you think that this is yours?”—“Yes.”

“But this is a son; therefore he is your son.”

The things that have accidentally been brought together are “yours” and “a son,” not “your son.”

 The same applies to “something evil being good,” as in “prudence is a discipline of evil things.” This is not said in several senses of those things themselves, but of possession. Perhaps it can be said in several senses—for example, we say that man belongs among animals—but not as a possession.

If something is said in relation to evils, or belongs to some things [Col. 1034A] because they are evils, it is “of evils” in that respect, but not “evil things.” Thus, although it may perhaps be possible for something belonging to evil things to be good in two senses, that is not the meaning in this argument. It would be more plausible if some slave belonging to a bad man were good.

Perhaps not even then. For if something is good and belongs to him, it does not follow that it is simultaneously “his good.”

 Nor is it the case that “man belongs to animals” is said in several senses. For an expression is not made ambiguous merely because we signify something after taking part of it away. The source gives the abbreviated example *dimidium … versus da mihi, Iliada significamus, Iram pande dea*—approximately: “give me half of the verse”; we signify the *Iliad* by “Unfold the wrath, goddess.” The syntax of this printed example is uncertain.

## CHAPTER V. On the Solutions of the Six Last Arguments Outside Expression

Arguments that arise because something is said in one respect, [Col. 1034B] or as something, or somewhere, or in some manner, or in relation to something, and not absolutely, must be solved by examining the conclusion in relation to the contradiction, if the thing in question can undergo such a qualification.

 Contraries and opposites, affirmation and negation, cannot belong absolutely to the same thing at the same time. But in a qualified respect, or in relation to something, or in some manner, or in one respect as opposed to another, nothing prevents both from applying. Therefore, if one predicate is absolute and the other qualified, there is not yet a refutation. This must be examined in the conclusion in relation to the contradiction.

All the following arguments have this character:

“Do you think that what is not can exist?” Yet what is not is not something.

Similarly, “what is” will not be; for when things exist, it will not be something that will exist.

 [Col. 1034C] “Can the same person simultaneously swear truly and perjure himself?”

“Is it possible simultaneously to persuade and dissuade the same person?”

“Is it not the same thing both to be something and to be?”

What is not, if it is something, is not therefore something absolutely.

Nor, if someone swears truly in one respect, is he necessarily a good swearer absolutely. A person who swears that he will perjure himself swears truly in saying this, but he does not therefore swear truly in the unqualified sense.

Nor does someone who dissuades also persuade; he persuades only in a certain respect.

 The same account applies to the claim that the same person is simultaneously lying and telling the truth. But because the qualification “in some respect” is not easily noticed, it is difficult to see whether someone is assigning to the person an absolute character—that he is truthful or a liar—or merely a qualified one.

Nothing prevents the same person from being absolutely neither a liar nor truthful in every respect, while being truthful in a particular matter, or from being truthful about something without being truthful absolutely.

[Col. 1034D] The same applies to relation, place, and time. All such arguments arise from this source.

 “Do you think that health or wealth is good?” Yet for a foolish person, or for one who does not use it properly, it is not good. Therefore it is both good and not good.

“Is being healthy, or having power in the city, good?” Yet sometimes it is not good. Therefore the same thing is both good and not good for the same person.

Or is there nothing to prevent what is good absolutely from not being good for this person, or what is good for this person from not being good now, or from not being good in this place?

 “Do you think that what the wise person does not wish is evil? But he does not wish to lose what is good; therefore what is good is evil.”

For “a good thing is evil” (*malum est bonum*) is not the same as “to lose a good thing” (*amittere bonum*).

[Col. 1035A] The same applies to the argument concerning the thief. For if a thief is evil, it does not follow that taking is evil, and therefore that he wishes for evil; rather, he wishes for what is good, since taking is good.

Illness is evil, but losing illness is not evil.

 “Do you think that the just is more choiceworthy than the unjust, and what is done justly more choiceworthy than what is done unjustly?” Yet to die unjustly is more choiceworthy.

“Do you think that it is just for each person to have his own property?” Whatever someone awards according to his own opinion, even if that opinion is false, is his by law. Therefore the same thing is both just and unjust.

“Should one judge the person who speaks justly or the person who speaks unjustly?” Yet it is just for the person who has suffered injustice to state fully what he has suffered, and what he suffered was unjust.

 For even if suffering something unjustly is choiceworthy, it does not follow that what is unjust is more choiceworthy than what is just. Absolutely, what is just is choiceworthy; [Col. 1035B] but there is nothing to prevent the question from being whether the act was done unjustly or justly.

It is just for each person to possess his own property, but not just to possess what belongs to another.

Nor is there anything to prevent a judgment from being just in a qualified sense—for example, because it accords with the opinion of the judge. For if a judgment is just in this way or just for this person, it is not thereby just absolutely.

 Similarly, there is nothing to prevent unjust things from being said to be just. For if it is just to say something, it does not follow that what is said is just, any more than if it is useful to say something, what is said is useful.

The same applies to things that are unjust.

Therefore, if someone says that certain things are unjust, he is not thereby convicted of speaking unjustly. He says things that it is just to say, although the things themselves may be unjust to suffer.

 Refutations that arise from a definition must be resisted, as was previously stated, by considering the conclusion in relation to the contradiction: the thing must be the same, in the same respect, in relation to the same thing, in the same manner, and at the same time.

[Col. 1035C] If the question is put at the beginning, one must not concede it—“For it is impossible for the same thing to be both double and not double”—but must answer in such a way that the person who makes the concession cannot be refuted.

All the following arguments arise in this way:

 “Do you think that one who knows a thing knows the thing which he knows, and that one who does not know it does likewise?”

Someone who knows Coriscus as Coriscus does not know him as musical; therefore he both knows and does not know the same thing.

“Do you think that a four-cubit object is larger than a three-cubit object?” A three-cubit object can become a four-cubit object in length; and what is larger is larger than what is smaller. Therefore the same thing is both larger and smaller than itself in the same respect.

 Arguments that arise from begging the question and assuming at the beginning what is at issue must be met as follows. If the point is evident to the person being questioned, [Col. 1035D] it must not be granted, even if the questioner appears trustworthy. If it is not evident, the ignorance resulting from the fault in such arguments must be turned against the questioner, as against someone who has not produced a refutation. For a refutation must not depend on the initial assumption; moreover, the assumption was granted not for the questioner to use as he pleased, but so that he might derive the opposite from it, as occurs in refutations that do not remove the initial assumption.

In arguments arising from the consequent, the relevant point must be shown within the argument itself. There are two kinds of consequence. One is when the particular follows the universal—for example, “man” follows “animal”; for the questioners assume that if one follows the other, the other also follows the one. The second arises from opposites: if this follows from that, then the opposite follows from the opposite. This is the basis of Melissus’ argument.

 [Col. 1036A] If what has come into being has a beginning, he assumes that what has not come into being has no beginning. Therefore, if the heavens have not come into being, they are infinite. But this is not so, since the consequence runs in the opposite direction.

In arguments that derive a conclusion from something added, one must examine whether, once that addition is removed, the same impossibility still follows. This must then be made clear. One must say that the respondent granted the point not because it appeared true in itself, but for the sake of the argument; what the questioner has actually used does not belong to the argument.

 In arguments that make several questions into one, the distinction must be made immediately at the beginning. A question is one when it has one answer. Therefore one must not affirm or deny several things of one thing, or one thing of several things, but one thing of one thing.

As with equivocal terms, sometimes the predicate belongs to both subjects, sometimes to neither. [Col. 1036B] Therefore, when the question is not simple, nothing follows against someone who gives a simple answer.

The same applies here. Whenever several predicates belong to one subject, or one predicate belongs to several subjects, or belong to neither, nothing contrary follows against someone who gives a simple answer and thereby commits this error.

 Sometimes, however, a predicate belongs to one subject but not to another; or several predicates belong to several subjects, so that in one respect they belong to both and in another they do not. This must be guarded against.

For example:

“If this is good and that is evil, it is true to say that these things are good and evil, and again that they are neither good nor evil.” For neither predicate belongs to both subjects. Thus the same things are good, evil, and neither good nor evil.

Again, if each thing is identical with itself but different from other things, then, since they are not identical with others but with themselves, and are different from those same things, they are both different from and identical with themselves.

 [Col. 1036C] Further, if good is evil and evil is good, there will be two things. And each of two unequal things will be equal to itself; therefore the two things are both equal and unequal to themselves.

Arguments of this kind also fall under other solutions, since “both” and “all” signify several things. It is therefore not the same thing, apart from the name, to affirm and deny the same predicate. But that was not a refutation; rather, it is clear that if several questions are not made into one, but one thing is affirmed or denied of one thing, no impossibility results.

## CHAPTER VI. Solutions of Arguments Involving Repetition and Solecism

In arguments that lead one to say the same thing repeatedly, it is clear that terms said in relation [Col. 1036D] to something must not be granted to signify predicates existing separately in themselves. Thus “double” implies its relation to “half”; “ten” is involved in what falls one short of ten; “to do” is involved in “not to do”; and, in general, an affirmation is involved in a negation. Yet someone who says, “This is not white,” does not thereby say that it is white.

Perhaps “double” signifies nothing independently, just as neither does what is contained in “half.” Even if it does signify something, what it signifies separately is not the same as what it signifies in combination. Nor does “knowledge” signify a species by itself, as in “medicine is knowledge”; the common term is knowledge of something knowable.

For predicates displayed in themselves, one must answer that what is displayed separately and what is displayed in the expression [Col. 1037A] are not the same. “Hollow,” taken generally, signifies the same thing in what is snub and what is curved; once it is added to another term, however, nothing prevents it from signifying a hollowing of the nose in one case and of the leg in the other. Nor is there any difference here between saying “a snub nose” and “a hollow nose.”

Moreover, the wording must not be granted in the nominative case, for that is false. “Snub” is not itself “a hollow nose”; rather, the hollowing is a condition of the nose. There is therefore nothing absurd in saying that a snub nose is a nose having a hollowing of the nose.

We have already explained why solecisms appear to arise. How they are to be solved will be clear in the arguments themselves. All arguments of this kind try to construct something like the following:

“Do you think that what you truly say to be something really is it? You say that something (*quidpiam*) is a stone (*lapidem*, accusative); therefore something is ‘a stone’ (*quidpiam lapidem*, retaining the accusative predicate).”

But to say *lapidem* (“stone,” accusative) is not to say “what” (*quod*) but “whom” (*quem*), not “this” (*hoc*) but “this one” (*hunc*). If someone therefore asks, “Do you think that the person whom (*quem*) you truly say to exist is that person (*istum*)?” [Col. 1037B] he does not appear to speak grammatical Latin. The same is true if he asks, “Do you think that the woman whom (*quam*) you say exists is this man (*iste*)?”

It makes no difference to call a piece of wood (*lignum*, neuter) “this man” (*iste*, masculine), or to do the same with anything signifying neither masculine nor feminine. Thus no solecism results if what you say exists is “this” (*istud*, neuter): you say that it is wood, and therefore the wood is this (*lignum istud*).

But *lapis* (“stone”) and *iste* (“this man”) have masculine declension. Suppose someone asks, “Do you think this man (*iste*) is that woman (*illa*)?” and then, “Is this man (*iste*) not Coriscus?” The conclusion “Therefore he is that woman (*illa*)” does not establish a solecism unless “Coriscus” signifies the same thing as *illa*. The respondent has not granted that identity; it must be asked beforehand. If the identity neither holds nor has been granted, no conclusion has been drawn, either about the existence of something or against the respondent.

Likewise, in the earlier argument, “this man” (*iste*) must signify “a stone” (*lapidem*) [Col. 1037C]. If it neither does so nor is granted to do so, the conclusion must not be stated. The inference merely appears to work because unlike noun cases look alike.

“Do you think it is true to say that this (*ista*, feminine nominative) is what you say it to be? You say it is an asp (*aspidem*, accusative); therefore this is an asp (*ista aspidem*, with an accusative predicate).”

Is it not necessary instead that *ista* signify *aspis* (“an asp,” nominative), while *aspidem* signifies *istam* (“this,” accusative)? The same failure occurs in the Cleon example. From “the man whom (*quem*) you say is this man (*istum*, accusative) is this man (*iste*, nominative)” and “you say that this man (*istum*) is Cleon (*Cleonem*, accusative),” it does not follow that “this man is Cleon” in the malformed form *iste Cleonem*. For *iste Cleonem* is not grammatical. What was granted was that the man whom I call *istum* is *iste*, not *istum*; the proposed question itself otherwise would not be grammatical Latin.

“Do you know this (*istud*)? But this (*istud*) is a stone (*lapis*); therefore you know ‘stone’ (*lapis*).” Does *istud* signify the same thing in “Do you know *istud*?” and in “*Istud* is *lapis*”? In the first it stands for *hunc* (“this one,” accusative); in the latter, [Col. 1037D] for *hic* (“this one,” nominative).

Again: “Do you know that (*illud*) of which you have knowledge? You have knowledge of a stone (*lapidis*, genitive); therefore you know ‘of a stone’ (*lapidis*).” But in “of this stone” one says *hujus lapidis*, whereas the object “this stone” is *hunc lapidem*. What was granted was “you know *illud*,” not “you know *illius*.” The conclusion must therefore use *lapidem* (“stone,” accusative), not *lapidis* (“of a stone,” genitive).

It is therefore clear from what has been said that arguments of this kind do not establish a solecism but only appear to do so; it is also clear why they appear so and how one must resist them.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Easy, Difficult, and Acute Argument

One must understand that some arguments are easy to recognize and others more difficult, because some deceive [Col. 1038A] the listener subtly in one respect, even though they arise from the same source.

The same argument must be called the same when it arises from the same cause. Yet the same argument may appear to one person to arise from wording, to another from accident, and to another from something else, because each of the indirect causes is not equally evident.

Thus, among arguments arising from equivocation—which appears to be the most inept form of captious reasoning—some are evident to everyone. Nearly all arguments arising from wording are ridiculous, such as:

“A man was carried in a cart to the stairs, where the slave arrived, at Cereas.”

“Is Boreas pure?”—“Certainly not, for he destroys the poor man and the buyer.”

“Which of the oxen will calve first?”—“Neither; both are behind.”

“Is it Evarchus?”—“Certainly not; it is [Col. 1038B] Apollonides.”

Most of the other arguments of this kind are similar.

Others, however, appear to escape even the most experienced. A sign of this is that people often dispute about names—for example, whether “being” and “one” signify the same thing in all cases or something different. Some think that “being” and “one” signify the same thing; others solve the arguments of Zeno and Parmenides by saying that “one” and “being” are used in several senses.
