The same applies to arguments from accident and to each of the other sources. Some arguments will appear easy and others more difficult. It is not equally easy in every case to determine the genus to which an argument belongs, or whether it is a refutation or not.

An acute argument is one that produces the greatest doubt. It bites most sharply, and doubt is of two kinds: in syllogistic arguments, doubt about [Col. 1038C] which of the questions one should choose; and in contentious arguments, doubt about how one should maintain the proposed position.

Consequently, among arguments that form syllogisms, the sharper arguments are those that produce the greatest uncertainty.

The sharpest syllogistic argument is one that, from premises that appear most plausible, refutes and establishes a conclusion with the greatest possible plausibility. Since there is one argument—with the contradiction transposed—all its syllogisms will be similar; for it will always refute or establish what is plausible from premises that are similarly plausible. Hence doubt is unavoidable.

The sharpest argument, then, is one that establishes its conclusion equally through the questions. The second is one that does so through all similarly plausible questions. This too produces similar doubt about which of the questions must be refuted. That is difficult, because although it is clear that something must be refuted, it is uncertain [Col. 1038D] what must be refuted.

Among contentious arguments, the sharpest is one in which it is immediately doubtful whether a syllogism has been formed or not, and whether the solution is based on falsity or on division.

The second sharpest is one in which it is clear that the solution depends on division or refutation, but it has not been determined through which question the refutation or division must be made—whether the solution concerns the conclusion or one of the questions.

Sometimes an argument that does not form a syllogism is easy to solve, if the premises assumed are extremely implausible or false. Sometimes, however, it is not fit to be dismissed. This happens when one of the relevant questions is missing—the question on which the argument depends and from which it arises—and the questioner forms a conclusion without asking it; in that case [Col. 1039A] the reasoning is inept.

When the missing premise is something that should in no way be dismissed because it is external to the argument, the argument may be sound, while the questioner has simply asked the question improperly.

The solution must sometimes be directed against the argument, sometimes against the questioner and the question, and sometimes against neither of these.

Similarly, the questioning and syllogistic process must be adapted to the position, the respondent, and the time available—especially when the solution requires more time than the present occasion of the debate allows.

## CHAPTER VIII. Epilogue to the Eight Preceding Books and the Two Present Books
[Col. 1039B] From what sources, then, and from which elements, the disputants’ deceptive reasonings arise; how we may show that they are saying what is false and contrary to expectation; further, from what sources a syllogism arises; how one should ask questions and what order the questions should follow; moreover, what use all such arguments have; and, finally, concerning every kind of response in general, and how arguments and syllogisms are to be resolved: all these matters have been discussed by us. It remains, recalling what was proposed at the beginning, to say something briefly about that subject and bring our discussion to an end.

We stated at the outset that there is a certain ratiocinative faculty for discovering, concerning a proposed matter, what is as probable as possible; for this is the proper work of dialectic in itself and of the tentative method. But because someone is first instructed by it on account of its proximity to sophistry, so that he may be capable of conducting not merely an experiment in the dialectical manner but also something approaching a scientific inquiry, for that reason we stated that the function of this discipline was not only to acquire an argument, but also, while maintaining an argument, to defend a position in a similar manner by means of what is as probable as possible. We explained that the reason for this was that Socrates also questioned for this purpose, but did not answer, for he confessed that he did not know.

It has been made clear in the preceding books from how many sources, and directed toward how many ends, this is to be done, and from where we shall be equipped for these tasks. It has also been explained how every question should be asked or arranged, and concerning the responses that are directed toward syllogisms. The other arguments belonging to this discipline have likewise been set forth, whatever they may be. In addition, as we already said earlier, we have treated deceptive reasonings and the manner in which they are to be handled.

That the matters we proposed have therefore sufficiently reached their end is clear.

## CHAPTER IX. Peroration.

[Col. 1040A]

It is worthwhile that we should not fail to recognize what has occurred in connection with this undertaking. For of all discoveries, those which have first been taken over from others gradually acquire elaboration and increase from those who receive them later; but discoveries made at the beginning generally make little initial progress, although that small increase is much more useful than the later growth produced by others. For, as the saying goes, the greatest beginning of everything is perhaps also the most difficult. The more powerful something is in potential, the smaller it is in bulk, and therefore the more difficult it seems. Once it has been discovered, however, it is easy to add to it and fit the remainder together.

The same thing has happened with rhetorical arguments, and almost with all the other arts as well. Those who first discovered their principles brought them to only a very small extent; but those now regarded as more celebrated, claiming material from many sources and gathering it piece by piece as though by succession, enlarged them in this way. Tisias came after his predecessors; Thrasymachus after Tisias; Theodorus after Thrasymachus; and many others assembled many parts. It is therefore no wonder that the art has grown to a considerable size.

In this undertaking, however, it was not the case that one part had been investigated while another had not; rather, almost none of it had previously existed. For among those who worked for hire on contentious arguments, there was a kind of instruction resembling the activity of Gorgias. Some taught people to memorize rhetorical speeches, while others taught interrogative speeches, into which the speeches of the two parties were accustomed to fall by turns.

Their instruction was therefore quick for learners, since it was without art. They did not think they were teaching an art, but merely providing the products of an art, and so teaching people to speak with sophistication. It would be just as if someone claimed to teach a discipline by which people would not suffer from sore feet, but did not teach shoemaking or indicate where such things could be obtained, while supplying a great variety of every kind of shoe. Such a person would certainly have contributed to practical use, but would not have transmitted the art.

There had been many and ancient statements concerning rhetoric; but concerning syllogisms we had absolutely nothing else to say beforehand. We had to search for them at length and labor over them for a very long time. If, however, this work appears, on the basis of our investigations—and as with discoveries made at the beginning—to possess sufficient superiority over the other disciplines introduced by tradition, it will remain for all of you, or for those who hear this work, to pardon what has been omitted from the art, and to pursue with abundant gratitude what has been discovered.

[Col. 1039]

# THE SIX BOOKS OF ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS’ COMMENTARIES ON CICERO’S TOPICS (C)

## BOOK ONE.

[Col. 1039D] I have considered nothing more important than your request, most accomplished of rhetoricians, Patricius—a request joined both to the honor of the present undertaking and to the usefulness of future generations. I have undertaken this task willingly, not because I believed that I was laboring over commentaries on M. Tullius’ *Topics* in order to instruct you—for I would be ridiculous if I wished, as they say, to teach letters to Minerva—but so that, drawn from the storehouse of the liberal disciplines, it might remain with you as a perpetual pledge of our friendship.

What gift can be found more pleasing to those who love one another sincerely than one that forms and instructs the faculties of the mind itself? Almost everything else is transient, weak, unstable, and, if one considers the vicissitudes of fortune, nearly always belongs to someone else. But the wealth of letters is not diminished by the present age; rather, antiquity—which itself brings all things to an end—strengthens and confirms their authority.

Receive, then, this work, undertaken not with confidence in my ability to execute it, but with confidence in our friendship. In friendship, I do not know how it happens, but it is not disgraceful to chatter; and since I have presented you with a gift, when I later ask you for one of your own works, you would be unjust if you refused.

But since the rhetorician Marcus Victorinus, highly knowledgeable in the art of discussion, composed extensive commentaries on M. Tullius’ *Topics*, I ought perhaps not to have attempted matters already handled better by another, unless there were something by which our own labor too could exercise itself and produce something. Victorinus composed four volumes on the *Topics*. In the first of them he occupies himself solely with explaining the beginnings of the book. He also adds whatever, in that same volume, he thought ought to be stated beforehand. Thus his exposition of the first volume ends with the passage beginning, “We have undertaken to write on greater matters, Gaius Trebatius,” and continuing through the passage, “But now it is time to approach what we have undertaken.”

In the second volume he treats the dialectical parts of judging and discovering, and the definition of a place and of an argument, beginning with the passage in the *Topics*, “Every systematic method of careful discussion has two parts: one of discovering, the other of judging,” and continuing through, “Thus one may define a place as the seat of an argument; and an argument as a reasoning that establishes belief in a doubtful matter.”

The third and fourth volumes then pursue the distinction among the places and their various examples in many forms. The third proposes Cicero’s own examples concerning law; the fourth displays the same places through other analogies, drawing from the poets Vergil and Terence and from the orators Cicero and Cato, so that what is demonstrated by precepts may shine forth through examples multiplied in many ways.

The exposition proceeds from the passage in the *Topics*, “But from these places in which arguments are contained,” and does not go beyond the passage, “May equity, which seeks equal laws in equal cases, prevail.” How large a portion remains is shown by the size of the *Topics* itself—a portion that Victorinus neither reached nor could have reached, since he lingered over minor matters, unless he had extended the work by the great number of his books.

We shall undertake carefully, as far as we can, this very section that Victorinus reached, and, proceeding farther in our exposition, shall continue until we come to the end of the *Topics*. Therefore, let us take a fitting beginning here from the whole plan of the work.

But before I discuss the nature of the topical faculty, I shall briefly conclude the preface that M. Tullius addresses to Trebatius. For he says:

“We had begun to write on greater matters, Gaius Trebatius, and on matters more worthy than the books which we have published in considerable number within a short time, when your wish recalled me from my course. For when you were with me at Tusculum, and each of us, separately in the library, was turning over whatever little books he wished for the sake of his own studies, you happened upon some of Aristotle’s *Topics*, which he explained in several books. Moved by their title, you immediately asked me what those books meant.

“When I had explained to you that the discipline of discovering arguments was contained in those books, so that we might reach, without any error, by a certain path the method discovered by Aristotle, you urged me to hand them over to you—modestly, as you do everything, but in such a way that I could easily see how passionately you desired them.

“When I urged you, however, not so much to avoid my own labor as because I thought it was in your interest, either to read them yourself or to receive the whole method from some highly learned rhetorician, you tried both, as I heard from you. But the obscurity of the books drove you away from them. The great rhetorician, however, in response to your inquiry, replied, as I suppose, that he did not know these Aristotelian matters.

“I was not at all surprised that this philosopher was unknown to a rhetorician, since he is unknown even to philosophers themselves, except for a very few. They are all the less excusable because they ought to have been attracted not only by the matters stated and discovered by Aristotle, but also by the extraordinary abundance and sweetness of his expression.

“I could not, therefore, continue to owe you an answer when you so often asked for it, while nevertheless fearing that you might be a burden to me—for I could easily see this. I did not wish to cause an injury to the very interpreter of the law. For since you had often taken precautions on behalf of me and mine, I feared that if I hesitated, it might appear either ungrateful or arrogant.

“But while we were together, you are the best witness of how occupied I was. After I departed from you and set out for Greece—when neither the republic nor my friends were making use of my services, and when I could not honorably remain amid the weapons, even if it had been safe for me to do so—when I came to Velia, as though I were seeing your own people, I was reminded of this debt. I did not wish to fail even your unspoken demand.

“Thus, since I did not have the books with me, I wrote this from memory during the voyage itself and sent it to you from the road, so that by my diligence in carrying out your instructions I might rouse you too to the memory of our affairs, even if you had not needed a reminder. But now it is time to approach what we have undertaken.”

Every preface, as is taught in rhetoric, aims to prepare the audience by winning goodwill, securing attention, or producing teachability. Cicero shapes Trebatius through these three parts.

By saying that he was recalled from beginning great works and turned instead to his friend’s request, he earns Trebatius’ favor, as though Trebatius were a judge, through the means of goodwill. The greater works from which he turned to his friend’s interest were treatises on moral philosophy. The study of morals is indeed greater than expertise in discussion. We infer that this was the period when, because of the turbulent condition of the republic, Cicero withdrew into leisure and devoted himself to the disciplines of philosophy.

But because the presumed belief in the truth of what an audience hears also wins its minds, Cicero uses this as a means of preparing goodwill. He does so by truthfully recalling matters that Trebatius knew, thereby lending credibility to things that later occurred and that might have been unknown to Trebatius. These matters are that, at Tusculum, each of them was turning over books for his own studies; that Trebatius happened by chance upon Aristotle’s *Topics*; and that, struck by the title of the work, he asked M. Tullius what the title meant.

Cicero also recalls that he explained to Trebatius that those books contained the knowledge of discovering arguments, so that one might reach the discovery of arguments without error, by a certain path, a straight line, and a method. This statement, briefly expressed, displays the purpose of the work and makes the audience teachable.

For it seems to encompass the purpose of the *Topics*: Cicero says that it is a discipline for discovering arguments, not so that arguments may be discovered at all—for nature supplies that—but so that the mind may reach them without labor or confusion, not by chance, but by a certain path and method.

After this appeal for goodwill, Cicero adds praise of Trebatius, mentioning his modesty in seeking what he requested. Had Cicero granted his friend’s request, he would have received both the reward of glory and the favor of gratitude; but he had not granted Trebatius’ request that he hand over the *Topics*. He insists that this was done not to avoid his own labor, but rather for Trebatius’ sake, so that Trebatius’ spirit, perhaps then irritated at having been rejected, might not now be alienated.

It was in Trebatius’ interest either to become more practiced by reading the books himself or to have a more learned rhetorician explain whatever he found doubtful. Cicero says that he heard from Trebatius that he had tried both. Trebatius had tried to read the books himself but had been repelled by their obscurity; and the rhetorician from whom he had sought an explanation of the *Topics* had confessed that he did not know those Aristotelian matters.

Because of the difficulty of the work, this circumstance necessarily makes the audience attentive. We inspect with care what we suspect will not be easy to understand. Cicero also says that he was not at all surprised that a philosopher should be unknown to a rhetorician when he seemed unknown even to many philosophers. He rightly censures their laziness, since they had not been attracted to Aristotelian philosophy either by the usefulness of its discoveries or by the brilliance of its expression.

This increases the audience’s attentiveness through a still greater insight: criticizing the sluggishness of others easily turns minds toward study. Wherever attention is present, teachability cannot be absent. Trebatius’ praise is also introduced covertly here. It is a great thing that, while philosophers neglect their own apparent duty, Trebatius, not even hindered by his own studies, should investigate the secrets of another’s knowledge.

The following passages seek goodwill even more clearly. Such is the elegant statement that Cicero feared that, if he had rejected the modest request of the petitioner, he would somehow appear to have wronged the very interpreter of the law. He also recalls and recounts Trebatius’ earlier merits in receiving a favor: Trebatius had often taken precautions on behalf of Cicero himself and those whom Cicero defended.

Cicero therefore says that he had to fear that, if he refused to repay the favor, the act would appear either ungrateful or arrogant: ungrateful if he seemed to value too lightly Trebatius’ great merits, from which he himself had benefited, by thinking that no gratitude should be returned; arrogant if he scorned them.

The remaining points return to the same purpose, namely, the winning of goodwill. Cicero supports this by Trebatius’ own testimony: while he was in Rome, he was constrained by the necessity of his occupations and could not repay the favor. But when he came to Velia, reminded by the gathering of Trebatius’ friends, he did not wish to fail even Trebatius’ unspoken demand. Although he had no supply of books available, he nevertheless wrote during the voyage from the storehouses of his recalled memory and sent the work to him from the road, so that the speed of obedience might be added to the accumulation of the favor.

Although all these things seem intended to win Trebatius’ favorable assent, the brevity of the *Topics*, recalled from memory, must nevertheless serve the purpose of attracting attention. For the very act of recalling it from memory shows that what he has gathered is brief. Cicero also says that Trebatius’ instructions had been entrusted to him and that he wished some pledge and memorial of himself to remain with his friend, as it were. He adds, “even if you do not need a reminder,” so as not to offend his friend by the assiduity of reminding him, lest someone whom he thinks needs reminding appear to be accused of forgetfulness.

All these matters, as I have said, are full of the means of winning goodwill. But enough has been said about the preface. Let us now proceed to what follows. And if anyone finds these matters treated at greater length in Victorinus, let him not attack us with the reproach of neglecting completeness. We do not wish, as he does, to linger over every individual word; we are hastening toward the larger purposes of this work.

“Every systematic method of careful discussion has two parts: one of discovering, the other of judging. Aristotle was, in my opinion, the principal author of both. The Stoics, however, labored over one of them. They diligently pursued the method of judging, the science that they call dialectic. But the art of discovering, which is called topical and was more important for practical use and certainly prior according to nature, they abandoned entirely.”

Since there is great usefulness in both, and since we intend, if we have leisure, to pursue both, we shall begin with the one that is prior.

Since philosophy devotes its labor and study to the greatest matters; since it applies observation and contemplation to natural matters, action to moral matters, and eagerly forms character according to what the true conduct of life has persuaded us to follow; it necessarily happens that, in accordance with what reason has decided ought to be held or abandoned, done or not done, either a judgment is established, or the ascent [the transmitted reading is uncertain] or intention of a life to be practiced is directed.

It will therefore be necessary, whether in natural contemplation or in reflection upon moral actions, for a certain method either to discover what must be contemplated in things or first to weigh what ought to be put into practice in life. Unless this method proceeds along a certain path, it must often fall into many errors.

To prevent this from happening indiscriminately, and to make the discipline stand upon definite rules, the leaders of ancient philosophy thought that they should first examine thoroughly the nature of the reasonings by which something was to be investigated, so that, once these had been purified and arranged, we could use them either in the contemplation of truth or in the practice of the virtues.

This, then, is the discipline that is, as it were, a teacher of discussion, which the ancient Peripatetics called *logice* [logic]. Cicero, defining it, called it “the systematic method of careful discussion.” It has been treated by many people in various ways and has been given various names.

As has been said, the Peripatetics call this careful method of discussion *logice*, and it contains expertise both in discovering and in judging. The Stoics treated this same method of discussion somewhat more narrowly. For, making no effort concerning discovery, they remain solely in the sphere of judgment; and, giving many kinds of precepts concerning it, they called it *dialectica* [dialectic].

Plato too calls dialectic the faculty by which what is one can be divided into many things, as a genus is accustomed to be separated by its proper differences down to its ultimate species, and by which what is many can be gathered together by reason into one genus.

Plato therefore calls this faculty dialectic; Aristotle calls it logic, which, as has been said, Cicero defined as the systematic method of careful discussion.

This method has a threefold division in one respect: for the whole power of logical discipline either defines something, divides it, or draws a conclusion. The power of drawing conclusions is treated in three different ways. For either a discussion proceeds through true and necessary arguments, and is called a discipline or demonstration; or through merely probable arguments, and is called dialectic; or through arguments that are most openly false, and is called sophistic—that is, contentious or captious reasoning.

Logic, then, which is expertise in discussion, treats either definition, division, or conclusion—that is, either true and necessary arguments, probable arguments (that is, arguments resembling the truth), or sophistic, that is, captious arguments. We have stated that these are the parts of conclusion-making.

This is one division of logic, in which Aristotle calls dialectic the faculty of drawing conclusions through probable arguments.

There is again another division of the same logic, by which the entire systematic method of discussion is divided into two parts: one of discovering and the other of judging.

The definition of logic itself also seems to show this. Since logic is a method of discussion, it cannot be separated from discovery. Since no one can discuss without discovery, the method of discussion is a method of discovery.

Again, since logic is a careful method of discussion, judgment cannot be absent from it. For the very care of reason placed in discussion is judgment. No one can discuss carefully unless he has judged what sort of thing is that which is taken up for debate.

If care of reason is applied to the order of discussion, there is no doubt that this judgment is adapted to the variety of discoveries.

These matters having therefore been clarified, we must see how these divisions are related to one another. Discovery is placed beneath all the others, as it were in the position of matter, in the following way.

Unless there has been discovery, there can be neither definition nor division, since we either divide or define each genus or difference through the discovery of differences, or through the gathering together of species.

If discovery is absent, there can be no conclusion either. There will therefore be neither necessary, nor probable, nor sophistic argumentation. For these three come after discovery, so that an argument may be necessary, probable, or captious.

Necessity, probability, and captiousness are certain forms. When they accompany discoveries, they make arguments necessary, probable, or captious.

The same reasoning also encompasses divisions and definitions. For the undifferentiated power of discovery can be called both definitional and divisional when it is applied to matters that are to be defined or divided.

In this way, composed from the matter of discovery and from the form of the differences mentioned above, these again become matter for judgment. For the earlier division of logic, separated into three parts, explains those parts in such a way that discovery supplies the matter of each, while the same division itself provides matter for judgment.

When someone defines or divides a proposed matter, he discovers the differences appropriate to the definition or division; but he weighs through judgment whether he defines or divides correctly.

Thus the earlier parts of logic’s second division join its members together: discovery is their matter, while they themselves become matter for judgment.

The same occurs in the remaining part concerned with drawing conclusions. The part that treats probable arguments has discovery as its underlying matter, since discovery finds arguments resembling the truth; judgment then weighs such an argument.

For judgment is precisely the act of distinguishing that which is not a necessary discovery but possesses probability.

The part concerned with necessary arguments likewise has beneath it the matter of necessary discovery, and its judgment determines whether what it discovers is also necessary.

The captious part contains both functions within itself, since false things can be discovered and can also be distinguished as false by judgment.

Consequently, the earlier division of logic also appears to contain the second. For definition, division, and conclusion contain both discovery and judgment, since they can neither exist apart from discovery nor be recognized apart from judgment.

But since every discovery is subject to judgment, and since the parts of the earlier division cannot exist without both, it follows that the first division joins discovery and judgment together. The second division, by which Cicero also divides logic, separates these faculties in such a way that it distinguishes the matter of discovery from the part concerned with judgment.

Judgment itself has its own parts in the method of drawing conclusions. For every argument and every syllogism is constructed from propositions, and everything composite retains within itself two elements that seem to require examination.

It contains, first, the things from which what is composite is understood to be joined; second, the manner in which it is composed through the connection of its parts.

Thus, if in a wall you inspect the stones themselves from which the wall has been built, you examine something like its matter; but if you consider the order and composition of the joining, you weigh something as belonging to the account of form.

Accordingly, in arguments—which, as we have stated above, are articulated and joined together by propositions—there will be two methods of investigation and judgment.

One distinguishes and judges the nature of the propositions themselves, determining whether they are true and necessary, probable, or applicable to sophistic reasoning; this is, as it were, an examination of matter.

The other part of judgment weighs the connections and compositions of the propositions with one another; it judges, as it were, the form of the arguments.

Since this is so, the division, carried through continuously, is made in the following way: the systematic method of discussion has one part concerned with discovery and another concerned with judgment—both with discovery itself and with the arrangement of discovery, which is the form of argumentation.

The part that teaches discovery supplies certain instruments for discoveries and is called topical. Why it has been given this name I shall explain later.

The part concerned with judgment supplies certain rules for distinguishing and is called analytic. If it considers the connection of propositions, it is called prior analytics; but if it treats the discoveries themselves, the part concerned with distinguishing necessary arguments is called posterior analytics, while the part concerned with false and captious—that is, sophistic—arguments is called the *elenchi* [refutations].

Nothing seems to have been treated concerning the judgment of probable arguments, because the method of judging the middle is plain and easy once one knows the extremes. If someone knows how to judge necessary arguments and is also capable of judging false arguments, he has no difficulty distinguishing probable arguments, which are situated in the middle.

It is therefore clear, I think, what Cicero means when he says that the systematic method of discussion has two parts: one of discovering and the other of judging.

It has also been explained more carefully what the method is that the Stoics call dialectic. For it contains expertise in judging, and Plato calls by the same name the faculty of dividing through differences and bringing things back to a genus.

Aristotle too uses the same name, not—as the Stoics do—for the whole art of discussion, but only for that part which draws arguments from probable premises concerning a proposed question.

Aristotle therefore treated logic more completely because, besides the two things beyond which there is nothing further, he discussed a third [the transmitted wording is uncertain], namely discovery and judgment. The Stoics, neglecting discovery, transmitted only the instruments of judgment.

Cicero therefore rightly reproaches them, because they abandoned precisely what was both prior by nature and more important in practice. It is prior by nature because it is impossible to judge discovery unless discovery itself has first existed.

It is more important in practice because it is far more useful to defend an undertaking often begun by natural discovery, even if it is bare and produced without art, than, when another person has made the discovery, to apply judgment to something that is itself mute, defenseless, and silent.

Cicero gives his opinion about both and says that the greatest usefulness rests equally in both, and that, if he has leisure, he wishes to discuss both. He thinks that one should begin with the prior of the two, namely discovery, which, as we have said, is called topical.

[Col. 1048A] Just as the discovery of hidden things is easy when their place has been indicated and marked, so, if we wish to investigate some argument, we must know the places. Aristotle called these places, as it were, the seats from which arguments are drawn.

Thus it is permissible to define a place as the seat of an argument, and an argument as a reasoning that establishes belief in a doubtful matter.

After the division of logic, which he defined as a careful method of reasoning, he undertakes to explain topical theory (*topice*), which has already been described as the art of discovery. First, he includes what places (*loci*) are within the terms of a definition, and with a certain illustrative clarity indicates the purpose of that art called topical theory. For the purpose of topical theory is the easy discovery of arguments. [Col. 1048B] Topical theory, therefore, does not teach discovery itself—for that belongs to natural talent—but easier discovery. For every art imitates nature and, having received its material from nature, shapes its own methods and path, so that whatever each art promises may be accomplished both more easily and more elegantly. Thus, building a wall belongs to natural talent, but it is done better by art.

An argument, however, is a reasoning that establishes the credibility of a doubtful matter. For many things establish credibility, but since they are not reasonings, they cannot be arguments. Sight, for example, establishes the credibility of things that are seen; but because sight is not a reasoning, it cannot be an argument either. He has taken up one difference, namely, that which establishes credibility, for every argument establishes credibility. If, then, we join the genus and the difference and say that an argument is that which is a reasoning that establishes credibility, has the whole [Col. 1048C] nature of an argument been displayed? Certainly not. What if someone wished by some reasoning to establish the credibility of a matter about which no one doubts? Would that reasoning therefore be called an argument because it establishes credibility? Not at all. For an argument is that which argues a matter, that is, proves it; but nothing can be proved unless it is doubtful.

Unless, therefore, there is an ambiguous matter and a reasoning establishing credibility is brought to bear upon it, it cannot be an argument. Thus, once another difference has been added—namely, “of a doubtful matter”—the complete definition of an argument has been produced, consisting of a genus and two differences: its genus is “reasoning”; one difference is that it establishes credibility; the other is that it concerns a doubtful matter. The complete definition is therefore: an argument is a reasoning that establishes the credibility of a doubtful matter.

Since this is so, wherever something is doubted, there must be a question. [Col. 1048D] And if an argument cannot exist apart from a doubtful matter, it cannot in any way exist apart from a question. A question is a doubtful proposition. A proposition is a reasoning that indicates what is true or false. Every proposition, therefore, whether it is uttered firmly and declaratively—as when someone says, “Every human being is an animal”—or directed toward an interrogation—as when someone asks, “Do you think that every human being is an animal?”—retains its proper name and is called a proposition. But when the same proposition is uttered as doubtful, it becomes a question, as when someone asks whether every human being is an animal.

At present this does not seem an appropriate place to explain in how many ways a question is divided; we shall discuss that in the books on the differences of topical theory that we are attempting to compose. [Col. 1049A] Every purpose of an argument, therefore, is directed toward a question—that is, toward a doubtful proposition—not so as to prove the question in its entirety, but to confirm one part of it by reasoning. For the whole question is not defended; rather, any one of its parts is strengthened by argumentation. No one defends both that the heavens are round and that they are not round; if someone defended both, he would appear to be proving the entire question. But when the matter is considered as whether the heavens are round or are not round, the defense rests upon only one part of the question, whether the part affirming or the part denying.

Every question consists of contradictions. For if one person affirms a matter and another denies it, the whole is called a contradiction. Thus, one person may say, “The heavens are round,” while another denies it, saying, “The heavens are not round.” The assertion that the heavens are round and are not round is called a contradiction.

[Col. 1049B] The doubtful proposition, which we have said is a question, contains both an affirmation and a negation. For by the very fact that it is doubtful, it appears to include a contradiction. When someone doubts whether the heavens are round—whether he adds “or are they not?” or leaves that unspoken—the doubt itself draws along with it the other part. For if the proposition upheld only one part, it would not be doubtful and therefore would not be a question.

Since every question consequently has two parts, one affirmative and the other negative, there must always be a defense of one or the other part: one person defends the affirmative part and another the negative, the former seeking whatever arguments may establish the affirmation, the latter whatever may destroy it. [Col. 1049C] It makes no difference whether someone posits the affirmation or destroys the negation, or defends the negation or attacks the affirmation.

Suppose, then, that the question is whether the heavens are round. If someone takes up for himself the part of the question that he defends, he must gather all the arguments necessary to establish it. In doing so, he posits the affirmation but destroys the negation. If someone else denies this and says that the heavens are not round, he takes up the other part of the question, the part that had remained, namely the negation, and rests upon it; to approve it, he relies upon arguments that he has sought out. Thus, whoever posits the negation weakens the affirmation.

[Col. 1049D] Since this is so, I think it has been demonstrated that it is not the whole question, but some part of it, that comes forward for defense. Yet each person seeks arguments for the matter that he defends. Arguments, therefore, are adopted for establishing or destroying one part of the question. If anyone understands this imperfectly, let him not complain that we have expressed ourselves obscurely. For if he is ignorant of what has been said in dialectic, whether by us in Latin or by the Greeks in writing, it is surprising if he can grasp any part of what we are saying—much less should we be astonished that he does not comprehend everything.

But since we have said that a doubtful proposition is a question, it follows that a question appears to retain the same parts as a proposition. [Col. 1050A] Every simple proposition, however, has two parts constituted by terms. A simple proposition is of this kind: “Every human being is an animal.” By “terms” I mean the simple parts of speech that contain the proposition, such as “animal” and “human being.” They are the predicate and the subject.

The predicate is the major term placed in the proposition; the subject is the minor term. The major term is predicated of the subject; the minor term is in no way predicated of the major. Thus, “animal,” because it is greater than “human being,” is predicated of “human being,” for we say, “Every human being is an animal.” “Human being,” however, is not predicated of “animal,” for no one truthfully says, “Every animal is a human being.” By this method, therefore, we can distinguish which term in a proposition is major and which is minor.

[Col. 1050B] Every question, as has been said, has doubtful parts, and arguments are adopted to prove those same parts. Whatever, therefore, is proved in questions must be established by the reasoning of arguments. But unless an argument is expressed in speech and arranged through a connection of propositions, it cannot establish credibility in a matter of doubt. Accordingly, that expression and arrangement of an argument through propositions is called argumentation, which is called an *enthymeme* or a syllogism. We shall explain its definition more fully in the Differences of Topics.

Every syllogism or enthymeme consists of propositions. Every argument, therefore, is expressed through a syllogism or an enthymeme. An enthymeme is an imperfect syllogism, in which some parts have been omitted, either for the sake of brevity or because they are already known. This argumentation, accordingly, does not depart from the genus of the syllogism.

[Col. 1050C] Since every syllogism consists of propositions, and propositions of terms, and since the terms differ from one another in that one is major and the other minor, it is impossible for a conclusion to arise from propositions unless propositions proceeding through their terms join their extreme terms by means of a third term. This is demonstrated by the easiest example.

Let the question be whether a human being is a substance or not. I take up for proof the one part of the question, namely, that a human being is a substance. There are therefore two terms in this proposition, “substance” and “human being.” “Substance” is the major term, and “human being” the minor. This can also be shown from the fact that “substance” is uttered later in the statement—or, as in the very proposition “A human being is a substance,” we name “human being” first and “substance” afterward.

[Col. 1050D] To join “substance” and “human being,” therefore, it is necessary to find a middle term that connects both terms. Let that term be “animal,” and let there be the proposition, “Every human being is an animal.” In this proposition, then, “animal” is predicated and “human being” is subjected. I add again, “Every animal is a substance.” In this proposition, “animal” is once more subjected and “substance” is predicated. I therefore conclude: “Every human being is a substance.”

Thus, “human being” is always the subject. “Animal” is predicated in relation to “human being,” but is the subject in relation to “substance.” “Substance” itself remains always the predicate. Hence “human being” is the minor term, “substance” is the major term in relation to “human being,” and “animal” is the middle term.

[Col. 1051A] Since the extreme terms are joined by the interposition of the middle term, and in this way the parts of the question are brought together, while doubt is resolved by the proof supplied, an argument is nothing other than the discovery of a middle term. For this middle term can either join the extremes, if the affirmation is defended, or separate them, if the negation is maintained.

Since this is so, among the two propositions and the third, concluding proposition, the major proposition is the one that contains the major term—that is, the one in which the major term is predicated and the middle term is subjected: “Every animal is a substance.” The minor proposition is the one that predicates the middle term but subjects the minor term: “Every human being is an animal.”

[Col. 1051B] But since lesser things must descend from greater things, the proposition that is first appears to be, as it were, the productive and proper proposition of the conclusion that arises from the two propositions. This proposition is: “Every human being is a substance.” Anyone who has read our *Prior* and *Posterior Analytics*, which we translated from Aristotle, has no doubt about this. But if someone ignorant of what is written there should rush to read this work, even if he has no understanding of the reasoning of matters he does not comprehend, nevertheless let him confidently believe that it is as stated here, and let him suppose that, if he reads Aristotle’s *Analytics*, he will find the matter treated more fully there.

The nature of things, therefore, dictates that wherever there is something greater and something lesser, there must also necessarily be something greatest. Hence there are certain greatest propositions, since we have shown that some propositions are lesser and others greater. Their nature must be derived from the division of simple propositions.

[Col. 1051C] Every simple proposition is either affirmative or negative. Some are universal, such as “Every human being is just” and “No human being is just”; some are particular, such as “Some human being is just”; some are indefinite, such as “A human being is just” and “A human being is not just”; and some contain something singular and individual, such as “Cato is just” and “Cato is not just.” Of all these, some are doubtful and others indubitable.

We therefore call supreme and greatest propositions those that are universal and so known and evident that they require no proof, but rather prove what is doubtful. For indubitable propositions ordinarily serve as principles for demonstrating ambiguities, as does the proposition “Every number is either even or odd,” and “When equals are subtracted from equals, equal amounts remain,” along with the other propositions whose acknowledged truth is not questioned.

[Col. 1051D] We have accordingly observed that the greatest propositions—that is, universal and most widely known propositions—from which the conclusion of syllogisms descends are called “places” in the *Topics* written by Aristotle. Because they are greatest, that is, universal propositions, they embrace the remaining propositions within themselves as the bodies of places; and because they are most widely known and evident, they provide credibility to questions and thereby contain proofs of doubtful matters.

Sometimes we see these propositions adhere within the syllogisms and argumentations themselves; at other times they are not contained in the argumentations themselves but supply force to the argumentations. For example, if we wish to show that kingship is better than the consulship, we may say:

“Since kingship is good, it is [Col. 1052A] more lasting than the consulship; but every more enduring good is better than what is confined to a short period. Therefore kingship is better than the consulship.”

Here the greatest proposition, both universal and known in itself, requiring no proof, has been inserted into the argumentation. It is this: “All more enduring goods are better than those that are restricted by the brevity of time.”

But if we wish to show that a wise person is not envious, we may say:

“An envious person is one who grieves at another’s happiness; but a wise person is not one whom another’s happiness saddens. Therefore a wise person is not envious.”

Here the greatest proposition does not appear to be included in the argumentation, but is placed outside it; nevertheless, it supplies strength to the syllogism. It is this: “When things have different definitions, they must necessarily be different substances.”

[Col. 1052B] Whoever, therefore, examines either Aristotle’s Greek text or our translation from Aristotle will find that these propositions are there called “places.” They are greatest and universal, and are either necessary in themselves or intrinsically probable and known.

But since these propositions must be numerous and almost innumerable, the reasoning of our investigation still has farther to ascend. For, with careful treatment and consideration, we can weigh the differences among all the greatest and universal propositions and gather the innumerable multitude of greatest propositions known in themselves into a few universal differences. Thus, we may say that some consist in definition, others in genus, and others in some other mode, as I shall demonstrate more clearly shortly.

[Col. 1052C] All greatest propositions, therefore, whatever fall under the account of definition, will be contained under the single name “definition.” And just as those propositions were said to be the places of the remaining propositions because they contained the latter within their scope, so the differences of those greatest and universal propositions—which we have said are the places of minor propositions—will appear to be, if not truly, at least in a kind of likeness, the places into which the propositions have been reduced by an appropriate method.

These differences of places—that is, of greatest propositions—which we also call places themselves, may likewise be called the genera of the propositions subjected to them. For containing differences can also commonly be regarded as genera. Thus, “irrational,” although it differs from “rational” as a divisive difference, is nevertheless the specific difference of a horse or a dog and occupies the place of a genus in relation to them. [Col. 1052D] For “irrational animal” is the genus of a horse.

The same applies to greatest propositions. Some propositions are derived from wholes, others from parts. Compared with one another, these are divisible differences; but in relation to the greatest propositions themselves, the containing differences have the position of a genus. For the genus of a proposition derived from a whole is precisely what is called “from a whole.” Likewise, propositions derived from parts, although they are known and evident, have as their genus what is called “from parts.” The other differences of those propositions, although they are greatest, nevertheless appear to be included within these differences as though they were certain genera. I shall discuss what these differences are a little later.

[Col. 1053A] Tullius therefore undertakes to discuss these places, which contain and include the greatest propositions mentioned above—that is, propositions known in themselves and universal. These are the differences of the greatest propositions. He discusses the differences of universal utterances that are known in themselves, so that a place may become a complete seat of an argument.

For if every argument is carried through propositions to a conclusion, and all the remaining propositions are contained in the first and greatest proposition, while that first and greatest proposition is sometimes part of the argumentation—that is, of the syllogism—and sometimes placed outside the argumentation but supplies it with force, then, since it completes the argument in both ways, it appears to be a certain part of the argumentation. There can be no doubt, therefore, that these differences, which contain the greatest propositions, also all contain the argumentations, so that the differences of the greatest propositions may rightly appear to be the places of arguments and, as it were, their final seats.

[Col. 1053B] Of the four possible meanings of the two terms “argumentation” and “argument,” one must necessarily apply. Either the very utterance and connection of the propositions, together with the greatest propositions—whether placed outside the syllogism or included within it—is called argumentation, while the argument is the thought and meaning of the syllogism. Or the utterance of the reasoning together with the greatest propositions and the meaning of the syllogism is called the argument, so that “argument” is identical with “argumentation.”

Or, again, the whole connection of the syllogism together with its meaning is called argumentation, but the greatest proposition is called the argument. Or the complete order of the reasoning apart from the greatest propositions is called argumentation, the meaning of the argumentation is called the argument, and the remaining greatest proposition is called the place.

[Col. 1053C] Since this is so, whether someone wishes to call the connection of the propositions—and the continuous progression through to the conclusion, together with the greatest proposition, whether placed outside or included among the propositions of the reasoning—“argumentation,” and wishes to call the meaning and thought of the reasoning “argument,” we nevertheless understand the places to be the differences of the greatest propositions; or whether someone calls the whole force and meaning of the reasoning, together with the greatest proposition, whether placed within or outside, the “argument,” there can be no doubt that the place of the whole reasoning is that which is the difference of the greatest proposition.

For it contains the greatest proposition, in which the remaining propositions are contained. Or, again, if it is preferred to call the entire connection of the reasoning “argumentation,” and the greatest proposition “argument,” the difference of the greatest proposition will again rightly be regarded as the place, since it encloses and contains the argument.

[Col. 1053D] If, however, the argument is understood as the very meaning of the entire reasoning, argumentation as the complete utterance of the reasoning, and something distinct from both and possessing an external function is considered as a kind of place—namely, the greatest proposition—even in this case the differences of the greatest propositions will appear to be places. For since the difference itself contains the greatest proposition and is its place, while the greatest proposition [Col. 1054A] supplies force either to the argumentation or to the argument, there can be no doubt that it appears to be the place of the entire argument, because it encloses the whole within the scope of the greatest proposition.

It has therefore been demonstrated what the seats of arguments are—that is, where arguments are enclosed. These are the differences of the greatest propositions, which are called places. It has also been demonstrated what an argument is, since it establishes the credibility of a doubtful matter; what the doubtful matter is, namely, one part of a question; what a question is, namely, a doubtful proposition; and what a simple proposition is, namely, an utterance containing a predicate and a subject term and indicating what is true or false. All these things must be remembered.

The differences of the greatest propositions, which we have said are places, take their names from those terms that occur earlier in the proposition but are considered later [Col. 1054B] in the question—namely, from the predicate and the subject.

From what was said above, the difference between Cicero’s *Topics* and Aristotle’s has also become apparent. Aristotle discusses the greatest propositions, for he established these as the places of arguments, as we also reported above. Tullius, however, calls not the greatest propositions themselves but the differences containing them “places,” and undertakes to teach about these.

“Of these places, in which arguments are enclosed, some adhere to the very matter under discussion, while others are taken from outside: within the matter itself, either from its whole, or from its parts, or from what is known, or from things that are in some way related to the matter being investigated. Those are said to be taken from outside that are distant and widely separated from it.”

After defining the locus and the argument, he gives a very full division [Col. 1054C] of the loci. First, since every division ought to embrace everything, introduce nothing superfluous, and omit nothing necessary, Marcus Tullius makes this clear in the division he proposes, saying: “Of these loci, in which arguments are contained, some adhere to the very matter under discussion, while others are assumed from outside.” Nothing, it seems, can be added to or removed from this division, since it briefly embraces everything. For every locus of arguments that is taken either adheres to the matter under discussion or does not. By saying “from outside,” he indicates those that do not adhere, because between saying that the loci of arguments adhere to the matter under discussion and saying that they do not adhere there is no middle position. Between affirmation and negation there is no intermediate state.

Since a locus of an argument’s not adhering to the matter under discussion means that it is assumed from outside, there is no doubt that there is no middle ground between those arguments whose loci adhere to the matter itself and those whose loci are assumed from outside. Things assumed from outside are those that are distant and widely separated.

But the matter under discussion itself is more easily explained if we remember what was said earlier. When we were speaking of the question, we said that a question is a doubtful proposition. Since a proposition consists of a subject and a predicate, we also said that a question is joined together by a subject and a predicate. The predicate or the subject, therefore, is the very matter under discussion. For when one or the other part of the question is doubtful, the issue in this ambiguity is whether the predicate seems to be present in the subject or not. Since every question is divided into affirmation and negation, if the predicate is present in the subject, a true affirmation results; if it is not present, a true negation results. In disputed questions, one party therefore defends the affirmation and the other the negation: one maintains that the predicate is present in the subject, the other that it is not. Whatever is defended on either side is the very matter under discussion.

Thus the matter under discussion is the predicate or the subject, whichever of the terms is being considered. To make this clearer by an example, let the question be whether Verres committed theft. Here Verres is the subject, and “to commit theft” is the predicate. If theft is joined to Verres and this is established by arguments, the affirmation of the question has been demonstrated. If theft is separated from Verres, the negation of the question is again established. The matter under discussion, then, is nothing other than either of the terms proposed in the question, whether predicate or subject.

These terms, however, cannot themselves be arguments, nor can they themselves provide arguments. If they could be arguments simply in themselves, or provide the material for arguments, they would leave no doubt in the question. But since it is still doubtful whether their conjunction can be valid, they can neither be arguments in themselves nor provide arguments in themselves. The things contained in them, however, or placed outside them, supply an abundance of arguments.

What Victorinus asks and explains at greater length does not even seem worthy of mention to me. He asks whether the question itself—namely, the matter under discussion—has a locus, which, as has been said, he ought not to have done. The locus with which we are now concerned is not the locus of just any thing, but the locus of an argument; an argument, however, establishes the credibility of a doubtful matter, and the doubtful matter is a part of the question. If an argument cannot be the question or a part of the question, and the locus of which we are speaking is the locus of an argument, there is no doubt that it cannot be the locus of a question.

Moreover, every question is doubtful, whereas every argument clears up the ambiguity of a question. Argument and question, therefore, are not the same. The loci are loci of arguments, not of questions. With this established, let us understand the matter under discussion to be any term proposed in the question, whether predicate or subject. These terms, although they are things in themselves, cannot themselves be arguments; but they can contain certain things in which arguments are located and which are understood to be the seats of arguments.

Although these things seem to adhere to the terms under discussion, they are not yet arguments. Rather, they are loci that already embrace arguments, so to speak, and contain them in a natural seat. The same must be said of the loci assumed from outside. They are placed externally and in some way removed from the terms of propositions; they too are things, but they enclose within themselves an abundance of arguments.

To gather the matter into a brief statement [Col. 1056A]: the matter under discussion is nothing other than any term placed in the question. These terms cannot be arguments, nor can any argument be drawn from them. Consequently, the terms placed in the question are neither arguments nor loci, but merely things.

Again, the things that adhere to the matters under discussion are plainly themselves things, but they contain within themselves an abundance of arguments, so that when some argument must be taken from them, they perform the function of loci. Thus, if someone considers them in themselves, they are things; but if someone seeks to draw an argument from them, they become loci.

These points may be said generally about the principal and greatest loci. They are those that adhere to the matters under discussion or are assumed from outside. In order, then, to give a complete division of the loci, he cuts the same loci that he simply and primarily called “greatest” into certain species, saying: “In the matter itself, partly from the whole, partly from its parts, partly from a note, and partly from things that are in some way related to the matter we are investigating.”

The loci established in the matter under discussion are thus divided into four parts. Those that adhere to the matter under discussion are understood to arise either from the whole term under discussion, from an enumeration of its parts, from a note, or from related things.

This can be confirmed by a brief argument. Every term placed in the question must have its own definitions, its parts, its names, and some connection and relation to other things. Therefore, the locus called “from the whole” occurs whenever an argument is developed from the definition of either term placed in the question, whether subject or predicate.

The locus “from an enumeration of parts” occurs whenever an argument is drawn from the parts of the term placed in the question. The locus “from a note” occurs whenever an argument arises from the name of that term. The locus “from related things” occurs whenever an argument proceeds from things that are brought into relation with the proposed term.

I shall explain examples of all these later, when I have discussed the examples Cicero gives to clarify these matters. For now, we must consider this point. Tullius says that of the loci in which arguments are contained, some adhere to the matter under discussion while others are assumed from outside. This seems to have been said as though the loci that adhere to the things under discussion were distinct from the things themselves.

Nothing can adhere to itself [Col. 1056D], and consequently whatever adheres to something is different from the thing to which it adheres. If there are loci that adhere to the things under discussion, there is no doubt that these loci are distinct from those things.

Again, when he says “in the matter itself, partly from the whole and partly from its parts,” he seems not to be speaking of distinct things, since he says that in the matter itself there are loci both from the whole and from the parts—as though the matter itself were not something different from the whole, or from all its parts taken together.

Every thing is identical with its whole. Rome, for example, is identical with the whole city. Likewise, every thing is identical with its individual parts taken together and brought into unity. A human being, for example, is identical with the head, chest, belly, feet, and the other parts joined and united into one.

How, then, did he first speak as though he were speaking of different things, when he said that loci adhere to the terms under discussion, and afterward speak as though he were speaking of the same things, when he proposes that in the matter itself there are loci from the whole and from the parts? There is no difference between saying “in the matter itself, from the whole and from the parts” and saying “in the matter itself, from the matter itself.”

For if the matter itself is identical with the whole and with the parts, saying that a locus adheres to the matter itself, from the whole or from the parts, is the same as saying that a locus adheres to the matter itself because it is from the matter itself. But it cannot even be understood how something could adhere to the matter itself when it is the matter itself, since nothing adheres to itself, as I explained above.

But, as I explained shortly before, every thing has both a definition and parts. If we understand the force of a definition and the nature of parts, the whole knot of ambiguity is untied.

A definition is an explanation of a thing gathered and folded together within itself. Thus, when we say that a human being is a rational, mortal animal, we explain and unfold what the name had briefly and narrowly designated, and the definition discloses it, so to speak, through its substantial parts.

The understanding of a thing that is folded together, compressed and reduced into unity, must therefore be one thing; the understanding of that same thing when unfolded and spread out must be another. For although the definition of a thing signifies the same as its name, what the name designates narrowly and obscurely, the definition discusses and reveals more openly.

It is therefore rightly the case that the thing itself and its definition are different, even though the same subject belongs to both. As has been said, the thing itself is singular, whereas the definition of that singular thing is its distribution and enumeration through parts.

By “parts” I now mean substantial parts, not those that join together a magnitude, but those that constitute the property and rational account of a substance. What was said in the definition according to the parts that constitute the substance must, in the case of parts, be understood according to those that join together a magnitude—for example, a house, which is joined together by its foundation, walls, and roof.

Although a house is nothing other than what is joined together from its parts, it is nevertheless one unified thing, while its division distributes it into particular members. Therefore, although what is itself the whole is one, and although there are as many parts as those that flow together from every side, the understanding need not be the same when the complete thing itself is considered and when it is distributed into the parts from which it is joined.

The locus “from a note” is plainly different from the term established in the question. Who would say that the name of any thing is the thing itself that it designates?

Things related to the matter under discussion, although they seem to be placed outside it, nevertheless face the term proposed in the question as though from the opposite side. These things must be divided into many parts.

Every thing, considered as what it is, is one; but it retains many things joined to itself. Such things are understood to differ from those that are altogether external in this respect: related things are placed in a relation, as will later be shown both by the presentation of the related things themselves and by the reasoning of the examples.

Things that are external, however, are established in no relation; for that reason they are called simply “external.” The others are called “related,” because they have some kind of kinship with that to which they are referred. Whatever is referred to something is related to it.

Nearly all the loci that he now presents as simple and undivided he divides in a later treatment. Thus he now distributes the loci that are in the matter itself, proposing that some arise from the whole, some from the parts, some from a note, and some from related things, and he divides the related things themselves into their own parts.

He confirms that the external locus is found in testimony, and that the force of testimony consists in authority; he then divides authority into its proper parts. This will become clear in the later treatment. For now he presents these loci as simple and undivided, and places examples under them as though they were simple.

There remains one point that seems to require investigation: whether these loci, which are divided into other loci, can themselves be called the loci of the loci that they contain—for example, whether the one locus “in the matter itself” is a kind of locus of those that arise from the whole, the parts, a note, or related things.

There would be no obstacle at all to calling loci the loci of other loci. A broader locus can contain narrower loci within itself, just as a province contains cities. But this comparison does not fit the present case.

A locus is that from which the thing in which an argument is located is drawn. If one locus could be the locus of another, and if the locus “in the matter under discussion” contained those that arise from the whole, the parts, a note, or related things as a kind of locus, then those loci would not be loci from the whole, from the parts, from a note, or from related things. They would be arguments, since they would adhere to the locus that was said to be in the very term under discussion.

A locus, therefore, cannot be the locus of a locus. Rather, the relation is like that between genera and species. This, then, is the division of loci. Nor should it seem contrary to what was said above, when we used the common name “loci” both for the greatest propositions and for the differences that contain them.

Although the greatest propositions, by the very fact that they are greatest, contain other propositions and are called loci, they can nevertheless be arguments in doubtful matters because they are very well known. Their differences are therefore rightly called loci. But in the case of the species of loci, the matter is different: they cannot be arguments at all. The locus “in the matter itself” is divided, as into species, into those that arise from the whole, from the parts, from a note, and from related things.

Each of these loci seems to bear the complete name of the first locus. Just as we call a human being an animal, and likewise call a horse and an ox animals, so the locus that arises from the whole is said to be “in the matter itself,” and likewise those that arise from the parts, from a note, and from related things are in the matter itself.

It is possible to draw arguments from these loci, but it is impossible for them actually to be arguments themselves.

When a definition is applied to the whole matter under discussion, it unfolds, as though from a wrapping, the matter being investigated. The formula of such an argument is as follows:

“Civil law is equity established for those who belong to the same state, for the purpose of obtaining their own property. Knowledge of that equity is useful. Therefore knowledge of civil law is useful.”

After dividing the loci into two—those situated in the matter under discussion and those placed outside it—he divided the locus situated in the matter itself into four members: from the whole, from an enumeration of the parts, from a note, and from related things.

Before dividing the locus that he proposed to derive from related things, therefore, he supplies examples of the preceding three, which in this first treatment he will not yet divide but will leave undivided. These are the loci from the whole, from the parts, and from a note.

Regarding the locus from the whole, he discussed and argued as follows: “We call a locus an argument from the whole whenever we encompass by a definition the whole thing placed in the question, and that definition establishes the credibility of the doubtful matter under discussion.”

But every definition, as was also said above, unfolds and explains what is obscurely designated by a name. Consequently, it is not the term placed in the definition itself that can provide material for arguments, but the things contained in that term.

Each thing has its own definitions. A definition is an expression signifying the substance of each thing. Since the proper substance does not depart from any thing, neither does its definition depart from it. There is therefore a definition in the very term under discussion, and that definition must encompass the whole term; it does not display a part of the substance but the substance of the whole term.

Since the doubtful matter is made credible through that definition, an argument is drawn from the definition. The definition is in the very term under discussion, and it is the whole of that term. Thus the argument drawn from the definition is drawn from the locus situated in the very term placed in the question. Since there are many loci in the matter itself, this is the locus from the whole.

A definition encompasses the whole term and unfolds and reveals what the name had designated obscurely. The formula of the argument is as follows:

“Civil law is equity established for those who belong to the same state, for the purpose of obtaining their own property. Knowledge of that equity is useful. Therefore knowledge of civil law is useful.”

The question is whether knowledge of civil law is useful. Civil law is therefore supplied as the subject, and “useful knowledge” is predicated of it. The question is whether what is predicated can truly adhere to the subject.

I cannot call civil law itself an argument, since the question has been established concerning it. I therefore consider what is contained in it. I see that every definition is inseparable from the thing of which it is the definition, and that the proper definition cannot be separated from civil law either.

I therefore define civil law and say: “Civil law is equity established for those who belong to the same state, for the purpose of obtaining their own property.” After this I consider whether this definition can be joined to the remaining term, “useful knowledge”—that is, whether equity established for those who belong to the same state for the purpose of obtaining their own property is useful knowledge.

I see that knowledge of the equity described above is useful knowledge. I therefore conclude: “Knowledge of civil law is useful.”

This argument is drawn from the locus situated in the matter itself, that is, in civil law, the term established in the question. This locus is called “from the definition,” because the definition is the whole of the question’s term; the argument is therefore from the whole. Every locus from the whole is in the matter itself.

Nor should any doubt trouble us because civil law and useful knowledge are expressions that we place among the terms. Not every term is expressed by a simple part of speech; sometimes complete expressions are established as terms.

In this argument the greatest and self-evident proposition is the one by which we understand that whatever is joined to the definition of something is necessarily joined also to the thing whose definition it is. For if the definition of civil law can be joined to useful knowledge, useful knowledge can also be joined to civil law.

This is therefore an argument drawn from the locus situated in the matter itself. Every definition is in the term that it defines, and it is in the same locus that is situated in the matter itself and from the whole. Every definition displays and reveals the whole.

The greatest proposition is this: “Whatever is joined to the definition of something is necessarily fitted to that thing itself.”

Next comes the enumeration of parts, which is treated as follows:

“If he was not made free by the census, by the rod, or by a will, he is not free; and he was made free by none of these means. Therefore he is not free.”

Let the question be whether someone who is known to have been a slave is free.

There are three methods of making someone free. The first is that he be made free by the census. In ancient times only Roman citizens were enrolled in the census. If someone, with the consent or at the command of his master, had entered his name in the census, he became a Roman citizen and was released from the bond of slavery. To be made free by the census, therefore, meant to enter one’s name in the census with the master’s consent and thereby become a Roman citizen.

There was also a second means of acquiring freedom, called manumission by the rod. The rod was a small staff which the lictor placed on the head of the slave being manumitted and by which he vindicated that slave into freedom, uttering certain solemn words. For this reason the staff was called the vindicta.

The third method of making someone free was for a person, in the exercise of his final wishes, to write in the text of his will that his slave was free.

Since these are the methods of making someone free, if one wishes to show that someone known to have been a slave was not made free, one says: “If he was not made free by the census, by the rod, or by a will, he is not free.” He was made free by none of these means. Therefore he is not free.

If you separate the whole from any thing by removing all its parts, you have necessarily separated the whole from it. Since the whole consists in its parts, if something is joined to it by none of its parts, it is also separated from the whole.

We speak of parts in two ways: as species or as members. A species is something that receives the complete name of the whole, as “human being” and “horse” are species of animal. Each is called an animal by the complete name in itself. A human being is an animal, and a horse is likewise an animal.

Members, however, are things which, when joined together, constitute the whole and receive the name of the whole collectively, but do not receive it individually. Thus the foundation, walls, and roof are members of a house; when taken together they are called a house, but the foundation alone is not called a house, nor are the walls or the roof alone.

In the case of parts that are species, since they receive the complete name of the whole, you cannot show that the whole is absent unless you remove every part individually from the thing under discussion. Each part, as has been said, receives the complete name of the whole.

Since there are three species of making someone free—census, rod, and will—if you remove any two, one will nevertheless remain, and you must necessarily admit that the person is free. Whether he was made free only by the census, by the rod, or by a will, it is established that he is free.

Therefore, in the case of species, unless you remove all of them, you cannot destroy what has been proposed in the question.
