If, however, you wish to affirm and establish that someone is free, it is enough to demonstrate any one species—for example, to show that he was made free by the rod, by the census, or by a will.

If you wish to disprove that he is free, it is not enough to show that he was not made free by the census, the rod, or the will individually. You must show that he did not attain freedom by any of these methods.

Thus, if you wish to destroy an assertion concerning parts that are species, all of them must be used; if you wish to establish it, one is sufficient.

Parts that are members, however, work in the opposite way. If you wish to disprove the existence of a whole, it is enough to separate one member from it; if you wish to establish the whole, you must prove that all the members are present.

If you wish to show that there is no house, it is enough to say either that there are no foundations, no walls, or no roof. If any one of these is missing, the thing cannot be called a house. But if you wish to show that there is a house, you cannot establish what you propose unless you join all the parts together.

All these loci are drawn from an enumeration of parts, because in the case of parts that are species all the parts are enumerated in order to destroy the assertion, whereas in the case of parts that are members all the parts are enumerated in order to establish it.

The question in Cicero’s proposed example is whether someone who is known to have been a slave is free. “Someone who is known to have been a slave” is the subject term, and “free” is the predicate. We cannot therefore draw either of these terms themselves into the argument. Things about which there is doubt cannot themselves establish credibility for the doubt.

I therefore consider what is contained in one of them. Since all the parts are in that of which they are parts, and since granted freedom has its own parts, I take and enumerate them and ask whether any one of these parts appears to be present in the subject. None is present. I shall therefore conclude that he is not free.

This more clearly demonstrates that arguments can be taken not only from the subject term but also from the predicate. In the earlier example, by which he demonstrated that knowledge of civil law is useful, he defined civil law, which was the subject, and the argument drawn from it established the credibility of the doubtful matter.

Here, however, the parts of freedom are enumerated, and freedom is the predicate term. The question, as has been said, is whether someone known to have been a slave is free. “Someone known to have been a slave” is the subject, while “free” is the predicate. In the predicate—that is, in the matter itself—there are parts, and these are enumerated. When an argument is drawn from that enumeration, the argument is situated in the matter itself and arises from an enumeration of parts.

The greatest proposition is this: “Whatever has none of the parts of the proposed thing joined to it cannot have the whole thing joined to it.”

Here one may wonder whether the locus from the whole and the locus from the parts are the same, since all the parts, when joined together, make the whole. The answer is that when the argument is from an enumeration of parts, the whole is divided rather than joined together; the argument proceeds by division.

Whoever takes any part of a thing thereby appears to have divided the thing. Whoever divides a thing disperses it rather than completing the whole.

But an ambiguity may still remain. A definition too explains the obscure signification of a name through a kind of enumeration of substantial parts. The enumeration of parts, however, is a kind of dispersal of the parts from one another.

It is one thing to enumerate the parts of a thing itself, and another to enumerate the parts of a definition. The parts of a thing are always smaller than the thing of which they are parts—for example, the head, chest, and other members are smaller than the whole human being.

The parts of a definition, however, are shown to be greater than the whole thing defined, if they are substantial parts. Thus “animal” is greater than “human being.” Likewise, “rational” and “mortal” contain the same human being as though they were greater things, and each is a part of the definition, “a rational, mortal animal.”

The division that takes parts of the thing being divided therefore always takes smaller parts. The definition, however, takes things that are universal in themselves, complete, and containing, although when placed in the definition they become its parts. This can easily be understood from the examples proposed above.

It is therefore clear that the locus from the whole, which belongs to definition, and the locus from an enumeration of parts are different.

Next comes notation, and an argument is elicited from the force of a word in the following way:

“When the Aelia Sentia law orders that an *assiduus* be guarantor for an *assiduus*, it orders a wealthy man to be guarantor for a wealthy man”—as Aelius says, an *assiduus* is so called from giving an *as*.

The third of the loci that are in the matter itself is constituted by notation. Notation is a kind of interpretation of a name. A name, however, is always in the matter itself. Just as a definition declares, unfolds, and spreads out what is folded within a name, so a name designates obscurely, in a folded and confused manner, what is expressed distinctly by the definition.

Since a definition is in the matter itself, there can be no doubt that a name too is in the matter of which it is the name. The locus is called “from notation” because a name notes and signifies the whole thing.

A *vindex*, then, is someone who undertakes to defend another person’s case, such as those whom we now call agents or representatives. The Aelia Sentia law therefore orders that an *assiduus* be guarantor (*vindex*) for an *assiduus*.

The question is whether, when the Aelia Sentia law requires that an *assiduus* be guarantor (*vindex*) for an *assiduus*, it requires that a wealthy man be guarantor for a wealthy man.

Here the subject term is “the Aelia Sentia law requiring that an *assiduus* be guarantor (*vindex*) for an *assiduus*,” while the predicate is “a wealthy man as guarantor for a wealthy man.” I cannot bring the terms themselves forward as establishing the credibility of the question. No credibility can be produced from the very things about which there is uncertainty.

I therefore ask what is contained in one of them. I see that one of the terms is the Aelia Sentia law, which decrees that an *assiduus* shall be guarantor (*vindex*) for an *assiduus*—that is, the subject. I interpret a part of this expression, namely *assiduus*. What else is *assiduus* than “one who gives an *as*”? But no one can give an *as* unless he is wealthy. Therefore an *assiduus* is a wealthy man.

Since the Aelia Sentia law establishes that an *assiduus* is to be guarantor (*vindex*) for an *assiduus*, it orders a wealthy man to be guarantor for a wealthy man, because an *assiduus* is a wealthy man, so named from giving an *as*.

This argument is therefore drawn from the locus situated in the matter itself, namely from the interpretation of the name. The name is in the very thing whose name it is, and its interpretation is called notation. The argument was made from this interpretation.

The argument therefore arises from the locus situated in the matter itself, that is, from the name; and among the loci situated in the matter itself, it arises from notation, that is, from the interpretation of the name.

The greatest proposition is: “The interpretation of a name has the same force as the name.”

But Cicero’s argument is expressed somewhat confusedly, and this produces a serious error. It ought to have been stated as follows:

“An *assiduus* is one who gives an *as*; whoever gives an *as* is wealthy; therefore an *assiduus* is wealthy. The Aelia Sentia law orders that an *assiduus* be guarantor (*vindex*) for an *assiduus*; therefore it prescribed that a wealthy man be guarantor for a wealthy man.”

If it had been stated in this way, the argument would have been clearer. But Cicero says:

“When the Aelia Sentia law orders that an *assiduus* be guarantor (*vindex*) for an *assiduus*, it orders a wealthy man to be guarantor for a wealthy man,” and so forth.

He added the explanation in order to show that an *assiduus* is a wealthy man. But this amounts to saying that, when the Aelia Sentia law ordered that an *assiduus* be guarantor (*vindex*) for an *assiduus*, it ordered a wealthy man to be guarantor for a wealthy man, as though he had said: “Whoever is an *assiduus* is wealthy.”

For unless the person who is an *assiduus* is wealthy, it does not follow that, when the Aelia Sentia law ordered that an *assiduus* be guarantor (*vindex*) for an *assiduus*, it ordered a wealthy man to be guarantor for a wealthy man. Cicero therefore placed the conclusion of the argument first and added the proof afterward.

The conclusion is: “When the Aelia Sentia law requires that an *assiduus* be guarantor (*vindex*) for an *assiduus*, it orders a wealthy man to be guarantor for a wealthy man.” This he placed first. The proof is the explanation that an *assiduus* is wealthy because he is named from giving an *as*, and this he appended after the conclusion.

There remains the locus among those that are in the matter itself, which is drawn from related things. Since its exposition involves a varied and manifold division, let us postpone it and bring the first book to an end here.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1063]

[Col. 1063B] In the course of so difficult a work I am not unaware, my Patricius, that this labor of ours—which we undertook at your urging—while it is either raised up or pressed down by the judgment of the unlearned multitude, can easily be attacked by various criticisms.

Those who dislike this entire mode of discussion as a superfluous pursuit disparage it with the familiar mockery of corrupt minds. Those who think that this discipline yields the greatest benefit, meanwhile, deceive others by their own laziness and do not consider us equal to so great an undertaking.

If the former do not diminish the value of another’s labor through envy but agree with the judgment that condemns it, I think they are wholly intolerable. I would much more willingly take upon myself the hostility arising from their corrupt opinion, and I would readily allow them to distrust our abilities, rather than permit them to trample upon the principles of so great a discipline.

But, by divine and human faith, what perversity is this in human beings, what blindness of such profound ignorance, that they almost condemn themselves by their own confession! There is no one who does not wish to appear highly skilled in discussion. Indeed, they even try to raise objections to the discipline itself and to resolve the objections they have raised. If this were easily accomplished, everyone would hasten to the science of logical discipline as to a common profit of wisdom.

What could be imagined more absurd than that they should try, by arguments that they themselves consider probable, to establish that the study of dialectic is useless? What is more inconsistent than to pervert the art of discussion through discussion itself, so that one despises the truth of the very discipline whose reputation one seeks?

But just as that singer ordered his pupil to sing for himself and for the Muses, so I too shall sing for myself and for you—not for the Muses, but for you as though you were their guardian—and I shall set down what I have gathered with much labor and study, not merely with rhetorical skill but also with dialectical subtlety.

What follows is of this kind:

Arguments are also drawn from things that are in some way related to the matter under investigation. This type, however, is divided into several parts. Some we call conjugates; others arise from a genus, others from a form, others from similarity, others from difference, others from contrariety, others from things conjoined, others from antecedents, others from consequents, others from things that conflict, others from causes, others from effects, and others from comparison with greater, equal, or lesser things.

[Col. 1064C] After distributing into a twofold division those topics from which arguments are drawn—saying that some adhere to the matter under discussion itself, while others are assumed from outside—and after dividing the topic that adheres to the matter under discussion itself into four kinds, namely, from the whole, from the parts, from the mark, and from related things, he added examples to the first three. We explained these as carefully as possible in the first book. There remains the fourth topic he established, namely, “from related things.” Since this has many kinds, he could not provide a single complete and undivided example. For matters that must be divided are better revealed by examples arranged according to their individual members.

He therefore divides this topic as follows: “The topic derived from related things proceeds partly from conjugates, partly from genus, partly from form, also from similarity, or from difference, or from contrariety, and likewise from things conjoined, from antecedents, consequents, and things opposed, also from causes and from the effects of causes, and from comparison of greater, equal, or lesser things.” Cicero illustrates all these shortly afterward with appropriate similarities among the matters concerned.

We must now explain what the nature of related things is and what property they possess. Related things are those which can in some way be referred to the thing to which they are related. All things that regard one another through some relation are compared either as mutually harmonious or as mutually opposed. If harmonious, they are so either substantially, as genus, form, antecedent, consequent, cause, and effect; or qualitatively, as conjugate, similar, and conjoined; or quantitatively, as equal things. Things that are compared as opposed to one another are partly merely different from one another and partly contrary. Among contraries, some are opposed in quality, such as contraries or repugnant things, and others in quantity, such as greater and lesser.

Since this is so, it is evident that harmonious things are joined to one another by a relation of kinship, while opposed things are compared with one another precisely insofar as they are opposed. For harmonious things are harmonious with harmonious things, and opposed things are opposed to opposed things. Thus genus is the genus of a form, and form is the form of a genus; antecedents are antecedents of consequents, and consequents are consequents of antecedents; a cause is the cause of effects, and an effect is the effect of causes; conjugates are conjugates of conjugates; similarity is similarity of similar things; a conjoined thing is conjoined with a conjoined thing; equals are equal to equals; differences are differences of different things; greater things are greater than lesser things, [Col. 1065B] and lesser things are lesser than greater things; contraries are contrary to contraries; and repugnant things are repugnant to repugnant things.

Related things, therefore, are things that, although different from one another, are nevertheless referred to one another. But in the order in which Cicero described the topics above, we shall append definitions to all of them.

Among those things said to be related to one another, the first in Marcus Tullius’s discussion are conjugates. I call conjugates whatever are inflected from one name by varying expression, as *justus* (“just”), *justum* (“a just thing”), and *juste* (“justly”) from *justitia* (“justice”). These are called conjugate with one another and with justice itself, from which their name has flowed.

Genus is what is predicated of many things differing in species with respect to what a thing is; for example, *animal* is predicated of a human being and a horse, which differ in species, and it is predicated of them with respect to what each is. For when we ask what a human being or a horse is, the answer is “an animal.” Although genus must necessarily be different from the thing of which it is the genus, it is nevertheless akin to it, because it is joined to it by a relation of substance.

A species is that of which the higher genus is predicated, which Cicero called a “form,” for example, a human being as a form of animal.

Similarity is unity of quality. For two things that are similar to one another must have the same quality; and since a thing cannot be similar to itself, something else must be considered similar. But it cannot be something else unless it differs in some respect. Therefore similar things are different from one another in one matter but agree in another. In the matter in which they agree according to quality, they are understood to be similar; through the bond of that similarity they are referred to one another.

[Col. 1065D] Difference is that by which each thing differs from another; for example, a human being differs from a horse by the difference of rationality. Thus, by the predication of its proper nature, difference is referred to the things of which it is the difference—for example, rationality to a human being—but by reason of dissimilarity it is referred to the things from which the thing possessing that difference differs—for example, rationality to an ox.

Contraries are things that, placed within the same genus, differ from one another as widely as possible, such as white and black. Although they are placed within one genus of quality, they nevertheless recede from one another as far as possible. Everyone also recognizes that they are referred to one another. For what they are is one thing, and what it is for them to be contrary is another. What is black has a certain quality; what is contrary is that which differs most from white.

Conjoined things are those that possess a nature bordering upon each individual thing; for example, pallor is joined to fear. Such things commonly adhere to those joined with them, yet they are not necessarily required to be present with the things near them. Pallor often accompanies fear, but not always, as when fear is suppressed by concealment. Hence probable arguments arise from conjoined things. For whatever things are conjoined commonly serve as an indication of the things to which they adhere. I shall discuss these more carefully in the later treatment.

Antecedents are things which, once posited, necessarily have something else follow, as, because there is war, there must be enmity. They possess the necessity of order. Consequents cannot be separated from antecedents; a consequent is whatever follows what precedes it, [Col. 1066B] as enmity follows war. For if there is war, there must be enmity.

This topic has a noteworthy and remarkable feature: things that are naturally prior are often themselves consequents. Things that naturally precede are also often prior in a proposition. Enmity, for example, usually exists before wars. Yet we cannot propose enmity in such a way that war follows it. We cannot truthfully say, “If there is enmity, there is war.” Instead, we put war first, and enmity, which is naturally prior, follows in the proposition: “If there is war, there is enmity.”

Thus enmity, which naturally precedes war, accompanies war in the proposition. But if I say, “If he is proud, he is hateful,” pride precedes hatred both naturally and in the proposition. Pride usually comes into existence first, and afterward hatred follows from that same pride.

It makes no difference whether a thing naturally precedes at some point or instead follows, provided that in the proposition we mark as antecedent the thing which, whether naturally prior or posterior, nevertheless necessarily draws the other thing along with it.

Things are understood to be repugnant whenever that which is naturally joined to one of two contraries is compared with the other contrary. Since friendship and enmity are contraries, and the desire to harm follows enmity, friendship and the desire to harm are repugnant. These too are referred to one another by a likeness of contrariety.

A cause is that upon whose precedence something is produced; for example, the rising of the sun is the cause of day. An effect is what the preceding cause accomplishes, such as the day that the rising of the sun brings forth.

Comparison of greater things occurs whenever what is greater is compared with what is lesser, as in: “If no innocent person ought to be driven into exile, then Tullius—who was not merely innocent but also the liberator of his fatherland—ought all the more not to be driven into exile.” For being the liberator of one’s fatherland is more than being innocent.

Comparison of equals occurs whenever equal things are compared with one another, as in: “If this innocent citizen ought not to be driven into exile because he is innocent, then neither can that innocent man justly be deprived of his fatherland.”

Comparison of lesser things occurs whenever lesser things are compared with greater ones, as in: “If no one thought Cicero, the liberator of his fatherland, worthy of a reward, let no one think worthy of a reward a man who, although merely innocent, contributed no services to the state.” [Col. 1067A]

No one is unaware that all these things are akin to one another, are mutually referred to one another, and, as it were, behold one another face to face. To speak first of conjugates, justice looks toward what is just and toward what can be done justly, and it perfects the person who is just. The others likewise possess toward one another not merely kinship of name but also a certain agreement of nature, while nevertheless differing from one another.

Justice is not the same thing as a just person. Everything that is inflected from something is different from that from which it is inflected, yet akin to it; and is shown to have been inflected from that source. It is likewise beyond doubt that genus is akin to the thing of which it is the genus, that is, to the species Cicero called the form. Genus is the genus of a species, and species is the species of a genus; thus they are mutually referred to one another, [Col. 1067B] although genus and species are not the same thing.

One point must be considered: the things we now call species Cicero calls forms. So long as I understand what he means, I shall gladly allow him to use whatever names he wishes; but the same concession cannot be made to me. One who professes to shed the light of explanation ought to use words that are established in ordinary usage. The usage of language, however, has established that what is subordinate to a genus as its species should be called a species rather than a form.

Now, a thing can be similar only to something similar, and it can differ only from something dissimilar. Contraries are also understood to be contrary to contraries, and conjoined things adhere to conjoined things. Antecedents precede something capable of following; a consequent follows what has preceded it. Everything repugnant is understood to be hostile to what is repugnant to it. A cause is also the cause of its effect. Whatever a given cause produces, it is the cause of that thing; and an effect is likewise the effect of some cause.

The comparison of greater things looks toward lesser things, that of lesser things toward greater things, and that of equals toward equals. In all these cases, the nature of the relation is found to be such that, although certain things are in themselves different from those to which they are referred, they nevertheless appear to be related when they are compared. Their difference from the things to which they are referred is demonstrated by the fact that nothing can be referred to itself.

Since this is so, they are rightly called related things. All these are species or forms of the topic drawn from related things, as Cicero himself also testifies when he says: “But this genus is distributed into several parts.” By saying “genus,” he indicated that the things into which he divides it are species of the genus.

Moreover, all these things receive both the name of a genus and a definition. Related things are things “toward something,” which can be referred to that to which they are related; conjugates, genus, form, and the rest are always referred to the things to which they are related.

But, as was said in the earlier topics, those topics that adhered to the matter under discussion itself were derived from the whole, from the parts, and from the mark: from the whole, so that the term proposed in the question might be understood; likewise from its parts and from its mark. In the same way, among related things we shall say that they are considered related to the term that, occupying the position of subject or predicate, contains the question.

It remains to say why related things are said to exist in the matter itself under discussion. Cicero indicated that there are four topics in the term under discussion itself: from the whole, from the parts, from the mark, and from related things. It is clear that the first three adhere to the term under discussion. For the definition of any thing, being its whole, exists in the thing itself that it defines. Its parts are also in that thing, which they join together by their collection. Its mark is likewise in the thing that it signifies by its designation.

Related things, however, appear to be placed externally, since they are referred to that to which they are related. If they were not referred to the matter under discussion, they would be understood as being placed externally. Why, then, did he also count related things among the topics adhering to the term under discussion itself?

The answer is that what is said to adhere is not identical with the thing to which it is said to adhere. Although these things are different, they are nevertheless understood to be joined by a certain kinship. Thus a definition is not the same as the thing described by the definition. If a definition makes what it defines clearer, while nothing can make the thing itself clearer than it is in itself, it is evident that what is defined is different from the definition. We nevertheless say that the definition adheres to what is defined because it is akin and joined to it: by signifying its property, it does not depart from its substance.

Parts and marks are likewise different from that which they either join together or designate. But because they join the proposed term or signify it, and because they possess some kinship with the proposed term, they are said to adhere to the matter under discussion.

So too with related things: although they are external—and are not the same as the things to which they are understood to be related—they are nevertheless necessarily said to adhere to those things because they are considered to have some kinship with them.

Although it would be more appropriate to explain their natural order, their differences, and the other division of the topics in the discussion of topical differences, I shall append that explanation after I have expounded Cicero’s examples, which he brought forward to clarify these matters.

Conjugates are said to be words belonging to the same genus. Words of the same genus are those that, derived from one source, undergo various changes, such as *sapiens* (“wise”), *sapienter* (“wisely”), and *sapientia* (“wisdom”). This conjugation of words is called *syzygia* (συζυγία) in Greek. From it comes the following argument: “If a field is common-pasture land, there is a right to pasture in common.”

[Col. 1068D] Cicero’s definition of conjugates is as follows: “Conjugates are words that belong to the same genus,” that is, words that are inflected in various ways from one word. For *justitia*, *justus*, *juste*, *justum*, and all other forms that can be inflected into different kinds of words are words from the same genus. Whatever things arise from one source and undergo various changes are called *syzygia* by the Greeks, but *conjugates* by the Latins. For what the Greeks call *syzygia*, we call *conjugatio*, “conjugation.”

These include *sapiens*, *sapienter*, and *sapientia*, and whatever words derived from one source are seen to belong to various parts of speech and to have various inflections.

An example of an argument arising from conjugates is the following. Suppose it is doubtful whether I may pasture livestock together with a neighbor in some field—that is, whether there is a right to pasture in common. The subject is therefore “the field,” while the predicate is “to pasture in common.” We shall construct the argument in this way: “This field about which the question is asked is common-pasture land; in common-pasture land it is permitted to pasture in common; therefore, in this field it is permitted to pasture in common.”

The argument establishing the right to pasture in common has thus been taken from *compascuum*, “common-pasture land,” and specifically from a conjugate. For *compascere*, “to pasture in common,” and *compascuum* are conjugates. The argument that there is a right to pasture in common has been taken from the fact that the field is common-pasture land; yet *compascuum* is conjugate with *compascere*. The argument has therefore been taken from conjugates, because the conjugate is present in the very matter under discussion, namely, in “pasturing in common.” For all these forms flow from the same source and contain and regard one another.

The argument has consequently been made from what is in the matter itself, from related things—that is, from conjugates. The maximal proposition is: “Conjugates have one and the same nature insofar as they are conjugates”; or, put another way: “Whatever something is applicable to, its conjugate can also be associated with that thing.”

An argument is drawn from genus as follows: “Since all silver was bequeathed to the woman, the money counted out and left at home cannot fail to have been bequeathed. For the form never separates from the genus so far as its name is concerned; the counted-out money retains the name of silver; therefore it appears to have been bequeathed.”

[Col. 1069C] Genus is what is predicated of any species with respect to what a thing is. To be predicated with respect to what a thing is means that, when someone asks what a particular species is, the genus is appropriately given as the answer and displays the substance of the species about which the answer is given.

A genus is always greater than its proper species and includes it within the scope of its predication. Thus, although a genus may also be divided into other things, it never abandons its own species; for example, *animal* is predicated of a human being and displays the substance of a human being. When we ask what a human being is, the answer is “an animal.” The same genus can nevertheless be extended to a horse, an ox, and other things, which are called animals. Yet it is extended to different things in such a way that it does not abandon any one of the species it contains.

[Col. 1069D] Wherever a human being exists, it is necessary that an animal exist, for a human being is an animal. The same applies to an ox and to the rest. It has therefore been clearly demonstrated that the name of the genus can in no way be separated from the species.

If the name of the genus is ever uttered universally, it is necessary that all the species be designated. Thus, if someone says “every animal,” he designates both human beings and oxen and all the other species included under the name *animal*.

Since this is so, someone had bequeathed to a woman all his silver by his will. The question is whether the counted-out money also had been bequeathed to her. The subject in this question is therefore “the counted-out money,” and the predicate is “bequeathed.”

I accordingly consider which of the two contains something from which I may seek an argument. I see that the subject term, “counted-out money,” has as its genus *silver*, which is related to its own species, to which it is referred. For things that are referred to one another are related things. Therefore, since all silver was bequeathed, and since the genus does not abandon its proper species, it is necessary that the counted-out money also was bequeathed.

When someone says “all animals live,” he does not, as I understand it, mean merely that a human being, an ox, or a horse, or individually some other animal, whether one or many, lives, while maintaining that certain animals nevertheless lack life. Rather, he asserts that absolutely everything that is an animal lives.

Since, therefore, every member of the genus—that is, all silver—was bequeathed, no species is excepted. But counted-out money is silver. It follows that counted-out money too can be included under the term “bequeathed.”

The question, then, as stated, is whether the counted-out money was bequeathed. The argument is drawn from what is in the matter itself, namely, from the genus that is present in its proper species—from related things, which are such because they are referred to that to which they are related. Here the related thing is silver, derived from the topic of related things, namely, genus. For silver is predicated as a genus of counted-out money. When we ask what counted-out money is, we properly answer “silver.”

The maximal proposition is: “To whatever the whole genus applies, each individual species also applies.” Marcus Tullius stated the same proposition in different words but with the same meaning when he said: “For the form never separates from the genus so far as its name is concerned; the counted-out money retains the name of silver; therefore it appears to have been bequeathed.”

From the form of a genus—which may sometimes, for the sake of clearer understanding, be called its part—an argument is made as follows: “If money was bequeathed to Fabia by her husband on the condition that she was the wife of that man and a *materfamilias*, and she had not entered into *manus*, nothing is owed to her.”

The genus is *wife*, and it has two forms: one, *materfamilias*, consisting of those who have entered into *manus*; the other, consisting of women who are merely regarded as wives. Fabia belonged to the latter class, and therefore the bequest does not appear to have been made to her.

A species is that which, formed by its proper differences, is placed under the predication of a genus. Its proper differences separate and distinguish it from the other species. Thus, although a human being is a species of animal, it is formed by the differences of rationality and mortality and is separated from animals that are eternal, such as the sun, which the Platonists are said to regard as an animal, and from animals that lack reason.

Since all species differ from one another through their proper differences, what is said of one species cannot be transferred to another. What is said specifically of a human being, for example, cannot be understood of a horse or an ox.

An argument is drawn from species whenever the genus itself is contracted, as it were, into a particular portion. If someone says that an animal must be brought to him which is rational and mortal, this is understood to have been said not of a horse, an ox, or any other animal, but only of a human being.

Just as a genus stated universally, when someone says “every animal,” embraces all species, so any designated animal establishes a species. Accordingly, from the form of the genus—that is, from the species of the genus—an argument is made of the kind that Cicero often calls the form of the genus a part, so that what is said may be clearer. The name “part” is more familiar than “form.” We briefly explained above how form differs from parts, and Cicero himself will explain it more fully shortly afterward.

Let us now examine the proposed example. There are two species of wife: one, *materfamilias*; the other, a wife by usage. Both are called by the common name of the genus, “wives.” It often happens that species are called by the same names as their genera. But a woman could not be a *materfamilias* unless she had entered into *manus*; this was a definite species of marriage.

[Col. 1071B] A wife was held in three ways: by usage, by *confarreatio*, and by *coemptio*. *Confarreatio* was appropriate only to priests. Women who had entered into *manus* through *coemptio* were called *matresfamilias*; those who had entered through usage or *confarreatio* were not.

*Coemptio* was carried out with particular solemnities. In the act of purchase the man and woman questioned one another. The man asked whether the woman wished to be his *materfamilias*, and she replied that she did. The woman likewise asked whether the man wished to be her *paterfamilias*, and he replied that he did. Thus the woman entered into the *manus* of the man. This marriage was called marriage by *coemptio*, and the woman became a *materfamilias* in relation to the man, in the position of a daughter. Ulpian explains this solemnity in his *Institutes*.

Someone therefore bequeathed all his silver to his wife Fabia in his final testament, provided that Fabia was not merely his wife but also a definite species of wife, namely, a *materfamilias*. The question is whether the silver was bequeathed to Fabia as wife.

“Fabia as wife” is the subject; “silver bequeathed” is the predicate. I therefore ask what argument I can take from the things posited in the question. I see that “wife” contains two forms, one of which is merely a wife, while the other is a *materfamilias*, which is achieved by entering into *manus*.

If Fabia did not enter into *manus* and was not a *materfamilias*—that is, if she was not the species of wife to whom all the silver was bequeathed—then, since what is said of one species is not appropriately said of another, and since Fabia belonged to the species that did not enter into *manus*, that is, that was not a *materfamilias*, while the husband bequeathed the silver to a *materfamilias*, the bequest does not appear to belong to Fabia.

The question, then, as stated, is whether all the silver was bequeathed to Fabia as wife. The subject is “Fabia as wife”; the predicate is “silver bequeathed.” The argument is drawn from what is in the matter under discussion, namely, from what is in the wife under discussion.

What is in the wife under discussion is a species of wife, specifically the one that did not enter into *manus*, which is related to that wife. For every species is referred to its genus, that is, to its form. The argument has therefore been made from what is in the matter itself, from related things, and from the form of the genus.

The maximal proposition is: “What is said of one species is not applicable to another.”

From similarity, as follows: “If buildings have fallen because they have decayed or have become defective, and their usufruct has been bequeathed, the heir is not required to restore or repair them, any more than he is required to restore a slave if the slave whose usufruct was bequeathed has perished.”

Things are called similar when they possess the same quality. From them an argument is taken in this way. Someone bequeathed the usufruct of buildings by will—that is, he granted the buildings so that another person might use them during his lifetime. These buildings began either to become defective, that is, to threaten collapse, or actually collapsed.

The person to whom the usufruct of the buildings was bequeathed therefore asks the heir to compensate him for the damage to the buildings bequeathed to him by the testator and to restore the buildings that had become defective or collapsed. The question is whether the heir is required to restore the defect or collapse of the buildings whose usufruct was bequeathed.

The subject expression, functioning as the term, is therefore “the collapse or defect of the buildings whose usufruct was bequeathed.” The predicate expression, established in the position of the term, is “restoration by the heir.”

I take an argument from similarity in this way: “If, when someone has bequeathed the usufruct of a slave and the slave has perished in some way, the heir is not required to restore the slave, then the heir will not now be required to restore buildings that were bequeathed in usufruct and have become defective or collapsed.”

The bequest of a slave’s usufruct is similar to the bequest of the buildings’ usufruct. It is also similar that a slave bequeathed in usufruct is not restored by the heir if the slave perishes, and that a defect or collapse of buildings bequeathed in usufruct is not repaired by the heir.

The question, then, is whether the heir is required to restore the defect or collapse of buildings bequeathed in usufruct. The subject term is “the defect or collapse of buildings bequeathed in usufruct”; the predicate is “restoration by the heir.”

The argument is drawn from what is in the matter itself, that is, from what inheres in the collapse or defect of the buildings bequeathed in usufruct. This is a related thing, namely, a similarity. For every similarity is understood to inhere in that which is similar. The similarity here is the usufruct of a slave who perishes, whom the heir is not required to restore.

The maximal proposition is: “The same things are applicable to similar matters.”

From difference: “If a husband bequeathed to his wife all the silver that belonged to him, it does not follow that the money recorded as debts was bequeathed. For it makes a great difference whether the silver is placed in a chest or is owed in accounts.”

What is said of two things that differ greatly does not appear to be applicable to the other. Since this is so, someone bequeathed all his silver to his wife. She also claimed as hers the money owed by debtors, because all money was called by the name of silver. The question is whether the silver owed in accounts was also bequeathed.

The subject term is therefore “the silver owed in accounts,” while “bequeathed” is the predicate.

We shall construct the argument from difference as follows: “The same thing cannot be understood of matters that differ greatly. Silver placed in a chest differs greatly from silver owed in accounts. Money placed in a chest is under our ownership; money owed in accounts is not ours. For what is given as a loan becomes the property of the recipient. Therefore the debtor is not required to return that very money to the creditor but another amount equal to it.”

Money placed in a chest and money owed in accounts are not species of silver or money but differences. The species of silver are said to be coined and uncoined. The quality of money held in possession or not held in possession, though not alienated in every respect, consists in these differences: one kind is placed in a chest, while the other is owed in accounts.

This has been stated so that no one might think the argument was drawn from species rather than from differences. For substantial quality is counted among differences, not among species.

Since the husband bequeathed to his wife all the silver that was his, and since it is evident that this applies to what was the legator’s—that is, to what had been stored in a chest—the same cannot be understood of what was owed in accounts. For, as has been said, what is owed in accounts differs greatly from what is placed in a chest.

The argument has therefore been made from what inhered in the matter under discussion. The question concerned silver owed in accounts. In this silver there inhered a proper difference by which it differed from other silver, namely, the fact that the other silver was placed in a chest. This is a related thing, namely, a difference.

The maximal proposition is: “The same thing cannot be understood of matters that differ greatly.”

From contrariety, as follows: “The woman to whom her husband bequeathed the usufruct of his property, leaving wine-cellars and oil-cellars full, ought not to think that their contents belong to her. For usufruct, not abuse, was bequeathed; these are contrary to one another.”

What is said of one thing cannot apply to its contrary. The same thing cannot in any way be understood of two contraries.

Someone therefore bequeathed to his wife, by an act of final testamentary intention, the usufruct of his property. The woman claimed the full wine-cellars and oil-cellars for her own usufruct. The question is whether the stores too were bequeathed in usufruct. “The usufruct of the stores” is therefore the subject, and “bequeathed” the predicate.

An argument is taken from contrariety in this way: “We use things that remain for us while we use them; we abuse things that perish for us while we use them. Therefore, since remaining and perishing are contraries, use and abuse must also be judged contraries.”

[Col. 1073D] If other things remain when used, while the contents of wine- and oil-cellars are consumed through use, the usufruct of the other things can exist; but the stores cannot be use, rather they are abuse. Therefore, since the husband bequeathed to his wife the usufruct of his property, he could not have bequeathed its contrary, which is abuse. The wine and oil constitute abuse; therefore wine and oil cannot belong to the woman’s usufruct.

The argument is drawn from what is in the matter itself under discussion, namely, from the bequest of usufruct, and from what is related to it, namely, contrariety. Contraries are not in contraries as a definition is in the thing defined, but as a relation. For every relation exists in relatives, and contraries are said to be in contraries not with respect to what they are—that is, their qualities—but with respect to the fact that they are contrary. They are compared with one another according to their greatest separation.

The maximal proposition is: “What is applicable to one thing is not applicable to its contrary.”

From adjuncts: “If a woman made a will who had never suffered a diminution of status, possession under that will does not appear to be granted according to the praetor’s edict; for it is added that possession under the wills of slaves, exiles, and children is granted according to the edict.”

Adjuncts are things that occupy a proximate and very close position, so that, if one of them has existed in any way, the other also appears either to have existed, to exist, or to be going to exist [Col. 1074B]; for they are, as it were, neighbors to one another. Things that are close to one another in existence either precede the matter, as love often precedes intercourse; exist simultaneously, as pallor and fear; or occur afterward, as slaughter after anger. Such is the nature of adjuncts that they can indeed be separated, yet they indicate one another. For the person who has loved has not necessarily possessed the object of his love, and often one who has possessed it has not loved. Nor does one who is pale necessarily fear, and often someone who is not afraid is pale. Nor will an angry person necessarily kill, and often someone has killed without being angry. Yet, if individual cases are investigated, it is plausible that the person who loved had intercourse, that the person who fears is pale, and that the person who was angry killed—not because this is necessary, but because we infer neighboring things from neighboring things.

[Col. 1074C] As for the example of this argument, the comparison is as follows. *Capitis diminutio* is an alteration of a former status. This usually occurs in many ways: it may be maximal, intermediate, or minimal. It is maximal when both liberty and citizenship are lost, as in deportation. It is intermediate when citizenship is lost but liberty retained, as in migration to the Latin colonies. It is minimal when neither citizenship nor liberty is lost, but the status of the former condition is diminished—for example, by adoption—or when, in any other way, the former status can be altered while citizenship is retained.

In ancient law women were held under perpetual guardianship. Those, however, who passed into the *manus* of a husband withdrew from the power of their guardian; thus an alteration of their former status occurred, and a woman who had passed into the *manus* of a husband had suffered *capitis diminutio*. [Col. 1074D] Accordingly, a certain woman who had never suffered *capitis diminutio*—that is, who had never passed into the *manus* of a husband—made a will without the authorization of her guardian. The question is whether possession should be granted under the praetor’s edict according to the provisions of her will.

Here the subject term is “the provisions of the will of a woman who had never suffered *capitis diminutio*”; the predicate is “the granting of possession.” An argument is therefore drawn from adjuncts, as follows. If possession is granted according to the will of a woman who had never suffered *capitis diminutio*, there is no reason why possession under the praetor’s edict should not also be granted according to the wills of children and slaves. What, indeed, could prevent possession from being granted according to the will of a woman who had never suffered *capitis diminutio*? [Col. 1075A] Clearly, the fact that the woman who made the will was not legally independent; and the same can be said of children and slaves. Their age and their condition are placed under another person’s authority.

The adjunct argument is therefore: if possession is granted according to the will of a woman who was not legally independent, possession should also be granted according to the wills of children and slaves, who are likewise by no means legally independent, since the former are under the power of a guardian and the latter under the power of a master. For what follows a matter in question and exists afterward is proximate to that matter. The question is whether possession should be granted according to the will of a woman who had never suffered *capitis diminutio*. It follows from this that, if this is done, possession should also be granted according to the wills of slaves and children. Since that ought not to occur [Col. 1075B], the precedent example ought not to exist either.

Yet the consequence is not necessary, but merely proximate. It is possible that the sole point accepted may be that possession is granted according to the woman’s will, without accepting that possession should also be granted according to the wills of slaves or children. Nevertheless, it is proximate that one who has now accepted the former will later admit the latter.

This, then, is an argument from adjuncts—that is, from something that inheres in the matter under investigation. The question concerns the will of a woman who had never suffered *capitis diminutio*, and the argument is drawn from its associated, or adjunct, circumstances. The principal proposition is: “Adjuncts are to be assessed from adjuncts.”

## From antecedents, consequents, and things incompatible

From antecedents: “If the divorce was caused by the husband’s fault [Col. 1075C], and if the woman sent the notice of repudiation, nevertheless nothing ought to remain on behalf of the children.”

Antecedents are things which, once posited, necessarily bring about something else, even though the antecedent is lesser or later. It is lesser in the case of “If he is a human being, he is an animal”: a human being is less than an animal, yet once a human being is posited, it follows that he is an animal. It is later in the case of “If she has given birth, she has had intercourse with a man,” for giving birth is later than intercourse with a man.

Sometimes what is equal, simultaneous, or prior is also posited as the antecedent. It is equal in “If he is a human being, he is capable of laughter.” It is simultaneous in “If the earth has been placed in the way, the moon is eclipsed.” These are convertible, so that consequents become antecedents: “If he is capable of laughter, he is a human being,” and “If the moon has been eclipsed, the earth has been interposed.” [Col. 1075D] The antecedent is prior in “If he is arrogant, he is hateful.” Arrogance is prior, hatred later.

One point nevertheless remains true in all cases: once the antecedents have been posited, the consequents necessarily follow.

The explanation by example is as follows. Under Roman citizenship law, children remain under their fathers’ authority until they are released by the third emancipation. Therefore, if a divorce had once occurred through the woman’s fault, she was fined a certain portion of the dowry according to the number of children. Paulus discussed this matter in the second book of his *Institutes*, under the title “On Dowries,” as follows:

> If the divorce is a dissolution of the marriage and has occurred without the woman’s fault, the dowry shall be reclaimed in full; but if the divorce has occurred through the woman’s fault, the husband retains one sixth of the dowry for each child, [Col. 1076A] up to one half of the dowry only.

Therefore, since what is acquired from the dowry belongs to the children, and the children are under their father’s authority, it is necessary that this remain with the husband.

After the divorce has occurred, the question is whether a portion of the dowry should remain with the husband on behalf of the children. Here the subject is “a divorce announced by the woman”; the predicate is “the retention by the husband, after the divorce, of one sixth of the dowry.” The question is whether, after a divorce has occurred and the woman has sent the notice of repudiation, one sixth of the dowry ought to remain with the husband.

If an argument is to be made from antecedents, I ask what is antecedent and what follows. If the divorce occurred through the husband’s fault, I see that the woman cannot be fined a portion of the dowry, even if she was the first to send the notice of repudiation. For the antecedent—that the divorce occurred through the husband’s fault [Col. 1076B]—does not permit the woman’s portion of the dowry to be forfeited, even though she was the first to send the notice of repudiation. She is not to be fined a portion of the dowry because she first announced the repudiation; rather, she is to be released from the loss, since the divorce occurred not through her fault but through the husband’s.

The antecedent, therefore, is that the divorce occurred through the husband’s fault; the consequent is that a portion of the dowry is not retained. For if this is the case, that is the case.

The argument may be made as follows:

> If the divorce occurred through the husband’s fault, the woman will in no way be fined a portion of the dowry, even if she sent the notice of repudiation. But the divorce occurred through the husband’s fault. Therefore, the woman will not lawfully be fined a portion of the dowry.

If she will not be fined a portion of the dowry, nothing will remain in the husband’s household on behalf of the children in the name of the dowry. But she will not be fined a portion of the dowry [Col. 1076C]. Therefore, nothing will remain with the husband from the dowry on behalf of the children.

The conclusion of both syllogisms is this: if the divorce occurred through the husband’s fault, nothing ought to remain on behalf of the children.

The argument is from something inherent in the matter under investigation. The issue concerns a portion of the dowry and its retention by the husband after the divorce, which the woman announced first. The antecedent is the husband’s fault; because it is prior, it is associated with the consequent. For everything that precedes must necessarily be referred to what follows.

The principal proposition is: “Where the antecedent is present, the consequent will also be present.” In this question the antecedent is present—namely, that the divorce occurred through the husband’s fault. Therefore the consequent will also be present there: the sixth portions will not be retained.

Why I have woven the preceding argument into the conclusions [Col. 1076D] will become clearer when I discuss these matters at greater length, as Cicero develops them.

### From consequents

“If a woman, having been married to a man with whom there was no right of *connubium*, sent the notice of repudiation, then, since children do not follow their father, nothing ought to remain on behalf of the children.”

Consequents are things that follow once antecedents have been posited, as when we say, “If he is a human being, he is an animal”: “animal” is the consequent. In the proposed example, however, the argument does not sufficiently appear to proceed from consequents, but rather from antecedents, as will shortly become clear.

Children born without a lawful marriage were not under their fathers’ authority; rather, they followed their mothers. Nor did all persons have *connubium* with Romans. Nor was a marriage legally contracted [Col. 1077A] if it was not entered into between a Roman citizen and a Roman citizen, or if the prince or the people had not permitted citizenship or *connubium*, specifically in such a way that the children would be placed under the authority of their parents.

It must also be considered that children born from an unequal marriage follow not their father but their mother. Thus a Roman woman married either a Latin, a foreigner, or a slave with whom she had no right of *connubium*. She provided a dowry, and after a divorce had taken place between them, the question was whether a portion of the dowry of a woman married to a man with whom she had no right of *connubium* should remain with the husband after the divorce.

Here the subject is “a woman married to a man with whom there was no *connubium*”; the predicate is “the lawful retention by the husband, after the divorce, of a portion of the dowry.”

An argument is therefore drawn from consequents [Col. 1077B], as follows. Since she married a man with whom there was no right of *connubium*, it follows that the children do not follow their father. But if the children do not follow their father, they are not under their father’s authority. If they are not under their father’s authority, they are attached to their mother, and a portion of the dowry cannot remain with the husband.

The antecedent here is the marriage with a man with whom there was no right of *connubium*; the consequent is that nothing ought to remain from the dowry on behalf of the children.

The argument may be concluded as follows:

> Since, when *connubium* has not been granted, the children who are born do not follow their father, not even a portion of the dowry ought to remain with the father on behalf of the children, since the children follow not their father but their mother.

It has therefore been proved that nothing ought to remain on behalf of the children from the fact that the woman married a man with whom she had no right of *connubium*. But this was the antecedent [Col. 1077C]. The argument, therefore, is found to have proceeded not from the consequent but rather from the antecedent.

If the proposition that nothing ought to remain in the name of the dowry had been proved by establishing that she married a man with whom she had no right of *connubium*, the argument would rightly be said to have proceeded from consequents.

The argument would proceed from consequents if it were stated as follows:

> If something ought to remain from the dowry on behalf of the children, it is proved that the woman was married to a man with whom she had the right of *connubium*, because the children follow their father.

I assume the consequent:

> But the woman was not married to a man with whom she had the right of *connubium*.

I conclude the antecedent:

> Therefore nothing ought to remain from the dowry on behalf of the children, because the children do not follow their father.

The argument is from something inherent in the matter under investigation [Col. 1077D]. The question concerns a marriage in which there was no lawful *connubium*. The argument is drawn from associated circumstances, for every consequent is referred to what precedes it.

The principal proposition is: “Where the consequent is absent, the antecedent cannot be present either.” There will be another, fuller opportunity to discuss these matters.

### From things incompatible

“If a head of household bequeathed to his wife the usufruct of female slaves from his son, but did not bequeath it from the second heir, the woman will not lose the usufruct when the son dies. For what has once been given to someone by a will cannot be taken away from the person to whom it was given against his will; for it is incompatible rightly to receive something and to return it unwillingly.”

A second heir is one who is substituted for the appointed heir. For example, if someone appoints his son as heir and writes that, if the son should die before reaching puberty [Col. 1078A], his grandson or anyone else is to be heir, then the grandson or whoever else is called the second heir.

Things incompatible are those which, as has been said, follow contraries when compared with those contraries.

Someone therefore named his son heir in his will, substituted a second heir for him, and bequeathed to his wife the usufruct of female slaves from the son. He directed that his son grant his wife the usufruct of the female slaves, but did not add that the second heir should likewise grant the same usufruct to the woman.

The son succeeded and granted the woman the usufruct of the female slaves. When he died before reaching puberty, the second heir brought an action and attempted to wrest the usufruct of the female slaves from the woman, saying that the usufruct had been bequeathed to her by the son, but not by himself.

[Col. 1078B] The question is whether the woman can lose, against her will, the legacy she had received under the will. Here the subject is “a legacy that she rightly received under the law of the will”; the predicate is “being able to lose it against her will.”

I therefore take the argument from things incompatible. What is incompatible is this: if what follows from one contrary is compared with another contrary. In the example under discussion, “to receive rightly” and “not to receive rightly” are contraries; but “to return unwillingly” accompanies “not to receive rightly.” For a person who did not rightly receive something justly returns it unwillingly. Thus “to return unwillingly” is incompatible with “to receive rightly.”

The argument will therefore be made as follows:

> Whoever received something by will received it rightly. But what is received rightly cannot be taken away against the will of the person who once rightly received it. The woman, however, received the usufruct of the female slaves by will. Therefore it cannot be taken away from her against her will [Col. 1078C].

The argument is from something inherent in the matter under investigation—namely, from what was rightly received. It is inherent in the matter as an associated circumstance in the manner of contrariety, as was said above. The argument is therefore from something incompatible.

The principal proposition is: “Things incompatible cannot be brought together.”

### From efficient causes

“The right belongs to everyone to attach a straight wall to a common wall, whether solid or vaulted. But if someone, while demolishing a common wall, has given a promise against threatened damage, he will not be required to make good the damage caused by the vault’s defect. For the damage was caused not by the fault of the person who demolished it, but by the defect of the work, which had been built in such a way that it could not be supported.”

There are many kinds of causes [Col. 1078D], which Cicero divides somewhat later. At present he is discussing the argument from efficient causes. An efficient cause is one whose preceding operation produces something—not in time, but by the property of its nature—as in the example we are now explaining.

A promise against threatened damage is made whenever someone promises that, if any damage occurs through his work, it will be compensated by his restoration. It is lawful, however, to attach to a common wall another wall, either vaulted—that is, having an arch—or straight, continuous, and level.

Someone therefore attached another wall externally to a common wall and gave security against threatened damage. The common wall, however, was vaulted—that is, it had an arch or supported a tile structure. The person who had given security attached his wall and, in order to attach it, demolished part of the common wall [Col. 1079A] so that the join might hold. The common wall’s defect caused the problem.

The question is whether the promise against threatened damage compels the person who made the promise to restore the damage.

The subject term is “the promise against threatened damage”; the predicate is “the restoration of the defect.”

We therefore take the argument from causes as follows. If the person who promised against threatened damage was the cause of the defect, he ought to restore the defect that occurred through his fault. But if the wall was of such a nature that it could not support or sustain the structure—the nature of a vaulted wall is not such that it can be suspended—then the form of the wall rather than the fault of the person who demolished it will appear to have caused the defect. Accordingly, the person who bound himself by a promise against threatened damage is not compelled to restore the defect.

The argument will therefore be made as follows:

> If the form of the wall was responsible for the defect occurring when the person who had promised against threatened damage attached another wall to it, the person who made the promise is not compelled to make good that defect. But the wall was the cause of the defect [Col. 1079B], since it was of such a nature that it could not support or sustain the structure. Therefore, the person who promised against threatened damage is not required to make good the defect caused by the vault.

The argument is from something inherent in the matter under investigation—namely, the restoration of the defect—and from the effect, that is, from the cause. The cause of the defect is the form of the wall, not the fault of the person who attached the other wall. Thus the vault caused the defect; and since the cause of the defect is absent from the person who attached the wall, the restoration of that defect is also absent from him.

The principal proposition is: “Each matter ought to be considered from its causes.”

### From effects

“When a woman passes into the *manus* of a husband, everything that belonged to the woman becomes the husband’s [Col. 1079C] in the name of dowry.”

Effects are things produced by certain causes—not causes preceding them in time, but causes that precede them by nature. For example, someone may ask, when a wife who had passed into her husband’s *manus* dies, whether her property belongs to the husband.

In this question, “the property of the deceased wife who had passed into her husband’s *manus*” is the subject; “belonging to the husband” is the predicate.

I therefore seek an argument from the effect and consider what the passage into the husband’s *manus* itself accomplished. I draw the argument from this: everything that belonged to the woman became the husband’s in the name of dowry.

The passage into the husband’s *manus* therefore made everything that had belonged to the woman the husband’s in the name of dowry—not by preceding it in time, but immediately, by the proper force of its nature. For as soon as a woman passes into a man’s *manus*, her property [Col. 1079D] follows the husband in the name of dowry.

I therefore make the argument as follows:

> If the woman who died passed into the *manus* of a husband, and the property of a woman who passes into a husband’s *manus* becomes the husband’s in the name of dowry, then this property also, which is under discussion, belongs to the husband.

The argument is contained in something inherent in the matter under investigation. The matter concerns the property of a woman who passed into *manus*, and the argument is drawn from effects—that is, from the effects of the cause. For the effect is that, by passage into *manus*, everything belonging to the woman becomes the husband’s in the name of dowry.

Nevertheless, here too the argument appears to have been made not from effects but from the cause. It was shown that whatever belonged to the woman becomes the husband’s in the name of dowry because the woman passed into *manus*. But this is the cause by which what belonged to the woman becomes the husband’s in the name of dowry.

[Col. 1080A] Someone might say that, from the proposition that what belonged to the woman becomes the husband’s in the name of dowry, one may prove that the deceased woman’s property ought to belong to the husband. But “what belongs to the woman becomes the husband’s in the name of dowry” and “the property belongs to the husband” are either the same thing, or neither is the cause of the other.

If someone says that the cause whereby the woman’s property ought to pass to the husband is that, through passage into *manus*, it became the husband’s in the name of dowry, he will think that the argument has again been made from the cause and not from effects—that is, from the dowry. From effects, however, only the cause ought to be proved.

The argument would be from effects if the cause were proved from the effect in this way. Suppose the question were whether the woman had passed into her husband’s *manus*, and it were established beyond doubt that everything that had belonged to the woman had become the husband’s in the name of dowry. One would say [Col. 1080B]:

> If everything that belonged to the woman became the husband’s in the name of dowry, the woman passed into her husband’s *manus*. But everything that belonged to the woman became the husband’s in the name of dowry. Therefore, the woman passed into her husband’s *manus*.

The principal proposition is: “Causes are not to be separated from their effects.”

### From comparison

Everything of the following kind is valid by comparison:

> What is valid in the greater matter should be valid in the lesser—for example, if boundaries are not regulated in the city, neither should water be confined in the city.

The converse also applies:

> What is valid in the lesser matter should be valid in the greater.

The same example can be reversed.

What is valid in an equal matter should be valid in this matter, which is equal. Since possession by use (*usus auctoritas*) of land lasts two years, it should also last two years for houses. But houses are not mentioned in the law, and they are among all the other things for which possession by use lasts one year. Equity should prevail, since it demands equal rights in equal cases.

[Col. 1080C] The topic called comparison is divided into three parts: it arises either from comparison with greater things, comparison with lesser things, or comparison with equal things.

Comparison with greater things occurs whenever greater things are compared with lesser things, as follows: what is valid in the greater matter should be valid in the lesser.

Suppose the question is whether water may be confined in the city. The subject term is “water in the city”; the predicate is “the right to confine it.”

Boundaries are said to be regulated whenever each field is enclosed by its own boundaries. A person confines water when he does not allow it to flow through his own property.

The argument may therefore be made as follows:

> Since regulating boundaries is the greater matter and confining water is the lesser, if boundaries are not regulated in the city—something greater—then the lesser matter will not occur either: water will not be confined in the city.

The argument here is taken from something inherent in the matter under investigation [Col. 1080D]. The question concerns the right to confine water; the argument is drawn from an associated matter, namely, the greater matter, which is referred to the lesser.

It should be noted that Tullius included the principal proposition within the argument in this form: “What is valid in the greater matter should be valid in the lesser.” Relying on this, he developed the argument so that what was mentioned in the first book might become clearer: these principal propositions are sometimes included within arguments, as in the present example, while at other times they give force to arguments, as in the preceding examples of topics.

If we reverse the same example, we shall say:

> What is valid in the lesser matter [Col. 1081A] should also be valid in the greater.

But water is confined in the city; therefore boundaries should be regulated.

Here, however, the question is altered. The question is whether boundaries ought to be regulated in the city. The argument is drawn from the lesser matter—that is, from the confinement of water—so that here too the argument is from something inherent in the matter under investigation, namely, from the regulation of boundaries, and from an associated matter, namely, the lesser matter.

For the lesser matter is the associated matter, since it refers to the thing with which it is compared. Here too Tullius supplied the principal proposition:

> What is valid in the lesser matter is also valid in the greater.

Comparison from equals is made in the same way. Equity must prevail, since it demands equal rights in equal matters.

Possession by use of many things lasts one year: if someone has used them continuously for a year, he possesses them with the firm authority of law [Col. 1081B]—for example, a movable object. Possession by use of land, however, is limited to a period of two years; the law says nothing about houses.

The question is therefore whether houses are acquired by use in one year or in two. We shall make an argument from equals. Since equal possession applies to immovables, and houses are immovable, just as land is acquired by use after two years, so too a person who possesses houses ought to acquire them by use after two years. Equity demands equal rights in equal matters.

Tullius also sets out this principal proposition very clearly, but his example is stated in a more restricted way and is not immediately easy to understand. He says:

> Since possession by use of land lasts two years, it should also last two years for houses.

Here he understands possession by use of houses to be acquired after two years, but he adds [Col. 1081C]:

> But houses are not mentioned in the law, and they are among all the other things for which possession by use lasts one year.

Here again he seems to place houses among the things acquired by use in one year, and he concludes without defining anything except that equity should prevail, since it demands equal rights in equal cases.

The statement appears to mean this: since houses are immovable, like land, and land is acquired by use after two years, houses too should be acquired by use after two years. He then sets this against itself again, saying that in the Law of the Twelve Tables nothing is written about houses, and that, by the silence of the law, they were left among the things for which possession by use lasts one year.

For when the law prescribed two years for the acquisition of land by use, it remained silent about houses and, by that silence, rather joined them to the things for which possession by use lasts one year.

He resolves the objection as follows: equity demands equal rights in equal matters. Therefore, since land and houses are equally immovable, both will be acquired by use after two years.

[Col. 1081D] Here too, then, the argument was made from something inherent in the matter under investigation, namely, from the associated matter, the equal. Since the issue concerns possession of houses, the argument was taken from the acquisition by use of land.

Having dealt with these topics, which inhered in the matter under investigation, he now gives an example of the topic that he said was external. This is the topic drawn from the authority of a judgment. It is highly persuasive, even if it does not possess the greatest necessity.

Necessary things are considered from their own nature [Col. 1082A]. Probable things, however, await the judgment of many. Things are probable when they appear so either to everyone, to the majority, to the most renowned and eminent persons, or to those learned in each particular art and science—for example, what is true for a physician in medicine, for a geometrician in geometry, and for others in their respective fields of study.

Concerning this external topic he speaks as follows:

> Things that are assumed externally are said chiefly to derive from authority. Therefore the Greeks call such arguments ἀτέχνους—that is, “without art” or “inartificial.”

Some arguments are those that the orator himself elicits and, in a certain sense, obtains for himself from the topics that have been identified, acquiring them through his own ability. Others are placed externally: the orator does not discover them himself but makes use of things present and prepared, such as testimony, documents, reputation, and other matters that M. Tullius will discuss at greater length.

The orator does not prepare testimony for himself; he makes use of testimony already prepared. Nor does he himself create a judgment; he uses a rumor that has already arisen and comes to him spontaneously [Col. 1082B] for the purposes of the case. For this reason the Greeks call these topics ἀτέχνους, that is, “inartificial,” and, as Tullius said, “without art.” Things that are not acquired through the orator’s own art but come from outside and supply themselves are rightly called without art.

An example is this:

> Suppose you answer as follows: Since Publius Scaevola said that the ground belonging to the circuit of a house extended only as far as the roof projected for the purpose of covering the common wall, so that water would flow from it onto the roof of the house that had been covered, this appears to you to be the law.

The ground belonging to the circuit of a house is as much ground as the circuit of the house encloses. Scaevola therefore said that the ground belonging to the circuit of a house was whatever was covered by the projection of the roof.

[Col. 1082C] For it is clear that roofs extend farther than the ground and are not aligned with the walls, so that rainwater may fall farther outward. Since this is so, someone was attempting to cover a common wall, and the question is whether there is a right to cover it.

“You should answer,” he says to Trebatius, “that there is a right to cover the common wall, provided that rainwater from the roof of the person who covers it is not discharged onto any other roof. Otherwise, there is no legal right for anyone to cover the wall if the rainwater flows down onto the neighbor’s roof. This servitude concerning the flow of rainwater is new and, unless the neighbor consents, has no legal force.”
