But if someone objects that even then there is no legal right to cover the wall, since the ground belonging to a house extends only as far as the walls of each house enclose, whereas the person who covers it projects the roof farther outward, “you,” he says, “will support your answer by the authority of Scaevola, saying that Scaevola responded [Col. 1082D] that the ground belonging to the circuit of the house extended as far as the roof projected, not as far as the walls enclosed.”

There is therefore a right to project the roof for the person who covers it within the circuit of his own house, but only so that the water flows onto his own roof and does not injure the neighbor by means of a new servitude.

In this question the argument was drawn neither from the subject nor from the predicate term, as is customary in those topics that inhere in the terms under investigation. This has been explained with the greatest care in all the examples. But because the argument is taken externally, the judgment of another person is set against the doubt—here, the judgment of Scaevola, whose authority supplied the response. For this reason the argument is said to have been taken from the topic called external.

[Col. 1083A] These topics, then, which have been set out, provide, as it were, the elements by which the indication and demonstration for finding every argument are supplied.

“Is this enough for now, then—for you, so sharp and so occupied?” “I think so. But since I have welcomed a man eager for these banquets of learning, I shall receive him in such a way that there will rather be something left over than allow you to depart unsatisfied.”

Every element is the principle of the thing whose element it is understood to be. For the elements themselves must occupy the place of principles of that which is made from elements. Therefore, since the topics identified above are, as it were, certain principles of arguments—for they contain the arguments, and whatever contains something is the principle of what it contains—Cicero says that these topics appear to be, as it were, certain elements of arguments.

He very cautiously [Col. 1083B] added “as it were, certain elements.” These topics are not elements in the full sense, but are used in producing arguments as something resembling elements. They appear to be certain principles of arguments; otherwise, every element is the smallest part of the thing of which it is an element [Col. 1084A], and what is made from elements joins its parts together, as letters join together to form speech.

A topic, however, is not a part of an argument but the whole of it. It is a certain indication and demonstration supplied for finding an argument, so that, if you attend to the topic, you will know where the argument is hidden and from what source it ought to be drawn.

The remaining remarks are addressed very succinctly to Trebatius. The author flatters him by suggesting that brevity may suffice for his intelligence, especially since he is occupied with legal matters and has no time to read more.

But since, as he says, he has welcomed a man extremely eager for study to these banquets of learning, he does not wish to leave him merely having tasted them, but satisfied, so that nothing will be lacking and something will even remain from a full meal. Thus a delightful transfer has been made from dining to intellectual instruction.

Having explained all the topics and carefully set out their examples [Col. 1084B], I shall discuss a few matters concerning their force and order. When these have been fully treated, I shall proceed to explain what remains. But this must be done in the third book, since the second book has its own proper limits.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1083]

[Col. 1083B] Before I undertake Marcus Tullius’ fuller division concerning the topics listed above, I think that, as I promised, a few points must be discussed concerning the force and order of the topics, so that, once their nature has been more carefully understood, a more abundant supply of arguments may present itself.

First, then, since all the topics have been divided into those that adhere to the matter itself about which the question is asked and those that are assumed from outside, we must see which topics are those that adhere to the matter itself about which the question is asked, and how they differ from the things themselves in which they are said to adhere. The former point has been explained most clearly: it was shown in the preceding discussion that the terms themselves involved in the question are spoken of, one being the predicate and the other the subject.

What, then, is the difference between a topic and the whole, when the topic is taken from the term under discussion? For the very thing that is the whole is identical with being the whole; indeed, for any term proposed in the question, being that term is nothing other than being the whole of the same term that has been established in the question. We say the same also of the parts. For if all the parts constitute that of which they are parts, and the parts of the term proposed in the question constitute that term, there is no doubt that all the parts taken together, insofar as they coincide, should rightly be understood as being the same as the thing itself that has been proposed in the question.

A notation likewise is, in the same way, the very thing that is proposed in the question. For every word designates and marks out the single thing in question. Thus the whole, the parts, and the mark appear to be the same as the very thing about which the question is asked.

Amid such great similarity among these things, a distinction must therefore be supplied. For, as has been said, if a topic adheres to the very thing about which the question is asked, and yet cannot be taken from that very thing about which the question is asked, it cannot follow that the topic can be identical with the very thing about which the question is asked.

The distinction is this: the very thing is understood confusedly and singly, as in the case of “human being”; in it there is contained its whole, which is its definition. The whole, therefore, is separated from the thing itself in our understanding: the thing itself is understood singly, whereas the whole is displayed through an enumeration of genera and differences. For definition divides and distributes, and lays open the whole that was understood singly in the thing itself. The same account applies to the parts. For if you refer the understanding of a single term to a multiplicity of members or to an enumeration of all the species, you immediately grasp the distinction between the thing itself and its parts.

A mark, too, is easily distinguished from that of which it is the mark, because the one is a word and a signification, while the other is the thing subjected to the signification. The differences between things that are related are likewise not doubtful in comparison with those to which they are shown to be related. Who would say that “conjugate” is the same as the thing to which it is conjugate? Who would say that “justly” is the same as justice? Who would say that genus is the same as form, or that contraries or similars are the same as the things of which they are contraries or similars? For neither can a contrary be contrary to itself, nor a similar similar to itself, nor can a genus be a genus of itself. The same reasoning applies to the rest.

Now we must state why we have prefaced these remarks. Whenever arguments are taken from those three topics that were posited first—that is, from the whole, from the parts, and from the mark—the term itself concerning which the argument is sought is contained within whichever of those things the topics are shown to be when they have been drawn into the argument.

For example, when an argument is made from the whole, the term itself to which credibility is being given is included within the whole. The whole itself, which is the definition, is a thing, provided that we agree to call an expression a thing. But when an argument is taken from it, it becomes a topic. Thus the very matter under discussion is enclosed within the whole; and when an argument is made from that whole, the whole itself becomes the topic. Since the whole encloses the term involved in the question, it appears to adhere to that term. Consequently, the topic that is from the whole also adheres to the same term about which the question is asked.

The enumeration of the parts likewise encloses the same term, which it joins together through the collection of its parts. The enumeration of the parts itself is also a thing, if an expression is to be counted among things. But when an argument is drawn from it, it becomes a topic. Since the multitude of parts is in the same term, which the coming together of the parts joins, the topic that is from the conjunction of the parts must also adhere to that same term about which the question is asked.

A mark, too, designates a thing and in some way comprehends it through its signification. If an argument is drawn from the mark, it becomes a topic. And since every name appears to belong to the thing whose understanding it signifies, the topic that is from notation also adheres to the matter about which the inquiry is concerned.

But this is not the case with the related attributes, which have been divided into thirteen parts. Since they in some way face toward the term and are, as it were, established externally, they do not appear to be joined to the term in the same way as are the topics said to be from the whole, from the enumeration of the parts, and from the mark. Nevertheless, that which is related is said in relation to something. That “something” is always joined to the thing toward which the relation is directed, and the one can never exist without the other, because it arises together with it, and in a certain way, when one is spoken, the other is understood.

For if you consider the matter about which the question is asked and its related attributes, and regard the things said to be related as placed outside the matter about which the doubt exists, nothing that is relative can exist from itself; it always exists from another. As is shown in the Categories, all things that are said relatively are opposed to one another, but they are not so separated that they are completely divided. Since they are joined by relative predication, they must in some way be in that to which they appear to be related.

For everything related receives its form from that to which it is related and cannot exist without it. When one is spoken, the understanding immediately submits itself to the other, as when I say “half,” “double” is understood, and when I name “father,” “son” comes into the understanding. All things that are relative depend upon one another and do not abandon one another.

Every related thing, therefore, both looks toward that to which it is referred and is in it. It looks toward it because it is referred to its correlate as to something in the manner of relative predication; and it is in it because the nature of related things is such that one exists from the other and they possess one another, since what is called a related attribute belongs to the term to which it is considered related, and the term proposed in the question is understood to be connected with its related attribute.

Accordingly, when an argument is taken from conjugates, since the conjugate is related to that which on the other side is conjugate to it, the matter about which the question is asked adheres to the conjugate placed on the opposite side. The topic from which the argument is drawn, however, is taken from the other conjugate. Thus, if “common-pasture land” (*compascuus ager*) exists, there is a right to pasture in common (*jus compascere*). “To pasture in common” and “common-pasture land” are therefore conjugates. But the question was whether there was a right to pasture in common; the argument was drawn from “common-pasture land.” Thus the term about which the question was asked is found in the other conjugate, namely, in “pasturing in common,” while the topic from which the argument was drawn is in the other, namely, in “common-pasture land.”

Likewise, whenever an argument is drawn from a genus, the matter about which the question is asked must adhere to the species, as when it is shown that coined money has been bequeathed because all silver has been bequeathed. The question concerns coined money, which is a species of silver, and the argument has been drawn from silver, that is, from the genus. Thus the matter about which the question was asked was in the species, while the argument was drawn from the related attribute, that is, from the genus.

If, however, an argument is made from a species to a genus, the arrangement is reversed: the matter about which the question is asked is shown to be in the genus, while the thing from which the argument is taken is found to be in the species. For when the question is whether silver was bequeathed to the wife, it is shown that it was not bequeathed because it was not bequeathed to the wife merely, but to the wife as *materfamilias*. “Wife” is the genus of “wife as *materfamilias*.” The question, therefore, concerns the wife, that is, the genus. The argument has been made from *materfamilias*, that is, from the species.

Whenever an argument is drawn from similarity, since what is similar is understood to be similar not to itself but to another, the thing about which the question is asked is placed in one of the similar things, while the topic is in the other.

For example, the question may be whether an heir is obliged to restore a defect or collapse of buildings left in usufruct. The question concerns this matter; the topic, however, is from similarity, because an heir ought not to restore a building any more than a slave, if the latter should perish for some reason. Since the usufruct of a building and that of a slave are similar, the matter about which the question is asked is placed in the usufruct of the building, while the topic is in the usufruct of the slave.

The same applies to difference. Of the things that differ, the matter about which the question is asked is placed in one, while in the other is that from which the doubtful matter is established. Thus the question may be whether the silver owed in accounts has also been bequeathed. Here lies the matter in doubt. The topic, however, is in that which differs from it, from which it is shown that the silver owed in accounts was not bequeathed, because it makes a great difference whether the silver has not been placed in a chest or has been entered in accounts.

The same applies to contrariety, as in the question whether a store of provisions has been bequeathed in usufruct. The question concerns usufruct, but it is proved that it was not bequeathed because there can be no use of things that perish through use, but rather abuse. The topic, therefore, is in abuse, one of the two contraries, while the question was in use.

The topic from adjuncts is likewise separated from the matter about which the question is asked in the same way: the question is in one adjunct, while the topic is in the other. Thus the question may be whether possession is granted according to the will of a woman who has never undergone a reduction in civil status. The question is whether it is granted; the topic is in its adjunct. For it is shown that possession ought not to be granted because it would be close to granting possession of goods according to the wills of children and slaves as well.

The topic from antecedents is arranged so that the question is in the consequents. Thus, when the question is whether something ought to remain from the dowry for the children, the argument is taken from the antecedent that it ought in no way to remain: the divorce was brought about through the husband’s fault. The topic, therefore, is in the antecedent, while the question is in the consequent. It follows that nothing remains with the father for the children when the divorce has occurred through the husband’s fault.

If an argument is drawn from consequents, the matter that is doubtful is found in the antecedents. For example, the question may be whether, after a divorce, something ought to remain from the dowry for the children when the woman had been married to a man with whom there was no right of intermarriage.

The argument proceeds as follows: if anything ought to remain from the dowry for the children, it would be because the children followed their father, provided that the woman had been married to a man with whom there was a right of intermarriage. Here the antecedent is “if anything ought to remain from the dowry for the children,” and in it lies the question whether anything ought to remain. The consequent is “the woman was married to a man with whom there was a right of intermarriage,” and from this the argument is taken, that is, from the consequent.

For since it is clear that she was not married to a man with whom there was a right of intermarriage, it is shown that the children do not follow their father and therefore that nothing ought to remain for the children. Here, then, the matter in doubt is in the antecedent—namely, whether anything ought to remain from the dowry for the children—while the argument is in the topic that is in the consequents, namely, in the woman who is married to a man with whom there were no rights of intermarriage.

Whenever arguments are taken from things that conflict, the doubtful matter is in one of the conflicting things, while the topic of the argument is in the opposing one. Thus the question may be whether a woman can, against her will, return a bequest that she rightly received once under a will. The topic is from the conflicting circumstance: she cannot, against her will, return what she rightly received. The question, therefore, lies in what is understood as “returning against her will,” while the argument is in the other conflicting circumstance, namely, in what is understood as “rightly receiving.” “Returning against her will” conflicts with “rightly receiving,” but the question is in one of them and the topic in the other.

Whenever an argument is drawn from efficient causes, the question must be in the effects. For example, the question may be whether a person who has given security against damage must be compelled to answer for a defect in a wall. The question is in the defect of the wall, but the argument is drawn from the cause. It is said that he ought not to answer for it because the nature of the wall was the cause of the defect, not the person who had given security against liability for the defect.

The effect of the cause, therefore, was the defect in the wall. Thus the question is considered to be in the effect, while the topic is from the cause.

But if something is established from effects, the topic is in the effect, while the question is situated in the cause. For example, the question may be whether a certain woman, whose property had become her husband’s, had come under her husband’s *manus* by way of dowry.

Since, then, the husband’s acquisition of the woman’s property after her death is accomplished by her entering into *manus*, the argument is drawn from the effects. For by entering into *manus* it is effected that whatever belongs to the woman becomes the husband’s as dowry. Therefore, when the husband acquires as dowry what formerly belonged to the woman, it is necessary that the woman should have entered into her husband’s *manus*.

The question, therefore, concerns the woman: whether she entered into her husband’s *manus*. The argument, however, is from the effect of the cause, that is, from the entry into *manus*. The effect is that the husband acquires as dowry what formerly belonged to the woman. Thus what is in question is in the cause, while the topic is in the effects.

If the argument is from the comparison of greater things, the question will be in the lesser things. For example, if the question is whether water ought to be restrained in the city, and the answer is defended that it ought not, since even boundaries are not governed, the question is in the lesser matter, the restraint of water, while the topic is in the greater matter, the governing of boundaries.

Conversely, if the argument is drawn from the lesser, the matter in doubt will be in the greater. Thus, if it is doubted whether boundaries are governed in the state, we answer that they are not, since not even water is restrained. The matter in doubt therefore lies in the greater matter, while that from which the argument is taken lies in the lesser.

The same reasoning applies to the comparison of equals. The question lies in one of the equal things, while the topic of the argument is understood to be in the other. Thus the question may be whether the usufruct of buildings is acquired by two years’ use; we establish that it is, because the same is true of estates. Since an estate and a building are equal in this respect, the question concerns the building, while the argument is drawn from the estate.

This is enough to have said concerning the force of the topics, and concerning how the questions and the topics of the arguments are separated from one another. I shall now recall their order as briefly as possible.

From this arises the whole method of judging which topic should be considered prior and which posterior, if we consider the terms involved in the proposed question. For whatever is closer to those terms is most properly counted as prior; whatever has receded farthest from the terms proposed is posterior.

This will become clear in the following manner. First, the plurality of topics is divided into those that are in the matter itself under discussion and those that are assumed from outside. In this division, we understand the topics that are in the matter itself to have been placed before those drawn from outside.

The topic that is in the matter itself is divided into four primary parts. The first is definition, which is called the topic from the whole. The topic from the whole is placed first because nothing is so close to anything as its proper definition.

Next comes the enumeration of the parts, because after definition the parts should hold the nearest place: they join together the whole of which they are said to be parts.

The mark is added after these. It is, as it were, a definition in reversed form. Just as definition explains what the mark designates implicitly, so the mark envelops and indicates confusedly what definition lays open and explains.

The mark is third because definition holds the substance; the enumeration of the parts counts those things that join together the composite whole; but the mark accomplishes nothing—it merely designates.

After these topics, which adhere principally to the terms themselves, the related attributes are counted. These are no longer contained in the terms themselves, but follow them as though placed externally. They are said to be in the terms only because they cannot exist without those of which they are primarily the conjugates.

Among related attributes nothing is so close as that which participates both in the thing and in the name, except that it is separated by a slight inflection of the name. For that which is just participates both in justice and is named by an inflected form of the name “justice.” The same applies to the other conjugates.

After these, genus is counted. Genus is that which displays the substance of anything universally and is the substantial likeness of many things differing in species. It is farther removed from the proposed terms than conjugates are, because although it displays the substance, it is not joined to the name of the term even by an inflected word, but by one that is altogether different and widely distinct.

Species is joined to genus. Tullius called species “form,” because nothing is so close to genus as species. Species is the substantial likeness of individuals and that which is placed under a genus.

After species, similarity is established. For after that which is understood in substances, what is rightly placed next is that which is perceived to exist in quality.

Gradually the matter begins to recede from similarity. It does not immediately arrive at contrariety, but first establishes the topic from difference. Once similarity has been removed, nothing appears first except difference.

After this, the topic is drawn from contrariety, that is, from the greatest difference. The order then turns again toward the related attributes that are akin to it. But they are not akin in the way that similars are: adjuncts are proposed, which do not possess complete similarity, but are connected with one another by judgment and by a kind of proximity among things that cohere with one another.

After adjuncts, Tullius placed antecedents. After something that is joined in some way, it is necessary that something be understood either as antecedent or consequent. The antecedent was therefore placed first, and the consequent afterward.

After these he spoke of things that conflict, so that a kind of double order of contrarieties and similarities might arise. First he proposed similarity, difference, and contrariety; this entire order belongs to similars and contraries. Then, again, there are adjuncts, antecedents, consequents, and conflicts. Here a second order of similars and contraries is detected.

The first order, however, is much more evident than the second. To be similar is more than to be adjunct; to differ is more than to precede or follow; and to be contrary is more than to conflict.

Each item also retains its full form within its own order. Similarity, for example, ought to possess a certain proximity: what is similar is closer to that to which it is considered similar than what is adjunct is to that with which it is joined by natural proximity.

Again, since difference is the source of similarity, what differs from something is more dissimilar to it than what follows or precedes it.

Again, since a contrary ought to withdraw as far as possible from that to which it is contrary, a contrary withdraws farther than something that merely conflicts.

After these, what else could remain except to seek the causes of effects? And after the causes of effects, what else except to investigate the effects of the causes themselves?

Moreover, the topics from comparison hold the final order, because whether they possess similarity or dissimilarity, they possess it only in quantity.

Enough has now been said about the order of the topics. I think, however, that this further point should be considered: whether those topics of arguments that adhere to the matter itself about which the question is asked ought also rightly to be counted among the related attributes.

Related attributes are called related because they are relative to something and are joined by their relation to the proposed terms. A definition, too, is always the definition of something; the whole is the whole of parts; and a mark is the mark of what is signified.

But we must examine the nature of each individually and see whether these are related to something in the same way as the others. Definition in a certain manner explains and shapes the thing it defines. The parts, too, complete the thing of which they are parts through their proper conjunction. A mark, however, holds its understanding in common.

Since these do not behave as the other things called related attributes do, they are rightly not placed among the related attributes. Rather, they are said to be in the very thing that they, as it were, complete and shape.

But since enough has been said concerning the force and order of the topics, let us now proceed to what follows.

Above all that has been said, this point must especially be noted: not everything that is taken into an argument should be called the topic of that argument, unless it is not only contained in the argument but also gives rise to the argument.

What I mean will become clear from a simpler example. Suppose an argument contains genus or species. It is not immediately said that the argument has been drawn from genus or species unless the force of the genus or species supplies strength to the argument.

Let the question be whether being an animal is the same as living, and let the argument proceed as follows: “Being an animal is not the same as living, because even being inanimate is not the same as dying; for there are many inanimate things, and they do not die. For it is clear that things that have never lived cannot die.”

Here “inanimate” is the genus of stones and cast metals, and it has been taken into the argument. But the argument has not been made from genus, although genus appears to be included in it; rather, it has been made from contrariety. Life and death are contraries, and animal and inanimate are contraries; but being inanimate does not entail dying. Therefore being an animal does not entail living.

The topic is not to be taken from genus here, but rather from contrariety, even though genus contains an argument of this kind. The topic would be from genus if the reasoning of the argument were drawn from the genus of animal or from the genus of living, as in the following argument: “Being an animal is being a substance; but living is not a substance; rather, it comes into a substance. Therefore living is not the same as being an animal.” The argument has thus been drawn from substance, that is, from the genus of animal.

This argument, therefore, both contains genus and has been drawn from genus; in the earlier argument, however, although it contains genus, it is nevertheless understood to have been drawn from contrariety.

The point that must always be examined is not what is in the argument, but from what the argument is drawn. The same reasoning must be maintained in the other cases as well, and there is no need to linger over each individually. Anyone who has applied careful attention to the exposition given above will easily gather the same conclusion in the remaining cases from the single example by which it has been explained.

Since each of the topics I have explained has certain members of its own, let us pursue them as precisely as possible, and let us speak first about definition itself.

Definition is an expression that explains what the thing defined is.

Having briefly set out the topics of arguments, he now establishes and divides them more subtly and distinctly according to their parts and appropriate members. For the nature of all the topics will be considered more carefully if they are known not only in a confused manner but also distributively, according to the properties of their parts.

This provides a great abundance for discovering arguments. To speak of definition: if someone recognizes all the parts of definitions, he will be able to seek arguments for himself from all of them, and he will be more abundant in discovering arguments than someone who does not know how many kinds of definition there are. For he will produce as many arguments from the parts of definitions as he has recognized those parts to be.

The person who is not unaware of the diversity of definitions will possess the greatest capacity for topics of this kind.

For this reason Marcus Tullius now divides, with more careful method, the topics that he previously set out confusedly and without arrangement.

First, however, we must examine with especially attentive consideration the point that, as has been said, the topics themselves are also things, but are understood to be topics only when an argument is drawn from them. Thus Cicero is not now dividing topics principally, but the things themselves, which, when drawn into an argument, assume the character of topics.

Definition, a part, and a mark are each things, but when an argument is drawn from them, they become topics. Since Marcus Tullius divides the things themselves according to their natural constitution, he simultaneously divides the topics along with the things.

If there is one thing from which an argument can be drawn, there is also one topic; but if that thing is divided, however many parts there are of that thing, there will also be that many topics of the same kind from which arguments arise.

Since this is so, and since the first of all the topics is the topic from the whole, that is, from definition, he first declares what definition is by means of a definition, so that, once the nature of the thing has been revealed, he may divide its species or members in an appropriate order.

“Definition,” he says, “is an expression that explains what the thing defined is,” as in the definition of a human being: “a rational, mortal animal.”

The statement is expressed with great care. For what a name announces confusedly, definition spreads out through certain substantial members. What is declared confusedly by the name “human being,” definition opens and explains by saying that a human being is a rational and mortal animal.

For if he had not said this, the definition could have been common even to a genus, as in the following form: “Definition is that which indicates what the thing it defines is.” Genus also indicates what the thing of which it is predicated is, but it does not explain what it is.

Only definition explains what the thing is, and it accomplishes this through an expression. Genus and the other things that are usually expressed by individual names do not do so.

Definition explains the thing defined not in just any way—not with respect to what it is like or how much it is, nor in any of the other categories—but with respect to what it is: that is, it displays the substance of the thing it defines.

The definition that lays out substance consists of genus and differences. These signify the substance of each individual thing, as was stated where genus, species, difference, property, and accident were discussed.

Every definition, therefore, explains what the thing defined is.

Aristotle determines definition in almost the same way when he says: “Definition is an expression signifying what it is to be.”

Marcus Tullius divides it as follows:

There are two primary kinds of definitions. One concerns things that exist; the other concerns things that are understood. By “things that exist” I mean those that can be seen or touched, such as land, a building, a wall, a drip of rainwater, a slave, livestock, household equipment, provisions, and the like. Some things of this kind must occasionally be defined by us.

By “things that do not exist,” in turn, I mean those that cannot be touched in a demonstrable way, although they can be perceived and understood by the mind, as when one defines usucaption, guardianship, a clan, or agnation. None of these things has anything like a body underlying it; nevertheless, there is a certain configuration marked out and impressed upon the understanding, which I call a conception. This often has to be explained in argumentation by means of a definition.

[Col. 1092B] It is clear that every definition is said in relation to something, for a definition is always the definition of something. Things that are said in relation to something must necessarily derive a certain property from the things to which they are referred.

Consequently, from the things that definition determines, a certain property is transferred into the definitions themselves. But because what is referred to something cannot be identical with that to which it is said to belong, the thing referred to another must also possess its own proper form.

Thus, in definitions, both their own form is present and the form they receive from the things they define must be considered.

Seeing this, Marcus Tullius first divides definitions according to the things defined, proposing two kinds: one concerning things that exist and the other concerning things that are understood. He appears to have taken these differences among definitions from what is displayed in the definition.

For everything that is defined is either corporeal or incorporeal. All things are first divided into these two classes. He calls corporeal things “things that exist,” and incorporeal things “things that do not exist”—not because incorporeal things do not exist at all, since otherwise they would not receive definitions.

For if definition explains what the thing defined is, there can be no explanation of what a thing is if that thing does not exist in any way whatsoever.

But because the human race lives through the senses, it considers most especially to exist what is subjected to the apprehension of the senses. Who would not seem to know a stone or a human being more readily than justice, inheritance, or anything else apprehended not by the senses but by the understanding?

Thus, because of the evident character of cognition, things subjected to the senses appear more truly to exist, while things grasped by the reasoning of the understanding appear least to exist.

It must be understood, however, that Marcus Tullius was speaking according to human opinion, not according to truth. For, as is agreed among the best philosophers, those things exist most truly that are farthest removed from the senses, while those exist less truly that supply opinions to the senses.

Hence Cicero himself, in Plato’s *Timaeus*, says: “What is that which always is and has no origin, and what is that which comes to be and never is?” The former is comprehended by the reasoning of the understanding; the latter produces opinion in the sense deprived of reason.

Here, therefore, he assigned that which always is to reason, while he joined that which never truly is to the senses.

But, as has been said, when he speaks of corporeal things as existing and incorporeal things as not existing, he is speaking not according to truth but according to the common opinion of ordinary people.

He therefore gives as examples of things that exist certain forms of corporeal things, such as land, buildings, walls, a drip of rainwater, and things of that kind. He shows that these are corporeal because they can be seen and touched.

As examples of things that do not exist, he gives usucaption, guardianship, a clan, and the rest—things that are incorporeal. He shows that they are incorporeal by saying that they cannot be touched demonstratively but can be comprehended by the understanding and the mind.

Why he said that these things do not exist, he explains by adding that none of them has anything like a body or any mass that strikes the senses.

For what body could usucaption possess? The things that are acquired by usucaption are corporeal, but usucaption itself is not corporeal. The firmness of possession produced by the practice of use—what body could it have?

Likewise, the thing governed by guardianship is corporeal, for it is a human being. But the care of guardianship itself, and the right of protecting another, cannot possess anything corporeal at all.

The people who belong to the same clan are also corporeal. But the clan itself—that is, the association of free people sharing a common name, such as the Scipios, Valerii, and Bruti—is certainly incorporeal.

It is, however, a certain incorporeal conception of the mind and understanding of these things, which he called a conception. For the imagination of usucaption or guardianship, and the understanding of an incorporeal thing, is called the conception of that thing, which the Greeks call **ἔννοιαν** (*ennoian*, “conception”).

He therefore divided definition into these two parts according to differences in the subject: some definitions, he said, concern things that exist, that is, corporeal things; others concern things that do not exist, that is, incorporeal things.

Here a question may be raised, which I also mentioned briefly above: how is definition not counted among the related attributes, when every definition appears to be relative to something?

Similarity, contrariety, and the rest are called related attributes precisely because they are always referred to something. If definition too is referred to something and is not an absolute and proper object of consideration, it too ought to be placed among the related attributes.

The answer is that related attributes are like shadows of a body: being placed outside it, they cannot leave the thing to which they are shown to be related. They either do not signify its substance at all, as in the case of contraries, similars, and the rest; or, when they do signify it, only some one part of its substance is understood, as in the case of genus, species, and difference.

Genus is not the whole substance of a species, since genus alone does not form the species; differences do so as well. Nor do differences contain the whole form of the substance, since difference alone does not complete the species; genus does so as well.

Species itself is a certain part of genus. Definition, however, although it is relative to something, displays the whole substance, is made equal to the thing it defines, and completes its substance. It is therefore neither placed outside it, as similarity and contrariety are, nor a part of the substance that it determines by definition; rather, it is that very substance itself.

Enough has been said about this matter.

The same may be said of parts. For joined parts produce the whole of which they are parts.

A mark also signifies the whole of what it designates. All these things are equalized: the defined thing with the definition, the parts with the whole, and the mark with the thing it declares by its signification—provided that the mark is not equivocal and that the thing designated is not multivocal.

A legitimate question may be raised, however, as to why, after saying that there are two kinds of definitions, he did not divide the definitions themselves, but instead divided the things defined, namely, corporeal and incorporeal things.

The reason appears to be that definition, since it is relative to something, as has been said, receives a certain quality from the things whose substance it determines.

Moreover, some definitions are definitions by partition, others by division. A definition by partition occurs when the matter proposed [Col. 1094B] is, as it were, torn apart into its members. For example, if someone says that civil law is that which consists in laws, decrees of the senate, judicial decisions, the authority of jurists, edicts of magistrates, custom, and equity. A definition by division, on the other hand, encompasses all the forms that fall under the genus being defined, as follows: Alienation is, in the case of a thing subject to mancipation, either its transfer to another by the formal act of *nexum*, or its cession before the court, among those between whom these acts can be performed according to civil law.

Since a definition derives its proper character from the subject matter that it defines, while nevertheless retaining its own proper form, after discussing those differences among definitions that were drawn from the things being defined, he now presents differences derived from the proper form of definitions. The proper form of each composite consists in its parts; accordingly, from the parts of definitions [Col. 1094C] he teaches that some definitions are made by division and others by partition. For a thing is defined either by enumerating all its species or by enumerating its parts. Shortly afterward I shall explain how parts differ from species.

For now, I think Cicero’s examples must be explained. He gives the following example of partition. Suppose that one has proposed to define what civil law is. We shall say: Civil law is that which consists in laws, decrees of the senate, judicial decisions, the authority of jurists, edicts of magistrates, custom, and equity.

A law is therefore what the people have enacted in the comitia of the centuries. Decrees of the senate are what have been decreed by the authority of the senate. Judicial decisions are matters settled by the judgment of judges between those who dispute about some matter, and by the example of which other cases too are judged. [Col. 1094D] The authority of jurists is the approved and trusted opinions of those who, from the Twelve Tables or from the edicts of magistrates, interpreted civil law and whose judgments were approved by the judgments of citizens and trusted opinions. The edicts of magistrates are the rules pronounced by the urban or foreign praetors, or by the curule aediles. Custom is what is habitually done in the state. Equity is what natural reason has persuaded us to accept.

All these things therefore produce one form of law, like its parts—just as a human being is composed of a head, arms, chest, belly, legs, and feet. For partition is, as he himself says, that which tears each proposed thing apart, as it were, into its members.

He demonstrates the other part of definition, which is made through the division of species, by the following example. He defines what the alienation of a thing [Col. 1095A] subject to mancipation is, saying: Alienation is, in the case of a thing subject to mancipation, either its transfer to another by the formal act of *nexum*, or its cession before the court, among those between whom these acts can be performed according to civil law.

For under civil law an act can be performed among no others than Roman citizens, whose law is also civil law, contained in the Twelve Tables. All things that can be alienated—that is, that can pass from our ownership into that of another—are either subject to mancipation or not subject to mancipation.

The ancients called things subject to mancipation those that were alienated in such a way that the alienation took place through a certain solemn form of *nexum*. *Nexum* is a certain legal solemnity, performed in the manner explained by Gaius in his *Institutes*. In the first book of Gaius’s *Institutes*, concerning the performance of *nexum*, these are the words:

“Mancipation, as [Col. 1095B] we also indicated above, is a certain imaginary sale, an institution belonging specifically to Roman citizens. It is conducted as follows: no fewer than five Roman citizens of full age are summoned as witnesses, and in addition another person of the same status who holds a bronze scale; he is called the *libripens*, or scale-holder. The person who receives the object in mancipation, holding the bronze, says: ‘I declare that this man is mine according to the law of the Quirites, and that he has been purchased by me with this bronze and bronze scale.’ Then he strikes the scale with the bronze and gives the bronze to the person from whom he receives the object in mancipation, as if in place of the price.”

Therefore, whatever things could not be alienated under the law of the Twelve Tables except through this solemn form were subject to mancipation. The remaining things of independent legal status were called *res nec mancipi*, or things not subject to mancipation; things subject to mancipation could also be ceded before the court.

Such cession was performed in the manner explained by the same Gaius in his second [Col. 1095C] commentary:

“Cession before the court is performed in this way. Before a magistrate of the Roman people, or before a praetor, or before the governor of a province, the person to whom the thing is being ceded before the court, holding the thing, claims it as follows: ‘I declare that this man is mine according to the law of the Quirites.’ Then, after he has made this claim, the praetor asks the person who is making the cession whether he makes a counterclaim. When that person denies it or remains silent, the praetor awards the thing to the person who made the claim; and this was called an action at law.”

Things subject to mancipation were therefore alienated either through *nexum*, as has been said, or through cession before the court. That these solemnities are matters of law is shown by Gaius’s preceding words.

But if a thing subject to mancipation is [Col. 1095D] handed over without the intervention of any solemn form, it cannot be alienated unless it is acquired by usucaption by the person to whom it was handed over. Since this is so, alienation of a thing subject to mancipation has rightly been defined according to division, namely as something completed either by transfer through *nexum* or by cession before the court. For by simple delivery the alienation of a thing subject to mancipation is not accomplished.

That these are species and not parts is understood from the following consideration. If someone alienates a thing subject to mancipation through *nexum*, he transfers into another’s power, with full legal title, what had been his own. If he also cedes it before the court, the full right of alienation was present. Whenever the parts take on the full name of the thing that they divide, the thing divided is the genus and the parts are species; even someone with only a little dialectical training understands this.

Since this is so, Cicero divided definition into two parts: one made by an enumeration of parts [Col. 1096A], the other by a division of parts. Yet both definitions enumerate parts. The difference is that the former partitions members, whereas the latter partitions species.

Here a very difficult question arises. For if definition is also partition, it may seem surprising how one topic can be “from definition” and another “from the enumeration of parts.” This produces considerable confusion. Earlier, in his enumeration of topics, he proposed one topic from definition and another from the enumeration of parts; now, however, he confirms that the enumeration or division of parts is a species of definition. There is no doubt, therefore, that since the enumeration of parts is the same as definition (for species is the same as genus), the topic from definition is the same as the topic from the enumeration of parts.

The solution to this very difficult [Col. 1096B] question becomes easier if we gather together the forms and distinctions of definitions themselves. Definition can be made in many ways. Among these there is one true and complete mode of definition, which is also called substantial; the others are called definitions only by abuse of the term. I shall give a complete division of all of them a little later.

For now I shall explain the matter generally as follows: [Note: [Col. 1095D] The words “for since” appear to be redundant.] Every definition explains what the thing being defined is. Explanation, however, is made in two ways: first, when something clearer is offered in place of a thing that is scarcely known; second, when a kind of enumeration of parts is made.

I shall discuss the former mode later. For now, regarding the enumeration of parts, we must say that every definition made through an enumeration of parts is rightly understood as a kind of partition. It has been said that what is signified confusedly by a name is opened up and explained in a definition made through an enumeration of parts. This cannot happen except through the naming of certain parts; for when something is explained in speech, the whole cannot be stated all at once.

Since this is so, and since every definition of this kind is a certain [Col. 1096C] distribution of parts, it can be made in four ways. Either substantial parts are explained, or parts of a property are stated, or members of a whole are enumerated, or species are divided as if they were parts.

Substantial parts are explained when a definition is constituted from a genus and differences. For a genus that is predicated of a species in the singular is the whole of that species. When that genus is taken into a definition, it becomes a certain part. It does not complete the species by itself [Col. 1096D] unless differences are also added, and the same account applies to the differences as to the genus. For when those differences, stated individually, encompass the whole species, once taken into the definition they become parts of the species, because they signify not only the species but also the genus.

An example is: “A human being is a rational, mortal animal.” Since the whole definition is equal to the human being, and since both “animal,” “rational,” and “mortal” are parts of the whole definition, each of these seems to be a part of the human being itself, insofar as each is a part of that definition. This, then, is called definition in the proper sense.

There is also the definition in which accidents are gathered into one and something single is produced from them [Col. 1097A]. This is a kind of enumeration of parts, not situated in substance but in a certain collection of accidents. An example is: “An animal is that which can move by its own will.” Movement, will, and capacity are all accidents of an animal; joined together, however, they complete the definition of animal—not by constituting it substantially, but by indicating through certain accidents what an animal is. They are, as it were, certain parts of the animal. This is called description.

But if we speak not of the accidents of a thing but of certain members, as it were, out of which it is composed and joined together, and attempt to make a definition from them, we say: “A house is that which consists of a foundation, walls, and roof.” Here certain members have been taken into the definition, by which the whole thing is joined together. This is called a definition by an enumeration [Col. 1097B] of parts.

If, however, someone defines a thing by placing in the definition not members but species, the definition is called a definition by division of species. Thus someone might say: “An animal is a substance that is sustained either by sensation alone or by sensation and reason.”

It is therefore clear that these four types differ from one another. In the definition made through substantial parts, the individual parts seem to be greater than, and substantially more universal than, the thing defined; thus “animal” is greater than “human being.” “Mortal” and “rational” likewise each exceed the nature of a human being, but when they are brought together they are equal to the thing of which they are individually greater.

The accidents placed in a definition, however, are entirely separate from the nature of substance. In the definition made through an enumeration of parts [Col. 1097C], the items enumerated are such that no single one of them can bear the name of the whole defined thing; for that reason they are smaller than it. Thus foundations cannot be called “a house,” since foundations are smaller than a house, and the same applies to the other parts.

In the definition made through division, by contrast, each individual part is indeed smaller than the whole thing defined, yet each receives the name of the thing defined. Thus both “rational” and “irrational” can bear the name “animal.”

Once these distinctions have been established, whenever an argument is drawn from the definition made through substantial parts, or from that gathered through an enumeration of accidents, it is said to be an argument drawn from definition—that is, from the whole. Whenever an argument is drawn from the definition made either through an enumeration of members [Col. 1097D] or through a division of species, it is said to be an argument drawn from the enumeration of parts.

But since Marcus Tullius had already begun discussing the partition of definition, he also inserted this latter type, although it belonged not to definition but to the topic of the enumeration of parts. The evidence for this is that later, when treating these same topics at greater length and speaking about the enumeration of parts, he posited no other enumeration of parts than the one that he now called a species of definition.

Nevertheless, one must not suppose that every partition can serve as the topic of definition. For example, if someone says, “A house is foundations, walls, and a roof,” this is not necessarily a definition. There may be a portico intended for public [Col. 1098A] use; there may likewise be something else, such as a theater, which is usually covered in order to produce louder sounds.

What we must understand for the present is that something can often be defined by partition when that collection of parts can produce only one thing. If nothing other than a house could have foundations, walls, and a roof, then the definition would rightly be made: a house is that which is formed by foundations, walls, and a roof.

There are also other kinds of definitions, but they do not pertain to the purpose of this book. It is enough to explain what the mode of definition is.

Victorinus undertook to explain this topic in the continuous treatment of a single volume and to enumerate all the differences among definitions. He inserts many things that [Col. 1098B] almost everyone denies to be definitions. Among definitions he places names as well, although this does not seem acceptable in any branch of learning to Aristotle, who was exceptionally expert in every kind of doctrine. In the *Topics* he emphatically denies that a definition can be made by a name. For example, if someone asks, “What is ‘to be silent’?” and the answer is, “To keep quiet,” these should in no way be regarded as definitions.

This can also be established from Marcus Tullius’s own definition, by which he shows what definition is. He says that a definition is an utterance that explains what the thing being defined is. But since a name is not an utterance, it is clear that a definition cannot be constituted by a name—especially since not everything expressed in an utterance and displaying something is designated by the proper name “definition.” Descriptions and every other kind of utterance that is formed not from substantial parts but [Col. 1098C] from parts joined together in some other way are examples; even Victorinus himself does not fail to recognize this.

Victorinus nevertheless seems to have adopted this as the basis of his own discussion: that whatever can in any way display the subject matter may be taken in place of a definition. For this reason he included a name among the number of definitions, because something previously hidden under a less familiar expression is often made clearer by a more familiar word.

For the same reason we said above that explanation takes place in two ways: first, when something clearer is supplied in place of a thing scarcely known; second, when it is made through a certain enumeration of parts. Thus an explanation in which something more familiar is supplied belongs to a name, whereas one made through an enumeration of parts belongs to an utterance—although even in utterances [Col. 1098D] something clearer is always supplied so that the matter under discussion may become better known.

Therefore, so that our exposition may omit nothing, so that the proper nature of definition may be evident, and so that everything may be brought to knowledge—so that the true definition may not remain unknown and what is not properly and truly a definition may nevertheless fall within the scope of understanding—the following distinction among definitions must be made.

Some definitions are definitions properly speaking; others are called definitions in an abusive sense. Proper definitions are those that consist of a genus and differences, as in: “A human being is a rational, mortal animal.” Here “animal” is the genus, while “rational” and “mortal” are the differences.

Among the definitions that are not properly definitions but are called so by abuse of the term, some are designated only by individual names [Col. 1099A], while others are explained and expressed in an utterance.

Among those definitions designated only by a name, some are made *κατ’ ἀντίλεξιν*—that is, “word for word”—when a name is returned for a name. For example, someone may ask, “What is ‘to be silent’?” and the answer is, “To keep quiet”; or, “What is ‘he draws’?” and the answer is, “He strikes.”

Others are given by way of example. Thus, when we wish to indicate what substance is, we may say by way of example, “For instance, a human being.” This is called in Greek *τύπος* (“type” or “example”). It is included among definitions for the reason already stated: it designates in some manner something of what is being designated, and although it is not properly a definition, it nevertheless appears to be a definition in some way.

Among the definitions that consist in an utterance but are not proper definitions, there are many varieties [Col. 1099B]. The common name for all of them is description. Some are made by partition, others by division, as explained above.

Others take substantial differences but do not add the genus. Victorinus calls this *ἐννοηματική* (“conceptual”), as containing a kind of common notion. For example: “A human being is that which flourishes through rational conception and is subject to mortality.” Here the genus has not been stated, but the substantial differences have.

Others are designated through several qualities, though accidental ones, in such a way that each quality, even if not joined to the others, can nevertheless produce what is being demonstrated. Thus: “A human being is wherever piety is found,” or “wherever equity is found,” and again “wherever wickedness and cunning may be found.” Even if no other feature is added [Col. 1099C], it is sufficient to indicate a human being to say “where piety may be present,” or “where justice,” or the other qualities may be found. This is called *ποιῶδες* (“qualitative”).

Others are made by joining several accidents together into one, as when someone wishes to define a luxurious person and says: “A luxurious person is one who pours himself into pleasures through many unnecessary expenditures and gives himself excessively over to lust.” All these features together seem to constitute a luxurious person; individually they do not. This is called *ὑπογραφική* (“descriptive” or “outline-defining”).

Others are made in such a way that differences are proposed to mark a distinction in things joined together at a discrete boundary. Thus, if someone doubts whether Nero was an emperor or a tyrant, one says that he was a tyrant because he was cruel and intemperate. This added difference separates the tyrant from the emperor.

Or [Col. 1099D] if there is doubt concerning the same person, whether he is a tyrant or a king, a joined difference designates both: one may say that temperance or piety belongs to a king, whereas intemperance and cruelty belong to a tyrant. This is called *κατὰ διαφοράν* (“according to difference”).

Another kind is made through metaphor, as in: “Youth is the flower of life.”

A definition is also said to be made from the privation of its contrary, as in: “Good is that which is not evil.”

Victorinus also includes among definitions one that can be applied only to proper names. This is called *ὑποτύπωσις* (“characterization” or “depiction”), as in: “Aeneas is the son of Venus and Anchises.”

Besides these there is also a definition made through the lack of what would complete a thing, as in: “A quarter is that which lacks a three-quarter measure in order to be an *as*.”

Victorinus also places among the differences of definitions [Col. 1100A] one that can be made through a kind of praise, as in: “Law is the mind, spirit, counsel, and judgment of the state.” This is especially unreasonable. The manner of praise does not create a difference in the definition. What must be considered are the things placed in the definition, not the intention with which they were formulated.

If the intention to praise were to be admitted among the differences of definitions, why should not the intention to blame likewise produce another difference of definition? But this is plainly inappropriate and seems contrary to truth.

Definitions are also made [Col. 1100B] through proportion, as when someone says: “A human being is a lesser world.” Just as the world is governed by reason, so too a human being, although joined together from many parts, has reason as its guide in all things; hence he may be called a lesser world.

Definitions are also made from relations, as when someone asks, “What is a father?” and the answer is, “One who has a son.”

Cause too can produce a definition, as when we ask, “What is day?” and the answer is, “The sun above the earth.” For we have inserted the cause—the sun—in place of the thing of which it is the cause, and have thereby indicated a definition of day.

These are the differences among definitions that Victorinus enumerated in the book he published *On Definitions*. Marcus Tullius omits them because he considered them entirely unnecessary. But so that nothing might be lacking from the completeness of the work, we have added what Cicero omitted.

Thus the ancients give the following instruction: when you have taken what is common to the thing you wish to define and to other things, pursue the inquiry until what is proper is produced and can be transferred to no other thing [Col. 1100C]. For example: “Inheritance is money.” This is still common, since there are many kinds of money. Add what follows: “Which comes to someone upon another’s death.” This is not yet a definition, since the money of the dead can be held in many ways without being an inheritance. Add one word: “By law.” Now the thing appears to have been separated from what is common, and the definition is explained as follows: “Inheritance is money that comes to someone upon another’s death by law.”

It is still not enough. Add: “And that has not been received either as a legacy under a will or by retaining possession.” The definition is complete.

Likewise, take the following: “Gentiles are those who share the same name among themselves.” This is not enough. Add: “Who are descended from freeborn ancestors.” That too is not enough. Add: “None of whose ancestors served in slavery.” Something is still lacking: “Who have not suffered a diminution of status.” This may perhaps be enough [Col. 1100D]. For I do not see that the pontiff Scaevola added anything to this definition.

This method applies to both kinds of definitions, whether what exists or what is understood is to be defined.

Having set forth the method of definition and divided it according to its several parts, both in respect of matter and of form—the matter, when he said that definitions concern either things that are corporeal or things that are incorporeal; the form, when he taught that definitions are made either by partitions or by divisions—and having passed over everything else that did not pertain to the work undertaken, he now proceeds to what is most useful and can most fully convey an understanding of the whole definition. This is: what the method of definition is in all things that are done in whatever way.

There is one method of defining, common to all: a definition of the thing is gathered from common features joined and combined into a single property. For everything that is common and universal is reduced by determination if something is added to it; it returns to particularity and is confined within the compass that previously encompassed all things, just as when a difference is added to a genus and a species results. For when a genus, by its own proper compass, contains many species, if one adds to it its proper difference, it is narrowed and returns, in a way, to a certain particularity. Thus, when we say “animal,” this name embraces many things. But if “rational” is added to it and we make “rational animal,” it will be less than the simple term. For “rational animal” is less than “animal” taken simply. Thus the addition of the difference reduces and confines what was greater into a kind of particularity.

Whenever, therefore, some thing is to be defined, what it has in common with many other things is taken; differences are added to this, and at once what had previously been common to many necessarily becomes narrower. If, by the addition of this difference, it has diminished to such an extent that it becomes equal to the thing being defined, it will not be necessary to gather and apply other differences; rather, that very thing which has been reduced so as to be equal to what is being defined must be the definition. But if it still extends beyond the thing being defined, we must seek another difference. When this is added, the number of things included increases, but the force of the common features decreases through the addition of the differences. This must continue until, as has been said, what is taken for the definition is made equal to the thing that is to be defined.

To make this clearer not only by reasoning but also by a fitting example, let the most familiar thing be taken for definition: namely, man. We seek his definition in this way. We take what he has in common with many other things, namely “animal.” We therefore say that man is an animal. This is not yet a definition, first because, as has been said, a definition cannot be rendered by a single name alone; and next because “animal” is greater than “man.” Therefore, so that “animal” may be reduced and made equal to man, we add a difference. By adding it, the number of things increases, but the force and extent of the thing diminish. I therefore add “rational” and produce “rational animal.” Thus “rational animal” is less than animal properly so called.

I say, then, that man is a rational animal. But this is not yet made equal to man, for there may be rational animals that are not human beings, as Plato also holds concerning the heavenly bodies. I therefore add another difference, so that the definition may again be contracted in whatever way and become equal to the man being defined. I add “mortal” and say that man is a rational mortal animal. This is equal to man. For whoever is a man is a rational mortal animal.

I therefore say that this is the definition of man: one formed from several common features joined together, yet producing something proper and equal to man. The same method applies to all other definitions: definitions are formed by collecting common features and joining them into one, since by that joining what is common must be contracted and confined within a narrower compass, and from the joined common features something proper and equal to the thing being defined is composed.

This, then, is what Cicero says the method of definition is: when one has taken those things that are common to the thing one wishes to define and to other things, one must pursue them until what is proper is produced, something that cannot be transferred to any other thing. In these words and in this judgment he seems briefly to signify that a definition is one which, joined from substantial common features and reduced to a narrower compass, becomes equal to the thing being defined.

The examples he gives are of this kind: one concerns the definition of inheritance, the other that of gentile status.

For inheritance, the process is as follows:

> Inheritance is money.

This is common and applicable to many other things that are not inheritances—for example, gifts, thefts, and any other pecuniary things that are not inheritances at all. Something therefore had to be added to this money, namely:

> Which comes to someone upon another’s death.

Inheritance, then, is money that comes to someone upon another’s death. But even this does not fully explain the meaning of inheritance. For it is common: the property of the dead may be held in several ways, for example if someone has been defeated and despoiled in war.

Something must therefore be added:

> Lawfully,

so that the definition is:

> Inheritance is money that comes to someone lawfully upon another’s death.

For inheritances are acquired lawfully. It might perhaps seem that the definition could stop at this point, [Col. 1102C] but it cannot. Why? If money has been left as a legacy, it cannot indeed be called an inheritance, yet it is money acquired lawfully upon another’s death. For if wills are made lawfully, money is also bequeathed lawfully. Something must therefore be added—namely, that by which legacies are separated from inheritances—so that we say that an inheritance is money that comes to someone lawfully upon another’s death and is not a legacy.

Is this sufficient for the definition? Not at all. What if the ownership of a farm, or of some pecuniary property, is mine, but another person has the usufruct? Upon the death of the person to whom the usufruct belongs, that property returns to me, although it had been held lawfully in my ownership and possession of the property-right; nevertheless, it cannot be an inheritance.

Something must therefore be added: it must not have been retained by possession. That is, what comes lawfully and not as a legacy upon another’s death must not be retained by possession of the ownership. This can be retained by possession when the ownership is ours but the usufruct belongs to the deceased.

All the elements, then, joined into one, produce the definition of inheritance in this form:

> Inheritance is money that comes to someone lawfully upon another’s death, neither bequeathed nor retained by possession.

This definition is equal to inheritance. For just as an inheritance is money that comes to someone lawfully upon another’s death, neither bequeathed nor retained by possession, so any money that has come to someone lawfully upon another’s death, provided it was neither bequeathed nor retained by possession, must be an inheritance.

But when Marcus Tullius, in defining, had reached the point at which he said that inheritance is money that comes to someone upon another’s death, he rightly says:

> Now the thing will appear to have been separated from what is common, so that the definition is explained in this form: Inheritance is money that comes to someone lawfully upon another’s death.

This is said as though the definition had already been made complete. For what else is it for a definition to be explained and separated from what is common than for it to be perfect and lacking nothing?

But then, as though the definition were not explained and not separated from what is common, he adds:

> It is not yet sufficient; add: Neither bequeathed by will nor retained by possession.

The reason for this addition is that he made the definition by joining some things and separating others. Thus he separated what he was defining from the commonality of all other things by means both of what he added and of what he separated.

He said that inheritance is money, and added that it comes to someone upon another’s death. He separated it from those monies that come to someone not upon another’s death but through a contract between living persons. He added “lawfully,” so as to separate it from monies that might come to someone by force upon another’s death.

By these two features—death and lawfulness—that money was made distinct from all others, although the lawful mode of acquisition was one that took place not between two living persons but between one living person and another who was dead. This, then, was one separation from other things; and therefore he says that the definition has been explained and separated from what is common.

But since, within that very money which comes to someone upon another’s death and lawfully, there were certain things that were not inheritances, the definition of inheritance became complete by their separation. When he said that inheritance is money, and likewise money that comes to someone upon another’s death, and likewise money that comes lawfully, all these elements that constitute the substance of inheritance were added. But since within this collection there were certain things to which the meaning of the collection could also be transferred, although they were not inheritances—for example, a legacy or retention by possession—once these had been removed, what remained was inheritance: money that can be understood to have come to someone lawfully upon another’s death.

A legacy or retention by possession therefore does not constitute the substance of inheritance; indeed, they would obstruct the demonstration of its substance unless they were removed. Yet neither does the negation of anything complete the substance; it merely shows what the thing is not.

If a legacy and retention by possession do not merely fail to complete the substance of inheritance but actually obstruct and corrupt it unless they are separated and set aside—and if their negation shows nothing belonging to the substance of inheritance but only what it is not—then the superior part remains: money that comes to someone lawfully upon another’s death. This shows the substance of inheritance; it is an explained definition separated from the rest.

But since, again, as has been said, the understanding of this definition could be extended to certain other things, the remaining part is added in order to mark the complete distinction. Thus, because these features demonstrate inheritance and constitute its substance, Cicero says:

> Now the thing appears to have been separated from what is common, so that the definition is explained: Inheritance is money that comes to someone lawfully upon another’s death.

But since this understanding could again apply to several things included within it, it was rightly added:

> It is not sufficient,

and the rest—those words that separate a legacy and retention by possession from the definition of inheritance. So much may be said about the first example, concerning inheritance.

Following its likeness, he treats the second example, which concerns the definition of gentile status. For gentiles are those who have the same name among themselves, such as the Scipios, the Bruti, and others. But what if they are slaves? Can there be any gentile status among slaves? Certainly not. Something must therefore be added:

> Who are descended from freeborn persons.

What if the grandsons of freedmen are called by the same name as Roman citizens? Is there then any gentile status? Not even that, since gentile status is derived from the antiquity of freeborn ancestors. Let this therefore be added:

> None of whose ancestors has served in slavery.

What if someone passes by adoption into another family? Then, even if he is called by the name of the group into which he has migrated, and even if he is descended from freeborn persons and from parents who never served in slavery, nevertheless, since he does not remain in the family of his own group, he cannot remain in its gentile status either. Something must therefore be added:

> And who have not suffered a diminution of civil status.

“This,” he says, “is perhaps sufficient,” according to the definition of the pontiff Scaevola; for he added nothing further. The definition of gentiles is therefore:

> Gentiles are those who have the same name among themselves, are descended from freeborn persons, none of whose ancestors has served in slavery, and among whom gentile status has not been destroyed by any diminution of civil status.

This definition too is made from several common features flowing together into one and producing a single property of the thing being defined, namely gentile status.

This method of definition applies to both kinds of things: both to things that are and to things that are not—that is, to corporeal and incorporeal things. For, as was shown above, Cicero says that what is, is corporeal, while what is not, is incorporeal.

Finally, the method of all definitions is this: some property is formed from several common features.
