Definitions, however, differ from one another because those properly called definitions are joined from substantial common features. Those which are not true definitions but are called definitions by abuse of the term are assembled from accidental common features.

We have shown what the kind of partitions and divisions is; but what difference there is between them must be explained more clearly. In a partition there are, as it were, members—for example, of the body: the head, shoulders, hands, sides, legs, feet, and so forth. In a division there are forms, which the Greeks call εἰδέας [eideās, “forms”]; our people, if any of them happen to treat this subject, call them species. This is not a bad usage, but it is inconvenient because of the changes of case in speech. I would not wish to say, even if the term could be expressed in Latin, *of species* and *to species*, since those cases must often be used; I would prefer *forms* and *of forms*. Since both words signify the same thing, I do not think convenience in speaking should be neglected.

They define genus and form in this way:

> Genus is a conception pertaining to several differences.  
> Form is a conception whose difference can be referred to the head of the genus, as to a source.

By “conception” I mean what the Greeks call both ἔννοια (*ennoia*, “conception”) and πρόληψις (*prolēpsis*, “preconception”). It is an innate and previously apprehended cognition of a given form that requires clarification.

Forms, then, are those into which a genus is divided without omitting anything—for example, if someone divides law into statute, custom, and equity.

Anyone who thinks that forms are the same as parts confuses the art, and, disturbed by a certain resemblance, does not distinguish sharply enough what must be distinguished. Orators and poets also often define by transferring a word from one thing to another on the basis of resemblance, with a certain elegance. But I shall depart from your examples only when necessary.

My colleague and friend Aquilius, then, when shores were under discussion—[the transmitted text is uncertain: “you wish all things to be public”]—used, when those concerned asked what a shore was, to define it as “that against which the waves play.” This is like someone who wished to define youth as the flower of life and old age as the setting of life. By using metaphor, he departed from the proper words belonging to the things themselves.

So much concerning definitions; let us examine what remains.

Since he divided the forms of definitions into partition and division, so that the hearer would not be confused by their resemblance, he discloses the differences between division and partition, and first demonstrates that parts and species are different. For species are often called parts, but parts are never called species. They differ because parts join together the members of a whole, whereas species divide and distribute a genus.

For, as was also said above, the parts of that which they join together do not take the name of the whole. The foundations or roof of a house cannot be called “the house,” for unless all the things that constitute something are joined together, the individual things will not possess the name of the whole. Species, on the other hand, each take the name of the genus, as man takes the name of animal.

From this it follows that another difference can also be recognized: parts are said to be parts of a whole, while species are not species of a whole—namely, of a universal thing—but species of a universal thing, that is, of a genus.

A whole differs from a genus because a genus is universal, whereas a whole is not universal. This is proved as follows. If what is called a whole—for example, a house—were universal, its parts too would take the name of that whole. But they do not, as has often been shown. Therefore what is a whole is not universal.

That a genus is universal is clear, since the forms derived from it take its name.

There is another difference as well. A genus is always prior to its species, whereas a whole is found to be posterior to its parts. For unless the parts have existed, the whole cannot be joined together. Hence, if the genus perishes, its species also perish; but if a species perishes, the genus remains. The same is true in the opposite relation between parts and a whole. If any one part perishes, the whole must perish; but if the whole that the parts had joined together is dispersed, the parts remain distributed. Thus, if a house, its roof, walls, and foundations are understood as separately placed outside one another, the house will not exist because its union has been destroyed, but the parts will remain.

M. Tullius therefore uses proper names: he calls parts the members of a whole, as it were, but species forms. This is because the inflection of the word “species” does not seem sufficiently suitable to him. Although, he says, many have used this word, because its inflection through the cases is harsh—*speciei*, *specierum*, *speciebus*—he did not think that convenience in speaking should be neglected, as he himself says, and therefore called them “forms,” in whose case-forms no harshness is felt.

And since a form cannot exist apart from a genus—for nothing can exist apart from its own principle—he supplied definitions of both, saying that genus is a conception pertaining to several differences.

A conception is a certain understanding and simple formation of the mind that pertains to several things differing from one another. That this is genus is clear from the most obvious example. The conception of animal pertains to several differences: to rational and irrational, to mortal and immortal, to walking, crawling, flying, and swimming. It is the genus of all things that fall under these differences.

This definition signifies the same thing as the older definition, which is as follows:

> Genus is what is predicated of several things differing in species, in answer to the question “what is it?”, as animal.

Animal is a genus predicated of several things differing in species—that is, of man and horse—in answer to the question “what is man?” or “what is horse?” The answer is “animal.”

He gave the following definition of form:

> Form is a conception whose difference can be referred to the head of the genus, as to a source.

And rightly so. For if forms are derived from a genus, species must be referred to the genus. If the genus is a kind of principle and source of form, the understanding of form must necessarily return to its origin, that is, to the conception of the genus. The conception of man is referred to animal, and likewise that of horse and of the other species.

He calls “conception” what the Greeks call ἔννοια (*ennoia*). Its definition is:

> Conception is an innate and previously apprehended cognition of a given form that requires clarification.

This definition is drawn from the fact that Plato posited certain Ideas—that is, incorporeal forms and enduring substances, separated from other things by the nature of reality itself—such as “man” itself, by participation in which other things would become human beings or animals.

Aristotle, however, thinks that no substances exist outside things. Rather, he holds that the substantial likeness conceived among several things differing from one another is genus or species.

For since man and horse differ in rationality and irrationality, their conceived likeness produces a genus. The substantial likeness of horse and man consists in this: each is a substance, each is animate, and each is perceptible. These features joined together produce animal, for animal is an animate perceptible substance. The likeness of man and horse, therefore, is animal, which is their genus.

Again, since Plato and Cicero differed in number and in accidental properties, their likeness—humanity, conceived and formed in the mind—is a species.

Thus conception is a certain commonality and likeness among several things that differ from one another. Of conception, one kind is genus and another kind is form.

But since every conception is an understanding of things that are similar, while in similar things a distinction of differences is necessary, conception still requires some clarification and division. The conception of animal, for example, is not sufficient by itself. For the mind is immediately led to inquire about some particular animal—either man or horse—and the conception of man is referred either to Tullius, Plato, or any of the individual persons.

Since this is so, whenever a genus is divided into forms, nothing must be omitted. It is a very serious fault if the person making the division passes over any form. Thus, if someone wishes to divide law, he must divide it into statute, custom, and equity. Statute, custom, equity, and each of them individually, as well as all of them collectively, are included under the name of law.

He censures the ignorance of those who think that species or forms are the same as parts, and says that their ignorance causes them confusion because they do not carefully and competently distinguish and separate things that differ greatly from one another.

Since he was speaking about definition, he adds another kind of definition, which we listed above: one accomplished not by the criterion of propriety and truth but by that of brilliance and ornament. He considers this the province of poets and orators, who care for polished speech.

Tullius takes his example of this definition from civil law, saying that he will depart from the better-known examples of Trebatius only if necessity compels him.

A metaphorical definition is found, for example, when Aquilius, wishing to define a shore, said that a shore is “that against which the waves play.” The word “play” has been transferred from things that move in some agitation for the sake of amusement. Likewise, “youth is the flower of life”; this expression is taken from trees, whose fruits are preceded by flowers. And “old age is the setting of life”; this is taken from the day, which ends when the sun has set.

These metaphors depart from proper usage and designate their subjects through a certain resemblance. For metaphor occurs whenever the name of one thing is imposed upon another because of the resemblance of the two. Movement has its proper name, and play is called by its own term; but when someone says “that against which the waves play,” he transfers a word from the resemblance of agitation to the movement of the waves.

Having concluded his discussion of definitions, he passes to partitions. But this is enough for the third book; let us defer the rest to another time.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1107]

[Col. 1107C] I cannot explain to you, my Patricius, how much strength the contemplation of friendship often supplies during the course of a very difficult work. We compose more diligently for those whom we love with deeply stored affection, and an abundant supply of material presents itself to those who desire to please. To this is added the fact that whatever comes into the mind is brought forth without judgment and even without correction, since in the secrecy of a dear heart there is no danger in expressing what one thinks.

Thus, when I look to your goodwill, everything that is expended according to the prescription of your pleasure is easy and, so to speak, delightful for me. But when I consider myself, I fear that I may not be equal to the task for which I was unprepared, and that the fault of my failure may redound to the discredit of the one who urged me on.

It follows that you must again and again take care lest, although you yourself have been corrected by your own character, you bear the burden of some error of ours. You know the bites of barking envy; you know how easily jealousy passes judgment in the most difficult cases.

I therefore ask you, as one devoted to our common undertaking, to lay the final hand upon our work: cut away what is excessive, fill what gapes open, criticize what is erroneous, and finally be the defender both of our labor and of your encouragement. Especially since the completion of the task leaves me secure, your friend’s shame, worthy of you, may properly meet you if the work displeases.

But more of this elsewhere. For now, let us follow the course of the work we have undertaken.

Since among the topics that adhere to the boundaries of the matters under inquiry some derive from the whole, others from the parts, others from a sign, and others from associated circumstances, he has sufficiently discussed in the preceding treatise the topic that derives from the whole and is established in definition. Now he undertakes to speak about the enumeration of parts, following the correct order, so that he may teach not only by an example what an enumeration of parts is like, but also show by reasoning how the enumeration of parts is to be used in arguments.

Partition must be used in such a way that no part is left out. Thus, if you wish to partition guardianship, you act ignorantly if you omit any part. But if you partition the forms of stipulations or lawsuits, it is not a fault, in an unlimited matter, to omit something. The same is faulty in division. For the number of forms subordinate to each genus is definite. The distribution of parts is often more unlimited, like the branching of streams drawn from a spring.

Thus, in rhetorical disciplines, when a kind of question has been proposed, the number of its forms is added in a complete statement. But when instruction is given concerning the ornaments of words and sentences, which the Greeks call σχήματα (*schēmata*, “figures”), the same does not occur. The matter is more unlimited. From this too it can be understood what difference we wish there to be between partition and division. Although the terms seem to have almost the same force, nevertheless, because the things differed, they wanted the names to differ as well.

The meaning is as follows. Of things joined together from parts, some contain only a few parts that are easy to understand and comprehend, while others contain more parts that are difficult to grasp intellectually. In the case of parts that are few and easily apprehended, it is a very serious fault if something is left out in partition. In the case of those whose number, as he himself says, is more unlimited and whose inspection is more confused, it is a less serious fault if the person making the division passes over some part in the enumeration.

This happens not only with things that consist of parts, but also often with the parts themselves that we divide in distribution. If we wish to separate the human body intellectually and rationally according to its proper members, we might do so as follows: head, shoulders, hands, chest, belly, shins, and feet. Since we have taken larger parts for division, nothing seems to have been omitted. But if we pursue the smallest particles, then the eyes, lips, nostrils, ears, and their parts must also be pursued, and this must be done throughout the whole body. In the same way, the partition will become more difficult as the number of parts becomes more unlimited.

Often, as has been said, the things themselves are joined from parts whose inspection is not easy—for example, if someone partitions the forms of stipulations and lawsuits, or if it is necessary to divide figures of speech, which the Greeks call σχήματα (*schēmata*).

If something is omitted here, it will not be a fault of the person making the partition, because the complex nature of the parts frequently conceals the error. But if someone divides a genus, it is disastrous to omit any form, since the number of forms is finite.

Because forms are always divided according to opposites, there are always either two species of a genus, or three. There are three when the third is produced by a mixture of the opposites. Thus, if we divide color, we must say:

> One kind of color is white, another black, and another intermediate.

The intermediate is formed by the mixture and combination of white and black, although the same principle can be transferred to any other kind of color, whether purple, red, or green.

Therefore, if what you are dividing is of this character, and the parts you take for division are such that they can be easily grasped by understanding, it will be a fault if you omit anything—for example, if you partition guardianships.

Guardianship is generally of four kinds: it is either assigned by a degree of kinship, conferred by the right of patronage, established by the father’s will through the appointment of a guardian, or constituted by the jurisdiction of the urban praetor. There may perhaps be more kinds, but these are sufficient for now. Here, then, the parts are few and easily comprehensible.

But if you wish to comprehend the forms of stipulations and lawsuits, since there are many parts in them, it will not be a fault if you omit something.

The example of parts just given concerning guardianships is readily available, but guardianship has been divided more as a genus into forms than as a whole into parts. For whether the guardian is appointed by kinship, by the right of patronage, or in one of the other ways, he possesses the complete right of guardianship; this does not usually happen with individual parts, so that they can each take the name of the whole.

But if the example is to be made fitting, such parts of guardianships must be sought as can, when joined together, produce guardianship—not such as are individually designated by the name “guardianship.” I do not know whether any teacher of legal knowledge has set out such parts of guardianship.

The rhetor Merobaudes, however, thought that the passage should be understood in this way: when Cicero says, “Partition must be used so that you omit no part,” he was speaking of division—that is, of one part of a proposed partition. For both division and distribution into members are called partition. In division it is faulty to omit anything; in the partition of members it is not. He therefore adapted the example of guardianships to that partition which is actually division.

But if you make a division—that is, a partition of forms from a genus—it is a very serious fault to omit anything. Since the number of forms is finite, anything omitted is omitted through ignorance.

Thus, if we wish to divide rhetorical questions into forms, we shall say that every rhetorical question concerns either fact, the quality of the fact, or the name.

But if I distribute figures of speech and of sentences, it will not be a fault, as has been said, to pass over something, since figures of sentences and expressions are numerous and differ from one another in various ways.

Here too, the parts of figures cannot be understood as parts of a whole but rather as species of a genus. For each of the figures, which are unlimited in number, is a species of the general figure. We can understand this from the words of the rhetoricians where they treat of style.

There are no parts of figures that join figures together in such a way that the individual figures cannot admit the name of the universal figure. But someone may object: How can figures be unlimited if they are species?

I shall answer briefly: when style is changed, the figure also changes. Therefore it lies within the power of the speaker to create figures that the person treating the subject can scarcely recognize before they have been made. These figures are not constituted by certain substantial differences but are rather explained through accidents.

Hence, when figure is divided, it seems to be a division of a common name into its meanings rather than a division of a genus into species. It is difficult to include all the meanings of any name in a division, because new meanings are usually devised; yet even this is not permitted by the nature of things. For every figure is comprehended by the name and definition of the general figure. Whatever definition is given of figure, the same definition will also be the definition of each individual figure. This shows that each figure is a species of the universal figure. For species and genus are univocal.

But it is more correct to say that Tullius referred the partition of figures to style itself, of which a figure is a part, not a species. For polished style is woven from various and manifold figures. If, therefore, someone wishes to partition style into figures, he will not cut a genus into species but a whole into parts.

Since this is so, the difference between division and partition also appears from this: partition is sometimes of such a kind that omitting something in it causes no fault, whereas division of forms is of such a kind that nothing can be omitted without blame. This has happened because, since the things differed, different terms also seemed appropriate to things that differed from one another.

Much is also derived from notation. Notation occurs when an argument is elicited from the force of a name. The Greeks call it ἐτυμολογία (*etymologia*), that is, *veriloquium*, “true-speaking,” a word derived from a word. We avoid this unfamiliar term because it is not sufficiently suitable, and call this kind of argument “notation,” since words are signs of things.

Aristotle likewise calls this σύμβολον (*symbolon*), which in Latin is *nota*, “a sign.” But once its meaning is understood, there is less need to be concerned with the name.

Many things are therefore elicited in argument by notation from a word. Thus, when the question is what *postliminium* is, I do not ask what things return by *postliminium*. That would fall under division, which would take this form:

> The following return by *postliminium*: a man, a ship, a pack-mule, a horse, and a mare accustomed to accept a bridle—that is, a tamed mare.

But when the force of *postliminium* itself is sought and the word itself is examined, our Servius, as I think, believes that nothing need be noted except *post*, while *liminium* is merely an extension of the word. He wants *finitimus*, *legitimus*, and *aeditimus* to contain no more of *-timum* than *meditullium* contains of *-ullium*.

P. Scaevola, son of Scaevola, however, thinks that the word is compounded, so that it contains both *post* and *limen*, “threshold.” Thus, things alienated from us, when they have reached the enemy and have gone out, as it were, from their own threshold, seem, when they return from there afterward to the same threshold, to have returned by *postliminium*.

In this connection the case of Mancinus can also be defended: that he returned by *postliminium* and was not surrendered, since he had not been received. For neither surrender nor gift can be understood without qualification.

After enumerating the parts in due order, he considers notation. Notation, then, occurs whenever an argument is drawn from some mark of a thing that is in doubt. A mark, however, is that which designates each thing. Thus every name is a mark, because it makes known the thing of which it is predicated; Aristotle called this a σύμβολον (*symbolon*). An argument is drawn from notation whenever something is inferred from notation, that is, from the interpretation of a name. [Col. 1111C]

The interpretation of a name is called ἐτυμολογία (*etymologia*) in Greek and *veriloquium* (“true-saying”) in Latin; for ἔτυμον (*etymon*) means “true,” while λόγος (*logos*) means “speech.” But since *veriloquium* was less commonly used in Latin, Tullius calls the interpretation of a name “notation.” It is of the following kind. Suppose one asks, “What is *postliminium*?” In this question, the inquiry does not seem to concern which things return *postliminio*; that would fall under division, since it would require an enumeration of all the things that return after crossing the boundary. Thus, if we say, “The following return *postliminio*: a human being, a ship, a pack-mule, a horse, and a mare accustomed to take the bridle,” that is, a tamed mare, the things that return *postliminio* have now been enumerated.

But when the question is what the right of *postliminium* itself is, it can be understood from the interpretation of the name itself. For whoever, having been captured by the enemy, returns to his country returns *postliminio*. While he suffers captivity among the enemy, he loses the rights of a citizen; but he recovers all his rights if he returns *postliminio*. Thus the right of *postliminium* can be clarified through the notation of the name: since *post* always signifies what has been left behind, the word *postliminium* signifies a return. This is the view approved by Servius, who interprets the force of the name from the adverb *post*, affirming that the remaining part of the word is merely an extension; for in *postliminium* he derives the interpretation of the name from the element *post*, and considers *liminium* to have been needlessly lengthened.

The same pattern appears in *meditullium*: the first part signifies “middle,” while *tullium* signifies nothing. The same applies to *legitimum* and *aeditimum*. In both cases *lex* (“law”) and *aedes* (“temple” or “building”) signify something, whereas *-timum* designates absolutely nothing.

As for the name *postliminium*, Scevola, son of Publius, thinks that it is composed of the adverb *post* and *limen* (“threshold”). Since the person who returns *postliminio* returns to the same threshold that he had previously left, he therefore believes that the name is composed from the meanings of both elements. For whatever things have been alienated from us and come into the possession of the enemy, once they have gone out from our threshold, return *postliminio* if they subsequently return to that same threshold.

In this way the case of Mancinus can also be defended. Although the Roman people surrendered him because of a treaty badly concluded, the enemy refused to receive him; when he returned, he seemed to have returned *postliminio*. For if the enemy had accepted someone surrendered by his fellow citizens, he would not have seemed to return *postliminio* even if he had somehow escaped from the enemy, since by the judgment of his fellow citizens he had been stripped of every right of freedom. But since neither surrender, nor transfer, nor gift seems able to exist without acceptance, one who has not been received cannot be understood to have been surrendered either. Mancinus, therefore, who had not been surrendered into the power of the enemy—if they had been willing to accept him—was rightly defended as having returned to his country *jure postliminii*, by the right of *postliminium*. [Col. 1112B]

Next comes the locus that consists of things in some way related to the matter in doubt, which I have just said is divided into several parts. The first of these is the locus from derivation, which the Greeks call συζυγία (*syzygia*). It is adjacent to notation, which has just been discussed. Thus, if we understood *aqua pluvia* (“rainwater”) only as water that we saw collected from rain, Mucius would appear and, because the words *pluvia* and *pluendo* (“by raining”) are related, would say that all water that had increased through rainfall ought to be restrained. [Col. 1112C]

When he divided into four differences above the locus inherent in the very things about which inquiry is made—namely, the locus from the whole, from the enumeration of parts, from a mark, and from related things—he dealt carefully a little earlier with the first three. He now pursues the fourth locus, that of related things. Since the locus from related things was divided into very many differences, and the first of these was proposed under derived forms, he first discusses derivation, which differs little from notation. For just as notation is drawn from the force of a name, so derivation is contained in the similarity of a word; hence the two possess, as it were, a common boundary. The difference is that notation is accomplished through the exposition of a name, whereas derivation is accomplished through the similarity and derivation of a word.

Since the locus is easy both to understand and to treat, it is enough to give an example of the following kind: Rainwater (*aqua pluvia*) is water that is collected and increases through rainfall. *Pluendo* and *pluvia* are related forms. In one and the same word, a different ending of the names creates the difference.

Likewise: “It is lawful to restrain rainwater”—that is, if rainwater is collected in someone’s field and flows into another’s field, where it accumulates in such a way as to harm the neighbor’s crops, the person who thinks it is in his interest that the water not flow onto his land may ward it off from his boundaries. If, then, a river has increased through rainfall, the question is whether it ought to be restrained. “Mucius,” he says, “replies that, since *aqua pluvia* is so called from *pluendo*, a river that has increased through rainfall is also rainwater and ought to be restrained.” [Col. 1113A]

When an argument is drawn from a genus, it is not necessary to retrieve it from the very beginning; it is often permissible to take it from a point short of the highest genus, provided that what is taken is higher than that to which it is applied. Thus, in the highest genus, rainwater is water that comes from the sky and increases through rain; but there is a more immediate level at which the right of restraint is, as it were, contained. The genus is “harmful rainwater,” whose forms are water harmful because of the location and water harmful because of human action. One of these is ordered by the arbiter to be restrained; the other is not.

The nature of genera and species is understood to be such that, when they are collected or divided, one can ascend from individuals through species and genera to the highest genera; likewise, one can descend from the highest genera through the genera placed below them to individuals. This will become clear from a single example. Cicero is an individual; his species is “human being”; the genus of this species is “animal”; the higher genus of animal is “animate body.” If one ascends farther, one finds “body” as another genus; if one proceeds still farther, “substance” appears as the genus at the final level.

Since there are many genera, if the genus of any species must be assigned, it will not always be necessary, he says, to seek the highest and primary genera. It will also be necessary to employ some of those situated in the middle, provided that the following rule is preserved: the genus must always be higher than that of which it is predicated as genus. It is the height of ignorance to place something lower in the position of genus, when by nature the genus is always placed above its proper species. Accordingly, it is erroneous to say that “animate body” is the genus of body.

Thus, if a genus is to be fitted to a species, we may fit to it something among the higher genera; it will not always be necessary to employ the ultimate genus. If we wish to place the proper genus above “human being,” we need not place “substance” above it; we may instead place “body,” “animate body,” or, as is most appropriate, “animal.” For the genera that should always be taken are those that adhere most closely to the forms; these are especially required in definitions. In arguments, however, it makes no difference whether one chooses the nearest genus or a higher genus. Since argument proceeds from what contains something, the higher genus contains more.

Accordingly, if something about a human being is in doubt and the locus of argument is taken from the genus, whatever is said of “animal” will also be predicated of “human being.” Likewise, if something is predicated of an animate body, the same can also be said of a human being. Thus, just as arguments are made from the nearest genera, so they may also be made from genera established at another level.

In all these matters, however, the point that seems most important to consider is that nothing interior should be placed above what is superior as its genus. This, then, is the principle.

As for the example, it will be clarified in the following way. Let rainwater be water collected from rain falling from the sky. Its species are twofold: one kind of rainwater is harmful, the other harmless. Harmful rainwater likewise has two species: one harmful by human action, the other harmful through the natural defect of the location.

Rainwater harmful by human action is water collected in some place in such a way that, when it flows from there, it harms a neighbor, provided that the place is not naturally of such a character but has been prepared by human action for receiving water. It is harmful through the defect of the location whenever the place is naturally so constituted that it can receive water and harm a neighbor.

If, then, someone wishes to discover the genus of the water that he wants a neighbor to restrain so that it will not harm him, he need not descend from the ultimate genus and say that the genus of the water he wants restrained is “rainwater.” He can find the genus he seeks at a somewhat lower level and say that the genus of the water he wants restrained is “harmful rainwater.” If he seeks the nearest genus, he can employ “rainwater harmful by human action,” since what someone is compelled to restrain is what has been made harmful by human action. What causes inconvenience through the form or defect of the location does not have to be restrained.

What we said—that the genus of the water that ought to be restrained is “rainwater harmful by human action”—is to be understood as applying when the water that ought to be restrained has beneath it many individuals and similar instances. Only then can “rainwater harmful by human action” be the genus of the water that ought to be restrained. If the water that ought to be restrained is not divided into any individuals, it is itself an individual; and “rainwater harmful by human action” is not its genus but its species. If this seems somewhat obscure to anyone, let him consult the five books in which we arranged our commentaries on genus, species, difference, property, and accident. Nothing of this kind will then arise that could leave him at a loss. [Col. 1114C]

This argument drawn from a genus can also be handled conveniently by pursuing the parts from the whole, as follows. If fraud is committed when one thing is being done and another is being pretended, one may enumerate the ways in which this occurs and then include the matter one is arguing was done fraudulently among one of them. This kind of argument is generally considered especially strong.

It has been explained how a genus ought to be fitted to a species, and it was prescribed that nothing except what is higher should be employed. It is now added how the locus drawn from a genus can be used more conveniently in argument. Whenever a matter is in doubt, if, after dividing some genus, we can include the matter in doubt under one of the parts of that genus, then the argument appears to have been drawn from the genus, as follows.

Let fraud be defined as occurring when one thing is being done and another is being pretended. If its species are divided, and we can add the act we are alleging to have occurred to one of the species derived from fraud, then whatever is thought about fraud must also be judged of the matter we are alleging; and the argument has been made from the genus. For the matter in question is a species, while that from which the argument is taken is the genus—namely, where fraud occurs in this way.

This locus differs from the locus drawn from the enumeration of parts. Nor, if we enumerate the parts—that is, the forms or species—does the argument for that reason derive from a genus rather than from an enumeration of parts. Whenever we use the enumeration of the parts itself for argument, we say that the argument has been drawn from that division, as in the following example: “If it has foundations, walls, and a roof, and the place is intended for habitation, it is a house.” By using the division itself, we have proved that it is a house.

But whenever something must be placed under a genus, and, after the parts have been divided, we attach the matter in question to one of those derived from the genus, as follows—“If we show that Cicero is an animal, we shall say: Every animal is either rational or irrational; but Cicero is rational; therefore he is an animal”—we are not using division principally to establish the argument. We have divided the genus so that what we were striving to demonstrate could be included under one of the divisions; that is, so that the matter in doubt might be brought within the scope of the assumed genus, and confidence in it might consequently be established through the nature of the genus. Thus the argument is rightly called an argument from the genus. [Col. 1115B]

Moreover, an enumeration of parts generally produces the substance of a whole, whether that whole is universal, as a genus, or is completed through the conjunction of parts, as an integral whole. But this division of a genus, under any part of which the matter in dispute must be included, does not constitute the substance of a whole; rather, it places within the genus what we seek to establish. M. Tullius confirms that this mode of argument is especially powerful. For the following rule is sufficiently true and necessary: Whatever is predicated of a genus is predicated in every respect of its species.

It is also very useful to ask, when something is proved concerning particular things from the proximate superior species—as when we prove that Socrates is rational because he is a human being, and a human being is rational—whether we should think that the argument has been drawn from a genus or from a form. If we say that it has been drawn from a genus, the ultimate species cannot be a genus; if from a species, the superior genus always seeks to prove the species.

But “human being,” which supports the claim that Socrates is rational, is not a genus of human beings. We must therefore say that the argument will appear to have been drawn, as it were, from a genus. For confidence in the predicate is derived from the genus as from something containing and more extensive, and from its substance. No one doubts that this relation belongs to its individuals as their species, since the genus both contains them and is predicated of their substance.

[Col. 1115D]

Similarity follows. It extends widely, but is more relevant to orators and philosophers than to you. Although all loci supply arguments for all debates, they occur more abundantly in some debates and more narrowly in others. Therefore, let the kinds be known to you; when to use them, the questions themselves will advise you.

There are similarities that reach their conclusion through several comparisons, as follows: “If a guardian ought to show good faith, if a partner ought to, if one to whom you have entrusted a commission ought to, if one who has received something in trust ought to, then a manager ought to do so as well.” That which reaches its intended conclusion through several instances is called induction, which in Greek is ἐπαγωγή (*epagōgē*); Socrates made extensive use of it in his conversations.

The second kind of similarity is taken from a comparison in which one thing is compared with one thing, like with like, as follows: Just as, when there is a dispute in a city about boundaries, because boundaries seem to belong more properly to fields than to a city, you cannot appoint an arbiter for regulating boundaries, so, if rainwater causes harm in a city, because the whole matter of restraining rainwater belongs more properly to fields, you cannot appoint an arbiter. [Col. 1116A]

Examples are also taken from the same locus of similarity. Thus Crassus used many examples in the Curian case, arguing about a man who had instituted an heir in his will on the condition that, if a son were born within ten months and died before reaching the age at which he came under his own guardianship, the second heir would obtain the inheritance. The recollection of these examples was effective, and you often make much use of them in giving legal opinions.

Fictional examples also possess the force of similarity. They are more characteristic of orators than of you, although you too make use of them, as follows: “Suppose that someone has transferred by *mancipatio* something that cannot be transferred by *mancipatio*. Did it thereby become the property of the person who received it? Or did the person who made the transfer thereby incur an obligation?” In this kind of argument, orators and philosophers are permitted even to make the mute speak, to raise the dead from the underworld, and to say something utterly impossible for the sake of enlarging a matter—or, for diminishing it, what is called hyperbole—and many other marvelous things. Their field is broader, but, as I said earlier, they draw arguments from the same loci in both the greatest and the smallest questions. [Col. 1116B]

He has discussed the locus of similarity clearly and efficiently, laid open its entire meaning, divided the forms of similarities, and prescribed with the greatest clarity the cases in which arguments arise more especially from similarity—namely, among philosophers and orators. Similarity is particularly suited to persuasion. For what tends to occur in one or several cases other than the case under inquiry can easily be believed to apply also to the case in doubt.

Accordingly, arguments drawn from similarity are of great use to orators and also to philosophers, since philosophers do not employ demonstration in every question but sometimes collect probabilities in order to persuade more easily of what they are attempting to show. Similarity between things must often be sought; therefore the locus from similarity is especially useful to orators and philosophers, though not to them alone. All loci are common to every subject, but they arise more abundantly in some and are found more narrowly in others. Thus, once the loci have been learned and understood in advance, the questions themselves that are to be handled will be able to remind an attentive mind which loci it should use.

Every similarity is twofold. Either similarity is collected from several instances and is called induction, which the Greeks call ἐπαγωγή (*epagōgē*), or individual things are compared through similarity.

The former is of the following kind: “If a guardian ought to show good faith, if a partner ought to, if one to whom you have entrusted a commission ought to, if one who has received something in trust ought to, then a manager ought to do so as well.” Since good faith ought to be shown in several cases, and there is one similarity in the showing of good faith by a guardian, a partner, one to whom something has been entrusted, and one who has received something in trust, the same similarity must also apply to a manager.

A person receives something in trust whenever a thing is transferred to him so that he may transfer it back to the person who transferred it to him. For example, if someone, fearing a dangerous period, transfers a landed estate by *mancipatio* to a more powerful friend so that the friend may return it to him after the feared period has passed, this transfer is called *mancipatio fiduciaria*, because an assurance of restitution is interposed. Socrates is said to have made extensive use of this collection of similarities, as is found in the works of Plato and of others belonging to his school. [Col. 1117A]

Whenever one thing is compared with another through similarity, the argument is collected in the following way. Arbiters for regulating boundaries are appointed to decide disputes about boundaries, so that, if a dispute has arisen concerning boundaries, it may be settled by their judgment. But boundaries are said to exist only in the limits of fields, and arbiters for regulating boundaries cannot be appointed in a city.

Likewise, water is ordinarily said to be subject to restraint only in the fields, where, if rainwater is collected in some place and, flowing from there into the countryside, damages a neighbor’s pastures or crops, magistrates appoint arbiters for restraining the water. The question therefore arises whether we can compel the appointment of an arbiter for restraining water in a city. The argument is taken from similarity: if, because boundary regulation belongs only to the fields, one cannot compel the appointment of an arbiter in the city for regulating boundaries, then, because restraining water likewise seems to belong only to the fields, one cannot compel the appointment of an arbiter in the city for restraining water. Here, therefore, one thing has been joined to another through similarity.

Cicero also proposes that the things called examples be taken from this same locus of similarity, as in the Curian case, which was as follows. A certain man, leaving behind a pregnant wife, appointed a posthumous son as heir and substituted another as second heir, named Curius, on the condition that, if the posthumous son—who was to be born within the following ten months—died before reaching the age at which he came under his own guardianship, and died before reaching the age at which he could legally make a will, the second heir would succeed. But if he reached the age at which, having been received into his own guardianship with a judgment now firmly established, he could legally perform the office of heir under civil law, the second heir, that is, Curius, would not succeed. This is what is called pupillary substitution. The question was whether an arrangement instituted in this way was valid.

Crassus, then, brought forward many examples in which an heir instituted in this way had obtained the inheritance, and the recollection of these examples moved the judges. He also says that legal experts themselves frequently use examples, as when a proposition is formulated—that is, imagined—so that the case under discussion may be understood through similarity, as follows.

Suppose a jurist adds that something not legally contracted is of no effect, and introduces an example such as this: “If someone has transferred by *mancipatio* a thing that is not subject to *mancipatio*, did he thereby alienate the thing, or could he thereby have bound himself by becoming liable?” Certainly not; for what has not been legally contracted retains no validity.

Similar examples are found among jurists. Orators are especially powerful in this respect, since they are permitted to invent to such an extent that through their speech the dead may often be raised from the underworld. Tullius does this in the speech in which he defends Caelius. But, he says, their field—the field of orators—is broader, since they may roam and wander freely. Similarities are nevertheless no less useful to others in their various capacities, because the same arguments apply to the greatest and the smallest cases. Thus the loci of arguments are also suited to questions belonging to different disciplines. [Col. 1118A]

The difference from similarity follows. This is greatly opposed to the preceding matter, but it belongs to the same capacity to discover what is dissimilar as well as what is similar. Examples of this kind include the following: “It is not the case that, just as you may rightly pay a debt owed to a woman directly to the woman herself without the authorization of a guardian, you can rightly pay in the same way what you owe to a ward, whether male or female.”

It belongs to the same capacity to recognize similarities and differences. For whoever knows what is the same will be able to know what is different. Every similarity establishes that something is the same in some respect; for whatever is the same in quality must be similar. Every thing is the same either in substance, in quality, or in the other categories. If this is so, the mind can recognize the same thing in several categories. But when the mind marks this very sameness in the categories, it likewise perceives in the same categories what is different. Similarity is sameness, while difference is otherness. Therefore the same mind and the same understanding recognize similarity and difference.

There are many species of differences. Some are substantial, such as rationality in a human being. Others are not substantial but inseparable, such as blackness in an Ethiopian and in a raven. Still others are changeable and unstable, such as sitting, standing, and other things of this kind, by which we often differ both from other people and from ourselves.

Again, some differences in a certain respect divide genera, while others in a certain respect constitute species. But if an argument is drawn from constitutive differences, it is drawn as from a genus. For just as a genus contains a species, so differences contain species. Certainly, if constitutive differences are understood as genera, confidence derived from them will be applied to the things they constitute. These are, as it were, the forms of such differences.

But if the differences are divisive, and confidence from them is drawn for proving the things they divide—that is, genera—the argument appears to be made from a form, since such differences are, as it were, forms of the things divided. If, however, they are referred to proving the things into which the genus is divided in the contrary direction, then the argument properly appears to be made from a difference, because contrary things are compared as quasi-differences.

As for Tullius’s example, it is of the following kind. In ancient times women were held under perpetual guardianship; wards likewise acted under guardians. But if something had been owed to a woman, it could be paid without the authorization of her guardian, whereas it could by no means be paid to a ward without such authorization.

Therefore, if the question is whether something owed to any ward may be paid despite the guardian’s refusal, the argument is taken from difference, as follows: “Just as you can pay a debt owed to a woman without the authorization of a guardian, so you cannot pay what you owe to a ward unless the guardian’s authorization has been given.” Women remain under perpetual guardianship even after they have reached mature age, whereas a fixed number of years brings a term to the guardianship of wards. For this reason, payment cannot be made to a ward without authorization.

The person of women differs from the person of wards, either in that wards are not governed by perpetual guardianship while women are, or in that a ward cannot possess any judgment useful for managing his own affairs, whereas some judgment—although not firm—may be found in women for the conduct of family business. [Col. 1119A]

Next comes the locus called “from contraries.” There are several kinds of contraries. One consists of things that differ greatly within the same genus, such as wisdom and folly. Things are said to belong to the same genus when, once one is proposed, its counterpart occurs as though from a certain opposite direction—for example, slowness in relation to speed, not weakness. From contraries of this kind arguments arise such as: “If we flee folly, let us pursue wisdom,” and “If we flee wickedness, let us pursue goodness.” Things that are contrary within the same genus are called opposites (*adversa*).

There are other contraries that we may call privatives in Latin; in Greek they are called στερητικά (*sterētika*). For the prefix *in-* deprives a word of the force it would have had if the prefix *in-* had not been present, as in *dignitas* (“dignity”) and *indignitas* (“indignity”), *humanitas* (“humanity”) and *inhumanitas* (“inhumanity”), and other words of the same kind. Their treatment is the same as that of the preceding category, which I called opposites.

There are also other kinds of contraries, such as those compared with something else: double and single, many and few, long and short, greater and lesser.

There are also very strongly opposed terms that are called negatives; the Greeks call them ἀποφατικά (*apophatika*), contraries to affirmatives: “If this is, that is not.” What need is there for an example? Let it simply be understood that, in seeking an argument, no contrary applies to all contraries.

[Note: [Col. 1119D] Should it be read, *ea ἀποωαοτικά Graecis aientibus*—“these are ἀποωαοτικά [probably ‘negative terms’] in Greek, contrary to affirmatives”?]

Division, in the place dealing with differences, now treats contraries. Therefore, so that the order of the subject may become clearer, I must take a few points from Aristotle, that man by far the most learned of all, which he discussed concerning this division, although Marcus Tullius in substance agrees almost entirely with Aristotle, but differs from him in the interpretation of the terms [Col. 1119C]. For what Aristotle calls “opposites,” that is, ἀντικείμενα (*antikeimena*), Tullius calls “contraries”; but more on this shortly.

Let us now consider Aristotle’s division. According to Aristotle, then, of opposites some are contraries, some are privation and possession, some are relatives, and some are contradictories. Contraries are, for example, white and black; possession and privation, sight and blindness, dignity and indignity; relatives, father and son, master and slave; contradictories, “it is day,” “it is not day.” The following distinctions are observed among all these.

Among things that are contraries, some have an intermediate state, while others lack an intermediate state. White and black, for example, have an intermediate state: some other color, such as red or pale, lies between them; and it is not necessary that one or the other of these contraries always be present in bodies [Col. 1119D]. For not every body is either white or black; sometimes it is situated in the middle between them, being red or pale.

Contraries without an intermediate state are those between which no middle can be found, such as heaviness and lightness. There is no intermediate state between these: what is light is carried upward, and what is heavy downward. No body that is carried neither upward nor downward can be found. Contraries without an intermediate state are such that one of them must always adhere to whatever is capable of receiving either one, as in the example just given. Every body must be either light or heavy, since lightness and heaviness have no middle that could additionally be present in bodies [Col. 1120A].

Things belonging to privation and possession, such as blindness and sight, differ from those contraries that enclose an intermediate state because they themselves have no intermediate state. But they differ from contraries without an intermediate state because, in the case of the latter, one of the two contraries is always present in the subject—for example, heaviness or lightness in a body—whereas privation and possession are not always present. Thus, when possession is sight and privation is blindness, not everything capable of seeing either sees or is blind. An infant not yet born neither sees, because it has not yet come forth into the light, nor is it blind, because it has not yet possessed sight that it could have lost. The same may be said of young animals, which cannot see immediately after birth: at that time we can call them neither blind nor seeing.

Finally, contraries are always considered in terms of their own qualities, whereas privations are understood not as themselves being something, but from the absence of a possession. Blindness, after all, is not something in itself; it is understood from the departure of sight. Both privation and contrariety also differ from opposition by relation, because neither contraries nor privative opposites can be present together. The same thing, at the same time and in the same place, cannot be both white and black, or both seeing and blind. Relatives, however, cannot be separated from one another: there can be no son without a father, nor a slave if there is no master.

Furthermore, contraries and privative opposites are not referred to one another. No one says “white of black,” or “black of white,” or “blindness of sight,” or “sight of blindness.” Things placed in a relation, however, consist in the very predication of that relation, such as “double of half,” “master of slave,” and other expressions of this kind [Col. 1120C].

Contraries and relations likewise differ from contradictories. Contradictories always consist in a sentence, and truth is found in one member of the pair, falsity in the other. Contraries, privations, and relations, however, are found in simple parts of speech [printed: *invenitur*; perhaps *inveniuntur*], and in these there is neither truth nor falsity. When I say “white,” “black,” “blindness,” “sight,” “master,” “slave,” these are simple parts of speech and contain neither truth nor falsehood. There is no truth or falsity in simple parts of speech. But when I say “it is day” and “it is not day,” both are propositions—one framed as an affirmation, the other as a negation—and they are sentences [Col. 1120D].

Marcus Tullius, however, uses terms that are not so proper but more familiar. He says that among contraries some are called adversarial, some privative, some comparative, and some affirmative and negative. But what he calls “contraries” would more properly be called “opposites”; what he calls “adversarial” would more appropriately receive the name “contraries”; what he calls “comparative” would more accurately be called “relative” or “related”; nevertheless, let him use the terms as he wishes, provided that the things themselves are marked according to the exact character proper to them. In the other books that we have published, we have used the terms in the manner stated above in Aristotle’s division.

According to Marcus Tullius, then, among contraries some are adversarial, such as wisdom and folly; some are privative, such as dignity and indignity; some are things compared with something else, such as double and single; and some are called negative, being set in opposition to affirmatives, as in “if this is, that is not” [Col. 1121A].

Adversarial opposites are things placed under one genus that differ greatly, such as white and black, which, although placed under one genus—that is, color—are very far apart. Similarly, slowness is adversarial to speed when both are placed under motion. Weakness must not be opposed to speed, since sound health is contrary to weakness. Cicero omitted this point in the division, but taught it by his example.

Those things are also called adversarial which, although situated in different genera, are understood to differ greatly from one another, such as wisdom and folly. Wisdom belongs under the genus of good, whereas folly belongs under that of evil [Col. 1121B]. Yet this example seems rather to concern privation, for folly is the privation of wisdom, and folly is nothing other than the absence of wisdom and reason. But what Cicero calls privative I shall demonstrate later.

From these adversarial opposites an argument is drawn in this way: If we flee folly, let us pursue wisdom; if we desire goodness, let us flee wickedness, although wickedness too can be included among privations according to the same principle stated above.

According to Cicero, privatives are those called στερητικά (*sterētika*) in Greek. They have prefixed to them a part of speech which, when added, almost always takes something away, such as the prefix *in-*. For this syllable, when prefixed to a word, usually removes something from the force that the thing would have had if it had not possessed the prefixed syllable. Thus, from *humanitas* (“humanity”) comes *inhumanitas* (“inhumanity”): the prefixed *in-* deprives the thing of the humanity of which it is said. So also *dignitas* (“dignity”) and *indignitas* (“indignity”) [Col. 1121C].

Tullius maintains that only those things are privative in which this syllable is prefixed. According to Tullius, the nature of privatives is defined by reference to this syllable. From the Peripatetics, however, we have learned that privations are expressed both by simple nouns and by privative syllables: by simple nouns, as in *caecitas* (“blindness”), and by privative syllables, as in *indignitas* (“indignity”) and *inhumanitas* (“inhumanity”).

Accordingly, according to Marcus Tullius, blindness will not be the privation of sight but its adversarial opposite. For that reason, perhaps, he numbered folly among adversarial opposites, since it does not contain the syllable from which privations are thought to arise [Col. 1121D]. Arguments are drawn from these in the same way as from the adversarial opposites mentioned above: “If humanity is to be pursued, let us shun inhumanity.”

Those contraries, says Tullius, which are compared with something else are such as “double of single.” This amounts to the same thing as saying “double of half,” since the single is half of the double. So too “father of son.” Such terms are always reciprocal, sometimes with the seventh case—that is, the ablative—and sometimes with the genitive. “The son is the son of the father” and “the father is the father of the son” constitute a conversion according to the genitive; “the double is double in relation to the single” is according to the ablative. There are also examples with the accusative, such as “few in relation to many” and “great in relation to small.”

Negatives are things placed in affirmations and negations, such as “if this is, that is not”—for example, “if it is day, it is not night.” Cicero says that this opposition is strongly contrary [Col. 1122A]. From all these, the means of constructing arguments is available in the manner stated above. From relative contraries we draw an argument as follows: “If he is a father, it is impossible that he should not have a son.”

From the negatives, which, as he says, the Greeks call ἀποφατικά (*apophatika*), the argument runs thus: “If the sun was above the earth, it could not have been night.” For this affirmation destroys that negation. But why he established these as negatives is surprising. Negatives are opposed to affirmatives and cannot exist together, as in “it is day” and “it is not day.” Yet the consequence is of this form: “If this is, that is not,” as in “if it is day, it is not night” [Col. 1122B]. Tullius says that affirmation and negation are strongly contrary; but in this consequence they cannot be contraries, for what is consequent is not contrary.

I gave an example of the place from adjuncts a little earlier: many considerations would have to be accepted if we decided that possession of an estate should be granted according to the tablets of a will drawn up by someone who had no legal capacity to make a will. But this place is more useful in conjectural cases brought before the courts, when the question is what is, what has happened, what will happen, or what might in general happen. The formula of the place itself is as follows.

This place advises that we inquire what happened before the matter, during the matter, and after the matter. It has nothing to do with law. “Go to Cicero,” our Gallus would say if someone brought him such a matter that a question of fact was involved. “Yet allow me not to pass over any part of the art I have undertaken, lest, if you think that I should write nothing except what concerns you, I should seem excessively devoted to you” [Col. 1122C].

This place is therefore for the most part oratorical, not merely outside the province of jurists but even outside that of philosophers. Before the matter are considered such things as preparations, conversations, the place, and a banquet arranged in advance. During the matter come the sound of footsteps, the noise of people, shadows of bodies, and anything else of that kind. After the matter come pallor, blushing, hesitation, and any other signs of disturbance and consciousness of guilt. In addition, there may be an extinguished fire, a bloody sword, and other things capable of arousing suspicion that the deed was committed.

The nature of the place from adjuncts was briefly demonstrated above by the example in which he said that, if possession of an inheritance were granted according to the tablets of a woman who had never suffered a reduction in civil status, it would follow that possession should likewise be permitted according to the tablets of children and slaves [Col. 1122D].

But now he proposes to display the actual form and, so to speak, subject matter of the place, which is as follows: The place from adjuncts arises when, from what is proposed, something else is inferred by argument to be, to have been, or to be going to be, as in the very example he set out earlier. It is proved that possession of an inheritance ought not to be granted according to the tablets of a woman who had never suffered a reduction in civil status, because, if this were established, it would follow that possession of an inheritance would also have to be permitted according to the tablets of children and slaves.

Such things are called adjuncts because they are generally found around the matter under investigation, although they need not always adhere to it. The form of this place is such that it may also admit the following definition: The place from adjuncts arises when, from certain things that are close to the matters under investigation, the matter under investigation is shown to have been, to be, or to be going to be. This place is especially necessary in conjectural cases.

For when a fact is under investigation, if the fact in doubt has occurred, it is customary to consider what preceded it, what accompanies it, or what will follow it. Many things are inferred from the various events in time that are adjuncts to each individual matter. For this reason, in conjectural cases—the cases treated only by orators—we ask what happened before the matter, during it, and after it. Jurists have no connection with rhetorical skill in such affairs, for a legal expert responds concerning the legal character of a fact, but not also concerning the truth of the fact itself [Col. 1123B].

Therefore, whenever a question of fact was referred to Gallus, the legal expert, he would say, “That does not concern us,” and would instead refer those consulting him to Cicero—that is, to the rhetorician. In this passage Tullius combined the place with Trebatius’ discussion, saying:

“Although this place from adjuncts is especially useful in conjectural cases and contributes nothing to the legal expertise of those consulted, yet allow me,” he says, “not to pass over any part of the work I have undertaken, lest, if I write in this book nothing except examples belonging to your own art, I should seem devoted solely to your favor.” The place from adjuncts, however, is open neither to jurists nor even to philosophers, except to orators, and must often be treated with reference to three times [Col. 1123C].

For if a fact is under investigation, it is necessary to inquire what occurred either before it, along with it, or after it.

Before the matter, for example, come preparations. It is likely that someone carried out what he had prepared beforehand. Conversations are another example: it may be inferred that someone was in love because he had often conversed with the person concerned. The place is another example, as when a location suitable for doing something is selected. A banquet arranged in advance is another, as when someone is accused of having done something at a banquet that had been arranged beforehand, and an inference concerning the deed is drawn from the very fact that the banquet had been arranged. All these are examples of what occurs before the matter under investigation.

During the matter, the process is as follows. The sound of footsteps may establish that someone went to a particular place, if he is accused of having gone there. Or, if the shadow of a body indicates that an adulterer was in a bedroom, these things are inspected along with the matters under investigation, although they are nevertheless understood as adjuncts to them [Col. 1123D].

After the matter, there are any stains of consciousness revealed by pallor, blushing, or hesitation. An extinguished fire may indicate that something was done secretly, when, after the fire had been put out, we wish to show that the darkness was used to conceal knowledge of the deed. Similarly, a bloody sword indicates that a crime has been completed.

All these are understood as adjuncts occurring after the deed. The expressions “before the matter,” “during the matter,” and “after the matter” must always be understood according to the order of time, and not in the same way as “antecedents” and “consequents.” In the latter case, the order of nature is considered. Everything is simultaneous: if what precedes is posited, what follows is immediately present. Thus, if you posit “human being,” it is immediately necessary that there be “animal”; “animal” cannot be said to follow “human being” according to temporal succession. By contrast, a preparation precedes in time, and the result follows afterward.

Accordingly, in the one case the terms are “antecedents” and “consequents”; here they are “before the matter,” “during the matter,” and “after the matter.” The antecedent is called antecedent not according to time, but according to the primacy of nature, because it draws something else along with itself at once; the consequent is what accompanies the antecedent. Things considered according to the earlier or later order of time, however, began to receive the name “adjuncts,” and thus are called “before the matter,” “during the matter,” and “after the matter.”

Next comes the place proper to dialecticians, that from consequents, antecedents, and repugnant terms. For the things joined together that were discussed shortly before do not always occur. Consequents, however, are always present. By consequents I mean things that necessarily follow a matter. The same applies to antecedents and repugnant terms. Whatever precedes any matter is necessarily connected with that matter, and whatever is repugnant to it is of such a kind that it can never be connected with it.

Having disposed of the topic of adjuncts, he now discusses antecedents, consequents, and incompatibles. This topic has been divided, as it were, into three members. Marcus Tullius did not mention the name of this topic, but it seems to me that it should be called wholly conditional. Once its nature has been made entirely clear, it will also become more evident that the name we have assigned to it was rightly given.

First, therefore, the definition of each individual part must be supplied. An antecedent, then, is that which, once posited, necessarily has something else following from it; similarly, a consequent is that which necessarily exists if it has been established that the thing of which it is the consequent preceded it. An incompatible is something that cannot exist simultaneously with that which it is said to oppose.

We have already stated that antecedents, consequents, and incompatibles constitute a single topic; I shall show briefly how it is one. When it was first being asked in what way the topic of consequents, antecedents, and incompatibles could be one, the answer was that it belongs to the same mind and understanding to foresee things that agree with one another as well as things that disagree. For this reason too the topic appears to be one. Things that agree have two parts: one is the antecedent, the other the consequent. For when one accompanies another as its predecessor, they must agree with each other in the very succession of nature. In the case of incompatibles, although there are two parts, there is nevertheless one name for both, since both are called incompatibles.

No one is unaware that the things that oppose and disagree with one another are two. They differ in this respect: antecedents and consequents have two names, although there is one agreement between them; incompatibles, however, have one name, since there is one disagreement in both. Therefore the same mind and the same mode of understanding apprehend both what precedes and what accompanies it. For it is impossible to understand an antecedent without considering in the same thing what its consequent is; likewise, [Col. 1125A] one cannot understand a consequent unless what precedes it is apparent. Similarly, no one can understand an incompatible without understanding that with which it is incompatible.

But since the same faculty can discern both similarities and dissimilarities, and since there is a certain agreement and harmony through natural similarity between antecedents and consequents, whereas disagreement in incompatibles is dissimilarity, it is necessary that one and the same faculty examine the nature of antecedents and consequents and of incompatibles. Hence they too constitute one topic, since they are comprehended by one act of understanding.

An objection was raised against this: Why, then, did Marcus Tullius earlier enumerate one topic from similarity and another from opposition? For, according to the reasoning proposed, since one faculty weighs similarity and opposition, there ought to have been one topic of similarities and opposites. The answer was that antecedents and consequents are not said to agree with one another in the same way as things called similar.

Among similar things there is only one quality, and they are called similar according to that same quality. In antecedents and consequents, however, there is not a similarity of quality but a certain agreement of nature. Moreover, things that are similar can exist without one another, whereas antecedents and consequents cannot exist without one another. For this reason, there seems to be no natural connection between consequents and antecedents and similarity.

This reasoning does not seem very adequate, nor does it explain what it was attempting to demonstrate. Yet this is certainly the firmest point: the treatment of this topic is always accommodated to conditional propositions. [Col. 1125C] A conditional proposition is one that asserts that something exists on condition that something else exists, as when we say, “If it is day, it is light.”

This consequence between things is easily turned into incompatibility. For if a negation is inserted into the consequent things, incompatibility is produced from the consequents, in this way: “If it is day, there is light.” The incompatible form is: “If it is day, there is no light.” For “it is day” and “there is no light” are incompatible.

This incompatibility consists in the condition. We say, “If it is day, there is no light,” because night is contrary to day. The consequent of night, however, is that there is no light; therefore, “it is day” and “there is no light” are incompatible.

The proof that this incompatibility consists in the condition is that, if the condition is removed, there is no incompatibility, as follows: “It is day; there is no light.” For the two disjoined propositions each express their own meaning, and they are not understood to have anything in common. Taken at different times, therefore, they are true and are not incompatible.

Just as in the propositions “It is day” and “There is light” there is no consequence, because the condition that makes the proposition connected is absent, but each proposition, disjoined from the other, completes its own meaning, so in the propositions “It is day” and “There is no light” there is no incompatibility, because each preserves its own meaning when separated from the other.

But if a condition is introduced into these propositions, then in the former case the meaning is joined so that the propositions become consequent, and in the latter so that they become incompatible. Thus: “If it is day, there is light.” This consequent proposition is produced as one proposition from two [Col. 1126A] through the intervening condition. But if it is put this way—“If it is day, there is no light”—the propositions are incompatible. For what follows from the antecedent, once negated, must necessarily be incompatible with it.

Furthermore, the argument that arises from antecedents and consequents is born from the parts of one connected proposition. For in a conditional proposition one part is the antecedent and the other the consequent. If an argument is made from incompatibles, then again such an argument must arise from the members of one proposition.

Thus the propositions “It is day” and “There is light” cannot be one proposition unless they are joined by a condition, so that one is the antecedent and the other the consequent. For this reason no argument from antecedent and consequent can be made from them as they stand. Likewise, the two propositions “It is day” and “There is no light” cannot be one proposition [Col. 1126B] unless, by the addition of a condition, they are reduced, as it were, to the meaning of a single proposition whose parts are incompatible.

For just as in a connected proposition one part is the antecedent and the other the consequent, so in an incompatible proposition both parts oppose and disagree with each other. Moreover, an incompatible proposition holds the contrary relation to a connected proposition: just as in the latter what precedes draws along with it what follows, so in the former the parts cannot exist together. Contraries, moreover, are usually placed under the same genus.

Therefore, if a connected proposition is constituted by a condition, an incompatible proposition likewise subsists in a condition. And if a condition produces both the consequence and the incompatibility of propositions, there can be no doubt that this topic is rightly called conditional and is established as one topic in a condition, with its parts divided into antecedent, consequent, and incompatible. For one part of a connected proposition is the antecedent and the other the consequent; but both parts of an incompatible proposition are incompatible and discordant. Thus the parts of a connected proposition are antecedent and consequent, whereas those of an incompatible proposition are incompatibles.

Nor should the following disturb our understanding: “It is day” and “There is light” agree with one another in a certain respect, while “It is day” and “There is no light” disagree and conflict with one another. A proposition is connected when, if one thing has preceded, another follows. Likewise, a proposition is incompatible when, once one thing is posited, something else is inferred that cannot exist—unless the force of the condition produces this result.

Accordingly, I believe it has been clearly demonstrated that this topic is called conditional and that Marcus Tullius rightly established it as one topic. How an argument is made from antecedents, consequents, and incompatibles I shall explain later.

But since it belongs to no other discipline to examine what follows what, or what is incompatible with what, except dialectic, which especially claims expertise in this matter, he says that this topic belongs wholly to the dialecticians and is also very different from adjuncts.

The first reason is that adjuncts can reveal and indicate one another, but cannot bring their nature to completion or fulfillment. For example, the sound of feet can indicate and announce walking, but it cannot produce walking. The sound of feet does not cause walking; nor, necessarily, does walking cause there to be a sound of feet.
