Often one walks without any sound of feet being heard; often the feet can be moved and make a sound without walking, when one does not change position. For this reason adjuncts are not always found. When a conclusion has been proposed that we are attempting to prove, arguments from adjuncts often fail because the adjuncts themselves also sometimes appear to be absent.

Antecedents, consequents, and incompatibles, however, are never absent. Everything that exists in reality has something that either naturally follows it or precedes it. It also has something from which it differs by a diversity of nature. Thus animal follows a human being, but precedes substance. We say, “If it is a human being, it is an animal”; animal precedes substance when we propose, “If it is an animal, it is a substance.” An animal is incompatible with a dead thing when we say, “If it is an animal, it is not dead.”

Furthermore, adjuncts are distributed according to time: before the thing, together with the thing, and after the thing. In the case of antecedents, consequents, and incompatibles, however, it makes no difference how they are related in time. For things earlier in time often accompany one another; things later in time precede one another; and things simultaneous in time sometimes precede and sometimes follow one another, as we have also often said above.

Moreover, antecedents and consequents cannot leave one another, nor can things incompatible with one another cohere. Incompatibles are necessarily unconnected with each other. Adjuncts, however, possess no necessity, since they can both be joined to one another and separated from one another.

When matters stand thus, a very difficult question arises. To those who look at the matter superficially, this topic seems to differ in no way from those previously mentioned—those from genus, species, or contraries. For a genus always follows a species, a species precedes a genus, and contraries cannot exist simultaneously.

This must be resolved as follows. First, not every consequent is a genus, nor is every species an antecedent. Incompatibles are not themselves contraries, but the consequents of contraries, as we showed in our exposition of the topics proposed by Marcus Tullius.

In addition, when an argument is made from a genus, the genus itself is assumed; likewise, the species is assumed when we wish to prove something from it. But when we attempt to demonstrate something from antecedents, we use in the assumption that which preceded in the conditional proposition, even if it was not a genus. Similarly, if an argument is made from a consequent, the argument is drawn from the consequent part of the conditional proposition, even if that part is not a species.

For example: “If it is fire, it is light.” Fire is antecedent; lightness is consequent. Neither is the genus or species of the other. Let us assume, then: “But it is fire.” I have assumed what was antecedent, from which the conclusion is demonstrated: “Therefore it is light.” But if we assume it in this way—“But it is not light”—I have assumed what was consequent. The conclusion is therefore drawn and demonstrated: “Therefore it is not fire.”

You see, then, that we are now speaking of antecedents and consequents as they are placed in a conditional proposition and understood either to precede or to follow.

When, however, an argument is made from a genus, the species is the thing about which we are attempting to prove something, while we assume the genus not as something preceding but as something containing it, so that whatever is considered to exist in the genus ought also to be applicable to the form. For as long as the genus remains, it does not depart from its species.

When we take an argument from a species, the genus is indeed the thing about which something is sought; but we strive to make what we are attempting to show concerning the genus more readily recognized from the species.

For example, suppose that a legacy had been left to Fabia as wife, if she were a materfamilias (“mother of a household”). Since she had not entered into manus—namely, by the conventio in manum (“entry into the husband’s legal power”), which is a species of wife—we separate “wife,” which is the genus of materfamilias, from the right to the legacy, and refer the legacy to the species, namely the materfamilias.

But it seems necessary to examine more deeply whether the topic of antecedents and consequents appears wholly superfluous, since arguments made from it in whatever way do not depart from the other topics described above. For whatever argument is drawn from antecedents and consequents is seen to have been drawn either from the whole, from the parts, from conjugates, or from some one of the remaining topics, as follows:

“If equity has been established as useful for obtaining one’s own property, civil law is useful.” The argument proceeds from what precedes to what follows: “Therefore”—that is, it is an argument from definition, specifically from the assumption of the antecedent.

But if I say, “Civil law is not useful; therefore equity has not been established as useful for obtaining one’s own property,” the argument has been taken from the topic of definition through the assumption of the consequent.

Likewise, from an enumeration of parts: “If he has been manumitted neither by census nor by the other means, he is not free; but if he has been manumitted by census or by the other means, he is free. Therefore he is free.” Or: “But he is not free; therefore he was manumitted neither by census nor by the other means.”

It should be noted what the force of each argument is and how it is presented. For there are arguments suited to categorical syllogisms. Thus an argument from definition may be made as follows: “Civil law is equity established for those who belong to the same state, for obtaining their own property. That is useful. Therefore civil law is useful.”

Likewise, from the parts: “He who has been manumitted neither by census, nor by vindicta, nor by a will has not been made free from slavery. Stichus, however, has been manumitted neither by a will, nor by census, nor by vindicta. Therefore Stichus is not free.” The same applies to the other cases.

Everything that can be expressed through a categorical syllogism can also be expressed through a conditional syllogism. For every categorical proposition can be converted into a conditional one. Thus, “Every human being is an animal” is categorical; it can easily be converted into the conditional form: “If it is a human being, it is an animal.”

Not every conditional proposition, however, can be converted into a categorical one, as in: “If she has given birth, she has had intercourse with a man.” No one can say that her having given birth is identical with her having intercourse with a man, in the way that we say that a human being is an animal.

There is a different principle in propositions expressed as follows: “She who has given birth has had intercourse with a man.” This is similar to the proposition “If she has given birth, she has had intercourse with a man.” But a categorical proposition says that what has been the subject is identical with what has been the predicate. A conditional proposition, however, posits that if what is the antecedent exists, what follows necessarily accompanies it.

When a proposition is categorical, therefore, if it is converted into a conditional one, a different proposition is produced. When it is said, “Every human being is an animal,” the human being himself is asserted to be an animal. But when it is said, “If it is a human being, it is an animal,” the meaning is not that the one who is a human being is an animal, but that, once being a human being has been posited, it follows that the thing is an animal.

A conditional syllogism, therefore, is established in antecedence and consequence. Although it may be made through definition, through an enumeration of parts, through conjugation, or by any other method, it nevertheless retains its proper form and is conditional—that is, it uses its own distinctive power. In a certain sense, the other arguments appear to be subordinate to it as to their own nature.

For example, when an argument is made from definition, if the syllogism has been constructed in categorical form, it is said to have been drawn from definition. But if the argument has been made through a hypothesis, it becomes a conditional syllogism, and the assumption distinguishes whether it is drawn from the antecedent part or from the consequent part.

Thus, even if a conditional argument is presented through the other topics, it nevertheless has a form of its own, since it is established in antecedence and consequence. Definition, parts, conjugation, and the other topics then become, as it were, the things themselves rather than topics when they enter into a condition; but if the condition is removed, the argument will appear to have proceeded from those topics themselves.

If a condition joins a proposition, then the things contained in the propositions are themselves, as it were, parts of the argument, while the topic is established in the condition. [Col. 1129C] These points have been stated as though this conditional topic could not be treated in any other way unless it included one of the topics mentioned above. But it can often be found apart from them, as when we say: “If it is a human being, it is capable of laughter”; “If it is a raven, it is black.” Here the argument contains neither a definition, nor parts, nor any other topic enumerated above.

Furthermore, it is easy to discern the differences among the individual topics. The topic from the whole is drawn from substance; that from the parts, from the composition of the thing. Such an argument cannot be found in simple terms. The topic from a characteristic is drawn from a sign; that from an interpretation, from an explanation. The topic from conjugates is drawn from what is derived from the same source in both cases. That from a genus is drawn from what contains; that from a form, from what is contained; that from a difference, from what differs; that from similarities, from the same quality; that from contraries, from things widely different from one another; that from causes, from things possessing the power of producing; that from effects, from things that have received the power of another’s productive activity; that from adjuncts, from proximity of nature; that from comparison, from greater, equal, or lesser things; and that from relation, from equal or unequal quantity.

The mode of antecedents is altogether different. It consists in this: if something has been posited, something else will exist in every respect; this is called the consequent. Its meaning consists in the fact that, whenever anything has preceded, something else has followed. The meaning of incompatibles consists not only in the fact that they can neither follow nor precede one another, but also in the fact that they cannot exist simultaneously. It is beyond doubt that these relations consist in a condition.

These matters having been settled, and since Marcus Tullius expressed the distinctive nature of the topic succinctly and clearly, as far as he could in passing, he now adds the ways in which it is appropriate to use the same topic. Since this part of the *Topics* requires a more careful explanation, I shall make it the conclusion of the fourth book and present the remainder in the fifth.

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 1129]

[Col. 1129C] We have treated fully and abundantly, most accomplished of rhetoricians, Patricius, all the hypothetical syllogisms in the books that we composed principally for their instruction. From them the reader will receive a complete and perfect doctrine, provided that he has leisure to resolve these matters. But since we have now undertaken to explain Cicero’s *Topics*, and since in it Marcus Tullius mentions certain modes, I think I should briefly discuss the nature of these seven conditional syllogisms and the way their propositions are joined, so that, once these matters have been properly introduced to their understanding, Cicero’s examples may be recognized more easily.

Everything that is questioned in an inquiry is proved either by probable or by necessary arguments. Every argument either falls into the order of a syllogism or derives its force from a syllogism. Every syllogism, in turn, consists of propositions. Propositions are either simple or compound. Simple propositions are joined from simple parts of speech. The simple parts of speech that join an uncompounded proposition are a noun and a verb, as when we say, “It is day,” or “It is spring day,” or “It is a clear day.” Here the noun and the verb together constitute the entire force of the proposition.

Every simple proposition consists of a subject and a predicate. The subject is that of which what is predicated is said. The predicate is what is said of that which is the subject. Sometimes the verb is joined to a predicated noun; sometimes the verb itself is predicated. It is joined to a predicated noun in the proposition “The day is clear”: “day” is the subject, “clear” the predicate, while “is” is the verb joined to “clear,” which, as we have said, is the predicate. But if the proposition consists only of a noun and a verb, as when we say “It is day,” then “day” is the subject, and “is” is undoubtedly predicated. A proposition cannot consist of a verb alone, for every proposition is either true or false; but unless some verb is added by which something is said to be or not to be, no truth or falsity can be discerned in propositions.

Often, too, propositions consist of entire expressions, as when we say, “Crossing into Africa is useful to the Romans.” Here “crossing into Africa” is the subject, “useful to the Romans” the predicate, and “is” is joined to the predicate. All propositions of this kind are therefore called predicative propositions. They are called predicative because they predicate one thing of another. Syllogisms formed from these propositions are likewise called predicative according to the forms of their enunciations.

From these predicative propositions arise compound propositions. Some are joined by a copulative conjunction, as in “Both it is day and it is light.” Others are formed through a condition; these are also called conditional enunciations. They are propositions in which the parts are led toward consequence and conditional connection by means of a conjunction placed between them.

Suppose, then, that there are two predicative propositions: one says, “It is an animal”; the other says, “It is a human being.” If, when these are joined, the conjunction “if” is placed between them, it produces: “If it is a human being, it is an animal.” You see, therefore, how a conjunction has joined two predicative propositions into one conditional proposition.

Since this is so, all such propositions are called hypothetical, that is, conditional, and syllogisms arising from them are called hypothetical or conditional syllogisms. Every hypothetical proposition is formed either by connection or by disjunction. By connection: “If it is day, it is light.” By disjunction: “Either it is day or it is night.”

Among those formed by connection, some are joined from two affirmative propositions, as in “If it is day, it is light,” for both “it is day” and “it is light” affirm something. Others are formed from two negative propositions, as in “If it is not light, it is not day,” since both “it is not light” and “it is not day” are negations. Others are joined from an affirmative and a negative proposition, as in “If it is day, it is not night.” Others are joined from a negative and an affirmative proposition, as in “If it is not day, it is night.” All, nevertheless, are formed by connection. For either an affirmation follows an affirmation, or a negation follows a negation and is connected with it, or an affirmation is followed by a negation, or a negation by an affirmation.

It is clear that repugnant propositions arise from connected propositions. Where an affirmation follows an affirmation, if a negation is inserted between them, it produces repugnance, as follows: “If it is day, it is light.” Here an affirmation follows an affirmation. But if I say, “If it is day, it is not light,” the connected parts of the proposition conflict because a negation has been inserted.

Likewise, whenever a negation follows a negation, if the negative adverb is removed from the latter part of the proposition, the parts become repugnant, as in “If it is not an animal, it is not a human being.” This connection is composed of two negative propositions. But if the negative adverb is removed from the latter part—that is, from “it is not a human being”—the result is “If it is not an animal, it is a human being,” which is repugnant.

Again, when an affirmation follows a negation, the parts become repugnant whether a negation is added to the latter part or removed from the former. For example: “If it is not day, it is night.” Here an affirmation follows a negation. If a negation is added to the latter part, namely “it is night,” the result is “If it is not day, it is not night.” If the negation is removed from the former part, the result is “If it is day, it is not night.” In either case the proposition necessarily becomes repugnant.

If a negation follows an affirmation and the negative adverb is removed from the latter part, the connected parts fall into repugnance, as in “If he is awake, he is not snoring.” Here a negation follows an affirmation. But if the negation is removed from the latter part, namely “he is not snoring,” the result is “If he is awake, he is snoring,” and this is repugnant.

In connected and disjunctive propositions, one must understand that both the force of the question and the force of the argument are contained in their parts. Suppose, for example, that it is doubtful whether there is light, and that this is to be established from the fact that it is day. If the proposition is “If it is day, it is light,” the latter part of the whole proposition, namely “it is light,” is the question. For what is asked is whether there is light. The former part, namely “it is day,” contains the force of the argument. From the fact that it is day, the existence of light will be proved. The same reasoning applies in all the other connected and disjunctive propositions.

Since in all these cases the syllogism and argument are adapted to demonstrate one part of the question, while every question is doubtful, the syllogisms adapted to an ambiguous question must themselves be certain and clear. To be such, they must consist of propositions that are clear, evident, and manifestly true. Some propositions are known in themselves; others require proofs.

Every syllogism, once its enunciation has been proposed, contains an assumption of one of its parts, so that it may conclude what is at issue. For example: “If it is day, it is light.” To demonstrate that there is light, I assume one part of the proposition just established and say, “But it is day”; then I conclude what is at issue: “Therefore, there is light.”

Since, then, in reaching the conclusion of a syllogism we use the whole enunciation in the proposal and one part of the enunciation in the assumption, the things we use must contain nothing doubtful, since the ambiguous receives its credibility from them. If the proposition is sometimes known and evident in itself but sometimes requires proof, the assumption likewise is sometimes recognized as true in itself but sometimes requires supporting evidence. Thus, if both the proposition and the assumption must be demonstrated, the syllogism becomes five-part, as Cicero also states in the *Rhetorics*: it consists of the proposition, its proof, the assumption, its proof, and the conclusion. If neither requires proof, it is three-part, consisting of the proposition, the assumption, and the conclusion. If one of them requires demonstration, it becomes four-part, consisting of the proposition, the assumption, the proof of one of them, and the conclusion. The proof of the conclusion itself is completed by the preceding proposition and assumption.

Since every hypothetical proposition is divided into connection and disjunction, in connected propositions we call one part the antecedent and the other the consequent. We also call the consequent the connected part, as in the proposition “If it is day, it is light.” “It is day” comes first; “it is light” is joined to it. In disjunctive propositions the reasoning is not the same, because the things proposed cannot exist simultaneously and therefore cannot in any way be called connected.

The antecedent and the subsequent are judged from their position: what is placed first is rightly called the antecedent, and what is placed later is rightly called the subsequent.

From connected propositions arise the first and second modes of hypothetical syllogisms. When a negation is added to a connected proposition formed from two affirmations, and that negation is itself denied, the third mode is added. From disjunctive propositions, with assumptions made in different ways, arise the fourth and fifth modes. When both are composed through negation, the sixth and seventh arise. These, then, are the seven hypothetical conclusions mentioned by Marcus Tullius in the *Topics*. Their order and examples must now be set out.

The first mode occurs when, in a connected proposition, we assume what comes first in order to show what follows and to establish that it must be as the connection states. If, however, we assume what is connected and follows, no syllogism at all results. An example is: “If it is day, it is light.” If we wish to demonstrate that it is light, we must assume that it is day, as follows: “But it is day; therefore, it is necessarily light.” If, however, we assume that it is light and say, “But it is light,” it does not necessarily follow that it is day; consequently, the conclusion has no necessity. Where there is no necessity, a syllogism cannot be understood.

The form of the first mode is therefore: “If it is day, it is light; but it is day; therefore, it is light.”

There are, nevertheless, cases in which the assumption is equally valid whether the antecedent or the consequent is assumed, as with “human being” and “capable of laughter.” For “If it is a human being, it is capable of laughter; but it is a human being; therefore, it is capable of laughter; but it is capable of laughter; therefore, it is a human being.” In these cases the reason is that “human being” and “capable of laughter” are equivalent terms, and therefore, when one is posited, the other necessarily accompanies it. But since this is not the case universally, we say that it is not universally valid to prove what preceded by assuming what follows.

The second mode occurs whenever, by assuming what comes later and is consequent, what preceded is removed, as follows: “If it is day, it is light.” Here, if we assume that it is not light, we assume the contrary of what was stated in the proposition, saying, “But it is not light”; consequently, it follows that it is not day. But if we deny the day—that is, if in the assumption we put forward the antecedent in the contrary form to that in which it was placed in the proposition—what is connected is not removed. If we say, “But it is not day,” it does not immediately follow that it is not light, for it is possible that it is not day and yet that it is light.

The form of the second mode is therefore: “If it is day, it is light; but it is not light; therefore, it is not day.”

The first mode assumes what preceded in order to establish what is connected; it cannot assume what is connected in order to establish what preceded. The second, conversely, assumes what follows in order to overturn what preceded; but it cannot assume what preceded in the contrary form in order to remove what is connected.

The third mode occurs when a negation is inserted between the parts of a connected proposition formed from two affirmations, and that very negation is itself denied. Such a proposition is called in Greek **ὑπεραποφαντική** (*hyperapophantic*, “super-negative”), as in the proposition given above: “If it is day, it is light.” If a negation is inserted between its parts, the result is: “If it is day, it is not light.” If this is then denied, the result is: “It is not the case that, if it is day, it is not light.” The meaning of this proposition is that, if it is day, it is impossible for there not to be light.

This is called a super-negative proposition; all propositions in which a negation is set against a negation are of this kind, as in “It is not day,” and again:

> And likewise the Ausonian colonists, a race sent from Troy.

In this former proposition, if we place the first part—that it is day—in the assumption, it follows that there is light, as follows: “It is not the case that, if it is day, it is not light; but it is day; therefore, it is light.”

This mode differs greatly from the preceding ones. In the mode arising from antecedents, the antecedent is posited so that what follows may be established. In the mode arising from consequents, the consequent is destroyed so that what preceded may be removed. Here neither occurs: the antecedent is not posited so that what follows may be confirmed, nor is the subsequent destroyed so that what preceded may be overturned. Rather, the antecedent is posited so that what follows may be destroyed.

This form of proposition contains mutually repugnant parts, for it is contrary to and conflicts with the proposition “If it is day, there is no light.” Yet the resulting assertion is valid because the repugnance of the consequents, produced by the intervening negation, is destroyed by another negation and entirely restored to the force of an affirmation. Since it is understood and true that, if it is day, there is light, it is repugnant and false to say, “If it is day, there is not light.” When this is denied, the true proposition is “It is not the case that, if it is day, there is not light.” It is equivalent to the affirmation “If it is day, there is light,” because a doubled negation produces an affirmation.

Arguments are similarly formed from the repugnant parts of propositions, whether two negations, a negation and an affirmation, or an affirmation and a negation are joined. How repugnant propositions are formed from such connected propositions has been stated above.

From a proposition joined from two negative parts, an argument from repugnance is formed as follows. Let the proposition be: “If there is no light, it is not day.” Let its repugnant form be: “If there is no light, it is day.” Let us add a negation to this, so that it becomes true: “It is not the case that, if there is no light, it is day.” We assume: “But there is no light”; therefore we conclude: “It is not day.”

Likewise, from a negation and an affirmation comes the proposition: “If it is not day, it is night.” A negation is added to its latter part, producing: “If it is not day, it is not night.” This is repugnant. Let it nevertheless be denied so that it becomes true: “It is not the case that, if it is not day, it is not night.” We assume: “But it is not day”; we conclude: “Therefore, it is night.”

Again, from the same proposition, which is joined from a negative and an affirmative and says, “If it is not day, it is night,” a negation may be removed from the former part, producing the repugnant proposition: “If it is day, it is night.” Let a negation be added to it so that it can be true: “It is not the case that, if it is day, it is night.” We assume: “But it is day”; we conclude: “Therefore, it is not night.”

If the connected proposition is formed from an affirmation and a negation, as in “If he is awake, he is not snoring,” the negation is removed from the latter part, producing: “If he is awake, he is snoring.” But this is repugnant. The whole proposition is again denied so that it becomes true: “It is not the case that, if he is awake, he is snoring.” We assume: “But he is awake”; it necessarily follows: “Therefore, he is not snoring.”

These four conclusions from repugnant propositions are understood to belong to the third mode. Tullius mentioned three of them: one he taught by rule, namely the one produced by a proposition joined from two affirmations; two by example, namely the one arising from a proposition joined from two negations and the one generated by a connected proposition formed from an affirmation and a negation. He passed over the remaining one, because by its similarity to the others it seemed also to fall under the third mode of conclusion.

The fourth mode consists in disjunction, as follows: “Either it is day or it is night; but it is day; therefore, it is not night.” The reasoning is that, once a disjunctive enunciation has been proposed, its first part is assumed affirmatively so that the subsequent part may be removed. From the proposition “Either it is day or it is night,” we assume, “But it is day,” affirming that it is day; from this affirmative assumption it follows that it is not night.

The fifth mode occurs when, in the same disjunctive proposition, what comes first is assumed by negation so that what comes later may be inferred, as follows: “Either it is day or it is night; but it is not day”; the assumption is made through negation, and it follows that it is night.

The sixth and seventh modes are derived from the disjunctive proposition of the fourth and fifth modes by adding one negation, removing the disjunctive proposition, and adding a copulative conjunction to the propositions previously placed in disjunction, as follows: “It is not the case both that it is day and that it is night.”

Earlier the disjunctive proposition was: “Either it is day or it is night.” From this we removed the conjunction “or,” which was disjunctive, added “and,” which is copulative, and placed a negation before the whole. Thus, from the parts of the disjunctive proposition joined together, with a negation added, we formed the proposition of the sixth and seventh modes: “It is not the case both that it is day and that it is night.” In this proposition, if we assume that it is day, it follows that it is not night: “But it is day; therefore, it is not night.”

The seventh mode occurs when the first part of the proposition is assumed by negation so that the latter part follows, as follows: “It is not the case both that it is day and that it is night; but it is not day; therefore, it is night.”

This mode of proposition can be found only in cases where one of two alternatives must exist, such as day or night, illness or health, and anything else that has no middle state.

We have explained most carefully in the books that we composed on hypothetical syllogisms how the truth of all conditional syllogisms is constituted. What we have added here is not the fullest possible treatment of the subject, but only what could serve to explain Marcus Tullius’ meaning.

To summarize briefly everything we have said: the first mode occurs whenever what is first in a connected proposition is assumed as it is placed in the proposition, so that what is second may follow, as in: “If it is day, it is light; but it is day; therefore, it is light.”

The second mode occurs whenever, in a connected proposition, what is second is assumed in the contrary form to that in which it was placed in the proposition, so that what is first may be removed, as in: “If it is day, it is light; but it is not light; therefore, it is not day.”

The third mode occurs when the parts of a connected proposition joined by affirmations are divided by a negation, and the whole proposition is again denied; what comes first is assumed just as it is stated in the proposition, so that what is second, as stated in the proposition, may be concluded in the contrary form, as follows: “It is not the case that, if it is day, it is not light; but it is day; therefore, it is light.”

Here, by positing what preceded—that is, that it is day—what followed—that is, that there is no light—is overturned; for every affirmation overturns a negation.

The same applies when the connected proposition is formed from two negations, the negation is removed from its second part, and the whole proposition is denied; once the first part of the proposition has been posited, what followed is destroyed, as follows: “It is not the case that, if there is no light, it is day; but there is no light; therefore, it is not day.”

Or it applies when the connected proposition is composed of a negation and an affirmation, a negation is added to its second part, the whole is then denied, and what comes first is posited so that what follows may be removed, as follows: “It is not the case that, if it is not day, it is not night; but it is not day; therefore, it is night.”

Or it applies when, in the same proposition joined from a negation and an affirmation, the negation is removed from the first part, the whole proposition is denied, and what comes first is posited so that what follows may be removed, as follows: “It is not the case that, if it is day, it is night; but it is day; therefore, it is not night.”

Or it applies when, in a connected proposition joined from an affirmation and a negation, the negation is removed from the latter part, the whole is then denied, and the former part is posited so that what follows may be destroyed, as follows: “It is not the case that, if he is awake, he is snoring; but he is awake; therefore, he is not snoring.”

All these are understood to belong to the third mode and to arise from repugnant propositions. In them the antecedent is always posited so that the consequent may be removed. For the assumption does not make the proposition true in the same way as the conditional proposition is made true by negating the repugnance of its parts. Rather, when the first part has been assumed, whether affirmatively or negatively, the remaining part is concluded in the contrary enunciation. If the assumption is affirmative, the conclusion will be negative; if the assumption is negative, the conclusion will be affirmative.

The fourth mode occurs when, in a disjunctive proposition, the first part is posited so that the second may be removed, as follows: “Either it is day or it is night; but it is day; therefore, it is not night.”

The fifth mode occurs whenever what comes first in a disjunctive proposition is removed so that what comes second may be posited, as follows: “Either it is day or it is night; but it is not day; therefore, it is night.”

The sixth mode occurs when a negation is placed before things that can enter into disjunction—that is, contraries or mutually repugnant alternatives lacking a middle state—and copulative conjunctions are added; what comes first is posited so that what follows may be removed, as follows: “It is not the case both that it is day and that it is night; but it is day; therefore, it is not night.”

The seventh mode occurs when, in the same proposition, what precedes is removed so that what follows may be posited, as follows: “It is not the case both that it is day and that it is night; but it is not day; therefore, it is night.”

With these matters thus established, let us turn to Cicero’s words.

Since this topic is divided into three parts—consequence, antecedence, and repugnance—the place from which an argument is found is one, but the ways of treating it are three. For what difference does it make, once you have assumed that the counted money is owed to the woman to whom all the silver was bequeathed, whether you conclude the argument in this way:

“If coined money is silver, it was bequeathed to the woman; but coined money is silver; therefore, it was bequeathed to her.”

Or in this way:

“If counted money was not bequeathed, counted money is not silver; but counted money is silver; therefore, it was bequeathed.”

Or in this way:

“It is not the case both that the silver was bequeathed and that the counted money was not bequeathed; but the silver was bequeathed; therefore, the counted money was bequeathed.”

It has been explained above that the place which arises from antecedents, consequents, and incompatibles appears properly to be one place, and that it is situated in a conditional proposition, but is distributed by a threefold division; and Marcus Tullius marks this more clearly when he says that its understanding and consideration are one, being situated in a conditional proposition, but that in the treatment of argumentation it is divided three ways. He appended examples of this matter according to the first, second, and third modes of hypothetical syllogisms, as we said a little earlier. Since these seem more intricate than can immediately be grasped at first hearing, it seemed useful to train the reader’s mind for a little while with clearer examples, so that, once its understanding had first been exercised on easier matters, it might weigh the more difficult ones without great trouble.

Argumentation from antecedents therefore occurs whenever, in a proposition stated conditionally, what precedes is assumed so that what follows may be inferred, as follows. Let there be doubt whether Tullius is an animal, and let it be granted that the same Cicero is a human being, and let this proposition be accepted: “If Tullius is a human being, he is an animal.” “Human being” is antecedent; “animal” is consequent. If, therefore, I wish to construct an argument from the antecedent, I shall assume what precedes, in this way: “But Cicero is a human being”; it follows that Cicero is an animal. This is the first mode mentioned above.

Again, argumentation from the consequent occurs whenever the assumption in the proposed conditional removes what follows, so that what preceded is destroyed, as follows: “If Cicero is a human being, he is an animal.” “Human being” precedes; “animal” follows. If, therefore, I wish to construct an argument from the consequent, I shall say: “But he is not an animal”; it follows that he is not even a human being. Yet this is plainly false, for it is established that he is a human being. It is therefore false that he is not an animal. Thus Tullius is an animal; and this is the second of the modes mentioned above.

But if the argument is made from incompatibles, in the third mode of the conclusions arranged above, we shall proceed as follows: “Not: if Tullius is a human being, he is not an animal,” for being a human being and not being an animal are incompatible. If we assume that he is a human being, we correctly conclude that he is also an animal, in this way: “But he is a human being; therefore he is an animal.” This mode is derived from a connected proposition composed of two affirmatives.

Thus, by these three modes, Tullius, who was a human being, was also shown to be an animal: first, when we assume what precedes, namely, that he is a human being; then, when in the assumption we deny what follows, namely, that he is not an animal; and finally, when, denying the incompatibility of things that follow one another, we infer what followed after positing what preceded.

With these matters understood beforehand, let us now consider the examples of Marcus Tullius. When he had said that the understanding of the place situated in consequence, antecedence, and incompatibility is simple in discovery of an argument but threefold in treatment, he added: “For what difference does it make, once you have assumed for the purpose of demonstrating that counted money is owed to the woman to whom all the silver has been bequeathed, whether you prove this from antecedents, consequents, or incompatibles?” For the same judgment is gathered in the conclusion, and the diversity of the arguments lies not in the matter itself but in the treatment of antecedents, consequents, and incompatibles.

First, then, let it be posited that someone has bequeathed all his silver to a woman, and let the question be whether counted money has also been bequeathed to the woman; and let it be granted that counted money is likewise called silver. The argument in the first mode, from antecedents, is then constructed as follows. We state it thus: “If stamped and counted money is silver, the same stamped and counted money has been bequeathed to the woman.” Here the antecedent is that stamped and counted money is silver; the consequent is that it has been bequeathed to the woman. We therefore assume what preceded, saying: “But stamped and counted money is silver”; and we conclude that stamped and counted money has been bequeathed to the woman. The whole argument will therefore run as follows:

> If stamped and counted money is silver, it has been bequeathed to the woman; but stamped and counted money is silver; therefore it has been bequeathed to the woman.

If the reader turns back to the material repeatedly presented above and clarified through many examples, he will recognize that this argument has been composed in the first mode, from antecedents.

From consequents, however, it proceeds in this way:

> If counted money has not been bequeathed to the woman to whom all the silver has been bequeathed, counted money is not silver.

Here the antecedent is that counted money has not been bequeathed, although all the silver has been bequeathed; the consequent is that counted money is not silver. If, therefore, we remove what is posterior—that is, that counted money is not silver—we shall say: “But counted money is silver,” for affirmation removes negation. It follows that the preceding part must also be removed, namely, that counted money has not been bequeathed to the woman, when all the silver had been bequeathed to her. Since every negation is consumed by affirmation, we say in the conclusion: “Therefore counted money has been bequeathed to the woman, since all the silver has been bequeathed to her.” The argument will therefore be as follows:

> If counted money has not been bequeathed to the woman, since all the silver has been bequeathed to her, counted money is not silver; but counted money is silver; therefore counted money has been bequeathed to the woman, since all the silver has been bequeathed to her.

What Tullius omitted for the sake of brevity—that is, the part of the proposition which says, “since all the silver has been bequeathed to the woman”—we have added for the sake of clearer understanding. Nor should it disturb the reader that, whereas in the examples above the assumption in the second mode was always made by negation, and the conclusion likewise inferred by negation, here both the assumption and the conclusion are made by affirmation. The reason is perfectly clear.

In the preceding examples, the first proposition was composed of affirmations, and in the second mode the assumption removed what followed and destroyed what preceded. It was therefore necessary for two affirmations to be consumed by a doubled negation, as follows: “If it is day, it is light.” Both parts are constituted by affirmation. In order, therefore, to destroy the latter part, “it is light,” which is affirmative, it must be denied. I shall therefore say: “But it is not light.” In this way we also remove by negation the preceding part, “it is day,” which is plainly affirmative, concluding: “Therefore it is not day.”

But in Cicero’s example both parts of the first, hypothetical proposition are expressed by negations, and in the assumption or conclusion they are removed only by affirmations, as follows. Cicero’s example is:

> If counted money has not been bequeathed to the woman, counted money is not silver.

Do you see that both parts are negative? Both “counted money has not been bequeathed to the woman” and “counted money is not silver” are placed in the form of negation. If, then, the consequent part of the proposition is to be removed by the assumption—namely, “counted money is not silver,” which is negative—we must say that counted money is silver. If the preceding part is to be removed in the conclusion—namely, “counted money has not been bequeathed to the woman,” which is also negative—we must say: “Therefore counted money has been bequeathed to the woman.” This, then, is properly the second mode made from consequents.

One point, however, must be noted more carefully. When Marcus Tullius briefly arranged examples for all the places, he appended to this place, which is derived from consequents, an example that belongs improperly to the second mode of conditional syllogisms and rather suits the first mode, because he makes the conclusion not from consequents but from antecedents. Thus he presented the example as being from consequents:

> If the woman, having married a man with whom the right of marriage had not been granted, sent him a divorce notice, since children born to such a union do not follow their father, nothing ought to remain as their portion.

Here the question is whether part of the dowry ought to remain with the husband. What precedes is assumed, so that the conclusion may be established, in this way: “But the woman married a man with whom the right of marriage did not exist.” The conclusion follows: “Therefore, since children born to such a union do not follow their father, nothing ought to remain for them.” This is not an argument from consequents, because what followed was not assumed, but what preceded. The antecedent was that the woman had married outside the right of marriage; what followed was that, since the children did not follow their father, nothing from the dowry should be retained for them. Thus Tullius gave, as an argument from consequents, an example that is rather from antecedents.

An argument from consequents can, however, be made if what is in question is placed first and what is to be assumed is placed afterward, as follows:

> If anything ought to remain from the dowry for the children, because the children follow their father, the woman married a man with whom the right of marriage existed.

I assume what follows by negation, thus: “But the woman did not marry a man with whom the right of marriage existed, and therefore the children born to her do not follow their father.” Thus, in the conclusion, what preceded in the proposition is destroyed. Therefore nothing ought to remain for the children.

Let this suffice concerning the second mode, for, as I think, nothing has been omitted.

The third mode, from incompatibles, is very clear, as follows:

> Not: all the silver has been bequeathed and counted money has not been bequeathed to the woman.

For the consequent was: “If all the silver had been bequeathed, counted money too would have been bequeathed.” In order, therefore, to make it incompatible, a negation was inserted into this consequent, and it was said: “If all the silver had been bequeathed, counted money would not have been bequeathed.” Since this conflicts with the truth and is false, it is restored to truth by another negation, as follows:

> Not: if the silver has been bequeathed, counted money has not been bequeathed,

so that it may correspond to the affirmation which says: “If the silver has been bequeathed, counted money has been bequeathed.”

We therefore assume for this proposition that all the silver has been bequeathed, and it follows that all the counted money has been bequeathed to the woman. The form of the argument is therefore:

> Not: if the silver has been bequeathed, counted money has not been bequeathed; but the silver has been bequeathed; therefore counted money has been bequeathed.

Tullius, however, formed the proposition in this way:

> Not: all the silver has been bequeathed, and counted money has not been bequeathed.

For this reason we inserted the conditional conjunction *if*, in order to show the kind of proposition this is. For it is made from a connected proposition with a negation added, and is thereby rendered incompatible. Nothing could show the connected character equally well as the conjunction *if*, although a copulative conjunction produces the same effect. For things that are connected are also understood to be joined, on the basis of what we said a little earlier: the argument proceeded from a proposition joined by two affirmations and then further denied by the addition of a negation.

In all this, therefore, the following has been established: counted money is owed to the woman, since all the silver has been bequeathed to her. In the examples above we assumed what preceded; then what followed; and finally what was incompatible. I think enough has now been said about explaining Cicero’s examples.

A matter may nevertheless cause some doubt. If an insufficiently discerning person looks at Cicero’s examples, he will think that the place we have said is from the genus is the same as the place from antecedents, consequents, and incompatibles, being misled by the fact that in both places Cicero uses the same example, namely, silver and counted money. But anyone who considers the matter more carefully will see that the treatment of the arguments is different even though the things are the same.

It is one thing to say that, since counted money is a species of silver, if the genus has been bequeathed, the species too has been bequeathed, because a species is never separated from its genus. It is another thing to set out a sequence in a conditional proposition and, after assuming the same parts, construct an argument by varied reasoning, as was demonstrated above. Especially since arguments of this kind can be made from consequents, antecedents, and incompatibles even apart from genera and species, as we indicated earlier in the case of day and light. For neither is day a species of light, nor light a species or genus of day. What must be considered in these cases is only that, when one has been posited, the other necessarily follows.

The places from genus or species therefore differ from the place established in a conditional proposition, because the former are derived from the relationship of universality, species, and part, whereas the latter is treated according to the order of consequence and incompatibility. After this, then, Tullius counts up the modes and conclusions of hypothetical syllogisms as follows:

Dialecticians call that conclusion of an argument the first mode of concluding in which, once you have assumed the first part, what is joined to it follows. When you deny what is joined, so that the thing to which it was joined must also be denied, this is called the second mode of concluding. When you deny something joined, and another negation is again added to it, and from these you assume the first part so that what remains must be removed, this is called the third mode of conclusion.

From these arise those conclusions from contraries used by rhetors, which they themselves call *enthymemata*—not because every judgment is not called by the proper name “enthymeme,” but just as Homer, because of his excellence, makes the common name of poets his own among the Greeks, so, although every judgment is called an enthymeme, because the judgment formed from incompatibles appears the most acute, it alone has properly acquired the common name. Examples of this kind are:

> You fear this man, but do not count the other as a source of fear.  
> You condemn the woman whom you accuse of nothing.  
> You think that the woman whom you say has deserved well has deserved ill.  
> What you know is useful; what you do not know is of no harm.

This kind of reasoning touches your own discussions in responding as well. It belongs more particularly to the philosophers, however, for with orators they share that conclusion from incompatible propositions which dialecticians call the third mode and rhetors call an enthymeme.

There are several remaining modes of the dialecticians, which consist of disjunctions, as in: “Either this or that; but this is the case; therefore that is not the case.” Likewise: “Either this or that; but this is not the case; therefore that is the case.” These conclusions are valid because in a disjunction more than one thing cannot be true. Of the conclusions I wrote above, dialecticians call the former the fourth mode and the latter the fifth.

Then they add a negative conjunction, as follows:

> Not both this and that; but this is the case; therefore that is not the case.

This is the sixth mode. The seventh is:

> Not both this and that; but not this; therefore that.

From these modes innumerable conclusions arise, and nearly the whole of dialectic is contained in them. Yet even those I have explained are not necessary for this present instruction.

Although above we have arranged all these matters in many ways, and a discussion repeated so often requires no further exposition, it will nevertheless be worthwhile, if I can do so very briefly, to insert a moderate illumination of the commentary in the words of Marcus Tullius.

When he enumerates seven hypothetical modes, he says that, in connected propositions, when what is first is assumed so that the second may be shown, this is called by dialecticians the first mode, as follows: “If this is the case, that is the case.” What he calls “this” is the first part; what he calls “that” is the second. The first is therefore assumed: “But this is the case”; and what is second is concluded: “Therefore that is the case.” For example: “If he is a human being, he is an animal”; it is assumed: “But he is a human being”; it is concluded: “Therefore he is an animal.”

Tullius says that the second mode is a structure of connected propositions in which, if the second is denied, it follows that the first also must be denied, as follows: “If this is the case, that is the case; but that is not the case; therefore this too is not the case.” In examples: “If he is a human being, he is an animal; but he is not an animal; therefore he is not a human being.”

Tullius said that, when you deny what is joined, the thing to which it was joined must also be denied, this is the second mode, as though the connected proposition were joined by affirmative parts. More generally, it would be more correct to say that when what is joined—that is, the second part—is destroyed, the thing to which it is joined—that is, the first part—is also destroyed. If the joined part is affirmative, it is destroyed by negation; if it is negative, by affirmation. The same applies to the thing to which it is joined, the first part: if that part is affirmed in the connected proposition, it is denied in the conclusion, as in Cicero’s example presently under discussion; but if the first part of the proposition is negative, it is removed in the conclusion by the contrary affirmation.

Cicero says that the third mode occurs when the things that are joined are denied, another negation is again added to them, and one of these is then posited so that what remains may be removed. Since an animal is joined to a human being, we may say:

> Not both a human being and not an animal,

and then posit one of these, so that what remains may be removed, as follows. We posit that he is a human being, saying: “But he is a human being.” Therefore what remains—“he is not an animal”—is removed, and we conclude: “Therefore he is an animal.” The argument is formed in this way:

> Not both he is a human being and he is not an animal; but he is a human being; therefore he is an animal.

He says that enthymemes arise from these conclusions from incompatibles, which rhetors commonly use. They are called *enthymemata* not because every invention cannot be called by the same name—for an *enthymema* is a conception of the mind, a term that can apply to all inventions—but because these inventions, which are briefly gathered from incompatibles, are especially acute. Because of the excellence and character of the invention, the common name of enthymeme became proper, so that rhetors call these by the quasi-proper name “enthymemes.”

The same is true among the Greeks: only the poet Homer is ordinarily called “the poet,” and whoever quotes something from Homer commonly says, “The poet said this verse.” No one then understands any poet other than Homer—not because the others are not poets, but because his excellence turned the common name into a proper one.

These enthymemes are formed as follows, being woven from contraries:

> To fear this man, but not to count the other as a source of fear.

For example, if the following were said about Lentulus, Cethegus, and the others:

> You fear killing a few citizens, lest the republic perish; yet you take no trouble over its destruction.

For it is connected that whoever did not wish a few citizens to perish would much more strongly not wish the republic to be destroyed. When a negation is inserted into this, an argument from incompatibles is formed.

Tullius expressed this briefly; let us reduce the argument to a syllogism, namely, to one from incompatibles, from which enthymemes are commonly born, as follows. Let the connection be: “If someone fears that a few citizens will be killed, he fears that the republic will perish.” A negation is inserted in this way: “If someone fears that a few citizens will be killed, he does not fear that the republic will perish.” Another negation is joined:

> Not: if someone fears that a few citizens will be killed, he does not fear that the republic will perish.

These two negations constitute the parts of one affirmation, which says: “If someone fears this, he also fears that.” Its assumption is: “But he fears this”; the conclusion follows: “Therefore he also fears that.” The same thing is expressed if the question is put negatively: “You fear this, but do you not fear that?”

But because the syllogism is not placed whole in these arguments, as we set it out above, but rather a proposition whose assumption and conclusion are understood, it is called an *enthymeme*, as though it were a brief conception of the mind. The same mode applies in the other examples.

This comparison by Cicero, however, is understood to contain an argument not so much from incompatibles as from contraries. “To fear” and “not to fear” are contraries, unless the very expression of the words draws the argument from contraries back to incompatibility. For what he says—“to fear this, but not to count the other as a source of fear”—is such that the terms appear incompatible. “To fear” and “not to fear” are indeed contraries. But “not to count as a source of fear” and “to fear,” by the very expression, are understood as both contrary and incompatible, although they are proved to have the same meaning.

He added further examples:

> You condemn the woman whom you accuse of nothing.

The complete syllogism of this enthymeme is:

> Not: if you accuse her of nothing, you condemn her; but you accuse her of nothing; therefore you do not condemn her.

This argument therefore arises from a connected proposition composed of two negatives, as follows:

> If you accuse her of nothing, you do not condemn her.

The negation is removed from the latter part, and the entire proposition is further denied, in this way:

> Not: if you accuse her of nothing, you condemn her.

When this is turned into a question, it produces the enthymeme:

> The woman whom you accuse of nothing, you condemn.

Likewise:

> You think that the woman whom you say has deserved well has deserved ill.

The complete structure of this enthymeme is:

> Not both you think that she has deserved well and she has deserved ill; but you think that she has deserved well; therefore she has not deserved ill.

This enthymeme is completed from a connected proposition consisting of an affirmation and a negation:

> If you think that she has deserved well, she has not deserved ill.

When the negation is removed from its latter part and the entire proposition is denied, the proposition becomes:

> Not: if you think that she has deserved well, she has deserved ill.

When this is turned into a question, it makes the enthymeme:

> The woman whom you think has deserved well, you say has deserved ill.

Likewise:

> What you know is useful; what you do not know is of no harm.

This too is linked by the following syllogism:

> Not: what you know is useful and what you do not know is not harmful; but what you know is useful; therefore what you do not know is harmful.

This argument is composed from a proposition which, having been joined by two affirmations, received a negation in the middle and was further denied. When put in the form of a question, it becomes the enthymeme:

> What you know is useful; what you do not know is of no harm.

The general meaning of all the examples above is this: one cannot properly condemn a woman whom one accuses of nothing; it is disgraceful to say that a woman whom one regards as having deserved well has deserved ill; and if what someone knows is useful in a case, what he does not know will be harmful if it is contrary to what he knows.

He says that this place is shared by orators and philosophers, but among the philosophers is called the third mode, and among rhetors an enthymeme.

“The remaining modes,” he says, “are several,” for after enumerating the three modes above and adding four, he called them “several.” They are established in disjunctions, as follows:

> Either this is the case or that is the case; but this is the case; therefore that is not the case.

This is the fourth mode, which we too set out above in this form:

> Either it is day or it is night; but it is day; therefore it is not night.

What Cicero says “this” refers to what precedes; what he says “that” refers to what follows, whether in connected or disjunctive propositions.

Likewise:

> Either this is the case or that is the case; but this is not the case; therefore that is the case.

This too is the fifth mode, as in the examples:

> Either it is day or it is night; but it is not day; therefore it is night.

He says that the necessity of these conclusions arises because things placed in a disjunction appear to admit no middle term, so that something other than one of the two can exist. Therefore, when one is removed, the other is concluded to exist; when one is posited, the other is concluded not to exist.

But if there is a middle term that can exist apart from either alternative, neither the proposition is true nor the conclusion valid. For example:

> Either it is white or it is black.

This is false, because it can be red, which is outside both alternatives. If we posit that it is white or remove whiteness, it will not be necessary that it is not black or that it is black, because what is red can occupy the middle position.

Then, says Tullius, they add a negation of conjunctions, namely in disjunctive propositions, as follows:

> Not both this and that; but this is the case; therefore that is not the case.

The same is expressed thus:

> It is not both night and day; but it is night; therefore it is not day.

This, then, is the previously mentioned sixth mode.

The seventh proceeds from the same proposition, as follows:

> Not both this and that; but not this; therefore that.

For example:

> It is not both night and day; but it is not night; therefore it is day.

Such propositions cannot have a valid conclusion unless they concern disjunctive things that admit no middle term. Let us suppose, for example:

> Not both white and black;

and let us posit that it is not white. It does not follow that it is black, for it may be what lies between them.

This kind of proposition involving the negation of conjunctions, as Tullius says, will produce valid conclusions only if it is applied to disjunctive things that admit no middle term; otherwise the conclusion will not be valid. The proposition of the third mode differs from the proposition of the sixth and seventh in that the proposition of the third mode arises from joined terms, whereas those of the sixth and seventh arise from disjoined terms, as is clear in the preceding examples.

“From these modes,” he says, “innumerable conclusions arise.” For any one mode can be applied to infinitely many conclusions: the first and second, to everything that is connected, the number of which is unlimited if one wishes to pursue them; likewise, there is an infinite multitude of incompatibles in which the third mode is useful; and there are many disjunctive matters in which the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh modes are especially effective.

“And in these,” he says, “nearly all dialectic consists.” But for the topical places the first three modes are necessary, since they contain antecedence, consequence, and incompatibility. The remaining modes seem to have been added more for the sake of completing the discussion than because they were necessary for this instruction.

The next place concerns effective things, which are called causes, and then things effected by effective causes. I gave examples of these and of the remaining places a little earlier, drawing them from civil law. But the matter extends more broadly. For there are two kinds of causes: one which by its own power certainly effects what is subject to it, as fire kindles; the other which does not possess the nature of effecting anything, but without which the effect cannot be produced, as when someone wishes to call bronze the cause of a statue, because without it a statue cannot be made.

Among causes of the latter kind—those without which an effect is not produced—some are passive and do nothing, inert in a way, such as place, time, matter, tools, and other things of the same sort. Others make a kind of preliminary contribution toward producing the effect and provide certain aids in themselves, although not necessary ones, as intercourse had supplied a cause for love, and love for a crime.

From this class of causes the Stoics construct fate, linking it from causes that depend upon one another from eternity. Just as the classes of causes without which an effect cannot be produced can be divided, so too the effective causes can be divided. Some causes plainly produce an effect without assistance from anything else; others require assistance, as wisdom produces wise people. Whether wisdom alone, by itself, produces happiness, or whether it does not do so by itself alone, is a question.

After the place established in a conditional proposition, the next in order was the place considered from causes; after this came the place situated in the effects of causes, which supplied arguments. Marcus Tullius presented examples of these above; now he treats the reasoning more fully.

Since Aristotle posited four causes by which each thing is produced—first, that which is the source of motion; second, that from which something is made, which he calls matter; third, the account and form by which each thing is shaped; and fourth, the end for the sake of which anything is produced—Marcus Tullius, by contrast, makes the principal division of causes between those that produce something and those without which it cannot be produced. Thus what produces something is referred to the cause in which the source of motion is established; while that without which something is not produced is referred either to the understanding of matter, or to things joined to matter that assist the power of the effective cause, or to the remaining causes, as will appear a little later.

Of the cause which by its own power effects what is subject to it, he offers the following example: fire kindles. For fire is the cause of the kindling itself, and it can produce that effect; it moves and changes the thing that is kindled.

He designates the cause without which the thing to be made cannot be made by one of its parts, as when he says that bronze is the cause of a statue, because without bronze a statue cannot exist. As will become clear when the division is carried out, this is not itself the whole cause without which the effect cannot be produced, but will be shown to be a part of it.

He divides the cause without which the thing to be made cannot be produced as follows. Some things are passive and do nothing, inert in a way, and by themselves motionless unless an external act of movement is added: examples are place, time, matter, and instrument. Everything that comes into being must have a place underlying it; unless something is made in that place, the place itself remains motionless and does nothing toward the unfolding of the thing. Likewise, matter and instruments naturally do nothing unless they are moved by the hand of the craftsman. Time too underlies the operation; if the operation is absent, time itself accomplishes nothing by the activity of its own nature.

These things, although doing nothing, are nevertheless causes if an effective operation comes upon them. Others, however, being situated in motion, seem to offer a kind of preliminary movement toward effectiveness and preparation, as intercourse, which preceded love, is the cause of love, and love is the cause of crime.

From these causes, he says, Stoic doctrine connects fate. For they say that fate is a certain intertwining of preceding and subsequent causes, and their continuity after the manner of a chain, as follows: “For this reason he went abroad, because he could not endure his parents’ anger; for this reason he could not endure his parents’ anger in succession, because he was held by love for his mistress; for this reason he loved, because he had often previously had intercourse; for this reason he had intercourse, because something had preceded that led him to have intercourse.” Thus, by the order of preceding and subsequent things, fate is woven together by the Stoics, as he says.

He likewise divides the cause which by its own power effects something into one that is sufficient in itself for producing the effect and one that requires external support. A cause is sufficient in itself for producing an effect when, for example, wisdom ordinarily makes people wise by itself, with absolutely no assistance. But whether wisdom alone can make people happy is questioned: whether external things that help must be added to it, whether goods of fortune or goods of the body.

Thus the cause which by its own power produces something is either such that it does not need to seek any external aids, or else it is like a craftsman who requires certain instruments with which to unfold and shape what is to be produced.

Of all the causes that Tullius establishes in one or the other division of causes, those which by their own power unfold the effects of which they are causes—including both those that possess the power of producing by themselves and those that require external assistance—will all be placed in that Aristotelian division of causes which is the source of motion.

The example of wisdom, however, does not properly belong to such a cause, but rather tends toward account and form. For wisdom makes people wise by means of a certain account and form.

As for the cause that Tullius classifies as one without which something is not produced, matter, time, and place—that is, that from which something is made or in which it is made—are the substance of the effective nature, so that they may be comprehended under one understanding; they are either matter or are substituted in the place of matter. Instruments, however, belong to the cause that looks toward the end, though they are not themselves the end, because the end does not look toward instruments; rather, instruments look toward the end. Instruments are prepared for the sake of some end.

It may seem surprising that he did not count intercourse as a cause of love among those causes that possess effective power, but placed it among the causes without which the effect cannot be produced, although it does something and produces motion. For intercourse itself seems to produce something and resembles the cause that indeed possesses effective power but cannot act without assistance, as when the question is whether wisdom alone can produce happiness.

But the rhetor Merobaudes argued as follows: the power of causes that possess effective force is such that, even if they require external assistance, their effects nevertheless tend toward the thing to be produced. In the case of preliminary causes, however, even if something comes into existence after them, what is understood to come into existence is not principally produced by that preliminary cause.

The preliminary cause runs ahead, as it were, under a certain occasion, whereas the thing said to come into existence is born through other agents. Thus, in the case of intercourse, it is [perhaps *an solitum?*] what occurs. For perhaps a person does not have intercourse because of love; rather, love comes into existence after intercourse, although intercourse itself was not principally directed toward producing it.

Therefore, since love could not have come into existence apart from intercourse, intercourse is rightly placed among the causes without which the effect is not produced. But since it does not produce the effect by its own power—for it is not directed principally toward producing it, but merely exists before something else—it is rightly placed among the preliminary causes and not among the effective causes.

When an efficient cause has entered into the discussion, it will necessarily be permissible, without hesitation, to draw the conclusion that something is brought about by that cause. But when the cause is of such a kind that it does not contain the necessity of producing an effect, a necessary conclusion does not follow. And, indeed, that class of causes which possesses a necessary productive power generally does not lead to error. But that without which something is not produced often causes confusion. For example, although sons cannot exist without parents, it does not follow that the parents constituted a necessary cause of begetting. What cannot occur without something must therefore be carefully distinguished from that in which the effect certainly occurs.

The former is illustrated by the line:

> Would that the fir-tree beams had not fallen to earth in Pelion’s forest!

For unless the fir-tree beams had fallen to earth, that Argo would not have been made; nevertheless, the beams themselves did not possess a necessary power of producing it. But when the flame-furrowing, fire-bearing thunderbolt was hurled into Ajax’s ship, the ship necessarily caught fire. [Col. 1148A]

According to Tully, the first division of causes was into those which produce something and those without which it could not be produced. He then divided that which produces something into two further kinds: first, that which possesses a necessary power of producing it and requires no external assistance; and second, that which cannot act and produce anything unless other things assist it.

He begins with the cause that possesses productive power. For that part of it in which the necessity of producing is present immediately draws its conclusion along with it. Once a cause that necessarily produces something has been stated, the effect must also follow—for example, if someone says that the sun is present, he will demonstrate that light is present as well; or if we say that wisdom is present in someone, we must acknowledge that the person is wise.

But the same reasoning does not apply to efficient causes that require external assistance. For whenever such a cause is stated, it does not necessarily follow that the effect exists. A cause of this kind does not necessarily produce what it intends unless it is aided by external supports. The same applies to a cause that itself lacks productive power but without which the effect does not come about. For, as Tully also points out, it introduces no necessity into the production of things; and therefore the effect does not immediately follow once the cause has been stated.

For if there has been a sexual union, it does not follow that love immediately arose; nor, if there was bronze, is it necessary that a statue also existed. From this arises a further division of causes. Some causes are necessary, others not at all. Among the non-necessary causes, some are efficient, while others are those without which an effect is not produced.

The conclusion from necessary causes ordinarily causes no confusion: once such a cause has been stated, its effects immediately follow in the conclusion. Non-necessary causes, however, some of which are efficient—something he has passed over here but mentioned shortly before—do not have a conclusion corresponding to the thing produced. For although children do not exist without parents, it does not therefore follow that the parents contained a necessary productive cause, since we see that it lies within human power not to beget.

A cause that itself does not produce something but without which it cannot be produced is illustrated in the following way, as the verse of Ennius makes clear. Unless the fir-tree beams had fallen to earth, that Argo would not have been made. Argo was indeed made from the beams, but there was no necessity in the beams that a ship should be made from them.

By contrast, the efficient cause that contains its own necessity is of the following kind. When the fire-bearing, flame-furrowing thunderbolt was hurled into Ajax’s ship, the ship immediately had to catch fire, because fire is a necessary cause of ignition.

The meaning is indeed this, but the order is somewhat confused. He says:

> That class of causes which possesses a necessary productive power generally does not lead to error; but that without which something is not produced often causes confusion.

After saying this, and although he ought to have supplied an example of either or both kinds, he gave an example that properly fits neither. For having proposed either a necessary efficient cause or a cause without which something cannot be produced, he supplied an example of a cause that does produce something, but not without external assistance:

> For although children cannot exist without parents, it does not therefore follow that the parents constituted a necessary cause of begetting.

The parents—especially the male parent—are an efficient cause, but not without the female, that is, not without a certain material cause, and without that cause nothing can be produced, although it itself lacks productive power. Thus he has supplied neither an example of a necessary and efficient cause nor of that without which nothing can be produced, but of an efficient cause that is nevertheless not necessary.

It appears, however, that he silently omitted in the proposition the matter of which he supplied the example. It could have been stated more clearly as follows:

> That class of causes which possesses a necessary productive power generally does not lead to error; but what does not possess a necessary productive power, or that without which something is not produced, often causes confusion.

It should therefore be understood as though this had been said, for he supplied no example of a necessary cause. What he added afterward applies to both kinds of causes subsequently enumerated: both to the non-necessary efficient cause and to that without which nothing is produced.

Parents are said to include both the male and the female sex. The male is the cause that produces, but not a necessary one; the female is the cause that does not produce, but without which production cannot occur. Since this is so, causes must be distinguished and their necessity carefully examined. Not every cause should be stated as though the effect must follow, but only that cause in which there is a necessity of producing—even if external assistance is lacking. [Col. 1149C]
