There is also a difference among causes: some produce, as though it were their own work, without any desire of the mind, without will, and without judgment—for example, everything that has come into being perishes. Others produce either by will, by disturbance of mind, by habit, by nature, by art, or by chance.

By will: for example, when you read this little book.

By disturbance: for example, when someone fears the outcome of the present times.

By habit: for example, when someone becomes angry easily and quickly.

By nature: for example, when a vice increases day by day.

By art: for example, when someone paints well.

By chance: for example, when someone has a successful voyage.

Nothing of this kind is without a cause—indeed, nothing at all is. Yet causes of this kind are not necessary. [Col. 1149D]

He makes another division of causes as follows. Some causes, by a certain power of their own, without desire, will, or judgment, maintain one and the same order in the production of things—for example, everything that has come into being perishes. Since it has come into being, it must also necessarily perish. Yet coming into being itself does not bring about the perishing of other things through desire, will, or judgment; rather, the eternal condition of things is such that whatever has come into being, because it has received existence, eventually ceases to exist.

Again, some causes consist in will, disturbance of mind, habit, nature, art, or chance.

In will: if someone asks why Trebatius is reading a book, the answer will be: because he has the will to read.

In disturbance of mind: if someone grows pale through fear, or flees the city because he has been thrown into confusion by civil wars.

In habit: if Trebatius answers easily concerning the principles of law because, through long practice, he possesses a settled habit of knowledge of civil law; or if someone becomes easily angry because his mind has been inflamed by the habit of anger.

In nature: if someone is said to become angry because he is naturally irascible, and this vice increases in him day by day.

In art: if someone paints well because he is recognized as skilled in that art.

In chance: when things that are in no way within our control nevertheless occur—for example, successful navigation at a particular time.

Nothing among all these things is without a cause, nor is there anything in the world that some cause does not bring about. [Col. 1150B] Everything that happens has some reason why it happened; if someone can provide that reason, he has also provided the cause. For a cause is that on account of which each thing occurs.

All causes that are understood as arising from will or disturbance of mind belong to the cause that is the principle of movement, as we explained in the Aristotelian division. These are the principles of movement by which something is produced. In art, habit, and nature, however, the cause consists in reason. The form and rationale of each thing to be produced are situated in art, habit, and nature.

Chance is an external cause and is not counted among the principal causes, according to Aristotle. According to Marcus Tullius, however, chance is the hidden cause of an accomplished event. What this means will be explained shortly.

[Col. 1150C] In some causes there is consistency; in others there is none. There is consistency in nature and art, but in the others there is none. Nevertheless, among causes that are not consistent, some are evident and others hidden.

Those are evident which affect the mind’s desire and judgment; those are hidden which lie subject to fortune. Since nothing happens without a cause, an event of fortune is itself brought about by an obscure and hidden cause.

Things that happen are also partly unknown and partly voluntary. Those are unknown which occur by necessity; those are voluntary which occur by deliberation. Things that occur through fortune, however, are either unknown or voluntary.

Throwing a weapon is voluntary; striking the person whom you did not intend to strike is a matter of fortune. Hence, in your legal actions, that defense is introduced: “The weapon slipped from his hand rather than that he threw it.” [Col. 1150D]

Disturbances of mind also fall under ignorance and inadvertence, although they are voluntary; for they are cast down by reproach and admonition. Nevertheless, they involve such powerful movements that things which are voluntary may sometimes appear either necessary or, at any rate, unknown.

Again, he sets out another clear and evident division of causes. Some causes are consistent, while others are inconsistent. Causes are consistent when their effects scarcely vary; inconsistent when they are easily transferred from one result to another by slight changes.

Everything, therefore, that proceeds from nature and art is consistent. Nature and art always produce their proper work unless some uncertainty in the underlying matter stands in the way. For when one and the same craftsman repeatedly forms statues that are not very similar from the same material, the variation is not in the art. It lies either in the craftsman’s hand, which cannot attain the full integrity of the art, or in the material itself, which does not yield equally to production and form. [Col. 1151A]

The same is true of nature. It preserves its consistency when it forms a human being from a human being, and thus produces like things from like things in other cases as well. But when something monstrous is produced, the fault is attributed not to nature but rather to the material, from which nature was unable to develop in the intended way what it was striving to produce.

Habit, too, ought to have been added among the consistent causes, for what comes about from anyone’s habit is ordinarily consistent and not subject to change. Habit is so called because, through the long possession of something, it is transformed into a likeness of nature.

Perhaps, however, Tully saw that nature and art are understood to be consistent not so much in their effects as in their own rational principles—so much so that what art and nature get wrong is often attributed to the material—whereas habit itself is gathered through a kind of practice. Habit produces something not by reason and its own consistency but by use. For that reason, perhaps, he separated habit from the consistent causes, although among the remaining causes it seemed more consistent than anything except art and nature.

He divides things that are not consistent into those that are evident and those that are hidden. Evident are those that proceed from any movement of the mind, whether desire or the reasoning of judgment; hidden are those subject to fortune.

The mind is not unaware of the direction in which it inclines. Even when it sometimes possesses a good judgment, it never entirely loses awareness of the thing it produces—except in those who are utterly overcome in mind and in whom no will remains. Things that arise from will or from the mind’s judgment must therefore be known. Fortune and chance, however, are always unknown. Their nature is as uncertain as the things that occur through chance itself.

Marcus Tullius defines chance as an event produced by hidden causes. This does not appear to be a complete definition. For what if it were still unknown by what causes eclipses of the sun or moon occur? Would they therefore occur by chance and fortune, although they are governed by the consistent movements of the heavens? Would an eclipse be considered chance by those who could not discover its explanation, while in itself it would in no way be chance?

Marcus Tullius was not explaining what appeared to be chance to those who had not understood its nature; rather, he was showing what, in general, an event of fortune is. Cicero concludes that an event produced by hidden causes is chance in the following way:

> Since everything happens for definite causes whose explanation is known, the events of such things are shown not to occur by chance. But some things are thought to occur by chance when their cause cannot be understood by any reasoning. Hence an event produced by hidden causes belongs to fortune.

He therefore places consistency in the things themselves, but measures chance not by reality, rather by opinion. Thus, if someone else knows the cause of an accomplished event, what happened is not an event of fortune for him; nevertheless, it is an event of fortune for another person if the latter does not know the explanation.

When he says that all things have causes, he does not determine what kind of causes they are. Therefore he does not show what fortune itself is, or of what things it is the cause of the event. [Col. 1152A]

Let not the savage minds of men accuse me of arrogance because, as though relying on assumed authority, I oppose Tullian opinions. If anything in them seems open to opposition, I can balance it not with my own views but with matters treated by the most ancient writers.

Even if we were to claim these points as our own, they ought nevertheless to consider not the antiquity of the persons but the reasoning of what is brought against them. They should not hate what is said against men of great reputation more than they should refute it, if they can, with contrary argument.

For if Marcus Tullius pleases them excessively in his definition of things, why should they begrudge us also our approval of Aristotelian reasoning? And if the most tiresome among them persist in being offensively contentious, let them hear Marcus Tullius in the second book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, encouraging and challenging them to a contest in these words:

> Yet we are so far from being unwilling that writings be produced against us that we even desire this most of all. Greek philosophy itself would never have stood in such honor unless it had grown through the contests and disagreements of the most learned. Therefore I urge all who can do so to wrest from Greece, now languishing, the glory of this kind as well, and transfer it to this city, just as our ancestors transferred all the other things that were worth seeking through study and industry, enlarging them here.

And again:

> We who follow what is probable, and cannot advance beyond what appears likely, are prepared both to be refuted without stubbornness and to refute without anger.

Why, then, should anyone wish to overturn Marcus Tullius’s own will and judgment, when they rely upon his opinions and authority against us?

But if anyone has leisure to inspect our commentaries, let him know that we have taken these observations from Aristotle’s second book of the *Physics*. Although they touch upon discussions of higher philosophy, we should not be begrudged for mixing with rhetorical and dialectical discussions matters that are deeper in nature. Nor is it fitting that minds should grow sluggish and weary when the very ambiguity of things and the knowledge of diverse investigations ought to make them more attentive and vigorous—especially since books are by nature such that they hold the diligent reader to reading while compelling no lazy person.

Let us therefore say what an event of fortune is, or of what things chance is said to be the cause.

Everything occurs either immutably and always, as when the sun rises; or frequently, as when a horse is born four-footed; or rarely, as when a horse is born with five or three feet; or equally, when it makes no difference in the production of things toward which our will inclines.

What always occurs has no opposite that could in any way occur differently. What frequently occurs has an opposite, namely what occurs more rarely; for it would occur always, not merely frequently, unless something different occurred rarely but occasionally.

Whatever occurs through fortune is therefore not among eternal things. Who would say that the sun rises by chance? Nor is it among things that occur more frequently, for no one would say that a horse is four-footed by chance. Nor is it among things that regularly occur with equal probability, for voluntary actions do not appear to be fortuitous.

It remains, then, that an event of fortune occurs among things that happen more rarely. [Col. 1153A]

Of the things that happen, some look toward a certain end, while others do not. What end could there be if I extend my hand, bend my knees, and pick up something lying on the ground without applying it to any use?

Things that look toward an end are partly matters of will and partly of nature. Matters of will include someone’s leaving his house in order to see a friend. Matters of nature include what occurs in animals. Everything nature does in animals looks toward a definite utility, and all its operations are ordered toward their welfare and the preservation of all their limbs.

We therefore place chance and fortuitous events among things that, although they occur more rarely, nevertheless occur accidentally in things that happen for some purpose. For example, if someone leaves his house in order to see a friend and, while passing by, is struck by a stone falling from above, the event must be placed among the rarer causes. It has been added to an act of will that was directed toward a definite end: the reason for leaving the house was to see the friend.

Again, since a stone is naturally heavy, and heaviness seeks the earth, the stone’s falling has naturally occurred for a purpose. The nature of the stone was tending toward this: that its weight, reaching its proper place, should come to rest. But to this natural tendency was added what happens more rarely—namely, that it struck someone’s head. Thus, according to Aristotle, fortune or chance is the accidental cause of events that occur more rarely in things that are done for a purpose.

Since this is so, and since the Aristotelian definition differs greatly from Tully’s, one point nevertheless remains common to both: what is subject to fortune is always exposed to uncertain events. For although fortune often exercises its power in things that arise from will and are directed toward some end, what belongs to fortune occurs outside that end and does not proceed from the end that the mind had previously foreseen for itself.

When Cicero divided causes into those that are evident and those that are hidden, and said that the evident causes are those that affect the mind’s desire and judgment, it is clear that he places art, will, disturbance, and habit among the evident causes.

Will and disturbance of mind belong to desire, since we often desire something as a result of disturbance. Art and habit belong to judgment. We judge by art, while habit belongs to both: habit supplies the will, and through long practice and experience a certain consistency of judgment is formed.

He placed chance among the non-evident causes.

It is uncertain whether he places nature among the evident or the hidden causes. If he places it among the hidden causes, he would seem to regard nature itself as chance, but there is no basis for this view. If he places it among the evident causes, what desire or judgment of the mind exists in nature? Nature does not act by desiring or judging anything—unless perhaps it is because a certain aptitude of mind and body often arises from nature, and this aptitude assists the will in each matter. For we especially desire what we are suited for.

Nature is therefore placed among the evident causes, since it is also joined with judgment—as when someone is naturally endowed with sound judgment—and with desire—as when the mind naturally seeks something.

He adds another division of causes. He says that some causes are voluntary and others unknown. Voluntary causes are all those that arise from the mind’s judgment; unknown causes are those in which necessity is dominant—that is, those in which we either do not will at all or, even if we will, cannot act otherwise. This is the case with nature and chance.

By a kind of necessity of nature, heavy things are carried downward. We also say that something happens by necessity when, for example, someone unknowingly kills a passerby by throwing a stone over a wall. [Col. 1154A]

That necessity is of the following kind: it is not that the event could not have happened otherwise except by striking the person with the thrown stone, but that the will was absent. He did not do it because he wanted to.

The earlier necessity is of a different kind: it is one in which there is no will, or in which the will that exists is constrained by a stronger necessity so that it cannot accomplish what it desires. When a stone is carried downward by its own weight, there is no will, but only the necessity of nature. If a human being falls downward, however, there is a will not to fall, but a stronger natural cause compels him to be carried where he does not wish to go.

He distinguished will from fortuitous events by one particularly apt and identical example: someone throws a weapon with his hand and, unwillingly, strikes a passerby. Throwing arises from the principle of will. He threw it because he wanted to. But he did not know whom he would strike; for he would not have thrown it if he had been able to foresee that he would strike someone. Nor did he throw it because he wanted to strike.

If he had not been ignorant, he could have avoided striking the person. Hence a certain device and defense is found in the responses of legal experts:

> The weapon slipped from his hand rather than that he threw it.

For if someone is accused of murder, the best defense, when no other is available, is often that the weapon slipped from his hand rather than that he deliberately threw it. Thus the act is attributed not to will—which is what is condemned in crimes—but to ignorance. [Col. 1154C]

His judgment concerning disturbances of mind is somewhat more confused. It may be questioned whether what is done under the influence of disturbance arises from will, necessity, or ignorance.

Sins committed under disturbance appear voluntary, since the disturbed person desires or flees from something. But his disturbance is revealed in this: he avoids what ought not to be avoided and desires excessively what ought not to be desired.

Furthermore, since judgments are confused in disturbances—for otherwise disturbed people would not often desire what ought to be avoided unless their judgment had been blinded and obscured—what is done in confusion of mind is often such that the person who did it would not have wished to have done it. Consequently, disturbance of mind belongs not among voluntary causes but among unknown or necessary causes.

Indeed, a disturbed person departs so far from true discernment that he can be brought back to it by the straightforward admonition of those who offer sound advice. Hence disturbance of mind is rightly separated from voluntary causes and placed either among ignorance or among necessity.

When he says:

> Nevertheless, they involve such powerful movements that things which are voluntary may sometimes appear either necessary or, at any rate, unknown,

this should be understood as follows. Every passion of the mind disturbs judgment; and if it is more violent than can be restrained by the bridle of reason, it confuses right discernment. Thus a kind of violent necessity arises from disturbances, and it becomes doubtful whether someone who does something while disturbed acts in ignorance—for example, whether he commits an offense unknowingly by failing to foresee what will happen—or acts knowingly, or is driven by necessity.

What he said—that such things are either necessary or unknown—and his separation of the unknown from the necessary does not conflict with what he said earlier, that things which are unknown are necessary. For he divides what is unknown in a certain way: some unknown things occur by a kind of necessity, when there is either no will or the will that exists cannot resist necessity; others occur by chance, when, in the performance of things that are unknown, there is no will.

When he said that disturbances of mind are to be placed either among necessary causes or among unknown causes, he is evidently understood to have meant that disturbances of mind belong either among unknown things in which necessity is so strong that the will cannot resist, or among things in which there is no will but an offense results from blindness of judgment.

This is the case with those who serve the desire of love without restraint. Either they depart from moral goodness because their judgment is confused, and, while desiring what seems good, fall unknowingly into evil—so that excessive love is placed among a kind of chance and error—or they know that what they desire ought to be avoided but are driven by the force of a greater passion. In that case it is placed among necessary things, which either have no will or possess one so weak and feeble that it cannot in any way resist stronger passions.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 1155]

[Col. 1155B] I would not doubt, most accomplished among rhetoricians, Patricius, that there are some who will criticize this more elevated treatment from philosophy in the *Topics* with various objections, because he has inserted physics into a logical discussion.

These people are either those who dislike philosophizing altogether or those who do not think that natural causes ought to be introduced among the places of argument.

Against the former, sufficient answers have often been given both by Marcus Tullius and, in a certain sense, by human reason itself, which, being situated in motion, is always investigating something and, through its love of knowledge, neither allows itself to be deceived nor permits itself to be led away from the path of truth.

To those who think that philosophical disciplines should be separated from the rhetorical art, I believe a brief answer should be given. Something can indeed be discovered by reason, but an artisan will do it better and more easily if, in constructing the work, he acquires the power and elegance of the art.

The same is evidently true of arguments. Arguments are produced by the power of natural talent. But art, imitating the power of nature, discovers a certain method and procedure by which the thing can be accomplished more easily and better.

In this matter, the error of those who have called rhetoric a natural faculty must necessarily be criticized. They say this because anyone wholly untrained in the art ordinarily tries both to direct an accusation against another, to defend himself, and to prove something by an argument.

Those too must be criticized who have said that the same faculty lies solely in art. They ought to have noticed that every art indeed receives the material of its work from nature, but nevertheless tests its own power and elegance in the rational method it applies to that material.

Thus the things that the method of the arts accomplishes can also be done by the untrained, however it may happen. But no one accomplishes them well and easily unless he has been instructed in the method of the art.

Since the purpose of the whole work is that arguments, which nature supplies in a confused and almost closed form, should be investigated by art, he demonstrates through an example what enables art to accomplish what it promises:

> In order that arguments may be found more easily, this will be achieved if the places in which arguments are located are pointed out.

Just as someone searching for something can investigate and find it more easily if he is shown the place where the object of his search has been put, so too, when someone is trying to find an argument, if the place where the argument is located is indicated to him, he will be able to find the argument he seeks more easily.

Aristotle, and Tully as well, therefore call the seats in which arguments are located “places”—*loci*, which Aristotle called *topica*.

But since we are speaking about the seats of arguments, let us explain somewhat more fully what kind of things these are. For “place” is understood in more than one way.

Let us leave aside the places that Victorinus unnecessarily and incongruously inserts—for example, those that enclose bodies—and simply understand the places of arguments to be those that contain within themselves the arguments. When these are explained later, it will become clearer what we mean.

For now, it seems that we should discuss generally the whole theory of places, argumentation, questions, propositions, and their terms.

First, since the place treated in the *Topics* is not the place of just anything but only the place of an argument, we shall first explain the meaning of “argument” and then discuss the theory of place.

Tully defines an argument as follows:

> An argument is a reasoning that produces belief concerning a doubtful matter.

He therefore took “reasoning” as the genus.

All those who separate the power of speech from the reasoning of wisdom are unjust, and who want the art of speaking to be one thing and the art of understanding another. For if we do nothing else through speech except make public what we have thought inwardly, what possible reason is there for separating elegance of speech from the weight of ideas?

And what weight could ideas possess without comprehension of the matters about which one must speak? What other discipline teaches the nature and properties of all things, or professes knowledge of anything that can be understood, except this philosophy from which we have ventured to draw a few points? It ordinarily discusses these very matters in a very different way in its proper treatment by the wise.

Nor does it proceed as hurriedly as we do. If I had undertaken to discuss these matters at greater length, as is customary in their books, who could endure the insolence of men who want to criticize the advances of others—advances by which they themselves could make progress if they preferred to be diligent rather than quarrelsome?

Neither did antiquity lack such disputes, nor are we so delicate that we refuse to endure what has often impeded the patience of the most learned, so long as we can benefit more people and attain the judgments of the wise.

To this end our labor and the whole purpose of the work are directed. But enough of this. Let us now continue the order of the exposition we have undertaken.

Having now fully explained the place of causes, we may say that from the differences among causes a great abundance of arguments is available in major cases, whether those of orators or philosophers, while in your cases the supply may be not more abundant but perhaps more precise. For private judgments concerning matters of the greatest importance seem, in my view, to depend upon the expertise of legal advisers.

They are often present, they are called into councils, and they provide weapons to diligent advocates who have recourse to their knowledge.

In all judgments in which the phrase “in good faith” has been added, the first use of causes is that good men ought to deal well with one another. Especially in the action concerning marital property, in which what is better and more equitable is at issue, the following matters must be prepared:

What constitutes fraud; what constitutes good faith; what is equitable and good; what one partner ought to provide to another; what the person who has managed another’s affairs ought to provide to the person whose affairs they were; what one who has given a mandate, or the person to whom the mandate was given, ought to provide to the other; what a husband has handed over to his wife, and a wife to her husband.

Thus, once the places of arguments have been carefully understood, not only orators and philosophers but also legal experts will be able to discuss their consultations at length. [Col. 1157C]

Having divided and arranged the topic of causes among its proper parts, he discusses the scope of that same topic and the matters to which it may be applied more fully or more narrowly, as Cicero often does. First, he says, a considerable abundance of arguments is supplied from the topic of causes to orators and philosophers, whose discussions offer ample material. For this topic, which proceeds from causes, appears to be common to orators and philosophers: the philosophers prove the natures of things, which is proper to philosophy, while the orators prove facts, which belongs to rhetorical skill. For whenever any matter is investigated, philosophers ordinarily seek out its causes. When these [Col. 1157D] have been established, as was said above, what must be concluded follows immediately; and orators likewise seek the causes of actions in order to arouse or dispel suspicion. For this conviction remains fixed in human minds: nothing—not an action, nor any other thing except nature, the first principle of all things—can exist without its own causes. Hence the use of causes is exceedingly abundant in the speeches of rhetors and in the discussions of philosophers.

But when Marcus Tullius writes this little work, so that he may appear to have assigned almost everything to Trebatius, he demonstrates that this topic has also been allotted to legal experts, saying: Although this topic does not offer opportunities quite so abundant in the responses of legal practitioners, it can nevertheless be treated more subtly and more sharply, in accordance with the nature of the art itself—plainly compensating by the subtlety that can be present for the abundance that is lacking. For they too possess their own field in which their ability may shine forth.

The private investigation of causes belongs to the expertise of legal advisers, especially in those transactions in which this topic of causes is examined, namely, in cases founded upon good faith. In such cases the state of mind of the contracting parties is ordinarily investigated, and it can scarcely be discovered unless it is understood through the causes that preceded it. Accordingly, in those judgments in which it is added that the judges are to judge according to good faith—that is, where judges are appointed to seek not strict stipulations between the litigants but good faith—the use of causes is very extensive. It is added that one ought to act well among good men; conduct is considered, intentions are investigated, and it is determined for whom and for what reasons a matter has been conducted.

Above all, the judgment concerning the wife’s property offers the richest treatment of causes. A judgment concerning the wife’s property occurs whenever, after a divorce, there is a dispute about the dowry. For although the dowry belongs to the husband’s property while the marriage continues, it nevertheless remains within the wife’s right and may be claimed after the divorce as the wife’s property. This dowry was sometimes given under conditions such as these: if a divorce occurred between husband and wife, whatever was better and more equitable was to remain with the husband, while the remainder of the dowry was to be restored to the wife. That is, whatever, according to the judgment concerning the dowry, was better and more equitable to remain with the husband, the husband was to retain; whatever it was not better or more equitable for the husband to retain, the wife was to recover after the divorce.

In this judgment, not only the nature of the good is ordinarily considered, but also a comparison of goods is made, so that what is to be followed is not merely what is equitable, but what is better and more equitable. All these matters are ordinarily investigated from the preceding causes. For if the divorce occurred through the husband’s fault, it is better and more equitable that nothing remain with the husband. If the fault is the woman’s, it is better and more equitable that a sixth part be retained.

In all these matters legal advisers must be exceedingly well trained. Hence he also urges Trebatius to undertake the study, for he says that many matters await their assistance. “To them,” he says, “belong the questions of fraud, good faith, equity and fairness; to them belongs the question of what one partner ought to provide for another, what a person who voluntarily undertook to manage another’s business ought to provide for the person whose business it was, what a person who entrusted the management of his affairs to another ought to provide for the person to whom he entrusted it, what the husband has entrusted to the wife and what the wife has entrusted to the husband.” All these matters are causes of subsequent matters, and judgments are derived from them. For example, the judge ought to pronounce whatever judgment is appropriate in the case of wife and husband because the husband ought to provide this for the wife. Likewise, the person to whom a matter has been entrusted must be judged bound by the mandate, because this is to be observed between the mandator and the person who undertook the business. Everything that one person ought to provide for another is therefore a cause in the conduct and judgment of transactions.

Accordingly, he concluded rightly that, once the topics of arguments have been carefully understood, arguments will not be lacking for orators, philosophers, or legal advisers.

Closely connected with this topic of causes is the topic that is produced from causes. For just as a cause indicates what has been produced, so what has been produced demonstrates what its cause was. This topic ordinarily supplies orators and poets, and often philosophers as well—those, that is, who can speak elegantly and abundantly—with a remarkable wealth of expression when they announce what will follow from each thing. For knowledge of causes produces knowledge of events.

Everything that is related to something else is rightly said to be connected with it; the relation itself of things produces their connection. If something is the cause of one thing and not of another, it is the cause only of its own effect; and likewise, if there is some effect, it proceeds from the principles of causes. Therefore the topic from effects ought rightly to be connected with the topic of causes. Since things that are related to one another are always equal in their relation, the abundance of effects must be the same as the abundance of causes. For since a cause cannot exist apart from its effect, and since it is a cause in relation to an effect, it is necessary that many arguments also be supplied from events and effects, if many arguments are indeed drawn from causes. For just as the cause of any effect may be examined, so the event arising from any cause may be shown; and he rightly says that knowledge of causes produces knowledge of events. As is shown in the categories, one relative cannot be known apart from knowledge of the other relative.

The remaining topic is that of comparison, whose type and example were given above; its treatment must now be explained. Everything that is said to be greater, lesser, or equal is compared. In these comparisons the following are considered: number, kind, power, and a certain relation to particular things.

In number, things are compared in such a way that more good things are preferred to fewer good things, fewer evils to more evils; goods that last longer to those of shorter duration; goods spread far and wide to those confined within narrow limits; things from which more goods are propagated to those from which fewer are propagated; and things that more people imitate and do to those that fewer imitate and do.

In kind, things are compared so that those desirable for their own sake are preferred to those desirable for the sake of something else; what is innate and implanted to what is acquired and adventitious; what is untainted to what is contaminated; what is pleasant to what is less pleasant; what is honorable even to what is useful; what is easy to what is laborious; what is necessary to what is unnecessary; what is one’s own to what belongs to another; what is rare to what is common; what is desirable to what one can easily do without; what is complete to what is begun; wholes to parts; what is governed by reason to what lacks reason; what is voluntary to what is necessary; living things to lifeless things; natural things to non-natural things; and things made by art to things not made by art.

Power in comparison is discerned as follows: an efficient cause is weightier than one that is not efficient; things sufficient in themselves are better than things that need others; things within our power are better than things in the power of others; stable things than uncertain ones; and things that cannot be taken away than things that can.

A relation to particular things is of this kind: the advantages of rulers are greater than those of others; likewise those things are greater which are more pleasant, approved by more people, or praised by the best people. Just as these things are better in comparison, so the things opposed to them are worse.

But equality has neither elevation nor subordination, for it is equal. There are many things that are compared precisely by their equality, and the argument is generally concluded in this way: If helping citizens by counsel and by assistance is to be assigned equal praise, those who give counsel and those who defend ought to have equal glory; but the first is the case—helping citizens by counsel and assistance is to be assigned equal praise—therefore the consequence follows.

[Col. 1160A]

Every comparison is twofold. Either equals are compared with one another, or unequals. Among equal things, equality is always noted as identical. Unequals, however, are divided, as it were, into two members: the lesser and the greater. For what is lesser is not lesser in itself, but by comparison with what is greater. Likewise, what is greater is called greater by comparison with what is lesser.

Since this is so, he divides and sets before our eyes the modes of all comparisons. In doing this he does something he rarely did in the preceding topics: he sets out the principal propositions themselves in the form of comparisons, so that, whenever we have to use comparison as a topic, we may have something like a model of invention toward which we may direct the inquiring mind.

Every comparison, then, consists either in number, in kind, in power, or in some relation situated externally. Whatever we try to compare, we either compare in number and thereby decide that one thing is greater and another lesser; or, looking to the kind itself and comparing it with another, we judge of excellence; or we consider what each thing can accomplish and how far its nature can advance; or we view the thing we compare with another through the containment, so to speak, of other things and through the relation of surrounding circumstances.

Things compared in number, if they belong to the same class, are judged by preferring more to fewer. For example, if all good things were equal, anyone would rightly prefer more good things to fewer.

[Col. 1160C]

This is the principal proposition: more good things are preferred to fewer. The same reasoning is evident in the other principal propositions. But if all the things belong to opposite classes, fewness must be preferred to multitude: thus few evils are preferred to many evils, while evils themselves are in no way compared with goods. For things that are in any way balanced against one another must belong to the same class, not to opposite classes. When opposites are set face to face against one another, they cannot be compared or weighed against one another, because they are understood to be hostile to one another.

There is also a comparison according to number in the matter of time. Since time is divided into certain spans—hours, days, months, and years—among equal goods those are more desirable that last longer, a matter that everyone knows belongs to number. For duration itself declares that there are more days, months, or years during which the chosen thing continues.

Goods spread far and wide likewise surpass those confined within narrow limits, by comparison according to number. For things spread far and wide are distributed among many peoples and regions; and plurality in any matter concerns number. Again, when more good things are propagated from something, who would not judge them better than those whose productivity in goods is poorer and more restricted? Who would not also judge a good that more people imitate and perform to be superior to other goods that are not so imitated, since no one can fail to understand that this belongs to number, when plurality belongs to number?

Things are compared in kind when, considered in themselves, they are preferred to others by reason, so to speak, of their own beauty. Things desirable for their own sake are better than things desirable for the sake of something else. Thus health is desirable for its own sake, while medicine is desirable for the sake of health; therefore health is better than medicine. In this judgment we are not referring to any number or, finally, to any quantity, but to the consideration of the very kinds of health and medicine.

Things that are innate and implanted are also judged better than things acquired and adventitious. Thus the gravity innate in one’s character is far superior to that pursued through imitation. What is untainted is likewise judged better than what is contaminated. For what is untainted preserves its own form, while what is contaminated and damaged in some part has lost whatever beauty of form it possessed.

The common nature of all living creatures judges pleasant things better than less pleasant things. The wise prefer honorable things to useful things. That easy things should be preferred to laborious ones is shown by the fact that no one wishes to pursue the same goal by a laborious and harsh road when it is possible to reach it by an easy and gentle route. All labor is unpleasant; ease is pleasant.

Necessary things must sometimes be preferred to unnecessary things and sometimes placed after them. Marcus Tullius left this unstated. Necessary things are preferred to those unnecessary things that are established not by consideration of the good but by the desire for pleasure. Thus no wise person would judge banquets prepared with royal luxury to be better than those that satisfy nature’s need.

Yet some things, although unnecessary, are better than necessary things by the very character of the good. Living is necessary, and without it an animal cannot continue to exist. Philosophizing, however, is not necessary; nevertheless, to live as a philosopher is far better and much more excellent than merely to live. The former has been granted only rarely and to a few who use reason; the latter is common to us and to beasts.

Things of one’s own are likewise rightly said to be better than things belonging to others. Thus reason is better for human beings than the desire for pleasure: reason is proper to a human being, whereas the desire for pleasure is alien. Rare things are also better than common things. This topic confirms what was said above, that the philosophical life is better than life itself, for rare things easily surpass what is common.

Desirable things are also shown to be better than things one can easily do without, because they are especially desired and life is anxious without them. For example, suppose someone compares sight with hair. We endure the loss of sight less easily than the loss of hair; thus we judge sight better than hair because we can do without the latter easily but cannot do without the former with equal composure.

Complete things naturally excel incomplete things, for the former have attained their form, while the latter have not. Wholes likewise seem to excel parts in the same way, for what is a whole possesses the form proper to nature. What is a part, however, and strives toward the perfection of the whole has not yet acquired the appearance of its own beauty unless it is referred to the integrity of the whole.

No one doubts that things using reason are better than things lacking reason. Voluntary things are also rightly preferred to necessary things, for voluntary things are free, whereas necessary things bind us, as it were, under the domination of necessity. Therefore we judge voluntary things better than necessary things. Yet here one may also understand what we said above: unnecessary things are often preferred to necessary things, since voluntary things are not necessary, while voluntary things are better than necessary ones.

Thus unnecessary things often surpass necessary things. Living things are also to be preferred to lifeless things, when considered through the denial of the soul itself. Reason persuades us that natural things are to be preferred to non-natural things, and things made by art to things not made by art. The best order here is to prefer nature to art, and art to inactivity, for art imitates nature. Hence whatever retains beauty in itself comes from nature, whose form it seeks to imitate. Things that lack art are the lowest of all, since they depart not only from the appearance of nature but also from imitation.

These, then, are the matters considered according to kind in comparisons.

Power consists in considering what each thing can accomplish, for what each thing can do is rightly called its power. An efficient cause therefore has greater power than one that accomplishes nothing. Thus an artisan is better than matter, for matter is dull and unmoving. Nor does it accomplish anything unless it has received form from the artisan, that is, from the efficient cause.

Likewise, things sufficient in themselves seem better than things that need others. Thus God, who is the best of all, needs nothing, while all things need him. Things within our power are more desirable than things placed in another’s hand, where they easily slip away. Hence virtue is better than riches: virtue is within our power, while fortune is mistress of riches.

Who does not understand that stable things are better than uncertain things, and, if they are good, that things which cannot be taken away are better than those which can? The contrary part of these topics holds the opposite judgment: when we inspect the things that are better and look at their opposites, the opposites are worse.

There remains the comparison situated in relation to something else. It is treated in such a way that the thing compared with another is not assessed in itself but according to the consideration of some other thing. This occurs, for example, with three things, when two are compared with each other according to the fact that they are joined to a third in greater or lesser degree.

Suppose there are two things suited to human affairs, one of which is more suited to rulers and even to the state itself. We shall then judge that thing better which benefits better persons—that is, we shall consider not how the thing stands in itself, but how much it is connected with the state or with rulers. This thing is therefore compared according to relation, and what is useful to rulers is judged better than what is useful to private individuals, since rulers also contain within themselves the condition of the rest.

The same applies to what follows: things that are more pleasant to more people, more renowned among many, or approved by more people are judged better. Even if they are not intrinsically of this nature, they must nevertheless, by relation—as was said—be judged better by those for whom they are more pleasant, among whom they are more renowned, or by whom they are approved.

Although he placed what is judged good by more people above in that part of comparison in which the comparison was according to number, nothing prevents the same topic from being assigned to different kinds according to different considerations. For example, although a wing of a bird belongs to substance, it is also understood to be relative if it is considered in relation to something winged.

Those things also seem better by relation that have been praised by the person against whom one is arguing through dialectical reasoning or rhetorical skill. To refute an opponent, it is enough to show that he has agreed with you and at some time praised as excellent the very thing that you are now trying to show is better in the matter before you.

Having now stated all the topics of better things, the topics opposed to them will contain the things that are worse. There is no distinction among equal things. What is equal can neither rise nor fall. By the same methods through which greater and lesser things are weighed against one another, equal things are compared with one another. Things that are equal in number, kind, power, or relation are called equal.

A common example of all these cases is what Cicero places under quality. Quality is equal in all equal things, but things are equal in number, kind, power, or relation. In the comparison of things that are greater or lesser, there is one quality, but additions to it produce variation. Those things in which there is a greater number, a more beautiful kind, a more effective power, or a relation more closely joined to what is valuable will be judged better. If these are equal, they are equal in quality.

The example he proposed serves to flatter Trebatius, since it joins Cicero’s own ability—that is, oratory—with the praise of legal experts, in this way: If helping citizens by counsel, which belongs to legal experts, and by assistance, which belongs to orators, is to be assigned equal praise, those who give counsel and those who defend ought to have equal glory. The first proposition is true: helping citizens by counsel and assistance is to be assigned equal praise. Therefore what follows is inferred—namely, that those who give counsel, that is, legal experts, and those who defend, that is, orators, ought to have equal glory.

The conclusion is the statement by which we say: Therefore those who give counsel and those who defend ought to have equal glory. He expressed this briefly, in the manner of dialecticians, who say: “If it is day, it is light.” But “the first proposition is true” amounts to saying: “It is day.” For in the proposition “If it is day, it is light,” the first proposition is “It is day.” They conclude what follows with “therefore,” namely, that it is light. That is what followed in the first part of the proposition, which was “If it is day.”

Thus Cicero too expressed himself as follows: “But the first proposition is true”—that is, helping citizens by counsel and assistance is to be assigned equal praise. This was the first part of the proposition that said: If helping citizens by counsel and assistance were assigned equal praise, orators and legal advisers would have equal glory. “Therefore what follows”—that is, those who give counsel and those who defend ought to have equal glory—was the consequence of the proposition that stated: If helping citizens by counsel and assistance were equal, those who give counsel and those who defend would be equal.

The entire instruction for discovering arguments is complete. Once one has begun from definition, partition, notation, conjugates, genus, species, similarity, difference, contraries, adjuncts, consequents, antecedents, incompatibles, causes, effects, and comparison of greater, lesser, and equal things, no further seat of argument need be sought.

[Col. 1164B]

Although it is understood from what has been said that no topic of argument has been omitted, I nevertheless think that Cicero’s conclusion—where he states that he has omitted nothing—should be briefly approved in order to strengthen confidence in the completeness of the doctrine. For nothing at all is omitted from matters treated according to a certain method. No method is more certain than division. Whatever anyone divides by leading from common matters to particular ones, while proceeding along a straight path, cannot slip or be led into error.

The first division of all topics was therefore into those that adhere within the things themselves and those that are assumed externally. No middle position can be found between these divisions: either something is within the thing being investigated, or it must necessarily be assumed from outside.

Let us now see how the discussion proceeds by means of a division that omits nothing. Among the topics that are within the things under discussion, the argument is now taken from the whole, now from the parts, now from a word, and now from relations. It is plainly evident that nothing has been left out in these categories. For in what is joined together there is a twofold distinction: one proceeds from the very thing that has been formed and composed, namely, the whole, in which definitions are also employed; the other proceeds from examining its parts, from which the form of the composite has been joined together.

But because human nature often reveals in speech what it understands, the name used to disclose an understanding must also show some property of the thing it signifies. For an understanding signifies the quality of the thing that it understands. Therefore a name also indicates the quality of an understanding. It was rightly said, then, that some property of a thing is signified by its name, and an argument can accordingly be drawn from it; this is called an argument from notation.

He also supplied further divisions of these topics, which we shall gather together more briefly below. Relations, which, as was said above, consist in relation, have themselves also been properly divided. For things related to something else are either substantial or accidental.

They are substantial as in conjugates: in “just,” insofar as he is just, justice constitutes the substance. I do not mean that a human being is constituted as such by justice, but that the just person is corrupted when justice departs from him. The same reasoning applies to the adverb “justly.”

Genus, species, difference, cause, and effect are also substantial. Accidental are contrary, similar, adjunct, equal, greater, and lesser. Consequents and incompatibles, since—as was said above—they are situated in a condition, are sometimes found among substantial things and sometimes considered among accidents. They are substantial when, for example, a genus precedes a species; accidental when blackness follows a preceding raven, although some causes too may be accidental. Cicero discussed the properties of all these above.

To gather the entire division of topics into the briefest description, it will be as follows. Every argument is drawn either from those topics that adhere within the thing being investigated or from those assumed externally.

The topic situated within the things about which there is doubt is divided into the topic from the whole, the topic from the parts, the topic from the mark, and the topic from relations. The topic from the whole is called the topic from definition.

Definitions are either proper or improper. Of the improper, some are indicated by individual words, while others are unfolded in an expression. Of those made by individual words, some substitute one name for another name; these are called κατ’ ἀντίλεξιν, “by opposition of terms.” Others introduce a name by way of example; these are called ὡς τύπος, “as a type” or “as an example.”

Of those explained in an expression, some arise from partition, some from division, and some from differences beyond the genus; this last kind is called ἐννοηματική, “conceptual.” Others are formed from several qualities, each of which individually signifies the whole that the collection of qualities expresses; these are called ποιώδης, “qualitative.” Others consist of accidents, not individually but all together producing one thing. Others are given by difference; others by metaphor; others from the privation of a contrary; others are adapted to proper names and are also called ὑποτυπώσεις, “sketches” or “representations”; others are formed through the lack of what is complete; others through proportion; others through relation; and others through cause.

There is also, according to Tullius, another principal division of definition: some definitions concern bodily things, others incorporeal things. The topic of definition is divided in this way.

The topic from the parts is divided into partition and division. The topic from a mark is simple. The topic from relations is divided into the topic from conjugates, the topic from genus, from species, from similarity, from difference, from contraries, from adjuncts, from consequents, antecedents, and incompatibles, from cause, from effects, and from comparison of equals, greater things, and lesser things.

Genus is divided into highest genera and into those that can also be species. Species is divided into lowest species and into those that can also be genera.

Of similar things, some are considered in individual cases and are called examples; others in several cases and are called induction; others in connected cases and are called proportion.

Differences are either substantial, or, although not substantial, inseparable, or neither substantial nor inseparable.

Contraries are called either adversative, privative, negative, or relative.

Adjuncts are either those that exist before the thing, those that exist with the thing, or those that exist after the thing.

The conditional topic is divided into antecedent, consequent, and incompatible.

The topic of causes is also manifold. Some causes produce by their own power; others are causes without which a thing cannot be produced. Of those that produce by their own power, some are necessary and need nothing in order to produce; others need something in order to produce; others need something but are not necessary. Of those without which a thing is not produced, some are changeable and others unchangeable.

Again, some causes are not spontaneous, some arise from volition, some from disturbance, some from habit, some from nature, some from art, and some from chance. Again, some causes are constant and others inconstant. Furthermore, some causes are voluntary and others unknown. Of the unknown, one part is constituted by chance and another by necessity. Of necessary causes, one part is situated in force and another in knowledge.

Effects can be divided only insofar as they are related to the causes mentioned above. The topic from comparison of lesser, equal, and greater things is divided according to number, kind, power, and relation to other things.

Since this is so, and since nothing has been omitted in the division, Marcus Tullius rightly concluded his partition by saying that no seat of argument had been passed over.

There remains the topic taken externally. Since it is of no use to legal advisers, he adds it not for Trebatius’ sake, but lest anything seem lacking from a finished work.

But since at the beginning we divided the topics in such a way as to say that some adhere within the very thing about which there is doubt, and enough has been said about these, let us say a little about those assumed externally, although they have no relevance at all to your discussions. Nevertheless, let us complete the whole subject, since we have begun it. For you are not a person who is pleased only by civil law; and since this is written to you in such a way that it will also come into the hands of others, care should be taken to benefit as much as possible those who take pleasure in honorable studies.

[Col. 1166C]

Lest a topic that would be of no benefit to a legal expert cause Trebatius to neglect it, the great orator makes him attentive, as he did in the preface. He says that at the beginning he divided the topics so as to say that some adhere within the very matters under discussion, while others are assumed externally; and since the preceding topics have been adequately discussed, the remaining part ought not to be passed over untreated.

For Trebatius is not a man who, content with his own art, neglects the studies of others. Rather, being exceedingly strong in diligence and intelligence, he considers everything belonging to the liberal studies to pertain to him. Cicero says at the same time that care should be taken because Trebatius would publish Cicero’s work with goodwill, so that, once it had come into the hands of many, it might be wholly useful to those devoted to honorable studies. He grants Trebatius this further benefit: that what was written to him and published through him would be written for the benefit of very many.

This argument, then, which is said to be without art, is placed in testimony. By “testimony” we now mean everything taken from some external thing in order to establish credibility.

[Col. 1167A]

He declares that the external topic of argument, which Marcus Tullius calls “without art,” is placed in testimony. One may wonder how this topic differs from the preceding topics, which he placed among relations. For just as relations are always established in reference to something else, testimonies too refer to the things of which they are testimonies. Every testimony is testimony of something attested.

Accordingly, one may ask why the things formerly called relations should not be placed externally, or why the things now called external should not be placed among relations, especially since the things we earlier said were adjuncts to a transaction often provide something like testimony for matters. For what has happened is ordinarily considered from the signs of things that preceded or followed it.

The common solution to all these questions is that the arguments made from relations are discovered by the orator and arise through his work and industry. Those placed externally, however, merely provide testimony for the matter. They are not discovered by the orator; rather, the orator uses them as things already established and prepared in advance.

Arguments from genus, species, and the other relations are in some way found by the orator himself. Testimonies, however, he does not create for himself; he uses them in the case as things already prepared. Hence arguments from relations arise immediately and spontaneously in the case, whereas those placed among testimonies precede the matter and, by confirming it, subsequently provide support for the transaction. In the case of adjuncts, the orator gathers an inference and impresses it upon the minds of his hearers.

Testimonies, however, do not consist in inferences or suspicions, but in an account of what has been done. He shows more emphatically what testimony is when he says that he calls testimony what is taken from some external thing. For relations do not seem to be external to the things to which they are related.

A witness, however, is joined to the matter testified to by no kinship, except knowledge alone. Knowledge has no bearing on the matter that was done, since, even if no one recognized that the transaction had occurred, the matter would nevertheless have occurred. This could also be brought into comparison with similarity. For what would be less than something if nothing similar to it were found? But what is similar is joined to that of which it is similar by the same quality, and that quality forms both things.

Knowledge, however, although it makes someone a witness, is not joined by any quality to the matter of which it is the knowledge. For the knowledge possessed by someone who knows cannot be called a quality of the matter that occurred. If knowledge could be understood as a quality of the thing, then, when those who know it perished, the thing itself would either perish or change. Neither outcome is necessary, since, once those who know have been removed, the matter may continue to exist even though it is unknown.

Yet not every person carries the weight of testimony; for establishing credibility, authority is required. Authority is supplied either by nature or by time. Authority arising from nature lies chiefly in virtue; but many things in time confer authority: talent, wealth, age, fortune, skill, experience, necessity, and sometimes even the coincidence of fortuitous events. For people consider the talented, the wealthy, and those tested by length of years worthy of belief—perhaps not rightly, but the [Col. 1168A] opinion of the common people can scarcely be changed, and both those who judge and those who form opinions direct everything according to it. For those who excel in the qualities I have mentioned seem to excel by virtue itself.

Yet the other qualities I have just enumerated, although they contain no appearance of virtue in themselves, sometimes strengthen credibility. This happens when either some skill is employed—for knowledge has great power to persuade—or experience. For people generally believe those who have undergone and learned through experience. Necessity also produces credibility, arising both from bodies and from minds. What those tortured by blows or exhausted by fire say seems to be spoken by truth itself; and what arises from disturbances of the mind—grief, desire, anger, fear—because it possesses the force of necessity, brings authority and credibility. The same applies to those conditions from which truth is sometimes discovered: childhood, sleep, [Col. 1168B] inadvertence, drunkenness, and madness. Children have often disclosed something relevant while unaware of its significance, and much has often been revealed through sleep, wine, and madness.

Many have also fallen unwittingly into hateful matters, as recently happened to Staterius. He said these things while good men were secretly listening from the other side of a wall; when these statements were disclosed and brought into court, he was lawfully condemned on a capital charge. We have heard of something similar concerning the Lacedaemonian Pausanias. The coincidence of fortuitous events is of such a kind that something happens by chance when either something is being done that ought not to be disclosed, or something is being said that ought not to be said. The multitude of suspicions brought against Palamedes for treason also belongs to this category, and truth can sometimes scarcely refute such a charge.

[Col. 1168C] Since he said that an artless source had been placed among the forms of testimony, while in the testimony of persons who lend their credibility authority is sought, it was necessary to explain the things by which authority is ordinarily produced. The remaining points have been stated with complete clarity and openness. But since he divided authority into nature and circumstance, and placed within circumstance talent, wealth, age, fortune, skill, experience, necessity, and sometimes the coincidence of fortuitous events, one may ask: What has talent to do with circumstance? What has skill? What has experience? Age, wealth, fortune, and the coincidence of fortuitous events are subject to time, since each of these changes through the varying turns of time. Talent, however, ought rather to have been attributed to nature, while skill and experience constitute a third category, since they are subject neither to time nor to nature.

[Col. 1168D] Although virtue itself, which Marcus Tullius placed within the domain of nature, may also seem to some to be acquired not naturally but through instruction and the proper practice of living, the division must nevertheless be understood as follows: all authority either comes from great and excellent things that are by nature best, or derives credibility from those things placed in a lower rank, not from a natural quality but from opinions implanted among the common people. He placed the greatest and most excellent things in nature, which, as Tullius himself maintains in many passages, is always desirous of the good. But he placed the secondary things in time because everything subject to time does not retain the stability of the highest good. [Col. 1169A] Virtue cannot be bent toward what is worse. Talent, however, wealth, fortune, skill, and experience are often corrupted through improper practice. For whatever of these is separated from virtue loses the dignity of true praise. He postponed speaking of virtue itself.

He divided the latter category—that is, authority placed in circumstance—and illustrated it with the clearest examples. Talent also commands credibility, and from it great authority is readily available. People believe that those whose talent is sufficient to deal with the matters they have undertaken speak more wisely. They judge those who are pre-eminent in wealth worthy of trust; and to those distinguished by fortune and rank they grant the majesty of authority—perhaps not rightly. Yet both judgment in affairs and estimation of a person’s life are governed chiefly by human opinion. Since that opinion can scarcely be changed, the orator will direct everything according to it and propose it as something to be managed and governed.

[Col. 1169B] Skill and experience likewise have great force. In both cases, knowledge produces credibility. Necessity too, as though wrenching out what was hidden, is supported by authority, which arises both from the mind and from the body: from the body, when what is hidden is revealed by fire, iron, and blows; from the mind, when the mind is confused by a certain necessity arising from disturbance or ignorance. For then, distinguishing least of all what ought to be said and what ought to be kept silent, it betrays and pours into the light what had been concealed. Anger and every disturbance of the mind often fail to restrain what ought to be hidden; they therefore carry authority for credibility because they are disclosed simply and brought forth without any artifice of cunning.

[Col. 1169C] Moreover, the ignorance of children, drunkenness, and sleep have often brought certain things into the open which, had any judgment been exercised, would not have been disclosed. Often, too, people, without any disturbance of mind, have been compromised by their own unwitting confession, while they simply pour out everything they do not think will harm them. This, he proposed, happened to Staterius, who, with a wall between him and his hearers, confessed these matters while unaware that he was being overheard by men lying in wait. When his words had been made public and brought into court, he was condemned by a capital sentence.

This ignorance is included under necessity. For one who does not know what he is ignorant of cannot avoid it, even if he wishes to do so. Whatever necessity extorts seems in a certain way to be spoken by truth itself; and therefore belief is granted to such statements as though they were supported by authority.

[Col. 1169D] The coincidence of fortuitous events also produces credibility. Although it sometimes points falsely, it is nevertheless so powerful that truth can scarcely extricate itself from it. Such is the story told about Palamedes: a Phrygian was killed, who appeared to have been sent by Priam; Priam's letters were discovered, the writing having imitated a Phrygian hand, and these circumstances occurring together gave credibility to the charge of treason. Hence Cicero says: “Such also is the coincidence of fortuitous events.”

[Note: [Col. 1169] The end of this sixth book and the whole of the seventh are missing; in them the following text of Cicero was explained.]

Popular rumor also belongs to this category: it is a kind of testimony provided by the multitude.

Those things that create credibility through virtue are divided into two parts. Of these, one derives its power from nature, the other from human effort. The virtue of the gods excels by nature, while that of human beings excels through effort. [Col. 1170A] The following are, for the most part, divine forms of testimony: first, speech—for oracles (*oracula*) were named from the fact that the speech of the gods is present in them; next, things in which certain works of divine power seem to be present: first, the universe itself and all its order and adornment; then the flights and songs of birds through the air; next, sounds and fiery manifestations in that same air; omens of many things on earth; and also the foreknowledge discovered through the entrails of sacrificial victims. Many things have also been signified to sleepers through visions, and testimony of the gods is sometimes drawn from these visions in order to establish credibility.

Among human beings, the reputation of virtue has the greatest force. Reputation has force not only in the case of those who possess virtue, but also in that of those who seem to possess it. Thus, those whom people see endowed with talent, zeal, and learning, and whose course of life—like that of Cato, Laelius, Scipio, and many others—they see as steadfast and approved, seem to them to be what they themselves would wish to be. They judge not only those who are engaged in public honors and public affairs to be such persons, but also orators, philosophers, poets, and historians; from their sayings and writings authority is often sought in order to establish credibility.

[Col. 1170B] Once all the places from which arguments arise have been set out, the first point to understand is that there is no discussion in which some such place does not occur. Nor do all the places occur in every question; rather, some places are more suitable for certain questions and others for different questions.

There are two kinds of questions: one unlimited, the other defined. The defined question is what the Greeks call a *hypothesis* (ὑπόθεσις), which we call a case; the unlimited question is what they call a *thesis* (θέσις), which we may call a proposition. A case is determined by particular persons, places, times, actions, and affairs, either by all of these or by most of them. A proposition concerns one or more of these, but not the most specific circumstances. Thus a proposition is part of a case, being concerned with one or more such elements, but not with the most important of them.

[Col. 1170C] Every question, however, concerns some matter by which cases are constituted—either one such matter, several, or sometimes all of them. Whatever the subject of the question, there are two kinds: one concerned with knowledge, the other with action.

Questions of knowledge are those whose end is knowledge, as when it is asked whether law proceeds from nature or from some sort of human convention and compact. Questions of action are of this kind: “Is it proper for a wise man to enter public life?”

Questions of knowledge are divided into three parts, according as one asks whether something exists, what it is, or what kind of thing it is. The first is explained by conjecture, the second by definition, and the third by the distinction between right and wrong.

[Col. 1170D] The method of conjecture is divided into four parts. The first is when one asks whether something exists; the second, from what it arose; the third, what cause produced it; the fourth, when one asks about a change in the thing: “Does it exist or not?” “Is anything truly honorable, and is anything truly just, or are these matters of opinion alone?” The question of origin is exemplified when one asks whether virtue can be produced by nature or by instruction. The question of the efficient cause is exemplified when one asks by what means eloquence is produced. The question of transformation is exemplified when one asks whether eloquence could, through some change, be converted into childish speech.

When one asks what something is, its conception, property, division, and partition must be explained; for these belong to definition. Description is also added, which the Greeks call *hypographē* (ὑπογραφή). A conception is sought in this way: “Is that just which is useful to the person who has greater power?” [Col. 1171A] A property in this way: “Does suffering fall only upon human beings, or also upon animals?” Division and partition in the same way: “Are there three kinds of goods?” Description asks what a miser is like, what a flatterer is like, and so forth of the same kind, in which both nature and life are described.

When one asks what kind of thing something is, the question is either unqualified or comparative. Unqualified: “Is glory to be desired?” Comparative: “Is glory to be preferred to wealth?” There are three kinds of unqualified questions: questions about what is to be sought and avoided, about what is just and unjust, and about what is honorable and shameful. Comparative questions are of two kinds: one concerns one thing in relation to another, the other the greater and the lesser.

An example of seeking and avoiding is: “Are wealth to be sought and poverty to be avoided?” Of justice and injustice: “Is it just to take revenge on anyone from whom one has received an injury?” Of honor and shame: “Is it honorable to die for one’s country?”

[Col. 1171B] Of the other kind, which was divided into two parts, one concerns one thing and another, as when one asks what difference there is between a friend and a flatterer, or between a king and a tyrant. The other concerns the greater and the lesser, as when one asks: “Is eloquence more valuable, or knowledge of civil law?”

So much for questions of knowledge. The remaining questions concern action, of which there are two kinds: one directed toward duty, the other toward producing, calming, or entirely removing an emotion of the mind. An example directed toward duty is: “Should children be undertaken?” Questions directed toward moving the emotions occur when exhortations are made to defend the republic, or to pursue glory and praise. Complaints, incitements, and tearful appeals for pity belong to this category. So too does speech that extinguishes anger, removes fear, restrains exultant joy, or wipes away grief.

[Col. 1171C] Although these are the kinds of questions in propositions, they are transferred in the same form to cases. We must next consider the places suited to each question. All the places are indeed suitable for most questions, but, as we have said, some are more suitable for certain questions than for others.

For conjecture, the places most suitable are those drawn from causes, effects, and associated circumstances. Definition concerns the method and knowledge of defining. Closely related to this is the category we called “one thing and another,” which is a kind of definition. If one asks whether obstinacy and perseverance are the same, the matter must be judged by definitions.

[Col. 1171D] The places appropriate to this kind of question are consequences, antecedents, and oppositions, together with the two places drawn from causes and effects. If this thing follows that one, it does not follow this one; or if that one precedes this thing, it does not precede this one; or if it is opposed to this thing, it is not opposed to that one; or if this thing is the cause of one, another is the cause of the other; or if this has been produced from one source and that from another—by any of these means it may be discovered whether the matter in question is the same or different.

For the third kind of question, in which one asks what kind of thing something is, the matters enumerated above under comparison apply. In the category concerned with what is to be sought or avoided, one employs things belonging either to the mind, the body, or external circumstances, whether advantageous or disadvantageous. When the question concerns what is honorable or shameful, the whole argument must be directed toward the goods or evils of the mind. When it concerns what is just or unjust, the places of justice are gathered.
