[Col. 1172A] These are divided into two parts: nature and institution. Nature has two parts: the protection of oneself and the right to take revenge. The institution of justice is threefold: one part is established by law, another by agreement, and the third by the authority of ancient custom.

Justice is also said to be threefold in another sense: one part concerns the higher gods, another the departed, and the third human beings. The first is called piety, the second sanctity, and the third justice and equity.

Enough has been said about the proposition. Next, a little less must be said about the case, for most matters are common to it and the proposition.

[Col. 1172B] There are three kinds of cases: judicial, deliberative, and praise. Their ends themselves indicate the places that must be used. The end of a judicial case is justice, from which it also receives its name. The parts of justice were set out earlier, when equity was discussed. The end of deliberation is utility, whose parts are those matters of things to be sought that were just described. The end of praise is honor, of which we have likewise spoken already.

But defined questions are constructed from their own, as it were proper, places and are divided into accusation and defense. In them the following forms arise: the accuser charges the person with an act, while the defender opposes one of three claims—that the act was not committed, that, if it was committed, the act has another name, or that it was committed lawfully. Thus the first is called the denial or conjectural issue, the second the definitional issue, and the third—although this is an awkward name—the juridical issue.

The proper arguments of these cases, drawn from the places we have explained, are set out in the rhetorical precepts. The refutation of an accusation, in which the charge is repelled, is called in Greek *stasis* (στάσις) and may be called in Latin the “issue” or “state” (*status*), at which the defense first takes its stand, as if entering into combat in order to resist.

[Col. 1172C] The same issues also arise in deliberative and laudatory speeches. For it is often denied that things predicted by someone in a proposal will occur, either because they cannot happen at all or because they cannot happen without the greatest difficulty. In such an argument the conjectural issue arises.

But when something is discussed concerning utility, honor, or justice, and concerning the things contrary to them, issues of law or of terminology arise. The same occurs in laudatory speeches. For one may deny that the praised deed was committed, or deny that it should be designated by the name given to it by the praiser, or argue that it is not praiseworthy at all because it was not done rightly or lawfully. Caesar used all these kinds of issues far too shamelessly against my Cato.

[Col. 1172D] The dispute produced by the issue the Greeks call the *krinomenon* (κρινόμενον). Since I am writing to you, I prefer that it be called “the matter at issue.” The elements by which this matter at issue is sustained may be called the “supports,” as it were, of the defense, since once they are removed no defense remains.

But since nothing ought to be stronger in the settlement of controversies than a law, we must take care to employ the law as both helper and witness. In this matter other, as it were new, issues arise, which are called legal disputes. For the defense then maintains that the law does not say what the adversary claims, but something else.

This occurs when the written text is ambiguous and two differing meanings can be accepted. Or the writer’s intention is set against the written words, so that the question is whether the words or the intention ought to have greater force. Or one law is brought forward against another law. Thus there are three kinds of matters capable of producing controversy in any written text: ambiguity, disagreement between the written text and the author’s intention, and contradictory statutes.

[Col. 1173A] It is clear that the same controversies can arise not only in laws but also in wills, stipulations, and all other matters conducted through writing. The treatment of these matters is explained in other books.

Not only continuous speeches but also their parts are assisted by the same places, partly by places proper to them and partly by common places. Thus, in the introductions, one must use the proper places to make the hearers benevolent, receptive, and attentive. Narrations likewise must be directed toward their proper ends: they should be clear, brief, evident, credible, restrained, and dignified. Although these qualities ought to be present throughout the speech, they are especially proper to narration.

The credibility that follows narration is produced through persuasion. Which places are most effective for persuading has been stated in the books in which we discussed the whole method of speaking.

[Col. 1174A] The conclusion has certain other functions, and above all amplification. Its effect should be either to disturb the emotions or to calm them; and if they are already disposed in one direction or another, the speech should either intensify their movement or quiet it. Precepts for the kind of speech in which pity, anger, hatred, envy, and the other emotions of the mind are stirred are supplied in other books, which you may read with me whenever you wish.

As for what I understood you to desire, your wish ought to have been fully satisfied. For, so that I might omit nothing relevant to the discovery of an argument in the whole method, I have included more than you had requested. I have done what generous sellers often do: when they have sold a house or an estate, they nevertheless, after reserving the removable fixtures [the text is uncertain], concede something to the buyer that seems suitably and appropriately placed for purposes of adornment. In the same way, once we had supplied what we were, as it were, required to give as the principal property, we wished certain ornaments not strictly due to accompany it.

[Col. 1173]

**ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS, FOUR BOOKS ON TOPICAL DIFFERENCES. (C)**

**BOOK ONE.**
[Col. 1173B] Every method of discursive inquiry, which the ancient Peripatetics called *logicē* (logic), is divided into two parts: one concerned with discovery, the other with judgment. That part which purifies and equips judgment they called *analytice*; we may call it “resolutory.” The part, however, which supplies the capacity for discovery is called by the Greeks *topice*, and by us “local.” Concerning that part which is the teacher of judgment we shall argue elsewhere. For now, however, our purpose is to disclose what the topics are, what their differences are, and which syllogisms they suit. Nor does this seem to be done simply and uniformly; rather, a twofold division must be presented: one drawn from Greek works, the other taken from the *Topics* of Marcus Tullius. In these matters, for the perfection of theoretical understanding, this must also be established: in what ways the two divisions differ, in what ways they agree, and how one may in turn include the other. For the present, however, we shall not linger over individual points, but shall discuss the whole division generally, gathering only the definitions, examples, and differences of the topics from which arguments arise.

The individual topics, according to the nature of the work, have been treated more carefully either in the eight volumes in which we translated Aristotle’s *Topics* into Latin, or in the seven in which we labored to shed the light of a full exposition upon Cicero’s *Topics*. There everything has been set out in its proper and clearly disentangled parts; here, however, matters that were elsewhere disclosed member by member are handled through a common theoretical survey. Our concern is to treat not only dialectical topics but also rhetorical ones, and to explain how these differ both from one another and from the dialectical topics, so that, once all the topics have been set forth for full consideration and their differences and common features have been carefully noted, both an abundance of arguments may be acquired and a clear distinction among the topics may be possible.

To ensure that everything rests upon lucid reasoning, we must begin somewhat higher up. A proposition is an utterance signifying truth or falsity; for example, if someone says, “The heaven is revolving,” this is called both an enunciation and a statement. A question is a proposition brought into doubt and uncertainty; for example, if someone asks whether the heaven is revolving. A conclusion is a proposition established by arguments; for example, if someone proves that the heaven is revolving by reference to other things. An enunciation, whether it is spoken merely for its own sake or brought forward in order to establish something else, is a proposition; if it is itself questioned, it is a question; if it is itself established, it is a conclusion. Proposition, then, question, and conclusion are the same thing, but they differ in the manner described above.

[Col. 1174C] An argument is a line of reasoning that establishes the credibility of a doubtful matter. Argument and argumentation, however, are not the same. The force and rational content of the judgment contained in an utterance when something doubtful is proved is called an argument; the verbal expression of the argument itself is called argumentation. Thus the argument is the power, mind, and meaning of the argumentation, while argumentation is the exposition of the argument through speech.

A topic, however, is the seat of an argument, or that from which a suitable argument is drawn for the question proposed. Since this is so, the nature of each element must be treated more carefully, and their division must be made according to kinds, parts, and figures, as we have said. First, then, we must discuss the proposition.

We said that it is an utterance containing truth or falsehood. It has two forms: one affirmation, the other negation. An affirmation is expressed as follows: “The heaven is revolving.” A negation is pronounced as follows: “The heaven is not revolving.”

Some of these are universal, others particular, others indefinite, and others singular. Universal propositions are such as: “Every human being is just”; “No human being is just.” Particular propositions are such as: “Some human being is just”; “Some human being is not just.” Indefinite propositions are expressed as follows: “A human being is just”; “A human being is not just.” Singular propositions propose an individual or some singular entity, such as: “Cato is just”; “Cato is not just.” For Cato is an individual and singular entity.

Some of these we call predicative, others conditional. Predicative propositions are put forward simply, that is, with no force of condition attached to them; for example, when someone simply says that the heaven is revolving. But if a condition is joined to this, one proposition becomes conditional out of two, as follows: “If the heaven is round, it is revolving.” Here the condition makes it understood that the heaven is revolving only if it is round.

Since some propositions are predicative and others conditional, we call the parts of predicative propositions “terms.” These are the predicate and the subject. By “terms” I mean the words and names by which a proposition is connected. Thus, in the proposition “A human being is just,” we call the two names—namely, “just” and “human being”—the parts of the proposition. We also call them terms, one of which is the subject and the other the predicate.

The subject is the term that is lesser; the predicate is the greater. Thus, in the proposition “A human being is just,” “human being” is less than “just.” Justice does not exist only in human beings; it may also exist in corporeal and divine substances. Therefore “just” is the greater term, while “human being” is the lesser. Consequently, “human being” is the subject term, and “just” is the predicate.

Because propositions of this kind have one term as predicate and the other as subject, the proposition is called predicative by the privilege of the greater term. It often happens, however, that these terms are found to be equal to one another, as in “A human being is capable of laughter.” For “human being” and “capable of laughter” are each an equal term with respect to the other: neither “capable of laughter” extends beyond “human being,” nor “human being” beyond “capable of laughter.”

It is necessary, then, that the following hold: if the terms are unequal, the greater is always predicated of the subject; if they are equal, each is predicated of the other through reciprocal predication. But for the lesser to be predicated of the greater never occurs in any proposition.

The parts of propositions, which we call terms, may be found not only in names but also in utterances. For an utterance is often predicated of an utterance, as follows: “Socrates conducts an inquiry into philosophy with Plato and his students.” The utterance “Socrates with Plato and his students” is the subject; “conducts an inquiry into philosophy” is predicated.

Again, sometimes a name is the subject and an utterance the predicate, as follows: “Socrates conducts an inquiry into philosophy.” Here “Socrates” alone is the subject; the utterance “conducts an inquiry into philosophy” is the predicate.

It also happens that an utterance is made subject and a simple word is predicated, as follows: “Socrates’ likeness to the higher and divine substances is justice.” Here the utterance by which “Socrates’ likeness to the higher and divine substances” is expressed is made subject, while “justice” is predicated.

We discussed propositions of this kind more carefully in the commentaries that we wrote on Aristotle’s book *Περὶ ἑρμηνείας* (*On Interpretation*).

The parts of conditional propositions—which the Greeks call hypothetical propositions—are simple propositions. The part stated first is called the antecedent, and the part stated afterward the consequent, as in the proposition: “If it is round, it is revolving.” “Being round” is antecedent; “being revolving” is consequent.

[Col. 1176B] Some of these are simple conditionals, others conjunctive. Simple conditionals have predicative propositions as their parts, as in the example given above: “If it is round, it is revolving.” For “It is round” and “It is revolving,” taken separately and individually, are both predicative propositions.

Conjunctive propositions have many differences; we treated them very carefully in the volumes that we composed on hypothetical syllogisms. Simple hypothetical propositions, however, have four differences. They consist either of two affirmative categoricals, as in “If it is round, it is revolving,” since both are affirmatives; or of two negatives, as in “If the heaven is not round, it is not revolving,” since “not being round” and “not being revolving” are both negations; or of an affirmative and a negative, as in “If it is square, it is not revolving,” since “being square” is an affirmation and “not being revolving” a negation; or of a negative and an affirmative, as in “If it is not round, it is stable”: “not being round” is a negation, while “being stable” is an affirmation.

Some propositions are also self-evident, so that no proof of them can be found; others, although the mind of the hearer approves and assents to them, can nevertheless be established by other, prior propositions. Those for which there is no proof are called primary and maximal, because the propositions that can be demonstrated must necessarily be established through them. A maximal proposition is, for example: “If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal.” This is so self-evident that there can be nothing else more evident by which it could be established.

Since such propositions carry their own credibility by nature, they not only have no need of an external argument for their credibility, but also commonly serve as the starting point of proof for other propositions. Thus self-evident propositions, than which nothing is more evident, are called indemonstrable, maximal, and primary.

Those propositions which, although approved by the judgment of the hearer, nevertheless have something naturally more evident from which—if they are questioned—they derive credibility as though from an external source, are called demonstrable, lesser, and subsequent propositions.

Let this suffice concerning propositions.

A question is a proposition open to doubt, in which nearly the same considerations must be examined as were previously stated concerning the proposition. Some questions are simple, others composite. Simple questions arise from a simple proposition, as when one asks whether the heaven is revolving. This comes from the proposition that says, “The heaven is revolving.”

But if a question takes its beginning from a composite conditional proposition—namely, “Whether, if the heaven is round, it is revolving”—it will be conditional and composite in the following way. It takes its beginning from the conditional proposition “If the heaven is round, it is revolving.” Thus a question is sometimes predicative and sometimes conditional. Consequently, the parts of a question are the same as those previously said to be the parts of a proposition.

Predicative questions therefore have a predicate and a subject, as in the question whether the heaven is revolving. “Revolving” is the predicate, while “heaven” is the subject. “Revolving” is the greater term than “heaven,” since it is not only the heaven that can be called revolving.

A conjunctive question, however, has as its parts that which is predicated and that which is made subject, that which is antecedent and that which is consequent, as in the question: “Whether, if the heaven is round, it is revolving.” “Being round” is antecedent; “being revolving” is consequent.

Accordingly, in a predicative question it is asked whether the predicate inheres in the subject term. In hypothetical questions, however, the only question is whether what is proposed as the consequent accompanies the matter that precedes it.

Everything said concerning predicative propositions—that some are universal, some particular, some indefinite, and some singular—may also, for the most part, be said concerning a predicative question. The only difference between a question and a proposition is this: a proposition, whether simply enunciated or brought forward to prove something else, is an utterance signifying truth or falsehood; a question, although itself an utterance, is nevertheless a proposition open to doubt. Once doubt has been added, the same features considered in a proposition must also be treated in a question.

A question has two forms. One is called by dialecticians a *thesis*. It asks and discusses a matter stripped of all other circumstances, as dialecticians especially take such questions for disputation: “Is pleasure the highest good?” “Should one take a wife?” We call this a proposition or proposed thesis.

The other is called by the Greeks a *hypothesis* and by us a “case.” This question is involved with persons, times, actions, and other circumstances. It is of the following kind: “Should Cicero be driven into exile by law at a time of crisis for the state, because he killed Roman citizens without the order of the people?”

These two kinds of question must necessarily have further subdivisions. The thesis has been assigned to philosophers, the hypothesis to orators. I shall give the divisions of the hypothetical question later; for now I shall discuss the division of the thesis, which is divided into four kinds.

In every dialectical predicative question it is asked whether what is predicated inheres in what is made subject. When something is proposed as inhering in something else, it will either be greater than that of which it is predicated and claimed to inhere in its substance; or it will be greater but will not be predicated of its substance; or it will be equal and will be predicated substantially; or it will be equal but will in no way contain its substance. For the lesser to be predicated of the greater occurs in no proposition.

If what is proposed in the question is greater than the subject and is predicated of the subject’s substance, it will be a genus. Every genus is greater than that of which it is predicated and is said of its substance, as “animal” is said of “human being.”

If it is greater but is not predicated of the subject’s substance, it will be an accident, as “white” is said of a human being.

If it is equal and substantial, it will be the definition of the subject, as “rational mortal animal” is the definition of a human being. For this is convertible and displays the account—that is, the substance—of the subject, “human being.”

[Col. 1178B] If it is equal but separate from the account of the substance, it will be a proprium, as “capable of laughter” is said of a human being.

Thus simple dialectical questions concern either genus, accident, definition, or proprium.

Questions may also concern differentia, as when one asks whether heavenly bodies are rational or not, or when one doubts whether the differentia of a tyrant and a ruler is that the latter has assumed authority through laws while the former oppresses the people by violent domination.

To ask about a differentia amounts to asking about a genus. For the differentia will either be constitutive or divisive. If it is constitutive, it occupies the place of a genus, as rationality does for a human being, or for heavenly bodies if heavenly bodies live by reason. But if it is divisive, it is considered in the manner of a species, since every species is accompanied by a divisive differentia.

Since we use differentia sometimes in the place of genus and sometimes in the place of species, there can be no doubt that when it is questioned, the question concerns genus.

It may also happen that something is brought into dispute through comparison, as when it is debated whether courage is better than justice. But this question must be placed among questions concerning accidents. For nothing except an accident enters into comparison, since only an accident admits of “more” and “less.”

Again, a dispute may concern what is identical, as in the question whether the useful is the same as the honorable. Here the question must be joined to definition. For things that have the same definition are themselves the same, whereas things whose account of substance is different are themselves different.

Thus simple dialectical questions are rightly said to have four kinds, concerning which enough has been said.

We must now treat conditional questions. One consists of two affirmatives, another of two negatives, another of an affirmation and a negation, and another of a negation and an affirmation.

If a conditional proposition consists of two affirmations, the question is whether an affirmation follows an affirmation. If a proposition is joined from two negations, the dispute concerns whether a negation accompanies a negation. If it is joined from an affirmation and a negation, or from a negation and an affirmation, the question is whether a negation accompanies an affirmation, or an affirmation a negation.

First, then, we must divide the question in which it is disputed whether an affirmation follows an affirmation; this division does not escape the division of predicative questions. For the things in which something precedes and something else follows are generally those that I mentioned shortly above.

A species is followed by a genus, a differentia, a definition, a proprium, or an inseparable accident. Likewise, a species follows a proprium and a definition; a differentia and a definition follow a proprium; and a proprium or a differentia follows a definition. Thus: “If it is a human being, it is an animal”; “If it is a human being, it is rational”; “If it is a human being, it is a rational mortal animal”; “If it is a human being, it is capable of laughter”; “If it is an Ethiopian, it is black.”

“If it is capable of laughter, it is a human being”; “If it is a rational mortal animal, it is a human being.” “If it is capable of laughter, it is rational”; “If it is capable of laughter, it is a rational mortal animal”; “If it is a rational mortal animal, it is capable of laughter or bipedal.”

Beyond these, sometimes an effect follows a cause, and sometimes a cause follows an effect. An effect follows a cause in this way: “If the sun is present, it shines.” A cause follows an effect in this way: “If something has been burned, fire was present”; or in this way: “If the sun is seen, it shines.”

The whole is likewise followed by its parts: “If a house is intact, its roof, walls, and foundations stand.”

A mode also follows the principal name: “If justice is good, what is just is good.” The principal name likewise follows the mode: “If what is just is good, justice is good.”

Accidents, too, are accompanied by that which is subject: “If it is white, it is a body.”

Since this is so, the division of a simple conditional question joined from two affirmations must generally be made according to whether the doubt concerns genus, differentia, species, proprium, definition, accident, cause and effect, whole and parts, or mode and principal name.

These observations are to be understood concerning a question that, although it is a simple hypothetical question, is nevertheless joined from two affirmatives.

Questions arising from propositions consisting of two negations must necessarily stand within the same differences. For: “If it is not a genus, it is not a species.” Likewise: “If there is no differentia, definition, or proprium, there will be no species.” The other matters stated above must be considered in the same way. Whatever precedes so that something else may follow: if that which follows is absent, then neither is that which precedes present.

The division of questions consisting of an affirmation and a negation is generally as follows: they are contained either in different genera, different species, contraries, or privation and possession. For a negation to follow an affirmation, either a different genus is posited, so that what differs from it is denied, as: “If it is a human being, it is not whiteness,” or “If it is substance, it is not quality”; or different species under the same genus are proposed, as: “If it is a human being, it is not a horse”; or contraries, as: “If it is white, it is not black”; or privations, as: “If he is blind, he does not see.”

Finally, this occurs in everything that is not the same: if one thing is present, the other is not. Thus, for a negation to accompany the proposed affirmation, there will be either different genera, different species, contraries, privations, or things incompatible with one another in some other way.

For an affirmation to follow a negation—which was the fourth difference of conditional propositions—this can occur only with contraries that have no intermediate and of which one must always be present, as: “If it is not day, it is night”; “If there is no darkness, there is light.”

Once the divisions of predicative and conditional questions have been made, one further point seems worth adding: every question is drawn either from the method of discursive inquiry, from natural speculation, or from moral speculation. From the method of discursive inquiry, for example: “Are affirmation and negation species of enunciation?” From natural speculation: “Is the heaven round?” From moral speculation: “Is virtue alone sufficient for happiness?”

Moreover, every question is either simple or composite. It is simple whenever it is divided by an affirmation and a negation, so that one side must affirm the whole and the other deny it, as: “Is the heaven round or not?” One part of this question contains an affirmation, the other a negation. For when one person maintains that it is so, he affirms; the other, by maintaining that it is not so, denies.

A composite question is one that is divided into several affirmations, as: “Is the heaven round, or square, or oblong, or of some other shape?” For here it is necessary to establish several affirmations defending different alternatives.

So much has been said concerning the question, insofar as it was relevant to the present undertaking.

[Col. 1180C] A conclusion is a proposition established by arguments, and nearly everything said concerning the proposition may also be said concerning it. Since these matters were carefully explained above, it now seems appropriate to treat the argument.

An argument is a line of reasoning that establishes the credibility of a doubtful matter. It must always be more evident than the question. For if unknown things are proved by known things, and an argument proves a doubtful matter, then what is brought forward to establish the credibility of the question must itself be more evident than the question.

Of all arguments, some are probable and necessary, some probable and not necessary, some necessary but not probable, and some neither probable nor necessary.

A probable argument is one that appears so either to everyone, or to the majority, or to the wise—either to all of them, to most of them, or especially to the most famous and distinguished—or one that appears so to each practitioner according to his own field, as medical matters to a physician and matters concerning the piloting of ships to a helmsman. It also includes what appears so to the person with whom the discussion is being held or to the person judging. In such cases it does not matter whether the argument is true or false, provided that it possesses verisimilitude.

A necessary argument is one that, as it is stated, is so and cannot be otherwise. An argument that is both probable and necessary is, for example: “If something is added to any object, the whole becomes greater.” No one will dissent from this proposition, and it is necessary that the matter stand so.

Probable but non-necessary arguments are those to which the mind of the hearer readily assents, but which do not possess the firmness of truth, as: “If she is a mother, she loves her son.”

Necessary but non-probable arguments are those that must be as stated, but to which the hearer does not readily assent, as the claim that an eclipse of the sun occurs through the interposition of the lunar body.

Neither necessary nor probable are those which stand neither in human opinion nor in truth, as: “Diogenes has horns,” on the ground that everyone possesses what he has never lost. Such things cannot even be called arguments, since arguments establish the credibility of a doubtful matter. There is no credibility in things founded neither upon human opinion nor upon truth.

One might nevertheless say that those things too are not arguments which, although necessary, are not at all approved by their hearers. For if credibility is to be established for a doubtful matter, the mind of the hearer must be compelled through things to which he himself assents, so that he may also approach a conclusion that he has not yet approved.

If the person judging does not approve what is merely necessary but not probable, he will necessarily fail to approve what is concluded from such reasoning either. It would therefore follow from this kind of reasoning that things merely necessary and not probable are not arguments.

But this is not so, and such an interpretation does not correctly grasp the meaning of probability. Probable things are those to which assent is given freely and spontaneously, so that they are approved as soon as they are heard. Things that are necessary but not probable, however, are first demonstrated by other probable and necessary arguments; once they have been understood and believed, they are brought forward to establish the credibility of another matter, as with the investigations—that is, the theorems—considered in geometry.

For the propositions made there are not such that the mind of the learner spontaneously assents to them. Rather, because they are demonstrated by other arguments, once they too have been learned and understood, they lead to the acceptance of further investigations.

Thus things that are not probable in themselves but are necessary cannot serve as arguments for establishing something else in the case of hearers to whom they have not yet been demonstrated. But for those who have gained belief through prior reasoning in matters to which they had not assented, such things may be called arguments if they are in doubt about something.

[Col. 1181C] Since the entire art of discursive inquiry is contained within four disciplines, we must say which of them knows how to use which arguments, so that it may clearly appear for which discipline the abundance of topics is prepared.

The whole method of discursive inquiry is subject to four disciplines and, as it were, their practitioners: the dialectician, the orator, the philosopher, and the sophist.

The dialectician and the orator operate within the common nature of arguments. Both pursue arguments that are probable, whether or not they are necessary. These two kinds of argument therefore serve them: the probable and necessary, and the probable and non-necessary.

The philosopher and the demonstrator, however, deal solely with truth. Whether arguments are probable or not is irrelevant to them, provided that they are necessary. They too use two kinds of argument: the probable and necessary, and the necessary and non-probable.

It is therefore clear in what respect the philosopher differs in his proper field of inquiry from the orator and the dialectician: probability is proposed to the latter, while truth is proposed to the former.

The fourth kind of argument, which we previously taught should not properly be called an argument at all, is usually assigned to sophists.

The purpose of the *Topics* is to display an abundance of arguments based on likelihood. Once the topics from which probable arguments are drawn have been identified, the material for discussion must become abundant and copious.

But since, as was said above, some probable arguments are necessary and others non-necessary, when the topics of probable arguments are set out, it follows that necessary arguments will also be taught.

Thus this capacity is provided primarily for orators and dialecticians, and secondarily for philosophers. Where all probable arguments are gathered, dialecticians and orators are assisted; where probable and necessary arguments are taught, abundance is supplied for philosophical demonstration.

Therefore not only the dialectician and the orator, but also the demonstrator and the producer of genuine argumentation, have something to draw from the topics that have been established, since the tradition contained within the topics of probable arguments also includes the principles of necessary arguments.

Those arguments, however, which are necessary but not probable, together with the final kind—namely, those that are neither probable nor necessary—are excluded from the consideration of the present work, except insofar as certain sophistical topics are sometimes introduced for the sake of exercising the reader.

Accordingly, the usefulness and purpose of the *Topics* have been made equally clear. Through them both the power of speech and the investigation of truth are increased. For the recognition of topics assists dialecticians and orators by providing abundance for speech through discovery; while the teaching of the topics of necessary arguments to philosophers illuminates, in a certain manner, the way of truth.

All the more, then, this discipline must be investigated and examined further, and once it has been grasped through understanding, it must be strengthened through practice and exercise. For the consideration of topics promises something great: namely, ways of discovering.

Those who lack this method attribute discovery wholly to natural talent and do not understand how much is sought through this study, which brings the power and force of nature into an art.

But enough of this. Let us now explain the remaining matters.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1181]

[Col. 1181D] Everything that was worked out in the preceding sequence of the volume will perhaps seem to certain learned readers somewhat superfluous and, as it were, merely auxiliary. For when they read the title “On the Differences of the Topics” in the books, they disregard the stages of instruction and immediately look to the end of the work. To me, however, it seems necessary that, unless what has been said is known beforehand, the learner’s mind cannot reach what follows. Those, too, who now consider the entire discussion of the first volume superfluous will certainly cease to judge it superfluous if they read everything through and illuminate the structure of the work with their mind and reason, when they see that what was necessary has been placed in its proper part.

So much for this. But since sufficient has already been said about what we set out earlier—that is, about proposition, question, conclusion, and argument—let us now discuss argumentation.

Argumentation is the explanation of an argument through speech. There are two kinds of it: one called syllogism, the other induction.

A syllogism is a discourse in which, once certain things have been posited and conceded, something else necessarily follows through those very things that have been conceded, and that something else is different from the things conceded themselves. The reasoning behind this definition is fully contained in the second book of the *Categorical Syllogisms*, which we wrote as an introduction to categorical syllogisms. But for ease of understanding, we shall briefly clarify the same point by an example.

Let this, then, be a syllogism: “Every human being is an animal; every animal is a substance; therefore every human being is a substance.” The whole of this is a discourse in which, once certain things have been posited and conceded—that is, the two propositions “Every human being is an animal” and “Every animal is a substance”—something else is produced through those very things that have been conceded, namely the conclusion: “Therefore every human being is a substance.” For through the conceded propositions, the consequent conclusion is necessarily inferred. These are the propositions: “Every human being is an animal” and “Every animal is a substance”; and from them something else is produced [Col. 1183C] than the things that were themselves conceded. The conclusion is: “Therefore every human being is a substance,” which is entirely different both from the proposition that says “Every human being is an animal” and from the one that proposes that “Every animal is a substance.”

Some syllogisms are predicative, and are called categorical; others are conditional, which we call hypothetical. Predicative syllogisms are those constructed from entirely predicative propositions, such as the one I noted above by way of example, since it is woven entirely from predicative propositions. Hypothetical syllogisms, on the other hand, are those whose propositions are connected by a condition, as in this example: “If it is day, there is light; it is day; therefore there is light.” The first proposition contains this condition: light exists only if it is day. Hence this syllogism is called hypothetical, that is, conditional [Col. 1183D].

Induction is a discourse by which a progression is made from particulars to universals, in this manner: “If, in directing ships, the helmsman is chosen not by lot but by skill; if, in driving horses, the charioteer is appointed not by the outcome of chance but by the recommendation of his skill; if, in governing the state, chance does not make the ruler, but expertise in directing it; and if similar cases are collected in many matters, then it follows that in every matter which one wishes to be seriously directed and administered, a ruler is appointed not by lot but by skill.”

You see, then, how the discourse proceeds through individual cases in order to reach the universal. For when he had gathered that ships, chariots, and the commonwealth are directed not by lot but by skill, he concludes, as though the same held true in other matters as well, what was universal in this way: “In every matter, too, a leader ought to be placed in charge not through chance but through skill.” Often, however, a collection of many particulars demonstrates another particular, as when someone says: “If rulers are not appointed by lot over ships, chariots, or fields, then rulers ought not to be chosen by lot for public affairs either.”

This kind of argumentation is usually highly probable, although it does not possess the same firmness as a syllogism. For a syllogism proceeds from universals to particulars, and, if it is constructed from true propositions, it contains a firm and unchangeable truth. Induction, by contrast, has probability but sometimes falls short of truth, as in this example: “Whoever knows how to sing is a singer; whoever knows how to wrestle is a wrestler; whoever knows how to build is a builder.” From many cases collected in a similar manner, one might infer: “Therefore whoever knows evil is evil,” which does not follow. For knowledge of evil cannot be lacking in the good person: virtue loves itself and rejects what is contrary to it, and one cannot avoid vice unless it is known.

Thus, besides these two principles and kinds of argumentation, two other modes of argumentation are discovered, one subordinate to the syllogism and the other to induction. In them it is easy to observe that one takes its beginning from a syllogism and the other from induction, yet the former does not complete a syllogism, nor the latter an induction. These are the enthymeme and the example.

An enthymeme is an imperfect syllogism, that is, a discourse in which the conclusion is hastily inferred without all the propositions having first been established, as when someone says: “A human being is an animal; therefore he is a substance.” For he has omitted the other proposition, namely: “Every animal is a substance.” Therefore, since an enthymeme strives to prove particulars from universals and is thus similar to a syllogism, but does not use all the propositions appropriate to a syllogism, it departs from the nature of the syllogism and is therefore called an imperfect syllogism [Col. 1184C].

An example is likewise connected with induction in a similar way and also differs from it. An example is that which seeks to demonstrate one particular through a proposed particular, in this manner: “Catiline ought to be killed by the consul Tullius, since Gracchus was killed by Scipio.” It has been approved that Catiline ought to be killed by Cicero because Gracchus was killed by Scipio. The insertion of the persons indicates that both of these are particulars and not universals. Therefore, since one particular is approved on the basis of another, what we call an example possesses something resembling induction. But because it does not gather several particulars by which to produce this result, it departs from induction.

Thus there are two principal kinds of argumentation: one called syllogism, the other induction. Beneath these, as though flowing from them, are the enthymeme and the example. All of these derive from the syllogism and receive their force from the syllogism. Whether it is an enthymeme, an induction, or an example, it receives its credibility most fully from the syllogism, as has been demonstrated in the *Prior Analytics* that we translated from Aristotle [Col. 1185A].

It is therefore sufficient to discuss the syllogism as the principal form, containing the other kinds of argumentation. It remains now to explain what a topic is.

A topic is, as Marcus Tullius holds, the seat of an argument. I shall briefly explain the force of this definition. The seat of an argument can be understood partly as a maximal proposition and partly as the difference of a maximal proposition. For there are some propositions that, since they are known through themselves, have nothing further by which they may be demonstrated; these are called maximal and principal propositions. There are others whose credibility is supplied by the first and maximal propositions. Consequently, among all matters that are in doubt, those propositions must hold the most ancient form of proof which can give credibility to others in such a way that nothing more evident than they can be found.

For if an argument is that which gives credibility to a doubtful matter, and if it must be more evident and more probable than the thing being proved, then all arguments must receive their credibility from those maximal propositions which are so self-evident that they do not require proof from elsewhere. But such a proposition is sometimes contained within the scope of the argument, while at other times, placed outside it, it supplies and completes the force of the argument.

An example of an argument containing a maximal proposition is the following. Let the question be whether kingship is better than the consulship. We shall say: “Kingship lasts longer than the consulship, since both are good; but what lasts longer is better than what lasts for a short time; therefore kingship is better than the consulship.” In this argumentation [Col. 1185C] the maximal proposition, that is, the topic, has been inserted: “Goods that last longer are of greater merit than those that last for a short time.” This is so evident that it requires no external proof, and it can itself serve as a proof for other things. Therefore this proposition contains the whole proof, and since the argument arises from it, it is rightly called a topic, that is, the seat of the argument.

For an example of a maximal proposition placed outside the argument but supplying force to it, let it be proposed to demonstrate that an envious person is not wise. “An envious person is distressed by the goods of others; a wise person, however, is not distressed by the goods of others; therefore an envious person is not wise.” In this argumentation the maximal proposition does not appear to be included, but the maximal proposition itself supplies force to the argument [Col. 1185D]. The syllogism derives its credibility from the proposition through which we know that things whose definitions are different are themselves also different. Now, part of the definition of an envious person is to waste away over the goods of others; and since this does not belong to the wise person, the wise person is consequently separated from the envious person.

Thus, in one sense, a topic is a maximal, universal, principal, indemonstrable, and self-evident proposition which, whether placed among the propositions in an argumentation or outside them, nevertheless supplies force to arguments and propositions. Universal and maximal propositions are therefore called topics, because they contain the other propositions, and through them a consequent and established conclusion is produced [Col. 1186A]. Just as a topic in itself contains the magnitude of a body, so these propositions, which are maximal, contain within themselves the whole force of the subsequent propositions and the consequence of the conclusion itself. In this sense, then, a topic—that is, the seat of an argument—is called a maximal and principal proposition supplying credibility to the others.

In another sense, the differences of maximal propositions are called topics. These are drawn from the terms established in the question, about which we shall discuss next. Since there are many propositions called maximal, and since they differ from one another, we call all the differences by which they differ from one another topics. For if the maximal propositions themselves are the topics of arguments, their differences must also be topics of arguments.

The substance of anything consists of its proper differences, as the substance of a human being consists in rationality, which is that person’s difference. These topics, which are the differences of propositions, are more universal than the propositions themselves, just as rationality is more universal than a human being. Hence the topics located in the differences are found to be fewer in number than the propositions of which they are the differences. For whatever is more universal is always found to be fewer in number. Therefore they can easily fall within the scope of knowledge, since their number is not so great that they quickly escape the learner’s memory.

What these differences are is better brought out by division. In predicative questions, one term is called the subject and another the predicate. For in predicative questions nothing else is asked except whether the predicate inheres in the subject. If it is established that it inheres, the question is whether it inheres as a genus, an accident, a property, or a definition. If it is shown not to inhere, nothing remains of the question. For what does not inhere cannot inhere at all as an accident, a definition, a genus, or a property. But if it is established that it inheres, the question remains as to which of the four modes of inherence it is.

Mere inherence pertains especially to the accident, for when something inheres neither as a genus, nor as a definition, nor as a property, but nevertheless inheres, it must inhere as an accident. Since this is so, a division must be made of those topics that we have established as the differences of maximal propositions. As we proceed through each one, it will become clearer by example that maximal propositions differ from their differences. We shall provide examples for each of the questions, arguments, maximal and principal propositions, topics, and their differences.

All topics—that is, the differences of maximal propositions—must be drawn either from the terms placed in the question, namely the predicate and the subject, or be assumed from outside, or arise from terms intermediate between the two. Of those topics that are drawn from the terms about which there is doubt in the question, there are two modes: one from their substance, the other from what follows upon their substance [Col. 1187A].

Those that arise from substance consist solely in definition. For definition displays substance, and a definition is the complete demonstration of substance. Let us clarify what we mean with examples, so that the whole reasoning of questions, argumentations, and topics may become plain.

Suppose, then, that it is asked whether trees are animals, and that the following syllogism is formed: “An animal is an animated, sensible substance; a tree, however, is not an animated, sensible substance; therefore a tree is not an animal.” This is a question concerning genus, for what is asked is whether trees are to be placed under the genus of animals. The topic that consists in the universal proposition is this: “That to which the definition of a genus does not apply is not a species of the thing whose definition it is.” The higher difference of the topic, which is likewise called a topic, is from definition [Col. 1187B].

You see, then, how the entire doubt of the question has been treated through the argumentation of the syllogism by means of suitable and congruent propositions. These preserve their force from the first and maximal proposition, namely, the proposition that denies something to be a species when the definition of the genus does not apply to it. The universal proposition itself has been drawn from the substance of one of the terms placed in the question, namely animal, or rather from its definition, which is “an animated, sensible substance.”

Thus, in the other questions as well, after the differences of the topics have been mentioned briefly and concisely, one must grasp the character of each with an alert and attentive mind. This topic, which is drawn from substance, has two modes: arguments are drawn partly from definition and partly from description.

Definition differs from description in that definition takes genus and differences, whereas description encompasses the understanding of the subject by combining certain accidents that produce one property, or substantial differences assembled apart from the appropriate genus. But although definitions formed from accidents seem in no way to demonstrate substance, nevertheless, because they are often put in place of a true definition that does demonstrate substance, even those proofs that are drawn from description appear to be assumed from the topic of substance. The following is an example.

Let it be asked whether whiteness is a substance; what is being asked is whether whiteness is subordinated to substance as to a genus. We say: “A substance is that which can be the subject of all accidents; whiteness, however, is subject to no accidents; therefore whiteness is not a substance.” The topic, that is, the maximal proposition, is the same as above: “Whatever’s definition or description does not apply to what is said to be a species is not the genus of that which is asserted to be a species.” The description of substance does not apply to whiteness; therefore whiteness is not a substance. The higher difference of the topic is from description, which we earlier placed under the account of substance [Col. 1187D].

There are also definitions drawn not from the substance of a thing but from the signification of a name, and applied in this way to the thing about which the question is asked. If, for example, it is asked whether one ought to study philosophy, the argumentation will be as follows: “Philosophy is the love of wisdom; no one doubts that this ought to be studied; therefore philosophy ought to be studied.” Here it is not the definition of the thing but the interpretation of the name that supplies the argument. Cicero also used this argument in defense of the same philosophy in the *Hortensius*. In Greek it is called ὀνοματικὸς ὅρος (*onomatikos horos*), and in Latin, “interpretation of the name.”

We have, I think, made sufficiently clear through evident examples these arguments that are assumed from the substance of the terms placed in the question. We must now discuss those that follow upon the substance of the terms.

Their variation is manifold, for many things adhere to individual substances. Arguments are therefore usually drawn from what accompanies the substance of anything, either from the whole, from parts, from causes—whether efficient, material, formal in the natural sense, or final—or from effects, corruptions, uses, and, beyond all these, from common accidents.

An efficient cause is one that moves and acts so that something may be brought forth. Matter is that from which something is made or in which it is made. The end is that for the sake of which something is made.

Let us first examine the topic that arises from the whole. “Whole” is generally said in two ways: either as a genus, or as that which, being integral, consists of several parts. The whole understood as genus often supplies arguments to questions in this way. Let the question be whether justice is useful; the syllogism is: “Every virtue is useful; justice is a virtue; therefore justice is useful.” Here the question concerns an accident, namely whether usefulness happens to belong to justice. The topic contained in the maximal proposition is: “What belongs to the genus belongs also to the species.” The higher topic is from the whole, that is, from the genus—namely virtue, which is the genus of justice [Col. 1188C].

Again, let the question be whether human affairs are governed by Providence. We shall say: “If the world is governed by Providence, while human beings are parts of the world, then human affairs are governed by Providence.” The question concerns an accident. The topic is: “What applies to the whole also applies to the part.” The supreme topic is from the whole, that is, from the integral whole composed of parts; this is the world, which is a whole in relation to human beings.

Arguments also arise from parts in two ways. They arise either from the parts of a genus, which are species, or from the parts of an integral whole, which are called parts in the proper sense. Concerning those parts that are species, let the question be whether virtue is the disposition of a well-ordered mind. The question concerns definition [Col. 1188D], namely whether “the disposition of a well-ordered mind” is the definition of virtue. We shall therefore construct an argument from the species as follows: “If justice, courage, moderation, and prudence are dispositions of a well-ordered mind, and these four are subordinated to virtue as to a genus, then virtue is the disposition of a well-ordered mind.” The maximal proposition is: “What inheres in each of the individual parts must inhere in the whole.” The argument is from the parts—that is, from the parts of the genus, which are called species—for justice, courage, moderation, and prudence are species of virtue.

Likewise, from those parts that are said to be parts of an integral whole: let the question be whether medicine is useful. This is a question concerning an accident. We shall say: “If driving away diseases, preserving health, and treating wounds are useful, medicine is useful; but driving away diseases, preserving health, and treating wounds are useful; therefore medicine is useful” [Col. 1189A].

Often, one particular part is sufficient for the firmness of an argumentation, as in the following case. If it is doubted whether someone has been made free, we can show that he was manumitted either by the census, by a will, or by the rod; once this has been shown, he has been proved to have been made free. These were the parts by which freedom was to be granted.

Again, if it is doubted whether what is seen from a distance is a house, we shall say that it is not, since it lacks either a roof, walls, or foundations; here again the argument has been made from one part.

The whole and the parts may be considered not only in substances but also in manner, time, quantity, and place. Whatever we state absolutely is a whole with respect to time; whatever we state as occurring at some time is a part with respect to time. Again, if we propose something simply, it is a whole in respect of manner; if we propose it with an addition, it becomes a part in respect of manner. Likewise, when we say “all” in relation to quantity, we speak of the whole; if we select something from a quantity, we posit a part of the quantity. In the same way, in relation to place, what is everywhere is plainly a whole, while what is somewhere is a part.

The following examples apply generally to all these cases: from whole to part in respect of time, “If God always exists, then he exists now”; from part to whole in respect of manner, “If the soul moves in some manner, then it moves absolutely; but it moves when it becomes angry; therefore it moves universally and absolutely.” Again, from whole to parts in respect of quantity: “If Apollo is truly a prophet in all matters, then it will be true that Pyrrhus will defeat the Romans.” Again, in respect of place: “If God is everywhere, then he is here as well.”

The topic from causes follows. There are several causes: those that furnish and produce the beginning of motion; those that cause subjects to receive the forms of species; those for whose sake something is made; and that which is the form of anything.

An argument from an efficient cause would be as follows. If someone wishes to show that justice is natural, he may say: “The gathering of human beings is natural; justice produced the gathering of human beings; therefore justice is natural.” The question concerns an accident. The maximal proposition is: “Those things whose efficient causes are natural are themselves also natural.” The topic is from efficient causes: “For what is the cause of anything produces that thing of which it is the cause.”

Again, if someone argues that the Moors do not possess weapons, he will say that they therefore make no use of weapons because they lack iron. The maximal proposition is: “Where matter is lacking, what is made from that matter is also lacking.” The topic is from matter. Both of these topics—from efficient causes and from matter—are called by one name, “from cause.” For what produces something and what receives the act of the producer are equally causes of the thing produced.

Again, from the end: let the proposal be whether justice is good. The argumentation will be: “If being happy is good, then justice is good; for this is the end of justice, namely that whoever lives according to justice may be led to happiness.” The maximal proposition is: “That whose end is good is itself also good.” The topic is from the end.

From that which is the form of anything, the argument is that Daedalus could not have flown because he had no wings of a natural form. The maximal proposition is: “Each thing can do only as much as its natural form permits.” The topic is from form [Col. 1190A].

Arguments from effects, corruptions, and uses arise as follows. If a house is good, its construction is good; conversely, if the construction of a house is good, the house is good. Again, if the destruction of a house is bad, the house is good; and if the house is good, its destruction is bad. If riding is good, the horse is good; and if the horse is good, riding is good.

The first example is from generations, which may also be called effects; the second is from corruptions; the third is from uses. The maximal propositions in all these cases are: “What is good in its production is itself also good, and conversely”; “What is bad in its destruction is itself also good, and conversely”; and “What is good in its use is itself also good, and conversely.”

Arguments from common accidents are formed whenever accidents are taken that either cannot or ordinarily do not leave their subject. Thus someone may say: “A wise person will not repent, for repentance accompanies an evil deed. Since an evil deed does not belong to a wise person, neither does repentance.” The question concerns an accident. The maximal proposition is: “That in which something does not inhere cannot possess what follows upon that thing.” The topic is from common accidents.

Having now completed those topics that are assumed from the terms themselves placed in the question, we must discuss those that, although placed externally, nevertheless supply arguments to questions [Col. 1190C]. These are from the judgment of the thing, from similarities, from the greater, from the lesser, from proportion, from opposites, and from transference.

The topic that contains the judgment of the thing is of this kind: we say that something is so because everyone or most people judge it to be so. These may be wise men or people thoroughly learned in each particular art. An example is that the heavens are revolving, as wise men and the most learned astrologers have judged. The question concerns an accident. The maximal proposition is: “One ought not to contradict what all, or most, or wise people judge.” The topic is from the judgment of the thing.

From similarities, the argument proceeds in this way. If it is doubted whether being two-footed is a property of a human being, we say: “Four-footedness belongs to a horse in the same way as two-footedness belongs to a human being; but four-footedness is not a property of a horse; therefore two-footedness is not a property of a human being.” The question concerns a property. The maximal proposition is: “If what inheres in a similar way is not a property, neither can that about which the question is asked be a property.” The topic is from similarities.

This topic is divided in two, for the similarity consists either in quality or in quantity. In quantity it is called equality, that is, parity; in quality, similarity.

Again, from what is “more”: if it is asked whether the definition of an animal is “that which can move itself,” we shall say: “It is more appropriate for the definition of an animal to be ‘that which lives naturally’ than ‘that which can move itself.’ But ‘that which lives naturally’ is not the definition of an animal; therefore neither should what appears less appropriate—‘that which can move itself’—be regarded as the definition of an animal” [Col. 1191A]. The question concerns definition. The maximal proposition is: “If what appears more appropriate to inhere does not inhere, neither will what appears less appropriate inhere.” The topic is from what is more.

From the lesser, the argument proceeds conversely. For if “a two-footed, walking animal” is the definition of a human being, and this appears less suitable as the definition of a human being than “a rational, mortal animal,” and if the definition of a human being is the one that says “a two-footed, walking animal,” then “a rational, mortal animal” will be the definition of a human being. The question concerns definition. The maximal proposition is: “If what appears less appropriate to inhere does inhere, what appears more appropriate will also inhere.”

There are many variations among the topics that supply arguments from what is more and what is less; we have treated them more carefully in our exposition of Aristotle’s *Topics*.

Likewise, from proportion: if it is asked whether magistrates ought to be chosen by lot in cities, we shall say that they ought not. For even on ships a helmsman is not appointed by lot. There is a proportion here: as the helmsman is related to the ship, so the magistrate is related to the city.

This topic differs from the one drawn from similarities. In the latter, one thing is compared with another. In proportion, however, there is not a similarity of things but a comparison of a certain relation. The question concerns an accident. The maximal proposition is: “What occurs in one thing must also occur in its proportional counterpart.” The topic is from proportion.

The topic from opposites is manifold. Four things are opposed to one another in four ways: either as contraries set against one another; or as privation and possession; or as relatives; or as affirmation and negation. Their distinctions were mentioned in the book written on the Ten Categories. Arguments arise from them as follows.

From contraries: if it is asked whether being praised is a property of virtue, I shall say that it is not, because being blamed is not a property of vice either. The question concerns a property. The maximal proposition is: “Contraries belong to contraries.” The topic is from opposites, that is, from contrariety.

Again, let the question be whether seeing is a property of those who have eyes. I shall say no, since it can happen that some who have eyes are also blind. For where possession exists, privation can also exist, and what is a property cannot depart from its subject. Since sight departs when blindness arrives, it is proved that seeing is not a property of those who have eyes. The question concerns a property. The maximal proposition is: “Where privation can be absent, possession is not a property.” The topic is from opposites according to possession and privation [Col. 1191D].

Again, let the question be whether it is a property of a father to be a procreator. I shall say that this appears correct, because it is a property of a son to be begotten: as a father is related to a son, so a procreator is related to one begotten. The question concerns a property. The maximal proposition is: “The properties of opposites that are related to one another are themselves also related to one another.” The topic is from relative opposites.

Likewise, let the question be whether moving is a property of an animal. Let the answer be no, because not moving is not a property of an inanimate thing either. The question concerns a property. The maximal proposition is: “Opposed things ought to have opposed properties.” The topic is from opposites according to affirmation and negation. For “to move” and “not to move” are opposed to one another according to affirmation and negation.

The argument from transference is formed as follows. The doubt is transferred from the terms in which the question has been established to something else that is more evident, and from the proof of that other matter the things placed in the question are confirmed. Thus, when Socrates was asking what justice could accomplish in each individual, he transferred the entire discussion to the greatness of the commonwealth, and from what justice accomplished there he confirmed that it was also effective in individuals.

This topic might perhaps appear to be from the whole. But because it does not inhere in the terms about which the proposition is made, and because the external matter is assumed only because it appears more evident, this topic is therefore appropriately called “from transference.”

This transference also occurs in a name whenever an argument is transferred from an obscure term to a more familiar one, as when it is asked whether a philosopher is envious and the meaning of the word “philosopher” is unknown. We transfer the argument to the more familiar term, saying that he is not envious because he is wise. The term “wise” is more familiar than the term “philosopher.”

We have now discussed clearly enough, I believe, those topics that are assumed externally. We must now discuss the intermediate topics.

Intermediate topics are taken either from a case, from cognate forms, or from division. A case is the inflection of a principal noun into an adverb, as *juste* (“justly”) is inflected from *iustitia* (“justice”). Thus the case of *iustitia* is the word *juste*.

Cognate forms are words derived from the same source in different ways, as *justum* (“just”) and *justus* (“just”) are derived from *iustitia* (“justice”). These are therefore called cognate both with one another and with *iustitia* itself [Col. 1192C], and arguments are readily drawn from all of them. For if what is done justly is good, and what is just is good, and if whoever is just is good, then justice is good.

These follow according to the similarity of their proper name. They are called intermediate topics because, when the question concerns justice and arguments are drawn from a case or from cognate forms, they do not appear to be drawn properly or directly either from the substance itself or from things placed externally, but from the cases themselves—that is, from things derived from them through a slight alteration. Hence these topics are rightly placed midway between those drawn from the terms themselves and those drawn from external matters.

The topic from division remains. It is treated in this way: every division is made either by negation or by partition. Division by negation is made when someone states: “Every animal either has feet or does not have feet.” Division by partition is made when someone divides as follows: “Every human being is either healthy or ill.”

Every division is made either of a genus into species, of a whole into parts, of a word into its proper significations, of an accident into its subjects, of a subject into its accidents, or of an accident into accidents. I explained the reasoning of all these more carefully in the book I composed on division. Examples appropriate to the understanding of all these matters should therefore be taken from that work.

Argumentations are formed through division, both by the separation made through negation and by that made through partition. Those who use these divisions either proceed by direct reasoning or lead the argument to something impossible or absurd, and then take up again what they had left aside. Anyone will understand this more easily if he devotes attention to the Prior Analytics. For the present, the following examples will provide knowledge of these matters.

Let the question be whether time has any origin. Whoever wishes to deny this will establish by reasoning that time did not arise, and will demonstrate it by direct reasoning in this way: “Time either has an origin or does not. But since the world is eternal—for the sake of the argument let this be conceded for a little while—and since the world could not exist without time, time too is eternal. But what is eternal lacks an origin; therefore time has no origin.”

But if the same point is sought to be demonstrated through impossibility, it will be stated as follows: “Time either has an origin or does not. But if time has an origin, it was not always present. Time, however, has an origin; therefore there was a time when there was no time. But to say ‘there was’ already signifies time; therefore there was a time when there was no time, which cannot happen. Therefore time has no beginning. For, if it is posited that it began from some origin, some absurdity and impossibility …

It may happen that there was a time when there was no time. We therefore return to the other alternative: that time lacks an origin. But this division by negation, whenever arguments are drawn from it, cannot allow both alternatives to be true, since they are divided by affirmation and negation. Thus, when one is removed, the other remains; when the other is posited, the first is eliminated. This is called the topic “from division,” situated midway between those topics that are usually derived from the matter itself and those assumed from outside.

[Col. 1193C] For when the question is whether time has any origin, the proposition that it has an origin is indeed assumed, and from it, through a proper consequence, a syllogism of impossibility and falsehood is constructed concerning the very matter under inquiry. Once this has been established, one returns to the former proposition, which must be true, since the proposition opposed to it has been driven to something impossible and absurd. Accordingly, because a syllogism is ordinarily constructed from the very matter under inquiry, the topic appears to have been derived from the matter itself; but because it does not remain with that proposition and instead returns to its opposite, it appears to be assumed from outside. For this reason the topic from division is placed midway between the two.

The topics derived from partition, however, are of two kinds. Sometimes the things into which something is divided can exist simultaneously: for example, if we divide a word according to its significations, all of them can exist at the same time. Thus, when we say *amplector* [Col. 1193D] (“I embrace”), it can signify either an action or a passion, and it can signify both simultaneously. Sometimes, as in the case of negation, the things into which something is divided cannot exist simultaneously, as when we say, “He is either healthy or ill.”

Reasoning proceeds in the first kind of division both because what is being sought is either present in all the alternatives or absent from all, and because it is present or absent in one alternative precisely because it is present or absent in the others. We shall not labor over the explanation of these matters at greater length, provided that the earlier *Analytics* or Aristotle’s *Topics* have instructed the diligent reader’s mind.

For example, if it is asked whether a dog is a substance, and the interlocutor proposes this division: “A dog is either the name of a barking animal, a marine creature, or a heavenly star,” and demonstrates in each case that the barking animal is a substance [Col. 1194A], that the marine creature too may be subsumed under substance, and that the star may likewise be posited as a substance, he has shown that a dog is a substance. Here, at least, he will appear to have drawn his arguments from the very alternatives proposed in the question.

But in syllogisms of this kind—“He is either healthy or ill; but he is healthy; therefore he is not ill”; or, “He is not healthy; therefore he is ill”; or again, “He is ill; therefore he is not healthy”; or, “He is not ill; therefore he is healthy”—the syllogism is drawn from things that are external, that is, from opposites. Hence this entire topic from division is said to lie midway between the two. If it is constituted through negation, it is in a certain way derived from the alternatives themselves, but in another way comes from external considerations. If, however, the arguments are derived from partition, it sometimes supplies them from the alternatives themselves and sometimes from external considerations.

[Col. 1194B] This, then, appears to be the division of topics given by the Greek Themistius, a most diligent and lucid writer who brought everything within the reach of easy understanding. Since this is so, I must briefly review the division of topics, so that nothing may be shown to remain outside it, but may be proved to be included within it. Whatever is in doubt in any question will be established by arguments drawn either from the very things posited in the question, from outside them, or from matters investigated as though placed on the boundary between the two. Beyond this definition nothing else can be found outside.

But if an argument is drawn from the things themselves, it must necessarily be drawn either from their substance, from what follows upon that substance, or from those things that occur inseparably or adhere to it and cannot—or ordinarily do not—be separated and detached from its substance [Col. 1194C].

Whatever is derived from their substance is found either in a description or in a definition, and, beyond these, in the interpretation of the name. Whatever follows upon them as though containing their substance consists in topics that stand in relation to the things under investigation as genus, difference, whole, species, or parts. Likewise, such topics include cause, efficient cause, matter, form, end, effect, corruption, use, quantity, time, and manner.

What is properly called an inseparable or adhering accident is included among common accidents. Beyond these, nothing else that could be inherent in anything can be found.

[Col. 1194D] With these matters established, let us now examine the topics that we previously declared to be assumed from outside. Things assumed externally are not so separate and detached that they do not in some way, as if from an opposing position, regard the things under investigation. For similarities and opposites are without doubt referred to the things to which they are similar or opposite, even though they properly and orderly appear to be placed externally.

These topics are similarity, opposition, greater, lesser, and the judgment of the thing. Similarity includes both resemblance to the thing and the relation of proportion, for everything possesses some similarity. Opposites consist in contraries, privations, relations, and negations. Comparison of the greater with the lesser is a certain dissimilarity among similar things. For distinguishing things that are similar in themselves produces the greater and the lesser [Col. 1195A]. Whatever is wholly separated from another in every quality and every relation cannot be compared with it in any way.

Arguments derived from the judgment of a thing provide something like testimony. They are inartificial topics, entirely detached, and follow not the thing itself so much as judgment and opinion. The topic of transference consists sometimes in equality and sometimes in comparison with what is greater or lesser. For the transfer of arguments and considerations is made either to what is similar or to what is greater or lesser.
