The topics that we said were mixed arise either from cases, from conjugates, or from division. In all of them, consequence and incompatibility are observed. Arguments drawn from definition, genus, difference, or causes supply force and order chiefly to demonstrative syllogisms [Col. 1195B]; the remaining arguments do so to probable and dialectical syllogisms.

Thus, the topics that chiefly concern the substance of the things about which the question is asked [Col. 1196A] look toward predicative and simple syllogisms; the remaining topics look toward hypothetical and conditional syllogisms.

The topics having now been set out, and their nature having been carefully illuminated both by definitions and by examples, it seems necessary to explain how these topics constitute the differentiae of maximal propositions—and to do so briefly, since the matter requires no lengthy discussion. All maximal propositions contain either a definition, a description, an interpretation of a name, a whole, parts, a genus, species, or the other features by which maximal propositions differ from one another. They do not differ in being maximal propositions; rather, one derives from a definition, another from a genus, and others from other topics. They properly differ in these respects, and these are called their differentiae.

But since Themistius’ division has been made clear [Col. 1196B], let us now proceed to M. Tullius’ division.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1195]

[Col. 1195B] That we treat the differences of the topics in many and varied ways should seem nothing surprising to diligent minds, since it is evident that each thing can often be divided according to many differences and into various forms of division. For because individual things are often comprehended not by one difference but by several, it is necessary that, according to the variety of the differences, there should also be a diversity of divisions: thus, for example, we now collect the differences of numbers according to the fact that some are even and others odd, and now according to the fact that some are prime and indivisible, others composite and divisible. The practice of the geometrical discipline also shows that triangles can be divided in many ways.

Yet in every case one must take care that nothing be left outside in any form of division and that nothing unnecessary or beyond what is required be added. Why, then, should it seem surprising that, after previously setting out the differences of the topics according to Themistius, I now bring forward different ones according to M. Tullius? After briefly presenting his division and clarifying it with suitable examples, I shall finally explain in what respect it differs from, or agrees with, the division set out above, and also how one division encloses the other.

For when M. Tullius proposed that the whole logical faculty—which he called the method of careful discussion—has two parts, one of discovering and the other of judging, and when he defined topics as the seats of arguments, from which arguments are drawn, and an argument as a line of reasoning that makes a doubtful matter credible, he divided all topics as follows. “Of these topics,” he says, “in which arguments are contained, some adhere in the very matter under discussion, while others are assumed from outside.” Thus he made two kinds of topics: he proposed that some adhere in the very terms of the questions, while others are assumed externally.

And those which adhere in the very things about which inquiry is made he divides in this way: “In the matter itself,” he says, “there are arguments drawn from the whole, from its parts, from its notation, and from those things which are in some way related to the matter under inquiry.” But those from outside [Col. 1196B] are called things that are distant and widely separated.

After this he divided the topic drawn from related things into corresponding members, as follows: “For some,” he says, “are conjugate, some are taken from genus, some from form, some from similarity, some from difference, some from contrariety, some from adjuncts, some from antecedents, some from consequents, some from repugnants, some from causes, some from effects, and some from comparison with greater, lesser, or equal things.” The nature of all these must be touched upon briefly, and examples must be supplied.

Of those topics which adhere in the matter itself under discussion, he said that the first is the topic from the whole. The whole of each thing consists in its definition. For every definition is equal to the thing it defines; and if each individual thing is a whole—for nothing can be integral unless it is whole—it is necessary that the whole should also exist in the definition, that is, in a statement embracing the entire substance of the thing defined.

A definition is a statement that indicates what each thing is. From this an argument is drawn as follows. Suppose the question is whether trees too are animals. I shall say: “An animal is an animated, sentient substance; a tree is not an animated, sentient substance.” I shall conclude: “Therefore trees are not animals.” The question concerns genus. The maximally general proposition is: “Where the definition is absent, that which is defined is also absent.” This is the topic from definition.

Parts are those whose coming together produces a whole. Parts are also called those things that divide a whole; these are commonly called species or forms. From the former kind of parts an argument is taken in this way. Suppose there is doubt whether the soul is corporeal. We shall divide the soul as though it consisted of three parts: the vegetative, the sentient, and the intellectual. But neither vegetating, nor sensing, nor understanding is corporeal. Since no part of the soul is corporeal, it has been shown that the soul as a whole is not corporeal. The question concerns genus, that is, whether the soul falls under body as under a genus. The argument is from parts. The maximally general proposition is: “From whatever the parts are absent, the whole is also absent.” This is the topic from parts that join together to constitute a whole.

Again, from those parts which divide a whole, an argument is taken as follows. Suppose the question is whether the soul moves with respect to place. I shall say: “There are three species of local motion: growth, diminution, and change of place. But the soul neither grows, nor diminishes, nor passes from one place to another. Therefore it does not move.” The question concerns an accident. The maximally general proposition is the same as above. This is the topic from parts that divide a whole.

From notation an argument is taken whenever credibility is sought from the interpretation of the name of a doubtful thing, as when it is doubted whether philosophy is a good. We shall say: “Philosophy is love of wisdom; but that is good; therefore philosophy is good.” Here, then, we have not defined the thing but disclosed the name by means of a definition. The question concerns genus. The maximally general proposition is: “The thing is clarified through the interpretation of its name.” This is the topic from notation.

Conjugates are words inflected from the same name, as from *iustitia* (“justice”) come *iustus* (“just”) and *iuste* (“justly”). An argument is taken from them as follows. Suppose it is asked whether laughing is rejoicing. We shall say: “If laughter is joy, then laughing is rejoicing.” The question concerns an accident. The maximally general proposition is: “Conjugate terms have the same nature.” This is the topic from conjugates.

Genus is that which is predicated of several species-different things in respect of what they are. From genus an argument is drawn as follows. Suppose it is asked whether the soul is a self-moving number, as Xenocrates held. We shall say: “The soul is a substance, whereas number is not a substance; therefore [Col. 1197C] the soul is not a number.” The question concerns definition. This is the topic from genus. The maximally general proposition is: “Things whose genera are different are themselves also different.”

Form is that which is predicated of several things differing in number in respect of what they are. From form an argument is made in this way. Suppose it is asked whether color exists in a subject. We shall establish this because white and black exist in a subject, proceeding from species to genus. The question concerns genus. For to exist or not to exist in a subject signifies an accident or a substance, which are the first genera of things. The maximally general proposition is: “The properties of genera are to be observed in forms.” This is the topic from form.

Similarity is the same quality in different things. From it an argument is judged to be made as follows. Suppose it is asked whether rulers ought to be assigned to cities by lot or by election. We deny that they should be assigned by lot, because even on a ship the skilled captain is chosen not by lot but by election. A ship is similar to a city, and a helmsman to a magistrate. The question concerns an accident. This is the topic from similarity. The maximally general proposition is: “The same judgment applies to similar things.”

Likewise, from difference: suppose it is asked whether a king is the same as a tyrant. We shall say: “Certainly not. In a king there are piety, justice, and gentleness; in a tyrant all these are different.” The question concerns definition. This is the topic from difference. The maximally general proposition is: “Different things are not subject to the same judgment.”

The contraries which Cicero calls contraries are divided in four ways. They are either opposed, such as white and black; privative, such as justice and injustice; relative, such as master and slave; or negative, such as living and not living. Arguments are drawn from all of them as follows: from opposed terms, “If health is good, illness is bad”; from privatives, “If we shun injustice, let us pursue justice”; from relatives, “Whoever wishes to be a father should have a son”; from negatives, “You do not accuse me of having done what you defend me as not having done.” The questions concern accidents. The maximally general proposition is: “In opposed, privative, and negative terms, contraries cannot belong to one another; in relatives, relatives cannot exist without one another.” This is the topic from contraries, which would more properly be called the topic from opposites.

Adjuncts are things that occupy a neighboring position, so that in time they may precede, as an encounter precedes love; adhere to the thing to which they are adjunct, as the sound of feet accompanies walking; or follow, as mental agitation follows a dreadful crime. Yet these things are not necessary; they occur frequently. For the person who has encountered someone has not necessarily loved that person in every case, and someone who has not encountered another may fall in love at a single glance. When someone is walking, the sound of his feet may be absent; and when he is not walking, his feet may make a sound if, while remaining in the same place, he moves them. Someone may tremble although he has done nothing dreadful, and someone who has done something dreadful may not tremble.

From these adjuncts an argument is drawn: either when we undertake to love someone because an encounter has preceded; or when, because the sound of feet has been heard, we infer that someone has walked to a place; or when we infer that someone has committed a dreadful crime because we see him trembling. In these cases the questions concern accidents, and the topic is from adjuncts. The maximally general proposition is: “Adjuncts are assessed from adjuncts.”

Antecedents are things which, once posited, necessarily bring about something else immediately, as when we say, “If he is a human being, he is an animal.” In these cases neither temporal relation nor the necessity of things varies; as soon as what precedes has been stated, what follows accompanies it.

This entire topic is constituted by a conditional relation. Once the condition has been posited—if the antecedent is present—what follows must be present, as in: “If she has given birth, she has had intercourse with a man.” “She has given birth” is the antecedent; “she has had intercourse with a man” is the consequent. The question is not which occurred earlier or later in time. Often these relations are arranged so that what is later in time appears as the antecedent in the proposition: giving birth is later than intercourse, yet if she has given birth, she has necessarily had intercourse with a man. When the former is posited first, the latter must nevertheless be understood.

Sometimes antecedent and consequent are simultaneous, as in: “If the sun has risen, it is day.” Sometimes what precedes is earlier and what follows later, as in: “If he is arrogant, he is hateful,” since a person becomes hateful through arrogance.

An argument is therefore drawn from the antecedent as follows: “If she has given birth, she has had intercourse with a man. I take what precedes: she has given birth; I conclude what follows: therefore she has had intercourse with a man.” From the consequent I reason in this way: “What follows is that she has not had intercourse with a man; I conclude what precedes: therefore she has not given birth.” The question concerns an accident. The topic is from antecedents and consequents. The maximally general propositions are: “When the antecedent is posited, what follows accompanies it”; and “When the consequent is abolished, what precedes is abolished.”

Repugnants are the consequences of contraries. Thus waking and sleeping are contraries, while snoring is an adjunct of sleepers. Snoring and waking, therefore, are repugnant. An argument is made from them as follows: “Would you call someone awake who is snoring?” The question concerns an accident. The argument is from repugnants. The maximally general proposition is: “Repugnant things cannot belong to one another.”

A cause is an efficient cause, which, preceding any thing, brings it about—not always in time, but by the property of its nature—as the sun brings about day. From this an argument is taken: “Why would you doubt that it is day, when you see the sun in the sky?” The question concerns an accident, for it is accidental to the air that it is day, that is, that it exists because of the shining sun. The argument is from efficient causes. The maximally general proposition is: “Where the cause is present, the effect cannot be absent.”

An effect is that which a cause produces. From this an argument is taken: “Would you doubt that he loved the woman whom he carried off?” The question concerns an accident. The argument is from effects. The maximally general proposition is: “Where the effect is present, the cause cannot be absent”; for example, the love that was the cause of his carrying her off was not absent.

Comparison with the greater occurs whenever what is lesser is compared with what is greater. From this topic an argument is taken as follows: “If the man who attacked his country in war eventually deserved pardon from his fellow citizens, why should not the man who was driven into exile because he had stirred up a sedition also deserve it?” The question concerns an accident. The argument is from comparison with the greater. The maximally general proposition is: “What holds in the greater case should hold in the lesser.”

Comparison with the lesser occurs whenever a greater matter is compared with a lesser. From it an argument is taken as follows: “If Scipio, as a private citizen, killed Gaius Gracchus when he was only moderately weakening the condition of the republic, why should the consuls not pursue Catiline, who desired to lay waste the whole world with slaughter and fire?” The question concerns an accident. The argument is from comparison with the lesser. The maximally general proposition is: “What holds in the lesser case should hold in the greater.”

Things are equal when they are of the same quantity, and equality is always similarity of quantity. From this an argument is made as follows: “If someone wishes to praise Demosthenes, why should he blame Tullius?” The question concerns an accident. The argument is from comparison with equals. The maximally general proposition is: “Equal things are subject to the same judgment.”

There remains the topic which he said is assumed externally. It rests on judgment and authority and is wholly probable, containing nothing necessary. That is probable which appears so either to everyone, or to the majority, or to the learned and wise—especially to those among them who are distinguished and eminent—or to those who have acquired expertise in a particular art, such as a physician in medicine or a geometer in geometry.

From this topic an argument is made as follows: “It is difficult to wage war against the Carthaginians, because Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus said so, and he had often had experience of it.” This topic is said to be external because it is not taken from the terms that have been predicated or subjected, but arises from a judgment posited outside them. It is also called inartificial and devoid of art, because the orator does not construct the argument himself from these materials but uses testimonies that have already been established and presented.

Having dealt with the differences of M. Tullius, by which he separated from one another the maximally general propositions that we have called topics, I think the division set out above should now be examined briefly, so that things that appear similar may be separated from one another by a fitting rationale.

The topic from the whole seems similar to that from notation, since both are constituted in definition. For the interpretation of a name is in a certain sense a definition of the name itself. But their principal difference is that the topic from the whole defines the thing, whereas the topic from notation does not define the thing but interprets the name. The thing and the name are different: the one signifies, while the other is signified.

Likewise, the topic from enumeration of parts seems similar to that from form. For form is also a part, and the person who divides a genus enumerates its parts. Nor can an argument be made from form in any other way than by division; form cannot be taken at all except through division.

Here too, however, there is a considerable difference. The enumeration of parts must necessarily divide the whole into its parts and assume all of them together for the credibility of the argument, whether they are parts properly so called or species—so that the genus is established by species, and the whole by parts. In form, however, one example is sufficient to demonstrate what is said of the genus.

Likewise, the topic from contraries and that from repugnants seem similar, but they differ because contraries are opposed face to face. Repugnants, however, prove themselves opposed through the conjunction of contraries. Sleeping and waking are immediately contrary to one another; snoring is repugnant to waking because it is joined to sleep.

Adjuncts, antecedents, and consequents are, as it were, neighboring. But they differ in this: in adjuncts there is no necessity, whereas in antecedents and consequents there is the greatest necessity. In adjuncts, moreover, temporal relations are highly important. For what is adjunct to a thing usually precedes it, exists with it at one and the same time, or follows it later.

But in antecedents none of these temporal relations is involved. Without considering time, as soon as the antecedent exists, the consequent must exist; and if the consequent does not exist, the antecedent must necessarily perish.

Enough has been said about M. Tullius’s topics. Let us now return to Themistius’s division, so that we may briefly explain how the divisions set out above can agree with one another. First, we shall collect the differences common to the whole division.

The preceding division taught that some topics of Themistius are present in the very terms about which the question is asked, that others are assumed externally, and that still others lie between the two. Thus it presents a threefold division.

M. Tullius’s division, on the other hand, displays topics in two ways. It proposes that some adhere in the very matter under discussion, while others are assumed externally. Thus he attached and joined all the topics which Themistius had placed in the middle to those which are constituted in the very terms under discussion. Such, in general, is the difference between the divisions; it will become clearer if we examine each case.

In the earlier division Themistius placed the topics that are situated in the terms about which the question is asked partly in substance and partly in what follows from substance. Definition, description, and interpretation of the name belong to substance. What follows from substance includes genus, whole, species, part, efficient cause, matter, form, effect, corruption, end, use, and common accidents.

Those topics which are assumed externally he divided into judgment, similarity, comparison of quantity, opposition, proportion, and transumption. Those which he placed between the two he assigned to cases, conjugates, and division.

M. Tullius, however, placed the topics that are in the matter under discussion under the whole, its parts, its notation, and those things which are in some way related to the matter under inquiry. He divided the related things by a manifold division, while he separated judgment alone as external. He also counted among the related things several of the parts that had been placed in Themistius’s division under what follows from substance. Likewise, he counted the middle topics among the related things.

In so varied a division it is necessary that the two systems should not agree in the same members. This can occur in all things divided in multiple ways. For example, someone might divide the forms of triangles as follows: some triangles are equilateral, some have only two equal sides, and some are joined by sides all unequal.

Again, the division might be this: some have a right angle and are called right-angled triangles; some are bounded by three acute angles and are called acute-angled triangles; and some extend toward an obtuse angle and are called obtuse-angled triangles.

It is therefore necessary that the two divisions agree with one another by different methods of classification. For what is right-angled is always bounded either by two equal sides or by three unequal sides. What is obtuse-angled, however, is likewise bounded either by two equal sides or by three unequal sides. What is acute-angled is bounded either by three equal sides or by two unequal sides.

Again, what is equilateral is always acute-angled; what is bounded by two equal sides may be right-angled, obtuse-angled, or acute-angled. What is bounded by three unequal sides must be either right-angled or obtuse-angled.

Accordingly, following this method, beginning together at the outset with the entire divisions of M. Tullius and Themistius, we shall show that they are mutually enclosed, bearing in mind throughout the examples and the explanation previously completed. Let us set out the whole of Themistius’s division, and after it let the Tullian division be placed, so that what must be said may become clearer when set before the eyes.

## Themistius’s Division

### In the Matter Itself

1. From substance.  
2. From definition.  
3. From description.  
4. From interpretation of the name.  
5. From consequents.  
6. From the whole or genus.  
7. From parts or species.  
8. From efficient causes.  
9. From matter.  
10. From form.  
11. From the end.  
12. From effects.  
13. From corruptions.  
From uses.  
14. From common accidents.

### Externally

1. From the judgment of the thing.  
2. From similar things.  
3. From the greater.  
4. From the lesser.  
5. From opposites, whether contraries, relatives, or terms distinguished according to privation and possession, or through affirmation and negation.  
6. From proportion.  
7. From transumption.

### Intermediate

From cases.  
From conjugates.  
From division.

## M. Tullius’s Division

### From the Matter Itself

From the whole.  
From parts.  
From notation.  
From conjugates.  
From genus.  
From form.  
From similarity.  
From difference.  
From contrariety.  
From adjuncts.

### From the Matter Itself

From antecedents.  
From consequents.  
From repugnants.  
From causes.  
From effects.  
From comparison:

- with greater things;
- with lesser things;
- with equal things.

### Externally

From authorit[lacuna]

[Col. 1203A] With these matters thus set out, let us now explain how the division of Marcus Tullius agrees with the division of Themistius.

The topic which Cicero called the topic from the whole Themistius proposed as the topic from substance. Both consist in definition, whether that definition is substantial or descriptive.

The topic from enumeration of parts, set out in Cicero’s *Topics*, is the same as the topic called “from division” among the intermediate topics in Themistius’s division. Whenever we try to demonstrate that something exists or does not exist, if we derive credibility from an enumeration of parts, this must necessarily be done by division. Division, however, is either of forms or of parts, although the topic derived from division, which Themistius placed among the intermediate topics, is placed by Cicero in his treatment of genus. For Tullius says, when speaking of genus, as follows:

“This argument is also suitably treated when it is taken from genus, by pursuing the parts from the whole, in this way: if fraud is a wrong, when one thing is being done and another is pretended, it is permissible to enumerate the ways in which this occurs and then to include under one of them the action that you allege was done fraudulently. This kind of argument is generally considered especially strong.”

The topic from notation in Tullius is the one which in Themistius is from interpretation of the name.

The topic from conjugates is common to both; Themistius placed it among the intermediate topics.

M. Tullius placed the topic from genus where Themistius placed the topic from the whole.

Cicero’s topic from form corresponds to Themistius’s topic from part, that is, from species.

The topic from similarity is common to both, except that M. Tullius includes proportion under it.

The topic from difference in M. Tullius can be understood as the topic from the whole or from the part in Themistius’s division: from the whole if the difference from which the argument is taken is constitutive; from the part if it is divisible.

[Col. 1204A] The topic from contrariety is the same as that which in Themistius is called the topic from opposites and is placed among the external topics.

The topic from adjuncts is the one which in Themistius’s division is called the topic from common accidents and is listed among what follows from substance.

The topic from antecedents and consequents is scattered in many ways. Definition and description, for example, can both precede and follow a thing. The same is true of interpretation of the name. Species precedes, while genus follows. An efficient cause also precedes, and the effect follows. Matter, however, is followed by the effect. Common accidents too, if they are inseparable, must follow. Conjugates likewise may precede or follow one another.

Thus this topic is mixed with many others and differs from the others not so much in its subject matter as in its treatment. For the very condition of consequence makes it a distinct topic, even when that condition of consequence is placed in definition, description, form, cause, or any of the other topics.

Repugnants are attached to opposites. Efficient things belong with efficient causes, and effects produced by matter are similar to the topic which Themistius placed under the heading of the end, for the effect of causes is their end.

The topic from comparison with the greater or lesser is the same as that which in Themistius is placed among the external topics under the greater and the lesser.

The topic from comparison with equals should be considered among those derived from similarity. For it has been said that in quantity there is similarity of equality.

There remains a topic common to both divisions, placed externally, which Cicero, like Themistius, proposed as the topic from the judgment of the thing.

M. Tullius’s division can therefore include the earlier division of Themistius in the following way, as may be seen from the table below:

| Tullian division | Themistian division |
|---|---|
| From the whole | From substance |
| From enumeration of parts | From division |
| From notation | From interpretation of the name |
| From conjugates | From conjugates |
| From genus | From genus or the whole |
| From form | From part or species |
| From similarity | From the similar |
| From difference | From the whole or the part |
| From contrariety | From opposites |
| From adjuncts | From common accidents |
| From antecedents and consequents | From definition, description, interpretation, species, cause, matter, common accidents, or conjugates |
| From repugnants | From opposites |
| From efficient causes | From causes |
| From effects | From the end |
| From comparison with the greater | From the greater |
| From comparison with the lesser | From the lesser |
| From comparison with equals | From similar things |
| From authority | From the judgment of the thing |

[Col. 1203D] The whole of M. Tullius’s division of topics appears to be contained in Themistius’s division by the formula of the preceding description.

The division of Themistius must now be reduced to the division of M. Tullius. Much of it corresponds to Cicero’s division, as the preceding description also shows. But if what remains from Themistius’s division is referred to the order of the Tullian division, it is easily shown how the divisions may be reduced to one another.

For the following topics from Themistius’s division corresponded to the continuous division of M. Tullius in the preceding description: Cicero’s topic from the whole corresponds to Themistius’s topic from substance. Cicero’s topic from enumeration of parts corresponds to Themistius’s topic from division. [Col. 1205A] Cicero’s topic from notation corresponds to Themistius’s topic from interpretation of the name. The topic from conjugates is common to both. Cicero’s topic from genus corresponds to Themistius’s topic from the whole. Cicero’s topic from form corresponds to Themistius’s topic from part, that is, species. The topic from similarity is common to both. Cicero’s topic from difference corresponds to Themistius’s topic from the whole or the part. Cicero’s topic from contrariety is the same as Themistius’s topic from opposites. Cicero’s topic from adjuncts is the same as Themistius’s topic from common accidents. The topics from antecedents and consequents are mixed with several others. Cicero’s topic from repugnants is likewise called by Themistius the topic from opposites. Cicero’s topic from efficient causes corresponds to Themistius’s topic from causes. Tullius’s topic from effects corresponds to Themistius’s topic from the end. M. Tullius’s topics from comparison with the greater and lesser are the same as Themistius’s topics from the greater and lesser. Cicero’s topic from comparison with equals corresponds to Themistius’s topic from similar things.

Since, then, the full division of M. Tullius can be fitted to certain members of Themistius’s division, it is impossible that the members of Themistius’s division should not immediately be reduced to those corresponding to them in Tullius’s division. Therefore, if anything remains in Themistius’s division that does not seem to have been assigned in the preceding formula, we shall be able to fit it into the complete division of M. Tullius. For the divisions are joined to one another by reciprocal interchange.

[Col. 1206A] The following topics remain from Themistius: from uses, from effects, from corruptions, from proportion, and from transumption.

The topic from uses, if the use of something is always productive of an effect, must be fitted to Cicero’s topic called “from efficient causes.” But if the use itself is produced, it must be assigned to Cicero’s topic called “from effects.”

As for the topic from effects, if an effect produces something, it belongs with efficient causes; but if the effect itself demonstrates something completed and perfected, it is the topic which Tullius called “from effects.”

The topic from corruptions can be called the topic from efficient causes. For since every generation produces something—that is, forms a substance—corruption likewise produces something, namely, strips and deprives a substance of its form, as death brings about the dissolution of the body.

The topic from proportion is the same as that which Tullius called the topic from similarities, since similarity among many things in many respects is proportion.

Transumption, if it is directed toward greater things, belongs to comparison with the greater; if toward lesser things, it belongs to comparison with the lesser; and if toward equals, it belongs to comparison with equals.

A sufficient example for reducing all these topics is the following description.

[Col. 1205B] Concerning the dialectical topics, we have explained as much as the purpose of the present work requires. Now it seems that we must discuss the rhetorical topics: what they are and in what respects they appear to differ from the dialectical topics. We shall reserve the complete discussion of this matter for the whole of the fourth book.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1205]

[Col. 1205C] If anyone carefully examines the title of the work, since we are writing about the differences among Topics, he must not expect from us merely that we set out the differences among dialectical places—or even among rhetorical places—but much rather that we separate dialectical places from rhetorical ones. We believe that we can undertake this more effectively if, beginning from the very nature of the faculties, we take the starting point of our discussion from the art of disputation.

For once the similarity and dissimilarity of dialectic and rhetoric have been demonstrated, it is necessary also to derive from the forms of the faculties themselves the common features and differences of the places that serve those same faculties. The dialectical faculty therefore considers only a thesis. A thesis is a question without circumstances. Rhetoric, however, treats and discusses hypotheses, that is, questions enclosed by a multitude of circumstances. The circumstances are: who, what, where, when, why, how, and by what means.

Again, if dialectic at any time takes circumstances—such as a person or some action—for discussion, it does not take them as primary, but transfers all their force to the thesis about which it is arguing. If rhetoric assumes a thesis, however, it draws it toward a hypothesis; and each treats its own subject matter, but assumes that of the other so that it may rely upon a faculty more readily suited to its own subject.

Again, dialectic is confined to question and answer. Rhetoric, however, runs through the proposed matter in continuous speech. Likewise, dialectic uses complete syllogisms, whereas rhetoric is satisfied with the brevity of enthymemes. There is also this difference: the rhetor has, besides the opponent, another judge to decide between the two. For the dialectician, the one who gives judgment is the opponent. From the opponent, a response resembling a judgment is elicited by the subtlety of questioning.

Since this is so, all their difference is established either in subject matter, use, or purpose: in subject matter, because thesis and hypothesis are subject to both; in use, because the one disputes by questioning and the other by continuous speech, or because the one delights in complete syllogisms while the other uses enthymemes; and in purpose, because the one seeks to persuade the judge, whereas the other seeks to force something from the opponent.

With these matters understood beforehand, a little later we shall enumerate both the rhetorical questions that are placed among the constitutions and the places belonging to each kind. For the moment, it seems that I should discuss the entire faculty very briefly—a great and difficult undertaking. For how closely rhetorical art is joined to itself by kinship cannot easily be considered, and it can scarcely even be perceived by hearing, much less easily discovered. On the transmission of this matter, at least, we have received nothing from the ancient teachers. For they give instructions about each individual subject, without laboring over what is common to all. Let us undertake, as best we can, this part of the doctrine, which has been left vacant.

We shall therefore discuss the genus of the art, its species, subject matter, parts, instrument, the parts of the instrument, the work and office of the speaker, and the end; after that, the questions and the places. Accordingly, since what is common must be examined, let us begin our discussion from this point.

The genus of rhetoric [Col. 1207B] is a faculty. Its species are three: judicial, demonstrative, and deliberative; and it is clear that its genus is what we have said. The species are those we mentioned above because the entire faculty of rhetoric is contained in them. The rhetorical faculty is complete in causes in the judicial genus, and likewise in the demonstrative and deliberative. These, however, are genera of causes. For all causes, whether special or individual, fall under one of these three genera: under the judicial, for example, special causes such as treason or extortion; under the deliberative, any causes involving consultation—for example, if one takes the matter specifically as concerning war or peace, or individually as concerning the war of Pyrrhus or a particular peace treaty. Likewise, in demonstrative causes, whatever falls under praise or blame is placed under demonstration: specifically, for example, the praise of a brave man; individually, the praise of Scipio.

The subject matter of this faculty is every matter proposed for speech. It is generally a civil question. The species proceeding from rhetoric take this matter for themselves, as it were, as forms, and hold it fashioned in a threefold shape, as will become clear later: a civil question that was previously formless with respect to the species becomes, once it has received an end, subject to each of the rhetorical species.

Thus, when a still formless civil question receives from the judicial species the end of what is just, it becomes a civil question established in the judicial genus. When it takes from the deliberative species what is useful or honorable, the civil question itself becomes established in the deliberative genus of causes. If it takes from demonstration what is good, then it becomes a demonstrative civil question.

The species proceed from rhetoric into the subject matter for this reason: no faculty can operate in its own subject matter unless it applies its own parts. When all its parts are absent, rhetoric itself is absent as well. But since we have spoken of the species of rhetoric, and since they are genera of causes, they are constituted in the following way: of all matters established in a civil question, those that have received the end of justice belong to the judicial genus; of all matters established in a civil question that have received an honorable or useful end, the deliberative genus is formed; and of all matters placed in a civil question that have taken only an honorable or good end, the demonstrative genus is formed.

But enough of this. We must now consider the parts [Col. 1208A] of rhetoric. The parts of rhetoric are five: invention, arrangement, expression, memory, and delivery. They are called parts because, if any one of them is lacking in the orator, the faculty is incomplete; and therefore it is right to call those things that form the whole oratorical faculty parts of that faculty.

But since these parts belong to the rhetorical faculty and together compose the whole rhetorical faculty, it is necessary that wherever rhetoric is complete, the parts themselves should also be present in their proper species. All the parts of rhetoric, therefore, will be present in the species of rhetoric. Accordingly, they are applied to the treatment of those civil matters that are shaped by the rhetorical species mentioned above. In the judicial, deliberative, and demonstrative case alike, invention, arrangement, expression, memory, and delivery are appropriate.

Since almost every faculty uses an instrument to do what it can do, the rhetorical faculty will also have an instrument. This is speech, which is partly concerned with the civil genus and partly not. We are now speaking of speech that contains some question or is adapted to bring a question to its conclusion. Speech that is concerned with the civil genus proceeds continuously; speech that is not concerned with civil causes is unfolded by question and answer.

The former is called rhetoric, the latter dialectic. They differ first in that the former considers a civil hypothesis, while the latter considers a thesis; next, in that the former is carried on in continuous speech, the latter in interrupted speech; and in that rhetorical speech has a judge besides the opponent, whereas dialectic uses the same person as both judge and opponent.

This rhetorical speech has six parts: the prooemium, which is the exordium; the narration; the partition; the confirmation; the refutation; and the peroration. These are the parts of the instrument of the rhetorical faculty; and since rhetoric is present in all its species, they will likewise be present in all of them. Nor will they be present merely as elements, but they will administer what those species accomplish. Thus, in the judicial genus of causes, the order of the prooemium, narration, and the remaining parts is necessary; and they are likewise necessary in the demonstrative and deliberative genera.

The work of the rhetorical faculty is to teach and to move; this too is administered by nearly the same six instruments, that is, by the parts of speech. But the parts of rhetoric, since they are parts of the faculty, are themselves also faculties. Accordingly, they too will use the parts of speech as instruments in turn, and in order to operate through them, they will contain those same parts.

For in exordia, unless the five aforementioned rhetorical parts are present—so that the orator invents, arranges, expresses, remembers, and delivers—he accomplishes nothing. The same is true of nearly all the remaining parts of the instrument: unless they possess all the parts of rhetoric, they are useless.

The effecter of this faculty is the orator, whose office is to speak appropriately for persuasion. Its end lies both in himself and in another. In himself, it is to have spoken well, that is, to have spoken appropriately for persuasion; in another, it is to have persuaded. For even if circumstances prevent the orator from persuading, the end is not thereby absent once the office has been performed. The end that is contiguous and related to the office is achieved when the office has been performed; the end that lies outside it is often not achieved. Nevertheless, this does not deprive rhetoric, content with its own end, of its dignity.

These matters are so interwoven that rhetoric is present in the species, while the species are present in the causes. The parts of causes are said to be constitutions, which may also be called by other names, both “constitutions” and “questions.” They are divided in accordance with the way in which the nature of things is also divided.

Let us arrange the differences among questions from the beginning. Since all rhetorical questions are wrapped in circumstances, they either concern a controversy over some written text or derive the beginning of their contention from the matter itself apart from the written text.

Those that concern a written text can arise in five ways. First, when one party defends the words of the writer and the other the intention; this is called the conflict between the written text and its purpose. Second, when laws disagree with one another through a certain opposition, and the parties defend them from opposite sides; this is called the constitution of conflicting law. Third, when the written text under dispute encloses an ambiguous meaning; this is called ambiguity by its proper name. Fourth, when something unwritten is understood from what has been written; because this is investigated through reasoning and a kind of syllogistic consequence, it is called reasoning or syllogism. Fifth, when a statement has been written whose force and nature cannot easily become clear unless it has been disclosed by definition; this is called the issue of definition, or the inscription.

It is not our task to demonstrate how all these differ from one another, but that is the task of rhetoric. We present these matters for the learned to contemplate, not for the inexperienced to learn, although we have discussed their difference briefly in passing in the commentaries on the Topics.

The differences among those constitutions that are placed in the contention over the matters themselves apart from a written text are separated according to the differing nature of the matters themselves. For in every rhetorical question it is asked whether something exists, what it is, of what kind it is, and, in addition, whether judgment may be exercised lawfully or according to custom.

If the act or matter being alleged is denied by the opponent, the question is whether it exists; this is called a conjectural constitution. If it is established that the act occurred but it is not known what the act was, because its force must be shown by definition, the constitution is called definitive. But if both its existence and the definition of the matter are agreed upon, while its quality is investigated, then, because it is uncertain under what genus it should be placed, it is called general qualification.

In this question the reasoning of quality, quantity, and comparison is involved. But since the question concerns genus, this constitution must be divided into several members according to the form of the genus. Every general question—that is, one in which the genus, quality, and quantity of an act are investigated—is divided into two parts. For the quality of the proposed act is asked either with respect to the past, the present, or the future. If it concerns the past, the constitution is called juridicial. If it concerns the present or future, it is called negotiative.

The juridicial constitution, whose investigation concerns the past, is divided into two parts: either the force of the defense lies in the act itself, and it is called absolute qualification, or it is assumed from outside, and the constitution is called assumptive.

The latter is divided into four parts: the crime is either conceded, removed, transferred, or, finally, compared. The crime is conceded when no defense of the act is introduced but pardon is requested. This can happen in two ways: by supplication or by excusing. You supplicate when you bring forward no excuse; you excuse when the blame for the act is assigned to circumstances that cannot be resisted or prevented, provided that they are not persons—for that will fall under another constitution. These circumstances are ignorance, chance, and necessity.

The crime is removed when it is transferred from the person who is attacked to someone else. The removal of the crime can occur in two ways: either the cause is removed or the act. The cause is removed when it is argued that something was done through another’s authority. The act is removed when it is shown that someone else either could or ought to have done it. This is especially effective when an action is brought against us on the charge that we failed to do what ought to have been done.

The crime is transferred when it is argued that an act was justly committed against someone, because the person against whom it was committed had often been unjust and deserved to suffer what is alleged. Comparison occurs when the act that the opponent accuses someone of having committed is defended on the ground that it was done for something better or more useful.

All these have their own distinctions, and therefore the books written by rhetoricians for teaching and explaining them contain very minute divisions in greater detail. For us, it is enough to have taken these matters from Marcus Tullius. The whole aim of our work is hastening toward something else.

The following point must be examined concerning all these matters. Marcus Tullius demonstrates that the parts of causes are constitutions in the passage where he attacks Hermagoras, saying that, if the parts of a genus of causes cannot properly be regarded as causes, much less will the parts of a part of a cause be properly regarded as causes. Every constitution, however, is a part of a cause; by this he indicates that constitutions are the parts of a cause.

The matter therefore raises a substantial question: how could they be regarded as parts of a cause? If they are parts in the sense in which species are parts, how can several constitutions exist in one cause? For species are not mixed with one another. Yet several constitutions enter into a cause; therefore constitutions cannot be parts of causes in the manner of species of a status.

There is also the fact that no species assists another opposed species in establishing its substance, whereas one constitution confirms another in establishing credibility. Nor can they be parts of causes as parts of a whole in such a way, for no composite made from a single part can be a whole and complete. And in a cause one constitution is sufficient to establish the cause.

What, then, must be said? The way is clear to reason. A constitution is not called a part of that cause which comes into controversy and which the status establishes, especially since a status added to a cause that has already been secured by a single constitution is not principal but accidental. Moreover, in one matter as many controversies arise as there are constitutions, and as many causes as there are controversies. Although one matter contains them, the causes nevertheless vary independently of one another:

A man saw a young man coming out of a brothel; shortly afterward he saw his own wife coming out of the same place, and he accuses the young man of adultery. There is one matter, namely the matter under dispute, but two causes: one conjectural, if the young man denies that he did it; the other definitive, if he says that intercourse in a brothel cannot be considered adultery.

The conjectural status is not a part of the same controversy in the case of the denier, nor is definition a part of it in the case of the person making a definition; each contains the entire cause. By “cause,” however, I mean not a cause in general, but a controversy formed by some constitution.

The parts of a general cause are constitutions in the following way. If every cause were conjectural and no other status could be found, the conjectural status would not be a part of the cause; the cause itself would undoubtedly be conjecture. But since all causes are held partly by conjecture, partly without it, partly by qualification, and partly by transference, the constitution is a part of the cause—not of the cause that it forms by taking hold of it, but of the general cause that it divides, each constitution cutting off, as it were, one of its members and making it its own.

Constitutions are therefore parts, like species, of the general cause, not of the cause that each one forms by taking hold of it.

Thus, the genus is the rhetorical faculty. The species of rhetoric are three: judicial, demonstrative, and deliberative. Its subject matter is a civil question, which is called a cause; the parts of this subject matter are constitutions. The parts of rhetoric are invention, arrangement, expression, memory, and delivery. Its instrument is speech; the parts of the instrument are exordium, narration, partition, confirmation, refutation, and peroration. Its work is [Col. 1211C] to teach and move; its actor is the orator; its office is to speak well; its end is both to have spoken well and to persuade. The whole of rhetoric is present in its species.

The species shape the whole subject matter in such a way that each in turn nevertheless claims the whole for itself. This can be understood from the fact that each species possesses all the parts of the subject matter. For in the judicial species you will find four constitutions, and you can find the same four in the deliberative and demonstrative species. Hence it is shown that, if the individual species possess all the parts of the general cause—which is the civil question—and if the cause itself is all its parts, then the cause, that is, the civil question, is in turn claimed in its entirety by the species in the same way that a voice reaches the ears of many people at one time together with all its parts, namely its elements. For at the same time the whole cause, with its parts, passes to different [Col. 1211D] species.

But when the species enter into the subject matter, that is, into the civil question, and possess it together with its parts, they bring with them the rhetorical faculty itself. Therefore the parts of rhetoric will also be present in each constitution. The subject matter, once brought in, brings its instrument with it; it therefore brings speech with it, and speech brings its proper parts. Thus, in the treatment of constitutions there will be exordium, narration, and the rest.

But when the instrument enters into the civil question, it also brings its work with it. It will therefore teach and persuade in every constitution. These things, however, cannot come by themselves unless there is someone to set them in motion as an artist and architect. This person is the orator. When he approaches the cause [Col. 1212A], he will perform his office; he will therefore speak well in every genus of causes and in every constitution, and he will also accomplish the end: both that he has spoken well in every constitution and that he has persuaded.

We have now discussed these matters individually in general. Later, if it is convenient, we shall discuss each one separately. Enough of this. We must now treat invention.

Earlier we presented the dialectical places; now we bring forth the rhetorical places, which must arise from the attributes of the person and the matter. The person is the one summoned to judgment, whose statement or action is criticized. The matter is the person’s act or statement on account of which he is summoned to judgment.

The entire division of places is therefore established in these two. For whatever provides an occasion for criticism, unless it tends entirely toward an inexcusable aspect, also supplies an opportunity for defense; accusation and defense alike consist entirely of these same places.

If a person is summoned to judgment and no act or statement is criticized, there can be no case. Nor can any act or statement be brought before judgment if no person exists. Thus, the whole structure of judicial proceedings turns upon these two things, namely the person and the matter.

But, as has been said, the person is the one summoned to judgment; the matter is the person’s act or statement on account of which he is made the defendant. Therefore the person and the matter cannot themselves supply arguments. For they are the very things about which the question is raised. Things that are in doubt cannot themselves lend credibility to the doubt. An argument, however, was a form of reasoning that makes a doubtful matter credible. What lends credibility to the matter is what is attributed to persons and matters.

If sometimes a person lends credibility to a matter—for example, if Catiline is believed to have held opinions against the commonwealth because his person is marked by the disgracefulness of his vices—then he does not lend credibility to the matter insofar as he is a person and is summoned to judgment, but insofar as, from the attributes of his person, he takes on a certain quality.

But so that the order of things may become clearer, I think we should discuss circumstances. Circumstances are those things that, when joined together, constitute the substance of a question. For unless there is someone who did something, something that he did, a reason why he did it, a place and time in which he did it, and also a manner and means, the case will not stand.

Cicero divides these circumstances into two groups, placing the circumstance “who” among the attributes of the person and establishing the remaining circumstances among the attributes of the matter.

He divides the first circumstance, “who,” because he attributes it to the person, into eleven parts: name, as “Verres”; nature, as “a barbarian”; way of life, as “a friend of the nobles”; fortune, as “wealthy”; interest, as “a geometer”; accident, as “an exile”; affection, as “a lover”; habit, as “wise”; purpose; actions; and speeches. These last three are those things outside the act or statement that is now being brought to judgment.

The remaining circumstances—what, why, how, where, when, and by what means—he places among the attributes of the matter. “What” and “why” he calls things accompanying the matter itself, placing “why” in the cause; for the cause of every act is that on account of which the act was done.

He divides “what” into four parts: the substance of the act, as “the killing of a parent”—from this source amplification is chiefly drawn; before the act, as “he hastily seized the sword”; while it is being done, “he struck violently”; after the act, “he buried him in a hidden place.”

Although all these are acts, they nevertheless belong to the action under investigation and are not the acts that are counted among the attributes of the person. The latter, being placed outside the matter under discussion and shaping the person, lend credibility to the matter at issue; the former acts, which accompany the matter itself, belong to the matter under investigation.

Cicero places the final four circumstances in the conduct of the matter, which is the second part of the attributes of the matters. He divides the circumstance “when” into time, as “he did it at night,” and opportunity, as “while everyone was asleep.” The circumstance “where” he calls place, as “he did it in a bedroom.” From the circumstances of “how” he derives manner, as “he did it secretly.” The circumstance “by what means” he calls means, as “with a large army.”

Although the distinction among these places is clear from the nature of the circumstances, we shall nevertheless act more helpfully if we show their differences from one another more fully. Marcus Tullius has sometimes classified certain things as accompanying the matter itself and others as belonging to the conduct of the matter. Among the things accompanying the matter itself he counted the place he called “while it is being done.” From the very meaning of the expression, this place seems to be the same as the one belonging to the conduct of the matter.

But this is not so. “While it is being done” means what was admitted at the time when the crime was being perpetrated, as “he struck.” In the conduct of the matter, however, are contained the things that preceded the act, occurred while it was being done, and followed the act that was performed. In all of these, time, place, opportunity, manner, and means are investigated.

Again, “while it is being done” is an act by which the matter was carried out. Therefore the things belonging to the conduct of the matter are not acts, but things attached to an act. No one would agree that time, opportunity, place, manner, or means are acts; rather, as has been said, they are attached to any act and do not in any way leave it, because they are related to and subordinated to the very matter that was performed.

Likewise, the things belonging to the conduct of the matter can exist without the things that accompany the matter itself. For the place, time, opportunity, manner, and means of any act can be understood even if no one performs the act that could be performed in that place, time, opportunity, manner, or by those means. Thus, the things belonging to the conduct of the matter can exist without those that accompany the matter itself, whereas the latter cannot exist without the former.

For an act cannot exist apart from place, time, opportunity, manner, and means. These things, which stand among the attributes of the person and the matter, resemble in the dialectical places those things that adhere to the very matters under investigation.

The remaining things, which are either attached to the matter or follow the matter that has been performed, resemble in the dialectical places those things that, according to Themistius, partly follow the substance of the matter, partly are external, and partly occupy an intermediate position. According to Cicero, however, they are counted among the affections or placed externally.

For things attached to the matter also lend credibility to the question itself; in a certain way they are affected toward and look back upon the matter under investigation. The seven circumstances counted among the attributes of the person or matter, when they begin to be compared and, as it were, enter into relation, produce the following results.

If what contains is referred to itself or to what is contained, the result is either a species or a genus. If it is related to something far removed from it, the result is a contrary. If it is related to its end and outcome, it is an event. In the same way, comparisons are made with greater, lesser, and equal things.

In general, such places are considered among things that are related to something else. For the greater, lesser, similar, equally great, or dissimilar arises from the circumstances counted among the attributes of the matter and the person, when the circumstances themselves are compared with other things, so that an argument may arise from them concerning the statement or act brought before judgment.

They differ from the preceding places in that the preceding places either contained acts or adhered to acts so closely that they could not be separated from them—for example, place, time, and the other things that do not leave the matter that has been performed. The things attached to the matter, however, do not adhere to the matter itself; they happen to the circumstances and provide an argument only when they enter into comparison.

Arguments are taken not from “contrariety” but from “the contrary,” and not from “similarity” but from “the similar,” so that it may be clear that an argument is not taken from relation but from things attached to the matter.

[Note: [Col. 1213D] This passage is resumed below, col. 1224, not in the same words, as follows: “so that it may be clear that the argument is taken FROM REVELATION in things attached to the matter.”]

The consequence, which is the fourth part of the things attributed to matters, is neither inherent in the things themselves in such a way that it does not leave the substance of the things [Note: [Col. 1214D] The sense seems to be: “nor is it inherent in the things themselves; for what is inherent in the things themselves belongs to the substance of the things,” etc.], nor is it derived from comparison. Rather, it either precedes the matter that has been performed or follows it.

This entire place is external. First, one asks what the act that was performed should properly be called; here the concern is not with the matter but with the word. One then asks who the authors of the act were, who approved its discovery, and who rivaled them. All this flows toward the support of the argument from an external judgment and, in a certain way, testimony.

Next, one asks what law, custom, agreement, judgment, opinion, or art belongs to the matter. Then one asks whether such a thing commonly happens by nature, or whether it is unusual and rare; whether people have been accustomed to approve and defend it on their own authority; and other matters that generally follow an act immediately or after an interval. These necessarily, being placed externally, tend more toward opinion than toward the nature of the things themselves.

Thus the things attributed to matters may be divided into four groups: some accompany the matter itself, and, as was said above, have been called acts; some belong to the conduct of the matter, and, as we recently demonstrated, are not acts but things attached to acts; some are attached to the matter. These, as has been said, are partly placed in relation and partly follow the matter that has been performed; their credibility is taken from outside.

Enough has been said about the rhetorical places. It must now be explained what similarity they have to the dialectical places and what their differences are. When I have shown this adequately and appropriately, the purpose of the proposed work will have been fulfilled.

First, just as in the dialectical places, according to Themistius, some adhere to the very things under investigation, others are assumed externally, and still others are placed between the two, so also in the rhetorical places some consist in the persons and the matter, about which the opposing side is disputing; others are external, such as those that follow the matter that has been performed; and others are intermediate.

Those nearest to the matter are the places that are considered from the remaining circumstances in the conduct of the matter. Those placed among the things attached to the matter are themselves also situated among the intermediate places, since they look back upon the matter under investigation through a certain affection.

Someone might instead say that the things attributed to persons, the things accompanying the matter itself, and the things considered in the conduct of the matter are similar to the places that, in dialectic, are drawn from the very things under investigation; that the consequences of the matter should be placed externally; and that the things attached to the matter should be placed between the two.

The correspondence with Cicero’s division is made in the following way. The things that accompany the matter itself and those considered in the conduct of the matter adhere to the things under investigation; those attached to the matter are placed among the affections; and those that follow the matter that has been performed are located externally.

Alternatively, one might think that the things accompanying the matter itself adhere to the things under investigation; that the things considered in the conduct of the matter, or attached to the matter, are affections; and that the things following the matter that has been performed are external.

The common features are already clear: the places occur almost equally in both faculties, such as genus, part, similarity, contrary, greater, and lesser.

Enough has been said about the common features. Their differences are these: dialectical places are also suitable for theses, whereas rhetorical places are assumed only for hypotheses, that is, for questions shaped by circumstances. For just as the faculties themselves are distinguished from one another by universality and particularity, so their places differ in scope and restriction.

The scope of the dialectical places is greater. Since they are independent of circumstances, which make causes individual, they are useful not only for theses but also for arguments placed in hypotheses; they enclose and encompass the places that arise from circumstances. Thus it happens that the rhetor always proceeds beyond the dialectical places, while the dialectician can be content with his own.

For the rhetor, because he treats causes arising from circumstances, takes arguments from those same circumstances; these must necessarily be confirmed by universal and simple arguments, which are dialectical. The dialectician, however, who comes first, does not need what comes later, unless a question concerning a person should arise. When a cause enclosed by circumstances occurs as an incidental matter for the dialectician in proving his thesis, only then does he use rhetorical places.

Thus, in dialectical places, when the situation requires it, arguments are taken from the genus, that is, from the very nature of the genus. In rhetoric, however, they are taken from that genus which is the genus under discussion—not from the nature of the genus, but from the matter belonging to the genus, namely from the very thing that is the genus.

The reasoning depends upon the fact that the nature of the genus has been previously understood. For example, if it is disputed whether someone was drunk, and we wish to refute this, we shall say that he was not drunk because no luxury preceded in him. This is evidently because, since luxury is something like the genus of drunkenness, where there was no luxury, there was no drunkenness either.

But this depends upon the other point. For since there was no luxury, drunkenness could not exist. What dialectical reasoning supplies is demonstrated from the nature of the genus. For wherever the genus is absent, the species must also necessarily be absent, since the genus does not leave the species behind.

The same applies to similarities and contraries; and in these there is the greatest difference between rhetorical and dialectical places. Dialectic seeks arguments from the qualities themselves, rhetoric from things that receive a quality. Thus the dialectician argues from the genus—that is, from the very nature of the genus—whereas the rhetor argues from the thing that is the genus. The dialectician argues from similarity, while the rhetor argues from the similar, that is, from the thing that has received similarity. In the same way, the former argues from contrariety and the latter from the contrary.

With everything proposed above now dispatched, I think it should be added that Marcus Tullius, in the Topics that he published for Gaius Trebatius, an expert in law, did not discuss the Topics in the manner in which one might debate the Topics themselves, but rather explained how arguments belonging to the rhetorical faculty could be derived. We have treated this more carefully in the commentaries that we wrote on Cicero’s Topics.

As for how these dialectical arguments should be discussed—in the commentaries which [were written] by us on Aristotle’s Topics—
we have written out the translated [texts]; it has been made clear.

# [TWO UNPUBLISHED OPUSCULA.]

## [Column 1215]

### ON TWO UNPUBLISHED OPUSCULA OF BOETHIUS AND ON A COMMENTARY ON SEVERAL OF BOETHIUS’ POEMS

[Column 1215D] I shall give this commentary below in an appendix. — **Editor**

Manlius Severinus Boethius, whose services to literature are brighter than the midday sun, wrote a considerable number of works that have not yet been printed with the others, either because they seem to have been consumed by the devouring power of time or because, through neglect, they lie hidden in manuscript in the shelves of libraries. Bibliographers nevertheless mentioned some of these works. Among them, Peter Bertius’ diligence in the prolegomena to his edition of Boethius’ *Consolation of Philosophy*—I scarcely know whether anyone surpassed it—deserves recognition, although even he did not record everything.

For my part, while examining ancient manuscripts, I long found nothing unpublished by Boethius. The Vatican manuscripts, which contain Boethius in great number, do not even fill the gap that mars the printed commentary of Boethius on Cicero’s *Topics*. At last, however, I came upon a very ancient manuscript which bestowed upon me two unpublished opuscula by so distinguished a writer.

Moreover, to remove any doubt about their authenticity, Sigebert of Gembloux served as a witness to both works. In chapter 37 I read these words: “Boethius wrote, among other things, on the kinship of dialectic and rhetoric and on the distinction of rhetorical topics.” The word “dialectic,” however, was inserted by Sigebert—or by someone else—for the title of my manuscript and the work itself reject it. In all other respects Sigebert’s statement is entirely correct.

Since Sigebert’s testimony is so clear, I am genuinely surprised that Trithemius, in chapter 201, and his follower Bertius, in the prologue cited above, mention only a book *On Rhetorical Topics*. Since I have begun to correct Bertius, I shall add that he is also wrong to place among Boethius’ lost writings a book *On the Squaring of the Circle*. This work is by Franco, who lived in the eleventh century. Because it is customarily placed after Boethius’ *Geometry* in manuscripts—as I know from a certain Vatican exemplar—it was wrongly attributed to Boethius by some reader whose hurried eye misread it; and, as commonly happens, the error passed into the accounts of others.

The noble, and perhaps unique, manuscript preserving these two opuscula is a parchment codex of 562 pages, written around the eleventh century. Its contents are as follows:

- Page 8: the end of the *Isagoge* of Porphyry, which is acephalous because of a defect in the manuscript; there also begin Aristotle’s *Categories*, translated by Boethius.
- Page 59: Aristotle’s *On Interpretation* (*περὶ ἑρμηνείας*), likewise translated by Boethius.
- Page 88: Cicero’s *Topics*.
- Page 181: Boethius’ four books of *Topical Differences*.
- Page 223: two books of the *Introduction to Categorical Syllogisms*.
- Page 300: three books *On Hypothetical Syllogisms*.
- Page 401: the *Book of Divisions*.
- Page 431: Victorinus’ *Book of Definitions*.
- Page 501: **ON THE KINSHIP OF RHETORIC**.
- Page 509: **THE DISTINCTION OF RHETORICAL TOPICS**.
- Page 512: the *Book before the Categories*.

Furthermore, while examining Boethian manuscripts, as I have said, a certain very ancient codex especially arrested my attention. Written approximately in the tenth century, it contains Boethius’ *Consolation of Philosophy*. It is noteworthy not so much for its excellent and ancient scholia on that work—for such scholia often occur in manuscripts—as for a certain lengthy and learned commentary on several poems in the Boethian work, sent to Bishop Bovo and, in my opinion, fully deserving the light of print.

There were three Bovos in the tenth century who were abbots of the monastery of New Corbie on the River Weser in Saxony, as Mabillon carefully relates in volume VII, page 706, of the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*. During the time of the second Bovo, Bruno flourished as a monk at New Corbie. Since the commentary we are discussing is addressed by its author, B., to Bovo, I strongly suspect that Bruno was the author of the commentary and that Bovo later became a bishop.

Moreover, the commentary’s mention of barbarian incursions suits that period extremely well. For in the work cited above, Mabillon, volume VI, page 489, quotes a passage from a certain history—now lost—by Adam of Bremen, whose author was Bovo, abbot of Corbie. Writing about the events of his own time, he said: “In our own times, a severe incursion of barbarians was raging throughout almost the entire kingdom of the Franks.”

## [Column 1217]

### AN. MANL. SEV. BOETHIUS’ *SURVEY OF THE KINSHIP OF RHETORIC* (S)*

#### 1

How closely rhetoric is joined to itself by kinship cannot easily be considered; indeed, it can scarcely even be noticed by hearing, much less readily discovered. The error concerning this matter is produced by a divided discussion of individual precepts: teachers give instructions about each subject separately, without undertaking anything concerning their common relationship.

Let us therefore undertake, as best we can, this neglected part of doctrine. We shall speak about the genus of the art, its species, parts, instrument, the parts of its instrument, its work, the function of its author, and its end. Accordingly, let us begin our discussion by considering what must be examined in common.

#### 2

The genus of rhetoric, then, is an ability; its species are three: judicial, demonstrative, and deliberative. [The author speaks in this way also at folio 11.] That its genus is what we have said is evident. Its species are those we listed above because the whole of rhetoric is contained in them. The entire power of rhetoric is present in the judicial kind of cases, and entirely in the demonstrative or deliberative kind.

These, however, are kinds of cases. For all cases, whether specific or individual, fall under one of these three kinds. Under the judicial kind fall specific cases such as cases of treason or extortion, and individual cases such as the treason case of Cornelius or the extortion case of Verres.

Under the deliberative kind fall all cases involving deliberation—for example, if considered specifically, a question concerning war or peace; if individually, a question concerning Pyrrhus’ war or peace.

Likewise, under the demonstrative kind fall all matters concerned with praise and blame: specifically, the praise of a brave man; individually, the praise of Scipio.

#### 3

The matter of this ability is every subject proposed for discussion, but especially a civil question. The species proceeding from rhetoric receive this matter as though they were certain forms and hold it in a threefold configuration, as will become clear later.

Thus, a civil question that is still unformed with respect to the species becomes, once it has received an appropriate end, subject to each rhetorical species. When an as-yet-unformed civil question receives from the judicial species the end of justice, that civil question itself becomes constituted in the judicial kind.

When it receives from the deliberative species what is useful or honorable, the civil question itself becomes constituted in the deliberative kind of cases. If, however, it receives from the demonstrative species what is good, then the civil question becomes demonstrative.

The species proceed from rhetoric into the matter because no ability can operate in its own matter in any other way than by applying its own parts. When all its parts are absent, rhetoric itself is absent.

#### 4

Since we have spoken of the species of rhetoric as kinds of cases, they are configured in this way with respect to all affairs established in civil business.

The kind is judicial wherever the end is justice. The deliberative kind belongs to all matters established in a civil question that have received an honorable or useful end. The demonstrative kind belongs to all matters placed in a civil question that have received an end involving the honorable, the just, or the good.

But enough on these matters for now.

#### 5

We must now consider the parts of rhetoric. The parts of rhetoric are five: invention, arrangement, expression, memory, and delivery.

They are called parts because, if any one of them is lacking in an orator, the ability is incomplete. Since these elements collectively form the oratorical ability, there is nothing absurd in calling them parts of that ability.
