But since these parts belong to the rhetorical ability and together compose the whole rhetorical ability, wherever rhetoric is present, they must also follow. Rhetoric is complete in its proper species; therefore all the parts of rhetoric will be present in the species of rhetoric.

Accordingly, these parts will also be applied to the treatment of those civil affairs that are formed by the rhetorical species mentioned above. In the judicial, deliberative, and demonstrative case alike, invention, arrangement, expression, memory, and delivery are equally appropriate.

#### 6

Since nearly every ability uses an instrument to accomplish what it can do, there will therefore be some instrument of rhetoric. This instrument is speech, which is partly concerned with civil matters and partly not.

We are speaking of speech that contains a question or that is adapted to bring a question to its conclusion. Speech that is concerned with civil matters proceeds continuously; speech that is not concerned with civil cases is explained by question and answer.

The former is called rhetoric, the latter dialectic. They differ in the following respects. First, rhetoric considers civil hypotheses (*ὑποθέσεις*), whereas dialectic considers theses (*θέσεις*). [The manuscript reads *illa* (“that one”) for *haec* (“this one”).] Second, rhetoric proceeds in continuous speech, whereas dialectic proceeds in interrupted speech. [The manuscript reads *illa* (“that one”) for *haec* (“this one”).] Third, rhetorical speech has a judge in addition to its opponent, whereas dialectical speech relies upon the same person as both judge and opponent. [Perhaps *utitur* (“uses”) should be read instead of *nititur* (“relies upon”).]

#### 7

This rhetorical speech has six parts: the proem, which is the exordium; the narration; the partition; the confirmation; the refutation; and the peroration.

Since these are parts of the instrument of the rhetorical ability, and rhetoric is present in all its species, they will likewise be present in those species. [The manuscript has *eisdem* (“the same”), whereas below it has *hisdem*.] Indeed, they will not merely be present in them; they will administer the matters carried out through them.

Thus, in the judicial kind of cases, the order of the proem, narration, and the other parts is necessary, just as they are necessary in the demonstrative and deliberative kinds. [The manuscript reads *et* (“and”) for *quae* (“which”).]

The work of the rhetorical ability is to teach and to move. This work is likewise administered through nearly the same six instruments, that is, the parts of speech.

The parts of rhetoric, however, since they are parts of an ability, are themselves also abilities. Accordingly, they too will use the parts of speech as instruments, in part, and will be present in them so that they may operate through them.

For unless the aforementioned rhetorical parts are present—so that the orator may discover, express, arrange, remember, and deliver—he will accomplish nothing. In the same way, those things that are generally parts of the instrument are useless unless they possess all the parts of speech. [The manuscript reads: “for unless they are in the exordia.”] [The manuscript reads *earum* (“of them”) instead of *eae* (“those”).]

The producer of this ability is the orator, whose function is to speak suitably for persuasion.

#### 8

The end lies both in the orator himself and in another person. In the orator himself, it is to have spoken well—that is, to have spoken suitably for persuasion. In the other person, it is to have persuaded.

For if some obstacles prevent the orator from persuading, then, although he has performed his function, the end is not attained. Yet the end that is contiguous and related to the function is attained by performing the function; the end that lies outside it is often not attained.

Nevertheless, rhetoric will not be deprived of honor because it is content with its own end. These things are so intermingled that rhetoric is present in the species and the species are present in rhetoric. [The manuscript lacks *rhetoricae* (“in rhetoric”).]

The parts of cases are said to be the constitutions of the case. This must be examined as follows. How can they be considered parts of cases if they are parts in the way that species are? How can several constitutions exist in one case, since species are mutually unmixed?

Yet several constitutions enter into a case. They are therefore not parts of cases in the way that species are parts. Furthermore, no species helps an opposed species toward its substance. A constitution, however, confirms another constitution for the sake of credibility.

Nor can they be parts of cases in such a way as to be parts of a whole. No composite made from a single part can be a whole and complete. Yet in a case one constitution is sufficient to establish the case. [The manuscript reads *causam* (“the case”) instead of *causa* (“in the case”).]

#### 9

What, then, should be said? The way is clear to reason.

A constitution is not called a part of the case that has come into dispute and that the status establishes, especially since a status added to a case already secured by one constitution is not principal but incidental. In one affair, as many disputes arise as there are constitutions.

But as many disputes as there are, so many cases there are. Even if one affair contains them, the cases nevertheless remain distinct and mutually unmixed.

Suppose, for example, that someone saw a young man coming out of a brothel and shortly afterward saw his own wife emerging from the same place. He accuses the young man of adultery. Here there is one affair at issue, but two cases: one conjectural, if the young man denies that he did it; the other definitive, if he says that intercourse in a brothel cannot be considered adultery.

Yet the conjectural status is not a part of the same dispute for the one who denies the act, nor is the definition a part for the one who defines it. Each contains the entire case.

By “case” I do not mean the term generally, but a dispute secured by some constitution.

#### 10

The constitutions are parts of a general case in the following way. If every case were conjectural and no other status could be found, the conjectural status would not be a part of the case; the case itself would undoubtedly be conjectural.

But since all cases are held partly by conjecture, partly [the text reads *sine*, uncertain], partly by quality, and partly by translation, the constitution is a part of the case—not of the case that it forms by holding it, but of the general case that it divides. Each constitution, as it were, cuts off a member of that general case and makes it its own.

Constitutions are therefore parts in the same way as species: they are parts of the general case, not of the particular case that each constitution forms by holding it.

#### 11

The genus of rhetoric is therefore an ability. The species of rhetoric are three: judicial, demonstrative, and deliberative. [Here the epilogue is made; see folio 2 again.] Its matter is a civil question, which is called a case. The parts of this matter are the constitutions.

The parts of rhetoric are invention, arrangement, expression, memory, and action. Its instrument is speech. The parts of the instrument are exordium, narration, partition, confirmation, refutation, and peroration.

Its works are teaching and moving. Its agent is the orator. His function is to speak well. Its end is both to have spoken well and to persuade.

#### 12

The whole of rhetoric is present in its species; the species, however, so form the whole matter that they also claim it wholly for themselves in return.

This can be understood from the fact that each species possesses all the parts of the matter. For in the judicial species one finds four constitutions, and one can likewise find the same four in the deliberative and demonstrative species.

Thus it is shown that, if the individual species possess all the parts of the general case—which is the civil question—and if all the parts constitute the case, then the case itself, that is, the civil question, is in turn wholly claimed by the species.

This occurs in the same way that a voice reaches the ears of many people at one time, complete with all its parts, that is, its elements. At the same time, the whole case passes to different species together with its parts.

#### 13

When the species enter into the matter—that is, into the civil question—and possess it together with its parts, they also bring with them rhetoric itself, and therefore its parts.

Thus the parts of rhetoric will be present in each constitution. But when rhetoric is brought into the matter, it brings its instrument with it. It therefore brings speech and its proper parts, so that in the constitutions there will be an exordium, narration, and the rest.

When the instrument enters into the civil question, it also brings its work with it. It will therefore teach and persuade in every constitution.

But these things cannot come by themselves unless there is someone to set them in motion, like an artisan and architect. This person is the orator, who, when he approaches the case, will perform his function.

He will therefore speak well in every kind of case and in every constitution. The orator will also achieve the end: both by speaking well in every constitution and by persuading.

We have now treated these matters collectively. Later, if convenient, we shall discuss each one separately.

**HERE ENDS THE GENERAL SURVEY OF THE KINSHIP OF RHETORIC.**

## [Column 1221]

### AN. MANL. SEV. BOETHIUS’ *DISTINCTION OF RHETORICAL TOPICS* (S)*

[Column 1221D] In the manuscript: “Mallius,” and shortly afterward “Boecius.” I give the more correct spelling of these names on the authority of the very ancient manuscript of Boethius’ *Consolation*, Vatican codex 3363. — **Editor**

#### 1

A person is someone summoned to court; the affair is the deed or statement of the person on account of which the person is summoned to court. The person and the affair cannot themselves supply arguments, for they are the subjects of inquiry.

Those things attributed to persons and affairs, however, establish the credibility of the affair. The person also establishes the credibility of the affair, but not insofar as he is a person; rather, insofar as he receives a certain quality from the attributes of the person.

Circumstances are those things which, when brought together, constitute the substance of the question. Unless there is someone who acted, something that he did, and a reason why he did it, as well as the place and time in which he did it, and unless manner and means are also present, the case and the affair will not stand.

Cicero divides these circumstances into two groups. [Compare Cicero, *Rhetoric* II.9 ff.] He places the circumstance “who” among the attributes of the person, and the remaining six among the attributes of the affair.

He divides the first circumstance, “who,” which he attributes to the person, into eleven parts: name, as in Verres; nature, as in barbarian; way of life, as in a friend of the nobles; fortune, as in a wealthy man; occupation, as in a geometer; accident, as in an exile; affection, as in a lover; disposition, as in a wise man; intention, as in “Come now, dear father, to place upon our neck”; and deeds, such as the speeches that lie outside the deed or statement now brought before the court.

#### 2

The remaining circumstances—what, why, when, where, how, and by what means—he places among the attributes of the affair.

By “what” and “why” he means the elements belonging to the affair itself, establishing them in the case. He divides “what” into four parts:

- the principal fact, as in the killing of a parent;
- before the deed, as in “he seized the sword in agitation”;
- while it is happening, as in “he struck violently”;
- after the deed, as in “he buried [him] in a hidden place.”

Although all these things exist, they belong to the act under investigation and therefore are not the deeds that belong among the attributes of the person, or that have been counted there.

Those deeds, because they are placed outside the affair under discussion and shape the person, establish credibility for the affair that is the subject of the inquiry. These deeds, however, because they belong to the affair itself, pertain to the affair under investigation.

Cicero places the final four circumstances under the conduct of the affair, which is the second part of the attributes of affairs.

He divides the circumstance “when” into time, as in “he did it at night,” and opportunity, as in “while everyone was asleep.”

For “where” among the circumstances, he gives place, as in “he did it in the bedroom.” For “how,” he gives manner, as in “he did it secretly.” For “by what means,” among the circumstances, he gives means, as in “with a large army.”

#### 3

To prevent what was said under “while it is happening” from being thought identical with what belongs under the conduct of the affair, the distinction is this:

“While it is happening” refers to what was committed at the time when the crime was perpetrated, such as the striking. Under the conduct of the affair, however, belong those things that include what occurred before the deed, while it was happening, and after the deed.

For in all these matters time, opportunity, place, manner, and means are investigated.

Again, “while it is happening” is the deed by which the affair was carried out. The things belonging to the conduct of the affair, however, are not deeds, but things attached to the deed and in a certain way subordinate to the affair that was carried out.

Moreover, the things belonging to the conduct of the affair can exist without the things that belong to the affair itself. The latter, however, cannot exist without them. [The word *sine* (“without”) is absent from the manuscript.] The things attached to the affair themselves also establish credibility for the question.

They are, in a certain way, effects that look back upon the affair being conducted, as follows.

#### 4

Seven circumstances have been counted among the attributes of the person or the affair. When these are compared with other things and, as it were, brought to light, they become genus, part, contrary, consequence, greater, lesser, similar, equal in magnitude, or different.

These therefore occur to the circumstances counted among the attributes of affairs. When they are compared with other things, arguments are drawn from them concerning the deed or statement brought before the court.

They differ from the matters mentioned above in this respect: the former either contained the deeds or adhered to the deeds so closely that they could not be separated from them—for example, place, time, and the other circumstances that do not leave out the affair being conducted.

The things attached to the affair, however, do not adhere to the affair; they occur to the circumstances. They provide arguments only when the things attached to the affair have entered into comparison.

#### 5

Arguments are drawn not from contrariety but from the contrary, and not from similarity but from the similar. It is therefore evident that arguments are drawn from revelation among the things attached to the affair, and that the things attached to the affair are those that are related to the affair itself under discussion.

Consequence, however, exists neither in the things themselves nor is it discovered through comparison. Rather, antecedents or concomitants attend the deed that has been done.

Since the distinction among these topics is easy, I have decided to bring the discussion to this point.

**HERE ENDS.**

# APPENDIX TO THE PHILOSOPHICAL WORKS OF BOETHIUS

## [Column 1223]

### AN. MANL. SEV. BOETHIUS’ *ON THE DISCIPLINE OF SCHOLARS* (G,S)*

## PROEM

[Column 1223D]

Your intention, as I understand it, asks for a concise treatise on the discipline of scholars. Would that, according to the capacity available to me, the weakness of my intellect, and the persistence of my troubles, I might attempt to comply with the requests of your friends, O Martianus.

Although I have been impeded by two kinds of commentary—not entirely unrelated kinds—on certain editions of Aristotle and other philosophers, and although I have been weakened by my own study and gnawed by the torture inflicted by the inhuman king of the Goths, philosophical consolation has gone before me, and the final depths of the profound Trinity have softened me.

For what is brighter than the knowledge appropriate to the gymnasium’s progress in the artificial and natural order, and than the gradual display of the powers of understanding? We know that the parts of eloquence are established by the fitting progression of artificial and natural things and by the clear apprehension of understanding.

First, therefore, the earliest amusements of children must be tasted. Second, the manner in which the pride of adults is to be subjected to the authority of teachers and joined to discipline. Third, the manner in which their pride is to be restrained, explained distinctly through the commendation of examples. Fourth, the prudent provision to be made for scholars and their gradual establishment. Fifth, the manner in which the scholars’ venerable and sincere devotion is to be directed toward teaching. Sixth, the rule of teachers, their threefold division, their condition with respect to their subjects, and the method of teaching that must first be understood.

We have undertaken these matters for the acquisition of understanding, largely setting aside the former method of treatment. We have never used a lighter style, since the execution is for the most part intended to instruct beginners, and the exposition ought therefore to be correspondingly clearer.

## CHAPTER ONE

When helpless infancy at the age of seven is indiscriminately led to instruction, care must be taken that there be no unsuitable condition of the limbs—for example, of the bodily members as a whole—and that the unhealthiness of the air, such as the dull severity of constricting winter and the oppressive intensity of burning summer, does not increase the danger.

For it is written that the son of Timothy, when leprosy had attacked him, was castrated, club-footed, swollen with a hump, and handed over to instruction; he became a disgrace among the common people and a laughingstock to his companions.

Likewise, we saw the son of a suburban praetor handed over to letters when the Dog Star was exerting its force. Since he did not enjoy his customary shade, deprived of his natural strength, softened by the punishment of jaundice, and finally weakened in his vital spirits, he died of a disorder of the lymph.

See how much difficulty the unsuitable condition of the limbs and the unhealthiness of the air brought upon childish tenderness.

There should be moderate provision of food.

His drink should be light, and he should be sparing in it.

Likewise, there should be no shortage of clothing.

First of all, then, love for the forms representing the elements must be impressed upon him, together with a sufficiently skillful joining of the letters to be connected.

He must neither be made to persist too long in such a laborious contest nor depart too quickly, as Servius recommends. For although one child may appear more ready in many matters, in others he may then be found more capable.

The structure of the second laborious contest rests upon the teachings of Probus, Didymus, and the other philosophers whose venerable authority commends them.

In such matters one must see to it that an extensive tradition be subjected to faithful analysis and that the learner’s idiom be explained word for word. For the firmness of the foundation must rest upon these things.

One must not depart with the monthly leap of Phoebe, nor be sustained merely by the course of the sun; rather, after completing Mercury’s interval, one must diligently linger for approximately twice as long.

Diligence softens the dullness of every task.

The teaching of Seneca, Lucan’s inexhaustibility, Virgil’s prolixity, Statius’ urbanity, the difficult translation of Flaccus, the still more difficult edition of Persius, Martianus’ not unworthy *laesio* (“injury”), and Ovid’s discrimination must be investigated and entrusted to the chamber of memory.

The moral teaching of the other philosophers, insofar as the capacity of the intellect permits, must not be passed over in silence, so that the serenity of sententious composition may flourish and the delight of meter may bloom.

O how highly must the venerable eloquence of Cicero be prized and placed among our greatest desires!

In such matters one must beware lest what happened to Iotarius happen again. For thirty years he taught his ignorance of the aforementioned philosophers in the schools.

When the day arrived for him to preside over ordinary students, he asserted that he had long been uncertain whom he had found in the clarity of Virgil’s half-lines: “whose wife you are” or “and Aeneas.”

When one of his students asked him how a teacher could turn the first syllable of this expression into a verse, he replied that it was absurd for the first syllable of so great a name to be shortened, and that it should instead be pronounced with an acute accent.

See how much time and expense the dullness of a stubborn neck squandered.

When the rudiment of this school has been completed in a fitting manner, one must proceed to the threshold of the knowledge of greater inquiry—knowledge, I say, which we know to be the investigator of truth and falsehood, and which alone is adorned, by the subtlety of its subject matter, with the title “science of sciences.”

This is, I say, the mistress of the scholar. By the penetrating nature of its garments [*vestium*, perhaps corrupt], she provides advances in virtues toward the summits of all the sciences.

What is brighter than the knowledge of the five universals, which is the teacher of the sciences of the trivium, the power of the quadrivial sciences, and the fullness of the collateral sciences?

To climb to the summit of this imperial mistress, one must proceed in the following order.

First, the inward knowledge of terms, their evident conjunction in a proposition, and the fitting connection of propositions must be supplied.

The determinations of terms, which we call syncategoremata, must be impressed upon the mind through memory, since they serve no little purpose for sophistical imagination.

We remember that Trebatius, a most prudent man but inexperienced in this matter, passed over knowledge of these things in silence, as though it were unworthy of mention.

When the day of conflict arrived, we saw the same unfortunate man held most miserably captive by sophistry’s victory over him and disgracefully separated from the company of his colleagues.

What more? Confounded by the anguish of shame, he afterward begged in company for what he had previously judged unworthy of expression.

The sophistical art, endowed with the fringes of this imperial mistress, confused by a petulant spirit, decked out with the praise of frivolous loquacity, and with its face covered by a woman’s cosmetic, looked askance at barbarian nations. We know it to have been adorned in the commentaries of Alexander and in our own works, and it must be cultivated with the utmost care and perfected through translation.

For the perfection of these and other matters, we customarily use three kinds of recollection. The first is vocal, the second mental, and the third common.

Vocal recollection makes a sophist; mental recollection makes judgment; common recollection, if continued, makes perfection.

The vocal produces blindness, the mental knowledge, and the common use.

Use hastens toward teaching. For just as prudence without justice is of little or no benefit, while justice without prudence is of great benefit, so knowledge without use benefits little, whereas use without knowledge benefits greatly.

If a beginner of good disposition cannot comprehend the whole speech in sequence, let him at least grasp the first pronunciation, until by proceeding gradually he can produce a continuous result.

Having considered the sciences of frivolous matters, we must attend to Porphyry’s speculation on the five universals, which Aristotle calls “monsters,” since they are necessary for his *Categories*. We have twice made them clear through the light of exposition in our commentaries.

O how much usefulness there is in these things if their inward knowledge is possessed!

Is not the literary ability of Sophronicus to be marked as defective? I say so.

Nor should our own volumes, adorned by the pattern of their style, be omitted.

The whole compressed brevity of Aristotle must also be considered—[the reading is uncertain: “dull in letter and voice,” or a similar phrase]—though it is not without usefulness. For I preferred to serve a faithful translation rather than be censured for the rashness of arrogance.

What could be more serene than Aristotle’s lucid truth?

While these matters are being undertaken, the fruitfulness of grammar must in no way be neglected. Through it, possession of any commendable art is made agreeable.

Nor should the charm of rhetoric or the honor of the quadrivial sciences, acquired through comparison of studies, be omitted insofar as possible.

In these matters, the insolence of study produces a flower and gives birth to fruit if it is mixed with doubt and exercised at the proper time.

## CHAPTER II
Having considered the rudiments of students and their progress in the virtues, we must now briefly begin speaking of their subjection to teachers, since one who does not know how to submit himself cannot know how to become a teacher. For it is wretched for a man to be a teacher who has never learned that he is a pupil. The pupil’s submission, moreover, consists in three things: attention, goodwill, and teachability. [Col. 1227A] Attentive, I say, in practice; teachable in understanding; benevolent in disposition. Attentive, I say, in listening; teachable in understanding; benevolent in retaining what he has learned. These three, when properly combined, contribute to perfection.

A student must not be *dyscolus*. For *dyscolus* is said to mean, as it were, “separated from the school.” *Schola* is Greek and means “leisure” in Latin; hence *dyscolus*, as though “separated from leisure.” A *dyscolus* is one who runs about through alleys, streets, and taverns; through brothels, public spectacles, processions and dances, banquets and public dinners—and does so with wandering eyes, an unbridled tongue, a wanton spirit, and an undisciplined countenance. All these things are placed after the school.

Once, when circumstances had caused us to travel to Gaul for the recovery of our health, because of the harshness of the climate, the pleasant customs of the Gauls, and the pious conversations of matrons, we observed, as I recall, many *dyscoli* in the city of Julius Caesar, which was called Lutetia of the Parisians. We saw many of them begging for the arts, although none supplied them with cups of philosophy; and we deeply lamented the fair-haired Britons traveling to Rome at the cost of their studies, because they were not nourished at all by the little sparks of the Athenians. At last they began to speak Greek in the Gallic tongue. If they had found anything in their own regions besides the twisted volumes of Lucretius, they would not, on our advice, have wasted so much labor. We saw a few Germans being given titles. By the art of magical deception, we saw many from Iberia being made teachers. As for our own men, the matter is evident from their bleary and twitching eyes. But let this suffice concerning the *dyscolus*.

A pupil must not be violent toward his teacher. Let Albinus, son of Albeus, serve as an example of violence. Although he was a son of affection—or rather, more truly, a precursor of misfortune—he once laid criminal hands upon his teacher Grillus, who was stammering, and stained his venerable gray hair with the shameful approach of his feet. The cause of so great a crime was that he had been unable to comprehend the whole constitution at the first impression of the air. Shame upon it! Shame upon the advance of an unhappy pupil against the head of felicity! May a Nero rejoice in so criminal an heir, and an Anetus in so polluted a successor. But may Grillus rejoice, together with Socrates, in Seneca’s eagerness.

Therefore, he is not worthy of knowledge who rises up against the teacher of knowledge.

Let the pupil strive to keep himself apart from luxury. The satirists divided it into three parts: one, they said, consists in the adornment of clothing; another, in sexual intercourse; and the third serves gluttony. We have often known subjects to suffer from the filthy frenzy of each of these.

All Rome mourned Lucretius’ blood-stained son, a disciple of Zeno, ensnared by an insulting appetite for sexual intercourse. He was born, nevertheless, of very distinguished parents: he was tall in stature, sanguine in complexion, and possessed remarkable eloquence and penetrating intelligence. Yet he rejoiced in daily marriages and in marriages beyond what was proper, while his father bore the penalty, for he was unlawfully consuming his parents’ patrimony and wealth and stood out among all jealous husbands. He was always eager for dice and for the brothels of prostitutes.

Still not freed from his own lust, he was later expelled by his parents. At last, abandoned by his friends and companions and harassed on every side by creditors, he secretly sought to remain among acquaintances and strangers alike. He was very frequently ransomed by his father from the torments of the cross, but finally he could no longer be redeemed with his parent’s money. When he was led to the cross, he compelled his father to come to him by his tears and asked for a kiss in a plaintive voice.

Moved by pity at his son’s request, the father rose up; but the son, after rising, cut off his father’s nose with a very sharp bite, saying: “Why did I escape uncorrected from my earliest errors? Why did I not obey the teachings of my teacher and why did I despise my companions?”

A father must correct his son, and a teacher must shape the character of his pupil.

Behold how detestable is the assault of prostitutes. A prostitute is the ninefold gate of hell, the road of iniquity, the sting of a scorpion, a reservoir of crimes, a well of destruction—and, if there is any other disgrace of luxury, every other such form is graver in crime and worse. The destruction of Hyacinthus and Jovinus is evident to all. Elsewhere, the lips of a prostitute are said to distill honey, but her final offerings are wormwood.

The second species of luxury, endowed with banquets and drunkenness, rejoices to be joined by turns to the preceding species, as cause to effect. For drunkenness arises in relation to sexual intercourse, and likewise the other kinds of vice. Wine taken in moderation seems to sharpen the intellect; but wine taken immoderately disturbs reason, dulls the understanding, weakens the memory, introduces forgetfulness, pours in error, and leads to ignorance. For where drunkenness is, there madness rules; where madness rules, there is no wisdom, but folly ranges everywhere.

The daily examples and the damage done to the virtues by this are evident. This plague is worse when joined to a drinking companion, because, if he is unable to study, he gnaws at the others who wish to devote themselves to the schools; he fosters the error of quarrels, or calls for assistance through blows. What a terrible mixture for students: association with a dissipated man! Therefore, the discretion of the prudent must expel such men from the integrity of their company by an irrevocable decision, at the appointed time. This second species is sometimes a preliminary to the first, but a follower of the third in its appetitive aspect. How much error drunkenness pours into a pupil’s mind, unless it is restrained to the last degree by the bridle of sobriety!

The third species of luxury is desire that longs for adornments and is joined in marriage to the offspring of parents, to whom the secure resources of poverty yield undefeated. It delights in frequent variety of clothing; in polishing the hair limb by limb at its parting with the aid of a comb; in making it luxuriant in winding curls and in successive varieties of flowers; in covering the throat with cosmetics; in longing for the frequent discipline of the razor; in filling the bosom with perfumes; in displaying to the crowd a disciplined belly, its neck adorned with jeweled necklaces and its waist with Parthian belts; in walking like a queen in beaked and boarded shoes; and in moving with raised neck, swollen throat, clipped eyebrow, shameless eye, and pompous semicircular gait.

It delights in speaking grandly with rare and scarcely modest words; in disdaining every food placed before it; in serving quarrels; in being allied with insults; in afflicting strangers with tortures; in attending the schools only rarely and contributing little, while hurrying first to be absent from them. What a mixture, and how great a mixture, of vices!

When I once withdrew to Athens for the sake of study, I observed Ganymede, the son of Pyrrhrus the dictator, suffering from all the faults mentioned above. Sometimes he went about in cloth slippers with embroidered edges, sometimes in spotted leggings; for an hour he strutted about in cedar sandals, and at other times proceeded barefoot. He attacked the Areopagus as though enraged, and I very carefully took precautions lest he rise up against me, since I was a foreigner.

What more shall I say? Although unwillingly, he eventually fell into such great poverty that, with the course of Fortune reversed, he obtained by begging and soliciting those things which he had previously despised out of fastidiousness. But let what has been said thus far suffice.

## CHAPTER III

Since a pupil is bound to strive toward perfection, he must recognize that the effective cause of perfection—namely, constancy of continuity—must be impressed upon his mind insofar as his ability permits. For what is brighter in the little work of love than constancy, and what is worse than inconstancy? The first produces; the second dissolves what has been produced. The first advances; the second retreats. The first gathers; the second scatters what has been gathered.

When we had resolved to devote ourselves diligently to the schools and had judged it worthy to obtain the office of teaching, Fortune assigned to our instruction a son of inconstancy—or, to speak more truthfully, inconstancy itself. He was monthly in his appetite for satirical writings, often daily in his appetite for historians, yearly for elegiac poets; in the method of disputation he lamented Aristotle at night; in philosophical editions he was monthly; in compilations of the Twelve Tables he was, as it were, instantaneous. In every subject he quickly became bored.

If he had given even a little attention to examining books and their writing, he would have inspected very many within an hour, yet never laid hands upon any of them long enough to bring it to completion. At last he began to be a merchant by ship. But when seasickness forced him during the first night to vomit into the bilge, and afterward he was terrified by the assault of the flooding deck, he wanted to become a gardener.

When he ran out of vegetables, he transferred himself to military service. But when he saw the enemy’s attacks, he entrusted his back to flight and turned more safely to the studies of Crato, whose semicircle’s capacity feared many questions. The breadth of the upper circle, formed as the plane of the zodiac, smiled upon sevenfold drachmas. The first extension of literal study asked whether the rule of the empyrean heaven could be obscured by any participating nature of earthly substance.

The second asked whether the vital service of spirits could be darkened by the surrounding impurity of earthly matter, with the support of nature. The third asked whether one should accept the triple division of the Jews concerning the poles, or Aristotle’s simple division. The fourth asked, concerning the Jewish division, whether the boundaries are from the things themselves or in the things themselves, or whether each is sealed; and, concerning Aristotle’s division, if the parts of the whole move locally, why does the whole not move?

The fifth asked why there is continuous transmutation of the elements, and whether the elements that existed at first are the same ones, or whether others come into being. The sixth asked: when one of the elements, such as water, receives an accidental quality—for example, heat—why does fire not receive accidental coldness? The seventh asked whether any zone of the earth is habitable from our point of view; what the original birth of its inhabitants is; what their approach is; and what sort of change their departure entails.

The map of the second circle, a ninefold arrangement, held the eyes of those who looked upon it. The first of its questions contained, with respect to the zodiac’s breadth, the quality of the circles in an observational account, the boundaries of the colures in a definitive account, and the quantity of the whole form progressively. The second asked whether the fixed stars are in the higher heaven, or whether, traveling in their own circles, they are perceived to wander like the planets.

The third asked whether comets, reddened portentously, travel circularly with the other planets, or whether they return to their own chaos as destructive creatures, by the permission of Nature who creates. The fourth asked whether lower nature, composed of elements, draws its power or eclipse from the planets or from the first generators. If from the planets, is this according to necessity or according to chance? But if from the generators, when one generator is white and another black, why is what is generated from them not both white and black? And why, when a generated thing resembles its father at its extremities and the mother in other respects, does it sometimes resemble neither of the generators?

The fifth asked what proportion one planetary motion bears to another and what their connection is. The sixth asked: since Saturn is the oldest among the planets and Venus the most benevolent, does the benevolence of one restrain the malignity of the other as it approaches from the opposite direction? The seventh asked: since the north wind is naturally cold and dry, why does it appear contrary to us? The eighth asked what the proportional connection of the elements is. The ninth asked what the course and effect of the sun and moon are.

The plane of the final semicircle proposed the following questions: Why is there trembling in the earth? Why does lightning burn the air? Why does the fury of the sea overflow? What is the harmful taste? What is the nature of the winged creatures that appear in summer and disappear in winter, and conversely? What is the roundness of hail, the length of snow, and the power of mist? Does the power of stones arise from their composition or from their matter? Does the attraction of the diamond arise from its components taken together, or only from the action of one of them? What accounts for the sweetness of rain, the warmth of a winter well, the coolness of a summer well, the threefold emission of sight, and the consolidation of colors?

Since the solution of these difficult questions could not satisfy his restless mind, he proposed to submit himself to a wife, setting the foregoing aside. After seeing virgins everywhere, he was brought to disgust and replied to his parents:

“I disapprove of the corrupted; I detest aged beds. I have nothing to do with a stern virgin; I shall remain alone.”

Having rejected the foregoing as, so to speak, solutions to difficult questions, he said, “From now on I shall devote myself to the teachings of Ptolemy. But the degrees of the signs and the courses of the planets cannot be easily grasped without the height of a tower. What shall I do henceforth? Wretched that I am to be a human being! If only I could shed my humanity and put on the nature of an ass, exchanging the form of a man!”

Let the pupil’s submission to the teacher therefore be complete: attention to practice, together with goodwill of spirit and teachability of intellect; avoidance of the forms of luxury; and the fitting profession of fortunate constancy.

## CHAPTER IV

Everything set forth above concerning the formation of students has been firmly established. We must now briefly discuss their prudent provision.

Since the constitution of the human body is supported by phlegm, blood, yellow bile, and melancholy, it is necessary that each person derive a predominance from one of these. A melancholic person, being subject to sluggishness and fear, ought to study in secret and secluded places, free from noise and receiving little light. He should avoid excessive fullness and late dinners, and enjoy moderate drinks according to the needs of study, insofar as the drying effect of study requires it. He should be sustained by a full intake of drink in due measure, lest excessive zeal in study produce consumption, breathlessness, and constriction of the chest.

A phlegmatic person, although he may be trained in studies and teachings in houses full of noise and rich in light, may be sustained by fuller cups and strengthened by all kinds of food; and, if it is permissible to say so, he ought to be softened monthly by sexual intercourse.

A sanguine person, whose bodily constitution is more favorably joined together, can be accommodated in any house or place. We have often known him to be strengthened by playing over a very serious question, provided that he alone were rocking the walls with sideways glances. Yet one must not always rely upon this. He should be cheered by lighter foods and very pleasant drinks.

A choleric person, usually subject to a pale appearance, should be assigned to solitude, lest excessive noise pour bile into the whole company by what he hears and thereby injure the venerable dignity of the teacher. How greatly the injury of a teacher’s dignity must be avoided! We have known such a person to be sustained by a larger dinner and soothed by stronger drink. Care must be taken, however, that the horror of quarrels not be drawn out of his raging mind by the administration of drink.

If the company is unable to determine these qualities, it should consult theorists and thereby come to know itself. The maxim *gnōthi seauton* (“know yourself”) has been impressed upon many minds. The fortunate pupil’s discretion should rejoice to submit to the teacher; he should love him while fearing him and should remain faithful. Nor should he resemble Albinus by detracting from him under the appearance of painted affection. For what is worse than a detractor? Woe to the detractor of a teacher!

Even if there are a thousand people with him, he should rise when the approaching teacher arrives, greet him according to place and time, and bow his head. If the teacher orders him, he should accompany him and, if possible, join him in his dwelling by living there with him, so that, once corrected, he may not only bite at himself inwardly but also, whenever an opportunity arises, come to him and inquire.

If a pupil cannot always, as is necessary, present himself to his teacher—whether because of the distance of his dwelling or because of some other circumstance—he should always keep at hand the notes dictated for his use, and from them diligently impress upon himself whatever he knows to have been entrusted to his conscience, while explicitly asking about whatever he finds doubtful.

When the annual association of table companions has been established in harmonious and suitable agreement—or sooner, according to the intended length of residence—he should gather fragments of salt and wood in summer, an abundance of the grape harvest in autumn, grain at harvest, and a heap of meat under Capricorn.

How beneficial and conducive to health it is, according to one’s means, to bring these things together, lest the mold of the vegetables weaken the anxious man’s breath, the sourness of tasteless wine disturb the heart’s secret places, the rancor of the butchered meat and the stench of crushed salt corrupt the intestines, and the shortage of wood contract the limbs—and, worse still, lest the anxious man become fat through continual attacks! It is a great convenience for a pupil, insofar as his means permit, to provide what the teacher needs, so that, while he is intent upon carrying out his duties, he may not have to devote himself to purchasing things for sale.

How absurd is the poverty of a teacher! The removal of old washerwomen must be valued above all, and their visits are the healthier the rarer they are, lest, when one comes, she suggest something polluted or extract something from a softened servant. For compassion is rarely found among servants, and constancy in distress is found even more rarely.

Woe to the servant who deceives the one in whom the master’s affection places full confidence! What is uglier than such a person, and what is more serious than such a crime?

A clean lodging, clean furnishings, and a whitened mattress should be arranged by the servant’s prudence, with attention to the outcome of affairs and constant attendance upon the master’s diligence, all in a seemly manner. What is uglier than a servant who withholds things?

Let the unhappy Elimax terrify everyone. His name, derived from *elimare*—“to scrape away”—was drawn from his deed. After he had received the gifts of Nicostratus, he first served him with a flattering expression, administering everything at his command and proving faithful in every matter, while promising to be still more faithful. Whatever Nicostratus’ fidelity possessed was entrusted to Elimax’s infidelity.

What more need be said? When the wretched foresight of the utterly wicked Elimax had seen that everything was being supplied to him—meat for food, fish for nourishment, and all other merchandise—he reported each item to his master’s ears at twice the price at which it had been bought. In this way he exhausted the increase of the entire substance, brought Nicostratus into the deepest poverty, and exposed him to the prolonged outcry of creditors. Nothing more bitter than this is impressed upon the mind. Woe to the madness of a creditor!

Nicostratus’ extreme poverty finally led him to recognize his servant’s error. He confronted Elimax late concerning his wrongdoing. When Elimax heard this, he immediately burst into insulting words, buried a dagger in his master’s entrails, carried away with him the things he had previously omitted to take, and left his master’s body to be devoured by dogs. Behold how much wickedness the impiety of a detestable traitor perpetrated!

A two-tongued servant must be driven far away, and his wickedness must immediately be cast off, even if he is related by close blood. For we have seen many companions suffer loss through the cruelty of servants.

The full amount of the entrusted debt must be presented to creditors, and payment of the debt fixed for each day must always be made insofar as possible.

For a student to whom abundance has not smiled with a full horn, how sweet is the transfer of a creditor’s claim and the support provided by relatives! The constancy of a prudent student should also always rejoice in some particular companion to whom he can reveal his conscience, who will diligently assist him when Fortune is clouded and show himself attentive when illness prevails.

If the dark shadow of death should appear, that companion should arrange the remaining resources. If the student survives, he should be sustained, fed, soothed, and consoled by him; taken to bed; and provided for in various ways. While health prevails, let them enjoy little books in turn; let them commend one another gradually through competitive little questions, with commendable recollection; let them correct one another in turn with the happiness of correction; and let them sweetly serve one another through diverse and varied kinds of jokes.

Thus let the integrity of mutual affection remain among them, so that the dew of their earliest time may be sprinkled upon it, flooding it in the middle and intoxicating it at the end. What is sweeter, what more excellent, what truly better? For no adoption of favor brings the love of excellence to an end.

Envy, if it occurs in a qualified form—namely, in learning—is harmless; but simple envy consumes its own author.

When the foresight of my parent, as is customary, promised to console me through his conversation for a few days, he said that he had sent me to Athens for the sake of study. There I found the sole guardian of my life, a man named Favonius—not named from the wind, but from favor.

When he saw me fatigued from the journey, considering many things and sighing frequently, he asked whose son I was. He took me with him and courteously consoled me, briefly asking whether I had come there for the sake of study, what profession I followed, and what my abilities were.

After three days, while showing me the names of the streets and the rough turns of the alleyways, he said:

“Here flourish the prophecies of the Chaldeans; the undisguised glory of Ptolemy; the sincere truth of Aristotle; the approved divinity of Plato; the synthesis of Zeno; the affection of Peribonius; the promise of Pythagoras; the *Iliad* of Homer; the labor of Theseus; the theorems of Euclid; the propositions of Dares; and the investigations of Hippocrates.

“Here flourish the effectiveness of the Areopagus; knowledge of the laws; the confused glory of the hippodrome; the victory of the circus; the power of the wrestling ground; the thunderbolt of the boxing glove; the elevation of missiles; the shouts of sailors; the wandering of youth; and the gathering of the dance.”

When Favonius’ generosity had disclosed these and many other matters to me, he asked what my abilities were, how much money my purse could supply for expenses, and toward which discipline the inclination of my mind was readiest.

After I had answered him in order on all these matters, he impressed upon the ears of his friends something worthy of remembrance: namely, that I should attend diligently to economy of money, since it is fitting to modesty not to squander foolishly what has been entrusted to one. If necessity compelled me, I should return to my homeland in confusion and shame.

He also disclosed something departing from the usual path of reasoning: if I were to enter any discipline, I should first examine carefully whether its teacher obeyed good morals and was distinguished by the abundance and titles of the liberal arts. Setting aside all negligence concerning his profession, I should listen to him attentively for three days and consider everything, so that, if he proved good, I would not leave him even if he stammered.

Fortified by these and other secrets, I flourished at Athens for twenty-two years, always striving toward the traces of the good, whatever evil I had experienced. For no one is worthy of the sharpness of sweetness who has been unable to be entangled in the burden of bitterness. I always adhered to the teachings of Herodian and Aristotle, and carefully entrusted the little sparks of others to my mind.

Lest the simplicity of the present work detract from the resources of poverty, or despair confuse it, or desolation afflict it, we have judged it worthy to submit for examination something common to the nature of all.

Although the poverty of a student proceeds from different causes—because of the tenacity of relatives, the poverty of their overflowing storm, the inconstancy of a stepfather’s assistance, the pressure of a sister’s marriageable age, the excessive negligence of the firstborn’s military service, and the cunning of a familiar’s hostility—we have judged it worthy to offer general advice.

The detestable hooked tenacity of parents is softened by the urgency of pleas, often dissolved by tiresome appeals, and soothed by timely tears. It is frequently stirred by deceptive promises, dissolved by affectionate little gifts, pierced by flattery if the time is right, or, if not, made more solid—even though it be adamantine. It is overcome by exemplary admonition and stirred by the requests of others.

The poverty caused by the overflowing storm must be endured through the increase of one’s own labor: by writing, gathering grain, cleaning threshing floors, and serving for a time. If, however, an ingenious ability to write compels a voluntary movement, we have judged it worthy to restrain the spur of necessity.

Care must nevertheless be taken lest a luxurious appetite stir the mind and weaken the common Siren-like profit of writers; lest lavish and rarely faithful flattery deceive; and lest a hostile familiar absorb, through sight or hearing, whatever the writer’s right hand has gently produced.

Notwithstanding the wickedness of Glebeon, the favor of kinship brought me how much inconvenience in learning and decline of the virtues while I was serving under Herodian! Since the little spark of paternal feeling frequently failed, we judged it safer, in the previously described manner, to mitigate our sorrow, thinking that it was safer to endure some want than, unwillingly, to return home and undertake the long roads of labor.

He told my relatives, through Glebeon’s wickedness, that I was being steeped in pestilential writing-houses and glorying too long in seductive profit. The father’s inclination, generally readier to evil, evaporated in its inward fire and deprived me of its customary assistance. Before events had proved their outcome, his madness did not turn aside, and the urgency of pleas accomplished nothing. After the notorious delivery of the informer, following two years [the text is uncertain here], the matter remained, but it did not depart unpunished.

If one’s resources cannot be consoled by obedience to a stepfather, let threats be employed against him and let him be broken by timely pressure, as the amusing transaction of Proculus teaches.

The negligence of a festive brother should be softened by exemplary praise, and his cunning should be corrected by reminding him of his kinship—or his madness should be brought low.

A sister who has reached marriageable years must be obeyed by her relative as quickly as possible, lest, through the fault of negligence, the first rose be plucked by an unworthy thumb. How worthy of recommendation is a sister’s profession of modesty, and how lamentable the commission of its opposite—like the cutting away of flesh full of shame that disfigures the face!

The insignia of obedience to one’s sister must not be silently entrusted to a second Theophrastus, Symmachus the steward. When both parents had entered the way of all flesh, he married his sister, whose constancy was threatened by impending disgrace, through the benefit of a dowry, and committed himself earnestly to the courses of Fortune.

After Elisia’s husband had been taken away by shipwreck, the sister pursued her brother Symmachus. Elisia, serving in many ways, supplied everything to Symmachus under the semblance of meritorious service. For, when opportunity for the pleasures of her own flesh was lacking, she secretly exposed her flower. For Elisia preferred, through the fault of negligence, secretly to yield [the Latin is syntactically corrupt here] rather than, while alive, break the bond of fraternal constancy; nor did she retreat from what she had begun until she brought what had been commenced to a suitable conclusion.

The domestic scorching must be assisted by the beginning of careful frugality, lest attention to borrowed money pour bile into the mind, or, distressed by another misfortune, one attribute the matter to it. Whatever is done in such circumstances must be done cautiously, lest a small parsimony in material things later stiffen the face under judgment of shame. For strong structures are often known to collapse through the injury of a single spark.

Let us consider what the gray-haired Calvus, a soldier endowed with the light of wisdom, thought. Passing beyond the first bloom of military service, he secretly carried with him beneath a *birrus* a certain amphora and entrusted it to the favor of a servant. After lightly changing his position, he chose the role of another cohort and approached a cook concerning an earthen pot.

When the bridle of quarrel and rancor had been loosened, the cook, unable to bear the rancor, struck the gray hair with the earthen vessel. Although afterward it was decorated with ivy, it could not thereafter restore the injury to its former condition or connection of sap; from the impact of the earthen vessel it incurred a mark for itself and for its lineage.

Let the resource of poverty therefore be safe, clean, and content with little; let it endure attacks bravely, always aspire to higher things, and obey everyone. Let it be ready for service and slow to speak; faithful in obedience, sincere in affection, sweet in conversation, and free from swelling of heart, since its opposite is not valued as a companion by the one who lives with it.

Although the reward of labor is often withheld by many, it will nevertheless earn the adoption of favor from someone. Does it not often happen through a slight slip that something cannot be accomplished even in the course of a year?

The duties of the flatterer and the companionship of the informer must be driven away according to the place, the business, and the occasion.

## CHAPTER V

When a young man of good disposition wishes to ascend to the excellence of teaching, it is necessary that he carefully understand the three kinds of condition which Aristotle indicates in assigning probability. Some people are exceedingly dull, others moderate, and a third group exceptionally keen.

We have never seen any of the exceedingly dull become greatly intoxicated with the philosophical nectar. Mechanical work rejoices in being joined to such men; politics belongs to those of moderate ability.

Among authors, however, we find three divisions: some are exceptionally keen, others moderate, and a third group exceptionally and supremely keen. Household management rejoices in the exceptionally keen; physics under the lunar sphere and the practice of apothecaries belong to those of moderate ability. To the exceptionally keen—whom Aristotle calls especially distinguished according to philosophy—belongs the knowledge of universals through experience of particulars. This is the mistress of the trivium (the three verbal arts), the power of the quadrivium (the four mathematical arts). Oh, how fortunate is its presentation!

The final division of mediocrity has sometimes acquired good and perfect men for itself with labor; nevertheless, teachers are endowed with honor after the flower of youth has been consumed. The following must be arranged for these men in the manner described.

First, each must know what belongs to the reverence due to so great a name, so that he may know how to express what he knows and may not commit himself entirely to the composition of writings, like Lucretius, who, whenever he investigated the knot of any question he had proposed, abandoned his companions and hurried to his notes.

Second, he must acquire an abundance of books for his own training, so that he may consult them when necessary. Yet he must not believe them absolutely, as Jugo did. He trusted so greatly in the admonitions of his teacher Montanus that he wrote down every word proceeding from Montanus’ mouth in little notebooks and regarded it as sacred. In the schools he proclaimed nothing except what served in place of his teacher; hence he frequently departed enclosed in shame.

For it is the mark of a most wretched intellect always to use discoveries rather than things that remain to be discovered. It is still more foolish for a teacher to trust entirely in speeches. At first, one should believe him, until it becomes clear what he thinks; afterward, one should pretend that he has erred in teaching, so that perhaps one may discover what objection he can bring against the diligence entrusted to him.

Third, he must have certain people whom he can teach his secrets, read books with, and train in other rudiments, so that he may know what he has understood, learn to express what he knows, and acquire practice through frequent expression. Practice provides mastery; for teaching others is properly to indulge one’s own ability.

Fourth, it must be arranged that he attract these and others to himself, so that, when the opportunity for teaching arrives, he may enjoy their inward presence.

What is more shameful than to be left alone at the very beginning of one’s undertaking? Such was Flavus, who, because of the authority of his lineage and the wealth of his ruling treasure, believed that everyone had been subjected to him. But after the time of the gathering had passed, he rarely found a companion who remained with him under a contract of employment, even if unwillingly, despite adding every kind of threat in a regal manner.

Nevertheless, according to the twofold division of kinship, it is consistent with generosity to support the presence of a teacher, at least for a time.

Fifth, he must walk about peripatetically in the schools, in favor of those by whose favor he is to be crowned; he must oppose them courteously, sharply bite those who behave arrogantly, and answer more diligently according to the occasion, lest, if his will has become mute, this be attributed to the blindness of ignorance or the rashness of arrogance.

We have seen many observers, because of the insolence of their answers, enjoy a fall—even unwillingly. For it is not fitting for a learner to provoke a ruler with insulting and abusive speeches.

Even if he is joined to the teacher by the greatest familiarity, he must not eagerly pursue the teacher’s secrets unless ordered to do so; and, when ordered, he should obey reluctantly.

Did not Fontinus’ insolence open the investigations of Zenocrates? After he had been taught, he first examined them publicly and believed that he had become a teacher if he had taken away all of Zenocrates’ Minerva—that is, all his wisdom. Once this had been taken away, Zenocrates ceased to study, while Fontinus, unknowingly deprived of his single resource, suffered from a greater frenzy.

Therefore, a pupil who trusts in his own labor will never envy another’s honor.

When the day of highest promotion has arrived, the venerable assembly of companions should be commended with brief expression and concise speech. Thus one should proceed fearlessly toward the beginnings and advancement of honor, with suitable clothing and festive equipment, if means permit, and with everything splendidly provided either for all or at least for those of the same profession, according to his wishes.

Before the elevation of the teaching office, however, he must carefully—and even more carefully—consider and investigate whether, during the course of the first year, he can support himself from his own resources if necessary. For it is shameful to beg at the very outset out of reverence for so great a name, as Strictonius did. After carrying out in a reverent manner everything pertaining to the teaching office, he began begging on the third day, and soon regretted having dared so much.

What wonder? Deceived as though by an instantaneous illusion, he departed and thereafter never acknowledged the heights of such an honor. Oh, how worthy of reverence is the commendation of a fortunate outcome!

## CHAPTER VI
Having disposed of the matters arranged for the instruction of students, observing moderation in making them clear, we take care neither to harass the reader with brevity of expression nor to confuse him by delay. We have never proceeded by a clearer style [Col. 1235A] or a lighter genealogical account, since the work is commended not only to the discerning but also to the unlearned, after the sequence of its riddles has been set aside.

Now we must hasten to the venerable majesty of masters. The following division of masters should be maintained. Some of them dwell in the two cities that shine more brightly than the rest, namely Rome and Athens, proceeding nowhere farther unless fortune advances them so that they may be held in higher honor. Others, abandoning the eminence of those aforesaid places, seek the profits of neighboring towns, both because of the stepmotherly poverty of their discipline and because of the resisting sweetness of their native country.

Among both the former and the latter, some assume authority on account of an attractive title, so that they may be honored. Others do so on account of their intelligence, lest their ignorance be exposed. A third group, observing more subtly, gathers the master’s robes for the advancement of both parties. Anyone of this kind who wishes to pursue the rewards of assumed elegance and duly performed office ought to excel most conspicuously in every form of moral uprightness [Col. 1235B]: he should be truthful in speech, just in judgment, prudent in counsel, faithful in what is entrusted to him, steadfast in countenance, kindly in conversation, distinguished by virtues, and worthy of praise for his goodness. If anything contrary occurs, it usually occurs through the appetite of human frailty.

He should also be good in his way of life. Nothing is more ruinous to a pupil than the teacher’s disgraceful life: what has been poured in seems very often to become confused, as in a foul vessel, because a foul vessel corrupts the waters poured into it.

These matters have been arranged for the formation of the teaching soul. Now we must discuss the remaining primary qualities—not, I mean, the first among the first, but the second among the first. An educated teacher must also be gentle, stern, ancient—not in years—free from negligence, and not arrogant.

Let him, I say, be educated. He must first learn before he teaches. For we know that the study of the Trivium is an aid to learning. It is exceedingly absurd and unjust that the unskilled should be preferred to the skilled, the young to the old, and the unlearned to those who have completed their service [Col. 1235C].

Gentle: for since it is sometimes necessary to endure the students’ arrogance, gentleness must therefore be employed. Let Master Franco serve as an example in his lack of gentleness. Because he could not restrain the unchecked arrogance of his students, who were taking advantage of his nobility, he hanged himself with a noose; he would have acted more wisely had he used gentleness.

Stern: for in the embrace of students it is most advantageous to enjoy sternness, so that he may impose punishment upon those who go astray, dissolve the disputes of sophists, bite back at those who bark, restrain those who contradict, chastise the insolent, and carry out every dialectical determination.

Ancient—not in years, but in perpetual knowledge. If both qualities are present, the condition will be sounder.

Not negligent: for just as constancy is found to be the mother of every individual work, so negligence is the stepmother of all teaching and discipline. It would be more fitting to serve the mechanical arts than to be burdened by the yoke of negligence.

Let him not be arrogant: for the lively little spark of the poor is extinguished by the teacher’s arrogance, and the will to learn is kept apart from the wealthy, since the diligence of an arrogant teacher has never faithfully instructed a person. These are the men who disdain to teach humbly what they know, and cannot properly show what they understand through reason, because, placed in a position of eminence, they look down upon the minds of the sorrowful. They do not refer the cause to the giver of knowledge, but look instead to their own excellence.

These are also the men who enlarge their fringes, magnify their phylacteries, seek the more elevated seats at public spectacles, and desire to be called and greeted by everyone with the name *rabbi*. Such a collection of all good things, once the obligation of diligence has been removed, will rightly banish itself from itself.

When a beginner in good inquiry has entered the schools for the sake of reading, having inwardly assumed sternness, care should be taken that he begin immediately at dawn in a subdued voice, rising moderately with rounded speech, and waiting unless great necessity urges him. For if the teacher’s diligence presumes to wait for certain people beyond the appointed time [Col. 1236A], delay caused by laziness confounds them, and he will wear himself down with the rancor of anger. When the student devoted to laziness, an artificer of drowsiness, has learned of the teacher’s diligence, he will either hurry more promptly or, confounded by shame, sleep to the teacher’s disgrace.

But he should not act as the poet Assuerus prescribes—Assuerus whom the laziness of Dromo, Castor’s student, could not move to laughter. Every day, when he was snoring until the first hour, with rough fingernails producing a musical melody limb by limb, and with bleary eyes searching out the light of morning work, he used to say to his companions arriving at the schools, lest the matter be carried out:

“Is the dawn of day still being confused by the redness of the light?”

When they denied it, he very often completed half the day in drowsiness, giving thanks to God. He preferred to have the hardness of a sound head rather than the skill of an unsound one. If he was generally present at the midday disputation, unable to depart from his accustomed way, he snored with his nose awake and caused annoyance to those nearby because of the noise of his porcine gnashing. Once, while he was swallowing vegetables [Col. 1236B], his mouth gaped open and he entrusted his eyes to sleep. His hands, although dirty, were grasping something in the dish, but sleep proved harmful to him when he tried to imprison the food.

To what fruit of maturity do you think this man would come, O Marcianus, dearest of companions? Your own intention knows.

If a teacher comes to the study at midday for the purpose of discussion, he must take care not to rely upon sophistical equipment or be stirred by gloomy difficulties. Armed instead with diligent forethought, let him approach disputes fearlessly and settle them with an untroubled mind. Let him arrange in his memory whatever each person has raised as an objection, so that when the time comes to uncover it he does not depart from the path of reason, but, having adopted a suitable order and moderation for clarifying the riddles, explicitly resolves them.

If, as often happens, the greatest doubt should arise in the minds of discerning people during a discussion, one must employ study by deliberating; and whatever the mind, agitated by natural impulses, has dictated should be deferred until the following day for examination by conscience. In the same way, if anyone has reflected upon something exceedingly difficult [Col. 1236C], it should be commended to discretion. For in discussion the little spark of difficulty is usually discovered more easily than if it were entrusted to the discipline of private study, since, as Aristotle says, the truth of knowledge is not found only in one of the two alternatives.

It must also be observed that the knowledge of discerning teachers customarily makes use of traditions in three ways: by boasting of new and unfamiliar editions; by concealing the minds of students beneath old and grimy materials; and by awakening the understanding of those who believe in very ancient things that have nevertheless been renewed and flow forth as though from their own streams.

If anyone is delighted by the sagacity of these students, he should be attached to the chief scholar, so that he may either faithfully impress upon them a sequence of recollection or commend diligence in writing things out. Great nourishment of usefulness will certainly be gathered from this.

For a student to reach the summit of teaching in due time, he must remain constant in study and persist in a more secluded retreat, even if he is of sanguine temperament, lest the noise of attendants dull his mind or the quarrel of those coming and going confuse his understanding [Col. 1236D], while no bonds impede the vital spirits. It is consistent with moral propriety that a teacher should be more solitary while examining secrets than that he should display his presence to everyone by bringing out little books. For, when the son of detraction sees a teacher’s diligence in bringing out books, what, and to what extent, would he meditate?

If, at the beginning, the teacher’s diligence does not have an abundance of learners, he should not therefore grow lukewarm or fade away after abandoning hope. Rather, let him devote himself to study all the more ardently and conduct himself vigorously in the contest, so that, even with only a few, he may attain honor. For we have often seen people, supported by the companionship of a few and strengthened by devotion to profound study, receive their titles with distinction.

Did not Theophrastus, an artificer of subtlety, supported by the adornment of a few and deprived of the hope of governing, abandon the undertaking? Yet he acted without prudence; he would have acted more wisely had he shown himself worthy of the discipline of study. By the gifts of Master Leontinus, however, the discernment of many acquired companionship for him [Col. 1237A]. He judged it more honorable to act in this way than to be deprived of a gathering of learners.

Won over by the circle of piety, the ruler of students must diligently soothe the hearts of pupils living in poverty and studying earnestly: if he has the means, he should assist them with food, shoes, at least worn clothing, and other gifts, as well as with suitably encouraging advice. What gift could be more splendid or sweeter by nature than a donation to genuine students? It is more excellent to warm a student with things in which the donor’s contribution is minimal but the poor recipient’s readiness is greatest than to be soothed by the detestable assaults of actors and prostitutes.

Even if fortune is sometimes clouded, the teacher’s care should not despair. Rather, by always conducting himself courteously, let him endure adversity manfully and await better things with patience.

Shame upon Coriandus’ disgraceful transaction!

If, because of the impulse of a festive season, he wishes to visit places of pleasure, the teacher’s discretion should always have with him the nobler and better-looking members of his group, lest he appear to many to be deprived of companionship [Col. 1237B] or lest he be exposed to danger. Maro regretted being deprived of the company of his fortunate students.

Although he ought to be stern in the schools, nevertheless, upon entering he should remain devout in greeting; in speech he should be pleasant to those coming and going, a companion to those who jest, faithful in admonition to those who remain, and cautious in chastity toward those nearby, lest, if anyone is present, a friendly intimacy drink in the stench of his sighing nose.

The final part of the present volume is a compilation concerning teachers whom poverty—stepmother to the liberal disciplines—has driven to invade the territories of others. Let us also say something briefly about those whom the natural sweetness of their homeland recalls.

When, because of poverty, someone seeks the sweetest scent of profit, he should take care, while preserving the honor of teaching, to devote himself as much as he can to frugality, to desire modest clothing, and especially to show indulgence in governing students. He should first present a kindly face to the children, an even kinder manner of speaking to their parents, and promise the most gracious willingness to hear them concerning instruction [Col. 1237C]. Thus he will soften not only the hearts of the children but also draw money from their parents and spread his reputation. He should, however, defend the rights of the school according to the rule, once he has first been taught the order of instruction.

Toward the same pupils, once they have grown somewhat older, he should show himself stern; he should shape their mouths for correct speech, constrain their fingers for writing, and thoroughly train them to read, accompanied by the sternness of justice. Thus he should be agreeable not only in teaching but also in wit, granting an opportunity for play at the proper time and never withdrawing the benefits of instruction.

If he finds someone stubborn and proud, let him chastise him gently and set before him examples of conduct by which he may be restrained. Otherwise, with the parents’ consent, he will be struck with rods, so that, chastised to the last detail, he may emerge corrected and not, in despair, fall into disgrace.

When the teacher’s affection has admitted among the participants in the school’s entrance ceremonies people grown cold with age, as well as *statuales* and *planetici*, and he cannot use the file of correction upon them, he should smile upon those worn out by old age, sigh over the *statuales*, and likewise rejoice with the *planetici* at the image of a honeycomb [the reading *favo is simulacro* is uncertain] [Col. 1237D]. He should singe those with curled, bristling locks and drench with streaming tears the throats of those smeared with cosmetics. He should cautiously expel the soft ones, lest, being disturbed, they share in the guilt of his mind.

It must also be observed that in those by whose contribution the laborious contest is soothed, the educational result must be demonstrated; for the result of a matter is revealed by the presentation of the work. They should therefore be summoned in suitable order, one after another, so that careful scrutiny may disclose what the daily labor of those supplying the resources has provided [Col. 1238A].

One cannot always trust those who provide assistance, for their greed is often softened when their coins are exhausted, their loyalty grows lukewarm when hope has been frustrated, or their power becomes harsh in order to appear faithful.

Just as fortunate poverty must mercifully be treated with consideration, so one must attend no less carefully to the learning of the poor person himself. When a poorer dinner has taken place, the means should be distributed among table companions and extended to familiar associates and unwilling neighbors, lest a familiar voice reveal secrets by slander, or some garrulous old woman draw near another old woman by attaching herself to her. What is more futile than an old woman who knows the secret? Let insolent greed in small matters remain far away, as well as the stepmother of hunger and hooked tenacity.

Care must also be taken that he not play there for more than three years in the feculent dust of children, even if the greatest abundance of companions or wealth is present, and even if the richness of affection has been considered—unless advancement in honor flourishes through affection, or elevation of resources through honor.
