When, because of the delights of his homeland’s sweetness and the venerable sight of his parents, someone accepts responsibility for governing in the vicinity of his native soil [Col. 1238B], he should persist in pompous speech. He should in turn smile upon elegant and splendid administration and rejoice in variety of clothing, since the beauty of embroidered dress and the insignia of rings compel many to obtain something other than what truth requires.

Adornment, favor, and charm of speech compel very many persons endowed with intelligence to appear to surpass Homer, though the prescribed order of teaching must nevertheless be carefully observed. The harmful desire for jokes should also be removed with the greatest care, so that the provincial honor—which rarely occurs—may spread his reputation in commendation of his title.

The more the title of elegance rises, the more diligently he must cultivate the favor of his subjects, so that what cannot be proclaimed amid the tumult of his own mouth may be conveyed through their timely utterances, and so that he may be seen to be commendable not only in the sweetness of his conduct but also in the acuteness of his own abilities.

When commendation both of his conduct and of his abilities has emerged publicly, he must take care [Col. 1238C] that incest does not stiffen his head, adultery confuse his speech, or the stench of illicit wickedness blacken his good reputation. Otherwise, he may seem to wither away like roses emitting the fragrance of spring, and the lilies sought through the sweat of chastity may appear to diminish.

The image of the venerable Craton caused grief and its increase to those associated with his own abilities and also to others who had encountered him only once. He fell asleep in Castor’s lodging because of the pleasures of Euphrasia, his wife, and was found embracing her. He was dragged by the hair, punished with blows, torn by wounds, rubbed with salt, drenched with the urine of slaves, thrown into corners, raised upon beams, and finally, when his torturers had grown weary, deprived of his genitals. He was placed beneath a dung heap and exposed to passers-by. He became the outcast of the populace, the desolation of the students, the disgrace of his fellow soldiers, and a raw and cruel, wretched and most wretched spectacle of sorrow to all; the favor of his connections and the glory of his family benefited him in no way.

For although the first signs may sometimes remain unharmed, the final stains of another flavor will endure [Col. 1238D], and so forth.

I was also considering how to release the song of the sons,

Deaf, with a sidelong face, I am carried from the citadel.

Let it not shame me to have constructed snares from a sown heap,

While the broad harvest stirs rumor-bearing sounds.

At times a madness bordering upon the sea was present.

While I speak, consult the work from the fourth chapter.

I beseech you, young men whose youth is to be celebrated:

May my lyre now suggest innocent melodies.

[Col. 1239]

COMMENTARY ON BOETHIUS, *ON THE CONSOLATION OF PHILOSOPHY*, BOOK III, METER IX.

[Col. 1239A] O You who govern the world by perpetual reason,

Sower of earth and heaven, who bid time

Proceed from eternity, and, remaining steadfast, grant all things to move [Note: [Col. 1239D] See the remainder in the preceding volume, col. 758.],

To the most beloved and most desired son in age, and, by the right of profession and kinship, sweetest brother, by the sublimity of merit and rank most reverend lord Bishop Bovo, B., an unworthy servant of the brothers serving Christ in New Corbie, wishes every good of temporal and eternal life in the Lord.

### 1.

Your charity instructed me to explain in writing a certain obscure passage from the book of Boethius, which I once expounded to you orally. I obeyed, I confess, with ready willingness, but with excessive difficulty, because amid the countless occupations—or rather, miseries and sufferings—which we endure without ceasing amid civil wars and the incursions of the pagans, which, to speak prophetically, are swifter than eagles, I scarcely applied my mind to writing at all.

The subject itself also frightened me, since it was contrary to my office and purpose: it necessarily required saying something about the vanity of Platonic doctrines rather than about the truth of evangelical teaching. Yet the vehement ardor of your affection—which the great distance of land separating us in absence has not diminished, but, through the increasing sorrow of desire, has kindled from day to day—compelled me to attempt to obey your will even beyond my strength.

Nor, I think, will they reproach me for having brought forward certain things from the books of secular authors, since our foremost teachers have often done this in order to refute them. Physicians, after all, not only recommend wholesome foods to be taken but also point out harmful ones to be avoided: while showing useful herbs, they also identify poisonous ones, lest the unfortunate be deceived when reading about aconites. What is more, they say that precious antidotes are made even from the poisons of serpents. From this practice, in ancient times, skilled enchanters gained profits from their art; from it, apothecaries obtained no small gain in their trade.

### 2.

Thus, excellent bishop and spiritual chief physician of souls [Col. 1239C], you ought to know salutary things so that you may recommend them, and harmful things so that you may prohibit them. For neither could Saint Augustine, writing *The City of God Against the Pagans*, so vehemently condemn their filthy and shameful rites unless he knew them thoroughly, nor could he have written such polished books against the Manichaeans if he had been ignorant of their most wicked errors.

Therefore I do not believe it will harm you to read these few things about philosophical doctrines. I declare that I have touched upon them much more sparingly than the necessity of the undertaking demanded. And I earnestly ask that you deign to examine this little book, which I have sent, privately with someone highly learned and especially familiar to you, so that, if it contains anything useful, it may not be denied to anyone; but, if it contains little or nothing, it may not afterward be published to anyone.

### 3.

Anyone who wishes to investigate the meaning of those verses of Boethius upon which your holiness, venerable bishop, has imposed upon me the task of commenting must first be warned that not only in these verses but also in many passages of the same work, entitled *The Consolation of Philosophy* [Col. 1239D], certain things contrary to the Catholic faith are found.

This is surprising because I have read a very distinguished little work by the same author on the Holy Trinity, as well as another against the heretics Eutyches and Nestorius. Anyone who devotes himself to reading his other books—as I have done since adolescence recognizes without doubt from the particular brilliance of their elegant style that these works too were composed by the same author [Col. 1240A].

However this may be, it is certain that in these books he did not debate ecclesiastical doctrine, but merely wished to disclose to his readers the doctrines of the philosophers, especially those of the Platonists. Hence he presents himself as questioning everywhere, while he introduces Philosophy herself as responding and teaching. In Book Three, in seeking the seat of the highest good, he describes her as invoking the Father of all things in these words:

### 4.

“O You who govern the world by perpetual reason,

Sower of earth and heaven . . . and the rest.”

Although *sower* (*sator*) here seems to be used metaphorically rather than properly for “creator,” authors frequently use it in this way. Thus Virgil also sings in the *Bucolics*:

“Seeds gathered through the great void—seeds of earth, of souls, of the sea, and of liquid fire together.”

Therefore, if the beginnings of the elements are rightly called seeds, their creator is also rightly called their sower.

### 5.

“Who bid time,” and so forth. These words evidently signify nothing other than the eternity and immutability of the Creator, and the temporality and mutability of creation. He used *aeon* (*aevum*) on account of eternity.

First, it must be understood that the philosophers defined the eternal as that which has neither beginning nor end—that is, which neither begins nor ceases. That which begins but does not cease, and remains immortal, they call everlasting (*sempiternum*).

When he wished to express that time begins from eternity, he used a very precise and vigilant formulation, saying, “You bid time proceed from eternity.” For all time swiftly passes through its moments, whereas the eternity of the Creator, remaining steadfast in itself, cannot be moved, increased, or made greater by any additions of time.

Every creature, from the moment it was created, began to be what it had not been, and thereafter, with each individual moment, acquired a greater span of time in its existence. To have more or less of something than one had previously, just as to be what one had not been, is a kind of movement. Hence change appears to have been called almost *motation* (*motatio*).

Thus every creature, from the moment it began to exist, took up a certain journey through time. The Creator of all things, however, remaining immovable and eternal, creates temporal things, and, being immutable, creates mutable things; he grants all things to move. For incorporeal creation moves in time but not in place, whereas corporeal creation moves both in place and in time.

If this seems less clear to anyone, let him read the books of Saint Augustine on *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, where he discusses the movements of creatures with the greatest clarity.

### 6.

“Whom no external causes impelled.” For a long time the leading philosophers inquired about the causes on account of which God wished to create the world. At last, however, it seemed to them—and our own authors follow them in this—that the sole cause of so great a work was the goodness of the Creator. Through it he wished rational creation to become a participant in his blessedness by contemplating him.

The remainder of the world’s adornment was intended partly for the service of the human race and partly for the display of his eternal wisdom, by which he created all things “very good,” so that, from considering them, the attention of the human mind might be raised to understanding and praising him [Col. 1240D].

### 7.

“You lead all things from a heavenly exemplar.”

Before discussing this, something must be said about Plato’s doctrine, which Boethius particularly follows in this work. Thus in this same book he says, “I strongly agree with Plato.”

Plato therefore asserted that a kind of triad existed in the beginning and persuaded his students to believe it: God, exemplar, and matter. God was the creator of all things; the exemplar was that according to whose form everything would be fashioned; matter was that from which he would create all things.

Above he spoke of matter as “the flowing matter.” Here he expresses the exemplar when he says, “You lead all things from a heavenly exemplar.” This is the Platonic doctrine about which Blessed Jerome speaks in the prologue to Genesis. He said that the Seventy Translators had taken care lest Ptolemy, a worshiper of one God, discover among the Jews also a divided divinity; he says that they did this especially because the matter seemed liable to fall into Plato’s doctrine.

Thus, whenever Scripture speaks in a sacred passage about the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, they either interpreted it differently or kept silent altogether. They feared, of course, that if Ptolemy should find the mystery of the Trinity in the divine books, he might suppose it to be the same Trinity Plato had taught and thereby be drawn more deeply into Plato’s error.

Accordingly, just as any craftsman who plans to make a work of any kind first carries its form and the likeness of its individual parts in his mind and contemplates it with a certain act of thought [Col. 1241B], so Plato asserted that God eternally carried in his mind the form and image of the future world. This is what he says: “The beautiful world, the most beautiful one,” and so forth—in order that the structure of the world might be perfect both as a whole and in its parts.

### 8.

“You bind the elements with numbers,” and so forth. We often find in Latin authors how much the Greek philosophers—and Plato, the most eminent of them, in his *Timaeus*—discussed the power of numbers and the divinely effected joining of the elements through them, indeed the structure of the whole world. These Latin authors treated the material translated from Greek and judged it to belong to the great perfection of learning.

Of this material I have thought it appropriate to insert here only as much as suffices for this little commentary. Ambrosius Macrobius, who splendidly explained in two books the *Dream of Scipio* described by Cicero, says in his first book:

“We know, according to Plato—that is, according to the secret of truth—that those things are joined together by a strong bond among themselves which have an intervening middle portion to provide the bond’s firmness. When the middle portion itself is doubled, the outermost things are bound not only firmly but also inseparably.

“Thus the number three was the first to receive three terms—two extremes and a mean—by which it might be bound. The number four was the first to obtain two middle portions. From this number God, the architect and creator of the world’s mass, borrowed them and bound the elements together with an inseparable bond.

“As Plato asserts in the *Timaeus*, things so divided from and opposed to one another, and refusing communion by nature—I mean earth and fire—could not have been mixed in any other way than by being joined through the two middle bonds of air and water.”

In these words of Macrobius it is evident, unless I am mistaken, what is meant by “you bind the elements with numbers.”

### 9.

What follows—“so that you join cold to flames,” and so forth—can easily be understood. For the elements themselves and their differences are established by the same number. Their differences too are four: cold and heat, dryness and moisture. When these pairs combine with one another throughout the individual elements, they produce a fitting concatenation even among things that appear opposed.

For example, beginning with earth, which is lowest, earth is naturally dry and cold. Since humid and hot air is contrary to it, water, cold and humid, has been placed between them; through its coldness it connects with earth, and through its moisture with air.

Likewise, because the cold and humid nature of water opposes hot and dry fire, air is placed between them and joins itself to water through moisture and to fire through heat. Fire, too, differs from earth in heat, but agrees with it in dryness.

Thus all the elements, varied and arranged according to a fixed law of numbers together with their differences, are joined by an indissoluble bond among themselves: opposites agree and things in conflict are bound together. Hence scarcely any earthly body, so long as it retains its natural condition, exists without the combination of these elements.

Since this is evident to almost everyone, I think this demonstration may be omitted.

[Col. 1242A] ### 10.

We must examine more attentively what follows: “lest purer fire fly away,” and so forth. Just as earth and fire are, more than the other elements, separated by their position in space—earth being lowest and fire highest among them, since fire’s natural place is in the ether, which is evidently fiery in nature, and which every flame striving upward appears to seek—so they are also separated by certain other differences besides those mentioned above: namely, lightness and heaviness, purity and coarseness.

Of these elements, fire is the purest and lightest; earth is known to possess more density and weight than the others. Therefore, lest this great difference also separate fire and earth completely through irreconcilable opposition, a doubled middle portion was provided. As shown above, such a middle normally joins the extremes with an indissoluble bond—namely, water and air. Tempered by an appropriate sharing in both forms of opposition, they reconcile the lightness of fire with the weight of earth.

Both possess something of lightness with fire and something of heaviness with earth. Air, however, is nearer to fire through its lightness, while water approaches the weight of earth more closely.

### 11.

Yet just as great as the difference between water and air on account of density and weight is the difference between air and fire. Again, the difference between air and water on account of rarity and lightness is the same as that between earth and water.

Likewise, the difference between earth and water on account of density and weight is the same as that between water and air; and the difference between water and air is the same as that between air and fire.

Nor are only neighboring and contiguous things compared; equality is preserved through alternating steps. For what earth is in relation to air, water is in relation to fire. However many times you reverse the comparison, you will find the same joinable correspondence, by which things differing equally are associated with one another.

This is what he says: “lest purer”—that is, lighter—“fire fly away” and become completely separated from earth, or lest earth, submerged by its own weight and no longer adhering to the other elements [Col. 1242C], fall away from its own stability.

### 12.

All the authorities on astrology testify that earth is situated in the middle of the entire heavenly sphere, like the center in the middle of a circle, and that the heavens themselves, together with the stars, are at equal distances from earth on every side.

If this is so, earth must be surrounded on all sides either by water or by air. Therefore, unless it is held in place by the divinely arranged connection of the elements, it would necessarily, as they supposed, slip from its position by a kind of submergence. This is what he wished to be understood by the words, “or let weights drag down the submerged earth.”

When we discuss, in accordance with the teachers of astronomy, the circuit of the heavens by which they think earth is surrounded on every side, though across immense and immeasurable spaces, let no one suppose that we are contentiously asserting even this, or that we accept the fables of the Antipodes, which are wholly contrary to the Christian faith [Note: [Col. 1241D] May allowance be made for the times.].

For this reason, we approach the following verses of this passage—which Philosophy addresses as though invoking Divinity itself—with very great hesitation [Col. 1242D], especially because these matters do not pertain to instruction in religious conduct or faith.

And because, when we devote even a little attention to these useless matters, we are hindered from examining the secrets of divine law, with whose sweetness devout minds cannot be satisfied in this life, I nevertheless do not consider my labor entirely useless if I have fulfilled the will of your most sweet affection. In particular, just as salutary things that should be retained must often be spoken, so harmful things that should be avoided must sometimes be spoken as well.

I shall therefore pass over the following verses with as much brevity as I can, so that I may make clear not what we ought to approve or follow, but what Boethius’ Philosophy thought.

### 13.

“You, the middle of the threefold,” and so forth. The philosophers, speaking of one great soul of the whole world, uttered many things about its supposedly divine nature and power—not according to truth, but according to the fabrications of their opinions [Col. 1243A].

Since these matters are alien to our doctrines, they must be touched upon briefly and mentioned only in passing, insofar as the necessity of this commentary requires. For just as the soul of any human being fills the entire body and supplies vital movement to all its members, so they thought that this soul, diffused throughout the whole mass of the world’s body, supplied its own movement to all the members, so to speak, of the entire world.

Maro too appears to hold this very view. It is established that he was highly skilled in philosophical disciplines, insofar as they concern the Epicurean school. His distinguished commentator Servius, when beginning his explanation of the sixth book of the *Aeneid*, writes:

“Virgil as a whole is indeed full of knowledge, and this book holds the chief place in it.”

In this book he says the familiar lines:

“First, heaven, earth’s fields, and the watery plains—  
the shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars—  
a spirit within nourishes, and a mind infused through the limbs  
moves the whole mass.”

Observe how Boethius says “soul,” Virgil “spirit,” and shortly afterward calls it “mind” [Col. 1243B]. What is said here—“you resolve the soul that moves all things through harmonious members”—is expressed there in the words, “a mind infused through the limbs moves the whole mass.”

### 14.

Concerning the generation of this soul, unusual excerpts from Plato’s *Timaeus* are read aloud to us in the aforementioned book of Macrobius. I shall summarize their meaning briefly rather than reproduce the words in order.

It is read there that God, through the abundant fecundity of his majesty, created from himself a mind, which is called *νοῦς* (*nous*, “intellect” or “mind”). Then from this mind the world-soul was created. Plato says that its generation was effected by the Creator’s command through a certain power of numbers.

“For,” he says, “with the monad placed at the summit, three numbers flowed from each side: even numbers from one side and odd numbers from the other. From the one side, after the monad, came two; then four; then eight. Likewise, the first even number and the first square; and from the even number, the first κύβος (*kybos*), that is, the first number producing a solid figure.

“From the other side came three, then nine, then twenty-seven: namely, the first odd number, the first square from an odd number, and the first κύβος (*kybos*) from an odd number.”

Let this suffice concerning the Platonic fictions.

15. It remains for us to try to explain why Boethius called this same soul of a threefold nature. For they say that from the mind from which it was born it possesses reason, and from its own nature the power of providing sensation and the seedbed of growth. The first of these is called λογικόν, that is, rational; the second αἰσθητικόν, that is, sensory; the third φυτικόν, by which is understood the nature that plants and increases bodies.

According to certain authorities, it is also said in another way to be of a threefold nature, in accordance with the likeness of the human soul: namely, rational, desiring, and spirited. But it seems to me that the former interpretation better expresses what this author intends. For, in order to move all things, it diffuses itself throughout all things, so that first it causes the heavenly bodies of all the stars—for they too are thought to have received certain souls of their own from God—as though capable of mind, [Col. 1243D] pure and whole in reason, to move in an established order. Next, because there are three orders of earthly bodies, which they assert are animated by it, in the first order, that of human beings, those three are recognized together, since human beings both use reason, possess sensation, and have a nature capable of growing and propagating. In the second order, that of beasts, cattle, and every kind of animate creature, because they lack reason, only two of these are found: sensation and growth. The third order consists of earthly bodies in trees and plants, which lack both reason and sensation; and because only the power of growth flourishes in them, they are said to live by this one faculty alone.

16. Therefore, if the philosophers speak truly, the world-soul, according to its threefold nature, moves all things in three ways: by reason, sensation, and growth. But it moves the heavenly bodies by stable reason alone; the lowest earthly bodies by growth alone; the first of the earthly bodies, [Col. 1244A] that is, the human, by all three of the aforesaid modes; and the intermediate bodies, namely, brute animals, by two.

Moreover, when he called the members of the world harmonious, this may be understood simply to mean that they are mutually fitting and concordant, and that each, in its own place and order, is beautiful or suitable and in no way discordant with the others. Or it may be understood that he wished to express what they say is present in the greatest parts of the world, namely, in the circles of the seven planets: a certain supreme harmony, although far removed from our ears. For the planets that are carried in the higher circle produce, by their course, the melody of a sharper sound, while those that are lower resound more deeply; yet all together accord in one harmony of musical modulation.

The treatment of this matter would require more leisure and time than we now possess, and it is recognized as useful only to those who desire to know the nature of the musical art. We nevertheless know that the greatest philosophers composed many volumes discussing the intervals and harmony of these circles.

[Col. 1244B] 17. Let us now examine the words of Boethius that follow, in which he continues to present certain astonishing speculations about this soul, saying: “which, having divided two,” and so forth. There might be some uncertainty about this soul’s division into two spheres, unless he himself resolved the matter by adding, “with a similar image he turns the heavens.” For it is evident that he means that the soul, first divided into two spheres, moves and revolves with a certain force, and in this way draws and turns the mass of heaven with itself into those same spheres.

How heaven revolves in two spheres and circuits opposed to one another is apparent to everyone’s eyes, though not to everyone’s understanding. There is, first, the best-known circuit of heaven, by which we see the aether, with all the stars fixed in it, revolve from east to west, so that, when we observe the pole placed at the very summit of the world, all the stars seem to rise on the right and set on the left, except those contained within the arctic circle. For these never undergo cosmical setting; they undergo only heliacal setting [Col. 1244C].

18. The other revolution of heaven is demonstrated to us by the courses of the planets, that is, the wandering stars. Although these are not fixed in heaven but are carried beneath heaven and counter to heaven, no one nevertheless hesitates to call them stars of heaven. The heaven in which they are carried many call the aetherial heaven, although, just as it is much higher than the air that supports the flight of birds, so it is incomparably brighter in purity. Its revolution, contrary to the upper one, always proceeds from west to east—that is, for those looking toward the southern region, from right to left.

Finally, the fact that the planets themselves, like the other stars, appear to proceed from east to west and to descend toward the setting during the daily or nightly intervals results from the more violent whirling of the aether, which drags them along with it as though against their will. Yet they themselves at every moment move in the opposite direction, as if going backward. This is most evident in the moon, which is the lowest and nearest to the earth of those seven, and traverses the smallest circle and therefore the more rapid course. When it is new, it scarcely appears around the sun’s [Col. 1244D] setting; on the following evening it is already brighter and has withdrawn farther from the west. Its daily withdrawal from the setting then increases by equal intervals, until on the fourteenth day, having traversed the entire upper hemisphere, it appears, with the sun sunk in the west, to advance in the east as a full lamp.

19. As for the course of the sun along the same path—that is, through the zodiac, measured out by the equal intervals of its twelve signs—since the matter is known to all who possess even a slight knowledge of computation and astrology, I consider it superfluous to say anything. Nor does it pertain to this work to mention the remaining five: the star of Saturn, and those of Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury, except merely to demonstrate that, since the two circuits of the stars are known to be opposed to one another, those seven are shown by careful observers to wander in a lower position and in a course contrary to that of all the others.

We must [Col. 1245A] therefore attend keenly to the truth of the matter at this point and separate it completely from philosophical fictions, so that we may believe that this marvelous revolution of heaven and the stars in opposite directions is produced not by the world-soul, which is unknown to us, but by the ineffable power of almighty God.

Certainly, when that soul is said to proceed in such a way as to return into itself, this signifies that the whole motion is continually repeated through the same circuits: whatever distance it appears to have traversed, it hastens to enter upon that very same course again. For whenever a circle revolves in a circuit, it turns back into itself. This does not differ from what is read in Solomon: “The spirit goes, turning and turning, and returns to its own circle.”

20. Nor should we pass over what he says, “it circles the deep mind.” For this signifies the mind given to human beings by God, but depressed and weighed down by the mass of bodily thought, as Cicero says in his books *On the Republic* [Note: [Col. 1245D] In my edition, book III, 1. I nevertheless think that our author took this passage from Augustine, who was reporting it, rather than from Tully himself [Col. 1246D]]: that it seemed to him that human beings had been generated by nature not as by a mother but as by a stepmother, with a body naked, fragile, and weak; but with a spirit anxious toward troubles, humbled by [Col. 1245B] fears, tender toward labors, and inclined toward lusts. In these conditions there was, as it were, a certain divine fire of intellect and mind buried beneath.

Behold in what depth the mind, endowed by God with the profoundness of intellect, is placed: it has observed, attended to, and grasped through calculation and understanding the circuit of heaven as it revolves along two contrary paths. It is rightly called profound, since without profound thought it could not investigate such matters.

Human thought may indeed be understood to be called profound in both ways: because of the profundity of its perception and intellect, and because it is weighed down by its earthly dwelling. For, on every side, the height from the earth to heaven is equal, and we know nothing deeper than the earth beneath heaven. According to this arrangement of places, therefore, every height is referred to heaven, and every depth to earth. For this reason the expression seems especially suited to the present meaning, since the entire revolution of both spheres is understood to circle the depth of the earth.

Hence it comes about that the inaccessible and swift rotation of so immense a [Col. 1245C] mass, by its violent force, compels all dense and heavy things from every side to be carried toward the earth, which alone remains motionless in the middle like a center. For whenever a sphere revolves in equal balance, nothing in it is immobile except the center. The earth itself does not move, because a sphere must necessarily move around something immobile. This motion, drawing downward everything that possesses any density, removes it far from the upper regions of heaven, so that even clouds are said to be unable to rise higher than ten stadia above the earth.

21. There follows: “You bring forth souls and lesser lives by like causes,” and so forth. The meaning of these words should be avoided rather than revealed through exposition. For, having explained the nature of the great world-soul, he now begins to speak of the condition of lesser souls, asserting that they were made by the same causes as the former.

But he wishes this to be understood about them, although the Christian faith by no means accepts it: namely, that from the beginning of their creation they were placed in heaven and lived blessedly through contemplation of the divine mind; that afterward some of them descended [Col. 1245D] into human bodies; and that, once those bodies had been dissolved and cleansed of earthly vices, they returned to their origin, went back to heaven, and, as Virgil says, wished to return once more into bodies.

He expresses the dignity of their first condition in these words: “You advance them and fit them to lofty, light chariots.” By this he signifies that, through the lightness of their incorporeal nature, they are carried forward as if by certain chariots into the seats of the stars.

When he says, “You sow them into heaven,” he wishes this to be understood of the lights of the world and of all the stars, which they endeavored to affirm live when implanted in heaven and make use of reason.

22. But “You sow them into the earth” is spoken only of human souls. As I said, they believe that these are sent down from heaven into bodies and, because they are of a fiery nature, are brought back there by that same nature, though, as they think, only after long [Col. 1246A] periods of time.

Regarding their descent to earth, they weave utterly empty fables: how, through desire for earthly bodies, they begin to slip away from contemplation of the divine mind; then, proceeding through the zodiac to the seven spheres of the planets, they receive from each sphere the particular motion that they will possess in the practice of earthly life. Thus, in the sphere of Saturn they exercise reasoning; in Jupiter’s, the power of action; in Mars’s, the heat of courage; in the sun’s, the nature of sensation and opinion; the motion of desire in Venus’s circle; the knowledge of pronouncing and interpreting in Mercury’s sphere; and, they say, the nature of planting and increasing bodies upon entering the sphere of the moon.

But who is so mad as not to remove these monstrous fictions far from his faith? Nevertheless, it is useful to know them for this reason alone: so that when someone reads them expressed in other words by very learned authorities, he may not be led by the sweetness of their composition into error, imagining that they are saying something true other than this.

For when the same Boethius says in the fifth book of this work [Col. 1246B] that human souls are freer when they preserve themselves in contemplation of the divine mind, less free when they descend into bodies, and still less free when they are joined to earthly limbs, who would understand him to be speaking there of the descent of souls into bodies unless he had first become acquainted with this philosophical sect?

23. Since above this author mentioned certain lives or souls of the heavenly bodies, that is, of the stars, we must not pass over the fact that some of our own authorities held the same view even concerning the principal lights of the world, the sun and the moon: namely, that at the consummation of the world they will receive the reward of their labor.

For Saint Jerome, in the ninth book of his exposition of the prophet Isaiah, where he explains this verse [Note: [Col. 1246D] Chapter XXX, 26, at the end of the book], “And the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, like the light of seven days,” says among other things:

“The light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun when the Lord makes a new heaven and a new earth, and [Col. 1246C] the form of this world passes away, so that the moon and the sun may receive the reward of their labor and their course. For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God, because creation itself will also be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the sons of God,” although some, understanding them to be instruments of light, maintain that they are insensible.

Therefore the moon will receive the sun’s splendor. Nor is it surprising to hold this concerning the most brilliant element, to which dominion over the night has been entrusted, when it is also written of the saints, “The righteous shall shine like the sun”; and the sun shall receive sevenfold light, like the light of seven days, when the world was created in the beginning.”

24. Since we do not read anything of this sort in our other authorities, and since Jerome himself did not conceal that some held contrary opinions, I do not think that these words of Saint Jerome should be defended contentiously. For, according to the authority of Scripture, I understand that no rational creature was created by God in the beginning except angels and human beings. Moreover, it does not seem at all credible that an angelic or human spirit has been mingled with these stars or dwells among them.

[Col. 1246D] Let it therefore be sufficient for us to know that Scripture says that the two great lights were made by God. To wish to investigate their nature more deeply is rash.

The few verses that remain require no exposition, since in them a pure and open prayer to God is poured forth. I nevertheless confess that certain words in these passages seem to me to carry the poison of the philosophers. But since Catholic ears are accustomed to receive such words more correctly and interpret them in a better sense, and since for this reason they do no harm to the faith, I accept them gladly and have judged it best to remain silent about them.

You now have, most beloved lord, the explanation of Boethius’ obscure verses that the feebleness of my intellect has been able to compose. If anyone finds in it something useful, he will rightly be grateful to your command.

## SECOND PART OF THE WORKS. THEOLOGICAL WORKS.

[Col. 1247]

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING BOOKS.

[Col. 1247] We undertook, at the exhortations and prayers of many, to explain the books of questions by Anicius. We have found the subjects of the matters treated in them exceedingly profound, their subtlety exceedingly obscure, yet the completion of the work exceedingly well established. For what is deeper than the infinite? What is more subtle than the ineffable and inscrutable? And what is more persuasive than that which, although established by invincible arguments, nevertheless rests upon the highest and most celebrated authorities?

God, of whom these books treat, is rightly understood and worthily proclaimed as immeasurable in greatness, incomprehensible in contemplation, and inexpressible in speech. Yet the ancient seers, inspired by him, understood certain of his mysteries and conveyed them to the unrefined people of their own time through various figurations of both things and words. Later writers spoke differently but with the same meaning; through carefully considered interpretations they disclosed the enigmas of those figurative expressions and confirmed them not only by their own authority but also by arguments that either the majesty of theology claims as its own or that human philosophy, in whatever proportion it bears to theology, admits as common to both.

Accordingly, the aforementioned author, as one privy to the secrets of the seers and not ignorant of these mysteries, wrote a little against the perverse doctrines of certain heretics. Yet he wrote in such a manner that he might close the approach to understanding for the negligent and presumptuous, while stirring the attention of the diligent and perceptive, and opening the way for those who knock with vehement application of mind.

For his concise discourse, without its own amplification; his exposition, obscure through a tacit method of reasoning; his indirect arrangement of meanings or words; and his novel syntax, contrary to the rule of the grammarians—these conceal meaning from the ignorant and proud, for whom they have been articulated. But to the wise, and especially to those who venerate the sacred Scriptures and examine them through constant practice and watchful attention, they permit the meanings to be seen within.

Appropriately, therefore, Anicius touches upon the secrets of higher theology through such mysteries and, so to speak, words of hidden meaning, by which he tests the learned and the unlearned, the humble and the proud. Worthily called Anicius for his strength, Severinus for his gravity, Boethius for his assistance, and Manlius for his merits.

As for us, wishing to contribute nothing on the authority of our own judgment but only to report the meanings of the author that we have apprehended through their prior significance, we attend not only to his words but also to the reasons for those words. And lest we seem either to be strangled into complete silence by the narrowness of timidity or loosened into chatter by the boldness of presumption, we neither say everything nor remain silent about everything that we have recognized the author to have intended.

There are two kinds of those who see: one consists of authors who advance their own judgment; the other of readers. Among readers, some are reciters, who pronounce the same words of the authors and for the same reasons as the authors themselves; others are interpreters, who explain what the authors have said obscurely in more familiar words.

We, performing the office of interpreters among readers rather than of reciters, restore transpositions of words to their proper order, figurative expressions to their sequence, and novelties to regular form, adding the causes of each. We explain the developed matter, according to the nature of the work, by divisions or definitions applied to all or some of its parts; by comparisons with matters taken from elsewhere; by the grammatical cases of expressions placed by the author; by the several multiple meanings of those expressions; or by the introduction of arguments. We carefully take heed that in no meaning we depart from the authentic writers of the holy prophecies.

What we have written appears not only firm in its arguments to readers well trained in the subject but also so consonant with the authentic Scriptures that it may be thought not so much our own discoveries as things stolen by us.

## [ON THE TRINITY.]

[Col. 1247]

## HOW THE TRINITY IS ONE GOD AND NOT THREE GODS. [Note: [Col. 1247] We have transcribed and prefixed this title in full from an older copy of the Royal Library and from the manuscripts of Saint Victor, which are of the highest reliability; of all the manuscripts, they alone had preserved this wording.] TO QUINTUS AURELIUS MEMMIUS SYMMACHUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS AND MOST ILLUSTRIOUS EX-CONSUL OF THE ORDER, AND HIS FATHER-IN-LAW. (C)

## PREFACE.

[Col. 1247]

I have taken care to offer and communicate to you a question investigated for a very long time, insofar as the divine light has deigned to illuminate the spark of our mind, and committed to writing in arguments and letters. In doing so, I have been as eager for your judgment as I am devoted to my own discovery.

What state of mind I experience whenever I entrust to writing what I have devised may be understood both from the difficulty of the subject and from the fact that I converse with only a few—in other words, with you alone. For we are not stirred by the pursuit of fame or by the empty shouting of the crowd. If there is any outward fruit to be hoped for, it can expect no judgment other than one resembling the subject itself.

Wherever, therefore, I have turned my eyes away from you, I have encountered partly sluggish indolence and partly cunning envy, so that one who has put such matters before these human monsters for trampling rather than recognition seems to inflict an insult upon divine studies.

For this reason I restrain my style through brevity and veil the principles drawn from the innermost disciplines of philosophy in the meanings of new words, so that these matters may speak only to me and to you, should you at some time turn your eyes toward them. We keep the others at such a distance that those unable to grasp them intellectually may seem unworthy even to read them.

Yet we must not demand more from ourselves than the vision of human reason is capable of ascending toward the heights of divinity. For in the other arts as well, a certain limit has been established: as far as the path of reason is able to approach. Medicine, for example, does not always bring health to the sick; nevertheless, there will be no fault in the physician if he has omitted nothing that ought to have been done. The same applies in the other arts.

And the more difficult this question is, the more readily it ought to obtain pardon. You must also examine whether the seeds of reasoning coming to us from the writings of blessed Augustine have produced some fruit in us. Let us take our beginning from the question proposed.

## CHAPTER ONE. The Catholic Judgment Concerning the Trinity and the Unity of God.

Many claim the reverence of the Christian religion, but that faith prevails most fully and exclusively which, both because of the universal precepts by which the authority of the same religion is understood and because its worship has spread through almost all the regions of the world, is called catholic, or universal. Its judgment concerning the unity of the Trinity is this:

They say: The Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God; therefore the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, not three Gods.

The principle of this conjunction is indifference—that is, absence of difference. Difference accompanies those who increase or diminish, such as the Arians, who vary the Trinity according to degrees of merit, divide it, and draw it into plurality.

For the beginning of plurality is otherness; apart from otherness, plurality itself cannot be understood. The diversity of three things, or of any number of things, is established either by genus, species, or number. For whenever something is said to be the same, something different is also predicated.

“Same” is said in three ways: by genus, as the same human being and horse, because they share the same genus, namely, animal; by species, as the same Cato and Cicero, because they share the same species, namely, human being; or by number, as Tullius and Cicero, because they are numerically one.

Accordingly, “different” is also said by genus, species, or number. Difference in number, however, is produced by variation in accidents. For three human beings differ neither in genus nor in species but through their accidents. Even if we mentally remove all accidents from them, their places are nevertheless different, and we cannot in any way imagine them as occupying one place. For two bodies cannot occupy one place, and place is an accident. Therefore they are numerically plural, because they are made plural through their accidents.

## CHAPTER TWO. The Divine Substance Is Form.

[Col. 1250A]

Come, then, let us enter upon the matter and examine each point insofar as it can be understood and grasped. For, as it seems to have been most aptly said, it belongs to an educated person to try to apprehend each thing as it is in itself.

There are three speculative disciplines: natural philosophy, which concerns motion and is unabstracted—ἀνεπεξαίρετος, that is, inseparable. For it considers the forms of bodies together with matter, and these forms cannot in actuality be separated from bodies. The bodies are in motion: earth is carried downward, fire upward, and form, joined to matter, possesses motion.

Mathematics is without motion but unabstracted. It considers the forms of bodies without matter and therefore without motion. Although these forms exist in matter, they cannot be separated from it.

Theology is without motion, abstract, and separable. For the substance of God is without both matter and motion.

In natural matters, therefore, we ought to proceed rationally; in mathematical matters, through disciplined study; in divine matters, intellectually. We must not be drawn away into imaginings but rather contemplate the form itself, which is truly form and not an image, which is being itself, and from which being derives. For all being comes from form.

A statue, for example, is called the likeness of an animal not according to the bronze, which is its matter, but according to the form impressed upon it. Bronze itself is spoken of not according to earth, which is its matter, but according to the shape of bronze. Earth itself is not called so according to formless matter—κατὰ τὴν ὕλην—but according to dryness and heaviness, which are forms.

Nothing, therefore, is said to exist according to matter but according to its proper form.

But the divine substance is form without matter; therefore it is one, and it is what it is. Other things are not what they are. For each thing has its being from the things of which it consists, that is, from its parts. It is this and that—that is, its parts joined together—but it is not this or that separately. Thus, since an earthly human being consists of soul and body, the human being is body and soul, but is neither body nor soul alone.

A part, therefore, is not what the whole is. But that which is not composed of this and that, but is simply this, truly is what it is. It is also most beautiful and strongest, because it depends upon nothing.

This, therefore, is truly one: in it there is no number, nothing else besides what it is, and it cannot become a subject. For it is form, and forms cannot be subjects. Other forms, such as humanity, are subjects to accidents, but humanity does not receive accidents insofar as it is itself; rather, it receives them insofar as the matter subject to it receives them. When the matter subject to humanity receives any accident, humanity itself appears to receive it.

But a form that exists without matter cannot be a subject, nor can it inhere in matter. Otherwise it would not be form but an image. From those forms that exist apart from matter have come these forms that exist in matter and constitute bodies. We misuse the term “forms” for the others that exist in bodies, since they are images; they resemble those forms that are not constituted in matter.

There is therefore no diversity in God, no plurality arising from diversity, no multiplicity arising from accidents, and consequently no number.

## CHAPTER THREE. There Is No Number in the Divine Substance.

God does not differ from God, neither through accidents nor through accidental differences posited in a subject. Where there is no difference, there is absolutely no plurality; therefore there is no number, but only unity.

When God is named three times—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—the three units do not produce a plurality of number in what they are, if we attend to the things that are counted and not to number itself. In the case of number, the repetition of units produces number. But in the number that exists among countable things, the repetition of units and plurality does not at all produce a numerical diversity of countable things.

For number is of two kinds: one by which we count, and the other that exists among countable things. One, in the first sense, is the unit by which we say “one.” Two, in the realm of things, are human beings or stones; duality is nothing, but only the duality by which two human beings or stones become two. The same applies to the other numbers.

Thus, in the number by which we count, repetition of units produces plurality. But in the number of things, repetition of units does not produce plurality. For example, if I say of the same thing, “one sword, one blade, one weapon,” the sword can be recognized by so many names. This repetition of units is rather a reiteration than a counting. Likewise, if we say “weapon, blade, sword,” it is a repetition of the same thing, not a counting of different things. Or if I say “sun, sun, sun,” I have not made three suns but have predicated the word repeatedly of one sun.

Therefore, when God is predicated three times of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the threefold predication does not thereby produce number. As has been said, this threatens those who introduce a difference of merits among them.

For Catholics, however, who establish no difference and posit the form as it is, believing that what it is is nothing other than the very being that it is, rightly regard the repetition of the same thing, rather than the enumeration of different things, when it is said: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit; and this Trinity is one God—like “weapon and blade,” one sword; like “sun, sun, sun,” one sun.

For the present, let this have been said to indicate and demonstrate that not every repetition of units produces number and plurality.

But the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not spoken of as though they were something merely multivocal. Blade and weapon are both the same thing and identical; the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are indeed the same, but they are not the same individual.

This point must be considered briefly. When asked, “Is the Father the same individual as the Son?” they answer, “Certainly not.” Again, “Is one the same individual as the other?” is denied. Therefore there is not complete indifference among them in every respect. Number consequently enters in, and it has been explained above that number is constituted by the diversity of subjects.

We shall consider this matter briefly, after first setting forth how each thing is predicated of God.

## CHAPTER FOUR. How God Exists in the Categories.

[Col. 1252A]

The ten categories are altogether handed down, which are universally predicated of all things: substance, quality, quantity, relation, place, time, having, being situated, doing, and undergoing. These categories, then, are such as their subjects permit them to be; for some of them belong to substance in the predication of other things, while others belong among the accidents. But when one applies these categories to divine predication, everything that can be predicated is transformed. Relation, however, cannot be predicated at all; for substance in that case is not truly substance, but is beyond substance. The same applies to quality and to the other categories that can occur. To make the point clearer, examples should be supplied. [Col. 1252B]

When we say “God,” we seem indeed to signify substance, but substance that is beyond substance. When we say “just,” we seem to signify quality, but not an accidental quality: rather, one that is substance and beyond substance. For God is not one thing as God and another thing as just; rather, being God and being just are the same. Likewise, when “great” or “greatest” is predicated, we seem to signify quantity, but a quantity that is itself the substance of the sort that we have said is beyond substance. For being God and being great are the same. Concerning his form it was demonstrated above that he is form and truly one, and that there is no plurality.

These categories, however, are such that, in other things, they make the thing in which they are to be what is predicated: in other things separately, but in God conjointly and inseparably. [Col. 1252C] Thus, when we say “substance,” as in “a human being” or “God,” this is said as though that of which it is predicated were itself substance—“the substance of a human being” or “the substance of God.” Yet there is a difference: a human being is not wholly identical with “human being,” and therefore is not wholly substance. What a human being is, depends upon other things that are not human being. God, however, is precisely what God is; for he is nothing other than what he is, and therefore is himself God.

Again, “just,” which is a quality, is said as though the subject of which it is predicated were itself just: if we say “a just human being” or “a just God,” we assert that the human being or God himself is just. But there is a difference, because in a human being the human being is one thing and the just is another; God, however, is himself precisely what is just. A human being or God is likewise said to be great, and this is said as though the human being itself were a great human being or God were a great God. But a human being is merely great, whereas God exists as greatness itself. [Col. 1252D]

The remaining categories are predicated neither of God nor of other things in the same way. For “where” can be predicated both of God and of a human being: of a human being, as “in the forum”; of God, as “everywhere.” But it is predicated in such a way that the thing of which it is predicated is not itself what is predicated. A human being is not said to be “in the forum” in the same manner as he is said to be white or tall. Nor is he said to be as though surrounded and delimited by some property by which he could be designated in himself; rather, this predication merely shows that he is informed by other things.

The case is different with God. When he is said to be everywhere, this does not mean that he is in every place—for he cannot be in a place at all—but that every place is present to him so as to receive him, whereas he himself is not received in a place. [Col. 1253A] Therefore he is said to be nowhere in a place because he is everywhere, but not in a place.

“When” is likewise predicated in the same way: of a human being, “he came yesterday”; of God, “he always is.” Here too, the thing to which yesterday’s coming is attributed is not said to be something in itself; rather, what has accrued to it in relation to time is predicated. But when it is said of God that he always is, this signifies one thing: that he has been throughout all the past, is present in every manner of the present, and will be throughout all the future. The same may be said, according to the philosophers, of the heavens and of the other immortal bodies.

But it is not said of God in that way. He always is because in him there is always present time. There is as much difference between the present of our things—the “now” that constitutes our flowing time—and the divine present as there is between a moving and a permanent present. The divine now, remaining without moving itself and standing firm, produces eternity. If one adds “always” to this name, one makes the now’s continuous, tireless, and therefore perpetual course—which is sempiternity.

“Having” and “doing” are likewise predicated in the same manner. Of a human being we say, “He runs clothed”; of God, “He governs while possessing all things.” Yet nothing concerning being itself has been said of either. All this predication is given to externals, and in some way everything is referred to something else. We can more easily distinguish the difference among these predications as follows.

One who is a human being, or God, is referred to the category of substance, by which something is what it is—namely, a human being or God. One who is just is referred to quality, by which he is something—namely, just. One who is great is referred to quantity, by which he is something—namely, great. [Col. 1253C]

In the remaining predications there is nothing of this sort. For one who says that someone is in the forum or everywhere does indeed refer him to the category of place, but not to that by which he is something, as justice makes someone just. Likewise, when I say “he runs,” “he governs,” “he is now,” or “he is always,” the predication refers either to doing or to time—if, indeed, that divine “always” can be called time—but not to that by which something is something, as greatness makes something great. There is no need to seek position or passion in God, for they do not exist in him.

Is the difference among predications now clear? Some of them point to a thing itself, while others point, as it were, to circumstances belonging to the thing. The former are predicated in such a way as to show that the thing is something; the latter in such a way as to attach to it, not something that it is, but rather something external.

[Col. 1253D] Let those predications that designate something as existing in itself be called predications according to the thing. When they are said of created subjects, they are called accidents according to the thing; when they are said of God, who is not a subject, the predication is called predication according to the substance of the thing.

## CHAPTER V. How God Is in Relation

Let us now examine relatives, on account of which we have undertaken the whole preceding discussion. For relatives especially do not seem to make a predication according to themselves; they are plainly seen to consist in the arrival of something else. Since “lord” and “servant” are relatives, let us see whether the predication is according to itself or not. [Col. 1254A]

If you remove the servant, you also remove the lord; but if you remove whiteness, you do not thereby remove the white. There is, however, a difference. Whiteness is an accident of the white, and when it is removed, the white naturally perishes. But in the case of a lord, if you remove the servant, the name by which the lord was called perishes. The servant, however, is not an accident of the lord in the way whiteness is an accident of the white. Rather, it is a certain power by which the servant is restrained. Since that power is lost when the servant is removed, it is clear that it does not belong to the lord in himself, but comes to him externally, in a manner of speaking, through the presence of servants.

A relative predication therefore cannot be said either to add anything to, or to subtract anything from, or to alter anything in, the thing of which it is predicated according to itself. It consists wholly not in being, but in having some relation to something in some manner of comparison; and it is not always directed toward another, but sometimes toward the same thing.

Suppose, for example, that someone is standing. If I approach him on his right, he will be on my left in relation to me—not because he himself is intrinsically on the left, but because I have approached on the right. If I approach on the left, he likewise becomes on the right—not because he is intrinsically right, as he is white or tall, but because, when I approach, he becomes right; and what he is in this respect comes from me and through me, not from himself.

Thus those things that do not make a predication according to the property of some thing in itself cannot alter or change anything, nor can they vary any essence whatsoever. Accordingly, if “Father” and “Son” are said relatively, and differ in nothing else, as has been said, except by relation—and if relation is not predicated of that of which it is predicated as though it itself were, according to the thing, what is predicated of it—then it will not produce an otherness in the things of which it is predicated. If it may be said, it produces only that by which the distinction of persons, otherwise scarcely intelligible, is interpreted.

For there is complete truth in the great rule that, in incorporeal things, distinctions are produced by differences, not by places. Nor can it be said that something came to God so that he might become Father. He never began to be Father, because the production of the Son is indeed substantial in him, whereas the predication of Father is relative.

If we recall all that was said earlier about God, let us think in this way: God the Son proceeded from God the Father, and the Holy Spirit from both. Since these are incorporeal, they are not separated by places. Since, however, the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and God has no differences by which he differs from God, none of them differs from any other. Where differences are absent, plurality is absent; where plurality is absent, unity is present. Nothing could be begotten from God except God; and, among things that can be counted, the repetition of units does not in every respect produce plurality. Thus the unity of the three has been suitably established. [Col. 1254D]

## CHAPTER VI. How Unity and Trinity Are in God

Since no relation can refer to itself—for that is a predication according to itself which lacks relation—there has been a numerical plurality of the Trinity in that which is predication of relation, while unity has been preserved in that which is indifference of substance, of operation, or altogether of the predication that is said according to itself. Thus substance contains unity, while relation multiplies the Trinity. Therefore the things that belong to relation are brought forward singly and separately. The Father is not the same as the Son, nor are both together the same as the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1255A]

Yet the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the same God; the same just, the same good, the same great, and the same in everything that can be predicated according to itself.

It must be understood, however, that relative predication is not always such that it is always predicated toward what is different. Every equal is equal to an equal; every similar is similar to a similar; and whatever is identical is identical to what is identical. The relation of the Father to the Son, and of both to the Holy Spirit, is of this kind: it is the relation of what is identical to what is identical. [Col. 1256A]

If this cannot be found in all other things, the reason is the kindred otherness that belongs to perishable things. We, however, must not be led astray by imagination, but must be raised up by simple understanding; and as each thing can be understood, so must we approach it intellectually.

Enough, then, has been said concerning the question proposed. Now the subtlety of the question awaits the standard of your judgment: whether it has been traversed correctly or not is established by the authority of your pronouncement. If, with divine grace assisting, we have furnished suitable supports of argument to a position already firmly established by the foundations of faith, the joy of the completed work will return to the place from which its result came. But if human ability has been unable to rise beyond itself, our prayers will make up whatever weakness has taken away.

[Col. 1255]

# GILBERT OF PORRETA’S COMMENTARY ON THE BOOK ON THE TRINITY

[Col. 1255B] Of all the principles that provide support for apprehending things, some are common to many genera, while others are proper to certain ones. Common principles include the following: whatever is present in something must necessarily be distinct from that in which it is present. This is true in every kind of thing.

The statement that a species is never predicated of its genus belongs to the genus of definitions, not of divisions. For just as, in a definitional demonstration, the species is explained through the genus, so in a divisional demonstration the genus is explained through the species.

Whoever has carefully investigated things rather than merely looking at them in passing is not ignorant of this commonality or propriety of principles. Such a person first fixes them in the mind, marks them with the mind’s acuity, grasps them by judgment, and entrusts them to memory for preservation. Then, lest anyone should think that they had either perished altogether through forgetfulness or languished in silence, he often expounded them: sometimes playfully, for the sake of practice, in the various constructions of sophists on the stage; sometimes while engaged with his associates in the serious tasks of philosophy.

For example, in the sphere of civil matters, the orator Tullius spoke more seriously in the cases for Sextus Roscius and for Marcus Marcellus. Likewise Quintilian, Seneca, and Menander were sophists and constructors of oratory: the first in legal cases, the second in declamations, and the third in fictional comedies. In these matters, however, they spoke from the principles of rhetoric about arguments concerning what could happen, and testified that they had kept those principles before their minds and held them not with a superficial disposition, but with a certain difficult and active habit of knowledge. [Col. 1255C]

Similarly, others in their own disciplines taught that they firmly understood and attentively considered either the theorems of measurements or the axioms of weights, or principles bearing other names—principles common to many things or proper to certain genera—whether they were seriously philosophizing or exercising themselves among sophists through invented likenesses.

In this way it came about that they neither used proper principles beyond the limits of their genera, nor narrowed common principles belonging to many things to some particular ones; and thus, in each discipline, they found the boundaries and functions proper to it.

Whoever is wholly ignorant of this difference among principles, or neglects to attend to it, often entrusts a matter to chance beyond the proper function of the discipline. Consequently, lacking an end to his task, he wavers uncertainly in amazement at some contradiction into which, unknowingly, he has fallen—which is dangerous. Or, presuming with a kind of security—in fact secure in his presumption—he asserts a false judgment, which is harmful. And, pouring forth every kind of utterance, with immoderate gestures and facial expressions, he shouts among a crowd of ignorant people, not without provoking the detestation of those who think otherwise. This is utterly shameless.

Such were the Arians, the Sabellians, and many others, who transferred the proper principles of natural things into theological matters and tore apart principles common to both. [Col. 1255D]

[Col. 1256B]

It is a proper principle of natural things that, just as the properties of things numerically distinct are distinct, so also their subsistences are numerically distinct; and that one individual subsistence makes only one thing subsistent. Thus the properties of Plato and Cicero are distinct—not only their accidental properties, but also their substantial properties, by which they are, for example, different bodies or different human beings. Every individual property that makes Plato a body or a human being makes no other person a body or a human being.

For even if the propagation of generation gives the generated being a body from the singular corporeity of transfused blood by which the generator had been a body, there is nevertheless a separation through division. By this separation the generator becomes one body, possessing the subsistence of the body that remains after the blood has been divided off, while the generated being becomes another body, possessing the subsistence of that to which the nourishment of temporal additions is given through the divided blood.

Understanding these principles of natural things correctly, as it seems, Arius, Aëtius, Eunomius, and likewise Noetus, Sabellius, Praxeas, Hermogenes, Priscillian, and many others, failed to attend to the fact that these principles were proper to natural things. They therefore appropriated them in theology. [Col. 1256C]

Because there is only one essence of the one principle from which, through which, and in which all things exist—an essence called οὐσία (*ousia*) in Greek—they thought that, just as there is only one God, so there is only one God who is alone.

Arius calls this one God the Father. In the proper use of the principle he says, “The Father is the only God”; but by abusing the principle he also says, “The Father alone is God.” From this he infers that neither Christ nor the Holy Spirit is God in the truth of essence. He says that Christ is a creature and that the Holy Spirit is a creature of a creature.

Following him, Aëtius, and Eunomius, the disciple of Aëtius, asserted that the Son was unlike the Father in every respect, and that the Holy Spirit was unlike the Son in every respect.

Noetus, his disciple Sabellius, Praxeas, Hermogenes, and Priscillian, employing a fanciful principle removed from its proper genus, likewise asserted that the one whom Arius believed to be the only God was alone God. They differed from Arius in this: they thought that this one alone was Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. They thereby opposed the principle that admits no exception in any genus of things—namely, that the distinct proper properties of distinct persons cannot belong to one person.

Many things that are different from one another in every respect and belong properly to different genera can, however, belong to one thing. Thus length and knowledge, which differ from one another in their whole genus and belong by their properties to different genera—for length belongs only to a body, while knowledge belongs only to a spirit—can belong together to one human being, who is simultaneously body and spirit. [Col. 1257A]

But the distinct proper properties of distinct persons cannot belong to one person. For although one thing may be constituted from parts belonging to different genera and from different properties, it is not thereby constituted from different persons as an integral whole. Every person is rightly understood as one in himself.

All these people, therefore, while correctly affirming the singularity of divinity, reasoned according to the principle of natural things. They held not only that there is one God alone, but also that God is only one.

Others, correctly understanding that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are numerically distinct persons through distinct properties, and that not only the Father is God but also the Son is God and the Holy Spirit is God, were nevertheless deceived by the principle proper to natural things according to which, just as the properties of numerically distinct things are distinct, so their subsistences are also numerically distinct. They therefore said that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not of the same essence, but of a similar essence.

Macedonius, correctly holding that the Father and Son are of one and the same substance or essence, and that both are one God, nevertheless said that the Holy Spirit is not God. But because the Holy Spirit is common to both, he supposed that the divinity of both is the Holy Spirit, and that the Holy Spirit has no substance. [Col. 1257B]

Others assert that God is so composed that they assign the one God’s diverse essences as though they were diverse parts: to one belongs what is the Father, to another what is the Son, and to another what is the Holy Spirit, while the same one and only God remains. Thus they assign omnipotence to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Holy Spirit.

They derive this also from a principle of natural things: that the diverse subsistences of one subsisting thing have diverse properties attached to them. Thus, in one human being, color belongs to corporeity, passion to sensibility, and discrimination to rationality.

Through such abuses of principles outside their proper genus, the people whom we have mentioned as examples, together with many others, were driven into various doctrines—that is, opinions of falsehood. Worse still, moved by presumption, they confidently spoke against the catholic faith concerning the number of persons and their simple and singular essence, and declared their errors to be the truth. [Col. 1257C]

Others, without in any way departing from the catholic faith, rightly believed both in the number of persons and in the singularity of the essence. Yet they were astonished that false conclusions could be drawn from true antecedent principles, and humbly asked how, while the foregoing principles of truth remained intact, there could be distinct persons of one simple and singular essence, and one singular and simple essence of distinct persons.

Boethius wished to destroy the detestable errors of the former and to assist the weakness of the humble. He therefore wrote to Symmachus and certain other wise men about the number of the three persons and their simple and singular essence, and about the three persons, numerically distinct, of one essence. He demonstrates both points by arguments, but by arguments drawn from different kinds of disciplines.

First he demonstrates the singularity and simplicity of the essence by theological principles; then he demonstrates the numerical diversity of the persons by natural principles. From this it can rightly be understood that the heretics mentioned above were deceived because they transferred the proper principles of natural things into theology. [Col. 1257D]

### “Investigated” (*Investigatam*)

He begins with a prologue in which he promises that, although the subject about which he is going to speak is obscure and entangled in many matters exceedingly difficult to understand, he will nevertheless not speak in wholly explicit terms. This is customary among orators when the kind of case is obscure. Indeed, he conceals the dignity of the subject from the unworthy, does not unfold it in a complete verbal exposition, and, if the speech of the speaker reveals anything to the understanding of the hearer, immediately covers it over by introducing a new meaning.

He especially stimulates attention both by the greatness of the subject itself and by the brevity and obscurity of his words, as we have said. He wins goodwill both from the dignity of the subject and from his own person, when he says without arrogance that he has written what he has long considered. He also wins goodwill from the persons to whom he writes: having rejected everyone else, he says that he most eagerly offers the work of his study to their authority and wishes to receive their judgment. [Col. 1258A]

Beginning, therefore, with praise of his own undertaking, he says: “Investigated,” and so forth.

Here it should be noted that a question consists of an affirmation and its contradictory negation. Not every contradiction, however, is a question. When one side of a contradiction appears true and the other has no arguments whatever for truth—for example, “Every human being is corporeal” and “Not every human being is corporeal”; likewise, “No human being is a stone” and “Some human being is a stone”—or when neither side can possess arguments for truth or falsity, as in “The stars are even” and “The stars are not even,” then the contradiction is not a question.

But when both sides appear to have arguments for truth, there is a question. This can occur in three ways: through the sophistical multiplicity of univocal and equivocal terms, modes, parts, times, and relations; through the quality of expression; or through the kind of principles from which speech is composed. [Col. 1258B]

The six kinds of sophistical multiplicity are known to many through the art and practice of sophists. The quality of expression is considered either in the sequence of things and words or in their tropes. If one of these occurs in the affirmation and the other in the negation, both may be true. Thus “The day is happy” is true through the trope of μετωνυμία (*metonymia*), that is, through transferring the name of what is made to what makes it. “The day is not happy” is likewise true if one denies the natural correspondence of such things.
