Again, both sides may be similarly true through different principles belonging to different genera. Thus, as we said above, “No species is predicated of its genus” is true in the genus of definitions, while “Every species is predicated of its genus” is true in the genus of divisions. [Col. 1258C]

Through the hidden multiplicity of these areas, whether the arguments are derived by art or arise by chance, a question is brought into ambiguity. It is therefore dissolved only by dividing the matters belonging to those areas.

When both sides of a contradiction appear to have arguments for truth, one must investigate with the greatest care which universality of these areas contains the expressions in which the proposed multiplicity consists. Once this is known, one can recognize what must be brought out through division, by what division it must be brought out, and how it must be adapted to the parts of the question.

This applies to the question concerning the singularity and simplicity of the essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and concerning their numerical diversity according to their different properties—a question whose two sides appear to have arguments for truth. It should not be doubtful that Boethius investigated this question, since he says, “Investigated.” Nor did he do so without diligent effort, since he says, “For a very long time.” He could not have quickly passed through so many areas of multiplicity without weighing whether the difficulty lay in signification, mode, or something else that had produced the question.

In other cases, a definite property of the thing or a definite position of a word arouses understanding. Thus, when one says “a white human being,” since it is certain that whiteness is proper to corporeity, one may think that the expression has been made according to some part of the human body. Or, when one says “a dog is sentient,” since it is certain to which species the word refers, whatever quality is signified by the word, the hearer knows that the statement concerns only something that has one of those kinds of sentience.

But when the principles of different genera are diverse and hidden, the investigation can require a longer labor. They are so hidden that their genera are always, and often the principles themselves together with their genera, completely left unspoken.

That is what occurs in this question. It is not entangled in signification, modes, parts, times, relations, or, finally, qualities of expression, but in diverse principles belonging to diverse genera. Silence had concealed these principles in both parts of the question so completely that, because of this concealment, Boethius rightly says that he investigated the question for a very long time. [Col. 1259A]

### “Having formed it by principles” (*Eam ergo formatam rationibus*, etc.)

A question is unformed while the multiplicity, still remaining in an unknown area, is undigested and covers over the form of truth, so that it is not known which side of the contradiction it belongs to. But when the question is brought out from the universality of the area that has been explained, and through division its signification and mode are brought forth, then the form of truth is brought to light. The division displays these and the other matters, and they are adapted to the parts of the question so that the question may be fully understood.

Yet the adaptation of the parts of the division to the parts of the question also contributes to its form, because it is confirmed by arguments. It is fitting that just as a question is brought into doubt by arguments, so it should also be made certain by arguments.

I therefore took care to offer and communicate this question to you—not as though I had discovered through investigation everything belonging to its solution, but only insofar as divine light deigned to illuminate the spark of our mind; that is, insofar as divine grace judged that my natural ability was worthy of being illumined by its radiance. I offer this question, I say, formed by principles in the manner described and committed to writing—that is, written down—for you to receive and share with me.

He then explains how and why it should be shared: “as desirous of your judgment,” that is, of your careful examination, “as devoted to our discovery.” For with as much zeal as I applied myself to finding the means by which I might solve this question, so eagerly did I wish to possess the judgment of your authority concerning it.

### “In this matter” (*Qua in re*, etc.)

By saying “investigated,” “for a very long time,” and “formed by principles,” he arouses attention through the greatness of the subject. Here he wins goodwill from his own person by speaking without arrogance about his deeds and undertakings, saying, as it were, “I offer it to be shared with you.”

What state of mind I have in this matter—that is, whose favor I seek—can be understood whenever I commend something to my writing, that is, whenever I write something that I have long considered. This can be understood both from the material itself, namely, from the difficulty of the subjects about which I continually write, and from the fact that I converse with only a few: with you alone, Symmachus, to whom I generally offer almost all my writings for examination, and with a few other prudent men.

We are not roused to do anything excellently by the throwing about of our reputation or by the empty shouts of the crowd—namely, so that our fame may pass to outsiders and, among our own people, theatrical and stage applause may exalt us, as it usually exalts comic poets and others who wish to entertain. The meaning is: I take pleasure not in external approval, but in the secrecy of conscience.

If we do gain any external benefit from the judgment of others, we cannot expect this to yield any judgment except one like the subject itself. That is, we cannot expect a judgment from anyone except from people of a kind appropriate to the material with which we are dealing—people whose authority is known to possess a certain dignity through excellence and singularity of virtue, just as the material itself possesses a certain dignity through its greatness and incomparable distinctiveness.

[Col. 1260A] Here he seeks the goodwill of those to whom he writes. Wishing their authority to be understood as singularly excellent, he says: [Col. 1259D]

### “Therefore, wherever” (*Quocunque igitur*, etc.)

The meaning is: So that I may hope for a judgment like the material itself, I speak only with you; therefore no similar judgment can be hoped for from others.

For wherever—that is, to whatever others—I might appoint as judges of my treatises, I did not say that I turned away from you, but that I cast my eyes down from you; there I encounter partly sluggish indolence—that is, people rendered sluggish by indolence and indolent through sluggishness—and partly cunning envy—that is, cunning and envious people.

Thus it seems that anyone who offers these writings not to be recognized, that is, examined, by such men, but to be trampled underfoot and cast aside like something for pigs, inflicts an insult on divine treatises. Their outward bodily form shows that they are human beings, but by the inner vices mentioned above they are more like beasts.

Whoever, then, reveals the secrets of philosophy to such people prostitutes philosophy, so to speak, and, insofar as he can, makes its dignity less worthy of admiration.

Because this usually happens through excessive talk and commonplace speech, I therefore contract my style through brevity. That is, I do not explain fully what I think about this question, but signify it through abbreviated marks of writing. I veil it with new meanings of new words drawn from the disciplines of philosophy—not from the external matters of physics, nor from the interior matters of mathematics, but from the innermost matters of theology.

Examples are: “A human being is not what he is”; and “A great human being is not the human being itself, nor is he greatness itself.”

Here he arouses attention: through brevity I contract, and through novelty I veil, so that these writings of brevity and novelty may speak by a mere sign to me and to you, if you turn your eyes to them from your other studies, rather than converse with us as familiar things.

We remove others from these writings so thoroughly that anyone who, stirred by their half-complete and unfamiliar signification, cannot grasp them intellectually appears unworthy not only of judging them, but even of reading them—not because of what the writings produce, but rather because of the source from which they were produced. [Col. 1260B]

There are three things: the thing, the understanding, and speech. The thing is conceived by the understanding and signified by speech. But neither the mark of speech can show everything that the thing is, nor can the act of understanding encounter everything that belongs to the thing. Therefore the concept does not retain everything.

Speech also remains around the concept. A word does not reveal as much through the signification of the thing as the understanding conceives. Similarly, the signification of writing is related to the conception of its author.

It is therefore clear that one who hears or reads weighs the conception of the orator or writer from what the signification reveals, but can rightly judge the thing only from the sense of that same orator or writer.

For this reason he rightly bars from reading this treatise those who despise the writer’s understanding, from which speech or writing is produced, and who think that signification is sufficient for judging the thing. [Col. 1260C] Or, if they attend to something toward which a determinate signification does not direct them, they strive not so much to refer to what accords with truth as to bring forward what accords with signification.

But since understanding cannot reach all the way to the fullness of the thing, he also warns those who judge words or writings from the author’s understanding not to suppose that the author has written perfectly about the thing or divided into words everything that it is. Rather, they should measure the perfection of the writings or statements by what can be conceived.

He therefore says:

### “But also only so much,” or “certainly only so much,” or “but lest only so much,” etc.

The meaning is: We remove from these writings those who cannot grasp them intellectually. But to those who can grasp them intellectually we also say: “Do not seek only so much,” or “Certainly seek only so much,” or “But lest you seek only so much”—that is, only so much.

For in this passage *ne* is a confirmative conjunction. Virgil likewise uses it when he says:

> Did such a love of life, my son, hold me,

> that I should endure defeat by an enemy’s hand in your place?

Here, they say, *ne* means “even.” [Col. 1260D] It is also found as a confirmative conjunction in many other passages.

Thus in this passage too it is used confirmatively, so that the meaning is: “But indeed only so much”; that is, “but we ought also to seek only so much of ourselves.” It is fitting for us to require of those who can grasp our writings intellectually, from the understanding out of which they were written, only as much as the gaze of human reason is able to ascend toward the heights of divinity—heights toward which it does not altogether aspire, even though it sees something of divinity as through a mirror.

To commend this in writing is to complete the task of writing with its proper end. This can be understood from the other arts. For the other arts too have a certain end established for them: namely, to pursue their activity as far as the path of reason is able to approach. Even if the result for the sake of which the activity is undertaken does not occur, the art nevertheless has not failed to attain the end of its function.

For, as the rhetor Marcomannus supposes, the end of every art should not be considered to be the occurrence of the result for whose sake it is performed.

[Col. 1261A] “For medicine does not always bring health to the sick, for the sake of which it is practiced. Yet there will be no fault on the physician’s part.” That is, an art has fulfilled its proper end if it has omitted none of the things that ought to be done—that is, which the art teaches ought to be done. The same applies to the other arts. For just as the duty of medicine is to apply a remedy toward health, so the end of its duty is not simply to heal, but to heal by applying a remedy. Similarly here, the author’s duty is to divide the multiplicity in which the intellect sees the question entangled, in order to disentangle it. The end is not, I say, simply to disentangle it, but to disentangle it by division. And in the other arts also, if what Marcomannus considers their end does not occur, the author earns pardon by doing what is appropriate. But the more difficult this question is—because it is entangled by the diversity of hidden reasons—the readier pardon ought to be. “For you”: as if he were saying, “If, in a matter so difficult, the art fails to achieve its result, I deserve easy pardon.” Yet not everything introduced for solving this question comes from me. You must also examine, and note with the greatest attention, whether the seeds—that is, the principles of reasoning—coming to us from the writings of blessed Augustine have brought forth any fruits: as if to say, “I have written with Augustine as my author.” For whatever I have said about this question, although it differs from his words in manner of expression, agrees with them in meaning and has been derived from the understanding by which he indicates that he wrote. Let us therefore take our starting point here concerning the proposed question.

“Of the Christian religion, etc.” Religion is placed by many as the first species of natural right. According to it, in human duties the virtue of justice gives to God what belongs to his singular dignity; while, according to the other species of the same genus—piety, gratitude, vengeance, observance, and truth—it gives human beings what belongs to their exceedingly well-ordered distinction under him. In all these, however, justice itself, according to the law of religion, refers the cause back to God; and this one end of all duties makes every part of the law a virtue.

In religion, faith comes first. Generally speaking, faith is the apprehension of the truth of any matter with assent; but usage has restricted this name, by excellence, to the apprehension especially of invisible things, so that faith is said to be that by which the rational mind truly and with assent apprehends what is the being of all things, and the worship by which he is to be honored by all, together with what rewards of his worshipers it hopes for in Greek. Religion also contains divine fear and divine love, and other such things, in which the Christian religion itself is greatly to be revered.

Yet many usurp its reverence, saying that they possess the Christian religion, while they not only do not fear the divine power over them or love the divine goodness toward them, but also do not rightly believe the things that belong to faith. But, to say nothing of the rest, that faith is especially and uniquely powerful, and is to be revered with singular and supreme dignity, which is called in Greek καθολική (*katholikē*), or in Latin *universalis*, “universal.” This is so for two reasons.

First, because of the precepts of universal rules—that is, because of the universal rules of the commandments. They are called universal here because they are imposed not upon one people, as the law was upon the children of Israel; nor upon one sex, as circumcision was upon males; but upon every people, every sex, every age, and every condition. One faith, one baptism, one rite of sacrifice, one love, and one hope are proclaimed to all. By these rules of the commandments, the authority—that is, the primacy—of the same Christian religion is to be understood, or may be understood.

Second, because the worship of that faith—that is, the worship by which faith venerates that which is the source of whatever exists—has spread through almost all the regions of the world, that is, has reached to the ends of the earth.

“Whose [faith] this is, etc.” Having commended the faith of Christians, he states what they themselves think concerning the essence and properties of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit of them both. First, he says that they think the essence of the three is singular and simple, and he proves by theological arguments that they think rightly.

As if to say: Universal faith is especially powerful. The judgment of this faith concerning the unity of the Trinity—that is, of three persons distinct in number—according to unity, or singularity, of essence, is as follows. For the faithful say: “The Father is God; the Son is God; the Holy Spirit is God”; and they infer: “Therefore the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God in the singularity of essence, not three Gods”—that is, they are one being of all, not three.

Observe that they draw this inference not according to the proper reasoning of natural things, but according to that of theological things. According to the reasoning of natural things, namely, that different things in number have different natures in number, the result is otherwise: “Plato is a human being; Cicero is a human being; Aristotle is a human being. Therefore Plato, Cicero, and Aristotle are three human beings, not one human being in the singularity of subsistence.”

For when it is said, “Plato is a human being; Cicero is a human being; Aristotle is a human being,” the second affirmation is stated not only of another individual, but also with the singularity of its own subject, differently from the first; and the third differently from both the first and the second. Although the second and third repeat the predicate name of the first, they do not repeat the thing predicated. Rather, although the things are alike, they are nevertheless different; indeed, because they are alike, they affirm of things different in number from one another natures that are different in number. This necessary difference among the three predicates concerning the three subjects does not permit them to be joined together so that one could say: “Plato, Cicero, and Aristotle are one human being in the singular.”

But when it is said, “The Father is God; the Son is God; the Spirit of them both is God,” although these statements concern things different in number, they do not state different things. Just as the name is repeated, so too the thing predicated is repeated. This necessary absence of difference in the one predicate concerning the three allows—indeed requires—the same three to be joined to the singularity of the essence predicated three times, as follows: “The Father, the Son, and the Spirit of them both are one God in the singular.”

Rightly, therefore, commending this inference of the faithful according to the proper reasoning of theological indifference, he says:

“Whose, etc.” As if to say: The faithful say separately: “The Father is God”; likewise, “The Son is God”; likewise, “The Holy Spirit is God.” From this they infer jointly: “Therefore the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God.” Certainly they do not do so without reason, since the reason for this conjunction is [editorial supplement: *sit*, “is”] the indifference of the one essence which they affirm separately of distinct things.

There are, however, some who think that, just as those distinct statements concern distinct things, so also they say distinct things—namely, those who suppose that the Son or the Holy Spirit is either other than the Father or is called God in a different manner from the Father. Difference undoubtedly accompanies those who, when they compare one with another, either increase one by calling the other greater, or diminish one by calling the other lesser.

For example, the Arians divide the Trinity—that is, these three, one of whom is called the Father, another the Son, and another the Holy Spirit—by varying them according to certain degrees of merit and saying that the Father is greater than the Son, and the Son greater than the Holy Spirit. They thus draw them apart, distinguishing them not only by the number of their personal properties but also by the number of their natures. They say that the Father alone is God in the truth of essence, but that the Son is a creature and the Holy Spirit a creature of a creature.

This difference is plainly understood from the degrees of merit, which cannot exist in things that are not different—even if they belong to the same genus—in nature. For one human being would not be greater or more worthy than another human being unless, through a difference of nature, one were something other than the other.

Therefore, when the Arians vary the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit according to degrees of merit, they necessarily separate them by a difference of nature and lead them into that plurality which is according to the form of a genus. In their view, then, when the Father is called God, the Son is called God, and the Holy Spirit is called God, the Son must be understood as another God than the Father, and the Holy Spirit as another God than the Son or the Father. Nor can there be the conjunction by which one says, “The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God”; rather, it must be understood that they are several gods, since the Son is another God than the Father, and the Holy Spirit another God than the Son or the Father.

For every plurality that is called by its true name has alterity—otherness—as its principle, and alterity is the principle of duality. Apart from this otherness of duality, plurality cannot even be understood, since every plurality is either wholly duality or is constituted from duality. The binary consists only of one and another; the ternary of a binary and one; the quaternary of two binaries; and thereafter every number contains a binary as one of its parts.

“Of three, therefore, etc.” He has said that plurality arises from otherness. Now he demonstrates, by division, according to what kind of otherness—or plurality—there is in natural things, in accordance with whose reasoning the Arians separate the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit according to the number of their natures.

As if to say: Plurality arises from otherness—truly so—for it arises either from otherness of genus, of species, or of number. The diversity of three, four, five, or however many subsistent things consists in genus, species, or number.

He proves this by comparison with the opposite as follows: Whenever “the same” is predicated, “different” is also predicated. “The same” is said in the three ways mentioned: either in genus, species, or number.

In genus, as when human being and horse are said to be the same, because the genus of human being and horse is the same—for example, animal. For the diverse subsistences from which human beings on the one hand and horses on the other are animals make those who subsist according to them conformable, not by imitation or imagination, but by substantial similarity.

Likewise, “the same” is said in species, as when Cato and Cicero are said to be the same, because the species of Cato and Cicero is the same—for example, human being. For the diverse subsistences that belong to one species, one of which is Cato and the other Cicero, make them substantially alike.

In number, “the same” is said of what, although it is called by many names, is nevertheless one according to the same singular quality—for example, Tullius and Cicero. For, from the one singular quality from which these names were given to one individual, I do not say that they are, but that he is numerically one—the person to whom they were given.

“Therefore, etc.” As if to say: As often as “the same” is said, “different” is also said. But “the same” is said in three ways. Therefore “different” is also said in those same three ways, either in genus, species, or number. Hence it is clear that “the same” and “one,” and likewise “different” and “another,” are said in natural things in many ways.

For one or the same subsistent is sometimes said according to the singularity of one nature alone: for example, Cicero is one human being and the same as Tullius, indeed the same person who is Tullius; and Plato is one rational being and the same as his own [spirit], indeed the same [being] as his own spirit. For Plato and his own spirit, from which Plato himself consists, are one rational being—not rationalities that are different, one of which is imagined to be Plato’s and the other a species of him by conformity, but one and the same singularity.

This unity does not admit number at all, either through a collection of units or through the proportion of bodily things. For Tullius and Cicero are neither two nor different. Plato and his spirit, however, are indeed different, but they are not two. They are different because Plato is whatever his spirit is naturally, whereas his spirit is not whatever Plato himself is; and they are altogether different in reason, because Plato consists of his spirit, while his own spirit constitutes Plato.

Yet they are certainly not two, because no account by which one could specify what the two are can be assigned through the similarity of certain features, one of which is said of Plato and the other of his spirit. This unity is not called union.

If, then, someone conceives in natural things something different from this one, it is appropriate, according to the proportion of reason, that he oppose to it another one in the singularity of nature, setting aside every consideration of similarity and dissimilarity—for example, this other human being to this human being, or this stone.

Many subsistents are also called one and the same, not through the singularity of one nature, but through a union of many natures produced by their similarity. Through this union, many human beings are called one or the same human being, and many animals one or the same animal.

Therefore, when someone conceives something different from this one, he must compare and oppose to it something contrary not only in essence but also in dissimilarity—for example, a horse to a human being, and a stone to an animal. These are called different and other in genus or species, just as those whose diverse natures are united by conformity are called one in genus or species.

In this unity produced by union, there is always number—not only of the subsistents but also of the subsistences. For just as things can be conformable only if they are different in number, so they can be different only according to numbers. Cato would not be human in the same way as Cicero unless the subsistences by which each is something were also different in number; and their numerical difference makes them different in number.

In natural things, the dissimilarity of the accidents present in those subsistences and in the same subsistents does not create this numerical difference—not only of subsistents but also of subsistences—but proves it. Nevertheless, because the dissimilarity of certain accidents is always the companion of numerical difference, he adds “proves” and “makes,” following the close association of these properties, in place of what he ought to have said.

But the variety of dissimilar accidents makes the difference that exists in number—truly so. For the dissimilarity of genera or species does not divide things united in this way into different things. For example, three human beings differ not in subsistences of one genus or of one species, but neither in genus nor in species—that is, they differ without any dissimilarity among their subsistences, and are distinguished by the dissimilarity of their accidents.

As has already been said, for some subsistents to be called different in genus or species, their subsistences must also be different through dissimilarity. When their diversity is without dissimilarity, the number of subsistents follows the number of those subsistences, indeed arises from their number.

Since subsistences are always accompanied by accidents that are diverse in some dissimilarity, the variety of the accidents is rightly said to produce, by reason of this association, the numerical difference of the subsistents—without those accidents, subsistences cannot exist at all in subsistents.

To make this clearer and more plausible by applying the example already introduced in the other cases: even if we separate from these three human beings all their accidents—not in reality, but at least in thought—imagining that they possess absolutely no other accidents, nevertheless the place, not the quantity by which something is said to be local in itself, but the relation of local things by which each of the things related locally is rightly called located, is different for all of them, even if not in genus, at least in species. We cannot possibly imagine this place as one either by singular unity or by the most specific union of similarity.

For two bodies will not possess one place by singularity or species when they are related to one another. Therefore the three human beings whom we introduced as an example are more numerous than the subsistences conforming them, because they become more numerous through accidents that are also diverse by some dissimilarity. That is, through this particular diversity of accidents, they are proved to be more numerous by the similarity of the subsistences united in them.

“Come, then, etc.” Above, after saying, “The Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God,” he added: “Therefore the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God.” He showed that he did this according to theological reasoning when he added: “The reason for this conjunction is indifference.”

He said that the Arians draw the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit into that plurality which is in the form of a genus—or rather, which is in the genus of form. He made clear that they did this according to the reasoning of natural things when he said: “The principle of plurality is otherness.” He then taught that this otherness of subsistents arises from the diversity of dissimilar or similar subsistences, when he added that it consists in genus, species, or number.

From these points it is clear that some of the principles of theology and physics are different. Therefore, since he is going to demonstrate by theological reasoning that the three mentioned above—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—have one singular and simple essence by which each of them is what he is, he shows that theological reasoning differs from the reasoning of natural things in this respect: he subjects natural things to one kind of speculation and theological things to another.

Since this can be better understood after the parts of speculation have been set forth, he enumerates how many of them there are, according to the properties of the things subjected to them, and shows to which of them the proper reasoning of theological things belongs.

As if to say: The judgment of the Catholic faith, according to the proper reasoning of theology, is this: it is truly said separately, “The Father is God; the Son is God; the Holy Spirit is God,” and jointly, “The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God.”

The judgment of the Arians, according to the reasoning of natural things, is that the Father alone is called God in the truth of substance, while neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit is called God in the truth of substance, either separately or jointly as one God with the Father.

“Come, then, let us enter and examine”—that is, let us begin and look at each thing according to different modes of speculation: natural things and theological things, insofar as they can be understood and apprehended—that is, natural things in their own way and theological things in theirs—and whatever else the division of speculations may contain for the completion of itself.

We ought certainly to do this. For, as Cicero seems to have said most excellently, it is characteristic of an educated person to attempt to arrive at belief concerning each thing as it itself is—that is, in the manner required by the property of the thing—by considering it according to that speculation to which the thing proposed for consideration is assigned by a definite distinction of reasoning. For not every matter belongs indiscriminately to every kind of speculation.

“For since there are three speculative parts, etc.” Knowledge has many kinds. Some kinds are theoretical, that is, speculative—those by which we contemplate whether created things exist, what they are, what qualities they have, and why each exists. Others are practical, that is, active—those by which we know how to carry out an activity rather than merely inspect it, as physicians, magicians, and others of this kind do.

But, to say nothing of practical disciplines, speculative disciplines derive their names from the things that we contemplate through them. Some are called physical, that is, natural; others ethical, that is, moral; and others logical, that is, rational.

And, again, leaving aside the moral and rational disciplines, the disciplines that are called natural by one name, and which are also more commonly called speculative, have three parts: one that is specifically called natural by the universal name of all; another, mathematics; and a third, theology.

He describes these by motion and separation, and by their opposites, placing two distinctions in the definition of each. Thus he says: That is called natural which is in motion and non-abstracted—in Greek ἀχώριστος (*achōristos*), that is, inseparable.

He explains why he says “non-abstracted,” or “inseparable”: it considers the forms of bodies together with matter. These forms cannot be separated from bodies, not, I say, in reason, but in actuality.

Here it should be said that “matter” is a name with many meanings, and “form” likewise. The origin or beginning of things, which Plato calls necessity, fraud, receptacle, womb, lap, mother, bosom, and place of all generation—while his students call it ὕλη (*hylē*), that is, “wood” or “forest”—Plato himself calls first matter, because whatever is received by it is formed in it, although it itself acquires no form from them.

The four elements also, which have mutual concretion in it, are known by the name “matter,” taken from the greater thing that contains all things. And thereafter the other kinds of matter in the genus of bodies are distinguished according to their species, such as bronze, wax, stone, and other things of this kind that are called matter.

The general and specific subsistences, too, which are said to be the being of the subsistents in which they exist, because they contribute to those subsistents’ being something, receive another designation from the same name, “matter.” For they too are called the subject matters of the things that are present to them and, in a certain way, follow them more closely, because everything whose being derives from something of this kind naturally receives something from it; and in this respect it is, by reason, the matter of what comes later.

For example, since corporeality—which is the being of the body in which it exists, and by which the body is something naturally—confers upon the body that it be something, such as a figure or other things of this kind, it is matter for the figures and other things attached to its power, since it contains them in itself; and it too is called their matter.

Hence a definitive demonstration of such a being first brings forward the primary element, and then adds what is adapted to its power. If one asks what a statue is, bronze, marble, or something of this kind is named first; then the things that accompany whichever of these is involved are enumerated according to what the property of the statue sought in comparison with something else requires.

“Form,” too, is said in many ways. The essence of God is called the first form: with God as maker, whatever is something exists; whatever has being has it from that essence, from which it is something; and everything that is present in a thing that is something is present to that which is its being.

The four pure substances—fire, air, water, and earth—are also called forms. These are not the things previously said to have mutual concretion in the forest or matter, but those that consist of the forest and an intelligible species, from which these perceptible matters—fiery, airy, watery, and earthy—were ultimately derived. They are exemplars of bodies, which the bosom of the nurse that contains all things receives; they are called in Greek εἴδεαι (*eideai*), and in Latin *formae*, “forms.”

The being of any subsistent, whatever it may be, from which each of them is something, and which, as has been said, is the matter of the things present to it, is also called the form of those subsistents—for example, corporeality, the form of all bodies.

The fourth genus of quality is also called form: namely, the figure of bodies and the other things that are present in subsistents in such a way that they follow the power of the subsistents from which they are something.

From these points it is clear that one kind of matter is formless and therefore simple, such as ὕλη (*hylē*); another is formed and therefore not simple, such as bodies. Their manifold being and the many things present in them by no means allow them to be simple. Both of these are called matter.

Those things that are the being of subsistents and are called both matter and form are nevertheless called so separately: they are matter in relation to the things present to them, and form in relation to the things that are something from them.

Likewise, one kind of form belongs to no matter and is therefore simple, such as the essence of the maker, by which he truly is. For it does not consist of many essences, nor are there present in the maker any things of which the maker—or its own essence—could in any respect be either the being or the matter.

Those pure substances that are the exemplars of bodies are also forms without matter and therefore simple. For they are not what they are said to be from a multiple essence, nor do they adhere to something in such a way that they themselves could be matter for the things in which they are present.

When they are said to be present in perceptible things, this does not mean that they are in them and adhere to them inseparably, as corporeality is in a body. Rather, although they are abstracted from perceptible things and in no way concretely joined to them, they are set before them, as it were, in opposition, so that perceptible things may be derived from them as images from exemplars by a maker. Through this shared process of derivation, not only are the forms said to be present in perceptible things, but perceptible things are also said to be present in the forms.

Those things that are the being of subsistents, as has already been said, are called not only forms but also matter. The figures of perceptible things, however, and the other things that follow their being in subsistents, are called forms only, not matter.

After making these distinctions, it must be added that primary matter, that is, ὕλη (*hylē*), and the primary forms—the οὐσία (*ousia*), or “essence,” of the maker, and the εἴδεαι (*eideai*) of perceptible things—because they are simple and abstracted, have no motion. For neither does the former owe what it is to forms, nor do the latter owe what they are to matters.

But things that are inseparable from one another and concrete—that is, perceptible things—are in motion. The forms of perceptible things, although inseparable and therefore possessing motion, are nevertheless said to be without motion when they are considered abstractly, in imitation of abstract things.

For things are often truly conceived not only as they are, but also otherwise than they are. For this reason the mind’s speculation itself is divided and receives its name either from the things it considers or from the manner of considering them.

When it considers natural things as they are—that is, concrete and inseparable—it is called reason, by the proper power through which the human mind has been enabled to reason about perceptible things with the preceding assistance of the senses and imagination. But, from the things it considers—natural things, namely, which are inseparable and in motion—it is called natural, in motion, and inseparable.

He clearly shows that this is the reason for the name when he says: “For it considers the forms of bodies”—that is, figures and other things of this kind—not only in the matter in which they exist, but together with the matter in which they are present. Hence it is called the concretion of all subsistents.

Creation makes something be present in a subsistent, so that that in which it is present is something from it. Concretion, however, adapts to the same subsistent the natures of a subsequent kind of being, so that that in which these things exist together with it is not simple.

Since these things cannot exist unless they are present in subsistents in such a way that they adhere to the subsistences of those subsistents, they are called inseparable. Hence he says: “The forms of a subsequent kind of being cannot be separated from bodies,” not by a disciplinary act of reason, but in actuality—that is, so that, once separated, they retain what they are when they are concrete.

The motion of bodies follows from the same concretion, since the change of things departing and succeeding alters what is concrete. For whatever is not simple through concretion—namely, bodies—is in motion. This is apparent, for example, in motion according to place: because of the property of their heaviness, earth is carried downward and fire upward, and thus they possess motion.

The motion in question is not that which is the being of subsistents, from which each of them is something—namely, first matter—but the motion of the form joined to that matter by concretion in the same subsistents.

Another kind of speculation considers the inseparable forms of natural things otherwise than they are—that is, abstractly—and, from the end for which it does this, is called in Greek μαθηματική (*mathēmatikē*), and in Latin *disciplinalis*, “disciplinary.”

This is entirely appropriate. Since these forms are inseparable—that is, since they do not exist except in concretion—it is nevertheless necessary to understand what they are there. For rational speculation does not perfectly grasp what it is to be something, while disciplinary speculation must firmly grasp what it is by which a thing is what it is.

For example, reason does not sufficiently determine what it is to be a body, to be colored, or to be broad unless discipline knows what corporeality, color, and breadth are. This cannot happen unless it separates and distinguishes these things, which are inseparable and concrete, both from the thing in which they exist and from one another.

Thus, because it separates inseparable things for the purpose of perceiving their nature and comprehending their properties, it is called mathematics, or discipline. It is nevertheless called inseparable because the things it perceives separately are inseparable.

This discipline contemplates the forms of bodies without matter. I do not mean that it contemplates their being without matter, but that it contemplates them without motion. If concretion confers motion upon things that are concrete, it is appropriate that separation remove motion from the things from which they derive their being.

This does not mean that movable things are without motion, any more than inseparable things can be separated. Rather, as has been said, mathematics contemplates them without matter and therefore without motion. For the actuality of a thing always contains its forms as inseparable.

Hence he adds that these forms, when they are in matter—that is, in bodies—cannot be separated from those bodies. Therefore, the designation “mathematical speculation” is derived from the fact that it considers what is inseparable from the actuality of the thing; the designation “without motion” is a metonymical name derived from the manner of speculation.

The third kind of speculation transcends all natural things and fixes its gaze upon the principle of each of them: either upon the maker, by whose authorship they exist; or upon the idea, from which they were derived as from an exemplar; or upon ὕλη (*hylē*), in which they are located. This kind is called, by excellence, intellectual.

What is simple, without motion, and always is, is apprehended more truly than perceptible things can be apprehended either by rational opinion—or rather, by an opinionative kind of reasoning—which do not always exist and are in motion, or than the inseparable forms of those same things, which are therefore in motion, can be considered separately and without motion.

From the nature of the thing itself that is apprehended, this speculation is called theological; and from its property it is called without motion, abstracted, and separable.

This is entirely appropriate. For God’s substance—that is, God or divinity—is without matter and without motion. Neither God nor his essence can be matter. For the essence by which he is, called in Greek οὐσία (*ousia*), cannot be non-simple, nor can anything else be present in that essence by which he is.

God would not be simple if either his essence consisted of many essences or forms were present in that same essence such that God himself truly was one of them, or such that his essence could in any respect be called their subject matter.

This, then, is the diversity of speculations arising from the diversity of the things that are apprehended. Although some principles are common to the things subjected to the various speculations, it is nevertheless necessary that most principles be proper to them.

Accordingly, in natural things—which must be apprehended as they are, namely, as concrete and inseparable—the philosopher ought to proceed rationally. Once the name has been posited by which both what a thing is and that by which it is are signified, he must carefully attend, by that power of mind through which concrete things ought to be considered, to what the concretion they share requires of the thing itself, whether of what it is or of that by which it is, and to what it shares with the other kinds of speculation.

In mathematics, however, where inseparable things are considered otherwise than they are—that is, abstractly—he ought to proceed disciplinarily. Since things that are nothing at all unless they are present in subsistents are taken separately from those subsistents, he must attend to what is proper to them for the production of discipline, without applying to them the principles they share with the other kinds of speculation.

In natural things, human being is said to be a species of a genus, that is, of animal or body. In mathematics, however, human being is said to be a species not of a genus but only of individuals. Therefore, by the property of natural concretion, a genus is said to be predicated of a species.

By the property of mathematical abstraction, however, not a genus but a genus of a genus is conceded to be truly and consequently predicated of that which is not a species of a genus but only of individuals.

In divine things, which are abstracted not only in discipline but also in reality itself, one ought to proceed intellectually: that is, one must conceive them from the proper principles of theological things and not judge them according to the properties of things naturally concrete or disciplinarily abstracted.

He makes clear that this is how he wants it understood when he adds: “Nor will it be appropriate to be drawn toward any created things, which are imaginations of things that truly exist, but rather to contemplate the singular and simple form itself from its own principles.”

What truly is, etc.] Thus far he has shown the parts of speculative knowledge and what is appropriate to contemplate in each. Now, employing theological speculation, he demonstrates that the Father, Son, and Spirit of them both have one singular and simple essence, by which alone each of them is what it is. [Col. 1268D] In this way Catholics, who say, “The Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God,” and consequently infer, “Therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, not three gods,” are understood to draw their conclusion correctly according to the proper account of the things about which they speak.

It is as though he said: In divine matters one must intellectually contemplate the form itself, which truly is form. Many things are called forms: the shapes of bodies, for example, and other features that arise in subsistent things through creation or concretion, by which what possesses them is demonstrated, in the orderly course of instruction, either to be something or to be something in a particular way. But all these have in themselves their own sources, from which they are derived in some respect or to which they refer. Therefore they are called forms by a borrowed designation rather than by the truth of the account.

Essence, however, which is the principle, precedes all created things, imparting to all of them that they may be said to exist, while receiving from nothing else the fact that it itself exists. [Col. 1269A] Therefore it is form in the true sense of the name, and not an image. When someone speaking of it says, “It is essence,” this ought to be understood as follows: Essence is that thing which is existence itself—that is, which does not borrow this designation from another—and from which existence comes, that is, which communicates the same to all other things by a certain extrinsic participation.

For “is” is not predicated of any arbitrary property of its essence, but the expression is transferred from that which properly exists by its own essence, not by another’s, to what, created by it, is something through form, and to the created form itself, and finally to everything that is truly predicated of them, since these exist from it as from a principle. Thus, through participation in the divine form, it is rightly said of each thing that it “is.” This is not altogether different from the account of natural things.

In natural things also, the existence of every subsistent thing comes from form: whenever “is” is predicated of a subsistent thing, it is predicated through participation in the form that it possesses. This may be understood from the following examples. A statue is said to be a statue not according to the bronze—for the bronze is its matter, and its existence as bronze comes from the form of bronze [Col. 1269B]—but according to the form by which the likeness of an animal has been impressed upon that bronze through human craftsmanship. This is done in order to designate and, through likeness, to demonstrate what a true animal is, whose image has been fashioned.

The bronze itself is called bronze not according to earth—for earth is its matter, and its existence as earth comes from the form of earth—but rather according to the figure of bronze, which is created in it when the stone is dissolved by heat. Earth itself is called earth not κατὰ τὴν ὕλην—that is, not “according to the matter,” literally, “according to the wood.” For κατὰ means “according to,” and ὕλη means “wood”; τὴν is the article. Or it is not ἀπὸ τῆς ὕλης, that is, “not from the wood.” For ἀπὸ is the preposition “from,” τῆς, as stated, is the article, and ὕλης means “wood.”

This is that first matter which Plato calls the receptacle. In it, as we mentioned above, whatever it receives is formed, although it itself acquires no form from those things and is altogether formless. Of this matter, then, he says that earth is not called earth according to it, but according to the forms that belong to earth—for example, according to its dryness and heaviness.

It is therefore clear that nothing is said to “be,” according to the matter underlying the form that is predicated, by the expression through which that form is explained. It is said to be only according to the form from which the proposed thing receives its name: the thing’s own proper form.

But the divine, etc.] He shows that what he had called the divine form the existence of all things is not foreign to natural things, whose existence altogether comes from form. He now returns to what he had begun to establish and demonstrates, by comparison with natural things—none of which is one through the simplicity of its nature—that the divine form is truly one.

It is as though he said: Whatever each subsistent thing is, it is so through its proper form, which is present in matter. But whatever each of those things, or any other things, is—not, I say, something according to natural or even mathematical speculation, but, as I say, something according to theological speculation—is simply from a form that is not in matter.

For the divine substance is [Col. 1269D] form without matter. The substance of the principle cannot have ὕλην, “matter,” as its principle and matter in which it must exist. Nor is it present in the principle—that is, in God—in such a way that it contains within itself natures of a later account, either composing it or being adjacent to it, from which it itself is constituted and through whose causality matter could belong to the power of a prior principle.

For the divine substance itself lacks both principle and composition. There is nothing by which it could be a principle—something from which, through which, and in which all things exist—except itself. It is therefore truly one, and so simple in itself and solitary, without those things that can be present, that what is said of the one may rightly be said of this one: “It is what it is,” which is said of the principle whose οὐσία it is.

Just as there is nothing by which God is except the simple and sole essence, that is, οὐσία, so there is nothing from which οὐσία itself is except that it is the simple and sole God. Hence it is also customary to say of God not only, “God is,” but also, “God is [Col. 1270A] essence itself.” This is entirely correct. If of someone who is not only wise but also colored, large, and many other such things, one says, on account of his abundance of wisdom above all else, “However great you are, you are wholly wisdom,” as though nothing else contributed to his being except wisdom alone, then God, to whom diverse things do not contribute in order that he may be, is much more properly called essence itself. He is likewise called by other names: God is his own divinity, his own wisdom, his own power, and so forth.

For the remaining things, etc.] It is as though he said: The divine substance is what it is. The remaining things—that is, whether things that subsist or things that are in them—are not what they are. In other words, that from which each of them is said to be something is not simple or solitary.

The entire substantial form of any subsistent thing is not simple. [Col. 1270B] The multitude of accidents that belong either to the whole of that form or to its individual parts is much greater; nevertheless, all these things are predicated of the subsistent thing. Thus, in the case of a human being, the entire substantial form by which he is a complete human being includes the whole genus and every difference from which that form is composed, such as corporeality, animation, and other things of this kind. It also includes everything that belongs either to the whole form—for example, risibility, which belongs to humanity—or to some of its parts, such as color, which belongs to corporeality, knowledge, which belongs to rationality, and innumerable things of this kind.

The things predicated of a subsistent thing are also multiple by nature according to their power of producing. The entire substantial form of a human being is rightly said to be something not only because, as a whole, it makes the thing in which it is a human being, but also because one part of it makes that same thing animated, another makes it sentient, and another rational. Likewise, each part of it, or any accident concreted with a part or with the whole, is said to be something by its productive power, either similarly or differently, both in common with many things and differently from many things.

[Col. 1270C] Thus rationality is called a quality in general and rationality in particular, because it makes its possessor qualified, as every quality makes the things in which it is present qualified; and it makes him rational, as every rationality makes those in whom it is present rational. The whiteness of something likewise makes it qualified, as all qualities do; colored, as all colors do; and white, as all other whitenesses do. Therefore it is called, generally, a quality among qualities, a color among colors alone, and, specifically, whiteness among whitenesses alone.

So many things are predicated of these that, often, through their productive power, a denominative transfer is made from co-accidents to the things in which they coexist: “The line is long,” “The whiteness is bright.”

Thus, what makes each of the things that are something is either not simple or not solitary. Each of them—that is, both subsistent things and subsistences, and the accidents belonging to them—has its existence from the things of which it is constituted. He seems to explain how this should be understood when he says, “that is, from its parts.”

The sense in which he says this must be carefully considered. Earlier, when speaking about the character of this work, he promised to contract his style through brevity and said that he was concealing the face of his meaning beneath the novelty of his words. He says, “The remaining things are not what they are,” and, as though he wished to uncover the meaning to some extent, adds: “For each thing has its existence from the things of which it is constituted.” Yet in the explanation that follows—an explanation through which he might have been expected to expound the matter completely, so that its dignity would not be exposed to the unworthy—he rather covers it over when he adds, “that is, from its parts.” [Col. 1270D]

The indefinite and ambiguous signification of the pronoun and the noun is also worth noting. With one he seems to point out what he wishes to be understood; with the other he refers back to it, saying, “from these” and “from which.” Although this does not fix the reader’s mind with a definite designation upon the property or genus of what “existence” is, it does not turn the reader away from it either. But the definite noun introduced in the supposed explanation—“that is, from its parts”—removes the matter altogether from what “existence” is.

For nothing is the existence of that of which it is a part. Existence and that which exists through it have no genus whatsoever in common. A part, however, and that of which it is a part are one, even individually, in many genera. [Col. 1271A] Indeed, the genus of every part of something that is constituted from that part must also be the genus of the whole. Likewise, whatever is the existence of something is either the whole substance of that whose existence it is said to be, or a part of that which is the whole substance.

The whole substance is the species predicated of the thing. Its part, however, is the genus or difference that constitutes the species itself. But no part of that of which it is a part can be its species, genus, or difference. Therefore no part is the existence of that of which it is a part.

When he says, then, “Each thing has its existence from the things of which it is constituted”—which can rightly be understood as meaning “from the species, which is the whole existence, and from the genus and difference,” for although these are not the whole existence, they are nevertheless something belonging to its existence—why does he add, as though explaining this, “that is, from its parts”?

But let us examine what follows. Perhaps through it the sense in which these words were spoken will become clearer. He continues:

And it is this and that.] [Col. 1271B] Someone interpreting this appropriately might say: “That is, it has its existence from these diverse things,” and might understand “these diverse things” as diverse genera, diverse differences, diverse species, genus and difference, or at least a numerical diversity within the very union that produces a genus or species.

But he again names these things, which are not existence, in his explanation, saying: “That is, its parts.” Whether these parts—as he seems to say—are the existence of that which is constituted from them, or something else, it is certain that the thing is not simple or solitary. Correctly understanding this, he adds, “joined together.” He explains what he means by this when he says: “But not this or that singly”—that is, no one thing alone makes something be what it is; rather, many things do so, each of which contributes to it.

He clarifies what these many things are by an example. At the same time, the sense in which, after saying “Each thing has its existence from the things of which it is constituted,” he added “that is, from its parts,” and likewise, after saying “It is this and that,” added “that is, its parts,” may be observed.

He says that when an earthly human being consists of [Col. 1271C] soul and body—that is, when a subsistent thing consists of subsistent things—the same human being is both body and soul. In other words, by the existence of the body, from which he is composed, he is also body; and by the existence of the soul, from which he is likewise composed, he is also soul.

This is evidently what he intended to be understood when he said, “Each thing is from its parts,” and “It is its parts.” This manner of speaking is common whenever rational speculation conceives natural things as they are, without abstraction.

Thus a certain second substance is said to be predicated of a species. The statement is not to be understood as predicating something of what the species is, but rather of the subsistent thing in which a specific subsistence exists. Nor is it to be understood as predicating of that thing what a second substance is—that is, something that subsists alone, which cannot possibly be predicated—but rather the subsistence that is in it.

In this way many things are said, so that although being and that which is are different, what is said, when the name of one is supplied, belongs not to it but to the other.

[Col. 1271D] It is from this association, then, that he said, “Each thing has its existence from its parts, and is its parts,” although he intends it to be understood not as the parts themselves, but as what belongs to those parts—namely, the subsistences that are the existence both of those parts and of the thing constituted from them.

Whatever is the existence of any part is also the existence of the thing constituted from that part, and it is truly predicated of that thing as it is predicated of the part. This is clearly shown by their proper properties.

Color, which belongs only to corporeality, is truly predicated both of a human being, who is constituted from body, and of the body itself, which constitutes him. Rationality, which follows the genus of spirits, and knowledge, which belongs only to rationality, are likewise truly predicated both of the human being, who is constituted from spirit, and of the spirit from which he is constituted.

Not only is the body from which a human being is constituted colored, but the human being himself, who is constituted from it, is colored. Although the human being and the body from which he is constituted are different—indeed, the body from which the human being is constituted is not a human being—they are not two bodies or two colored things. Rather, they are one body, not through the conformity of universals but through the singularity of subsistence, and one [Col. 1272A] colored thing through the singularity of the accident.

Similarly, not only is the spirit from which a human being is constituted rational or knowing, but the human being who is constituted from it is rational or knowing. Although the human being and the spirit from which he is constituted are different—indeed, the spirit from which the human being is constituted is not a human being—they are not different spirits, different rational beings, or different knowing beings. Rather, they are one spirit through the singularity of subsistence, one rational being through the singularity of one power, and one knowing being through the singularity of one accident.

The supreme dialectical proposition is self-evident: “Of whatever the proper attribute that belongs to one thing alone is predicated, that of which it is the proper attribute is also predicated of the same thing.”

[Col. 1272B] Since color belongs only to that from which whatever is truly said to be a body derives its status as body, color is predicated not only of that part of a human being which is body but also of the human being himself. It follows necessarily that the existence of body to which color alone belongs—that is, corporeality—is predicated not only of that part of the human being which is body but also of the human being himself.

Since rationality belongs only to that from which whatever is truly a spirit derives its status as spirit, and knowledge belongs only to that from which whatever is rightly called rational derives its status as rational, they are predicated not only of that part of the human being which is spirit but also of the human being himself. It follows necessarily that the subsistence of spirit to which rationality alone belongs—that is, what one might call spirituality—is rightly predicated not only of that part of the human being which is spirit but also of the human being himself.

A human being is therefore body, not because of the body from which he is constituted, but because of the existence of that body. The same human being is also spirit, not because of the spirit from which he is constituted, but because of the existence of that spirit.

Thus the existence of a human being is not simple or solitary. As has been said, he is body through the existence of his body, from which he is constituted, and soul through the existence of his soul, from which he is constituted—not body alone or soul alone.

[Col. 1272C] Some inexperienced people suppose from the statement “not either body or soul” that neither of these may be mentioned without the other; that is, they suppose that it is not a true statement to say “A human being is body” without adding “and soul,” or to say “A human being is soul” without adding “and body.”

They imagine that because diverse things are joined together to compose one thing, the existence of both becomes so confused through their union that, just as when white and black are mixed, what results is called neither white nor black but rather some other color produced by the mixture, so what is constituted from diverse things thereafter receives the name of neither, but is something resulting from the mixture.

According to this interpretation, “A human being is body and soul” would mean not that the human being is body or soul, but that he is something produced from the mixture resulting from the conjunction of body and soul. But the fact that conjunction does not always result in a confused mixture will be discussed sufficiently in the book he writes against this error of Eutyches. [Col. 1272D]

Here, however, where it is being shown that the source from which each thing is something is simple or not solitary, we say that just as both of the following are true—conjunctively, “A human being is colored and wise,” and disjunctively, “A human being is colored” and “A human being is wise”—so both conjunctively, “A human being is body and soul,” and disjunctively, “A human being is body” and “A human being is soul,” are true, according to the dialectical rule stated above: of whatever the proper attribute is predicated, that of which it is the proper attribute is also predicated.

Therefore, when he says “not either this or that,” and specifically “not either body or soul,” this should not be understood to mean that one statement is not true without the addition of the other. Rather, neither one nor the other, in making a human being—of whom it is also said separately that he is something—can be solitary.

To be solitary is one thing; to be called solitary is another. What is called solitary need not actually be solitary, and what cannot be solitary in existence can nevertheless be called solitary. [Col. 1273A]

Those who say that neither statement can be made solitary seem, as an argument for their error, plausibly to assume for themselves and for others of lesser understanding the confusion of white and black mentioned above. Those, however, who reject one statement while accepting the other chatter so baselessly in support of their error that they speak not only against the truth but also against themselves.

They concede “A human being is body” while rejecting, even in form, “A human being is soul.” Yet they do not consider how the existence of one part can also be the existence of what is constituted from that part and can therefore be predicated of it by itself, while the existence of the other part is neither the existence of the thing similarly constituted from it nor capable of being predicated of that thing.

This is especially absurd since they concede that the power belonging to this same kind—namely, rationality—and its accidental affection, namely, knowledge, are truly affirmed of the composite thing whose existence they deny can be predicated from that kind.

[Col. 1273B] Some of them are eager to say that a rationality other than that which belongs to the human spirit is predicated of a human being, and likewise another knowledge and another corporeality than that which belongs to the human body. We reject this so completely that we shall pass over in silence everything that could be said against it.

Against their objection that the human spirit is incorporeal, whereas a human being is not incorporeal, and that therefore whatever is affirmed of a part cannot be affirmed of what is composed from that part, we respond as follows. When they say, “The spirit is incorporeal,” they are rather denying of the spirit something belonging to the power of its genus than affirming its nature of it. Every privation removes what is naturally due.

We do not say that whatever is removed from a part must necessarily be removed from the whole. We say that whatever is naturally predicated of the part must also be affirmed of the composite.

In the part, then.] It is as though he said: A human being is both body and soul. In one part, then, there is not what is in the other. That is, the existence of one part is at least numerically other than the existence of the other part; [Col. 1273C] from the existence of the one part the composite is likewise something, and from the existence of the other part the composite is similarly something, whether this is said conjunctively or disjunctively.

This applies not only to subsistent things composed from diverse subsistent things, such as a human being or a stone, but also to simple things, such as the soul of a human being, which is a subsistent thing composed from no subsistent things. It applies likewise to all subsistences, accidental affections, and, finally, to everything that exists from a principle in such a way that it is not itself the principle. As stated above, there are many things from which each of these is something.

For this reason, properly speaking, none of them is what it is.

But whatever is not from this and that—that is, not from diverse things, but only from this one thing, which has only one existence—is truly what it is and is not other than itself. Such is God, or his divinity.

For there is nothing other than divinity by which God is, nor is there anything from which divinity itself is, except that God is divinity. Whatever is thus singularly and simply one through the singularity and simplicity of its kind [Col. 1273D] is most beautiful through the proper form of supreme dignity and most powerful through its incomparable power. This is rightly said of God, since he rests upon nothing that he needs as support.

Therefore.] It is as though he said: Since only that which is this one thing is truly what it is, therefore it is truly one—and such a one that there is no number of essences in it, because there is no other existence in it apart from the one by which it alone is.

Indeed, it cannot become a subject by possessing something in itself according to its principal essence. Why? Because it is form. He demonstrates by a self-evident mathematical proposition that this proves it cannot be a subject, saying: “Forms cannot be subject,” that is, they do not receive any accident in themselves according to some subsistence that they possess in themselves.

If someone objects that the other forms which mathematical [Col. 1274A] speculation considers abstractly are subject to accidents, and proves this with the example of humanity, we say that his statement is true, but not in the sense in which a human being is said to receive accidents.

Humanity does not receive accidents in the way a human being does. Humanity is not something through a subsistence that it possesses in itself, according to whose principal character it has certain appropriate accidents in itself. Rather, the matter subjected to humanity, and called matter through it, is something from humanity. Humanity gives that matter, through its own property, the concretion by which it is present, while the matter itself is capable of receiving it.

Whatever is truly called a subject of accidents and their matter must first, if not in time then at least in account, be from some subsistence, so that through this it possesses its own properties.

Since, as has been said, subsistence is the cause by which that which exists through it is subject to its own properties, subsistence itself is also said, by denomination, to be subject to those properties and to be their matter.

[Col. 1274B] For when matter, which subsists subject to humanity—that is, which possesses humanity in itself—is said to receive something accidental to it, humanity itself seems in a certain way to be the accident; or rather, a denomination transferred from effect to cause is said to receive this.

But whatever form exists without matter cannot be a subject even μετωνυμικῶς, “metonymically,” nor can it be in matter. Even if it happens to be said to be in something, as divinity is often said in theological writings to be in the Father, or ideas in the elements, this is not said in the sense of being in matter.

Divinity is said to be in the Father as essence is in that which truly is. Ideas are said to be in the elements as exemplars are in the things that are their images. Neither ideas in the elements nor οὐσία in the Father are created subsistences in which accidents are concreted, so that the accidents would exist from their causes and the causes be called their matter as an effect.

Thus neither the Father is matter of any accidents whatsoever, nor are the elements matter of accidents arising from ideas. Therefore neither οὐσία nor εἰδέαι are called matter.

[Col. 1274C] He explains why form without matter is not only not matter but is not even called matter by denomination, saying: “For otherwise it would not truly be form, but rather an image.” This is entirely correct.

From those forms that exist apart from matter—that is, from pure substances, namely fire, air, water, and earth, not from those that have mutual concretion in ὕλη, but from what consists of matter and intelligible form, which are the ideas of sensible things—the forms that are in matter and that come to the matter’s existence to constitute body have proceeded through a certain conforming derivation from their exemplar.

Therefore those pure ideas, which are exemplary, are called forms in the true sense of the name. When we call the others that are in bodies forms, we misuse the name, since they are not ideas but εἰκόνες of ideas—that is, images. This name suits them better.

They resemble those forms that are not constituted in matter—namely, as stated, pure substances and eternal ideas—not by a complete likeness throughout their substance, nor by a substantial likeness that is half-complete in some part of their substance, since temporal things cannot in any way be compared with eternal things, but by a certain imitation outside their substance. [Col. 1274D]

No one, then, etc.] Earlier, after saying that what is not this and that but only this is truly what it is, he added: “Therefore this is truly one, in which there is no number.” To establish this further, he said: “For it cannot become a subject.”

Having demonstrated this, he again draws the same conclusion, as though saying: Since that which is only what it is is neither a subject nor in a subject, there is therefore in it no diversity arising from differing existences, no plurality arising from this diversity, and no multiplicity arising from accidents. Consequently, it has neither the number that is ordinarily produced by diverse things, nor the number produced by one thing’s being diverse, nor the number produced by diverse accidents, nor that produced by existence and accident.

For being at least numerically different, or different even by dissimilarity, and the accident belonging to it, always pertain to diverse things. Thus every being of human beings is diverse not by dissimilarity but by number alone. [Col. 1275A]

Some accidents are different by number alone, as the whiteness of two white things is one whiteness and another whiteness. Others are different also by dissimilarity, as in the case of white and black. Whiteness and blackness are different. The being of human beings and horses, and the accidents belonging to them, are different not only by number but also by dissimilarity.

Even in one thing, such as any individual human being, there is much existence and many accidents. These are diverse not only numerically under one genus but also by dissimilarity, according to some or all of their genera: animation, sensation, rationality, colors, lines, and things of this kind.

God, however, does not differ from God—that is, the Son and the Holy Spirit do not differ from the Father, nor does the Holy Spirit differ from the Son—in any of these ways.

I say this so that God and God may not be thought to differ through various things posited in God as in a subject—namely, so that they may not be understood to differ through differences of any kind, whether accidental or substantial. Since reason assigns these, like accidents, to the power of some determinate genus, [Col. 1275B] they are said to be in the same thing in which the genus itself is, as in a subject, although they too, because they constitute the whole existence, are rightly denied to be in a subject.

No one who understands why the Father is said to be what he is will fail to know that in the Father there are neither plural essences, nor plural accidents, nor an accident together with essence. The same must be understood of his Son and of the Spirit of them both.
