Wherever, then—that is, whether in one thing or in many—there is no difference of essence from essence, accident from accident, or essence from accident, there is no source from which either the one or the many could be understood as plural.

Therefore none of the things that contribute to the one or to the many their being what they are contributes a number to them.

There is thus one essence of the many as well as of the one—namely, one essence alone—by which the Father, his Son, and the Spirit of them both exist, are one, and are what they are; by which they exist together and equally, are one together and equally, and are what they are together and equally.

Their essence, which in Greek is called οὐσία, is essence, singular, and simple. [Col. 1275C] Therefore each of them individually and all of them together are said to exist, to be one, and to be what they are.

No one should be disturbed by the fact that in natural things, when there are three individuals—Plato, Aristotle, and Cicero—there is a threefold designation of human being corresponding to their number: Plato is a human being, Aristotle is a human being, and Cicero is a human being. These three designations are combined into a certain number under the same name, according to which Plato, Aristotle, and Cicero are rightly called three human beings.

The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, however, are not similarly three, although there are three of them, nor is there, corresponding to their number, a threefold act of designating God. Although the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, this threefold designation cannot be combined into a number under the name “God,” so that one could rightly say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three gods.

When “human being” is said three times of these individuals, [Col. 1275D] the individual designations are gathered into a number because the forms predicated of them under one name are diverse and because each is called a human being from a subsistence of his own, which does not belong to another. Thus they are collectively said to be three human beings.

Although, according to the signification of the appellative noun—which is said to signify something qualified—the repetition of the same name occurs, the things predicated under that name nevertheless possess a numerical diversity.

When the name “God” is repeated three times—when the Father is called God, the Son is called God, and the Holy Spirit is called God—the repetition occurs not only according to the manner in which the name signifies but also according to the account of that thing from which each of them is called God.

Therefore these, who appear through repetition to be three units, do not produce a plurality of number—that is, a numerical plurality—in the fact that they appear to be three. For they are not truly three.

[Col. 1276A] This can be understood by comparison if we attend to numerable things—that is, to those from whose diversity number ordinarily arises—and do not attend to the very act of counting, through which a multitude is represented by imitation as a number.

In counting, the diversity of many things, and sometimes merely the repetition of one thing, produces a kind of number of diverse units. But in the number that is not spoken by imitation, but consists in the things themselves through a true diversity of properties among things that are numerable from that diversity, the repetition of one thing—which occurs as though it were the counting of many units and as though plurality arose from the diversity of things—does not produce the true numerical diversity of genuinely numerable things.

It is rather the diverse property of things that produces their numerical diversity.

It therefore appears from this that when, in counting, we say “one, one, one,” or “human being, human being, human being,” or something similar, we say it either with the understanding of diverse properties, which always accompany a diversity of units, or through a repetition of one thing that imitates number.

[Column 1276B] “For number is twofold, that is, in ordinary speech it is said in two ways: one is enumeration, by which we count; the other, etc.” By saying “one” and “another,” he does not intend us to understand that the number by which we count is always different in reality from the number that consists in numerable things. For it is by the latter—the number that consists in numerable things—that we count. But they say “one” and “another” because there is one account of number’s being present in things, and another of counting the things themselves by number.

Enumeration too occurs in different ways: sometimes by division, sometimes by collection. For one who divides also counts; hence number is said of any multitude of diverse things, diverse from one another in their properties. And one who collects also counts; hence number is said of a quantity’s heap and of a collection of units.

We count by division when we say “one, one,” and this occurs in two ways: either by signifying the unit itself, or by signifying that which is one by the unit. We signify the unit itself when we say its name more than once—“one, one,” or “unit, unit.” We signify that which is one by the unit when either we say each of things that are wholly different only once; or when we say more than once things that are the same in their mode of signification, while counting things that are wholly different; or when we say “man, beryl,” in which both the things that exist and that from which they exist are understood to have been counted by division; or when we say “white man,” where it is not the man who is man, nor the white thing that is white, but the singular humanity that is man and the singular whiteness by which the same thing is white, that have been counted.

We count by division when we say more than once things that are the same in their mode of signification. This is a real division, in the proper sense of the word, when, speaking of Plato and Cicero, we say “man, man,” counting both the men who exist and the different humanities, one of which is predicated of one and the other of the other as “man.” Or it is a division that is not real but is said by a certain imitation. For example, when, understanding one thing alone that exists and one thing alone from which it exists, we say “man, man” under one name, as when we understand Cicero and some singular property of his; or under different names, “Marcus Tullius Cicero”; or “sword, blade, weapon”; or when we understand different things mentioned above, from which nevertheless they are one—for example, when we say “white, white,” speaking both of the body from which man consists and of man himself, who consists from it. Likewise, “rational, rational,” speaking both of the spirit of man and of man, who consists from it.

This division, however, which is not real but is said by imitation, is properly called iteration, or repetition.

We count by collection when, under one name and at one time, we say either several units, as “two,” or several things as one, as “men.” In the latter case both the things that exist and that from which they exist are always counted under one of their names, whether naturally common or plural. This enumeration, which occurs by collection, consists of the parts of division.

This too must be carefully observed. For the parts of that division which are counted as diverse both in names and in properties—both the things that exist and that from which they exist, as “man, beryl”—or the parts in which it is not the thing that exists but that from which it exists that is counted, as “white man”—are not counted by any collection of a plurality of the name in question. In the former two cases, diversity without union, and in the latter, unity without diversity, prevents enumeration by collection from taking place.

The parts of that division therefore remain for collection in which, by saying more than once things that are the same in their mode of signification, we count both, as in the case of different men, “man, man,” both the things that exist and that from which they exist. Thus, what is distributed as different both in reality and in name in the first two cases—one and another one—is not made “two” by collection; and what is repeated twice as one in the third case is nothing but one. But what is distributed under the same name in the fourth case is, because of the different property of the things that exist and of that from which they exist, one and another one, and, because of the sameness of the signification of the name, twice one; thus, “man, man,” “two men.”

[Column 1277B] Thus number is one and the same both in things and as that by which we count—whether by collecting, by dividing, by a division using the proper name, or by repetition. But since, as has been said, there is one account of number’s consisting in things themselves and another of counting things by the same number, the author rightly says, distinguishing the two: “One is that by which we count, and another that which consists in numerable things, truly distinct from the things in which it exists.”

For what is one is a thing subject to unity: either unity is present in it, as in a white thing, or is present to it, as to whiteness. Unity is that by which we call both the thing in which it is present and the thing to which it is present “one”: thus, “one white thing,” “one whiteness.”

Again, the things that we say are two are things in reality; that is, they are things similarly subject to duality, which is two: “two men” or “two stones.” Duality, however, is nothing; that is, it is not something to which duality is either present or attached, because nothing can either be present in it or present to it. Rather, it is simply duality by which two men or two stones become two.

For just as through quality it is not quality itself but the subject of which it is the quality that is qualified, so through quantity it is not quantity itself but what is subject to it that is quantified. Therefore it is not unity itself but what is subject to unity that is properly called one; nor is it duality itself but what is subject to duality that is properly called two.

By a trope, however, in which the name of the effect is transferred to the cause, unity itself is called one, and duality itself—that is, unity and unity—is called two. The same applies to the other numbers, namely three, four, and so forth. For truly every number is not a number of the number itself but of the things subjected to it. These, as we have often said, we count either by collection—which is always a true plurality both of the things that exist and of that from which they exist—or by division, which is not always so.

Thus, in the number called enumeration, by which we count, repetition of one, as though of many units, often produces the plurality that is said by imitation alone. But in the number of things, which is truly constituted by the diverse properties of the things themselves, repetition of one, as though it were many units, does not produce plurality. For example, if, speaking of the same thing, with diversity in the matter of sound but not in signification, I say: “one sword, one blade, one weapon.” I rightly prefaced this with “if I speak of the same thing.” Since any such name is naturally common to many things, both to things that exist and to that from which they exist, these same names can indeed be uttered from the understanding of different things or of the same things; but they can be said from the understanding of one thing, because one individual sword can be recognized as having been called by so many names, with such diversity of words, by one singular nature.

This enumeration, which might perhaps be thought to be an enumeration of different units, is not an enumeration of many, but rather a repetition of one alone. He repeats the same example, saying: “Or if, from the understanding of one alone—both what exists and that by which it exists—we should say in different words, ‘blade, weapon, sword,’ it is a certain repetition of the same thing, not an enumeration of different things.” And by another example, in which both the sound and the signification are the same, he shows the same point, saying: “Or if, contracting a naturally common appellation through customary usage, I apply it to one thing alone in my understanding and say ‘sun, sun, sun,’ I have not made three suns by enumerating a plurality of the things that exist and of that by which they exist; rather, concerning one thing that exists and one thing by which it exists, I have predicated the same thing three times through repetition.”

“Therefore not,” etc. From these examples he infers, as though saying: By saying “blade, weapon, sword,” with names different in sound but not in signification, and by saying “sun, sun, sun,” with a name one both in sound and in signification, a triple predication by repetition does not produce a number. Likewise, then, if “God” is predicated three times of the Father, of his Son, and thirdly of the Spirit of both, this triple predication does not thereby produce a number of predicates.

This—the number, that is, of things, under the name “God”—is a triple predication that applies only to those who, as was said above, appear to establish some distinction of merits among them, namely, those who say that the Father is greater than the Son and the Son greater than the Holy Spirit. Since Catholics establish no such distinction of merits, and do not derive from this diversity of merits—which is fabricated by others—a diversity of the predicates bearing the name “God,” but posit the aforesaid form as it is in itself, namely, as singularly one, and judge that it is nothing other than what it is—that is, wholly simple οὐσία, “essence”—the repetition of the same predicate rightly seems to have been made, rather than an enumeration of different predicates, when it is said: “The Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God.”

For different essences have not been predicated in these three propositions. Rather, this Trinity—that is, these three, diverse from one another in certain properties—is singularly and simply one God, like “blade,” “weapon”: one singular sword, with one singular predicated quality of names. Likewise, “sun, sun, sun” is one sun under one singular form.

“Yet this for the moment,” etc. Up to this point he has demonstrated by theological arguments the singular and simple essence of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, by which each of them both exists and is God, and the three are one God. Now he wishes to demonstrate by arguments drawn from nature that these same persons are diverse through different properties, although their essence is singular and simple.

In order that this diversity within their unity might be understood to some extent, he recalls all the genera of the natural categories and first explains what they are and how they are predicated of creatures and of God. It should be observed how skillfully he moves toward demonstrating the diversity of those whose unity he had demonstrated, taking his opportunity from the examples he had introduced to make their unity intelligible.

He had said: “When it is said, ‘God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit,’ it seems more a repetition concerning the same thing than an enumeration of something different.” And, lest anyone doubt this, he had confirmed it by a comparison of equivocal and univocal terms, saying: “Like blade, weapon, sword,” and “like sun, sun, sun.” In these examples, repetition has been made both of what exists and of that by which it exists.

But when it is said “God, God, God”—the first concerning the Father, the second concerning the Son, the third concerning the Holy Spirit—he himself clarifies this by saying: “God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit.” An enumeration has been made of those who are God, but a repetition of that by which they are God.

This will be better understood by division. In natural things, what exists is one thing, and that by which it exists is another. Enumeration is likewise one thing, and repetition another. When these are joined to one another, a division into four parts arises. For in the utterance of the words, either both what exists and that by which it exists are counted, or both are repeated; or what exists is repeated but that by which it exists is counted; or what exists is counted but that by which it exists is repeated.

Both are often counted under different names, as “man, stone”; often under the same name, as “man, man” concerning Plato and Cicero, or “men.” Both are often repeated under different proper names, as “Marcus, Tullius, Cicero,” or under appellative names, as “blade, sword, weapon”; often under the same proper name, as “Cicero, Cicero,” or under the same appellative, as “sun, sun.”

What exists is repeated but that by which it exists is counted when someone speaks of one man—for example, Plato—and says “rational animal.” What exists is counted but that by which it exists is repeated when someone speaks of different things—for example, of the soul of a man and of the man who consists of that soul—and says “rational, rational.”

Once these distinctions have been made, if someone, wishing something to be understood by comparison with something else, says “animal, rational,” he is correctly making a comparison with “man, stone,” which is enumeration. For although, when one says “man, stone,” both what exists and that by which it exists are counted, when one says “animal, rational,” it is not indeed what exists but that by which it exists that is counted. Nevertheless, the likeness of the comparison remains in those respects for which the comparison is made. For these two names, “animal” and “rational,” truly count that by which one thing exists, just as the two names “man” and “stone” count both what exists and that by which it exists.

Likewise, one correctly compares the following: “Just as there is enumeration when ‘man, man’ is said of Plato and Cicero, or ‘rational animal’ of Plato alone, so there is enumeration when one says ‘rational soul, rational man.’” For although it is not that by which they exist—that is, rationality—that is counted, the things that exist—that is, soul and man—are counted in a certain way when “man, man” is said of different things, both what exists and that by which it exists being counted; and when “rational animal” is said of one thing alone, only that by which it exists is counted.

Similarly, if someone wishes to make repetition understood by comparison with repetition, he correctly compares any of the three foregoing kinds of repetition, whether with repetition of the same genus or of another genus. He may compare it with what repeats only that by which it exists, as “rational soul, rational man”; or with what repeats something of the same kind, namely that by which it exists, as “long human body, long man”; or with what is of a different kind, namely what exists, as “rational animal”; or with both the same and the different, that is, both what exists and that by which it exists, as “Cicero, Cicero.”

Some, however, err in comparisons—or rather, on the basis of comparisons—when they either think that, if anything in them is dissimilar, the comparisons should be rejected altogether, or use them in respect of things for which they were not introduced. Such are the Sabellians. When they hear that there are three persons of one substance, and read the comparisons introduced to demonstrate, on the basis of their properties, either equality, or comparison, or co-eternity, or procession—namely, “the mind, knowledge, and love of one soul”; “the memory, understanding, and will of one mind”; “the radiance and heat of one ray”; or similar examples—they suppose that just as there is one ray alone, of which heat and radiance are predicated, or one mind alone, of which memory, understanding, and will are predicated, or one soul alone, of which mind, knowledge, and love are predicated, so there is likewise one subsisting entity alone who, being by nature God, is himself, through personal properties, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Their very error plainly shows that they are wholly ignorant of the multiple use in natural things of the name “substance”: namely, that not only what exists but also that by which it exists is called by this name. They are entirely ignorant, moreover, of the manner in which any property of something is called “personal” when it is so designated, and of the fact that the same thing is called “singular,” “individual,” and “personal” in different senses. We reserve the task of distinguishing these terms for a later place.

For the moment, however, we have mentioned the introduction of comparisons and the error of the Sabellians, which could arise from comparisons and from the multiplicity of the name “substance.” We have done so lest anyone, following them, should suppose from comparisons involving the equivocal terms “blade, weapon, sword,” or the univocal terms “sun, sun, sun”—comparisons in which both what exists and that by which it exists, that is, both the subsisting thing and subsistence, are repeated in signification—that, in the statement “God, God, God” concerning the Father, the Son, and the Spirit of both, a repetition of one subsisting entity has been made.

Rather, only subsistence is repeated: subsistence predicated as one and individual of different persons, namely, the Father, the Son, and their Spirit. The author himself makes clear that he wished this repetition alone to be understood through the comparisons, and that he introduced the comparisons for this reason, when he says:

“But this which we introduce—‘blade, weapon, sword,’ and ‘sun, sun, sun’—for the moment, while we are still investigating not in what properties the Father, his Son, and the Spirit of both are diverse but in what they are one, is to be taken as having been said with reference to that signification and demonstration—that is, to a demonstrative signification—in which not only is something signified by words but also shown by the proportionality of the comparisons: namely, that not every repetition of units in signification completes a number and plurality through the diversity of the things themselves—that is, a truly numbered plurality.”

The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not said to be one thing and from one thing, as though they were something equivocal. Rather, these are names of different things and from different things. For blade, weapon, and sword are the same through the singularity of subsistence and through the property itself.

The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, however, are the same in this respect: the plural verb “are,” predicated of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who are numerically plural, ought to signify the essence by which they are what they are. For, according to the rule of the grammarians, the person of the verb is determined not by what is said but by that of which it is said.

Therefore, when the utterance concerns one thing, whether one or many things are said, the singular verb is used: “Plato is a man,” or “Plato the man is white.” But when the utterance follows an enumeration of many, both one and many are enunciated of them with a plural verb: “Plato and Cicero are rational,” and “Plato and his spirit are one rational thing.”

Thus, since the enumeration “the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit” had preceded the utterance, the proper sequel should have been: “They are the same.” Yet because the essence by which the many are the same is one, singular, and individual, he refers the number of the verb not to the plurality of the subjects but to the unity of the essence predicated of them, so that the singularity of the essence might be understood from the verb rather than the singularity of the verb from the essence. He therefore says:

“The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are indeed the same”—by the singularity of the οὐσία, that is, of the essence, which is truly predicated of them—“but he is not himself,” namely, there is not one ὑπόστασις subject to these names: one subsisting entity, one and alone, with one solitary property, who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in different respects.

For the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not ὁμοϋπόστατοι, “of one subsistence,” but ὁμοούσιοι, “of one essence”: not of one subsisting entity or one being, but of one subsistence or one essence.

When I say “not of one subsisting entity or one being,” I do not say this because I want it understood that these three are not one subsisting entity or one being. For they truly are one subsisting entity or one being, through the one οὐσία, “essence,” by which they are what they are. Rather, I say it because the personal property predicated of one of them is never predicated of another. [The text is corrupt here; he continues:]

“In this matter,” that is, whether these different predicates are said of one alone, we must consider briefly, on the authority of the Catholics. When some ask the Catholics whether the one who is Father is himself the one who is Son, the Catholics reply: ‘By no means is the one who is Father himself the one who is also Son.’ Again, when some ask these same Catholics whether one of them is the same as the other—not, I do not say, by singularity, as one is the other, but by the property of one subsisting entity who is the other—they deny this.

It is therefore clear from this that they are not indifferent in every respect. Although in that by which they are what they are—that is, in the essence predicated of them—there is indifference among them, there is nevertheless, in certain properties that cannot be predicated of one and therefore must be predicated of different persons, a difference among them.

Accordingly, in accordance with their diversity, the number of those of whom these things are said enters into the discussion. Those who are one through the singularity of the one essence predicated of them are nevertheless numerically many through different properties, which cannot suitably be predicated of one alone.

That this number is constituted—or, as you may say, demonstrated—from the subjects or subsisting entities, or from subsistences substantially conformable to one another, through the diversity produced by dissimilar accidents, was explained above when we were discussing the numerical plurality of natural things.

Of this matter—that is, of their number, although through one singular and simple essence, solitary from all those things by which things that come later are accustomed to be accompanied by things that precede, they are singularly and simply one, and nothing but God—we shall speak briefly, provided that before considering it we first set out how each thing that is said of God is predicated of him.”

“Ten,” etc. Here it must be recalled that although the disciplines differ according to the genera of things with which they deal—namely, natural philosophy, mathematics, theology, civil philosophy, and logic—there is nevertheless one discipline, natural philosophy, which is more readily available in human speech and is prior in the proportional transfer of expressions.

For example, “how large” and “what sort” are properly said in natural things: “how large a man or stone,” “what sort of man or stone.” These same terms are transferred from natural things to other disciplines by way of some proportional relation: thus one speaks in mathematics of how large and what sort of line; in theology of how great and what sort of God; in civil affairs of how large and what sort of office; and in logic of how great and what sort of moral goodness.

The same applies to terms derived from the relations of natural things. “Contrary” is first and properly said in natural things of white and black; then in mathematics of whiteness and blackness; in theology and civil affairs of evil and good; and in logic of falsehood and truth. In this way, many terms proper to natural things, taken from them through some proportional relation, are transferred to other disciplines.

This philosopher, therefore, adopting this usage of words not only from the everyday speech of all people but also from the authority of the Scriptures produced by the most diligent and reputable men, had shown in what respect the Father, his Son, and the Spirit of both are one. Since he was about to say in what respects they, who are without number in being one, are nevertheless numerically many—for both that in which they are one and those respects in which they are many are predicated of them—he rightly enumerates all the genera of the natural categories and explains by a division in what sense each is said either of subsisting things or of God.

He therefore says: “The philosophers, especially Aristarchus and Aristotle, hand down ten categories in all, according to the number of their genera. Apart from these, nothing is predicated in any discipline; and these are predicated universally of all things, that is, with no thing of which something may suitably be said excepted, either properly or by some transference.” He then lists what they are.

“That is, substance,” etc. The name “substance” was not imposed by the discipline of natural philosophy, but by the common account of all things that exist as subsisting entities. It was imposed not only on those things that are the being of subsistences, but also on those whose being consists in being present in all subsisting entities.

Nevertheless, since there is no most general name, common to all subsisting entities—both corporeal and incorporeal—derived from their common subsistence, the Latins often use “substance” in its place. Thus Porphyry, in the *Isagoge*, says: “Substance is something,” and goes on to posit it as a genus. This philosopher follows him and says “substance” as the most general genus of all subsisting entities.

“Quality” is the most general of all qualities in mathematics, and “quantity” the most general of all quantities. They are called what they are not from causes understood to be in them, but from their producing the subsisting things in which they are: the former produces things qualified, the latter things quantified.

It should be observed that if he had said “what sort” and “how much,” he would have supplied examples no less appropriate. For although quality and “what sort” are different, they are not different genera; likewise quantity and “how much.”

Accordingly, he illustrates the remaining genera not with the names of mathematical abstraction but with the names of natural participation. For he does not say “relation” but “relative,” which cannot be said of relation. No relation is itself relative; only that of which it is predicated is relative. Just as no quality itself is qualified, but only that of which the quality is said. The quality itself, I mean, is not the genus of that thing; for it is impossible for the genus of something to be predicated of that same thing.

Thus quality is a quality in the genus of every quality, whereas “what sort” is qualified by the quality of every genus. Consequently, no “what sort” is a quality, and no quality is a “what sort.” Similarly, nothing that is relative is relation, and no relation is relative. Rather, as has been said, that of which relation is predicated is relative, that is, related. Relation itself is relation, not the related thing; nevertheless, relation and the related thing belong to the same genus.

Likewise, “where,” “when,” “having,” “being situated,” “doing,” and “being acted upon” are most general names, not of the things that are predicated but of the things of which they are predicated. Therefore they are named from the categories of genera, not from the genera of categories.

For place is not in a place, nor time in time; possession does not possess; situation is not situated; action does not act; and passion is not acted upon. Rather, the things subject to these are said, by reference to them, to be in a place, to be in time, to have, to be situated, to act, and to be acted upon.

“Thus these,” etc. He has posited all ten genera of the categories. Now he gathers all of them—not, I say, as genera but as categories—into two places in natural philosophy: substance and accident.

Whatever constitutes the being of subsisting entities is called their substance. These are, in every subsisting entity, its special subsistences, and all those from which these are composed—namely, the general properties by which the subsisting entities themselves are conformed to one another, and the differentiae by which they are dissimilar.

If someone asks what these things, which logicians call subsistences or substances, are by genus among mathematicians, we reply that simple subsistences are subjected to one of the nine genera: animation, for example, is subject to the category of having, and rationality to quality. Composite subsistences, such as humanity and the other special subsistences—which everyone knows to consist of general properties and differentiae—we say belong by genus to those same genera to which the simple parts composing them belong. Thus humanity belongs by genus to the same genus as animation, and likewise to the same genus as rationality; and similarly, according to its other parts, it belongs to whatever genera those parts themselves belong to.

In this way, then, logicians call some of the categories subsistences or substances—those that mathematical abstraction subjects to its genera—while they call all the others, of whatever genera, accidents.

But since these terms derive their names from the logical account of categories, it must be observed whose substances are the categories called substances, and whose accidents are those called accidents.

We say that subsistences, and the things whose being they are, are called substances. Thus corporeality is the substance of all bodies—that is, it is the being by which each of them is something. And the same corporeality is also the substance of colors, although colors are not beings of which corporeality constitutes the being by which each color is something; rather, colors follow being corporeal, even though they are not the being of some other thing.

For no color can be predicated of a body except through corporeality. Thus corporeality is the substance of colors, not because it is their being but because without it no color could be said of a body.

Accidents are predicated of those substances that consist in being, whether they are created in them or attached to them from outside. But accidents occur only to those that are beings, because of the latter it is correctly said that accidents are not in them but present to them.

Accordingly, introducing the categories themselves under these two natural places of all the categories—substance and accident—the author says: “These categories, then, are such, in relation to the logical discipline, as those subjects of which they are suitably predicated permit them to be.”

Part of the categories, in the place of the account of substance, occurs not only in the supposition of subsisting entities, by which it is made clear whose being they are—for example, “Plato is a body”—but also in the predication of other things, by which it is shown, as a consequence of the combination, what is present to that which constitutes being: “The body is colored.”

But part of the categories is in the place of the account of accidents, namely, when they are said of subsisting entities and nevertheless accompany their subsistences.

Thus, in the genus of natural things, whatever is predicated according to the proper accounts of natural things is called either a subsistence or an accident.

But when someone transfers these categories to divine predication—that is, when they are said to be predicated of God—everything that can be predicated imitates them. That is, although what is predicated of God is called substance, quality, quantity, or by some other natural name, it is not nevertheless what the name signifies; rather, it receives that name by some proportional relation of reason.

“Relative,” however—that is, relation—cannot in any way be predicated of God as that by which God is what he is.

“For substance.” The meaning is: Truly, the things predicated of God are not what they are called. For what is called his substance is indeed in him of whom it is predicated, but it is not truly substance in him. That is, it is not substance with the same rational truth by which anything is called substance—namely, the being by which a subsisting thing is something. Rather, it is called substance by some proportional relation of reason.

For example, a body is something: it is a body, and colored, and bounded by lines. But we must further distinguish by what it is a body, by what it is colored, and by what it is bounded by lines. It is a body through corporeality, colored through color, and bounded by a line through line.

We must still distinguish in what rational categories these things are contained. We say that it is not corporeality that follows color or line, but color and line that follow corporeality. For corporeality is not caused by these; rather, they are caused by corporeality. In this respect corporeality is the being of the body, while these are present to the same body.

Therefore, first corporeality, and then the body insofar as it is corporeal, is, in the true sense, the substance of these things. Corporeality, however, is first the substance of the body’s accidents, for the accidents truly stand under it; and corporeality, to which they are present, and the body, in which they are present, stand under them.

But what God is—not only is he simple in himself, but he is also so solitary from those subsistences to which things that exist are accustomed to be present that, apart from that one property by which he is, he has absolutely nothing else by which he may be understood to exist. Therefore neither he himself nor that by which God is what he is stands under anything by the relation of subjection.

Consequently, he is not called substance by the proper account of reason. Rather, since God properly is by that which he is, he is rightly called essence.

Nevertheless, since there is not such an abundance of words that everything can be designated by its own name—as we said above—human speech transfers names from other disciplines, especially from natural philosophy, to other disciplines by some proportional relation of reason.

Thus, just as we say “body,” “white,” and “large”—body by substance, white by quality, large by quantity—so we also say “God,” “just,” and “great.” It is as though we had said: “God by substance, just by quality, great by quantity.”

We use these names when we designate God by “substance,” the just by quality, and the greatest by quantity, although we say none of these according to the proper account either of a genus or of reason, but only by proportional transference.

Therefore, what we call substance in God is not substance according to the relation of subjection. It is essence beyond every substance subject to accidents, utterly solitary from all things that can occur.

Likewise, quality and the other things that can occur, such as quantities, are not in God what they are called. For a fuller understanding of all this, examples must be added, of the following kind.

When, speaking either of the Father, the Son, or the Spirit of both, we say “God,” we seem to signify the substance by which each of these three is what he is; and indeed we do signify it, but not a substance of the kind whose rational character belongs to those things that are called by this name in the genus of natural things. Rather, we signify the principal and eternal essence, beyond every natural substance that has a beginning in time.

When, however, we say “just” of any one of them, we seem to signify quality, and we do call that by which he is said to be just a quality. Yet we do not mean it according to the mathematical sense of an accident; rather, we mean that which is substance—not according to the relation of subjection but, as was said above, beyond the substance that is called substance from subjection.

“For neither.” The meaning is: Truly, we do not say “just” of any one of them by quality, but by substance in the sense just explained. For it is not one thing that he himself is and another thing that he is just. That by which he is just is not other than that by which he is himself; rather, God’s being is identical with his being just. That is, by the same thing by which he is, he is just.

Likewise, when he is called “great” or “greatest,” through this term—which properly belongs to the quantity of magnitude—we seem to signify quantity. And indeed we signify it, but not an accident; rather, we signify that which is itself substance, specifically substance of the kind we have described, beyond substance.

This is certainly so. For God’s being is identical with his being great: each of these three is great by the same thing by which he is.

**Concerning form, etc.]** As though he were saying: What is called quality or quantity in him is not what is being said, but that singular, simple, and solitary [Col. 1284B] essence which we have described as separated from everything that is accustomed to occur; and thus, most correctly, whatever is predicated of him as though after substance, like a form distinct from that substance, is called by that name. For above the same point was demonstrated concerning his form: namely, that he—that is, God—is the true form, and that by his singularity he is truly one, and so simple in himself and solitary from those things that are accustomed to be present, that there is no plurality belonging to him, either from his parts or from those accidents which, on that account, make him what he is.

**But these, etc.]** As though he were saying: Substances, qualities, and quantities are said of those things that subsist, and also of God. But one must carefully observe that they are said of them in a different sense from that in which the predicates of the other genera are said of them. For these categories are such that they inhere in the things of which they are predicated and also make that very thing in which they are present be what they are called.

In other things, which are not [Col. 1284C] God, they are divided—that is, when by predicating many things of the subject under discussion, the predication is distributed in such a way that, by predicating one thing, it leaves many others that can be predicated of the same subject. In God, however, they are joined and conjoined: that is, every predication, whether we say that substance, quality, or quantity is predicated, leaves nothing still to be predicated whereby the subject under discussion is what he is.

The matter is as follows. When we say, “Something is a substance,” or “Something is a man” or “God,” this is said as though the very thing of which this or that substance is predicated were a substance—that is, as though it made the subject of which it is said be what is stated: namely, as though it made that thing be a substance, that is, be a man or God. And this it does.

Yet although the manner of speaking is the same when it is said of something, “It is a man,” and when it is said of something, “It is God,” the sense in which the statement is made distinguishes one from the other. For the subject that is predicated to be a man, although it is a man, is nevertheless not completely what is predicated of it as man. That is, it is not predicated to be what it is in its [Col. 1284D] entirety in the statement that it is a man. Rather, the person who says this leaves many things still to be said of the same subject—namely, qualities, by which it is qualified, and quantities, by which it is quantified. Consequently, even in the statement that it is a substance, the whole of what it is is not fully predicated.

Whatever it is together with that by which it is what it is, it owes to other things that do not become man—that is, things which the person who says “He is a man” by no means predicates of him. But the subject of whom it is said, “He is God,” is perfectly what he is said to be, namely God; the statement leaves absolutely nothing further to be said of him whereby he is what he is. For he is altogether nothing other than that one singular and simple thing which he is. He has nothing whereby he is what he is except a singular and simple essence. For by that essence he both is and is God.

Therefore, since the person who says of him “He is God” has left nothing whereby he is what he is, it can rightly be said that he is only that which is predicated of him as being, when it is said of him, “He is God.” And in this sense the category called substance, whether it is predicated of God or of other things, is understood.

[Col. 1285A] Again, when someone is said to be just, since in mathematics this belongs to the genus quality, it is said in this way—that is, in this sense—as though the subject of which this quality is predicated were, in the true account of being, what it is said to be. For example, if we say “A man is just” or “God is just,” we maintain that the man or God himself is just, not by participation in something external to the thing of which we predicate justice and in no way inherent in it, but truly.

Although, in this sense of the true account of being, the predication properly applies in both cases, to man and to God, one differs from the other in that one leaves nothing, while the other leaves many things of which the subject under discussion can truly be predicated. When it is said, “A man is just,” he is not said to be just in the entirety of what he is; rather, in a divided manner, justice alone is said to make him just. Many things differ from justice—not only in their individual properties, but also in species and genus—by which the same subject is what it is in the same manner, such as the form by which a man is a man.

[Col. 1285B] To put it in new words: one thing is man, another is just; that is, one thing is what he is as man, another is that by which he is just. But when it is said, “God is just,” he is said to be just in the entirety of what he is. The statement leaves nothing at all whereby he is what he is. For God is the very same thing as what is just: by the same thing by which he is God, he is just.

The same man or God is also said to be great. Thus both are said to be great in this sense, as though the man himself were, in the true account of being, great, or as though God himself were, in the true account of being, great. But just as was said concerning quality and substance, this statement differs from the former in that, when it is said “A man is great,” greatness is divided among the things by which the man is what he is. For by this proposition he is not proposed to be great in the entirety of what he is and is said to be; rather, with many other things by which he is likewise what he is left aside, the man alone is proposed to be great.

But the proposition by which God is proposed to be great leaves [Col. 1285C] nothing whereby God is what he is, since God himself is great: that is, he is great by the same thing by which he is God.

These, then—substances, qualities, and quantities—are such that whatever is proposed to be by them truly is; and therefore they are rightly said to be predicated of them. The accidents of the remaining seven genera, however, are predicated neither of God nor of other things according to the true account of being.

For “where,” that is, place, can indeed be predicated either of a man or of God: of a man, when we say “A man is in the forum”; of God, when we say “God is everywhere.” But “a man is in the forum” and “God is everywhere” are said in such a way that, although the word *is* occurs in the predication, it is not said as though the thing of which it is said were that which is predicated—that is, as though it had its being by what is predicated.

For whatever is in a place certainly is something; nevertheless, to be in a place is not to be in the way in which being qualified or quantified is being. A man who is white or long is such, and for him to be white or long is to be what he is. But to be in the forum is not to be, although whoever is in the forum truly is.

Thus [Col. 1285D] “A man is in the forum” is not said in the same way—that is, in the same true sense of being—as it is said that the same man is white or long. For when he is said to be in the forum, he is indeed understood to be surrounded and bounded; yet this being is not understood as arising from some property by which he could be designated in himself—that is, without a comparison extending beyond him and made with something else—just as, without comparing himself with another, a man is designated in himself by his human form, and as white by the quality of his body, and as long by the quantity of that same body, which is called a line.

Conversely, the fact that he is said to be surrounded and bounded, in the statement that he is in the forum, is not said in itself but through comparison with those things by which he is surrounded and contained outside himself, and by which he is bounded when the ends of his intervals meet them.

Nevertheless, this fact—that he is in the forum, surrounded and bounded by external things—would not be predicated if he had not first been formed by his own intrinsic properties. Thus, by saying that a man is in the forum, no property inhering in the man, by which he truly is what he is, is indicated in the proper significance of grammarians or dialecticians. Rather, this alone is shown by the [Col. 1286A] predication: what must exist by nature is first revealed through association with what follows—namely, that the thing said to be surrounded and bounded by being in the forum is truly formed by things other than surrounding or bounding. In this sense place is predicated of man; but it is not predicated of God in this sense.

For when it is said “God is everywhere,” this seems to be said in the following sense: not that he is in every place, as though he were enclosed by being surrounded, or as though the extension of his intervals ended by encountering some exterior things. He cannot be said to be in a place at all in this sense of surrounding and bounding. Rather, he is said to be everywhere in the sense that every place whatsoever is present to him, capable of containing him within itself without limit—although he himself is not received into the place of anything external as though he were surrounded or bounded by exterior things.

Therefore, since he is neither surrounded by other things placed around him outside himself nor bounded by the ends of his supposed spaces, he is said to be nowhere as being in a place, because he is truly wholly everywhere—but, as has been said, not as being in a place.

[Col. 1286B] When “when,” that is, time—which is said not under the genus of quantities but through comparison among things that are quantities—is predicated, it is predicated in the same way as “where,” which is said not under the genus of quantities but through a comparison made among things that are quantities in relation to one another. Thus one says of a man, “He came yesterday,” and of God, “He always is.”

Here too, as in the predication of place, the thing of which a yesterday’s coming is said is not said by this expression to be something according to the true account of being—as though it were something in itself, although that whose coming it was yesterday is something through many things that are predicated of it in itself. Rather, by this expression something else is predicated as having been added to it through an external comparison according to time: namely, its own time, according to its coming, and the time of something else, according to something that could then truly be said of it.

[Col. 1286C] The sense, for example, might be: “Yesterday, while the sun was rising, the man came,” or something similar. In this way one thing is compared with another according to time, whether the time is the same or different.

But when it is said of God “He always is,” this expression, according to the usage by which philosophers predicate it of natural things, signifies only one thing. For whenever “He always is” is said of any natural thing, it is understood as though one were saying: what was throughout every past time, is throughout every present time—however that particular present time may be—and will be throughout every future time; that is, while all the other things were, while they are, and while they will be, he was, is, and will be.

From this it can be understood that when, in natural things, mathematics, and many other matters, one says “He will be,” “He was,” “He is today,” “He will be tomorrow,” or “He always is,” the understanding is neither absolute nor simple. Rather, it is a comparison and gathering together of different times.

[Col. 1286D] For when someone says of something “Yesterday it was white,” the time in which he predicates that it was white yesterday is compared neither with any present times, nor with any future times, nor with all past times, but only with those times in which either the same thing in other respects, or any other things in any respects, existed as yesterday within the boundaries of the beginning and end of that same day, whether simultaneously or successively.

When someone says of something “Today it is white,” he compares the time in which he proposes that it is white today neither with any past times nor with any future times, but only with all those times in which either the same thing in other respects, or any other things in any respects, are “today.”

Similarly, when someone says of anything “Tomorrow it will be white,” he signifies tomorrow by gathering together all the times of other things and of the same thing in other respects in which they will be tomorrow.

In these comparisons, its time is compared with other times, since by saying “not all times” but “many times” are gathered together, one time is compared with another. For nothing in any genus of things can be compared with itself. Hence, if one says “Plato is sitting while he is sitting,” the statement is absurd.

[Col. 1287A] But whoever, excluding the three principles posited by the philosophers—namely οὐσία (*ousia*, substance), εἴδεα (*eidea*, forms), and ὕλη (*hylē*, matter)—says of something “It always is,” gathers together all the times of all things that were, are, and will be: both all the times in which the thing proposed to be always was, is, or will be, and the names of all other things in any manner whatsoever that were, are, or will be; and he compares these with it by saying “It always is.”

For whenever a comparison is made either among past times themselves or between past times and others, or among present times, or among future times, the gathering together of many things leaves many others over. Thus when one says “yesterday,” “today,” “tomorrow,” “the day before yesterday,” “the day after tomorrow,” “formerly,” “before,” “after,” “now,” “once,” “just now,” and any other expression that properly signifies the present, past, or future, or any of these generally, the comparison expressed by “never” or “always,” as has been said, gathers together all times in their entirety, leaving none at all out. Hence he rightly says:

**When something is said always to be, it signifies that it was throughout every past time, etc.]** [Col. 1287B] “Always to be,” in this sense of comparison and gathering, can, according to the philosophers, be said of heaven and the other bodies that are immortal through the perpetuity of their motion.

For in none of them is that by which it is something solitary. Rather, in every one of them there are diverse things—not only in properties but also in genera. As some of these depart, others succeed them; and thus they are said to be and to move through the diversity of times.

For according to the number of things that endure through times, there is also a number of the times through which they endure. Yet some of these times are joined together by the continuity of things departing and succeeding, or by their sharing in existence at the same time; and thus many times are called one time: one year, one month, one day, one hour, one moment.

But God is not said to “always be” in this way. A comparison and gathering is indeed understood, but the matter differs. In the other things said always to be, times are compared with times. In this case, however, eternity is compared with times. For God is what he is not by a duration of time but by eternity.

[Col. 1287C] The other things that are joined together with one another in any manner—whether by an internal mode of concretion or by the external condition of some addition—endure through the durations of times, which the author of all things himself assigns to different things through different conditions.

This gathering of God’s eternity also exceeds all times. God is said to always be not only because he was in every past time, is in every present time, and will be in every future time, but also because he was before and will be after all times, either actually and naturally, or at least naturally in relation to temporal things.

For everything that was, is, or will be either had, has, or will have a beginning of being; but as regards its actual existence, not everything has an end, while as regards its nature and the power of him by whose authorship it exists, everything has an end. For all things are equally subject to his power, so that just as whatever has not been could have been, and whatever is not or will not be could be, so whatever has been could not have been, and whatever is or will be could not be.

[Col. 1287D] For by nature no interval is simply terminated by a single end. Hence an interval is called an interval because, lying between different boundaries, it is enclosed by their plurality. Thus a γραμμή (*grammē*), that is, a line, is enclosed by different points; an ἐπιπολή (*epipolē*), that is, a surface, by different lines; and a στερεόν (*stereon*), that is, a solid, by different surfaces. Each lies between boundaries and is itself bounded by them.

Similarly, since the eternal law of nature has established that no generated thing subsists, intervals of time are likewise terminated not by one boundary but by different ones—namely, by a natural position and beginning of being. For whatever endures through a duration of time—not merely in actuality but by nature—naturally begins, exists, and ceases.

But what endures through a duration of eternity, just as it does not begin in actuality, so neither does it begin or cease by nature. Therefore it cannot be called an interval; and without the motion of things departing and succeeding, it extends farther than every temporal interval.

[Col. 1288A] Thus, when God is said to always be, “to be” is understood as οὐσία (*ousia*, substance), while “always” is understood as eternity. The comparison of eternity with times is understood in this sense: by the expression “always,” he is understood to have been not only while the things said to have been existed, but also before they existed, without any actual or natural beginning; to be while each present thing is, whether actually or at least naturally; and to be future not only while the things that are future will exist, but also, without an actual or natural end, before those things will fail to be, whether actually or at least by nature.

In this way the comparison made by the expression “always,” which is said of God, shows eternity to exceed times in relation to them. The gathering gathers together all the times of all things that were, are, or will be, whether actually or naturally. Looking toward these things in their common relation, he says: “God always is.”

[Col. 1288B] But since there are not many things—whether simultaneous, or departing, or succeeding—by which God exists, there is also no plurality of durations through which the being signified when we say “God is” endures.

Therefore, when someone says “God always is,” although he gathers together the infinite multitude of temporal durations with which temporal things are compared, he cannot in any way gather together a multitude of those durations through which that which is compared endures, because there is no such multitude.

God always is because, whenever temporal things are compared with temporal things, the expression “always” gathers together the times of both things being compared. Here, where the eternal is compared with temporal things, the diversity of all past, present, and future times is understood as gathered together among the things with which he is compared.

But in that with which they are compared, although he is said to have been, to be, and to be future, he is nevertheless understood to have been and to be future by the same singular and simple duration of eternity by which he is present in this instant, without any gathering of present diversity. To make the statement clearer by comparison: between the present of our things—that is, temporal things—and the divine present, both of which are called “now,” there is this difference.

[Col. 1288C] Our “now,” that is, the instant of any natural thing, produces something like a running time through the natural departure and succession of things, or through the sharing of things that do not actually move with things that do move; and through the gathering of different durations among themselves it produces a kind of sempiternity.

The divine “now,” that is, the instant signified when it is said “God now is,” truly remains. No actual or natural departure and succession of any thing by which God is understood to be moves him; rather, he remains in such a way that when it is said “God was” or “God will be,” he is proposed to have been and to be future by the same singular duration by which he is thought to be when it is said “God is.” This makes eternity.

For it is not through the departure of that by which he is said to have been, or through the arrival of that by which he is proposed to be future, but through the permanence of that by which he is said to be, that he is pronounced to have been and to be future just as he is.

Consequently, just as there is one singular, undivided, simple, and solitary essence by which God himself, the eternal one, was, is, and will be God, so there is one singular, undivided, simple, and solitary duration called eternity by which God himself was, is, and will be eternal.

[Col. 1288D] For he both is, and is God, and is eternal. But he is God by essence, whereas he is eternal by duration.

Thus, by the word *now*, when it is said “God is now,” only one singular duration is understood, which is called eternity, by which he is also predicated to have been without beginning and to be future without end.

But when something temporal is proposed, as in “A man is now” or “Heaven is now”—since these things exist not in only one duration but in many, either simultaneously or through natural motion by which things depart and succeed—there is not merely one duration but many. Of these, sometimes different ones are present simultaneously, and sometimes one and sometimes another is present. By these, or by this one, whatever is said to be now is pronounced to be now; and the same thing is often said to have been at one time and to be future at another.

[Col. 1289A] To the word *now*—which is used in one sense of the single eternity belonging to God, as described above, and in another sense of the many times belonging to temporal things—if, when speaking of temporal things, you add *always*, you will produce this proposition: the succession of those durations that fall under the expression *now* changes what is now, through the motion of all things departing and succeeding, into something like a continuous course, uninterrupted, tireless, without termination, and therefore perpetual, in a kind of imitation of eternity.

This perpetual continuity of the course, gathered from the durations through which the motion exists, is properly called *sempiternity*.

It nevertheless differs from *perpetuity*, because by the word *perpetuity* a gathering is understood without comparison, whereas by *sempiternity* a gathering is understood with comparison. By the word *eternity*, however, neither is understood—that is, neither comparison nor gathering.

For, as was said above, God is properly predicated to be eternal by one singular, undivided, simple, and solitary duration called eternity. This is said to lack both beginning and cessation and continuation because God, by the simple essence through which he was, is, and will be, neither ceases to be nor begins to be, either in actuality or by nature.

[Col. 1289B] Nevertheless, *perpetuity* and *sempiternity* are often substituted for it, since both, through the endlessness of their course, imitate the endless instant of eternity, which is without motion—namely, when God is called perpetual and sempiternal.

**Again, etc.]** Up to this point he has said that no thing is something by the place in which a man and other such things are said to be somewhere, or by the time in which a man and anything similar is said to be at some time, while God is said to be everywhere and always.

Now he says the same thing concerning habit and action: “Again, to have and to do”—that is, habit and action—“are predicated of God and of other things in the same way as place and time.”

For example, we say of a man, predicating habit, “He is clothed,” and, predicating action, “He runs.” Of God, predicating habit, we say “He possesses all things,” and, predicating action, “He rules.”

[Col. 1289C] Behold that by these words “again,” as though according to what we said concerning place and time, nothing has been said of either—that is, neither of man nor of God—in such a way that the statement should be understood as concerning being: that is, in such a sense that to be clothed or to run would be for a man himself to be something, or that for God to possess all things or to rule would be for him to be something.

Nevertheless, whoever is clothed or runs is something, and whoever possesses or rules all things is something. But all this predication of habits and actions is assigned to external things.

To put the matter in other words: all these things—habits and actions of which we are now speaking, as well as places and times of which we spoke above—are in some way referred to something else. That is, rational thought supposes that some subsisting thing is somewhere, or sometime, or does something, by reference to things other than those by which any subsisting thing is something; and it supposes God to be everywhere or always, or to possess or rule the things that he possesses or rules.

For even if someone considers a natural habit, which many philosophers have said is a substance, and through whose arrival generation or through whose departure corruption occurs—for example, being animate, having a head, or having a hand—even in that case the thing whose conjunction with another is called a habit is not understood to be something by virtue of that habit.

[Col. 1289D] For although being animate, having a head, or having a hand contributes or removes something from the being of a man—being animate in one respect, having a head in another, and having a hand in another—nevertheless neither the body to which the soul is joined, nor the trunk of the human body to which the head is joined, nor the arm to which the hand is joined, is something by this conjunction. Through their conjunction, however, the man who consists of them is said to have the corresponding habit: animate because he has a soul joined to his body, head-bearing because he has a head joined to the trunk of the human body, and hand-bearing because he has a hand joined to his arm.

From this it is clear what things are something as a whole in such a way that, when someone thinks that any of them is something as a whole, there is no part of them toward which alone the mind directs its attention. If, for example, someone thinks that the soul is a spirit, he does not, by thinking this, suppose that it is a spirit according to one of its parts.

[Col. 1290A] Hence it is clear that the soul is not a spirit because it has a spirit in itself; likewise, a man is not a man because he has a man in himself.

Thus one kind of predication is that by which something truly inhering is predicated as inhering; another is that which, although it becomes the form of things in which something inheres, is nevertheless assigned to external things in such a way that nothing is understood to inhere in anything.

We can more easily distinguish the difference between these kinds of predication—one belonging to things in which something inheres, the other to things in which nothing inheres—by bringing together in one place the examples already given of both.

Notice that he does not say “we recognize” (*noscimus*), but “we distinguish” (*internoscimus*). For in opposites, and especially in those opposed as relatives, as habit and privation, or as affirmation and negation, since the account of one in some way depends on the other, and knowledge of both is more easily attained and their difference becomes clearer when one attends now to one and now to the other in turn, it is useful to set both out in comparison with one another and remove something from one in order to attribute it to the other, or attribute something to one in order to remove it from the other.

[Col. 1290B] For example, among those who are human are Plato, Cicero, and Typhon; among those who are God are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

When it is said that any of them is a man, or that any of them is God, this refers to substance—not the substance that is, but the substance by which something is: that is, not to the subsisting subject but to subsistence.

For substance is called not only the subsisting thing but also subsistence, because each supports accidents, although in different ways.

A subsisting thing is therefore substance—not the substance by which any thing is something, for nothing is something by virtue of a subsisting thing, but the substance that itself is something.

Subsistence, however, is substance—not that on which something rests so that it itself may be something, but that by which the subsisting thing alone is something: that is, by which it is a man or is God, as any of those mentioned above.

[Col. 1290C] Similarly, when someone is just, the statement that he is just refers to quality. He is understood to be just by a quality—not by a quality that is something through resting upon something else, but by that through which the subsisting thing on which it rests is something: that is, by which it is just according to the true account of being.

In the same way, when someone is great, the statement that he is great refers to quantity—not to a quantity that is something through anything else, but to that by which the subsisting thing on which it rests is something: that is, by which it is great according to the true account of being. This is understood according to quantities of intervals, that is, lines, surfaces, and solids.

For nothing is great by virtue of a point, a unit, a number, a place, or a time.

These, then, are the things—subsistences, qualities, quantities of intervals—by which alone a subsisting thing is predicated to be something. In the other cases, that is, in the predications belonging to the other categories, there is nothing of this kind. No subsisting thing is something by any of them: neither by those quantities by which nothing is great, nor by the predications of the other genera.

For example, whoever says that someone is in the forum, as a man, or that someone is everywhere, as God, does indeed refer the statement to the category *where*, that is, to place, which is usually understood through comparison as an accident. He understands “to be” in this way; but not as though that place in which the person is—whether the man whom he says is in the forum, or God whom he says is everywhere—were something according to the true account of being, as a man is truly just through justice.

[Col. 1290D] Likewise, when I say “The man runs,” or “God rules,” or “The man is now,” or “God is always,” the statement refers either to action, as in “runs” and “rules,” or to time, as in “now” and “always.”

That divine time, however—that is, simple eternity—can meanwhile be called *always*, while we are unable to explain in words of proper signification what we are thinking and transfer words according to some proportion. The word *always* is used here not only in the sense of comparison but also in the sense of gathering.

But the point is not that “runs” and “rules” refer to action, and “now” and “always” to time, because a man runs or God rules by an action, and a man is now or God is always by time. Rather, none of these—that is, neither a man by running, nor God by ruling, nor a man or God by time—is something in the way that each of them is something by greatness, that is, in the way that each is great.

[Col. 1291A] Similarly, habit contributes nothing to being something for any of those through whose conjunction the habit is said to exist. He does not repeat this point here, where, for example, he recalls the other matters that seemed more deserving of mention. He will speak more fully about relation below.

Situation and passion likewise do not confer being something upon the things of which they are predicated, since they do not inhere in them—and especially not in God. For situation and passion need not be sought in God; they are not in God, just as they are not in other subsisting things.

**Is it now clear, etc.]** Up to this point he has demonstrated the difference among predications by examples from categories of different genera. He now concludes generally that predications differ, repeating the same distinction in other words.

He says, therefore: “Is it now clear, from the examples that have been set out, what the difference is among all predications?”

As though he were saying: It is certainly clear that some of them, as it were, show the thing—that is, show it to be whatever it is by that through which it is what it is—while others do not show the thing, that is, do not show it to be anything by that through which it is what it is, but rather show, as it were, certain circumstances of the thing.

[Col. 1291B] He rightly calls places, times, actions, passions, habits, and situations circumstances of a thing. For although to be in a place or in time is not to be something, nevertheless nothing is in a place or in time unless it is itself something.

Similarly, although to act, suffer, have, or be situated is not to be something, nevertheless whatever acts, suffers, has, or is situated is something.

Therefore, since nothing is something by place, time, action, passion, habit, or situation, while the things of which these are predicated are all something through subsistences and qualities, and some also through the quantities of their intervals, it is clear that these three predications show the thing, while the others show the circumstances of the thing.

The three are predicated in such a way as to show that the subsisting thing is something through them. The others are indeed predicated, but not in such a way as to show that the subsisting thing is something through them. Rather, from outside—that is, through comparisons with other things and associations of a different kind—they somehow attach to it something assigned to it.

They are therefore not rightly called predications according to the thing, but [Col. 1291C] predications externally compared.

Those, however, that designate the thing of which they are said—that is, the subsisting thing—as being something through themselves, not through other things opposed to them, are called predications according to the thing.

These predications according to the thing, when they are said of things because of their subsistences, through which they are present in their underlying subjects, are called accidents, since they are present in the subsistences of those things. Nevertheless, they are according to the thing because they also inhere in the subsisting things themselves and make them be something.

But when they are said of God, who, because he is simple, is not subject to an accident, the predication is called not only according to the thing but also according to the substance of the thing of which it is said.

### “Come now, etc.”

Up to this point he has divided the categories according to the various ways of predicating; now he shows according to which of these ways relations are predicated. He therefore says: “Come now, let us consider relatives,” that is, let us see in what manner relations are predicated of those things that are referred through them. For it is on their account—that is, so that it may be understood how they themselves are predicated—that we have undertaken to discuss everything said about the diversity of the categories and of predication. We say, then, that relations are predicated of those things referred through them by relational names in the same way as places, times, and the other things mentioned above as circumstances of a thing are attached to it externally: namely, they contribute nothing to those of which they are predicated by making them something, although whatever is referred through them cannot fail to be something.

For especially these things—that is, relatives—do not seem to produce predication in themselves. That is, no relation is predicated of anything in such a way that the thing of which it is predicated is understood to be something by virtue of that relation, since relations are plainly seen to consist through the arrival of something else. He rightly says both “through something else” and “to consist.” For, strictly speaking, they are not predicated in themselves but rather through others; and this is true not only of things that are called relatives, but of whatever exists in relation to something.

Let us consider, then: since “lord” and “servant” are relative names by which relations are predicated of things that exist in relation to something, let us see whether their predication is in itself or not—in itself, or rather through the arrival of something else. This can be understood by comparing something predicated in itself with something attached externally through the arrival of something else.

If, by an act of understanding, you remove from someone the fact of being a servant, I do not mean that you will remove it, but that by the same act of understanding you will already have removed from another the fact of being a lord. For “lord of a servant” is said not merely because the one who is lord has a servant, but also because to be a lord is to have a servant.

Someone may object: when something is white by whiteness, is it not similarly the case that, if you remove whiteness, you have at the same time removed the white thing? We reply that, once whiteness has been removed, the white thing too has thereby been removed, just as, when the servant is removed, the lord too is thereby removed. Yet although these things follow one another, there is nevertheless a difference: the manner in which they follow one another differs because the things connected with each other are connected differently.
