Whiteness, namely, is an accident of the white thing. Nothing other than whiteness is understood by “whiteness” which, having come upon the white thing, would cause whiteness to be called its whiteness; rather, whiteness is called the whiteness of the white thing because the white thing is white through that very whiteness. When it is removed—that is, when the thing itself, and not something else, departs—the white thing necessarily perishes.

With the lord, however, the matter is not as it is with the white thing. If, as has been said, you remove the fact that someone is a servant, the term by which someone else was called a lord does indeed perish—that is, someone ceases to be a lord. But the servant is not an accident of the lord. That is, the reason why, when someone ceases to be a servant, another ceases to be a lord is not that servitude is an accident of the lord in the same way as whiteness is an accident of the white thing. Rather, according to the arrangement considered in civil affairs, a certain power accrues to the lord, by which the servant is restrained from presuming beyond what is permitted.

Since this power, accruing to the lord, perishes—that is, withdraws from the lord—when the servant is removed, that is, when the servitude of the other is removed, it is clear that this power, I do not say does not accrue to the lord, but does not accrue to him in itself in the way whiteness accrues to the white thing. It accrues through the arrival of servants, in a certain manner—that is, through another mode than that by which the arrival of places, times, dispositions, or anything else occurs externally through comparison.

### “Therefore not, etc.”

The sense is: Since a relation is predicated through something externally arriving and being compared, a relative predication—that is, a relation predicated—cannot in itself add anything to, diminish anything from, or alter anything in the thing of which it is predicated.

As was said above, this entire relative predication consists not in what it is to be—for it confers being upon nothing—but rather in nothing other than having oneself in relation to something else, in the comparison of one thing with another. Nor does it consist in just any manner of having oneself, but in a particular manner: not in the manner in which things have themselves through comparisons with places, times, or other things attached externally, as was already mentioned, but in the manner in which they have themselves in relation to each other.

The latter things truly both are said and are what they are in relation to others; and they often possess a reciprocal relation resembling a certain change, whereas those that stand in relation through the arrival of relations often do not possess such reciprocity. For the father of someone cannot be that same person’s son, and what is someone’s double cannot be that same person’s half. In this way many things are related to something else: they are said here to stand in relation to another because, through the mutual alteration of their relations, the comparison conferred upon them by such relations does not return in the opposite direction.

Yet things related to another do not always stand in relation without reciprocal alteration. Sometimes, after the relations have been exchanged, they stand in relation to the same thing. This can be seen from the following example.

Suppose someone is standing. If I approach him on his right, he will be situated in relation to me on the left. I say that he will be so situated, but not because he himself, in the true manner of being—that is, by something inhering in him—is what he is said to be, namely, left. Rather, he is left because I, who am right, have externally approached him, who already subsisted perfectly through the things truly inhering in him.

Again, I compare the same things—that is, myself to him and him to me—after exchanging the relations, so that the relation by which he had stood toward me now applies to me toward him, and the relation by which I had stood toward him now applies to him toward me. For I approach him on the left. See again: he stands in relation to me, but by the opposite relation from that by which he had previously stood toward me.

Now he is situated toward me and is predicated as right—not because of the understanding that he is so in himself, that is, in the true manner of being and by something inhering in him, as something is white by a quality inhering in it or long by a quantity inhering in it, but because, when I externally approach him, who already subsisted through the things truly inhering in him, he is right.

Thus what is right is right from me—or, if one prefers to say so, from the fact of me: that is, from my approaching him, through which I too become more than I am, and do not become left. Yet he is by no means right from himself, that is, from anything by which he either is something or could be something.

Therefore being right or left neither adds anything to the thing of which it is predicated, nor diminishes it, nor alters it in any way. Consequently, it is certain that those things which do not produce predication—that is, which are not predicated according to a property that belongs to some thing in such a way that it is said of that thing in virtue of what it is, so that, when predicated, the thing of which it is predicated is something—can alter nothing at all, nor change anything through any genuine change, nor alter any essence whatsoever.

For whatever these things are said of, they contribute nothing to making the thing of which they are said something other than it was before they were said of it.

### “For this reason, etc.”

From the place where he said, “Ten categories altogether are handed down,” up to this point he has divided all the categories both according to their genera and according to their modes of predication, whether they are predicated of created subsistents or of God. Now he returns to the matter for the sake of which he inserted his discussion of the distinction between the categories and between modes of predication, and he says how the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who are one without number, are nevertheless also numerically many.

The sense is: Since none of those things that are not predicated of a thing in virtue of what it is can alter the thing of which they are predicated, if the Father and the Son are said to be related—as indeed they truly are—and differ in no other way, that is, in no category of nature, except by relation, by which the Father is called Father in relation to the Son and the Son is called Son in relation to the Father; and since relation is not predicated of the thing of which it is predicated as though that thing were what it is by that relation, and is in no way predicated of the thing according to the predication called “according to the thing,” because by it the thing of which it is predicated cannot be or be something—it is clear that relation does not produce that otherness which is called the otherness of things, namely, the otherness produced by those things that are said to be predicated according to the thing, each of which makes the thing of which it is predicated something.

Rather, if it may be said so, relation produces the otherness called the otherness of persons.

Nor should anyone blow away this interpretation as a word of profane novelty. For I have interpreted in this way the otherness of the Father and the Son by which the Father both is and is called other than the Son, and the Son other than the Father—an otherness arising from no difference of any natural category except relation—just as many others before me have interpreted it. Yet this could scarcely be understood. Therefore, when I was about to express and state it, I prefaced the phrase “of persons” with “if it may be said.”

Observe that he rightly says “if it may be said,” and likewise that it “could scarcely be understood.” He does not say “it cannot be said,” but “if it may be said.” Nor does he say “it could not be understood,” but “it could scarcely be understood.” By these words he shows that this expression is not wholly alien to our manner of speaking, nor is the matter wholly removed from human understanding. Rather, a transferred expression, taken from some proportion of reason, cannot explain the matter as it is, and the mind’s understanding labors short of the fullness of reason over that which can be conceived only in part.

Therefore, so that the transference of the name “person” from natural things to theological things may be understood not through the fullness of reason but through some proportion of it, as has been said, it seems necessary to explain in what manner subsistents are called persons.

To make this more easily understood, let us distinguish what we reserved above for distinction at this point: namely, that the property of something is called singular in one respect, individual in another, and personal in another.

Although everything that is individual is singular, and everything that is a person is singular and individual, not everything singular is individual, nor is every singular or individual thing a person.

In natural things, whatever exists is something through something other than itself. And since that by which it is something is singular, that which is something through it is also singular. For just as several things numerically cannot be something through one singular thing, so one thing cannot be something without number. Thus, by the singularity of that through which it is, the thing that is something through it is also singular.

Often, however, numerically distinct singular things are alike according to some of the things through which they are what they are. Therefore, not only the things that exist, but also the things through which they are alike, are one individual. Consequently, neither of those things through which they are alike is itself an individual of the things that exist. For if likeness produces divisibility, it follows that unlikeness produces individuality.

It should be observed, however, that the things through which that which exists is something are either simple, such as rationality, or composite, such as humanity. All simple things are alike either in actuality or in nature, and therefore none of them is individual by any true account of unlikeness. Composite things, however, are some composed from only certain elements and others from all elements. Those not composed from all elements are, like simple things, alike either in actuality or in nature, and therefore none of them is individual.

It remains, then, that only those things are individuals which are composed from all elements and cannot as a whole be like any others—such as Plato’s Platonity, gathered from everything that was, is, or will be both in actuality and in nature.

With these matters established, we must add that every subsistent subsists through the conjunction of many things through which it is what it is—that is, through genus, difference, and accident—and consequently is something through one thing and also through another.

Nor is it necessary that the thing which is thus something should therefore be another thing, merely because it is something through not only one thing but also another, and is likewise something other through another. Thus Plato’s soul is not only, through its genus, a spirit—which is to say that it is something—but through another thing, namely rationality, it is other, that is, rational; and through many other things it is something else and something else. Yet it is not for that reason another thing, for it is something else through one thing and something else through another, while it itself remains one thing.

Conversely, it can be said generally that whatever subsistent thing, when compared with another, is numerically other than it, is not something through any of those things through which the thing from which it is other is something. For although both subsist through certain things and are alike to one another in those things, they are never one in the singularity of the same essence.

One thing is said to be numerically other than another only if it is different from it in all the things through which it is what it is. Thus each thing is, through each of the things by which it is something in itself, something other than any other thing from which it is other.

And since whatever is something is one through that by which it is, just as a thing is in itself something other than another, so also it is in itself one.

For this reason, this quality is in itself one thing distinct from another quality, and this quality-bearer is in itself one distinct from another quality-bearer. Yet this account is not sufficient for any thing that is in itself one to be called a person.

Many things that are thus individually one exist in one thing—for example, in one human being there are body and soul, and everything through which body and soul are what they are. Although, therefore, the human soul is not something through any of the things through which its body is something, and is therefore other than the body and individually one in itself, nevertheless, since there is one human being constituted from all the things through which the soul is something and all the things through which the body is something, and since this human being is something other than those things, neither of them—that is, neither the human body nor the human soul—is called a person, because neither exists wholly in itself.

Although each is other than all the other things through which it is something, they nevertheless exist in one human being, who is whatever body and soul are, and is something other than body and soul. Body and soul, however, are not everything that the human being himself is.

Plato is other than Cicero in such a way that neither is any of the things by which the other is other, and there is nothing that is the same in all the things through which both are what they are. Therefore Plato in relation to Cicero, Cicero in relation to Plato, and each of them in relation to all those from whom it is similarly distinct, is truly one in itself and, in the proper sense, a person.

The same applies to all other things that are other than one another in this way: every animal, every tree, and infinitely many such things. Although philosophers have restricted the use of the name “person” to rational subsistents, as will be said in the book Against Nestorius and Eutyches, in natural things any thing that is called a person is in itself one in such a way that it is one by the singularity of each of the things through which it is what it is, individual by the unlikeness of that through which it cannot be united with any other thing like itself, and simultaneously and individually is not any one of the things through which it is something, while it is other than that thing in the genus of natural things.

We say “simultaneously” because, although it is generated from something, it is individually the same as its generator, but not at the same time. For it is something through that corporeality of paternal blood through which its generator was individually something—not, I say, still is, but was something.

We say “individually” because, by conformity with many things through which it is what it is, those things that are other than it are the same.

We speak of the genus of natural things because, in mathematics and in other genera, several things are other both from one another and from natural things in such a way that they are one through different properties, are individuals through their unlikeness, and whatever one of them is, none of the others is; and then they are not persons—as, for example, the property of any person gathered from all [its constituents].

In theological things, however, it is certain that the Father is other than the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Son is other than the Father and the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is other than the Father and the Son. Yet each of these three, though other, is what it is by that singular, simple, individual, and sole οὐσία—that is, essence—one God, simple, individual, and without participation in another essence.

Thus the three together are God himself: one by the property of essence, simple without composition, individual through its unlikeness, and alone through separation from other essences.

From these considerations it is clear that the name “person” does not fit theological things according to the fullness of the account from which the name derives, but has been transferred from natural things to them according to a proportion that agrees with one part of the same account.

For what was said of natural things—that a person is so individually one that it is not other than any of the things through which it is—is not applicable to theological persons. Indeed, by the same thing by which each is one, each is also other.

There are, nevertheless, certain things which cannot belong to one theological person any more than to one natural person. Rather, just as the persons themselves are other than one another, so these things are said of different persons: generation, birth, and connection.

These cannot be said of one and the same person. For the begetter is not the begotten; the begotten is not connected to the begetter in the same way; nor is the begetter begotten, nor does the begotten connect the begetter and the begotten. The one proceeding from both, who is their connection, is neither of them—that is, neither begotten nor begetter—but is another: one is the begetter, another is the begotten, and another is the connection of begetter and begotten.

Thus theological things are understood to agree with natural things in part of that account—namely, personality—for the fullness of which the name was given to natural things, and to differ in another part.

Here one point above all must be observed: natural persons are first other than one another through the things by which each is something; then, through these things, categories externally attached to them are predicated. Through the opposition of these categories, although the persons are not themselves other, they are rightly proved to be other through the opposition of the things of which they are predicated.

Theological persons, however, since they are one by the singularity of that through which they are and are simple in what they are, cannot be other than one another through opposition of essences. Rather, through the opposition of the externally attached things just mentioned, they are both proved to be and are other than one another.

Therefore, when the author, admiring the name and number of persons in theological things—the secret both ineffable in words and incomprehensible to reason—was about to call that otherness by which the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are other than one another “the otherness of persons,” he rightly prefaced it with “if it may be said,” and added that it “could scarcely be understood.”

### “For altogether, etc.”

He continues to demonstrate that this otherness, by which the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are predicated as being other than one another, is not an otherness of things—that is, it is not according to the things through which the things of which they are predicated are what they are—but rather according to relations.

Whatever things, whether corporeal or incorporeal, are distinct, are distinct through the things by which they are what they are, whether those things are substantial or accidental. Corporeal things are also distinct through places, which are understood by comparison: places in which one body is said to be before another, beyond it, outside it, inside it, or in some similar relation.

Incorporeal things, however, are never distinct through places, but only through the differences mentioned above.

For this is altogether a great truth and rule: in incorporeal things, numerical, individual, or personal distinctions are produced not by places but by differences through which the things subject to them subsist.

The different property of such differences makes things numerically many; their unlikeness makes them individuals; and their incompatibility—by which they cannot belong to one thing—makes them persons. There can be no plurality of such differences in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who are one essence and nothing else.

For it is certain that they are not constituted by several substantial things, nor by accidental things. It cannot truly be said that something came to God according to time, so that he became Father. The Father never began to be Father through the arrival of something, just as he never began to be Father through the departure of something.

I say this because the production of the Son is substantial to him—that is, to the Father: the thing into which he produced the Son from himself through generation is nothing other than substance.

The matter is otherwise in natural things, since production occurs through generation. A human being produces his son through generation not only as a subsistent human being, but also as affected by color, length, and other accidents. Therefore the production of natural generation is partly substantial and partly accidental, especially since through generation certain accidents that were not previously present begin to exist in the begetter or the begotten.

In theological things, however, the production that occurs through generation is purely substantial. For the Father produced the Son through generation into nothing other than that in which the Father himself eternally existed by substantial essence—that is, into God. Through this production neither of them began to be something.

The Son has always existed as the one who received birth from the Father. It is in this sense that the statement is understood: “The production of the Son is substantial to the Father.”

Accordingly, it has been rightly shown that the otherness of theological persons is not an otherness of things—that is, it is not according to certain things through which they are what they are.

Nevertheless, the name “production” is not the name of the divine essence, since only the Father is said to have produced the Son from himself through generation. The essence through which he granted the Son to be God through generation is substantial not only to the one who generated, but also to his Son and to the Spirit, who proceeds from both.

The predication of the Father, however, by which the one who generated is called Father alone, is relative.

### “And if we remember, etc.”

What he said above at greater length about the unity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit according to essence, and about their numerical diversity according to relations, together with certain other matters inserted for this purpose, he here briefly recapitulates.

The sense is: The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit differ only through relations. If we recall all the statements made about God in the earlier parts of this work, let us think about them as we shall now state them briefly: from God the Father proceeded God the Son, and from both proceeded God the Holy Spirit.

Let us understand that these do not differ by places. This is certainly the correct understanding, since they are incorporeal. Since the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, let us also understand that God has no differences whatsoever of similar or dissimilar essences by which he differs from God: neither God the Father from God the Son, nor the same God the Father from God the Holy Spirit, nor God the Son from God the Holy Spirit.

The meaning is that each of the three differs from none of the others in that by which they are what they are.

Wherever such differences are absent, that plurality which ordinarily arises from their diversity is absent. Where this plurality is absent, there is unity of essence. By this unity of essence each of those who possesses it, and all of them together, are one.

Therefore the Father is one God, the Son is one God, and the Holy Spirit is one God; and the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together are only one God.

### “But nothing, etc.”

The sense is: Where plurality is absent, unity is present. In the matters now under discussion, however, there is no other unity than that which derives from the singularity of divinity.

For nothing other than God could have been generated from God. Yet the one generated from the Father is neither another God nor the Father himself; and the one who could proceed from both could be nothing other than God. Yet he is neither another God distinct from them nor they themselves.

“God, God, God” is said distributively of those who are God: the first is said of the Father, the second of the Son, and the third of the Holy Spirit. But the expression by which they are God is not distributive, but imitates distribution—an expression more properly called repetition of unities than distribution.

In numerable things, such repetition does not in every respect, or rather in no respect, produce plurality in the things repeated.

### “Therefore of the three, etc.”

The sense is: Since “God, God, God” is a distribution of those who are God, but a repetition of that by which they are God, the unity of essence of the three—that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—has therefore been rightly established.

But since no relation can be referred to itself—that is, since nothing can be referred to itself by any relation, but always to something else—therefore the predication that lacks relation, namely, that by which something is not referred to anything, is in itself.

The numerical plurality called the Trinity has been constituted in that respect—that is, according to that which is the predication of relation—while their unity has been preserved in that respect which is their lack of difference: whether the one substance, called such in relation to those three; the one operation, by which they operate equally; or altogether the lack of difference in any predication that is said in itself.

By “predication in itself” we must understand here the predication by which, as was said, either essence itself is predicated, or something according to essence is predicated, whether this is said in itself or in relation to something else.

It is said in itself in the examples already given: “to exist always,” “to be everywhere,” and “to operate.” It is said in relation to something else in the case of authority and primacy, which, like essence itself, are predicated indifferently of the three and therefore singularly.

Each of the three, and all three together, is one author and one principle of all creatures. We think that this lack of difference in authority and primacy derives from their essence, according to which these things are predicated of them.

Accordingly, according to the account of personality—which follows the difference of properties and is predicated of each of them not relatively but in itself—there is no such lack of difference that each individually and all three together are one person.

For the Father, because he is God, is the author and principle of all creatures; likewise the Son and the Holy Spirit. But because the Father is called Father by the property through which, as we said above, he is other than the Son and the Holy Spirit, he is a person; and likewise the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Therefore the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three authors of all things, but one sole author; not three principles, but one sole principle. Yet together they are not one person, but three persons.

From these considerations we understand that authority and primacy are predicated of the Father, his Son, and the Spirit of both not plurally but singularly, because of the singularity of their essence, according to which these things are predicated of them.

Personality, on the contrary, is predicated of them not singularly as a collective, but plurally, because of the diversity of their properties, through which they are other than one another.

Therefore he rightly concludes: “Thus, then,” that is, through these considerations, “it is clear that substance,” which in Greek is called οὐσία—that is, essence—“contains unity,” that is, makes the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit the same essence.

Through the singularity of that essence there is one God, one great one, one good one, and so forth; and among the things predicated according to essence there is one lord, one author, and one principle.

Relation multiplies the Trinity—that is, it makes those who are one through the singularity of essence many. Through the diversity of relations, which cannot be said of one and the same person, it makes them many and specifically three.

Therefore, since the relations that must be said of different persons make them many, only those categories that belong to dividing relations are brought forward individually and separately: what is said of one is not said of another.

For the Father is not the Son; that is, the one who is Father is not the Son, and the one who is Son is not the Father. Nor are both together the Holy Spirit. Nor is the one who is the Father the one who is called the Spirit of both—that is, of the Father and the Son—and the one who is the Son is not the one who is called the Holy Spirit. Nor is the Holy Spirit of both one of those from whom he proceeds—that is, he is neither the Father nor the Son.

Only the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are the same God, the same just one, the same good one, the same great one—in short, the same in all those respects that can be predicated in themselves.

He ought therefore to have used the plural verb “are,” since those of whom he predicated one essence under so many names—God, good, great—are many through the diversity of relations. Yet he used the singular “is,” measuring the unity of the verb according to the οὐσία that he was predicating.

This manner of speaking is often found in human writings, as in the phrase: “The angers of lovers are the restoration of love.” He did not say “are” in the plural, as he ought to have done, since he had prefaced the noun that contains both the person and number of the verb according to the grammarians’ rule by using the plural “anger.” Yet he said “is” in the singular because of the singularity of the noun “restoration,” although it is understood to have been used not according to the person and number of the verb, but according to the quality through which the demonstration is made.

Similarly, it is said: “All things was Caesar,” and many other such expressions.

### “Certainly, etc.”

He said that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are altogether the same according to that by which they are what they are—things that cannot be related to one another in the way that subsistents are related.

For whatever subsistents are related to one another differ according to the things through which they are what they are. Nevertheless, so that he might indicate by whatever likeness is possible that which is ineffable—namely, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who are the same in that by which they are what they are, are related to one another by different relations—he says:

[Sane, etc.] It is as though he had said: The Father, with whom the Son is identical, is predicated relatively to the Son as “Father.” This is entirely proper. For it must be understood that, even in created things, relative predication—that is, predication by which something is shown to stand in relation to something else—is not always such that it is invariably predicated in relation to something differing from it both in name and in reality, as “servant” is predicated in relation to “master.” For these names and the realities signified by them—that is, servitude and mastery—and the things of which they are predicated, differ.

But, as has been said, relative predication is not always made in relation to something different. For “every equal is equal to an equal,” and “every similar is similar to a similar.” These are relations bearing the same name. The quantities and qualities themselves according to which the things in which they exist are equal or similar are likewise of the same kind. Even if, by the property whereby they belong respectively to their subjects—one to this subject and the other to that—they are understood to be distinct, they are nevertheless not so distinct as the quantities of the double and the half, and of other unequal things; or as the qualities of white and black, triangular and square, and other contraries or disparate things.

And, not to depart from the example already proposed, the quantities and qualities according to which things are called equal and similar are not so different as the power and baseness according to which one is called master and the other servant. In a certain way they are one—not with the unity that results from singularity, but with the union that is measured by proportion.

Relative predication sometimes occurs even where there is not a union of collection but a unity of property: “The same is the same as that which is the same.” This is not only an identity of union, as when a human being is the same as a human being—for Plato and Cicero are the same human being by the union of species—but also an identity that is truly a unity arising from property: for example, “the rational is the same as the rational,” as the soul of a human being and the human being himself are one rational thing, not by a union of species but by a unity of property, although they stand in relations of partiality and totality to one another. For the soul is part of the human being, and the human being is the whole of the soul, although the human being is whatever the soul is. For although the soul is not altogether that which the human being is, the human being is nevertheless the same as the soul.

And, to come to the matter for which we spoke of relations among things that are thus not different, a similar relation exists in the Trinity especially under discussion—that is, in the three: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. It is the relation of the Father to the Son, and likewise of both to the Holy Spirit. It is similar, I say, to the relation of that which is the same to that which is the same. Just as, in the examples given, whatever identity they possess does not remove their relation, so the identity by which the three are individually one God does not remove the relation of the Father to the Son, or of both to the Holy Spirit.

But the relation of things to one another when they are identical in everything by which they are what they are—or the identity of things that are related to one another in everything by which they are what they are—cannot be found in any other things; that is, there are no other things in which this can be found. If this is so, as indeed it is, the reason is truly the otherness that is akin to perishable things. No subsistent thing is distinct from another without the otherness of those things by which they are what they are; nor can things be related to one another except insofar as they are distinct through this otherness.

But since, among all perishable things, whatever is related to another is made other than that other thing by this otherness, we who think theologically on the basis of some proportion drawn from them must not, in our imagination, be led away from what properly belongs to theological matters. Thus, because by transferring natural names to theological matters we say that the Father is related to the Son, the Son to the Father, the Holy Spirit to both, and both to the Holy Spirit, we must not suppose that they are other than one another in any of the things by which they are what they are. Rather, withdrawing from the property of natural things, we ought to raise our understanding in simplicity, so that we may understand that these three, although related to one another and distinct by the properties of their relations, have one single and simple essence by which each is what he is and all together are one and simple God; and that none of them is in any respect other than another.

Finally, whoever undertakes to understand anything—whether theological, natural, or of any other kind—must approach it in such a way that no fantasy of the imagination deceives him in comparing proportions beyond the things for the sake of which the comparisons are introduced.

But concerning the question proposed—whether there is one essence belonging to those who are other than one another through mutually distinct properties, and whether the diversity of properties makes those whose essence is not diverse other than one another—it has been sufficiently said that, according to theological reasoning, those who are other than one another are nevertheless, in what they are, altogether identical in one singular, undivided, and simple essence; while according to natural reasoning, those who are what they are through one essence are other than one another through diversity of properties, without that distinction which is properly called “otherness.”

Now, Symmachus, and all other wise men to whom, in my desire for your judgment, I have undertaken to submit this investigation of the question, the subtlety of the question as formulated and argued awaits the standard—that is, the rule—of your judgment. By its application, as it were, the things said concerning the question will be shown to have been said truly and in proper order.

He himself implies this when he says: The authority of your pronouncement alone will determine whether this subtle question has been traversed correctly or not, in due order and with a complete exposition—that is, whether it has been brought to the end of its explanation.

If, with the help of divine grace, we have supplied fitting aids of argument to the Catholic position—firmest of its own accord, that is, without rational arguments, in the foundations of faith, that is, because it is founded upon faith—the joy of our completed work will return whence its effect came. That is, we shall rejoice in God, namely the Trinity, by whose authorship we have brought it to completion. But if humanity—that is, the weakness of human nature—has been unable to rise beyond itself so as to demonstrate the ineffable by means of rational arguments, then, to the extent that the weakness of understanding detracts from the perfection of the work, the desires of a will that always clings to incomprehensible things will supply what is lacking.

# On the Predication of the Three Persons

[Col. 1299]

**The Book of Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, Whether the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit Are Predicated Substantially of the Divinity, Addressed to John, Deacon of the Roman Church**

[Note: [Col. 1299D] At that time he was a deacon of the Roman Church, and afterward, namely in the year 523, its pontiff. After returning from the East, where he had been sent as Theoderic’s ambassador to Justin, he was handed over by Theoderic to custody at Ravenna. Shortly afterward he obtained, for a similar reason, a similar palm with his friend Boethius. Hence Boethius’s antiquarian copyist—such was the writing of their best manuscripts—called him “holy” in order to designate him ἰδίως, that is, distinctively; and so also Anastasius the Librarian does in his Life. As a passing correction, in our revision of the Life of Boethius from an old manuscript of that same Anastasius, we have written that he died on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, as the Roman Breviary also has it, not on the fifteenth. From the same manuscript of Anastasius we have likewise restored the statement that his body was received at Rome on the Kalends of June, not on the sixth day before the Kalends, as it stood in the printed editions; the latter was the day of his death.]

(C)

[Col. 1299D] I ask whether the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are predicated substantially of the divinity, or in some other manner. I think that the path of investigation must be taken from the point where the manifest beginning of all things is established—that is, from the very foundations of the Catholic faith.

If, then, I ask whether the one who is called “Father” is substance, the answer is that he is substance. If I ask whether the Son is substance, the same answer is given; and no one will doubt that the Holy Spirit too is substance.

But when I collect the matter again, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit appear to be not several substances but one substance. Therefore the one substance of the three can in no way be separated or divided, nor is it joined together as though from parts into one; rather, it is simply one.

Whatever, therefore, is predicated of the divine substance must be common to the three. This will be a sign of what things are predicated substantially of the divinity: whatever is said in this way of the individuals taken together will be predicated in this way of the three as one. Thus, if we say, “The Father is God,” “The Son is God,” and “The Holy Spirit is God,” we also say, “The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God.”

If, then, their deity is one and their substance is one, the name “God” may properly be predicated substantially of the divinity.

[Note: [Col. 1301C] In explaining these words, Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers, fell into the error condemned by the Council of Rheims in 1148, and acknowledged by Gilbert himself. Saint Bernard reports the character of the man who relates his words in this way in Sermon 80 on the Song of Songs:

“If, therefore,” he says, “anything can properly be said of God, it will be said more correctly and suitably that God is greatness, goodness, justice, and wisdom than that God is great, good, just, or wise. Hence, not without reason, at the council recently held by Pope Eugenius at Rheims, that exposition in Gilbert’s book, by which he commented on Boethius’s words—words wholly sound and Catholic—appeared to him and to the other bishops perverse and altogether suspect. He explained them in this way: ‘The Father is truth,’ that is, true; ‘the Son is truth,’ that is, true; ‘the Holy Spirit is truth,’ that is, true; and these three together are not three truths but one truth, that is, one who is true.

“O obscure and perverse explanation! How much more truly and soundly he should have said the converse: ‘The Father is true,’ that is, truth; ‘the Son is true,’ that is, truth; ‘the Holy Spirit is true,’ that is, truth itself! He would have done this had he deigned to imitate Saint Fulgentius, who says: ‘For the one truth of the one God—or rather, the one truth that is one God—does not permit the service and worship of the Creator and the creature to be joined together.’”

Gofridus gives a fuller account of the whole matter in the third book, chapter 5, of the Life of Saint Bernard.]

Thus, the Father is truth, the Son is truth, and the Holy Spirit is truth; the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three truths but one truth.

If, then, there is one substance in them and one truth, truth must necessarily be predicated substantially. The same is clearly true of goodness, immutability, justice, omnipotence, and all the other things that we predicate individually of each and collectively of all.

It therefore appears that those things which may properly be said separately of each individual, but cannot nevertheless be said of all together, are not predicated substantially but in some other manner. What that manner is, I shall ask later.

For the one who is Father does not transmit this name to the Son or to the Holy Spirit. Consequently, this name is not a substantial name. If it were substantial, then, like “God,” “truth,” “justice,” and substance itself, it would be said of the others as well.

Likewise, only the Son receives the name “Son,” and it is not joined with the others, as are “God,” “truth,” and the other names mentioned above. The Holy Spirit also is not the same as the Father and the Son.

From these considerations, therefore, we understand that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not predicated substantially of the divinity itself but in some other manner. For if they were predicated substantially, they would be said both of each individual and of all together. But it is clear that these names are said relatively: the Father is the father of someone, the Son is the son of someone, and the Spirit is someone’s spirit. Consequently, even “Trinity” is not predicated substantially of God.

For the Father is not the Trinity: the one who is Father is not the Son and the Holy Spirit. Nor is the Trinity the Son, nor the Trinity the Holy Spirit, according to the same reasoning. Rather, the Trinity consists in the plurality of persons, while unity consists in the simplicity of substance.

If the persons are divided while the substance is undivided, then the name that originates from the persons must not belong to the substance. But the diversity of persons produced the Trinity; therefore, the Trinity does not belong to the substance.

Consequently, neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit, nor the Trinity is predicated substantially of God; rather, as has been said, they are predicated relatively. God, truth, justice, goodness, omnipotence, substance, immutability, power, wisdom, and anything else of this kind that can be conceived are said substantially of the divinity.

If these things are correct and accord with the faith, I ask you to instruct me. But if in any respect you happen to disagree, consider more carefully what has been said, and, if you can, join faith to reason.

# Gilbert of Poitiers’s Commentary on the Book on the Predication of the Three Persons

[Col. 1301]

[Col. 1301D] From the investigation of the question that Boethius had written to Symmachus about, it was sufficiently clear that the categories of natural things, diverse in their genera and rational accounts, are transferred by certain propositions and arguments to theological matters; and that, concerning God also, as concerning subsistent things, some things are predicated according to themselves, while others are predicated by comparison of one thing with another. Moreover, even those things which, according to themselves, demonstrate qualities—as though they were circumstances of a thing—are predicated by comparison.

Because, however, some people of limited understanding, hearing that God is simple and that whatever is said of him under a diversity of names—such as God, one, eternal, person, principle, author, Father, Son, connection, and other terms of this kind—is nevertheless one, interpret these names as having the same nature and the same account, they suppose that the essence by which he is said to be God is also the unity by which he is one, and the eternity by which he is eternal, and likewise with the rest. Conversely, they suppose that the Father himself is paternity, the one is unity, and the eternal is eternity, and similarly and reciprocally in all the other things predicated of him in any manner.

The same Boethius writes specifically to John, Roman deacon, about those things predicated under the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. He shows that these names are predicated of different things and that they are distinct not only from one another but also from the essence which, under diverse names, is said to be one in them, while these diverse names are predicated of them without compromising God’s simplicity.

Although this diversity may appear impossible, or scarcely possible, to demonstrate completely, nevertheless, since theological speculation does not altogether admit the laws of natural things, and since, as has been said, the childish error recoils from the name of any diversity in the simple God, Boethius does not seek to establish it—as is usual with a matter obscure because of its difficulty and difficult because of its obscurity—by many testimonies from approved writings, prove it by connections of necessary inferences, or explain it by expanding matters that might arise incidentally and, as it were, from the side of the discussion. Rather, because his addressee is neither malicious nor slow of understanding, he demonstrates each point solely by the proper manner of predication.

For the property of predication whereby, when one of these is predicated of something, another cannot be predicated of it, clearly shows that these names are distinct not only from one another but also from all those things that are said commonly of their substances, and especially from the one thing that is predicated substantially of the three under many names.

This diversity is not merely numerical—that is, that this is one while any other is another—but also a diversity of the nature of the genus and of the place of the rational account. For now remaining silent about natural diversity, and about the diversity that belongs to the genus, he first investigates diversity according to reason; toward the end he will mention the diversity according to genus, which necessarily follows numerical diversity.

Thus, as though on the stage of the sophists, adapting himself to genuine doubts while himself remaining free from doubt, he says:

**“I ask whether the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit …”**

That is, I ask whether the things signified by these names—things which grammarians call qualities according to different rational accounts, and which dialecticians call categories, that is, predicaments—are predicated substantially. In other words, I ask whether they are predicated of the divinity according to the proportion of those things which, in natural matters, are called the being of subsistent things; that is, whether they are predicated of those who, because they are what they are solely by divinity, are called not only God but also Divinity. Or are they not predicated substantially of it, but in some other manner?

He adds “in any other manner” because, in natural things—from which the use of such words has been transferred to theological matters according to some proportion of reason—there is not only one manner of predication. For even among things that are not the being of something else, some are understood according to themselves, that is, not through comparison with anything else: for example, white is called white without comparison with anything else. Others, however, are predicated in such a way that, through their predication, the things of which they are predicated are compared with other things: for example, a place, by which something is said to be beyond something; time, by which something is said to be today; possession, by which someone is said to be wearing a helmet; and relation, by which something is said to be of a certain kind or quantity. In all these cases certain other things are implicitly understood.

Again, among these, some are according to the thing itself, such as white; others are attached externally, such as the place just mentioned and the other things named, as well as corresponding examples from the other genera. Many things are said of subsistent beings according to these and other modes that can be shown through divisions of other kinds. Therefore, when these are transferred to theology, there too the mode of predication is manifold.

**“And I think the path of investigation …”**

It is as though he had said: As a sophist, I ask whether these things are predicated of God—that is, of those who are one God, or rather one divinity—substantially, or in some other way, and what that other way is. But as a more serious investigator, I am greatly concerned to discover which of these is true of them. I therefore think that the path of investigation must be taken from the point where the manifest—that is, manifestly certain—beginning of all things is established: from the very foundations of the Catholic faith.

In the other disciplines, in which generality and necessity are always adapted to custom, reason does not precede faith; faith follows reason. And since, in temporal matters, nothing is not subject to mutability, the necessity adapted entirely to their custom wavers. For whatever is called necessary in them, whether to be or in some manner not to be, is neither necessarily to be nor necessarily not to be. What custom alone gives the name of necessity to is not absolutely necessary.

In theological matters, however, where there is necessity in the true and absolute sense, reason does not precede faith; faith precedes reason. For in these matters we believe without first knowing, but by believing we come to know. Without the principles of reason, faith conceives not only those things which human reason cannot supply the means to understand, but also those things for which reason itself can provide principles.

The Spirit who is from God gives faith this dignity above reason, both in theological matters and even in the things below theology—natural things and others of that kind—whose rational accounts the spirit of this world has subjected to the faith of philosophers. For in natural matters and in other matters, faith precedes every rational account of spiritual things, so that people judge everything by faith before they judge it by reason.

Accordingly, Catholic faith is rightly called the beginning not only of theological understanding but of the understanding of all things: it is not merely an unshaken foundation in the face of uncertainty, but also the most certain and firm foundation concerning mutable things.

Beginning, therefore, from this beginning or foundation of the investigation under discussion, he says:

**“If, then, I ask …”**

He asked whether the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are predicated substantially of the things of which they are said, or in some other manner. This question is not simple but composed of several questions. By these words he is understood to have asked three distinct questions concerning the three: first, whether they are predicated substantially or not substantially, but in some manner other than substantially; and finally, in what other manner.

He seems, however, first to have needed to ask whether they are predicated at all. He could properly have asked this, since some things are predicated and others are not. If it were established that they were not predicated, nothing further would remain to be asked. If it were established that they were predicated, it would rightly be asked how they were predicated: whether substantially or in some other way. And if not substantially but rather in some other way, it would remain to ask in what other way.

He himself, however, omitting the first question—because it is certain to everyone that the things from which the threefold naming by these names arises are predicated—joins the second and third questions into one. But in the investigation by which he dispels doubt concerning both, he separates them. First he explains what must be thought about the question whether they are predicated substantially or not substantially, by the reasoning that Cicero calls a simple conclusion, as follows:

Whatever is predicated substantially of God is said both of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, separately of each and simultaneously of all. But none of the things from which those three names—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—arise is predicated of all, either individually or collectively. Therefore none of them is predicated substantially.

He confirms the first part of this reasoning—the part which dialecticians call a proposition or assumption and rhetoricians call an exposition—by the authority of the Catholic faith.

“Taking the path of investigation from this point,” he says, “if I ask whether the one who is called Father is, according to the οὐσία [ousia], that is, according to his essence, substance or subsistent, the authority of the Catholic faith answers that he truly is substance. If I ask whether the one called Son is substance, the same authority of the Catholic faith gives the same answer: he is substance. No one who adheres to the Catholic faith will doubt—that is, will be able to doubt—that the Holy Spirit too is substance.”

Thus substance is predicated of each individually and separately. It is not only predicated separately of each, but the same substance is also predicated collectively of the three. For when I gather them together, jointly positing the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the same faith presents not several essences in number but one essence in the singularity of essence, entirely without number, by which they are said to be substance; and therefore it presents them as truly one substance.

It is therefore clear that these three have only one substance. In Greek this is called οὐσία [ousia], while in Latin it is called, as has been said, substance or subsistence, or, to speak more precisely, essence. This one substance can in no way be separated or divided, nor is it joined together into one as though from parts.

For when it is said that the essence is one, this must be understood through the singularity or property of the reality predicated of them, not through the union of different things, by which it often happens that many things are called one. Nor is it to be understood through a conformity such as that by which several human beings are called one human being: those who, by their subsistences—which mathematicians may call “humanities”—are human beings are many through the numerical diversity of those subsistences, but similar and conformable through their conformity.

Nor is it to be understood through integrity, as when body and soul are called one animal—not because those things from which the animal consists are, or could be, an animal (for the parts of anything never constitute the whole form of the whole), but because the animal itself, which consists of them, is an animal through the form constituted from all the subsistences of that soul and that body. The individual parts are likewise predicated of the whole, each according to its own subsistence, without confusion with the other part or with both together.

This will be discussed more fully in the exposition of the book written against Eutyches.

There are also other unions among things that are distinct from one another through their own properties, based on other forms of association. But since the author appears to reject, against the errors of certain people, these unions in favor of the unity of the divine essence, we have taken care to mention them so that the exposition might correspond to the character of this work, while passing over the others that do not pertain to this place.

For certain heretics, whose error Epiphanius mentions without naming its author, say that the Son is *similis essentiae*—“of an essence similar to that of the Father.”

[Note: [Col. 1305D] Perhaps *similis* should be read instead of *simul*. Let the more learned judge.]

In this they partly agree with the Arians and partly disagree with them, and for that reason they are called Semi-Arians. For the Arians, with whom Eunomius agrees, deny that the Father and the Son are of one substance, both through the union of diverse essences and through the singularity of one essence. Since a creature cannot be similar to its principle, they consider the Son, whom their doctrine unequivocally confirms to be a creature in his entire nature, altogether unlike the Father.

These Semi-Arians, however, deny that the Son and the Father are of one substance according to the singularity of essence, but affirm it according to the conformity of diverse essences. Thus they in a certain way separate and divide the substance—that is, the essence—of the Father and the Son, which is understood to be one by singularity, because they regard it as one through a union of similarity. For just as things that are similar are themselves distinct, so the things according to which they are similar must necessarily be distinct.

Other heretics, whom Philaster likewise mentions without naming their author, assert God to be threefold in such a way that one part of him is the Father, another the Son, and another the Holy Spirit. That is, the parts of the one God constitute this Trinity, or God is completed from these three parts, so that neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit is perfect in himself.

According to this error, some people, reading that the Son is in the Father, interpret it as though a smaller vessel were contained in a larger vessel. Hence Philaster calls them *metangismonitae* (μεταγγισμονῖται). For ἄγγος (*angos*) is Greek for “vessel,” while μετάγγισμος (*metangismos*) means the entry of one vessel into another.

These people therefore join the substance—that is, the essence—of God together from parts, according to their opinion. For if God is joined together from parts, then the essence by which he is what he is is also joined together from the essences that constitute the parts of God. Whenever one subsistent thing is composed from subsistent things, its whole being—that is, the subsistence by which it is made complete—must be composed from all the subsistences of all its parts.

We do not, however, say conversely that whenever the being of something is composed of many things, the thing which exists through that being is likewise composed of many things. For it can happen that a subsistent thing is simple—that is, not composed from subsistent things—even though its being is multiple. Thus the soul is simple, yet through many subsistences it is something.

In the same way, some people who imagine God to be multiform attribute power, wisdom, and goodness to the one simple God as though they were distinct things. They assert by sophistical devices—not so much arguments as verbal cleverness—that the one and same God is the Father according to power, the Son according to wisdom, and the Holy Spirit according to goodness.

He destroys all these errors when he says: The one essence of the three, by which they are what they are, can neither be separated nor divided in any way, nor is it joined together as though from parts into one; rather, it is simply one, by which those three are one, simple, and altogether what they are. For there is nothing else by which they are what they are except that undivided and simple essence.

That essence is predicated of the three commonly, separately, and collectively, as has been said. Therefore whatever is predicated substantially of the divine substance—that is, of God—must be common to the three, namely to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Strictly speaking, he ought to have said in the singular that the thing which is predicated is also common, since, as has been said, there is only one thing substantially said of them. Nevertheless, because that one thing is often displayed by the proportions of various rational accounts through different modes of signification—whether by a change of genera, qualities, quantities, or the like—when we say “God is good,” “God is great,” and by other names of this kind, he spoke in the plural: “Whatever things,” “which are predicated,” and “which are common.”

Nor is it surprising that in theological matters, where we cannot possess modes of speech naturally related to the things of which we speak, we signify the same thing by many names and in different ways, transferring to its signification the expressions of the other disciplines according to some proportion of reason. We often do the same in natural matters, where there is no such poverty of names: “body,” “bodily,” and “corporeal” signify the same thing in different ways. Likewise “animal” and “animate,” “human being” and “human,” and very many similar expressions.

**“And this will be a sign,” etc.]** This is as though he had said: Whatever is predicated of the divine substance is common to the three. And this will be a sign—that is, this will be an indication—from which it may reasonably be understood what things are predicated substantially of the subsistence of the Divinity, that is, of God: namely, that whatever things, etc. What he calls a “sign” he takes from the rhetoricians. Cicero, among probable arguments, places the sign—things which ordinarily occur—for he says that it indicates in some way the thing of which it is called a sign, but that it requires greater testimony and stronger confirmation. Thus here also the commonality of the predication made of the three together and separately of each is called a sign of the substantiality of the predicate.

For bloodshed, flight, pallor, dust, and similar things are indeed signs of certain actions that ordinarily occur in circumstances accompanying affairs or in the conduct of affairs; yet they are weak signs, since they also occur apart from the affairs to which they are attributed. So too, the commonality of the things predicated—both separately of the three and jointly—is indeed a sign of the substantiality of the predicates, since many predicates are commonly applicable in this way; yet it is a weak sign, since there are certain things that are predicated separately of each and jointly of the three, with singularity both of reality and of name, but that cannot belong to their substance, because they are not predicates according to the thing itself but are externally attached categories, such as principality and activity.

For it is true in itself that the Father is a principle; likewise, in itself, the Son is a principle; and likewise, in itself, the Holy Spirit is a principle. Moreover, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together are one principle. Similarly, the Father in himself is an agent; likewise, the Son is an agent; and likewise, the Holy Spirit is an agent. Moreover, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together are one agent.

Yet neither principality nor activity is their essence, by which they are what they are. Rather, those who are what they are through their own essence are related to creatures by a relation called “principality,” and they are said to be their principle; while through activity they are said to make them. It should also be noted that they did not begin to be a principle, whereas they did begin to make. From this it is evident that some things belong commonly to these three eternally, while others belong to them according to time; yet neither sort is predicated substantially of them. Therefore the commonality of the predicates is a weak sign of their substantiality.

To demonstrate, then, which things are predicated substantially of God, the commonality of predication is useful: for every substantial predicate is truly common to the three. But substantiality itself requires the testimony of another argument and the place of a weightier proof, since not everything that is said commonly of them must be said substantially of them.

Accordingly, when this author had said that this—that is, the commonality of predication—would be a sign of what is predicated of the substance of the Divinity, he did not say that whatever is predicated individually of the three taken together is said of each separately in this way, that is, substantially; for that would be false. Rather, he said: Whatever is said of each separately—that is, in itself—will also be predicated substantially of the three taken together, that is, considered jointly.

This is also confirmed by the testimony of examples, as follows. If we say separately: “The Father is God,” likewise, “The Son is God,” and likewise, “The Holy Spirit is God,” then collectively also: “The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God.” This example makes clear that the Godhead, which is predicated separately of each, is predicated of the same three taken together.

Therefore, if their one Godhead—that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is, as it certainly is, their one substance, which in Greek is called *οὐσία* (*ousia*) and in Latin *essentia* (“essence”), it is clear that the name “God,” that is, “Godhead,” may be predicated substantially of the Divinity—that is, of God, namely, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Thus we have said that the Godhead, which is predicated substantially, is predicated separately of each and collectively of the three. Likewise, we have said that truth, which is their essence and is no other than the Divinity, is predicated of them separately and collectively. For separately: “The Father is truth,” that is, “is true”; likewise, “The Son is truth,” that is, “is true”; likewise, “The Holy Spirit is truth,” that is, “is true.” Collectively, however, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three truths, but are one truth, singly and simply—that is, one who is true.

Thus, because of the plurality of persons, he ought to have made the verb plural and said *sunt* (“are”); but because of the singularity of the truth predicated, he said in the singular, *est* (“is”). Here again this example makes clear that truth, which is predicated separately of each, is predicated of the same three taken together.

Therefore, if the one truth of these three is, as it certainly is, one substance in them—that is, one essence—it is necessary that the same truth be predicated substantially of them. The same applies to goodness, immutability, justice, omnipotence, and all the other things that we predicate singularly both separately of each and together of all.

**Supply:** We say of these what was said of the Godhead and of truth: namely, that if they are, as they certainly are, one substance of the three, it is clear that the same thing is predicated substantially of them, though under a diversity of names.

**“Whence,” etc.]** Up to this point he has confirmed by the authority of the Catholic faith that part of his reasoning which says: Whatever is predicated substantially of God is said both of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, separately and collectively, when they are considered together.

Now he is about to assume that none of those names by which the three are designated—namely, “Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit”—is said either separately or collectively of all three, and to conclude: therefore none of them is predicated substantially. He will demonstrate this point one by one. First, setting aside these particular names—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—he speaks generally of the things included under this general class. As though inserting briefly into his reasoning the place of an assumption and conclusion, he says generally: “Whence it appears that these things…” He is as though saying:

“Godhead, truth, goodness, and whatever else is predicated substantially of the three are said both separately of them and jointly when they are considered together. Hence it appears generally that whatever things are appropriately said separately of each, yet cannot be said of all under one singular name, are not predicated substantially, but rather in another way.” What that way is, I shall inquire later.

**“For that which,” etc.]** This is as though he had said: Whatever is said separately of any one of these three but is not said of all under the same singular name is not predicated substantially of them. For these names—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—when they are predicated of separate individuals but not of all, are plainly not predicated substantially.

For the one who is the Father does not transmit to the Son or to the Holy Spirit the name by which he himself is called Father, so that either the one who is the Son or the one who is the Holy Spirit might be called by the same name “Father.” Consequently, the name “Father,” which is attributed to him alone who is called Father, is not a substantial name. That is, the thing predicated by this name is not truly the substance of the one of whom it is predicated.

For if this name were substantial—that is, if the thing predicated by it were like “God,” that is, “Godhead,” or like “truth,” “justice,” or substance itself, that is, *οὐσία*—then, since we predicate by the name “substance,” it would also be said of the others, namely, of the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Likewise, the Son alone receives the name “Son.” He does not join this name to the others, namely, the Father and the Holy Spirit; nor is the one who is the Father or the one who is the Holy Spirit said to be the Son. This is unlike the case with “God,” that is, with the name “God”; with “truth,” that is, with the name “truth”; and with the other names mentioned above, by which the one *οὐσία* signified by them is predicated separately and collectively of the three whose essence it is.

The one who, although he is called “Holy” together with the Father and the Son—not only in distinction from the *οὐσία* of the Spirit, but also in distinction from the use of the office, which proceeds equally from the three, and from the eternity by which they always are what they are through their *οὐσία*—is nevertheless named “Spirit” through the appellations of these names, which have been drawn together to indicate the property by which he is understood to be distinct from the same Father and Son, is not the same as the Father or the Son. The Holy Spirit is not identical with the Father or with the Son.

Then he concludes his reasoning and says:

**“From these things, therefore,”** that is: Since whatever is predicated substantially of God is also said of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, both separately and collectively when they are considered together, while neither “Father,” nor “Son,” nor “Holy Spirit” is said of all the same beings, either separately or collectively, we rightly understand that “Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit”—that is, the things from which these three names arise—are not said substantially of the Divinity itself, that is, of those who, since they are God by the Divinity alone, are also called “Divinity,” but rather are understood to be said in another way, which will now be explained.

**“For if,”** that is: We have rightly inferred that these things are not said substantially from the fact that they are not said of all three—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—either separately or collectively. For if any one of these were predicated substantially, it is certain that it would be said separately of each and singularly of all three considered together, since the substance by which all of them are what they are is one alone.

**“But these are said relatively.”** He said that these things are not said substantially but in another way. Now he discloses what that way is, saying: It is evident that these things are said relatively—that is, according to what is predicated by these names, those of whom they are said truly possess the very relation signified by the predicates.

For the Father is the Father of someone, namely, of the Son; and conversely, the Son is the Son of someone, namely, of the Father. The Spirit likewise is the Spirit of someone, namely, of the Father or the Son—or rather, of both the Son and the Spirit: that is, the bond or connection.

**“Consequently,” etc.]** Here it seems worth recalling that the unity of all things divided from one another accompanies predicates in every kind of discipline. For whatever is predicated of anything is, with respect to the predicate, that which is signified by the name imposed on it and by the composition of the substantive verb through which it is predicated; but, through a unity that accompanies it, it is one.

Thus what is white is white through whiteness, but through the unity accompanying whiteness it is one; and through both whiteness and the unity accompanying it, it is one white thing. Accordingly, when many things are predicated of one thing, that one thing is in a certain way many, since it is many things. Although it is not the number of that which is by many things, it is nevertheless the number both of the things by each of which it is and of the unities accompanying them, each of which is one.

When one thing is predicated of many, many things are one; and when many things are predicated of many, many things are many. For corresponding to the number of the single things that are predicated there is, through a certain conformity, also a number of the unities that accompany them. Unity is without number when there is no number of the one predicate that it accompanies.

Since paternity, sonship, and connection are diverse, the unities that accompany them must also be distinct from one another. And although substance may be present to substantial things, or an accident to an accident—for example, animation to corporeality and color to an accident—substance itself cannot be present. Therefore the unities present to paternity, sonship, and connection, through which these predicates are three, and also those of which they are predicated—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—can in no way be substances.

Hence the author rightly concludes, saying:

**“Consequently, not even the Trinity is predicated substantially of God.”** This is also evident from the fact that it is not said separately of each one of them, namely, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

For the Father is not the Trinity—that is, the Father is not these three. The one who is the Father is indeed the Father, but he is not the Son or the Holy Spirit. This proof is entirely necessary. For since unities belong only to the things that are predicated and can be said of subjects only according to those predicates, it is impossible for them to be predicated of things in whose absence they are supposed to exist.

Therefore there cannot be one Son who is not the Son, nor one Holy Spirit who is not the Holy Spirit. In the same way, the Son is not the Trinity—that is, he is not these three—because the one who is the Son is indeed the Son, but is not the Father or the Holy Spirit. Nor is the Holy Spirit the Trinity—that is, he is not these three—because the one who is the Holy Spirit, that is, the connection, has this proper name, while he does not receive the other two names: he is neither the Father nor the Son.

Since the three have one Divinity, it is necessary that those who are God through the unity corresponding to that Divinity be one, and that, together with the Divinity and the unity corresponding to it, they be one God. Thus the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are both three and one.

But, as has been said, the Trinity consists in the plurality of persons: that is, a number of unities is predicated of them according to the number of their properties. These properties are distinct from one another and are predicated of distinct subjects, so that the full collection of properties belonging to one of them—together with all the other predicates—is never said of one subject. Hence each of them is another person, distinguished from the other by his own property, considered in itself as one.

Their unity, however, consists in the simplicity of the substance—that is, of the *οὐσία*—predicated of them: unity is predicated of them according to their singular and simple essence, by which they are what they are.

**“But if,” etc.]** He continues to say the same thing: namely, that those things which are not common to the three—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and the Trinity are not predicated substantially; whereas those things that belong to the substance are said commonly of them. Thus the Trinity consists in the diversity of persons, while unity consists in the simplicity of substance.
