If the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are distinct persons, as they certainly are, through properties that cannot be said of one alone, while the substance—that is, the *οὐσία*—by which they are what they are is undivided, then any name that originates from the persons—that is, from a personal property—does not belong to the substance, and is not predicated substantially.

Such a name may arise from one person, as “Father”; from two, as “proceeding,” which is said not of the Father but of the Son and the Holy Spirit; or “sending forth,” which is predicated not of the Holy Spirit but of the Father and the Son; or from all three, as “three,” which is not enunciated separately of any one but collectively of all three.

The Trinity—that is, the unities by which they are collectively said to be three—is produced by that diversity of properties from which arises the diversity called “persons.” Since these properties are not substances, as is most clearly established by the fact that they are not said singularly of all three, separately and collectively when they are considered together, still less does the Trinity belong to substance—that is, the unities by which those properties and those whose properties they are are numbered. These unities are neither predicated of all three together nor separately of each.

To repeat the point again and again: the most certain rule is that whatever is not predicated of the three separately and collectively when they are considered together is not substance. Consequently, neither Father, nor Son, nor Holy Spirit—that is, any of the properties from which these names have been given—nor the Trinity, according to which the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three, is predicated substantially of God, namely, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Rather, as was said above, these things are predicated relatively.

For the Father and the Son are related to one another through paternity and sonship, while the Holy Spirit is related to them through connection. The Trinity, by which they are called three, is not itself a relation—for every number exists in itself—but accompanies the relations by which they are related. Therefore, through its association with those relations, it is said to be predicated relatively.

God—that is, the Divinity understood by this name—and truth, justice, goodness, omnipotence, substance, immutability, power, wisdom, and whatever else of this kind can be conceived—diverse in name but identical in reality—are predicated substantially of the Divinity, that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. With one *οὐσία*, they are predicated, separately or together, as being God, true, just, good, omnipotent, subsistent, immutable, strong, wise, and so forth, being what they are by that same *οὐσία*.

**“If these things,” etc.]** This is as though he had said: I believe that I have demonstrated, by the preceding arguments—which take their beginning from the Catholic faith—that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not predicated substantially of the Divinity. Nevertheless, John, I await your judgment on these matters.

If these conclusions are correct according to the principles of reasoning appropriate to theological matters, and if the arguments are also derived from faith—that is, are consistent with the Catholic faith—I ask you to instruct me by the authority of your testimony; that is, confirm me in my understanding of what has been said.

Or, if perhaps you differ from me by thinking otherwise about some matter—that is, about one of the things stated—I ask you not to prejudice reason through a fabricated faith, or faith through a contrived argument. Rather, examine more carefully—that is, with the greatest diligence—whether what has been said is Catholic faith or follows from what the Catholic faith holds. And, insofar as you are able, join faith and reason together, so that first authority from faith may be furnished to reason, and then assent to faith may be obtained from reason.

# HOW SUBSTANCES ARE GOOD

[Col. 1311]

## HOW SUBSTANCES ARE GOOD IN THAT THEY ARE, ALTHOUGH THEY ARE NOT SUBSTANTIAL GOODS: A BOOK TO JOHN, DEACON OF THE ROMAN CHURCH (C)

[Col. 1311A] You ask me to set out, [Note: He was evidently intending to divide these shorter writings into “weeks,” as Titus Livy divided his great work into decades and Sabellicus into enneads.] in the form of our “weeks,” the obscurity of that question which concerns the manner in which substances are good in that they are, although they are not substantial goods, and to make it somewhat clearer. You say that this should be done because the method of these writings is not known to everyone.

You yourself, however, are my witness as to how vividly you previously grasped these matters. I devise these “weeks” for myself, and preserve what I have contemplated chiefly for my own memory rather than sharing it with anyone, since the frivolity and insolence of such people cannot endure anything detached from jest and laughter.

Therefore do not be hostile to the obscurities of brevity. They are at once a faithful guardian of secrets and possess this advantage: they converse only with those who are worthy.

As is customary in mathematics and in the other disciplines as well, I have set forth terms and rules by which I shall establish everything that follows.

A common conception of the mind is a proposition that anyone approves once he has heard it. There are two kinds of these. One is so common that it belongs to all human beings, as when one proposes: “If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal.” No one who understands this would deny it.

The other belongs only to the learned, although it arises from such common conceptions of the mind; for example: “Things that are incorporeal are not in a place,” and other propositions that are approved not by the common people but by the learned.

“Being” and “that which is” are different. For being itself does not yet exist; but that which is, having received the form of being, exists and subsists. That which is can participate in something; being itself, however, in no way participates in anything. For participation occurs when something already is; something is when it has received being.

That which is can have something in addition to what it itself is; being itself, however, has nothing mixed into it apart from itself. It is different merely to be something and to be something in that which is: in the former, an accident is signified; in the latter, substance.

[Col. 1311C] Everything that is participates in being, so that it may be; but it participates in something else so that it may be something. Accordingly, that which is participates in being so that it may be; but it exists so that it may participate in anything else.

Every simple thing has its being and what it is as one. In every composite thing, its being is one thing and what it is another. Every difference is discordant, whereas similarity is to be desired; and whatever desires something else naturally shows itself to be such as that very thing which it desires.

What we have set out is sufficient. A prudent interpreter of reason will fit each point to its proper arguments.

The question is as follows. Things that are are good. For the common opinion of the learned maintains that everything that is tends toward the good; and everything tends toward what is like itself. Therefore, things that tend toward the good are themselves good. But we must inquire how they are good: whether by participation or by substance.

If they are good by participation, they are in no way good in themselves. For what is white by participation is not white in itself, in that which it is; and the same applies to the other qualities. Therefore, if they are good by participation, they are in no way good in themselves. Yet this has been granted.

They are not good, therefore, by participation, but by substance. And when the substance of things is good, what they are is good; but they have what they are from being. Therefore their being is good. The being itself of all things is therefore good.

But if being is good, then things that are are good in that they are; and their being is the same as being good. Therefore they are substantial goods, since they do not participate in goodness.

But if being itself is good in them, there is no doubt that, since they are good, substantial things are first like the good; and consequently they will themselves be the good. For nothing is like it except itself. Hence it follows that everything that is is God, which is impious to say.

They are not therefore substantial goods; and consequently being is not good in them. They are therefore not good in that they are. But neither do they participate in goodness, for they would then in no way tend toward the good. Thus they are in no way good.

A solution of this kind may be applied to the question. Many things cannot be separated in actuality, but are separated by the mind and by thought. Thus no actual operation separates a triangle, or other things, from the underlying matter; nevertheless, by mentally separating it, the mind contemplates the triangle itself and its property apart from matter.

Let us therefore remove for a while from the mind the presence of the first good. That it exists is certain, and this can be recognized from the opinion of all the learned and unlearned, even from the religions of barbarian peoples.

With this temporarily removed, let us suppose that all things that are are good, and consider how they could be good if they had not flowed forth from the first good.

I observe that there is one thing in them by which they are good and another by which they are. For let one and the same substance be supposed to be good, white, heavy, and round. Then the substance itself would be one thing, its roundness another, its color another, and its goodness another.

For if each of these were identical with the substance itself, heaviness would be identical with color, with goodness; and goodness would be identical with heaviness. Nature does not permit this. Thus there would then be one thing in them by which they are, and another by which they are something; and then they would indeed be good, but their being itself would not be good.

Therefore, if they existed in any way apart from the good and were good, and if they were not identical with what is good, but their being were one thing and being good another, then, if they were nothing whatever except good—neither heavy, nor colored, nor distinguished by spatial dimensions, nor possessing any quality, but merely good—they would seem not to be things but the principle of things. Indeed, they would not seem to be a principle, but one principle: for there is only one thing of this kind, which is merely good and nothing else.

Since these things are not simple, they could not exist at all unless the one who alone is good had willed them to exist. Therefore, because their being flowed from the will of the good, they are called good.

The first good, because it is, is good in that it is. The second good, because it flowed from that whose being itself is good, is itself also good. But the being itself of all things flowed from that which is the first good, and which is such a good that it is rightly said to be good in that it is.

Their being itself is therefore good. For they would not be good in that they are if they had not flowed from the first good.

The question is thereby solved. For although they are good in that they are, they are not like the first good. They are not good because, in whatever way things may exist, their being itself is good; rather, their being itself is good because the being of things cannot exist unless it has flowed from the first being, that is, from the good.

Therefore their being itself is good, but it is not like that from which it derives. For that first good, however it exists, is good in that it is; it is nothing other than good. The latter, however, could perhaps be good if it existed apart from the former, but it could not be good in that it is. It would then perhaps participate in the good; but the being that it did not receive from the good could not itself possess goodness.

Therefore, when the first good is removed from these things in mind and thought, although they might be good, they could not be good in that they are. And since they could not exist in actuality unless that which is truly good had produced them, their being is therefore good, yet what flowed from the substantial good is not like it.

If they had not flowed from it, although they might be good, they could not be good in that they are, because they would exist both apart from the good and not from the good, whereas the first good is itself being, itself goodness, and itself good being.

But must not those things that are white also be white in that they are, since they flowed from the will of God so that they might be white? Not at all. Being is one thing, and being white another. This is because the one who made them exist is indeed good, but is not white.

They therefore followed the will of the good so that they might be good in that they are; but they did not follow the will of a non-white being so that this property might belong to him, namely, that he should be white in that he is. For they did not flow from the will of what is white.

Thus, because the one who was not white willed them to be white, they are merely white; but because the one who was good willed them to be good, they are good in that they are.

According to this reasoning, then, everything ought to be just, since he himself is just who willed them to be. Not even this follows. For being good concerns essence, whereas being just concerns activity. But being and acting are the same in him; therefore being good and being just are the same in him.

For us, however, being and acting are not the same, since we are not simple. Therefore, for us, being good and being just are not the same; but for us, being is the same in all good things, in that we are.

All things are therefore good, but not all are just. Moreover, goodness is general, whereas justice is particular, and a species does not descend into all things. Therefore some things are just and others are something else; but all things are good.

[Col. 1313]

# GILBERT PORRETA’S COMMENTARY ON THE BOOK *HOW SUBSTANCES ARE GOOD*
[Col. 1313C] What in Greek is called φιλοσοφία (*philosophia*), and in Latin “love of wisdom,” is a discipline whose entire form pleases philosophers—that is, lovers of wisdom—although they do not display the whole of it to everyone. For they observe among those who are what they are, namely, among the human race, very many who, like brute animals, have surrendered themselves wholly to the senses or to the imagination; and many others who, by the first movement, as it were, of reason, strive toward those things that must be conceived beyond the senses and imagination. [Col. 1313D] Philosophers utterly despise the former; but the latter they instruct through certain elementary principles and, as it were, signs of outward expressions. These, having received such signs through the discipline called in Greek σχολή (*scholē*, “school”), desire to express themselves. But because they attempt this beyond the rules of expression, they often fall into errors; and often they stammer out things that are incongruous, incomplete, or excessively wordy.

Some of them are held fast to these elementary signs of outward expressions either by the torpor of negligence or by dullness of intellect. Others, however, are drawn toward the very truth of things, which the mind’s acuteness naturally perceives beyond expressions, by their desire for that truth. The philosophers assign these also to duties appropriate and suited to them. For they allow the dull to labor constantly in an uncultivated and—as one might say—rustic style, in which the meaning is more enveloped than unfolded; but they do not expose to them the splendid form of wisdom, lest it should be prostituted. [Col. 1314C]

Others they direct toward a certain path called that of reason; yet they do not admit everyone equally to it. They lead the greater number, running along common arguments known to all as along a public road, toward an image of wisdom, which is in some manner sketched out in the combinations of natural things. But many who have become accustomed to these mirrors of nature they summon to those things that a higher discipline, called in Greek μάθησις (*mathēsis*, “learning”), draws away from the combinations of natural things, so that there they may more purely comprehend the nature and property of things and, through this, the form of wisdom that is more fully reflected in such matters. A few, however, whom they see to be attentive with more concentrated study, sharper in the acuteness of their minds, and drawn not so much upward by the frivolity of personal praise as by the beauty of truth itself—truly worthy persons in whom the dignity of wisdom may be exercised—they lead into a kind of retreat outside the public road of rational disciplines, into θεωρήματα or ἀξιώματα, that is, the speculations or dignities of the disciplines.

There, in a kind of secret recess, they reveal to them a certain dignity of wisdom itself surpassing that of others. These few, therefore, contemplating it for a long time and with great devotion in that acuteness of mind called intellect—in every kind of subject, namely, in natural philosophy, mathematics, and above all theology—marvel that its arguments differ from the arguments of others, and that the expressions by which they can be explained are not kindred with them. And whenever words must, or even necessarily do, get transferred from another argument to it by some proportion of reason, they produce exceedingly intricate questions. [Col. 1315A]

These, then, are the hidden matters of wisdom known to only a few in each discipline, but especially in theology. Because the glory of their dignity draws the admiration even of the greatest philosophers, they are called by them παράδοξα (*paradoxa*), “paradoxes.” And because they produce questions when expressions are transferred and employed in them, they are called ἐμβλήματα or ἐνθυμήματα (*emblēmata* or *enthymēmata*), that is, “propositions.” Since this higher understanding perceives them through excellence, they are called ἑβδομάδες (*hebdomades*), that is, “conceptions,” altogether different from those conceptions that are called ἐνθυμήματα.

For there is one kind of argument in which, before the conclusion, a λόγος with a λόγος—that is, one statement with another—is joined as an assumption to a proposition; and therefore the whole expression is called συλλογισμός (*syllogismos*), that is, a “joining together in discourse.” There is another kind of argument in which something is indeed stated before the conclusion, but something else that ought similarly to have been expressed in words is retained in the soul without expression, as in: “There is a human being; therefore there is an animal.” Here, from what has been stated—“there is a human being”—and from what is thought without expression, namely, that a human being is naturally an animal, the conclusion is reached: “Therefore there is an animal.” For this reason the whole expression is called an ἐνθύμημα (*enthymēma*) from that part of the antecedent which is held in the soul without exposition.

There are also other enthymemes, which either leave something in the mind in accordance with the quality of rhetorical summaries, as in “A mother loves,” or, by including something placed under an interrogation, wish the contrary to be understood, as in “What you know is beneficial, and what you do not know is not harmful.” But such conceptions possess no dignity. They do not depart from reason or from the custom of ordinary speech; and the orator holds them more firmly in the mind for the very reason that he judges it superfluous to set forth in speech things so familiar to everyone.

But those that are called hebdomades are entirely remote from the understanding of ordinary people. Even those who have studied many subjects and have been tested and disciplined through sophistical exercises are moved by the wonder of them; and, as has been said, they admit only a few, and those thoroughly approved, to their contemplation. The lover of wisdom Boethius held many such matters before his mind and, for the deacon John, who had long been knocking and was worthy that it should at last be opened to him, brought some of them forth as he was able, in natural—and therefore constructed and artfully fashioned—discourse.

Among them was one conception according to which the things that are are good in that they are, although they are not substantial goods. John revered this wonder, but a certain conflict of arguments that seemed to be present in it excluded him from understanding its meaning through the truth of his own perception. At his request, therefore, Boethius first proposed this conflict to him: he concluded, through certain apparent arguments, that the things that are are not merely good in that they are, but are in no way good at all. Then he cut through the entire cloud of this riddle by means of a division and thus admitted him to an understanding of the dignity of the hebdomades, that is, of conception.

[Col. 1315D] “You ask,” etc.]: He first sets forth, as a brief prologue, what the deacon John is asking and what Boethius promises to do about it, so as to stir his attention, which was especially necessary for presenting and resolving the proposition. He says:

“You ask”—as though requesting something owed by our friendship to you—that I should set out one of our hebdomades, namely, the obscurity of the question contained in it: the manner in which substances—that is, things subsisting in nature—are good in that they are, although they are not substantial goods. This means that goodness itself is not the being of the subsisting things of which it is predicated. I shall arrange this matter and, a little later, display it more clearly—that is, make it clear to some degree—by showing which arguments appear capable of proving the affirmation and which the negation, and by explaining at what point in the multiplicity of meanings, through division, error gives way to true knowledge.

“And you say that this ought to be done”—that is, that the obscurity of this question ought to be arranged in this way—because the path of writings of this kind is not known to everyone: that is, not many people have been accustomed to write about such matters, or even know how to write about them. For although Socrates, Cato, and many others sometimes inserted into their speeches these matters, which they called “weighty topics,” they nevertheless devoted themselves very little to treating them.

I have learned from the examples you sent to me, so that I might write about this question, that this path of such writings is known to only a few and that you have truly paid attention to it; indeed, I have learned that you have been so greatly pleased by it lest, if such matters were treated by many in ordinary usage, they should become cheapened. For from what I read in it I myself am your witness as to how vividly you had formerly embraced—that is, how much you had approved—these points: that, as has been said, the path of such writings is known to only a few.

You therefore ask that the aforementioned hebdomad be set out in this manner. I myself, however, do indeed meditate on this and other hebdomades—that is, I frequently call them to mind—but only for myself. What I have contemplated I preserve in my memory [Col. 1316B] rather than share—that is, communicate it to any of those whose inward frivolity and outward insolence allow nothing to remain joined, that is, complete in itself and harmonious with others, which the Greeks call ἁρμονικόν (*harmonikon*). This arises not from rational reflection of the mind but from the sport of frivolity and the laughter of their insolence. Such people customarily praise only their own inventions, while disparaging those of others and mocking them as though they belonged to no one.

For their sake, then—since we cannot remain altogether silent on account of those who appear worthy—we cover the secrets of wisdom with an appearance fashioned from multiplied topics, or at least with some compression of words. Therefore I warn you not to be hostile toward the obscurities of brevity, that is, toward those that may arise from brevity. These obscurities, besides being a faithful safeguard of the secret against the crooked bites of detractors—which is no small benefit—also possess this natural advantage: they converse only with those who, insofar as they can, trace out the path of fitting arguments and acquire, through the expenditure of unfailing study, the secrets of conceptions; such people are truly worthy to be admitted to them.

[Col. 1316C] “Therefore, so that,” etc.]: It is as though he had said: “You ask me to arrange and display more clearly the obscurity of the question,” and so forth. “Therefore, in order to satisfy your request, I proceeded as is customary above all in the mathematical discipline—that is, in arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy—and also in many other disciplines, as in the Categories and the Analytics, in which certain things necessary for the subsequent discussions are placed beforehand. Thus I placed the terms and rules first.”

He calls the same things “terms” and “rules”: “rules,” because by a local analogy they contain many things; “terms,” because from their principles the demonstration of the propositions is derived and by their final inductions, as by boundaries, it is terminated. These, therefore—whether terms or rules—I placed first. Through them I shall accomplish everything that follows: by them I shall show both that the proposed hebdomad can be brought into doubt and that, by dividing the point of multiplicity, I can confirm it.

“Common,” etc.]: The first rule he sets forth is the foundation of all that follows—indeed, of all general propositions, whatever discipline they belong to—which he also calls “conceptions” in this passage. To say nothing of the positive rules of grammar, it is certain that the common topics of rhetoricians, the maximal propositions of dialecticians, the theorems of geometers, the axioms of musicians, and the general propositions of ethicists or philosophers are all contained in the universality of this rule, which says:

“A common conception of the mind is a statement that everyone approves when he hears it.”

He calls the conception under discussion “a conception not merely of one mind, but of a common mind,” that is, of many minds, because it is a topical principle concerning innumerable, particular, conceded, or doubtful matters, and is so familiar to many either by nature or through the artificer Logic, that when it is brought forward to confirm something, it does not require the testimony of proof. Hence elsewhere it is called indemonstrable and self-evident, and here “a statement that everyone approves when he hears it.” This is why it is either frequently inserted among other discoveries or set forth after speeches that are already complete and concluded: because it is altogether beyond doubt to those with whom discourse is conducted, either naturally or through the discipline of logic.

Nor should it trouble you that a conception is called a statement, or that, conversely, a statement is called a conception, since we both state what we conceive and conceive what we state.

There are two kinds of these things called common conceptions of the mind. One is so common to the mind that it belongs to everyone—that is, all human beings know it naturally. For example, if you propose this geometrical conception: “If you subtract equal things from two equal things, the things that remain are equal,” no intelligent person—that is, no sane human being—would deny it. For all people, even apart from the discipline of logic, naturally recognize it as true.

Another is common to the mind not in the sense that it belongs to all human beings, but only to the learned; nevertheless, it arises from such conceptions as, in the manner described above, are common to the mind. An example is: “Incorporeal things are not in a place.”

This is not itself a topic belonging to what is called the universal realm of logical reasoning, but it is a natural principle proceeding from a logical topic. For among dialecticians there is a general topical principle known to all: what belongs properly to something alone cannot exist without that thing. For example, color, because it belongs as an accident only to a body, exists only in a body. From the universality of this topic, which is naturally known even to all human beings, comes this natural conception or statement: “Incorporeal things are not in a place.”

For place, whether it is understood as the local container or as something located, properly belongs only to bodies. The delimitation of a solid interval, which in the genus of quantities is called “place,” exists only in bodies. Likewise, that place which is called *collocation*—an arrangement arising from a certain ordered comparison of intervals with one another—belongs only to bodies. According to it, bodies alone are properly said, in general, to be located, and specifically to be within and outside, beyond and this side of, beneath and above, and in other such relations. This collocation applies to all the parts of the world’s structure.

The world’s structure itself, taken as a whole, is certainly local, since its extension in intervals is held within certain boundaries—in other words, it is circumscribed. Yet it cannot, considered as a whole, itself be located. For on account of it there is no other body in relation to which it could be said to be outside or inside, beyond or this side of, beneath or above, beside or around, or to receive any such predications. In this respect it agrees with incorporeal things: because they are not local, they cannot in any way be understood as located.

But, as has been said, although that maximal proposition and general topical principle from which this natural proposition proceeds, and in which it is contained together with infinitely many others, is naturally known even to all people, this particular proposition that proceeds from it is said to belong only to the learned. This is rightly so. For the rest, deceived by the usage of words—which often extends beyond nature for some reason—understand the following expressions according to the same sense: “The soul is inside the body of an animal and outside the body of a stone”; “a line is situated in a body and is outside the soul”; and similar expressions. They hear these according to the sense in which one body is inside or outside another body.

The learned, however, whom the single appearance of different expressions does not deceive, distinguish the senses that differ beneath the same verbal form; and therefore they recognize what others do not at all perceive. This, then, is that common conception or statement of the mind which belongs only to the learned, together with other such conceptions that the common crowd does not approve, but which the learned approve through long use of different disciplines and through both examples and rules.

“Second rule: Being and that which is are different. For being itself is not yet; but that which is, having received the form of being, is and subsists.”]

Here it seems necessary to note that, through differing usage among different philosophers in different disciplines, “being” and “being something” are called different things. In theology, the divine essence that we predicate of God when we say “God is” is said to be the being of all created things. For when we say “a body is,” or “a human being is,” or something similar, theologians understand this “being” as stated by an extrinsic denomination from the essence of its principle.

They do not say that a body is through corporeality, but that it is something; nor that a human being is through humanity, but that he is something. Similarly, they say that each subsisting thing is predicated through the essence of its principle not to be something, but to be. The subsistence created in the thing itself, however, they say not to be, but to be something. In the same manner, whatever exists through the operation of the supreme principle they say to be through that same principal and uncreated essence, but to be something through its own particular genus.

Among those philosophers whose disciplines have their own genera, some say that only those things that began to exist from a principle are “being”; others say that whatever subjects of their discussions—that is, the matters about which they speak—are both “being” and “being something” in the same sense in which they say that they are. Hence they also say that the verb “is” is predicated equivocally of all things. Others make a distinction: they say that subsisting things are through their subsistences, and that they are something through what accompanies their subsistences, namely, intervallic dimensions and qualities. They do not grant to the remaining seven genera of the categories that, through the same subsistence, they are either “being” or “something.” Similarly, they do not agree that any of the things separated by mathematical abstraction from the things of which they are predicated is either “being” or “something.”

Therefore, when it is said that “being” and “that which is” are different, according to theologians “being” is understood as that which is the principle, while “that which is” is what proceeds from the principle. According to other philosophers, “being” is the subsistence of those things that are predicated, while “that which is” is only those things that subsist by possessing those subsistences in themselves. Thus, according to both theologians and other philosophers, it can rightly be said that “being” and “that which is” are different.

But the subsequent discussion will teach us that this rule, as well as those that follow it apart from the seventh, must here be understood according to the usage both of theologians and of other philosophers. Nevertheless, for the sake of making them more significantly clear, we shall illustrate all of them except the seventh with examples from natural things.

He therefore says: “Being is different”—that is, the subsistence that is in a subsisting thing—“from that which is”—that is, from the subsisting thing in which subsistence exists: for example, corporeality and body, humanity and human being.

“For being itself, which the intellect in a certain manner separates by abstraction from that in which it exists, is not yet.” He does not say “is not,” but “is not yet.” For when we contemplate that simple and pure form as it is in itself—which is to attend to it in a way other than the way in which it exists—it is, in a certain respect, not, because it is not in the manner in which it is attended to. For although it is attended to abstractly, it nevertheless exists unabstracted.

“But that which is, having received in itself the form of being”—that is, the subsistence which the intellect conceives abstractly—“is.” This reception, which is called generation, consists in the concurrence of matter, called ὕλη (*hylē*), and this form, called in Greek οὐσιώδης (*ousiōdēs*), “essential.” The form called οὐσία (*ousia*), “essence,” brings it to subsistence according to the exemplar called εἰδέα (*idea*), “form,” as εἰκών (*eikōn*), that is, as the example and image of that exemplar. Thus a body, because it has corporeality as its mode of being, is a body; and a human being, because he has humanity—

“Third rule: That which is can participate in something; but being itself in no way participates in anything. For participation occurs when something else already is; and something is when it has received being.”]

The meaning is this: that which is—that is, the subsisting thing—is able to participate in something because the subsistence that it has in itself can contain within itself something else belonging to the potentiality of that subsistence. Thus a body, which is through the corporeality it has in itself, can have in itself color, a line, qualities of different genera, and other quantities belonging to the potentiality of corporeality, through which it is itself qualified and quantified.

But being itself—that is, the subsistence present in a subsisting thing—in no way participates in anything. For what does not have in itself the being by which it is cannot in any way, together with being, have in itself that by which it is qualified or quantified. Being is subsistence, not substance. Thus, since it cannot have in itself that by which it is, it will truly have nothing else in itself through participation.

For when something—that is, a subsisting thing—is already some subsistence, then participation occurs in another nature belonging to the potentiality of that subsistence, through which the subsisting thing is qualified or quantified. Among things that are predicated there is a certain order—not of time but of reason—in which that which is being naturally comes first, and what is attached to it by reason of a certain property follows. Hence, when something already is, one then asks what it has by which it participates in being with something else. That something is present when a thing, as was said in the second rule, has received being—that is, the form of being.

“Fourth rule: That which is can have something besides what it itself is; but being itself has nothing else mixed with it besides itself.”]

This rule in a certain way explains the meaning of the preceding one. That which is was said to participate in something because that which is itself can have something besides what it is—that is, besides the being through which it is. Thus a body can have color in addition to corporeality, through which corporeality it is.

Being itself, however, does not participate in anything because it has nothing else besides itself mixed within it together with whatever it might hypothetically be conceived to be.

“Fifth rule: Being something merely and being something in that which is are different; in the former an accident is signified, in the latter a substance.”]

As we said above, certain philosophers say that subsisting things are through subsistences alone and are something through certain things that are other than subsistences, namely, through accidents. According to this usage, in this passage only the subsisting thing is said to be something through accidents.

We also say that something which is something is sometimes said to be something in that which is, and this too in two ways; at other times it is simply said to be something, in no way in that which is. For example, a certain work is called bronze, human, and triangular.

“Bronze” and “human,” however, are said to be in that which is, though in different ways; “triangular,” by contrast, is said to be in no way in that which is, but merely to be triangular. The work is said to be bronze in that which is because, precisely by being what it is—namely, by its own genus—it is called bronze. It is said to be human in that which is, not because it is human through the genus by which it itself is, but because this work, which is predicated to be bronze, is human for the reason that its maker is truly human in that which he is, according to his own proper genus. For color came to the stone—after it had been dissolved and thus become bronze—through a human intermediary and, in a certain manner, through a human maker.

The same work is indeed called triangular, but in no respect in that which is. For it is not triangular by the very fact that it is—that is, by its own genus. Nor is it triangular because the being of the work, through which the work itself is said to be, is triangular on account of its maker, namely, a human being, being triangular. Thus it is called triangular solely through an accidental figure, which is the being neither of the work nor of its maker.

It is therefore clear that “being something merely”—that is, being something to which “in that which is” cannot be added when it is predicated—and “being something in that which is”—that is, being something to which “in that which is” can be added—are different.

In the former case, when something is said to be something in such a way that “in that which is” cannot be added, an accident is signified: that through which the thing is said to be something, as when a work is said to be triangular. In the latter case, when something is said to be something in such a way that “in that which is” can be added, a substance—that is, a subsistence—is signified: that through which the thing is said to be something.

This may signify either the subsistence of the being itself that is stated to be something—for example, “the work is bronze”—or the substance of that being, by whose maker there is the being of that which is stated to be something, through which both its being and the thing itself are affirmed to be something by the maker’s same subsistence—for example, “the work is human.”

“Sixth rule: Everything that is participates in that which is being, in order to be; but it participates in something else in order to be something. And therefore that which is participates in that which is being in order to be; but it is in order to participate in anything else.”]

Above, in the third rule, where it was said that “that which is can participate in something,” he called participation the having by that which is, together with its being, of something else. Hence in the fourth rule he explicitly said: “That which is can have something besides what it itself is.” In this he also clearly showed, both in what he placed at the end of the third rule—“something is when it has received being”—and in what he added at the end of the second—“that which is, having received the form of being, is”—that to have being itself is participation.

Thus, in this sixth rule he clearly calls both kinds of possession participation: the possession by which being itself is possessed, and the possession by which something else is possessed together with it, both by one subject—that is, by that which is. He says:

“Everything that is”—that is, every subsisting thing—“participates in that which is its being,” not indeed in order to be something through it, but only in order to be through it. Together with the same being, however, the same subsisting thing participates in something else, so that through it it may be something.

The participation by which it participates in being is prior by nature; the other is posterior. Hence he concludes: “And therefore,” as though to say: Since a thing cannot be something unless it first naturally is, that which is, as has been said, participates in being in order to be. It is naturally prior to participate afterward in anything else through which it is something.

“Seventh rule: Every simple thing has its being and that which it is as one.”]

This can be illustrated only in theological matters. For all natural things are not merely created but also concrete. Mathematical things, although they are said to have in themselves neither in reality nor according to proportion that by which they are or are something, nevertheless have certain parts according to which they consist in their own rational structure. Examples include the complete property of first substances, which is gathered from all their parts, both innate and externally attached, and the special subsistence that consists of the general nature and its potentialities.

The effect of these things, and of all other things that are called simple because they do not have parts of this kind, is multiple. God, however, is altogether simple. Since we do not have expressions cognate with him by which we may speak about him, we transfer words to him from natural things, saying: “In God there is an essence by which he is, a power by which he is powerful, a wisdom by which he is wise,” and so forth. Yet we do not conceive that his power or wisdom—which we use to say that he is something—differs, in the manner of being, from the essence by which we predicate him to be, although we neither know nor can know at all what he is in that respect.

Under the diversity of these names there is in him not merely a union of things, but the unity of a singular, simple, and undivided thing, so complete that the following may truly be said of him: not only “God is,” “God is powerful,” and “God is wise,” but also “God is the very essence,” “God is the very power,” “God is the very wisdom,” and so forth.

For he alone, whatever he is according to the diversity of such names, is truly in that which he is, and is himself that which he is, through the diverse use of one gift of his, namely, the Holy Spirit. Whoever else, through a different use of the aforementioned gift, is powerful, wise, or something of this kind, is indeed in some manner this in that which he is, but is in no way himself that which he is. For he is several things and is something through several things; but God, through the same thing by which he is, is something and is truly in that which he is, and is truly that which he is.

Therefore it seems rightly said that every simple thing has its being and that which it is as one. That is, if someone says of what is truly simple, “It is,” and then also says, “It is something,” no one should understand that in the second statement he has predicated of it some property different from what he predicated in the first.

Thus, if someone says of either the Father, the Son, or the Spirit of both: “He is”—for example, “The Father is,” “The Son is,” “The Spirit of both is”—and afterward says of the same Father, the same Son, or the same Spirit of both: “He is something”—for example, “The Father is powerful,” “The Son is powerful,” “The Spirit of both is powerful”—it should in no way be understood that the being by which he is is one thing and the being by which he is powerful another. For in the Father, the Son, and the Spirit of both, being and being powerful are altogether the same. Likewise, in each of the three, being and being wise are the same; and similarly, in each of them, being and being good are the same, and so forth. This is not at all true of non-simple things, which include everything created that subsists.

Hence there is also the eighth rule:

“Eighth rule: In every composite thing, its being is one thing and it itself is another.”]

Composition is understood in two ways. One is the composition by which a subsisting thing is said to be composed of subsisting things that are different from one another and from which the composite itself is something else. Thus a human being is composed of flesh and bones, or of body and spirit.

Of this kind of composite it is beyond doubt that many things are predicated. For everything by which any component is what it is, everything by which it is something, and the being that is composed from the being of all the components together with certain other things—through which the composite itself subsists and through which that same composite is something in accordance with its composite being—are all predicated of the human being. Thus: “A human being is flesh and bones”; “a human being is body and spirit”; “a human being is colored”; “a human being is capable of understanding”; “a human being is suited for laughter”; and many similar predicates.

There is another kind of composition in which a subsisting thing is not composed from subsisting things—for in this respect it is simple—but its property consists both of many things through each of which it is and of many things through each of which it is something. For example, the spirit of a human being is one and simple insofar as it does not consist of different subsisting things; yet it is through many subsistences and is something through many accidents of those subsistences. Therefore it is composite, and it is not itself that which it is.

For we do not attend to composition in it in this way: one thing is that which it is, and another is that through which it is. If, just as that which it is were one thing only, that through which it is were likewise one simple thing only—through which it both was and was something—it would in no respect be composite.

Therefore, since it is through one thing and is something through another, even if it does not consist of different subsisting things, the subsisting thing itself is concrete and composite. Since every subsisting thing is of this kind, he says generally:

“In every composite”—that is, in every subsisting thing—“its being is one thing,” namely, that through which it is; “but it itself is another thing, through some other thing,” namely, that by which it is something.

### Ninth Rule: Every diversity is discordant, but likeness is to be desired; and whatever desires something else naturally proves itself to be such as that very thing is which it desires.

Identity is contrary to diversity; likeness, however, is contrary to dissimilarity. Therefore, although “the same” is said in certain respects, and “different” likewise in those same respects, here he has taught that diversity is to be understood in the respect in which likeness is understood. For, having prefaced the statement “Every diversity is discordant,” he did not add “but identity,” but rather “but likeness,” and so forth.

Likeness is a certain comparison arising from the proportion of contraries or of equals, or of things falling under the same account. That meaning has nothing to do with the present passage. [Col. 1321D] There is also another kind of likeness relevant here, which is more properly called likeness: namely, a certain union of diverse things. I say “union,” not “unity,” and “a certain union,” not just any union.

For that which is called unity in the proper sense is produced solely by the property of a singular nature. Sometimes that nature exists in only one thing, as does any nature by which some heavenly spirit is one particular thing; sometimes it exists in many things, which, although they may not be diverse in number from one another, are at least diverse in number from something else. Such is any nature of the human body, which is said to exist not only in the body of a human being but also in the human being himself, who consists of a body, and which is predicated of that human being. Yet the human body and the human being differ numerically not as body and human being, but only as two human things.

For the human body is not, by the property of its nature, one thing other than the human being; rather, the human being, by the properties of his many natures, is one thing other than the human body. Hence the human being and the body of which he consists are said not to be united to each other, but truly to be one and the same—not, however, because that body is altogether the same as the human being, but because the human being is altogether the same as that body.

[Col. 1322A] Union, on the other hand, always belongs to things that are diverse from one another in number. But such union occurs in different ways, according to the different accounts arising from diversity. Matter and form are said to be united to each other in one way, so that what consists of them is one subsistent thing by a certain rational arrangement. Part and part are united in another way, so that what consists of them is one whole by a natural or rational arrangement, or through associations of other kinds. Thus, in civil matters, or in language, custom, law, place, or affection, many are said to be one nation, one people, one assembly, or one heart through a shared unity. None of these matters concerns the present passage.

There is, however, a union of things diverse in number from one another that is produced by the account of conformity, and this concerns the present passage. This union is called likeness, and it is either according to nature or according to certain extrinsic features.

[Col. 1322B] According to nature, it is of two kinds. It is either according to the fullness of the nature proposed, and is called substantial likeness—as white is like white and a human being like a human being—or according to certain parts of the proposed nature, and is called imaginary likeness—as a human painting is said to be like a real human being.

That likeness which is according to extrinsic features is called imitation. Thus one craftsman is said to be like another craftsman, or a human being like God, when he does something according to God’s will.

Therefore, wishing “every diversity is discordant” to be understood against this union of likeness as a diversity of dissimilarity, he says: “Every diversity of dissimilarity is discordant.” For contraries in a certain way recoil from and flee one another.

Thus, in the sphere of the world, fire, which is sharp, subtle, and mobile, is highest; earth, however, is lowest, being dull, dense, and immobile. Likeness, on the other hand, is to be desired—or rather, it is desired.

[Col. 1322C] Hence, in that same sphere of the world, air and water occupy the middle positions, but air is more like fire than water is, since it is similarly subtle and mobile and is therefore nearer to it. Likewise, water is nearer to earth in place than air is, since by its likeness it is more closely joined to earth than air is.

That is why, if someone attempts to place earth above fire, the proper heaviness of each causes fire to be carried upward by its lightness and earth to sink downward by its heaviness. Likewise, when a passage is found beneath water or earth, air is expelled by its own weight; striving upward as far as fire, it is held beneath it. And when water is placed above air or fire, its own heaviness similarly causes it to flow downward toward earth, where it is held and settles above it.

Each thing flees whatever, within its own kind, is diverse from it by dissimilarity; but it approaches that which is in any way conformed to it by likeness, and conversely, whatever is conformed in any way approaches it.

Hence he adds: “Whatever desires something else, by the very fact that it desires it, proves itself naturally to be such in some respect of the various kinds of likeness described above as that very thing is—namely, that other thing which it desires.”

### “These things, therefore, are sufficient,” etc.

[Col. 1322D] Up to this point he has proposed the rules or terms by which he will establish what follows. Since he does not doubt that by these rules he can bring the proposed “week” into question and confirm what he thinks about it, he says: “These things which we have set forth are sufficient for producing what follows.”

Nevertheless, I have deliberately refrained from indicating how these rules can be applied to the demonstrations or discoveries that follow, because of those whose captiousness permits nothing to remain connected, while attending to the obscurities caused by brevity. I have not said that this or that follows from the reasoning of this or that rule.

But a prudent interpreter of the reasoning—one who carefully observes, from the discoveries themselves and from the form of the argument, the rational topics from which these conclusions have been derived—will fit each of the foregoing matters to its proper arguments; that is, he will assign this or that matter to whichever of the rules mentioned above it belongs.

[Col. 1323A] ### “The question, however,” etc.

About to demonstrate that the things which exist are good in that which they are, although they are not substantial goods, he first asks whether the things that exist are good or not. So that this may appear to be a question designated not by a fabricated term and a mere form apart from the truth of reason—as is customary among sophists—he brings it into doubt through what appear to be the supports of both sides.

First he proves the side that says, “The things that exist are good,” and then the side that says, “The things that exist are not good.” In this way, while taking the opportunity to resolve the question, he explains how the hidden meaning of the proposed “week” can be grasped by a wise person.

For he shows not only that the things that exist are good, but also how they are good. In doing so, he defines them as not being substantial goods and yet as being good in that which they are.

He therefore says: “The question concerning this week is as follows”—that is, through this question and through the arguments that will now be stated, another matter is brought into uncertainty.

“I say that the things that exist”—that is, that subsist, as is clear from what follows—“are good.” It is certain, and this is the common opinion—not indeed of all human beings, but of all learned people—that everything that exists tends toward the first and highest good.

[Col. 1323B] Although the manner differs from one thing to another, and the objects differ, the intention of all hastens toward that which is the highest and perfect good. For irrational creatures, such as brute animals—or rather insentient things, such as trees and plants—and even inanimate things, such as stones, naturally tend toward the highest good, which truly and properly both exists and is one. In their own manner, and in the manner granted to them by the supreme maker, they desire both to exist and to be one, and they resist so as not to lose this altogether.

Rational creatures do this not only naturally, like the rest, but also by their proper activity. They desire not merely to exist or to be one; they also honor the principle of their life through their conduct, recall it through the understanding of their mind, and seek with their whole effort of love that it be given to them as a reward.

Therefore this opinion of the learned—that everything that exists tends toward the good—is supported by many and very firm arguments, and no contrary consideration overturns it. Indeed, whatever may seem to dissent from it, such as what is called evil, entirely agrees with it if one examines the matter more carefully and deeply.

[Col. 1323C] He adds: “Everything, moreover, tends toward what is like itself.” As we said above, likeness is either a comparison of proportion or a certain union of things diverse in number. Wishing the latter kind of likeness to be understood here, he says: “Everything that exists”—that is, every subsistent thing—“tends toward that which is like it through a certain union.”

This too is the common opinion of all learned people. It is the common rule and conception of all philosophers and moral thinkers. From this proposition and from the preceding one, which belongs specifically to moral philosophy—namely, “Everything that exists tends toward the good”—he could have inferred: “Everything that exists is like the good.” But since this was sufficiently evident from the premises, he omitted it.

Nevertheless, so that the reasoning would not remain divided into two parts, following Cicero’s instruction he infers the consequence and says: “Whatever things, therefore, exist”—that is, “the things that tend toward the good”—“are themselves good.” In drawing this inference, he repeats the first proposition within the conclusion itself, saying: “Those which tend toward the good.”

[Col. 1323D] It should be noted that the necessity of this argument derives from the first and ninth rules. For what he calls the common opinion of the learned functions as the mode of assumption belonging to the first rule, where it was said: “A common conception of the mind is a statement that everyone approves when he hears it.” The assumption in which he said, “Everything tends toward what is like it,” belongs to that part of the ninth rule where it was said: “Likeness is to be desired.”

### “But how,” etc.

Up to this point he has proved the part of the question that says: “The things that exist are good.” He now proceeds to demonstrate the other part, namely: “The things that exist are not good.”

The argument is as follows: “Those things that tend toward the good are good. But we must inquire in what way they are good—namely, whether by participation or by substance.”

[Col. 1324A] Here he wishes “substance” to be understood not as that which is, but as being itself; that is, not as the subsistent thing, but as the subsistence itself, which the subsistent thing possesses within itself and by participating in which it subsists.

For the sixth rule expressly says: “Everything that exists participates in being, in order that it may exist.” Yet he seems to hold that a subsistent thing does not participate in being when he says: “Whether by participation or by substance?” It is as though he were saying: “Or by that which is not possessed through participation.”

To this we reply that “participation,” as was indicated in the rules already set forth, is said in several ways.

When a subsistent thing possesses something within itself—such as a nature by which it exists or is something—it is said to participate in that nature. Now, since a nature is present in a subsistent thing and is therefore said to be participated in by it, one such nature is primary, having no cause before it that it follows except a primordial cause.

For example, the most general subsistence, which is present in every subsistent thing, is in a certain way accompanied by another nature. After the primordial cause, it has that cause also in such a way that it belongs to the power of that cause and adheres to it by a property without which it cannot exist.

[Col. 1324B] Such are all those differences which, whether they are closest to the most general genus or, together with it, constitute genera of narrower likeness, are called by logicians subordinate genera—“subnatural,” as the logicians themselves call them, by the designation of subsistent things—or which, similarly adhering to subordinate genera, compose some special subsistence beneath them.

All these are said to be possessed not only by that mode in which they adhere to the subsistent thing, but also by that mode in which they adhere to its genera through the power and property described above. Consequently, they are participated in for a double reason.

Nevertheless, because through the addition of these the subsistent thing in which they come to be is generated, and through their removal is corrupted, they are said to inhere not so much by participation as by substance, just as the genera themselves in which they are present, or the species of which they are composed, are said to inhere in a subsistent thing.

[Col. 1324C] Besides these, however, mathematical science recognizes another class of things which logicians call in Greek συμβεβηκότα (*symbebēkota*), and in Latin *accidentia*, “accidents.” These are differences attached by their property not only to the power of genera but also to the power of differences and species. They cannot be either species of subsistent things or parts of species.

Therefore they are in no way the being of subsistent things. Rather, they differ from them in every genus and property, and from their whole being they are often different in genus and always different in their entire property. These are properly said to be according to participation, and in no way according to themselves—that is, they are not said to be their being.

Hence he rightly says: “If the things that exist are good by participation, they are in no way good through themselves”—that is, by their own subsistence.

This can be made clear by an example. What is white by participation—which is, of course, everything white, since whiteness is predicated of a subsistent thing as an accident of that subsistence—is not white through itself, in that which it is; that is, it is not white through its own subsistence, by which it exists. For whiteness is in no way the subsistence of a white thing.

[Col. 1324D] The same is to be understood of the other qualities that accrue accidentally to that which exists. Likewise, then, if the things that exist are good by that kind of participation which we now wish to understand—namely, accidental participation—the things themselves are in no way good through themselves; that is, the things understood as their subsistence are in no way good.

And if this is so—as indeed it is—that the things which exist are not good through themselves, then they do not tend toward that highest good which is truly good through itself.

Here too it should be noted that the division—“Are the things that exist good by participation or by substance?”—and the consequence—“If by participation, they are in no way good through themselves”—have been derived from certain parts of the third, fourth, and sixth rules as from rational topics.

That being by participation differs from being by substance was clearly taught in the third rule, where he said: “Participation occurs when something already exists”; and in the fourth, where he says: “That which exists can have something besides what it itself is”; and at the end of the sixth, where, speaking of everything that exists, he said: “It exists in order to participate in something else.”

[Col. 1325A] But the consequence that he subsequently inferred in the second place—“Therefore they do not tend toward the good”—belongs to the first part of the ninth rule, which says: “Every diversity is discordant.”

### “But it has been granted,” etc.

He said that if the things that exist are good by participation, they are not good through themselves; and if they are not good through themselves, they do not tend toward the good.

He now assumes the contrary of the last consequence and says: “But they do tend toward the good.” This requires no proof, he says, because it has already been granted by the irrefragable authority of the learned, whose common opinion this is, when that proposition was introduced to prove that the things that exist are good.

### “Therefore not,” etc.

Here he concludes the argument from the contrary of the preceding premise:

“The things that exist, if they are good by participation, are not good through themselves; and if they are not good through themselves, they do not tend toward the good. But they do tend toward the good. Therefore they are not good by participation, but rather by substance”—that is, by subsistence—“since there is nothing intermediate between these two accounts of whatever is naturally predicated of a subsistent thing.”

[Col. 1325B] For whatever is naturally said of a subsistent thing is predicated either as its being or by the participation described above. Therefore, if goodness is not predicated by participation, it must necessarily be predicated as being.

Things whose substance is good—that is, whose subsistence is their goodness—are good in that which they are; that is, goodness is what they are. What they are, moreover—that is, what is rightly said of them—they derive from that which is their being, according to that part of the sixth rule which says: “Everything that exists participates in being, in order that it may exist.”

From these premises it is accordingly inferred that the good—that is, goodness itself—which is predicated of things as good, is their being. It is therefore clear that the good is the being of all things; that is, the goodness of all things of which it is predicated is their being.

But if the good—that is, the goodness by which existing things are called good—is their being, then the things that exist are good, so that they are said not merely to be good without qualification, but also to be good “in that which they are.”

This is genuinely different from saying that they are good in such a way that the addition “in that which they are” could not be made, according to the fifth rule: “It is one thing merely to be something, and another to be something in that which it is.”

[Col. 1325C] Although the expression “in that which it is” can be understood in different ways, it may signify either what a thing’s being is, or what constitutes the being of the thing of which it is predicated. Thus a work may be called bronze “in that which it is,” or it may signify that which is the being of the thing through which it exists, by whose authorship it both exists and is something. Thus a work may be called human “in that which it is.”

Here one point must be carefully observed. When that which is predicated is the being of the thing of which it is predicated, as in the statement “the work is bronze,” it may be said not only that “the work is bronze in that which it is,” but also that “the being of the work is the same as being bronze.”

I do not mean that the work’s being bronze is the same as being itself, but that its being is the same as its being bronze. For that by which it is bronze is not its entire being, even though it is being in its entirety.

[Col. 1325D] Being always belongs wholly to the genus whose being it is, but it is never the whole of being, since the many divided powers of that genus—or rather, all the powers which, together with the genus itself, constitute a species—have the being of the same genus to which the genus itself belongs.

Therefore, if goodness is the being of the things that are good, it is rightly said of them: “They are good in that which they are.” This means that their being is the same as being good—that is, as being good things.

This must be understood despite the similarity of case endings in the expression *bonis*, just as in the verse:

> Mediocribus esse poetis  
> Non di, non homines, non concessere Camenae.

“Neither gods, nor human beings, nor the Muses have allowed mediocre poets to exist.”

Although the sense is “They have not allowed poets to be mediocre,” the poet used *mediocribus*, “to mediocre ones,” in agreement with the case of *poetis*, “poets.”

### “Therefore they are substantial,” etc.

The argument is as follows: “Since the things that exist are good in such a way that they are not only good in that which they are, but their being is also the same as being good, they are therefore substantial goods”—that is, goodness is predicated of them substantially.

[Col. 1326A] For, as has been said, things that are not merely good but also good in that which they are, and whose being is the same as being good, do not participate in goodness by the kind of participation described above, as a bronze work participates in triangularity.

If the good—that is, goodness itself by which they are good—is their being within them, then there is truly no doubt—[the text has “that, since they are, etc.,” or “that, since they are good”]—that they are similar to the first substantial good, whose goodness is truly its essence.

For if goodness is the essence of things that are good in the same way as it is the essence of the first good, it is clear that they are good in the same way that the first good is good. Accordingly, in this respect they will be the first good itself.

He then supplies the reason: “For nothing other than itself is substantially similar to that first good.”

[Col. 1326B] The addition “other than itself” is not made because he wishes it to be understood that the first good is similar to itself in some respect. In no genus of things is anything said to be similar to itself, for every likeness is likeness to another. Nor are the things that are similar different only from one another; they also differ according to the respects in which they are similar.

But there is a customary way of speaking by which we say, “Nothing is similar to the highest good except itself,” intending to signify that nothing at all is similar to it. It is like a situation in which, while the master is absent, the master says, “Who is master here except me?” The one who says this does not wish it to be understood that he is the master, but only that the one who is master is absent.

Likewise, when he says, “Nothing is similar to the first good except itself,” he does not wish it understood that it is similar to itself, but that nothing can be compared with it by substantial likeness. Rather, if something should appear to be substantially like it, it would be what it is through the property of its essence itself, rather than being compared with it through conformity to a different essence.

From this it follows that all things that exist are God. For there is no doubt that, if they are that first good, they are one and simple. The seventh rule expressly stated that every simple thing possesses its own being and what it is as one.

[Col. 1326C] Therefore, since everyone grants that the first good is simple, its being is the same as its being good, and thus its being God is the same as its being good. To say this of any composite thing, for which according to the eighth rule being is one thing and the thing itself another, would even be impious.

Accordingly, it is now clear that things are not substantial goods; that is, existing things are not called substantially good. Consequently, the good—that is, the goodness by which existing things are called good—is not in them as their being.

It therefore appears that they are not good in that which they are. Yet it also appeared to have been proved earlier that they do not participate in goodness; that is, that they are not good by accidental participation. For, as was stated and as appears to be the case, they would in no way tend toward the good.

If, therefore, they are good neither by substance nor by participation, they are in no way good.

Here the second part of the question has been concluded: the question asked whether the things that exist are good or not. He will subsequently resolve it in such a way that he also reveals to those who understand intelligently the hidden meaning of the “week” about which John was asking. He shows that existing things are not only good, but also good in that which they are, although they are not substantial goods.

He therefore says:

### “A solution can be applied to this question,” etc.

[Col. 1326D] The argument is as follows: “It appears possible, by the arguments we have given, to bring into doubt the question whether the things that exist are good or not good. But a solution such as the following can be applied to this question.”

Beginning from a general conception of the mathematicians, he says: “Many things, indeed all things, that are said to be without motion and non-abstract”—that is, inseparable in actuality—“exist.” Although they cannot be separated in actuality from those things in which they exist, so that they could exist without them, they are nevertheless separated in the mind and in thought—that is, by the mind’s act of thinking—so that the nature and property both of the things separated in this way and of the things from which they are separated may be understood.

[Col. 1327A] For example, consider a triangle: that is, the quality which, by co-occurring with a surface, makes the matter subject to it triangular; or consider the other things that exist in the body of any genus. No one separates them in actuality from the matter subject to them, since in this respect they are non-abstract.

Yet by separating the matter itself from its subject matter in thought—that is, in contemplation—the mathematician considers the triangle and its property in a scientific manner as though apart from matter. I do not mean that it exists apart from matter, but that the triangle itself—which cannot exist apart from matter—and its property are considered as divided from matter.

The sense is this: he considers the triangle and its property—that is, the property of the triangle—or the triangle as derived from its property, which amounts to the same thing. In this way mathematicians abstract what is non-abstract.

Therefore we moral philosophers, following the mathematicians by imitation within our own discipline, should for a short time—that is, until the reasoning reaches its conclusion—remove the first good in the mind’s thought from the goods that have flowed from it.

That is, we should provisionally agree to posit that the good from which they have flowed is not good, although this cannot in any way occur according to the nature of things. This is the meaning.

[Col. 1327B] But instead of saying that we should remove the first good from them—for this removal takes place mentally and only for the present, until the reasoning has reached its proper conclusion—he says: “Let us remove the presence of the first good from the mind.”

The first good is certainly established as truly existing. This can be known both from the judgment of all human beings—learned and unlearned—for this is truly a common conception of the mind according to the first mode of the first rule—and from religions, that is, from the fear and ceremonies of barbarian peoples.

[Col. 1327C] ### “Having therefore removed this,” etc.

The argument is as follows: “Let us remove the first good in this way from those things that are good. Having thus removed the first good from them for a short time, let us posit something else: namely, let us posit that all things that exist—that is, that truly subsist—are good.”

Having posited these two things, let us consider the things we call good: in what way—that is, how—could they be good if they had not flowed from the first good in order to exist? This means: if their being were indeed being and subsistence, but they existed without the first good as author or maker.

From this—that is, from the very proposition “Let us posit that all things that exist are good”—I observe in them that being good is one thing and being is another; that is, their being is one thing and their being good another.

For if they were good by the same thing by which they exist, we would not divide them from what we truly judge while positively agreeing to the proposition. Yet we do make this division when we say: “Let us posit that the things that exist”—that is, the things we rightly understand to exist—“are good,” after removing the first good.

The meaning is: “They are not in fact so, but we provisionally agree in a certain way that they are.” Nor should it be doubted that their being is one thing and their being good another.

To make this clear from other examples, let us posit that one substance—that is, one thing truly subsisting, with one and the same property of subsistence—is good, just as we have now posited that all things that exist are good after removing the first good. Let us also posit the other things that had not been posited: namely, that it is white, heavy, and round.

### “Then it would be one thing,” etc.

[Col. 1327D] The argument is as follows: “After removing what we have mentioned, these are the things we ought to posit. For if we posited them in this way, it would then be clear, both concerning goodness and concerning the other qualities, that the substance itself would be one thing—that is, that the subsistent thing would be one thing—and its roundness another, by which it is round; its heaviness another, by which it is heavy; its color another, by which it is white; and its goodness another, by which it is truly good.”

For if each of these were not one and the same as the substance itself through a general union, but through the unity belonging to the property of the individual thing, then heaviness would, by the unity of property, be the same as color, roundness, and goodness—that is, goodness itself.
