Goodness would likewise be the same as heaviness, and similarly in the other cases.

Nature does not permit this—that is, it does not permit these things to be identical by property—for nature has divided them not only by their properties, as commonly happens within the same genus, but also by the diversity of their genera.

### “Therefore it would be one thing,” etc.

The argument is as follows: “If we posit them in this way, these things would be diverse from that by which the subsistent thing exists. Therefore the goodness by which existing things are good would similarly be diverse from the being of all subsistent things.”

[Col. 1328A] Accordingly, in keeping with the sixth rule, which says, “Everything that exists participates in being, in order that it may exist, but participates in something else in order that it may be something,” and with the eighth rule, which says, “In every composite thing being is one thing and the thing itself another,” it would most correctly be said that in them being would be one thing and being something another—that is, they would be subsistences in one respect and would be something through goodness in another.

They would then be good through the goodness by which, as has been said, they would be something, but they would not possess the good itself—that is, goodness itself—as the being by which they existed.

Therefore, if, after removing the first good in the manner described, they existed in any way according to the provisional position to which we have agreed for a short time, they would be good without being from the good, and yet they would be good. They would not be identical with what they are good—that is, their being would not be identical with their goodness.

Rather, according to the rules mentioned above, namely the sixth and eighth, their being would be one thing and their being good another: that is, their existence would be one thing and their existence as good another.

[Col. 1328B] If they were nothing other than good—if they were neither heavy through weight, nor colored through quality, nor extended by any dimension of space, whether length, breadth, or height, and if there were no quality at all in them, and no quantity, but only goodness, through which they were good—then, according to the seventh rule, which says, “Every simple thing possesses its being and what it is as one,” their being and their being good would be the same.

In that case they would not appear to be numerically diverse things according to their different properties, by which subsistent things ordinarily become diverse; rather, they would appear to be the principle of all things.

It is more correct not to say “they would appear,” in the plural, but “it would appear,” in the singular.

Quite rightly. For there is one and only one good of this kind, which is merely good and nothing else, since it is truly simple. Therefore, according to the seventh rule mentioned above, its being is the same as its being good.

[Col. 1328C] Subsistent things, however, are such that each of them both is through many things and is something through many things. Therefore it is not simple but composite, and according to the eighth rule its being is one thing and it itself another.

Nor could there be such a multitude in one thing—both of the things in relation to which it exists and of the things in relation to which it is something—unless one principle had joined these things together in it.

For just as the natural derives from the genuine, the temporal from the eternal, and the alternating from the one, so every composite thing must derive from a simple author.

All subsistent things, therefore, since they contain so many things within themselves and are not simple, could neither fail to be composite nor exist at all unless that which is good in such a way that it is only good and nothing other than good had willed them to exist, and had willed them to be what they are.

Consequently, since the being of any one of them—that is, not only that which it is and by which it is something, and that by which it exists or by which it is something, but also its being and its being something—has flowed from the will of the good, they are called good denominatively.

[Col. 1328D] Thus a bronze work, which exists in its genus through that by which it is, and is triangular through the quality by which it is something, is also called “human” denominatively, from the being of that through whose authorship, according to a certain account, it is both bronze and triangular.

For “human” is said in two ways: first, through the property of a genus, as in “a human animal”; and second, denominatively, because it has flowed from that whose being is human, as in “a human work.”

Likewise, “good” is said in two ways: first, of the good that is truly good because it is good in that which it is, through the truth of its own essence; and second, of that which is also called good, not through the truth of its own essence, but through a certain denomination called in Greek μετωνυμία (*metonymia*), “metonymy.”

Hence it is clear that, according to the rule of natural things, he previously divided the matter when he said: “I ask whether the things that are good are good by participation or by substance.”

[Col. 1329A] Whatever is naturally predicated of a subsistent thing is rightly understood either as its subsistence or as its accident. Besides these, however, many things are said of it outside the scope of natural science, including those that are predicated of it denominatively.

By this mode of predication, moral philosophers declare every created thing to be good—namely, by a denomination that occurs because that which is called good in this way has flowed, in order both to exist and to be something, from the true author and cause whose being is good; that is, from the one whose very goodness is essence.

But not only that which is and is something, and that by which it exists or by which it is something, but also the being itself of all things—which we signify when we say of something “it is” or “it is something”—has flowed from that author and maker in the true sense, namely, the first good, which is truly good in this way.

Thus that thing is said to be good in such a way that “in that which it is” can rightly be added, because it is good through the goodness of its own substance, not through the goodness of something alien.

This name, which it possesses from its own substance, is transferred denominatively to the things that have flowed from it, so that not only the things that exist and are something, and the things by which they exist or are something, but also their very being—which is signified when we say “they are” or “they are something”—is called good.

[Col. 1329B] This transferred denomination from the essence of the first good to the being of those things that exist and are something—or rather, this denominative transference—makes whatever is good by this denomination not only good, but also good in that which it is.

For although the goodness of things called good in this way is not their essence, it is nevertheless rightly added that they are good “in that which they are,” since this goodness, transferred through denomination from that original goodness, derives from the essence of their author, namely, the first good.

### On This Point, etc.

Earlier, having rightly proved that things which exist are good, he wished to appear able to establish that things which exist are not good. He therefore began with a division and asked whether they were good by participation or by substance. He then disproved both parts of this division in the form of indirect arguments: taking the assumptions themselves as premises, he first derived from one, and then from the other, through various multiple constructions drawn from the devices of sophistic art, impossible conclusions— in the first case, that they do not tend toward the good; in the second, that God exists. Since these conclusions cannot be true, he first inferred the opposites of the aforementioned parts of the division; then he brought both arguments to the conclusion he wished to seem to establish—namely, that things are in no way good.

Because, therefore, the parts of the arguments are true in themselves, but through the manyfold combination and combined multiplicity of sophistic art neither are nor appear to be regularly connected, he divided the multiple constructions according to the modes of their signification, in order to show that the form of the connection was contrary to the truth of the matter. For he says that “good” is understood in two ways, and consequently that the expression added to this noun when one says, “It is good in respect of what it is,” can also be taken in more than one way.

There is, he says, a first good, and there is also a second. The first is that which is good alone and nothing else; the second is that which flowed from the will of the first good so that whatever exists might exist. Of both, however, it is said that their being is the same as their being good, and that what is good is good in respect of what it is. Yet this too is said in two different ways. The first is said to be good in respect of what it is because goodness is its essence. The second is said to be good in respect of what it is—not because goodness is its essence, but because the one who caused it to be whatever it is is good in essence, and that second cannot be substantially like the first good.

In this matter both questions have been resolved: both the question whether things that exist are good, and the question on account of which the former was raised—namely, whether things that exist are good in respect of what they are, although they are not substantial goods. This has been done by distinguishing the noun “good” and the expression “in respect of what it is.”

For when “good” is said in two ways—either so that the goodness of what is called good is itself its essence, or by a denomination made because all its being flowed from that whose essence is goodness—it is clear that things which exist, although they are not good in the manner in which the first good is good, that is, substantially, and are not good by participation either, are nevertheless good in another manner. Consequently, he was wrong to infer earlier, when he said: “If they are good neither by substance nor by participation, then they are good in no way.”

Likewise, although they are not good in respect of what they are in the manner of the first good, they are good in another manner and therefore are themselves good in respect of what they are. Hence he was also wrong to say above: “If they are good in respect of what they are, then they are substantial goods and are like the first good.” They will not be substantially like the first good merely because they are good in respect of what they are.

Yet this was the connection sophistically constructed in the second argument. Things may indeed be good in respect of what they are, but they are not like the first good for this reason: it is not true in just any manner that things are such that their very being is good.

It is as though he said: “It is indeed true that their very being is good, but it is not true in every manner. It is not true because goodness is their subsistence, by which they naturally exist; rather, their very being is truly said to be good because the being of things cannot be whatever sort of being it might be unless it has flowed from the first being, that is, from the first good. Yet it is not substantially like that first being from which it comes.”

That first being, however it may be, is good, whatever is predicated of it as existing; thus it is good in respect of what it is. He could have added: “and thus its being is the same as its being good.” This is entirely correct, since what follows is: “For it is not something other than good itself”—that is, there is no essence predicated of it that is distinct from its goodness. It is simple, for, according to the seventh Rule, it has its being and what it is as one.

But whatever the being of things might be, if it were not from that first good—if, with the first from which it comes removed, that first were not good—it might perhaps be good in the way that what exists is white, heavy, or round; but it could not truly be good in respect of what it is. For then, if what is predicated as existing in whatever manner were not from it, it might participate in the good, that is, be good by participation, like something white or of that kind. But the goodness it possessed could not be possessed as though it possessed its very being—that is, in the manner in which its particular being is possessed, namely, in respect of what it is—since it would not have this from the good, that is, because that from which it had it would not itself be good.

It is therefore clear that, if the first good is removed from these things in thought and conception—so that it is posited by thought as not being good—the source from which they are whatever they are would remain; and although the things derived from it might be good, they could not be good in respect of what they were.

Conversely, it is evident that, since they could not actually exist unless what is truly good had produced them—that is, unless what produced them were truly good—their very being is therefore good. In other words, the same is said of them as of being: they are good in respect of what they are. Consequently, they are in some manner like the first good toward which they tend; yet what has flowed from it as good is not substantially like the first substantial good.

It is the same good, and it is good in respect of what it is; but this is true denominatively, not substantially. And unless all such good things had flowed from that first good, although they would still be good, as was stated above, they could not be good in respect of what they are. He then explains why: because they would be good both apart from the good and not from the good, whereas the first good itself truly is, and is so in such a way that its very being is its very goodness, and conversely its goodness is its very being.

### “But is it not also so,” etc.

Earlier, when he divided the good into a first and a second, he said that the second good is good because it flowed from that whose very being is good. For this reason, the same is said of the second as of the first: namely, that it too is good in respect of what it is.

It is certain, however, that whatever things are, they are whatever they are from the same cause—that is, they flowed from the same principle so that they might exist. Consequently, whatever they are, they appear to be that in respect of what they are.

Hence he rightly asks, saying: “When we also call things white, must not those that are white likewise be white in respect of what they are, by the same reasoning—namely, because they flowed from the will of that same principle so that they might be white?” He answers: “Not at all.”

And why not? He says: “For their being is one thing, and their being white another.” Here the nominative case is required by both the sense and the verb of demonstration, as was said above; but preserving here as well the correspondence of case with case, he says: “It is one thing for white things to be.”

That is, the fact that their being is one thing and their being white another, whereas with things that are good their being and their being good are the same, is due to this: the one who made the things called good and white so that they might be whatever they are is indeed good, but is not white.

Thus the fact that existing things should be good accompanied the will of the good, and consequently they are said to be good in respect of what they are. The will of one who is not white was indeed accompanied by the property that they should be white, but not by the property that this should be true in respect of what they are.

He adds the reason: “For they did not flow from the will of one who is white in order to be white.” Hence he rightly concludes: “Therefore, because the one who willed them to be white was not white”—that is, because the one who willed them to be white was not himself white—they are merely white, that is, white but not white in respect of what they are.

But because he who willed them to be good was good—that is, because the one who willed them to be good was good—they are good, so that one may add: “in respect of what they are.”

Their being called good is a denomination, just as their being called existent is, since the one from whom they are and from whom they are good is truly and substantially good, just as he truly and substantially exists. But their being white is a property, not a denomination, because the one from whom they are white is not white in substance in the same way that he exists in substance.

### “Accordingly, on this account,” etc.

Above, after saying that things which exist are good and adding “in respect of what they are,” and after giving as the reason for this addition that they flowed from the first good, he asked why they are also said to be white, without the addition “in respect of what they are,” since they flowed from the same cause so that they might be white.

He answered that the one from whom they are good and white is good but not white.

Now, from what he had said above—namely, that the second good is good because it flowed from that whose being is good—it might be supposed similarly that all things are just because they flowed from one who is truly just. He therefore asks and says:

“Therefore, if things which exist are good because the one who willed them to exist is good, I ask whether, by the same reasoning—that is, according to the proportion of the same reasoning—all things that exist must be just because the one who willed them to exist is himself just?”

He answers: “Nor is this necessary,” just as it was previously said that it was not necessary that things which are white should be white in respect of what they are because they flowed from God’s will in order to be white.

### “For to be good,” etc.

Here it seems necessary to say that “good” is used in two ways: in one way in itself, and in another according to the use that proceeds from what is called good in itself. The former is therefore said absolutely, just as it is when one says that something exists; the latter is not said absolutely, but by comparison with another, for whom some use proceeds from that good.

Thus one finds it said of many things: “This is good for that person,” or “This is good for this purpose.” This is said not only of creatures but also of God, who, although he is good in himself, is also good for us.

Just as, from the one who truly exists, “exists” is predicated denominatively of anything whatsoever according to ethical or theological usage, so also “good” is predicated in itself of anything whatsoever according to the same usages. But if something else is affirmed to be good, this, as was said, is not predicated in itself but by comparison of one thing with another. Hence one thing is understood to be more good, less good, equally good, or more good than another—or even more good now than it was previously. God is understood to be better than all, indeed best of all.

“Just,” however, is in no way predicated in itself of things that exist; this term is always understood either from the virtue of acting or from an act of virtue. It is from the virtue of acting that someone is called just when he possesses the settled disposition of a rightly ordered mind. When, however, someone does something through the duty of such a disposition and through the proper end of that duty, he is called just through an act of virtue.

Not only the one who acts but also what is done is called just by a kind of denomination. When a wicked person is called just through remission, this too occurs through the act of the one who justifies; yet for that one, being and being just are the same, and, in a certain respect, being and acting are also the same.

From these considerations it is clear that this term is applied neither only to creatures nor to all creatures, since God too is called just, while only rational creatures, and certain works of theirs, are called just. These are called just, as has been said, either through the virtue of acting, through an act of virtue, through the grace of the one who justifies in addition to these, or through a denominative transfer of the term.

Thus something is said to be just in a very different way from that in which it is said to be good. For “to be good,” in the sense in which good is predicated in itself—whether truly of God or denominatively of anything else—has reference to the essence by which God is good in what he is. As the author of all things, because they flowed from him, he communicates to all the being truly predicated of him when one says, “God exists.” Accordingly, things are called not merely good but also good in respect of what they are, and their being is the same as their being good.

“To be just,” however, has no reference to essence at all, but only to the act of the one who justifies, of one possessing the virtue of acting, or of one who acts through duty and its end. Consequently, things called just are not just in respect of what they are, nor is their being the same as their being just; in a certain respect, however, their being is the same as their acting.

Although the one who is the principle of all things never began to exist, but began to act at some point, because the virtue of acting never began to exist in him, it is said that in him being and acting are the same. By the same reasoning, therefore, being good and being just are the same for him.

For us, however—who are called just not so much from his virtue as from his act, or rather from the effect that proceeds from his justifying us, from rightly ordering our mind for the duty of acting and the end of that duty, or from moving the mind itself to act in this way—being and acting are not the same.

He explains why: “For we are not simple, as he is, but composite.” That is, according to the seventh Rule, he is rightly understood to have his being and what he is as one; whereas we, according to the eighth Rule, have being as one thing and something else as what we are.

Therefore, according to the same eighth Rule, for us being good and being just are not the same. But since, when we are said to exist from him who truly exists, we say this denominatively, it is certain from what was said above that, whatever we are, our being is the same in respect of what we are.

Since, then, in a certain respect our being and our being good are the same, just as for him they are the same in another respect, it is clear that everything we are, we are good in respect of what we are. We are not all just as well; only some are, because things are not thereby just merely because they exist or are good.

### “Furthermore,” etc.

He shows that not all things are just. From this it can without doubt be understood that the proportion of the reasoning given above was incorrectly drawn: it seemed necessary to say that, just as all things are good because he who willed them to exist is good, so all things would be just because he who willed them to exist is just.

For the same reason, in order to show that this proportion has been improperly established, he proves that although all things are good, not all things are just. He says:

“Furthermore, we have shown from this also that not all things are just, although all things are good: among ethical writers, good is general because it applies to everything by an entirely uniform denomination; but just, because being just is in some respect the same as being good, although being good is not the same as being just, is particular.”

Nor does a species descend into all things in such a way that, according to the rule of dialecticians and rhetoricians by which a species divides a genus, it is predicated of everything subsumed under the genus. Accordingly, among all things that exist, according to their rules, some are just, as belonging to one species of the good; others are something else, as belonging to another species of the same genus; but all are good according to the genus of these species.

### [Col. 1333]

## ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS  
### A Brief Summary of the Christian Faith (C, S)

[Note: This short work, which we now publish for the first time, is confirmed as belonging to Boethius by the very style of its discourse and by the concise sequence of the mysteries of the Christian religion, so firmly that it is hardly necessary to add that it exists under his name in my Fossatensis, Regius, and Saint Victor manuscripts, to say nothing of those from which Trithemius long ago gave the same information. He calls the book *On Faith*.]

[Col. 1333A] The authority of the New and Old Testament unfolds the Christian faith. Although the old Scripture itself contained the very name of Christ within it and always signified that he would come—the one whom we proclaim to have already come through the Virgin’s childbirth—it is nevertheless proved to have spread throughout the world through the wondrous advent of our Savior himself.

Our religion, which is called Christian and Catholic, rests principally upon these foundations, affirming that from eternity—that is, before the foundation of the world, before anything that can properly be called temporal—the divine substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit existed. Thus it calls the Father God, the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God; yet not three Gods, but one.

The Father therefore has a Son begotten from his own substance and coeternal with him according to a manner known to himself. Faith confesses this Son in such a way that he is not the same as the Father, nor was the Father ever the Son, lest the human mind should again imagine a divine progeny extending to infinity. Nor can the Son, in the same nature in which he is coeternal with the Father, ever become the Father, lest the divine progeny should again extend infinitely.

The Holy Spirit, moreover, is neither the Father nor the Son; and therefore, in no nature being either begotten or begetting, he proceeds from both the Father and the Son. We cannot explain the precise manner of this procession any more clearly than the human mind can comprehend the generation of the Son from the Father’s substance.

The Old and New Testaments provide instruction for believing these things. From this, as though from the citadel of our religion, many have spoken contrary opinions, thinking in a human and, so to speak, carnal manner. Arius, for example, although he calls the Son God, nevertheless confesses him in many ways to be lesser than the Father and outside the Father’s substance.

The Sabellians likewise dared to affirm not three existing persons but one, saying that the Father is the same as the Son, that the Son is the same as the Father, and that the Holy Spirit is the same as the Father and the Son. Consequently, they say that there is one person marked by a diversity of names.

The Manichaeans, who profess two principles coeternal and opposed to each other, do not believe him to be the only-begotten Son of God. They consider it unworthy that God should appear to have a son, thinking of the matter only carnally: since human generation proceeds from the commingling of two bodies, they believe that it is likewise unworthy to apply such an understanding to God. For this reason they neither accept the Old Testament nor accept the New in its entirety. Just as their error wholly rejects the former, so they refuse to admit the generation of the Son from a virgin, lest the divine nature appear to have been polluted by a human body. But enough concerning these matters; they will be placed in their proper location as the necessary order requires.

Therefore the divine nature, existing from eternity and enduring eternally without any change, by a will conscious only to itself freely willed to fashion the world. When it did not exist at all, it caused it to exist. It did not bring it forth from its own substance, lest the world be believed to be divine in nature; nor did it construct it from something else, lest something should already have existed whose existence in its own nature assisted its will—something that had not been made by him and nevertheless existed.

Rather, by his word he produced the heavens and created the earth, making heavenly natures worthy of a heavenly dwelling and joining earthly things to the earth.

Among the heavenly natures universally called angelic, although everything there is beautiful in its distinct orders, a certain portion desired more than nature and the author of nature had granted it, and was cast down from its heavenly seat. Since the Creator did not wish the number of angels—that is, of that higher city whose citizens are angels—to remain diminished, he formed man from the earth, animated him with the spirit of life, endowed him with reason, and adorned him with freedom of choice. After establishing a law, he placed him amid the delights of Paradise, so that, if he wished to remain without sin, he might associate both himself and his descendants with the angelic choirs.

Thus, because the higher nature had sought the lowest through the evil of pride, the lower substance might ascend to the heights through the good of humility. But the author of envy could not bear that man should ascend to the place where he himself had not deserved to remain. By introducing temptation, he caused man and his companion—the woman whom the Maker had produced from his side for the purpose of generation—to become subject to the punishment of disobedience. He also promised that divinity would come to man; but while arrogantly claiming it for himself, he was cast down.

God revealed these matters to his servant Moses, to whom he also wished the condition and origin of the human race to become known, as the books brought forth by him testify. All divine authority appears to be structured in these ways: either it is historical, so that it relates nothing other than events that occurred; or allegorical, so that the order of the history cannot stand literally; or composed of both, so that it appears to remain valid both according to history and according to allegory. These matters shine forth sufficiently and abundantly for those who understand them devoutly and hold them with a truthful heart. But let us return to the order of the account.

[Col. 1335A] Before the fall, the first man was an inhabitant of Paradise with his wife. But when he lent his ear to the persuader and neglected to heed the Creator’s command, he became an exile and was ordered to cultivate the earth. Excluded from the bosom of Paradise, he transferred the posterity of his kind to unknown regions, and through begetting transmitted to his descendants the punishment that he, the first man and guilty transgressor, had received.

From this it came about that corruption of bodies and souls and the destruction of death arose. He first deserved to experience death in his son Abel, so that he might learn in his offspring how great was the punishment he himself had received. If he himself had died first, he would in a certain way not have known it; and, if one may say so, he would not have felt his punishment. For this reason he experienced it in another, so that he might recognize what was justly owed him as a transgressor and, while enduring the punishment of death, be tortured more intensely by the expectation of it.

Pelagius, refusing to admit this evil of transgression, which the first man had naturally poured into his descendants, established a heresy named after himself. The Catholic faith is known to have immediately rejected it from its fellowship.

The human race, proceeding from that first man and increasing in manifold numbers, broke out into quarrels, stirred up wars, and occupied the misery of earth, having lost the happiness of Paradise in its first father. Nevertheless, there were not lacking those whom the grace of the Creator set apart for itself and who served his commands. Although the merit of nature condemned them, he wished to restore the ruined nature by making them participants in the future sacrament, which was to be revealed much later.

The world was therefore filled with the human race, and man entered upon his own ways, having despised the Creator through the wickedness of his own obstinacy. Then God, wishing to restore the human race through a righteous man rather than allow it to remain rebellious, permitted the sinful multitude to perish through the outpouring of the flood, except for Noah, a righteous man, with his sons and with those things that he had brought into the ark.

Why he wished to rescue the righteous through the wood of the ark is known to minds instructed in the divine Scriptures. Thus, as it were, the first age of the world passed away through the flood’s punishment.

[Col. 1335D] The human race was restored, yet it did not cease to embrace the defect of its nature that the first author of transgression had infused into it. The obstinacy that the floodwaters had once punished grew again; and although human life had previously been permitted to continue through a long succession of years, it was now confined to a short span.

God preferred no longer to punish the human race by a flood, but, while it remained, to choose men through whose succession a lineage might continue, from which, at the end of the world, he would grant us his own Son clothed in a human body.

The first of these was Abraham. Although he was advanced in age and his wife was aged, they deserved, in their old age, to have a son through the generosity of the promise. This son was called Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob. Jacob likewise begot twelve patriarchs, God not counting among their number those whom nature had produced in the ordinary way.

Jacob therefore wished to dwell in Egypt with his sons and household in order to complete his affairs. There, as the multitude grew through the succession of years, the Egyptians began to regard them with suspicion; and Pharaoh resolved to burden them with a great weight of oppression and afflict them with heavy labor.

At last God, disregarding the domination of the Egyptian king, divided the Red Sea—a thing that no natural power had ever previously known—and led his people across, with Moses and Aaron as leaders. Afterward, because Egypt refused to release the people, it was devastated by great plagues.

Having crossed the Red Sea, as was said, they came through the wilderness to the mountain called Sinai. There the Creator of all, wishing to instruct the peoples for the sake of the future sacrament, established through Moses, by the law he gave, how both the rites of sacrifices and the customs of the peoples should be ordered.

After they had waged war against many nations for many years along the way, they finally came to the river called the Jordan. Under the leadership of Joshua son of Nun, the waters of the Jordan were dried up for their crossing, just as the waters of the Red Sea had been. By it they arrived at the city that is now called Jerusalem.

While God’s people remained there, kings are recorded as having been established after the judges and prophets. After Saul, David of the tribe of Judah is recorded as having first attained the primacy. The royal line descended from him through successive generations and continued down to the time of Herod, who is recorded as the first foreigner to rule the aforementioned peoples.

Under Herod appeared the blessed Virgin Mary, who had come from the stock of David and who gave birth to the Creator of the human race. This occurred because the world, infected by many crimes, lay in death. One people was therefore chosen in which God’s commandments might shine forth. Prophets and other holy men were sent there, through whose admonition that very people might be recalled from the swelling of its obstinacy. Instead, by killing them, the people chose to remain in the perversity of its wickedness.

[Col. 1336C] In the final times God determined that not prophets or other persons pleasing to him, but his only-begotten Son himself, should be born through a virgin, so that the salvation of humanity, which had been lost through the disobedience of the first man, might be restored once again through the man who is God.

And because there had been a woman who persuaded the first man to bring about death, there would be a second woman who would bring the cause of life into human flesh. It should not seem unworthy that the Son of God was born from a virgin, since he was conceived and brought forth beyond the ordinary course of nature.

The virgin conceived the Son of God incarnate from the Holy Spirit; the virgin gave birth; and after his birth she remained a virgin. The same person became both the Son of man and the Son of God, so that in him both the splendor of the divine nature might shine and the assumption of human weakness might appear.

Yet many arose against this sound and most truthful faith, babbling various opinions. Among others, Nestorius and Eutyches became originators of heresy. One of them held that Christ was man alone, the other that he was God alone; neither acknowledged that the human body Christ had assumed came from participation in human substance. But enough of this.

Christ therefore grew according to the flesh. He was baptized so that he who was to give the form of baptism to others might himself first receive what he taught. After his baptism he chose twelve disciples, one of whom became his betrayer. Because the Jewish people could not endure sound doctrine, they laid hands on him and killed him by the punishment of the cross.

Christ was therefore killed; he lay in the tomb for three days and nights; he rose from the dead, as he himself had decreed with the Father before the foundation of the world; and he ascended into heaven, where, insofar as he is the Son of God, he is known never to have been absent. Thus the Son of God raised with himself to a heavenly dwelling the man he had assumed, whom the devil had not allowed to ascend to the heights.

He therefore gave his disciples the form of baptizing, of teaching the things that bring salvation, and also the power to perform miracles. He commanded them to enter the whole world for the sake of life, so that saving preaching would no longer be proclaimed only to one people but to the entire world.

Because the human race, by the desert of the nature it had contracted from the first transgressor, had been wounded by the arrows of eternal punishment and was not capable of its own salvation—having lost it in its ancestor—he bestowed certain medicinal sacraments. Through them humanity might recognize that one thing was owed to it through the merit of nature and another through the gift of grace: nature contributed nothing but subjection to punishment, whereas grace, which is bestowed on no merits—for it would not be called grace if it were bestowed because of merits—brought about the whole of its salvation.

[Col. 1337B] That heavenly doctrine was therefore spread throughout the world; peoples were united; churches were established; and one body was formed that would occupy the breadth of the world. Christ, its head, ascended into heaven, so that necessarily the members would follow their head.

This doctrine both forms the present life through good works and promises that, after the completion of the age, our bodies will rise again and, freed from corruption, be restored to the heavenly kingdoms. Thus whoever has lived well here, by his gift, will be supremely blessed in that resurrection; but whoever has lived badly will appear miserable after receiving the gift of resurrection.

This is the principal point of our religion: that we believe not only that souls do not perish, but also that the very bodies which the arrival of death had dissolved will be restored to their original state in future blessedness.

The Catholic Church, spread throughout the world, is proved to exist in three ways. Whatever is held within it is either the authority of the Scriptures, universal tradition, or a particular and local instruction. By authority the whole Church is bound; by the universal tradition of the ancestors it is likewise entirely bound; but by private constitutions and particular teachings each church exists and is governed either according to the diversity of places or as seems best to each.

The sole expectation of the faithful now is therefore this: that we believe the end of the world will come, that all corruptible things will pass away, that human beings will rise for examination at the future judgment, that each will receive according to his merits, and that each will remain forever and eternally within the limits allotted to him.

The sole reward of blessedness will be contemplation of the Creator—only as great as can be achieved by a creature in relation to the Creator—so that, through the restoration of the angelic number, that heavenly city may be filled, where the King is the Son of the Virgin.

There will be everlasting joy, delight, nourishment, and the work of perpetual praise of the Creator.

[Note: To praise God in heaven is an especially widespread Christian view of the blessed, arising naturally from admiration for his divinity and goodness. This praise is joined to the supreme contemplation of God by the angels and the blessed. Their single work, Athanasius says, is “an unceasing hymn and an inexhaustible praise of the magnificence of God” (*Ὕμνος ἄληκτος καὶ αἶνος ἄπαυστος τῆς μεγαλοπρεπείας τοῦ Θεοῦ*). Nor is the work of the blessed any less so: “For the greatest and only rest of the saints is to utter with unwearied voice in heaven the praise of the supreme Trinity, which is God,” says Junilius Africanus, if indeed this attribution is correct.

Nor is that their work only in the heaven of the blessed; it ought also to be the work of mortal human beings on earth. This can be demonstrated not only from the countless testimonies of the sacred Code and of the Fathers, but also from the words of the pagan yet most wise Epictetus, as transmitted by Arrian:

“Indeed, if we had understanding, what else ought we to do, both publicly and privately, than hymn the divine power, praise it, and render thanks”—*Εἰ γὰρ νοῦν εἴχομεν, ἄλλο τί ἔδει ἡμᾶς ποιεῖν καὶ κοινῇ καὶ ἰδίᾳ, ἢ ὑμνεῖν τὸ Θεῖον καὶ εὐφημεῖν, καὶ ἐπεξέρχεσθαι τὰς χάριτας*—“and what else can I do, an old and lame man, except hymn God? If I were a nightingale, I would perform the work of a nightingale; if a swan, that of a swan; but now I am a rational being. I must hymn God. This is my task; this is what I do. I will not abandon this station so long as it is permitted, and I exhort you also to the same song”—*τί γὰρ ἄλλο δύναμαι γέρων χωλός, εἰ μὴ ὑμνεῖν τὸν Θεόν; εἰ γοῦν ἀηδὼν ἤμην, ἐποίουν τὰ τῆς ἀηδόνος· εἰ κύκνος, τὰ τοῦ κύκνου· νῦν δὲ λογικός εἰμι· ὑμνεῖν με δεῖ τὸν Θεόν· Τοῦτό μου τὸ ἔργον ἐστί, ποιῶ αὐτό, οὐδ’ ἐγκαταλείψω τὴν τάξιν ταύτην, ἐφ’ ὅσον ἂν δίδοται, καὶ ὑμᾶς ἐπὶ τὴν αὐτὴν ταύτην ᾠδὴν παρακαλῶ*.

Latin rendering: “For what else can I do, an old and lame man, except celebrate God with praises? If I were a nightingale, I would perform the duty of a nightingale; if a swan, that of a swan. Since I now share in reason, God must be celebrated by me. This is my duty; this is what I carry out. I will not abandon this station so long as I am permitted, and I exhort you to the same song.”]

## ON THE PERSON AND TWO NATURES

### Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, *Book on the Person and Two Natures against Eutyches and Nestorius*, to John, Deacon of the Roman Church (C)

### Preface
I had long and anxiously waited for you, so that we might discuss the question raised at the meeting. But since you have been prevented from coming by your occupations, and I too shall be occupied with business arranged for tomorrow, I commit to writing what I had reserved for discussion in person. You remember that, when the letter was read in the council,

> [Note: Martianus Rota is dreaming when, in his *Life of Boethius*, he asserts that Pope Leo of Rome was present at the Council of Chalcedon, when he presided over it only through legates. Further, the person who here thinks that the matter concerns the same letter sent from Chalcedon to Rome, whereas the opposite is true—that it was sent from Rome to Constantinople to Flavian and was later approved and praised by the entire Council of Chalcedon. Finally, the person who believes that Boethius is speaking here of that council which was convened in the city while the Acephali were causing disturbances: if such a council existed (and there was none), it is nevertheless clear that Boethius did not attend it, since we think he was scarcely born at that time, whereas that heresy especially revived in the year 482, not in the Western but in the Eastern Church. Since the matter therefore stands otherwise, it is a plausible conjecture that he wrote the treatise *On Two Natures and One Person of Christ* in the year 512, and that the following was its occasion. The emperor Anastasius, an Arian, was savagely persecuting the Catholic bishops of the East through deposition, imprisonment, and exile. When they saw that they and the Catholic religion were being utterly destroyed and would be utterly destroyed, they sought help and assistance from Pope Symmachus by a written letter of exceptional learning, which is found in Baronius. After receiving it, Symmachus read it at a meeting, or council, held at Rome of the bishops then in the city and of other men devoted to religion, among whom were Symmachus and Boethius. While it was being examined, and they came to these words:

> “For we, O most holy and most blessed Symmachus, believe him to be the same from two natures and in two natures; and we do not, as they say, confess that after the union there is one nature from two natures, or that he does not suffer in two subsisting natures united together—thus showing themselves to be imitators of the Arians, who say that the Father is glorified through the Son, but do not allow themselves to say that he is glorified with the Son. But, just as your most holy fathers, our brothers, taught against them, we say that he suffers equally ‘through whom’ and ‘with whom’: ‘through whom’ signifying the humanity, and ‘with whom’ the divinity, of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. Thus, whereas they now say ‘from two natures’ but do not confess ‘in two,’ we say equally ‘from two’ and ‘in two.’ For by saying ‘from two,’ we confess the sources from which unity subsists; and by saying ‘in two,’ we confess the natures in which he was seen, seen and touched, and assumed after the passion and resurrection, and in which he will come to judge the living and the dead.”

> Many of those present, being insufficiently educated in theological matters, discussed the subject without even lightly touching upon it. Boethius then wrote down for John, at that time a deacon of the Roman Church and later its pontiff, what he thought about the question, against Nestorius, who joined two persons to the two natures, and Eutyches, who maintained one nature and one person.

> That meetings or councils of this kind were customarily held in the city—where bishops and distinguished members of the clergy were present, as well as many senators and other serious men who, on account of their exceptional piety, were called religious men, and before whom anything difficult in religion that arose at that time would be discussed, or any pious work written by learned men for publication would be read—is demonstrated, among other things, by the subscription to the works of Arator. D. Sirmond had long ago published part of it in his edition of Ennodius; we have copied it in full from our old manuscript.

> “With the assistance of blessed Peter, a codex of this kind was presented by Arator, *vir illustris*, former commander of the household troops and former commander of the private troops, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, an apostolic man, to Pope Vigilius; and it was received by him on the seventh day before the Ides of April in the presbytery before the Confession of blessed Peter, while many bishops, priests, deacons, and clerics, indeed the greater part, were present there. After the venerable Surgentius, first secretary of the school of notaries, had caused some portion of it to be read there, he placed it in the archives for preservation in the church. All the most learned men of letters immediately begged his Blessedness to order that it be publicly read. When he had commanded this to be done in the church of blessed Peter called *ad Vincula*, a crowd of religious people assembled, and, Arator himself reading, both books were heard on seven separate days; only half of one book was read, because of the frequent repetitions which they requested with great enthusiasm. The same repetition took place on these days: first, the Ides of April; second, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May; fourth, the third day before the Kalends of June, in the third year after the consulship of Basiliscus, *vir clarissimus*, in the seventh indiction—or rather, of Basilius; that is, plainly, in the year 544.”]

the letter was read, stating that the Eutychians confessed Christ to subsist from two natures but denied that he was in two natures, whereas Catholics gave equal credence to both expressions: among those who followed the true faith, he was believed both to subsist from two natures and to be in two natures. Struck by the novelty of this statement, I began to investigate the differences between these conjunctions—“from two natures” and “in two natures”—thinking that the distinction mattered greatly and that what the bishop who wrote the letter had not wished to pass over, as something of the utmost importance, should not, I thought, be passed over through careless negligence.

At this, they all clamored, in a confused and disorderly fashion, that the difference was plain and that there was nothing obscure in it; yet amid so great a tumult no one was found who even lightly touched upon the question, much less anyone who resolved it.

> [Note: Evidently this refers to his father-in-law Symmachus, whom Boethius, because of his learning in both languages and his mastery of every secular and sacred discipline and science, appointed everywhere as the critic of his writings. Ennodius bears witness to his great dignity and wisdom in his *Didactic Exhortation*, where one finds this eulogy of him: “The patricians Festus and Symmachus, the substance of all disciplines and steadfast embodiments of wisdom, do not withdraw from the most sacred city. In them lies the leadership of the noble senate; to have seen them is to have been educated. Among them there is no talk of frivolities, nor any mention of the scarcely pardonable performances of pantomimes. They do not seek popular favor at the cost of modesty; content to please the upright rather than the many, they obtain from blameless conduct the testimony it deserves. Although their commands must be followed in all things, they possess also a teacher’s silence and the model of learned reserve.” Pope Symmachus experienced his piety when he defended him against the schismatic Laurentius; Avitus of Vienne writes to him about this. It is therefore not surprising that he is called holy by his son-in-law, a man wholly formed by wisdom and virtues, and finally “the most precious adornment of the human race.”]

I was seated farther away from the man whom I most wished to observe—and indeed, if you recall the arrangement of those seated, turned away from him and with several people between us—so that, even if I had desired it most earnestly, I could not look upon his face or gesture in the hope of receiving from him some indication of his judgment.

For my part, I contributed nothing more than the others; indeed, I contributed something less. With regard to the matter proposed, I was no more informed than the others, but I contributed less than they did in one respect: I made no presumptuous claim to false knowledge. I endured this very painfully, I confess; crushed among the ignorant crowd, I fell silent, fearing that I should rightly appear insane if I tried to be considered sane among madmen.

From that point onward, therefore, I turned all the questions over in my mind. I did not swallow what I had received, but chewed it over by repeatedly deliberating upon it. At last the doors opened to my searching mind, and truth, discovered by one who sought it, dispersed all the clouds of Eutychian error.

I was therefore especially led to wonder at the audacity of ignorant men who try to cover the fault of ignorance with a cloud of presumption and shamelessness, although they often do not know even what is being proposed, and in disputes of this kind do not even understand what they themselves are saying—as though the cause of ignorance became worse when it was concealed.

But I now turn from them to you, to whom I send this work, however slight it may be, for examination and prior consideration. If you declare that it is correct, I ask you to insert this also among the writings bearing my name. But if something must be removed, added, or altered in some way, I ask you to send that back to my copies as well, so that it may return from you for transcription. When these have been brought to completion and established, only then shall I send them for the judgment of the person whose judgment I customarily follow.

But since the matter is now being transferred from conversation to writing, let the opposing errors of Nestorius and Eutyches first be removed; afterward, with God’s help, I shall set out the middle way of the Christian faith. Since throughout the whole question of these mutually opposed heresies there is uncertainty concerning persons and natures, these must first be defined and separated by their proper distinctions.

## CHAPTER I. What Nature Is

Nature, then, can be spoken of either of bodies alone, or of substances alone—that is, corporeal and incorporeal substances—or of all things that are said to exist in any way whatsoever. Since, therefore, nature can be spoken of in three ways, it must doubtless be defined in three ways.

For if it is agreed that nature is spoken of all things, a definition must be given that can include all things that exist. It will therefore be as follows:

> Nature is that which can in any way whatsoever be grasped by the intellect, among those things that exist.

In this definition, therefore, both accidents and substances are defined, for all these can be grasped by the intellect. The words “in any way whatsoever” have been added because God and matter cannot be understood by a complete and perfect intellect, but they are nevertheless grasped in some way through the privation of knowledge of other things.

> [Note: Thus all the old manuscript books read, not “God and nature.” Our inability to know God acknowledges that he cannot be known by a perfect act of understanding; and true is John’s statement: “No one has ever seen God” (*Theon oudeis pōpote tethéatai*). St. Paul likewise declares that we now see or know God “through a mirror in an enigma” (*di’ esoptrou en ainigmati*): “For his invisible things,” he says, “are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made; likewise his eternal power and divinity.” Plato too says that it is difficult to find God (*heurein ou rhadion*). As for what matter is, no mortal fully knows that either; and all philosophy admits that it cannot be apprehended by either sense or intellect. For Plato and Aristotle it is not *sōma* (“body”) but *sōmatikē* (“corporeal”); Zeno calls it *aidios* (“eternal”), because it “neither increases nor decreases” (*oute pleiōn gignomenē, oute elattōn*). Plato says in the *Timaeus* that, since it is known only insofar as it is the subject and place of forms, and therefore is known not through itself but through something else, there is no knowledge of it except by “a kind of bastard reasoning” (*logismō tini nōthō*). Aristotle likewise regards it as knowable, but “according to proportion” (*kat’ analogian*), that is, by comparison. St. Augustine too, in Book XIII of the *Confessions*, asserts that after the human mind has labored long and hard in investigating the knowledge of matter, it achieves only this: that it attempts either to know it by not knowing, or to not know it by knowing.]

We added the words “which exist” because even “nothing” signifies something, but not nature. For it signifies not that something is, but rather that it is not; whereas every nature exists. If, therefore, it is agreed that nature is spoken of all things, let this be the definition of nature that we gave above.

But if nature is spoken of substances alone, since all substances are either corporeal or incorporeal, we shall give the following definition of nature insofar as it signifies substance:

> Nature is either that which can act or that which can be acted upon.

That which can both act and be acted upon includes all corporeal things and the soul of corporeal things; for the soul acts and is acted upon in the body and by the body. That which can act only includes God and the other divine beings.

You therefore have the definition of that meaning of nature which applies only to substances. In this connection the definition of substance has also been supplied: for if the word “nature” indicates substance, then, when we have described nature, we have also provided a description of substance.

But if the name “nature,” leaving incorporeal substances aside, is extended to corporeal substances alone, so that only corporeal substances are thought to possess nature—as Aristotle and others belonging to various philosophical schools hold—we shall define it as those who have posited nature only in bodies do.

Its definition is as follows:

> Nature is the principle of motion in itself, not accidentally.

When I said “the principle of motion,” I meant that every body has its own proper motion: fire moves upward, earth downward. Likewise, when I proposed that nature is the principle of motion in itself and not accidentally, the point is this: a wooden bed must also be carried downward, but it is not carried downward accidentally. It is drawn down by weight and heaviness because it is wood, and wood is earth; it does not fall downward because it is a bed, but because it is earth—that is, because it happens to earth to be a bed. Hence we say that wood exists naturally, but a bed artificially.

There is also another meaning of nature, by which we say that the nature of gold differs from that of silver, wishing to indicate the property of things. This meaning of nature may be defined as follows:

> Nature is the specific difference that informs each thing.

Since nature is therefore spoken of or defined in so many ways, both Catholics and Nestorius, according to the last definition, maintain that there are two natures in Christ; for the same differences cannot belong to God and man.

## CHAPTER II. What Person Is

But the question of person is especially difficult: what definition can properly be applied to it? For if every nature has a person, it is impossible to determine what distinction can exist between nature and person. But if person is not equal to nature, and person subsists within the boundary and extent of nature, it is difficult to say how far person extends among natures—that is, which natures should be said to have person and which should be excluded from the term “person.” One point, however, is clear: person is subject to nature, and person cannot be predicated apart from nature.

These matters must therefore be investigated by those who inquire into them as follows. Since person cannot exist apart from nature, and since the things called natures are some substances and some accidents, we see that person cannot be constituted in accidents. For who would say that there is a person of whiteness, blackness, or size? It remains, therefore, that person properly belongs to substances.

But some substances are corporeal and others incorporeal. Of corporeal substances, some are living and others not. Of living things, some are sentient and others not. Of sentient things, some are rational and others irrational. Of rational things, one is by nature immutable and impassible, as God; another is mutable and passible by creation, unless it is transformed by the grace of the substance into the firmness of impassibility, as with angels and the rational soul.

From all this it is clear that person cannot be predicated of nonliving bodies: no one calls a stone a person. Nor, again, can it be predicated of living beings that lack sensation, for no tree is a person. Nor can it be predicated of what lacks understanding and reason: no horse or ox is a person, nor any of the other animals that live a mute and irrational life through the senses alone.

But we say that a person belongs to man; we say that a person belongs to God; we say that a person belongs to an angel.

Again, some substances are universal and others particular. Universal substances are predicated of individuals, such as “man,” “animal,” “stone,” “wood,” and other things of this kind, which are either genera or species. For “man” is said of individual human beings, “animal” of individual animals, and “stone” and “wood” of individual stones and pieces of wood.

Particular substances, however, are not predicated of other things, such as Cicero, Plato, this stone from which this statue of Achilles was made, or this wood from which this table was made.

Among all these, person can nowhere be predicated of universals, but only of singulars and individuals. There is no person of “animal” or of “man” in general; rather, the individual persons are called the persons of Cicero, Plato, or of the separate individuals.

## CHAPTER III. The Difference between Nature and Person

Accordingly, if person exists only in substances, and only in rational substances; if every substance is a nature; and if person is constituted not in universals but in individuals, then the definition of person has been found:

> Person is an individual substance of a rational nature.

By this definition we have defined what the Greeks call *hypostasis* (*hypostasis*). The name “person” appears to have been transferred from elsewhere, namely from the masks through which actors in comedies and tragedies represented the human beings whose roles they played. The word *persona* is said to derive from *personando*, “sounding through,” with the penultimate syllable circumflexed. If the antepenultimate syllable is given the acute accent, it will clearly appear to have been derived from *sonus*, “sound.” It is called this because the sound necessarily reverberates more fully in the concavity of the mask itself.

The Greeks likewise call these masks *prosōpa*, because they are placed upon the face and cover the countenance before the eyes—from the expression *para tou pros tous ōpas tithesthai*, “from being placed before the eyes.”

But since, after putting on the masks, actors represented in tragedy or comedy the individual human beings whose roles they played, as was said—Hecuba, Medea, Simon, or Chremes—the other human beings as well, whose recognition was certain according to their individual form, were called by the Latins *personae* and by the Greeks *prosōpa*.

The Greeks, however, with far greater precision, called the individual subsistence of a rational nature *hypostasis*. But because of our poverty of significant terms, we have retained the transferred designation and call what they call *hypostasis* “person.”

Greece, more expert in language, calls an individual subsistence *hypostasis*. To use Greek terminology in matters discussed by the Greeks and rendered in Latin translation:

> *Hai ousiai en men tois kath’ holou einai dynantai, en de tois kata meros monois hyphistantai.*

That is:

> “Essences can exist in universals, but subsist only in individuals and particulars.”

For the understanding of universal things is derived from particulars. Accordingly, since subsistences exist in universals but receive substance in particulars, they rightly called subsistences that subsist particularly *hypostases*.

For one who examines the matter more carefully and precisely will not think that subsistence and substance are the same. What the Greeks call *ousiōsis* or *ousiōsthai*, we call “subsistence” or “to subsist”; but what they call *hypostasis* or *hyphistasthai*, we render “substance” or “to underlie.”

That subsists which does not require accidents in order to exist. But that underlies which supplies a subject to other accidents so that they may exist; for it stands beneath them insofar as it is subject to accidents.

Thus genera and species merely subsist, since accidents do not belong to genera and species. Individuals, however, not only subsist but also underlie: they themselves do not require accidents in order to exist, and, having already been formed by their proper and specific differences, they supply a subject for accidents insofar as they exist.

Accordingly, *einai* and *ousiōsthai* mean “to be” and “to subsist”; *hyphistasthai* means “to underlie.”

Nor is Greece poor in verbs, as Marcus Tullius suggests; rather, it renders “essence,” “subsistence,” “substance,” and “person” by four distinct names: it calls essence *ousia*, subsistence *ousiōsis*, substance *hypostasis*, and person *prosōpon*.

The Greeks called *hypostases* individual substances because they underlie other things and are placed beneath and subject to them as though to certain accidents. For this reason we too call them substances, as though they were placed beneath; and since they also call these same substances *prosōpa*, we too may call them persons.

Thus *ousia* is the same as essence; *ousiōsis* the same as subsistence; *hypostasis* the same as substance; and *prosōpon* the same as person.

The reason the Greek does not speak of *hypostasis* with reference to irrational animals, as we predicate the name “substance” of those same animals, is that this name has been applied to superior things, so that something might be distinguished by the terms *hypostasis* or substance as something more excellent, even though this is not according to the description of nature and according to what it means to subsist (*hyphistasthai*) and underlie.

Thus man has an essence—that is, *ousia*—and a subsistence—that is, *ousiōsis*—and a *hypostasis*, that is, a substance—and a *prosōpon*, that is, a person.

He has *ousia* and essence because he exists; *ousiōsis* and subsistence because he exists in no subject; *hypostasis* and substance because he underlies other things that are not subsistences, that is, *ousiōseis*; and he is *prosōpon* and person because he is a rational individual.

God likewise is *ousia* and essence, for he exists—and he exists supremely, being the source from which the existence of all things proceeds. He is *ousiōsis*, that is, subsistence, for he subsists, needing nothing; and he is *hyphistasthai*, that is, he underlies.

Hence we say that there is one *ousia* or *ousiōsis* of the deity—that is, one essence or subsistence—but three *hypostases*, that is, three substances. In this way ecclesiastical usage has spoken of one essence of the Trinity, three substances, and three persons.

If ecclesiastical usage did not exclude speaking of three substances in God, one might think that substance was predicated of God not because he was placed beneath other things as their subject, but because, while ruling over all things, he also in a sense underlies them as their principle, supplying them all with *ousiōsthai*, or subsistence.

## CHAPTER IV. Against Nestorius: That There Is One Person

All this has been said so that we might show the difference between nature and person—that is, between *ousia* and *hypostasis*. The authority of ecclesiastical usage must determine what name ought to be applied to each.

For the present, let this be established: nature is the specific property of any substance, whereas person is an individual substance of a rational nature.

Nestorius posits two persons in Christ, led into this error because he thought that person could be predicated of all natures. Having assumed this, and believing that Christ had two natures, he also confessed that he had two persons.

That he is wrong in this matter is shown both by the definition given above and by the following argument, which will plainly reveal his error.

If Christ is not one person, and it is evident that there are two natures—namely, man and God (for no one is so foolish as to separate either of them from the other by reason)—it follows that there appear to be two persons. For person, as has been said, is an individual subsistence of a rational nature.

What, then, was the union of man and God? Was it like the joining of two bodies, so that they were connected only by occupying adjacent places and nothing from the quality of one passed into the other? The Greeks call this mode of union *kata parathesin*, “by juxtaposition.”

But if humanity was joined to divinity in this way, nothing was formed from both, and therefore Christ is nothing.

But if, while the two persons remained, the union of the natures took place in the manner described above, nothing could be made one from the two; for nothing can ever be made from two persons.

According to Nestorius, therefore, Christ is nothing one, and consequently he is altogether nothing. For what is not one cannot exist at all. To be and to be one are convertible, and whatever exists is one. Even things joined from many parts, such as a heap or a chorus, are nevertheless one.

But we plainly and truly confess that Christ exists. Therefore we say that Christ is one.

If this is so, it is necessarily the case, beyond doubt, that Christ is also one person. For if there were two persons, he could not be one. To say that there are two Christs is nothing other than the madness of a mind rushing headlong.

Why would anyone dare to call two persons “Christs”—one man and the other God? Or why call the one who is God “Christ,” if he is also going to call the one who is man “Christ,” when they have nothing similar and nothing joined together through their union?

Why misuse the same name for utterly different natures, when, if he is compelled to define Christ, he cannot apply one substance of definition to both Christs, as he himself calls them?

For if the substance of God and man is different, while the name “Christ” is one in both, and the union of different substances is not believed to have made one person, then “Christ” is an equivocal name and cannot be confined by any definition.

In what Scriptures, however, is the name “Christ” ever doubled?

And what new thing was accomplished by the coming of the Savior? For Catholics recognize both the truth of the faith and the extraordinary character of the miracle.

How great and how new is this: that once, and in no other age, the one who by nature alone is God should be joined with humanity, which was utterly different from him, and that from natures so far apart there should arise, through one union, a single person.

But according to Nestorius’s opinion, what new thing occurred? “Humanity and divinity,” he says, “retain their proper persons.”

When was there ever a time when divinity did not have its own person and humanity its own person? And when will there not be such persons? Or what more occurred in the birth of Jesus than in the birth of anyone else, if, with the two persons separated, the natures too remained separate?

For, with the persons remaining, there could be no union of natures any more there than in any human being, whose own person subsists, while no divinity of the highest substance is joined to him.

Very well, then: why does he call God himself “Christ”? And why does he not dare to apply the same name to the elements themselves, through which God performs remarkable works by their daily motions?

Is it because irrational substances cannot have a person capable of receiving the name “Christ”?

Is not the manifest action of divinity recognized in holy men distinguished by piety? If, in the assumption of humanity, there is not one person in the union, why should he not honor holy men also with the same name?

Perhaps he will say that they too are called Christs. I admit it—but according to the likeness of the true Christ.

If no one person was formed from man and God, we shall regard all of them as true Christs in the same way as we regard him who is believed to have been born from the Virgin. For no person has been united in him through the joining of God and man, just as no person was united in those who, by the Spirit of God, prophesied about the Christ who was to come—which is why they too were called Christs.

It now follows that, if the persons remained, humanity cannot in any way be believed to have been assumed by divinity. For things that are separated equally in person and in nature are completely disjoined. I say, they are utterly disjoined. Humanity and divinity in Christ would be no less separate than men and oxen, if the persons remained.

Men and oxen, after all, are joined by one common animal genus: they have a substance common according to genus, and the same nature when gathered into universality.

But what would not be separated by a different mode of being between God and man, if, beneath the difference of nature, the distinction of persons too is believed to have remained?

The human race, therefore, has not been saved; no salvation has proceeded to us through the birth of Christ; the Scriptures of so many prophets have mocked the believing people; and all the authority of the Old Testament, through which salvation for the world is promised by the birth of Christ, is rejected.

That this has not occurred is clear if the difference in person is the same as the difference in nature. For he saved the same one whom he is believed to have assumed; but no assumption can be understood if the distinction of nature and person remains equally.

Therefore, since the one who could not be assumed while his person remained cannot rightly be thought capable of saving us through the birth of Christ, human nature has not been saved through the birth of Christ. This is impious to believe.

Although there are many arguments capable of attacking and overturning this position, it is sufficient for now to have drawn this small selection from the abundance of arguments.

## CHAPTER V. Against Eutyches: That Christ Truly Assumed a Body from Mary
It is necessary to turn to Eutyches, who, having strayed from the paths of the ancients, ran into the opposite error. He asserted that it was so far from being necessary to believe Christ to have a twofold person that one ought not even to confess in him a twofold nature. He held that the man had been assumed in such a way that the union with God was effected so completely that the human nature did not remain. His error flows from the same source as that of Nestorius. For just as Nestorius thinks that there cannot be a twofold nature without a twofold person, and therefore, when he confessed a twofold nature in Christ, believed the person also to be twofold, so Eutyches likewise did not think that there could be a twofold nature without a doubling of the person; and since he did not confess the person to be twofold, he judged it to follow that the nature must be regarded as one.

Thus Nestorius, rightly holding that Christ has a twofold nature, sacrilegiously confesses that there are two persons; while Eutyches, rightly believing that there is one person, impiously believes that there is also one nature. When compelled by the evidence of facts—for it is clear that the nature of man is one thing and that of God another—he says that he confesses two natures in Christ before the union, but one after the union. [Col. 1348A] This statement does not openly express what he intends. Yet, if we examine his madness, this union must have taken place either at the time of the generation or at the time of the resurrection.

But if it took place at the time of the generation, he seems to suppose that, before the generation, there was human flesh—not taken from Mary, but prepared in some other way—and that the Virgin Mary was brought in, from whom flesh would be born although it had not been taken from her. He would then hold that the flesh which had previously existed was divided and separated from the substance of the divinity, but that, when he was born from the Virgin, it was united to God, so that it appeared to have become one nature.

Or, if this is not his position, it could be the position of one who says “two before the union, one after the union,” if the union was completed by the generation: namely, that he did indeed take a body from Mary, [Col. 1348B] but that, before he took it, the nature of deity and that of humanity were different; once taken, however, they became one and the human nature passed into the substance of the divinity.

But if he thinks that this union was effected not by the generation but by the resurrection, he will again suppose that it occurred in one of two ways: either Christ was born without assuming a body from Mary, or, having assumed flesh from her, the two natures remained until he rose, but became one after the resurrection.

From these alternatives arises the question that we shall put in this form: Did Christ, born from Mary, derive human flesh from her, or not? If he does not confess that he derived it from her, let him say with what man’s flesh he came clothed—whether with that of the man who had fallen through the transgression of sin, or with that of another.

If it was that man from whose seed mankind was derived, the one with whom the divinity was clothed? [The Latin wording is corrupt.] For if it was not the flesh of Abraham, David, and finally Mary, let him show from whose human flesh it was derived, since, after the first man, all human flesh is derived from human flesh. But if he names some man other than the Virgin Mary from whom the Savior’s generation was taken, he is himself confounded by error and, having been deceived, will appear to stamp the highest Divinity with the mark of falsehood, since he assigns to others what is promised to Abraham and David in the sacred prophecies, namely, that salvation should arise from their seed for the whole world. This is especially impossible because, if human flesh was assumed, it could have been assumed from no source other than the one from which it was also generated.

If, therefore, the human body was not taken from Mary but from someone else, though it was nevertheless generated through Mary—the body that had been corrupted by transgression—it is refuted by the argument stated above. But if Christ was not clothed with the man who had endured death as the penalty of sin, it follows that no such person could have been born from any man’s seed who was without the punishment of original sin.

No such flesh, then, was taken from anyone; hence it appears to have been newly formed.
