But this flesh either appeared to human eyes in such a way that it was thought to be a human body although it was not truly human—for it was subject to no punishment of original sin—or a new and genuine human nature, not subject to the punishment of original sin, was formed for a time.

If it was not a true human body, the divinity is plainly charged with deceit, since it displayed to human beings a body which, because it was not real, deceived those who believed it to be real. But if new and genuine flesh, not taken from a human being, was formed, what need was there for so great a drama of generation? What need was there for the scale of the passion? For even among human beings I do not think that what was done uselessly was done intelligently.

For what useful purpose would such great humility of the Divinity be brought forth, if the human being who had perished was not saved by the generation and passion of Christ, since he was denied to have been assumed? Thus, just as the error of Eutyches took its beginning from the same source as that of Nestorius, so it falls back into the same conclusion: according to Eutyches too, the human race was not saved, because the one who was sick and needed salvation and healing was not assumed.

He appears to have adopted this view—if indeed this was the character of his error—because he believed that Christ’s body was not truly from a human being, but had been formed elsewhere, by God, in heaven; for it is believed to have ascended into heaven with him, and the example contains this principle: no one ascends into heaven except the one who descended from heaven.

## CHAPTER VI. That neither the divinity was changed into humanity, nor humanity into divinity, nor were the two mixed together.

Enough seems to have been said about that matter, if it is not believed that the body which Christ received was assumed from Mary. But if it was assumed from Mary, and the perfect human and divine natures did not remain, this could have occurred in three ways: either the divinity was changed into humanity, or humanity into divinity, or the two were so blended and mixed together that neither substance retained its proper form.

But if the divinity was changed into humanity, something occurred which it is impious to believe: the divinity was converted into humanity, although its substance did not remain immutable; and what naturally existed as subject to suffering and change remained immutable, while what is naturally believed to be immutable and incapable of suffering was converted into a changeable thing.

This cannot occur in any way. Perhaps, then, the human nature may seem to have been converted into deity. But how could this happen, if in Christ’s generation the divinity assumed both a human soul and a body? For not every thing can be converted and transformed into every other thing. Since some substances are corporeal and others incorporeal, neither can a corporeal thing be changed into an incorporeal thing, nor an incorporeal thing into one that is a body.

Nor do incorporeal things change their proper forms into one another. Only those things can be changed and transformed into one another which have a common underlying subject of the same material; and not even all of these, but only those which can both act upon and be acted upon by one another.

This is demonstrated as follows. Bronze cannot be changed into stone, nor can the same bronze be changed into a plant, nor can any one body be transformed into any other body unless the things passing into one another have the same matter and can both act and be acted upon by one another. Thus wine and water, when mixed, are both of such a kind that they share action and passivity with respect to one another.

The quality of water can undergo something from the quality of wine. Therefore, if there is much water but little wine, they are not said to be mixed; rather, one is corrupted by the quality of the other. If someone pours wine into the sea, the wine is not mixed with the sea; it is corrupted in the sea. This is because the quality of the water, by the multitude of its body, suffers nothing from the quality of the wine, but instead, by its own greater quantity, changes the quality of the wine into itself.

If, however, the natures are moderate and equal to one another, or only slightly unequal, and can act and be acted upon by one another, they are mixed and tempered by qualities intermediate between them.

These principles apply to bodies—and not to all bodies, but only to those which, as has been said, can both act and be acted upon by one another while sharing a common and identical matter. Every body that exists in generation and corruption appears to have matter in common, but not every body can act upon or be acted upon by every other, or in every other.

Corporeal things, however, cannot in any way be changed into incorporeal things, because they do not participate in a common underlying matter which could, after receiving their qualities, be changed from one into the other. For the whole nature of incorporeal substance rests upon no material foundation; whereas there is no body without an underlying matter.

Since this is so, and since even things which naturally possess common matter do not pass into one another unless they have the power both to act upon and to be acted upon by one another, still less will those things be changed into one another which not only have no common matter, but of which one—such as a body—rests upon matter as its foundation, while the other—an incorporeal thing—has no need at all of an underlying material subject.

It cannot, therefore, happen that a body is changed into an incorporeal form; nor can incorporeal things be changed into one another through any mixture. For things which have no matter in common cannot be converted and changed into one another. Incorporeal things have no matter; therefore they cannot be changed into one another.

The soul and God are rightly believed to be incorporeal substances. The human soul, therefore, was not changed into the divinity by which it was assumed. Since neither the body nor the soul could be changed into divinity, it could in no way happen that humanity was converted into God.

Still less can it be believed that the two were confused into one another, since incorporeality cannot pass into a body, nor, conversely, can a body pass into incorporeality. For they have no common underlying matter which could be changed according to the qualities of either substance.

Yet these people say: “Christ consists from two natures, but not in two.” Their intention is evidently this: something that consists from two things can become one in such a way that the things from which it is said to consist do not remain. Thus, when honey is mixed with water, neither remains; one, corrupted by union with the other, produces a third thing. Accordingly, the third thing produced from honey and water is said to consist from both, but is denied to exist in both; for it cannot consist in both when the nature of both does not remain.

It can consist from both, although the things from which it is joined have been corrupted by one another’s quality. But it cannot consist in both in this sense, because the things poured into one another do not remain, and the two things from which it appears to consist are no longer both present, since they have been poured into one another through a change of qualities.

Catholics, however, reasonably confess both: that Christ is from both natures and consists in both. I shall explain shortly how this is to be understood. For now, it is clear that Eutyches’ position has been refuted on this ground: since there are three ways in which one thing could subsist from two natures—either the divinity could have been changed into humanity, or humanity into divinity, or the two could have been mixed together—the argument given above shows that none of these ways could have occurred.

## CHAPTER VII. That Christ consists in both and from both natures.

It remains for us to teach how the catholic faith says that Christ consists both in both natures and from both natures.

For something’s consisting from both natures has two meanings. The first is when we say that something is joined from two natures, as from honey and water. This means that the two have been confused in some manner, whether one has been changed into the other or both have been mixed together, with neither remaining in any way. It is in this sense that Eutyches says Christ consists from both natures.

The second way of consisting from both is when something is joined from two things in such a way that the things from which it is said to be joined remain and are not changed into one another, as when we say that a crown is composed of gold and gems. Here neither has gold been changed into gems nor gems into gold; both remain and do not abandon their proper form.

Thus, of things which consist from something, we say that they consist in those things from which they are said to consist. We can therefore say that a crown consists in gems and gold, for gems and gold are what constitute the crown. In the first case, however, honey and water are not the things in which that which is joined from both consists.

Since the catholic faith confesses that both natures remain in Christ and persist as perfect, neither being changed into the other, it rightly says that Christ is both in both natures and from both natures: in both, because both remain; from both, because through the union of both remaining natures there arises the one person of Christ.

The catholic faith does not, however, maintain that Christ is joined from both natures in the sense in which Eutyches declares it. For Eutyches gives such a meaning to the joining from both natures that he does not confess that Christ consists in both, nor that both remain. The catholic, by contrast, adopts that meaning of “consisting from both” which is closest to and preserves the meaning of “consisting in both,” which he confesses.

“Consisting from both,” then, is equivocal—or rather amphibolous—and designates different things under a twofold meaning. In one sense it means that the substances from which the joined thing is said to be constituted do not remain; in another, it means that it is joined from both in such a way that both remain.

Once this knot of equivocation and ambiguity has been untied, nothing further can be brought forward against what the firm and true catholic faith contains: that the same Christ is a perfect human being, the same is God, and the same one who is perfect man and God is one God and Son of God.

Nor is a quaternity of the Trinity asserted when a human being is added to perfect God. Rather, one and the same person completes the number of the Trinity, so that, although humanity suffered, God is nevertheless said to have suffered—not because the divinity itself became humanity, but because humanity was assumed by the divinity.

Likewise, the one who is man is called the Son of God—not in respect of the substance of divinity, but of humanity, which nevertheless has been joined to divinity by a natural unity.

Although these matters are distinguished and combined in understanding in this way, the same one is nevertheless both perfect man and God: God, because he himself was begotten from the substance of the Father; man, because he was born from the Virgin Mary.

Likewise, the one who is man is God because he was assumed by God; and the one who is God is man because he was clothed with man. Although in the same person the divinity that assumed is one thing and the humanity that was assumed another, the same one is nevertheless God and man.

For if you understand Christ as man, he is the same man and God, because he is man by nature and God by assumption. If you understand him as God, he is the same God and man, because he is God by nature and man by assumption.

In him there is a twofold nature and a twofold substance, because he is man and God; and one person, because the same one is man and God.

This is the middle path between the two heresies, just as the virtues also occupy the middle. Every virtue consists in a mean placed in the beauty of things: if it is exercised either beyond or below what is fitting, one departs from virtue. Virtue therefore holds the mean.

Accordingly, since these four possibilities cannot all be true of Christ, they are as follows: either there are two natures and two persons, as Nestorius says; or one person and one nature, as Eutyches says; or two natures but one person, as the catholic faith believes; or one nature and two persons.

We have refuted the view of two natures and two persons in the response directed against Nestorius, and, when Eutyches proposed that there was one person and one nature, we have shown that this too is impossible. Nor has anyone yet been so mad as to believe that there was one nature in him while still maintaining that there were two persons. It remains, therefore, that the true position is the one proclaimed by the catholic faith: a twofold substance, but one person.

Since shortly before we said that Eutyches confessed two natures in Christ before the union but one after the union, and since we interpreted this error as concealing a twofold meaning—either that the union occurred through the generation, with no body being taken from Mary, or that, although it was taken from Mary, the union occurred through the resurrection—we have, as I think, argued adequately on both points.

Now it must be asked how it could have happened that two natures were mixed into one substance.

## CHAPTER VIII. What the condition of Christ’s life was.

[Col. 1353A]

There is, nevertheless, another question that can still be raised by those who do not believe that the human body was taken from Mary, but think that it had been separated and prepared elsewhere, so that at the union it might appear to have been generated and brought forth from Mary’s womb.

They say that, if the body was taken from a human being, and every human being, from the first transgression onward, was held not only by sin and death but also entangled in sinful passions—and if this was the punishment of sin imposed upon him, that although bound by death he was also guilty through his will to sin—why was there in Christ neither sin nor any will to sin?

Such a question certainly requires careful consideration. For if Christ’s body was assumed from human flesh, it may be questioned what sort of flesh this assumed flesh appears to have been: he saved the very one whom he also assumed.

But if he assumed a man of the kind Adam was before sin, he appears to have assumed a complete human nature, yet one that had no need at all of medicine. How, moreover, could he have assumed a man such as Adam was, when in Adam there could be a will and inclination to sin? This is why, even after transgressing the divine commands, he was held bound by the offense of disobedience.

In Christ, however, no will to sin is believed to have existed—especially since, if he assumed such a human body as Adam had before sin, it should not have been mortal, because Adam, if he had not sinned, would in no way have experienced death.

Since Christ did not sin, it must therefore be asked why he experienced death if he assumed Adam’s body before Adam sinned.

But if he assumed the human condition that Adam had after sin, it appears that in Christ too there should have been the necessity of being subjected to offenses and overwhelmed by passions, and that, with the rules of judgment obscured, he should not distinguish good from evil with undivided integrity, since Adam received all these punishments through the transgression of his offense.

To these objections we must reply that three conditions of human beings can be understood. The first is Adam’s condition before the offense. Although death was absent from him and he had not yet defiled himself with any offense, there could nevertheless be in him a will to sin.

The second is the condition into which he could have been changed if he had chosen to remain firmly in God’s commands. In that case it would have been added that he not only would not sin or wish to sin, but would not even be able to sin or wish to commit an offense.

The third condition is after the offense, in which death necessarily followed him, together with sin itself and the will to sin.

These are the two extremes and opposites; between them lies the condition that would have been the reward if Adam had wished to remain in God’s commands, and the condition that became his punishment because he did not wish to remain. In the former there would have been neither death, nor sin, nor any will to sin. In the latter there were death, sin, every inclination toward wrongdoing, and everything tending toward destruction, with nothing in itself possessing the power to rise again after the fall.

The intermediate condition, in which the presence of death and sin was absent but the power of both was present, was placed between the two.

From these three conditions, therefore, Christ in some way took the respective elements for his bodily nature. The fact that he assumed a mortal body, in order to drive death from the human race, must be assigned to the condition imposed as punishment after Adam’s transgression.

The fact that there was in him no will to sin was taken from the condition that could have existed if Adam had not applied his will to the deceits of the tempter.

There remains the third, intermediate condition: that which existed at the time when death was absent but the will to sin could be present.

In this condition Adam was such that he could eat and drink, digest what he had taken, fall asleep, and perform the other activities that were not lacking in him—human activities, certainly, but permitted ones, and ones that did not bring upon him any punishment of death.

There is no doubt that Christ possessed all these things. He ate and drank and performed the functions of a human body.

We should not suppose that Adam had such great need that he could not have lived unless he ate. Rather, if he ate from every tree, he could have lived forever and would not have died through these things; therefore he satisfied his need with the fruits of Paradise.

No one is unaware that this need existed in Christ, but by power, not by necessity. This very need was in him before the resurrection. After the resurrection, however, his condition was such that the human body was changed in the way Adam’s could have been changed, apart from the bond of transgression.

The same Lord Jesus Christ himself taught us through our prayers to desire that his will be done “as in heaven and on earth,” that his kingdom come, and that he deliver us from evil. For all these things are sought in prayer by that most blessed transformation of the human race that faithfully believes.

These are the matters concerning my belief in the faith that I have written to you. If anything has been said incorrectly in this, I am not so enamored of myself as to insist on preferring what I have once poured forth to a better judgment.

For if nothing good comes from us, there is nothing in our opinions that we ought to love. But if all good things come from him who alone is good, that should rather be believed good which that unchangeable goodness, the cause of all good things, sets down in writing.

[Col. 1353]

## GILBERT OF POITIERS’ COMMENTARY ON THE BOOK ON THE TWO NATURES AND ONE PERSON OF CHRIST

[Col. 1353D]

I am not unaware that orators sharp in talent, previously trained and long and extensively practiced among sophists, carefully attend to the kinds of cases in their own— that is, civic—subject matter. According to the importance or insignificance of the matters, they bring the more obscure points to light by means either of induction or of reasoning; they pass over matters that are less obscure by mentioning a few examples or enthymemes; but in matters that are evident, they both disregard every kind of argument by remaining silent and remain silent by disregarding it.

Noble philosophers too are known to have done this in their disciplines. In matters where understanding is obscured by what appears to be a conflict among many arguments, they disprove the false parts of questions by numerous demonstrations and confirm the true ones. But in matters where one side of a question is scarcely shaken by a few and weak arguments, they do not labor much to demonstrate its falsity and the truth of the other side.

If, however, one side of a contradiction has no reasons whatsoever in support of truth, and the other therefore seems to need none, they set out in briefer words what they understand about the matters, without any presentation of argument. If someone demands arguments of this kind from them, or offers them himself, they disregard them in silence.

Yet because some unskilled people—and the more they boast of being something, the less they are—chatter against the most obvious truth and eagerly assert with contentious shouting, as though they were outstanding “hebdomads” and paradoxes (*paradoxa*) worthy of admiration, things that are plainly false and beyond any resemblance to reason, philosophers are compelled to strengthen their case against sophists and sometimes to demonstrate with many arguments, as though they were doubtful, things that are entirely beyond doubt.

Their arguments on such matters must not be called frivolous or superfluous. For just as, among the wise, arguments by which both sides of a contradiction appear capable of being proved bring an affirmation and its negation into doubt, so among the foolish the presumption of those who shamelessly claim authority for themselves in their eyes produces a similar effect. I do not mean that the proposition itself comes into doubt—for the common people pass beyond doubt—but that they swear that what is false is true and what is impossible is necessary.

By these arguments, through which certainties are seriously demonstrated as though they were doubtful, provision is made for the less educated: the impudence of such people is blunted by their arguments, and the authority acquired through presumption is nullified.

Boethius, a Catholic through sound faith in invisible things and a philosopher through true knowledge of things, rightly considered this. He demonstrated by many arguments what was certain concerning the unity of Christ’s person and the diversity of his nature, against Nestorius the bishop and Eutyches the archimandrite (*archimandritan*).

Nestorius, who did not understand the meaning of “person,” and Eutyches, who did not understand the meaning of “nature,” chattered most shamelessly, each against the other and both against the catholic faith and against philosophical reasoning—reasoning which rests upon the foundation of the Christian faith concerning the unity of person and the diversity of natures in Christ.

Nestorius, not understanding by what reasoning the name “person” is imposed upon any individual, falsely claimed that Christ consisted of two persons. Eutyches, however, entirely denied the diversity of natures in Christ after the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

Nestorius, in opposition to Eutyches, professed the truth concerning the diversity of natures; Eutyches, in opposition to Nestorius, professed the truth concerning the unity of person. But they did so, as it appears, not so much through the movement of reason as through a natural accident.

Often, like people dreaming, they burst forth amid many things they stammer out from confused elements of speech into words of truth through some inarticulate force of nature, entirely without the understanding of their minds.

Boethius rightly disproves them with firm and evident arguments—not in order to offer the wise an ambiguity concerning some question, but to remove authority, and consequently error, from simple people who might presume to speak—because Nestorius and Eutyches, drawn not by any appearance of reason but corrupted by presumption alone and deceived by the opinion of their own ingenuity, did not blush to say openly false things about the diversity of persons and the unity of nature in Christ, and, still more shamelessly, to write them.

He confirms the ecclesiastical faith, which stands between these two heresies, concerning the unity of Christ’s person and the diversity of his nature.

He addresses this work to John, the Roman deacon. And because what he demonstrates is certain both to philosophers through reason and to Catholics through faith, he does not conceal his judgment, to be learned by a few, in novel or truncated expressions, as is his custom. Rather, he treats the matter in an elegant, pure, and open style.

### “Indeed, I anxiously awaited you,” etc.

He first sets down a long prologue in which he explains the reason and manner of his writing. He engages the reader’s attention—not because he says that the matters he discusses are new or incredible, but because they are great and concern God and the whole Church.

He wins goodwill from the person of his opponents by making them objects of hatred through recalling their presumption, and objects of contempt through recalling their ignorance. He also seeks goodwill from his own person and that of his audience: he mentions his own actions and duties without arrogance, praises John, to whom he is writing, as the corrector of his work, and appoints Symmachus, to whom he dedicates the same work, as its judge.

When he openly and briefly explains what he is discussing and in what order, he makes the reader attentive and receptive.

The reason for writing is as follows. At a certain council attended by Boethius and John, a bishop’s letter containing the Eutychian heresy was read. After the Eutychians and the Catholics had argued against one another amid contentious and confused shouting, Boethius waited for John for a long time that day and even longer afterward, so that he might discuss with him what they had heard.

But then John’s affairs, and afterward his own, prevented Boethius from enjoying his conversation in any way. He therefore took care to communicate in writing, while absent, what he had wished to say in person while present.

This is what he means by: “Indeed, I anxiously and for a long time awaited you”—that is, “I waited for you, weighed down as though by the burden of prolonged longing”—for this reason: so that you and I might speak together about the question which is not truly said to arise among the wise from arguments contending against one another, but among the foolish from their opinions, without any conflict of arguments—a question stirred up in the assembly by the arrogance of certain people presuming upon themselves, through which they claim authority for themselves among the ignorant.

### “But since,” etc.

As though he were saying: “I did indeed await you so that we might speak about the question. Yet even then, after my waiting, we did not speak. You were distracted by the demands of your affairs, and for the present we cannot converse, because I too shall be entangled in business tomorrow—that is, in the future—with matters I have arranged to undertake.

“Since, therefore, your occupations prevented us from having time together for conversation, and mine will prevent it, I am sending you in writing, while absent, what I had preserved to discuss with you face to face—that is, what I had intended to say in person while awaiting your arrival.”

He recalls what these matters were, saying:

“For, as I think, you remember that when the bishop’s letter was read at the council, it was reported that the Eutychians—that is, the followers of Eutyches—confessed that Christ consisted from two natures before the incarnation, but denied that after the incarnation he consisted in two; whereas the Catholics gave credence to both statements. For they confessed that he was from two before the incarnation and likewise believed that he consisted in two natures after the incarnation.”

### “Struck by the novelty of this statement,” etc.

As though he were saying: “It was reported that the Eutychians confessed that Christ consisted from two natures, but not in two. Struck by the profane novelty of this statement—that is, moved in spirit as though by a sudden blow—I began to inquire, speaking as if to others and questioning myself, into the differences between these unions—that is, compositions—of natural things.

“I was asking which unions were such that the things joined consisted from two natures but not in two, and which were such that they consisted both from two and in two.

“I did not inquire into these differences without reason. I was compelled to investigate them by the authority of the bishop who had written the letter read at the assembly. I judged that the matter was of great importance—that is, greatly useful—and not to be passed over through sluggish negligence.

“As though he were saying: ‘What the bishop [Col. 1357A] has said must be considered with great vigilance.’ As though he were saying: ‘The writer of the letter, whose judgment should settle every controversy by both authority and reason and bring deliberations to an end with the certainty of his statement, would not have wished to pass over, as something highly necessary and especially important for understanding the nature of this union, what he had not uttered in a sudden movement of spirit into passing words, but had entrusted to a page destined to remain through the deliberate understanding of reason.’”

### “Then everyone,” etc.

As though he were saying: “It was reported at the council that the Eutychians confessed Christ to consist from two natures, but not in two. Then, when this had been reported, everyone began to make a commotion—that is, they expressed through the movement of their bodies the madness of their hastened minds—and, shouting in confusion, said that this difference was obvious, that it was correctly stated that Christ consisted from two natures and not in two, and that it was so obvious that, although some things are clear and others are not in other matters, in the difference signified by these words—‘from two,’ not ‘in two’—there was not even the least obscurity, much less a great deal: nothing disordered that could not be understood in any way, and nothing confused that might appear in one respect to exist and in another not to exist.”

### “No one was found,” etc.

As though he were saying: “Everyone was shouting that the difference was obvious. Yet amid such a tumult of people chattering without reason, no one was found who even lightly touched upon the question through some conception of reason, much less anyone who clarified it by distinguishing its multiple aspects.

“I was seated at that assembly with the person whom I most wished to observe, Symmachus, but at a considerable distance—that is, very far away—and turned from him. You can understand this if you recall the arrangement of those seated at the assembly: several people were seated between him and me and stood in the way.

“I could not, although I desired it most earnestly, look upon his face and gestures, from which observation of his face and gestures might give me some indication of his judgment—that is, might show me what he himself judged concerning the difference mentioned above.”

**“And I,” etc.]** As if to say: The others did not address the question, yet they loudly proclaimed that the distinction was clear. I, for my part, contributed nothing more than the others—indeed, something less, or rather, truly nothing more. For concerning the matter proposed, that is, the distinction between the aforesaid conjunctions, I understood no more than the others, that is, no more than they did. I contributed less than they did, as has been said; and he explains what this was: namely, the presumption of false knowledge. I did not presume to assert what I did not know.

I confess that I was deeply distressed that I understood nothing about the matter in question. And when I wished to inquire about it from others, I was silenced by the tumultuous babbling of the unlearned described above, fearing that I should rightly appear insane if, by investigating the truth, I insisted on being considered sane among madmen who, without reason, asserted what they had not understood—indeed, what they could not understand. [Col. 1357D]

**“I was therefore considering,” etc.]** As if to say: I was silent. Thereafter I considered inwardly all the questions that had arisen from the words of the letter read at the aforesaid assembly—whether concerning natures, persons, or their unity or diversity—not so much from the multiplicity of sophistical expressions or from the diversity of arguments according to their various kinds, as from the corruption of minds and the presumption of foolish men. I did not, through lack of attention, swallow what I had received according to that first sense which normally accompanies a signification, or, so to speak, according to an imaginative understanding; rather, I chewed it over through repeated and frequent reflection.

I therefore thought that the manifest matter should be deliberated upon in view, on the one hand, of the confession of the Catholics and, on the other, of the number and authority of those who contradicted them; and, having consulted the arguments, I sought an end to my deliberation. At last, when these arguments had repeatedly struck my mind, the doors opened to me, [Col. 1358A] that is, neither the multitude nor the authority of those contradicting the Catholics stood in the way. Thus the truth of the Catholic confession, when I sought it, that is, opened up all the clouds, or obscurities, of the Eutychian error. For the manifestation of truth through arguments revealed both the error of Eutyches and his followers and the causes of that error.

From this discovery of the truth of the Catholics and the error of the Eutychians there arose in me—that is, it entered my mind without prior deliberation—a great wonder at what this could be: namely, at such audacity among unlearned men, who attempted to cover over, that is, conceal, the defect of their ignorance beneath a cloud of presumption and shamelessness—in other words, beneath shameless presumption. For inwardly they presume upon these matters through the arrogance of their hearts, and outwardly they shamelessly display, through excessive utterance and bodily gesticulation, what they do not know. Hence he adds:

Although they often not only fail to know what is proposed by others, but also, in such loud disputes—where one expression is confused with another and therefore one signification with another—do not even understand what they themselves are saying. [Col. 1358B]

**“As if,” etc.]** As has been said, they attempt to cover over the defect of their ignorance with a cloud of presumption and shamelessness, as though the cause of ignorance were not made worse when ignorance itself is concealed. The cause of any ignorance is simple when it arises from neglect of one’s own study; but it is doubled, and therefore worse, when contempt for another’s learning is added to one’s own negligence.

But from those shameless men I turn to you, humble as you are. I send you this small work—however slight—which I have written against the aforesaid Eutyches and also against Nestorius, for examination and careful consideration. The order of the words is reversed: “for careful consideration and examination.” By “careful consideration” I mean the attentive inspection of what has been written; by “examination,” judgment according to reason—before I submit it either to Symmachus for judgment or expose it for reading to others.

If you pronounce that it is sound both in its rule of expression and in its statement of truth, I ask that you insert this also, as you do the other things that I write to you, into the books bearing my name. But if anything should be reduced, because it exceeds what is needed either in words or in meaning; or if something should be added, because it is similarly deficient in words or meaning; or if anything should be altered by a change of wording or sense, I ask that this too be sent back to my copies, from which the other books are to be transcribed. Thus, of course, it should return from you ready to be copied without any further correction.

When these have been brought to the end—that is, to completion—the meaning is this: once they have been found to be perfectly corrected and henceforth not subject to alteration by any further correction, then at last let them be sent, to be judged by his judgment, that is, by Symmachus’s, according to whose judgment I customarily send whatever is to be judged.

And indeed, while the discussion concerns various words, matters are first expressed with the addition of certain expansions and with frequent repetitions of meanings and words out of their proper order. Then, if it happens that the discourse reaches its conclusion, what has been stated diffusely and confusedly is brought into order through the brevity of an epilogue.

But since a matter is not written down as many times as it is spoken—indeed, it is transferred from conversation to writing only once, and what has been said in many ways is committed simply to writing—it is as though he were saying: everything is arranged briefly and orderly in writing. Therefore, in this work also, in which we write concerning nature and person against Nestorius and Eutyches, so that each matter may be treated in its proper order, the errors of Nestorius and Eutyches must first be removed.

I call them the extreme errors, because they are contrary to one another. Afterwards, with God’s help—God alone being the author of all things—I shall temper the exposition, that is, place nothing less and nothing more than is appropriate to our purpose, and shall explain moderately the middle position of the Christian faith.

It is as if he were saying: I shall not treat all the parts of the faith, but only that part which lies between the aforesaid extreme and contrary errors: namely, the unity of Christ’s person, with Eutyches against Nestorius, and the diversity of natures in Christ, with Nestorius against Eutyches.

Since, however, in the entire question that must here be treated—concerning αἱρέσεις, that is, heresies, opposed to one another—the doubt concerns natures and persons, these matters, namely nature and person, must first be defined and separated from one another by their proper differences. Through these differences it may be understood not so much why the things to which these names have been given are called by them, as what the usage of philosophers has reduced these terms to signify. Nevertheless, in what follows he explains in a certain manner the reason for the name “person.”

# ON NATURE

**“Nature, therefore,” etc.]** He defines nature first and person afterwards, using the familiar term “nature” as his starting point. This is entirely appropriate, because, according to the philosophers, the being of all natural things—and therefore of all persons, which have some existence from natures—is nature. Every being, insofar as it is being, is naturally prior.

Here we should recall what Marcus Tullius says in these words: “It is difficult to define nature itself. But it is easier to enumerate its parts, the parts of which we need for this instruction.” He speaks correctly. For “nature” is a name of many meanings, so that it is spoken not only in many ways but also with many significations concerning things of different kinds in different disciplines. Philosophers, ethicists, and theologians all make extensive use of this name.

Therefore Boethius does not here define nature in general, but enumerates the parts of it that appear relevant to his purpose, saying:

“Nature, therefore, can be spoken of either only of bodies, or only of substances”—that is, corporeal or incorporeal substances—“or of all things that are said to be in any way.”

Here he wants “substances” to mean those things that subsist, not the substances by which they subsist. By “things that are said to be in any way,” he understands both subsisting things and subsistences, as well as things that happen to them; he also includes God and ὕλη, that is, matter, as becomes clear from what follows. The other matters belonging either to ethics or to logic do not appear to belong to this division at all.

Here it must be carefully noted that a subsisting thing has no genus or rational principle whatsoever in common with subsistence or accidents. Both subsisting thing and subsistence are called substances, or subjects, but for different reasons. Much less, therefore, is there any community of genus or rational principle between God and primordial matter, on the one hand, and subsisting things, subsistences, and accidents, on the other.

It is therefore clear that the name “nature” cannot be understood as the general topic—that is, the common place—of all these things. Consequently, all the things designated by this name cannot be enclosed within a single definition. Hence he says:

“Since, then, nature can be said”—so far as it is relevant to recall for the present work—“in three ways,” that is, since the three things mentioned above are called “nature” in three ways, it must undoubtedly be defined in three ways.

**“For if it is said of all things,” etc.]** Reversing the order, he defines first what he had placed last in the division. He says:

“If it is considered appropriate to speak of nature with reference to all things”—as we read that many philosophers considered appropriate—“a definition will be given that can include all things that are.”

Here it should be said that some definitions show not only what thing is called by a name, but also what it is to be what is so called; others show only what thing is called by a name, and by no means what it is to be what is so called.

For by the definition “man is a rational animal,” not only is it shown what thing man is, but also what it is to be man. For not only is whoever is a man a rational animal, but being a man is itself being a rational animal.

By contrast, in the definition “difference is that by which a species exceeds its genus,” what is shown is what thing difference is; it is not merely shown what it is to be a difference. The thing by which a species exceeds its genus is undoubtedly a difference; it is not merely the case that its being a difference consists in the species exceeding its genus.

He defines nature by definitions of this kind, namely, definitions that demonstrate what things are natures, not merely that they are natures. If, therefore, nature is said of all things, as was stated above, the definition of nature will be of this kind:

“Nature is of those things”—that is, those things are natures—“which, when they exist, can in some way be grasped by the understanding.”

By this definition it has been shown what things are natures, but not that they are natures. For it has not been shown that they are natures by the fact that they can be grasped by the understanding.

He explains what a manifold name “nature” is, and what he wants understood as included under this definition, by saying:

“In this definition, therefore, accidents and substances are defined.”

This is not because, as has been said, “these things can be grasped by the understanding” means that they are natures, but because these are the things that can be grasped by the understanding. Hence he adds:

“For all these things”—that is, accidents and substances, both subsisting things, in which accidents exist, and subsistences, to which accidents belong—“can be grasped by the understanding.”

Then he explains why he added “in some way” and “when they exist,” saying:

**“But the addition ‘in some way,’” etc.]** It should be known that the movement of the mind sometimes encounters what exists and sometimes what does not exist, and thus apprehends either what exists or what does not exist.

Any conception of what does not exist is called an opinion, such as the conception of a two-bodied Centaur or a three-bodied Chimaera. The conception of what exists is divided according to the kind of thing conceived and the modes of conceiving it.

Natural things are conceived through some property of themselves, either an efficient property or a property of producing an effect: for example, white through whiteness, and whiteness through the nature by which it makes something white. Nothing natural can be conceived except through a cause, and nothing mathematical except through the power of producing an effect.

But just as, in perceiving external things, the sense first hesitates and then becomes fixed with certainty upon what is presented to it, so the mind too, when its own movement is directed toward something, first thinks its nature in a mixed and confused way; then, by a certain abstraction proper to reason, it separates it from the other things with which it had encountered it simultaneously, and marks it with a fixed gaze just as it is.

This is clear in the things perceived externally. The sight, which perceives colors with the assistance of figures, and the bodies subject to them, if it encounters red and reddish at the same time through its movement, initially does not distinguish them at all, and afterwards distinguishes them only with difficulty. The same is true of white and whitish and other such things.

It likewise distinguishes figures less readily when one is longer in front and longer in another respect, in proportion as one exceeds the other by a smaller margin. Hearing either does not distinguish or distinguishes only with difficulty those sounds—φθόγγοι, that is, tones or sounds—the proportion of whose parts is marked by an extremely small difference.

For the similarity of all things that stand in proportion is closer where the differences are smaller, just as their dissimilarity is more remote where the differences are greater.

In things that the mind perceives inwardly, not only similarity but also the multitude of things causes it first to weigh, as though with foreknowledge, what it is acting upon, and then to perceive it with increasing attention, although it does not yet assent to it.

This anticipatory weighing, or perception without assent, is not called opinion, because it concerns what exists rather than what does not exist. But because it concerns what exists, whose truth assent does not yet possess, it is called “imagination” by a certain transference of the name.

An image is a thing, but not the truth of that of which it is an image. Therefore the perception of a thing without assent to its truth is rightly called imagination.

If, however, the mind first weighs and then perceives what lies within the similarity or multitude of things, and selects it from among those similar or otherwise numerous things, and, having marked it with the fixed gaze of the mind according to its own property, assents to the perception, this is called understanding.

Rightly so. For the similarity of a thing should truly be said to exist in the mind when the mind has selected the thing from among the other things by the aid of its own property and has thereby assented to the preceding perception.

Natural things are conceived through the aids belonging to what they are; fictitious things are conceived through the aids belonging to what they are imagined to be.

But the two principles of natural things—God and primordial matter—are conceived in a very different way. [Col. 1361A] They are not something through the subsistences, quantities, or qualities by which natural things truly are something, nor through those by which things that are not something are imagined to be something.

God is essence; he is not “something,” nor is he imagined to be something through a created subsistence. Therefore none of the things that accompany subsistences can exist in him. Thus, although he is great, he is not so through quantity; although he is of some character, he is not so through quality; although he endures, he does not do so through time.

Therefore, when the movement of the human mind acts upon him in the desire to conceive him, it cannot find anything of this kind to assist its conception. Consequently, it cannot comprehend him through those things by which something is something or is imagined to be something.

Nevertheless, by selecting him from among other things through the removal from him of all these things, and by perceiving with assent that he truly exists, the mind understands him in some manner. But since it perceives neither what he is according to genus, nor how great he is according to measure, nor what sort he is according to form, nor anything of this kind through any property of his, it does not comprehend him at all. For he is intelligible, but not comprehensible.

The philosophers likewise considered primordial matter to be incomprehensible yet intelligible. In it, they say, all nature was made by the craftsman. Thus things that do not exist are conceived through opinion, while things that exist are conceived through imagination or understanding.

In many writings, however, imagination and understanding are also called opinion. Likewise opinion and imagination are called understanding.

Hence in this definition of nature, where he says, “Nature is of those things that can be grasped by the understanding,” he has used “can be grasped by the understanding” as though it were predicated more universally of nature.

For according to the rule of dialecticians, if a true universal affirmative, when converted with the same quantity, is false, its predicate is truly more extensive than its subject. For example: “Every man is corporeal” is a true universal affirmative; “Everything corporeal is a man” is false. It is therefore clear that “corporeal” is more extensive than “man” and exceeds it.

Similarly, “Every nature can be grasped by the understanding” is a true universal affirmative; “Everything that can be grasped by the understanding is a nature” is false. It is therefore certain that “can be grasped by the understanding” is more universal than “nature.”

For just as truly, so also fictitiously, the mind selects by the aids of properties and by removing all other things—whether they exist or can be imagined—something that does not exist, and grasps it. Therefore what it opines is said to be understood.

But since it neither exists nor is anything, it is in no way a nature. Therefore, having begun the definition of nature from the universal by saying, “Nature is of those things that can be grasped by the understanding,” he rightly added, against fictitious things—which, as has been said, can also be grasped by the understanding but are not natures—“which, when they exist.”

Since things that exist are sometimes conceived confusedly through imagination, and sometimes through the aid of the property of the thing itself toward which the mind is directed, he explained how he wished “can be grasped by the understanding” to be taken, saying “in some way”—that is, either through imagination, or through the mere removal of other things without conceiving the property of the thing itself that is being considered, or through a fixed and complete understanding that also includes the conception of its property.

Explaining this himself, he says:

**“But the addition ‘in some way.’ Why?”** Because God, the creator of all natural things, and primordial matter—which in Greek is called ὕλη and in Latin silva, “wood” or “forest,” in which philosophers say that all things were created by the craftsman—cannot be understood by a complete and perfect understanding, that is, by an understanding perfected in completeness and complete in perfection.

An understanding is complete and perfect when it conceives a thing not merely through the removal of other things, but also through some property of the thing itself, with assent. This is how God and the primordial matter mentioned above cannot be understood.

For although the mind’s assent establishes and fixes their conception, it does not do so through any properties known to it in them, but solely through the removal from them of those things that belong to other things.

Hence he adds:

**“But in some way.”** As if to say: God and matter cannot be understood through a complete and perfect understanding, but they are nevertheless grasped in some manner—namely, through the privation of all other things, that is, through the privation of what belongs to other things—and thus they are perceived with the assent of the mind.

He says nothing here about imagination, which is one mode of understanding, by which a thing is perceived with the mark of its own property but without assent; nor does he speak of perfect understanding, which is constituted by both property and assent. An explanation made by example does not enumerate all the parts, but illustrates a few, especially those through which the others may be understood.

This is sufficiently apparent here: “understanding” ought properly to be called perfect understanding, although the name also applies to imperfect understanding.

**“But for this reason,” etc.]** He has explained why he added “in some way” to the definition of nature. Now he shows why he added “which, when they exist,” and says:

“We added ‘which, when they exist,’ in order to distinguish nature from those things that do not exist, although they agree with nature in this respect: that they can be grasped by the understanding.”

For, as was stated above, even things that do not exist can be grasped by the understanding, since even the very indefinite name “nothing” signifies something—not as a substance, but not a nature either.

We say “as a substance” because it signifies both what is nature and what is not nature according to quality. For it signifies the same quality as the indefinite name “something,” and that quality may belong both to what exists and to what does not exist.

The meaning is this: among grammarians, “something” and “nothing” signify exactly the same quality, but they do not signify exactly the same substance. Whatever belongs to the things that exist, and whatever quality is imagined to belong to things that do not exist, is the quality of both names.

But the substance signified by “something” is both what exists and what is imagined but does not exist. By contrast, the substance signified by “nothing” is only what is imagined and is in no way something.

For even if it exists, if it is not something either by nature or by productive efficacy, it is nothing. Such is ὕλη, which, according to the philosophers, exists but is in no way something, because it is neither nature, as white is a quality by being something qualified, nor productive efficacy, as whiteness is a quality because it makes something qualified. [Col. 1362C]

These names also differ in their mode of signifying quality. “Something,” through its lexical signification, assigns a true or fictitious quality of one of the things that exist or are imagined to a similarly true or fictitious substance. “Nothing,” however, removes every true or fictitious quality from a substance that is not true but fictitious.

For when something is called “nothing,” it is signified as being affected by no quality of either true or fictitious efficacy. Nothing fictitious is what is imagined. Therefore, rightly, through this infinitive negative term “nothing,” even a fictitious quality is signified as absent from the substance of the same name.

Hence he adds:

“For the name ‘nothing’ does not signify that something”—that is, that the substance of the name—“is something according to the quality of the same name; rather, it signifies that its substance is not something according to the quality from which the name is derived.”

But every nature is something that exists. He could have completed the syllogism in this way:

“Therefore what signifies nothing as a substance is not a nature.”

But because, once the preceding propositions have been set forth, this conclusion is certain, he leaves it unstated.

Thus, if it is considered appropriate to speak of nature with reference to all things—that is, substances and accidents, and also God and matter—this is the definition of nature that we proposed above.

But if, as some have thought, nature is understood not of all things but only of subsisting substances, then, since all subsisting substances are either corporeal or incorporeal, we shall give a definition of nature signifying substances—that is, according to the signification of this name by which it is said to signify subsisting things. The definition is as follows:

“Nature is either what can act or what can be acted upon.”

Here the conjunction “or” is used subdisjunctively: it signifies both alternatives. Hence he adds:

**“To be acted upon and to act,” etc.]** The division would be complete if he had said:

“Either what can act and not be acted upon; or what can be acted upon and not act; or what can both be acted upon and act; or what can neither be acted upon nor act.”

But it must be carefully observed that “to act” and “to be acted upon” are said in several ways.

According to the usage of certain philosophers, “to act” belongs only to living things—that is, to God, spirits, animals, and their souls. “To be acted upon” belongs only to sensible things, such as animals, their souls, and certain spirits.

According to the usage of other philosophers, however, acting and being acted upon belong to all corporeal things and to the souls of sensible things. For all corporeal things, and the souls of some corporeal things, are causes of things that come to be through generation or corruption; therefore they too are said to act, while those that receive their activities are said to be acted upon.

Following this usage, Boethius says:

“To be acted upon and to act is what nature can do,” meaning that nature can do this in all corporeal things and in the souls of corporeal things.

In the case of corporeal things it is certain that they both act and are acted upon. In the case of the soul of a corporeal thing, which is an incorporeal substance, it is not so entirely certain, but it is nevertheless true that it both acts and is acted upon.

For in the body the soul both acts and is acted upon apart from the body's causation, and also from the body—that is, from a bodily cause. Rational souls, not only outside bodies but also while remaining in bodies, understand not through the power of the body but through their own rational activity.

In perceiving bodies, however, whether through sight, hearing, taste, or other senses of this kind, although this sensibility belongs properly to the soul, bodies can nevertheless be perceived through these senses only, and only through corporeal instruments. Therefore the soul is said to derive from the body what it senses, and in the extensive usage of Scripture the senses themselves are called corporeal.

Similarly, souls are affected by passions of pleasure or sadness not only outside bodies but also in bodies—not by the bodies, but solely according to their own nature. It is also certain that certain passions of the soul arise from the quality or imbalance of bodies, such as [the effects of] drunkenness and feverish heat. Therefore the soul’s own passions are said to arise from bodies and are also called corporeal.

**“To act, however,” etc.]** All corporeal things and the souls of corporeal things can be acted upon and act. But nature can be what acts alone and is not acted upon, as God and the other divine beings are.

Here “divine beings” seems to mean all things that are perpetual: things that, once created, are thereafter changed neither by generation nor by corruption. This is also certain of the eternal principle, God, who did not begin to be through generation and does not cease to be through corruption.

Since these things do not change, they are not acted upon. Nevertheless, as the author of all things, God acts; and the other divine beings act greatly either through causation or through service. No agent undergoes change through its action. Therefore the immutable God, and those perpetual things that do not change, act alone and are in no way acted upon.

**“You have, therefore,” etc.]** According to the signification of nature by which the name “nature” is applied to all substances and to substances alone, he has defined nature by a division, saying:

“Nature is either what can act or what can be acted upon.”

The logic of the division, as was stated above, requires four parts:

“Nature is either what can act and not be acted upon; or what can be acted upon and not act; or what can both be acted upon and act; or what can neither be acted upon nor act.”

Of two parts of this division he gives examples: of what can both act and be acted upon, and of what can act and not be acted upon. Of what can be acted upon and not act, or of what can neither be acted upon nor act, he says nothing.

This is because there is no subsisting thing that can merely be acted upon and not act, or that can neither be acted upon nor act. Every subsisting thing is either temporal, perpetual, or eternal.

Every temporal thing, as has been said, both acts and is acted upon. Every perpetual and eternal thing can act and not be acted upon. Therefore no subsisting thing at all remains for the other two parts of the division.

Having briefly indicated, then, according to which signification of nature he has just given this definition, he proceeds to define the same nature according to another signification, which he had placed first in the division above, saying:

“You have, therefore, the definition of that signification also,” that is, according to the signification of nature that applies only to substances.

Because what has been said about nature in that definition applies only to substances, a definition of substance has also been supplied in this definition of nature.

Pay careful attention to his statement that substance has been defined by the definition of nature. He himself shows why he said this, adding:

“For if the name ‘nature’ indicates substance”—as the usage of certain people, mentioned above, maintains—“when we have described nature, a description of substance has also been supplied.”

This would truly and without any doubt have to be acknowledged if the names “nature” and “substance,” in naming the same substance, were multivocal and derived from the same quality. But they are not.

Even if, according to some, the substance of these names is understood to be the same, their quality is never the same. For it is one thing to be nature and another to be substance, just as it is one thing to be human and another to be capable of laughter, although the same substance is both human and capable of laughter.

Therefore, just as the definition of “human” differs from the definition of “capable of laughter,” so the definition of nature cannot be the same as the definition of substance.

Since “nature” and “substance” are names derived from different qualities and are therefore diversivocal, we must ask in what way he has said that they have the same definition.

There are four kinds of names: univocal, equivocal, multivocal, and diversivocal. Univocal and multivocal names are demonstrated by one definition; equivocal and diversivocal names by different definitions.

Yet the difference between definitions that occurs in the case of diversivocal names does not prevent the same names from having one and the same definition. Whoever recalls what was said above concerning definitions will not doubt that diversivocal names can be explained not only by different definitions but also by one definition.

For some definitions show not only what thing is called by a name, but also what it is to be what is so called; others show only what thing is called by a name, and by no means what it is to be what is so called.

If diversivocal names must be demonstrated by the first kind of definition, this must be done through different definitions. But if they are demonstrated by the second kind, they can be shown through one definition.

Therefore, although “nature” and “substance” are different names imposed according to different rational principles, their description is rightly said to be one, because it declares what is nature and substance, but not what it is to be nature or to be substance.

Nature is indeed described in the way stated, whether the name is used of all things or only of substances.

But if, excluding incorporeal substances, the name “nature” is restricted to corporeal things, so that only corporeal substances are thought to possess nature and are called by the name “nature”—as Aristotle and others of this kind, that is, followers of Aristotelian and diverse philosophies, believe—we shall define it in the same way as those who, according to their opinion and judgment, held that nature, that is, the name and signification of nature, exists only in bodies, defined it.

According to this signification of bodies, its definition is as follows:

“Nature is the principle of motion in itself and not accidentally.”

Here we should recall what Aristotle says: that there are six species of motion. [Note: [Col. 1363D] The words placed between brackets seem to be redundant.] [which are species of motion], namely generation, corruption, increase, decrease, alteration, and change of place.

Of these, five belong not only to corporeal things but also to incorporeal things. Generation is an entrance into substance. Therefore whatever begins through creation to belong to some genus is rightly said to be generated; and this applies to all temporal and perpetual things. None of these always existed, and therefore whatever they are according to any genus, they began to be so through generation.

Since, however, it has been established by an eternal law that nothing generated is imperishable, the motion of corruption also naturally belongs to all created things, incorporeal as well as corporeal. For just as everything ungenerated is incorruptible, so everything generated is corruptible.

Increase and decrease belong not only to corporeal and incorporeal subsisting things but also to subsistences and the accidents belonging to them. For increase and decrease occur according to the quantity of space, time, and number.

Those according to the quantity of space—that is, according to line, surface, solidity, or place—belong only to corporeal things. Those according to the quantity of time or number belong to all things that have time and number; and these are truly all natural things, both incorporeal and corporeal.

Alteration also belongs not only to corporeal but to incorporeal substances. Certain qualities arise in the soul, which Aristotle calls habits, dispositions, passive qualities, and passions.

Motion according to place, however, belongs only to corporeal things. Since place, which is called a quantity in genus, belongs only to corporeal things, place, which accompanies it, can belong only to corporeal things.

Thus, according to those who assigned the name “nature” only to bodies, he defines nature through motion, understanding only the motion that belongs exclusively to bodies—namely, local motion—when he says:

“Nature is the principle of motion.”

For, as has been said, local motion alone is proper to bodies; and, in general, local motion belongs to bodies, while its species belong to the species of bodies according to the property mentioned above.

Therefore, further showing the causes of each of the elements he included in the definition, he says:

“I said ‘the principle of motion.’”

As if to say: I described nature through motion—that is, I did so because every body, according to the species of its element, has its own proper motion.

He makes this clear through examples, saying:

“Fire is moved upward by a motion proper to this kind according to its species, while earth is moved downward.”

For in the world-sphere fire is highest and earth is lowest. Therefore, if fire is forced by some cause to be below the highest place, or earth above the lowest place, once left to themselves the elements seek their proper places by their own weight: fire seeks the higher regions, and earth the lower.

Again, when I stated that nature is the principle of motion in itself and not accidentally, after saying in the definition of nature that it is the principle of motion I added “in itself and not accidentally.” This means the following.

The point can be understood through the example that follows. A wooden bed, like earth, if it is placed in the air by some force, must fall downward when left to itself.

But although it is both a bed and wooden—the wooden character belonging to it through subsistence, while “bed” belongs to the subsistence accidentally—it is not carried downward accidentally in virtue of being called a bed; rather, it is carried downward through the subsistence to which the wood belongs.

For this reason, because it is wood, which is earth, etc.] He rightly said “because it is wood” and added “which is earth,” since things that are said to inhere in particular subsistences do not so much inhere in the subsistences themselves as in certain parts of them [Col. 1365D]—or rather, they are said to inhere in the subsistences because they are attached to their parts. Thus, when color, health, and knowledge are said to be present in us through that particular subsistence by which we are human beings, they are so called because, by reason of their properties, color belongs to corporeality, health to sensibility, and knowledge to rationality.

Likewise, therefore, what is carried downward belongs to that particular subsistence by which a bed is wood, insofar as the bed is earth. For it is because the bed is wood—or rather because, in part of its species, it is earth—that it is drawn downward by weight and heaviness, that is, by the weight of heaviness. Hence it is clear that it is not carried downward accidentally. It does not fall downward because it is a bed, but—as we have said—because it is made of earth.

For just as something is said to be “very white” because its surface is large, and an action is said to be “long” because its duration is long—that is, not because the cause is whiteness or action, but rather because multiplicity or length follows from the cause of the surface or of time—so a bed is said to fall downward not because it is a bed, but because its being earth becomes the cause of its falling. [Col. 1366A]

And if someone asks, “Why, then, when the cause is left unmentioned—namely, earth or wood—is the bed said to fall?” the answer may be: because being a bed also belongs to that same cause, that is, because it happened accidentally to earth or wood that it should be a bed.

The sequence of things is not always expressed in words, so that predicates are assigned in their propositions to their causes. Rather, there is often in words what dialecticians call an accidental and merely true connection: namely, when, in predicating consequences of causes, a thing is made the subject, whether the predicate follows from the same causes—as in “the hard is white”—or from causes different and contrary to those of the predicates, as when “something rational is white,” for rationality, although it is the cause of many things, is by no means the cause of colors; or from the consequences of alien causes, as when “something musical is white.” For musical knowledge is neither the cause of whiteness nor does it follow its cause, which is certainly found in body alone. Whiteness is solely an affection of body; musical knowledge, on the other hand, occurs in the spirit and follows there upon the cause of rationality. [Col. 1366B]

Likewise, therefore, when it is said that a bed is carried downward, the connection is accidental, in that particular class of accidental connections in which both what is predicated and what is made the subject are referred to the principle of the same cause—namely, the species by which the bed is wood, or the genus by which it is earth.

Thus, although a bed is truly said to be carried downward, the principle of this motion—that is, its cause—is not its being a bed, but rather its being earth in genus, or wood as a species of that genus. The definition of nature that we have just illustrated contains the statement that nature is what is the principle of motion. Hence it follows that we say that the bed, which is said to be carried downward, exists naturally, whereas we say that wood is a bed not naturally but rather artificially.

“It is also,” etc.] Up to this point he has defined nature according to the use of this term whereby it is said of bodies alone; according to the use whereby it is said of all subsistences; and according to the use whereby it is said of all substances and accidents, and even of the principles of these. But it must be noted that the application of this term is altogether removed from principles that do not proceed from anything by a creative birth.

It approaches more closely to things that are born, according to the proper character of grammatical derivation, whereby a name is taken from some word without being assumed independently of participation in the thing signified. Thus it is called *natura* from *nativum* (“born”), although it is understood that this name does not properly apply to everything born.

For what is called nature appears to be the nature of something. Hence those things that truly are something—that is, things that, although they are themselves something in relation to other things, nevertheless truly subsist—are not the natures of something; rather, certain things are their natures. Body or spirit, for example, is not the nature of something else; rather, certain things are the natures of body or spirit. And I think that this term is more appropriately applied to their subsistences than to the accidents of those subsistences. [Col. 1366C]

For although accidents are both born and belong to something—namely, to the things in which or upon which they inhere, or to which they are attached externally in any manner—nevertheless, because they are not the being of subsistent things, and therefore generation cannot arise through their approach nor corruption through their departure, they are rarely called natures in the usage of more subtle logic.

Those things, however, that are born in the sense that they are the being of born subsistent things, and are so implanted in them that they either remain in them perpetually or destroy them by their departure, are more properly and much more commonly called natures. Among these, since some precede by reason while others follow, and since the latter are assigned, by reason of their properties, to the power of the former, the latter rather than the former are called the natures of the former; for example, the differences of genera.

This is entirely correct, since they are both born, belong to something, and, through their approach, generation always occurs in the things in which they are, while through their departure corruption often occurs. Moreover, in the subsistent things in which they inhere, and in the genera to which they belong, they follow the power of those things, as has already been said. [Col. 1366D]

Considering this proper meaning of the term *nature*, the author says:

“But there is another signification of nature,” namely, that according to which, in the common usage of many people, we say that the nature of gold differs from the nature of silver.

By this expression we do not mean the subsistent corporeal thing—that is, the thing itself that is gold or silver; nor the particular subsistence constituted from genus and difference, by which it is gold or silver; nor the general subsistence, which in a certain way is the principle of the species whereby each of these is metal, earth, body, or some other such thing; nor any of the accidents that are present in subsistences or inhere in them; nor, finally, some eternal principle of these things. Rather, by the term *nature* we wish to point out the substantial property of things that are something through their genera and species, or the substantial property of the genera and species themselves.

Such is, for example, rationality. For rationality is neither a subsistent thing, nor a genus, nor a species, nor an accident of a subsistent thing, nor the eternal principle of any of these. Rather, it is the consubstantial property of the species that it constitutes together with a genus, or of the genus whose power it follows in a subsistent thing or in the species of a subsistent thing. [Col. 1367A]

This, then, is the proper meaning of nature, according to which nature will be defined in the following way:

> Nature is that which informs each thing with a specific difference.

According to this definition, no principle, no corporeal or incorporeal subsistent thing, no genus or species of a subsistent thing, and no accident whatsoever is called nature. For, according to the philosophers, *ὕλη* (*hylē*), which is called “wood” or “forest,” namely primordial matter, is indeed, according to them, the receptacle of all forms, but it itself informs nothing.

God, the author of all things, even if, according to the theologians and in another sense, he is rightly called the nature of all things created by him and the form of the rational creature that lives rightly, is nevertheless not, in the sense in which logicians call the forms of subsistent things their general, specific, or differential subsistences—or, under the fourth genus of quality, certain accidents—the form of the things of which he is something. [Col. 1367B]

A corporeal or incorporeal subsistent thing has within itself the aforementioned forms by which it is something; but it itself informs nothing.

The species called “most specific,” although it is the form of individuals or even of a genus, nevertheless occupies the place of matter in the description of individuals and cannot be specific to anything. A general subsistence, although it is the form of the subsistent things in which it is present and constitutes forms of a lesser likeness than itself, nevertheless, when placed before the definitions of species with substantive signification, has a certain likeness to matter. In definitions it cannot be assigned, without an accidental connection, to any genus above itself whose entire substance is different from it; and therefore no genus rightly informs the understanding of its species.

That form which Aristotle calls a genus of quality cannot be specific, since it is accidental in character. Therefore none of the things mentioned is nature according to the foregoing definition.

It follows, then, that the name *nature* belongs to specific differences. These are both natures and the natures of something—namely, of subsistent things in which they are, whose forms and being they are; of species, whose constitutive parts they are; and of genera, to whose power they are assigned by reason of their properties and whose forms they are, likewise, in the definitions of species. [Col. 1367C]

“When, therefore,” etc.] The meaning is as follows: The name *nature* is said either of all things, or of subsistent things alone, or of bodies alone, or of specific differences alone.
