Since, therefore, nature is spoken of in so many ways, either by different people according to different uses or even by way of different definitions, both the Catholics and Nestorius rightly maintain—that is, they say without any hesitation in their understanding—that there are two natures in Christ. They do not mean this according to any of the three definitions stated above, according to which either all things, or subsistent things alone, or corporeal things alone are defined as natures, but according to the final definition, according to which the name *nature* belongs only to specific differences.

Nevertheless, it must be carefully observed that, since a specific difference constitutes a species together with a genus, no particular subsistence can be simple. The essence of God, however, is altogether simple. It is not to be understood in any way as composed of diverse things. Hence, in the first book, God himself is rightly called “that which is,” or being itself.

God, therefore, is not something that is either a particular subsistence or a specific subsistence. Consequently, even if one says that the nature of God is one and that the nature of man is another, the latter must in no way be understood as a form of a genus, nor as a specific difference joined to that genus as its form in the constitution of a species.

Thus, when the author says that both the Catholics and Nestorius maintain two natures in Christ according to the final definition of nature, this appears to be understood as follows: although there is not one specific difference of God and another specific difference of man, nevertheless one is called “another” because what is specific to man is not specific to God, and what belongs to God, being non-specific, does not belong to man. [Col. 1367D]

[Col. 1368A] This usage of language is also often found in human writings. For Aristotle, after saying in the *Prolegomena to the Categories*, “The species and differences of different genera that are not subordinated to one another are different,” illustrated this by saying, “as in the case of animal and knowledge.”

After listing certain differences that truly belong to animal, he listed none belonging to knowledge, nor could he do so, since among those things that mathematical science contemplates as abstract, though separately from the things in which they are, there is no genus that divides them and no species that a specific form constitutes. For abstract mathematical things are not something in subsistences.

[Col. 1368B] Thus, after listing the differences of animal, he did not add, “But these are the differences of knowledge”; rather, he said, “Knowledge has none of these,” although he had said that different genera have different differences.

Likewise here, when the author said that the Catholics and Nestorius maintain two natures in Christ according to the final definition, he did not say, “For these are the natures of man, and those are the natures of God.” Rather, he said, “For they do not maintain that the same differences belong to God and man”—with “the Catholics and Nestorius maintain” understood. [Col. 1368C]

By saying this he wishes it to be understood not that there are specific natures belonging separately to man and to God, but that those which belong to man by no means belong to God, although he had said that there are two natures in Christ, and that this is according to the final definition of nature.

## ON PERSON

[Col. 1368D] “But concerning person,” etc.] Up to this point he has distinguished the meanings of the term *nature* insofar as they pertain to this work. According to each meaning he has defined what nature is, and he has taught in what sense the Catholics and Nestorius wish *nature* to be understood.

Now he investigates, first by dividing things themselves, what things the name *person* applies to; afterward he explains this by means of definition, usage, and the interpretation of the name itself. The meaning is as follows:

It is uncertain how nature is to be defined because of the different uses of the term. But with *person* there is even greater room for doubt: namely, what definition can be applied to it? He then sets forth the cause of this doubt.

“If, then,” etc.] As has been said, nature is spoken either of specific differences alone, or of bodies alone, or of all substances, or of all things.

The name *person*, however, is either predicated of those things to which the name *nature* applies or of those things to which it does not apply. But among those things to which the name *nature* is predicated according to any of the meanings stated above, *person* is predicated either of all or of some.

If every nature has a person—that is, if person is predicated of everything that is called nature according to any of the meanings stated above—then there is an insoluble knot. It will scarcely, or perhaps not at all, be possible to understand [Col. 1369A] what distinction there can be between nature and person.

For even if, according to different qualities, *nature* and *person* are different names, and if on this account there is a considerable distinction between nature and person, and if the definitions by which they are displayed are different—not merely the definition of what is said to be nature or person, but also the definition of what the thing itself is—the thing that is called by both names will nevertheless be the same, and no definition will be able to show that it is different.

This is like the fact that “man is capable of laughter” and conversely, although being a man is one thing and being capable of laughter is another.

Or, if person is not equated with nature, so that the two names are said conversely of the same thing, but person subsists within the limits and extent of nature—that is, if person is predicated not of all natures but of some—then, because of the different uses of the terms, it is difficult to say how far person extends among natures.

He explains in what sense this is to be understood: namely, which natures are suitable for having a person and which are excluded from the term *person*. The meaning is: of which natures [Col. 1369B] the name *person* is predicated and of which it is not.

For the thought that someone might perhaps entertain—that the name *person* is predicated of absolutely nothing to which the name *nature* applies in any of its meanings—is untenable. It is clear that nature is subject to person; that is, person cannot in any way be predicated apart from nature, but only of something that is called nature according to some meaning.

Since, therefore, person is predicated neither of no natures nor of all natures, but only of some according to one of the meanings of nature stated above, those some must be investigated by those who inquire what they are, in the following way: namely, through a division of natural things.

For, as has been said, person cannot exist apart from nature. Rather, whatever is a person must be called nature according to some meaning of the term. But, according to the definition by which those things are called natures which, insofar as they exist, can in some manner be grasped by the intellect, some natures are substances and others are accidents.

We see that person cannot be constituted in accidents; that is, no accident is a person. Who, for example, would say that there is a person of whiteness, blackness, or magnitude? That is, who could say that whiteness, blackness, or magnitude is a person? If anyone should say this, the answer is: no one.

For these things sometimes belong to persons, and therefore they are never persons. Whatever exists—whether it is a part, a nature, or a property of some person in any genus or by any account—can never be a person. [Col. 1369C]

“Therefore it remains,” etc.] The meaning is as follows: Person cannot exist apart from nature; and among natures some are substances and others accidents. Accidents cannot be persons. Since this is so, it remains that person is properly said of substances—that is, that substances alone are persons—but not all substances.

Therefore he continues his investigation by division, asking which substances are persons. Note that here he intends by “substances” not subsistences but things that subsist. This is apparent from what follows, for he says:

[Col. 1369D] “Among substances, some are corporeal and others incorporeal. Among corporeal things, some are living and others are not. Among living corporeal things”—that this is how the statement must be understood will become clear from the divisions that follow—“some are capable of sensation and others are not; among those capable of sensation, some are rational and others irrational.”

“But among rational things,” etc.] Note that in all the preceding subdivisions he intended the genera of the prior divisions to be understood. In the division that follows, however, he includes not only corporeal things, nor merely those subsistences that are subject to accidents, but also incorporeal subsistences, as well as the principle of all these things.

He says:

“Among rational things, one kind is by nature immutable and impassible, such as God; another is mutable and passible by creation—unless it is transformed by the grace of the impassibility of the substance, that is, of the principal essence, which is God, into the firmness of impassibility—such as the nature of angels, that is, of heavenly spirits, and the nature of the human soul.”

God cannot be changed in any way, nor can he be affected by any sensation of animal passion. The heavenly spirits who attend him, however, are not stable but naturally corruptible, and the same is true of human souls.

For whatever, when it did not exist, could come to exist through divine power can also, while it exists, through that same power cease to exist. Divine power would not be immutable if what began to exist could not cease to exist, since, when such things did not exist, it was possible for them not to exist.

But, as has been said, divine grace establishes some mutable things, insofar as they have been made through creation, so firmly that thereafter they are not changed at all; consequently they are called incorruptible and immortal. [Col. 1370A]

[Col. 1370B] “From all these things,” etc.] The meaning is as follows: We have displayed the parts of nature through the divisions stated above. From all these divisions it is clear that person cannot be said to exist in nonliving bodies. No one says that there is a person of a stone, nor again of living things that lack sensation.

There is no person of a tree, nor of a living thing that is deprived of understanding and reason. There is no person of a horse or ox, or of the other animals that, being naturally mute and without reason, lead their lives solely through the senses.

Pay close attention to the fact that when he says that there is no person of a stone or tree, he says this not only according to the usage of philosophers but also according to the property of the thing that is rightly called a person. For no person can in any way be constituted from something whose entire continuum consists either actually or potentially of a single whole. The reason for this will be stated below.

When he says that there is no person of a horse, ox, or any irrational animal, however, he says this not according to the property of the definition by which anything is a person, but according to the usage of philosophers [Col. 1370C], who, although they could rightly have called such animals persons, nevertheless did not wish to do so. He himself will state this clearly below.

“But of a human being,” etc.] The meaning is as follows: According to the usage of philosophers, we say that no mute animal is a person. But we say that a human being is a person; we also say this of God and of an angel—that is, of any heavenly spirit. We say that such a being is a person both naturally and according to the usage of philosophers.

“Again, among substances,” etc.] Since personhood belongs not to all natures but only to certain ones—namely, those that are substances—and since it does not belong even to all of these, but only to some, he divided natures and substances by several differences. He also showed through examples to which things, according to those divisions, it is appropriate or inappropriate to say that they are persons.

Now he divides substances again for the same reason. But note that whereas earlier he divided only subsistent things by natural differences, he now divides both subsistent things and subsistence by rational and topical differences. He says:

“Again, among substances, some are universal, by the likeness of a substantial form; others are particular, that is, individual, by the dissimilarity of their complete properties.”

He demonstrates by descriptions and examples which are universal and which are particular, saying:

“Universal things are those which, being wholly similar to one another in their effects, are predicated of several individual subsistent things that are truly similar to one another: for example, *man*, *animal*, *stone*, *wood*, and other such things.”

With respect to subsistences, which are the qualities signified by these names, some are genera, such as *animal*, *stone*, and *wood*, while others are species, such as *man*. For *man*—namely, the particular subsistence that is the quality signified by this name—is predicated of individual human beings: one in conformity, but many in the singularity of their essences. Similarly, *animal* is predicated of individual animals, and *stone* and *wood* of individual stones and pieces of wood, in a general manner. [Col. 1370D]

“Particular things,” that is, individuals, which by their dissimilarity divide among themselves those things that substantial likeness makes divisible, are those that are said of one thing in such a way that they are not predicated of other things numerically distinct from that one. [Col. 1371A] Examples are Cicero, Plato, this stone from which this statue of Achilles was made, and this wood from which this table was made.

Note that proper names are assigned to certain particular things from their own proper qualities; he wishes all such things to be understood when he says “Cicero” and “Plato.” For others, no proper names have been assigned; they are understood through a demonstrative pronoun and an appellative noun, as when one says “this stone,” “this wood,” and similar expressions.

“But among these,” etc.] The meaning is as follows: Some substances are universal and others particular. But among all of these—universal and particular alike—if someone asks to which the name *person* applies, I say that it is nowhere applicable among universals: that is, nothing universal can be called a person. It applies only among singular things [Col. 1371B], and among these only to those that are actual and naturally individual.

Pay close attention to the fact that, after saying that person is predicated of singular things, he added “and individual,” thereby indicating that not every singular thing is an individual.

For just as every person is an individual, but not every individual is a person, so every individual is singular, but not every singular thing is an individual. Whatever exists is singular, but not everything that exists is individual.

Among singular things, some are wholly similar to others in their entire property. All such things are collectively called one divisible thing by reason of this conformity—for example, the different qualities of different bodies that are equal in their entire species. Others are dissimilar from all the rest in some part of their property. Such things alone, and all of them, are individual by reason of this dissimilarity—for example, this stone, this wood, this horse, and this human being.

As has been said, the name *person* applies to some of these, but to none of the universal things.

[Col. 1371C] “For there is no person of a general animal or of a general human being, but of Cicero or Plato,” etc.] Note the examples of individuals that he gives. He does not say “of this stone” or “of this wood,” although above, when giving examples of particulars that he wished to be understood as individuals, he had said “this stone” and “this wood.”

For such individuals cannot in any way be persons; the reason why they cannot will be stated shortly. But Cicero, Plato, and similar individual singular things are called individual persons.

“Accordingly,” etc.] Up to this point he has investigated, by dividing things themselves, which things the name *person* applies to. Now he explains this by a definition. It must be carefully observed what he says according to reason and what he says according to the usage of philosophers.

[Col. 1371D] Briefly recalling the parts of the preceding divisions to which he said the name *person* applies, he proceeds to define it and says:

“Accordingly, if person exists only in substances—that is, in subsistent things—as it truly does according to reason, and among these only in rational things, as is said according to common usage; and if every substance, both subsistent thing and subsistence, is called nature according to certain uses; and if, according to any account or usage, person is not found in universals but only in individuals, then the definition of person has been discovered through the divisions stated above:

> Person is an individual substance of a rational nature.”

According to this definition, the human soul appears to be a person. For it is not, as some have said, an *ἐντελέχεια* (*entelecheia*), that is, a form; rather, it is a substance—that is, something subsisting and possessing forms and accidents of different genera within itself—and it is of a rational nature.

It understands and distinguishes both when separated from the body and when placed in the body. Indeed, the human being, who consists of soul and body, is extended by the body’s proper position, while distinguishing by the soul’s proper power.

The soul of each human being also falls under the genus spirit and, by the species of soul proper to it, is an individual divided from all things that are not that soul by its property.

Thus the soul, which is a constitutive part of a human being, appears rightly to be a person. Yet that this is impossible is understood from the fact that no part of a person can be a person. [Col. 1372A]

For every person is so far one in itself that the complete property of any person, gathered from all the things that belong to that person, cannot be predicated of one true individual together with the similarly complete property of another person, gathered from all the things that belong to the other. Thus the personal properties of Plato and Cicero cannot be said of one individual.

But the whole property of Plato’s soul—that is, whatever is naturally affirmed of it—is predicated of Plato himself. We say “naturally” because what is not said naturally of the soul need not be predicated of Plato. For example, the topical relation by which Plato’s soul is called a part of him is not said of Plato himself.

We also say “affirmed” because what is denied of Plato’s soul need not be denied of Plato himself. For example, if the soul is said to be incorporeal—a privative term by which the subsistence of bodies, namely corporeality, is removed from it—Plato is not thereby said to be incorporeal.

Thus the human soul appears to be a person according to the definition stated above. [Col. 1372B]

To settle the conflict of words by agreement in meaning, it must be said that just as something is called an individual not only by actual likeness but also by natural likeness, so too something is called an individual not only by actual dissimilarity but also by natural dissimilarity. Whatever possession contributes, privation removes.

This will become clearer through examples. *Man* and *sun* are called appellative nouns by grammarians but divisible things by dialecticians. Plato and his particular whiteness are called proper nouns by those same grammarians but individuals by dialecticians.

Of these, *man* is appellative or divisible both in actuality and in nature; *sun*, however, is so only in nature, not in actuality. For many have been, are, and will be human beings who are alike in substantial likeness not only naturally but also actually. There have also been many suns that never existed actually but are always alike in nature.

For just as *man* is not named from the entire property of one human being, so *sun* is not named from the entire property of this sun that we see. *Man* is a name taken from certain human subsistences that are alike both actually and naturally; *sun* is a name taken from certain things that are not actually but only naturally alike to one another in their entire substantial form.

There have been those who are no longer present, and there will be those who do not yet exist; and there have been and now are infinitely many human beings alike both actually and naturally. Hence their forms are many and alike naturally, actually, in the past, in the future, and in the present. From these, by their complete conformity with one another, the truly divisible name *human being* has been imposed on the human beings themselves.

There is only one sun in actuality; apart from it, no other sun either was, is, or will be actual. Nevertheless, infinitely many suns have existed, exist, and will exist by nature alone. Thus, because these subsistences are alike to one another only naturally, the name *sun* is truly divisible and universal by nature alone.

For just as no part can be conformable either actually or naturally to the complete property of a true individual, so, with respect to any part of a complete property, there is at least a natural likeness.

Therefore the whole property of Plato, gathered from all the things that belong to him, is conformable to no other thing either actually or naturally, nor is Plato himself, through it, conformable to anything else. [Col. 1372D] His whiteness, however, and whatever part of his property is under consideration, is understood to be conformable either both naturally and actually or at least naturally.

Therefore no part of the property of any creature is naturally individual, although by reason of singularity it is often called individual. But that property of any creature which, by natural dissimilarity, differs from all things that have been, are, or will be either actually or potentially is not merely singular or particular; it is also truly called and is individual.

Things of this sort are called individuals because each of them consists of such properties that, when all of them are collected in thought, the same collection will never be naturally conformable in any other individual of either number. [Col. 1372C]

For this reason, Plato’s whole form, being naturally conformable to no other thing, is truly individual. Every part of it, however, is singular but not truly individual, because it is at least naturally conformable to many things.

Thus his soul, which is a part of his whole form, is called individual with respect to Plato’s form, but not with respect to the name. Therefore, although it is a substance of a rational nature, it cannot in any way be a person. In general, as has been said, no part of any person is a person, because the property of that part, gathered from all the things understood to belong to it, is naturally individual. [Col. 1373A]

From these considerations it is understood that a person is so far one in itself that its whole property cannot be compared with the whole property of anything else by any likeness in itself, nor can it be joined to anything else in order to constitute a personal property.

“But we, by this definition,” etc.] Up to this point he has investigated by divisions and by a definition—partly drawn from nature and partly from usage—which things the name *person* applies to. Now he shows the reason for this name: namely, why that to which the stated definition applies is called a person.

The meaning is as follows:

“Person is an individual substance of a rational nature.”

But it must be carefully noted that by this definition we have delimited not what the Greeks call *πρόσωπον* (*prosōpon*), but rather what they call, according to usage, *ὑπόστασις* (*hypostasis*).

For the name *persona* seems to have been transferred from elsewhere by a kind of metaphor—namely, from those persons who, in the performance of comedies and tragedies, represented those people who differ in age, sex, condition, and property: sad or happy, rich or poor, noble or ignoble, and people of similar kinds. [Col. 1373B]

In comedies and tragedies, the term *persona* was appropriately and properly derived from *personare* (“to sound through”), with the penultimate syllable circumflexed, according to the rule concerning the accents of words that says:

> In trisyllabic and tetrasyllabic words, and in words of more syllables, if the final syllable is short but the penultimate syllable is naturally long, the penultimate is circumflexed, while the remaining syllables receive the grave accent.

Hence the word *persona* does not appear to have been derived from *personare*. For in this word, namely *sonus* (“sound”), [Col. 1373C] the first syllable is naturally short and is therefore pronounced with the acute accent, according to the rule that says:

> In disyllabic words, if the first syllable is naturally short, it receives the acute accent, while the second receives the grave accent.

*“But if…”*] Or rather: “As if.” This name *persona* (“person”) is said to derive from *personando* (“sounding through”), although this scarcely seems true, since the penultimate syllable, as though naturally long, is circumflexed before a shortened final syllable. But if the antepenultimate syllable is given the acute accent, according to the rule which says, “In trisyllabic and tetrasyllabic words, and in longer words, if the penultimate syllable is short, the antepenultimate receives the acute, while the remaining syllables receive the grave,” then it will most plainly appear that *persona* is derived from *sonus* (“sound”).

The reason, then, why the mask used in the performance of comedies and tragedies to represent some person seems to have been called *persona* from *sonus* is that, because of the concavity of the mask placed before the face for representing the person, a louder sound necessarily reverberates through it. This was certainly useful for those in the amphitheater who were attentive to what was being said.

The Greeks likewise called the masks used in the performance of comedies and tragedies *πρόσωπα* [*prosōpa*], [Col. 1373D] not indeed from the sound—which truly became louder because of the concavity of the mask placed before the face—but from the fact that those concave masks, placed on the face and before the eyes of the spectators in order to produce a louder sound, covered the face of the speakers who wore them. He also expresses this in Greek words, saying: *Παρά τοῦ πρὸς τοὺς ὦπας τίθεσθαι*, that is, “from placing it before the face.” For *παρά* means “from”; *πρός* means “at” or “before”; *ὦπας* means “the face”; *τίθεσθαι* means “placing”; while *τοῦ* and, meanwhile, *τοὺς* are articles. Since, therefore, *πρός* means “at” or “before,” and *ὦπας* means “the face,” *πρόσωπα* unquestionably means “at the face” or “before the face.”

Thus these two names—*persona* and *πρόσωπα*—are properly names for those who, in the amphitheaters, represented different people through the diversity of masks and sounds. One name, namely *persona*, derives from the sound produced by the concavity of the mask placed before the face; the other, *πρόσωπα*, derives from the mask placed before the face, from whose concavity the sound was produced. [Col. 1374A]

But since, as has been said, when the actors had introduced persons differing in voice and appearance, they represented in tragedy or comedy the individual persons concerned—for example, Hecuba or Medea in tragedy, and Simon or Chremes in comedy—they consequently also called the other people whose identity could be certainly recognized, according to each person’s natural distinctiveness, “individual form.” That is, they named them not by a natural or proper designation, but by a conventional and improper one: the Latins called them *personae*, and the Greeks *πρόσωπα*.

Far better, and more precisely according to the truth of the matter, the Greeks called the individual substance of a rational nature by the name *ὑπόστασις* [*hypostasis*], though they contracted the term from the broader range of things to which this name naturally applies. We Latins, however, through a scarcity of words properly signifying the things themselves, have retained a transferred designation: namely, the one which they—the Greeks—properly call *ὑπόστασις*, calling it *persona*, a name derived from sound. [Col. 1374B]

*“But the more learned…”*] As if to say: What we defined above as an individual substance of a rational nature, certain Greeks call *ὑπόστασις*. But Greece, which is more skilled in language, calls *ὑπόστασις* not only any rational individual substance but also any non-rational individual substance.

And, to use Greek speech concerning matters that were long debated by the Greeks and later transferred into Latin translation, they say: *Αἱ οὐσίαι ἐν μὲν τοῖς καθ’ ὅλου εἶναι δύνανται, ἐν δὲ τοῖς κατὰ μέρος μόνοις ὑφίστανται*—that is: “Essences can exist in universals, but subsist only in individuals and particulars.”

This translation was made word for word. For *αἱ* is the article; *οὐσίαι*, “essences”; *ἐν*, “in”; *μέν*, “indeed”; *τοῖς*, the article; *καθ’ ὅλου*, “according to the whole.” In place of this, because every universal is a whole, the translator puts “in universals.” *Εἶναι* means “to be”; *δύνανται*, “can.” Again, *ἐν* means “in”; *δέ*, “but”; *τοῖς*, the article; *κατὰ μέρος*, “according to the part.” In place of this, because every particular and individual is called a part, the translator puts “in individuals and particulars.” [Col. 1374C] *Μόνοις* means “alone”; *ὑφίστανται*, “subsist.”

From these Greek words, and from the Latin translation that followed, it is clear that not only a rational but also a non-rational individual substance of nature is called *ὑπόστασις*. For there are certain universals not only of rational but also of non-rational individual substances, which the human intellect in a certain way abstracts from the individuals themselves, so that it may discern their nature and grasp their properties. Indeed, in accordance with truth, the intellect of universal things is drawn from any particulars whatsoever—that is, not only from rational but also from irrational particulars. In other words, the intellect derives universal concepts from any particulars.

*“Accordingly, since the substances themselves…”*] Since the substances themselves are indeed in universals, as is understood from the foregoing Greek words and their Latin translation, but in particulars [Col. 1374D] I do not say that they are, but that they “take substance,” and so forth.

He observes that, although above he said “essences,” he now says “substances” in particulars. Since “to be” and “that which is” cannot exist apart from one another by reason of a certain association, as corporeality and body illustrate: corporeality in actuality is nothing unless it is in a body, and a body is not what it is called unless corporeality, which is its being, is in it. Accordingly, once either of these two names—whether “essence” or “substance”—has been supplied, the meaning of the following expression is properly referred to either one, either consequently or accidentally.

Thus, after saying, “Essences exist in universals but subsist in particulars,” he rightly also says, “Substances exist in universals and take substance in particulars,” that is, “subsist.” The meaning is this: The universals which the intellect gathers from particulars exist, because they are said to be the being of particulars, by which the particulars themselves are something.

Particulars, however, not only are—for they are so through this being of theirs—but also subsist, because, by receiving within themselves or having externally attached to them the accidents that attend upon universals, they are subject to them. [Col. 1375A] Accordingly, they rightly called particular subsistents *ὑποστάσεις* (“hypostases”). For whatever is said to be either is the essence of something or exists from an essence. But whatever is said to underlie must underlie accidents. By having accidents either within itself or externally attached to it, it underlies them.

Observe that, after first saying, “Essences subsist in particulars,” and then, with the same meaning, “Substances take substance in particulars,” he now wishes the same thing to be understood when he says, “Particular subsistents that underlie.” Nevertheless, essence, subsistence, and substance are different things.

For, leaving essence aside for the moment, anyone who examines the matter more carefully—that is, more certainly and subtly, in accordance with the properties of things and the causes of words—will see that subsistence is not the same as substance. This can be understood from the diversity of the Greek terms. What the Greeks call *οὐσίωσις* or *οὐσιῶσθαι* [Col. 1375B], we call “subsistence” or “to subsist.” But what they call *ὑπόστασις* or *ὑφίστασθαι*, we translate as “substance” or “to underlie.”

He then explains why we call one thing “subsistence” and the other “substance.” That which subsists is, in a certain respect, through itself, and does not need accidents in order to be. Rather, accidents need it so greatly—precisely because it is said to subsist and exist through itself in this respect—that unless it is present, they cannot exist in anything. Every accident is added to the capacity of some subsistence, and therefore it is called an accident: it is present to that which subsists when it inheres in something substantial, as color is present to corporeality so that it may inhere in a body.

That which underlies, however, supplies a subject to other things—that is, to accidents—so that they may exist, as a body does for color. I rightly say “underlies,” for in a certain manner it stands beneath them, being subject to accidents according to a rational order by which it receives them in itself, in accordance with the subsistences to which they alone belong.

[Col. 1375C]

*“Thus…”*] As if to say: That which does not itself need accidents in order to exist subsists. Thus genera and species—that is, general and specific subsistences—only subsist; they do not truly underlie. For accidents do not occur to genera or species, so that they would owe their being to accidents. Genera and species do not need accidents in order to be.

Individuals, however, truly subsist. For individuals, just like genera and species, do not need accidents in order to be. He explains why individuals likewise do not need accidents in order to exist: “For they have already been formed by their proper and specific differences, through which they subsist.”

Individuals not only subsist but also underlie, because they furnish a subject for accidents so that those accidents may exist. They are, namely, subjects for accidents, as though they were the causes and principles of those accidents according to the rational order of created things.

Accordingly, so that the diversity of things may appear more clearly through the richness of the Greek language, we say [Col. 1375D] that *εἶναι* and *οὐσιῶσθαι* are understood in Latin as “to be” and “to subsist,” whereas *ὑφίστασθαι* is understood as “to underlie.” For, as Marcus Tullius playfully alludes with a figurative and witty bite disguised as praise, Greece is not poor in words. Rather, here it renders four names by four names: *essentia*, “essence,” as *οὐσία*; *subsistentia*, “subsistence,” as *οὐσίωσις*; *substantia*, “substance,” as *ὑπόστασις*; and *persona*, “person,” as *πρόσωπον*.

To return to the matter for which we made the foregoing division of things and names: the Greeks called all individual substances *ὑποστάσεις*, as has been said, because they underlie other things. Repeating the same meaning, he explains how he wishes “underlie” to be understood and what those “other things” are, saying: “They are as though placed beneath and subjected to certain things which are said to have accidents attached to them either within themselves or externally.”

For this reason we Latins also call them *substantiae*, as though they were placed beneath [Col. 1376A]—or rather, as though they were *ὑποστάσεις*, that is, things that underlie. And since the Greeks likewise call these same individual substances *πρόσωπα* by “placing them before the face,” although they do not call all such substances by this name but only rational ones, as has been said, we Latins too can call them *personae*, deriving the name from sound.

Thus, as is clear from what has been said, *οὐσία* is the same as essence; *οὐσίωσις* is the same as subsistence; *ὑπόστασις* is the same as substance; and *πρόσωπον* is the same as person.

*“But why…”*] That Greece, being more skilled in language, calls not only a rational but also an irrational individual substance *ὑπόστασις*, distinguishing it from the things designated by the other names, is shown by the force and proper meaning of the word itself. For just as the Greek *ὑπόστασις*, so the Latin *substantia*, derives its meaning from “underlying.”

This is entirely proper, since an irrational *ὑπόστασις* or substance, just like a rational one, underlies the accidents it contains or has externally attached to it. Later, however, [Col. 1376B] Greek usage contracted this same name from the genus to the species, calling only a rational substance *ὑπόστασις*, whereas Latin usage still retains the name *substantia*, according to the nature and force of the word itself, for everything that underlies accidents.

If someone asks why Greek usage now does not call irrational animals *ὑποστάσεις*, as we Latins predicate the name “substance” of those same irrational beings, we reply that this is for a reason. The name *ὑπόστασις*, which by current usage, as we have said, is now a name for a superior nature, was contracted from the genus of all things that underlie and applied to the species of rational beings, so that what is more excellent—namely, rational substance—might be distinguished by a certain description.

This distinction is not a description of nature according to what it truly is, namely *ὑφίστασθαι* or “to underlie”—for, in this respect, anything that underlies accidents can be understood in the same way—but rather a distinction by vocabulary, that is, by the usage of the words *ὑπόστασις* or, if one prefers the Latin term, *substantia* [Col. 1376C]. Through this usage it is distinguished from non-rational beings, although according to the nature of the matter the interpretation of the name belongs to them as well, both in Greek and in Latin.

There are many such words which, although by the nature of their signification they can apply to many things, are nevertheless used in practice not of all those things but only of some.

*“Therefore there is…”*] Since we have said that among both Greeks and Latins there is a distinction of things and names—*οὐσία*, *οὐσίωσις*, *ὑπόστασις*, *πρόσωπον*; essence, subsistence, substance, person—although these names are all predicated of one man, one angel, or God, there is therefore in man an essence, that is, *οὐσία*; a subsistence, that is, *οὐσίωσις*; a *ὑπόστασις*, that is, substance; and a *πρόσωπον*, that is, person.

He shows how it is certain that these belong to man, saying: “*Οὐσία* and essence belong to man because he possesses an immutable conformity of species”; *οὐσίωσις* and subsistence belong to man because man is in no subject. That is, the subsistence by which he himself is and is called man has no prior subject in which it inheres [Col. 1376D], in the man who is man through it. *Ὑπόστασις* and substance belong to man because he underlies other things that are not subsistences, that is, that are not *οὐσιώσεις*.

The meaning is: He underlies accidents, because accidents are in him in such a way that they naturally have in him a prior subject in which they inhere. The same man also has *πρόσωπον* and person, because according to the natural distinctiveness of his property he is an individual, and not an irrational being to which the term could apply by nature, but a rational being, to which usage has restricted the names *ὑπόστασις* and person.

The name person belongs not only to man but also to an angel, as was said above, because an angel is likewise a rational individual. For the same reason the other terms—*οὐσία* or essence, *οὐσίωσις* or subsistence, and *ὑπόστασις* or substance—belong to an angel. Each of the heavenly spirits possesses an immutable conformity of species [Col. 1377A]; and because its special subsistence has no prior subject in which it inheres, it is in no subject. It subsists through that subsistence and underlies the accidents that follow in it naturally, after those things that are prior to them.

But he says nothing about the angel because this work is concerned not with the nature and person of an angel but only with the nature and person of man and God.

Therefore, after saying “essence” and “the being of man,” he also says that the same things belong to God. They do indeed belong to God, although not all for the same reason that they belong to man. Essence is predicated of man because of the immutable conformity of the subsistences that are universally predicated of him; it is also predicated of God, but not because of an immutable likeness among his subsistences.

For there are not several essences substantially conformed to one another, one of which is predicated of the Father, another of his Son, and another of the Spirit of them both. For then the Father, his Son, and the Spirit of them both would be many gods rather than one singular and individual God. Although “is” is predicated of each individual man, it is never said that he is [Col. 1377B] essence itself, in the way in which, through the likeness of the many universals we have mentioned, he is.

But there is only one singular and individual essence of God, which is predicated of the Father, the Son, or the Spirit of them both when it is said, “God is.” Therefore we say not only “God is,” but also “God is essence.” With this understanding he says: “God also—that is, the Father, his Son, or the Spirit of them both—is *οὐσία* and essence.” This is entirely right. For God is without beginning and without end, one, individual, and simple.

Although everything that exists from him, through him, and in him is said by theologians to exist because it exists through him alone as its author, he himself is especially the one from whom the being of all things proceeds. Whatever is said to be something—whether through subsistences, accidents, proper effects, logical reasons, or moral qualities—exists through him as its author, and through him is what it is said to be.

He is also truly *οὐσίωσις*, that is, subsistence. For he subsists through himself and needs nothing. The divine essence cannot be present in anything as an accident. [Col. 1377C]

He is also rightly said to *ὑφίστασθαι*, that is, to underlie. Although nothing is present in God as an accident of the divine essence, he underlies all things of which he is the true cause, true being, and true principle. For if, among created things, some are called the causes, being, principles, and therefore subjects of others, then God, who has no prior cause, being, or principle of any essence other than the one he himself is, and who is the true and sole cause, being, and principle of all created things, is much more rationally said to underlie those same things.

There are, however, three who share one singular, simple, and individual essence but differ in properties: namely, the Father, his Son, and the Spirit of them both. Each of them is the cause and principle of the being of all created things, while together they are one cause and one principle of being.

Hence we also say that there is one *οὐσία* or *οὐσίωσις* of the Deity—that is, one essence or subsistence, namely, the Deity—but three *ὑποστάσεις*, that is, three substances. [Col. 1377D] This does not mean that those three, through their distinct properties, are three causes or three principles of created things. Rather, each one of the three is the cause, being, and principle of all things, and in this respect underlies them all.

Just as, although there is only one divinity and one eternity of the three, if one nevertheless says “three divine and eternal persons,” the plurality of the added names—“divine” and “eternal”—is rightly matched to the plurality of the nouns to which they are attached in the same clause, namely, “three” and “persons,” which are truly plural in both things and words, while the singularity of divinity and eternity remains intact:

so, although there is only one reason by which each of them exists through himself, and although the three together are, by the force of all of them, one cause, one being, and one principle of all created things, the singularity of this reason nevertheless remains intact, while the plurality of the names *ὑποστάσεις*, or “those who underlie,” is rightly matched to the plurality of the word “three,” [Col. 1378A] to which they are attached in the same clause.

Accordingly, in this sense the Latins have said that there is one essence of the Trinity—that is, of the Father, his Son, and the Spirit of them both—and three substances and three persons. The truth of things, theological reasoning, and the usage of ecclesiastical authority all affirm that the three mentioned persons have one singular and individual essence, and that the same three, sharing one essence, are three persons.

But since both “to subsist” and “to underlie” are predicated of one subsistence, although in different senses, according to what that same subsistence truly is something—for example, a man subsists because the subsistence by which he is and is called a man, namely, humanity, is not present in the man in whom it exists as an accident.

He underlies, however, because various kinds of accidents are present in that same subsistence in the same man. Yet neither according to the truth of things nor according to philosophical usage is he called “many substances” merely because he underlies through the one singular subsistence of one species. For one man, by one singular humanity, underlying many accidents that belong to him, [Col. 1378B] is through that humanity called only one man and one substance.

Those things that are said to subsist and underlie through several subsistences of the same species are numerically many substances, and are so called: for example, through several humanities there are several men and substances.

In the same way, since each of the three persons mentioned is one essence, and the three together are nothing other than that same essence, although they underlie the many—or rather, all—created things, as was explained above, because they are the principle of those things, they will not be many who underlie or many substances, but only one who underlies or one substance. For, according to the unity of their essence, they are one and only one principle of all things.

But if there were several essences of the three—one belonging to the Father, another to the Son, and another to the Spirit of them both—then, just as there are many subsistences of one species among human beings, one of which is one man and another another man, so, according to the plurality of essences, the Father, the Son, and the Spirit of them both would be [Col. 1378C] many principles of created things. Consequently, they would be many who underlie those things, and their substances would be many, just as, according to the plurality of subsistences of that species, several men underlie the many accidents that belong to their subsistences and are called their substances.

But because, according to theological reasoning, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have only one singular and individual essence, and therefore can be only one principle of all things, and because by reason of this principality they can be said, in the language of human philosophy, to be beneath or to underlie those things, ecclesiastical usage excludes the expression “three substances” of God.

For unless it excluded—or rather, accepted—the plurality of substances in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, what might perhaps be understood from that plurality would be that they derive from different essences: that the Father derives from one essence and is one principle, the Son from another and is another principle, and their Spirit from another and is another principle.

In that case it would rightly seem possible, on the basis of that plurality by which they would be three substances, to say of each one what is now said, because of the singularity arising [Col. 1378D] from the unity of their essence, of God the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit—namely, that he is substance. This would not be because he is placed beneath other things as their subject, so that they might exist in him and accidents of his essence—rather, of the essence that he himself is—might inhere in him, as various kinds of accidents inhere in the subsistences of one man. Rather, it would be because that same God, the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, just as he is above all things, is also beneath them, as their principle—which he truly is, since he supplies to all things their *οὐσίωσθαι*, or subsistence.

*“But here too…”*] Since, in speaking about essence, subsistence, and substance, he seems to have departed from his purpose—namely, to demonstrate the differences between nature and person—he says that what has been said about them pertains to those differences.

As if to say: Much has been said about essence, subsistence, and substance [Col. 1379A], but everything has been said for this reason—that is, I want it to be understood as having been said with the intention of demonstrating the differences between nature and person, that is, between *οὐσία* and *ὑπόστασις*.

As for which name ought to be used among the Latins for each of them—that is, whether what is called *οὐσία* in Greek should be called in Latin “essence,” “subsistence,” or “nature,” and whether what is called *ὑπόστασις* in Greek should be called in Latin “subsistent,” “substance,” or “person”—this is left to the judgment of ecclesiastical usage, that is, to the judgment of those who know the usage of ecclesiastical language.

For the present, however, let this remain certain and beyond doubt: nature and person, as we have already stated, are different, that is, distinct. For, according to the final meaning of “nature” given above, nature is the specified property of any substance. [Col. 1379B]

He uses different words from those used above, but the meaning is the same. Earlier he said: “Nature is the specific difference that informs each thing.” Here, instead of “each thing,” he says “any substance.” By the equivocal word “thing” he wished substance to be understood. And where he earlier said “specific difference,” he now says “specified property,” quite properly. For the difference he named there he had shortly before called a property, saying: “We say that the nature of gold differs from that of silver,” wishing by this to point out the property of things.

*“But person…”*] As if to say: Nature is the specified property of any substance, whereas person is an individual substance of a rational nature.

*“This in Christ…”*] Up to this point he has shown that nature and person are distinct through their proper differences. He now begins to set forth and refute the errors of Nestorius and Eutyches. First he presents and destroys the error of Nestorius.

As if to say: Person is an individual substance of a rational nature. Nestorius, in his opinion, made this person—that is, person itself—twofold in Christ: one, namely, God; the other, man. For he says that in Christ there is one person who is God and another who is man, and that Christ is composed from these two. [Col. 1379C]

He was led to this assertion by the error of supposing that person could be predicated of all natures, however they might be defined—that is, because he supposed that every nature was also called a person. Having assumed this, and rightly judging that there are two natures in Christ, he also confessed that there are two persons in him.

The definition of person stated above—“an individual substance of a rational nature”—proves him wrong in this matter. The definition does not say plurally, “Person is an individual substance,” but singularly, “an individual substance.” Although this definition of person proves him wrong, the argument that follows also clearly exposes his error.

*“Truly. For if…”*] Here “argumentation” is called *ὑπόθεσις* (“hypothesis”) with respect to its manner, through a kind of apparent agreement; in genus it is a syllogism, and in species a hypothetical argument. For it does not confirm its conclusion by taking something from outside, but, as though agreeing with the opponent’s statement that Christ is not one person, it takes [Col. 1379D] that statement as its premise in order to show what falsehood follows from it.

Once that premise has been refuted, it concludes the argument through the evident truth of its own position. He therefore says:

### If Christ is not one person, it follows, etc.

But because Nestorius, who thinks that every nature is a person, measures the number of persons by the number of natures, he adds, after what was assumed above: “It is evident that there are two natures in Christ,” namely, that of man and that of God. And because it has not yet been sufficiently established that he may necessarily draw the conclusion he is about to draw, he adds further:

“Nor will anyone be so foolish as to separate from reason either of them”—that is, in some way or other, either one of the two, namely, the human and the divine natures—“saying that one of those two natures is a person, but the other is not. It follows that they appear to be two persons in him”—that is, that Christ is not one person [Col. 1380A], but two.

That this is false is demonstrated, as was said above, by the definition of person previously given. For a person is, as stated, “an individual subsistence of a rational nature.” But if Christ is two persons, what, then, is the union made between man and God? Was it made, perhaps, as when two bodies—that is, two stones, or two pieces of wood, or a stone and a piece of wood, or other bodies of this kind—are placed beside one another, so that those bodies are joined only in position, namely, so that nothing of the quality of one passes into the other? The Greeks call this mode of union κατὰ παράθεσιν, that is, “according to juxtaposition” or “by apposition.” For κατά is *according to* in Greek, παρά is *to*, and θέσις is *position*.

Pay close attention to what is briefly and obscurely signified by these words: namely, that there are different modes of joining things together. He says that two bodies are joined to one another in such a way that nothing of the quality of one passes into the other. By this he implies that some things are also joined to one another in such a way that something of the quality of one passes into the other.

A black stone placed beside a white stone is indeed next to it in position; but neither is the black stone called white by the quality of the white stone, nor is the white stone called black by the quality of the black stone. Iron or gold is placed upon wood, and by the condition of apposition the wood itself is indeed called iron-clad or gilded; but the quality of iron or gold is not yet predicated of the wood. Nevertheless, in such forms of apposition the name of a quality is sometimes transferred from one thing to another by a kind of denomination, although the quality itself by no means becomes present in the other thing, as happens in the apposition of clothing or weapons. The person to whom clothing or weapons are applied is called dirty, beautiful, or painted by the dirt or beauty of the clothing and the painting of the weapons, although these qualities do not at all come to exist in that person's substance.

Sometimes not only the name of one thing is denominated in another, but the quality of one thing actually becomes present in the other—for example, the sweetness or sourness of something placed in a vessel, or the scent of an apple in a hand. In all these cases, however, one must observe that no single thing is made from what is placed upon another and from that upon which it is placed. No single thing is naturally formed from stones placed together, one white and one black [Col. 1380C]; nor from wood and iron, or wood and gold; nor from a human being and his garment or weapons; nor from an apple and a hand.

But from flesh and bones, together with certain other things, one body—that of an animal—is formed; and from body and soul, one animal is formed. Therefore, in order that this may be more readily understood with respect to the composition of any person from the elements of which that person consists, we must begin at a higher level.

Everything that exists is either simple or composite. What the simple and the composite are was explained in the book *On the Hebdomads*. There, in the seventh of the preceding propositions—or rules—he defines the simple in this way: “The simple is that which has its being and what it is as one.” In the eighth proposition, concerning the composite, he says: “In every composite, its being is one thing, and it itself is another.”

In what sense these statements are to be understood has been explained. From this it is clear that there is something in which different things are said to be joined to one another, and to which all the special subsistences belong as their being—both those from which the special subsistences of the things joined together in it consist, and also those which arise in the same thing from the condition of the things joined together.

Thus, a human being, who is one because body and spirit are joined together, has as his being all the subsistences of body and spirit, as well as certain others that arise within him from their conjunction [Col. 1380D]. The same human being is something constituted by the qualities belonging to these subsistences and by their measurable intervals. And because the composition of a human being from body and spirit is such that neither both together nor either one is confused in him, all the subsistences, qualities, and interval-measures that we have just mentioned—and indeed the boundaries of the intervals themselves—are rightly predicated of the human being.

The union of spirit and body is therefore a composition, not a commixture. For not every composition is a commixture, just as not every union is a composition. Every commixture, however, is a composition. For things mixed together compose one thing within themselves; but the mixture confuses some qualities of one or of both of them. Thus, when white and black are mixed, neither the components nor the composite retain the qualities of white and black, but they are affected with a color of another kind.

A composition formed without commixture, however, allows the components to retain their respective natures and makes those same natures predicable of the composite. Thus the natures of body and spirit are truly predicated not only of body and spirit, but also of the human being; and the other features that arise in him from their coming together in composition are predicated of him as well, as was said.

Here one must carefully observe that although the things joined together in compositions are sometimes not of the same genus, they are always of the same kind in some respect. For although body and spirit are different in genus, they are of the same kind in this respect: both are subjects of what is predicated, while they themselves cannot be predicated. For what a thing is is never predicated; rather, its being and what belongs to it are predicable, and they are predicable without metaphor only of what the thing is.

Simple subsistences are likewise of different genera—for example, rationality and animation—but they share one account, by which they are said to be the being of things that exist; and therefore they together compose the entire being of what exists.

Being and what a thing is, however, are neither of the same genus nor of the same kind; therefore their union cannot be a composition. Yet, when a certain rational disposition intervenes, there is one thing, whether simple or composite, which the mind conceives in such a way that it assents to the perception that in it what a thing is and its being—or what belongs to it in genus and kind—are distinct.

For the mind sees in that one thing both the being by which what it is exists and also what it is, which exists through that being. It also sees certain other features which, by reason of their properties, belong to the being itself, but inhere in what the thing is or are attached to it externally.

In this one thing, therefore, what it is has the being by which it exists, together with the things that in any way follow upon that being. Being itself, too, and the things that follow upon it have what the thing is, of which they are truly predicated. Unless these were distinct, they could neither possess nor be possessed. For nothing can exist in itself or possess itself, nor can it in any way be joined to itself. Therefore the things joined to one another are distinct from one another.

But if they are joined in one thing according to every genus and every kind, nevertheless they cannot be mixed together in it or compose it. From this it is evident that there are different modes of joining different things to one another: sometimes there is one thing in which different things are joined, and sometimes there is not one thing. The one thing in which different things are joined is sometimes simple and sometimes composite. In what is composite, sometimes one component, sometimes both, and sometimes neither, is confused with the composition by commixture. But things that are different from one another in every genus and in every kind can in no way be composed together. A composite, moreover, can never be different from its components in every genus, much less in every kind. Rather, if the composition is without commixture, the composite naturally belongs to the same genera as its components [Col. 1381D].

We wish all these statements to be understood only of created things. In theological matters, some things will be shown to be similar and others different. We do not think that everything—or nothing—that is understood in natural or mathematical matters should be applied to theological matters. For this reason, it belongs to the most subtle and highly practiced philosophy to distinguish the accounts common to both domains from those proper to each.

We have touched upon these matters for the sake of the unlearned, who either transfer the principles proper to different disciplines to one another or make common principles peculiar to one discipline. Returning now to the subject at hand, we say that although there are so many modes by which things may be joined to one another, the union of the two natures in Christ—namely, the divine and the human—is shown below, against Eutyches, not to be by commixture; here, against Nestorius, it is shown not to be by apposition.

It is as though he were asking: Was the union of God and man made κατὰ παράθεσιν, that is, according to apposition?

### But if humanity was joined to divinity in this way, that is, according to apposition, etc.

One must carefully observe that although he previously said, “What union was made between man and God,” he now does not say “man was joined to God,” but “humanity was joined to divinity.” By this he indicates that when he said “of man and God,” he intended “of humanity and divinity.”

This is entirely correct, since he had previously said that both the Catholics and Nestorius established two natures in Christ according to that meaning of *nature* by which it is defined as “the specific difference informing each thing.” Nor can the statement that the union of man and God was made in Christ be understood in any other way.

There is a general rule—not confined to any single genus of things or to any one discipline, but evident and necessary in every discipline and every genus of things—that whatever things are joined to one another are distinct from one another in their properties.

Therefore, in Christ, the one who is God cannot be joined to the one who is man. For there is no one in Christ who is man; rather, just as he is God in essence, so he is man in subsistence. But he cannot be joined to himself, since he is not distinct from himself by his own property.

When, therefore, it is said that the union of man and God was made in Christ, the understanding both of the speaker and of the hearer must move from the one who is man to that by which he is man—that is, to the nature and subsistence of man, which is called *humanity*. Mathematical speculation likewise abstracts this from the one who is man. The understanding must therefore grant, and believe, that humanity is joined in Christ to divinity—Christ being the one who alone is both God and man.

The reader’s vigilance must attend to the meanings of words, so that the relation of the things signified may correspond to the subject under discussion, and so that one may understand what the interpreter explains the statement to mean. For example, if someone says, “Man is capable of laughter,” and also, “Man is the form of individuals,” the word *man* signifies the same thing in one affirmation as in the other: both what is understood as man and that by which man is what he is [Col. 1382C].

Of these significations, the first, which we have explained, grammarians call substance. The second, which we have explained, they call quality, whatever its genus may be, in every discipline. In the first affirmation, it is not that by which man is man—that is, the quality of the name—but the one who is man by that quality—that is, the substance signified by the name—who is proposed as capable of laughter. In the second affirmation, it is not the one who is man, but that by which he is man—that is, the quality of the name—which is called the form of individuals.

Likewise, if someone says, “Animal is sentient,” and “Animal is the genus of human beings”; “Sentient is a body,” and “Sentient is a difference”; “Capable of laughter is a human being,” and “Capable of laughter is a property of man”; “White is corporeal,” and “White is an accident”—although the supposition of things under the same names is made in the proposed statements, the first statements are to be understood of the substances of the names, while the second are to be understood of their qualities.

There are infinitely many statements of this kind in which, under the same names—not only names that are equivocal or transferred by any kind of figure, but even univocal names—the very nature of things and the rule of speech teach the prudent interpreter that different things are to be understood.

Every name signifies different things, namely, substance and quality. Thus *white* signifies both what is called white, which is the substance of the name, and that by which it is called white, which is the quality of the same name.

If, therefore, under the same name, *white*, someone says, “White is a body,” and “White is an accident,” the interpreter, following the nature of things, will understand the first statement, as was said, of what is called white, which truly is a body, and the second of that by which it is called white, which truly is an accident. For the nature of the things themselves does not permit what is white to be an accident, or that by which something is white to be a body.

Likewise, when it is said that a union of man and God was made in Christ, it should not be understood that the one who is man and the one who is God were joined in Christ. For in him there is nothing that is man which can be understood as joined to the one who is God in him [Col. 1383A]. Rather, Christ himself, who is God, is also man, and he cannot in any way be joined to himself.

In him, therefore, the divine essence, by which Christ is God, and the human subsistence, by which he himself is man, are rightly understood to be joined; and the statement that a union of man and God was made must be understood in this sense. The author himself, as we have already said, made this clear when he repeated the same meaning and said, “But if humanity was joined to divinity.”

Therefore, lest any word deceive the reader—any word which, wherever it is placed in a statement, arouses in the ears a meaning through its sound—let him recall the nature of things, which he has learned from the philosophers, and attend to the rules of speech supplied by logic. Considering the σύνταξις (*syntaxis*, arrangement) from the grammarians, the λέξις (*lexis*, diction) from dialecticians or sophists, and the ῥῆσις (*rhēsis*, expression) from rhetoricians, let him select, from among the many things signified, that which pertains to the subject, with the support of the accounts appropriate to it.

To say nothing of the other forms of speech, in affirmations he should endeavor to notice, among the other things signified, which thing, as subject, receives the name of which predicated thing; there he should establish the understanding of his mind. This is something that the most shameless of men—who understand nothing yet judge everything, who are most wise in folly and most eloquent without any method of argument—do not think worth attending to.

Therefore they take the sense from the words rather than the words from the sense of the speaker, and often derive a different sense from the one to which the words are articulated. Even in what they themselves utter, they do not understand the words, nor what they are saying, nor the things of which they make affirmations.

Thus, when they hear that a union of man and God was made in Christ, they think that the one who is man and the one who is God are said to have been joined in Christ.

Similarly, if one spoke of the union made in Christ of the human spirit, which is called the soul, and of the body, it would rightly be understood that not only that by which the soul is spirit and that by which flesh is body—that is, the natures of spirit and body—but also the soul itself, which is spirit, and the flesh itself, which is body, are in Christ and are joined there [Col. 1383C].

But this cannot be understood in the same way when one says that a union of man and God was made in Christ—namely, so that the one who is man and the one who is God are understood to have been joined. Rather, only the divine essence and the human subsistence—that is, divinity and humanity—are so understood.

Nor were these joined by apprehension. If so—that is, if humanity was joined to divinity by apprehension—then nothing one would have resulted. For he himself will add in what follows: “Nothing”—I repeat—“naturally one has been made from both of these.” That is, no single property is constituted from them.

Consequently, neither is there anything of Christ. And hence Christ is nothing—that is, he is not something naturally one, although he exists. For the name itself, *Christ*, signifies one thing: namely, the one who is called Christ, together with the property gathered from many things by which he is called Christ. This is understood from the singularity of the word *Christ*.

### As if he were saying,

The singularity of the word indicates one thing. But we must see in what way it is one. For he is not simply one who, according to Nestorius, has been joined from the one who is God and the one who is man.

It is certain, however, that the one who is God is also a person. But one person cannot be joined to another except by apposition. If, therefore, while the two persons remain—the one who is God and the one who is man—the union of the natures, that is, of divinity and humanity, was made in the manner described above, namely, according to apposition, then, while the persons of God and man remained, this union could not have been made otherwise, and no single thing could have been produced from the two.

Observe that he says: “If humanity was joined to divinity according to apposition, no one thing was made from both”; and he shows when the union is to be understood as having taken place according to apposition when he says: “If the union of the two takes place while the two persons remain.” By this he plainly demonstrates that there is no union of natures according to apposition unless the subjects in which those natures exist, or of which they are predicated, have themselves been joined to one another according to apposition.

Thus, in the body of an animal, the natures of flesh and bone are said to be joined not by apposition but by composition, because flesh and bone in the body of an animal are joined not by apposition but by composition. For whenever things that constitute some subsistent compose one another, the things by which they are themselves compose the property of that whole subsistent.

The converse, however, does not hold universally. Often the property of some subsistent is composed from many natures, while the subsistent itself consists of no subsistents. Thus the special subsistence of the soul, by which it is and is called a soul, consists of different subsistences.

Observe also that he does not say, “If two things that exist remain”; rather, he says, “If, while two persons remain, that union takes place.” For there are many things that are not persons, some of which are joined to one another according to apposition and others according to composition—for example, stone to stone. Sometimes stones are joined only by apposition, and sometimes by composition.

But one person is never composed with another. For absolutely nothing can ever be made from two persons. Therefore their natures cannot compose any nature. Rather, according to the apposition of persons to one another—which sometimes occurs—their natures too are said to be placed beside one another.

If, therefore, while God and man remain as two persons, the natures of God and man were joined to one another in Christ according to apposition, no single property of Christ was made from them. And since nothing is one except by the singularity of its own property, it follows that, according to Nestorius—who, as has been said, thinks that the two natures in Christ were joined to one another not by composition but by apposition, while God and man remain as two persons—Christ is nothing one.

And consequently he is altogether nothing, truly. For what is not one cannot exist at all, just as what does not exist is not one [Col. 1384C]. Among philosophers there is a common place and a proposition evident in itself: being and unity are universally convertible. Whatever is, is one; and whatever is one, is.

For the singularity of a verb requires the singular property of the singular thing placed beneath it. Likewise, the plurality of a verb requires that diversity of properties which cannot belong to one thing. Thus, if someone speaks of Plato, whether he affirms or denies one thing or many things about him, he will do so with a singular verb. He will not say, “Plato are running,” but “Plato is reading.” Nor will he say, “Plato are a human being, white, an astrologer,” and so forth, but “Plato is a human being, white, an astrologer.”

If, however, he takes Plato and Cicero as the subjects, he will not say, “Plato and Cicero is this or that,” but “they are this or that.” Unless, perhaps, by a figure of speech, the singularity of the predicate noun is matched by the singularity of the verb, as in the statement, “All things was Caesar.”

Therefore, whoever says “they are” signifies, according to the grammatical rules, that he is speaking of many; whoever says “he is” signifies that he is speaking of one.

That one is sometimes simple, as the soul; sometimes composite, as an animal; sometimes continuous, as the body of an animal; and sometimes discrete, as a heap. Nevertheless, just as the simple is one by the singularity of its property, so too is the composite one.

Not only things that are continuous through the intervening boundaries of their lines, such as the body of an animal, or things joined together in some other way without separation, such as the animal itself without the dissolution of spirit and body, are one. Even things composed from many things separated from one another—such as a heap of stones, or a cluster of things of this kind, a heap of grain, legumes, or other such things—are nevertheless one by the singularity of their own property.

### But being, etc.

Whatever is, is one. But we openly and truly confess, before everyone and without any multiplicity of meaning or mixture of falsity, that Christ is—that is, that *is* is said of Christ with the singularity of a verb. Since whatever is, is one, and Christ is, we therefore say that Christ is one by the singularity of his own property.

If this is so—and it certainly is—then God and man are not two persons in Christ. Rather, just as he himself is one by the singularity of his property, so, too, owing to the natural dissimilarity of that same property, it is necessary beyond doubt that God and man be one person of the same Christ.

And truly: if Christ, who is both God and man, is one in the manner we have described, then God and man are not two persons in him. For if God and man were two persons in him, he could not be one Christ.

It is as though he were saying: There would instead be two Christs—one who was one God, and another who was man.

To say that there are two Christs, one who is God and another who is man, is nothing other than the madness of a mind rushing down from its own supposed height of reason. For why should Nestorius dare to call those two—namely, one man and the other God—Christs at all? There is no reason whatsoever.

He repeats the same question with equal astonishment, in order to remove from them the principle by which any things that possess the same principle might be called two. He therefore says [Col. 1385B]:

Or why should he call the one who is God Christ, if he is also going to call the one who is man Christ, when the one who is God by nature and the one who is man by nature have nothing naturally similar, and—if the same thing is to be expressed by another name—have nothing joined together from the union made between God and man, but, if the two persons remain, have only a fictitious association?

The meaning is this: Why does he misuse the same name for natures that are utterly different? If he is compelled to define Christ, he cannot, according to his own account, apply one substantial definition to both Christs—that is, at least one definition according to the substance of the form, even if not according to the form of the substance.
