For this alone is the principle by which the designation of any name is naturally common: namely, that the quality according to which something is named should be wholly common to the substance of the form in those things of which it is the name, as with *man* or *white*.

Such a community between God and man cannot exist either according to any subsistence or according to any accident, since God and man cannot be conformed in any genus or in any accident. Therefore the name *Christ* cannot be predicated univocally of God and man, that is, of persons different from one another both in genus and in individual property.

Truly, if the substance of God and man is different according to genus—as it certainly is—and one name, *Christ*, is applied to both, so that each is called by that name, then the name *Christ* is neither the union of different substances—that is, of the divine essence and the human subsistence—nor something believed to have made one person from what was not one at the beginning, namely, a giant of two substances. Rather, the name *Christ*, that is, the word *Christ* itself, is equivocal and cannot be enclosed within one definition.

But this is not true.

The meaning is: The name *Christ* is neither a univocal nor an equivocal designation of two persons in Christ.

### But by what Scriptures, etc.

Up to this point he has shown by dialectical reasoning that Christ is one person, not two. Now, using the support of rhetoric, he briefly touches on many considerations by which he demonstrates the same point with the greatest firmness.

It is as though he were saying: There is no reason to speak of two Christs, one God and the other man. Nor is there any authority by which this might appear capable of being established. For in what Scriptures has the name *Christ* ever been doubled in order to signify God and man? He might as well say: In none.

What novelty, then—that is, what new thing was accomplished by the coming of the Savior—if, whenever the human being is believed to have been assumed by God, God and man remained different persons?

If someone asks here whether any novelty was effected in this assumption, we answer: Certainly. For among Catholics the truth of the faith and the extraordinary character of the miracle are established by the claim that God assumed man.

This miracle belongs to those things that ordinarily produce wonder, namely, things distinguished by greatness and novelty. For how great—and how new—this is!

It is as though he were saying: Nothing is so new and so great as this: that which happened once and could occur in no other age, namely, that the nature of the one who alone is God should be joined by composition to human nature, which was utterly different from him, so that from natures separated by such distance one person should be made by union [Col. 1386A].

Pay close attention to his statement that “one person was made by union.” Do not understand this to mean that the person was made by the union of the natures, but that he was made one by union. For Christ was not made what he already was, but what he was not.

He was God and the Son of God, and he was a person and one, but without the union of different natures. If someone therefore asks what Christ was made, no one will answer that he was made God, or that he was made the Son of God, or that he was made a person, or that he was made one. Rather, he was made one through the union of different natures.

One what? One whole, one composite, and things of this kind. This is the wonderful novelty.

Through the ordinary process of generation, which is called nature, many things of different species are customarily joined in one person: flesh, bones, blood, bile, and things of this kind, together with the soul. Yet these things agree with one another in some genus and in some respect.

Likewise, there are general and differential subsistences, which are parts of spiritual subsistences, and accidents, which are also counted among the parts of personal properties. These sometimes agree with one another in some genus, and always in some respect.

But no natural process of generation has ever produced one thing composed of elements different in every genus and in every respect. This nevertheless occurred in the person called Christ, in whom human subsistence was joined to divine essence. Human subsistence is understood to differ from divine essence not only in every genus but also in every respect: the one is essence, the other subsistence; the one is without beginning, the other from a beginning; the one is Creator, the other is a creature.

Hence the union made between them in Christ is a novelty.

According to Nestorius’s view, however, just as divinity and humanity existed before Christ’s incarnation—namely, without any union with one another—so he says that they remained after Christ became incarnate. What new thing, then, occurred?

He might as well say: Nothing. This is clear from his own words, for he says: “Humanity and divinity preserve their own persons,” that is, just as before Christ’s incarnation God and man were different persons, so they are after the incarnation.

And as though this ought to be beyond doubt to everyone, he confirms it in a form of rhetorical astonishment, saying: “When was there ever not one proper person of divinity and another proper person of humanity?” In other words: When was God ever not a different person from man, and man a different person from God? “When will this not be so?” That is: It has always been so and will always be so; the one will always be different from the other.

Or what more has occurred? That is: What new thing has happened?

Or what more occurred in the generation of Jesus than in the generation of any other human being, if, while both persons remained distinct—that is, God and man—the natures also remained distinct—that is, divinity and humanity?

For in that case, with the persons remaining distinct, namely God and man, there could be no union of the natures—divinity and humanity—in the generation of Jesus, any more than in the generation of any other human being.

Every human being is generated with God as author and agent, yet his own person subsists, and subsists so distinctly by its own property that no divinity—not, I say, divinity in the Greek sense according to any gift or use of a gift, but divinity in the sense of the most excellent substance, that is, essence—is joined to his human nature by any composition.

For God, who is nowhere absent, is wholly present everywhere in the fullness of his substance. Therefore he is in every human being, and the Father and the Son also give their Spirit to human beings for certain purposes. But none of them is God because the essence of his divinity has been composed with the humanity by which he is man.

Jesus alone, however, is the one in whom the whole fullness of divinity exists. For just as the Father, the Son, and their Spirit are wholly everywhere and beyond all things, so they are wholly in his human body and spirit. The Spirit of the Father, and his own Spirit, is in him for whatever purposes Jesus wills [Col. 1387A].

The Father is also in him by his personal property and is other than him, just as the Holy Spirit is in him and is personally other than him. He himself, however, cannot be in himself, since by his personal property he cannot be other than himself. Thus, when he himself said, “The Father is in me,” he did not add, “and I am in myself,” but rather, “and I am in the Father.”

The Father and the Holy Spirit are therefore in the Son, being personally other than him there, just as they are everywhere. He himself is not in himself, since by his personal property he cannot be other than himself. Nevertheless, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are wholly in his body and soul, as was said, and they are personally distinct from his body and soul.

For neither his body nor his soul is the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit.

But the essence by which the Son is, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one in a singular and individual way, has been joined to the subsistences of his body and soul—indeed, to the whole of his humanity—in him. This has happened in no other human being [Col. 1387B].

Therefore none of the others, although the Father, the Son, and their Spirit are in their bodies and souls—or rather, in the persons themselves—and although the Holy Spirit has been given to them by the Father and the Son, together with many graces in that same Spirit, is ever God by the essence of divinity.

He alone, whose human subsistence has been joined to the divine essence, is both God and man.

But [Note: [Col. 1387D] In the text above, col. 1316, it reads: “Granted, however, [that it is] God.”] perhaps Jesus, etc.] Earlier, while wondering why Nestorius would say that there are two Christs, one God and the other man, he asked whether they ought to be called two Christs, since they could be called neither by a univocal designation nor by an equivocal one, except contrary to the usage of Scripture. Now he shows that they cannot properly be called two Christs—even by a transferred use of the name—namely, God and man. As if he were saying:

“I am astonished that Nestorius calls God and man, whom he says are two persons in Christ, Christs, since they have nothing in common, and so forth. But perhaps he calls Jesus—that is, the person of the man, namely the person whom he thinks to be the man in Christ—a Christ for this reason: because some divinity has performed wondrous deeds through him.”

As if he were saying: “Just as the Scriptures had promised concerning the coming Messiah.” Granted. As if he were saying: “Let this be conceded.” But why does he call God himself—a reference, namely, to the person whom he thinks to be God in Christ—by the name “Christ”? As if he were saying: “Does he call that person a Christ also for the same reason? Namely, because some divinity has performed wondrous deeds through him?” It is as though he were saying: “That is not fitting.”

But if Nestorius says that the person whom he thinks to be the man in Christ is rightly called a Christ for this reason, namely, because some divinity has performed wondrous deeds through him, I ask why he does not also dare to call the elements themselves—that is, earth, water, air, and fire—by the same name, since through them God performs wondrous deeds by their daily movements of generation, corruption, increase, diminution, alteration, and even change of place.

Or will he weaken the force of the comparison by saying that what we object concerning the elements is irrelevant, because irrational substances cannot, as was said above, have a person—that is, be persons capable of receiving the designation “Christ”? It will not avail him. For there are also many irrational substances that are persons, and through them divinity performs wondrous deeds; yet none of them is called Christ.

Indeed, in certain human beings—holy in themselves and conspicuous, in relation to others, for the devotion of divine worship—an evident act of Divinity is recognized; yet, as he might say, none of them is called Christ. Therefore the person in Christ whom he thinks to be the man will not be called Christ for the reason that divinity has performed wondrous deeds through him. For there would be no reason why holy men also, through whom God performs wondrous deeds, and whose subsistences—through which they are something—are not united to divinity, should not be honored with the same designation, so that they too might be called Christs, if the person who is Christ—who, just as he was always God, was always a person—is not, in the assumption of humanity, one through the union of divinity and humanity.

But perhaps, etc.] As if he were saying: “There would be no reason why holy men also, and so forth.” But perhaps Nestorius will say that those men too—that is, the holy men through whom Divinity has performed wondrous deeds—are called Christs. I admit it, but not true Christs; rather, they are Christs in the image of the true Christ. Why they are so called “in his image,” he will say shortly.

But if no single person is united from man and God—that is, if the property of one person does not arise from human and divine nature—we shall judge that all those who are called Christs are not called Christs in the image of the true Christ, but are true Christs in such a way that we would judge this one to be the true Christ who is believed to have been born of the Virgin.

He adds the reason why we judge this: according to Nestorius, no person in this true Christ has been united from the conjunction of God and man. That is, the individual property of this person who is Christ, who never began to be a person, must not be understood to consist of divine and human nature; rather, God and man in Christ are different persons.

The same is true of those holy men who, through the Holy Spirit of God the Father and of Christ himself, his Son—the Spirit given to them by grace—preached the Christ who was to come in the flesh. Their personal properties were in no way composed of divine and human nature. Each of them was a person, while the Spirit of the Father and the Son, given to them by the same Father and by the Son, was another person distinct from them. It was truly given to them for various uses, and especially for this purpose: that, as has already been said, they might preach the Christ who was to come.

For this reason—that is, because of the basis of their fellowship with Christ—they too were called Christs, because through this they were, in a certain way, an image of him whom they revealed by their preaching.

Now, etc.] As if he were saying: “From what we have said, it is clear that God and man are not two persons in Christ.” Now what follows is entirely beyond doubt: if, according to Nestorius, God and man remain different persons in Christ, then in no way can it be believed that humanity was assumed by divinity. Yet this is precisely what the faith of those who rightly believe maintains.

Pay close attention to the expression “humanity was assumed by divinity.” Do not judge the meaning merely from the words, but the words from the meaning; and learn from the properties of the things themselves what, according to grammarians, the expression and, according to rhetoricians, the phrasing are intended to convey to readers. Authors are accustomed to express different meanings through the same words, and the same meanings through different words.

The same meaning is found in the statements “God assumed man” and “divinity assumed humanity”: the former uses the names of a person, the latter the names of natures. For the names “God” and “man” arise from different natures, but they are nevertheless names of one person. “Divinity” and “humanity,” on the other hand, are names of natures. Yet “God” and “man” are sometimes used with the meaning of a person and sometimes with the meaning of natures; and in either case one term may be understood as referring to a person and the other to a nature.

The same applies here: “divinity” and “humanity” may both be used for natures, both for a person, or one for a person and the other for a nature. Thus, when we say “God assumed man” and “divinity assumed humanity,” we use the same sense in both statements: in the first, “God,” and in the second, “divinity,” are expressed in order to signify the person; while “man” and “humanity” are expressed in these sentences in order to signify the nature.

For a person did not assume a person, nor a nature a nature, nor a nature a person; only a person assumed a nature. For Christ alone received the form of a servant.

But when Nestorius hears “God assumed man,” he thinks it must be understood to mean that the one who was God assumed the one who is man. This cannot be so, for it is one and the same Christ—namely, the one who was God and is man—and he could not in any way assume himself, since assumption can occur only between distinct things.

If, however, he thinks that in Christ the one who was God is one person, while the one who is man is another person, and that the one who was God assumed the one who is man, this too is impossible. For just as something absolutely identical cannot be assumed, neither can something absolutely different be assumed. Nothing is more different from one another than things that differ in every genus and in their personal properties.

We do not say merely “in a genus,” but “in every genus.” Nor do we say “in any properties,” but “in personal properties.” Some things differ in genus, but not in every genus: stone and wood, for example, are nevertheless bodies in one genus. They differ in properties, but not in personal properties, and therefore they can compose something unified, such as a house or some similar object.

There are also things that differ in every genus, and therefore in their entire range of properties, but not in personal properties; consequently they can exist in one thing. Color and surface are examples: they have no genus in common and no part of their natural properties in common, yet they are in one thing because their properties are not personal. Color is not, by itself, one thing apart from a surface in such a way that its property prevents it from existing together with a surface.

Again, some things differ even in personal properties and yet agree in their entire genus and even in their species, such as Plato and Cicero.

There are also things that agree—not, I do not say, through an imaginary or substantial likeness of numerically different natures, but through the singularity of one simple and individual essence—while they differ in personal properties: God the Father, his Son, and the Spirit of both.

But, as we have already said, none of all these things is as different from one another as things that differ in every genus and in their entire personal properties. Things are wholly disjoined when they are separated equally in person and in nature; that is, when they are distinguished by personal properties and by dissimilarity of nature, they are, I say, completely disjoined.

Human beings and oxen are not more—indeed, not even as much—disjoined from one another as divinity and humanity are distinct in Christ, if, in the assumption by which God is believed to have assumed man, divinity and humanity themselves—that is, God and man—remained persons.

Human beings and oxen, though separated from one another by properties and species, are joined by one animal nature—that is, by a common genus, which exists through substantial likeness in the thing itself. For human beings and oxen, although different according to their properties and species, nevertheless possess a substance common according to genus.

He explains how this should be understood in other words, repeating the same meaning as follows: “And by the same collection of universality, nature.” What he had called “substance,” he here calls “nature”; what he had called “common,” he here calls “the same”; and what he had called “according to genus,” he here calls “by the collection of universality.”

In the more proper usage of Scripture, substance—which is called subsistence by another name—is the nature of those things that subsist through it. Genus, however, should be understood as nothing other than a collection formed by comparing the subsistences of things differing according to their species, on the basis of their likeness in their entire property.

Through this comparison of likeness, all those subsistences are called one universal, one divisible whole, one common thing, one genus, and one identical nature.

By this common nature, therefore, human beings and oxen are joined, as has been said. But what will not be disjoined in a different way between God and man, if, in addition to the diversity of their nature—which is certain, since no subsistence of a created thing can be substantially like the essence of the Creator—the distinction of persons in Christ is also believed to have remained?

Therefore it is not, etc.] As if he were saying: “If God and man remain persons in Christ, humanity cannot in any way be believed to have been assumed by divinity.” Therefore the human race has not been saved.

And again, he says the same thing in other words: “No salvation has come to us through Christ’s birth if humanity was not assumed by divinity.”

[Tot?] As if he were saying: “The writings of many prophets have deceived the people who believed that salvation had come to them through Christ’s birth. The entire authority of the Old Testament is rejected—an authority by which salvation for the world through Christ’s birth is promised.”

It is evident from what Nestorius thinks that this salvation did not occur, if in Christ the difference between God and man in person is the same as the difference in nature; that is, if God and man in Christ are different persons in the same way that divinity and humanity in him are different natures.

For he saved the very one whom he is believed to have assumed, not with original concupiscence serving as intermediary, but with divine grace preceding.

Notice that he says “the same one” and “whom.” Do not understand this to mean that Christ, who is God and the Son of God, assumed the one who is man. The author of this treatise explains this through argument: Christ could in no way have assumed either himself or another person distinct from himself.

Rather, he who was God by nature, the Son of God the Father by relation, and by individual property also man, assumed the things that belong to man—that is, a human body, a human soul, and even a human form resembling that of a servant—and, in himself, glorified this form, cleansed by grace from every guilt and necessity of vice. For this reason he is said both to have assumed man and to have saved him.

But if what Nestorius thinks is true—that is, if in Christ the distinction of the persons of divine and human nature remains equally, then no assumption of man by God can be understood at all. Since, therefore, the person of man could not be assumed while remaining a person, it will rightly be thought that man could not have been saved through Christ’s birth.

Therefore this too—the belief rightly held and desired by Catholics, namely, that through Christ’s human birth the nature of human beings was saved—is not the case, a conclusion that it is impious to accept.

From these considerations it is therefore clear that there are not two persons in Christ, God and man, but that Christ himself is one person: truly God through the divine essence, and truly man through the human subsistence.

But although there are very many arguments capable of attacking and shattering this Nestorian understanding of the diversity of persons in Christ, for the present it is enough to have drawn these few from the abundance of arguments.

For we must pass on to Eutyches, who, etc.] Up to this point he has stated and refuted the error of Nestorius. Now he first states the error of Eutyches in a similar manner and then refutes it.

For when Eutyches had strayed from the paths of the ancients—that is, when he had abandoned the tracks of the forefathers—he ran, that is, quickly fell into an error contrary to Nestorius’s error. He asserted that what Nestorius thinks is so far from the truth of the Catholic faith—namely, that one should believe there are two persons in Christ—that one ought not even to confess that Christ has a dual nature.

For Eutyches says that man was assumed by God—that is, human nature was assumed—in such a way that the union of this man with God was made such that human nature did not remain in him after the union.

This error, however, will be shown to arise from the same source as Nestorius’s error. Just as Nestorius thinks that there cannot be a dual nature in anything without there being a dual person—a view he holds because, as was said above, he thinks that “person” can be predicated of all natures—and therefore, when he confessed that Christ had a dual nature, he believed him also to have a dual person, so Eutyches likewise did not think that there could be a dual nature in anything without a doubling of the person. Consequently, when he did not confess that Christ had a dual person, he thought it followed that Christ must appear to have only one nature.

Thus Nestorius, rightly maintaining, both according to natural reasoning and according to theological reasoning, that Christ has a dual nature—that is, divine and human nature—nevertheless falsely, against the truth of philosophy, and impiously, against the religion of Christian faith, confesses that there are two persons in him: one who is God and another who is man.

Eutyches, on the other hand, rightly believes, so far as the truth of the matter and the Catholic faith are concerned, that Christ is only one person; but falsely, against sound reasoning, and impiously, against religion, he believes that Christ likewise has only one nature, namely, the divine nature.

Eutyches was convicted not by an argument that would clear up the ambiguity of the question, but by the evident facts themselves. This is rightly said, since it is manifest to everyone, without introducing anything discovered from outside, that the nature of man is one thing and the nature of God another.

He then said that he confessed two natures in Christ before the union of the divine and human nature, but only one after the union.

His statement, however, does not clearly express what he intends: that is, it does not make certain in what sense the words “before” and “after” are articulated in his mind, or from what meaning he uttered them with a definite force of signification. For “before” can be understood from a preceding time that is different, and “after” from a following time that is different.

Nevertheless, in order to examine his madness, we explain this difference of times by division. We shall show that, whichever of the times distinguished by this division he wishes to be understood by saying “before” and “after,” the union of divinity and humanity that he imagines is impossible.

We therefore say that this union of the divine and human nature in Christ occurred either at the time of his birth—namely, in the Virgin’s womb, since then the Word became flesh—or at the time of the resurrection, since then the human soul, which had been separated from his body by Christ’s true death, was reunited with it.

But if the union occurred at the time of his birth, then when he says that before the union Christ possessed two natures, namely divine and human, he says this because, convicted by the evidence of the facts, he rightly holds that the flesh Christ assumed from the Virgin—as was stated above—was different from the divine nature before Christ assumed it.

But concerning that flesh, he appears to hold one of two opinions. For he seems to think what the Valentinians thought: that even before Christ’s birth there was human flesh, not taken from Mary but prepared for his incarnation in some other manner; that the Virgin Mary was then brought in, from whom that flesh—which had not been taken from the Virgin—would be born; and that this flesh, which, as has been said, existed before the birth, was divided and separated from the substance of divinity—that is, from divinity—and was wholly different from it.

When Christ was born from the Virgin, he thinks that this flesh was united to God—that is, to the divine nature—in such a way that the two natures, divine and human, appeared to have become only one nature.

Or, if this is not his opinion concerning Christ’s flesh—namely, that it was not taken from Mary—his view could be the following, if, as has been said, the union occurred at the birth: Christ did indeed assume a body from Mary, as the Catholic faith maintains; but before he assumed it, the nature of divinity and the nature of humanity were distinct from one another. Once the human nature had been assumed, it became one with the Deity and wholly passed over into the substance of divinity—that is, into divinity itself.

But if he does not think that this union occurred at the birth but at the resurrection, we shall again suppose that it occurred in one of the two ways mentioned above: either the flesh was assumed from Mary or it was not.

For after Christ had been born—whether he did not assume a body from Mary or did assume flesh from her—we shall suppose that his natures, which we have often mentioned, namely divine and human, remained two until he rose again; after the resurrection, however, they became one out of two, in such a way, as was said above, that the human nature did not remain.

Concerning these matters, etc.] Up to this point he has stated Eutyches’ error concerning the unity of Christ’s nature. Now, before refuting it, he argues against the opinion by which someone might think that Christ’s human nature was not taken from Mary, and he demonstrates that this could in no way have happened.

As if he were saying: “Whether Christ assumed a body from Mary or did not assume it,” and so forth.

From these words arises the following alternative question, which we shall formulate in this way: “Christ, born from Mary, either derived flesh from her or did not derive it from her.”

If Eutyches does not confess that Christ derived human flesh from her, let him say what man he came clothed in—that is, whose human substance made him appear as man—and according to what distinction of man he wishes him to be said to have come. He himself indicates this by dividing the alternatives and saying: “Was it in the man who, through the transgression of sin, fell from the honor of the human condition, or was he clothed in another?”

If he says that Christ came clothed in the one from whose seed, through something like the propagation of generation, man was derived, let him say whose substance, other than Mary’s, divinity put on.

And rightly I ask, “Whose other substance?” For if that flesh by which Christ was born from Mary was not from the seed of Abraham and David, and finally of Mary—of whom this had been promised—let him show from whose human flesh it was derived.

I speak properly when I say “derived,” because after the first man, Adam, all human flesh is drawn from human flesh through a kind of propagation. For the woman who was given to him as a helper is read to have been formed from his rib. From these two, and thereafter from male and female, with original concupiscence serving as intermediary and the bodies of both being divided, everyone is generated except Christ.

Christ too became man through the division of a human body—not with original concupiscence serving as intermediary, but solely through the ineffable and inscrutable operation of divine grace.

But if Eutyches names some man other than the Virgin Mary from whom the human generation of the Savior was taken, from whom does he say that it was taken?

Two consequences appear to follow from this: he himself will be confounded by his error, and, deceived by the error of his false opinion, he will appear to those who know the Scriptures to have branded the supreme Divinity, which cannot lie, with the mark of falsehood through his own assertion.

He will rightly appear to have done so, since in the holy prophecies—that is, in predictions made firm by their unchangeability, through which many things hidden from human understanding were plainly revealed by the divine power—it is promised to Abraham and David that salvation for the whole world, that is, the one through whom salvation comes, would arise not merely from them, but from their seed.

For something is said to be promised not only when what will happen is promised, but also when it is promised that it will happen, provided that the event necessarily follows the promise itself. I do not say merely that it follows as something necessary, but that it follows necessarily. This occurs when the promise is made by one who cannot lie—that is, by God.

Therefore it is rightly promised that salvation would arise from their seed, and so forth, especially since, if the Savior’s human flesh was taken through conception from someone, it could have been taken from no other source than that from which it was also begotten by the truth of the promise—indeed, by the truth of the promise—namely, from Abraham and David.

If, therefore, the human body was not taken from Mary but from some other man through Mary, nevertheless what had been corrupted by the transgression of the first parents was begotten. If Eutyches thinks this, he is refuted by what was said above, which is an argument drawn from what follows.

But if Christ was not clothed in that man—that is, not in the body of the man who endured death as the punishment for sin—then the following conclusion will arise from an argument drawn from the proper meaning of the passage: such a man, one who was without the aforesaid punishment of death, which is the due punishment of original sin, could not have been born from the seed of any man.

The meaning is this: no one ever begotten through the concupiscence of intercourse could be without the punishment of death.

Therefore, if such flesh was taken from no one subject to the punishment of death on account of original guilt, it rightly follows that it was taken from no human being.

Hence it comes about that it appears to have been newly formed. But this, etc.] Here it seems necessary briefly to touch upon a point that will be understood more clearly in the final chapter [Col. 1393A] of this book concerning the condition of human nature: namely, that in the case of every subsistence, one thing is nature and another is condition. For the nature of a subsistent is that by which the subsistent itself is something. These are substantial forms, together with the qualities and measurable intervals that are present in them within the subsistent. The other things that are naturally predicated of it are called certain conditions of it, because, while retaining now one set and now another of the measures and qualities by which it is something—and especially of the subsistences—it is determined in one condition or another.

For while the color remains, and the lines of three, four, or however many cubits remain, and while the subsistences in the proper sense always remain, a man is nevertheless determined now in this, now in that position, place, state, relation, time, action, or passion; and, while remaining the same, he is varied according to the accidents external to him. The same man is a man sitting and standing, outside the house and inside it, unarmed and armed, a lord and a servant, in the morning and in the evening, at rest and at work, joyful and [Col. 1393B] sad.

It must nevertheless be understood that, although certain things belong to one of these classes, generation and corruption of the subsistent are said to occur according to them—for example, incorporation and animation, which belong generically to condition. For when a body is animated, or a soul is incorporated, the animal is generated through this conjunction of body and soul; and likewise, through the separation of body and soul, the same animal is corrupted. Thus the animation of the body and the incorporation of the soul appear to be subsistences; and so indeed they are, but not subsistences of the soul or of the body, rather of that animal which is composed of them. For the soul is perfectly a soul apart from its incorporation, and the body is perfectly a body apart from its animation; but the animal neither is nor can be an animal apart from the incorporation of the soul and the animation of the body. Therefore these are external conditions of the soul and body, but subsistences of the animal’s generation and corruption.

I speak of generation and corruption because there are other subsistences in the truer sense, which never depart from the subsistent and are called perpetual: for example, corporeality and that by which the soul is a soul, namely what is called generically spirit; and these are perpetual subsistences not only of body and soul but also of man. For just as the soul of a man never ceases to be, generically, a spirit, nor his body to be, generically, a body, so man, although when the condition of body and soul is removed he ceases to be a man and an animal, nevertheless never ceases to be a body and a spirit.

Just as, by divine power, these perpetual things, before they were anything, could be something through these perpetual subsistences, and afterward, with God alone as author, became what they could be and, with him alone sustaining them, remained perpetually in these subsistences—and therefore are said necessarily to be destined thus to be—so also, by divine power, the subjects of the aforesaid and other such conditions of generation and corruption, together with those things that follow upon the power of those conditions, could be generated, exist, and be corrupted at the time of their generation or corruption. Afterwards, however, when God, for the sole reason of his will, brought about the movements of generation and corruption, they had diverse conditions.

For, to say nothing of the rest, through the animation of the body and the incorporation of the rational soul, man becomes an animal and a man. The faith of those who believe rightly holds that God’s will would have preserved this union of body and soul in man without any corruption, had man kept the commands of his Maker. But when he incurred punishment through transgressing the commandment, God’s justice, solely because of his own will, afflicted him with sufferings of many kinds and also with the dissolution of body and soul.

Afterward, however, it pleased God to justify the sinner, to take up the fallen, to restore the corrupted, and henceforth to preserve him forever in that nature of restoration. Before sin, therefore, man was—and after restoration will be—immortal: before sin, because he could avoid dying; after restoration, because he will not be able to die. Before sin, however, he could die; after sin, he could not not die. Thus, before sin, neither dying nor not dying was impossible. But, as has been said, after sin he cannot not die, and after perfect restoration he will not be able to die.

Accordingly, among the subsistences of man by which he truly is something, philosophers have counted this necessary mortality after sin and placed it in the definition by which his being is explained. For when they are asked what it is to be a man, they answer: to be a rational mortal animal. Deceived by this usage of the philosophers, certain people of our own time and Christian profession have doubted whether true men will exist after the resurrection, since it seemed to them that they would lack a part of human subsistence, namely mortality.

It seems to us, however, that neither mortality nor immortality is a subsistence of man. Rather, man is called mortal because, by divine power, he can be dissolved: before sin, without any necessity; after sin, necessarily. He is likewise called immortal because the same divine power, while he was without sin, preserved him so that he would not be dissolved; after restoration, it will preserve him so that he will never thereafter be dissolved. Hence he is said to be unable to be dissolved.

He is not said to be unable either to be dissolved or not to be dissolved because God could not bring these things about, but because the divine will determined that man should be in this condition—before sin, after sin, or after the resurrection. In this sense the sun is said to be unable not to move, although divine power could make it stand still so that it would not move. There are infinitely many examples of this kind.

Therefore, to say nothing of the rest, man’s mortality and immortality, whether necessary or unnecessary, are not subsistences by which he is something, but conditions of his existence at different times, according to divine power or will. Nevertheless, he would not have been called a true man before sin if he had been subject to the punishments inflicted on account of sin, even though he could have died and not died. Nor after sin would he be considered a true man unless he experienced those punishments even to the dissolution of soul and body. After the resurrection, moreover, the conjunction of body and soul will always remain.

Thus mortality and immortality—according to which, at different times and for the reasons stated above, man is said to be able or unable to die or not to die—are certain powers known to us from the customary course of events. For this reason they are often taken as evidence of the truth of human substance, according to the diversity of the times mentioned.

It must nevertheless be carefully observed that, if someone is a man outside the law of human generation, these discoveries concerning mortality and immortality do not establish or disprove the truth of his human substance. For if someone says that Christ is not a true man because, after the sin of the first parents, he is not held by any necessity of dying, or that before his resurrection he was not such as the blessed will be after the common resurrection of all, on the ground that he suffered, the argument does not follow.

For he was not generated by the law of sin—that is, by human concupiscence as its instrument—from a male and a female. Therefore he is subject neither to original guilt nor to any necessity of sinning or suffering, either before or after his passion. But just as he became flesh by his will, so by his will he suffered, rose again, and thereafter remained without any suffering.

Nevertheless, since by divine arrangement all human flesh comes to be either from a male and a female, or from a male without a female, or from a female without a male, or without either male or female, Christ had to become flesh either not at all or in one of these four ways. Since examples of three of these modes had already occurred through God’s own action—Adam, for he fashioned him neither from a male nor from a female but from the clay of the earth; Eve, from a male without a female, from Adam’s rib; and all the others from a male and a female—he displayed in himself the remaining fourth mode, becoming flesh without a male from a female. Nevertheless, certain people, as we have already said, falsely claimed that his flesh had been newly [Col. 1395A] formed.

This can be refuted by the following argument. For this supposedly newly formed flesh was either seen by human eyes in such a way that it was thought to be a body of the kind that would be called human because it had been assumed from a man by original assumption, although in reality—that is, in the truth of the origin just mentioned—it was not human, since, I do not say that it was subject to no punishment, but that it was subject to no original punishment, which we may plausibly add according to the condition of the present age; or else, apart from the original assumption just mentioned, it was formed for a time as some new thing which was not merely said to be true human nature by opinion, but was in reality true human nature, and yet was not subject to the punishment of original sin—that is, the punishment inflicted for the sin of the first parents upon all who are begotten from them through concupiscence and who are therefore also held by original guilt.

Meaning: According to some, this newly formed flesh of Christ was either seen to be what it was not—namely, a human body assumed from a man by original assumption—or, although it was not such, it was not seen to have been from a man. But if it was seen to be what it was not—or rather, if what was seen was not what it was, namely, a true human body assumed from a man—then the Divinity is plainly shown to have lied, since it displayed it; as if to say: by displaying to human beings, through the properties ordinarily belonging to men originally assumed, a body that was not truly, in the manner stated, a body assumed from a man, it would have deceived those who on this basis thought it true.

But if a new and genuinely real flesh was formed apart from assumption, and was not taken from a man, for what purpose—that is, to what end—and for whose benefit was so great a tragedy of his generation, that is, of so many persons, from Abraham or from Adam down to Christ, fabricated as though it were a thing made? Why was there such a great humiliation of something so exalted—that he whose generation was without time should be generated in time? Where, then, is the purpose for which there was such a great course of suffering, to which he is said to have been offered because he willed it?

Meaning: For what benefit did he will to suffer? For I think that not even in a man who can err—much less in God, who cannot—is something uselessly done without folly.

But if someone says that this incarnation of Christ, which was not made from a man, and his voluntary suffering were beneficially accomplished, I ask for what benefit such a great humiliation of the Divinity can be shown to have occurred: namely, that the eternal God was temporally generated and suffered, if the man who perished through the sin of the first parents was not saved through the temporal generation and suffering of Christ. According to some, this is indeed the case, since they deny that Christ was assumed in the generation that is according to the flesh.

Thus again, just as Eutyches’ error—which was discussed above—took its beginning from the same source of causation as Nestorius’ error, since neither of them thinks that there can be a dual nature in anything without a duplication of person, so it returns to the same conclusion: namely, that, just as according to Nestorius, so also according to Eutyches, the human race was not saved. And this one conclusion is drawn. He repeats it, saying:

For, according to him—if this was indeed his opinion—the one who was sick was not assumed in Christ’s incarnation; that is, human substance, which in the first parents and thereafter in all who were begotten from them through concupiscence was held by original guilt and, weakened by original defect, had suffered under its passions. Therefore it needed both salvation and healing (the order of the words is reversed: “healing and salvation” should be understood). Healing was needed so that it might be instructed in how to worship its Maker, that its guilt might be remitted by a sure promise, that the heat of concupiscence might be diminished, and finally that all its movement toward sinning, as well as its defect, might be removed entirely. Salvation was needed so that it might not be punished for sin and might thereafter be preserved not only without sin but also without any disturbance.

Eutyches appears to have drawn this opinion—that Christ did not assume a body from a man—from the words of the Gospel of John, where the Lord himself is read to have said:

[Col. 1396A] “No one has ascended into heaven,” etc.] If this was indeed the nature of his error—that he believed Christ’s body not truly to have been from a man, but to have been taken from the earth elsewhere and formed by God in heaven—this seems to have appeared so to him because Christ is rightly believed to have ascended into heaven with his body, and he supposes that Christ ascended with the same body with which he had descended from heaven. This is the example contained in the words of the Gospel, which Christ himself is seen to have spoken as follows: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven.”

This is understood in a very different way. For it was said of Christ and of all who are to be saved, and the truth of the words is irrefragable if one is not ignorant of that closest unity which exists by reason of the fellowship of head and members.

“But enough,” etc.] Above, the author, wishing to argue against the opinion by which someone might perhaps suppose that Christ’s human nature was not taken from Mary, divided the matter as follows: “Christ, born from Mary, either drew human flesh from her or did not.” He then argued against those who think that he did not draw it from Mary, and by pointing out several inconveniences that appear to follow from that view, entirely rejected the opinion.

Now, therefore, wishing to pass to the other part of the division mentioned above and to destroy Eutyches’ error concerning the union of the natures in Christ after the resurrection, he says as follows: “Enough seems to have been said about that part of the division according to which the body that Christ received is not believed to have been assumed from Mary. But if it was assumed from Mary”—he uses “if it was assumed” affirmatively in place of “because it was assumed,” as though to say: “Which is certainly the case”—“then neither did the perfect human and divine nature remain as Eutyches says, in three,” etc.

He begins his discussion from the division, and shows that the conjunction of the divine and human nature in Christ, which above he demonstrated against Nestorius not to be by addition, is here demonstrated against Eutyches not to be by mixture. For mixture is a confusion through composition, and it occurs only in three ways.

If, therefore, the divine and human nature in Christ were joined by mixture, this could have occurred in only three ways. He explains these by division, saying: “Either the Divinity was transferred into humanity, or humanity into the Divinity, or both were so tempered and mixed into each other that neither substance retained its proper form.”

Here it seems necessary to say that the natures of bodies that are truly mixed are said to be mixed only by denomination; but, through the mixture of the bodies that underlie them, they are rightly said to be confused, without any trope of denomination. Thus whiteness and blackness are not at all mixed, since they are incorporeal, but white and black things are confused by mixture. Therefore it happens that only those things which exist are mixed, while those by which they exist are confused.

It is therefore clear that the Divinity and humanity, which are truly predicated of Christ, cannot be said to be mixed into one another—not merely not properly, but not even by denomination. Nor are God and man in the same person confused by any mixture, since he himself is God and man, and even if he were corporeal in his entirety according to himself, he could not be mixed with himself. For every mixture is of different things.

Nor are there in him one who is God and another who is man, so that—if this were possible—the Divinity and humanity could be said to be mixed by denomination and rightly confused through the mixture of those two, as though there were in him one thing that was God and another that was man.

Thus, in any human being there is something that is soul and something else that is body. In discussing the mixture of God and man in Christ, he says: “Either God was transferred into man, or man into God, or both were so tempered and mixed into one another that neither retained its proper form.” Thus he speaks denominatively of the Divinity and humanity when he says, “Either the Divinity was transferred into humanity,” and so forth.

“But if the Divinity,” etc.] If Christ’s body was assumed from Mary, and the perfect human and divine nature did not remain after the resurrection, he divided the possible ways in which this could occur, if it were true, according to the manner in which things that are genuinely mixed or confused into one another are ordinarily related.

Now, in the order in which he enumerated those modes, he removes them one by one through different arguments from the divine and human nature that truly and perfectly exist in Christ. It is as though he were saying: “If the perfect human and divine nature did not remain in Christ, either the Divinity was transferred into humanity,” and so forth.

But if the Divinity was transferred into humanity—that is, if Christ, before assuming a body from Mary, was God without beginning, and when he rose, through the conversion of the Divinity into the nature of the body, ceased to be God—then something occurred in that transfer which it is impious to believe: namely, while humanity, that is, human nature, remained in an unchangeable substance, the Divinity, that is, the divine essence, was changed.

How absurd and contrary to reason this is, he indicates by saying that what existed—or ought naturally to have existed—as possible and changeable would itself, with every sophistical evasion removed, remain actually unchangeable; while what is rightly believed to be naturally unchangeable and impassible would be changed into a mutable thing.

This, then—namely, that the unchangeable should become changeable and the changeable unchangeable—can occur in no way except, perhaps, by a sophistical argument.

“But human nature,” etc.] He has shown that the Divinity could not be transferred into humanity. He now proceeds to demonstrate that humanity likewise could not be changed into the Divinity.

It is as though he were saying: “The Divinity was not transferred into humanity. But human nature may perhaps appear to have been changed into the Divinity,” that is, it may seem to follow from the words of Athanasius. For after saying of Christ that, although he is God and man, there are nevertheless not two but one Christ, and explaining how he is one, Athanasius added that this was not through a conversion of the Divinity into flesh, but through an assumption of humanity into God.

He seems to wish it understood that the Divinity in Christ remained as it was, without beginning, whereas humanity was converted into the Divinity, at least after the resurrection. The words of Hilary also seem to confirm this meaning: “Before the passion, partly man and partly God; in the passion, entirely man; after the resurrection, entirely God.”

For this reason, in the regions of Germany, someone wishing to establish that not only Christ’s human substance but also the human substance of all the saved, ceasing after the resurrection to be human, would become divine—so that, just as God is wholly everywhere, each of the blessed might likewise be wholly everywhere—brought forward, among many words of Sacred Scripture by which he thought he could support this error, the aforesaid words of Athanasius as an argument for the same opinion.

Had he sought distinction under the title of his own name as a heretic, he might have been made famous by the judgment of ecclesiastical authority. But because, under his concealed name, he secretly sowed the tares of a new heresy in the noble seed of the divine word, not so much by writing as by erasures, he will remain unknown and unharmed among men.

The words of Athanasius, however, must not be understood in the sense intended by the author of this error. For when that sound-minded man said, “not through a conversion of the Divinity into flesh,” he did not add, “but through a conversion”—rather, “but through an assumption of humanity into God.” This was entirely true and carefully expressed. For conversion changes a substance, whereas assumption does not change it.

The assumption is of something cast down, so that what abasement had made base, assumption might render glorious. Thus human nature in Christ is rightly understood not as taken up through conversion, but as assumed into God through glorification.

The words of Hilary that we mentioned above seem to be understood according to this principle. For Christ, both before he suffered on the cross, while he suffered, and after he had been raised from death, truly was and is God and man. He is said to have been “before the passion partly man and partly God” because at that time, in his humanity, insofar as he willed, he truly suffered the weaknesses of our condition: fasting, he hungered; walking, he grew tired; and he endured other such infirmities. In his divinity, insofar as it was fitting, he exercised power: he drove the merchants from the temple, healed the sick, forgave sins, [Col. 1398A] and raised the dead.

When he was betrayed by his disciple, seized by the servants of the rulers, judged by the rulers, and killed among thieves, showing almost nothing then of divine power but enduring only those things that belong to our weakness, he appeared, as it were, entirely man.

But when, rising from the dead, he no longer dies and death no longer rules over him; when he abstains from food and eats without hunger; when he leaves the sealed tomb and enters through closed doors; when all that he lives, he lives to God; and when he displays none of the things belonging to our weakness but only those belonging to divine glorification—then he is, as it were, entirely God. Nevertheless, by the truth of human subsistence he is true man, and by the truth of the divine essence he is true God.

The words of Athanasius and Hilary, therefore, must not be understood in such a way that Christ is thought to have alternated within himself between different modes of existence at the times mentioned. Rather, he exercised the properties of one or the other substance, according to the circumstances. Thus, although human nature was assumed into God, it was not converted into the Divinity.

But how could this happen—that it should at some time be converted into the Divinity? As if to say: “In no way.” Wishing to demonstrate this, he enumerates the parts of man that Christ assumed when he became man and shows that they could not be converted into the Divinity.

He therefore says: “The Divinity”—that is, God the Son, namely Christ—“in the generation by which he himself became man, assumed both a human soul, that is, a rational soul, and a body.” Supply: “Neither of these could be changed into the Divinity.”

For although one thing can be changed and transformed into another, not everything can be changed into everything. What can be changed into what, and for what reason, and what cannot, he first explains by division and then by examples, saying:

“For since some substances of subsistents are corporeal and others incorporeal, we say generally that neither can a corporeal thing be changed into an incorporeal thing, nor an incorporeal thing into that which is a body. Nor do incorporeal things change their proper forms into one another, whether substantial or accidental.”

True. For only those things can be changed and transformed—that is, changed by transformation or transformed by change—into one another which have a common subject of one thing, namely matter.

As if to say: “Corporeal and incorporeal things do not have this in common, nor do corporeal things among themselves.” For, as he is about to say, the nature of incorporeal things rests upon no foundation of matter, whereas all bodies alone have matter subject to their nature. Therefore only bodies can be changed into one another.

Yet not all bodies can be so changed, but only those which can not merely act or be acted upon, but both act and be acted upon with respect to one another. That not all things which have a common subject of one matter can do this, but only those which can both act and be acted upon—and I do not mean in just any other thing, but in one another—will be proved in the following way, namely by the examples that follow.

“For neither…”] As if to say: “Truly, not all things,” and so forth. Bronze cannot, by the ordinary course of nature, be changed into stone, although stone can be changed into bronze. For stone can be acted upon, not by bronze acting upon it, but by fire: stone, dissolved by heat, is changed into bronze. Thus fire acts upon stone, but stone does not act upon fire; stone is acted upon, but not by bronze; while bronze neither acts upon stone nor is acted upon by stone.

Accordingly, they do not exchange the roles of acting and being acted upon except where a thing can both act and be acted upon with respect to the other.

Nor can the same bronze be changed into grass. Grass both acts and is acted upon, but not into bronze or by bronze; bronze likewise both acts and is acted upon, but not into grass or by grass.

“Nor can just anything,” etc.] As if to say: “Bronze can be changed neither into stone nor into grass, nor can any one body be transformed into just any other body. In general, no thing can be changed into another unless the same matter belongs to the things that pass into one another, and unless they can also act upon and be acted upon by one another.”

He illustrates this clearly with the two final examples, saying: “When wine and water are mixed, both are such as to share activity and passivity with each other”—that is, both act upon one another and are acted upon by one another.

Indeed, the quality of water can undergo something from the quality of wine; likewise—that is, similarly—the quality of wine can undergo something from the quality of water. When he says that a quality undergoes something, this is a denominative expression: because that which has the quality undergoes such change that its quality departs from it, the quality itself is said to undergo the change.

This alteration occurs either in one alone or in both. But if in one alone, that which has undergone the change is said to be corrupted, not mixed; if in both, both are called mixed. He demonstrates how this occurs by the same examples of wine and water, saying:

“And therefore,” etc.] As if to say: “The quality of wine can…” And therefore, if there was much water but little wine, wine and water are not called mixed; rather, one—that is, the wine—is said to be corrupted by the quality of the other, namely water.

For it is clear that if someone pours a small quantity of wine into the sea, which is very great in quantity, the wine is not mixed with the sea but is corrupted in the sea. The sea retains its former quality and name, whereas the wine retains neither the name of wine nor its quality. He then adds the reason why this occurs, saying:

“This is certainly because the quality of the water, by reason of the quantity of the body in which it is present, suffered nothing from the quality of the wine; but, on the contrary, the quality of the wine was changed by that quantity of its own body into the quality of the water.” Thus, among things which can both act upon and be acted upon by one another, one is called corrupted, not mixed.

But if the natures that can act upon and be acted upon by one another are moderate in quantity—and, explaining how this occurs, he adds—“and equal or only slightly unequal to each other,” then they truly are mixed. And, as though defining what it is to be mixed, he adds: “They are tempered by qualities moderate in relation to each other.”

Now this—that is, either the corruption of one or the mixture of both—occurs among bodies, but not among all bodies. It occurs only among some, namely those which, as has been said, can act upon and be acted upon by one another, and which also have, as has been said, a common matter of the same kind subject to the qualities of the things that are to be corrupted or mixed.

For in general every body which truly subsists according to all that is in it, and which in generation and in certain respects in corruption appears—and truly does—have a common matter, possesses not only **ὕλη** (*hylē*, “matter”), which Plato calls “wood” or “forest,” and which according to the philosophers exists but is not something, but also that which is not called matter by its proper name yet, according to its own perpetual subsistence, is said to be something.

Only these properly bear the name of matter. For nothing is truly called matter by its proper name except **ὕλη**, which exists but is not something, and the body which does not exist as a particular thing but is something.

The former, therefore, is the matter of all bodies and of the things that are in bodies; the latter is the matter of all things that follow within it upon its first and perpetual subsistence.

But when this matter is called common and the same for all bodies, this must not be understood with regard to its numerical individuality, but rather with regard to the one conformity of diverse substances in number. Thus, when the author says “common and the same,” this should be understood as “the same through the commonality of substantial likeness.”

Different bodies, therefore, receive the matter of those things which, after the first subsistence, are received into them according to one conformity; one acts in another, and one is acted upon by another. But, as has often been said, not everything can act upon everything, or in everything, or be acted upon by everything.

Observe carefully that, although acting belongs only to living things and being acted upon only to things capable of sensation, he nevertheless says that insensible and lifeless things act and are acted upon. He does not do so contrary to the usage of Scripture, in which it is often read that causes act and that the things which receive their actions undergo them—especially when some change occurs in that which is said to receive the action.

“But corporeal things,” etc.] He has shown both by examples and by reasoning that certain bodies are mixed with one another, or that, while one remains, the other is corrupted in it. He now shows that neither incorporeal things can be changed into one another, nor corporeal things into incorporeal things, saying:

“Corporeal things cannot in any way be changed into incorporeal things.” He then adds why the possibility of such a change is absent from them: “Because corporeal and incorporeal things do not share any common matter subject to them—matter which, remaining according to the kind of its own subsistence, by which it is something in both, could be changed into one or the other through the reception of the qualities of one upon the other, or of both upon one another.”

“For every…”] As if to say: “There is no common matter for bodies and incorporeal things.” Indeed, for there is absolutely no matter belonging to incorporeal things. He states it as follows:

“For every nature of incorporeal substance is such that it rests upon no foundation of matter.” For **ὕλη** itself cannot be their matter. But there is no body to which matter is not subject—that is, to whose nature matter does not belong. For **ὕλη** is subject to bodies, while bodies themselves are subject to the other natures of bodies from the first subsistence onward.

[Col. 1400B] “Since this is so,” etc.] Briefly gathering together what he had said, he concludes that corporeal and incorporeal things cannot be changed into one another. He therefore says:

“Since this is so, and since even those things which naturally have matter in common do not pass into one another unless they possess the power to act upon and be acted upon by one another, much less will those things be changed into one another which not only have no common matter but for which it is also impossible that there should be common matter.”

This is clear because one thing rests upon a foundation of matter, as a body does, while another has no need whatsoever of matter as a subject—that is, it cannot even need such a subject—as is the case with an incorporeal thing.

Since, therefore, the incorporeal thing cannot possess the foundation of matter upon which the body rests, it cannot happen that a body is changed into an incorporeal form. Hence it is as though he were saying: “It is clear that the body which God the Son, namely Christ, assumed could not become God according to essence.”

“Nor indeed,” etc.] He has proved that Christ’s body could not be changed into the Divinity. He now wishes to prove that his soul likewise could not be changed into it. He derives this proof from the same principle by which he also demonstrated the point concerning the body: namely, that incorporeal things have no common matter.

It is as though he were saying: “A body cannot be changed into an incorporeal form. Nor can incorporeal things be changed into one another through any mixture, whether the kind in which, while one remains, the other is corrupted—as was said above concerning wine and the sea—or the kind in which both are changed, as was said concerning wine and water.”

Why incorporeal things cannot be changed into one another can be established from the principle of the following major proposition: “Those things which have no common matter cannot be changed and transformed into one another.” But there cannot be common matter where there is none at all. It is certain, however, that there is no matter whatsoever in incorporeal things, as was stated above. It is therefore clear that they cannot be changed into one another.

Recall, if you have learned the art of necessary argumentation, and see what kind and figure of syllogism he uses to prove the proposition. For he has now established as certain the major proposition: “Those things which have no common matter cannot be changed into one another,” namely by establishing that no incorporeal things are changed into one another. Taking this as certain, he adds the minor premise: “But the soul and God are incorporeal substances,” and they are rightly believed to be so.

Since this requires no proof—although the **Ἄνθρωπομορφῖται** (*Anthropomorphites*, those who imagined God in corporeal form) imagined God corporeally—he draws the conclusion, saying:

“Therefore the human soul was not changed into the Divinity, by which, as was said above, it was assumed.”

“But if,” etc.] At last he concludes the entire argument with respect to the proposition he had set out—namely, that human nature was not converted into the Divinity. Briefly gathering together what he had previously inferred by necessary reasoning concerning the body and now concerning the soul, he says:

“If neither the body nor the soul of Christ could be changed into the Divinity”—as indeed, as has been shown, they could not—“then it could in no way happen that humanity,” that is, human nature, which is understood through these parts, “was converted into God.”

*“Much less, however,” etc.]* If the divine and human natures in Christ were joined through mixture, he said above that this could happen in only three ways: namely, if either the divinity were transferred into humanity, or humanity into divinity, or both were so mixed together that neither substance retained its proper form. He has shown by manifest arguments that divinity cannot be transferred into humanity, nor humanity into divinity. If, then, it is not believed that one can pass into the other, much less can it be believed that their transfer occurred in the manner explained by the third possibility in the division just mentioned: namely, that both—the divinity and the humanity—were confused into one another. For, as was demonstrated above, neither incorporeality, that is, something incorporeal, can pass over into a body so as to become a body, nor, conversely, can a body pass over into incorporeality so as to become incorporeal. Here too he repeats the reason already stated several times, saying: “Since no common matter is subject to these”—that is, to body and incorporeal substance—“which, while retaining its existence according to the kind of its perpetual subsistence, might be changed into either of them, that is, into the qualities of either one.”

*“But they,” etc.]* Thus far he has demolished Eutyches’ error; now he briefly recalls it, so that it may become clearer in what the Catholics agree with him and in what they differ, by bringing together a comparison of their truth and his fiction. It is as though he said: “Divinity and humanity cannot pass into one another.” But they—that is, the Eutychians—say this: “Christ consists indeed from two natures, but by no means in two.” He then reveals the sense in which they say this:

“This is what they mean: that what consists from two natures before their conjunction can through conjunction become one in such a way that those things from which it is said to consist no longer remain.”

He adds the example by which they wish to demonstrate this:

“For example, when honey joined to water is confused, neither remains”—that is, neither does honey retain the state of being honey, nor water the state of being water—“but one, corrupted through the union of the other, produces something like a third thing of I know not what name.” In other words, neither is it honey nor water, but something one made from them.

Thus, according to this account, that which becomes a third thing from honey and water is said by them to consist from both, but is denied to exist in both. He then explains why it is denied to exist in both:

“For that third thing cannot consist in both, since the nature of both does not remain.”

“But,” they say, “it is rightly said to be from both. For it can consist from both, even though the things from which it is joined do not remain with either of their qualities.”

He repeats the same point in partly different words, lest he appear, as a perverse interpreter of another’s meaning, either to have passed over the reasons by silence or to have distorted them by abridging them or expressing them improperly. He therefore says:

“But,” they say, “such a one cannot consist in both natures, since the things that have been poured into one another do not remain; and, since they do not remain, they do not exist. Therefore they cannot rightly be called by this name, namely, ‘both,’ in which it appears to consist, although it does not consist in both but truly consists from both—yet with those two having been poured into one another by a change of qualities, or rather with the qualities of both having been changed through their mutual transfusion.”

The Catholics, however, partly affirm and partly contradict what the Eutychians maintain; for they rationally confess both things. They confess that Christ consists both from the two natures and in the two natures. I shall explain shortly afterward in what sense this is said.

*“Now that,” etc.]* Just as he recapitulated the arguments by which Eutyches seemed able to establish his error, so he also recapitulates his own arguments by which he destroyed that error, and says:

“Now it is manifest that Eutyches’ position has been refuted by this consideration”—that is, by this argument known to all—“namely, that since it is possible for one substance to subsist from two natures in only three ways, either divinity must have been transferred into humanity, or humanity into divinity, or both must have been mixed into one another, the argument given above declares that none of these modes could have occurred.”

What remains now is what we promised to explain shortly afterward: namely, that we should show how the Catholic faith says that Christ consists both from the two natures and in the two natures.

*“From the two natures,” etc.]* Above, when arguing against Nestorius and saying that the union of God and man does not occur *κατὰ παράθεσιν*—that is, “according to juxtaposition”—I recall that it was stated that there are different ways in which different things are joined to one another. Some are joined through apprehension, and from these no single thing is made; others are joined through composition, and from these something one is made. Of things joined through composition, some are joined through the mixture of one or both components, and others without mixture.

It is therefore clear that every composite, or a property of it, is said to consist from the natures of both its components. But this is said in several ways, as the preceding subdivision makes clear. He explains it as follows:

“To say that something consists from the two natures signifies two things. One meaning occurs when we say that something is joined from two natures through confusion, as something is joined from honey and water. Such a composite is of a kind that, however the things confused into it may have been composed—whether one nature is changed into the other or both are mixed into one another—neither remains in any way.”

*“But another mode is,” etc.]* He first inserts the point that Eutyches, according to this mode, says that Christ consists from both natures. Then he says:

“Another mode of something’s consisting from both natures is this: that the thing is joined into one through composition from two natures in such a way that the things from which it is said to be joined nevertheless remain and are not changed into either of the two in any way—neither one into the other nor both into one another.”

He clarifies this with an example suited to human workmanship:

“As when we say that a crown is composed from gold and gems.”

This example properly serves the purpose for which it was introduced. In the crown, neither has gold been transferred into gems, nor has a gem been changed into gold; both remain what they were before the crown was made from them. This is understood from what he adds:

“Nor do they abandon their proper form”—either gold the form by which it was gold, or the gem the form by which it was a gem.

Thus in all composites, not only those made by human agency but also those produced naturally through God’s operation without the confusion of any component, the components are what they were, and predicates are made of the composites from them—whether one thing is similar to other things, whether one thing exists by itself, or whatever genuine subsistences the components may be, together with those properties proper to them that always and universally belong to things of their kind. They are components not only while they remain in the condition of that composition, but also before they are combined, when they already exist, and after they have been separated from one another.

For anyone who has not yet been generated but will be a human being is already a body, as Antichrist is. Whoever, however, is no longer a human being because soul and body have already been separated is still both body and spirit. This is proved by those properties of body and spirit that belong only to these general subsistences, from which these names are derived. But the things said of what has not yet been conceived and of what has already been separated—such as what is said of Antichrist, that he is in his father’s loins, and of Phaethon, that he is lying in the tomb—would not be said either of the former or of the latter unless the former already existed and the latter still existed as body in kind.

For although the parts withdraw from one another through separation, they do not withdraw from that of which they are parts—not with respect to the integrity of the composite, but at least with respect to their own number.

We therefore say that things consisting from something consist not only from those things but also in those things from which they are said to consist. For then—that is, if they are not corrupted in the composition itself but retain the existence they had—we can say that a crown consists in gems and gold. The gems are gems, and the gold is gold; the crown consists in them, as it were, while they remain in their own substance. We could not speak in this way if either one or both were corrupted in the composition. For in the earlier mode of composition, there is neither honey nor water in which that thing joined through composition from both could consist.

*“Since, therefore,” etc.]* The sense is: when both components remain, then the composite is said to consist in those things from which it consists.
