Since, therefore, the Catholic faith confesses that both natures—the divine and the human—remain in Christ, and that they persist perfect and without any corruption, so that neither is changed into the other, it rightly says that Christ consists both in the two natures and from the two natures.

Just as above he repeated Eutyches’ words together with the arguments that seemed persuasive to him, so that his error might be more clearly exposed, so he also repeats the Catholics’ words together with their arguments, so that the faithful may hold them as certain. He says:

“The Catholic faith says that Christ consists in both natures because both remain; but it says that he consists from both because the person of Christ, which existed from eternity, becomes one without any composition—not one in what it was, that is, in person or unity, but one in what it was not, namely, through the union of both natures. I speak of the natures not as corrupted by that union, but as remaining without any corruption.”

From this it is clear that although Eutyches’ perfidy and the Catholic faith both say that Christ has been joined from the two natures, the Catholic faith does not hold this according to the meaning in which Eutyches declares it. For he, that is, Eutyches, takes “from both natures” to signify such a union that he does not confess Christ to consist in both. He then explains why he does not confess this:

“For he does not confess that both remain.”

The Catholic, however, takes “consisting from both” in a sense that is prior to and preserves the meaning in which he confesses that Christ consists in both.

It is therefore evident that the expression “to consist from both” is equivocal, or rather amphibolous, designating different things through a double meaning, according to the way in which the *σύνθεσις*—the combination—of the words rationally functions. He shows what these different meanings are by division:

“On the one hand, it signifies that the substances do not remain”—that is, to consist from both in such a way that the substances from which the joined thing is said to be composed do not remain. “On the other hand, it signifies that it is joined from both in such a way that both remain.”

*“This having been clarified,” etc.]* Thus far he has both explained and removed the mutually opposed errors of Nestorius and Eutyches. Now he presents the position held midway between them by the Catholic faith. The sense is:

“To consist from both” is equivocal or ambiguous. Once this equivocation and ambiguity has been resolved by division, there is nothing further that Eutyches or anyone else can bring forward against the firm and true faith—which, with the word order reversed, means “true and firm.” It is true because the matter is so; it is firm because the Catholic faith, proved by arguments, contains it: namely, that Christ himself is a man perfect in the integrity of human substance, and the same Christ is God true in the reality of divine essence. This is directed against Eutyches together with Nestorius.

The same one who is man, as was said above, perfect and truly God in essence, is one God by the property of person, true in essence and, by personal property, the Son of God. Nor, as it may perhaps seem to those who understand less well, is a quaternity of the Trinity asserted when man—that is, human nature—is added to perfect God. Rather, one person is asserted by individual property, the same person who, like the Father, or his Son, or his Holy Spirit, existed without beginning. This person does not complete—that is, fill out—the number of the Trinity as another person. He is the same person, so that when humanity has suffered—that is, when suffering belongs not to the divine but to the human nature, and Christ has suffered according to that nature alone—it is nevertheless truly said that God has suffered.

This could in no way be said if God and man had been joined together in Christ *κατὰ παράθεσιν*, that is, according to juxtaposition. But since, as Holy Scripture testifies, “as the rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ,” divine and human nature are truly and without any figure of transference predicated of one singular and individual Christ, through the names given to Christ from those natures—namely, “God” and “man”—just as, of any human being, the natures of soul and flesh are called by the names derived from them, namely “soul” and “flesh.”

With the same Christ as subject, if one of these predicative names is posited, the other may be predicated, together with whatever naturally accompanies the cause signified by that other nature. For when a man is soul and body, the properties of both soul and body may truly be predicated of him under the name “man”—that is, under the name “animal” or “rational”—with the same subject understood.

Not only those properties proper to souls may be predicated, but also those proper to bodies, as in the statement: “Eight souls entered the ark.” Here the author uses the plural noun “souls” not to mean the souls of human beings but the human beings themselves as subject, and he predicates of them what belongs not to souls but only to bodies, namely, entering.

Similarly, one may say, “A certain rational being is white,” so that by the name “rational”—which derives from the power of the soul and is the name not only of the soul itself but also of a human being—the human being himself is understood as subject; yet, with this subject, whiteness, which is a quality not of the soul but of the body, is truly predicated.

Likewise, under the human name “body” or “white,” with the same human being as subject, properties belonging not only to bodies but also to souls may truly be predicated of him, such as “rational,” “musical,” or other such predicates.

In general, whenever one thing is called by many names according to the same capacity, any of those names may be used to posit the thing of which they are names, and the remaining names may then truly be predicated of it. But not every predicate would produce a consequent connection with the things of which the subject is posited. For one must know that among predicative connections some are consequential and others accidental.

Consequential connections include “what is corporeal is colored”; accidental connections include “what is corporeal is rational.” Color is due to corporeality, not the power of discernment, which belongs to spirits alone just as color belongs to bodies alone. But since it happens that body and spirit exist in one thing, whatever belongs naturally to body and spirit may truly be predicated of that one thing, as has often already been said.

Nor can the truth of the connection be hindered in any way by the accidental character mentioned, provided that both what is predicated and what serves as the subject belong to that one thing according to the same account.

We say “according to the same account,” lest someone, hearing it said of something that “what is a body is white” and “what is white is contrary to black,” should think that one may say “body is contrary to body.” Although “body,” “white,” and “contrary” are all names of the same thing, they are not names according to the same account: “body” and “white” derive their names from natures, whereas “contrary” derives its name from the reasoning process.

Therefore “contrary” cannot truly be predicated of that thing unless it is posited under the name imposed on it from the cause of contrariety: thus, “white is contrary,” or under some other name imposed on any thing from the cause of its contrariety.

For whiteness and blackness are not contrary to one another, except perhaps through a trope of denomination; rather, the causes of the contrariety of white and black are truly contrary to one another.

One must also carefully observe that when it is said “white is an accident,” it is not white, from the cause of whiteness, that is called an accident, but whiteness itself. Hence it is clear that, in the reasoning process, we cannot truly predicate something of anything unless the predicate is connected with the subject by a certain consequence of the things signified.

Accordingly, the connection expressed by “God has suffered,” although accidental, is nevertheless true—not because the divinity itself has become humanity through any change of itself (for it is inconvertible, that is, wholly unchangeable), but because humanity was assumed by the divinity, that is, by God, and thereby was truly joined in the Son of God, namely Christ.

Because of this union, there is rightly formed not only in natural matters but also in theological matters an accidental and nevertheless true connection of expressions. Since Nestorius does not think that this can truly occur, having already illustrated it with the accidental and true connection “God has suffered,” in which the person of Christ, posited under this name derived from the essence of his divinity—namely “God”—is said to possess a suffering that belongs not to divinity but to animal, sentient nature, he gives another example of the same kind: an accidental yet true connection in which the same person of Christ, made subject under that name derived from the subsistence of his humanity—namely “man”—is said to be the Son of God. This is not according to human generation but according to divine generation.

He therefore says:

“He who is man is called the Son of God.”

And this is not because the substance of divinity has come about through the conversion of humanity into it, but while the substance of humanity remains. Although humanity has not been converted into divinity, it has nevertheless been joined to divinity by a natural union.

Although these—that is, divinity and humanity—are distinguished and mixed by understanding, whose power it is both to divide what is joined and to join what is divided, nevertheless one and the same person, by personal property, is both a man perfect without corruption of human nature and true God without any transformation of divine nature.

He is God because he is from the substance of God the Father—that is, from God the Father—not created according to substance but begotten. He is man because he was brought forth from the Virgin Mary according to the substance of the body that he assumed from her and according to the soul that he received in her.

*“Likewise,” etc.]* He has said that although it is spoken accidentally, “God has suffered” and “man is the Son of God” are true statements. He then removes the opinion by which someone might perhaps concede that this is true while thinking that humanity itself had become divine, saying:

“Not because divinity itself became humanity and thus became not of divine substance but of human substance.”

He likewise says that it is accidental but true that he who is man is God, and he explains why:

“Because the man was assumed by God, the Son of God, that is, by Christ.”

This is what he had said above about humanity: “because it was assumed by the divinity.” Conversely, he who is God is man. He then explains why:

“Because he has been clothed with man”—that is, with human nature—“as with a suitable garment.”

This is what he had said earlier: “because the substance of humanity has been joined to divinity by a natural union.”

Although within the same person one thing is divinity, which assumed, and another thing is humanity, which was assumed, nevertheless the same person—that is, Christ—is both God and man. This is what he had said before: although these things are distinguished and mixed in understanding, one and the same person is nevertheless both perfect man and God.

Observe that he says “the divinity which assumed,” and understand that Christ, who was God before this assumption, assumed humanity. Hence it is said that “the divinity assumed,” because it was not nature but the person that assumed a nature.

*“For if,” etc.]* What he had said—“he who is man is God, and he who is God is man”—together with the reasons he had supplied, namely that the man was assumed by God and that God was clothed with man, he continues to press against the Nestorians. He also continues to insist against the Eutychians that although within the same person divinity is one thing and humanity another, the same person is nevertheless both God and man.

Let the one who speaks remember, or let the one who does not know learn, that a speaker must keep in mind not only the persons about whom he speaks but also the principles of speaking, and must form his words accordingly.

To pass over the other matters in the page that do not contribute to the present exposition, in predicative statements we do not so much predicate something already posited as posit something in order to predicate it. First we choose the thing of which we are going to say something; then we either affirm or deny something of it. In this process, because every expression signifies different things, the attentive listener considers both what is signified and of what it is signified.

For example, when we make the noun “body” the subject, since it designates both that which is a body and that by which something is a body, we posit either the subsistence itself or that which subsists through it; either a part of some substance that is a body, or that body of which it is itself a part.

Therefore, when we are going to predicate something of Christ, we first choose one of his names under which to posit him. Thus, when we think of him as man, we posit him under the name “man” and predicate of him the divinity that is his essence. This is entirely correct.

For if you first understand him under the aspect of subject as man, it can truly be said that the same person is both man and God—that is, that he who is man is God—because he is man by nature, while he is likewise God by nature, but it happens that together with the human nature by which he is man he also has the divine nature by which he is God. This occurs through the assumption by which, while he was God, he assumed human nature.

If, however, you understand the same Christ first as God under the aspect of subject, then he is the same God and man—that is, he who is God is man—because he is God by nature, while he is likewise man by nature, but it happens that together with the divine nature by which he is God he also has the human nature by which he is man. This occurs through the assumption by which, while he was God, he assumed human nature.

Thus in him there is a twofold nature without any confusion, and, if you prefer to say so, a twofold substance, since, as has been said, he is both man and God. Yet there is one person in true individual identity, since the same person is both man and God.

The Catholic faith is a middle way between the two heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches, just as virtues also occupy the middle between contrary vices. Every virtue consists in being situated in what is fitting—in being fittingly placed at the middle point of things.

It is rightly said that virtue is situated in the middle of things. For whenever something is done either beyond or below what ought to be done, one departs from virtue.

Thus generosity is intermediate between extravagance and avarice. Generosity gives what ought to be given and keeps what ought not to be given. Extravagance goes beyond what is proper, giving both what ought to be given and what ought not to be given. Avarice falls short of what is proper, keeping both what ought to be given and what ought not to be given. There are very many examples of this kind.

Virtue therefore holds the middle position; and by its likeness the Catholic faith described above occupies the middle between the heresies just mentioned.

*“Therefore, if these four,” etc. . . . “it remains that this is the true one,” etc.]* Here is the order of the words. From the combination of nature and person, and likewise of one and two, four classes arise. Nestorius contends that the first belongs to Christ, Eutyches the second, the Catholics the third, and no one the fourth.

He has already destroyed by arguments the opinions of Nestorius and Eutyches. Against the position that no one has yet proposed he has brought no arguments; after removing the errors, he finally set forth the true Catholic position, as he had promised in his prologue.

Recalling all this in a brief summary, he says:

“These four possibilities, and no more according to the customary course of things, can exist. When persons and natures are proposed, either the natures are different and the persons are different, as Plato and Cicero are different persons and their natures are different; or there is one person and one nature, as God the Father is one person and his nature is one; or there are different natures and one person, as Plato is one person but has different natures, namely those of soul and body; or there is one nature and different persons, as the Father, the Son, and the Spirit of both are different persons but have only one nature.”

Since this is the true and complete division of persons and natures into one and many, when the matter proposed for discussion is Christ and his nature, it is necessary that in Christ either there be two natures, divine and human, and two persons, one God and the other man, as Nestorius says; or one person, Christ, and one nature, arising from the conversion of the human into the divine, as Eutyches says; or two natures, divine and human, but one person, Christ, who is one God and man, as the Catholic faith believes; or one nature and two persons, which no one has yet asserted.

We have shown, in the response given against Nestorius, that there cannot be two natures and two persons in Christ. We have shown, when Eutyches proposed it, that there cannot be one person and one nature. Nor has anyone yet appeared so insane as to believe that in Christ there is one nature but two persons.

If these four possibilities, and no more, can exist in Christ—if there are either two, and if we have refuted the two possibilities just mentioned—then it remains that the faith proclaimed by the Catholic Church is true: namely, that in Christ there is a twofold substance, that is, divine essence and human subsistence, but that he himself is one person.

A little earlier, when explaining Eutyches’ error, we said that Eutyches confessed that before the union there were two natures in Christ, divine and human, but that after the union there was only one, namely the divine. When we interpreted this error as concealing, in the multiplicity of the expressions “before” and “after,” a double meaning—namely, that the union either occurred through generation, that is, at the time of his generation, when the human body was by no means assumed from Mary, or that, although assumed from Mary, the union occurred through the resurrection, that is, at the time of the resurrection—the two alternatives have been discussed sufficiently, as I think, and it has been demonstrated that this union could have occurred at no time and in no way whatsoever.

*“Now it must be asked,” etc.]* What he promised in the preface to his prologue he has thus far carried out while preserving the order of his division. First he set forth and removed the mutually contrary errors of Nestorius and Eutyches; then he taught what the Catholic faith holds as the middle position.

Philosophers, whenever they see that something is necessary for their treatises, or perceive that something worthy of inquiry may arise from their words, customarily place it either at the beginning, in the opening pages, as a prologue, or after everything has been explained, at the end, or even after brief epilogal recapitulations of the Trinity.

Since the author of the work under discussion had learned this both from reading many treatises and through the considered reasoning of his own mind, he wished to touch at the conclusion of the completed work upon matters that seemed in some way useful to his argument but that, if treated in its course, would disturb its sequence, and thus, because they are extremely necessary, to commend them to memory.

These matters are the different states of human nature: namely, the state before man sinned, the state after he sinned, and the state that would have been given to him as a reward if he had not sinned.

Since, therefore, the arguments already stated make it clear that Christ is one person and that in him human nature is joined to divine nature without any confusion, it is rightly asked in which state of human nature Christ became man.

He therefore first brings this question into apparent doubt by arguments, and afterward dispels the doubt through a division of the states. He says:

“Now, as though the errors of Nestorius and Eutyches had been explained and destroyed, and the Catholic faith of those who confess that Christ is one person but has a twofold nature had been demonstrated, it must be asked how it could have happened that two natures so different—divine and human, which are not alike to one another in any respect or according to any account—were mixed, that is, came together in a certain union without confusion of themselves, into one substance, so that they might exist together in one subsistent thing and be truly predicated of that one thing both together and separately, just as the natures of soul and body are predicated of any human being, some of which agree in some respect and all of which agree together in some way.”

*“Nevertheless,” etc.]* The sense is: Now it must be asked how this happened, and so forth. Nevertheless, after what has been said, there is also another question that can reasonably be inferred from the preceding discussion by those who do not believe that Christ’s human body was assumed from Mary. They think instead that it was, at another time and in another place, either in heaven, as the Valentinians suppose, or separated and prepared for Christ’s incarnation in some other place apart from other bodies. At the union—that is, when the union of the divine and human natures had taken place—it would then have seemed to be born and brought forth from Mary’s womb.

The question is as follows. They say:

“If Christ’s body was assumed from a human being, as you Catholics believe, and if every human being, as you say—and as is true—was, from the first transgression, that is, from the transgression of the first parents, held not only by sin, so that he might actually do what ought not to be done, and by death, so that he would necessarily be dissolved, but was also entangled by a certain necessity in sinful affections, that is, in desires for sinning, which was the penalty of the sin of the first parents—so that, although bound by death, as has been said, he was nevertheless also guilty through his will to sin—how, that is, on what grounds, can it be maintained that in Christ, from such a man as you say he assumed his body, there was neither the sin of any act nor any will to sin? According to the consequence of what applies to others born from sinners, this would seem, and indeed absolutely ought, to have been the case.”

The sense is: Those who do not believe that Christ’s human body was assumed from Mary raise the question in this way. In reality, such a question contains a doubt that must be taken seriously, so that just as the ambiguity appears to have been brought forward by arguments, it may likewise be cleared away by arguments.

He has already touched upon the arguments by which the doubt may appear to have been raised, and he reinforces them as follows:

“For if Christ’s body was assumed from human flesh—as indeed it was—it may be questioned what kind of flesh the assumed flesh seems to have been: whether such as Adam was after sin, or such as he himself was before sin.”

And indeed the flesh assumed appears to have been such as Adam was after sin. Christ saved the one who was in need of medicine, and he assumed him—that is, he assumed the body separated by grace alone from the mass of sinners and freed from every guilt and necessity of vice. Likewise, with respect to the human soul that he assumed in the same way, that is, through grace alone, he glorified it by the same grace.

But if he assumed such a man—that is, such a human nature—as Adam was before sin, which he certainly could have done, since, although he assumed a human body from sinners and from those generated through sin, he did not assume it through sin, that is, through the agency of original concupiscence, then he seems indeed to have assumed a complete human nature, but one that in no way needed medicine, by which it might be said to be saved or to have been saved.

If it is granted that he assumed one such as Adam was before sin, it is asked how he could have assumed a man—that is, a human nature—such as Adam was before sin, since it was then shown by what occurred in Adam that the will and inclination to sin existed in him.

From this will an act proceeded: he transgressed not only in a matter concerning which he had received no commandment, but also, after violating the divine commands that had been given to him—“You shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil”—he became bound by the sins of disobedience.

In Christ, however, it is believed that there was not even any will to sin, much less the act of sin itself. Nor ought this to be believed, especially since, if Christ assumed a body such as Adam’s was before sin, he ought not to have been mortal through any necessity. For Adam too, if he had not sinned, is believed to have experienced death in no way.

The necessity of dying is undoubtedly the penalty of sin, as the Lord says: “At whatever hour you eat, you will die.”

Since, therefore, Christ did not sin—which indeed he did not—if he assumed Adam’s body as it was before Adam sinned, it must be asked why he experienced death.

But if he assumed the state of man—that is, human nature in the state—in which Adam was after sin, then it seems that, just as Adam was, Christ too was not without the necessity of being subjected to sins and of being overwhelmed involuntarily by sufferings, and, with the judgments of necessary ignorance imposed upon him—that is, with the rules by which things are rightly discerned—of failing to distinguish good from evil with the undivided integrity of reason.

For it is certain that Adam, through the transgression of sin—that is, because by sinning he transgressed, or rather because through transgression he sinned—received all these penalties: the penalty of sinning, the penalty of suffering, and the penalty of ignorance.

Against whom, etc.] That is to say: those who do not believe that Christ’s human body was taken from Mary—such as the Valentinians—seem to think that they can, by these arguments, confirm their own position and weaken that of the Catholics. To them the reply must be made that three states of human beings, or rather of human nature, can be understood. I remember having said above that, in the case of every subsistent being, one thing is its nature and another its state; that its nature is what the subsistent being itself is as something. The remaining features, which are said to be externally attached to it, are called its state, because, retaining them now in one way and now in another, it is established by the divine will in the conditions by which it is something, and especially in its enduring subsistences.

Leaving aside, then, other subsistent beings and their states, let us consider the human being and those states of his whose knowledge is relevant to the present discussion. Thus the human being, who from the moment he began has never ceased to be body and spirit in enduring subsistence, was established by divine power and will in the condition constituted by the union of these two, a condition called the subsistence of a living animal in generation and corruption, so that he may properly be said first to have been able, and then not to have been able, to be dissolved and not to be dissolved. This does not mean that God ever in any way begins or ceases to be able; his power is eternal power. Rather, among all things subject to his power, he established some as changeable and others as unchangeable, solely by the cause of his eternal will.

According to this established condition, therefore, the human being, made through the union of body and rational soul, was able both to be dissolved and not to be dissolved. In this state he received God’s commandments, through obedience to which he would merit rewards and through disobedience to which he would merit punishments. By obeying, he would have merited not being able to be dissolved or to sin—or rather, to be glorified—which is another state. By disobeying, he merited being unable not to be dissolved or not to sin, but to be utterly confounded; and this is the third state.

We therefore understand three states of human beings—that is, of Adam and thereafter of those generated from him according to the law of human generation, through the original sin of concupiscence. The author himself explains them as follows:

“One state, namely that of our first parent Adam, can be understood as having existed before his sin of disobedience. In that state, although death—that is, the dissolution of body and soul—was absent from Adam, and although he had not yet defiled himself with any offense for which he would have deserved punishment, there could nevertheless be in him a will to sin; and consequently, as though he were saying this, there was in him the power to die.

“Another state is that in which he could have been changed from this will to sin and power to die, if he had wished to remain firmly in God’s commandments, so that his mind would not even waver toward transgression under the impulse of any temptation. Truly, then, he would have acquired this additional condition: not merely would he not sin or wish to sin, but he would not even be able to sin or wish to commit an offense; and consequently, as though he were saying this, he could neither die nor be affected by sufferings.

“This must nevertheless be understood correctly—not as though God, whose power is eternal, as we have already said, ever ceased to be able to do what he had been able to do, but as meaning that, if the human being did not sin, the divine will established that this should be so. To the power of committing an offense, in which even those who stand by it are not steadfast, there is present the power of punishment, by which he found perversity even in his angels.

“The third state is that after the offense, in which death followed him necessarily, by the ordinance of the divine will, and likewise sin itself and the will to sin.”

These, then, are the three states of human beings according to what has been said. Of these states, the following are the locations of the highest points and opposites—that is, of the extremes opposed to one another: the state that would have been the reward if Adam had wished to remain in God’s commandments, and the state that became his punishment because he did not wish to remain in them. These two are truly, in a certain sense, the locations above the mutually opposed extremes. In the state that would have been the reward, as has been said, there would have been neither the death of dissolution, nor the sin of transgression, nor any will to sin. In the state after the offense, however, there are death, sin, every inclination to commit an offense, and everything which, to put it briefly, through original fault inclines toward destruction; and it is so weak that after the fall it has no power in itself to rise again. The intermediate state, in which the actual presence of death or sin was absent, but the power of both—of sin and of death—was established, is placed between the two states just mentioned.

From these things, therefore, etc.] Up to this point he has divided the states of Adam, or of those who have been propagated according to the law of human generation—that is, through the sin of original concupiscence. He now begins to say that something of all these states existed in Christ, who indeed assumed his body from sinners, but not according to the law of sin: absolutely nothing in him arose from necessity, to which the sin of their generation subjects others, but everything from the will alone.

He says this so that they may understand that the arguments stated above by those who do not believe that Christ’s body was taken from Mary in no way establish their conclusion in Christ. Such people do not recognize that, although certain reasons are admitted in the case of various kinds of things or capacities, there are nevertheless others assigned to particular kinds which do not extend beyond them, whether in universality, probability, or even necessity.

It is as though he were saying: These are the three states of human beings. From these three states, therefore, Christ—who did not become human according to the law of human generation—introduced into his bodily nature, in a certain manner, not all the causes but individual ones, that is, some causes; and he shows both which they were and from which states they came, saying:

“Since he assumed a mortal body—and he did this in order to drive death away from the human race—it must be placed in that state; that is, it must be understood to have come about according to what was inflicted, after Adam’s transgression, upon Adam himself and upon the entire human race propagated from him through concupiscence as a punishment: namely, so that death would be in it as the punishment of its own sin.

“But because there was no will to sin in him, namely in Christ, insofar as he is God such a will was naturally absent from him; and insofar as he was made human by grace, it was taken from that state—that is, according to that state it was granted to him—which would have been Adam’s had he not attached his will to the snares of the devil lying in wait for him.”

These, then, existed in Christ according to those states which are mutually opposed as the locations of the extremes. There remains the third, intermediate state: the state in which death was not present, yet could be present—not only death, but also its precursor and cause, namely the will to commit an offense.

In this state Adam was such that he ate and drank, digested what he had taken in, was released into sleep, and performed other such acts which were not lacking in him. These acts belonged to human life—that is, to the human life for which he had been made a living soul—but they were granted to him, and were of such a kind that they imposed no punishment of death as though for sin.

There is no doubt that Christ possessed all these things. For although Christ was made a life-giving spirit, nevertheless, just as Adam was made, as has been said, a living soul, so Christ ate and drank and, in the other matters that the first state of human nature required, performed the functions of a human body without necessity arising from any need.

Nor should we believe that Adam’s need at that time was as great as it became after sin—namely, that if he had not eaten he could not have lived. Rather, it was such that, if he took food from every tree, he could always have lived and, by taking these things—that is, by consuming them—would not die. Therefore, in order that he might always have been able to live by them, he satisfied that need, as it has been described, with the fruits of Paradise.

Even in this punitive state, not everything which we are said to need is of such a kind that, although it in some way supports those living in this life, it is necessary to die without it. Such are clothing, vehicles, and the many other things of this kind and of varied character: without them we can indeed live, yet at the same time we need them.

Much more, therefore, in the state that existed before sin, Adam could live even without food, and yet he needed it. No one is unaware that Christ possessed this same need—that is, a need of this kind—according to that state which Adam possessed before sin; but in Christ it existed by his power alone, not through any necessity beyond his will.

From these considerations it can clearly be understood how, although Christ’s body was taken from a human being and every human being was held by sin and death from the first transgression, there was nevertheless no sin in Christ and no will to sin; and although he himself did not sin, he nevertheless experienced death, which is the punishment of sin. He became human not according to the law of human generation—that is, through the sin of concupiscence—but by the will alone; and, in order to rescue us from our necessities, he freely assumed from the states of human nature described above whatever he willed, without any necessity of this kind.

Therefore, when the reasoning or rule proper to the class of transgressors is brought forward as an argument outside that class, it proves nothing. Thus, according to the state that would have been the reward of the obedient, he was free from every sin; according to the state that is the punishment of the disobedient, he rightly endured many sufferings even unto death; and according to the state in which Adam was before sin, when he satisfied the need described above with the fruits of Paradise, he performed the functions of a human body by power, not by necessity.

This very need existed in him before the resurrection. After the resurrection, however, the condition of that human body, in accordance with the human uses which he himself had willed it to possess, became such that it was changed as Adam’s body could have been changed apart from the bond of transgression. In him was fulfilled what the Lord Jesus Christ himself taught us not merely to proclaim with the outward sound of words, but also to desire in the prayers of our inmost affection: that his will be done on earth—that is, in human beings—as it is in heaven—that is, in angels; that his kingdom may come, in which the spirit rules the flesh in all things; and that it may free us from every evil of this world.

For this is what Christ himself, as it were, taught us to desire, and we should act accordingly, as he taught us. All these things are implored by that most blessed transformation of the human race—not, indeed, of everyone, but of those who faithfully believe this with right faith. That is, it is they themselves who, in being transformed, implore all these things.

These are the matters, O John, which I have written to be sent to you concerning the credibility of my faith—that is, concerning the things which I believe ought rightly to be believed. In this matter.] In effect: Since I have sent these things to you, I wish you to correct anything you may discover that I have said otherwise than is fitting. For if anything has been wrongly—that is, perversely—said by me, I am not so enamored of myself as to insist on placing before every better judgment what I once poured forth without reason; nor ought I to contend for it and defend it as though it were mine.

For if nothing good comes from us—that is, if there is no good thing of which we are the authors, as indeed there is not—there is nothing in our opinions which we ought to love as ours. But if all good things come from him—that is, from him alone, who alone is good, not through an accidentally acquired goodness but through the truth of his essence—then that should rather be believed good which unchangeable Goodness, namely God, who is unchangeably good and the cause of all good things, prescribes by the unchangeable purpose of his will.

# APPENDIX

[Note: [Col. 1411C] This little work bears, in French, the title: *History of Boethius, Roman Senator, with an Analysis of All His Works, Notes, and Historical and Theological Dissertations, Divided into Two Parts*. [Col. 1412C]]

## TO THE WORKS OF BOETHIUS

Containing the history of Boethius and an analysis of his works, together with notes and historical and theological dissertations, composed in French by Gervais, priest of Tours.

[Col. 1411]

## [LIFE OF BOETHIUS]

### DEDICATORY EPISTLE

#### TO HIS ROYAL HIGHNESS MONSEIGNEUR THE DUKE OF ORLÉANS, GRANDSON OF FRANCE, REGENT OF THE KINGDOM

My Lord,

The late king had permitted me to place his august name at the head of this *History*. Two months ago, when the Epistle included in it was read to him, he approved it and received it graciously; but since its printing was completed only at the time of his death, I am deprived of the honor of offering it to His Majesty.

I would believe, my Lord, that I was failing in what I owe to the memory of this great prince if, in giving the work to the public, I suppressed this final mark of my zeal; and I would commit a kind of theft against the royal family if I did not return to it what so legitimately belongs to it.

[Col. 1413] Since the work was dedicated to Louis the Great, to whom should it return except to the depositary of his sovereign authority? To whom could the history of Boethius be presented more justly than to a prince who bears such marked similarities to this illustrious Roman?

Boethius possessed all the brilliance, solidity, and breadth of mind that France admires in Your Royal Highness. He loved the sciences and the fine arts; he was an enemy of oppression and injustice; he devoted all his power to calming the troubles that had arisen in the Church and to making his country happy and flourishing.

France, my Lord, flatters itself that under your administration it will enjoy all the blessings that constitute the glory of states and the happiness of peoples. Justice and peace follow your steps: they are the soul of your counsels and the rule of your decisions. Everything promises us equal tranquility at home and abroad. The foreigner who might envy our happiness will fear disturbing it. Witness to your intrepidity in battle, he has more than once yielded before your valor; and all Europe knows that you have been victorious everywhere whenever you have been permitted to fight.

Continue, great prince! All our hearts belong to you; all our wishes are for you. The offspring of the august line of Louis the Great is the precious pledge of our confidence and our love.

This young monarch, raised under your eyes, will learn from your example all that he must know to make his reign as glorious for His Majesty as your administration is about to make it beneficial to his subjects.

I remain, with complete submission and the deepest respect,

My Lord,

Your Royal Highness’s

Most humble and obedient servant,

GERVAISE, provost of Suèvre in the church of Saint-Martin of Tours.

### PREFACE

[Col. 1413A] Since Boethius lived in an age when letters were not cultivated, few writers recorded his actions; nor was it easy to penetrate the obscurity of a time so distant from our own and gather enough facts to form an historical account. Nevertheless, this has been attempted, and through careful and persistent inquiry what is now presented to the public has been found.

First, the works of this great man were examined exactly, and from them most of the circumstances of his life—at least the most important—were drawn. Next came the works of Cassiodorus, secretary to Theodoric, and of Ennodius, bishop of Pavia, both of whom had close relations with Boethius; the Greek and Latin historians who were his contemporaries or lived nearest to his age—Jornandes and Procopius; the miscellaneous history of Paul the Deacon; the anonymous history of M. de Valois; the general and particular councils; the letters of the popes; and the ancient compilers of Boethius’s works, who at different times gave us summaries of his life drawn from manuscripts appended to the beginning or end of his works.

To the search for ancient monuments has been added that for modern ones: Baronius, Bollandus, his continuators Father Sirmond and Father Pagi, M. de Tillemont, M. Fleury, M. Baillet, M. Dupin, and several others. From all the collections made by these writers, this historical account has been formed, with nothing added except the reflections and explanations that were necessary.

It is therefore offered to the public as a certain and authentic history drawn from contemporary and original authors, at least with regard to the most considerable events. We do not possess the same certainty concerning some less important circumstances that we have nevertheless thought it necessary not to omit, because they shed considerable light on the history and contribute greatly to its ornament. But the love of truth and the respect due to it oblige us to warn the reader that these circumstances have appeared to rest more on probability than on certain monuments, from which the authors who first inserted them into the history of Boethius derived them.

For example, it has been said, on the authority of Cardinal Baronius, that Boethius spent eighteen consecutive years at Athens training himself in the sciences. Yet, as proof of this fact, Baronius cites only the *Treatise on the Discipline of Schoolboys*, which he says was by Boethius but which is rejected as a spurious work wholly unworthy of him. Since it is nevertheless certain that Boethius spent a considerable time at Athens, we have thought it possible to defer to Baronius’s authority and determine from it the number of years he remained there. The determination is not far from probability, and this learned cardinal may have possessed information that we no longer have, since he very often cites treatises and historians that he apparently had in his hands but which have escaped us or have not yet been printed. Some relatively unimportant circumstances may therefore occur in this work for which one should not hold us responsible; but they are neither numerous nor significant enough to cast the slightest doubt on the substance of the history.

The same love of truth has obliged the author to examine several treatises and a number of events reported by writers suspected of partiality with less fidelity and accuracy than they should have shown. The reader who approaches the matter without prejudice will readily judge for himself and recognize without difficulty on which side the truth lies.

This work is divided into two parts. The first [Col. 1415A] contains the life of Boethius and is divided into three books. The first leads the reader from Boethius’s birth to his consulship. The second recounts what occurred from his consulship until he was made prefect of the praetorium, shortly before his disgrace. The third presents all the circumstances of that disgrace and of his death, what followed it, and the honors paid to him at different times thereafter.

The second part is an abridgment of the Philosophy, Mathematics, Morals, and Theology extracted from Boethius’s works. Explanations and several theological and historical dissertations concerning various events belonging to his history have been added; these could not have been given a place in the first [Col. 1415B] part without interrupting the continuity of the narrative for the reader.

Two short treatises by Boethius have nevertheless been analyzed in the first part, because it was thought that the chronological order of his life and works required their placement there, and because this could be done without diverting the reader from the attention owed to the principal subject.

All the other treatises are deferred to the second part; and it may be said that the analyses of Boethius’s theological and moral treatises provided there may serve in place of the translation that might otherwise have been made of them.

It was also thought necessary to anticipate and answer two objections that the reader might raise: first, that the digressions are too frequent and the episodes too long; second, that since the public in France is not accustomed to revering Boethius as a saint or martyr, it will always believe that the author gives him those titles merely to make his history more readily accepted.

To the first objection we answer that, since most of the events in Boethius’s life have not come down to us with all their circumstances, it was necessary to supplement them with circumstances from the history of his time that are related to them and could help bring them into clearer light. If attention is paid to this, they will appear less like digressions than essential parts of the history.

As for the episodes, it is admitted that they are somewhat [Col. 1415D] long; but there are only two or three of them. They flow naturally from the substance of the subject as from their source, and the importance of their matter amply compensates for their length. Indeed, they could not have been omitted without doing Boethius an injustice. [Col. 1416A] Could one have refrained from making known the difficulties encountered in the conversion of the Burgundians, and the most important events in that affair, without diminishing the glory that belongs to Boethius, the first instrument God used to bring these peoples to knowledge of the truth? Could one likewise have been silent about the origin, progress, and extinction of the great Eastern schism, which the Church owes to Boethius’s zeal and vigilance, without depriving him of the honor that should result from it? To understand the merit of an action, one must know the difficulties and opposition that had to be overcome, as well as the advantages that followed it.

In these episodes those limits have not been exceeded. Had the history of Boethius been presented stark naked [Col. 1416B] and stripped of these circumstances, it might have pleased a small number of scholars more, but it would have been little appreciated by most people in the world, who read only to occupy a few hours pleasantly.

To the second objection we answer that public prejudice must not prevail against the truth; and that there are several great men honored as saints in the Church whom people do not ordinarily call “saint” when speaking of them. Without straying from our subject, we find an example in Ennodius, whom we have just mentioned. He has been canonized, yet he is not ordinarily called Saint Ennodius. There are several other examples, which would take too long to report.

The reader should therefore suspend his judgment, at least until the end of the first part, where he will find the titles of saint and martyr sufficiently established as applied to Boethius. To remove any remaining scruple, we shall add to the proofs in the first part that Cardinal Baronius—who could not have been unaware of the saints whom the Church honors with public worship in Italy—compares Boethius in his *Ecclesiastical Annals* with Saint Denis the Areopagite in doctrine, holiness, and the manner of his martyrdom.

After reporting these words from a historian of Boethius’s life, Martianus Rota—“After his death, he received divine honors from our people”—this pious and learned cardinal adds, under the year 526: “Namely, those which we are accustomed to render to holy martyrs”; because Boethius had always defended the Catholic faith with invincible courage against the perfidy of the Arians and had lost his life in its defense.

# HISTORY OF BOETHIUS

[Col. 1415]

## FIRST PART

### BOOK ONE

[Col. 1415D] Until now, people have formed an idea of Boethius only from the qualities that could make him esteemed in the eyes of the world, without giving sufficient attention to those that distinguished him infinitely more before God.

In the life of this incomparable man, everything combines to form a Christian hero: illustrious birth, [Col. 1416D] (2) great alliances, superior genius, sublime knowledge, profound learning, consummate prudence, and perfect integrity in the most brilliant and difficult offices. A wise magistrate; an enlightened, provident, and faithful minister; protector of the laws; father of the people; defender of the oppressed; guardian of his country; philosopher, theologian, orator, and poet; a humble Christian amid splendor; solitary amid the tumult of the world and the court; enemy of falsehood and error; support of the Church; a model of firmness and patience in the greatest adversities; finally, a generous martyr of Jesus Christ: such was Boethius, known in antiquity by the names Anicius Manlius Torquatus Severinus Boetius.

He was born in Rome in the year of Our Lord 470. [Note: [Col. 1417D] Martianus Rota was mistaken when he said that Boethius was born a few years after the capture of Rome by Alaric. Since this event, by the agreement of all historians, occurred in the year 409 of Jesus Christ, Boethius, on that supposition, would have lived nearly one hundred and twenty years. Moreover, it is certain that he was no more than fifty-five years old at most when Theodoric had him put to death in 525. See the dissertation on the year of his death in the second part.]

The Western Empire was then (3) in a deplorable condition. The barbarians had poured into its finest provinces and divided them among themselves after overthrowing the oldest monuments of Roman power; everywhere they had left traces of their avarice and cruelty. The Huns and Vandals had begun, the Cimbri and Alans continued; finally, the Herules, Visigoths, and Goths brought its misfortunes to their culmination by making themselves masters of Rome and all Italy.

It is impossible to imagine what change these barbarian incursions produced among the Romans. Not only did religion suffer, but their morals were altered by them. With everyone occupied by his calamities and groaning in slavery, the fine arts were neglected, justice oppressed, and emulation at the bar ceased; little by little Rome became barbarian.

Arianism, which the Goths professed and which had been almost extinct (4) in Italy, regained new strength there; and since the religion of the prince is ordinarily the most widely followed, people no longer felt as much horror of heresy. If they did not openly embrace it, considerations of interest and policy nevertheless caused them continually to favor it.

God caused Boethius to be born at this time and gave him to his Church to be one of its firmest supports.

From childhood, his promising dispositions for the sciences and for virtue were recognized. As he advanced in age, the precious gifts of nature and grace unfolded. Flavius Boethius, his father, omitted nothing that could cause them to grow in his son. Having himself passed through the first offices of the republic and finding himself endowed with riches, he had nothing left to desire except to leave a worthy heir to his possessions and virtues.

This desire overcame the paternal tenderness that urged him to keep his son near him. But seeing clearly that Rome, in the condition to which it had been reduced, was no longer a suitable place for his education, he consulted Pope Simplicius and sent him to Athens, although he was still only ten years old.

(5) Soon the breadth and elevation of his mind became apparent; his liveliness and penetration were astonishing. A happy imagination, suited to grasping the most abstract matters, was accompanied by admirable grace and ease of expression in Greek and Latin. This superior genius was especially noticeable in his studies of philosophy and mathematics.

The inner beauty of his soul became still more evident. That zeal for justice of which he later gave such brilliant proofs already distinguished him among young men of his age. He always supported the cause of the innocent, praised virtue, and condemned vice. Little affected by insults directed only at himself, he showed resentment only toward those he saw committed against God or his neighbor.

Although Athens had always been the school of wisdom and the dwelling place of the fine arts, Boethius found it greatly fallen from its former reputation. After a year or two, he developed such a profound distaste for it that he would have left had he followed his inclination. Respect for his father kept him there; he (6) forced himself to remain, and, moving from one science to another, eighteen years passed without the pleasures or all the advantages he might have expected in Rome being able to call him back.

This long course of study may surprise, but if it is compared with the progress he made in every science, it will still not appear proportionate; for he learned by rules and principles all those disciplines that can be acquired only through continual reflection and long practice (Cassiodorus, book I, letter 45). He gathered into himself everything that had been most admired in all the teachers of Greece.

He was not accumulating all these treasures for himself alone; he was gathering them to enrich Rome and all the nations that spoke her language. Through elegant and faithful translations, he made available to them the finest works of the Greeks: the music of Pythagoras, the astronomy of Ptolemy, the arithmetic of Nicomachus, the geometry of Euclid, the theology of Plato, the logic of Aristotle, and the mechanics of Archimedes. In the judgment of Theodoric and Cassiodorus (Theodoric, apud Cassiodorus, book I, letter 45), these translations were so perfect that they surpassed the originals and would have been preferred (7) [Col. 1418C] by their authors themselves, had those authors known Latin as they knew Greek. He added several treatises of his own composition on these various subjects, and what remains of them fully justifies the testimony of Theodoric and Cassiodorus.

These same works further prove that he was a good poet, an excellent orator, a subtle philosopher, and a profound theologian. His style is pure and elevated, far above the barbarism of his age. Scaliger (*Hypercriticus*, book VI) compares his prose with Cicero’s and his verse with Virgil’s. Some scholars nevertheless maintain that he excels more in poetry than in prose. Yet if in poetry he commands admiration through the elevation of his mind and the richness of his striking and surprising thoughts, in prose he persuades with extraordinary gentleness.

Hence a skillful critic of the last century, Antonius Sabellicus (*Aenead.*, 8, book II), was unable to decide whether Boethius had been the last author to speak the Latin language in all its purity or the first of those who worked to restore its former beauty.

[Col. 1418D] Boethius’s reputation flew from Athens to Rome, where people soon learned how brilliantly he shone among the learned. (8) It was a great consolation to his family when it lost Flavius Boethius: too early a death had taken him away as early as 490, shortly after his last consulship, which ended in 487.

There was no position in the city that did not promise itself great advantages from his return. The Senate regarded him as a man destined to be its chief ornament; the lesser magistrates as aid sent from heaven to maintain justice [Col. 1419A] and the laws; men of letters as a light destined to restore their original brilliance to the sciences and arts; and the Church and all good people as a sure protector.

Yet, despite his initial distaste for Athens and the eagerness of his fellow citizens, his love of letters and his desire to perfect the knowledge he had acquired there kept him in Athens for several more years.

Ever since the great Constantine, after founding Constantinople, had transferred the seat of the empire there, one might have said that all Rome’s glory had followed him. Rome soon lost what distinguished it from the other cities of the world. Like lands too far removed (9) from the sun to be warmed by it, receiving the influence of its rays only rarely, and where nature never brings her fruits to happy maturity, everything there languished.

Those who governed Rome in the emperors’ name, instead of maintaining justice and peace there, ruled it as tyrants. Hence arose those seditions and [Col. 1419B] civil wars in which it was more than once stained with the blood of its citizens. Disorder was sustained by jealousy among the great families, each wishing to rise above the others; offices were no longer assigned on merit, nor were they even granted through favor: arms decided everything.

Odoacer, king of the Thuringians, accompanied by the Heruli and other barbarian nations that had emerged from the depths of Pannonia, had seized Italy. After dethroning the young emperor Romulus [Note: [Col. 1419D] He is better known in history by the name Augustulus.], he had established the seat of his dominion at Ravenna (Mez. on Child.). Zeno, emperor of the East, watched him there with grief (Daniel, ibid.), but was not in a position to drive him out. He was forced to call upon the power (10) of the Ostrogoths, whom he had already employed very successfully against other barbarians who were ravaging the provinces of the empire (Procopius, final book of *The Gothic War*). Theodoric, their king, had also contributed greatly to his restoration to the imperial throne, through the timely assistance he had given him against the unfortunate Basiliscus. Wishing to reward his services, but also placing rather too much confidence in his loyalty, Zeno sent him into Italy to reduce Odoacer, and secured its possession for him, so that he might live there under his obedience and govern it in his name (Jordanes, *On the Gothic Deeds*, 86 and following).

Theodoric left Thrace, followed by his entire nation. He defeated an army of Gepids who disputed his passage at Sirmium, entered Italy through the Julian Alps, won three battles against Odoacer, who had come to meet him with a formidable army, and forced him to withdraw into Ravenna, where he besieged him. The siege lasted three years; and although the city was then considered one of the strongest in the world, Odoacer was finally compelled to surrender at the victor’s discretion. Yet a few days later Theodoric killed him with his own hand at a banquet, on the pretext of forestalling a plan he had formed against [Col. 1419D] his person.

(11) Thus having become master of Italy, he nevertheless did not assume the title of king, out of consideration for Zeno, who, after adopting him as his son, had honored him with the rank of patrician, made him ordinary consul, bestowed upon him the honors of a triumph, and erected an equestrian statue of him in the Palace Square at Constantinople.

So many benefits moved Theodoric to show his gratitude toward him. He was naturally inclined to do so; for, having been carefully brought up from the age of eight at the emperors’ court, nothing of his former origin remained to him except the name of barbarian, and there he had acquired all the sentiments of a great [Col. 1420A] prince. But as soon as he learned of Zeno’s death, he had himself proclaimed king of Italy without seeking the consent of Anastasius, who had just succeeded him (Procopius, *The Gothic War*, book I, chapter 1).

Rome alone still stood firm, acknowledging no master other than the emperor of the East. It could have held out against Theodoric’s efforts if the hatreds and divisions prevailing among its citizens had not hastened its ruin. Some factions appealed to the conqueror and called him to their aid. The ecclesiastics were the (12) first to set so pernicious an example.

Symmachus and Laurentius, deacons of the Church of Rome, disputed the chair of Saint Peter after Anastasius’s death (Baronius, under the year 498). Each had powerful factions among the clergy and in the Senate. Symmachus had first been elected by a plurality of votes, but Laurentius refused to yield to him. The whole city became divided on this account; and, seeing no prospect [Col. 1420B] of resolving the dispute, the two parties agreed to refer its decision to Theodoric. Thus, to the shame of the Church, a heretical prince was seen entering into the most important affairs of religion and becoming judge of those whom Jesus Christ had established as the oracles of the world.

Theodoric decided in favor of Symmachus, and the schism ended. But the prince knew perfectly well how to profit from the Romans’ misguided action. It persuaded him that they did not feel as much aversion toward him as he had thought, and that Rome was not so far from recognizing him as sovereign. He made further attempts; they succeeded; and all the city’s corporate bodies, by common (13) consent, as though they had recognized themselves as unworthy of liberty, surrendered themselves to a shameful slavery.

Boethius returned from Athens at this juncture. Rome thought it saw the father revived in the son. It was not mistaken, since he even surpassed him, and to his father’s rare [Col. 1420C] qualities he added the deepest learning and the most eminent holiness.

Festus and Symmachus, heads of the Senate and the foremost men of the city, were struck by the splendor of so many virtues. They had attended to his affairs since his father’s death, and wished to make him their friend (Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, book II). The choice made by these two great men is itself sufficient praise of Boethius; for they were the admiration of their age, and no one could see them without being moved to imitate them. In their persons, Ennodius has traced the image of the most accomplished magistrate. Festus had been consul, and since the year 472 had stood at the head of the Senate and of the republic’s greatest affairs (Ennodius, *Panegyric*, *Didascalia*). As for Symmachus, known in history as Quintus Aurelius Memmius Symmachus, he had been ordinary consul without a colleague in (14) 485, under Odoacer. He was a man of ardent zeal for the glory of God and immense charity toward his neighbor (Cassiodorus, *Chronicle*). He distributed his possessions among the poor without measure; he was generous toward pilgrims and strangers; and, content with the inner testimony of his conscience, he thought only of pleasing God, never seeking anything for himself. Yet the more his humility led him to disregard worldly glory, the more it seems that God wished to raise him up through the praises of the holy Fathers.

On his return from Athens, Boethius was made patrician (Ennodius, book VIII, letter 1). Descended from the Manlii and the Anicii, he could trace his nobility back to the foundation of Rome. His father, Flavius Boethius, as has been said, had been consul in 487. His mother, of the house of the Severini [Note: [Col. 1419D] It is believed that the surname *Severinus*, added to [Col. 1420D] Boethius’s name, was his mother’s family name, because the Romans often joined the mother’s name to the father’s.], was also of consular descent (Synod of Rome, under the year 487; Onuphrius, *On the Fasti*).

[Col. 1421A] Boethius, his grandfather, had held the office of praetorian prefect with great distinction under Valentinian III (Cassiodorus, *Chronicle*). Having taken part in the campaigns (15) and victories of the general Aetius, he perished with him, and the majesty of the Western Empire seemed to be buried beneath their ruin. It would therefore have been an insult to Boethius to deny him this honor; but another was added to it, one that openly acknowledged his merit and the esteem in which he was held. Although he was not yet thirty, he was admitted to the Senate and entrusted with the most important affairs.

Yet ambition never led him to seek advancement to high office. He calls God to witness (Boethius, book I, *Consolation*) that his modesty was violated when he was compelled, at so early an age, to accept offices that were often refused to the oldest senators, who eagerly sought them. Only concern for the public good, and fear of leaving them to citizens capable of abusing them, could induce him to accept them despite all the dangers [Col. 1421B] he foresaw in them (Boethius, book II, *Consolation*).

The Senate, as well as the family of Boethius, had an interest in preserving a bloodline so noble and so dear to the republic. It therefore joined with the family in urging him, through their common entreaties, to establish a household. He (16) preferred the alliance of Festus to all those proposed to him.

Festus had a daughter named Elpis, who united every charm of mind with bodily beauty. Rome regarded her as a learned woman; she loved poetry, and the hymns that the Church still sings on the feast of Saint Peter and Saint Paul are attributed to her (Boethius, book II, *Consolation*). Piety gave new brilliance to her merit; indeed, it was almost hereditary in her family, for Elpis’s sister was the mother of Saint Placid, one of the first disciples of the great Saint Benedict. Boethius therefore married Elpis as his first wife, but the outcome of this much-desired marriage was unhappy. A few years later [Col. 1421C] she died at Pavia without leaving any offspring.

She was universally mourned. The most celebrated poets of Italy honored her memory, and Boethius, philosophical though he was, needed considerable time to console himself. History does not record the affairs that had called him to Pavia, but the epitaph engraved on Elpis’s tomb, which has survived to our own time, tells us that she was (17) a native of Sicily, and that the love she bore her husband had separated her from her homeland to follow him there.

L. Giraldus gave us the first three verses of this epitaph. Monsieur Pithou, in his *Ancient Poems*, gave us four, without following the order in which they had been composed. But it was later found in its entirety in very ancient manuscripts of Boethius’s works, and it was not thought that these verses were unworthy of being attributed to him. If they are not by him, they are at least from his time. Here they are:

[Col. 1421D]

*Elpes dicta fui Siculae regionis alumna,*  
*Quam procul a patria conjugis egit amor,*  
*Quo sine moesta dies, nox anxia, flebilis hora;*  
*Nec solum caro, sed spiritus unus erat.*

*Lux mea non clausa est, tali remanente marito,*  
*Majorique animae parte superstes ero.*

I was called Elpis, a daughter of the Sicilian land;  
The love of my husband drove me far from my homeland.  
Without him, the day is sorrowful, the night anxious, the hour tearful;  
For we were one not only in body, but in spirit.

My light has not been extinguished, since such a husband remains;  
I shall survive as the greater part of his soul.

(18)

*Porticibus sacris jam nunc peregrina quiesco,*  
*Judicis aeterni testificata thronum.*  
*Neu qua manus bustum violet, nisi forte jugalis*  
*Haec iterum cupiat jungere membra suis;*  
*Ut thalami tumulique comes nec morte revellar,*  
*Et socios vitae nectat uterque cinis.*

Now, a stranger, I rest in the sacred porticoes,  
Having borne witness to the throne of the eternal Judge.  
Let no hand profane this tomb, unless perhaps my husband  
Should wish once more to join these limbs with his,  
So that I may be the companion of his chamber and his tomb,  
And death itself may unite the ashes of those who shared life.

The same reasons of state and the same family interests that had led him into this first alliance led him into a second. The patrician Symmachus, that famous Roman senator of whom we have just spoken, had three daughters, all perfect imitators of his virtues.

Galla, the eldest of the three, whom Saint Gregory the Great praised in the fourth book of his *Dialogues*, had married young. But after losing her husband in the first year of her marriage, she generously renounced the world and all the advantages of a brilliant fortune, wishing to please God alone in the secret of a solitude she had created for herself (19) near the Vatican basilica. The reading of the holy books and prayer sustained by fasting were interrupted there only by the practice of the most heroic charity.

So secluded and penitential a life produced an extraordinary effect on her body. In addition to the pallor and thinness, faithful companions of Christian penance, her blood, still boiling in the vigor of early youth, became so heated that her cheeks and chin soon became completely covered with a beard. She became unrecognizable; perhaps God permitted this in order to strengthen her in the resolution she had taken to divorce herself from the world forever (Baronius, [Col. 1422B] under the year 504).

Saint Fulgentius, of whom we shall have occasion to speak later, had a particular esteem for her. From the exile to which he had been banished by the Vandals, who had seized Africa, he wrote to her several times to console her and instruct her in the duties of a Christian widow. Galla nobly completed her course, and after several years of so penitential a life went to be reunited with Jesus Christ (20). The Church honors her memory with public worship on October 5.

The second was called Proba. From her youth she had consecrated herself to God and embraced celibacy. The same Saint Fulgentius, who was closely bound in friendship with the entire family of Symmachus, addressed to her two excellent treatises that we still possess: the first entitled *On Virginity and Humility*, the second *On Prayer*. The Church honors her, together with her sister, as a saint.

[Col. 1422C] Rusticiana, the youngest of the three, still remained in the world. She was destined to be Boethius’s wife, but she had difficulty resolving to marry because she attributed the misfortune that had befallen her sister Galla to marriage and feared that she might suffer the same fate. She was made to understand that, since her constitution differed from her sister’s, she need not fear a similar disgrace. Thus at last she yielded to her father’s entreaties and gave way to the attractions and advantages she found in an alliance with Boethius.

She was as holy as she was happy. Each vied with the other in serving (21) God with greater fidelity and fervor, in being more generous toward the poor, and in providing greater examples of virtue. God blessed them and gave them several children who upheld the dignity of their family with honor. Rusticiana became the admiration of Rome, and her virtue made her respected by Theodoric, Totila, and the other tyrants who successively oppressed [Col. 1422D] Italy.

Nothing would have been lacking from Boethius’s happiness had he been less sensitive to the republic’s misfortunes. The condition to which it had been reduced had inflicted a wound on his heart all the more difficult to heal because he was obliged to conceal it, since the evil was without remedy. The fatal moment when Rome was to fall into slavery had arrived. Theodoric, assured of a powerful faction, had chosen the day on which to enter it as though in triumph. Considering the conquest of Ravenna and the rest of Italy as of little importance so long as Rome remained unsubjugated, he left Ravenna toward the end of the year 500 (Procopius, *The Gothic War*, as above; Cassiodorus, *Chronicle*). To risk nothing in an undertaking of such importance, he sent part of his troops ahead of him. They seized (22) all the approaches, and a few days later he himself appeared, followed by his nobles and the leading men of his [Col. 1423A] nation, escorted by a numerous, nimble, and well-mounted cavalry.

The Romans were no longer in a position to oppose such forces; and, even if they had possessed the power, their minds were divided. Most of them, disgusted with the weak and languishing government of the emperors of Constantinople, desired Theodoric’s arrival. The wisdom and moderation he had displayed since being proclaimed king of Italy led them to hope for a happier reign. They therefore decided to receive him with every mark of honor. The young men were ordered to take up arms as for a day of triumph. The Senate went a long way out to meet him (Procopius, ibid.). Boethius, as the most eloquent of the senators, spoke on their behalf; and he did so with such dignity that he pleased Theodoric, the Goths, and the Romans alike (Baillet, *Life of Boethius*).

The prince was led to the Capitol amid the sound of fanfares and trumpets and the acclamations of the people. There Boethius once again delivered in his presence [Col. 1423B] that excellent (23) panegyric which caused him to be admired by both nations. He spoke with such wisdom and tact that, without offending the prince, he maintained the Senate’s dignity; and, while giving Theodoric the just praises he deserved without descending into base flattery, he skillfully exalted the freedom of his country and the ancient majesty of Rome at the very moment when nothing of them remained but their shadow and appearance.

On leaving the Capitol, Theodoric entered the Senate. There, with great skill, he bestowed on each senator the praise appropriate to him; he applauded the body’s general zeal for justice; assured it of his protection; promised under oath to preserve all Rome’s ancient privileges and to govern it as a good prince—or rather, as the father of his country. At the same time, he made great distributions to the people and assigned the city considerable revenues for the maintenance of its walls and public buildings. When he learned that scarcity there [Col. 1423C] was extreme, he had such a quantity of grain purchased from every direction that the city immediately found itself in abundance (Cassiodorus, *Chronicle*).

(24) However splendid this triumph was, something was lacking from its glory. It was an ancient custom among the Romans (Martianus Rota, *Life of Boethius*) to give the people and the entire army a magnificent feast when the honors of conquerors and emperors were decreed. They called this a *triumphale convivium*—a “triumphal banquet.” Whether Theodoric had not been informed of this custom, or whether, on entering Rome, he deliberately refrained out of moderation from taking the title of conqueror, he had given no order to entertain either the people or his troops. Boethius noticed this; and, following the inclination of his generous heart, without considering that the expense exceeded the means of a private individual, however wealthy he might be, he immediately had tables set up everywhere, where sumptuousness and abundance, [Col. 1423D] combined with the delicacy of the dishes, produced a delightful surprise. Rome admired the foresight and magnificence of its magistrate, but good men admired his modesty even more. In order to leave all the glory to the Senate, as though he had had no part in the undertaking, he persuaded the ordinary consuls to preside over it [Col. 1424A], contenting himself with following them (25) wherever his presence was necessary.

Theodoric realized that Boethius was the person to whom this was owed. Since he possessed great penetration of mind, he immediately recognized the vast extent of his genius. At that moment he resolved to win him over. Shortly afterward he gave him a place on his council and made him master of the palace and of the offices [Note: [Col. 1423D] Theodoric, having become king of Italy, changed almost nothing in the state’s external administration. He preserved the same dignities and titles that he found established by the emperors. Boethius held the office of master of the offices for several years, but it is certain that he ceased to exercise it several years before his death, for in very ancient manuscripts and in several addresses he is designated *Exmagist. Off.*, that is, former master of the offices. He perhaps ceased to hold it when he was appointed consul, because the master of the offices, being the judge of all the king’s officials and of the palace staff and the members of the court’s retinue, could not be absent from them. He also had oversight of the superintendents assigned to the manufacture of weapons, received complaints coming from all the provinces, and reported on them to the king.
