The obligation imposed on Boethius by his office to render justice to those who were oppressed earned him the enmity of several powerful persons, as will be seen later.]. These (26) two offices were among the most important at court; they conferred the greatest influence and authority in the state, as well as the greatest access to the prince. Thus Boethius found his elevation amid the deepest abasement of his country.

God, whose infinite wisdom orders all events for his glory and for the good of his chosen ones, made beneficial use of Theodoric’s triumphal entry into Rome to lead two men, by two different paths, to the highest sanctity (Baronius, under the year 500): Boethius, by placing him in the state’s highest offices so as to make him the support of truth and religion; and Fulgentius, by making him one of the most brilliant lights of his Church, inspiring him with a generous contempt for the world (Life of Fulgentius).

Gordian, his grandfather, one of the foremost senators of Carthage and a member of one of Africa’s oldest houses, had been driven from his homeland by the Vandals after being stripped of his possessions. But Fulgentius, having risen above the (27) misfortunes of his ancestors, flattered himself that he would soon restore it to its former splendor. At the age of twenty-two he already saw himself superintendent of the province of Byzacena and chief collector of the estates of Gombaud, Huneric’s successor as king of the Vandals. Amid his offices, he did not lose the pious sentiments that his mother, Mariana, had carefully engraved in his heart from his earliest youth. The severity he was sometimes unable to avoid using in exacting tribute [Col. 1424C] did not always agree with the goodness and gentleness of his disposition; and the difficulty he found in reconciling the maxims of the Gospel with those of the world, and the humility of Jesus Christ with the greatness of the age, had begun to make him uneasy and somewhat disgusted with his profession. His private affairs brought him to Rome at the time when Theodoric was making his entry. He saw him in all the splendor of royal majesty. As a spectator of the almost divine honors paid to him, and indignant at the Romans’ softness and luxury and at the baseness with which (28) they crawled before a man, he could not help lamenting it in the depths of his heart. Comparing Rome with itself—what it then was with what it had once been—he uttered profound sighs and said to himself what a wise Roman had said to himself long before on an almost similar occasion:

> This is no longer that Rome, so holy and so pure;  
> Her chaste desires outrage nature;  
> And that harsh virtue, so dear to our ancestors,  
> So fertile in heroes, is a monster in her eyes.  
> (Lucan, book I.)

Such were Fulgentius’s thoughts at that moment, if these were not his actual words. Finally, [Col. 1425A] considering the instability of human affairs and how short the distance is between the most sublime virtue and the excess of vice, and seeing that in less than a century this unfortunate city—which within its walls had counted almost as many saints and martyrs as it had inhabitants—had become the dwelling place of worshipers of fortune, he resolved to renounce the world and give himself wholly to God. He (29) hastened to visit the tombs of the apostles and martyrs and immediately afterward returned to Africa, where he carried out the plan he had formed.

Meanwhile Boethius advanced daily in Theodoric’s favor. His wisdom in council, his penetration in affairs, his uprightness—which did not permit him to conceal evil, much less flatter the prince’s passions—and his disinterestedness, which always moved him toward the public good without any thought of himself, were the chains that bound Theodoric to him so closely.

[Col. 1425B] Because this prince’s education had been very fortunate, although he was a Goth and an Arian, he nevertheless had a love of glory. He even possessed judgment sufficiently sound and solid to esteem virtue wherever he found it. He was captivated by Boethius’s virtue and soon perceived the difference between the Romans and the Goths. Little accustomed to finding in his ministers the fidelity, skill, and ability he found in Boethius, he congratulated himself on his choice and enjoyed with (30) pleasure the fruits of this wise minister’s labors and the charm of his conversation.

Although Boethius was wholly occupied with public affairs, he still found time for study. He managed it so well that, without neglecting the duties of his office, whose extent was infinite; without being absent from the council, which met every day and which the prince attended; because he had no wasted moments, he still had as much time for his study as a private man, [Col. 1425C] removed from all worldly affairs, would have had (Sidonius Apollinaris, *Life of Theodoric*, *Agricola*). One would have said that he had discovered the secret of multiplying himself, so as to be at once entirely devoted to himself, entirely devoted to his prince, entirely devoted to the state, entirely devoted to the public, entirely devoted to God in the exercises of piety, and entirely devoted to his neighbor in the works of charity.

He could not do this without taking much from his rest and eliminating every amusement. He therefore used to say that the present life was not the time for such things (Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*), and that a Christian philosopher ought to have no other recreation than faithfully fulfilling all his duties and, during his moments of (31) rest, conversing with divine wisdom, listening to it or questioning it. It was in his study or library [Note: [Col. 1425D] Boethius’s library was magnificently decorated, according to the taste of that age. The paneling consisted of compartments of ivory, mirrors, or thick glass representing various figures, some enlarging and others diminishing objects. The walls were faced with marble, porphyry, and other precious stones, among which those brought from Egypt—some kind of black marble as lustrous as glass (Seneca; Pliny, book I, *Natural History*)—were particularly distinguished. The ancients called these stones *obsidiana*, after the name of Obsidianus, who first brought them to Rome (Horace, *Odes*, book II).] that he enjoyed these gentle pleasures of the mind. Wisdom had established her throne there, as he himself says, from which she instructed him in nature’s most hidden secrets [Col. 1425D] and in all that a mortal is capable of knowing about divinity. There she taught him to regulate his conduct and to measure the whole course of his life according to the model of those celestial spirits who have the advantage of drawing truth from its source (Boethius, book I, *Consolation*, prose 4).

He was never seen at the Circus, never at the Theater, never at the baths (32), nor at any of those pleasure gatherings so frequent in Rome. With admirable skill, without appearing ill-tempered, he even found a way to avoid the banquets that the great occasionally held and to which he was invited. Though sumptuous and magnificent when necessity required it, his household table was among the most frugal. Everything that might soften courage or blunt the edge of the mind was banished from it. Thus always ready to pass from the table to contemplation of nature’s works and to the most serious conversations, he resumed the ordinary thread of affairs without difficulty. Dawn never found him in bed, although he always retired very late and had spent most of the night studying, attending to affairs, or contemplating the courses of the heavenly bodies, the number and magnitude of the stars. In them he perceived marvelous outpourings of God’s beauty, which transported his mind (Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, book, prose 2).

He had already published several volumes, the least of which would have been capable of occupying a man’s entire life, given the difficulty and (33) abstraction of the subjects treated in them. I do not count among these volumes [Col. 1426B] the translations he made, as we have already noted, while still at Athens. Those immense labors were, so to speak, only a sketch of what he was one day to accomplish, and the amusements of his youth (Glareanus, Preface to Boethius’s works). I count only the treatises that came from his own resources and that may be regarded as the genuine productions of his admirable genius. Such are his treatise on Geometry in two books, that on Music in five books, that on Arithmetic in two books, and that on Unity in a single book. He had published them shortly after returning to Rome and had thereby acquired a reputation as one of the finest minds and deepest thinkers of the age. But reflecting that a Christian philosopher ought to use human sciences and natural knowledge only as a step by which to rise toward knowledge of God, he devoted himself wholly to the study of eternal truths and soon appeared as profound [Col. 1426C] a theologian as he was already regarded as a subtle philosopher. He pursued this study not only (34) in order to exercise or edify himself through the examination of these admirable and profound truths, which are the principal object of our faith, but also because the Church at that time needed it.

She had protected herself from the poison of Arianism and had discovered all the devices of those enemies of Jesus Christ’s divinity (Bollandists, under May 27, no. 12). Despite the influence of the error’s adherents, who were always numerous and very powerful at court, the faithful were secure doctrinally, since the doctrine had been sufficiently established by the councils. It had nothing to fear except the cowardly and weak compliance of her children, who might allow themselves to be overcome by the flatteries of the Arian powers.

Pope Celestine I, who had opposed Nestorius’s heresy with all apostolic vigor, had also preserved her from it. But, as it happens all too often that one falls into the opposite extreme when attacking an opinion passionately, many of the faithful in the East were in danger of falling into the error of Eutyches. Here is the occasion.

(35) After Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople, had been condemned at Ephesus, and Saint Cyril’s firmness had triumphed over the malice and stratagems of the heretics, the multitude of the faithful thought only of submitting to the council’s decisions. It was no longer difficult to acknowledge in Jesus Christ [Col. 1427A] two natures subsisting in a single person. It was taught in the Church that divinity and humanity were truly distinct in Jesus Christ. But, fearing that this distinction might be abused to divide Jesus Christ himself and to make two persons out of his two natures, as Nestorius had done, people sought suitable and unambiguous terms to express the union of the natures without fear of falling into division of the person.

They had difficulty finding such terms, and at first adopted several expressions that led people to believe that they were embracing the union and confusion of the two natures in Jesus Christ. Such was the expression used by Saint Cyril of Alexandria and most of the bishops of Egypt (Cyril, *On the Twelve Chapters*): “One incarnate nature” (36) in Jesus Christ. For, as Saint Isidore of Damietta very well observed (Letter to Cyril), by saying “one nature,” one seems to exclude the existence of two and to acknowledge [Col. 1427B] only one.

Indeed, Eutyches, who appeared somewhat later, having paid attention to the expressions used by Catholics on this subject, and seeing moreover that their entire aim had been to condemn the opinions of Nestorius, who had made two persons out of Christ’s two natures, persuaded himself that the divine nature and the human nature were so thoroughly confused in him that the two natures had become only one. At the moment of the Word’s incarnation, he thought, the human nature had become so completely mingled with the divine that it was as if absorbed by it—much as a drop of wine that had fallen into the ocean would be.

One could say to him: “Then Jesus Christ is not both God and man at once?” “He is both,” he would reply. “But how can he be God and man if he is not composed of the nature of man (37) and that of God?” “He is of two natures,” he said, “[Col. 1427C] but he does not subsist in two natures”—much as if two portions of wax were melted and reduced to one: they could no longer be distinguished, and, although composed of two portions, they would subsist only in one. Eutyches’s reasoning went no further; and this was all that could be drawn, after many disputes, from that impudent and obstinate old man, as Saint Leo calls him (*Ep.* 25, *ad Jul. de Cos.*). For he was already more than seventy years old and strongly attached to his opinions.

The disturbances caused by his heresy in the East are well known, as is the number of bishops and monks who took his side under the pretext of defending the honor of Saint Athanasius and Saint Cyril. They falsely attributed this erroneous opinion to those saints, although it was precisely the opinion of the Apollinarians, from which those two holy teachers were very far removed.

Several councils were held on this subject. Theodosius the Younger, otherwise a religious prince and zealous for [Col. 1427D] the glory of God, himself leaned (38) toward Eutyches, together with his entire court. This wicked monk had imposed upon him by a great outward show of piety. Supported by so powerful a party, he found a way to have his doctrine approved by an assembly of bishops commonly known as the Robber Council of Ephesus. It was only under Marcian, Theodosius’s successor, that the [Col. 1428A] Council of Chalcedon—composed of more than six hundred bishops, and the largest ever held—finally caused the truth to triumph by pronouncing anathema upon all who should say that, after the Incarnation, Jesus Christ was not composed of two truly distinct natures subsisting in one person.

But when the acts of the council had been sent to Rome, and Eutyches’s proposition—“Jesus Christ is of two natures, but he does not subsist in two natures”—was found to have been expressly condemned, great difficulties arose, and minds in the West grew almost as heated over this expression as they had in the East over the substance of the matter. Some maintained (39) that the proposition was true; others said that it was false; most claimed that the terms were synonymous and that there was no difference between these two propositions: “to be composed of two natures” and “to subsist in two natures.”

[Col. 1428B] These disputes continued for several years afterward. When Boethius was at Theodoric’s court, the same question was being debated with great vehemence; it was the customary subject of conversation in social gatherings. Everyone took part in it because each believed that his faith was at stake.

Some Eastern bishops then wrote to Pope Symmachus to inform him of the disorders that the Eutychians were causing in their dioceses. “These heretics,” they said, “claim to conceal their errors and evade the decisions of the Council of Chalcedon by new artifices. While admitting that Jesus Christ is of two natures, they deny that he subsists in two natures.” They asked the pope to suggest what answer they ought to make to them. Symmachus (40) assembled the bishops [Note: [Col. 1427D] Public conferences of this kind were often held in Rome. Whenever some new difficulty arose in the Church, or whenever new works on religious subjects were to be made public, they were presented there. Thus Arator’s works were presented to Pope Vigilius in the presbytery, before the Confession of Saint Peter, in the presence of several bishops and the clergy. Part of them was read; and, when the writing was about to be returned to the archives, all the men of letters rose [Col. 1428D] and begged His Holiness to have the entire work read to them. The Church of Saint Peter in Chains was appointed for the assembly. All the distinguished people of Rome attended, and Arator himself read or declaimed his two books before them in seven sessions held on different days, because he was obliged to repeat several passages that had pleased the assembly especially, at its request (Jac. Sirmond, note on Ennodius).] who were then in Rome, the principal members of his clergy, and those senators and people who professed piety and learning, in order to [Col. 1428C] communicate the Eastern bishops’ letter to them and learn their opinions.

Boethius and Symmachus, his father-in-law, (41) always zealous for the Catholic faith, were present at the conference; but they were so far apart from one another that they could neither speak nor even communicate their thoughts by signs or gestures. When the letter had been read, a confused uproar suddenly arose in the assembly. “This is not a question; the difference is obvious,” they said to one another. By this, as Boethius observes, these people made it clear both that they were ignorant and that they had not even understood what the matter concerned (*Boeth.*, *tract. de duab. Nat.*). Boethius grieved in the depths of his heart; and, believing that he ought not to compromise himself in the midst of this tumult, he resolved to remain silent and carefully examine the Eutychians’ proposition.

John, archdeacon of Rome, who succeeded Pope Hormisdas under the name of John I, was not far from Boethius at the conference. Since he was one of Boethius’s friends, [Col. 1428D] Boethius stopped him as he was leaving and asked him to come and see him the following day so that they might examine the matter together. John promised to come; but unforeseen business prevented him from doing so. Boethius, after waiting for him a long time—and himself having important affairs (42) that would occupy him entirely the next day—thought he ought to write to the archdeacon to set out his opinion.

After mature reflection upon the two [Col. 1429A] propositions, he found in fact that the second destroyed the first, that it was the source of all Eutyches’s errors, and that the Council of Chalcedon had rightly condemned it. He perceived the horrible consequences that could be drawn from it, and that it tended no less than to overturn the entire structure of our holy religion and undermine at its foundations the mystery of the Incarnation of the Word and the redemption of the human race.

Then the blindness of his fellow citizens aroused his compassion. His desire for their salvation and his zeal for the strengthening of the faith inspired him to compose the short treatise *On the Two Natures and One Person in Jesus Christ, against Eutyches and Nestorius*, which is still among his works. He addressed it to this same John, archdeacon of Rome.

After learnedly refuting Nestorius’s errors, he shows how the two natures are united (43) in a single person. He does so in a manner so sublime and precise that one does not know [Col. 1429B] which to admire more: the solidity of his reasoning or the penetration of his mind. There he makes admirable use of Aristotle’s philosophy to explain the terms substance, person, hypostasis, nature, and subsistence. I believe that he was the first to treat these matters with all the precision of the schools, and in the manner in which they could still be treated today. He thereby shows us how useful this philosophy can be for explaining properly the mysteries of our holy religion. This has been recognized so fully ever since that today one could scarcely distinguish his work from the theological lectures delivered in the schools. An analysis of it, together with that of his other treatises, will be found at the end of this work, since it could not have been given here without interrupting the sequence of the history.

Gilbert [Note: [Col. 1429D] M. Dupin (first volume of his *Twelfth Century*, p. 414), relying too heavily on the unreliable memoirs supplied to him, believed that Gilbert of Poitiers’s books had not yet been printed and that only his letter concerning the Eucharist, which Dom Luc d’Achéry gave us, existed. Yet they are found among Boethius’s works printed at Basel in 1570.] de la Porrée, bishop of (44) Poitiers, so famous for the great controversies he had with [Col. 1429C] Saint Bernard, gave us an extensive commentary on this short treatise by Boethius; but the gloss is even more obscure than the text.

In this same work, *On the Two Natures in Jesus Christ*, Boethius left us a lofty impression of his virtue and of the humble opinion he had of himself. He fears, he says, that John, to whom he addresses it, will find nothing in it deserving of his approval. He asks him to correct it without any restraint if he sees that Boethius departs even slightly from the Church’s constant doctrine. He concludes with a reflection worthy of the soundness of his judgment and one that could be suggested only by the deepest humility. Here it is:

“I cannot understand,” he says, “where the disordered attachment that one observes in certain authors to the productions of their minds can come from, since whatever is good and well said does not come from us but from God, who is the fullness of all goodness and the source from which it flows upon us. Why, then, display [Col. 1429D] such violent love for something that does not belong to us and that we cannot appropriate without sacrilegious theft?”

Such holy dispositions were capable of drawing down upon him and upon everything he wrote powerful heavenly assistance, guiding his pen and preserving it from error. Indeed, none is found in his works; and, like those of the great Hilary, they could be offered for reading without fear of encountering anything objectionable. People rose up against Gilbert’s commentaries and claimed that they were filled with blasphemies: that it was blasphemous to say that the divine essence is not [Col. 1430A] God, that the properties of the divine persons are not the persons themselves, that the divine nature was not incarnate, and so forth. But Boethius’s text has always been respected, and for nearly twelve hundred years it has remained beyond attack. This writing was followed by so many (46) blessings that a great number of Eutychians, after reading it, renounced the heresy; and several Catholic teachers who had been perplexed by the captious proposition, “Jesus Christ is composed of two natures, but he does not subsist in two natures,” were strengthened in the faith in which they had been wavering and were given the means to silence those imprudent men who wished to revive errors proscribed by the Church.

State affairs interrupted these labors of Boethius [Col. 1430B], so useful to religion. Theodoric entrusted him with a commission that required all his care and attention. This was the occasion. The officers and soldiers of his guard, with a bold and mutinous air, came to him while he was at Ravenna and presented a petition filled with bitter complaints and written in disrespectful terms. They intimated that they would abandon him if he delayed giving them satisfaction.

The subject of their complaint was fairly legitimate. They claimed that the currency with which they were paid had been debased and was of less weight than it customarily had been (47). The loss was considerable and amounted each year to at least one-third of their pay.

Theodoric at first imagined that this was a pretext for having their wages increased. Irritated by their insolence, he had resolved to punish them. Before resorting to punishment, however, he wanted to ascertain the truth of the matter. He actually found that the coins, and especially the gold solidi, were underweight; therefore, concealing his anger, he promised to remedy the [Col. 1430D] abuse as soon as possible.

Finding no one more capable of doing so than [Col. 1430C] Boethius, he wrote to him in Rome, where he had left him. The letter is highly flattering (*apud Cass.*, book I, letter 10). After praising his virtues and abilities, he charged him with reforming all the coins circulating in the empire, restoring to each the weight and value it had formerly possessed, and especially ensuring that the gold solidus should again be worth six thousand denarii, as in former times.

It is not easy to understand what these denarii were to which Theodoric here refers (48). According to Budé, the lowest-valued denarius among the Romans was worth approximately three and a half sous in our currency; and it does not appear that their gold solidus ever equaled the one thousand and fifty French livres that would result from six thousand pieces worth three sous and six deniers each. Moreover, Justinian’s Code, almost contemporary with Theodoric, observes that a pound of gold contained twelve gold solidi; consequently, the gold solidus weighed scarcely more than ninety grains. But if these are valued according to their present worth among us, the six thousand that made up the gold solidus would be worth approximately twenty-five pounds in our currency.

Theodoric also asked him in this letter to extend his care to the reform of weights and measures and to regulate them so that the pound would consist of twelve ounces. He claimed that neither caprice nor chance had determined this arrangement, and that there was a mystery in the number: the ancient legislators had established it to leave the people with a perpetual reminder of the six (49) different [Col. 1431A] ages of the world and of its duration, which they had limited to six thousand years. “The world,” he said, “is signified by the brilliance of the metal and by the roundness of the coin; its six-thousand-year duration, by the six thousand denarii of which the gold solidus is composed; and the twelve months of the year, by the twelve ounces of the pound.”

Finally, Theodoric ended his letter by telling Boethius that he took singular pleasure in conversing with him in this way because he knew that he was speaking to someone ignorant of nothing in all these matters and perfectly instructed in every divine and human science.

The famous Cassiodorus was then Theodoric’s secretary. This may lead us to believe that the entire letter was written by him and that Theodoric merely signed it. It is too witty and its style too brilliant to be Theodoric’s own production. Besides Cassiodorus’s style, which is recognizable in it, one finds there all the playfulness of his mind.

Boethius discharged his commission with all the [Col. 1431B] care and skill that could have been expected of him. The reform (50) of the currency, weights, and measures was completed in a very short time and implemented throughout the furthest reaches of the empire. Order in commerce was thus restored, and Theodoric’s troops were pacified. Boethius’s wisdom in government and his skill in every kind of art and science contributed greatly to extending Theodoric’s reputation and causing neighboring princes to seek his friendship. Clovis, informed of the magnificence of his court and table, asked him to send a musician who could sing and play instruments perfectly. Theodoric addressed Boethius as the most accomplished musician in his dominions and charged him with making the selection. From the letter he wrote to him, it appears that Clovis was not yet a Christian, for Theodoric led Boethius to hope that he would have the advantage of softening the fierce hearts of the [Col. 1431C] pagan Franks and taming them, as Orpheus had once tamed animals and monsters through the harmony of his instruments and the sweetness of his voice. He further assured him that he would receive as many thanks from Clovis for carrying out his orders well as Theodoric himself would receive from Clovis (Cassiod., *Var.*, book II, letter 40).

Boethius found a musician of the kind Theodoric desired, and quickly enough to send him with the two ambassadors whom Theodoric was dispatching to Clovis to congratulate him on the great victory he had just won over the Germans at Zülpich, which the ancients called Tolbiac. It would have been impossible to praise the victory in more pompous terms than those Theodoric used, while also asking Clovis to spare the remnants of that fugitive nation, which had come to seek refuge in his territories. However skillful he was, Theodoric nonetheless allowed it to be seen that he already feared the power and valor of Clovis and his troops. Our historians have hitherto seemed to pay little attention [Col. 1431D] to Theodoric’s letters to Clovis [Note: [Col. 1431D] The heading of Theodoric’s letters to Clovis is as follows: “To Luduin, king of the Franks” (*ibid.*, letter 41). From this name, Luduin, which was Clovis’s family name, the Latins later formed *Ludovicus*, *Clodovecus*, and *Clodovaeus*, according to the differing pronunciation of nations and centuries. Jordanes also calls him Lodoin (*De rebus Geticis*, 88).]; yet there are few monuments in history more certain or more glorious to France. Theodoric ended his first letter by expressing the hope that the musician he was sending—and whom he assured him to be highly skilled—would be fortunate enough to charm Clovis’s power through the sweet harmonies of his voice and instruments.

Almost at the same time Boethius was entrusted with a third commission [Col. 1432A] from Theodoric, which he carried out with no less success. Gondebaud, king of Burgundy, had sent ambassadors to him, perhaps to request one of his daughters in marriage for Sigismund, his son. The purpose of this embassy is not sufficiently clear in history; but it is certain that, around this time, Sigismund married Ostrogotha, one of Theodoric’s natural daughters and Alaric’s sister-in-law (Jordanes, *De rebus Geticis*, 88).

The Burgundians, then a crude people, had seen sundials and water clocks in Rome, which they admired because they did not understand their construction. They asked Theodoric to send some to Gondebaud, as something that could (53) give him the greatest pleasure. To satisfy them, Theodoric searched throughout his territories for the people most capable of producing such works. He again wrote to Boethius as the most skillful mathematician in Italy. His letter, like the preceding ones, is in Cassiodorus’s style and filled with everything capable of flattering an accomplished mind and touching a good heart. To persuade him of the [Col. 1432B] importance of the commission with which he was entrusting him, he first represented that it was a prince’s duty never to neglect rendering his neighbors every good service within his power and which they expected from him, because the pleasure he gave them, even in a matter of little importance, often had more power over their minds than the full force of arms. Second, he said that the smallest actions of sovereigns were always very great, not excluding even their entertainments, because all of them bore an immediate relation to the government of the state [Note: [Col. 1432D] “Let it therefore be for the commonwealth even when we seem to be at play” (*Theod.*, apud Cass., book II, letters 4–5).]. Finally, after a long enumeration of Boethius’s talents, he particularly praised his skill in (54) mathematics; and, in order to encourage him to undertake more willingly the works requested by Gondebaud’s ambassadors, he appealed to his glory and personal reputation.

“Your name,” he said, “[Col. 1432C] will become famous throughout Burgundy. You will have the honor of introducing the fine arts to this renowned nation, and the glory will rebound even upon Rome; for it will be no small glory for her to have contributed through you to civilizing peoples so renowned. Therefore spare neither effort nor expense; my treasuries are open to you.”

Boethius took pleasure in contributing to the satisfaction of Theodoric and Gondebaud. He summoned the most skilled craftsmen from every direction and worked himself on the water clocks and sundials with such success that they became the admiration of the Romans and Burgundians. He made sundials for all the different positions of the sun. As for the water clocks, they accurately indicated the course of the sun, the moon, and all the stars, without wheels, weights, or springs (55), through the power of a certain quantity of water enclosed in a spherical tin vessel that turned continually, driven by its own weight.

In Burgundy they were regarded as marvels. [Col. 1432D] The Burgundians could not understand how these machines could mark every hour of the day and night so accurately without being moved or without the pointer being advanced. For a long time they kept watch beside them to make sure that no one touched them; and, finally recognizing the truth of the matter, they believed that some divinity animated them inwardly and gave them all the precise and measured movements that could be observed in them.

But if there was nothing divine in the movement of these machines, then unknown to the Burgundians, there certainly was something divine in the [Col. 1433A] circumstances and consequences of Theodoric’s gifts. Since God ordinarily pours a particular blessing upon everything the saints undertake for his glory, Boethius’s labors on this occasion were not (56) deprived of it. From this the Burgundians gradually took occasion to become familiar with the Romans. These curiosities, having drawn them to Italy, brought them into contact with Boethius, who, always animated by an ardent zeal to extend the faith of Jesus Christ, used the opportunity advantageously to insinuate the truth into their hearts.

The greater the extent of the kingdom of Burgundy, the more ardently Boethius desired to deliver it from the darkness of paganism and heresy. Not only did this kingdom then include the duchy and county of Burgundy, but also the Lyonnais, the Dauphiné, Savoy, and several other neighboring provinces. Two kinds of peoples inhabited it: the native inhabitants of the country, called Gallo-Romans since they had been subjected by Julius Caesar; and the Burgundians, [Col. 1433B] fierce and barbarous peoples who had come out of Germania during the decline of the Empire, seized these great provinces, and established their domination there. They held sovereign power, and Gondebaud was already the sixth of the kings who had ruled them.

(57) Among the excellent qualities that shone in this prince, there was an inconceivable mixture of vices that obscured all his virtues. Most of the Gallo-Romans were already Christians; the others were pagans. Gondebaud and his Burgundians were not only obstinate Arians but also Photinians, whose errors were more opposed to Catholic doctrine than those of the pure Arians. The Catholic Gauls suffered greatly under his rule. Several yielded to torture; a greater number preferred to lose their lives rather than defile themselves by a sacrilegious communion with the prince and his bishops (Bail., *Life of Saint [Col. 1433C] Sigismund*, 1 May). Since nothing lay closer to their hearts than enlarging their authority by spreading their heresy, they took every opportunity to embitter Gondebaud’s mind against the Catholics.

Chilperic, his own brother, and the princess, his wife, were among the first to experience this. He had the former put to death by the sword and had the latter thrown into the river with a stone around her neck. Two of Chilperic’s children were caught up in this massacre; as for the two daughters (58) who remained, it was thought sufficient to send them into exile. The elder, named Saëdeluba, having laid aside her secular clothing, consecrated herself to God. The younger, called Clotilde, was reserved as a gift from heaven to become the wife of Clovis and the first instrument of his conversion (Gregory of Tours, *History*, book II).

Gondebaud’s fear that his children might one day be deprived of his succession if Chilperic survived him, together with his hatred of the Catholic religion they professed, led him to commit these crimes.

[Col. 1433D] Since Boethius was therefore obliged to maintain many relations in the kingdom of Burgundy, he had occasion to form friendships with its Catholic bishops. He already had a very close friendship with Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne, his close relative, who, like him, descended from the emperor Avitus. He often stimulated their zeal by his letters and urged them to work seriously for the conversion of their prince. No one took the matter more to heart than the holy bishop of Vienne (Fleury, *History*, vol. VII, p. 3 ff.).

Lyon was then the capital of this (59) kingdom and the usual residence of its kings. One day Saint Avitus found himself there with several other bishops of the province to celebrate the feast of Saint Just. He urged them to come with him to the palace to greet Gondebaud and request a public conference with the bishops of his party.

The saint’s purpose was at the same time to persuade the [Col. 1434A] king to attend, so that he might disabuse him of the error in which his false shepherds were holding him. The veneration felt for Avitus was so great that everyone deferred to his judgment, but on condition that he would speak for them. This honor was accorded him although he was neither the oldest nor the first in rank. Despite the opposition of the most powerful supporters of the heresy, they obtained an audience with the king. He received them with great honor; but after the initial compliments, he did not fail to call them idolaters and reproach them for worshiping three gods. This was the customary reproach that the Arians made against the Catholics.

Avitus then heaved a profound sigh and lamented the thick darkness (60) spread over the king’s mind. Taking this as an opportunity to explain the Catholic faith to him, he did so in a manner so clear and moving that the prince appeared affected. Seizing this favorable moment, the holy bishop added: “If you wished, great king, to discover for yourself upon [Col. 1434B] what foundations our faith rests, you would soon be disabused. What benefits would this not bring to you and to your entire people? But your bishops, enemies of Jesus Christ, are drawing God’s anger down upon you. This would not happen if you were willing to listen to us and command them to enter with us into a public conference in which the truth would be fully brought to light.” Then, throwing himself at the king’s feet with all the other Catholic bishops, he embraced him, and they all tearfully begged him to allow himself to be moved. Gondebaud could not prevent a few tears from falling. Having had the bishops raised with every possible expression of humanity, he assured them that he would give them his answer the following day.

No sooner had they withdrawn than he assembled the bishops of his communion (61) and made them understand so clearly that their honor was at stake in accepting the challenge presented by the Catholics that they did not dare refuse it. The king immediately informed the [Col. 1434C] holy bishop of Vienne and the bishop of Lyon and had them told to come to his palace the next day, accompanied by a small number of their colleagues. To avoid disorder, the prince did not think it appropriate for the conference to be held publicly.

Six bishops were chosen. After spending the entire night in prayer at the tomb of Saint Just, they went to the king at the appointed hour, followed by a very small number of Catholics, all people of distinction. Placide and Lucain, two of the principal officers of the court, were conspicuous among them. An equal number of Arian bishops and officers accompanied the king. Boniface, the most important man in their party, was ordered to open the dispute. But Saint Avitus rose with that air of confidence inspired by truth and had scarcely demonstrated, by sound arguments and the authority of Scripture, that the Catholics did not worship three gods (62), although they worshiped the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit equally, and acknowledged that the Son was God like the Father and the Holy Spirit God like the Father and the Son, when Boniface, overwhelmed by the authority and majesty shining from Saint Avitus’s face, had nothing to oppose him. Instead of answers, the Arians offered only insults and abuse. The Catholics were called sorcerers, as though by their enchantments they had deprived them of the use of speech. Gondebaud perceived the embarrassment of his bishops and, to save their honor, rose and postponed the contest until the following day.

The Arians, so badly handled in this conference, no longer wished to return to the contest. Yet, since their withdrawal would make the weakness of their cause too obvious to the king, they maintained a bold appearance in his presence, claiming that they were fully resolved to prove to the Catholic bishops the next day that they were genuine idolaters. But while they pretended to [Col. 1435A] prepare for the dispute, they were cultivating Arédius in order to induce him to refuse them entry to the (63) palace when they presented themselves there the following day. Arédius was a courtier, the king’s favorite, a great politician, and a supporter of the Arians on every occasion, although he claimed to be Catholic. As soon as he saw the orthodox bishops in the king’s antechamber, he did not fail to urge them to leave. His pretext was that such disputes merely embittered minds instead of producing anything beneficial to religion. But since he was known to be a false brother and was dealing with intelligent men, his remonstrances had no effect. The bishops stood firm and boldly replied that they had come by order of the king.

At these words the courtier no longer dared insist. They went forward, and when the king saw them, he rose and came to meet them. At first they spoke only of affairs of state. The prince complained that the king of the Franks was openly favoring his enemies (Gregory of Tours, *History*, book II, chapter 32), that he was even in league with his brother to invade his territories, and that such conduct gave him a poor opinion of their faith, since true religion did not permit one to desire another’s possessions or thirst for the blood of peoples. Thus people often condemn in others the evil of which they themselves feel most guilty.

Indeed, if someone had asked Gondebaud on what grounds his fathers, Arians like himself, had seized the vast provinces that obeyed him, he might have found himself greatly embarrassed. But the bishops, in order not to waste time on useless speeches, contented themselves with telling him that Holy Scripture teaches us that the overthrow of kingdoms is often the punishment due to contempt for religion; that the best way to be at peace with the king of France was to agree with him concerning the faith; that it would never depend upon them that the two kings should not live in perfect [Col. 1435C] harmony; and that, if he approved, they offered their mediation with Clovis wholeheartedly.

When this conversation was over, they went to the conference, and each took his place. The Arian bishop, whose aim was to avoid the principal difficulty, opened it by proposing several abstract questions, in order to weary the prince and (65) bring the assembly to an end without reaching any conclusion. But Saint Avitus, instead of answering them, insisted especially on the divinity of the Word and on the unity of God, thereby forcing his opponent to restrict himself to this essential point. Having demonstrated clearly that the Catholic Church, in worshiping the three persons of the august Trinity with equal worship, did not worship several gods but one alone, he won the admiration of the entire assembly. Only Boniface, unable to bear the disgrace under which he found himself, broke out in insults even more violently than on the preceding day. He did so with such fury and vehemence that, having made himself hoarse by shouting, he rendered himself incapable of speaking any further in defense of his party.

Since no one on the Arian side dared to speak, lacking reasons with which to oppose those of the great Avitus, the king, wearied by the vehemence of his bishop and by the length of the dispute, rose abruptly, showing his indignation toward the leaders of his party. But Saint Avitus, inspired from above, stopped him. Animated by the same spirit that once inspired the prophet Elijah (III Kings, chapter XVIII), when he proposed to the priests of (66) Baal that they build a pyre and prepare victims upon it, so that the truth of the God who would consume them by heavenly fire might be recognized, he cried out:

“It is not enough, great king, that I have proved in your presence the truth of the Catholic faith in such a way that nothing more can be opposed to it; I also offer to make the dead speak in its favor. Let us all go together to the tomb of Saint Just; let us question him about our faith [Col. 1436A] and about that of your bishops, and let us all follow whichever one God approves through the mouth of his servant.”

The Arian bishops, more prudent than the priests of Baal, took care not to accept Avitus’s proposal. They were not unaware of the credit he enjoyed with God, nor that he was capable of obtaining from Him whatever seemed most impossible to human beings.

Since it is rare to find bishops of good faith attached to a false belief, they never dared put theirs to the test, although the king, better disposed than they, seemed willing to consent. Thus, as far as the prince was concerned, the conference achieved no other result than to leave him more undecided than he (67) had been beforehand. It did, however, open the eyes of several people, who asked to be reconciled to the Catholic Church.

Boethius was informed of everything that had taken place, and he grieved over Gondebaud’s blindness; but he still did not believe that he ought to abandon his efforts for his conversion. Not content with asking God for it with [Col. 1436B] tears, when he had occasion to send Gondebaud new gifts on Theodoric’s behalf, he wrote at the same time to the Catholic bishops of Burgundy, and especially to Saint Avitus, imploring them to labor anew for this purpose. History does not indicate, however, that Saint Avitus afterward made any further effort for his conversion. Perhaps he believed that Gondebaud had already rendered himself unworthy of heaven’s new graces by abusing those previously granted to him, and that he had fallen into final hardness of heart, since, after having so clearly recognized the truth in the two conferences held in his presence, he had not had the courage to embrace it.

Nevertheless, it seems that God, earnestly entreated on his behalf by the tears of (68) Boethius, still wished to touch that hardened heart. For after receiving Theodoric’s gifts, Gondebaud himself sent for the holy bishop of Vienne, showed him signs of particular esteem and confidence, and, after acknowledging and confessing in his presence the divinity of the Son of God and of the Holy Spirit, and their perfect equality with the Father, he earnestly begged him to reconcile him secretly to the Catholic Church through anointing with the holy chrism. These are the terms used by Gregory of Tours (*History*, book II, chapter 34). They have given the theologians of our century occasion to debate several questions concerning the manner of reconciling heretics to the Church. Since we could not examine them here without a lengthy digression that would cause us to lose the thread of the history, we refer the reader to a dissertation that will be found at the end of the work (see the second part).

But Saint Avitus did not believe that he ought to yield to Gondebaud’s entreaties.

“Prince, if you truly believe,” he said to him, “follow the precept of the Lord, who said: ‘Whoever confesses my name before men will be acknowledged and recognized by me (69) before my heavenly Father.’ You are a king, and you have no reason to fear being persecuted as the apostles were. You fear, you say, the people’s revolt; but it is for the people to follow you, and for you to support their weakness by your example. God is not mocked: He cannot love the one whom fear of losing an earthly kingdom prevents from confessing His name before men.”

These words struck the prince like a thunderbolt. He remained speechless, not knowing what to answer, and never had the courage to make a public profession of the Catholic faith. Who knows whether the many murders committed to preserve a temporal crown had not rendered him unworthy of the grace being offered to him, so that he might secure another whose duration would have been eternal? Saint Avitus had rightly foreseen that one who had not hesitated to stain his hands with the blood of his own brothers, or to cause so many innocent people to perish in order to secure it, would never risk losing it by the slightest action that might contribute to that loss. Thus this (70) unfortunate prince died soon afterward in his hardness of heart.

Boethius’s prayers for the conversion of the kingdom of Burgundy were eventually answered. If Gondebaud died committed to error, his son Sigismund worked to raise the Catholic faith upon its ruins. During his father’s lifetime, although Gondebaud was convinced of the impiety of his heresy, Sigismund was reconciled to the Church by Saint Avitus, without Gondebaud opposing it (Gregory of Tours, cited above). He profited so well from the instruction of this great bishop that, not content with embracing orthodox belief in all its purity, he also devoted himself to the most exact practice of the Gospel’s most sublime virtues. After departing from them on one occasion because he had yielded too much to the resentment of a second wife, he was seen courageously to enter upon the path of the most arduous penance: assiduous in prayer, exact in vigils and fasts, generous toward the poor, and magnificent toward God in the construction of his churches and monasteries.

Having ascended the throne of Burgundy after his father’s death, he (71) appeared to change nothing in his conduct except by renewing his zeal for the conversion of his subjects. He entrusted the instruction of his children to the holy master who had formed him in virtue, and, after long and arduous labors, went to receive his reward in heaven.

The good understanding between Theodoric and Clovis did not last long. Alaric, who had married Theudgote [Note: [Col. 1437D] Some historians call her Theudieusa.], one of Theodoric’s natural daughters and the sister of Ostrogotho, the wife of Sigismund, Gondebaud’s son, was the cause of this (Jordanes, *On the Origin and Deeds of the Goths*, 88). His territories bordered those of Clovis. The officers of the two princes had several disputes. Clovis believed himself insulted; a few words escaped him against Alaric, who immediately began to think of taking up arms to avenge himself. Theodoric was informed of this. He wrote about it to Clovis, Alaric, and Gondebaud. He exhorted the first two to peace, urged Gondebaud to bring them to it, and asked them to agree upon arbitrators to settle their disputes, threatening to declare war on whoever refused to heed his advice.

(72) An island situated in the middle of the Loire, near Amboise, on the frontier between Clovis’s territories and those of Alaric, was chosen as the place of the conference. The princes went there, and their disputes were settled; but Alaric did not remain long without giving Clovis new cause for complaint. Religion also supplied him with very plausible grounds: for Clovis, having become a Catholic Christian after the celebrated victory he had won over the Germans through a very special protection from heaven, could scarcely tolerate the Arians so close to his territories. Moreover, the ancient Gauls, Alaric’s subjects, almost all Catholics and dissatisfied with his rule, leaned toward Clovis and wished to have him as king. Finally, having been miraculously [Col. 1437D] cured by Saint Severinus of Agaunum of a very long and dangerous illness, he believed that he ought to show his gratitude to God through some outstanding enterprise. Having nothing more to fear from Theodoric, he declared war on Alaric and resolved to drive the Arians from this beautiful part of (73) France that they occupied.

Full of confidence in the one who had inspired him with so generous a purpose, he advanced toward Poitou and entered the plains of Vouillé at the head of a powerful army. Alaric awaited him there with a formidable army of his own. Giselic, his natural son, commanded part of it. They engaged in battle; the outcome was uncertain, and extraordinary acts of courage were performed on both sides. Clovis narrowly escaped perishing there; but at last, having [Col. 1438A] killed Alaric with his own hand, he left nothing but a rout in the Arian army. The slaughter was so great that Giselic had difficulty gathering a handful of men to support his retreat.

Amalaric, Alaric’s legitimate son, was still only a child; for this reason the troops recognized Giselic as king. He took possession of the territory that remained to him in Gaul and ruled there until Theodoric, who did not love him, deprived him of both it and his life. As for Amalaric, some troops that remained loyal led him into Spain, a considerable part of which obeyed him, while Clovis, who knew better (74) than anyone how to exploit the advantages of a victory, conquered all Aquitaine. He advanced as far as Toulouse, where Alaric had held his court, took possession of it and of the defeated king’s treasures.

Theodoric did not remain long without learning of his son-in-law’s defeat. The nobles who had remained loyal to Amalaric omitted nothing in their efforts to persuade him to enter into his master’s quarrel: blood spoke in his favor. Theodoric was quite willing to do so, but he believed that he ought to submit the matter to his council before undertaking it. All his generals knew the prince’s passion for war, and knew that it yielded nothing to the passion he had for his grandson’s fortunes. They advised him to send immediate assistance and declare war on Clovis. Boethius alone held the opposite view. The difficulty of moving troops into Gaul, the valor of Clovis’s forces, with whom everything succeeded, and the interests of the religion that God was visibly protecting made him fear an unfortunate outcome. He could not conceal his feelings from Theodoric; he even ventured to predict to him (75) that the outcome of this war would be disastrous and would tarnish the glory of his first conquests.

“My lord, if you love war,” he said to him, “turn your arms against this multitude of barbarians who threaten you [Col. 1438C] on every side. Is it not more appropriate to secure your former conquests than to think about making new ones?”

He was not heeded. The Roman troops stationed in Gaul were ordered to join those of Amalaric and his brother Giselic. Others came from Italy, and within a short time an army of eighty thousand men had assembled there. Ibba, one of the most experienced commanders, was placed in command (Jordanes, 88, *Mez* [the reference is uncertain]).

At first he won great advantages over Clovis’s forces. He even reconquered everything they had taken in Provence and Languedoc, with the exception of Toulouse, Uzès, and a few other places; and he raised the siege of Arles and Carcassonne, which the French and Burgundians were besieging (Procopius, *The Gothic War*, book I; Jordanes, cited above).

Whatever Procopius may say, there is no appearance that Theodoric was personally present on this expedition. Ibba had its entire direction [Col. 1438D] and all the honor, and from the subsequent course of the history it appears that Theodoric had remained in Italy, where he awaited the outcome. Since Thierry, also called Theodoric, Clovis’s son, commanded the army that his father had sent into the Albigeois and Quercy, this historian must have confused the king of Italy with the son of the king of the Franks.

No sooner had news of these successes been brought to Ravenna than Theodoric, unable to contain his joy, made Boethius feel it through a pointed jest.

“Where are your predictions, Boethius?” he said to him. “My troops are victorious everywhere. Arles has just put up a vigorous resistance; its inhabitants have already paid me the precious tribute [Note: [Col. 1438D] *Pretiosum vectigal jam nobis dederunt suae fidei* (“They have already given us the precious tribute of their fidelity”), etc. In Cassiodorus, book III, letter 32.] of their fidelity. As a reward, I grant them [Col. 1439A] a four-year exemption from every kind of tax.”

“I rejoice in it, my lord,” Boethius replied with great modesty, “but the war is not (77) yet over,” whether he was inspired from above or whether, through his insight, he knew well that it would prove fatal to Theodoric. The outcome confirmed his prediction, and the prince did not have long to regret failing to follow the advice of his faithful minister. His troops, although frequently reinforced by a multitude of Goths and Gepids, were thereafter always defeated by Clovis’s forces; and the Franks remained peaceful possessors of the provinces from which they had driven Alaric. Theodoric was compelled to withdraw his army and to content himself with the small portion that Giselic held in Gaul. After taking his life, he reunited that territory with his kingdom of Italy, together with what his grandson Amalaric possessed in Spain, pending the time when he would be old enough to govern them himself.

During this expedition, which occupied Theodoric greatly, Boethius was engaged in other struggles more useful to the Church. The heresies of Arius, Nestorius, and Eutyches having refined men’s minds, reasoning had been pushed to its ultimate limit. Since the Catholic dogma (78) was highly elevated, all the subtlety of logic and the abstractions of metaphysics were needed to understand anything of it. Every day people practiced seeking new terms and new ways of expressing themselves, in order to bring our faith closer to ordinary ideas and to the common capacity of human beings.

But by dint of reasoning and subtilizing these matters, they eventually came to maintain the proposition that, in the holy Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit could be predicated substantially of the Divinity. That is, that the Divinity was substantially the Father, that it was the Son, and that it was the Holy Spirit. Boethius could not accept this; he immediately perceived its falsehood and malignity and resolved to combat it.

Thus, in the course of time, according to the Angelic Doctor, the following propositions were advanced in treating the mystery of the Incarnation: “The divine nature is the human nature”; “the Divinity suffered”; “the Divinity is humanity.” All these must be rejected as false and dangerous, (79) because, as this holy doctor says, since the natures remain distinct in Jesus Christ, their properties may indeed belong and be attributed to the one person, but not indifferently to both natures (Thomas Aquinas, *Summa theologica*, part III, question 16, article 5).

On this principle Saint John Damascene rightly observes that, in speaking accurately of the Divinity, one must not affirm of it or attribute to it what properly belongs to humanity (Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book III, chapter 11). Thus, he says, one must take great care not to assert that the Divinity is passible, that the nature of the Word suffered, or that the flesh is uncreated. These and similar expressions are contrary [Col. 1439D] to the purity of the faith.

It was upon these same foundations that Boethius established the principles he set forth to prove that none of the divine persons can be predicated substantially of the Divinity. He did so in the short treatise addressed to that same John, archdeacon of Rome, under the title: “Whether the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit can be predicated substantially of the Divinity.” Properly speaking, it is only a fairly short letter, but it contains great difficulties. An analysis of it and explanations will be found in the final part of this work. He concluded it by asking the archdeacon to let him know his opinion on the question.

“Although it seems to me,” he said to him, “that I have advanced nothing that is not of the faith, or that does not necessarily follow from the principles of the faith, I nevertheless submit myself to your judgment. Instruct me, then; teach me what I must believe in order to be a good Catholic, [Col. 1440A] and try, if possible, to support the dogma by reasoning, so that faith and reason, lending each other mutual assistance, may establish the truth more firmly.”

Nothing better indicates the high esteem Boethius had for the virtue and ability of the archdeacon John, since he surrendered himself entirely to his judgment and made him the arbiter of his faith; nor does anything better indicate at the same time this great man’s profound humility, and that he never wrote or disputed in order to have the honor of defeating his opponents, but solely to clarify the issues and make the truth triumph.

(81) Gilbert also wrote long commentaries on this letter, but in his customary manner—that is, with obscurities and abstractions that distress the reader and oblige him to read the same thing several times without understanding it. We do not know what John replied to Boethius; but when this archdeacon found himself perplexed, at approximately this time, by a question proposed to him by a certain Manichaean philosopher, he turned to Boethius and asked him [Col. 1440B] to provide its solution.

The Manichaean asked how it could be that every being was good, and that goodness, which is not a substantial being, could belong to substances by virtue of their being. The Manichaean’s aim was to draw from the archdeacon’s answer some proof with which to establish his error concerning the two first principles he admitted, one of good and the other of evil. Boethius noticed this, and, in order to confound the Manichaean’s pride in answering him, did so in a manner so subtle and elevated that, as he himself says, only learned people entirely devoted to the study (82) of wisdom can understand it. He proceeds in this way so as not to expose the precious treasures of wisdom to the mockery of profane and ignorant people, and so as not to blind altogether the diseased eyes of those who would be dazzled by an entirely divine light.

Indeed, nothing is more subtle or abstract than his answer. One is stopped at the opening of the book. The title *Hebdomades* that he gives it is unknown to the most skillful grammarians, for he does not take it in the sense in which Livy takes his *Decades*, as a work divided into weeks or as a collection made over the course of several weeks, but as referring to the loftiest conceptions of the mind. This is the meaning Boethius attaches to the Greek word Ἐβδομάδες (*Hebdomades*), quite different from the simpler conceptions that the ancient Greeks called Ἐνθυμήματα (*Enthymemata*).

He first establishes nine general rules, which he claims are so many axioms received from the philosophers. The first is that “what is” is different from “being”: that is, essence is not existence.

The second is that there is a great difference between being something and being something in that which is: that is, between substance and accident.

The third is that what is may participate, but being may not: that is, one must exist in order to participate in something, whereas essence in itself is incapable of receiving anything.

The fourth is that what is may have something other than being, but being has nothing except itself: that is, essence in itself is so simple that it admits no composition, whereas what exists may be composed at least of essence and existence.

The other five rules turn upon these and are, as it were, their necessary consequences. Having established these principles, he proceeds to examine the proposition; and, in order to bring the difficulty fully to light, he has the Manichaean reason as follows:

“If everything that has being is good, it can be good in only two ways: either by essence or by participation, since one cannot conceive any other kinds of goodness. Now, what is good only by participation is not good in itself, because it receives this goodness from another—just as something that is white only by participation is not white in itself, for if it were, it would not need to receive whiteness from another. Therefore, if everything that has being is good, it must be good by a substantial goodness; that is, its essence or substance must be the goodness attributed to it, so that there is no distinction between its being and this goodness. But if this is so, all creatures will be gods, which cannot be said without blasphemy, since only of God can one assert that His essence is goodness. Consequently, it is not true to say that everything that has being is good.”

To answer this difficulty and show the origin and principle of this goodness inseparable from created beings, which philosophers call transcendent goodness, he separates the supreme good from other goods, the first being from secondary beings, God from the creature. Although this is not possible in reality, since there is no created being that does not stand in relation to the Creator and does not presuppose Him, being an emanation from Him, they can nevertheless be distinguished by the understanding; the mind can consider one without the other, just as it can consider a triangle solely with respect to its triangular form, abstracting from its matter, although the triangle cannot really be separated from it.

If, then, we come to consider creatures apart, as though they were not emanations or outpourings of the first being, we may affirm of them that they are good, white, round, and heavy. My mind will then necessarily be compelled to agree that this goodness, whiteness, roundness, and heaviness are not their essence, but something distinct from it that has accrued to them as an accident. Otherwise these qualities would all be identical, since they would be the essence of the things themselves: heaviness would be color, color [Col. 1441C] would be goodness, and goodness would be roundness. (86) From this it necessarily follows that the goodness of creatures is not their essence, and that they are good only because their being is an outflow and participation of uncreated being, which is goodness itself. Now, just as something that participates in whiteness cannot participate in it without becoming white, so creatures that participate in God’s goodness by virtue of their being cannot participate in it without becoming good.

From this established truth he draws two consequences. The first is that this goodness found in all created beings is not an accidental goodness, because it does not come upon the created being afterward; rather, it is, so to speak, infused into its essence, from which it cannot be separated, since it is its essence itself insofar as that essence is a participation in the first goodness.

The second is that this goodness, although essential to the creature—since it is essential to created goodness to emanate from uncreated goodness—is nevertheless very different from that infinite goodness which constitutes God’s nature: not only because this first goodness is not a participation in any other goodness, and not only because this divine goodness is immense and without any limits, qualities that do not belong to the goodness of creatures, any more than does existing through themselves, but also because, whatever supposition one makes, whatever distinction or abstraction the human mind may make in God and in His attributes, it can neither make nor conceive that God’s nature is not goodness itself. By contrast, the essence of earthly beings is good only on the supposition that it proceeds from this first goodness; and if, impossibly, it derived its origin from elsewhere or from some other attribute of God, this created essence would no longer be essentially [Col. 1442A] good. In this way Boethius overturned the entire reasoning of the Manichaean.

These labors of the mind were, so to speak, this great man’s recreations. By means of them he relaxed from his endless occupations, under whose weight many ministers might have succumbed. In addition to the administration of the cities, the general oversight (88) of the arts and buildings, and the supervision of all the judicial officers attached to his office, Theodoric also relied upon him to maintain good order among the troops, secure abundance in the provinces, ensure the people’s peace, provide for the safety of commerce and of the frontiers, maintain good relations with his neighbors, and consolidate peace with them.

But in how many other cares did his zeal for religion involve him! He could say, like Saint Paul, that he became weak with the weak; that the scandals he saw among Christians [Col. 1442B] filled his heart with bitterness and sorrow; and that concern for all the Churches brought him a multitude of thorny affairs that besieged him on every side.

He was continually attentive lest the Catholics be perverted through association with the Arians, and lest the purity of Christian virgins suffer from the licentiousness of those barbarians. The bishops of distant provinces called upon his authority whenever their Churches found themselves oppressed; he was obliged continually to set himself against this torrent of injustice, which swept everyone along. Each person had recourse to him in his calamities, and he would have believed that he was being insulted if anyone had appealed to others rather than to him. In Rome he demonstrated what a single good man can accomplish when he wishes to devote himself to banishing vice from his homeland and making virtue flourish there.

Two things in particular dishonored this great city, and both had been introduced there [Col. 1442C] along with the barbarian nations that had seized control of the government. A great number of Manichaeans had come to settle there and were daily seducing several of the faithful through their devices, especially people of the lower classes, who had become admirers of their fantasies.

There were no fewer magicians, who had already managed to draw several people of rank, and even senators, into their superstitions. Boethius had long groaned in the depths of his heart over these disorders and sought means (90) of stopping their progress. At last his zeal prevailed over all the considerations that had hitherto restrained him. He went to the pope—Symmachus was still pope—and described to him so movingly the miserable state of Christianity in Rome that no one could fail to be touched by it.

After making the Holy Father aware of the magnitude of the wound, he spoke to him of the remedy (Anonymous of Valesius):

“We need remedies quite different from those used until now,” he said to him. “A desperate illness requires extreme measures. If we were dealing with reasonable people, we might hope to bring them back through reason. Your paternal exhortations, your charitable admonitions, the zeal of your preachers, and the disputations of your theologians might remove the bandage that this abominable sect wears over its eyes and make it perceive the truth. But what can reason do against people who have none left and who utter nothing but extravagances? If their impiety had not reached its height and had not rendered them unworthy of God’s mercies, we might still flatter ourselves that the fervor (91) of your holy prayers and the groans of so many good souls concerned with their conversion would do violence to heaven on their behalf and perhaps bend the divine justice angered by their disorders. But the monstrous mixture they make of Christianity with idolatry, of Jesus Christ with Belial, of the Supreme Being with the demon, to whom they give more power [Col. 1443A] than to God Himself, no longer permits us to hope for their change. Everything that indulgence and charity have been able to inspire until now in order to bring them back to themselves has been useless; the evil, instead of diminishing, grows from day to day; error, feeling itself supported by human authority, [Note: [Col. 1443D] He is referring to the emperor Anastasius, who openly favored the Manichaeans, as the pope reproaches him for doing in his letter found in volume I of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.] triumphs insolently. Leniency is therefore now out of season; iron and fire are needed to extirpate so great an evil.”

The pope agreed, but it was a matter of finding a prompt and decisive means that could remedy these evils without bringing about still worse ones. Sedition was to be feared. Boethius told him that all the Manichaeans ought to be expelled from Rome and that, so that nothing of their impiety might remain there, a great fire should be lit in one of the public squares and their idols and writings burned in it.

It is not easy to guess where Boethius could have derived the confidence to carry out so bold a design. The popes did not possess the sovereign authority they have at present; the emperor Anastasius openly favored the Manichaeans [Col. 1443B] at Constantinople and throughout the empire, while persecuting the Catholics. Nor does it appear that Boethius had recourse on this occasion to Theodoric’s authority. Nevertheless, the matter was carried out as he had planned (Baronius, under the year 503). Whether Theodoric had given him a secret order, or whether what passed between that prince and Boethius on this occasion had been buried in oblivion, it is certain that, when the Manichaeans least expected it, their books and images were seized; a pyre was erected before the door of the Basilica (93) of Saint John Lateran; they were thrown upon it and consumed there. They were then all expelled from the city and sent into exile in various very distant places.

The magicians were not spared any more; but since the number and rank of the guilty required great precautions, these are the measures Boethius believed he ought to take.

[Col. 1443C] He knew that Theodoric detested them and that, when renewing the ancient laws of the Christian emperors, he had expressly forbidden all his subjects to practice any magical art. But, following the policy usual to a prince who feels his throne insecure and fears giving newly subjected peoples the slightest occasion for revolt, he affected to leave everyone complete freedom in matters of religion; and, content with having issued very wise ordinances, he took little trouble to punish those who violated them. It was therefore necessary to renew the prince’s attention and stir him to action.

One day Boethius, while speaking with him about what the magicians were doing in Rome, (94) represented to him that it was the indispensable duty of a Christian king to punish crimes that directly attacked the majesty and independence of God, as magic did; that he could not be as just as he wished people to believe if the most enormous abominations found impunity beside his throne; that such conduct debased sovereign authority and opened the way to revolt, toward which peoples are all the more readily inclined when they know that the laws can be violated with impunity. “Most of the barbarian nations that seek to invade the lands of the Empire also practice magic,” he added. “If you allow your peoples to devote themselves to it, they will be more disposed to join your enemies. The most virtuous men who attach themselves to Your Majesty do so because you fear God; if they come to perceive that, through your silence, you are fostering these abominable impieties, their zeal for your service [Col. 1444A] will inevitably cool. If you dissemble, everything is to be feared.”

“That is not my intention,” Theodoric replied, “and I certainly intend that the laws I have made shall be observed to the letter.”

“They will never be observed,” Boethius answered, “unless Your Majesty makes an example that inspires terror. You must begin with the persons of highest rank, who are, as it were, the leaders of this impious sect.”

The king was astonished to hear Boethius say that the nobility of Rome and the principal members of the Senate had defiled themselves with these abominations (Cassiodorus, Letter 22). After having Argolicus, prefect of Rome, make still more exact inquiries into all the circumstances of the affair, he ordered him to conduct a thorough investigation of the guilty parties. Basilius and Praetextatus, two distinguished senators, were accused. At the same time Theodoric ordered Count Arigerne to seize them (Cassiodorus, Book IV, Letter 22). [Col. 1444B] He did so without difficulty, because the inquiries had been conducted very secretly.

Under the ordinary laws, these senators were to be judged by the entire Senate. But, since they had too much influence there, being related by marriage to most of the senators, and since there was reason to fear that they would not be judged as severely as they deserved, Theodoric selected six men of acknowledged probity from the Senate and sent them a formal commission to judge the accused as a final court, according to the full rigor of the laws.

Symmachus, Boethius’s father-in-law, was appointed president of the commission (ibid., Letter 22). Decius, Volusianus, Caelianus, Maximianus, Count Arigerne, and Argolicus were the other judges. As for Boethius, he did not think he ought to serve, since he had acted as their accuser.

The criminals understood from the rank of the judges assigned to them that there was no mercy [Col. 1444C] to hope for. Having learned that the court’s orders expressly required proceedings against them according to the full rigor of the laws if they were found guilty, instead of thinking about a just defense, they believed it safer to seek their salvation in flight.

It is not known whether the jailers and guards were bribed, whether their friends forced open the prisons, or finally whether magic gave them some assistance, as Argolicus believed and reported to Theodoric. But it is certain that they found a way to escape, and that two days later the prefect informed the king that the prisoners had fled, and that, despite every effort that could have been made to guard them or pursue them after their escape, it had been impossible to discover what had become of them (ibid., Letter 23).

Theodoric gave orders that they be sought everywhere, but without success: Praetextatus was never seen again (Cassiodorus, Book IV, Letter 23). Long afterward [Col. 1444D], Basilius was discovered and punished. He had left Rome disguised as a monk and, in that garb, had gone to the bishop of Amiternum (St. Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 4). This was an ancient city of the Abruzzo, a province of the Kingdom of Naples, of which only the ruins now remain. This prelate [Note: [Col. 1444D] He had been in Rome several years earlier at the council convened there by Theodoric to judge the great affair of Pope Symmachus, who had been falsely accused by his enemies.] had a reputation for receiving graciously those who professed piety.

In the bishop’s presence (98), Basilius perfectly played the part of a solitary and asked the bishop to point out to him an enlightened superior who could guide him along the paths of the highest perfection. There was no one in his diocese more famous than the holy abbot Equitius, who had long governed a [Col. 1445A] celebrated monastery. Basilius earnestly begged the bishop to give him letters of recommendation so that he might be received there. But the bishop did more: he himself took him to the monastery. When they arrived, he took him by the hand and, presenting him to the abbot, said:
