“Here, Father, is a good solitary whom I am bringing to you. He greatly desires to live under your guidance and benefit from your holy instruction. You would give me great pleasure by receiving him into your community.”

Equitius looked at the solitary and, enlightened from above, immediately exclaimed:

“This is not a monk, but a demon, whom you are bringing to me.”

The bishop, taking the abbot’s reply as a rebuff, expressed his displeasure. But Equitius, far removed from the duplicity attributed to him, yielded at once to the bishop’s entreaties.

“He shall be received, since you wish it,” he said, (99) “but I could not refrain from revealing to you what I perceived in his eyes.”

[Col. 1445B] Some time afterward, an incident exposed the hypocrisy of the false solitary. The abbot Equitius, whose zeal was not confined within the bounds of his monastery, sometimes left it to proclaim the word of God to peoples who requested him. He even supported his preaching with striking miracles, and everyone eagerly hastened to hear him. At the same time, he governed a monastery of consecrated virgins devoted to Jesus Christ.

One of the youngest of them suddenly appeared dangerously ill and became convinced that she could be cured only by the monk Basilius, who had recently been received into the holy abbot’s monastery. She called for him with loud cries and earnestly begged the superior and the other sisters to send for him. They hurried to the monastery door and asked the man governing it during the abbot’s absence for Basilius. But this novelty seemed so strange to all the (100) brothers who had gathered that they did not believe they should decide the matter [Col. 1445C] on their own. They therefore resolved to send to Saint Equitius to learn what he wished them to do.

When the saint had heard them, he smiled. Then, addressing those who had come to him, he said:

“Did I not tell you clearly that this man was a demon and not a monk? Return quickly, and as soon as you arrive, let him be driven from the monastery. As for our sister, do not trouble yourselves about her: she will be healed immediately and will think no more of Basilius.”

It happened as the saint had predicted. When the brothers returned to the monastery, they shamefully expelled the magician. He readily admitted that the nun’s apparent illness had been the effect of his art, and that he had even used it several times since joining them in attempts upon the holy abbot’s life, but that his enchantments had always been ineffective. He said that he had possessed the power to carry the abbot into the air together with his cell, but [Col. 1445D] that (101) he had never possessed the power to harm his body. Perhaps he attributed to himself still greater power than he had actually possessed.

Thus expelled, Basilius did not know where to find refuge. He thought that he was no longer being remembered in Rome and that it would be easy for him to hide there. But it was precisely there that divine justice awaited him. He was recognized, and the people, inflamed by his presence, seized him without waiting for new orders from the court or the magistrate, erected a pyre, set it alight, and had him burned alive.

The zeal that the Romans displayed on this occasion in avenging the honor of God, together with the severity of the punishment, so astonished the other magicians that thereafter none were seen in Rome. Such were those zealous Levites of old to whom Moses said, on returning from an almost similar action, that they had consecrated their hands to the Lord by dipping them [Col. 1446A] in the blood of those idolatrous Israelites who had kindled his anger against his people.

Already, in the time of Pope Gelasius, there had been many complaints that the city (102) was infected with such abominable men. This pope had bitterly reproached the unfortunate Andronicus, who, by virtue of his office as prefect of Rome, ought to have stopped the course of these disorders, but in vain (St. Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 4). They had reached such an excess that even the pagans detested them and publicly expressed their fear that their gods might swiftly avenge themselves by means of the ordinary scourges with which they were accustomed to punish the most enormous crimes. Gelasius, lacking power in his hands, had contented himself with complaining and lamenting. Whether the leading members of the Senate were themselves stained by the same abominations, or whether at that time there was no physician firm or skillful enough to apply a suitable remedy to so great an evil, people tried to conceal it rather than undertake [Col. 1446B] to cure it. Boethius alone dared to undertake the task and successfully brought it to completion.

Not content with having halted the course of these abominations, he omitted nothing that could protect the Romans from such deadly assaults in the future. (103) He believed that he had found the source of these disorders in the ignorance in which most people were buried. The sciences were no longer cultivated. Far from displaying the noble emulation that their ancestors had shown for letters, the Romans took pride in having become stupid, following the example of the barbarians whose yoke they had endured. Military exercises, gaming, good food, sensual pleasures, and shameful idleness occupied their entire lives. Boethius believed that the young ought to be occupied from an early age, their minds opened and formed through knowledge of the workings of nature, which raises human beings to knowledge of their Creator and leads them there, as it were, [Col. 1446C] by the hand.

With this aim he conceived the plan of giving the public a complete philosophy. He had already translated Aristotle’s *Ethics* from Greek into Latin, together with his eight books of *Physics*, and had also supplied them with highly learned notes. These were supported by several clarifications and by another treatise reconciling the views of Plato with those of this philosopher. This work was (104) of great importance, because Plato was then universally esteemed and even venerated among the Romans. Aristotle’s philosophy would have run the risk of being poorly received if they had recognized that his views diverged from those of Plato, whom they called the Divine.

Boethius had found a way to reconcile the principles of the two philosophers, to show that both established the same foundations, and that the opposition observed between them was only apparent [Col. 1446D], arising merely from a failure to understand them properly.

To succeed more fully, he also wrote a very extensive commentary, of profound learning, on all the other parts of Aristotle’s philosophy. It contained everything necessary for forming morals, inspiring elevated sentiments, and raising human beings above themselves by giving them a correct idea of the supreme Being. But since all this knowledge presupposes the exercise of sound reasoning, without which it cannot be acquired, he composed an exact *Logic* to teach people to detect the illusions of false reasoning and resolve the difficulties that arise in the search for truth.

Aristotle had fallen far short of fulfilling the idea of a perfect logic. Two considerable defects [Col. 1447A] were found in it. The first concerned understanding terms. This philosopher had done for his disciples what a teacher would do who presented a book for a pupil to read before teaching him to recognize the letters. The second was that he had treated in a manner too general and too confused the different natures of which all beings in the world are composed.

Porphyry, once a Christian and a fellow student of Origen, had perceived this defect very clearly. He had tried to remedy it through the treatise on the Universals, which he composed as a kind of introduction to Aristotle’s *Categories*. But it was so obscure that nothing could be understood from it. Boethius explained it in an excellent commentary, just as he also explained Aristotle’s *Categories*.

His entire *Logic* is divided into two books. In the first he treats (106) the ante-predicaments—that is, the preliminaries that serve as a better entrance into knowledge of the predicaments [Col. 1447B], or universal natures. He thus explains univocal, equivocal, analogous, demonstrative, and other terms. In the second and third books he explains Aristotle’s ten Categories. He proves that substance, taken in itself and properly speaking, cannot have a true definition, and that one can only make a portrait of it drawn from its properties. Whereas philosophers ordinarily define substance as that which is not received in any subject, Boethius maintains that this is only its first and most essential property. He then proves that it would itself be invisible without the accidents with which it is clothed. This opens an easy way for us to answer the doubts of those who find it difficult to understand how Jesus Christ can truly be present in the holy Eucharist without being perceived there. Finally, in the fourth book he explains [Col. 1448A] certain affections that naturally follow substances when compared (107) with one another—what philosophers call the post-predicaments. This method appeared so correct that it has been followed to the present day in all schools.

While Boethius was using so profitably the moments left to him by the duties of public office, he was suddenly appointed consul by a joint decision of the king and the Senate (Boethius, Preface to Book II of Aristotle’s *Predicaments*). The occupations inseparable from this new dignity came very near to making him leave the work unfinished. But his desire to contribute to the formation of his fellow citizens’ minds enabled him to find resources where no one else could have found them. This new office, on the contrary, acted as a spur that animated him to the task. He explains himself in the following manner in the preface to the second book of his *Logic*:

[Col. 1448B] “Although the duties inseparable from the consulship in which I am engaged do not allow me to devote myself entirely to study, I nevertheless believed that the instruction of my fellow citizens formed part of the duties of my office, and that they would owe me some gratitude if, leaving to those who preceded me in these high offices the glory of having acquired for the Republic sovereignty over so many cities and vast provinces, I enriched Rome with the spoils of Greece and communicated to her all the light and wisdom that Greece possessed. Thus our ancestors made it both their duty and their honor to take and imitate whatever they found honest and praiseworthy among the nations they had subjected.”

Animated by these motives, he overcame every difficulty that might have stopped him and put the finishing hand to this work, most of which has escaped us.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1447]

[Col. 1447C] (109) The news of Boethius’s consulship had scarcely spread through Rome when all the city’s men of merit and distinction came in crowds to congratulate him. These were not the compliments inspired by a political and ever-self-interested spirit among courtiers: few people of that character appeared at his house. Instead, one saw those who were most distinguished by their piety, their zeal for religion, and their love of the public good.

As soon as he had received the purple robe, raised with embroidery and strewn with palms—the insignia of his dignity—the clergy and the Senate came to fetch him from his home. With a magnificence almost equal to that of the emperors, they led him amid the acclamations of the people to the great basilica and from there to the Capitol. But the joy occasioned by his elevation did not remain confined to Rome: the most distant provinces and the holiest bishops of the time shared in it. They did not conceal from him the great hopes that [Col. 1447D] all good people had conceived, nor what the Church and the Republic expected from him.

“Virtue,” they said, “is now secure beneath so powerful a protection. It may appear boldly, without fear of oppression, and abandon that timid and stern air that has until now kept it hidden, afraid to show itself. The insignia of the consul’s dignity—those fasces and weapons carried before him—are for it pledges of victory. It will triumph everywhere, because it is certain that he will use the authority in his hands only for its defense, and that every blow [Col. 1448C] he strikes will be aimed only at overthrowing its enemies.”

Ennodius [Note: [Col. 1447D] Ennodius was canonized by John VIII. His feast is celebrated on 17 July. See M. Baillet. He wrote an apology for Pope Symmachus in which he says that the supreme pontificate makes those who are elevated to it holy, or finds them already so, because most of the popes up to that time had in fact been holy. See M. Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. VII, p. 119.], bishop of Pavia, so well known in history for the embassies on which he was sent to the emperor and for the famous apology he published in defense of Pope Symmachus, wrote him on this occasion a letter that has been preserved to us. Here, approximately, are the sentiments of this great man:

“I rejoice,” he said to him, “at the honor conferred upon you, and I give thanks to God for it—not because he raises you above others, but because you are truly worthy of it. This is not a consulship given to an illustrious birth without any other merit (Ennodius, Book VIII, Letter 1). Whoever obtains it on that basis is unworthy to succeed the great Scipio. It is the reward of his ancestors’ virtue, not his own. Your consulship was indeed owed to the nobility of your origin, but it was owed still more to your virtue and to the many rare and eminent [Col. 1448D] qualities that shine in you. No blood is seen to have been shed, no provinces subdued, no peoples enslaved or fastened to your chariot, as was once seen at the entrance of those elevated to this high dignity—a sad prelude to an office that ought to be entirely devoted to preserving peoples, not destroying them.

“Now that Rome enjoys profound peace, and has herself become the prize and reward of the courage of our conquerors, a different kind of virtue is required in her consuls. Those warlike virtues are no longer appropriate. What is wanted are peaceful virtues. This [Col. 1449A] does not mean that your consulship lacks that advantage: it contains battles and victories won in very great number, since your entire life until now has been nothing but a continual struggle and a series of victories over error, vice, and ignorance—monsters infinitely more dangerous and more to be feared than all the barbarians who threatened the Empire [Note: [Col. 1449D] This letter provides certain proof that Boethius had not been designated consul as early as the year 487, as some historians have maintained, for Ennodius was not then a bishop or even involved in the clergy. He was scarcely fourteen years old at that time, since he died in 521 at only forty-eight years of age. Moreover, the whole course of the letter suggests that it was written to someone who had not yet held the office of consul, since it gives him the title of candidate, which would in no way suit a person designated consul for the second time. This led Cardinal Baronius to assign the letter to the year 510, the year in which Boethius was in fact designated consul by the Senate and appointed by King Theodoric.].”

(114) The hopes that had been formed regarding Boethius’s elevation, magnificent though they were, did not prove vain: he fully answered the expectations placed in him. From that moment he regarded himself as a man who ought to live only for his country and have no other interest (Book I of *The Consolation of Philosophy*, p. 4). All his views and all his actions aimed only at the welfare of the people, the peace, and the contentment of good men. To profound ability in affairs he joined inviolable integrity; thus he was proof against surprise and corruption. The firmness and courage with which he [Col. 1449B] maintained the sanctity of the laws and defended the poor and weak against the oppression of the wicked inspired even libertines with reverence for virtue. Raised above the fear of quarrelling with the ministers and favorites of the prince, who abused his confidence, anyone who attacked justice or innocence could expect to find in the new consul an inflexible man whom nothing could shake. He no longer recognized his relatives, his family (115), or his friends when the public good was at stake. Here is a remarkable example.

Ennodius, whom we have just mentioned, was closely united to him by the bonds of blood and friendship. Their union was founded not only on sympathy and the virtuous sentiments they shared, but also strengthened by a literary correspondence that bound their hearts and minds still more closely. It happened that the magistrates of Milan, intending to build or enlarge a [Col. 1449C] public square for the adornment of their city, demolished several houses. Since the space was still not sufficiently large, they took another house belonging to the bishop of Pavia. He had inherited it from one of his aunts, who had served as father and mother to him in his youth and whose memory was very dear to him [Note: [Col. 1450D] It appears that Boethius also had some claim to it, but that he had relinquished it to Ennodius as property of little use to him. Ibid., Ennodius, Book VIII.].

The bishop was distressed to see a patrimony taken from him to which he was deeply attached (Ennodius, Letter VIII, Letter 37). He complained several times to the consul and pressed him by letter to order that his house be preserved. But Boethius gave him no answer on this point, whether because he believed his relatives as detached from earthly possessions as he himself was, or because the affairs surrounding him prevented him from giving the attention he owed to the request. Boethius’s silence obliged the bishop to take another course and address the magistrates of Milan directly. He made it known to them that he was the consul’s close relative [Col. 1449D] and friend. At this name the magistrates immediately replied that they were ready to compensate him, but that they could not dispense with the house, because it absolutely had to be demolished in order to make the square regular. Since it had the honor of belonging to Boethius, they were willing to leave it to him to set the price. Ennodius accepted [Col. 1450A] this arrangement, but was greatly surprised when the consul informed him that he ought not only to consider it an honor and a pleasure to dedicate his house to the public good, but that it was unworthy of him to demand compensation for it, since (117) he did not need it to live, the bishopric of Pavia providing him with more than sufficient income for his maintenance.

What is most admirable in this conduct is that he was the first to do what he advised others to do. For if he urged detachment, it was only after lavishly distributing his possessions among the poor (Procopius, *The Gothic War*). Everyone had free access to him; it was enough to be unfortunate to be heard. He regarded citizen and foreigner with the same eye, because in their poverty he saw only Jesus Christ. Entering even the most secret and remote houses, those hospitals where infirmity joined to poverty makes the [Col. 1450B] members of Jesus Christ a spectacle deserving Christian compassion, and those solitary places, those sacred retreats where greed and love of the world had not yet gained entry, where people thought only of serving God and singing his praises, without anxiety about life or the morrow—there he distributed with open hands the immense possessions left to him by his (118) fathers, as well as everything that the prince’s favor and the emoluments of his dignities and offices could bring him. He was one of those men of mercy of whom Scripture speaks (Ecclesiasticus XLIV), whose piety was inexhaustible. One would have said that God had filled him with the goods of fortune only to show, in his person, how far the charity of a true Christian could extend.

One of his principles (Boethius, Preface to the Book of Aristotle) was that persons invested with dignity occupy Christ’s place in this world and must consequently model their conduct on his example. This divine Savior, not content with having given us everything, [Col. 1450C] also gave himself and spent his entire life relieving the unfortunate, healing the sick, and consoling the afflicted. It was therefore just that those who represented him here below should imitate him less in his power and greatness, of which he had rarely given signs, than in his infinite charity, which he had displayed on a thousand occasions. For great men, he added, are fathers of the people not only in order to command them, but also to nourish and relieve them. When one has received much from God, one must also give much; and it is inconceivable ingratitude toward him to pour out consolations and benefits upon the poor only little by little, as though drop by drop, when God has poured them upon us with such profusion. This led a writer of our own day (Baillet, for 23 October) to say that Boethius, in his magistracy, had conducted himself as the holiest bishop might have done in governing his diocese.

[Col. 1450D] In their processions the consuls were always surrounded by a large number of officials and preceded by their guards. As for Boethius, he allowed only those who carried the insignia of his dignity, and one saw around him only a crowd of poor people who gave him a thousand blessings, praised his charity, [Col. 1451A] or asked him for new proofs of it.

Rome was not the only city to experience its effects; all the provinces of the Empire shared in them. Whatever he could not do from his own resources, great though they were, he supplied through his influence, authority, counsel, or remonstrances. More than once he was seen to expose not only his peace of mind but also his property and his life for the relief of the people.

Campania and the provinces neighboring Rome had for several years suffered a cruel scarcity. Since grain was lacking, the price of wheat rose day by day, and famine, with all that it brings of horror, was already making itself felt everywhere (Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book I, prose 4). The prefect of the praetorium [Note: [Col. 1451D] This prefect may well have been Faustus, to whom Theodoric addressed several rescripts and whom he honored with the title “Your Illustrious Magnificence” (*Illustrem Magnificentiam tuam*). He even ordered him to put an end to certain new exactions on the grain of Apulia and Calabria, of which the merchants complained (Cassiodorus, Book II, Letter 26).], who had supervision of the royal revenues and responsibility for supplying the armies, nevertheless ordered a very considerable quantity to be transported out of these provinces.

[Col. 1451B] This could not be done without reducing them to the utmost extremity, and Boethius could not learn of it without being deeply moved by the deplorable condition to which they were about to be reduced. He opposed the execution of the prefect’s orders and reproached him so vigorously for his injustice that the man did not dare proceed. But the consul had to endure all the fury and outbursts of which this avaricious and cruel man was capable. Since he cloaked his undertaking in the specious pretext of the prince’s interests and the needs of the state, the affair caused a great stir and reached Theodoric’s ears. The king wished to investigate it himself, and Boethius defended the public cause so well that the king was compelled to yield to his arguments.

This brilliant action won him such authority over people’s minds and such confidence among the populace that he began to become formidable to Theodoric. But the consul did not for that reason relax any of his customary firmness; indeed, he gave a new impetus to his zeal: [Col. 1451C] the more credit and authority he possessed, the more obliged he believed himself to be to employ them for the relief of his neighbor. In his view, it was to make oneself unworthy of God’s favors not to use them to undertake great things for His glory. Sustained by this thought, he conceived great designs and embarked upon still greater enterprises for the public good.

The provinces of the Empire were then exposed to great vexations; the taxes were excessive, and commerce had been ruined by the severity of the conditions imposed upon it. The officers charged with collecting the royal revenues, finding impunity with the prince by sharing the proceeds of their exactions with his favorites, everywhere left traces of their avarice (Bail. as cited above). Boethius, who had long groaned at the sight of so many injustices, resolved to put an end to them. He first tried to inspire the Senate with the same sentiments, but found few senators capable of them. Symmachus, Tertullus, and a few others, it is true, [Col. 1451D] lamented with him the deplorable condition in which the Republic found itself; but since they were his allies, their sentiments made no more impression on people’s minds than Boethius’s own. Besides, they were few in number, and their voices scarcely gave (123) any greater weight to his undertakings.

Since they could not openly declare themselves without risking the burial, in the ruin of a single man, of several great families—and consequently depriving the State of the hope that it might one day recover through the courage and good government of these virtuous senators—Boethius believed that he ought to sacrifice his interests, his family, and his life for the good of his country. He took upon himself alone the entire burden of the office and all the risk, and began to act for the public good with all the ardor of his zeal. His remonstrances were not fruitless, for among Cassiodorus’s letters one finds several rescripts from Theodoric addressed around this time to the prefects and superintendents of the provinces, ordering them to put an end to the disorders of which merchants had complained to him, particularly the exactions and monopolies practiced in connection with grain.

There were at Theodoric’s court two notorious leeches who devoured the substance of the people and fed upon the blood of the unfortunate. Both were Goths by nation and had acquired absolute power over the king’s mind. One was called Conigast: his possessions were immense and his authority boundless, but his pride was greater still, and his avarice more insatiable. The other was named Triguille: he had charge of the king’s household. Although he did not love Conigast—for there can be no true friendship among the wicked—he nevertheless came to a perfect agreement with him whenever plunder was at issue (Boethius, *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, book I, 4). Then they combined all their strength and assisted one another; one had to be very powerful or very skillful to escape them. Triguille possessed all Conigast’s bad qualities, and if one noticed any difference between them, it was that one was more deceitful and the other more cruel.

The entire occupation of these criminals was to search everywhere, in the provinces and even in Rome, for those who possessed property but lacked the credit and support needed to defend it. They especially targeted widows and orphans. Without any legal proceedings and on their own authority, they seized their estates, or, on some false accusation, had them condemned to exile, and then easily obtained from the prince the confiscation of their property. They had made themselves so fearsome that [Col. 1452C] no one dared oppose their tyranny. Those who had attempted to resist it had unfortunately learned what these men were capable of; consequently, people preferred to let themselves be stripped of their possessions rather than defend themselves and, by defending themselves, risk losing their liberty or their lives along with their property.

It was against these two public scourges that the consul believed he ought to rise up most vigorously. At the first injustice they committed, they found him confronting them; believing that they had to deal only with a poor widow whom they were oppressing, they discovered that the consul himself had taken up her cause. He pressed them so forcefully that they were compelled to return what they had usurped. He would have ruined them utterly if Theodoric had been less prejudiced in their favor.

Boethius showed the king that they had diverted and concealed immense sums; that less than a tenth of what was collected in his dominions ever entered his coffers; that during the past four or five years these two criminals had ruined, through their vexations, violence, or [Col. 1452D] false accusations, more than sixty families; that their cruelty was driving the people to despair; and that there was reason to fear that it would lead them to revolt if the matter were not remedied as quickly as possible.

But how difficult it is to open the eyes of a prince who finds himself obsessed by men of Triguille’s and Conigast’s character! Prejudiced in favor of a minister whose skill has made him indispensable and whom he believes he cannot do without, he is incapable of being moved in the least by the most urgent motives or the strongest reasons. He fears being deceived and deprived of the assistance he needs. These two criminals had the skill to ward off the blow that should have [Col. 1453A] struck them down. They were Goths, as has been noted, whereas Boethius was a Roman. They made the king understand that this was a Roman scheme intended to place him under guardianship: after removing his most faithful servants and managing to distance from his person those of his own nation who were capable of serving him in the ministry, the Romans would reduce him to having only Romans around him. Once he had entrusted them with all his authority, they would seize control of the government and leave him nothing but the shadow of kingship.

Whether Theodoric believed them or simply did not wish entirely to lose men whom he had honored with his confidence, he left them unpunished. Nevertheless, he appeared so convinced of the consul’s uprightness and integrity in administering his office, and so astonished by the firmness of his zeal for justice, that they clearly saw they must not fall into his hands a second time. They restrained themselves for some time; the public benefited from their well-founded apprehension; and they concealed their hostility toward Boethius while awaiting an opportunity for revenge. Thus passed the year of his consulship, which won him much glory before men and infinitely greater merit before God, whom he had always kept in view in all his undertakings.

(128) What particularly distinguished Boethius in this consulship was that he exercised it alone (Papebroch, on 27 May, p. 704). This was not only a mark of very particular honor but also proof of his outstanding ability and certain testimony to the confidence that the prince and the Senate placed in him (Baronius, under the year 510). I therefore cannot see what reason could have led the annalist of Rome, contrary to the judgment of the authors, to give him Eutharic as a colleague, since Eutharic was not designated consul until 517 (Cassiodorus, *Chronicle*).

Boethius would have had much to suffer from such a colleague [Note: [Col. 1453D] He was the king’s son-in-law, having married his daughter Amalasuntha, and consequently enjoyed great influence at Theodoric’s court. Some Jews of Ravenna came to insult the Catholics in the church where they had assembled to sing the praises of God. After the service, the Catholics went and set fire to the synagogue. The Jews brought their complaint to the king, and on Eutharic’s advice he ordered that the synagogue be rebuilt at the Catholics’ expense, and gave the Jews, as compensation, the chapels of Saint Stephen and Saint Sylvester of Verona.] He was a very wicked man, a sworn enemy of the Catholics, always (129) ready to harm them whenever an opportunity arose, as he showed only too clearly in the affair of the Jews of Ravenna when he was made consul.

The court, tired of staying in Rome, went to spend some time at Ravenna, and Boethius was ordered to follow it. Hardly had he arrived there when Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, was brought before Theodoric to answer an accusation of treason. Arles then belonged to Theodoric, as we have already noted; he maintained there a strong Gothic garrison to defend it against the Franks, who had already made several attempts to seize it. I do not know by what chance they attempted to scale the walls at a time when the city was poorly guarded. The storehouses lacked all the provisions and military supplies that were necessary, and it came very close to succumbing to the efforts and valor of the Frankish troops; nevertheless, they were repulsed.

After the Franks withdrew and the alarm had subsided (*Life of Saint Caesarius*, book I, no. 9), [Col. 1453D] so bold an action gave rise to much reflection. People believed (130) that the Franks would never have dared undertake such an enterprise unless they had some intelligence within the city. At that point, two ecclesiastics dissatisfied with their bishop came before the governor and accused him of maintaining secret communications with the enemy, adding that it was highly probable that through him they had learned the condition of the fortress. The officers did not investigate the matter further. Without considering that the two accusers might be suspect, since they had long displayed their resentment toward Caesarius, who had often reproved them for their misconduct, they seized him and sent him to Italy.

The affair was delicate, and the saint had everything to fear from a heretical court. He needed a protector who would take up his defense and make his innocence known. But where could one find such a person, and who would dare at court to take the side of a man accused of a crime against the state? Could this be done without making one’s loyalty suspect and exposing oneself to disgrace? The (131) court is ordinarily a foreign land to the saints, and Theodoric’s court was more foreign than any other to the holy bishop of Arles. He knew only Boethius, by the reputation that his virtue had won for him throughout all the provinces of the Empire; so he appealed to him.

Although this minister knew that Theodoric was prejudiced against the bishop and that the officers of the garrison at Arles had given him a highly unfavorable account of him, he was not guided by the false maxims of worldly sages and was willing to take responsibility for the accused man’s defense. Anyone other than Boethius would have refused it. Caesarius was the bishop of a frontier city, accused by his own ecclesiastics and certainly known to have close relations with the sons of Clovis, who, like him, professed the Catholic religion. This was a strong prejudice against him. One would initially have thought that he might well have informed them of the condition of the city and invited them to conquer it.

But the saints reason in a wholly different manner from worldly people. Since they know (132) that whoever is faithful to God is also faithful to his prince, and that one withdraws from the obedience owed to the Creator as soon as one withdraws from temporal authority, Boethius knew the bishop of Arles to be a man of eminent holiness, far removed from all secular intrigues and [Col. 1454C] entirely occupied with the care of his flock. He was soon persuaded of his innocence and believed himself obliged to make it known to the king.

But God, who reserved to Himself the task of making it known—He who holds the hearts of kings in His hands—so turned Theodoric’s heart in Caesarius’s favor that the bishop’s journey to court won him infinitely more glory than his enemies had intended to bring him shame.

No sooner had the holy bishop been admitted to the king’s presence than the prince felt seized by holy fear and profound veneration for him. He rose from his throne, uncovered his head, and received him so favorably that the entire court was astonished. Without saying a word to him about the complaints that had been made against him, he asked whether he was not very tired from the journey, what his Goths were doing in Arles, whether he was satisfied with them, whether the people were not being oppressed by his officers, and whether they were observing [Col. 1454D] exactly the discipline and orders he had prescribed for them.

This was a strange surprise for the entire court, which had expected nothing less than so favorable a reception. But its astonishment was even greater when, after the bishop had withdrawn, the king addressed the courtiers surrounding him and said: “May God punish those who have caused this holy man to make such a long journey for nothing! I trembled when he entered; he has an angelic face. It is not permissible to think ill of so venerable a prelate.”

The prince did not stop there. As soon as he learned that the bishop had returned to his lodging, he sent him, through one of his principal officers, a silver vessel weighing sixty pounds, together with a purse containing three hundred gold sous [Note: [Col. 1455D] Valuing the gold sou according to the standard previously established, which is the lowest estimate, the three hundred sous amounted to nearly seven thousand livres in our currency.] (134) The bearer was instructed to accompany the gift with a message, whose exact wording was as follows: “The king asks you, holy bishop, to accept this vessel, which he gives you, and to use it for love of him.”

Caesarius smiled and, without explaining what he intended to do with the gift, received it respectfully. But since the spirit of poverty that animated him did not permit him to keep it for his own use, he had it sold and immediately used the proceeds to ransom several captives. His friends were alarmed by this conduct; they feared that, if it came to the prince’s knowledge, he might be offended. But the saint’s charity produced the opposite effect.

The king was informed of it. It was even added that the entrance to the lodging where the holy bishop was staying was surrounded by so many poor people that no one could approach it, and that he had already distributed among them all the gold His Majesty had sent him. [Col. 1455B] Theodoric could not help admiring such great disinterestedness. He praised him again in the presence of his entire court and acknowledged that he regarded as a very (135) particular favor from heaven the grace God had granted him of seeing this apostolic man.

Nothing more was needed to set many courtiers into motion. It became a contest to see who would hasten to show him the greater honor and bring him alms to distribute to the poor with his own hands. But nothing was more admirable than the contest of humility between Boethius and Caesarius. The latter attributed the favorable reception he had received entirely to the minister’s zeal and to the gracious words he had spoken to the king. The former, on the contrary, maintained that the bishop owed it solely to his virtue. Neither could believe that he had played any part in an event so extraordinary and unexpected, and both agreed that it was the work of Him who turns human wills as He pleases, and who knows, whenever He wishes, how to make what seems destined to cover His chosen ones with shame and confusion serve their glory and sanctification. God did even more and wished to confirm by a miracle the opinion held at court of the great holiness of the bishop (136) of Arles. At his mere prayer he perfectly healed a young Goth, a servant of the praetorian prefect and greatly dear to him, from whom nothing more than his last breath had been expected.

These events made Caesarius’s name so famous throughout Italy that there can be no doubt that he would have brought great advantages to the Catholic religion there had the needs of his Church allowed him to remain for a long time. But duty continually called him back. The young man whom he had snatched from the shadows of death wished to follow him and, out of gratitude, devoted the rest of his days to his service.

However eager Caesarius was to rejoin [Col. 1455D] his beloved flock, Boethius could not consent to his departure until he had promised to pass through Rome and inform the pope of the state of religion in Gaul. Caesarius was sufficiently inclined to do so, both to satisfy his devotion to visiting the holy places and to have the pope settle certain disputes he had with the bishop of Vienne in Dauphiné concerning the extent of his jurisdiction. But this desire yielded to (137) his longing to return to his Church, from which he had been violently torn away. He knew how distressed it had been when it saw him loaded with chains and taken to Theodoric’s court; it still did not know [Col. 1456A] what the outcome of his journey had been, and it was only right to relieve its anxiety.

Boethius, who always preferred the general good of the Church to the particular good of some of its members, was convinced that the holy bishop’s presence would accomplish in Rome what letters and recommendations could not, and would further cement the union—so necessary—between the Church of Gaul and the Apostolic See. He therefore did not believe that he ought to yield to the bishop’s wishes. He continued to insist upon the journey to Rome and, to remove the difficulty Caesarius raised, advised him to send one of the priests accompanying him back to Gaul to inform his Church of what had happened at Theodoric’s court while Caesarius himself departed from Rome.

Caesarius accepted this compromise, and hardly had he arrived in Rome when, through the benefits he derived from his journey—whether (138) for his Church and for himself personally or for all the Churches of Gaul collectively—he recognized how right Boethius had been to urge him to undertake it. The letters of this faithful friend to the pope and the Senate had preceded him, and contributed greatly to the favorable reception he received from the vicar of Jesus Christ and the leading senators.

In Rome he was regarded as an angel sent by God and treated with the same honors that had been shown him at Theodoric’s court. The pope granted him everything he could desire for the peace and honor of his Church and confirmed its privileges. Concerning the disputed jurisdiction between the bishop of Arles and the bishop of Vienne, he ordered that the regulations established by Pope Saint Leo should be followed. Accordingly, the bishop of Vienne was to exercise jurisdiction only over the Churches of Valence, Tarentaise, Geneva, and Grenoble, while the bishop of Arles was to have jurisdiction over all the others that the bishop of Vienne disputed with him.

At the same time, it was ordered that the bishop of Aix should submit (139) to the mandate of the bishop [Col. 1456C] of Arles, both in matters concerning councils and in other ecclesiastical affairs. His Holiness also condemned several abuses that had arisen in Gaul, including the alienation of Church property, except when such property was granted for life only to clerics, in consideration of their services, or to monks and certain outsiders who had likewise rendered important services to the Church (vol. IV of the Councils, epistle 5, p. 1295).

There is reason to believe that this was the origin of ecclesiastical benefices, since before that time clerics possessed no property individually and received only manual distributions for their subsistence, weekly or monthly, from the property that the Church held in common.

To all these marks of honor, the pope added others on his own initiative. He gave Caesarius the pallium, an ornament of distinction, for himself and his successors in perpetuity. He permitted his deacons to wear dalmatics [Note: [Col. 1456D] Saint Gregory, book VII, epistle 113, says that the deacons, and even the bishops, still had only tunics with narrow sleeves.] (140) similar [Col. 1456D] to those worn by the deacons of the Church of Rome. Finally, he made him and his successors, as bishops of Arles, his legates by birth in Gaul and Spain, and granted them a right of precedence in all the ecclesiastical affairs of those kingdoms.

To preserve for posterity the memory of what he had established, he issued authentic bulls that would be everlasting monuments to the veneration that the pope and Rome had for Caesarius’s eminent holiness. He entrusted him with a brief addressed to all the bishops of Gaul (vol. IV of the Councils, epistle 9, p. 1309), in which he again praised their colleague, the bishop of Arles. He declared that he had appointed him his vicar in their provinces [Col. 1457A] and exhorted them each to remain content with the rights anciently attached to their sees, without seeking to enlarge them through the favor of the great.

Some of them had already appealed to secular powers in order to acquire new rights. This was something of which the bishop of Arles had complained (141), particularly to the pope. Nothing seemed to him more unworthy of the episcopal character, or more degrading to it, than the eagerness he had observed in some of his colleagues to court the great in order to obtain from them, through base compliance, favors that they would more willingly grant to the holiness of their lives and the eminence of their character if they knew how to sustain it through truly apostolic virtues.

These regulations of the Holy See made in favor of the bishop of Arles are contained in two decretals: one dated 6 November, during the consulship of Probus, in the year 513; the other dated 11 June of the following year, 514, during the consulship of the Senator—the same person as Cassiodorus.

It was a great consolation to Boethius when he learned of the reception given to the holy bishop of Arles in Rome. He had played a significant part in it, for the pope, Symmachus, could not have honored or loved Caesarius more. Through such brilliant actions this holy pontiff brought his life and pontificate to an end. God took him from this world one month later, and the deacon (142) Hormisdas, born at Trucinoné in Campania, was elected in his place. He was no less closely united to Boethius than his predecessor had been, and Boethius, for his part, rendered him no less important services than those he had rendered to Symmachus.

During Hormisdas’s pontificate, Boethius was the soul of his council. No important matter arose in the Church without his participation. But his zeal for the glory of God and the exaltation of the faith was not limited to Rome’s needs alone; his care extended to the most distant kingdoms. If he grieved over the losses suffered by the Church through the schisms [Col. 1457C] that divided her and through the particular quarrels and disputes that impaired the charity of the faithful, he regarded her advantages as his own and, so to speak, triumphed in all her victories.

He therefore saw with infinite joy, at the feet of Pope Hormisdas, the envoys of the Cimmerians, newly converted to the faith, pay homage to him and ask him for a bishop (Theodoret the Reader, book II, p. 567). But he never experienced greater joy than when he saw the end of the schism of Constantinople (143), which had divided the entire East for so many years. Since the extinction of this schism was the fruit of his counsels and labors, we cannot dispense with giving a summary of it and tracing it back to its origin.

After the Council of Ephesus had condemned Nestorius, the troubles did not thereby cease. His supporters were too powerful and still possessed too much influence not to make new efforts [Col. 1457D] whenever opportunities arose to recover their position. The heresy of Eutyches provided them with one of the most favorable such opportunities, and the division then broke out more violently than ever.

The Robber Council of Ephesus was one of its first and most disastrous consequences. The unfortunate Dioscorus, patriarch of Alexandria, who presided over it, caused error and impiety to triumph there for a second time, so that Saint Flavian, patriarch of Constantinople, became its victim, and all the Catholics remained for a long time in cruel oppression. Rome, despite all its power, could accomplish nothing in that tumultuous assembly; on the contrary, the Holy See was treated with the utmost (144) indignity in the persons of its legates.

The Council of Chalcedon, which assembled some time afterward, treated the matters with great moderation and equity and expressed itself on the disputed points in terms that were exceptionally clear [Col. 1458A] and intelligible. It therefore seemed destined to reunite minds and end the disputes. The emperor Marcian, who had convened it, had almost all the Churches receive it with respect; and since he was absolute in the Empire and knew perfectly how to make himself obeyed, no one dared rise against its decisions while he lived.

Everything was calm in appearance. But it is to misunderstand a person whose mind has once been corrupted by error to expect such prompt submission from him and to rely upon the peace that authority—however just it may be when acting alone—has established. People remain silent as long as they see that breaking the silence is dangerous. Once the danger has passed, they speak more loudly and rise up with greater insolence than ever. Ill will erupts in proportion to how long it has been restrained by fear of punishment: such has been the character of heretics in every age.

Human beings, in fact—and Easterners more than anyone else—are so excessively attached [Col. 1458B] to their own opinions and endure the affront of a just condemnation with such difficulty that, instead of submitting to the most legitimate authority, they first begin to regard their judges as their adversaries. Then, setting up an entirely new tribunal, they not only appeal there from their decisions but would also like to summon them before it and have them condemned as the teachers and patrons of error.

This is what happened particularly with regard to the Council of Chalcedon. The emperor Marcian, who kept the heretics under restraint, had no sooner died than the troubles began again, and the Church found herself shaken with greater violence than before. Here is the reason.

Although the Council of Chalcedon had acted with extreme moderation in all its decisions, and had even pardoned the bishops who had brought about or consented to Flavian’s deposition in the Robber Council of Ephesus, restoring them to their sees after they had represented that they had been compelled to subscribe by violence and had asked forgiveness for their cowardice, the Fathers nevertheless did not believe that they could refrain from punishing the author of the disturbance, who remained obstinate and rebellious. This was the unfortunate Dioscorus, patriarch of Alexandria.

After several petitions had been read in which he was accused of numerous crimes, he was summoned three times. When he refused to appear, the legates of the Holy See and the Fathers pronounced against him a sentence of deposition couched in these terms:

“Leo, archbishop of Old Rome, through us and through the synod, with the authority of Saint Peter, who is the rock and foundation of the Church and the foundation of the faith, strips Dioscorus of the episcopal dignity and declares him unworthy of all priestly functions.”

The Fathers unanimously confirmed the sentence. In consequence of this decree, the emperor Marcian exiled Dioscorus to Gangra and ordered the people and clergy [Col. 1458D] (147) of Alexandria to proceed with the election of a new patriarch.

However absolute the emperor’s power was, he nevertheless encountered resistance there, because Dioscorus had a powerful party in the city. Proterius was appointed in his place, but he could maintain himself there only with the assistance of guards whom the emperor was obliged to provide to defend him against the violence of the populace, which several times attempted his life.

As soon as news of the death of this deeply religious prince reached Alexandria, the people no longer restrained themselves and proceeded to the utmost extremes. It was Holy Week, three days before Easter in the year 457. While Proterius was in the baptistery performing the sacred functions appropriate to the season, the rebels came armed to the great church, selected a priest of Dioscorus’s party named Timothy Aelurus, had him ordained [Col. 1459A] bishop, installed him in the see of Saint Mark, and immediately went to the baptistery to find Proterius. They pierced him with a thousand blows, dragged his body through the streets with unparalleled inhumanity, burned it, and scattered his ashes to the winds.

Without showing any fear of the punishment deserved by so outrageous an act, they sent an insolent petition to the emperor Leo, who had just succeeded Marcian. They asked that the Council of Chalcedon be abolished, its decisions destroyed, and the sentence it had issued against Dioscorus annulled. This is what the Alexandrians did, and this too is what should be expected of every heretical party that has been treated with excessive leniency and allowed to gather strength when it could have been strangled at its birth.

The Emperor Leo found himself not a little embarrassed, seeing so many affairs upon his hands at his accession to the crown. There was no prospect of assembling a new council, since the disputed points of doctrine and faith had been fully [Col. 1459B] decided: nothing remained but submission, and it would have been needless to weary the bishops, who had scarcely returned to their homes. He therefore thought he ought to content himself with (149) consulting them by a circular letter; and, finding them all of one mind, he sent to Alexandria, expelled Timothy Aelurus, relegated him to the Chersonese, and installed in his place a Catholic priest named Timothy Salophaciolus.

The Alexandrians, naturally inclined to revolt, did not dare to stir so long as Leo lived, nor during the first years of the reign of his successor Zeno. But when that unfortunate prince was driven from his throne by Basiliscus, the latter, in order to win supporters, openly declared himself the protector of the party of Dioscorus. He expelled Salophaciolus from Alexandria, restored Aelurus after eighteen years of exile, and caused a decree to be published throughout the Empire that destroyed the Council of Chalcedon and the doctrine taught in the letter of the great Saint Leo. Most of his bishops, [Col. 1459C] cowardly and timorous men whose religion was regulated by self-interest or by the prince’s favor, subscribed to it—more than five hundred of them, including Peter Mongus, patriarch of Antioch. Although most of them had attended the Council of Chalcedon and had issued or confirmed its (150) decrees, they were sufficiently base, in condemning those decrees, to condemn themselves and cover themselves with eternal disgrace by destroying what they had established so wisely.

Salophaciolus was obliged to flee Alexandria and seek refuge in a remote monastery. It was then that the whole Eastern Church found itself torn by schism, for the uprising of its treacherous bishops only strengthened the courage of the defenders of the truth. The lower clergy, the monks—whose number was almost infinite—and the greater part of the people, strengthened by the bishops who had remained firm in the faith of the Council of Chalcedon, did not fear exposing themselves to the most violent persecutions in order to [Col. 1459D] maintain its decisions. A very large number of these generous defenders of the truth were driven from their churches and withdrew to Rome, the customary refuge of piety and the support of the faith.

Rome therefore could not remain ignorant of what was happening in the East, for the Holy See was too deeply concerned. The issue was not only to uphold the doctrine of the great Saint Leo, received with (151) universal acclaim by all the churches, but also to maintain the authority and dignity of a general council over which he had presided through his legates, and at which the impious Dioscorus—who wished to revive the errors of Eutyches—had been canonically deposed. [Col. 1460A] Communion was therefore broken between the churches of the East and those of the West. At Rome, all relations with the court of Constantinople ceased; and when the Westerners excommunicated the enemies of the Council of Chalcedon, some of the Eastern bishops were rash enough to carry their insolence so far as to excommunicate Pope Saint Leo by name.

Matters remained in this condition until the year 477 (Baron., under the year 477), when the unfortunate Basiliscus, who had become an object of universal horror—not only on account of his heresy, but still more because of his greed and cruelty—was abandoned by his troops, who went over to Zeno and restored him to the throne. No punishment seemed more appropriate to Basiliscus’s crime than to let him die of hunger. His wife and children (152) were caught up in his downfall, and the Catholics began to breathe a little more freely.

Peter Mongus was expelled from Antioch, and Salophaciolus was restored to the see [Col. 1460B] of Alexandria, although after the death of Aelurus the Alexandrian schismatics had elected this same Peter Mongus patriarch of Alexandria. But this calm did not last. The Emperor Zeno, who until then had favored the Catholics, suddenly changed course; and, by the strangest caprice ever seen, he conceived the idea of restoring Peter Mongus to the see of Alexandria.

[Note: [Col. 1459D] M. Dupin claims in his *Sixth Century*, p. 438, that Mongus, or Peter Mongus, was restored to the see of Antioch; but it was to that of Alexandria, [Col. 1460D] and this author contradicts himself. See M. Fleury, vol. VII, p. 37.]

This was so although, only a few years earlier, Zeno himself had expelled him from that see, as well as from the see of Antioch, where the schismatics had installed him. To disguise so rash an undertaking and to avoid provoking the Catholic party, he devised a decree of union couched in the most deceptive terms. It did indeed treat the mystery of the Incarnation (153) in a thoroughly orthodox manner; it accepted the chapters of Saint Cyril and recognized the Nicene Creed as an infallible rule of faith. But it said not a word about the Council of Chalcedon or the letter of Saint Leo.

The Emperor wanted people to be satisfied with this decree, without pressing the matter further, and wanted those who subscribed to it to be recognized as orthodox. Mongus, who knew the purpose for which it had been drawn up, was among the first to subscribe it. The Emperor immediately declared that, since Mongus had been expelled from the see of Alexandria only because he was believed to be a heretic, and since he had now given certain proofs of the purity of his faith, there was no longer any reason to deprive him of it; and he gave orders for his restoration.

This is the decree called Zeno’s *Henotikon*. Those who conformed to it formed a third party in the Church. Some accepted the Council of Chalcedon; others rejected it entirely; while these people adhered to the edict of union without either accepting or rejecting the council, for which reason they were called *hesitants*. This last party inflicted a greater (154) wound upon the Church, and the Catholics suffered much more from it than from the others, because authority was on their side.

All the West rose up against Zeno’s decree. It was impossible to see without horror a prince who called himself Catholic arrogating to himself a right reserved to the Church and making himself judge of the most important matters of religion. In short, people said no less against it than, in later centuries, they would say against the Interim of Charles V.

But because they wished to spare the Emperor personally, all the thunderbolts of the Vatican fell upon Acacius, patriarch of Constantinople, who had approved the *Henotikon* and consented to the restoration of Peter Mongus to the see of Alexandria. He was expressly cut off from communion with the Roman Church; and the Emperor, finding himself offended in the [Col. 1461A] person of his patriarch, took cruel revenge upon all the Catholics in his dominions who refused to subscribe to his decree. All this occurred during the pontificate of Pope Simplicius.

Felix, who succeeded him, eagerly sought some favorable opportunity to bring the Emperor back to his senses and inspire him with more reasonable and just sentiments. He thought he had found one by sending to ask the Emperor’s protection for the Catholics and for the bishops of Africa, whom the Vandal king Huneric was cruelly persecuting. Huneric was an Arian, while Zeno was a sworn enemy of Arianism. For this purpose he sent a solemn embassy. Vitalis, bishop of Emesa; another bishop whose name is unknown; and Felix, a priest and defender of the Roman Church, were deputed.

[Col. 1461B] The stated purpose of this legation appeared to be solely to implore the Emperor’s protection for the Catholics against the Arians, as has just been said. But its true purpose was to strengthen the Eastern peoples in the faith of the Council of Chalcedon and, if possible, to recall the Emperor himself to that faith during the conferences the legates would hold with him.

But the Emperor—whether he had penetrated the intentions of the holy pontiff (Felix, Letter 6 to Acacius), or whether he had resolved to have (156) no further communication with the Roman See—far from receiving them with honor, as ancient custom required, had them arrested as they came ashore from their ships; and, at his command and at the urging of the patriarch Acacius, they were thrown into a dark prison. Their papers were seized, lest they should deliver to the Catholics of Constantinople the letters with which they had been entrusted for them, and nothing was omitted that might shake their constancy.

Threats and the harshest treatment were used to compel them to communicate with the patriarchs of Constantinople [Col. 1461C] and Alexandria. But the fear of a violent and imminent death, which was several times placed before their eyes, could not intimidate them.

The Emperor and his schismatic patriarchs then saw that they had to adopt other measures and try an entirely different course. They attempted to overcome by kindness and promises those whom threats and tortures had been unable to shake. A terrible example of human weakness: these two bishops (157), legates of the Holy See, wearied by the horrors and length of their imprisonment, at last allowed themselves to be ensnared by the attractions of freedom and by the caresses of worldly powers; they promised whatever was demanded of them.

They were immediately conducted with honor to Constantinople. There they publicly communicated with Acacius and recognized Peter Mongus as the legitimate bishop of Alexandria. They were then showered with gifts and honors and sent back to Rome, laden [Col. 1461D] with letters of compliment to the Pope from the Emperor and the patriarchs.

But Rome had already been informed of their conduct by letters from the Catholic bishops of the East and by those of the abbots and monks of Constantinople, who were dismayed by their fall; and even more accurately by the priest Felix, who had escaped from prison (Gelasius, *To the Dardanian Bishops*, Letter 13; Evagrius, Book III, chapter 20). The two episcopal legates, convicted of their prevarication, were deposed and excommunicated.

Far from Felix’s legation producing any benefit for the Eastern Church, it only increased [Col. 1462A] its evils. For the Pope, believing that he could not tolerate such insolence, assembled a council at which sixty-seven bishops were present (Volume IV of the Councils, p. 1073); there he again condemned the patriarch Acacius, who was deposed and excommunicated.

A cleric of the Roman Church, a bold and courageous man, willingly undertook to carry the sentence to Constantinople and formally notify Acacius of it. He did so by fastening it to the patriarch’s cloak [Note: [Col. 1461D] Some writers say that this cleric, the defender of the Roman Church, having gone to the monastery of Saint Dius, persuaded the Ace­mete monks to take charge of his commission; that they carried it out in the church itself; and that Acacius’s men, unable to tolerate their boldness, killed some of them, wounded others, and imprisoned several. Victor of Tunnuna, p. 487; Theophanes, p. 114; Nicephorus, Book XVI, chapter 17, etc.], as the patriarch was entering the church one Sunday to celebrate the divine mysteries.

Meanwhile the Emperor Zeno died in his schism, and Anastasius succeeded him. He was already sixty years old, and, wishing to live in peace, he left all the churches in the condition in which he had found them, leaving each bishop free to act (159) as he pleased with regard to the Council of Chalcedon. Never was confusion greater in the Church. In the East, the bishops anathematized one another, each following his own whim, with very little regard [Col. 1462B] for the rules of justice and truth.

Pope Felix died soon afterward and did not have the consolation of seeing peace restored. Before his death, however, he had taken the precaution of drawing up accurate memoranda, invested with authentic formalities, of everything that had occurred in the affair of Acacius, in order to inform his successors and posterity. They remained obscure for a long time, and we owe it to the learned Father Sirmond that they were brought to light and published together with the letters of this holy pontiff.

Gelasius succeeded him. During the five years he occupied the see of Rome, the affairs of the East remained in the same condition as under Felix. Anastasius, who followed him, was no more successful. Nevertheless, at the beginning of his pontificate, he thought that by writing courteously to the Emperor Anastasius he might induce him to procure peace for the Church (Cedrenus, p. 337).

The piety of which this Emperor had given great [Col. 1462C] examples during his private life may have led this Pope to entertain some hopes. But Anastasius had greatly changed his conduct since ascending the throne. Previously, he had risen punctually before daybreak to go to church, where he remained in prayer until the end of the offices; he fasted very frequently and gave great alms. The historians of his time, however, portray him as an exceedingly impious man who lived a highly disordered life.

Since Pope Anastasius had not obtained the satisfaction he had hoped for, nothing more could be expected but that God Himself would provide remedies for the evils overwhelming the Eastern Church, by delivering it from Anastasius, who only aggravated them from day to day. It would be difficult to say how many holy bishops he persecuted, how many he expelled from their sees under various pretexts—but in truth because they refused to anathematize the Council of Chalcedon and subscribe to Zeno’s *Henotikon*—how many others he drew into schism by corrupting their faith with [Col. 1462D] gifts or threats, or how many unworthy bishops he placed in the principal sees of the Eastern Church.

As for Anastasius himself, no one knew what religion he professed: a Christian in name, but in fact a Manichaean like his mother, and an Eutychian like his uncle, he was equally favorable to both parties. Only the party of truth and the Catholics could find no protection with him.

God allowed His Church to groan for twenty-seven years under this Emperor’s tyranny. No day of deliverance appeared during the pontificate of Pope Symmachus. But in the first years of the pontificate of Hormisdas, [Col. 1463A] his successor, people believed that God had raised up Count Vitalian, prefect of the army, to rescue the Catholics from oppression (Theophanes, year 23; Marcellinus, *Chronicle*, 514).

Indeed, after the count had revolted and routed the imperial troops, the Emperor Anastasius was forced to ask for peace. It was granted on these conditions: that Macedonius, patriarch of Constantinople, and Flavian of Antioch should be restored to their sees; (162) that a general council should be assembled without delay; and that the Pope should be invited to attend in person in order to examine and judge the abuses committed against the Catholics.

In consequence of this treaty, which the Emperor, the Senate, and the magistrates of Constantinople promised and swore faithfully to execute, Anastasius finally wrote to Pope Hormisdas. He began by excusing the length of his silence on the harshness of the preceding popes and asked the Pope to come to Heraclea in Thrace on 1 July of the year 515, where, he said, he had summoned a [Col. 1463B] general council to calm the disturbances in Scythia [Note: [Col. 1463D] He apparently means the disturbances caused by the proposition “One of the Trinity suffered,” and by certain similar propositions advanced by the monks of that province. The subsequent outcome of these propositions will be seen later.], without saying a word about the disturbances in the other churches.

The least discerning people immediately realized that the Emperor was not acting in good faith and that he only wished to gain time in order to compel Vitalian (163) to withdraw and dismiss his troops. Nevertheless, Pope Hormisdas, so as to have nothing for which to reproach himself, sent him legates (the *Liber Pontificalis*, under Hormisdas). The famous Ennodius, bishop of Pavia, was placed at the head of the legation. His assistants were another bishop named Fortunatus, Venantius the priest, Vitalis the deacon, and Hilarus, notary of the Roman Church.

At the same time, an excellent set of instructions was placed in their hands, in which prudence and charity shone equally. This document is one of the oldest and finest surviving works of its kind. But everything proceeded through legations and embassies on both sides, without any conclusion being reached.

The Pope rightly wanted, as a preliminary to peace, the name of Acacius, [Col. 1463C] the first author of the schism, removed from the Diptychs, or sacred tablets, of the Church. The Emperor resisted this on weak and wholly groundless pretexts, such as, perhaps, fear of a sedition in Constantinople.

But at last God cast a merciful glance upon His afflicted Church by exercising His just vengeance against its persecutor. Tired, so to speak, of waiting for him to repent, He struck him with lightning while he was in his palace, on the night of 10 July 518, at the age of eighty-eight (Marcellinus, *Chronicle*, p. 330; Baronius, under the year 518, p. 693).

His constitution was not impaired by so advanced an age. He was so robust and of so strong a constitution that he might still have expected a long succession of years. Proclus, a skilled mathematician, had predicted to him some time earlier that he would perish by fire. To make this prediction false, Anastasius had caused an enormous cistern to be dug in the middle of his palace; every apartment opened into it by a gallery. He thus [Col. 1463D] believed himself protected from accidents of fire, whatever direction the flames might take in his palace.

But there is no wisdom against God; only repentance could have stayed His raised arm, ready to punish him. Thunder had rumbled throughout the preceding day, and all Constantinople seemed to be on fire, so fiercely had the storm gathered. Toward evening the thunderclaps grew more frequent, with terrifying crashes. The Emperor was frightened; running from apartment to apartment and from chamber to chamber, he sought a refuge where he might be (165) safe from the avenging hand of God that pursued him.

When he reached the place where his destruction had been decreed, he was struck alone, and afterward the storm ceased.

Justin, whose head Anastasius had resolved to have cut off, was elected in his place. He was captain of the guards. Having begun military service as a simple soldier, he had risen to this dignity through every rank of the army. He could neither read nor write, but he was a good Catholic and exemplary in piety. God, it seems, chose him to restore peace to His Church; and Boethius contributed greatly to this through the wisdom of his counsel and the firmness of his conduct.

Although schism had prevailed under the Emperors Zeno and Anastasius, the greater part of the clergy and people had remained Catholic in their hearts. Convinced of the doctrine of the Council of Chalcedon, they suffered the oppression of the Church with extreme anguish, and only fear of persecution had kept them silent.

As soon [Col. 1464B] as it became known that Justin had ascended the throne and was truly orthodox, they no longer thought they ought to conceal their convictions. The Church of Constantinople was the first to make them manifest. Its patriarch, having entered the great church with his clergy according to custom on the Sunday immediately following the Emperor’s election, was proceeding toward his throne when the people stopped him and cried aloud:

“Long life to the patriarch! Long life to the Emperor and the Empress” (Volume V of the Councils, p. 178 and following)! “Why should we remain excommunicated any longer? Ascend, great patriarch, to the ambo and instruct your people. You are Catholic—what do you fear? Publish the holy Council of Chalcedon at once. Mary is the Mother of God; the faith of the Trinity is victorious; the Emperor is Catholic—what do you fear? Long life to the new Constantine!”

Repeating these acclamations several times, they pressed the patriarch [Col. 1464C] either to leave the church or to publish without delay the Council of Chalcedon and anathematize all heretics. John—that was his name—wanted them to await the Emperor’s consent, but the people gave him no opportunity. Seizing the doors, they declared that he would not leave the church until he had done what they wished.

There was no further possibility of hesitation. After consulting the twelve bishops who accompanied him, he finally ascended the ambo and addressed the people in these terms:

“You know, my very dear brothers, what struggles I endured for the Catholic faith when I was only a priest, and that I continue to uphold it, even to the point of exposing myself to death in its defense. Why are you alarmed? End the tumult. We recognize as orthodox all the councils that confirmed the faith of Nicaea, especially the Council of Ephesus and the great Council of Chalcedon.

“Following the canons and ordinances of the Fathers, we regard Severus [Note: [Col. 1464D] Severus was a monk whom the party of Dioscorus had installed in the see of Antioch after expelling its lawful patriarch. He had had the temerity to anathematize the Council of Chalcedon and the patriarch of Constantinople, who defended that council’s decisions.] as an intruder in the Church of Antioch; we regard him as an outsider, justly condemned on account of his blasphemies, and we anathematize him.”

The twelve bishops accompanying the patriarch likewise anathematized him. To make this declaration more authoritative, the people further demanded that a solemn feast be appointed for the following day, at which all the holy bishops who had attended the Council of Chalcedon, or who had suffered death or exile in its defense, would be commemorated. The archdeacon announced it.

The Emperor attended. When he arrived at the church with the patriarch, he was greatly surprised to hear [Col. 1465A] the people making new acclamations, as on the preceding day, and additionally demanding that the bones of Nestorius, Eutyches, and their most famous partisans be disinterred; that all those exiled in defense of the truth be recalled; that synodal letters be sent to Rome; and finally that the four general councils, together with the name of the great Saint Leo, be entered in the sacred Diptychs (169).

The patriarch might protest that, in order to proceed canonically, it was necessary to convene all the bishops of his patriarchate, but he was not heard. The people’s cries grew louder, the doors were closed, and the entire assembly declared that no one would leave the church until everything it had demanded had been done.

The patriarch could not avoid having the Diptychs brought and having entered in them the four general councils—Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon—together with the name of Pope Saint Leo. When this had been done, the people cried out with one voice:

“Blessed be the God of Israel, who has visited and delivered [Col. 1465B] His people!”

They continued this hymn, singing it antiphonally for a considerable length of time. Then the chanters were brought up to the ambo to intone the *Trisagion*. The Emperor and his entire court were deeply moved by the spectacle and could not restrain their tears.

Since all this had taken place in a somewhat tumultuous manner (Volume V of the Councils, p. 170), the patriarch John, who was a wise and well-intentioned man, thought he ought to confirm (170) by the authority of a canonical assembly everything that seemed to have been done merely through the violence of the people.

To make his proceedings more advantageous for the reunion of the Empire’s other provinces, he immediately assembled the bishops who were in Constantinople and its environs, together with the abbots of the monasteries, all of them honored with the priesthood except Enécius, superior of the Ace­metes, who was only a deacon.

The council was held on 20 July. But the patriarch, out of prudence, did not preside over it, nor even attend it, in order to leave the bishops and abbots who composed it freer to express their opinions and decree whatever they judged appropriate.

The monks, in great numbers, first presented a petition containing all the demands the people had made in the church during the preceding days. It was subscribed by fifty-four abbots. The Fathers granted their requests and consequently ordered that the memory of the patriarchs Euphemius and Macedonius—who had been unjustly driven from the see of Constantinople and sent (171) into exile by the Emperor Anastasius, where they had died—should be restored to the sacred tablets; and that, with regard to those who had been banished for the good cause and were still living, the Emperor should be asked to recall them; that the sacred tablets, with the name of Saint Leo—and then, in a syntactically defective surviving clause, “and received unanimously with submission and respect.”

As for Severus, the intruder in the patriarchate of Antioch, it was thought proper to judge him formally and with full consideration of the matter concerning him. One of his sermons was read before the assembly, in which he had pronounced an anathema against the Council of Chalcedon and against what it had defined. Nothing more was necessary.

The Fathers declared him himself worthy of an eternal anathema, deprived of all ecclesiastical functions and of the name of priest and Christian, and excluded from communion as a blasphemer (Volume V of the Councils, p. 186).

A synodal letter was drawn up in the name of the assembly. It was then presented to the patriarch of Constantinople, to the Emperor, to the Empress, and to the Senate, who received it respectfully and approved it by (172) their subscriptions. Authentic copies were made and sent to the patriarch of Jerusalem and to the bishops assembled with him, who likewise received them.
