Thus, in the East, the only patriarchates remaining to be brought back to the unity of the Church were those [Col. 1466A] of Alexandria and Antioch.

But the most difficult task was to reunite Constantinople with the West and with Rome, from which it had been separated for thirty-four years, ever since Acacius, patriarch of Constantinople, had been condemned by the Holy See. Although several of his successors had been thoroughly orthodox and had even suffered greatly in defense of the faith, they had always been deprived of communion with Rome because they had been ordained by Acacius or had not subscribed to his condemnation. This was precisely what prevented the reunion of the two churches.

The matter was among the most delicate and difficult to negotiate. Nevertheless, the Emperor Justin had taken the first steps by informing Pope Hormisdas of his election and asking him to contribute to the reunion sought by John, patriarch of Constantinople, and his other bishops. He had even already urged him to send capable men to the East to bring this great affair to its conclusion.

But the Pope was so discouraged by the bad faith of the Easterners [Col. 1466B] and by the useless legations sent to Constantinople, where the dignity of the Holy See had been dishonored and his predecessors and himself, in the persons of their legates, had been treated in the most outrageous manner, that he did not think he ought to yield to the Emperor’s first requests.

He regarded them as mere courtesies and replied to them in the same spirit. He remained convinced that most of the Eastern bishops did not sincerely desire reunion and would never do what was absolutely necessary to achieve it, even if they wished for it.

Pope Hormisdas’s decision grieved all good Catholics, and Boethius more than anyone else (the *Liber Pontificalis*, under Hormisdas). Since he loved God and the Church above all things, he was deeply distressed to see it torn apart by so cruel and long-standing a schism. He perceived some glimmer of an approaching peace in the advances [Col. 1466C] being made by the Easterners and believed that these advances should be handled with great prudence.

He spoke to the Pope and represented to him on this subject everything that his zeal could suggest that was most forceful and moving, in order to persuade him to respond to the Easterners’ overtures. But he could gain nothing over his mind. The Pope was inflexible.

The reasons he alleged were strong, and it was difficult to answer them:

“How,” he said, “can we act in this affair in a manner honorable to the Holy See? Let us suppose that the Emperor’s intentions are good and upright; that Counts Justinian and Vitalian, whose religion and faith cannot be suspected by us, support him; that he possesses over his bishops all the influence and authority you claim; and that the patriarch of Constantinople himself desires peace as sincerely as you believe.

“But can we grant them peace unless they condemn Acacius and everything he did, and submit to the anathema our council pronounced against him? They will never do so. For if Acacius is excommunicated and degraded from the priesthood, as the council decreed, then all the patriarchs of Constantinople who succeeded him, including the one who presently occupies that see, were intruded into it.

“They are excommunicated, since they communicated with Acacius while retaining his name in the Diptychs. What an outrage they committed against the legates of the Holy See! Has the law of nations ever been violated more insolently than it was in the persons of those whom my predecessor sent to them? Can I refrain from demanding reparation for this injury before listening to the peace proposals they make to us? Who knows whether those whom I send to them will not be treated in the same way again?”

Boethius clearly saw that the Pope was not entirely wrong, but his reasons did not seem conclusive to him, because affairs in the East had taken a different turn and he believed that something more should still be risked for the good of peace.

Thus, after several conferences, having been unable to influence the mind (176) of Hormisdas, and convinced moreover that reconciliation was much easier to accomplish than His Holiness believed, the general welfare of the Church led him to take measures at court to induce the Pope to be less exacting.

Justin claimed already to have received some grounds for displeasure from Theoderic, and on both sides preparations were being made for war. Boethius therefore went to Theoderic at Ravenna, reported to him all the steps the Easterners had taken to reunite with the Western Church, and what he himself had done to persuade Hormisdas to respond to them. He made him perceive the interest he had in maintaining good relations with the court of Constantinople, and how greatly it was to be feared that the emperor, angered by the refusal of the peace proposals he had caused to be made to the pope, might wish to avenge himself by ravaging [Col. 1467B] the undefended coasts of Italy. Finally, he presented the matter in so favorable a light that Theoderic resolved to compel the pope to yield to the Easterners’ requests. He had him come to Ravenna and, after speaking with him (177) about the necessity of preserving peace with Justin, finally persuaded him to send to Constantinople one of the most distinguished embassies that had yet been seen.

It consisted of five persons of outstanding merit. Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua, was its head—the very man whom Pope Saint Gregory mentions so honorably in the second book of his *Dialogues* (c. 35). Another bishop named John was assigned to him as associate, together with the priest Blandus and the deacons Felix and Dioscorus, all three from the clergy of Rome. For his part, the pope took every precaution imaginable not to expose the honor of the Holy See further and to prevent the Easterners, of whom he had every reason [Col. 1467C] to be suspicious, from taking his legates by surprise. He had a formulary drawn up and placed in their hands, ordering them to admit no one to their communion unless that person had first signed it.

This formulary expressly anathematized the patriarch Acacius and all his followers, established submission to the decisions of the councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon, and generally settled all the difficulties that (178) the Easterners might raise in order to evade those decisions. The legates departed bearing the instructions of the Holy See. Their journey was highly successful: the Easterners signed the formulary and subscribed to everything the legates required. In truth, this did not happen without a kind of miracle, and grace had to act very powerfully upon their hearts to overcome all the difficulties involved in concluding a peace so greatly desired.

The difficulty did not concern the condemnation of Acacius. The Easterners themselves agreed that it was just and that he had richly deserved it, because his whole life had been nothing but hypocrisy, [Col. 1467D] continual dissimulation, and a false policy that had led him to sacrifice everything to his interests and ambition: at one time condemning heretics when he saw that their party was not the stronger, and at another declaring himself for them when he noticed that the court favored them. In short, although he had appeared to take great care of his diocese and of all the churches subject to his jurisdiction, people nevertheless remained convinced that he had been a man without (179) religion.

But those most inclined toward peace and best disposed could not bring themselves to condemn the patriarchs Euphemius and Macedonius, Acacius’s successors, who were acknowledged to have been great defenders of the truth and who had even suffered exile, in which they died, in defense of the Council of Chalcedon, while Acacius was anathematized by most of the Eastern bishops and by the court of Constantinople. [Col. 1468A] To resolve this difficulty, which was no small one, it was agreed that they would be content to anathematize Acacius by name, say nothing about his successors, and merely erase their names from the sacred Diptychs. Thus the reunion of the two Churches was concluded, to the incredible joy of every rank of the empire, and the great Eastern schism, which had lasted thirty-five years, reckoned from the excommunication pronounced at Rome against Acacius in 484, was happily extinguished.

The patriarch John, to demonstrate to the pope his complete reconciliation and the union in which he wished to live with the Holy See, entrusted his legates with rich gifts for His Holiness, among them a gold chalice with its paten, adorned with jewels; two silver chalices; and two embroidered veils. The joy at Rome after the legates’ return was no less than it had been at Constantinople. Since it was known that the Church owed to Boethius’s zeal and vigilance [Col. 1468B] the conclusion of so difficult and important an affair, everyone came to congratulate him. It was then understood more clearly than ever that the faith of the saints often knows how to overcome the greatest obstacles and find openings where human reason and policy are helpless.

It is astonishing that M. Dupin (*Fifth Century*, p. 612), who could not have been ignorant of the entire course of this history, should have done so little justice to the memory of the popes who governed the Church during those unhappy times. Does he not, on the contrary, seem intent on placing all the blame upon them and making them responsible for the evils she suffered? For this is what he says:

> Even if Acacius had been more culpable than he was, something should have been conceded to the interests of peace, and the memory of a bishop whose beliefs were Catholic, and whose only fault was having displeased the bishop of Rome and shown a little too much compliance with the wishes [Col. 1468C] of his prince, should not have been persecuted with such severity.

If M. Dupin had taken the trouble to examine this point of history more carefully, or if he had wished to discuss it without prejudice against the Holy See, he would have spoken of it quite differently.

The simple account of what occurred during this schism would have shown him how culpable Acacius was, and that his entire crime did not consist in having displeased the bishop of Rome. For was it not Acacius who, after first condemning Peter Mongus and denouncing his impieties and errors to the Holy See, was the first to assist in restoring him out of compliance with the emperor? Was it not he who, instead of firmly opposing Zeno’s *Henotikon*, was among the first to embrace and sign it? Did he not even support it with all his strength and influence? Was it not he who imprisoned the legates of the Holy See and had them (182) treated in the most disgraceful manner, as has been noted, violating all the canons, all [Col. 1468D] the Church’s holiest rules, and the most inviolable law of nations? Did he not throughout his life make a disgraceful game and traffic of the episcopate, deposing and restoring countless bishops without any judicial form, according as his interests required?

Is it not just that, after so many excesses, he should at last have experienced the severity of the Apostolic See and felt the firmness of that solid and unshakable rock upon which Jesus Christ founded his Church, and against which all errors and everything that rises against God must be shattered? After so many excesses, can it be said that Acacius’s only crime was having displeased the bishop of Rome? Were not the sovereign pontiffs right to demand, as a preliminary to peace, the condemnation of a man so justly cut off from the body of the Church, and to refuse communion to anyone who refused to subscribe to it? [Col. 1469A] There was nothing excessive in this conduct; it was full of justice and wisdom, and M. Nicole speaks of it quite differently. (183) Since his opinion may carry great weight with M. Dupin, I thought I ought to report word for word what he says about it in his *Treatise on the Unity of the Church* (Book II, ch. 10).

> It is certain, he says, that the excommunication pronounced by Pope Felix III against Acacius, patriarch of Constantinople, was in itself entirely just in substance; for Acacius’s crimes were very evident, especially to the Roman Church. He himself had written to Pope Simplicius against Peter Mongus, depicting him as a heretic, a usurper, a child of darkness, and an adulterer who had attempted to usurp the Church of Alexandria during the lifetime of its lawful pastor, Timothy Salophaciolus. Indeed, it was on the basis of this information that Acacius had sent to Pope Simplicius that the pope condemned Mongus, whose crimes were otherwise quite evident, since he had been the agent of Dioscorus’s violence against Saint Flavian, archbishop of [Col. 1469B] Constantinople; of Timothy the Cat against Saint Proterius, archbishop of Alexandria; and was an avowed enemy of the Council of Chalcedon.

(184) Yet Acacius, notwithstanding an excommunication so lawfully procured by himself in order to drive John Talaia, elected archbishop of that city, from Alexandria—because John had not shown him sufficient deference and had failed to render him certain courtesies—nevertheless had Peter Mongus restored there by the emperor Zeno and communicated with him without the pope’s participation. According to the canons, he could not do this, since a legitimate excommunication by the first See, namely Rome, could not be lifted by a lower-ranking bishop such as Acacius.

It is true that he required Mongus to promise not to condemn the Council of Chalcedon. But, apart from the fact that there was no reason to trust his word, which he in fact violated repeatedly by anathematizing the Council of Chalcedon whenever he judged it useful [Col. 1469C] to his interests, it is certain that so avowed a heretic as Mongus, marked by such grave excesses, could be received only into lay communion, according to the order of the canons. Thus it was a highly irregular undertaking for Acacius to communicate with him as with the legitimate archbishop of Alexandria.

There were also several other clear violations of the canons in Acacius’s conduct, above all the violence he used against two bishops, legates of Pope Felix, which was utterly inexcusable. Thus M. Nicole spoke of the affair of Acacius; and so will all who love the truth and write without self-interest or passion always speak of it.

While the Church was being shaken by such violent storms and torn apart by the schisms and heresies of which we have just spoken, Boethius enjoyed in his heart the peace given by a pure faith and a good conscience. But, not content with the inward testimony borne to him by his conscience, he thought it necessary, for the edification of the faithful [Col. 1469D] in the circumstances in which they then found themselves, to make known his faith through a public profession, as he had received it within the Catholic Church, where he had the advantage of having been born (*Exposition of the Catholic Faith by Boethius*).

He did so in a short treatise found among his works under the title of his profession of faith: *Confessio* (186) *Boetii*. It is an excellent compendium of all the mysteries of the Christian religion and its principal doctrines, of the establishment of the Church from the creation of the world, and of the most important events that occurred within it up to the condemnation of Nestorius and Eutyches. He acknowledges sacraments instituted [Col. 1470A] by Jesus Christ as certain remedies for the wounds sin has inflicted upon human nature, particularly those caused by the sin of our first father; that since this sin man is by nature worthy only of punishment, and that he is delivered from it only by the grace of the Savior—a grace, he says, that cannot be attributed to any merit existing in man, for if it were owed to his merits, it would no longer truly be grace:

> *Ut natura nihil aliud nisi poenae submitteret. Gratia vero quae nullis meritis attributa est, quia nec gratia diceretur si meritis tribueretur*  
> “So that nature would be subject to nothing but punishment. But grace is attributed to no merits, since it could not be called grace if it were attributed to merits.” (*Boethius, ibid.*), etc.

He then establishes the necessity of good works, the immortality of the soul, and the catholicity, or universality, of the Church spread throughout the world: (187) two incontestable proofs of his doctrine, namely the authority of Scripture and universal tradition. The particular traditions of each Church follow, as do their private constitutions authorizing practices proper to them and different from those [Col. 1470B] generally received by the entire body of the Church. From there he passes to the account that every person must render to God after death for his entire life; to the general resurrection; to the particular resurrection of the righteous for eternal and blessed life; to the expectation of the Second Coming of Jesus Christ, in which the faithful must live; to the general destruction of everything corruptible; to the reward corresponding to the various merits of human beings; and to the assignment to each person, according to his works, of a place in which to dwell throughout eternity, immediately after the universal judgment.

He asserts that the blessedness of the saints consists in the vision of God, and that they will know and possess him clearly, insofar as a creature is capable of knowing and possessing him.

(188) That man was created to repair the loss of the angels; that he will be received into the heavenly city until the number of its citizens is complete; [Col. 1470C] that there God manifests himself in all his glory; that the Son of the Virgin is the king of that holy city; that joy there will be eternal; and that the continual praise of the Creator will be the delight, food, and occupation of all those blessed citizens throughout eternity:

> *Ut ex eis reparato angelico numero superna illa civitas impleatur, ubi rex est Virginis Filius, eritque gaudium sempiternum delectatio, cibus, opus, laus perpetua Creatoris.*  
> “So that, the number of the angels having been restored through them, that heavenly city may be filled, where the Son of the Virgin is king; and there will be everlasting joy—the delight, food, work, and perpetual praise of the Creator.”

Vallin, who gave us an accurate edition of Boethius’s short works in 1656, justly calls this treatise a little book wholly of gold, *libellus vere aureus*. It had not previously been printed, and he supplied it from two ancient manuscripts in the Royal Library, which he assures us are among the most authentic [Note: [Col. 1469D] “Of better quality.”]; from one in the library of Saint-Victor; from another in his own private collection; and from a fifth in the library of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, which he likewise says is very ancient. This little work was not unknown to Trithemius, since he cited it under the title *The Faith of [Col. 1470D] Boethius*.

Hardly had the Church begun to enjoy the calm secured for it by Boethius’s wise counsel and firmness when it found itself exposed to a new storm (*Vol. IV of the Councils*, p. 1612). Certain monks who had come from Scythia [Note: [Col. 1469D] This was European Scythia, now known by the name of the eastern part of Bulgaria.] stirred it up while the legates of Pope Hormisdas were at Constantinople. Imagining that Nestorius’s errors could not be properly refuted without receiving the following proposition as orthodox—“One of the Trinity became incarnate and suffered”—they wished to have it approved by the Church. Although they cited no explicit passage from the Fathers except one from Proclus [Note: [Col. 1469D] Proclus lived at the beginning of the fifth [Col. 1470D] century. He left several sermons found in the *Library of the Fathers*. He is honored as a saint in the Church.], patriarch of Constantinople, [Col. 1471A] they presented it as one of their purest expressions.

These (190) monks were led by Leontius and Maxentius. The latter was regarded as learned; the former was related to Count Vitalian, whom we have already mentioned and who had shown such zeal in maintaining the decisions of the Council of Chalcedon. Vitalian openly declared himself for their party and became its protector. But, since Count Justinian, the emperor’s nephew, always regarded him with a jealous eye, these monks found in Justinian, while Vitalian lived, a very powerful opponent.

Nevertheless, supported by Count Vitalian’s favor, they were bold enough to present a petition to the pope’s legates and to the patriarch of Constantinople. In it they accused Paternus, metropolitan of Scythia, and several other bishops of his province of heresy because they refused to admit their proposition. The legates could not hear this without sorrow. Fearing that it was a new device of the Greeks to prevent or delay the reunion, they avoided as much as possible entering into this new dispute, which they clearly foresaw would [Col. 1471B] require lengthy discussion and have no connection with the affairs entrusted to them.

But since the monks’ proposition had already divided all opinion at court, and since the emperor, who was well informed about it, wished their petition to be examined in order to calm the disturbances it had caused there, it became necessary to confer with them. The conference took place in the patriarch’s palace in the presence of the court. The Council of Chalcedon and the letters of Saint Leo were read; and, since nothing had been decided in them concerning the proposition, the legates declared that they could add nothing to the holy council, and thus dismissed the matter.

The monks did not stop there. Dissatisfied that the emperor had summoned them in order to compel them to submit to the bishops—among them their metropolitan Paternus, who had [Col. 1471C] come expressly to Constantinople and defended the opposing cause—they immediately set out for Rome. They hoped by their intrigues to secure acceptance there for the proposition the legates had rejected, together with several other propositions of a similar kind that they had advanced with equal rashness.

(192) The legates had already informed the pope by letter. Count Justinian had likewise written to him. He described these monks in their true colors, as disturbers who sought only to trouble the peace of the Church through innovations and empty subtleties. He asked the pope to make them feel the full force of his indignation by shamefully expelling them from Rome. He named only four of them—Achilles, John, Leontius, and Maurice—although they were far more numerous, as appears from the subscriptions to the letter they wrote shortly afterward to the bishops of Africa in order to draw them into their party.

Count Vitalian, who had declared himself their protector, neglected nothing to support them. He wrote forcefully to the pope on their behalf; and, since he had [Col. 1471D] great influence over the pope’s mind, his letter produced all the effect they could have expected. This pope, who possessed consummate prudence, seeing that the affair was becoming serious because of the rank of the persons involved, thought it necessary to proceed with great caution. Without disregarding either the reports of his legates or those (193) of Count Justinian, he first attempted to win the monks over through gentleness and bring them back to the truth by the force of his arguments (*Hormisdas*, Letters 66 and 67).

They were admitted to his audience. He listened to them very patiently and did not even appear surprised at the boldness with which they branded as heretics the bishops who refused to accept their doctrine. But since they offered no evidence for many other facts they alleged—facts of which it was difficult for anyone at Rome to have knowledge—he proposed that the matter be referred to the patriarch of Constantinople. Since the patriarch was closer to the scene, [Col. 1472A] he could be informed about it more surely and easily. But they took care not to accept this course. They knew the patriarch’s views and that their condemnation would be virtually certain if they recognized him as judge.

They therefore persisted in demanding to be judged by the pope himself. They hoped to take him by surprise and that the distance from the place of events would prevent him from discovering the substance of the affair. They therefore began, in his presence, to utter deep sighs; and, striking their foreheads and breasts violently with groans capable of arousing his compassion, they called God to witness that, if they ever returned to Constantinople, their lives would not be safe.

The pope was moved by their tears and resolved to summon to Rome those whom they accused, in order to give a canonical judgment. Meanwhile, he had the proposition they wished to have accepted as orthodox examined with great care. All the skilled theologians in Rome were summoned. Hormisdas asked Boethius [Col. 1472B] to attend the conferences. He spoke there with such learning and eloquence that it had to be acknowledged that he understood these matters better than the theologians who made them the subject of their study and entire occupation. The subtlety of philosophy was not useless to him on this occasion.

Accustomed to distinguish everything with exact precision, he first pointed out that there was a very great difference between affirming that “a person of the Trinity was crucified” and saying that “one of the Trinity was crucified”; that the word “one” seemed to signify and combine nature and person, thereby causing suffering and death to fall upon the divine nature, which is incapable of them. Since all actions are attributed to the suppositum, or person, there was much less danger in saying, “A divine person,” or “A person of the Trinity, suffered.” Yet, to remove all ambiguity, one ought to add: “A person of the Trinity suffered in the flesh.”

[Col. 1472C] Second, he pointed out that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three but one God in three persons. Now, when one says “one of the Trinity,” it seems that one means one of three gods, which sounds improper on a Christian’s lips.

He then showed that this proposition had originally come from the Arians, who had advanced it to prove that the Son was a creature; that it favored every heresy; and that the Eutychians also used it to establish the confusion of the two natures in Jesus Christ and to prove that the human nature had been absorbed into the divine. With this aim they had proposed it at the Council of Chalcedon and had made every effort to have it approved there (196), being fully convinced that, if it once passed, they would thereafter have no difficulty establishing their principal doctrine.

The emperor Anastasius, who had always been an Eutychian, asked nothing more of the Catholics whom he persecuted than that they accept it; and he ceased persecuting them as soon as they had subscribed to it. This was clear evidence, Boethius said, that the prince regarded it as the strongest support of Eutyches’ doctrine. Finally, the proposition was found in none of the Fathers received by the Church, and the passage from Proclus cited by the monks had been truncated and falsified. Saint Leo, by contrast, expressly rejected it in his letter to the emperor Marcian, as did Saint Cyril in his letter to John. If one carefully examined the proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon against Carosus and Dorotheus, one would notice the horror the Fathers had expressed toward it.

However strong Boethius’s arguments were, the assembly still included learned men who contradicted them and even undertook to refute them. For while Count Vitalian was acting powerfully (197) at Constantinople and throughout the East on behalf of the monks, a [Col. 1473A] powerful party was forming in Rome. It was greatly strengthened by the letter that the emperor Justin wrote to the pope, asking him not to condemn the proposition.

Ferrandus, a deacon of the Church of Carthage, defended it. In a writing addressed to the scholastic Severus and to Anatolius, deacons of the Church of Rome (Dupin, *Sixth Century*, pp. 44 and 57), he maintained that it was entirely orthodox. Since it was certain, he said, that Jesus Christ was one of the Trinity and that he had suffered, one could not, without contradicting oneself, deny that one of the Trinity had suffered.

The matter did not end there. These monks, stubbornly attached to their opinions, had written a long letter to the bishops of Africa exiled in Sardinia by the Vandals. Under an appearance of zeal and piety, they had managed to draw these illustrious confessors of Jesus Christ into their party.

Saint Fulgentius, one of them, was charged with replying. Although he was so enlightened, he could not avoid falling into the trap (*Fulgentius*, Letter 17): for in his reply he confirmed their profession of faith without [Col. 1473B] making scarcely any alteration, subject only to the restriction that one should say “a person,” and not “one of the Trinity suffered”—something the monks themselves did not even approve.

At Rome, several senators had allowed themselves to be taken in by the great outward display of piety they cultivated, among them a man named Faustus, one of the senate’s most illustrious and distinguished members on account of his virtue. But because this magistrate was acting in good faith, before becoming more deeply involved in their party he thought he ought to consult the priest Trifolius, who had a reputation for being one of the most learned men of his age. Trifolius replied plainly that the proposition was not orthodox and that one ought to adhere to Boethius’s view.

That was enough to decide Faustus. He abandoned the monks’ party, but they did not thereby become more tractable, and the news they received from the East made them still more arrogant. They were told that the entire people were [Col. 1473C] on their side and that, when the priests began the *Trisagion* [Note: [Col. 1473C] The Greeks do not say this sacred hymn as it is recited in the Latin Church. We simply say: “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth”; they say: “Holy God, Holy Strong One, Holy Immortal One, have mercy on us,” etc. Some churches then added: “You who suffered for us, have mercy on us.” This innovation had not, however, been made in Constantinople or in the churches dependent upon it. Since they understood the *Trisagion* as referring to the Holy Trinity, as had always been done until then, they could not tolerate the addition of the words “who were crucified,” or “who suffered for us.” It was apparently to counter these Easterners, who applied it to Jesus Christ contrary to the ancient usage of all the Churches, that several Western Churches, after saying the *Sanctus* at Mass, added: “Holy Trinity, have mercy on us.”] in the sacred liturgy, those present replied by adding these words: “You who have been crucified for us, have mercy on us.”

But while these questions were being debated at Rome with great intensity on both sides, God took Count Vitalian away. He was consul in that year, 520, with Rusticus as his colleague. In the seventh month of his consulship (*Marcellinus, Chronicle; here; Evagrius, Ecclesiastical History* 4.3), he was killed in (200) the emperor’s palace and pierced by seventeen blows. This tragic death was attributed to the machinations of Count Justinian, who had always regarded him with jealousy.

Although the emperor had on every occasion given Vitalian signs of very special confidence, people nevertheless believed that he had had a part in his death. For it is unlikely that anyone would have dared to commit such a murder in his palace, almost before his eyes, unless he had at least tacitly consented to it. Moreover, there is no indication that he took pains to discover the perpetrators [Col. 1473D] or to avenge Vitalian as he ought to have done.

But if the court of Constantinople was very glad to be rid of a man whom it feared because he was too powerful and universally loved and honored throughout the Empire, all the distinguished people in Rome mourned him. Boethius was deeply distressed by his death. Although he had opposed Vitalian in the dispute over the Scythian monks, he nevertheless regarded him [Col. 1474A] as a zealous defender of the Church and one of the firmest supports of the Catholic faith.

This unexpected blow finally humbled the monks’ pride. (201) They were no longer heard speaking with such insolence, and the pope—whom consideration for Count Vitalian alone had until then restrained—sent the Defenders of the Church to drive them shamefully from the city.

They did not, however, leave without publicly displaying the violence of their anger and the passion that impelled them. The pope himself wrote the following about them to an African bishop named Possessor, who had been driven from his see by the Vandals and had withdrawn to Constantinople (*Vol. IV of the Library of the Fathers*, p. 547):

> We wished by our patience to heal these false monks, who, under the pretext of religion, sought only to satisfy their deep-rooted hatred. But they are too accustomed to disputes, too fond of novelties, and too firmly attached to their opinions. They refuse to recognize as Catholics those who follow the tradition of the Fathers unless they yield to their views. They are so accustomed to calumniating, slandering, murmuring, and fomenting seditions that we have been unable to restrain them either by gentleness or by our charitable admonitions (202), not even by our authority. They went so far as to rush into the assembly of the people, shouting and making a disturbance beside the statues of the emperors; and, had they not been stopped, they would have stirred up a sedition there. But at last they were expelled from Rome. We write these things to you because we fear that, if they come into your region, they may again deceive those who do not know how they behaved among us.

It would be difficult to understand what the pope meant here when he spoke of the tumult these monks caused beside the statues of the emperors (*ibid.*), if they themselves had not explained it in a writing they published shortly [Col. 1474C] after their return to Constantinople.

Bishop Possessor having made public the letter the pope had written to him concerning them, they did not think they ought to remain silent. John Maxentius, sometimes given the title of abbot, took up his pen in the name of them all. With a device quite usual among people of his character, who intrigue and plot in order to secure acceptance for a bad doctrine, he began by supposing that the letter being circulated was not from the pope but from some enemy of the monastic state.

He then complained bitterly about the pope himself: after the fourteen months they had spent in Rome, the pope had never been willing to give them any answer, although he had kept them throughout that time in his communion. Out of consideration for his legate, who had prejudiced him against them quite unjustly and was about to return, and in order to spare the legate the embarrassment of being convicted of heresy in their presence, he had sent the Defenders of the Church to drive them out by force.

[Col. 1474D] Finally, since they had been unable to make themselves heard or obtain justice from the Holy See, they had been compelled, before leaving Rome, to make their protestations in a public square where the statues of the emperors stood. There, in the presence of the entire people, they declared how they were being treated, so that no one could suspect them of having withdrawn secretly or abandoned their cause.

[Col. 1475A] The conclusion of this manifesto was (204) that anyone who did not accept the proposition “One of the Trinity suffered” was a Nestorian and a heretic, as were those who wished to add the words “One person of the Trinity” and say, “One person of the Trinity suffered.” It was precisely in this that the monks’ impudence was most apparent. Nor were these their final efforts. Supported by everything capable of making a party formidable—the protection of army generals, of princes, and even of the emperor, whom they had managed to enlist in their cause—they continued for two years to have Pope Hormisdas petitioned to pronounce in their favor.

Count Justinian, whose attitude toward them had completely changed after Vitalian’s death, also wrote to him several times. The emperor sent him a special ambassador to make this request; but, however insistently they pressed him, the pope refused to decide the matter. He was convinced that, since the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon had sufficiently explained everything that ought to be believed, no new decisions were needed; and he believed, on the contrary, that it was extremely dangerous to accept new expressions in matters of faith when no trace of them could be found in antiquity:

> [Note: [Col. 1475D] “What, then, after that fountain of faithful decrees, could the most inquisitive investigator seek that would be more perfect either in practice or in formulation—provided only that he preserves the boundary of faith? Unless, perhaps, someone would rather doubt than believe, contend than know, follow uncertainties than preserve decrees . . . . . . There is one holy Trinity; it is not multiplied by number, etc.” *Epist. Hormisd. ad Just.* 79, from Vatican Codex 4961.]

“You have in your hands,” he replied to Justin, who had pressed him once again to decide the question, “the decrees of the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon and the letters of the great Saint Leo. What can be added to them? What can one ask for after this so fruitful source of faithful decrees? Whoever is not satisfied with them departs from the rules of faith. He prefers to doubt rather than believe, to dispute rather than be instructed, to prefer what is uncertain to what is established and decided.”

He then added the reason that prevented him from accepting and approving this entirely new manner of expression. For if the Holy Trinity, namely the Father, the Son (206), and the Holy Spirit, is one God, as the supreme Legislator himself says—“Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God”—then necessarily whoever wishes to say that one of the Trinity suffered must either divide the Godhead into several parts or believe that the divine essence is capable of passion and suffering . . . . . . The Holy Trinity is one reality; it is not multiplied by number. And although, with regard to the persons, it may be counted, with regard to its essence it is one and indivisible (*Noris, Hist. Controversiae*, chap. 10).

There were still many other reasons for rejecting the proposition as it had initially been stated without qualification. Boethius had touched upon them in the first conference held in the presence of Pope Hormisdas. Peter the Fuller, the famous Eutychian who had seized the see of Antioch, had abused his position to introduce into the faith of the believers the unity of nature in Jesus Christ, in which he claimed that the Savior had suffered; accordingly, he had added to the *Trisagion* the words “who suffered for (207) us.” The Severians, another and even more pernicious sect of Eutychians, also embraced this doctrine and carried it so far as to say that the entire Trinity had suffered and had been crucified, because they made no distinction between nature and person in Jesus Christ. The Apollinarists likewise maintained that one of the Trinity had suffered, because, denying that Jesus Christ possessed a soul and understanding like other human beings, and maintaining that the divinity took the place of his soul and understanding, they found this proposition favorable to their doctrine.

After this, is it surprising that the pope and the most enlightened persons hesitated to accept it as Catholic? In truth, they did not condemn it as heretical, because it could be understood in a sound sense; but they rejected it as suspect, dangerous because of its novelty and because of the meaning that heretics had attached to it. However, once Justinian had attained the empire and redoubled his efforts with Pope John II to have it declared Catholic, the pope had it examined anew in a synod and, finding less danger in accepting it as it was being proposed—and because the sects that had abused it had almost disappeared—[Col. 1476B] declared it Catholic. Pope Agapetus confirmed it, and afterward Pope Vigilius; it was also confirmed by the Fifth General Council, in the Catholic sense that it contains, by taking the word “one” personally rather than substantially—that is, with reference to the person and not to the substance of God. The latter was the sense given it by the heretics and the sense in which Pope Hormisdas, Boethius, and the most enlightened Catholics of their time had rejected it.

Since the Scythian monks had not initially received all the satisfaction they expected concerning the proposition “One of the Trinity suffered,” they turned to questions of free will and grace when they returned to Constantinople. Bishop Possessor, whom we have already mentioned, had shown great zeal in having their proposition rejected; and on several occasions he had defended Faustus, bishop of Riez, whose writings were beginning to attract attention. The Scythians, claiming to be zealous defenders [Col. 1476C] of the doctrine of Saint Augustine, thought they had found an opportunity for revenge by portraying Possessor as a heretical Pelagian on the pretext that he supported Faustus’s teaching.

Constantinople was again divided by this new controversy. Not only the clergy and the monks, but even the laypeople and the lords of the court, took the liberty of expressing their opinions; and the dispute caused no less commotion there than the controversy that has arisen in our own day in France over the doctrine of Jansenism. When Pope Hormisdas was informed of it by letters from Bishop Possessor, he again assembled the theologians of Rome to learn their views on these new difficulties. Boethius’s opinion prevailed, and through the wisdom of his counsels the Church soon found peace. But in order to understand what happened on this occasion, and the part Boethius played in the affair, it is necessary to take the matter up from a more distant point (210) and to give a proper account of Faustus and his writings. This will be done in the final part of this work, under the title “Clarifications concerning Faustus, Bishop of Riez, and His Doctrine,” to which we refer the reader so as not to interrupt the sequence of the history.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1475]

[Col. 1475D] (211) Peace having been strengthened between Justin and Theodoric through the efforts of Boethius and Symmachus, the emperor and the king sought an opportunity to acknowledge the services they had rendered them; they offered them the consulship a second time. But, as it were satiated with these honors, they [Col. 1477A] asked the princes and the senate to confer them upon their children.

Symmachus had no sons. Boethius had two by Rusticiana (*Boeth. De Cons. Phil.*, book II, p. 4). Although they were still very young, one could already discern in their faces and throughout their conduct traces of the spirit and virtue of their grandfather and father.

Boethius, full of gratitude and respect for Symmachus, wished to preserve a name so dear to him and gave it to his eldest son. He was called Quintus [Note: [Col. 1477D] Martianus Rota, who had read in the *Consolation of Philosophy* that Boethius had seen his two sons made consuls in the same year and had delivered a speech in their presence praising Theodoric; and who had elsewhere found that, when Theodoric made his first entry into Rome, Boethius had delivered another speech in his presence, while Cassiodorus designates Patricius and Hypatius as consuls for the year 500, when Theodoric made his first entry into Rome: from all these circumstances, badly put together, he imagined that these two consuls were Boethius’s two sons, although apparently he had not yet married their mother. This misled several other historians, who imprudently named Patricius and Hypatius as Boethius’s two sons.] Aurelius Anicius (213) Symmachus; the second son retained his father’s name and was called, like him, Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius. No patrician family had ever yet seen two brothers so young designated consuls in the same year; that privilege had hitherto been reserved for the imperial family. Nevertheless, both of Boethius’s sons were appointed consuls in 522, and their father had the joy of seeing them leave his house at [Col. 1477B] the head of the senate, amid the acclamations of the people, and take their places in those seats of honor reserved for the foremost [Note: [Col. 1478D] The ancient Romans called *curules* the chief magistrates who sat in ivory seats, as in a kind of throne. These seats were placed in their chariots, and they sat in them when they appeared in public. The term comes from the Latin word *currus*, meaning a chariot.] magistrates, while he himself acquired immense glory through the panegyric he (214) delivered in praise of Theodoric. When the speech was over, Boethius, between his two consular sons, was led to the circus, where, according to custom, he provided games and spectacles for the people and gave them gifts equal in magnificence to those of a sovereign (*Consolation of Philosophy*, book II, p. 3). It was this happy day, the most glorious of his entire life, that Wisdom placed before his eyes to console him in the time of his disgrace.

Because no example had ever been seen of so extraordinary a distinction, several historians who had not sufficiently examined this circumstance in Boethius’s history convinced themselves that Boethius the father and Symmachus the grandfather had been designated consuls in the year 522 (Onuphrius Panvinus). But Boethius’s text is explicit on this point and explains itself so clearly and precisely that there is no reason to doubt that the consulship was conferred upon his sons in that year. Moreover, these writers failed to notice that, as the learned Father Sirmond observed, the grandfather Symmachus was called Aurelius Memmius Symmachus, whereas Boethius’s son was Aurelius Anicius Symmachus, and that it is the latter who is recorded in the consular fasti for the year 522. This is established not only by the consular fasti but also by several surviving inscriptions—one of which Father Sirmond reports—that are dated by the consulship of Anicius Symmachus and that of Boethius.

Finally, Paul the Deacon (*Book VII, ad Eut.*; Pagi, *Critique* at the year 522; Baronius, *Annals*) makes it sufficiently clear that he had no doubt on the matter, since he thought it necessary to distinguish Boethius the father from Boethius the son not only by the title of former consul that he gives him, but also by calling him “Boethius the elder, former consul” (*Boetium seniorem exconsulem*). If the son had not been consul during his father’s lifetime, it would have been unnecessary to distinguish him by anything other than the consulship. Although Murmelle and Martianus Rota often confuse events in Boethius’s life and place the consulship of his children very incorrectly, they nevertheless agree with modern historians that both were consuls during their father’s lifetime, and nowhere else are they found recorded in the consular fasti except for the year 522. Therefore Father Pagi, in his critique of Baronius at this point (*ad ann. 522*), Vallin, M. Dupin, and all the learned men of the present day have adopted Father Sirmond’s view [Note: [Col. 1478D] See his notes on Ennodius’s letters, *ad lib. VII, ep. 25*, and *ad l. VIII, ep. 1*.].

But since Boethius’s sons were too young to discharge so important an office, there can be no doubt that Symmachus the grandfather and Boethius the father exercised it throughout the year; and that the services the state could expect from these great men led Justin, Theodoric, and the senate to confer the honor of the consulship upon their sons at so young an age. Never had Roman purple been seen more honored, nor the office of consul exercised with greater dignity; nor had there ever been a consulship more glorious or more advantageous to the Church.

Africa had been subject to the Vandals for sixty-six years. Genseric and Trasamond, their kings, had successively made the Catholics feel everything that Arian fury could devise. Their churches closed, their bishops exiled, and the loss of liberty and property had not satisfied the hatred they bore toward the defenders of Christ’s divinity; they had employed the most extraordinary tortures and everything that paganism had invented of most inhuman against Christians, in order to force the Catholics to embrace heresy. There was no hope of seeing an end to so many evils; but God, who knows how to set limits to impiety whenever he wills, suddenly overthrew this formidable power.

[Col. 1478C] Of all the African coast, only the city of Tripoli [Note: [Col. 1478D] This is Tripoli in Barbary, called *Laca* by the ancients. Procopius calls its inhabitants *Mauressii*; they were idolaters. The Saracens, who had embraced the religion of Muhammad, seized these regions at the beginning of the eighth century, and they were then called Moors.] and its dependencies were not subject to the Arians. Trasamond, determined to subjugate it, besieged it with a powerful army. The Tripolitans [Note: [Col. 1478D] The Tripolitans were still pagans.] were dismayed at his approach and on the point of surrender when Cabaon, who (218) commanded in the city, was inspired to lead out all the inhabitants and seek help from a power superior to that of earth.

“Citizens,” he said to them, “we are being unjustly attacked; they wish to reduce us to slavery. Yet do not lose courage. I have learned that the God of the Christians, against whom our enemies have been waging war for so long, is a just God, full of goodness and mercy toward those who have recourse to him and live under his laws. Let us not doubt that he will humble the pride of our enemies and deliver us from them if, for his honor, we do the exact opposite of what they do to dishonor him. Believe me, then: let us form two camps separated from each other. Let the women and children shut themselves in one; we, who are capable of bearing arms, will withdraw into the other. Let no one leave it until further orders, unless he wishes to risk losing his life. Let us live there in continence; let us banish injustice, perjury, intemperance, and excess. Let us send out some of our men dressed as Vandals, speaking their language, and unable to be recognized. Let us follow their army at a distance and repair the disorders these impious men commit in the temples of the Christian God and the outrages they inflict upon his ministers.”

They believed him, and everyone obeyed. At once they selected officers and soldiers capable of carrying out this plan. By circuitous routes they reached the rear of the Vandal army, and wherever it had profaned churches, overturned altars, or insulted priests, they repaired these offenses by cleansing the holy places of the filth that the impious men had left there, since they ordinarily quartered their cavalry in them. They restored the altars, burned incense upon them, and gave substantial gifts [Col. 1479B] to the Lord’s ministers.

The Vandal army meanwhile drew near. It was already facing the Tripolitans and preparing to surround them when Cabaon arranged his troops in the following order of battle. Having a large number of camels, he had the most skillful archers mount them and formed a large square body, facing the enemy on every side; between the camels he placed the remainder of his men. As soon as the Vandals came within range of the arrows, since they were armed only with spears and swords, which could be used only at close quarters, they were halted. Feeling themselves pierced from every side, they were soon thrown into disorder. Their horses, driven mad by the pain caused by the enemy’s arrows, threw their riders or furiously charged one another. Thus, in less than three hours, the entire army was defeated, and Trasamond, having gathered its remnants, was forced to withdraw in disgrace. He was so [Col. 1479C] grieved by his defeat that nothing could console him. A few days later he died of sorrow. But in those moments when the most violent passions usually leave men, his passions flared up again. The hatred he bore toward the Catholics followed him to the grave; for, having summoned Hilderic, whom he had designated as his successor, he made him swear that during his reign the Catholic churches would not be reopened, (221) their exiled bishops would not be recalled, and the defenders of the consubstantiality of the Word would not be restored to their former privileges. Hilderic swore this; but whether he was convinced that all the misfortunes that had befallen Trasamond at the end of his reign were a just punishment for the crimes he had committed against the Catholics, or whether these severities were contrary to his gentle temperament and natural goodness—for he inherited much from his mother Eudocia [Note: [Col. 1479D] Genseric had taken her captive when he plundered Rome.], daughter of the emperor Valentinian—he did not wish to commit perjury. As soon as Trasamond lost consciousness, he issued orders to restore the Catholics to all their rights before ascending the throne. Once the order was published, the exiled bishops set out for Carthage, arriving there in great numbers. The faithful people went far out along the seashore to meet them, some carrying lamps, others torches or palms. They escorted them to the great church, singing God’s praises in as many different languages as there were nations inhabiting that great city.

News of this event reached Rome just after the public celebrations [Col. 1480A] held there for the consulship of Boethius’s sons had ended. It was regarded as the first fruits of the graces that God was to pour out during the course [Note: [Col. 1479D] M. Fleury, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, assigns this event to the year 523, under the consulship [Col. 1480D] of Maximus; but he was mistaken, and the other historians who preceded and followed him were correct in assigning it to the year 522.] of a magistracy exercised by two men who seemed born solely for the good of the Church.

It was followed by another event no less astonishing. The Lazi, inhabitants of ancient Colchis and tributaries of the Persians, suddenly submitted to the faith of Jesus Christ; and their king, converted by a miracle of grace of which there are few examples, at the same time sent ambassadors to Pope Hormisdas to pay homage to Jesus Christ in the person of his vicar on earth. (223) This sudden change may appear incredible, but it is too well attested to be dismissed as doubtful; and this is how it occurred.

When Canax, their king, died, it was expected that Cat, his son, would go to the court of the Persian king to receive from him, according to custom, the scepter and crown (*Theophanes*, year 5 of Justin, p. 144). For some time he appeared undecided about what he ought to do, and the nobles of his realm could not discover the cause of his indecision. Some imagined that he was considering handing the kingdom over to his brother; but they were greatly surprised when they suddenly saw him take the road to Constantinople and throw himself into the arms of the emperor Justin.

“Already a Christian in my heart,” he said to him, “I could not bring myself to receive the crown or investiture of my kingdom from the Persians. I could not have done so without defiling myself through the profane sacrifices and other impious ceremonies that ordinarily accompany this act; I detest them. It is from you that I have come to receive these things; this is what brings me here, together with my desire to receive baptism.”

No one knew (224) who had inspired him with so pious a purpose. There were no Christians in his kingdom, and all his subjects were idolaters. Yet how can anyone believe if he has not heard of the mysteries of faith, and how can he hear of them if they are not proclaimed by ministers of the Gospel? But the grace of the Most High is not always bound to ordinary rules. The supreme Shepherd, who knows all his sheep by name, knows how to call them whenever he wishes and through whomever he wishes, and to make them hear his voice without the ministry of human beings. Perhaps this prince had heard of Jesus Christ from the Iberians, Catholic peoples neighboring his kingdom; this is the most certain thing that can be said about it. There is no likelihood that he had come to Constantinople under the reign of Zeno for particular affairs, nor that he owed his conversion to the miracles of the holy solitary Daniel, as Cardinal Baronius claims. For the historians speak of him as a young prince who was not yet married when he came to Constantinople to receive the crown (225) from the hands of the emperor Justin; this could not be true if he had already made a journey there under the reign of Zeno.

Justin, a zealous Catholic, joyfully embraced the opportunity that presented itself to extend the kingdom of Jesus Christ. [Col. 1480D] He received the king of Colchis with honor, had him baptized, and adopted him as his son (*Theophanes*, ibid.). He had him marry Valeriana, a woman of distinction; declaring him king of the Lazi, he gave him a crown like those of the Roman emperors, magnificent white garments bearing the emperor’s image raised in embroidery, and several other objects of great value. He then sent him back honorably to his own country. His subjects soon followed his example, and in a short time all Colchis became Christian. This happened under the reign of Cabades, king of Persia, and caused the war that broke out between him and Justin and lasted for a long time.

[Col. 1481A] The cross of Jesus Christ was therefore shining everywhere, and the Church, enjoying a fairly profound peace, gained new (226) advantages every day. That same year God made it triumph in a manner no less astonishing over the impious Dounoas, called “the scourge of Christians,” who had long persecuted them; it was believed that the Church owed this victory to Boethius’s prayers. Dounoas was Jewish by nation; I do not know by what turn of fortune he had attained the crown of Himyar. This was a province of Arabia Felix, whose inhabitants were called Homerites by the Greeks and Sabaeans by us [Note: [Col. 1481D] It is believed that the queen of Sheba had led them to embrace Judaism; that they later abandoned it and became pagans, remaining so until the time of the emperor Constantius.]. In the fourth century, under the emperor Constantius, they had received the light of the Gospel through the efforts of an apostolic man named Theophilus, who had been sent to them. But two hundred years later Dounoas placed himself at the head of a band of Arabs and Jews, invaded their country, and compelled them to submit. He had promised to allow them the free exercise of their religion (*Phil.*, book III, [Col. 1481B] p. 477). As soon as he felt himself secure, he mocked all his promises and made known his hatred of the Christian name by the inhuman manner in which he treated all who refused to renounce it. By his orders, deep pits were dug and great fires lit in them; everyone who refused to embrace Judaism was thrown into them without exception. This is why he was given the surname “Author of the Pits.”

Najran, which some geographers call Nageran or Nagran, one of the principal cities of the Sabaeans, outraged by the treatment this tyrant inflicted upon his new subjects, refused to submit. The famous Arethas, one of the great commanders of that time, was its governor. Dounoas besieged it; and, seeing that the courageous Christians’ strong resistance made his efforts useless, he despaired of taking it by force and tried to capture it through deception. A capitulation was concluded. The tyrant confirmed everything he had promised by the most terrible oaths; but as soon as he had entered the city, he spared no effort to induce its inhabitants to embrace Judaism (Baronius, ibid., p. 93; Baill., October 24). Since caresses and temporal advantages could do nothing (228) to move the hearts of these faithful Christians, he displayed his cruelty toward them in the most horrifying manner. Convinced that the clergy and monks were the authors of this admirable constancy, which he regarded as unbearable obstinacy, he had a pyre erected in the middle of the square. After gathering all the priests, monks, and virgins consecrated to God who were in the city and its surroundings, he had them all burned together. Far from shaking the Christians’ steadfastness, this deed only increased their courage: each competed to run most quickly toward martyrdom. Three hundred and forty of the city’s principal inhabitants were beheaded, together with their governor Arethas [Note: [Col. 1482D] The Church honors him with public veneration as a martyr on October 24.].

The tyrant’s rage was not yet satisfied. Without distinction of sex or age, he likewise had most of the inhabitants massacred, and he ordered that those who remained and had escaped his cruelty should be sold and reduced to slavery. If on this occasion one saw unheard-of excesses of cruelty, one saw no fewer miracles of the grace of Jesus Christ or of these Christians’ invincible courage. Children ran to martyrdom with their fathers and mothers, preferring fire and torture to the tyrant’s caresses.

News of so many outrages soon spread. People began to fear the power of the cruel Dounoas; in Rome it was believed that the end of the world was near and that this tyrant might well be the Antichrist. [Col. 1482A] Indeed, he possessed almost all the characteristics by which the prophets designate him. But while everyone reasoned about the matter according to his own ideas and showed his anxiety and apprehension, Boethius remained tranquil. Often prostrate at the foot of the altars, he tearfully asked God either to put an end to this bloody persecution or to take him from this life, sparing him the pain of seeing his Church treated with such indignity and its true worshipers become the playthings and prey of the enemies of God’s holy name.

“These are not, Lord,” he said to him, “the promises you made to us, nor what your prophets foretold concerning the perfidious Jews: that they would be scattered throughout the earth, treated as slaves, without a king, without states, without priests, and without altars, as punishment for the horrible deicide they committed. Here they are masters of a kingdom of vast extent; they have a king of their own nation seated upon the throne, armed with power and threatening soon to destroy the empire of your [Col. 1482B] Son Jesus Christ.”

After continuing his prayers in this way for some time, he rose full of confidence that an end to these evils would soon be seen. Whether God had revealed to him what was soon to happen to the impious Dounoas, or whether, through his naturally penetrating intelligence, he had discerned the future, he consoled his friends, dismayed by such tragic events, assuring them that they would soon learn how faithful and unchanging God is in his promises.

Indeed, before the year of his consulship had ended, it was learned that Elesbaan, [Note: [Col. 1482D] He renounced his kingdoms toward the end of his life in order to embrace the monastic life.] king of Axum in (231) Ethiopia, a very zealous Christian and an old enemy of Dounoas, stirred by the prayers of the emperor Justin and supported by forces from Egypt and the East, had come to attack the tyrant, finally defeated him, captured him in battle, and taken his life. The Arab writers tell the story somewhat differently [Col. 1482C] (*Theophanes*, year 5 of Justin, ibid.; Baronius, ibid.). They claim that, finding himself hard-pressed by the Abyssinians, Dounoas drove his horse forward with such speed that he could neither restrain it nor prevent it from plunging into the sea, which was near at hand. The tyrant’s entire family experienced the conqueror’s just severity. He avenged upon them the crimes Dounoas had committed against the Christians, took possession of his entire country, and restored Christianity there. Thus God, after using the impious to punish the sins of his people or to test their faith, casts into the fire the instruments he has used to chastise them and, in their defeat, makes his Church—purified by persecution—more glorious and triumphant than it had been before.

From that moment Boethius was no longer seen to act as an ordinary man. Raised by his faith above the weak lights of reason, infinitely removed from all those low and earthly perspectives by which human wisdom is measured, he had only God as the object of all his enterprises, and against all hope he expected success from him alone. Having surpassed all the other consuls during his own consulship, one may say that in the exercise of his sons’ consulship he surpassed himself. Never had one seen in a man greater disinterestedness, greater elevation of soul, greater zeal for religion, or greater love of the public good.

The courtiers of Theodoric, ever insatiable and ready to seize the property of those who were unable to resist them (Boethius, Book I, *On the Consolation*, p. 4), gave him more than one further opportunity to display his character in its full extent. The patrician [Col. 1483A] Paulinus, who had been consul in 498, or, according to Cassiodorus, in 499—a man distinguished by his virtue and nobility, and respected on account of his age—found himself in his old age prey to the avarice of these hungry wolves, as Boethius calls them. They had seized this former consul’s property and were beginning (233) to divide it among themselves. They devoured him with all the greater confidence because his extreme old age rendered him incapable of opposing them. But no sooner had Boethius learned of this than, without regard or consideration for the influence these public pests enjoyed at court, he went to Theodoric. He depicted in such vivid colors the abuse these courtiers made of the protection he granted them, and the harm this inflicted upon him personally in the eyes of his subjects—who were led to hate him by such tyrannical conduct—that the king was finally obliged to put an end to these acts of brigandage, and the patrician Paulinus was restored to all his property (Book I, *On the Consolation*, p. 4). The law of charity [Col. 1483B] and zeal for justice were the only motives that could have moved Boethius on this occasion; for there is no indication that Paulinus had any particular connection with him. On the contrary, history tells us that Paulinus had had serious disputes with Festus and Symmachus, Boethius’s fathers-in-law, which could be settled only through commissioners appointed for them by Theodoric (Cassiodorus, Book I, Letter 23). This greatly heightens (234) the significance of this episode in his life.

The wicked trembled with rage in their hearts and secretly tore apart this holy man’s reputation through the most atrocious calumnies. But he knew that the first duty of a Christian magistrate was to rescue from oppression all who groaned beneath the tyranny of the powers of this world: friend as well as the indifferent, foreigner as well as citizen; and that a man makes himself unworthy of so respectable a name and so elevated a rank when he fears human resentment while [Col. 1483C] justice and truth are at stake. Therefore he despised their efforts, and, feeling the injury done to each individual as though it had been done to himself, he joyfully sacrificed his dearest interests, even his life, by opposing injustice everywhere.

Several earlier historians who wrote about Boethius believed that on this occasion he was removed from court as an inconvenient man who wearied the prince with his continual and excessively frank remonstrances, or as a suspicious man who too readily believed he found extortion (235) and injustice where none existed. They add (Palmerius, *Florentine Chronicle*; Marius of Rome, *Life of Boethius*) that Theodoric was seduced by the stratagems of his enemies and by the jealousy of certain senators, who could not see without envy the great elevation and almost sovereign authority that Boethius and Symmachus possessed in Rome. But, they say, after Theodoric recognized the injustice of his favorites and the oppression they had inflicted upon Paulinus, he [Col. 1483D] recalled Boethius shortly afterward and then honored him with the office of prefect of the praetorium.

It is true that Boethius [Col. 1484A] himself complains (Book I, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, p. 4) of an injustice committed against him by the senate, which would have caused him to withdraw his support from its interests had he possessed less zeal for its glory. He even says that he wrote an account of this first persecution and of all that he then had to suffer from human injustice; and there is reason to believe that he meant this first exile. But since that writing has been lost, like many of his other works, we are deprived of knowledge of what occurred in this intrigue.

Some writers have thought it necessary to reject as uncertain so important (236) an episode in Boethius’s life, on the grounds that the office of prefect of the praetorium, which he was supposedly honored with by Theodoric after his return, was a military office unsuited to a magistrate who had spent his entire life engaged in civil functions. But those who reason in this way show little familiarity with history. For the office of prefect of the praetorium was, in its origin, no less civil than military; and even if one granted that it had once been exclusively military, it is certain that from the reign of the great Constantine onward it became a civil magistracy and the first dignity of the Empire.

That prince created another office for warfare, [Col. 1484B] which he gave to a military officer called *comes belli*, “count of war,” roughly what the constable was formerly in France. Yet the prefect of the praetorium still possessed the power of the sword and decided, as the final court of appeal, the most important affairs. He received honors owed to sovereignty and even bore all its insignia, as can be seen in Justinian’s *Code* [Note: [Col. 1483D] Book I of the *Code*, Title 26]. Thus Boethius could have been prefect of the praetorium without ever commanding armies or exercising any military office.

Palmerius [Note: [Col. 1483D] “Boethius, recalled from exile some time ago and made prefect of the praetorium,” etc. Matthew Palmerius of Florence, in his *Chronicle*] expressly states in his *Chronicle* that, having been recalled from exile by Theodoric almost immediately, Boethius was honored with [Col. 1484C] this office. This is all the more credible because Boethius himself tells us, after discussing the first offices he had held, that Theodoric gave him another which he had great difficulty accepting. One of the reasons that most strongly dissuaded him was that he would have as his assessor [Note: [Col. 1483D] “You too, then, could at last have been brought by so many dangers to think that you were holding office with Decoratus, while recognizing in him the spirit of a most wicked buffoon and informer.” *Consolation of Philosophy*, p. 4, line 3] a certain Decoratus, whom he knew to be a rogue, an enemy of all good men, and an accuser of the senate.

[Note: This Decoratus survived Boethius by many years. He appears to have been the son of Decoratus the quaestor and elder brother of Honoratus, who is mentioned in Cassiodorus (Letters 3 and 4, Book V) and in Father Sirmond’s notes on the seventeenth letter of Ennodius’s fourth book, addressed to Decoratus the elder. Among Cassiodorus’s letters there is a rescript of Theodoric addressed to this Decoratus, a vicar or deputy, in which he is called *vir devotus*, “a devout man”; but this did not make him any more virtuous. It was merely an honorific title assigned especially to those inferior magistrates whose duty was to assist at the judgments delivered by the prefect of the praetorium, draw up the records, and, in the prefect’s absence, even pronounce judgment and administer justice. This is shown by an ancient subscription to a document reported by Cujas, in which Flavius Theodorus, who held a similar office, is called *vir devotus, memorialis sacri scrinii epistolarum exadjutor*, “a devout man, assistant to the keeper of the memorials of the sacred bureau of letters.” It is in this sense that Decoratus, Boethius’s accuser, is called *V. D.*, that is, *vir devotus*, “devout man,” and *devotio tua*, “your Devotion” (Letter 31, in Cassiodorus, Book V).]

This circumstance gives considerable weight to Palmerius’s view, for there is no likelihood that Boethius had such a wicked man as his assessor in the office of master of the palace, or in that of master of the offices. At that time no question had yet arisen concerning his loyalty or that of the senate; no courtier had yet dared to make him suspect in Theodoric’s eyes, and Boethius had no reason at that time to fear finding an informer in the magistrate who was to assist him in the duties of his offices.

In any case, Boethius had reached the highest degree of distinction to which a private citizen in the Empire could aspire. Everything bowed before him: regarded [Col. 1484D] [Col. 1485A] by his prince as the firmest support of his crown, feared by his enemies, who, after so many fruitless attempts, seemed no longer to dare attack him; honored and respected by all good people as the protector of innocence; loved by everyone as the father of his country; supported by the wishes and prayers that all the Churches continually offered to God for the preservation of so dear a protector—yet his heart was not exalted by this lofty fortune. He was not touched by worldly greatness, nor was it capable of inflating him. In his person people found what the Fathers had always regarded as one of the rarest marvels: profound humility amid honors and (240) applause. It seems that Saint Augustine had drawn Boethius’s portrait in advance when he gave us the image of a truly Christian magistrate.

“There are,” says this Father (Augustine, on Psalm 51, Book 8), “two kinds of people mingled together in the world. [Col. 1485B] One is occupied with heavenly things, the other with earthly things. The hearts of the latter are buried in earthly concerns; the hearts of the former are united in heaven with the blessed spirits. The latter place all their hope in treasures and worldly greatness, which are unstable and perishable; the former direct their desires toward heavenly goods, which cannot fail.

“But since it is impossible for those whose office charges them with administering divine matters not sometimes to incline their hearts toward earth, even though they preach entirely heavenly truths every day, so it also often happens that those engaged in administering temporal affairs nevertheless keep their hearts raised toward heaven. Thus one may see a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem clothed in purple, a consul (241) charged with governing the republic, hold the greatness that accompanies him in contempt and continually sigh [Col. 1485C] for blessed eternity.”

Indeed, all the splendid insignia of his dignity were burdensome to him. He endured them only with difficulty and abandoned them as soon as he could. Thus he could truly say with Esther: “You know, Lord, that I hate the glory of the wicked and detest all their pomp. If on certain days I appear in public with splendor and magnificence, it is not the inclination of my heart that leads me there, but the unavoidable obligation imposed upon me by my station. My own glory is a burden that crushes me, and I long only for the days when I shall be able to enjoy you in retreat and silence” (Esther, chapter 15).

Indeed, whenever Boethius could withdraw from court, he immediately fled into solitude. The desert of Sublaqueum [Note: It is now called Sollagoa. It was not Monte Cassino, as some writers [Col. 1486D] on the life of Boethius have believed, since that famous monastery was not founded until 529, four years after his death], a day’s journey from Rome, where the great patriarch Saint Benedict had retired, possessed for him charms that cannot be expressed (Murmus, *Life of Boethius*), and the admirable man who lived there possessed even greater charms. [Col. 1485D] They had formed a very close friendship (John Trithemius, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*).

Another senator named Tertullus, believed to have been the father of Saint Placid, usually accompanied him there. Forgetting what they were according to the world, they took pleasure in mixing with these humble solitaries and joining them in fasts and vigils, prayer and the chanting of psalms. Rejoicing to appear as the least among that company of earthly angels, they would have wished to spend the rest of their lives there; but this was not God’s design for them. After gaining new strength through contemplation of heavenly things, Saint Benedict sent them back filled with ardor and zeal for the Lord’s glory, to continue the [Col. 1486A] duties of their offices.

Under his direction Boethius (243) made those marvelous advances in virtue that enabled him to rise above all the persecutions being prepared for him. There he clothed himself in a strength and courage that nothing could shake. There he learned the perfect contempt a Christian should have for all passing things, and learned to value properly the happiness of risking everything, losing everything, and even giving one’s life in defense of God’s interests.

He needed this assistance, for the time of those harsh trials was approaching, when he would have to struggle against all that nature, flesh, and blood possess that is most flattering and most capable of seduction. He was about to find himself in those delicate circumstances in which a Christian, in order to give God proof of his fidelity, must lose everything so as not to lose himself.

Since the earlier writers on Boethius’s life have introduced confusion [Col. 1486B] into this most important part of his history by mingling, as they did, the sacred and the profane, the interests of the state with those of the Church, and the glory of dying for one’s country with that of giving one’s life (244) for the faith, we are obliged to clarify all the circumstances surrounding his persecution and to show its origin.

Theodoric had already ruled Italy for more than thirty years with as much justice as prosperity. Although involved in heresy, he had always made a point of treating Catholics with great moderation. Until then his conduct had shown none of the ferocity natural to his nation. On the contrary, he had abolished certain barbarous customs that the Romans had still retained from paganism (in Cassiodorus, Book V, Letter 42). Among his letters are those he wrote to the consul Maximus, urging him to abolish the cruel spectacles offered to the people, in which human lives were, so to speak, made sport of by forcing men to fight against [Col. 1486C] beasts.

Recently he had even given signs of his piety by presenting the church of Saint Peter in Rome with two silver candelabra weighing seventy pounds (Baronius, 16).
