It was not thought dishonorable to God’s majesty to accept them or to use in his holy temple gifts from an Arian prince, whom people believed they had to thank for the liberty and peace enjoyed by the Church under his reign.

Indeed, far from ever interrupting ecclesiastical assemblies, diminishing the privileges of the Church or clergy, he had increased them and, by his authority, upheld all the rules established there concerning morals and discipline. Finally, the Churches fortunate enough to be under the rule of Catholic princes were no more peaceful than those of Italy under Theodoric.

It is true that Boethius had contributed greatly to making him so tractable; while he retained influence over the prince’s mind, and Theodoric willingly allowed himself to be guided by the wisdom of his [Col. 1486D] counsels, his reign was prosperous and the Church was at peace. But whether the Romans’ sins had made them unworthy of enjoying this happiness any longer, or whether God knew that this calm was harmful to the piety of the faithful, whose fervor was daily declining, and that persecution would awaken it, he permitted Theodoric to change everything (246) at once by abandoning him to himself. This was the occasion of so sudden a change.

Pope Hormisdas died a few months after Boethius had completed his sons’ consulship. John, a deacon of the Church of Rome, was elected in his place by the unanimous consent of the clergy, after the Holy See had remained vacant for seven days. He came from an illustrious family of Tuscany. He was the very man [Col. 1487A] with whom Boethius had formed a close friendship long before, and to whom he had dedicated several of his works.

Boethius consulted him about all his conduct. Both burned with zeal for the glory of God, and their conversations ordinarily concerned the means of advancing it, whether by uprooting heresies, removing everything that could foster vice among the faithful, or establishing good order within the clergy. When John found himself raised to the chair of Saint Peter, and Boethius had reached the highest degree of power and influence, their zeal acquired new strength, and there was nothing that could not be expected from their union.

(247) At that time the Emperor Justin, who likewise thought of nothing but making God reign throughout his dominions, enacted new laws against heretics, in order to purge the Lord’s threshing floor of the tares mixed with the good grain. With this aim he ordered that an exact search be made for all the [Col. 1487B] Manichaeans whom his predecessor Anastasius had not merely spared but favored, and that they be punished with death.

Regarding pagans and the other heretics, he contented himself with declaring them incapable of holding any office, fearing, he said, that they might use such positions to oppress Christians, especially bishops (Book XII, title *On Heretics*). At the same time, so as not to offend Theodoric, he excepted from the general law the heretical Arian Goths allied with the Empire.

This was to give free rein to Arianism, which had already made far too much progress in both East and West. It was to encourage the cowardice of certain Catholics who, already shaken by the Arians’ efforts, would inevitably embrace their party upon seeing it authorized by the civil laws, with its adherents admitted to the honors and offices of the state and supported by the two princes who divided almost the entire Eastern and Western Empire between them.

The [Col. 1487C] fear of punishment had until then restrained several bad Catholics; but once that fear was banished from their hearts by the law Justin had just published, it seemed that nothing could any longer contain them. This caused mortal grief to the holy pontiff and to Boethius. They resolved to employ all their influence to persuade Justin to revoke the exception he had made in favor of the Arian Goths, and to use the power God had placed in his hands against the Arians as well as against the other heretics.

They wrote to Justin about this. They set in motion the friends they had in Constantinople; and the empress Euphemia, a princess of admirable piety and zeal for the glory of God and the purity of the faith, having been fully informed of the pope’s and the patrician’s intentions, pursued the matter with such ardor that she soon obtained what they desired.

She represented so vividly (249) to the emperor the prohibitions God had given his people against entering into any alliance with [Col. 1487D] his enemies, and the danger that he would draw upon himself and his family the disasters threatened against those who violate his law, that, without fearing the consequences or worrying about losing the friendship of the Arian princes, he ordered by another law that the churches usurped by these heretics be returned to the Catholics, and that the Catholic bishops seize those that the Arians had built in their dioceses and consecrate them according to the usage of the Church. This was to undermine Arianism at its foundations; for once a sect has no place in which to assemble or practice its religion, it cannot long survive.

The moment Theodoric learned the news, he appeared transported with fury. His rage burst forth against Justin in insults and invectives; he threatened nothing less than to go burn him in [Col. 1488A] his palace and reduce all Constantinople to ashes.

Since his court was full of Arians, there was no shortage of people who approved his resentment and incited him to vengeance. It was not that these courtiers cared greatly about the interests of their religion—they had no such concern. Rather, they believed they would profit by breaking the peace with the emperor. The prospect of plunder and pillage in so wealthy a city animated their savage temperament and made them ardently wish for war.

When Theodoric’s first movements of anger had passed, he turned to complaints and reproaches against the Catholics (Baronius, year 524). Addressing those who were at his court—for Catholics, like Arians, held all the offices of the state—he said:

“Is this how you acknowledge all the services I have rendered you? Is there any prince of your communion—not even excluding the emperor himself—who has done for you what I have done over the last thirty years? Have I ever disturbed anyone on account of his religion? Have I not left you [Col. 1488B] all the liberty you could desire? Who suppressed the schism that divided you? Who delivered the Church of Rome from (251) the oppression in which it lay? Finally, who restored justice and peace among you? Are you not indebted to me alone for all these advantages?

“Will you abuse my goodness and patience in this way, insulting me in the place where I am most sensitive, without regard for my person and without respect for the authority God has placed in my hands? I swear to you: if the emperor does not retract his unjust edicts, and if I do not promptly receive satisfaction, not one man of your sect will remain in my dominions before the year has ended.”

All the courtiers remained in gloomy silence, and no one dared show the slightest involvement in the matter. Almost at the same time, Theodoric received letters from the Arians in Constantinople [Col. 1488C], informing him of the oppression under which they suffered and imploring him, by everything capable of moving him, to come quickly to their aid and restore to them the liberty of which Justin’s latest edicts had deprived them.

These letters were delivered by distinguished persons from the heretical party. It is believed (252) that they were bishops, and this is likely, since they had all the more at stake in the matter because their dignity was virtually annihilated by the loss of their churches. Everything they added orally to the letters did nothing but further inflame Theodoric’s anger.

Nevertheless, he did not follow its first impulses. To act in a manner befitting royal majesty, he thought he should write to the emperor before undertaking anything.

These letters were among the most vehement, full of urgent pleas mingled with threats. The two sides exchanged letters, and the negotiation continued for some time. [Col. 1488D] But finally, seeing that Justin continually evaded the matter and would not revoke his edicts, Theodoric resolved to try another course, which seemed to him more effective for compelling him to do so.

The court was then at Ravenna. Pope John was summoned there, and Theodoric declared to him that it was his intention that John go to Constantinople with the principal members of the Roman senate as his ambassadors, to ask (253) the emperor on Theodoric’s behalf to restore the freedom of conscience he had taken from the Arians, and to declare to him that, if he refused this justice, Theodoric would treat all the Catholics in Italy as Justin treated the Arians in his dominions.

At these words the holy pontiff was overcome with grief. He did what he could to calm the prince’s mind and to free himself from a commission so unsuitable to his dignity. He even had enough firmness and courage to tell him that if, by the sovereign authority he possessed, he [Col. 1489A] compelled him to carry out his orders, he could not guarantee the outcome. This answer came very close to costing him his life on the spot. But Theodoric calmed down, and the pope, considering the danger threatening all Italy, submitted to his will. He believed that he could serve as custodian of the promises these two princes would exchange with one another in order to preserve peace in their dominions, without promising anything further.

No one can imagine Rome’s astonishment when it saw the pope compelled by Theodoric’s authority to depart for Constantinople, (254) charged with such a negotiation. They did not part from him without shedding many tears, and never were tears shed with greater reason or justice; for whatever direction the affair took, it could only be highly damaging to the Church and to its supreme pastor.

If the Emperor Justin granted Theodoric what he requested, Arianism would triumph and the Church would be humiliated. If, [Col. 1489B] on the contrary, the emperor remained firm in his resolution not to return to the Arians the churches he had taken from them, everything was to be feared for the Catholics in Italy. There was reason to fear that Theodoric would carry his resentment all the farther because he might believe that the pope had deceived him by secretly opposing the success of the matter he had ordered him to pursue on his behalf.

Although the holy pontiff was in a state of indescribable turmoil and agitation, he nevertheless decided to show nothing of it outwardly. Convinced that this new form of persecution, far from degrading his dignity, would make it still (255) more illustrious if he took care to obey God rather than men, he consulted for some time with his closest friends, especially Boethius, and prepared to depart.

The king had ships fitted out with every possible magnificence to carry him and his other ambassadors to Constantinople. Nothing had been omitted that might give the Orientals a grand impression of Theodoric’s power and wealth. To make his embassy more splendid, he required the pope to be accompanied by five bishops (Paul the Deacon, Book VII). The principal ones were the bishop of Ravenna and Eusebius of Fano, who was honored with public veneration in the Church.

He added four Roman senators: Theodoric, Importunus, and Agapitus, together with another also named Agapitus. The latter died at Thessalonica on the return journey; he was a patrician, while the other three had been consuls.

The particular orders entrusted to them were terrible. The king, newly angered because, before his departure, the pope—far from guaranteeing the success of his negotiation—had not even wished (256) to promise to help bring it to a favorable conclusion, added to his earlier threats the threat of putting to death [Col. 1489D] all the Catholics in his dominions if Justin did not restore the Arians to all their rights.

These threats could not shake the holy pontiff’s constancy, and the king could obtain no other words from him than these: that he would do his duty according to his conscience. Although the pope was ill and unable to undertake so long a journey, he forgot his own interests in thinking only of those of the Church and entrusted himself entirely to divine providence, as Boethius had continually urged him to do throughout this sorrowful affair. Nevertheless, he embarked and set sail at the beginning of the year 525.

At that time there were prodigies in heaven and on earth, which were regarded as so many omens of the misfortunes threatening humanity. For fifteen days a comet appeared, of prodigious size and extraordinary shape and position. It was not, like ordinary comets, [Col. 1490A] in the middle region of the air, but much higher; it appeared as though it were attached to the firmament (Baronius, year 525). Its form was that of a great star with a flaming tail, and it cast such a powerful light that the night was almost as bright as day.

At the same time there were several earthquakes, felt particularly in Greece and Illyria. Corinth and several other cities were severely damaged. But none felt the anger of God more visibly than Antioch, which had long since become the center of heresy and the refuge of all schismatics.

Around midday, at the moment when its inhabitants were preparing food, a wind arose with such fury that most of the houses were overthrown. Since there was scarcely a house in which a fire was not burning, the wind ignited the flames and carried them so far that everything that had withstood the wind’s violence was reduced to [Col. 1490B] ashes.

Such tragic events spread consternation (258) through all the provinces. The court at Constantinople was astonished by them, and the pious Emperor Justin, in order to urge his people to repentance, was the first to put on sackcloth and resort to prayer and fasting, seeking to soften God’s anger. The people of Constantinople followed his example, and these days of penance and mourning did not end until the arrival of the pope and Theodoric’s ambassadors.

They were shown every honor imaginable. The entire city went twelve miles out to meet the pope, carrying crosses and candles, in order, as they said, to honor in his person the Apostles Peter and Paul, whose successor he was. Everyone congratulated one another on the happiness of receiving the bishop of ancient Rome in the new Rome, for the East had not enjoyed this privilege since the imperial seat had been transferred to [Col. 1490C] Constantinople.

The supreme pontiff’s talents and holiness contributed as much as his eminent dignity to winning him the people’s veneration. God himself deigned to bear witness to him (259) through several miracles performed at his prayer or in his favor. After setting foot on land at the Isthmus of Corinth, he mounted a horse to continue his journey by land. But the horse that carried him could never afterward endure being mounted by another rider. And when he entered Constantinople through the Golden Gate, he found there a blind man to whom he restored sight simply by laying his hands upon him.

These two events are reported by Saint Gregory the Great, who lived shortly afterward and whose testimony deserves respect. The emperor, together with the imperial family, was present at the same place. Justin, then forgetting what he was on earth and seeing through the eyes of faith only Jesus Christ in his vicar, humbly prostrated himself before him and, with the most unmistakable demonstrations of respect and honor, led him [Col. 1490D] into his palace.

Although he had already been crowned by John, patriarch of Constantinople, shortly after his election, Justin wished to be crowned again by the hands of the holy pontiff. The ceremony took place in the great church on Easter Day, which that year fell on March 30. The pope performed the entire service in the language and according to all the ceremonies of the Roman Church.

Epiphanius, then patriarch of Constantinople, entirely forgetting the secret jealousy that his predecessors had long felt toward the greatness of the bishops of Rome, gladly paid him on this occasion all the honors due to the primacy of his see, and always yielded to him the right-hand side and his place.

But while Theodoric’s ambassadors were being treated with such distinction at Constantinople, that prince—who until then had been regarded as [Col. 1491A] moderate and equitable—who until then had been regarded as moderate and equitable—so completely changed his sentiments and conduct that nothing was henceforth visible in him but the cruelty of a tyrant (Anonym. apud Vales.). On mere suspicions, vague accusations, and uncertain rumors, he had Rome’s most eminent citizens arrested and subjected to all the rigors of a dreadful prison. From the reports of certain flatterers at his court, who had connections with the court of Constantinople, he learned (261) that Boethius, acting in concert with Pope John, had urged the emperor Justin to revoke the liberty that he had granted the Arians by his first edicts. Yet this was still not enough to turn him against his faithful minister; but a new affair that arose shortly afterward caused him to set aside all the considerations that had restrained him until then.

Among all the distinguished persons unjustly oppressed by the calumnies of his courtiers, there was one whose innocence was known to [Col. 1491B] Boethius. This was Albinus. He had been consul twice, and his virtue made him esteemed by all good men. Boethius especially honored him as one of the most accomplished magistrates and loved him as a friend; his advanced age even made him respected in the senate. But he was rich, and that was the cause of his ruin. Cyprian, Theodoric’s *referendarius* [Note: [Col. 1491D] Gomez was mistaken when he said that the *referendarii* were established by Justinian, who did not attain the empire until after Theodoric’s death], one of the most powerful and wicked men of those unhappy times, (262) looked upon his possessions with covetous eyes. For several years he had been seeking pretexts to satisfy his avarice. He found none more effective than to charge him with a crime against the state, thereby causing him to lose both his property and his life. He accused him before Theodoric of maintaining secret understandings with the emperor Justin, in order to make him master of Rome and drive the Goths from Italy. This was to seize the prince at his weakest point. In his old age he had become suspicious and imagined that at every moment some disturbance or sedition was arising [Col. 1491C] to drive him from a throne he had usurped.

Not only was Albinus about to be condemned on Cyprian’s sole accusation, but Theodoric also wished to involve the entire senate in his ruin as an accomplice to the same crime, when Boethius, informed of so flagrant an injustice, hastened to his aid. The king was at Verona, and the accusers, wishing to make the success of their plot more certain, had chosen the time when Boethius was absent (Boet. *Cons. Phil.*, bk. I, prose 4). But his zeal for the senate, his love of justice, and the strength of his friendship (263) gave him wings and made him despise the danger. He appeared at Theodoric’s throne when no one expected him. There, animated by the zeal he had always shown in defending oppressed virtue, he pleaded Albinus’s cause himself, and did so in a manner so affecting and moving that the king was stirred and the accusers confounded. He showed that if Albinus was guilty, he too was guilty with him, and that the entire senate was likewise guilty, since they [Col. 1491D] had never done anything except in concert. Since the king had no reason to suspect either his loyalty or that of the senate, it was unjust to make him suspect Albinus’s loyalty (Anonym. apud Vales.). He then gave him a detailed account of everything that the senate as a whole, and Albinus and he in particular, had done in his service [Note: [Col. 1491D] Since Albinus was consul when Theodoric made himself master of Ravenna, he had contributed more than anyone else to bringing Rome under his authority and securing him in the kingdom of Italy (Cass. *Chron.*)], how much they had labored to maintain his authority, and the submission they had always shown to his wishes, which the senate (264) had studied—or rather anticipated—in all its deliberations.

Then, addressing the king himself, he said:

“Is this, then, how your most faithful servants are treated? Are those who have voluntarily sacrificed [Col. 1492A] their liberty to you regarded as rebels and traitors? Who among us has not considered it a pleasure to employ his strength and his life to keep you upon the throne and support your interests? Were it the Romans who enriched themselves at the expense of the Goths, or the Goths who profited from the spoils of the Romans? What was all of Albinus’s consulship but a succession of important services rendered to Your Majesty and to the state? Would to God that all those honored by proximity to him had the same zeal for his glory and service; but far from it. Their ambition, cruelty, and avarice dishonor your reign, and it is not their fault if it does not degenerate into tyranny. Yes, Cyprian is a calumniator, and Albinus is falsely accused. Cyprian vainly attempts to cover his crime with the most specious pretexts and with an appearance of zeal for your (265) service; greed alone conceived this plot. Albinus would be innocent if he were less wealthy.”

All who were present had no doubt that the prince would consider himself offended [Col. 1492B] by the freedom with which Boethius spoke to him. But virtue, supported by so many eminent qualities shining in that great man, possesses hidden charms that make it respected even by the most barbarous souls. It is like a sanctuary that one approaches only with trembling; certain traces of divinity accompanying it are like flashes of lightning that strike and dazzle those who behold them and fill them with terror. Theodoric respected it and was moved by it. Albinus seemed less guilty to him; and, perhaps wishing to find him entirely innocent, he contented himself for the moment with saying that he would examine the matter at leisure and render justice to everyone.

Cyprian immediately understood that he was lost unless he found means to sustain his accusation, whose falsehood was revealing itself: for even the least religious princes do not tolerate with impunity (266) being deceived, or having their ministers [Col. 1492C] abuse their confidence in order to use their name for oppression and injustice; it is a crime that is never forgiven. Haman might perhaps have found favor with Ahasuerus if he had not entered so deeply into his confidence, and if that faithless courtier had not employed against Mordecai, to satisfy his passion, the authority his master had entrusted to him.

In the agitation in which Cyprian found himself, he turned to Triguille and Conigastus, those two palace officers whose avarice and injustice Boethius had so vigorously curbed while he was consul. They had not forgotten it and had long been seeking an opportunity for revenge. They gladly embraced the opportunity Cyprian offered them. It was agreed that they would not appear in the proceedings against Albinus, nor in the case they intended to bring against Boethius, lest they arouse the suspicion of Theodoric, who knew how hostile they were toward him. But they supplied memoranda designed to implicate him in Albinus’s accusation and make both of them appear [Col. 1492D] guilty.

(267) Cyprian therefore represented to the king that one ought not to be surprised if Boethius defended Albinus’s interests so warmly; that he was not merely part of the conspiracy but even more guilty than Albinus, since he was its author; and that letters written to the emperor Justin were in their possession, in which every circumstance of his treason was so distinctly marked that there could no longer be any doubt (Boet. *de Consol.*, bk. I, prose 4). At the same time he presented Theodoric with two counterfeit letters.

In the first, Boethius was made to give an account of the king’s tyrannical government and to portray [Col. 1493A] the oppression under which the senate and people were groaning.

In the other, the Romans implored the emperor, in the strongest and most urgent terms, to deliver them from it. The means were suggested to him: all the coasts of Italy, it said, were undefended and without protection; it would be easy to land troops there. They would immediately be joined by another, more considerable force, commanded by Albinus. The provinces, which awaited only this moment, would rise up. The young men would take up arms, while the senate would issue thunderous decrees against the Goths and against those who wished to aid them. The sums collected to bring this project to success were then specified.

At once Theodoric, without examining the matter further, lost all the confidence he had placed in his minister, forgot all the services he had rendered him, and, resolved not to hear his defense, judged him guilty.

[Col. 1493B] Who can comprehend the darkness that spreads over the eyes of a prince when one knows how to strike at his weakness? The least plausible things, the most remote from reason and common sense, pass in his mind as established and genuine facts; he sees dangers where there is not even an appearance of danger. Nothing was easier than to discover Cyprian’s imposture and deceit: it was enough to compare Boethius’s handwriting and style with letters known to be unquestionably his, and to ask the accuser where he had obtained the letters he produced. If Boethius had written letters of such importance to the emperor Justin, should one not have believed that he would have placed them in the hands of the pope and of his senatorial friends, who had recently departed for Constantinople? Where were the troops that were supposed to assemble at the first signal? How could Albinus have commanded them at his decrepit age, when he had never [Col. 1493C] borne arms or known what war was? The slightest reflection on these circumstances would have been enough to open Theodoric’s eyes and make him recognize the imposture of Boethius’s accusers. But at that moment he remembered only what could confirm him in his false prejudices. He recalled what had already been told him: that Boethius had written to Justin, in concert with the pope, urging him to destroy Arianism in his dominions; that on many occasions he had shown his aversion to the sect; and that he had always zealously embraced the Catholic cause. The freedom of the remonstrances he had made to him (270) several times appeared to him a criminal insolence and the true mark of a mind inclined to revolt. Nothing more was needed for him to believe Boethius guilty, just like the bishop of Rome. Indignation seized his heart and anger was kindled. From anger he passed to desires for vengeance: his mind revolved only fatal thoughts against these two great men [Col. 1493D], and he regarded them only as irreconcilable enemies of his state and his person.

The impostors triumphed and already congratulated themselves on having mastered the prince’s mind, but they feared a reversal. A single moment would be enough to disabuse him, and then all their iniquity, once exposed, would fall back upon their own heads: this was what they dreaded. They therefore had to add crime to crime and employ yet another means of confirming Theodoric in his belief. They thought that if they had other persons, especially Catholics, assure him of the same things they had told him, not only would the king never be disabused, but they would also protect themselves if the affair were brought to trial, by shifting all the iniquity of the accusation onto witnesses whose depositions they were merely reporting.

[Col. 1494A] A few days earlier, two notorious brigands, Opilio and Gaudentius, had been condemned to exile (Boet. *de Consol.*, bk. I, prose 4). Their principal crime was having diverted to their own use considerable sums entrusted to them for the needs of the state. To escape justice, they had fled into a church as into an asylum that no one dared violate. But since these criminals had themselves been the first to violate public faith, Theodoric had no hesitation in ordering that they be violently torn from the very altar they were embracing and, after being branded on the forehead with a hot iron, led to the place of their exile if they did not leave Ravenna on the appointed day. His orders were about to be carried out when Cyprian had their execution suspended. He secretly gave these criminals to understand, as though he had received the prince’s order, that they would be pardoned if they testified against Boethius. What are criminals not capable of doing to escape the punishment due to their crime? [Col. 1494B] They promised everything, asking only that the substance of the deposition they were expected to make be given to them in writing and be fully detailed, so that they could make it more credible through the uniformity it would display and would not risk contradicting themselves if questioned separately.

Basil, formerly steward of the royal household, had been expelled from the palace for his misconduct. Finding himself burdened with debts and reduced to the greatest extremity, he was easily corrupted. Won over by Cyprian’s money, he joined Opilio and Gaudentius and promised to appear with them as Boethius’s accuser. Assured on this point, Cyprian went to Theodoric ( *Cons. Ph.*, bk. I, prose 14) and, after protesting by everything most sacred and holy in religion that zeal alone for His Majesty and for the preservation of his person moved him on this occasion, begged him not to rely solely on what he had had the honor of telling him about Boethius’s conspiracy, but to listen to those who were better informed than [Col. 1494C] he.

“What, then?” cried the king in anger. “Are there subjects in my kingdom wicked enough to conceal from me a conspiracy formed against me? If there are any, whoever they may be, they must die.”

That was not what Cyprian wanted. Therefore, to avoid this reaction, which thwarted all his plans, he immediately resumed speaking:

“No, my lord; they would already have done so if they had not been restrained by Boethius’s violence and intimidated by his threats. Since then they have not even dared approach the palace. It is Gaudentius, Opilio, and Basil whom people have represented to Your Majesty as criminals. The mere names of these wretches should make their testimony suspect; for can one expect truth from the mouth of a man convicted and condemned for his crimes to undergo the [Col. 1494D] just punishment he deserves?”

But whether Theodoric was seeking only a pretext to rid himself of Boethius and free himself from a man whom he regarded as a stern censor of his conduct, or whether he wished to avenge himself for everything Boethius had done toward the destruction of Arianism, he ordered these witnesses to be brought in and their depositions received.

The first declared that he had heard Boethius say several times that the Romans would not continue much longer to groan beneath the tyranny of the Goths, and that he had often heard him express wishes for the liberty of the senate and people.

The second added that Symmachus, Albinus, and several other senators often assembled at Boethius’s house and at improper hours; that they then shut themselves in and excluded all their servants from their presence; that they composed writings there that they kept highly secret; and that on the eve of the pope’s departure [Col. 1495A] for Constantinople, their conference had lasted throughout the night.

Finally, the third protested that he had often heard Boethius speak of the king in an offensive manner, while praising instead, in the most pompous terms, the piety and clemency of the emperor Justin. He declared that Boethius had strongly criticized the prohibition [Note: [Col. 1495D] Theodoric had imposed this prohibition on the Romans at Eutaric’s instigation in 518] by which the king had forbidden the Romans to bear arms or keep them in their homes, calling it an injustice and a tyranny; and, finally, that all the Orientals who came to Rome went to Boethius’s house, where they found a secure refuge and were always treated magnificently.

This was enough to turn Theodoric’s suspicions against Boethius into complete conviction of the crimes imputed to him. The false witnesses were acquitted and released, while orders were simultaneously issued for the arrest of Boethius and Albinus. But since senators could be judged only by the senate [Col. 1495B] itself when assembled, Theodoric, in order to preserve at least some appearance of justice, wished the case to be brought before it, and the accusers and witnesses to be heard and confronted there.

When it became known in Rome that Boethius had been arrested, no one failed to feel deeply the injury done to virtue itself by its oppression in the person of this great man. The whole city was plunged into desolation, and everything was seen to be the opposite of what ordinarily occurs in the misfortunes of courtiers and ministers. When they incur the prince’s displeasure, everyone disowns them and each person avoids them; people even discover new crimes in their persons and conduct of which they had never before been accused. The wisest remain silent and consider it a great deal if they do not join their enemies.

All who were eminent in the senate, distinguished in the clergy, or notable in the state for virtue and [Col. 1495C] merit—except the Arians—shared in Boethius’s disgrace; each felt it as though it had happened to him personally. The poor, the widows, and all who were oppressed lamented it still more. But Triguille and (277) Conigastus, seeing him unable to oppose their injustices, no longer feared joining Cyprian and his accusers openly. They appeared in the full senate with the *referendarius*, escorted by a large band of armed men and followed by several companies of soldiers, in order to inspire fear in the judges and forestall the just resentment of a people outraged by the loss of its father and protector.

Never had the senate found itself more embarrassed. Convinced of Boethius’s innocence, it seemed unable to acquit him without condemning itself, or to give grounds for believing that it had shared in the conspiracy of which he was accused. The first charge brought against him was that he had abused his authority to [Col. 1495D] prevent the king from being informed of the steps the senate had taken to shake off the Gothic yoke and restore Rome to the hands of the Eastern emperors, its former masters.

The second was that he had written to Justin to urge him to come and deliver the senate from Theodoric’s tyranny. (278) To acquit a man accused of such crimes was to reveal that one had participated in them and to make oneself guilty. To condemn him was to act against one’s own conscience and to put virtue itself on trial. But how could they have declared him innocent? He was not even given the freedom to [Col. 1496A] defend himself; his condemnation was pursued with arms in hand, and the prince declared himself his adversary. What courage and firmness would the senate have needed to refuse to provide some satisfaction to the sovereign’s vengeance?

[Note: [Col. 1495D] “But the king was laying a snare for the Romans and seeking how he might kill them” (Anonym. apud Vales.).]

It is even claimed that Theodoric was setting a trap for the senate, which had become suspect to him, so that whatever judgment it rendered in the case, he would have a pretext for destroying it entirely. For if it condemned the accused—since they were the senate’s principal members and leaders, and those most capable of opposing the prince’s unjust wishes—he could easily reduce the other senators to the condition he desired. And if it acquitted them, he would have grounds to accuse their judges of being accomplices in the crime of which they were accused and of having dared not condemn them lest they be forced to condemn themselves. Whatever course the senate took, it always risked much (Boet. *l. de Cons. Ph.*, bk. I, prose 4; Bail. *in vit. Boet.*).

[Col. 1496B] The senators clearly perceived the danger threatening them; the question was how to avoid it. After several deliberations, they thought they could do so by concluding in favor of banishment. Convinced that time might bring some change in affairs, that Boethius’s absence might soften the minds of Theodoric and his enemies, or that, since the prince was already old, the exile would be brief, they believed they could choose no better course.

Yet nothing was more unjust than the sentence pronounced by the senate. If Boethius was guilty of the crime of which he was accused, banishment was too light a punishment: he deserved death. If he was not guilty, was there anything more unjust than to proscribe an innocent man? Such are most of the judgments rendered by the world’s false justice, whose only rules are political considerations; one always finds in them (280) a core of iniquity that cannot escape human eyes.

Once the sentence had been pronounced, Theodoric’s passion was still not [Col. 1496C] satisfied. He had Boethius and Albinus taken to Pavia and confined in the tower [Note: [Col. 1495D] It is made of brick and is round in shape; but the cathedral church, which was then very near it, has been changed into a monastery called the Annunciation, and the principal church has been transferred to another part of the city. Boethius was confined in the highest part of the tower] of the church’s baptistery, which then served as a prison. It still exists and is still known by the name of Boethius’s prison. From that moment he was so closely guarded that his relatives and friends were no longer permitted to approach him to offer consolation; no one was allowed to accompany him to Pavia. Only wisdom and the Muses, as he himself says (Boet. bk. I, *de Cons. Ph.*, meter 1), could not be prevented from accompanying him; they remained his faithful companions until his death.

Although, by the king’s order, everything capable of increasing the prison’s (281) horror had been gathered there, Boethius was not frightened. At first he had several petitions presented to the king in his defense, but they were not heard, because nothing was feared more than that he might not be found guilty. This denial of justice made him understand that his ruin had been decided (Boet. ibid.); for [Col. 1496D] Theodoric had never condemned anyone without hearing him. He always left the accused complete freedom to defend themselves, and often indicated to them himself the persons whom he believed most capable at the bar of presenting their case advantageously. This extraordinary conduct led many people to believe that the king was convinced of Boethius’s innocence, but that certain secret reasons, which he wished to conceal because they would not have honored him, made him seize upon this pretext to rid himself of Boethius.

Indeed, once his flatterers had gained the [Col. 1497A] upper hand in his mind, he regarded Boethius only as the greatest enemy of his sect and a severe censor of all his actions. Thus it is truly dangerous to speak too freely of the truth (282) to earthly kings when it does not accord with their passions, and it always costs much to good men who possess sufficient strength and courage to do so. For there are few princes like the great Theodosius (Paulin. *in vit. Ambr.*), who regret having found only one Ambrose in their dominions—that is, only one bishop who never concealed the truth from him.

For the rest, Boethius never appeared so great as he did in chains. There, awaiting death with the tranquility of a philosopher and the submission of a perfect Christian, he composed various works in which piety and the purest virtue are joined to profound learning. The treatise *On the Trinity of God*, which he addressed to Symmachus, was the first fruit of his imprisonment. From the beginning of [Col. 1497B] this work he makes it clear that it is especially the impiety of the Goths that he attacks and that he has only the destruction of Arianism in view, as though he wished to consecrate his final thoughts and devote the last strokes of his pen to defending the divinity of the Son of God, for whom (283) he was soon to give his life.

In the preface he laments the calamities of his time and the fact that, wherever he turns his eyes, he sees only cowardly Christians unworthy of the name they bear, or wretched heretics who dishonor God’s majesty by their blasphemies. Neither group, he says, deserves to have this work addressed to them, since it would be like casting precious pearls before swine to expose such sublime truths to profane eyes. But he rejoices to have found in Symmachus a soul sufficiently holy to receive the mystery of our religion with respect, a mind sufficiently [Col. 1497C] enlightened to discern its beauty, a heart sufficiently pure to savor its principles and its unction, and a Christian sufficiently faithful to transmit the sacred deposit of the faith to posterity without alteration.

He asks him to examine whether he has faithfully followed the thoughts and principles of Saint Augustine, whose works he had studied closely, and to attribute to the difficulty of the subject whatever defects he may find, since he is certain that the sublimity (284) of the subject infinitely surpasses the weakness of the human mind. An analysis of this treatise will be found in the second part of this *History*.

Symmachus received it at Rome, where he was overwhelmed with grief at the disaster suffered by his son-in-law and occupied in consoling his daughter Rusticiana over her separation from her husband, and his grandchildren over their separation from a father who was so dear to them. It was no small consolation amid their troubles to learn of the firmness and constancy with which Boethius endured his misfortunes, and of the peace and tranquility [Col. 1497D] enjoyed by his soul in the obscurity of his prison and in the continual expectation of death. Never did they better understand the truth of Saint Paul’s words: that the spirit of God cannot be held captive. Indeed, what holy freedom Boethius must have enjoyed to be able to compose a work such as the one he had just sent to Symmachus! What detachment, concentration, and elevation of mind were necessary for him to write on so sublime and abstract a subject?

If one gives even a little thought (285) to the multitude of passions that arise, to the succession of convulsive movements by which the human heart, reduced to the condition in which Boethius found himself, is ordinarily agitated—the oppression of the present, fear of the future, memory of the past, a devastated family, a beloved wife and children exposed to the fury of his enemies and on the point of being crushed [Col. 1498A] beneath the ruins of his fortune; that dreadful fall from the highest degree of honor, wealth, and greatness into an abyss of misery; innocence oppressed, iniquity applauded, falsehood and calumny triumphing over truth—one will agree that the perfect freedom of mind Boethius enjoyed in his chains could only have been the effect of extraordinary grace, and that it was at the same time the mark of a heroic soul.

Knowing, then, that Boethius regarded all these tragic events with a tranquil eye and with that holy indifference by which a perfect Christian receives alike the good and the evil of this life as coming from the hand of God, they (286) were ashamed to entertain feelings different from his. His example taught them to abandon themselves entirely to divine providence and to leave it complete control of the affair.

Theodoric displayed far greater anxiety and impatience concerning the outcome of the embassy [Col. 1498B] he had sent to Constantinople. He continually inquired what his ambassadors were doing there, whether they were faithfully carrying out their commission, and what relations and conferences they had with the emperor Justin. The Arians of Constantinople regularly gave him a faithful account of it. At first they informed him of the extraordinary honors paid to the pope and the senators accompanying him, and of the universal joy of the clergy, court, and people at their arrival. Far from being alarmed by this, Theodoric conceived good hopes. But some time afterward he learned that the pope had reconciled all the churches the emperor had taken from the Arians; that the Catholics were in possession of them; and that, far from persuading Justin to revoke the edicts issued specifically against members of his sect, the holy pontiff had instead confirmed him in his resolve to have them executed to the [Col. 1498C] letter. Theodoric then fell into such a fury that people thought he would lose his mind (Greg. Tur. *de Glor. Mart.*, ch. 40).

In the first movements of his passion he ordered armed troops to be made ready to go throughout his dominions and massacre the Catholics. But shortly afterward, having recovered from his initial outburst and reflecting that such unheard-of cruelty might cause a general uprising, since the Catholics greatly outnumbered the Arians, he revoked the order and contented himself with having the most distinguished persons arrested, so that they could be put to death separately and without public display, as will be seen in what follows.

He did not even wait for Pope John’s return before displaying his resentment against Boethius, his pious and faithful minister. As soon as he had been informed of what had occurred at Constantinople against the Arians, he no longer doubted that everything there had been done (288) in concert with Boethius. He regarded him as the author [Col. 1498D] of the persecution the emperor was inflicting upon his impious sect and as the guiding force behind the conduct of his ambassadors in the East. For these reasons he resolved to have him put to death.

He gave the order to Eusebius, governor and chief magistrate of Pavia, where Boethius was still being held prisoner, commanding him to condemn Boethius to death without hearing him and without even allowing him to say a word in his defense; to strip him of all his offices and dignities; to declare his property confiscated; and to formally announce his sentence in the customary manner, but to suspend the execution of the death sentence until further orders.

The motives Theodoric may have had for such extraordinary conduct are unknown. There is reason to believe that his only purpose was to make Boethius suffer more, and, if possible, cast that great soul into impatience and despair—or, if he did not yet wish to destroy him completely, to break him so as to subject him to all his wishes. For is it not to die a thousand times a day, and, so to speak, to taste death in long draughts, to survive so long after the sentence of one’s condemnation?

Eusebius, delivered over to injustice, obeyed the prince’s orders without delay. He pronounced Boethius’s sentence and immediately had him loaded with irons and chains so heavy that they kept him bent toward the ground. This was no light punishment for a man accustomed to looking toward heaven, where his heart continually turned; he himself admits that it was among the sufferings most keenly felt by him (*Consolation of Philosophy*, Book I, prose 4). He heard his sentence without being shaken by it, and all his misfortunes could not draw from him the slightest complaint. Since he had never been attached to the goods of this world, and had always regarded the splendor of human greatness with contempt, he saw himself unjustly stripped of them without concern. Raised above everything that passes with time, [Col. 1499B] he regarded all these losses as a sure gain acquired for eternity, and as a means of completing his course with greater lightness and of being united all the more closely to his Creator, since his soul (290) was freed from all the bonds that keep human beings so immoderately attached to life.

In this condition, as though he were the happiest of mortals or already freed from the human condition, he had no conversation except with God, and sought in the treasures of divine wisdom alone the strength and consolation he needed. This gave him occasion to compose those admirable books of the *Consolation of Philosophy* [Note: [Col. 1499D] We owe it to Nicolas Crescius, a Florentine monk of the Cistercian order, that Boethius’s books of the *Consolation* were restored to their original purity on the basis of the best and oldest manuscripts, which he sought out with great care in all the libraries of Italy. Before the edition he had produced in Florence, they could scarcely be recognized, so corrupt and different were they from the originals.]. One cannot read them without being astonished by the tranquillity of his soul and the profound peace it enjoyed amid so many misfortunes. They are interwoven with prose and poetry, and this agreeable mixture, sustained consistently from beginning [Col. 1499C] to end, has always caused them to be regarded as one of the most accomplished works of its kind and as the author’s masterpiece. It is divided into five books, and one cannot tell what deserves the greater admiration: the variety of its arguments, its thoughts—each finer and more elevated than the last and filled with piety—or the beauty of its style, its choice of words, and the sweetness of its expressions. For twelve centuries it has delighted all people of intelligence, and it has been translated into as many different languages as there are nations in Europe. But since the translators did not feel in their hearts that living flame of the love of God which animated Boethius when he composed it, and were not as deeply penetrated as he was by the great truths treated in it, they do not convey the same charms and attractions, and much of the original’s grace is lacking.

The learned Murmell [Note: [Col. 1499D] Murmell was rector of the college of Münster, and a friend [Col. 1500D] and fellow student of Erasmus. He worked extensively to restore distinction to humane letters in his age, which may be called an age of ignorance. He died in 1517.] wrote a (292) commentary on the five books of Boethius’s *Consolation*, and his observations greatly assist in achieving a more perfect understanding [Col. 1499D] of the author’s thoughts, because he shows the connection between several passages that at first seemed unrelated, and explains many things that are not easily understood without a thorough familiarity with the poets and with the customs of the ancient Romans.

[Col. 1500A] Those who love humane letters will always read them with pleasure, because they are full of learning. At least as much learning is found in those that Wallin published in 1656; they are much clearer, more reliable, and less diffuse.

Denis the Carthusian had also written a commentary on the same work a hundred years earlier; it is not to be despised. If it contains less profane learning than Murmell’s (293), it displays more piety and offers more instruction concerning morals. They were formerly attributed to Saint Thomas Aquinas, but without foundation.

In the second part of this work an analysis will be given of the five books of Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*, more extensive than those of his other treatises, because it contains several circumstances of his life that will have to be developed, and that will shed considerable light on his history.

Boethius, having therefore begun his books of the *Consolation of Philosophy* in the prison at Pavia, [Col. 1500B] did not have time to complete them there; for after his death sentence had been pronounced, he was transferred to a castle situated in the territory of Calvance (*Anonymus apud Valesium*, p. 485, no. 30) [Note: [Col. 1500D] “But now, removed almost five hundred thousand paces away and without defense.” *Consolation of Philosophy*, Book I, prose 4. Boethius means the wilderness of Calvance in this passage, for from Rome to Pavia one counts only about three hundred miles.], about five hundred miles from Rome and almost as far from Pavia, in the midst of a dreadful desert (294). God permitted this in order to test his servant’s constancy still further through the complete deprivation of all human consolation, while Theodoric acted thus to exhaust his patience and, if he remained unyielding, to have him killed without publicity or danger of provoking unrest in the state. He would have found this difficult to avoid had he had him executed publicly in Rome or Pavia, and the senate might perhaps not have tolerated it.

It was in this solitude, in this general abandonment by all creatures, that divine Wisdom communicated herself more familiarly to our philosopher, and it was there that he completed his books of the *Consolation [Col. 1500C] of Philosophy*. He himself reports that Theodoric omitted nothing during this sad sojourn that he thought capable of making him change his mind. First, they wanted him to acknowledge the letters attributed to him; second, to declare that Theodoric’s conduct toward the senate was entirely equitable and just, and that, far from having governed his states as a tyrant, he had left the senate and (295) the peoples subject to him all the liberty and advantages they had enjoyed under the emperors who had governed them since Constantine. If he admitted these two facts, he was promised life and freedom.

However pressing the solicitations made to him, they could never soften his courage. Unable to betray the truth or conceal his convictions through cowardly compliance, he stood firm to the end, always protesting that the letters attributed to him were false and fabricated, and, on the other hand, that he would never cease to [Col. 1500D] pray for the freedom of his country and for the growth of the Catholic faith and religion, which they were attempting to oppress.

Several months passed in these entreaties. Theodoric, seeing that they were useless, resolved to obtain by the force of torture what he had been unable to obtain by threats; but they had [Col. 1501A] no greater success. So sincere a confession and so generous a resistance made his enemies blush. They were ashamed to put (296) to death a man who had been convicted of no crime, and against whom none could bring any charge other than that of having shown too much zeal for the public good and for the honor of the senate. He had to be made odious in order to disguise the injustice. They charged him with an infamous crime, and the connection between ancient pagan philosophy and magic provided Boethius’s enemies with a pretext for accusing him of being a magician because he was a philosopher. They spread among the people the claim that he had risen to the state’s most important offices and posts, which he had held from his youth, only through magical illusions and by the aid of demons. The very name of magic horrified him, for no one had ever been farther than he from defiling himself with so detestable a profession.

“Do you not remember,” he said to Wisdom, whom he calls as his witness, “that from my tenderest years you had insinuated yourself [Col. 1501B] into my heart, had made yourself its mistress, and had uprooted from it the desire for the perishable things of this world? That the first lesson you gave me was (297) that it was unworthy of your disciples to secure the protection of those vile and contemptible spirits of darkness, and that the person whom you carefully formed to be raised to the lofty dignity of likeness to God through imitation of his virtues should never lose sight of that divine model? If the innocent life led within my household, and my choice of friends, all people of acknowledged integrity, were not enough to shield me from suspicion of so heinous a crime (*Boethius*, cited above, Book I, prose 4), should not the name of Symmachus, my father-in-law, with whom I always lived in the closest union and under whose eyes I continually remained—the name, I say, of a man as worthy of respect as virtue itself—have protected me from it? But through an injustice that cannot be understood, they take as an occasion to accuse me of sorcery the fact that I had the advantage of being educated in your school, O most loving Wisdom, and of having learned from you to regulate my conduct. Was it not enough that, in my person, you had been covered with disgrace and contempt (298)? To increase my sorrow, did you also have to be torn apart and treated with equal indignity because of me and the designs formed against my life?”

This is what Boethius alleged in his defense and for his own consolation. But although the accusation contained no plausibility, he was not heard; they silenced him, and Theodoric ordered that he be put to torture. They devised a wholly new torture, and one of the most cruel. It is not known precisely whether Theodoric invented it or whether Cyprian suggested it (*Anonymus*, Valesius, p. 485, no. 30). A large wheel was set up and turned by a crank. A rope was fastened to it and wrapped around the martyr’s head; as the wheel turned, the rope tightened more and more.

[Col. 1501D] This repeated torment could draw no complaint from the mouth of that innocent victim. Absorbed in the greatness of the eternal goods he was about to possess, he appeared insensible to the cruelties inflicted upon his body. They were such that his eyes were forced from their sockets. They then subjected him to another torment no less infamous or painful. He was stretched out on a beam, and after being tied to it, two executioners beat him for a long time with sticks over every part of his body, from his neck to the soles of his feet. Some historians (*Anonymus*, as above; the manuscript *Life of the Pontiffs* in the Vatican Library; Anastasius on John; and Cossinus, Baronius) believed that he died in this torment, but others, more numerous and with much stronger grounds, maintain that he survived it and ended his life by the axe or the sword.

Thus died this great man, the ornament of his age, the firmest support of the [Col. 1502A] Catholic faith, the protector of innocence and the laws, in his fifty-fifth year, on 23 October 525, the eighth year of Justin’s empire, the thirty-third year of Theodoric’s reign, and the second year of the pontificate of Pope John I, under the consulship of Probin and Philoxenus. His labors, continual application, affliction, misfortunes, and the horrors of his imprisonment—which lasted seven months and perhaps longer—had made him old before his time, as he himself says (*Boethius*, *Consolation of Philosophy*, Book I, meter 1). His hair was completely white, and his skin was dried and marked (300) with wrinkles. The thought of an approaching death was, during the final months of his life, the only consolation he could find for his sufferings.

He appears to have been taller than average. He had a broad, high forehead; lively, slightly sunken eyes; a long, aquiline nose; hollow cheeks; a pleasant mouth; and well-proportioned features. Integrity was depicted on his face [Col. 1502B], and even his appearance inspired respect. This was apparent in his statues and busts, which were still preserved in Rome when I was there in 1691. One was preserved in the Justiniani Palace, from which Wallin had a portrait of Boethius made, had it engraved, and placed it at the beginning of his works when he had them printed in 1656. The inscription that could be read on it stated that it had been erected when he was fifty years old. Nothing is said of this in his history, but that was precisely the period of his greatest fortune and highest elevation. Moreover, an ancient author (Raphael Volaterranus) assures us that the princess Amalasuntha, after the death of her father Theodoric, had the statues of Boethius and Symmachus, which had been overturned at the time of their condemnation, re-erected in (301) Rome. This implies that statues had been erected to them during their lifetimes.

Although Theodoric tried to cloak so odious an act [Col. 1502C] under the specious pretext of justice punishing the alleged infidelity of his minister, it is nevertheless certain that he began to hate him and resolved to have him killed only after discovering that the emperor Justin, at Boethius’s urging, had taken away from the Arians the free exercise of their religion. That was the cause of this holy man’s death, and no other should be sought, even though Theodoric had different causes published so as not to give the Romans an opportunity to revolt. Julian the Apostate acted in the same way: he never appeared to have Christians put to death out of hatred for their religion; he had them all perish under various pretexts, and the Church nevertheless honored them as true martyrs because it was convinced that they would have been found innocent had they not been Christians (302). For this reason antiquity did not deny Boethius the honor of martyrdom, any more than it denied it to the holy Pope John, who was involved in the same conspiracy and suffered [Col. 1502D] for the same cause.

Boethius appears to have deserved it even more justly than that holy pope, for Theodoric allowed Pope John to waste away miserably in prison, and his death was not so violent; it cannot be determined whether illness and the hardships of the journey contributed more to his death than hunger and ill-treatment. What is distinctive in Boethius’s case, and what makes it impossible to deny him the title of martyr without injustice, is that no one can dispute that he died in defense of justice and truth, and that Cyprian, Triguille, and Conigastus brought about his death solely out of resentment. Had he quietly allowed them to oppress the innocent and devour the substance of orphans and widows, they would never have plotted his death. That is why modern writers such as Baronius, Bollandus and his continuators, and even M. Baillet, after [Col. 1503A] (303) Pierre des Noels, Canisius, and others, have not hesitated to give him, like the ancients, the title of martyr.

Indeed, if antiquity did not deny it to King Sigismund or to several other persons who, having lived piously, were unjustly killed, although this was not out of hatred for the faith (*Gregory of Tours*, Book III of the *History*, no. 6), should it be denied to Boethius, who, after fighting until the last moment of his life for truth and justice, had the glory of shedding his blood in that glorious struggle? No Christian has ever been more worthy of it.

Since Theodoric had an interest in keeping his death secret, he had him executed in the prison at Calvance. The ministers of his cruelty would naturally have buried him immediately in some obscure place near the prison. Nevertheless, his body was handed over that very day to the Catholics, who carried it to Pavia, where it was buried beside Elpis, his first wife. Papebroch believes that this was in the church near the Baptistery tower, which had served as his prison; [Col. 1503B] this led several historians to say that it was in Pavia itself that Theodoric had him put to death.

Fear of arousing the prince’s indignation caused him to be given a burial far less honorable than he deserved. Nevertheless, an epitaph was made for him and engraved upon his tomb; it has been preserved to the present day. It says much in few words, although in a barbarous style. Here it is:

> Behold Boethius, great in heaven, and visible  
> To the whole world, a man worthy of wonder.  
> Betrayed to the unjust King Theodoric,  
> He spent his old age in exile at Ticinum;  
> In that city, consoling himself in sorrow, he composed a little book,  
> Then, struck by the sword, he departed from this life.

It is found somewhat differently in Papebroch under 27 May, but the meaning is entirely the same. The version reported by that author was apparently placed there instead of the older one when Boethius was given a more honorable burial [Col. 1503C]; for it is noticeable that Pavia, called Ticinum by the ancients (305), is there named Papia, which is what the Lombards called it. This leads one to believe that it is no older than their age.

Father Mabillon, in his *Journey through Italy*, says that he saw Boethius’s tomb in Pavia, in the church of Saint Augustine, at the foot of the steps by which one ascends into the sanctuary on the southern side, raised upon four columns. He adds that, in place of the ancient leonine verses just quoted, Balthasar Taconus had substituted others of his own composition, as follows:

> Most illustrious in city walls and in the Latin tongue, and I who  
> Was consul, here perished, sent into exile;  
> And whatever death snatched away, integrity lifted me to heaven;  
> Now my fame flourishes greatly, and my work lives.

It would have been desirable that so learned a man as Father Mabillon had been willing to tell us how Boethius’s tomb was transferred to the church of Saint Augustine of Pavia, where it now stands, since that church was built only about two hundred years (306) after his death. Since he did not do so, we shall try to make up for the omission.

Theodoric’s cruelty was not yet satisfied. It went so far as to have Symmachus killed, that senator so worthy of respect for his age and virtues, who brought honor to Rome and was the head and glory of the senate. Fearing that he might wish to avenge his son-in-law’s death (*Anonymus apud Valesium*, p. 486, no. 20), Theodoric summoned him to Ravenna several months later, had him arrested there, and beheaded him in prison. Such grievous blows could deeply affect Rustician, his daughter and Boethius’s wife, but they were not capable of crushing her. Never had such religion and greatness of soul appeared amid so complete an overturning of fortune.

By losing her father and husband she was deprived of all their possessions, and, after having held the first rank among the Roman ladies, [Col. 1504A] she soon found herself reduced to begging. Her faith sustained her in this prostration; and the more she saw human assistance withdraw from her, the more her confidence in God increased. (307) It was not in vain, for a few days after Symmachus’s death, once Theodoric’s iniquity had reached its fulfillment, God exacted from him the vengeance it deserved.

While he was at table, the head of a monstrous fish was served to him. He imagined that in this head he saw the head of Symmachus threatening him with its eyes and teeth, biting his lower lip like a man in the height of anger. Fear seized him and caused a general trembling. Convulsions followed and became so continual that in a short time his face was disfigured and he found himself at the point of death. The remorse of his conscience agitated him inwardly with equal violence; and, unable any longer to conceal what he felt in his soul, while Elpidius, his physician, employed all his skill to warm his limbs, already half dead, he [Col. 1504B] uttered deep sighs and bitterly lamented the crime he had committed in causing Boethius and Symmachus to die. He praised those two great men and condemned himself for having too readily believed the reports made to him.

But his regret (308) could not appease God’s justice; the moment of divine vengeance had come, and he died amid suffering. The event is too important for us not to report Procopius’s complete testimony, on which it particularly rests. Several historians have confirmed it, and there is no indication that it was ever called into question in antiquity.

> Symmachus and his son-in-law Boethius were patricians of distinguished ancestral blood, leaders of the Roman senate, and consuls. They had devoted themselves to philosophy and equity above all other mortals, and with their resources had assisted many needy people, both Romans and foreigners. Having risen to immense glory, they aroused the worst men against themselves out of envy. Persuaded by these informers, King Theodoric killed the illustrious men as though they were plotting revolution [Col. 1504C], and confiscated all their property. But a few days later, when his attendants had placed before him at dinner the head of a huge fish, Theodoric thought it was the head of the recently murdered Symmachus. With its teeth fixed into its lower lip and its eyes staring at him darkly and furiously, it seemed to threaten him greatly (309). Terrified by the strange portent and trembling and shuddering beyond measure, he withdrew hastily to his bedchamber. Ordering large quantities of clothing to be heaped upon him repeatedly, he obtained a little relief. Then, after explaining to the physician Elpidius everything that had happened, he bewailed the crime he had committed against Symmachus and Boethius. Finally, overwhelmed with immense grief after lamenting their deaths, he died not long afterward. This was the first and last example of injustice he exercised against his subjects, because in this case he had passed judgment on such eminent men without investigating the matter carefully, as was his custom.  
> *Procopius, History of the Gothic War*, Book I.

Before this event, Theodoric had suffered an excessive discharge of bile for two or three days, which had greatly weakened him. This gave some historians occasion to say that he had died in the same manner as Arius, confusing an aspect of his illness with the true cause of his death. A few days earlier he had issued an order depriving the Catholics of their (310) churches throughout his dominions and handing them over to the Arians (*Paul the Deacon*, *History*, Book XV, p. 437, and elsewhere). This order was to be carried out the following Sunday, which was to be for the Arians a day of celebration and rejoicing because of the victory they expected to achieve over idolatry—for that is how they described the Catholic religion. But that Sunday was changed for them into a day of mourning and sorrow by the death of their most powerful protector, and God’s justice visibly halted him at the very moment when he was becoming most threatening to the Church.

[Col. 1505A] He nevertheless received the most magnificent burial honors. During his lifetime he had had a splendid mausoleum built for himself, the largest ever seen in Italy; he was carried there with truly royal pomp. His daughter Amalasuntha, niece of Clovis, the first Christian king, succeeded him in the kingdom of Italy. Having built at Ravenna the magnificent church of Our Lady of the Rotunda in place of that great mausoleum, which was only of stone, she had another made of porphyry and raised beneath the dome of the cathedral in an admirable manner (311), so that it appeared to be suspended in the air, with Theodoric above life-size, seemingly ready to ascend into heaven.

It remained there until the time of Caesius, archbishop of Ravenna. This prelate, rightly indignant to see the ashes of an Arian heretic placed with such honor in a holy place, had the mausoleum demolished and the tomb moved to the entrance of the church of Saint Apollinaris. It is a great porphyry urn still visible there, above which [Col. 1505B] the following inscription appears:

> This porphyry vessel once contained, at the summit of the Rotunda, the ashes of Theodoric, Emperor of the Goths. With the favor of Peter Donatus Caesius, bishop, it was transferred here, for perpetual remembrance, by the wise men of the commonwealth.  
> R. P. P. C.  
> 1564.  
> (*Papebroch*, under 27 May, p. 710.)

But while such great honors were being paid in this world to Theodoric’s ashes, his soul in the next was treated very differently by God’s avenging justice. He (312) wished to make something of this known to a holy solitary who had withdrawn to the island of Lipari near Sicily (*Paul the Deacon*, *History*, Book XV, pp. 467, 475). On the very day Theodoric died, God showed the solitary in a vision Theodoric covered with a sackcloth garment, barefoot, and with his hands bound behind his back like a criminal; Pope John, Boethius, and Symmachus were leading him and casting him into the flames.

Two of Theodoric’s officers, Goths by nation, who had come to Sicily on his behalf [Col. 1505C] to collect taxes and had been obliged to remain there in order to have their ships repaired, went to Lipari that very day to visit the holy solitary. During the conversation he told them of Theodoric’s death and of what God had revealed to him concerning the king’s fate the previous night. Since they had left the king in perfect health only a few days earlier, they believed none of it. But when they returned to Ravenna, they learned that Theodoric had indeed died on the day and at the hour the solitary had indicated. This event is reported by Pope Saint Gregory, who assures us that he learned it from the two officers themselves.

The Arians, in order to conceal from the public eye the signs of divine vengeance that had appeared upon Theodoric at the moment of his death, announced that he had been carried off by apoplexy; others said by dysentery. But his daughter Amalasuntha [Note: [Col. 1505D] Cassiodorus speaks of Amalasuntha in these terms: “She must be counted among the foremost and rarest of women; to behold her was venerable, and to hear her speak was a marvel.”], a princess among the most virtuous and accomplished of her age and an eyewitness to everything that had [Col. 1505D] occurred, made it sufficiently clear by her conduct that she was fully convinced that God had then wished to avenge the unjust deaths of Boethius and Symmachus.

Theodoric, having declared Atalaric, his grandson, his successor in his dominions under the guardianship of Amalasuntha, his mother, she governed them for several years with great wisdom. First, she had the property of Rustician’s husband Boethius and of her father Symmachus, which had been confiscated, restored to her. Then, in order, if possible, to erase the memory of Theodoric’s crime (*Raphael Volaterranus*, in the *Anthropology*), she had their statues re-erected in the squares of Rome with (314) inscriptions containing their praises.

For her part, Rustician displayed no less generosity through the contempt she showed for worldly greatness [Col. 1506A] and advantages. After dividing among her children what belonged to them in the inheritance of their grandfather and father, she distributed the remainder to the poor and devoted herself entirely to relieving the sick and undertaking the most arduous works of charity. By this way of life she showed that Theodoric, in depriving her of her possessions, had not been able to disturb the peace of her soul, and had merely anticipated what she herself would soon have done. Entirely occupied with the loss of a father and husband so worthy of respect and so dear to her, she counted as nothing all the other losses she might suffer in this world. Thus she became Rome’s example and the perfect model of Christian widows.

Deprived of all human assistance, her virtue served as a rampart against her husband’s enemies, who were cowardly enough to persecute him even after his death in his children and his widow. More than once they (315) suggested to Amalasuntha that she have Rustician killed, or at least condemned to perpetual imprisonment [Col. 1506B]. The reasons they offered her might have been accepted by a soul less great and generous than that of this princess.

“Everything is to be feared from Rustician,” they told her. “One must even distrust her alms and her tears: by these means she is stirring up the people to avenge the death of her husband and father. She will never cease sowing a spirit of revolt against the government.”

But far from allowing herself to be guided by such base and shameful political principles, Amalasuntha redoubled her efforts to give Rustician greater marks of esteem and consideration. Had she lived longer, Rustician would have found in her a sure protector against the disasters that soon afflicted Italy and against the implacable hatred of her family’s enemies.

Italy did not deserve so gracious a sovereign. Since the people’s sins had reached excess, God had resolved to punish them (316) with the most terrible scourges of his justice. A premature death [Col. 1506C] carried off the young prince Atalaric within a few days. And Amalasuntha, long widowed, finding herself without children and beyond the age at which she could hope for any—even if she had wished to enter a second marriage—wished, in order to avoid the civil wars that might disturb the peace of her people after her death, to provide them during her own lifetime with a successor who would govern them in the justice and peace that her wise conduct had secured for them.

She chose Theodahad, her first cousin, the son of Amalafrida, the sister of King Theodoric, and handed over her dominions to him. But this treacherous man, instead of acknowledging the favor, soon had her confined in a castle situated in the middle of Lake Bolsena, and while she was bathing, had her suffocated there. All good people mourned her death; the emperor Justinian, with whom she had maintained a faithful correspondence, was inconsolable. He had unparalleled respect and esteem for her. Since Amalasuntha knew Greek perfectly, as well as Latin and all the languages in use within the empire, they maintained a regular exchange of letters. Resolved to avenge her death, he sent Belisarius, the general of his armies, against Theodahad.

Everything yielded before Belisarius: the treacherous ruler was killed in battle, his army was scattered, and the principal cities of Italy submitted to the victor. Rome was among the first to open its gates to him, and the Goths were about to be driven entirely from Italy when God—who sets bounds to empires, preserving and destroying them whenever he wills—permitted the Persians to invade the finest provinces of the East at the same time. Justinian was forced to recall Belisarius with part of his troops. Taking advantage of his [Col. 1507A] absence, the Goths summoned the famous Totila. The sufferings he inflicted on Italy cannot be expressed: its most beautiful cities were sacked; Rome was abandoned for forty days to the soldiers’ fury and greed; and after the siege of Jerusalem, history presents us with nothing more terrible than the sack of Rome that he carried out.

(318) Rusticienne, like all the other Roman ladies, was reduced to asking the conquerors for bread (Procopius, *The Gothic War*, book III). She was recognized by the Goths who had served under Theodoric and brought before Totila to be condemned to death, on the pretext that she had incited the senate to tear down the statues of the prince who had murdered her husband and her father. She did not deny it; the matter was public. But Totila, moved by her virtue and still respecting in her the memory of those great men, ordered that she be set free. Some time afterward, she peacefully ended her [Col. 1507B] days in the practice of every kind of good work.

Although God uses the wicked to punish the sins of his people, he did not leave their crimes unpunished. Other peoples, still more savage, came to punish the outrages that the Goths had committed in Italy. Totila was killed, the Goths were scattered and finally driven from those provinces. The Lombards settled there. After spending several years in Italy, they all embraced the (319) Catholic faith, and they even had several kings of exemplary piety.
