Aripert II, who began to reign in the year of Our Lord 702, distinguished himself by his zeal for religion. Near Pavia he founded a celebrated monastery and a church dedicated under the name of Saint Peter. It was called the church of Saint Peter in the Golden Heaven, because gold shone there everywhere, especially on the vault.

Luitprand succeeded him and seemed to surpass still further the [Col. 1507C] piety of his fathers. Not only did he confirm to the church of Saint Peter all the gifts Aripert had made to it, but he increased them and enriched it with an inestimable treasure: the body of Saint Augustine, which he redeemed from the Saracens for a very considerable sum. At that time they were masters of the island of Sardinia, where the bishops of Africa had transported it when they were driven from their country by Thrasamund, around the year 506.

Luitprand had it placed with great honor beneath the high altar of this church, where it is believed still to rest. This is what an authentic charter (320), preserved in the archives of this monastery, teaches us. Father Mabillon (*Iter Italicum*, p. 221), during his journey through Italy, states that he read it and reports its final words:

> *Haec omnia quae supra diximus, adjudicamus venerabili monasterio Sancti Petri in Coelo Aureo, in quo sanctum ac venerabilem Augustinum adduximus. Datum XL non. Aprilis regni Luitprandi I, indict. 10.*

> “All these things that we have stated above we adjudge to the venerable monastery of Saint Peter in the Golden Heaven, in which we brought the holy and venerable Augustine. Given on the fortieth day before the Nones of April, in the first year of the reign of Luitprand, indiction 10.”

This indicates the year 712 from the Incarnation of Our Lord. The end of this document clarifies three points of history. First, it teaches us that Luitprand’s reign did not begin in 713, as Moréri and certain historians maintain, since public acts were already being dated at the beginning of April 712 by the first year of his reign. Second, Luitprand was not the founder of the monastery of Saint Peter in the Golden Heaven, as Papebroch, followed by M. Baillet and others, has claimed, since in the first year of his reign he confirmed the donations that Aripert, his predecessor, had already made to it. Finally, the translation of the (321) body of Saint Augustine from Sardinia to Pavia took place before the beginning of 712, since Luitprand states in this charter, dated at the beginning of that year, that he had already enriched the monastery with this [Col. 1508A] precious deposit. From that time onward, the practice in Italy was to reckon the years from March to March.

Peter, bishop of Pavia, at whose urging Luitprand had had Saint Augustine’s body transferred to the church of Saint Peter, also advised him to enrich it with the other relics of the saints that he might gather from various places. He had the relics of Boethius removed from the place where he had first been buried and placed there, and Luitprand had a magnificent mausoleum erected for him—magnificent for that time, though it would now appear quite simple. It stood on four stone columns, and bore the inscription that we have reported. It was placed at the foot of the steps leading up to the high altar, where it still remains. Luitprand appointed religious men to keep vigils there day and night, as at the tomb of Saint Augustine, and ordered in his (322) testament that after his death he should be buried at Boethius’ feet, because, when he ceased to live, he did not wish to cease honoring him. And so that no one might mistake the matter in later centuries, and so that the just might always be distinguished from the sinner—these are his own words—he wished no other inscription to be placed on his tomb than this:

> “Here lie the bones of King Luitprand.”

This was carried out as he had ordered, and after so many years no change has yet been made there. This circumstance led M. Baillet, in the *Life of Boethius*, to say that in the time of King Luitprand people began to render Boethius a kind of religious worship.

Around the twelfth century, the monks who possessed the church of Saint Peter were expelled from it; regular canons living under the rule of Saint Augustine were substituted in their place. Pope Honorius III, who explains at length in one of his bulls the reasons for this change (*Bull of Honorius III*, year 1220, apud Mabillon, *Itinerarium Italicum*, p. 222), identifies the causes that ordinarily make monks lose their possessions and monasteries: the relaxation of regular (323) discipline, the squandering [Col. 1508C] of their resources, and the corruption of their morals. Their abbot himself had recently been killed in a scandalous manner.

When its inhabitants changed, its name changed as well, and it was called the Abbey of Saint Augustine. Every year, on October 23, the feast of Boethius is celebrated there with great solemnity. Several churches in Italy commemorate him on the same day as a holy martyr. The city of Pavia claims him as one of its principal patrons and as a powerful protector before God. Papebroch believes that this day is the day of his translation, carried out by King Luitprand and the bishop of Pavia; but the tradition of that church teaches us that it is also the day of his martyrdom. Since Papebroch’s opinion rests on no authority, we prefer to it the ancient tradition of the churches. It is always dangerous to depart from traditions, whatever they may be, and one should never do so without evident reasons.

Because he did so in the case of Elpis, Boethius’ first wife, Papebroch certainly fell into a manifest error: he (324) attacks this tradition and calls faith and public notoriety as witnesses. He says that it is well known that Boethius’ wife was named Rusticienne, that she came from Rome, and that she survived her husband by several years; yet in the epitaph still visible at Pavia, this woman, said to have been Boethius’ wife, is named Elpis. The epitaph tells us that she came from Sicily and that she left her husband full of life. He cites several authorities to confirm his claim, and then triumphs over so fortunate a discovery at the expense of tradition.

Yet the tradition is constant, and Papebroch was mistaken because Boethius had married Elpis first and Rusticienne second. Both facts agree perfectly with the authorities he cites, with the epitaph, and with the tradition.

What has been reported above sufficiently proves the antiquity [Col. 1509A] of the worship rendered to Boethius as a true martyr. But, to give it still greater authority, it was thought necessary to add that, according to the Milan Breviary printed in 1539, that church appears to have celebrated a solemn commemoration of him on October 23 under the name of Saint Severinus, martyr—the name by which Boethius is best known in the Church and among the compilers of martyrologies.

The ancient historians of his life expressly say that after his death the Church rendered him the honors customarily paid to holy martyrs, because he had suffered for defending the Catholic faith against the perfidy of the Arians. (*Martyrologium of Rota, in the Life of Boethius.*) They even add that the inhabitants of Pavia have always been so filled with respect for their holy patron that, by a constant tradition transmitted from century to century, they have handed down a fact for which I would not wish to vouch. It is almost like what simple antiquity once reported about Saint Denis, the patron of Paris.

They regard it as certain [Col. 1509B] that, after Boethius had been struck by the executioner, he had received or supported his head between his two hands; that when he was then asked by whom he believed he had been struck, he replied that it was by the impious; and that he had come, carrying it thus between (326) his hands, as far as a neighboring church. Having knelt at the foot of the altar, he received the divine mysteries there and expired a moment later. If this event does not appear credible, the ancient tradition concerning the martyr’s holiness and veneration nevertheless remains constant.

The emperor Otto III wished to signal his devotion to this holy man by having a richly ornamented marble mausoleum erected for him. He had his eulogy engraved above it. Gerbert, philosopher and poet, who was later raised to the supreme pontificate under the name Sylvester II, composed it in verse. Here it is:

> *Roma potens dum jura suo declarat in orbe,*  
> *Tu pater, et patriae lumen, Severine Boeti,*  
>   
> *Consulis officio, rerum disponis habenas;*  
> *Infundis lumen studiis, et cedere nescis*  
> *Graecorum ingeniis: sed mens divina coercet*  
>   
> [Col. 1509C] (327) *Imperium mundi. Gladio bacchante Gothorum*  
> *Libertas Romana perit: tu consul et exsul*  
> *Insignes titulos praeclara morte relinquis.*  
>   
> *Nunc decus Imperii summas qui praegravat artes*  
> *Tertius Otto sua dignum te judicat aula.*  
>   
> *Aeternumque tui statuit monumenta laboris,*  
> *Et bene promeritum meritis exornat honestis.*

> “Powerful Rome, while she declares her laws throughout the world,  
> You, father and light of your fatherland, Severinus Boethius,  
>   
> In the office of consul, you guide the reins of affairs;  
> You pour light upon learning and do not yield  
> To the genius of the Greeks; but the divine mind restrains  
>   
> The empire of the world. While the Goths’ sword rages,  
> Roman liberty perishes; you, consul and exile,  
> Leave behind illustrious titles through your glorious death.  
>   
> Now Otto the Third, the glory of the Empire,  
> Who surpasses the highest arts, judges you worthy of his court.  
>   
> He establishes an eternal monument to your labor  
> And adorns one who has deserved well with honorable distinctions.”

His cult became still more celebrated in the fourteenth century, after hermits living under the rule of that holy doctor were joined to the regular canons who served the church of Saint Augustine. Since the church became common to them and to the canons, and since the side of the Epistle, where Boethius’ tomb is located, fell to their share—the canons having retained the side of the Gospel—these hermits, who believe they possess a special right over Boethius’ relics, took particular care to adorn his (328) tomb and to maintain the people’s devotion there.

The Council of Trent contributed no little to this. Having ordered that all tombs raised above the ground in churches should be leveled, except those of recognized saints, and apostolic commissioners having been sent to enforce its decree throughout Italy, some tombs in the church of Saint Augustine at Pavia were demolished. But Boethius’ tomb was religiously preserved (Sylvester, *Moralium in Mariocam Religionem*, book IV, p. 271): clear proof that he was regarded as a saint in possession of the glory from which one might claim his assistance before God.

For this reason the Holy See leaves the churches of Italy complete freedom to render him public worship, and does not disapprove [Col. 1510B] of martyrologies and ecclesiastical writers giving him the title of saint and martyr, although no other ceremonies were ever performed for his canonization than that of raising his body from the ground, which was the ancient manner of canonizing saints. It was judged that the voice of the people, supported by a tradition of (329) twelve centuries, was sufficient to authorize the worship rendered to him. For these reasons, historians who have written the Acts of the Saints with the greatest accuracy, and the most rigorous critics of our century, after a strict examination of those concerning Boethius, have been unable to deny him the title of saint and martyr.

It is a great honor to have given one’s life and shed one’s blood for justice, truth, and the defense of the faith. But it is even more glorious for Boethius to have reached that point through an inviolable fidelity to all his duties, through an innocent life, purity of morals, and an exact, faithful, and constant correspondence with all the graces with which God’s goodness had anticipated him. (Can. I Gren. Ferrar.; par. Natal. Baillet, *Life of Saint Augustine*.)

It is in order to honor the memory of this great man and perpetuate his cult that all the circumstances of his life and death have been carefully gathered. I hope that the faithful will be edified by them and will find in them great reasons for consolation amid the adversities and persecutions inseparable from true piety. Since during his life he loved the Church so tenderly and so often displayed his zeal for its defense and for the reunion of its divided members, we should not doubt that, freed from the bonds of the body and favorably heard by God, he still powerfully entreats him, asking for the perfect unity of all its members and for its preservation from the evils that threaten it.

## SECOND PART

[Col. 1509]

[Col. 1509D] (3) To know a person only by his outward actions is to know him only superficially. To penetrate his feelings, unfold his intentions, and discover the motives of his conduct is to know him according to the noblest part of himself. But to add to knowledge of outward actions and the feelings of the heart knowledge of the products of the mind is to know him entirely.

In the first part of this History, everything that the injury of time and a long succession of centuries had not been able to bury in oblivion concerning Boethius’ actions was carefully collected. A natural portrait of this great man was placed before the public. In this second part, however, Boethius himself paints his own portrait: it is his mind that he reveals to us, and that we are about to come to know through his writings.

It has already been noted what the productions were of this superior genius, whom the greatest men who followed him all equally admired, including even those who shone most brightly in the less remote periods of our own age, such as Albert the Great, Saint Thomas Aquinas, his disciple, and the most skilled theologians who came after them. They made a particular study of Boethius’ works. Saint Thomas cites him in a thousand places, and one may say without flattery that they drew, as from a pure and fertile spring, what they gave us that was most solid and complete on the matters of religion that Boethius had occasion to treat. They merely extended and developed the principles he had established too concisely to be readily understood by people less experienced than he in the divine and human sciences.

Since it was possible, without distracting the reader from the course of the history that he was meant to follow, to give him a proper idea of the treatise on the Goodness of Being, of the treatise on Faith, and of several explanations concerning the Philosophy that Boethius left us—for these works were not very extensive—an extract was provided according to their relation to the chronological order of the events of his life, while all the other treatises were reserved for the second part of this work. These are the works that remain for us to discuss.

The first is that on the two natures and one person in Jesus Christ, against Eutyches and Nestorius, addressed to John, deacon of the Church of Rome.

The second is entitled: “Whether the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit can be substantially predicated of the Divinity,” addressed to the same deacon.

The third is that on the Holy Trinity, addressed to Symmachus, his father-in-law, entitled: “How the Trinity is one God and not three Gods.”

The fourth comprises the five books of the *Consolation of Philosophy*. We give these treatises first place among Boethius’ works because of the dignity and importance of the subjects they treat, although we have observed that most of them were his final productions.

[Col. 1512A] An analysis of his mathematical books will follow: that of the book on Arithmetic, of the five books on Music, and of the two on Geometry. Next, a brief account will be given of what remains of his commentaries on Porphyry’s *Introduction*, on the various parts of Aristotle’s Philosophy, and on Cicero’s *Topics*. Finally, the works attributed to him will be examined, and an attempt will be made to distinguish the genuine products of his mind from the spurious works.

(7) After these analyses, a brief historical dissertation will be given on the year of his death. Another, much more extensive theological dissertation will follow on these words of Gundobad, king of Burgundy: “Give me the anointing with chrism in secret.” This second part will conclude with two explanations: the first concerning Faustus, bishop of Riez, and his doctrine; the second concerning the opinion of Anastasius the Librarian, adopted by M. Dupin, regarding the conduct of Pope John toward King Theodoric, which we had occasion to discuss in the first part. This, then, is the subject of the second part, which will be neither less useful nor less interesting than the first.

[Col. 1511]

## ANALYSES OF THE WORKS OF BOETHIUS

### ANALYSIS OF THE TREATISE ON THE TWO NATURES AND ONE PERSON IN JESUS CHRIST, AGAINST EUTYCHES AND NESTORIUS: TO JOHN, DEACON OF THE CHURCH OF ROME

(8) Boethius first observes that the inadequate knowledge people possessed of the terms was what most divided minds concerning the mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God. Indeed, it is certain that the word “person,” which the Latins use, does not signify among the Greeks what they understand by ὑπόστασις (*hypostasis*). For hypostasis is a rational substance made singular and individual, whereas among them the word “person” signifies those comic actors who represent the actions of men, whether real or imagined. From this came the word “character,” and the expression “to play a character,” which they expressed by the term πρόσωπον (*prosopon*). But since the Latins had no word to signify what hypostasis means, scarcity of language caused them to use the word “person.”

Boethius observes, secondly, that the Latins often confuse the words essence, substance, subsistence, and person; whereas the Greeks, whose language is extremely rich, have proper terms for signifying each thing. They call essence οὐσία (*ousia*), subsistence οὐσίωσις (*ousiosis*), substance ὑπόστασις (*hypostasis*), and person πρόσωπον (*prosopon*). Thus, from the beginning, he assigns each term its proper value and (10) meaning, in order to remove confusion and ensure that the dispute may no longer concern words but the [Col. 1511D] thing itself under discussion.

Having established these principles, he shows the source of Nestorius’ error. It arises, he says, from his confusing nature with person. Wherever there is a nature—that is, a substance specified by its properties—he believes there is also a person. And since he saw two natures in Jesus Christ, the divine nature with all its properties and the human nature with all its own, he drew the conclusion that there were also two persons in Jesus Christ, one divine and one human.

[Col. 1512B] On this basis, the heretic imagined that there was no longer any difficulty in the mystery of the incarnation and that what had until then seemed incomprehensible had become very easy to understand. What revolts the human mind more in this mystery, he said, than hearing Christians say that a God was born of a woman, that he was a child, that he grew with time like (11) other children, that he advanced in age, wisdom, and prudence; that he was hungry and thirsty, suffered heat, cold, and sleeplessness, and finally died amid pains and humiliations? Faith as well as reason teaches us that God is eternal, that he has neither beginning nor end, that he is immortal and impassible, and that all his perfections are as ancient as he is, since they are not distinct from him himself. Faith would oppose faith and destroy on one side what it establishes on the other if all these expressions could apply to God. But, by acknowledging two persons in Jesus Christ, nothing remains that conflicts with common sense. It is the man who was born, advanced in age, grew in wisdom and experience, and was subject to all the weaknesses and infirmities common to men; it is the man who died for us. Thus reasoned Nestorius.

[Col. 1512D] “Then Mary will no longer be the mother of God,” people said to him. “She will be the mother of Christ,” he replied, “that is, of this man who is united to the divine Word; (12) for to claim that the Divinity can be born is a horrible blasphemy,” against which Augustine rose when he said that Mary was not the mother of the Divinity: *Non erat illa mater Divinitatis*—“She was not the mother of the Divinity.”

[Note: [Col. 1511D] These treatises were composed in 417, and the authority of Saint Augustine was cited even by Saint Leo and [Col. 1512D] by Theodoret (*Theodoret, Dialogue* 2, p. 108; Saint Leo, p. 134).]

Boethius overturns all the false arguments of this heresiarch by showing him not only the difference between nature and person but also that, through his absurd suppositions, he entirely destroys Jesus Christ. For Jesus Christ [Col. 1513A] is one, he says, and no one has yet thought to say that there were several Christs. Now, if he is composed of two natures and two persons, somewhat as two bodies would be, each occupying its own place, he is no longer one and consequently no longer exists at all, since unity is inseparable from being, and since God himself, by his omnipotence, cannot make what is one not to be one. Thus Nestorius, instead of establishing the mystery of the incarnation as he imagines, annihilates it (13) and gives men as savior a phantom capable of existing only in a diseased imagination.

He presses him still further, asking him in what the union of two natures as different as the divine and human consists if they are not united by one person. For if this entire union consists in the divine person lending his assistance and power to the human person so that he may perform miracles and receive supernatural knowledge not otherwise due to him, then the prophets had as much.

Moreover, either Nestorius calls the divine nature Jesus Christ, or only the human nature, or both together. This name cannot apply to both together, for two natures as dissimilar as the divine and the human—two natures that have nothing in common and that, according to him, are not joined by a hypostatic union—cannot have the same name or the same definition. If he says that the divine nature is what is called Jesus Christ, then Jesus Christ is God alone and is no longer man. If, on the contrary, he maintains that the human nature is called Jesus Christ, then he is man alone and is no longer God.

Thus this unheard-of miracle, this mystery that astonishes men and angels, this wonder of which there had never before been an example, is reduced to nothing; and Mary, in bringing the Savior into the world, did nothing other than what all women do. Where, then, is now this great object of our faith, which confesses that the divine Word was incarnate and became man? If each nature retains its own person, Boethius continues, there will be less union between the divine nature and the human nature than there is between a man and a beast, which at least agree with each other in the degree of animality.

He then turns to the heresy of Eutyches, which he combats with equally solid arguments. He shows that Eutyches went astray by the same path on which Nestorius was lost, and that both erred only because they imagined that there could be no existing nature without personality—that is, without subsisting in a (15) person. On this false principle Nestorius said: Faith teaches us that there are two natures in Jesus Christ, the divine and the human; therefore there is also a divine person and a human person.

[Col. 1513D] On the same basis Eutyches said: Faith teaches us that there is only one person in Jesus Christ, and the Church anathematizes the impiety of Nestorius, who maintained that there were two. Therefore, he concluded, there is also only one nature; otherwise one falls into the heresy of Nestorius. But it is impossible, he was told, for the divine nature to be the human nature, or for the human nature to be the divine nature. The point is self-evident, just as it is impossible for a man to be a beast or for a beast to be a man. “I admit it,” Eutyches replied. “It is likewise true that before the hypostatic union the human nature of Jesus Christ was very different from the divine nature. But since that union, these two natures form only one, just as a drop of water poured into a barrel of wine becomes one nature with the wine.”

It is into this final refuge (16) that Boethius drives him, leaving him nothing more to answer:

“At what time did this union—or rather, this confusion of natures—take place?” he asks Eutyches. “Was it at the instant of Jesus Christ’s conception, or at the moment of his resurrection? If it was at the instant of his conception, then the one who was later called Jesus Christ was already man before being conceived in Mary’s womb. This human nature that was to be joined to the divine therefore already existed, since you say that before the union there were two distinct natures. Thus Mary is not his mother; she merely lent her womb, like a channel through which this humanity, formed in heaven or elsewhere, passed in order to be joined to the divine Word.

“Consequently, all those magnificent promises that God had made to Abraham and David—that Christ would be born from their own flesh—are vain. Jesus Christ lied when he called himself the Son of Man, for to be the son of man one must derive one’s flesh from man.

[Col. 1514B] “If it was after the resurrection that these two natures were confused, then (17) man was not redeemed, Adam’s sin still remains, and the Passion of Jesus Christ is useless, since it is certain that man alone could neither satisfy the justice of God nor give infinite merit to his actions and sufferings. Besides, Jesus Christ redeemed only what he assumed. If he assumed nothing from man, if his flesh does not derive its origin from Adam’s flesh, then Adam was not redeemed, nor was his posterity. Jesus Christ himself ought not to have died, since man was subjected to death only through sin.”

Finally, Boethius adds, this mixture of natures could have occurred in only three ways: either the divine nature was transformed into the human nature, or the human nature was changed into the divine nature, or a third nature was formed from the two, properly neither one nor the other, much as mixed substances are not elements, although they are formed from them. No other transformation can be imagined.

Now all three possibilities are equally impossible. The first contains an evident contradiction, namely, that a nature essentially immutable and impassible should become passible and subject to change. The second is no less fanciful. Can one conceive of a bodily nature becoming a purely spiritual nature, of a body becoming spirit, or of spirit becoming body? Since substance in general is divided into corporeal and spiritual, the spiritual can never become corporeal, nor the corporeal spiritual. Thus, just as animal is divided into rational and irrational, one can never become the other.

Even spiritual substances cannot be changed into one another, for such a change can occur only between things that have a subject or matter in common, in which these transformations take place. It is also necessary that they possess qualities [Col. 1514D] capable of acting upon one another, altering and destroying one another; finally, after several struggles, the stronger must remain victorious by taking the place of the vanquished. Hence these changes are impossible even in corporeal substances, where such conditions are absent. Thus copper can never be changed into stone, nor can a stone become a plant. Therefore no third nature, mixed or composed of the two, could have been formed from the divine and human natures.

Having thus refuted the errors of Nestorius and Eutyches, Boethius establishes the position of the Catholic Church, which believes that Jesus Christ is not only composed of two natures but subsists in two distinct natures, without mixture or confusion. To prove the possibility of this mystery, he gives two examples.

The first is a crown composed of gold [Col. 1515A] and pearls, in which the gold is not changed into pearls, nor the pearls into gold. Each retaining its own nature, their union produces a whole that constitutes the crown. Although the gold and the pearls could subsist separately if they were no longer united, nevertheless, insofar as they form a crown, they have only one existence, namely, that of the whole and of the crown.

The other example is taken from the remedy that the charitable Samaritan—an evident figure of Jesus Christ, the Savior and Redeemer of man, covered (20) with wounds by sin—applied to the wounds of the unfortunate man who had fallen among robbers on the road to Jericho: he poured oil and wine upon them. However closely these two liquids may be united, they always preserve their particular being and are never mixed or confused. Nevertheless, they still constitute a unity insofar as they compose a remedy.

[Col. 1515B] This learned man does not claim that these examples perfectly represent the hypostatic union in question. He knew, like Saint Augustine, that there is no example in nature of a mystery infinitely elevated above all nature. If there were one, it would be neither admirable nor unique. He offers them only to provide a general idea of the incarnation and to show that it is not impossible for two entirely different natures to unite under one subsistence, without mixture or confusion, and that it is not always necessary to multiply hypostases when multiplying natures.

He then explains the communication of the properties of these two natures (21), and how God became man and man became God; how the same Jesus Christ who is man is God, the Son of God, and at the same time the son of man. He attributes this wonder to personality alone, which, by causing these two natures to subsist, makes all their properties common to them through an appropriation that theologians call the communication of idioms.

He then responds to one of the most subtle objections that the Valentinians were accustomed to raise against the reality of Jesus Christ’s flesh. “The flesh of Jesus Christ,” these heretics said, “was not formed in Mary’s womb and does not derive its origin from Adam’s flesh; it was formed immediately by God himself and is entirely different from ours.” This is how they proved their position. Our flesh can be considered in only two ways: either in the state of Adam’s innocence, or in the condition to which it has been reduced since his sin. Jesus Christ did not assume the flesh of holy and innocent Adam: that is not ours; it no longer suits us; and, if he had assumed it, he would not have saved or redeemed us, because he saved and redeemed only what stood in need of salvation. Although Adam, in that state, was stained by no sin, he nevertheless still had the power to sin, as he made all too clear afterward. [Col. 1515D] Now Jesus Christ not only never sinned, but did not even have the power to sin; therefore he did not assume Adam’s flesh as Adam was before his fall. Finally, Adam in that state was not subject to death, which was a punishment for his sin, whereas Jesus Christ was subject to it; therefore he did not clothe himself with Adam’s innocent flesh.

Nor did he assume the flesh of Adam as a criminal and guilty man, for that flesh is not only infected with the general corruption spread among all his descendants, but also has a natural tendency and inclination toward sin, which is a punishment for his sin. Now there was never in Jesus Christ any tendency or inclination toward sin; therefore Jesus Christ did not assume Adam’s guilty flesh. [Col. 1516A] And since he assumed neither the flesh of innocent Adam nor that of guilty Adam, it necessarily follows that he did not assume ours. [Col. 1516A]

Boethius refutes these heretics. First, he considers human nature under the three different conditions it can possess: before Adam’s sin, on the supposition that Adam had not sinned but had remained obedient to God’s commands, and after his sin and disobedience. The first state is real. In it, since man was stained by no sin, he did not die either; nevertheless, he could die, could will to sin, and could actually sin. The second is hypothetical. If Adam had remained in the obedience he owed to God, he would not only not have sinned in that state, but could not have sinned, because he would have been confirmed in grace. Finally, in the third state, which is the one in which we find ourselves, man can not only [Col. 1516B] sin and die, but actually sins and is placed under the unavoidable necessity of dying.

These last two states are like the two extremes of human nature. One would have been the reward of the submission and obedience of the righteous man: there would have been neither death, nor sin, nor the will to sin. The other is the just punishment of his rebellion, and it is accompanied by death, sin, a tendency toward every kind of evil, and above all the inability ever to rise again by his own strength from so wretched a condition. [Col. 1516B]

The first state stands, as it were, midway between these two extremes. In it there is neither death nor sin, but only the power to sin and the danger of being subjected to death. What did Jesus Christ do, Boethius continues, to save human nature and give our redemption all the scope it could have? From all these states he took what could suit his humanity in relation to the purpose he had set himself: to withdraw us from the abyss into which we had fallen. To destroy death and restore to us the blessed immortality of which we had been deprived as punishment for our sin, he subjected his humanity to death; this is what he took from the last state. And because the one who came to destroy the reign of sin, far from being subject to it, had to possess an infinite distance from it, he found the means of making his humanity impeccable by uniting it to the divine nature. This impeccability he took from the first state, in which man, had he remained faithful to God, would have become impeccable.

There remains a third state, which is intermediate between these two: the state in which death and sin are absent, though they could nevertheless occur. In that state Adam drank and ate, digestion took place in his stomach, he slept, and performed all the other functions proper to human beings. These were not burdensome necessities then, but rather innocent occupations of which he could have dispensed; for one must not imagine that Adam would have died in that state had he abstained from drinking or eating. Nevertheless, he felt hunger, and that hunger led him to nourish himself with the fruits of the earthly Paradise, which would have preserved his life and health. This is what Jesus Christ took from that state. He drank and ate like other men, felt hunger, and allowed his body to sleep. From this the learned man concludes that Jesus Christ assumed not only the flesh of sinful Adam, but also that of innocent Adam—what he was—and of impeccable Adam—what he ought to have been. This work is learned and elevated, written in an extremely concise style: it says a great deal in very few words. Yet it is infinitely abstract, and unless one is a good theologian, it appears obscure; at first, one understands nothing of it.

## (27) ANALYSIS OF THE TREATISE ENTITLED: “Whether the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit Can Be Substantially Predicated of the Divinity,” TO JOHN, DEACON OF THE CHURCH OF ROME, WITH SOME CLARIFICATIONS OF THIS DIFFICULTY

[Col. 1517]

[Col. 1517A] In this treatise Boethius lays down as the foundation of his doctrine that everything predicated substantially of the Divinity, or divine nature, must apply to all the divine persons. Since all three possess the whole of divinity in substance, as well as all the perfections of that nature, everything predicated substantially of the nature must also be predicable of each person individually. Now, since one cannot say of the Son that he is the Father, nor of the Holy Spirit that he is the Father or the Son, it follows that one cannot say that the Divinity is the Father, that the Divinity is the Son, or that the Divinity is the Holy Spirit, although the whole of divinity is contained in these three persons.

The same does not apply, he says, to the other divine attributes—truth, wisdom, goodness, justice, and so forth. These can be predicated substantially of the Divinity because they apply equally to each divine person, to the Father as to the Son, and to the Son as to the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1517B] Moreover, Boethius adds, every substantial attribute is something absolute. For to speak of substance is to speak of a being subsisting through itself, without dependence, relation, or reference to anything else. But to speak of a father is not to speak of something absolute. It is a term relative to a son: there is no father without a son, nor son without a father. It is therefore impossible, he concludes, for the Father to be predicated substantially of the Divinity, any more than the Son or the Holy Spirit.

M. Dupin (sixth century, p. 91) did not understand Boethius’s reasoning in this way. In attempting to explain it, he gives it an entirely opposite meaning. “The question,” he says, “was whether one could say that the Father is the Divinity.” But that is not Boethius’s thought when he examines whether the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit can be predicated substantially of the Divinity. He takes “the Divinity” as the subject of his proposition, in the manner of the philosophers, and “the Father” as its predicate. M. Dupin, on the other hand, makes the Divinity the predicate of his proposition and takes the Father as its subject. A little reflection on the rules of logic would have saved him from this error. [Col. 1517C]

In fact, the question was not whether the Father is the Divinity, but whether the quality of being Father belongs substantially to the Divinity. The first proposition could be true, whereas the second is always false; this is what that author has not yet noticed. He proposes a new question, and not at all the one debated in Boethius’s time.

M. Dupin (twelfth century, vol. I, p. 411) was no more successful when he maintained that the question debated in Boethius’s time was one of the propositions condemned at the Council of Reims, held in 1148 against Gilbert of Poitiers. The difference is clear.

[Col. 1518A] Gilbert maintained that the essence or nature of God—his divinity and greatness—is not God, but his form, by which he is God, just as his wisdom was the form by which he was wise. Saint Bernard, arguing against him, maintained on the contrary that the divine essence, form, nature, divinity, goodness, and wisdom were God himself, because, he said, if God’s form were not God, it would be more perfect than God.

As is evident, this concerns only absolute attributes, not relatives. Now far from denying that absolute attributes are God himself, Boethius maintains that they can be predicated substantially of God; and this is one of the reasons he adduces for proving that no divine person can be predicated substantially of the Divinity. For why, he asks, are truth, wisdom, goodness, justice, and omnipotence God and substantially predicated of the Divinity, unless it is because all these attributes apply equally to all the persons of the august Trinity? The Son is truth by essence, wisdom, goodness, justice, and mercy just as much as the Father and the Holy Spirit. From this he concludes, by an argument drawn from the rule of contraries, that since paternity, filiation, and procession are not common to the three divine persons—for the Father cannot be the Son, nor the Son the Father or the Holy Spirit—it follows that what these terms signify cannot be predicated substantially of the Divinity. [Col. 1518B]

The only proposition of Gilbert’s that could have any relation to Boethius’s is this: “The one God is not the three persons, nor are the three persons one thing, although they are one God through one and the same divinity.” Yet on close examination, one still finds an infinite difference between these two theologians. Gilbert reasoned in accordance with his great principle, namely, that humanity is not man but the form by which he is man; likewise, divinity is not God but the form by which he is God. On this principle, he wanted the Divinity to be like the form that made the three persons one God; consequently, they did not constitute one God through themselves, but by reason of the Divinity, with which they were identical. [Col. 1518C]

Now although Boethius maintains that the Trinity cannot be predicated substantially of God—because the Father is not the Trinity, nor the Son the Trinity, nor the Holy Spirit the Trinity, and because nothing can be predicated substantially of God that does not apply to all three divine persons—[Note: [Col. 1517C] “The Trinity consists in the plurality of persons, whereas unity consists in the simplicity of substance. If the persons are divided while the substance is undivided, it is necessary that a term deriving its origin from the persons should not belong to the substance. But the diversity of the persons produces the Trinity; therefore the Trinity does not belong to the substance. It follows that neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit, nor the Trinity is substantially predicated of God.” Boethius, above, col. 1362.] he nevertheless never said, as Gilbert did, that the three persons were not one God through themselves. It is therefore unreasonable to confuse his propositions with those of the bishop of Poitiers.

## (33) ANALYSIS OF THE TREATISE ON THE HOLY TRINITY, TO SYMMACHUS: “HOW THE TRINITY IS ONE GOD AND NOT THREE GODS”

[Col. 1517]

[Col. 1517C] Boethius begins by acknowledging that several sects have usurped the name of Christian, which properly belongs only to the Catholic Church; that this Church, or this faith, as he calls it, is named Catholic because it is spread everywhere, even to the ends of the world, and because its doctrines [Col. 1519A] and laws extend generally to all human beings; and that the faith of this Church is to recognize and adore one God the Father, one God the Son, and one God the Holy Spirit. From this it draws a conclusion quite different from that drawn by the Arians: therefore the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, not three Gods.

The proof of this Catholic conclusion constitutes the entire subject of his treatise. He proves it by arguing that there can be no diversity in the divine nature, because it contains neither genus, species, nor accident, which are the only sources of diversity. He immediately turns against the Arians the consequence they drew from the Catholic proposition and shows them that it applies exclusively to themselves. It is the Arians, he says, who admit degrees and diversity within the Trinity, and to them one may attribute the worship of three Gods. For since they attribute merits and perfections to the Father that they say do not belong to the Son, it necessarily follows that the Son is something other than the Father. And if he is something other, there is diversity and plurality in God. Therefore the Arians worship several Gods. [Col. 1519B]

If they attribute the divine nature to the Word, or make him merely a highly perfect creature, they cannot avoid either worshiping several Gods or worshiping a monster. If they attribute the divine nature to him, he is God—but a God different from the Father, since, according to them, he is less perfect than the Father. Thus there is diversity and plurality, as with two men, who remain several persons although united in the same nature because of the different qualities distinguishing them. If, on the contrary, they make the Word a creature, the God they worship is a monster. For it is certain that the difference between God and a creature is greater than that between a man and a beast. Just as a man whose word or intellect were, for example, a horse would be a horrible monster in human nature, so there would be a similar—and indeed much greater—monster in the Divinity if God had a Word who were a creature. [Col. 1519C]

The Catholics do not fall into this abyss, he says, because they admit no quality in the Father that is not also in the Son and the Holy Spirit. There can be neither diversity nor plurality where there is no difference of quality. In the three divine persons there can be no generic, specific, or numerical difference; consequently, they preserve among themselves perfect unity and complete equality.

He appropriately observes that what makes this mystery so incomprehensible is that our imagination finds no foothold in it. Since there is in the divine nature neither matter nor motion, but only an utterly simple form, it cannot send images to our imagination. The intellect alone, he says, could act upon this object; but since, in our present life, all its knowledge depends upon imagination and the senses, whenever these can provide it with no assistance, it must necessarily remain inactive—and this is what causes its incapacity. [Col. 1519D]

He then enters into the heart of the mystery and first establishes what God is. He finds no truer or more perfect idea than the one God gave of himself when he said: “I am the one who is.” By this, the learned theologian adds, God makes us understand that he is an utterly simple form without parts and therefore indivisible, because only form gives being. A statue, for example, is not a statue by virtue of the bronze or stone of which it is made, but by virtue of the form and figure impressed upon that matter. Moreover, if matter cannot give being, it necessarily follows that God has no matter, but is pure spirit, since he is being in its entirety. [Col. 1520A]

This is not so with creatures. None is what it is through itself, because it is such by virtue of the parts composing it, not through itself; and these parts, united together, are properly what it is. Body and soul united make a human being, and a human being is neither his body nor his soul.

From this spiritual form without parts and without matter flow all the prerogatives of the Divinity. Hence his independence, since he subsists through himself. Hence his invincible power, or, if one prefers, his omnipotence, since he rests upon nothing different from himself. Hence his indivisible unity, since he has no parts that could become the members of a division and give rise to plurality. Hence the impossibility of receiving any accidental form, as all creatures do, because he has no subject or matter capable of receiving it. For all accidental forms are received in matter [Note: [Col. 1519D] When he says that all accidental forms are received in matter, this must be understood *per distributionem accommodam*, that is, corporeal accidents are received in corporeal matter, and spiritual accidents in metaphysical matter, otherwise called potentiality.], and this is the source of God’s immutability and, consequently, of his eternity. [Col. 1520B]

But if God is one and indivisible, as we have just proved; if there can be in him neither number nor plurality, as we maintain, why then do we repeat God’s name three times by saying, “the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God”? For unity repeated several times produces a number and therefore plurality. He answers this objection by saying that numerically repeated unity truly produces number, but not the counting unity, as the philosophers express it. That is, to produce number it is not enough to multiply the unity that counts; one must also multiply the unity of the thing being counted. For example, if I were to say three times, “sun, sun, sun,” that would not make three suns; it would merely be a repetition of the same thing. Likewise, when I say, “the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God,” this does not thereby make three Gods; it is a repetition of the same divinity attributed to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1520C]

(40) It does not nevertheless follow that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are synonymous terms, as are the terms “sword,” “blade,” and “cutlass.” The reason is that a sword, a blade, and a cutlass are not only one and the same thing, but one is also the other. In God, by contrast, although the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one and the same thing, one is nevertheless not the other. For in relative terms, although one cannot exist without the other, it is nevertheless impossible for one to be the other: there is no father without a son, but it is impossible for the father to be the son, or for the son to be the father. [Col. 1520D]

He then goes at length to show the distinction of the persons within the unity of the divine nature, and how all the attributes of that nature—goodness, wisdom, power, justice, mercy—apply equally to the three persons. These are merely accidents in creatures, but in God they are God himself and his own nature.

One cannot say that God began to be Father, he continues, because the production of his Son proceeds from his substance, and the attribute or quality of being Father is purely relative. The Son is therefore God [Note: [Col. 1521B] Boethius uses the term “procession” to express the generation of the Word and the breathing forth of the Holy Spirit: “The Son God proceeded from God the Father, and the Holy Spirit from both.” Boethius, above, col. 1254.], having proceeded from the substance of the Father; and the Holy Spirit is God, having likewise proceeded from the Father and the Son. The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, because there is in God no difference by which God could differ from God; and this is why the three persons are only one God. For there is no diversity where there is no plurality, and where there is no plurality there is perfect unity.

Nothing, therefore, could have been begotten from God except God: *nihil aliud gigni potuit ex Deo nisi Deus*—“nothing other than God could have been begotten from God.” And just as, in things that are counted, the repetition of units does not produce their plurality, the unity of the three persons remains indisputably established. But because no relation is relation to itself and must necessarily refer to another, this gives rise to the plurality of persons. The Trinity is therefore counted, and is plural, with respect to relation; but unity always remains the same with respect to substance, because there is no difference in substance or operation. The divine substance therefore contains unity, while the relation of the persons produces the Trinity. [Col. 1521B]

This is why we name the three divine persons separately: the one who is the Father is not the Son, and neither the one nor the other is the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, the same God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; the same is just, great, and almighty; and his justice and omnipotence are his being. He always remains the same in everything that can be predicated substantially of God.

Moreover, just as it is not necessary, in order to establish a perfect relation, that the two terms of the relation be different from one another—as, for example, master and servant, or father and son in human nature, since relation can also be found between two equal things that are equal to a third by virtue of the relation established by their equality, according to the axiom *aequale omne aequali aequale est*, “everything equal is equal to an equal”—so it is not necessary that the terms of divine relations be substantially different from one another in order to establish a perfect relation. The relation between them is that of an equal to an equal. [Col. 1522A]

He concludes by leaving Symmachus to judge his work. He declares that he did not undertake it to give greater weight or firmness to his faith, which can receive none from any human reasoning, but to support by reason what faith teaches, and to show that although faith rises above reason, it does not destroy reason or propose anything contrary to it. [Col. 1522B]

This treatise of Boethius is among the most sublime. Since it is infinitely abstract and expressed in terms understood only by those well versed in the subtleties of Aristotelian philosophy, few people will be capable of understanding anything in it. Gilbert of Poitiers, however skilled he was in this science, failed in it; and it is claimed that in the extensive commentary he wrote on this short treatise, he fell into several errors. By attempting to refine the matter too excessively, he gave God a form that was not God himself, but by which he was God, and which Gilbert designated by the name “Deity.”

## (45) ANALYSIS OF BOETHIUS’S FIVE BOOKS OF THE CONSOLATION OF PHILOSOPHY

[Col. 1521]

[Col. 1521C] *The Consolation of Philosophy* is a treatise in dialogue form, which Boethius, oppressed by calumny and close to succumbing beneath the weight of his affliction, imagines himself holding with Philosophy, or Wisdom. This man, born for the public good and an enemy of idleness, did not think he ought to let the few days remaining to him pass uselessly in prison; he used every moment to leave posterity this excellent work. He divided it into five books.

### BOOK ONE

In the first book he describes the deplorable condition in which he found himself: that inconceivable fall from the highest degree of honor and glory into the deepest abyss of disgrace and misery. He begins it with elegiac verses, most suited to express the complaints and sighs of a man in distress. He ends this elegy with a brief reflection highly useful for morals: “There is therefore nothing on which one should place less reliance than the splendor of fortune and the applause of men.” He certainly was not firmly established who could not avoid falling:

*Qui cecidit stabili non erat ille gradu.*

“He who fell was not standing on a firm foundation.” [Col. 1521D]

While, reclining upon his bed, he was occupied with these sad thoughts, Wisdom appeared to him. He was astonished by this vision. The oppression under which he labored initially prevented him from recognizing her, but after recovering his senses, he cast upon her a sufficiently steady gaze to describe her. “I thought,” he says, “that I saw above my head a maiden of extraordinary beauty and majestic bearing. Modesty was painted upon her face, grace spread across her lips, and her eyes were brilliant and full of fire. Her complexion was ruddy, like that of a person in the vigor of age and perfect health, although it was otherwise easy to recognize that she belonged to a period very remote from our own. Everything about her seemed beyond the human. Her stature was not fixed, for it changed from one moment to the next. Sometimes she appeared to me of human height; at other times I would have thought that her head touched the heavens and that she was about to withdraw into them.

“Her garments were of the finest material and of marvelous workmanship, embroidered by her own hands, as she later told me. The garment was cut in the ancient style, and the faded color of its folds made this unmistakable. At the bottom of her robe was engraved the Greek character π [Note: [Col. 1521D] The π signifies practical philosophy, the θ theoretical or speculative philosophy.], and at the top was this one, θ; between the two were painted steps by which one ascended from the first character to the second. Her cloak, made of the same material, appeared torn in several places. In her right hand she held several books, and in her left she carried a scepter.” [Col. 1522C]

After looking at me fixedly, Boethius continues, she found me surrounded by Muses—for at that time I was occupied in composing verses—and cast an indignant glance at them. “What are these theatrical women doing here?” she said. “Who allowed them to approach this sick man? Do they wish to prolong his illness through their enchantments and poisonous sweetness? Leave this place and let me care for my pupil.”

The Muses did not need to be told twice and disappeared at once. With my eyes bathed in tears and my head bowed toward the ground, crushed beneath the weight of my chains, I still did not recognize her, and could not imagine who this imperious woman might be, one whose commands were obeyed with such authority. [Col. 1522D] In a gloomy silence mingled with respect and fear, I awaited what she would do.

At last she approached me, sat down at the foot of my bed, and, moved by the extreme dejection in which she saw me, began to console me by addressing me in verse with these gentle reproaches:

“Is this really you?” she said. “Can your mind, once raised to the highest heavens, have fallen so far as to become wholly earthly? Can your eyes, accustomed to contemplate the course of the stars and the sun and to observe the movements of the heavens, be so firmly fixed upon the earth? You whose ordinary occupation was to study the marvelous effects of nature and discover their reasons and most hidden operations—can you now have nothing in your mind but thoughts so base, unworthy of so great a soul as yours? But what use are these complaints, which can only increase your pain? You must think seriously about curing yourself, not about quarreling with yourself.

“Is it not you, my dear child,” she continued, “whom I nourished with my own milk, whom I formed in my womb, and who through my care had become a strong and perfected man? Had I not given you weapons capable of defending you? What has become of them? They would have made you invincible if you had wished to use them. The mind, like the body, has its illnesses and its lethargy. You have forgotten yourself; you must gradually bring yourself back to yourself and remove from your soul’s eyes this veil of sensible objects that covers them.” [Col. 1523B]

She approached and, having caressed me with a fold of her cloak, wiped away my tears. At that moment, just as a gentle zephyr rising from the east disperses the clouds covering the sun and gladdens all nature, the darkness that clouded my mind disappeared. I recognized my true mother, to whom I owed all my education.

“Who has brought you down from the heights of heaven,” I said to her, “into this place of misery and sorrow, O gracious mistress of the virtues? Is it to be persecuted here by the calumnies of the wicked?”

“Could I have abandoned you?” she replied. “Was it not just that I should come and share with you the sufferings you endure because of me and in my defense? Could I abandon your innocence? Would you not have thought that I feared the accusations of the wicked, or that I was astonished by them as by something new and extraordinary?

“It is not today that the impious have declared war against me. I am accustomed to withstand the assaults they make upon me. These torn portions of my cloak that you see are signs of this. But I have never abandoned those who have fought for me and under my laws.” [Col. 1523C]

This speech deeply moved me. The tears flowed from my eyes again, more abundantly than before. Since I remained in profound silence, Wisdom urged me to answer her.

“You must reveal to me the wounds of your heart,” she said, “if you want me to heal you.”

Then, having recovered my senses and gathered together the little strength that remained to me, I said: “Do I need to reveal to you the sufferings that overwhelm me? Do you not see them yourself? Is the injustice of Fortune not sufficiently evident in my case? Do you not yourself feel the immense difference between this dungeon to which I have been reduced and that library where you used so often and so pleasantly to converse with me? Was I burdened with chains and oppressed as you see me now—exiled, proscribed, stripped of my possessions, condemned to death—when you gave me your lessons and instructed me in your maxims? This is the reward of those who follow them.”

He then explains to her what occasioned his disgrace, and that the offices for which she had prepared him, together with the love of justice that she had [Col. 1524A] inspired in him, were its sole causes. “Had I been less faithful to it,” he tells her, “I should be less unhappy.” He gives her the details of the conspiracy formed against the senate and against himself; he reveals to her the full disgracefulness of his accusers, men burdened with crimes and already condemned. “If Fortune,” he adds, “was not ashamed to expose innocence to calumny, she ought at least to have blushed to employ instruments so deserving of contempt. *Itane nihil fortunam puduit? si minus accusatae innocentiae, at accusantium vilitatis?*—Was Fortune then ashamed of nothing? If not of the innocence accused, at least of the baseness of the accusers?”

He goes into the details of the accusation and the stratagems his enemies had used to ruin him; but he always speaks of them with the utmost moderation, contenting himself with reporting the facts briefly and in the most plausible manner. He observes that all the services he rendered to the republic and to the senate were repaid only with ingratitude; and the senate’s conduct toward him is one of the things that grieve him most. “Through cowardly compliance,” he says, “it condemned me to exile for having defended [Col. 1524B] its interests.” He then protests against the refusal to hear him in his defense. “Had I been accused of burning temples, murdering the Lord’s priests, and attempting the lives of all good men, I would not have been condemned until after I had been questioned and convicted. There is no crime so obvious or so enormous that its condemnation is not submitted to the judgment of men, and in which some diversity of opinion is not found. My entire crime, they say, is that I wished to save the senate and (54) to prevent an informer from approaching the king to tell him that we were guilty of having wished to secure liberty for the Roman people, and, in order to accomplish this, of writing several letters. I shall never deny that I wished to preserve the life and honor of the senate; it has always been too dear to me. I did so, and I shall do so insofar as it depends on me; but it will never be proved that I prevented the informer from approaching the king, or that I wrote letters against the king’s service. [Col. 1524C] Had I done so, I am not so imprudent as to have done it in such a way that he could ever have discovered it. But since these crimes still do me too much honor, it was necessary to resort to falsehood and invent others more shameful: I am accused of magic, for which you had inspired in me, from my earliest youth, an extreme horror. It is you, therefore, lovable Wisdom, whom they attack in my person, because these brutal men persuade themselves that there is only one step from the study of wisdom to magic. But what completes my misery is that most people, who judge things only superficially, (55) readily accept the first impressions given them, and that the esteem which the practice of your principles had won for me in the world will easily be lost. This will give occasion for virtue itself to be degraded, mocked, insulted, and iniquity applauded.”

Wisdom, having listened with great patience to the complaints of her afflicted disciple, appears [Col. 1524D] moved by them and attempts to console him. “I knew well, from the sadness depicted on your face and from the tears continually flowing from your eyes,” she tells him, “that you were exiled, proscribed, condemned, and unhappy; but I could not have known what your exile was if you yourself had not told me that you were five hundred miles distant from your homeland. Ah! how mistaken you are, my dear child, to think yourself banished! You yourself have gone astray; there is no power on earth that can banish you from your true homeland, if you know it well. One of the fundamental laws of that city in which your name has been written is that no citizen can be banished from it unless he has first banished himself; he can be expelled from it only when he ceases to wish to dwell there.”

She then takes up again all the subjects of grief that Boethius had laid before her and begins to place before his eyes the admirable order by which [Col. 1525A] the world is governed. “Do you believe,” she asks him, “that everything that happens in the world happens by chance and recklessly, and that there is no supreme reason governing it?” “I am convinced,” Boethius replies, “and I know that God, who made it, preserves his work, and regulates and directs everything that happens within it; I have never doubted this for a moment.” “I was afraid,” Wisdom replies, “that you had forgotten this important truth when I heard you say that only human beings failed to perceive the care of Providence; but since you admit the contrary to me, how can you be afflicted to the extent that you appear to be? You know that nothing happens except by God’s command, that he directs this world, and that all things proceed from him and flow from him as from their source. Having agreed to this principle, can you deny its consequences? Since you know that God is the beginning and end of all things, and since you are convinced of it, it will not be difficult to restore you to the right path. Passion had agitated you; it [Col. 1525B] had filled your mind with clouds that caused you to stray from the straight road you had been following.

“If you wish to return to it, calm these passions, shun joy, banish hope and fear, and your sorrow will soon cease. Wherever these passions reign, the mind is always in turmoil and agitation; but peace will follow when they have been removed.”

> Drive joy away,  
> Drive fear away,  
> And banish hope,  
> So that pain may not be present;  
> The mind is clouded  
> And bound with reins  
> When these things reign.  
>   
> (*Book I, meter 7*)

## BOOK TWO

“You complain of Fortune,” Wisdom continues, “as though something new had happened to you that was not accustomed to happen to all men, and you are mistaken if you [Col. 1525C] believe that she has changed (58) toward you. Her nature is to be changeable, and by what has now happened to you she shows that, in her inconstancy, she is always the same. Yesterday, when she smiled upon you more generously, she was what she is today; at that time she flattered you with the idea of a false happiness, and you saw her only from one side, as she still conceals herself from many others; but since then she has shown herself to you openly. If you regard her as treacherous, despise her who plays tricks on you and prides herself on being unfaithful. What is now the cause of your affliction ought therefore to be the cause of your soul’s tranquillity. This Fortune, on whom no one can ever rely, has abandoned you; can you persuade yourself that your happiness has gone away with her? Prudence ought to have revealed to you what her nature was, so as to place you in a position neither to fear her misfortunes nor regret her caresses. You gave yourself over to Fortune; you must submit to the one you chose as your mistress, for that is how one behaves: when one embarks [Col. 1525D] upon the sea, one abandons oneself to the will of the winds and waves. The farmer acts in the same way when he casts seed into the earth; he expects good years to compensate him for the bad.

“But if you, in turn, were willing to listen to the complaints Fortune might make against you, could she not justly complain of your ingratitude? ‘What injury have I done you?’ she would say. ‘Of what benefit have I deprived you? After receiving you naked from your mother’s womb, did I not exhaust myself on your behalf? My wealth, my influence—everything was employed for your advancement. Am I not now free to withdraw my hand, and ought you not to thank me for having lent you for so long what did not belong to you? The goods, honors, and all the things of this kind in the world belong to me. If they had belonged to you, you would have brought them with you when you entered the world, and you would not have lost them. What then? Is the [Col. 1526A] sky permitted to change, to make dark and cloudy days follow the fairest days; is the year permitted to cover the earth (60) with flowers and adorn it with its fruits, then strip it bare and cover it with snow and frost; is the sea permitted to be calm and, a moment later, to raise its storms; while the insatiable greed of mortals would impose upon me a law so contrary to my nature? Is it not my duty to play different parts in this world, to turn continually the wheel upon which I am supported, to bring down what is highest and, in an instant, raise what is lowest? Climb with me if you wish, but always on the condition that you descend when I please; and do not think that I ever wrong you when I make you descend with me.’

“Wisdom next sets before her pupil all the advantages he had enjoyed in the world: the noble and fortunate education that had been given him; the protection of the most powerful persons in the [Col. 1526B] state, who had chosen him as their friend and with whose families he had entered into alliance; the extraordinary honors that had always been shown him; the glory with which he had lived; the esteem and (61) respect of all good people that he had acquired; the distinction—one that no private individual had ever enjoyed before him—of seeing his two sons named consuls on the same day, while they were still almost children; the privilege of still having Symmachus, his father-in-law, alive; Rusticiane, his wife, that most virtuous woman; and children so accomplished, all concerned with his misfortunes and disgraces. ‘Compare all this,’ she tells him, ‘with what you claim to suffer at Fortune’s hands, and you will see that you have more reason to thank her than to complain of her. Could you not have died in an instant? And then, would Fortune have left you, or would you yourself have left Fortune? Trust, then, if you wish, in these passing goods that continually flee [Col. 1526C] before you like a shadow; but never forget that there is an eternal and immutable law ordering that everything created be subject to inconstancy. Dry your tears, then, since Fortune has preserved more good for you than she has taken away.’

“To confirm him in this thought, Wisdom makes all the various conditions of men pass in review before him; among them there is not one who is perfectly happy, and none from whom much is not lacking for happiness. ‘This man,’ she says, ‘has wealth and overflows with possessions, but his birth is obscure; that one is of higher rank, but lacks the means to sustain it; he is so unfortunate that he is ashamed to show himself. Here are some who have both, but have no heirs. Others are advantageously married and possess great wealth, but do not know how to use it; they save in order to leave a rich inheritance to a stranger. Others have children, but this is to their misfortune: the disorderly conduct and [Col. 1526D] debauchery of these children cover them with shame, and their children are for their fathers a continual cause of tears and sorrow. How many would consider themselves very fortunate if they possessed the least of the advantages that remain to you! Is this very place, which you regard as your exile, not the homeland of its inhabitants? Believe me, no one is unhappy except insofar as he believes himself to be so (63) and makes himself so. On the contrary, nothing is happier than the wise man, even though he suffers, because he receives everything with equanimity and perfect peace of mind.

“Draw from all that I have just told you this just and necessary conclusion: the sweetnesses of human happiness are always mingled with bitterness, and earthly blessedness is always accompanied by misery, and is consequently false and contemptible, since no stability is found in it. Why, then, mortals, do you seek happiness outside yourselves? It is an ancient error [Col. 1527A] that deceives you. Do you possess anything dearer than yourselves? No, surely. If you possess yourselves, you will have what you will never wish to lose and what Fortune will never be able to take from you. But I shall go further, and, to make you understand that human happiness cannot consist in what is frail and perishable, you must know that only the supreme good can make you truly happy. This supreme good is such that it depends on nothing, is subject to no change, (64) and can never be taken from you. To be perfectly happy, one must be assured of the immutability and perpetuity of one’s happiness; for if one fears losing it, what kind of happiness can it be?”

After Wisdom has dwelt at length on this subject, she tells her pupil that she knows he has been convinced by several demonstrations that the human soul is immortal, and that, moreover, the happiness of this world ends with its separation from the body; and that [Col. 1527B] if there were no other happiness, there could be no doubt that the whole human race would fall into extreme misery through death. She then enters into a detailed examination of the things that man regards as capable of producing his happiness here below, and makes him feel their utter nothingness.

First, she proves that happiness cannot be found in riches, since nothing is viler than their material; and if they have any appearance of goodness, it is only when they are distributed, not when they are locked away. Besides, this happiness ought to be common to all men, and one man cannot grow rich without impoverishing another:

> “O, then, how narrow and destitute are those riches which several people cannot possess in their entirety, and which cannot come to anyone without the poverty of the others!”

Nor does happiness consist in a large retinue of slaves and servants; for if their morals are corrupt, what a burden they are to a master, what a weight upon a household, and to how many disorders and misfortunes does it become [Col. 1527C] exposed! If they are well governed, their integrity ought not to be counted among the goods belonging to you, since it belongs to them and not to you. Do luxury and the beauty of furnishings not also have their inconveniences? Nothing is more certain than the maxim that those who possess many things are reduced to greater poverty; on the contrary, the person who measures abundance by the necessities of nature, rather than by the desires of greed, needs far fewer things. How, then, can you believe that you will become happy through possessing earthly things?

You who resemble God through your immortal soul, what an injury you do to your Creator and to yourself by placing your happiness (66) in things so vile and contemptible! You lower him and debase yourself below these worthless creatures, since you believe them capable of making you happy, and therefore superior to you. [Col. 1527D] The whole greatness of man consists in the rank he holds above all earthly things, and he preserves it only when he recognizes his excellence. He ceases to occupy it and becomes inferior even to the beasts when he ceases to recognize it; and he ceases to recognize it by believing that he can find happiness in things beneath him. What strange blessedness would riches be if they plunged a man into anxiety and fear as soon as he became happy!

> “O splendid blessedness of mortal wealth: once you have attained it, you cease to be secure!”

Dignities, offices, and power are incapable of making those who exercise them good; on the contrary, they cover them with contempt when they are unworthy of them. Reputation, and the glory of making a name for oneself among posterity, are likewise a vain and deceptive happiness. Compare the infinite stretches of eternity with the entire duration of a man’s reputation: will it not be less than a minute compared with ten thousand years?

[Col. 1528A] Fortune therefore shows herself less the enemy of man when she strips him of these apparent goods and appears hostile to him than when he believes her favorable to him. When she smiles upon him, she seduces him by the appearance of happiness; but when she is harsh or inconstant, she shows herself as she truly is. Smiling Fortune deceives; adverse Fortune instructs. Adverse Fortune reveals true friends, who cannot be distinguished when Fortune is favorable. When Fortune leaves a man, she leaves him only what truly belonged to him, and carries away everything that belonged to her.

## BOOK THREE

Wisdom having instructed and consoled her pupil, he acknowledges what he owes her. “O supreme consoler of afflicted men,” he tells her, “how powerful are your arguments! How sweet are your charms! I feel entirely changed, and it seems to me that now Fortune, through her most capricious reversals, will no longer have power over me. Far from fearing the austerity of your principles and the bitterness of the remedies that you (68) apply to me, I savor them; they are my delight, and in them I find complete consolation. Continue, then, to instruct me.”

After remaining silent for a time, Wisdom continues speaking. “Men,” she says, “are restless and entangled; each imposes a thousand troubles upon himself in his own way. Yet all have one and the same end: to make themselves happy. But they often lose their way along the various paths they take to reach it. They wear themselves out uselessly in their searches because they do not know what this happiness is, and because it consists only in the supreme good: that good, the greatest of all goods, which contains them all within itself, so that if any one of them were lacking, it would no longer be the supreme good, because there would be something outside it that it could desire and did not possess.

“From this conclude that true blessedness is a perfect and permanent state in which [Col. 1528C] all goods are united:

> *Status bonorum omnium aggregatione perfectus.*  
> “A state made perfect by the aggregation of all goods.”

“It is toward this supreme blessedness that men naturally tend and move, but by such different paths; for the desire (69) for blessedness is naturally engraved in their hearts, and only greed causes them to go astray in seeking it.

“Wisdom next surveys the various opinions—or rather the errors—of the ancient philosophers concerning blessedness, and continues to show the nothingness of all the creatures in which they have made it consist: the emptiness found in them, their weakness and powerlessness, even in sovereignty itself, which is not exempt from these defects, since it alone is not sufficient to itself, and since kings upon their thrones need foreign assistance more than men in any other condition need it in order to support, defend, and preserve it.

“She then unfolds the nothingness and vanity found in glory and reputation. ‘Some,’ [Col. 1528D] she says, ‘have acquired it through the false opinion of the public and without deserving it. Even if it were founded upon true merit, how far would it extend? To one point of the world, one province, one kingdom; and there will be a thousand places elsewhere on earth where the man who is its slave will be unknown. Its duration cannot extend beyond time, (70) which will end and will always be very brief.’
