“She shows the disastrous consequences of bodily pleasures, and the cares and anxieties inseparable even from those called respectable and permissible. ‘Pleasure,’ she says, ‘has its sting, like the bee, which always leaves it in the one it tickles.’

> Where it has poured forth its pleasant honey,  
> It strikes the wounded hearts with its bite.

“She then reveals the causes of men’s illusion in seeking blessedness; and, to make her disciple understand wherein true blessedness consists, [Col. 1529A] she urges him to have recourse to prayer and to implore God’s help, without which one cannot attain it (*Book III, meter 9*):

> “The Father of all things must be invoked, I say, for without him no beginning can rightly be established.”

And she herself addresses this admirable prayer to God:

> “O you who govern the world by everlasting reason, etc.

“Creator of heaven and earth, who govern the world by eternal reason, who, while remaining forever immutable and unmoved within yourself, give motion to everything and change all things; you whom no external cause moved to create this fluid matter that composes the universe, but only the essential goodness of your nature—a goodness that you continually communicate, without jealousy and without diminution; you who create all things according to that eternal model which you carry within yourself, who, being beauty itself, bear this admirable world in your mind and produced it according to that eternal image, in all the beauty that we admire: grant to my spirit, beloved Father, that it may rise [Col. 1529B] to the throne of your awe-inspiring majesty, draw from the very source of goodness, and contemplate you openly and in the full daylight of your glory. Dispel by your divine light the darkness that envelops it; free me from this mass of flesh that prevents it from rising to you; cause the radiance of your wholly divine light to shine upon me. For you are the true rest of righteous souls; their end is to see and possess you. O beloved principle of all things, you alone raise us to that end—you who are our guide, our way, and our goal.”

> You are tranquil rest for the devout; to behold you is their end,  
> The same beginning, guide, driver, path, and goal.

After this prayer, Wisdom examines whether there truly is a blessedness such as she previously defined. “It cannot be denied,” she says, “that there is a source from which all good flows. The very imperfection found in creation proves it, since [Col. 1529C] this imperfection is the diminishment of something supremely perfect. If, then, there is an appearance of happiness in the world, there must somewhere be a solid and perfect blessedness. But where is it? Since God is the source and beginning of all good, and since the supreme and most perfect good is true blessedness, it follows that blessedness can be found only in God.

“This she continues to prove through a series of inferences, from which she concludes that goodness and blessedness have one and the same essence, and that true blessedness and God are one and the same thing. ‘It is this supreme good,’ she says, ‘that governs all things with strength and wisdom (73), and disposes of everything with gentleness.’

“She then establishes God’s omnipotence on the ground that there is nothing he cannot do; from this she takes occasion to instruct her pupil more fully by asking whether God can do evil. Boethius answers in the negative, and she appears to draw from this the conclusion that evil is therefore nothing, and is not a positive and real being, but a privation of [Col. 1529D] being, since God, who can do everything, cannot do it.”

## BOOK FOUR

Boethius, delighted by the sweet conversations he has with Wisdom, appears insensible to all his misfortunes. Recalling everything he had formerly learned from her, he says to her: “You have told me nothing new; you had already revealed all these secrets to me. It is true that my affliction did not allow me to reflect upon them, but the true cause of my sorrow is that God, who is the supreme arbiter and immutable rule of all things, and who is goodness itself, incapable of doing evil, can permit evil to exist in the world or allow it to go unpunished. For then virtue is not only unrewarded as it ought to be (74), but is also trampled underfoot by the impious, and often suffers the punishment that crime ought to bear. Who can understand how this can happen [Col. 1530A] in the state of a just king, a king who can do everything and knows everything—in the state of a good God, who can will nothing but good? This is the subject of my astonishment and my grief.”

“You would have reason to be astonished,” Wisdom replies, “and certainly it would be a horrifying thing if, in the household of so wise and just a father, regard were paid only to the vilest furniture and vessels, while everything most precious were cast aside. But it is not so in the kingdom of this great king, nor in the household of this great father whom we are discussing. I shall make you understand that good people are always honored and influential there, while criminals are always weak, powerless, and despised; that crime is never without punishment, nor virtue without reward; that happiness always follows virtue, and adversity and misfortune are the faithful companions of the sinner. This I shall prove to you with sound arguments.

“(75) To [Col. 1530B] make you understand these things, I must give wings to your spirit, so that it may rise to the highest heavens; and, having passed beyond this region of air in which you dwell, you may happily return to your homeland by following me along the path I am about to trace for you.”

Wisdom uses the same expressions that she had employed shortly before when speaking of God himself. This persuades me that the Wisdom with whom Boethius converses is not philosophy or created Wisdom, but uncreated Wisdom, the eternal Word clothed in human flesh, to whom alone it belongs to reveal the secrets of the abyss of knowledge and the depths of God’s judgments.

Wisdom therefore first proves that powerlessness is the portion of the wicked. Since good and evil are contrary, and true good is omnipotence itself, sin must necessarily be weakness and frailty itself. “All human actions,” [Col. 1530C] she continues, “proceed from will and power. When will is absent, a man undertakes nothing. Through lack of power, the will becomes vain and useless; and the person who cannot accomplish what he wills is recognized as weak and powerless. Yet all men, wicked and good alike, strive for happiness, and only good people attain it. Therefore only good people are powerful, and weakness is the portion of the impious, since he cannot attain possession of the object of his desires.

“The power that appears in the wicked is therefore the effect of their weakness. One cannot even say that they truly are what they appear to be, just as one cannot say of a dead man that he is truly a man, but only a corpse. So it is with the wicked and their actions: they may indeed do what they will, but they do not do what they desire. For [Col. 1530D] they desire, against their will, to be happy, and they cannot become so through their actions. On the contrary, they are reduced to servitude as soon as they fail to do what they desire; and, against their will, they are enslaved to evil masters:

> He does not do what he desires,  
> Himself oppressed by unjust masters.

“What are most of those rulers of the world whom you see seated upon thrones with all the splendor of gold and purple, with anger and indignation depicted upon their faces even as glory and majesty shine there? Once the veil is lifted from the outward pomp that surrounds them with armed men ready to obey them, you will find them vile slaves. You will see these very kings loaded with chains, their hearts torn by a thousand different passions. At one moment a shameful fire devours them; at another, anger inflames them. Now sadness overwhelms them; a moment later hope raises and agitates them, and, when it [Col. 1531A] leaves them, breaks them through their fall. These are as many tyrants under one head, each commanding them in turn and preventing them from ever doing what they desire:

> He does not do what he desires,  
> Himself oppressed by unjust masters.

“This is what Jesus Christ admirably expressed in two words: every sinner makes himself the slave of sin.

“(78) Do you see into what dreadful abyss crime casts man? And with what glory, by contrast, virtue shines, surrounded by what light? This alone would suffice to prove that the good are never without reward, nor criminals without punishment. For the thing proposed as the end of an action is the reward of the action itself. For example, the prize proposed in a race is the end and reward of the one who has run. Since, then, the supreme good—or blessedness, which is the same thing—is the object and end of the actions of the virtuous man, [Col. 1531B] it is also the reward of his action, and remains inseparable from it so long as he remains virtuous. Let the wicked rise against him and attack his virtue as much as they please: the wise man will not lose his reward; his crown will never wither, because чужая malice will never tarnish the glory proper to virtue.

“Virtue changes, so to speak, the substance of man into its own, by assuring him possession of the supreme good. For by making him participate in it through goodness, it in some way makes him divine and transforms him into God through possessing it.

“(79) The exact opposite occurs with the wicked. As they depart from good, they also depart from blessedness; the farther they depart from it, the more they cease to be what they previously were. By degrading themselves from their condition through crime, although they retain the outward form of man, they are changed into the nature of beasts. Indeed, can one not say that this miser, always intent on seizing [Col. 1531C] another’s property and ready to take it away by force, is a wolf rather than a man? That the person who gives himself over to rage, whose tongue is accustomed to disputes, invectives, insults, and quarrels, is a dog that continually barks and yelps? That this other person who deceives skillfully, this trickster who knows so well how to disguise himself in order to catch his neighbor unawares, is a true fox? Do you not think you see a lion in the man who gives himself over to fury and anger? In the timid person who fears where there is no danger, always ready to flee, do you not find the image of the stag? Does this coward, this idler, this dullard, not partake of the nature of the ass? Is this flighty and ever-inconstant person, who changes his purpose at every moment, not like the birds? And does this voluptuary, plunged into infamous pleasures, not live like the pig that delights in mud and wallows in filth?

“This is how man, who through virtue could acquire likeness to God and be transformed into [Col. 1531D] him, by turning away from virtue is unhappily reduced to the condition of the beasts.”

Wisdom carries her reasoning further and even maintains that if God prevented the wicked from carrying out their evil desires, He would punish them less than by allowing them to fulfill them; and although it may seem incredible that the wicked become more wretched by accomplishing their evil will than when they are unable to accomplish it, nevertheless this is true. For, she says, if it is a great misery to desire evil, it is an even greater one to commit it. The misery of the wicked is increased by three circumstances inseparable from their evil deed: it is one evil to wish to commit the crime, another to be able to do so, and a greater one to commit it. (81)

She adds that the wicked are even more wretched when their crimes remain unpunished than [Col. 1532A] when they receive their just punishment; for, when they receive punishment, their misery is diminished by their participation in some good that comes to them. Now when punishment follows the crime, and justice draws from it the vengeance the crime deserves, the criminal, by reason of the justice that accompanies the crime in the punishment drawn from it, participates in justice to some degree and consequently becomes less wretched than he was before being punished. Hence the criminal who remains unpunished suffers a double misery: the misery inseparable from his crime and that of his impunity.

Once these maxims have been established, Boethius asks Wisdom whether, if justice has punished the crimes of the wicked in this world, or has postponed punishing them, they have nothing more to fear after death, and whether the souls of the dead are exempt from every kind of torment. “No,” Wisdom replies; “very great punishments remain, some administered with penal severity, others with purifying mercy. Two kinds of torment are reserved in the other world to expiate the penalty due to sin: one is the pure punishment of sin without mercy; the other expiates the sin while at the same time purifying the sinner.” And this justice, however severe it may appear, Wisdom says, is full of mercy and goodness; but this is not the place to discuss these different punishments at length. (82) [Col. 1532B]

*Nullane animarum supplicia post defunctum morte corpus relinquis? Et magna quidem, quorum alia poenalia acerbitate, alia vero purgatoria clementia exerceri puto*—“Do you leave no punishments for souls after the body has died? Yes, indeed, very great ones: some, I think, are administered with penal severity, others with purgatorial mercy” (*Book IV of the Consolation*, prose 4).

She then proves that the person who inflicts an injury is much more wretched than the person who suffers it, since a human being becomes truly wretched only through sin. From this she concludes that the wise person never gives way to hatred and can hate no one. He does not hate the good, since only a madman could hate them; nor does he have cause to hate the wicked, because he knows that [Col. 1532C] malice is to the soul what illness is to the body. Just as no one hates a sick person, but instead considers him worthy of compassion, so, far from hating the sinner, one ought to be moved by compassion for his misery—especially since the sin oppressing him is a more dangerous and more dreadful disease of the soul than any illness from which he might suffer in his body. (82) [Col. 1532C]

She ends her reasoning with a maxim truly worthy of Wisdom: “Do you wish to render to each person, with exact justice, what you owe him according to his merit? *Dilige jure bonos, et miseresc[e] malis*—“Love the good rightly, and have compassion on the wicked”: Love the good with justice, and have compassion on the wicked.” (83)

Boethius returns to the question he had raised at the beginning. Whatever one may allege, he says, there is nevertheless something good or evil in what the people call fortune. For in truth there is no wise person who would prefer disgrace to glory, poverty to riches, or exile to the pleasure of appearing with distinction in his native country; and it is precisely through this preference that Wisdom makes herself particularly known and succeeds more effectively in governing peoples. For prisons, tortures, punishments ordained by the laws, and the laws themselves are established only against bad citizens, not against the good. How, then, does the exact opposite so often occur in the order of God’s providence—that good people are found exposed to the punishments ordained for criminals, while the wicked seize the prize intended only for virtue? Such an unjust confusion fills me with astonishment; I beg you to reveal its cause to me. I would be less astonished if I could persuade myself that everything that happens here below were the effect of chance; but I cannot recover from my astonishment, knowing that it is God who governs all things, and who often afflicts good people with every kind of evil, sometimes more severely than sinners, while I see the sinner often happier than the just person. (84) [Col. 1532D]

“This should not astonish you,” Wisdom replies, “nor make you believe that chance decides everything in the world. Although the reason for so extraordinary a disposition is unknown to you, you should not doubt that it is entirely just, since God Himself governs and ordains it. Moreover, the question you raise is among the most difficult; for scarcely shall I have satisfied you concerning one difficulty before an infinite number of others arise. By compelling me to answer the first, you immediately place me under the necessity of unfolding to you the marvels of the simplicity of divine Providence; what destiny and chance are (*Repentinus casus*), and what are God’s knowledge and predestination and the human free will. You are not unaware of the extent and depth of these matters; nevertheless, since your healing depends in some measure upon knowing them, I cannot avoid touching upon them, and I shall do so as far as the little time I have to spend with you permits. (85) [Col. 1533A]

“The generation of creatures subject to change, the development of mutable natures, or secondary causes—in short, everything that moves—derives its origin, form, motion, disposition, and order from the immutable stability of God’s spirit. Remaining always the same in the most perfect simplicity, it has determined the particular manner in which each agent acts. This manner, considered within the simplicity of divine intelligence, is called Providence: a term expressing that God sees and orders all things from afar and, as it were, from a very lofty place. But when it is related to secondary causes and to the order established among creatures to which God has imparted motion, the ancients called it Destiny. (86) [Col. 1533B]

“The difference between the two will clearly appear to anyone who examines them closely. Providence, then, is the divine reason residing in that first principle of all things and ordering everything. Destiny is the disposition inherent in mobile things, or secondary causes, by which Providence has bound each thing and each event together through the chain and order it has established within them. Providence embraces all things in general, however diverse they may be, whereas Destiny concerns particular things, whether with respect to motion, form, or time—Destiny, as though one were to say ‘designation.’ Although these two realities are very different, one nevertheless depends upon the other, and the order of Destiny necessarily flows and proceeds from the simplicity of God’s Providence. (87)

“Just as an architect who has conceived the design of a great building in his mind brings it forth externally and, through a regulated sequence of operations, makes visible the idea he had formed in his understanding, so God’s Providence, having in its simplicity established in a stable and immutable manner the subordination and manner of acting of creatures, makes manifest through Destiny the motion and order it has impressed upon them. This Destiny is exercised sometimes through the obedience that the blessed spirits render to Providence and through the submission owed by all nature to its Creator; sometimes through the movements of the stars and the power of the celestial virtues; and sometimes through the cunning of demons. Thus all things subject to Destiny are also subject to Providence, to which Destiny itself is subject. (88) [Col. 1533C]

“In this admirable order, Wisdom recognizes different degrees of dependence according to the dignity of creatures: the most perfect and those nearest to God depend immediately upon His Providence and are governed by it immediately, while all the others are subject immediately to Destiny. What the lower celestial spheres are, approximately, in relation to the higher spheres and to the first mover; what reasoning is in relation to understanding; time in relation to eternity; and the extremities of lines drawn from the center of a circle in relation to the center itself—such is the order of mutable Destiny in relation to the immutable simplicity of God’s Providence. [Col. 1533D]

“It is this order, this arrangement of Destiny, that moves the heavens and the stars; that produces the mixture and transformations of the elements, births and deaths; and that renews creatures through seeds. It also governs human fortune through an indissoluble chain of causes, all of which derive their origin from the simple and immutable Providence of God. Thus everything is accomplished with wisdom and in the order we admire. By this means, God’s spirit, remaining in its perfect simplicity, reveals without changing the inevitable order of causes and fixes the inconstancy and fluidity of creatures, which would fall back into chaos without this immutable arrangement God has established among them. (89) [Col. 1534A]

“Those who do not understand this admirable order believe that everything here below is confused, although everything is in fact regulated and tends only toward the good. Indeed, everything tends toward it in such a way that the wicked do nothing except for the sake of some good they seek, although error and blindness make them seek it where it is not.

“But,” you may say, “can anything more grievous happen than this confusion, this mingling of good and evil that occurs alike to the good and the wicked?” I shall answer by asking whether you believe that human beings possess a sufficiently sound judgment to form a true assessment of the quality and order of each thing and of each person in particular, so that each might truly be what they think it is. This is impossible, for people often hold different opinions: those whom some consider worthy of the greatest honors, others consider worthy of the deepest contempt. (90) [Col. 1534B]

“I grant you, if you wish, that a person may be sufficiently enlightened to distinguish the good from the wicked; but can he attain to a perfect knowledge of each person’s soul? The soul has, so to speak, its temperament, just as the body does. Someone who is ignorant of the different temperaments of bodies is surprised to find two people enjoying equal health, when acids suit one and sweet things the other; or that one sick person is relieved by gentle remedies while another is relieved by remedies that are harsher and more bitter. But the physician who knows the difference between the temperaments of a healthy person and a sick one is not surprised and can form an equitable judgment. The same is true of souls.

“Virtue and integrity are their health, while vices and passions are their diseases. God, who created them, who is the Father of all spirits, and who governs them, is their true physician. By observing them all attentively from the highest heavens, through His divine Providence, He knows and understands what suits each one and gives each what He knows to be suitable. Human beings do not know this, and that is what causes their astonishment. But since the temperaments, diseases, and qualities of souls are perfectly known to God, it is impossible for Him to err in the manner in which He governs them. (91) [Col. 1534C]

“You may consider a certain person, for example, a good person of outstanding virtue; yet he may appear entirely different in the eyes of God, who knows all things thoroughly. But suppose that this person’s conduct is so orderly and his virtue so perfect and pure that the judgment people have formed of him agrees with God’s judgment. Perhaps he does not possess a sufficiently strong spirit or sufficiently manly a virtue to bear adversity properly and derive some benefit from it. If God allowed him to be afflicted, perhaps he would depart from virtue. God spares him because He foresees that adversity would make him wicked. (92) [Col. 1534D]

“Here is another person of more heroic virtue, a saint of the highest order, perfectly united with God. Providence finds that he has no need to be tested by adversity or even by any bodily illness, and allows him to pass his days peacefully. It foresees that another would be ruined by uninterrupted prosperity, and permits him from time to time to experience some slight adversity, lest he become elated through too prolonged happiness. Another appears to possess a firm and robust temperament; he needs to be strengthened in virtue, so Providence subjects him to harsher trials and allows him to be tested by continual tribulations, so that through the practice of patience he may become established in every virtue. [Col. 1535A]

“Some allow themselves to be too easily overcome by fear; others presume too much upon their own strength. Providence regulates goods and evils—what we call the accidents of fortune—according to their needs. Foreseeing that a certain man, wicked though he is, would become still more wicked if he fell into poverty and would resort to even greater excesses, God allows him to become rich, to prevent him from becoming worse. His attachment to his possessions and his fear of losing them serve as a restraint upon his passions. Often he will change his morals and conduct because he fears losing his fortune and becoming wretched. (93) [Col. 1535B]

“Others have been plunged into the abyss of misery by a continual prosperity they abused. God alone, who can use both goods and evils equally to produce good effects, employs the greatest misfortunes to draw them out of it. He has often used the wicked to make others, still more wicked, become good. Finally, the order He has established is such that whoever departs from it always falls back into that admirable order. Thus nothing ever occurs in the world rashly or by chance. [Col. 1535C]

“O depth of God’s judgments! Inconceivable workings of His Providence, unknown to human beings, which they can never penetrate, still less explain in words!”

Boethius next considers with Wisdom what ought to be thought of people’s ordinary opinions concerning good and bad fortune. “What can this bad fortune be?” Wisdom replies. “As it is, does it not serve either to exercise a person or to correct him, and consequently is it not always good, since it is always useful? Fortune can be bad only for the wicked. (94) [Col. 1535D]

“If a person possesses virtue, he should not think it bad to be summoned or challenged to combat, any more than a courageous man fears going to meet the enemy; for it is through resisting vice and adversity that he can become established in virtue. Just as the resistance of the enemy brings glory to the victor, so the more resistance a good person encounters from fortune, the more glory and merit he will gain by overcoming it.

“Do not think,” Wisdom adds, “that those who profess to follow virtue have embraced it in order to be softened by pleasure. They have embraced it in order to enter the lists, to fight continually against fortune and against the passions, so as never to be oppressed by life’s most grievous misfortunes, never cast down by sorrow, and never seduced by pleasures, but to learn to remain always in a just and perfect equanimity of mind amid the most painful reversals and the disorders of fortune. It lies in your hands to make fortune what you wish, even the fortune that appears worst to you; for it either exercises, corrects, or punishes, and by this you should always find it good, since it is always useful to you.” (95) [Col. 1536A]

Boethius asks Wisdom what she thinks of chance and whether chance truly exists. Although the question may seem to depart from the goal she had set herself, Wisdom is nevertheless willing to instruct him further because the matter is highly useful. “If by chance,” she says, “you mean an event produced by a rash movement and without any concurrence of causes, I answer that there is no chance in the world; it is an empty name signifying nothing. For it is an axiom accepted by all philosophers that nothing comes from nothing. We understand this, as the ancients did, only of the material subject, and not of the first operating principle or efficient cause of all things. [Col. 1536B]

“If some event were produced in nature without the concurrence of causes, something would come from nothing. Consequently, there can be no chance in the world if you understand the term in this way. But chance, or the fortuitous event, as philosophers have defined it—and as the common people do not understand it—is an unforeseen event that occurs through the concurrence of secondary causes acting toward some end.

“For example, a man goes to plow his field and finds a treasure there: that is chance. But it does not happen from nothing. The event has its causes; for if someone had not hidden money in that field, and if a man had not gone there to plow it, the treasure would not have been found there.” (96) [Col. 1536C]

“I readily agree with you,” Boethius says to Wisdom, “concerning the admirable chain observed in the concurrence of secondary causes and that inevitable order Providence has established in the world. But if things are as you say and as I believe, human will is inevitably subjected to it, just like all other creatures. It will therefore be carried along inevitably in their fixed and determined course, and thus humanity will no longer possess freedom.”

Wisdom answers that no rational creature is without freedom, because it is rational only insofar as it can use its natural reason; and as soon as it can use it, it can form a judgment and discern for itself what it ought to flee and avoid and what it ought to seek. A person asks for and takes what he believes suits him, and flees what he believes harmful to him. Whoever can make this discernment possesses freedom, which consists in willing or not willing, in willing one thing or another. Yet this freedom is proportioned to the different rational natures. (97) [Col. 1536D]

For in spiritual and celestial substances, such as angels and saints, there is a lively and penetrating judgment, a will wholly free from corruption, a ready facility, and absolute power to do whatever they desire.

[Note: [Col. 1535D] It seems that Boethius, using these terms in speaking of souls—*cum dilabuntur ad corpora* (“when they descend into bodies”)—believed in their pre-existence, like the Platonists. Nevertheless, they may be explained as referring to the sensible and earthly affections of souls united to bodies. But if this explanation does not appear sufficiently natural, one may say that this opinion was not peculiar to him, but was held by several Christian philosophers, and that the contrary was not clearly defined until the Lateran Council under Innocent III, which decided as an article of faith that God creates souls by uniting them to our bodies and unites them to our bodies in creating them. [Col. 1536D]]

Holy souls, although still surrounded by mortal flesh, enjoy greater freedom in proportion as they are more detached from sensible and earthly things, because they are continually occupied in contemplation of the Divinity; yet their freedom is less perfect than that of the saints. (98) If they attach themselves to material and sensible things, their freedom diminishes in proportion to their attachment, and they fall into servitude and slavery as soon as they surrender themselves to them and abandon themselves to iniquity. [Col. 1537A]

They then deprive themselves of the use of their own reason; for as soon as they cease to look toward the light of supreme Truth, they fall into darkness and go astray. The disordered affections of the passions throw their minds into confusion and produce ignorance in them; and by giving themselves over to their passions, they strengthen the servitude to which they have subjected themselves. Thus they make themselves captives through the misuse of their freedom. (99)

But the eye of divine Providence, which from all eternity sees all these things, disposes and regulates them according to the way it has predestined them in relation to their merit: *Suis quaeque meritis praedestinata disponit*—“It disposes each thing as predestined according to its merits.”

“But how can you say,” Boethius replies, “that, since God has known all things from eternity, human beings nevertheless remain free? This appears contradictory. For if God sees everything from eternity and is infallible in His knowledge, then what His Providence has known will one day exist must necessarily come to pass. Thus, since not only human actions but also their intentions and wills are known to God, no freedom can remain to them. And if their wills can be bent or turned elsewhere, in a manner different from what divine Providence has foreseen, God will no longer be infallible in His foreknowledge—something that cannot be said without blasphemy. (100) [Col. 1537B]

“Nor can I approve the opinion of those who believe they answer the difficulty by saying that what happens does not happen because Providence foresaw that it would happen, but because divine Providence could not be ignorant that it would happen, since it was going to happen. That does not resolve the difficulty. The question is not what the true cause of the necessity of each thing is—whether it is the foreknowledge of the necessity of future things or the necessity imposed upon future things to occur according to the order established by Providence. Rather, the difficulty is to show that, within the order established by Providence, the occurrence of known things is infallible even though God’s foreknowledge imposes no necessity upon them. [Col. 1537C]

“An example will make this proposition clear. Suppose that a person is seated. It is necessary that the judgment of someone who believes that person to be seated is true; and likewise, if the judgment that a person is seated is true, it is absolutely necessary that the person be seated. In both operations there is an equal necessity: the necessity of being seated in the person who is seated and the necessity of the truth of the judgment in the person who believes that the other is seated. Is this not approximately how one must reason concerning divine Providence and God’s foreknowledge of future things? (101) [Col. 1537D]

“Moreover, it seems to me that this would make future things the cause of God’s knowledge, or would say that the past in God is the cause of His knowledge of the future—something entirely unworthy of God. But however the matter may occur, if, as you admit, everything issuing from the certain source of all things is certain and infallible, then the occurrence of things God has foreseen will be infallible. Consequently, human beings will no longer be free in their intentions and actions, because they are constrained by these events that God foresees with certainty and infallibly.

“If this is so, into what confusion does human nature fall, and to what injustice is it subjected? Would it not plainly be unjust to offer rewards to the good and punishments to the wicked when none had deserved them? For without freedom there is no merit. What we consider most just in God would become the very essence of injustice. It would be unjust to punish the wicked for crimes they had not committed voluntarily, but through the fatal necessity by which they had been carried along. It would likewise be unjust to reward those whom we consider good, since without freedom they would possess no merit in their supposed virtue. (102) [Col. 1538A]

“It is therefore a horrible blasphemy to maintain that all things are necessarily ordered by God’s Providence and to leave human beings no freedom in choosing their actions. This makes God, who is goodness and holiness itself, the author of all crimes and casts all our iniquity upon Him. If this were so, we would have nothing to ask of Him and nothing to expect from Him. For if things are so determined that they can never be changed, and if the order established by God is immutable, our wishes and prayers will never change it, and our hope will have nothing left to sustain it.

“Thus the only relationship that remains to human beings with God—through hope and prayer—is taken away. For as a reward for a just humility, when we bow beneath His almighty hand, await everything from Him with steadfast confidence, and ask Him in faith and perseverance for what we need, we believe that, in return for His immeasurable goodness toward us, we obtain the precious gift of His grace to act and do good. This is the only way in which we can converse with God and draw near to that inaccessible light, even before obtaining what we wish to ask of Him. (103) [Col. 1538B]

“It is therefore impossible for human freedom to accord with God’s foreknowledge; one absolutely destroys the other. For once the necessity of divine foreknowledge is admitted, all things appear bound together by an indissoluble, necessary, and inevitable chain. And if this is so, human beings hope in God in vain and address their wishes to Him in vain, since once things have been fixed by an eternal and immutable law, they can no longer be changed.”

Before answering these great objections, Wisdom tells Boethius that the complaints he raises against divine Providence are not new, and that it is true that no one has ever answered them with such precision and clarity that some obscurity did not remain concerning this matter. But this obscurity arises from the difficulty of making the human understanding grasp the simplicity of God’s knowledge and foreknowledge; and no difficulty would remain concerning the matter if it could once understand it fully. (104) [Col. 1538C]

Second, she says that she is surprised that the reasoning Boethius has presented does not seem sufficient to him to preserve free will and prevent human beings from becoming subject to a fatal necessity. “You believe,” he has said, “that the will is subject to this fatal necessity only because the things God has foreseen must infallibly occur. But if I prove to you that this foreknowledge imposes no necessity upon future things, from where could the unavoidable necessity you attribute to them arise? Let us suppose for a moment that there were no foreknowledge: could things done freely thereby be reduced to an infallible necessity? Certainly not. Let us suppose further that foreknowledge exerts no necessity upon things that occur: will you not agree that freedom remains wholly intact? Yes, certainly. (105) [Col. 1538D]

“But you will say to me that foreknowledge, although it does not impose the necessity of being upon future things, is nevertheless a certain sign that future things will necessarily occur. How, then, can it be that things God has foreseen as destined to occur might fail to occur? We do not claim this, Wisdom replies; we agree that they will occur infallibly. But we say that God’s foreknowledge imposes no necessity upon them, because we see many things occurring before our eyes without our knowledge making them necessary. And just as knowledge of present things imposes no necessity upon them to exist, so God’s foreknowledge of future things cannot impose any necessity upon those that are to exist. [Col. 1539A]

“But if foreknowledge imposes no necessity upon them, you will again say, God cannot have knowledge of them—that is, certain knowledge—since knowledge can concern only a certain object. You are mistaken. The source of your error is that you believe the knowledge we have of objects comes only from the nature of the object itself, which is entirely false. For everything known is not known solely through its object and the force of its nature, but rather according to the faculty and power of the one who knows it. (106) [Col. 1539B]

“The senses, for example, can judge only of figure and form united to matter. Imagination can represent form without matter, because imagination is superior to the senses. Since reason is superior to imagination, it knows, through a more universal and extensive knowledge, the species communicated to several individuals. And intelligence, which is the highest part of reason, surpasses it still further and knows the simplest forms, which are unknown to the senses, to the imagination, and to reason.”

Boethius, who maintained that free will was destroyed by God’s foreknowledge, reasoned as follows:

Everything that is future is either necessarily future or contingently future: if it is necessary, there is no longer any free will; if it is contingent, there can (107) be no foreknowledge of it in God: this foreknowledge is nothing more than a simple conjecture, since there is no knowledge of contingent things; and even if foreknowledge imposed no necessity upon future things, it would always be a certain sign that they will occur.

But Wisdom destroys this false reasoning and proves to him, first, that God’s foreknowledge imposes no necessity upon future things; second, that there is in God [Col. 1539C] certain foreknowledge of future and contingent things; third, that a sign, however certain it may be, does not determine the being of the thing it signifies. This last point, she says, is self-evident. Indeed, a *bouchon* (a wine-shop sign) attached to a house, for example, does not produce the wine sold there, nor does it exert any influence upon the nature of the wine; it merely indicates that wine is available there and that it is for sale.

But this is how she proves her other two propositions: if knowledge of things came from the things themselves and not from the faculty of the one who knows them, things would be known equally by all those (108) capable of knowing them, and in the same manner. Now this is entirely false; for there would then be no difference between God’s intelligence and man’s, or between the manner in which one knows and that in which the other knows.

If you believe that one cannot have knowledge of future and contingent things, that is true [Col. 1539D] with regard to man, whose faculty of knowing is limited; but not with regard to God, whose knowledge is infinite; to God, who knows uncertain and future events just as certainly as things that are present, although the human mind cannot comprehend this. Since knowledge therefore follows the nature of the one who knows, there are different ways of knowing, according to the diversity of intelligent substances, some higher and more perfect than others; and inferior intelligent substances can never attain the sublimity of the knowledge possessed by superior substances.

Just as our senses and imagination never rise as high as our reason, so our reason can never rise high enough to comprehend the manner in which God (109) [Col. 1540A] knows future things as absolutely certain, whereas we know them only as highly uncertain. Let us therefore, if we can, raise the point of our minds toward this sublime intelligence. There our reason will see what it cannot comprehend within itself: how God, through his foreknowledge, knows the least certain events with the greatest certainty; that he has not merely an opinion about them, but genuine knowledge; and that he knows them in this way through the simplicity of his knowledge, which is infinite and without limits.

Here is the reason: you agree that God is eternal; now eternity is the complete, simultaneous, and perfect possession of a life without end or limit [Note: [Col. 1539] *Aeternitas est interminabilis vitae tota simul et perfecta possessio*: “Eternity is the complete, simultaneous, and perfect possession of an unending life.”]. In this eternity there is nothing past and nothing future, but everything is always present all at once.

For there is a great difference between what is eternal, what is perpetual, and what exists in time. What exists in time passes from the past to the present and from the present to the future, and there is nothing in time capable of embracing all the moments of its duration simultaneously. [Col. 1540B] Man, for example, does not yet possess (110) tomorrow; yesterday is lost to him; and of the day in which he lives, only the instant in which he is living belongs to him.

Even if the perpetual had had no beginning—as Aristotle believed of the world—and its duration were to extend into eternity, it would not for that reason be eternal, because it does not possess all at once, in the same instant, the entire extent of the perpetual duration it might have, since it does not yet possess its future duration.

Only the eternal possesses and comprehends, in the same instant, the whole fullness of eternity: everything past, everything future, and everything present. It is impossible that it should not always possess itself, that it should not always be present to itself, or that it should not always have present to it all the infinite parts of time that flow onward. [Col. 1540C] But this eternity belongs to God alone.

Since knowledge, as has just been said, is always proportioned to the nature of the one who knows, and since God’s manner of knowing is eternal, God must know all things as present. (111) This is why his knowledge is called providence rather than foresight: God looks upon and sees all things as though he were placed in an infinitely elevated position from which he could see everything from a great distance.

And just as knowledge of present things imposes no necessity upon them—for our seeing them does not make them more necessary—so divine Providence, by looking upon future things that are present to it, imposes no necessity upon them. The manner in which it knows them in its eternity has no more influence upon creatures than our manner of knowing them in time. Consequently, it brings about neither any change nor any alteration in the nature of things themselves, nor in the judgment that ought to be formed concerning them. [Col. 1540D]

“But how, then,” you will reply, “can you say that God foresees future things, since he knows them only as present, since nothing past or future exists before him, and since everything is present to his eyes in his eternity? This knowledge is rather ordinary knowledge than foreknowledge.”

I will answer (112) that we call it foreknowledge because the things that are continually present to him are future with respect to us.

To shed more light on this subject, Wisdom next distinguishes two kinds of necessity: one simple and absolute, the other conditional.

A simple necessity is, for example, the necessity of dying imposed upon all human beings. A conditional necessity is, for example, this: [Col. 1541A] if you know that someone is walking, it is necessary that he walk, for it cannot be the case that a thing is other than one knows it to be.

But this conditional necessity does not entail absolute necessity, because it does not arise from the nature of the thing, but from the hypothesis and condition that have been posited. There is no necessity compelling someone who walks voluntarily to walk, although, while he is walking, he necessarily walks. Such is the necessity that God’s foreknowledge can impose upon the things it knows.

It knows what will occur through the free will of human beings, and these things become necessary only with respect to God’s knowledge, (113) but not absolutely or considered in themselves. All things foreseen by God therefore occur infallibly; but some occur because they proceed from human freedom, without losing anything of their own nature, since before occurring they [Col. 1541B] could have failed to occur; while others occur through an absolute and unavoidable necessity.

What does it matter in what manner they are necessary, provided that they occur infallibly, as God knew they would? Man himself finds within him an image of what takes place in God: with the same eye and the same glance he sees two things that are necessary in different ways. For example, he sees the sun rise—which rises by an absolute and unavoidable necessity—and at the same time, in the same instant, he sees a man walking, who walks only by a conditional and hypothetical necessity: a necessity imposed upon him solely by his free choice and by the voluntary decision he has made to walk.

“But if it depends upon me,” you will say, “to change God’s decree, then I can render his foreknowledge vain.” (114)

No. You can indeed change your purpose and your decision, but [Col. 1541C] divine Providence knows—and has known—that you have the power to do so, and whether you will do so or not. It cannot be ignorant of the choice you will make, and you can never render its foreknowledge vain, any more than you can escape the gaze of a keen and far-seeing eye fixed upon you, even though you may freely turn toward different actions.

But will divine knowledge be changed [Col. 1542A] by a change in our dispositions? When I desire one thing at one moment and another thing at another, will it change in the same way?

Not at all. God’s eye sees everything—the future as well as the present—and, remaining always the same, knows all your changes in a single glance. This manner of knowing present things does not arise from the occurrence of future things, but from the inherent simplicity of God’s knowledge and nature. Therefore one cannot say that future things are the cause of his foreknowledge, since his foreknowledge derives nothing from the future.

Within the extent of his knowledge, simple though it is, (115) God contains the entire order that he has prescribed for all creatures. Once things are thus ordered, man’s free will nevertheless remains inviolable, and the laws God has made are entirely just, as are the punishments and rewards he has prepared for human actions, upon which no necessity is imposed.

Thus God, contemplating from his eternal vantage point and foreseeing everything that is to happen in the presence of his eternity, concurs with our actions without imposing any necessity upon them. Thus the hope we place in him and the prayers we address to him are not vain; and if they are just and in accordance with reason, they cannot even be ineffectual. [Col. 1542B]

“Withdraw yourselves, then, mortals, from vice,” Wisdom concludes; “flee from it and embrace virtue. Lift your minds through noble hopes, and raise your humble prayers to God’s throne. You have, if you do not wish to conceal it from yourselves, a very pressing necessity to be good people, knowing that God’s eye is continually attentive to you and that you cannot escape the (116) sight of a just judge who knows and sees everything.”

This work is Boethius’s masterpiece. It has always been regarded as one of the most accomplished works of its kind, not only because of the admirable variety of reasons and subtle [Col. 1542C] and pious thoughts it contains, but also because of the beauty of its style, the gentleness of its expressions, and the pleasing mixture of verse and prose, which is maintained with equal strength throughout.

In its poetry one finds verses of twenty-six different meters, whose force and beauty yield nothing to those of Virgil and Horace.

(117) **EXAMINATION OF GLAREANUS’S OPINION concerning the author of Boethius’s books of the *Consolation of Philosophy*.**

[Col. 1541]

It is astonishing that Henry Lorit, better known in the republic of letters by the name Glareanus, should have wished to persuade the people of his century—contrary to the common opinion then prevailing and still prevailing—that the books of the *Consolation of Philosophy*, of which we have just spoken [Col. 1541D], were not by the Boethius whose life we are writing, but by another author of the same name.

He himself anticipates the objection based on the universally accepted presumption that ought to be set against him (118), and speaks of it as follows:

“What shall we say of the opinion of so many learned men who preceded us? And who has ever doubted that these works were by Boethius?”

But how does he answer this objection?

“Did they all examine them? I do not say so. But what does it matter? They did not think about it.”

He himself had not thought about it when he answered his objection in so weak and childish a manner. For, after all, an opinion accepted by everyone and confirmed by the unanimous consent of so many centuries ought not to be rejected so rashly, and one cannot wish to substitute one’s own opinion for it without displaying considerable presumption.

The style of the work, by his own admission, accords with that of Boethius. What, then, does he find in it that makes it [Col. 1542C] unworthy of being recognized as the production of this great man?

He says that not once does one find in it the name of Jesus Christ. And can one readily believe that a Christian as devout as Boethius, in the condition in which he found himself, awaiting from one moment to the next the execution of the death sentence pronounced against him, would have directed his thoughts [Col. 1542D] not toward Jesus Christ, (119) the supreme model of Christian patience and the abundant source from which all who suffer unjustly must draw the motives for their consolation—but toward empty arguments more suitable to a pagan philosopher?

But this reason would also prove that the treatise on the Trinity, which Boethius composed in prison, is not his work, since the name of Jesus Christ does not appear there even once.

Would it be possible, reasoning according to the same principle as Glareanus, that a man as devout as Boethius would not, in the condition in which he found himself, have directed his thoughts toward the crucified Jesus Christ rather than toward an infinity of other subjects capable of drying up the heart, and would have occupied himself solely with metaphysical abstractions and barbarous, almost unknown terms such as *hypostasis*, relation, identity, [Col. 1543A] opposition, incommunicability, and so many others with which his work is filled?

Yet this reasoning made no impression upon Glareanus’s mind regarding the treatise on the Trinity. Why, then, should it make an impression regarding (120) the *Consolation of Philosophy*?

The latter work is far more moral, instructive, and moving than the former. If Boethius speaks there as a philosopher, his thoughts, reflections, and sentiments are all those of a perfect Christian. It is easy to perceive that, under the name of Philosophy, he skillfully conceals uncreated Wisdom, and that the speeches he places in her mouth make this sufficiently clear.

Did not the Fathers of the early centuries call Christianity the most excellent philosophy, and Christians true philosophers? Their works are filled with similar expressions.

And is it not evident that those who excel particularly in some art ordinarily express their thoughts through terms belonging specifically [Col. 1543B] to that art? If a painter, musician, physician, or mathematician happens to discuss God and matters of religion, it will [Col. 1544A] almost always be through figures and comparisons drawn from his art, with which he is most familiar.

This conduct is natural to human beings. Can one be surprised (121) that Boethius, raised from his earliest youth in the school of the philosophers, and whose life had been a continual philosophy—that is, a constant and faithful study and love of true wisdom—should have expressed his final thoughts in terms proper to the science in which he had most excelled?

If the Word of God, this uncreated Wisdom, made himself the milk of children by clothing himself in our humanity, he nevertheless remained, according to his divinity, the nourishment of the strong and of the loftiest souls.

Since Boethius belonged to their number, one should not be surprised that he attached himself solely to the divinity of the Word. It is with that divinity that he conducts these conversations, so gentle and consoling; it is that divinity that his faith renders present to him and almost perceptible under the idea of Philosophy or Wisdom.

Have these not always been the sentiments of the most perfect Christians and of those most detached from everything [Col. 1544B] that can fall under the senses?

## ANALYSIS OF BOETHIUS’S MATHEMATICS

[Col. 1543]

[Col. 1543B] Boethius divides his *Mathematics* into four parts: Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, and Astronomy. The last of these parts is lost, and its loss cannot be sufficiently regretted.

He shows that Arithmetic is independent of the other three, and that the latter depend upon it entirely, both for their existence and for their perfection.

## ON ARITHMETIC

### FIRST BOOK

Boethius’s *Arithmetic* comprises (123) two books. It is a complete work, from which those who came after him drew [Col. 1543C] everything most subtle, profound, and useful in this science.

He himself praises it at the beginning of his books. Transported with admiration when considering its essence, properties, and relations, he does not hesitate to say that it existed before all times, and that the Creator, as an infinitely perfect geometer, used it as a model in forming all creatures.

He apparently alludes to the unity of nature and the Trinity of Persons that exists in God from all eternity. Elsewhere he calls arithmetic a divine work, one that was not invented by human beings.

He first divides numbers into even and odd and gives various definitions of them, reporting the different opinions of the authors on the subject.

He distinguishes three kinds of even numbers: evenly even, even-odd, and unevenly even.

An evenly even number is one that can always be divided equally [Col. 1543D] into two without a fraction until one reaches unity. Such is the number (124) 128.

An even-odd number is one that can first be divided into two equal parts without a fraction, but afterward cannot be divided without a fraction before reaching unity. Such is the number 30.

An unevenly even number is one that can initially be divided and subdivided equally into two without a fraction, but that afterward cannot be so divided without a fraction before reaching unity. Such is the number 120.

The author has made two tables to render what he has said more intelligible. One will admire the ingenuity with which they are composed, and in them one will see how these three kinds of numbers arise from one another, as well as their properties, relations, progressions, arithmetical and geometrical proportions, and proportional means.

An odd number is opposed to an even number [Col. 1544B] and cannot initially be divided equally into two without a fraction, because of the intervening unit, which is indivisible by nature.

The author gives three kinds of odd numbers.

The first consists of a number that can be divided only by units; it is called a prime, non-composite odd number. Such are the (125) numbers 3, 5, and 7.

The second kind consists of numbers that can be divided equally by 3 and by 1. He calls this kind a secondary, composite odd number.

The third kind partakes of the first and second. It consists of a number that, with respect to itself, is a secondary and composite odd number, but, with respect to [Col. 1544C] another number, is prime and non-composite, having no common measure with it except unity.

Such is the number 9 in relation to 25: 9 cannot be divided by 5, which divides 25, and 25 cannot be divided by 3, which divides 9, but 25 can be divided equally only by units.

The author then shows how the first two kinds arise from one another and teaches the method of finding a number belonging to the third kind.

After this, Boethius divides even numbers into perfect and imperfect numbers.

Imperfect numbers are those whose aliquot parts do not equal the whole they divide, but fall short of it or exceed it. Such are the numbers 8 and 12.

Perfect numbers are those whose aliquot parts, when added together, equal (126) the whole they divide. Such are the numbers 6, 28, 496, and so forth.

He observes that only one occurs in each decade and moralizes on this point: “Why,” he says, “are there so few perfect numbers and so few elect?”

He also shows [Col. 1544D] that perfect numbers always end alternately in 6 or in 8.

M. Prestet, in his *Elements of Mathematics*, nevertheless gives two in succession ending in 6 and two in succession ending in 8, which contradicts Boethius’s principles, which are infallible. He also prescribes the sure and invariable method for finding perfect numbers.

The author next turns to the division of relative numbers, some of which are equal and others more or less unequal.

Equal numbers are indivisible by nature; for if they were divisible, they would cease to be equal. Thus 4, for example, which is equal to 4, ceases to be equal to it as soon as it loses its integrity.

As for numbers that are more or less unequal, he gives five kinds. He gives them in Latin the name *duces*, meaning the greater numbers, and sets them against five others, which he calls in Latin *comites*, as being inseparable from the former; these are the lesser numbers. (127) It is upon these relative numbers that the different proportions are founded. [Col. 1545A]

The first kind is called multiple, and from it arise double, triple, quadruple, and other proportions.

It consists of a number that contains a lesser number more than once, without anything remaining over or falling short.

Boethius prefers this first kind to the others because of its antiquity, excellence, and usefulness. He says that it is the principle of the celebrated table of multiplication and division attributed to Pythagoras, whose ingenuity and properties he cannot admire sufficiently.

He also shows how this first kind is formed and the uniformity it preserves in this respect to infinity.

The second kind consists of a number that contains a lesser number and, in addition, an aliquot part of that lesser number. He calls it *superparticular*.

If, in addition to the lesser number, the greater contains (128) half of it—for example, 6, which contains 4 plus 2, half of 4—that number is called in Latin *sesquialter*.

If, in addition to the lesser number, it contains a third—for example, 4, which contains 3 plus 1, a third of 3—he calls it *sesquitertius*.

If, in addition to the lesser number, it contains a fourth—for example, 5 contains 4 plus 1, which is one-fourth of 4—it is a *sesquiquartus*; and so on to infinity.

The designations will be derived from the excesses of the lesser number that the greater number contains together with it.

These first two kinds are of great use for musical harmonies, as will be seen in its proper place.

The third kind of relative numbers consists of a [Col. 1545C] number that contains a lesser number and, in addition, certain parts of that lesser number that cannot be aliquot parts of the greater number—that is, cannot divide it equally.

Boethius calls this kind in Latin *superpartiens*, which could be called in French *surdivisante*. It receives as many different designations as there are different excesses of the lesser number that it contains.

If, in addition to the lesser number, the greater contains two-thirds of it, it is called *superbipartiens*. Such is the number (129) 5 in relation to 3: 5 contains the whole of 3 plus two-thirds of 3, namely 2, which cannot divide 5 equally.

If, in addition to the lesser number, the greater contains three-fourths of it, it is called *supertripartiens*. Such is the number 7 in relation to 4, and so on to infinity.

The fourth kind partakes of the first two and is called by the author multiple-superparticular.

It is nothing other than a greater number that contains a lesser number several times and, in addition, one of the parts of that lesser number, whether a half or a third.

Such is the number 5 in relation to the number 2, which it contains twice plus one-half of 2.

This kind receives as many different designations as the excesses are different and as the quantity of the lesser numbers it contains varies.

[Col. 1545D] The fifth kind partakes of the first and third and could be called multiple-superpartient.

It consists of a greater number that contains a lesser number several times and, in addition, some of its parts—two-thirds or three-fourths, and so forth.

Such is the (130) number 24 in relation to 9; such also is the number 44 in relation to 16, which it contains twice plus 12, or three-fourths of 16.

The author teaches how these different kinds are formed and provides tables to make this more easily understood; he marks their properties in them.

He sets against these five kinds of greater unequal numbers five corresponding kinds of lesser, likewise unequal numbers, which the former contain and to which they are correlated. He gives them names indicating their inferiority, such as submultiple, subsuperparticular, and so forth.

[Col. 1546A] Boethius ends his first book of *Arithmetic* with a demonstration intended to prove that all unequal numbers derive their origin from equal numbers.

The tables he provides for this purpose are very clear, and they were necessary for understanding a subject that he himself says is very profound.

They are formed upon three infallible principles, which can also serve to extend the tables. By means of them one sees how all the proportions contained in the five kinds of relative numbers (131) are formed, and how one of the five preceding kinds is transformed into another by transposing the two extremes, without moving the number or term in the middle.

### SECOND BOOK

At the beginning of the second book of his *Arithmetic*, which he calls an introduction to the other parts of his *Mathematics*, he shows that all unequal numbers, whatever kind they may be, can be reduced to the equal numbers from which they originated.

For this purpose he gives three [Col. 1546B] infallible rules. He then shows, through very curious and instructive tables, from what principles the proportions of the second kind of relative numbers proceed, and how many subordinate proportions these principles can contain.

Afterward he gives other tables by means of which one discovers how the subdivisions of these proportions produce others of the first kind, according to the manner in which they are combined.

These tables are very necessary for the various proportions found in the different harmonies of music.

The author next establishes the principles of geometry. He speaks of the point (132), the line, and the surface, for which he gives definitions.

He then proves that the triangle is the origin of all rectilinear plane figures and teaches the method by which triangles are formed through numbers placed in their natural order and added according to the rules he prescribes.

He observes that there are as many units in each side of an equilateral triangle [Col. 1546D] as there are units in the last number used in forming it. This can be seen in the figures he drew for this purpose.

After triangles, he discusses square figures and square numbers and shows the uniform manner in which they are formed through odd numbers set out in their natural order.

He observes that each side of a square contains as many numbers as there were terms involved in the formation of cubes and polygonal figures.

The tables he composed for this purpose equally convince and satisfy the mind.

He then discusses circular and spherical numbers and gives a table in which one sees how the numbers 5 and 6, by multiplying themselves or by multiplying their products, always end in 5 or 6.

(133) After warning that triangles are the principles of plane figures, the author proves that pyramidal figures are the principles of solid figures [Col. 1546D] and that they multiply their triangles in proportion to the different bases supporting them.

He gives tables to make it clear how these figures are formed uniformly through numbers. He then discusses truncated pyramids and various other figures that approach the cubic.

He next says that elongated squares are formed by subtracting a square’s root from it or by adding the root to it.

He gives very useful tables to show that from square and elongated-square numbers—the former odd and the latter even—various proportions and even various figures are formed, the triangular figure being their principle.

He further proves that if these square and elongated-square numbers are successively interwoven and mutually compounded, they will be equal on one side with respect to proportion and unlike with respect to difference.

[Col. 1547A] In the continuation of his work, after showing that in nature there are (134) two kinds of substances—one immutable, such as spirits, and the other changeable, such as bodies—and that numbers partake of one or the other in their own manner, he says that unity properly partakes of immutability.

Then come odd numbers, followed by squares, and finally cubes.

Among things of a changeable nature, duality occupies the first place, followed by even numbers and then elongated squares.

Since some difficulty might be raised concerning squares that end in an even number, such as 4, 16, 36, and 64, he first shows that these squares are formed from odd numbers.

Second, he proves through specially constructed tables that if several numbers in double proportion and others in triple proportion are arranged, all the squares—whether even or odd—beginning with one, will always be found [Col. 1547B] in an odd-numbered rank, that is, in the first, third, fifth, or seventh rank, and so on to infinity.

After this he treats of arithmetical, geometrical, and harmonic proportions (135) and teaches how to find their proportional means.

He shows their differences and properties.

These three different proportions were known to Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle, as were three others, two of which are contrary to geometrical proportion and one opposed to harmonic proportion.

He says that four other unnamed proportions were added to these six in order to make the number ten, a number favored by the Pythagoreans.

But since they are of little use, he discusses them only in passing; nevertheless, he provides tables for the satisfaction of the curious.

The author ends his second book with a geometrical-harmonic proportion containing four terms [Col. 1547C] and entering into the composition of the most perfect harmony.

In this respect it corresponds to the cubic proportion, which contains three intervals.

Since it will be discussed again in connection with Pythagoras’s tetrachord, it will suffice to observe here that these four terms are 6, 8, 9, and 12.

In them one first sees an arithmetical progression: the numbers 6, 9, and 12 differ (136) equally by 3, whose proportional mean is 9, half of the sum of the two extremes, 6 and 12.

One also sees a geometrical proportion, since the product of 6 multiplied by 12—namely, 72—is equal to the product of 8 multiplied by 9.

Finally, one discovers the harmonic proportion in 6, 8, and 12, of which 8 is the proportional mean.

Just as the two extremes, 6 and 12, are in double proportion, so the differences 2 and 4 are in double proportion: 6 differs from 8 by 2, and 8 differs from 12 by 4.

(137) ## ON MUSIC
[Col. 1547D] **FIRST BOOK.**—At the beginning of his first book, Boethius dwells on the excellence and usefulness of music, toward which even the most barbarous nations have felt an inclination, and whose efficacy is so great that it has been able to calm the most violent passions. He gives several examples of this, while not concealing that one may also abuse this divine art. This led several republics to banish those soft and effeminate (138) symphonies that serve only to kindle the passions. He believes that the reason music pleases all human beings so greatly lies in the admirable harmony that the Creator has placed between soul and body, between spirit and matter—two things equally opposed.

He divides music into three kinds. The first is nothing other than the harmony formed among themselves by the many different parts composing the entire structure of the great world, all of which tend toward [Col. 1548A] the benefit of the little world, that is, humanity, and toward the glory of their Creator, who has made everything according to number, weight, and measure. The second kind consists in the harmony formed within human beings by the many different and opposed parts of which they are composed, whose perfect agreement enables them to live. The third kind of music is nothing other than the symphony produced by instruments or voices. He gives its elements and principles, then distinguishes it into various species according to the equality or inequality of the intervals.

After observing that consonance (139), which directs harmony, presupposes sound, just as sound presupposes percussion, and percussion movement, without which everything would be silent, he says that sound is nothing other than the percussion of the air continued until it reaches the sense of hearing. He later compares it to the uniformly non-uniform circles produced by a stone thrown into still water. Now, the slower the movement of this percussion, the lower the sound [Col. 1548B]; and the faster this movement, the higher the sound. It is the proper joining of the low and high tones, entering the ear with a non-uniform uniformity, or a uniform and pleasant non-uniformity, that produces consonance. As for unison, it consists of sounds that are either equally high or equally low. Although the ear does not perceive the different vibrations or the unequal movements caused, for example, by the striking of a string, such differences are nevertheless present. But because the sense of hearing, like sight, is liable to deception, he determines that judgment concerning the accuracy of harmonies should be governed not by the senses but by the science of numbers and by their relations and proportions.

(140) On this subject Boethius repeats what he said in his books on Arithmetic concerning the five species of relative numbers. He says that only the first two species—the multiple and the superparticular—[Col. 1548C] are suitable for composing harmonies, and even then he uses only their simplest proportions. Thus, the double proportion corresponds to the harmony of the octave, the triple proportion to the consonance of the octave and fifth, and the quadruple proportion to the harmony of the double octave. These proportions belong to the multiple genus, which is the most perfect. For the simple consonance of the fifth and fourth, he assigns proportions belonging to the second species.

He then explains what gave Pythagoras the occasion to invent the four-stringed instrument, in which the tone, fourth, fifth, and octave are found. This philosopher, he says, after having wearied his mind in vain while trying to discover whether the nature of harmonies was founded on quantity or quality, happened to pass by a blacksmith’s shop. Noticing that the workmen’s hammers produced a harmony when they struck, he had them weighed. From their weights he discovered the principle of consonances (141), and that they were founded solely on quantity. Some [Col. 1548D] weighed six pounds, others eight, others nine, and others twelve—all numbers corresponding to those mentioned above at the end of the second book of the Arithmetic.

The author then discusses Mercury’s tetrachord, which is the same as Pythagoras’s. This instrument, he says, was enlarged by Chorœbus, son of Athis, king of the Lydians. Hyagris, a Phrygian, added a sixth string, and Terpander a seventh, modeled on the seven planets, just as Mercury’s tetrachord had been modeled on the four elements. Later, people were not content with this heptachord. Samius of Lycaonia added an eighth string, Prophrastus a ninth, Hestiocus a tenth, Timotheus an eleventh, and others eventually increased the number of strings to two full octaves. Boethius gives the names of every string in these various instruments and provides [Col. 1549A] an explanation of them, showing their properties and the kind of music to which they belong: some being suited to the diatonic, others to the chromatic (142), and others to the enharmonic. He prefers the last of these three kinds, since the diatonic seems too harsh to him and the chromatic too soft.

He ends his first book of Music by reporting the differing opinions of Plato and Nicomachus concerning the essence of consonances. He also shows the views held by Nicomachus, Ptolemy, Eubulides, and Hippasus regarding which harmony should be given precedence. Some place the octave first, followed by the harmony of the octave with the fifth, then the double octave, and finally the fifth and fourth. Others alter this order, placing the octave first, then the fifth, then the harmony of the fifth with the octave, followed by the fourth and finally the double octave. The author also observes that, to be a perfect [Col. 1549B] musician, it is not enough to sing a piece of music well or to play instruments well—activities belonging only to mechanics. One must know how to judge theoretically and rationally all the different harmonies, the accuracy of the consonances, and every kind of poetry, and understand all their properties, principles, and consequences. By this standard, true musicians are very rare.

**SECOND BOOK.**—The author begins his second book with a definition of philosophy, which, following Pythagoras, he makes consist in the perfect knowledge of things that properly and truly exist: things that are stable, independent of accidents, and always the same. Such are forms, magnitudes, qualities, relations or proportions, and other entities, insofar as speculation detaches them from all matter. Among these, arithmetic holds first place, together with the sciences that depend on it. He then observes that, according to Pythagoras, all quantity is either discrete or continuous, and that their properties are different and almost opposed. For numbers have their principle in what can be conceived as smallest—that is, in unity, which by its nature is indivisible—and they find no limit in their progression: however large a number may be, it can always be increased to infinity. Solid bodies, by contrast, whatever extent they may have at their beginning and throughout their existence, once divided, multiply so greatly through the diminution of the whole that their parts, even when apparently invisible, remain divisible to infinity.

He then shows that mathematics is rightly divided into four parts, since a thing may be considered either as immobile or mobile, or as absolute and independent or relative and dependent. The first consideration [Col. 1549D] belongs to geometry, the second to astronomy, the third to arithmetic, and the fourth to music.

He next recapitulates everything he said in the second book of his Arithmetic concerning proportions and relative numbers, and rejects Ptolemy’s opinion, according to which the third species of relative numbers entered into the composition of harmonies, from which it followed that the consonance of the octave with the fourth was valid. Boethius destroys this view by demonstrations founded on the proportion of numbers, and by the same means overturns the system of Aristoxenus, who divided the tone into two equal parts (145) and assigned six whole tones to the octave. The author supplies tables that are highly curious and demonstrative, which may satisfy those who wish to exercise themselves in this science. They will not find much difficulty [Col. 1550A] once they have thoroughly mastered the principles established in the two books of the Arithmetic. (144)

**THIRD BOOK.**—In the third book he continues to destroy the system of Aristoxenus, who, making the ear alone the judge of consonances, assigned six whole tones to the octave. He opposes it with new demonstrations founded, like the preceding ones, on the proportion of numbers, which is an infallible science quite different from mechanics.
