Mechanics is subject to error because it relies only on the senses, whereas the science of numbers relies on reason, which is independent of accidents. Such accidents often produce contrary effects in voices and instruments as well as in the sense of hearing. This leads the author to prefer above all others the view of the Pythagorean Philolaus concerning the division of the tone. Philolaus makes it consist of two minor semitones and one common semitone, or of a minor semitone and a major semitone, which he calls the apotome (146). He then divides the minor semitone into two diaschismata, and the comma into two schismata; and the apotome [Col. 1550B], or major semitone, into a minor semitone and a comma, or into two diaschismata and two schismata. It follows that the exact half of a tone contains a minor semitone and a schisma.

But Boethius does not accept this exact division of the tone in consonances. Thus he assigns to the fourth two whole tones and a minor semitone; to the fifth, three tones and a minor semitone; and to the octave, five tones and two minor semitones. Consequently, the octave falls short of containing six whole tones by one comma. He also supplies tables by which he demonstrates his claims, showing through the proportion of numbers that the minor semitone, or diesis, exceeds three commas and is less than four; that the apotome, or major semitone, exceeds four commas and is less than five; and that the whole tone contains more than eight commas but not nine.

**FOURTH BOOK.**—In his fourth book Boethius gives several tables confirming what he [Col. 1550C] stated in the preceding book, and represents by figures the method (147) used by the ancient Greeks to mark the different consonances and various kinds of harmony. He also sets out all the different stringed instruments, together with the mixture of minor and major tones and semitones entering into the composition of the diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic genera. He then divides tones into mobile and stable tones—that is, those that always remain within the same kind of symphony and those that pass from one genus to another.

After this he explains two tables containing all the modes by which the ancient Greeks distinguished their songs, just as we distinguish ours by the various dominants and finals. He names seven: Hypodorian, Hypophrygian, Hypolydian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, and Inquolydian, all modes named after the places where they were most popular. In the tables he adds an eighth, which he calls Hypermyxolydian. He [Col. 1550D] concludes his fourth book by teaching how to make a monochord, by means of which one may, insofar as this can be done through the senses, judge the accuracy of harmonies.

(148) **FIFTH BOOK.**—He begins his fifth book with a definition of harmony, and again proves, through comparisons drawn from geometry, that the senses alone are not competent or infallible judges of the accuracy of harmonies. Reason must be joined to them, and reason employs demonstrations drawn from the nature and different proportions of numbers.

He then reports the differing opinions of various authors. Some, such as Aristoxenus, maintained that consonances should be judged solely by the sense of hearing and by mechanics, without any relation to reasoning. Others, such as the Pythagoreans, assigned almost all authority in judgment to reason and almost none [Col. 1551A] to hearing and mechanics. Ptolemy held that, after the ear had provisionally judged consonances, reason should have the right to deliver a definitive judgment, and that it belonged to reason to correct or perfect whatever might be defective in the discernment of hearing and mechanics. This last opinion is Boethius’s.

He also discusses the differing opinions of the same authors concerning (149) the nature of sound. Some, such as the Pythagoreans, made it consist in quantity; others, such as Aristoxenus, in quality. He then gives tables showing Ptolemy’s view concerning the difference between tones, and reports the arguments he used to prove that the harmony of the fourth with the octave was a valid consonance, and that the third species of relative numbers therefore had to be admitted for the proportion of harmonies. Boethius had already opposed this in advance in the preceding books through his demonstrations.

He also describes Aristoxenus’s various tetrachords, which [Col. 1551B] show how he organized the tone and which consonances he included in the enharmonic, chromatic, and diatonic genera. He gives this author’s arguments by which he maintained, as many musicians still do, that the octave contained six whole tones—arguments that Boethius again combats as he had done earlier, without considering the view of Archytas, who confused proportions that ought to be distinguished in the various kinds of harmony.

(150) **ON GEOMETRY.**

We shall not dwell at length on these two books, since one is merely a faithful Latin translation of the books Euclid wrote in Greek concerning geometry. Boethius limits himself to clarifying certain passages that seemed obscure and confused to him. Toward the end he gives definitions of right, obtuse, and acute angles [Col. 1551C], and of the various kinds of signs. He then divides numbers into digital, articulate, composite, non-composite, multiplicative, and divisive numbers, and shows that in the table of Pythagoras one finds the proportions of the five species of relative numbers discussed in his first book of the Arithmetic. He then details all the measures used by the ancients, from the greatest to the smallest, and provides a table of them.

In the other work, which he himself composed on geometry, after giving its definition he proves by several arguments that it is useful to those who apply themselves to mechanics, particularly (151) architects and surveyors, and even physicians and philosophers. He adds that no natural science develops the mind more or raises it more greatly toward knowledge of the Creator, because geometry, supported by the principles of arithmetic, daily reveals something new [Col. 1552A] about the wonders that God has enclosed in the construction of this entire visible structure.

Boethius next reports what gave rise to the origin of geometry. Some, he says, attribute its origin to the inundations of the Nile; others, such as Varro, to the love of peace. For as human beings multiplied more and more, they resolved to divide the lands in order to remove every cause of dispute; this is no minor concern of geometry. They also divided the year into twelve months according to the same principles: *Menses a mensura quia metiuntur annum*—“Months are so called from measurement, because they measure the year.”

This treatise shows how highly geometry was once esteemed, since, according to Boethius, emperors and the most learned men considered it almost a duty to apply themselves to it. On this subject he reports (152) a letter of Julius Caesar, in which we see that this great conqueror paid particular attention to ensuring that everything throughout the empire was regulated geometrically—whether concerning possessions and their boundaries, public and private buildings, the fortifications of cities, or the great roads.

Boethius then reports the various matters that may become subjects of dispute and that fall within the province of surveyors, who in former times were people of great distinction. On this subject he reports the decree of the famous jurist Cassius Longinus, by which it was ordered that, when waters gradually wore away part of someone’s land through their ordinary course, the owner would bear the loss, because he ought to have protected and fortified his estate—even though the loss he suffered might benefit his [Col. 1552B] neighbor. But if an extraordinary and unforeseen flood caused the river to change its bed and form an island, then the owner of the estate damaged by the river would have the right to take, as compensation for his loss, as much (153) land as the river occupied through the new course it had taken across his estate.

The author then observes what qualities a surveyor must possess; gives the names of the ancient and most celebrated surveyors; names the emperors under whose authority the ancient divisions were made; and describes the various kinds of boundary markers placed to distinguish provinces, highways, and private possessions. He enters into detail concerning the knowledge necessary to become a perfect geometer, and ends his treatise with a dialogical recapitulation of everything he has said before. He also answers an objection he raises himself concerning Euclid’s book: namely, whether Euclid was truly [Col. 1552C] its author. He says that several learned men believed that Euclid had merely been its compiler, having collected it from various authors.

Nothing better reveals the vast extent of Boethius’s intellect than his mathematical treatises. They were admired by the most learned men of earlier centuries, and there can be no doubt that those who brought this science in our (154) own age to the perfection it has now attained drew all their principles from these sources.

**CONTINUATION OF BOETHIUS’S WORKS.**

Before producing these works, so important and useful to religion and the arts, whose contents have just been analyzed, Boethius had composed two dialogues on Porphyry’s *Introduction to Philosophy*. Here is the occasion for them.

After returning from Athens, he spent part of the winter at a country house he possessed in the mountains of ancient Tuscany [Note: [Col. 1551D] *In montibus Aureliae.* The ancients called *Aurelia* that region of Italy extending toward the Apennines along the Mediterranean coast, from the Aurelian Way, on leaving Rome, to the Maritime Alps [Col. 1552D]; the road leading there from Provence is still called *lou Camin Aurelian*. Lexicon Ferr.; Baud’s Dictionary.]. This region now forms part of the Papal States. [Col. 1552D] One night a south wind arose with such violence that it was impossible for him to sleep. He then recalled to mind the maxims that the ancient philosophers had left to posterity in order to enlighten the human mind and dispel the darkness in which it is (155) enveloped.

When day came, fatigue obliged him to lie down on his bed. A young friend named Fabius, whom he had brought with him, came to ask him how he ought to conduct himself in order to cultivate his mind and preserve himself from error. Since they were alone—the bad weather having prevented the numerous visitors who were always present at Boethius’s house from coming that day—[Col. 1553A] Fabius presented him with a translation that Victorinus had made from Greek into Latin of Porphyry’s *Introduction* to Aristotle’s *Categories*, and asked him to explain it.

Victorinus was a famous orator from Africa who, after teaching rhetoric for a long time at Rome, deserved to have a statue erected to him in the Forum of Trajan. Some time later, in his old age, he was converted to the faith of Jesus Christ through the exhortations of the holy priest Simplician, who succeeded Saint Ambrose. It is this Victorinus’s conversion and baptism that Saint Augustine describes so vividly and movingly (156) in the fifth chapter of the eighth book of his *Confessions*.

Victorinus had therefore made a translation of Porphyry’s *Introduction*, now known in the schools under the name of the *Isagoge*, or *Introduction to the Philosophy of Aristotle*. For Porphyry’s sole purpose in this treatise had been to explain the five universals—that is, genus, species, difference, proper accident, and common accident [Col. 1553B]—the knowledge of which is absolutely necessary for properly understanding Aristotle’s *Categories*, which form the first part of his philosophy.

Boethius, always ready to communicate the gifts he had received from God, willingly went through Porphyry’s translation with Fabius and, in two conversations that have survived under the name of *Dialogues*, explained all its difficulties to him. But having observed that Victorinus’s translation was not faithful—for Victorinus, accustomed to speaking as an orator, had given free rein to his style and paid little attention to Porphyry’s expressions—he resolved to make a new and more faithful translation. To it he added an excellent commentary divided into five books, which we still possess in its entirety.

(157) He next explained Aristotle’s *Categories* and composed four books on *Interpretation*, that is, on words that signify something by themselves—for example, “man,” “I run,” “I [Col. 1553C] read,” and so forth. He added two kinds of commentary. One he calls the commentary of the first edition, because in it he aims only to instruct beginners. It is very concise and does little more than give the literal meaning of Aristotle’s text. The other belongs to the second edition. It is much fuller, and explains the difficulties in a manner suited to more advanced students.

After these works, he translated Aristotle’s prior and posterior *Analytics* into Latin, in order to teach how to make a correct definition, a sound division, a formal syllogism, and reduce a proposition to its first principles. He did not comment on them; instead, he produced an excellent work in which he treats at length of the categorical and hypothetical syllogism, definition, and division. This work is divided into seven books.

The first is merely an introduction in which he gives the elementary principles of the art of reasoning well. It may be regarded as [Col. 1553D] (158) the first compendium of logic ever to appear in the world; and those that masters of philosophy produced afterward, when compared with it, are only imperfect copies of a very perfect original. The next two treat of the categorical syllogism; the fourth [Note: [Col. 1553D] These two treatises are dedicated to Symmachus.] and fifth explain the hypothetical syllogism; the sixth treats of division, and the seventh of definition.

He then translated Aristotle’s eight books of the *Topics*, that is, probable arguments drawn from various circumstances of a case, as well as his two books of *Sophistical Refutations*, that is, deceptive arguments. His translation contains no commentary.

Cicero had also written on the *Topics* and, with his natural eloquence, had explained how to construct probable arguments concerning every kind of subject. Boethius commented on Cicero’s *Topics* and brought all their contents into full light. This work was divided into seven books; the seventh is lost, together with part of the sixth, so that only four or five pages of Cicero’s text (159) remain without commentary. But we possess four books that he composed on *Topical Differences*, in which he shows the difference between Aristotle’s *Topics* and Cicero’s; the sources from which a philosopher should draw his probable arguments; and those from which an orator may draw his.

We also possess a short treatise by Boethius, *On the One and Unity*, in which he compares unity with matter and form, insofar as each thing is one through unity, just as white is white through whiteness. It appears that he intends to treat only of the transcendent unity common to all beings; nevertheless, he also says something about numerical and quantitative unity.

Trithemius, in his catalogue of [Col. 1554B] Boethius’s works, mentions a collection of several letters written to different people, which no longer exists. In addition to these works, which have survived the ravages of time and come down to us, Boethius had composed several others, both in verse and prose, which are lost, or at least have not yet been recovered (Murm. in *vit. Boet.*). We do not know precisely what subjects they treated. Nevertheless (160), it appears to us from the works that remain of this great man that he had produced a complete reconciliation of Aristotle’s philosophy with Plato’s; commentaries on Aristotle’s *Physics* and *Ethics*; and a Latin translation of Plato’s dialogues (Murm. pref. in *vit. Boet.*).

Baronius (*ad ann. 510*, p. 601) speaks of a book of commentaries on the *Enunciation* composed by Boethius—*in Commentariis de Enuntiatione*—and speaks as though he had seen it. Yet no treatise by Boethius bearing this title currently [Col. 1554C] exists. Perhaps Baronius confused it with his *Introduction*.

He also attributes to Boethius the book *On the Discipline of Scholars*, as do several other writers. It is indeed found among his works, even in the latest, most complete, and most accurate edition of all. But it would be an insult to Boethius to attribute such a poor work to him. It is enough to read it to recognize that it is neither in his style nor even from his period. The title alone can prove this. The word *scholaris*, which the author uses for young people who study, is new and considerably later than Boethius’s age (161). And although the Greeks called the halls where philosophers gave their lectures *scholarioi* (Σχολάριοι), there is no evidence that they ever called those who came to hear them *scholares*. They used this word to designate the soldiers of the emperor’s guard. It is in this sense that it is found in the Theodosian Code, in Sulpicius Severus, and in Procopius (see Ducange’s Glossary [Col. 1554D], under *SCHOLARIS*).

Moreover, the author of this treatise mentions the University of Paris, which was founded only several centuries after Boethius. He says that he had come to Paris to enjoy its air, and calls it the city of Julius Caesar, as though Julius Caesar had founded it. It would be a waste of time to continue proving that such a wretched work cannot be the product of a mind as excellent and sound as Boethius’s.

Father Labbe, and after him Moréri, attribute it to Denis the Carthusian, who lived toward the end of the fifteenth century. But I believe that they too were mistaken and confused it with another treatise entitled *On the Doctrine of Scholars*, which Denis the Carthusian himself acknowledges as his work in (162) the catalogue he left of his writings.

[Col. 1555A] Father Cossin (*apud Papebroc. ad 27 Maii*, p. 706) agrees that only a madman could have composed the book *On the Discipline of Scholars*. This certainly does not describe Denis the Carthusian, who was a very wise and enlightened man.

It is more likely that the work was produced by a professor of law at the University of Douai named Boethius Epo. The careless style, commonplace thoughts, and low expressions found in it could well be the work of Epo, who was born in Frisia and, by his profession, would often have been exposed to insults from his pupils. To make the instructions he gave them more respectable, he may have authorized his own name with that of Boethius, the Roman senator, and pretended that he was imprisoned by order of Theodoric and suffered greatly at the hands of the Goths.

This treatise began to appear among Boethius’s works only in the edition published at Basel in 1546, precisely the period in which Boethius Epo was living. Those who [Col. 1555B] undertook that edition, having carefully searched for all Boethius’s works and found this treatise, may have been (165) mistaken and presented it to us, without examining it, as a genuine work of Boethius the Roman senator.

What led me to assign this work to the sixteenth century is that it mentions the famous Franco, a man of intelligence and merit who lived at that time and had the misfortune to be hanged. The author says that he hanged himself out of despair and overwhelming grief at the disobedience and insolence of his pupils. The common opinion, however, is that Franco was hanged at Rome by judicial authority for publishing highly biting satires against certain princes of Italy.

This is all that we have been able to discover concerning Boethius’s works. We did not think we ought to deprive the public of what has survived. They are monuments of antiquity too precious not to be carefully preserved; moreover, they contribute greatly [Col. 1555C] to showing the breadth of his mind and his depth in every kind of science.

If Saint Augustine surpassed him in matters of religion, one may say that Boethius surpassed Saint Augustine by much in all (164) other matters. One could fill a volume with the praises bestowed upon him throughout the various centuries for his piety and learning. Even Theodoric, who unjustly put him to death, had often praised him during his lifetime and continued to praise him after his death. Theodoric himself died, compelled by a hidden virtue, while rendering the justice owed to Boethius’s virtue and ability.

Cassiodorus raised him above the greatest men of his age in several of his letters. [Col. 1556A] Paul the Deacon, Procopius, Marius, Anastasius the Librarian, Adon, Aimoin [Note: [Col. 1555C] “How eloquent he was in secular letters and how Catholic he was is demonstrated by his books . . . His book on the consubstantiality of the Holy Trinity clearly shows how outstanding he would have been, had he been permitted, in his time, as a cultivator of the holy Church.” Aimoin, *De Gestis Francorum*, I, II, chap. 1. [Col. 1556C]], Baptista of Mantua, Politianus [Note: [Col. 1556C] “Boethius, a most serious and most holy man, and the most skilled and outstanding in all the sciences, a seeker after and discoverer of truth.” Angelus Politianus.], Platina, Volaterranus, Palmerius, Sabellicus, Hermolaus Barbarus, Crescius, Valla, Trithemius, Giraldus, Baronius, Bellarmine, and many other ancient and modern writers have all praised him and made (165) highly honorable mention of him in their chronicles and writings.

Angelus Politianus (*Miscellanea*, chap. 1) gathers together all the praises that the ancients bestowed upon him in the highly glorious testimonies given him by Saint Thomas Aquinas and Albert the Great.

Even the later philosophers, by far the most discerning of all, held him in such high esteem that he deserved to have as his interpreters Thomas Aquinas, the divine man, and that great teacher of Thomas—good heavens, what men!

Sabellicus says that his writings are so polished and elegant that he is entitled to dispute first place with all the ancients: “In all respects so chaste and elegant that he can compete with any of the great men of old.”

[Col. 1556B] Adon (in his *Chronicle*) asserts that Theodoric had him put to death out of hatred for the Catholic faith: “Theodoric put to death Symmachus and Boethius, men of consular rank, for the sake of the Catholic faith.”

Giraldus says that Boethius was placed among the martyrs by most historians: “Boethius Severinus, a Roman patrician and former consul, who is entered by most of our historians in the catalogue of martyrs.”

But Trithemius gives him a complete eulogy in a few words—there is not a word in it that does not tell. “Boethius Manlius Severinus,” he says, “ordinary consul, Roman philosopher, excellent orator and poet, learned in divine and human letters, the most learned man of his age, was the son-in-law of the patrician Symmachus. He knew Greek and Latin perfectly. He translated several volumes of Aristotle and of other philosophers from Greek into Latin. He possessed a lively, subtle, and highly elevated mind, which grasped the most difficult matters with admirable ease. He is thoroughly Catholic [Col. 1556C] in his expressions and yields nothing to Cicero in eloquence. He was bound by close friendship to Saint Benedict, whom he frequently visited in his solitude and at whose table he ate, accompanied by another senator named Tertullus, the father of the monk Placidius. He composed several excellent works. I have found the following, whose catalogue is here given . . . But it is said that he composed several others, which have not come to my knowledge. He died in the same year as Symmachus and Pope John—that is, eight or nine months earlier—and was slaughtered in prison by order of King Theodoric. It is said that he was placed among the saints under the name Severinus” (Johannes Trithemius, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 238 ff., Wechel edition, 1601).

# Dissertation on the Year of Boethius’s Death

[Col. 1555]

[Col. 1555C] (167) There are almost as many different opinions concerning the year of Boethius’s death as there are writers who have discussed it. Bellarmine maintains that he died in 521; M. Fleury and M. Dupin, in 524; Baronius, in 526; and M. Baillet, in 524 or 525. Yet nothing in the historical record seems more clearly marked. To establish it, one must begin from a date on which all these authors agree, and I do not believe that one can find a more secure one than the election and death of Pope John I. They all agree that he succeeded Pope Hormisdas in August of the year 523 and that he died in May of the year [Col. 1556C] (168) 526, so that he occupied the Holy See for only about two years and nine months. M. Fleury agrees on this in his *Ecclesiastical History*, M. Dupin in his *New Library*, M. Baillet in his *Lives of the Saints* under 27 May, and Baronius in the seventh volume of his *Annals*. They also all agree that Boethius died during the pontificate of this pope.

Bellarmine was therefore plainly mistaken when he said that Boethius died in 521, since Pope John was not elected until 523. Moreover, the *Fasti of the Church* testify that Boethius died on 23 October, [Col. 1557A] and all the authors of his time, as well as those who wrote shortly afterward, expressly say that Theodoric put him to death after Pope John’s departure for Constantinople. Bellarmine therefore had no grounds for saying that he died in 521.

It remains only to examine the opinion of M. Fleury and M. Dupin, who agree with each other, and that of Baronius and M. Baillet. We may use their own writings to bring the truth of this matter to light.

“While the pope”—M. Fleury is speaking of Pope John—“was at [169] Constantinople, King Theodoric had the two most illustrious senators, Symmachus and Boethius, his son-in-law, imprisoned. Both had been consuls. They were accused of a crime against the state, that is, of wishing to uphold the dignity of the senate against Theodoric’s encroachments. Besides, Boethius was extremely zealous for the Catholic religion, which he defended in several writings, two of which he sent to Pope John, then a deacon of the Roman Church” (M. Fleury, vol. VII, p. 285).

M. Dupin (ibid., p. 89) expresses himself in much the same way. Their opinion is supported by the testimony of Anastasius the Librarian, by that of Baronius, and by that of the author of the *Miscellaneous History*, from whom this learned cardinal cites extracts. They likewise all agree that Boethius was arrested while Pope John was in Constantinople. Now Pope John did not arrive in Constantinople until March of the year 525, as M. Fleury expressly assures us in the seventh volume of his *History* (p. 284). How, then, can he afterward say that Boethius died in 524? The contradiction is manifest, and it is clear that M. Fleury paid no attention to it. Add to [170] this that a considerable time elapsed between the moment when Boethius was arrested by Theodoric’s order and condemned to exile by the sentence of the senate and the day on which Theodoric had him put to death. He was held prisoner at Pavia for several months; in his prison he composed his treatise on the Trinity and began his books of the *Consolation of Philosophy*; from there he was transferred to Calvance, where he had time to complete them. This gives reason to believe that he was arrested at the beginning of the year 525, shortly after Pope John’s departure for Constantinople, and that Theodoric had him put to death only much later. I do not believe that M. Fleury or M. Dupin can oppose anything to so evident a demonstration.

Baronius and those who have adopted his opinion and assign the year 526 have been no more successful. For he admits in the seventh volume of his *Annals* that Boethius was arrested and imprisoned at the beginning of the year 525, when news reached Rome of the extraordinary honors that the emperor Justin was showing the pope; and afterward he adds [171] that Theodoric had him put to death on 23 October of the year 526. Consequently, he must maintain that Boethius spent a year and eight months in prison. Elsewhere, however, he says that only ninety-eight days elapsed between the death of Pope John and that of Theodoric, supporting his assertion with the testimony of Anastasius the Librarian. No one contradicts Anastasius on this point, and his calculation is correct to within two days.

According to Baronius, then, since Pope John died on 27 May 526, Theodoric must have died on 2 September of the same year. The calculation is correct, and Baronius acknowledges it. Here are his words: “As for the day of Theodoric’s death, it is found to have been 2 September, if we believe Anastasius himself, who records that he died ninety-eight days after the death of Pope John, which we have said occurred on 27 May.”

But if Theodoric died three months and six days after 27 May—that is, on 2 September—how could he have had Boethius put to death on the following 23 October, as Baronius claims? To reconcile him with himself, it would be necessary not only to change the day [Col. 1558A] but even the month of Boethius’s death and advance it by about five months, as Papebroch did when he fixed it on 27 May, the day before the death of Symmachus, whom Theodoric had beheaded shortly before he himself died.

But all the historians of Italy would contradict him, for they unanimously place it, together with the martyrologies, in October. His feast is celebrated on the twenty-third of that month at Pavia, with great solemnity, in the church of Saint Peter, where his ashes rest. It was formerly celebrated on the same day in the church of Milan under the name of Saint Severinus, martyr, before the calendar was reformed by Saint Charles Borromeo in 1585. Symmachus’s feast is celebrated on 28 May at Ravenna, where he was buried, and it is believed that this was also the day of his death.

It is astonishing that so enlightened a man could, within fewer than three or four pages, say things so contradictory to one another. For on page 112 of his seventh [Col. 1558B] volume, he seems to wish to say that Boethius died at the same time as Symmachus. Here are his words: “Since Anastasius has recorded that ninety-eight days elapsed between the death [173] of Pope John and the pitiable death of King Theodoric . . . it must be related what that wicked and savage barbarian cruelly did against the noble and pious patricians Boethius and Symmachus during that interval.”

Two pages later he admits that Boethius was executed first, that a considerable interval separated his death from that of Symmachus, and that during his imprisonment he composed several works: “That Boethius’s death, like his imprisonment, preceded [Symmachus’s], we can understand from what has been said; for while Boethius was in prison, he wrote the book on the Trinity, and so forth.”

Then he says that Theodoric died on 2 September and that he died while the memory of Symmachus’s murder was still very recent: “Since the memory of the murdered consul Symmachus was still fresh.” This expression [Col. 1558C] suggests that Symmachus had been arrested and executed shortly before Theodoric’s death. Since, according to Baronius and by the agreement of all who wrote the history of that period, Symmachus was not arrested until after Boethius’s death, and since, according to Baronius, Boethius himself was not arrested until after Pope John’s return to Ravenna, it would follow that Boethius spent only a short time in prison—contrary to what Baronius himself said and to what Procopius and Anastasius wrote—and that Boethius could, in so brief a period, have composed his admirable books on the Trinity and the *Consolation of Philosophy*, as well as several others that Baronius attributes to him. Who does not see the impossibility of these claims?

We must therefore adhere to what we have said and fix Boethius’s death in October of the year 525 as its true date. Indeed, since Pope John arrived in Constantinople at the beginning of Lent that year, and since Theodoric learned shortly afterward what was taking place there between the emperor [Col. 1558D] and his ambassadors, he no longer doubted that they were in league with him, and that Justin had secret dealings with the entire senate. He then resolved to put to death the principal members of that illustrious body and all those whom he believed to have particular connections with the Easterners.

Albinus and Boethius were arrested first. After spending several [175] months in the prison at Pavia, where Boethius composed his treatise on the Trinity and began his books of the *Consolation of Philosophy*, Theodoric had the sentence of death pronounced against him by the judge of Pavia. He was then transferred to the prison at Calvance, where he had time to complete them. There he was long pressed, on Theodoric’s behalf, to acknowledge the letters attributed to him and to admit the acts of which he was accused. But when they could not compel him to do so, Theodoric had him executed, as has been related.

[Col. 1559A] When Pope John and the other ambassadors returned from Constantinople at the end of that year, Theodoric had them arrested at Ravenna and kept them in prison, where they perished from hunger and misery and from other tortures. Pope John died on 27 May, not on the eighteenth, as Anastasius is made to say; his body was carried to Rome and buried there on 1 June. This is expressly stated by a very ancient manuscript of Anastasius, against which the printed editions should be corrected. It is also on that day, 2 May [sic], that his feast is celebrated at Rome, as Walin rightly observes in his notes (p. 97) on Boethius’s minor works.

(176) Symmachus had also been arrested a few days earlier, and on the day after Pope John’s death he was executed at Ravenna, where his feast is celebrated on that day. As for Theodoric, he died in the tragic manner we have related, on 2 September according to Anastasius’s calculation, or, more probably, on 30 August. For although Anastasius expressly says [Col. 1560A] that ninety-eight days elapsed between the death of Pope John and that of Theodoric, there is considerable reason to think that Anastasius miscalculated by two days. M. de Valois’s anonymous author, believed to have been a writer of the period—or at least of the same century, and consequently more reliable in what he reports than Anastasius, who lived several centuries later—states positively that Theodoric died on a Sunday. In 526, 2 September was not a Sunday but a Wednesday. Therefore, according to this author, Theodoric died on 30 August, which fell on a Sunday that year; and the same anonymous writer expressly confirms this elsewhere.

But Anastasius’s error is not consequential, since it amounts only to two [177] days. It changes neither the year nor the month of Boethius’s death, and in no way weakens the evidence we have presented for fixing the date of his death on 23 October 525, or the reasons by which we have opposed the contrary opinions.

# Theological Dissertation on These Words of Gondebaud, King of Burgundy, to Saint Avitus, Bishop of Vienne: “Give me the anointing with chrism privately.”

[Col. 1559]

(178) **First Part**

[Col. 1559B]

We observed in the first book of the *History of Boethius* that King Gondebaud, finally convinced of the truth of the Catholic faith, detested in his heart the impiety of Arius and had insistently asked Saint Avitus to reconcile him secretly to the Church by anointing him with chrism. He did not wish this to be done publicly because he feared the Arian bishops [179] and feared that his conversion might provide his subjects with a pretext for revolt. “Having confessed Christ the Son of God and the Holy Spirit to be equal to the Father, he secretly requested to be anointed,” says Saint Gregory of Tours (*History of the Franks*, II.34).

These words have occasioned several disputes among theologians concerning their meaning. Some have maintained that Gondebaud was asking for baptism under the name of chrism, because in that sacrament the crown of the baptized person’s head is anointed with chrism. Others have believed [Col. 1559C] that it was the sacrament of confirmation, which the ancients designated by this name because, they say, they regarded chrism as the matter and the most essential part of that sacrament. These two opinions still divide theologians today. But Gondebaud was asking for neither one nor the other; it will be shown that he was asking only for a ceremony formerly established in the Church for the reconciliation of heretics.

The theologians who maintain that Gondebaud was asking for baptism in the Catholic Church base their opinion on the invalidity of the Arians’ baptism. This prince, they say, was abjuring a heresy that was erroneous at its foundation; he was abandoning a sect in which only a false baptism was administered and which consequently could produce only false Christians. He was therefore right to ask for the baptism of the Catholic Church, as the sole gate by which one can enter it. “One must be born of water and the Spirit,” says Jesus Christ, “in order to enter the kingdom of God.” Of [Col. 1559D] what use could confirmation be to a man who was not a Christian? The growth and perfection of the spiritual creature, which is the particular effect of this sacrament, necessarily presuppose the existence and production of that creature within the order of grace. It is through baptism alone that it receives this new being, which makes us children of God and gives us a share in the adoption of Jesus Christ. Gondebaud could not have been ignorant of these first [Col. 1560B] elements of Christianity. The Arians’ principles did not differ from ours concerning the necessity of this sacrament. Even if he had been ignorant of them, there can be no doubt that Saint Avitus instructed him in the conversations he had with him. There is therefore no reason to doubt, these theologians continue, that at the moment of his conversion, when grace had dispelled the darkness of error and he began to see the light of truth, he could have asked for anything other than the baptism of the Catholic Church.

But all this presupposes the invalidity of the Arians’ baptism, and they claim to prove it both by authority and by reason. As for authority, without relying on the famous dispute that arose in Saint Cyprian’s time between the bishops of Asia and Africa and Pope Stephen concerning the validity of heretics’ baptism in general, they cite the opinions of several holy doctors, particularly Saint Basil and Saint Athanasius. Since the decision of that pope, these doctors maintained that the baptism of the Arians was invalid, as was that of all other heretics who held erroneous opinions concerning the faith of the mystery of the Holy Trinity, even though, in administering this sacrament, they used the matter and form customary in the Catholic Church.

Indeed, Saint Basil says expressly, speaking of the baptism of the Pepucians [182], a particular sect of the Priscillianists, that it was entirely worthless because, he says, the ancients had always believed that only baptism which deviated in no respect from the faith should be admitted: “As for the baptism of the Pepucians, it seems to me to have no validity. For the ancients judged that baptism should be accepted which deviates in nothing from the faith” (Basil, *Letter to Amphilochius*, canon 1).

Elsewhere he declares that in the Church of Alexandria the Manichaeans, Novatians, and other heretics whom he names were baptized anew when they sought admission to Catholic communion: “The Encratites and the Saccophori are subject to the same rule as the Novatians, because a canon has been issued concerning them. And if [the reading is] different [*diversus*, sense uncertain], we nevertheless rebaptize them all on one and the same ground” (*Idem*, *Letter to Amphilochius*, canon 47).

And lest anyone should say that he assumed all these heretics failed to preserve, in administering baptism, the essential form, namely, the distinct invocation of the three persons of the Holy Trinity, here is what he adds (*ibid.*): “It is useless for you to tell us that you were baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, since you believe that the Father is the author of evil, as the Marcionites believe.”

Moreover, neither Saint Basil nor any Father of the Church ever accused the Novatians of failing to preserve the true form of this sacrament in the administration of baptism. Nevertheless, whenever a Novatian or any other heretic whose faith concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity was unorthodox asked to be received into the Catholic Church, he baptized them anew. Saint Basil therefore believed that baptism administered by these heretics—even in the form customary in the Catholic Church—was invalid and had to be repeated. For this reason he often calls the Arians pagans and unbelievers, as having had no share in Christian regeneration.

It is no less certain that this was also Saint Athanasius’s opinion, since he teaches on several occasions that the Arians’ baptism was vain and useless, merely a semblance of baptism, and [Col. 1561B] that the difference between their baptism and that of the Catholic Church was as great as the difference between the Creator and the creature. “Who, I ask, would not conclude that the baptism given by them was plainly vain and useless, since it is nothing but an appearance and an empty imitation? Just as the creature is something different from the Son, so what they consider baptism is something different from true baptism” (Athanasius, *Third Discourse against the Arians*).

But perhaps it will be said that these heretics corrupted the form prescribed by Jesus Christ in the administration of baptism and that this defect rendered it useless. Antiquity, however, agrees that the Arians made no change in its form during Saint Athanasius’s lifetime and that it was only long after his death that certain Arians thought of changing it in order to express, within the administration of baptism itself, their impious doctrine opposed to the consubstantiality of the Word.

Saint Athanasius acknowledges that in his time they used no other words [Col. 1561C] than those prescribed to us in the Gospel. But while recognizing that these words are holy because they were prescribed by Jesus Christ, he reproaches them for rendering the words useless in their mouths, just as the name of God is rendered useless in the mouths of those impious men who often cry, “Lord, Lord,” yet will be forever banished from the kingdom of heaven: “Although they pretend to name the Father and the Son, because they see these names in the Scriptures . . . even if they recite the Scriptures and utter the very names, they deceive and mock those who receive baptism from them. For it is not the one who simply says, ‘Lord,’ who bestows legitimate baptism, but the one who utters the name and possesses the right faith” (*Idem*, *ibid.*).

In Saint Athanasius’s view, it is not enough to pronounce the words that the Gospel gives us as the form of this sacrament. The person who pronounces them must also understand them in a Catholic sense, just as one who wishes to share in the kingdom of God must not content himself with saying merely with his lips, “Lord, Lord,” but must pronounce that adorable name with the love and reverence that charity forms in the heart.

Thus, continues this holy doctor, the Son of God did not simply say to his apostles, “Go and baptize”; rather, he commanded them first to instruct the peoples and, when they found them properly disposed through instruction and faith, to baptize them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: “So that from right teaching faith might arise, and with faith an integral initiation through baptism might be completed” (*Idem*, *ibid.*).

Saint Cyril of Jerusalem (*Preface to the Catechetical Lectures*) expresses himself no differently and states plainly that the baptism of heretics was not true baptism: “Only heretics are rebaptized, since their former baptism was not baptism.”

This opinion soon passed from the East into the West, and we see that the famous Optatus, bishop of Milevis in Africa (*Against Parmenianus*, I), exempts from the general rule of rebaptizing all heretics received into the Catholic Church only the schismatics, because, he says, all the sacraments are held in common by them and by us; and since they received them in the Catholic Church, they can confer them upon others.

In addition to the Fathers’ authorities, these theologians offer reasons that appear no less solid. Faith, they say, teaches us that there is only one baptism. But the baptism administered by the Arians was different from ours; therefore it could not be true baptism. It was certainly different from ours, since they rebaptized Catholics who joined their sect, as Saint Ambrose and Saint Augustine assure us (Ambrose, *Sermon on Basil*, not transmitted; Augustine, *On This Heresy*, 49). They would not have rebaptized them [187] if they had administered the same sacrament that is given in the Catholic Church.

[Col. 1562B] In the second place, they baptized only in the name of a false Trinity, since they regarded the Son of God as a creature. Finally, since there is only one God, one faith, and one Church, there is likewise only one baptism. Outside the Church there is only a false and corrupted faith, incapable of saving a person; consequently, outside that Church there can only be a false baptism, entirely useless for salvation. This led Saint Ambrose to say that the Arians destroyed the baptism of Jesus Christ: “Auxentius has dissolved Christ’s baptism” (Ambrose, as above).

Moreover, the Council of Trent, following several earlier councils, defined that it is not enough to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit if the minister who confers the baptism does not intend to do what the Catholic Church does. And can one say that the Arians had this intention? Did they not, on the contrary, make it clear that they had the opposite intention by [Col. 1562C] rebaptizing Christians who deserted the true faith?

Is it not acknowledged that the Church has [188] always rejected the baptism of the Sabellians because those heretics held erroneous opinions concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity (First Council of Constantinople, canon 7)? The Arians’ opinions were even more monstrous. It is therefore evident that the Church rejected their baptism, as it did that of the Sabellians.

“They shall be received,” says the First Council of Constantinople, speaking of the Sabellians, “when they ask to enter the Catholic Church, in the same manner as pagans are received. First, hands shall be laid upon them so that they may receive the name of Christians; then they shall be placed among the catechumens; they shall be exorcised by blowing three times upon their faces and into their ears; they shall be catechized; they shall be allowed for a long time to come to church to hear the word of God; and finally they shall be baptized.”

Yet what comparison is there between the Sabellians and the Arians? The former, while confusing the persons, nevertheless acknowledged that the Word was God, just as the Holy Spirit was; they merely refused to call them persons, so as not to be obliged to say that there were three Gods. The Arians denied the divinity of the Word [189] and consequently admitted neither Father nor Son. For, as Saint Athanasius very judiciously observes, he is not a father who does not produce a son of the same nature as himself, and he is not a son who is not consubstantial with his Father.

If this is true of all the Arians who lived in Saint Athanasius’s time and baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, what must be said of those who followed them and changed the form of this sacrament, substituting a new one in its place—one that was an explicit profession of their impiety, which the neophyte made by consenting to be baptized in the name of the greater Father and the lesser Son: “in the name of the greater Father and of the lesser Son”?

It was particularly toward the beginning of the sixth century that the Arians employed these sacrilegious words in the form of baptism, in order to distinguish themselves from the Catholics. Since this was the period in which Gondebaud, king of Burgundy, lived, he would have been baptized in the manner then practiced by the Arians. The baptism he received from them having been invalid, there is no doubt that, wishing to embrace the orthodox faith after all Saint Avitus’s instruction, he would have asked him for baptism, expressing it by the name of chrism when he made the request. He did so to indicate that he was asking for the baptism of the Catholic Church, distinct from that of the Arians by the ceremony of anointing the crown of the baptized person’s head with chrism, a practice not used among them.

These reasons are certainly very plausible, and I do not even see how the passages from the Fathers cited by these theologians to support their opinion can be explained by restricting them to those Arians who had corrupted the form of baptism. For when their authorities are compared with what precedes and follows, it becomes clear that these Fathers anticipated and refuted the explanation one might wish to give them, as though they had foreseen that in later centuries people might persuade themselves that this was the sense in which they had advanced their doctrine.

We must therefore indeed agree that these holy doctors believed the baptism of heretics whose error attacked [191] the mystery of the Holy Trinity to be invalid, and that they maintained this opinion until their deaths. But one cannot say that this was a culpable error in them, since the Church had not yet determined in a general council, as it did later, that the Arians’ baptism was valid. They followed the practice of their particular churches; these were remnants of the ancient dispute that Saint Cyprian had once had with Pope Saint Stephen concerning the repetition of heretical baptism.

All that can be said of Saint Athanasius, Saint Basil, Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, and the others who held the same opinion is that, given their piety, one may presume—as Saint Augustine said of Saint Cyprian—that they would have submitted to the Church’s decisions had they lived until the time when it assembled to decide this great question: “He too would undoubtedly have yielded to it, if by that time the truth of this question had been sifted and declared and established by a plenary council” (Augustine, Letter 48).

But since the entire Church recognized as early as the end of the fourth century, in canon 7 of the First Council of Constantinople, [192] that the baptism of the Arians, given in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, was valid; and since this same council distinguishes the heretics who must be rebaptized when they ask to be received into the Church from those from whom only a profession of faith is required; and since it places the Arians, Macedonians, Novatians, and Apollinarists among the latter, and the Eunomians, Montanists, and Sabellians among the former, I am astonished that Catholic theologians should still dare to call the validity of Arian baptism into question and, supposing it invalid, insist that Gondebaud asked Saint Avitus to baptize him a second time.

They may object that the canons of the First Council of Constantinople were not accepted in the West and were rejected by Saint Leo, Pope Gelasius, and Saint Gregory himself. But they may be answered that these canons are now included among those universally received by the Church; that this council was subsequently approved by the Council of Chalcedon; and that the Westerners did not reject the decisions concerning [193] the faith made by the Council of Constantinople.

If these popes and the bishops of the West [Col. 1564A] refused to accept the decisions concerning discipline, it was only with regard to the fifth canon, which assigned the patriarch of Constantinople first rank after the bishop of Rome, contrary to the regulations established by earlier councils.

It seems so certain that the West had accepted the Council of Constantinople’s decision concerning the validity of Arian baptism that Pope Siricius, the successor of Damasus, who had convened it, speaks of the matter as wholly decided and no longer open to doubt. This is how he explains himself (Siricius, *Letter to Himerius of Tarragona*, chapter 1) to a bishop who had consulted him on the matter:

“You inform me that several persons who were baptized by the Arians are eager to join the Catholic Church, and that some of our brothers wish to rebaptize them. I declare to you that this is not permitted, since the Apostle forbids it, as do the canons of the general council, authentic copies of which my predecessor sent to all the provinces. [Col. 1564B] We ourselves obey what was decreed in that assembly; and whenever an Arian or a Novatian asks to be received into the unity of the Catholic Church, we content ourselves with laying hands upon him and invoking the Holy Spirit over him—a practice observed throughout both the East and the West, ‘which the whole East and West likewise maintain.’ If you refuse to submit to this ordinance, I declare to you that we shall be compelled to excommunicate you in a council.”

Saint Gregory, who appeared most opposed to the bishop of Constantinople, offended by the violation he had committed against the ancient statutes in his fifth canon, out of complaisance toward the patriarch of that city, nevertheless accepted his regulations concerning the validity of the Arians’ baptism. He expressly told the bishops of Hibernia that all those who had been baptized in heresy in the name of the Holy Trinity were to be received into the Church by the imposition of [Col. 1564C] hands, or by a profession of faith, or by anointing with chrism (Gregory, Book IX, Letter 61, to Quirinus). And Saint Jerome (Dialogue against Lucifer) assures us that the whole of the West reconciled the Arians by the imposition of hands alone, without repeating their baptism.

(195) At the Council of Capua, held in 390 to settle the dispute between Flavian and Evagrius, Paulinus’s successor in the see of Antioch, the question of repeating baptism in the case of heretics was again debated, and the council prohibited it under very severe penalties, just as it prohibited reordination.

The Third Council of Carthage, assembled seven or eight years later, adopted this decision. “We have recalled,” it says, “what had already been decreed in the general Council of Capua: that it was not permitted either to rebaptize or to reordain” (Canon 48 in *The Code of the Councils of the African Church*, vol. II of the Councils, p. 1702). It is true that the canon names no particular heretic; but since Arianism was then at the height of its power, the [Col. 1564D] Fathers would never have failed to name the Arians expressly if there had been any exception to be made on their behalf. It is even very probable that they had no other heresies in view than Arianism, just as, in the century when their errors were most fashionable and virtually dominant, the terms “heretics” ordinarily meant only the Lutherans and the Calvinists.

(196) Some time afterward, Saint Augustine (*The Ninth Tome, On Baptism against the Donatists*), having again examined the question, stated precisely that baptism, insofar as it is a sacrament, is always valid, whoever administers it—heretic or Catholic—provided that it is given in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This baptism must not be repeated, because neither the faith nor the holiness of the minister contributes to the sacrament’s validity. Since it is not the minister but God alone who gives the [Col. 1565A] Holy Spirit and grants the remission of sins, it makes little difference who the minister is. If the person receiving baptism has faith and is properly disposed, he will receive not only the sacrament but also the sacrament’s effect, which is grace. Saint Thomas later used the same arguments to establish the same truth. Pope Innocent I gathered them all into his letter to Victricius, bishop of Rouen:

“You must receive all the Novatians, Montanists, and others by the imposition of hands alone, because they are baptized in the name of Jesus Christ—that is, with the baptism instituted by Jesus Christ—even though they (197) were baptized by heretics: *Quia quamvis ab haereticis, tamen in Christi nomine sunt baptizati*”—“For although [they were baptized] by heretics, nevertheless they were baptized in the name of Christ.”

Finally, the Council of Trent—which may be said to have adopted the spirit and understanding of the first Fathers of the Church and of the ancient councils—pronounces anathema against those who say that the baptism of heretics conferred in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1565B] is not true baptism (Council of Trent, session 7, canon 4). Since the Arians baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as the Second Council of Arles expressly declares, it cannot be denied that their baptism was valid. There is not even any evidence that they later changed the form of baptism. The formula that some theologians attribute to them—“in the name of the greater Father and in the name of the lesser Son”—is found in neither any Father nor any ancient ecclesiastical author. On the contrary, Theodoret, who lived only forty or fifty years after Saint Athanasius, expressly says (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 1) that Arius would have greatly wished to change the invocation of the Holy Trinity in the baptismal form, but that he did not dare openly to oppose the sacred text; instead, he retained the words of that invocation in baptism, although (198) he contradicted its meaning.

What may have led these theologians [Col. 1565C] to assert that the Arians had changed the form of baptism is that Saint Athanasius had said that they baptized in the name of the Creator and the creature. But it is a misunderstanding of this holy doctor to imagine that he meant that, when baptizing, the Arians pronounced these words: “I baptize you in the name of the Creator and the creature,” since he himself assures us in the same place that they used the words expressed in the Gospel, “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Because they understood the name “Son of God” to designate a creature, Saint Athanasius inferred that they baptized in the name of the creature, and that the names “Father” and “Son” were in their mouths only false names, a mask concealing their error, although they used no other baptismal form than the one customary in the Catholic Church:

“For they do not confer baptism in the Father and the Son, but in the Creator and the creature, the Maker and what was made, although, because they see the name of Father and Son in the Scriptures, [Col. 1565D] they pretend to pronounce it as well” (*Athanasius, Third Oration against the Arians*): *Non enim in Patre et Filio tribuunt baptisma, sed in Creatore et creatura, factore et factura, tametsi nomen Patris et Filii, quia illa in Scripturis vident, simulant se nominare.*

“But,” it may be said, “far from intending to do what the Catholic Church did, they had the opposite intention. That is why they rebaptized Catholics who embraced their error; consequently, their baptism was invalid, since, for baptism to be valid, one must intend to do what the Church does, as the Council of Trent declares.”

This is not sound reasoning, for the council does not say that one must intend to do what the Catholic Church does, but simply that one must intend to do what the Church does. The Arians had that intention: they wished to do what the true Church does, what Jesus Christ had instituted, and what the apostles had done, although, through an error that made them culpable, they believed themselves to be in the true Church and believed Catholics to be idolaters who worshiped three gods. That is why, through another error that made them no [Col. 1566A] more excusable, they rebaptized Catholics.

Thus Saint Augustine, when asked (200) what he thought of baptism received in the Church or in a society of heretics who believed themselves to be the true Church, replied that it was valid and must not be repeated, as the ancient canons prescribe:

“As has already been established by the statutes of our predecessors, I have no doubt that even those have baptism who, although they receive it deceitfully, nevertheless receive it in the Church, or where those in whose fellowship it is received believe the Church to be” (Augustine, Book VII, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 53): *Sicut jam praeteritis majorum statutis, non dubito etiam illos habere baptismum qui quamvis fallaciter accipiant, in Ecclesia tamen accipiunt, vel ubi putatur esse Ecclesia ab eis in quorum societate id accipitur.*

Saint Avitus, perfectly instructed in all these principles, could not have failed to make them known to Gundobad after the many conferences he had held with him. There is therefore no apparent reason why this prince should have asked him for a second baptism. Moreover, antiquity offers no trace of baptism’s ever having been designated by the symbol of chrism. Consequently, if Gundobad had asked Saint Avitus to baptize him again, he would have made the request in intelligible and customary terms, since one speaks in order to be understood.

Finally, Gregory of Tours, who has told us what took place between Saint Avitus and the king of Burgundy, [Col. 1566B], leaves us (201) no grounds for doubting either the validity of Arian baptism or the constant practice then followed by the Churches of Gaul of reconciling heretics by the imposition of hands and the anointing with holy chrism. For after reporting (*History of the Franks*, Book II, chapter 22) how Clovis, the royal family, and more than three thousand Franks in his retinue were regenerated by baptism on the same day, he expressly says that the king’s sister, named Lantilde, who had already received baptism in the Arian communion, was merely reconciled to the Catholic Church by anointing with chrism, after making her profession of faith:

“She confessed the Son equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit, and was anointed with chrism”: *Quae confessa aequalem Filium Patri et Spiritum sanctum, chrismata est.*

The anointing with chrism included the imposition of [Col. 1566C] hands, as confirmation does at present, although this was not expressly mentioned. It was never omitted, because it was the sign of the imposition of penance. “The Church used it in this way,” says Saint Augustine, so that no one would believe that the person presenting himself had been without sin: *Ne tanquam extra omnem culpam esse judicaretur* (Augustine, Book V, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 23).

(202) **SECOND PART**

**Refutation of the opinion of the theologians who maintain that the Arians were reconciled to the Catholic Church through the sacrament of confirmation**

It is no less certain that the sacrament of confirmation was not what Gundobad was asking Saint Avitus for, as some other theologians still maintain. In the first place, the Arians received [Col. 1566D] confirmation among the sacraments, just as did the whole Catholic Church. “Heretics,” says Saint Cyprian, “having been raised in the bosom of the Church, must be presumed to believe everything that we believe and to receive everything that we receive, except for those doctrines that the Fathers or ecclesiastical historians have identified as the cause of their separation.” Yet no Father or ecclesiastical historian is to be found who says that the Arians rejected the sacrament (203) of confirmation. I venture even to say that, before Luther and Calvin, no heretic had thought of doing so.

Theodoret observes that the Novatians did indeed neglect this sacrament and did not receive confirmation because their teacher Novatian had never received it. But he does not say that these schismatics denied confirmation to be a true sacrament instituted by Jesus Christ. Gundobad, although an Arian, was sixty years old when he asked Saint Avitus for confirmation; he had undoubtedly received the sacrament of confirmation at the hands of the bishops of his [Col. 1567A] sect. How, then, could he have asked for it a second time? Could he have been unaware of the constant practice of all the Churches, which was not to repeat this sacrament any more than ordination or baptism? How, then, after the Council of Trent pronounced anathema against those who would say that these three sacraments, which imprint an indelible character on the soul, can be repeated, can theologians maintain that Gundobad was asking for confirmation a second time?

“But,” they say, “the Council of Trent speaks only of confirmation received in the Catholic Church, not of confirmation received in heretical societies.” If that were so, then only baptism and ordination given and received in the Catholic Church could not be repeated, while these sacraments administered in a heretical society could always be repeated. For the council joins them to confirmation and makes a single decree concerning all three, based on the same reason: the character that [Col. 1567B] these three sacraments imprint on the soul. (204) If the Fathers and the ancient councils so strongly opposed the repetition of baptism—a sacrament necessary for human beings with the necessity of means for salvation—what would they not have said against repeating confirmation, whose necessity is not so absolute?

To support their opinion, they object that the Second Ecumenical Council orders that the Arians, Macedonians, and others, after abjuring their errors, be received into the Church by the anointing of the Holy Spirit and with chrism, with which they are to be anointed on the forehead, the eyes, the hands, the mouth, and the ears, while these words are pronounced: “This is the seal (205) of the Holy Spirit” (First Council of Constantinople, canon 7). The form and matter of the sacrament of confirmation are plainly found in this ceremony. Who, then, can doubt that it was administered to these heretics when they were reconciled to the Catholic Church, and that it was confirmation that Gundobad was asking Saint [Col. 1567C] Avitus to give him when he begged him for anointing with chrism?

The canon of this council is supported by many others and by several Fathers who say the same thing, such as Gennadius (*Gennadius, On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapter 52) and Saint Isidore of Seville (Isidore, Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 24). Canon 17 of the Second Council of Arles and canon 16 of the Council of Epaon explain the matter in the same way. The latter adds that the bishop, and no other minister, must perform this ceremony. Thus we have not only the matter and form but also the minister of the sacrament of confirmation.

The first answer is that these theologians assume as an established fact that anointing with chrism constitutes an essential part of the sacrament of confirmation and is its principal matter. Yet this is not the opinion of our most learned theologians. M. de Sainte-Beuve (*Treatise on the Sacrament of Confirmation*, articles 1 and 2, disputation 3), Father Sirmond, Father Morin, and several (206) others rightly maintain that the imposition of hands alone is, as it were, the essential matter of this sacrament, and that the anointing with chrism was added only long after the apostles and their first successors. (206) [Col. 1567D]

Indeed, not only did the apostles confirm and give the Holy Spirit by the imposition of hands alone, as may be seen in the Book of Acts, but the most ancient Fathers of the Church used no other term than “imposition of hands” to express the sacrament of confirmation. “After we have been baptized,” says Tertullian (*On Baptism*, chapter 8), “hands are imposed upon us, and through the blessing that calls upon and invites the Holy Spirit, we receive the Holy Spirit”: *dehinc manus imponitur, per benedictionem advocans et invitans Spiritum sanctum.*

“What did Peter and John do,” asks Saint Cyprian (Letter 73), “when, through their prayers and the imposition of their hands, they caused the Holy Spirit to descend upon these newly baptized Samaritans, except give them the perfection they lacked?” This is still done among us. The newly baptized are presented to the bishop; he imposes his hands upon them, and they receive the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1568A] In this way they are marked with the Lord’s (207) seal, and the work of their perfection is accomplished:

“Only that which was lacking was done by Peter and John,” and so forth: *Tantummodo quod deerat id a Petro et Joanne factum est, etc.*

The custom of the Church, says Saint Jerome (*Dialogue against the Luciferians*), is that in villages and small towns where the bishop does not ordinarily reside, deacons and priests baptize the catechumens, and afterward the bishop comes expressly to give them the Holy Spirit by the imposition of his hands: “so that the bishop may hasten to those who, in the smaller towns far away, have been baptized by priests and deacons, in order to impose his hand upon them for the invocation of the Holy Spirit”: *ut ad eos qui longe in minoribus urbibus, per presbyteros et diaconos baptizati sunt, episcopus ad invocationem Spiritus sancti manum impositurus excurrat.*

Saint Augustine, Saint Chrysostom, Saint Gregory, and almost all the Fathers use only the expression “imposition of hands” to signify the sacrament of confirmation. It would never end if we wished to report all their testimonies individually.

As for the form of this sacrament, [Col. 1568B] is it not known that the form now used, which bears considerable relation to the words cited from the seventh canon of the First Council of Constantinople, is very recent? I do not believe (208) that any trace of it can be found before Eugenius IV. At least it is certain that during the first six centuries of the Church a prayer was used that is reported in Saint Gregory’s Sacramentary; they did not say, as they do now:

“I mark you with the sign of the cross, and I confirm you with the chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”: *Signo te signo crucis, et confirmo te chrismate salutis, in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus sancti.*

If the bishop has always been the minister of the sacrament of confirmation, at least its ordinary minister, the reconciliation of heretics has likewise always been reserved to him. One does not enter a house without the consent of the head of the household, and one must approach the shepherd in order to enter [Col. 1568C] the sheepfold. At present heretics are not even reconciled by priests without a special commission from the bishops.

Finally, if the ceremony by which the Arians were formerly reconciled to the Church had been the sacrament of confirmation, that ceremony would have been uniform and constant everywhere. Yet it is certain that the Arians were not reconciled everywhere with anointing by chrism. In some Churches they were reconciled by the imposition of hands alone; in others, by a profession of faith and the abjuration of their errors; in some, by these two acts together; and in still others, by the anointing with chrism that was added to them. Nothing, therefore, is more false than what these theologians assert: that the First Council of Constantinople required the Arians to be reconciled to the Church through the sacrament of confirmation, and that the ceremony established by this council for their reconciliation was that sacrament.

[Col. 1568D] There can be no doubt about the diversity of the Churches’ practices concerning the reconciliation of heretics. Pope Siricius, in his letter to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, expressly says that the Novatians and other heretics are reconciled by the bishop’s imposition of hands, invoking the Holy Spirit upon them, as had been ordered by the synod. He is referring to the Council of Rimini, held under Pope Liberius in the year 359.

The First Council of Arles, held in 314, says that if a heretic presents himself to enter the Church, the priests must question him concerning (210) the creed. If he says that he believes in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, hands are to be imposed upon him in order to give him the Holy Spirit. But if he does not confess the Holy Trinity, he must first be baptized.

The Second Council of Arles, held in 350, says that the [Col. 1569A] Arians who baptize in the name of the Trinity are to be received by chrism and by the imposition of hands when they return to the Catholic Church, after making their profession of faith. Thus there are three different ways of reconciling heretics. The method mentioned by Pope Siricius, and followed at Rome, speaks only of the imposition of hands. The second, reported by the First Council of Arles, adds a profession of faith to the imposition of hands. The third, from the Second Council of Arles, adds the anointing with chrism to the profession of faith and the imposition of hands.

This is how Pope Saint Gregory explained the matter when instructing the bishops of Hibernia (Gregory, Book IX, Letter 61, to Quirinus):

“We have learned from our fathers and ancestors that those who, while in heresy, were baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity must be reconciled to the Church either by anointing with chrism, or by the imposition of [Col. 1569B] hands, or by a profession of (211) faith. Throughout the West, the Arians are reconciled by the imposition of hands.”

[Note: [Col. 1569A] Saint Gregory is speaking of Italy; for it is certain from the testimony of his contemporary, Saint Gregory of Tours, that in France the Arians were reconciled [Col. 1570D] by the imposition of hands and by anointing with chrism.]

Saint Gregory does not combine these different ceremonies for the reconciliation of heretics. Rather, he uses the disjunctive particle *aut*—“or”: either chrism, or the imposition of hands, or the profession of faith—and indicates which practice was used in the East and which was followed by the West, or at least by Italy.

If, then, the ceremony by which the Arians were reconciled had been our sacrament of confirmation, as these theologians maintain, that sacrament, according to them, would consist either in the imposition of hands alone, or in the anointing with chrism alone, or in the profession of faith alone, since the heretics were reconciled indifferently by any one of these three ceremonies. They will not accept this conclusion.

Moreover, if the ceremony mentioned by the Council of Constantinople for the reconciliation of heretics (212) is the sacrament of confirmation [Col. 1569C], I ask these theologians whether it is confirmation as it is administered today or as it was administered in the time of the apostles and during the first centuries of the Church. If they say that it is confirmation as it is administered today, it is easy to prove the contrary. At present we are confirmed by a single anointing on the forehead with chrism: that is the matter of the sacrament; and by these words, “I mark you with the sign of the cross, and I confirm you with the chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father, and so forth”: that is the form.

But the ceremony mentioned by the Council of Constantinople consisted of several anointings, on the forehead, the eyes, and several other parts of the body, while saying, “This is the seal of the Holy Spirit.” Who does not see the difference between these two ceremonies?

It is also agreed that the anointing with chrism, although according to some theologians an essential part of the sacrament of confirmation, is not sufficient by itself, and that it must be joined to the imposition of hands in order to constitute the complete matter of this [Col. 1569D] sacrament, as is done in the Catholic Church. (213) But these two ceremonies are not essentially joined in the ceremony used for the reconciliation of heretics. They were employed separately, according to the diversity of the Churches’ practices, as has been observed. Therefore this ceremony is not the sacrament of confirmation as we now receive it in the Catholic Church.

Nor is it confirmation as it was administered in the time of the apostles. At that time it was administered by the imposition of hands alone, of which the seventh canon of the Council of Constantinople makes no mention in its account of the reconciliation of heretics. Therefore this ceremony, however one understands [Col. 1570A] the sacrament of confirmation, is entirely different from it.

But if one considers that this canon was enacted at a council held in Constantinople, and that the Greek Church has never omitted the imposition of hands when administering confirmation—as appears certain from the testimony of the Greek Fathers, particularly Theodoret’s commentary on chapter 6 (214) of the Epistle to the Hebrews [Col. 1570B]—there can be no doubt that the Council of Constantinople never intended this ceremony to designate the sacrament of confirmation.

Even if anointing the forehead with chrism, accompanied by the necessary form, were its essential and complete matter, one would still find no sacrament in this ceremony. For, as a theologian of our own century very judiciously observes (M. Nic.), not every anointing of the forehead with holy chrism by a bishop is the sacrament of confirmation. It is also necessary that, in making this anointing, the bishop intend to confer that sacrament. If he performed the ceremony in order to heal a sick person or to exorcise one possessed—as Ageric, bishop of Verdun, did, according to Gregory of Tours—he would not confer the sacrament of confirmation, even though the matter, form, and minister all came together in the ceremony.

This is more or less like the action of a newly ordained priest practicing how to offer the sacrifice solemnly. He has the matter present; he pronounces the words that constitute its form; (215) he performs all the ceremonies that should accompany it. [Col. 1570C] Yet there is no sacrament, because his intention is only to practice and not truly to offer the sacrifice.

The anointing with chrism and the imposition of hands may be ordained by the Church to produce different effects, and these ceremonies are determined by the application made of them by the Church as a whole and by its ministers. For example, the imposition of hands is sometimes performed for the ordination of clerics, sometimes to confirm the faithful, sometimes to absolve penitents, and sometimes to reconcile heretics. It is the general intention of the Church that determines this ceremony to produce the effect for which it is performed.

The Churches of the East, which used chrism for the reconciliation of heretics, had several purposes in this ceremony. First, they intended to supply the holy anointing that most heretics had not received in baptism or confirmation. Second, they intended to give them the Holy Spirit, whom they supposed these persons could not have received from a (216) heretical hand. Third, they intended to purify all their senses, defiled by heresy, so as to make them receptive to the sound doctrine they were about to hear in the Catholic Church.
