This was precisely what the bishop who performed these anointings asked God to grant them in the prayer he pronounced aloud: [Col. 1570D]

“Give them, Lord, the true knowledge of yourself, as your holy apostles taught it, and deign to grant them your Holy Spirit through the sign of this divine chrism.”

This prayer is still found in an ancient ritual of the Church of Constantinople, preserved in the King’s Library, whose handwriting appears to date from the eighth century. M. de Marca extracted several passages from it and inserted them into his notes on the Council of Clermont.

This same ritual, under the heading “The Manner of Reconciling the Arians, Macedonians, Apollinarists, and Novatians,” says that the bishop recites over the new convert, who is deeply bowed, the prayer just quoted. Immediately afterward [Col. 1571A] he gives him the same (217) anointings that are given to neophytes, pronouncing the same words:

“After this he anoints him with ointment as he does the neophytes, pronouncing the same form over him”: *Post hoc ungit eum unguento sicut neophytos, eamdem super ipsum formam pronuntians.*

If other Churches added a profession of faith to the imposition of hands and the anointing with chrism, this was in order to obtain greater assurance of the new convert’s convictions and for the edification of the faithful. As for the Churches of the West, which are more particularly subject to the Church of Rome, they conformed to its practice and now require only the abjuration of errors and a profession of faith. The Church believes that by this means it is assured of the new convert’s horror of the impious doctrines he had professed and of the purity of his faith. After this, it reconciles him by absolution and the imposition of hands.

**THIRD PART**

[Col. 1571B]

**The anointing with chrism that Gundobad requested from Saint Avitus was the imposition of penance**

What, then, was this anointing with chrism that Gundobad requested from Saint Avitus, if it was neither baptism (218) nor confirmation? I answer that it was the imposition of penance, which was administered indifferently either by this anointing or by the imposition of hands, as has been demonstrated.

The practice of admitting converted heretics to public penance was constant throughout the West and was observed during the earliest centuries. Pope Saint Stephen expressly communicated this to Saint Cyprian: “If any heretic returns to you, whoever he may be, let nothing be changed in the Church’s ancient practices; let it suffice to impose hands upon him for penance.” He speaks neither of baptism nor of confirmation.

Saint Cyprian understood this so well that, being astonished by it, he represented to the pope that it was insufficient [Col. 1571C] to halt the spread of heresies and that, with this penance, he saw them multiplying every day. Eusebius says (Book VII, chapter 2) that this already ancient custom had become general and had acquired, as it were, the force of law throughout the Church:

“For an ancient tradition had prevailed, namely, that in the case of such persons only the imposition of hands with prayers should be employed”: *Quippe antiqua traditio invaluerat ut in ejusmodi hominibus sola manuum impositio cum precationibus adhiberetur.*

Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, whom some believe to have been the compiler (219) of the Code of the African Church, reports that some young Donatists were reconciled to the Church by the imposition of hands, according to the ancient custom:

“They were received according to the ancient practice through the imposition of hands”: *More antiquo per manuum impositionem recepti sunt* (vol. II of the Councils, African Code, canon 57).

Saint Jerome establishes the same truth in several places, particularly in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*. He asks the Luciferians why their sect did not admit Arian clerics to penance, although it admitted laypeople:

“Why does it not receive clerics when it receives laypeople as penitents?”: *Cur non recipit clericos qui recipit laicos poenitentes?*

The Luciferian replies that they do not wish to receive Arian priests [Col. 1571D] or bishops into penance because they do not wish to renounce the priesthood or clerical status, and because it is unbecoming to see a bishop in humiliation and tears, prostrate at the feet of the faithful, and shortly afterward offering and distributing the body of Jesus Christ, raised upon a throne above all those at whose feet he had recently been seen:

“It is not fitting for a bishop to shed tears for his sins, to handle the Lord’s body, to fall prostrate at his brothers’ knees, and from a lofty place to administer the Eucharist to the people. It is one thing to mourn what you have been; it is another (220) to live gloriously in the Church while neglecting sin.” If you repent of having sinned, lay down the office of priest”: *Non est episcopi lacrymas fundere pro peccatis, et corpus attrectare Domini, ad fratrum genua provolvi et de sublimi loco eucharistiam ministrare populo; aliud est lugere quod fueris, aliud neglecto peccato in Ecclesia vivere gloriosum. Si peccasse poenitet, officium depone sacerdotis.*

This is assuredly public penance, marked out with complete clarity. [Col. 1572A] What does Saint Jerome reply to the Luciferian? Does he say that this is not how Arians are received when they abjure their errors? Does he say that they are merely confirmed without being subjected to public penance? Not at all. He agrees that they are received into the Church through penance; at the same time, however, he maintains that this does not destroy the priesthood of bishops or priests, any more than it destroys baptism, which he calls the priesthood of laypeople.

And when Saint Optatus replies to the calumnies of the Donatists, who accused Catholics of rejecting the sacraments—particularly baptism and confirmation received among them—does he agree that these sacraments should be repeated? Not at all. On the contrary, he cries out against the calumny and complains that they imputed to Catholics a crime of which they were innocent, a crime committed only in the Donatist sect:

“Do we destroy your oil, and so forth? If anyone passes from you to us, he is treated by us as he is dismissed by you. (221) But you destroy the thing where there was oil and sweetness; you anointed men, rebaptized them, and anointed them again” (Optatus, Book VII, *On the Donatist Schism*): *Nunquid nos exterminamus oleum vestrum, etc. . . . Si a vobis ad nos aliquis transitum fecerit, sic a nobis servatur, quomodo a vobis dimittitur. . . . Sed vos exterminatis rem ubi oleum fuit et suavitas, sed unxistis homines, rebaptizastis, iterum unxistis.*

And so that no one may doubt that by the word “oil” [Col. 1572B] he means holy chrism, which is the matter of the sacrament of confirmation, he declares that he uses this term only to accommodate himself to the way of speaking of these schismatics, who call “oil” the liquid prepared in the Catholic Church and which, from the name of Christ, is called “chrism” after it has been consecrated:

“They call oil that liquid, namely, which is prepared from the name of Christ; once it has been prepared, it is called chrism”: *Oleum nominant illum scilicet liquorem qui ex nomine Christi conditur, quod chrisma postquam conditum est nominatur.*

The anointing with chrism performed upon heretics who were abjuring their errors was therefore neither baptism nor confirmation, but only the imposition of penance and a preparation for their reconciliation.

Pope Innocent I (Ep. 18, c. 3) gives us, in a few words, a perfect idea of this ceremony. “We receive,” he says, “the Arians and other similar pests, [Col. 1572C] and their laypeople who convert to the Lord, under the appearance or image of penance”: *Arianos caeterosque hujusmodi pestes, et eorum laicos conversos ad Dominum sub imagine poenitentiae recipimus.* Indeed, it was only an image of the ancient public penance, and it was much less rigorous than that imposed upon apostates, for those who had been born in heresy and asked to be received into the Catholic Church were always treated with far greater gentleness than deserters from the faith when they came to repentance. Pope Siricius thus reconciled all heretics by the imposition of hands alone (Ep. 4, c. 8). And the author of the *Pontifical*, known under the name of Damasus, says that this pope ordered heretics to be received and reconciled throughout the whole Western Church by the imposition of hands and in the presence of the people: *Hic constituit haereticos in manus impositione recipi et reconciliari praesente cuncta ecclesia*—which clearly indicates penance according to the ancient custom of the Church. Finally, all the Latin Fathers and the most ancient ecclesiastical authors speak only of the imposition of hands for penance in the reconciliation [Col. 1572D] of heretics; (223) and if confirmation had formerly been administered to reconcile heretics to the Church, how could it later have been considered sufficient merely to abjure their errors and to make a profession of faith before the assembly of the faithful, *coram sanctae fraternitatis congregatione*, as Saint Gregory the Great informs us (Book IX, Ep. 61)?

I conclude, therefore, that the ceremony which was in use during the first centuries of the Church for reconciling heretics, and which continued until the end of the sixth century, was neither baptism nor confirmation, but a simple ceremony by which they were placed among the penitents, either through the imposition of hands or through the anointing with chrism that they received from the bishop; and that either one or the other, or both together, were administered in order to begin restoring in these new converts the Spirit of God, the grace of baptism, and that of confirmation, [Col. 1573A] which had, so to speak, been stifled by the evil dispositions in which they had received these sacraments within a heretical society. This was called receiving the imposition of hands for the Holy Spirit. This expression was preferred to (224) that of the imposition of hands for penance because it was gentler and less likely to repel heretics who wished to draw near to the Church, although in fact the two things were identical.

If they had not yet received the sacrament of confirmation, they were confirmed only after passing through all the stages of the penance to which they had been subjected. They were reconciled on Maundy Thursday together with the other penitents. This penance itself made them irregular—that is, incapable of being promoted to ecclesiastical orders, or of exercising them if they had already been promoted to them. The Church did not dispense them from this irregularity without good reasons; but she believed that she almost always had sufficient reasons to grant such a dispensation to [Col. 1573B] bishops and clerics born in heresy who asked to be received into the Catholic faith. Once their penance had been completed, they were restored to the rank they had held and admitted to the functions of the priesthood, and even to the episcopate if they were bishops, as before their penance. This is clear proof that, far from considering the baptism, confirmation, and ordination of these heretics invalid, people did not even doubt their validity. Indeed, why would a member of the faithful regenerated by a second baptism have been subjected to public penance, or one in a condition to receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit through the sacrament of confirmation? There would have been nothing in such conduct that did not offend right reason, common sense, and the constant practice of the Church.

Saint Augustine, in the letter he wrote to Count Boniface concerning the Donatists, thoroughly instructs us about the conduct she followed on these occasions. A Donatist objected to him that it was unjustified [Col. 1573C] for the Church to subject members of their sect who wished to convert to penance, and to require it of them as necessary for their salvation, since priests and bishops could be seen retaining their rank and exercising the sacred functions of their ministry, contrary to the ancient canons, which require that clerics who have been subjected to public penance [Col. 1574A] be excluded forever from clerical functions: “If, then, we must repent of having been outside the Church and against the Church in order that we may be saved, how is it that, after this penance, priests or even bishops remain among you?” (*Si ergo oportet ut nos extra Ecclesiam et adversus Ecclesiam fuisse poeniteat, ut salvi esse possimus, quomodo post istam poenitentiam apud vos clerici vel etiam episcopi permanemus?*)

The holy doctor replied that this should not be so, and that the Church would not tolerate in the exercise of the sacred ministry those priests or bishops who had been subjected to public penance, if the great advantages arising from union and peace—which had led her to set aside those holy and just rules—did not in some way compensate her for the loss that this caused her in discipline. But this very fact, continues the holy doctor, should confound you Donatists all the more: you should see that the state of death in which you are is so terrible that, in order to restore you to life, the Catholic Church, your mother, does not fear inflicting so great a wound upon her discipline. On this occasion, he says, she acts much as a skilled gardener would when grafting a branch separated from one tree onto a foreign stock. That branch, separated from the trunk and root, would inevitably dry up; to preserve it and give it life, he makes an incision in the tree [Col. 1574B] onto which he wishes to graft it. In this way he not only preserves its life but gives it a better one and makes it bear more excellent fruit. This is the Church’s intention in the wound she inflicts upon the severity of her discipline: “For when a severed branch is grafted, another wound is made in the tree so that the branch that was perishing without the life of the root may be received and live” (*Cum enim praecisus ramus inseritur, fit aliud vulnus in arbore quo possit recipi, ut vivat qui sine vita radicis peribat*) (Augustine, Ep. 185).

All this clearly proves that heretics were not reconciled by repeating baptism or confirmation, but only through public penance, to which they were subjected by the imposition of hands or, in some Churches, as has been noted, by the anointing with chrism, and in others by both ceremonies together. This was the reconciliation that Gondebaud requested from Saint Avitus; and, since it always presupposed public penance, from which he had a strong aversion, he would have preferred to perform it privately and to profess the Catholic faith secretly—something Saint Avitus did not believe he could grant him.

## CLARIFICATIONS CONCERNING FAUSTUS, BISHOP OF RIEZ, AND HIS DOCTRINE

[Col. 1573]

(228) Faustus, originally from the islands of Great Britain, had withdrawn to the famous monastery of Lérins, recently founded by Saint Honoratus on the coast of Provence, while Saint Maximus, who was its second abbot, governed it (Eusser, *British Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, c. 3). After giving great examples of virtue there, he was appointed in Maximus’s place when the latter became bishop of Riez, around the year 433. For several years he governed this monastery with great prudence; and after Maximus’s death (229), his merit caused him to be appointed Maximus’s successor in the bishopric of Riez as he had been in the abbey of Lérins.

This new dignity brought about no change in Faustus: he always appeared the same, bishop and abbot (Sidonius, Book IX, Ep. 3). In the midst of a city and amid the labors of the episcopate, he relaxed none of the rigor of his former discipline, and he transferred [Col. 1574C] from Lérins to Riez the practice of continual prayer, to which he had been accustomed in his monastery.

[Note: [Col. 1573D] With what appearance of justice can Faustus’s enemies accuse him of failing to instruct those under his direction about the necessity or the benefits of Christian prayer, when they themselves acknowledge that Saint Sidonius of Clermont, his contemporary, testifies that prayer was the most ordinary and continual exercise of his life, and that he transferred its practice from the monastery of Lérins to the Church of Riez? A man who prays continually and inspires his people with the desire for continual prayer is very far from attributing salvation to the powers of free will and despising the grace of Jesus Christ. Had these writers been a little less impassioned, they would have noticed the manifest contradiction into which they were falling.]

He (230) was present with several other bishops of Gaul at a council held in Rome under the pontificate of Hilary, the immediate successor of Saint Leo. On returning from Rome he composed various works, [Col. 1574D] and acquired considerable reputation through his writings and learned preaching. He was consistently regarded as a man of superior intellect, highly skilled and thoroughly learned, and as one of the most accomplished bishops of his age. This is the testimony borne to him by Saint Sidonius of Clermont, Gennadius, and almost all the ancient authors who were his contemporaries.

This is what Saint Sidonius wrote to him personally: “Whoever hears your discourses and instructions learns from them equally how to speak well and how to live well. You alone speak better than the teachers who taught you, and you live still better than you speak. All good people will justly praise you and raise you above all who have spoken in your time.”

Some modern writers who attack his doctrine are not so favorable toward him. Although they cannot deny that, by the holiness of his life, he deserved all the praise bestowed upon him by the ancients, they believe themselves entitled to penetrate into his innermost thoughts and condemn him as a hypocrite whose virtue was merely external and apparent, inwardly corrupted by the worm of pride. Without blushing at treating so disgracefully a bishop whose memory is still venerated in the Church, they dare to assert that the monastery of Lérins ought to have been ashamed to give him to Saint Maximus as his successor, and that in the world he received, through the esteem his virtue earned him among men, all the reward it deserved. This is how certain writers of our century have spoken—writers attached to a [Col. 1575B] doctrine repeatedly proscribed by the Church, because they believe that it was first condemned among the Predestinarians through the zeal and vigilance of this bishop.

Since the most enlightened people are not surprised to see, in the lives of the greatest saints, shadows that sometimes tarnish the brilliance of their holiness, because they were human, they are even less surprised to find in their writings on delicate matters that had not yet been decided certain errors into which they were imperceptibly led by the insufficiently measured zeal with which they defended the truths opposed by those errors. These writers seem more inclined to spare him concerning other, cruder errors regarding the nature of angels and souls, in which he appears less excusable; but concerning those into which they claim he fell while opposing the views they attribute to Saint Augustine on the [Col. 1575C] grace of Jesus Christ and human freedom, “it is, according to them, a sin against the Holy Spirit, which is forgiven neither in this world nor in the next.”

The two books Faustus had written on these subjects were what most inflamed the zeal of the Scythian monks, whom we discussed in the first part of this work, and whom they wished to have condemned as Pelagians. He had undertaken them to refute the heresy of the Predestinarians.

[Note: [Col. 1575C] In his fifth century, page 596, M. Dupin calls the Predestinarian heresy a chimera. This is not what has been believed in Rome until now, nor what a learned cardinal told Father Mabillon. [Col. 1576C] See Father Mabillon’s *Journey through Italy*, p. 135, and Father Sirmond’s *History of the Predestinarians*.]

(233) It had spread into Gaul and acquired a powerful following there, having arisen in the time of Saint Augustine himself from misunderstandings of his writings on grace and predestination—writings that Faustus says were regarded with suspicion by the most learned people of his age (Faustus, *To Gerontius*, p. 45). The monks of Hadrumetum were the first to give them a meaning entirely different from that intended by this holy doctor, and to draw from his principles exaggerated consequences capable of driving people to despair or into a dangerous security. This is how one must understand what Tiro Prosper says about this heresy in his chronicle, and restore to purity the passage that has been corrupted, as Sigebert did. God forbid that the beginning of this heresy should be attributed to the holy Doctor of Grace: it could only have been one of his enemies or an ignorant copyist who added these words to Tiro Prosper’s chronicle: *quae ab Augustino dicitur accepisse initium*—“which is said to have taken its beginning from Augustine.”

(234) As soon as this heresy appeared in Gaul, Saint Hilary of Arles and Saint Prosper vigorously opposed it and learnedly refuted it in their writings. Pope Saint Celestine subsequently condemned it, but it nevertheless continued to have many adherents. One of its most outspoken partisans in the time of Faustus of Riez was a certain priest named Lucidus. Since he persisted in dogmatizing and spreading his errors, the bishop of Riez took up the matter and sought to compel him to retract. After failing to do so through several conferences, he finally wrote him a very urgent letter, in which he set out all the propositions he had to condemn and warned him that, if he did not do so promptly, he would be obliged to summon him before the council that was soon to assemble at Arles. Indeed, in the early months of the year 475, thirty bishops of Gaul assembled there. Lucidus was summoned and appeared; and after the questions had been thoroughly debated and decided, he was compelled to retract, as the Fathers had ordered. He did so in writing. Here are Faustus’s letter and Lucidus’s retraction.

## LETTERS

[Note: [Col. 1575C] The Latin and French versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

## FAUSTUS’S LETTER TO LUCIDUS

Faustus to my very dear and most respected brother Lucidus, priest.

[Col. 1575D] It is a great act of charity to employ the help and grace of God to bring back into the way of truth a brother who has strayed from it through imprudence, rather than to cut him off from the unity and charity of the faithful, as the bishops are considering doing. You wish me to write to you; but since I was unable to persuade you in several conferences, in which I spoke to you with all the gentleness and cordiality of a friend, can I add anything in my letters to all that I have already told you, or anything capable of moving you? Nevertheless, I am willing to do so again. Since I am to speak of the grace of God and human obedience, we must set before ourselves as an inviolable rule the royal way, which is the middle way, without turning aside either to the right or to the left.

I was astonished that you could advance what no Christian before you had yet dared to say against the Catholic faith, although a very great number of those who pride themselves on that name have published countless [Col. 1577A] errors and have even taught them in their writings. I shall therefore set out briefly, as far as one can speak to an absent person, what you must believe with the Catholic Church, so that, always joining human cooperation and labor to the grace of God, you may detest the impious doctrine of Pelagius, which establishes predestination while excluding human labor and effort.

Anathema, therefore, to anyone who, with criminal presumption, maintains that man is born without sin, can be saved by his own labor alone, and can be delivered without the grace of God, as Pelagius asserts along with many other impieties.

Anathema to anyone who maintains that a person solemnly baptized with true faith, and having professed the Catholic religion, may subsequently be carried away by the pleasures of the world without any longer bearing original sin, and that Adam and original sin have entirely perished and been extinguished in him.

[Col. 1577B] Anathema to anyone who says that man is hurled into death by God’s foreknowledge.

Anathema to anyone who says that the one who perishes was not given what would have enabled him to be saved, whether he be a baptized person or a pagan who has reached the age of discretion, who could have believed but did not wish to do so.

Anathema to anyone who says that a vessel of dishonor cannot be changed or become a vessel of honor.

Anathema to anyone who says that Jesus Christ did not die for all and does not wish all human beings to be saved.

When you come to us in the name of Jesus Christ, or when you are summoned by the holy bishops, then, with the Lord’s help, we shall show you for each article the testimonies on which the Catholic doctrines are established and those by which the errors opposed to them are destroyed.

For our part, enlightened by the light of Jesus Christ, [Col. 1577C] we truthfully and confidently assure you that the one who perished through his own fault could have been saved by grace if, in addition to the assistance of grace, he had not refused to join the obedience of labor; and that the one who through grace reached the end of a blessed completion, cooperating with that same grace through his labor, could have fallen through negligence and laziness and perished through his own fault. Walking, therefore, along the just middle path and following Jesus Christ and his grace, without which we are nothing, we affirm the labor of an obedient and active servitude, while entirely excluding the arrogance and presumption of human labor. Thus, exerting ourselves with all our strength lest grace be rendered fruitless in us, we acknowledge and say that everything we have received from God’s hand is his gift, not the just reward of our labor. Knowing well that the fruit of our labor results from his mercy and [Col. 1577D] goodness, not from our merits, we always say, as Jesus Christ commands us in the Gospel: “We are unprofitable servants; we have done only what we ought to have done.”

You must answer me precisely whether you accept or reject all the articles I have briefly proposed to you, as far as I could do so in a letter. Moreover, know that anyone who does not follow this rule of truth with the preceding assistance of grace and with the efforts that ought to follow it will deserve to be barred from entering the holy places. For my part, I hope that, sincerely rejecting your error, you will remain in the bosom of the Church our mother. This hope comes from the depths of my heart and from the tender and sincere affection I have always had for you. If you promptly reject the error, people will have reason to believe that you fell into it through surprise or ignorance; but (242) if you remain in it and stubbornly maintain it, people will be unable to avoid regarding and treating you as a blasphemer. Indeed, is it not a great insult to God to say that he did not wish to give the power of attaining salvation to the one who perished and who possessed the use of reason and freedom? For, since we cannot deny that he will condemn such a person as a transgressor of his commandments in the examination of his judgment, while one who has not received grace is not indebted for it and consequently cannot be condemned as guilty of having lost it, by asserting this impious doctrine we rise up against God himself; and, by wishing to attribute too much to his grace, we attack his justice.

I retain a copy of this letter in my possession, so that I may have it read, if necessary, in the assembly of the holy bishops. If you judge it appropriate to accept it and embrace the doctrine it contains, return it to me signed in your own hand. If you do not wish to assent to it, inform me of that as well. But if you do not return it to me signed, you will make known to me by your silence [Col. 1580A] that you remain obstinately attached to your errors, and you will oblige me to denounce you and make known what you are in the assembly of the bishops. Therefore, reply to me according to what I have written, without concealment or ambiguity: indicate whether you assent to it or reject it, and so forth.

(235) FAUSTUS’S LETTER TO LUCIDUS THE PRIEST

[Col. 1576C]

Faustus to his most devoted lord and brother Lucidus the priest, whom he reveres and welcomes with special affection.

[Col. 1576D] Great charity consists in wishing, through God’s help and grace, to heal the error of a brother insufficiently cautious rather than, as the chief bishops are contemplating, to exclude him from communion. What can I say about this matter, since you wish to speak with me in agreement through letters, when, though present, I was never able to draw you back to the way of truth through much gentle and humble conversation? Speaking, then, of God’s grace and human obedience, we must establish this above all: that, neither leaning toward the left nor straining toward the right, we should rather walk along the royal way.

I was astonished that your Reverence said that no one had ever, under a religious profession, either written or preached against the Catholic faith, since many who nevertheless gloried in the Christian name believed that their manifold and profane errors should even be inserted into written records. I shall therefore say briefly, as far as I can speak with an absent person, what you ought to believe with the Catholic Church: namely, that you should always join the work of the baptized servant to the Lord’s grace, [Col. 1578A] and should detest, together with the doctrine of Pelagius, the one who asserts predestination while excluding human labor.

Anathema, therefore, to anyone who, among Pelagius’s other impieties, maintains with damnable presumption that man is born without sin and can be saved through labor alone, and who believes that he can be delivered without the grace of God.

Likewise, anathema to anyone who maintains that, in a person solemnly baptized with a faithful confession, professing the Catholic faith and later falling through the various pleasures of this world, Adam and original sin have perished.

Likewise, anathema to anyone who says that man is thrust into death through God’s foreknowledge.

Likewise, anathema to anyone who says that the one who perished did not receive what would have enabled him to be saved—that is, a baptized person, or a pagan of the age at which he could believe but did not wish to do so.

Likewise, anathema to anyone who says that a vessel of dishonor cannot rise up to become a vessel of honor.

Likewise, anathema to anyone who says that Christ did not die for all, (239) nor wish all human beings to be saved. [Col. 1578B]

When you come to us in the name of Christ, or when you are summoned by the holy priests, then, if the Lord so orders, we shall appropriately produce the testimonies in their proper places, by which what is Catholic may be made manifest and what is opposed to Catholic teaching may be destroyed.

For our part, through the illumination of Christ, we truthfully and confidently affirm both that the one who perished through his fault could have been saved by grace if he had not refused obedience in labor to the service of grace itself, and that the one who, through grace and obedient service, reached the goal of a good completion could have fallen through indolence and could have perished through his fault. Walking, therefore, along the middle path under Christ’s guidance, after grace, without which we are nothing, we affirm the labor of dutiful servitude but entirely exclude the arrogance and presumption of labor, so that, laboring with all our strength lest grace be emptied in us, we may declare that whatever we have received from the Lord’s hand is a gift, not a price, knowing that the fruit of this labor is a matter of duty, [Col. 1578C] not of merit, saying with the Evangelist: “We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done.”

(241) Let your unanimity reply in a subsequent letter whether you accept or reject these things that have been stated briefly for the sake of the letter’s concision. Moreover, whoever does not follow this measure of truth, with grace preceding and effort rising to meet it, will be worthy of being barred from the sacred thresholds. For my part, retaining your goodness with me on the way in the full embrace of sincere kindness, I desire that, having rejected this error, you remain in the bosom of the mother Church. If it is quickly rejected, it will appear to have arisen from ignorance. But if it is stubbornly defended, it will be reckoned blasphemy. For we bring serious reproach upon the author when we say that he did not wish to give the possibility of grasping salvation to the one who perished—namely, to one who was already capable of grasping the freedom of choice—since we certainly cannot deny that he will condemn him as a transgressor of the commandment in the examination of his judgment. For how can one who is not liable on account of what he has received be guilty on account of what he has lost? And thus, by sinning against God, whose grace we have rashly asserted at the outset, we shall finally appear to attack his justice. I retain a copy of this letter with me, to be produced at the gathering of the holy bishops if it should be necessary. If your fraternity considers that it ought to be accepted, let it promptly return it signed in its own hand; otherwise, let it reply in a subsequent letter that it has entirely rejected it. But if you do not wish to send it signed, as I have said, you will openly prove by that very silence (243) that you still persist in error; and consequently you will compel me to expose your person in public assemblies. Therefore, in accordance with what I have sent you, write back whether you acknowledge or reject these propositions, without evasions.

And the bishops who follow in order subscribed; they too had been present at that synod.

Auxanius, bishop in the name of Christ: I reread it and subscribed.

Faustus: I reread the copy of my letter and subscribed.

[Col. 1580A] (244) Paul, bishop in the name of Christ: I reread it and subscribed.

Eutropius, bishop in the name of Christ: reread and subscribed.

Pragmatius, bishop in the sign of Christ: reread and subscribed.

Patient, bishop in Christ: reread and subscribed.

Euphronius: reread it, and I was astonished at its holy fullness.

Megetius, bishop: reread and subscribed.

Claudius, in the name of Christ, bishop: reread and subscribed.

Leucadius, in the name of Christ, bishop: reread and subscribed.

Julianus, in the name of Christ, bishop: reread and subscribed.

Lucidus the priest: reread and subscribed.

[Note: [Col. 1579B] The Latin and French versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

## LETTER OF THE PRIEST LUCIDUS

[Col. 1579B]

To the most holy lords and most reverend Fathers in Jesus Christ: Euphronius, Leontius, Fonteius, Viventius, Mamertus, Patient, Verianus or Veranus, Auxanius, Faustus, Paulus, Megetius, Graecus, Eutropius, Leontius, Claudius, Marcellus, Crocus, Basilius, Claudius, (246) Ursicinus, Praetextatus, Pragmatius, Theoplastus, Leocadius, Viventius, Julianus, Amicalis, Joannes, Opilio, and Licinius or Lesinus, bishops.

Your charitable admonitions are always salutary, and the judgments you render are effective remedies that you apply. I therefore regard it as a sovereign remedy for my ills to excuse my past errors by accusing them and to cleanse myself of them through a humble confession. Accordingly, submitting respectfully to the new decrees of the council that has assembled:

1. I condemn with you the opinion of those who maintain that man is not obliged to join the labor of obedience to the grace of God.

[Col. 1579C] 2. That after the fall of the first man his free will was entirely extinguished.

3. That Jesus Christ our Savior did not suffer death for the salvation of all.

4. That by God’s foreknowledge man is violently driven to death, or that those who perish do so by God’s will.

5. That Adam has entirely perished in the person who sins after having properly received baptism.

6. That some are destined for death and others predestined for life.

7. That from Adam until Jesus Christ none of the nations were saved through faith in the coming of Jesus Christ and through God’s first grace—that is, through the law of nature—because they all lost free will in their first father.

(248) 8. That the patriarchs and prophets, or the greatest saints, before the time of redemption, were received into paradise.

[Col. 1579D] 9. That there are neither fires nor hell.

I condemn all these things as impious and sacrilegious. I acknowledge and confess the grace of God in such a way that I always join the assistance of the Lord’s grace to human efforts. I acknowledge that the freedom of the human will has not been extinguished, but only weakened and diminished by the sin of our first father; and that the one who has been saved was in danger, while the one who perished could have been saved. I acknowledge that Jesus Christ our God and Savior, in accordance with the riches of his infinite goodness, offered the price of his death for all, and that he does not wish anyone to perish—he who is the Savior of all human beings, especially of the faithful, liberal and magnificent toward all who invoke him.

[Col. 1581A] And because I am obliged to satisfy my conscience concerning all these important articles, I remember having previously said that Jesus Christ had come only for those whom he had foreseen would believe in him, because I had adhered literally to these words of the Lord: “The Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve and to give his soul for the redemption of many”; and to these others: “This is the cup of my blood of the New Testament, which is poured out for many for the remission (250) of their sins”; and to this other passage of the Apostle: “Just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, so Christ also offered himself once to destroy and erase the sins of many.” But now, instructed by the authority of the sacred testimonies found throughout the divine Scriptures and informed about the sense in which the ancient Fathers understood them, I openly and sincerely acknowledge and confess that Jesus Christ came even for the damned, because they perished against his will, and that it is not permissible to restrict his benefits or the immense riches of his goodness and mercy to those alone who are saved. For if we say that Jesus Christ healed and redeemed only those who are saved, we will appear to wish to absolve and declare innocent those who are damned and who will certainly be punished for having despised their salvation.

I further acknowledge that, in the succession of the ages under the law of nature, which God engraved upon the hearts of all human beings, some were saved through the faith and hope they placed in the coming of Jesus Christ, although no one could be delivered from original sin except through the merit of his precious blood.

I further confess that there are eternal fires, and that the flames of hell are prepared to expiate capital offenses, because divine justice equitably pursues vengeance against the crimes of those who persist in them to the end; and those who do not believe all these things with their whole heart are rightly subjected to them and cannot escape them. [Col. 1582B] Pray for me, my lords and holy Fathers . . . . . I, Lucidus, priest, have subscribed this letter with my own hand. I (252) believe and confess the doctrines established in it, and I condemn those who are condemned in it.

(245) **Copy of the Letter of the Priest Lucidus**

[Col. 1580B]

To the most blessed and most reverend fathers in Christ, Euphronius, Leontius, Fonteius, Viventius, Mamertus, Patien­tius, Verianus, Auxanius, Faustus, Paulus, Megetius, Graecus, Eu­ropius, Leontius, Claudius, Marcellus, Crocus, Baselius, Claudius, Ursicinus, Praetextatus, Pragmatius, Theoplastus, Leocadius, Viventius, Julianus, Amicalus, John, Opilio, and Licinius, bishops: Lucidus, priest.

Your correction is the public welfare, and your judgment is medicine. Therefore I regard it as the supreme remedy to excuse my past errors by accusing them, and to cleanse myself through a salutary confession.

1. Accordingly, in conformity with the council’s recently published statutes, I condemn with you the opinion that says that human effort in obedience must not be joined to divine grace.

[Col. 1580C]

2. The opinion that says that, after the fall of the first man, the freedom of the will was entirely extinguished.

(247) 3. The opinion that says that Christ the Lord, our Savior, did not undergo death for the salvation of all.

4. The opinion that says that God’s foreknowledge violently compels a human being to death, or that those who perish perish by God’s will.

5. The opinion that says that, after lawfully receiving baptism, whoever sins dies in Adam.

6. The opinion that says that some are appointed to death and others predestined to life.

7. The opinion that says that, from Adam to Christ, no one from among the nations was saved by God’s first grace—that is, through the law of nature—in hope of Christ’s coming, on the grounds that they had all lost free will in their first parent.

8. The opinion that says that the patriarchs and prophets, or any of the greatest saints, dwelt in paradise even before the time of redemption.

[Col. 1580D]

9. The opinion that says that fires and hell do not exist.

I condemn all these things as impious and filled with sacrilege.

I nevertheless affirm God’s grace in such a way that I always join grace to human striving and effort.

And I declare that the freedom of the human will has not been extinguished, but weakened and enfeebled; that the person who is saved was in danger, and that the person who perished could have been saved.

I also affirm that Christ, our God and Savior, insofar as concerns the riches of his goodness, offered the price of his death for all.

And because he does not wish anyone to perish—he who is the Savior of all human beings, especially of believers—and is rich toward all who call upon him.

And because in such important matters one must satisfy the conscience, I remember having said earlier that Christ had come only for those whom he had foreseen would believe, following the Lord’s statements in which he says: “The Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” And this: “This is the cup of my blood of the New Testament, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins.” Or that statement of the Apostle: “Just as it has been appointed once for human beings to die, so Christ was offered once to remove the sins of many.” But now, instructed by the authority of the sacred testimonies that are found abundantly throughout the divine Scriptures, and by the teaching and reasoning of the elders through which their meaning has been made clear, I willingly confess that Christ also came for the lost, because they perished against his will. For it is not right to confine the immense riches of his goodness and his divine benefits solely to those who appear to have been saved. For if we say that Christ brought remedies only to those who have been redeemed, we shall appear to absolve the unredeemed, who are known to be punished for having despised redemption.

I also affirm that, according to the course and order of the ages, others were saved under the law of nature—which God wrote in the hearts of all—in hope of Christ’s coming.

[Col. 1582B]

Nevertheless, from the beginning of the world no one was released from the bond of original sin except through the intervention of the sacred (251) blood.

I further profess that there are eternal fires and that infernal flames are prepared for capital offenses, because divine judgment rightly follows human sins when people persist in them to the end. Those who have not believed these things with their whole heart justly incur that judgment.

Pray for me, holy and apostolic lords and fathers.

I, Lucidus, priest, have subscribed this letter with my own hand; and I affirm the things established in it, and condemn the things condemned in it. (From the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyon edition, p. 524.)

[Col. 1581C]

But the bishops did not think they had done enough to halt the course of this pernicious doctrine. Before separating, they commissioned Faustus of Riez to write on the subject and to maintain such a balance between the errors of the Pelagians and those of the predestinarians that he would avoid falling into either danger: that is, that he would not give so much to grace as to destroy human freedom, as the predestinarians did, nor so much prominence to the powers of free will as to make the Savior’s grace useless for human salvation, as the Pelagians did. This therefore became the subject of the two books that Faustus composed on free will and grace. But since the council’s order was not among the easiest to carry out, and since Faustus’s books were apparently corrupted by his enemies, while he himself may, in the heat of controversy, have carried his opinions too far, we ought to judge this bishop’s faith less by those books [Col. 1581D] than by the (253) letter he wrote to Lucidus and by the recantation that he made him sign—both of which appear to have expressed the consistent doctrine of the bishops of Gaul at that time.

During Faustus’s lifetime, few people nevertheless dared to oppose the doctrine he had taught in his two books. He governed his diocese irreproachably and ended his life most devoutly, in peace and in communion with the Catholic Church, esteemed, praised, and mourned by the greatest men of his time. He is still honored by public worship as a saint throughout his diocese, and his feast is celebrated there on 16 January. Several ancient churches dedicated to God under his name are also found there. The ancient martyrologies of France, according to Baronius, those of Ireland and Scotland, and, in more recent times, Bollandus, du Saussay, and M. Baillet, did not hesitate to place him among the saints recognized by the Church. Cardinal Baronius, in the year 490, having failed to reflect upon all these circumstances or to examine his doctrine sufficiently, inconsiderately treated him as a heretic and struck him from his sacred annals. But later, having paid attention to these matters, he believed himself obliged, before his death, to retract what he himself admitted he had advanced too rashly; and in his additions he repaired, with a humility of which authors provide few examples, the injury he had done to Faustus’s memory in his *Ecclesiastical Annals* (In the appendix to volume VI of the *Annals*, after volume X).

It would be desirable, for the salvation of modern writers who followed this pious and learned cardinal in his error, that they had likewise imitated him in his retraction; but they write in a spirit quite different from that which animated this great cardinal.

[Col. 1582D]

Faustus thus died in the peace of the Church toward the end of the fifth century, and as his writings spread in every direction—in Italy, Africa, and the East—they began to cause a stir there. Each person formed a very different judgment of them and, following the principles in which he had been raised, praised, approved, or condemned them. Meanwhile, Pope Gelasius deemed it appropriate to compile a catalogue of apocryphal books and a decree that was approved by a council of seventy bishops held at Rome in 494. The works of Faustus of (255) Riez were included in it. This did not prevent people from reading them, however, nor did it prevent continued great veneration for his person, because the censure that this pope pronounced against the works of the authors included in his catalogue—even assuming that the decree was his—does not declare them heretical or make them so. Indeed, he included several authors whom the Church recognizes as thoroughly Catholic, such as Lactantius, Clement of Alexandria, Africanus, and several others. Thus, if they are marked there, it is only to indicate that in some respect these authors departed from the views then upheld by the Church of Rome, and to warn readers to be wary of them and to read them cautiously.

Moreover, since other errors are found in Faustus’s works concerning the nature of angels and souls—for he believed, like Origen and several of the ancients, that they were composed of a very subtle matter different from that of our bodies, God alone being, in his view, a pure spirit—Gelasius may justly have placed his works on the index without intending specifically to condemn his books (256) on free will and grace, which were not yet at issue and perhaps had not yet been corrupted. For if they had already been condemned by the Holy See, the Scythian monks would not, twenty-four years after the publication of this decree, have pursued their condemnation so vigorously. Nor would the Church of Constantinople and almost the whole East have been divided on their account, or a great number of distinguished people—among the clergy, in the monastic state, and in the world—have taken their defense against the small number of monks who pursued their condemnation.

This is what we learn from Bishop Possessor, whom we have already mentioned, and from the letter he wrote to Pope Hormisdas at the urging of several distinguished persons who wished to know his opinion and what the views of his fellow bishops of Africa were on these matters. “When the health of the members of the body is at stake,” Possessor wrote to that pope, “one must have recourse to the head” (vol. IV, *Councils*, p. 1529). [Note: Observe the ancient practice of bishops and particular Churches of having recourse to the Holy See when a doctrine affecting the Church in general is at issue, and of referring the decision to it.]

Some of our brothers (257) are scandalized by Faustus’s writings on grace, while others defend them. They consulted me; I told them that the writings of bishops do not have the force of law, as do the canonical Scriptures or the decrees of councils, but that they should be valued according to their worth, without prejudice to the faith. They took my answer as an excuse. Therefore I am sending you my deacon Justin, asking you to declare by apostolic authority what you think of this author’s writings, especially since your sons Vitalian, master of the soldiers, and Count Justinian also desire to be instructed by your reply.

This letter was written before July of the year 520, since Bishop Possessor speaks in it of Count Vitalian as still alive; he was killed in that same month, as has been said.

Since the Scythian monks, who claimed to be zealous disciples of Saint Augustine, were among the most ardent opponents (258) of Faustus’s doctrine, they for their part wrote to various Churches, ostensibly to consult them but in reality to obtain testimonies conforming to their prejudices and placing among the Pelagians all those who held the views of the bishop of Riez. They particularly opposed Possessor; and, since he appeared inclined toward Faustus’s doctrine, they would have been pleased to obtain grounds for having him condemned as a heretic.

They first addressed themselves to the Church of Africa. The invincible courage of its confessors and martyrs, who every day won new victories over the enemies of the faith, together with the great number of learned prelates it then possessed, made it one of the most illustrious Churches in the world. They sent it Faustus’s books and addressed them to the exiled bishops. Saint Fulgentius was charged with replying, and his reply was exactly what they could have desired. One cannot be sufficiently astonished that these prelates, who certainly did not lack illumination and who were numerous enough to examine thoroughly the books sent to them—for fifteen of them subscribed to Saint Fulgentius’s reply—should have approved the profession of faith that the Scythian monks had sent them. For among the many pious and Catholic opinions it contains are some very bad and notoriously heretical ones. Such, for example, are the propositions: “By sin, human beings lost their freedom”; and: “God does not wish to save everyone”; along with several others.

The reply of the African confessors made the Scythian monks prouder and more insolent; and although it made no mention of Faustus’s books, they nevertheless did not cease proclaiming that it constituted their condemnation. [Col. 1584B] The quarrel grew hotter than ever, and the pope found himself compelled to pronounce on these questions, which were causing so much commotion, in order to prevent consequences that could only be most disastrous for the Church.

The theologians of Rome were assembled again and found themselves divided over the means to be adopted to settle the dispute. Some wanted Faustus’s books (260) to be declared heretical and his memory prosecuted. Pope Gelasius, they said, had paved the way for this condemnation by placing his works among the apocryphal books; and they considered it important to uphold the judgment that the Holy See had already rendered. Others, more moderate, said that the example of the African bishops should be followed, and that, like them, they should be content to establish sound doctrine concerning grace and freedom without mentioning Faustus or his writings. [Col. 1584C] Still others, without expressly declaring their own views, represented that it was regrettable to mark the memory of a holy bishop who had always been deeply zealous for the honor of the Holy See, who had appeared with distinction in Rome, and who might be regarded as the soul of all the councils held in the West during his lifetime; by condemning him, they would condemn the Churches of Gaul, which held almost no other views on grace than his.

Finally, others, more political than these, wishing to manage people’s feelings and avoid assigning blame to anyone, advised (261) adhering to Bishop Possessor’s reply and saying, as he had, that an individual bishop did not establish the faith of the Church; his testimony had authority and was admissible only insofar as it conformed to the truths revealed by God in the Scriptures and to the decisions of the ecumenical councils.

The pope, weary of so many disturbances [Col. 1584D] that had already agitated his pontificate, leaned rather toward this position. But when Boethius had explained himself on these extremely thorny and delicate matters and stated his opinion, he changed the pope’s mind and brought him around to his own view, which was the wiser and more suitable one in so difficult a circumstance. It did honor to the Holy See through a preliminary decision and preserved the precious deposit of faith and doctrine in its purity, without staining the memory of a learned bishop who had died in the odor of sanctity and in communion with the Catholic Church.

Boethius’s opinion was therefore to refer the parties back to the ancient decisions; to declare that the Church had already expressed itself sufficiently on these matters and that it was not (262) worthy of her dignity to pronounce [Col. 1585A] several times on the same question; and, for the rest, to reserve the explanation of Saint Augustine and the declaration of the true meaning of his writings on grace and free will, should any difficulty be found in them.

This did not cut off the source of the controversies, but it remedied an immediate evil, checked the greatest conflagration of the dispute, and, while each party congratulated itself on victory, allowed time for a more precise decision to be accepted and for people’s minds to be prepared to submit to it.

The pope therefore adopted this opinion and gave Bishop Possessor the following reply (vol. IV, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 556):

“As for those who consulted you about the writings of a certain Faustus, bishop of Gaul, they shall receive this answer: We do not number him among the Fathers, and none of those whom the Catholic Church does not number among the Fathers can cause ambiguity in doctrine or bring harm to religion. Those who read such books are not blamed, since they can be used profitably to refute errors. As for what the Roman Church—that is, the Catholic Church—follows and maintains concerning free will and the grace of God, there are explicit articles on these matters in the archives of the Church, which I shall send you if you do not have them and if you consider them necessary.”

Although this reply appeared sufficiently favorable to the Scythian monks, they were nevertheless not satisfied with it, and Abbot Maxentius immediately opposed it in his writings. He first complained that the pope had permitted the reading of Faustus’s books, continuing to maintain that they were heretical. To prove this, he cited several passages that certainly betray Pelagianism and could cause the books to be rejected, had he not falsified them. [Note: Those who recently published Abbot Maxentius’s work in the great *Bibliotheca Patrum* assure us that it is entirely filled with lies, impieties, blasphemies, and calumnies. Note on the reply of Maxentius, vol. IX, new edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyon, p. 539.]

Maxentius then turned to invectives against Bishop Possessor, whom he claimed was the principal support of this bad doctrine, and he showed as much aversion to his person [Col. 1585C] as he appeared (264) satisfied with his fellow bishops of Africa. He had good reason to praise the latter highly, for Saint Fulgentius, not content with the letter he had written in the name of all the holy confessors exiled with him in defense of the faith, also composed seven books refuting Faustus’s. They have not been printed, and M. Fleury (*Ecclesiastical History*, vol. VII, p. 267) believes them lost. It is nevertheless claimed that Father Vignier of the Oratory had them in manuscript shortly before his death.

If they are lost, the loss is not irreparable, since we still possess the books *On Predestination* and *On Grace*, which this saint composed somewhat later on the subject and according to the same principles. He addressed them to the priest John, believed to be Abbot Maxentius, and to the deacon Venerius, who may have been one of the Scythian monks. These books are nothing but a fabric of the doctrine that he attributes to Saint Augustine on these matters. He establishes predestination as purely gratuitous, without any consideration of merits; [Col. 1585D] he asserts that the human will always follows God’s victorious grace, which precedes it; that God converts us, makes us desire the good, (265) and gives us the desire and will to pray. He regards calling, justification, and glory as effects of this gratuitous predestination, which he believes to be so infallible and certain that it is impossible for anyone to be added to or removed from the number of the predestined, which was determined from all eternity.

He then raises the great objection customarily made against gratuitous predestination and answers it with greater precision and plausibility than any of the ancient authors who treated these matters. [Col. 1586A] “If it is as you say,” he objects to himself, “if this predestination is so effective and infallible, then we need no longer trouble ourselves to watch, pray, or fast; we need only follow the inclination of our desires and do our own will. For if we are among the predestined, we shall certainly be saved, and if we are not, whatever we may do, we cannot be saved.”

But those who reason in this way, Saint Fulgentius replies, are like someone to whom God had promised a long life, and (266) who, relying on that promise, no longer wished to take nourishment. But just as the love of life, he adds, causes the person to whom God has promised it to seek the necessities for sustaining it, so the grace that God has prepared for us through his predestination infallibly causes us to watch, pray, fast, and so forth. The clearest sign that someone is not among the predestined is that he neglects these holy exercises.

[Col. 1586B]

However beautiful and eloquent these works may have been, they nevertheless met the same fate as those of many other authors who had written with the same convictions: they only further outraged the minds of those who did not appreciate this doctrine. The more he wrote, the more the difficulties increased; the more he explained himself, the farther people moved from his principles, because they became convinced that he was destroying free will and introducing a fatal necessity from which human beings could not escape.

Then the pope understood how wise Boethius’s advice had been when he urged him to decide nothing new concerning these great difficulties (267), but merely to declare that the Roman Church adhered to her ancient decisions on grace and, for the rest, left Christians free to think about it as they wished, provided that they condemned all the errors that the Church had condemned [Col. 1586C] in Pelagius, his disciples, and the predestinarians.

Pelagius’s errors are chiefly reduced to two. One concerns original sin, which he denied; the other concerns the necessity of interior grace for salvation, which he likewise rejected, attributing to the powers of nature what can only be an effect of God’s goodness and mercies and the fruit of the Savior’s Passion. We cannot sufficiently acknowledge what we owe to Saint Augustine for having established these two great truths of religion so well and so firmly against Pelagius’s impieties.

But perhaps it would have been desirable to stop there. For as soon as people sought to investigate further and examine how this grace was given to us and how it acted in the human heart, God permitted these excessively curious questions to become a seed of quarrels, divisions, and hatred among Catholic people; and they have remained so ever since, whenever anyone has sought to reopen them. This was Boethius’s opinion, and it has always been that of the most disinterested persons, including Saint Francis de Sales in more recent times, when the sovereign pontiffs, pressed to decide something on this subject, asked his advice.

“I find difficulties on both sides that frighten me,” he said (Augustine de Sales, book VII of his *Life*; and Anonymous, book II). “The times are not suitable for making a decision, because minds are too heated to submit peacefully to a condemnation. In truth, one ought to expect this submission from their respect for the Holy See; but that is not always [Col. 1587A] certain, and it is not appropriate to put their submission to such a test. It is far better to devote oneself to making good use of grace than to turn it into disputes that have always damaged charity and disturbed the peace of the Church. Party spirit,” he added, “often transforms hatred of opinions into hatred of persons. In this way, (269) the law of charity so strongly commended in Holy Scripture—the supreme law to which everything ought to yield, the most inviolable of all laws—is not merely violated but seemingly destroyed and annihilated. Christian is my name; Catholic is my surname. I do not wish to know anything more about this matter.”

This does not mean that the great saint, who was a skilled theologian, did not know everything that can be known about it. Rather, he was convinced that human understanding is too limited to attain perfect knowledge of a mystery that will be fully revealed to us only in the next life, and that it is a lack of humility to pass beyond the limits prescribed for us by faith on this subject.

Indeed, how rash it is for human beings to wish to know what God absolutely intended to remain hidden from them: to uncover a secret he reserved for himself, to penetrate an abyss without a bottom. God’s grace is like God himself and his spirit. Only that divine spirit can comprehend and fathom itself; and, in the words of the Savior, we cannot know where it goes or from where it comes.

“I have clearly felt that it was at the depths of my heart,” Saint Bernard said (*Sermon 74 on the Song of Songs), “but when and how it entered there, and how it departed, I have not yet been able to know. From where his grace came into my soul, and where it went when it left; by what path it entered and by what path it departed—I do not know, in accordance with the saying that its steps and footprints cannot be known. It did not enter through my eyes, for it has no color; nor through my ears, [Col. 1587C] for it has no sound; nor through my nostrils, because it does not mingle with the air, but it insinuates itself imperceptibly into the spirit. Nor did it enter through my mouth, for it cannot be eaten; nor through my touch, for it cannot be touched. By what route, then, did it enter? Could it be that it does not enter at all, since it cannot come from outside? To say that it comes from within me is likewise impossible, because it is the true good, and I know, as Saint Paul says, that there is no good in me.

“Yet you ask me how I could know that it was within me, since its ways are unknown and imperceptible. I answer that I recognized its presence solely by the movement of my heart and by the various effects it produced there. When I was inwardly urged to flee vice and restrain my passions, then I recognized the power of grace.”

Although the sovereign pontiff’s reply to Bishop Possessor, given in accordance with Boethius’s advice, was not capable of ending all these dangerous disputes, it nevertheless moderated their fervor and at least temporarily halted all the harmful consequences that might have been feared from them. The Church would apparently have remained with her ancient decisions, following Boethius’s opinion, if the enemy—always attentive to finding the moment to cover the Lord’s field with weeds—had not in recent centuries stirred up an infinite number of restless people and those children of darkness of whom the Apostle speaks, who are always wanting to learn but never arrive at knowledge of the truth.

For by reviving the old errors condemned in the predestinarians, they advanced new ones that naturally followed from the principles of those heretics, and finally compelled the Church, after mature examination and lengthy discussions, to pronounce definitively as she did on these delicate questions and, so as not to defile herself, to expel from her bosom by striking them down all those who had defiled themselves through the corruption of their opinions and faith.

If one cannot give too many thanks to the holy pontiffs and bishops who for more than seventy years have worked with tireless care and diligence to purge the Lord’s threshing floor of such bad grain, neither can one give too much praise to the zeal and piety of our kings, who have so consistently used their authority to support and secure respect for the Church’s decisions. Since it is now known what must be believed and rejected concerning these matters, after the Church has explained herself with such precision, there is reason to hope that the disturbances that have agitated her for so many centuries will finally cease. And if disputes continue, it will no longer be in order to receive instruction, but to enjoy disputing and to display a spirit of pride and rebellion that authority alone can restrain.

## Clarification concerning the Opinion of Anastasius the Librarian and that of M. Dupin regarding Pope John’s Conduct toward King Theodoric during the Embassy He Undertook on Theodoric’s Behalf to the Emperor Justin

[Col. 1587D]

(273) The reasons are unknown that led Anastasius the Librarian to assert (*Life of Pope John*) that the emperor Justin had granted Theodoric, at Pope John’s advice and request, not only everything that did not concern the Catholic religion but also the revocation of his edicts against the Arians; and that the pope, the bishops, and the senators accompanying him, finding no other way to protect the Catholics in Italy from the Goths’ fury, had believed they could ask the emperor, out of consideration for them, to relax the severity of his edicts.

For there is no plausibility in this, and there is every reason to believe that Anastasius, living nearly four hundred years after the period under discussion, had been badly informed. M. de Valois’s Anonymous explicitly says the contrary. [Note: “To this Pope John replied: ‘What you are going to do, O King, do quickly; I do not promise that I shall do this for you.’” p. 186, no. 5.]

Indeed, if Pope John had fulfilled his commission, and if everything had succeeded according to Theodoric’s wishes, what cause would that prince have had for complaint? Why would he have repaid so important a service with such appalling ingratitude? Scarcely had this holy pontiff landed in Italy when the king had him arrested, together with the other ambassadors and their entire retinue, without even allowing them to go to Rome. He had them all thrown into horrible prisons, where he had them starved to death [Col. 1589A], and gradually destroyed by every kind of misery and by various tortures. Aimoin adds that he even had some of them burned alive. [Note: “Some of those who were with Pope John he burned with fire, and others he killed with various tortures.” (*Aimon, Deeds of the Franks*, book II, chapter 1; Gregory of Tours, same passage).]

Authors contemporary with Anastasius and more worthy of belief assure us, on the contrary, that Pope John had not treated with the emperor Justin as the ambassador of an Arian prince, but as the pastor of the Catholic Church; (275) that, far from being intimidated by all the threats Theodoric had made against him, he had increasingly confirmed Justin in his generous resolve to prefer the glory of God to all the interests of the world; and that, instead of having the churches from which the Arians had been expelled restored to them, this holy pope had reestablished the practice of the Catholic religion in those where it had not yet been restored. This is what Gregory of Tours, who lived in the same century, teaches us, reporting it as a public and established fact attested by the testimony of all the Catholics of the East. He even adds that he was still awaiting from Rome, concerning [Col. 1589B] this important matter, fuller and more detailed accounts. The letter that Pope John wrote from prison to all the bishops of Italy teaches us the same thing; it breathes only the spirit and piety of the earliest centuries and is filled with learning (*Tom. I Conc. vet. edit. in Joan. Pont.*).

After exhorting them not to fear those who can kill only the body and have no power over the soul, he inspires them and urges them to martyrdom; he earnestly entreats them to arm themselves with strength and courage in order (276) to complete the destruction of the remnants of Arian impiety, so often condemned by the holy councils, which seemed, like a hydra, to have revived entirely anew in Italy through Theodoric’s protection. He very earnestly asks them to take from the Arians as many churches as they can and to consecrate them anew with prayers and the customary ceremonies of the Roman Church, as he himself had done, he says, while he was at Constantinople, aided by the protection of [Col. 1589C] the emperor Justin. He then adds that this is the surest means of extirpating the heresy, because a sect must necessarily collapse of itself when it no longer has a church or public place in which to assemble or perform its religious exercises. Could one have a better witness to what took place between the emperor and him at Constantinople? He is a pope, a saint, and a martyr writing to the bishops of his province when he is about to give his life in defense of the faith.

A critic of our own day (Dupin, *Sixth Century*, p. 99), having no means of opposing proofs so clear and certain, thought he could evade the authority of this testimony by (277) rejecting the letter of Pope John I as a spurious document. But on what grounds? “It is,” he says, “because it is contrary to history, good faith, and common sense.” Contrary to history, because Anastasius the Librarian assures us that John fulfilled his legation. But Saint [Col. 1589D] Gregory of Tours assures us of the contrary, and a contemporary author will always be more readily believed than another who lived only four hundred years later.

Besides, could not Pope John have fulfilled his legation and at the same time reconciled or reconsecrated the churches that had been taken from the Arians? What was the purpose of his embassy? Simply to present to the emperor Justin the requests and wishes of Theodoric: this he could do in his capacity as Theodoric’s ambassador. But, as head of the Catholic Church and as a private person, could he not have held opinions opposed to those of that prince, and even represented to the emperor that his requests were harmful to the honor of God and the welfare of the [Col. 1590A] Church? “But that would have been acting in bad faith,” the critic replies, “for Pope John should not have undertaken this negotiation if he intended to urge Justin to do the exact opposite of what Theodoric wanted.” He will forgive me for saying that this is not sound reasoning. This holy pontiff had done everything within his power to be relieved of this commission. Finding himself compelled by sovereign authority to go to a Catholic prince, he could consent to go; he could even tell Justin the subject of his embassy. But when Theodoric pressed him to urge Justin to grant what he requested, neither threats nor fear of death were able to draw this promise from his lips. On the contrary, as has been noted, he repeatedly declared to him that he would do nothing of the sort: *Non promitto me facturum nec illi dicturus sum* (“I do not promise that I will do it, nor will I say it to him”) (Anonym. apud Vales. p. 486, no. 5).

Regulus, taken prisoner by the Carthaginians, was subsequently sent by them to the Roman Senate to [Col. 1590B] request an exchange of prisoners. His freedom was to be the reward for the success of his negotiation; but at the same time he was made to promise that, if he did not succeed, he would return and put himself back in chains. He accepted this arrangement. Having entered the Senate, he explained his commission and the (279) Carthaginians’ wish. But when he saw that most of the senators were dismayed by the magnitude of the loss they had just suffered—for more than forty thousand Romans had remained on the battlefield—and that they were inclined toward peace, he showed them, by arguments so convincing, that the Carthaginians, exhausted on their side, could no longer sustain the war, and that the interests of the Republic required its continuation, that the exchange of prisoners they were requesting was even refused them. Regulus returned joyfully to Carthage, where he knew that death awaited him.

Such, in approximate terms, was Pope John’s conduct in the embassy entrusted to him by Theodoric. And since Regulus was never accused [Col. 1590C] of having acted in bad faith on that occasion, why should this holy pope be accused of it on another occasion entirely similar? Is it less noble to sacrifice one’s life for the interests of God and the Church than to give it for those of one’s country? And does the same act of courage and generosity, considered worthy of praise and admiration in a pagan whose intentions are wholly (280) earthly, deserve only blame in a holy pope whose motives are entirely divine?

Where is common sense offended when Pope John, in this letter, exhorts the bishops of Italy to do under an Arian prince what he himself had done at Constantinople under a Catholic and most devout emperor? If the pope had expected to remain all his life in the territories of the emperor Justin, the example he proposed to them might perhaps not have been entirely imitable, and one might have told him that, since he risked nothing, he was exposing his [Col. 1590D] brothers, the bishops of Italy, to great danger by exhorting them to do what he did. But, given his intention of returning to Rome and placing himself again in Theodoric’s hands, as he did, was the danger not equal for them and for him? And did he not have the right to exhort them to follow his example, to despise life and not fear death while defending the interests of religion, just as he himself had despised the one and in no way feared the other for the same cause? These generous sentiments are certainly worthy of a pontiff whom the Church has placed (281) among the saints, and they characterize him so well that, instead of causing this letter to be rejected as a foreign interpolation, they demonstrate on the contrary that it is the work of a truly apostolic man, filled with the spirit that [Col. 1591A] animated those great bishops, the immediate successors of the apostles.

The other reasons he adduces against it are no better. “This letter,” he says again, “begins with scraps from the letters of Saint Leo, and the rest is merely a fabric of passages drawn from Saint Paul’s Second Epistle to the Corinthians.” What, then? Are the purest expressions of the Spirit of God unworthy of being used in the letters of holy pontiffs, the successors of the apostles and of the great Saint Leo? Have they not always deliberately expressed themselves in the same terms as those great men? Could they have chosen expressions more appropriate, more forceful, or more authoritative and powerful for convincing and persuading? This critic’s reflections would lead to the rejection of all the most certain letters of the popes, in which we everywhere find these same expressions employed.

But (282), he will say at last, the date is manifestly false. It is dated under the [Col. 1591B] consulship of Maximus and Olibrius: the former was consul in 523 and the latter in 526, and they were never consuls together. I admit that this objection appears better founded than all the others; but it will have no more solidity once the origin of the error has been discovered. This pope wrote two letters: one to Bishop Zacharias, a few months after his election, in October of the year 523, dated under the consulship of Maximus; the other from his prison in May 526, dated under the consulship of Olibrius. Those who later copied these letters, finding only one consul named at each date, apparently imagined that this was an omission, because it was customary to name two consuls for each year. To correct what they regarded as an error, they joined the two consuls, and from the two different dates of the two letters they made a single date, without reflecting that Maximus and Olibrius had held the consulship separately, three years apart, [Col. 1591C] and without any colleague. Thus they dated (283) the two letters to the consulship of Maximus and Olibrius. Such blunders by copyists are so common that those who are even slightly versed in history and have some acquaintance with ancient manuscripts are not surprised by them and readily correct them.
