What reason would the Church have had to place Pope John among the saints and martyrs if he had not been thrown into chains for having courageously defended the interests of God and religion before the emperor Justin and against Theodoric’s intentions? There is no indication that he had any other occasion to distinguish himself by his zeal. The [Col. 1592A] question embarrasses the modern critic, and he found no better way out of the difficulty than to rob this pontiff both of the honor of sanctity and of the glory of martyrdom. He does so against the testimony of all antiquity and against the authority of the universal Church. Yet both have led the most learned critics of recent centuries (*Vide Baron. ad an.* 525 and 526) unanimously to reject Anastasius’s testimony and embrace that of Saint Gregory of Tours.

And although M. Baillet, whose examination is among the most rigorous, finds (284) difficulty in the matter, nevertheless, after comparing the opinion of Saint Gregory, followed by Cardinal Baronius, with that of Anastasius, and simply setting out what might lead one to reject the former in favor of the latter, he concludes in favor of the holy pontiff and expresses himself as follows (M. Bail., *Life of Saint John*, P., 17 May):

> “But on the other hand,” he says, “the event and the consequences of the embassy would seem to suggest that Anastasius, who lived only 350 [Col. 1592B] years after our saint, may have been misinformed when he believed that the emperor Justin had restored throughout the empire to the Arians the churches that he had taken from them, following the advice of our holy pope and the other Roman ambassadors.”

And despite this doubt, he concludes his account as follows:

> “When the pope arrived in Italy from his embassy to Constantinople and was preparing to come and report the outcome of his negotiation to the king, the prince sent men to seize him and had him taken to the prisons of Ravenna; he also had the three ambassadors from the Senate arrested. His fear of openly provoking a revolt among the Romans and part of Italy, which was already reaching out its arms toward the emperor, prevented him from having so many illustrious prisoners put to death by the sword. Instead, he chose an even greater cruelty, causing them to suffer every sort of hardship in order to rid himself of them without public commotion. Thus the blessed pope, within a few days, was consumed by hunger and [Col. 1592C] misery in that prison until, overcome by the weight of so many sufferings, he was happily freed from the bonds of the body by a death precious in the sight of God and went to receive from his hands the crown of martyrdom.”

M. Baillet therefore acknowledges, together with all antiquity, religious causes—not merely political aims and reasons of state, as M. Dupin argued—in the death of this holy pope. And since Boethius [Note: [Col. 1591] M. Fleury admits that Theodoric had Pope John arrested because he believed him to be Boethius’s accomplice. *History*, vol. VII, p. 286.] was involved in the same affair and put to death for the same reason, as all historians agree, one cannot regard one as a martyr without granting the other the same distinction.

Gundobad, king of Burgundy, an Arian, 57, 58. His cruelty, *ibid.* He asks Saint Avitus to reconcile him to the Church. Saint Avitus refuses him, and why, 68, 69. He dies hardened in his obstinacy, *ibid.* Dissertation on the reconciliation of heretics by anointing with chrism, which he requested from Saint Avitus. See the second part, 78.

The Goths make themselves masters of Italy, 4 ff. Their fierce and barbarous character, 102, 103.

## H

*Hebdomads*. Boethius’s treatise on the *Hebdomads*, 82. Different explanations of the term, *ibid.*

Heretics. Their character, 145. Restrained by fear, they rise up as soon as they have nothing left to fear, 148. Outrages they committed against Proterius, 147. The heretical party, always dangerous in a state, must be suppressed at its birth, *ibid.*

Hilderic, successor of Trasamund, 220. He is favorable to the Catholics, *ibid.* and following. He recalls the exiled bishops, 221.

Hormisdas, pope. His election, 142. His union with Boethius, who urges him to reunite the Churches of the East, *ibid.* His difficulties concerning the reunion, 172, 173 ff. He is summoned to Ravenna by Theodoric, 176. He is induced to send a celebrated legation to Constantinople to settle the matter of reunion, 177. The instructions he gives his legates, *ibid.*

## J

John, archdeacon of Rome, Boethius’s particular friend, 41. Boethius addresses several treatises to him. Boethius’s special esteem for him, 80. He asks Boethius to answer the difficulty proposed by a Manichaean concerning the goodness of being, 81. He succeeds Pope Hormisdas, 246. His zeal for the glory of God, *ibid.* The resistance he offers Theodoric in the matter of the Arians, 253. His conduct on that occasion. He is sent to Constantinople, *ibid.* Extraordinary prodigies occurring at the time of his departure, *ibid.* Extraordinary honors paid to him upon entering Constantinople, 259. Miraculous events that make him noteworthy, *ibid.* He celebrates the Easter office in the church of Constantinople according to the Latin rite and crowns the emperor Justin there, 259, 260. His return to Italy. See the second part, 273 ff. He is arrested by order of Theodoric, *ibid.* His death, precious in the eyes of God, *ibid.*, 283 ff.

John, patriarch of Constantinople, a zealous Catholic, 166, 167. He publishes the Council of Chalcedon, 168. He works with great wisdom for the reunion of the Church of the East with that of the West, 169, 170 ff. He concludes the reunion, 179. He sends gifts to Pope Hormisdas, 180.

Justin, a thoroughly Catholic emperor, succeeds Anastasius. His zeal for the purity of faith and morals, 165. He works zealously to end the Eastern schism, 168, 170 ff. He sends to ask Pope Hormisdas for the reunion of the Churches, 172. He receives the king of the Lazians with great honor and serves as his sponsor at the baptismal font, 225 ff. His edicts against heretics and magicians, 247. He exempts the Arians out of consideration for Theodoric, *ibid.* At the request of Pope John and Boethius, he issues new edicts against them, 248, 249.

Justinian, the count, declares himself against the Scythian monks, 192. Secret enemy of Count Vitalian, 190. Accused of being the author of Count Vitalian’s murder. He changes his opinion after Vitalian’s death and defends the Scythian monks, 204, 205. He pursues at Rome the definition of the proposition “One of the Trinity suffered,” 206. He succeeds Justin in the empire and has the proposition declared Catholic.

## L
The Lassians: They embrace the faith of Jesus Christ, 222. Leo (the emperor) succeeds Marcian, 148. He expels Elurus from Alexandria and protects the Catholic faith, 149. Lombards: Establishment of their kingdom in Italy, 318. They embrace the faith of Jesus Christ, 319. The piety of their kings, ibid. They found the church of Saint Peter in Ciel d’Oro at Pavia, ibid. Luitprand, king of the Lombards: His piety, 319. His burial, 322. He has the body of Saint Augustine transferred to Pavia and has that of Boethius raised from the ground, 321. Lyon, capital of the kingdom of Burgundy, 59. The bishops assemble there for the feast of Saint Just, ibid.

[Col. 1597]

## M

The magicians are expelled from Rome, 94. Several senators accused of magic are arrested. Their trial, 93 and following. The Manichaeans are expelled from Rome, 91. Their books and images are publicly burned, ibid.

Weights and measures are reformed by Boethius, 49. The opinions of the ancients concerning the twelve ounces in a pound, ibid.

The Scythian monks disturb the peace of the Church, 189. Their particular opinion concerning the Trinity, ibid. Their proposition—“One of the Trinity is incarnate and has suffered”—is examined and rejected, 190, and subsequently approved, 207, 208. Their conduct at Rome, 193, 201. Their writings, 202, 203. They provoke new disturbances concerning liberty and grace, 208, 209. They attack Possessor, the bishop, and the writings of Faustus of Riez, ibid. See the second part: *Clarifications concerning Faustus of Riez*, 228 and following.

Peter Mongus, patriarch of Antioch, receives Zeno’s *Henoticon*, 149. He is expelled from Antioch, 152. He is elected patriarch of Alexandria, ibid. He is expelled from the see of Alexandria and restored by the emperor Zeno, ibid.

Debased coinage: It gives occasion for Theodoric’s troops to mutiny, 46. Boethius is charged with reforming it, 47. The value of the gold solidus, 48. The opinions of the ancients concerning the roundness and other qualities of coinage, 49.

## N

Nestorius: His heresy. The difficulty of finding terms to express the union of the natures in Jesus Christ without dividing the person is its origin, 35 and following. He is condemned at the Council of Ephesus, ibid., 143. Boethius writes against his errors, 42, 43. See the second part, 8 and following.

## O

Odoacer seizes Italy, 9.

Opilio and Gaudentius, notorious brigands, 271. Their punishment, ibid. and following. They obtain pardon by joining Cyprian and become witnesses against Boethius, 272.

Otho III, the emperor, has a new mausoleum erected for Boethius, 326.

## P

Paulinus, a patrician, is oppressed by Theodoric’s courtiers, 322. His disputes with Festus and Symmachus, 323. Boethius defends him against the oppression of Theodoric’s courtiers, ibid.

Persia: Cabades, king of Persia, declares war on Justin, 225. Cat, tributary of the Persians, 223.

Philosophy: Boethius composes a course of philosophy, 103. His aims in this work. Defects found in Aristotle’s *Philosophy*, 105. Division of Boethius’s philosophy, 105, 106. See the second part, 154, 155 and following.

The prefecture of the praetorium: Its institution, 276. It is a civil magistracy, ibid., and a military office, ibid.

Praetextatus, a Roman senator, is convicted of magic, 95. He escapes from prison and disappears, 97.

Proba (Saint), the second daughter of Symmachus, 20.

Proterius is elected patriarch of Alexandria in place of Dioscorus. He is murdered in the baptistery by the heretics, 147, 148.

## R

The Romans: They display their zeal against magicians, 101.

Rome: Disorders in Rome, 9, 102, 103. It voluntarily submits to Theodoric, 21, 22. It is sacked by Totila, 317.

Rusticiana, the third daughter of Symmachus and the second wife of Boethius: Her virtues, 20, 21. Her steadfastness during her husband’s misfortunes, 284. After his death, she renounces the world and her possessions and gives great alms, 306. She is protected by Amalasuntha, 313, 314. She is persecuted by Boethius’s enemies, who demand her death, 315. Her steadfastness on this occasion. She is reduced to begging during the sack of Rome and brought before Totila to be condemned to death, 118. Totila respects her virtue and sends her away with honor, ibid.

## S

Salophaciolus, the Catholic patriarch of Alexandria, 149. He is expelled from his see by Zeno, ibid.

The schism of the Church of Rome after the death of Anastasius, 12.

The great schism of the East, 173. Its origin and progress, ibid. and following, up to p. 165. Its extinction, 166–185.

[Col. 1598]

Sigismund, king of Burgundy: His conversion, 70. His virtues, ibid. His penance and death, 71.

Father Sirmond, a learned Jesuit, makes public the memoirs left by Pope Felix, 159. His notes on Ennodius, 40, 216.

Sovereigns: All their important actions, even their amusements, 53.

Substance: Its invisible nature apart from the accidents with which it is clothed, 106.

Pope Symmachus: His election is confirmed by Theodoric, 12. He grants great privileges to Saint Caesarius of Arles. He opposes the ambition of certain bishops of Gaul who arrogated new rights over neighboring churches, 140, 141. His death, ibid.

Symmachus, a Roman senator and Boethius’s father-in-law: His virtues, 13, 14. He is appointed head of the commission to judge the senators accused of magic, 93. His steadfastness during Boethius’s misfortunes, 84. His zeal for the Catholic faith; he is arrested by order of Theodoric, 300. Theodoric has him killed in prison, ibid. God avenges his death, 307, 308. He is honored as a holy martyr at Ravenna. See the second part, the *Dissertation on the Year of Boethius’s Death*, 176.

## T

Tertullus, a Roman senator and friend of Boethius, accompanies him in his retreats in the desert of Subiaco, 242.

Theodoric: He is sent to Italy by Zeno, 10. He contributes to Zeno’s restoration, and Zeno overwhelms him with favors, 10, 11. He makes himself master of Italy. His good qualities. His education, ibid. He is appointed judge of the schism of the Church of Rome after the death of Anastasius, 12. He decides in favor of Symmachus, ibid. He enters Rome in triumph, 22. The honors paid to him, ibid. His pomp, ibid. His generosity and magnificence, 23. His conduct in governing Italy, 25. His letters to Boethius, 48, 50, 55. His letters to Clovis, glorious monuments for France, 51, 52. He sends ambassadors to Clovis, ibid. He declares war on Clovis, 74. He sends troops into Gaul under the command of Ibba, 75. Success of his first campaign, 76. The failure of the second campaign. He recalls his troops from Gaul, 77. He incorporates into his Italian kingdom what remained to Amalaric, his grandson, in Gaul, ibid.

His consideration for the Catholics at the beginning and throughout his reign, 244. He suddenly changes his conduct toward them during the final years of his life, 245. His outbursts against Justin on account of the edicts published against the Arians, 250. He makes great threats against the Catholics, 252. He summons Pope John to Ravenna and sends him, together with bishops and senators, to Constantinople to request freedom of conscience on behalf of the Arians, 253, 254 and following. The threats he makes against Pope John, 256. He has Boethius imprisoned, along with several distinguished senators, 260. He has Boethius condemned to death, 288. His cruelty toward Boethius, Symmachus, Pope John, and other distinguished persons, ibid. and through p. 306. God takes vengeance on him, 307. He confesses his crime and repents of it as he dies, 307, 308. His tragic death, from 307 through 311. His hatred of the Catholics is shown especially in his attempt to hand over their churches to the Arians, 309, 310. His burial, 311.

Totila is called into Italy by the Goths; he sacks Rome, 317.

Thrasamund, king of the Vandals, comes to besiege Tripoli, 217. His tragic death, 221. At his death, he reveals more clearly than ever his hatred of the Catholics.

Triguille, steward of Theodoric’s household, and Conigastus: Their injustices, 124. Boethius openly opposes them and puts a stop to them, 125 and following. They join Cyprian in bringing about Boethius’s destruction, 266.

The Holy Trinity: Whether, in the Holy Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit can be substantially predicated of the Godhead, 78. Boethius’s treatise on this question, 79, 80. See the second part, 27 and following. The Trinity is one God, not three Gods. See the second part, 33 and following.

The tunics of deacons: Their ancient form, 140.

## V

Vitalian, the count, a zealous Catholic, takes up arms against the emperor Anastasius in defense of the Catholics, 161. He declares himself the protector of the Scythian monks, 192. His tragic death, 199.

Vitalis, bishop of Emesa and legate of Pope Felix at Constantinople, 155. He is taken prisoner, 156. His constancy amid the harsh treatment inflicted on him by the emperor Zeno and the patriarch Acacius, ibid. He allows himself to be seduced by their caresses and gifts, 157. His fall and deposition, ibid.

Volusianus, a Roman senator and commissioner against the magicians, 96.

Wallin: His 1656 edition of Boethius’s *Opuscula*, 188.

## Z

Zeno, the emperor, succeeds Leo, 110, 111. The weakness of his reign, ibid. He is driven out by Basiliscus, 149. He calls the Ostrogoths to his aid; they serve him usefully under the command of Theodoric, 10. He sends Theodoric to Italy, ibid. He is restored to the throne, 151.
